Applicants should demonstrate a combination of academic readiness, analytical ability, interpersonal skills, professional maturity, and interest in financial markets.

The listed requirements include:

August 2026 and July 2027

Candidates should be able to examine information, identify relationships, evaluate problems, and develop practical solutions. Logical reasoning and analytical thinking are important because the role involves research, financial analysis, investment strategies, and complex client needs.

Candidates should have a desire to eventually work with external clients in a relationship-building and sales-oriented capacity. This does not mean applicants must already be experienced financial advisors, but they should be interested in developing client-facing skills.

Collect information on all aspects of remote and digital access across domains through workshops and expert groups

TITLE: ACET Graduate Intern – Gender Equality Program 2026: Six-Month Opportunity Supporting Gender Equality and Women’s Economic Empowerment in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Center for Economic Transformation (ACET) Graduate Intern – Gender Equality Program 2026 is an opportunity for graduates interested in gender equality, women’s economic empowerment, development policy, research and programme management to gain practical professional experience while contributing to programmes focused on advancing gender equality across Africa.

ACET is recruiting a motivated Graduate Intern for its Gender Equality Program (GEP) to provide programme coordination and delivery support across a portfolio of initiatives. The successful candidate will also contribute to research, monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL), procurement, stakeholder engagement and general programme administration.

The internship is particularly relevant for graduates from fields such as gender studies, economics, development studies, public policy and the social sciences who want to strengthen their professional experience while working on issues affecting gender equality and economic transformation in Africa.

Applications must be submitted by Thursday, 17 September 2026. The internship will initially run for six months, with the possibility of an extension depending on the intern’s performance and the needs of the programme.

About the African Center for Economic Transformation

The African Center for Economic Transformation works on issues connected to Africa’s economic transformation and development. Its areas of work include economic management and governance, gender equality, green industrial transformation, innovation and digital policy, private-sector development, regional integration, and youth employment and skills.

Through the Gender Equality Program, ACET maintains a portfolio of programmes and projects designed to advance gender equality and women’s economic empowerment across Africa.

The current Gender Equality Program portfolio includes:

African Women’s Inclusion Index (AWII)

Shared Power

Care Economy in Africa

Gender-Responsive Budgeting (GRB)

Gender Mainstreaming

These initiatives form the broader environment in which the selected graduate intern will work and provide programme support.

About the ACET Graduate Intern – Gender Equality Program 2026

The Graduate Intern will support the coordination and delivery of activities across ACET’s Gender Equality Program portfolio.

One of the central purposes of the position is to improve visibility and coordination across GEP’s different workstreams by ensuring that reliable and up-to-date information is maintained concerning programme activities, deadlines, deliverables and outstanding actions.

Rather than being limited to one narrow function, the internship covers several aspects of programme implementation. The successful candidate will have opportunities to contribute to programme coordination, research, MEL, procurement, stakeholder engagement, events and programme administration.

Because several tasks and projects may be taking place simultaneously, ACET is looking for a graduate who is highly organised, proactive and capable of managing multiple responsibilities. The successful candidate should also communicate effectively with colleagues across different teams and be comfortable working with limited day-to-day supervision.

Key Responsibilities of the Graduate Intern

The selected intern will undertake responsibilities across six major areas.

1. Programme and Workplan Coordination

Programme coordination will form an important part of the internship.

The intern will help the GEP team maintain visibility over its various activities and deadlines by keeping the programme tracker updated. This will include information relating to:

Programme activities

Key milestones

Deliverables

Responsible team members

Deadlines

The intern will also prepare short weekly overviews identifying upcoming deadlines, overdue tasks and matters requiring the team’s attention.

Another responsibility will involve following up with relevant team members concerning outstanding actions. This means the intern will need to communicate proactively and ensure that important activities do not remain unresolved without appropriate follow-up.

The intern will additionally monitor GEP’s work with other ACET functions, including Finance, Procurement, MEL and Communications.

Support will also be provided for GEP team planning and programme review meetings.

2. Procurement and Consultant Coordination

The internship provides exposure to procurement and consultant management processes within a development-focused organisation.

The successful candidate will support the preparation, submission and tracking of procurement requests and their supporting documentation.

The intern will liaise with the Procurement team to follow up on routine requirements and timelines, helping ensure that programme-related procurement activities move forward as required.

The intern will also provide support during consultant recruitment and contracting processes. Responsibilities may include:

Coordinating interviews

Supporting shortlisting processes

Coordinating feedback

Tracking consultant contracts

Monitoring consultant deliverables against agreed timelines

This aspect of the internship can provide useful experience for graduates interested in programme administration, project management and international development operations.

3. Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning and Programme Reporting

Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning, commonly referred to as MEL, is another important component of the internship.

The intern will assist with collecting and consolidating information needed for quarterly MEL reporting.

Information may relate to:

Programme activities

Outputs

Events

Stakeholder engagements

Cross-team collaborations

The successful candidate will also maintain relevant records and trackers throughout each reporting period.

In addition, the intern will follow up with project leads to help ensure that required inputs are submitted on time for MEL and other programme reporting requirements.

4. Programme and Research Support

Graduates interested in research and policy will also have opportunities to support research activities associated with GEP’s programmes.

Responsibilities may include conducting targeted literature and evidence searches and helping prepare research summaries.

The intern may also support:

Organisation of datasets and research materials where appropriate

References and research documentation

Background research ahead of policy engagements

Short policy-facing outputs where appropriate

This combination of research and programme responsibilities makes the internship particularly relevant to candidates seeking practical exposure to the relationship between evidence, policy engagement and programme implementation.

5. Events and Stakeholder Coordination

The Graduate Intern will also contribute to stakeholder engagement and event coordination.

The successful candidate will help plan and coordinate GEP activities such as:

Workshops

Stakeholder meetings

Validation sessions

Dissemination events

The intern will work with ACET’s Communications team and other relevant teams when coordinating these activities.

Additional responsibilities will include participant coordination, preparing meeting materials, scheduling and conducting post-event follow-up.

The intern may also prepare meeting notes and monitor outstanding actions arising from meetings or events.

Maintaining stakeholder databases and engagement tracking will form another part of this responsibility.

6. General Programme Support

Beyond the specific areas outlined above, the intern will provide general programme support to the Gender Equality Program.

An important responsibility will be maintaining organised project documentation.

The successful candidate will also support the effective flow of information between GEP projects and between the Gender Equality Program and other relevant ACET teams.

Required Qualifications for the ACET Graduate Internship 2026

Candidates interested in applying should hold a relevant undergraduate or postgraduate degree.

Relevant academic disciplines include:

Economics

Development studies

Public policy

Social sciences

Other related fields

ACET is seeking candidates with strong organisational and coordination abilities. Applicants should demonstrate the capacity to manage several tasks and deadlines simultaneously.

Candidates should also be proactive and detail-oriented. The role requires someone capable of anticipating requirements, following up on outstanding activities and identifying potential delays without requiring constant supervision.

Applicants must also be proficient in Microsoft Excel and comfortable using digital tools for project tracking and documentation.

Areas of Interest and Experience

Previous experience is not stated as an absolute requirement in the announcement. However, experience in certain areas will be considered an advantage.

Candidates who have gained relevant experience through academic projects, internships, professional roles or related activities may therefore find their background relevant to the responsibilities of the position, although applicants should represent their experience accurately in their applications.

Skills ACET Is Looking For

The vacancy places considerable emphasis on organisation, initiative and the ability to coordinate multiple activities.

An ideal applicant should therefore be able to demonstrate:

Importantly, ACET states that there is a possibility of extension. Any extension will depend on the intern’s performance and the needs of the programme.

TITLE: Upfront Ventures Founder Fellows 2026: $75,000+ Startup Backing for the Next Generation of Technical Builders and Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Upfront Ventures Founder Fellows programme is inviting applications for its second cohort, offering an eight-week fellowship designed for the next generation of technical builders, engineers, researchers and aspiring startup founders.

The programme is aimed at highly capable individuals who are already building, researching or working in high-growth technology environments and are considering starting a venture-backed company.

Over the course of eight weeks, selected Fellows will receive exposure to Upfront Ventures partners, participate in the Upfront Summit, take part in intimate conversations with category-defining founders and gain access to a network of builders and operators.

A major feature of the programme is the opportunity for Fellows to receive $75,000 or more in backing when they incorporate a venture-backable startup.

This makes the fellowship particularly relevant to technically strong individuals who may already have significant experience but are at different stages of deciding when and how to launch a company.

What Is the Upfront Ventures Founder Fellows Programme?

The Upfront Ventures Founder Fellows is an eight-week programme created by Upfront Ventures for individuals who represent the next generation of technical founders and researchers.

The fellowship is designed around exposure, relationships and preparation for entrepreneurship.

Rather than requiring every participant to already have an incorporated company, the programme appears to target people who are at different stages of their transition toward becoming founders.

The profiles highlighted by Upfront include:

Recent graduates with experience at hyper-growth startups.

Individuals who have left school to work full-time at leading AI laboratories.

Highly accomplished technical builders.

Engineers working at rapidly growing technology companies.

Individuals who want to start a company but are not yet ready to take the leap.

Technical researchers and builders with the potential to create venture-backable startups.

The second cohort therefore brings together people who may have different educational and professional paths but share an interest in building significant technology companies.

What Does the Founder Fellows Programme Offer?

The fellowship lasts for eight weeks.

During this period, Fellows receive opportunities to interact with Upfront’s investment network and the broader technology and startup ecosystem.

The programme includes several key components.

1. Direct Exposure to Upfront Partners

Fellows receive direct exposure to Upfront’s partners.

This gives participants an opportunity to engage with people at the venture capital firm and gain exposure to perspectives surrounding technology, entrepreneurship and company building.

For aspiring founders, access to experienced investors can provide an opportunity to better understand how venture-backed companies are developed and supported.

2. Attendance at the Upfront Summit

Fellows will also attend the Upfront Summit.

The summit is an important part of Upfront’s wider network and provides Fellows with an opportunity to interact with people across the startup and investment ecosystem.

For participants considering founding a company, attending a major gathering connected to investors, founders and technology leaders can provide opportunities for conversations and relationship building.

3. Fireside Chats With Category-Defining Founders

Another feature of the programme is access to intimate fireside chats with category-defining founders.

These sessions are intended to expose Fellows to the experiences and perspectives of founders who have built companies that have established significant positions within their respective categories.

For technical builders who are considering entrepreneurship, these conversations can provide insight into the realities of starting and developing a company.

4. Access to a Network of Builders and Operators

Fellows will also be able to plug into Upfront’s network of builders and operators.

This is an important component of the fellowship because startup creation is not limited to technical development.

Building a company can involve product development, hiring, operations, fundraising, go-to-market strategy, partnerships and many other areas.

Access to a network of people who have experience building and operating companies can therefore expose Fellows to perspectives beyond their own technical discipline.

$75,000+ Startup Backing

One of the most significant elements highlighted in the programme announcement is Upfront’s commitment to back Fellows with $75,000 or more when they incorporate a venture-backable startup.

The announcement states:

“we’ll back you with $75,000+ when you incorporate a venture-backable startup!”

This means the fellowship is connected directly to potential financial backing for Fellows who go on to incorporate a startup that meets the relevant venture-backability criteria.

It is important to distinguish this from a general cash award or unrestricted fellowship stipend. The information provided describes the $75,000+ support specifically in connection with incorporating a venture-backable startup.

Applicants should review the official fellowship terms and application information for the precise conditions associated with this backing.

Who Is Upfront Looking For?

The programme announcement identifies several types of candidates.

Rather than describing a single conventional applicant profile, Upfront highlights three examples of the kinds of people it wants to attract.

The Founder

The first profile is the aspiring founder who is already demonstrating strong professional experience.

According to Upfront, this person may be:

Graduating from university.

Equipped with multiple internships at hyper-growth startups.

Preparing to start a company as soon as possible.

Already oriented toward entrepreneurship.

Interested in building a venture-backable startup.

This profile is particularly relevant to technically talented graduates who have used internships to gain experience inside rapidly growing startups and are now considering founding their own company.

TITLE: Harvard G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Training 2027 Opens Applications with Full Tuition Coverage

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027 G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Professional Training programme, an intensive, one-week learning opportunity delivered by the FXB Center for Health and Human Rights at Harvard University.

The programme is designed for experienced, mid-career professionals working to prevent and respond to child abuse, violence, exploitation and neglect. It brings together cross-sectoral country teams representing government, international organisations and local civil society.

Selected teams will attend the training from June 7 to June 11, 2027, at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts, United States.

All Harvard University course fees will be covered for admitted participants through support from the G. Barrie Landry Fund for Child Protection Professional Training and UNICEF USA. However, participants remain responsible for their travel, accommodation, living expenses, visa arrangements and meals that are not included as part of the training.

Applications must be submitted by December 1, 2026. Importantly, individual applications are not accepted. Each application must be submitted by a three-member, cross-sectoral country team.

The programme details and deadline are confirmed in the official Harvard FXB programme announcement and the official 2027 programme brochure.

G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Training 2027 at a Glance

Programme detail
Information

G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Professional Training

Organiser
FXB Center for Health and Human Rights at Harvard University

Academic location
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

About the G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Professional Training Programme

The G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Professional Training is an on-site course for professionals who work to protect children from abuse, exploitation, violence and neglect.

Participants may work for:

Government ministries, departments or agencies

International organisations

United Nations bodies or development organisations

Local or national nongovernmental organisations

Child protection and social welfare institutions

Human rights organisations

Public health, education or justice-sector bodies

Organisations working with displaced, vulnerable or marginalised children

The programme is based on the understanding that risks facing children are diverse and interconnected. Children may experience displacement, child labour, abuse, neglect, exploitation, early marriage, violence, inadequate care, discrimination or the consequences of armed conflict and natural disasters.

Regardless of their legal status or personal circumstances, children have rights to health, education, protection and access to justice. Realising these rights requires more than the work of a single organisation or government department.

Effective child protection depends on cooperation among:

Social welfare agencies

Health institutions

Education systems

Justice-sector institutions

Civil society organisations

Community-based organisations

International development partners

Human rights institutions

Policymakers and legislators

Child protection researchers and practitioners

The programme therefore promotes an integrated and multisectoral approach in which government and civil-society actors work together to build and maintain effective national child protection systems.

Purpose of the Training

The training seeks to deepen participants’ understanding of child protection challenges while strengthening the leadership, negotiation and coalition-building skills required to improve national protection systems.

It is not designed solely as a theoretical classroom course. Participants must work together on an actual child protection problem from their own country and develop practical options that can be applied after the programme.

The training combines:

Academic research

International human rights principles

Child-development science

Evidence-based advocacy

Leadership development

Negotiation techniques

Policy analysis

Legal and institutional frameworks

Multisectoral collaboration

Case-study development

Peer learning between countries

Individualised feedback from specialists

The programme aims to help professionals connect academic knowledge with real institutional and policy challenges.

Main Goals of the Programme

1. Understanding the Effects of Violence and Exploitation on Children

Participants will examine how abuse, violence and exploitation can affect children’s:

Emotional development

Intellectual development

Social development

Physical and psychological well-being

Ability to learn and participate in education

Family and community relationships

Long-term health and life opportunities

The programme also examines the traumatic effects of armed conflict, war and natural disasters on children.

2. Learning Multidisciplinary Child Protection Approaches

Participants will be introduced to multidisciplinary approaches for preventing and responding to child-specific harms.

These approaches may draw on:

Public health

Social work

Education

Psychology

Law and justice

Human rights

Public policy

Data and research

Community development

Digital technology

The programme emphasises that complex child protection problems cannot usually be resolved by one professional discipline or institution acting alone.

3. Understanding Legal and Human Rights Principles

The training introduces participants to legal principles and analytical frameworks relevant to child protection, including those based on international human rights standards.

Participants will consider how laws, policies and institutions can be used to prevent harm, protect children and provide appropriate responses when violations occur.

4. Examining Effective Child Protection Systems

Participants will study the components required for a well-functioning child protection system.

These components may include:

Appropriate laws and regulations

Clearly defined institutional responsibilities

Skilled social-service professionals

Case-management and referral systems

Reliable administrative information

Sustainable public financing

Coordination across government departments

Participation by civil society and communities

Accountability and monitoring arrangements

Child-sensitive justice procedures

Prevention and early-intervention mechanisms

Participants will assess how these components work together and why gaps in one area can weaken an entire national protection system.

5. Strengthening Data and Evidence-Based Advocacy

The programme will introduce participants to data sources used in child protection systems and the challenges involved in developing reliable information.

Participants will consider how evidence can be used to:

Identify the scale and nature of child protection problems

Understand which children are most at risk

Design appropriate interventions

Monitor institutional performance

Evaluate whether policies are working

Advocate for legal or administrative reforms

Secure financial and political support

Hold relevant institutions accountable

The course also explores ways digital solutions may help address child protection challenges.

6. Building Leadership and Negotiation Skills

The training will help participants develop leadership, negotiation and coalition-building skills for advancing child protection reforms.

These capabilities are essential when reforms require cooperation across multiple areas of government, including:

Education

Health

Social services

Justice

Public finance

Local government

Disaster management

Digital regulation

Participants will examine how professionals can build agreement, manage competing priorities and secure institutional support for child protection initiatives.

7. Developing Country-Specific Solutions

A central objective is to help each participating team develop practical options for strengthening its country’s child protection system.

Teams will use the knowledge gained during the course to improve the quality of national child protection policies, strategies or plans of action.

Who Should Apply?

The programme is intended for mid-career professionals working in fields where child protection is a central or important concern.

Suitable applicants may include:

Child protection specialists

Social welfare professionals

Government policymakers

Human rights practitioners

Public health professionals

Social workers

Education-sector professionals

Justice-sector officials

Programme managers

Policy and advocacy specialists

Researchers

International development professionals

NGO leaders

Professionals supporting vulnerable or displaced children

Applicants should already be involved in child protection or a closely connected field. They should also be committed to strengthening their leadership skills and working collaboratively across institutional and professional boundaries.

No particular university degree, academic discipline, age limit or minimum number of years of experience is stated. However, the programme is explicitly designed for experienced, mid-career professionals rather than students or entry-level applicants.

Applications Must Be Submitted by Country Teams

One of the most important eligibility conditions is the country-team requirement.

Applications must be submitted by a three-member, cross-sectoral team representing the same country. Applications from individuals will not be considered.

The preferred team composition is:

One professional employed by a government agency

One professional employed by an international organisation

One professional employed by a local NGO

This composition is described as preferred rather than an absolute requirement. Nevertheless, teams should reflect the programme’s multisectoral purpose and demonstrate how different institutions can work together on a common national child protection challenge.

A strong team should include members who:

Represent different institutional perspectives

Have relevant child protection responsibilities

Can work collaboratively before, during and after the training

Possess sufficient institutional knowledge to analyse the selected problem

Can influence policies, programmes or professional practice

Are able to apply the programme’s lessons in their home country

An organisation should not submit a single employee independently. It must coordinate with professionals from other sectors to form a complete three-person country team.

English-Language Requirement

Fluency in written and spoken English is required for all three team members.

Participants must be able to:

Understand lectures and technical discussions

Participate actively in group sessions

Read programme materials

Discuss complex child protection issues

Prepare and deliver presentations

Work with professionals from different countries

Respond to questions from Harvard-affiliated specialists

Write and refine their team’s case study

No English-language test such as IELTS or TOEFL is mentioned. However, every applicant must possess sufficient practical English fluency to participate fully in the programme.

Programme Curriculum

The course is organised thematically, with related subjects distributed across the training week.

Examples of previous sessions include:

Leveraging Science to Protect the Developing Brain from Violence, Abuse and Neglect

Engaging and Strengthening the Social Service Workforce

Climate Change, Disasters and Child Well-Being

Negotiation for the Child Protection System

Child Protection in a Digital World

Measurement and Evidence Generation in the Child Protection System

Juvenile Justice: Practice, Research, Policy and Advocacy

Social and Structural Inequalities and Children’s Health

The exact 2027 timetable may differ from previous years. These subjects are presented by Harvard as examples of past course sessions rather than a confirmed session-by-session schedule for 2027.

Developing-Brain Science and Childhood Trauma

The course examines scientific evidence concerning children’s development and the effects of violence, abuse and neglect.

This area helps participants understand why early exposure to harm may have lasting consequences and why timely prevention and intervention are essential.

Participants may consider how evidence from child-development science can inform:

Prevention programmes

Social-service practice

Health interventions

Education policy

Justice-sector responses

Family support

Community-based protection measures

Strengthening the Social-Service Workforce

A functioning child protection system requires trained, supported and appropriately distributed professionals.

The course examines how countries can strengthen the workforce responsible for:

Identifying children at risk

Assessing protection concerns

Managing individual cases

Coordinating referrals

Supporting families

Responding to violence

Monitoring children in alternative care

Connecting children with health, education and justice services

This subject is particularly important for countries facing shortages of qualified social workers or fragmented professional standards.

Climate Change, Disasters and Child Well-Being

Climate change and disasters can expose children to displacement, interrupted schooling, family separation, exploitation, violence and inadequate access to health and protection services.

The programme considers how child protection systems can prepare for and respond to these risks.

This may be relevant for teams working in countries affected by:

Flooding

Extreme heat

Drought

Severe storms

Earthquakes

Food insecurity

Conflict-related displacement

Climate-related migration

Child Protection in a Digital World

Digital technologies create both opportunities and risks for children.

The programme examines ways technology may support protection systems while also considering threats such as online exploitation, harmful content, privacy violations and technology-facilitated abuse.

Participants will consider how digital tools can contribute to:

Data collection

Case-management systems

Referral mechanisms

Professional training

Public education

Reporting protection concerns

Evidence-based advocacy

Measurement and Evidence Generation

Child protection decisions require credible information. However, many countries lack consistent administrative data, coordinated monitoring systems or reliable evidence about the scale of abuse and exploitation.

The programme explores how participants can improve data collection, measurement and evidence generation while recognising ethical, privacy and safeguarding considerations.

Juvenile Justice and Child-Sensitive Legal Systems

The course may examine how justice institutions interact with children who are victims, witnesses or accused of offences.

Participants may consider how legal systems can uphold children’s rights while ensuring that procedures are appropriate for their age, needs and circumstances.

Social and Structural Inequalities

Poverty, discrimination, social exclusion and unequal access to services can increase children’s exposure to harm.

The programme considers how structural inequalities affect children’s health, development and access to protection.

The Country Case-Study Requirement

A defining feature of the programme is its practical country-team case study.

Before travelling to Harvard, each team must work collaboratively to prepare a case study describing a genuine child protection challenge in its country.

The case study should outline:

The child protection problem

The groups of children affected

The institutional and legal context

Existing national responses

Weaknesses or gaps in the current system

Relevant government and civil-society stakeholders

Possible solutions the team wants to explore

Training organisers will provide admitted participants with preparation materials to guide the development of their case study.

Each team presents its initial case at the beginning of the training week.

Examples of Previous Case-Study Topics

Past teams have examined specific child protection concerns such as:

Child marriage

Alternative care

Violence against children

Other teams have focused on broader systemic problems, including:

Inadequate legal frameworks

Insufficient social-service workforces

Weak coordination between institutions

Lack of reliable child protection administrative data

These examples demonstrate that teams may focus on either a defined harm affecting children or an institutional weakness affecting the wider protection system.

Refining the Case Study at Harvard

Throughout the training week, country teams use research, classroom discussions and concepts presented by instructors to improve their case studies.

The process allows teams to:

Reassess their understanding of the problem

Identify missing evidence

Examine the roles of different institutions

Compare their experience with other countries

Consider alternative policy options

Improve the practicality of proposed solutions

Develop a more coordinated approach

Strengthen their advocacy strategy

On the final day, each country team presents its conclusions and proposed options to a panel of Harvard-affiliated child protection specialists.

The panel provides individualised feedback and suggestions to each team.

Benefits of the Country-Team Model

The country-team model helps ensure that programme learning is not limited to individual professional development.

By bringing together representatives from government, international organisations and local NGOs, the programme seeks to strengthen national collaboration and increase the likelihood that participants can implement or advocate for solutions after returning home.

The model may help participants:

Understand the perspectives of other institutions

Build professional relationships across sectors

Identify overlapping responsibilities

Reduce fragmentation

Develop more realistic policy proposals

Establish a foundation for future national cooperation

Translate international evidence into locally appropriate reforms

Programme Impact and Participant Feedback

Harvard reports that 100% of surveyed previous participants said the programme met or exceeded their expectations.

Past participants have highlighted:

Access to leading child protection specialists

Learning with professionals from diverse countries and backgrounds

The balance between evidence and practical application

Leadership development

Opportunities to examine national system strengths and weaknesses

Increased awareness of challenges facing children in other countries

Stronger advocacy and communication skills

A more holistic understanding of child protection

The programme was also featured in a UNICEF story concerning efforts to strengthen child protection systems.

Cohort Size

Enrollment is limited to:

30 individual participants

10 country teams

Three participants per team

The small cohort is designed to support close interaction, team-based work and individualised feedback.

Because only 10 country teams can be selected, applicants should demonstrate clearly why their proposed case study is important and how participation could strengthen national capacity.

Training Dates and Schedule

The 2027 programme will take place from:

June 7 to June 11, 2027

The course runs from Monday midday until Friday midday.

The on-site format means participants must be physically present in Boston for the training week. The programme is not advertised as an online or hybrid course.

Training Location

The programme will be held at:

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Boston, Massachusetts

United States

The official brochure provides the following FXB Center contact address:

651 Huntington Avenue

7th Floor

Boston, MA 02115

United States

The listed international telephone number is:

+1 617 432 0656

Tuition Coverage

All Harvard University course fees will be covered for admitted participants through the support of:

The G. Barrie Landry Fund for Child Protection Professional Training

UNICEF USA

This means selected participants will not be required to pay the tuition charged for the Harvard training itself.

However, this opportunity should not be described as completely funded because several major expenses remain the responsibility of participants.

Costs Participants Must Pay

Participants are responsible for:

International or domestic travel to Boston

Return travel

Accommodation

Living expenses

Visa application costs

Other required travel documentation

Meals not included as part of the training

Any other personal or incidental expenses

No travel allowance, accommodation subsidy, daily allowance or living stipend is promised in the official announcement or brochure.

Country teams should therefore confirm that they or their organisations can cover these expenses before applying.

Visa and Travel Responsibilities

Participants must secure their own United States visa and any other required travel documentation.

Admission to the programme does not guarantee that a visa will be issued.

Teams should consider:

Passport validity

United States visa requirements

Visa interview availability

Travel time to the nearest visa-processing location

Accommodation costs in Boston

Institutional travel approvals

Travel insurance

Budget approval from employers

Time required to complete government or organisational procedures

Admitted teams will be notified during or before the week of January 25, 2027, providing several months to make travel and visa arrangements before the June training.

How to Request an Application

There is no public online application form linked on the programme page.

Interested organisations or teams must request the application form by contacting:

Rebecca Shin

Director, Child Protection Program

Email: rebeccashin@hsph.harvard.edu

The request should clearly identify:

The applicant’s country

The organisations represented

The intention to form a three-member cross-sectoral team

A request for the official 2027 application form

Applicants should use the form and instructions provided directly by the FXB Center rather than preparing an unofficial application.

Application Process

The general application process is expected to involve the following steps:

Identify an important national child protection challenge.

Form a three-member, cross-sectoral country team.

Confirm that all members are mid-career child protection professionals.

Confirm that all three members are fluent in written and spoken English.

Obtain support or approval from the participating organisations.

Email the programme director to request the official application form.

Review the application instructions carefully.

Develop the country case and proposed area of work collaboratively.

Complete all required sections of the official application.

Submit the completed team application by December 1, 2026.

Await the admission decision during or before the week of January 25, 2027.

If admitted, begin case-study preparation and make visa, travel and accommodation arrangements.

Applicants should request the form well before the deadline to allow sufficient time for coordination among the three organisations.

Application Deadline

The deadline to submit a completed application is:

December 1, 2026

The brochure does not specify a closing time or time zone. Teams should therefore avoid submitting on the final day.

A team application requires coordination among three professionals and their respective institutions. Applicants should begin forming their teams, securing organisational approvals and requesting the official form as early as possible.

Admission Decision Timeline

Candidates will be notified of the admission decision during or before the week of:

January 25, 2027

The official materials do not describe separate interview, shortlisting or wait-list stages. Applicants should rely on subsequent instructions issued directly by the FXB Center.

How to Prepare a Strong Team Application

Although Harvard does not publish a detailed scoring framework, a strong application should reflect the programme’s stated objectives.

Teams should clearly demonstrate:

A significant national child protection challenge

The relevance of the challenge to children’s rights and well-being

Evidence that the problem requires multisectoral action

The complementary roles of all three team members

Strong institutional commitment

Practical opportunities for reform or improvement

The potential to apply learning after returning home

The ability to influence national policies, systems or professional practice

A commitment to collaboration

Strong English-language ability

Realistic expectations about travel and participation costs

The proposed case should be specific enough for meaningful analysis during the programme but significant enough to contribute to wider national child protection improvements.

Important Points to Confirm Before Applying

Prospective teams should confirm the following:

The application will include exactly three team members.

The team represents more than one sector.

Individual applications will not be submitted.

Every participant is a mid-career professional.

Every participant works in child protection or a closely connected field.

Every participant is fluent in written and spoken English.

All participants can attend in person in Boston from June 7 to June 11, 2027.

The team can cover travel, accommodation and living expenses.

Each participant can obtain the necessary visa and travel documents.

The team can complete and submit the application by December 1, 2026.

Conclusion

The 2027 G. Barrie Landry Child Protection Professional Training offers an important opportunity for experienced professionals to strengthen their knowledge, leadership and ability to build effective child protection systems.

Through an intensive week of instruction, case-study development, peer learning and specialist feedback, participants will examine the scientific, legal, institutional and policy dimensions of protecting children from violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect.

The programme’s country-team model is central to its design. Applications must be submitted by a three-member, cross-sectoral team, preferably comprising representatives from a government agency, an international organisation and a local NGO. Individual applications will not be considered.

Selected participants will receive full coverage of Harvard University course fees. Travel, accommodation, living expenses, visas and meals not included in the training remain the responsibility of participants.

The programme will take place at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston from June 7 to June 11, 2027. Applications must be submitted by December 1, 2026, and admission decisions are expected during or before the week of January 25, 2027.

TITLE: Advanced Moodle Practitioner Workshop | 1-2 August 2023

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Introduction

In lieu of the current technical models across the continent, with Africa in focus, the training workshop is drafted uniquely to fulfil and satisfy the continental demand for locally sourced talents to support the technical architectural demands of emerging universities.

As we approach the 21st century, institutions and corporate campuses continue to see a drastic divergence from the traditional modus operandi to more refined, sustainable framework solutions to address and automate manually defined processes within the academic administrative management and training workflow.

The formal classroom instructional environment has been challenged with an online contemporary to often replace or augment the structural brick and classroom environment. While the instruments for learning are being replaced, the underlying instructor-led, peer-based collaborative environment remains unthreatened. This workshop serves as a recurring medium to promote learning technology standards and use of eLearning solutions within the African Continent.

AAU invites you to attend a 2-day working session themed ‘Advanced Moodle Practitioner Workshop.’

The workshop is scheduled for 1st and 2nd August 2023 in Accra, Ghana at the AAU Secretariat.

Training Workshop

The workshop promises to be a hands-on experience with breakout sessions to provide comprehensive networking opportunities between learning enthusiasts. The breakout sessions will offer short, 30-minute sessions to collaborate and explore the following broad categories:

Technical knowledge transfers and how-to documents. Example: How to create a course

Best practices, use-cases and product sustainability. Example: Defining product roadmap and software lifecycle.

Frontend Administration. Example: Site configuration and settings available

Upgrades and Server Administration. Example: Managing your Moodle Server

Learning Outcomes

At the end of this workshop, the learner should be able to:

Describe an LMS?

Explain available features and functionalities.

Configure your site via front-end settings.

Manage your Moodle server via backend scripts.

Describe sustainability within the context of application management and adoption.

Audience

This event targets the following:

Learning Management Systems Administrator

Instructional Designer

Course Designer/Administrator

ICT Support Personnel

The event offers two specific training opportunities suitable for both front-end and back-end support personnels. With a keen focus on achieving defined learning outcomes, the training workshops lay the foundation for developing learning plans to support a career as a Moodle Administrator.

Front-End Administration

This section describes the management of the application through the graphical front-end user interface, or the application website. This section targets staff members who fit into one of the following categories:

Teaching Staff

Non-Teaching Staff

Teaching Staff

This cohort of learners reflects faculty or learners who interact with the application to create courses, add content, grade courses, etc.

Non-Teaching Staff

This cohort of learners reflects the faculty and academic support group; teaching assistants, help desk support representatives, etc.

Back-End Administration

This section describes the management of the application, database and web server.

This section targets staff members who fit into one of the following categories:

Server Administrator

Database Administrator

Linux Administrator

ICT Administrator

With a very mature marketing department dedicated to controlling AAU’s academic narrative on the web, we will work with AAU to:

Create and disseminate digital marketing materials: flyers, pdfs, etc.

Promote the event via social media outlets: Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, etc.

The workshop registration fee of US $350 for AAU Member Institutions and US $400 for Non-AAU Member Institutions per person and would cover tuition, programme materials, tea/coffee and lunches over the period of the event. Your nominees have to pay for the other expenses separately and these include travel, accommodation, local transport, visas and upkeep.

We recommend subscribing to the training workshop which can be held two to three times annually. AAU to spearhead this engagement and appropriate to handle registration and payment related communications.

TITLE: HWCC Conference Travel Grants 2027: Apply for Free Registration or Up to US$1,000 to Attend the Bangkok Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for a limited number of travel grants supporting participation in the 2nd International Conference on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence, which will take place from March 2–4, 2027, in Bangkok, Thailand.

Successful applicants may receive either a conference registration fee waiver or financial assistance of US$500 or US$1,000 toward travel costs. Applicants can request only one of these three support options.

The application window runs from September 1 to October 31, 2026. All applications must be submitted in English through the official online form by 23:59 GMT on October 31, 2026. Applicants are expected to receive the outcome of their applications by November 15, 2026. The official travel-grant page confirms the deadline, support options and priority criteria.

Travel Grant Opportunity at a Glance

Detail Information

Opportunity name
Travel Support for the 2nd International Conference on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence

Conference dates
March 2–4, 2027

Location
Bangkok, Thailand

Venue
Avani+ Riverside Bangkok Hotel

Application opening date
September 1, 2026

Application deadline
October 31, 2026, at 23:59 GMT

Notification date
By November 15, 2026

Application language
English

Available support
Registration waiver or reimbursement, US$500 toward travel, or US$1,000 toward travel

Number of options allowed
Applicants may request only one support option

Conference registration required before applying
No

Application method
Online Google application form

Host
IUCN SSC Human-Wildlife Conflict & Coexistence Specialist Group

About the 2nd International Conference on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence

The 2nd International Conference on Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence will bring together people working across conservation, research, policy, development, agriculture, technology and community-based practice.

Human-wildlife conflict can occur when interactions between people and wildlife create actual or perceived negative consequences for human livelihoods, safety, well-being, conservation objectives or animal welfare. Addressing these challenges requires more than biological research. It frequently involves community participation, governance, economic incentives, land-use planning, communication, behavioral science, conflict resolution and public policy.

The conference is being organized by the IUCN Species Survival Commission’s Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence Specialist Group. It will build on the first international conference, held in Oxford in 2023, which brought together nearly 600 participants from 70 countries and all continents.

The second conference will be held over three days in Bangkok from March 2–4, 2027. It is expected to convene Indigenous and local community leaders, conservation practitioners, researchers, government representatives, grant-makers, policymakers and professionals from other relevant sectors. The official conference overview explains its international, cross-sectoral focus.

Main Objectives of the Conference

The conference aims to improve international cooperation and learning on human-wildlife conflict and coexistence.

Its stated objectives include:

Promoting a shared understanding of human-wildlife conflict and coexistence through new perspectives, scientific knowledge, practical insights and technological advances.

Supporting the development of frameworks and approaches that improve research, management and mitigation.

Encouraging approaches that can influence national and international policies concerning human-wildlife conflict.

Facilitating dialogue and learning between different professional sectors and academic disciplines.

Examining emerging dimensions of human-wildlife conflict and coexistence.

Supporting local, national and international collaboration between practitioners, policymakers, researchers, communities and other stakeholders.

Advancing interdisciplinary approaches that consider the ecological, social, economic, cultural, political and behavioral dimensions of human-wildlife interactions.

The event is intended to provide a platform for practical discussion, knowledge exchange, professional networking and the development of new collaborations.

What Support Is Available?

Applicants must select only one of the following three options in the application form.

Option 1: Free Conference Registration

Successful applicants under this option will have their conference registration fee waived.

The organizers will send successful recipients a registration form so that they can register and confirm their place at the conference.

If a successful applicant has already registered and paid for a conference ticket, the organizers state that the ticket cost will be reimbursed.

This option may be useful for applicants who can arrange their own transportation and accommodation but cannot afford the conference registration fee.

Option 2: US$500 Toward Travel Costs

Applicants may request US$500 toward the costs of travelling to Bangkok.

The official page states that successful recipients will receive the amount in cash and in person at the conference on March 3, 2027.

The webpage does not state that the organizers will purchase airline tickets, reserve accommodation or provide the US$500 before the conference. Applicants should therefore plan on arranging and initially financing their travel unless their award letter expressly states otherwise.

Option 3: US$1,000 Toward Travel Costs

Applicants from eligible locations may request US$1,000 toward travel expenses.

As with the US$500 option, the amount will be provided in cash and in person at the conference in Bangkok on March 3, 2027. The award letter issued to each successful applicant will confirm the payment arrangement.

The US$1,000 option is not available to applicants based in:

Bangladesh

Bhutan

Brunei

Cambodia

China

India

Indonesia

Laos

Malaysia

Maldives

Myanmar

Nepal

Philippines

Singapore

Sri Lanka

Taiwan

Thailand

Vietnam

Applicants from these locations may still select the free conference registration option or the US$500 travel-support option, provided they otherwise satisfy the requirements.

Important Funding Limitation

The travel-grant programme is not described as full sponsorship.

Applicants should understand the following points:

Only a limited number of awards are available.

Submitting an application does not guarantee funding.

Applicants may request only one support option.

A US$500 or US$1,000 travel award is not described as including free conference registration.

A registration waiver is not described as including airfare, accommodation or other travel expenses.

The travel money is scheduled to be distributed in person on March 3, 2027.

The webpage does not promise advance payment or direct flight booking.

The webpage does not specify whether visa costs, accommodation, insurance or local transportation qualify as travel expenses.

The final award letter will confirm the arrangement offered to each recipient.

Applicants should prepare a realistic financial plan covering any costs not included in their selected support option.

A Critical Cash-Flow Consideration

The timing of the travel-grant payment is particularly important.

The main conference starts on March 2, 2027, while the US$500 or US$1,000 award is scheduled to be paid in person on March 3, 2027. This means recipients may need to purchase their tickets, obtain a visa, arrange insurance, book accommodation and reach Bangkok before receiving the money.

Applicants should not assume that selection will remove the need for advance funds. Before accepting an award, recipients should confirm:

Whether they must purchase their own airline ticket.

Whether any payment can be made before departure.

Whether the award may be used for accommodation.

Whether proof of expenditure will be required.

Whether conference registration must be purchased separately.

Whether payment will be made in U.S. dollars or an equivalent local currency.

Whether identification or a signed receipt will be required to collect the cash.

What happens if the recipient experiences a visa refusal or travel disruption.

Unless the award letter states otherwise, applicants should treat the funding as a contribution toward attendance rather than complete coverage of every cost.

Who Receives Priority?

The official page does not state that applicants must meet every priority criterion. It says priority will be given to applicants who meet any of the following:

Residents of countries not classified as high-income under the World Bank country classification.

Students from any country.

Applicants who submitted an abstract for a talk, poster or session.

Individuals included in a conference session submitted by another person.

These are priority factors rather than clearly stated absolute eligibility restrictions.

Therefore, the published information does not explicitly exclude:

Non-students.

Applicants from high-income countries.

Applicants who did not submit an abstract.

Applicants who are not presenting at the conference.

People working outside universities.

Independent practitioners and consultants.

Private-sector professionals.

Government employees.

Members of nonprofit or intergovernmental organizations.

However, applicants who do not meet any priority criterion may face stronger competition because the available funding is limited.

Do Applicants Need to Register for the Conference First?

No. Applicants do not need to register for the conference before submitting a travel-support application.

This is important because one of the available options is a registration fee waiver. Applicants seeking this option do not need to pay the registration fee merely to qualify for consideration.

Those who have already purchased a ticket may still apply. If they are selected for the registration-support option, the organizers state that the ticket will be reimbursed.

Applicants should keep their:

Registration confirmation.

Payment receipt.

Invoice.

Card or bank transaction record.

Any correspondence with the conference organizer.

These records may be needed to arrange reimbursement.

Status of the Call for Contributions

The conference’s separate call for abstracts and session contributions closed on August 31, 2026.

The travel-grant application opened on September 1, 2026. Consequently, applicants who submitted an abstract, poster, talk or session proposal before the contributions deadline may receive priority during travel-grant consideration.

Someone who did not submit a contribution may still apply for travel assistance because submitting an abstract is not stated as a mandatory requirement. However, the person cannot now rely on that particular priority factor unless the organizers reopen the contributions process.

The conference accepted proposals across a broad range of subjects, including:

Human, cultural and behavioral dimensions of coexistence.

Landscape-scale, climate and ecological issues.

Development, livelihoods, food security, poverty and well-being.

Communications and media.

Technology, artificial intelligence and scientific innovation.

Compensation, insurance, incentives and other financial instruments.

Practical conflict resolution and peacebuilding.

Policy and governance.

Connections between science and policy.

Lived experience and traditional knowledge.

One Health approaches.

Animal behavior, ethics and animal welfare.

The contribution formats included symposia, panels, reverse panels, interactive sessions, workshops, film screenings, individual presentations, speed talks and posters. The official contribution page confirms that submissions are now closed.

Application Form Requirements

The official application form is relatively short. It currently requests the following information:

Personal and contact information

Applicants must provide:

First and last name.

Email address.

Main country of residence.

Employment and affiliation

Applicants must identify the type of organization with which they work. The form provides the following options:

Government.

Private sector.

NGO or nonprofit organization.

Intergovernmental organization.

Academia or research institution.

Independent or consultancy.

Other.

Applicants must also state their organization or professional affiliation.

Student status

The application asks whether the applicant is currently a student.

Students from any country are one of the groups given priority, but the form also allows non-students to apply.

Conference contribution status

Applicants must state whether they submitted an abstract to the conference.

The form also asks whether they have been included as a panelist or speaker in a proposal submitted by another person. Available responses are:

Yes.

No.

I do not know.

Funding justification statement

Applicants must respond to the following substantive question in no more than 150 words:

Explain how attending the conference will further your work in human-wildlife conflict and coexistence and why you need financial support to attend.

This is the main written justification on the current form. Applicants should use the limited word count carefully.

Requested grant option

Applicants must choose one of the following:

Free conference registration.

US$500 toward travel costs.

US$1,000 toward travel costs, where geographically available.

The current form does not display a requirement to upload a curriculum vitae, passport, recommendation letter, academic transcript, detailed budget or copy of an abstract. Applicants should nevertheless recheck the live form before submission in case the organizers make changes.

How to Write a Strong 150-Word Funding Statement

The 150-word response should address both parts of the question:

How attending will advance the applicant’s work.

Why the applicant cannot attend without financial assistance.

A practical structure could be:

Opening: Professional or community context

Briefly introduce your work and the human-wildlife conflict issue you address.

For example, explain whether you work in conservation, research, agriculture, public policy, local government, community development, animal welfare, livelihoods or another related area.

Current challenge

Identify the specific problem, knowledge gap or implementation challenge affecting your work.

Avoid relying only on broad statements such as “human-wildlife conflict is important.” Describe the particular problem your community, institution or project is facing.

Value of conference participation

Explain how the conference will help you:

Learn a specific approach.

Connect with relevant specialists.

improve an existing intervention.

Strengthen policy development.

Develop a collaboration.

Share community knowledge.

Apply research findings.

Bring practical lessons back to your institution or community.

Financial need

State clearly why assistance is necessary. Where relevant, mention limited institutional funding, student status, unfavorable exchange rates, long-distance travel costs or lack of access to professional-development funding.

Applicants should remain factual and avoid making unsupported claims.

Suggested 150-Word Allocation

Applicants may use the following approximate structure:

30–40 words: Your role and the human-wildlife issue you address.

35–45 words: The practical problem or knowledge gap affecting your work.

40–50 words: How conference learning and connections will improve your work.

20–30 words: Why financial support is necessary.

10–20 words: The outcome you intend to deliver after returning.

This is application guidance rather than an official scoring formula.

How Applications Are Expected to Be Reviewed

The organizers have not published a numerical scoring system, detailed assessment rubric or weighting for each criterion.

The official information only confirms that:

Funding is limited.

Applications will be assessed against available resources.

Priority will be given to the specified applicant groups.

Selection is not guaranteed.

Applicants should therefore avoid claims that meeting one priority criterion guarantees an award.

A strong application should demonstrate:

A clear connection to human-wildlife conflict and coexistence.

A practical reason for attending the conference.

A realistic benefit to the applicant’s work, organization or community.

Genuine financial need.

A credible plan to apply or share knowledge gained from the conference.

Accurate information about student, residence and contribution status.

Travel-Grant Application Timeline

August 31, 2026

The separate call for abstracts and session contributions closed.

September 1, 2026

Travel-grant applications opened.

September 15, 2026

The conference’s early-bird registration deadline was extended to this date. Applicants do not need to register before applying for travel support.

October 31, 2026

Travel-grant applications close at 23:59 GMT.

November 15, 2026

All applicants are expected to be notified of the result by this date.

March 1, 2027

Optional pre-conference short courses are scheduled. These courses are separately ticketed and are not automatically included in the main registration fee.

March 2–4, 2027

The main conference takes place in Bangkok.

March 3, 2027

Successful US$500 and US$1,000 recipients are scheduled to receive their awards in cash and in person. The separately ticketed conference dinner is also scheduled for this date.

Conference Venue

The conference will be held at:

Avani+ Riverside Bangkok Hotel

257 Charoen Nakhon Road

Samre, Thon Buri

Bangkok 10600

Thailand

The hotel is a riverside venue overlooking the Chao Phraya River. It can be reached from both Suvarnabhumi Airport and Don Mueang Airport using taxis or ride-hailing services.

Delegates arriving at Suvarnabhumi Airport may also use the Airport Rail Link, connect to the BTS Skytrain and travel to Saphan Taksin Station before using the hotel’s shuttle boat. Complete venue and transportation information is available on the official conference website.

What Conference Registration Includes

According to the registration page, the main conference registration fee includes:

Access to sessions in the main conference programme.

Tea, coffee and snacks twice each day.

Lunch on all three conference days.

Admission to the conference reception.

The following are optional or separately ticketed:

Conference dinner.

Pre-conference short courses.

Other separately advertised activities.

Registration does not automatically cover international travel, accommodation, visas, insurance or other personal expenses. The official registration page explains what the ticket includes.

Visa, Passport and Insurance Responsibilities

International participants are responsible for checking the entry requirements that apply to their nationality and travel documents.

Delegates should plan for:

A passport valid for the required period.

A Thai visa or electronic visa where applicable.

Thailand’s entry and arrival requirements.

Travel and health insurance.

Cancellation insurance where appropriate.

Vaccination or health documentation if required.

Sufficient funds for accommodation and daily expenses.

Contingency costs caused by delays or cancellations.

Thailand requires international visitors to complete the Thailand Digital Arrival Card before arrival. Entry rules can change, so selected applicants should verify requirements through official Thai government sources before booking travel.

The conference terms state that the organizer may issue visa-support letters only after registration and payment have been completed. A support letter does not guarantee visa approval. Applicants should review the conference’s current visa guidance.

How to Apply

Follow these steps:

Read the official travel-grant information.

Decide which single support option best matches your financial situation.

Open the official travel-grant application form.

Enter your name, email address and main country of residence.

Select your organization type.

Provide your institutional or professional affiliation.

Confirm whether you are a student.

State whether you submitted a conference abstract.

State whether you are included as a speaker or panelist in someone else’s proposal.

Prepare a focused statement of no more than 150 words.

Select only one grant option.

Review every response carefully.

Submit the form before 23:59 GMT on October 31, 2026.

Save evidence that the form was submitted.

Monitor your email, including spam and junk folders, for the outcome.

Google sign-in is offered as a way to save application progress. Applicants should still prepare the 150-word response in a separate document before entering it into the form.

Application Preparation Checklist

Before starting the online application, prepare:

Your name exactly as used in professional correspondence.

A reliable email address.

Your country of residence.

The name of your employer, university, organization or professional affiliation.

Your organization type.

Confirmation of your current student status.

Details of any conference abstract or session proposal.

Confirmation from a session organizer if you may have been included as a speaker.

A 150-word funding justification.

A realistic estimate of your overall attendance costs.

A decision on which one of the three support options to request.

A plan for financing travel before the in-person payment date, if requesting travel funding.

Practical Tips for Applicants

Choose the appropriate grant option

Do not automatically select the highest amount.

If you can fund your travel but cannot afford conference registration, the registration waiver may be the most suitable request.

If you need help with airfare or another travel cost, select either US$500 or US$1,000, subject to the geographical restriction on the US$1,000 option.

Address both elements of the main question

A response that only explains your professional work is incomplete. You must also explain why you need funding.

Similarly, a response that discusses only financial hardship without demonstrating a meaningful connection to the conference may be less persuasive.

Emphasize a practical post-conference outcome

Explain what you will do with the knowledge and contacts gained. Examples could include:

Updating a community conflict-management programme.

Sharing lessons with colleagues.

Improving a research method.

Developing a policy recommendation.

Organizing a local training session.

Strengthening a cross-border collaboration.

Integrating community perspectives into a conservation programme.

Do not assume the grant is paid before travel

The official payment arrangement states that travel-grant recipients will receive cash in Bangkok on March 3, 2027. Prepare accordingly.

Submit early

The deadline is fixed at 23:59 GMT on October 31, 2026. Submitting early gives applicants time to address internet, form or email problems.

Keep the statement within 150 words

Exceeding the maximum length may weaken the application or result in text being cut off. Draft and count the words before pasting the response into the form.

Travel-Grant Sponsors

The sponsor logos displayed on the official page identify:

Fondation Segré.

Golden Triangle Asian Elephant Foundation.

The conference is organized by the IUCN SSC Human-Wildlife Conflict & Coexistence Specialist Group.

Other Funding Opportunities Listed by the Conference

The official page also refers applicants to two external funding sources:

British Ecological Society travel-grant opportunities.

Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture travel grants.

These are separate programmes with their own eligibility rules, application procedures and deadlines. Applicants should not assume that the HWCC Conference application automatically places them under consideration for either external opportunity.

Conclusion

The 2027 HWCC Conference travel-support programme provides an important opportunity for people working on human-wildlife conflict and coexistence to participate in an international gathering in Bangkok.

Applicants can request one of three forms of support: free conference registration, US$500 toward travel expenses or US$1,000 toward travel expenses. Priority will be given to residents of countries not classified as high-income, students and people contributing to the conference programme, but the published information does not restrict applications exclusively to these groups.

Applicants should carefully consider the payment arrangement before applying. Travel awards are scheduled to be paid in cash at the conference on March 3, 2027, rather than before departure. Successful recipients may therefore need to finance their initial travel and attendance expenses independently.

The main application requirement is a concise 150-word explanation of how conference participation will advance the applicant’s work and why financial assistance is needed. Clear, specific and honest responses will be more effective than broad descriptions of conservation challenges.

Applications must be submitted in English through the official online form by 23:59 GMT on October 31, 2026. Applicants are expected to receive the outcome by November 15, 2026.

TITLE: Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 12, 2026

Applications are open for the Zukunftskolleg Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026. The Zukunftskolleg offers postdoctoral researchers independence for their research, interdisciplinary and intergenerational exchange as well as intra-university integration and international contacts.

Each fellow is a member of both a university department and the Zukunftskolleg. Additionally, fellows of the Zukunftskolleg can be affiliated to the Clusters of Excellence at the University of Konstanz: “Politics of Inequality” or to the “Centre for the Advanced Study of Collective Behaviour”. The target group consists of excellent early career postdoctoral researchers who demonstrate scientific excellence, research independence, and a strong capacity for teamwork, indicating high potential for a successful academic career.

Responsibilities

Develop and implement your research project

Build up your own research profile

You are expected to participate actively in the regular weekly meetings of the Zukunftskolleg and to contribute to the Zukunftskolleg in creating a team of exciting interdisciplinary postdoctoral researchers

Have your place of residence in Konstanz or its surroundings

Benefits

Postdoctoral Fellows profit from all support measures available at the Zukunftskolleg:

they receive an annual research allowance e.g. for funding research assistants or equipment;

they are eligible to apply for co-funding;

Senior Fellowships and the Mentorship Programme give them the opportunity to invite distinguished colleagues to Konstanz;

they can go on a temporary Research Visit abroad or nominate international early career researchers for a Research Visit at the Zukunftskolleg;

they are eligible to apply for funding for cooperative initiatives or for funding for particular career stages;

they receive non-monetary support like coaching, professional career counseling or in grant proposal writing;

they get financial support to organise and run a scientific retreat.

Eligibility

You should be in possession of a doctoral degree granted between 30 September 2024 and 1 October 2026. Earlier graduation dates may be accepted in case of maternity/paternity leave, or working contracts outside academia.

Candidates must not hold a permanent professorship, or have a habilitation or equivalent (Venia legendi).

Candidates with their own position funded by another programme, which can be transferred to Konstanz, are also eligible.
