TITLE: NASA Texas Aerospace Scholars 2026–2027: Apply for the TAS Junior Experience for Texas High School Juniors

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2026–2027 Texas Aerospace Scholars Junior Experience, a NASA STEM education programme designed for high school juniors in Texas who want to explore aerospace, engineering, science and technology while engaging directly with NASA scientists and engineers.

The Texas Aerospace Scholars programme, commonly known as TAS and formerly called High School Aerospace Scholars or HAS, provides eligible Texas students with a structured pathway to explore real-world STEM concepts while learning how those subjects connect with NASA missions and careers in the aerospace industry.

The Junior Experience is a year-long commitment beginning with an online learning programme called Launch Pad. Students develop transferable skills in areas including:

Coding

Computer-aided design

Engineering

Earth science

Space exploration

Technology

Collaborative problem-solving

Students who perform strongly during Launch Pad may be invited to the next stage, a five-day virtual challenge called Moonshot, where participants work in teams with support from NASA scientists and engineers to develop an Artemis-inspired mission to the Moon and Mars. The highest-performing Moonshot teams may then be invited to Base Camp, an in-person residential experience at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

The programme is open only to students who meet specific requirements. Applicants must be U.S. citizens, residents of Texas, enrolled as juniors in a Texas high school, interested in STEM, able to access the internet and prepared to complete the online course requirements.

The application window runs from:

July 1 to September 16, 2026

Students must complete their application through NASA STEM Gateway.

What Is the Texas Aerospace Scholars Programme?

Texas Aerospace Scholars is a NASA educational initiative that gives Texas high school students an opportunity to explore science, technology, engineering and mathematics through activities connected with actual aerospace research and exploration.

Rather than introducing STEM only through traditional classroom lessons, TAS incorporates:

NASA mission concepts

Engineering challenges

Interactive online learning

Teamwork

Career exploration

Contact with NASA scientists and engineers

The Junior Experience is specifically designed for students who are currently entering or enrolled in their junior year of high school.

The programme aims to help students understand how subjects studied in school connect with careers in:

Aerospace

Engineering

Science

Technology

Space exploration

Computer-aided design

Related STEM industries

Texas Aerospace Scholars Junior Experience

The TAS Junior Experience is not simply a short summer programme.

It is described by NASA as a year-long commitment during which students progress through several stages.

The pathway begins with:

Launch Pad

Moonshot

Base Camp

Not every participant automatically progresses through every stage.

Students begin with Launch Pad, and later opportunities depend on performance.

Stage 1: Launch Pad Online Course

The first stage of the Junior Experience is:

Launch Pad

Launch Pad is an online course beginning in the fall.

Students work through four mission-inspired modules involving subjects connected with:

Earth science

Space exploration

Technology

Engineering concepts

NASA designed the modules to help participants see how STEM knowledge is applied to challenges associated with space exploration.

The official 2026–2027 calendar shows that the Launch Pad online course runs from:

September 28, 2026 to March 6, 2027.

Because the programme is online during this stage, students need reliable access to the internet through:

Home

School

Public library

or another available source.

Internet access is specifically listed as an eligibility requirement.

Four Engineering Design Challenges

Launch Pad includes a series of engineering design challenges during the academic year.

For the 2026–2027 programme, the currently published dates are:

Engineering Design Challenge #1: November 7, 2026

Engineering Design Challenge #2: December 5, 2026

Engineering Design Challenge #3: January 23, 2027

Engineering Design Challenge #4: February 27, 2027

These challenges allow students to move beyond reading about aerospace concepts and begin applying problem-solving and engineering principles themselves.

The programme may therefore be especially useful for students considering future study in fields such as:

Aerospace engineering

Mechanical engineering

Computer science

Physics

Earth science

Robotics

Space science

Other STEM fields

Coding and Computer-Aided Design Skills

One of the distinguishing features of the TAS Junior Experience is that students build practical and transferable skills.

NASA specifically identifies:

Coding

Computer-aided design, or CAD

Engineering

as areas in which Junior Experience participants develop skills.

These abilities can be valuable well beyond aerospace.

For example, CAD is widely used in:

Engineering

Product development

Manufacturing

Architecture

Aerospace design

Mechanical systems

Coding also plays a growing role in scientific research, engineering analysis, aerospace systems and technology development.

Stage 2: Moonshot Virtual Summer Experience

Students who demonstrate high achievement during the online programme may be invited to:

Moonshot

Moonshot is a:

Five-day virtual summer challenge

Participants work in teams while receiving mentorship from NASA scientists and engineers.

The challenge is themed around NASA’s Artemis programme, with students working collaboratively to develop a mission concept involving exploration of:

The Moon

Mars

NASA’s programme description emphasizes teamwork and mission planning rather than individual competition alone.

Moonshot Dates for 2027

The current programme schedule identifies two potential Moonshot weeks:

Week 1: May 31–June 4, 2027

or

Week 2: June 7–11, 2027

Selection for Moonshot is expected in:

April 2027.

Students should therefore understand that participation in the Junior Experience can continue well beyond the school-year online course.

What Students Do During Moonshot

During Moonshot, participants work collaboratively to develop an Artemis-themed mission to the Moon and Mars.

The experience allows students to practice:

Teamwork

Engineering thinking

Problem-solving

Mission planning

Technical communication

Collaborative decision-making

The involvement of NASA scientists and engineers also gives participants exposure to professionals working within aerospace and STEM careers.

Stage 3: Base Camp at NASA Johnson Space Center

The highest-performing Moonshot teams may receive invitations to:

Base Camp

Unlike Launch Pad and Moonshot, Base Camp is a:

Residential experience

held at:

NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

For the 2026–2027 cycle, NASA’s current schedule lists:

July 25–30, 2027

for the residential experience.

This means top-performing students can progress from an online statewide programme to an in-person NASA experience.

Why NASA Johnson Space Center Matters

NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston is closely associated with American human spaceflight.

For students interested in aerospace careers, participating in a residential activity connected with the Center can provide important exposure to the environment surrounding NASA’s work.

However, applicants should understand that Base Camp is not guaranteed to every student admitted to Launch Pad.

The pathway is selective:

Launch Pad → high achievement → Moonshot → top team selection → Base Camp

This distinction is important when describing the programme.

Who Is Eligible for the TAS Junior Experience?

NASA publishes several mandatory eligibility requirements.

Applicants must satisfy all of them.

1. U.S. Citizenship

Applicants must be:

U.S. citizens.

This means the programme is not open generally to international students studying temporarily in Texas if they do not hold U.S. citizenship.

2. Texas Residency

Applicants must be:

Residents of Texas.

This is a statewide programme specifically designed for Texas students.

3. Texas High School Junior

Applicants must be:

Enrolled as a junior in a Texas high school.

The programme is therefore not open to:

High school freshmen

High school sophomores applying outside the specified transition requirements

College students

Students who have already graduated from high school

The application transcript must demonstrate the student’s current school status.

Are Homeschool Students Eligible?

Yes.

NASA specifically states that students may attend different types of schools, including:

Homeschool

Public school

Private school

Charter school

Online school

The important requirement is that the school must be based in Texas.

NASA may request proof of enrollment.

This makes the programme accessible to students across several different education models.

STEM Interest Requirement

Applicants must demonstrate interest in:

Science

Technology

Engineering

Mathematics

NASA does not require students already to be experts in aerospace engineering.

The programme is designed partly to help students explore STEM pathways.

Therefore, students who are curious about aerospace or science but are still deciding what they may want to study after high school can still potentially be strong applicants.

Internet Access Requirement

Applicants must have access to the internet through:

Home

School

Public library

or another suitable location.

This requirement exists because the core Launch Pad component is completed online.

Programme Commitment

Applicants must commit to completing the online course in order to qualify for Moonshot.

NASA’s FAQ further describes participants as needing to commit to the programme duration, including the virtual summer experience.

Students should therefore consider their academic and extracurricular schedule before applying.

This is not simply a single online seminar or one-day NASA event.

Application Window

The Junior Experience application window is:

July 1–September 16, 2026.

Students who meet the requirements should submit well before the closing date to reduce the risk of technical difficulties.

How to Apply for Texas Aerospace Scholars

Applications are completed through:

NASA STEM Gateway

NASA outlines several application steps.

Step 1: Create or Access a NASA STEM Gateway Account

Applicants must either:

Log into an existing NASA STEM Gateway profile, or

Create a customized profile

The STEM Gateway provides access to NASA education and STEM opportunities.

Step 2: Find the TAS Launch Pad Opportunity

Once logged in, students should visit the:

TAS Launch Pad Opportunity Page

The opportunity is accessible only while the application window is active.

Step 3: Upload a Texas High School Transcript

Applicants must upload a transcript from a:

Texas high school.

The transcript should:

Clearly show the student’s name

Match the name registered on the NASA STEM Gateway account

Demonstrate that the applicant is currently enrolled as a junior or has completed sophomore year

Students should therefore check their transcript before submitting.

If the name on their STEM Gateway profile differs from the name shown on the school transcript, they should resolve the discrepancy before completing the application.

Step 4: Complete the Expression of Interest Essay

Applicants must complete an:

Expression of Interest essay

NASA states that this essay may be shared with:

State legislators.

Students should therefore treat this as an important part of the application.

The essay is an opportunity to communicate:

Why STEM interests them

Why they want to participate in TAS

What they hope to learn

How NASA or aerospace relates to their goals

What qualities they would bring to the programme

Applicants should answer authentically rather than trying to imitate highly technical aerospace writing.

Step 5: Submit the Application

After completing all required components, applicants should click:

Apply

in the upper-right corner of the opportunity page and complete the submission process.

Students should verify that all required materials have been successfully uploaded before considering the application complete.

Orientation Dates

Students selected for the programme should be aware of two scheduled orientation dates:

September 22, 2026 – Student Orientation #1

September 24, 2026 – Student Orientation #2

These occur shortly before Launch Pad begins on September 28.

What Skills Can Students Develop?

The TAS Junior Experience provides opportunities to strengthen several transferable skills.

Engineering Skills

Students work through engineering-oriented activities and design challenges that encourage them to move from abstract concepts toward practical solutions.

Coding

Coding experience can help students build computational thinking and become more comfortable with technology-focused problem-solving.

Computer-Aided Design

CAD introduces students to digital design tools used widely across engineering and technical industries.

Teamwork

Moonshot involves collaborative mission planning, requiring participants to:

Share responsibilities

Communicate ideas

Evaluate alternatives

Solve problems collectively

Communication

Participants also need to explain technical ideas clearly and participate in collaborative discussions.

Time Management

Because Launch Pad runs alongside the normal academic year, students must balance the programme with:

School

Homework

Exams

Extracurricular activities

Exploring STEM Careers

A major objective of the programme is helping students understand how their interests connect with aerospace and broader STEM careers.

Students may gain a clearer understanding of fields including:

Engineering

Earth science

Space exploration

Technology

Aerospace

Computer science

Scientific research

This exposure can be valuable before students begin applying to universities and deciding on potential majors.

Direct Engagement With NASA Professionals

A particularly distinctive component of TAS is the opportunity to interact with:

NASA scientists and engineers.

High-achieving students selected for Moonshot receive mentorship from NASA professionals while completing the Artemis-themed summer challenge.

For high school students, this can provide a clearer picture of what professional STEM work actually involves.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

1. Do Not Wait Until September 16

The programme requires:

NASA STEM Gateway registration

Transcript upload

Essay completion

Formal application submission

Completing everything early gives applicants time to resolve any technical or documentation problems.

2. Check Your Transcript

Make sure:

The name matches your Gateway account

Your grade-level status is clear

NASA specifically identifies these requirements.

3. Make the Essay Personal

Do not write only:

“I like NASA and space.”

Instead, explain what actually interests you.

You might discuss:

An engineering challenge you enjoyed

A science class that influenced you

A coding project

Curiosity about space exploration

An interest in solving complex problems

A future STEM career you want to explore

A concrete example can make the response much stronger.

4. Show Willingness to Learn

You do not need to arrive already knowing how to design spacecraft.

The programme exists to help students develop STEM skills.

A strong application can communicate curiosity, commitment and willingness to challenge yourself.

5. Understand the Time Commitment

The Junior Experience extends from fall 2026 through potentially summer 2027.

Students should make sure they can commit to completing Launch Pad and, if selected, the later stages.

Application Checklist

Before submitting, students should confirm that they:

Are U.S. citizens.

Are Texas residents.

Are enrolled as juniors in a Texas high school.

Have an interest in STEM.

Have reliable internet access.

Can commit to the online programme.

Conclusion

The NASA Texas Aerospace Scholars Junior Experience 2026–2027 provides Texas high school juniors with an exceptional opportunity to explore STEM through a year-long programme connected directly to NASA.

Students begin with Launch Pad, an online course covering mission-inspired topics in Earth science, space exploration and technology while developing practical skills in coding, computer-aided design and engineering.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Rainer Weiss

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Rainer Weiss ’55, PhD ’62 has established a fellowship in the Physics Department because he is eternally grateful to his advisor, the late Jerrold Zacharias, for all that he did for Rai, so he knows firsthand the importance of supporting graduate students.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2018

© Bryce Vickmark. All rights reserved. www.vickmark.com 617.448.6758
Rainer “Rai” Weiss was born in Berlin, Germany in 1932. His father was a physician and his mother was an actress. His family was forced out of Germany by the Nazis since his father was Jewish and a Communist. Rai, his mother and father fled to Prague, Czechoslovakia. In 1937 a sister was born in Prague. In 1938, after Chamberlain appeased Hitler by effectively giving him Czechoslovakia, the family was able to obtain visas to enter the United States through the Stix Family in St. Louis, who were giving bond to professional Jewish emigrants. When Rai was 21 years-old, he visited Mrs. Stix and thanked her for what she had done for his family.

The family immigrated to New York City. Rai’s father had a hard time passing the medical boards because of his inability to answer multiple choice exams. His mother, who Rai says “held the family together,” worked in a number of retail stores. Through the services of an immigrant relief organization Rai received a scholarship to attend the prestigious Columbia Grammar School. At the end of 1945, when Rai was 13 years old, he became fascinated with electronics and music. As World War II ended a lot of surplus Navy and Army electronic parts became available. Rai bought some of the equipment and began making ham radio transmitters and an audio system for his school. Then, after a movie theater in Brooklyn had a fire behind the screen, he was able to acquire broken but repairable loud speakers and began making high-fidelity equipment. At this time concerts were broadcast via FM radio with high fidelity. Rai invited some family friends to listen to these concerts on his equipment. He was asked to build a comparable system by one of his guests. That began a chain of people via word-of-mouth who all wanted to have such systems. In Rai’s senior year of high school he had more orders than he could handle and the beginning of a pretty good business. Eventually he ran into a problem that was past his ability to solve with the “street” electronics he knew: trying to reduce the hissing noise on the shellac phonograph records, then available by using adaptive filters. That problem convinced Rai he would do well to go to college.

Rai attended MIT because of his strong interest in electrical engineering. He admits that MIT scared him when he received the course catalog of everything he had to take, all listed in numbers. When he came to MIT in 1950 there were 400 freshman, and only one was a woman. He picked electrical engineering as a major, but was disappointed since he was not able to do electronics and had to take a number of classes before he was able to get to it. He ultimately choose physics since the curriculum seemed less rigid. At the beginning of his junior year, Rai took a trip to Nantucket and met an interesting woman who was a pianist. He fell for her and followed her to Chicago. He took about two months off from MIT since he did not think they took attendance and thought he could get by just by taking the exams. He ended up flunking out of MIT.

Rai found a job as a technician in Building 20, which had housed the WWII Radiation Laboratory that had developed radar. It was there that he met Professor Jerrold Zacharias, who Rai says “was the person that had the biggest influence on my life.” Zacharias had carried out fundamental measurements of the properties of individual atoms and had used the techniques to develop an atomic clock with unprecedented precision of an error of 1 second in 10,000 years. When Rai joined his lab he was thinking of making an even more precise clock that could measure a prediction of Einstein’s that clocks in strong gravitational fields ran more slowly than those in weak fields. It was through Zacharias that Rai was able to get back into MIT and finish his undergraduate degree, and later a graduate degree in physics.

During his graduate years Rai began to study the piano and rebuilt a Steinway grand in a garage where he lived and worked. Also at that time he met his wife Rebecca, a graduate of Radcliffe College, who was working as a botanist for Harvard. Rai and Rebecca have two children, Ben, an art historian, and Sarah, who is an ethnomusicologist. Rai became an assistant professor at Tufts University while still a graduate student but then left to become a postdoc at Princeton University. Then, Zacharias called him and asked if he would come back to MIT to be an assistant professor in MIT’s RLE (Research Laboratory of Electronics). So, Rai came back and started a research group in cosmology and gravitation. The group was engaged in experimental research to determine if G, the Newtonian constant, was changing with time, as well as studies of the spectrum and angular distribution of the recently discovered cosmic background radiation. Rai got the idea for LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational- Wave Observatory) when the Physics Department asked him to teach a graduate course on general relativity. He teamed up with Professor Kip Thorne at Caltech and formed a collaboration between MIT and Caltech with the late Scottish physicist Ronald Drever, also with Caltech.

Anything you can do to help advance students, because they are our future.
Rainer Weiss ’55, PhD ’62, Professor of Physics Emeritus and 2017 Nobel Laureate.

After a gravitational wave—a ripple from the distant part of the universe—was detected by the LIGO team, Rai received a number of awards for the discovery. At first, he was not sure what to do with the prize money. He was committed to his grandson’s education and he wanted to give back to MIT. He was so grateful for what Jerrold Zacharias had done for him that in many ways this gift is a tribute to him. Rai also thought about the importance of supporting graduate students. As a faculty member, he would see MIT losing some of the best graduate student applicants to other universities that had the capability of offering graduate student fellowships.

Rai decided to establish a fellowship in the Physics Department and to name it the Barish–Weiss Fellowship. It was important to Rai to include Barry Barish in the name since he was instrumental in the success of LIGO by knowing how to make the transition from “table top” to the large-scale physics required to detect gravitational waves.

On October 3, 2017, Rai Weiss won the Nobel Prize in Physics along with Emeriti Professors of Caltech, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish. They were honored for their “decisive contributions” to the Laser Interferometer Gravitational–Wave Observatory (LIGO) detector and the observation of gravitational waves.

Rai is happy that he had the opportunity to give back to MIT. He is eternally grateful for all that Jerrold Zacharias did for him, and that MIT has allowed him to still work in the Department. He works every day, even on Saturdays, because he loves his work and being involved with students. When asked what he would say to encourage others to support MIT, he replied, “Anything you can do to help advance students because they are our future.”

TITLE: 2026–2027 Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants for Journalists and Storytellers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Better Life Lab at New America is inviting journalists and storytellers to apply for its 2026–2027 Multimedia Reporting Grants, an opportunity designed to support powerful, solutions-oriented stories about caregiving, child care, family support, disability care, elder care, and end-of-life care.

The reporting grants are intended for storytellers who can use journalism and creative storytelling to explore the challenges surrounding care in the United States while highlighting practical solutions, innovations, and possibilities for building stronger care systems.

Selected storytellers will have their stories commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026. In addition to funding for reporting, successful applicants will be invited to participate in the Better Life Lab’s reporting cohort and receive editorial guidance and placement assistance.

The program welcomes both new and experienced reporters and particularly encourages applications from people with perspectives that have traditionally been underrepresented in the media.

About the Better Life Lab Multimedia Reporting Grants

The Better Life Lab, a program at New America, focuses on issues connected to work-family justice, gender equity, and the value of care.

The Lab recognizes that care is a universal part of human life. People provide or receive care in many different circumstances, including raising children, supporting family members during illness, caring for older relatives, assisting people with disabilities, and providing comfort at the end of life.

However, the source notes that care infrastructure in the United States faces significant challenges. The Better Life Lab therefore sees storytelling as an important way to examine these challenges, highlight solutions, influence policy discussions, and help audiences understand why care systems matter.

Through the 2026–2027 reporting grants, the Lab is seeking journalists and storytellers who can develop compelling stories that do more than describe problems. The program emphasizes reporting that identifies approaches that are already being tested or implemented and examines what could be learned from them.

What the 2026–2027 Reporting Grants Are Looking For

The Better Life Lab is particularly interested in stories addressing two major pillars of the care crisis:

1. Innovations in Child Care

One major focus of the reporting grants is innovation in child care.

Applicants are encouraged to develop stories about real-world efforts that are already underway and that could contribute to a more equitable and accessible child care system.

The goal is to identify and explore promising approaches while helping audiences envision what a stronger child care system could look like.

Stories in this area may examine child care solutions or address fundamental questions about how early childhood education and care can be improved.

The source specifically identifies several areas that storytellers can explore, including:

Rethinking when learning begins.

Examining who is served by child care systems.

Exploring the quality of care provided.

Examining the costs associated with child care.

Exploring how child care is financed and paid for.

Highlighting innovations that could contribute to a more equitable child care system.

Examining approaches that could provide families with greater choices.

Exploring ways of supporting living wages for child care educators and providers.

The initiative’s child care reporting component is supported by the Bainum Family Foundation and other funders.

Applicants interested in this area can therefore consider reporting that moves beyond identifying shortcomings and instead investigates programs, models, practices, policies, or community efforts that could offer useful lessons for the future.

2. Investments in Care Infrastructure

The second major focus is the broader issue of investment in care infrastructure.

This area recognizes that caregiving extends throughout the life cycle and is not limited to early childhood.

The Better Life Lab is seeking multimedia stories examining both challenges and potential solutions affecting caregivers and people who depend on care, including:

Infants and young children.

Families requiring child care.

People with disabilities.

Older adults.

Families caring for aging relatives.

People approaching the end of life.

Caregivers supporting family members across different stages of life.

The reporting can explore how investments in care infrastructure could strengthen families, communities, and gender equality.

The Lab’s call also points to the relationship between caregiving and women’s lives, noting that care is often treated as a private family responsibility and frequently falls disproportionately on women.

Stories can therefore examine how better care infrastructure could affect families and communities while also considering the broader economic and social implications of care.

Solutions-Oriented Journalism Is at the Heart of the Opportunity

A defining feature of these reporting grants is the emphasis on solutions-oriented storytelling.

Rather than focusing exclusively on what is broken within care systems, the Better Life Lab wants stories that investigate how and why care issues matter and what can be done about them.

The program describes its approach as solutions journalism: reporting that emphasizes not only problems but also possible ways of addressing them.

For applicants, this means that a strong reporting proposal should ideally have a clear connection between the issue being examined and potential solutions, innovations, or approaches that can be explored through reporting.

The stories should help audiences understand:

Why care matters to families.

Why care matters to children.

Why care matters to communities.

Why care matters to the economy.

What innovative approaches are already being attempted.

Whether particular innovations could be expanded or replicated.

What a better future for care could look like.

The Better Life Lab says this approach is intended to help build the energy and public demand necessary to support solutions to care challenges.

Who Can Apply for the Reporting Grants?

The opportunity is open to journalists and storytellers, with applications welcomed from both new and experienced reporters.

The source specifically states that:

New reporters are welcome to apply.

Experienced reporters are welcome to apply.

People with perspectives traditionally underrepresented in the media are especially encouraged to apply.

The program is therefore not restricted solely to established journalists with long professional careers. The invitation explicitly includes newer reporters and storytellers.

What Types of Stories Can Be Submitted?

The Better Life Lab is open to a broad range of storytelling formats.

Applicants are not limited to conventional written journalism. The program welcomes multiple forms of media, including

Print stories.

Online articles.

Photojournalism.

Graphic stories.

Podcasts.

Audio stories.

Multimedia projects.

Videography.

The Lab also expresses interest in new and creative storytelling methods that can reach broad and diverse audiences.

This provides applicants with considerable flexibility in how they approach a proposed story. Rather than requiring every applicant to use the same medium, the program allows storytellers to select a format that fits the subject and intended audience.

Creative Storytelling and Reaching Diverse Audiences

The Better Life Lab is interested in stories that can communicate complex care issues to broad and diverse audiences.

Applicants should therefore consider how their proposed reporting can make care-related issues understandable, engaging, and relevant to people beyond a specialized professional audience.

Creative approaches may be particularly relevant where they help audiences understand:

The realities faced by caregivers.

The experiences of families seeking care.

The importance of child care systems.

The challenges associated with aging.

Disability and care needs.

End-of-life care.

The economic importance of care.

Innovative solutions being tested in communities.

The Lab also wants stories that can paint a vision of what is possible in the future and examine whether promising innovations have the potential to scale.

What Selected Storytellers Receive

Successful applicants will receive more than an opportunity to develop a story.

According to the Better Life Lab, selected journalists and storytellers will benefit from several forms of support.

Reporting Commissions

Stories will be commissioned on a rolling basis beginning in October 2026.

This means selected storytellers will have an opportunity to develop reporting around the care-related topics identified by the program.

Participation in a Reporting Cohort

Selected journalists will also be invited to participate in the Better Life Lab reporting cohort.

This creates an opportunity for participating storytellers to engage with others working on care-related reporting and become part of a broader group supported by the Lab.

Editorial Guidance

The program will provide selected journalists with editorial guidance.

This support can be particularly relevant for storytellers developing complex stories that require careful reporting, framing, research, and presentation.

Placement Assistance

Selected storytellers will also receive placement assistance.

The source indicates that the Lab works with its grantees to support the publication and placement of their stories.

Track Record of the Better Life Lab Reporting Grants

The Better Life Lab has an established history of supporting storytellers.

Since 2021, the Lab reports that it has supported more than 30 different storytellers.

Together with its team, it has produced nearly 100 stories on child care innovations, with those stories appearing in nearly 40 different publications and media outlets.

This previous work demonstrates the program’s focus on taking care-related reporting to established media audiences.

Examples highlighted by the Lab include stories published by outlets such as Slate, Wisconsin Examiner, and Vox.

The examples cover topics including elder care, child care differences across countries, and challenges facing caregivers who simultaneously support aging parents and children.

Previous Better Life Lab Care Story Collections

The Better Life Lab has also published collections of stories from previous reporting grant periods.

Applicants interested in understanding the type of work previously supported by the program can review its earlier collections, including:

These previous collections can provide useful context about the themes and approaches that have been explored through the reporting initiative.

One resource focuses specifically on telling stories of care through video.

The resource provides guidance for reporters who want to create videos, including practical considerations such as writing a script and preparing for presentation on camera.

Applicants interested in producing video or multimedia reporting may find these resources particularly relevant when developing their storytelling approach.

Why Caregiving Stories Matter

Caregiving affects virtually every stage of life.

Families may need child care when children are young, support for relatives dealing with illness, assistance for people living with disabilities, care for aging family members, or support during the end-of-life stage.

Because these needs affect individuals, families, communities, workplaces, and economies, reporting on care can extend beyond personal stories and examine wider social and economic systems.

The Better Life Lab’s reporting grants provide a platform for exploring these connections through journalism and creative storytelling.

The program’s emphasis on solutions also means that applicants can investigate not only the challenges people experience but also the initiatives attempting to address those challenges.

TITLE: J-PAL 2026–2027 Recruitment Drive: Apply for Research Associate Jobs and Join a Global Network Advancing Evidence-Based Policy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) is opening its 2026–2027 recruitment cycle, providing an opportunity for qualified candidates interested in research, data, fieldwork, development economics, public policy, and evidence-based approaches to poverty reduction to apply for positions across its global network.

The recruitment drive is particularly relevant for candidates seeking to build careers in international development research and work alongside researchers, academic institutions, and organizations conducting rigorous evaluations of policies and programs designed to improve people’s lives.

J-PAL and professors at affiliated research institutions around the world are accepting applications for General Data Research Associate and General Field Research Associate positions during the early phase of the recruitment cycle. The wider recruitment drive will subsequently open applications for additional positions.

About J-PAL

The Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) is a global research network that works with researchers and policymakers to generate evidence and translate research into policy and practice.

Its work focuses on using rigorous research and data to understand which approaches can effectively address challenges associated with poverty and social and economic development.

J-PAL works through a network of affiliated researchers, regional offices, academic institutions, governments, and partner organizations around the world. This makes its recruitment opportunities particularly valuable for individuals who want to gain experience in international development, empirical research, policy evaluation, data analysis, and field-based research.

Working within the J-PAL network can also provide exposure to multidisciplinary research projects and collaboration with researchers and organizations operating in different countries and sectors.

J-PAL 2026–2027 Recruitment Drive

J-PAL conducts recruitment throughout the year, but a substantial number of positions are filled during its annual recruitment drives.

The annual recruitment drive is therefore an important period for people seeking employment with J-PAL and its affiliated organizations. Applying during the recruitment drive can increase the likelihood that an application will be considered by multiple researchers and hiring managers within the network.

For the 2026–2027 recruitment cycle, J-PAL has introduced an early launch for two major categories of research positions:

General Data Research Associate

General Field Research Associate

The early recruitment period runs from September 8, 2026, through October 9, 2026.

The full recruitment drive will then open on November 25, 2026, with applications remaining open until January 13, 2027.

Key Recruitment Dates

Early launch: September 8, 2026

Early launch closes: October 9, 2026

Full recruitment drive opens: November 25, 2026

Final application deadline: January 13, 2027

Expected interview period: From the end of January through spring 2027

Typical start period: Many positions begin around June, although start dates vary by position and organization

Applicants interested in the General Data Research Associate or General Field Research Associate opportunities should therefore pay particular attention to the early application period rather than waiting until the full recruitment drive opens.

General Data Research Associate Positions

The General Data Research Associate recruitment track is intended for candidates interested in research work involving data, quantitative analysis, research implementation, and evidence generation.

Data Research Associates can work on projects where researchers use data to evaluate development programs, public policies, and interventions.

Depending on the specific position and research project, the work may involve activities such as:

Collecting and managing research data

Cleaning and organizing datasets

Conducting quantitative analysis

Supporting research design and implementation

Assisting researchers with empirical research

Preparing research materials and documentation

Working with statistical or analytical tools

Contributing to research outputs

Supporting rigorous impact evaluations

Helping transform research findings into evidence that can inform policy

Candidates interested in economics, statistics, data science, public policy, social sciences, development studies, and related fields may find this recruitment track particularly relevant.

General Field Research Associate Positions

The General Field Research Associate track is focused more directly on implementing and supporting research activities in the field.

Field-based research is an important component of many J-PAL projects because rigorous evaluations frequently require researchers and research teams to work directly with communities, institutions, governments, businesses, or other stakeholders.

Depending on the particular project, field research responsibilities may include:

Supporting field research operations

Coordinating research activities

Assisting with data collection

Working with local research teams

Supporting surveys and field experiments

Coordinating with project stakeholders

Monitoring field activities

Helping ensure that research protocols are followed

Supporting the implementation of impact evaluations

Contributing to the accurate collection and management of research information

Field research positions may be especially attractive to candidates who enjoy practical, project-based work and are interested in understanding how development programs operate in real-world settings.

Who Can Apply?

The recruitment drive is intended for qualified candidates interested in research and development-related employment opportunities within the J-PAL network and its affiliated research institutions and organizations.

Applicants should carefully review the requirements of each individual position because eligibility, academic qualifications, technical skills, language requirements, geographic requirements, and other selection criteria can differ between jobs.

The General Data Research Associate and General Field Research Associate positions are particularly relevant to candidates with backgrounds or interests in areas such as:

Economics

Development economics

Statistics

Data science

Econometrics

Public policy

Political science

International development

Social sciences

Research methods

Quantitative research

Other related academic and professional disciplines

Candidates should not assume that every J-PAL position has identical requirements. The appropriate qualifications will depend on the particular researcher, project, institution, location, and position.

Geographic Eligibility

J-PAL is a global research network, with affiliated researchers and partner organizations located in different parts of the world.

The recruitment information indicates that hiring managers may consider applicants based on factors including geographic location, alongside the strength of their applications, flexibility, and language skills.

This means applicants from different countries and regions may be considered where their qualifications and circumstances align with available positions.

Importantly, the recruitment information does not establish a blanket race- or continent-specific restriction for the overall recruitment drive. Applicants should instead examine the eligibility requirements of the specific job they wish to pursue, as some positions may have location-specific or language-related requirements.

Candidates from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East, Oceania, and other regions may potentially find relevant opportunities within the broader J-PAL network, subject to the requirements of individual vacancies.

How the J-PAL Recruitment Drive Works

J-PAL’s recruitment process allows researchers and affiliated organizations to identify candidates for research positions through the network’s recruitment system.

During the annual recruitment drive, J-PAL publicizes available opportunities and solicits applications from candidates interested in joining its research network.

Applicants submit a Common Application, selecting the jobs for which they are interested and qualified.

The application process is designed to make it easier for researchers and affiliated organizations within the network to identify suitable candidates.

What Happens After You Apply?

After applications are submitted, J-PAL staff, researchers, and hiring managers may review candidates based on several considerations.

According to the recruitment information, these include:

Strength of the application
The quality and relevance of a candidate’s academic background, professional experience, skills, and application materials can influence their prospects.

Geographic location
Some research projects require candidates to be located in particular countries or regions, making geographic considerations relevant to recruitment.

Flexibility
Candidates’ flexibility may be considered depending on the needs of the position and research project.

Language skills
Language capabilities can be important, particularly for field research and projects involving local communities or institutions.

Candidates who are shortlisted may be contacted for interviews.

J-PAL Interview and Selection Timeline

Shortlisted candidates may begin receiving interview invitations from the end of January through spring 2027.

One notable feature of the J-PAL recruitment process is that candidates may receive interviews from several researchers or organizations during the selection process.

This means a candidate’s application may potentially attract interest from more than one research team or affiliated organization.

Candidates should therefore ensure that their applications clearly communicate their qualifications, technical abilities, research interests, geographic flexibility, language capabilities, and relevant experience.

Potential Start Dates

Start dates vary depending on the position, research project, and employing organization.

However, J-PAL indicates that many positions have start dates in June.

Applicants should therefore carefully check the start date associated with individual positions when considering opportunities available through the recruitment drive.

A candidate who is successful in the recruitment process may need to make arrangements around employment transition, relocation, academic commitments, or other responsibilities depending on the position.

J-PAL Common Application

A central component of the recruitment drive is the Common Application.

Candidates interested in participating in the drive should submit the Common Application and select the positions they are interested in and qualified for.

Applicants should avoid selecting positions simply because they are available. Instead, they should identify opportunities where their academic qualifications, professional experience, technical abilities, research interests, language skills, and geographic circumstances closely match the requirements.

This approach can help candidates present a more targeted and credible application.

Other Organizations in the J-PAL Recruitment Network

The recruitment drive is not limited exclusively to positions directly employed by J-PAL.

Organizations affiliated with J-PAL, as well as researchers and organizations associated with other major research networks, may participate in recruitment.

The recruitment information specifically notes that organizations affiliated with J-PAL, IPA, EPoD, and CEGA may choose to post jobs on the Common Application.

This makes the recruitment platform a potentially valuable resource for candidates seeking research positions beyond a single institution.

Rolling Recruitment Outside the Annual Drive

Candidates should also understand that they do not necessarily have to wait for the annual recruitment drive to find opportunities.

J-PAL conducts rolling recruitment throughout the year, with positions recruited individually according to the needs of specific projects.

For these positions, recruitment timelines depend on the project and employing organization.

Individual vacancies may include:

A proposed start date

A specific application deadline

Position-specific eligibility requirements

Project-specific qualifications

Geographic requirements

Language requirements

Other selection criteria

Because rolling recruitment operates independently of the annual recruitment drive, candidates should regularly monitor J-PAL’s careers opportunities.

Why Applicants Should Apply Early

J-PAL recommends applying as soon as possible, particularly for positions recruited outside the main annual drive.

For specifically posted positions, the majority of finalists are generally contacted by hiring managers within a month of applying.

For the annual recruitment drive, early application is also strategically important because applicants may be reviewed by multiple researchers and hiring managers across the network.

Candidates should therefore avoid waiting until the final day of the application period if they already have the necessary information and documents prepared.

How to Strengthen Your J-PAL Application

Competition for international development research positions can be significant. Candidates can improve their applications by ensuring that they demonstrate a clear connection between their background and the requirements of the positions they select.

1. Match Your Background to the Position

Before applying, carefully examine the responsibilities and requirements of each job.

Your application should demonstrate how your education, research experience, analytical skills, professional experience, and other competencies relate directly to the position.

2. Highlight Quantitative and Research Skills

For Data Research Associate positions, candidates should clearly present relevant experience with:

Data analysis

Statistical analysis

Econometrics

Research methodology

Data management

Statistical software

Programming or data science, where applicable

Quantitative research

Where possible, applicants should demonstrate how they have used these skills in actual projects rather than simply listing them.

3. Demonstrate Field Research Experience

Candidates applying for Field Research Associate opportunities should highlight experience involving:

Fieldwork

Surveys

Data collection

Community engagement

Research implementation

Project coordination

Stakeholder engagement

Monitoring research activities

Relevant experience does not necessarily have to come from a job specifically titled “Field Research Associate.” Academic research, internships, development projects, and other practical research experiences may be relevant where they demonstrate transferable skills.

4. Highlight Language Skills

Language ability can be important for research conducted in different countries and communities.

Applicants should clearly identify languages they speak and their proficiency levels where relevant to the position.

5. Demonstrate Flexibility

Because J-PAL works across different countries, projects, and research environments, flexibility can be an important consideration.

Applicants should clearly communicate relevant geographic, professional, or project flexibility when appropriate.

6. Prepare for Multiple Interviews

Because candidates may potentially be contacted by several researchers or organizations during the recruitment process, applicants should be prepared to discuss their experience and suitability for different research projects.

A strong candidate should be able to clearly explain:

Why they are interested in J-PAL

Their research interests

Their relevant academic background

Their technical skills

Their field or project experience

Their career goals

Their interest in evidence-based policy

Why their skills are relevant to the particular research project

Conclusion

The J-PAL 2026–2027 Recruitment Drive presents an important employment opportunity for candidates seeking careers in international development, research, data analysis, field research, economics, public policy, and evidence-based policymaking.

The recruitment process is particularly significant because applicants are not necessarily applying to a single research team. Through the J-PAL network and Common Application, candidates may be considered by multiple researchers and affiliated organizations looking for research talent.

The early recruitment period for General Data Research Associate and General Field Research Associate positions runs from September 8 to October 9, 2026, while the full recruitment drive opens on November 25, 2026, and closes on January 13, 2027.

Candidates interested in these opportunities should begin preparing their applications early, carefully select positions for which they are qualified, and ensure that their academic background, research experience, technical capabilities, language skills, geographic circumstances, and career interests are clearly presented.

For aspiring researchers and development professionals, joining J-PAL or one of its affiliated research organizations can provide valuable exposure to rigorous research, international development projects, data-driven policymaking, and collaboration with researchers working to generate evidence on some of the world’s most important social and economic challenges.

TITLE: 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship at the African Development Bank: Eligibility, $100,000 Stipend, Requirements and How to Apply

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship Program at the African Development Bank (AfDB) is now open to qualified African professionals seeking high-level experience in development policy, strategy, leadership and institutional decision-making.

The program provides an opportunity for an outstanding African professional to spend up to 12 months working with the African Development Bank in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, contributing to strategic assignments and gaining direct exposure to senior-level leadership within one of Africa’s major multilateral development institutions.

The fellowship is funded by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation and is designed to help develop a pipeline of future African leaders with the professional, analytical and leadership capacity needed to contribute to the governance and socioeconomic development of African countries.

For the 2027 intake, the African Development Bank states that the fellowship will focus particularly on four priority areas: mobilizing resources to finance Africa’s development, reforming Africa’s financial architecture, harnessing Africa’s demographic dividend to support economic growth, and building climate-resilient infrastructure and value addition to natural resources.

The application deadline is 20 November 2026.

About the Mo Ibrahim Leadership Fellowship

The Mo Ibrahim Leadership Fellowship Programme was established to help identify, develop and mentor the next generation of African leaders.

The program is based on the idea that Africa’s future leadership requires professionals who possess not only strong academic credentials but also practical experience, strategic thinking, policy knowledge and the ability to work effectively within complex institutions.

According to the Mo Ibrahim Foundation, the fellowships were established in 2011 to identify and mentor future generations of outstanding African leaders. Fellows work in the executive offices of institutions such as the African Development Bank, the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa and the International Trade Centre. The Foundation describes the program as a 12-month professional development opportunity combining technical and leadership development with exposure to senior institutional leadership.

For the 2027 fellowship cycle, the Foundation states that the program is open to young professionals, mid-career professionals and new executives from Africa who have relevant professional experience and a Master’s degree.

2027 Mo Ibrahim Fellowship at the African Development Bank

The African Development Bank is hosting one of the 2027 Ibrahim Leadership Fellowship positions at its headquarters in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire.

The official AfDB vacancy identifies the position as the 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship Program, with position number 50100504. The vacancy was posted in September 2026 and has a closing date of 20 November 2026.

The Fellow will work with the Bank for a period of up to 12 months. The fellowship is intended to provide practical exposure to strategic development work at a senior institutional level while allowing the Fellow to strengthen professional and leadership capacity.

The Fellow will receive guidance from senior leadership, including the President, Managing Directors, Chief of Staff and Director of Cabinet, or a designated representative. This places the Fellow within an environment where they can observe and contribute to high-level strategic work.

What Is the Purpose of the Fellowship?

The fellowship has both a professional development and African leadership development purpose.

Rather than being structured simply as an academic scholarship, the program provides an opportunity for a qualified professional to work directly within a major African development institution.

The Fellow is expected to contribute to real institutional assignments while developing a deeper understanding of:

Development policy and strategy

Financial and economic issues affecting Africa

Institutional decision-making

Strategic planning

Policy formulation

Project implementation

Development financing

Climate-resilient development

Regional and continental development priorities

Leadership within complex organizations

High-level policy and institutional discussions

The broader objective is to strengthen the Fellow’s ability to contribute to the governance and development of their country and the African continent.

The Mo Ibrahim Foundation describes its fellowship model as a way of preparing future African leaders through practical experience at senior levels of prominent African institutions and multilateral organizations.

Key Priority Areas for the 2027 African Development Bank Fellowship

The 2027 AfDB fellowship places particular emphasis on four areas described by the Bank as its Four Cardinal Points.

1. Mobilizing Resources to Finance Africa’s Development

The first priority focuses on increasing the resources available to finance Africa’s development.

This includes issues surrounding development finance, investment, financial mobilization and innovative approaches to funding infrastructure and socioeconomic development.

Applicants whose professional experience involves development finance, investment, banking, financial institutions, resource mobilization or related areas may therefore find a strong connection between their experience and this priority area.

2. Reforming Africa’s Financial Architecture

The second priority concerns the financial systems and institutional structures that support economic development across Africa.

This may involve areas such as financial policy, development finance, capital markets, financial institutions, international financial systems and strategies for improving the continent’s ability to finance sustainable development.

Strong analytical experience in finance, economics, policy or development strategy can be relevant to this area.

3. Harnessing the Demographic Dividend

The third priority focuses on Africa’s large and growing population, particularly the economic opportunities associated with its youthful population.

This includes issues relating to employment, productivity, skills development, entrepreneurship, human capital, economic participation and policies that can support inclusive economic growth.

Professionals working in economic development, public policy, private-sector development, youth employment, human capital or related areas may be able to connect their experience with this priority.

4. Building Climate-Resilient Infrastructure and Value Addition to Natural Resources

The fourth priority focuses on infrastructure that can withstand climate-related challenges while increasing the economic value derived from Africa’s natural resources.

This brings together areas such as climate resilience, infrastructure development, natural resource management, industrialization, value chains and sustainable economic development.

The Bank specifically identifies building climate-resilient infrastructure and robust value addition to natural resources among the priorities for the 2027 Fellow.

Learn More HERE

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is aimed at experienced professionals rather than applicants who are just beginning their careers.

The African Development Bank specifically describes the opportunity as being for young professionals, mid-career professionals and/or new executives.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate substantial professional experience, leadership capacity and a clear connection between their career background and the Bank’s development activities.

The official eligibility requirements include the following.

African Nationality

Applicants must be nationals of an African country and may be residing anywhere in the world.

This means that an eligible African professional does not necessarily have to be living in Africa at the time of application.

The AfDB vacancy additionally states that applicants must be nationals of an African Development Bank member country.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be:

40 years old or younger for men and women; or

45 years old or younger for women with children.

Applicants should carefully consider the applicable age requirement when preparing their application.

Master’s Degree

Applicants must have at least a Master’s degree from a recognized institution.

The Bank lists several relevant academic backgrounds, including:

Banking

Business

Economics

Social sciences

Finance

International development

Other disciplines relevant to the African Development Bank’s business

Having a degree in one of these areas does not by itself guarantee eligibility. Applicants must also demonstrate the professional experience, leadership and technical competencies required by the Bank.

At Least Seven Years of Relevant Work Experience

A minimum of seven years of relevant work experience is required.

This is an important distinction because the opportunity is not designed primarily for recent graduates or professionals with only a few years of experience.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate how their professional background relates to the Bank’s activities and the priorities identified for the 2027 fellowship.

Leadership Experience

Applicants are expected to demonstrate proven leadership and consultative abilities.

Communication Skills

Ability to Work With Diverse Stakeholders

The Bank expects the Fellow to be able to communicate and interact with government officials at different levels and work effectively with a wide range of constituencies in a diverse environment.

This requirement makes interpersonal skills, diplomacy, consultation and stakeholder management important elements of the application.

Applicants should demonstrate an ability to motivate teams while simultaneously managing several projects.

This requirement is particularly relevant for professionals who have worked in environments involving multiple deadlines, stakeholders and strategic priorities.

Who Is Not Eligible?

The AfDB vacancy identifies several categories of people who cannot apply for this fellowship.

These include:

Government officials

Active military personnel

Political party leaders

Current AfDB staff

Non-active, retired or separated AfDB staff

Individuals with close family relations with an active or non-active AfDB staff member, such as a mother, father, sister or brother

Applicants should review the complete official vacancy carefully before submitting an application.

Fellowship Duration

The fellowship will run for one year, or up to 12 months.

The AfDB states that the contract is for one year and is not renewable.

The fellowship is therefore a defined professional development assignment rather than an open-ended employment position.

Fellowship Stipend and Financial Support

The Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s current fellowship information states that Ibrahim Fellows receive a stipend of US$100,000 for the fellowship period. The Foundation describes the program as a 12-month fellowship and states that each year three Fellows have opportunities to work at participating host institutions.

For the AfDB-hosted position, the Bank’s vacancy states that the Fellow will receive an annual stipend paid monthly by the Bank from funds provided by the Foundation.

The fellowship also provides specific support related to travel and other arrangements.

According to the AfDB vacancy:

The Fellow’s official mission travel expenses are covered by the Bank.

Travel insurance associated with official mission travel is covered by the Bank.

Travel and shipping costs associated with taking up the appointment are funded by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation.

Travel and shipping costs associated with repatriation at the end of the fellowship are also funded by the Foundation.

The Foundation will ensure that arrangements are made for the Fellow’s medical insurance, child education and retirement needs.

Applicants should distinguish these benefits from those available to regular AfDB staff because the Ibrahim Fellow is not considered a regular Bank employee.

What Will the Ibrahim Fellow Do?

The successful candidate will contribute to strategic work within the African Development Bank.

The main responsibilities include the following.

1. Develop Innovative Approaches to Strategic Issues

The Fellow will design, develop and help implement innovative approaches to strategic issues relevant to the Bank’s mission and objectives.

The work is expected to draw on international best practices and contribute to addressing important development challenges.

2. Conduct Research and Analysis

The Fellow will undertake research and analysis of existing and emerging strategy, programme and policy areas relevant to the Bank.

This may require the ability to examine evidence, interpret data, understand development trends and translate research into useful policy or strategic recommendations.

3. Monitor Bank Initiatives and Prepare Briefs

The Fellow will assist with monitoring and analysing the implementation of Bank Group initiatives and the Bank’s regular work programme.

The role also includes preparing:

Briefs

Memoranda

Analytical documents

Other strategic documentation

An important part of this responsibility is communicating the likely impact of initiatives in language that is understandable to non-technical audiences.

4. Participate in High-Level Discussions

The Fellow will participate in high-level discussions and contribute to preparations for the President’s meetings and missions.

This can provide direct exposure to senior-level institutional processes and strategic decision-making.

5. Undertake Other Strategic Assignments

The Fellow may also be assigned other responsibilities by relevant senior staff within the President’s Office.

This means applicants should be prepared for a dynamic role that may involve different strategic assignments during the fellowship period.

Professional Development Opportunities

The fellowship provides a practical environment for developing both technical and leadership capabilities.

The Mo Ibrahim Foundation states that Fellows develop technical and leadership skills while contributing directly to research and policy design. Fellows can also become members of the Now Generation Network, through which they can continue contributing their skills and insights to African development after the fellowship.

For a professional interested in African development, the experience can provide exposure to areas such as:

Development policy

International development

Economic strategy

Development finance

Institutional leadership

Policy analysis

Strategic planning

Multilateral cooperation

African economic transformation

High-level stakeholder engagement

The program’s structure also places the Fellow close to senior institutional leadership, making it different from a conventional academic fellowship or entry-level internship.

Important Note About Employment at the African Development Bank

Applicants should understand that selection for the fellowship does not constitute permanent employment with the African Development Bank.

The AfDB explicitly states that the Fellow is not a regular employee of the Bank and is not given a right to employment with the Bank.

There is also no presumption that the Fellow will be hired by the Bank after completing the fellowship.

In addition, the vacancy states that the Fellow will not be eligible for recruitment as an AfDB staff member for one year following the termination or expiry of the fellowship, whichever occurs first.

This is an important distinction for applicants who may otherwise assume that the fellowship is an alternative route into permanent AfDB employment.

What Documents Are Required?

Applicants should prepare their application materials carefully before beginning the online application.

The African Development Bank requires applicants to submit a comprehensive Curriculum Vitae containing information including:

Date of birth

Nationality

Academic qualifications

Relevant professional experience

Other information demonstrating suitability for the fellowship

Applicants must also attach:

Academic transcripts

Three letters of recommendation

The CV should clearly demonstrate how the applicant’s professional experience aligns with the fellowship’s requirements and the Bank’s priority areas.

How the Selection Process Works

The selection process involves several stages.

According to the AfDB:

Stage 1: Initial Human Resources Review

The Bank’s Human Resources Department will conduct an initial review of applications.

Stage 2: Shortlisting

Human Resources will develop a shortlist of 10 applicant files.

Stage 3: Mo Ibrahim Foundation Review

The shortlisted files will then be reviewed by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation.

Stage 4: Final Shortlist

A shortlist of three candidates will be presented to the President of the African Development Bank or the President’s designate.

Stage 5: Final Selection

The final candidate will be selected from the shortlisted candidates.

Only applicants who fully meet the Bank’s requirements and are considered for further assessment or interview will be contacted.

The deadline to apply for the 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship Program at the African Development Bank is 20 November 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit their applications, particularly because the application requires several supporting documents, including academic transcripts and three recommendation letters.

How to Apply

Official application page:

Apply for the 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship at the African Development Bank

Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowships

Application Preparation Tips

Applicants can take several practical steps to strengthen the clarity and completeness of their applications.

Development policy

Economic development

Instead of simply stating that you “managed projects,” explain the nature of the projects, your responsibilities, the stakeholders involved and the results achieved.

This can help demonstrate the leadership, strategic planning and execution competencies required by the Bank.

3. Connect Your Experience to the Four Cardinal Points

The 2027 fellowship has clearly identified four priority areas.

Applicants should therefore understand the relationship between their professional experience and:

Development finance and resource mobilization

Financial architecture

Demographic dividend and economic growth

Climate-resilient infrastructure and natural-resource value addition

4. Prepare Your Recommendation Letters Early

Three recommendation letters are required.

Because obtaining recommendation letters can take time, applicants should approach potential referees well before the deadline and provide them with relevant information about the fellowship.

5. Prepare Your Academic Transcripts

The application requires academic transcripts.

Applicants should make sure their transcripts are accessible and ready to upload before beginning the final application process.

6. Demonstrate Leadership Clearly

Leadership does not necessarily mean having held a senior executive title.

Applicants can demonstrate leadership through strategic projects, team management, policy initiatives, stakeholder coordination, organizational change, programme implementation and other situations where they were responsible for achieving important outcomes.

7. Highlight Analytical Experience

The Bank specifically emphasizes strong analytical skills and the ability to analyse and interpret financial and other data.

Applicants should therefore make their analytical experience visible rather than leaving it implicit.

Important AfDB Application and Fraud Warning

Applicants should be cautious of fraudulent recruitment communications.

The African Development Bank states that it does not request payments from applicants during the recruitment process, including application, CV review, interviews or final processing.

The Bank also states that it does not request applicants’ bank account information as part of its recruitment process.

Applicants should therefore use official African Development Bank channels when applying and should be cautious about third parties claiming to represent the Bank or requesting money in exchange for recruitment assistance.

Nationality and Dual Nationality Note

The vacancy contains an important nationality requirement.

The Bank states that it does not accept dual nationality and requires applicants to declare the nationality under which they would be considered.

Applicants are also instructed to provide supporting government-issued identification documents such as a passport, national identity card or certificate.

Applicants with questions about their nationality status should carefully review the official AfDB requirements before submitting an application.

Why This Opportunity Matters for African Professionals

The 2027 Mo Ibrahim Foundation Leadership Fellowship combines professional experience with leadership development in an African multilateral institution.

Instead of limiting participants to classroom-based learning, the program places the selected Fellow within the working environment of the African Development Bank.

The Fellow will participate in strategic assignments, undertake research and analysis, contribute to high-level discussions, prepare policy and strategic documentation and work under the guidance of senior Bank officials.

The Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s broader fellowship programme is intended to help build a pipeline of African leaders who can contribute to governance and development.

For professionals with substantial experience in development policy, finance, economics, strategy, project management, private-sector development or related areas, the fellowship provides an opportunity to deepen their understanding of how major development institutions operate while contributing to issues affecting Africa’s economic and social development.
