TITLE: United Nations Free Online Air Pollution Courses: Learn Air Pollution Monitoring, Transboundary Pollution and Emissions Reporting

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations system, through the UN SDG:Learn platform, offers a collection of free, self-paced online courses designed to strengthen knowledge and practical understanding of air pollution, climate action, emissions reporting, environmental policy and international cooperation.

Among the available learning opportunities are three courses focused specifically on air pollution and the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution. These courses cover the effects of air pollution on human health and the environment, methods for monitoring those effects, international frameworks for reducing pollution, emission inventories, reporting requirements and emission estimation methods.

The courses are delivered online and can be particularly useful for policymakers, government officials, technical experts, academics, students, NGO professionals, private-sector practitioners and other individuals interested in environmental protection and clean-air policy.

Importantly, the courses are free to take, are self-paced and offer certificates to learners who successfully complete the applicable assessment requirements.

There is no application deadline stated for these courses in the supplied course information. Learners can access the courses online according to the availability and registration requirements of the respective course platforms.

1. Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention

Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention is an introductory, self-paced online course designed to help learners understand the effects of air pollution and the importance of monitoring those effects for human health, ecosystems and environmental policymaking.

The course is offered through the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) and made available through the UN SDG:Learn/UN CC:Learn learning ecosystem.

It focuses on how information about the effects of air pollution can be collected, assessed and used to support the development of effective clean-air policies.

Course Details

Course: Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention

Format: Self-paced e-learning

Level: Introductory

Duration: Approximately 1.5 hours

Effort: Approximately 1.5 hours for the complete course

Venue: Online

Language: English

Cost: Free

Certificate: Yes

Subject: Air pollution

SDGs: SDG 3 – Good Health and Well-being; SDG 13 – Climate Action

Offered by: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and UN CC:Learn

The course is designed to provide learners with foundational knowledge about why monitoring the effects of air pollution is important and how such information can contribute to policymaking.

What Does the Monitoring Air Pollution Course Cover?

Air pollution can affect human health, ecosystems, agriculture, climate and the broader environment. Understanding these effects is an important component of developing policies and measures designed to improve air quality.

The course introduces learners to the major effects of air pollution and explains how monitoring and assessment can provide evidence for environmental decision-making.

It also introduces the work undertaken under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution and helps learners understand how effects-related information contributes to international and national clean-air efforts.

The course contains four modules.

Module 1: Major Effects of Air Pollution

The first module introduces the major effects associated with air pollution.

Learners explore why air pollution is an important environmental and public-health concern and examine the different ways pollutants can affect people and the environment.

Module 2: Effects-Related Work under the Convention

The second module introduces effects-related activities conducted under the Convention.

Learners gain an understanding of the purpose of this work and how international cooperation contributes to understanding and addressing the effects of air pollution.

Module 3: Methodologies to Monitor Effects

The third module focuses on methods used to monitor the effects of air pollution.

This section helps learners understand the importance of collecting and assessing information that can demonstrate how air pollution affects health and environmental systems.

Module 4: Use in Policy-Making

The fourth module examines how information generated through effects monitoring and assessment can be used to support policymaking.

Learners are introduced to the relationship between scientific and technical information and the development of clean-air policies.

Interactive Learning and Assessment

The course uses a combination of learning tools and interactive educational content.

The modules contain:

Interactive learning features

Quizzes

Additional resources

Structured learning content

Explanatory materials

Clear learning storylines

The modules are recommended to be completed in sequence, because the material builds progressively from basic concepts toward the application of effects-related information in policymaking.

Learners are also encouraged to complete all four modules before attempting the final assessment.

Certificate of Completion

Learners who successfully meet the certification requirements can obtain a certificate.

To receive the certificate, participants must achieve a passing score of 70% in the end-of-course assessment and complete the required course evaluation form.

Once the requirements have been fulfilled, the certificate can be downloaded from the course webpage.

Learning Objectives

After completing Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention, learners should be able to:

Identify the major effects of air pollution.

Explain the objectives of effects-related work under the Convention.

Describe methods used to monitor the effects of air pollution.

Explain how effects assessments can contribute to policymaking.

Understand the importance of evidence-based information in clean-air policy development.

Recognize how monitoring activities can support environmental decision-making.

Who Can Benefit from the Monitoring Air Pollution Course?

The course is primarily intended to strengthen the capacity of employees working in ministries and technical institutes dealing with the Convention and its protocols.

However, the course is also designed for a wider group of learners interested in air pollution and environmental policy.

Potential participants include:

Government employees

Environmental ministry officials

Technical institute employees

Environmental specialists

Academics

Researchers

NGO professionals

Environmental practitioners

Students

Individuals interested in air pollution effects

Professionals working on clean-air policy

The course can therefore be useful even for people who do not directly work under the Convention but want to develop knowledge of air pollution effects and environmental policy.

2. Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution Course

The Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution course is another free, self-paced online learning opportunity available through the UN CC:Learn ecosystem.

While the first course focuses specifically on monitoring the effects of air pollution, this course provides a broader introduction to air pollution, pollution prevention and reduction, and the international cooperation framework established through the Convention.

The course explains why air pollution requires cooperation across national borders and introduces the Convention and its major protocols.

Course Details

Course: Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution

Format: Self-paced online learning

Level: Introductory

Duration: Approximately 3.5 hours

Venue: Online

Languages: English and Russian

Cost: Free

Certificate: Yes

Subject: Air pollution

SDG: SDG 11 – Sustainable Cities and Communities

Provider: UN CC:Learn

Why Transboundary Air Pollution Matters

Air pollution does not necessarily remain within the geographical area where it is produced.

Pollutants can originate from sources such as:

Road and other transportation activities

Industrial facilities

Agriculture

Energy production

Other human activities

Once released into the atmosphere, some pollutants can travel considerable distances and cross national borders.

This means that addressing air pollution can require cooperation between countries, sectors and institutions.

The Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution provides an international framework through which countries in the relevant region cooperate to reduce air pollution and its harmful effects.

The course introduces learners to this framework and explains the role of international cooperation in achieving cleaner air.

Four Modules on the Convention and Its Protocols

The course consists of four major modules.

Module 1: The Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution

The first module introduces the Convention itself.

Learners gain an understanding of the Convention’s role in international cooperation on air pollution and the fundamental concepts associated with transboundary air pollution.

Module 2: The Gothenburg Protocol

The second module focuses on the Protocol to Abate Acidification, Eutrophication and Ground-Level Ozone, commonly known as the Gothenburg Protocol.

Learners are introduced to the role of the protocol in addressing specific environmental impacts associated with air pollution.

Module 3: The Protocol on Heavy Metals

The third module covers the Convention’s work concerning heavy metals.

The module helps learners understand the significance of heavy-metal pollution and the international framework established to address relevant emissions.

Module 4: The Protocol on Persistent Organic Pollutants

The fourth module focuses on persistent organic pollutants and the associated protocol.

Learners explore the basic principles and obligations associated with addressing these pollutants within the Convention framework.

What Learners Will Gain from the Convention Course

The course is intended to increase awareness of:

Major air pollutants

Sources of air pollution

Effects of air pollution

Measures for preventing and reducing harmful emissions

International cooperation on air pollution

The Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution

The Convention’s protocols

Stakeholders involved in the Convention

Processes established under the Convention and its protocols

The knowledge can help participants understand the relationship between air pollution, environmental protection and international policy.

Learning Objectives

After completing the Convention course, learners should be able to:

Identify important air pollutants and their sources.

Explain the effects of air pollution.

Recall measures used to prevent and reduce air pollution.

Recognize the value of the Convention as a framework for international cooperation.

Define basic principles under the Convention and its protocols.

Explain basic obligations under the Convention’s protocols.

Identify important stakeholders involved in the Convention and its protocols.

Understand how international cooperation can contribute to cleaner air.

Target Audience for the Convention Course

The course is designed for a broad audience.

It can be particularly relevant to:

Policymakers

Government officials

Staff working for intergovernmental organizations

Staff working for non-governmental organizations

Private-sector professionals

Students

Academics

Environmental professionals

Other stakeholders interested in air pollution and clean-air action

Because the course is introductory, it can provide a useful starting point for individuals who want to develop an understanding of the international framework for addressing transboundary air pollution.

3. How to Report Emissions under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution

The third learning opportunity is How to Report Emissions under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution.

This course is designed for learners who want to understand emission inventories, emission reporting requirements and methods for estimating emissions.

Unlike the introductory Convention course, this course is classified at the intermediate level and focuses more specifically on the technical and reporting aspects of air pollution management.

Course Details

Course: How to Report Emissions under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution

Format: Self-paced e-learning

Level: Intermediate

Duration: Approximately 1.5 hours

Effort: Approximately 1.5 hours

Venue: Online

Languages: English and Russian

Cost: Free

Certificate: Yes

Subject: Air pollution

SDG: SDG 13 – Climate Action

Provider: UN CC:Learn

What Is an Emission Inventory?

An important concept introduced by this course is the emission inventory.

An emission inventory provides information about pollutants and/or greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere from different sources within a defined geographical area and during a specified period.

Emission inventories are important because they can help governments and other stakeholders understand where emissions originate, how emission patterns change over time and how pollution-control measures are performing.

The information can be used to:

Study trends in major sources of air pollution.

Evaluate pollution-abatement measures.

Develop national environmental policies.

Develop local clean-air policies.

Evaluate the effectiveness of environmental policies.

Assess impacts on populations and ecosystems.

Demonstrate compliance with emission-reduction targets.

Provide information to the public.

The course therefore connects technical emission reporting with wider environmental policymaking.

Why Countries Report Emissions

Under the Convention, reporting emission inventories is a basic obligation.

Reliable emissions information provides a foundation for understanding air pollution and developing appropriate responses.

Without reliable information about the quantity and sources of pollutants being released into the atmosphere, it becomes more difficult to evaluate pollution trends, identify major sources and assess whether emission-reduction measures are producing the desired results.

The course introduces learners to the processes and principles involved in developing and reporting these inventories.

Three Modules and a Final Assessment

The emissions-reporting course is divided into three modules followed by a final assessment.

Module 1: Purpose and Scope of Emission Inventories

This module introduces the purpose of emission inventories and explains their scope.

Learners explore what emission inventories are, why they are important and how they support clean-air policy development.

Module 2: Reporting Process and Templates

The second module focuses on the reporting process and templates used under the Convention.

Participants learn about the principles behind completing reporting templates and the information required for effective emissions reporting.

Module 3: Emission Estimation Methods

The third module examines different methods used to estimate emissions.

This gives learners an introduction to how emissions can be quantified from different sources and how estimation methods contribute to the development of reliable inventories.

Final Assessment

After working through the course material, learners can undertake the final assessment associated with the course.

Successful completion can lead to the award of a certificate, subject to the course’s certification requirements.

Learning Objectives for the Emissions Reporting Course

After completing the course, learners should be able to:

Explain what an emission inventory is.

Identify substances released into the atmosphere by different human activities.

Explain how emission inventories contribute to clean-air policy development.

Explain the role of emission inventories at national and international levels.

Outline the objectives, scope and principles of reporting guidelines developed under the Convention.

Identify different source categories covered by reporting obligations.

Explain the basic principles involved in completing reporting templates.

Describe different emission-estimation methods used under the Convention.

Understand why accurate emissions information is important for environmental policymaking.

Recognize how emissions reporting can contribute to evaluating pollution-control measures.

Who Can Take the Emissions Reporting Course?

The course is primarily designed to build the capacity of people involved in air pollution management and reporting.

The target audience includes:

Employees of ministries dealing with the Convention

Technical institute employees

Academics

Researchers

NGO professionals

Environmental practitioners

Professionals involved in emissions reporting

Individuals interested in emission inventories

People seeking knowledge about air pollution reporting under the Convention

The course can be particularly relevant to individuals whose work involves environmental data, air pollution policy, emissions monitoring, environmental regulation or clean-air strategies.

Benefits of Taking These Free United Nations Air Pollution Courses

Taken together, the three courses provide learners with a structured introduction to several interconnected areas of air pollution management.

Participants can develop knowledge in:

1. Air Pollution and Its Effects

Learners can develop a better understanding of how air pollution affects human health, ecosystems, agriculture, climate and the wider environment.

2. Air Pollution Monitoring

The monitoring course introduces methods and approaches for assessing the effects of air pollution and understanding how evidence can support policymaking.

3. International Environmental Cooperation

The Convention course explains how countries cooperate to address air pollution that crosses national boundaries.

4. Clean-Air Policy Development

The courses demonstrate how scientific, technical and emissions-related information can support the development of policies designed to improve air quality.

5. Emission Inventories

Learners can gain an understanding of how emission inventories are developed and why they are important for environmental management.

6. Emissions Reporting

Participants can learn about reporting processes, templates, source categories and estimation methods under the Convention.

7. Climate and Sustainable Development

The courses connect air pollution management with broader sustainable-development and climate objectives, including SDG 3, SDG 11 and SDG 13.

8. Professional Development

Because the courses are free, online and self-paced, they can provide an accessible way for students and professionals to expand their knowledge without the costs associated with conventional classroom training.

9. Certificates

The courses provide certificate opportunities for learners who satisfy the relevant assessment and completion requirements.

How the Three Courses Complement Each Other

Although each course can be taken independently, the three learning opportunities cover different aspects of air pollution management.

A learner interested in developing a broader understanding could approach them as follows:

First, understand the broader international framework.

The Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution course provides introductory knowledge about air pollution, its sources and effects, and the international framework for cooperation.

Next, understand how air pollution effects are monitored.

The Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention course focuses on assessing the effects of air pollution and understanding how monitoring information can support policymaking.

Finally, explore emissions reporting.

The How to Report Emissions under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution course provides more technical knowledge about emission inventories, reporting processes and emission-estimation methods.

This creates a learning pathway covering air pollution fundamentals, international cooperation, effects monitoring, emission inventories and environmental policymaking.

Course Format and Accessibility

All three opportunities are delivered through online learning platforms and are designed as self-paced courses.

This means learners do not need to attend conventional classroom sessions at a specified physical venue.

The supplied information identifies the courses as:

Online

Self-paced

Free

Available in English, with some courses also available in Russian

Designed for relatively short completion periods

Supported by learning materials and assessments

Certificate-bearing, subject to completion requirements

The first and third courses require approximately 1.5 hours each, while the broader Convention course takes approximately 3.5 hours.

Certificate Information

Certificates are an important feature of these courses.

For Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention, learners can take an assessment at the end of the course. To satisfy the stated certification criteria, participants must achieve a 70% passing score and complete the course evaluation form before downloading the certificate.

The other courses also indicate that a certificate is available, subject to their respective completion and assessment requirements.

Learners should therefore complete the required modules and assessments rather than assuming that simply registering for a course automatically results in certification.

Deadline

No application deadline is stated in the supplied information.

These are online learning courses rather than conventional competitive applications. Prospective learners should nevertheless check the relevant official course page for the current registration status, access requirements and any platform-specific conditions before beginning the course.

APPLY HERE

How to Access the Courses

Interested learners can begin by visiting the relevant course pages through the UN SDG:Learn and UN CC:Learn platforms.

The supplied course information provides the following course pages:

Monitoring Air Pollution Effects under the Convention: available through the UN CC:Learn course platform.

Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution: available through the UN CC:Learn course platform.

How to Report Emissions under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution: available through the UN CC:Learn course platform.

Learners should register or log in where required and follow the instructions provided on the respective course page.

It is also advisable to download and review the relevant syllabus where available before starting, particularly for learners who want to understand the complete course structure and learning outcomes.

Visit HERE to learn more about the United Nations Free Online Air Pollution Courses.

Conclusion

The United Nations air pollution courses available through UN SDG:Learn and UN CC:Learn provide accessible opportunities for learners to develop knowledge about one of the major environmental and public-health challenges facing societies.

The three courses cover complementary areas: the international framework for transboundary air pollution, monitoring the effects of air pollution, and reporting emissions through emission inventories.

With free online access, self-paced learning, relatively short completion times and certificate opportunities, the courses can be useful for students, environmental professionals, government officials, policymakers, researchers, academics, NGO practitioners and anyone seeking to strengthen their understanding of air pollution and clean-air policy.

For learners interested in climate action, environmental governance, public health, sustainable development or emissions management, these courses offer an opportunity to build practical foundational knowledge while becoming familiar with the international systems used to address air pollution and support evidence-based environmental policymaking.

TITLE: Leading for Humanity 2027: Fully Funded Leadership Programme for Global Changemakers in South Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation Leading for Humanity Programme 2027 is inviting nominations for individuals who demonstrate courageous, values-based leadership and a strong commitment to truth, justice, human rights, reconciliation, and societal healing.

This immersive leadership programme brings together a diverse group of emerging and established changemakers for an intensive residential experience focused on personal reflection, courageous conversations, peer learning, Ubuntu, forgiveness, and compassionate leadership.

The programme will take place in South Africa in April 2027 and is open to both South African and international nominees who can travel to Cape Town and Hermanus and participate fully in the residential experience.

The Foundation will cover the programme costs, accommodation, and meals. However, participants or their sponsors will be responsible for travel expenses to and from South Africa.

Application deadline: 14 October 2026

About the Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation

The Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation was established to preserve and advance the values, principles, and legacy of Archbishop Desmond Tutu and Leah Tutu.

The Foundation works to nurture courageous leadership, promote social healing, encourage dialogue, and support a more just, inclusive, and humane society. Its work is rooted in the belief that meaningful social change requires not only technical solutions and institutional action but also moral courage, compassion, accountability, and a commitment to shared humanity.

The Foundation’s programmes seek to inspire people to challenge injustice, overcome social divisions, and contribute to positive change in their communities and wider society.

The Leading for Humanity Programme is one of its flagship initiatives. It reflects Archbishop Tutu’s belief that the world can be transformed through a “million ripples” of courageous action.

What Is the Leading for Humanity Programme?

Leading for Humanity is an immersive leadership-development programme designed to nurture individuals who want to lead with courage, compassion, integrity, and a commitment to justice.

The programme is built around the idea that effective leadership begins with personal transformation. Participants are encouraged to examine their own experiences, assumptions, relationships, and responsibilities before considering how they can contribute to healing and change in society.

The programme combines:

Residential learning;

Courageous conversations;

Peer-to-peer exchange;

Personal reflection;

Storytelling;

Leadership development;

Exploration of Ubuntu;

Discussions on justice and reconciliation; and

Engagement with a diverse community of changemakers.

Rather than focusing only on conventional leadership skills, the programme explores the moral and human dimensions of leadership. It encourages participants to consider how they can act meaningfully in their workplaces, communities, organizations, and wider societies.

The programme’s central premise is that leaders who want to contribute to societal repair must also be willing to engage in the work of self-repair.

Key Themes of the Programme

The Leading for Humanity experience focuses on several interconnected themes that are central to the leadership philosophy of Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

1. Self-Repair for Societal Repair

The programme explores the relationship between personal healing and social transformation.

Participants are encouraged to reflect on their own experiences, wounds, privileges, assumptions, fears, and responsibilities. This process is intended to help them understand how personal experiences influence the way they relate to others and respond to injustice.

The concept of self-repair does not suggest that individuals must be perfect before contributing to social change. Instead, it emphasizes the importance of self-awareness, accountability, emotional honesty, and the willingness to continue growing.

Participants examine how personal transformation can strengthen their ability to contribute to healthier relationships, communities, and institutions.

2. Ubuntu and Compassionate Leadership

Ubuntu is an African philosophy that emphasizes interconnectedness, shared humanity, mutual responsibility, and the idea that people’s lives are deeply connected.

Within the Leading for Humanity Programme, Ubuntu encourages participants to understand leadership as a responsibility to others rather than merely a position of authority.

The programme explores questions such as:

How can leaders recognize the humanity of others?

How can leadership become more inclusive and compassionate?

How can people work across social, professional, cultural, and ideological differences?

How can communities build relationships based on dignity, respect, and mutual responsibility?

Through peer exchange and group reflection, participants explore how Ubuntu can inform leadership decisions and social action.

3. Forgiveness, Indignation, and Righteous Anger

The programme also examines the complex relationship between forgiveness, anger, injustice, and social change.

Participants are encouraged to explore how anger can emerge from experiences of oppression, discrimination, inequality, and injustice. The programme considers how righteous anger can be transformed into constructive action rather than hatred, violence, or division.

Forgiveness is approached as a complex process rather than a simple requirement to forget harm or excuse wrongdoing. Participants are invited to reflect on how forgiveness, accountability, justice, and reconciliation may interact in personal and social contexts.

4. Finding Purpose and Building a Circle of Courage

Another central theme is the exploration of purpose.

Participants consider what motivates their leadership, what values guide their decisions, and how they can translate their convictions into meaningful action.

The programme also encourages the development of a “Circle of Courage”—a supportive network of people who share a commitment to courageous, compassionate, and justice-oriented leadership.

This community can help participants continue learning, reflecting, collaborating, and acting beyond the residential programme.

Programme Format and Duration

The Leading for Humanity Programme is an 8-day residential leadership journey.

The residential experience is designed to provide an intensive environment in which participants can step away from their normal routines and engage deeply with the programme’s themes.

The programme will take place in April 2027 in South Africa, with activities associated with Cape Town and Hermanus.

Full attendance is mandatory. Nominees should therefore ensure that they can commit to the entire residential programme before being nominated.

The programme may include a combination of:

Facilitated discussions;

Group activities;

Personal reflection;

Peer exchange;

Storytelling;

Leadership exercises;

Courageous conversations; and

Engagement with other leaders and thought partners.

The immersive format is intended to create space for meaningful learning and relationship-building among participants from different backgrounds and sectors.

What Participants Will Gain

Successful participants will become part of a carefully selected community of individuals committed to courageous leadership and social change.

The programme is designed to provide several important benefits.

1. Values-Based Leadership Development

Participants will have the opportunity to strengthen their understanding of leadership rooted in:

Integrity;

Justice;

Compassion;

Accountability;

Courage;

Inclusion;

Human dignity; and

Shared responsibility.

The programme encourages participants to consider how these values can shape their decisions and actions in real-world situations.

2. Personal Reflection and Self-Awareness

Through guided reflection and challenging conversations, participants will have opportunities to examine their personal leadership journeys and better understand their motivations, strengths, challenges, and areas for growth.

This self-awareness can help participants become more intentional and thoughtful in their leadership roles.

3. Peer Learning and Exchange

The programme brings together individuals from different sectors, professions, communities, cultures, and life experiences.

This diversity creates opportunities for participants to learn from perspectives different from their own, challenge assumptions, and develop a deeper understanding of complex social issues.

4. Exposure to Diverse Changemakers

Participants will connect with people working in different areas of social change, including sectors and communities that may not normally interact with one another.

These relationships can encourage collaboration, knowledge exchange, and the development of new approaches to social challenges.

5. A Lifelong Community of Purpose

Successful participants will become part of an enduring alumni network connected by shared values and a commitment to leading with humanity.

This network may provide opportunities for continued engagement, collaboration, peer support, and collective action after the residential programme.

6. Fully Funded Programme Participation

The Foundation will cover:

Programme costs;

Accommodation; and

Meals.

This support allows selected participants to focus on the learning experience without bearing the direct costs of the programme itself.

However, travel expenses to and from South Africa are not covered by the Foundation and must be paid by participants or their sponsors.

Who Should Be Nominated?

The Foundation welcomes nominations of individuals who demonstrate the potential and willingness to lead with courage, compassion, and a commitment to justice.

Nominees should ideally demonstrate several of the following qualities.

Leadership Potential and Courage

Nominees should be individuals who are willing to stand up for:

Truth;

Human rights;

Justice;

Equality;

Freedom;

Human dignity; and

Social responsibility.

They may already be leading initiatives or communities, or they may be emerging leaders who have demonstrated the courage to act on their values.

Leadership does not necessarily mean holding a senior institutional position. The programme recognizes that meaningful leadership can take place in communities, workplaces, civil society, educational institutions, businesses, grassroots movements, and personal networks.

Diversity of Backgrounds and Experiences

The Foundation welcomes individuals from different sectors, professions, age groups, communities, and life experiences.

The programme seeks to build a diverse cohort capable of learning from different perspectives and experiences.

Potential nominees may come from fields such as:

Civil society;

Education;

Business;

Entrepreneurship;

Human rights;

Law;

Public policy;

Government;

Community development;

Arts and culture;

Media;

Research;

Youth development;

Environmental action;

Health;

Social justice;

Faith-based organizations; and

Other areas of public and community life.

The supplied call does not specify a particular academic qualification or professional credential as a mandatory requirement.

Commitment to Societal Repair

Nominees should be willing to engage seriously with the programme’s themes, including personal reflection, difficult conversations, forgiveness, justice, compassion, and social healing.

The programme is intended for individuals who are open to examining their own perspectives and experiences while listening respectfully to others.

Nominees should be prepared to participate in an intensive residential experience and contribute constructively to a diverse learning environment.

South African and International Applicants

The Foundation welcomes nominations from both South Africa and other countries.

International applicants are encouraged to apply, provided they can:

Travel to South Africa;

Reach the programme locations in Cape Town and Hermanus;

Participate fully in the residential programme; and

Meet any applicable travel and entry requirements.

The Foundation does not state a restriction based on nationality, race, or continent in the supplied call for nominations.

Eligibility and Geographic Scope

The Leading for Humanity Programme is open to individuals from around the world.

The eligibility information indicates that nominees may be:

South African citizens or residents;

Applicants from other African countries;

Applicants from Europe;

Applicants from Asia;

Applicants from North America;

Applicants from Latin America and the Caribbean;

Applicants from Oceania; or

Applicants from other regions globally.

However, all nominees must be able to travel to South Africa and participate fully in the required residential programme.

The call does not state a specific age limit, academic degree requirement, professional sector restriction, or nationality quota. Instead, selection emphasizes leadership potential, alignment with the values of Archbishop Desmond Tutu, commitment to social justice, diversity, and readiness for deep engagement.

Learn More Here

Self-Nominations and Nominations by Others

The programme accepts both self-nominations and nominations submitted by other people.

Individuals may nominate themselves, or they may be nominated by:

Colleagues;

Mentors;

Employers;

Community members;

Professional networks;

Organizational leaders; or

Other people familiar with their leadership work and potential.

This flexible nomination process allows individuals who recognize their own readiness for the programme to apply directly, while also enabling others to recommend promising leaders.

How to Nominate Someone

Applicants and nominators should prepare a nomination package containing the information required by the Foundation.

Step 1: Prepare a Motivation

The nomination should include a motivation explaining:

Why the nominee demonstrates courageous leadership;

How the nominee reflects the values associated with Archbishop Desmond Tutu;

The nominee’s commitment to truth, justice, human rights, or societal healing;

Why the nominee would benefit from the programme; and

How the nominee could contribute to the cohort and the wider community.

The motivation should be specific and supported by examples. Rather than relying only on general statements such as “the nominee is a great leader,” the submission should describe concrete actions, initiatives, achievements, or experiences that demonstrate leadership and social commitment.

Step 2: Include the Nominee’s Contact Details

The nomination should provide the nominee’s relevant contact information so the programme team can communicate with them if they are shortlisted.

Step 3: Provide a Brief Biography

The biography should summarize the nominee’s background, leadership experience, community involvement, professional work, and relevant achievements.

It should help the selection team understand who the nominee is and why they may be a strong fit for the programme.

Step 4: Add Supporting Materials

Where available, nominators may include supporting documents such as:

Curriculum vitae;

Reference letters;

Links to relevant projects;

Evidence of community engagement;

Leadership portfolios;

Publications;

Media coverage; or

Other materials demonstrating the nominee’s impact and commitment.

Supporting materials should be relevant and should strengthen the nomination rather than overwhelm the selection team with unnecessary information.

Step 5: Submit the Nomination by Email

Nominations should be sent by email to:

shanti@tutu.org.za

The subject line should read:

Leading for Humanity nomination – 2027 cohort

Applicants should ensure that all required information and supporting materials are attached before sending the nomination.

Selection Process

Nominations will be reviewed by the programme team.

The selection process will consider factors such as:

Demonstrated leadership;

Alignment with Archbishop Desmond Tutu’s values;

Commitment to social justice;

Potential to contribute to societal healing;

Openness to personal reflection and courageous conversations;

Diversity of the overall cohort; and

Ability to participate fully in the residential programme.

The Foundation aims to create a cohort that brings together individuals with different backgrounds and experiences while maintaining a shared commitment to humane, inclusive, and values-based leadership.

Shortlisting and Interviews

Shortlisted nominees will be contacted for interviews and may be asked to provide additional information.

Being nominated does not automatically guarantee selection. Nominees should therefore be prepared to explain their leadership journey, motivation, values, community or professional contribution, and interest in the programme.

Final Cohort Announcement

The final cohort is expected to be announced in early 2027.

Successful nominees will then receive further information about programme arrangements, participation requirements, travel planning, and other relevant details.

Important Funding and Travel Information

The Leading for Humanity Programme is described as fully funded in relation to the residential programme itself.

The Foundation covers:

Programme costs;

Accommodation; and

Meals.

However, participants or their sponsors must cover:

Flights or other international travel to South Africa;

Return travel from South Africa;

Any visa-related costs, where applicable;

Personal expenses; and

Other costs not explicitly covered by the Foundation.

International nominees should begin considering travel requirements early, including passport validity, visa eligibility, travel insurance, and the ability to reach Cape Town and Hermanus.

Programme Location

The residential programme will take place in South Africa, with the call specifically referring to Cape Town and Hermanus.

Cape Town is a major cultural, political, and historical center in South Africa. Hermanus, located in the Western Cape, is known for its coastal setting and natural environment.

The locations provide an appropriate setting for a programme focused on reflection, dialogue, leadership, reconciliation, and social healing.

Participants should be prepared to travel between or participate in activities associated with these locations as directed by the Foundation.

Application Deadline

The deadline for nominations is:

14 October 2026

Nominations open on 11 September 2026.

Because places are limited and shortlisted nominees may be invited for interviews or asked to provide additional information, interested applicants and nominators are encouraged to submit their nominations as early as possible.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Nomination

A strong nomination should show more than the nominee’s job title or academic achievements. The selection team is looking for evidence of courage, values-based leadership, and a commitment to justice and societal healing.

Consider the following recommendations:

Use specific examples.

Explain what the nominee has done, whom they have served, and what changed as a result of their actions.

Demonstrate moral courage.

Highlight situations in which the nominee stood up for truth, human rights, justice, equality, or dignity.

Explain alignment with the programme.

Connect the nominee’s experience and values to themes such as Ubuntu, forgiveness, self-repair, compassion, and social healing.

Show openness to learning.

Identify why the nominee is ready to engage in personal reflection, courageous conversations, and peer exchange.

Explain the nominee’s potential contribution.

Describe the perspectives, experiences, and knowledge the nominee could bring to a diverse cohort.

Confirm availability.

Ensure the nominee can attend the full residential programme in April 2027.

Address travel requirements.

International nominees should confirm that they can travel to South Africa and make the necessary arrangements.

Keep supporting materials relevant.

Include a concise CV, references, or evidence of impact that strengthens the nomination.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Leading for Humanity Programme a scholarship?

No. It is a leadership-development programme rather than an academic scholarship. Participants receive a fully funded residential learning experience, but the programme does not provide a university degree or academic qualification.

Is the programme open to international applicants?

Yes. The Foundation welcomes South African and international nominations. International nominees must be able to travel to South Africa and participate fully in the programme.

Can I nominate myself?

Yes. Self-nominations are welcome.

Can someone else nominate me?

Yes. Nominations may be submitted by colleagues, mentors, employers, community members, or other individuals familiar with the nominee’s leadership potential and work.

Is there a specific academic qualification required?

The supplied call does not specify a mandatory academic degree or professional qualification. Selection is based primarily on leadership potential, values, commitment to social justice, diversity, and readiness to participate fully.

What costs are covered?

The Foundation covers programme costs, accommodation, and meals.

Applications are open for the Southeast Asia Research Group (SEAREG) Postdoctoral Fellowship Program 2027. The Southeast Asia Research Group (SEAREG) is launching a Postdoctoral Fellowship program that will begin in the summer of 2027 with one Fellow holding a 12-month position at one of four partner institutions located in Southeast Asia.

The program aims to provide scholars of Southeast Asia with opportunities for training, networking, and field research to improve competitiveness for the academic and non-academic job markets. The appointment will allow the Fellow to strengthen their research agenda while also contributing to the academic life of the host institution. The Fellow will receive mentoring from a member of the SEAREG Executive Council and will have their work showcased at SEAREG’s annual Southeast Asian workshop in the summer of 2027.

Benefits

The Postdoctoral Fellowship offers a competitive salary and a small fund to support research expenses. It will also support travel ahead to SEAREG’s Southeast Asian workshop at the start of the Fellowship.

Eligibility

To be eligible for consideration, all applicants must have:

Completed their PhD in a three-year window that precedes the start of the Postdoc Fellowship (May 2024-May 2027)

Received their PhD from an institution based in North America (the United States, Canada or Mexico)

Engaged with Southeast Asia seriously as a region in the course of their dissertation research, and their ongoing research agenda should align with SEAREG’s priorities as outlined in the organization’s constitution.

Eligible applicants will have completed their PhD in a social sciences discipline—political science, sociology, economics, or a related discipline. The researcher will not necessarily be expected to conduct research on the country of their host institution, but their two-page research proposal should indicate how the host university is nonetheless an excellent fit for their postdoc agenda.

Application

All application materials must be submitted by Sunday, Nov. 1 at 12 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (U.S.).

Required application materials include the following:

A one-page cover letter

A two-page research proposal that outlines:

What you hope to accomplish during the Postdoctoral Fellowship;

How you are going to engage the host institution;

Who your mentor at the host institution will be and the rationale for the pairing;

Your intended outputs from the Fellowship

A letter of support from your mentor at the host institution (two-page maximum). Mentors must be full-time, permanent faculty; each mentor can only support one application.

Two writing samples, which may include published articles, working papers, or dissertation chapters highlighting your scholarship on Southeast Asia

Two letters of recommendation

TITLE: FCDO Research Advisory Group 2026: Part-Time Remote Opportunity for Senior Global Research and Policy Experts

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The FCDO Research Advisory Group (RAG) is seeking experienced experts to join its advisory group and provide independent scientific and research advice to the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).

This is a senior-level, part-time advisory opportunity for individuals with substantial expertise in areas such as health, agriculture, climate, energy, water, economic growth, humanitarian affairs, education, governance, conflict, social development, data for development, big data and artificial intelligence.

Members will contribute strategic advice on FCDO’s research priorities, funding portfolio, evidence use, research quality, value for money, emerging global challenges and connections with the wider UK and international research community.

The position is remote, part-time and unremunerated, although FCDO will reimburse reasonable economy travel and incidental expenses associated with the role.

About the FCDO Research Advisory Group

The FCDO Research Advisory Group was established in 2022 to provide strategic guidance, rapid insight and independent challenge to FCDO’s research funding portfolio.

The Group supports the work of the FCDO Chief Scientific Adviser (CSA), who is also the Director of the Research and Evidence Division.

Its role is to help assure the quality, relevance and appropriateness of FCDO’s research portfolio.

The Group brings together experts with thematic and geographic knowledge covering a wide range of global development and international policy issues.

Its areas of expertise include:

Health

Agriculture

Climate

Energy

Water

Economic growth

Humanitarian affairs

Education

Governance

Conflict

Social development

Data for development

Big data

Artificial intelligence

Innovation and related research areas

Members are expected to contribute their expertise while also engaging with issues that extend beyond their own individual academic discipline.

What Is the Role of an FCDO Research Advisory Group Member?

Members provide independent scientific and research advice to FCDO.

The role is not simply about advising on an individual’s specialist field. Members are appointed in a personal capacity, meaning they serve as independent experts rather than representatives of their employer, profession, institution or an interest group.

Members are also expected to contribute across the Group’s broader agenda.

Their responsibilities include providing insight into how research and evidence can support international development and wider foreign policy objectives.

Key Responsibilities

1. Advising on FCDO Research Priorities

Members will contribute to discussions concerning:

FCDO’s research priorities

Research activities

The relationship between FCDO research and the wider UK science base

Connections with international research communities

Emerging areas where additional research may be required

Their advice can help FCDO consider whether its research portfolio is addressing important global challenges and research needs.

2. Supporting Evidence-Informed Policy

A central responsibility of the Group is helping ensure that FCDO policy is informed by the best available research and evidence.

Members may therefore be asked to consider the quality, relevance and usefulness of research being used to inform policy.

This requires an understanding of how research can be translated into practical policy and development impact.

3. Reviewing Research Programme Effectiveness

Members will comment on the:

Effectiveness of research programmes

Value for money of research investments

Funding mechanisms for research and development

Performance and relevance of research activities

This means applicants should be able to engage with questions concerning not only academic quality but also the practical impact and effectiveness of research funding.

4. Advising on the Research Portfolio

Members will help assess the overall balance and adequacy of FCDO’s research portfolio.

This includes identifying:

Research gaps

Areas requiring greater attention

Areas that may deserve less emphasis

Emerging research priorities

Opportunities for strengthening the overall portfolio

Members therefore need to be able to think beyond individual research projects and consider research strategically at portfolio level.

5. Horizon-Scanning and Scenario Planning

The Group also participates in horizon-scanning and long-range scenario planning.

This involves considering emerging global challenges and developments that could have implications for research, international development and policy.

Experts should therefore be comfortable thinking about future trends and possible challenges rather than focusing exclusively on current issues.

6. Connecting FCDO With Specialist Expertise

Members can provide advice and connections to specialist expertise across:

The UK research community

International research institutions

Academic networks

Relevant specialist fields

Global research communities

Their networks and understanding of the international research environment can therefore contribute to the Group’s advisory role.

7. Emergency Response and Disaster Preparedness

Where required, members may also provide advice on scientific inputs to FCDO’s emergency response and disaster preparedness.

This responsibility highlights the importance of having experts who can apply research and evidence to rapidly changing international situations.

Time Commitment

The position is designed to be compatible with other professional responsibilities.

Members are expected to participate in:

Four meetings per year

Approximately 2.5 to 3 hours per meeting

Approximately 2 to 3 hours of reading and preparation for each meeting

Occasional additional meetings or direct engagement when FCDO requires specific expert advice

Meeting papers are expected to be circulated approximately one week before each meeting, allowing members time to review the material and prepare.

Meeting dates will be confirmed as far in advance as possible.

There may also be occasional ad hoc requests for expert input between scheduled meetings.

Length of Appointment

The appointment is for:

Three years

The term is renewable once, with a maximum of:

Two terms

This means a member may potentially serve for up to six years if their appointment is renewed.

Remuneration and Expenses

The position is unremunerated.

Members do not receive a salary for serving on the Research Advisory Group.

However, the information provided states that reasonable travel expenses and incidental expenses will be reimbursed by FCDO.

Where travel is required, the stated provision is for economy travel.

Applicants should therefore understand that this is a professional advisory appointment rather than a salaried part-time employment position.

Employment Arrangement

The position is listed as:

Employment Type: Part Time

Location: Remote

The remote nature of the role means that members can participate without being based at a particular FCDO office.

However, applicants should take into account that the role may involve meetings or activities requiring travel, with reasonable eligible travel and incidental expenses reimbursed according to the stated arrangements.

Who Is FCDO Looking For?

The Research Advisory Group is seeking individuals with a combination of subject-matter expertise, senior professional experience, international perspective and the ability to provide independent advice.

The selection criteria emphasize several important characteristics.

Selection Criteria

1. Relevant Thematic Expertise

Applicants should have expertise, skills and experience in a relevant thematic area.

The identified thematic areas include:

Health

Agriculture

Climate

Energy

Water

Growth

Humanitarian affairs

Education

Governance

Conflict

Social development

Data for development

Applicants whose expertise relates to broader research, innovation, technology or evidence issues may also be relevant where their expertise connects with the Group’s agenda.

2. Seniority and International Reputation

The Group is looking for individuals with an appropriate level of seniority and international reputation.

This is therefore a senior expert/advisory appointment rather than an entry-level opportunity.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate a substantial record of expertise and contribution in their relevant field.

3. Familiarity With Government Processes

Applicants should have familiarity with:

Government processes

Key government policies

Policy development

The relationship between research and government decision-making

Experience of working with government, public institutions or policy environments can therefore be relevant to the role.

4. Independence and Fairness

Members must be committed to a fair and independent process.

Because the Group provides independent advice, members are expected to approach issues objectively and contribute professional judgement without allowing personal or institutional interests to determine their advice.

5. Breadth of Academic Discipline

The selection process values breadth across academic disciplines.

Applicants should have an understanding of transdisciplinary approaches to global challenges.

This is important because many of the issues addressed by FCDO cannot be examined through one discipline alone.

For example, challenges involving climate, health, development, conflict or technology can involve multiple scientific, social, economic and policy perspectives.

6. International and Global Perspective

Applicants should have an international and global perspective.

Particular emphasis is placed on:

Capacity strengthening in the Global South

Translation of research into impact

Research partnerships

Working with international partners

Understanding how research can contribute to development outcomes

Experience working across countries, regions or international research networks may therefore be relevant.

FCDO Research and Development Context

The Research Advisory Group operates within a broader FCDO research and development environment.

Following publication of the Global Research and Technology Development (GRTD) Approach Paper, launch of the GRTD website and confirmation of long-term funding, FCDO’s research and development portfolio now includes:

A large Official Development Assistance (ODA) programme

A smaller but growing non-ODA portfolio

The non-ODA component is focused on broader foreign policy and national security objectives.

This means the Group’s work extends across a diverse research portfolio involving development, international policy and other strategic priorities.

Appointment in a Personal Capacity

A significant condition of the appointment is that members serve in their personal capacity.

They are not appointed as representatives of:

Their employer

Their university

Their profession

An interest group

Another organization

Members are also expected to contribute across the full agenda of the Research Advisory Group, rather than restricting their contribution exclusively to their own academic discipline.

This makes breadth of perspective and the ability to engage with multidisciplinary issues particularly important.

Principles and Standards Expected of Members

Members must abide by the Seven Principles of Public Life, commonly known as the Nolan Principles.

They are also expected to take account of the Government Chief Scientific Adviser (GCSA)’s Principles of Scientific Advice to Government.

These expectations reinforce the importance of:

Independence

Integrity

Evidence

Professional conduct

Responsible advisory practice

Transparency around interests

Declaration of Interests

Successful members must complete a declaration of interests when appointed.

The declaration must also be kept up to date throughout their appointment.

This is important because members may be involved in discussions concerning research programmes, funding mechanisms and research priorities.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to disclose relevant interests and maintain accurate declarations during their term.

Confidentiality and Information Security

Members will have responsibilities concerning FCDO information and documentation.

FCDO documents and information used by the Group are Official UK Government papers and must not be shared outside the Group.

Members will therefore be responsible for safeguarding:

FCDO documents

Research-related information

Meeting papers

Advisory materials

Other official information provided to the Group

Applicants should be comfortable working within appropriate confidentiality and information-security requirements.

Selection Process

The selection process involves several stages.

Step 1: Submit an Application

Interested applicants are required to submit:

A CV

An expression of interest

The application should demonstrate how the applicant’s experience, expertise and perspective correspond to the requirements of the Research Advisory Group.

Step 2: Shortlisting

Applications will be reviewed and suitable candidates will be shortlisted.

The selection criteria include thematic expertise, seniority, international reputation, government familiarity, independence, multidisciplinary perspective and international experience.

Step 3: Panel Interview

Shortlisted candidates will be invited to a panel interview.

The panel will be led by the Co-Chairs and will include the:

Chief Scientific Adviser (CSA), and/or

Deputy Chief Scientific Adviser (Deputy CSA)

Candidates should therefore be prepared to discuss their expertise, experience, understanding of research-policy relationships and ability to contribute to the Group’s broader agenda.

Application Deadline

The stated application deadline is:

30 September at 11:59 PM UK time

Important Application Form Instruction

Because this is a part-time and unremunerated position, applicants are specifically instructed to enter:

N/A

in both the:

Notice period field

Applicants should follow this instruction rather than entering a salary expectation or employment notice period.

How to Apply

Applicants interested in joining the FCDO Research Advisory Group should prepare a strong CV and expression of interest addressing their suitability for the position.

The application should demonstrate relevant evidence of:

Thematic expertise

Senior professional experience

International experience or perspective

Understanding of government and policy processes

Independent and fair judgement

Multidisciplinary or transdisciplinary experience

Research translation and impact

Capacity strengthening, particularly in the Global South

Relevant professional and academic networks

Ability to contribute to the Group beyond a narrow disciplinary area

Applicants should also ensure that the salary expectations and notice period fields contain N/A, as instructed in the vacancy announcement.
