TITLE: Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab 2027: Apply for CHF 10,000 Grant and 10-Month Incubation Programme

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab 2027, an alternative incubation programme supporting innovators and early-stage initiatives working to transform humanity’s relationship with nature and society.

Organised by Unearthodox, the Exploration Co-Lab is designed for changemakers addressing complex environmental and social challenges at their root. The programme seeks applicants whose work goes beyond short-term or incremental solutions and instead explores new systems, worldviews, relationships, and pathways for a more just, vibrant, and regenerative future.

Selected participants will receive CHF 10,000 in grant funding, a 10-month incubation journey, tailored non-financial support, peer learning, coaching, expert guidance, systems mapping, visibility opportunities, and access to a global community of innovators.

The programme will run from 1 March to 31 December 2027.

Application deadline: 16 November 2026.

What Is the Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab?

The Exploration Co-Lab is an alternative incubator for what Unearthodox describes as “edge-walkers”—innovators whose work challenges conventional approaches and does not fit easily into traditional categories.

The programme is intended for people and initiatives exploring the deeper causes of nature-society challenges. Rather than focusing only on treating visible symptoms, the Co-Lab encourages participants to question the systems, assumptions, institutions, and relationships that have contributed to environmental and social problems.

The programme is particularly interested in work that:

Reimagines the relationship between humans and the natural world.

Challenges dominant systems based on commodification or exploitation.

Questions anthropocentric assumptions.

Examines the effects of coloniality and unequal systems.

Develops new ways of thinking about ecological and social wellbeing.

Builds more regenerative, equitable, and community-centred futures.

Creates stronger relationships with the more-than-human world.

Explores new approaches to systems change and collective transformation.

The Co-Lab recognises that deep systems change often requires time, experimentation, trust, reflection, relationships, and support for ideas that may initially appear unconventional or difficult to categorise.

Key Details About the Exploration Co-Lab 2027

Programme: Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab 2027

Organiser: Unearthodox

Opportunity type: Incubator and grant-supported fellowship-style programme

Grant funding: CHF 10,000

Programme duration: 10 months

Programme dates: 1 March–31 December 2027

Application period: 15 September–16 November 2026

Application deadline: 16 November 2026

Format: Primarily online

Working language: English

Geographic scope: Global

Target applicants: Early-stage initiatives and innovators working at the intersection of environmental and societal change

What Does the Programme Offer?

The Exploration Co-Lab combines financial support, learning, coaching, community, visibility, and strategic development.

1. CHF 10,000 in Grant Funding

Selected initiatives will receive a grant of:

CHF 10,000

The funding is intended to help participants move their initiatives forward. Applicants should be able to explain how the grant will contribute to the development, testing, deepening, or transformation of their work.

The grant may help an initiative:

Conduct further research.

Test or refine a pilot.

Engage communities.

Develop new tools or approaches.

Strengthen project implementation.

Explore new pathways for systems change.

Build partnerships.

Develop a more sustainable operating model.

Expand the initiative’s capacity to create impact.

Applicants should connect their proposed use of funds to the stage and needs of their initiative.

2. A 10-Month Incubation Journey

The programme offers a structured 10-month incubation journey beginning in March 2027 and ending in December 2027.

Participants will join a cohort of changemakers in an online environment focused on:

Systems transformation.

Collective learning.

Collaboration.

Connection.

Experimentation.

Changemaker wellbeing.

Strategic development.

Regenerative approaches to impact.

The incubation is designed to provide participants with space to think deeply, learn from others, and develop their work in a supportive environment.

3. Tailored Non-Financial Support

Participants will have access to a shared pool of non-financial support estimated at up to:

CHF 60,000 in value

This support is tailored to the needs of the cohort and may include:

Peer learning.

Shared exploration.

Individual coaching.

Expert guidance.

Systems mapping.

Futures thinking.

Strategic positioning.

Regenerative approaches to defining and measuring success.

The support is not necessarily provided as a cash award. Instead, it is intended to give participants access to knowledge, expertise, relationships, and tools that can help them develop their initiatives.

4. Peer Learning and Shared Exploration

Participants will become part of an interdisciplinary cohort of innovators working on complex challenges.

Peer learning may help participants:

Exchange experiences.

Learn from different approaches.

Identify new possibilities.

Reflect on challenges.

Test assumptions.

Build relationships with other changemakers.

Discover potential collaborators.

Develop a stronger understanding of systems change.

The Co-Lab values shared learning and collective problem-solving rather than competition between participants.

5. Individualised Coaching and Expert Guidance

The programme provides access to individualised coaching and expert guidance.

This support may help participants clarify:

Their initiative’s purpose.

The systems they are trying to influence.

Their theory of change.

Their strategic priorities.

Their approach to collaboration.

Their methods for measuring progress.

Their long-term sustainability needs.

The specific support available may depend on the needs of each participant and the expertise within the programme’s wider network.

6. Systems Mapping and Futures Thinking

Participants will have opportunities to explore practical approaches such as systems mapping and futures thinking.

These approaches can help innovators understand:

The relationships between different actors.

The structures that maintain a problem.

The assumptions underlying existing systems.

Possible future scenarios.

Points where change may be possible.

The conditions required for an initiative to thrive.

This is especially relevant for applicants whose work addresses complex challenges that cannot be solved through a single intervention.

7. Strategic Positioning

The Co-Lab will also support participants in thinking about the strategic positioning of themselves and their initiatives.

This may include clarifying:

What makes the initiative distinctive.

Which audiences and partners need to understand the work.

How the initiative can communicate its purpose.

What networks could support its development.

How the initiative can become more visible, findable, and fundable.

8. Regenerative Approaches to Measuring Success

Unearthodox encourages applicants and participants to think beyond conventional measures of growth and success.

The programme includes support for regenerative approaches to defining and measuring success. This may involve considering:

Ecological wellbeing.

Community resilience.

Relationships.

Equity.

Long-term systems change.

Collective capacity.

Quality of participation.

The sustainability of the work itself.

This approach recognises that meaningful change cannot always be captured through short-term numerical indicators alone.

9. Visibility and Amplification

Selected initiatives will be showcased through Unearthodox’s communication channels.

This may help participants become:

More visible to relevant audiences.

More discoverable by potential partners.

More credible to prospective supporters.

More connected to wider networks.

More fundable over time.

Visibility and amplification are intended to help promising initiatives gain recognition and access to further opportunities.

10. Global Community and Collaboration

Participants will gain access to a global network of:

Systems innovators.

Mentors.

Network weavers.

Changemakers.

Potential collaborators.

People working on related environmental and social challenges.

Unearthodox describes this community as a space for belonging, mutual support, deep allyship, and collaboration.

Who Is the Exploration Co-Lab For?

The Exploration Co-Lab is open to people who share a commitment to reimagining systems for a:

Just future.

Vibrant future.

Regenerative future.

The programme is intended for innovators who are willing to challenge conventional thinking and explore new possibilities with an engaged and interdisciplinary cohort.

Applicants should value:

Participation.

Trust.

Empathy.

Critical thinking.

Creative thinking.

Collective learning.

Community engagement.

Long-term change.

Collaboration across disciplines and backgrounds.

The programme is particularly suitable for people who do not necessarily have a straightforward or conventional career or project journey, but who are actively working on meaningful environmental and societal transformation.

Eligibility and Stage of Initiative

Applicants should be working on an early-stage initiative at the intersection of environmental and societal change.

The initiative does not need to be fully developed or have every detail resolved. However, applicants must be beyond the basic idea stage.

Some groundwork should already exist, such as:

Initial research.

Early testing.

A pilot project.

Community engagement.

An emerging intervention.

A developing model or approach.

Early evidence of a problem-solution relationship.

A concept that exists only on paper, without any research, testing, engagement, or practical development, may not be suitable for this call.

Initiative Development Stages Considered

Unearthodox recognises that initiatives may be at different stages of development. Applicants may identify with one of the following phases.

1. Testing

At the testing stage, an initiative may have limited resources and be exploring what works through direct engagement with:

Communities.

People affected by the issue.

Local environments.

Living systems.

Relevant stakeholders.

The focus is on learning, experimentation, and understanding whether the proposed approach is appropriate.

2. Proving

At the proving stage, an initiative has a tangible proof of concept demonstrating that its central idea may work.

The applicant may be seeking support to:

Continue testing.

Refine the approach.

Improve implementation.

Collect evidence.

Build momentum.

Strengthen the model.

3. Deepening

At the deepening stage, the initiative has begun to demonstrate what it can make possible.

The applicant may now be ready to:

Explore new pathways.

Adapt the approach.

Deepen community relationships.

Strengthen systems understanding.

Develop more meaningful impact.

Expand the depth rather than simply the size of the work.

4. Pivoting

Some applicants may be leading more established initiatives that require a meaningful change in:

Direction.

Strategy.

Approach.

Operating model.

Theory of change.

Relationship with communities or ecosystems.

The Co-Lab may be suitable for initiatives that need to rethink their existing model in response to new learning or changing conditions.

5. Other Development Stages

Applicants who do not fit neatly into one of these categories are still encouraged to apply if their work aligns with the programme’s purpose.

They should explain their current stage of activity and describe what kind of support would help the initiative move forward.

Diversity, Inclusion, and Participation

Unearthodox welcomes underrepresented voices from the global majority and historically excluded communities.

The programme embraces diversity across:

Age.

Gender identity.

Geographic location.

Cultural background.

Professional background.

Lived experience.

Social and community context.

As a Swiss-founded organisation, Unearthodox also seeks to deepen exchange between Swiss-based innovators and innovators from other parts of the world working on regeneration.

The organisation aims to include at least one Swiss-based initiative in each annual cohort. However, Swiss-based initiatives will be selected based on the strength and relevance of their work alongside other applicants.

The programme does not indicate that applicants must belong to a particular race, ethnicity, gender, or nationality. Instead, it expresses a particular welcome toward underrepresented and historically excluded communities.

Programme Language and Time-Zone Considerations

All programme activities are conducted in:

English

Regular online group calls are scheduled within the time range of:

UTC−6 to UTC+6

Applicants and participants located within these time zones may find it easier to participate synchronously in group sessions.

People outside these time zones may still consider applying, but they should assess whether they can participate effectively in the scheduled online activities.

What Counts as a Nature-Society Challenge?

Unearthodox defines nature-society challenges as issues arising from the ways human societies and natural systems interact.

These challenges may include:

Climate change.

Biodiversity loss.

Habitat destruction.

Environmental degradation.

Unsustainable resource use.

Human-centred systems that disregard other forms of life.

Social inequalities connected to environmental systems.

Extractive economic and institutional structures.

Disconnection between people and the more-than-human world.

The Co-Lab is interested in initiatives that explore new possibilities at this intersection and seek to create conditions in which both people and living systems can thrive.

Questions Applicants Should Consider

Applicants should reflect on the deeper purpose and potential of their work.

Useful questions include:

What future is the initiative helping to create?

What kind of future is the initiative trying to move away from?

How does the initiative encourage people to see, act, connect, or live differently in relation to the more-than-human world?

How does the work challenge existing systems, assumptions, or norms?

How could the initiative help all life on Earth thrive together?

What conditions are needed for the work to flourish?

What deeper purpose connects the applicant with others working on similar challenges?

How are communities involved in shaping the work?

What has already been tested, learned, or developed?

What kind of support would make the greatest difference at this stage?

These questions can help applicants determine whether their initiative aligns with the programme’s focus on deep systems change.

Types of Work the Programme Is Looking For

The Exploration Co-Lab does not appear to be restricted to one specific sector or discipline.

Potentially relevant initiatives may work in areas such as:

Environmental justice.

Climate action.

Biodiversity conservation.

Regenerative agriculture.

Ecological restoration.

Community resilience.

Alternative economic systems.

Indigenous and traditional ecological knowledge.

Environmental education.

Sustainable livelihoods.

Social innovation.

More-than-human relationships.

Systems transformation.

Food systems.

Urban ecology.

Environmental governance.

Community-led conservation.

Post-growth approaches.

New models of collective wellbeing.

However, an initiative’s relevance will depend on whether it addresses the deeper relationship between nature and society and demonstrates a commitment to justice, regeneration, and systemic transformation.

Work That May Not Align With the Call

Unearthodox explains that the Exploration Co-Lab is not intended for projects that:

Reinforce extractive or dominant systems.

Prioritise profit, speed, or growth above purpose.

Address only surface-level symptoms.

Seek individual advantage without genuine collective learning.

Lack meaningful interest in allyship.

Focus exclusively on short-term outcomes without considering deeper conditions.

Treat communities as passive recipients rather than active participants.

This does not mean that every applicant must reject all existing institutions or economic activity. Rather, the programme seeks initiatives that critically examine harmful systems and work toward more equitable and regenerative alternatives.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should begin by reviewing the official applicant information document. The document includes:

Application form preview.

Eligibility information.

Evaluation criteria.

Frequently asked questions.

Terms and conditions.

Guidance based on previous applications.

Additional application tips.

Applicants can access the Official Applicant Information Document.

Applications can be submitted through the Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab 2027 application portal.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

1. Clearly Explain the Problem

Describe the nature-society challenge your initiative addresses.

Explain:

Who or what is affected.

Why the challenge exists.

What systems or assumptions contribute to it.

Why conventional solutions may be insufficient.

Why the issue requires deeper transformation.

2. Demonstrate That You Are Beyond the Idea Stage

Provide evidence of groundwork, such as:

Research.

Pilot activities.

Community engagement.

Early testing.

Partnerships.

Initial results.

Existing prototypes.

Practical experimentation.

The initiative does not need to be fully mature, but the application should demonstrate that meaningful work has already begun.

3. Explain Your Approach to Systems Change

Describe how your initiative seeks to influence underlying systems rather than only treating symptoms.

You may discuss:

Institutional structures.

Cultural assumptions.

Economic incentives.

Power relationships.

Environmental relationships.

Community practices.

Governance systems.

Dominant narratives.

Social norms.

4. Show Community Participation

Explain how the people most affected by the issue participate in:

Identifying the problem.

Designing the solution.

Making decisions.

Implementing activities.

Evaluating progress.

Adapting the initiative.

Community participation should be demonstrated through actual practices rather than presented only as a general principle.

5. Identify What You Need to Develop

Be specific about the support your initiative needs.

For example, you may need:

Strategic guidance.

Systems mapping.

Research support.

Community engagement resources.

A new pilot.

Partnership development.

Coaching.

A revised theory of change.

New ways to measure impact.

Time and space for reflection.

6. Explain How the CHF 10,000 Grant Will Be Used

Provide a realistic explanation of how the grant will contribute to the initiative.

Potential uses may include:

Research and testing.

Community activities.

Materials.

Travel connected to the project.

Specialist support.

Pilot implementation.

Communications.

Monitoring and learning.

Project coordination.

Applicants should ensure that proposed expenditure is directly connected to the initiative’s development and intended outcomes.

7. Demonstrate Openness to Collective Learning

The Co-Lab is cohort-based. Applicants should show that they are willing to:

Share learning.

Receive feedback.

Collaborate.

Question assumptions.

Learn from other disciplines.

Participate in group activities.

Contribute to a supportive community.

8. Consider Accessibility and Participation

Since the programme operates online and uses English, applicants should consider their ability to participate in group sessions and complete programme activities.

Those outside the UTC−6 to UTC+6 range should assess how they will manage time-zone differences.

Application Deadline

The application period runs from:

15 September 2026 to 16 November 2026

The official application deadline is:

16 November 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit. Reviewing the applicant information document and preparing a thoughtful application may require time, particularly for initiatives that need to gather evidence of community engagement, project development, and existing work.

Email: colab@unearthodox.org

sofia.papadakaki@unearthodox.org

About Unearthodox

Unearthodox is an organisation focused on supporting unconventional approaches to environmental and social transformation.

Its work explores how innovation, relationships, systems change, regeneration, and collective learning can contribute to more just and sustainable futures.

The Exploration Co-Lab is part of this wider approach. It seeks to create a supportive environment for innovators whose work may be difficult to place within traditional funding or incubation structures.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab, 2027.

Conclusion

The Unearthodox Exploration Co-Lab 2027 is an opportunity for innovators and early-stage initiatives working on the deeper relationship between nature and society.

The programme offers a combination of CHF 10,000 in grant funding, a 10-month incubation journey, tailored coaching, expert guidance, peer learning, systems mapping, futures thinking, strategic positioning, visibility, and access to a global community of changemakers.

It is particularly suited to applicants whose work goes beyond incremental environmental or social interventions and seeks to challenge underlying systems, assumptions, and relationships. Initiatives should already have some groundwork in place through research, testing, pilot activities, or community engagement.

The programme welcomes applicants from diverse backgrounds and particularly encourages applications from underrepresented voices and historically excluded communities. Activities are conducted in English, with online group calls generally scheduled within UTC−6 to UTC+6.

Applications are open from 15 September to 16 November 2026. Interested applicants should review the official guidance, assess how their initiative aligns with the programme’s focus, and prepare a clear explanation of their work, community relevance, systems-change approach, development stage, and funding needs.

TITLE: Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 15, 2026

Applications are open for the Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship 2026-2027. The Polyfoni Fellowship is a four-month part-time research collaboration for social scientists with fieldwork experience in regions where AI products are being deployed. Fellows join remotely from November 2026 to March 2027 and conduct a cultural audit of a real AI product in their region of expertise.

Fellowship Details

Fellows conduct a cultural audit: an empirical analysis of how a specific AI product encodes assumptions about the context it is deployed in, and where those assumptions break. Each audit follows Polyfoni’s Cultural Audit Method: assumption mapping, contextual failure identification, severity assessment, and recommendations.

Polyfoni supervisors propose audit themes aligned with the research priorities. Fellows choose and shape their project in close collaboration with their academic and industry mentors. The output is a report written for a product team, published on Polyfoni’s Substack under the fellow’s name.

The audit target should be a real AI product in a region the fellow has genuine contextual knowledge about. Your fieldwork experience is the data. You are not starting from scratch. You are applying what you already know through a structured method.

Examples of audit targets:

A health AI chatbot in East Africa

A ocean AI tool in Southeast Asia

An agricultural AI tool in West Africa

An LLM deployed in a non-English-dominant market

Benefits

Dual mentorship from an academic collaborator and an AI industry professional

Training in Polyfoni’s Cultural Audit Method

Online masterclasses and monthly group sessions, supported by our partner AI Mission Lab

A published research on Polyfoni’s website and Making AI Listen (open access publication) under your name

Eligibility

You can apply if you are interested in using your social science training to contribute to how AI products are built, evaluated, and governed.

They are interested in candidates from a broad set of disciplinary backgrounds, including anthropology, sociology, STS, development studies, political science, humanities, and area studies. There are no strict degree requirements, although we expect that the most promising candidates will have fieldwork experience in a Global South context and an interest in technology careers. Prior AI experience is not required.

When assessing applications, they will be looking for:

Regional expertise with evidence of fieldwork: Deep contextual knowledge of a place, community, or sector where AI is being deployed. Priority regions: East Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, China.

Clear motivation: A specific reason for wanting to work at the intersection of social science and AI, and a concrete idea of which AI product you would audit. They expect the fellows to work on the audit 5 hours a week.

Language: Comfortable working in English. Additional languages are an advantage.

They select for diversity of region and discipline.

Application

Application is now open. The selection process has two steps:

Step 1: Initial application. Submit a short application with motivation (500 words maximum). Successful candidates will be contacted for a CV review.

Step 2: Interview. Final candidates will have an interview and a research discussion with the Polyfoni team.

Polyfoni matches fellows with mentors based on regional expertise alignment (your fieldwork region and the mentor’s company market) and sector alignment (health, fintech, content moderation, etc.).

For more information, visit Polyfoni Social Sciences for AI Fellowship.

TITLE: WomHub Accelerating African Female Founders to Capital Programme 2026

Applications are open for the WomHub Accelerating African Female Founders to Capital Programme 2026. This is an ambitious business growth and investment readiness programme designed to support high-potential women entrepreneurs across Southern Africa.

Delivered by WomHub, in partnership with AfricaGrow Technical Assistance Facility, KfW DEG Impact, and the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), the programme supports women-led businesses operating within the STEM sectors (Science, Technology, Engineering and Manufacturing) to become investment-ready, scale sustainably, and access catalytic funding.

The programme is designed for women entrepreneurs who are building innovative, revenue-generating businesses with strong potential for growth and impact. Through a combination of expert-led training, mentorship, technical assistance, business diagnostics, and investor engagement, participants will strengthen their business foundations, enhance their growth potential, and prepare to attract investment.

Phase 3: Capital Deployment – Businesses that successfully complete the investor readiness journey and due diligence process will become eligible to pitch for catalytic funding, with between five (5) and ten (10) businesses receiving investment together with ongoing post-investment support.

Benefits

Beyond funding, participants will gain access to a dynamic network of mentors, industry experts, ecosystem partners, and investors committed to supporting the growth of women-led STEM enterprises across the region. The programme seeks to create lasting impact by strengthening founder capabilities, improving investment readiness, enabling access to capital, driving revenue growth, creating quality jobs, and accelerating innovation within the STEM ecosystem.

Must be a female founder;

Participant must be from across Southern Africa – Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Madagascar, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe;

TITLE: Australian Government DFAT Vienna Traineeship 2027: Paid 5–6 Month Internship in Austria

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Australian Permanent Mission to the United Nations and International Organisations in Vienna is offering a valuable 5–6 month traineeship in Vienna, Austria, for Australians interested in international relations, multilateral diplomacy, international organisations, security, nuclear issues, drugs and crime, and international affairs.

The traineeship provides participants with the opportunity to gain first-hand experience working within a busy Australian overseas mission while supporting Australia’s engagement with Vienna-based multilateral organisations.

Participants will work under the guidance and mentorship of Australian diplomats and will have opportunities to develop practical skills in research, reporting, program development, public diplomacy, digital communication, meeting support, and international engagement.

The program is expected to offer two traineeships in 2027.

The application deadline is 22 September 2026.

Australian DFAT Vienna Traineeship 2027 Overview

Opportunity: DFAT Vienna Traineeship

Department: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)

Organisation: Commonwealth Government of Australia

Location: Australian Embassy, Vienna, Austria

Address: The Icon, Gertrude-Fröehlich-Sandner-Str. 2, Vienna 1100, Austria

Duration: Approximately 5–6 months

Expected intake: 2027

Number of traineeships: Two traineeships are envisaged

Workplace type: Onsite

Compensation: EUR 1,523.15 per month

Employment type: Internship/traineeship

Application deadline: 22 September 2026

Nationality requirement: Australian citizenship is mandatory

About the Australian Permanent Mission in Vienna

The Australian Permanent Mission to the United Nations and International Organisations in Vienna undertakes a broad range of multilateral diplomatic functions.

The Mission is accredited to several major international organisations based in Vienna, including:

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)

Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO)

United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)

Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)

The Permanent Mission is co-located with the Australian Embassy in Vienna. The Embassy is responsible for Australia’s bilateral relations with Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Hungary, Slovakia and Slovenia.

This makes the traineeship particularly relevant for people seeking practical exposure to both multilateral diplomacy and Australia’s broader international engagement.

About the DFAT Vienna Traineeship

The traineeship is designed to provide participants with practical experience supporting Australia’s interests at the international level.

Successful trainees will work under the guidance of experienced officers and Australian diplomats.

The experience is intended to provide exposure to how an overseas diplomatic mission operates and how Australia engages with international organisations and other stakeholders.

The traineeship covers a particularly busy period in the calendar of Vienna-based multilateral organisations, including major meetings concerning nuclear issues and transnational crime.

Participants may therefore gain first-hand exposure to international meetings, diplomatic processes, research, reporting, public diplomacy, and stakeholder engagement.

What Will Trainees Do?

The role involves a range of research, administrative, communications, diplomatic-support, and program-related responsibilities.

Potential duties include, but are not limited to, the following.

1. Support Multilateral Meetings and Conferences

Trainees may assist with the preparation for and attendance at multilateral meetings and conferences.

Responsibilities can include:

Preparing for meetings

Attending relevant meetings

Taking notes

Supporting meeting documentation

Contributing to the drafting of reports

Helping officers follow up on relevant issues

This provides trainees with an opportunity to understand how international meetings are prepared for and documented.

2. Conduct Research and Present Information

Trainees may support research and the presentation of information concerning:

Multilateral issues

Bilateral issues

Public diplomacy

International affairs

Other issues relevant to Australia’s interests

This component can help participants strengthen their analytical, research, writing, and information-presentation skills.

3. Support Official Visits

The traineeship may involve assisting with preparations for official visits and contributing to program development.

This can include supporting the planning and organisation of activities involving Australian officials and international stakeholders.

4. Digital Communication

Trainees may contribute to content development for the Permanent Mission’s digital platforms.

Potential channels include:

The Permanent Mission’s website

X (formerly Twitter)

This means applicants with strong writing, digital communication, social media, and content-development skills may find this component particularly relevant.

5. Outreach and Events

Trainees may also support engagement and outreach activities and contribute to Mission events.

This provides exposure to public diplomacy and stakeholder engagement in an international setting.

Skills You Can Develop

The traineeship offers the opportunity to develop a broad range of professional skills.

These include:

International relations research

Multilateral diplomacy

Policy research

Analytical thinking

Report writing

Meeting documentation

Program development

Public diplomacy

Digital communication

Strategic thinking

Stakeholder engagement

Event support

Teamwork

Organisation

Problem-solving

Working under pressure

Participants will also gain practical insight into the operation of an Australian diplomatic mission overseas.

Who Is the Australian Government Looking For?

The Mission is looking for an undergraduate or postgraduate student or recent graduate with an enthusiasm for multilateralism and international affairs.

Candidates should have relevant education and abilities that can contribute to advancing Australia’s national interests.

Preference is given to applicants who have recently completed, or who have completed at least four semesters of tertiary studies, in relevant areas.

These areas include:

Political science

International relations

International law

International security

Defence studies

Science and technology

Prior exposure to, or demonstrated knowledge of, the United Nations system is highly desirable.

The opportunity may therefore be particularly suitable for students and recent graduates seeking to establish a career in:

Diplomacy

International relations

Foreign affairs

International organisations

Government

International security

Public diplomacy

Multilateral affairs

Policy research

Personal Qualities and Professional Skills

Beyond academic qualifications, DFAT is seeking candidates who demonstrate strong professional and interpersonal qualities.

Applicants should be:

Highly Motivated

Candidates should demonstrate enthusiasm for international affairs and a commitment to contributing to Australia’s national interests.

Strong Communicators

Excellent oral and written communication skills are expected.

This is particularly important because the traineeship involves research, reporting, meetings, stakeholder engagement, and digital communication.

Strategic Thinkers

Applicants should demonstrate the ability to analyse situations, identify relevant issues, and think strategically.

Practical Problem-Solvers

The Mission is seeking people who can approach challenges constructively and identify practical solutions.

Team Players

The role involves working with diplomats, officers, other staff, international organisations, and external stakeholders.

Good teamwork and organisational skills are therefore important.

Flexible and Adaptable

The environment of an overseas diplomatic mission can involve changing priorities and time-sensitive activities.

Applicants should be flexible, adaptable, resourceful, and able to work under pressure.

Respectful and Ethical

Applicants should demonstrate respect for others, ethical conduct, and an appreciation of diversity.

Mandatory Eligibility Requirements

Before applying, candidates should carefully check the mandatory eligibility criteria.

Australian Citizenship

Applicants must be Australian citizens.

This is explicitly stated as a mandatory requirement.

Non-Australian citizens are therefore not eligible for this particular traineeship.

Right to Work in Austria

Successful applicants must obtain, or be able to obtain, an appropriate visa giving them the right to work in Austria for the duration of the traineeship.

Relevant Qualifications and Background

Applicants must possess relevant qualifications and background.

Preference is given to candidates who have completed, or are currently completing, tertiary studies in areas such as:

Political science

International relations

International law

International security

Defence studies

Science and technology

Interest in Multilateralism

Applicants must demonstrate a genuine interest in multilateralism.

It is not enough simply to state an interest; candidates should be able to demonstrate this interest through their academic background, experience, activities, or responses to the application questionnaire.

Police Check

Successful applicants must be willing to undergo a mandatory police check.

Relocation to Vienna

Applicants must be willing to relocate to Vienna, Austria, for a period of up to six months.

The relocation is primarily self-funded.

Travel

Visa

Passport

Accommodation

Health insurance

EUR 1,523.15 per month

08:30–16:30, Monday to Friday

UN meetings are usually held between:

10:00–18:00

Trainees should therefore expect a professional working environment connected to the schedules of the Mission and Vienna-based international organisations.

The Australian Permanent Mission expects high standards of professional conduct from its staff and trainees.

Ethical behaviour is considered important not only for the effective operation of the workplace but also for maintaining the reputation and standing of the Mission and its employees in Australia and internationally.

Trainees participating in the program will be required to comply with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s Locally Engaged Staff Code of Conduct.

The Code takes into account the particular responsibilities associated with representing Australia outside the country.

Applicants must submit several documents as part of their application.

1. Resume

Applicants should submit a resume of no more than two pages.

The resume should clearly communicate the applicant’s:

Education

Relevant experience

Skills

Other relevant qualifications

Because the resume is limited to two pages, applicants should prioritise information directly relevant to the traineeship.

2. Written Reference

A written reference must be included with the application.

Applicants should select a referee who can provide meaningful evidence of their academic, professional, research, communication, teamwork, or other relevant abilities.

3. University Letter of Support

A letter of support from the applicant’s university is optional but encouraged where appropriate.

Students may therefore wish to explore whether their university can provide an appropriate supporting letter.

4. Traineeship Questionnaire

Applicants must complete a questionnaire designed to assess their suitability for the position.

The questionnaire evaluates qualities, experience, skills, and knowledge relevant to working as a trainee at the Mission.

Questionnaire Questions

Applicants are asked to respond to six questions.

Each response should be no more than 150 words.

Question 1: Motivation

Applicants must explain:

Why are you applying for this traineeship?

This response should clearly communicate the applicant’s motivation and demonstrate why the opportunity fits their academic and career interests.

Question 2: International Relations and DFAT

Applicants must:

Question 3: Analytical and Research Skills

Applicants must briefly describe a recent:

Achievement

Project

Task

that demonstrates their:

Analytical skills

Research skills

Strategic thinking

A strong response should provide a specific example rather than simply listing skills.

Question 4: Teamwork

Applicants must demonstrate their ability to:

Work effectively as part of a team

Build strong working relationships

Applicants should use a concrete example where possible.

Question 5: Problem-Solving Under Pressure

Applicants must demonstrate their ability to solve problems under pressure.

A practical example from university, employment, volunteering, research, leadership, or another relevant setting can be used.

Question 6: Additional Languages

Applicants may optionally state whether they speak languages other than English.

This question is optional.

Cover Letter Is Not Required

An important point for applicants is that cover letters are not required.

The announcement specifically states that cover letters will not be considered as part of the application.

Applicants should therefore focus their effort on preparing:

A strong two-page resume

A written reference

A university support letter where appropriate

Strong questionnaire responses

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the DFAT Vienna traineeship is:

22 September 2026

Applicants should submit their applications before the deadline and allow sufficient time to prepare the required documents and questionnaire responses.

Where Is the Traineeship Based?

The traineeship is based at the:

Australian Embassy, Vienna

The Icon

Gertrude-Fröehlich-Sandner-Str. 2

Vienna 1100

Austria

Who Should Consider Applying?

This traineeship may be particularly relevant to Australian students and recent graduates interested in international careers.

Political science

International security

Science and technology

Australian foreign affairs

Travel costs

Visa costs

Passport costs

Health insurance

Why This Traineeship Is Valuable

The DFAT Vienna traineeship provides more than classroom-based exposure to international relations.

Participants can gain practical experience within an actual diplomatic mission and work alongside experienced Australian diplomats.

The combination of research, reporting, international meetings, public diplomacy, digital communication, program development, outreach, and stakeholder engagement can provide a broad understanding of how Australia’s international interests are represented and advanced overseas.

The location is also significant because Vienna hosts several major international organisations, including the IAEA, CTBTO, UNODC and OSCE.

For someone considering a future career in diplomacy or international affairs, exposure to these institutions can provide valuable professional experience.

About the Commonwealth Government of Australia

The Commonwealth Government of Australia employs staff overseas to support the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and other Australian Government agencies at overseas posts, including:

Embassies

High commissions

Consulates

Locally Engaged Staff support and complement Australian Public Service employees by providing important in-country knowledge, skills, networks, and continuity.

The Australian Government’s overseas workforce operates across more than 100 locations and contributes to Australia’s international objectives and national interests.

TITLE: How to Create the Right Business Strategy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Starting a new business can be exciting, but a good idea alone is rarely enough to build something that lasts. Many businesses begin with enthusiasm, energy and ambition but struggle because there is no clear strategy behind the idea. A strong business strategy helps you understand what your business is trying to achieve, who it is serving, how it will make money and what you need to prioritise in order to grow. For a new business, strategy does not have to be complicated. It simply needs to provide direction and help you make better decisions from the beginning.

Start With the Problem You Want to Solve
One of the first things every entrepreneur should understand is the problem the business is trying to solve. Many people begin by thinking about the product they want to sell rather than the problem customers are experiencing. However, successful businesses are usually built around real needs. Before developing your product or service, ask yourself what challenge people are facing, how they currently deal with that challenge and what is missing from the existing solutions. You should also consider whether people care enough about the problem to pay for a solution. A business becomes stronger when it is addressing a problem that is clear, specific and important to its target customers. For example, instead of simply deciding to start a food delivery business, you may discover that young professionals in a particular city struggle to find affordable and healthy meals during working hours. That insight gives the business a clearer focus. Your strategy can then be built around providing convenient, affordable and nutritious meals to this specific customer group rather than trying to serve everyone.

Know Exactly Who Your Customer Is
Every business needs customers, but trying to serve everybody can make it difficult to serve anyone properly. A strong business strategy identifies the specific people most likely to need and pay for what the business offers. Think about their age, location, occupation, lifestyle, income level, challenges and buying habits. You should understand where they spend their time, how they make purchasing decisions and what matters most to them when choosing a product or service. The more specific you are, the easier it becomes to make good business decisions. Instead of saying that your business serves young people, you could identify your target customers as university students between the ages of 18 and 25 who need affordable professional clothing for internships and job interviews. This level of clarity can influence your pricing, branding, marketing, communication and even the type of products you develop.

Create a Clear Value Proposition
Your value proposition explains why customers should choose your business. It should clearly communicate the benefit you provide and what makes your business different from the alternatives already available. New entrepreneurs sometimes assume that saying they offer good quality or excellent customer service is enough, but these are things customers already expect. Your strategy should identify something more meaningful. Perhaps your business is more affordable than competitors. Perhaps it provides faster delivery, better convenience, locally produced goods, personalised services or products designed specifically for an underserved group. Whatever makes your business valuable should be easy to explain. If customers cannot quickly understand why your business matters to them, your message may need to be clearer.

Understand the Market Before You Enter It
Before investing heavily in your business, take time to understand the market. Research businesses already offering similar products or services. Look at what they sell, how much they charge, how they communicate with customers and what people say about them. Customer complaints can be particularly useful because they often reveal gaps in the market. If people constantly complain about high prices, slow delivery or poor customer service, there may be an opportunity for your business to provide a better experience.
Market research does not always require a large budget. You can speak directly with potential customers, conduct small surveys, observe buying patterns, review social media conversations and study competitors online. The goal is to gather enough information to make informed decisions rather than building your business entirely on assumptions.

Decide How the Business Will Make Money
A business strategy must clearly explain how the company will generate revenue. You should know exactly what customers will pay for, how much they will pay, how frequently they are likely to buy and how much it will cost you to provide the product or service. Revenue can come from direct sales, subscriptions, commissions, memberships, service fees, licensing or several different sources depending on the nature of the business. It is also important to understand the difference between sales and profit. A business can generate a lot of revenue and still struggle financially if its costs are too high. If it costs almost as much to produce and deliver a product as the amount you charge customers, there may not be enough money left to support staff, marketing, technology, rent and future growth. Understanding your financial model early will help you build a more sustainable business.

Focus on What Matters Most
One of the most important parts of business strategy is deciding what not to do. New entrepreneurs often want to launch many products, target multiple customer groups and enter several markets at the same time. This can quickly stretch limited resources. A new business usually benefits from focusing on one clear opportunity and doing it well before expanding. You may eventually want to offer ten different products, but beginning with one strong product can help you build trust and understand your customers. You may have ambitions to operate nationally or internationally, but starting in one location can allow you to test your model and develop strong systems before expanding. Focus allows a new business to use its money, time and energy more effectively.

Build a Competitive Advantage
Your business strategy should identify what gives your company an advantage. This is something that makes it difficult for competitors to simply copy what you are doing. It could be your expertise, relationships, technology, community knowledge, supplier network, location, intellectual property, brand reputation or understanding of a particular market. For many new businesses, a competitive advantage can come from understanding customers better than larger competitors. Entrepreneurs who are close to the communities they serve often recognise problems and opportunities that bigger companies may overlook. The important thing is to understand what makes your business valuable and continue strengthening that advantage as the company grows.

Decide How Customers Will Find You
Having a good product does not automatically mean customers will discover it. Your business strategy should include a clear plan for reaching your target market. Consider where your customers already spend their time and which channels are most likely to influence their purchasing decisions. Depending on the business, customers may discover you through social media, Google, online marketplaces, physical stores, referrals, networking events, community groups, partnerships or direct sales. You do not need to use every available marketing platform. Instead, focus on the channels that are most relevant to your customers. A business targeting corporate professionals, for example, may benefit more from LinkedIn, networking and referrals than from trying to become active on every social media platform.

Test the Idea Before Spending Too Much
One of the smartest approaches for a new business is to test the idea before making major investments. You do not necessarily need an expensive office, a large stock of products or a sophisticated website at the beginning. Start by creating the simplest version of your product or service and see how customers respond. If you are planning to start a catering business, for example, you could begin with a small menu and serve a limited group of customers. If you want to develop an online platform, you may be able to test the service manually before investing heavily in technology. These early tests help you understand what customers actually want. You can then improve the business based on real feedback rather than assumptions.

Set Clear and Measurable Goals
A business strategy becomes more useful when it includes specific goals. Instead of saying that you want the business to grow, define what growth means. You might want to gain your first 100 customers, generate a certain amount of monthly revenue, secure five major clients or increase the number of customers who return to buy again. Your priorities may also change as the business develops. During the first few months, your focus might be testing the product, building a customer base and generating consistent sales. Later, you may focus on hiring employees, improving systems, expanding into new locations or attracting investment. Clear goals help you understand what deserves your attention at each stage.

Understand Your Business Numbers
Every entrepreneur should have a basic understanding of the financial performance of the business. You do not have to be an accountant, but you should know how much money the business is making, how much it is spending and whether it is actually profitable. Important figures to monitor include revenue, costs, profit margins and cash flow. Cash flow is especially important because a business can appear successful while still struggling to pay its bills. For example, you may have customers who owe you money, but if that money has not yet entered your bank account, you may not have enough cash to pay suppliers or staff. Regularly reviewing your financial position will help you identify problems early and make better decisions.

Build the Right Team and Partnerships
No founder can do everything alone. As the business develops, think about the skills and expertise needed to achieve your goals. You may be very good at developing products but less experienced in finance, sales, marketing or operations. Understanding these gaps allows you to bring in the right people. A new business does not always need to employ a large team immediately. You can work with freelancers, consultants, service providers and strategic partners when necessary. The goal is not to have the biggest team but to make sure the business has access to the skills it needs to operate effectively.

Listen to Your Customers
Your customers are one of your most valuable sources of information. Speak with them regularly and ask about their experience. Find out why they chose your business, what they liked, what they found difficult and what they would change. Customer feedback can help you improve your products, services and overall strategy. You should also pay attention to behaviour. Sometimes what customers do provides more useful information than what they say. If one product consistently sells while another is ignored, that tells you something about what the market values. A business that listens and adapts is more likely to remain relevant.

Build for Sustainable Growth
Growth is an important goal, but growing too quickly without the right systems can create serious problems. Before expanding, make sure the core business works well. Ask whether customers are satisfied, whether your products are profitable and whether your team and systems can manage increased demand. If you expand a business that already has operational problems, those problems are likely to become bigger. Sustainable growth means building strong foundations first and expanding when the business is ready. This may sometimes mean growing more slowly, but it can create a healthier and more resilient company.

Keep Your Business Strategy Simple
A new business does not always need a long and complicated strategy document. In the beginning, you should be able to explain your strategy clearly and simply. You should know the problem you are solving, the customers you want to serve, the product or service you are offering, why customers should choose you, how you will reach them and how the business will make money. You should also know your biggest costs, your competitive advantage and the main goals you want to achieve within the next year. If you can answer these questions clearly, you already have the foundation of a strong business strategy.

Review and Adjust Your Strategy
Your first strategy should not be permanent. Markets change, customer needs evolve, competitors enter the market and new opportunities emerge. A good entrepreneur regularly reviews the strategy and makes changes when necessary. Ask yourself what is working, what is not working and what you have learned since launching the business. Some of the assumptions you made at the beginning may turn out to be wrong. Changing direction when you have better information is not a sign that the business has failed. It shows that you are learning and adapting.

Final Thoughts
Creating the right business strategy for a new business is about making deliberate choices. You need to understand the problem you are solving, know your customers, offer something valuable and create a realistic way to generate income. You also need to understand your market, focus your resources, track your finances and continue learning from your customers. You do not need to have everything figured out before starting. What matters is having a clear direction and being willing to test your ideas, learn from the market and improve as you go. The businesses that grow successfully are often not the ones that started with the perfect plan. They are the ones that understood their customers, remained focused and continued making better decisions as they grew.

Study materials funding

Research funding

Visa support

Providing students with access to available financial assistance.

Supporting the university’s mission of providing quality education to a diverse student population.

Enhancing diversity in student enrolment.

Supporting student career development through campus work opportunities and graduate assistantships.

Follow the required application procedures.

Submit applications within the prescribed deadlines.

Maintain good conduct.

Satisfy academic requirements.

Meet any additional requirements attached to the specific financial-aid programme.

How to Apply

The university’s financial-aid process generally involves several stages.

Step 1: Complete the Application Form

Applicants should download and complete the relevant scholarship application form.

All information should be provided accurately and completely.

Academic information is complete.

Required questions have been answered.

Supporting information is consistent.

All required documents are available.

Step 2: Prepare Supporting Documents

Opportunities for Women, Persons with Disabilities and Disadvantaged Applicants

What Makes the Scholarship Different?

TITLE: Fostering the Future Together: $15 Million U.S. Grant Opportunity to Protect Children Online and Empower Youth Globally

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB) has announced the Fostering the Future Together: Empowering Youth for a Safe Digital World funding opportunity, supporting projects that promote child well-being, online safety, positive youth development, education, digital skills, and protection from child labor and online exploitation.

The funding opportunity, FOA-ILAB-26-43, provides approximately $15 million in total funding through cooperative agreements. Up to five organizations are expected to receive awards ranging from $2 million to $3 million each.

This is an organization-focused funding opportunity rather than an individual grant. Eligible organizations from the United States and other countries may apply, provided they satisfy the detailed requirements in the official Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA).

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity
Fostering the Future Together: Empowering Youth for a Safe Digital World

Funding opportunity number
FOA-ILAB-26-43

Agency
U.S. Department of Labor

Bureau
Bureau of International Labor Affairs

Assistance Listing
17.401 – International Labor Programs

Funding instrument
Cooperative Agreement

Total funding
Approximately $15 million

Expected awards
5

Award amount
$2 million–$3 million

Cost sharing
Not required

Deadline
September 10, 2026

Application deadline time
11:59 p.m. Eastern Time

Project duration
Up to 27 months

Application platform
Grants.gov

Opportunity type
Discretionary

The opportunity was posted on August 11, 2026, and the current announcement lists September 10, 2026 as the closing date.

What Is the Fostering the Future Together Grant?

The Fostering the Future Together (FTFT) initiative is designed to support international projects addressing challenges affecting children and young people in the digital era.

The U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of International Labor Affairs is making approximately $15 million available for five cooperative agreements. The projects are intended to support the FTFT global coalition’s goals related to:

Child well-being

Online child protection

Positive youth development

Prevention of child labor

Prevention of online exploitation

Access to quality education

Digital skills development

Safe pathways into employment

Apprenticeships and skills training

Strengthening government capacity

Collaboration with the private sector

The full FOA indicates that projects are expected to operate internationally and complement or build upon relevant country commitments under the Fostering the Future Together global coalition.

What Will the Funding Support?

The funding is intended for projects that address interconnected challenges facing children and youth, particularly the risks associated with digital technologies, child labor, exploitation, education, and transitions into employment.

According to the FOA, proposed projects should focus on several major areas.

1. Expanding Access to Quality Education

Organizations may develop projects designed to connect children who are at risk of or have withdrawn from education with quality education opportunities and technology-enabled learning.

The objective is to help vulnerable children access educational opportunities that can support their development and future prospects.

Projects should consider the specific circumstances of the country where they will operate and demonstrate how proposed activities respond to local needs.

2. Connecting Youth With Skills and Apprenticeships

Another major focus is connecting young people of legal working age with safe, market-relevant apprenticeship and skills-training opportunities.

The program particularly emphasizes:

Digital skills

Workforce preparation

Apprenticeships

Dignified employment

Market-relevant training

Technology-enabled learning

Introduction of America EdTech tools and training

The objective is to help young people develop skills that can improve their employment prospects while ensuring that pathways into work are safe and appropriate.

3. Protecting Children From Online Exploitation

The opportunity also focuses heavily on online safety.

Funded projects may develop and implement:

Child-centered online safety protocols

Online safety tools

Training modules

Educational resources

Awareness initiatives

Protection mechanisms

These interventions are expected to address risks including online exploitation, predatory practices, and the recruitment or involvement of children in harmful labor activities through digital platforms.

The FOA specifically highlights the importance of developing resources for educators, parents, and children.

4. Strengthening Government Capacity

The program recognizes that preventing child labor and online exploitation requires strong national and local institutions.

Projects may therefore work with governments to strengthen their capacity to:

Prevent online exploitation

Enforce child labor laws

Respond to emerging digital threats

Protect children and young people

Improve relevant systems and policies

This makes government engagement an important component for organizations developing their project proposals.

5. Working With the Private Sector

The funding opportunity also encourages partnerships with private-sector stakeholders.

These partnerships can help develop sustainable, market-driven solutions addressing child labor and online exploitation risks.

Applicants should therefore consider whether businesses, technology companies, educational organizations, employers, or other private-sector actors can contribute meaningfully to their proposed intervention.

Learn More Here

Where Will Projects Be Implemented?

The funding is intended for international implementation.

The FOA states that up to $15 million will support projects implemented in five countries, with at least one project in each of the following regions:

Africa

Asia

Latin America and the Caribbean

The project must comply with the FOA’s country eligibility and geographic requirements. Applicants should therefore consult the full announcement carefully before selecting a proposed implementation country.

This means that organizations should not assume that every country worldwide is automatically eligible.

The geographic focus must correspond with the countries and requirements specified in the official FOA.

Who Can Apply?

The funding opportunity is designed for organizations rather than individual applicants.

The eligibility information published by Simpler.Grants.gov states that eligible applicants may include:

Commercial organizations

International organizations

Educational institutions

Non-profit organizations

Faith-based organizations

Community-based organizations

Public international organizations (PIOs)

Faith-based organizations are specifically encouraged to apply.

The Department of Labor also states that it will not discriminate in the selection or administration of awards based on an organization’s religious character, affiliation, exercise, or lack thereof, where the organization is otherwise similarly situated to eligible secular organizations.

Important Eligibility Point

Although the public eligibility summary identifies broad categories of organizations, applicants must satisfy all applicable requirements in the full FOA, including country, project, partnership, and technical requirements.

Organizations should therefore not rely solely on the short eligibility summary when determining whether they qualify.

International and U.S. Organizations Can Apply

The eligibility structure is broader than many U.S.-only government funding opportunities.

The published eligibility information includes international organizations and non-U.S. organizations, in addition to U.S.-based entities.

Therefore, eligible organizations from Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the United States, and other relevant locations may potentially participate, subject to the specific country and project requirements of the FOA.

This is particularly significant for organizations already working on:

Child protection

Digital safety

Youth development

Education

Child labor prevention

Workforce development

Digital skills

Online exploitation

Public policy

Labor rights

Letter of Support Requirement

One of the important requirements identified in the FOA is that applicants must obtain a letter of support from the relevant country’s Office of the First Spouse or an appropriate designee.

An appropriate designee may include institutions such as:

The Foreign Ministry

The Ministry of Labor

Another designated government authority

This requirement means organizations should not wait until the final days before the deadline to begin preparing their government engagement and supporting documentation.

Applicants should review the full FOA for the exact requirements concerning the letter and the relevant government authority in the proposed implementation country.

Project Duration

The FOA anticipates a project period of up to 27 months from the award date.

Applicants may propose a shorter implementation period if that better aligns with their strategy and project design.

A strong proposal should therefore demonstrate how activities can be realistically implemented, monitored, and evaluated within the proposed period.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The program has an estimated total funding pool of:

$15,000,000

The Department expects to make:

5 awards

Each award is expected to fall within the range of:

Minimum: $2,000,000

Maximum: $3,000,000

No cost-sharing or matching contribution is required according to the funding announcement.

This makes the opportunity particularly significant for organizations capable of implementing large-scale international projects.

What Is a Cooperative Agreement?

The funding instrument is a cooperative agreement, rather than a conventional grant.

A cooperative agreement generally involves substantial involvement by the awarding federal agency during the implementation of the funded project.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to work closely with the U.S. Department of Labor and comply with applicable federal requirements throughout the project.

Key Program Themes

Organizations considering an application should ensure that their proposed project clearly connects with the central objectives of the funding opportunity.

Key themes include:

Child Well-Being

Projects should contribute to improving children’s safety, development, education, or overall well-being.

Online Safety

Projects should address the growing risks children face through digital platforms and online environments.

Child Labor Prevention

Proposals should contribute to preventing child labor and addressing factors that place children at risk of exploitation.

Positive Youth Development

Projects should help young people build skills, resilience, opportunities, and pathways toward productive futures.

Digital Skills

The opportunity places particular importance on preparing youth for a rapidly changing digital economy.

Safe Employment

Young people of legal working age should be connected to safe and dignified employment pathways.

Government Capacity

Projects should contribute to stronger systems for addressing child labor and emerging online threats.

Private-Sector Partnerships

Organizations are encouraged to engage private-sector actors to support sustainable solutions.

Why This Opportunity Matters

The digital transformation of society has created significant opportunities for children and young people, but it has also introduced new forms of vulnerability.

Children can encounter exploitation, predatory behavior, harmful content, recruitment into labor, and other risks through online platforms.

At the same time, young people need relevant skills to participate successfully in modern labor markets.

The Fostering the Future Together opportunity attempts to address these challenges through an integrated approach combining:

Education;

Digital safety;

Child protection;

Skills development;

Apprenticeships;

Government capacity;

Private-sector collaboration; and

Prevention of child labor and exploitation.

This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to organizations working across multiple sectors rather than only traditional labor-focused organizations.

Learn More HERE

Potentially Relevant Organizations

Organizations whose existing work aligns with the program may include:

Child protection organizations

Youth development organizations

Education-focused nonprofits

Digital literacy organizations

Technology organizations

Community-based organizations

Faith-based organizations

Labor rights organizations

Workforce development organizations

International development organizations

Research and policy institutions

Educational institutions

Public international organizations

Organizations working on online safety

Organizations addressing child labor

Organizations supporting vulnerable children and youth

Eligibility, however, depends on the full requirements of the FOA and the proposed project.

What a Strong Project Proposal Should Demonstrate

Given the scale of the funding, applicants should develop proposals that are specific, measurable, realistic, and closely aligned with the FOA.

A competitive proposal should clearly explain:

1. The Problem

What specific child, youth, labor, education, or online safety problem exists in the proposed country?

2. The Target Population

Who will benefit from the intervention?

This could include children, adolescents, youth of legal working age, educators, parents, government officials, employers, or other stakeholders.

3. The Proposed Solution

What will the organization actually do to address the identified problem?

4. The Country Context

Why are the proposed activities appropriate for the selected country?

5. Government Alignment

How does the project complement existing national priorities and the country’s commitments under the Fostering the Future Together global coalition?

6. Partnerships

Which government, private-sector, educational, community, or international partners will participate?

7. Measurable Results

What specific outcomes will be achieved, and how will progress be measured?

8. Sustainability

How will the project’s impact continue beyond the period of federal funding?

Application Requirements

The full FOA requires a substantial application package.

According to the available FOA summary, applications include a detailed technical proposal of up to 50 pages, addressing areas such as:

Project design

Milestones

Targets

Monitoring and evaluation

Work plans

Organizational capacity

Key personnel

Management plans

Applicants must also provide detailed cost proposals using the applicable SF-424 family of forms.

Because this is a multi-million-dollar cooperative agreement, organizations should allow sufficient time to prepare the technical and financial components.

No Matching Requirement

A significant advantage of this funding opportunity is that cost sharing or matching is not required.

Applicants therefore do not have to provide a mandatory matching contribution as a condition of applying.

Nevertheless, applicants should prepare a realistic and well-justified budget that demonstrates responsible use of federal funds.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

September 10, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applications must be submitted electronically by the stated deadline.

Organizations should not wait until the final day because preparing a large technical proposal, securing required supporting documentation, completing federal forms, and submitting through Grants.gov can require significant time.

The Department of Labor’s FOA indicates that award decisions are expected between September 30, 2026, and December 31, 2026, although this timeframe may change.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted electronically through grants.gov in response to funding opportunity number:

FOA-ILAB-26-43

Applicants should:

Review the complete Funding Opportunity Announcement.

Confirm that their organization meets the eligibility requirements.

Confirm that their proposed country is eligible.

Review the programmatic priorities.

Develop a project that directly responds to the FOA.

Identify appropriate government and implementation partners.

Obtain the required letter of support.

Prepare the technical proposal.

Prepare the monitoring and evaluation components.

Develop the required work plan.

Prepare the organizational capacity and key personnel sections.

Complete the required federal application forms.

Develop the detailed cost proposal.

Review all requirements for completeness.

Submit the application electronically through Grants.gov before the deadline.

Applicants should use the official funding announcement and its attachments as the authoritative source for all application requirements.

Important Documents

The funding opportunity provides supporting documents that applicants should review carefully.

These include:

FOA-ILAB-26-43_FTFT.pdf — the primary Funding Opportunity Announcement.

Financial System Risk Assessment Form — a required supporting financial document where applicable.

The official opportunity page also provides access to updates and the Grants.gov application system.

Contact Information

Questions regarding the Funding Opportunity Announcement may be directed to the Bureau of International Labor Affairs.

Email: OGM_ILAB@dol.gov

Applicants should review the FOA for instructions concerning the submission of technical questions and applicable deadlines for questions.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Organizations should pay particular attention to several issues.

This Is Not an Individual Grant

The funding is intended for organizations capable of designing and implementing substantial international projects.

Country Eligibility Matters

An organization cannot simply choose any country. The proposed project must meet the geographic requirements of the FOA.

Government Support Is Important

Applicants must secure the required letter of support from the relevant country’s Office of the First Spouse or appropriate government designee.

The Proposal Is Substantial

The application requires extensive technical and financial information. Organizations should begin preparing well before the deadline.

Alignment Is Essential

A project should directly respond to the objectives of the Fostering the Future Together initiative rather than simply being a general youth-development project.

Partnerships Can Strengthen Implementation

Organizations should consider relevant government, educational, private-sector, and community partners that can contribute to successful implementation.

Visit HERE for more information about the Fostering the Future Together: $15 Million U.S. Grant Opportunity.

Conclusion

The Fostering the Future Together: Empowering Youth for a Safe Digital World funding opportunity provides approximately $15 million for projects addressing child well-being, online safety, child labor, education, digital skills, youth development, and safe pathways to employment.

The U.S. Department of Labor expects to make five cooperative agreements, with individual awards ranging from $2 million to $3 million. Projects may operate for up to 27 months, and no cost-sharing requirement applies.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations working in child protection, education, youth development, digital safety, workforce development, labor rights, technology, and international development. It also provides an opportunity for organizations to collaborate with governments and private-sector stakeholders to address emerging challenges facing children and young people in the digital age.

Eligible organizations should carefully review the complete Funding Opportunity Announcement, confirm the eligibility of their proposed country and project, secure the required government support, and prepare a strong technical and financial application.

Application deadline: September 10, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Official application platform: Grants.gov — Fostering the Future Together funding opportunity
