Course Name: Water Catchment Management

Duration: 6 weeks

Target group:

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

Water resources are under increasing stress from growing populations, intensification of agriculture, and climate change. Catchment management is vital to water use permitting, setting allocation limits, defining permissible loads and environmental impacts, and making water-sharing strategies. To achieve holistic integrated catchment management, water managers and planners must address groundwater and surface water interaction as well as the impact of land use and climate change on water resources. This thematic course will aim to enable participants to address suitable holistic integrated catchment management. The course focuses on the challenges of surface water and groundwater resources management at the catchment scale, as well as managing competing uses and environmental impacts. Catchment hydrology and its implications on water management are discussed. Decision support tools and modelling tools are introduced through examples and project cases.

Area of Physics

Astrophysics (Instrumentation/Observation/Experiment)

Research Interests

Rohan Naidu is broadly interested in the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang. His research addresses when these galaxies emerged to illuminate the universe, how they ionized the intergalactic reservoirs of hydrogen, and how they synthesized the elements that would one day seed life on Earth.

Rohan pursues these galaxies with a near-and-far approach. As one of the first users of NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, he is leading direct studies of galaxies at the highest redshifts.

And through archaeological studies of our own galaxy, aided by ESA’s Gaia satellite, he has excavated some of the most ancient systems that lie buried within the Milky Way.

Biographical Sketch

Rohan grew up in Hyderabad, India. In a Bollywood-esque plot twist, at age 18 he dropped out of engineering school, bought his first-ever plane ticket, and joined the founding class of 150 students at Yale-NUS College, Singapore.

He discovered the joys of astronomy studying blazars in the Chilean Andes with Prof. Charles Bailyn and as an exchange student with Dr. Iva Momcheva and Prof. Pascal Oesch in the van Dokkum group at Yale.

For his Ph.D. thesis supervised by Prof. Charlie Conroy at Harvard, Rohan surveyed the Milky Way’s farthest reaches to excavate ancient, immigrant galaxies that have been assimilated by our galaxy as a core member of the H3 Survey.

Outside astronomy, Rohan is a quiz-bowl/trivia enthusiast, published poet, and is always down to watch test cricket.

Since 1974, the European Science Foundation (ESF) has cultivated a strong network of international academics, science policy experts, and key stakeholders across the European and global research landscape. TITLE: Kehang Bai, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Kehang Bai
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2026-2029
Email: kehangbai@gmail.com
Phone: TBA
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, 4-304
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Experimental Particle Physics

Research Interests

Kehang Bai is an experimental particle physicist who seeks to discover new fundamental particles and forces at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The LHC collides protons with the highest energies ever achieved in terrestrial experiments, recreating particle interactions from the first picosecond of the universe’s existence. Data from these collisions may reveal answers to some of the deepest questions about the fundamental laws of nature and uncover rare phenomena beyond the Standard Model of particle physics.

With the ATLAS experiment, Kehang specializes in searching for unconventional signatures from hidden-sector physics using novel analysis techniques. She initiated and led the first ATLAS search for low-mass, long-lived dark photons with displaced vertices in the silicon tracker. She also developed weakly supervised learning methods to identify semi-visible jets from strongly interacting hidden sectors. Moving forward, she aims to study the Higgs boson as a portal to new physics by measuring its fundamental properties at the CMS experiment.

Kehang’s research also focuses on instrumentation, with expertise in front-end electronics and track reconstruction using silicon detectors. She contributed to the operation and ongoing upgrade of the ATLAS pixel detector. She is currently interested in advancing silicon tracking detector technology through continued work on High-Luminosity LHC upgrades and targeted R&D efforts to enable future discoveries.

Biographical Sketch

Kehang (可航), whose name in Chinese means “able to voyage”, grew up in Inner Mongolia, China, and has followed her curiosity across the world in the pursuit of fundamental science. She received a B.Sc. in Physics from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in 2020 and began her Ph.D. at the University of Oregon under the supervision of Prof. Laura Jeanty. During her Ph.D., she was an affiliate at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, contributing to the ATLAS Inner Tracker upgrade for the High-Luminosity LHC and designing state-of-the-art machine learning applications for particle physics. She subsequently continued her work at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland, leading a team of 20 researchers to search for unconventional dark sector signatures and serving as Run Manager for ATLAS Pixel detector operations.

Selected Publications

Kehang Bai, Radha Mastandrea, and Benjamin Nachman. “Non-resonant anomaly detection with background extrapolation”. JHEP 04 (2024) 059. arXiv: 2311.12924.

ATLAS Collaboration. “A search for R-parity-violating supersymmetry in final states containing many jets in pp collisions at √s = 13 TeV with the ATLAS detector”. JHEP 05 (2024) 003. arXiv: 2401.16333.

Chiara Arina et al. “t-channel dark matter models – a whitepaper”. Eur.Phys.J.C 85 (2025) 975. arXiv: 2504.10597.

TITLE: UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo 2026/2027: Business Bootcamps, Mentorship, Investment Pitching and Networking for Women Entrepreneurs in Europe and Central Asia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo 2026/2027 is bringing together women entrepreneurs and business partners from Europe and Central Asia for a regional platform focused on entrepreneurship development, business networking, capacity building, mentorship and investment readiness.

The Expo is designed around the principles of inclusivity, diversity and leaving no one behind. It will combine local and interregional business-building activities, networking opportunities and capacity-building workshops, giving women entrepreneurs the opportunity to strengthen their businesses, connect with peers and business partners, receive expert support and prepare for potential investment opportunities.

The programme will culminate in Expo Capital Quest, a physical event planned for Spring 2027, where selected participants will have the opportunity to take part in networking and investor pitching, subject to an additional selection process.

What Is the UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo 2026/2027?

The UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo 2026/2027 is a regional entrepreneurship initiative designed to support women entrepreneurs and women-owned businesses in Europe and Central Asia.

Rather than being a single conference or exhibition, the Expo consists of several interconnected activities intended to help participating entrepreneurs develop their businesses and expand their networks.

The programme includes:

Local business-building activities.

Interregional networking activities.

Capacity-building workshops.

Business bootcamps.

Mentorship.

Investment-pitch preparation.

Feedback from experts.

Online business exhibition opportunities.

Networking with entrepreneurs from across the region.

Potential participation in a physical investor-focused event.

The programme is therefore particularly relevant to women entrepreneurs who are already developing a product or service and want to improve their business capabilities, visibility, networks and readiness for future growth or investment.

Key Highlights of the UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo

The Expo provides women entrepreneurs with access to several forms of business development support.

Main opportunities include:

Online business exhibition: Participants can showcase their businesses through an online exhibition space.

Business bootcamps: Selected entrepreneurs will have the opportunity to participate in bootcamps managed by leading companies.

Mentorship: Participants can receive support and guidance from mentors.

Investment preparation: Entrepreneurs can prepare their investment pitches and receive feedback.

Regional networking: Participants can connect with entrepreneurs and peers from countries across Europe and Central Asia.

Expo Capital Quest: Selected participants may take part in a physical event in Spring 2027 focused on networking and investor pitching.

Who Is the UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo For?

The Expo is primarily intended for women entrepreneurs and representatives of women-owned businesses.

The programme is open to women entrepreneurs working across all sectors of the economy.

Applicants are expected to provide information about themselves and their businesses, including their business ownership, location, business development stage, sector, online presence, revenue, financing history, business challenges, training needs and future growth plans.

This means the application process is designed not simply to collect basic registration information but also to help the Expo organisers understand each entrepreneur’s business needs and tailor the programme’s content accordingly.

Business Stage Requirements

One of the most important aspects of the Expo is the stage of business development.

The programme states that, to be eligible for all phases of the Expo, a woman entrepreneur or representative of a women-owned business should be at one of the following stages:

Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

Early Stage, where the business is already selling

Growth Stage, where the business is generating revenue

These stages indicate that the Expo is particularly focused on entrepreneurs who have moved beyond the purely conceptual stage and have something tangible to develop, sell or scale.

However, the application questionnaire also allows applicants to identify themselves as being at:

Idea Stage

Working on Prototype

Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

Early Stage

Growth Stage

Not applicable

The form explains that entrepreneurs who meet the applicable criteria can participate in the virtual Expo capacity-development and networking component, while virtual booths will be allocated to entrepreneurs who already have an MVP, are already selling, or are at the Growth Stage.

This distinction is important for applicants because being at an earlier stage may affect the specific elements of the Expo in which they can participate.

Countries Eligible for the UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo

The Expo focuses on Europe and Central Asia.

The application form specifically lists the following countries:

Albania

Armenia

Azerbaijan

Bosnia and Herzegovina

Georgia

Kazakhstan

Kosovo (under UNSCR 1244)

Kyrgyzstan

Moldova

Montenegro

Türkiye

Ukraine

The questionnaire also includes an “Other” option for the country where the applicant’s company is registered or operating.

The programme description refers to networking with peers from 12 countries of Europe and Central Asia, while the application questionnaire itself lists 15 named countries plus an “Other” option. Applicants should therefore carefully provide their actual country and business location when completing the form.

Learn More HERE.

Business Sectors Eligible for the Expo

Women entrepreneurs from all sectors of the economy can apply for participation in the Expo.

The application form provides a broad list of sectors, including:

Agriculture

Building and construction

Media and communication

ICT and telecommunications

Training and education

Clothing, fashion and textiles

Trade, transport and logistics

Healthcare

Tourism and hospitality

Finance

Water, sanitation and waste management

Energy

Food products

Retail

Sports

Jewellery and accessories

Environment

Paper products

Electronics

Other sectors

This broad sectoral approach means that the Expo is not restricted to technology startups or a single industry. Women building businesses in traditional industries as well as innovative, technology-driven and sustainability-focused sectors can potentially benefit.

UN Women also states that it reserves the right to exclude certain products from the Expo following careful consideration.

Benefits of Participating in the UN Women Entrepreneurship Expo

1. Showcase Your Business Online

Participants can showcase their businesses through an online exhibition space.

This provides entrepreneurs with an opportunity to increase the visibility of their products or services and present their businesses to a wider network of potential partners and other stakeholders.

For entrepreneurs looking to strengthen their digital presence, the online exhibition component can be an important opportunity to communicate their value proposition and business story.

2. Participate in Business Bootcamps

Selected women entrepreneurs will be invited to participate in business bootcamps managed by leading companies.

These bootcamps are intended to support business development and help entrepreneurs strengthen practical capabilities relevant to running and growing a business.

Participation in bootcamps will vary by country, and selected participants will receive additional information from the organisers.

3. Receive Mentorship

The Expo provides opportunities for entrepreneurs to receive support from mentors.

Mentorship can be particularly valuable for entrepreneurs dealing with challenges such as business strategy, market access, financing, marketing, technology adoption, operations and growth.

The questionnaire also asks applicants about their current levels of knowledge in areas such as financial management, marketing, networking, branding, distribution, international markets and competitiveness.

This information is intended to help the organisers better understand participants’ needs.

4. Prepare an Investment Pitch

Another major benefit is the opportunity to prepare an investment pitch and receive feedback.

Investment readiness is especially relevant for entrepreneurs who want to attract capital to expand their businesses.

Applicants are asked about their business objectives, including whether they want to find investment to move to the next phase of development and whether they want to become more attractive to investors.

The Expo therefore provides a platform for entrepreneurs to improve how they communicate their business opportunity to potential investors.

5. Build Regional Business Networks

Participants will have opportunities to network with other entrepreneurs and business partners from the Europe and Central Asia region.

Networking can help entrepreneurs identify:

Potential business partners.

New buyers.

Suppliers.

Investors.

Mentors.

Industry experts.

Other entrepreneurs.

Regional and international opportunities.

For businesses seeking to expand beyond their existing market, regional networking can be particularly valuable.

Learn More HERE.

Expo Capital Quest 2027

One of the major planned components of the programme is the Expo Capital Quest, a physical event expected to take place in Spring 2027.

The event will provide opportunities for networking and investor pitching.

However, participation in Expo Capital Quest is subject to an additional selection process. Therefore, completing the initial Expo application does not automatically guarantee participation in the physical Capital Quest event.

Entrepreneurs interested in investment should therefore treat the initial application as an opportunity to demonstrate the strength and potential of their business while recognising that additional selection may apply for the Capital Quest component.

Regional Virtual Expo 2026

The Regional Virtual Expo 2026 is scheduled to take place in November 2026.

According to the programme information, this virtual component will be open to all women entrepreneurs interested.

The virtual Expo forms part of the broader regional programme and provides an opportunity for entrepreneurs to engage in online capacity development and networking.

Selected entrepreneurs may subsequently be invited to participate in country-specific bootcamps and satellite events.

Country-Specific Bootcamps and Satellite Events

The Expo is not limited to one uniform programme for every participant.

Selected women entrepreneurs will be invited to participate in Bootcamp and Satellite Events, with activities varying from country to country.

Participants who are selected for these activities will receive additional information regarding the specific opportunities available to them.

This structure allows the programme to respond to different business environments, sectors and needs across the participating countries.

What Information Do Applicants Need to Provide?

The application questionnaire is comprehensive and asks applicants to provide detailed information about themselves and their businesses.

Applicants should be prepared to provide information covering several areas.

Personal and Contact Information

The form requests:

First name

Surname

Contact phone number

Country and city, town or village

Email address

Gender

Age category

Geographic location

Applicants are asked to provide a full telephone number with the country code, and the programme indicates that having a number available on WhatsApp is preferable.

Business Ownership and Location

Applicants will be asked whether they:

Own or co-own the registered business.

Have participated in a previous Expo.

Operate or have a company registered in a particular country.

The form asks applicants to identify the country where their company is registered or operating.

Online Business Presence

Applicants are also asked whether they currently sell products or services online.

The available responses distinguish between:

Businesses that operate entirely online.

Businesses that sell some products or services online.

Businesses that do not currently sell products or services online.

This information helps the organisers understand participants’ current level of digital business activity.

Business Description

Applicants must provide a description of their company in fewer than 150 words.

The description should explain:

What the business offers.

Who the customers are.

What traction the business has achieved.

What the entrepreneur wants to accomplish through the business.

Links to any existing articles about the company, where applicable.

Entrepreneurs should therefore prepare a concise but compelling description before starting the application.

Business Size

Applicants will also be asked to indicate the size of their business:

Solo entrepreneur or micro business: 1–10 employees

Small business: 11–50 employees

Medium business: 51–250 employees

This enables the organisers to understand the scale of participating enterprises.

Annual Business Revenue

Applicants are asked to identify their approximate average annual revenue in US dollars.

The available categories are:

Less than US$50,000

US$50,000–100,000

US$100,000–500,000

More than US$500,000

This information can help the programme assess the different stages and financial profiles of participating businesses.

Business Challenges

Applicants are asked to identify up to three of the biggest challenges they experienced when starting their businesses.

Potential challenges include:

Accessing financing

Getting support from family

Finding a suitable business location

Finding information about starting a business

Registration and regulatory requirements

Other challenges

This section is particularly relevant because it allows the Expo organisers to identify common barriers facing women entrepreneurs and tailor support accordingly.

Possible sources include:

No trade fairs or exhibitions

Previous Training and Business Support

Connect with other women entrepreneurs.

TITLE: Max Planck Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships 2027 in Germany: Up to 4 Months of Funded Support for Final-Stage PhD Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships 2027, offering doctoral candidates in the final stage of their PhD an opportunity to spend up to four months at the Institute in Halle (Saale), Germany, while completing their dissertations.

The fellowships are offered by the Law & Anthropology Department of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology and are designed specifically for advanced doctoral researchers who are close to completing their manuscripts and whose research is directly relevant to the Department’s academic programme.

For the 2027 cycle, fellows may choose between two possible residency periods:

Spring 2027: March 1 to June 30, 2027

Fall 2027: September 1 to December 31, 2027

The fellowship may be awarded for a maximum of four months.

Successful candidates will receive a monthly living stipend from the Institute. According to the announcement, the stipend is not taxable and is free of social security obligations. The exact stipend amount is not specified in the information provided.

While applicants from relevant disciplinary backgrounds may be considered, the call explicitly states that priority will be given to candidates pursuing PhDs in anthropology.

The application deadline is September 15, 2026.

About the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology

The Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, located in Halle (Saale), Germany, is an internationally recognized research institution specializing in social anthropology.

Research at the Institute is broadly concerned with the comparative analysis of social change.

Across its different programmes and projects, researchers investigate changing social relations, institutions, legal systems, political arrangements, cultural practices and economic structures.

The Institute’s research contributes to anthropological theory while frequently engaging with questions that have significant practical, political and policy relevance.

Its institutional setting provides doctoral and postdoctoral researchers with access to:

An international scholarly community

Research seminars

Academic discussions

Specialized expertise

Institutional resources

Interdisciplinary exchange

Research networks

For doctoral candidates finishing their dissertations, a short period of concentrated residence at the Institute can provide valuable time, intellectual engagement and access to a highly specialized research environment.

About the Law & Anthropology Department

The fellowships are offered specifically by the Law & Anthropology Department of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology.

The Department operates as an interdisciplinary space connecting:

Social anthropology

Legal anthropology

Law

Socio-legal studies

Related interdisciplinary fields

Its research is particularly concerned with the interactions among legal systems, communities, institutions and societies.

The Department seeks to create a setting in which anthropologists and legal scholars can engage with one another and undertake research with both scholarly and policy relevance.

Law, Society and Increasing Legal Pluralism

One major intellectual concern of the Department is the increasing intensity of encounters between:

Different legal systems

National legal frameworks

Communities

Institutions

Social groups

Forms of normative ordering

Contemporary societies are frequently characterized by overlapping legal systems and normative frameworks.

These interactions can become especially visible in areas involving:

Migration

Religious law

Family law

International law

Customary law

Minority rights

Citizenship

Human rights

Transnational communities

Legal pluralism

The Department is interested in research that helps explain these complex interactions empirically and theoretically.

Empirically Grounded and Ethnographic Research

The call emphasizes a growing demand for empirically grounded knowledge, particularly ethnographic research, about contemporary legal and social processes.

Anthropological research can make important contributions because it examines not only what laws formally say, but how legal rules, institutions and normative expectations are actually experienced, interpreted and negotiated in everyday life.

The Department is therefore particularly interested in research capable of connecting empirical findings with broader questions of:

Law

Policy

Governance

Rights

Social transformation

Institutional decision-making

Translating Empirical Knowledge into Normative Thinking

A central concern of the Law & Anthropology Department is the challenge of translating empirically grounded research into forms of knowledge that can contribute to normative thinking and decision-making.

The Department recognizes that anthropological findings and legal reasoning operate through different intellectual traditions.

Nevertheless, there is growing demand for scholars who can help connect detailed empirical understanding with discussions occurring within:

Policymaking

Law

Courts

Governance institutions

Civil society

International organizations

Public debate

The Department therefore prioritizes research addressing this demand for translation, particularly within an increasingly plural European context.

Applicants should carefully consider how their dissertation relates to this broader research agenda before applying.

What Are the Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships?

The fellowships are designed for doctoral researchers who have already completed most of their PhD research and are now working toward the finalization of the dissertation manuscript.

They are not intended primarily to support:

Beginning-stage doctoral students

Major new fieldwork

Initial research design

Extensive new data collection

Instead, the fellowship provides advanced doctoral candidates with a temporary academic base where they can focus on writing and completing their dissertations.

The call specifically states that candidates should be in the final stage of their doctoral programme.

Fellowship Duration

Each fellowship may last for:

Up to four months

Applicants can choose between two fellowship periods.

Spring Fellowship Period

March 1 to June 30, 2027

This option may be particularly suitable for candidates expecting to complete their dissertations during the first half of 2027.

Fall Fellowship Period

September 1 to December 31, 2027

This provides a second opportunity for researchers whose dissertation schedules align better with the latter part of the year.

The maximum duration remains four months.

Financial Support

Successful candidates will receive a:

Monthly living stipend

The Institute states that the stipend is:

Not taxable

Free of social security obligations

The specific monthly amount is not stated in the information provided.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming a particular stipend value unless the Institute provides one directly through the application system or subsequent correspondence.

What Fellows Are Expected to Do

Although the principal purpose of the fellowship is dissertation completion, fellows are expected to engage actively with the Department during their residency.

The fellowship is therefore not simply a private writing grant.

Selected doctoral researchers should be prepared to:

Work intensively on completing their dissertation

Participate in Law & Anthropology Department activities

Contribute a working paper

Present their doctoral research

Engage with the Department’s scholarly community

Participation in Department Activities

Fellows are expected to take part in activities organized by the Law & Anthropology Department during their fellowship period.

These may provide opportunities to interact with:

Senior researchers

Visiting scholars

Postdoctoral researchers

Doctoral researchers

Anthropologists

Legal scholars

Participation can help fellows receive intellectual feedback and situate their own research within broader interdisciplinary conversations.

Working Paper Requirement

Successful fellows are expected to submit:

A working paper addressing the topic of their research

This requirement demonstrates that the fellowship involves active academic contribution in addition to dissertation writing.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to develop part of their dissertation research into a form suitable for circulation as a departmental working paper.

Research Presentation

Each fellow will also present their doctoral research as part of the Department’s:

Seminar series

This offers an opportunity to:

Present findings

Receive feedback

Discuss methodology

Refine arguments

Engage with scholars from different disciplinary traditions

Strengthen the final dissertation manuscript

Applicants should therefore be comfortable discussing their research in an interdisciplinary academic setting.

Relationship With the Home University

One particularly important requirement concerns coordination between the Max Planck Institute and the candidate’s existing doctoral institution.

Before the fellowship begins, a clear understanding must be reached between the Director of the Law & Anthropology Department and the candidate’s principal doctoral supervisor.

The purpose is to determine:

How the candidate can make the fullest possible use of the writing period

How the home university and Max Planck Institute can cooperate

How the fellowship can contribute effectively to dissertation completion

How the arrangement can benefit both institutions and the candidate

This is important because the fellowship does not replace the candidate’s existing doctoral supervision.

The researcher remains embedded in their home doctoral programme while spending a temporary period at the Max Planck Institute.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is intended for advanced doctoral candidates.

Applicants should normally:

Be enrolled in a doctoral programme

Be in the final stage of the PhD

Be sufficiently advanced to complete or substantially finalize the manuscript during the fellowship

Have a dissertation topic immediately relevant to the Law & Anthropology Department’s research programme

Be able to spend up to four months at the Institute in Halle (Saale)

Be willing to participate in departmental activities

Be prepared to submit a working paper

Be able to present their doctoral research during the Department seminar series

Priority for Anthropology PhD Candidates

For the 2027 call, the Department explicitly states that:

Priority will be given to applicants working toward PhDs in anthropology.

This does not necessarily mean that every applicant must be formally enrolled in an anthropology department.

However, candidates whose projects are strongly grounded in anthropology, social anthropology or legal anthropology are likely to have the closest alignment with the call.

Applicants from adjacent fields should make the anthropological or interdisciplinary relevance of their work especially clear.

Research Fit Is Essential

The candidate’s dissertation topic must be of immediate relevance to the Department’s research programme.

This is a central requirement.

Applicants should therefore avoid treating the fellowship as a general dissertation-writing opportunity available for any PhD topic.

Before applying, candidates should review the research agenda of the Max Planck Institute and, in particular, the activities and publications associated with the Law & Anthropology Department.

A competitive applicant should be able to explain:

How their dissertation connects to law and anthropology

Why their research would benefit from the Department’s expertise

What they could contribute to Department discussions

Why a residency at the Institute is intellectually appropriate

Examples of Potentially Relevant Research Themes

The call itself does not provide an exhaustive list of acceptable dissertation topics.

However, research fitting the Law & Anthropology agenda may potentially engage with themes such as:

Legal pluralism

Anthropology of law

Migration and law

Human rights

Religious law

Customary law

Minority rights

Legal institutions

Citizenship

Governance

Transnational legal processes

Dispute resolution

Social change and legal systems

Empirical approaches to law

Law and community

Normative orders

Legal translation

European legal pluralism

Applicants should not assume that every topic in this list is automatically eligible. The central requirement remains direct relevance to the Department’s current research programme.

Application Materials

Applicants must prepare several documents.

1. Cover Letter

A cover letter is required.

A strong cover letter should explain:

Current doctoral status

Dissertation topic

Progress toward completion

Why the Max Planck Institute is an appropriate environment

How the research fits the Law & Anthropology Department

Which fellowship period is preferred

What the applicant hopes to achieve during the residency

The letter should make clear that the candidate is sufficiently advanced to benefit from a writing-up fellowship rather than still being in an exploratory research stage.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit an academic CV.

The CV should clearly present:

Education

Doctoral programme

Research experience

Publications

Conference presentations

Teaching where relevant

Research projects

Grants and awards

Relevant methodological skills

Candidates should make their anthropological and law-related experience easy to identify.

3. Dissertation Writing Sample

Applicants must submit:

A chapter of the PhD dissertation

This document gives reviewers direct evidence of:

Academic writing ability

Research quality

Theoretical sophistication

Methodological competence

Dissertation progress

Applicants should choose a chapter that best represents the quality and relevance of their doctoral research.

4. One-to-Two-Page Dissertation Summary

Candidates must submit a:

1–2 page summary of the PhD work

This summary should provide reviewers with a concise overview of the dissertation.

It should ideally explain:

Central research question

Research context

Theoretical framework

Methodology

Main argument

Findings or emerging findings

Contribution to the field

Relevance to the Department

Because reviewers will use this summary to understand the entire project quickly, clarity is especially important.

5. University Degrees and Transcripts

Applicants must provide photocopies of:

University degree certificates

Academic transcripts

These documents allow the selection committee to verify academic qualifications and background.

6. Supervisor Recommendation Letter

A recommendation letter from the candidate’s:

Principal doctoral supervisor

is mandatory.

The supervisor must specifically confirm that the applicant is:

Advanced enough to finalize the doctoral manuscript within the period financed by the Law & Anthropology Department.

This is an important requirement because it directly verifies that the applicant has reached the appropriate dissertation stage.

How the Recommendation Must Be Submitted

The supervisor recommendation should be sent directly to the Department, rather than simply uploaded by the applicant.

The specified email address is:

marencakova@eth.mpg.de

Candidates should contact their supervisors well before the application deadline so the recommendation can be prepared and submitted on time.

Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, candidates should make sure they have prepared:

Cover letter

Curriculum vitae

Dissertation chapter as writing sample

One-to-two-page dissertation summary

Copies of university degrees

Academic transcripts

Supervisor recommendation letter sent directly to the Department

Applicants should also ensure that their proposed research clearly fits the Law & Anthropology Department’s research agenda.

How to Apply

Application materials must be submitted electronically through the Max Planck Institute’s official vacancy and recruitment system.

Applicants can access vacancies through the Institute’s Career section or use the recruitment platform indicated in the call.

More information:
https://lnkd.in/dim6R52d

Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology:
http://www.eth.mpg.de

Candidates should use the official online application system rather than sending the complete application directly by email unless specifically instructed otherwise.

APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

September 15, 2026

Applicants should ensure that both their own application materials and the supervisor recommendation are arranged well ahead of this date.

Fellowship Timeline

The two possible fellowship periods are:

Spring 2027

March 1–June 30, 2027

Fall 2027

September 1–December 31, 2027

Each award can last for a maximum of four months.

Contact for Application Questions

Questions concerning the application process can be directed to:

Carolin Klevenow
Human Resources Management

klevenow@eth.mpg.de

Applicants with administrative questions should use this contact rather than relying on unofficial information.

Gender Equality and Diversity

The Max Planck Society states that it strives to ensure:

Gender equality

Diversity

Applicants from eligible backgrounds are therefore encouraged to consider the fellowship where their academic profile and dissertation topic match the programme.

The supplied call does not state any gender-specific application restriction.

Why This Fellowship Can Be Valuable

Completing a dissertation can be one of the most demanding phases of doctoral study.

By the final stage, researchers may already have:

Completed fieldwork

Gathered data

Conducted archival research

Finished major analysis

Drafted several chapters

Yet transforming these components into a coherent final manuscript requires sustained concentration.

A dedicated writing fellowship can provide:

Protected writing time

Distance from routine obligations

Access to scholarly resources

New intellectual feedback

Engagement with specialists

Structured deadlines

The Max Planck fellowship is especially valuable because it combines concentrated dissertation writing with integration into an internationally recognized research environment.

Benefits of Spending the Fellowship at the Max Planck Institute

Successful fellows will have the opportunity to use Institute resources while finalizing their dissertations.

The intellectual environment may help candidates:

Strengthen theoretical arguments

Refine chapters

Receive interdisciplinary feedback

Develop future publications

Build international scholarly connections

Prepare for postdoctoral or academic careers

The requirement to present research and prepare a working paper can also help fellows transform dissertation material into future scholarly outputs.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Demonstrate That You Are Truly at the Writing-Up Stage

This is perhaps the most important consideration.

The fellowship is not aimed at students who still need extensive data collection or major fieldwork.

Applicants should clearly show:

What chapters are already drafted

What research has been completed

What remains to be written

Why four months is sufficient to make substantial progress toward completion

The supervisor recommendation must confirm this readiness.

2. Make Your Research Fit Explicit

Do not assume that reviewers will identify your connection to the Department automatically.

Clearly explain how your dissertation relates to:

Law

Anthropology

Legal systems

Social change

Legal pluralism

Translation between empirical and normative knowledge

where applicable.

3. Explain Why Max Planck Is Necessary

A strong application should communicate why spending four months in Halle would materially improve the dissertation.

Possible reasons might include:

Relevant faculty expertise

Departmental research themes

Interdisciplinary exchange

Research resources

Seminar participation

Use reasons specific to your own project.

4. Select Your Writing Sample Carefully

The dissertation chapter should showcase your strongest research and writing.

Ideally, it should also demonstrate a close relationship with the Law & Anthropology Department’s intellectual agenda.

5. Keep the Dissertation Summary Focused

In only one or two pages, explain:

The problem

The question

The method

The argument

The contribution

Avoid using too much space on general background.

6. Contact Your Supervisor Early

Your principal supervisor must submit the recommendation directly.

Give them sufficient time and clearly explain what the letter must confirm.

Important Details at a Glance

Host institution: Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology

Department: Law & Anthropology Department

Location: Halle (Saale), Germany

Opportunity: Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships

Target stage: Final-stage doctoral candidates

Priority discipline: Anthropology

Maximum duration: Four months

Spring period: March 1–June 30, 2027

Fall period: September 1–December 31, 2027

Financial support: Monthly living stipend

Tax treatment: Stipend described as non-taxable and free of social security obligations

Department participation: Required

Working paper: Required

Research presentation: Required

Application deadline: September 15, 2026

Application contact: klevenow@eth.mpg.de

Supervisor recommendation: marencakova@eth.mpg.de

Conclusion

The Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology Dissertation Writing-up Fellowships 2027 provide an excellent opportunity for advanced doctoral researchers to spend up to four months in Germany concentrating on the final stages of their dissertations.

Hosted by the Institute’s Law & Anthropology Department in Halle (Saale), the fellowship is particularly relevant to researchers whose projects examine relationships between law, society, legal pluralism, social change, anthropology and related interdisciplinary questions.

For the current call, priority will be given to PhD candidates in anthropology, and applicants must be sufficiently advanced in their doctoral programme to make meaningful progress toward completing their manuscript during the funded period.

Selected fellows will receive a monthly living stipend while benefiting from the resources and intellectual environment of one of the world’s leading institutes for social anthropology.

The fellowship is not solely a private writing residency. Fellows are expected to participate actively in departmental activities, prepare a working paper and present their doctoral research through the Department’s seminar series.

Applicants can choose between a spring residency from March 1 to June 30, 2027, or a fall residency from September 1 to December 31, 2027, with funding available for a maximum of four months.

Applications require a cover letter, CV, dissertation chapter, one-to-two-page research summary, academic certificates and transcripts, as well as a recommendation from the principal doctoral supervisor confirming that the candidate is advanced enough to finalize the dissertation during the fellowship period.

TITLE: Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant 2026: $2,000 Grants for U.S. Organizations to Build Youth Leadership and Decision-Making Opportunities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant 2026 is a new funding opportunity from Youth Service America (YSA), supported by an AmeriCorps MLK Day of Service grant, designed to help organizations create or strengthen formal structures through which young people can participate in leadership, decision-making, community service, and civic engagement.

The grant will provide $2,000 to selected organizations that want to develop a new Youth Council or a similar youth leadership structure, or expand an existing one. In addition to establishing or strengthening youth leadership structures, grantees will be expected to organize a citywide, regional, or statewide Youth Leadership Summit around Martin Luther King Jr. Day and create continuing opportunities for youth voice, leadership, and decision-making through The Civic Season, from Juneteenth through July 4.

The program is particularly focused on ensuring that young people are not simply consulted occasionally but have meaningful opportunities to participate in organizational and community decision-making. YSA states that the grant program is intended to support the development or expansion of youth councils and similar structures while engaging at least 200 youth and adults in training or youth voice, leadership, and decision-making opportunities.

Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant 2026: Overview

Youth Service America is accepting applications from eligible U.S.-based organizations seeking funding to strengthen youth participation and leadership.

The opportunity is connected to the MLK Day of Service, which will take place on January 18, 2027. YSA’s MLK Day of Service campaign describes the holiday as a national day of service focused on community action, service, and honoring the legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

For this particular grant, organizations will use the funding to create or expand structures that give young people a more formal role in organizational and community decision-making.

Key details at a glance

Opportunity: Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant

Organizer: Youth Service America (YSA)

Funding: AmeriCorps MLK Day of Service grant

Grant amount: $2,000 per selected grantee

Total funding available: $50,000

Number of organizations expected to receive grants: 25

Required local match: $1,000 in cash or in-kind support

Minimum engagement requirement: 200 youth and adults

Main focus: Youth voice, leadership, decision-making, youth councils, youth leadership structures, and community service

MLK Day of Service: January 18, 2027

Application deadline: Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time

Geographic eligibility: United States organizations meeting the program’s organizational eligibility requirements

Application format: Online application

Contact: Mike Minks at mminks@ysa.org

YSA’s official MLK Day of Service page confirms that the program will award $2,000 grants, with $50,000 available overall and 25 citywide, regional, or statewide organizations expected to receive funding.

What Is the Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant?

The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant is designed around the idea that young people should have meaningful opportunities to contribute to decisions affecting their organizations and communities.

Rather than supporting only a one-time service event, the grant focuses on developing or expanding ongoing youth leadership structures. These can include Youth Councils or other formal youth leadership groups that allow young people to contribute ideas, participate in planning, advise organizations, and take part in decision-making processes.

According to YSA, grant recipients will use the funding to support the development of new Youth Councils or similar youth leadership structures, or the expansion of existing ones.

This makes the opportunity relevant to organizations that already have some youth engagement experience but want to create a more formal mechanism for youth participation, as well as organizations that are ready to establish a new youth leadership structure.

What Will Grant Recipients Be Expected to Do?

Receiving the $2,000 grant comes with specific expectations. Organizations should therefore consider whether they have the capacity to develop a youth leadership structure and sustain youth engagement beyond a single event.

1. Create or Expand a Youth Leadership Structure

Applicants will need to describe their plans for establishing or strengthening a formal youth advisory or leadership board, council, or similar group.

The application asks organizations to explain:

Their current programs and organizational work.

Their existing experience with youth engagement.

Their experience with youth voice and leadership.

Their experience involving young people in decision-making.

Whether they plan to create a new youth advisory structure or expand an existing one.

What they hope the youth leadership structure will accomplish.

How youth participation could strengthen the organization.

The emphasis is therefore not simply on recruiting young people for an event. Applicants are expected to demonstrate how youth leadership can become part of their organization’s continuing work.

2. Organize a Youth Leadership Summit Around MLK Day

Each grantee will be expected to organize a citywide or statewide Youth Leadership Summit on or around MLK Day.

YSA indicates that the Summit should be organized with the organization’s youth leadership group. The program is therefore designed to give young people an active role in shaping the event rather than having adults independently plan the entire experience.

The Summit can be scheduled between January 11 and January 25, 2027, although YSA says it should take place as close as possible to MLK Day on January 18, 2027.

The Summit should provide training connected to:

Youth-adult partnerships

Youth voice

Youth leadership

Community service project design

Future youth-led service opportunities

The 200-Person Engagement Requirement

One of the most important requirements applicants need to understand is the minimum engagement target.

Grant recipients are expected to engage at least 200 youth and adults through the Youth Leadership Summit and/or related youth voice, leadership, and decision-making opportunities.

The application specifically requires applicants to acknowledge this requirement and provide an estimate of how many youth and adults they expect to engage in relevant training or opportunities.

The goal is not simply to establish a small internal youth council. The youth leadership group should also help broaden youth participation and encourage other young people and adults to become involved.

YSA describes the program as requiring grantees to organize a Youth Leadership Summit and ongoing opportunities through The Civic Season while engaging a minimum of 200 youth and adults in commitments to future or ongoing service and related training.

Continuing Youth Engagement Through The Civic Season

The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table initiative extends beyond MLK Day.

Applicants are asked to explain how their youth leadership group could continue engaging other young people after the Summit during the remainder of the 2026–2027 academic year and through The Civic Season, from Juneteenth through July 4.

This means applicants should think about a longer-term engagement strategy rather than proposing a single event.

Potential activities described in an application could include continued youth leadership meetings, peer engagement, youth-led service projects, community conversations, leadership training, youth advisory activities, or other forms of participation that are consistent with the organization’s mission.

The key consideration is that the youth leadership group should help create opportunities for its peers as well.

Who Can Apply for the Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant?

The application identifies several types of organizations as eligible.

These include:

K-12 schools

Higher education institutions

Out-of-school-time programs

Afterschool programs

Summer learning programs

Positive youth development organizations

Community-based organizations

Faith-based organizations

State governments

Local governments

YSA’s official program information confirms these organizational categories as eligible for the Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grants.

The application form also asks organizations to provide their organization name, organization type, contact information, mailing address, state, ZIP code, and website.

Youth Representation and Inclusive Recruitment

A major part of the application concerns how an organization will recruit young people who reflect the diversity of the community it serves.

Applicants are asked to explain how they will recruit youth who are representative of their organization’s or community’s youth/student population.

The application specifically identifies groups that applicants should consider reaching, including:

Young people of color

Young people from low-income families and neighborhoods

Young people from rural areas

Youth with disabilities

Young people who are unhoused

Young people in foster care

Young people involved in the juvenile justice system

Immigrants and refugees

English Language Learners

LGBTQ+ young people

Young people from military families

Other young people who are not typically asked to participate in leadership opportunities

This component is important because the application is not simply asking organizations to create a youth council. Applicants must also explain how they will ensure that the council and related activities include young people whose perspectives may otherwise be overlooked.

What Should Organizations Explain in Their Application?

The application contains several substantive questions. Organizations should be prepared to address each area clearly and specifically.

1. Describe the Organization and Its Youth Engagement Experience

Applicants must describe their organization, current programs, and previous experience with:

Youth engagement

Youth voice

Youth leadership

Youth decision-making

This section provides an opportunity to demonstrate that the organization understands the needs of young people and has some capacity to work with them.

2. Explain the Youth Advisory or Leadership Structure

Applicants must describe their plans and goals for creating or expanding a formal youth advisory board, leadership board, council, or similar group.

The application asks organizations to explain:

What they want to establish or expand.

What they are excited about doing.

What the youth group will contribute.

How the planned actions will strengthen the organization.

A strong response should therefore connect youth leadership directly to the organization’s existing work rather than treating the youth group as a completely separate activity.

3. Explain How Youth Will Be Recruited

Organizations must describe their recruitment strategy and explain how they will reach young people who represent the broader population they serve.

This includes thinking about barriers that can prevent certain young people from participating and explaining how the organization will reach people who are traditionally underrepresented in leadership opportunities.

4. Describe the Youth Leadership Summit

Applicants must provide preliminary ideas for a citywide or statewide Youth Leadership Summit taking place on or around MLK Day.

The application emphasizes that the plans are preliminary because the event will ultimately be planned with the youth leadership group.

Applicants should also explain how they intend to provide training to at least 200 youth and adults and encourage participants to commit to future or ongoing service.

5. Explain How Youth Will Engage Their Peers

The application specifically asks organizations to consider what happens after the Summit.

Applicants should provide ideas for how members of the youth leadership group can engage other young people throughout:

The remainder of the 2026–2027 academic year

The Civic Season from Juneteenth through July 4

This requirement reinforces the program’s broader objective of expanding youth participation beyond a small leadership group.

Grant Amount and Available Funding

Each successful organization will receive a $2,000 grant.

YSA states that $50,000 in total funding is available and that 25 citywide, regional, or statewide organizations will receive grants.

The grant is funded through a federal AmeriCorps MLK Day of Service grant.

Required $1,000 Match Funding

Organizations applying for the grant must also be prepared to provide a $1,000 local match.

The match can consist of:

Cash contributions

In-kind contributions

Donated event supplies

Food

Recognition items for youth leadership group members or Summit participants

Meeting space

Event space

Equipment

Other qualifying local contributions

Applicants must indicate whether they agree to meet the matching requirement and identify potential sources of the match.

This means an organization applying for the $2,000 grant should consider how it will document an additional $1,000 in local support.

What Can the $2,000 Grant Be Used For?

The application asks applicants to submit a tentative $2,000 budget.

A full budget will be submitted later if the organization is selected and enters into a grant agreement.

However, the application clearly states that grant funds cannot be used for staff salaries and benefits.

The funds also cannot be used for AmeriCorps-prohibited activities, including:

Lobbying

Partisan political activities

Voter registration

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed budget is directly connected to allowable activities supporting youth leadership, youth voice, decision-making, training, and related program implementation.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant is:

Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time.

YSA’s official MLK Day of Service page confirms the October 25 deadline and specifies that the deadline is based on the applicant’s local time.

Organizations should not wait until the final day if they need time to develop their youth leadership plans, identify match funding, prepare the preliminary budget, and collect organizational information.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the Youth Service America online application.

The application requires organizations to provide organizational and contact information and answer questions about their current programs, youth engagement experience, proposed youth leadership structure, recruitment strategy, Youth Leadership Summit, continuing engagement plans, anticipated participant numbers, budget, and match funding.

The application also provides options to:

Save progress and return later.

Resume a previously saved application.

Applicants with questions about the application can contact Mike Minks at mminks@ysa.org.

Apply through the Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant application

Important Note About AI and the Application

The application itself contains a specific request that applicants not use AI to prepare their application responses.

YSA says it wants to hear about the applicant organization and its own ideas in the organization’s own words. It also states that it does not use AI to review applications.

Applicants should therefore treat the application questions as an opportunity to describe their actual organization, existing youth engagement work, local community, proposed plans, and ideas rather than submitting generic or AI-generated responses.

For this reason, organizations should make sure that their final application responses genuinely reflect their own experience and plans.

MLK Day of Service and the Wider Program Context

The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant is part of YSA’s broader MLK Day of Service programming.

The next MLK Day of Service will take place on January 18, 2027. YSA describes MLK Day as a federal holiday designated as a National Day of Service and encourages Americans to participate in service and community action.

YSA’s broader work focuses on helping young people find their voices, take action, develop civic skills, and contribute to their communities. The organization says its campaigns and events have engaged more than 3.2 million young people in service over the past decade.

The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant fits within this broader approach by emphasizing not only youth service but also youth voice, leadership, participation, and decision-making.

Why the Youth Council Component Matters

One of the distinctive features of this opportunity is its emphasis on establishing a formal youth leadership structure.

A one-time event can create an opportunity for young people to participate on a particular day. A youth council or similar structure can provide an ongoing mechanism through which young people can:

Share perspectives with organizational leaders.

Help identify community needs.

Participate in planning.

Develop leadership skills.

Help design service projects.

Engage their peers.

Build relationships with adult partners.

Continue participating in decision-making beyond MLK Day.

The grant therefore combines organizational development, youth leadership development, community service, and ongoing civic participation.

Suggested Areas Organizations Should Think About Before Applying

Although the application requires organizations to provide their own responses, prospective applicants may find it useful to think through several practical questions before beginning.

Organizational readiness

Consider whether your organization already has:

Youth programs

Youth volunteers

Youth advisory structures

Adult staff or volunteers who work with young people

Community partnerships

Experience organizing service activities

Youth leadership structure

Consider:

Whether a new Youth Council is needed

Whether an existing youth group could be expanded

How youth members would be selected

How often the group would meet

What decisions young people could influence

How adult leaders would work with the youth group

Recruitment

Consider how the organization can reach young people who may not normally volunteer for leadership opportunities, particularly those identified in the application.

Summit

Consider:

Where the Summit could take place

Who should participate

What training participants need

How young people will help design the event

How the organization can reach 200 or more participants

How participants will be encouraged to continue serving afterward

Long-term engagement

Consider how the Youth Council could continue its work after MLK Day and through The Civic Season.

Budget

Consider how the $2,000 grant and $1,000 match could support allowable activities without being used for prohibited expenses.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much funding does the grant provide?

Each selected organization will receive $2,000.

How much funding is available overall?

YSA states that $50,000 is available and that 25 organizations will receive grants.

Is matching funding required?

Yes. Applicants must provide and document $1,000 in local match funding, which may include cash or qualifying in-kind contributions.

Who can apply?

Eligible organizations listed by YSA include K-12 schools, higher education institutions, out-of-school-time/afterschool programs, positive youth development organizations, community-based organizations, faith-based organizations, state governments, and local governments.

Learn more HERE

Does the organization need an existing Youth Council?

Not necessarily. The grant can support the development of new Youth Councils or similar youth leadership structures, as well as the expansion of existing ones.

Is there a minimum number of people that must be engaged?

Yes. The program requires engagement of at least 200 youth and adults through the Summit and/or related youth voice, leadership, and decision-making opportunities.

When is MLK Day of Service?

MLK Day of Service will be held on January 18, 2027.

When is the application deadline?

The application deadline is Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time.

Can grant money pay staff salaries?

No. The application specifically states that grant funds cannot be used for staff salaries or benefits.

Can the funding be used for lobbying or partisan political activities?

No. The application identifies lobbying and partisan political activities among the prohibited uses of AmeriCorps funding.

Conclusion

The Youth At Every Decision-Making Table Grant 2026 provides an opportunity for eligible U.S. organizations to strengthen how young people participate in leadership, service, and decision-making. With $2,000 available to each selected organization, the program is designed to support the creation or expansion of Youth Councils and other formal youth leadership structures while connecting those structures to a broader Youth Leadership Summit around MLK Day and continuing engagement through The Civic Season.

The opportunity goes beyond funding a single youth event. Applicants are expected to demonstrate how they will establish meaningful youth leadership, recruit participants who reflect the diversity of their communities, engage at least 200 youth and adults, provide relevant training, and continue creating opportunities for youth voice and leadership after the MLK Day period.

Organizations considering applying should pay particular attention to the $1,000 match requirement, the 200-person engagement requirement, the restrictions on how grant funds can be spent, and the expectation that youth leadership structures will contribute to ongoing engagement throughout the 2026–2027 academic year and The Civic Season.

The application deadline is October 25, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time, giving eligible organizations a clear opportunity to prepare their organizational information, youth leadership plans, recruitment strategy, Summit concept, preliminary budget, and match-funding plan before submission.

TITLE: Strong M&E helps track DLIs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Strong Monitoring, Evaluation & Learning Systems and Processes Helps Track the Status of the ACE Impact Project’s Implementation & Achievement of Disbursement-Linked Indicators (DLIs)

To promote greater transparency, data-driven decision making, improved project performance and learning, as well as effective resource allocation among several other reasons, ACE Impact places a high premium on Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL). The project’s MEL Specialist, Mrs. Adeline Addy presented the status of implementation and achievement of the Disbursement Linked Indicators at the ongoing 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop, in Cotonou, Benin. As a results-oriented project, the Disbursement Linked Indicators are project requirements that centres must attain before receiving funds.

The 53 Centres of excellence are divided into two groups, 1st ACE Impact and 2nd ACE Impact centres, depending on when their projects were approved for implementation. Centres from Burkina Faso, Djibouti, Ghana, Guinea, and Senegal are in the 1st ACE Impact group while Centres from Benin, Gambia, Niger, Nigeria, Togo and Cote d’Ivoire are in the 2nd ACE Impact group.

Process-wise, the results achieved by centres from both groups are initially submitted to the AAU as the Regional Facilitating Unit through an online digital reporting system. After this, an external verification agency is appointed to verify the results. Verified results lead to the Centres receiving funds for the results achieved.

The presentation by the Project’s MEL Specialist focused on the status of the project development objectives (PDO) for both the 1st and 2nd ACE Impact Centres, as well as for the overall project. She also shared the country-level status per DLI​ and provided an overview of the highlights and challenges. The presentation concluded by sharing the schedule for results reporting and verification.

The highlights were that the 1st ACE Impact Centres had achieved 51% of the DLIs, with three (3) out of five (5) PDO indicators on target including student enrollment, programme accreditation and student and faculty internships. Strong performance had also been recorded under PhD training (74%); External Revenue Generation (74%), Masters level training (73%); and Research Publications (72%). The areas of concern with the 1st ACE Impact Centres were the generally low achievement rates under Overall Fiduciary (20%), Programme Accreditation (19%), Infrastructure (16%) and Overall Institutional Impact (8%) – however some Centres individually did well in these areas of concern.

The presentation pointed out that the 2nd ACE Impact Centres had achieved 32% of the DLIs. Noteworthy performance was also highlighted under Masters enrolment and training (56%), Short Courses (55%), PhD (54%), Research Publications (53%) and External Revenue (44%). The areas of concern with 2nd ACE Impact Centres were the overall low achievements on Fiduciary (13%) and Institutional Impact (0.3%). However, some Centres individually did well in the indicated areas of concern. Apparent lack of progress was noted under DLR 4.1 (Number of internationally, regionally/sub-regionally accredited education programs), DLR 4.3 (Improved teaching and research environment as per approved proposal) and DLR 5.3 (Number of new entrepreneurships, innovation, start-up companies, and commercialization support programs). Worth noting is the fact that some of the processes towards achieving some of these DLRs, for instance DLR 4.1 related to accreditation takes quite some time, and the centres were working hard to achieve the expected results. Centers were also encouraged to step up their efforts in some of these areas.

Mrs. Addy also indicated that the Results Verification Schedule for June 2022 to August 2022 includes the following key milestones:

Completion of results submissions by 30 June 2022

Verification of results from 1 to 30 July 2022

Finalization of results 1 to 10 August 2022

Issuing of verification notices/letters by the RFU, the Association of African Universities by 15 August 2022

Project Performance & Disbursement – Ms. Maud Kouadio-IV

Ms. Maud Kouadio-IV, the Education Consultant and ACE core team member with the World Bank reported that most of the 1st ACE Impact Centres had exceeded their project average for DLI achievements and most of the 2nd ACE Impact Centres had also exceeded their project average. It was reported that the performance of some of the Centres had been negatively affected by delays at a national level in approving the projects, the COVID-19 pandemic, and coup d’etats in some countries.

For the 1st Group of ACE Impact Centres, as at end of May 2022, the total International Development Association (IDA) funds received project wise was 40% – with Ghana Centres topping in terms of IDA funds that they have received to date – 51%. For the 2nd Group of ACE Impact Centres, as at end of May 2022, the total IDA funds received project wise was 22% – with Benin Centres topping in terms of IDA funds that they have received to date – 27%.

The International Development Association (IDA) is the portion of the World Bank that aids the world’s neediest countries. Created in 1960, IDA aims to reduce poverty by providing zero to low-interest loans (called “credits”) and grants for programs that increase economic growth, reduce inequalities, and advance people’s living conditions.

Ms. Kouadio-IV stated that the first Group of ACE Impact Centres had completed their mid-term review (MTR) process, whilst the 2nd group were scheduled to conclude theirs in November 2022.

The project-wide recommendations include project extension to June 2025 because of COVID-19 related implementation delays, and procurement delays beyond the control of the centers. Ms. Kouadio-IV noted that there were disruptions to the academic calendar, regional student enrollment, internships, and staff mobility. She advised that discussions needed start at national level to prepare and submit official requests for extension to the Bank.

On project fund reallocations, she said that these would follow agreed criteria to ensure optimum use of project funds. The criteria for fund reallocations would include merit, the Centers’ needs, planned activities, expected results, and case-by-case reallocation.

It was mentioned that some disbursement-linked indicators (DLIs) would change, and these include DLI2 (Development Impact of ACE Center), DLI6.4 (Quality of Procurement planning) and DLI7.4 (ACE host university participate in PASET ). The changes are meant to reflect the challenges that have arisen in the project and to ensure that centers still have the chance to earn 100% of project funds in the remaining project time.

Ms. Maud Kouadio-IV

Ms. Kouadio-IV said that the parameters for the additional financing for Centres would consider the DLI achievement rate, fund utilization rate, implementation performance rate and qualitative assessment of the Centres.

Wrapping up, the Centres were advised to accelerate the implementation of their project “as if there would be no project extension”, since this was not currently assured. The RFU and the Subject Matter Experts have been assisting the Centres to develop and implement accelerated implementation plans aimed at guiding the Centres to fully deliver the expected results.

TITLE: Chapter 7 Impacts of the Indian Ocean on regional and global climate

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ummenhofer, C. C., Taschetto, A., Izumo, T., & Luo, J.-J. (2024). Chapter 7 Impacts of the Indian Ocean on regional and global climate. In C.C. Ummenhofer & R. R. Hood (Eds.), The Indian Ocean and its Role in the Global Climate System (pp. 145–168). Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-12-822698-8.00018-4

(a, b) Teleconnection mechanisms to a positive Indian Ocean Dipole and Indian Ocean Basin Mode. Illustrated in the schematic are changes in local Walker circulation (dashed brown cells), areas of above (green patch) and below (brown patch) precipitation, warm (red patch) and cool (blue patch) sea surface temperature anomalies, Rossby wave train emanating from the Indian Ocean (high and low centers and dashed yellow arrow), and the capacitor effect onto the Northwest Pacific anticyclone (purple dashed arrow and yellow circle). (Figure reproduced from Ummenhofer et al., 2024)

The impact of Indian Ocean variability on regional and global weather and climate across a range of timescales is increasingly recognized. Large strides have been made in understanding and predicting such impacts (e.g., droughts, floods, wildfires), which can have considerable societal relevance, especially in the densely populated Indian Ocean rim with agrarian societies vulnerable to changes in climate. Atmospheric teleconnections triggered by Indian Ocean conditions can impact variability in other ocean basins, including the tropical Pacific and the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or affect the higher latitudes of both hemispheres, including the North Atlantic Oscillation, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, as well as Antarctic sea-ice. Understanding feedbacks and interactions among the tropical ocean basins can aid seasonal prediction efforts. Being particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic climate change, the Indian Ocean exhibits strong warming trends that can further modulate how the Indian Ocean affects regional or global climate and weather patterns.

TITLE: FARA visits AAU

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Monday 21st March 2022

The Executive Director of the Forum for Agricultural Research in Africa (FARA), Dr. Yemi Akinbamijo, paid a courtesy call on the Secretary-General of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Prof. Olusola Oyewole, for bilateral talks between the two continental bodies. Accompanying the FARA boss was Ms. Ama Pokua Asenso, Human Resource and Administration Manager. From the AAU side, the Director of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management , Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, joined the Secretary General to receive the delegation.

FARA is Africa’s apex organization responsible for coordinating and advocating for agricultural research for development and also serves as the technical arm of the African Union Commission on agriculture science, technology and innovation.

According to Dr. Akinbamijo, despite Africa’s huge natural resources, the continent remains brain rich but pocket poor because agriculture, the mainstay of the African economy, loses its graduates to other sectors. He expressed the fear that unless there is a paradigm shift towards the application of science, technology and innovation in the agriculture sector, the continent would continue to be a net importer of food. It is in light of these sector challenges that FARA has committed to raise the quality of post graduate education to strengthen agricultural production in Africa and seeks a collaboration with the AAU to actualize this vision.

Prof. Oyewole expressed the AAU’s readiness to partner with FARA on this noble course. The two organizational heads agreed to implement this through a memorandum of understanding which will establish the key initiatives to be undertaken towards achieving the set targets.
