It explores how people can think more effectively together and how creative, culturally responsive, and critically informed discussions can contribute to stronger communities.

The 2027 Emerging Fellowship seeks to expand awareness and engagement with the Collaborative Discussion Project among diverse communities.

Through the fellowship, Emerging Fellows will be paired with Senior Fellows, who are experienced leaders in collaborative discussion. Together, they will explore ways to strengthen dialogue and take meaningful action within communities over the course of a year.

The fellowship is particularly suited to individuals who want to develop their leadership abilities while applying collaborative discussion approaches to real-world community challenges.

What Is the 2027 Emerging Fellowship About?

The fellowship focuses on the practical application of collaborative discussion skills and mindsets.

Rather than being solely an academic or classroom-based program, fellows will be expected to work on a project that advances collaborative discussion within a community or among a particular audience.

Potential projects could include:

Designing and delivering a workshop.

Creating a Collaborative Discussion certificate program.

Developing a new activity for the Collaborative Discussion Project Toolkit.

Introducing the Collaborative Discussion Project to new audiences.

Developing innovative approaches for strengthening dialogue within a community.

Creating educational or community resources that encourage constructive discussion.

In addition to their community project, fellows will produce a publication, video, or new curriculum that contributes to the mission of the Interactivity Foundation.

Key Benefits of the Collaborative Discussion Emerging Fellowship

Selected fellows will have access to several financial, professional, educational, and networking benefits.

$6,000 Fellowship Stipend

Each selected Emerging Fellow will receive a $6,000 stipend, which will be paid in three installments during the fellowship.

This provides financial support while fellows participate in the year-long program and undertake their collaborative discussion project.

Full Collaborative Discussion Coach Training Scholarship

Fellows receive a full scholarship to the Collaborative Discussion Project Coach Training, valued at $495.

The training is intended to help participants develop practical knowledge and skills for facilitating collaborative discussions.

Travel and Expenses Covered

The fellowship includes two in-person gatherings, with travel and related expenses covered for participating fellows.

This provides opportunities for fellows to meet other participants, mentors, and leaders working in the collaborative discussion field.

Real-World Community Project

Fellows will complete a project designed to bring collaborative discussion skills and approaches into a real community setting.

This could allow participants to translate the knowledge gained through the fellowship into practical community impact.

Co-Author Opportunity

Fellows will receive co-author credit on a deliverable. Depending on the project, this could take the form of:

A written publication.

A new curriculum.

An audiovisual media project.

This can provide participants with a tangible professional output from their fellowship experience.

Mentorship and Professional Network

Each Emerging Fellow will be partnered with a Senior Fellow who will provide mentorship and support throughout the program.

Participants will also take part in monthly virtual meetings with a network of mentors and peers working in collaborative discussion and efforts to strengthen democracy.

Who Should Apply?

The Interactivity Foundation is seeking individuals who have a demonstrated commitment to collaborative discussion and/or strengthening democracy within a particular community.

The organization welcomes applicants from a broad range of backgrounds, careers, ages, identities, political affiliations, racial and ethnic backgrounds, religions, socioeconomic backgrounds, and lived experiences.

The fellowship is also intended to help nurture new and diverse leadership. Applicants who have not previously had an opportunity of this kind are specifically welcomed.

Potential applicants may therefore include individuals involved in:

Community leadership.

Civic engagement.

Dialogue and deliberation.

Education.

Youth development.

Community organizing.

Social-impact initiatives.

Public engagement.

Democratic participation.

Facilitation and discussion.

Community-based projects.

Other activities focused on strengthening constructive discussion within communities.

The central consideration described by the Interactivity Foundation is a demonstrated commitment to collaborative discussion and/or strengthening democracy within a particular community.

U.S. Work Authorization Requirement

One of the most important eligibility requirements is related to employment authorization.

The fellowship requires compensated services to be performed in the United States.

Therefore, selected fellows must be legally authorized to work in the United States for the entire fellowship period.

The Interactivity Foundation explicitly states that it is unable to sponsor or obtain employment authorization for fellows.

Applicants who are outside the United States should therefore carefully consider this requirement before applying.

Fellowship Activities and Responsibilities

The 2027 Emerging Fellowship is structured around several activities that take place throughout the year.

Participants will be expected to participate in required virtual sessions, meetings, training, project work, and in-person gatherings.

The program includes:

In-person Fellows Launch

Monthly virtual meetings

Progress reporting and deliverables

Final reporting

In-person Fellows Showcase

Applicants must be able to participate in all required virtual and in-person dates.

However, applicants must also meet the fellowship’s U.S. work authorization requirement because the fellowship involves compensated services performed in the United States.

The fellowship does not state a conventional country or continental restriction such as “open only to citizens of specific countries.”

Instead, the critical geographic and employment requirement is that selected fellows must be legally authorized to work in the United States for the entire fellowship period.

The Interactivity Foundation does not provide sponsorship or obtain employment authorization for participants.

Race, Ethnicity and Diversity

The fellowship is open to people from a wide range of racial and ethnic backgrounds.

What Will Fellows Work On?

Mentorship Through Senior Fellows

Training and Professional Development

TITLE: WTO SPS Mentoring System 2026: Applications Open for Government Officials Working on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Matters

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for government officials interested in joining the 2026 World Trade Organization Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Mentoring System as mentees, an international professional development initiative designed to strengthen practical knowledge, peer learning, coordination and engagement on sanitary and phytosanitary issues.

The WTO SPS Mentoring System connects government officials who need support on particular SPS challenges with experienced officials who can provide practical guidance through an informal, flexible mentoring relationship. The initiative is particularly intended to assist developing and least-developed country (LDC) WTO members, including in areas such as SPS transparency, participation in the WTO SPS Committee, implementation of SPS Agreement provisions, domestic coordination, leadership and other operational SPS issues.

Applications for the current call must be submitted by:

Friday, 25 September 2026

The WTO’s current implementation timeline indicates that mentees will be selected during the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a call for mentors and mentor–mentee matching. The new mentoring relationships are then expected to operate from the first quarter of 2027 onward, with the duration determined by the individual mentoring participants.

The programme is not a scholarship, grant or funded training course. The WTO states that mentoring does not imply a financial commitment unless the participants agree otherwise. Instead, the programme focuses on professional knowledge exchange and practical institutional capacity-building between government officials.

Apply for the 2026 WTO SPS Mentoring System

Official WTO SPS Mentoring System information

About the WTO SPS Mentoring System

The SPS Mentoring System was created by the WTO Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures as a practical mechanism for supporting government officials who work with SPS matters.

It was established following recommendations arising from the Sixth Review of the Operation and Implementation of the SPS Agreement, adopted in March 2025.

The system was originally launched as a pilot in June 2025.

Its purpose was to provide developing and LDC members with additional practical support, particularly concerning:

SPS transparency

Timely engagement in SPS matters

Participation in the SPS Committee

Implementation of SPS requirements

Domestic institutional coordination

Knowledge-sharing between governments

The pilot created mentoring relationships between government officials from different WTO members, including through South-South cooperation.

Following the pilot, the SPS Committee agreed in June 2026 to extend the initiative for another two years, with a mid-term review planned for 2027.

What Are Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures?

Sanitary and phytosanitary measures are government measures intended to protect:

Human health

Animal health

Plant health

Food safety

In international trade, these rules can affect products such as:

Food

Agricultural commodities

Plants

Animals

Meat

Fish

Fruit and vegetables

Seeds

Animal products

SPS policy can involve issues including:

Food safety standards

Pest controls

Animal disease measures

Plant health regulations

Quarantine

Import inspections

Risk assessment

Certification

Maximum residue limits

Disease-related import restrictions

The WTO SPS Agreement establishes disciplines governing how members use such measures in international trade.

International standards in the SPS field are closely associated with organizations including:

The Codex Alimentarius Commission for food safety

The World Organisation for Animal Health for animal health and zoonoses

The International Plant Protection Convention for plant health

Government officials working in these areas may therefore encounter highly technical questions alongside complex institutional and trade-policy challenges.

The mentoring system is intended to help officials learn from peers who have already dealt with comparable problems.

Why Was the SPS Mentoring System Created?

The WTO SPS Committee recognized that developing and least-developed members may face practical challenges when participating in the SPS system.

These can include:

Limited institutional capacity

Difficulties coordinating agencies domestically

Limited experience preparing SPS notifications

Challenges using WTO transparency mechanisms

Limited familiarity with SPS Committee procedures

Difficulties implementing specific SPS Agreement obligations

Technical problems associated with sanitary or phytosanitary controls

The mentoring system offers a relatively flexible mechanism through which government officials can discuss those practical challenges with peers who have relevant experience.

The aim is therefore not simply to provide theoretical training on the SPS Agreement.

It is intended to facilitate problem-oriented learning.

How the Mentoring System Works

The WTO describes mentoring as an:

Informal, ad hoc supportive relationship between government officials.

Its purpose is to facilitate:

Knowledge-sharing

Peer learning

Practical discussion

Engagement on SPS-related issues

A mentoring arrangement does not have to consist only of one mentor and one mentee.

Depending on the issue, it may involve:

One mentor and one mentee

Several mentees

Several mentors

A wider peer-learning relationship

This flexibility allows the mentoring arrangement to be adapted to the SPS challenge involved.

Mentoring Is Not Formal Consultancy

Participants should not view this programme as equivalent to hiring a technical consultant.

The mentor is primarily a peer professional who can:

Share experience

Explain approaches used in another administration

Discuss institutional practices

Suggest useful tools

Help the mentee think through practical challenges

Share lessons learned

The exact relationship will depend on the needs identified by the mentee and the experience of the mentor.

Possible SPS Mentoring Topics

The WTO identifies several broad areas that may form the basis of a mentoring request.

These include:

SPS Transparency

Transparency is a major component of the WTO SPS system.

Mentoring may help an official understand areas such as:

Notifications

National enquiry points

National notification authorities

Information-sharing

Changes in SPS regulations

Timely communication with trading partners

Officials who are newly responsible for SPS transparency may benefit particularly from practical guidance from another administration.

Participation in the WTO SPS Committee

Another mentoring objective may involve:

SPS Committee participation.

Officials may need support understanding:

Committee procedures

How to prepare for meetings

How to coordinate positions domestically

How to raise an SPS issue

How to respond to questions

How to engage with other WTO members

The mentoring system may therefore support officials who want to strengthen their government’s effective participation in WTO SPS processes.

Operational Implementation of SPS Issues

Officials may also request mentoring concerning the implementation of specific SPS matters.

For example, a government agency could seek peer support concerning:

Import inspection

Risk categorization

Food safety controls

Animal health measures

Plant health systems

Regulatory implementation

The exact issue should be identified in the mentee’s request.

Implementation of the SPS Agreement

Mentoring may concern a particular:

SPS Agreement provision

or a broader implementation problem.

This can be valuable where officials understand the formal legal requirement but need practical examples of how another WTO member has operationalized it.

Leadership and Domestic Coordination

SPS policy frequently involves several government institutions.

Depending on the country, these might include:

Ministry of Agriculture

Ministry of Health

Ministry of Trade

Food safety authorities

Veterinary authorities

Plant protection authorities

Customs

Standards agencies

Poor coordination can create problems in:

Notification

International representation

Inspection

Risk management

Trade negotiations

Regulatory implementation

The WTO therefore identifies leadership and coordination on SPS matters as a potential mentoring objective.

South-South Cooperation

An important feature of the mentoring system is that it can support:

South-South cooperation.

This means expertise does not need to flow only from high-income countries to developing economies.

Officials in one developing country may have highly relevant experience that can benefit counterparts in another country dealing with a similar institutional or regulatory issue.

For example, the pilot included Morocco providing mentoring on transparency, domestic coordination and SPS Committee participation to officials from Cameroon, Djibouti and Tunisia.

Examples From the First SPS Mentoring Pilot

The 2025–2026 pilot provides useful examples of the kinds of issues that can be addressed.

Belize and the European Union

The Belize Agricultural Health Authority was matched with the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety.

Their mentoring topic focused on:

SPS risk categorization and/or risk-based inspection.

Cameroon, Djibouti and Tunisia With Morocco

Officials from trade ministries in:

Cameroon

Djibouti

Tunisia

were connected with Morocco’s:

National Office for Food Safety

The mentoring focused on:

SPS transparency

Domestic coordination

SPS Committee participation

Namibia and the United Kingdom

Namibia’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform was matched with the UK’s Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs.

The mentoring focus was:

SPS Committee participation.

Pakistan and Canada

Pakistan’s Animal Quarantine Department was connected with the:

Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The mentoring addressed:

Operational implementation

Domestic coordination

Peru and the European Union

Peru’s National Authority for Health and Safety in Fisheries and Aquaculture was matched with the European Commission.

The mentoring explored:

Artificial intelligence and predictive models based on historical sanitary control data for assessing health risks related to hydrobiological products.

These examples demonstrate the considerable range of issues that may be appropriate for mentoring.

Results of the 2025–2026 Pilot

The initial pilot generated significant interest.

The WTO reported receiving:

56 mentoring requests

from:

23 WTO members and observers.

From those requests:

Nine applications were selected

Five mentoring partnerships were established

The most common mentoring topics included:

Transparency

SPS Committee participation

Implementation of specific SPS issues or Agreement provisions

Leadership

Domestic SPS coordination

The positive experience and feedback from participants contributed to the SPS Committee’s decision to continue the programme for another two years.

Who Should Apply in 2026?

The current call is directed at:

Government officials working on SPS matters who want mentoring assistance to address SPS issues at the domestic level.

The programme’s broader purpose is to support:

Developing and least-developed country WTO members.

Potential applicants might therefore work in institutions such as:

Ministries of Agriculture

Ministries of Trade

Ministries of Health

Food safety authorities

Veterinary services

Plant protection agencies

Fisheries authorities

Quarantine agencies

SPS national notification authorities

SPS enquiry points

Other government regulatory agencies

The key issue is that the applicant should have official responsibilities connected with sanitary or phytosanitary matters.

This Call Is for Mentees

It is important to distinguish between:

Mentees

and:

Mentors

The current application form is specifically for officials requesting mentoring.

The 2026 timeline indicates that:

Mentee applications are collected during Q3 2026.

Mentees are selected during Q4 2026.

A call for mentors follows.

Mentors and mentees are matched.

Mentoring begins afterward.

Government officials who are interested in providing mentoring rather than receiving it should therefore follow the subsequent mentor call rather than complete the mentee form.

What Makes a Strong Mentee Request?

The first pilot indicates that selection can consider factors such as:

The mentoring objective

Commitment of the mentee

Language

Region

The suitability of available mentors

A strong application should therefore identify a specific SPS challenge rather than requesting general professional development.

For example, compare these two requests:

“Help me learn more about SPS.”

versus:

“Our agency wants to strengthen its coordination between the national notification authority and veterinary and plant health regulators so that SPS notifications are submitted more consistently and on time.”

The second request provides a much clearer basis for identifying a suitable mentor.

What Applicants Should Explain

Although applicants should follow the actual online application questions, a useful mentoring request will normally make clear:

What SPS issue the official is working on

What specific problem they are trying to solve

Why mentoring would be useful

What outcome they hope to achieve

What their role is within the responsible government institution

How they intend to participate actively

Any relevant language or regional considerations

The programme is based on active peer learning, so mentees should be prepared to engage consistently rather than simply receive information.

There Is No Financial Award

Applicants should understand that the WTO SPS Mentoring System is:

Not a financial assistance programme.

The WTO states that:

Mentoring does not imply any financial commitment unless otherwise agreed.

Therefore, applicants should not expect:

A stipend

Salary

Scholarship

Research grant

Travel allowance

Cash award

The value of the programme lies primarily in:

Professional mentoring

Knowledge exchange

Peer learning

Institutional capacity-building

International SPS networking

Mentoring Duration

The programme does not prescribe one universal duration for every mentoring relationship.

According to the current implementation timeline:

The duration will be decided by each mentoring pair.

The new 2026 cohort is expected to begin mentoring from:

Q1 2027 onward.

This flexibility allows different SPS problems to receive different levels of support.

Why the WTO Extended the Programme

The pilot generated positive feedback from WTO members involved in the mentoring partnerships.

At the June 2026 SPS Committee meeting, several participating members shared their experiences, and the Committee agreed to extend the programme for two additional years.

The extension suggests that WTO members see peer mentoring as a useful complement to more conventional forms of:

Technical assistance

Training

Workshops

Capacity-building

Mentoring allows officials to engage with a colleague over time rather than receiving information only during a short formal training event.

Why SPS Capacity Matters for International Trade

SPS measures play an important role in determining whether agricultural and food products can enter international markets.

Weak SPS capacity can affect a country’s ability to:

Export agricultural products

Respond to trading partner requirements

Demonstrate food safety

Control pests and animal diseases

Participate effectively in international rule-making

Respond to SPS trade concerns

At the same time, governments need to protect:

Consumers

Agricultural production

Animal health

Plant health

Officials therefore often need to balance:

Trade facilitation and market access

with:

Legitimate health protection.

The mentoring programme can help officials learn how other administrations address this balance.

Transparency as a Major Priority

Transparency has been one of the recurring priorities of the SPS Committee.

WTO members are expected to communicate relevant SPS measures and provide mechanisms through which trading partners can obtain information.

For developing and LDC members, effective transparency may require:

Strong domestic coordination

Clear institutional responsibility

Trained staff

Reliable information flows

Familiarity with WTO systems

This explains why transparency has featured prominently in both the programme’s objectives and its pilot mentoring relationships.

Connection With SPS Committee Participation

The SPS Committee provides a regular forum in which WTO members discuss:

Implementation of the SPS Agreement

Specific trade concerns

Transparency

International standards

Technical cooperation

Emerging SPS issues

Officials who understand how to participate effectively can better represent their government’s interests.

The mentoring system can therefore support institutional capacity not only at the domestic level but also in multilateral trade diplomacy.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the current mentee call is:

Friday, 25 September 2026.

The WTO’s official current timeline explicitly lists this date for the Q3 2026 mentee call.

Applicants should submit early rather than waiting until the final day.

How to Apply

Government officials interested in receiving SPS mentoring should complete the official:

2026 SPS Mentoring System – Form to Request Mentoring for Mentees

Complete the WTO SPS Mentoring application form

Applicants should also review the programme information before submitting.

Read the official WTO SPS Mentoring System information

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

1. Identify One Concrete SPS Problem

Avoid requesting mentoring on “SPS generally.”

Instead, identify a specific problem such as:

Improving SPS notification procedures

Strengthening domestic coordination

Improving risk-based inspections

Preparing for SPS Committee participation

Implementing a specific Agreement obligation

Specificity makes it easier for the WTO to identify a relevant mentor.

2. Explain the Institutional Context

Explain what your agency does and what role you personally play.

For example:

Are you responsible for notifications?

Do you work on veterinary import controls?

Do you coordinate plant health regulation?

Do you represent your government in WTO meetings?

This context helps demonstrate why the mentoring request is relevant.

3. Define a Practical Objective

A good mentoring objective should be achievable.

For example:

“Develop a more effective national SPS coordination procedure involving the trade, agriculture and health ministries.”

is stronger than:

“Improve SPS capacity.”

4. Show Willingness to Participate Actively

The pilot considered mentee commitment as part of the selection process.

Mentoring works only when both sides actively participate.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to:

Attend agreed meetings

Share relevant information

Follow up on discussions

Test proposed approaches

Report progress

5. Think About Language

Language is one factor considered when matching mentors and mentees.

Applicants should accurately indicate which languages they can use professionally.

This increases the likelihood of an effective mentoring relationship.

6. Explain the Wider Institutional Benefit

Where possible, show how mentoring could benefit more than one person.

For example:

Improved procedures

Better coordination

Knowledge transferred to colleagues

More effective WTO participation

Stronger national transparency

This can make the request more strategically valuable.

Key Details at a Glance

Conclusion

The WTO SPS Mentoring System 2026 provides government officials working on sanitary and phytosanitary matters with an opportunity to receive practical, peer-based professional support on specific SPS challenges.

Established following the Sixth Review of the SPS Agreement and first piloted in 2025–2026, the system was created to assist developing and least-developed WTO members, particularly in strengthening transparency and timely engagement on SPS matters.

The programme is deliberately flexible. Mentoring can involve one mentor and one mentee or several participants and can address issues ranging from SPS transparency and WTO Committee participation to domestic coordination, risk-based inspection and practical implementation of SPS obligations.

The first pilot received 56 requests from 23 members and observers, resulting in nine selected applications and five mentoring partnerships. Following positive feedback from participating members, the SPS Committee agreed in June 2026 to extend the system for a further two years.

This is not a financial award. Mentees should not expect a stipend, salary or travel grant. Rather, the value lies in access to peer experience, professional knowledge, practical problem-solving and stronger engagement with the international SPS community.

For government officials in developing and least-developed countries who are currently dealing with a specific sanitary or phytosanitary challenge, the programme can provide a relatively personalized form of capacity-building that complements formal WTO technical assistance.

Applications for the current mentee cohort must be submitted by:

25 September 2026.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Juan Carlos Torres

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Juan Carlos Torres (SM ’79)
MIT Sloan School of Management

Juan Carlos Torres, SM ’79
MIT Sloan School of Management

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2009

Juan Carlos Torres has had a long interest in physics, which started in his last two years of high school. He had a wonderful physics teacher who sparked his interest in finding out how things work.

He earned a master’s degree in physics from Universidad Complutense de Madrid, where he specialized in geophysics. After working for several years in the petroleum industry, he found himself drawn increasingly to management, and in 1979 he obtained an SM in Management from the MIT Sloan School. Following consultant work with McKinsey and corporate leadership positions in the pharmaceutical industry, he joined the private equity firm Advent International in 1988. Since 1995, he has been the Managing Director and Senior Partner in charge of Advent’s investment activities in Latin America. Juan Carlos has led or co-led Advent’s investments in 30 companies in several countries, including Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Spain, France, and the U.S. He has also sponsored six other investments in the information technology services, pharmaceutical and retail sectors.

Juan Carlos Torres’s interest in physics was rekindled when he and his wife Ann Kreis, who also has a degree from Sloan, attended the 2006 MIT Alumni Travel Program trip to Chile led by MIT Physics Department Head Ed Bertschinger. Lectures on dark matter and dark energy, gravitational waves and black holes, and planets around other stars, brought back Juan Carlos’s fascination with the frontiers of physics. A glimpse through a 15-inch telescope of the globular star cluster 47 Tucanae — with its hundreds of thousands of stars blazing in a tiny corner of the Milky Way — was enough to whet his appetite for more.

Since Juan Carlos’s first trip with Ed Bertschinger, he has gotten even more involved with the Department. He and Ed have shared several trips since 2006, including a visit to the Large Hadron Collider in Geneva in 2008 and a night-time visit to the Magellan Telescopes in Chile in 2009.

I cannot think of anybody that visits the place that would not be interested in the Magellan Telescopes. It’s a rare privilege to have a small window into the universe.
Juan Carlos Torres (SM ’79)

His appreciation for the Physics Department is what led him to offer his assistance. He has generously supported operations costs for MIT’s partnership in the Magellan Telescopes consortium and has also provided two graduate fellowships. Juan Carlos was in a position to be able to give back and knew what an impact his gift could have. Juan Carlos has become further involved with the Department and is a member of the MIT Corporation Visiting Committee for the Physics Department. Juan Carlos’s most recent adventure with the Physics Department was in July 2009 for the Japan Total Solar Eclipse trip, also led by Ed Bertschinger. Juan Carlos brought along his three daughters; his hope was that seeing the solar eclipse would spark their interest in the subject. Juan Carlos says, “for me, it was a once in a lifetime experience that I will always treasure.”

TITLE: EY Foundation Policy and Research Officer 2026: Permanent Career Opportunity in London, Birmingham, Manchester or Glasgow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:

The organisation was founded by EY, the professional services firm, which continues to serve as its primary funder.

The Foundation’s ambition is for young people who are eligible for Free School Meals to have employment and earnings potential that is equitable with that of other young people across the United Kingdom.

Its approach is informed by an understanding of both sides of the labour market. By bringing together young people and employers, the Foundation seeks to address barriers to employment while helping young people develop skills and access opportunities.

Its activities include:

Delivering employability skills programmes.

Developing scalable digital interventions.

Collaborating with a wide range of organisations.

Bringing employers and young people together.

Using its convening power to influence systemic change.

Building evidence that can support improvements in employment and skills outcomes.

London

Birmingham

Manchester

Glasgow

Staff ordinarily work from the office for at least one day each week. However, depending on the responsibilities associated with the position and specific organisational requirements, employees may occasionally be expected to attend an office or external events more frequently.

About the EY Foundation Policy and Research Officer Role

The Policy and Research Officer will become part of the EY Foundation’s Influence Team and report to the Policy and Public Affairs Manager.

The position is national in scope and is closely connected to the Foundation’s ambition of helping young people from low-income backgrounds access meaningful employment opportunities.

The successful candidate will contribute to the implementation of the Foundation’s influence strategy by designing and coordinating impactful research projects and ensuring that research is robust, relevant and informed by the lived experiences of the young people the organisation supports.

The Policy and Research Officer will also help shape the Foundation’s policy agenda.

The Foundation describes the opportunity as particularly suitable for someone who thrives in a dynamic and purpose-led environment and is passionate about using evidence to advance equity and opportunity.

A strong commitment to social mobility, diversity and inclusion is also expected.

The responsibilities associated with the EY Foundation Policy and Research Officer position span research, project management, policy development and stakeholder engagement.

The successful candidate will undertake comprehensive landscape reviews.

Political factors

Social factors

Technological factors

Environmental factors

This analysis will be used to inform the Foundation’s research priorities, policy positioning and approach to stakeholder engagement.

Candidates should therefore be comfortable analysing external developments and understanding how wider political, economic and social changes may affect the organisation’s priorities and the young people it supports.

TITLE: Impact of atmospheric circulation variability on U.S. Midwest moisture sources

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Carr, T., & Ummenhofer, C. C. (2024). Impact of atmospheric circulation variability on U.S. Midwest moisture sources. Journal of Climate, 37, 59-75. https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-23-0178.1

Estimates of future changes in precipitation over land are poorly constrained owing to uncertainty about changes in atmospheric circulation and specific humidity over land. Recent work suggests one way to better-constrain these land precipitation estimates is to consider humidity changes over the land’s oceanic “moisture sources”, as future projections of humidity are more robust over the ocean than over land. As a first step to imposing such an ocean-based constraint, we estimate how much moisture from U.S. Midwest rainfall events originates from oceanic vs. land sources using an atmospheric moisture tracking model. We find that on daily timescales, almost all anomalous rainfall in the Midwest originates over the ocean. This is shown in the above figure, where we analyze a “composite” rainfall event (averaging over ~600 individual events from 1979-2020). Read from top-to-bottom, Panels. a-d show tracked moisture (blue colors) traveling from the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea northwards to the Midwest as an atmospheric Rossby wave propagates from west to east across the continent (open contours show geopotential height at 200 hPa). Panel e shows the Midwest precipitation anomaly as a function of time (blue curve) along with the global-integral of tracked evaporation (orange curve, representing evaporation which contributes to subsequent precipitation in the Midwest). Panel f shows how much of the tracked evaporation occurs over the ocean (blue curve), over land (green curve), and within the Midwest (orange curve). Finally, Panel g shows how much of the oceanic contribution originates from the Atlantic vs. the Pacific Oceans.

TITLE: Finding Yourself in a Busy World

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
We live in a world that is constantly moving. There is always somewhere to be, something to achieve, someone to respond to and another goal waiting to be reached. Social media makes it even easier to compare our lives with other people’s progress, careers, relationships and achievements. In all this noise, it is possible to become so busy living that you lose touch with yourself. Finding yourself does not necessarily mean disappearing to somewhere quiet or completely changing your life. Sometimes, it simply means creating enough space to understand who you are, what matters to you and the kind of life you genuinely want to build.

Slow Down Enough to Listen
Busyness can become a distraction. When every moment is filled with work, messages, meetings and responsibilities, there is little room to reflect. Creating moments of silence can help you reconnect with yourself. This could mean taking a walk without your phone, journalling, praying, sitting quietly or simply spending time away from constant notifications. Ask yourself important questions. Am I happy with the direction of my life? What gives me energy? What drains me? What am I doing because I truly want to, and what am I doing because other people expect it? The answers may not come immediately, but asking the questions matters.

Stop Measuring Your Life Against Others
Comparison is one of the easiest ways to lose yourself. Someone will always appear to be moving faster, earning more, travelling more, achieving more or living a more exciting life. But you rarely see the complete picture of another person’s journey. Your life does not have to follow someone else’s timetable. Instead of constantly asking whether you are ahead or behind, focus on whether you are becoming the person you want to be. Progress is deeply personal.

Remember What Makes You Feel Alive
Think about the things that once brought you joy before life became filled with responsibilities. Perhaps you loved writing, painting, dancing, volunteering, reading, travelling, creating things or simply spending time with people you love. Growing older does not mean abandoning the parts of yourself that make life meaningful. Make room for them again. Sometimes finding yourself is not about discovering someone new. It is about returning to parts of yourself you neglected while trying to survive, succeed or meet everyone else’s expectations.

Learn to Say No
Finding yourself also requires boundaries. You cannot say yes to everything and still have enough time and energy for what truly matters. Not every invitation must be accepted. Not every opportunity is right for you. Not every relationship deserves unlimited access to your time. Saying no can sometimes be an act of self-respect. Protect your time, your energy and your peace.

Accept That You Are Still Becoming
There is no final version of you. Your priorities may change. Your dreams may evolve. Things that mattered deeply five years ago may no longer feel important. That does not mean you are lost. Growth often involves letting go of identities, relationships, expectations and ambitions that no longer fit who you are becoming. Give yourself permission to change.

Spend Time With the Right People
The people around you can either help you become more yourself or make you feel as though you constantly need to perform. ay attention to the relationships where you feel safe enough to be honest, imperfect and fully present. Healthy friendships and communities remind you of your values, challenge you when necessary and encourage your growth without asking you to become someone else. Sometimes finding yourself also means recognising the environments where you can truly flourish.

Define Success for Yourself
The world has many definitions of success: money, titles, followers, houses, recognition and influence. But none of these automatically creates fulfilment. Ask yourself what success genuinely means to you. It might mean meaningful work, financial stability, a peaceful home, strong relationships, freedom, service to others or enough time to enjoy your life. When you define success for yourself, you stop spending your life chasing goals that were never truly yours.

Make Space for the Life You Want
Finding yourself is not one dramatic moment of discovery. It is a series of small decisions. It is choosing what deserves your attention. It is walking away from what constantly diminishes you. It is making time for what gives your life meaning. It is becoming comfortable with your own voice in a world filled with opinions. The world may never become less busy. There will always be deadlines, responsibilities, expectations and distractions. The challenge is learning how to remain connected to yourself within all of it. Because sometimes the most important journey is not towards the next achievement, opportunity or destination. It is the journey back to yourself.

TITLE: On the vertical structure of deep ocean subinertial variability

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Toole, J. M., Musgrave, R. C., Fine, E. C., Steinberg, J. M., & Krishfield, R. A., 2023. On the vertical structure of deep ocean subinertial variability. Journal of Physical Oceanography. https://doi.org/10.1175/JPO-D-23-0011.1

The vertical structure of subinertial variability is examined using full-depth horizontal velocity and vertical isopycnal displacement observations derived from the Ocean Observatory Initiative (OOI), contrasted with moored observations on Line W in the Gulf Stream. Observed structures are compared to theoretical mode profiles for flat, sloping and so-called rough-bottom solutions. The map shows the locations of the four OOI Global Site moored arrays and of Line W moorings #5 and #6 where colors indicate the logarithm (base 10) of the bathymetric slope on 100 km scale calculated from ETOPO-2 (NOAA National Geophysical Data Center, 2006). Regions with steeply sloping bottom are shown in red, flatter regions are colored blue/green. Looking across the observations, no universal vertical structure is found that characterizes the subinertial variability at the five sites examined; regional bathymetry, stratification, baroclinicity, nonlinearity and the forcing (both local and remote) likely all play a role in shaping the vertical structure of the subinertial variability in individual ocean regions. (Image provided by John Toole)

TITLE: AAU and Afrobarometer hold strategic dialogue to explore areas of collaboration

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Prof. Olusola Oyewole, the Secretary-General of the Association of African Universities, on Thursday 3rd March 2022 paid a courtesy call on the Chief Executive Officer of Afrobarometer, Dr. Joseph Asunka at the latter’s office in Accra, Ghana.

The visit was at the invitation of Dr. Joseph Asunka for the two organisations to explore possible areas of mutual interest for collaboration. Present at the meeting were Prof. Emmanuel Gyimah-Boadi, Board Chairman of Afrobarometer, Maame Akua Amoah Twum, Communications coordinator for Anglophone West and North Africa, Ms. Linda Theresa Abbey, the executive assistant to the CEO and Dr. Hamadziripi Tamuka Moyo, Ph.D Moyo, Director of Capacity Building who joined the meeting virtually from Southern Africa.

The AAU delegation, which was led by Prof. Oyewole, comprised the Project Director of the World Bank ACE for Development Impact Program, Dr. Sylvia Mkandawire, and the AAU TV Manager, Mr. Ransford Bekoe.

The AAU delegation was briefed by Prof. Gyimah-Boadi on the aims and objectives of the organisation and its impact in Africa since its establishment in 1999. He explained that the organization sets out to Africanise the study of African society through ordinary African citizens to enable them speak for themselves on matters of common interest to society. From a humble coverage of 12 African countries, Afrobarometer will be rolling out its 9th round of a standardized survey instrument on democracy, governance, the economy and society, and is set to cover almost 40 African countries. The standardization of the survey instruments is to allow for comparability and trends analyses over time.

The CEO of Afrobarometer, Dr. Asunka intimated that while Africa is still deficient in quantitative data analysis skills, Afrobarometer offers a platform for academics and students to train and upgrade their skills and use its free data for teaching, research and scientific publication. Afrobarometer highlighted that due to the continental reach and wide membership of African universities to the AAU, the Association of African Universities is a suitable partner to training the African faculty and students in quantitative data analysis. The AAU can also be a collaborative partner in Afrobarometer’s Summer School programmes which is run on selected themes such as gender, democracy and governance, taxation and climate change at the University of Cape Town campus.

Prof Oyewole, AAU’s Secretary-General, reiterated the roles of universities in the development agenda of Africa and noted that the AAU’s mission is to enhance the quality and relevance of higher education on the continent and strengthen its contribution to development hence the opportunities offered by Afrobarometer to build capacity in higher education are very laudable. The Association with therefore leverage its role as the African Union’s lead agency on higher education in the implementation of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA) to draw academics to adopt data from Afrobarometer for their academic teaching and research.

On AAU’s specific areas of interest for collaboration, the Secretary-General identified tracking of the SDGs as a priority. The other areas of interest noted were:

Demographics on higher education in Africa

Capacity building of African faculty and students on quantitative data analysis

Summer school collaborations on thematic topics such as gender, climate change, governance and democracy.

Capacity building to improve the skills of African academic faculty

To move this expression of interest forward, Prof. Olusola Oyewole voiced out the need for the two organisations to develop a defined project (s) to implement these. The two organisations agreed on the need to change the narrative by presenting home-generated data to governments so that policy decisions are based on verifiable data.

_

Afrobarometer is a non-partisan, pan-African research institution that conducts public attitude surveys on democracy, governance, the economy and society in 36 countries, repeated on a regular cycle. Find out more about Afrobarometer here – https://afrobarometer.org/about

TITLE: University of Cape Town PhD Scholarships 2027: Two Funded Health Research Positions Worth R315,000 Per Year

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for two funded PhD scholarship opportunities at the University of Cape Town (UCT) for 2027, offered through the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre and the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation (DTHF) in collaboration with the University of Cape Town in South Africa.

The scholarships are designed for research-ready candidates who want to pursue rigorous doctoral research while contributing to established and actively funded global health research programmes. Successful candidates will undertake their PhDs through the UCT Department of Medicine and will work within multidisciplinary research environments emphasizing publication, analytical skills, academic development, mentorship, and increasing research independence.

Each successful candidate will receive funding valued at:

R315,000 per year

The scholarship provides core funding for the first three years of the PhD. A fourth year may be supported, but this additional year is conditional on satisfactory academic progress, including evidence of manuscript development and progress with thesis completion. The scholarship contributes toward tuition and living costs and must be held together with formal PhD registration at the University of Cape Town.

The opportunity is restricted geographically: applicants must be South African citizens or permanent residents of South Africa. Candidates must also hold a completed Master’s degree or equivalent qualification in an appropriate discipline and demonstrate previous experience with qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods research analysis.

The final deadline to apply is:

14 September 2026

Late or incomplete applications will not be considered.

About the University of Cape Town PhD Scholarship Opportunity

The scholarship call is a collaboration involving:

University of Cape Town

Desmond Tutu HIV Centre

Desmond Tutu Health Foundation

The programme is designed to support candidates seeking to complete doctoral research within active global health research programmes rather than undertake an isolated or entirely self-directed doctoral project.

This structure means successful scholars will enter research environments where there are already:

Established research programmes

Multidisciplinary research teams

Active data collection

Existing publication pipelines

Academic mentorship structures

Regular research meetings

Opportunities to produce scholarly outputs

The scholarship therefore combines doctoral funding with a highly structured research-development model.

Two PhD Scholarships Are Available

The official call provides:

Two PhD scholarship awards

Both opportunities are associated with doctoral registration at the University of Cape Town.

The scholarships are intended for candidates who have already developed the academic and research skills necessary to begin doctoral-level research.

Applicants are therefore expected to demonstrate more than general interest in public health. They should be able to show evidence of previous research experience and readiness to operate within a research-intensive doctoral environment.

Scholarship Value: R315,000 Per Year

Each scholarship is valued at:

R315,000 annually

The scholarship may potentially be available for up to:

Four years

However, the funding structure is important to understand.

Years 1–3

The first three years represent the:

Core PhD funding period

Successful candidates are expected to use this period to progress through their doctoral research milestones and develop their publication portfolio.

Possible Year 4

Funding during a fourth year is:

Optional and conditional

It depends on satisfactory progress.

Candidates seeking fourth-year funding will need to demonstrate progress such as:

Manuscript development

Thesis writing

Progress toward doctoral completion

The fourth year should therefore not be interpreted as an unconditional guaranteed additional year of funding.

What Does the Scholarship Cover?

The official call states that the funding contributes toward:

Tuition costs

Living costs

and that the scholarship must be held alongside formal registration for the PhD at the University of Cape Town.

Although the promotional announcement describes the opportunities as fully funded, the detailed official call specifically says that the R315,000 annual award contributes to tuition and living costs.

Applicants should therefore use the official funding amount when budgeting rather than assuming that every possible personal, research, travel, insurance, or relocation expense will necessarily be separately covered.

Duration of the PhD Scholarship

The normal funded doctoral period is:

Three years

with the possibility of a:

Fourth year subject to satisfactory progress

This means the overall scholarship tenure may be between:

Three and four years

depending on academic progress and the conditions attached to fourth-year funding.

Research Environment

A particularly important feature of these scholarships is the research environment into which successful candidates will be integrated.

The official call states that selected scholars will work within:

Established multidisciplinary research programmes with active data collection and publication pipelines.

This means candidates can expect their doctoral development to take place within an existing research ecosystem.

The structure emphasizes four major areas.

1. Regular Academic Oversight

Doctoral scholars will receive academic oversight aligned with the formal requirements of UCT.

Candidates will therefore be expected to work consistently toward defined doctoral milestones.

2. Structured Academic Writing Support

The programme emphasizes:

Manuscript development

Academic writing

Publication planning

This is significant because the PhD is specifically described as publication-oriented.

Candidates should therefore expect scholarly publication to form an important part of their doctoral development.

3. Interdisciplinary Research Engagement

Successful candidates will work with multidisciplinary research teams.

Global health research frequently requires engagement across fields such as:

Epidemiology

Public health

Biostatistics

Medicine

Behavioural science

Psychology

Sociology

Implementation research

Applicants who can work effectively across disciplinary boundaries may therefore be especially well positioned.

4. Research Independence

The programme seeks to develop candidates’:

Analytical capacity

Conceptual capacity

Scholarly skills

Research independence

The purpose is not simply to train candidates to perform predefined research tasks.

Rather, scholars should progressively develop the ability to formulate, analyze, interpret, publish, and communicate research independently.

Career Development Focus

The scholarship is described as an academically rigorous programme intended to help candidates progress toward:

Postdoctoral research

Research-intensive careers

Academic careers

The programme may therefore be particularly attractive to applicants who want to remain involved in health research after completing their doctorate.

Candidates are specifically expected to demonstrate a:

Clear motivation to pursue an academic or research-focused career.

Applicants whose main motivation is simply earning another qualification may find it difficult to demonstrate the long-term research orientation expected by the programme.

Who Can Apply?

Candidates must meet the University of Cape Town’s requirements for PhD registration in the:

Department of Medicine

They must also demonstrate strong potential to undertake research at doctoral level.

Several specific requirements apply.

Master’s Degree Requirement

Applicants need to have completed:

A Master’s degree or equivalent qualification

in a relevant discipline.

Examples specifically listed in the official call include:

MBChB

Public Health

Psychology

Sociology

Epidemiology

Biostatistics

Behavioural Science

Related disciplines

The inclusion of “related fields” means the list is illustrative rather than necessarily exhaustive.

However, candidates from another discipline should be able to demonstrate how their academic training provides appropriate preparation for the proposed doctoral research.

South African Citizenship or Permanent Residency Is Required

This is one of the most important eligibility requirements.

Applicants must have:

South African citizenship or South African permanent residency.

Therefore, this is not an internationally open scholarship.

Citizens of other African countries or countries outside Africa who do not have South African permanent residency are not eligible under the criteria published in the scholarship call.

Research Methods Experience

Applicants need demonstrated experience with at least one of the following:

Qualitative data analysis

Quantitative data analysis

Mixed-methods data analysis

This is an important requirement because selected candidates will work within active health-research programmes.

Applicants should therefore make their methodological expertise especially visible in their CV.

For example, relevant experience might involve:

Master’s dissertation research

Research assistant positions

Academic research projects

Health research projects

Statistical analysis

Interview or focus-group analysis

Survey analysis

Mixed-methods research projects

The call specifically requires the one-page CV to include details of the applicant’s qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods experience.

Interest in an Academic or Research Career

Candidates should demonstrate a clear motivation to pursue:

An academic career, or

A research-focused career

This aligns with the broader structure of the programme, which emphasizes publications and doctoral research independence.

Applicants should therefore use their application documents to communicate a credible research trajectory.

Additional Qualifications That Are Advantageous

Several qualifications are not stated as compulsory but may strengthen an application.

Previous Publications

Previous:

Peer-reviewed publications

Manuscripts in preparation

are considered advantageous.

Candidates do not appear to need an existing publication to be eligible.

However, evidence of academic publishing experience can help demonstrate readiness for the programme’s publication-oriented model.

Applied Health Research Experience

Previous experience in applied health research is also advantageous.

The official call provides examples including:

HIV

PrEP

Mental health

Men’s health

Infectious diseases

Non-communicable diseases

Related areas

These areas indicate the type of health-research environment in which the PhD opportunities are situated.

However, the call does not state that every applicant must already specialize in HIV.

Candidates from related health-research areas may therefore also be competitive.

Strong Academic Writing and Conceptual Thinking

Applicants should demonstrate evidence of:

Strong academic writing

Strong conceptual thinking

These qualities will be evaluated partly through the required writing sample.

This is particularly important because successful candidates will be expected to produce manuscripts and develop a publication trajectory throughout the PhD.

Expectations of Successful PhD Scholars

Successful candidates will be expected to perform several responsibilities throughout the programme.

According to the official call, scholars must:

Maintain progress toward their PhD milestones.

Contribute toward a publication trajectory during the doctorate.

Participate in academic activities.

Engage actively with supervision and mentorship.

Maintain Progress Toward PhD Milestones

Candidates should expect their progress to be formally monitored.

Milestones may relate to areas such as:

Research development

Ethics approvals

Data analysis

Training

Writing

Manuscripts

Thesis development

The precise milestones will depend on UCT doctoral requirements and the candidate’s project.

Publication Expectations

The programme explicitly expects scholars to contribute to a:

Publication trajectory during the PhD.

The doctoral experience is therefore strongly oriented toward producing scholarly outputs.

Applicants should demonstrate that they understand publication as an integral part of doctoral research rather than something considered only after graduation.

Participation in Academic Activities

Candidates will participate in activities such as:

Seminars

Research meetings

This helps integrate doctoral researchers into the wider intellectual environment of the programme.

Participation may also provide opportunities to:

Present work

Receive feedback

Learn from colleagues

Engage with multidisciplinary researchers

Build professional networks

Active Engagement With Supervision and Mentorship

Successful scholars are expected to work actively with:

Supervisors

Mentors

Structured academic oversight

The programme therefore combines independent research development with regular guidance.

Candidates should demonstrate that they can receive feedback productively while increasingly taking ownership of their own research.

Application Requirements

The application process is deliberately structured to evaluate:

Research readiness

Academic initiative

Ownership

Capacity for doctoral planning

The official call describes its application model as aligned with training and capacity-building principles.

Applicants must prepare six major documents.

1. One-Page Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a:

One-page CV

This is a much shorter format than many conventional academic CVs.

Candidates must therefore prioritize highly relevant information.

Importantly, the CV should explicitly include experience in:

Qualitative methods

Quantitative methods

Mixed-methods research

where applicable.

A strong one-page CV could prioritize:

Education

Master’s qualification

Research methods

Research employment

Publications

Relevant health research

Statistical or qualitative-analysis skills

Key awards

Avoid filling the limited space with unrelated experience.

2. One-Page Research Concept

Applicants need to prepare a:

One-page Research Concept

The document should include:

Background

Problem statement

Research aims

Significance

Alignment with a publication-focused PhD

This is likely to be one of the most important components of the application.

Candidates have only one page to demonstrate that they can identify an important health-research problem and transform it into a viable doctoral research direction.

How to Structure the One-Page Research Concept

A useful structure could be:

Background

Briefly establish the health issue and what is already known.

Problem Statement

Identify the unresolved problem or knowledge gap.

Research Aim

Explain what the proposed PhD seeks to investigate.

Significance

Explain why the research matters to:

Health outcomes

Research

Policy

Clinical practice

Programme delivery

depending on the topic.

Publication Potential

Show how the project could generate several related scholarly outputs rather than a single broad thesis product.

3. One-Page Proposed PhD Plan

Applicants must also submit a:

One-page structured three-year PhD plan.

The plan should identify:

Milestones

Outputs

Manuscripts

Coursework or training

Mentorship

Supervisory support

This requirement is unusual and important.

The selection committee is not only evaluating whether the research idea is interesting. It is also evaluating whether the applicant understands how to organize a doctoral project strategically.

Example Structure for the Three-Year PhD Plan

Year 1

Potential activities might include:

Refining research questions

Literature review

Methodological training

Ethics processes

Data preparation or collection

Initial analyses

Year 2

Potential milestones could include:

Major data analysis

Manuscript development

Conference presentation

Advanced methods training

Year 3

Potential objectives may include:

Final analyses

Additional manuscripts

Thesis integration

Submission preparation

Applicants should design their plan around their own proposed research rather than treating these examples as formal requirements.

4. Academic or Technical Writing Sample

Applicants must submit:

One example of academic or technical writing.

Acceptable examples listed in the call include:

Published paper

Thesis

Manuscript draft

Candidates should ideally choose a sample that demonstrates:

Strong analytical reasoning

Clear structure

Academic writing

Conceptual thinking

Appropriate use of evidence

Where applicants have several options, the strongest relevant research piece will generally be preferable.

5. South African ID

Candidates must submit:

A copy of their South African ID.

This corresponds with the citizenship/permanent residency eligibility condition.

Permanent residents should follow the application instructions concerning appropriate proof of status if their documentation differs.

6. Certified Master’s Certificate

Applicants must provide a:

Certified copy of their Master’s certificate.

Candidates should arrange certification early rather than waiting until the application deadline.

Application Checklist

Before submitting, applicants should ensure that they have:

A one-page CV

A one-page Research Concept

A one-page three-year PhD plan

One academic or technical writing sample

A copy of South African ID

A certified copy of the Master’s certificate

Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted by:

14 September 2026

The deadline is clearly stated both in the scholarship announcement and the detailed call documentation.

Candidates should aim to submit before the closing date, particularly because several documents require careful preparation.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted using the dedicated online application link:

APPLY HERE

The link is provided in the official scholarship call.

Applicants should complete the online process and upload all required documents before the deadline.

Selection Process

Following the initial application review:

Shortlisted candidates will be invited to an interview.

Late or incomplete applications will not be considered.

Applicants should therefore prepare not only a strong written application but also be ready to discuss:

Proposed research

Research methods

Previous research experience

Academic goals

Publication plans

Motivation for a research career

during a possible interview.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Demonstrate Research Readiness

This opportunity is explicitly aimed at research-ready candidates.

Use your CV, research concept, PhD plan, and writing sample collectively to demonstrate that you already understand how research is developed and conducted.

2. Make Your Methodological Skills Visible

Qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods experience is a formal requirement.

Do not hide this experience inside a generic description of your Master’s project.

State clearly:

Which methods you used

What data you analyzed

Which analytical tools you know

What outputs resulted

3. Develop a Focused Research Concept

A one-page research concept cannot support an overly broad project.

Instead of proposing something such as:

“Improving HIV prevention in South Africa,”

a stronger concept would identify:

A specific population

A particular intervention

A defined knowledge gap

A researchable outcome

The exact project should be tailored to the research environment and applicant’s expertise.

4. Show Publication Potential

Because the programme is explicitly publication-oriented, explain how the project could produce several coherent manuscripts or academic outputs.

Your three-year plan should reinforce this.

5. Choose the Writing Sample Carefully

The writing sample is being used as evidence of your:

Academic writing

Analytical ability

Choose your strongest relevant piece rather than simply the most recent document available.

6. Demonstrate Long-Term Research Motivation

The programme is intended to prepare researchers for postdoctoral or research-intensive career pathways.

Applicants should therefore explain how the PhD fits within their longer-term academic or research trajectory.

Why This PhD Opportunity Stands Out

Several aspects make the scholarship particularly attractive for emerging South African health researchers.

It combines:

Substantial annual financial support

Formal doctoral registration at UCT

Established global health research programmes

Multidisciplinary research teams

Active data pipelines

Publication opportunities

Structured mentorship

Academic writing support

Research-methods development

Clear doctoral milestones

A pathway toward research independence

Rather than simply providing a stipend and leaving the scholar to develop independently, the programme emphasizes an integrated research and mentorship structure.

Important Details at a Glance

Deadline: 14 September 2026

Application: https://redcap.link/8fn2m1jl

Conclusion

The University of Cape Town PhD Scholarships 2027, offered through the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre and Desmond Tutu Health Foundation, provide two promising South African researchers with substantial financial and academic support to pursue doctoral research in global and applied health.

Each award is valued at R315,000 annually, with core funding available for three years and the possibility of a fourth year where satisfactory progress is demonstrated. Funding contributes toward tuition and living expenses while candidates remain formally registered for their PhDs at UCT.

To help meet this need the MMF annually awards a small number of Morland Writing Scholarships, with the aim being to allow each Scholar the time to produce the first draft of a completed book. The Scholarships are open to anyone writing in the English language who was born in Africa, or both of whose parents were born in Africa.

Miles Morland set up the foundation which bears his name in 2013, after a career investing in Africa via two companies he created, Blakeney Management and DPI (Development Partners International). Based in London, the Miles Morland Foundation (MMF) is a UK registered charity which makes grants in areas reflecting its founder’s interests.

Grant

Scholars will receive a grant of £18,000, paid monthly over the course of twelve months. At the discretion of the Foundation, Scholars writing non-fiction, who require additional research time, could receive an additional grant, paid over a period of up to eighteen months.

Eligibility

Open to anyone writing in the English language who was born in Africa, or both of whose parents were born in Africa.

There are no age restrictions for applicants.

Application

Application must include:

A submission of between 2,000 to 5,000 words as a Word document of work that has been published and offered for sale.

Proof of publication and proof of sale.

A scan of an official document showing that you, or both of your parents, were born in Africa.

Tell them how you heard about the Morland Writing Scholarships.
