TITLE: OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship 2026 in Warsaw: Applications Open for a Six-Month Placement

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe is accepting applications for its 2026 Human Rights Internship at the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights in Warsaw, Poland. This full-time, six-month placement is expected to begin in November 2026 and will give a graduate-level student or recent graduate the opportunity to support ODIHR’s Human Rights Department.

The placement is particularly relevant to emerging professionals interested in international human rights, political science, law, international relations, human rights monitoring, democratic governance and related disciplines. Interns will support research, analysis, written reporting, event organization and the implementation of human rights programmes across the OSCE region.

According to the official OSCE vacancy announcement, applications must be submitted by 3 September 2026. Candidates must also state their availability dates in their cover letter.

OSCE ODIHR Internship 2026 at a Glance

Official position title: Intern

Issuing office: Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights

Department: Human Rights Department

Duty station: Warsaw, Poland

Requisition number: ODI000321

Job field: Human Rights

Schedule: Full-time

Employment status: Short-term

Grade: No grade

Internship duration: Six months

Expected starting period: November 2026

Issue date: 20 August 2026

Application deadline: 3 September 2026

Number of posts: The vacancy metadata lists two posts, although the main description says that the department is seeking one intern. Applicants should consult the official vacancy page for any clarification or subsequent correction.

Application method: Online through the OSCE recruitment portal

About the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights

The Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, commonly known as ODIHR, is one of the principal institutions of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

ODIHR is responsible for supporting the human dimension of the OSCE’s comprehensive approach to security. The human dimension recognizes that lasting peace and security depend not only on political and military stability, but also on democracy, respect for human rights, the rule of law and strong public institutions.

ODIHR provides assistance, expertise and practical support to governments, public institutions and civil society organizations. Its activities include:

Observing elections and assessing electoral processes;

Supporting the development of democratic institutions;

Reviewing legislation and advising governments;

Promoting the rule of law;

Monitoring and strengthening respect for human rights;

Supporting tolerance and non-discrimination;

Conducting training for government officials, law-enforcement personnel and civil society representatives; and

Helping participating States implement their OSCE human dimension commitments.

ODIHR’s activities are implemented across the OSCE’s 57 participating States. More information about its institutional mandate is available through ODIHR’s official human-dimension overview.

About the ODIHR Human Rights Department

The successful intern will be placed in ODIHR’s Human Rights Department. The department provides expert advice to OSCE participating States, organizes capacity-building initiatives and monitors the implementation of human dimension commitments.

Its work involves engagement with State authorities, national institutions, civil society representatives, human rights defenders, researchers and other stakeholders.

The department’s programmes cover a broad range of thematic human rights priorities, including:

Human rights defenders

ODIHR works to strengthen the ability of human rights defenders to conduct their legitimate activities safely and effectively. This includes monitoring the challenges defenders face and supporting participating States in fulfilling their responsibilities to protect them.

Human rights education

Activities in this area seek to improve awareness, understanding and practical application of human rights standards among public officials, law-enforcement personnel, educators, civil society organizations and other groups.

Human rights and counter-terrorism

ODIHR promotes approaches to preventing and countering terrorism that comply with international human rights standards and OSCE commitments.

Torture prevention

The department contributes to work intended to prevent torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. This may involve research, monitoring, institutional support and capacity-building.

Anti-trafficking work

ODIHR addresses the human rights dimensions of trafficking in human beings, including the protection of victims, access to justice and the development of rights-based responses.

Freedom of religion or belief

Programmes in this area support the right of individuals and communities to adopt, practise, change or manifest their religion or belief without discrimination or unjustified interference.

Freedom of peaceful assembly

ODIHR monitors developments and supports participating States in protecting the right to organize and participate in peaceful assemblies.

National human rights institutions

The department supports institutions mandated to promote and protect human rights at the national level, including through capacity development and the promotion of institutional independence.

Human rights, gender and security

This area considers the relationship between human rights, gender equality and security policies, including the need to incorporate gender perspectives into institutional and programme activities.

The selected intern may contribute to one or several of these programmes depending on departmental priorities and operational needs.

Main Responsibilities of the Human Rights Intern

The intern will assist with the implementation of activities conducted by the Human Rights Department. The responsibilities combine research, writing, project support and administrative coordination.

1. Conducting desk research and human rights analysis

The intern will research human rights developments relevant to OSCE participating States. This research will assist ODIHR in monitoring how States implement their OSCE human dimension commitments.

The work may require the intern to:

Identify relevant information from credible public sources;

Review laws, policies, reports and institutional developments;

Follow country-specific and regional human rights developments;

Organize research findings in a clear and accessible format;

Distinguish between verified information and unconfirmed claims; and

Support the preparation of internal or public-facing analysis.

The vacancy therefore requires someone who can work carefully with complex information, recognize relevant developments and communicate findings accurately.

2. Assisting with reports, briefing papers and other documents

The intern will help prepare reports, briefing materials and other written products dealing with thematic, national or regional human rights issues.

Assignments may include:

Collecting and organizing background information;

Summarizing longer reports and source materials;

Preparing initial drafts or sections of documents;

Editing and formatting written materials;

Checking facts, references and consistency;

Supporting the development of country or regional briefings; and

Contributing to documents on specific human rights themes.

Strong analytical writing is therefore central to the placement. Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate that they can convert research findings into structured, concise and evidence-based written material.

3. Supporting meetings, conferences, workshops and events

The intern will assist with the preparation and organization of activities managed by the Human Rights Department.

This may involve support before, during and after events, including:

Conducting background research;

Helping prepare agendas and supporting materials;

Organizing documents for participants;

Assisting with logistical or administrative preparations;

Supporting communication with relevant colleagues and stakeholders;

Helping ensure that event materials are properly organized; and

Contributing to follow-up documentation.

The role consequently requires attention to detail, reliability, communication skills and the ability to manage multiple tasks within established deadlines.

4. Taking notes and contributing to event reports

During meetings, conferences, workshops and other activities, the intern may be asked to take accurate notes and help prepare written records.

Effective note-taking in this context means identifying:

The central issues discussed;

Significant observations made by participants;

Recommendations or proposed actions;

Areas of agreement or disagreement;

Follow-up responsibilities; and

Information that should be reflected in an event report.

Applicants with previous experience preparing meeting minutes, workshop reports, academic summaries or conference documentation may be especially well positioned for this responsibility.

5. Supporting additional programme and department-wide activities

The intern may also support other projects, tasks and department-wide activities as assigned.

This provision reflects the varied nature of work in an international organization. The selected candidate should therefore be flexible, able to respond to changing priorities and willing to assist across different human rights themes when necessary.

Educational Requirements

Applicants must fall within one of the academic categories specified in the vacancy notice.

Eligible candidates include:

Students in the final year of higher education at the graduate or postgraduate level in a university or another accredited institution; or

Recent graduates or postgraduates who completed their studies within the previous two years.

Relevant fields of study include:

Political science;

International relations;

Law;

International human rights law; or

Another closely related discipline.

A qualification in a different field may still be relevant if the applicant can demonstrate a clear connection between their studies and ODIHR’s human rights mandate. Candidates should explain that connection directly in their application rather than expecting recruiters to infer it.

Age and Nationality Requirements

Applicants must meet the following mandatory conditions:

They must not be older than 30 years.

They must be nationals of an OSCE participating State.

Nationality is the controlling requirement. Living, studying or working in an OSCE participating State does not necessarily make someone eligible if they are not a national of one of the participating States.

The complete and current list is available on the official OSCE participating States page.

Required Skills and Competencies

In addition to meeting the academic, age and nationality conditions, applicants should demonstrate the following qualifications.

Excellent English-language proficiency

An excellent command of spoken and written English is required. The intern will undertake research, prepare written material, communicate with colleagues and contribute to reports in an international professional environment.

Applicants should be able to:

Read and understand complex human rights material;

Write clearly and accurately;

Summarize detailed information;

Communicate professionally; and

use appropriate terminology consistently.

Russian-language knowledge

Knowledge of Russian is considered an asset rather than a mandatory requirement. Candidates without Russian-language ability are not automatically excluded if they meet the essential requirements.

Applicants who speak Russian should clearly state their proficiency level and indicate whether they can use the language for research, reading, writing or professional communication.

Research and analytical writing ability

Candidates must demonstrate competence in research and analytical writing. Relevant evidence could include:

Academic research papers;

A thesis or dissertation;

Policy briefs;

Legal research;

Human rights reports;

Country or regional analysis;

Research assistance;

Monitoring reports; or

Publications produced through employment, volunteering or civil society work.

Organizational, communication and reporting skills

The successful candidate must be capable of organizing information and supporting activities in a structured manner.

Applicants should provide examples showing that they can:

Work according to deadlines;

Prioritize assignments;

Communicate with different audiences;

Prepare accurate written reports;

Maintain organized records; and

Contribute to meetings, workshops or projects.

Cultural sensitivity and sound judgment

Because ODIHR works across a diverse regional and institutional environment, the intern must demonstrate cultural sensitivity and good judgment.

This includes respecting different experiences and perspectives, communicating professionally and handling sensitive human rights information responsibly.

Understanding of gender mainstreaming

Applicants should understand the importance of integrating gender perspectives into policies, programmes, analysis and organizational activities.

This does not necessarily require a specialized gender-studies degree, but candidates should be able to demonstrate awareness of how laws, policies and security or human rights developments can affect people differently.

Computer proficiency

Applicants must be able to use Windows-based applications, including:

Word-processing software;

Microsoft Excel;

Email applications; and

Other basic office productivity tools.

The role may involve drafting and formatting reports, organizing information, maintaining records and communicating electronically with colleagues and stakeholders.

Is Previous Human Rights Experience Mandatory?

Previous exposure to or experience in human rights issues is identified as an asset, not as an absolute requirement.

Potentially relevant experience could come from:

A university research project;

A human rights course or academic specialization;

An internship with a civil society organization;

Volunteer work;

A legal clinic;

Student leadership;

Election observation;

Work with a national human rights institution;

Participation in advocacy or awareness campaigns;

Research on democracy, governance, equality or fundamental freedoms; or

Professional work involving related policy or legal questions.

Applicants with limited formal work experience should not automatically assume they are unqualified. Academic research, volunteering and extracurricular activities can help demonstrate a serious engagement with human rights issues.

Professional Development Value of the Placement

The OSCE Internship Programme is designed to expose graduate-level students and recent graduates to the Organization’s work while allowing its institutions and departments to benefit from specialized assistance.

Through this placement, the selected intern can gain practical exposure to:

International human rights monitoring;

Research on the implementation of political commitments;

The preparation of reports and briefing papers;

Country-specific and thematic analysis;

International meeting and event organization;

Professional note-taking and reporting;

Multicultural teamwork; and

The operations of an international security and human rights institution.

The OSCE’s official internship information explains that its internship programme is intended to help graduate and postgraduate students or recent graduates develop professional skills and obtain practical experience in an international environment.

However, applicants should understand that the internship does not create a commitment or guarantee of future employment with the OSCE.

Duration, Schedule and Expected Starting Date

The internship will last for six months and is expected to begin in November 2026.

The position is full-time and based at ODIHR in Warsaw, Poland. The vacancy does not describe the placement as remote or hybrid, so applicants should prepare on the basis that they will need to be available at the duty station.

The announced starting date is subject to change. Applicants must state their availability dates in their cover letter. This should be done clearly and specifically.

For example, candidates can indicate:

Their earliest possible starting date;

Whether they are available from November 2026;

Whether they can remain for the full six-month period; and

Any academic or administrative obligations that could affect their availability.

Remuneration and Living-Cost Support

Applicants should review the financial terms carefully before applying.

The OSCE states that it is not in a position to:

Pay remuneration to the intern;

Cover expenses incurred during the internship;

Pay relocation costs; or

Reimburse travel expenses.

The placement should therefore not be treated as a salaried position.

Nevertheless, interns who do not reside at the duty station may receive some compensation toward their cost of living. The stated amount is equivalent to 10 per cent of the applicable Daily Subsistence Allowance rate for Warsaw.

This contribution should not be interpreted as a salary or as full financial support. Applicants should assess whether they can cover accommodation, food, local transportation, visa-related expenses where applicable, travel to Warsaw and other personal costs.

The notice does not promise accommodation, relocation support or full living-cost coverage.

Health, Life and Accident Insurance

The selected intern may participate in the OSCE group health insurance scheme at their own expense.

Alternatively, an intern who arranges independent medical insurance must provide evidence that the coverage is valid for:

The Warsaw duty station; and

Any destinations connected with possible official duty travel.

The OSCE will cover life insurance and accident or disability insurance for the intern.

Candidates should examine the scope, exclusions and duration of any personal medical policy before the placement begins. Insurance should remain valid throughout the internship period.

How to Apply for the OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship

Applications must be submitted through the OSCE’s online recruitment platform. Interested candidates should access the official vacancy page and select the application option provided there.

A practical application process is as follows:

Review the complete vacancy notice

Confirm that you meet the academic status, age, nationality, language and skills requirements before beginning the application.

Create or update your OSCE applicant profile

Enter accurate personal, academic and professional information. Ensure that dates, qualification titles and institutional names are consistent throughout the application.

Tailor your application to the Human Rights Department

Explain how your studies, research, employment, volunteering or extracurricular activities relate to ODIHR’s human rights programmes.

Demonstrate the required skills with examples

Instead of merely stating that you have research, writing or organizational skills, describe a project or assignment through which you used them.

Prepare a focused cover letter

The cover letter should explain your motivation, relevant background and potential contribution to ODIHR. Most importantly, it must state your availability dates.

Check your language and supporting information

Proofread the application carefully. Human rights research and reporting require accuracy, so errors in the application could weaken the evidence of your written communication skills.

Submit before the deadline

Complete the online submission by 3 September 2026. The notice does not specify an exact closing time or time zone, so candidates should avoid waiting until the final hours.

How to Strengthen Your Application

The following measures are not additional eligibility requirements, but they can help applicants present their experience more effectively.

Connect your background to specific ODIHR themes

Rather than discussing human rights only in general terms, identify the areas most closely connected to your studies or experience, such as:

Human rights defenders;

Freedom of peaceful assembly;

Freedom of religion or belief;

Gender and security;

Torture prevention;

Anti-trafficking;

Human rights education;

National human rights institutions; or

Human rights-compliant counter-terrorism.

Provide evidence of analytical writing

Mention specific written work you have completed, such as a dissertation, research paper, legal memorandum, policy brief or monitoring report. Explain the subject, research method and final output.

Show that you can support events and teamwork

If you have helped organize a seminar, student conference, workshop, advocacy event or public discussion, describe your responsibilities and the result.

Address the financial conditions realistically

Because the placement is not salaried and the possible living-cost contribution is limited, applicants should make an informed plan for spending six months in Warsaw.

State your availability precisely

Do not use vague wording. Clearly confirm whether you can begin in November 2026 and remain for the full placement.

Selection Process and Communication

Only candidates selected to participate in subsequent stages of recruitment will be contacted.

Submitting an application does not guarantee an interview or further communication. Applicants should ensure that the email address and telephone details provided in their profile remain active.

The OSCE also retains the discretion to:

Re-advertise or repost the vacancy;

Cancel the recruitment process;

Offer an internship with modified terms of reference; or

Change the duration of the internship.

Applicants should monitor their email and the official recruitment portal for updates.

Important Clarification About the Number of Positions

The official listing contains an apparent inconsistency concerning the number of available places.

The main description says that the Human Rights Department is seeking to recruit one intern. However, the “Additional Information” section lists the number of posts as two.

Applicants should not rely on an unofficial interpretation of this difference. The vacancy remains a valid opportunity regardless of whether one or two candidates are ultimately appointed, and any updated information published by the OSCE should take precedence.

Diversity, Inclusion and Professional Conduct

The OSCE states that it is committed to diversity and inclusion within its workforce. Qualified female and male candidates from different religious, ethnic and social backgrounds are encouraged to apply.

Candidates selected by the Organization are expected to conduct themselves in a manner appropriate to the status of international civil servants. This includes avoiding conduct that could undermine the integrity, independence or impartiality of their official functions.

The OSCE Competency Model identifies commitment, diversity, integrity and accountability as core organizational values. It also emphasizes communication, collaboration, planning, analysis, sound decision-making, initiative and flexibility.

Application Fee and Fraud Warning

The OSCE does not request payment at any point in the application or review process.

Candidates should submit their information only through the official OSCE recruitment system and should be cautious of individuals, websites or messages requesting money in exchange for application processing, interviews or guaranteed selection.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship is:

3 September 2026

Because the official announcement does not provide an exact closing time or time zone, applicants should submit well before the deadline.

Applications should be made through the official OSCE internship vacancy page.

Final Application Checklist

Before submitting, confirm that:

You are in the final year of graduate or postgraduate study, or graduated within the previous two years;

Your academic field is political science, international relations, law, international human rights law or another related discipline;

You are not older than 30;

You are a national of an OSCE participating State;

You have an excellent command of written and spoken English;

You have described any Russian-language ability accurately;

You have provided evidence of research and analytical writing skills;

You have demonstrated organizational, communication and reporting abilities;

You have addressed cultural sensitivity and gender mainstreaming where relevant;

You can use standard Windows and Microsoft Office applications;

Your cover letter states your exact availability;

You have considered the financial and insurance conditions;

Your contact information is accurate; and

You have submitted the application by 3 September 2026.

Conclusion

The OSCE ODIHR Human Rights Internship 2026 offers graduate-level students and recent graduates an opportunity to contribute to research, reporting, events and programme implementation within one of Europe’s leading human rights and democratic institutions.

The placement is especially suitable for candidates seeking practical exposure to international human rights monitoring, analytical writing, democratic governance and the implementation of OSCE human dimension commitments. It can also provide valuable experience working in a multicultural institutional environment and engaging with complex country-specific and thematic human rights questions.

Candidates should nevertheless consider the terms carefully. The internship is full-time, based in Warsaw and not salaried. Travel and other personal expenses will not be reimbursed, while the possible living-cost contribution is limited to qualifying non-resident interns.

Eligible candidates who can commit to the full six-month period should prepare a tailored application, state their availability clearly and submit through the official OSCE portal no later than 3 September 2026.

TITLE: PALOMERA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Science Policy Support

Image:

Policy alignment of open access monographs in the European Research Area

Academic books continue to play an important role in scholarly production and research communication, particularly in the social sciences and humanities. As an important output of scholarly production, academic books must be included in open science/open access policies and strategies developed by research funders and institutions, to ensure that open science becomes the modus operandi of modern science across all disciplines. However, contrary to article publishing in journals (especially in the areas of Science, Technology, and Medicine) academic books have not been a focus point for open access (OA) policymakers. Consequently books are only rarely mandated to be published OA by research funders and institutions.

PALOMERA will investigate the reasons for this situation across geographies, languages, economies, and disciplines within the European Research Area (ERA). Through desk studies, surveys, in-depth interviews, and use cases, PALOMERA will collect, structure, analyse, and make available knowledge that can explain the challenges and bottlenecks that prevent OA to academic books. Based on this evidence PALOMERA will provide actionable recommendations and concrete resources to support and coordinate aligned funder and institutional policies for OA books, with the overall objective of speeding up the transition to open access for books to further promote open science. The recommendations will address all relevant stakeholders (research funders and institutions, researchers, publishers, infrastructure providers, libraries, and national policymakers).

The PALOMERA consortium broadly represents all relevant stakeholders for OA academic books, but will facilitate co-creation and validation events throughout the project to ensure that the views and voices of all relevant stakeholders are represented, promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion. This will assure maximal consensus and take-up of the recommendations.

TITLE: ActHIVate Fund Grants 2026–2028: €2 Million Funding for MSM and Trans-Led Organisations Advancing HIV Services, Advocacy and Inclusive Healthcare

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Aidsfonds has announced the upcoming launch of the ActHIVate Fund Request for Proposals, a new funding opportunity designed to strengthen community-led HIV responses for men who have sex with men (MSM) and trans communities in countries and settings where access to healthcare remains highly restricted.

With a total of €2 million available in the first funding round, the ActHIVate Fund will provide flexible support to established MSM- and trans-led community organisations delivering HIV-related healthcare, conducting strategic advocacy, and working to integrate inclusive services into existing health systems.

The first full Request for Proposals is scheduled to open on 21 September 2026, with applications due by 25 October 2026.

The funding will cover an implementation period of approximately one year and nine months, from April 2027 to December 2028, and Aidsfonds expects to award funding to up to 20 organisations.

About the ActHIVate Fund

The ActHIVate Fund has been developed in response to increasing challenges faced by community-led organisations working with MSM and trans communities.

MSM and trans people continue to experience disproportionately high levels of HIV infection in many parts of the world. At the same time, they can face significant barriers when attempting to access healthcare, including stigma, discrimination, criminalisation, hostile political environments and limited availability of inclusive health services.

For many years, community-led organisations and peer outreach initiatives have played a critical role in addressing these challenges. These organisations have helped communities access HIV prevention, testing, treatment linkages, follow-up support and other essential health services while also advocating for human rights and more inclusive healthcare systems.

However, the organisations providing these services are increasingly operating under financial and political pressure.

The ActHIVate Fund has therefore been created to provide flexible and accessible funding to organisations that are already doing this critical work and need resources to maintain services, strengthen their organisations and advocate for sustainable changes within health systems.

Why the ActHIVate Fund Is Needed

The global HIV response has entered a challenging period as international development funding has declined and several major funding streams have experienced significant disruptions.

According to information provided by Aidsfonds, official development assistance from OECD Development Assistance Committee members decreased by 23.1%, representing the largest single-year decline recorded.

Funding disruptions have also had a direct effect on HIV services.

Cuts and changes affecting PEPFAR-supported programmes have particularly affected prevention and community-based HIV services. Aidsfonds cites findings from amfAR’s PEPFAR Pulse Study indicating that prevention investment declined sharply, with 51% less funding available and 43% of service providers forced to stop providing at least one prevention service.

The funding crisis has also contributed to the closure of health facilities and the discontinuation of HIV programme components. According to Aidsfonds, at least 1,700 health facilities have closed, while 73% of service providers have discontinued at least one component of their HIV programmes.

These changes can disproportionately affect key populations, including MSM and trans people, who may already experience significant difficulties accessing mainstream health services.

The ActHIVate Fund seeks to help address this situation by supporting organisations that are embedded within the affected communities and have the experience and relationships necessary to provide services effectively.

Objective of the ActHIVate Fund

The central objective of ActHIVate is to support community-led HIV responses for MSM and trans communities in restrictive and criminalised environments.

The fund will focus on three major areas:

Community-led HIV-related healthcare service delivery

Strategic advocacy

Integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing health systems

The programme is not intended simply to provide short-term emergency funding.

Instead, it aims to support organisations in addressing immediate health needs while also generating evidence and strengthening approaches that can influence healthcare systems over the longer term.

Successful applicants are therefore expected to demonstrate how their community-led work can contribute to stronger, more inclusive and sustainable HIV and healthcare responses.

How the ActHIVate Fund Was Developed

The fund was developed through extensive consultations with representatives of MSM and trans communities.

These consultations highlighted the urgent need for funding that is:

Flexible

Accessible

Responsive to community needs

Capable of sustaining essential HIV-related services

Supportive of advocacy and human rights efforts

Suitable for organisations working in difficult or restrictive environments

Community representatives emphasised that organisations already working within these communities understand their needs and are often best positioned to deliver effective services.

As a result, ActHIVate places community organisations at the centre of both implementation and decision-making.

What Activities Can the ActHIVate Grant Support?

The ActHIVate Fund has a broad scope covering HIV services, advocacy and organisational strengthening.

1. Community-Led HIV Service Delivery

Funding can support community-led HIV-related healthcare services, including:

HIV prevention

Linkages to HIV treatment

Follow-up support

Other allied health services that are particularly important to MSM and trans communities in the applicant’s context

Applicants should demonstrate a clear understanding of the health needs of the communities they serve and explain how their proposed activities will address barriers to accessing appropriate services.

2. Building Evidence for Advocacy

Organisations can use their service-delivery experience to build evidence that can strengthen their advocacy efforts.

This may involve documenting:

Service gaps

Community healthcare needs

Barriers to accessing healthcare

Experiences of MSM and trans communities

Lessons learned from community-led service delivery

The evidence generated should contribute to advocacy for policy and health-system improvements.

3. Advocacy for Better Healthcare Access

The fund can support advocacy aimed at reducing barriers preventing MSM and trans communities from accessing HIV and other essential health services.

This may include efforts to:

Promote more inclusive healthcare policies

Address discriminatory barriers

Improve access to HIV services

Advocate for more responsive healthcare systems

Strengthen recognition of the healthcare needs of MSM and trans communities

4. Integration of Inclusive Services Into Health Systems

Another important area of ActHIVate is advocacy for better integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing healthcare systems and policies.

The long-term objective is to demonstrate approaches that can influence and strengthen mainstream health responses rather than operating entirely outside existing systems.

5. Organisational Core Strengthening

ActHIVate recognises that organisations require more than project-specific funding to remain effective.

The fund can therefore provide support for core organisational strengthening, enabling organisations to build their capacity to undertake critical HIV service delivery and advocacy work.

This flexible approach recognises that strong community organisations require adequate organisational resources to sustain their work and respond effectively to changing circumstances.

Intersectionality and Other Key Populations

ActHIVate recognises that MSM and trans communities are not homogeneous groups and that individuals may experience multiple vulnerabilities simultaneously.

The fund specifically recognises the intersection between MSM and trans communities and other key populations.

For example, proposed work may take into account the experiences of:

MSM and trans people who are sex workers

MSM and trans people who use drugs

Other community members facing overlapping barriers to HIV prevention, treatment and healthcare

Applicants should consider the realities of the communities they serve and demonstrate how their proposed work responds to the specific context in which they operate.

Activities That Are Outside the Scope of the Fund

Although the ActHIVate Fund covers a range of HIV, advocacy and organisational activities, certain activities are specifically excluded.

Multi-Country or Regional Projects

The fund does not support multi-country or regional projects that engage more than one country.

The grant is intended to support work within the individual country of implementation described in the application.

Large-Scale Health-System Improvements

The fund does not cover large-scale health-system infrastructure or technology projects such as:

Establishing health information technology systems

Clinical software

Digital databases

Laboratory systems

Projects exclusively focused on community-led monitoring

Managing or building supply chains

Facilitating task shifting

Procurement of Health Products

Grant funding cannot be used for the procurement of:

Medicines

Vaccines

PrEP

ART

Applicants should ensure that their proposed budgets do not rely on the grant to purchase these products.

Conference Attendance and Hosting

The fund does not support:

Attendance at conferences

Hosting conferences

Large Capital Purchases

Large capital expenditures are outside the scope of the fund.

Examples include:

Buildings

Large equipment

Facilities

Research Without a Clear Advocacy or Service-Delivery Purpose

Research activities are not eligible where they do not have a clear connection to either:

Advocacy

Service delivery

Applicants should demonstrate how any research-related component directly contributes to their HIV services or advocacy objectives.

Who Can Apply for the ActHIVate Fund?

The primary applicants are registered local community organisations led by MSM and trans community members.

Organisations must have substantial demonstrated experience in relevant areas.

Eligible organisations should be able to demonstrate experience in:

Providing critical HIV services to MSM and trans communities

Conducting advocacy relating to MSM and trans health and rights

Engaging with local and/or national governments

Engaging with health systems

Addressing healthcare barriers affecting MSM and trans communities

Can Unregistered Organisations Apply?

Yes.

Unregistered organisations can also apply if they already have an established fiscal host.

This provides an opportunity for community organisations that may not have formal legal registration but have an appropriate fiscal-hosting arrangement in place.

Applicants should carefully review the full Request for Proposals once it is released because the complete eligibility criteria and detailed requirements will be provided at that stage.

Eligible Countries and Regions

The first ActHIVate Fund call will support organisations operating in:

Uganda

Ugandan community-led organisations meeting the programme’s requirements can apply.

Nigeria

Nigerian MSM- and trans-led community organisations that meet the eligibility requirements can also apply.

Eastern Europe and Central Asia

The fund will cover selected countries in the Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA) region.

The specific eligible countries should be confirmed in the full Request for Proposals.

Southwest Asia and North Africa

The fund will also operate in selected countries in the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region.

Applicants should consult the full RFP when it is released for the definitive country list.

Important Country Restriction

The grant supports work within one country of implementation.

Multi-country or regional projects involving more than one country are outside the scope of this funding opportunity.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The first ActHIVate Fund Request for Proposals has a total funding envelope of:

€2,000,000

The funding will cover an implementation period running from:

April 2027 to December 2028

This represents approximately one year and nine months of implementation.

Aidsfonds expects that up to 20 applications will receive funding.

The exact amount available to each successful organisation and the detailed budget requirements will be specified in the full Request for Proposals.

Community-Led Decision-Making

A significant feature of the ActHIVate Fund is its approach to decision-making.

Aidsfonds states that communities should play a central role in decisions about funding and investment because community members have direct knowledge of the challenges they face and the approaches that work in their contexts.

Grant decisions will therefore be made by an ActHIVate Grantmaking Committee.

The committee will consist of external members who are community leaders and experts from the regions and communities covered by the Request for Proposals.

The aim is to develop a balanced portfolio of funded organisations based on factors such as:

Objectives

Countries and regions

Populations

Budgets

This community-centred approach is intended to ensure that funding decisions reflect the realities and priorities of the communities the programme seeks to support.

ActHIVate Fund Application Timeline

Applicants should take note of the following important dates:

Application Stage
Date

Full Request for Proposals published and grants portal opens
21 September 2026

Full proposal submission deadline
25 October 2026

Funding decision
Mid-December 2026

Implementation begins
March/April 2027

Funding period
April 2027 – December 2028

Application Deadline

The deadline for submitting the full proposal is:

25 October 2026

Organisations interested in applying should begin preparing early rather than waiting until the application portal opens.

Visit the official website HERE

Click HERE for more global grant opportunities

What Should Potential Applicants Prepare?

Because the complete RFP has not yet been released, applicants should wait for the official requirements before finalising their applications.

However, based on the announced scope of the fund, prospective applicants can begin organising information about the following areas.

1. Organisational Information

Applicants can prepare information about:

Registration status

Leadership structure

Community ownership and leadership

Fiscal host arrangements, where applicable

Organisational experience and capacity

2. Previous Experience

Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate previous experience in:

HIV service-delivery programmes

Prevention activities

Treatment linkages

Follow-up services

Advocacy initiatives

Government engagement

Health-system engagement

3. Communities Served

Applicants should clearly understand and be able to describe:

The MSM communities they serve

The trans communities they serve

Intersectional populations within their communities

Specific healthcare barriers in their local context

4. Proposed Activities

Applicants should consider how their proposed project will address relevant areas such as:

HIV service delivery

Strategic advocacy

Evidence generation linked to advocacy or services

Integration of inclusive services into health systems

Organisational strengthening

5. Expected Impact

Applicants should consider how their proposed project will:

Improve access to healthcare

Strengthen community-led HIV responses

Generate useful evidence for advocacy

Reduce barriers to HIV and health services

Improve integration of inclusive services into health systems

Contribute to longer-term health-system change

6. Budget Planning

Applicants should prepare realistic budgets covering eligible activities and organisational strengthening needs while ensuring that proposed expenditures comply with the fund’s restrictions.

Applicants should ensure that their plans do not include activities specifically listed as out of scope.

Q&A Session

Aidsfonds has indicated that a Q&A session will become available only after the full Request for Proposals is published.

Organisations with questions about detailed eligibility requirements, budgets, application procedures or other technical aspects should consult the full RFP and accompanying Q&A materials once they are released.

Why This Grant Opportunity Matters

The ActHIVate Fund represents an important funding opportunity for community-led organisations working at the intersection of HIV, healthcare access and human rights.

MSM and trans-led organisations often have direct relationships with communities that mainstream healthcare systems struggle to reach. Their peer-led approaches can help individuals overcome stigma, discrimination, fear and other barriers that may prevent them from seeking HIV prevention, testing, treatment or other health services.

At the same time, these organisations are operating in an increasingly difficult funding environment.

By providing flexible funding that combines service delivery, advocacy and organisational strengthening, ActHIVate aims to support organisations not only in responding to immediate healthcare needs but also in building stronger systems for the future.

Conclusion

The ActHIVate Fund is a major new grant opportunity from Aidsfonds designed to strengthen HIV responses led by and for MSM and trans communities in restrictive and criminalised settings.

With €2 million available in the first funding round, the fund will support up to 20 organisations working in Uganda, Nigeria and selected countries in Eastern Europe and Central Asia and Southwest Asia and North Africa.

The programme places particular emphasis on three interconnected areas: community-led HIV service delivery, strategic advocacy, and the integration of MSM- and trans-friendly services into existing health systems. It also provides support for organisational core strengthening, recognising that sustainable community-led responses require strong organisations and flexible resources.

Eligible organisations should have substantial experience serving MSM and trans communities, delivering HIV-related services, conducting advocacy and engaging with governments or health systems. Unregistered organisations may also be eligible where they have an established fiscal host.

The full Request for Proposals and grants portal are scheduled to open on 21 September 2026, while the full proposal submission deadline is 25 October 2026.

Prospective applicants should use the period before the launch to review their organisational experience, proposed activities, evidence, partnerships and budgets so they are prepared to respond when the complete requirements become available.

The ActHIVate Fund ultimately seeks to ensure that community-led organisations have the resources needed to continue providing essential HIV services today while helping create more inclusive and sustainable healthcare systems for MSM and trans communities in the future.

TITLE: Press Release: A Free Open-Source Digital Grants Management System Developed for Science Granting Councils in Sub-Saharan Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana and Nairobi, Kenya (October 12, 2021) – A digital grants management system has been developed and positioned for adoption by Africa’s Science Granting Councils. This forms part of activities being implemented by the Research Management Project under the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI).

The Research Management Project of SGCI, seeks to strengthen the capacities of Africa’s Science Granting Councils to play their essential roles in research, knowledge generation and innovation through training, technical support, and peer-to-peer learning.

In an increasingly digitalized world, the development of the online system is critical and aims at improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the SGCs’ grants management processes. The partners involved – the Association of African Universities (AAU), the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) developed the system as part of activities outlined in a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed by the parties.

The AAU, AAS and UNCST undertook to upgrade the UNCST grants management system and strategically position it for adoption by all the 15 SGCs participating in the SGCI. These are the Science Granting councils in Ghana, Burkina Faso, Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal, Botswana, Malawi, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Ethiopia, Namibia, and Rwanda.

Working collaboratively with the Councils, the system development partners ensured that the online grants management system is well equipped with multi-lingual functionalities and the flexibility to accommodate the different needs of the SGCs.

“To promote quick adoption of the system, an engagement process with key stakeholders and the SGCs has been carefully executed by the partners to ensure clarity concerning the differences that exist amongst the SGCs in terms of managing granting processes” said Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management at the AAU.

In ensuring that all requirements were met for the different groups of stakeholders who will be utilizing the system, the team put together for its development comprised of Project Management and Oversight; Grants Management Experts; Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Experts; Systems Engineering and Software Development Experts; as well as Finance and Audit personnel.

“The team was cognizant of the need to promote standardized processes among all the SGCs while preserving requirements for the grants management processes of the individual SGCs” she added.

The digitalized grants management system broadly encompasses functions such as Calls for Proposals (publication and receipt of applications); Reviewers Database Management; Proposals Completeness Check and Criteria Establishment; Technical Review of Proposals and Criteria Establishment; Grants Awarding and Contracting; Grants Monitoring, Progress Reporting, Evaluation, and Learning. Other functions include Financial Management and Monitoring; Rolling out and implementation of the system; Knowledge Transfer and Continuous improvement of the Grant Management System.

The implementation of the digital grants management system by the SGCs will contribute towards integrated national data systems and facilitate the flow of data among diverse users and stakeholders.

The SGCI is a multi-funder initiative that is funded by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC), South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF) and the German Research Foundation (DFG).

The Association of African Universities, the African Academy of Sciences and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) are strongly committed to working closely with the Science Granting Councils to ensure full adoption of the system and optimum derivation of the benefits therein.

A copy of the Press Release can be downloaded from here – https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Press-Release-_Digital-Grants-Managment-System_-SGCI-Research-Management-Project.pdf
