TITLE: Alpha Fellowship 2026: Join a Breakout a16z Startup or Get Up to $250,000 to Build Your Own Company.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Highly technical students and recent software engineering graduates looking for an opportunity to accelerate their careers in the startup ecosystem can apply for the Alpha Fellowship, a programme designed to place exceptional early-career engineers into full-time roles at fast-growing companies within the Andreessen Horowitz ecosystem or provide aspiring founders with capital to begin building their own company.

The Alpha Fellowship is designed for ambitious technical builders who do not want to wait years before taking on meaningful responsibility.

Participants can follow one of two pathways. The Startup Track connects successful fellows with fast-growing portfolio companies for full-time engineering positions that include salary and equity. The Founder Track is designed for individuals who want to build their own startup and provides early capital even when they do not yet have a formal company, established team or fully developed idea.

Both pathways begin with an approximately two-month, eight-week, in-person fellowship experience that includes an immersive retreat, founder discussions, curated dinners, small-group conversations and opportunities to interact with engineers, startup founders, operators and investors.

The programme also provides fellows with access to the broader a16z speedrun and EO Ventures communities and events.

For applicants who want to work at a rapidly growing technology company, become a founder or gain exposure to experienced entrepreneurs and investors, Alpha offers a potentially significant early-career pathway.

What Is the Alpha Fellowship?

The Alpha Fellowship is an early-career programme focused on highly technical software engineers who have demonstrated an ability and desire to build.

Its central proposition is straightforward: rather than waiting for an opportunity to emerge, technically strong students and recent graduates can use Alpha as a direct route into either a high-growth startup or entrepreneurship.

The programme offers two main choices:

Join a breakout portfolio company through the Startup Track.

Start your own company through the Founder Track.

The fellowship component provides an intensive in-person experience, while the two tracks provide different long-term outcomes.

For Startup Track participants, the fellowship is combined with a full-time engineering position.

For Founder Track participants, the fellowship is combined with the opportunity to build a startup and access early-stage funding.

Who Is Alpha Looking For?

Alpha is looking for people who are highly technical and have demonstrated that they can build.

The programme specifically targets:

Highly technical software engineers

Exceptional students

Recent graduates

Recent graduates within approximately three years of leaving school

People with a track record of building

Individuals with strong technical curiosity

People who want to move quickly into startups or entrepreneurship

The programme is not designed as a general graduate fellowship for applicants from every professional background.

It is specifically focused on software engineering talent.

A Programme for Builders

A central theme of Alpha is building.

The programme is intended for people who do not simply want to learn about startups but want to participate directly in building products, companies and technology.

For applicants joining the Startup Track, this means becoming a full-time engineer at a rapidly growing company.

For Founder Track applicants, it means having the opportunity to begin building a company full-time.

This makes Alpha particularly relevant to technically skilled individuals who want their early careers to involve substantial hands-on work.

The Two Alpha Fellowship Tracks

Startup Track: Join a Fast-Growing Portfolio Company

The Startup Track is designed for technical students and recent graduates who want to gain experience inside a high-growth startup.

Successful candidates can take full-time engineering roles at fast-growing companies within the a16z portfolio.

The fellowship portion lasts approximately two months, but the employment opportunity continues beyond the fellowship.

What the Startup Track Provides

Participants can receive:

A full-time engineering position

Employment with a fast-growing portfolio company

Salary

Equity

An eight-week in-person fellowship experience

A kickoff retreat

Founder AMAs

Small-group dinners

Access to members of the a16z speedrun community

Exposure to engineers, founders and investors

Continued employment after the fellowship

The role is not simply an internship or temporary placement.

Fellows are hired directly by the matched company and continue in their full-time roles after the fellowship concludes.

How Startup Matching Works

The matching process is designed around mutual fit between candidates and participating companies.

Candidates and companies rank their preferences, after which matches are made.

If a candidate is matched with a company and accepts the opportunity, the fellow becomes an employee of that company.

This is an important distinction: fellows who join startups are not employees of a16z simply because the company is part of the a16z portfolio.

Instead, the successful fellow is hired directly by the participating company.

Founder Track: Start Your Own Company

The Founder Track is designed for technically strong individuals who want to become entrepreneurs.

Its most distinctive feature is that applicants do not necessarily need to have already established a conventional startup.

Alpha states that it is willing to back founders at an extremely early stage, including before they have:

A legal entity

A complete startup idea

A founding team

This makes the programme particularly interesting for technical builders who have the ambition to become founders but are still at the beginning of the process.

Apply as an Individual

Founder Track applicants apply individually.

If an applicant already knows who they want to build a company with, each potential founder should submit their own application and identify the person or people they intend to build with.

This means that an applicant does not need to wait until they have assembled a complete founding team before applying.

Founder Track Funding

The Founder Track provides significant early-stage financial support.

Accepted founders receive an initial:

$20,000 grant

The programme also makes available:

Up to $250,000 in total investment

This gives accepted founders capital to begin working full-time on their company.

The programme’s stated timeline explains that accepted founders receive their initial $20,000 grant and begin working full-time on their idea, with up to $250,000 in total investment available.

This is particularly significant because Alpha is willing to support founders at a stage when they may not yet have a traditional venture-backed startup.

Potential Access to a16z Speedrun

Alpha also provides a potential pathway into a16z speedrun, described by the programme as its flagship startup programme.

Once Alpha fellows complete the fellowship with a team and company formed, they receive priority consideration for a16z speedrun.

The programme states that speedrun can provide:

Up to $1 million in investment

For aspiring founders, this means Alpha can potentially serve as an early step in a larger startup-building and fundraising journey.

The pathway can therefore look like:

Apply to Alpha as a technical builder.

Join the Founder Track if selected.

Receive initial funding.

Build a team and company.

Complete the Alpha fellowship.

Receive priority consideration for a16z speedrun.

Potentially access further investment through speedrun.

The Eight-Week In-Person Fellowship

Both tracks include an approximately two-month, eight-week fellowship experience.

The programme is conducted in person and is designed to surround fellows with experienced technical and startup leaders.

The fellowship includes:

An immersive kickoff retreat

Curated dinners

Founder AMAs

Small-group discussions

Conversations with engineering leaders

Meetings with portfolio founders

Interactions with investors

Access to selected a16z speedrun events

Participation in the broader startup community

Rather than functioning solely as classroom-based training, the fellowship is designed around direct exposure to people building and funding technology companies.

Founder AMAs and Community Events

One of the programme’s notable features is access to founder conversations.

Fellows participate in founder AMAs, allowing them to learn directly from people who have built technology companies.

They also gain opportunities to participate in small-group dinners and discussions with people working across the startup ecosystem.

The objective is to give fellows exposure to the practical realities of building and scaling technology companies.

Speakers and Mentors

The Alpha Fellowship lists a range of technology founders, investors and leaders among its speakers and mentors.

These include:

Marc Andreessen

Marc Andreessen is listed as a co-founder and general partner at a16z.

Chris Best

Chris Best is listed as founder and CEO of Substack.

Michael Lingelbach

Michael Lingelbach is listed as founder and CEO of Hedra.

Lisha Li

Lisha Li is listed as founder of Rosebud AI and formerly of Pinterest.

Maxwell Wang

Maxwell Wang is listed as founder of Dispatcher and formerly of SpaceX.

Elena Wagenemas

Elena Wagenemas is listed as founder of Taya and formerly of Apple.

Andrew Chen

Andrew Chen is listed as a general partner at a16z.

Roland Fryer

Roland Fryer is listed as founding general partner at EO Ventures and a Harvard professor.

These connections provide fellows with exposure to experienced technology entrepreneurs, investors and operators.

Previous Speakers

The programme also highlights previous speakers associated with major technology companies.

These include:

Dylan Field, co-founder and CEO of Figma

Jeff Lawson, co-founder and CEO of Twilio

Adam D’Angelo, founder of Quora

Rahul Vohra, founder of Superhuman AI

Bobby Murphy, CTO of Snap

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel

Kevin Weil, VP of OpenAI for Science

Emmett Shear, founder of Twitch

Fellows will also be invited to selected a16z speedrun events.

Career Opportunities Through the Startup Track

For early-career software engineers, the Startup Track offers more than a short-term fellowship.

The successful candidate receives a full-time role at a participating portfolio company.

This can provide experience in:

Product development

Software engineering

Startup environments

Rapid product iteration

Working with technical teams

Building products at high-growth companies

Collaborating with founders and operators

Because the role continues after the fellowship, fellows have the opportunity to build a longer-term career within their matched company.

Salary and Equity

Startup Track participants receive a full-time engineering position with:

Salary

Equity

Compensation is determined by the hiring company.

This means applicants should not assume that all fellows will receive an identical compensation package. The actual terms depend on the company and position into which they are matched.

The Founder Opportunity

For those who want to build rather than join an existing company, the Founder Track offers a different type of opportunity.

Instead of being matched to an established startup, the participant works full-time on creating a company.

The programme can support founders even before they have:

Incorporated a company

Developed a final product

Built a team

Fully defined the startup idea

This makes the Founder Track particularly relevant to technical people who have strong entrepreneurial ambitions.

Who Can Apply as a Student?

Students are eligible to apply.

However, the full-time nature of the programme is important.

Students selected for the Startup Track must be prepared to take on a full-time engineering position.

Founder Track participants are expected to work full-time on their company.

Therefore, students should consider whether they can make the required commitment before applying.

Recent Graduate Eligibility

Recent graduates can also apply.

The programme specifically focuses on recent graduates who are within approximately three years of leaving school.

This makes Alpha primarily an early-career opportunity rather than a programme for experienced engineers who have already spent many years in the industry.

Applicants should therefore consider how recently they completed their studies when assessing their eligibility.

U.S. Work Authorization Requirement

One of the most important requirements for prospective applicants is U.S. work authorization.

Applicants must have valid authorization to work full-time in the United States.

This requirement is especially important for international candidates.

Simply being a highly skilled software engineer or graduating from a university outside the United States does not remove the work authorization requirement.

Applicants who do not have the required U.S. work authorization should carefully review the official eligibility requirements before applying.

Geographic Eligibility

The programme information does not identify a specific race, nationality or continent as an eligibility category.

However, the U.S. work authorization requirement is a major practical eligibility condition.

The fellowship is also conducted in person, meaning successful candidates need to be able to participate physically in the programme and relocate near the relevant a16z office.

Consequently, prospective international applicants should evaluate both their work authorization and ability to relocate.

Is Alpha Only for Software Engineers?

Yes.

The programme states that Alpha is exclusively for software engineers.

It is therefore not intended as a general technology fellowship for every technical profession.

Applicants whose primary background is in areas such as:

Graphic design

Marketing

Communications

Sales

Finance

General business

Non-technical operations

should not assume that the programme is suitable for them unless they also meet the software engineering requirements.

What Does “Track Record of Building” Mean?

Alpha is looking for people who can demonstrate that they build.

For applicants, this could mean being able to show evidence of:

Software projects

Products

Applications

Technical experiments

Startup projects

Open-source work

Other substantial technical projects

The exact evidence will vary from applicant to applicant, but the underlying idea is that Alpha wants people who demonstrate initiative and technical execution.

For more information on Alpha Fellowship 2026, VISIT HERE.

How the Application Process Works

The Alpha Fellowship selection process has several stages.

Stage 1: Submit an Application

Applicants submit their application through the official Alpha application portal.

The programme encourages candidates to apply early.

The current programme information states that Cohort 1 applications have closed and that applicants can submit applications to be considered when Cohort 2 opens in September 2026.

Early applicants receive priority review.

Stage 2: Technical Assessment and Interviews

Selected applicants proceed to a technical assessment and live interviews.

This stage allows the programme to evaluate the applicant’s technical ability and overall fit.

Stage 3: Begin Full-Time

Successful candidates then proceed according to their selected track.

Startup Track

Candidates and companies rank preferences and matches are made according to mutual fit.

Successful candidates are hired directly by their matched company.

Founder Track

Accepted founders receive their initial $20,000 grant and begin working full-time on their startup idea.

They can potentially receive up to $250,000 in total investment.

Stage 4: The On-Ramp

The fellowship begins with an immersive retreat.

During the retreat, fellows meet one another and spend time with the a16z speedrun team.

Stage 5: Fellowship Programming

From the beginning of the fellowship through its completion, fellows participate in weekly small-group conversations with engineers, operators and investors.

These conversations take place alongside the fellows’ normal full-time work.

Stage 6: Completion

The fellowship concludes with a capstone event.

Fellows present to the a16z speedrun team and broader community.

Startup Track fellows continue working in their full-time positions after the fellowship.

Founder Track participants continue building their companies.

Fellowship Timeline

The programme information provides a six-step timeline:

01. Application

Submit an application and be considered for the relevant cohort.

02. Interview and Assessment

Complete the technical assessment and live interviews if selected.

03. Full-Time Start

Begin either the startup role or full-time company-building journey.

04. On-Ramp

Participate in the immersive kickoff retreat.

05. Fellowship Programming

Take part in weekly discussions, dinners and conversations with leaders from the technology and startup ecosystem.

06. Completion

Complete the fellowship through the capstone event and continue along the selected career or founder pathway.

Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 Application Status

Applicants should pay close attention to the cohort information.

The programme states that:

Cohort 1 applications have closed.

The application information directs candidates to submit applications for consideration when:

Cohort 2 opens in September 2026.

The programme also states that early applicants receive priority review.

This means applicants interested in Cohort 2 should not wait until the last possible moment.

Is There a Final Application Deadline?

The information provided does not give a specific final closing date for Cohort 2.

Instead, the website states that Cohort 2 opens in September 2026 and encourages applicants to apply early because early applicants receive priority review.

Therefore, prospective applicants should not invent or assume a September 30 deadline.

The safest approach is to monitor the official Alpha application page and apply as soon as the Cohort 2 application window becomes available.

How Many Fellows Will Be Selected?

The programme indicates that it may admit up to 10 fellows per track.

This means the programme could have up to approximately 10 participants in the Startup Track and up to approximately 10 in the Founder Track, although the exact number selected may vary.

Given the technical requirements and the benefits attached to both tracks, applicants should expect a competitive selection process.

Benefits of the Alpha Fellowship

The Alpha Fellowship combines professional experience, community, mentorship and potential financial support.

Key benefits include:

1. Full-Time Startup Employment

Startup Track fellows can receive full-time engineering positions at fast-growing portfolio companies.

2. Salary and Equity

Successful startup-track candidates receive salary and equity through their matched employer.

3. Startup Experience

Participants gain direct experience working in a fast-growing technology company.

4. Founder Opportunity

Technical builders can use the Founder Track to start their own company.

5. Initial $20,000 Grant

Accepted Founder Track participants receive an initial $20,000 grant.

6. Up to $250,000 in Investment

The Founder Track offers up to $250,000 in total investment.

7. Potential $1 Million Investment Pathway

Founder Track participants receive an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun, which can provide access to up to $1 million in investment.

8. Access to Experienced Founders

Fellows participate in conversations with technology founders, investors and engineering leaders.

9. Strong Startup Network

Participants gain access to the a16z speedrun and EO Ventures communities and events.

10. In-Person Community

The programme provides opportunities to build relationships with other technically strong builders in person.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Alpha Fellowship may be especially relevant to a person who can say:

“I am a strong software engineer.”

“I have already built meaningful technical projects.”

“I am a current student or recent graduate.”

“I want to work at a high-growth startup.”

“I want to become a founder.”

“I want direct access to experienced founders and investors.”

“I am prepared to work full-time.”

“I have valid U.S. work authorization.”

“I can participate in an in-person programme.”

If these characteristics describe an applicant, Alpha may be worth serious consideration.

Who Is Less Likely to Be Eligible?

The programme is not designed for everyone.

Applicants may not be suitable if they:

Are not software engineers

Do not have strong technical skills

Have no evidence of building

Are not students or recent graduates within the relevant early-career window

Cannot work full-time in the United States

Cannot participate in person

Cannot relocate as required

Are seeking a part-time opportunity

Are specifically looking for a remote fellowship

Why Apply Early?

The programme explicitly encourages early applications.

According to the application timeline, early applicants receive priority review.

This is important because waiting until the end of the application period could put an applicant at a disadvantage compared with candidates who submit earlier.

Since Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026 and a specific closing date has not been provided, prospective applicants should prepare their materials in advance.

What Applicants Should Prepare

Although applicants should follow the official application requirements, candidates can prepare by gathering:

An updated software engineering resume

A clear record of technical projects

Links or documentation demonstrating what they have built, where appropriate

Information about educational background

Evidence of technical achievements

Details about startup or product-building experience

A clear explanation of their career ambitions

Their preferred pathway, where applicable

Information regarding U.S. work authorization

Availability for the full-time and in-person requirements

A strong application should make it easy for the selection team to understand what the candidate has built and why they are ready for an opportunity of this scale.

Application Link

Interested applicants can access the official application portal here:

APPLY HERE.

Because the programme encourages early applications and gives early applicants priority review, prospective candidates should avoid waiting until the last minute.

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: Alpha Fellowship

Focus: Early-career software engineering and startup building

Tracks: Startup Track and Founder Track

Target applicants: Highly technical students and recent graduates

Graduate window: Within approximately three years of leaving school

Technical field: Software engineering

Format: In person

Duration: Approximately two months / eight weeks

U.S. work authorization: Required

Startup Track: Full-time engineering role

Startup compensation: Salary and equity

Founder Track: Build your own startup

Initial Founder Track grant: $20,000

Potential Founder Track investment: Up to $250,000

a16z speedrun pathway: Automatic final interview

Potential speedrun investment: Up to $1 million

Estimated cohort size: Up to 10 fellows per track

Cohort 1: Applications closed

Cohort 2: Opens in September 2026

Early applications: Receive priority review

Final Cohort 2 deadline: Not specified in the provided information

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Alpha a fellowship, job or startup accelerator?

Alpha is structured as a fellowship with two distinct pathways. The Startup Track connects fellows to full-time jobs at portfolio companies, while the Founder Track supports participants who want to start their own companies.

Do I have to be a software engineer?

Yes. Alpha states that it is exclusively for software engineers.

Can current students apply?

Yes. Students are among the target applicants.

However, selected participants must be prepared to make the necessary full-time commitment.

Can recent graduates apply?

Yes. The programme is intended for recent graduates, generally within three years of leaving school.

Do I need a startup idea?

No, not for the Founder Track.

Alpha states that it can back founders before they have an entity, idea or team.

Can I apply with my co-founder?

You apply individually. If you already know who you want to build with, each person should apply separately and identify the person they intend to build with.

How much funding does the Founder Track provide?

Accepted founders receive an initial $20,000 grant and can have access to up to $250,000 in total investment.

Can founders receive more funding?

Founder Track participants receive an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun. The speedrun programme can provide up to $1 million in investment.

Will Startup Track fellows work for a16z?

No. Fellows are hired directly by the portfolio company they are matched with.

Is the programme online?

No. The fellowship is in person.

Do I need U.S. work authorization?

Yes. Applicants must have valid authorization to work full-time in the United States.

Is there a specific nationality requirement?

The provided information does not specify a nationality, race or continent restriction. However, the U.S. work authorization requirement applies.

When does Cohort 2 open?

Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026.

What is the application deadline?

A specific final deadline for Cohort 2 has not been provided. Early applicants receive priority review, so candidates are encouraged to apply early.

Conclusion

The Alpha Fellowship is designed for highly technical early-career software engineers who want to accelerate their path into the startup world.

The programme offers two very different but potentially powerful routes.

The Startup Track gives selected engineers an opportunity to join fast-growing portfolio companies in full-time engineering positions with salary and equity. The fellowship experience adds access to founders, investors, engineering leaders, retreats, dinners and the broader a16z speedrun community.

The Founder Track is aimed at technical builders who want to create something of their own. Rather than requiring an incorporated company, established team or fully developed startup idea, Alpha is willing to support founders at a very early stage. Accepted founders receive an initial $20,000 grant and can have access to up to $250,000 in total investment, while also receiving an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun, which can provide access to up to $1 million in investment.

However, prospective applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements. Alpha is specifically for software engineers, with a focus on exceptional students and recent graduates, generally within three years of leaving school. Applicants must have valid U.S. work authorization and be able to participate in the programme in person.

The application timeline also requires attention. Cohort 1 applications have closed, while Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026. A specific final deadline for Cohort 2 is not currently provided in the supplied information, but early applicants receive priority review.

For a technically strong student or recent graduate who wants to join a breakout startup or take the first serious step toward becoming a founder, the Alpha Fellowship could provide an unusually direct combination of employment, startup exposure, mentorship, community and potential investment.

Interested candidates should prepare early and monitor the official application page so they can apply as soon as Cohort 2 opens.

TITLE: Monash University Graduate Research Scholarships 2026–2027: Funding Opportunities for Master’s and PhD Students in Australia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Monash University offers a wide range of scholarships, grants and funding opportunities designed to support graduate research students undertaking higher degree research at its campuses in Australia and selected international locations. These opportunities can help eligible students manage tuition fees, living expenses, research costs, travel and other expenses associated with postgraduate research.

For students planning to pursue a research-based master’s degree, doctoral degree or other graduate research qualification, Monash University provides several centrally managed scholarships, faculty-supported awards, industry-funded opportunities and scholarships specifically designed for international students.

The available funding varies considerably depending on the scholarship. Some awards provide a living stipend, while others cover tuition fees, Overseas Student Health Cover or provide additional funding on top of an existing scholarship.

Opportunity Category

Category: Scholarship and Graduate Research Funding Opportunity

The information below covers multiple Monash University graduate research scholarships, grants and related funding opportunities rather than one single scholarship programme.

About Monash University Graduate Research Scholarships

Monash University is a major Australian research institution offering graduate research opportunities across a broad range of academic disciplines. Its graduate research funding system includes scholarships funded by the Australian Government, Monash University, faculties, academic units, industry partners, philanthropic organisations and external sponsors.

The university’s graduate research funding opportunities are particularly relevant to students who want to undertake research in areas such as:

Engineering

Science

Medicine

Information Technology

Business and Economics

Social sciences

Humanities

Sustainability and environmental studies

Social justice

Human rights

Social policy

Energy and low-carbon technologies

Other research disciplines available through Monash graduate research programmes

The funding arrangements differ according to the scholarship, applicant category, research area, citizenship status and funding source.

Who Can Apply for Monash Graduate Research Scholarships?

Eligibility depends on the individual scholarship.

International Students

Several Monash graduate research scholarships are specifically available to international students. International applicants can therefore be considered for selected funding opportunities when they meet the academic, research, admission and scholarship-specific requirements.

The Monash International Tuition Scholarship (MITS), for example, is designed for international graduate research students and can cover tuition fees and single Overseas Student Health Cover. It is generally awarded alongside a stipend scholarship.

Other international opportunities have more specific nationality requirements. These include scholarships for students from Indonesia, China, Vietnam and Thailand.

Domestic Students

Australian and New Zealand citizens and Australian permanent residents may be eligible for scholarships and government-supported funding designed for domestic graduate research students.

Domestic students may also benefit from the Australian Government’s Research Training Program arrangements, including fee offsets for eligible students.

Important Eligibility Point

There is no single nationality or academic eligibility requirement that applies to every scholarship listed by Monash University. Each funding opportunity has its own criteria.

Applicants should therefore identify the specific scholarship they intend to apply for and carefully check:

Citizenship or residency requirements

Academic qualifications

Previous research experience

Proposed research area

Degree requirements

English-language requirements where applicable

Admission requirements

Scholarship-specific conditions

Whether a supervisor or research proposal is required

Whether the scholarship is available to domestic or international students

Major Graduate Research Scholarships Available at Monash Australia

Monash University lists a number of scholarships for graduate research students studying at an Australian campus.

1. Research Training Program Stipend

The Research Training Program (RTP) Stipend is funded by the Australian Government and supports students undertaking higher degree research at Australian universities.

At Monash University, RTP funding forms part of the university’s graduate research scholarship system and can provide financial support to eligible research students.

Students interested in this funding should review the specific Monash RTP requirements because eligibility and scholarship conditions apply.

2. Monash Graduate Scholarship

The Monash Graduate Scholarship (MGS) is funded by Monash University to support graduate research students.

It is one of the university’s central graduate research scholarship schemes and is intended to provide financial assistance to students undertaking eligible research degrees.

Applicants should review the current scholarship conditions and application process to determine whether they qualify.

3. Co-funded Monash Graduate Scholarship

The Co-funded Monash Graduate Scholarship (CF-MGS) is jointly funded by the Monash Graduate Research Office and a faculty or academic unit.

This arrangement allows research students to receive scholarship support through collaboration between central university funding and academic units.

Because the funding is connected to faculties and academic areas, applicants should pay close attention to available research projects and faculty-specific requirements.

4. Sir James McNeill Foundation Postgraduate Research Scholarship

The Sir James McNeill Foundation Postgraduate Research Scholarship (SJMN) is a prestigious scholarship established in memory of Sir James McNeill, who had a long association with Monash University.

The scholarship supports research in selected areas, including:

Music

Engineering

Science

Medicine

Applicants interested in these disciplines should examine the individual scholarship requirements and research eligibility criteria before applying.

5. Maxwell King PhD Scholarship

The Maxwell King PhD Scholarship (MKS) is named after Professor Maxwell King, who made significant contributions to graduate research at Monash University, including serving for eight years as Pro Vice-Chancellor for Research and Research Training.

The scholarship is intended to support eligible PhD research students.

Candidates should confirm the current eligibility requirements, scholarship value and application arrangements through Monash University’s official scholarship information.

6. Monash Graduate Impact 2030 Scholarship

The Monash Graduate Impact 2030 Scholarship supports research aligned with one of Monash University’s identified Global Challenges under its Impact 2030 framework.

This opportunity may be particularly relevant to applicants whose proposed research addresses major societal, environmental, technological or global challenges.

Applicants should demonstrate how their proposed research connects with the relevant Monash Global Challenge.

7. Raydon Scholarship

The Raydon Scholarship provides top-up funding for graduate research students undertaking research in areas connected to social and environmental improvement.

Relevant research areas include:

Social justice

Social inclusion

Human rights

Sustainability

Environment

Social policy for the betterment of society

Because this is a top-up scholarship, applicants should also examine the requirements concerning their primary scholarship or existing funding.

8. Monash-Museums Victoria Scholarship

Monash University has partnered with Museums Victoria to encourage and facilitate new research projects and initiatives.

The partnership includes two scholarship schemes:

MMV Honours

MMV PhD

These opportunities can be particularly attractive to students interested in research connected to museums, collections, cultural institutions, heritage or other relevant research themes supported through the partnership.

9. Monash Graduate Research Equity Supplement

The Monash Graduate Research Equity Supplement is intended to help eligible graduate research students meet additional expenses associated with undertaking their research.

The supplement is aimed at students with a disability or long-term medical condition where additional costs are incurred during their research degree.

Eligibility conditions apply, and applicants should consult the official Monash requirements for the current application process.

Scholarships for Domestic Graduate Research Students

Monash University also provides funding opportunities specifically aimed at domestic graduate research students.

Monash Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Scholarship

The Monash Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Scholarship is awarded on equity grounds to students whose academic careers have been adversely affected.

The scholarship recognises circumstances that may have affected an applicant’s educational progression and provides support to eligible students undertaking graduate research.

Monash Humanitarian Scholarship

The Monash Humanitarian Scholarship is intended for eligible humanitarian visa holders whose academic careers have been adversely affected.

This scholarship is therefore subject to specific residency or visa requirements and is not a general scholarship open to all international applicants.

Monash Indigenous Research Scholarships

Monash University provides scholarships specifically for Indigenous Australian students undertaking research degrees.

These scholarships include targeted support intended to assist eligible students with living costs while undertaking their research.

Industry and Partner-Funded Research Scholarships

Monash University also collaborates with industry and external organisations to support research addressing real-world challenges.

Woodside Monash Energy Partnership Research Scholarship

The Woodside Monash Energy Partnership is a major research collaboration between Monash University and Woodside Energy.

Research scholarships under the partnership support projects aligned with:

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals

Strategic research themes of the Woodside Monash Energy Partnership

Energy solutions

Lower-carbon technologies

Engineering and scientific innovation

Relevant study areas include:

Engineering

Science

Business and Economics

Information Technology

This opportunity can be particularly relevant to applicants whose research has a strong connection to energy, sustainability, technology or the transition toward lower-carbon systems.

Zema Energy Studies Scholarship

The Zema Energy Studies Scholarship, supported by the Australian Energy Market Operator, is designed to support multidisciplinary research.

The scholarship covers research areas including:

Engineering

Information Technology

Business and Economics

Its multidisciplinary nature makes it potentially suitable for research projects examining energy systems from technical, technological, economic or business perspectives.

International Graduate Research Scholarships

Monash University has several funding opportunities specifically for international graduate research students.

Monash International Tuition Scholarship

The Monash International Tuition Scholarship (MITS) can cover:

Tuition fees

Single Overseas Student Health Cover

The scholarship is generally awarded together with a stipend scholarship.

For international students, this distinction is important because tuition funding and living-cost support may come from separate scholarship arrangements.

Applicants should therefore determine whether they are applying for a tuition scholarship, a stipend scholarship or a combination of both.

Indonesian Women Impact Scholarship

The Indonesian Women Impact Scholarship supports high-achieving female graduate researchers from Indonesia.

The scholarship is designed for Indonesian women who intend to undertake graduate research with meaningful impact.

Because this is a targeted opportunity, applicants should ensure that they satisfy the nationality, gender, academic and research requirements before applying.

Monash University-China Scholarship Council Joint Scholarship

Monash University has established a collaborative scholarship programme with the China Scholarship Council (CSC) to attract high-achieving Chinese students who wish to undertake a PhD at Monash University.

This opportunity is therefore specifically relevant to eligible Chinese applicants pursuing doctoral research.

Applicants should review both Monash University and China Scholarship Council requirements before beginning the application process.

Monash University-Vietnam Government Joint Scholarship

The Monash University-Vietnam Government Joint Scholarship, associated with Project 89, is offered in partnership with the Vietnamese Government.

The programme supports high-achieving Vietnamese students undertaking graduate research at Monash University.

Vietnamese applicants should verify the current Project 89 requirements as well as Monash University’s admission and scholarship conditions.

John Bush Memorial Top-Up Scholarship

The John Bush Memorial Top-Up Scholarship provides additional living-cost support for Thai-born graduate research students.

It is designed as a top-up scholarship and is intended to supplement a centrally allocated Monash scholarship.

Applicants should therefore understand that the scholarship is not necessarily intended to replace a primary graduate research scholarship.

Scholarships That Are Not Currently Available

Applicants should pay attention to the status of individual scholarships because not every opportunity appearing on the university’s scholarship information is currently accepting applications.

For example, the Monash Graduate Excellence Scholarship (MGES) Top Up is identified by Monash University as not currently offered.

Similarly, the Monash University-Pakistan Higher Education Commission Joint Scholarship is identified as not currently accepting applications because the relevant agreement has expired.

Applicants should always confirm the current status of a scholarship before preparing an application.

Graduate Research Travel Grants

In addition to scholarships, Monash University provides travel grants to support eligible graduate research students undertaking essential research-related travel.

The university states that travel grants can provide:

Up to AUD 2,300 for international study away

Up to AUD 900 for domestic study away

The funding may help cover flight-related expenses and can also support activities such as:

Attending seminars

Attending conferences

Conducting fieldwork

Conducting research away from the student’s home campus

However, these grants are subject to specific conditions.

Applicants must generally be:

Presenting at a conference, supported by an acceptance or invitation to present; and/or

Undertaking approved fieldwork relevant to their research project, supported by confirmation or planned activities.

Students must also have successfully completed confirmation and must complete the approved travel before thesis submission.

Students who are eligible for a staff travel grant or who have applied for an annual mandatory period of residency at a campus for external students may not be eligible.

Joint research award students may be eligible where the travel relates to their Monash Australia campus stay component.

Externally Funded Scholarship Opportunities

Monash University also directs graduate research students toward scholarships funded by external organisations.

These scholarships must generally be applied for through the relevant external organisation.

Examples listed by Monash include:

A*STAR – Agency for Science, Technology and Research

AusIMM Education Endowment Fund

Australia Awards Scholarships

Heart Foundation

National Health and Medical Research Council

Westpac Future Leaders Scholarships

Other externally funded opportunities

Applicants should carefully investigate the individual conditions of each external scholarship because eligibility, deadlines, funding amounts and application procedures are determined by the respective funding organisation.

Funding and Tuition Fees for Domestic Students

Eligible domestic graduate research students may benefit from the Australian Government’s Research Training Program Fees Offset.

The fee offset covers graduate research course fees for eligible students, including:

Australian citizens

New Zealand citizens

Australian permanent residents

The fee offset applies for the specified duration of an eligible research course.

Domestic students may also be required to pay the Student Services and Amenities Fee, commonly known as the SSAF. The amount can depend on the student’s annual research load.

Tuition Fees for International Students

International graduate research students should pay particular attention to tuition fees.

International students are generally required to pay tuition fees unless those fees are covered by:

A Monash scholarship

An external scholarship

Sponsorship

Another approved funding arrangement

Students should use Monash University’s course information to determine the applicable tuition fees for their selected research degree.

If an external sponsor provides a fee-paying scholarship, the student may need to submit a financial guarantee letter when accepting their offer.

The guarantee letter should identify:

Costs covered by the sponsor

Duration of sponsorship

Other relevant financial commitments

If the scholarship does not cover the entire duration of the research programme, the student may be responsible for paying the remaining fees after the scholarship ends.

International students without a sponsor may also be required to pay a deposit equivalent to one semester’s fees when accepting their offer.

Overseas Student Health Cover

International students must have Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) for the period required by their Australian student visa.

Where a scholarship covers only single OSHC, students who require family or multi-family coverage may have to pay the difference.

This is an important cost for international applicants to consider when developing their overall postgraduate funding plan.

Monash Graduate Research Scholarships in Malaysia and Indonesia

Monash’s graduate research funding opportunities are not limited to Australia.

Monash Malaysia

Monash Malaysia offers a range of tuition-fee and stipend scholarships for graduate research students.

Students considering research study at Monash Malaysia should consult the campus’s current scholarship information and postgraduate fee information because eligibility and funding arrangements may differ from Monash Australia.

Monash Indonesia

Monash Indonesia offers a range of partially and fully funded scholarships for Graduate Research students.

Students interested in undertaking a PhD or other graduate research programme at Monash Indonesia should review the available scholarships and current programme-specific requirements.

How to Apply for a Monash Graduate Research Scholarship

The application process varies according to the specific scholarship, but prospective applicants should generally follow a structured approach.

Step 1: Identify Your Research Degree

Determine whether you are applying for:

A research master’s programme

A PhD

Another eligible graduate research programme

Your intended degree will determine which scholarships you may be eligible to pursue.

Step 2: Identify Your Research Area

Review Monash University’s research areas and determine whether your proposed research fits within the university’s available disciplines and research strengths.

This is particularly important for scholarships that target specific areas such as:

Energy

Engineering

Science

Medicine

Sustainability

Social justice

Human rights

Information Technology

Business and Economics

Step 3: Determine Your Applicant Category

Establish whether you are applying as:

A domestic student

An international student

A student from a scholarship-specific country

A student eligible for a targeted equity programme

A student eligible for an industry or partner-funded scholarship

Your nationality, residency status and academic circumstances can significantly affect which funding opportunities are available.

Step 4: Review Academic Requirements

Make sure your previous academic qualifications meet the requirements for the research programme and scholarship.

Applicants should also consider whether their academic background demonstrates sufficient preparation for advanced research.

Step 5: Develop Your Research Proposal

Where required, prepare a strong research proposal explaining:

The research problem

Background and context

Research objectives

Research questions

Proposed methodology

Expected contribution

Significance of the research

Relevant literature

Potential impact

For impact-focused scholarships, applicants should clearly explain how their proposed research addresses the objectives of the relevant funding programme.

Step 6: Identify Potential Supervisors

For research degrees, identifying suitable academic supervisors can be an important part of the application process.

Applicants should investigate researchers whose expertise aligns with their proposed topic and review the university’s supervision requirements.

Step 7: Prepare Supporting Documents

Depending on the scholarship, applicants may need documents such as:

Academic transcripts

Degree certificates

Curriculum vitae

Research proposal

Evidence of English-language proficiency

Identification documents

References or referee reports

Publications or evidence of research experience

Scholarship-specific documentation

Applicants should rely on the individual scholarship page for the definitive list of required documents.

Step 8: Submit the Application

Applications should be submitted according to the instructions provided by Monash University or, for externally funded scholarships, by the relevant funding organisation.

Applicants should not assume that all scholarships use the same application procedure.

Is There a Single Deadline?

No single deadline is provided for all of the Monash graduate research scholarships listed above.

The scholarships have different application processes and availability periods. Some may be offered through particular rounds, while others may depend on faculty, research project or external funding arrangements.

Applicants should therefore check the individual scholarship page for the current closing date before applying.

For opportunities that do not display a deadline in the supplied information, applicants should not assume that applications remain open indefinitely.

Why Consider Monash University for Graduate Research?

Monash University’s broad scholarship portfolio offers several advantages for prospective research students.

1. Multiple Sources of Funding

Funding can come from:

The Australian Government

Monash University

Faculties

Academic units

Industry partners

Government agencies

Philanthropic organisations

External scholarship providers

This creates multiple potential pathways for students seeking postgraduate research funding.

2. Opportunities Across Multiple Disciplines

The scholarships cover a broad range of academic areas, from engineering and science to medicine, information technology, business, sustainability, social justice and human rights.

3. Support for International Students

International students can access several dedicated funding opportunities, including tuition scholarships and nationality-specific joint programmes.

4. Additional Research and Travel Support

The session broadly featured an interactive discussion on how the 53 Centres of Excellence are progressing with entrepreneurship and innovation, building on lessons from both within and outside the African continent.

The Disbursement Linked Indicator (DLI) 5.3 – Key Observations and Next Steps

Making a presentation on DLI 5.3 which focuses on innovation and entrepreneurship, Dr. Danica Ramljak took participants through the key targets of the implementation plan, including a focus on innovation-oriented cooperation in research infrastructures and collaboration with the private sector. Centres had earlier been given opportunities to develop implementation plans on how to accomplish the activities related to innovation and entrepreneurship as part of DLI5.3. Dr. Danika used the opportunity to provide feedback to the Centres on their applications.

She called on the centres to pay special attention to the established criteria for the review process of applications under this indicator, which included – quality background description of institutional and innovation ecosystems. Others included justification for the proposed activity and a detailed explanation of the proposed implementation plan with specific descriptions of each activity, highlighting the goals, timelines and person (s) responsible. The verification criteria and budget as well as the justification for the budget were said to be part of the criteria.

Commenting on the general results from the review process, it was mentioned that the quality of applications significantly differed, in ways which cannot be attributed to the country of origin or scientific research interest areas of the Centres. The number of improved resubmissions were also noted to have been significantly increased during the resubmission stage. Again, it was observed that the Centres were at different levels in terms of institutional innovation ecosystem.

Participants were reminded of the key roles of higher education in the areas of knowledge generation, training of skilled human resource and the development of technology that can be transferred to industry among others. Based on these roles, including others such as undertaking research for industry and the development of competitive products, the session participants were encouraged to advocate and engage the authorities in their institutions and at the country levels to prioritise innovation.

They were also encouraged to measure and determine the technology readiness level of their institutions for innovation and commercialisation as this was an important step towards planning and putting measures in place to foster the readiness of their systems for full scale deployment.

Key among the recommendations towards becoming fully blown entrepreneurial and innovative institutions, the importance of having appropriate Science Technology Innovation (STI) policies in place and ensuring its effective implementation was underscored. Other recommendations outlined included – ensuring institutional capacity building for STI management and governance, the establishment of efficient models for knowledge transfer and the provision of institutional capacity building. It was also recommended that centres define their research and development priorities, develop a roadmap for research infrastructure and provide sustainable support for innovation development. Equally important to fostering innovation and entrepreneurial activities were the recommendations to attract the private sector to collaborate and invest in HEIs research and development (R&D), the need to strengthen international collaborations, a well as inform the general public about the importance of the Centres’ work.

Experience Sharing on Entrepreneurship and Innovation by Three Centres of Excellence – ACECoR, CERSA and OAU-OAK PARK

A high-level panel composed of Mr. Joshua Adotey from the Africa Centre of Excellence in Coastal Resilience (ACECoR), Ghana, Prof. Adesola Aderounmu from OAU ICT-Driven Knowledge Park, Nigeria and Dr. Edoh representing the Regional Center of Excellence on Avian Sciences (CERSA), Togo discussed key issues and shared their experiences on how to excel and meet the requirements of DLI 5.3.

Speaking on the key challenges encountered in their institutions’ ecosystems which inhibit their work in this area, CERSA identified the lack of a technology transfer office to facilitate their commercialisation process, and the low marketing of results generated by the researchers. For ACECoR, there was the lack of entrepreneurship policies at the initial stage of developing the framework for the DLI. Limited engagement and collaboration between industry and the university was also a challenge, however this has been improved drastically and currently industry members are engaged closely in various ways, including in remodeling some programmes and courses. ACECoR highlighted how the support from university authorities, especially the vice-chancellor helped them overcome some of their challenges, leading to the strengthening of their technology office.

For OAU-OAK PARK, the focus on developing the skills of students had been prime on their agenda, however the development of IT entrepreneurs had not been prioritised, thus they identified the need to train the youth in this area for wealth creation and capacity development among others. Having done all these however, the key challenge of their inability to attract investors to fund the innovations and products including spin off institutions, remains. Another challenge faced related to intellectual property rights issues which come up as they partner with industry in generating some innovations. Participants were told that the centre has put in place pragmatic measures to overcome these challenges, including training students to develop business plans, providing seed funding for the innovations, engaging the University’s intellectual property rights office from the start of discussions with industry players.

Speaking on how to be successful in innovation, the experienced panelists advised centres to strengthen their engagement with the private sector, implement measures to motivate their researchers, and to develop and implement institutional manuals and procedures to guide various processes. Again, the Centres were encouraged to ensure that there is a fully functional entrepreneurial ecosystem which has people with the right skills, a pool of investors supporting their research work, a ready market to uptake developed innovations and the sensitisation of stakeholders to embrace entrepreneurship. Additionally, commitment from institutional authorities toward innovation and entrepreneurship was said to be key, just like having an Intellectual Property Technology Transfer Office (IPPTO) and a sustainability plan.

Centre’s Impact on University Systems

Tackling the discussion on how Centre’s activities impact and strengthen the university system, numerous contributions were shared. Among these, ACECoR for instance is engaging the University’s Directorate of Research, Innovation and Consultancy (DRIC) in operationalising the formulation on Innovation, thereby building capacity in the team. It is also creating an enabling environment for the service incubation centre of the institution.

Similarly, OAU- OAK is supporting capacity building of the institution’s Business Resource Centre, linking this centre to industry players and also collaborating with them to organise technology focused conferences. Again, some spin off companies from the centre’s activities now serve as places for practical skill acquisition for the University’s students, through internships.

Leveraging ACE Impact Project to strengthen innovation and entrepreneurship in African HEIs

Following a question-and-answer session from participants, Dr. Danica Ramljak wrapped up the session by calling on the centres to leverage the opportunity presented by the project to improve their institutions’ innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem. Centres were encouraged to for instance draw on the project to beef up capacity in their technology transfer offices, if they are understaffed. They were urged to strengthen partnerships among themselves as centres and with other international partners, advocate for the development and implementation of Intellectual Property Policies among others.

Finally, the centres of excellence were called upon to lobby and engage their ministries and universities to recognise innovation and entrepreneurship activities of researchers as part of career progress and promotion indicators, and equally work hard to bring in money from other external sources to support innovation and entrepreneurship as these are key ingredients to economic growth of countries across the continent.

Written By: Mrs. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, Senior Communications and Publications Officer, AAU

TITLE: 2027 Summer Philanthropy Internship at Constellation: Paid 10-Week Opportunity for Students in the United States

Nuclear

Natural gas

Geothermal

Hydroelectric power

Wind

Solar

Interns will join Constellation’s Philanthropy Team and work on specific projects during the summer.

Develop professional communication skills

Start date: June 7, 2027

TITLE: World Future Policy Award 2027: Call for Nominations for Education for Sustainable Development in Cities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Future Council (WFC) has opened nominations for the World Future Policy Award (WFPA) 2027, focusing on Education for Sustainable Development in Cities. The prestigious global policy award seeks outstanding laws, policies, provisions and frameworks that use education, lifelong learning and community participation to help cities become more inclusive, sustainable, resilient and peaceful.

Unlike awards that primarily recognise individual personalities, the World Future Policy Award focuses on exemplary policy solutions that can inspire governments, communities and decision-makers around the world. The 2027 edition is particularly interested in policies that demonstrate how cities and communities can empower people of different ages and backgrounds to participate meaningfully in sustainable urban development.

The call is open to nominations from a broad range of organisations and stakeholders, including international organisations, governments, government agencies, parliaments, academia, non-governmental organisations, Indigenous communities, local communities and other relevant actors. Policies may operate at national, regional, subnational or local levels.

Nomination deadline: 31 October 2026.

About the World Future Policy Award 2027

The World Future Policy Award is presented by the World Future Council to raise international awareness of policies that provide effective solutions to major challenges facing present and future generations.

The award aims to identify and showcase policies that are not only effective in their original contexts but also have the potential to inspire action elsewhere. According to the World Future Council, the award’s mission is to raise global awareness of exemplary policies while educating and inspiring policymakers, civil society and the wider public.

For 2027, the award turns its attention to the relationship between education, sustainable development and cities.

This focus recognises that cities are increasingly at the centre of environmental, social, technological and economic transformation. As urban populations grow and societies face increasingly complex challenges, cities need approaches that allow residents to acquire the knowledge, skills and values required to participate in creating sustainable futures.

The World Future Council is therefore looking for policies that demonstrate how education and learning can become an integral part of urban development.

What Is Education for Sustainable Development in Cities?

Education for Sustainable Development, commonly known as ESD, seeks to equip individuals and communities with the knowledge, skills, values and attitudes needed to make informed decisions and contribute to sustainable development.

Within cities, this concept extends beyond traditional classrooms and formal education systems.

It can include:

Community-based learning.

Lifelong learning programmes.

Intergenerational learning.

Environmental education.

Digital inclusion.

Civic education and participation.

Skills development for sustainable lifestyles.

Community engagement in local decision-making.

Learning initiatives supporting climate action.

Programmes that promote inclusive and equitable urban development.

The 2027 World Future Policy Award is particularly interested in policies that demonstrate how these approaches can be embedded into the way cities are governed and developed.

The World Future Council notes that cities can create inclusive, lifelong and intergenerational learning opportunities that allow residents to contribute to sustainable, regenerative and just futures.

Why Cities Are Central to Sustainable Development

Cities face many of the world’s most significant development challenges, but they are also important places where solutions can be tested and implemented.

Rapid urbanisation, technological change, environmental pressures and social inequalities are changing the way people live and interact with their communities. These developments create an urgent need for urban populations to have access to learning opportunities that enable them to understand challenges and participate in solutions.

Education can help residents:

Understand environmental and climate-related challenges.

Adopt more sustainable lifestyles.

Participate in local decision-making.

Develop digital skills.

Engage with public institutions.

Understand their rights and responsibilities.

Contribute to community development.

Support inclusive and peaceful communities.

Adapt to technological and economic changes.

Build stronger relationships between generations.

The award therefore recognises that sustainable cities cannot be created solely through infrastructure, technology or environmental regulation. People also need opportunities to learn, participate and shape the future of their communities.

Key Areas of Policy the Award Is Looking For

The World Future Council has identified several areas of particular interest for the 2027 award.

1. Greening Cities

The first focus area is policies that support the greening of cities through community-based learning and participation.

This could include policies that help residents understand and participate in:

Urban environmental protection.

Climate action.

Sustainable transportation.

Urban agriculture.

Biodiversity conservation.

Green public spaces.

Sustainable waste management.

Energy efficiency.

Nature-based solutions.

Sustainable urban planning.

The strongest nominations are likely to demonstrate how learning and public participation contribute to measurable environmental improvements.

2. Digital Inclusion Strategies

Digital technologies increasingly influence access to education, employment, public services and civic participation.

The award therefore welcomes policies addressing digital inclusion, particularly where such policies help communities overcome barriers to participation.

Relevant policies could involve:

Digital literacy.

Access to digital learning.

Digital skills development.

Affordable access to technology.

Inclusive digital public services.

Digital opportunities for disadvantaged communities.

Programmes supporting older people or marginalised groups.

Community-based digital education.

A strong policy could demonstrate how digital inclusion allows residents to participate more effectively in sustainable urban development.

3. Civic Participation and Participatory Budgeting

The third highlighted area concerns civic participation, with particular attention to participatory budgeting.

Participatory budgeting gives residents opportunities to participate in decisions concerning the allocation of public resources.

Policies in this area may demonstrate how cities educate and empower residents to:

Understand public budgets.

Identify community priorities.

Participate in decision-making.

Propose projects.

Deliberate with other community members.

Monitor implementation.

Hold local institutions accountable.

Such approaches can transform residents from passive recipients of public services into active participants in shaping their communities.

What Makes a Strong Policy Nomination?

The World Future Council has identified several characteristics that it wants to see in nominated policies.

Transformative

The policy should demonstrate meaningful potential to change the way communities address sustainable development.

Innovative

Nominations should showcase creative approaches that provide new or particularly effective ways of connecting education, learning and sustainable urban development.

Inspiring

The policy should provide lessons that can motivate other cities, communities or policymakers to take action.

Inclusive

The World Future Council is particularly interested in approaches that recognise diverse perspectives and ensure that different communities can participate.

Replicable

One of the most important considerations is whether a policy can provide lessons for other places facing similar challenges.

The award specifically encourages nominations of policies that are replicable in similar contexts.

Indigenous and Local Community Policies Are Particularly Welcome

An important feature of the 2027 call is its emphasis on Indigenous and local communities.

The World Future Council is particularly interested in policies that reflect the perspectives, worldviews, cosmologies, cultural traditions and socio-legal perspectives of Indigenous and local communities.

This means that nominations do not have to rely exclusively on conventional government or mainstream educational approaches.

Policies that incorporate locally developed knowledge systems, cultural practices and community perspectives may be particularly relevant when they demonstrate how these approaches contribute to sustainable, inclusive and resilient communities.

What Types of Policies Can Be Nominated?

The World Future Council states that eligible policy instruments can include:

Laws.

Policies.

Provisions.

Frameworks.

These can operate at different levels, including:

National.

Subnational.

Regional.

Local.

This broad scope means that relevant examples do not necessarily have to be nationwide programmes.

A city policy, municipal framework, regional strategy or community-oriented legal provision may also be relevant if it demonstrates strong connections between education for sustainable development and urban or community development.

Who Can Submit a Nomination?

The call is open to nominations from representatives of a wide range of institutions and organisations.

The World Future Council specifically welcomes nominations from:

International organisations.

Academic institutions and researchers.

Non-governmental organisations.

Parliaments.

Governments.

Government agencies.

Indigenous communities.

Local communities.

Other relevant stakeholders.

This broad approach means that the opportunity is not restricted to government officials or policymakers alone. Organisations and institutions working with communities, education, sustainability, urban development and public policy can also identify and nominate relevant policies.

International Context of the Award

The 2027 focus is connected to broader international commitments concerning education, sustainability and future generations.

The World Future Council highlights the 1997 UNESCO Declaration of the Responsibilities of the Present Generations Toward Future Generations, which emphasises education as a means of promoting peace, justice, tolerance and equality for present and future generations.

The award also connects strongly with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly:

SDG 4: Quality Education, which focuses on inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities for all.

SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities, which focuses on making cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable.

Education for Sustainable Development provides an important connection between these two areas by helping communities acquire the knowledge and capabilities needed to participate in sustainable urban transformation.

Partnership Behind the World Future Policy Award 2027

The 2027 World Future Policy Award is being developed with important international partners.

The World Future Council is working together with the UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning (UIL) and the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).

The UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning works with UNESCO Member States on lifelong learning, learning ecosystems, skills for life and work, and inclusive learning. The institute also focuses on research, capacity-building, networking and publications relating to lifelong learning.

The Inter-Parliamentary Union is the global organisation of national parliaments and works on areas including democratic governance, human rights, gender equality, youth empowerment, climate action and sustainable development.

This partnership gives the award a strong connection to international policy, lifelong learning, parliamentary engagement and sustainable urban development.

Why This Award Matters

The World Future Policy Award is significant because it focuses on policy solutions rather than individual achievements.

Many cities around the world are experimenting with innovative approaches to sustainability, education and community participation. However, effective local policies can remain relatively unknown outside their immediate communities.

By identifying and showcasing exemplary policies, the award seeks to help successful approaches gain wider international attention.

A recognised policy can potentially provide useful lessons for policymakers in other cities and countries facing similar challenges.

The award therefore serves several purposes:

Identifying effective policy solutions.

Raising international awareness.

Sharing lessons between cities and communities.

Encouraging policymakers to take action.

Highlighting innovative approaches.

Supporting sustainable development.

Promoting lifelong learning.

Encouraging inclusive civic participation.

Amplifying Indigenous and local perspectives.

Demonstrating how policy can support future generations.

How to Prepare a Strong Nomination

Anyone considering submitting a nomination should carefully assess whether the policy demonstrates the characteristics sought by the World Future Council.

A strong nomination should clearly explain the policy and its relevance to the award theme.

Consider addressing the following questions:

1. What is the policy?

Clearly identify the law, policy, framework or provision being nominated.

Explain where it operates and which institution or authority is responsible for it.

2. What problem does it address?

Describe the social, environmental, educational or urban challenge that the policy was designed to address.

3. How does education or learning contribute?

Explain how the policy creates opportunities for people to learn, develop skills, participate or exchange knowledge.

4. Who benefits?

Identify the communities, residents, learners, organisations or groups affected by the policy.

5. Is the policy inclusive?

Explain how the policy addresses the needs and perspectives of different groups, including Indigenous and local communities where relevant.

6. What results has it achieved?

Where evidence is available, provide concrete information about outcomes and impact.

This might include improvements in participation, environmental outcomes, digital inclusion, education, community engagement or other measurable areas.

7. Can the approach be replicated?

Explain why the policy could provide useful lessons for other cities or communities.

8. What makes it innovative?

Highlight the elements that distinguish the policy from conventional approaches.

9. How is the policy transformative?

Explain how it has changed systems, institutions, behaviours, participation or community outcomes.

Nomination Deadline

The official nomination deadline for the World Future Policy Award 2027 is: 31 October 2026

Potential nominators should therefore begin preparing their submissions early rather than waiting until the final days of the call.

The World Future Council states that finalists are expected to be announced in May or June 2027. The winning policies will subsequently be celebrated at a high-level award ceremony held jointly with the UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning during the International Conference on Learning Cities (ICLC) in 2027.

How to Apply or Submit a Nomination

The process is a nomination, rather than a conventional individual job or scholarship application.

Interested organisations, institutions and stakeholders should first review the official nomination criteria and then complete the nomination form.

The official World Future Council page provides the nomination form as well as translations of the nomination materials in Arabic, French, German, Hindi, Kiswahili, Portuguese and Spanish.

Before submitting, nominators should make sure that the proposed policy clearly relates to Education for Sustainable Development in Cities and demonstrates relevance to one or more of the priority areas.

A stronger nomination should demonstrate why the policy matters, what it has achieved and why other communities could learn from it.

In particular, nominators should connect the policy to the central idea of empowering people through lifelong and intergenerational learning. The strongest examples are likely to show a clear relationship between learning, community participation and sustainable urban outcomes.

It is also useful to demonstrate evidence of implementation rather than presenting only a theoretical policy proposal. Evidence of community involvement, measurable results, institutional adoption, innovation and potential for replication can make a nomination more compelling.

Conclusion

The World Future Policy Award 2027: Education for Sustainable Development in Cities provides an important international platform for highlighting policies that place learning, participation and people at the centre of sustainable urban development.

As cities confront rapid urbanisation, environmental pressures, technological change and growing social complexity, education can play a critical role in helping communities understand challenges and participate in building solutions.

The 2027 award is particularly relevant to policies focused on greening cities, digital inclusion and civic participation, including participatory budgeting. It also provides an important opportunity to showcase Indigenous and local approaches that reflect diverse cultural, social and legal perspectives.
