TITLE: Third Wave Fund Mobilize Power Fund 2026: Rapid Response Funding for Gender Justice Organizations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the Third Wave Fund Mobilize Power Fund 2026, a rapid-response funding opportunity designed to support gender justice organizations and groups in the United States and U.S. territories that need to respond quickly to unexpected, time-sensitive opportunities or threats affecting their communities, movement-building activities, or organizing conditions.

Through the Mobilize Power Fund, eligible organizations can receive grants of up to $10,000 USD, while partnerships or coalitions involving two or more groups can request up to $20,000 USD. The programme is specifically intended for organizations that need to significantly adapt or pivot their work because of an unforeseen incident or change in circumstances that occurred within the previous six months.

The Mobilize Power Fund is not intended to finance ordinary organizational activities or compensate for routine budget shortages. Instead, it provides flexible resources that enable gender justice movements to respond to rapidly changing circumstances through activities such as community organizing, direct action, healing justice, mutual aid, conflict resolution, legal or bail support, leadership development, and unexpected legislative or ballot initiative campaigns.

The September 2026 application cycle is currently open, with applications due by September 8, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time. Organizations that cannot apply during the September cycle will have another opportunity when the October cycle opens on September 9, 2026.

About the Third Wave Fund Mobilize Power Fund

The Mobilize Power Fund is a rapid-response grantmaking programme operated by Third Wave Fund to provide gender justice organizations with resources when unforeseen developments require an immediate or significant change in their work.

The fund recognizes that movement-building does not always happen according to predictable schedules. Organizations working directly with communities affected by gender oppression can encounter unexpected political developments, safety concerns, community crises, organizing opportunities, legislative changes, or other circumstances requiring an immediate response.

Rather than requiring organizations to wait for conventional long-term funding cycles, the Mobilize Power Fund provides a mechanism through which qualifying groups can seek resources to respond to these situations.

Third Wave Fund describes the programme as a resource for organizations needing to adapt or pivot their work when faced with unanticipated and time-sensitive opportunities or threats to their movement-building work and organizing conditions.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The amount organizations can request depends on whether they are applying individually as a group or organization or jointly through a partnership or coalition.

Funding is available as follows:

Individual organizations or groups: Up to $10,000 USD

Partnerships or coalitions involving two or more groups: Up to $20,000 USD

This makes the programme particularly relevant for organizations that require relatively small but timely grants to respond to circumstances that could not reasonably have been anticipated through their normal programming or budgeting processes.

What Is the Purpose of the Mobilize Power Fund?

The Mobilize Power Fund was established around the understanding that effective movements need the ability not only to plan long-term strategies but also to respond to immediate opportunities and threats.

Third Wave Fund explains that the programme was created because movements need flexible and responsive funding to both respond to and heal from urgent circumstances.

The first iteration of the Mobilize Power Fund supported organizers responding to HB2, the North Carolina legislation widely known as the “Bathroom Bill,” in 2016.

The fund has subsequently developed into a broader rapid-response funding mechanism for qualifying gender justice organizations confronting unexpected developments.

Who Is the Mobilize Power Fund For?

The Mobilize Power Fund supports gender justice organizations and groups whose work is rooted in and accountable to communities directly affected by gender oppression.

These organizations must be adapting or pivoting their work in response to an unexpected and time-sensitive opportunity or threat affecting their movement work or organizing conditions.

This means applicants should be able to clearly demonstrate both:

Their existing connection and accountability to the communities they serve; and

Why a recent development requires them to substantially change or expand their planned activities.

Geographic Eligibility: Where Must Applicants Be Based?

The Mobilize Power Fund is geographically restricted.

Third Wave Fund states that funding is provided only within the United States and U.S. territories.

Eligible locations include:

United States

American Samoa

Guam

Northern Mariana Islands

Puerto Rico

U.S. Virgin Islands

Groups based outside the United States and U.S. territories are not prioritized by the fund.

International organizations operating entirely outside these eligible geographic areas should therefore not consider this a global grant opportunity.

Organizational Budget Requirement

One of the most important eligibility requirements is the organization’s budget.

To qualify for a Mobilize Power Fund grant, an organization must have an annual organizational budget of less than $500,000 USD.

Third Wave Fund additionally prioritizes organizations and groups that:

Operate in areas where access to philanthropic resources is limited; and

Do not have access to 501(c)(3) status or fiscal sponsorship.

The lack of 501(c)(3) status or fiscal sponsorship therefore does not automatically exclude a group from consideration. In fact, organizations facing these structural funding barriers are specifically identified as a priority.

Core Eligibility and Selection Criteria

Third Wave Fund identifies several important areas that organizations should demonstrate through their applications.

1. Accountability to Communities

Leadership and decision-making structures should demonstrate meaningful accountability to communities directly affected by gender oppression.

The programme specifically references communities including:

Young women of color

Trans youth

Queer youth

Intersex youth

Gender non-conforming youth

People of color under the age of 35

Organizations should demonstrate alignment between their leadership, governance structures, and the communities they serve.

2. Gender Justice

Applicants need to demonstrate a clear gender justice analysis.

Their political analysis should explain how the issue being addressed connects to one or more areas such as:

Patriarchy

Transphobia

Homophobia

Gender inequity

Gender-based violence

Simply responding to an urgent situation is therefore not sufficient. The organization should also demonstrate how that situation relates to gender justice.

3. Rapid Response

The organization must be responding to a specific incident or change in circumstances that occurred within the previous six months.

The situation should require the organization to significantly pivot from its ongoing and regularly planned activities.

4. Community Power Building

The strategies and activities proposed should strengthen the organizing and movement-building power of the communities involved.

The proposed activities should also directly contribute to the overall objectives described in the application.

5. Organizational Need

Organizations must have budgets below $500,000 USD to qualify.

Priority is additionally given to organizations operating in areas with limited access to philanthropic resources and organizations without access to 501(c)(3) status or fiscal sponsorship.

What Types of Activities Are Prioritized?

The Mobilize Power Fund is intended to respond to unexpected circumstances rather than support routine activities.

Third Wave Fund identifies several examples of work that may receive priority, including:

Unexpected and time-sensitive community organizing

Direct action

Participatory Action Research

Healing justice work

Conflict mediation

Conflict resolution

Legal fees

Bail fees

Marches

Rallies

Leadership training

Skills building

Mutual aid

Unexpected legislative campaigns

Unexpected ballot initiative campaigns

These examples illustrate the programme’s emphasis on rapidly mobilizing resources where organizations need to respond to a new circumstance rather than simply continue activities they had already planned.

What Types of Applications Are Not Prioritized?

Organizations should carefully consider whether their proposed activities genuinely fit the rapid-response purpose of the fund before applying.

Third Wave Fund states that the Mobilize Power Fund does not prioritize applications involving:

Budget shortfalls

Ongoing or regularly scheduled programmes

Start-up or seed costs

Fundraising

Previously planned campaigns

Long-term campaigns

Projects led by individuals

Charity

Groups based outside the United States and U.S. territories

For the purposes of this programme, Third Wave Fund defines long-term programming as programming extending beyond six months.

Applicants should therefore clearly establish that their proposed work represents a genuine response or pivot rather than an attempt to finance existing activities.

Mobilize Power Fund 2026 Application Deadlines

The Mobilize Power Fund is no longer accepting applications on a rolling basis.

Applications must instead be submitted during specific funding cycles, and all deadlines are at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

June 2026 Cycle

Applications opened: May 5, 2026
Deadline: June 2, 2026

July 2026 Cycle

Applications opened: June 3, 2026
Deadline: July 7, 2026

September 2026 Cycle

Applications opened: August 5, 2026
Deadline: September 8, 2026

October 2026 Cycle

Applications open: September 9, 2026
Deadline: October 6, 2026

Organizations planning to apply should make sure they submit within an active funding cycle.

Application Materials Required

Applicants need to gather several pieces of information and documentation before completing their submission.

Basic Information

Applicants must provide:

Contact information

A description of the group or organization

A brief one-to-two-sentence description of the application

Group or Organizational Budget

Applicants should provide the group’s or organization’s total budget for the current calendar or fiscal year, where applicable.

Third Wave Fund provides an organizational budget template for this purpose.

Independent 501(c)(3) Organizations

Applicants operating as independent 501(c)(3) organizations should provide their organization’s IRS letter.

Fiscally Sponsored Organizations

Fiscally sponsored applicants should provide:

The fiscal sponsor’s organizational budget

The fiscal sponsor’s 501(c)(3) IRS letter

A current fiscal sponsor agreement signed by both parties

Applicants must also provide responses to the required application narrative questions.

Three Ways to Complete the Application Narrative

An important feature of the Mobilize Power Fund application is the flexibility provided for completing the narrative component.

Applicants can provide their narrative through:

A written application

A selfie video submission

A Zoom or phone interview

Written Applications

Written narratives should be no longer than one page and must be uploaded through the grant portal.

Video Applications

Video narratives can be up to 10 minutes long.

Applicants should upload a link to their video through the grant portal.

Phone or Zoom Applications

Organizations wishing to complete their narrative through an interview should contact Third Wave Fund to schedule a Zoom or phone call.

Interview calls must be scheduled and completed at least one week before the relevant application deadline.

Because Third Wave Fund has limited staff capacity, it may not be able to accommodate every interview request.

The fund aims to prioritize phone interviews for:

Groups for which a written narrative is inaccessible

Groups led by BIPOC trans people

Groups led by young people under 25

Groups without tax status

Spanish-speaking groups

Groups based in U.S. territories

Mobilize Power Fund 2026 Narrative Questions

Third Wave Fund updated its narrative proposal questions in April 2026. Previous applicants should therefore carefully review the current questions rather than relying on earlier versions of their applications.

Applicants are asked to address the following areas:

1. Purpose and Structure

Describe the purpose and structure of the organization and provide an overview of its regular activities.

Partnerships or coalitions should briefly describe each participating organization.

2. Accountability

Explain how the organization’s leadership is rooted in and accountable to the communities it serves, including young women of color and trans, queer, intersex, and gender non-conforming youth under 35.

Applicants should explain how their leadership aligns with the communities being served.

3. Context

Explain the specific incident or change in circumstances that occurred within the previous six months.

Applicants should clearly demonstrate how their proposed response relates to gender justice.

4. Pivot

Explain how the organization has pivoted or intends to pivot in response to the situation.

Applicants should explain how the proposed response differs from their existing work and provide a detailed timeline showing how their strategies and activities address the relevant incident or change.

5. Impact

Describe the impact the organization hopes to achieve within approximately six to eight months.

Applicants should also explain how young BIWOC and/or TIGNCBIPOC communities will benefit from the proposed work.

6. Partnerships

Applicants submitting a partnership or coalition proposal must explain the role each participating organization will play.

How to Apply for the Mobilize Power Fund 2026

Applications are submitted through the Proteus Fund Fluxx online grant portal.

Step 1: Access the Portal

Visit:

proteus.fluxx.io

Step 2: Create or Access Your Account

The procedure depends on whether you are a new or returning applicant.

Returning Applicants and Grantees

Organizations that have previously applied to a Third Wave Fund or Proteus Fund grant programme but have not used the new application system should use the Forgot Password function with their email address to regain access.

New Applicants

New applicants should request a new account at least three business days before the application deadline to allow time for approval.

Applicants should:

Select “Register Now.”

Complete all required fields on the registration form.

Select “Submit Request.”

Wait for a verification email.

Follow the verification link to create a password.

Log into the application system.

Select “Open Grant Opportunities.”

Choose “Third Wave Fund – Mobilize Power Fund.”

Begin the application.

The verification link sent to new applicants is valid for only 24 hours.

Third Wave Fund also recommends setting up the portal account in advance to allow time to resolve potential technical difficulties.

What Happens After Submitting an Application?

After submitting an application through Fluxx, applicants should receive a confirmation email.

The application will also appear under “Submitted Requests” within the applicant’s Fluxx account.

If Third Wave Fund requires clarification, additional information, or supporting documentation, the applicant will be contacted through the email address connected to their account.

The application may then be moved to “Requests to Edit”, allowing the applicant to review what additional information is required and submit the requested changes.

Applicants can also use the Fluxx portal to follow their application through the decision-making process.

When Will Applicants Receive a Decision?

Applicants are generally notified within four to six weeks after the monthly review deadline.

The notification may indicate that the application:

Has been recommended for funding

Has not been recommended for funding

Requires additional follow-up information

Third Wave Fund indicates that grant payments typically occur up to two months after the monthly review deadline, after the applicant has been notified and all necessary paperwork has been completed.

Payments are generally made through ACH direct deposit where applicable.

Third Wave Fund notes that it may be able to process requests more quickly in emergency situations.

Accessibility and Applicant Support

Third Wave Fund aims to make the application process accessible.

English applications use a screen-reader-compatible online portal. Applicants who require accommodations or have feedback concerning accessibility can contact the organization directly.

For application questions or support:

Email: mpf@thirdwavefund.org
Phone: 917-387-1262 x 920

For technical problems involving the Fluxx application system, applicants can contact:

fluxx@proteusfund.org

Important Tips for Applicants

Organizations interested in applying should carefully evaluate their circumstances before beginning an application.

First, make sure the issue being addressed occurred within the previous six months and represents an unexpected development rather than a previously planned activity.

Applicants should then demonstrate why this development requires a significant pivot from their organization’s normal work.

The proposal should also clearly establish the relationship between the issue and gender justice, particularly areas such as gender inequity, patriarchy, transphobia, homophobia or gender-based violence.

Organizations should demonstrate meaningful accountability to the communities they serve and explain how the proposed activities will build community organizing and movement power.

Applicants should also remember that:

Organizational budgets must be below $500,000.

Individual organizations or groups can request up to $10,000.

Partnerships or coalitions of at least two groups can request up to $20,000.

The proposed response should address an incident or change occurring within the previous six months.

Long-term programming extending beyond six months is not prioritized.

New applicants should request a Fluxx account at least three business days before the deadline.

Phone or Zoom interviews must be scheduled and completed at least one week before the application deadline.

APPLY NOW

Conclusion

The Third Wave Fund Mobilize Power Fund 2026 offers an important rapid-response funding opportunity for gender justice organizations and groups facing unexpected circumstances that require immediate adaptation, organizing, or action.

With grants of up to $10,000 USD for individual organizations and groups and up to $20,000 USD for partnerships or coalitions, the programme can provide timely financial support for organizations undertaking activities such as direct action, mutual aid, healing justice, conflict resolution, legal or bail support, leadership development, community organizing, and unexpected legislative or ballot initiative campaigns.

However, this is a highly targeted funding programme. Applicants must be based within the United States or U.S. territories, have organizational budgets below $500,000, demonstrate accountability to communities directly impacted by gender oppression, and be responding to a specific incident or change in circumstances that occurred within the previous six months.

Organizations interested in the September funding cycle should prepare their applications as soon as possible. The September 2026 deadline is September 8, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time. The October cycle will then open on September 9, with a final deadline of October 6, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Brooke Russell
Title: The Neil and Jane Pappalardo Special Fellow in Physics, 2024-2026
Email: russell3@mit.edu
Phone: (617) 253-8538

Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Experimental Nuclear and Particle Physics, Instrumentation

Research Interests

Brooke Russell is an experimental nuclear and particle physicist. Her research focuses on elucidating the landscape of beyond the Standard Model (BSM) physics brought about by massive neutrinos. This work currently involves neutrino property characterization and the study of neutrino interactions with matter.

Neutrinos are the most abundant massive particle in the universe. Ubiquity notwithstanding, much remains unknown about their underlying properties. With the DUNE experiment, Brooke aims to observe neutrino and antineutrino oscillation patterns to precisely measure neutrino mixing parameters. She is actively involved in the design, testing, and analysis of the liquid argon DUNE near detector (ND-LAr), which will measure and constrain the neutrino flux and constrain the response for a near-far detector oscillation measurement. Brooke’s work currently focuses on measuring neutrino-nucleus interactions and making detailed detector performance evaluations with small-scale demonstrators to mitigate cross section and detector systematic uncertainties, respectively, in future long-baseline neutrino oscillation analyses.

Biographical Sketch

Brooke earned an A.B. in physics from Princeton University in 2011. In her senior year, she was a co-captain of the women’s varsity track and field team. From 2011 to 2013, she was a research assistant in the Particle and Nuclear Astrophysics group in the Princeton Physics Department, using chemical engineering techniques to remove radon daughters from liquid scintillator for the low-background Borexino solar neutrino experiment. Brooke earned her Ph.D. in physics from Yale University in 2020. Her dissertation work focused on novel signal processing and imaging techniques for liquid argon time-projection chambers (LArTPCs) with the MicroBooNE experiment. She was awarded the Gertrude Scharff-Goldhaber Prize from Brookhaven National Laboratory for her work. From 2020 to 2023, Brooke was an Owen Chamberlain postdoctoral fellow in the Physics Division at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. At Berkeley, she helped develop low-power, cryo-compatible pixelated charge and light detector system-on-a-chip readout. In 2021, Brooke was a recipient of the L’Oreal USA Women in Science Fellowship.

TITLE: Safeguarding Consultant Jobs in Southeast Asia 2026: Cowater International Opens Regional Safeguarding Roster

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Cowater International is inviting qualified safeguarding professionals to join its Safeguarding Roster of Consultants for Southeast Asia, an opportunity focused on strengthening organisational safeguarding systems among organisations working to prevent gender-based violence (GBV) across the region.

The consultancy is part of the Southeast Asia Gender-based Violence Prevention Platform, a regionally led and Australian-funded initiative designed to increase investment, coordination, evidence-based practice, advocacy, and capacity for the primary prevention of gender-based violence against women and girls across Southeast Asia.

The position offers experienced safeguarding specialists an opportunity to provide technical assistance to civil society organisations, women’s rights organisations and other local partners while contributing to stronger safeguarding policies, systems, and practices across the region.

About the Southeast Asia Gender-Based Violence Prevention Platform

The Southeast Asia Gender-Based Violence Prevention Platform was established in response to the need for greater investment and coordination in gender-based violence primary prevention initiatives across Southeast Asia.

The initiative is built around a shared commitment to ending gender-based violence against women and girls in all their diversity. It seeks to strengthen locally led approaches by promoting evidence-based advocacy, dialogue, policy development, and programming.

The Platform is led by a regionally based Secretariat and works in collaboration with Cowater International, Social Development Direct and the Equality Institute. These collaborating organisations provide organisational development and technical assistance to support the Platform’s work.

The programme operates through three major pillars:

1. Demonstrate

This pillar focuses on generating and sharing evidence about what works in preventing gender-based violence in Southeast Asia.

The objective is to ensure that evidence on effective GBV prevention approaches is accessible and applied by practitioners and policymakers across the region.

2. Advocate

The Advocate pillar seeks to expand regional and bilateral cooperation among multiple stakeholders working on GBV prevention.

It aims to strengthen collaboration and commitment to gender-based violence prevention among governments, organisations, practitioners, policymakers, and other relevant stakeholders.

3. Facilitate

The Facilitate pillar is designed to strengthen the capacity of practitioners and policymakers to develop, implement, and monitor high-quality, evidence-based GBV prevention policies and programmes.

The Platform also provides competitive grants to civil society organisations and women’s rights organisations in Southeast Asia. These grants are offered through several funding cycles and range from AUD 20,000 to AUD 150,000.

About the Safeguarding Consultant Position

The Safeguarding Consultant will provide tailored technical assistance to a portfolio of Platform grantees to help them strengthen their organisational safeguarding systems and practices.

The work is intended to ensure that participating organisations operate in accordance with DFAT safeguarding standards and the safeguarding standards established by the Platform.

The consultant will work under the overall guidance of the Platform’s Safeguarding Specialist, with technical support from the Safeguarding Adviser of the Technical Partner.

Rather than simply producing safeguarding documents for organisations, the consultant will act as a technical partner throughout the grant lifecycle. The approach is intended to help organisations build sustainable safeguarding capacity based on their existing systems, strengths, risks, and organisational context.

Key Responsibilities of the Safeguarding Consultant

Successful consultants will be expected to undertake responsibilities across grant assessment, safeguarding planning, technical assistance, monitoring, and coordination.

Grant Assessment and Onboarding

At the beginning of the grant process, the consultant will contribute to safeguarding-related assessment and onboarding activities.

Key responsibilities include:

Providing technical input into the safeguarding review of grant applications.

Supporting due diligence processes.

Contributing to safeguarding risk assessments.

Helping identify safeguarding risks associated with proposed projects.

Recommending appropriate measures for mitigating identified risks.

Helping grantees understand DFAT safeguarding standards.

Ensuring grantees understand their safeguarding responsibilities throughout the grant period.

This means candidates should be comfortable assessing organisational risks and translating safeguarding standards into practical requirements that local organisations can understand and implement.

Safeguarding Action Planning

Another major responsibility will involve helping grantees develop and strengthen their safeguarding action plans.

The consultant will be expected to:

Review safeguarding policies, procedures, and supporting organisational documents.

Assess existing organisational safeguarding capacity.

Compare existing systems against DFAT and Platform safeguarding standards.

Facilitate the development or refinement of risk-proportionate Safeguarding Action Plans.

Build on the organisation’s existing safeguarding systems, strengths, and priorities.

Help grantees identify realistic and achievable safeguarding priorities.

Ensure agreed priorities are aligned with relevant DFAT standards and expectations.

The emphasis is therefore not on imposing a standardised safeguarding model. Instead, consultants are expected to help organisations strengthen systems that are appropriate to their specific circumstances and levels of risk.

Ongoing Technical Assistance and Capacity Strengthening

The successful consultant will provide continuing technical support throughout the grant lifecycle.

This may include:

Providing tailored safeguarding advice and technical accompaniment.

Reviewing safeguarding policies and procedures.

Providing feedback on safeguarding tools and resources developed by grantees.

Supporting organisations to operationalise safeguarding systems.

Strengthening reporting mechanisms.

Supporting risk management processes.

Advising on safe recruitment practices.

Supporting safeguarding training and governance.

Delivering or facilitating safeguarding learning sessions.

Providing coaching or mentoring where necessary.

Working with grantees, mentors, mentees, and other Platform partners.

Identifying emerging safeguarding concerns.

Working with the Platform Secretariat to develop appropriate responses to emerging issues.

The position therefore requires more than theoretical knowledge of safeguarding. Candidates need to demonstrate an ability to work directly with organisations, understand their practical challenges, and help them implement workable solutions.

Monitoring, Documentation, and Coordination

The consultant will also be responsible for following up on safeguarding progress and maintaining effective communication with assigned organisations.

Responsibilities include:

Maintaining regular communication with grantees.

Monitoring progress against agreed Safeguarding Action Plans.

Documenting progress and emerging challenges.

Recording agreed next steps and technical assistance provided.

Identifying situations where safeguarding priorities or action plans need to change as projects evolve.

Escalating complex safeguarding concerns, incidents, or significant organisational risks to the Platform Safeguarding Specialist.

Ensuring that technical advice remains consistent with DFAT safeguarding requirements and Platform guidance.

A Facilitative and Locally Led Approach

One of the most important aspects of this consultancy is the expected working approach.

Consultants are expected to use a facilitative, collaborative, and capacity-strengthening approach. Rather than taking over the safeguarding responsibilities of partner organisations or simply writing policies on their behalf, consultants should help organisations develop and implement their own safeguarding systems.

This makes experience in organisational development, mentoring, coaching, and locally led development particularly relevant.

Candidates should therefore be able to work respectfully with different types of organisations and support them to build on their existing strengths and systems.

Qualifications Required for the Safeguarding Consultant Role

Educational Requirements

Applicants should have at least a Bachelor’s degree in a relevant discipline.

Acceptable fields include:

Social work

Gender and development

International development

Community development

Human rights

Social sciences

Another relevant field

A postgraduate qualification is desirable but not essential.

Additional training or professional certification can strengthen an application. The position particularly values training or certification in areas such as the following:

Safeguarding

Child protection

Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (PSEAH)

Gender-based violence

Protection

Investigations

Related safeguarding fields

Professional Experience Requirements

Candidates must have a minimum of five years of relevant professional experience in safeguarding, child protection, PSEAH, gender-based violence, or related areas.

Importantly, this experience should include providing technical assistance, organisational capacity strengthening, or safeguarding support to:

Civil society organisations

NGOs

Development partners

Women’s rights organisations

Community-based organisations

Other local partners

Specific Skills and Experience

Applicants should be able to demonstrate experience in developing, reviewing, and strengthening organisational safeguarding systems.

Relevant experience includes:

Developing and reviewing safeguarding policies.

Strengthening safeguarding procedures.

Developing or reviewing codes of conduct.

Establishing reporting mechanisms.

Strengthening case-handling mechanisms.

Developing safeguarding prevention and response systems.

Conducting safeguarding risk assessments.

Developing risk mitigation measures.

Implementing and monitoring risk mitigation measures.

Providing technical assistance and mentoring.

Facilitating safeguarding training and workshops.

Providing safeguarding coaching and organisational mentoring.

Candidates should also have a strong understanding of:

Safeguarding principles.

Victim-survivor-centred approaches.

Child safeguarding.

PSEAH.

International donor safeguarding standards.

DFAT safeguarding requirements or comparable standards.

Locally led development principles.

Interpersonal and Professional Competencies

The role requires strong interpersonal and analytical abilities because consultants will work with organisations that may have different levels of safeguarding capacity and different operational contexts.

Applicants should demonstrate:

Strong analytical skills.

Excellent facilitation skills.

Strong interpersonal and communication skills.

The ability to explain complex safeguarding concepts in practical and accessible language.

Sound professional judgement.

The ability to maintain confidentiality.

The ability to manage sensitive safeguarding information with professionalism and integrity.

Experience working with diverse organisations is also highly desirable. This includes experience with women’s rights organisations, organisations of persons with disabilities, LGBTQIA+ groups, and other organisations representing or supporting different communities.

Language Requirements

Applicants must have proficiency in English and at least one Southeast Asian language, both written and oral.

This requirement is important because the consultant will work with organisations and stakeholders across Southeast Asia and will need to communicate technical safeguarding concepts effectively in relevant local contexts.

Who Can Apply?

Diversity and Equal Opportunity

The opportunity places emphasis on diversity, inclusion, gender equality, and intersectionality.

Women in all their diversity, persons with disabilities, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and people from historically marginalised or underrepresented communities are strongly encouraged to apply.

The organisation also states that it is committed to hiring based on merit and qualifications and does not discriminate on the basis of race, religion, sex, gender identity, disability, age, or other legally protected grounds.

Graduate students and alumni from WHOI’s Physical Oceanography Department recently joined more than 5,000 attendees at the 2026 Ocean Sciences Meeting in Glasgow, Scotland, for a week filled with science and discussions about the future of ocean research. TITLE: Call for Consultants: Mid-Term Review of the AAU 2016 – 2020 Strategic Plan

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities is calling for applications from consultants to undertake a mid-term review of its 2016-2020 Strategic Plan.

The Mid-Term Review (MTR) will assess the progress of AAU 2016 – 2020 Strategic Plan. It will also highlight issues and challenges affecting effective and efficient implementation of the Strategic Plan and recommend changes where necessary.

The review is being undertaken at the midpoint of the Strategic Plan’s implementation and will pave the way for improved delivery for the remaining Plan’s duration and propose amendments (if any) required in the Strategic Plan’s implementation arrangements and/or institutional linkages in order to effectively and sustainably contribute to improved performance of African Higher Education Institutions and the AAU Secretariat.

SCOPE OF THE EVALUATION

The evaluation will review the performance of the AAU 2016 – 2020
Strategic Plan since its inception to date. Specifically, it will review the Plan’s
goal and strategies, objectives, outcomes and impact as outlined in the
Strategic Plan and other relevant documents to determine their relevance and
compatibility with the constitutional mandate and mission of the AAU. It will
cover work done by AAU in line with the three broad goals, seven key result
areas and 29 strategic objectives of the AAU 2016 – 2020 Strategic Plan.

The assessment will focus on but not be restricted to the issues
outlined below:

Relevance

Assess the contribution of the Strategic
Plan towards the achievement of organizational mandate of AAU.
Analyze whether the Strategic Plan’s
implementation strategies address the needs and demands of the African higher
education stakeholders.
Assess the relevance of the Strategic
Plan’s activities, including capacity building for higher education leaders and
managers, and AAU Staff.

Effectiveness

Review whether the Strategic Plan has accomplished its outputs. In particular
the mission should:

Assess the qualitative and quantitative
achievements of objectives, strategies, activities, targets, indicators, and
partners as defined in the Association’s Strategic Plan Matrix, as well as
other documents and work-plans.
Based on the progress so far suggest /
recommend any changes to the current arrangements.

Efficiency

Analyze the role of the AAU Governing Board
as the Supervisory Organ of the Secretariat and assess whether this body is
optimally being used for Strategic Plan implementation and decision making.
Assess the timeline and quality of the
reporting followed by the Association.
Analyze the performance of the Monitoring
and Evaluation mechanism of the Association and the use of various M&E
tools.
Assess the qualitative and quantitative
aspects of management and other inputs (such as equipment, monitoring and
review and other technical assistance and budgetary inputs) provided by the Association vis-à-vis
achievement of objectives, strategies, activities, targets, indicators of the
Strategic Plan.
Identify factors and constraints which have
affected the Strategic Plan’s implementation including technical, managerial,
organizational, institutional and socio-economic issues in addition to other
external factors.

Sustainability and Impact

Assess preliminary indications of the
degree to which the Strategic Plan’s results are likely to be sustainable and
provide recommendations for strengthening sustainability.
Based on the findings (relevance,
efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability and impact) as well as taking into
account new emerging initiatives at both regional and continental level, recommend whether continuation of the
Strategic Plan is warranted.

Lessons Learnt/ Conclusions

Analyze areas for improved programme
planning, especially with respect to setting targets, relevance and capacity of
AAU for decision making and delivery.
Identify significant lessons or conclusions
which can be drawn from the Strategic Plan in terms of effectiveness,
efficiency, sustainability and networking.

EXPECTED OUTPUTS

The Mission’s findings and recommendations will be thoroughly discussed with AAU. The Mission will complete and submit a draft final report in soft copy at the end of the mission. Key stakeholders (AAU Secretariat and the Governing Board) will provide comments on the Draft Final Report, based on which the Mission will finalize the report.

All applications should be sent to secgen@aau.org not later than 31st January, 2019.

TITLE: NASA Fellowships: Research, STEM Graduate Education and Fellowship Opportunities for Aspiring Scientists and Engineers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The NASA Fellowship Activity provides opportunities designed to strengthen the next generation of scientists, engineers, researchers and other STEM professionals while supporting research and education that contribute to the missions of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).

Through its fellowship activities, NASA supports research, graduate-level education, hands-on experience and workforce development in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). The initiative forms part of NASA’s wider commitment to developing a highly skilled workforce capable of contributing to research, innovation, aeronautics, science and the continued advancement of space exploration.

Each year, NASA Fellowships awards research grants, as authorized by Congress, to Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs) through funding from the Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP). The fellowship activity is intended to help prepare graduate-level students for research careers by combining academic development with practical experience and workforce training.

NASA also partners with The National GEM Consortium, providing another important pathway for undergraduate and graduate students pursuing disciplines relevant to NASA’s missions.

For students interested in engineering, computer science, physical sciences, mathematics, data science, environmental science and numerous other STEM disciplines, NASA’s fellowship ecosystem provides a valuable starting point for identifying graduate education, research and professional development opportunities.

About the NASA Fellowship Activity

NASA Fellowships are designed to help develop a well-trained STEM workforce capable of contributing to the United States’ scientific, technological and space exploration priorities.

The fellowship activity has a strong emphasis on preparing graduate-level students for careers in research. Participants and institutions can benefit from opportunities that connect academic learning with practical research experience, workforce preparation and exposure to areas relevant to NASA’s work.

NASA’s fellowship activities also support the broader development of:

Faculty members;

Undergraduate students;

Graduate students;

Researchers;

STEM professionals; and

Academic institutions involved in research and education.

Through NASA’s partnership with The National GEM Consortium, students in disciplines needed to advance NASA’s missions can gain access to graduate education, industry experience and professional development opportunities.

The overall goal extends beyond providing financial assistance. NASA Fellowships contribute to the development of a pipeline of talented scientists, engineers and researchers who can potentially advance innovation and discovery in areas connected with NASA’s work.

NASA Fellowships and the Minority University Research and Education Project

An important component of NASA’s Fellowship Activity is its relationship with the Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP).

Each year, NASA awards research grants to Minority Serving Institutions using MUREP funds. These investments are authorized by Congress and are intended to strengthen research capacity, STEM education and workforce development.

MUREP supports NASA’s efforts to engage academic institutions and students while building pathways into STEM research and related careers.

Prospective applicants should understand that these institutional research grants are distinct from individual graduate fellowship opportunities. Students looking for an individual fellowship should carefully review the specific program through which they intend to apply.

NASA and The National GEM Consortium Partnership

One of the major pathways highlighted through NASA Fellowships is its partnership with The National GEM Consortium.

GEM provides opportunities for students pursuing master’s and Ph.D.-level education in engineering and science. The program connects graduate education with employers, universities and practical professional experience.

The GEM Fellowship Program is designed to promote opportunities for individuals to enter industry at the graduate level, particularly in areas including:

Research and development;

Product development;

Engineering;

Scientific research;

Advanced technical careers; and

Academia.

GEM provides MS and Ph.D. students with access to participating engineering and science employers and universities.

This structure can be particularly valuable for students seeking a graduate education experience that combines academic study with professional exposure.

GEM Fellowship Programs

The National GEM Consortium identifies fellowship opportunities at both the Master’s and Ph.D. levels in engineering and science.

Through the program, eligible fellows may receive financial support for graduate education while gaining practical work experience with participating employers.

The structure helps connect three important components of STEM career development:

Graduate-level academic education;

Financial support for advanced study; and

Practical industry experience.

This combination allows fellows to develop academic expertise while simultaneously gaining experience that may prepare them for research, engineering, technology and other highly technical careers.

GEM Fellowship Benefits

The exact financial package and benefits depend on the fellowship classification and sponsorship arrangement.

Employer Fellows

For Employer Fellows, university sponsorship is required, and applicants must be available for selection by a participating employer.

According to the GEM Fellowship Program information, benefits can include:

A minimum total stipend of $16,000 over the entire Master’s program;

Up to two paid summer internships with a GEM Employer Member; and

Full tuition and fees provided by a GEM University Member.

The combination of tuition assistance, stipend support and paid internships makes the fellowship particularly valuable for students seeking both academic and professional development.

University Fellows

University Fellows may receive:

Full tuition and fees provided by a participating GEM Member University.

Associate Fellows

Associate Fellows may receive:

Full tuition and fees from the GEM Member University;

At least $8,000 per year in stipend support for Master’s students; and

At least $16,000 per year in stipend support for Ph.D. students.

Applicants should note that University and Associate Fellows are nominated by participating universities rather than selected as an applicant-chosen fellowship classification.

Practical Summer Internship Experience

Practical professional experience is an important component of the GEM Fellowship.

For applicable GEM Fellows, the summer internship with a GEM Employer represents the initial phase of the fellowship program. Acceptance of the relevant employment validates the fellowship.

Confirmed GEM Fellowship internships generally must be completed over a 10- to 12-week period during the summer, normally between May and August, or potentially into September for universities operating on a quarter system.

This work experience gives fellows an opportunity to apply their academic knowledge in professional environments while building experience relevant to advanced STEM careers.

General GEM Fellowship Eligibility Requirements

Students interested in the GEM pathway highlighted by NASA should carefully review its eligibility requirements.

For the program described by GEM, applicants must:

Be a senior or graduate of an accredited engineering or computer science program at the time of application;

Have a minimum cumulative GPA of 2.8 on a 4.0 scale; and

Contractually agree to intern for two summers with the sponsoring GEM Employer, beginning in the summer following sponsorship.

Additional requirements apply elsewhere in the program rules and should be reviewed before an application is submitted.

Citizenship Requirement

The GEM Fellowship has an important citizenship requirement.

Applicants must be either:

A United States citizen; or

A United States permanent resident

at the time they submit their application.

International students who do not hold U.S. citizenship or U.S. permanent resident status therefore do not meet this stated GEM citizenship requirement.

Applicants should not automatically assume that this citizenship rule applies to every NASA graduate or postdoctoral opportunity. Other NASA opportunities may establish their own eligibility requirements, and candidates should review the specific solicitation or program before applying.

Is the GRE Required?

The Graduate Record Examination, commonly known as the GRE, is not required for the GEM Fellowship application.

However, GEM strongly encourages students considering STEM graduate programs to take the GRE because individual universities or graduate programs may have their own admissions requirements.

Applicants who already have GRE results may submit their scores. Candidates should therefore separately review the admission requirements of every graduate program to which they intend to apply.

University Application Requirement

Applying for the fellowship does not replace applying to graduate school.

Applicants are required to apply directly to a minimum of three GEM Member Universities’ STEM graduate departments.

The deadline identified for applying to the three GEM Member Universities is January 15 or the relevant STEM graduate department’s deadline, whichever comes earlier.

Applicants must ultimately be admitted to a GEM Member University’s graduate program with confirmed departmental funding support before the GEM Fellowship can be awarded.

This requirement is particularly important because submitting only the GEM Fellowship application is not sufficient.

Even undergraduate students whose current university has indicated that it may support them as a GEM Fellow are generally still required to apply to three GEM Member Universities. A limited exception exists for certain applicants already matriculating in the same graduate program for which they are seeking financial support.

Eligible STEM Disciplines

The GEM Fellowship covers an extensive range of science, technology, engineering and mathematics disciplines.

Examples identified by GEM include, but are not limited to:

Aeronautical Engineering;

Aerospace Engineering;

Agricultural Engineering;

Analytical Chemistry;

Anatomy;

Automotive Engineering;

Biochemistry;

Bioengineering;

Biology;

Biomedical Engineering;

Chemical Engineering;

Chemistry;

Civil Engineering;

Computer Engineering;

Computer Science;

Data Science;

Electrical Engineering;

Environmental Engineering;

Environmental Science;

Industrial Engineering;

Information Systems;

Inorganic Chemistry;

Manufacturing Engineering;

Materials Engineering;

Materials Science;

Mathematics;

Mechanical Engineering;

Metallurgical Engineering;

Nuclear Engineering;

Operations Research;

Organic Chemistry;

Petroleum Engineering;

Physics;

Robotics and Engineering;

Structural Engineering; and

Systems Engineering.

Because this list is not exhaustive, students in related STEM fields should review the current eligible disciplines and program rules before determining whether their program qualifies.

How to Apply for NASA Fellowship Opportunities

NASA directs prospective applicants to different resources depending on the type of opportunity they are seeking.

1. GEM Fellowship Opportunities

Students interested in GEM Fellowship opportunities should visit The National GEM Consortium’s GEM Fellowship Program.

The current program information indicates that the GEM application is open and provides access to the eGEM application system.

Applicants should carefully review:

Fellowship options;

Application instructions;

Rules and requirements;

Eligible disciplines;

Available resources;

Internship requirements; and

Frequently asked questions.

2. Planned NASA Solicitations

Applicants and institutions interested in planned NASA funding opportunities should consult NASA’s EONS Grant Forecasting webpage.

This resource provides information concerning planned solicitations and can help prospective applicants anticipate upcoming opportunities.

3. Graduate and Postdoctoral Opportunities

NASA directs individuals looking for other graduate and postdoctoral opportunities to its Learner Opportunities resources.

Because requirements can vary significantly between programs, prospective applicants should review each individual opportunity rather than assuming that GEM’s requirements apply to all NASA-supported fellowships.

Important Application Deadlines

The NASA Fellowship Activity information provided does not state one universal application deadline for all NASA Fellowships.

Similarly, the supplied GEM Fellowship Program information indicates that the GEM application is currently open but does not provide a single closing date for the fellowship application itself. Applicants should therefore check the current eGEM application portal and official program instructions for the applicable application-cycle deadline.

One important deadline is explicitly identified for the university application component:

GEM Member University application deadline: January 15 or the relevant STEM graduate department deadline, whichever is earlier.

Applicants should not wait until January 15 without checking their chosen departments because a department may impose an earlier deadline.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should carefully understand the commitments associated with accepting a GEM Fellowship.

Employer Selection

Applicants may be contacted by multiple GEM employers during the selection process. However, the employer ultimately selects the applicant for sponsorship rather than the applicant selecting the sponsoring employer.

Once an applicant has been selected for sponsorship by a GEM Employer, another GEM Employer cannot subsequently select that applicant. If the applicant rejects the internship and sponsorship offer, this can amount to declining the GEM Fellowship.

Graduate School Commitment

Applicants should be prepared to begin or continue their graduate education as required.

GEM indicates that an applicant cannot knowingly accept the fellowship with the intention of deferring the beginning of graduate school to a later date. Candidates uncertain about their graduate education plans should communicate with the relevant employer and university representatives before making a commitment.

Fellowship and Other Funding

Receiving another funding opportunity does not necessarily mean a student cannot participate in GEM. However, GEM states that fellows cannot accept a competing fellowship alongside the GEM Fellowship, although certain supplemental fellowships may be permitted.

Applicants receiving multiple funding offers should confirm compatibility before accepting them.

Why Consider NASA-Connected STEM Fellowship Opportunities?

For aspiring scientists, engineers and researchers, NASA-associated fellowship pathways can provide more than financial assistance.

Depending on the specific program, potential advantages can include:

Support for graduate education;

Research experience;

Exposure to NASA-relevant STEM disciplines;

Workforce training;

Professional development;

Industry experience;

Paid internship opportunities;

Connections with participating employers;

Access to universities and research environments;

Opportunities to develop advanced technical skills; and

Preparation for careers in research, engineering, science, technology and academia.

NASA’s broader objective of preparing graduate students for research careers means these opportunities can serve as an important bridge between university education and advanced STEM careers.

About NASA

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is the United States government agency responsible for the nation’s civilian space program as well as major work in aeronautics and space research.

NASA describes its mission as exploring the unknown in air and space, innovating for the benefit of humanity and inspiring the world through discovery.

Its work spans areas including space exploration, Earth science, planetary science, astrophysics, aeronautics, technology development and human spaceflight.

Developing future generations of STEM professionals is therefore an important component of NASA’s long-term mission.

Where to Find More Information

Prospective applicants should use the official NASA and GEM resources for current requirements and application information.

For NASA Fellowship information, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources/internship-programs/nasa-fellowships/

For GEM Fellowship opportunities and application information, visit:

https://www.gemfellowship.org/gem-fellowship-program/

The GEM application portal is available through the eGEM system.

For planned NASA solicitations, applicants should consult NASA’s EONS Grant Forecasting webpage.

For other NASA graduate and postdoctoral opportunities, candidates should explore NASA’s Learner Opportunities resources.

Questions specifically concerning NASA Fellowships may also be directed to:

Fellowships@mail.nasa.gov

Conclusion

The NASA Fellowship Activity represents an important component of NASA’s investment in STEM education, research and workforce development. Through research grants to Minority Serving Institutions, graduate-level development activities and partnerships such as the collaboration with The National GEM Consortium, NASA helps create pathways for students, researchers and academic institutions to contribute to the future of science, technology, engineering and space exploration.

For eligible graduate students, the GEM Fellowship pathway can be particularly valuable because it combines academic financial assistance with practical industry experience. Depending on fellowship classification and sponsorship, support can include full tuition and fees, stipends and paid summer internships with participating GEM employers.

Prospective applicants should nevertheless distinguish between the broader NASA Fellowship Activity and specific programs such as GEM. Eligibility, citizenship, funding, academic requirements and deadlines can vary depending on the particular fellowship or solicitation.

Students interested in the GEM pathway should pay particular attention to the U.S. citizenship or permanent residency requirement, academic eligibility, internship commitments and the requirement to apply to at least three GEM Member University STEM graduate departments.

Most importantly, applicants should consult the official NASA and GEM websites before submitting an application to confirm the current application cycle, deadlines and program requirements.

For students who meet the applicable requirements and are serious about building advanced careers in engineering, science, research and technology, NASA-connected fellowship opportunities offer a pathway to combine graduate education, professional experience and participation in the broader STEM workforce supporting future innovation and exploration.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.

TITLE: In Memory of Fanyi Zhao

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Postdoctoral Researcher Dr. Fanyi Zhao, a rising star in the area of nuclear and particle theory, tragically passed away on January 24, 2024 at the age of 27. She had joined MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics (CTP) (now MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)) in September 2023.

Born in 1996 in China, Fanyi received her B.S. in Physics in 2018 from the University of Science and Technology in Anhui, China before heading to UCLA where she completed her PhD in Physics under the supervision of Professor Zhong-bo Kang. Her PhD thesis was titled “3D Imaging via Polarized Jet Fragmentation Functions and Quantum Simulation of the QCD Phase Diagram.”

During her time, at UCLA, she impressed in many ways with her research in QCD theory and phenomenology, and in quantum simulation to QCD and strong interactions. She was a recipient of the Mani L. Bhaumik Institute Nina Byers Summer Fellowship in Theoretical Physics and a fellowship in quantum information science. In addition to efforts in conference organizing and diversity and outreach she also found time to mentor undergraduate students at UCLA, a number of whom went on to PhD programs in Physics, including one at MIT.

Joining the CTP (now CPT-LI) in the September 2023, Fanyi’s research involved using quantum field theory to investigate nucleon structure, including things like transverse momentum distributions, energy-energy correlators, and jets as a member of the research team of Professor Iain Stewart. Her work also continued to involve a significant component on quantum information science as applied to problems in nuclear physics.

She is remembered by Center members and other colleagues outside of MIT as a funny, generous, kind and thoroughly committed scientist with a great love of physics. Beyond her scientific passion, she embraced life fully, with passions ranging from music and martial arts to running and drawing. We are all greatly saddened by her passing.

In May 2024, the Center for Theoretical Physics will honor Fanyi’s memory with the announcement of the recipient of the first Fanyi Zhao Award for postdoctoral researchers in the CTP who have promoted collaboration and interactions between different CTP research groups, including scientific and/or social connections.

In the Fall of 2024, there will also be the Fanyi Zhao Memorial Lecture established at the UCLA Department of Physics and Astronomy. This lecture series will be awarded yearly to a young physicist, recognizing outstanding achievements in nuclear and particle physics.

Any donations made to the CTP-LI to honor the memory of Fanyi Zhao will be used to support the award named in her honor.

A reminder to all that MIT’s MyLife Services for staff, postdocs and faculty (844-405-5433), and Student Mental Health and Counseling for students (617-253-4481, Option 2), are available 24/7 including on the weekend.

TITLE: AAU advocates for top-level support for the Open Science Agenda

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
As part of the Open Science Day holding on the sidelines of the World Science Forum and the Science Granting Councils Initiatives’ Annual Forum in Cape Town, South Africa, the Association of African Universities (AAU) has made a high-level presentation on why Open Science is important for African Universities and the AAU’s role in institutional policy dialogue.

Addressing participants, Mrs. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, the Senior Communications and Publications Officer, who spoke on behalf of Mr. Abednego Corletey, the Senior IT Officer for AAU, highlighted the importance of top-level support at both the University and National levels to foster the adoption and advancement of Open Science. She indicated that the Registry of Open Access Repository Mandates and Policies (ROARMAP) states that out of 1,225 African universities, only 36 have Open Access Mandates and none have Open Science ones, and therefore it was urgent for key players advancing the course of Open Science to implement strategic approaches to increased awareness and buy-in from the key decision makers in African Universities.

The AAU’s presentation underscored the fact that Open Science presents enormous benefits to the research ecosystem, including promoting access to knowledge, ensuring efficiency and quality of research, promoting innovation and collaboration, garnering increased visibility for both African Researchers and their Research. Mrs. Nkrumah Kuagbedzi mentioned that Open Science, by its very nature requires researchers to make their data, processes for data analysis and findings readily available to others, from the very start of their research, thus promotes transparency in the research process, and assures the reproducibility and replicability of research.

Key intervention by the AAU and its Partners – PLOS, TCC & UNESCO

The presentation to participants at the forum highlighted some of the various interventions being implemented by the Association of African Universities and its partners – the Public Library of Science (PLOS), The Training Centre in Communications (TCC) and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), in promoting the adoption of Open Science by African Universities.

The initiatives, being championed with an overall goal of increasing awareness and getting the buy-in from the higher education leaders (both top and mid-level management), include institutional policy dialogues, advocacy, and capacity building among others. Regional meetings and workshops have been hosted for the East and Central Africa Regions and the Northern Africa Region. Both events, hosted on the theme – ‘Open Science Policies and Mandates in African Higher Education Institutions’, were highly successful and had over 650 participants in attendance. The East and Central Africa event was hosted by the University of Dar-es-Salaam, in Tanzania, from 14th -15th July 2022, while the Northern Africa Regional event was hosted by the British University in Egypt from 26th – 27th October 2022.

The Association of African Universities also focused its 2022 Africa Universities Day Celebrations (a week-long statutory celebration to mark the establishment of the AAU), on the theme ‘Open Science – Bringing Equity to Research and Publishing’. The weeklong celebration featured key events from November 7 -12, 2022, and convened various higher education stakeholders, including African Universities, ministries of education, industry, and development partner institutions as well as others for dialogue on the important topic of Open Science.

Participants were also told that the AAU established a Knowledge Management Unit in 2005 to improve and put in place mechanisms to ensure that the knowledge generated by African Universities are properly managed. This unit had since then focused on creating the requisite platforms, for instance it introduced and managed the Database of African Theses and Dissertations -Including Research (DATAD-R) Platform. The DATAD-R platform was set up to help increase visibility and improve access to research emanating from African Higher Education Institutions and can be accessed from here – http://datad.aau.org:8080/xmlui/. The Unit has also been engaging in capacity building and helping institutions to set up their repositories, among others.

The presentation made by the AAU on the Open Science Day also highlighted the key roles of the National Research and Education Networks (NRENs) in terms leveraging their infrastructure, resources, and expertise to support the Open Science agenda. AAU spearheaded the NREN agenda with partners as far back in 2005 and has partnerships with the various networks, including – the West and Central Africa Research and Education Network (WACREN), UbuntuNet Alliance for Research and Education Networking, and the Arab States Research and Education Network (ASREN).

Planned Events and Upcoming Engagements

Beyond the policy dialogues and current engagement by the AAU and partners, it was emphasized that the focus going forward is to present the value proposition of Open Science to more stakeholders at the topmost level of African Higher Education, including University Senate bodies. So far, institutions have invited the partners to present the Open Science discourse to their senate members as part of ensuring buy-in.

Events are also planned for 2023 in South Africa to be hosted by the University of Cape Town for the entire Southern African Universities.

Other Presentations and Discussions by Participants

The session on Open Science which was facilitated by Dr. Ezra Clark of UNESCO and Ms Joy Owango of the Training and Communication Centre, Africa, also featured key presentations by other institutions as well as a question-and-answer session with experts.

Dr. Jo Havemann, of AfricArXiv elaborated on the various platforms, infrastructures and networks that exist on the continent, while Dr. Justine Germo Nzweundji, of the Global Young Academy also engaged participants on the various opportunities and challenges for early career researchers.

The expert panel that delved deep into discussing various topical issues, including strategies for overcoming some unintended consequences of Open Science – article processing charges, commercial exploitation of data, predatory behaviors, and other topics, included Roheena Anand, PLOS; Prof. Arianna Becerril-García, AmeliCA; Dr. Andrés Izeta, National University of Cordoba; Dr. Bianca Amaro, LA Referencia; Maria Cotera, Figshare; Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, AAU; Dr. Peggy Oti-Boateng, African Academy of Sciences; Susan Veldsman, InterAcademy Partnership & ASSAF; and Dr. Mathieu Denis, International Science Council.

Dr. Ezra Clark, of UNESCO also briefed participants about the UNESCO Recommendation Checklist on Implementing Open Science at Universities and referred them to access this important document via the UNESCO website – https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000379949.locale=en

Overall, participants unanimously agreed that there’s a great deal that needs to be done by Africa and its Higher Education Institutions and stakeholders to leapfrog its Open Science adoption rates. The raising of funds locally to support Open Science also came tops as priority during the discussions. Similarly, the importance of partnering with researchers from other continents, and working to gain the necessary political will in our various countries and institutions were highlighted as being critical. Participants and researchers, generally, were called on to be ambassadors of Open Science wherever they find themselves.

About the SGCI Annual Forum Platform

The SGCI Annual Forum is part of the series of high-level dialogues and engagements hosted by the National Research Foundation (NRF) of South Africa, on the side-lines of the World Science Forum. The SGCI holds these dialogues annually as part of its strategy to strengthen partnerships, share experiences and practices on a range of emerging topics, and network amongst themselves and with other science system actors within and outside the African continent.

Written By: Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, Senior Communications and Publications Officer, AAU

Reviewed By: Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management, AAU

TITLE: Wallace Fellowships 2027-2028 at Harvard University (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 16, 2026

Applications are open for the Wallace Fellowships 2027-2028 at Harvard University. The Wallace Fellowships are designed for scholars who explore the historiography and impact of the Italian Renaissance in the Modern Era (19th-21st centuries). They are made possible by a generous grant from The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund.

Projects could address a range of topics from historiography to the reaction to, transformation of, and commentary on the Italian Renaissance and its ties to modernity. Also, welcome are projects on museum and collecting history and on the survival of the Renaissance in modern art and architecture (including photography and landscape architecture), in literature and music, and in philosophy and political thought.

I Tatti offers Fellows the precious time they need to pursue their studies with a minimum of obligations and interruptions together with a maximum of scholarly resources—a combination that distinguishes the Harvard Center from similar institutions. Each year, a limited number of activities organized at I Tatti are reserved for the Fellows, and they are expected to join the wider community at conferences, lectures, and concerts.

This is a residential fellowship of 4 or 6 months in length. Up to four fellowships will be awarded every year.

Benefits

The grant is USD $5,200 per month, plus a one-time supplement (maximum USD $1,800) towards relocation expenses. In light of the residential nature of the fellowship Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days a week at the center. When possible, an apartment will be set aside for the Fellow’s use, rent free, but with charges for utilities. If an apartment is not available, a housing subsidy will be offered to help offset rental costs.

Eligibility

At the time of application, scholars must have a PhD in hand and will be asked to upload a scan of the certificate.

They may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application. They should work solely on the project with which they applied and are not permitted to work simultaneously on editing other book or article projects. The proposed research project may represent a segment of a larger project.

Applicants must be conversant in English and have familiarity with Italian.

Priority will be given to early and mid-career scholars.

Projects can address the historiography or impact of the Renaissance on any field, including art and architecture, landscape architecture, history, literature, material culture, music, philosophy, religion, and science. It must be possible for applicants to carry out most of their research in Florence.

I Tatti welcomes applications from scholars from all nations and gives special consideration to candidates without regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy.

Application

Applications can be written in English or Italian and must be submitted electronically by midnight (Cambridge, MA time) on November 16, 2026. Scholars can apply for only one type of fellowship at I Tatti per academic year.
