TITLE: 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day: SG Prize for Outstanding AfCFTA Intellectual Property Innovation and Impact

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day (#2026AIPD) is highlighting the growing importance of intellectual property in strengthening African businesses, innovation, trade and economic development under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

Under the theme “Growing Business Under The AfCFTA IP Ecosystem,” the initiative seeks to recognize exceptional accomplishments involving intellectual property, particularly achievements that contribute to the implementation and operationalisation of the AfCFTA Protocol on Intellectual Property Rights.

A central component of the 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day initiative is the SG Prize, which recognizes an outstanding individual or entity whose work demonstrates meaningful use or generation of an intellectual property right, process or mechanism in the context of the AfCFTA.

The recognition is intended to celebrate African innovators, creators, entrepreneurs, institutions and other stakeholders whose intellectual property-related work produces tangible economic, social or cultural value and has the potential to inspire similar achievements across the continent.

2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day

Africa’s expanding continental market presents significant opportunities for businesses, innovators, creators and institutions. However, intellectual property protection and effective use are important components of ensuring that African innovation can generate sustainable value within this market.

The 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day focuses attention on the relationship between intellectual property and the implementation of the AfCFTA. Its theme, “Growing Business Under The AfCFTA IP Ecosystem,” reflects the role intellectual property can play in helping African enterprises develop, protect and commercialize their ideas, brands, inventions, creative works and other forms of intellectual assets.

The initiative also provides an opportunity to showcase accomplishments that demonstrate how intellectual property can contribute to:

Business growth and competitiveness

Cross-border trade within Africa

Innovation and technology development

Employment creation

Export growth

Community development

Cultural preservation

Recognition of African creativity and invention

Greater use of intellectual property systems across African markets

What Is the SG Prize?

The SG Prize is a recognition for an exceptional accomplishment by an individual or entity in any domain involving technology, cooperation, economy, trade, law or business where the achievement involves or targets the use or generation of an intellectual property right, process or mechanism in the context of the AfCFTA.

The prize is designed to celebrate individuals and organisations contributing to the development and operationalisation of the AfCFTA IP Ecosystem.

Rather than simply recognizing an idea or an untested concept, the SG Prize places emphasis on verifiable intellectual property use and demonstrable impact.

This means that nominees should be able to show evidence that their intellectual property has been formally registered and applied and that it has generated a concrete outcome.

What Types of Intellectual Property Can Be Considered?

The SG Prize guidelines identify several forms of intellectual property that may qualify, including:

Trademarks – intellectual property associated with brands, names, symbols, signs and other identifiers.

Patents – protection associated with qualifying inventions and technological innovations.

Geographical Indications (GIs) – intellectual property connected to products whose characteristics, reputation or qualities are linked to a particular geographical origin.

Plant Variety Rights – intellectual property protection associated with qualifying new plant varieties.

Applicants and nominees should therefore identify the relevant intellectual property right associated with the achievement and provide appropriate evidence demonstrating that it has been formally registered and used.

Key Eligibility and Evaluation Criteria for the SG Prize

The SG Prize guidelines establish several important criteria that submissions should satisfy.

1. Verifiable Intellectual Property Use

The first requirement is that the nominee must have formally registered and applied intellectual property.

The relevant IP may involve:

Copyright

Trademark

Patent

Geographical indication

Plant variety right

Importantly, the guidelines require evidence supporting the intellectual property claim. Such evidence should either be publicly available or submitted alongside the nomination.

This requirement means that applicants should avoid relying solely on general descriptions of an invention, business, creative project or innovation. The submission should demonstrate that the intellectual property exists within an identifiable and verifiable protection or registration framework and that it has actually been applied.

2. Demonstrable Impact

The intellectual property must have produced a concrete outcome.

The guidelines recognize three broad forms of impact:

Economic impact

Examples may include:

Increased income

Export growth

Business expansion

Job creation

Commercialisation of an innovation

Increased market access

Improved business competitiveness

Social impact

Examples may include:

Community benefits

Increased public access

Improved services

Support for communities

Wider access to useful products or innovations

Cultural impact

Examples may include:

Preservation of cultural heritage

Protection or promotion of cultural expressions

Recognition of artistic achievements

Strengthening of African cultural identity

The application should therefore move beyond simply stating that an innovation has been successful. The impact statement should explain what changed as a result of the intellectual property and provide evidence supporting that change.

The guidelines specifically indicate that vague claims are insufficient.

3. African Origin and Reach

Another important criterion is the African origin of the work, innovation or creation.

The work must originate in an African Union (AU) Member State.

The guidelines also indicate that achievements demonstrating cross-border or AfCFTA-relevant impact score more highly.

This makes the relationship between the intellectual property achievement and the broader African market particularly important.

For example, a submission can be strengthened if it demonstrates how an intellectual property asset:

Expanded beyond its original national market

Supports African cross-border commerce

Facilitates trade between African countries

Creates opportunities under the AfCFTA

Demonstrates potential for wider continental adoption

4. Role-Model Potential

The SG Prize also considers whether the innovation or achievement can serve as an example for other Africans.

The guidelines emphasize that the innovation should be transferable and inspiring.

This means that a strong submission should demonstrate not only what the nominee achieved but also why the achievement matters to other entrepreneurs, innovators, creators, businesses or institutions across Africa.

A successful nominee should ideally demonstrate that their experience can provide a model that others can learn from, adapt or build upon.

5. Consent and Verifiability

Nominees must consent to being:

Publicly named

Quoted

Featured

In addition, all claims associated with the nomination must be verifiable through either:

Publicly available information, or

Supporting documents submitted with the nomination

Applicants should therefore ensure that information included in the submission is accurate and supported by appropriate documentation.

Who Can Be Nominated for the SG Prize?

The submission form provides two types of submission:

Individual

Institution

The recognition therefore accommodates both individual accomplishments and institutional achievements.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to individuals or entities that have developed, registered and applied intellectual property in an African context and can demonstrate measurable economic, social or cultural impact.

Potentially relevant nominees may include innovators, entrepreneurs, creators, technology developers, businesses, institutions and other organisations whose intellectual property-related accomplishments satisfy the stated criteria.

What Should the 200-Word Impact Statement Include?

One of the most important parts of the submission is the 200-word impact statement.

The form specifically asks applicants to provide a 200-word impact statement based on the SG Prize criteria.

A strong statement should therefore focus on evidence rather than general descriptions.

Applicants should consider addressing the following questions:

What intellectual property was developed or used?

Clearly identify the relevant IP right, process or mechanism.

For example, explain whether the achievement involves a patent, trademark, copyright, geographical indication or plant variety right.

Has the intellectual property been formally registered?

Explain where and how the IP has been registered, where relevant, and provide supporting evidence.

How has the intellectual property been applied?

Describe how the intellectual property is being used in practice rather than simply describing the idea behind it.

What measurable impact has it created?

Explain the concrete results generated by the IP.

Depending on the achievement, this could include:

Income generated

Jobs created

Export opportunities

Business growth

Community benefits

Public access

Cultural preservation

Artistic recognition

How is the achievement relevant to Africa and the AfCFTA?

Applicants should explain the African dimension of the achievement and, where applicable, demonstrate cross-border or AfCFTA-related relevance.

Why can the achievement inspire others?

Explain what makes the innovation transferable, scalable, replicable or inspirational for other Africans.

Supporting Documents and Evidence

Applicants are required to upload relevant supporting evidence.

The submission system allows supporting evidence to be provided in either of two formats:

One ZIP folder, or

Up to 10 separate PDF files

The maximum total file size for the uploaded evidence is 100MB.

Applicants should organize their supporting documentation carefully so that the evidence directly supports the claims made in the nomination.

Possible supporting documentation may include relevant official registration evidence, documentation demonstrating application or use of the intellectual property, evidence of impact, publicly verifiable records and other materials that substantiate the submission.

The strongest supporting evidence should directly connect the intellectual property to the claimed economic, social or cultural outcomes.

Information Required in the Application Form

The submission form requires applicants to provide several key details.

These include:

Email address

Full name of the applicant

Type of submission

Individual

Institution

Country of origin of the applicant

200-word description of impact

Relevant supporting evidence

Applicants should ensure that all information entered in the form is accurate and consistent with the supporting documentation.

SG Prize Submission Deadline

The deadline for submitting nominations for the SG Prize is: 31 August 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day to prepare their submissions, particularly where supporting documents need to be collected, converted into PDF files or compressed into a ZIP folder.

Early preparation can also provide an opportunity to review the 200-word impact statement and ensure that it addresses the eligibility and evaluation criteria.

How to Prepare a Strong SG Prize Submission

Applicants can improve the quality of their submission by taking a structured approach.

Step 1: Identify the Intellectual Property

Begin by clearly identifying the intellectual property associated with the achievement.

Determine whether the relevant asset involves a:

Patent

Trademark

Copyright

Geographical indication

Plant variety right

Step 2: Gather Verification

Collect documentation demonstrating that the intellectual property has been formally registered and applied.

The evidence should be clear enough to allow the claim to be verified.

Step 3: Quantify the Impact

Where possible, use specific evidence to demonstrate results.

For example, instead of simply stating that an innovation created economic benefits, explain the measurable outcome, such as increased income, additional employment, export activity or expansion into new markets.

Similarly, social and cultural impact should be explained through concrete results rather than broad statements.

Step 4: Establish the African Connection

Explain where the innovation or creation originated and how it relates to an AU Member State.

If the achievement has reached multiple African markets or has a clear relationship with AfCFTA implementation, make this connection explicit.

Step 5: Demonstrate Role-Model Potential

Explain why other African innovators, businesses, institutions or creators could learn from or adapt the achievement.

This is particularly important because the SG Prize seeks to recognize achievements that are transferable and inspiring.

Step 6: Prepare the 200-Word Statement

The impact statement should be concise but evidence-driven.

Because the form specifically limits the impact statement to 200 words, applicants should prioritize:

The intellectual property

Verification

Application

Measurable impact

African origin and reach

AfCFTA relevance

Role-model potential

Step 7: Organize the Supporting Evidence

Ensure that all supporting documents are readable and relevant.

Applicants can submit either one ZIP folder or up to 10 PDF files, with a maximum combined file size of 100MB.

Why Intellectual Property Matters Under the AfCFTA

The AfCFTA is intended to strengthen economic integration and create greater opportunities for trade across African markets. Intellectual property is an important part of this ecosystem because businesses and innovators depend on intellectual assets to distinguish products, protect inventions, develop brands, preserve creative works and commercialize innovations.

For African businesses seeking to expand beyond their domestic markets, intellectual property can provide an important foundation for protecting and developing their competitive advantages.

The 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day theme therefore draws attention to the connection between intellectual property, business growth and continental trade integration.

Recognizing successful examples can help demonstrate how intellectual property can be transformed from a legal concept into a practical tool for economic, social and cultural development.

APPLY HERE

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity: 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day – SG Prize

Theme: “Growing Business Under The AfCFTA IP Ecosystem”

Recognition: SG Prize

Submission types: Individual or Institution

Focus: Intellectual property use or generation in the context of the AfCFTA

Eligible IP areas: Copyright, trademarks, patents, geographical indications and plant variety rights

Impact areas: Economic, social and cultural

Geographical requirement: Work, innovation or creation must originate in an AU Member State

Supporting evidence: One ZIP folder or up to 10 PDF files

Maximum evidence size: 100MB total

Impact statement: 200 words

Deadline: 31 August 2026

Conclusion

The 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day SG Prize provides an opportunity to recognize exceptional intellectual property achievements that contribute to Africa’s economic, social and cultural development under the AfCFTA framework.

The initiative goes beyond recognizing ideas alone. The SG Prize emphasizes formally registered and applied intellectual property, verifiable evidence, measurable impact, African origin, AfCFTA relevance and the ability to inspire other Africans.

Individuals and institutions with qualifying achievements should carefully document their intellectual property, demonstrate the concrete results it has produced and clearly explain its relevance to the wider African market.

With the submission deadline set for 31 August 2026, eligible applicants and nominees should begin preparing their 200-word impact statement and supporting evidence as early as possible. A well-organized submission that directly addresses each SG Prize criterion can effectively communicate the significance and wider potential of an intellectual property achievement.

The 2026 Africa Intellectual Property Day theme ultimately highlights an important message for African innovators and businesses: intellectual property can be more than protection for an idea or creation; when effectively developed and applied, it can become a tool for business growth, innovation, employment, trade, cultural preservation and stronger participation in Africa’s emerging continental market.

TITLE: UPSA Requests for PHD Collaboration with Sister African Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), Ghana, is keen to exploit the prospects of international educational partnerships and collaborations in PhD studies with sister African Universities across the continent. UPSA is a full member of the Association of African Universities (AAU) and part of AAU’s mandate is to foster mutually beneficial relationships for its member institutions. Founded in 1965 as an institute for professional studies training, UPSA has grown to become a full-fledged University, and accredited with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission. UPSA offers business programmes in undergraduate, graduate, diploma, professional courses and recently PhD. Along with two other universities in Ghana, UPSA made the 2021 Times Higher Education Impact Rankings. UPSA is an accredited member of Accreditation Council for Business Schools and Programs.

The Office of Doctoral Programmes (ODP) is the mandated office responsible for the development and administration of PhD programmes at UPSA. Currently, the office is superintending over the PhD in Marketing programme and is close to securing accreditation for PhD in Accounting and PhD in Finance.

In line with UPSA’s mission, the doctoral programme has been designed with inputs from practicing academics in the field and external academic partners. It hinges on a foundation of in-depth knowledge in the core areas of the relevant discipline area, facilitated by experienced academic mentors and rigorous independent student research with a developing economy and sustainability perspective, and applicable in both the public and private sectors. It is a blend of research and course work, designed to equip students with the requisite theoretical background and methodological skills necessary for carrying out industry-relevant research and the development of successful careers at institutions of higher learning. This approach will be a precursor for students to contribute meaningfully and scientifically to the generation of new knowledge.

Informed by the above, and working with AAU, the ODP seeks partnerships from sister universities across Africa with the objective of working collaboratively for mutual benefits. The areas for potential collaboration and partnership include:

Faculty exchange programmes

Student exchange programmes

Co-hosting of PhD programmes

Joint PhD student or faculty research collaboration

Joint seminars for faculty and students

Joint supervision for PhD Thesis

The UPSA Office of Doctoral Programmes welcomes proposals for collaboration in PhD education with the potential to promote synergy for both institutions. If your institution is keen to collaborate with the University of Professional Studies, Office of Doctoral Programmes, please contact:

TITLE: DA Young Leaders Programme 2027: Applications Open for Young South Africans Interested in Political and Public Service Leadership

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027 Democratic Alliance (DA) Young Leaders Programme (YLP), a one-year political leadership learning and development programme designed for young South Africans who are passionate about leadership, public service, politics and creating positive change in their communities.

The programme provides an opportunity for motivated young people to strengthen their political knowledge, critical-thinking abilities, communication skills and personal leadership capabilities while gaining practical experience through a dedicated leadership project.

For young South Africans considering a future in politics, government, public service or community leadership, the DA Young Leaders Programme offers structured leadership development designed to help participants understand their leadership potential, identify areas for personal growth, and develop the skills required to become effective changemakers.

About the DA Young Leaders Programme 2027

The DA Young Leaders Programme is described as a political leadership learning and development programme for South Africans aged between 18 and 35 who align themselves with the Democratic Alliance’s values of Freedom, Fairness, Opportunity and Diversity.

The programme is aimed at highly motivated individuals who are interested in pursuing a career in politics or the public service and who want to contribute to building what the DA describes as “One Nation with One Future.”

Rather than focusing only on theoretical leadership concepts, the programme combines political learning, personal development, communication development and practical leadership experience. Participants are expected to develop a stronger understanding of politics while also gaining greater insight into their own leadership style, strengths and development needs.

Over the course of one year, Young Leaders participate in activities intended to broaden their political knowledge and critical-thinking capabilities. They also develop communication skills and take part in dedicated sessions focused on leadership and personal development.

A central component of the programme is the requirement for each participant to conceptualise and undertake a leadership project. This gives participants an opportunity to apply what they learn in a practical setting while addressing an issue within their community.

Who Should Apply for the DA Young Leaders Programme?

The programme is designed for young people who are not only interested in leadership but are already demonstrating a commitment to making a positive difference in their communities.

According to the programme information, successful applicants are expected to demonstrate qualities such as

Integrity and a strong commitment to serving others.

Leadership potential and motivation to create meaningful change.

A desire to continue developing their personal and professional potential.

An interest in politics, public service or government as a potential career path.

A passion for contributing to a better future for South Africa.

The ability to align their personal values with the Democratic Alliance’s liberal values and principles.

An interest in strengthening their critical-thinking, communication, writing, public-speaking, and leadership skills.

The programme therefore goes beyond identifying young people who simply have an interest in politics. It seeks individuals who demonstrate leadership potential, community commitment and a willingness to take responsibility for creating meaningful change.

What Participants Can Gain from the Young Leaders Programme

The DA Young Leaders Programme provides a combination of political education, leadership development, personal development and practical experience.

1. Political Knowledge and Understanding

Participants have the opportunity to broaden their understanding of politics and develop greater political knowledge. This can help them better understand the issues affecting South Africa and the role that effective leadership can play in addressing national and community challenges.

The political learning component is particularly relevant for young people considering future careers in political leadership, government or public service.

2. Critical-Thinking Skills

Critical thinking is another important area of development within the programme.

Participants are challenged to think critically and develop the ability to engage with issues in a thoughtful and informed manner. These skills can be valuable for people interested in policy, public leadership, government and community development.

3. Communication Development

Communication is a major component of effective leadership, and the programme provides participants with opportunities to strengthen their communication abilities.

Participants are expected to develop their:

Writing skills

Public-speaking abilities

General communication skills

Ability to express ideas effectively

Capacity to engage with political and community issues

These skills can be particularly valuable for aspiring public representatives and future leaders.

4. Personal Leadership Development

The programme also places considerable emphasis on personal development.

Participants are given opportunities to understand themselves better, including their individual leadership styles and areas where they need further development. Dedicated leadership and personal-development sessions are intended to support this process.

This emphasis means that the programme is not solely focused on external leadership responsibilities. It also encourages participants to develop self-awareness and understand how their individual characteristics can influence the way they lead.

5. Practical Leadership Experience

One of the distinguishing elements of the programme is the leadership project that every participant is required to undertake.

Through this project, participants are able to move beyond classroom or theoretical learning and apply their leadership skills to a real-world challenge.

The programme states that these projects provide experience in areas such as:

Planning

Collaboration

Community engagement

Leadership

Problem-solving

Public leadership

This practical experience can help participants build confidence and develop a stronger understanding of what effective leadership looks like in real communities.

Leadership in Action: The Programme’s Community Projects

The leadership project component is intended to create meaningful impact within participants’ communities.

According to the programme information, previous projects have addressed a range of social and community challenges. Examples provided by the programme include initiatives focused on gender-based violence awareness, school support, youth employment, housing and education.

Examples include:

Anti-Gender-Based Violence Awareness

Some Young Leaders have developed campaigns focused on raising awareness about gender-based violence. These initiatives have included empowering young women and organising public gatherings against gender-based violence.

Such projects demonstrate how leadership development can be connected to advocacy and community mobilisation.

School Support Initiatives

Other projects have focused on supporting disadvantaged schoolchildren.

The examples include initiatives that provided children with essential items such as proper shoes, with the broader aim of supporting their confidence and sense of pride.

Female Youth Employment Projects

Some participants have worked on projects designed to address youth employment challenges among disadvantaged girls.

These initiatives have sought to help bridge the gap between secondary education and full-time employment, demonstrating how Young Leaders can use community projects to address barriers facing young people.

Housing and Education Projects

Other leadership projects have addressed housing and community resilience.

The programme highlights projects involving the construction of houses in vulnerable areas of the Western Cape, alongside efforts to educate local communities about the use of sandbag systems for flood protection.

These examples illustrate the practical dimension of the Young Leaders Programme: participants are expected to use their leadership skills to engage with genuine challenges and develop initiatives that can produce tangible community benefits.

The DA Young Leaders Programme’s Long-Term Impact

The Young Leaders Programme has already developed a substantial alumni network.

According to the programme’s information, more than 330 graduates have completed the programme since its launch. These alumni are described as making an impact across South Africa in public office, within the Democratic Alliance and through community initiatives.

The programme reports the following impact figures:

330+ graduates have completed the Young Leaders Programme.

84 alumni are currently serving in public office, including as Members of Parliament, Members of Provincial Legislatures, councillors and other elected representatives.

7 members of the Democratic Alliance’s leadership are alumni of the Young Leaders Programme.

Alumni continue to contribute through community initiatives, public service and policy development across South Africa.

These figures demonstrate the programme’s stated role in developing a pipeline of young people who can go on to participate in political leadership, public service and community development.

The Programme’s Vision for South Africa

The Young Leaders Programme is connected to the DA’s broader vision for South Africa.

The programme’s stated vision is for a South Africa in which individuals have the opportunity to live lives that they value. It describes a country characterised by a dynamic and innovative society, an inclusive and growing economy, and a capable government that protects the Constitution and promotes equal opportunity.

The vision emphasises equal opportunity regardless of where people are born, how they look or other arbitrary characteristics.

The programme argues that achieving such a vision requires excellent leaders who are prepared to step forward and lead.

Consequently, the Young Leaders Programme is positioned as part of the effort to prepare young South Africans for future leadership responsibilities.

Eligibility for the DA Young Leaders Programme 2027

The source identifies the programme as being open to South Africans between the ages of 18 and 35 who align with the DA’s stated values of Freedom, Fairness, Opportunity and Diversity.

Potential applicants should therefore carefully consider whether they meet the programme’s stated target profile before submitting an application.

The programme is particularly relevant to individuals who:

Are South African.

Demonstrate leadership potential.

Demonstrate integrity and a commitment to serving others.

Want to strengthen their political knowledge and critical-thinking skills.

Want to improve their writing, public-speaking, and communication abilities.

Are willing to undertake a leadership project.

Can align their personal values with the DA’s stated liberal values and principles.

Is a Tertiary Qualification Required?

However, the supplied material lists the question without providing an answer. Therefore, the source does not establish that a university or college qualification is either required or not required.

Previous Applicants and DA Programme Participants

Again, the supplied source lists these questions but does not provide their answers. Applicants in either situation should therefore consult the official programme information or contact the YLP Office for clarification.

What Makes the Programme Relevant to Aspiring Public Leaders?

Leadership in politics and public service requires more than an interest in public affairs. Effective leaders need to communicate ideas, understand complex issues, work with others, engage communities and develop the confidence to make decisions.

The Young Leaders Programme brings these areas together through political learning, critical thinking, communication development, personal leadership sessions and practical community projects.

For young people considering a future in political or public leadership, the programme can therefore provide a structured environment in which to explore leadership ambitions while developing practical skills.

Its emphasis on leadership projects is particularly significant because participants are expected to translate their learning into action. Rather than limiting leadership development to discussions and training sessions, the programme provides an opportunity to work on a real community challenge.

Why Community Leadership Experience Matters

The programme’s emphasis on community projects reflects the importance of practical experience in leadership development.

Working on a community initiative can require a participant to identify a problem, understand the people affected, develop an approach, work with others and implement activities. Such an experience can strengthen a range of leadership capabilities.

The examples provided by the programme show that leadership projects can cover diverse areas, including social justice, education, employment, housing, gender-based violence awareness and community resilience.

This provides participants with an opportunity to connect leadership development with issues that affect communities directly.

TITLE: IAS CEU Global Invisible University Fellowships 2027/28: Residential Research Opportunities for Scholars and Artists in Budapest

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University (IAS CEU) is inviting applications for its 2027/28 Global Invisible University Fellowship Program, offering an exceptional opportunity for scholars, researchers, writers and visual artists to pursue independent work within an international and interdisciplinary academic community.

Hosted primarily in Budapest, Hungary, the IAS CEU fellowship programme brings together highly accomplished senior academics, promising early-career scholars, threatened scholars, writers and visual artists whose work connects with some of the most pressing intellectual, political, social, environmental and institutional challenges facing societies today.

For the 2027/28 academic year, the Institute is offering several fellowship pathways, including the Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship, Artist in Residence Fellowship, Residential and Non-residential Fellowships for Threatened Scholars, and Residential Affiliated Fellowships.

Depending on the fellowship, successful applicants may spend between three and nine months at IAS CEU, while non-residential opportunities for threatened scholars can extend from six to 12 months.

The fellowships form an important part of the Global Invisible University (GIU), a wider CEU initiative that integrates research, teaching, mentoring and civic engagement while seeking new ways of responding to challenges affecting universities, scholars and access to knowledge around the world.

About the IAS CEU Global Invisible University Fellowship Program

The Institute of Advanced Study at CEU provides an intellectual environment in which fellows can concentrate on their individual research and creative projects while participating in a broader interdisciplinary community.

IAS CEU is seeking scholars who are interested not only in advancing their own research but also in contributing to conversations about new approaches to producing, sharing and transferring knowledge.

The fellowship programme is envisioned as the principal research arm of the Global Invisible University.

The initiative draws on approximately 15 years of institutional experience and practices developed by IAS CEU and combines this established research infrastructure with GIU’s broader ambition to rethink higher education in response to contemporary global challenges.

These include challenges arising from:

War and armed conflict;

Forced displacement;

Autocratization and democratic decline;

Restrictions on academic freedom;

Political repression;

Commercial pressures affecting higher education;

Inequalities in the production and accessibility of knowledge;

Threats faced by scholars and academic institutions; and

Wider transformations affecting universities and research communities globally.

Through this programme, CEU aims to bring together researchers and creative practitioners who can contribute to an international academic environment centred on rigorous research, interdisciplinary exchange and new approaches to knowledge production.

What Is the Global Invisible University?

The Global Invisible University (GIU) is a strategic initiative intended to develop a new model of a “university for the future.”

Rather than approaching research, teaching and public engagement as entirely separate activities, GIU seeks to integrate them.

The programme combines university-level education, mentoring and research involving students and scholars, including academics affected by authoritarianism, war, displacement and other crises that constrain academic life.

The wider objective is to contribute to more resilient, democratic and open societies and academic institutions.

The 2027/28 IAS CEU fellowships therefore offer more than simply time away from normal professional responsibilities. Fellows are expected to become members of an experimental academic community in which independent research, intellectual collaboration and discussions about the future of knowledge and higher education can reinforce one another.

IAS CEU Fellowship Duration for 2027/28

Residential fellowships are available for different periods, allowing fellows to participate for between three and nine months depending on the fellowship type and approved arrangement.

Potential residential periods include:

Nine-month fellowship: October 2027 to June 2028.

Three-month short fall semester: October to December 2027.

Five-month fall semester: October 2027 to February 2028.

Six-month spring semester: January to June 2028.

Separate arrangements apply to some fellowship categories, particularly the Artist in Residence and Threatened Scholars programmes.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the individual call corresponding to the fellowship for which they intend to apply.

Types of IAS CEU Fellowships Available for 2027/28

There are several fellowship pathways within the IAS CEU programme. Candidates should select the opportunity that most closely corresponds to their academic background, professional situation and proposed project.

1. Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship

The Junior and Senior Residential Fellowship, also described as the core fellowship programme, is designed for scholars who want to spend between three and nine months in Budapest pursuing their own research.

Both junior and senior scholars are considered within this programme.

Core fellows are given an opportunity to work on their research while becoming part of the interdisciplinary intellectual community at IAS CEU.

Importantly, Junior and Senior Core Fellows receive:

A fellowship stipend;

Accommodation at the Raoul Wallenberg Guesthouse;

An opportunity to pursue their own independent research;

Access to the IAS CEU intellectual community;

Research support and institutional resources; and

Opportunities for interdisciplinary exchange with other fellows and the wider CEU community.

Applicants should consult the dedicated Residential Core Fellowship call for the detailed eligibility criteria, financial terms and application requirements.

2. Artist in Residence Fellowship

IAS CEU also recognises creative practice as an important component of intellectual and societal engagement.

For 2027/28, the Institute offers two Artist in Residence opportunities:

One Writer in Residence Fellowship

One Visual Artist in Residence Fellowship

These fellowships are offered competitively to writers and visual artists whose work engages with the objectives of the Global Invisible University in innovative and convincing ways.

Eligible areas of creative practice may include, among others:

Poetry;

Prose;

Drama;

Screenwriting;

Playwriting;

Film;

Digital applications; and

Other forms of visual media.

Artist in Residence fellowships may last for up to five months, with a minimum residence period of three months.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate how their creative work connects meaningfully with the broader intellectual and societal aims of GIU.

3. Residential and Non-residential Fellowships for Threatened Scholars

An especially important component of the programme is dedicated to scholars facing serious threats to their ability to work, research or participate freely in academic life.

The Fellowships for Threatened Scholars are intended for scholars at risk because of circumstances including:

Loss of employment;

Harassment;

Violence;

Legal persecution;

Political or civic positions of dissent;

Identity;

Critical scholarship;

Exercise of academic freedom; or

Immediate exposure to active military conflict.

The programme therefore recognises that academic freedom and the ability to conduct research cannot be taken for granted in many parts of the world.

Scholars living in or coming from areas affected by active military conflict may also qualify where the conflict directly affects them.

In addition to residential opportunities, IAS CEU provides non-residential fellowships exclusively for Threatened Scholars.

These non-residential fellowships are available for periods ranging from six to 12 months, during the period from August 2027 to July 2028.

Candidates interested in this pathway should carefully consult the specific Threatened Scholars fellowship call because eligibility is linked to the applicant’s circumstances as well as their scholarly work.

4. Residential Affiliated Fellowships

IAS CEU also welcomes a limited number of Affiliated Fellows each year.

These opportunities differ significantly from the funded core fellowships.

Affiliated Fellows typically have their own external fellowship or other funding and use that support to spend all or part of their research period at IAS CEU.

The minimum stay for an affiliated fellowship is three months.

Prospective applicants should note that:

Affiliated Fellows do not receive a stipend from IAS CEU;

Housing may or may not be provided by the Institute;

Applicants typically rely on external fellowship funding or another independent source of financial support; and

The fellowship allows researchers to become part of the IAS CEU academic environment during their research period.

Applicants requiring full financial support should therefore pay close attention to the differences between the Affiliated Fellowship and the funded fellowship categories.

Research Areas for the Global Invisible University Fellowships

A major component of the selection process is the relationship between an applicant’s proposed project and the intellectual priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Applicants are expected to connect their research or proposed work with at least one of eight key GIU thematic areas.

1. Democratization, De-democratization and Re-democratization

This thematic area addresses processes through which democratic systems emerge, weaken, transform or recover.

Projects may explore questions surrounding democratic institutions, political participation, authoritarian tendencies, democratic resilience and transitions between different political systems.

2. Politics of History, Memory and Culture Wars

This area encompasses the political use and interpretation of history and collective memory, as well as contemporary cultural conflicts.

Relevant work may examine:

Historical narratives;

Collective memory;

Culture wars;

Nationalist discourse;

Transnationalist discourse; and

The relationship between identity, politics, culture and interpretations of the past.

3. Political Economy and Global Inequalities

Researchers working on political economy, economic structures, inequality and related global challenges may find this thematic area particularly relevant.

Projects could address the relationships between political institutions, economic systems, distribution of resources and inequalities within or between societies.

4. Human Rights and Justice

This research priority focuses on human rights and justice in the context of international and comparative law.

Researchers may investigate legal institutions, rights protection, comparative legal systems, international law and broader questions surrounding justice and accountability.

5. Crisis of Multilateralism and Global Institutions

This area examines the changing role and effectiveness of international and regional institutions and alliances.

Potential research subjects may include:

Multilateral organisations;

International cooperation;

Regional institutions;

Global institutions;

Political alliances;

International governance; and

Contemporary challenges facing multilateralism.

6. Politics of the Anthropocene, Climate Justice and Natural Resources

Environmental and climate-related research is another important GIU priority.

Relevant research may explore:

The politics of the Anthropocene;

Climate justice;

Environmental governance;

Natural resources;

Political and social responses to climate change; and

Inequalities associated with environmental change and resource distribution.

7. Old and New Media and Their Networks

This theme examines both established and emerging media environments and the networks through which information is created, circulated and contested.

Topics may include:

Information warfare;

Media networks;

Digital communication;

Safer use of media and digital systems;

Securitization; and

Transformations in information ecosystems.

8. Epistemological Problems of Social Sciences in the Digital Age

The eighth thematic area addresses fundamental questions about how knowledge and evidence are created and evaluated in an increasingly digital environment.

The programme specifically identifies areas such as:

Evidentiary procedures;

Truth claims;

Archival practices;

Digital transformations of research;

Epistemological challenges in the social sciences; and

“Forensic social sciences.”

Applicants do not necessarily need to address all eight areas. However, their proposed work is expected to demonstrate a meaningful relationship with at least one of these priorities.

Who Is IAS CEU Looking For?

IAS CEU describes its residential fellowships as opportunities for both highly accomplished senior scholars and promising younger scholars.

The programme is particularly relevant to individuals who want concentrated time to advance an independent research project while also participating in an interdisciplinary academic environment.

Depending on the specific fellowship, IAS CEU is seeking:

Junior scholars;

Senior and established scholars;

Researchers in the social sciences;

Researchers in the humanities;

Scholars whose research addresses GIU thematic priorities;

Writers;

Visual artists;

Scholars facing threats to their academic freedom or personal safety;

Scholars affected by active military conflict; and

Externally funded scholars interested in becoming Affiliated Fellows.

Applicants should not assume that general alignment with social sciences or humanities is sufficient. The proposed project should also demonstrate clear relevance to the broader goals and thematic priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Selection Process for the IAS CEU Fellowships

Applicants should be aware that admission to the IAS CEU fellowship programme is highly competitive.

Applications undergo a rigorous peer-review process, with the final decision made by an independent Selection Committee.

According to IAS CEU, major considerations include:

Excellence of the proposed research

The intellectual strength and overall quality of the research proposal are central to the assessment.

Applicant’s track record

The Selection Committee considers the applicant’s previous scholarly or professional accomplishments.

Thematic relevance

Proposed research must demonstrate relevance to the broader objectives and research priorities of the Global Invisible University.

Because the fellowships are highly competitive, applicants should ensure that their proposals clearly communicate the importance, originality and feasibility of their proposed work rather than relying solely on academic credentials.

Why Budapest Is Important to the Fellowship Experience

Although Central European University’s main campus is located in Vienna, Austria, CEU maintains a significant research presence in Budapest, Hungary.

Several CEU research institutes, centres and resources operate in Budapest, including:

The Institute of Advanced Study;

CEU Democracy Institute;

Blinken OSA Archivum;

Center for Ethics and Law in Biomedicine;

Artistic and cultural programmes;

Non-degree educational programmes; and

The Budapest branch of the CEU Library.

The fellowship programme is therefore situated within a broader intellectual ecosystem rather than functioning as an isolated research residency.

IAS CEU also views Budapest as an important environment for thinking about political and social transformation, including processes of re-democratization.

The programme aims to encourage new relationships and synergies not only among IAS fellows but also between fellows and educational and civil society organisations in Hungary and the broader region.

Benefits of Joining the IAS CEU Intellectual Community

While exact financial benefits depend on the fellowship category, participation in IAS CEU offers fellows an opportunity to become part of a multidisciplinary and international research environment.

Potential advantages include:

Dedicated time to pursue independent research or creative work;

Participation in an interdisciplinary community;

Interaction with scholars working across social sciences and humanities;

Engagement with CEU institutes, research centres and intellectual networks;

Opportunities for scholarly exchange and collaboration;

Access to research support infrastructure;

Participation in conversations around research, teaching and civic engagement;

An opportunity to explore new approaches to knowledge production and transfer; and

Residence in Budapest for eligible residential fellows.

For Junior and Senior Core Fellows specifically, IAS CEU states that fellows receive a stipend and accommodation at the Raoul Wallenberg Guesthouse.

Benefits and financial conditions vary across fellowship categories, so candidates should review the individual call before applying.

Application Deadline for IAS CEU Fellowships 2027/28

Application deadlines vary according to the individual IAS CEU fellowship call.

The general programme information provided by IAS CEU directs applicants to its dedicated fellowship and open-call pages for the applicable application deadlines and detailed instructions.

Applicants should therefore check the official IAS CEU Open Calls page and the individual fellowship call before submitting an application, rather than assuming that all 2027/28 fellowships share one closing date.

Because individual fellowship programmes may have different requirements, funding arrangements and deadlines, prospective applicants should begin reviewing the appropriate call as early as possible.

How to Apply for IAS CEU Fellowships 2027/28

Candidates should apply through the official Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University fellowship portal and relevant fellowship call.

Official fellowship information and open calls are available through:

IAS CEU Fellowships:

https://ias.ceu.edu/fellowships-ias-ceu

Applicants should first identify which fellowship best matches their circumstances:

Junior or Senior Residential Fellowship;

Writer in Residence Fellowship;

Visual Artist in Residence Fellowship;

Residential or Non-residential Fellowship for Threatened Scholars; or

Residential Affiliated Fellowship.

They should then open the corresponding official call and carefully review its eligibility requirements, application documents, financial conditions, residence requirements and deadline.

Given the competitiveness of the programme, applicants should allow sufficient time to prepare a strong research or creative proposal that clearly demonstrates both the quality of the proposed project and its relevance to the Global Invisible University.

Important Points Applicants Should Remember

Before applying for an IAS CEU fellowship for 2027/28, prospective candidates should keep several important points in mind:

The programme is centred primarily on the social sciences and humanities.

Proposed work should connect with at least one of the eight GIU thematic areas.

Residential fellowship periods generally range from three to nine months.

Artist in Residence fellowships are available for a minimum of three months and up to five months.

Non-residential fellowships lasting six to 12 months are available exclusively to eligible Threatened Scholars.

Junior and Senior Core Fellows receive a stipend and accommodation.

Affiliated Fellows do not receive a stipend from IAS CEU.

Housing for Affiliated Fellows is not guaranteed.

Applications are assessed through rigorous peer review.

Final decisions are made by an independent Selection Committee.

Research excellence, applicant track record and thematic relevance are major selection considerations.

The programme is highly competitive.

Applicants should consult their specific fellowship call for exact application requirements and deadlines.

Conclusion

The IAS CEU Global Invisible University Fellowships 2027/28 provide an important opportunity for scholars, researchers, writers and visual artists seeking dedicated time and an interdisciplinary environment in which to advance ambitious research or creative projects.

Through its different fellowship pathways, the Institute of Advanced Study at Central European University accommodates applicants at different career stages and in different circumstances—from promising junior researchers and established senior academics to creative practitioners, threatened scholars and externally funded researchers.

At the heart of the programme is the Global Invisible University’s ambition to rethink how research, teaching, mentoring and civic engagement can respond to the profound pressures currently affecting higher education and knowledge production worldwide.

Applicants whose work examines democracy, history and memory, inequality, human rights, international institutions, climate justice, media, digital society or changing methods of knowledge production may find particularly strong alignment with the programme’s research priorities.

Because admission is highly competitive, prospective applicants should carefully identify the most appropriate fellowship, study its individual requirements and develop a compelling proposal demonstrating research excellence, a strong track record and clear relevance to the Global Invisible University.

Interested applicants should visit the official IAS CEU fellowship website for the individual 2027/28 calls, detailed eligibility conditions, application procedures and applicable deadlines:

Over the past three years, 56 Global Youth Leaders from 38 countries and regions have been invited to attend the Youth Forum at the Wuzhen Summit, engaging in in-depth exchanges with leading figures across the global internet community. In 2025, the program attracted outstanding young applicants from nearly 120 countries and regions, receiving widespread attention and recognition.

The program aims to select outstanding young people in the global Internet field on a regular basis, closely follow the frontier trends of Internet technology, industry and governance, carry out a series of youth activities around Forum, Training, and Research, and build an international exchange and cooperation platform for young people to learn from each other.

Benefits

Receive an official Global Youth Leader certificate from the WIC.

Attend the 2026 WIC Wuzhen Summit and speak at the Youth Forum. Round-trip airfare, complimentary catering and accommodations are available upon application. You will have the opportunity to engage in in depth exchanges with high-level representatives of other international organizations, governments, global leading Internet companies, well-known experts and scholars, and senior officials of the WIC international organization.

Gain opportunities to organize workshops or activities at other WIC summits and thematic and regional forums.

Youth-led forums and activities initiated by Global Youth Leaders aligned with the WIC Global Youth Leaders Initiative will be eligible for inclusion in the program and may receive support from the WIC Secretariat. Outstanding outcomes may be featured in the program’s Collection of Practical Outcomes.

Receive priority access to internship and job opportunities within the WIC international organization.

Outstanding candidates advanced to the final review but not ultimately selected will receive a Nominee Certificate of the WIC Global Youth Leadership Program and be invited to join the WIC’s youth community, where they can participate in discussions, contribute ideas to conference activities, and enjoy priority access to WIC internship opportunities.

Eligibility

Embrace the mission of the WIC international organization. Be willing to engage with the vision of building a community with a shared future in cyberspace, and contribute ideas or perspectives that support this vision.

Be under the age of 45.

Have notable accomplishments in one or more internet-related or ICT-related fields:

In the policy field, they may hold positions in government or international organizations involved in digital governance or internet policymaking.

In the business sector, they may serve as senior executives in established internet companies or founders/leaders of innovative startups, with strong leadership, innovation, and influence.

In the research field, they may have made contributions to artificial intelligence, big data, and other internet-related technologies, industries, or governance through publications, awards, patents, or recognized academic achievements.

In the public interest field, they may lead NGOs or social organizations with expertise in digital inclusion, digital literacy, or the application of technology for public welfare and sustainable development.

Possess an international perspective and be willing to contribute to the growth of WIC’s youth community.

Demonstrate interdisciplinary and diverse thinking.

Exhibit strong public speaking and presentation skills.

Application

Ready to shape the future of the internet? Complete your personal information and submit the following materials through the online system:

TITLE: IPDE

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The European Post-Doctoral Institute for mathematical sciences (EPDI) was created in October 1995 by IHES, the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences (INIMS Cambridge) and the Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik (MPIM Bonn) in order to encourage young scientists’ mobility across Europe, in both basic and applied research.

The founding circle was enlarged with the arrival of the Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik in den Naturwissenschaften (MIS Leipzig) in 1998 and of the Erwin Schrödinger Institut (Vienna), the Institut Mittag-Leffler (Djursholm, Sweden) and the Banach Center (Warsaw) the following year.

With the addition in 2000 of the Centre de Recerca Matemàtica (Barcelona, Spain), and the Forschungsinstitut für Mathematik (Zürich), EPDI had nine European partners engaged in the pursuit of excellence.

In June 2007, the EPDI Directors invited the Mathematisches Forschungsinstitut Oberwolfach (Oberwolfach, Germany) to join the network, offering prospective candidates a broader choice for their itinerary. The Alfred Renyi Institute of Mathematics (Budapest) was the latest to join in 2014, bringing the number of EPDI institutes to 11.

From 1996 to 2014, EPDI made 20 calls for applications. Each year, it recruited 5-7 European postdocs (or holders of a European PhD) and one Japanese laureate. They came from all mathematical backgrounds and were able to work in the research centres of their choice.

The directors of EPDI are currently considering redesigning the programme. As a result, no call for applications was made in 2015.

TITLE: Universal Acceptance (UA) Day Celebrations – Tuesday March 28, 2023

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The maiden edition of the Universal Acceptance (UA) Day celebrations by AAU was held successfully on Tuesday 28 March 2023 to create awareness about Universal Acceptance as a prelude to the launch of the Universal Acceptance Readiness project, a new initiative between the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN).

The event which was collaboratively organized by the partners, AAU and ICANN, saw various stakeholders from the African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) participating both physically at the AAU Secretariat in Accra and virtually via the AU Zoom platform. These stakeholders included Vice Chancellors, Rectors, Deans and Heads of Departments, Technical staff, lecturers, and students of various HEIs on the continent and beyond. Directors and IT Professionals from various private sector organizations and institutions were also in attendance.

The theme for the event, “Universal Acceptance (UA) and What it Means”, provided an opportunity for participants to be educated on the meaning of Universal Acceptance. Universal Acceptance principles ensure that email addresses and all valid domain names, including long new top-level domains like .org, .net, .com, and .info which are part of Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), can be used by all internet-enabled applications, devices, and systems regardless of script, language and character length. UA generally supports the ability for email mailbox names to use characters in local languages and scripts through Email Address Internationalization (EAI) standards.

Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, the Director of ICT Services, Communications, and Knowledge Management at the AAU, delivered a speech on behalf of the Secretary-General of the AAU and began by giving a brief history of the AAU as an institution and its vision of being a lead advocate for higher education on the African continent. AAU’s strategic priorities are to promote a favourable policy environment, strengthen institutional capacity of stakeholders, promote harmonization standardization for competitiveness and collaboration, and mobilize resources to help sustain its programmes.

Ms. Dhlamini reiterated the partnership that was established in December 2022 between ICANN, AAU, and other organizations which launched the Coalition for Digital Africa Initiative, during the Internet Governance Forum themed, “Connecting All People and Safeguarding Human Rights” in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. She went on to explain the concept of Universal Acceptance and the need for its adoption in our various higher education institutions. She concluded her speech by expressing excitement about the participation of students in the event saying that they would go into the industry after school as champions of Universal Acceptance principles.

The Senior IT Officer at the AAU, Mr. Abednego Corletey, who was the main speaker for the event, made a presentation on the theme, “Universal Acceptance of Domain Names and Emails”, stressing what Universal Acceptance meant to the continent. He stated that, “Through Universal Acceptance, all those who develop, provide or manage online websites and applications will have the opportunity to enable users globally to experience the social and economic power of the internet through making their systems universally compliant”. Mr. Corletey engaged participants in hands-on tasks through case studies and the self-verification of the compliance of their institutional websites using the EAI checker.

Some comments and recommendations were made by some of the 48 representatives from various stakeholder institutions in Ghana who participated physically at the Secretariat and over 150 participants who connected via the AAU Zoom Platform. These comments included a proposal for a collaboration between the AAU and the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) toward the incorporation of the Universal Acceptance concepts in the IT Curriculum in Ghana. Another proposal of collaboration between the AAU and various institutes of languages such as the Ghana Institute of Languages to sensitize the public on the use of scripts in local languages, an extension of UA Day outreach to other parts of the continent, and the introduction of UA on assistive technologies for the visually impaired.

The Universal Acceptance Day celebration ended with closing remarks from the Mistress of the Ceremony and an official announcement of the launch of the Universal Acceptance Readiness project, slated for Thursday, April 13, 2023, at the AAU Secretariat in Accra, Ghana. A follow-up workshop is expected to be held at the same venue on Friday 14 April 2023 to give participants hands-on experience with the latest tools and technologies in the areas of making email systems and other communication platforms within Africa’s higher education institutions, ready for Universal Acceptance (UA) and Email Address Internationalization (EAI).

Article by – Ms. Naomi Darko, Communications Assistant, AAU.

TITLE: Selection and Review Process

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
USIEF follows a multi-tier selection process for all fellowships. After the application deadline, no applications will be accepted. The submitted applications move through the following stages of the selection process:

Technical Review: USIEF staff screen all the applications for eligibility and completeness before sending them to the reviewers/screening committees. Application that are deemed ineligible or do not meet the award requirements are not moved forward in the review process. Only complete applications (including all the required documents ) received by the deadline are considered in the review process. USIEF has created a checklist to ensure the applicants do not miss any mandatory documents.

Screening/Review Committees: Technically eligible applications are reviewed by subject experts. Reviewers include academicians and professionals from both U.S. and India who have discipline or field-specific experience. The committee/reviewers read and rate applications and make recommendations for further consideration.

National Selection Committee: Applicants who are short-listed in the review process are then invited for virtual interviews. Based on the fellowships available and priorities, final recommended list is drawn.

Screening/selection committees will generally use the following criteria to evaluate applications:

Academic credentials and professional ability

Merit of the proposed Fulbright project

Communication skills

Commitment to community or national service

Need to conduct research in the U.S. and relevance to the Indian context

Outcomes, Potential Impact and Benefits

Motivation, Seriousness of Purpose, Maturity, Leadership, Cultural Adaptability

Ability to contribute as a cultural ambassador beyond his/her specific field of study

Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board (FFSB): All final shortlisted applications are forwarded to FSSB for final approvals

Note: It is the policy of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board that reasons for non-recommendation and non-selection of applications are not given. Decisions taken by the reviewers/committees in connection with the selection process will be final and requests for reconsideration will NOT be entertained.

USIEF organizes mentoring workshops for potential Fulbright applicants, offering guidance on how to create a strong application. These workshops cover key elements of the application process and provide valuable insights to enhance your submission.

For more information on upcoming workshops in your region, please contact your local USIEF office.

TITLE: Call for Participation : The African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN) Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN) is organizing a hybrid conference that will be hosted physically in Maputo, Mozambique and virtually from – 25th to 27th October, 2022. This event is supported by the HAQAA2 initiative and is being held under the theme: ‘Post COVID-19: Emerging Developments in Quality Assurance in Africa – ‘Towards strengthening synergies between Quality Assurance Agencies and accelerating regional integration’ .The conference will create the much needed platform to to share new developments in quality assurance in Africa and to strengthen synergies between quality assurance agencies and networks, in pursuit of the harmonization of quality assurance systems in Africa, the mutual recognition of qualifications and enhanced mobility of academics and labor. The REGISTRATION LINK is made available here for stakeholders’ attention – https://www.research.net/r/AfriQCon22

Background

Over a decade, quality assurance in higher education in Africa has registered tremendous changes. Cognizant of the important role of quality assurance agencies, the continent continue to register an increase in the number of new agencies that are being created. On the other hand, the already established agencies continue to strengthen their quality assurance activities, notably by undergoing external quality assurance evaluations and by joining and participating in the activities and key programmes of different quality assurance networks, such as the African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN), the Francophone Network of Quality Assurance Agencies (RAFANAQ), the East African Quality Assurance Network (EAQN), among others. These quality assurance collaborations are fostering the establishment of compatible and comparable quality assurance systems to facilitate the recognition of qualifications and mobility of labor on the continent.

In the same line, the HAQAA (Harmonisation of African Higher Education Quality Assurance and Accreditation) initiative that was launched in 2016 and funded by the European Union in partnership with the African Union, has been established to support the development of a harmonised quality assurance and accreditation system at the institutional, national, regional, and Pan-African continental levels.

Despite the above positive developments, African higher education has faced different challenges including the recent effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, and therefore the need to relook the emerging developments (both positive and negative) and to strengthen the efforts by the different players to overcome the challenges and accelerate regional integration is critical now, more than ever.

The conference will highlight key emerging developments in quality assurance in Africa and take a deep-dive into discussing issues/questions such as – how can African quality assurance agencies and higher education institutions also capitalize on the available opportunities, whether it is from enhanced digitalization, or from the plethora of quality assurance initiatives that are being funded and implemented? What is the role of quality assurance (QA) in supporting higher education to be competitive in a global market? How can African higher education institutions leverage QA to positively contribute to the socio-economic transformation of the continent?

Objectives of the Conference

The conference will:

i) Document and discuss quality assurance developments in all African regions, including common challenges and best practices

ii) Provide a platform for the dissemination of the quality assurance initiatives under HAQAA 2

iii) Strengthen synergies between quality assurance agencies, across regions and linguistic lines

iv) Strengthen and support quality assurance networks’ collaboration

v) Revisit AfriQAN’s vision and mission and define the road map for the future

Who should attend?

Vice-Chancellors; Rectors and Provosts of higher education institutions ; AfriQAN members; Quality Assurance Agencies; Officers in charge of higher education at the African Union Commission; UNESCO officials from the regional and muti-sectoral offices in Africa ; Regional bodies (CAMES, SARUA, IUCEA, etc); Regional networks (RAFANAQ, EAQAN, SAQAN, INQAAHE, etc); Higher Education Policy and Decision Makers and Experts; Quality Assurance practitioners; University Academic, Research and Administrative Staff; Professional bodies; Students and student unions and, Development Partners; Stakeholders in higher education in Africa and from other regions of the world.

The working languages of the meeting will be English, French, and Portuguese

What Is the EAC Scholarship Programme?

The EAC Scholarship Programme (EACSP) is a regional scholarship initiative intended to support postgraduate education among citizens of East African Community Partner States.

Under the current call, the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) is inviting suitably qualified EAC nationals to apply for Cohort 4 of the KfW-funded scholarships for Master’s studies at USIU-Africa in Kenya.

The current call is specifically for applicants interested in three approved Master’s programmes:

Master of Arts in Communication Studies

Master of Science in Information Systems & Technology

The scholarship enables successful applicants from eligible EAC countries to study in an EAC Partner State other than their country of citizenship.

This means that applicants from the eligible countries cannot use this particular scholarship to study in their own country. For example, an eligible Ugandan applicant would study in Kenya under this call, while a Kenyan citizen is not eligible for this specific EAC scholarship because Kenya is the host country for this particular opportunity.

EAC Scholarship 2026 Benefits

1. Full Tuition Fees

Accommodation

Other day-to-day living expenses

3. Return Air Ticket

4. Arrival Allowance
