TITLE: GIFTS Global Institute Fellowship 2026–2027: Global Opportunity for Education System Leaders to Transform Education at Scale

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The GIFTS – Global Institute Fellowship for Transforming Systems is a new global fellowship designed for influential education system leaders who are working to reshape education systems and create better futures for children and young people.

The fellowship brings together a carefully selected group of education system leaders from different countries for a year-long, cohort-based leadership and learning experience. Participants will have opportunities to engage with leading voices in education, collaborate with peers from around the world, receive mentoring and coaching, explore complex system-change challenges and participate in an in-person education-system immersion.

The programme is designed around the idea that education systems must evolve in response to major economic, technological and climatic changes while ensuring that every child has the opportunity to learn, thrive and develop the purpose, agency and abilities needed to shape a better future.

For education leaders working at a national or regional system level, the GIFTS Fellowship offers an opportunity to strengthen their leadership capabilities, expand their international networks, and develop locally rooted but globally informed approaches to education-system transformation.

What Is the GIFTS Global Institute Fellowship?

GIFTS stands for the Global Institute Fellowship for Transforming Systems.

It is a new fellowship created to address a gap experienced by education-system leaders who are working to transform complex education systems but may have limited opportunities to connect with other leaders facing similar challenges.

Education-system transformation can involve working across ministries, government institutions, schools, teachers, communities, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. Leaders responsible for this work must often navigate competing interests, political realities, changing technologies, economic pressures and evolving expectations about what education systems should deliver.

The GIFTS Fellowship is intended to create a global community in which such leaders can learn from one another, exchange experiences and develop the capabilities required to lead system-wide transformation.

The fellowship will bring together 20 influential education system insiders from diverse countries for a year-long experience combining virtual learning, peer engagement, mentoring, coaching and an in-person immersion.

Why Was the GIFTS Fellowship Created?

Education systems around the world are operating in an increasingly fast-changing environment.

Economic developments, technological advances and climate-related changes are creating new challenges and opportunities for education. At the same time, education systems are expected to ensure that children and young people develop not only academic capabilities but also the purpose and agency required to navigate an uncertain future.

The fellowship recognises that education-system leaders play a critical role in responding to these changes.

These leaders are expected to:

Chart new paths for their education systems.

Adapt institutions and strategies to changing realities.

Improve the performance of complex systems.

Mobilise people at different levels of the education system.

Inspire students, teachers and school leaders.

Work with government and other partners.

Address difficult system-level challenges.

Develop strategies capable of producing sustainable change.

Despite the importance and complexity of this work, education-system leaders may have relatively few opportunities to connect with peers, reflect on their experiences and share practical lessons about what it takes to transform education systems.

The GIFTS Fellowship has been launched to help address this gap by creating a structured global learning environment for education-system leaders.

What Will GIFTS Fellows Explore?

The fellowship will encourage participants to investigate fundamental questions about education-system transformation.

Among the questions highlighted by the programme are

What outcomes should education systems achieve for all students today?

How can the practices, structures and culture of an education system be aligned around its core purpose?

What are the most effective strategies for improving the quality of learning in classrooms?

What does improving classroom learning require from education-system leaders themselves?

These questions place system leadership at the centre of the fellowship.

Rather than looking only at individual schools or isolated education interventions, the programme focuses on the broader structures, practices, cultures and leadership approaches that determine how education systems operate.

Who Is the GIFTS Fellowship Designed For?

The GIFTS Fellowship is intended for influential and innovative education system leaders.

The programme specifically identifies leaders working within:

Ministries.

Political offices.

Civil society roles involving long-term partnerships with government.

This means the fellowship is targeted primarily at people who have the ability to influence education systems at a significant level.

It is not presented as a general scholarship or fellowship for students, recent graduates or people simply interested in education. Instead, the target participants are individuals already positioned within education systems or closely connected to government and capable of contributing to system-level transformation.

The programme seeks leaders who can demonstrate both a track record of commitment and the potential to influence education beyond their immediate organisation or role.

Qualities Expected of GIFTS Fellows

According to the fellowship information, successful fellows will demonstrate several important characteristics.

1. Commitment to Improving Systems Around Children

Fellows should have a lifelong commitment to improving the systems that shape children’s lives and educational experiences.

This means the programme is interested in leaders whose work goes beyond individual short-term interventions and is connected to improving the broader systems surrounding children.

2. Commitment to Holistic Student Development

Applicants should align with the purpose of developing all students holistically, regardless of their background or economic circumstances.

This reflects the fellowship’s emphasis on creating education systems that provide opportunities for every student rather than benefiting only particular groups.

3. Collective Leadership

Education-system transformation rarely happens through the work of one individual.

The fellowship therefore seeks leaders with the capacity to develop collective leadership and work effectively with others.

This can involve bringing together different stakeholders, building shared ownership and navigating the relationships necessary to move system-level initiatives forward.

4. Ability to Navigate Complex Politics

Transforming education systems can involve complex political and institutional environments.

The fellowship therefore looks for individuals capable of navigating political complexity while maintaining focus on system-level objectives.

5. Ability to Influence System-Level Change

Applicants should have the ability to influence significant change at a national or regional scale.

This is an important distinction because the fellowship is designed for system leaders whose influence extends beyond a single classroom, school or small community initiative.

6. Potential for Global Education Leadership

The programme also seeks individuals who have the potential to become influential leaders within the wider global education ecosystem.

This suggests that the fellowship is designed not only to strengthen participants’ current leadership but also to contribute to the development of a broader international community of education-system leaders.

What Does the GIFTS Fellowship Offer?

The fellowship provides a comprehensive learning and leadership experience lasting approximately one year.

The programme will combine several components, allowing fellows to learn through formal sessions, peer interaction, coaching, mentoring and practical exploration.

The major components include

A curated international cohort.

System Change Labs.

Virtual masterclasses.

Roundtables with senior education leaders.

Peer-learning groups.

Leadership sessions.

Mentoring.

Coaching.

A four-day in-person immersion.

The Better Future Forum.

Continued participation in a global community of system leaders.

Cohort-Based Learning Experience

The GIFTS Fellowship will bring together 20 education system leaders from diverse countries.

The cohort model is designed to create an environment in which participants can build trusting and enduring relationships with peers.

This peer network is particularly important because education-system leaders often face similar challenges even when they work in very different national contexts.

Through shared learning and reflection, fellows can exchange experiences and gain perspectives from leaders operating in other education systems.

The programme aims to create relationships that extend beyond the formal fellowship period and contribute to a lasting global community.

System Change Lab

The System Change Lab is a practical component of the fellowship.

Participants will explore and address a problem of practice during the fellowship. Rather than simply discussing system transformation at a theoretical level, fellows will have an opportunity to work on an issue connected to their own professional context.

The lab will use:

Action.

Reflection.

Peer feedback.

Exploration of practical challenges.

Generation of new insights.

This approach is intended to help fellows connect leadership learning with real system-level challenges.

Four-Day Education System Immersion

Another major component is the Immersion Event.

Fellows will participate in a four-day in-person immersive learning experience within an education system undergoing transformation.

The immersion will give participants opportunities to engage with:

Ministers.

Schools.

Practitioners.

Fellow participants.

Other education-system stakeholders.

The programme identifies the four-day immersion as required.

This practical exposure can enable fellows to observe system transformation in action and examine how leadership, policy, institutions and educational practice interact.

Masterclasses and Roundtables

Fellows will also participate in curated masterclasses and roundtable sessions involving senior global education leaders.

These are described as closed-door sessions where participants can engage in honest conversations about the realities of system transformation.

Topics can include:

Difficult trade-offs.

Failures.

Breakthroughs.

Leadership decisions.

System-level challenges.

Strategies for transformation.

The focus on honest dialogue is intended to create a learning environment where leaders can discuss not only successful initiatives but also the difficulties and failures that accompany complex system change.

Shared Inquiry and Peer Learning

The fellowship places significant emphasis on learning with and from peers.

Participants will form a curated cohort of education-system leaders and develop trusting relationships that support deeper learning.

Peer interaction can help fellows compare experiences across different contexts, question assumptions and explore alternative approaches to leadership and system transformation.

Triad Model Coaching

GIFTS will use a three-part coaching and support model.

The model brings together:

Policy Mentors

Policy mentors provide subject expertise and help participants think through policy-related questions and challenges.

Leadership Coaches

Leadership coaches support fellows as they navigate execution, uncertainty and difficult trade-offs associated with leadership.

Peer Coaches

Peer coaches contribute shared learning, accountability and feedback.

Together, these three forms of support are intended to provide a more comprehensive development experience, combining technical or policy expertise with leadership guidance and peer support.

The Better Future Forum

Fellows will also have an opportunity to participate in the Global Institute’s annual Better Future Forum.

The forum is an in-person event that provides an opportunity to connect with leaders from the global education ecosystem.

Participation in the Better Future Forum is listed as optional, unlike the four-day January immersion, which is specifically identified as required.

Building a Lifelong Global Community

The fellowship is designed to extend beyond the formal learning sessions.

Participants will have opportunities to exchange practices across geographical boundaries and may have the option of visiting other fellows.

The programme aims to build a lifelong global community of education-system leaders who can continue learning from one another and sharing practices after the formal fellowship concludes.

This international network is potentially one of the most valuable aspects of the programme for leaders working on complex education-system challenges.

The GIFTS Fellowship does not rely solely on self-nomination.

The organisers also welcome nominations of exceptional system leaders who are working at the forefront of education-system transformation and shaping a better future for children and young people.

This nomination route creates an opportunity for organisations, colleagues and other stakeholders to identify education leaders whose work deserves consideration.

Global Eligibility and Geographic Reach

The GIFTS Fellowship is explicitly described as a global fellowship.

The programme aims to bring together education-system leaders from countries around the world and states that the cohort will include leaders from diverse countries.

The supplied information does not provide a specific list of eligible countries or continents. It also does not identify any race or ethnicity restrictions.

Therefore, the opportunity should be understood as internationally oriented, while applicants should consult the official application guidance to determine whether any additional eligibility conditions apply.

What Kind of Leader Is Best Suited to GIFTS?

The GIFTS Fellowship is particularly suited to an education professional who is already working on system-level change rather than someone who is simply beginning a career in education.

TITLE: Press Release – Commemoration of the 2021 Africa Universities’ Day will focus on Building Technology Based Resilient Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra-Ghana, October 11, 2021 – The Association of African Universities (AAU) is inviting all Higher Education Institutions across the continent to celebrate the 2021 Africa Universities’ Day which comes off on November 12, 2021, under the theme “Building Technology Based Resilient Universities, Now!”.

Africa Universities’ Day is commemorated each year to celebrate the day of the AAU’s establishment on November 12, 1967, and to highlight the contributions of the Higher Education Sector to the development of the African continent. It is also a day when critical dialogue on how to improve the quality of Africa’s higher education is promoted.

The theme for this year’s celebration – Building Technology Based Resilient Universities, Now!, seeks to throw more light on the effects the COVID-19 pandemic has had on higher education, and the urgent need for stakeholders to find ways to improve the modes of education delivery, especially based on the experiences and innovations that emerged as positives from the pandemic era. The concept note for the 2021 Africa Universities’ Day celebration is accessible at – https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Final-Concept-Note-Africa-Universities-Day-2021.pdf

A rich bouquet of the programme lined up to be hosted in the week of November 8 -12, includes high-level presentations and panel discussions on the need for African Higher Education Institutions to collaborate and share technological resources and expertise in online content preparation and delivery. Other aspects will focus on the needed management and stakeholder support (policy and financial) and commitment towards building a technology based resilient higher education system. Having such systems in place is critical in promoting development and the attainment of the “Africa we want” by 2063. Please download the programme from here: 2021 AU Day Program Line Up

The Registration Link is found here: https://meet.aau.org/auday-2021

“The 2021 celebration also seeks to bring together the entire higher education community and major stakeholders in Africa to respond to salient questions and issues such as: How are HEIs leveraging on partnerships to share resources? How are they capitalizing on technological innovations to enhance the achievement of their core mandates? What can African Universities do to promote equitable access to higher education and inclusion for Africa’s youth bulge?”, said Prof. Olusola Oyewole, the Secretary General of the AAU. “Answers to the above questions and the conversations around the theme of the Africa Universities’ Day Celebrations are critical and fall in line with the Continental Education Strategy for Africa 2016-2025 (CESA 16-25) and the AAU Strategic Plan (2020 – 2025)”, he added.

From topical seminars, debates, exhibitions, social media conversations, conferences, webinars and several interesting events, the variety of events hosted by Higher Education Institutions over the years continue to be colourful and educative. The 2021 celebrations promise to be even more insightful. Aside the events lined up by the AAU Secretariat headquartered in Accra, Ghana, the AAU East Africa Regional Office at the University of Khartoum in Sudan, the North Africa Regional Office at Al-Azhar University, Egypt, and individual AAU member institutions will also be hosting events to mark the Africa Universities’ Day.

AAU encourages the management of universities, to circulate information concerning the 2021 Africa Universities’ Day celebrations to the Ministries of Education, University Councils, Committees of Vice-Chancellors and all institutions involved in the management of Higher Education Institutions for their attention and participation in the events. Other public and private universities in each country which are non-members of the AAU, research institutions, the media and general public should also be invited to join the celebrations to give visibility to the Africa Universities’ Day and promote the activities of Higher Education Institutions in each country.

Applications are invited for the Max Kampelman Fellowship Program 2026. Named for a longtime U.S. Ambassador to the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, Kampelman fellows represent the next generation of American leaders in security policy, human rights, and strategic communications.

Kampelman fellows join a team of world-class experts at a U.S. government commission that advances national security by promoting human rights, military security, and economic cooperation in 57 countries in Europe, Eurasia, and North America.

Fellowship Details

Policy Fellowships: Policy fellows will work in political and military affairs, economic and environmental matters, and human rights and fundamental freedoms, based on their areas of interest, expertise, and needs of the Commission. Under the direction of commission policy advisors, policy fellows research topics and trends relating to international military, economic, and human rights issues throughout the 57-country OSCE region; assist staff advisors with hearings, briefings, congressional delegations, legislation, and publications; attend congressional hearings, panels, and events; and perform administrative duties. Each fellow is expected to write at least one article for potential publication on the commission website during his or her fellowship period.

Communications Fellowships: Communications fellows support projects and initiatives in all areas of the commission’s portfolio. Communications fellows assist with media outreach activities; help publicize Commission hearings and briefings; staff Commission events; develop web content; and craft creative and engaging content to be shared on social media. They also assist with other special communications projects and perform administrative duties. Each fellow is expected to write at least one article for publication on the commission website during his or her fellowship period.

Benefits

Kampelman fellowships last three months, with fellows expected to work 30 hours per week in-person at the office in Washington DC. Fellows are paid $27 per hour and are offered ongoing enrichment, professional development, and networking opportunities facilitated by senior commission staff.

a citizen of the United States;

a person who is admitted as a refugee under 8 U.S.C. 1157 or is granted asylum under 8 U.S.C. 1158 and has filed a declaration of intention to become a lawful permanent resident and then a citizen when eligible; or

a person who owes allegiance to the United States.

Brief cover letter indicating the following:

Why you want to work for the Commission, including relevant background or personal experiences

Your specific areas of interest as they relate to the work of the Commission

Your availability (start and end dates, as well as hours per week)

Resume of no more than two pages

Writing sample of three pages or less

TITLE: Continental Workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
CONTINENTAL WORKSHOP FOR DIRECTORS OF ICT / CHIEF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY OFFICERS

INTRODUCTION

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is a membership-based network of 425 plus universities covering the 5 regions of Africa and its mission is to enhance the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development. Since 1967 the AAU has been the leading advocate for higher education in Africa, demonstrating the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting their national, continental, and global needs.

As part of creating value for its members the AAU regularly runs various capacity building programs for the benefit of various thematic groups within the member universities. These capacity building programs offer discounted fees to staff from the member universities to demonstrate the value of their loyal membership to the AAU.

The AAU also hosts various diverse forums for exchanges, discussions, engagements, collaborations, and advocacy for the purpose of fulfilling its mission and to improve the functions of its member universities. The AAU has created the Africa Research, Innovation and Development Network (AFRID) to promote the establishment of thematic networks representing the diverse functions and research interests of member universities, individual researchers, and individual administrative staff.

WHY THE WORKSHOP

The continental workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers will be hosted by the AAU for the purpose of strengthening collaborations among the Africa-wide Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers (DICT/CITOs). The workshop also aims to build the capacities of DICT/CITOs in emerging areas of leadership and strategic management; IT governance; business acumen; technology trends and innovation; cybersecurity; data management and analytics; cloud computing; digital transformation; vendor management; regulatory compliance; communication and stakeholder management; project management; and personal and professional development.

The plans are that the continental workshop will be an annual gathering of DICT/CITOs modelled around the computer society summer/winter schools, higher education information technology South Africa (HEITSA) and EDUCAUSE. The purpose of the continental annual DICT/CITOs workshop will be to serve as a joint voice for the Africa-wide IT profession in African Universities. The annual workshop will promote best practices and standards through the sharing of expertise among participating DICT/CITOs. The long-term goal of the continental DICT/CITOs workshop will be to support the sustainable application of digital tools, platforms, and strategies to transform African Higher Education.

OBJECTIVES AND INTENDED OUTCOMES OF THE ANNUAL WORKSHOP

The initial objectives of the annual workshop for Directors of ICT / Chief Information Technology Officers are:

To develop strategies for guiding the integration and adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) by African Universities.

To develop strategies for developing and deploying AI Literacy training programs for universities.

To build capacities of DICT/CITOs in key emerging areas such as IT governance, cybersecurity, vendor management, ERP implementation, cloud computing and digital transformation.

To initiate strategies for monitoring ICT development in African Higher Education Institutions.

To deliberate on opportunities (and implement) for joint purchases of technology licenses and equipment to reduce the costs to individual universities.

The expected outcomes from the annual workshops include:

Strengthened collaboration and networking among DICT/CITOs in the African continent.

Developed action plans and strategies for guiding AAU Member Universities to harness the benefits from Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies.

A program developed for monitoring the development of ICT in African Universities through annual surveys.

Agreement on future focus areas of the continental workshops of DICT/CITOs.

WORKSHOP FACILITATORS

High profile, experienced and well-respected IT professionals and thought leaders from industry and academia will be identified to facilitate these workshops. The workshops will be organized in such a way that practical case studies are shared, current information is provided, and participants are guided in terms of post-workshop action planning.

TARGET PARTICIPANTS

These workshops are strictly for Senior Leaders in African Universities that are responsible for the running and management of the Information and Communication Technology role and related infrastructure and systems. The target participants are:

Directors of Information and Communication Technology

Chief Information Technology Officers

Deputy Vice Chancellors responsible for Information technology

Senior Project Management Officers responsible for high-level IT projects implementation

DATES AND VENUE FOR THE 2024 WORKSHOP

The inaugural workshop will be hosted from 27-29 February 2024 in Accra Ghana.

LANGUAGE OF THE WORKSHOPS

The workshops will be delivered in the 4 languages of the Association of African Universities – Arabic, English, French and Portuguese. Interpretation will be available in the 4 languages.

HOW TO PARTICIPATE

The participation fees for DICT/CITOs from AAU member universities in good standing are US$800 per participant and these include facilitation fees, workshop materials, interpretation services, excursion within Accra and lunches, and refreshments during the workshop days.

DICT/CITOs from non-AAU member universities and DICT/CITOs whose universities are in bad standing will pay US$1,000 per participant.

Participants are responsible for their airfares, accommodation, visas, and general upkeep.

Please register to participate via this link: https://forms.office.com/r/x35b0UvyDJ

Please pay for your participation from this online link: https://pay.aau.org/cwd-accra

CONTACT DETAILS

If you have any questions, please contact Miss Nodumo Dhlamini on ndhlamini@aau.org or call her on +233553019588. Please also copy Mr Abdul Manaf Sulemana on amsulemana@aau.org

DOWNLOAD THE WORKSHOP CONCEPT NOTES IN THE FOUR AAU LANGUAGES

Arabic: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/PKikYmTs9zRjgfL

English: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/zmt6oPG3xxyHjXZ

French: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/Ebos58JzXtnPR9s

Portuguese: https://repo.aau.org/index.php/s/opm786eZWmS4ey3

SELECTION OF MODULES TO BE COVERED

A) Leadership and Strategic Management of AI in African Higher Education by DICT/CITOs

The recent webinars organized by the AAU revealed a great need for DICT/CITOs to take fore-front leadership in supporting their universities to understand what opportunities and challenges are posed by Artificial Intelligence. DICT/CITOs should lead the discourse, strategy formulation and capacity building within their universities. This module will cover the following:

Change management, policies, and strategies for AI adoption.

Driving AI innovation within the university.

Evaluating and adopting AI technologies that align with your university goals.

Developing AI literacy training programs.

B) Information Technology Governance

IT governance is part of corporate governance, and its goal is to improve the overall management of information technology (IT) and generate improved value from investments made in information technology. IT governance frameworks help universities manage their IT risks effectively and ensure that the activities associated with information technology are aligned with their overall objectives. IT governance enables a university to demonstrate measurable results against the broader university’s strategies and goals; respond to relevant legal and regulatory obligations; assure higher education stakeholders that they can have confidence in the university’s IT services; and facilitate an increase in the return on IT investment. This module will cover the following topics:

Strategic alignment with the university’s objectives

Achieving value delivery and optimization

Risk management and mitigation

Performance measurement and monitoring

Resource management and optimization

C) Cybersecurity

In the quickly evolving digital landscape, Africa is experiencing significant advancements in technology adoption and connectivity. However, these advancements come with increased cybersecurity threats that can undermine the region’s progress. This module will discuss the challenges and solutions relevant to cybersecurity in African higher education institutions and will explore practical strategies to safeguard African HEI networks and promote a secure digital culture. The module will include:

The complexities of cybersecurity in African HEIs, including the challenges, solutions, and emerging trends.

Developing and implementing robust cybersecurity strategies.

Managing cyber risks and ensuring compliance with regulations.

Incident response and crisis management.

Cybersecurity advocacy, awareness campaigns, and capacity-building activities, and achieving the digital resilience of African HEIs.

D) Cloud Computing

African Universities are subscribing to various models of cloud computing infrastructure to host their digital management information systems, manage their email servers and other key resources. Cloud computing needs to be managed appropriately so that the university data and information are secure. This module will cover the following:

Cloud strategy development and implementation.

Cloud security and compliance.

Managing and optimizing cloud resources.

E) Communication and Stakeholder Management

The IT function is normally viewed as a technical function that works in the background to service the institution. Because of the growing importance of IT, it is now critical for DICT/CITOs to become proficient in communication and stakeholder management so that they obtain the buy-in and support for the digital transformation initiatives. This module will cover the following:

Effective communication with both technical and non-technical stakeholders.

Building relationships with other Senior Leaders in the university and elsewhere

Advocating for the IT department’s role in achieving business objectives.

F) ERP Implementation and digital transformation: lessons and pitfalls

African universities are investing significant financial and human resources in implementing university-wide enterprise resource planning digital systems. These ERPs focus on student information systems, financial management, library management, university hospitals management, dormitory management, and others. Some of the systems are developed in-house and others are purchased off the shelf. This module will cover the following:

Case studies of in-house developed ERPs

Case studies of off the shelf ERPs

Funding and sustaining ERP implementations.

Driving digital initiatives and transformations.

Integrating digital technologies into university business processes.

Enhancing university customer experiences through digital channels.

G) Strategies for monitoring ICT development in African Higher Education Institutions.

Data and information are critical for informing university top leadership and governments about the development of ICT in higher education institutions. When data is available the senior leaders can make informed decisions on how to support ICT development. This module will discuss the following:

Strategies for data collection about ICT development in African Universities

What data to collect

How to incentivize African universities to share ICT related data

H) Vendor Management and opportunities for joint purchases of technology licenses and equipment

Some of the potential benefits of speaking with one voice to vendors is the reduction of financial investments, better services, and standardization of services. This module will discuss the following:

Effective negotiation and relationship management with technology vendors.

Evaluating and selecting technology solutions.

Ensuring vendor compliance and performance.

Opportunities for continental level negotiations with technology vendors

I) Personal and Professional Development

Continuous learning and adaptability are crucial for Directors of ICT / Chief IT Officers to thrive in their roles, because of the quick pace of technological advancements and the evolving nature of higher education challenges. This module will cover the following topics

Continuous learning and staying abreast of industry trends.

Networking and participation in professional organizations.

Mentoring and coaching to develop the next generation of IT leaders.

J) Emerging Issues in ICT for Universities

This module will cover emerging issues, strategies, tools, and opportunities that benefit African higher education institutions. The module would also provide new information to Directors of ICT / Chief IT Officers so that they are most impactful in their roles.

TITLE: World Bank Small AI for Development Hackathon 2026: Build Inclusive AI Solutions and Win Sponsored Travel to Seoul

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026, a global innovation opportunity inviting young people to develop practical artificial intelligence solutions for communities and economies facing limited connectivity, infrastructure and access to digital technology.

Participants will compete during a two-day hackathon on 3–4 October 2026, developing a working “Small AI” solution addressing a real development challenge in one of three sectors:

Health

Agriculture

Tourism

Three winning entries will be selected, with one winner representing each sector. The winners will be invited to present their solutions at the Global AI and Digital Summit 2026, taking place from 19–22 October 2026 in Seoul, Republic of Korea.

The final deadline to apply for the hackathon is 26 September 2026. Applications and all competition submissions must be completed in English.

Key Information at a Glance

Programme: Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026

Related event: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026

Hackathon dates: 3–4 October 2026

Hackathon format: Hybrid, with online participation and physical hubs

Application deadline: 26 September 2026

Summit dates: 19–22 October 2026

Summit location: Grand Hyatt, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Winner presentations: 21 October 2026

Challenge sectors: Health, agriculture and tourism

Application language: English

Team size: Individual applications or teams of up to four people

Number of World Bank challenge winners: Three

Competition partner: Hack-Nation

Referral code: WBGSmallAIGADS

Application form: Apply through the official Google Form

Official information: Global AI and Digital Summit 2026

The application form currently requires applicants to sign in to Google. Candidates should therefore ensure that they have access to an active Google account before starting.

About the Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge

The Small AI for Development Hackathon is organized by the World Bank Group’s Digital and AI Vice Presidency in collaboration with the World Bank Group Youth Summit, Development Economics Vice Presidency and Information and Technology Solutions.

Hack-Nation is responsible for managing the competition platform and administering the hackathon process. The World Bank Group serves as the sponsor and final judging authority.

The challenge is intended to encourage artificial intelligence development that responds to the actual conditions experienced in developing economies. Instead of assuming that every user has reliable broadband, an advanced smartphone and strong digital literacy, participants must consider environments where access to technology remains constrained.

The organizers are looking for solutions that can translate artificial intelligence into practical development outcomes rather than demonstrations of technology without a clearly defined problem or target user.

Why This Challenge Matters

The competition has been launched against the backdrop of significant global connectivity and employment challenges.

According to the official World Bank event page, more than two billion people remained offline as of 2025. At the same time, approximately 1.2 billion young people in the Global South are expected to reach working age during the coming decade, while current trends indicate that substantially fewer jobs will be created.

Artificial intelligence may support economic growth, better services and new employment opportunities. However, many existing AI applications have been designed for environments with advanced devices, dependable internet connectivity and users who already understand how to communicate with AI systems.

This challenge asks young innovators to reconsider those assumptions and create technology that can function under real development constraints.

What Is “Small AI”?

Small AI is a targeted and use-case-driven approach to artificial intelligence development.

Unlike general-purpose AI systems that require extensive computing and data-centre infrastructure, Small AI focuses on using specific capabilities to solve a clearly defined problem.

A Small AI solution may operate through accessible technologies such as:

Basic mobile phones

Sensors

Microcontrollers

Locally operated models

SMS-based interfaces

Voice-based systems

Devices with limited processing capacity

Systems that function with intermittent or restricted connectivity

A solution may use predictive, generative or agentic AI. The decisive issue is not the size or complexity of the model but whether the technology addresses a real problem within the operating environment of its intended users.

Effective Small AI solutions should be designed around:

A specific development problem

Clearly identified users

Local data and knowledge

Limited or unreliable connectivity

Affordable and accessible devices

Familiar communication channels

Measurable development outcomes

Responsible and inclusive implementation

Realistic infrastructure and institutional conditions

The World Bank also stresses that Small AI still depends on enabling foundations such as broadband access, digital literacy and trusted local institutions. Without these foundations, even technically promising solutions may remain isolated pilots instead of becoming sustainable and scalable interventions.

Challenge Areas

Every applicant must select one of the three official sector challenges.

Health

Applicants selecting health must develop an AI solution that responds to the relevant development challenge and operating conditions identified in the official sector brief.

Solutions will need to demonstrate how Small AI can contribute practical value in contexts where communities may face limitations in connectivity, devices, infrastructure, information or access to services.

Agriculture

Agriculture applicants must consider how targeted AI applications can create measurable value for agricultural stakeholders in resource-constrained environments.

The proposed technology should be grounded in a specific problem and should account for the digital tools, data, infrastructure and institutional conditions that must be present for the solution to work.

Tourism

Applicants selecting tourism must develop a practical solution that responds to the official tourism-sector challenge.

The proposal should show how AI can produce meaningful benefits within the sector while remaining accessible, context-specific and realistic about connectivity and technology constraints.

Applicants should consult the official sector briefs and avoid attempting to address all three sectors in one entry. The World Bank’s rules require each entry to respond to one sectoral challenge.

What Participants Must Build

The hackathon requires participants to build a working Small AI solution during the official competition weekend.

The proposed solution should:

Address one clearly defined challenge in health, agriculture or tourism.

Operate within the realities of a constrained environment.

Demonstrate a clear advantage over existing approaches.

Produce measurable or credible development value.

Consider accessibility and inclusion.

Reflect local needs, users and operating conditions.

Explain the infrastructure and preconditions required for implementation.

Acknowledge relevant technical, social and development trade-offs.

Comply with the technical and submission rules published by Hack-Nation.

Be submitted through the official competition platform during the prescribed window.

The broader Hack-Nation programme describes the event as a 24-hour global building experience delivered online and through physical hubs. Participants are expected to move from identifying a problem to developing and presenting a working AI product.

How to Apply

Participation involves two separate and mandatory stages.

Step 1: Apply for the Hackathon

Applicants must complete the official Hack-Nation application process by 26 September 2026.

The direct application form is:

Small AI for Development Hackathon 2026 Application Form

Applicants may also visit the Hack-Nation Hackathon 7 page, select “Apply” and enter the following referral code:

WBGSmallAIGADS

The application must be submitted in English.

Applicants should understand that submitting this initial form only applies for admission to the hackathon. It is not the final competition submission.

Step 2: Develop and Submit the Competition Entry

Registered and accepted participants must develop their Small AI solution during the official hackathon window on 3–4 October 2026.

The final entry must be submitted through the designated Hack-Nation competition portal and comply with all published requirements concerning:

Submission deadline

Technical format

Team composition

Originality

Challenge selection

Demonstration materials

Video submission

Use of the referral code

English-language requirements

Intellectual-property compliance

Only entries formally submitted and confirmed as received through the official competition platform will be considered for judging.

Applications or entries submitted through email, social media, messages to World Bank Group staff or unofficial channels will not be accepted. Late, incomplete or incorrectly submitted entries will not be considered.

Rules for Individual and Team Participation

Applications may be made individually or as a team of up to four members.

For team applications:

Every team member must register individually.

Every member must independently satisfy all applicable requirements.

All members must identify themselves as belonging to the same team before the application deadline.

A participant may be associated with only one competition entry.

Team membership cannot be changed after the hackathon begins.

A team submission will be evaluated as one entry.

A winning team will collectively receive one of the three winning places.

A winning team must nominate one member to represent it in Seoul.

The World Bank Group judging panel will make the final determination regarding the traveling representative.

Teams should finalize their membership, roles and sector selection before submitting their applications.

How Entries Will Be Evaluated

Hack-Nation will evaluate eligible entries and prepare a shortlist for the World Bank Group.

The World Bank Group will then act as the final judging authority and select the three winners.

Entries will not be assessed solely on technical sophistication. The organizers will also consider:

Development relevance

Quality of problem definition

Suitability for constrained environments

Measurable potential impact

Design quality

Accessibility

Inclusivity

Practicality

Local relevance

Responsible use of AI

Awareness of infrastructure requirements

Recognition of trade-offs

Potential for implementation or expansion

Applicants are encouraged to explain what localized AI development means within their particular setting. They should demonstrate how their perspective or direct understanding of a local challenge has shaped the proposed solution.

The organizers are interested in entries that recognize tensions between technological capability and accessibility, as well as between ambition and responsible risk management.

Applicants should therefore rely only on the World Bank’s expressly stated Seoul presentation and travel benefits unless Hack-Nation confirms additional awards.

About the Global AI and Digital Summit 2026

The Global AI and Digital Summit is a high-level forum hosted by the World Bank Group together with the Republic of Korea’s Ministry of Finance and Economy and Ministry of Science and ICT.

It will take place from 19–22 October 2026 at the Grand Hyatt in Seoul.

The Summit will examine how artificial intelligence and digital transformation can help countries:

Generate more and better jobs

Raise productivity

Expand economic opportunity

Improve public services

Strengthen businesses

Develop trusted digital ecosystems

Expand affordable digital access

Build AI readiness

Mobilize investment

Deliver practical development outcomes

The programme will bring together government leaders, development partners, private-sector executives, investors, technology innovators, researchers, civil-society representatives and youth leaders.

In-person participation in the Summit is by invitation only. Selected sessions will be open to the public and streamed online, with livestream information expected as the programme is finalized.

Wednesday, 21 October 2026

The Small AI challenge winners are scheduled to present their solutions on this day.

The closing day is expected to include study tours and consultations with participating clients and stakeholders.

Intellectual Property and Submission Rights

Participants retain ownership, copyright and other rights in their entries.

However, submission of an entry grants the World Bank Group a worldwide, non-exclusive and royalty-free licence to:

Review and evaluate the submission

Reproduce relevant materials

Display or record the submission

Publish summaries

Present the solution publicly

Use the entry for competition administration

Use materials for educational, promotional and knowledge-sharing purposes

Participants must possess all rights necessary to submit their materials. Entries must not knowingly violate another party’s:

Copyright

Trademark

Privacy

Confidentiality

Intellectual property

Contractual rights

Applicants should document the sources of datasets, code, models, images, audio, research and other materials used in their solution.

Restrictions on World Bank and Partner Branding

Participants may not independently place the names, titles, acronyms, logos or branding elements of the World Bank Group or its partners on their entry materials without prior written consent.

This restriction also covers branding associated with:

Hack-Nation

World Bank Group Youth Summit

Development Economics Vice Presidency

Information and Technology Solutions

Other programme partners

Applicants should describe the challenge accurately without creating materials that imply official endorsement, partnership or organizational approval beyond what has been expressly authorized.

Data Protection

Information submitted during registration and the hackathon may be shared with the World Bank Group, Hack-Nation and relevant stakeholders involved in:

Competition administration

Hosting

Participant coordination

Judging

Winner notification

Summit participation

Follow-up communication

Personal data will be handled in accordance with the World Bank Group Privacy Notice.

Applicants should review the privacy terms of both the World Bank Group and the external application or competition platforms before providing personal information.

Other Important Conditions

By participating, applicants accept the official competition terms and acknowledge that:

The organizers may verify compliance at any stage.

Ineligible candidates may be disqualified.

Incomplete or non-compliant entries may be removed.

The organizers are not responsible for lost, late, corrupted or misdirected submissions.

Illegal or rights-infringing content may be excluded.

Final decisions concerning judging and winner selection rest with the organizers.

The competition may be modified, suspended, shortened, cancelled or terminated.

An alternate winner may be selected if a winner is ineligible, unavailable or unable to participate.

The privileges and immunities of the World Bank Group remain reserved.

Submissions must not be used for purposes inconsistent with the World Bank Group’s mandate and mission.

Participants should read the complete terms on the official event page rather than relying only on promotional summaries.

Practical Application Advice

Applicants can strengthen their preparation by taking the following actions:

Apply during the earliest available batch.

Form the complete team before registration.

Confirm that every team member registers individually.

Select only one official sector challenge.

Study the relevant sector brief.

Define one specific user and problem.

Identify the actual connectivity, device and data constraints.

Explain why AI is necessary for the solution.

Build around locally available technology.

Define measurable indicators of impact.

Incorporate accessibility and inclusion from the beginning.

Prepare a realistic working prototype rather than an overly broad concept.

Plan the demonstration and video submission early.

Verify all intellectual-property permissions.

Avoid unauthorized World Bank or partner logos.

Monitor the World Bank and Hack-Nation pages for updates.

Keep evidence that both the application and final entry were successfully submitted.

Ensure that a potential team representative could travel to Seoul at short notice.

Application Deadline

The final deadline to apply is:

26 September 2026

The official page does not specify a deadline time or time zone. Applicants should submit well before the final date.

The actual competition entry must subsequently be developed and submitted during the official hackathon window on 3–4 October 2026.

Global AI and Digital Summit 2026 and Small AI Hackathon Challenge

Apply through the official Google Form

Hack-Nation Global AI Hackathon 7

WBGSmallAIGADS

Due to the anticipated volume of applications, the organizers state that they cannot respond individually to questions concerning competition eligibility, application status or judging results. Applicants should monitor the official World Bank and Hack-Nation pages for announcements.

Conclusion

The World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026 provides young innovators with an opportunity to rethink how artificial intelligence can serve people living and working in environments with limited connectivity, devices and digital infrastructure.

The strongest entries will not necessarily be the largest or most technically complex. Successful solutions will need to address a well-defined health, agriculture or tourism challenge, demonstrate measurable development value, respond to local realities and function through accessible technology.

Three winners will earn the opportunity to present their work at the Global AI and Digital Summit in Seoul, with reasonable travel, accommodation and designated participation expenses covered under the organizers’ conditions.

Prospective applicants should apply early, finalize their teams, review the relevant sector challenge and prepare for an intensive development and submission period on 3–4 October 2026. The final application deadline is 26 September 2026.

TITLE: Experiencing an International Geophysics Conference as a Postdoc by Maurice Huguenin

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Last month, I had the privilege to help convene, present my science and attend the European Geophysical Union (EGU) annual meeting in Vienna, Austria. What an experience it has been! This was my third time attending this international conference, this year together with over 18’000 other attendees. Having been to Vienna before, I was ready to jump right in – armed with my program on the phone, my badge printed and my coffee mug ready to battle the jetlag.

Getting ready for the conference. Photo by Maurice Huguenin.

The week started strong for me. I had a job interview at 8 am on Monday. How nice, perfect to adapt to the jetlag. I made it to the conference a bit later, making use of the free public transport that comes with the conference badge. Thank you EGU! On the underground, I already met a researcher I knew from my time in Australia – how nice to be able to catch up with others who I have not seen in years. Monday afternoon was my first session where I was actively involved in. As a convener of our ‘Southern Ocean in a changing climate’ session, I helped announce speakers, made sure they kept to their eight minute presentation limit and thought about questions to ask in case the audience did not raise any. The after-session drinks and dinner of our Southern Ocean community are always great. It is nice to catch up with others and also get to know new scientists from around the world in a relaxed way. I was surprised by how many in our ~40 people group I knew from previous times. It really is a small world!

With two of my Postdoc advisors. Photo by Maurice Huguenin.

On Tuesday, it was time for posters in our Southern Ocean session. Lots of interesting new science on new observational data from moorings (stationary instrument lines in the ocean) and Weddell Seal CTDs (data from tiny sensors we put on top of a seal’s head) as well as new insights from changing heat and carbon fluxes down South. I also saw my PhD advisor present our study on the drivers of the extreme 2023 North Atlantic marine heat wave. For lunch, I came prepared this time, bringing a sandwich with me to avoid the long queue times at food stalls around the conference center. Tuesday’s lunch was another type of ‘job-interview’. I had the opportunity to get to know a scientist to whom I sent in my job application for a postdoc position on ocean modelling a few days earlier. Drinks on Tuesday after the sessions ended were followed by a typical Viennese dinner (Wienerschnitzel mit Preiselbeeren + Almdudler) together with a geologist friend of mine from my Bachelor’s education at ETH.

Wednesday came around and it was time to present again. This time I talked about my own research in the ‘Under Cover: The Southern Ocean’s connection to sea ice’ session. My results on the (not so large) impact of the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation on Weddell and Ross Sea dense shelf water formation were well received and I was able to talk in more detail about my science with multiple people who saw my talk. It is such a rewarding feeling when people approach me and want to learn more about my science. It is also a big motivation moving forward.

Visiting Schönbrunn Palace just outside Vienna the Sunday before the conference. The mountain range to the left is where 1683 the polish Winged Hussars arrived to lift the siege of Vienna by the Ottoman Empire. This event inspired J.R.R. Tolkien to write a similar cavalry charge in his epic fantasy novel The Lord of the Rings. Photo by Maurice Huguenin.

Thursday morning was exciting too; I had time to catch-up with another scientist friend from my Bachelor’s in Switzerland. These are times I value as they allow me to chat with others who are at the same career stage as me. On this day, I also presented my research in a ‘fun session’ where I was only allowed to use the 1’000 most common English words in the dictionary. That was challenging to prepare because words like ‘ocean’, ‘temperature’ and ‘salinity’ that I use often were not allowed. Instead, I had to refer to descriptions of ‘the big blue body’, ‘hot stuff’ and ‘the white fluffy thing we put on food’. Thankfully, my basic English presentation pitch was only two minutes. It was then followed by a presentation at a touchscreen with slides that also only used those basic words. I had more fun in this session than I anticipated and was impressed by the creativity of other presenters. Thursday evening was another highlight of the week. I was invited for dinner with scientists from Germany and the Netherlands, most of whom I have not met before. It was great learning about their work on sea level rise and the impacts of microplastics focusing on the European region, while sharing my own experience and insights from my PhD and postdoc so far.

Presenting my science in the Up-Goer Five Challenge session, where I was only allowed to use the 1,000 most common English words. Photo provided by Maurice Huguenin.

Tips on what helped me manage the huge program at EGU in Vienna:

Looking at the session program well in advance and blocking out important sessions.

Reaching out in advance to people with whom I really wanted to talk (about science but also just about live in academia).

Scheduling time for myself to recharge. I went to the Post office & a chocolate cake store in the city center during a time when no session on my own science field was running. Well worth it!

Trying to meet at least one new person a day.

Keeping an open circle (like a Pacman) for people to join a discussion when talking in a group.

Buying lunch in advance to skip the 40 minute food stall queues.

I am grateful for the funding provided by the Australian Centre for Excellence in Antarctic Science, the European Geophysical Union and the Polar Science Early Career Community Office that allowed me to attend this conference.

Having the, what I deemed myself obligatory, Apfelstrudel in Vienna.

TITLE: The National Lottery Community Fund Grants 2026: UK Community Funding Opportunities for Stronger, Fairer Communities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The National Lottery Community Fund is a major source of community funding in the United Kingdom, supporting projects designed to help people connect, develop, overcome disadvantage and create stronger communities.

Through funding generated by the National Lottery, the organisation supports community-led initiatives that seek to make a meaningful and lasting difference to people’s lives. Its overall focus is on building stronger, fairer and more inclusive communities, with particular attention given to people experiencing poverty, disadvantage or discrimination.

The National Lottery Community Fund has set an ambitious long-term goal: by 2030, it plans to distribute more than £4 billion to help create stronger and fairer communities across the UK.

This makes the fund an important potential source of support for organisations, community groups and initiatives working to address social, economic, environmental and wellbeing challenges.

Rather than focusing on only one type of project, the organisation supports a broad range of community-led activities. These can include initiatives that bring people together, improve outcomes for children and young people, strengthen physical and emotional wellbeing, protect the environment and help communities respond to climate change.

What Is The National Lottery Community Fund?

The National Lottery Community Fund is the UK’s largest community funder, distributing money raised through National Lottery funding to support projects that benefit communities.

Its approach is strongly centred on community-led change. This means that the organisation backs projects developed around the needs, priorities and aspirations of local communities.

The fund’s work is based on the understanding that communities can create better outcomes when people have opportunities to:

Build meaningful connections with one another.

Reduce isolation and loneliness.

Create welcoming and inclusive community spaces.

Support children and young people to thrive.

Improve physical, mental and emotional wellbeing.

Protect nature and the environment.

Respond to environmental challenges and climate change.

Address poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.

Develop stronger and more resilient communities.

For organisations seeking community funding in the UK, understanding these priorities is important because successful projects are expected to demonstrate how their work can contribute to positive outcomes for people and communities.

National Lottery Community Fund’s Long-Term Vision

The organisation’s overarching vision is built around the belief that stronger communities create brighter futures.

Its funding strategy therefore places community-led initiatives at the centre of its work. Rather than simply providing financial support, the fund aims to contribute to broader social change by investing in projects that can improve people’s experiences and strengthen communities.

By 2030, the National Lottery Community Fund intends to share over £4 billion to help build stronger and fairer communities throughout the United Kingdom.

This long-term commitment creates significant opportunities for community organisations and groups whose projects align with the fund’s priorities.

The Four Community-Led Missions

The National Lottery Community Fund has identified four major community-led missions that guide the outcomes it wants to see from the projects it supports.

These missions provide an important framework for understanding the types of projects that may be relevant to its funding programmes.

1. Communities Come Together

The first mission focuses on helping communities become more connected, welcoming and inclusive.

Social connection is an important part of building healthy communities. Projects under this broad area can help people develop relationships, participate in community activities and feel that they belong.

The fund highlights outcomes such as:

Building stronger connections between people.

Reducing loneliness and social isolation.

Creating spaces where people feel welcome.

Encouraging participation in community activities.

Helping people develop stronger relationships within their communities.

Creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to interact and work together.

Community organisations working to tackle loneliness, isolation or social exclusion may therefore find this mission particularly relevant.

The emphasis is not simply on bringing people together for individual events. The broader objective is to create stronger and more connected communities where people feel included and able to participate.

2. Communities Help Children and Young People Thrive

The second mission focuses on babies, children and young people.

The National Lottery Community Fund recognises that communities can play an important role in helping younger people grow, connect and build positive futures.

Projects in this area may seek to improve opportunities and outcomes for children and young people by helping them:

Develop relationships and social connections.

Participate in positive community activities.

Access supportive environments.

Build confidence and skills.

Feel connected to their communities.

Develop healthier and brighter futures.

Organisations working with children, young people and families should therefore consider how their proposed project could demonstrate meaningful and measurable benefits for its participants.

3. Communities Are Healthier

The third mission focuses on community health and wellbeing.

Health is considered broadly within this mission, including physical, mental and emotional wellbeing.

Projects can contribute to healthier communities by creating opportunities for people to become more active, improve their wellbeing, access supportive environments and develop healthier lifestyles.

Potential areas of relevance include:

Physical wellbeing.

Mental wellbeing.

Emotional wellbeing.

Community-based health initiatives.

Activities that encourage healthier lifestyles.

Programmes that help people participate in supportive social environments.

Initiatives designed to improve overall community wellbeing.

Projects addressing health and wellbeing challenges should clearly explain the problem they are responding to and demonstrate how their activities could result in positive outcomes for the people involved.

4. Communities Are Environmentally Sustainable

The fourth mission focuses on environmental sustainability and the ability of communities to respond to environmental challenges.

The National Lottery Community Fund is interested in projects that can help communities protect nature, reduce environmental harm and respond to climate change.

Relevant initiatives may include projects focused on:

Protecting nature.

Improving local environments.

Reducing environmental harm.

Community sustainability.

Responding to climate change.

Encouraging environmentally responsible behaviour.

Helping communities become more resilient to environmental challenges.

This means environmental and climate-focused community projects may be able to align with the fund’s sustainability priorities where they demonstrate clear community benefits.

Who Can Benefit From The Funding?

The National Lottery Community Fund is focused on community projects rather than personal financial support for individuals.

Its funding is intended to support initiatives that create positive outcomes for people and communities across the UK.

The organisation places particular emphasis on supporting people experiencing:

Poverty.

Disadvantage.

Discrimination.

Social isolation.

Other barriers that can prevent people from participating fully in community life.

A strong project proposal should therefore demonstrate a clear community need and explain how the proposed activities will address that need.

Applicants should also show that their project is genuinely connected to the community it intends to serve.

Where Is The Funding Available?

The National Lottery Community Fund operates across the United Kingdom.

Its website identifies four geographical funding areas:

England

Northern Ireland

Scotland

Wales

However, applicants should not assume that every funding programme has identical geographical eligibility requirements.

Different programmes can have different rules concerning location, applicant type, project size, eligible activities and funding amounts.

Applicants should therefore check the specific requirements of the programme they intend to apply for before preparing a full application.

What Types of Projects Could Be Relevant?

Because the National Lottery Community Fund operates multiple funding programmes, the precise activities supported can vary.

Nevertheless, the organisation’s four missions provide a useful indication of the broad areas in which community projects may have potential relevance.

Examples of potentially relevant project themes include:

Community connection projects

These may include initiatives designed to:

Reduce loneliness.

Bring residents together.

Build community relationships.

Create inclusive spaces.

Encourage participation.

Support people who are socially isolated.

Children and youth projects

These may include initiatives that:

Support young people.

Improve community participation.

Provide positive activities.

Build confidence and connections.

Help children and young people develop.

Strengthen support networks for younger people.

Health and wellbeing projects

These may include programmes focused on:

Physical activity.

Mental wellbeing.

Emotional wellbeing.

Healthy lifestyles.

Community-based wellbeing.

Social activities that contribute to healthier communities.

Environmental projects

These may include initiatives focused on:

Nature conservation.

Community environmental action.

Climate change.

Sustainability.

Reducing environmental damage.

Improving local natural spaces.

These examples should be treated as broad areas of alignment rather than a guarantee that a particular activity will qualify for funding. Applicants should always check the eligibility criteria for the specific funding programme.

Why Community Organisations Should Consider This Funding

The scale and breadth of the National Lottery Community Fund make it a potentially important funding source for eligible community initiatives across the UK.

One of the major advantages is that the organisation does not focus on a single social issue.

Instead, its four missions cover several areas that are central to community development:

Social connection.

Children and young people.

Health and wellbeing.

Environmental sustainability.

The fund also has a strong focus on communities experiencing poverty, disadvantage and discrimination.

This makes it particularly relevant to organisations that are developing projects to address real community needs rather than simply seeking funding for general organisational expenses.

How To Find The Right National Lottery Community Fund Programme

The National Lottery Community Fund provides a dedicated section where applicants can browse its funding programmes.

This is an important stage of the application process because there is not necessarily one universal grant application that applies to every organisation or project.

Applicants should review the available programmes and filter them according to relevant criteria.

When looking for a suitable programme, consider:

Your project’s location

Confirm that your project operates in an eligible part of the UK.

The type of organisation applying

Check whether the programme accepts your particular organisation or community group structure.

The people your project supports

Clearly identify who benefits from your work.

The community problem you are addressing

Explain why the project is needed and what challenge it seeks to solve.

Your project’s objectives

Establish what you want to achieve through the funding.

The relevant community mission

Consider whether your project contributes to stronger connections, better outcomes for children and young people, healthier communities or environmental sustainability.

The programme’s individual requirements

Read the full eligibility rules, application guidance and funding conditions before applying.

Preparing A Strong Application

Getting ready before beginning an application can significantly improve the quality of a funding proposal.

The National Lottery Community Fund provides guidance designed to help applicants understand the funding process and complete applications with greater confidence.

Before applying, organisations should consider preparing the following information.

A clear description of the project

Explain what the project is, what activities will take place and how the project will operate.

Avoid describing the idea only in general terms. Give the funder a practical understanding of what will happen if funding is awarded.

Evidence of community need

Explain the problem that the project is designed to address.

A strong proposal should answer questions such as:

What problem exists?

Who is affected?

Why is the issue important?

What evidence demonstrates the need?

Why is the proposed project an appropriate response?

Clearly identified beneficiaries

Explain who will benefit from the project.

TITLE: Anthropogenic fingerprint detectable in upper tropospheric ozone trends retrieved from satellite

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Yu, X., Fiore, A. M., Santer, B. D., Correa, G. P., Lamarque, J.-F., Ziemke, J. R., Eastham, S. D., & Zhu, Q. (2024). Anthropogenic fingerprint detectable in upper tropospheric ozone trends retrieved from satellite. Environmental Science & Technology. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c01289

Image provided by Xinyuan Yu

Tropospheric ozone is a strong greenhouse gas, particularly in the upper troposphere. Limited observations point to a continuous increase in upper tropospheric ozone in recent decades, but the attribution is complicated by large internal climate variability. Here we derive a time-invariant fingerprint of human-caused upper tropospheric ozone changes from a 16-member initial-condition ensemble performed with a chemistry-climate model (CESM2-WACCM6). We then search for this pattern in a product obtained from the OMI and MLS satellite instruments. Although the satellite retrieved upper tropospheric ozone record began in 2005 and is only 17 years in length, we found that the model-simulated fingerprint is detectable with high statistical confidence after only 13 years of monitoring, revealing a unique pattern of human influence on Earth’s atmospheric chemistry in the upper troposphere.

The Opportunity and Innovation Grants are designed to enable CSOs to leverage modest funding into larger impacts, and to incubate promising new approaches — topics, methodologies, and formats for fostering dialogue between local communities in the Western Balkans.

Some examples may include preparing an application for larger funding opportunities, conducting pilot projects or feasibility studies, reacting to political developments within communities, or taking proactive action in response to anticipated developments. Applicants will be asked to specify the local community and type of divide they would like to address. The latter may include identities such as national, ethnic, racial, religious, gender, or sexual orientation.

Grant

The maximum grant amount is €4,500. There will be a total of 20 grants available in 2026.

Eligibility

Open to civil society organizations working on peace, dialogue, and social cohesion in the Western Balkans registered in Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia.

Informal (unregistered) organizations, collectives, or ad hoc groups may apply in a coalition with a registered organization, or with a fiscal host.

Selection Procedure

Applications will be reviewed on an ongoing basis internally by at least two EFB staff members based on the following criteria:

Strategic & Values Fit (30%): Successful applicants will be small and medium local organizations, collectives, or ad hoc groups working on bridging divides within a local context, or on topics that have the potential to unite communities and build trust.

Opportunity or Innovation Argumentation (30%): Applicants will be asked to provide a brief description of the context they would like to address, their proposed intervention, an activity description, and a clear, well-argued rationale as to why these constitute an innovative or promising approach to the problem.

Estimated Impact (25%): This criterion is based on the evaluators’ estimation of the intervention’s impact; in other words, how likely it is to produce the social results represented by the applicant.

Feasibility & Proportionality (15%): While all types of costs are admissible, applicants will be asked to briefly argue as to how each budget line specifically contributes to the opportunity or innovation being applied for, rather than the applicant’s everyday work.

Application

In addition to the application form, applicants will be required to submit the following documentation:

Valid registration documentation of the applicant or fiscal host;

Statute of the applicant or fiscal host;

A list of staff members and their roles within the applicant or fiscal host;

For coalitions or entities using fiscal hosts: a duly signed Memorandum of Understanding between the relevant parties on the distribution of roles and responsibilities and the use of funds.
