TITLE: TradeRoots Africa 2026–2027: ICC Programme Helping African SMEs Become Export-Ready and Access Regional and Global Markets

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) seeking to expand beyond their domestic markets can now apply for TradeRoots Africa, an initiative of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Centre of Entrepreneurship designed to help businesses become export-ready and compete more effectively across African and international markets.

The programme is particularly focused on helping African SMEs navigate the practical challenges associated with regional and international trade, including export compliance, trade documentation, market access, digital trade, logistics, customs, trade finance, mentorship and business development.

Applications for TradeRoots Africa are currently open, with the application deadline set for 15 October 2026. The programme is scheduled to officially launch in November 2026 and continue through August 2027.

What Is TradeRoots Africa?

TradeRoots Africa is an SME-focused trade development programme established by the ICC Centre of Entrepreneurship to help African businesses translate regional and continental trade opportunities into practical business growth.

The initiative was launched at the 2025 B20 Summit in South Africa and is designed around the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the Regional Economic Communities (RECs).

Rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge about international trade, TradeRoots Africa takes a practical approach. The programme aims to help participating businesses develop the knowledge, capabilities, connections and resources needed to move towards actual export activity.

According to the ICC, African SMEs represent approximately 90% of businesses on the continent and employ around 70% of the workforce, yet fewer than 20% formally export. The programme therefore seeks to address some of the barriers preventing otherwise viable African businesses from accessing regional and international markets.

Why TradeRoots Africa Was Created

Expanding a business into another country can involve considerably more than simply finding international customers.

African SMEs can face multiple interconnected barriers when attempting to enter regional and global markets. These include:

High costs associated with international trade.

Complex regulatory and customs requirements.

Limited access to digital trade tools.

Infrastructure constraints.

Difficulty accessing appropriate financing.

Limited knowledge of export procedures.

Challenges understanding regional and international markets.

Limited access to potential buyers and business networks.

The ICC notes that these challenges are interconnected, meaning that addressing one obstacle in isolation may not be sufficient to turn an SME into a successful exporter.

TradeRoots Africa therefore brings several forms of support together in a structured programme intended to take participating businesses from foundational trade knowledge towards export acceleration.

The Six Key Pillars of TradeRoots Africa

TradeRoots Africa is structured around six major areas of support. Together, these pillars are intended to provide participating SMEs with practical capabilities for regional and international trade.

1. Trade Knowledge and Market Access

Businesses will receive support in understanding trade requirements and identifying opportunities to access markets beyond their domestic market.

This pillar is particularly important for SMEs that may have a product or service with growth potential but lack sufficient knowledge of export procedures, market requirements and regional trade opportunities.

2. Trade Finance

Access to finance can be an important factor in a company’s ability to enter new markets.

TradeRoots Africa incorporates trade finance into its support framework, helping businesses develop greater readiness around financing requirements associated with international trade.

3. Logistics, Customs and Air Transport

Cross-border trade requires businesses to understand how goods move between markets and how customs and logistical processes affect exports.

The programme therefore includes logistics, customs and air transport as one of its six central pillars.

4. Digital Trade Tools

Digital technologies are increasingly important for businesses seeking customers and opportunities beyond their domestic markets.

TradeRoots Africa includes digital trade tools among its core areas of support, with later programme activities also focusing on e-commerce and related digital capabilities.

5. Mentorship

Participating SMEs will have access to mentorship as part of the programme’s broader support ecosystem.

Mentorship can provide businesses with practical guidance as they work through trade-related challenges and develop their internationalisation strategies.

6. Business Development

The programme also focuses on business development, helping participating SMEs strengthen their commercial readiness and move towards concrete market opportunities.

These six pillars collectively form the foundation of the TradeRoots Africa SME support system.

How the TradeRoots Africa Programme Works

TradeRoots Africa is organised into three progressive tiers.

The structure means that participation can develop from foundational trade education to more specialised support and ultimately to export acceleration.

Tier 1: Trade Foundations

Period: November 2026 – March 2027

The first tier is designed to establish the fundamental knowledge SMEs need before entering regional and international markets.

The ICC states that 1,000 SMEs will participate in this stage.

Participants will learn about areas including:

Export compliance.

Trade documentation.

AfCFTA.

Regional trade fundamentals.

Other foundational aspects of exporting.

The training will be delivered through a combination of:

Virtual and blended webinars.

Practical sessions.

Capacity-building activities.

The programme identifies Modules 1–14 as part of this foundational stage.

For SMEs that are still developing their understanding of international trade, this first tier provides an opportunity to strengthen the foundational knowledge required to operate across borders.

Tier 2: Digital and Sector Skills

Period: April – June 2027

The second tier moves beyond basic trade foundations and focuses on more advanced capabilities.

The programme expects 200 SMEs to participate at this stage.

Businesses selected for Tier 2 will receive support in areas including:

E-commerce.

Sustainability-related trade.

Trade finance.

Market adaptation.

Regional and trade-corridor bootcamps.

Targeted technical support.

Mentorship.

Buyer connections.

Digital trade readiness.

Trade finance readiness workshops.

Modules 16–19 are identified for this stage, alongside additional technical and business support activities.

This stage is particularly relevant to SMEs that have progressed beyond basic export knowledge and are looking to develop more specialised capabilities for entering or expanding within regional markets.

Tier 3: Export Acceleration

Period: July–August 2027

The third tier focuses on turning export readiness into practical commercial opportunities.

The programme expects 50 SMEs to participate at this stage.

Businesses reaching Tier 3 will receive support related to:

Developing export plans.

Accessing new markets.

Securing trade finance.

Transaction support.

Buyer engagement.

Trade finance facilitation.

One-to-one sessions.

Continued business development.

The ICC specifically identifies Module 18 on transaction support as part of this stage.

Important Progression Requirement

An important point for prospective applicants is that the three tiers are not presented as separate, independent opportunities.

The ICC states that only SMEs that participate in Tier 1 are eligible for Tier 2 and Tier 3.

This means that SMEs interested in progressing to the more advanced digital, sector-specific and export acceleration support should understand that participation begins with the foundational stage.

Who Is TradeRoots Africa For?

TradeRoots Africa is designed for African small and medium-sized enterprises that have potential to scale across African markets.

The programme specifically seeks a balanced cohort comprising:

Emerging SMEs

Growth-stage businesses

Established SMEs

The common factor is the potential for these businesses to expand and scale across African markets.

This means the opportunity is not limited exclusively to newly established businesses. More established SMEs can also be considered where they demonstrate the potential to expand across African markets.

TradeRoots Africa and the African Continental Free Trade Area

A significant component of the programme is its connection to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

AfCFTA is referenced by the ICC as one of the key frameworks within which TradeRoots Africa will help SMEs become export-ready.

The programme also considers the role of Regional Economic Communities (RECs), recognising that African businesses can operate within both continental and regional trade frameworks.

For SMEs, understanding these frameworks can be important when considering expansion into markets beyond their home country.

TradeRoots Africa therefore seeks to make trade policy more practical for businesses by connecting knowledge of continental and regional trade arrangements with practical capabilities such as export compliance, documentation, market access, logistics, digital trade and finance.

What Businesses Can Gain From TradeRoots Africa

The programme provides several potential areas of development for participating SMEs.

Export Readiness

One of the central objectives is to help businesses become better prepared for exporting.

This includes understanding export compliance and documentation, as well as gaining knowledge of regional trade requirements.

Market Access

Businesses can develop greater awareness of opportunities to access regional and international markets.

Later programme activities also include buyer connections and market adaptation support.

Trade Finance Readiness

TradeRoots Africa incorporates trade finance into its support framework, including dedicated trade finance readiness workshops and facilitation during the export acceleration stage.

Digital Business Capabilities

Businesses participating in later stages can develop capabilities relating to digital trade and e-commerce.

These skills can be particularly relevant to SMEs seeking to reach customers and commercial partners beyond their traditional geographic markets.

Mentorship and Technical Support

Participants can benefit from mentorship and targeted technical support as they develop their trade capabilities.

Buyer Connections

The programme’s advanced stages include buyer connections and buyer engagement, creating opportunities for participating businesses to move beyond training towards practical commercial relationships.

Export Planning

At the export acceleration stage, selected SMEs will work on export plans and receive support related to entering new markets.

These components demonstrate that TradeRoots Africa is structured around progression from learning and capacity building towards practical export activity.

Why Export Readiness Matters for African SMEs

For a business seeking to expand internationally, export readiness involves more than having a product that can be sold in another country.

TITLE: Celebration of International Women’s Day (IWD) and Consultative Forum for the Launch of the African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
March 8th, 2021 | 10am – 1pm GMT

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the apex continental organisation and voice of higher education in Africa established 53 years ago. The AAU prioritises strengthening intellectual engagement and discussions on topical issues that addresses Africa’s developmental goals, and generally global issues – be it already existing or emerging issues.

One of such key issues relates to gender inclusiveness, and AAU has been taking the lead to drive women and young girls’ equal participation in the higher education sector . As the forum for consultation, exchange of information and co-operation among institutions of Higher Education in Africa, AAU is cognisant of the gender imbalances in African higher education and has thus been dedicated to ensuring gender inclusiveness in its various initiatives and projects, including hosting its flagship Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) Conference regularly. The promotion of gender equality is firmly rooted in the AAU’s Strategic Plan, which was carefully crafted to help Higher Education Institutions respond to the realisation of the targets of continental and global strategies, agenda’s and frameworks such as the Africa Union’s (AU) Agenda 2063, the Continental Education Strategy for Education (CESA 16 -25) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Every year, 8th March is set aside as International Women’s Day by the global community. The day celebrates the social, economic, cultural, and political achievements of women and also underscores the call to action for accelerating gender parity, raising awareness about women’s equality and fundraising for female-focused activities.

The theme for the 2021 celebration is ” Choose To Challenge”. This year, stakeholders are encouraged to use the day to choose to challenge and call out gender biases and inequalities.

In line with AAU being a key player and advocate in issues of women empowerment, the Association is marking the international Women’s Day on March 8th by hosting a virtual discussion session on the theme, as well to consult and engage the African Higher Education Community to input into the establishment of the African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN), which will be launched by the AAU in July 2021. The network shall among others, engage similar minded bodies to ensure that it adds value to issues related to all women, teaching and non-teaching in the African higher education space. The detailed concept note for WoHEN and programme for the International Women’s Day event will be made available to all registered participants.

TITLE: The 6th ACDE General Assembly and Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Overview of the 6th ACDE General Assembly and Conference

Theme: Open and Distance Learning, The Continental Education Strategy for Africa and The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG4).

Convener: African Council for Distance Education (ACDE)

Host Institutions: Association of African Universities (AAU), All-Africa Students Union (AASU), Laweh Open University College, Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), Ministry of Education, Ghana and the International Council for Open & Distance Education (ICDE)

Venue: LIVE ON ZOOM

The ACDE 2021 Quality Assurance pre- conference Workshop requiring a US$50 fee payment will be held on the 27th September 2021. You can download the pre-conference concept note from here: Pre-Conference Workshop Document

Register for it via this link: https://flutterwave.com/pay/qaaareg

The free to attend Main ACDE Conference will be held from 28-29 September 2021. Register for it via this link: https://bit.ly/ACDE2021

The 6th General Assembly and Conference of the African Council for Distance Education, Accra invites scholars, policy makers, students, professionals and other stakeholders to send original research abstracts, case studies and proposals formatted according to the conference guidelines. The conference will be held from 27th-29th September, 2021 via the ZOOM PLATFORM under the theme “Open and Distance Learning, The Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA) and the Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG4)”. Additional information concerning the conference can be found from this link: https://acdeconf.laweh.edu.gh/

The African Council for Distance Education (ACDE) is a Continental Educational Organization comprising of African Universities and other Higher Educational Institutions, which are committed to promoting quality education and training through Open and Distance Learning. Every four years, the ACDE organizes its General Assembly and Conference to take stock of its activities in the last four years and to plan for the next four years (http://acde-afri.org/). The Assembly brings together Vice Chancellors, Rectors and Presidents of Universities and other tertiary institutions providing Open and Distance Education on the continent and in the diaspora to deliberate on key issues affecting ODL on the continent by partnering with host countries. In line with the aspirations of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa, the ACDE has embarked on a number of initiatives geared at ensuring that, the strengths of ODL is harnessed towards the achievement of both the strategic focus of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA, 2016-2025) and ultimately the SDG4. This focus has necessitated a stakeholder conference to review and share experiences on the progresses chalked by diverse stakeholders in the Open and Distance education space in Africa, in a bid to fulfill the goals of the CESA and SDG4.

The 2020 conference will bring together Leaders and Managers of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), Policy Makers, scholars, students, educational professionals, development agencies and educational technology investors and private sector committed to sustainable open and distance learning education in Africa. We welcome submissions that address wider distance

learning and open education contexts including methodological approaches and technological infrastructure. Scholars, practitioners and upcoming scholars with conceptual and empirical papers as well as teaching case studies are invited to submit their abstracts online under the following conference themes.

Conference Themes and Tracks Chairs

1. Infrastructure, ODL Resources and Adoption Techniques for Open and Distance Education

African Virtual Universities and Ubuntu Net

2. Quality Assurance in Open and Distance Learning

Dr. Beatrice Njenga (International Expert, Development Management)

3. Teaching and Learning Methodologies in Open andDistance Learning

Professor Peter Akinsola Okebukola (National Open University of Nigeria)

4. Academic Misconduct and Open and Distance Education

Prof. Goski Alabi (Laweh Open University College, Ghana)

5. Students’ and other Stakeholders Perceptions of Open and Distant Learning

Professor Etienne Ehile (Association of African Universities)

Submission Guidelines

The deadline for submission of abstracts is extended to 20th September 2021

Abstracts must not exceed 300 words

Competitive papers must not exceed 10,000 words and must comply to the APA style requirements. Please refer to 6th edition of APA guidelines.

Interactive papers should be between 2,000 –5,000 words. Submissions should clearly state the research questions, methodology and knowledge contribution. The main results and implications for open and distance learning research and practice should be discussed, if available/applicable.

Teaching case should be between 2,000 – 5,000 and no more than 10,000 words for competitive cases.

Panel proposals should have 3 – 5 scholars and/or students and a common theme, as well as a chair/discussant. We welcome a variety of proposals (paper presentations, roundtable, and professional development workshop). The names of participants and the discussant should be disclosed for this type of submission.

Competitive papers, interactive papers and teaching cases will be double-blind reviewed. Please do not include any author-identifying information. Authors are strongly encouraged to abide by these instructions to facilitate the review process. Please submit online through this ink: https://event-mgt.aau.org/event/15/

Please state the submission type (competitive, interactive or panel) and track title on the front page at the top right. In addition, if you are a student, kindly indicate the type (graduate or undergraduate)

Participation at the ACDE is limited. Hence, presenters will be selected based on the quality of their submitted work. Submissions should be submitted online: https://event-mgt.aau.org/event/15/ and include the workshop title as the subject

We are expecting two types of submissions:

Full, competitive research papers – Should not be more than 10,000 words in length.

Interactive papers – Should be no more than 3,000 words in length and include a theoretical framework, propositions, and proposed research design.

Doctoral Consortium

The aim of the doctoral consortium is to develop the research ideas of doctoral students especially as it pertains to conducting open and distance learning research in African higher education Institutions. The consortium also aims to create a platform for the development of professional networks and to highlight some of the opportunities and challenges of developing a successful academic career. Interested doctoral students must have successfully defended their proposals and are asked to submit a five-page maximum double spaced document detailing their research. Only defended proposals will be considered for the doctoral award. Submissions should be submitted online via https://event-mgt.aau.org/event/15/ and include the workshop title as the subject as well as the following:

What are you studying?

What is known and unknown about what you are studying?

What is unique about what you are studying?

What is your chosen research methodology?

What are the findings from the research?

Networking & Field Visits

The host University had planned a visit to historical and landmark sites in Ghana such as Mampong Cocoa Plantation, Cape Coast Castle, Elmina Castle, Kakum National park among others. But because of the COVID19 these field visits will no longer take place

Conference Awards

Several prizes will be awarded at the conference:

Best Competitive Paper Award, Best Thematic Conference Paper Award

Best Teaching Case Award, Best Conference Paper Prize for Practice / Policy Implications Award

Best Promising Doctoral Paper Award

Best Graduate Student Paper Award

Publication Opportunities

All accepted conference papers will be published as an abstract in the 6th ACDE General Assembly and Conference (with ISBN).

A selection of papers that are aligned with the conference theme may be considered for inclusion in Huria: Journal of the Open University of Tanzania, ISSN: 0856-6739

TITLE: Jack and Doris Shadbolt Fellowship in the Humanities 2027–28 at Simon Fraser University: Eligibility, Benefits, Application Process and Deadline

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Jack and Doris Shadbolt Fellowship in the Humanities 2027–28 at Simon Fraser University (SFU) is now accepting applications from emerging and established academic scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers working in the humanities and arts.

Hosted by the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences (FASS) at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, Canada, the fellowship provides an opportunity for talented and engaged individuals to develop a meaningful project within an academic and intellectual environment.

The fellowship supports creative practice and publicly engaged scholarship while encouraging applicants to explore major concerns affecting society and contribute to conversations around decolonization, Indigenization, culture, creativity and social change.

For scholars, artists, writers, knowledge keepers and practitioners whose work connects intellectual inquiry with creative practice or public engagement, the Shadbolt Fellowship offers an opportunity to develop an important project while becoming part of the Simon Fraser University community.

About the Jack and Doris Shadbolt Fellowship

The Jack and Doris Shadbolt Fellowship in the Humanities is supported by the Jack and Doris Shadbolt Endowment for the Humanities.

The fellowship reflects the vision of Jack and Doris Shadbolt, who viewed the humanities and arts as deeply connected to the natural and social worlds inhabited by artists, scholars and thinkers.

The programme seeks to promote the humanities and arts as important sites of:

Creative practice

Critical engagement

Public scholarship

Cultural reflection

Intellectual inquiry

Social engagement

Decolonization

Indigenization

Creative world-making

Engagement with major concerns of contemporary society

Rather than restricting the fellowship to traditional academic research, SFU takes a broad approach to the humanities and arts. Potential fellows may be academic scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners or writers.

This makes the opportunity relevant to individuals working across a wide range of intellectual, artistic, cultural and publicly engaged fields.

2027–28 Fellowship Opportunity

The Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences at Simon Fraser University is inviting applications for the 2027–28 academic year.

Applicants are expected to propose a project that they intend to undertake during the fellowship.

The proposed project should be clearly explained and demonstrate why the applicant’s work would benefit from a fellowship at Simon Fraser University.

Applicants should clearly communicate:

The project they intend to undertake.

The purpose and importance of the project.

What they hope to accomplish during the fellowship.

How the project relates to the humanities and/or arts.

Their preferred primary unit affiliation within FASS.

Any desired secondary affiliation within SFU.

The length of fellowship they are requesting.

Why the requested fellowship duration is appropriate for the project.

Who Can Apply?

The Shadbolt Fellowship is intended for emerging or established engaged academic scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers in the humanities and arts.

Potential applicants may include people whose work involves:

Humanities research

Arts and creative practice

Writing

Cultural knowledge

Public scholarship

Community-based intellectual work

Creative research

Socially engaged artistic practice

Critical humanities scholarship

Indigenous knowledge and cultural practice

Interdisciplinary humanities and arts projects

Publicly engaged research and creative work

The fellowship is therefore not limited exclusively to conventional university academics.

Emerging Applicants

The programme welcomes emerging scholars, artists, writers, practitioners and knowledge keepers.

Applicants who are at an earlier stage of their careers may be considered if they have a strong project and demonstrate the experience and preparation necessary to undertake it.

Established Applicants

Established scholars, artists, practitioners, writers and knowledge keepers are also eligible to apply.

The programme seeks a diverse group of resident fellows representing different stages of professional and intellectual development.

International Applicants

The official announcement does not specify a nationality or citizenship restriction.

Therefore, the opportunity is not presented as being limited to Canadian citizens or residents.

Applicants from outside Canada may apply if they satisfy the fellowship’s eligibility requirements and are suitable candidates.

This means applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions may consider applying.

International applicants should, however, separately consider any immigration, visa, travel or residency requirements that may apply if they are selected.

Indigenous Applicants Are Particularly Encouraged

The Shadbolt Fellowship has a specific commitment to decolonization and Indigenization.

SFU states that the programme especially welcomes Indigenous applicants.

The fellowship is not restricted to Indigenous applicants, but the university’s commitment means that Indigenous scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers are particularly encouraged to submit applications.

Applicants whose proposed projects engage meaningfully with Indigenous knowledge, decolonization, Indigenization or related areas may find strong alignment with the programme’s stated mission.

Commitment to Equity, Inclusion and Diversity

The selection of resident Shadbolt Fellows will be guided by considerations of equity, inclusion and diversity.

SFU also aims to ensure that its group of resident fellows represents a broad range of humanities and arts areas.

The fellowship seeks to include:

Indigenous applicants

Emerging scholars and practitioners

Established scholars and practitioners

Academic scholars

Artists

Knowledge keepers

Practitioners

Writers

Applicants working across different humanities and arts disciplines

Candidates belonging to underrepresented groups are particularly encouraged to apply.

These groups include:

Indigenous peoples

Persons with disabilities

Racialized persons

Women

People representing gender and sexual diversity

Applicants should nevertheless focus on presenting a strong project, relevant experience and a clear explanation of why SFU is an appropriate environment for their work.

What Does the Fellowship Support?

The Shadbolt Fellowship is designed to support projects that contribute to the humanities and arts as important spaces for creative practice and critical engagement with major concerns of our times.

The programme aims to support work that can help society imagine better ways of understanding and shaping the world.

Supported approaches may include:

Creative arts

Humanities research

Publicly engaged scholarship

Critical inquiry

Cultural work

Intellectual engagement

Creative practice

Socially engaged projects

Decolonization

Indigenization

Interdisciplinary work

Applicants should focus on the project they intend to undertake during the fellowship rather than simply describing their previous accomplishments.

Their previous work should instead demonstrate their preparation and ability to successfully undertake the proposed project.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit a complete application package containing the required documents.

The application should include:

1. Completed Application Form

Applicants must complete the official Shadbolt Fellowship Application Form for the 2027–28 academic year.

The application form provides the required structure for the submission and should be completed accurately and thoroughly.

2. Current CV

Applicants must provide a current curriculum vitae.

The CV should clearly demonstrate the applicant’s academic, artistic, professional, creative and/or public engagement background.

Depending on the applicant’s field, relevant information may include:

Education

Academic appointments

Research experience

Publications

Books

Articles

Creative works

Exhibitions

Performances

Professional experience

Awards

Fellowships

Community engagement

Public scholarship

Artistic achievements

Presentations

Relevant projects

Other professional or intellectual accomplishments

3. Cover Letter

Applicants must also submit a cover letter.

The cover letter should specifically address three areas identified by Simon Fraser University:

The project the applicant intends to undertake during the fellowship.

The desired primary unit affiliation in the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and, where applicable, a secondary unit affiliation.

The length of fellowship desired and why that duration is appropriate.

Applicants should therefore avoid submitting a generic cover letter.

The letter should be tailored specifically to the Shadbolt Fellowship and explain the applicant’s proposed project, experience and connection to SFU.

Choosing an SFU Primary Affiliation

An important part of the application is identifying the academic unit where the applicant would like to be primarily affiliated.

The primary affiliation should be within the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences.

Applicants should consider which department or programme best matches their proposed project and intellectual interests.

A suitable affiliation can help demonstrate that the applicant has carefully considered how their work would fit within SFU’s academic environment.

Secondary Unit Affiliation

Applicants may also identify a secondary affiliation if appropriate.

Importantly, SFU states that secondary units may be any unit within Simon Fraser University and are not restricted to FASS.

This creates an opportunity for applicants whose projects are interdisciplinary to identify another relevant academic unit that could contribute to their work.

Applicants should only identify a secondary affiliation where it has a meaningful connection to the proposed project.

Contacting an SFU Department Before Applying

Before submitting an application, candidates are strongly encouraged to contact the FASS department or unit with which they wish to work.

This is an important preparatory step.

Applicants can use the opportunity to discuss:

Their proposed project

The relevance of the project to the department

Potential academic connections

Their proposed primary affiliation

Possible secondary affiliations

Interdisciplinary opportunities

The fit between their project and SFU’s academic environment

Candidates can consult the official FASS departments and programmes list to identify the most appropriate unit.

Fellowship Duration

Applicants must indicate the length of fellowship they would like.

They must also explain why the requested duration is appropriate.

When determining the requested length, applicants should consider:

The scope of their project

Research requirements

Creative development

Writing requirements

Public engagement activities

Collaboration

Access to university resources

Expected project outcomes

The amount of work that can realistically be completed

The requested fellowship length should therefore be justified by the proposed project rather than selected without explanation.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the 2027–28 Shadbolt Fellowship is:

October 23, 2026 at 9:00 a.m.

Applicants should ensure that their complete application package is submitted before the stated deadline.

Applications should be emailed to:

shadbolt_fellows@sfu.ca

Simon Fraser University states that a single PDF is preferred.

Applicants should also include their name in the filename.

For example:

FirstName_LastName_Shaddbolt_Fellowship_2027-28.pdf

Applicants should follow the official application instructions when preparing and submitting their documents.

Application Timeline

The official timeline for the 2027–28 fellowship is as follows:

September 21, 2026 — Online Q&A Information Session

An online question-and-answer information session will be held on September 21, 2026.

Time: 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Format: Online via Zoom

This session provides prospective applicants with an opportunity to learn more about the fellowship and ask questions before submitting their applications.

October 23, 2026 — Application Deadline

The complete application must be submitted by:

9:00 a.m. on October 23, 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final minutes to submit their applications.

Late November — Shortlisted Candidates Notified

Shortlisted candidates are expected to be notified in late November.

December 7, 2026 — Reference Letters Deadline

For shortlisted candidates, reference letters must be submitted by December 7, 2026.

Applicants should therefore consider potential referees before the application deadline so they are prepared if shortlisted.

Important Eligibility Restrictions

Although the fellowship has broad eligibility in terms of professional background, SFU has identified important restrictions.

Current SFU Students

Individuals who are students at Simon Fraser University are ineligible for the fellowship.

Continuing SFU Appointments

Individuals who hold a continuing appointment at Simon Fraser University are also ineligible.

Relationship to Degree Requirements

SFU states that the project proposed for the fellowship will normally not be related to work being undertaken to fulfill the requirements of a degree programme in which the applicant is enrolled.

The fellowship project should therefore generally be independent from an existing degree requirement.

What Could Make an Application Strong?

While applicants should follow the official requirements rather than trying to predict the selection committee, a strong application should be clear, focused and closely aligned with the goals of the fellowship.

Present a Clearly Defined Project

Explain exactly what you want to accomplish during the fellowship.

The selection committee should be able to understand the project’s purpose, objectives, intellectual direction or creative contribution.

Demonstrate Humanities or Arts Relevance

Clearly explain how the proposed work contributes to the humanities and/or arts.

Explain the Broader Significance

Where appropriate, demonstrate how the project engages with important cultural, social, intellectual or public issues.

Show Why SFU Is a Good Fit

Explain why Simon Fraser University is an appropriate environment for the proposed work.

Identify the relevant primary unit and, where applicable, secondary affiliation.

Demonstrate Feasibility

The project should be realistic within the fellowship period requested.

Applicants should demonstrate that they have thought carefully about what they can accomplish during their time as a fellow.

Connect Your Experience to the Project

Your CV and cover letter should establish a logical connection between your previous experience and the proposed fellowship project.

Your past work should demonstrate that you have the skills, knowledge or creative experience necessary to undertake the project successfully.

Recommended Preparation Checklist

Applicants can prepare for the competition by following these steps:

Read the official fellowship application form carefully.

Develop a clear and meaningful fellowship project.

Identify the most appropriate FASS department or unit.

Consider whether a secondary SFU affiliation would strengthen the project.

Contact the relevant department before submitting the application.

Update your CV.

Prepare a fellowship-specific cover letter.

Clearly explain your desired fellowship duration.

Review all eligibility restrictions.

Complete the application form carefully.

Combine the required documents into a single PDF where possible.

Include your name in the PDF filename.

Email the completed application to shadbolt_fellows@sfu.ca.

Submit before October 23, 2026 at 9:00 a.m.

If shortlisted, ensure that reference letters are submitted by December 7, 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Shadbolt Fellowship a scholarship?

No. It is a fellowship supporting emerging and established scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers in the humanities and arts.

Who is the fellowship designed for?

The fellowship is designed for engaged academic scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers working in the humanities and arts.

Can international applicants apply?

The announcement does not specify a nationality restriction, so the opportunity is not limited to Canadian applicants. International candidates may apply provided they satisfy the stated eligibility requirements.

Are Indigenous applicants encouraged to apply?

Yes. SFU explicitly states that the programme especially welcomes Indigenous applicants and supports work connected to decolonization and Indigenization.

Can current SFU students apply?

No. Individuals who are students at SFU are ineligible.

Can someone with a continuing SFU appointment apply?

No. Individuals who hold a continuing appointment at SFU are ineligible.

Do applicants have to be university professors?

No. The fellowship specifically includes artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers in addition to academic scholars.

Does the primary affiliation have to be within FASS?

Yes. Applicants are asked to identify their desired primary unit affiliation within the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences.

Can the secondary affiliation be outside FASS?

Yes. SFU states that secondary units may be any unit within Simon Fraser University.

Should applicants contact a department before applying?

Yes. SFU strongly encourages candidates to contact the FASS department or unit with which they wish to work before submitting their applications.

What documents are required?

Applicants must submit:

A fully completed application form

A current CV

A cover letter

A single PDF is preferred.

What is the application deadline?

The application deadline is October 23, 2026 at 9:00 a.m.

When will shortlisted candidates be notified?

Shortlisted candidates are expected to be notified in late November.

When are reference letters due?

Reference letters for shortlisted candidates are due December 7, 2026.

Official Application Information

Prospective applicants should carefully review the official Simon Fraser University fellowship information and application materials before submitting their applications.

Official application page

Official 2027–28 application form

More fellowship available on the OFY Website HERE

Conclusion

The Jack and Doris Shadbolt Fellowship in the Humanities 2027–28 at Simon Fraser University provides an important opportunity for emerging and established academic scholars, artists, knowledge keepers, practitioners and writers to develop meaningful work within a university environment dedicated to the humanities and arts.

The fellowship stands out because of its broad understanding of who can contribute to the humanities and arts. Applicants do not have to fit exclusively within the traditional academic model, as the programme welcomes artists, writers, practitioners and knowledge keepers alongside academic scholars.

The programme also places strong emphasis on creative practice, publicly engaged scholarship, critical engagement with major concerns of our time, decolonization and Indigenization. Indigenous applicants are particularly encouraged to apply, while candidates from underrepresented groups are also strongly encouraged to consider the opportunity.

Applicants should prepare a complete application consisting of the official application form, a current CV and a tailored cover letter. The cover letter should explain the proposed fellowship project, desired primary and secondary affiliations and the requested fellowship duration.

Candidates are also strongly encouraged to contact their preferred FASS department or unit before submitting their application.

The key deadline to remember is October 23, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. Shortlisted candidates are expected to be notified in late November, while reference letters for shortlisted candidates will be due on December 7, 2026.

For individuals whose work combines humanities, arts, culture, scholarship, creativity or public engagement, the Shadbolt Fellowship could provide a valuable platform to develop an ambitious project, engage with an academic community and contribute to broader intellectual, cultural and social conversations.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Carol Alonso and Jose Alonso

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Carol Alonso PhD ’70 and Jose Alonso ’62, PhD ’67 have made a gift to the Physics Department to support a fellowship.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2014

Carol and Jose Alonso

Carol and Jose started their physics careers in the heady years immediately following Sputnik, during the wake-up call that first satellite provided for youngsters interested in science and engineering.

Jose’s personal interest in physics came from a one-day visit in 1958 to the Lawrence Berkeley Lab (then the “RadLab”) where, wide-eyed, he was introduced to fascinating and fabulous machines such as the Bevatron, the 184-foot Synchrocyclotron and the Heavy-Ion Linac (HILAC), all working furiously to discover new elements and unravel the newly developing field of particle physics. The serendipity of that visit came home when, 20 years later, after finishing his bachelor’s and PhD degrees at MIT, Jose returned to Berkeley and assumed the directorship of those same machines that had turned him on to the field.

Carol and Jose pursued different paths to their professional physics careers: she through a double major in physics and math at Allegheny College, and Jose through an undergraduate degree at MIT. In Jose’s 1958 freshman class, fully 50% of the students intended to major in physics or electrical engineering, but while many later diverged to other specialties, he continued to enjoy physics. As a senior, Jose joined Prof. Lee Grodzins’ group and conducted a thesis experiment on the newly-discovered Mossbauer effect. Later, when accepted into MIT’s physics graduate program, he continued with Prof. Grodzins in his hyperfine interactions group.

Carol and I owe so much to MIT for the formation of our professional careers and this gift is a small token showing our appreciation. We understand that fellowship support is a top need in the Department, allowing it to recruit the best students and give them flexibility in their first year.
Jose Alonso ’62, PhD ’67

Carol joined the same MIT group about two years later, after finishing a master’s in biophysics at Bryn Mawr. Her MIT PhD thesis on “Perturbed Angular Correlations” landed her in European conferences, as she had discovered a new selection rule. They then both worked as postdoctorates at Yale, transferring a year later to Prof. Glenn Seaborg’s group at Berkeley for another two years of postdoc research. There, their team discovered Element 106, subsequently named Seaborgium after their mentor. During that period Carol also fielded a hydrodynamics experiment on the Space Shuttle Challenger with astronaut Taylor Wang.

Carol then transferred to Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, managed by the University of California, where she pursued a productive career in Defense Sciences, including management of joint U.S. – U.K. programs in the field and early laser fusion experiments. She was the Deputy “A” Division Leader for several years, then promoted to Assistant Associate Director for National Security in the Director’s Office and Assistant to the Deputy Director. Carol was honored with a United States Medal for Outstanding Service during the Gulf War.

After early retirement in 2001, Carol took on her current career, the training and competing of dressage horses with a specialty in freestyle to music. She has been fortunate to win several awards riding her own horses. In 2009 she earned a Bronze Medal from the United States Dressage Federation and in 2011 was the California Reserve Champion for Second Level Freestyle. Riding, her daily passion, keeps Carol fit and healthy.

Jose remained at Lawrence Berkeley Lab in the Accelerator Division, and pursued a productive career in the development of new applications for particle accelerators, in many of the fields pioneered by the Bevatron and Bevalac. Examples include the use of particle beams for cancer therapy, beams up to uranium for relativistic heavy-ion research, and as part of the SNS project at Oak Ridge, megawatt proton beams as neutron sources for materials research.

After “retirement” in 2002, Jose did a stint at CERN working on the ATLAS detector, then was appointed director of the newly-established Sanford Underground Laboratory in the Homestake mine of Lead, South Dakota. It was there that he met MIT professor of physics Janet Conrad, becoming fascinated with the maelstrom of neutrino physics. Using his expertise in particle accelerators, he is currently helping Prof. Conrad develop a new generation of cyclotrons, primarily as neutrino sources (involving striking targets with megawatt proton beams), but with far-reaching applications in medical isotopes and so-called ADS* areas.

The DAEδALUS Collaboration that Prof. Conrad leads includes scientists, engineers and students from almost 50 institutions and laboratories in the U.S., Japan and Europe, and is a resourceful and dynamic group. Currently, plans are being developed for deployment of experiments at two deep underground sites—in mines in Japan and the U.S.—and this is only the beginning!

Jose comments, “This reconnection with MIT through Prof. Conrad’s research has been a marvelous experience, and it is with great pleasure that we are able to provide a gift that benefits the Physics Department in supporting graduate fellowships. We understand that fellowship support is a top need in the Department, allowing it to recruit the best students and give them flexibility in their first year. Carol and I owe so much to MIT for the formation of our professional careers, and this gift is a small token showing our appreciation.”

* Accelerator Driven Systems (ADS): use of high-energy, high-power beams for nuclear waste transmutation, driving of sub-critical thorium reactors, and other novel applications of particle accelerators in the field of nuclear power.

TITLE: AAU Participates in the PRICNAC Micro-Projects Kick-Off Meeting,  21-23 March 2022, Yaoundé Cameroon

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Partners of the project titled – the “Promotion of Research, Innovation and Digital Culture in Central Africa (PRICNAC)”, have organized a kick-off meeting for the implementation of five (5) micro-projects which were selected following a call for proposals launched in July 2021. Aside the Association of African Universities (AAU), the other project partners include the Agence universitaire de la Francophonie (AUF), OBREAL Global Observatory, African and Malagasy Council for Higher Education (CAMES), and the Network of Experts in Training Engineering of Central Africa and the Great Lakes (REIFAC). The highly successful kick-off meeting was hosted in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from March 21 to 23, 2022.

Before the effective start of the micro-project activities, the PRICNAC Project Consortium considered it necessary to organize a meeting to sensitize and train the project leaders on the financial and administrative management of the grant and to outline and discuss/clarify expectations of the Consortium members and the development partners (the project is funded by the African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) Group of States and the European Union under the ACP Innovation Fund). The overall objective of the meeting was to allow stakeholders to exchange information to ensure a smooth start and implementation of the micro-projects.

The meeting also offered the opportunity for the micro-projects teams to present the details and focus of their respective projects to the consortium and other participating stakeholders.

Through a competitive process, five (5) out of twelve (12) micro projects were selected for funding by PRICNAC. The five institutions involved in the selected micro-projects (two from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and three from Cameroon) are:

TITLE: International Physics Competition 2026: Join the Global Online Physics Challenge for Cash Prizes and Certificates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Submissions are open for the International Physics Competition 2026, also known as IPhyC 2026. Officially described as the “Education Program & Talent Search in Physics,” IPhyC is an international online initiative that allows participants to test their physics knowledge, strengthen their scientific reasoning and engage with problems extending beyond the conventional classroom curriculum.

The competition is conducted online, meaning participants can enter without travelling to another country or attending an in-person international event. It combines accessible introductory problems with advanced calculations, research-based questions and fast-paced assessments across three progressive rounds.

The Qualification Round is free to enter. Participants must download the official problem sheet, solve the questions and submit their work online by Sunday, 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0. Successful participants can progress to the Semi-Final and Final rounds, where they may compete for cash prizes, international honours, national awards and verifiable certificates.

What Is the International Physics Competition?

The International Physics Competition is an independent educational programme designed to make international physics challenges accessible through digital technology. It is coordinated by Edu.Harbour and brings together participants, teachers, schools and local representatives from different parts of the world.

Its purpose goes beyond ranking competitors. IPhyC aims to encourage curiosity about physics, introduce participants to unconventional problem formats and help them develop skills that can support future studies in science, technology, engineering and research.

According to the organizers, the programme is intended to supplement established national and international physics Olympiads rather than replace them. Its focus is broader accessibility, educational development and exposure to scientific research. Read more about IPhyC’s mission and structure.

Why Participate in IPhyC 2026?

IPhyC provides an opportunity to apply theoretical physics knowledge to diverse and unfamiliar problems. Participants are expected to combine calculations, logical reasoning, reading comprehension and scientific interpretation.

The principal features include:

A globally accessible online format.

The same problems for participants around the world.

Separate age and academic groups with adjusted qualifying scores.

A free Qualification Round.

Research-based problems connected to real scientific publications.

A structured pathway from an open Qualification Round to supervised examinations.

Participation certificates for all valid participants.

Cash prizes and special certificates for leading finalists.

National awards for strong performers from individual countries.

Online accounts through which participants can access results, performance reports and certificates.

Resources for teachers, schools and local physics groups.

An alumni network through which former participants may receive information about scholarships, sponsored events and other academic opportunities.

Academic Areas Covered by IPhyC

The competition can draw on a wide range of theoretical and applied physics subjects. The official website’s learning and preparation resources cover areas such as:

Astrophysics

Participants should not assume that every topic will appear in every round. Instead, they should prepare broadly and practise applying fundamental principles in unfamiliar contexts.

IPhyC is designed to develop several transferable academic skills:

Logical reasoning and creative problem-solving

Knowledge of physical laws, concepts and definitions

Mathematical calculation

Scientific reading comprehension

Analytical thinking

Application of theoretical knowledge

Time management

Adaptability to different question formats

Clear presentation of scientific solutions

The official IPhyC training and preparation page provides preparation advice, recommended reading and previous competition material.

How the International Physics Competition 2026 Works

The competition consists of three stages:

Qualification Round

Semi-Final Round

Final Round

Participants must achieve the prescribed score for their age group before progressing to the next stage.

Stage One: Qualification Round

The Qualification Round is the open-entry stage of IPhyC 2026. It contains five physics problems identified as Problems A, B, C, D and E.

The problems vary in subject, difficulty and format. Some primarily assess physics knowledge, while others require mathematical calculations, interpretation and structured reasoning.

Qualification Round scoring

Each of the five problems carries a maximum of five points, creating a total possible score of 25 points.

The minimum scores required to advance are:

Qualification Round deadline

The final submission deadline is:

Sunday, 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0

The organizers recommend submitting earlier to avoid last-minute internet, file-upload or website-related problems.

Submission format

Solutions may be:

Written by hand and uploaded as clear scanned images or photographs.

Digitally typeset solutions may receive a special honorary note on the participant’s certificate.

Qualification Round participation cost

Participants should receive the result by email. They can also log in to their participant accounts to access:

Qualified and registered participants will receive it through email and their participant accounts. Participants may use translation tools and artificial intelligence tools during the preparation period to help them understand the research paper.

However, these tools cannot be used to obtain assistance during the supervised examination itself.

Semi-Final examination period

The examination can be taken at any selected time during the following window:

Once started, the participant has 60 minutes to complete the examination. After the examination ends, a further 10 minutes is provided to scan and upload the written answers. This upload period remains supervised.

Supervision options

Participants have two supervision options.

Option One: Teacher supervision

Teacher supervision is recommended. The supervising teacher must:

Be employed by a government-accredited school or university;

Be an active teacher or professor rather than retired;

Not be related to the participant;

Register with IPhyC; and

Receive approval before supervising the examination.

The teacher must also document the examination conditions as required by the organizers.

Option Two: Online supervision

Participants without an eligible teacher may use IPhyC’s online supervision system. This requires:

A computer, laptop or phone with a webcam as the examination device;

A separate phone with a camera and microphone as the supervision device;

A valid government-issued identity card or passport;

A stable internet connection; and

An appropriate private examination environment.

Semi-Final registration cost

Qualified participants who choose to enter the Semi-Final Round must pay EUR 12. The general rules describe this payment as non-refundable.

The Semi-Final registration deadline is Tuesday, 8 December 2026.

Semi-Final results are expected on Monday, 28 December 2026. Complete information is available on the official 2026 Process and Rounds page.

Financial Aid for Semi-Finalists

IPhyC offers limited financial assistance for qualified participants who cannot afford the EUR 12 Semi-Final fee.

Two forms of assistance are available:

A 50% reduction in the registration fee; or

A complete fee waiver.

Financial aid is limited and depends on sponsorship funding. Receiving support is therefore not guaranteed.

Applicants must generally submit:

A written explanation of their financial circumstances; and

Evidence of household income, such as a salary slip, tax statement or official income certificate.

The financial-aid request deadline is Monday, 23 November 2026. Requests are assessed according to demonstrated financial need and the quality of the applicant’s Qualification Round work. Review the official financial-aid conditions.

Stage Three: Final Round

Participants who achieve the required Semi-Final score progress to the Final Round.

The Final Round is scheduled for:

Tuesday, 12 January 2027

The current 2026 information describes it as a digitally monitored online examination with approximately 30 questions. It takes around 30 minutes and may contain:

Multiple-choice questions;

Short-answer questions;

Questions connected to previous rounds;

Questions requiring knowledge from different branches of physics; and

Problems related to the Semi-Final research material.

Final rankings are determined primarily by performance in the Final Round. If two or more participants obtain the same Final Round score, Semi-Final and Qualification Round scores may be used as tie-breakers.

Final Round results are scheduled for Monday, 18 January 2027.

Local IPhyC representative’s name, if applicable.

The teacher’s email address and local representative selection are optional.

Participants must enter their names and dates of birth accurately because these details are used on certificates. The organizers may verify the ages of prize winners.

How to Enter the International Physics Competition 2026

Follow these steps:

Visit the official IPhyC website.

Download the 2026 Qualification Round problem sheet.

Review all five problems carefully.

Solve as many problems as possible and show the reasoning behind each answer.

Type the solutions or prepare clear scans of handwritten work.

Combine everything into one accepted file.

Ensure that the file is smaller than 10 MB.

Open the official submission form.

Enter the required personal and academic details accurately.

Upload the solution file.

Read and accept the competition rules and data policy.

Submit before 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.

Monitor the registered email address and participant account for confirmation and results.

Submissions are not accepted by email.

Collaboration, Academic Integrity and Cheating Rules

Every participant must submit an individual solution.

During the Qualification Round, participants may:

Work with classmates or friends to explore possible approaches;

Receive basic guidance from a teacher;

Consult books and online material for general definitions and scientific background; and

Discuss the underlying concepts.

They may not:

Copy another person’s exact solution;

Copy a completed solution from the internet;

Ask users on an online platform to solve the problems for them; or

Submit work that is not their own.

During the Semi-Final examination, participants cannot use external websites, books, notes or assistance from another person. A calculator is permitted in the Semi-Final Round, but artificial intelligence and translation tools are limited to understanding the research paper during the preparation period.

During the Final Round, calculators, external sources and assistance from others are prohibited. Only blank paper and a pencil may be used for notes.

Cheating, plagiarism, impersonation or the submission of falsified information can result in immediate disqualification and loss of any registration fee. Participants should read the complete IPhyC cheating policy before entering.

How to Prepare for IPhyC 2026

A strong preparation strategy should include the following:

1. Understand the three-round structure

The Qualification Round rewards complete reasoning and clear written solutions. The Semi-Final adds a supervised, time-limited research component, while the Final requires faster responses across different physics fields.

2. Review fundamental physics

Focus on essential principles in mechanics, electricity and magnetism, thermodynamics, optics, modern physics, fluids and related topics.

3. Practise presenting complete solutions

Do not provide only a numerical answer. Define the variables, identify the relevant physical law, show the calculations and state the final result clearly with the correct units.

4. Strengthen scientific reading skills

Practise reading research abstracts, identifying a paper’s main finding and connecting unfamiliar terminology to familiar physics principles.

5. Solve problems under time limits

Timed practice is particularly important for the supervised Semi-Final and fast-paced Final Round.

6. Learn from errors

After attempting a problem, compare the approach with an official or trusted solution. Identify whether the mistake came from conceptual understanding, algebra, units, interpretation or time management.

7. Use official preparation materials

Consult previous IPhyC problems, recommended textbooks and the resources available through the official training page.

Role of Teachers and Schools

Teachers are not required for the initial Qualification Round, but they can play a valuable role in sharing the competition, guiding students and supervising later stages.

Registered teachers may be able to:

View their students’ results and certificates;

Download teacher reports;

Pay Semi-Final fees for multiple students as a group;

Supervise Semi-Final examinations; and

Access educational materials.

IPhyC also offers honorary awards for teachers and schools with significant participation, strong student performance or notable contributions. These awards do not include cash payments.

Language and Global Accessibility

English is the original language of IPhyC. The website also provides translated interfaces in German, Arabic, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian, Russian, Portuguese, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean and Turkish.

The organizers indicate that non-English versions may contain automatic translations. Participants using a translated version should therefore compare any uncertain scientific wording with the original English material.

Because the competition is mainly online, no international travel is required. Participants should nevertheless ensure that they have reliable internet access and the necessary devices before any supervised examination.

Important Points to Remember

The Qualification Round is free, but the Semi-Final costs EUR 12.

Limited financial aid is available for eligible Semi-Finalists.

The Qualification Round deadline is 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.

One solution file must be uploaded in an accepted format.

The file must be under 10 MB.

The same problems are given to all age groups.

Older groups have higher qualifying thresholds.

Personal information must be entered accurately for certificates.

All entries are individual, even where limited Qualification Round discussion is allowed.

Applicants should rely on the official website for any timetable changes.

Conclusion

The International Physics Competition 2026 offers an accessible way to test physics knowledge in an international setting without the cost and logistical burden of travelling overseas. Its three-round structure combines open-ended problem-solving, engagement with scientific research and supervised online assessments.

Participants can earn internationally verifiable certificates, compete for cash prizes and national recognition, and develop practical skills in scientific reasoning, analytical thinking and research comprehension. Anyone planning to enter should download the Qualification Round problem sheet immediately, prepare a complete and clearly presented solution, and submit well before the official deadline of 1 November 2026 at 23:59 UTC+0.
