TITLE: PPG Research Fellowship 2026 in the USA | $50 Per Hour for Early-Career Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Partners for Public Good (PPG) is accepting applications for its 2026 Research Fellowship, a six-month, project-based opportunity for early-career researchers interested in improving government effectiveness through rigorous, policy-relevant research.

The fellowship is designed for researchers who want to contribute directly to research on public procurement, local government operations, technology, regulatory systems, infrastructure and government capacity.

Selected fellows will work remotely from within the United States for approximately 15 to 25 hours per week and will receive compensation of $50 per hour, with benefits as required by applicable state or local law.

The fellowship is expected to begin in October 2026, and applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis. The final application deadline is September 28, 2026, at close of business.

About the PPG Research Fellowship

The PPG Research Fellowship is a six-month programme that provides early-career researchers with dedicated time, mentorship and practical experience conducting research connected to government effectiveness.

Fellows will work on one of five predetermined high-priority research topics related to public procurement and local government operations.

Throughout the fellowship, participants will conduct policy-relevant background research, apply rigorous research methods to collect and analyse data, and collaborate with PPG staff and other fellows.

The programme is designed not only to generate useful research for governments but also to help fellows develop their own research portfolios through publications, policy briefs, datasets and other professional outputs.

About Partners for Public Good

Partners for Public Good (PPG) is a nonpartisan organisation that works alongside state and local governments to strengthen the operational systems that determine whether policies translate into results for residents.

Its work covers areas including:

Procurement

Staffing

Budgeting

Technology

Government operations

Applied research

Implementation

Rather than simply providing recommendations, PPG works directly with government staff during implementation and remains engaged until meaningful changes have been achieved.

Through its implementation work, applied research and Procurement Excellence Network, PPG shares knowledge and tools that can be applied across different jurisdictions.

The organisation’s Procurement Excellence Network includes more than 3,000 government professionals.

Why the Fellowship Focuses on Local Government

Local governments play a critical role in translating public policy into services and outcomes that residents experience every day.

Areas such as transportation, infrastructure, emergency services and school food depend on effective local government systems and operations.

However, there remains a need for more rigorous research examining how local governments manage procurement, budgeting, technology and staffing capacity, as well as how these operations are influenced by state and federal policies and regulations.

The PPG Research Fellowship aims to support a new generation of researchers who are interested in using evidence and research to improve government effectiveness.

The programme provides fellows with an opportunity to investigate practical government challenges while producing research that can contribute to broader discussions about public-sector reform.

Fellowship Structure

The fellowship lasts for six months.

Fellows will work on a defined research project under the guidance of PPG staff and alongside two other fellows.

The programme combines independent research with collaboration and professional development.

Participants will take part in activities such as:

Coaching calls

Research team meetings

Collaborative research activities

Professional development opportunities

Research discussions with PPG staff

Fellows will also receive support in translating their research into public-facing outputs, including draft publications and policy briefs.

Before the fellowship begins, PPG and each selected fellow will agree on:

Work hours

Project goals

Expected deliverables

Data access

Data use

Data rights

Data ownership

The work schedule is flexible within the agreed 15–25-hour-per-week commitment.

Five Research Topics

Applicants can express interest in one or two of the five research projects available through the fellowship.

1. Understanding Public Procurement Through Municipal Data

Public procurement is an important mechanism through which governments use public resources to provide services, infrastructure and other outcomes for residents.

However, procurement practices, systems and publicly available information can differ significantly from one jurisdiction to another.

This research project will examine publicly available information about local government procurement to develop a better understanding of procurement practices across U.S. cities.

The fellow will contribute to research designed to strengthen understanding of how governments purchase goods and services while identifying opportunities for further research and analysis.

2. The Compliance Web: Layered Governance and Local Implementation

Local governments operate within a complex system of federal, state and local laws, regulations, funding requirements and administrative procedures.

While these requirements can establish important protections and standards, they can also create administrative burdens, uncertainty and challenges for effective implementation.

This project will focus on one area, such as permitting, transit infrastructure or school food procurement, to examine how the complex “compliance web” affects local government operations and project delivery.

The research will explore where federal and state policies support or constrain local implementation and how policy design could better support effective government delivery.

3. Emerging Technology and Government Operations

State and local governments are increasingly exploring artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies to support internal operations and their workforce.

These technologies may also provide new ways to understand how public servants interact with government systems and processes.

This research project will explore what the use of AI and emerging technologies can reveal about government operations, organisational capacity and opportunities for improvement.

The fellow will contribute to developing and testing new approaches to studying how government work is performed.

4. Innovative Approaches to Public Purchasing

Governments have multiple tools and approaches available for purchasing goods and services.

Different purchasing approaches can involve different advantages, limitations and trade-offs.

This project will examine emerging procurement trends, with particular attention to cooperative purchasing.

The research will explore how and why different approaches are being used across jurisdictions and consider their implications for:

Government efficiency

Market participation

Public procurement systems

The broader procurement ecosystem

5. Building Local Capacity for Stormwater Management

Communities across the United States are exploring different ways to improve their ability to manage stormwater and respond to infrastructure and resilience needs.

Approaches vary depending on local circumstances, governance structures and state and federal policy environments.

This research project will examine how communities develop and finance stormwater management capacity.

Fellows will identify patterns across jurisdictions and generate insights that can inform future research and practical approaches to stormwater management.

Fellowship Deliverables

Each fellow will be expected to complete approximately two to three deliverables during the fellowship.

Depending on the research project, deliverables may include:

A topic-specific literature review

A dataset compiled from publicly available information and supporting documentation

A dataset developed through primary data collection

Survey or interview instruments

A draft research publication

A policy brief

A conference submission

These outputs can provide fellows with practical research experience while strengthening their professional and academic portfolios.

Fellowship Location and Working Hours

The fellowship is a remote opportunity.

The position can be undertaken from a flexible location within the United States, but fellows must have access to a major U.S. airport because the programme includes an in-person research retreat.

Fellows will work between 15 and 25 hours per week.

The exact working hours will be agreed upon between PPG and each selected fellow before the fellowship begins.

Fellowship Compensation

Selected fellows will be compensated at a rate of:

$50 per hour

The fellowship requires approximately 15–25 hours of work per week.

Benefits will be provided where required by applicable state or local law.

The compensation structure provides fellows with paid research experience while allowing them to maintain other academic or professional commitments within the requirements of the programme.

Who Can Apply?

The fellowship is intended for early-career researchers and professionals with relevant research or policy experience.

Potential applicants may include:

Graduate students

Postdoctoral researchers

Early-career faculty

Research staff

Policy staff

Researchers affiliated with universities

Researchers affiliated with think tanks

Researchers affiliated with nonprofits

Professionals with comparable research or policy experience

Applicants may maintain an affiliation with a university, think tank, nonprofit or other research or policy organisation during the fellowship, provided they can meet the required time commitments and deliverables.

Applicants who do not have an institutional affiliation are also welcome to apply.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit the following materials:

1. Resume or CV

Applicants must submit a resume or curriculum vitae of no more than two pages.

The document should clearly present the applicant’s relevant academic, research, professional and policy experience.

2. Letter of Interest

Applicants must submit a letter of interest addressing specific questions.

The letter should explain:

Which one or two research projects the applicant is interested in and why.

Why the applicant is qualified to undertake the selected project.

How the applicant would approach the proposed research.

Applicants interested in two projects may submit a letter of up to three pages and should clearly identify their first-choice project.

Applicants interested in only one project should follow the two-page limit.

3. Work Sample

Applicants must provide a work sample demonstrating their research skills and expertise.

The work sample may be:

A published research publication

A research publication under review

Another relevant research product

Applicants should select a work sample that provides strong evidence of their ability to conduct and communicate rigorous research.

Application Deadline

The final deadline to apply for the PPG Research Fellowship is:

September 28, 2026

PPG will review applications on a rolling basis.

All applications received by the close of business on September 28, 2026 will be considered.

Applicants are encouraged to submit their materials as early as possible because applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Expected Start Date

The desired start date for the fellowship is:

October 2026

Selected fellows will work with PPG before the start of the programme to establish expectations regarding working hours, research goals, deliverables and data-related matters.

Equal Employment Opportunity

Partners for Public Good is an equal opportunity employer.

The organisation states that all qualified applicants will receive consideration without regard to race, colour, religion, sex, national origin, disability status, protected veteran status or any other characteristic protected by law.

PPG is also committed to including qualified individuals with disabilities in its hiring process.

Applicants who require reasonable accommodation to participate in the application or interview process can contact the organisation through the contact information provided in the original application announcement.

How to Apply for the PPG Research Fellowship

Interested applicants should prepare all required materials before submitting their application.

The application process includes:

Review the five available research topics.

Select the one or two projects that best match your interests and experience.

Identify your first-choice project if applying for two.

Prepare a resume or CV of no more than two pages.

Prepare the required letter of interest.

Select an appropriate research work sample.

Review all application requirements carefully.

Submit the complete application before the September 28, 2026 deadline.

Conclusion

The PPG Research Fellowship 2026 offers early-career researchers an opportunity to gain practical experience conducting policy-relevant research focused on government effectiveness and local government operations.

Over six months, fellows will work alongside PPG staff and other researchers on one of five research topics covering public procurement, regulatory compliance, emerging technology, public purchasing and stormwater management.

The programme combines independent research, collaboration, mentorship and professional development, while giving participants opportunities to produce literature reviews, datasets, publications, policy briefs and conference submissions.

Selected fellows will work remotely for 15–25 hours per week and receive $50 per hour, with benefits as required by applicable law. The fellowship is expected to begin in October 2026.

Researchers interested in contributing to evidence-based improvements in government operations should consider preparing their application early. The final deadline is September 28, 2026.

TITLE: ACU Early Career Conference Grants 2026–27: Up to £2,000 for Early Career Researchers to Attend Conferences in Commonwealth Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) Early Career Conference Grants 2026–27 provide financial support for emerging researchers and academics who want to attend and actively participate in academic conferences in Commonwealth countries outside their country of work.

For early career academics, conferences can be an important part of building a successful research and teaching career. They provide opportunities to present research to an international audience, learn about new developments in a field, exchange ideas with other researchers, establish professional connections and bring new knowledge back to their universities.

Through the Early Career Conference Grants, the ACU is offering seven grants of up to GBP 2,000 each to eligible early career researchers and academics at ACU member universities.

The funding can contribute towards major costs associated with conference participation, including conference registration, international travel, accommodation, visa expenses and travel and health insurance.

Applications for the 2026–27 round open on 18 August 2026 and close on 13 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC.

Overview of the ACU Early Career Conference Grants

The Early Career Conference Grants are designed to help emerging academics gain valuable international conference experience.

Attending an academic conference is more than simply travelling to an event. For researchers who are still establishing themselves in their academic careers, a conference can provide an opportunity to:

Present research findings to other academics and specialists.

Receive feedback on research ideas and findings.

Discover the latest developments in their area of research.

Develop international professional networks.

Identify potential research collaborators.

Learn from established academics and researchers.

Exchange knowledge and ideas with colleagues from other institutions.

Strengthen their academic profile.

Bring new knowledge and perspectives back to their home university.

Improve teaching and research through exposure to current developments in their discipline.

The ACU states that conference participation can have a significant impact on both emerging academics and the universities that employ them.

What Is the Association of Commonwealth Universities?

The Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) is an international network of universities across the Commonwealth. Its programmes and funding opportunities support collaboration, professional development, research and knowledge exchange among universities and academics.

The Early Career Conference Grants form part of this broader effort to support emerging researchers and enable academic communities to benefit from international exchange.

What Funding Is Available?

For the 2026–27 funding round, seven grants are available, with each grant providing a maximum of:

GBP 2,000 per awardee

The grant can be used to help cover eligible expenses connected with attending and participating in the proposed conference.

Eligible costs include:

Conference registration feeFunding can contribute towards the cost of registering for the conference.

FlightsThe grant can be used towards flight costs associated with travelling to the conference.

AccommodationAwardees can use the funding to help cover accommodation expenses during the conference trip.

Visa costsWhere a visa is required for travel to the conference country, visa expenses can be covered by the grant.

Travel and health insuranceFunding can also contribute towards travel and health insurance associated with the conference trip.

Applicants should carefully review the official application guidance and FAQs for further information about eligible expenses and funding conditions before submitting an application.

Who Can Apply for the Early Career Conference Grant?

The grant is specifically intended for early career researchers and academics at ACU member universities.

Applicants must satisfy the eligibility requirements established for the programme.

1. Applicants must be early career researchers or academics

An applicant must be an early career researcher or academic working at an ACU member university.

For the purposes of this grant, early career researchers and academics are generally defined as those who are within seven years of the start of their academic research or teaching career.

This means that applicants should consider when they began their academic research or teaching career when determining whether they fall within the seven-year early career period.

2. Career breaks may be considered

The seven-year criterion does not necessarily exclude applicants who have experienced a career break.

The ACU recognises that researchers and academics may take time away from employment for personal or professional reasons.

Examples of career breaks can include periods away from employment to:

Care for children.

Address personal circumstances.

Take time away from academic employment for professional reasons.

Deal with other circumstances that result in a temporary period away from employment.

Applicants who have experienced a career break should review the official guidance to determine how their circumstances affect their eligibility.

Applicants Must Identify a Suitable Conference

Applicants must identify a conference that they would like to attend as part of their application.

The proposed conference must satisfy important requirements.

The conference must take place in a Commonwealth country

The conference must be held in a Commonwealth country.

In addition, the conference must take place outside the applicant’s country of work.

This requirement makes the grant particularly valuable for academics seeking international exposure and opportunities to engage with researchers in other Commonwealth countries.

Conference dates

The proposed conference must take place between:

February 2027 and January 2028

Applicants should therefore identify a suitable conference falling within this period before submitting their application.

Applicants Must Actively Participate in the Conference

Simply attending a conference is not sufficient for this grant.

Applicants must have an active role in the proposed conference.

They must be doing at least one of the following:

Chairing a session

Presenting a paper

Presenting a poster

This requirement means applicants should already have identified an appropriate opportunity to contribute academically to the conference.

Researchers should therefore consider conferences that are directly relevant to their research interests and where they can demonstrate an active contribution.

Why Conference Participation Matters for Early Career Researchers

Academic conferences can be particularly valuable during the early stages of a research career.

For researchers who are still developing their academic networks and professional reputation, presenting at an international conference can create opportunities that may not be available through their normal university environment.

Conference participation can help early career academics to:

Share research

Presenting a paper or poster allows researchers to communicate their findings to academics working in related areas.

The feedback received during conference discussions can also help researchers identify strengths, weaknesses and potential improvements in their research.

Learn about new developments

Academic disciplines continuously evolve. Conferences bring together researchers who are working on current issues and emerging areas of research.

Participation can therefore help early career researchers remain informed about developments in their field.

Build professional networks

Meeting academics from other universities and countries can help researchers establish professional relationships that may continue after the conference.

These connections can potentially lead to research collaboration, knowledge exchange and other academic opportunities.

Strengthen research and teaching

Knowledge acquired through conference participation can be shared with colleagues and students at the researcher’s home university.

The benefits of the grant can therefore extend beyond the individual awardee and contribute to the wider academic community.

Important Ineligibility Conditions

Although the grant is intended to support international conference participation, there are important restrictions that applicants must understand.

Applicants must not have previously travelled outside their region of employment for work purposes

Applicants cannot have previously travelled outside their region of employment for work purposes, including conferences, since the start of their academic career.

This is an important eligibility requirement.

Applicants who have already travelled internationally for work or conference purposes during their academic career should carefully check the ACU’s definition of the relevant employment region and the application guidance before applying.

Previous ACU grant recipients cannot apply

Applicants who have previously received an ACU Early Career Conference Grant are not eligible to receive another award under this programme.

The programme was previously known as the Early Career Academic Grants, so previous recipients of the earlier version of the grant are also excluded.

Application Requirements

Before applying, prospective applicants should ensure they have identified an appropriate conference and understand the programme requirements.

Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate that:

They are an early career researcher or academic.

They work at an ACU member university.

Their academic career falls within the applicable seven-year period, taking eligible career breaks into consideration.

They have identified a suitable conference.

The conference is taking place in a Commonwealth country.

The conference is outside their country of work.

The conference will take place between February 2027 and January 2028.

They will actively participate by chairing a session, presenting a paper or presenting a poster.

They meet the ACU’s requirements concerning previous international work travel.

They have not previously received an ACU Early Career Conference Grant or its previous Early Career Academic Grant equivalent.

How to Apply for the ACU Early Career Conference Grant

Applications are submitted online through the ACU application system.

APPLY HERE

Applicants can also visit the official website HERE

Applicants should first review the official application guidance and frequently asked questions before completing the application.

Applicants with an existing MyACU account

If you already have a MyACU account, you can access the application form through the ACU’s online grant application system.

Applicants without a MyACU account

Applicants who do not already have a MyACU account must first register for an account.

After registering, applicants should follow the instructions contained in the registration email to log into the system and access the application form.

Applicants should ensure that they provide accurate information and carefully follow the application instructions.

Application Timeline

The application period for the 2026–27 Early Career Conference Grants is:

Applications open: 18 August 2026

Applications close: 13 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC

Applicants are strongly encouraged to begin preparing early rather than waiting until the final day.

This is particularly important because applicants need to identify an appropriate conference and demonstrate that they will actively participate through a presentation, poster or session chairing role.

Conference Period

The conference proposed in the application must take place between:

February 2027 and January 2028

Applicants should therefore look for conferences whose dates fall within this specified period.

Grant Conditions After Selection

Successful applicants will have responsibilities after receiving the grant.

All awardees are required to complete a report after completion of their award.

This reporting requirement means recipients should retain relevant information and documentation associated with their funded conference participation and be prepared to report on their experience and use of the award.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although meeting the eligibility criteria is essential, applicants can also take practical steps to make their applications clear and well prepared.

1. Choose a conference closely connected to your research

Select a conference that is directly relevant to your research or academic work.

A strong connection between your research and the conference can help demonstrate why participation would be valuable.

2. Confirm your participation role

Do not select a conference simply because it is interesting.

The programme requires applicants to actively participate by:

Chairing a session;

Presenting a paper; or

Presenting a poster.

Applicants should therefore have a clear understanding of their intended role.

3. Check the conference location

Confirm that the conference is being held in a Commonwealth country outside your country of work.

This is one of the central requirements of the grant.

4. Check the conference dates

Make sure the conference takes place between February 2027 and January 2028.

5. Confirm your university’s ACU membership

Before investing significant time in the application, verify that your university is an ACU member university.

6. Review the eligibility restrictions carefully

Applicants should pay particular attention to the rules concerning previous international work-related travel and previous receipt of an ACU Early Career Conference Grant.

7. Prepare early

Because applications close at a specific UTC time, applicants should avoid submitting at the last minute.

Early preparation also gives applicants time to review their information, confirm conference details and resolve any account or application issues.

Benefits of the Early Career Conference Grant

The ACU Early Career Conference Grant can provide several important benefits to emerging academics.

Financial support

The grant provides up to GBP 2,000, helping reduce the financial barriers associated with international conference participation.

International academic exposure

Participating in a conference in another Commonwealth country can expose researchers to different academic communities, approaches and research perspectives.

Research presentation experience

Applicants can gain experience presenting their research through papers or posters or by chairing academic sessions.

Professional networking

International conferences provide opportunities to meet academics, researchers and potential collaborators from different institutions.

Knowledge exchange

Awardees can bring knowledge gained at the conference back to their universities and share it with colleagues and students.

Career development

Conference participation can contribute to the professional development of early career researchers by increasing their exposure to the wider academic community.

Final Thoughts

The ACU Early Career Conference Grants 2026–27 represent a valuable opportunity for emerging researchers and academics to gain international conference experience without having to personally cover all of the associated travel and participation costs.

With seven grants of up to GBP 2,000, successful applicants can receive financial support for conference registration, flights, accommodation, visa expenses, and travel and health insurance.

More importantly, the programme can help early career academics share their research, learn about developments in their disciplines, establish professional networks and bring new knowledge back to their universities.

The applicant must be an early career researcher or academic at an ACU member university, the conference must be in a Commonwealth country outside the applicant’s country of work, and the applicant must actively participate by chairing a session, presenting a paper or presenting a poster.

TITLE: Strengthening Quality Assurance  in Higher and Tertiary Education – The Association of African Universities builds  capacity of African Higher Education institutions in Online Teaching and Learning in the post COVID-Era

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Quality Assurance in Higher and Tertiary Education: Online Teaching and Learning (OTL) in the post COVID- Era Workshop was a four-day capacity building event hosted by the Association of African Universities in Accra, Ghana.

This face-to-face workshop, held from the 28th – 30th of March 2022 , covered broad topical areas which included the online teaching and learning delivery space and landscape; quality assurance issues and standards, strategies for online teaching and learning management as well as delivery technologies in higher education institutions. Other content areas covered included student assessment systems & protocols.

A total of eleven (11) top leadership personnel from Higher Education Institutions in Ghana, Nigeria and Zimbabwe participated in this training session. In her welcoming remarks, Dr. Violet Makuku, the Workshops Coordinator and Quality Assurance Specialist at the AAU, commended the participants as well as the institutions that funded and facilitated their participation for their efforts to attend the workshop. The AAU’s Director of Research and Programmes, Prof Damtew Teferra, who gave the opening remarks for this workshop encouraged participants to network and actively engage in the discussions and key issues during the sessions.

The facilitators for this important capacity building event were – Dr Violet Makuku (AAU), Mr. Abednego Corletey (Senior IT Officer, AAU), Prof. Clement Dzidonu (the President of the Accra Institute of Technology, Ghana) and Mr. Christopher Addo (Kwame Nkrumah University of Science & Technology, Kumasi, Ghana).

In an interactive session, the participants discussed key concerns and challenges related to quality assurance and online teaching and learning in the post COVID-19 pandemic era. Possible solutions in response to the identified challenges were mapped out by all present, with guidance from the facilitators.

Key Challenges Affecting the Attainment of Quality Online Teaching and Learning

One of the major issues identified during the discussions was related to the lack of attitudinal change in moving from the traditional ways of teaching (face-to face teaching in a classroom environment) to the full adoption and support of online teaching and learning. In addition, the lack of specific ICT and digital skills as well as the insufficient knowledge of the different tools, platforms and software and how they are used by both students and lecturers was also another issue of concern.

The other identified challenges were related to the inadequate and/or lack of financial support to establish and maintain technological infrastructure and facilities and to support the implementation processes, human and other resources that are needed in the execution of the online teaching and learning. Government and other sources of higher education funding , generally continue to dwindle.

Furthermore, institutionalization and effective implementation of policies that enable OTL, coupled with the unstable Internet access and erratic power (electricity) supply in many African countries continue to be key challenges. All these tend to have a negative impact on the quality of OTL in African Higher Education Institutions.

The Way Forward – Proposals for Addressing the Challenges

In addressing the challenge of attitudinal change, the workshop delegates proposed a focus on awareness creation and continuous demonstration of the benefits of OTL to institutions. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) could institute benefits such as additional points for promotion, certificates, commendation letters and the recognition of individuals and departments/units that promote and adopt the OTL tenets .

Institutions were encouraged to adopt the blended approach as opposed to heavy reliance on the face -to- face mode of teaching and learning because of the 4th Industrial Revolution which led to the automation of the industry where graduates would go to work. OTL would help them to acquire the requisite skills for university graduates to work in digitalized workspaces. Capacity building of both faculty and students was suggested as a response to solving the skills and knowledge gaps. A proposal that the Vice-Chancellors of African universities should advocate and strategically engage governments to prioritize its investment and funding to HEIs was also brought forward. African Universities were encouraged to expand their funding sources and also explore partnerships with industry and other HEIs to leverage existing digital/OTL infrastructure, among others.

Continuous engagement of institutional heads to enforce OTL policies and awareness creation on those policies among faculty and students were also identified as being key. Finally, regarding the challenge of erratic power supply and unstable Internet access, the AAU encouraged HEIs to engage their respective governments to operationalize their national development plans, as most of these plans have components related to improving such infrastructure.

Wrapping up the Capacity Building Workshop

The key messages from all the facilitators and participants were that the workshop was forward looking and timely in bridging the gap between the pre-and post-COVID-19 pandemic eras. They all agreed that Online Teaching and Learning had come to stay with or without the pandemic because no one could tell when other disasters that would disable the face to face teaching and learning would happen. It was also observed that OTL could increase access of schooling by the disadvantaged communities and differently abled people. Therefore, its significance could not be over-emphasized.

The participants felt that the workshop content and delivery were excellent because they addressed current topical issues in Online Teaching and Learning in universities. They suggested the repetition of the workshop for policy and decision makers in higher education with an extra day for real practical experiences and engagement of participants. Such participants should include university leaders, quality assurance (QA) managers, quality assurance agencies and accreditation agencies, ministers of education, information and communication, finance and other relevant ministries.

Bringing the 4-day training to an end, the AAU Secretary General, Prof. Olusola Oyewole encouraged institutions of higher learning and African governments to prioritize investments in ICT infrastructure and Internet services to facilitate successful digitalization processes. Certificates of participation were issued to all participants at the end of the workshop.

TITLE: James Kane Foundation Grants 2026: Up to £400,000 Annual Funding for Education, STEM and Employment Pathways in Northern Ireland

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The James Kane Foundation has opened its 2026 Expression of Interest process for organisations seeking funding for projects that improve access to education, STEM opportunities, career development, work experience, training and pathways into employment across Northern Ireland.

Established in 2016 through the legacy of the late James “Jim” Walker Kane, owner of JW Kane Precision Engineering Limited, the Foundation supports initiatives designed to help people develop the education, skills, competencies and career opportunities needed to progress into employment, further study or professional life.

For the 2026 funding round, the Foundation expects to allocate approximately:

£400,000 per year

across its grantmaking programme.

Funding may include both:

Large grants

Small grants below £25,000

The Foundation indicates that approximately:

75% of its annual budget will be allocated to large grants

25% will be allocated to small grants of under £25,000

Multi-year funding may also be considered.

The current application process begins with a mandatory Expression of Interest, commonly referred to as an EOI. Organisations whose EOIs are assessed positively may then be invited to submit a full application during Stage 2.

The deadline for the 2026 Expression of Interest round is:

Friday, 16 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Applicants should note carefully that the closing time is midday, not midnight.

Projects funded through this round will normally be expected to commence from:

June 2027

The Foundation particularly welcomes projects aligned with two priority themes:

Enabling STEM-related education and career opportunities

Helping students make informed choices between employment, career and higher-level education pathways

Applications are open to eligible organisations including:

Schools

Colleges

Third-level institutions

Employers

Private-sector companies

Charities

Social enterprises

Priority may be given to projects benefiting people living in the Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon Council areas, although the Foundation’s broader area of benefit extends across Northern Ireland.

About the James Kane Foundation

The James Kane Foundation was established in 2016.

Its funding comes from the legacy of the late James Walker Kane, also known as Jim Kane, who owned JW Kane Precision Engineering Limited.

The Foundation was created with a strong connection to:

Education

Skills

Employment

Engineering

Career development

Training

Economic opportunity

Its charitable objects focus on advancing education for public benefit, particularly in Portadown and surrounding areas, while also allowing support for projects elsewhere in Northern Ireland.

The Foundation may support people and organisations through activities connected with:

Work experience

Employment opportunities

Training

Career preparation

Skills development

Professional development

Preparation for entry into occupations, trades or professions

However, the Foundation does not intend to replace funding for services that schools, colleges, government bodies or other public authorities already have a legal obligation to provide.

Who Governs the James Kane Foundation?

The Foundation is governed by a:

Board of Trustees

with experience across:

Business

Education

The Trustees collectively make decisions concerning:

Grant awards

Funding priorities

Project support

Strategic direction

The Foundation is administered by:

Belfast Charitable Society

which supports the Trustees in delivering the Foundation’s aims and charitable objectives.

This governance structure means applicants should prepare proposals that are not only socially valuable but also:

Clearly structured

Financially credible

Educationally relevant

Deliverable

Capable of demonstrating measurable outcomes

Purpose of the 2026 Funding Round

The Foundation’s core mission is to:

Progress and facilitate education and career opportunities.

Projects seeking support must clearly demonstrate how they contribute to this mission.

Applications that fall outside education, career development, STEM access or transitions into employment are unlikely to be competitive.

The Foundation has identified two principal themes for eligible projects.

Theme 1: Enabling STEM-Related Education and Career Opportunities

The first funding theme focuses on improving access to opportunities connected with:

Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics

or:

STEM

Projects under this theme may seek to help participants:

Discover STEM careers

Develop technical skills

Gain practical experience

Engage with employers

Access engineering opportunities

Understand pathways into STEM education

Build confidence in science and technology

Prepare for technical employment

Access skills training

Participate in work experience

The Foundation’s origins in the legacy of a precision engineering business make STEM and employment development particularly relevant to its charitable objectives.

What Could a STEM Project Look Like?

The Foundation does not provide an exhaustive list of eligible activities, but qualifying projects might potentially include initiatives such as:

Engineering outreach

STEM career programmes

Employer engagement

Robotics programmes

Coding opportunities

Technology workshops

Practical engineering experience

STEM mentoring

Career fairs

Skills development programmes

STEM-related work placements

Technical training

The important consideration is not simply whether a project uses the label “STEM.”

Applicants need to show how their activity creates additional and meaningful education or career opportunities.

Theme 2: Helping Students Make Informed Education and Career Choices

The second priority theme concerns helping students make informed decisions between:

Employment

Career pathways

Higher-level education

Many young people face uncertainty when deciding what to do after:

School

College

Training

Further education

The Foundation is interested in projects that help students better understand the options available to them.

This could include initiatives helping participants understand:

University pathways

Apprenticeships

Vocational training

Employment opportunities

Professional careers

Technical careers

Further education

Skills requirements

Why Career Decision-Making Matters

Students may have limited information about:

Different industries

Entry requirements

Apprenticeships

Career progression

Workplace expectations

Alternative pathways to university

Good career guidance can help individuals make choices aligned with their:

Skills

Interests

Strengths

Ambitions

Financial circumstances

Projects under this theme should therefore demonstrate how they improve the quality of information, experience or support available to learners.

Additionality Is a Key Requirement

The James Kane Foundation specifically states that it seeks:

Additionality

in the projects it funds.

This means funding should create something additional to what is already available.

Applicants should demonstrate clearly:

What currently exists

What gap remains

What the proposed project adds

Why Foundation funding is necessary

A project that simply continues standard activity without adding something new may be less competitive.

What Additionality Could Mean

Additionality may involve:

Reaching a new group of participants

Expanding access to an existing opportunity

Introducing an innovative programme

Creating a new employer partnership

Developing a new training pathway

Providing an opportunity not previously available

Testing a new model

Bringing STEM resources to underserved communities

Applicants should explain additionality directly rather than expecting Trustees to infer it.

Projects the Foundation Will Not Fund

The Foundation states that it will not support activities that Trustees believe are the responsibility of:

Local authorities

Government

Public bodies with statutory obligations

This means funding cannot simply substitute for services that should already be delivered through public funding.

The Foundation will also avoid funding projects that:

Duplicate existing provision.

Applicants therefore need to research existing services and demonstrate that their project fills a genuine gap.

Avoiding Duplication

A strong application should explain:

What similar services currently exist

How the proposed activity differs

Which participants are currently underserved

Why another service is necessary

Whether the project complements rather than duplicates other organisations

This is particularly important in areas where several organisations are already delivering similar education or employment programmes.

Geographic Priority: Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon

The Foundation may give particular priority to projects benefiting people in the:

Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon Council areas.

This geographic priority reflects the Foundation’s historical connection to:

Portadown

Surrounding communities

However, the Foundation’s objects allow activity elsewhere in:

Northern Ireland

Projects outside the priority council area may therefore still be eligible where they fit the wider mission and criteria.

Approximately £400,000 Available Annually

The James Kane Foundation intends to allocate approximately:

£400,000 per year

through its grantmaking.

This does not mean a single organisation can apply for £400,000.

Rather, this is the approximate total annual funding envelope available across funded projects.

Applicants should request only what is justified by:

Project scope

Delivery plan

Outputs

Outcomes

Budget

Large and Small Grants

The Foundation plans to divide its annual budget broadly as follows:

Large Grants

Approximately:

75% of the annual budget

will be allocated to larger grants.

The information provided does not specify a single maximum amount for a large grant.

Applicants considering a substantial request should therefore review the detailed guidance carefully rather than assuming a particular upper limit.

Small Grants

Approximately:

25% of the budget

will be allocated to:

Small grants below £25,000

This makes the programme potentially suitable for both:

Smaller pilot projects

Larger strategic initiatives

Multi-Year Funding Is Possible

The Foundation states that it will consider:

Multi-year funding

This can be valuable for projects requiring more than one year to:

Develop

Recruit participants

Deliver training

Measure outcomes

Establish partnerships

However, multi-year funding should not be assumed automatically.

Applicants should provide a clear case for why several years of funding are necessary.

When Can Projects Begin?

Projects supported through the current round will normally be funded only if they commence from:

June 2027

Applicants should therefore plan:

Recruitment

Staffing

Procurement

Partnerships

Programme delivery

around the expected funding commencement date.

Projects requiring funding significantly before June 2027 may not align with the Foundation’s normal timetable.

Match Funding Is Allowed

The James Kane Foundation allows its grants to be combined with:

Match funding

Other secured funding sources

This means applicants do not necessarily need the Foundation to finance the entire project.

Indeed, applications that can demonstrate:

Secured match funding

may be viewed more favourably.

Why Match Funding Can Strengthen an Application

Match funding can demonstrate:

Wider confidence in the project

Shared commitment

Financial sustainability

Partnership

Lower dependence on one funder

Stronger leverage of Foundation resources

Applicants should clearly state:

How much match funding has been secured

Who is providing it

What costs it will cover

Whether it is confirmed or pending

Do not describe unconfirmed funding as secured.

Partnership Funding Is Encouraged

The Foundation states that it is willing to work with:

Other organisations

Other funders

where collaboration can:

Maximise impact

Increase resources

Improve project delivery

This may be particularly useful for larger education or STEM initiatives involving:

Schools

Universities

Employers

Charities

Industry bodies

Community organisations

Eligible Project Costs

The Foundation may support several types of direct project costs.

These can include:

Project Costs

Funding may support costs directly required to deliver the proposed programme.

Salary Costs

The Foundation may support salary costs where they are clearly connected to the project.

This could include staff required specifically for:

Project coordination

Training

Delivery

Participant support

Equipment Costs

Equipment may also be eligible where it is clearly required for project delivery.

For STEM programmes, this could be particularly relevant where projects need technical equipment.

Funding Requests Must Be Clearly Connected to Outcomes

Every cost should be linked to:

Project activities

Outputs

Outcomes

Applicants should avoid submitting broad or poorly justified budgets.

For example, instead of requesting a generic equipment budget, explain:

What equipment is required

Who will use it

Why it is necessary

What educational outcome it enables

Overhead and Indirect Costs Are Normally Not Funded

The Foundation generally does not seek to fund:

General overheads

Indirect organisational costs

because its priority is supporting:

New and/or innovative projects

that directly align with its mission.

Applicants should therefore avoid including large general administrative charges unless there is a compelling project-specific justification.

Organisational Reserves May Be Reviewed

The Foundation may request further information concerning:

Organisational reserves

Applicants should therefore be prepared to explain:

Current reserves

Financial position

Why Foundation support is necessary

This helps Trustees understand whether the requested funding represents appropriate use of philanthropic resources.

Who Can Apply?

The James Kane Foundation accepts applications from several categories of organisations.

Eligible applicants include:

Education Bodies

Such as:

Schools

Colleges

Third-level institutions

Employers

Including:

Private-sector companies

Charities

Eligible charitable organisations may apply where the project aligns with the mission and themes.

Social Enterprises

Social enterprises can also apply if they meet the programme requirements.

Can Individuals Apply?

The information provided describes eligible applicants as organisations rather than individuals.

It does not list:

Individual students

Individual researchers

Individual jobseekers

as direct applicants.

The funding is therefore primarily designed to support organisations delivering projects for beneficiaries.

Individuals may benefit from funded projects but are not identified as direct applicants under the published eligibility categories.

One Application Per Organisation

The Foundation will consider:

Only one application per organisation in each grant round.

This is an important restriction.

Organisations with multiple possible projects should decide internally which application represents their strongest fit with the Foundation’s priorities.

Submitting several applications from different departments of the same organisation may not be accepted.

Can an Organisation Receive Funding More Than Once?

Yes.

The Foundation may fund the same organisation more than once over time.

However:

It will not provide multiple awards to the same organisation within the same funding cycle.

Future applications from previous grantees are considered on a:

Case-by-case basis

and are usually dependent on satisfactory performance against previous:

Outputs

Outcomes

Organisations that have previously received funding should therefore be prepared to demonstrate the impact of earlier awards.

The Application Process

The James Kane Foundation uses a:

Two-stage application process

consisting of:

Expression of Interest

Full Application

The purpose of the two-stage structure is to allow the Foundation to assess project fit before asking applicants to prepare a more detailed full submission.

Stage 1: Expression of Interest

The first stage is the:

Expression of Interest

or:

EOI

This allows applicants to present:

Their project concept

Relevant organisational information

Supporting evidence

The EOI is therefore an important screening stage.

Applicants should not treat it as an informal preliminary note.

Expression of Interest Form Requirements

The Foundation has strict formatting instructions.

Applications must be completed using the official forms provided.

They must be submitted in:

Microsoft Word format

Applicants must:

Leave the form formatting unchanged

Not add photographs

Not add images

Not insert extra text boxes

Applications submitted:

In another format

With altered formatting

will not be accepted.

Word Limits Must Be Followed

Many questions in the EOI form include:

Maximum word counts

Applicants must not exceed these limits.

Information provided beyond the stated limit may:

Be treated as ineligible

Not be considered

This means applicants should write strategically.

Prioritize:

Need

Project design

Outcomes

Fit

Evidence

rather than lengthy background information.

No Unrequested Additional Documents

Applicants cannot attach additional supporting papers unless the Foundation specifically requests them.

Do not attempt to strengthen an application by sending:

Extra brochures

Large reports

Promotional materials

Unrequested case studies

The application should stand on the evidence permitted within the formal process.

Required Supporting Documents

The EOI form sets out the supporting documentation required at Stage 1.

Applicants must submit:

All requested information

for the EOI to be accepted.

Incomplete submissions will:

Not be assessed and will be rejected.

Applicants should therefore use a checklist before sending their application.

Data Sharing and Due Diligence

The Foundation notes that information supplied through the application process may be shared with:

Other funders

Government departments

Agencies

for purposes such as:

Audit

Research

Statutory obligations

Crime prevention

Crime detection

Applicants should therefore ensure all information submitted is:

Accurate

Complete

Verifiable

Stage 2: Full Application

EOIs undergo assessment after the October deadline.

Applications will either:

Be rejected, or

Proceed to Stage 2

Only successful Stage 1 applicants will move to:

The Full Application stage

This means applicants should not prepare a complete second-stage application unless invited.

When Will EOI Applicants Hear Back?

The Foundation expects applicants to be notified approximately:

8–10 weeks after the Expression of Interest deadline

Given the deadline of October 16, applicants should therefore expect initial decisions later in 2026.

No Appeal Process

The James Kane Foundation’s funding decisions are:

Final

There is:

No right of appeal

Applicants should therefore ensure their EOI is as complete and persuasive as possible at the time of submission.

No Feedback Will Be Provided

The Foundation states that:

Feedback will not be provided

to unsuccessful applicants.

Because of this, organisations should carefully self-assess against the eligibility criteria before applying.

Expression of Interest Deadline

The deadline is:

Friday, 16 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Applicants should not assume that the form can be submitted at the end of the business day.

The deadline is specifically:

12 PM

rather than 5 PM or midnight.

Submitting at least a day early is advisable.

Download the 2026 EOI Guidance

Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the full guidance before preparing their submission.

2026 EOI Guidance

The guidance should be reviewed carefully for:

Eligibility

Funding priorities

Application questions

Supporting documents

Assessment requirements

Download the Expression of Interest Form

The official 2026 EOI form

Applicants must use this form and preserve its original formatting.

Key Dates at a Glance

EOI forms available: 2026

EOI deadline: Friday, 16 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

EOI decision: Approximately 8–10 weeks after the deadline

Stage 2: By invitation

Normal project funding commencement: June 2027

Funding at a Glance

Foundation: James Kane Foundation

Approximate annual grant budget: £400,000

Large grants: Approximately 75% of the annual funding budget

Small grants: Approximately 25% of the annual budget

Small grant threshold: Under £25,000

Multi-year funding: May be considered

Match funding: Permitted and potentially advantageous

Eligible project costs: Project costs, salary costs and equipment costs where clearly related to the project

General overheads: Normally not funded

How to Prepare a Strong James Kane Foundation EOI

1. Start With the Foundation’s Mission

Your application should clearly demonstrate how the project will:

Progress and facilitate education and career opportunities.

Do not make the connection vague.

State directly what educational or employment outcome the project will create.

2. Align Clearly With One or Both Themes

Identify whether the project fits:

STEM education and careers

Education/employment decision-making

or both.

Do not submit a general youth programme and assume the Foundation will identify the connection.

3. Demonstrate Additionality

Explain:

What currently exists

What is missing

What your programme adds

Why it cannot be delivered through existing provision

This is one of the Foundation’s explicit priorities.

4. Avoid Statutory Activity

Do not apply for services that schools, government or local authorities are already required to provide.

The Foundation wants philanthropic funding to create:

Additional opportunities

rather than replace statutory provision.

5. Demonstrate Need

Use evidence to show:

Who needs the project

What barrier exists

How many people are affected

Why the issue matters

Evidence can make the difference between a general idea and a credible project proposal.

6. Define Outputs

Outputs describe what the project will deliver.

For example:

Number of workshops

Number of participants

Number of placements

Number of mentoring relationships

Number of employer sessions

These should be realistic and measurable.

7. Define Outcomes

Outcomes describe the change created.

Examples might include:

Improved STEM confidence

Increased career awareness

Improved technical skills

More students entering apprenticeships

Better understanding of higher education pathways

Increased employment readiness

Trustees will want to understand what changes because of the grant.

8. Explain Why Your Organisation Is Well Placed to Deliver

Applicants should demonstrate organisational capacity.

This may include:

Relevant experience

Staff expertise

Partnerships

Existing relationships with schools

Employer networks

Previous programme outcomes

9. Use Match Funding Strategically

If match funding has already been secured, state it clearly.

The Foundation says confirmed match funding may be viewed more favourably.

Explain:

Funding source

Amount

Confirmation status

How it complements the Foundation request

10. Follow the Form Instructions Exactly

Technical compliance matters.

Do not:

Alter the form

Add photographs

Add text boxes

Exceed word limits

Submit unrequested documents

Even a strong project can be rejected if the application does not comply with formal requirements.

Important Details at a Glance

Organisation: James Kane Foundation

Funding round: 2026

Primary location: Northern Ireland

Priority geography: Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon

Funding focus: Education and career opportunities

Theme 1: STEM-related education and career opportunities

Theme 2: Supporting informed decisions between employment/career and higher-level education

Eligible applicants: Education bodies, employers, charities and social enterprises

Approximate annual funding: £400,000

Small grants: Under £25,000

Multi-year funding: Possible

Application process: Two stages

Stage 1: Expression of Interest

Stage 2: Full application by invitation

EOI deadline: 16 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Normal funded project start: June 2027

EOI Form:
https://jameskanefoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/JKF-Expression-of-Interest-2026.docx

Guidance:
https://jameskanefoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/JKF-EOI-Guidelines-2026.pdf

Main information:
https://lnkd.in/eWWsuMfC

Conclusion

The James Kane Foundation 2026 grant round offers an important funding opportunity for eligible organisations delivering education, STEM and career-development projects across Northern Ireland.

The Foundation expects to allocate approximately £400,000 per year, with around 75% directed toward larger grants and 25% toward grants below £25,000. Multi-year funding may also be considered.

Applications should support the Foundation’s mission of progressing and facilitating education and career opportunities and must align with at least one of two priority themes:

Enabling STEM-related education and career opportunities.

Helping students make informed choices between employment/career pathways and higher-level education.

Eligible applicants include schools, colleges, third-level institutions, employers, private-sector companies, charities and social enterprises.

The Foundation places strong emphasis on additionality, meaning funded programmes should create opportunities beyond what is already available. It will not fund activities that public bodies have a statutory responsibility to deliver or projects that unnecessarily duplicate existing services.

Priority may be given to projects benefiting people in Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon, although the Foundation’s remit extends more broadly across Northern Ireland.

Funding may cover project, salary and equipment costs where clearly connected to project outputs and outcomes. General overheads are normally not funded.

Match funding is allowed, and applications demonstrating confirmed match funding may receive more favourable consideration.

The application process has two stages. Organisations must first submit an Expression of Interest. Successful applicants will then be invited to complete a full application.

EOIs must be submitted using the Foundation’s official Word document without modifying its formatting, adding images or exceeding stated word limits.

The deadline for Stage 1 is:

Friday, 16 October 2026 at 12:00 noon.

Applicants are expected to receive an EOI decision approximately 8–10 weeks after the deadline.

TITLE: Future for Nature Awards 2027 (up to €50,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 23, 2026

Are you a young (between 18 to 35 years old) and dedicated nature conservationist committed to protecting wild species? Do you combine passion with action to create concrete results in nature conservation? Are you the Future for Nature? Apply now for the Future for Nature Awards 2027.

The Future for Nature Foundation (FFN) supports young, talented, and ambitious nature conservationists committed to protecting wild species. Therefore, they select and build a new generation of nature conservationists who they believe make the difference for the future of nature. Natural leaders who inspire and with their drive and ‘stubbornness’ achieve impressive results. Annually, they put three of these promising young people in the spotlight.

Award

The winners each receive 50,000 Euros and the prestigious FFN Award. The winners may spend the money at their own discretion in the service of nature conservation; after all, they know better than anyone where the money is most needed. Additionally, Future for Nature offers much more than one-off financial support.

Winning the FFN Award gives the winners international recognition for their work and opens doors that were previously closed.

Celebrating their work and passion at a prestigious Awards event in Arnhem and broadcasted to an international audience.

FFN offers the winners a platform and brings their stories to the attention of conservationists, donors, and a wide audience, allowing them to increase their impact and gain more access to funds.

Connecting winners to a peer-network of fellow conservationists for mentoring and growth.

Winners will present their work at the Future for Nature Awards event at Royal Burgers’ Zoo in Arnhem, the Netherlands. The event will take place in May 2027. Travel and accommodation expenses will be covered by the Future for Nature Foundation.

Eligibility

The candidate:

Must be an individual, not an organisation, programme, or group of individuals.

Must be born on or after the 31st May 1992 (Maximum age of 35 years old at the 2027 FFN Awards event) and before the 31st of August 2008 (minimum age of 18 years old at the time of submitting your application).

Has achieved substantial and long-term benefits to the conservation status of one or more wild species.

Has demonstrated commitment, determination, and passion for conservation work.

Has demonstrated leadership, entrepreneurship, and a clear view of conservation work.

Has been creative and innovative in their work.

Has demonstrated to be honourable in the conservation work performed.

Must be determined to continue their conservation work, as the Award aims to stimulate the winner’s future work. It is not an “end of career” prize.

Is able to explain their conservation work in proficient English (written and spoken).

The application:

Must be based on the ongoing conservation work of the candidate and not a project proposal. Future For Nature is a foundation that presents Awards to individual nature conservationists and is not a project funding organisation. Therefore, we do not evaluate project proposals.

Must be written by the applicant and reflect the work and conservation vision of the applicant in their own words. The use of AI tools is permitted for guidance only; when direct copying or pasting of AI-generated content is suspected, the application can be excluded from the selection process.

Application

Click here to apply

For more information, visit Future for Nature Awards.

TITLE: A Message from the director

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
« The Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques is an international mathematics and theoretical physics research center. Free of teaching duties and administrative tasks, its professors and invited researchers carry out their work in complete independence and total freedom, at the highest international level.

Ever since it was created, IHES has cultivated interdisciplinarity. The constant dialogue between mathematicians and theoretical physicists has led to particularly rich interactions. In more recent years, IHES has turned its attention to the interface between mathematics and biology and the theoretical issues arising from high technology.

A limited number of permanent professors and researchers from prominent French organizations (Collège de France, CEA and CNRS) are based at IHES. These very senior scientists attract some 200 visiting researchers each year, who also benefit from the high concentration of mathematicians present in close proximity to the Institute. The scientific emulation resulting from the interactions between researchers in different disciplines and from different countries contributes to the vitality of basic research globally.

The Institute’s originality also lies in its capacity to take scientific risks and I would like to thank here all those who have helped us maintain this unique model. IHES continues to seek new partners to share in what is both its essence and its success: giving the most prominent and the most promising researchers an opportunity to travel down as yet unexplored intellectual avenues. »

Emmanuel Ullmo, mathematician and IHES Director

TITLE: Skolem, Lump Bumps and Windy Figures

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The mathematical sculpture Skolem, Lump Bumps & Windy Figures is the culmination of a mathematical project, “Mathématiciens en culottes courtes” (Budding Mathematicians). It was offered by Max Leguem, then director of the youth and cultural center in Bures-sur-Yvette, to the French equivalent of third and fifth graders, in 1999. For this educational initiative aimed at raising awareness of mathematics in young students, he called on Jean Brette, then Director of the mathematics section at the Palais de la Découverte, and Jean-Pierre Bourguignon, then Director of IHES, to visit these classes regularly during the school year with sessions involving mathematics in a fun format.

In the second year, children who had reached grade 5 became “tutors” of sorts for grade 3 students, who were discovering this new approach to mathematics. That year, the project took on a new dimension: in addition to mathematics, art was added to the mix.

The « Jeu des Cavaliers » (Knights’ Game) became the most studied game. The meeting with artists enabled the same game to be imagined from different angles. The game then moved from a flat representation to a 3D one. Some of the students worked on a set of specifications for an artist, who were then inspired to create their own version… which would become a sculpture. It needed to be mobile, as the public had to be able to play with it, while respecting the rules of the « Jeu des Cavaliers ».

Once the specifications had been finalized, they decided to commission a work of art. Contact was made with Mari Linnman of the 3-CA association, mediator for the Fondation de France’s « Nouveaux commanditaires » program in the Ile-de-France region, who proposed that the project be entrusted to American sculptor Jessica Stockholder.

On May 19, 2005, Jessica Stockholder’s mathematical sculpture: Skolem, Lump Bumps and Windy Figures, was thus born in the grounds of IHES and inaugurated. The launch was attended by the artist, the organizations which financed the piece (Fondation de France, Conseil Régional Ile-de-France, Conseil Général de l’Essonne, Communauté d’Agglomération du Plateau de Saclay, Fondation Électricité de France, Lafarge Bétons, Délégation Régionale à la Recherche et à la Technologie d’Ile-de-France, and Les Amis de l’IHÉS) and all those involved in the project, including children and teachers.

Since then, the sculpture has been presented every time the Institute welcomes students or opens its doors to the general public. The interest and questioning surrounding this work are as lively as ever.

For further information, please contact Valérie Touchant.

TITLE: United Nations Shadowing Programme 2026: Master’s and PhD Students Can Virtually Shadow UN Professionals in Vienna

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations Shadowing Programme 2026 is now accepting applications from eligible Master’s and PhD students who want to gain first-hand insight into professional life within the United Nations and other Vienna-based international organizations.

Coordinated by the United Nations Information Service (UNIS) Vienna, with support from the United Nations Information Centre (UNIC) Kyiv, the 2026 programme will take place virtually from 24 October to 24 November 2026. Selected students will have the opportunity to participate in a one-hour virtual encounter with a staff member from a participating Vienna-based organization and attend a virtual career workshop.

The programme brings together several prominent organizations operating in Vienna, including the International Atomic Energy Agency, Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs, United Nations Industrial Development Organization and United Nations Information Service Vienna.

Applications are particularly aimed at students enrolled in Master’s or PhD programmes at universities in Armenia, Austria, Czechia, Georgia, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Türkiye and Ukraine.

Application Deadline: 27 September 2026

Applications opened on 14 September 2026 and will remain open until 27 September 2026. As only a limited number of applications can be accommodated, eligible students are encouraged to apply as early as possible.

About the United Nations Shadowing Programme 2026

The United Nations Shadowing Programme is designed to give university students a closer look at the professional work carried out by United Nations personnel and employees of other international organizations based in Vienna.

Rather than being a conventional lecture or general information session, the programme provides selected participants with direct virtual interaction with an international-organization professional.

Each selected student will have the opportunity to participate in a one-hour virtual encounter with a staff member. This creates space for students to learn about areas such as the staff member’s work, responsibilities, professional environment and organizational context.

Participants will also join a virtual career workshop, adding a broader career-development component to the experience.

The programme is therefore particularly relevant for postgraduate students who are exploring careers connected with international organizations, multilateral cooperation and the work of the United Nations system.

Programme Dates

The virtual edition of the United Nations Shadowing Programme will take place between:

24 October and 24 November 2026.

The programme begins around United Nations Day, which is observed annually on 24 October.

The organizers specifically note that the Shadowing Programme is held in connection with the commemoration of United Nations Day.

Programme Format

The 2026 Shadowing Programme is being conducted virtually.

Participants do not need to travel to Vienna in order to take part.

The two principal components are:

A one-hour virtual encounter with a staff member from a participating organization.

A virtual career workshop.

The virtual structure provides postgraduate students in the participating countries with access to professionals working in Vienna-based international organizations without requiring international travel.

Language of the Programme

The official language of the Shadowing Programme 2026 is:

English.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating and participating in professional discussions in English.

The announcement does not specify a formal English-language certification such as IELTS, TOEFL or another standardized examination.

Participating Vienna-Based Organizations

Students can apply to shadow a professional from one of several participating international organizations.

The 2026 programme includes the following organizations.

International Atomic Energy Agency

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is participating in the 2026 Shadowing Programme.

Applicants interested in the IAEA should submit their application to:

N.Wright@iaea.org

Students whose academic or professional interests align with the work of the organization may select the IAEA as the organization they wish to shadow.

Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) is another participating organization.

Applications for the CTBTO should be sent to:

info@ctbto.org

The inclusion of CTBTO gives students another opportunity to gain insight into the work of a major Vienna-based international institution.

United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) is participating in the programme.

Students wishing to apply to shadow UNODC should send their application to:

unodcadvocacysection@un.org

Applicants should choose the organization that most closely corresponds with their academic interests and career aspirations.

United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs

The United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) is also participating.

Applications should be sent to:

unoda-viennaoffice@un.org

The programme can provide selected participants with an opportunity to better understand the working environment of professionals involved with Vienna-based multilateral institutions.

United Nations Industrial Development Organization

The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) is participating in the 2026 programme.

Students who wish to apply for UNIDO should send their application to:

R.WICKREMASINGHE@unido.org

UNIDO has separately promoted the programme as an opportunity for Master’s and PhD students to virtually meet a staff member and participate in a career workshop.

United Nations Information Service Vienna

Students can also apply to shadow the United Nations Information Service (UNIS) Vienna.

Applications should be sent to:

unis.vienna@un.org

The International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River (ICPDR) is among the participating Vienna-based organizations.

Applications should be submitted to:

helene.masliah-gilkarov@icpdr.org

United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation

The United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (UNSCEAR) is also participating.

Applications should be sent to:

unscear@un.org.

Complete List of Participating Organizations

The organizations taking part in the United Nations Shadowing Programme 2026 are:

International Atomic Energy Agency

United Nations Industrial Development Organization
