TITLE: Royal Holloway University of London Announces 10 Funded PhD Studentships for 2027 Through the Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Royal Holloway, University of London is inviting applications for 10 funded PhD studentships through its Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training (CDT), offering doctoral researchers the opportunity to undertake research designed not only to generate new knowledge but also to deliver tangible benefits for society, communities, organisations or the environment.

The 2026–27 competition supports doctoral research across an unusually broad range of disciplines, including artificial intelligence, computer science, engineering, economics, business, law, psychology, health, sociology, geography, politics, literature, culture, environmental science and biological sciences.

Successful applicants will receive funding for 3.5 years full-time equivalent, covering UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees together with a UKRI-rate stipend of £23,805 for the 2026/27 academic year, including London Allowance. The studentships can support full-time or part-time study, subject to the funding terms. Applicants must be eligible for UK Home fee status, and the University explicitly states that applicants assessed as overseas students are not eligible for this particular funding competition.

The application deadline is 20 October 2026, with successful candidates expected to begin their doctoral studies on 11 January 2027.

About Royal Holloway, University of London

Royal Holloway, University of London is a research-intensive UK university with a substantial postgraduate research community and involvement in multiple Doctoral Training Partnerships, Doctoral Landscape Awards and Centres for Doctoral Training.

The University participates in doctoral training structures including programmes associated with the Arts and Humanities Research Council, Economic and Social Research Council, Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, Natural Environment Research Council and other UK research-funding initiatives.

Beyond discipline-specific doctoral training, Royal Holloway operates researcher-development programmes intended to help postgraduate researchers build transferable professional capabilities alongside their academic expertise.

The Social Purpose CDT forms part of this wider institutional approach to postgraduate research but has a distinctive requirement: doctoral research must clearly demonstrate why the research matters outside academia and how it can contribute to positive social, economic, environmental or public outcomes.

What Is the Royal Holloway Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training?

The Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training is designed around the principle that research should have a clearly articulated purpose beyond academic knowledge production alone.

In this competition, Royal Holloway defines social-purpose research as work directed toward addressing a real-world challenge, injustice, unmet need or opportunity and capable of producing a tangible public benefit.

This does not mean every project must immediately result in legislation, a new product or a direct policy intervention. Social impact can be immediate or longer-term.

For example, a doctoral project might contribute to:

Improving health and wellbeing

Reducing economic, social or digital inequalities

Addressing climate change or biodiversity loss

Improving the responsible use of artificial intelligence

Supporting vulnerable or marginalised communities

Developing more equitable business practices

Improving public policy

Strengthening environmental sustainability

Addressing gender inequality

Developing safer digital technologies

Improving access to healthcare

Supporting responsible innovation

Advancing cultural inclusion and community cohesion

Developing technologies that can subsequently support industry, public services or society

Applicants therefore need to explain not only what they want to research, but also why the research should be undertaken and who could ultimately benefit from it.

10 Funded PhD Studentships Available

Royal Holloway is recruiting 10 doctoral researchers for the latest cohort of its Social Purpose CDT.

These are not limited to one academic department or narrow field. Applicants can pursue research across the University’s arts and humanities, social sciences, business and law, and science disciplines, provided an appropriate Royal Holloway supervisory team can support the project and the proposal demonstrates a credible social-purpose dimension.

Candidates can take one of two broad approaches.

They may develop their own doctoral research proposal and identify suitable Royal Holloway academics to supervise it.

Alternatively, candidates can explore one of the project ideas already proposed by Royal Holloway academics and work with the relevant potential supervisor to develop that proposal into a doctoral research project.

In either case, applicants cannot simply submit an application without making supervisory arrangements first.

Funding Package

The Social Purpose CDT studentship provides funding for 3.5 years on a full-time-equivalent basis.

The award covers UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees and provides a stipend set at the applicable UKRI rate.

For the 2026/27 academic year, Royal Holloway states that the stipend is:

£23,805 per year FTE, including London Allowance.

Funding also incorporates time for a career-enhancing research placement or challenge-led activity of up to three months.

Applicants should note that this award is specifically tied to UK Home tuition-fee eligibility. Royal Holloway’s current applicant guidance states that it is unable to accept overseas students for this funding scheme.

This restriction relates to fee status rather than race or ethnicity.

Full-Time and Part-Time Study

The official studentship information states that the award can fund full-time or part-time UK-rate tuition fees, with the funding period calculated on a full-time-equivalent basis.

Applicants considering part-time registration should discuss the structure and feasibility of their proposed programme with the relevant department and supervisory team before applying.

Mandatory Three-Month Placement or Challenge-Led Research

A major feature of the Social Purpose CDT is its emphasis on applying research outside conventional academic settings.

Successful postgraduate researchers are expected to undertake either a placement or a piece of challenge-led work lasting up to three months.

This activity may involve a:

Business organisation, public-sector institution, charity, community organisation, third-sector organisation or another relevant external partner.

The objective is to allow researchers to experience how research evidence can be translated into practice while developing transferable capabilities such as leadership, stakeholder engagement and policy communication.

The placement must be incorporated into the doctoral timetable so that the PhD can still be completed within the funded 3.5-year period.

Training and Professional Development

The Social Purpose CDT is not structured solely around the completion of a thesis.

Award holders are expected to participate in the wider postgraduate researcher community and undertake additional professional and researcher-development activities.

Each funded postgraduate researcher is expected to complete at least 10 days of development and training activities every year, including Social Purpose CDT cohort training.

Researchers will also be expected to participate in relevant on-campus activities, cohort-development opportunities and broader programmes covering areas such as researcher development, knowledge exchange, teaching preparation and wellbeing.

Royal Holloway’s applicant guidance also indicates that researchers will be expected to demonstrate their learning and skills development through the University’s permitted alternative thesis format.

Research Supervision Requirements

Every proposed project must have a supervision team consisting of at least two Royal Holloway supervisors.

Applicants must therefore identify an appropriate primary supervisor and communicate with potential supervisors before submitting the formal application.

The proposed supervisory team must agree that it is willing to support the application.

Royal Holloway specifically instructs candidates to contact prospective supervisors directly before preparing the final submission.

Applicants should not treat this as an optional networking step. Securing supervisory support is an integral component of the application process.

Proposed Research Areas

The current call demonstrates how broad the concept of social-purpose research can be. Royal Holloway academics are inviting applications across subjects ranging from public health and inequality to AI, economics, sustainability, digital rights and cultural studies.

Examples currently highlighted by the University include research into children’s education and mental health, using large administrative datasets to investigate whether educational attainment can influence later mental-health outcomes; migration, humanitarianism, reparation and cultural practice; relationships between opera, politics and society; care politics and the human right to care; violence, gender inequality and social policy; and the use of intergenerational and intercultural creative practices to strengthen community cohesion.

Business and management possibilities include AI adoption among SMEs, political economy, migrant and refugee entrepreneurship, precarious employment, fintech, mergers and acquisitions, banking regulation, behavioural finance, the macroeconomics of AI and geopolitics, global production networks, international migration, digital consumer behaviour, entrepreneurial learning, gig work, algorithmic management, fraud, organisational accountability, sustainability accounting, platform economies and digital technologies affecting marginalised workers.

Law-focused proposals can investigate subjects including medical-device regulation, digital healthcare, telemedicine and predictive AI, including questions concerning regulation, clinical practice, patient autonomy and rights.

Science and engineering opportunities include projects addressing sea-ice reflectivity and climate change, climate-resilient renewable-energy microgrids for AI data centres, eyewitness identification and face recognition, inequality in access to depression treatment, artificial intelligence for early detection of mental and metabolic disorders, lower-cost and lower-energy deep learning, secure and privacy-preserving digital communication, and vitamin-A biofortification of food crops.

These topics are illustrative rather than meaning that every applicant must select one exactly as published. Royal Holloway explicitly permits applicants to develop their own proposals where an appropriate supervision team can be identified.

Social Purpose Must Be Clearly Demonstrated

Applicants should not treat the phrase “social purpose” as a generic statement about research being beneficial.

Royal Holloway’s guidance specifically requires proposals to demonstrate a clear connection between:

The proposed research → a significant social challenge → identifiable potential beneficiaries.

Applicants are expected to explain why the work matters.

Examples given by Royal Holloway include research that could support sustainability, reduce inequality, respond to mental-health challenges, promote innovation or contribute to improved public or organisational outcomes.

A technically strong project that fails to articulate this social-purpose relationship risks performing poorly against the competition’s assessment criteria.

Who Can Apply?

Candidates must be capable of meeting the admission requirements of the relevant Royal Holloway MPhil/PhD programme and must be eligible for UK Home tuition-fee status.

There is no single degree-subject requirement applying to all 10 studentships because proposals are being accepted from many departments.

Qualifications therefore depend heavily on the chosen discipline and project.

For example, the sea-ice project welcomes applicants from fields including physics, engineering, chemistry and Earth sciences, while a proposed AI-based health-detection project specifies a strong Computer Science or Engineering background with machine-learning and deep-learning expertise.

Candidates should consequently check the normal PhD entry requirements of the department to which they intend to apply and discuss their academic fit with the proposed supervisor.

Current Royal Holloway PhD Students Can Also Apply

The competition is not restricted to completely new applicants.

Royal Holloway states that currently registered, unfunded first-year PhD students may also apply. The current call gives students who began around September or October 2026 as an example of those who may qualify.

Existing eligible students use a separate application route specified by the University.

Application Documents Required

Applicants need to prepare a substantial doctoral application. Royal Holloway’s current guidance requires:

Personal Statement — maximum 500 words. It should explain the candidate’s motivation for doctoral study, interest in the specific project, relevant previous experience, preparedness for a PhD and what the applicant hopes to gain from doctoral training.

Research Proposal — maximum four pages plus one page of references. The proposal should state that the applicant is applying for an RH PhD Social Purpose Studentship, provide a project title, include a social-purpose statement of no more than 250 words, establish the background and research gap, explain the research aim and design, provide a 3.5-year timeline including the placement, identify the supervisory team, explain required research or training resources, discuss relevant external partners where applicable and include ethical considerations of no more than 250 words.

Supervisor Letter — maximum one page. The primary supervisor must assess the applicant’s readiness for doctoral research, explain how the supervision team will support the researcher, address project feasibility and explain how the research connects with Royal Holloway’s social-purpose objectives.

Curriculum Vitae. The CV can include academic qualifications, paid and unpaid experience, publications, conference presentations, awards, recognition, training and relevant technical or professional skills.

Qualification Transcripts. Applicants must provide the academic records required by the University.

Applicants are also asked to complete a separate “Getting to know our applicants” form. Royal Holloway states that information collected through this form is intended to support monitoring of diversity and equality initiatives and does not form part of the assessed application.

How to Prepare the Research Proposal

The research proposal is particularly important because it carries a substantial proportion of the assessment.

Applicants should clearly demonstrate that their project is intellectually credible, methodologically realistic and achievable within the funding period.

The proposal needs to account for the three-month placement or challenge-led activity rather than constructing a 3.5-year research plan and attempting to add the placement afterward.

Applicants should also discuss expected training, laboratory work, fieldwork, research visits or data requirements where relevant.

Where external resources will be necessary, the proposal should explain where the required support is expected to come from.

How Applications Will Be Assessed

Royal Holloway has published a transparent weighting system for the competition.

Applicant preparedness accounts for 40% of the assessment. Evaluators will consider previous academic achievements, the CV, personal statement, relevant academic, professional and life experience, and the supervisor’s supporting statement.

Quality and feasibility of the PhD proposal accounts for another 40%. Reviewers consider the strength and novelty of the research ideas, methodology and design, feasibility within the funded period, inclusion of the placement, potential impact, proposed supervisory expertise and practical feasibility of required research activities.

Fit with Social Purpose accounts for the remaining 20%. The panel evaluates how convincingly the proposal aligns with Royal Holloway’s commitment to research with meaningful societal value.

This means that applicants should not concentrate solely on academic grades. A competitive submission needs to combine candidate preparedness, a credible research design and a convincing explanation of social impact.

How to Apply

New applicants must submit their PhD application through the Royal Holloway Applicant Portal.

Before doing so, candidates should:

Identify the appropriate Royal Holloway PhD programme, research potential supervisors, contact the proposed supervisor directly, develop the research proposal with an appropriate supervision team, obtain agreement from that team to support the application, prepare the required documents and complete the University’s diversity-monitoring form.

Applicants may submit either an independently developed proposal or one developed from a project idea advertised by an interested supervisor.

Important Dates

The principal dates published on Royal Holloway’s current Social Purpose CDT webpage are:

Application deadline: 20 October 2026
Applicants notified of outcome: 1 December 2026
Required start date: 11 January 2027

There is, however, a discrepancy worth noting. The current applicant-guidance PDF lists shortlisted interviews between 20 October and 3 November 2026 and refers to decision letters being issued on 6 November 2026, whereas the main Royal Holloway funding page lists 1 December 2026 as the outcome-notification date. The application deadline and start date are consistent across both sources. Candidates should therefore treat 20 October 2026 as the firm application deadline and follow subsequent timing communicated directly by Royal Holloway.

Applicant Information Events

Royal Holloway has also scheduled online information sessions for applicants who want to better understand doctoral study or the application process.

The current funding page lists sessions on:

24 September 2026, 1:30 PM–3:00 PM, and
30 September 2026, 12:30 PM–2:00 PM.

The sessions cover the studentship and doctoral application process and are particularly useful for candidates preparing an application before the October deadline.

Why the Placement Component Matters

One of the strongest features of this competition is the deliberate link between doctoral research and organisations outside academia.

A PhD candidate studying digital inequality, for example, may have an opportunity to work with a public institution or community organisation affected by technological change.

A candidate researching environmental sustainability could work alongside an environmental organisation or industry partner.

A researcher examining public policy, health or social inequality could engage with a government, charity or policy-oriented organisation.

The purpose is not simply work experience. The placement is intended to help doctoral researchers understand how evidence is interpreted, implemented and communicated within real-world institutional settings.

This practical dimension is integral to Royal Holloway’s concept of a Social Purpose PhD.

What Makes a Strong Application?

A strong application should establish a convincing relationship between the applicant, the proposed research question, the supervisory team and the societal value of the project.

The candidate should be able to explain why the research problem matters, what gap in existing knowledge will be addressed, how the research will answer the proposed question, why Royal Holloway is an appropriate environment for the project and how the findings could ultimately benefit identifiable stakeholders.

Candidates should also ensure their research plan is realistic within 3.5 years.

Highly ambitious projects that require inaccessible datasets, excessive fieldwork or resources without credible funding arrangements may struggle against the competition’s feasibility criteria.

Similarly, simply describing a project as socially important without identifying likely beneficiaries or routes to impact may not adequately address the programme’s Social Purpose requirement.

Deadline

Applications for the 10 Royal Holloway Social Purpose CDT PhD Studentships must be submitted by 20 October 2026.

Applicants must also be able to begin the PhD on 11 January 2027.

Because applicants need supervisory agreement before applying, prospective candidates should contact potential supervisors well ahead of the deadline instead of waiting until the final days of the competition.

Conclusion

The Royal Holloway Social Purpose Centre for Doctoral Training 2027 PhD Studentships provide a significant funded doctoral opportunity for researchers interested in combining rigorous academic research with demonstrable public or societal impact.

Ten studentships are available across a wide range of disciplines, extending from artificial intelligence, computer science, engineering and environmental science to business, economics, law, psychology, sociology, politics, culture and the humanities.

Each award provides 3.5 years of funding on a full-time-equivalent basis, covers UK-rate MPhil/PhD tuition fees, and offers a 2026/27 UKRI-rate stipend of £23,805 FTE including London Allowance. Successful candidates will also undertake a placement or challenge-led project lasting up to three months and participate in structured researcher-development activities.

Prospective applicants should first identify a suitable Royal Holloway supervisor and secure support from a supervision team. They must then prepare a detailed research proposal, personal statement, CV, academic transcripts and supervisor supporting letter before completing the online application.

The deadline is 20 October 2026, with funded candidates required to start on 11 January 2027.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Jonathan Rothberg

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Jonathan Rothberg supports Professor Max Tegmark’s research.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2013

Jonathan Rothberg
What fascinates Jonathan Rothberg about science is the ability to either learn something no one knew before or to create an instrument that enables the discovery of something new. He is a serial entrepreneur best known for inventing high-speed, massively parallel DNA sequencing. The company he founded, 454 Life Sciences, brought to market a new method for sequencing genomes. After creating the next generation sequencing, he went on to develop the first sequencing on a semiconductor chip, thus enabling the $1,000 genome. With this discovery he founded Ion Torrent, where they actually sequenced Gordon Moore.

The idea for the high-speed sequencing came to him when his infant son was rushed to intensive care and he realized how critical personal genomes were to human health. That invention is now in use at major pharmaceutical companies, universities, genome centers, and medical centers around the world—and his son, Noah, lived to inspire yet another company.

Jonathan’s generous support has been invaluable for our Omniscope project, which is developing technology to help make the largest-ever 3D map of our universe.

He is an inspiration to me, with his knack for overcoming daunting challenges through outside-the-box technological innovation.

Professor Max Tegmark

Rothberg has supported Professor Max Tegmark’s research; he decided to get involved because of the tremendous scope of the project and the vision behind it. Tegmark notes that “Jonathan’s generous support has been invaluable for our Omniscope project, which is developing technology to help make the largest-ever 3D map of our universe. He is an inspiration to me, with his knack for overcoming daunting challenges through outside-the-box technological innovation.” Rothberg says about Tegmark: “he is one of those people who, as Steve Jobs was fond of saying, is actually putting a dent in the universe” and that “he intends to map the universe at a resolution never before obtainable.”

Although Rothberg’s undergraduate degree in chemical engineering is from Carnegie Mellon University and his PhD in biology from Yale, he encourages others to support science at MIT. “Ultimately, it is research that raises the quality of life, and if you love science and discovery and people, then you should support basic research.”

Ion Torrent was acquired in 2010 by Life Technologies. Rothberg also founded CuraGen Corporation, a company dedicated to using genome technologies in drug development; RainDance Technology, a company developing general droplet microfluidic lab-on-chip technologies; and Clarifi Corporation, an analytical software company. Jonathan Rothberg is inspired to create companies that impact the quality of life and he is always looking for like-minded people to join him.

Core components

the University Composition Fee at the appropriate rate*

a maintenance allowance for a single student (£23,152 for 12 months at the 2026-27 rate; pro rata for courses shorter than 12 months) – for PhD scholars the award is for up to 4 years

academic development funding – from up to £750 to up to £4,000, dependent on the length of your course, to attend conferences and courses.

fieldwork – you may apply to keep up to your normal maintenance allowance while on fieldwork as part of your PhD (the Trust does not fund other fieldwork costs as these should be funded by the University Composition Fee).

hardship funding – for unforeseen difficulties facing the scholar

a citizen of any country outside the United Kingdom

PhD (full-time or part-time*)

MLitt (full-time)

one-year postgraduate course (full-time), with some exceptions.

outstanding intellectual ability

reasons for choice of course

a commitment to improving the lives of others

leadership potential

TITLE: AAU/Stellenbosch University Capacity Building Workshop for University Registrars and Administrators

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Background and Rationale

For every Higher Education Institution (HEI), the registrar’s office is the axis on which every activity spins. It is also the hub of a student’s education. Due to the vital role of the registrar’s office in administrative excellence and students’ academic success, the registrar, who is one of the principal officers, should see himself/herself as a peer of academics and a partner in the delivery of educational programs. As the steward of the academic record and the keeper of institutional data, the registrar is in a unique role at the institution. An institution needs good data to advance its initiatives. The registrar, who sits at the crossroads between student service and academic programming, is distinctly suited to use the data at hand to help shape discussions and decisions in the context of desired educational outcomes for the institution and students alike.

While serving and advancing higher education by safeguarding the academic integrity of the institution, there are broad professional principles of good practice, management, and conduct that should be followed. When these principles are not being followed, those served by the registrar’s office, majority of whom are students, are the ones that bear the consequences of a disengaged office. The registrar must be current, consistent and professional to ensure the integrity of degrees and maintain the ability to accurately advise students about degree requirements and other administrative requirements. Continuous professional development is central to enabling the registrar perform at optimal level for the overall benefit of his/her institution.

It is against this backdrop that the Association of African Universities (AAU) is organizing a capacity building workshop for university registrars in universities and colleges in Africa. The workshop addresses one of AAU’s strategic goals of strengthening the delivery capacity of HEIs through enhanced leadership and management capacity development.

The modules for this Capacity Building Workshop for University Registrars include:

Module 1: Students’ records management: Retention, Transcript Guide, Disposal, and Archive of Students’ records

Module 2: Managing Student Recruitment/Admission, Registration and Displacement

Module 3: Examination Management

Module 4: Curriculum Management and the Role of the Registrar

Module 5: Student Online Services

Module 6: Professional Development of Registrars and Administrators

Module 7: Graduation and Commencement

Objective and Expected Outcomes

The overall goal of the Workshop is to enhance the capacity of Registrars and HEI Administrators to deliver on their position as custodians of records in HEIs in Africa. To this end, AAU and Stellenbosch University, South Africa expect that at the end of the workshop the participants would return to their institutions with:

Improved knowledge about student records management and processes of records retention, disposal, transcript guide and records archiving.

Improved knowledge of innovative approaches to student recruitment, admission, registration and displacement.

Enhanced awareness of examination management processes and best practices.

Improved knowledge on how to organise effective online support services for students.

Methodology

The workshop will be held over a period of four days and would comprise the use of case studies, focused group discussions, experiential learning, presentations and ideas sharing. The workshop will develop a strategy of follow-up to ensure that university registrars are implementing good practices learned from the workshop at their various institutions of higher learning. The participants will have the opportunity to engage in dialogue with peers on the various challenges at their universities and strategies to overcome those challenges.

A post workshop report will be compiled and recommendations made will be integrated into improving subsequent workshops.

Registrars

Enrollment Managers

TITLE: International Conference on Education and Restitution  – 30 August – 1 September 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: The past, the present and the future – Afrofuturism and Africa’s Development

The Association of African Universities (AAU), the Pan African Heritage World Museum (PAHWM) and UNESCO, under the auspices of the Government of Ghana and the African Union Commission, are organizing a Special Diaspora Conference titled: The Past, The Present and the Future – Afrofuturism and African Development. The other collaborators are PANAFEST, Ghana National House of Chiefs, GHANA Cultural Forum, Diaspora African Forum, the African Private Sector Summit (APSS), the Global Institute of Planning and Sustainable Development (GIPSD), and the All-African Students Union (AASU).

The joint conference from 30th August – 1st of September 2022, aims to reclaim and recontextualize Africana education, technology, politics, languages, histories, arts, culture, music, and spirituality toward a conscious effort of unification and rapid development of Africa. The reappropriation of African heritage and education is key to telling and retelling the African’s own stories to disrupt the master inaccurate narratives as handed down mainly from Global Northern (Western) perspectives.

Please Register for this conference via this link – https://bit.ly/3sClx5U

For further information also contact Ransford Bekoe at – ransford@aau.org or call – +233 244736280

The conference will reflect on the concept of Sankofa, an Akan philosophical symbol, which illustrates the necessity of “going back to retrieve and reclaim the enduring values of the past to forge a viable and owned future. It will also discuss the new paradigm of Afrofuturism, which highlight the potential of African resilience and creativity in using new technologies to build innovative alternatives to the global crisis of the dominant model of development.

Essential to the restoration of Africa’s dignity, self-confidence and creativity, is the decolonization of the mind through a renewed effort of reconceptualization from a Global African perspective of dominant paradigms about development, politics, education, culture and sciences. African worldviews, humanism and spirituality, offer a rich heritage of principles, values, symbols, rituals and practices to build meaningful thought and imagination that can guide our efforts for emancipation, innovation and recreation.

The importance of using the African academic Diaspora in helping build a robust and resilient African higher education system that responds to scientific inquiries has been rigorously expressed by the Association of African Universities (AAU), Africa’s apex higher education organization. Under the African Union’s Science, Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa 2024 (STISA-2024), mobilizing and widening the involvement of relevant segments of Africa’s population (private sector, civil society, parliamentarians and the Diaspora) is paramount to support the continent’s renaissance and development agendas.

It is on the basis of this recontextualization and reconceptualization that African nations can build the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which aims to create a single market to deepen the economic integration of the continent. The AfCFTA is arguably Africa’s most important development initiative in the 21st century and a more responsive African higher education sector is required to provide the skillsets for its implementation: i.e. to support infrastructure (transportation, laboratory engineering, etc.), services (reliable electricity, water, healthcare, manpower training, Internet access, etc.); and provide consultancy (strengthening legal frameworks on intellectual property rights, harmonising tax systems, arbitration and dispute resolution, etc.).

The conference will bring together scholars, artists, political and economic decision-makers, traditional leaders, civil society activists, professionals and practitioners from across the continent and from the African diaspora to share the results of their research, collaborative work, and practices, that squarely address the above-mentioned issues.

The conference will be a hybrid one to be hosted at the Secretariat of the Association of African Universities in Accra, Ghana and online. Besides the main theme, the three sub-themes adopted and the various topics for this three-day summit are:

Subtheme 1: Addressing the prerequisites for the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area

Topics to be addressed:

Connecting African Peoples: Infrastructures and Traffic Policies

Rules, Processes and Procedures: Harmonizing Trade Governance

Interdependency and Complementarity between African economies

The Question of African Common Currencies

Developing Continental Legal Recourses and Fair Arbitration

Subtheme 2: Rethinking Education: Towards Achieving African Renaissance

Topics to be addressed:

African Endogenous Systems of Teaching of Learning

Reshaping Education Systems in Africa

Building Pan African Citizenship through Education

Revising the Contents of History Education

Regional Integration and Curriculum Harmonization

Reorienting African Higher Education

Education about African Future

Subtheme 3: Reclaiming and Reconceptualising African Arts, Culture and Heritage

Topics to be addressed:

Reconceptualizing Cultural Heritage

Decolonising Museums

Afrofuturism and African Contemporary Creation

Return of Looted Cultural Properties: A Pan African Vision and Framework

Cultural Sovereignty and Intellectual Property

Handicraft and Cultural Industries

TITLE: The Association of African Universities (AAU) Launches the African Quality Rating Mechanism (AQRM) Institutional Assessment & Evaluation for  Self-Improvement

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Quality Rating Mechanism (AQRM) institutional assessment and evaluation for self-improvement has been launched by the Association of African Universities in a virtual event hosted on 3rd June 2022 and attended by close to 400 higher education stakeholders. The objectives for organizing the AQRM launch were to i) educate and make Africa’s Higher and Tertiary Education aware of the existence of the AQRM and its importance; ii) make the African Higher and Tertiary Education Community understand the processes and procedures involved in the implementation of the AQRM institutional evaluation for self-improvement iii) make known the benefits of the AQRM and iv) advocate for and encourage African Higher Education institutions to start making use of the AQRM institutional evaluation regularly, at least two (2) times a year

The AQRM is a self-assessment, rating and evaluation tool that African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) can use to rate the quality of their institutions. This important tool supports continuous quality improvement and the building of a quality culture in Africa’s HEIs. Additionally, the AQRM can be used as a means to assess and fulfil Part A of the African Standards and Guidelines for QA (ASG-QA) which focuses on Internal Quality Assurance (IQA). It is also a vital tool to aid strategic planning in quality assurance for African higher and tertiary education institutions.

In his remarks, the Secretary General of the AAU, Prof. Olusola B. Oyewole continued to encourage and urge the participants to disseminate information on the AQRM to their institutions and other institutions as well. He also emphasized the need for the institutions to also participate in the self-assessment and evaluation process in order to improve the quality of service provision and consequently the quality of graduates and research for Africa’s transformation. The event was coordinated by Dr. Violet Makuku, the Quality Assurance Specialist, Workshops Coordinator and Project Officer at the AAU.

Participants who attended the AQRM launch consisted of all higher education stakeholders including Vice Chancellors (VCs), Deputy VCs, Deans and Directors from Higher Education Institutions and other HE stakeholders. The event was truly global and international because participants were from different parts of the world including; Ghana, Nigeria, Zimbabwe, Cameroon, United Kingdom, Lesotho, Canada, Mozambique, Kenya, Sierra Leone, Ethiopia, Namibia, Botswana, Uganda, Malawi, Zambia, USA, Libya, and Burkina Faso. Others were from Egypt, Guinea, Spain, Somalia, Tanzania, Ivory Coast, South Africa, Portugal, Angola, Mali, Eswatini, Mauritius, Turkey, France, Benin, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Malaysia, Switzerland, South Sudan, Tunisia, Cape Verde, Senegal, Burundi, Qatar and Israel.

As background, the African Quality Rating Mechanism was developed by the African Union Commission (AUC) through extensive dialogue with the African Higher Education community, including the Association of African Universities (AAU) and quality assurance experts across the world. It was then adopted by the Conference of Ministers of Education of the African Union (COMDAF) in 2007.

It was announced during the launch event on the 3rd June 2022, that the link for the AQRM questionnaire is available online at https://aqrm.aau.org , while the online expression of interest form was also available at this link: https://www.research.net/r/AAUEva .

African Universities were encouraged to begin using the AQRM tool immediately to benefit from the enormous advantages that it offers towards quality services and products as well as self -improvement. Participants were alerted, that the commitment of the leadership of their institutions and universities, as well as the preparedness of HEIs to undertake the evaluation exercise were very important to the success of the AQRM institutional assessment and evaluation process. They were also informed that there were no opening and closing dates, and thus, institutions could express interest at any time of the year.

Success Stories Showcased During the Launch

Two institutions (Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Kumasi, Ghana and The Redeemer’s University, Edo State, Nigeria), were picked as case studies to explain the process, describe their experiences and demonstrate the benefits of undertaking the AQRM institutional assessment and evaluation for self-improvement. They both acknowledged that the thorough processes and procedures of undergoing such an exercise were highly beneficial to them. The institutions narrated how the whole AQRM institutional assessment and evaluation for self-improvement brought immediate, medium and long-term benefits with tangible positive impacts to their institutions. They also highlighted their challenges which were mainly in relation to data collection from the various departments to the AQRM central committee. Institutions were strongly warned, that to access real and total transformation of their institutions, they needed to pay due diligence to this key aspect of the whole exercise. According to them, their respective institutions’ involvement in the whole AQRM exercise resulted in drastic and better rankings both at national and continental levels. They also won grants and generally had their systems and policies strengthened, among others.

More than 15 other African institutions that were part of the initial pilot study as well as those who undertook the AQRM assessments and evaluations under the HAQAA1 Initiative had similarly shared positive feedback and outcomes with the Association of African Universities earlier. They reported that the exercise was useful in helping them to plan using real data and information as opposed to using their own perceptions, judgements and conceptions. The universities also reported the value that such data collected as part of the assessment brought to their overall ratings in their respective countries (Nigeria and Ghana), as well as in Africa and the world at large. In short, the benefits from the process, as reported by the African HEIs which had used the AQRM self-assessment and evaluation tool, are enormous. Among others, their participation in the assessment had helped these institutions to attract regional and international students.

Written by Dr. Violet Makuku, Quality Assurance Specialist, AAU

TITLE: Strengthening connections in observing the North Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation: Outcomes from a Joint RAPID-OSNAP Workshop

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Foukal, N., Le Bras, I., Fu, Y., Petit, T., Bilo, T. C., Elipot, S., & Moat, B. (2026). Strengthening Connections in Observing the North Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation: Outcomes from a Joint RAPID-OSNAP Workshop. Oceanography, 39(1), 44-49. https://doi.org/10.5670/oceanog.2026.e110

In July 2025, we organized a hybrid workshop based in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, that brought together 45 oceanographers and marine technicians involved in the RAPID and OSNAP arrays. Though previous meetings had focused on the scientific findings of these arrays, this workshop was the first to focus on their operational logistics and data handling. Specifically, the workshop sought to: (1) facilitate discussion and knowledge sharing between the RAPID and OSNAP groups, (2) improve awareness within the RAPID/OSNAP community of alternative observational technologies and techniques, and (3) move toward common measurement techniques where possible. Its research contributes to the broader work of the United Nations and its Member States and covers issues connected to the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

UNU brings together researchers working across different countries and disciplines. The university also maintains collaborations with United Nations agencies, universities and research institutions around the world.

This makes a UNU internship particularly valuable for individuals seeking exposure to international research, evidence-based policymaking, sustainable development and the United Nations system.

About UNU Institute in Macau

The United Nations University Institute in Macau is one of the research and training institutes within the UNU system.

UNU Macau focuses on the relationship between digital technologies and sustainable development, undertaking research designed to address challenges identified within the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

The Institute emphasizes:

Digital technology and sustainable development

Evidence-based policymaking

Data-driven approaches

Applied research

Innovation and emerging technologies

ICT for development

Interdisciplinary research

Policy impact at international, regional and national levels

One of the Institute’s objectives is to help nurture the next generation of interdisciplinary researchers, including computing, information and social scientists and engineers working in ICT for development.

The Institute’s location in Macau also places it within the broader Greater Bay Area, a major technology and innovation hub with connections to China, Hong Kong SAR and several other Asian countries.

For the selected intern, this provides an opportunity to participate in research connected to major technological and educational developments while working within a United Nations research environment.

About the Research Internship

The Research Intern – Neuroscience, Learning and AI in Higher Education will support ongoing research under the supervision of the Institute Director.

The internship is connected to a forthcoming Springer publication on artificial intelligence and higher education, meaning the successful candidate will have an opportunity to contribute to research that may ultimately inform an academic publication.

The role combines several areas of expertise, including:

Neuroscience

Learning science

Education

Artificial intelligence

Higher education

Social science research

Education policy

Academic writing

Knowledge translation

Evidence-based policymaking

The position is therefore well suited to candidates who enjoy interdisciplinary research and are interested in translating academic evidence into practical policy and educational recommendations.

Key Responsibilities

The selected Research Intern will undertake a range of research and knowledge-production activities.

1. Conduct Literature Reviews

A major responsibility will involve conducting literature reviews and research relating to:

Neuroscience

Learning

Education

Artificial intelligence

Higher education

The intern will be expected to identify relevant academic literature, examine existing evidence, synthesize findings and help establish an evidence base for ongoing UNU research.

Strong literature-review skills will therefore be important because the role requires the ability to navigate academic research and identify information relevant to specific research questions.

2. Support Research for the Springer Book

The intern will support research and analysis contributing to a forthcoming Springer book focused on AI and higher education.

This could involve reviewing academic literature, organizing research materials, synthesizing findings and supporting the development of content for the publication.

The opportunity may therefore be particularly attractive to candidates who want experience contributing to an international academic publication.

3. Explore Neuroscience and Learning Science

The intern will examine how findings and insights from neuroscience and learning science can contribute to better educational policies and practices.

This involves exploring the relationship between how people learn, what research says about learning and cognition, and how these insights can be incorporated into education systems.

The role therefore goes beyond simply studying artificial intelligence. It requires an interdisciplinary understanding of how AI, learning, neuroscience and education intersect.

4. Contribute to Education Policy Recommendations

Another important responsibility will be contributing to policy outputs and recommendations.

The intern will explore how evidence from neuroscience and learning science can potentially inform policymaking within education.

This may include helping translate academic findings into practical recommendations that policymakers and other stakeholders can understand and potentially apply.

5. Write Blogs and Research Publications

The selected candidate will also contribute to various written knowledge products.

These may include:

Blog articles

Research papers

Journal articles

Policy outputs

Other knowledge products

This means candidates should be comfortable communicating complex academic information clearly and accurately.

Strong academic and analytical writing will be particularly important for this aspect of the internship.

6. Prepare and Analyze Research Materials

The intern will assist with the preparation, organization and analysis of research materials and evidence.

This responsibility requires attention to detail and the ability to work systematically with academic information.

Expected Outputs

During the internship, the successful candidate is expected to contribute to several research and knowledge products.

These include:

Research Briefs and Literature Reviews

The intern may contribute to research briefs and comprehensive literature reviews examining neuroscience, learning, AI and higher education.

Policy Recommendations

The intern will contribute to recommendations examining how neuroscience and learning science can be incorporated into educational policymaking.

Blog Articles and Public-Facing Content

The internship also provides an opportunity to contribute to blogs and other materials designed to communicate research findings to broader audiences.

Academic Publications

The intern may contribute to drafts or research supporting journal articles and other academic publications.

Springer Book Research

A significant component of the internship will involve research and analysis contributing to the forthcoming Springer book on artificial intelligence and higher education.

Learning Opportunities and Professional Development

The internship is designed not only to support UNU’s research activities but also to provide professional development for the selected intern.

1. Strengthen Research Skills

Interns will gain practical experience conducting research in a professional international research environment.

This can strengthen abilities in:

Literature reviews

Evidence synthesis

Research analysis

Academic writing

Research organization

Knowledge production

2. Learn to Translate Research Into Policy

One of the most valuable learning objectives is developing the ability to transform research findings into policy-relevant outputs.

This is particularly useful for individuals interested in careers involving:

Public policy

International development

Education policy

Research

Think tanks

Academia

International organizations

Technology policy

3. Gain United Nations Experience

The internship provides exposure to the working environment of the United Nations University.

Experience within a UN institution can help candidates better understand how international organizations conduct research, generate evidence and contribute to global policy discussions.

4. Work in a Multicultural Environment

UNU operates within an international and multicultural environment.

The internship therefore offers an opportunity to develop experience collaborating across different cultural, academic and professional backgrounds.

Required Qualifications

Applicants must meet the academic and professional requirements outlined for the position.

Educational Requirements

Candidates must have a Master’s degree or higher in one of the following areas:

Neuroscience

Education

Learning sciences

Psychology

Artificial intelligence

Social sciences

A related field

The interdisciplinary nature of the position means that candidates from different academic backgrounds may be considered, provided their expertise is relevant to the research focus.

Required Skills and Experience

Applicants should demonstrate strong capabilities in research and academic writing.

Key requirements include:

Strong Research Skills

Candidates should have experience conducting structured and rigorous research.

Analytical Skills

The position requires the ability to analyze academic evidence, identify important findings and synthesize information.

Academic Writing

Applicants should be capable of producing clear, well-structured academic and research-oriented writing.

Literature Review Experience

Candidates should demonstrate the ability to conduct literature reviews and synthesize findings from academic research.

Interest in Interdisciplinary Research

Applicants should have a strong interest in the intersection of:

Neuroscience + Learning + Artificial Intelligence + Higher Education

Ability to Work Independently

Because the position is remote, applicants must be able to organize their workload, manage deadlines and work effectively with limited direct supervision.

Language Requirements

Candidates must have:

Excellent written English

Excellent spoken English

Knowledge of another United Nations official language is considered an advantage.

Applicants who can demonstrate multilingual communication skills may therefore have an additional strength, although English proficiency is the primary language requirement specified for the position.

Core Values and Competencies

The internship follows UNU’s core values and competency framework.

Core Values

Candidates are expected to demonstrate:

Respect for diversity

Integrity

Professionalism

Core Competencies

The position also emphasizes:

Awareness and sensitivity regarding gender issues

Accountability

Creative problem solving

Effective communication

Inclusive collaboration

Applicants should consider demonstrating these competencies through their cover letter, CV and examples of previous research or professional work.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is open to qualified candidates who meet the stated academic and skills requirements.

Applicants should have:

A Master’s degree or above

A background in neuroscience, education, learning sciences, psychology, AI, social sciences or a related field

Strong research and analytical abilities

Strong academic writing skills

Experience conducting literature reviews

An interest in neuroscience, learning, AI and higher education

The ability to work independently in a remote environment

Excellent written and spoken English

UNU specifically states that it welcomes applications regardless of gender, nationality, religious or ethnic background, and encourages applications from persons living with disabilities.

The organization also strongly encourages applications from developing countries and women.

Therefore, the announcement does not restrict applicants to a particular continent or nationality. Qualified candidates from around the world can apply, subject to meeting the academic, skills and other requirements.

Application Requirements

Interested applicants must submit an application containing the following materials:

1. Cover Letter

Applicants should submit a brief cover letter written in English.

The cover letter should explain:

Why the applicant is interested in the internship

Their relevant qualifications

Their suitability for the research position

Their interest in neuroscience, learning, AI and higher education

The cover letter should be specifically tailored to the position rather than being a generic application letter.

2. Current CV

Applicants must submit a current and complete CV in English.

The CV should clearly demonstrate relevant:

Academic qualifications

Research experience

Publications or academic writing

Professional experience

Analytical skills

Relevant projects

Research interests

3. Examples of Relevant Research Work

Applicants must provide examples of relevant research work in English.

This could be particularly important because the internship is heavily research-focused. Candidates should therefore select examples that demonstrate their ability to conduct research, analyze evidence and communicate academic findings effectively.

Documents Required if Invited for an Interview

Candidates who are invited for an interview will be required to submit additional documentation before the interview.

These include:

Proof of Education Status

Applicants may provide documents such as:

Academic transcripts

Proof of enrollment

Other documents confirming their education status

Health and Life/Accident Insurance

Selected candidates must have health and life/accident insurance valid for the duration and location in which the internship is carried out.

This requirement should be taken seriously when preparing for the internship because the selected intern is responsible for having the required insurance coverage.

Selection and Assessment Process

UNU may assess qualified applicants through one or more stages.

The assessment process may include:

Desk review of applications

Competency-based interview

Reference checks

Candidates should therefore prepare to discuss their academic background, research experience, analytical abilities, writing skills and motivation for joining UNU.

A competency-based interview may also explore examples of how candidates have demonstrated communication, accountability, problem solving, collaboration and other relevant competencies.

Important Information About the Remote Internship

The position is explicitly described as a remote internship.

This means applicants do not need to relocate to Macau to carry out the internship.

However, candidates should understand that remote work still requires:

Reliable communication

Independent time management

Consistent availability

Ability to meet deadlines

Strong written communication

Ability to collaborate virtually

Access to an appropriate working environment

Visa and Employment Considerations

UNU states that it does not sponsor a working visa for this position.

Because this is a remote internship, applicants should carefully consider the location from which they will undertake the internship and ensure they can legally participate from that location.

The internship is also intended to complement an intern’s studies and is not intended to lead directly to further employment with UNU.

Therefore, candidates should not regard the internship as a guaranteed pathway to a permanent or temporary position within the organization.

Status of Interns at UNU

Interns should also be aware that they do not have the same status as United Nations staff members.

According to the vacancy information:

Interns may not represent UNU in an official capacity.

Interns do not hold international civil servant status.

Interns are not considered staff members under the UN Staff Rules and Regulations.

Applicants should therefore distinguish between gaining experience through a UNU internship and being employed as a member of the United Nations international civil service.

Insurance and Personal Responsibility

UNU states that it accepts no responsibility for costs arising from accidents, illness or death incurred during the internship.

Selected interns must therefore ensure that they have the required health and life/accident insurance coverage for the relevant period.

Why This Internship Could Be Valuable for Researchers

This opportunity offers several potential benefits for postgraduate researchers and early-career professionals.

International Research Exposure

Working with a United Nations University institute can provide experience in an international research environment.

Interdisciplinary Experience

The internship brings together several rapidly developing fields, including artificial intelligence, neuroscience, learning sciences and higher education.

Academic Publication Experience

Contributing to research associated with a forthcoming Springer publication can provide valuable exposure to the academic publication process.

Policy Research Experience

The role emphasizes translating research into policy recommendations, making it relevant to candidates interested in evidence-based policymaking.

Writing and Knowledge Production

Interns can gain experience producing research briefs, blogs, academic papers and other knowledge products.

Remote International Collaboration

The position provides an opportunity to develop experience working remotely in an international and multicultural setting.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants can improve their applications by making sure every document directly reflects the requirements of the internship.

Tailor Your Cover Letter

Your cover letter should clearly connect your academic background and research experience to the internship’s focus.

Rather than simply stating that you are interested in AI or education, explain how your previous work relates to the intersection of neuroscience, learning, AI and higher education.

Highlight Research Experience

Your CV should make research experience easy to identify.

Include relevant:

Research projects

Literature reviews

Publications

Academic papers

Policy research

Research reports

Data analysis

Conferences or research presentations

Select Strong Writing Samples

Because academic writing is an important requirement, choose research samples that demonstrate your ability to synthesize evidence and communicate complex ideas clearly.

Demonstrate Independent Working Ability

Since this is a remote position, applicants should demonstrate examples of successfully managing research or professional responsibilities independently.

Show Policy-Relevant Thinking

Candidates can strengthen their application by demonstrating that they understand the importance of translating research into practical recommendations for policymakers, institutions and other stakeholders.

Application Deadline and Key Dates

Applicants should take note of the following dates:

Application deadline: September 18, 2026

Deadline time: 11:59 p.m. Macau time (GMT+8)

Expected start date: October 5, 2026

Expected end date: December 4, 2026

Duration: 2 months

Mode: Remote

Because the application page will no longer be operational after the deadline, applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their materials.

Scam Warning

Applicants should be alert to recruitment scams.

UNU states that it does not charge application, processing, training, interviewing, testing or other recruitment fees.

Applicants should therefore be cautious of anyone requesting payment in exchange for:

Application processing

Interview invitations

Recruitment

Training

Testing

Selection

Placement

Applicants should also be careful when providing personal information because organizational names, logos, addresses and other identifying information can be copied and misused by scammers.

Applications should be submitted through the official UNU recruitment platform.

Visit HERE for more information about the Remote Research Internship at United Nations University.

Application Link

Interested candidates should apply through the official United Nations University careers platform and carefully review the vacancy requirements before submitting their application.

Apply for the UNU Remote Research Internship

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The United Nations University Remote Research Internship in Neuroscience, Learning and AI in Higher Education offers an interdisciplinary research opportunity for Master’s-level and above candidates interested in the rapidly evolving relationship between artificial intelligence, neuroscience, learning and higher education.

The two-month remote internship will allow the successful candidate to contribute to research supporting a forthcoming Springer publication while developing practical skills in literature reviews, evidence synthesis, academic writing, policy research and knowledge production. The opportunity also provides exposure to a United Nations research environment and experience working within an international, multicultural setting.

With applications closing on September 18, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Macau time (GMT+8), eligible candidates should prepare their cover letter, CV and relevant research samples early and ensure that their application clearly demonstrates the research and academic capabilities required for the role.

TITLE: Advancing Gender Equality in Sport: Highlights from the SUPPORTER Final Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
News

As coordinator of the EU-funded SUPPORTER project, the European Science Foundation (ESF) has been proud to lead efforts to advance gender equality in sports higher education institutions across Central and Eastern Europe. Drawing on its extensive expertise, ESF also led the communication work package and successfully organised the final conference, which brought together 160 participants to share achievements, lessons learned, and commitments for the future.
The project aims to support 8 partners developing their own Intersectional, Innovative, Inclusive and Impactful Gender Equality Plans (4I-GEPs), explicitly addressing gender-based violence and sexual harassment.

Conference highlights

On 4-5 June 2025, the SUPPORTER community gathered in Prague for its Final Conference, hosted by Charles University. The participants included students, researchers, university staff, policymakers, and gender equality practitioners. The event offered two days of insightful exchange and learning.

4 June – Creating safe and inclusive ecosystems in sports and higher education: How students can make a difference

This session explored how students are shaping change within their institutions and communities. From student-led initiatives to peer-to-peer interventions, participants shared practical strategies and personal experiences demonstrating the power of youth-led advocacy in preventing gender-based violence and promoting inclusive practices.

Watch the recording

5 June – Advancing Gender Equality Plans in widening higher education institutions: challenges, insights, and strategies

The second day brought together diverse voices from the SUPPORTER consortium and sister projects to reflect on GEP implementation in sports, agriculture, and research-focused institutions. The sessions provided valuable insights into overcoming structural and cultural barriers and highlighted adaptable models for institutional transformation.

Building Gender Equality in Sports Higher Education

The reflections and shared experiences from the Final Conference reinforced the need for ongoing, practical support in transforming institutions. To this end, SUPPORTER has developed a series of capacity-building and mentoring videos designed to help sports higher education institutions create or strengthen their Gender Equality Plans (GEPs).

Watch the videos and learn more on the SUPPORTER website

To make its work widely accessible , SUPPORTER has produced a set of resources to support institutional transformation:

Training materials and tools for institutional transformation– A comprehensive overview of existing approaches and gaps in gender equality within sports higher education.

Training materials and tools for institutional transformation – Practical tools for building institutional capacity and fostering inclusive change.

Capacity Building Scheme – A structured approach to strengthen skills and knowledge among project partners and stakeholders.

Report on the design of the institutional roadmaps – Insights and strategies for co-designing (4I-GEPs).

Policy Brief 1 – Key recommendations and policy messages to support gender equality in sports education.

TITLE: Fulbright Global Scholar Award

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Fulbright Global Scholar Award allows U.S. academics and professionals to engage in multi-country, trans-regional projects. As a truly worldwide award, U.S. scholars will be able to propose research or combined teaching/research activity in two to three countries within two different world regions with flexible schedule options; trips can be conducted within one academic year or spread over two consecutive years.

Applications are welcome from a wide range of scholars – early career, professor emeriti, independent scholars – and from all disciplines, including those with an interdisciplinary focus.
