TITLE: How to Apply for Postgraduate Research at the University of Sydney: Complete Guide to PhD, Joint PhD and Research Master’s Applications

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Sydney offers a range of higher degree by research (HDR) opportunities for students seeking to undertake advanced academic research, including Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), Joint PhD, Master’s by Research, and Master of Philosophy (MPhil) programs. These research degrees are designed for students who want to develop substantial expertise in a particular field while conducting an original research project under academic supervision.

For prospective research students, applying successfully involves more than simply submitting an online application. Applicants are expected to demonstrate previous research experience, strong academic performance, the ability to develop a meaningful research proposal, and a suitable relationship with a potential academic supervisor.

This comprehensive guide explains the University of Sydney postgraduate research application process, including eligibility requirements, research proposal development, finding a supervisor, required documents, application timing, scholarships and financial assistance, and additional requirements for international students.

University of Sydney Postgraduate Research Opportunities

A higher degree by research at the University of Sydney can include:

Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)

Joint PhD programs

Master’s by Research

Master of Philosophy (MPhil)

The University states that the general application process applies to most research courses and is intended for both domestic and international research students. However, individual faculties and schools may have additional admission requirements or variations in their procedures.

Applicants interested in research degrees in areas such as architecture, arts and social sciences, business, engineering and computer science, law, medicine and health, music, and science should therefore check the requirements of their intended course and faculty carefully.

Important Exception: Sydney Law School and Business School

Applicants interested in postgraduate research through the Sydney Law School or Business School should note that their application process differs from the general process.

For these schools, applicants first apply for their course. If they are successful, a supervisor will then be allocated to them. This differs from the general process, where applicants normally need to secure a supervisor before submitting their application.

Step 1: Check Your Eligibility

One of the most important parts of preparing an application is determining whether you meet the University’s academic and research requirements.

For postgraduate research study, the University states that applicants need previous research experience and a high academic record.

Previous Research Experience

Applicants should have completed a significant research project or thesis during their previous university-level studies.

Acceptable preparation may include:

An Australian honours degree

A master’s by research degree

A master’s by coursework that includes a substantial thesis or dissertation component

The purpose of this requirement is to demonstrate that applicants have already developed experience conducting academic research and are prepared for the demands of a higher research degree.

This means that prospective PhD or research master’s applicants should not focus only on their final grades. Their previous research experience is also an important part of demonstrating research capability.

Academic Requirements for Postgraduate Research

The University also places considerable importance on academic performance.

For the general postgraduate research requirements, applicants are expected to have a bachelor’s degree with first-class honours, with equivalent standards determined for students from other institutions. The University provides the following guide based on its grading system:

WAM of 75 over the degree

Honours Class I: WAM greater than 80

Honours Class II: WAM between 75 and 80

Equivalent qualifications from other institutions may be assessed according to the University’s requirements.

PhD Eligibility

Applicants seeking admission to a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) need to demonstrate sufficient previous research experience and capability.

In most cases, applicants will have one of the following:

A bachelor’s degree with first-class honours;

A master’s degree completed to a high academic standard that contains a substantial research component; or

An equivalent qualification demonstrating research experience, academic excellence and research capability.

Therefore, prospective PhD applicants should be prepared to demonstrate not only academic excellence but also their ability to undertake independent and substantial research.

Eligibility for a Master’s by Research or Master of Philosophy

Applicants interested in a Master’s by Research or Master of Philosophy (MPhil) will generally need one of the following:

A bachelor’s degree with first- or second-class honours from the University of Sydney or another approved institution; or

An equivalent qualification demonstrating sufficient research experience and capability.

Applicants should still check the individual course requirements because specific faculties or programs may have additional admission criteria.

English Language Requirements

English language requirements vary depending on:

The specific course;

The applicant’s country of origin; and

Their previous educational background.

Applicants whose circumstances require proof of English proficiency should determine what evidence is required for their particular course.

International applicants should therefore check the English-language requirements well before submitting their application, particularly if their previous education was not conducted in English.

Joint PhD Opportunities

Students interested in a Joint PhD must initially follow Steps 1 to 3 of the University’s standard PhD application process.

There is an additional process for Joint PhD applicants. The proposed supervisor must complete a proposal to negotiate a student agreement form. If the proposal is accepted, the student must also sign an individual student agreement.

Once the student agreement has been finalised, the applicant will receive an application form for the Joint PhD program.

Applicants interested in this route should therefore allow additional time for discussions with their proposed supervisor and the formalisation of the relevant agreement.

Step 2: Develop a Strong Research Proposal

After establishing eligibility, the next major step is to develop a research proposal.

The University recommends carefully considering the subject of the proposed research project and beginning to develop a proposal that can be shared with potential academic supervisors.

A research proposal is important because it allows you to communicate:

What you want to research;

Why the topic is important;

What you intend to investigate;

Why your proposed research is worthwhile;

How the project relates to existing academic work; and

How your proposed research aligns with the research interests of a potential supervisor.

The University also notes that an initial proposal will likely evolve as discussions with the supervisor progress. Therefore, applicants should not necessarily expect their first version to be the final version.

The important point is to begin with a clear research idea and demonstrate why the proposed project is significant and appropriate for postgraduate research.

Step 3: Find a Suitable Research Supervisor

For most postgraduate research applications at the University of Sydney, applicants need to secure a supervisor before submitting their application.

The main exceptions are applicants to the Sydney Law School and Business School, where students apply for the course first and are allocated a supervisor if successful.

Finding an appropriate supervisor is therefore one of the most important stages of the application.

How to Search for a Supervisor

The University provides Sydney Profiles, where prospective research students can identify academics and explore research supervision opportunities.

Applicants can search using:

The name of a particular academic; or

A general keyword related to their research area.

For example, an applicant researching a particular scientific or engineering topic could use relevant keywords to identify academics working in that area.

The search can then be refined using filters such as:

Faculty and School;

Availability; and

Research supervision.

Applicants can also combine multiple keywords to make the search more specific.

What to Include When Contacting a Potential Supervisor

Finding an academic whose research interests match your proposed topic is only the beginning. Applicants should prepare a professional enquiry explaining why they are contacting that particular academic.

The University recommends providing information about:

Your academic background;

Your previous research experience;

The research topic you want to investigate;

How your proposed research aligns with the supervisor’s research;

Your CV or resume;

Academic transcripts for all degrees; and

Your initial research proposal.

This alignment is particularly important. A strong academic record alone does not necessarily demonstrate that a particular supervisor is suitable for your project. Your proposal should connect meaningfully with the academic’s research interests, projects or expertise.

Step 4: Submit the Application Online

Postgraduate research degree applications at the University of Sydney are open throughout the year.

However, most research intakes begin during:

Research Period 2 — March

Research Period 3 — July

Applicants should check the research periods available for their specific faculty and course because not every program necessarily follows exactly the same schedule.

The University recommends applying as early as possible before the intended start date.

Applicants should also discuss their intended start date with their proposed supervisor.

Is There a General Application Deadline?

The source does not state one single general deadline for all postgraduate research applications.

Instead, applications are described as being open throughout the year, while individual research periods and funding opportunities may have their own relevant dates.

Important Scholarship Deadline Consideration

Applicants who want to be considered for the Research Training Program (RTP) stipend must submit their application by the relevant RTP dates.

The University explains that applicants may still submit their course application after an RTP deadline, but their stipend outcome will not be provided until the next round of RTP rankings.

Therefore, students seeking funding should not wait until the last possible moment to submit their research degree application.

Deadline: No single general postgraduate research application deadline is stated in the provided source. RTP scholarship applicants must follow the applicable RTP dates.

Documents Required for a University of Sydney Research Degree Application

Once a supervisor has been secured and the research project has been refined, applicants need to prepare the required supporting documentation.

The University identifies several important categories of documents.

1. Research Proposal

The research proposal should be finalised in conjunction with the supervisor.

The University specifies a proposal of up to 2,000 words, covering the objectives and significance of the proposed research.

The proposal should therefore communicate the central purpose and value of the research project clearly.

2. Evidence of Supervisor Agreement

Applicants need evidence that a primary supervisor has agreed to supervise them.

This may take the form of email correspondence showing that the staff member has agreed to supervise the applicant.

The Sydney Conservatorium of Music may have an additional interview requirement.

3. Referee Reports

Applicants must provide two referee reports using the University’s specified forms.

Applicants should therefore identify appropriate academic referees in advance and allow enough time for them to complete and submit their reports.

4. Academic Transcripts

Applicants must provide official academic transcripts.

These transcripts need to be supplied:

In the original language; and

With an English translation where applicable.

5. English Language Evidence

Applicants must provide proof of English language proficiency if English is not their first language and the course requires such evidence.

6. CV or Resume

A curriculum vitae or resume is also required as part of the application documentation.

The CV should provide a clear picture of the applicant’s academic background and relevant research experience.

7. Additional Course-Specific Documents

Some courses may require additional materials.

Depending on the program, these could include:

A portfolio;

An audition; or

Other documents specified in the relevant course listing.

Applicants should therefore check their specific degree page rather than assuming that the general documentation list covers every requirement.

General Documents Applicants Need to Prepare

The application also requires proof of identity.

Examples include:

A valid passport biodata page;

An Australian birth certificate; or

An Australian or New Zealand citizenship certificate for domestic students.

Domestic applicants seeking part-time study also need to provide a statement demonstrating that they have sufficient time available to conduct their research under University supervision and complete the degree within the maximum permitted period for part-time PhD enrolment.

Additional Requirements for International Students

International applicants should pay particular attention to the additional requirements associated with studying in Australia.

According to the provided information, international students will need to address immigration and application requirements after receiving an admission offer or an electronic Confirmation of Enrolment (eCoE).

They will need to apply for the appropriate student visa after receiving the necessary admission documentation.

Application Processing Fee

International applicants are also required to pay a non-refundable application processing fee.

However, the source states that this fee can be waived in certain circumstances, including where:

The applicant is a sponsored student; or

A University staff member grants an exemption during an office interview or recruitment event.

International applicants may also use an authorised University of Sydney agent where appropriate. The University has partnered with authorised agents who can assist with applications and arrangements on behalf of students.

Scholarships and Financial Assistance for Postgraduate Research

Funding is an important consideration for students pursuing research degrees.

The University of Sydney states that it has one of the largest research scholarship schemes in Australia. Research scholarships may help students finance their research or meet living costs while undertaking their studies.

Scholarships may be:

Specific to a particular research project;

Specific to a particular discipline; or

Awarded based on academic merit and research potential.

This means that prospective applicants should investigate available funding opportunities alongside their course application.

Stipend Scholarships

The University also offers competitive stipend scholarships designed to provide an allowance that assists with living costs.

These awards are based on factors including:

Academic merit; and

Research potential.

Applicants seeking these scholarships must complete the additional scholarship form as part of the course application process.

Funding for Domestic Students

Domestic students do not pay tuition fees and are awarded an RTP Fees Offset under the Australian Government’s Research Training Program.

Funding for International Students

International students are required to pay tuition fees, with fee estimates available through the individual course pages.

However, international applicants can apply for scholarship packages that may provide:

A stipend scholarship to assist with relocation and living costs; and

A tuition fee scholarship.

These scholarship packages are described as highly competitive and have limited places.

Applicants who require financial assistance should therefore research funding opportunities early and pay close attention to scholarship-specific deadlines.

Research Ethics and Additional Approvals

Some research projects may involve additional ethical or institutional requirements.

For example, applicants conducting research involving fieldwork in the New South Wales hospital and education systems may be required to pass health and security checks. Additional admission criteria may also be specified by the individual course.

Depending on the nature of the research, students may also need approval from relevant ethics committees.

The University specifically notes that research involving human participants or animals may require approval from:

The Animal Ethics Committee; and/or

The Human Research Ethics Committee.

This is particularly important for applicants whose proposed research involves people, personal information, clinical environments, animals, or other ethically sensitive research activities.

Which Faculties Offer Postgraduate Research Opportunities?

The University provides faculty-specific information for postgraduate research across a wide range of academic disciplines.

Applicants can find additional information for:

Architecture, Design and Planning

Arts and Social Sciences

Business

Engineering and Computer Science

Law

Medicine and Health

Music

Science

Because individual faculties may have different admission requirements or application procedures, prospective students should use the relevant faculty or course page to confirm their requirements before applying.

How to Make Your Application Stronger

Although meeting the formal requirements is essential, prospective applicants should also approach the application strategically.

1. Start With a Clear Research Idea

Before approaching supervisors, develop a research idea that clearly identifies the issue you want to investigate.

Your idea should be specific enough to form the basis of a research project but flexible enough to evolve through discussions with your supervisor.

2. Demonstrate Research Experience

Previous research experience is a major component of the University’s eligibility requirements.

Applicants should therefore clearly communicate relevant:

Theses;

Dissertations;

Research projects;

Academic research experience; and

Other substantial research work.

3. Choose Supervisors Carefully

Do not simply contact academics because they work within your general discipline.

Instead, look for meaningful overlap between:

Your proposed research + the academic’s research expertise + the academic’s current research projects.

The University specifically encourages applicants to explain how their proposed research aligns with the work of their proposed supervisor.

4. Prepare Your Documents Early

Applicants should begin preparing transcripts, CVs, research proposals, referee reports and evidence of supervisor support well before the intended submission date.

This is especially important for international applicants who may also need to consider English-language evidence, application processing requirements and visa processing times.

The University recommends international applicants factor Department of Home Affairs visa processing times into their planning when considering a likely start date.

5. Consider Funding at the Same Time as Admission

Students who require financial support should not treat scholarship applications as an afterthought.

Because RTP and other scholarship opportunities can have separate deadlines and competitive ranking processes, applicants should investigate funding requirements before submitting their course application.

Application Timeline: What Prospective Students Should Do

A practical approach to the University of Sydney postgraduate research application process is:

Stage 1: Identify your research area

Determine the discipline and broad subject you want to investigate.

Stage 2: Confirm eligibility

Check your academic qualifications, research experience, academic performance and English-language requirements.

Stage 3: Develop an initial research proposal

Create a clear proposal explaining the research problem, objectives and significance.

Stage 4: Search for potential supervisors

Use Sydney Profiles to identify academics whose research interests align with your proposed project.

Stage 5: Contact potential supervisors

Send a professional enquiry accompanied by your CV, transcripts and initial research proposal.

Stage 6: Refine the research project

Work with the prospective supervisor to improve and finalise your research proposal.

Stage 7: Prepare supporting documentation

Gather transcripts, referee reports, proof of English proficiency where required, identity documents and any course-specific materials.

Stage 8: Apply online

Submit your postgraduate research application through the University’s online application process.

Stage 9: Apply for relevant funding

Complete the additional scholarship requirements if you wish to be considered for available research scholarships.

Stage 10: Prepare for additional requirements

International applicants should plan for visa requirements, while applicants whose research involves humans, animals or certain fieldwork environments should consider the relevant ethics and approval requirements.

Deadline for University of Sydney Postgraduate Research Applications

There is no single general deadline stated in the provided source for all postgraduate research degree applications.

Instead, applications are open throughout the year, with research intakes generally taking place in March and July. Applicants are advised to check their specific course and faculty requirements and apply as early as possible before their intended start date.

However, applicants seeking consideration for an RTP stipend must follow the applicable RTP submission dates. Applications submitted after the relevant RTP deadline may still be considered for admission, but the applicant’s stipend outcome will be considered in a subsequent RTP ranking round.

Deadline: No universal postgraduate research application deadline is specified in the source; scholarship applicants should check the applicable RTP and course-specific deadlines.

Who Can Apply?

The University of Sydney’s postgraduate research application process is available to both domestic and international research students.

Academic qualifications

Depending on the degree, applicants generally need:

Previous significant research experience;

A strong academic record;

Appropriate bachelor’s honours or master’s-level qualifications for PhD study; or

A bachelor’s degree with first- or second-class honours, or equivalent research capability, for a research master’s/MPhil.

LEARN MORE HERE

Geographic eligibility

The provided source does not identify a restricted list of countries or a particular continent from which applicants must come. It explicitly describes the process as being open to both domestic and international research students.

Race or ethnicity

The provided source does not specify a race or ethnic group restriction for postgraduate research admission.

International applicants

International students can apply, but they may have additional requirements involving:

English-language proficiency;

Application processing fees;

Student visa arrangements;

Tuition fees; and

Potential international scholarship opportunities.

Conclusion

Pursuing a postgraduate research degree at the University of Sydney can provide an opportunity to undertake advanced independent research through a PhD, Joint PhD, Master’s by Research or Master of Philosophy. However, applicants should understand that the process involves considerably more than completing an online form.

A competitive application begins with the right academic preparation and research experience, followed by the development of a strong research proposal and identification of an appropriate supervisor. Applicants then need to refine their project with their supervisor and prepare the required academic, research and personal documentation before submitting the application.

The University accepts postgraduate research applications throughout the year, although individual courses and research periods may have specific requirements. Students seeking scholarships, particularly RTP funding, need to pay close attention to the relevant funding deadlines because scholarship consideration may operate on a different timeline from general course admission.

For international applicants, additional planning is particularly important because English-language requirements, application fees, tuition costs, scholarships and visa processing may all affect the application timeline.

Ultimately, prospective applicants should begin early, carefully examine their intended course and faculty requirements, identify supervisors whose research aligns with their interests, develop a well-defined proposal, and prepare all supporting documentation before submission. With careful planning, the University of Sydney’s postgraduate research pathway can provide a structured route toward advanced academic research and higher-degree study.

TITLE: CTP-LI Guidelines for Graduate Students

Fall 2026

Students in the CTP-LI should always be in close contact with their academic advisor, even more so before they join a research group. You should also consult the Department’s PhD guidelines and be in contact with the Department’s Academic Programs Office should you have questions/concerns going forward. If not specified, the information applies to both groups.

Students often have a fellowship their first year, in which case no teaching is required.

Fall:

Take written exams (strongly recommended).

Depending on preparation, either take Quantum Field Theory II (8.324) at MIT, or else take QFT 1 at Harvard, or Quantum Theory I (8.321) at MIT.

Take one breadth class.

Take classes to cover written exams (8.309 for Classical Mechanics, 8.321 for Quantum Mechanics, 8.333 for Statistical Mechanics).

Attend seminars, meet fellow graduate students, postdocs and faculty in the Department.

Spring:

In January, must take written exams for any parts not yet passed; can take 8.311 for Electromagnetism during spring term.

If prepared, take QFT III (8.325) at MIT. Otherwise take QFT I (8.323) at MIT or maybe QFT 2 at Harvard. If taking QFT 3, maybe also listen to QFT 1 at MIT, or QFT 2 at Harvard.

Take breadth class.

Meet with potential PhD research advisors.

Prepare research project for summer with one or more research supervisors.

Summer:

Start research project.

Study for written exam if you still have some subjects to take.

Second Year (N&P)

Fall:

Take written exam if needed.

Take QFT 2 at MIT if needed.

If ready, think about taking oral exam.

Work on research, TA if required to.

Spring:

Take QFT 3 at MIT if needed

Summer:

RESEARCH

Finish any required classes you might have left.

Work on research, TA if required

Second and final opportunity to pass oral exam, if needed.

Students should expect to graduate in their fifth year. Should circumstances arise that may affect this time frame, the students needs to discuss the matter with their research advisor and Scott Morley.

Classes (Nuclear and Particle theory):

Please refer to the Department web sites on PhD requirements, but classes required in the CTP-LI are:
• QFT 3 at MIT
• Two additional specialty (specialty= depth)classes, most often satisfied by selecting two from the following list:

8.334 Statistical Mechanics II

8.821 String Theory

8.831 Supersymmetric Quantum Field Theory

8.841 Electroweak Interactions

8.851 Effective Field Theory

8.701 Intro to Nuclear and Particle Physics

8.952 Particle Physics of the Early Universe

8.962 General Relativity.

Several of these courses are only offered every two or three years, including 8.821, 8.831, 8.841, 8.851, and 8.952. The course 8.701 is most often taught by an experimental nuclear or particle physicist, and hence is a good way for theorists to get exposure to an experimental point of view. Other special topics courses relevant for CTP-LI students are also occasionally offered, and can be used to satisfy a specialty requirement with permission from a student’s academic advisor, and subsequent approval by the CTP-LI director.

● Two breadth classes: Breadth courses are intended to provide a broad introduction to a field other than the student’s specialty. Subjects that are designed for specialists in an area are not appropriate for the breadth requirement. Possible courses include Quantum Computation, Astro I or II (I is not a prerequisite for II, despite what the course catalog says), Theory of Solids I, Plasma Physics, a Biophysics course, or Atomic & Optical physics I or II. Courses not on the list can be approved with permission of your academic supervisor, and the department’s General Exam and Requirements Coordinator; if you have any questions about the process for requesting a substitution, be sure to check with the Academic Programs Office request.

Students are encouraged to visit the website for more information about the course requirements.

Oral Qualifying Exam (Nuclear and Particle theory):
NOTE: Information on the exam which was updated in 2023 is here.

Nuclear and Particle Theory (NUPAT) students, like all students in the Physics Department, are required to pass an oral examination in their sub-field.The first attempt at the oral exam must be taken by the end of the first term of the third year. Two attempts are permitted, with the second attempt scheduled in the subsequent term. If the subsequent term precedes the third year, a student may postpone the second attempt until the beginning of the third year.

The exam is administered by the Oral Exam Committee, composed of three faculty members. Should the student’s research advisor be a member of that committee, another faculty member will be substituted in place of the advisor.

The exams are scheduled at the beginning of the Fall or Spring term and will take place in December and May, respectively. The NUPAT oral exam consists of two parts:

(1) A short exposition on a question or topic assigned to the student by the Head of the Oral Committee no later than two weeks before the exam.

(2) A set of questions on theoretical nuclear and particle physics posed by the committee.

Passing of the exam will depend on the student’s performance in the assigned question, as well as their proficiency in theoretical nuclear physics and theoretical particle physics. The topics and questions are drawn primarily from material covered in NUPAT graduate classes, with emphasis on 8.325 and Field Theory of the Standard Model. If you have a question about whether some particular material should be studied for the exam, then you should ask the current head of the NUPAT Oral Exam committee.

The exam is most often 120 minutes in duration and results are communicated to the student at the completion of the exam.

Furthermore, please note that more senior CTP-LI students have a list of suggested books, material, and a shared Dropbox with previous questions that is helpful for studying. Additional suggestions:

Students are encouraged to form study groups for the oral exam. It is an excellent way to learn.

Students should talk to more senior graduate students about what the exam has covered in past years, and consult the above-mentioned documents.

Talk to your committee before taking your exam to discuss your topic and any suggested material.

Ask faculty if you have questions. If they have time, they are always happy to help.

TITLE: Tracking a large‐scale and highly toxic Arctic algal bloom: Rapid detection and risk communication

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Fachon, E., Pickart, R., Sheffield, G., Pate, E., Pathare, M., Brosnahan, M., Muhlbach, E., Horn, K., Spada, N., Rajagopalan, A., Lin, P., McRaven, L., Lago, L., Huang, J., Bahr, F., Stockwell, D., Hubbard, K., Farrugia, T., Lefebvre, K., & Anderson, D. (2024). Tracking a large‐scale and highly toxic Arctic algal bloom: Rapid detection and risk communication. Limnology and Oceanography Letters. https://doi.org/10.1002/lol2.10421

Surface currents associated with initial bloom detection (23–28 July 2022) of a toxic bloom of the dinoflagellate Alexandrium catenella in the northern Bering Sea. Alexandrium catenella cell abundance is indicated by colored points and black arrows indicate surface (top 25 m) current velocities measured by the shipboard acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP). This study tracked the bloom over six weeks as it advected northward into Arctic waters. Figure provided by Evie Fachon.

Climate warming is expanding the potential for harmful algal blooms (HABs) to occur in polar waters, raising significant concerns about emerging human and ecosystem health impacts. Recent observations of HAB species and algal toxins in Arctic waters have established a clear need for a better understanding of bloom dynamics coupled with detection and mitigation strategies. During summer 2022, a massive bloom of the toxic dinoflagellate Alexandrium catenella was detected as it moved through the Bering Strait region. This bloom was exceptional in scale, density, and toxicity, far exceeding any events reported previously in Arctic waters. This unprecedented risk to the remote coastal communities of the region was communicated in near real time, providing the opportunity for rapid mobilization and establishing a framework for future event response. This research represents a highly interdisciplinary collaboration between biological and physical oceanography, as well as coastal stakeholders.

TITLE: Africa Economic Analyst Job at NRGI in Ghana: Earn $34,236 Per Year and Work on Natural Resource Governance

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Natural Resource Governance Institute (NRGI) is inviting applications for an Africa Economic Analyst position based in Accra, Ghana. The role presents an opportunity for an experienced economic and policy professional to contribute to research, technical assistance, policy reform, advocacy, and capacity development relating to natural resource governance in Ghana and across Africa.

The position is particularly relevant to professionals with substantial experience in economic analysis, extractive industry governance, revenue management, oil and gas, mining and minerals, energy transition, transition minerals, public financial management, taxation, or related policy fields.

The successful candidate will join NRGI’s Regional Programs team, work closely with the Ghana Country Manager, and have matrix reporting responsibilities to a Senior Economic Analyst. The position combines economic research, quantitative and qualitative analysis, policy advice, stakeholder engagement, project management, technical assistance, and strategic communications.

The advertised starting salary is US$34,236 gross per year, in addition to a range of employee benefits, including health insurance, a 10% employer pension contribution, extensive leave, and two weeks of annual office closure.

Applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, meaning applicants are encouraged to submit their applications as soon as possible. No specific closing date is provided in the vacancy information.

About the Natural Resource Governance Institute

The Natural Resource Governance Institute (NRGI) is an international non-profit organization focused on helping countries rich in oil, gas, and minerals achieve sustainable and inclusive development.

NRGI works on improving the governance of natural resources by combining country-level expertise with international policy engagement. Its work is particularly relevant in a period when the global energy transition is changing the way economies approach oil, gas, minerals, energy systems, investment, and public revenues.

The organization draws on extensive experience in natural resource governance and works with a wide range of stakeholders, including:

Government institutions and policymakers

National institutions

Civil society organizations

Development partners

Private-sector organizations

Communities affected by natural resource development

Women and youth groups

Media organizations

Climate and development-sector actors

Other policy and economic stakeholders

Through its work, NRGI seeks to support effective policies, stronger institutions, informed decision-making, and better outcomes from natural resource wealth.

About the Africa Economic Analyst Position

The Africa Economic Analyst will be based in Accra, Ghana, and will work within NRGI’s Regional Programs team.

The position has a strong focus on economic and policy analysis related to natural resources and the changing economic environment created by the global energy transition.

The successful candidate will contribute to NRGI’s analytical and policy work in Ghana while also supporting selected initiatives across Africa.

The role will involve examining issues such as:

Revenue management

Optimal utilization of natural resource revenues

Oil and gas

Mining and minerals

Extractive industry governance

Energy transition

Transition minerals

Economic and financial analysis

Public policy

Extractives-sector developments

Natural resource governance at national, regional, and global levels

The analyst will be expected to turn complex economic information and datasets into useful analysis that can support policy development, institutional capacity, advocacy, and decision-making.

Key Areas of Work

The Africa Economic Analyst will contribute to both research and practical policy engagement. This makes the position suitable for an experienced professional who can move between detailed economic analysis and communication with policymakers and other stakeholders.

1. Economic Research and Analysis

A major component of the position involves conducting strategic economic research and quantitative and qualitative analysis.

The analyst will examine issues connected to:

Extractive industries

Natural resource governance

Energy transition

Transition minerals

Revenue management

Mine and mineral economics

Project economics

Related economic and policy issues

The successful candidate will need to work with complex information and translate research findings into practical insights that can support policy and institutional decisions.

2. Economic and Financial Modelling

The role requires experience with economic and financial analysis, including the ability to develop or adapt models.

The analyst will work with complex datasets relating to mines, minerals, and project economics. This requires the ability to collect information from multiple sources, analyze it systematically, identify important trends, and synthesize the findings into meaningful conclusions.

Strong quantitative skills will therefore be important for successfully performing the role.

3. Research and Thought Leadership

The Africa Economic Analyst will produce a variety of written materials to communicate research and policy findings.

These may include:

Research reports

Policy briefs

Blog articles

Opinion pieces

Thought-leadership materials

Other analytical and communications outputs

The successful candidate must therefore be capable of explaining complex economic and policy subjects clearly to different audiences.

4. Policy Advice and Technical Assistance

The analyst will provide economic analysis, policy advice, and technical assistance in support of NRGI’s Ghana program.

This will involve helping decision-makers and other stakeholders understand economic and policy issues and supporting practical approaches to improving natural resource governance.

The position also involves contributing to regional work where the analyst’s expertise is relevant.

5. Training and Capacity Development

Another important responsibility will be supporting capacity-development initiatives.

The analyst may be involved in designing and delivering:

Technical-assistance activities

Training programs

Workshops

Conferences

Stakeholder dialogues

Other capacity-building interventions

The ability to communicate technical economic concepts to stakeholders with different levels of expertise will therefore be important.

6. Project Management

The successful candidate will also be responsible for managing different aspects of projects.

This can include:

Managing project activities

Coordinating consultants

Managing budgets

Tracking timelines

Preparing reports

Monitoring project progress

Supporting monitoring, evaluation, and learning activities

Applicants should therefore be comfortable managing multiple responsibilities while maintaining quality and meeting deadlines.

7. Funding and Donor Engagement

The role includes contributing to funding proposals and donor engagement.

The analyst may support the development of proposals, provide relevant technical information, and help ensure that projects comply with donor requirements.

An understanding of development-sector processes and the ability to work with institutional partners will therefore be useful.

8. Stakeholder Engagement

The Africa Economic Analyst will build and maintain relationships with a wide range of stakeholders in Ghana and across relevant regional initiatives.

These stakeholders may include:

Government officials

National institutions

Civil society organizations

Development partners

Media organizations

Women and youth groups

Private-sector representatives

Policy experts

Other organizations involved in natural resource governance

Strong interpersonal and relationship-building skills will be important because the position requires regular engagement with people from different professional and institutional backgrounds.

9. Advocacy and Communications

The successful candidate will also contribute to advocacy and communications strategies.

This includes helping communicate research findings to diverse audiences and ensuring that technical economic research can contribute to broader policy discussions.

The ability to present complex information in an accessible and persuasive manner will therefore be valuable.

10. Representation of NRGI

The analyst may represent NRGI at relevant:

Conferences

Policy forums

Networking events

Stakeholder meetings

Other professional and policy engagements

This responsibility requires confidence in communicating NRGI’s research and policy perspectives in professional settings.

Required Professional Experience

The Africa Economic Analyst position is intended for an experienced professional rather than an entry-level applicant.

Applicants must have a minimum of five years of experience working as an economic analyst in international development.

TITLE: AAU President, Prof. Kenneth Matengu and AAU Ambassador Prof. Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, Attain Key Global Leadership Roles on ACU Council

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) celebrates a proud and historic moment for African higher education. Two of our most distinguished leaders have ascended to high office within the Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU), placing the continent’s voice at the very heart of one of the world’s oldest and most influential university networks. This dual achievement highlights the global recognition of the leadership cultivated within the AAU’s membership and underscores our collective commitment to shaping the future of higher education worldwide.

Professor Kenneth Matengu, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Namibia and the elected President of the AAU Governing Board, was elected to the ACU Council in July 2025. He currently serves as a Council Member and Trustee, representing Constituency III – comprising East, West and Southern Africa – for a three-year term from 01 August 2025 to 31 July 2028. In a related recent and prestigious development, Professor Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ghana and the AAU Ambassador for Gender Equity & Social Inclusion, has been elected as the Chair of the ACU Council. She will provide strategic leadership for an initial two-year term, effective 1 January 2026, after having served as a valuable member of the Council since August 2024.

A Powerful Convergence of Governance and Advocacy

These appointments are not just personal accolades; they represent a strategic alignment of the AAU’s core missions on a global platform. Prof. Kenneth Matengu brings to the ACU Council his dynamic vision as the youngest-ever AAU President and his deep commitment to pan-African collaboration. His leadership is instrumental in driving initiatives that strengthen universities across the continent. Upon his election, Prof. Matengu stated his focus would be on “supporting postgraduate education and research, especially as Africa works to produce the next generation of doctoral graduates needed to realise our continent’s vision for the future.”

Prof. Nana Aba Appiah Amfo ascends to the ACU Chairmanship as a proven leader and a powerful voice for the values the AAU champions. Her role as our Ambassador for Gender Equity & Social Inclusion is a testament to her lifelong commitment to these principles. In her new role, she aims to “strengthen collaboration, advance equity and inclusion and ensure that higher education continues to serve as a powerful force for sustainable development and societal transformation.”

A Statement from the AAU Secretariat

The AAU community is immensely proud of Professors Matengu and Amfo. Their elections are a resounding endorsement of African leadership and the relevance of our continental agenda. To have our Board President on the ACU Council and our Ambassador for Gender Equity assuming its Chairmanship creates a unique and powerful synergy. It ensures that Africa’s priorities, from building research capacity to championing inclusive education, will be advocated for at the highest level of Commonwealth dialogue. This is a victory for every AAU member institution.

Celebrating Our Members, Elevating Our Continent

As the apex organisation for higher education in Africa, the AAU exists to connect, support, and celebrate the achievements of its members. The global recognition of Prof. Matengu and Prof. Amfo is a direct reflection of the excellence nurtured within the University of Namibia and the University of Ghana. We extend our heartfelt congratulations to these esteemed institutions for fostering such exemplary leadership.

We look forward to the strengthened partnership between the AAU and the ACU under this joint leadership. Their roles promise to foster greater collaboration, drive innovative solutions to shared challenges, and ensure that African universities continue to play a pivotal role in the global knowledge ecosystem.

We champion quality higher education and research and strengthen the contribution of higher education to Africa’s development. Visit our website for more information

TITLE: Artists’ Contacts 2026: Apply for ifa International Arts and Cultural Exchange Funding for Projects in 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen (ifa) Artists’ Contacts programme 2026 is offering funding for international artistic and cultural exchange projects connecting Germany with countries of the Global South and countries in transition. The programme is designed to strengthen international collaboration, encourage knowledge exchange, support artistic mobility and create sustainable networks among artists and cultural practitioners across borders.

Eligible applicants can seek support for a wide range of international visual arts and cultural activities, including working visits, research trips, exhibitions, artist-in-residence programmes, workshops, lectures, conferences, performances and other international exchange initiatives.

The application deadline is 30 September 2026, while supported projects are scheduled to take place between March and November 2027. Applicants who are interested in using art and cultural exchange to promote diversity, democratic values, human dignity, social cohesion and environmental responsibility are particularly encouraged to consider the programme.

About the ifa Artists’ Contacts Programme

The Artists’ Contacts programme is an international funding initiative of the Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen (ifa) that supports artistic and cultural exchange between Germany and countries in the Global South and countries in transition.

Rather than treating international mobility simply as an opportunity to travel, the programme places emphasis on meaningful cooperation, mutual learning and the creation of long-term relationships between cultural practitioners and institutions.

The programme is particularly relevant to artists and cultural professionals who want to work across national and cultural boundaries, develop collaborative artistic projects, undertake research, participate in international exhibitions or residencies, and build sustainable professional networks.

According to ifa, international artistic encounters can create spaces for dialogue, encourage different perspectives and contribute to mutual understanding. The programme therefore recognises art and culture as important tools for strengthening democratic values, social participation and responsible engagement with global challenges.

What Is the Main Focus of Artists’ Contacts 2026?

The central focus of the programme is intercultural exchange and networking in the visual arts.

The funding supports projects that place collaboration and knowledge exchange at the heart of international artistic engagement. Applicants are therefore encouraged to develop projects that go beyond one-time travel or isolated activities and instead demonstrate the potential to establish lasting relationships and professional networks.

The programme is especially interested in projects that contribute to:

International artistic and cultural cooperation

Knowledge exchange between cultural practitioners

Sustainable international networks

Diversity and inclusion

Democratic values

Human dignity

Social cohesion

Social participation

Environmental sustainability

Regional connections

Long-term international partnerships

Projects should demonstrate strong artistic quality while also reflecting the broader values promoted by ifa.

Who Can Benefit From the Artists’ Contacts Funding?

The programme is open to a broad range of professionals and organisations working in the arts and cultural sector.

Potential beneficiaries include:

Artists

Curators

Art mediators and art educators

Art theorists

Architects

Designers

Photographers

Media artists

Institutions working within the arts and cultural sector

The programme is therefore not limited to one particular artistic discipline. Instead, it provides opportunities for a variety of visual arts and cultural practitioners to participate in international exchange and collaborative projects.

Applicants should, however, ensure that their proposed project meets the programme’s artistic, collaborative and international eligibility requirements.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

A major feature of the Artists’ Contacts programme is its focus on international cooperation between Germany and countries included on the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) list of developing and transition countries.

Applications can be submitted from countries on the DAC list for projects taking place in Germany. Applications from Germany can also be submitted for projects taking place in eligible countries on the DAC list.

This means that the programme provides a two-way framework for cultural exchange:

Artists and cultural practitioners from eligible DAC countries can participate in projects in Germany.

Artists and cultural practitioners based in Germany can undertake eligible projects in countries appearing on the DAC list.

Applicants should consult the current official list of eligible countries before preparing their applications because eligibility depends on the country’s inclusion on the relevant DAC list.

Importantly, eligibility is not determined by race or ethnicity. The programme’s geographic eligibility is based on the relevant DAC country classification and the applicant’s location or residence in accordance with the programme rules.

Key Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the programme requirements before submitting a proposal. The following conditions are particularly important.

1. The Project Must Demonstrate High Artistic Quality

The planned project should have a strong artistic or cultural concept and demonstrate a high level of artistic quality.

Applicants should clearly communicate what they intend to achieve, why the project is artistically significant and how the proposed international collaboration contributes to the development of the work or professional practice.

2. Projects Should Reflect ifa’s Values

In addition to artistic quality, ifa considers broader values when assessing applications.

These include:

Social relevance

Diversity

Environmental sustainability

Regional connections

International cooperation

Social cohesion

Democratic values

Applicants should therefore avoid presenting international travel as an end in itself. A stronger application should explain the artistic, cultural and social value of the proposed exchange.

3. International Artistic Cooperation Is Required

The project must involve artistic and content-based cooperation between Germany and eligible countries in transition or countries of the Global South listed under the DAC framework.

The international dimension of the project is therefore fundamental to the programme.

4. Special Residence Requirements Apply to Projects in Germany

For projects involving travel to Germany, the participating artistic and cultural workers from eligible developing or transition countries must come from a country on the DAC list and must currently live there.

This requirement is important for applicants who may have nationality from an eligible country but currently reside elsewhere.

5. Additional Residence Requirement for Projects Outside Germany

For projects taking place in an eligible DAC country, artistic and cultural workers who do not have German citizenship must have lived in Germany for at least five years.

The programme does not fund trips to the applicant’s country of origin under this arrangement.

6. An Institutional Invitation Is Generally Required

Applicants normally need an invitation from a non-commercial cultural or exhibition organisation or an artist-in-residence establishment.

The organisation should not be a profit-oriented gallery.

An invitation is not required for research trips.

The foreign institution issuing the invitation must also provide significant financial and/or other services as part of the project.

7. Commercial Projects Are Not Eligible

The project must not be organised within a commercial context.

For example, projects connected to commercial art fairs are not eligible. The sale of artworks also excludes a project from funding.

This means applicants should clearly distinguish an artistic or cultural exchange project from a commercial activity.

8. Students Cannot Apply

Projects by students are not eligible for Artists’ Contacts funding.

ifa recommends that students seeking relevant international academic opportunities instead explore programmes offered by the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD).

What Activities Can the Funding Support?

Artists’ Contacts funding can support a wide range of artistic and cultural exchange activities.

Eligible activities can include:

Exhibitions

Performances

Artist-in-residence programmes

Workshops

Preparatory trips

Research trips

Working visits

International symposia

Conferences

Lectures

Other international exchange initiatives

This broad range of activities makes the programme relevant to artists and cultural professionals at different stages of an international project.

A research-oriented applicant, for example, may use the opportunity to undertake an international research trip, while another applicant may use the programme to participate in an exhibition, workshop, residency or international cultural event.

What Costs Does the Programme Cover?

The Artists’ Contacts programme provides support for travel and accommodation costs in accordance with the applicable Federal Travel Expenses Act.

For artistic and cultural workers travelling from countries in transition and developing countries to participate in eligible projects, ifa can cover a number of expenses.

These may include:

Flight expenses

Travel expenses

Accommodation costs

Visa costs

Overseas health insurance

Daily food allowance of EUR 28 per day

The programme does not cover travel and care expenses for family members.

For Germans and artistic and cultural workers who have lived in Germany for at least five years and are travelling to eligible countries outside Germany, support can include the following:

Flight expenses

Travel expenses

Accommodation costs

Visa costs

Applicable daily food allowances

Again, family members’ travel and care costs cannot be covered by the programme.

Environmental Sustainability Is an Important Consideration

The programme recognises that international cultural exchange often requires travel, which can have an environmental impact.

For this reason, ifa encourages applicants to consider environmental sustainability from the earliest stages of project planning.

Applicants are encouraged to:

Consider the environmental impact of international travel.

Prioritise sustainable forms of mobility where practical.

Reduce the carbon footprint of their projects.

Incorporate environmental considerations into project planning.

Demonstrate responsible use of environmental resources.

Environmental sustainability is also one of the aspects considered when assessing the overall quality and relevance of proposed projects.

How to Apply for the Artists’ Contacts Programme

The application process involves four main steps.

Step 1: Request Access to the Online Application

Applicants must first request access through the official Artists’ Contacts application system.

Step 2: Open the Link Sent by Email

After requesting access, applicants receive an email containing a link through which they can create their online application.

Step 3: Complete the Application

Applicants should complete all required sections of the application.

The system allows applicants to save their work and return to it later, meaning the application does not necessarily have to be completed in a single session.

Step 4: Submit the Online Application and Send the Signed Hard Copy

After submitting the online application, applicants must print it, sign it and send the hard copy by post to:

ifa – Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen

Artists’ Contacts

Charlottenplatz 17

D-70173 Stuttgart

Germany

Applicants should allow sufficient time for the physical application to reach the organisation because the postmark deadline applies.

APPLY HERE

Documents Required for the Application

Applicants should prepare the required supporting documents before submitting their application.

The official programme lists the following key documents:

Invitation Letter

Applicants generally need an invitation from the relevant foreign cultural or exhibition organisation, unless the application concerns a research trip.

Description of the Host Institution

Applicants should provide information describing the cultural or exhibition institution involved in the project.

Curriculum Vitae

CVs should be submitted for all applicants for whom funding is being requested.

The CVs should help demonstrate the applicants’ artistic or professional backgrounds and their suitability for the proposed project.

Visual Material

Applicants should provide visual material relating to the proposed project and/or examples of previous artistic work.

This is particularly important because the programme evaluates the artistic quality of applications.

Airfare Quotations

Applicants must provide three quotations for airfare based on current fares.

Applicants should therefore obtain current and credible flight quotations when preparing the budget and supporting documentation.

Sound and video works can be provided as links in the upload section of the application system.

Application Deadline for Artists’ Contacts 2026

The official application deadline is 30 September 2026.

The funding is for projects taking place between March and November 2027.

Applicants should pay close attention to the deadline because ifa states that no additional applications for projects taking place in 2027 will be accepted after 30 September 2026.

The date of the postmark applies, and applications sent after the deadline will not be considered.

Important Deadline Information

Application deadline: 30 September 2026

Eligible project period: March to November 2027

Notification of decision: February 2027

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the process involves both an online submission and a signed hard-copy application sent by post.

Visit HERE for more information about the Artists’ Contacts Programme 2026.

What Happens After You Apply?

Once applications have been submitted, they are assessed through the programme’s annual selection process.

An expert jury meets once a year to decide which projects will receive funding.

Funding decisions and the amount awarded depend on the available IFA budget and the applications received.

Applicants will receive written notification of acceptance or rejection in February 2027.

Applicants should also be aware of several important conditions surrounding the decision-making process:

No reasons for funding or rejection decisions will be provided.

Rejected applications cannot be resubmitted.

There is no legal recourse against the decision.

Additional materials submitted with an application will not be returned.

Projects that begin before approval cannot receive retrospective funding.

Expenses incurred before approval cannot be reimbursed retrospectively.

These conditions make it particularly important for applicants to wait for formal approval before beginning activities for which they expect to receive funding.

How Can Applicants Strengthen Their Proposals?

Although funding decisions are made by an expert jury and no outcome can be guaranteed, applicants can improve the clarity and competitiveness of their proposals by presenting a well-developed project.

A strong proposal should clearly explain:

What the project is about – Describe the artistic or cultural concept in clear terms.

Why international cooperation is necessary – Explain why collaboration across Germany and the partner country adds value.

Who is involved—Introduce the artists, cultural practitioners and host institutions.

What the project will achieve – Define the expected artistic and cultural outcomes.

How knowledge will be exchanged – Explain how participants will learn from one another.

How the project can create lasting relationships—Demonstrate potential for continued cooperation after the funded activity.

How the project reflects IFA’s values—Address diversity, social relevance, environmental sustainability and regional connections where appropriate.

How the budget will be used – Ensure requested travel-related costs are clearly justified.

Why the proposed activities are appropriate – Link each activity to the project’s objectives.

How environmental impacts will be considered – Explain efforts to make international mobility as sustainable as reasonably possible.

Applicants should also ensure that all required supporting documents are complete and consistent with the project proposal.

Why Artists and Cultural Practitioners Should Consider This Opportunity

International collaboration can be expensive, particularly when it involves air travel, accommodation, visas and other international mobility costs.

The Artists’ Contacts programme can reduce some of these financial barriers and make international artistic cooperation more accessible.

The opportunity can be particularly valuable for professionals seeking to:

Expand their international networks.

Collaborate with artists and cultural organisations across borders.

Develop new artistic projects.

Participate in exhibitions or performances.

Undertake international research.

Join artist-in-residence programmes.

Organise workshops and knowledge-sharing activities.

Participate in international conferences, symposia and lectures.

Establish long-term institutional partnerships.

Explore new cultural perspectives.

Connect artistic practice with social and environmental issues.

Beyond the immediate financial assistance, the programme’s emphasis on sustainable international networks means that applicants can frame their projects around longer-term professional and cultural relationships rather than short-term travel alone.

Important Restrictions Applicants Should Know

Before applying, prospective applicants should carefully consider the programme’s restrictions.

The following are particularly important:

Commercial projects are not eligible.

Art fairs and similar commercial activities do not qualify.

Selling artworks excludes funding.

Student projects are not eligible.

Trips to an applicant’s country of origin are not permitted in the relevant projects involving non-German citizens residing in Germany.

Projects that have already started cannot receive retrospective funding.

Expenses incurred before approval cannot be reimbursed retrospectively.

Family members’ travel and care expenses are not covered.

Applicants cannot resubmit rejected applications.

Funding is subject to the available budget.

Approved funding represents the maximum amount payable subject to the relevant rules and receipts.

Applicants should comply with the applicable German Federal Budget Code requirements when spending programme funds.

A Global Opportunity for Visual Arts and Cultural Exchange

The Artists’ Contacts programme stands out because it combines artistic mobility with broader objectives around international cooperation and intercultural understanding.

For artists and cultural practitioners in eligible countries, the programme can provide an avenue to establish professional connections in Germany. For Germany-based practitioners, it can facilitate collaborations and exchange projects in eligible countries of the Global South and countries in transition.

The programme’s approach reflects a wider understanding of the role of culture in international relations. Artistic exchange can provide opportunities for people from different backgrounds to meet, share ideas, challenge assumptions and develop new approaches to common challenges.

The emphasis on democracy, diversity, human dignity, social cohesion and environmental responsibility also means that projects with wider cultural or social relevance may be particularly well aligned with the programme’s objectives.

Where to Apply

Interested applicants should use the official ifa Artists’ Contacts application system and carefully review the programme’s eligibility conditions and supporting documents before submitting their applications.

The official application process requires applicants to request access, create their online application, complete and submit it electronically, and then print, sign and send the application by post to ifa in Stuttgart.

Application deadline: 30 September 2026

Project period: March to November 2027

Conclusion

The ifa Artists’ Contacts 2026 funding programme presents an important opportunity for artists, curators, art mediators, art theorists, architects, designers and cultural institutions seeking to develop meaningful international collaborations between Germany and eligible countries in the Global South and countries in transition.

Through support for travel, accommodation, visas, insurance and daily allowances, the programme can help reduce some of the financial barriers associated with international artistic mobility. It also supports a wide range of activities, from exhibitions and performances to research trips, workshops, artist residencies, lectures, conferences and other forms of cultural exchange.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. Projects must demonstrate high artistic quality, involve genuine international cooperation and generally have a non-commercial cultural context. Residence requirements also apply depending on whether the project takes place in Germany or an eligible DAC country, while student projects are specifically excluded.

With the 30 September 2026 deadline approaching, eligible artists and cultural practitioners should begin preparing their project concept, invitation documentation, CVs, artistic materials, budget information and airfare quotations as early as possible.

Ultimately, the Artists’ Contacts programme is more than a travel funding opportunity. Its central objective is to encourage sustained international cooperation, knowledge exchange and cultural dialogue. For applicants with strong artistic projects and a clear commitment to meaningful intercultural collaboration, it offers an opportunity to build connections that can extend well beyond the funded project period.
