TITLE: ACE for Impact Centers respond to COVID19

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Overview

The life-threatening nature of the COVID19 pandemic has been felt globally – its influence on global education systems is also being felt in Africa. Activities in African higher education institutions (HEIs) were suspended by various governments in order to contain the spread of the virus. Many of these institutions are host universities of the Africa Centers of Excellence for Development Impact project (ACE Impact) and as a result, activities of these Centers were slowed down. However, as part of their objectives to address regional developmental challenges, the ACE Impact Centers initiated measures to support the containment and management of the virus in all 11 participating countries within the West African sub region.

What is an Africa Center of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE for Impact Center)

These are largely competitively selected faculties, schools or colleges within an African University. The ACE Impact Centers focus on STEM, Agriculture, Environment, Health and applied Social Sciences / Education thematic areas. As part of the ACE for Development Impact project they are mandated to deliver quality undergraduate and post-graduate programs, promote regional academic mobility, address national and regional problems through research and promote best practices to their entire university systems.

Challenges faced by the ACEs for Development Impact Centers

The Association of African Universities, which is the Regional Facilitation Unit for the ACE Impact project, in collaboration with the World Bank conducted a survey to understand steps taken by the ACE for Impact Centers in addressing the pandemic to ensure continuous teaching and learning. Subsequently, a virtual meeting was held with the Centers to validate information collected through the survey. The survey results indicated challenges faced by the Centers and they pertain to infrastructure ; skills ; e-Platforms; limited time to plan and implement alternative solutions; limited commitment of staff and students to online learning; funding challenges and infection risks.

A review of how the ACE for Development Impact Centers in West Africa are responding to COVID19

Even though the ACE Impact Centers are facing numerous challenges, they are still contributing their quota in helping countries within the West African sub-region manage the crisis. The Centers have so far responded to the COVID19 pandemic by using technology for teaching, learning and research; engaging in innovative and groundbreaking research activities and participating in community outreach activities and services.

Notably, there has been groundbreaking research going on in different centers to provide immediate solutions that can support the management of the pandemic. The researches have so far led to the sequencing of the virus, abilities to carry out massive testing and online screening of individuals’ risk levels, among others.

In line with the ACE for development impact project objective to contribute to regional development through applied research, the centers are doing research to address societal needs. These efforts have included the production of personal protection equipment such as face shields through 3D printing, manufacturing of ventilators, production of nose masks, production of alcoholic gels and hand sanitizers and manufacturing of hand washing equipment for communities in their respective countries.

Several Centers have also created mathematical models to help assess and predict the spread of the virus and the possibility of confinement in certain cities.

These initiatives are all key towards preventing the rapid spread of the coronavirus.

DOWNLOAD Table that profiles individual ACE for Impact Centers’ Efforts towards responding to COVID 19

About the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence Project

The Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence (ACE) Project is a World Bank initiative in collaboration with governments of participating countries to support Higher Education institutions in specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Environment, Agriculture, applied Social Science / Education and Health. It is the first World Bank project aimed at the capacity building of higher education institutions in Africa. The first phase (ACE I) was launched in 2014 with 22 Centers of Excellence in nine (9) West and Central African countries; Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Togo. The Project aims to promote regional specialization among participating universities in areas that address specific common regional development challenges. It also aims to strengthen the capacities of these universities to deliver high quality training and applied research as well as meet the demand for skills required for Africa’s development. The second phase (ACE II) was launched in East and Southern Africa with 24 centers across Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia.

Based on the initial successes, the World Bank and the French Development Agency (AFD) in collaboration with the African governments, launched the ACE Impact Project in 2018 to strengthen post-graduate training and applied research in existing fields and support new fields that are essential for Africa’s economic growth. There are 43 ACEs (25 new ones and 18 from ACE I); 5 Emerging Centers;1 “top up” center in Social Risk Management; and 5 Colleges and Schools of Engineering. The new areas include sustainable cities; sustainable power and energy; social sciences and education; transport; population health and policy; herbal medicine development and regulatory sciences; public health; applied informatics and communication; and pastoral production.

The grant also includes a workstation at the Conservation Institute, an apartment in the Getty scholar housing complex, research assistance, a travel stipend, and an available healthcare option.

Eligibility

Applications are welcome from researchers and practitioners of all nationalities working in cultural heritage conservation or preservation, including objects, collections, architecture, and sites.

Applicants should have at least seven years of professional experience and should have an established record of publications and other contributions to the field.

Individuals from groups underrepresented across the field of cultural heritage conservation are encouraged to apply.

Proposals for postdoctoral research or research that contributes to a PhD or other academic degree will not be considered. Recent PhDs in chemistry and other physical or material sciences should apply to the Postdoctoral Fellowship in Conservation Science.

The Conservation Institute will consider proposals that require use of its science laboratories; however, use is dependent upon availability of lab facilities and staff time and cannot be guaranteed. If selected, Scholars should be prepared to conduct research independent of Science department staff.

Previous Conservation Guest Scholar Grant recipients are eligible to reapply after a waiting period of six years.

TITLE: Universal Acceptance (UA) Readiness Project Launched-13 April 2023

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), has launched the Universal Acceptance Readiness Project, an initiative under the Coalition for Digital Africa.

The project seeks to promote the adoption of Universal Acceptance (UA) standards in African higher education institutions which will improve access to online services and content, promote multilingualism and inclusion, and ultimately enhance the quality of education on the continent. It is aimed at making websites, applications, and email systems within Africa’s higher education institutions ready to support all domain names and email addresses in different languages and scripts.

In attendance at the launch were the Deputy Minister for Education in Ghana, Hon. Rev. John Ntim- Fordjour, the Executive Director of the Ghana Domain Name Registry, Nana Kofi Asafu-Aidoo, Vice Chancellors, stakeholders of Higher Education Institutions in Ghana, Directors of IT institutions and students.

Hon. Ntim-Fordjour who represented the Ministry of Education in Ghana delivered a speech on how the government is preparing for digital inclusion through capacity building and educational programs. He stated that the Government of Ghana is committed to developing the education system and has initiated some key education reforms to transform teaching and learning and improve educational outcomes under the Education Strategic Plan (ESP 2018-2030). The ESP’s three main priorities are improved learning outcomes, enhanced accountability, and equity at all levels of the education sector. He concluded by expressing gratitude to ICANN, AAU, Vice Chancellors, and all higher education stakeholders for their support and contribution to the project.

Nana Kofi Asafu-Aidoo also gave remarks on how the Ministry of Communications and Digitalization in Ghana is committed to supporting this project and ensuring that policies and strategies are aligned with the goals of the Universal Acceptance initiative. He tagged the project as a timely intervention, aimed at unlocking the potential of local language content and ensuring that African communities can fully participate in the digital economy. He pledged on behalf of the government to work with partners in the private sector, civil society, and academia to create an enabling environment for the development of local language content and the adoption of Universal Acceptance standards.

Professor Olusola Bandele Oyewole, the Secretary-General of the AAU thanked ICANN for the partnership which has birthed this novel project that seeks to strengthen the accessibility of the internet across the continent, with a specific focus on making email systems and other communication platforms of Africa’s higher education institutions ready for Universal Acceptance (UA) and Email Address Internationalization (EAI).

During an engagement with the media, the Vice President of Global Stakeholder Engagement (Africa) at ICANN, Mr. Pierre Dandjinou, said that the project is a fundamental requirement for achieving a multilingual internet where internet users around the world can navigate entirely in their local languages and scripts.

In a press statement released by ICANN, Sally Costerton, the Interim President and CEO of the corporation said, “ICANN is committed to ensuring that the internet continues to grow safely in Africa, to bring communities, cultures, and economies together and that is why collaboration among internet access providers, manufacturers, content providers, and academia is so important. We must work together to support the development of Africa’s digital economy.”

Sarmad Hussain, Senior Director of IDN and UA Programs at ICANN took participants through a presentation on Universal Acceptance and its Readiness in African Universities. He mentioned that though the rapid expansion of digital technologies had revolutionized the way we access and share information, this expansion had also highlighted a critical issue which is the lack of Universal Acceptance of domain names and email addresses in many countries, particularly in Africa. This has created significant barriers to the use of digital technologies by those who do not speak or write in English, French, or other common languages.

Universal Acceptance is the principle that all domain names and email addresses should be treated equally by software applications and online services, regardless of the language, script, or encoding they use. For example, an email address written in Arabic or Chinese characters should be able to receive and send emails just like an email address written in English. Similarly, a website address written in a non-Latin script, such as Arabic or Chinese, should be treated as equally as a website address written in English.

The Universal Acceptance Readiness project will address this issue by promoting the adoption of Universal Acceptance standards by African countries and institutions. The project will bring together governments, universities, and other stakeholders to raise awareness of the importance of Universal Acceptance and will provide training and technical support to enable the adoption of Universal Acceptance standards.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) are leading this initiative under the Coalition for Digital Africa Initiative. The Coalition for Digital Africa brings together like-minded organizations committed to building a robust and secure Internet infrastructure to bring more Africans online. The Coalition recognizes the critical role that digital technologies play in the development of education and seeks to ensure that African countries and institutions are fully equipped to harness the benefits of these technologies. In partnership with governments, regional and international organizations, and the local Internet community, the Coalition provides investments in Internet infrastructure, offers capacity-building workshops, and facilitates participation in the multistakeholder policymaking process.

Article by Ms. Naomi Darko

Communications Assistant,

AAU.

TITLE: Invitation to the Launch of the AAU Strategic Plan (2024–2030)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
On behalf of the governing board, members, secretariat, and staff of the Association of African Universities (AAU), we cordially invite all higher education stakeholders to the virtual launch of the AAU Strategic Plan (2024–2030), holding on Wednesday, August 14, 2024, from 10:00 AM to 11:00 AM GMT. Please register to participate in this event via this link – https://tinyurl.com/StrategicPlanLaunch

Since its founding in November 1967, the AAU has played a pivotal role in coordinating and networking Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) across Africa, while leading the charge in developing and promoting a unified vision for higher education on the continent. Currently, the AAU has a membership of about 450 HEIs from 48 African countries. Guided by a series of strategic plans, the AAU has remained committed to serving its community with excellence.

In line with best practices, we continuously review our strategic plans to stay attuned to global trends and enhance our service delivery to member universities. The disruptions caused by artificial intelligence (AI) and the implications of generative AI tools for higher education have necessitated critical reflections within the global higher education community. Our previous strategic plan (2020–2025) was revised to incorporate emerging trends in African higher education, particularly considering the lessons learned and new priorities that arose post-COVID-19.

The new strategic plan, to be launched on August 14, 2024, reflects a comprehensive, bottom-up approach in its development. The AAU Secretariat staff convened at a retreat to discuss the previous strategic plan and identify necessary revisions. A dedicated task force was established to lead the review process, which was further enriched by an online survey targeting Vice Chancellors of AAU member universities and other key higher education stakeholders. Their insights and suggestions have shaped the direction of this revised plan, ensuring it meets the dynamic needs of our community. In the face of changing global trends and increasing competition in higher education, we are prioritizing intellectual engagements on critical issues that address Africa’s developmental aspirations.

The AAU remains committed to providing a platform for discussions on African higher education, with key resolutions shared and disseminated to relevant stakeholders. The revised strategic plan places a strong emphasis on the contribution of African higher education to international development agendas, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the African Union’s Agenda 2063. The plan also aligns with the ongoing evaluations of the CESA 16-25 and STISA 2024 frameworks as they transition into their next phases.

We extend our deepest gratitude to everyone who contributed to the various stages of revising this strategic plan and look forward to the continued support of the African higher education community in making this plan a success.

For the 2024-2030 period, the AAU will focus on five key strategic areas:

A favorable higher education policy environment promoted in Africa at national, regional, and continental levels supported by evidence-based advocacy.

The capacities of AAU Member Universities strengthened to deliver on their mandates.

Higher education in Africa harmonized and standardized to enhance inter-institutional collaboration, networking, and competitiveness.

Research Excellence and Management advanced as a mechanism of impacting Africa’s development.

Innovations promoted to impact African Higher Education Systems and Africa’s Development

New AAU Focal Areas:

Research

Higher Education Access and Mobility

Responding to Emerging Issues

Higher Education Capacity Building and Empowerment

Building the African Higher Education Space (Quality Higher Education for Skills and Competencies)

Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence

Advocacy Platform for Collaboration

AAU Diaspora Programme

AAU Television and Public Broadcasting

Continental Initiatives

Collaboration and Partnerships for Higher Education Development

African Research Innovation and Development Network (AfRID)

We look forward to your participation in the launch of our new strategic Plan

TITLE: EGEN Research Prize 2026: Win Up to $3,000 for Cutting-Edge Research on Gender and Politics

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The EGEN Research Prize 2026, presented by EGEN in collaboration with Johns Hopkins University, is now accepting applications from graduate students and very early career scholars conducting innovative empirical research on gender and politics.

The research prize is designed to recognize and encourage emerging scholars producing high-quality, original research that advances understanding of gender and political issues. The organisers support empirical scholarship across a wide range of methodological approaches and academic subfields, with particular interest in developing research in comparative politics and international relations.

Selected researchers will receive financial awards ranging from $1,000 to $3,000, while several additional applicants will receive $500 honorable mentions. Winners will also receive an opportunity to be matched with a mentor from the EGEN executive board for the following year.

About the EGEN Research Prize

The EGEN Research Prize is part of EGEN’s efforts to support and recognize junior scholars working on important questions surrounding gender and politics.

The prize focuses on empirical gender scholarship, meaning research that uses evidence and systematic research approaches to examine political questions related to gender.

The organisers welcome research across different methodological approaches and subfields rather than limiting applicants to one particular research method.

This makes the prize potentially relevant to researchers working with:

Quantitative research

Qualitative research

Mixed-method research

Comparative research

International relations research

Political science research

Other empirical approaches to studying gender and politics

The organisers are particularly interested in encouraging emerging work in comparative politics and international relations.

EGEN Research Prize 2026 Awards

Successful applicants can receive one of several financial prizes.

Main Research Prizes

Several selected researchers will receive awards ranging from:

$1,000 to $3,000

The exact amount awarded may vary among the selected prize recipients.

Honorable Mentions

In addition to the main prizes, several applicants will receive:

$500 honorable mentions

These awards provide additional recognition for promising research that demonstrates quality, innovation and relevance to the field.

Mentorship Opportunity for Winners

One of the notable benefits of the EGEN Research Prize is that winners are not only recognized financially.

Prize winners will also be matched with a mentor from the EGEN executive board for the coming year.

This provides an opportunity for emerging scholars to receive guidance and build a professional relationship with an established member of the EGEN leadership network.

For graduate students and very early career researchers, mentorship can be valuable for developing research ideas, strengthening academic work and navigating the early stages of an academic career.

Research Areas of Interest

The 2026 prize focuses on gender and politics.

Applicants should therefore submit research that makes a meaningful contribution to understanding the relationship between gender and political processes, institutions, behaviour, outcomes or international affairs.

The organisers support research across methodological approaches and subfields.

However, particular interest is placed on research that can help incubate emerging scholarship in:

Comparative Politics

Research may examine political processes and gender-related questions across countries, political systems or societies.

International Relations

Research may explore gender within international political institutions, global political processes, international security, diplomacy, conflict, foreign policy or other areas of international relations.

Applicants should ensure that their research clearly demonstrates its relevance to gender and politics.

Who Can Apply?

The EGEN Research Prize is intended specifically for:

Graduate students

Very early career scholars

The opportunity is therefore aimed at researchers who are still in the early stages of their academic careers rather than established senior academics.

Graduate students should provide their advisor’s contact information as part of the application process.

APPLY HERE

Coauthored Research

Coauthored work is eligible for consideration.

However, there is an important condition:

Every co-author must also be eligible for the prize.

Applicants submitting coauthored research should therefore ensure that all individuals listed as co-authors meet the eligibility requirements for graduate students or very early career scholars.

Original Research and AI Requirement

The submitted work must be original.

The organisers specifically state that submissions must not be generated by AI.

Applicants should therefore submit their own original research and writing and ensure that their work complies with the prize’s requirements concerning originality and authorship.

What Applicants Must Submit

Applicants are required to submit several materials as part of the 2026 application.

1. Application Form

Applicants must complete the official EGEN Research Prize application form.

The application form collects the information required for consideration and also asks applicants to identify potential mentors.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide their CV as a PDF.

The file should be named:

lastname_firstname_CV.pdf

Applicants should ensure that the CV clearly presents their academic background, research experience, publications and other relevant scholarly achievements.

3. Anonymized Writing Sample

Applicants must submit an anonymized version of their most polished piece of writing.

The writing sample must be provided as a PDF and should be named:

lastname_firstname_writing sample.pdf

The sample should be anonymized, meaning identifying information should be removed where appropriate so that the research can be evaluated without unnecessary identifying details.

Applicants should choose a piece of work that best demonstrates the quality of their research, writing and analytical abilities.

4. Advisor Contact Information

Graduate students must provide their advisor’s contact information.

This information is entered directly into the application form.

How the Documents Are Submitted

There are two different submission processes that applicants need to pay attention to.

The application form is completed online, while the CV and writing sample are uploaded separately through a Dropbox file request.

Applicants must therefore make sure they complete both parts of the submission process.

The application form asks applicants to confirm that they have uploaded both required documents.

Failure to complete the document-upload portion could result in an incomplete application.

Potential Mentors

The application form also asks applicants to identify three potential mentors from the EGEN executive board, either past or present.

Applicants should therefore review the EGEN executive board and select three potential mentors whose academic interests or expertise are relevant to their research.

Choosing appropriate mentors can help demonstrate that the applicant has considered how mentorship could support the development of their research and academic career.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2026 EGEN Research Prize is:

15 October 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (ET).

Applicants should submit all required materials before the deadline and should not wait until the final hours to upload their documents.

Submission Language

All submissions must be made in:

English

Applicants should ensure that their application materials and submitted writing sample meet this language requirement.

How to Apply

Applicants should follow these steps:

Complete the official EGEN Research Prize application form.

Prepare a current CV in PDF format.

Name the CV according to the required format: lastname_firstname_CV.pdf.

Select your most polished research or writing work.

Anonymize the writing sample.

Save the writing sample as a PDF.

Name it according to the required format: lastname_firstname_writing sample.pdf.

Upload both the CV and anonymized writing sample through the designated Dropbox file request.

Confirm in the application form that both documents have been uploaded.

Graduate students should provide their advisor’s contact information.

Identify three potential mentors from the EGEN executive board, past or present.

Submit the completed application before 15 October 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Visit HERE to learn more about the EGEN Research Prize 2026

Important Application Requirements

Before submitting an application, candidates should carefully review the following requirements:

The applicant must be a graduate student or very early career scholar.

The research must focus on gender and politics.

Empirical research is encouraged.

Multiple methodological approaches and subfields are supported.

Comparative politics and international relations research is particularly encouraged.

Submissions must be in English.

The work must be original and must not be generated by AI.

Coauthored work is permitted only when every co-author is eligible.

Graduate students must provide advisor contact information.

A CV must be submitted as a PDF.

An anonymized writing sample must be submitted as a PDF.

The CV and writing sample must be uploaded through the specified Dropbox file request.

Applicants must identify three potential mentors from the EGEN executive board.

The application must be submitted by the stated deadline.

Why Researchers Should Consider Applying

The EGEN Research Prize offers more than financial recognition.

For emerging scholars, receiving a research prize can provide recognition for their academic work while also creating opportunities to develop professional connections within the field.

The combination of financial awards, academic recognition and mentorship makes the opportunity particularly relevant to graduate students and researchers at the beginning of their careers.

The prize can also provide encouragement for scholars developing innovative research on gender and politics, particularly those working in comparative politics and international relations.

Conclusion

The 2026 EGEN Research Prize provides an opportunity for graduate students and very early career scholars to gain recognition and financial support for innovative research on gender and politics.

With several awards ranging from $1,000 to $3,000, additional $500 honorable mentions, and a mentorship opportunity with members of the EGEN executive board, the prize offers both financial and professional-development value to emerging researchers.

Applicants should ensure that their research aligns with the focus on gender and politics, carefully prepare their CV and anonymized writing sample, follow the required file-naming and submission procedures, and identify three potential EGEN mentors.

For more global grants, scholarships, fellowships, internships, jobs, conferences, competitions, and other career opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities for Youth (OFY) website at www.opportunitiesforyouth.org.

TITLE: Canvas FAQs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Below are frequently asked questions regarding the new Canvas LMS.

General FAQs

Who should instructors, TAs, and/or graders contact regarding questions about their Canvas course site?

If you can’t find an answer to your question on this page or via MIT Canvas Resources for Instructors or Canvas Guides, you can contact canvas-support@mit.edu.

Please also CC Physics Course Administrator Kim Heatley (kheatley@mit.edu), and our Course Manager (physicscoursemanager@mit.edu) on that message.

Can I read a Canvas guide in another language?

Yes. Below is a list of Canvas guides in other languages.

Canvas 指南中文版 (Chinese)

Canvas Guider (Danish)

Canvas-guider (Swedish)

Canvas-guider (Norwegian)

Canvas Gidsen (Dutch)

Guías de Canvas (Spanish)

Guias Canvas (Portuguese – Brazil)

Manuels Canvas (French)

Canllaw Canvas (Welsh)

How long will I be able to access a Canvas site?

Courses will enter a read-only state within a few weeks after the semester ends. Students will be able to view course content after this point, but will be unable to interact with the course site.

Likewise, instructors and course admins will lose the ability to edit their course site after this point. The site will remain available in a read-only state and all course content will be accessible and downloadable by class staff, but no further changes or additions can be made.

Class staff may extend or shorten the time a course remains open in advance. If you wish to set a later end date, make a course site read-only sooner, or restrict student access entirely after the term ends (rather than allowing read-only access), these can be configured via the Settings page.

We highly recommend setting an appropriate end date if you want your Canvas site to remain open beyond the end of the term.

More information on configuring this setting is available from Canvas here.

If your site has closed and you need to make a change to it, please contact canvas-support@mit.edu.

For Students

Getting started as a student with Canvas?

Here’s a list of guides you can read to help:

Getting Started

Canvas Basics Guide

Student Guide

Observer/Parent Guide

Troubleshooting Guide

Video Guide

How do I set my Canvas notification preferences as a student?

Canvas includes a set of default notification preferences you can receive for your courses. However, you can change the default settings by setting your own notification preferences.

See “How do I set my Canvas notification preferences as a student?” for more info.

Where on Canvas can students see their recitation schedule?

Students can see their section enrollment in the “people” tab if it is also enabled.

Can I obtain access to prior-semester course content, and if so, for how long?

If you no longer have access to a past course, please contact that course’s instructor or the relevant department for guidance.

For Instructors/TAs

Getting started as an instructor with Canvas?

Here’s a list of guides you can read to help:

Getting Started

Semester Startup Essentials

Canvas Basics Guide

Instructor Guide

Instructor Cheat Sheet

MIT Canvas Resources for Instructors

Troubleshooting Guide

Video Guide

How do I create a Canvas site for my course?

Canvas course sites are created automatically each semester from Registrar data. Instructors are added to and removed from these sites daily based on the information in the MIT’s Instructor Assignment application so that info should be kept as up-to-date as possible. When necessary, additional instructors can be added manually to a site by anyone with permission to do so, or by request to canvas-support@mit.edu.

How do I opt-in to teach my course using Canvas?

Canvas courses are created before the next semester (should you choose to use them), and will display as tiles on lead faculty dashboards immediately upon login. They will also be listed under “Courses” on the left-hand sidebar once you login to Canvas. To start, your course is just a shell with a basic course template; no actual course content or membership has been populated, integrations enabled, and the course will not be visible (outside of your view) until it is published. If you are logging into Canvas, and do not see your course on either the dashboard or in the “Courses” tab, please email canvas-support@mit.edu.

Can I migrate my course content from a previous Stellar course?

Yes, and the team that is working to launch Canvas available to the MIT community is here to help. A number of students were hired to serve as Learning Technologists to support each academic department at MIT. These Learning Technologists are available to work with you personally to ensure that your course content is imported and displaying correctly. They will also ensure that all integrations are in place for your course site ahead of the start of the semester. You will receive an email from the point person in your department who is collecting requests to opt in to Canvas, and who will help to coordinate the work of these Learning Technologists to ensure that all course instructors receive the help that they desire. If you are not familiar with who the point person for your department is, please email canvas-support@mit.edu.

Can I request a Canvas course outside of the current semester?

The team that has been working to launch Canvas to the MIT community has been working tirelessly to make Canvas available for all academic courses that wish to utilize this learning management system, will be initiating a process for the creation of course sites for future semesters. All requests can be submitted via email to canvas-support@mit.edu.

When will course membership populate?

Course membership will begin to populate along in the registration cycle once the data is available in the system, usually within a week of registration changes (add/drop). If you believe your membership should already be populated and it is not, please contact canvas-support@mit.edu.

Pre-Registered students are converted to student status or removed from the course starting on Registration day and the conversion or removals should be complete within one week.

How to auto-populate recitation sections from registrar?

An instructor can navigate to their course “settings” and then to the navigation tab found within. You should see a new tool called “MITSIS Section Import” which once initiated by faculty will sort students into the sections they are in from the registrar (similar to tool in Stellar). Let me know if you have an questions, this system was only rolled out over the weekend and there have been some bugs so far but hopefully no more large ones appear.

How can instructors add students to their Canvas website?

To manually add students, instructors can click on the “People” link and then add students by their MIT emails.

Need help with Assignments?

Read these Assignment FAQ’s (Assignment not displaying in the Gradebook, delete a student submission?, what are differentiated assignments, exclude assignments from Gradebook)

Section Management in Canvas

Two tools are available in Canvas to instructors, TAs, and admins to allow finer control of section management. A MITSIS section import tool will enable instructors to import student section enrollments based on pre-registration data. A section self-signup tool will enable instructors to set section caps and a signup window for students to select or change their assigned section.

For more information, please read “Section Management in Canvas“.

How to allow your students to change their recitation section?

An instructor can navigate to their course “settings” and then to the navigation tab found within. You should see a new tool called “Section Signup”. Faculty can enable this in their course and then configure student ability to move between sections, enable section caps, etc.

How can instructors change students recitations sections?

Faculty can manually move students to different sections. Going into the “people” tab and hitting the 3 dots to the right of a student’s name allows instructors to edit their section assignments.

How can instructors message the entire class?

Canvas provides many avenues of communication with students and allows customization of notifications (text, push notif, email). It is up to the student to choose notification settings that work for them but it is highly suggested that students at least keep “Announcements” and “Conversation Message” on at all times.

Notification preferences as a student

Notification preferences as an instructor

There are two main communication options once a course is published, announcements and inbox messages:

Announcements are site-wide or section-wide rich text editor objects that are located in the core Canvas shell and can be scheduled.

Inbox Messages (or “conversations”) are plain text editor messages that are located outside of the core Canvas shell. Inbox messages can be specified much more than announcements down to groups, roles, and individual students.

If you do not want everyone to see all recipients and replies in the message, click the “Send an individual message to each recipient” checkbox. This box will be automatically checked for recipient lists of 100+ users

As a general rule, consider using Announcements to share time-sensitive, urgent information that does not necessarily require a response (e.g. a class cancellation, or a new Assignment posting), but should be received by every student/member of the Canvas course site. Or for information that requires the complexity of the rich text editor (multiple files, Canvas Objects, pictures, videos, etc.) Conversation messages, however, can be used for lengthier, sustained exchanges between instructors and their students/lab partnerships(e.g. questions about a class discussion, or something that should only be shared individually or on a group level).

For an unpublished course or if there arises some need to use direct email, WebMoira automatically creates Canvas student emails similar to how Stellar did.

For example: For 8.01 students: canvas-2021fa_8.01-st@mit.edu, for 8.286 students: canvas-2021fa_8.286-st@mit.edu.

How can instructors add something in the calendar and have students be emailed reminders about it?

Students have to opt-in to these notifications by going into their Canvas “account” and then “notifications” and manage what they would like to get emailed or texted about. Faculty will have to ask students to opt-in.

How do instructors get the Canvas calendar to show MIT holidays?

FYI, currently there is no way to import the MIT academic calendar into the Canvas calendar but The Office of Online Learning is working on implementing this function in the future.

Can students see their total grades in Canvas?

For academic courses, total grades are hidden from the student grades summary by default. You may change this setting by unchecking the box “Hide totals in student grades summary” under “more options” in the course Settings page.

How to Submit Canvas Grades to OGS at the End of the Term

Instructions for instructors and others with permission to assign grades in Canvas and OGS can be accessed at “How to Submit Canvas Grades to OGS at the End of the Term.”

What happens to Canvas sites after a term ends?

Canvas courses change to a read-only state within a few weeks after the end of a term. Instructors and admins may adjust the end date in their course settings if they would like a course site to be open for more or less time. More information about adjusting the end date for a Canvas site can be found here.

After the term ends, past courses will no longer appear in your current course list or dashboard. Past courses are located in “All Courses” via the Courses tab in the main menu. More details are available here.

If you need to add someone to membership for a past Canvas site that has entered read-only mode, please contact canvas-support@mit.edu.

TITLE: Invitation to contribute to international collaboration in doctoral education

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
INVITATION TO RESPOND TO SHORT SURVEY ON DOCTORAL EDUCATION

The International Association of Universities (IAU) and partners (KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Sweden; University of Bergen; NORDUnet and Nordic Insight), invite you to contribute to a short survey on international collaboration in doctoral education: https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/IDOCOS1

The Covid-19 pandemic has exposed significant deficiencies in virtually all countries when it comes to remote learning. When universities overnight pivoted from campus-based education to digital and remote solutions, this very often meant emulating what used to happen on campus and not necessarily quality online learning and teaching. Despite the challenges that the pandemic has caused, it also represents an opportunity to reconsider practices and processes and to reform the university education. The partners behind this survey seek to leverage this opportunity by proposing an innovative approach to co-creation and sharing of doctoral courses among universities in different countries. It proposes a structured process and comprehensive guidance supporting the move towards more internationally co-created and shared resources for doctoral education to enhance reciprocal exchange of research capacity, resources, to increase competencies and ultimately strengthening high-quality research education through international collaboration.

In order to build the methodology, it is essential to take stock of the current situation and address the needs and expectations of the higher education institutions. We have already received numerous replies from higher education institutions in Europe for a first part of the project; but the group is building a second part with partner universities in Africa with a view to enhance research capacity and international collaboration in doctoral education. For this second part of the project, we need more information about the current situation in Africa.

We therefore invite you to send this invitation to colleagues in charge of doctoral education within your institution. It will take between 10-15 minutes to respond to this quick survey which will be of tremendous support in order to further respond to the specific needs in Africa.

It is not important whether you institution is already participating in co-sharing and co-creation of doctoral courses; the most important for us is to get a clear picture of the current situation in order to address it through collaboration.

For any questions regarding the survey; please contact Trine Jensen at the International Association of Universities (IAU) t.jensen@iau-aiu.net

We thank the Association of African Universities (AAU) for their support in disseminating this survey and we thank you for contributing to the survey!

ACCESS the survey here: https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/IDOCOS1

TITLE: ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 in Belgium: Fully Funded Study and Professional Training Opportunities for Applicants from 32 Eligible Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 offer an opportunity for qualified graduates and working professionals from selected developing and partner countries to undertake specialised higher education and professional training in Belgium.

The programme is administered by the Académie de Recherche et d’Enseignement Supérieur (ARES) and supports specialised academic and professional programmes within the higher education system of the Wallonia-Brussels Federation in Belgium. For the 2027–2028 call, applicants can choose from one specialised bachelor’s programme, eight specialised master’s programmes, and one continuing education programme.

Applications opened on 3 August 2026, and the application deadline is Friday, 18 September 2026 at 12:00 noon Belgian time (UTC+1). Applicants are strongly advised to begin the process early because the application requires account creation, documentation, eligibility checks and submission through the ARES GIRAF platform.

ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 at a Glance

Host country: Belgium

Organiser: Académie de Recherche et d’Enseignement Supérieur (ARES)

Academic year: 2027–2028

Application opening date: 3 August 2026

Application deadline: 18 September 2026 at 12:00 noon Belgian time (UTC+1)

Study location: Institutions within the Wallonia-Brussels Federation

Available programmes: 1 specialised bachelor’s degree, 8 specialised master’s degrees and 1 continuing education programme

Duration: Up to 12 months for the specialised bachelor’s and master’s programmes; up to 6 months for continuing education

Eligible applicants: Residents and workers from 32 eligible partner countries, with a special provision for Palestinian nationals

Application platform: ARES GIRAF

Application limit: One programme per applicant

Funding: International travel, living/subsistence support, applicable tuition fees, insurance and certain visa-related or other eligible costs

What Are the ARES International Training Scholarships?

The ARES International Training Scholarships are designed to strengthen the academic knowledge, technical expertise and professional capacity of people from eligible partner countries.

Rather than being a general scholarship open to applicants from every country, the programme targets candidates from a defined group of partner countries. Applicants are expected to demonstrate both academic preparation and professional experience relevant to the programme they wish to pursue.

The 2027–2028 call provides specialised training in areas connected to major development and professional challenges, including:

Human rights

Public health

International and development economics

Microfinance

Food-chain safety

Supply-chain management

Cybersecurity

Health-risk management

Cultural conservation and collections management

Disaster and risk management

The programme therefore has potential relevance to professionals working in government, development organisations, NGOs, healthcare, finance, supply chains, technology, public administration, humanitarian work, research, education and other related fields.

Programmes Available Under the ARES 2027–2028 Call

Applicants should carefully examine the admission requirements of their preferred programme before beginning the application because academic and professional requirements can differ between programmes.

1. Specialised Bachelor’s Degree

The 2027–2028 call includes one specialised bachelor’s programme:

Specialised Bachelor’s in Digital Integrated Supply Chain

This programme is particularly relevant to candidates interested in modern supply-chain systems, logistics, digital transformation, procurement, international business and integrated supply-chain management.

The programme may be particularly attractive to professionals whose careers involve logistics, procurement, supply-chain operations, business management, international development or related areas.

The specialised bachelor’s programme has a maximum duration of 12 months.

2. Eight Specialised Master’s Programmes

Applicants can also choose from eight specialised master’s programmes covering a broad range of development-oriented disciplines.

The available programmes include:

Specialised Master’s in Human Rights

Specialised Master’s in Integrated Health Risk Management

Specialised Master in International and Development Economics

Advanced Master in Microfinance

Specialised Master’s in Public Health Sciences – Analysis and Evaluation of International Health Policies, Programmes and Systems

Specialised Master’s in Food Chain Safety Management

Specialised Master’s in Preventive Conservation and Collections Management

Specialised Master’s in Risk and Disaster Management in the Anthropocene Era

These programmes provide opportunities for professionals to deepen their expertise in fields that have significant relevance to sustainable development, public policy, health systems, economic development, food security, cultural heritage, disaster preparedness and humanitarian responses.

The specialised master’s programmes have a maximum duration of 12 months.

3. Continuing Education Programme

The call also includes a continuing education opportunity:

Certificate in Cybersecurity Operations and Risk Governance

The programme focuses on cybersecurity operations and the governance of digital risks. It may be particularly relevant for professionals working in information technology, cybersecurity, digital governance, risk management and related fields.

The continuing education programme has a maximum duration of six months.

Who Can Apply for the ARES Scholarships?

The ARES scholarships have specific eligibility requirements. Meeting one requirement alone does not necessarily make an applicant eligible. Candidates should satisfy the residency, employment, academic, professional experience and programme-specific admission requirements.

1. Applicants Must Be Connected to an Eligible Country

Candidates must be permanent residents and workers in one of the 32 eligible countries.

There is a specific exception for Palestinian nationals, who may qualify even when they do not reside in one of the 32 listed countries.

This means that simply holding nationality from an eligible country may not be sufficient in every case. The call specifically refers to residence and employment requirements, so applicants should carefully review their circumstances before submitting an application.

2. Applicants Must Hold an Appropriate Higher Education Qualification

Candidates must have an appropriate higher education qualification and satisfy the admission requirements of the programme they select.

The relevant qualification must generally have been obtained no more than 20 years before the start of the programme.

The maximum period can be extended by one additional year for each childbirth and/or adoption, according to the eligibility conditions provided in the call.

Applicants should therefore examine the academic requirements of their selected programme rather than assuming that every university degree will automatically qualify them.

3. Professional Experience Is Required

Applicants must demonstrate at least two years of relevant professional experience in one of the eligible countries.

The experience must have been acquired after completion of the most recent graduate degree and before the application deadline.

This requirement makes the scholarship particularly relevant to working professionals who already have experience in their field and want to acquire specialised international training that can strengthen their contribution to their organisations and communities.

4. Language Proficiency

Applicants must complete their application in the language in which their chosen programme is taught.

Candidates are expected to demonstrate good written and spoken command of the relevant teaching language.

Applicants should therefore check the language requirements of their specific programme before applying.

The scholarship information also notes that having a basic knowledge of French can be helpful for integration into everyday life in Belgium, even where the programme itself may have different language requirements.

5. Applicants Can Apply for Only One Programme

One of the important rules of the ARES call is that an applicant may apply for only one programme.

Applicants should therefore research the available courses carefully before submitting their application.

Choosing a programme should involve considering:

Academic background

Professional experience

Career objectives

Programme admission requirements

Language requirements

Relevance to the applicant’s professional field

Long-term career plans

Submitting applications for multiple programmes is not an appropriate strategy under this call.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

The ARES International Training Scholarships are open to applicants connected to 32 eligible partner countries across Africa, Asia, Southeast Asia, South America and the Caribbean.

Eligible African Countries

The African countries included in the call are:

Benin

Burkina Faso

Burundi

Cameroon

Democratic Republic of the Congo

Ethiopia

Guinea

Côte d’Ivoire

Kenya

Madagascar

Mali

Morocco

Mozambique

Niger

Rwanda

Senegal

South Africa

Tanzania

Tunisia

Uganda

Zimbabwe

Eligible Countries in South America and the Caribbean

The eligible countries listed in this region are:

Bolivia

Cuba

Ecuador

Haiti

Peru

Eligible Southeast Asian Countries

The eligible Southeast Asian countries are:

Cambodia

Indonesia

Nepal

Philippines

Vietnam

Eligible Asian Country

Palestine

Therefore, applicants from Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ethiopia, South Africa, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and the other listed partner countries can potentially apply, provided they satisfy all other eligibility requirements.

Importantly, this is not a scholarship open to all African countries. Applicants should check the official country list before investing time in preparing an application.

What Does the Scholarship Cover?

The ARES International Training Scholarships provide substantial financial support to successful applicants.

The support listed in the call includes several major categories.

International Travel Expenses

Scholarship recipients receive support for international travel expenses associated with their studies or training in Belgium.

This can significantly reduce one of the major financial barriers faced by international applicants who need to travel to Europe for their programme.

Subsistence Allowance

The scholarship includes a subsistence allowance to help recipients meet living expenses during their period of study or training.

This is particularly important for international students who may otherwise need to finance accommodation, food and other daily expenses independently.

Tuition Fees

For the specialised bachelor’s and specialised master’s programmes, the scholarship includes support for tuition fees.

This means successful recipients can undertake their eligible programme without having to independently finance the applicable tuition costs covered by the scholarship.

Visa-Related Expenses

For specialised bachelor’s and specialised master’s recipients, the scholarship can cover exceptional costs associated with visa applications, subject to the conditions of the programme and scholarship.

This provides additional financial support during the relocation process.

Insurance

Insurance costs are also included in the scholarship support.

This provides an additional layer of financial protection for recipients while they are undertaking their programme in Belgium.

Continuing Education Support

For the continuing education programme, the financial package includes indirect mission expenses, alongside the applicable scholarship support described in the call.

Because funding arrangements can differ depending on the programme type, applicants should consult the official call documentation for the exact financial conditions applicable to their selected programme.

How Long Are the ARES Programmes?

The duration depends on the type of programme selected.

Specialised Bachelor’s and Master’s Programmes

The specialised bachelor’s and specialised master’s programmes have a maximum duration of:

12 months

Continuing Education

The continuing education programme has a maximum duration of:

6 months

Applicants should distinguish these programmes from conventional multi-year undergraduate or master’s programmes. The ARES International Training call is focused on specialised training and academic programmes designed to strengthen the expertise of candidates who already possess relevant educational and professional backgrounds.

How to Apply for the ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028

Applications are submitted electronically through the ARES GIRAF platform.

The application process involves several stages.

Step 1: Create or Access Your GIRAF Account

Applicants who already have a GIRAF account created and validated by ARES can log in using their existing account.

Candidates who do not have a validated GIRAF account must complete the account creation request process.

It is advisable to do this well before the deadline because applicants should not leave account creation and validation until the final hours of the application period.

Step 2: Access the International Training Application

After logging into GIRAF, navigate to:

Competitive Calls

Then select:

Application – International Training 2027–2028

Applicants should click the application button only once, according to the application instructions.

Step 3: Complete the Application Form

Applicants should carefully complete all required sections of the form.

Certain fields marked with an asterisk are mandatory and must be completed before the application can initially be saved.

The system allows applicants to work on the application over multiple sessions.

This means candidates do not necessarily need to complete everything in one sitting.

Step 4: Save Your Application as a Draft

If an applicant needs additional time to gather information or documents, the form can be saved as a draft.

To continue a saved application, applicants should go to:

Competitive Calls → My Tasks

They can then select the relevant application and click:

Open

The applicant can continue editing the form as long as it remains a draft and has not been submitted.

Step 5: Review the Application Carefully

Before submission, applicants should check:

Personal information

Academic qualifications

Employment history

Professional experience

Programme selection

Language information

Supporting documentation

Eligibility information

Contact details

Any programme-specific requirements

A careful final review is important because errors or missing information can affect the application.

Step 6: Submit the Application

Once everything has been completed and reviewed, the applicant can select:

Submit my application

After submission, the application will appear under:

Competitive Calls → My Submitted Applications

A crucial point is that an application cannot be modified after it has been submitted.

Applicants should therefore avoid submitting prematurely.

Important Application Deadline

The deadline for the ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 is:

Friday, 18 September 2026 at 12:00 noon Belgian time (UTC+1).

Applications opened on 3 August 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final day to create their GIRAF account, upload documents or submit the application.

Because the deadline is based on Belgian time, international applicants should also account for the time difference between Belgium and their home country.

Important Documents and Preparation

Although exact documentation can depend on the selected programme, applicants should be prepared to provide evidence supporting their eligibility and application.

Potentially relevant materials include:

Academic certificates and diplomas

Academic transcripts

Evidence of professional experience

Employment information

Proof of residence

Proof of nationality

Language-related documentation where applicable

Programme-specific documents

Recommendation or reference information where required

Any additional documentation requested by the selected programme

Applicants should use the official ARES candidate guide and call documentation to determine exactly what must be submitted.

It is also advisable to ensure that documents are clear, valid and prepared in the required language or format before beginning the final submission process.

How to Strengthen Your ARES Scholarship Application

Meeting the minimum requirements does not automatically guarantee selection. Applicants should therefore approach the application strategically.

1. Select a Programme That Matches Your Background

Do not choose a programme simply because it is fully funded.

Your academic background and professional experience should make sense in relation to your chosen field.

For example, someone with professional experience in logistics, procurement, operations or supply-chain management may find the Digital Integrated Supply Chain programme particularly relevant.

Similarly, someone working in public health should carefully examine the public-health and health-risk programmes.

2. Connect Your Professional Experience to Your Career Goals

Your professional experience should demonstrate why the programme is useful for your career.

Explain the skills you have already developed and identify the knowledge gaps that the programme will help you address.

A strong application should create a logical connection between:

Past experience → Current professional responsibilities → Selected programme → Future impact

3. Demonstrate Development Impact

Because the programme is designed around international cooperation and capacity building, applicants should clearly demonstrate how advanced training could contribute to their institution, sector or wider community after completion.

Think beyond personal advancement.

Consider how the knowledge gained in Belgium could be applied to:

Improve organisational systems

Strengthen public services

Develop innovative programmes

Improve professional practices

Address development challenges

Build institutional capacity

Transfer knowledge to colleagues

Support sustainable development

4. Check Programme-Specific Admission Requirements

One of the most important steps is to review the detailed admission requirements for the programme you intend to select.

Different programmes can have different academic prerequisites and professional expectations.

A candidate who meets the general ARES requirements may still fail to meet the admission conditions of a particular programme.

5. Start Early

Do not treat the deadline as the date to begin the application.

A better approach is to:

Check eligibility.

Research the programmes.

Select one suitable programme.

Create and validate your GIRAF account.

Gather supporting documents.

Complete the application.

Review the information.

Submit before the deadline.

Starting early also gives you time to address technical or documentation problems.

Why This Scholarship Is Valuable

The ARES International Training Scholarships can provide more than financial assistance.

For successful candidates, studying or undertaking professional training in Belgium can provide opportunities to:

Gain specialised international academic training

Develop advanced professional expertise

Study in a European higher education environment

Build international professional networks

Learn from specialists and academic institutions

Strengthen career prospects

Acquire knowledge that can be applied in the home country

Gain exposure to international approaches and practices

Develop skills relevant to development challenges

Expand professional and academic perspectives

For mid-career professionals, the opportunity can be especially valuable because it combines international exposure with specialised training rather than simply providing a general academic qualification.

Key Mistakes Applicants Should Avoid

Applicants should be particularly careful to avoid the following mistakes:

Applying for More Than One Programme

The call permits applicants to apply for only one programme.

Ignoring the Residency and Employment Requirement

Being from an eligible country does not mean every applicant automatically qualifies. The residency and employment conditions should be carefully checked.

Applying Without the Required Professional Experience

The call requires at least two years of relevant professional experience under the stated conditions.

Choosing a Programme Without Checking Academic Requirements

Every programme can have specific admission requirements.

Submitting an Incomplete Application

Missing information or documentation can weaken an application or make it ineligible.

Waiting Until the Deadline

Technical issues, account validation, missing documents or last-minute errors can create serious problems.

Forgetting That Submitted Applications Cannot Be Edited

Applicants should review everything carefully before clicking the final submission button.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity may be particularly suitable for:

Professionals from eligible developing and partner countries

Graduates seeking advanced specialised training

Mid-career professionals who want to strengthen their expertise

Professionals working in development-related fields

Public-sector employees

NGO and civil-society professionals

Health professionals

Supply-chain and logistics professionals

Economists and development practitioners

Human-rights professionals

Financial and microfinance specialists

Food-safety professionals

Disaster-risk and humanitarian practitioners

Cybersecurity and technology professionals

Professionals working in cultural heritage and collections management

However, applicants should not rely solely on their professional field. They must also satisfy the official ARES eligibility requirements and the admission requirements of their selected programme.

APPLY HERE

Application Resources

Applicants should consult the official ARES application information, candidate guidance and call documentation before submitting.

The ARES candidate guide should be used to understand the GIRAF application process and submission requirements.

Applicants should also consult the official 2027–2028 call reference document for the authoritative eligibility, programme and funding conditions.

For questions concerning the scholarship call, the provided contact is: Maryvonne Aubry Email: scholarships-cooperation@ares-ac.be

Visit HERE to learn more about the ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 in Belgium.

Final Thoughts

The ARES International Training Scholarships 2027–2028 represent a significant opportunity for qualified professionals and graduates from 32 eligible partner countries to undertake specialised academic or professional training in Belgium with substantial financial support.

The programme stands out because of the range of disciplines available. Applicants can pursue training connected to human rights, public health, international and development economics, microfinance, food-chain safety, cultural conservation, disaster and risk management, supply-chain management and cybersecurity.

The scholarship is particularly suited to candidates who already have relevant academic qualifications and professional experience and who can clearly demonstrate how specialised international training will contribute to their professional development and wider impact.

For eligible applicants, the most important next step is to verify the requirements of the specific programme they wish to pursue, prepare the required documentation and establish or validate their GIRAF account well before the deadline.

Application deadline: 18 September 2026 at 12:00 noon Belgian time (UTC+1).

Applicants should submit their applications before the deadline and remember that once an application is submitted, it can no longer be modified. Always verify the latest requirements and instructions through the official ARES documentation before submitting.

TITLE: Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027: Fully Funded Leadership Programme for Mid-Career Security and Defence Professionals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027, hosted by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom in Shrivenham, offers a specialised opportunity for experienced professionals working in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, resilience, civil protection, and related international organisations.

Funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and delivered by Cranfield University, the six-week fellowship is designed to strengthen the leadership, strategic decision-making, organisational resilience, cyber resilience, and emerging-technology capabilities of mid-career professionals from across Europe.

The programme brings together professionals who have demonstrated leadership potential and who have the ability to influence policy, strategy, organisational capability, or operational effectiveness within their organisations and countries.

Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027 at a Glance

Programme: Chevening Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

Host institution: Cranfield University

Host location: Defence Academy of the United Kingdom, Shrivenham

Funding: UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)

Duration: Six weeks

Cohort 1: 25 January – 5 March 2027

Cohort 2: 15 March – 23 April 2027

Application deadline: 27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC

Target applicants: Mid-career European professionals in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, resilience, and international organisations

Programme format: Teaching, discussions, practical exercises, site visits, individual research, simulations, workshops, and collaborative learning

About the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

The Chevening Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is designed for professionals who operate in environments where security and defence challenges are becoming increasingly complex and interconnected.

Modern security challenges can involve traditional defence concerns alongside cyber threats, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, organisational vulnerabilities, governance challenges, and international cooperation.

The fellowship therefore takes an interdisciplinary and applied approach.

Rather than focusing on a single area of defence or security, participants will explore how leadership, organisational culture, governance, technology, resilience, and strategic decision-making interact.

The programme is intended to help fellows become more effective leaders who can operate within rapidly changing security and defence environments.

Participants will engage in:

Teaching and academic learning

Group discussions

Practical exercises

Workshops

Simulations

Practitioner-led sessions

Site and institutional visits in the United Kingdom

Individual research

Collaborative learning

International professional networking

A major component of the fellowship will be the opportunity to develop a research project addressing a relevant policy, leadership, organisational, or security challenge.

What Is the Aim of the Fellowship?

The programme aims to develop professionals who can operate effectively in complex security and defence environments.

Through the fellowship, participants will strengthen their ability to understand and respond to challenges affecting:

Governments

International organisations

Public institutions

Defence organisations

Security institutions

Civil protection systems

Resilience structures

The programme places particular emphasis on practical leadership and strategic thinking.

Fellows will be encouraged to examine problems from different perspectives and consider how decisions made under uncertainty can affect organisations, governments, and societies.

Six-Week Fellowship Programme

The fellowship lasts for six weeks and is offered through two cohorts in 2027.

Cohort 1

25 January – 5 March 2027

Cohort 2

15 March – 23 April 2027

Applicants should therefore consider which cohort best fits their professional circumstances when applying.

Key Learning Areas of the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

The programme is organised around six integrated themes.

1. Global Leadership in an Era of Complexity

The first theme focuses on leadership within an increasingly complex international environment.

Security and defence professionals frequently need to make decisions while dealing with multiple stakeholders, competing interests, uncertainty, and rapidly changing circumstances.

Through this theme, fellows will examine leadership challenges and consider approaches for operating effectively in complex environments.

2. Understanding People, Culture, and Organisations

Security and defence organisations are influenced not only by policies and structures but also by people, organisational culture, behaviour, and governance.

This theme examines how these factors can influence:

Institutional effectiveness

Organisational resilience

Vulnerability

Decision-making

Leadership

Organisational performance

Understanding organisational culture and human behaviour can help leaders identify both strengths and vulnerabilities within their institutions.

3. Cyber Resilience and Information Threats

Cybersecurity and information threats are increasingly important components of national and international security.

The fellowship will provide fellows with an opportunity to explore cyber resilience and understand the challenges associated with information threats.

Participants will consider how organisations can better understand and respond to emerging cyber-related risks.

This theme is particularly relevant to professionals whose responsibilities involve security policy, resilience, defence, intelligence, technology, or organisational risk.

4. Artificial Intelligence, Governance, and Emerging Technology

Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are changing the way organisations operate and make decisions.

At the same time, these technologies create new governance, security, and ethical challenges.

The fellowship will examine both the opportunities and risks associated with artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies.

Participants will be encouraged to consider how governments and organisations can respond to technological change while maintaining effective governance and resilience.

5. Strategic Decision-Making Under Pressure

Security and defence professionals may be required to make important decisions in circumstances characterised by:

Uncertainty

Incomplete information

Competing pressures

Rapidly changing conditions

The fellowship will explore strategic decision-making approaches that can help professionals respond effectively in such environments.

The focus is not simply on making decisions, but on understanding the conditions under which strategic decisions are made and the factors that can influence their effectiveness.

6. Building Resilience and Future Leadership

The final theme brings together the fellowship’s emphasis on resilience and leadership.

Participants will explore how organisations can prepare for future challenges while developing leaders who can operate effectively in changing environments.

This theme connects leadership development with organisational resilience and the ability to anticipate and respond to future security challenges.

What Will Fellows Do During the Programme?

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship uses a variety of learning methods rather than relying exclusively on classroom teaching.

Participants will have opportunities to engage in:

Lectures

Fellows will receive structured academic and professional input covering the programme’s major themes.

Workshops

Workshops will provide opportunities to explore issues in greater depth and apply concepts to practical situations.

Simulations

Practical simulations will allow fellows to engage with scenarios that reflect complex decision-making environments.

Practitioner Speakers

Fellows will hear from practitioners and professionals with relevant experience in defence, security, leadership, policy, and related areas.

Research Activity

Each fellow will work on an individual research project addressing a relevant challenge.

UK Institutional Visits

The programme includes visits to relevant institutions in the United Kingdom, providing participants with additional opportunities to understand institutional practices.

Collaborative Learning

Participants will learn alongside professionals from different European countries and professional backgrounds, creating opportunities for the exchange of ideas and experiences.

Fellowship Research Project

A significant component of the programme is the individual research project.

Throughout the fellowship, participants will work on a research project addressing a relevant:

Policy challenge

Leadership challenge

Organisational challenge

Security challenge

Fellows will receive academic support while developing their research.

At the conclusion of the programme, participants will have the opportunity to present their findings to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) in London.

This gives fellows an opportunity to connect their research to real-world policy and institutional challenges.

International Networking Opportunities

The programme brings together professionals from across Europe and the UK, creating opportunities to establish relationships across:

Countries

Professional sectors

Government institutions

Security organisations

Defence communities

International organisations

The fellowship is designed to create enduring professional networks that can continue beyond the six-week programme.

For professionals working in security and defence, these international relationships can be valuable for exchanging knowledge, experiences, and perspectives on shared challenges.

The fellowship is specifically intended for mid-career professionals from eligible European countries who demonstrate leadership potential in security and defence.

Applicants must meet the programme’s additional eligibility requirements as well as the standard Chevening eligibility criteria.

Academic and Professional Requirements

In addition to meeting the standard Chevening eligibility criteria, applicants must meet several fellowship-specific requirements.

Postgraduate Qualification

Applicants must hold a postgraduate qualification, or have equivalent professional training or experience in a relevant field.

Professional Experience

Applicants must have at least five years of relevant professional experience.

Relevant Professional Sector

Applicants must be mid-career professionals employed within areas such as:

Government

Defence

Security
