Resilience

International organisations with responsibilities for national or international security

Leadership Potential

Applicants must be able to demonstrate leadership potential.

The fellowship is aimed at professionals who have the potential to contribute to organisational and national security-related priorities through their leadership.

Ability to Influence

Applicants should be working in roles that have the potential to influence:

Organisational capability

Policy

Strategy

Operational effectiveness

This influence may be within the applicant’s organisation and/or country.

Commitment After the Fellowship

Applicants must demonstrate a commitment to applying the knowledge, experience, and professional networks gained through the fellowship after completing the programme.

This means applicants should be able to explain how the fellowship could contribute to their future professional work and wider organisational or national impact.

Funding and Benefits

The fellowship provides financial support to successful participants.

According to the provided information, each fellowship includes:

Full Programme Fees

The fellowship covers the full programme fees.

Living Expenses

Fellows receive living expenses for the duration of the fellowship, including pre-arranged accommodation close to Oxford, as stated in the provided programme information.

Return Economy Airfare

The fellowship also includes return economy airfare.

These provisions are intended to support fellows throughout their participation in the six-week programme.

Why This Fellowship Is Relevant to Today’s Security Environment

Security and defence professionals increasingly need to understand issues beyond traditional security structures.

A contemporary security environment can involve interconnected challenges relating to:

Cybersecurity

Artificial intelligence

Governance

Human behaviour

Leadership

Information threats

International cooperation

Strategic decision-making

The fellowship’s interdisciplinary structure reflects this broader environment.

By bringing these subjects together, the programme aims to help professionals develop a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced by modern governments, organisations, and institutions.

Application Deadline

Applications for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship are open until:

27 September 2026 at 11:00 UTC

Applicants should ensure that their application is submitted before the stated deadline.

Late applications may not be considered, so prospective applicants should allow sufficient time to review the eligibility criteria and prepare their application.

How to Apply

Eligible applicants can apply through the official Chevening application system.

Apply for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship

Before applying, prospective candidates should carefully review both the standard Chevening eligibility requirements and the additional requirements for the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship.

What Makes a Strong Candidate for This Fellowship?

Based on the requirements provided, a strong candidate would be someone who can demonstrate several important characteristics.

1. Relevant Professional Experience

The applicant should have substantial experience in a relevant security, defence, government, resilience, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, or international organisation environment.

2. Leadership Potential

Applicants should demonstrate that they have the potential to become or continue developing as influential leaders within their professional environment.

Important Information for Applicants

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is a specialised programme with specific professional requirements.

The fellowship specifically targets mid-career professionals whose current employment and responsibilities are connected to security, defence, resilience, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, or relevant international organisations.

Applicants should also pay attention to the requirement concerning the ability to influence organisational capability, policy, strategy, or operational effectiveness.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Europe Defence and Security Fellowship?

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship is a six-week Chevening fellowship funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and delivered by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom in Shrivenham.

Conclusion

The Europe Defence and Security Fellowship 2027 offers a specialised six-week professional development experience for mid-career European professionals working in defence, security, government, law enforcement, intelligence, civil protection, resilience, and relevant international organisations.

Delivered by Cranfield University at the Defence Academy of the United Kingdom and funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, the programme combines academic learning with practical exercises, simulations, workshops, institutional visits, research, practitioner engagement, and international networking.

Fellows will also undertake an individual research project and present their findings to the FCDO in London at the end of the fellowship.

The opportunity is particularly suited to professionals who already have substantial experience and responsibilities within the defence and security environment and who can demonstrate the potential to influence policy, strategy, organisational capability, or operational effectiveness.

TITLE: Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership 2026–2027: Access Training, Seed Funding and Awards of Up to $10,000

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership 2026–2027, an initiative supporting young people who want to create positive change in their schools and communities.

Developed through a partnership between the Andrew Carnegie Foundation and Ashoka, the challenge invites young changemakers from Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, the United States and U.S. territories to submit either a new idea or an existing youth-led initiative that addresses a community problem and strengthens meaningful civic participation.

Successful applicants can access seed funding, peer feedback, training, application support and financial awards. Depending on the applicant’s country and selection level, funding ranges from $50 in early-entry seed support to a top award of $10,000 in the United States. Selected participants may also attend an in-person civic leadership convening in 2027, with eligible travel and participation expenses covered by Ashoka.

The final application deadline is January 31, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Earlier deadlines apply to applicants who want to be considered for Civic Seed Grants. Applications are currently open through the official Changemakers platform.

Important Accuracy Note

As of September 3, 2026, the challenge’s main webpage and its legal Terms and Conditions publish a matching award structure. However, the separate FAQ page still contains a different award breakdown that appears not to reflect the current figures.

The funding details in this article therefore follow the current main challenge page and official Terms and Conditions. Applicants should recheck the official page before submitting because the organizers reserve the right to revise award details.

The official materials also contain minor inconsistencies concerning applicants who are exactly 20 years old, parent or guardian consent thresholds, and certain event dates. These discrepancies are explained below so applicants can take the safest approach.

What Is the Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership?

The Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership is designed to help young people recognize their ability to lead change within their own communities.

For the purpose of this challenge, civic leadership means identifying a meaningful school or community problem and working with other people to develop solutions, inspire action and produce a positive outcome.

Applicants do not need to be elected representatives, government officials or members of a formally registered organization. The opportunity is intended for young people who are taking action—or are ready to begin taking action—on issues affecting their communities.

The organizers are looking for ideas and initiatives that:

Address an identifiable community-based challenge or opportunity.

Encourage people to participate in solving local problems.

Strengthen communities and civic participation.

Mobilize other people around a common purpose.

Offer a new idea or a creative approach to an existing issue.

Demonstrate the potential to produce positive social change.

Are led primarily by young people.

Operate or will be implemented in an eligible country.

Both early-stage ideas and projects already producing results are welcome. An applicant does not need to have a long-established organization or an extensive impact record to participate.

Examples of Projects That Could Fit the Challenge

The official page does not restrict applications to one social issue or project sector. A suitable initiative could therefore address a wide range of local concerns, provided that it is youth-led, community-focused and connected to civic participation.

Potential areas may include:

Youth participation in local decision-making.

Community education and civic awareness.

Environmental protection and community resilience.

School safety and student well-being.

Disability inclusion and accessibility.

Gender equality and social inclusion.

Community health education.

Digital literacy and responsible technology use.

Peacebuilding and conflict resolution.

Voter or civic education, where legally appropriate.

Food security and community-based agriculture.

Support for refugees, migrants or underserved communities.

Volunteerism and neighborhood improvement.

Access to education and youth development.

Community storytelling, journalism or public information.

Intergenerational dialogue and social cohesion.

These are illustrative possibilities rather than an official list of approved themes. Applicants should concentrate on a real issue they understand personally and explain how their proposed action will involve others in creating change.

Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership Deadlines and Timeline

Applicants should distinguish between the early-entry deadlines and the final application deadline.

Early-entry deadlines

Young people who submit an eligible application by the applicable early deadline may be considered for a Civic Seed Grant:

Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa: October 10, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

United States and U.S. territories: November 17, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applicants who miss an early deadline can still apply before the final deadline, but they may lose the opportunity to be considered for the corresponding early-entry seed funding.

Final deadline

Final application deadline: January 31, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Published challenge timeline

The main challenge page presents the following schedule:

September 2, 2026: Applications open.

October 10, 2026: Early-entry deadline for Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa.

November 17, 2026: Early-entry deadline for the United States and U.S. territories.

January 31, 2027: Final application deadline.

February 1–March 5, 2027: Review period.

June 1, 2027: Winners expected to be announced.

July 2027: In-person convenings and summit activities.

The prize section provides more specific convening periods:

The United States convening is expected during the week of July 12, 2027.

The Kenya convening for selected participants from Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa is expected during the week of July 26, 2027.

Applicants should rely on communications from the organizers for final travel dates and arrangements.

Benefits Available to Eligible Participants

The Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership offers more than financial prizes. All eligible participants can potentially benefit from learning, feedback and community-building opportunities.

1. Peer feedback and applicant connections

Participants can engage through the online challenge platform, connect with other applicants and review applications submitted by their peers.

This process can help young changemakers:

See how other young people define community problems.

Learn from different approaches to civic leadership.

Improve their own project descriptions.

Build connections with applicants working on similar issues.

Develop confidence in giving and receiving constructive feedback.

2. Training and live application support

Applicants can access on-demand training intended to support their changemaking journey. The organizers also plan information sessions, office hours and other live support opportunities.

These resources can assist applicants with understanding the challenge, developing their ideas and strengthening their submissions.

3. Opportunity to become an Ashoka Youth Venturer

Every applicant has the opportunity to work toward becoming a certified Ashoka Youth Venturer, even if the applicant is not selected for a financial award.

Applicants who have already taken action on an idea that creates positive change in their school or community may be eligible for a Youth Venture Certificate. Those who have not yet reached the certification criteria may receive guidance intended to help them progress.

4. Multiple pathways to funding

The challenge provides separate funding opportunities for:

Eligible early applicants.

Civic Promise Award recipients.

Civic Impact Award recipients.

Civic Leadership Award recipients.

Receiving early seed funding does not automatically make an applicant a finalist. Early recipients can continue revising their applications until the final deadline and remain eligible for later-stage awards.

Early-Entry Civic Seed Grants

United States and U.S. territories

Up to 600 eligible applicants who submit by November 17, 2026, may each receive a $100 Civic Seed Grant.

Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa

Twenty-five eligible applicants in each participating African country who submit by October 10, 2026, may each receive a $50 Civic Seed Grant.

That represents:

25 potential recipients in Kenya.

25 potential recipients in Nigeria.

25 potential recipients in South Africa.

The seed grants are intended to help applicants take a practical next step toward testing, starting or developing their civic initiative while continuing through the challenge.

Financial Awards for Applicants in the United States

The main challenge page publishes the following award structure for the United States:

12 recipients: $500 each through the Civic Promise Award.

10 recipients: $1,000 each through the Civic Impact Award.

2 recipients: $10,000 each through the Civic Leadership Award.

Anyone receiving an award of at least $500 may be considered for an invitation to the United States convening. A total of 10 selected challenge winners are expected to receive invitations.

The gathering is scheduled for the week of July 12, 2027. It is intended to provide opportunities for participants to connect with other young civic leaders, develop skills and celebrate their work.

Financial Awards for Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa

A total of 66 published awards are to be distributed equally across Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa:

30 recipients: $250 each through the Civic Promise Award.

30 recipients: $1,000 each through the Civic Impact Award.

6 recipients: $5,000 each through the Civic Leadership Award.

When distributed equally, the published structure amounts to the following in each country:

10 Civic Promise Awards of $250.

10 Civic Impact Awards of $1,000.

2 Civic Leadership Awards of $5,000.

Anyone receiving an award of at least $250 may be considered for an invitation to the in-person convening in Kenya. Thirty selected participants from the three countries are expected to attend the gathering during the week of July 26, 2027.

Travel and Convening Support

For participants invited to an in-person gathering, Ashoka states that it will cover eligible travel and participation expenses, including:

Airfare.

Hotel accommodation.

Ground transportation.

Meals provided during the convening.

Eligible chaperone travel for participants under 18, in accordance with the challenge rules.

The Terms and Conditions state that 40 challenge winners across the four participating countries are expected to attend the 2027 gatherings.

Applicants selected for the relevant finalist or winner pathway must be able to participate in the convening. The FAQ states that a person who cannot attend will not be eligible to become a challenge finalist.

If circumstances require the organizers to cancel an in-person event, they may replace it with a virtual event. Under such circumstances, an all-expenses-paid trip would not be provided.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy the challenge’s age, residency, language and youth-leadership requirements.

Age requirement

The main eligibility summary says that participants must be 20 years old or younger by January 31, 2027.

However, another statement on the same page says that the “primary project lead” must be under 20. Because those two statements could be interpreted differently for applicants who are exactly 20, anyone who will be 20 on the final deadline should contact the organizers for written clarification.

Residency requirement

Applicants must currently reside in one of the following eligible locations:

Kenya.

Nigeria.

South Africa.

United States.

A U.S. territory.

Citizenship is not required. For example, an eligible young person may be a legal resident, migrant or citizen of another country, provided the individual currently resides in an eligible location and satisfies all other requirements.

The initiative must also be designed and delivered in one of the eligible countries.

English-language requirement

Applications must be completed and submitted in English.

Youth-leadership requirement

The submitted initiative must be youth-led. The young applicant should be the person driving the idea, project or initiative, even when adults provide administrative, safeguarding or technical support.

New ideas and existing projects

Applicants may enter:

A new idea they are preparing to put into action.

An early-stage initiative that has begun testing its approach.

An existing project already producing community impact.

A youth-led organization or group helping community members participate in positive change.

Individual and team applications

Applicants do not need to have a teammate before applying. Nevertheless, “Team” is one of the evaluation criteria. A solo applicant should therefore explain how other people will be involved or provide a credible plan for building a team.

Previous Ashoka challenge winners

Young people who previously won another Ashoka youth challenge may apply if they meet all the requirements of the Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership.

Excluded applicants

Employees of the Andrew Carnegie Foundation or Ashoka are not eligible. Their children and grandchildren are also excluded.

Parent or Guardian Support: Use the Stricter Interpretation

The main eligibility page and FAQ state that:

Applicants aged 17 or younger in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa need adult assistance.

Applicants aged 12 or younger in the United States need adult assistance.

However, the legal Terms and Conditions use stricter thresholds. They indicate that parent or legal guardian consent is required for:

Applicants aged 18 or younger in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa.

Applicants aged 13 or younger in the United States.

Because the legal terms are stricter, the safest approach is for applicants aged 18 or younger in the three participating African countries and applicants aged 13 or younger in the United States to arrange adult or guardian support before submitting.

Adults are permitted to assist or apply on behalf of an eligible young person. The project must still genuinely be led by the young applicant.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

The organizers identify four principal evaluation areas: Dream, Team, Creativity and Changed World. No public weighting is provided, so applicants should address all four areas clearly.

1. Dream

Reviewers want to understand the challenge or opportunity the initiative addresses and the applicant’s vision for positive change.

A strong submission should explain:

The specific problem affecting the community.

Who experiences the problem.

Why the issue matters.

What personal experience, observation or insight motivated the applicant.

What a successful outcome would look like.

Why the proposed initiative can contribute to that outcome.

Applicants should avoid describing only a broad global problem. They should connect the issue to a particular school, neighborhood or community.

2. Team

The initiative should mobilize people around a shared purpose. Reviewers want to see that the applicant can involve others, encourage collaboration and create opportunities for additional people to contribute or lead.

Applicants may describe:

Existing team members and their responsibilities.

Community partners, schools or organizations involved.

People the project hopes to recruit.

How young participants will help make decisions.

How affected community members will shape the solution.

How responsibilities will be shared.

A formal team is not mandatory at the application stage, but an applicant without one should present a practical team-building plan.

3. Creativity

The project should introduce a new idea, offer a fresh perspective or apply an inventive variation to an existing solution.

Creativity may appear in:

The proposed solution.

The method used to deliver activities.

The way participants are recruited or engaged.

The use of available technology or community resources.

The way an existing model is adapted to local circumstances.

The project’s willingness to test, learn and improve.

Applicants do not need to claim that nobody has ever attempted a similar initiative. They should instead explain what is distinctive or contextually relevant about their approach.

4. Changed World

The organizers apply this criterion differently to new ideas and existing projects.

For a new idea, reviewers are looking for:

Potential to make a positive difference.

A realistic path from idea to action.

Evidence of the applicant’s commitment.

Early learning, testing or traction where available.

For an existing project, reviewers are looking for:

Progress already achieved.

Evidence of positive change.

Potential for the impact to continue.

Opportunities to deepen or expand the work.

A sustainable plan for the next stage.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the Ashoka Changemakers online platform.

Step-by-step application process

Visit the official Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership page.

Select the “Apply Now” button.

Create a Changemakers account using an email address, username and password, or sign in if an account already exists.

Access the Carnegie Challenge application form.

Complete the application in English.

Follow the word limit displayed beside each question.

Save the application as a draft regularly.

Review all responses before submitting.

Submit before the appropriate early deadline if seeking seed-grant consideration.

Make any necessary corrections before the final deadline.

The verified direct account-registration route is available on the Changemakers application portal.

The FAQ states that applicants can save drafts and edit a submitted entry until the final deadline. Applicants should nevertheless avoid waiting until the closing hours because account, consent or technical issues may take time to resolve.

What Applicants Should Prepare

The complete application questions are displayed after applicants create an account and enter the application form. Based on the published evaluation and platform information, applicants should be prepared to provide:

A clear project or initiative title.

A concise description of the community problem.

The applicant’s personal motivation or defining insight.

A description of the proposed solution.

The initiative’s sector, theme or focus area.

The project’s current stage.

Information about the people or community affected.

Details about existing or planned team members.

An explanation of how other people will participate.

Evidence of progress if the project already exists.

A realistic plan for creating, continuing or expanding impact.

An explanation of what is innovative about the approach.

A suitable cover image.

School or organizational information where applicable.

A presentation video if included or requested.

Adult or guardian information where required.

Applicants should not invent statistics or exaggerate results. For an early-stage idea, a credible plan is more useful than unsupported claims of large-scale impact.

Information Sessions and Applicant Support

The organizers plan information sessions for the United States and the three participating African countries.

Published United States information sessions

September 13, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

October 5, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

November 3, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

December 17, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

Published sessions for Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa

September 13, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. East Africa Time.

October 5, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. East Africa Time.

November 3, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. East Africa Time.

December 17, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. East Africa Time.

United States application-assistance office hours

The webpage also lists two-hour office-hour sessions for United States applicants:

September 27, 2026, from 7:00–9:00 p.m. Eastern Time or 4:00–6:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

November 1, 2026, from 7:00–9:00 p.m. Eastern Time or 4:00–6:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

The page contains inconsistent weekday labels beside some support-session dates. Applicants should therefore confirm the date, weekday, time zone and registration status directly on the live resources section of the challenge page.

Funding Conditions and Recipient Responsibilities

Financial support is intended to advance the initiative described in the recipient’s application.

Seed-grant recipients and later-stage award recipients may be required to:

Sign a funding agreement.

Explain how the money was used.

Submit progress and impact updates.

Provide expenditure information.

Participate in monitoring and evaluation.

Meet reasonable publicity and communications requirements.

Use the award to advance the submitted initiative.

Comply with applicable national and local laws.

Awards are provided as gross amounts. Recipients are responsible for understanding and paying any applicable income, social-security or indirect taxes in their country of tax residence.

The organizers retain discretion over awards and reserve the right to change award details. Applicants should read the full Terms and Conditions before accepting funding.

Privacy and Public Application Information

Applicants should understand that parts of their submissions may be made visible to other applicants or the public.

According to the Terms and Conditions, publicly displayed information may include:

Username.

Profile photograph.

Country, city and state.

Initiative title.

Initiative cover image.

Project description.

Sector, theme or focus.

Project stage.

School information.

Project category.

Presentation video, if included.

Challenge jurors and peers involved in community review may access application information during the review process.

Bank details requested from awardees are intended for grant disbursement and are not listed as public information. Applicant information may be retained for up to seven years or for any longer period required by applicable law.

Applicants, particularly minors and their supporting adults, should review the platform’s privacy policy and avoid placing unnecessary private information in publicly visible project descriptions.

Intellectual Property and Communications Rights

Applicants retain their individual intellectual-property rights in original work submitted through the challenge.

However, every applicant must ensure that:

The submitted work is original, or the applicant has permission to use it.

Photographs, music, video and written materials do not violate another person’s rights.

Written consent has been obtained for protected material where required.

The entry complies with applicable laws.

The Terms also allow the challenge partners to share and promote publicly submitted entry information. This may include the applicant’s name, likeness, project information, photographs, recordings and other publicly provided materials through websites, publications, journalism and social media.

Applicants should read these provisions carefully before submitting media involving children or identifiable community members.

Contact and Technical Support

Questions about eligibility, consent, application problems or technical difficulties can be directed to:

Email: civicleadershipchallenge@ashoka.org

Instagram: @ashokachangemakers

United States text support: (571) 622-1066 for young people aged 13 and older

Applicants should contact the organizers directly if they:

Will be exactly 20 years old on January 31, 2027.

Are uncertain whether adult consent is required.

Cannot access or submit the form.

Do not receive an expected guardian-consent email.

Need clarification about convening attendance.

Find that a support-session date or registration link does not match the published schedule.

Practical Application Tips

To develop a stronger application:

Start with a specific community problem rather than a broad global issue.

Explain the personal observation or experience that led to the idea.

Show that affected community members will participate in shaping the solution.

Describe what makes the proposed approach different or locally appropriate.

Include evidence where available, but do not exaggerate early results.

Present realistic next steps, responsibilities and timelines.

Explain how seed funding or a larger award would move the initiative forward.

Address all four evaluation areas: Dream, Team, Creativity and Changed World.

Arrange parent or guardian support early if it may be required.

Save the application frequently and submit before the final hours.

Apply by the regional early-entry deadline to preserve seed-grant eligibility.

Recheck the live challenge page for corrections or changes before submitting.

Conclusion

The Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership 2026–2027 offers young people an opportunity to turn community concerns into practical action. It welcomes both new ideas and existing initiatives, making it relevant to applicants who are just beginning their changemaking journey as well as those already leading community projects.

Participants can benefit from training, peer engagement, feedback, potential Ashoka Youth Venturer certification and multiple funding pathways. Early applicants may receive small seed grants, while later-stage recipients can access awards of up to $10,000 in the United States and up to $5,000 in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa. Selected young leaders may also participate in fully supported in-person gatherings during July 2027.

Eligible applicants should review the legal conditions, prepare a clear explanation of their community problem and solution, and apply early whenever possible. The final deadline is January 31, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Official reference and application page: Carnegie Challenge for Civic Leadership

TITLE: Byron Drury, Academic Staff

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Dr. Byron Coffin Drury
Title: Lecturer
Email: bdrury@mit.edu
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, 26-331
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:

Physics Education Group

Area of Physics

Condensed Matter Theory, Quantum Information Science, Physics Education Research

Research Interests

Dr. Drury’s primary research interest is the factors that influence student learning, sense of belonging, self efficacy, and interest in undergraduate physics courses. He studies the effects of peer mentorship and other novel pedagogical techniques on student behaviors, attitudes and performance.

Other research areas include the application of machine learning to educational assessment and the quantum behavior of classically chaotic systems.

Biographical Sketch

Byron received a BS in Physics from Haverford College in 2008 and completed a Masters in Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics at Cambridge University as a Churchill Scholar in 2009. He earned his PhD in Physics from MIT in 2017, studying condensed matter theory. Since then, he has spent his time teaching and performing Physics Education Research as a postdoc and then lecturer at MIT.

TITLE: Statement by the Association of African Universities (AAU) on the Passing of Professor Christine Dranzoa, Vice Chancellor of Muni University, Uganda

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the entire African higher education community are deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Professor Christine Dranzoa, the Vice-Chancellor of the Muni University, which occurred on June 28, 2022.

As the first female Professor and Vice-Chancellor of the Muni University, she was a trailblazer and role model to many, especially young girls who aspire to climb the ladder and occupy top leadership roles in African Higher Education Institutions. Prof. Dranzoa was a woman of several talents and capabilities and had a rich experience serving as a wildlife ecologist, conservationist, educationalist, facilitator and an administrator.

Due to her strong track record as a zealous advocate for the girl child’s education, she was nicknamed “the defender of the girl child”. She was also awarded a medal of excellence in education by the Forum for African Women Educationists-Uganda chapter in 1999, for mentoring the girl child, and went on to become the honorary secretary for the pan-African body. In 2002, the Dierenpark Amersfoort of the Netherlands awarded her the Wankele Aarde (Unbalanced Earth Trophy) for her contribution to wildlife conservation. She served as the Executive Committee chairperson of Inter University Council of East Africa (IUCEA), at the time of her death.

On behalf of the Governing Board of the AAU, the 400 plus member universities of the Association, Staff of the AAU and all the stakeholders of the African Higher Education community, the Association of African Universities extends its heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family, and commiserates with the Uganda Ministry of Education, the Muni University community, as well as the entire citizenry of Uganda, and Africa on this sad event.

We will fondly remember Prof. Dranzoa for her immense contribution to wildlife, the girl child education and academic leadership in Africa. Indeed, Africa has lost a great mentor, scholar, and leader.

May Her Dear Soul Rest in Perfect Peace!

TITLE: Choosing the Right University and Course for Your Study Abroad Degree

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Studying abroad is a major investment in your education, career and future. Beyond earning an international degree, it can expose you to new cultures, professional networks, opportunities and ways of thinking. However, with thousands of universities and courses available across the UK, United States, Canada, Australia, Europe and other destinations, deciding where and what to study can quickly become overwhelming. It is easy to begin with university rankings or familiar names such as Edinburgh, Oxford, Harvard,Toronto or Melbourne. But a famous university is not automatically the right university for you, and a popular course is not necessarily the course that will move you towards your goals. The best choice is one that connects your interests, career ambitions, finances and the opportunities you hope to access after graduation.

1. Start With Where You Want the Degree to Take You
Before searching for universities, think about what you want your degree to help you achieve. You do not need to know exactly what job you will have in five years, but you should have some idea of the sector, profession or problem you want to work on. For example, imagine that you are passionate about improving healthcare in your country. Your first thought might be to study Public Health. However, if your ambition is specifically to influence national health policies, a programme combining Public Health and Health Policy might be more useful. If you want to manage large health programmes for international organisations, Global Health or International Development with a health specialisation might be a better fit. The same applies to someone who wants to work in international development. You may encounter master’s degrees in Development Studies, International Development, Public Policy, International Relations and Social Policy. Although these programmes overlap, they can lead you towards different skills and career pathways. Instead of asking only, “What do I want to study?”, ask, “What do I want to be able to do after studying this?”

2. Look Beyond the Course Title
One of the easiest mistakes to make is choosing a programme because its title sounds impressive. Suppose you receive offers for an MSc International Development from two different universities. At first glance, they may appear almost identical. However, when you examine the modules, one programme may focus strongly on economics, quantitative methods and development policy, while another emphasises gender, politics, inequality and community-led development. The same principle applies to courses such as Data Science, Business Analytics or Artificial Intelligence. One programme may expect significant previous programming experience, while another may be designed for students transitioning from non-technical backgrounds. Always examine the compulsory modules, optional courses, assessment methods and dissertation requirements. If a university offers ten modules and eight of them do not genuinely interest you, the attractive course title should not persuade you otherwise.

3. Research the University’s Strength in Your Field
University rankings can be helpful, but overall rankings should not make the decision for you. Imagine choosing between University A, which is ranked highly overall, and University B, which has a particularly strong research centre in your area of interest. If you want to specialise in climate finance and University B has academics researching climate finance, partnerships with relevant organisations and regular industry events, that environment may be more valuable to your career than the difference between the universities’ overall rankings. This becomes even more important for master’s and doctoral students. If you hope to research gender-based violence, for example, finding a university with academics and research centres working specifically on gender, violence, feminist policy or human rights could provide access to supervision, networks and opportunities directly connected to your interests. You are therefore not simply choosing a university. You are choosing an academic and professional ecosystem.

4. Think About Your Career Before You Arrive
Career planning should begin before you accept your university offer, not three months before graduation. Suppose you want to move into philanthropy after completing your master’s degree. Before choosing a university, investigate whether its careers service works with foundations, charities, social-impact organisations and international development institutions. Look for professional events, internships, mentorship programmes and opportunities to meet employers. Graduate outcomes can also tell you a great deal. If you are considering an MSc in Finance, for example, search for graduates of that exact programme on LinkedIn. Are they working in banks, investment firms, consulting companies and financial institutions? If you want to work in international development, are graduates progressing into organisations such as the United Nations, international NGOs, government agencies, foundations or development consultancies? Do not assume that a degree automatically creates these opportunities. Investigate the evidence.

5. Choose Your Location Strategically
Where you study can influence the opportunities you encounter outside the classroom. Consider someone hoping to build a career in international affairs. Studying in Washington, D.C., Geneva, Brussels or London could provide proximity to international organisations, think tanks, government institutions, NGOs and policy events. Someone interested in technology might consider the technology ecosystem surrounding cities such as San Francisco, London, Berlin or Toronto. But location must also be balanced against affordability. A university in London, for example, may offer access to an enormous professional network, but accommodation and everyday living costs can be considerably higher than in many other UK cities. Imagine choosing between a one-year master’s degree in London and another in a smaller city. If the London option costs several thousand pounds more in accommodation alone, ask whether the additional professional access genuinely justifies that cost for your particular career. The best location is not necessarily the biggest city. It is the place where academic opportunity, career access, affordability and quality of life come together for you.

6. Understand the Full Financial Commitment
Never look at tuition fees in isolation. Imagine University A charges £20,000 in tuition while University B charges £24,000. University A initially appears cheaper. However, if living expenses around University A are approximately £1,500 per month while you could realistically live on £900 per month around University B, your total expenditure could tell a very different story. Calculate accommodation, food, transportation, flights, visa expenses, immigration-related health charges where applicable, study materials and an emergency allowance alongside tuition. Scholarships should also be researched early. Depending on your nationality, destination and programme, funding may come from the university itself, government scholarship programmes, foundations or international schemes. Some scholarships require applicants to secure university admission first, while others operate according to completely different timelines. Do not wait until you have accepted an expensive offer before asking, “How am I going to pay for this?”

7. Speak to People Who Have Actually Studied There
Sometimes the most useful university research comes from a simple conversation.
Suppose you are considering a master’s programme that promises “excellent industry connections”. Instead of accepting that statement at face value, find two or three graduates on LinkedIn and ask about their experiences. You could ask whether they found the programme practical, whether they had meaningful access to employers, what they found most challenging and, importantly, whether they would choose the same programme again. If several graduates tell you that a supposedly practical course was predominantly theoretical, that is useful information. Equally, you may discover opportunities that are barely mentioned on the university website, such as excellent mentorship, accessible professors, student consulting projects or strong alumni networks. Speak to people, but remember that one person’s experience is not universal. Look for patterns across several conversations.

8. Consider What Happens After Graduation
For international students, your plan should extend beyond graduation day. Suppose you are choosing between programmes in two different countries and hope to gain professional experience abroad after completing your degree. The availability and conditions of post-study work routes could significantly affect your decision. You should therefore investigate current immigration rules, the length and conditions of any post-study work permission, employment restrictions and the longer-term requirements for remaining in the country if that matters to you. More importantly, separate permission to work from the likelihood of finding suitable work. A country may allow international graduates to remain temporarily after university, but that does not guarantee employment. For example, if your target profession requires employer sponsorship after your graduate permission expires, understanding which employers in your industry sponsor international workers can help you make a much more informed decision before investing in the degree. Always verify immigration information through the relevant government’s official website because these policies can change.

9. Compare Offers Based on Value, Not Prestige
Imagine receiving three offers. The first comes from a globally famous university but offers no scholarship. The second comes from a strong university offering you a substantial scholarship. The third is from a less internationally recognised university but has an outstanding programme in your field and excellent connections with the industry you want to enter.Which one should you choose? There is no universal answer. This is where you need to consider the complete picture: what you will learn, what the degree costs, who will teach you, where you will live, what networks you can access and what opportunities previous graduates have secured. Prestige has value, but prestige without alignment can become a very expensive purchase.

Most importantly, choose intentionally.

Strengthening CoARA and Enabling Systemic Reform of Research Assessment – A Booster

CoARA is a global initiative focused on improving research assessment and is hosted by ESF – elected as its secretariat – since December 2022. CoARA’s vision is that the assessment of research, researchers and research organisations recognises the diverse outputs, practices and activities that maximise the quality and impact of research. This requires assessments primarily based on qualitative judgement, for which peer review is central, supported by responsible use of quantitative indicators. Each CoARA member is expected to implement an action plan towards changing their practices following the ten commitments establishing a common direction for research assessment reform and listed in the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment. The Coalition has been set to facilitate information and sharing of practices and eventually help members to reach their objectives.

As an enabler deeply rooted in the CoARA structure, the CoARA Boost project strengthens the ramp-up of CoARA, enhancing its operational capacity and providing means to investigate and implement new models for research assessment. By amplifying its spectrum of actions and providing the additional capacity to implement a Cascade funding programme, CoARA Boost allows to develop a critical mass for reforming research assessment, generate gravitas for new members and facilitates the leveraging of additional sources of funding.

The overarching objective of the CoARA Boost Project is to contribute to enabling systemic reform of research assessment following the principles and commitments of the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment. CoARA Boost’s objectives are to

strengthen CoARA’s operational capacity,

catalyse knowledge development, policy evolution and institutional change in research assessment,

facilitate collection and exchange of information and

widen the Coalition’s membership in Europe and beyond.

TITLE: Call for host – AAU General Conference 2025

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
INTRODUCTION

The Association of African Universities (AAU) will hold its 16th Quadrennial General Conference (QGC) in July 2025. The QGC, comprising representatives of members, associate members and observers, is the supreme authority of the Association and is responsible for determining the general policies of the Association. It is normally a five-day event centered around issues of relevance to higher education in Africa.

The QGC comprises two parts; the first is the business session which evaluates the performance of the AAU in the preceding four years and approves of the programmes for the subsequent four years. The business session also incorporates the election of a new 15-member Board to steer the affairs of the Association for the next four years.

The second part of the QGC is the scientific discussions of the theme and sub-themes of the Conference under the biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and Rectors of African Universities (COREVIP). At the 16th General Conference, the 23rd COREVIP will be held.

These events are jointly organised by the AAU and a member institution in good standing with the Association (i.e. having zero arrears in annual subscription payment). It should be noted that the co-hosting of this most important event on the calendar of the African higher education community provides very high-level visibility and exposure to the host institution and country because of the calibre and number of academic leaders, policymakers, researchers, development partners, industry, and other stakeholders that usually attend it, and it is, therefore, a highly sought-after event.

2025 QGC THEME

Yet to be finalized.

CALL FOR HOST

The AAU hereby invites applications from member institutions for the co-hosting of this prestigious quadrennial Conference.

The Host’s Responsibilities

The host university will be expected to contribute to the organisation of the Conference, financially or in kind, in the areas of:

Local transportation for participants.

Airport “meet and greet” (reception and facilitation of immigration procedures).

Traditional items as gifts to presenters and sessional chairs.

Welcome Reception or Dinner for participants.

Publicity and media coverage (local press, radio and TV, conference photographer).

Arrangement of courtesy calls by the Governing Board on appropriate government authorities in the host country.

Arrangement of excursion visits by delegates.

Providing the Secretariat for the Conference (equipment and supplies).

Decorations, banners, invitations to Opening/Closing Ceremony and receptions.

Cultural display during open and closing ceremonies.

Institutions interested in co-hosting the 16th Quadrennial General Conference should officially apply by filling this form: https://www.research.net/r/HostAAUGC25

The deadline for the receipt of the official application is Friday, 28, June 2024.

Freelancers, gig workers, independent contractors, artists, researchers, organizers, policymakers, advocates, entrepreneurs, technologists, community leaders, and others interested in the changing nature of work are among the people the program seeks to engage.

Selected fellows will participate in a year-long learning and collaboration experience while receiving a $30,000 stipend for their participation.

Applications opened on September 8, 2026, and the application deadline is October 26, 2026. Applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, meaning interested candidates are encouraged to apply early rather than waiting until the final deadline.

About the Work//Shift Fellowship

The Work//Shift Fellowship is built around the changing nature of employment.

Many traditional social protection systems were developed around stable employer-employee relationships. However, millions of people earn income through arrangements that do not necessarily fit that model.

These include:

Freelancers

Independent contractors

Artists and cultural workers

Domestic workers

Care workers

App-based workers

Rideshare and delivery workers

Temporary workers

Project-based professionals

On-demand workers

Other people working outside traditional employment structures

The Work//Shift Fellowship creates a collaborative environment in which participants can examine these realities and explore new approaches to worker protection and economic security.

Instead of beginning with predetermined answers, fellows will engage in inquiry, shared learning, experimentation, imagination, and cross-sector collaboration.

The fellowship is particularly interested in creating relationships among people who might not normally work together but who bring different forms of professional knowledge, community experience, lived experience, and expertise to questions about the future of work.

Why the Work//Shift Fellowship Was Created

The nature of work continues to evolve.

Freelance, contract, temporary, platform-based, project-based, and other nontraditional forms of employment have become important parts of modern economies. At the same time, many systems providing benefits and protections remain closely connected to traditional employment arrangements.

This creates important questions about how workers outside conventional employment structures can obtain the security and support they need.

The Work//Shift Fellowship provides a space for people to examine these challenges collectively.

Rather than focusing exclusively on one profession, policy area, or industry, the program deliberately brings together people from multiple disciplines and sectors.

The goal is to develop the relationships, knowledge, imagination, and collaborative capacity needed to explore new approaches to worker protections, economic justice, and social safety nets.

Who Should Apply for the Work//Shift Fellowship?

The program is looking for people who are already thinking seriously about the future of work, particularly freelance, gig, independent, and other forms of nontraditional work.

Applicants do not need to have all the answers or arrive with a fully developed project.

Potential applicants may include:

Organizers and movement builders

Policy advocates

Researchers

Storytellers

Cooperative entrepreneurs

Systems entrepreneurs

Artists

Cultural workers

Labor advocates

Worker advocates

Community leaders

Academics

Technologists

Journalists

Policymakers

Disability rights advocates

Domestic workers

Home healthcare workers

App-based workers

Builders working on emerging models of care

People developing new ownership models

People exploring alternative economic systems

Freelancers and independent contractors

Applicants can approach the fellowship’s central questions from many different professional and community perspectives.

What matters is having a meaningful connection to the issues being explored and an interest in contributing to a more equitable future of work.

What the Fellowship Is Looking for in Applicants

The Work//Shift Fellowship is seeking applicants who demonstrate a genuine commitment to improving conditions for gig workers, freelancers, artists, independent workers, and other workers who may lack traditional employment protections.

Successful applicants are expected to demonstrate characteristics including:

Commitment to Worker Well-Being

Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in improving conditions for freelancers, gig workers, artists, independent contractors, or other workers operating outside conventional employment arrangements.

Curiosity

The fellowship is designed for people willing to ask difficult questions rather than simply defend existing systems or assumptions.

Willingness to Challenge Assumptions

Participants should be prepared to reconsider conventional ideas about employment, worker benefits, institutions, economic security, and social safety nets.

Openness to New Perspectives

Because fellows will come from different sectors and backgrounds, participants should be comfortable learning from perspectives that may differ substantially from their own.

Collaborative Mindset

The fellowship emphasizes collective learning rather than isolated individual work. Applicants should therefore demonstrate an ability and willingness to collaborate across sectors and disciplines.

Community or Professional Relationships

Strong candidates are expected to have meaningful relationships within their communities, industries, professions, or fields.

Interest in Economic Justice and Worker Protection

Applicants should be interested in contributing to a broader ecosystem of people developing new ideas around worker protections and economic justice.

Work//Shift Fellowship Learning Journey

The 12-month fellowship is structured around four major stages of collective learning.

1. Unlearning

The first stage encourages fellows to question existing assumptions about work, institutions, employment structures, and the systems that influence economic life.

Participants will examine ideas that may traditionally have been accepted as fixed or inevitable and consider whether different arrangements are possible.

2. Sensemaking

Fellows will work toward developing a shared understanding of the political, economic, social, and cultural forces affecting today’s workers.

This stage is intended to help participants understand the broader environment in which employment systems and worker protections operate.

3. Envisioning Possibilities

Participants will examine historical examples, community innovations, emerging models, and other approaches that demonstrate alternative ways of organizing work, support, ownership, care, and economic security.

The objective is to expand the range of solutions participants believe may be possible.

4. Building

The final stage focuses on turning learning and relationships into new ideas and opportunities for collaboration.

Fellows may develop new concepts, partnerships, projects, or other initiatives that contribute to improving the future of work.

What Fellows Will Receive

One of the most significant features of the Work//Shift Fellowship is its financial support.

$30,000 Fellowship Stipend

Each fellow will receive a $30,000 stipend for participation in the 12-month fellowship.

The stipend supports participation in fellowship activities, including meetings and assigned reading, writing, planning, reflection, and other program-related work.

12-Month Fellowship Experience

The fellowship lasts approximately one year, giving participants sufficient time to engage deeply with the program’s questions and build meaningful relationships with other fellows.

Hybrid Participation

The program combines virtual programming with selected in-person gatherings.

This structure enables fellows to participate remotely in much of the program while still having opportunities for face-to-face collaboration.

Cross-Sector Network

Participants will build relationships with people working across different sectors and disciplines.

This network is an important part of the fellowship because the program emphasizes relationships and shared learning as major outcomes.

Access to Guest Practitioners

Fellows will learn from guest practitioners as well as from members of their cohort.

Participants will also bring their own professional knowledge, community experience, and expertise into the learning environment.

Fellowship Duration and Time Commitment

The Work//Shift Fellowship will run for 12 months.

Fellows should expect a baseline commitment of approximately 10 hours per month.

This time may include:

Virtual cohort meetings

Reading and learning materials

Written assignments

Planning activities

Individual reflection

Discussions with other fellows

Collaborative activities

Relationship building

Fellowship-related preparation

The fellowship has intentionally been structured so participants can remain engaged in existing professional or community work.

According to the program’s FAQ, applicants can participate while working full-time.

Cohort Size

The Work//Shift Fellowship is expected to select approximately eight fellows.

The relatively small cohort is designed to facilitate deeper collaboration, relationship building, discussion, and collective learning among participants.

In-Person Convenings

Fellows will participate in two in-person cohort convenings during the fellowship.

The first gathering is scheduled to take place in Southern California on January 29–30, 2027.

Travel days for the first gathering are scheduled for January 28 and January 31, 2027.

Information about the second in-person convening will be communicated to fellows in advance.

Fellowship Start Date

The fellowship will begin in January 2027, starting with an in-person cohort gathering.

Selected applicants should therefore consider their availability for the January 2027 launch when applying.

Do Applicants Need a Fully Developed Project?

No.

Applicants do not need to enter the Work//Shift Fellowship with a fully developed project.

This is an important feature of the program.

The fellowship is designed for people who may already have significant questions, early-stage concepts, lived experience, professional expertise, or emerging ideas but who want an environment where those ideas can evolve through collaboration.

The program deliberately creates space for projects and partnerships to emerge through the fellowship experience.

Consequently, applicants should not feel that they need to present a complete solution to the challenges facing gig workers or freelancers before applying.

Can New Projects Emerge From the Fellowship?

Yes.

The organizers expect that new ideas, initiatives, collaborations, and potentially projects may emerge as fellows learn and work together.

However, producing a particular project is not the sole purpose of the fellowship.

The program places significant emphasis on relationships, learning, exploration, and collective imagination.

Depending on the ideas that emerge, opportunities to explore additional resources or implementation support may potentially become available. However, fellows should not assume that additional project funding is guaranteed beyond the $30,000 participation stipend.

Is Work//Shift Only a Policy Fellowship?

No.

Policy is one part of the fellowship, but Work//Shift is not exclusively a policy program.

Its interdisciplinary approach is one of its distinguishing characteristics.

The fellowship welcomes perspectives from people working in areas such as:

Public policy

Organizing

Research

Arts and culture

Technology

Entrepreneurship

Worker advocacy

Community development

Economic development

Cooperative models

Journalism and storytelling

Emerging systems of care and ownership

The program’s underlying idea is that meaningful approaches to the future of work may emerge when people from different sectors learn together.

Do Applicants Need Direct Experience Working With Gig Workers?

Not necessarily.

Applicants do not have to currently work directly with freelancers or gig workers.

However, some present or previous connection to gig work—whether through personal experience, professional work, research, advocacy, policymaking, community engagement, or another indirect connection—may strengthen an application.

The key requirement is having a meaningful connection to the issues the fellowship addresses.

How the Fellowship Defines Gig Work

Work//Shift uses a broad definition of gig work.

It generally refers to work occurring outside a traditional, ongoing employer-employee relationship.

This can include:

Freelance work

Contract work

Temporary employment

Project-based work

On-demand work

Platform-based work

Independent contracting

Examples of workers who may fall within this broad category include rideshare drivers, delivery workers, freelancers, artists, cultural workers, caregivers, domestic workers, and other people whose income is derived from short-term or nontraditional working arrangements.

Because applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, prospective applicants should consider applying as early as possible.

How to Apply for the Work//Shift Fellowship

Prospective applicants should first review the complete fellowship information and eligibility expectations before preparing their application.

Applicants should pay particular attention to demonstrating their:

Commitment to improving worker conditions.

Ability to collaborate across disciplines and sectors.

Existing relationships within relevant communities or professional fields.

Interest in contributing to new approaches to worker protections and economic justice.

Applicants do not need to submit a fully developed project simply to fit the fellowship’s mission. The program explicitly welcomes people whose ideas are still emerging.

Why the Work//Shift Fellowship Is Worth Exploring

Work//Shift stands out because it approaches the future of work as a collaborative systems challenge rather than focusing narrowly on a single profession or predefined policy solution.

The combination of a small cohort, year-long learning experience, interdisciplinary participation, hybrid programming, in-person gatherings, and a substantial $30,000 participation stipend gives selected fellows the opportunity to dedicate meaningful time to exploring complex questions surrounding work and economic security.

The fellowship may be particularly relevant to people who believe existing worker protection systems need to evolve alongside changing employment models and who want to explore those questions with others from different professional and community backgrounds.

Conclusion

The Work//Shift Fellowship 2027 offers gig workers, freelancers, independent contractors, researchers, artists, organizers, advocates, entrepreneurs, policymakers, technologists, and other future-of-work leaders an opportunity to participate in an intensive year-long exploration of worker protections and economic security.

Approximately eight fellows will participate in the 12-month hybrid program and receive a $30,000 stipend, while engaging in virtual programming, collaborative learning, relationship building, and two in-person convenings.

Importantly, applicants do not need to arrive with a complete project or ready-made solution. Work//Shift is designed to provide the intellectual and collaborative environment in which new relationships, ideas, and initiatives can emerge.

TITLE: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS) AI Policy Fellowship 2027 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 27, 2026

Applications are open for the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS) AI Policy Fellowship 2027. The IAPS AI Policy Fellowship is a fully funded, three-month program for professionals from varied backgrounds seeking to strengthen practical policy skills for securing a positive future in a world with powerful AI.

The IAPS Policy Fellowship is designed to cultivate the talent needed to ensure AI policy can meet the magnitude of challenges emerging from the frontier. Participants embed into the live AI policy field, responding to priority policy windows, and developing the skills to further their careers at leading organizations in the field.

Fellowship Tracks

Two tracks are available to participants:

Research Track: The Research track pairs you with an IAPS researcher (or an external supervisor at a partner organization) to produce a substantive piece of AI policy research over the course of the Fellowship. You will scope a question with your supervisor in the first weeks, then take primary ownership of the analysis and writing, with regular feedback on research direction, methods, and drafting for a policy audience. The goal is developing the ability to carry a research project from open question to evidence-based conclusions, and to produce a publishable output. Former Fellows have published reports written during their time with IAPS.

Applied Track: The Applied track focuses more on hands-on policy work rather than a single research output. You will work with a supervisor on projects closer to the practice of AI policy that will require adaptability to real-life, evolving situations rather than building deep specialization on a research question. This track would suit people coming from an adjacent field (government, programs, operations, event organizing, grantmaking, etc.) who want to fast-track the conversion of existing professional skills into AI policy experience, or researchers who want to transition to practitioner roles. Former Fellows have run policy workshops, assisted in evaluating grant applications, and collaborated on policy memos.

Financial Support

Senior Fellows will receive $24,000 and Fellows $18,000 as a stipend to work full-time during the three-month program.

Fellows on the DC or London track will also receive an additional $3,000 stipend.

They can provide part-time options for exceptional candidates.

They will provide financial support for travel and accommodation for the two-week D.C. event.

Eligibility

They are looking for people who want to develop a career in AI policy and address the lasting implications of frontier AI.

They encourage applicants to familiarize themselves with IAPS’s areas of focus by checking out their research.

Applicants with policy, technical, academic, and government backgrounds are strongly recommended, but they are open to a wide variety of backgrounds.

Application

The application takes about 45 minutes, in five sections:

About you (5 min): basic details and eligibility.

Your experience (5 min): where you have worked, for how long, and what you did.

Your motivation (10 min): rank the AI policy issues that motivate you, then two short written answers – a research interest (up to 300 words) and your career goals (150-200 words).

Communicating with stakeholders (10 min): one written reply to a policy conversation (100-200 words).

Timed reasoning (15 min): logic and reasoning questions with a timer. This comes last, and you start it when you are ready.
