TITLE: York University YSpace Venture Catalyst 2026: Free Startup Program for Early-Stage Technology Founders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the York University YSpace Venture Catalyst 2026, a highly practical entrepreneurship program designed to help early-stage technology founders transform innovative ideas into stronger, validated, and potentially market-ready ventures.

Delivered through YSpace, York University’s entrepreneurship and innovation hub, the Venture Catalyst program provides founders with structured business development support, expert mentorship, interactive workshops, peer-to-peer learning, and access to an entrepreneurial ecosystem designed to help startups avoid common early-stage mistakes and accelerate progress.

For the current Fall 2026 cycle, applications officially opened on August 25, 2026, and interested founders must submit their applications by September 25, 2026. Successful applicants are expected to receive final acceptance decisions by October 9, 2026, with programming beginning on October 21, 2026 and concluding with Demo Day on December 10, 2026.

One of the strongest features of the York University YSpace Venture Catalyst is that participation is free, and YSpace states that it does not take equity in participating companies. The program is also not restricted solely to York University students or alumni, making it accessible to eligible founders from the wider entrepreneurial community.

About the York University YSpace Venture Catalyst Program

The Venture Catalyst is an intensive early-stage startup development program that supports entrepreneurs who are still shaping their business concept, validating an idea, developing a proof-of-concept, or refining an early minimum viable product.

The program is operated by YSpace at York University in partnership with the Black Entrepreneurship Alliance (BEA). YSpace describes itself as York University’s pan-university entrepreneurship and innovation hub, supporting startups, scaleups, students, researchers, entrepreneurs, and founders from different sectors and communities.

The Venture Catalyst is particularly relevant for technology entrepreneurs who have an innovative concept but need structured guidance to determine whether the concept has genuine commercial potential.

Instead of focusing only on theoretical entrepreneurship education, Venture Catalyst is structured around practical venture development. Participants are expected to work directly on their companies, test assumptions, improve their business models, develop customer strategies, and make measurable progress toward launching or strengthening their products.

The current program is described as a two-month program for early-stage founders, whether they are developing their first concept or already refining an MVP.

What Is the Main Purpose of Venture Catalyst?

Many promising technology startups fail during their earliest stages because founders begin developing products without adequately validating the customer problem, target market, value proposition, business model, or go-to-market strategy.

The York University Venture Catalyst aims to address these challenges.

During the program, entrepreneurs are supported in critically testing and improving different components of their ventures.

The program is intended to help founders:

Validate whether their startup idea addresses a meaningful market problem.

Test important assumptions behind their business model.

Better understand potential customers and users.

Strengthen their value proposition.

Develop practical customer development strategies.

Improve their go-to-market strategy.

Establish measurable venture development milestones.

Refine or prepare an MVP.

Generate early market traction.

Learn from experienced entrepreneurs and industry professionals.

Avoid potentially expensive mistakes during the early development stage.

Prepare the venture for longer-term growth.

According to YSpace, the program goes beyond simple idea validation. Founders are expected to stress-test their business models, sharpen their go-to-market strategies and strengthen early traction so their ventures are built on stronger foundations.

Who Is Venture Catalyst Designed For?

The Venture Catalyst is primarily intended for early-stage technology founders.

The ideal applicant is not necessarily expected to operate an established or profitable business. In fact, the program specifically targets entrepreneurs who may still be working through the ideation and early validation stages.

According to the official eligibility information, Venture Catalyst serves founders who are:

Going through the ideation process.

Validating the feasibility of their business concepts.

Developing innovative technology-based ideas.

Motivated to transform those ideas into viable ventures.

Coachable and receptive to advice.

Collaborative and willing to participate in the startup community.

Demonstrating a growth mindset.

Prepared to commit the necessary time to developing their venture.

YSpace further explains that an ideal participating company is likely to still be in the ideation or early validation phase, with the objective of validating its target market and launching an MVP within approximately three months.

Technology Startups Across Different Industries Can Apply

A major advantage of Venture Catalyst is that the program is sector-agnostic within technology.

This means applicants do not necessarily have to operate within one specific technology vertical.

Technology-enabled businesses operating across different industries may potentially qualify, provided the venture meets the program’s early-stage and innovation requirements.

This could potentially include ventures operating in areas such as:

Artificial intelligence

Software and SaaS

FinTech

EdTech

HealthTech

Climate and sustainability technology

Digital platforms

E-commerce technology

Enterprise software

Consumer technology

Data and analytics

Smart infrastructure

Mobility technology

Transportation technology

Electric vehicles

Automation

Internet of Things

Other technology-enabled sectors

Applicants should, however, demonstrate that technology forms a meaningful component of the business concept rather than merely being incidental to the venture.

YSpace explicitly states that Venture Catalyst remains sector-agnostic and supports technology-based ventures operating across industries.

Specialized Support for Black-Led Ventures

The Venture Catalyst is delivered in partnership with the Black Entrepreneurship Alliance, or BEA.

YSpace indicates that specialized support is available to Black-led businesses participating in the program.

The Black Entrepreneurship Alliance is an initiative developed to strengthen entrepreneurship opportunities for Black founders through entrepreneurship education, mentorship, networking and business development support.

YSpace’s wider BEA programming has historically focused on helping Black entrepreneurs develop, launch, validate and scale their businesses.

Importantly, the general Venture Catalyst program itself is not described on the current official application page as being restricted exclusively to Black founders. Specialized support is available for Black-led businesses, while the broader program welcomes qualifying early-stage technology entrepreneurs.

Mobility Innovation Support

Technology entrepreneurs working in mobility-related areas may also find the Venture Catalyst particularly relevant.

YSpace has expanded its entrepreneurship ecosystem to support mobility ventures working on areas including:

Transportation

Electric vehicles

Smart infrastructure

Mobility technologies

Automotive technologies

Related technology solutions

The main Venture Catalyst webpage states that the Winter cohort includes dedicated mobility innovation support through the Venture Mobility Catalyst.

YSpace’s broader SmartTO programming also supports innovation involving smart mobility, transportation, materials, energy systems, automotive technologies and related sectors.

Founders specifically interested in the mobility stream should verify the availability of specialized mobility places for the relevant cohort when applying.

What Participants Can Expect

Successful applicants receive access to a structured venture development ecosystem rather than simply attending a series of lectures.

The program combines several forms of support to help participating entrepreneurs systematically develop their companies.

1. Expert Mentorship

Participants receive access to experienced mentors who can provide guidance on the strategic and operational challenges involved in developing an early-stage startup.

Mentorship can be particularly valuable for founders who have strong technical ideas but limited experience commercializing products.

2. Hands-On Workshops

Venture Catalyst includes workshops delivered with industry experts.

These workshops are intended to provide founders with practical knowledge that can be immediately applied to their startups rather than remaining purely theoretical.

3. Peer-to-Peer Founder Sessions

Entrepreneurship can be highly isolating, particularly during the ideation and validation stages.

The Venture Catalyst incorporates peer-to-peer sessions that allow founders to learn from one another, share challenges, exchange experiences and build relationships within the startup ecosystem.

4. Office Hours with Subject-Matter Experts

Participants can gain access to a private network of subject-matter experts through dedicated office hours.

This can help founders obtain targeted advice relating to specific business challenges.

5. Dedicated Mentorship

The program identifies a dedicated mentor as one of its key components, providing participants with additional guidance throughout their entrepreneurial journey.

Leadership Development

Venture Catalyst also places emphasis on strengthening founders themselves rather than focusing exclusively on the startup.

Participants receive access to curated leadership content, personal-growth accountability and peer-to-peer support.

This is significant because startup development frequently requires founders to develop new leadership competencies alongside their businesses.

Entrepreneurs may need to learn how to communicate their vision, receive critical feedback, make difficult strategic decisions, manage uncertainty and eventually lead teams.

The leadership-development element therefore complements the technical and commercial aspects of the program.

Customer Development and Go-to-Market Strategy

A core component of Venture Catalyst involves developing practical frameworks for bringing products to customers.

Founders receive guidance related to customer development and go-to-market strategies.

This can help entrepreneurs answer fundamental questions such as:

Who is the ideal customer?

What problem is the venture solving?

How significant is that problem?

Who currently pays to solve the problem?

What alternatives or competitors already exist?

Why would customers choose the new solution?

What channels can be used to acquire customers?

What assumptions must be validated before investing additional resources?

What should be included in the first MVP?

How can the startup generate meaningful early traction?

Developing answers to these questions can significantly reduce the risk of building a product that ultimately lacks market demand.

A Milestone-Driven Approach

The Venture Catalyst uses a milestone-driven approach.

Instead of simply completing classes, participating founders are expected to actively work toward developing and launching their technology ventures.

YSpace describes its programs as goal-driven and based on established frameworks that place founders in control of their development while providing the ecosystem and guidance needed to help them progress.

For applicants, this means Venture Catalyst should be approached as an active venture-building commitment rather than a passive educational course.

How Much Time Must Participants Commit?

Prospective participants should carefully consider whether they have enough time to participate meaningfully in the program.

YSpace states that ventures should devote at least five hours per week to:

Workshops

Mentorship sessions

Venture development activities

This represents a minimum expected commitment.

Founders actively conducting customer interviews, developing an MVP, conducting market research or testing different business models may need to devote considerably more time outside formal programming.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they have sufficient availability to make meaningful progress during the program.

How Much Does Venture Catalyst Cost?

One of the strongest benefits of the York University Venture Catalyst is that the program is free.

YSpace states that there is no participation fee.

Even more importantly for startup founders, the program does not take equity in participating companies.

This means selected founders can access entrepreneurial training, mentorship, workshops and ecosystem support without having to surrender an ownership stake simply for participating in the program.

For founders at the earliest stages of building their businesses, maintaining ownership while gaining professional startup support can be particularly valuable.

Is Venture Catalyst Only for York University Students?

No.

The official Venture Catalyst FAQ specifically addresses this issue.

Applicants do not have to be York University students or alumni to participate.

YSpace states that Venture Catalyst is open to the broader community, provided founders are dedicated and willing to commit the necessary time to developing their ventures.

YSpace more broadly serves entrepreneurs from multiple backgrounds, including students, alumni, faculty members and external community founders.

This makes Venture Catalyst considerably more accessible than university entrepreneurship initiatives that restrict participation to current students.

How Many Startups Will Be Selected?

Selection is competitive because each cohort has limited capacity.

According to the current official information, approximately 15 to 20 ventures may be admitted to each cohort.

The program information also references approximately 5 to 10 ventures in its mobility innovation stream.

Applicants should therefore avoid submitting generic startup descriptions.

A strong application should clearly communicate:

The problem being addressed.

Why the problem matters.

Who experiences the problem.

How the proposed technology solves it.

Why the solution is different or innovative.

The current development stage of the venture.

What validation has already been completed.

What the founders want to accomplish during Venture Catalyst.

Why the founding team is capable of executing the idea.

Why mentorship and program support are needed at this stage.

Venture Catalyst 2026 Timeline

Applicants should carefully note the official Fall 2026 schedule.

Applications Open: August 25, 2026

Application Deadline: September 25, 2026

Final Acceptance: October 9, 2026

Programming Starts: October 21, 2026

Demo Day: December 10, 2026

Application Deadline

The official deadline to apply for the current Venture Catalyst cohort is:

September 25, 2026

Applicants should preferably submit their applications before the final day rather than waiting until the deadline.

Venture Catalyst Application Process

The official selection process consists of several stages.

Step 1: Submit the Online Application

Interested entrepreneurs must complete the Venture Catalyst application while applications are open.

Applicants should provide accurate and well-developed information about their venture, founders, current development stage and business concept.

The official application page describes Venture Catalyst as supporting early-stage technology ventures in developing, validating and refining their startups from an idea toward proof-of-concept.

Step 2: Video Meeting with the YSpace Team

Applicants who progress through the initial review may be contacted by the YSpace team to schedule a video call.

This meeting allows the program team to:

Review the business.

Understand the company’s present development stage.

Learn more about the leadership team.

Evaluate the business concept.

Assess the viability of the proposed venture.

Determine whether Venture Catalyst is appropriate for the founder’s current needs.

Applicants invited to this stage should therefore be prepared to explain their venture clearly and concisely.

Step 3: Admission to the Cohort

Companies accepted into the program are invited to join the Venture Catalyst cohort.

Participants then receive access to the program’s resources and venture-development support.

The official program information highlights resources including:

Curated startup programming

Industry experts

Startup perks

Peer founder circles

Mentorship

Workshops

Venture development support

Opportunity for Continued YSpace Support

Participation may potentially lead to further involvement within the YSpace ecosystem.

According to YSpace, after completing the two-month cohort, selected companies may receive an opportunity to join the YSpace Virtual Membership Program for continued support and growth.

This can be important because startup development rarely ends when an accelerator or entrepreneurship program concludes.

Continued access to a startup ecosystem can help founders maintain momentum, expand their professional networks and access future entrepreneurial resources.

Demo Day

The Fall 2026 Venture Catalyst concludes with a Demo Day scheduled for December 10, 2026.

Demo Day represents an opportunity for participating founders to demonstrate the progress they have made throughout the program and communicate their business concepts more effectively.

Previous YSpace Venture Catalyst showcase events have featured cohort founders presenting their startups through short pitches while connecting with entrepreneurs, mentors, partners and members of the wider innovation ecosystem.

For early-stage entrepreneurs, learning to communicate a startup clearly can be nearly as important as developing the underlying technology.

Why Founders Should Consider Applying

The Venture Catalyst can be particularly valuable for founders who have identified a promising problem but are not yet certain how to turn the solution into a commercially viable business.

Its main advantages include:

Free participation.

No equity surrendered to the program.

Access to York University’s YSpace entrepreneurship ecosystem.

Expert mentorship.

Hands-on startup workshops.

Customer-development guidance.

Go-to-market strategy development.

Peer-to-peer founder learning.

Leadership development.

Office hours with subject-matter experts.

A milestone-driven venture development structure.

Support for entrepreneurs in the ideation and early validation stages.

Opportunities for selected businesses to access continued YSpace support.

Specialized support for Black-led businesses.

Support within YSpace’s wider mobility and technology ecosystem.

Participation open beyond York University students and alumni.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Venture Catalyst Application

Because the cohort accepts a limited number of companies, applicants should make their submissions as specific and evidence-based as possible.

Clearly Define the Problem

Avoid describing only the technology.

Explain the real-world problem being addressed and why solving it matters.

Identify Your Customer

Specify who would actually use or purchase the product.

A narrowly defined target customer is often more convincing than claiming that a product is useful to everyone.

Explain Your Innovation

Applicants should clearly demonstrate what is innovative about their technology, product, business model or approach.

Show Evidence of Validation

Even at the earliest stage, founders can demonstrate progress through:

Customer interviews.

Surveys.

Prototype testing.

Letters of interest.

Pilot discussions.

Waiting lists.

Early users.

MVP development.

Research demonstrating the problem.

Explain What You Want to Achieve

Because Venture Catalyst is milestone-driven, applicants should identify tangible objectives they want to accomplish during the program.

For example:

Complete customer validation.

Refine an MVP.

Secure initial pilot users.

Develop a go-to-market strategy.

Test pricing.

Improve customer acquisition.

Prepare for commercialization.

Demonstrate Coachability

YSpace specifically identifies coachability, collaboration and a growth mindset among the qualities it seeks in applicants.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate that they are willing to test assumptions, receive feedback and adapt their ideas based on evidence.

September 25, 2026

Conclusion

The York University YSpace Venture Catalyst 2026 provides an attractive opportunity for early-stage technology founders seeking structured assistance in transforming an innovative concept into a viable business.

Through mentorship, practical workshops, customer-development frameworks, leadership development, peer learning, expert office hours and milestone-driven venture building, the program addresses many of the most difficult challenges entrepreneurs encounter between developing an idea and successfully taking it to market.

Its free and equity-free structure makes the opportunity especially attractive because successful applicants can obtain significant entrepreneurship support without paying participation fees or surrendering ownership in their companies.

The program is particularly suitable for founders who are still validating their ideas, developing an MVP or preparing for their first meaningful steps into the market.

The Commonwealth Foundation says its grants programme supports civil society, grassroots communities and creative actors working to advance meaningful social, cultural and political change.

About the Commonwealth Foundation Grants

The Commonwealth Foundation has announced its 2026–27 open grants call, providing funding for projects that seek to influence public policy, public discourse, behaviours and decision-making.

The programme supports projects using constructive engagement with governments and decision-makers and/or creative advocacy to achieve positive social, cultural or political change.

A major change for 2026–27 is the introduction of the new Collective Action Grants, expanding funding opportunities beyond individual civil society organisations to networks, coalitions, alliances, platforms and creative collectives.

Commonwealth Foundation Grant Funding 2026–27

There are two funding streams available.

1. Individual Organisation Grants

Eligible not-for-profit civil society and creative organisations can apply for:

£15,000 to £30,000 per year for up to two years.

These grants are designed for organisations delivering standalone projects aligned with the Foundation’s strategic priorities.

2. Collective Action Grants

The new Collective Action Grants provide:

£15,000 to £20,000 per year for up to two years.

They are intended for eligible networks, coalitions, alliances and platforms of civil society actors, including creative collectives, working together to strengthen participation and collective action.

Funding Priorities

Projects must address at least one of the Commonwealth Foundation’s three strategic impact areas:

Climate and Environmental Justice

Projects may address climate and environmental injustice, participation in climate decision-making, environmental rights, just energy transitions, indigenous and local knowledge, environmental accountability and access to justice.

Economic Inclusion

This priority includes work promoting:

Sustainable livelihoods and entrepreneurship

Decent jobs and labour rights

Economic opportunities for young people

Reduced socio-economic inequality

Women’s and youth participation in economic policymaking

Inclusive economic policies

Creative industries and the creative economy

Youth-led economic initiatives

Freedom of Expression

Projects can focus on freedom of expression, association and assembly, access to information, media freedom, digital rights, online safety, civic participation and transparent governance.

Cross-Cutting Priorities

Applicants must also demonstrate how gender and intersectionality have been considered throughout project design and implementation.

The Foundation also identifies Commonwealth small states as a cross-cutting priority and strongly encourages applications from eligible organisations in small states.

Young People and Youth-Led Organisations

Young people remain central to the Foundation’s mission. The 2026–27 call welcomes projects that meaningfully involve young people and strengthen their leadership, agency and participation in public discourse, policy processes and decision-making.

Youth-led organisations are encouraged to apply.

Who Can Apply?

Individual Organisation Grants

Applicants must generally:

Be a not-for-profit civil society or creative organisation

Be registered in an eligible Commonwealth Foundation member country

Have been registered and operating for at least three years

Have at least three years of relevant experience

Have significant experience working in the communities where the project will be delivered

Have an average annual income below £2.5 million

Request no more than 70% of their average annual income over the previous two years

Collective Action Grants

The Collective Action stream is open to eligible networks, coalitions, alliances and platforms. An unregistered network or collective can nominate an eligible registered member organisation to serve as the lead applicant.

Applicants should also have at least three years of demonstrable experience relevant to the proposed project and strategic impact area.

What Projects Will the Commonwealth Foundation Not Fund?

The Foundation will not fund:

Projects involving electioneering or partisan political communications

Activities promoting hatred, discrimination or violence

Projects primarily focused on service delivery

Activities solely designed to build the capacity of government officials or private-sector actors

Creative projects without a social or political change objective

Projects primarily designed to generate private profit

Exchanges between developed countries

Applicants should carefully review the full exclusions before preparing their application.

Applicants must submit an online application together with supporting documentation.

Required documents include:

A completed logic model

Registration certificate

Board or trustee information, including names, roles and responsibilities

Relevant financial accounts

Additional governance and membership information for Collective Action Grant applicants

A portfolio of previous or current work for eligible creative applicants

For grants exceeding £15,000 per year, applicants must provide their most recent audited accounts, including the external auditor’s opinion.

Changes to our open call grants

What has changed this year

In response to the Foundation’s new strategic plan, the 2026–2027 open call marks an evolution in how the Foundation supports communities, collectives and creative practitioners. Our Individual Organisation Grants will continue the work of our previous open call grants by providing support for projects delivered by civil society organisations, including creative organisations. From this year, we will also provide support for networks, coalitions, alliances, platforms and creative collectives through our Collective Action Grants.

Can I apply for an Individual Organisation Grant AND a Collective Action Grant?

No. An organisation, network or collective may only be included in one application under this open call, whether as a lead applicant or partner.

Can we deliver in partnership?

Yes. Partnerships are welcome where they enhance the scale, depth, reach, or impact of the proposed work. For a Collective Action Grant, partners are defined as those directly involved in delivering the work; you do not need to list every member of the network or collective.

Do partners need to be registered?

No. While the applicant or lead applicant must meet the relevant registration requirements and be registered in an eligible Commonwealth Foundation member country, partners may be registered civil society or creative organisations, grassroots or community-based groups, informal groups, social movements, networks, artists, storytellers, creative practitioners or advocates. An Individual Organisation Grant may be delivered by the applicant organisation alone or in partnership. The lead applicant should explain each partner’s role and contribution.

Can I partner with unregistered organisations, actors or collectives?

Yes. However, the grant agreement will be with the registered applicant or lead applicant, which will be responsible for the funding and delivery of the project.

I am an artist (creative actor or creative practitioner). How can I engage?

If you are a member of a registered organisation, non-for-profit organisation, you can apply to either type of grant as long as you meet the eligibility criteria. You can also be a partner in a proposal that uses creative advocacy to advance one or more of the Foundation’s strategic impact areas.

What is creative advocacy?

Creative advocacy is the intentional use of creative practices to influence public discourse, policy, behaviours or decision-making in pursuit of positive social, cultural or political change.

What should creative organisations or collectives submit?

Submit a small selection of previous or current work that demonstrates your creative practice and its relevance to the project. Use one or a combination of the following: up to six images, up to five minutes of video or audio, up to five pages of writing or other relevant material, or links to digital, interactive or web-based work. For each example, provide the title, date, your role and a short description of no more than 75 words.

You do not need to create a new portfolio for this application. Existing documentation is welcome, and production quality will not be assessed. If the work was collaborative, briefly explain your contribution.

You may include a link to a wider portfolio, but assessors will only be expected to review the material submitted within these limits.

Frequently asked questions

Is my organisation eligible to apply?

To be eligible for a grant under this call, the following criteria must be met:

For an Individual Organisation Grant, the applicant must be a not-for-profit civil society organisation or creative organisation registered in an eligible Commonwealth Foundation member country.

For a Collective Action Grant, the applicant must be a not-for-profit network, coalition, alliance or platform of civil society organisations, community-based organisations, groups, creative actors or creative collectives, registered in an eligible Commonwealth Foundation member country. The list of eligible countries can be found on this page. An unregistered network or collective must nominate an eligible registered member organisation to act as lead applicant.

Newly registered organisations, networks, coalitions or collectives that have been registered and operating for less than three years are not eligible to apply.

The proposed project must be implemented in the applicant’s or lead applicant’s country of registration but may also include activities in additional eligible Commonwealth Foundation member countries. Projects can a national, sub-national, regional or international remit. For multi-country projects, strong local participation in each country of implementation is required.

The project must seek to advance at least one of the Foundation’s strategic impact areas (freedom of expression, economic inclusion, or climate and environmental justice) through constructive engagement between civil society and governments or other decision-makers and/or, the use of creative practice to influence public discourse or decision-making, policy or behaviours in pursuit of positive social, cultural, or political change (creative advocacy).

The applicant, network or collective must have at least three years’ demonstrable experience relevant to the proposed project and strategic impact area, as well as significant experience in the communities where the project will be delivered.

The grant requested must be between £15,000 and £20,000 per year for a Collective Action Grant, or between £15,000 and £30,000 per year for an Individual Organisation Grant.

Grants may be requested for a maximum of two years.

The requested grant amount should not exceed 70% of the applicant’s or lead applicant’s average annual income over the past two years.

The applicant’s or lead applicant’s average annual income over the past two years must be less than £2.5 million.

The proposal must demonstrate how gender and intersectionality have informed its design and will be integrated throughout implementation, including consideration of factors such as age, disability, race, ethnicity, socio-economic status and geographical location.

Organisations that are currently implementing a Commonwealth Foundation grant, or have recently completed a grant but have not yet received their final payment, are not eligible to apply.

Applications should relate to projects that are expected to begin between 1 August 2027 and 30 September 2027.

Note that applications not meeting the above eligibility requirements will not be considered.

What documents must we submit?

All applicants must submit a completed online application form. All applications must include the following additional documentation:

A logic model (using the template provided).

A clear copy of the applicant’s or lead applicant’s registration certificate. If it does not state that the entity is not-for-profit, include other evidence such as articles of association. Shortlisted applicants whose original documents are not in English will be expected to provide a certified translation.

A document listing the names, roles, responsibilities and contact details of the applicant’s or lead applicant’s board members or trustees. If there is no board or trustee structure, upload the relevant governance structure, including roles and responsibilities.

Applicants based in India should comply with the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA), or have preparations in place to obtain valid FCRA registration to receive charitable funding from outside India.

For grants of exactly £15,000 per year, the applicant may choose to submit either the latest audited accounts or the most recent annual accounts. Annual accounts must include a balance sheet, profit and loss statement and notes, and be signed off by the Board or principal executive officer. The accounts must not be older than December 2024.

Grants exceeding £15,000 per year, the applicant must submit the most recent audited accounts, including the accounts and the external auditor’s opinion. They must be signed by the auditor and the Board or principal executive officer and must not be older than December 2024.

Collective Action Grant applicants must also provide the collective’s structure, governance, secretariat organisation where applicable, and a full list of current members. Creative organisations and collectives must provide the required portfolio or equivalent digital evidence.

All organisational and financial documents must relate to the same legal entity named as the lead applicant.

Additional information on accounts is provided below. Note that incomplete applications will not be considered.

What type of projects is the Commonwealth Foundation seeking to fund?

The Foundation will support projects advancing one or more of three strategic impact areas: freedom of expression; economic inclusion; and climate and environmental justice. Priority will be given to applications that facilitate constructive engagement between civic actors, governments and other decision-makers and/or use creative advocacy. All projects must integrate gender and intersectionality into their design and implementation.

Can we apply for funding in relation to a project that has already started?

The Foundation may support work that is not entirely new but builds on, extends or adds a component to an existing initiative that meets the open call grants criteria. Applicants should identify existing work in the application and explain the value and expected impact of the proposed extension. If the applicant is not a creative organisation or collective, a creative advocacy component added to an existing project will not be considered for funding.

What kind of audit report do we need to submit?

For grants exceeding £15,000 per year, applicants must submit their most recent audited accounts, including the accounts and the external auditor’s opinion. They must be signed by the auditor and the Board or principal executive officer and must not be older than December 2024.

Project audits and independently verified accounts will not be accepted in place of the organisation’s audited accounts. Audited accounts for an affiliated organisation registered in a different country will not be accepted.

What kind of annual accounts do we need to submit?

For grants of exactly £15,000 per year, applicants may submit audited accounts or their most recent annual accounts. Annual accounts must include a balance sheet, profit and loss statement and notes, be signed off by the Board or principal executive officer, and must not be older than December 2024.

Can we submit the audited accounts/annual accounts after we have submitted the application?

No. The required financial documentation must be submitted together with the application form. Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Can an organisation apply for funding for a project that is to be implemented in a country that is not the country of the registration?

The project must be implemented in the applicant’s or lead applicant’s country of registration, but may also include activities in other eligible Commonwealth Foundation member countries. Strong local participation is required in each country of implementation (please refer to the full list of eligible countries above).

Are partnerships part of the selection criteria?

Partnerships are not compulsory, but the Foundation welcomes grant applications for partnerships that aim to enhance the scale, depth, reach or impact of the proposed work. Please note that partners do not have to be registered organisations. They may include not-for-profit community-based organisations/groups, informal alliances, social movements, individual activists or creatives such as artists, musicians, writers, poets or performers’ activities.

Applicants should clearly explain each partner’s role and contribution. If a proposed partner is a registered organisation in a country of implementation, its registration certificate should be submitted with an Individual Organisation Grant application; for Collective Action Grants, certificates for registered partners will be requested if the application is shortlisted.

Who can we partner with?

Partners may include registered civil society or creative organisations, grassroots or community-based groups, informal groups, social movements, networks, artists, storytellers, creative practitioners or advocates whose contribution will strengthen the project.

Can two or more organisations submit an application?

Yes. One eligible organisation must be nominated as lead applicant and the others identified as partners. For an unregistered network or collective, the lead applicant must be an eligible registered member organisation.

The lead applicant will enter into the grant agreement with the Commonwealth Foundation and will hold the relevant rights and responsibilities under that agreement.

Can an organisation be an applicant in one application and a partner in another? Or a partner in more than one application?

No. An organisation/partner can only be included in one application.

Can an organisation apply for more than one grant?

No. An organisation can only apply for one grant under this call.

Can an organisation that has previously been awarded a grant by the Commonwealth Foundation (as either lead applicant or partner) apply for another grant under this call as either a lead applicant or a partner?

Organisations that have previously received a Foundation grant may apply only after that earlier grant has ended and the final payment has been received. Applicants currently implementing a grant, or awaiting final payment, are not eligible.

We are planning to partner with another organisation whose average total income is more than £2.5 million. Does that affect eligibility?

No. The income requirement applies only to the applicant or lead applicant.

Can a government or business entity be a partner in the project?

No. Partners nominated by an applicant should not be government or business entities. However, the Foundation does welcome informal collaborations–including with government and the private sector–that might enhance the project’s effectiveness and impact.

Can a project funded under this call provide training or other support to government officials?

No. While the Foundation is seeking to support constructive engagement with government, project funds cannot be used to provide training to government officials. If such training is considered necessary for project aims, an alternative source of funding for those costs should be secured and this should be explained clearly in the application.

How should grant partners monitor and report on their projects?

Successful applicants will be required to develop a monitoring plan for their project. The Foundation will provide guidance for grant partners, including through the use of simplified versions of the Results Based Management and Outcome Harvesting methodologies that we use for all our work.

For projects of one year duration, grant partners are required to provide an end of project report and a corresponding financial report. For projects of more than one year duration, grant partners are required to provide an annual report including a financial report and, at the end of the project, an end of project report and corresponding financial report.

Reporting schedules will be agreed between the grant partner and the Foundation and set out in the grant agreement.

Why is my country not included in the list of eligible countries?

The Foundation’s arrears policy restricts eligibility for the open call to organisations from member countries that are in good financial standing with the Foundation. As in previous years, this excludes applications from several countries that are in serious arrears with respect to their contributions.

See our map of eligible countries for more information.

Can I apply for an open call grant to strengthen organisational capacity or support my organisation in other ways?

No. Open call grants are awarded for specific projects and do not cover core organisational costs.

The Foundation does appreciate the importance of strengthening organisational capacity. For Individual Organisation Grants, shortlisted applicants will be invited to propose capacity strengthening initiatives as part of their project budget, costed at up to 5% of the grant amount requested. These funds may be used to cover organisational needs that are broader than the project that enhance organisational effectiveness. For Collective Action grants, shortlisted applicants are welcome to suggest capacity strengthening initiatives that support collective action work. There is no need to include capacity-strengthening proposals in the first-stage application.

Can I look at examples of projects funded by open call grants in previous years?

Past and current projects funded by the Commonwealth Foundation can be found on our website: commonwealthfoundation.com/projects

While these provide an overview, applicants should note that requirements and focus areas differ from year to year. Please also note that collective action grants are new for 2026-2027, so you will not find examples of projects funded under this grants stream.

How do I apply for a grant?

Login and create your Survey Monkey Apply account to complete and submit an online application. Only applications submitted through the online application system will be considered.

Can I submit an application via email or post?

No. Only applications submitted using the online application system will be considered.

Who are SurveyMonkey Apply?

SurveyMonkey Apply is the provider of the online platform used for Commonwealth Foundation grant applications.

I don’t have a SurveyMonkey Apply account; how do I get one?

You can find out how to register for an account here.

I’ve applied for a Commonwealth Foundation grant in the past, do I still need to create an account?

No. You should already have an account. Please log in using your email address and password. If you have forgotten your password, follow the guidance provided on screen to set a new one.

Who do I contact if I can’t log into my account?

If you have login problems, please send an email to: cfgrants@commonwealth.int.

Why am I receiving emails from noreply@mail.smapply.io?

This is the email address from SurveyMonkey Apply, the providers of the grants online application system. All emails relating to the submission of your grant application will be sent from this email address. Please do not reply to this email address as it’s not monitored. Send any queries to cfgrants@commonwealth.int and a staff member of the Foundation will get back to you.

What do I do if I have problems with my application?

If you have problems with your application, please contact cfgrants@commonwealth.int and a staff member of the Foundation will assist you.

We strongly advise that applicants requiring help reach out to us as soon as possible. We receive a large volume of last-minute requests for help and we cannot guarantee responding to them all in time; you could miss the deadline. Submission after the deadline is not possible, and you should not rely on people being available to assist in the final days.

How do I know if my application was successfully submitted?

You will receive an email from noreply@mail.smapply.io acknowledging receipt of your application soon after it is submitted. If you do not receive this acknowledgement email one of three things may have happened:

your application was not successfully submitted

the email was sent to a different email that was provided in the form

your email is in your spam box

Please check out all these options and if you are still experiencing problems contact the grants team at cfgrants@commonwealth.int.

When will I find out if my application was successful?

Shortlisted applicants will be contacted by the end of February 2027 and invited to provide further information, including a detailed project budget. If you have not been contacted by then, it means that your application has not been shortlisted.

Shortlisted applicants will be informed of the outcome by the end of June 2027. Grant agreements are expected to be concluded soon afterwards, allowing implementation to begin between August and September 2027.

Can I request feedback on my application?

The Foundation receives a large number of applications each year and is therefore unable to provide individual feedback for unsuccessful applicants.

If you have not been contacted by the end of February 2027, it means your application has not been shortlisted.

Ethical considerations

Safeguarding

The Foundation is committed to ensuring all activities supported through its grants protect the safety, dignity and wellbeing of the people involved. Applicants are expected to identify any safeguarding risks associated with their proposed project and explain how these risks will be prevented, managed and responded to. Safeguarding measures should be appropriate to the nature of the project, the people involved and the context in which activities will take place.

Shortlisted applicants will be required to provide relevant safeguarding policies or procedures or, where these are not already in place, to develop appropriate safeguarding measures as a condition of funding.

Guidance on the use of AI

The Foundation’s grants programme exists to support civil society and creative voices to constructively engage in policy processes; to help people to participate in and transform the policies and systems that shape their lives. We are conscious that many potential applicants are drawn to these tools to prepare applications more quickly and with less effort.

The Foundation would like to advise prospective applicants to use AI merely as a support tool for editing, grammar, research, improving readability, and summarising.

The Foundation values proposals that are grounded in the knowledge, experience and perspectives of the communities affected, not generic narratives. Consequently, applications must still demonstrate organisational understanding of the problem being addressed, institutional knowledge of the community being served as well as the organisational journey to grow and create change for beneficiaries.

The Foundations assessment process remains centred on human judgement, expertise, and decision-making, to preserve the integrity of the process. The use of AI tools will neither disadvantage nor advantage applicants in our assessment process.

Good applications are grounded in verifiable evidence, real lived experience in the thematic area, genuine community engagement, realistic planning, and the insight that only comes from the organisation’s direct experience, learning and knowledge.

The application process

23 September 2026

The call opens for applications.

26 October 2026

The call closes for applications and assessment begins.

February 2027

Shortlisted applicants will be contacted by Foundation staff. If you haven’t been contacted by the end of February, your application has been unsuccessful.

June 2027

Successful applicants will be informed before the end of the month.

What happens next

Assessment criteria

We typically receive around 3000 applications which are assessed in line with the eligibility criteria.

The assessment criteria for applications are as follows:

Your organisation meets all eligibility criteria

Your organisation has a good track record of advocacy work

Your application provides a clear description of the problem that the applicant is seeking to address

Your application provides a clear explanation of how you plan to address the problem and contribute to its resolution

Your organisation provides good evidence of having consulted with the project’s supposed beneficiaries

Your application makes a persuasive case for the proposed approach to the problem. It is timely, relevant and feasible.

Your organisation demonstrates that it has the capacity to undertake the project and complete it successfully within the stipulated time

Your organisation demonstrates a serious commitment to gender equality.

Shortlisting

Shortlisted applicants will be contacted by Foundation staff by the end of February 2027. These applicants will be invited to provide further information in support of their application, including a detailed project budget.

If you have not been contacted by the end of February 2027, it means that your application has not been shortlisted.

Approval process

Shortlisted applicants will be informed of the result of their application by the end of June 2027, and it is expected that grant agreements will be concluded soon thereafter, allowing for implementation to begin in the third quarter of 2027 (August- September).

Monitoring and reporting

Successful applicants will be required to develop a monitoring plan for their project. The Foundation will provide guidance and support to grant partners as required.

Reporting schedules will be agreed between the grant partner and the Foundation and set out in the grant agreement.

Grant partners who are implementing a one-year project will be asked to provide an end of project narrative report, along with a financial report. Grant partners who are implementing a two-year project will submit a narrative and financial report at the end of the first year as well as an end-of-project narrative and financial report. Reporting schedules will be agreed between the grant partner and the Foundation and set out in the grant agreement.

TITLE: AREF Towards Leadership Programme 2026/2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 8, 2026

Applications are open for the AREF Towards Leadership Programme 2026/2027. The Africa Research Excellence Fund (AREF) Towards Leadership programme aims to empower talented, emerging scientists in Africa to compete successfully for UKRI MRC and other major funding opportunities in global health research. Together they are investing in talented African scientists in Africa, enhancing their global health research and leadership potential.

The programme will run in March 2027 consisting of two residential workshops (opening and closing) and one virtual workshop.

The curriculum is designed to support engage and enhance the participants’ capabilities and to empower talented, emerging scientists in Africa to compete successfully on a level playing field for UKRI MRC and other major funding opportunities in global health research. The programme is directed towards to winning grant funding, empowering effective teams, collaborating internationally, influencing stakeholders, and building rewarding research careers.

Programme Outline

The Programme comprises the following elements:

Three inspiring and practical blended workshops at six-monthly intervals

Supplementary webinars, tutorials, and online resources

Baseline and end-of-programme assessments and evaluation

Collaboration between participating individuals

The Programme has the following themes tailored to meet the needs of each cohort:

The Researcher as a Leader focusing on learning & leading in a complex world; raising the cohorts’ self-awareness, and mindfulness while also building their coaching, influence, and leadership capabilities.

The Effective Researcher develops the individual’s ability to envision, plan and action career goals and development trajectory through personal development planning, time management, and mentorship.

The Researcher as a Communicator augmenting the individual’s leadership, authorship & authority skills through the use of effective presentations, storytelling and messaging while refining their engagement with research users.

The Compelling Applicant: Understanding funders. Proposal development and writing skills: formulating a research question; justifying the design/strategy; concept notes and full proposals. Data sharing. Understanding peer review. Fellowship interviews.

The Researcher as a Manager: Building a great team. Effective collaboration. Implementation planning. Working with Research Support and Finance departments. Managing a budget. Managing intellectual property.

The five themes will be integrated across the three workshops. The balance of the curriculum will be determined by the participant’s needs.

Costs

The costs of the workshops and associated accommodation and travel of selected nominees will be met by MRC and AREF.

Eligibility

You are a citizen of a country in Africa.

You are currently employed in Africa by a recognised university and/or specialist research institution.

You are an early career researcher, having completed your research education and are now at the early stages of leading your own research group.

You will hold a research doctorate (PhD/DPhil/MD) from a recognised academic institution OR you have a medical/clinical qualification PLUS a research-relevant Master’s degree, both usually within the last 10 years. If it has been longer than 10 years since your last degree, please explain in your application why you should still be considered an early career researcher (i.e. caring responsibilities or career break/change impacting your research career).

You are currently responsible for managing/supervising one or more research students and/or research staff members and are involved in building research collaborations.

Organized by the Division of Biostatistics within the Department of Population Health Sciences at Weill Cornell Medicine, this paid summer internship provides students with practical exposure to health research, statistical analysis, R programming, professional development, and mentorship from experienced biostatisticians.

Participants will work on real-world health research questions while developing skills that can support future studies and careers in biostatistics, data science, epidemiology, public health, healthcare analytics, and related fields.

About the Weill Cornell Medicine Biostatistics Summer Internship

The Weill Cornell Medicine Biostatistics Summer Internship is designed to expose students to the practical application of statistics and data analysis in healthcare research.

Rather than focusing only on classroom instruction, the program gives interns an opportunity to participate in an applied research experience. Students work with data connected to genuine healthcare research questions and learn how statistical methods can be used to generate evidence that may ultimately contribute to better healthcare access and outcomes.

The 2027 internship is scheduled to run for approximately seven weeks, from:

Program Start Date: June 7, 2027

Program End Date: July 23, 2027

Location: New York City, United States

What Will Interns Do During the Program?

Participants in the Weill Cornell Medicine Biostatistics Summer Internship will have several opportunities to develop their research and analytical capabilities.

The program consists of four major components.

1. Complete a Real-World Health Research Project

One of the main components of the internship is an applied health research project.

Students work in small groups to investigate a real-world healthcare research question using data and statistical analysis. The experience is structured to expose interns to several important stages of the research process.

Participants may work through activities including:

Understanding and conceptualizing a research question

Developing a statistical analysis plan

Preparing and cleaning research data

Performing statistical analyses

Interpreting analytical results

Drawing evidence-based conclusions

Communicating findings effectively

Preparing a research poster

Presenting their final project

The process gives students experience beyond simply running statistical models. They learn how an analytical project develops from an initial research question through to the communication and presentation of results.

This type of experience can be particularly useful for students considering future graduate education or careers in biostatistics, statistics, public health, epidemiology, healthcare analytics, data science, medical research, or related quantitative disciplines.

2. Participate in Educational Lecture Series

Interns will also participate in several educational lecture series designed to increase their understanding of biostatistics, public health research, data analysis, and related career opportunities.

The educational component includes the following areas.

R Programming Crash Course

During the first week of the program, participants will receive an R crash course covering important R programming fundamentals.

This is particularly important because R is widely used in statistical analysis, biostatistics, epidemiology, public health research, and data science.

Applicants should note that although previous R experience is identified as a preferred qualification, R coding experience is not mandatory for applicants. The introductory training helps participants develop or strengthen the R skills required for the internship.

Fundamentals and Hot Topics in Biostatistics

Interns participate in weekly lectures covering important statistical methods and current topics relevant to public health data analysis.

These sessions are intended to expand students’ knowledge of how biostatistics is applied to contemporary healthcare and public health problems.

Research Spotlight Series

Participants will also attend weekly research spotlight sessions featuring projects involving Weill Cornell Medicine biostatisticians.

These lectures are designed to show students the range of research areas in which biostatistical expertise can be applied.

For students who may understand statistics academically but have limited exposure to its practical use in medical and public health research, these sessions can provide valuable insight into potential research and career pathways.

Career Development Series

The program also includes weekly career-focused sessions addressing careers available to biostatisticians and professionals working in related health data analysis disciplines.

Participants therefore receive not only technical training but also exposure to the professional opportunities associated with quantitative healthcare research.

3. Individualized Professional Development and Mentorship

Another major feature of the program is personalized professional development support.

Participants receive weekly one-on-one meetings where they can discuss their career objectives and future professional development.

Topics can include:

Career goals

Academic planning

Professional development

Networking

Resume building

Soft skills

Possible next steps following the internship

Participants also receive mentorship support from a biostatistician during the program.

This component can be particularly valuable for undergraduate students who are still deciding whether to pursue graduate studies, professional research positions, biostatistics, healthcare analytics, data science, epidemiology, or other quantitative careers.

4. Community-Building Activities in New York City

The internship is located in New York City, and the program incorporates community-building events and activities.

These opportunities are intended to help participants engage with one another beyond their academic and research responsibilities while developing connections within the internship cohort.

The combination of collaborative research projects, lectures, professional development sessions, mentorship, and community activities creates a broader internship experience than a purely technical data-analysis placement.

No.

Previous experience using R is listed as a preferred qualification, but it is explicitly not required.

Additionally, interns participate in an R crash course during the first week of the program.

Applicants with previous R experience may therefore have an advantage when beginning the technical components of the internship, but students should not assume that a lack of advanced R knowledge automatically makes them ineligible.

before beginning the internship.

TITLE: Who Teaches the Teachers and Who Will?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Daniel Omanyo and Izel Kipruto

Kenya’s education reforms are ambitious, but their success hinges on a question too often overlooked: Who Teaches the Teachers and Who Will? Behind every well-trained teacher stands a university lecturer shaping the quality of learning for millions. Yet evidence shows our higher education system is straining under growing demand and shrinking faculty capacity. Kenya faces a critical shortage of university faculty to prepare teachers for the Competency-Based Education (CBE). Investing in those who teach the teachers is important for lasting reform.

What the data show

Recent findings from the Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community (DAF-EAC) project, a collaboration between Education Sub Saharan Africa (ESSA), the Inter-University Council for East Africa, the Association of African Universities, and the Population Reference Bureau, paint a clear picture of this challenge.

Across East Africa, student enrolment in universities has surged over the past decade, but faculty recruitment has not kept pace. In Kenya, for instance, the DAF-EAC study shows that no discipline currently meets the student–teacher ratio targets set out in the 2014 Universities Regulations. The situation is most pressing in Faculties of Education, where the Commission for University Education recommends a ratio of 15 students per lecturer. In reality, the average ratio stands at 53 to 1.

Put simply, one lecturer may be responsible for teaching and mentoring more than fifty students, over three times the recommended number. This makes it difficult to give students the personalised attention they need, engage in quality research, or develop innovative teaching methods. Yet, this data also highlights an opportunity: investing in and strengthening faculty capacity can directly improve the quality of university education, research, and innovation across Kenya and the region.

Why it matters

Teacher educators sit at the heart of Kenya’s education system. They are the ones who prepare teachers to bring our education reforms to life, from early childhood to tertiary and technical training. Their ability to provide quality instruction, mentorship, and research guidance directly shapes the quality of learning in classrooms across the country. At the recent Education Evidence for Action conference held at Embu University, under the theme “Reimagining Teacher Education for Sustainable Development in Africa,” this issue took centre stage. In his keynote remarks, the Cabinet Secretary for Education referenced the DAF-EAC findings, noting that Kenya may need to recruit about 35,000 new faculty members by 2030 to meet university staffing norms. This acknowledgement is a positive sign that policy decisions are increasingly being guided by evidence. Strengthening the higher education workforce is not just about numbers, it is about ensuring that the next generation of teachers, and in turn learners, receive the quality education they deserve. Building a stronger faculty base today will make Kenya’s education system more resilient, responsive, and ready for the future. The urgency of this issue is clear. The recent lecturers’ strike laid bare long-standing concerns about pay, workload, and morale across universities. It echoes the DAF-EAC findings and reminds us that lasting education reform depends not only on policy and staffing targets, but also on valuing and supporting those who teach the teachers.

Learning from broader trends

Kenya’s experience reflects a wider continental pattern. A recent study by the Research on Socio-Economic Policy at Stellenbosch University found that half of South African teachers are considering leaving the profession within the next decade, largely due to burnout and heavy workloads. While the contexts differ, the lesson is universal: when educators, whether in schools or universities, feel overstretched and undervalued, the quality of education inevitably suffers. Preventing similar pressures within higher education must therefore be a national priority.

Pathways forward

Addressing the faculty shortage requires more than filling vacancies. It demands a comprehensive, long-term strategy that balances recruitment with sustained investment in professional growth and institutional support. Kenya can take several key actions to strengthen its higher education workforce. This includes building robust data systems to guide evidence-based planning and forecasting, improving working conditions and incentives to make academic careers more attractive to young professionals, and expanding professional development opportunities in pedagogy, research, and technology. Equally important is promoting mentorship and succession planning to nurture the next generation of scholars and leaders within universities. As Kenya embraces digital learning and the opportunities of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, teacher educators must be equipped to integrate emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, into their teaching. By doing so, they can help ensure that Africa’s young people are not only consumers of technology but also creators of innovation.

Building a sustainable future

Budget limits are real, but DAF-EAC data show that targeted, evidence-led planning can direct scarce resources where they matter most. The cost of inaction is far higher: overcrowded classes, falling quality, and an education system struggling to meet its promise. Kenya has expanded access and reformed its curriculum. The next step is clear, invest in the people who make that system work: those who teach the teachers. By prioritising faculty recruitment, development, and wellbeing, Kenya can rebuild the foundation of its education system and ensure every learner is guided by a motivated, well-prepared, and innovative teacher. Because the real question isn’t whether we can afford to invest in teacher educators, but whether we can afford not to.

Daniel Omanyo is the Research Manager, and Izel Kipruto is the Head of Communications at ESSA

TITLE: 22nd AAU COREVIP Sets Stage for Advancing Excellence in African Higher Education – July 4-7, 2023

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The biennial Conference for Rectors, Vice Chancellors, and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) is underway in Windhoek, Namibia, under the theme: “Advancing Excellence in African Higher Education”. Organised by the Association of African Universities (AAU) and hosted by the University of Namibia, the conference has assembled over 400 chief executive officers of African universities and other high-profile representatives from industry, development partner institutions, and strategic partner organisations from Africa and beyond. AAU’s capacity to convene Africa’s higher education community remains unmatched, as demonstrated at the ongoing COREVIP, through its ability to bring together stakeholders with diverse backgrounds from 52 countries, for purposeful deliberations on transforming the landscape of higher education across the continent.

The critical sub-themes guiding discussions at the conference are – Doctoral Education; Partnerships/Cooperation and Internationalisation; Institutional Differentiation; University-Industry Linkages; Role of the Intellectual Diaspora; and Funding and Financing. By addressing these topics during the diverse range of interactive sessions, including sessions for scientific paper presentations, the 22nd COREVIP is expected to shed light on the current challenges faced by African universities while celebrating the successes achieved thus far. The primary focus remains on generating tangible outcomes and sustainable solutions that will shape a brighter future for the continent.

AAU President Appreciates Stakeholders for Supporting the Advancement of African Higher Education

In his welcome address, Professor Saeed Bakri Osman, the President of the Governing Board of AAU, expressed his gratitude to attendees, esteemed partners, and stakeholders for their unwavering support towards the Association and its mission of enhancing the African higher education sector. He highlighted the importance of the conference through its provision of a unique platform to foster engaging discussions, spotlight successful initiatives, and generate key recommendations towards ensuring sustainable progress in Africa’s higher education sector.

Professor Oyewole Emphasises Global Collaboration and Highlights the Launching of Key Initiatives

For his part, the Secretary-General of AAU, Prof. Olusola Oyewole, said the conference also provides an opportunity to strengthen collaboration within and outside Africa. According to him, the participation of delegates from Latin America, the Republic of China, and other non-African countries demonstrates AAU’s commitment to foster global partnerships. He highlighted some key launch events taking place at the conference in collaboration with various partner organisations, including the launch of the Harmonisation of African Higher Education, Quality Assurance and Accreditation (HAQAA3) programme, a flagship initiative of the Global Gateway Package of the European Union and African Union Commission. The Africa Charter for Transformative Research Collaborations co-created by the University of Bristol, African higher education and research bodies and the China-Africa Consortium of Universities Exchange Mechanism, were all highlighted.

Namibia’s Commitment to Higher Education highlighted by Dr. Itah-Kandji Muragi as she addresses challenges and prioritization of investment

Declaring the conference open, on July 4, 2023, the Minister of Higher Education, Innovation and Technology of the Republic of Namibia, Dr. Itah-Kandji Muragi, emphasized the deep sense of honor experienced by the country, represented by the esteemed University of Namibia (UNAM), in being selected as the host for the conference. She reminded the delegation about the role of higher education systems as seats of knowledge creation, skills development, invention generation, especially through research and innovations.

In her speech, Dr. Itah-Kandji Muragi informed the gathering that since its independence in 1990, Namibia has prioritised investment in higher education. She cited the example of an allocation of 3.8 billion Namibian dollars, representing 28.4% of the national budget for education. According to her, this investment makes Namibia one of the countries with the highest expenditure on education in the world. She reflected that despite this investment, access with equity remains a challenge, as funding to meet the demand for quality and equitable higher education still requires attention to effectively respond to the need to produce the requisite workforce in this digital era. She therefore concluded that “the conference has come at an opportune time to foster the sharing of international experiences, forge links and collaboration as we interrogate the challenges that confront the African higher education system”.

Prof. Kenneth Matengu Urges Action to Advance Excellence in African Higher Education

Addressing participants in a presentation titled, “Why Advancing Excellence in Higher Education Is Important”, Prof. Kenneth Matengu, the Vice Chancellor of the University of Namibia profiled and examined Africa’s position, vis-à-vis the rest of the world on key issues including research production, literacy rate, enrolment in higher education, university ranking performance, higher education spending, access to electricity, and the number of African Noble Prize Laureates. Africa’s scores, percentages, and numbers unfortunately remain weak, even lower than the global average in most instances, as Prof. Matengu showed in his presentation.

Highlighting the huge youth population of Africa, Prof. Matengu called on the gathering of intellectuals to put in place drastic and strategic measures to change the narrative and prepare for the future.

Concluding his delivery, he stressed the need for stakeholders to advance excellence in higher education and to share best practices on increasing doctoral education, strengthen south-south-north cooperation, and move away from being technology consumers to being its producers. Prof. Matengu also appealed to African governments and other key stakeholders to commit to financing Research and Development and student and staff mobility and for the diaspora to play its part, too.

Distinguished Academics Honoured with Recognition Awards for Making Impact on Africa’s Higher Education

Day one of the gatherings of academics, national leaders, and distinguished guests featured the presentation of awards to exceptional individuals who have made impactful contributions to Africa’s higher education. These were Honourable Prof. Peter Hitjitevi Katjavivi (former Vice Chancellor of the University of Namibia, and speaker of Namibia’s National Assembly) and Honourable Angula Nahas Gideon Angula (first Minister of Education, Culture and Sport in independent Namibia). The Association of African Universities also honoured key individuals and presented awards to its regional and some thematic focused Ambassadors. These were Emeritus Professor Peter Okebukola, AAU Higher Education Ambassador for West Africa; Professor Kenneth Matengu, Vice Chancellor, University of Namibia and AAU Higher Education Ambassador for Southern Africa; and Professor El Meteini Mahmoud, President of Ain Shams University, Egypt, and AAU Higher Education Ambassador for North Africa. The distinguished academics awarded also included Emeritus Professor Olugbemiro Jegede, AAU Higher Education Ambassador for Open and Distance Learning, and Professor Peter Katjavivi, AAU Goodwill Ambassador.

Looking Ahead – COREVIP holds the Promise of Igniting Transformative change in African Higher Education

The conference proceedings and resulting recommendations are anticipated to serve as a catalyst for the realization of a shared vision, driving the growth and development of African higher education. With eager anticipation, conference participants are poised for fruitful engagements and meaningful collaborations that will undoubtedly shape the trajectory of African higher education. As the conference sets the stage for advancing excellence, it is expected to play a crucial role in realizing the aspirations of “The Africa We Want“.

The journey has just begun, and the stage is set for the next three days of COREVIP —a transformative event that paves the way for advancing excellence in African higher education.

As the conference continues, the participants eagerly look forward to the forthcoming days, brimming with productive engagements, knowledge sharing, and collaborative endeavours.
