TITLE: Life at IHES

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Location

Operating from the premises of the Fondation Thiers in Paris for the first three years of its existence, IHES moved to Bures-sur-Yvette in 1962. It has remained on the same site ever since. Bures-sur-Yvette is 23 kms away from Paris and an integral part of the Paris conurbation.

From an academic point of view, the Institute is located in the Saclay area, at the heart of the largest concentration of mathematicians in the world.

Work environment

The IHES site, Bois-Marie, offers all visitors comprehensive research facilities and high-quality services. Wherever possible, each researcher has their own office at the Institute. IT equipment and the library are freely accessible 24/7.

The quiet 10-hectare park is an invitation to deep thoughts and inspiring walks.

Accommodation

The Ormaille residence contains approximately 60 accommodation units. It is also located in Bures-sur-Yvette near the RER train station and close to the local shops.

The residence not only welcomes IHES visitors and their families, but also, when possible, other visiting scientists in need of housing.

This is because IHES belongs to the « Science Accueil » association, the mission of which is to help house foreign researchers staying in the area for varying lengths of stay.

In addition, since 2010, six newly built apartments at Ormaille have been allocated to the Université Paris-Sud mathematics department, following a partnership agreement between IHES, the Conseil Général de l’Essonne and Université Paris-Sud 11.

More information on the Ormaille residence and the childcare

Combating discrimination and gender-based and sexual violence

No form of discrimination is tolerated at IHES and the Institute is actively engaged in combating gender-based and sexual violence. As mentioned in its ethical charter adopted by the IHES Board of Directors and its visitors’ guide, moral harassment, sexual harassment and sexism are illegal and subject to penalties.

IHES has developed a specific procedure to support any person affiliated with the Institute who may be the victim or witness of harassment or gender-based and sexual violence.

Elisabeth Jasserand, Head of Scientific Administration at the Institute is the contact person for matters relating to combating sexual harassment and sexist behavior. Elisabeth Jasserand can be contacted by mail (jasserand@ihes.fr), in person at her office or by telephone (+33 60 92 66 04). Anyone affiliated with the Institute can approach her (in French or English) regarding topics related to harassment or sexual and gender-based violence. If required, support can be provided, with the guarantee of confidentiality and discretion.

At Université Paris-Saclay, of which IHES is a founder member, a prevention initiative and helpline has been set up to welcome, support, listen to and guide anyone who may be a victim or witness in order to end all forms of harassment (sexual, moral and cyber harassment, sexist behavior, sexual assault, rape, exhibitionism etc.). Contact: contact.dalida@universite-paris-saclay.fr, for more information here.

In order to raise awareness of sexual harassment and how to tackle it, and provide training on these issues, IHES has also made available here a guide on sexual harassment in higher education and research. This guide was produced by the CLASCHES collective (Anti-sexist collective combating sexual harassment in higher education).

This policy of raising awareness and combating discrimination, harassment and gender-based and sexual violence, forms part of IHES’ broader gender equality plan which can be found here.

Acknowledgments

IHES has gradually acquired the real estate that it needs to host researchers. These assets contribute to the Institute’s endowment funds and thus to its long-term mission.

The Sénat, the Conseil Régional Ile de France, the Conseil Général de l’Essonne and the Caisse des Dépôts are among the major contributors to the maintenance of buildings and sites. A great many individual donors have also contributed to renovation and refurbishment programmes.

For more information on the practical aspects of your research visit, please check the Intranet.

TITLE: Harvard Berenson Fellowship 2027-28 in Italy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a scholar interested in Renaissance studies and want to explore the connections between Italy and other cultures? The Harvard Berenson Fellowship 2027-28 in Italy is an excellent opportunity for you. This funded fellowship in Italy supports scholars whose research explores “Italy in the World” and focuses on the transnational dialogues between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance. The European fellowship welcomes scholars working in architecture and the arts, history, philosophy, literature, music, and history of science. The Harvard Fellowships provide scholars with valuable time, resources, and a supportive academic environment to advance their research. Make sure you read till the end and apply for this Harvard Fellowship 2027.

The Harvard Berenson Fellowship in Europe is a residential fellowship offered for four or six months at the Harvard Center for Italian Renaissance Studies at Villa I Tatti in Florence. These fellowships in Europe encourage research that takes a broad geographical view of the Renaissance, including connections with Latin American, Mediterranean, African, and Asian cultures. Fellows can focus on their proposed research project with a minimum of obligations and interruptions while accessing extensive scholarly resources. They are also expected to take part in the wider intellectual community through conferences, lectures, concerts, and other activities.

Moreover, the Harvard Berenson Fellowship 2027-28 provides a monthly grant of USD 5,200 along with a one-time relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800. Fellows must live in the Florence area and spend at least three days a week at the center. When available, the Harvard Center may provide an apartment rent-free, with fellows responsible for utility charges. If an apartment is unavailable, fellows can receive a housing subsidy to help with rental costs. Hence, making it one of the valuable Harvard fellowships in Italy for scholars working on Renaissance studies.

The Harvard Paid Fellowship is made possible by The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund and honors Bernard Berenson, who supported a geographically broad understanding of the Renaissance. These paid fellowships encourage scholars to examine Italy’s relationship with the wider world and contribute to the intellectual life of the Harvard Center. Up to four fellowships are awarded each year. Therefore, if you are a scholar with a strong research project related to the Renaissance and Italy’s global connections, you must apply for this Fellowship in Italy.

TITLE: IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 31, 2026

Applications are now open for the IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme (MSCFP). The fellowship seeks to inspire and support young women to pursue a career in the nuclear field. To that end, the MSCFP provides scholarships to selected students studying towards a master’s degree in nuclear related subjects as well as limited internship opportunities facilitated by IAEA.

The programme supports young women studying in nuclear related fields relevant to the IAEA’s work to advance the safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology such as nuclear engineering, nuclear physics and chemistry, nuclear medicine, isotopic techniques, radiation biology, nuclear safety, nuclear security, non-proliferation and nuclear law. More examples of related fields are listed here.

MSCFP award

The students are awarded up to €20,000 for tuition costs and up to €20,000 for living costs for the master’s programme. Applicants are obliged to declare if they have additional scholarships and to provide relevant documents, in which case the IAEA’s financial support would be reduced accordingly, i.e. only covering tuition costs, not living costs, for the duration of the programme. Failure to provide such information in a timely and transparent manner may lead to suspension of the IAEA’s financial support.

Eligibility

The IAEA MSCFP is open to students from IAEA Member States who meet the following entry requirements:

Female candidates;

Accepted by or enrolled in an accredited university in master’s programme in a nuclear related field.

Preference will be given to applicants with above average academic credentials (75% or above or GPA > 3.0 out of 4.0).

Application

The documents required in addition to completed online application form are:

Copy of the Passport/National ID

Official acceptance/admission letter from university into the master’s programme indicating the nuclear related field of study and duration of the programme

Statement of tuition fees/confirmation of tuition costs

If applicable, documents about other scholarships you have for the master’s programme for which you are seeking MSCFP support.

Completed reference templates sent directly to MSCFP by referees by the application deadline (download the form here). One reference is MANDATORY, second is preferred.

TITLE: Invitation to Participate in the International Deaf Blind Conference, Nairobi, Kenya, May 12 -14, 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Deaf Blind International (DBI), USA and the Maseno University, Kenya, in collaboration with their partners are inviting individuals who are deaf blind along with their families, professionals, researchers, developers, service organizations, libraries, universities, national and international agencies and any other relevant partners in the field of Deaf blindness, to a conference dubbed “Deaf blind Reality in Africa: Meeting the Sustainable Development Goals- Opportunities and challenges”.

This conference is to raise awareness among Ministry officials that Deaf blindness is a distinct disability, and to promote the development of appropriate services through policy and practice to benefit deaf blind people and their families around the world. The conference comes off from 12th – 14th May 2022 at the Kenya Institute of Special Education (KISE), Nairobi, Kenya, and will include over 200 delegates from around the world. It aims to interrogate issues and share promising interventions on Deaf blindness; Publish the journal on Deafblind International based on the Conference papers; and issue a communique on Action Oriented Resolutions to inform policy and practice. This will be a hybrid conference where participants will be engaged in both face to face and online sessions.

Call for Papers

Stakeholders interested in presenting papers at this conference are encouraged to submit their papers on the following themes:

Education and Transition of persons with Deaf blindness.

Families and Community based Rehabilitation (CBR) for persons with Deaf blindness.

Research, Policy and Advocacy for persons with Deaf blindness.

Deafblind International cordially invites you to submit your research papers, survey papers, case studies and academic papers in the aforesaid area from the 1st of February to 18th February 2022.

For more information about the conference kindly visit https://www.deafblindinternational.org/conference/africa/ . For enquiries , please write to africaconference@deafblindinternational.org /vc@maseno.ac.ke / poracha@maseno.ac.ke

TITLE: Call for Co-Hosting by the Association of African Universities – 2023 Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The AAU will hold its Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors, and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) in July 2023. The COREVIP is an assembly of the Chief Executive Officers of AAU member institutions or their representatives. It is held once every two years with the purpose of:

collectively examining themes identified as common concerns and priorities for the development of higher education in member institutions and Africa in general,

making recommendations primarily to members, as well as to the Governing Board of the Association, and to the Secretariat, and

acting as a mid-term forum for taking stock of the implementation of the decisions of the previous AAU General Conference and recommending corrective actions.

The main theme for COREVIP 2023 is Advancing Excellence in African Higher Education. Supporting this main theme are the following sub-themes:

Doctoral education

Institutional differentiation

Partnership/cooperation and internationalization

University-industry linkages

Role of intellectual diaspora

The overall concept note for the Conference can be accessed from this link: COREVIP 2023 Concept Note __ The AAU’s statutory Conferences such as the COREVIP are normally jointly organized with a member institution in good standing (not owing more than two years in subscription arrears). In light of this, the AAU invites applications from its member institutions in good standing for the co-hosting of this prestigious biennial Conference.

The Host’s Responsibilities

The host university will be expected to contribute to the organization of the Conference, financially or in kind, in the areas of:

Local transportation for participants.

Airport “meet and greet” (reception and facilitation of immigration procedures).

Traditional items as gifts to presenters and sessional chairs.

Welcome Reception or Dinner for participants.

Publicity and media coverage (local press, radio, social media and TV, conference photographer).

Arrangement of courtesy calls by the Governing Board on appropriate government authorities in the host country.

Arranging excursion visits by delegates – to be funded by the delegates.

Providing the Secretariat for the Conference (equipment and supplies).

Decorations, banners, and invitations to Opening/Closing Ceremony and receptions.

Cultural display during open and closing ceremonies.

It should be noted that the co-hosting of this most important event in the calendar of the African higher education community provides very high-level visibility and exposure to the host institution and country because of the calibre and number of academic leaders, policymakers, researchers, development partners, and other stakeholders that usually attend it, and it is, therefore, a highly sought-after event.

Institutions interested in co-hosting the 2023 COREVIP, should contact the Secretary General at their earliest convenience.

Applications to host the conference should be addressed to:

The Secretary-General

Association of African Universities (AAU)

Accra, GHANA.

Email: secgen@aau.org and copy ransford@aau.org

The deadline for the receipt of the official application to host the 2023 COREVIP is Friday, 25 November 2022.

While thanking you in anticipation of your positive and expeditious response, please accept the assurances of my highest esteem.

Yours in the service of higher education in Africa,

Professor Olusola Bandele Oyewole

Secretary-General

TITLE: Nordic Scholarship Programme 2027: Funded One-Month Africa Research Stay at the Nordic Africa Institute in Sweden

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the Nordic Scholarship Programme 2027, a funded research opportunity offered by the Nordic Africa Institute in Uppsala, Sweden. The programme gives eligible students and researchers working on Africa-focused topics in the social sciences or humanities an opportunity to spend one month at the Institute, use its specialist library collections, work in a scholarly environment, and connect with research hosts whose work relates to contemporary Africa.

The programme is open to master’s students, PhD candidates, postdoctoral researchers, and mid-career researchers. Citizenship is not a restriction. However, applicants must be both affiliated with and based at a university or research centre in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland when applying and when taking up the award. This institutional and geographic requirement is central to eligibility and should be checked before an applicant spends time preparing the research proposal.

Selected participants receive return travel at the least expensive available fare from their residential address in one of the four eligible Nordic countries to Uppsala, free centrally located accommodation, a desk and computer in a shared office, and a subsistence allowance of SEK 450 per day. The programme does not include health care insurance or any other insurance, so successful applicants must make their own arrangements for adequate coverage.

The application deadline for the 2027 programme is October 11, 2026. The official call does not publish a specific closing time or time zone, so applicants should submit well before the final day rather than relying on a last-minute upload.

About the Nordic Scholarship Programme

The Nordic Scholarship Programme is an annual initiative of the Nordic Africa Institute. Its purpose is to strengthen capacity for producing knowledge about Africa and to promote relationships within and between Nordic research communities. Rather than financing a complete university degree, it offers a concentrated one-month research period at the Institute.

The visit is intended to help a successful applicant advance a defined part of an existing Africa-oriented research project. Scholars can consult NAI’s library materials on contemporary Africa and relate their work to research already taking place at the Institute through an appropriate NAI research host.

This structure makes the programme particularly useful for applicants who already have a clear project but would benefit from dedicated research time, specialist material, a professional workspace, and intellectual connections. The programme is not described as a general study tour, introductory training course, conference, or open-ended residency. Every application must be built around a serious research project and a realistic plan for what the applicant will accomplish during the one-month stay.

About the Nordic Africa Institute

The Nordic Africa Institute conducts research and provides resources intended to deepen understanding of contemporary Africa. It presents research-based knowledge and analysis as a foundation for informed decision-making and progress toward the global development agenda. The Institute is located in Uppsala, Sweden, and maintains a specialist library focused mainly on contemporary Africa within the social sciences.

According to NAI, its library serves Nordic users and provides printed and digital resources supporting African studies. The scholarship call specifically highlights books, academic periodicals, newspapers, and government publications. These collections are a central reason for the one-month placement: scholars are expected to use the stay purposefully to advance the part of their research described in their work plan.

Applicants can learn more from the Nordic Africa Institute’s official website and NAI Library page.

Purpose of the One-Month Research Stay

The Nordic Scholarship Programme has two closely connected goals:

Strengthen Africa-focused knowledge production. The programme gives scholars time and institutional resources to develop research about Africa within the social sciences or humanities.

Build Nordic research relationships. The programme seeks to promote and establish connections with and among research communities in the Nordic region.

During the stay, a scholar may use specialist collections, work on analysis or writing, and connect with a relevant NAI research host. The exact activity should be defined by the applicant rather than left vague. A successful work plan should identify the segment of the larger research project that can be meaningfully advanced in one month and explain why working at NAI will make that progress possible.

Because the award is offered only once each year, applicants should treat the 2027 call as a distinct annual competition and follow the published deadline carefully.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

Applicants must satisfy all of the core conditions below.

1. The research must be Africa-oriented

The proposed work must concern Africa and fall within the social sciences or humanities. The call does not provide a closed list of acceptable topics, but the subject must be clearly identifiable and placed within its academic discipline in the research outline.

Potential disciplinary areas may include political science, sociology, economics, development studies, anthropology, history, human geography, public administration, peace and conflict studies, gender studies, cultural studies, law, media studies, or related social-science and humanities fields. These are illustrative areas rather than an official exhaustive list. Eligibility ultimately depends on whether the proposed project is Africa-focused and academically situated within the required broad fields.

2. The applicant must be at an eligible academic or professional stage

The programme accepts applications from:

Master’s students

PhD candidates

Postdoctoral researchers

Mid-career researchers

The call does not state that an applicant must be an African national, a Nordic citizen, or enrolled at a particular named university. It also does not advertise a fixed age limit. The decisive questions are the applicant’s research focus, career stage, current institutional affiliation, and physical base.

3. The applicant must have the correct institutional affiliation

An applicant must be affiliated with a university or research centre in one of these countries:

Sweden

Finland

Denmark

Iceland

Affiliation must exist both when the person applies and when the scholarship period begins. A signed letter from the applicant’s supervisor or head of department must confirm the current affiliation and research field.

4. The applicant must also be based in an eligible country

Institutional affiliation alone is insufficient. The applicant must also be based in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland at the time of application and when taking up the award.

This means, for example, that a person of any nationality who is genuinely based at and affiliated with an eligible institution may apply. Conversely, a researcher living elsewhere who has no qualifying current base in one of the four countries should not assume eligibility merely because the project concerns Africa or because the person collaborates informally with a Nordic scholar.

5. Citizenship is unrestricted

NAI expressly allows applications regardless of citizenship. This creates a globally inclusive nationality rule within a geographically limited institutional framework. An applicant may hold citizenship from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, or Oceania, provided all other requirements are met.

6. Certain former or current NAI affiliates are excluded

Anyone who is currently or was previously employed by the Nordic Africa Institute, or who is or was otherwise professionally affiliated with the Institute, is not eligible for this programme.

Applicants who are uncertain whether a past relationship counts as professional affiliation should request clarification from the programme contact before submitting.

An Important Geographic Clarification

The eligibility list includes Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Iceland. Norway is not included in the published scholarship criteria, even though Norway is generally recognised as a Nordic country and NAI’s library serves users across the Nordic region. Applicants based at Norwegian institutions should therefore not infer eligibility from the programme’s name. They would need confirmation from NAI if they believe an exceptional rule applies.

Similarly, citizenship in one of the four eligible countries is not enough if the applicant is neither based at nor affiliated with a qualifying university or research centre there. The programme applies two tests simultaneously: institutional affiliation and physical base.

Financial Support and Programme Benefits

The Nordic Scholarship Programme provides several forms of support for the one-month stay.

Return travel to Uppsala

The scholarship covers travel expenses using the least expensive fare from the recipient’s residential address in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland to Uppsala and back. Applicants should understand that the policy is based on economical travel rather than unrestricted route, class, airline, or ticket selection.

The official call does not specify reimbursement procedures, booking responsibility, baggage allowances, local transfers, or change-fee rules. Selected scholars should obtain written instructions before purchasing tickets or making non-refundable arrangements.

Free accommodation in Uppsala

Scholarship holders receive free accommodation in a central location in Uppsala. This substantially reduces the cost of a one-month research visit. The call does not promise a particular property type, room size, family accommodation, or facilities, so recipients with accessibility, caregiving, or other specific requirements should contact NAI in advance.

Daily subsistence allowance

The award includes a subsistence allowance of SEK 450 per day. This daily support is intended to help with ordinary costs during the stay. The official call does not explain the payment schedule, tax treatment, eligible expense categories, or whether the amount changes with arrival and departure times. Those details should be confirmed after selection.

Workspace and computer

Each scholarship holder receives a desk and computer in a shared office at the Institute. This creates a dedicated environment for reading, analysis, writing, and engagement with the NAI research community.

Access to specialist research material

The Institute’s contemporary Africa collections include books, periodicals, newspapers, and government publications. Access to these materials is one of the programme’s defining academic benefits and should be connected directly to the applicant’s research objectives and proposed work plan.

Links to NAI research hosts

The programme supports connections to existing work at the Institute through NAI research hosts. Applicants should study NAI’s current research themes and researchers so that they can explain genuine academic alignment. They should not claim a confirmed host or collaboration unless the Institute has actually provided that confirmation.

What the Scholarship Does Not Cover

NAI explicitly states that the scholarship does not include health care insurance or other insurance. Successful applicants are responsible for ensuring that they have adequate coverage for the entire visit.

The official announcement also does not list the following as guaranteed benefits:

Visa or residence-permit costs

Travel insurance

Health care costs

Family or dependent expenses

Childcare

Salary replacement

Research fieldwork expenses

Special equipment purchases

Conference fees

Publication charges

Items not listed should be treated as unconfirmed rather than assumed to be covered. Applicants with questions should contact NAI before accepting the award or incurring costs.

Required Application Documents

Applications must be submitted online and include all required material. Incomplete applications will not be considered.

1. Updated curriculum vitae

The CV must be current and should include a list of publications, if the applicant has publications. It should make the applicant’s academic stage, institutional affiliation, education, research experience, and Africa-related work easy for the selection committee to understand.

Applicants should not pad the publication section. If they have no publications, the official wording allows for that by stating “if any.” Relevant theses, research assistance, working papers, conference presentations, fieldwork, professional research, or policy outputs can be presented accurately in appropriate sections of the CV.

2. Research project outline of three to five pages

This is the most important application document because NAI says applications are primarily evaluated on the research-project outline. The outline must address three components.

Research objective and disciplinary context

The research topic must be clearly identified and placed within its academic discipline. The reader should be able to understand the issue being investigated, why it matters, the part of Africa concerned, and the research problem or question.

Method and time frame

Applicants must explain how the project will be carried out, including the research method, data-gathering techniques, and overall time frame. The method should fit the research question and reflect the project’s current stage.

Theoretical explanation

The outline must briefly identify the theoretical basis of the project. Applicants should show how the chosen concepts or framework support the analysis instead of merely listing theoretical names.

The three-to-five-page limit requires discipline. A proposal should be detailed enough to demonstrate scholarly quality while remaining focused and readable. Applicants should follow any formatting instructions in the application portal and avoid shrinking text or margins simply to exceed the stated length.

3. One-page work plan

The work plan must be specific to the month at the Nordic Africa Institute. It should clarify exactly which part of the larger research project the applicant will work on during the stay.

A useful plan may identify:

The research material to be consulted

The analytical, reading, or writing tasks to be completed

How NAI’s collections relate to those tasks

The expected engagement with relevant Institute research

Realistic weekly milestones

A tangible output or stage of progress to be achieved by the end of the month

The official call does not require this exact list or format; these points are practical guidance for presenting a concrete and feasible plan.

4. Signed reference or letter of support

Applicants must submit a signed letter of support from their supervisor or head of department. The letter must confirm:

The applicant’s current institutional affiliation

The applicant’s field of research

Because the affiliation requirement applies at application and when the award begins, the letter should be current, accurate, and issued by someone authorised to verify the applicant’s status.

5. English-language application and appendices

The application and every appendix must be in English. Applicants whose original documents are in another language should check the portal or ask NAI whether a translation, certified translation, or additional original-language copy is required. The public call states the language rule but does not provide detailed translation procedures.

How to Apply for the Nordic Scholarship Programme 2027

Follow these steps:

Read the complete official Nordic Scholarship Programme call.

Confirm that the research is Africa-oriented and within the social sciences or humanities.

Verify that the applicant is at one of the four eligible career stages.

Confirm current affiliation with and physical base at a university or research centre in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland.

Prepare the updated CV and publication list, where applicable.

Write the three-to-five-page research-project outline.

Prepare the one-page work plan for the proposed month at NAI.

Obtain the signed support letter from a supervisor or head of department.

Ensure the application and all attachments are in English.

Use the application link on the official call page to open the external recruitment portal.

Upload every required document and review the submission for completeness.

Submit before October 11, 2026, and retain the application confirmation.

The online application system requires JavaScript for full functionality. Candidates should use a compatible browser, allow enough time for account or upload issues, and avoid waiting until the deadline day.

Deadline and Selection Timeline

The closing date for the Nordic Scholarship Programme 2027 is:

October 11, 2026

NAI states that applicants will be informed as soon as the selection process is finalised and no later than the end of November 2026.

The programme’s separate selection-process page explains that scholarship applications are assessed rigorously by a selection committee working under ethical and professional rules. Committees include staff members with varied experience and diversity across background, profession, gender, and other considerations. The Institute says its selection processes emphasise transparency, equity, fairness, and respect for candidates.

For this particular programme, the research outline is the primary basis of evaluation. Applicants should therefore allocate substantial preparation time to the substance, structure, clarity, originality, and feasibility of that document.

NAI’s Warning About Artificial Intelligence in Applications

The Institute states that it reads proposals carefully and wants to understand each applicant’s research in that person’s own words and framing. It warns that using artificial intelligence to develop the application text may place the applicant at a disadvantage during assessment.

Applicants should take this warning seriously. Any submitted proposal should authentically reflect the researcher’s own thinking, disciplinary judgment, project design, and language. Automated text can introduce generic claims, fabricated references, unsuitable methods, or a voice that the applicant cannot defend. The safest approach is to write the substantive application independently and use only forms of assistance that comply with NAI’s expectations and the applicant’s institutional rules.

How to Make the Research Outline More Competitive

NAI does not publish a numerical scoring rubric, and no strategy can guarantee selection. The following recommendations are therefore practical editorial guidance grounded in the published requirements, not additional official criteria.

Define a precise research problem

Avoid describing only a broad topic such as development, democracy, conflict, migration, health, agriculture, or climate change in Africa. State the specific problem, context, location, population, period, and analytical question.

Explain why the project belongs at NAI

Connect the one-month visit to identifiable collections, themes, or research expertise at the Institute. A strong application should show why the project will advance through a stay in Uppsala rather than merely state that access to a library would be helpful.

Keep the method credible

Explain how evidence will answer the research question. Identify the type of material to be gathered or analysed and ensure that the proposed activities are realistic for the project stage.

Align the outline and work plan

The research outline explains the full project, while the work plan explains what will happen during the one-month visit. These documents should reinforce one another without becoming duplicates.

Define a realistic one-month result

A plan to complete an entire major research project in one month may appear unrealistic. A defined literature review, archival search, analytical chapter, dataset assessment, article section, comparative framework, or policy-paper draft may be more credible if it fits the project and available material.

Use clear academic writing

The selection committee should not have to infer the research question, contribution, method, or purpose of the stay. Direct writing and logical organisation are more persuasive than unnecessary complexity.

Common Application Mistakes to Avoid

Applying without being both affiliated with and based at an eligible institution.

Assuming that citizenship in a Nordic country is enough by itself.

Assuming that affiliation in Norway meets the published four-country rule.

Submitting a project that is not clearly Africa-focused.

Proposing work outside the social sciences or humanities without confirming eligibility.

Sending a research outline shorter than three pages or longer than five pages.

Writing a generic work plan that is not specific to the NAI stay.

Omitting the research method, data-gathering approach, time frame, or theoretical basis.

Providing an unsigned or unclear support letter.

Failing to include a publication list in the CV when publications exist.

Uploading appendices in a language other than English.

Submitting an incomplete application.

Assuming that insurance is included.

Leaving document uploads until the final day.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the programme open only to Nordic citizens?

No. Citizenship is unrestricted. Applicants must instead meet the institutional affiliation and location requirements in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland.

Can an African student or researcher apply?

Yes, nationality is not restricted. An African national can apply if pursuing eligible Africa-oriented social-science or humanities research and currently based at and affiliated with a qualifying institution in one of the four named countries.

Can someone based at a university in Africa apply directly?

Not under the published rules unless that person also meets the stated requirement of being affiliated with and based at a university or research centre in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland at application and when taking up the award.

Are bachelor’s students eligible?

The official list names master’s students, PhD candidates, postdoctoral researchers, and mid-career researchers. Bachelor’s students are not listed.

Are natural-science projects eligible?

The published call specifies social sciences or humanities. Applicants with interdisciplinary work that includes natural-science elements should ask NAI whether the project falls within scope before applying.

Is Norway included?

Norway does not appear in the four-country eligibility list. The official call names Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Iceland.

How long does the scholarship last?

The research stay lasts one month.

How much is the subsistence allowance?

The scholarship includes SEK 450 per day.

Does the scholarship provide accommodation?

Yes. Scholarship holders receive free accommodation in a central location in Uppsala.

Is travel covered?

Yes. The programme covers the least expensive fare from the recipient’s residential address in an eligible country to Uppsala and return.

Is insurance included?

No. The official call expressly excludes health care insurance and other insurance.

What is the most important application document?

NAI states that applications are primarily evaluated on the three-to-five-page research-project outline.

When will applicants receive a decision?

Applicants should be informed as soon as selection is completed and by the end of November 2026 at the latest.

Can current or former NAI employees apply?

No. People currently or previously employed by, or otherwise professionally affiliated with, the Nordic Africa Institute are ineligible.

Final Application Checklist

Before submitting, confirm that:

The proposed research is focused on Africa.

The project falls within the social sciences or humanities.

The applicant is a master’s student, PhD candidate, postdoctoral researcher, or mid-career researcher.

The applicant is currently affiliated with a university or research centre in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland.

The applicant is also based in one of those four countries.

The affiliation and base will continue when the scholarship is taken up.

The applicant has no disqualifying current or previous professional affiliation with NAI.

The CV is current and includes publications, if any.

The research outline is between three and five pages.

The outline clearly explains the objective, disciplinary context, method, data-gathering techniques, time frame, and theoretical basis.

The one-page work plan is tailored to the month at NAI.

The supervisor or head of department has signed the support letter.

The support letter confirms current affiliation and field of research.

The application and all appendices are in English.

Every required file has been uploaded successfully.

The application is submitted before October 11, 2026.

The applicant understands that health care and other insurance are not included.

Contact for Further Information

Questions about eligibility, previous NAI affiliation, research scope, documentation, or programme arrangements may be directed to:

Marie Karlsson

Email: marie.karlsson@nai.uu.se

Telephone: +46 (0)18 471 52 54

Applicants should consult the official programme page before contacting the Institute, as it remains the authoritative source for the current call.

Important Programme Contingency

NAI notes that, in the extraordinary event that the programme does not receive full funding or cannot be implemented in 2027 for another unforeseen reason, applicants will be informed. Selection and planning should therefore not be treated as an unconditional guarantee that the visit will proceed until the Institute confirms the final arrangements.

Conclusion

The Nordic Scholarship Programme 2027 offers a valuable funded research stay for master’s students, doctoral candidates, postdoctoral scholars, and mid-career researchers developing Africa-oriented work in the social sciences or humanities. A one-month placement at the Nordic Africa Institute can provide concentrated research time, access to specialist contemporary-Africa collections, a professional workspace, engagement with relevant NAI research, free accommodation, economical return travel, and a daily subsistence allowance.

The eligibility rules are precise. Applicants may hold any citizenship, but they must be both affiliated with and based at a university or research centre in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, or Iceland when applying and when taking up the scholarship. The research outline carries particular weight in selection, all materials must be in English, and incomplete applications will not be considered. Applicants must also arrange their own health care and other insurance.

Candidates who meet the conditions should begin early, obtain the signed institutional support letter, develop the research outline in their own authentic words, and produce a realistic one-page plan for the NAI visit. The deadline is October 11, 2026, and the Institute expects to communicate outcomes by the end of November 2026 at the latest.

TITLE: Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship 2027: Prestigious African Leadership Fellowship for Emerging Leaders Across Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship Programme 2027 is inviting nominations for the next generation of high-potential African leaders who are expected to take on significant leadership roles and contribute to Africa’s transformation over the coming years.

Organised by the African Leadership Institute (AFLI), the Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship is the organisation’s flagship leadership development programme. The programme has been offered since 2006 and is designed to identify, develop and connect promising young African leaders across different sectors of society.

For the Class of 2027, approximately 25 high-potential individuals from across Africa will ultimately be selected through a rigorous and competitive process. However, unlike many fellowship programmes, individuals cannot directly apply or nominate themselves. Candidates must first be nominated by another person and, following the nomination and screening stages, eligible nominees will be invited to complete the full fellowship application.

The programme is designed for Africans between 30 and 39 years of age who demonstrate strong leadership potential and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to Africa’s social, economic and political transformation.

Nomination deadline for the Class of 2027: September 20, 2026, at midnight Johannesburg, South Africa time.

The subsequent candidate application process is scheduled to begin around September 25, 2026, with applications and letters of recommendation due by October 25, 2026, at midnight Johannesburg time.

About the African Leadership Institute

The African Leadership Institute (AFLI) is focused on nurturing and strengthening leadership capabilities across Africa, particularly among young people who demonstrate exceptional leadership potential.

The Institute’s broader objective is to develop a network of high-potential African leaders who can progress into senior leadership positions within their respective fields over the following five to ten years.

AFLI seeks to develop leaders who will not only advance professionally but also remain actively engaged in creating positive change across Africa.

The Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship is the Institute’s flagship programme through which it pursues this objective.

The fellowship has been running since 2006, creating a network of alumni who have participated in leadership learning and development activities designed to strengthen their experiences, insights, leadership tools and confidence.

What Is the Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship?

The Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship Programme is a prestigious leadership development programme aimed at identifying and developing the next generation of African leaders.

Each year, approximately 25 high-potential individuals from across Africa are selected following a rigorous competitive selection process.

The programme targets individuals who are expected to become influential leaders in their respective fields over the next five to ten years.

Importantly, the fellowship is not limited to one profession or sector.

The programme is intended for emerging leaders across all sectors of African society, meaning that candidates can come from different professional, social, economic, public, private, civil society and other leadership backgrounds.

The central question is not simply what sector an individual works in, but whether the person demonstrates the leadership potential, experience and commitment necessary to contribute to Africa’s transformation.

The Purpose of the Tutu Fellowship

The fellowship is designed around the idea that Africa’s future depends significantly on the development of capable, ethical and transformative leaders.

AFLI therefore seeks individuals who have already demonstrated leadership potential and who can develop into influential leaders in their respective fields.

Through the fellowship, selected participants receive leadership learning activities intended to strengthen:

Leadership experience

Strategic insight

Personal confidence

Leadership tools

Understanding of complex African challenges

Capacity to influence positive change

Professional networks

Collaboration across sectors and countries

The programme also seeks to create a lasting network of fellows who can support one another and contribute to Africa’s transformation beyond the fellowship itself.

Approximately 25 Fellows Will Be Selected

The Archbishop Tutu Fellowship is highly selective.

For each annual class, approximately 25 individuals are selected from across Africa.

This means that becoming a Tutu Fellow is a competitive achievement.

The programme describes its selected participants as some of the continent’s most promising future leaders and specifically targets individuals expected to rise into top leadership positions within their areas of activity over the next five to ten years.

Applicants and nominators should therefore understand that meeting the basic age and geographic requirements does not automatically result in selection.

The selection process is designed to identify candidates who demonstrate exceptional leadership potential and a strong capacity to contribute to the transformation of Africa.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The programme is designed for high-potential African leaders between 30 and 39 years of age.

The fellowship is not restricted to one professional discipline.

Potential candidates may come from sectors such as:

Government and public service

Business and entrepreneurship

Education

Other sectors of society

The key consideration is the candidate’s leadership potential and capacity to contribute to positive change.

Age Requirement for the Class of 2027

Candidates must be between:

30 and 39 years of age.

The nomination form explicitly requires the nominator to confirm the candidate’s age.

Applicants outside the specified age range should not be nominated for the programme.

Prospective candidates should therefore verify their age eligibility before approaching a potential nominator.

An Important Difference: You Cannot Apply Directly

One of the most important aspects of the Archbishop Tutu Fellowship is that direct applications are not accepted.

Individuals interested in becoming Tutu Fellows must first be nominated by another person.

This means:

You cannot nominate yourself.

You cannot submit a direct application without first being nominated.

You need someone else to put your name forward.

Only one nomination is necessary.

Multiple nominations may be regarded as abuse of the nomination process.

The programme specifically advises interested individuals who wish to be considered to read the relevant candidate guidance and seek nomination.

How the Nomination Process Works

The nomination process is designed to identify individuals who have demonstrated strong leadership potential.

A nominator must provide information about both themselves and the candidate.

Instead, the nominator should provide personal insight that selectors would not obtain simply by reading a résumé.

The Fellowship Is Not Limited to One Career Path

Conclusion

The Archbishop Tutu Leadership Fellowship 2027 represents a major leadership development opportunity for high-potential Africans who are already demonstrating the capacity to influence their organisations, communities, sectors and societies.

Run by the African Leadership Institute, the fellowship has been offered since 2006 and seeks to build a network of emerging African leaders who are expected to rise into significant leadership positions over the next five to ten years.

For the Class of 2027, approximately 25 individuals will be selected through a rigorous process. The programme is open to emerging leaders across sectors rather than being restricted to a particular profession. Candidates must be between 30 and 39 years old and must first be nominated by another person.

TITLE: FWF Cluster of Excellence funding programme

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Blog | GE News | Grant Evaluation

Our Grant Evaluation Partnerships Manager, Julia Boman, had the opportunity to connect with Tina Olteanu, Unit Head of Program Management Coordination at the Austrian Science Fund (FWF).

Tina shared insights into the role of FWF’s Cluster of Excellence funding programme and how ESF supports FWF in achieving its objectives.
Can you tell us briefly about FWF funding programmes and what makes FWF unique in the Austrian research funding landscape ?

The Austrian Science Fund (FWF) is Austria’s central funding organization for basic research. The purpose of the FWF is to support the ongoing development of Austrian science and basic research at a high international level. In this way, the FWF makes a significant contribution to cultural development, to the advancement of our knowledge-based society, and thus to the creation of value and wealth in Austria.

Clusters of Excellence (COE) are the first of three pillars of the excellent=austria funding initiative to strengthen Austria’s position as a top location for research within the international scientific community. The dimension and scope of the research conducted in a cluster go far beyond what was previously possible within the FWF’s existing program portfolio.

COEs enable groups of researchers at Austrian research institutions to achieve outstanding cooperative research results (including arts-based research) in one area or interdisciplinarily and to firmly establish this research area in Austria in the long term at a top international level. COEs thus play a central role in shaping and strengthening core research areas at the participating research institutions.

How does FWF stay ahead in the dynamic research assessment landscape ?

The FWF is involved in various working groups and platforms that put current evaluation procedures to the test and discuss or try out new formats. The FWF strives to test innovative review formats in programmes that lend themselves to new approaches based on the specific programme objectives.

For example, in the 1000 Ideas Programme, which focuses on exceptional ideas and high-risk research, the FWF uses a random selection procedure when it is no longer possible to distinguish between projects on the basis of excellent scientific quality, but the budget is not sufficient for all fundable projects. Here, too, we are in close exchange with other funding organisations that follow this path.

How did partnering with ESF support FWF in achieving its goals for the COE programme ?

The COE programme brings together large groups of researchers at Austrian research institutions. At the same time, FWF funding decisions are made in the FWF Board, where researchers from Austrian research institutions are also represented. Due to the large number of people involved at the research institutions and on the FWF Board, the FWF has decided to externalise the review process to the ESF in order to ensure that transparency and the rules regarding conflicts of interest can be complied with without any problems.

Why did you choose ESF to support you with your evaluation processes? And how has this impacted your organisation ?

It was an unusual step for the FWF to hand over part of its core acitvity to another organisation. However, the above considerations convinced us that this was the best way to implement a transparent decision-making process with the same high scientific evaluation quality.

What aspects of the ESF support did you appreciate the most ?

The cooperation with the ESF was very straightforward and goal-oriented, and flexible when it came to implementing our premises and specifications within the framework of the COE review. Most applicants were satisfied, but there were also a few critical voices that questioned the competence of the reviewers. However, from the FWF’s perspective, this is not unusual for such review processes.

TITLE: CERHI/ACEGID Partnership Wins Grant for Validation of Rapid Diagnostic COVID-19 Test Kits

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Centre of Excellence in Reproductive Health Innovation (CERHI), University of Benin in collaboration with the African Centre of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) hosted by the Redeemer’s University and the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) have been awarded a Grant to validate Rapid Diagnostic Tests kits (RDT) for COVID-19 testing in Nigeria.

The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a research consortium between CERHI and UBTH for the testing of the SARS COV-2 virus. With CERHI’s laboratories and facilities, including RT-PCR machine for testing for the virus and UBTH’s expertise in managing infectious diseases, the unit was validated by the Nigerian Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) to become the second testing unit in Edo State, and one of the few in Nigeria. Similarly, the African Centre of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) successfully sequenced the genomes of the COVID-19 virus and was the first institution to do so in Africa. Considering this knowledge and expertise, the three institutions partnered to apply for a Grant on the validation of RDTs in Nigeria. Led by Professor Friday E. Okonofua, Centre leader of CERHI and Professor Christian Happi, Centre Leader of ACEGID, the team’s proposal was selected for funding and implementation. The CERHI/UBTH/ACEGID team is one of the 5 teams selected to develop and implement a national protocol for the validation of RDT kits for COVID-19 in Nigeria. The projected timeline for completion of this project is four months.

The importance of this project stems from the fact that available rapid tests for COVID-19 in Nigeria have not been validated and as a result, this project will contribute to the validation of the rapid COVID-19 tests, comparing the sensitivities and predictive results obtained from their use with the gold standard and the PCR test. If the rapid tests are found to be sensitive and accurate, it will expand access to COVID-19 testing to millions of Nigerians, and the continent at large.

The Centre of Excellence in Reproductive Health Innovation (CERHI) and Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) are part of the 53 Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) supported by World Bank through the coordination of the Association of African Universities as the Regional Facilitation Unit. The ACE Impact project aims to address regional developmental challenges through quality post-graduate education and applied research (https://ace.aau.org/).

CERHI implements high quality training and applied research for reproductive health professionals. The centre is also a leading name in the development and implementation of several ground-breaking researches in the field of sexual and reproductive health and population studies within the continent (https://www.cerhiuniben.edu.ng/).

ACEGID focuses on capacity building of African scientists in the field of genomics. The centre aims to translate the research outcome to products that can be deployed to the field to contribute to the control, management and elimination of infectious diseases in the continent (https://acegid.org/).

Her leadership was defined by her passion for empowering others and fostering unity within the academic community. Professor Mahmoud’s legacy will continue to inspire us as we build upon the solid foundations she established, carrying forward her mission to strengthen higher education across Africa.

TITLE: Workshop on Online Teaching and Learning Management

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Background and Rationale

The beginning of the twenty-first century is being perceived as an information period, of which advanced education assumes a critical role. The essential objectives of advanced education foundations are improving and keeping up scholastic greatness, grant, and open administration. Desires for training quality and, the changing standards in educating and learning are a portion of the difficulties that instructing clique faces constantly. These when combined with enormous increment sought after for advanced education calls for concerns with regard to how institutions can suit the majority without bargaining the nature and quality of instructing and learning.

With the above patterns happening in almost every establishment of higher learning, it has turned out to be basic that staff build up a fitness life-long learning and have an introduction to new changes/patterns in their field through continuous training and presentation to new information, for example, web based instructing and management. Web based learning and digitized training are developing exponentially consistently, also the propagation of worldwide massive open online courses (MOOC). Understudies of today, alluded to as “digital natives” access free courses from adroit subject experts everywhere throughout the world without limits to space and time. As students endeavor to improve learning results; faculty has to upgrade its skills and knowledge to perform in the digital age institution and work environment.

Many universities and learning organizations are adopting the new trend of e Learning to increase students’ enrollment and achievements. However, many faculties fail to recognize the changing roles of academic faculty members, the “digital immigrants.” Conventional faculty pedagogical role has changed to e-pedagogy, managerial, social and technological roles in the virtual learning environment.

Workshop Goals

This workshop is intended to help participants in building up the required aptitude/expertise in theory and practice to work viably in the e-learning environment. The spotlight isn’t just on the technical side, yet on the changing roles to suit the requests of the creative framework, developing technologies and address diverse learning styles. The workshop will explore several key issues that educators need to understand about teaching and learning in the digital age. It will also consider; how online learning is different from traditional methods of learning and examinations ; how the digital practices of young people are continually changing; and explore some key considerations that need to be addressed while designing learning environments that are engaging and student centered.

Training Outcomes

By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to:

1. Apply evidenced-based approach to design, develop and manage online courses reflectively and pragmatically for teaching online or in a blended learning environment.

2. Recognize and be able to describe the characteristics of effective online and blended learning programmes.

3. Be able to explain how the Community of Inquiry framework, and similar perspectives can help promote successful learning in online programmes.

4. Understand the needs and nature of online learners.

5. Appreciate the range of available technologies and learn how to maintain knowledge of emerging technology trends, identifying those systems most appropriate to the needs of your courses and students.

6. Demonstrate knowledge of ethical and legal issues relating to online teaching.

Target Groups

All academic faculty lecturers, learning and training instructors, educational researchers and administrators, directors and coordinators of distance education, curriculum designers and developers, e Learning managers and coordinators, I.C.T program directors and managers, and general practitioners of scholarship and teaching.

Date and Venue
