TITLE: 2021 AAU GENERAL CONFERENCE COMMUNIQUE

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
15th General Conference of the Association of African Universities

July 5-8, 2021 (Virtual)

Click to download a version of the Communique HERE

The Association of African Universities (AAU) held its 15th Quadrennial General Conference of African University leaders on July 5-8, 2021. This was a virtual meeting of academic leaders, policy makers, funders, educational ministers and educational stakeholders across the African continent, the African diaspora and beyond.

The main theme for the General Conference was “The Future of Higher Education in Africa”. In addition to keynote presentations on the main theme of the Conference, papers delivered under the following six sub-themes framed the deliberations of the conference :

Sub-Theme 1: The Future of African Higher Education Post-COVID-19

Sub-Theme 2: Contributions of African Higher Education Institutions to Addressing the

Challenges linked to the COVID-19 pandemic

Sub-Theme 3: Contributions of African Higher Education Institutions in Achieving

Sustainable Development Goals

Sub-Theme 4: Funding of African Higher Education Institutions in the face of

unpredictable Economy

Sub-Theme 5: Mainstreaming e-learning and the digital divide

Sub-Theme 6: Contributions of the Diaspora to African Higher Education

The Conference was held under the Patronage of His Excellency Nana Addo Danquah Akuffo Addo, President of the Republic of Ghana.

We, participants at the Conference,

Appreciate the President of the Republic of Ghana for hosting this Conference.

Welcome the support of sponsors, donors and development partners, including the African Union, the European Union, the African Development Bank, and the Carnegie Corporation of New York, in the organization of this Conference.

Acknowledge the numerous programmes generously funded by these organizations to support African higher education institutions, agencies, staff, students and researchers.

Appreciate the numerous goodwill messages delivered at the Conference by key partners across the African continent and beyond.

Are aware of the challenges confronting higher education across the African continent such as limited student enrolment; inadequate financial resources; deficient human capital; low research output; suboptimal physical and electronic infrastructures; and poor leadership and governance, among others.

Resolve to accelerate activities at the higher education institutional level that can help to overcome the challenges identified by the numerous presenters.

Acknowledge the fact that COVID-19 has disrupted teaching and learning, stalled research and threatened the much-needed skills to enhance Africa’s teaching and research competitiveness.

Recognize the fact that the majority of African universities do not have the necessary infrastructure to adequately respond to the challenges that have emerged with the onset of the novel COVID-19 pandemic.

Acknowledge the fact that while COVID-19 has disrupted traditional learning systems and changed the educational trajectory on a scale never experienced before in higher education, it has at the same time created new opportunities for Africa to innovate rapidly.

Are conscious of the fact that COVID-19 has raised our awareness and created the need for African higher institutions to transition to areas such as: digital content creation, online instructional design; training of staff on online teaching, provision of e-Learning infrastructural facilities, support to connect to learning management systems and assistance with online learning strategies, methods and resources.

Recognize the need for African universities to urgently resolve the challenges posed by COVID-19 such as infrastructural deficit, limited access to affordable high-speed internet connectivity, poor access to and/or unreliable electricity, recalibration of research, among others.

Support the design of home-grown solutions in response to the pandemic and appreciate the role of Africa Centers of Excellence in undertaking high-end research to develop a cure for COVID-19.

Are aware of the need to partner with prominent Regional Research Education Networks (RRENs) that champion educational and research infrastructure including internet connectivity, cloud services and other platforms to enable African researchers collaborate across the world.

Appreciate the importance to leverage the AAU African Research & Education Network (AfREN) project to facilitate improved teaching, learning and research collaborations, as well as use network economies of scale to reduce the cost of highspeed internet access and promote linkages of academics to industry, government and other international research/educational networks.

Aim to subscribe to large scale academic research infrastructures, such as Africa Light Source Initiative, to encourage African scientists to undertake research in Africa.

Recognise the need to cultivate and deepen mutual trust among governments at the continental level, understanding and respect for educational systems, as well as mobility opportunities within Africa and other countries.

Undertake to leverage international mobility mechanisms such as the European Union initiatives and inter-institutional joint degree programmes, in a manner that strategically benefits Africa.

Resolve to work with the AAU to support further initiatives with a focus on academic mobility such as the African Jobs Board.

Undertake to promote university-industry linkages with the objective of creating an “entrepreneurial university” to help transform African universities.

Will promote universities’ contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals and their potential to develop local, national, regional and global economy, to create employment, to improve education in terms of curricula, teaching and learning, research and community engagement activities.

Resolve to explore creative ways to fund African higher education.

Undertake, consistent with the AAU strategic plan, to promote evidence-based advocacy to ensure a favourable policy environment and prioritization of higher education at national, regional and continental levels.

Urge African institutions of higher learning to harmonize their quality assurance frameworks and develop a quality culture that is embraced by all members.

Resolve to explore the adoption of the African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN), a network for quality assurance practitioners in African higher education initiated by the AAU with the support of the Global Initiative for Quality Assurance Capacity (GIQAC) as a model in promoting a culture of quality assurance in higher education in Africa.

Undertake to determine the level of readiness for e-learning across Africa and implement measures to mainstream e-learning among higher education institutions in Africa in order to overcome the digital divide among countries and institutions.

Recognize Open, Distance and e-Learning (ODeL) and the establishment of virtual and open universities as an innovative way of delivering education to the majority of Africans in need of higher education.

Acknowledge the role of the African diaspora in serving as a focal point for rebuilding the global African community and championing several developmental initiatives at the intercontinental level.

Agree to take measures to reverse the brain drain which has deprived the African continent of the kind of intellectual capacity the continent needs.

Recognize the role of the diaspora in promotion higher education in Africa, and undertake to develop strategic partnerships between African HEIs and, in particular, diasporas in North America and Europe, including the Historically Black Colleges and Universities in the USA, to contribute to the African Union’s Africa educational agenda.

Undertake to implement a coordinated and focused approach to bring back the children of Africa in the diaspora to help achieve the vision of the Africa we want.

Recognize the immense contribution that the diaspora can make in leading Africa to the next frontier of its development.

In closing,

We, participants at the Conference,

a. Applaud the AAU for successfully organising the 15th Quadrennial General Conference of African University leaders which has profoundly refocused higher education institutions in Africa to commit to addressing the core challenges created by the COVID-19 pandemic.

b. Resolve to work together to surmount the real challenges hindering the growth and relevance of Africa’s institutions of higher learning for continental relevance within a globally competitive environment.

c. Acknowledge the pivotal role played by Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education as the foundation for the development of other academic disciplines.

d. Urge the AAU to create a platform that will enable African universities store all their research online within their institutions and to provide the expertise to transfer the knowledge useful for the development of Africa.

e. Undertake to contribute collectively to the attainment of the goals of policies such as the African Union’s Agenda 2063, the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25), the Science Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024), and the Global 2030 Sustainable Development Goals Agenda, among others, for the benefit of the people of Africa and the World at large.

f. Acknowledge the fact that the Africa We Want can be achieved by undoing the miseducation Africans have received from colonial masters.

g. Urge the AAU to admit diaspora institutions that have 50% of its members with African decent as AAU members, and encourage them to join AAU conferences and activities.

h. Urge the AAU to undertake a review of the implementation of this Communiqué and report the progress achieved at the next General Conference.

Nana Professor Osei Darkwa

Rapporteur General

TITLE: Call for Participants – 3rd International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: Women’s Participation in Science Programmes in Africa

November 26 -29, 2019

Abuja, Nigeria

Host: African University of Science and Technology (AUST)

The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the African University of Science and Technology (AUST) is inviting the Higher Education Community to participate in the upcoming 3rd International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) being organised in Nigeria, under the theme Women’s Participation in Science Programmes in Africa.

Background: World over, the issue of inclusiveness of women, especially in leadership remains a major challenge. To date, women continue to have unequal opportunities as their male counterparts. African higher education, for instance, continues to see fewer women occupying leadership positions in the universities, polytechnics and research institutions among others. Indeed, very few women have risen to positions such as Vice-chancellors, Heads of Departments, Deans and Registrars across the continent.

The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 4 and 5 on Quality Education, and Women and Girl’s Empowerment respectively recognise the importance of advancing gender parity in the process of striving to achieve the SDGs.

Similarly, the African Union Commission (AUC) established its Centre for Education of Girls and Women in Africa (AU-CIEFFA) to, among others, provide guidance for Africa Member States to integrate gender perspectives in their programmes and in the implementation of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 2016-2025).

Taking the lead to drive women and young girls’ equal participation in the higher education sector has been prime on the agenda of the Association of African Universities (AAU). As the apex organization and forum for consultation, exchange of information and co-operation among institutions of Higher Education in Africa, AAU is cognisant of the gender imbalances in African higher education and has thus been leading the campaign on gender inclusiveness in its various initiatives and projects. The promotion of gender equality is firmly rooted in the AAU’s Strategic Plan (2016 – 2020) where reference is made to expanding gender programmes to facilitate the attainment of objectives spelt out in the African Women’s Decade (2010 -2020) Plan of Action.

In this Strategic Plan, the AAU set out to organise special events and create platforms for higher education institution (HEI) stakeholders to discuss topical issues which serve as catalysts for Africa’s development, including Gender, Science, Technology and Innovation.

The International Conference for Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) is one of such key platforms provided by AAU for the discussion of innovative and creative ways of empowering women, especially young women in higher education to reach their full potential and aspire to the topmost leadership positions in their chosen fields. The WoLPHE maiden edition, which was held in Accra, Ghana was highly successful and brought women across national and international boundaries together to share knowledge, ideas and strategic management skills required for success in various leadership positions.

The WoLPHE second edition, held in Nairobi, Kenya attracted mostly women in academia, politics and business as well as few men who share the grand vision of women advancement in science-based careers. In attendance were various dignitaries including the Kenyan government representation through the Cabinet Secretary, Professor Margaret Kobia, the Head of Education Division at the Human Resources, Science and Technology (HRST) Department of the African Union Commission, Dr. Beatrice Njenga, and former Vice Chancellor of Kenyatta University and Director of the Centre for Innovative Leadership and Governance, Prof Olive Mugenda. The conference drew participants from higher education institutions in Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania, Burkina Faso, Uganda, South Africa, Mauritius, Sudan, Egypt among others. Key organisations such as the Forum for African Women Educationalists (FAWE) and the Organisation for Women in science in the Developing World (OWSD) were also present.

Focus on Women in STEM

As reflected by the theme, the focus of this upcoming WoLPHE conference to be held in Abuja is on the theme Women’s Participation in Science Based Programmes in Africa.

Africa’s progress is challenged by a myriad of problems ranging from lack of employment for its youth, the existence of tropical diseases, weak entrepreneurial drive and low levels of university-industry linkages, among others. It is widely accepted, that Science and Technology do have a key role to play in overcoming the continent’s developmental challenges.

However, studies have revealed that though the number of women in science and engineering is growing, men continue to outnumber women, especially at the upper levels of these professions (AAUW, 2010). With only 24% of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) occupations being filled by women, various barriers, ranging from culture, implicit bias and subtle stereotyping to willful ignorance and blatant discrimination have been identified as contributing factors (Pierce, Margo, 2013).

Africa needs to ensure that its human resource – both men and women, are fully engaged in the STEM fields in solving its developmental challenges, and thus should make significant investment into women in STEM to increase their contribution to solving the continent’s challenges. The promotion of Women in Science to contribute massively and equally to a developed Africa must therefore form an integral part of various plans and strategies aimed at achieving the African Union’s vision of ‘Africa We Want’ by the year 2063. This conference will therefore create the right platform for the analysis and discussion of women participation in science programmes in Africa- what the key challenges are; what institutions can do to ensure that more women are encouraged to take up STEM courses; how young Women faculty members can be motivated to move up the academic ladder among others.

Aim

The WoLPHE International Conference seeks to:

 Create the platform for the presentation of findings on a commissioned study on the key challenges faced by women in the science fields.

 Inspire and empower the next generation of African women in STEM to actively and effectively contribute to solving Africa’s Challenges.

 Provide the platform for women in STEM to share their cutting-edge research as a way of inspiring others.

 Build the leadership capacity of women in STEM to drive change and innovation in the STEM field.

 Draw attention to the important role of mentorship, through the provision of the platform for young scientists to interact with accomplished women scientists.

 Create the platform for various actors – educators, policy-makers and partners -to debate on pertinent issues related to the promotion of Women in STEM.

Conference Theme and Subthemes

The Conference Theme is: Women’s Participation in Science Programs in Africa.

Based on the Conference theme, the AAU is calling for papers under the following subthemes:

a) Current Developments on Women Participation in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics in Africa.

b) Key Challenges Faced by Women in Science.

c) Gender Mainstreaming in STEM programmes in Africa.

c) Resource Mobilization Strategies to support STEM research

d) Policies, Strategies and Mechanisms to support Women in STEM.

Activities

-Presentation of Commissioned Studies and Research Papers on the Conference subthemes

– Panel Discussions on Topical Issues

-Leadership Training Sessions

-Networking and Speed Mentoring Sessions

Expected Participants

-Accomplished women in various leadership positions in STEM fields from Africa and beyond.

– STEM women academics and researchers in African HEIs.

-Women in industry, government and partner institutions involved in promoting STEM.

– STEM men academics and researchers in African HEIs.

Sponsorship

Authors whose papers are accepted for presentation will be provided with a roundtrip economy ticket and accommodation to make their presentation at the conference.

Participation Fee

The Conference Registration fee is $200 for women participants; $50 for female students; and $300 for other participants

TITLE: Mapping the Capabilities of Using Data in African Higher Education Institutions: A case Study of 36 ACE Impact Host Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Written By: Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini – Director ICT Services, Communications and Knowledge Management at AAU

Background

The ability of any institution to use data is critical because when data is well managed, it can be used to support decision making through the mapping and understanding of emerging data trends. Well managed data facilitate key strategic initiatives and actions that help improve business performance and relationships with stakeholders.

African Universities collect great amounts of data on students, staff, curricula, research, partnerships, and other areas – but more still needs to be done for African Universities to benefit from the data that they collect. Issues hindering them from maximizing the benefits from their data, include weak management information systems, limited data skills, gaps in the data collected, inadequate human resources to manage data functions, and limited institutional policies to promote data prioritization.

In addition, this century is characterized by the prevalence of new data sources that is sometimes referred to as Big Data. This new data emanates from the social media, various online systems, and many ‘silent’ data collection processes. In line with these developments, it is very important that African Universities sift through such data and turn useful and important new data into a resource that informs curricula, student services, partnerships, resource mobilization, among several other important functional areas of universities.

Benchmarking Initiatives for African Universities

There are two major benchmarking initiatives that were initiated for African Universities – the PASET (Partnership for Applied Skills in Engineering and Technology) Regional Benchmarking Initiative developed by the World Bank and the AQRM (African Quality Rating Mechanism) developed by the African Union Commission. Both benchmarking initiatives aim to strengthen the capacities of African Universities to self-study, self-analyze and self-assess using set standards and ultimately use these results to improve their processes and performances. Both the PASET Regional Benchmarking Initiative and the AQRM have a set of indicators that universities use to self-report on their status in relation to these indicators.

The PASET Regional Benchmarking methodology is based on five institutional performance and eight institutional health indicators. The five institutional performance indicators concentrate on Inclusion and Equity; Learning Achievement; Labor Market Outcomes; Research Results; and Technology Transfer Results. The eight institutional health indicators focus on Inclusion and Equity; Quality of Teaching and Learning; Relevance; Internationalization; Research; Community Service & Technology Transfer; Governance & Management; and Financing.

The AQRM benchmarking methodology has three parts, namely institutional general information, institutional level self-rating and programme level self-rating. The institutional general information indicators include Institutional Profile; Student Profile; Facilities; Faculty / Staff Profile; Governance & Management; Teaching & Learning; Linkage with the Industry Sector; Research & Community Outreach; Internationalization; and Rating of Best Three Departments /Subject Areas. The self-rating indicators at institutional level concentrate on Governance & Management; Infrastructure; Finance; Teaching & Learning; Research, Publication & Innovation; and Community/Societal Engagement. The self-rating indicators at programme level focus on Programme Planning & Management; Curriculum Development; Teaching & Learning; Assessment; and Programme Results.

PASET Regional Benchmarking Initiative

At the just ended 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop that was hosted in Benin, Dr Jingwen Mu from the University of Auckland, New Zealand, spoke on the progress that the ACE Impact Host Universities have made towards achieving the goals of the Disbursement Linked Result 7.4 (DLR7.4) which encourages the Host Universities to participate in the PASET Regional Benchmarking initiative. DLR7.4 is one of the sub- indicators that is used by the ACE Impact Project to measure the impact of the project on the overall universities’ functions, that is, how the project is impacting the processes at the universities’ institutional levels.

The first PASET benchmarking pilot in 2014 involved seven universities, the second round in 2016 involved 31 universities, and the third round in 2018 involved 26 universities. These earlier benchmarking activities revealed that the participating universities were challenged with reporting and finding the data that was required as part of self-benchmarking. For example, during the 2018 and 2021 PASET Benchmarking exercises, the participating universities said that they needed support in the areas of institutional research, quality assurance, MIS (management information systems) capacity development and conducting benchmarking and graduate tracer studies. These declared needs by the universities proved that they were facing difficulties in meeting the full benchmarking data requirements of the PASET self-benchmarking methodology. MIS support was identified by participating institutions as a top critical area where support was most needed.

‘As part of revising the PASET self-benchmarking methodology, the project team decided to initially assess the data systems maturity of ACE Impact Host Universities – instead of requiring that they respond to the set self-benchmarking questions’, said Dr Jingwen Mu. ‘It was within this context that DLR 7.4 proposed a two-phase approach, in which Phase 1 asked ACE Impact host institutions to complete a self-assessment of their institutional data systems’, added Dr Jingwen Mu.

Data System Maturity Survey involving 36 ACE Impact Host Universities

It was reported that a free open source data maturity framework called DataOrchard was chosen and adapted to assess the “data maturity journeys” of all the ACE Impact Host Universities. The data maturity assessment aimed to inspire the universities to work “towards improvement and increased capability in using data”. This Framework, created by Data Orchard CIC, has been developed specifically for the non-for-profit sector and has seen its adoption by higher education institutions. It was mentioned that the adapted version of the Framework for ACE Impact institutions is a simplified version that encourages participants to focus on three key themes of a healthy data system – People, Technology, and Culture. The host institutions’ survey responses were aggregated and rated at both the ‘theme-level’ and the ‘overall level’ and classified into one of the five stages of data system maturity: Unaware, Emerging, Learning, Developing, and Mastering.

Dr. Jingwen Mu reported that 36 ACE Impact host institutions had participated in the Data System Maturity Assessment as part of preparing them for the PASET self-benchmarking. The findings from the data system maturity assessment were that the participating universities fell into three categories – 14 host universities were found to be in the Learning Group in terms of their data systems maturity; 19 host universities were placed in the Developing Group and 3 host universities were placed in the Mastering Group.

Three Host Universities graded in the mastering group were said to be most advanced in the way that they collect, manage, and use their data. Mastering Universities are very comfortable using data to ask difficult and complex questions, explained Dr. Mu.

Nineteen Host Universities in the developing group were reported to be starting to use and share data at institutional levels. People from various teams and levels of seniority in these institutions regularly discuss data and how to use it, expounded Dr. Mu.

Fourteen Host Universities in the learning group were said to be characterized by the fact that data was beginning to be recognized as important at more senior levels, however access to data was still challenged.

Dr. Jingwen Mu said that even those universities that were graded to be masters, also have much more to learn towards improving their data management systems. Dr. Jingwen Mu also cautioned that the results of the ACE Impact Data System Maturity Assessment needed to be interpreted in the context of the adapted version of the data maturity framework and in the context of the PASET DLR 7.4 objectives.

As a follow up to the Data System Maturity Assessment, the ACE Impact host universities were given a personalized report that indicated areas of strengths and weaknesses. Currently these institutions are developing institutional intervention plans as their responses to the outcomes of the Data System Maturity Assessment, said Dr Jingwen Mu.

During the question-and-answer session, the participants asked for advice on how to handle resistance by team members to new ways of handling data. Dr. Jingwen Mu said that in the context of Africa, it was important to demonstrate what faculty currently do and what they can do with data or how they can improve their processes because of data. She advised that staff needed to be educated about the importance of data in helping universities better engage students and stakeholders. Such efforts in demonstrating the usefulness of data would reduce their resistance, advised Dr. Jingwen Mu.

Key Lessons for other African Universities

Data capability is very important for the sustainability and relevance of African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs); thus, it is important that HEIs strengthen their data skills, transform their data cultures and reinforce their data management technologies.

Assessing the data systems maturity of African Universities might be an important starting point as opposed to insisting that the universities move straight into self-benchmarking. The value of the data systems maturity assessment is that it prepares the universities to provide the required data during self-benchmarking.

There is an opportunity for the two benchmarking methodologies (PASET and AQRM) to integrate the good aspects of the other – and for the universities that have used these methodologies to share experiences.

The adapted data systems maturity assessment could be deployed across all interested universities in Africa – and this would assist the universities to advance their journeys towards data systems maturity.

TITLE: EY Foundation Smart Futures 2026/27 | Paid Work Experience, Training and Mentoring for Young People in the UK

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The EY Foundation Smart Futures programme is a career development opportunity designed to help young people gain practical experience of the workplace, develop employability skills and receive professional mentoring before they leave school.

The programme combines paid work experience, interactive employability skills training and business mentoring, with opportunities across different sectors and locations in the UK. The EY Foundation currently lists 2026/27 Smart Futures programmes as open for applications, with programmes available in locations including London, Birmingham, Manchester, Liverpool, Bradford, Newcastle and Aberdeen, among others.

Unlike a traditional work-experience placement, Smart Futures combines workplace exposure with structured training and mentoring. Participants can explore different industries, develop transferable skills, build professional networks and receive guidance as they consider their next steps into employment or higher education.

About the Smart Futures Programme

Smart Futures is an EY Foundation programme for young people in Year 12 in England or S5 in Scotland.

Participants receive paid work experience with employer partners, employability skills training and support from a business mentor. The programme is designed to help young people understand the world of work and develop skills that can support their transition into employment, apprenticeships or university.

The EY Foundation describes its wider programme offer as supporting young people with paid employability training and work experience, alongside mentoring and, where needed, support with travel costs.

What Does Smart Futures Offer?

Successful participants can benefit from several components throughout the programme.

1. Paid Work Experience

Participants receive real-world experience with one of the programme’s employer partners.

This provides an opportunity to experience a professional working environment, understand workplace expectations and gain practical knowledge that can strengthen future applications for jobs, apprenticeships or university.

The work experience can also help participants understand what different careers are actually like before making important decisions about their future.

2. Employability Skills Training

The programme includes up to two weeks of employability skills training and interactive workshops.

Training can include activities designed to develop:

Communication

Teamwork

Confidence

Networking

Workplace awareness

Professional skills

Career planning

Understanding of different industries and organisations

Participants also have opportunities to meet other young people taking part in Smart Futures.

3. Business Mentoring

Participants receive support from a business mentor who can help them understand their options and prepare for the transition into professional working life or higher education.

Mentoring can provide guidance around career decisions, workplace expectations and the first steps towards a future career.

4. Alumni and Networking Opportunities

Participants can also be invited to alumni events through the EY Foundation’s Limitless Series during their final year at school or college.

The programme provides opportunities to practise networking and build connections with professionals and other young people.

Smart Futures Career Areas

One of the major strengths of Smart Futures is the range of career-focused programmes available.

The programme is not limited to students who already know exactly what career they want. The EY Foundation states that its different programmes can provide workplace experience and transferable skills even for young people who are still exploring their options.

Some of the programme areas include:

Smart Futures Business and Finance

Sector: Professional Services

This programme is aimed at young people interested in careers such as accounting, consulting and other professional services.

It is particularly relevant to students considering a high-level or degree apprenticeship after school or college.

Secure Futures

Sector: Security

Secure Futures introduces participants to careers within the security sector, including work connected to keeping people safe online, in workplaces, homes and public spaces.

Tech Futures

Sector: Technology

Tech Futures provides exposure to the technology and digital sector.

Participants can gain insight into technological careers while receiving work experience and mentorship from professionals working on digital developments.

Smart Futures Banking and Finance

Sector: Banking

This programme introduces participants to different careers within banking and finance.

Areas covered can include:

Branch banking

Technology

Sustainability

Marketing

Risk

Relationship management

Smart Futures Business and Technology

Sectors: Professional Services, Finance and Technology

This programme is designed for young people interested in exploring career opportunities across professional services, finance and technology.

Impactful Futures

Sector: Charity

Impactful Futures provides young people with an opportunity to explore careers in the charity sector and understand the range of professional roles that contribute to positive social change.

STEM Futures

Sectors: Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics

STEM Futures provides insight into careers connected to science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

Data Driven Futures

Sectors: Data, Business Analysis and Risk

This programme introduces young people to data-focused careers, including the work of actuaries and professionals who use mathematics, data and risk analysis to help organisations make informed decisions.

Private Equity Futures

Sector: Private Equity

Private Equity Futures provides an introduction to the private equity sector and the role investment can play in supporting business growth and innovation.

Real Estate Futures

Sector: Real Estate

Real Estate Futures introduces participants to the property sector and careers connected with the development and management of buildings, communities and cities.

The EY Foundation notes that applicants must be based in the relevant delivery location for the programme they select. The full list of programmes, locations and dates is available on the official application page.

Who Can Apply?

The Smart Futures eligibility criteria are designed specifically for young people who may face financial or socioeconomic barriers to accessing professional work experience.

Applicants must meet the following requirements.

Financial Eligibility

Applicants must either:

Have been eligible for Free School Meals at any time during the previous two years, or

Be eligible for a college bursary or Education Maintenance Allowance (EMA).

Age and Education

Applicants must also:

Be in Year 12 in England or Fifth Year (S5) in Scotland.

Be 16 or 17 years old during the programme.

Attend a state school.

Be studying an eligible combination of qualifications, including A-levels, International Baccalaureate, BTEC Level 3s, National 5s or Highers.

Have achieved at least Grade 4 in English Language or English Functional Skills Level 2, subject to programme-specific exceptions.

Applicants should also be ambitious and motivated to learn about the world of work and interested in gaining paid work experience that could support their future employment or university plans.

Additional Requirements for Business and Finance

The Smart Futures Business and Finance programme has additional academic requirements.

Applicants must have:

At least Grade 6 in GCSE Maths for London-based programmes.

At least Grade 5 in GCSE Maths for other locations.

Be on track to achieve 112 UCAS points from their top three A Levels or five Highers.

Have a strong interest in applying for a high-level or degree apprenticeship after school or college.

The EY Foundation also states that there is no GCSE English Language or English Functional Skills requirement for relevant North/Newcastle-based Smart Futures programmes for applicants living in Newcastle.

Does Your Subject of Study Matter?

For most Smart Futures programmes, applicants do not need to be studying business-related subjects.

The programme is designed to give young people exposure to different industries and transferable skills, meaning students from different academic backgrounds can apply if they meet the relevant eligibility requirements.

However, individual programmes such as Business and Finance can have additional qualification requirements, so applicants should always check the requirements for their chosen programme.

How to Apply

The current application process involves two main stages.

Step 1: Complete the Online Application

Applicants first need to register and complete a short online application form.

The EY Foundation recommends using a personal email address rather than a school email address where possible.

Applicants will select their preferred programme and location and provide information about their background and circumstances.

The Foundation states that most Smart Futures programmes do not depend on previous work experience, grades or qualifications beyond the specific eligibility requirements.

Step 2: Telephone Interview

Applicants who successfully progress from the initial application will be invited to a short telephone interview.

The interview can take up to 30 minutes.

Candidates may be asked about:

Their experiences

Their strengths

Their motivations

Their future aspirations

Examples from school or home life

The interview is intended to help the EY Foundation understand each applicant’s individual strengths and motivation for joining Smart Futures.

Application Deadline

There is no single overall deadline stated for all Smart Futures 2026/27 programmes on the current application page.

Instead, applications are listed according to individual programme dates and locations, with several 2026/27 programmes currently marked Open. Applicants should therefore check the specific programme they want to join and apply as early as possible.

How to Choose the Right Smart Futures Programme

Applicants should consider their career interests when selecting a programme.

For example:

Interested in technology and digital careers? Consider Tech Futures or Business & Technology.

Interested in banking and finance? Consider Banking & Finance.

Interested in accounting or consulting? Consider Business and Finance.

Interested in STEM careers? Consider STEM Futures.

Interested in investment? Consider Private Equity Futures.

Interested in property and urban development? Consider Real Estate Futures.

Interested in charities and social impact? Consider Impactful Futures.

Interested in data, mathematics and risk? Consider Data Driven Futures.

You do not necessarily need to have your entire career mapped out before applying. The programme is also designed to help young people explore different professional environments and develop transferable skills.

Evidence of Programme Impact

The EY Foundation reports that 96% of young people surveyed said they were extremely or very confident that the support they received would help them get a job after education.

The Foundation also reports that 99% of respondents rated Smart Futures as Good or Excellent after taking part. These figures were based on 284 respondents.

How to Apply for Smart Futures

Young people interested in the programme should review the available 2026/27 programme dates and locations and select a programme for which they meet the eligibility requirements.

The official EY Foundation application page contains the current programme schedule and application process.

Apply here:

EY Foundation Smart Futures – How to Apply

Conclusion

The EY Foundation Smart Futures programme provides eligible young people with an opportunity to gain paid work experience, develop workplace skills, receive professional mentoring and explore different career sectors.

With programmes covering areas such as technology, banking, finance, professional services, STEM, data, private equity, real estate, security and charity work, participants can choose an opportunity aligned with their interests while gaining practical exposure to the world of work.

The 2026/27 programme cycle is currently open, with different dates and locations available across the UK. Because individual programmes have different schedules and locations, prospective applicants should check the official application page carefully and submit an application for a suitable programme.

Discover more opportunities on the OFY Webpage.

TITLE: Call for EOIs: To support the development of Research Management Frameworks, Manuals & Procedures for SGCs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
CALL FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST: SUPPORT THE DEVELOPMENT OF RESEARCH MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORKS, MANUALS AND PROCEDURES FOR SGCs

About the SGCI

The Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI) is a multi-donor Initiative with Phase 2 (SGCI-2: 2020-2023) supported by Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC) and South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF).

The overall goal of the SGCI-2 Research Management project is to fortify the capability of Science Granting Councils in explicit areas of research management, namely research excellence (particularly the knowledge and use of tools such as Research Quality Plus framework), research ethics, emerging scientific practices (especially open data, open access and citizen science) Good Financial Grant Practice (GFGP) benchmarking exercise and development of online grant management systems (including databases of peer reviewers).

The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) are the consortium partners for the SGCI-2 Research Management project. Both AAU and AAS are two continental higher education and research bodies with experience in research management. AAU has participated in the SGCI-1 as part of the “Theme 3” Consortium. The SGCI-1 provided the AAU with invaluable experiences and lessons of working with and being part of activities taking place at the level of national science systems.

The SGCI-1 experiences and lessons learnt have been brought to bear on the SGCI-2 and are helping strengthen the capacity of Science Granting Councils to effectively and efficiently play their essential roles in research, knowledge and innovation

Why the focus on Research Management Frameworks for SGCs

Research management involves “all strategic, administrative and operational functions dealing with the management of research except conducting research itself”. It covers, inter alia, pre- and post-award management, research governance and planning, strategy and policy; research ethics and integrity, partnerships and collaboration; managing funded research; research data and information management; research uptake and utilization. It also covers development and delivery of research strategies and associated reporting and oversight.

As part of the SGCI Phase One project some manuals, procedures and frameworks were developed to guide quality research management processes within the SGCs. Some of these manuals, procedures and frameworks include the Good Practice Guidelines on the Quality of Research Competitions; Training Manual on Engagement with the Private Sector; STI Policy Handbook; Checklists for an MoU / a partnership agreement; and several others. These existing manuals, procedures and frameworks will further be reviewed and adapted by the SGCs. The existing manuals, procedures and frameworks will all be translated to French.

In addition, the manuals, procedures and frameworks will be developed in the areas of research excellence, research ethics, data and information management and digitization of management information systems for SGCs. Specifically, the following activities will be implemented in this work area:

Review and technical support towards the customization and adoption of existing research manuals, procedures and frameworks.

Needs analysis and development of new manuals, procedures and frameworks in the areas of research excellence, research ethics, data and information management and digitization of management information systems for SGCs.

Peer review, publication and dissemination of the new manuals, procedures and frameworks.

In the Development of frameworks, manuals and procedures, the frameworks, manuals and procedures developed under SGCI-1 would be reviewed and new ones developed – e.g. the Good Practice Guidelines on the Quality of Research Competitions developed by SARIMA; a participatory process will be used to prioritize the frameworks, manuals and procedures that require development; and a participatory process will be used to develop the agreed frameworks, manuals and procedures – e.g. a framework for monitoring research ethics. This action will lead to the development of frameworks – e.g. framework for monitoring research ethics adherence; development of Manuals – e.g. how to use the RQ+ framework; and to the development of Procedures – How to lead a digitization project in a Science Granting Council.

The Call for request for proposals to support the development of research management frameworks, manuals and procedures for the SGCs

The AAU is therefore calling on consultants / resources persons to formally express interest in undertaking the assignment of supporting the development of research management frameworks, manuals and procedures for the SGCs.

The Consultant / resource person should have an understanding of current international and pan-African challenges in research management and knowledge of the current research landscape in Africa. Should have a broad understanding of national funding systems and an understanding of research management as both a strategic and administrative function.

How to submit the Expression of Interest

Consultants / resource persons are requested to submit their interests by completing the online form via this link: [https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/JBTM6HG]

Deadlines

The deadline for submission of the expressions of interest is close of business on Thursday, 15th October 2020.

TITLE: Mascarene High Variability Shapes the Demography of a Wind-Reliant Marine Top Predator

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Sun, R., Rouby, E., Barbraud, C., Weimerskirch, H., Delord, K., Krumhardt, K., Ventura, F., Ummenhofer, C. C., & Jenouvrier, S. (2026). Mascarene High Variability Shapes the Demography of a Wind-Reliant Marine Top Predator. Geophysical Research Letters, 53(11), e2026GL122317. https://doi.org/10.1029/2026GL122317

Subtropical anticyclones are semi‐permanent atmospheric high‐pressure systems located in all five major ocean basins and are associated with large‐scale wind and weather patterns. They shape the physical environments of many species, yet their impacts on wildlife remain unexplored. We combined population and climate analyses to investigate the demographic effects of the Mascarene High, the Southern Indian Ocean subtropical anticyclone, on a wind‐reliant marine top predator. Using 39 years of population data for wandering albatrosses (Diomedea exulans) breeding in the Southern Indian Ocean, we explored the mechanisms linking variability in the subtropical anticyclone to demographic rates. We found that an intensified and poleward-shifted Mascarene High toward Antarctica enhances westerly winds, increasing survival and reproduction probability across all life stages of wandering albatrosses. These findings uncover a direct link between subtropical anticyclones and population dynamics, highlighting subtropical anticyclones as important drivers of the responses of wind‐reliant taxa to climate variability and change.

Mechanisms linking Mascarene High variability to demographic rates of wandering albatross. Schematic illustrating how changes in the intensity and position of the Mascarene High affect wind conditions for wandering albatrosses breeding on Crozet. A stronger, poleward‐shifted Mascarene High enhances westerly winds, creating favorable conditions that improve albatross survival and reproduction. Figure from Sun et al. (2026).

TITLE: How do marine animals hear?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
If you’ve ever plunged your head underwater and listened, you’ll know that sounds are muffled. But why? The reason is that your ears are adapted to hear in air, not water. Many marine animals do hear well underwater. For whales, crabs, and corals, detecting the sounds around them is a matter of survival.

Sound radiates through air or water in waves, like ripples on a pond. But it travels much more efficiently in water. It also travels faster, in part because water is denser than air. As the ocean gets deeper, the pressure increases water’s density, causing sound to travel even faster. In the ocean, variations in pressure can bend sound and make it hard to determine its source.

A humpback whale surfacing to breathe between bouts of song off Maui, Hawaii. This song contains high levels of acoustic particle motion, the vibratory component of sound, which may be used in both communication and hearing. (Photo by T. Aran Mooney, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution/NMFS permit #: 1468)

Whales are experts at detecting and deciphering sound in the ocean. They use sound for socializing, breeding, navigation, and feeding. The two main types of whales-baleen whales and toothed whales-use sound differently.

Baleen whales include humpback whales and blue whales. They communicate by making low-frequency sounds called songs, which can travel long distances.

Toothed whales, such as sperm whales and dolphins (known as odontocetes), have hearing that’s tuned to high-frequency sounds. They echolocate like bats, producing high-pitched clicks that bounce off elements in their environment. These echoes help them discern fish and other items in their surroundings.

Whales and dolphins (collectively known as cetaceans) have ears that are similar to ours, but with key differences. Humans have fleshy outer ears (called pinna) for capturing sounds, whereas cetaceans do not. Instead, dolphins have pads of fat along their lower jaws that collect sounds. These vibrations then travel into the labyrinth of the middle and inner ear to the cochlea, a snail-shaped organ that also exists in humans.

This organ transforms sound waves into electrical signals for the brain to process. Unlike humans, a dolphin’s cochlea contains far more nerve cells, reflecting the dolphin’s ability to process complex auditory signals. This allows odontocetes to hear much higher frequencies in the water. The cochlea of baleen whales, on the other hand, is more sensitive to low-frequency sounds.

Biologists at WHOI understand the importance of sound in the marine environment and are studying how it can be used as a remediation tool for critical ecosystems such as coral reefs. Here, MIT-WHOI student Nadége Aoki installs a hydrophone on a reef in the U.S. Virgin Islands to record the local soundscape. (Photo by Austin Greene, © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Corals, the animals that form the foundation of coral reefs, can also hear. These sessile animals reproduce by spawning, releasing sperm and eggs into the water, which mix to create larvae. A free-floating coral larva, roughly the size of a grain of sand, uses sound to select a spot where it will settle and spend its adult life. The larva is covered with microscopic, sound-sensitive hairs. A healthy reef is alive with the grunting and chirping of fish and the crackling of snapping shrimp. A damaged or dying reef is much quieter. Coral larvae can hear the difference. They are attracted to the sound of a healthy reef.

Crustaceans, like crabs and lobsters detect sound using thousands of microscopic hairs, called setae, which line their bodies. They also use internal fluid-filled sacs called statocysts, and stretch receptors located in the joints of their legs and antennae.

Like corals, crustaceans use sound to select a home. Some species live in coral reefs. Others avoid reefs, possibly to steer clear of predators. Sound helps guide these animals to a suitable home, either toward a reef or safely away.

TITLE: Giving Joy Grant 2026: Apply for Up to $500 to Launch or Expand a Women-Focused Business or Community Project Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Women entrepreneurs, aspiring business owners, nonprofit founders, and community changemakers around the world can now apply for the Giving Joy Grant 2026. The initiative provides microgrants of up to $500 USD to support innovative ideas that create meaningful economic and social benefits for women, girls, families, and communities.

Giving Joy receives thousands of applications during each grant cycle, making the program highly competitive. However, the organization emphasizes that applicants do not need polished proposals or sophisticated business plans to stand out. Instead, successful applications are expected to demonstrate practical ideas, creativity, initiative, feasibility, and a clear potential for community impact.

Beginning in 2026, Giving Joy has introduced a simplified global grant model with two grant cycles per year. Unlike previous regional rounds, each cycle is now open to eligible women entrepreneurs and changemakers from anywhere in the world.

The Fall 2026 Giving Joy Microgrant Round opened on September 1, 2026, offering women globally an opportunity to secure funding to start or expand businesses, nonprofit organizations, NGOs, charities, projects, and other initiatives focused on improving the lives of women, girls, families, and communities.

About the Giving Joy Grant

Giving Joy is an organization committed to supporting women entrepreneurs and empowering women to transform innovative ideas into initiatives that generate meaningful social and economic impact.

The Giving Joy Grant provides financial support to women who have practical and creative ideas but may lack the resources needed to take the next step. The funding can support a wide range of initiatives, provided they are legal and demonstrate benefits beyond individual financial gain.

Applicants are encouraged to think broadly about how their ideas can contribute to positive change. A proposal may involve launching a new business, expanding an existing enterprise, establishing a nonprofit organization, implementing a community project, delivering skills training, or developing an innovative initiative that benefits women and families.

The program is particularly interested in projects that create multiplied impact. This means that successful proposals should demonstrate how a relatively small amount of funding can create benefits that extend beyond the applicant herself.

For example, a woman may use the grant to organize skills training for unemployed women, establish a community-based initiative that creates income opportunities, conduct educational workshops, or develop a project that improves access to knowledge, leadership opportunities, safety, or economic independence.

Giving Joy Grant 2026 Funding Amount

Successful applicants may receive grants of up to $500 USD.

The exact amount awarded may be determined by Giving Joy based on several factors, including:

The proposed activities.

The applicant’s project budget.

The feasibility of the proposal.

The potential social and economic impact.

The availability of funding.

How effectively the proposed grant amount will support the initiative.

Applicants should therefore provide a clear and realistic explanation of how they intend to use the requested funding.

A strong application should not simply state that the applicant needs money for a business or project. Instead, applicants should clearly demonstrate exactly how the funding will be spent and what outcomes are expected.

For instance, applicants may need to explain:

What materials they intend to purchase.

What activities they plan to organize.

Who will participate.

How many people are expected to benefit.

What the estimated costs will be.

How the grant will contribute to long-term impact.

2026 Giving Joy Grant Cycle

Beginning in 2026, Giving Joy has moved to a new grant structure consisting of two global grant cycles each year.

The organization previously conducted multiple regional grant rounds. However, after reviewing feedback from applicants and volunteer reviewers, Giving Joy determined that operating four cycles created unnecessary administrative complexity.

The new approach is designed to create a simpler, more transparent, and more effective application process.

According to the organization, the new structure will help:

Provide clearer timelines for applicants.

Improve the quality and depth of application reviews.

Reduce administrative burdens.

Allow the organization to provide better support to grant recipients.

Improve communication and fundraising efforts.

Ensure women entrepreneurs from all regions have access to the same global application opportunities.

Most importantly, each cycle is open to eligible women entrepreneurs and changemakers worldwide without dividing applicants into regional categories.

Giving Joy Grant 2026 Timeline

Cycle 1 – Spring 2026

The first Giving Joy Grant Cycle for 2026 has already closed.

The timeline was as follows:

Applications opened: April 1, 2026.

Application deadline: April 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST.

Awards announced: August 2026.

The Spring 2026 round attracted significant global interest, receiving 6,423 applications from women entrepreneurs around the world.

Despite the extremely competitive application pool, Giving Joy awarded 10 microgrants during the cycle.

This demonstrates both the global popularity of the program and the importance of submitting a clear, specific, and impactful application.

Cycle 2 – Fall 2026 Giving Joy Microgrant Round

The second and current Giving Joy Grant Cycle for 2026 opened in September.

The Fall 2026 Microgrant Round follows the schedule below:

Applications open: September 1, 2026.

Application deadline: September 30, 2026.

Review period: October 1 to November 30, 2026.

Shortlisted applicants notified: During the review period.

Unsuccessful application notification: Applicants who have not heard from Giving Joy by December 1 should consider their applications unsuccessful.

Awards announced: Beginning of December 2026.

Giving Joy Grant 2026 Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Fall 2026 Giving Joy Microgrant Round is:

September 30, 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their applications. Given the high number of applications received during each grant cycle, it is important to carefully complete all sections of the online application form and ensure that the proposed project is clearly explained.

Who Can Apply for the Giving Joy Grant?

The Giving Joy Grant is designed to support women aged 18 years and above.

One of the major strengths of the program is its global accessibility. Applicants are not restricted to specific countries, regions, continents, or territories.

Eligible women can apply from anywhere in the world.

Applicants may include women who want to:

Start a new business.

Expand an existing business.

Launch a nonprofit organization.

Develop an NGO initiative.

Establish a charity project.

Implement a community-based initiative.

Organize a training program.

Create employment opportunities.

Develop an innovative social enterprise.

Implement a specific activity benefiting women or families.

Applicants do not necessarily need to own an existing business before applying.

This means that women with innovative ideas who are still at the planning stage can also submit applications.

What Types of Projects Can Be Funded?

Giving Joy does not limit applications to a specific industry, professional sector, trade, occupation, or craft.

Applicants can propose projects from a wide range of fields.

However, the proposed business, organization, project, or initiative should demonstrate clear benefits for women, girls, families, or communities.

Potential areas may include:

Women’s entrepreneurship.

Skills development.

Vocational training.

Community development.

Education.

Social enterprises.

Employment creation.

Women’s leadership.

Economic empowerment.

Legal awareness.

Community workshops.

Professional training.

Creative enterprises.

Agriculture.

Technology initiatives.

Crafts and trades.

Environmental projects.

Family support initiatives.

All proposed activities must be legal.

Giving Joy is particularly interested in projects that create opportunities beyond the applicant’s individual financial interests.

For example, a business that creates employment or training opportunities for other women may demonstrate stronger community impact than a proposal focused solely on personal income.

What Giving Joy Looks for in Grant Applications

Giving Joy evaluates applications based on several important criteria.

Applicants should carefully consider these factors when developing their proposals.

1. Alignment With Giving Joy’s Mission

The proposed initiative should support the broader mission of empowering and inspiring women.

Projects should ideally contribute to areas such as:

Women’s leadership.

Economic independence.

Dignity.

Opportunity creation.

Entrepreneurship.

Community empowerment.

Applicants should demonstrate how their idea contributes to positive outcomes for women and their communities.

2. Social and Economic Impact

Giving Joy places significant emphasis on projects that can create meaningful benefits.

A strong application should explain how the proposed activities will positively affect:

Women.

Girls.

Families.

Communities.

Applicants should clearly identify the people who will benefit and explain the expected outcomes.

For example, rather than simply stating that a project will empower women, applicants should provide specific details about what empowerment will look like in practice.

This could include:

Training 20 women in a professional skill.

Creating income opportunities for mothers.

Providing educational workshops.

Supporting women to understand their legal rights.

Establishing a community enterprise.

Creating employment opportunities.

Developing leadership programs.

Specific and measurable impact is generally more compelling than broad statements.

3. Innovation and Creativity

Giving Joy prioritizes creative and innovative ideas.

Applicants are encouraged to propose approaches that address genuine challenges faced by women and communities.

Innovation does not necessarily mean using advanced technology or creating something that has never existed before.

Instead, applicants can demonstrate innovation by:

Developing a creative solution to a local problem.

Combining existing approaches in a new way.

Creating a practical community-based model.

Identifying an overlooked challenge.

Designing an initiative with multiplied benefits.

The key is to demonstrate initiative and thoughtful problem-solving.

4. Effective Use of the $500 Grant

Applicants must explain how the grant funds will be used.

Giving Joy expects applicants to provide a practical and specific budget.

A strong budget should identify:

The materials or resources required.

Estimated costs.

Planned activities.

Expected outputs.

Number of beneficiaries.

Applicants should avoid vague statements such as “the money will help grow my business.”

Instead, they should provide concrete information.

For example:

Purchase training materials for a vocational workshop.

Rent a venue for community training sessions.

Purchase equipment necessary to provide a service.

Develop educational resources.

Support the implementation of a specific community activity.

The proposed use of funds should be realistic within the $500 funding limit.

5. Clarity and Feasibility

The application should be easy to understand.

Applicants do not need to use complicated language or highly polished writing.

Giving Joy specifically emphasizes that practical ideas and real community impact are more important than sophisticated writing.

However, the application should clearly explain:

What the applicant intends to do.

Why the project is needed.

Who will benefit.

How the grant will be used.

What outcomes are expected.

The proposal should also be realistic and achievable within the six-month grant period.

How to Write a Strong Giving Joy Grant Application

Given the high number of applications received during each grant cycle, applicants should take time to develop clear responses.

Here are some important strategies for preparing a competitive application.

Be Specific About Your Project

Avoid general statements.

Clearly explain what you plan to do and how you intend to implement the activities.

For example, instead of saying:

” I want to empower women through training.”

Explain:

” I plan to organize a practical skills training program for 15 unemployed women in my community, focusing on a specific skill that can help participants generate income.”

Specific proposals help reviewers understand the project and evaluate its feasibility.

Clearly Identify the Beneficiaries

Explain exactly who will benefit from the project.

Consider questions such as:

Are the beneficiaries unemployed women?

Young women?

Mothers?

Girls?

Rural communities?

Women entrepreneurs?

Families facing economic challenges?

Also explain approximately how many people will benefit.

Demonstrate Community Impact

Giving Joy is interested in projects that create benefits beyond personal business growth.

Applicants should explain how the initiative can generate wider social or economic impact.

For example, an applicant might propose:

Training 10 women in construction skills.

Providing legal education workshops for 20 women.

Establishing a community initiative that creates income opportunities.

Creating skills programs that enable participants to support their families.

The stronger the explanation of multiplied impact, the stronger the proposal may be.

Develop a Clear Budget

Applicants should show exactly how they plan to spend the funding.

A simple budget may include:

Equipment or materials.

Training resources.

Venue costs.

Transportation directly related to project activities.

Implementation costs.

Every expense should connect directly to the proposed project.

Focus on Practical Impact

Giving Joy values real-world outcomes.

Applicants should therefore focus on practical questions such as:

What problem does the project solve?

Who experiences the problem?

What activities will address it?

What changes will happen after implementation?

How many people will benefit?

A proposal that clearly answers these questions will be easier for reviewers to evaluate.

Activities Giving Joy Does Not Primarily Fund

Applicants should carefully review the restrictions before submitting their applications.

Giving Joy indicates that it does not primarily fund activities focused mainly on:

Purchasing merchandise or inventory for resale.

Advertising.

Marketing activities.

Personal expenses that are not connected to broader community impact.

This does not mean applicants cannot propose business-related ideas.

However, the proposal should demonstrate that the funding will contribute to wider economic or social benefits rather than simply supporting individual commercial activities.

Applicants should therefore carefully explain the community value of their projects.

Grant Duration

Successful applicants will have up to six months to implement their proposed projects.

The six-month grant period gives recipients time to organize activities, use the awarded funds, and deliver the proposed outcomes.

Applicants should therefore develop projects that can realistically be implemented within this timeframe.

When planning an application, it may be helpful to create a simple implementation schedule covering:

Project preparation.

Purchase of necessary materials.

Participant identification.

Activity implementation.

Community engagement.

Monitoring of outcomes.

Completion of project deliverables.

A realistic implementation plan can demonstrate that the applicant has carefully considered how the project will move from idea to execution.

Can Applicants Apply in Languages Other Than English?

Yes.

Giving Joy accepts applications in any language that can be translated using Google Translate.

This significantly improves accessibility for women entrepreneurs and changemakers from different linguistic backgrounds.

Applicants should still ensure that their responses are clear and understandable.

Simple and direct language may be particularly useful because the organization emphasizes that clear, practical ideas are more important than polished writing.

How Does the Giving Joy Application Process Work?

The Giving Joy application process involves several stages.

Step 1: Submit the Online Application

Applications must be submitted online through the official application platform.

Giving Joy does not accept proposals or funding requests submitted through email.

Applicants must therefore use the designated online application form.

Step 2: Application Compliance Review

After submission, Giving Joy reviews applications to ensure they meet the basic requirements.

The organization may contact applicants if additional information or clarification is needed.

Applicants may also be asked to provide supporting information, including photos of themselves or their businesses or organizations.

Step 3: Application Evaluation

Giving Joy staff evaluate eligible applications based on criteria such as:

Alignment with the organization’s mission.

Innovative use of grant funding.

Social and economic impact.

Community benefits.

Feasibility.

Clarity of the proposed activities.

Step 4: Shortlisting

Based on the evaluation process, Giving Joy may shortlist approximately 10 applications per grant round.

Due to the large number of applications received, the organization only contacts shortlisted applicants.

Step 5: Final Evaluation

Giving Joy Board Members evaluate shortlisted applicants using similar assessment criteria.

Board members may contact applicants to request additional information or clarification.

Step 6: Grant Notification

Successful applicants are notified individually via email.

If an applicant does not receive communication from Giving Joy within the stated notification period, the application should be considered unsuccessful.

For the Fall 2026 cycle, applicants who have not heard from Giving Joy by December 1, 2026, should consider their applications unsuccessful.

Step 7: Grant Agreement and Project Implementation

Successful applicants will participate in discussions with Giving Joy regarding:

Grant terms and conditions.

Project deliverables.

Implementation guidelines.

Grant agreement requirements.

Once the grant agreement is signed, recipients will have up to six months to implement their proposed projects.

Can You Apply More Than Once?

Applicants can only submit one application per grant cycle.

Women who are unsuccessful may apply again during future grant cycles.

However, applicants who have already received a Giving Joy grant cannot apply again.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they submit their strongest possible proposal during each application cycle.

What Happens if You Win the Giving Joy Grant?

Successful applicants may receive funding of up to $500 USD.

The award amount will depend on:

The proposed activities.

The project’s financial requirements.

The availability of funding.

Giving Joy’s funding decision.

Successful grantees will also receive guidance regarding grant implementation requirements.

Recipients will need to review and sign a grant agreement before beginning implementation.

The organization will then expect grantees to implement their proposed activities within the designated six-month period.

Why the Giving Joy Grant Is a Valuable Opportunity

The Giving Joy Grant is particularly valuable because it provides accessible microfunding to women with ideas that may otherwise struggle to secure traditional investment or large grants.

Many funding opportunities require applicants to have established organizations, extensive financial records, or complex proposals.

Giving Joy offers a different approach by emphasizing initiative, creativity, practical planning, and community impact.

Key advantages of the program include:

Funding of up to $500 USD.

Open to women worldwide.

Applicants do not need to own an existing business.

Supports businesses, nonprofits, NGOs, charities, and community projects.

No restriction to a specific professional field.

Applications accepted in multiple languages.

Focus on innovative and creative ideas.

Six months available for project implementation.

Opportunity to create social and economic impact.

Accessible online application process.

Although the funding amount is relatively modest, the program recognizes that small amounts of capital can create significant change when used strategically.

Important Tips Before Applying

Before submitting your Giving Joy Grant application, consider the following checklist:

Confirm that you are eligible to apply.

Ensure you are applying only once during the current cycle.

Complete every section of the application form.

Clearly explain your proposed project.

Identify the women, girls, families, or communities who will benefit.

Explain the social and economic impact.

Provide a realistic budget.

Show exactly how the grant funds will be used.

Demonstrate creativity and initiative.

Ensure your project is legal.

Avoid proposals focused primarily on inventory resale, advertising, marketing, or unrelated personal expenses.

Ensure your project can be implemented within six months.

Submit your application before the deadline.

Keep your project description practical and easy to understand.

APPLY HERE

How to Apply for the Giving Joy Grant 2026

Interested applicants must submit their applications online through the official Giving Joy Microgrant application form.

Email applications and funding proposals are not accepted.

Applicants should carefully review the application questions and provide complete, specific, and practical answers.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Giving Joy Grant 2026.

Conclusion

The Giving Joy Grant 2026 presents an important funding opportunity for women entrepreneurs, aspiring business owners, nonprofit founders, and community changemakers who have innovative ideas capable of creating meaningful social or economic impact.

With grants of up to $500 USD, the program supports initiatives that go beyond individual financial growth and demonstrate clear benefits for women, girls, families, and communities. The opportunity is particularly accessible because applicants do not need to own an existing business, proposals can come from any legal field, and women from countries around the world are eligible to apply.

However, competition is expected to be intense. Giving Joy receives thousands of applications during each grant cycle and awards only a limited number of microgrants. Applicants should therefore focus on presenting a clear, specific, creative, and practical project with measurable community benefits.

For the Fall 2026 cycle, eligible applicants should submit their online applications by September 30, 2026, and ensure that their proposals clearly demonstrate how the funding will create meaningful and lasting impact.

TITLE: Register now for the Introduction to Circular Economy course

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Course Name: Introduction To Circular Economy

Duration: 6 weeks

Target group:

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

Today, economic growth is primarily contingent on increased resource consumption. In this linear economic approach, organizations harvest or extract materials, use them to create products and then sell those products to consumers who generally incinerate or send to landfills the materials that no longer serve their original purpose. As the population grows and the negative environmental impact of resource extraction continues, this “take, make, waste” model is quickly reaching its limits. The circular economy, by contrast, is one that is “restorative and regenerative by design, and aims to keep products, components, and materials at their highest utility and value at all times” (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2013). The circular economy philosophy is an emerging field of study, promoting a systemic, cross-disciplinary approach. This course explores how these various disciplines come together to promote a sustainable economic model.
