TITLE: Finland-Africa Platform for Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Innovation) convenes key stakeholders to deliberate on practical steps towards the achievement of SDG9 –  AAU Participates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Over 100 participants from Finish Universities and Ministries, Universities and Private Sector stakeholders from 15 African Countries, UN Agencies and Business Organisations in Finland gathered at the University of Turku, Finland from August 26 -27, 2019 to deliberate on the effective implementation and functioning of the Finland – Africa Platform for Sustainable Development Goal 9 (innovation). The meeting sought to come up with practical steps on how the parties involved can strategically work together towards the achievement of this SDG before the end of 2030.

The platform is an initiative of the University of Turku and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. An MoU signed between the two parties assigned the University of Turku the role of acting as the node and platform for supporting and advancing SDG9 of the United Nations in Africa, through research, education and capacity building in innovation.

The two-day event featured high level panel discussions, and over 20 plenary and parallel session presentations to showcase potential projects and existing initiatives which can be boosted or adopted to contribute to enhancement of the economic, scientific and technological transformation of Africa.

One key presentation at this seminar was the presentation by the Association of the African Universities, which was made by the Communications and Publications Officers, Mrs. Felicia Kuagbedzi. AAU’s presentation titled ‘North-South Partnership of the AAU and the potential role of Finland’ focused on introducing the Association to the over 100 participants, discussing the current programmes being implemented by the Association, key partners of the Association, challenges faced by African Universities and where Finland can partner with the association in dealing with these issues towards the achievement of SDG9. Aside the AAU, other African Institutions that made presentations at the event included the Next Einstein Forum (Rwanda), the University of Cape-Coast (Ghana), the Scinnovent Center (Kenya) and Sahara Ventures (Tanzania) among others.

The seminar was presided over by Li Anderson, Minister of Education for Finland and Jukka Kola, Rector of the University of Turku, Finland. Also in attendance was the Ambassador for Innovation in Finland and representatives from various ministries.

At the end of the two-day deliberations, participants recommended that SDG 9 (Innovation, industralisation and infrastructure and their relationship with research and education) be recognized as Finland’s competitive advantage and area which the country can focus on to create significant impact in Africa. Participants unanimously acknowledged that Africa is the continent of the future and Finland had the potential to contribute to the continent, especially towards the attainment of SDG9. Participants also appreciated the inter-ministerial involvement (Ministries of Education, Science and Culture, Foreign Affairs and Development Cooperation) in the takeoff of the platform and called for their continuous support to the platform as well as facilitate the synergy around SDG9 towards Africa. This includes aligning the vision and mission of the platform to their respective ministerial and national Africa Strategy, facilitating its functioning and funding.

Participants also thanked the delegation from the United Nations Economic Commission for their leadership and commitment through the Partnership agreement with the University of Turku.

TITLE: 30 Interns Undergo Practical Training at AAU

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), the voice of higher education in Africa, has opened its doors to thirty students from various universities in Ghana to undergo a three-month internship programme at its Secretariat, located in Accra, Ghana.

The students, who are currently on vacation, started their practical training through the flagship programme; Graduate Industrial Training and Placement (GITP) under the Youth and Students Affairs. The thirty (30) interns who went through a rigorous interview and selection process begun their training on Thursday, June 6, 2019 and will end it in August 2019.

The key tasks of the interns are among others, to develop a database of research problems dubbed the “African Research Bank” and website for the African Universities Olympics. The African Research Bank will house research needs and problems from industries and key sectors. Its goal is to provide students and researchers with critical research topics, that can help solve practical industrial and societal needs when investigated.

The target of the assignment related to the African Universities Olympics, is to develop a website, market and increase the number of participating institutions at the next event, taking place in August 2020.

Speaking at the orientation programme, Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of Knowledge Management and ICT Services, and Dr. Violet Makuku, Quality Assurance Specialist emphasized that “Africa is going to be driven by the youth and women” and therefore charged the interns to take the opportunity given them seriously, and give off their utmost best.

She encouraged the interns to network and work in a unified team to achieve set objectives at the end of the three months training.

The interns are being supervised by staff from the Directorate of Research and Academic Planning; Mr. Kwesi Acquah Sam (Team Lead) and Mr. Schenineda Kwaku Ankomah, as well as staff from the Directorate of ICT Services, Communications and Knowledge Management; Mr. Frank Asefuah, Mrs. Felicia Kuagbedzi, Miss Georgina Diana Maison and Mr. Enoch Kpani.

As part of the orientation, the interns were each given a book titled, “Empowering Dreamers to Become Achievers” and encouraged to read it daily, ahead of each day’s tasks. This book, authored by Ramsey Jay Jr, a Wall Street trained Finance Executive is targeted at helping young people to develop an optimistic mindset to achieve more and reach their full potentials.

About the AAU

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the Voice of Higher Education in Africa, created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. AAU aims to improve the quality of African Higher Education and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher educational Institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting African higher education. It was founded in 1967 and currently has over 400 member Universities across Africa.

Communications Intern

Applications are open for the Atlantic Fellows for Equity in Brain Health Program 2027-2028. Join a global community of more than 300 Atlantic Fellows from over 65 countries worldwide, dedicated to protecting the world’s aging populations from threats to brain health.

The Atlantic Fellows for Equity in Brain Health program at the Global Brain Health Institute (GBHI) provides innovative training, networking, and support to emerging leaders focused on improving brain health and reducing the impact of dementia in their local communities and on a global scale. It is one of seven global Atlantic Fellows programs to promote societies that expand opportunity, improve health, and foster belonging.

Fellowship Sites

Atlantic Fellows for Equity in Brain Health complete their fellowship year at one of two sites: University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) or Trinity. Both sites share a commitment to advancing equity in brain health and follow a common program structure while drawing on their unique institutional and regional strengths.

Fellows at UCSF complete a part-time, global hybrid fellowship that blends weekly online learning with international in-person sessions and optional visits to San Francisco. Fellows at Trinity complete a full-time, in-person fellowship based in Dublin.

Career Development and Pilot funding: Throughout the program and beyond fellows will receive career mentorship from faculty at GBHI and in their local community. Mentors will help fellows to realize their goals and be transformative and will assist them in applying for competitive pilot awards of up to $25,000 to begin an ambitious project in their home community.

Lifelong Fellowship: Becoming an Atlantic Fellow for Equity in Brain Health doesn’t end upon completion of the program. The inter professional and interdisciplinary nature of the program encourages collaborations across sectors and each fellow contributes greatly to the cohort through sharing their experience and expertise.

Applications are open for the U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027-2029. The Junior Fellowship program is a highly selective, fixed two-year program for new college graduates to work shaping international economic policy for the United States in Treasury’s Office of International Affairs. Fellows have left the program to pursue a range of opportunities, including employment at Treasury and elsewhere in the U.S. government, work in the private sector, and graduate study (e.g., law, public policy, international relations, and finance and business).

Junior Fellows have exposure to multiple policy issues and opportunities to enhance their knowledge and skills. They typically perform a variety of tasks that include developing policy proposals, analyzing international economic and financial developments, and conducting analytical studies. Fellows also support bilateral and multilateral meetings for senior Treasury officials engaging counterparts at the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20 – to name a few. Junior Fellows often participate in such meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad.

Junior fellows will be placed in either a regional or functional office. Regional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries across the world. Functional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with international financial institutions and structure broader Treasury policy on issues ranging from international trade to export credits, to foreign exchange.

Benefits

Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits.

Eligibility

Applicants must be U.S. citizens.

Strong candidates will have recently received – or will soon receive – a bachelor’s degree with relevant coursework in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields.

Note that due to the structure of the program, preference is given to undergraduates.

Application

In the email, candidates must also:

indicate a desired start date;

confirm they hold U.S. citizenship (must be able to provide documentation);

note veterans’ preference, if applicable; and

include a resume that demonstrates 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience relevant to the duties described above.

TITLE: Sustainable Research Pathways 2026–2027: U.S. Research Collaboration and Paid Summer Experience Opportunities for Students, Faculty and Project Leaders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Sustainable Research Pathways (SRP) 2026–2027 program is inviting applications from eligible students, faculty members, principal investigators, and project leaders across the United States and its territories for a research collaboration and professional development opportunity designed to connect emerging researchers with established scientific projects.

The program provides a structured environment for participants to build research collaborations, explore career opportunities, develop professional networks, and potentially participate in a 10-week paid summer research experience in 2027. Through workshops, mentoring, cohort activities, and research engagement, SRP aims to help students and faculty connect with projects led by researchers working with U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories and the National Science Foundation (NSF) National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) pilot, among other participating projects.

Applications for the 2026–2027 cycle are currently open, with applications for principal investigators/project leaders, faculty, and students due September 30, 2026.

What Is the Sustainable Research Pathways Program?

Sustainable Research Pathways is a comprehensive research collaboration program created to connect U.S.-based researchers and project leaders with students and faculty from academic institutions throughout the United States and its territories.

The program is designed around the idea that meaningful research collaborations can help students launch scientific and technical careers while also giving researchers and faculty access to new talent, perspectives, and collaborative possibilities.

Rather than functioning solely as a traditional internship or academic placement, SRP provides opportunities for participants to meet potential collaborators, explore research projects, participate in professional community-building activities, and potentially continue their engagement through a summer research experience.

The 2026–2027 program brings together several tracks, allowing participation from different groups within the research ecosystem.

History and Development of Sustainable Research Pathways

Sustainable Research Pathways was initially established in 2015 through a partnership with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL).

Since its creation, the program has expanded considerably.

In 2022, SRP developed into a multi-laboratory program through the U.S. Department of Energy’s Exascale Computing Project (ECP).

In 2023, the program expanded beyond ECP projects to include additional computational and data science projects. These activities were coordinated through the Computational Research Leadership Council (CRLC).

The program has continued to receive support from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research through the Partnering for Scientific-Software Ecosystem Opportunities (PESO) project and the Consortium for the Advancement of Scientific Software (CASS).

In 2025, SRP expanded further by incorporating projects associated with the National Science Foundation’s National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) pilot and the High Performance Software Foundation (HPSF).

The 2026–2027 cycle therefore represents a broader research collaboration environment involving students, faculty, project leaders, and projects connected with major U.S. scientific and computational research initiatives.

SRP 2026–2027 Project, PI and Mentor Track

The Project/PI/Mentor Track is intended for principal investigators and project leaders who have active projects funded through eligible NAIRR Pilot or U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories Computing Sciences programs.

Researchers and project leaders participating in this track can potentially be matched with students and faculty interested in contributing to research projects.

For participating project leaders, the program provides an opportunity to:

Connect with exceptional students and faculty.

Explore potential research collaborations.

Introduce students to active scientific and computational projects.

Build longer-term academic and professional relationships.

Participate in the SRP Matching and Exploratory Workshop.

Identify potential collaborators for summer research activities.

If a successful match is established, project leaders may have the opportunity to work collaboratively with selected faculty members and students.

Faculty Track

The Faculty Track is designed for full-time faculty members who are interested in leading student teams and potentially collaborating with projects connected to NAIRR and DOE National Laboratories.

Faculty members working with students from different academic institutions are particularly encouraged to participate.

This track can provide faculty with a structured mechanism for connecting their students to broader research projects and professional communities.

Faculty participants may have the opportunity to:

Lead student teams.

Connect students with research project leaders.

Explore collaborations with NAIRR-related projects.

Explore collaborations with DOE National Laboratories projects.

Participate in the November 2026 Matching Workshop.

Build relationships with researchers and other faculty members.

Support students as they explore research and career pathways.

The cross-institutional nature of the program also provides an opportunity for faculty and students from different academic environments to engage with one another.

Student Track

The Student Track is intended for eligible students who are studying at accredited U.S. academic institutions and who are not applying as part of an SRP faculty team.

The program specifically identifies the following student groups as eligible to apply:

Community college students.

Undergraduate students.

Graduate students.

Students can apply independently rather than having to participate through an SRP faculty team.

For students interested in research, computational science, data science, artificial intelligence, scientific software, or related areas, the program provides an opportunity to explore potential research collaborations and develop professional relationships with researchers and faculty.

Potential 10-Week Summer Research Experience

One of the significant opportunities associated with SRP is the potential for matched faculty and students to participate in a 10-week onsite summer experience in 2027.

Participants who are successfully matched with project leaders may have the opportunity to spend the summer working on research activities connected to their selected project.

The experience is described as potentially paid, meaning eligible participants may have access to a paid summer research opportunity depending on the specific match and arrangements.

The summer experience is expected to provide participants with exposure to real research environments while allowing them to work with project leaders and other members of the research community.

Matching and Exploratory Workshop

A central component of SRP is the Matching and Exploratory Workshop, scheduled for November 3–6, 2026.

The workshop is designed to give project leaders, faculty, and students an opportunity to meet, communicate, discuss research interests, and explore possible collaborations.

Rather than participants being matched without interaction, the workshop creates a dedicated environment where individuals can learn more about available research projects and potential collaborators.

The workshop can therefore play an important role in helping participants determine whether their research interests and skills align with particular projects.

SRP Program Benefits

The Sustainable Research Pathways program offers several activities and potential benefits throughout the 2026–2027 cycle.

1. Pre-Workshop Q&A Webinar

Participants will have access to a Q&A webinar before the main matching workshop.

This provides an opportunity for prospective participants to better understand the program and ask questions about participation.

2. Matching and Exploratory Workshop

The interactive workshop gives participants an opportunity to meet researchers, faculty members, project leaders, and students and discuss potential collaborations.

3. Potential Paid Summer Experience

Students and faculty who are successfully matched with project leaders may have the opportunity to participate in a 10-week onsite summer experience in 2027.

The summer experience may be paid, providing participants with both research exposure and potential financial support for their summer participation.

4. Professional Community Onboarding

SRP includes onboarding into a professional community, helping participants become familiar with the broader network associated with the program.

This can help participants establish relationships beyond their immediate academic institution.

5. Summer Kick-Off Event

The program includes a summer kick-off event intended to bring members of the cohort together as summer research activities begin.

6. Midterm Practice and Check-In

Participants will take part in a midterm practice and check-in during the summer. This provides an opportunity for members of the cohort to reflect on their experiences and remain connected throughout the research period.

7. End-of-Summer Celebration

The program also includes an end-of-summer celebration marking the conclusion of the summer research experience.

8. CULTIVATE Conversations

After the summer program, participants can continue engaging with the SRP community through CULTIVATE Conversations, which are described as virtual seminars and meet-ups.

This post-summer engagement can help maintain relationships established during the program.

9. Potential Conference Presentation Funding

Some funding will be available to support participants in presenting their summer research results at a scientific conference.

This provides an additional opportunity for participants to share their research outcomes with the wider scientific community and gain experience communicating research findings in a professional setting.

Who Can Apply for Sustainable Research Pathways 2026–2027?

The program has separate participation tracks, and eligibility depends on the applicant’s role.

Principal Investigators and Project Leaders

The Project/PI/Mentor Track is intended for principal investigators and project leaders with active NAIRR Pilot or U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories Computing Sciences funded projects.

Faculty Members

The Faculty Track is open to full-time faculty who can lead student teams and potentially collaborate with NAIRR and DOE National Laboratories projects.

Faculty working with students from a variety of institutions are encouraged to apply.

Students

The Student Track is open to:

Community college students.

Undergraduate students.

Graduate students.

Students must be studying at an accredited U.S. academic institution and must not be applying as part of an SRP faculty team.

Country and Geographic Eligibility

Sustainable Research Pathways is specifically designed for the United States and its territories.

The program description states that it connects U.S. researchers and project leaders with students and faculty from across the United States and its territories. Student applicants must attend an accredited U.S. academic institution.

Therefore, this is not presented as a general worldwide opportunity. Prospective applicants should carefully review their institutional and program eligibility before applying.

The available information does not specify eligibility based on race or ethnicity.

How the SRP Program Can Support Career Development

A major objective of Sustainable Research Pathways is to help participants build pathways toward research and scientific careers.

For students, participating in research activities can provide exposure to professional research environments, while interaction with project leaders and faculty can help them better understand potential career directions.

For faculty, the program can facilitate collaboration between institutions and research teams.

For project leaders, SRP can provide a structured environment for engaging with students and faculty who may contribute new perspectives and skills to their research projects.

The combination of research activities, professional community-building, workshops, mentoring, and potential conference participation makes the program broader than a single summer placement.

How the Matching Process Can Create Collaboration Opportunities

The matching component is particularly important because SRP is structured around connecting participants with potential research collaborators.

During the November 2026 workshop, participants can meet and discuss potential research interests and collaborations.

This interaction allows students and faculty to learn more about research projects while allowing project leaders and mentors to identify potential participants whose interests and backgrounds align with their work.

Successful matches may subsequently lead to the 10-week summer research experience planned for 2027.

Application Process

Applications for the three main tracks are submitted through the SRP application system.

Applicants should select the appropriate track based on their role:

Project/PI/Mentor Track for eligible principal investigators and project leaders.

Faculty Track for eligible full-time faculty.

Student Track for eligible community college, undergraduate, and graduate students.

Applicants should provide accurate information and ensure that they meet the relevant requirements before submitting their applications.

The Participant Q&A Webinar is scheduled for 10:00 AM PT, while the DOE Mentor Q&A Webinar is scheduled for 1:30 PM PT.

Prospective applicants who have questions about participation, tracks, matching, or program activities can use the relevant registration pages provided by the organizers.

Why Applicants Should Review Their Eligibility Carefully

Because Sustainable Research Pathways contains multiple tracks, applicants should not assume that the same eligibility requirements apply to everyone.

A student applicant, for example, must meet the requirements for the Student Track, including enrollment at an accredited U.S. academic institution.

Similarly, faculty applicants must meet the requirements specified for the Faculty Track, while project leaders and principal investigators must have qualifying active projects for the Project/PI/Mentor Track.

Reviewing the appropriate track before applying can help applicants submit their applications through the correct pathway.

Conclusion

The Sustainable Research Pathways 2026–2027 program provides a structured platform for connecting students, faculty members, principal investigators, and research project leaders across the United States and its territories.

Through its Project/PI/Mentor, Faculty, and Student Tracks, the program creates opportunities for participants to explore research collaborations, develop professional relationships, participate in an interactive matching workshop, and potentially take part in a 10-week paid onsite summer research experience in 2027.

The program also extends beyond the summer through professional community onboarding, cohort-wide activities, CULTIVATE Conversations, and potential financial support for presenting summer research results at scientific conferences.

TITLE: An Open Call to Higher & Tertiary Education Institutions in Africa to Apply for the 2021 AAU Facilitated Institutional Workshops

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
THE CALL

The Association of African Universities (AAU) (www.aau.org and www.blog.aau.org) is pleased to invite all African Higher and Tertiary Education Institutions to apply for Institutional Workshops for the 2021/2022 Academic Year.

Interested HEIs are requested to apply online through this link to provide further information on their specific needs, and to ensure that the workshop(s) focuses on identified capacity development area(s) which requires urgent attention – https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/AAUWORKSH19TO20

The AAU is the Apex Body and Voice of Higher Education in Africa. It is also the implementing arm of the African Union on Higher and Tertiary Education matters. Furthermore, the AAU is the Coordinator for the African Union Commission’s Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 2015-2025) Cluster on HE. This activity seeks to fulfil some of CESA’s 12 strategic objectives which are in line with revitalizing the quality of all aspects of Higher Education in Africa.

The Association of African Universities has extensive experience in organizing and delivering high-quality workshops, and has been implementing numerous workshops and webinars tailored to institutional, national and international needs, over the years.

WHAT IS AN INSTITUTIONAL WORKSHOP?

An Institutional Workshop is a capacity building workshop organized by the AAU for staff of a particular institution. The workshop content is designed in collaboration with the institution in order to meet its specific needs. In terms of duration, they take between 3-10 days and are normally delivered in that institution or at a selected venue outside the campus. It can also be conducted online upon request by an institution. The cost of delivering the Institutional Workshop is negotiated between the AAU and the concerned institution. Below are the contact details for inquiries and further communication:

CONTACT INFORMATION

Violet Makuku vmakuku@aau.org; vmakuku@gmail.com +233 263 129 798

Pamela H. Boamah: adomboamah1@gmail.com+233 249 644 795

Agnes Apedoe: secgen@aau.org+233 20 815 2735 +233 55 349 5797

Frank Asefuah (Technical Challenges): fasefuah@aau.org +233 548 880 855

WHY PARTNER AAU FOR YOUR CAPACITY BUILDING NEEDS?

The AAU has extensive experience in organizing and delivering high-quality workshops tailored for the needs of higher and tertiary education practitioners. The AAU has effectively trained over 63,000 academic staff since its founding in 1967. The AAU has a vast database of higher education experts that it mobilizes to support the delivery of the required workshops – including Francophone, Arabic, Lusophone and Anglophone experts. The AAU is ready to design and deliver workshops that are customized to the specific needs of institutions.

ADVANTAGES OF INSTITUTIONAL WORKSHOPS

A follow-up research and impact assessment by AAU indicated that there are more benefits from implementing institutional workshops which include, but not limited to:

i) The creation of a common understanding of concepts, themes and areas being covered by the workshops;

ii) The institution’s community ends up with a shared vision which they can all rally behind and support with adequate understanding of the concerned aspects;

iii) One key advantage this type of workshop has over the others is that many employees can be trained at once at a highly affordable and more competitive rate as opposed to sending individuals to attend workshops outside the institution. There is a realization of economies of scale since unlimited numbers of participants can be trained at once in one institution;

iv) Institutional workshops eliminate travel, accommodation and subsistence costs, which normally prohibit the sending out of more personnel to attend relevant capacity building activities.

v) This model encourages quick implementation of recommendations agreed upon during the workshop with less to no resistance from employees because of a common realization of the need to act once the workshop is over.

vi) Such workshops enable management and staff to freely deliberate on key issues and make meaningful as well as objective decisions within a relaxed learning environment with an external facilitator (expert in the area concerned) as the moderator.

vii) The workshops are tailor-made to address the key areas of concern indicated by the institution and prospective participants during the online registration.

viii) There is ample time for the institution to plan and properly budget for all the workshops that are needed for each academic year.

ix) It becomes easy for the AAU and the institutions to assess, later on, the impact and implemented key recommendations.

ABOUT THE ASSOCIATION OF AFRICAN UNIVERSITIES

The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa. AAU aims to improve the quality of African higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education.

It is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 400 HEIs and has three regional offices – North Africa Regional Office (NARO) in Cairo, Egypt; East Africa Regional Office (EARO) in Khartoum, Sudan; and North America Office (NAMO) in Washington DC, USA. The Association is the technical implementing arm of the African Union in higher education – with coverage and mandate across the language divide of Africa. We have influence in the francophone, anglophone, lusophone and arabophone regions.

The AAU is the coordinating agency of the Higher Education Cluster of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25) of the African Union Commission (AUC). Through our guidance, our member universities are responsible for implementing the Science, Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024) of the AUC. (Website – https://www.aau.org/ blog – blog.aau.org |Facebook – Association of African Universities| Twitter -@aau_67)

Vision

To be the leading advocate for higher education in Africa, with the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting national, continental and global needs.

Mission

To enhance the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development.

Core Values

Transparency and Accountability

Equity and Inclusiveness

Excellence and Professionalism

Responsiveness

Sustainability

Teamwork and Collegiality

Objectives of the Association

To promote interchange, contact and cooperation among universities and other institutions of higher education in Africa;

To collect, classify and disseminate information on higher education and research, particularly in Africa;

To promote cooperation among African higher education institutions in curriculum development, post graduate training, research, quality assurance, recognition of qualifications, the determination of equivalence of degrees, and other matters of special policy or practical interest to African higher education;

To encourage and empower members of the Association to address developmental challenges and become an effective voice in national, regional and global institutions;

To study and make known the educational and related needs of African universities and other institutions of higher education and, as far as practicable, co-ordinate the means whereby those needs may be met;

To contribute to the improvement of leadership, institutional management and the policy environment of African higher education;

To organise, encourage and support public fora for information dissemination and exchange and policy dialogue on issues of higher education;

To promote gender and social equity in policies on higher education and in the delivery of higher education services; and

To promote linkages with the international higher education community.

ESF has reinforced its commitment to an inclusive, diverse, and innovative culture in Research and Innovation through the development and implementation of a Gender Equality Plan (GEP)

ESF’s GEP ambitiously covers all the Building Blocks and Recommended Areas brought forth by the European Commission in the frame of Horizon Europe, but it is also going a step further by integrating an intersectional approach, in line with its far-reaching ambition to keep its important position in strengthening European research and ensure a continuous development of the state-of-the-art of gender equality in Europe and beyond.

8.044 In-Class Scribe

Disability & Access Services is seeking a scribe for a student with a disability. The employee(s) will assist the student with specific tasks related to in-class assessments. As a scribe, you must adhere to the academic integrity of the institution; you may not use your own words (numbers), interpret, prompt, or offer suggestions to the student whom you are scribing for.

Requirements:

Proficient knowledge of upper level physics and successful completion of 8.044

Task-oriented and able to sustain courtesy and concentration over extended sittings with breaks determined by student

Ability to read and write clearly

Excellent organizational skills

Guidelines for Scribing:

Use a clear voice when reading each exam question verbatim.

If the student needs clarification on any exam questions, please ask the instructor or TA to assist you.

The student will likely talk through their thought process, if they want, you should write down all of their steps.

If you are unsure of the student’s final answer, explicitly ask them to please state their final answer.

TITLE: Team Turns Around Internal Wave Resolving Array West of California

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
As part of the National Ocean Partnership Program (NOPP) Global Internal Wave study (NGIW) https://nopp-giw.ucsd.edu, the Internal Wave Resolving (IWR) Array team https://nopp-giw.ucsd.edu/teams/waterhouse/, funded by the Office of Naval Research, successfully turned around the IWR Array deployed west of California in the SWOT cal/val crossover site. The data from the central mooring and one of the nine PIESs continue to come back in real time: https://mooring.ucsd.edu/nopp1/nopp1_02/, building on the data collected for the first 7 months of the deployment: https://mooring.ucsd.edu/nopp1/nopp1_01/ . Cruise participants on the on the RV Sally Ride SR2405 included engineers, technical staff and scientists from Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO) and WHOI as well as postdocs from SIO, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the University of Michigan. The full IWR Array will be recovered in fall 2024. A second array will be deployed in the equatorial Pacific in fall 2024, partnering with the NSF-funded MOTIVE project, and the third array will be deployed off the Aleutian Islands in summer 2025. Photo provided by Magdalena Andres.

TITLE: Morgan Stanley Legal and Compliance Internship 2026 in Budapest

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Good news for students interested in international internships in Europe. The Morgan Stanley Legal and Compliance Internship 2026 in Budapest is an excellent opportunity for students who want to gain real-world experience in a global financial institution. This legal internship in Europe takes place in Budapest, Hungary, and gives students exposure to one of the most important areas in banking such as risk management, legal compliance, and operational control.

This European internship program is offered by Morgan Stanley, one of the world’s leading investment banks. It is open to students currently pursuing a bachelor’s degree or higher in finance, economics, business, law, or a related field. Through these internships in Europe, candidates will learn how global financial institutions identify risks, build compliance systems, and maintain regulatory standards. It is a strong opportunity for students who want to build a career in legal risk, operational risk, or compliance roles in the financial sector.

Moreover, the Morgan Stanley Legal and Compliance Internship 2026 provides hands-on experience in the Non-Financial Risk (NFR) team. Interns will support operational risk control testing and framework development activities. They will work on real projects that help the firm manage risk across different departments and global offices. This international internship in Hungary allows students to understand how large banks operate under strict regulations while still driving innovation and growth.

In addition, interns will gain exposure to analytical tasks, documentation processes, and risk reporting systems used in international banking. The European program also includes training sessions, teamwork activities, and networking events. Interns may also get the chance to extend their internship or receive a full-time job offer after graduation based on performance. Therefore, this legal and compliance internship in Budapest is not only a learning opportunity but also a potential career pathway in the financial industry. TITLE: Thesis Information

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Upcoming Thesis Defenses

If you are defending this term and do not see your information listed, please contact Jennifer Roesch in the APO.

Forming a Thesis Committee

When: The thesis committee should be formed within four weeks of passing the oral exam. If the form is not submitted by the end of the following semester, the student’s registration will be held until the form is submitted.

Forming their committees at this stage will allow students to consult with all members of the committee during their studies and can provide additional advice and mentorship for them.

How: Register for thesis research under subject number 8.ThG, form a thesis committee, meet with full committee.

Thesis Committee Formation

Student should consult with their Research Supervisor to discuss the Doctoral Thesis Committee Proposal Form which will solicit the committee chair and selected readers of the Physics Doctoral Committee and a descriptive preliminary thesis title.

Doctoral Committee must include 3 members with MIT Physics faculty appointments:

Committee Chair: Research Supervisor from MIT Physics Faculty or Research Supervisor from outside MIT Physics + Co-Supervisor/Chair from MIT Physics Faculty. Senior Research scientists may also serve as research supervisor.

Selected Reader: from MIT Physics Faculty (in the same/similar research area, selected by student and supervisor) Senior Research scientists may also serve as selected reader.

Assigned Reader: from MIT Physics Faculty (in different research area, selected by the Department’s faculty Graduate Coordinator.)

The Form should include the names of the Student, Chair, and Selected Reader and a Preliminary Thesis Title, when it is submitted. The Graduate Coordinator will then work with Faculty Graduate Coordinator Will Detmold, to identify the Assigned Reader.

It will take approximately 2-3 weeks before an Assigned Reader will be added and the Gradate Coordinator will provide an introduction to this final member of your Doctoral Committee.

Please note: you may not form your committee and defend your thesis in the same semester.

Thesis Committee Meeting and Proposal

When the departmentally-assigned reader has been selected, it is the student’s responsibility to convene an initial thesis committee meeting no later than four weeks before the last day of classes.

At that meeting the student makes an oral presentation to the thesis committee of a detailed proposal for a research program that would subsequently become the Ph.D. thesis. The student should demonstrate a thorough knowledge of relevant literature, explain the significance of the research to progress in the field, and present a well-thought-out program of research, including contingency plans. After that meeting, and based on the discussion, the student may develop a written proposal consisting of a one- or two-page description of the body of work that is to comprise the thesis.

Thesis Research

Following the formation of the doctoral committee and submission of the thesis proposal, the student will continue to work on their thesis research in consultation with their Research Supervisor and other members of their Committee. This important communication paves the way for the thesis defense and degree completion.

When students are ready to defend, they should complete an ‘Application for Advanced Degree’ with the Registrar and schedule a thesis defense with all committee members attending in real time, whether in person or by video. Announcements for the defense will be coordinated by the Academic Programs Office and students should be in close contact with Jennifer Roesch during their final term or study.

Further details about this last stage of your studies will be available separately.

Thesis Defense

If there is even a slight possibility that you may finish this term, please complete an Application for Advanced Degree at the Registrar’s website at the beginning of the term. It is easy to remove your name if your plans change, but this timely step will avoid late fees!

Thesis Defense

Once you have scheduled your defense, please send this information to Jennifer at physics-grad@mit.edu:

Date:

Time:

Thesis Title:

Committee Members:

Meeting Details: (can be sent in the final week before the defense)

She will create the email notifications for our physics community and the MIT Events and Physics Calendar listings. This information you provide her is also used to generate the defense grade sheet for your defense.

Please send your committee members a thesis draft to help them prepare for your defense and plan to spend around two weeks making thesis revisions after your successful defense. The date you submit your thesis document to the department will determine whether it is for a Fall, Spring, or Summer degree.

Thesis Formatting

Archival copies of all theses must adhere carefully to principles specified by the MIT Libraries for formatting and submission. For complete information about how to format your thesis, refer to the Specifications for Thesis Preparation.

Graduate Program Coordinator Jennifer Roesch can review your title page and abstract for accuracy before you submit the thesis. You may send these to her at physics-grad@mit.edu.

Required Signatures and Documentation

Signatures: The MIT Archives require an electronic PDF document and the Department needs a separate additional stand-alone title page with electronic/scanned signatures of the student, research supervisor, and co-supervisor (if applicable). Theses are accepted by Associate Department Head, Professor Scott Hughes. Please send your documents to physics-grad@mit.edu and the APO staff will forward your thesis submitted to the MIT Library Archives.

Thesis defense grade sheets: Before accepting a PhD thesis, the Academic Programs Office must have a signed thesis defense grade sheet from the research supervisor indicating a “Pass” on the thesis defense.

Thesis letter grade: Before accepting an SM thesis, Academic Programs must have received a letter or email from the research supervisor, assigning a final thesis grade of A, B, or C.

Finalizing and Submitting your Thesis to MIT

Departments collect the thesis documents on behalf of the MIT Thesis Library Archives and Physics graduate students will submit their thesis to Jennifer Roesch. Review overall information from MIT about thesis specifications and format.

Please see the attached doctoral title page format for Physics and send your draft of the title/cover page and abstract to Jennifer for review and any necessary edits. Once these are approved, please prepare the full document, with pagination appropriate for double-sided printing.

Theses may be completed and signed on any date of the year and the degree requirements are completed when the thesis is submitted. This is the final day of student status and payroll. (International students are eligible for Optional Practical Training starting on the following day.)

Research assistants should be aware that their appointment will be terminated on the day they submit their thesis.

MIT awards degrees at the end of each term:

Fall Term degree is in February. (Theses due second Friday in January.)

Spring Term degree is in May. (Theses due second Friday in May.)

Summer Term degree is in September. (Theses due second Friday in August.)

Thesis submissions are electronic files and you will submit the following to Jennifer:

A complete thesis document, without signatures

A title page with electronic signatures from yourself, your supervisor (and co-supervisor, if required). Jennifer Roesch will work with the Associate Head, Scott Hughes, whose signature is required for the department and this will be added after you submit your document to the department and Jennifer.

A separate abstract page

Digital Submission Guidelines

All theses are being accepted by the MIT Libraries in digital form only. Digital theses are submitted electronically to the Physics Department, along with a separate signed title page. Students on the degree list will receive specific guidance about submission from the Academic Programs Office.

General Thesis Policies

All theses are archived in the MIT Libraries.

After all required materials have been submitted to the Academic Programs Office, a thesis receipt will be sent by email.

Thesis Due Dates

Check the MIT Academic Calendar for deadlines to submit your online degree application.

Thesis submission deadlines
Graduating in May: Second Friday in May
Graduating in September: Second Friday in August
Graduating in February: Second Friday in January

We strongly recommend that your defense be scheduled at least three weeks prior to the submission date. Consult with Academic Administrator Shannon Larkin to determine your thesis submission timeline.

Thesis FAQs

The information on this page is applicable for both PhD and Masters (with the exception of an Oral defense) degree candidates.

How do I submit a Thesis Proposal? When is it due?

Students register for thesis research units and assemble a thesis committee in the term following passing the Oral Exam.

The first step is for the student and research supervisor to agree on a thesis topic. An initial Graduate Doctoral Thesis Committee Proposal Form (Master’s Degree candidates should see process in section below) must be submitted to Academic Programs by the second week of the term.

The form requires

an initial thesis title

the name of the research supervisor

the name of one additional reader for the thesis committee agreed upon by the student and advisor

A third reader from the MIT Physics faculty, who is not in the same research area but whose background makes him or her an appropriate departmental representative on the committee, will be assigned by the Graduate Program Faculty Coordinator. If a student has a co-supervisor (because the main supervisor is from outside the MIT Physics faculty), the thesis committee will consist of four people: research supervisor, co-supervisor, selected reader, and assigned reader.

After the student is notified of the assigned reader, he or she should convene an initial thesis committee meeting within the same term. The student should also register for 8.THG beginning in this term, and in each term thereafter. 8.THG registration should be for up to 36 units, depending on whether the student is also still taking classes and/or receiving academic credit because of a teaching assistantship. All post-qual students should routinely register for a standard total 36 units.

Master’s degree candidates should complete an SM Thesis Proposal Cover Sheet (PDF). A second reader for the Master’s degree thesis committee is assigned by the Graduate Program Faculty Coordinator. Note that there is no public defense required for an SM degree.

See the Doctoral Guidelines for additional information.

I am going to graduate soon–what do I have to do in terms of paperwork etc.?

Please reference the Registrar’s complete graduation checklist. Students should reference this list at the START of the semester prior to graduation. Your research area’s administrative office and the Physics APO will also help you manage the final stage of your degree.

How do I get on/off the Degree List?

Fill out the Degree Application through the student section of WebSIS. Petitioning to be on the degree list for a particular commencement is required. Note that it is easier to be removed from the degree list to be added, so students are encouraged to apply for the degree list if there is any reasonable chance they will complete the PhD in the coming term.

The WebSIS degree list is used to communicate information about thesis defense announcements and grade sheets, thesis formats, and completion dates, so it is important to file a degree application to be on the list in a timely way. The standard deadline for filing a degree application without being assessed a late fee is the Friday of the first week of the term in which a student anticipates graduating. Removing oneself from the degree list requires an email to Academic Programs.

When is my thesis due? Can I get an extension?

Students can defend and submit their thesis on any dates that work for their committees, but MIT confers degrees only 3 times each year: in May, September and February.

Thesis submission deadlines
Graduating in May: Second Friday in May
Graduating in September: Second Friday in August
Graduating in February: Second Friday in January

We strongly recommend that your defense be scheduled at least three weeks prior to the submission date. Consult with Assistant Director Shannon Larkin to determine your thesis submission timeline.

Note that these deadlines are already more generous that the Institute thesis deadline. Students desiring extensions should contact the Assistant Director, Shannon Larkin.

How do I find a room for my Thesis Defense?

Many Divisions have conference and/or seminar rooms which can be used for oral exams and defenses. These locations are recommended to keep your Thesis Defense comfortable and in familiar territory. Students who cannot book a room in their research area should contact Jennifer Roesch in the Physics APO to check availability of a Physics departmental conference room (often difficult to schedule due to heavy demand) or to help schedule a classroom through the Registrar’s Office.

When I submit my thesis to Physics Academic Programs, what do I need to bring?

Please refer to the Graduate Thesis Submission Guidelines.

TITLE: ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarships 2027 in Germany for PhD Students from Developing Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Global Water and Climate Adaptation Centre – Aachen, Bangkok, Chennai, Dresden (ABCD-Centre) has opened applications for the ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarships 2027, an opportunity designed to support doctoral researchers from developing countries whose work addresses pressing challenges related to water security, climate change adaptation, ecosystem resilience, sustainable development, and environmental management.

The 2027 scholarship call will support two doctoral students through a nine-month research stay in Germany. Successful applicants will have the opportunity to conduct research at one of three participating host institutions: RWTH Aachen University in Aachen, Technische Universität Dresden, or UNU Resource Nexus in Dresden.

The research stays are scheduled to take place from March 1, 2027, to November 30, 2027.

The programme is particularly valuable for PhD researchers who want to strengthen their academic and research experience in an international environment while developing research that can ultimately be translated into practical solutions, policy recommendations, and real-world approaches to water and climate adaptation challenges.

About the Global Water and Climate Adaptation Centre

The Global Water and Climate Adaptation Centre – Aachen, Bangkok, Chennai, Dresden (ABCD-Centre) is an international collaborative initiative bringing together leading academic and research institutions in Europe and Asia.

The consortium includes:

RWTH Aachen University

Asian Institute of Technology

Indian Institute of Technology Madras

United Nations University – Institute for Integrated Management of Material Fluxes and Resources (UNU Resource Nexus)

Technische Universität Dresden

The Centre seeks to address some of the world’s most urgent and interconnected environmental challenges, particularly those involving water security and climate adaptation.

Its work combines research, education, international collaboration, and knowledge transfer, with a strong emphasis on ensuring that scientific findings can move beyond academic publications and contribute to practical solutions.

A major objective of the ABCD-Centre is to develop the next generation of Future Environmental Leaders. These researchers are expected not only to produce high-quality scientific work but also to help translate research findings into applications that can benefit communities, institutions, policymakers, and other stakeholders.

About the ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarships 2027

For the 2027 cycle, the ABCD-Centre is offering two scholarships, each supporting a nine-month research stay in Germany.

The scholarships are intended for doctoral students from developing countries who are already undertaking PhD studies at universities in developing countries.

The programme provides selected researchers with an opportunity to temporarily conduct part of their doctoral research at an internationally recognised German research institution.

Applicants are required to indicate their preferred host university when applying.

The available host institutions are:

RWTH Aachen University – Aachen, Germany

Technische Universität Dresden – Dresden, Germany

UNU Resource Nexus – United Nations University Institute for Integrated Management of Material Fluxes and Resources, Dresden, Germany

The research stay is planned for:

March 1, 2027 – November 30, 2027

Applicants who are able and willing to spend the full nine-month period in Germany are given preference during the selection process.

Research Areas and Thematic Clusters

Applicants are encouraged to develop research proposals that fit within the three interconnected research clusters of the ABCD-Centre.

Cluster I: Water Security and Water Resources Management

The first cluster focuses on challenges surrounding water security and the sustainable management and provision of water resources.

Research areas include:

Water security

Water resources management

Secure water supply

Water treatment

Innovative approaches to water management

Technologies and approaches for improving access to and sustainability of water resources

This cluster may be particularly relevant to researchers investigating how societies can improve water availability, water quality, infrastructure, and resource management in the context of growing environmental pressures.

Cluster II: Ecosystem Resilience and Nature-Based Adaptation

The second cluster focuses on strengthening ecosystems and exploring nature-based approaches to climate adaptation.

Potential areas include:

Ecosystem resilience

Nature-based solutions

Climate adaptation

Environmental restoration

Sustainable ecosystem management

Innovative monitoring systems

Adaptation measures that work with natural processes

Researchers working on environmental systems and solutions that use or strengthen natural ecosystems to address climate risks are encouraged to consider this research cluster.

Cluster III: Transfer Strategies for Climate Adaptation

The third cluster focuses on how climate adaptation research can be transferred into society and translated into practical action.

It includes areas such as:

Traditional knowledge

Local economies

Societal acceptance

Climate adaptation strategies

Knowledge transfer

Policy development

Community-based approaches

Translating scientific findings into practical solutions

This cluster recognises that effective climate adaptation requires more than scientific innovation. Solutions must also be socially acceptable, economically realistic, culturally appropriate, and capable of being implemented by communities and institutions.

Priority Research Topics for the 2027 Scholarship

Although the scholarship is open to a broad range of research topics connected to the ABCD-Centre’s thematic clusters, priority will be given to proposals addressing five specific areas.

Topic A: Modelling Water Infrastructure, Digitalization and Habitat Modelling

This area includes research into:

Water infrastructure modelling

Innovative digitalisation methods

Digital twins

Habitat modelling

Applicants working on the use of digital technologies, modelling systems, simulations, or related tools to improve water infrastructure or environmental management may find this theme particularly relevant.

Topic B: Innovative Monitoring for Ecosystem Resilience and Nature-Based Adaptation

This topic focuses on improved methods for monitoring ecosystems and understanding their resilience to environmental change.

Research could address:

Innovative environmental monitoring

Ecosystem resilience

Nature-based adaptation measures

Monitoring tools and technologies

Assessment of environmental adaptation strategies

Topic C: Climate-Driven Water Extremes in Urban Areas

This theme addresses the increasing risks that climate change creates for urban water systems.

Potential research may focus on climate-driven:

Flooding

Water scarcity

Extreme rainfall

Urban water challenges

Other water-related climate extremes

Researchers investigating how cities can prepare for, manage, and adapt to increasingly severe water-related climate events are encouraged to consider this topic.

Topic D: Sustainable Business Models for Unconventional Water Resources

This research area focuses on developing sustainable approaches for the use and management of unconventional water resources.

Applicants may explore:

Sustainable water business models

Alternative water resources

Economic approaches to water management

Resource efficiency

Innovative approaches to water supply

The theme highlights the importance of developing solutions that are not only environmentally sustainable but also economically viable.

Topic E: Eco-Friendly Materials and Sustainable Building Solutions for Climate Adaptation

This topic focuses on sustainable materials and construction approaches that can contribute to climate adaptation.

Research may involve:

Eco-friendly materials

Sustainable building solutions

Climate-resilient construction

Environmentally sustainable infrastructure

Materials that support climate adaptation

Who Can Apply?

The scholarship is specifically designed for doctoral students from developing countries.

Applicants must satisfy the programme’s stated eligibility requirements.

Applicants must:

Be doctoral/PhD students.

Have commenced their PhD studies within the last three years.

Be registered as full-time PhD students.

Be enrolled at a university in a developing country.

Have a research topic that can be aligned with the thematic areas of the ABCD-Centre.

Be able to demonstrate strong academic and research potential.

Be prepared to undertake the proposed research stay at the selected German host institution.

Have the necessary support and agreement from their home institution and doctoral supervisor.

The call does not specify eligibility according to race or ethnicity. Rather, its geographic eligibility is framed around doctoral students from developing countries/Global South countries who are studying at universities in developing countries.

Applicants should therefore carefully establish that their home country and institution meet the programme’s definition or requirements for developing-country eligibility before submitting an application.

What Does the Scholarship Cover?

The ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarship provides financial support intended to cover key expenses associated with the research stay in Germany.

The scholarship typically includes support for mobility, accommodation and living expenses, insurance, and travel.

The stated financial components include:

Monthly accommodation and living expenses

Selected scholars will receive:

€1,200 per month

This allowance is intended to contribute towards accommodation and living costs during the research stay.

Insurance allowance

The scholarship provides an insurance allowance of up to:

€105 per month

The exact amount is subject to the programme’s stated maximum.

Travel allowance

A one-time travel expense stipend of up to:

€1,000

is available to support travel expenses associated with the research stay.

Research materials and equipment

In addition to the personal allowances, up to €1,000 may be allocated for research project materials and equipment through the host institution.

This additional funding can provide valuable support for researchers who require specific materials, equipment, or other research-related resources to conduct the approved project.

Duration of the Research Stay

Each scholarship lasts for nine months.

The research stay is scheduled to run from:

March 1, 2027, to November 30, 2027.

Applicants are encouraged to demonstrate their willingness to spend the complete nine-month period in Germany.

Preference is given to candidates who are willing to undertake the full research stay rather than only a shorter period.

Available Host Institutions

Applicants must identify their preferred host institution as part of the application.

RWTH Aachen University

The first option is RWTH Aachen University, located in Aachen, Germany.

Applicants interested in undertaking their proposed research at RWTH Aachen should identify a suitable host scientist and, preferably, obtain an invitation letter from the prospective host.

Technische Universität Dresden

The second option is Technische Universität Dresden (TU Dresden).

Researchers whose projects align with the university’s relevant expertise may select TU Dresden as their preferred host institution.

UNU Resource Nexus

The third option is the UNU Institute for Integrated Management of Material Fluxes and Resources (UNU Resource Nexus), located in Dresden.

This option may be particularly relevant for applicants working on integrated approaches to resources, environmental management, water, sustainability, and related areas.

Application Documents

Applicants are required to compile their application materials into one single PDF file.

The application should contain the following documents:

1. Personal motivation for the research stay

Applicants must provide a 2–3 page motivation statement explaining their motivation for undertaking the research stay.

The statement should clearly communicate why the applicant wants to participate, how the research stay fits into their doctoral project, and how the proposed experience will contribute to their academic and professional development.

2. Sample of a scientific paper

Applicants must provide a sample of a written scientific paper.

This gives the selection committee an opportunity to assess the applicant’s academic writing and research capabilities.

3. Recent Curriculum Vitae

A current CV should be included, highlighting relevant:

Academic qualifications

Research experience

Publications

Professional experience

Awards

Projects

Skills

Other achievements relevant to the proposed research

4. Preferred host university

Applicants must clearly indicate which of the three participating institutions they prefer:

RWTH Aachen University

Technische Universität Dresden

UNU Resource Nexus

5. Support letter from the home institution

A support letter from the applicant’s home institution is required.

This is important because the research stay forms part of the applicant’s ongoing doctoral work and requires institutional support.

6. Invitation letter from a host scientist

An invitation letter from a prospective host scientist is preferably included.

While the wording indicates that this is preferred rather than listed as an absolute mandatory document, applicants should make every reasonable effort to establish contact with an appropriate host researcher before applying.

7. Statement regarding online work

Applicants must provide a statement demonstrating their ability to work online if remote work is required.

This requirement is relevant to the practical organisation of the research stay and any circumstances in which some research activities may need to be undertaken remotely.

8. Enrollment certificate and transcript

Applicants must submit:

An enrollment certificate from their home institution

A current transcript of records

These documents must be no older than six months.

9. Passport copy

A copy of the applicant’s passport must also be included in the application.

Agreements Required Before Applying

Before submitting the application, the applicant’s doctoral supervisor and home university must agree on several important aspects of the proposed research stay.

These include the following.

Research topic

The applicant, supervisor, and home institution should agree on a research topic that is aligned with the ABCD-Centre’s research clusters and priorities.

Doctoral project timeline

A detailed timeline of the entire doctoral project must be established.

This should show how the proposed nine-month research stay fits into the applicant’s broader PhD programme.

Research project in Germany

Applicants must describe the specific research project they intend to conduct in Germany.

This description should include:

The research objectives

Activities to be undertaken

A timetable

How the research contributes to the overall PhD

Plans for future third-party funded research projects

Outreach contributions

Applicants should also describe their planned contributions to the ABCD-Centre’s outreach activities.

This highlights the programme’s emphasis on knowledge sharing and communication beyond the immediate research project.

How Will Applicants Be Selected?

Selection is based on several factors.

The ABCD-Centre’s Steering Committee is responsible for carrying out the selection process.

Key selection considerations include:

Academic merit

Applicants should demonstrate strong academic performance and research potential.

Motivation

The committee will consider the applicant’s motivation to contribute meaningfully to the relevant environmental field.

A strong application should therefore explain not only why the applicant wants to travel to Germany, but also why the proposed research matters and what impact it could have.

Quality of the research proposal

The quality and relevance of the proposed research project are central to the selection process.

Applicants should demonstrate:

A clear research problem

Well-defined objectives

A logical methodology

Relevance to the ABCD-Centre

Potential practical applications

A realistic timeline

Potential contribution to policy or practice

Commitment to the full research stay

Preference is given to candidates who are willing to spend the full nine months in Germany.

Policy relevance

Applicants who are interested in translating research findings into policy papers are also given preference.

This reinforces the programme’s objective of connecting academic research with practical environmental and policy solutions.

English proficiency and communication

Proficiency in English is considered important.

Applicants should also demonstrate effective communication skills because the programme involves international academic collaboration, research exchange, and outreach activities.

Adaptability

The ability to adapt to conducting research in Germany is another important consideration.

Successful applicants should be prepared to work within an international research environment and collaborate with researchers from different academic and cultural backgrounds.

Reporting Requirements

Successful scholarship recipients will have responsibilities beyond simply completing their research stay.

Scholarship and experience report

A mandatory scholarship and experience report must be submitted three months before the scholarship ends.

Recipients should therefore keep records throughout the research stay that can help them prepare the required report.

Scientific draft paper

Before the end of the research stay, scholars must submit a scientific draft paper based on the research conducted during the fellowship.

The paper should demonstrate the scientific outcomes of the research stay.

The draft may subsequently be developed further into a publication.

This requirement means that applicants should approach the nine-month stay with a clear plan for generating tangible research outputs.

Rules and Regulations

The scholarship operates under the applicable rules and regulations of:

The German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD)

The German Federal Foreign Office

The relevant host institutions

Upon selection, scholarship recipients will be required to sign a contract with their host institution.

The contract will outline the terms of the scholarship and expected conduct during the research stay.

Advice for Prospective Applicants

Applicants should begin preparing well before the deadline because the application requires multiple documents and institutional coordination.

A strong applicant should consider the following steps:

Confirm your eligibility by checking that you are a full-time PhD student at a university in a developing country and that your PhD began within the last three years.

Review the ABCD-Centre research clusters and identify where your doctoral research fits.

Consider the five priority topics and determine whether your project can directly address one of them.

Identify your preferred German host institution based on research fit rather than simply selecting an institution because of its reputation.

Identify potential host scientists whose research interests align with your proposed project.

Seek a host invitation letter early, since the call preferably requests one.

Discuss the proposed research stay with your PhD supervisor and home university and obtain the required institutional support.

Develop a strong research plan showing what you will accomplish during the nine months.

Prepare your motivation statement carefully, explaining the academic, research, practical, and policy value of the proposed stay.

Update your CV and select a strong scientific paper that demonstrates your research and writing ability.

Obtain recent academic documents, making sure the enrollment certificate and transcript are not more than six months old.

Prepare the required statement about online work if remote work becomes necessary.

Ensure all documents are combined into one PDF file before submission.

Submit the application before the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarships 2027 is:

October 31, 2026

Applications must be submitted by email to:

abcd-centre@rwth-aachen.de

Applicants should compile all required documents into a single PDF file and send it to the stated email address before the deadline.

Contact and Further Information

For questions concerning the scholarship and application process, applicants can contact the ABCD-Centre directly at:

abcd-centre@rwth-aachen.de

Applicants are also encouraged to seek guidance from their local International Office and DAAD office, particularly regarding questions related to the research stay in Germany.

For more scholarships opportunities visit OFY Website HERE

Why This Scholarship Is a Valuable Opportunity

The ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarship offers more than financial assistance.

For a doctoral researcher from a developing country, a nine-month research stay at a leading German academic or research institution can provide exposure to international research networks, specialised expertise, new methodologies, research infrastructure, and potential future collaborations.

The programme is also strongly focused on translating research into practical solutions. This makes it particularly suitable for researchers who want their work to influence environmental policy, planning, technology, community-level solutions, or sustainable development practices.

The opportunity can also help scholars develop research outputs, international connections, and experience that may support future academic collaborations and third-party research funding.

Conclusion

The ABCD Future Environmental Leaders Scholarships 2027 provide an international research opportunity for doctoral students from developing countries working on important challenges related to water security, climate adaptation, ecosystem resilience, nature-based solutions, sustainable infrastructure, and environmental management.

With two nine-month scholarships available, successful applicants will be able to conduct research at RWTH Aachen University, Technische Universität Dresden, or UNU Resource Nexus in Germany from March 1 to November 30, 2027.

The scholarship provides €1,200 per month for accommodation and living expenses, an insurance allowance of up to €105 per month, a one-time travel stipend of up to €1,000, and potentially up to €1,000 for research materials and equipment through the host institution.

Candidates should pay particular attention to the quality and practical relevance of their research proposal, their motivation, academic record, institutional support, and potential contribution to the ABCD-Centre’s work.

Eligible doctoral students should begin preparing their applications early and submit the complete application as one PDF to abcd-centre@rwth-aachen.de by October 31, 2026.
