TITLE: Ross Dempsey, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Ross Dempsey
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2025-2028
Email: rossd97@gmail.com
Phone: TBA
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, TBA
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

High Energy and Particle Theory

Research Interests

Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) was established as the gauge theory governing the strong nuclear force over 50 years ago. Despite this long history, it remains very difficult to make predictions about the strong nuclear force by starting from QCD, because many of our best-understood methods for studying quantum field theories are only applicable to weakly-coupled interactions. Even the most apparent feature of QCD, the robust confinement of quarks and gluons into color-neutral hadrons, remains stubbornly impervious to analytic approaches.

Driven by this central puzzle in theoretical particle physics, Ross Dempsey’s research focuses on tools for making predictions about the observable data of strongly-coupled gauge theories. During his Ph.D., he worked on augmenting conformal bootstrap methods with input from supersymmetric localization; this provided a new window into N = 4 super-Yang-Mills theory, a frequently-studied cousin of QCD. He also worked extensively on Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory, developing a significant improvement to a decades-old method for simulating two-dimensional quantum electrodynamics and extending this method to two-dimensional QCD.

Ross is now working to leverage these non-perturbative techniques for various important physical questions about strongly-coupled gauge theories. In particular, he is interested in simulating real-time processes, such as particle collisions.

Biographical Sketch

Ross Dempsey grew up in Virginia near Washington, DC, and was an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins. He was introduced to the joys of astrophysics research by Prof. Nadia Zakamska, with whom he worked on quasar winds and a spectacular system in the Orion Nebula. He was slowly but steadily coaxed into pursuing high-energy theory by Prof. Ibou Bah, with whom he studied hidden structure in the Einstein equations.

He moved to Princeton for his Ph.D., where he was advised by Prof. Silviu Pufu. There he worked on a variety of analytic and computational tools for probing the non-perturbative dynamics of strongly-coupled gauge theories. In particular, he collaborated extensively with Prof. Igor Klebanov as well in research on two-dimensional gauge theories.

Ross is passionate about physics education and outreach, and is always looking for ways to engage with students of all levels. He especially enjoys working with the Department of Energy’s National Science Bowl competition for middle- and high-school students.

Selected Publications

Ross Dempsey, Igor R. Klebanov, Silviu S. Pufu, and Bernardo Zan. “Discrete chiral symmetry and mass shift in the lattice Hamiltonian approach to the Schwinger model”. In: Phys. Rev. Res. 4 (4 Nov. 2022), p. 043133. arXiv: 2206.05308

Ross Dempsey, Igor R. Klebanov, Silviu S. Pufu, Benjamin T. Søgaard, and Bernardo Zan. “Phase Diagram of the Two-Flavor Schwinger Model at Zero Temperature”. In: Phys. Rev. Lett. 132.3 (2024), p. 031603. arXiv: 2305.04437

Shai M. Chester, Ross Dempsey, and Silviu S. Pufu. “Bootstrapping N = 4 super-Yang-Mills on the conformal manifold”. In: JHEP 01 (2023), p. 038. arXiv: 2111.07989

Ross Dempsey, Silviu S. Pufu, Benjamin T. Søgaard, and Igor R. Klebanov. “More About the Lattice Hamiltonian for Adjoint QCD2”. arXiv: 2409.19164

TITLE: Duke University Global Health Innovation and Policy Faculty Position 2026: Associate Professor or Professor Opportunity in the United States

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Duke University is inviting applications for a senior faculty position in Global Health Innovation and Policy at the Duke Global Health Institute (DGHI) in Durham, North Carolina, United States. The position is being jointly conducted by the Duke Global Health Institute, Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy, and Duke Global Health Innovation Center. Duke is seeking an experienced professional with significant expertise in global health innovation, health policy, health financing, or closely related areas to strengthen research, policy and leadership activities at Duke. The successful candidate will be appointed at the Associate Professor or Professor level and will have opportunities to contribute to research, policy engagement, teaching, mentorship, partnership development, external funding, and leadership within the Duke Global Health Innovation Center and the wider university.

Duke University Global Health Faculty Position: Key Details

This is a senior-level academic and professional opportunity for an established global health expert with a strong record of research, external funding, publications, stakeholder engagement and leadership.

The main details of the position include:

Institution: Duke University

Institute: Duke Global Health Institute

Position title: Faculty Position in Global Health Innovation and Policy

Academic level: Associate Professor or Professor

Position type: Non-tenure-track faculty

Location: Durham, North Carolina, United States

Primary appointment: Duke Global Health Institute

Track: Research or practice track

Appointment: Full-time, 9- or 12-month appointment

Initial appointment: Three years

Reappointment: Possible at the conclusion of the initial three-year term

Position ID: Duke-DGHI-FACULTY [#32464]

Subject area: Global Health

The position is intended for a senior individual who can combine academic excellence with practical impact in global health innovation and policy.

What Is Duke Looking For?

Duke is looking for a candidate with significant expertise and experience in one or more of the following areas:

Global health innovation

Health policy

Health financing

Policy analysis

Operational research

Research on health innovation

Development and introduction of health innovations

Scaling health innovations in low-resource settings

Policy engagement

Global health systems

The institution is particularly interested in professionals who have demonstrated the ability to move beyond research alone and translate knowledge into practical solutions that can be implemented in real-world settings.

Duke describes innovation broadly. It may involve something entirely new or something that has been newly adapted to a particular local context and produces meaningful impact.

Such innovation could take the form of:

A product

A service

A programme

An enterprise

An applied solution

The university emphasizes that successful innovation should be effective, scalable, sustainable and equitable.

Experience in Low-Resource and Global Settings

Although the position allows flexibility regarding specific topics, populations and contexts, Duke has a particular interest in candidates who have worked on health innovation in low-resource contexts globally.

Relevant experience may include leading:

Research on health innovations

Policy analysis

Operational research

Development of health innovations

Introduction of health innovations

Scale-up of health innovations

Policy engagement activities

Experience across different low-resource settings is particularly relevant because the successful candidate will be expected to understand how innovations can be adapted to different environments rather than assuming that one solution will work identically everywhere.

Duke Welcomes Non-Traditional Career Paths

An important feature of this opportunity is Duke’s openness to candidates who have followed non-traditional professional paths.

The position specifically welcomes team-science-oriented professionals who have moved between different sectors during their careers.

Examples include professionals with experience across:

Universities and academic institutions

Government

Multilateral organizations

Social enterprises

Implementation organizations

Practitioner settings

This means candidates do not necessarily need to have followed a purely academic career trajectory if they can demonstrate strong relevant expertise, leadership, research, policy and practical experience.

Leadership and Management Responsibilities

Duke is also seeking an individual with substantial management and leadership experience.

The successful candidate could serve in a faculty leadership capacity at the Duke Global Health Innovation Center.

Leadership responsibilities may include:

Managing people

Managing budgets

Managing organizations or programmes

Representing the Center externally

Engaging funders

Working with governments

Engaging implementation partners

Supporting business development

Developing partnerships

Advancing funded programmes

Traveling domestically and internationally when necessary

The position therefore goes beyond traditional teaching and research responsibilities. It is designed for a senior professional who can help build partnerships, attract resources, manage programmes and represent Duke in global health innovation activities.

Research, Policy and Practical Impact

One of the central features of the position is the connection between research, policy and practical implementation.

The successful candidate is expected to contribute to research and policy efforts while also demonstrating an understanding of how evidence can influence real-world health systems and programmes.

This makes the position particularly relevant to professionals who can demonstrate that their work has moved from academic research into areas such as:

Government policy

Health programme implementation

Innovation scale-up

Public-sector decision-making

Stakeholder engagement

Health financing

Health-system improvement

Partnerships with implementation organizations

Duke is looking for someone who can understand both the academic and practical dimensions of global health innovation.

External Funding Experience

A significant record of extramural funding is one of the required qualifications for the position.

Duke is particularly interested in applicants who have obtained funding from diverse sources, including:

Governments

Foundations

Industry

The position’s long-term salary support will come predominantly from extramural grant funding, although additional internal sources may contribute over time through activities such as teaching and administrative responsibilities.

Because of this funding model, competitive candidates must be able to demonstrate their ability to communicate the value of their work and develop funded programmes that are sustainable and add value to the Duke Global Health Innovation Center’s portfolio.

Duke Global Health Institute and Duke-Margolis will support the successful faculty member in transitioning into the institution and developing successful programmes.

Teaching and Mentorship Opportunities

The position also places considerable importance on teaching and mentorship.

Duke is seeking an applicant who is passionate about mentoring students and developing the next generation of global health professionals alongside their research and policy activities.

The successful faculty member may mentor:

Undergraduate students

Global Health majors

Graduate students in the Master of Science in Global Health programme

Graduate students in other Duke programmes

Doctoral students across the university

Medical school doctoral students

Postdoctoral scholars

Junior faculty

The faculty member may also participate in students’ ongoing research and studies.

In addition, the successful candidate could develop new courses related to:

Global health systems

Innovation

Health policy

Health financing

They may also teach existing courses in these areas.

Appointment Structure and Work Location

This is a full-time 9- or 12-month appointment at the rank of Associate Professor or Professor.

The primary appointment will be within the Duke Global Health Institute, and the position will be a regular-rank non-tenure-track appointment in either the research or practice track.

The initial appointment is for three years, with eligibility for reappointment at the end of that period.

Rank and salary will be determined based on the successful candidate’s qualifications and experience.

There is also potential for a joint appointment in another department or school at Duke University.

Because the role involves extensive collaboration, teaching, mentoring and partnership responsibilities, candidates are expected to be able to work in the United States and maintain regular presence in Durham, North Carolina.

Relocation or substantial on-campus engagement is expected.

About the Duke Global Health Institute

The Duke Global Health Institute (DGHI) was established in 2006 as a university-wide institute bringing together faculty from across Duke.

Its vision is focused on achieving health equity for vulnerable populations around the world.

The institute works across several areas, including:

Preparing global health leaders through interdisciplinary education.

Conducting research into major global health challenges.

Designing policies.

Developing evidence-based interventions.

Partnering with international and local organizations.

Supporting locally grounded and collaborative projects.

Developing innovative solutions to global health challenges.

The DGHI community includes staff, primary and secondary faculty, affiliate faculty and adjunct faculty. The institute also emphasizes values including humility, compassion, respect, cultural sensitivity, collaboration, diversity, inclusion and commitment to impact.

Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy

The position is also connected to the Robert J. Margolis, MD, Institute for Health Policy at Duke University, commonly referred to as Duke-Margolis.

Duke-Margolis brings together expertise from the Washington, DC policy community, Duke University and Duke Health.

Its work focuses on important health-policy challenges and aims to improve:

Health

Health equity

The value of health care

Health policy

Health-care implementation

The institute combines interdisciplinary research, education and engagement to help inform policymaking and implementation.

Duke Global Health Innovation Center

The position is also closely connected to the Duke Global Health Innovation Center (Duke GHIC).

Duke GHIC works at the intersection of:

Health innovation

Health policy

Global health

The Center collaborates closely with its partner organization, Innovations in Healthcare, a Duke-affiliated nonprofit organization.

According to the vacancy information, Innovations in Healthcare works with more than 100 healthcare innovators across more than 90 countries as well as public and private sector organizations.

Together, the organizations work to:

Improve access to quality healthcare.

Improve affordability of healthcare.

Scale promising health innovations.

Study health innovations.

Connect health innovators with experts.

Provide opportunities for students to engage with global health innovation.

This broader institutional environment provides an important context for understanding why Duke is seeking someone with both research expertise and practical experience in innovation and policy.

Required Qualifications

Applicants must meet the stated required qualifications.

1. Doctoral or Terminal Degree

Candidates must hold a doctoral or terminal degree in a relevant field.

Examples specifically provided in the position description include:

PhD

ScD

DrPH

MD

The degree should be relevant to the applicant’s area of expertise and the responsibilities of the position.

2. Research Experience

Applicants must have experience conducting either quantitative or qualitative research related to global health innovation and policy.

Candidates should therefore be able to demonstrate a substantive research record connected to the subject areas of the position.

3. Experience Across Low-Resource Contexts

Applicants must have experience, or a credible pathway, for translating their work across multiple low-resource contexts globally.

The position specifically identifies:

Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)

Low-resource settings in the United States

This requirement emphasizes the importance of understanding how global health solutions can be adapted and implemented across different settings.

4. Significant Extramural Funding Record

Applicants must have a significant record of extramural funding.

This is an important requirement because the position’s long-term salary support will rely predominantly on external grant funding.

Candidates should therefore be able to demonstrate a history of successfully developing, securing or contributing to externally funded programmes.

5. Academic and Non-Academic Publications

Candidates must have a record of publishing in both academic and non-academic formats.

Examples listed by Duke include:

Journal articles

Op-eds

Policy papers

Open letters

Blogs

This demonstrates that Duke is looking for someone who can communicate research and policy ideas to both academic and broader public audiences.

6. Policymaker and Stakeholder Engagement

Applicants must also have a record of engaging with policymakers and stakeholders.

Relevant stakeholders may include:

Government agencies

Advocacy groups

Public-sector organizations

Private-sector organizations

Other policy and implementation partners

Candidates should therefore be able to demonstrate that their work has involved engagement beyond academic institutions.

Preferred Qualifications

In addition to the required qualifications, Duke identifies several preferred qualifications that could strengthen an applicant’s profile.

These include:

Deep expertise in health financing.

Deep expertise in policy analysis.

Academic teaching experience.

Experience supervising faculty.

Experience supervising staff.

Experience mentoring trainees.

While these are listed as preferred rather than required qualifications, applicants who possess them may be particularly well aligned with the position.

What Type of Candidate Is Duke Seeking?

The overall profile described in the vacancy is that of a senior global health professional who can operate across several domains.

An especially strong candidate would be able to combine:

Academic expertise through advanced qualifications and research.

Practical experience applying global health innovation in real-world settings.

Policy expertise and experience engaging policymakers.

External funding success from governments, foundations, industry or other sources.

Leadership experience involving people, budgets and organizations.

Communication expertise demonstrated through academic and public-facing publications.

Teaching and mentorship ability.

International experience, particularly across low-resource contexts.

Partnership-building skills with governments, funders and implementation organizations.

The position is therefore intended for an established professional rather than an early-career applicant.

Application Deadline

The application process is already open, and the university states that review of applications will begin immediately.

Applications submitted by 15 September 2026 are guaranteed consideration.

Review will continue until the position is filled. The position listing itself gives an application deadline of 16 September 2026 at 7:59 AM United Arab Emirates Time, while the detailed position description states that applications submitted by 15 September 2026 will be guaranteed consideration.

For applicants, the safest approach is to submit the application by 15 September 2026 rather than relying on the later listing date, because Duke explicitly guarantees consideration for applications received by that date.

How to Apply

Applicants must apply online through Academic Jobs Online here

At the first stage, candidates are required to submit:

A cover letter

A curriculum vitae

The cover letter should explain the applicant’s:

Interest in the position

Relevant experience

Qualifications

Skills

Additional materials, including a list of references, will be requested from a smaller group of candidates after the initial review.

Duke states that references will not be contacted without advance notice.

The application materials required are also listed as:

Cover letter

Curriculum Vitae

Any other materials requested in the position description

Application Preparation Tips

Because this is a senior faculty position, applicants should ensure that their application demonstrates not only eligibility but also the depth and impact of their professional record.

Highlight Your Global Health Innovation Experience

Applicants should clearly explain how their previous research, programmes or professional activities have contributed to global health innovation.

Where possible, candidates should demonstrate measurable outcomes and explain how innovations were developed, adapted, implemented or scaled.

Demonstrate Experience in Low-Resource Settings

Since Duke specifically emphasizes low-resource contexts and LMICs, applicants should clearly identify relevant geographic and professional experience.

This could include work involving research, implementation, health systems, policy, innovation or operational programmes.

Explain Your Funding Record

A significant extramural funding record is required.

Applicants should therefore make their funding experience easy to understand and demonstrate their role in funded programmes.

Show Policy Impact

Candidates should highlight experience working with:

Governments

Policymakers

Advocacy organizations

Public-sector organizations

Private-sector stakeholders

Implementation partners

The goal is to demonstrate the ability to translate evidence and research into policy engagement and practical impact.

Demonstrate Leadership

Applicants should explain any experience involving:

Team leadership

Staff management

Budget management

Organizational leadership

Programme management

Partnership development

Business development

These experiences are particularly relevant because the successful candidate may take on a leadership role within the Duke Global Health Innovation Center.

Include Both Academic and Public-Facing Work

Because Duke requires a record of academic and non-academic publishing, candidates should make their publication record comprehensive.

Relevant examples include journal publications as well as policy papers, op-eds, blogs and other public-facing contributions.

Equal Opportunity and Inclusion

Duke University states that it is an Equal Opportunity Employer.

The university is committed to providing employment opportunities without regard to factors including:

Age

Color

Disability

Gender

Gender expression

Gender identity

Genetic information

National origin

Ethnicity

Race

Religion

Sex

Pregnancy and pregnancy-related conditions

Sexual orientation

Military status

Duke also emphasizes collaboration, innovation, creativity and belonging and seeks to create an environment where diverse perspectives and experiences can contribute to the university community.

Additional Disclosure Requirement

The application process includes a specific disclosure concerning past misconduct or policy violations.

Duke states that it seeks information about relevant misconduct or policy violations from the past 10 years, as well as relevant pending investigations.

The university explains that such disclosures are not automatically a reason for rejection. Instead, they initiate further discussion concerning the past actions and steps taken to address them.

The information disclosed will not be shared with search committees during the initial application review process.

Who Qualifies to Apply?

This opportunity is primarily designed for senior global health professionals, academics, researchers, policy experts and experienced practitioners with an established record in global health innovation and policy.

The minimum profile includes:

A doctoral or terminal degree such as a PhD, ScD, DrPH or MD in a relevant field.

Experience conducting quantitative or qualitative research related to global health innovation and policy.

Experience, or a credible pathway, for translating work across multiple low-resource contexts globally, including LMICs and/or low-resource settings in the United States.

A significant record of extramural funding.

A record of academic and non-academic publications.

A record of engagement with policymakers and stakeholders.

Preferred candidates may additionally have deep expertise in health financing or policy analysis, academic teaching experience, and experience supervising or mentoring faculty, staff or trainees.

Learn more:https://globalhealth.duke.edu

/send further question to this email:globalhealth.duke.edu

Nationality, Race and Geographic Eligibility

The vacancy does not specify a nationality, race, ethnicity or particular continent as an eligibility restriction.

Duke explicitly states that it provides employment opportunities without regard to national origin, ethnicity, race, religion and several other protected characteristics.

The position is based in Durham, North Carolina, United States, and candidates are expected to be able to work in the United States and be regularly present in Durham, with relocation or substantial on-campus engagement expected.

The position description particularly values professional experience involving low- and middle-income countries and other low-resource settings, but this is an area of professional experience sought by Duke rather than a nationality or citizenship restriction.

Conclusion

The Duke University Faculty Position in Global Health Innovation and Policy is a senior-level opportunity for an accomplished global health researcher, academic, policy expert or practitioner who wants to contribute to research, innovation, policy and practical health-system impact.

The position offers the opportunity to work across the Duke Global Health Institute, Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy and Duke Global Health Innovation Center while contributing to research, policy engagement, teaching, mentorship, fundraising, partnerships and organizational leadership.

Duke is particularly interested in professionals who understand how health innovations can be developed, adapted, implemented and scaled in low-resource settings. Candidates with experience across academia, government, multilateral organizations, social enterprises, implementation organizations and other practitioner environments are also explicitly welcomed.

The position requires a doctoral or terminal degree, relevant research experience, experience working across low-resource contexts, a significant extramural funding record, academic and non-academic publications, and demonstrated engagement with policymakers and stakeholders.

Applications should be submitted through Academic Jobs Online. Applications submitted by 15 September 2026 are guaranteed consideration, while the listing gives 16 September 2026 at 7:59 AM UAE Time as its stated application deadline. Given the discrepancy, applicants should aim to submit no later than 15 September 2026 to ensure guaranteed consideration.

TITLE: 1834 Global Fellowship 2027 for Black Canadians

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 13, 2026

Applications for the 1834 Global Fellowship 2027 are now open. 1834 Global is a transformative 9-week fellowship that supports the skill-building and career development of high-potential Black Canadians aged 20–30 who aspire to lead in global civic and international affairs. Through a dynamic blend of expert mentorship, intensive virtual mixers, and real-world policy research with leading international organizations, Fellows gain the tools, training, and networks needed to understand and shape the global systems that impact Black communities in Canada and around the world.

This program offers more than education, it’s a launchpad for emerging leaders to imagine bold governance solutions, collaborate with high-profile clients, and step confidently into careers as diplomats, policy analysts, and global change-makers. 1834 Global nurtures a new generation of Black visionaries ready to shape the future of global affairs from the inside out.

The 1834 Global program is offered in collaboration with the Centre for Diaspora and Transnational Studies at the University of Toronto.

Program Overview

1834 Global will achieve its objectives through the delivery of the following program activities:

1834 Global Mixers: Weekly facilitated sessions expose Fellows to a broad range of global issues and leadership challenges. Each session is designed to strengthen both personal and professional competencies, creating space for critical dialogue, reflection, and growth in areas such as diplomacy, governance, advocacy, and policy design.

1834 Global Research Projects: Fellows are grouped into policy teams that collaborate throughout the program on research projects tied to real-world global issues. Each team is paired with an experienced Coach—an expert in global affairs—who provides ongoing mentorship and guidance. These Champions help Fellows sharpen their strategic thinking, refine their communication, and apply their learning to practical outcomes.

1834 Global Summit: The program culminates in a high-impact capstone experience that brings together public policymakers, analysts, nonprofit leaders, and civically engaged Black youth. The Summit offers Fellows a platform for Fellows to present their research, gain professional exposure, and connect directly with institutions shaping global policy—while centering Black voices and leadership in the global conversation.

TITLE: JET Programme 2027: Apply to Teach English in Japan for at Least One Year as an Assistant Language Teacher

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Government of Japan is inviting applications from young South Africans interested in gaining international teaching and cultural exchange experience through the Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme 2027. The programme offers successful participants an opportunity to spend at least one year in Japan working as Assistant Language Teachers (ALTs) while contributing to internationalisation, foreign-language education, and people-to-people exchange at the local level.

Administered through a collaboration involving Japanese government ministries and agencies, the JET Programme is one of the world’s largest international exchange programmes. It brings university graduates from participating countries to Japan to work with local governments, schools, boards of education, and other organisations.

For South African graduates with an interest in education, language, Japanese culture, international relations, community engagement, and cross-cultural communication, the JET Programme provides an opportunity to live and work in Japan while developing professional and intercultural skills.

JET Programme 2027 Overview

The Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme was established to promote grassroots internationalisation in Japan. Participants work with local communities and educational institutions, helping strengthen understanding between Japan and other countries.

For the 2027 intake, the Embassy of Japan in South Africa is calling for applications from young South Africans who would like to spend at least one year in Japan as Assistant Language Teachers.

Key details

Programme: Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme

2027 Position: Assistant Language Teacher (ALT)

Host country: Japan

Recruiting country: South Africa

Duration: Generally one year

Target applicants: Young South African university graduates

Work environment: Elementary, junior high and senior high schools, local boards of education and related institutions

Application method: Courier with a tracking number or hand delivery

Application deadline: 4:00 PM, 16 October 2026

Application location: Embassy of Japan, 259 Baines Street, Groenkloof, Pretoria, 0181

Selection notification: Successful and unsuccessful applicants will be contacted by email

What Is the JET Programme?

The JET Programme is an international exchange initiative administered through cooperation among several Japanese institutions, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC), Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), and the Council of Local Authorities for International Relations (CLAIR).

Its primary objective is to promote grassroots internationalisation at the local level.

Rather than focusing only on international exchange at the national or diplomatic level, the programme places participants directly within Japanese communities. Participants interact with students, teachers, local government employees and community members, allowing cultural exchange to take place through everyday professional and community activities.

The programme also seeks to create long-term international networks. Participants are expected to contribute positively to mutual understanding between Japan and their home countries while gaining a deeper understanding of Japanese society and culture.

JET Programme History and Global Reach

The JET Programme has developed considerably since its establishment in 1987.

According to the Embassy of Japan in South Africa, the programme began with participants from only four countries. Over the years, it has expanded to include participants from 54 countries, with 5,993 participants as of 2025.

Across the history of the programme, more than 80,000 people from 82 countries have participated.

This extensive international participation demonstrates the scale of the JET Programme and its emphasis on creating connections between Japan and communities around the world.

The programme has also developed a strong reputation both within Japan and internationally. Participants are regarded as representatives of their respective countries and are therefore expected to conduct themselves responsibly and contribute constructively to international understanding.

Assistant Language Teacher Position

The 2027 opportunity highlighted by the Embassy of Japan in South Africa is for applicants interested in serving as Assistant Language Teachers (ALTs).

ALTs are primarily placed in educational settings, including:

Local boards of education

Elementary schools

Junior high schools

Senior high schools

Participants work under the guidance of language-teacher consultants, Japanese teachers of foreign languages, school principals, boards of education, or other designated supervisors.

The precise working environment and responsibilities can vary depending on the Contracting Organisation to which an individual is assigned.

Duties and Responsibilities of an ALT

The role is broader than simply standing in front of a classroom and teaching English. Participants can become involved in different educational and cultural activities depending on the needs of their school or Contracting Organisation.

Typical responsibilities may include the following.

1. Assisting with foreign-language classes

ALTs assist Japanese teachers with foreign-language lessons in elementary, junior high and senior high schools.

This can involve supporting classroom activities, language practice, communication exercises and other activities designed to help students develop their foreign-language abilities.

The exact nature of classroom involvement may depend on the school, teaching arrangements and instructions provided by the relevant supervisor.

2. Supporting foreign-language activities in elementary schools

Participants may also assist with foreign-language activities for younger learners.

This gives ALTs an opportunity to introduce language learning in engaging and accessible ways while interacting directly with Japanese pupils.

3. Helping prepare teaching materials

ALTs may contribute to the preparation of materials used for foreign-language education.

This could involve helping teachers develop language-learning resources or providing information and examples that support classroom instruction.

4. Supporting language training for teachers

Participants may assist with language training for Japanese teachers of foreign languages or other language-related activities.

Their perspective as international participants can be useful in providing practical language knowledge and insights into how English and other foreign languages are used.

5. Participating in extracurricular and club activities

The JET Programme can extend beyond formal classroom instruction.

ALTs may cooperate with extracurricular activities and school clubs, allowing them to interact with students in less formal educational environments.

6. Providing language-related information

Participants may provide information to teachers and language consultants on matters such as:

Word usage

Pronunciation

Language expressions

Other language-related subjects

This responsibility allows participants to contribute their knowledge of their own language and culture to the Japanese education system.

7. Supporting foreign-language speech contests

ALTs may also assist with foreign-language speech contests.

This could include helping students prepare, providing language-related guidance or supporting the organisation of such activities, depending on the requirements of the school or Contracting Organisation.

8. Supporting local international exchange activities

One of the most important elements of the JET Programme is international exchange.

Participants may cooperate in local international exchange activities, helping communities develop greater awareness and understanding of other countries and cultures.

9. Performing other duties as required

Participants may be assigned additional duties considered necessary by their supervisor or school principal.

Because assignments differ between Contracting Organisations, applicants should understand that the precise responsibilities of an ALT can vary.

Where Do JET Participants Work?

JET participants are generally appointed by Japanese prefectures, municipalities, private schools and other Contracting Organisations.

This means that successful applicants are not necessarily assigned to one specific city or region in Japan. Their eventual placement depends on the organisation to which they are appointed.

Participants can therefore expect their experience to be shaped partly by their assigned community, school and local working environment.

For someone interested in experiencing Japanese life beyond major tourist destinations, this aspect of the programme can be particularly significant because placements can connect participants with local communities and educational institutions.

One-Year Participation Period

Participants are generally appointed for a one-year period.

The programme is therefore designed as a substantial international experience rather than a short-term visit. Successful applicants should be prepared to live and work in Japan for the duration of their appointment.

The Embassy of Japan also emphasises that participants should avoid withdrawing from the programme after receiving an assignment or ending their participation early, as doing so can create significant difficulties for the Contracting Organisation and affect the administration of the programme.

Applicants should therefore consider the commitment carefully before applying.

Financial Support and Transportation

According to the Embassy of Japan’s information, the cost of transportation from the participant’s place of origin to Japan, as well as remuneration, is funded by Japanese taxpayers through the Contracting Organisation where the participant is appointed.

This means successful participants receive financial support connected to their participation and employment under the programme.

Because participants serve as staff members of their respective Contracting Organisations, they are expected to observe applicable rules and behave responsibly.

The financial arrangements therefore form part of a broader employment and public-service structure rather than being simply a study-abroad scholarship.

Professional and Personal Development Opportunities

The JET Programme can provide participants with an opportunity to develop skills that extend beyond language education.

Living and working in another country can expose participants to new professional environments, educational systems and cultural practices.

Participants can potentially develop experience in areas such as:

Classroom support and education

Public speaking and communication

Cross-cultural communication

Community engagement

International relations

Cultural exchange

Teamwork

Adaptability

Interpersonal communication

Working in a foreign professional environment

Understanding Japanese society and culture

For graduates interested in careers involving international development, education, communications, diplomacy, international organisations, cultural exchange or global affairs, such experience can provide useful exposure.

Expectations of JET Participants

JET participants are regarded as representatives of their respective countries.

The Embassy of Japan therefore stresses the importance of responsible behaviour and mutual understanding.

Applicants should understand that the programme is not solely about travelling to Japan. Participants are expected to make a meaningful contribution to the communities in which they live and work.

The Embassy indicates that desirable participants should be:

Adaptable

Mentally capable of performing their duties

Physically capable of performing their duties

Deeply interested in Japan

Responsible in their activities

Committed to promoting mutual understanding between nations

Participants should therefore be prepared to adapt to a different cultural and professional environment.

Why the International Exchange Element Matters

International exchange is central to the JET Programme.

An ALT from South Africa, for example, does more than assist with language education. Their presence can give Japanese students and community members opportunities to learn about South Africa and interact with someone from a different cultural background.

At the same time, the participant gains first-hand exposure to Japanese culture and society.

This two-way exchange is one of the fundamental purposes of the programme.

Participants are encouraged to build relationships with the communities where they are placed, contributing to a broader international network that can continue beyond their period in Japan.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity is particularly relevant to young South African university graduates who are interested in combining professional experience with international cultural exchange.

Potentially suitable applicants may include graduates interested in:

Teaching and education

English-language education

International exchange

Japanese culture

International development

Global communication

Community engagement

Cross-cultural relations

International careers

Applicants should also be comfortable with the responsibilities associated with representing their country in an international programme.

Application Deadline for JET Programme 2027

The deadline is 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.

Importantly, applications must arrive at the Embassy of Japan by the deadline. Applicants should therefore not wait until the final day to send their documents.

The Embassy specifically instructs applicants to either courier their complete application package with a tracking number or hand deliver it to the designated address.

Application address

Embassy of Japan

JET Programme

259 Baines Street

Groenkloof

Pretoria

0181

South Africa

Applicants using courier services should allow sufficient time for the package to arrive before the stated deadline.

How to Apply for the JET Programme 2027

Applicants should carefully review the official JET Programme information and application documentation before preparing their submissions.

The basic submission process indicated by the Embassy is:

Review the official JET Programme information and application requirements.

Complete the required application documentation.

Prepare the complete application package.

Check that all required documents have been included.

Submit the package by courier with a tracking number or hand deliver it to the Embassy of Japan in Pretoria.

Ensure that the application arrives by 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.

Wait for notification by email regarding the outcome of the application.

Applicants should ensure that their submissions are complete and comply with the instructions in the official application documentation.

Selection Results

The Embassy of Japan states that both successful and unsuccessful applicants will be contacted by email.

Applicants are specifically requested not to contact the Embassy to enquire about the outcome of their application.

It is therefore important for applicants to monitor the email address provided in their application after submission.

To APPLY download the application form HERE.

Important Considerations Before Applying

The JET Programme can be a major international and professional opportunity, but applicants should understand the commitment involved.

Before applying, prospective participants should consider whether they are prepared to:

Live in Japan for at least one year.

Adapt to a different cultural and social environment.

Work within the Japanese education system.

Follow the instructions of their supervisors and Contracting Organisations.

Interact professionally with students, teachers and community members.

Represent South Africa responsibly.

Participate actively in international and cultural exchange.

Accept the responsibilities associated with their assigned position.

Commit to the programme rather than treating it simply as an opportunity for travel.

The programme is intended for individuals who can make a meaningful contribution while adapting to life and work in Japan.

Visit HERE to learn more about the JET Programme 2027.

Conclusion

The JET Programme 2027 offers young South African university graduates an opportunity to spend at least one year in Japan while working as Assistant Language Teachers and contributing to international exchange.

The programme combines language education, professional experience, community engagement and cultural exchange. Participants can work alongside Japanese teachers and educational authorities, support foreign-language classes, assist with teaching materials and extracurricular activities, contribute to speech contests and participate in local international exchange initiatives.

Beyond the professional responsibilities, the programme provides an opportunity to experience Japanese society from within a local community while helping Japanese students and residents learn more about South Africa and the wider world.

Interested South African graduates should begin preparing their applications well before the deadline. The complete application package must arrive at the Embassy of Japan in Pretoria no later than 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.

For the official application instructions, detailed information and application forms, applicants should consult the Embassy of Japan in South Africa’s official JET Programme information before submitting their documents.

TITLE: 3rd WACCBIP Research Conference

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The West Africa Center for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP) hosted its third annual Research Conference from July 18 – 20, 2018 at its new office complex in the University of Ghana.

The Conference which aims to showcase the talent and quality of young African scientists and to provide a platform for the dissemination of research conducted by fellows at the Centre and by visiting scientists from its global network of collaborators.

The three-day conference held under the theme “Translating Molecular Research into Healthcare Solutions for Africa”, brought together world-class scientists from Africa, Europe, and North America, who conduct research into tropical diseases, including malaria and Buruli ulcer, that are prevalent in Africa. The conference afforded young scientists at the Centre the opportunity to interact with seasoned scientists, giving them better insight into their research projects and opening them up to new perspectives from experienced researchers.

In his welcome address, Director of WACCBIP, Prof. Gordon Awandare, explained that the Centre was established with the vision to build and support development of dynamic and internationally competitive talent. He reiterated the Centre’s commitment towards the provision of high-end facilities suitable for advanced training and research and cited the construction of the new WACCBIP building as one of the key achievements towards reaching the Centre’s overarching goal.

He also highlighted the achievements of the Centre saying, “Since we started, we have given fellowships to 90 master’s students, 50 PhD students, and 12 postdocs. That is the largest biomedical training research programme in West Africa. Nobody has done that in the last four years.”

He further entreated Government to provide incentives to encourage the creation of research units in the private sector to absorb the pool of research scientists produced by research institutions across the country.

Also speaking at the event, Professor Keith Gull, Professor at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at the University of Oxford and Chair of the WACCBIP International Advisory Board, was impressed with WACCBIP’s sustained development of its research and training activities since its establishment.

He explained that WACCBIP’s vision does not end at training scientists but extends to ensuring that their training is translated to relevant research output for the future.“It has always been the vision of WACCBIP and the Department to balance research and teaching, and that is really a critical part of a research-led education. Some of you are here for a degree; a master’s or a PhD. I think that’s one of the least important things about what you’re doing at WACCBIP. You’re not here [only] to get a degree; you are here to engage and end up with something far more precious; it’s called an education.” Prof. Gull said.

Prof. Francis Dodoo, Pro-Vice Chancellor of Research, Innovation and Development at University of Ghana, who chaired the opening ceremony, expressed his delight at the impact WACCBIP has made in mobilising resources to attract a high calibre of scientists to the University.

He said, “WACCBIP is demonstrating precisely the impact an African Centre of Excellence can have by way of contributing to the transformation of our University. This is in line with [the University’s vision of] attaining world class status with respect to quality, quantum, and impact of research.

He added that WACCBIP played an important role in the reorganisation of ORID’s activities as they allowed for collective cultivation of the Centre’s resources within the University.

Other speakers at the event were Dr. Ben Botwe, President of Pharmaceutical Society of Ghana and Dr. Lydia Mosi, Head of Department of Biochemistry Cell and Molecular Biology.

The West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP) was set up in 2013 with funding from the Government of Ghana through World Bank’s Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence (ACE) Project. Since its inception, WACCBIP has grown into a leading Centre of Excellence, building global partnerships with world-class research institutions and funding organisations. The Centre aims to improve diagnosis, prevention, and control of infectious diseases in sub-Saharan Africa by providing advanced-level training and research excellence on the cell and molecular biology of infectious pathogens.

TITLE: ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027: Paid Public Health Traineeships in Stockholm, Sweden

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) Traineeship Programme 2027 offers recent university graduates an opportunity to gain practical professional experience within a European Union agency working to prevent and control infectious diseases.

The programme is designed for graduates who are beginning their professional careers and want to develop practical knowledge, understand the work of an EU public health institution, and apply the knowledge gained through their university studies in a professional environment.

For the 2027 cohort, ECDC is offering 12 traineeship positions across different professional areas and functions of the Centre. The traineeships will last between five and nine months, depending on the placement and applicable arrangements.

The programme is based at ECDC in Stockholm, Sweden, and provides selected trainees with a monthly traineeship grant and a travel allowance. The programme is particularly relevant to graduates interested in public health, epidemiology, infectious diseases, data and digital solutions, science communication, social and behavioural sciences, administration, and related fields.

About the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, commonly known as ECDC, is an agency of the European Union that works to strengthen Europe’s defences against infectious diseases.

ECDC supports European countries and public health institutions by:

Monitoring infectious disease developments.

Collecting and analysing public health information.

Identifying emerging and cross-border health threats.

Assessing risks associated with communicable diseases.

Supporting outbreak preparedness and response.

Providing scientific and technical advice.

Strengthening disease surveillance.

Promoting public health cooperation.

Supporting training and professional development.

Communicating reliable information about infectious disease risks.

Through its traineeship programme, ECDC gives recent graduates the opportunity to gain first-hand knowledge of how a European public health agency operates and how scientific, technical, administrative, and communication functions contribute to public health protection.

What Is the ECDC Traineeship Programme?

The ECDC Traineeship Programme is a professional development opportunity aimed at recent university graduates who are entering the early stages of their careers.

The programme is intended to help trainees:

Gain a practical understanding of ECDC and its role within the European Union.

Learn about the Centre’s work in identifying, assessing, and communicating current and emerging threats to human health.

Acquire practical knowledge of the day-to-day work of ECDC units.

Apply academic knowledge and technical skills in a professional setting.

Develop professional competencies and workplace experience.

Improve their understanding of European public health procedures and institutional cooperation.

Build a foundation for future professional opportunities in public health, science, policy, administration, communications, and related areas.

Trainees work within a specific ECDC unit or function and are expected to contribute to activities relevant to their educational background and placement.

Duration: Five to nine months

The ECDC recruitment portal lists traineeship positions across a range of professional and scientific areas. The available positions include opportunities related to infectious diseases, public health, digital services, social sciences, communication, and organisational support.

Epidemiological information.

Disease monitoring.

Risk assessment and communication.

Information systems.

Public health.

Infectious diseases.

Food.

Water.

Animals.

Environmental exposure.

Benefits of the ECDC Traineeship Programme

The ECDC traineeship provides a combination of professional experience, financial support, international exposure, and practical learning.

1. Monthly Traineeship Grant

Selected trainees receive a monthly grant from ECDC to help cover living expenses during the traineeship.

The exact monthly grant for 2027 has not yet been established. ECDC determines the amount annually, and the revised amount applies from 1 January of the relevant year.

For reference, the monthly traineeship grant for 2026 was EUR 2,205.72. This figure is provided for information only and should not be treated as the confirmed grant amount for 2027.

2. Travel Allowance

ECDC provides a travel allowance intended to compensate for expenses incurred at the beginning and end of the traineeship when travelling from the trainee’s place of residence.

Applicants should review the applicable guidelines and employment conditions to understand how the travel allowance is calculated and administered.

3. Practical Professional Experience

Trainees gain first-hand experience within an EU public health agency. This may help them understand how scientific, technical, administrative, and communication activities are organised in an international institutional environment.

The experience may be particularly useful for graduates planning careers in:

Public health.

Epidemiology.

Infectious disease prevention.

Microbiology.

Health policy.

Scientific research.

Data analysis.

Science communication.

International development.

Public administration.

Digital services.

Programme management.

4. Exposure to European Public Health Work

The programme provides trainees with an understanding of ECDC’s role in identifying, assessing, and communicating infectious disease threats in the European Union.

Trainees may learn how public health evidence is developed, interpreted, communicated, and used to support decision-making and cooperation among European institutions and national authorities.

5. Opportunity to Apply Academic Knowledge

The traineeship allows graduates to apply skills acquired during university studies in a professional environment.

Depending on the placement, trainees may use skills in:

Research.

Data analysis.

Scientific writing.

Project coordination.

Public health assessment.

Communication.

Information technology.

Administration.

Policy analysis.

Programme evaluation.

Behavioural research.

6. International and Multicultural Work Environment

ECDC operates in a European and international environment involving professionals from different countries and disciplines. Trainees may work with colleagues and stakeholders from across Europe, gaining experience in multicultural teamwork and institutional cooperation.

7. Professional Networking

The traineeship may enable participants to develop professional relationships with ECDC staff, public health experts, researchers, administrators, and other professionals working in European public health.

These connections may support future learning, collaboration, and career development, although participation does not guarantee future employment with ECDC or another EU institution.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet all formal eligibility requirements by the application deadline.

1. Nationality or Citizenship

Candidates must be nationals or citizens of one of the following:

A Member State of the European Union.

Norway.

Iceland.

Liechtenstein.

Applicants from countries outside these territories are generally not eligible for this specific traineeship programme.

A residence permit, work permit, or long-term residence status in one of the eligible countries is not sufficient if the applicant does not hold the required nationality or citizenship.

2. Completed University Degree

Applicants must have completed their university education and been awarded a full university degree or equivalent qualification by the closing date for applications.

Proof of the degree must be submitted with the application.

This requirement means that applicants who are still studying and have not yet received their degree by the deadline may not qualify. The ECDC FAQ specifically states that medical students who have not completed their studies and obtained a full university degree are not eligible.

3. English Language Requirement

Applicants must have a very good command of English because English is the main language used in ECDC’s day-to-day operations.

Knowledge of additional official EU languages is considered an asset and may strengthen an applicant’s profile, although the precise language requirements may depend on the traineeship area.

4. No Previous Employment or Traineeship in an EU Institution

Applicants must not have previously benefited from a formal traineeship or held employment, whether formal or informal, paid or unpaid, within:

An EU institution.

An EU agency.

An EU body.

An EU delegation.

An EU representative office.

Another relevant EU institutional entity.

This restriction may include previous roles such as temporary staff, contract staff, auxiliary staff, or assistants to Members of the European Parliament.

Applicants should carefully review the official guidelines if they have previously worked with or completed a traineeship at a European institution.

5. Relevant Educational Background

Successful candidates are expected to have an education and background relevant to the activities of ECDC.

Depending on the vacancy, relevant academic backgrounds may include:

Public health.

Epidemiology.

Medicine, where the applicant has completed the required degree.

Microbiology.

Infectious diseases.

Biology.

Veterinary public health.

Environmental health.

Statistics.

Mathematics.

Data science.

Information technology.

Social sciences.

Behavioural sciences.

Communications.

Journalism.

Health policy.

Public administration.

Business administration.

Human resources.

Finance.

Law.

Project management.

Other related disciplines.

The relevant degree or background must correspond to the requirements of the specific traineeship vacancy.

The application period for the ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027 runs from:

8 September 2026 to 5 October 2026

Final Deadline

5 October 2026 at 12:00 noon, Stockholm time

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit their applications. The application must be completed and submitted through the official e-recruitment platform before the stated deadline.

Because the deadline is specified in Stockholm time, applicants from other countries should convert the closing time to their local time zone and submit early.

Selection and Interview Timeline

ECDC indicates the following expected timeline for the 2027 traineeship selection process:

Applications open: 8 September 2026.

Applications close: 5 October 2026 at 12:00 noon, Stockholm time.

Shortlisted applicants may be contacted for interviews: From mid-October 2026 onwards.

Interviews: Expected to take place by mid-December 2026.

Traineeship start: Applicants should follow the official communication issued to selected candidates regarding the start date.

Being invited to an interview does not guarantee selection. Candidates must successfully complete the selection process and satisfy all required conditions before receiving a traineeship offer.

Reserve List

Following the interviews, ECDC may establish a reserve list of suitable candidates.

The reserve list may be used if additional traineeship opportunities become available. For the 2027 cohort, the reserve list is expected to remain valid until:

31 December 2027

Placement on a reserve list does not necessarily guarantee that a candidate will receive a traineeship offer. It means that the candidate may be considered for additional opportunities if they arise.

Tax and Employment Arrangements

The ECDC traineeship is a non-statutory traineeship and does not create a conventional employment relationship between the trainee and ECDC.

Trainees receive a monthly grant, but ECDC is not considered the employer for the purposes of the traineeship. Therefore:

ECDC does not pay social security contributions related to the traineeship.

Trainees are responsible for determining whether they must pay income tax.

Tax obligations depend on the trainee’s individual circumstances and the applicable national rules.

Applicants should seek appropriate tax advice where necessary.

The monthly grant should therefore not automatically be treated as a conventional salary.

Accommodation and Health Insurance

Accommodation

ECDC does not provide accommodation or arrange housing for trainees in Stockholm.

Trainees are responsible for finding their own accommodation. However, ECDC may provide practical advice about where to look for housing and how to approach the accommodation search.

Applicants should plan for the cost and availability of accommodation before accepting a traineeship offer.

Health Insurance

All trainees are provided with accident insurance through the programme.

However, trainees must obtain health insurance that is valid in Sweden before starting the traineeship. Proof of valid health insurance will be requested before the traineeship begins.

Applicants should confirm their health insurance arrangements early, particularly if they are relocating to Sweden.

Equal Opportunities

ECDC applies equal-opportunity principles in its traineeship programme. Applications are considered without distinction based on factors such as:

Age.

Race.

Ethnic or social origin.

Political, philosophical, or religious convictions.

Sex.

Sexual orientation.

Disability.

Marital status.

Family situation.

Applicants must still meet the formal nationality, degree, language, and previous-employment requirements of the programme.

Applications must be submitted online through the Official ECDC e-recruitment Platform.

Step 1: Review the Available Traineeship Vacancies

Visit the ECDC recruitment portal and review the available traineeship positions for the 2027 cohort.

Hold the nationality of an eligible country.

Applicants should prepare the documents requested in the relevant vacancy notice. These may include:

Curriculum vitae.

Motivation letter.

University diploma or degree certificate.

Academic records, where requested.

Evidence of relevant experience.

Language information.

Other supporting documents required by the application platform.

Applicants should ensure that all information is accurate and consistent across their documents.

Step 4: Complete the Online Application

Create or access an account on the ECDC e-recruitment platform and complete the required application fields.

Use clear descriptions of your academic background, technical skills, relevant projects, professional experience, research activities, volunteering, and other achievements related to the selected traineeship.

Step 5: Submit Before the Deadline

Submit the completed application through the official recruitment platform no later than:

5 October 2026 at 12:00 noon, Stockholm time

Applicants should retain confirmation of submission and monitor their email or recruitment account for further communication.

Explain why you are interested in the specific ECDC traineeship and how your academic background, skills, and career goals relate to the selected area.

Avoid using a generic motivation letter for every position. Highlight relevant subjects, research, internships, projects, volunteer activities, or work experience.

Data analysis and statistics.

Scientific writing.

Public health knowledge.

Digital and IT skills.

Project coordination.

Teamwork.

Problem-solving.

Stockholm is the programme location, and trainees are responsible for finding accommodation. Applicants should consider housing, transportation, food, insurance, and other living expenses when evaluating the opportunity.

Apply Early

Submit your application well before the deadline. Early submission allows time to correct missing information, upload documents, resolve technical problems, and confirm that the application has been successfully received.

The ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027 offers recent university graduates an opportunity to gain practical experience within a European Union agency focused on infectious disease prevention, public health preparedness, scientific analysis, and health protection.

These fellowships are designed for scholars, researchers, academics, and professionals interested in contemporary Asia and provide opportunities to conduct research, develop academic work, engage with other scholars, and contribute to research on major political, economic, social, health, and policy issues affecting the Asia-Pacific region.

Through its research programs, APARC provides opportunities for scholars and researchers to investigate important developments across the region, including political and economic change, healthcare policy, international relations, social issues, technology, development, and regional policy challenges.

Taiwan Program Kwoh-Ting Li Visiting Fellowship

Each fellowship has its own research focus and eligibility requirements.

How to Choose the Appropriate Fellowship

Applicants should first identify their research topic, geographical focus, and career stage.

If your research covers contemporary Asia broadly

The Shorenstein Postdoctoral Fellowship may be relevant for recent PhD recipients researching political, economic, or social change, international relations, or international political economy in Asia.

If your research focuses on health

The Asia Health Policy Program Postdoctoral Fellowship is specifically focused on contemporary health and healthcare policy in the Asia-Pacific region.

If you study Southeast Asia

The Lee Kong Chian NUS-Stanford Fellowship is designed for scholarship concerning contemporary Southeast Asia and is open to candidates at all career stages who meet its professional requirements.

If your research fits emerging Asian policy challenges

The Stanford Next Asia Policy Lab fellowships provide opportunities across four research themes, including talent flows, nationalism and racism, U.S.-Asia relations, and democratic crisis and reform.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Because these are different fellowship programmes, applicants should not assume that meeting the requirements for one automatically means they qualify for all of them.

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should:

Identify the fellowship that corresponds to their research area.

Check whether the opportunity is intended for recent PhD recipients, visiting researchers, or established scholars.

Review the specific application requirements.

Confirm the fellowship duration and expected start period.

Prepare the required academic and research materials.

Ensure that the research proposal or project aligns with the fellowship’s stated focus.

The fellowship portfolio covers broad regional research as well as specialized areas including health policy, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, higher education and research policy, economic security, international relations, political change, and social development.

The opportunities also differ considerably in terms of career stage. TITLE: Building the Capacities of African Universities in Research and Project Proposal Grants Writing: AAU Takes the Lead

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) is leading the retooling and upskilling of staff from African Universities in Research and Project Grants writing through hosting a series of capacity building workshops.

The workshops, which started on February 17th -March 10th, 2021 attracted participants from Kenya, Zambia, Nigeria, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Eswatini, Uganda, among other African countries.

Dr. Violet Makuku, the Quality Assurance Specialist, Workshops Coordinator and facilitator of the workshop, encouraged participants to be vigilant and always be on the lookout for opportunities as there are many grant calls which are frequently released that a lot of stakeholders in African HEIs, including the workshop participants, do not get to know of.

Even in cases where they were aware of such calls and respond to them, some knowledge and skills gaps have led to their inability to win those grants. This trend forms part of the background which informed the AAU to move to improve capacity in this area, with an ultimate target of helping more African Universities to actually win the grants when they submit their proposals in response to a specific call.

Taking participants through the sessions, Dr. Makuku highlighted that both Solicited and Unsolicited Proposals require high levels of dedication, knowledge, skills, time and hard work to win them. She explained that with Solicited Proposals, a taskforce need to devote quality time to search for them (via the internet and other sources). The need to also subscribe to some channels/websites so that stakeholders are notified immediately there is a call for proposals was shared by her.

She also stressed the following key issues to consider when writing proposals and these include but are not limited to, having a policy in place, building good track records, adopting multi-disciplinary and inter-disciplinary approaches, teamwork and collaboration, monitoring and evaluation as well as effective communication. Participants were encouraged to, “Build strong grant proposal writing teams which are so strong to an extent that no one will know who the leader of the team is.” She stated this when she spoke about teamwork and collaboration.

She explained that the Multidisciplinary and Interdisciplinary Approaches cover gaps and strengthen the case in a proposal. Citing an example of a research proposal on “Causes of increase in Malaria deaths in a given Community”, she explained that if the writing of a proposal only include a team from the medical field, it will not help much, because other people like religious leaders, communication personnel, Accountants, Demography Experts, Traditional Healers, Policy Makers, Environmentalists, Community Based Organizations (CBOs), Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) are key players, and therefore should be involved so that they work hand in hand to win the grant.

Several other examples were cited to drum home the message that multi and interdisciplinary approaches were strategic choices. One of such was the example of a proposal on, “The Cause of High Mortality Rate due to Malaria in a given Community.” She intimated that such a proposal would require among others, an environmentalist, to research on mosquito breeding places in that area and an editor to check and correct grammatical, typographical and other errors in the proposal.

Overall, she stressed on the need for hard work in the pursuit of grants and in the entire process of grant writing – “It is only through hard work and dedication that we can deliver a strong economy and create opportunities for all”, she remarked. Dr Makuku cited how in 2020, Prof. William Bazeyo, an academician in Uganda won a UGX 185 billion grant which benefited his country through the Makerere University and the Ministry of Health by determination and hard work, as an example. According to her, this was an unprecedented situation.

At the end of the session, Dr. Makuku highlighted the need to have sound knowledge and skills in academic writing and research methodology. She indicated that these are some of the workshops the AAU offers at international and institutional levels. She also urged institutions who are non- AAU members to register and become members to help take African Higher and Tertiary Education to the highest level. Participants and stakeholders in general, were also encouraged to visit the AAU website (www.aau.org) and blog (blog.aau.org) for further information on the Association, and its various initiatives.

By Pamela H. Boamah (Association of African Universities Workshops Unit)

TITLE: African Ministers of Higher Education and Key Stakeholders Meet in Banjul for the 8th Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) Regional Workshop

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana (November 8, 2022) – Stakeholders of the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) project will be convening in Banjul, The Gambia, for the 8th bi-annual meeting to be held from 14th-17th November 2022. The meeting will bring together Ministers of Higher Education and project government representatives from the 11 participating African countries, the leaders of the fifty-three (53) Centers of Excellence, subject matter experts, key higher education stakeholders, policy think tanks, and partners such as the World Bank, the French Development Agency (AFD) and the Association of African Universities (AAU).
