The workshop fosters an environment of knowledge sharing and networking between the centers and relevant agencies, and provides in-person collaborative opportunities for the exchange of regional knowledge. The necessary tools and guidelines to facilitate effective project implementation and sustainability are shared with all centers, strengthening partnerships and networks whilst ensuring quality standards are maintained. The meeting seeks to provide implementation support and share global best practices with centers on the project objectives, especially development impact, entrepreneurship and innovation, gender initiatives, digital transformation, and institutional impact activities.

In line with students’ participation in this high-level meeting, winners of the maiden edition of the Student Innovation Research Award (SIRA) will be recognized. At least the best 15 ACE Impact students competitively selected for the SIRA will be awarded during the closing ceremony for outstanding competitive projects that offer solutions and innovative ideas in transformative research and interdisciplinary collaborations. Furthermore, students from the University of Applied Science, Engineering, and Technology (USET) in The Gambia will be given the opportunity to share their innovative research outputs through a poster exhibition to be held on November 15, 2022.

All activities, including the Opening and Closing ceremonies will be hosted at the OIC Conference Centre in Banjul, The Gambia. Virtual participation is available for stakeholders that may want to join online. The opening and closing sessions of the workshop will be held on the 15th and 18th of November, respectively, at 8:00 GMT. The special guest-of-honor for the opening session is His Excellency Adama Barrow, the President of the Republic of The Gambia.

The workshop will be preceded by a closed-door Ministerial/Steering Committee meeting on 14th November 2022. The Ministers of Higher Education and project government representatives from the 11 participating countries together with key partners will take stock of the progress made thus far and make recommendations towards the sustainability of the project.

The ACE Impact project remains committed to training the next generation of experts in priority areas such as Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM); Agriculture, Environment, Applied Social Science, Education, and Health with the aim of promoting sustainable growth and development in Africa.

Please visit the event website for details of the meeting Agenda among other relevant information.

– END –

For further information, contact

The World Bank: Hadijja Jawara, hjawara1@worldbank.org

The AAU: Millicent Kyei, makyei@aau.org

The Gambia: Maya Faal, mayafaal10@gmail.com

Background Information

The Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence (ACE) is a World Bank initiative in collaboration with governments of participating countries to support higher education institutions specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Agriculture, Health, Environment and Social Science/Applied Science and Education. It is the first World Bank project aimed at building the capacities of higher education institutions in Africa through the promotion of regional specialization among participating universities in areas that address specific common regional development challenges. It further aims to strengthen the capacities of these universities to deliver high-quality training and applied research, as well as meet the demand for skills required for Africa’s development. The first phase (ACE I) was launched in 2014 with 22 Centers of Excellence in Nine (9) West and Central African countries; Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, and Togo. The second phase (ACE II) was launched in East and Southern Africa with 24 centers across Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. Based on the initial successes, the World Bank, and the French Development Agency (AFD) in collaboration with the African governments, launched the ACE Impact Project in 2019 to further strengthen post-graduate training and applied research in existing fields and support new fields that are essential for Africa’s economic growth. Under ACE Impact, there are 53 ACEs specializing in the broad thematic areas of STEM, agriculture, health, environment and social/applied science and education. For more information on the ACE Impact Project, visit https://ace.aau.org

About the Organizers

Association of African Universities (AAU): The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the Voice of Higher Education in Africa. AAU aims to improve the quality of African Higher Education and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of Higher Education Institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting Higher Education in Africa. The AAU is the Regional Facilitation Unit of the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence for Development Impact project.

World Bank Group: The World Bank Group is a multilateral development institution that works to reduce poverty and boost shared prosperity. Its subsidiary IDA (International Development Association) finances the Africa Centers of Excellence series of projects. The World Bank’s International Development Association (IDA), established in 1960, helps the world’s poorest countries by providing grants and low to zero-interest loans for projects and programs that boost economic growth, reduce poverty, and improve poor people’s lives. IDA is one of the largest sources of assistance for the world’s 74 poorest countries, 39 of which are in Africa. Resources from IDA bring positive change to the 1.3 billion people who live in IDA countries. Since 1960, IDA has provided $458 billion to 114 countries. Annual commitments have averaged about $29 billion over the last three years (FY19-FY21), with about 70 percent going to Africa.

French Development Agency (AFD): For more than 75 years, the French Development Agency (AFD) has been fighting global poverty by supporting policies and investments that benefit the poorest populations. Strengthening the social link between individuals, groups, and territories are now at the heart of its actions in education, health, employment, urban planning, climate, and biodiversity. The French Development Agency (AFD) is the ACE Impact project co-financier.

TITLE: Impact100 DC Fellowship 2026: Fully Funded Philanthropy Fellowship for Women Ages 21–39 in the Washington, DC Region

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Impact100 DC Fellowship 2026 offers an opportunity for women between the ages of 21 and 39 who are interested in philanthropy and community impact but may not have the financial resources to become full members of Impact100 DC.

The fellowship allows participants to experience collective giving firsthand, take part in the organization’s grant review process, contribute to community activities, and develop their leadership and philanthropic skills. Fellows become full members from the beginning of the fellowship at no cost, allowing them to participate alongside other Impact100 DC members without having to pay the standard membership contribution.

Applications for the fellowship are currently open, with applications due October 15, 2026.

What Is the Impact100 DC Fellowship?

The Impact100 DC Fellowship is designed for women who want to learn about philanthropy through direct participation rather than simply observing from the sidelines.

The program gives Fellows the opportunity to become actively involved in how philanthropic resources are distributed and how grants can contribute to positive change in the community.

Through the fellowship, participants experience the process of collective giving and help shape how Impact100 DC grants affect the community.

Rather than requiring Fellows to make the standard financial contribution associated with membership, the fellowship provides qualifying participants with full membership at no cost.

This creates an opportunity for women who are interested in philanthropy but may not have the financial resources to join Impact100 DC through the regular membership route.

Experience Collective Giving Firsthand

One of the central features of the Impact100 DC Fellowship is the opportunity to experience collective giving directly.

Collective giving involves people coming together to pool resources and participate collectively in decisions about how those resources are distributed through grants.

For Fellows, this means gaining practical exposure to the grantmaking process and understanding how philanthropic decisions can influence organizations and communities.

Fellows are not passive participants. They are expected to become involved in the organization’s activities and contribute to the grant review process.

Full Membership From Day One at No Cost

A major feature of the fellowship is that Fellows become full members from the beginning of the fellowship at no cost.

The program emphasizes that Fellows do not simply observe Impact100 DC’s activities. Instead, they participate as members and contribute to the organization’s work.

Fellows are expected to:

Serve on at least one grant review committee.

Contribute their skills to outreach, events, or communications.

Connect with Impact100 DC members.

Attend events and member activities.

Participate actively in the community.

Develop their leadership experience through involvement in the organization.

This structure allows Fellows to gain practical experience while also contributing their own skills and perspectives.

Grant Review Committee Participation

Participation in the grant review process is a required component of the fellowship.

Each Fellow must serve on at least one grant review committee.

This gives Fellows direct experience with an important aspect of philanthropy: reviewing grant opportunities and participating in the process through which philanthropic resources can support community organizations.

For women interested in nonprofit organizations, social impact, community development, charitable giving, or philanthropy, this experience can provide an opportunity to better understand how grantmaking works in practice.

Outreach

Events

Communications

This means the fellowship is not limited to grant review. Fellows can also become involved in activities that help build and maintain the Impact100 DC community.

Networking and Community Building

Another component of the fellowship is the opportunity to connect with existing Impact100 DC members.

Fellows are encouraged to:

Attend organizational events.

Participate in member activities.

Build relationships within the Impact100 DC community.

Develop their leadership abilities.

NASA is offering an exciting opportunity for students interested in communications, journalism, multimedia production, public engagement, digital media, photography, marketing, graphic design, and science communication to gain hands-on professional experience through its Multimedia, Social Media, Public Engagement, and Internal Communications Internship.

Hosted at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) in Greenbelt, Maryland, the internship provides students with the opportunity to work alongside experienced writers, multimedia producers, public affairs professionals, and experience designers. Successful interns will contribute to communications activities connected to some of NASA’s most significant scientific missions and discoveries.

The opportunity is designed for students who are passionate about storytelling and interested in translating complex scientific information into engaging content for diverse audiences. Interns may work on content and campaigns related to NASA missions such as the Hubble Space Telescope, James Webb Space Telescope, Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, Artemis lunar exploration, Earth observation satellites, and solar science missions.

The application deadline is September 14, 2026.

About the NASA Communications Internship

NASA internships provide educational, hands-on experiences that allow students to explore research, operations, technology, communications, and other professional fields connected to the agency’s work.

This particular internship focuses on science communication and public engagement. NASA is seeking students who can help communicate scientific discoveries, space exploration activities, technological developments, and educational initiatives to the public through compelling stories and creative media.

Students will become part of a dynamic communications environment where storytelling intersects with science, technology, creativity, and public engagement.

Gain Experience Communicating NASA’s Scientific Discoveries

One of the most exciting aspects of the internship is the opportunity to contribute to communications surrounding major NASA science missions.

NASA’s communications teams are responsible for helping the public understand scientific discoveries and exploration activities. Interns may gain exposure to projects involving some of the world’s most recognized space science programs.

These may include stories and communications related to:

Hubble Space Telescope

The Hubble Space Telescope has transformed humanity’s understanding of the universe through decades of observations and discoveries. Communications professionals help translate complex astronomical research into stories that can be understood and appreciated by global audiences.

James Webb Space Telescope

The James Webb Space Telescope is one of NASA’s most significant scientific observatories. Its discoveries generate enormous public interest, requiring skilled communicators who can explain groundbreaking research through articles, videos, graphics, social media, and other forms of media.

Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

Students may also gain exposure to communications related to NASA’s Roman Space Telescope and its mission to explore fundamental questions about the universe.

Artemis Program

NASA’s Artemis missions represent a new era of lunar exploration. Communications surrounding Artemis involve public engagement, multimedia storytelling, digital campaigns, educational outreach, and media relations.

Earth Science and Remote Sensing

NASA’s Earth-observing satellites provide critical information about our changing planet. Communicators play an important role in sharing scientific findings about climate, weather, environmental change, ecosystems, and other Earth science topics.

Solar Science

NASA also studies the Sun and regularly communicates discoveries from solar missions. Students interested in translating complex scientific concepts into engaging stories may find this area particularly rewarding.

TITLE: PRESS RELEASE – The Association of African Universities (AAU) to Organise its 20th COREVIP on ‘The Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16 – 25)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the Arab Republic of Egypt and Al-Azhar University, is organising its 20th biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) at the Al-Azhar International Conference Centre, in Cairo, Egypt from 8-11 July 2019.

Conference Theme and Subthemes

This year’s conference is being held under the theme ‘The Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting the Continental Education for Strategy for Africa’ and is set to convene distinguished scholars and practitioners to discuss and exchange experiences on the main conference theme and the subthemes indicated below;

Sub-Theme 1: Focus on the science and mathematics curricula in youth training and disseminate scientific knowledge and culture in society

Sub-Theme 2: Expand TVET opportunities at tertiary levels and strengthen linkages between the world of work and education and training systems

Sub-Theme 3: Revitalize and expand tertiary education, research and innovation to address continental challenges and promote competitiveness.

Sub-Theme 4: Promote peace education and conflict prevention and resolution at all levels of education and for all age groups.

Sub-Theme 5: Improve management of education systems as well as build and enhance capacity for data collection, management, harness the capacity of ICT to improve access, quality and management of education and training systems.

Sub-Theme 6: Promote mobility through harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation systems.

Sub-Theme 7: Identify new directions in improving management of education through enhanced capacity for data collection and management, research and scholarship and efficient governance of HEIs in Africa.

The over 1500 expected participants of the COREVIP will comprise executive heads of AAU member institutions, top-notch African scholars, representatives of student bodies, as well as representatives of sub-regional, regional and international organisations. Members from the donor and development agencies that partner with the AAU in carrying out its mandate of improving the quality of higher education in Africa will also be in attendance.Additionally, Ministers of Higher Education and other higher education policy think tanks will partake in this august conference.

The Conference will provide an excellent opportunity for leaders of African higher education institutions, particularly the current member institutions of the AAU, to exchange experiences and draw on the lessons from the theme as well as serve as an opportunity to hear from both regional and international organisations involved in higher education initiatives.

About COREVIP

The Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) is an assembly of the Chief Executive Officers of AAU member institutions or their representatives. The Conference is held every two years with the purpose of collectively examining themes identified as common concerns and priorities for the development of higher education in member institutions and Africa in general; making recommendations primarily to members, as well as to the Governing Board of the Association, and to the Secretariat; and acting as a mid-term forum for taking stock of the implementation of the decisions of the General Conference and recommending corrective actions.

For further information on COREVIP 2019 – participation, exhibitions and sponsorship, please visit: https://events.aau.org/corevip/

About The Association of African Universities

The Association of African Universities (AAU), is an international non‑governmental organization set up in November 1967 by universities in Africa to promote cooperation among themselves and between them and the international academic community. With a current membership of 400 institutions of higher learning drawn from all regions within the continent, the AAU is the representative voice of the African higher education community.

The mission of the AAU is to raise the quality of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to African development by fostering cooperation and collaboration among its member institutions, providing support to their core functions of teaching, learning and research.

TITLE: Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program, Spring 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Application now open for the next competition of the
Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program (CADFP)
DEADLINE: February 28, 2022 at 11:59 PM EST

The Institute of International Education (IIE) is pleased to announce that the next round of competition for the CADFP is now open.
Apply now or share this message with those who might be interested.

What is the CADFP?
The CADFP is a scholar exchange program for African higher education institutions to host a diaspora scholar for 14-90 days for projects in curriculum co-development, research collaboration and graduate student teaching and mentoring.

Who is eligible?

Accredited universities in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania and Uganda, and member institutions of the African Research Universities Alliance (ARUA) (including Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia; the University of Rwanda; Cheikh Anta Diop University, Senegal; and University of Mauritius) can submit a project request to host a scholar.

Scholars born in Africa, who live in the United States or Canada and work in an accredited college or university in either of those two countries, can apply online to be placed on a roster of candidates for a fellowship. Scholars must hold a terminal degree in their field and may hold any academic rank.

How do I apply?
Links and information about the African host institution project request application, scholar roster application and review guidelines are posted on the CADFP website. Interested parties are invited to register for one of the informational webinars:

Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #1: Thursday, January 13 at 11 AM Eastern US Time
Information for Potential Hosts: Wednesday, January 19 at 10 AM South Africa Standard Time
Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #2: Thursday, January 27 at 12 noon Eastern US Time

After the webinars, the recordings will be posted via the YouTube Channel.

Timeline
The deadline for project requests from host universities and scholar applications for diaspora scholars is February 28, 2022 at 11:59 pm EST. Selection decisions will be made in March-April 2022; project visits can begin as early as June 1, 2022 and must be completed by November 30, 2023.

Benefits
Selected fellows receive a $150/day stipend, visa costs, limited health insurance, round-trip international air travel and ground transportation costs to and from home and the U.S./Canadian airport. Selected Host Fellows and Diaspora Fellows can apply for supplemental funds to be used for fieldwork, publication costs and workshops. The CADFP Team manages the fellowships and payments to fellows. Host institutions are encouraged to provide cost-share for the fellow’s meals, lodging and in-country transportation.

For more information on the fellowship program and application process, as well as the projects of current fellows, please write to AfricanDiaspora@iie.org visit their website and communities on Facebook and Twitter.

TITLE: Jens Hertkorn, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Jens Hertkorn

Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics

Research Interests

Jens’ research interests lie broadly at the interdisciplinary interface between atomic and condensed matter physics and in quantum simulation.

During his PhD Jens used Bose-Einstein condensates of strongly magnetic atoms to investigate the formation of an exotic quantum phase known as supersolid where the frictionless flow of a superfluid and the crystalline order of a solid coexist. Jens investigated the collective excitations of such magnetic supersolids and showed that the crystallization mechanism is similar to that of liquid helium. He also predicted that these magnetic Bose-Einstein condensates can self-organize in honeycomb or labyrinthine structures which are candidates for new types of supersolids.

In general the possibility of using a quantum many-body system for realizing different phases of matter relies on a strong and controllable coupling between particles. Jens is interested in building interactions from a single- or few-particle level by trapping particles in optical lattices or tweezers enabling the quantum simulation of strongly correlated condensed matter systems. Using such bottom-up approaches, Jens is interested in understanding and engineering correlations connected to exotic behaviour such as induced superconductivity seen in the field of twistronics. Jens also sees potential in improving the preparation of the quantum state and the classification of correlations using neural networks.

Biographical Sketch

Jens grew up in Stuttgart, Germany. Fascinated by the way humans reason Jens wondered how accurate statements could be made about systems as complex as a human brain. During his teenage years the precise language used in a physics colloquium excited Jens to pursue physics for understanding such complexities in nature.

Jens received his BSc in physics in 2017 from the University of Stuttgart working with Maria Fyta, using density functional theory to understand the electronic structure of defective nanodiamonds. For his MSc in physics Jens joined Tilman Pfau’s group in Stuttgart investigating supersolidity of quantum droplets in ultracold dipolar gases theoretically and graduated 2019 with distinction. Jens continued his PhD in Pfau’s group investigating self-organization of dipolar quantum gases beyond the quantum droplet regime, built a new quantum gas experiment within the group, and independently received funding to probe such self-organization experimentally. Jens graduates with his PhD in physics in 2024.

Timing of academic requirements:

Please be sure to carefully examine each advisee’s progress chart with particular attention to Specialty and Breadth requirements not yet satisfied, and encourage your students not to postpone taking the subjects needed to satisfy these requirements.

Requests for substitutions of academic requirements:

Your advisee may enquire about the possibility of substituting another subject either for one of the two (or three, for NUPAT and NUPAX students) designated specialty subjects, or for one of the required two breadth subjects. Information about requesting substitutions is available in detail here, but in brief:

Specialty subjects: Approval comes from the Division Head; the student should obtain the academic advisor’s permission in writing, and then forward the request to the Division Head. This process holds even for Harvard subjects that have been routinely substituted for MIT subjects.

Breadth subjects: Approval comes from the Graduate Requirements Coordinator (Mehran Kardar); the student should obtain the academic advisor’s permission in writing, and then forward the request to Prof. Kardar. No student may receive approval for a substitution until one of the pre-approved breadth subjects has been completed successfully. Note: an appropriate breadth subject is not simply one that is different in nature from the student’s area of specialty; the approved subjects were selected based on being broad overviews of the fields we teach, and subjects that are intended only for specialists in an area are generally not appropriate as breadth subjects.

TITLE: WHOI deploys ocean sensors ahead of Hurricane Erin as part of the SASCWATCH project funded by the Office of Naval Research

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The next frontier in understanding the coupled ocean–wave–atmosphere system requires detailed investigations of turbulence and wave dynamics within tropical cyclones, using a combination of observational and modeling approaches. To address this need, a new research initiative — the Study on Air–Sea Coupling with Waves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High Winds (SASCWATCH) — was launched this year with funding from the Office of Naval Research. The goal of SASCWATCH is to advance understanding of air–sea–wave interactions under extreme wind conditions through coordinated in situ observations, mesoscale coupled modeling, and high-resolution turbulence simulations. The observational program centers on co-located measurements of ocean, wave, and atmospheric turbulence properties using an integrated system of ocean drifters with wave measurement capabilities, profiling floats equipped with ocean currents and waves, and uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) for direct flux measurements in the boundary layer. In 2025 ahead of Hurricane Erin, a major hurricane in the western Atlantic, we deployed a large (200 km × 200 km) array of wave drifters, profiling floats, and AXBTs in its path. Erin generated an exceptionally large wave field, with observed significant wave heights exceeding 10 meters and an extensive cold wake.

Video credit: US Air Force

For more information, visit Air-Deployed Profiling Instruments Group and SASCWATCH: Study on Air-Sea Coupling with WAves, Turbulence, and Clouds at High winds

Each accepted student will be eligible for up to $500 in financial assistance, dramatically reducing the cost barrier to advanced business education for public sector professionals across Africa.

Nations that have achieved rapid and sustainable economic growth have done so by developing the most productive resource in any nation: human capital.”

Vice-Chancellor Prof. Bashiru Koroma reinforced this commitment, “Collaborating with eLearnLXD enables us to deliver an MBA that is both accessible and aligned with the region’s economic and professional priorities. This initiative represents our dedication to building public sector capacity through targeted educational opportunities that support the nation’s human capital development agenda.”

“This initiative shows what’s possible when African institutions embrace technology for inclusion. We are particularly focused on creating pathways for civil servants who represent the backbone of public service delivery across the continent,” Brook Negussie, CEO of eLearnAfricaLMS, noted in highlighting the transformative potential of the partnership.

The program has already garnered positive feedback from current participants, with one student noting, “This is a different ball game. The quality is exceptional — the standard is on another level.”

Aligning with both ECOWAS Vision 2050 and the African Union’s Agenda 2063, the online MBA program emphasizes education and innovation as key drivers of sustainable development. The curriculum strategically integrates core business subjects with essential modern competencies in digital leadership, ethics, and applied research, preparing graduates for critical leadership roles, including Operations Manager, CFO, HR Director, IT Project Manager, and Policy Advisor.

TITLE: UK MEET Fellowship 2026 for Journalists and Digital Content Creators in Ghana and Nigeria: Science, Technology and Emerging Media Training with Imperial College London

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the UK–West Africa Media Excellence in Emerging Technologies (MEET) Fellowship 2026, a professional development programme designed to strengthen the capacity of journalists and digital content creators in Ghana and Nigeria to report accurately, creatively and responsibly on science, innovation and emerging technologies.

The programme is delivered by the British High Commission, working through its teams in Accra, Lagos and Abuja, in partnership with Imperial College London through Imperial Global Ghana.

The UK MEET Fellowship responds to a growing need for media professionals who can take complicated scientific and technological subjects and translate them into accurate, engaging and accessible journalism for diverse audiences.

Selected participants will take part in online preparation and an intensive six-night residential training programme in either Ghana or Nigeria. The Fellowship combines science and technology reporting with practical digital storytelling and opportunities to engage directly with researchers, policymakers, innovators and industry professionals.

Participants will also develop an original story concept during the programme. On the final day of the residential training, Fellows will pitch their stories for the opportunity to receive funding to produce and publish them. A subset of participants selected through the pitch process will subsequently take part in a fully funded, week-long knowledge-exchange visit to London, including engagement with Imperial College London.

The programme particularly encourages applications from women, journalists and creators outside major urban centres, applicants from underrepresented regions, and marginalized groups.

The application deadline is:

22 September 2026 at 23:45 GMT

Applications must be submitted through the official online form.

About the UK Media Excellence in Emerging Technologies Fellowship

The Media Excellence in Emerging Technologies Fellowship, commonly referred to as the MEET Fellowship or UK MEET Fellowship, is designed to strengthen media professionals’ ability to communicate developments in science, innovation and technology, referred to throughout the programme as SIT.

Scientific and technological developments increasingly influence almost every part of public life. Artificial intelligence is changing work, education and communication. Climate and environmental risks affect communities, infrastructure and national planning. Biomedical technologies raise new possibilities and difficult ethical questions. Electronic waste and circular-economy approaches influence environmental policy, health, employment and manufacturing.

Yet these subjects are often difficult to report well.

Journalists and digital storytellers need to understand enough of the underlying science and technology to distinguish evidence from hype, identify credible experts, ask informed questions, explain uncertainty and communicate technical information without making it inaccessible to general audiences.

The UK MEET Fellowship is built around this challenge.

Rather than focusing only on conventional journalism techniques, the programme brings together science understanding, public communication, emerging technology, ethics and digital storytelling.

What Is the Main Goal of the Fellowship?

The programme aims to build the capacity of media professionals for excellence in:

Science reporting

Innovation reporting

Technology reporting

Digital storytelling

Public communication of technical information

Its central purpose is to help participants translate complex scientific and technological ideas into content that is:

Accurate

Accessible

Engaging

Relevant

Responsible

Useful to diverse audiences

The Fellowship therefore combines subject knowledge with practical media skills.

Participants are not expected simply to become experts in one technology. Instead, the programme aims to give journalists and digital creators a stronger framework for approaching unfamiliar and rapidly changing scientific subjects.

Who Is Behind the UK MEET Fellowship?

The programme is delivered through a partnership involving major UK institutions.

British High Commission

The British High Commission is a funding and delivery partner for the Fellowship.

Applications from Ghana and Nigeria will be reviewed through the appropriate British High Commission teams associated with the applicant’s country track.

The official application information explains that participant information will be shared between Imperial College London and the relevant British High Commission teams for purposes including:

Eligibility screening

Shortlisting

Selection

Programme auditing

Evaluation

The initiative also connects with broader UK objectives around innovation, science partnerships and evidence-informed policymaking.

Imperial College London

Imperial College London participates through Imperial Global Ghana.

Imperial brings substantial scientific and technological expertise to the Fellowship, creating opportunities for journalists and creators to interact with researchers rather than learning about science communication only through conventional media-training approaches.

The programme’s UK knowledge-exchange component also includes time at Imperial College London for selected pitch award winners.

What Will Participants Learn?

The Fellowship is organized around several thematic areas and five core skills.

The major themes include:

Artificial intelligence

Climate and environmental risk

Biomedical innovation

Circular economy and electronic waste

Other related science, innovation and technology issues

Across these subjects, participants will develop five central competencies:

Understanding complex scientific and technological concepts

Effective science communication

Navigating emerging technologies for the public good

Understanding ethical considerations in science, innovation and technology reporting

Engaging directly and effectively with experts

These competencies are intended to be transferable across different media beats.

A journalist may currently focus on health but later need to report on AI. A digital creator may focus on climate but encounter new questions around technology, agriculture or energy. The Fellowship therefore aims to strengthen the underlying skills required to approach complex evidence responsibly.

Theme 1: Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence has quickly become one of the most important emerging-technology reporting areas.

Journalists increasingly need to understand issues connected with:

Generative AI

Automation

Algorithmic decision-making

AI policy

Data

Misinformation

AI and employment

AI and education

AI in healthcare

Governance

Privacy

Bias

Ethics

Public-sector uses of AI

Good AI reporting requires more than repeating claims from technology companies or presenting every new tool as revolutionary.

Journalists need to ask questions such as:

What can the technology actually do?

What evidence supports the claims being made?

Who developed it?

What data does it use?

Who may benefit?

Who could be disadvantaged?

What safeguards exist?

What are the relevant regulatory debates?

The Fellowship aims to equip participants with stronger tools for addressing questions of this kind.

Theme 2: Climate and Environmental Risk

Climate and environmental reporting often involves complicated data, scientific uncertainty and long-term trends.

Potential reporting issues may include:

Climate change

Flooding

Extreme heat

Pollution

Coastal risks

Environmental degradation

Climate adaptation

Resilience

Energy transitions

Environmental health

Journalists need to communicate these issues without either overstating evidence or minimizing genuine risks.

For Ghanaian and Nigerian media professionals, these subjects can also be connected to very local questions affecting communities, livelihoods and public policy.

Theme 3: Biomedical Innovation

Biomedical innovation creates important opportunities for journalism at the intersection of science, health and society.

Relevant subjects may include:

Medical technologies

Diagnostics

Biotechnology

Public health innovation

Pharmaceutical research

Genomics

Health technology

Digital health

Clinical research

Reporting on these issues requires journalists to understand not only what a new technology promises, but also what evidence exists, which stage of development it has reached and what uncertainties remain.

Theme 4: Circular Economy and E-Waste

The Fellowship also addresses the circular economy and electronic waste.

A circular-economy approach seeks to reduce waste and extend the useful life of materials through practices such as:

Reuse

Repair

Recycling

Resource recovery

More sustainable production

Better product design

E-waste introduces additional questions around:

Environmental contamination

Informal recycling

Health

Technology consumption

International waste flows

Regulation

Employment

Industrial policy

These subjects illustrate why emerging-technology journalism increasingly requires reporters to connect science with economics, politics, health and social issues.

Five Core Skills Used Throughout the Programme

The programme does not treat each thematic topic as an isolated subject.

Instead, five skills are applied throughout the training.

1. Understanding Complex Concepts

Participants will strengthen their ability to understand scientific or technological concepts well enough to report them accurately.

Journalists do not need to become scientists themselves, but they should be able to recognize:

What they understand

What they do not understand

What questions need to be asked

Which experts should be consulted

Which claims require verification

2. Effective Science Communication

Participants will work on communicating technical subjects clearly without sacrificing accuracy.

This is especially important when producing material for audiences that may have little specialist knowledge.

Effective science communication involves finding the balance between:

Technical precision and public accessibility.

3. Emerging Technology for the Public Good

The Fellowship also encourages participants to consider how new technologies affect society.

Rather than presenting innovation as automatically positive or negative, journalists can investigate:

Who gains access

Who is excluded

What risks emerge

What policy choices are involved

Whether technology addresses an actual public need

4. Ethics in Science and Technology Reporting

Ethical considerations are explicitly included in the programme.

These may involve questions around:

Accuracy

Source selection

Sensationalism

Privacy

Conflicts of interest

Representation

Uncertainty

Public harm

Responsible use of digital tools

Ethical reporting becomes particularly important where scientific issues involve health, vulnerable populations or technologies whose long-term effects remain uncertain.

5. Direct Engagement With Experts

Participants will learn through direct interaction with:

Researchers

Policymakers

Innovators

Industry professionals

This can help journalists build confidence in interviewing experts and develop relationships that may continue after the Fellowship.

Six-Night Residential Training

One of the major components of the UK MEET Fellowship is an intensive:

Six-night residential training camp.

The programme runs from Sunday evening through Friday evening.

Participants attend the residential programme in their country of residence.

Therefore:

Ghana-based Fellows attend the Ghana residential programme.

Nigeria-based Fellows attend the Nigeria residential programme.

Applicants may only apply through the country track in which they are currently based.

Programme Dates

Applicants need to be available for all relevant programme components.

Online Pre-Training

The programme begins with:

Two short online sessions plus pre-reading

during the:

Week of 5 October 2026

This is referred to as Phase 0.

Ghana Residential Programme

The official detailed call identifies the Ghana training as the:

Week of 12 October 2026

Because the residential runs from Sunday evening to Friday evening, participants should expect the residential period to begin around Sunday, 11 October, followed by the training week beginning Monday, 12 October.

Nigeria Residential Programme

The Nigeria training is scheduled for the:

Week of 19 October 2026

With the Sunday-evening residential structure, participants should expect arrival around Sunday, 18 October, followed by the programme week beginning Monday, 19 October.

UK Knowledge Exchange

For selected pitch award winners, the UK visit is planned for the:

Week of 30 November 2026

Applicants should note carefully that the UK knowledge-exchange visit is not automatically guaranteed to everyone who attends the residential training.

It is intended for a selected subset of participants associated with the story-pitch award stage.

Digital Skills Development

An important part of the Fellowship is hands-on digital storytelling.

Training includes areas such as:

Platform strategy

Short-form video

Data storytelling

Visual design

These skills reflect the rapidly changing ways audiences consume journalism.

Media professionals increasingly need to understand how the same story may need to be adapted for:

News websites

Social media

Short-form video

Visual platforms

Mobile audiences

Data-led storytelling formats

The Fellowship therefore recognizes that strong science communication depends not only on the accuracy of information but also on how that information is presented.

Networking Opportunities

Participants will have structured opportunities to engage with:

Leading researchers

Policymakers

Innovators

Industry professionals

Fellow journalists

Digital content creators

These relationships can be particularly valuable for science and technology journalists because reliable reporting often depends on access to credible specialist sources.

A journalist who develops a network of researchers during the Fellowship may later be better positioned to obtain:

Expert interpretation

Background briefings

Technical clarification

Alternative perspectives

Leads for future stories

Pitch for Story Funding

The Fellowship moves beyond classroom-style training by asking participants to develop an original journalism story concept.

On the final day of the residential programme, participants will pitch their developed idea for a chance to receive an award to:

Produce and publish the story.

This creates a direct bridge between training and real media output.

The public call does not state the monetary value of the pitch award.

Therefore, applicants should not assume or advertise a specific amount unless organizers subsequently provide one.

What Could Make a Strong Story Pitch?

Although the programme does not prescribe one formula for a successful pitch, a promising story concept would likely benefit from having:

A clear science, innovation or technology connection

Strong relevance to the public

A clearly identifiable audience

Evidence of a genuine problem or question

Potential access to credible experts

Original reporting potential

Clear public-interest value

An appropriate digital storytelling approach

Candidates may benefit from thinking about possible story ideas even before entering the programme.

Fully Funded UK Knowledge-Exchange Visit

A selected subset of participants will have the opportunity to join a:

Fully funded, week-long knowledge-exchange visit to London.

The programme includes time at Imperial College London.

The visit is scheduled for the week of:

30 November 2026

The detailed eligibility guidance also requires applicants to hold, or be capable of obtaining in time, a valid international passport because some participants may be selected for this international component.

Again, the distinction is important:

Residential Fellowship participation does not automatically guarantee selection for the UK visit.

Minimum Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy all seven minimum eligibility requirements.

The organizers explicitly state that applicants who do not meet every minimum requirement will not be able to submit a complete application.

1. Applicants Must Be at Least 18

Applicants must be:

18 years old or above.

There is no maximum age stated in the official call.

2. Applicants Must Be Based in Ghana or Nigeria

Applicants must currently be based in:

Ghana, or

Nigeria

Candidates must apply through the country track where they are currently based.

Applicants cannot choose another country’s track simply because its residential dates are more convenient.

3. Applicants Must Be Journalists or Eligible Digital Content Creators

Applicants must currently work as one of the following:

Journalists

Working in:

Print media

Broadcast media

Online media

or:

Social Media Content Creators

Creators must have an:

Active and publicly viewable presence

on at least one relevant platform.

The official call specifically names:

TikTok

Instagram

YouTube

For creators, that public presence must feature content relevant to science, innovation or technology.

This is an important expansion beyond conventional newsroom journalism.

The Fellowship is therefore open not only to journalists employed by traditional media organizations, but also to qualifying digital-first creators.

4. Applicants Need at Least Five Recent SIT Content Pieces

Applicants must have produced at least:

Five original pieces of content

on science, innovation or technology-related themes within the:

Previous 12 months.

Applicants must have links available to share.

Eligible subject matter can include areas such as:

Climate

Health

Technology

Agriculture

Energy

Related science and innovation themes

This requirement demonstrates that the programme is looking for applicants who already have some practical engagement with relevant subjects.

It is not simply an introductory programme for someone who has never produced any science- or technology-related content.

5. Full Attendance Is Mandatory

Applicants must be able to participate in:

Phase 0 online preparation

Full in-country residential programme

The official call clearly states:

Partial attendance is not possible.

This means applicants should compare the programme schedule carefully against:

Work obligations

Travel

Other professional commitments

Personal responsibilities

before submitting an application.

6. International Passport Requirement

Applicants must either:

Already hold a valid international passport, or

Be capable of obtaining one in time

This is necessary because selected participants may travel to the United Kingdom for the knowledge-exchange component.

Applicants without a passport at the application stage are not necessarily automatically excluded, provided they are genuinely able to obtain one within the required timeframe.

7. Professional English Ability

Applicants must be comfortable:

Working and communicating professionally in English.

The programme does not state that candidates need to submit an IELTS, TOEFL or other formal English-language certificate.

The requirement concerns functional professional communication.

Selection Criteria and Scoring

Candidates who satisfy all seven eligibility conditions move to competitive evaluation.

The official call provides a clear weighted selection framework.

Relevance to SIT Themes – 35%

This is the largest component of the assessment.

Applicants will be evaluated on demonstrated experience reporting or creating content on:

Science

Innovation

Technology

Related subjects

This means applicants should choose previous work examples strategically.

Quality of Previous Work – 30%

Nearly one-third of the evaluation is based on the quality of the applicant’s previous journalism or digital content.

Applicants will provide links to their work.

Reviewers can therefore examine actual evidence of the candidate’s:

Reporting

Storytelling

Accuracy

Audience communication

Digital media skills

Potential for Impact – 25%

Applicants need to explain clearly how participating in UK MEET could:

Improve their work

Expand their reach

Strengthen their journalism

Help communicate science more effectively

The programme will also consider alignment with broader FCDO goals, including:

Fostering innovation

Strengthening UK–Ghana partnerships

Strengthening UK–Nigeria partnerships

Promoting evidence-based policymaking

Applicants should therefore think beyond personal career development and explain how the programme could improve their wider professional impact.

Collaboration Readiness – 5%

Applicants may receive additional credit for demonstrating readiness to collaborate.

The call particularly mentions applicants who have already identified:

Researchers

Research areas

Research topics

whose work they would like to amplify.

This accounts for 5% of the assessment.

Diversity and Inclusion – 5%

The final weighted component considers:

Gender balance

Regional representation

Participation outside major urban centres

Inclusion of underrepresented voices

The programme aims for:

At least 40% women in its cohorts.

This does not mean that only women are eligible.

It means gender representation forms part of the cohort-building process.

Selection Criteria at a Glance

Criterion
Weight

Relevance to science, innovation and technology themes
35%

Quality of previous work
30%

Potential for impact
25%

Collaboration readiness
5%

Diversity and inclusion
5%

Applicants can use this weighting strategically.

Because 65% of the score comes from thematic relevance and previous work quality, choosing strong published work examples is likely to be particularly important.

Women Are Strongly Encouraged to Apply

Women applicants are explicitly encouraged.

The programme targets at least:

40% female representation

within its cohorts.

This is an encouragement and selection consideration rather than a women-only eligibility condition.

Applicants of other genders remain eligible if they satisfy the programme requirements.

Applicants Outside Major Cities Are Encouraged

The selection framework specifically values:

Regional representation, including locations outside major urban centres.

This is significant for journalists who might assume that applicants in Accra, Lagos or Abuja automatically have an advantage.

Media professionals based elsewhere in Ghana or Nigeria are expressly encouraged to participate.

Marginalized and Underrepresented Applicants

The programme also strongly encourages applications from:

Marginalized groups

Underrepresented voices

Underrepresented regions

The call does not restrict eligibility to any one racial, ethnic or social group.

Instead, diversity is treated as part of building a broader and more representative cohort.

How to Apply

Applicants must submit the official online application form.

Application form:
https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/ugjTfMLCWQ

The application begins with an eligibility screening process.

Applicants should therefore verify that they meet all seven minimum requirements before beginning.

The organizers also provide a detailed Call for Applications explaining:

Programme objectives

Benefits

Dates

Eligibility

Selection criteria

Application requirements

Information Provided Through the Application

The application process begins with basic information such as:

First name

Last name

Email address

Gender

How the applicant heard about the programme

Country track

The application then determines eligibility before allowing applicants to proceed with the full submission.

Because prior science and technology work forms a major part of selection, candidates should prepare links to at least five qualifying pieces of original work produced within the previous 12 months.

Data and Privacy

Imperial College London states that information collected through the application form will be used to:

Assess applications

Screen eligibility

Shortlist candidates

Make selection decisions

Conduct programme auditing

Conduct programme evaluation

Application information will also be accessible to the relevant British High Commission teams in accordance with the applicant’s country track.

Candidates should review the privacy information linked in the application before submission.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

1. Choose Your Five Strongest Work Samples Carefully

Do not simply submit the first five SIT-related pieces you can find.

Because previous work quality and thematic relevance together represent 65% of the selection weighting, choose examples that demonstrate:

Strong reporting

Originality

Public relevance

Clear explanation

Good sourcing

Appropriate use of evidence

2. Show Breadth or Depth in SIT Reporting

If you have reported repeatedly on one topic, demonstrate clear subject knowledge.

If your work covers multiple themes, explain how the Fellowship would help you build a more coherent science and technology reporting practice.

3. Explain Your Potential Impact Specifically

Avoid generic statements such as:

“I want to improve my journalism skills.”

Instead, explain what will change.

For example:

Will you establish a regular technology column?

Produce more evidence-based climate journalism?

Expand science reporting in your regional newsroom?

Build short-form video explainers?

Train colleagues?

Reach audiences currently underserved by science journalism?

Concrete plans make potential impact easier to understand.

4. Identify Researchers or Research Topics

Because collaboration readiness is assessed, applicants may strengthen their submission by identifying:

Researchers whose work interests them

Universities or laboratories

Emerging technology questions

Research fields deserving wider media coverage

This shows that the applicant is already thinking about journalism-research collaboration.

5. Think About Your Story Pitch in Advance

You do not need to arrive with a finished story.

However, having a promising direction can help you take fuller advantage of the residential programme.

Consider:

What emerging-technology issue affects your audience?

Who is missing from current coverage?

Where is there a gap between research and public understanding?

What question deserves original reporting?

6. Check Your Passport

Since pitch winners may travel to London soon after the residential training, passport preparation should not be left until the last minute.

The UK exchange is scheduled for the week of 30 November 2026, only several weeks after the Ghana and Nigeria residential programmes.

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted by:

22 September 2026 at 23:45 GMT

The call identifies GMT/Accra time for the deadline.

Applicants should submit early enough to avoid technical difficulties close to closing time.

imperialglobalghana@imperial.ac.uk

Conclusion

The UK Media Excellence in Emerging Technologies Fellowship 2026 offers journalists and digital content creators in Ghana and Nigeria an intensive opportunity to strengthen the quality of science, innovation and technology reporting in West Africa.

The programme goes considerably beyond a short journalism workshop. Participants will complete online preparation, join a six-night residential training programme, build practical skills in digital storytelling and engage directly with researchers, policymakers, innovators and industry professionals.

Training will address some of the most consequential emerging issues facing contemporary media, including artificial intelligence, climate and environmental risk, biomedical innovation, circular economy and electronic waste. At the same time, participants will develop transferable skills in interpreting complexity, communicating science, considering ethical questions and reporting emerging technologies in the public interest.

The programme also creates a practical pathway from learning to publication. Fellows will develop and pitch original stories, with selected pitches receiving an award to support production and publication. Selected participants will subsequently join a fully funded, week-long UK knowledge-exchange visit, including engagement at Imperial College London.

Eligibility is more specific than simply being a journalist in Ghana or Nigeria. Applicants must be at least 18, be currently based in one of the two countries, work as an eligible journalist or digital creator, have produced at least five original SIT-related pieces within the previous 12 months, commit to the entire training schedule, be able to obtain an international passport and work professionally in English.

Selection is competitive. Relevance to science, innovation and technology accounts for 35% of the assessment, quality of previous work for 30%, potential impact for 25%, collaboration readiness for 5%, and diversity and inclusion for 5%.

Women, applicants from underrepresented parts of Ghana and Nigeria, people outside major media centres and marginalized groups are particularly encouraged to apply.

The final deadline is:

22 September 2026 at 23:45 GMT

Apply through the official form.

TITLE: Manki Kim, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Manki Kim
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics, 2021-2024
Email: mk2427@mit.edu
Phone: (607) 261-9367
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, 6c-433
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

String Theory; Cosmology

Research Interests

Manki Kim’s research is centered on string theory and its applications in the physics of the early universe.

Despite the heroic achievements of string theory, fully explicit experimental predictions in string theory have been out of reach. To understand if string theory can describe our universe, or how it fails to do so, Manki thinks we should bring string theory under the scrutiny of experimental tests. Thus, his long-term goal is to experimentally test string theory through the physics of the early universe such as inflation, which is highly sensitive to the Planck scale physics.

The first step towards this direction is to show or disprove the existence of cosmologically realistic vacua in string theory. Manki has been working on string compactifications and topological string theory in efforts to construct cosmologically realistic string vacua, such as the de Sitter vacua of string theory.

Biographical Sketch

Manki was born and raised in South Korea. In 2016, he received a BS degree in physics and mathematics from KAIST (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology).

Later that year he went to Cornell University for PhD studies, working on particle phenomenology, and flavor and neutrino physics in particular.

A few months later, he switched his research field to string theory to work with Professor Liam McAllister. Manki is expected to complete his PhD in mid-2021.
