TITLE: Embracing Excellence and Empowering African Higher Education: Association of African Universities (AAU) Reflects on 2024 with Appreciation to Stakeholders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Dear Esteemed Members, Development Partners, and Stakeholders,

As we stand at the threshold of a new year, we take a moment to reflect on the transformative power of partnerships and collaboration. The AAU extends its heartfelt appreciation to all our stakeholders for your tireless support and unwavering commitment to our shared vision of empowering African higher education. Together, we achieved significant milestones in 2024, driving meaningful impact and progress. Our accomplishments would not have been possible without your dedication and contributions. With renewed energy and purpose, we look forward to building on our successes in the years to come. Our efforts will continue to focus on advancing the AAU’s new Strategic Plan (2024-2030), the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16–25), Agenda 2063, and the Global Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) among other key targets. We are deeply grateful for your immense contributions, which have been instrumental in our successes throughout 2024.

Looking ahead to 2025, we are thrilled to invite you to the AAU’s General Conference, scheduled to take place in July 2025 in Morocco. This premier gathering of higher education stakeholders in Africa promises to be an impactful and unforgettable experience. We encourage you to mark your calendars and join us to connect, share knowledge, and chart the course for the future of African higher education together.

In the spirit of the holiday season, we wish you joy, peace, and happiness. Please receive our Season’s Greetings Card (French, English, Arabic & Portuguese) and Video, accompanied by a summary of our notable accomplishments in 2024, outlined below:

Key Highlights of 2024

Thirteen Higher Education Institutions Successfully Joined AAU’s Membership in 2024: Between November 2023 and May 2024, the Secretariat received several applications through its online submission form. Following the review of these applications, and in line with the AAU’s Constitution, a total of 13 Universities were admitted as Full and Associate Members by the AAU’s governing structures. Furthermore, in line with our membership benefits commitments, the AAU organized a face-to-face capacity-building workshop targeting university Librarians. This event was hosted at the AAU’s Secretariat in Accra, Ghana, from 28th –31st May 2024 and brought together several of our members across the continent. Another capacity building activity focusing on Fostering International Partnerships in Higher Education Institutions in Africa, was organised jointly with the Women’s University in Africa in Harare, Zimbabwe from 24th – 26th September 2024. Other capacity building efforts for AAU members focussed on ICT Directors, Social Media Officers, Legal Officers in universities and Quality Assurance Units.

Toluca Cape Town Declaration on Diamond Open Access, 13 December 2024: The AAU Secretary General, Professor Olusola Oyewole led a large delegation of the African Research & Education community from the AAU member institutions and the secretariat to participate in various activities associated with Open Science in the South and Diamond Open Access hosted by the University of Cape Town (UCT) in Cape Town, South Africa from 8-14 December 2024. The Toluca Cape Town Declaration on Diamond Open Access was made – with the participants affirming that sharing knowledge was a human right. “As such scholarly knowledge must be a public good. It must be accessible to all communities, including readers and authors, without barriers and paywalls. Participation in knowledge production and communication must be free of prejudice and bias. Social justice, equity and inclusivity are fundamental to Diamond Open Access, enabling it to be a driver of decolonization and demarginalization”. The AAU is grateful for this partnership championed by the University of Cape Town (a proud member of the AAU). The AAU and UCT are also jointly supporting the growth of open science in Africa in several ways – one of which is through the African Online Platform that consists of open access journals and open access monographs and textbooks – aimed at supporting open scholarship and infuse quality control measures into the publishing processes of African higher education institutions and help establish world class HEI journals across the continent. As part of the events in Cape Town, the AAU also partnered with COPIM to host the Open Monograph Publishing workshop from 9-10 Dec 2024 and Professor Oyewole used this opportunity to underscore several activities that the Association is involved in to support Open Science, including partnerships with SCOSS, TCC Africa and PLOS.

The AAU Governing Board Meeting was hosted by Badr University, Egypt, June 2024: Badr University (BUC), a proud member of the Association of African Universities (AAU), successfully hosted the 83rd AAU Governing Board Meeting from June 24–26, 2024, at its campus in eastern Cairo, Egypt. The Governing Board, a key organ of the AAU, is tasked with implementing decisions from the General Conference and reporting on its activities. This body convenes at least once annually for an ordinary session, with the date and venue determined by its members. The Directorate of International Affairs at Badr University spearheaded the organization of the event, managing all aspects of logistics and on-site coordination.
Ahead of the official sessions on Monday, June 24, 2024, a special meeting was held between the AAU Governing Board and Badr University’s leadership, chaired by the university’s president, Prof. Dr. Ashraf Mohamed El-Shihy. During the meeting, Prof. El-Shihy expressed pride in BUC’s membership in the AAU and emphasized the university’s commitment to strengthening cooperation with African universities. Following the board meeting in Egypt, the AAU President Professor Bakri Osman Saeed and the Secretary General Professor Olusola Oyewole travelled to Morocco at the invitation of the Ministry of Higher Education and Research. In Morocco, they engaged with Vice Chancellors of public universities to explore opportunities for enhanced collaboration with African universities. Discussions also included plans for Morocco to host the 2025 AAU General Conference.

Collaboration with the African Union Commission: The AAU is recognized as the technical implementation arm of the African Union Commission for strategies and programs concerning higher education in Africa. The AAU leads the Higher Education Cluster responsible for implementing Strategic Objective 9, which focuses on revitalizing and expanding tertiary education under the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25). The AAU also chairs the Knowledge Generation Working Group of the African Union CESA Early Childhood Education Development Cluster. During 2024 the AAU played a key role in guiding African higher education institutions to actively contribute to the development of the new African Union Commission strategies – the CESA 26-35; the STISA 2034 (Science Technology Innovation Strategy for Africa) and the TVET 25-34 (Continental Strategy for Technical and Vocational Education and Training) strategy. This guidance was provided through organizing virtual meetings and ensuring the participation of the African higher education stakeholders, as well as facilitating the completion of relevant surveys.

The AAU also collaborated with the AUC as part of the implementation of the HAQAA3 project, and participation in various strategic events organized by the AUC in collaboration with diverse partners.

We inaugurated three regional offices, expanding the AAU’s global presence and strengthening ties with international partners. The Europe Regional Office (ERO), hosted by the University of Nottingham, was inaugurated on March 6, 2024, with key officials from the AAU and European higher education bodies in attendance. The ERO has already begun implementing impactful higher education initiatives. The Latin America Regional Office (LARO), hosted by the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), was officially inaugurated on April 25, 2024. This launch also led to the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the AAU and the Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro (UFRRJ) to enhance collaboration in agricultural development. The Southern Africa Regional Office (SARO) was inaugurated on September 27, 2024, following a 3-day workshop at the Women’s University in Africa (WUA) in Zimbabwe. This event brought together heads and officials from higher education institutions across Africa to share best practices and address common challenges.

Celebration of Africa Universities’ Day 2024 and AAU at 57 Years: The Association of African Universities (AAU) proudly commemorated the 2024 Africa Universities’ Day, marking its 57th anniversary. This year’s theme, “Educate an African fit for the 21st Century: Building resilient education systems for increased access to inclusive, lifelong, quality, and relevant learning in Africa,” aligned with the recognition of the year 2024 as the African Year of Education. A week-long celebration took place from November 11 to 15, 2024, featuring various activities that highlighted the contributions of higher education institutions to Africa’s development. The event brought together academic leaders, policymakers, students, and industry experts to discuss key challenges and opportunities facing African universities.

Significant Milestones Recorded by The Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) Project:  This year marks a significant milestone for the Africa Higher Education Centers of Excellence (ACE) Project—10 years of transformative impact in higher education across Africa. Over the past decade, the project has consistently advanced higher education, making tangible contributions in research, societal impact, and sectoral development. It has expanded partnerships to a global scale, strengthened university-private sector collaborations, and established bold strategies for sustainability. As part of this journey of excellence, the ACE Impact project held its Second International Partnership Meeting from May 8–10, 2024, in Mauritius. This event, aligned with the AU-EU Innovation Agenda, provided a peer-learning platform for centers to explore common interests in key priority research areas and identified potential collaborations in research and innovation. Additionally, the project hosted the 12th Virtual Regional Workshop 21st – 22nd October 2024 to consolidate achievements and address outstanding challenges. This workshop focused on ensuring the timely completion of critical activities and achieving project objectives as the initiative approaches closure.
A significant highlight of the year was the completion and validation of the Nimble Evaluation Impact Assessment, which provided valuable insights into the project’s impact at all levels. Additionally, the Graduate Tracer Study was concluded, offering comprehensive data on program and job relevance, and placement over the past decade. An assessment of the ACE Impact thematic networks further underscored their meaningful contributions to regional development. Notably, six Centers of Digital Competence have been piloted and fully equipped with state-of-the-art facilities, marking a significant milestone in innovation and capacity building. In relation to the project’s development objectives, performance across key indicators showed remarkable improvement over the year. Targets for 10 out of the 15 indicators were not only achieved but exceeded. Indicators related to PhD Enrolment, International Program Accreditation, Regional Strategy, Research Publications, and External Revenue are also progressing well, with performance levels ranging between 86% and 99%. For more detailed information and updates, please visit the project website for more information.

Enhancement of Quality Assurance in African Higher Education through the HAQAA3 Initiative: In 2024, the Harmonisation, Accreditation, and Quality Assurance in African Higher Education Initiative (HAQAA3) marked significant milestones in its third phase. The initiative facilitated workshops and training programs across Africa, bolstering the internal and external quality assurance capabilities of higher education institutions.
HAQAA3 advanced the African Standards and Guidelines for Quality Assurance (ASG-QA) by coordinating reviews and integrating feedback from diverse stakeholders, enhancing harmonization across the continent. The initiative also made progress in implementing the African Credit Transfer System (ACTS), which aims to facilitate student mobility and academic recognition between institutions across Africa. Furthermore, HAQAA3 explored mechanisms for establishing the Pan-African Quality Assurance and Accreditation Agency (PAQAA), laying the groundwork for improved regional integration. Additionally, the initiative played an active role in hosting regional focus group discussions, focusing strengthening on the role of data in transforming African higher education and strengthening cross-regional partnerships. The 4th HAQAA3 Steering Committee meeting was hosted by the DAAD Brussels office on the 12th November 2024 to review project implementation updates and provide necessary guidance. Visit the project website for more information.

Research Collaborations Deepened through the University Experts Initiative: The Association of African Universities (AAU) has been promoting research partnerships among universities and thematic experts under the African Research, Innovation and Development (AfRID) Network. In July 2024, the AAU launched its first thematic university experts’ networks, aiming to accelerate research collaborations among African researchers. Two networks were established: the Agro-Processing and Food Network, and the African Universities Experts in Climate Resilience, Oceans, Sustainable Water Use, Marine Resources, and Fisheries network. These networks facilitate joint research, proposal writing, student and staff mobility, and other activities that elevate the interests of the network.

Research and Innovation Management Strengthened through the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI):
The AAU received an 18-month grant from the IDRC and FCDO to strengthen Africa’s Science Granting Councils in research and grants management. This grant supports the development of digitized online grant management systems, training in research excellence, emerging scientific practices, financial management, and the integration of gender equality and inclusivity considerations in all aspects of research and grants management. . Under the Research and Innovation Management project (RIM), the AAU impacted research and education stakeholders in 17 countries across Eastern, Southern, and Western Africa. The RIM project is funding 81 research and innovation projects in areas such as agriculture, circular economy, renewable energy, emerging technologies, and health.

Additionally, under the SGCI project titled ‘Supporting African Science Granting Councils (SGCs) to Develop Policy Frameworks and Enabling Structures for Public – Private Partnerships in Research and Innovation’, the AAU collaborated with the Scinnovent Centre and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST) to hold two capacity building workshops. These focused on Research Infrastructure Management and were held in Kampala, Uganda and Lilongwe, Malawi in August 2024. A research infrastructure sharing platform called ‘Technomart’ being championed by the AAU and the UNCST was also launched in 2024 and is being positioned for adoption by the 17 participating countries of the SGCI.

Highlights of the SEADE Project’s 2024 Impacts: This year’s milestones highlight the commitment of the project to enabling digital transformative collaborations that prioritize human-centered approaches, policy alignment, and market-ready innovation. Through an extensive actor mapping and needs assessment, we engaged stakeholders across Ghana and Kenya, identifying critical barriers within the Research and Innovation in Digital Ecosystems. This analysis provided actionable insights for shaping policies that respond to the needs of diverse actors, setting a robust foundation for ecosystem resilience and growth.
By collecting and analysing AU-EU R&I and digital policies and strategies, we uncovered key gaps and opportunities, ensuring alignment with the Global Gateway principles. These insights not only support sustainable partnerships but also position stakeholders to harness transformative opportunities across both continents. With impactful programs like the Learning Expeditions from 1st – 5th October 2024, the Research “Route-to-Market” Webinar on 23rd October 2024, and the Piloting of the Enrich in Africa (EiA) Digital platform (tools and services) on 12th November 2024 and 25th November 2024 in Ghana and Kenya respectively, we introduced the SEADE Project’s tools, services, and pilot region ecosystems (Ghana, and Kenya) to hundreds of stakeholders. These initiatives bridged knowledge gaps, inspired international cooperation, and equipped participants with the skills to expand their innovations to new markets. The SEADE R&I Summit 2024 in Cape Town on 3rd December 2024, crowned the year by awarding five outstanding EU-AU R&I success stories. This event not only celebrated impactful collaborations but also distilled invaluable lessons and recommendations, serving as a beacon for future EU-AU R&I Cooperation. Through dedicated content creation and dissemination by the AAU TV, we amplified the SEADE Project’s activities, reaching a wider audience and elevating awareness about the transformative potential of AU-EU R&I collaboration.

Cultivating a Culture of Data-Driven Faculty Planning in the East African Community: The Demographics of African Faculty—East African Community (DAF EAC) Project, Phase 2, made significant progress in 2024. Implemented by a consortium consisting of the Association of African Universities, Inter-University Council for East Africa, Education Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Population Reference Bureau, the project is focusing on cultivating a culture of data collection, analysis, and management for faculty planning in the East African Community. A consultative co-creation workshop in Nairobi, Kenya, gathered insights for developing harmonized higher education data collection and management guidelines. The AAU further engaged by working to set up a technical data working group, comprising experts from across Africa, to provide a continental perspective. Additionally, the project released policy briefs highlighting key statistics and recommendations to address critical faculty challenges, including gender parity, staffing, and funding in higher education.

Implementation of the China-Africa Consortium of Universities Exchange Mechanism: The AAU, in collaboration with the China Association of Higher Education (CAHE), successfully began implementing activities under the Exchange Mechanism Between Chinese and African Universities, earlier launched at the AAU’s COREVIP in 2023. This initiative aims to foster partnerships between 50 African and 50 Chinese universities, promoting collaborations in higher education. A major milestone was achieved with the inauguration of the annual conference of the China-Africa Consortium of Universities Exchange Mechanism in Beijing, China, on September 5, 2024. The conference brought together representatives from 35 African and over 50 Chinese universities, resulting in the signing of 14 China-Africa educational cooperation projects and the launch of the Digital Cooperation Platform.

Enhancing Internet Inclusivity and Accessibility through the Universal Acceptance (UA) Project: As part of the ongoing Universal Acceptance (UA) project, a significant milestone was achieved through a pilot study involving 23 member universities. Through a collaborative effort with Automattic, the parent company of WordPress, and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), 23 AAU member universities piloted the Universal Acceptance (UA) configuration steps for WordPress websites. The institutions provided valuable feedback, informing Automattic’s efforts to ensure future WordPress configurations are UA-compliant by default. This enhancement will make the platform more inclusive and accessible worldwide. By participating in the pilot, AAU member universities contributed to the global movement for internet inclusivity, paving the way for improved WordPress compatibility and functionality. The pilot’s success will yield seamless user experiences, promoting broader adoption of non-Latin and internationalized domain names (IDNs) across the web.
Additionally, the Universal Acceptance project made significant strides in integrating UA principles into academic curricula. Participating universities’ computer science departments were engaged to embed UA education into their programs, ensuring future graduates possess the necessary skills to develop and maintain UA-compliant digital platforms. This initiative addresses a critical need for professionals who can design systems that accommodate diverse scripts and languages, ultimately supporting a global internet where language barriers are minimized.

Advancing Online Education in Africa via the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS Project: The AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS project successfully organized two flagship events: the e-Learning Summit 2024, which fostered discussions on advancing online education, and the Academic Leadership Summit (ALS) 2024, which explored strategies for transforming higher education through digital innovation. The project also expanded its portfolio of online degree programs, including an Online Master of Business Administration (MBA) program developed with Rhodes Business School and Njala University, a Master of Public Administration (MPA) program developed with the University of Nigeria, and a Master of Public Health (MPH) program developed with Nexus International University. Furthermore, the project commenced the onboarding process for various qualified applicants across the online MBA programs, demonstrating its commitment to delivering innovative, flexible, and accessible higher education solutions.

As we reflect on the accomplishments of 2024, we are reminded that our collective efforts have brought us closer to achieving our vision for African higher education. We extend our deepest gratitude to all stakeholders, partners, and team members who have contributed to the AAU’s success this year. Together, we will continue to drive innovation, excellence, and inclusivity in African higher education. THANK YOU ALL!

Yours in the Service of Higher Education in Africa

Professor Olusola Bandele Oyewole

SECRETARY GENERAL

Association of African Universities

AAU – The Voice of Higher Education in Africa!

TITLE: Women’s Fellowship on Human Mobility in the Context of Climate Change (HMCCC) 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 19, 2026

Applications are open for the Women’s Fellowship on Human Mobility in the Context of Climate Change (HMCCC) 2026. The Women’s Fellowship on Human Mobility in the Context of Climate Change (HMCCC) is a regional leadership and capacity-strengthening programme designed to empower young women across the ECOWAS region to advance gender-responsive solutions to climate-induced human mobility challenges.

Implemented by the Women Environmental Programme (WEP) under the GIZ-led Human Mobility in the Context of Climate Change (HMCCC) Programme, the fellowship seeks to strengthen women’s participation in climate and migration policy processes, support community-led initiatives, and foster regional collaboration among emerging women leaders.

The Fellowship Programme will recruit dynamic young women leaders from the following ECOWAS Member States: Nigeria, Gambia, Ghana, Liberia, and Sierra Leone for Anglophone countries; Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, Senegal, and Togo for Francophone countries; Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau for Lusophone countries.

Objectives of the Fellowship

The objectives of the fellowship are:

Strengthen women’s leadership and participation in climate mobility governance and policy processes.

Build the capacity of young women to address climate-induced migration and displacement through gender-responsive approaches.

Support fellows to design and implement community-based pilot projects that address climate mobility challenges.

Foster regional collaboration, peer learning, and knowledge exchange among women leaders across the ECOWAS region.

Increase women’s representation in regional and global climate, migration, and development dialogues.

Eligibility

They are seeking applications from young women aged 18–35 years from ECOWAS Member States who are passionate about climate action, human mobility, gender equality, and community development.

The candidates must be young women who:

Have demonstrated leadership experience in climate change, migration, gender advocacy, environmental sustainability, youth engagement, or community development.

Are actively engaged in community initiatives, civil society, research, policy advocacy, or related fields.

Have a project idea or ongoing initiative that addresses climate-related human mobility and can be further developed through the fellowship.

Are committed to influencing policy, driving community impact, and collaborating across cultures and languages.

Are available to fully participate in all fellowship activities.

Possess good communication skills and a willingness to engage in cross-cultural and multilingual collaboration.

Application

Applicants must submit the following documents compiled into a single Word or PDF file:

Motivation Letter outlining interest in the fellowship and how it aligns with personal and professional goals (maximum 1 page).

Curriculum Vitae (CV) highlighting relevant experience and achievements (maximum 2 pages).

Brief Project Proposal describing an initiative to be developed or scaled during the fellowship (maximum 3 pages).

Interested applicants should submit their application to the email: Fellowship.HMCCC@wepnigeria.net. Using the email subject line: HMCCC Fellowship Application – Applicant Name – Country e.g. HMCCC Fellowship Application – Amina Diallo – Senegal

For more information, visit HMCCC.

TITLE: EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGIES (EdTech) WORKSHOP

Understand the relationship between educational technology and other terms in the learning situation;

Examine the development of educational technologies over the years.

Review ethical issues in the use of educational technologies

Apply technology resources and tools appropriately when implementing administrative practices, instruction, assessment and evaluation

The workshop targets Information technology (e-learning) administrators, university administrators, faculty members and academic professionals who are interested in acquiring pedagogical and technical skills needed to successfully integrate technology in their classroom and those responsible for the training of instructors involved in creating online courses.

TITLE: The University of London Awards Professor Bakri Osman Saeed the Degree of Honorary Professor

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Professor Bakri Osman Saeed, President of the Association of African Universities (AAU) Governing Board and President of Sudan International University, has been appointed an honorary Professor by Queen Mary College – University of London (QMUL). The AAU congratulates Prof. Saeed for his remarkable contributions and outstanding efforts in elevating the AAU’s presence on the global stage.

In the United Kingdom, this is the highest title bestowed by a British university on individuals whom the university wishes to appoint, honor and work with. Queen Mary College – University of London considers this appointment an important means that enables the university to establish relationships with people who are distinguishing themselves either in their own academic disciplines or in fields of activities where QMUL would benefit from association. Through this means, QMUL enriches the breadth of its community and the breadth of people making contributions to its endeavours, as the university benefits from their skills and experience in contributing to university activities such as teaching, scientific research and community participation, in addition to contributing to the design and development of the university’s strategy for internationalization and global engagement.

Profile of Prof. Bakri Osman Saeed – President of the AAU Governing Board

Prof. Bakri Osman Saeed obtained a Bachelors degree in Medicine and Surgery from the University of Khartoum, a PhD from the University of Leeds in the UK, a Doctor of Medicine from the University of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, a Fellowship of the Royal College of Pathologists, and a Fellowship of the Royal College of Physicians, London, UK. He is currently the President of the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the President of Sudan International University. He is a UNESCO Chair in School Health Education. Before that, he was the Founding Dean of St. George’s International Medical School, which is a partnership between St. George’s University in Grenada and Northumbria University in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. He started his career as a lecturer at the University of Khartoum, and then worked for many years as a Medical Consultant and Associate Professor at the University of Newcastle-upon-Tyne and the University of London (UCL).

He has been a Visiting Professor for University of Northumbria in Newcastle and St George’s University in Grenada, where he was a Consultant to the Caribbean Reference Laboratory. He has been involved with many higher education and training bodies in the UK and in many other countries. In Sudan, he contributed significantly to the development of higher education as a Chair or member of important bodies and committees, including: the committee for revising the Higher Education Act, the committee for the evaluation of research proposals, the Ministry of Higher Education, Sudan, and the committee for the regulation of private higher education. He was involved in conflict resolution and peace promotion in Africa through his appointment as Special Advisor to the United Nations University for Peace.

Applications are open for the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) Fellowship 2026. The African Academy of Sciences (AAS) recognizes scientific excellence by electing to its membership outstanding scholars who have attained the highest level of excellence in their scientific field and have made significant contributions to the advancement of science regionally and globally.

AAS Fellows are elected for life through a rigorous peer review process on the basis of excellence in their publications record, innovations, leadership roles and contribution to policy and society.

There is no age limit and AAS encourages nomination of female scientists and deserving scholars from under- represented disciplines. Candidates may be nominated from all scientific disciplines grouped into ten AAS scientific clusters:

Agricultural & Nutritional Sciences.

Biosciences.

Chemical Sciences.

Cultural Humanities & Social Sciences.

Engineering, Technology & Applied Sciences.

Mathematical Sciences.

Geological, Environmental, Earth & Space Sciences.

Medical & Health Sciences.

Physical Sciences.

Policy Sciences.

Eligibility

Have obtained a PhD or equivalent qualifications no less than 10 years before the year of nomination

Have an H-index of 20 and above in either of (Scopus, Google Scholar, Web of science and ResearchGate) and not necessarily all. However, this is NOT applicable to social scientists.

Have at least one journal article with 100 or more citations.

Be a first author, senior or corresponding author or last author in at least 50% of the 10 submitted articles.

Candidates for Associate Fellows who are members of an Academy in their home country or region will have an added advantage.

Candidates for Associate Fellowship must:

Demonstrate contributions that they have made to Africa. For example, they can demonstrate supervision of several African masters and doctoral students and published papers based on research in Africa with a substantial number of the African research papers having African first authors. Demonstrate outstanding scientific leadership and citizenship and, if applicable, contribution to policy.

Demonstrate evidence of recognition by their peers in the field such as active peer review of journal articles, membership of scientific advisory committees, invited lectures, awards, prizes, membership in other academies or professional bodies. TITLE: Introduction to the Indian Ocean

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Hood, R. R., Ummenhofer, C. C., Phillips, H. E., & Sprintall, J. (2024). Introduction to the Indian Ocean. In C. C. Ummenhofer & R. R. Hood (Eds.), The Indian Ocean and its Role in the Global Climate System (pp. 1–31). Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-822698-8.00015-9

Indian Ocean main oceanographic features and phenomena. The surface circulation seasonally reverses north of 10°S under the influence of monsoons. The summer monsoon also promotes the intense Somali current as well as upwelling and high productivity in the western Arabian Sea. High surface layer productivity, sinking of biomass, and its remineralization at depth also lead to the formation of subsurface oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The Indo-Pacific warm pool is a region of intense air-sea interactions, where the Madden-Julian oscillation, monsoon intraseasonal oscillation, and Indian Ocean dipole develop. The Indian Ocean is a gateway of the global oceanic circulation, with inputs of heat and freshwater through the Indonesian Throughflow, which exit the basin though boundary currents, mainly the Agulhas Current along Africa, but also the Leeuwin Current along Australia. There are two vertical overturning cells connecting subducted waters south of 30°S to the tropical Indian Ocean: the shallow subtropical overturning cell where water upwells in the “thermocline ridge” open-ocean upwelling region, and the cross-equatorial cell where water upwells farther north in the Arabian Sea of the coast of Somalia and Oman. These cells are the main source of subsurface ventilation due to the presence of continents to the north. (Figure reproduced from Hood et al., 2024)

This chapter provides an overview of the research history, geology, and physical and biogeochemical variability in the Indian Ocean. A major theme that emerges from this book, is that there is a very strong link between atmospheric forcing and physical, biogeochemical, and ecological responses in the Indian Ocean, as observed everywhere in the global ocean. However, the Indian Ocean is unique in that the atmospheric forcing due to the monsoon winds is particularly strong and periodic. The low-latitude land boundary to the north and the tropical connectivity to the Pacific in the east via the Indonesian Throughflow further make it distinct. The Indian Ocean also has remarkably complex bottom topography. These attributes combine to give rise to circulation patterns and physical variability that are not seen in the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, which, in turn, give rise to strong and unusual biogeochemical and ecological responses. For example: 1) the South Asian monsoon represents the largest monsoon system on Earth, the Indian Ocean has the world’s largest southward meridional heat transport, and the Indian Ocean is characterized by unusually active intraseasonal variability; 2) the Arabian Sea has the thickest oxygen minimum zone in the world and some of the lowest pH values in the world have been measured in surface waters of the Indian Ocean; and 3) tuna catches in the Indian Ocean represent a large fraction of the world tuna and billfish catch, with 90% of the neritic tunas caught by the coastal/artisanal fisheries. All of this makes the Indian Ocean a fascinating place for atmospheric and oceanographic study where many important research questions still remain unanswered.

TITLE: Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships 2027: Up to £70,000 for Experienced Researchers in Any Discipline

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships 2027 provide funding for experienced researchers who need dedicated time to complete a programme of original research. The scheme is particularly aimed at researchers whose routine teaching and administrative responsibilities have limited their ability to undertake research in recent years.

The fellowship offers up to £70,000 and can support research periods lasting between 3 and 24 months. Researchers from a wide range of academic disciplines can apply, making this an opportunity for established scholars seeking protected time to develop and complete substantial research projects.

About the Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships

The Research Fellowships are offered by the Leverhulme Trust, a UK charitable organisation that supports research and education.

The fellowship is designed around a specific challenge faced by many experienced academics: although they may have strong research ideas and established research records, their ability to conduct research can be restricted by teaching, administration and other routine institutional responsibilities.

The programme therefore provides financial support that can enable successful applicants to devote a significant period of time to their research.

The Trust gives particular priority to applicants whose teaching and administrative duties have significantly affected their capacity to conduct research during the three years before applying.

This makes the fellowship especially relevant to experienced researchers who can demonstrate that institutional responsibilities have prevented them from giving sufficient attention to an important original research programme.

Fellowship Value

Successful applicants can receive funding of up to:

£70,000

The maximum value gives researchers substantial flexibility to structure an appropriate period of research leave and cover eligible costs associated with undertaking the proposed research.

Applicants should nevertheless ensure that their requested budget is appropriate to the scale and requirements of their proposed project rather than simply requesting the maximum amount available.

Duration of the Fellowship

Research Fellowships can be held for:

A minimum of 3 months

Up to a maximum of 24 months

The duration should correspond to the amount of dedicated research time genuinely required to complete the proposed programme.

A project requiring a shorter period of concentrated research may therefore be proposed for a shorter fellowship, while a more substantial programme may require a longer period, subject to the scheme’s conditions and assessment.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The Research Fellowships are intended for experienced researchers who want to complete a defined piece or programme of original research.

The scheme is particularly relevant to researchers who:

Have an established research background.

Have developed an original research project that requires dedicated time to complete.

Have been unable to devote sufficient time to research because of routine academic responsibilities.

Have significant teaching commitments.

Have substantial administrative responsibilities within their institution.

Can demonstrate that these responsibilities have affected their research activity during the three years preceding the application.

Are able to undertake the proposed research within the fellowship period.

The Trust’s emphasis on the impact of teaching and administration means that applicants should clearly explain how their professional responsibilities have constrained their research time and why the fellowship would make a meaningful difference.

Research in Any Discipline

One of the notable features of the Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowship is its broad disciplinary scope.

The opportunity is available to researchers working across disciplines rather than being restricted to a single academic field.

Depending on the nature of the proposed project, this can include research areas within fields such as:

Humanities

Social sciences

Arts and related disciplines

Natural sciences

Other eligible academic research fields

The breadth of the scheme means that the quality and originality of the proposed research, together with the applicant’s experience and eligibility, are important considerations.

Applicants should consult the official scheme guidance carefully to determine whether their particular discipline and research proposal satisfy the Trust’s requirements.

Why the Fellowship Is Important for Experienced Researchers

Academic researchers often have responsibilities extending well beyond conducting research. Teaching, student supervision, administration, committee responsibilities, institutional projects and other duties can substantially reduce the amount of time available for original research.

The Leverhulme Research Fellowship is structured to address this problem by providing support for a period in which an experienced researcher can concentrate on a specific research programme.

For an applicant, the fellowship may therefore provide an opportunity to:

Create dedicated research time

The fellowship can help an experienced researcher obtain a sustained period away from routine responsibilities so that they can concentrate on their research.

Complete an existing research programme

Researchers who have already developed a substantial body of work but have struggled to bring it to completion may use the fellowship period to make significant progress.

Develop original research

The scheme is intended for original research, making the research question, methodology and anticipated contribution important elements of an application.

Advance an established research career

A successful fellowship can provide researchers with additional time and resources to develop significant scholarly work.

Address research interruptions caused by academic duties

Researchers whose teaching and administrative workload has reduced their research capacity can explain this context as part of their application.

Priority for Researchers Affected by Teaching and Administrative Duties

A particularly important feature of this fellowship is the Trust’s stated priority for applicants whose research has been affected by routine institutional responsibilities.

The Trust specifically indicates that priority will be given to applicants whose teaching and administrative duties have significantly impacted their ability to undertake research during the three years before the application.

This means applicants should pay close attention to explaining their circumstances.

Rather than simply stating that they are busy, applicants should demonstrate the relationship between their professional workload and their reduced research activity.

For example, an applicant may need to explain:

The nature of their teaching responsibilities.

The extent of their administrative workload.

How these responsibilities have affected their available research time.

The period over which the impact occurred.

How dedicated fellowship time would allow them to complete the proposed research.

The purpose should be to establish a clear connection between the applicant’s current circumstances and the need for the fellowship.

What Type of Research Can Be Proposed?

The fellowship is intended to support a piece or programme of original research.

Consequently, applicants should have a clearly defined research objective rather than presenting a general desire to undertake academic work.

A strong proposal should communicate:

The central research question or problem.

The significance of the research.

The originality of the proposed work.

The approach or methodology to be used.

The work that will be undertaken during the fellowship.

The expected scholarly contribution.

Why the proposed fellowship period is necessary.

How the research will progress during the requested period.

The research programme should also be realistically structured around the amount of time and funding requested.

Internationally Focused Projects

The fellowship information also contains guidance concerning projects with an international focus.

Researchers whose proposed work involves international subjects, locations, sources, collaborations or comparative research should carefully review the Trust’s specific guidance on projects with an international focus before submitting an application.

This is particularly important for researchers whose projects extend beyond the UK or involve research activities in multiple countries.

Applicants should make sure that the international dimension of their proposal is clearly justified by the research itself and that all relevant eligibility and funding conditions are satisfied.

Application Preparation

The Leverhulme Trust advises prospective applicants to read the available information before beginning the application.

The Trust has provided Application Help Notes 2027 to assist researchers in preparing their submissions.

The guidance should be reviewed carefully because it contains information about the requirements and information applicants need to prepare.

Applicants should ideally begin preparation well before the closing date, allowing enough time to develop their research proposal, assemble supporting information and review their application before submission.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the Leverhulme Grant System.

Prospective applicants should:

Review the Research Fellowships information provided by the Leverhulme Trust.

Read the Application Help Notes 2027.

Develop a clearly defined original research programme.

Confirm that they meet the fellowship’s eligibility requirements.

Consider the appropriate duration of the proposed fellowship.

Prepare the information and supporting material required by the application system.

Prepare a realistic funding request, taking into account the maximum fellowship value.

Submit the completed application through the Leverhulme Grant System before the deadline.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit, particularly where institutional approval or additional information may be required.

APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

The deadline for the Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships 2027 is:

5 November 2026

Applicants should ensure that their applications are submitted before the stated closing date and should check the official application system for any submission-time requirements.

Feature

What Applicants Should Emphasise

Applicants should ensure that their proposal presents a convincing and coherent explanation of the research they intend to undertake.

Several areas deserve particular attention.

1. Explain the originality of the research

The application should make clear what is new about the proposed research and what contribution it is expected to make.

2. Demonstrate research experience

Because the fellowship is intended for experienced researchers, applicants should present their relevant research background and demonstrate their ability to undertake the proposed work.

3. Explain the need for dedicated research time

Applicants should clearly explain why the research cannot easily be completed alongside their existing teaching and administrative responsibilities.

4. Address the three-year context

Researchers who have been significantly affected by teaching and administrative responsibilities should clearly explain how those duties have constrained their research activities during the relevant three-year period.

5. Develop a realistic timetable

The proposed research should be achievable within the requested fellowship period. Applicants should demonstrate how the available research time will be used.

6. Prepare an appropriate budget

Although the maximum award is £70,000, applicants should request an amount that is justified by the needs of their specific research programme.

Research Fellowship Application Strategy

A prospective applicant can strengthen the preparation process by treating the application as a coherent research case rather than simply a request for funding.

The application should connect four central elements:

Research problem → Original contribution → Need for dedicated time → Achievable research programme

The research problem establishes what the applicant wants to investigate. The originality explains why the research matters academically. The explanation of the applicant’s workload establishes why dedicated fellowship time is necessary. Finally, the research plan demonstrates that the proposed work can realistically be completed during the fellowship.

This structure can help ensure that the application remains focused and that the need for fellowship support is clearly communicated.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is designed for experienced researchers. The information provided by the Leverhulme Trust does not describe the fellowship as a general scholarship for undergraduate or newly enrolled students.

Applicants should therefore assess their level of research experience and their ability to demonstrate a substantive programme of original research.

The Trust’s emphasis on applicants affected by teaching and administrative responsibilities also means that the fellowship is particularly relevant to established researchers working within academic or research institutions.

Who Is Not the Main Target of the Fellowship?

Based on the stated purpose of the scheme, this opportunity is not primarily presented as a general funding programme for:

Undergraduate students.

Students seeking tuition funding.

Applicants without an established research background.

Individuals seeking general professional development funding.

Projects that are not based on original research.

The fellowship is specifically framed around experienced researchers seeking time to complete a programme of original research.

Official Application Resources

Prospective applicants should review the Leverhulme Trust’s official Research Fellowships information and the Application Help Notes 2027 before preparing their application.

The application is made through the Leverhulme Grant System.

The Trust also provides a dedicated contact for Research Fellowship enquiries, which applicants can use if their questions are not answered in the published guidance.

Visit HERE for more information about the Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships 2027.

Conclusion

The Leverhulme Trust Research Fellowships 2027 offer experienced researchers an opportunity to obtain dedicated time and financial support to complete original research. With funding of up to £70,000 and fellowship periods ranging from 3 to 24 months, the scheme can provide substantial support for researchers whose teaching and administrative responsibilities have limited their ability to pursue research.

The fellowship is particularly relevant to applicants who can demonstrate that their routine academic duties have significantly affected their research capacity during the previous three years. Researchers should therefore carefully explain their research experience, the originality and importance of their proposed project, the effect of their existing responsibilities, and why a dedicated fellowship period is necessary.

Interested researchers should begin preparing early, read the 2027 application guidance carefully and submit their applications through the Leverhulme Grant System before the 5 November 2026 deadline.

TITLE: Mycelia Fellowship 2026: $2,000 Remote Fellowship for Ethical Storytelling, Arts, Civic Engagement and AI Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mycelia Fellowship 2026: An Opportunity for Ethical Storytelling Practitioners

The Social Resonance Lab (SRL) Mycelia Fellowship 2026 is an exciting new opportunity designed to support practitioners working at the intersection of storytelling, arts, humanities, civic participation, technology, community engagement, and intersectional practice.

The inaugural fellowship cohort will select two fellows whose existing projects demonstrate innovative approaches to ethical storytelling. Rather than supporting entirely new ideas that have not yet begun, the Mycelia Fellowship focuses on strengthening, documenting, refining, extending, or scaling projects that are already underway.

Selected fellows will receive a $2,000 stipend alongside direct advisory support from the Social Resonance Lab team. Participants will also gain opportunities to increase the visibility of their work, share their knowledge with wider audiences, contribute to discussions on ethical storytelling, and engage with other practitioners working across creative, civic, technological, and community-centered spaces.

The fellowship is built around an important idea: stories do not exist in isolation. Stories travel between people, communities, generations, technologies, and institutions. As they move, they can change shape, acquire new meanings, and influence how individuals and communities are understood.

Through the Mycelia Fellowship, participants will be encouraged to explore important questions surrounding storytelling, including who has the power to tell stories, who receives recognition when stories are adapted, what responsibilities storytellers have toward communities, and how ethical practices can be maintained when narratives continuously evolve.

The application deadline for the inaugural Mycelia Fellowship cohort is September 13, 2026, at 11:59 PM.

About the Social Resonance Lab

The Mycelia Fellowship is organized by the Social Resonance Lab, a collaborative research studio focused on understanding how ethical storytelling can contribute to stronger human connection.

Through creative inquiry, partnerships, research, experimentation, and collaboration, Social Resonance Lab explores how stories can be developed and shared in ways that promote:

Human connection

Empathy

Trust

Community understanding

Ethical representation

Shared learning

Creative collaboration

Responsible narrative practices

The organization’s work recognizes that storytelling is not simply about producing compelling narratives. Stories influence public understanding, shape collective memory, affect political and social perceptions, and determine whose experiences become visible or invisible.

For this reason, ethical storytelling requires practitioners to think critically about issues such as:

Power

Representation

Attribution

Ownership

Consent

Community relationships

Narrative responsibility

Technology

Digital platforms

Algorithmic influence

The Mycelia Fellowship provides a structured environment for practitioners to investigate these issues while advancing their existing projects.

Understanding the Concept Behind the Mycelia Fellowship

The fellowship takes inspiration from mycelium, the complex underground network of fungal structures that connects and supports ecosystems.

Mycelium operates largely beneath the surface, creating interconnected networks that allow nutrients and information to move throughout an ecosystem. Social Resonance Lab uses this concept as a metaphor for storytelling.

Stories, like mycelial networks, rarely exist independently.

A story may:

Originate from an individual experience

Be shared within a family or community

Be documented by researchers

Be adapted by artists

Spread through digital platforms

Be transformed by audiences

Influence political conversations

Become part of collective memory

As stories move between people and contexts, important ethical questions emerge.

For example:

Who should receive credit for a story?

What happens when someone else’s story is retold?

How should storytellers acknowledge the communities from which narratives originate?

What responsibilities exist when adapting historical or community narratives?

How can storytelling avoid exploitation?

How do digital technologies influence ownership and attribution?

What happens when algorithms amplify some stories while suppressing others?

The Mycelia Fellowship encourages fellows to examine storytelling as a living and interconnected ecosystem.

Participants are expected to understand that individual creative work can have broader consequences. A story can influence communities far beyond its original context. Therefore, practitioners must consider both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with storytelling.

The fellowship emphasizes the idea that practitioners are simultaneously:

Influenced by broader storytelling ecosystems.

Contributors to those ecosystems.

Responsible for the impacts their storytelling practices may create.

Through this framework, the fellowship seeks to transform individual artistic, archival, civic, and technological initiatives into work capable of generating sustained collective impact.

What Is the Purpose of the Mycelia Fellowship?

The primary goal of the Mycelia Fellowship is to support innovative practitioners advancing ethical storytelling interventions.

The fellowship provides several forms of support designed to help participants deepen and strengthen their work.

These include:

1. Financial Support

Each selected fellow will receive a stipend of $2,000.

The financial support is intended to help practitioners continue advancing work that is already underway.

Unlike programs that require participants to create completely new projects, the Mycelia Fellowship recognizes that meaningful projects often require additional support to:

Expand their reach

Improve documentation

Develop stronger strategies

Refine methodologies

Increase visibility

Strengthen community engagement

Explore new applications

Build sustainable approaches

2. Professional Advising and Consultancy

Selected fellows will receive direct support from the Social Resonance Lab team.

Areas of expertise available to fellows include:

Project management

Evaluation

Communications

Design

Community storytelling

This advisory support can help fellows think strategically about the development and future direction of their projects.

For practitioners working independently or within small organizations, access to specialized expertise can be particularly valuable.

The consultancy component of the fellowship may help participants better understand how to:

Organize and manage projects

Evaluate impact

Communicate complex ideas

Present work to different audiences

Strengthen storytelling strategies

Improve public engagement

Document learning

Build sustainable practices

3. Visibility and Knowledge-Sharing Opportunities

The Mycelia Fellowship also provides fellows with opportunities to share their work publicly.

This is an important component because the program is not only focused on supporting individual projects. It also aims to contribute to broader conversations surrounding ethical storytelling.

Fellows will have opportunities to share their experiences, methodologies, insights, and learning with:

Other practitioners

Researchers

Creative professionals

Community members

Storytelling organizations

Public audiences

By creating spaces for knowledge exchange, the fellowship seeks to advance broader field practice.

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Duration and Structure

The inaugural Mycelia Fellowship will run for eight weeks.

Fellowship Period

November 1 – December 31, 2026

Cohort Size

Only two fellows will be selected.

The small cohort structure may provide participants with opportunities for more direct engagement and personalized support.

Fellowship Format

The fellowship will be conducted remotely.

Activities will include:

A lightweight virtual kickoff

Semi-regular check-ins

Advisory support

Collaborative discussions

Presentations

Knowledge-sharing activities

Because the program is remote, fellows will not need to relocate for the fellowship. However, applicants must meet the residency and payment requirements outlined by the organizers.

Mycelia Fellowship Stipend and Benefits

Each selected fellow will receive a $2,000 stipend.

In addition to the financial award, fellows will benefit from professional support and opportunities for public engagement.

Key benefits include:

Financial Support

$2,000 stipend per fellow

Professional Advising

Support from the Social Resonance Lab team in areas such as:

Project management

Evaluation

Communications

Design

Community storytelling

Increased Visibility

Professional Development

Participants can further develop their thinking and practice around:

Ethical storytelling

Community engagement

Power dynamics

Intersectional practice

Digital storytelling

Civic participation

Knowledge Exchange

Fellows will engage with other practitioners and audiences interested in ethical storytelling and related fields.

Platform for Public Engagement

Selected participants will have opportunities to present their work and participate in conversations with the public.

Required Deliverables for Mycelia Fellows

Selected fellows will be expected to complete a short set of shared deliverables during the fellowship period.

These deliverables are designed to help participants document their work, share insights, and contribute to broader discussions about ethical storytelling.

1. Written Contribution to the SRL Substack

Each fellow will produce one written piece for the Social Resonance Lab Substack.

This contribution may provide fellows with an opportunity to:

Document their project

Share research insights

Reflect on ethical storytelling practices

Introduce audiences to their work

Discuss challenges and lessons

Contribute to public conversations

Strong writing skills will therefore be particularly valuable for applicants.

2. Podcast Participation

Fellows will participate as guests in an episode of Social Resonance Lab’s upcoming podcast series focused on ethical storytelling.

The podcast opportunity will allow fellows to discuss their projects and perspectives with wider audiences.

Participants may have an opportunity to share:

Their professional journey

Their project methodology

Key challenges

Ethical questions

Community experiences

Lessons learned

Future directions

3. Co-Leading a Workshop

Each fellow will participate in a workshop activity.

The workshop will involve:

Co-leading a session

Delivering a 30-minute presentation

Presenting their work

Engaging in dialogue with practitioners

Participating in discussions with SRL

Interacting with public audiences

This component means successful applicants should be comfortable communicating their ideas and engaging with diverse audiences.

Thematic Tracks of the Mycelia Fellowship

Applicants must identify which thematic track best aligns with their project.

The fellowship contains two major thematic tracks:

Arts as a Civic Tool

AI and the Digital Landscape

Both tracks share an interest in ethical storytelling, intersectional practice, and power dynamics.

Importantly, the fellowship considers not only how stories are produced but also how they are experienced by audiences and communities directly affected by the narratives.

Track A: Arts as a Civic Tool

The first thematic track focuses on the use of art and narrative as forms of civic participation.

Projects under this track explore how artistic and storytelling practices can contribute to public engagement and responses to social issues.

The fellowship is particularly interested in work that represents ongoing and complex forms of:

Injustice

Resistance

Identity

Social transformation

Civic participation

Community engagement

Rather than reducing complex issues to simplified narratives with clear resolutions, Track A encourages projects that recognize the ongoing nature of social and political experiences.

This is especially relevant to issues sometimes described as “slow” forms of injustice.

These may involve challenges that develop gradually or persist over long periods, making them difficult to communicate through traditional storytelling formats.

Projects can explore how art and storytelling help communities understand and engage with such issues.

Examples of Projects Suitable for Track A

Potential projects may include:

Phygital Civic Activities

Projects that connect physical and digital participation while linking democratic engagement with artistic practice.

Examples could include initiatives involving:

Community art

Digital storytelling

Local democracy projects

Interactive public engagement

Hyperlocal creative participation

Artistic Responses to Local Issues

Projects that engage with specific local challenges through creative and humanities-based approaches.

These may include:

Community storytelling initiatives

Public art projects

Participatory cultural activities

Creative research

Narrative-based advocacy

Creative Placemaking

Digital campaigns or creative initiatives centered around clearly defined geographic communities within the United States.

These projects may explore how storytelling and creativity contribute to:

Community identity

Local engagement

Public participation

Cultural preservation

Civic dialogue

Track B: AI and the Digital Landscape

The second thematic track focuses on the relationship between technology, storytelling, power, collective memory, and political agency.

This track is particularly interested in projects that critically examine how:

Digital infrastructures

Artificial intelligence

Algorithms

Social media

Data systems

Platform governance

Digital surveillance

shape human narratives and social experiences.

The fellowship does not treat technology as neutral.

Instead, Track B encourages applicants to examine the real-world consequences of data-driven systems.

Technology increasingly influences:

Which stories become visible

Which voices are amplified

Which narratives are suppressed

How historical information is preserved

How misinformation spreads

How communities communicate

How personal data is collected

How digital surveillance affects communities

Projects under this track should critically investigate these dynamics.

Examples of Projects Suitable for Track B

Eligible or relevant projects may include the following.

Digital Archives and Oral History Projects

Projects documenting community histories while addressing challenges associated with automated moderation or content suppression.

Such initiatives may explore how digital platforms influence historical preservation.

Counter-Surveillance Documentation Tools

Projects documenting how communities navigate surveillance and information control.

Examples could include research or tools examining:

Encrypted communication

Informal information networks

Digital security practices

Community communication strategies

Community-Led Data Preservation

Projects that protect local knowledge and narratives from algorithmic erasure.

These initiatives may focus on preserving:

Community histories

Cultural knowledge

Oral traditions

Local archives

Marginalized narratives

Creative Storytelling Platforms

Projects that help communities maintain control over their narratives in environments shaped by digital oversight and platform power.

These projects may investigate how communities can preserve narrative autonomy when interacting with large technology platforms and algorithmic systems.

Research Questions Driving the Fellowship

The Mycelia Fellowship is grounded in a broader research agenda focused on ethical storytelling.

The central research question is:

How do power dynamics shape who gets to tell stories and how those stories are received?

This question recognizes that storytelling is influenced by unequal access to:

Media platforms

Financial resources

Technology

Institutional recognition

Cultural authority

Publishing opportunities

Political influence

The fellowship encourages practitioners to investigate these dynamics through their existing work.

Arts as a Civic Tool Research Question

Applicants under Track A are encouraged to consider:

What methods can organizations and creators use to practice ethics in their storytelling?

This question invites practitioners to explore practical approaches to responsible storytelling.

Potential areas of exploration include:

Community participation

Consent

Attribution

Collaborative authorship

Representation

Long-term community relationships

Responsible documentation

Participatory creative processes

AI and the Digital Landscape Research Question

Applicants under Track B are encouraged to investigate:

How does the digital landscape, including social media, AI-generated content, and virality, complicate or enable ethical storytelling?

This research question is increasingly relevant as artificial intelligence and algorithmic platforms influence the production and distribution of information.

Potential areas for exploration include:

AI-generated narratives

Algorithmic bias

Digital misinformation

Viral storytelling

Platform moderation

Content suppression

Digital memory

Automated representation

Narrative manipulation

Who Should Apply for the Mycelia Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for individuals who are already actively engaged in storytelling or arts and humanities work.

The organizers are not seeking applicants who simply have an idea for a completely new initiative.

Instead, they want to support projects that are already in progress and have the potential to be:

Scaled

Documented

Extended

Strengthened

Refined

Ideal applicants are likely to have experience in fields such as:

Storytelling

Arts

Humanities

Creative practice

Research

Community organizing

Movement building

Civic engagement

Digital culture

Archives

Oral history

Technology and society

Ethical communications

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet several important eligibility criteria.

1. Applicants Must Have Existing Work in Progress

The fellowship supports practitioners who are already advancing storytelling or arts-humanities projects.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate evidence that they have already begun meaningful work.

The fellowship is suitable for projects seeking:

Expansion

Documentation

Scaling

Extension

Refinement

Completely new projects developed from scratch are not the primary focus of this opportunity.

2. Applicants Must Demonstrate Intersectional Practice

The fellowship is specifically interested in storytelling and arts-humanities work grounded in intersectional practice.

Applicants should demonstrate awareness of how multiple social identities and systems of power influence human experiences and storytelling.

3. Strong Writing Skills Are Important

Selected fellows will be required to produce a written piece for the SRL Substack.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate strong abilities in:

Writing

Research

Analysis

Communication

Critical thinking

4. Applicants Should Be Skilled Researchers or Practitioners

The fellowship seeks people capable of exploring complex questions with nuance.

Strong applicants may demonstrate experience in:

Research

Creative inquiry

Documentation

Community engagement

Storytelling practice

Arts and humanities work

5. Applicants Should Demonstrate Leadership

The fellowship seeks practitioners capable of independently advancing projects.

Applicants should demonstrate the ability to:

Lead initiatives

Manage responsibilities

Work independently

Develop ideas

Complete projects

Engage communities

6. Applicants Must Be United States Residents

The fellowship is currently only open to residents of the United States.

Applicants must be based within:

The United States

US Territories

The application specifically states that fellowship activities must be based domestically.

7. Applicants Must Meet Payment Requirements

Successful fellows must be able to:

File a W-9 form

Receive stipend payments

Access a domestic United States bank account

Applicants who cannot meet these requirements may not be eligible for the fellowship.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Applications will be assessed according to several criteria.

Understanding these criteria can help prospective applicants prepare stronger submissions.

Creativity

Applicants will be evaluated based on the originality of their approach and voice.

Strong applications should demonstrate:

Innovative thinking

Original approaches

Creative methodologies

Distinct perspectives

Leadership

Applicants should demonstrate their ability to independently lead and advance their projects.

The selection committee will likely consider:

Previous leadership experience

Initiative

Project ownership

Ability to execute ideas

Evidence of Prior Execution

Because the fellowship focuses on existing work, applicants must demonstrate evidence of previous or ongoing execution.

Strong evidence may include:

Completed projects

Ongoing initiatives

Research

Publications

Community programs

Digital platforms

Archives

Creative works

Campaigns

Understanding of the SRL Research Agenda

Applicants should demonstrate familiarity with the fellowship’s central themes.

This includes understanding questions related to:

Ethical storytelling

Power

Narrative responsibility

Intersectionality

Technology

Community engagement

Attribution

Digital storytelling

Fit With a Thematic Track

Applicants must demonstrate a strong connection between their project and either:

Arts as a Civic Tool, or

AI and the Digital Landscape

Applicants should clearly explain why their work fits within their selected track.

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Timeline and Key Dates

Applicants should pay close attention to the fellowship timeline.

Application Window Opens

August 31, 2026

Application Deadline

September 13, 2026, at 11:59 PM

Review Period

September 14 – September 27, 2026

Interviews

Final Selections Announced

Fellow Onboarding
