Fellowship Period

November – December 2026

More specifically, the fellowship will run from:

November 1 – December 31, 2026

Because only two fellows will be selected, interested applicants should ensure that their applications clearly demonstrate the strength, progress, and relevance of their existing projects.

How to Prepare a Strong Mycelia Fellowship Application

Given the highly selective nature of the fellowship and the small cohort size, applicants should carefully prepare their submissions.

Here are several strategies that may strengthen an application.

1. Clearly Explain Your Existing Project

Since the fellowship does not primarily fund brand-new ideas, applicants should provide clear evidence that their work is already underway.

Explain:

What your project is

When it began

What you have accomplished

Who the project serves

What challenges exist

What the next stage of development involves

2. Demonstrate Ethical Storytelling Practice

Applicants should go beyond simply describing their project.

They should explain how their work engages with ethical questions.

Consider discussing:

Community relationships

Consent

Representation

Attribution

Ownership

Power dynamics

Accountability

3. Select the Most Appropriate Track

Applicants should carefully determine whether their project fits better under:

Arts as a Civic Tool, or

AI and the Digital Landscape

Avoid forcing a project into a track.

Instead, clearly explain the relationship between your existing work and the fellowship’s thematic focus.

4. Provide Evidence of Execution

Selection criteria emphasize evidence of prior execution.

Applicants should highlight tangible examples of their work.

Depending on the project, this could include:

Publications

Research findings

Websites

Digital archives

Community events

Artistic work

Campaigns

Workshops

Documentation

5. Demonstrate Independent Leadership

Explain your specific role in the project.

The fellowship seeks practitioners capable of independently advancing their work.

Applicants should demonstrate:

Initiative

Decision-making

Project ownership

Leadership

Problem-solving

6. Connect Your Work to the Research Questions

A strong application should demonstrate that the applicant understands the fellowship’s intellectual focus.

Consider how your work addresses:

Who gets to tell stories

Who controls narratives

How stories are received

How technology influences storytelling

How ethical practices can be strengthened

7. Highlight Your Writing and Communication Skills

Since fellows must write for the SRL Substack and participate in public discussions, applicants should demonstrate strong communication abilities.

Experience in the following areas may be relevant:

Writing

Public speaking

Research communication

Workshop facilitation

Community engagement

Important Privacy Considerations for Applicants

Applicants submitting information to Social Resonance Lab should understand how personal information may be handled.

According to the organization’s privacy policy, information collected may include:

Information Provided Directly

Such as:

Names

Email addresses

Contact details

Fellowship application information

Usage Information

Website-related information may include:

IP addresses

Browser information

Website interaction data

Voluntary Submissions

This may include:

Survey responses

Research participation

Stories voluntarily shared with the organization

The organization states that personal information is not sold, rented, or traded.

Information may be used for purposes such as:

Communicating about programs

Processing applications

Improving websites and content

Conducting research

Analysis and reporting

Applicants may also have rights to access, correct, or request deletion of personal information depending on applicable laws and circumstances.

How to Apply for the Mycelia Fellowship 2026

Interested and eligible applicants should complete the official Mycelia Fellowship application form before the deadline.

Applicants should carefully review the full program overview before submitting their responses.

The application will ask candidates to provide information including their:

Email address

City or town of residence

US State or Territory of residence

Professional background

Existing project

Thematic track alignment

Experience and qualifications

Before submitting an application, candidates should ensure that they:

Meet all residency requirements.

Have an existing project already in progress.

Select the appropriate thematic track.

Demonstrate evidence of prior execution.

Explain their approach to ethical storytelling.

Highlight leadership and research abilities.

Confirm their ability to meet the W-9 and US bank account payment requirements.

Submit before the September 13, 2026 deadline.

APPLY HERE

Why the Mycelia Fellowship Is an Important Opportunity

The Mycelia Fellowship stands out because it addresses a growing need for ethical approaches to storytelling.

In an era shaped by artificial intelligence, social media, digital surveillance, misinformation, and rapidly changing communication technologies, storytelling has become increasingly complex.

Stories can now travel globally within seconds.

However, rapid distribution creates important challenges.

For example:

Narratives can be removed from their original context.

Community stories can be appropriated.

Algorithms can determine which voices receive visibility.

AI systems can generate narratives without meaningful accountability.

Viral content can spread misinformation.

Historical information can disappear from digital platforms.

The fellowship creates space for practitioners to investigate these challenges while continuing their own work.

Its interdisciplinary structure also creates opportunities for collaboration between people working across:

Arts

Humanities

Research

Civic engagement

Technology

Community organizing

Storytelling

Visit HERE to learn more about the Mycelia Fellowship 2026.

Conclusion

The Mycelia Fellowship 2026 represents a unique opportunity for practitioners working at the intersection of storytelling, arts, humanities, civic engagement, and technology to deepen and expand projects that are already making an impact.

With only two fellows selected, the inaugural cohort will be small and highly selective. Successful applicants will receive a $2,000 stipend, direct advisory support from the Social Resonance Lab team, opportunities for increased visibility, and platforms to share their knowledge through writing, podcast participation, workshops, and public dialogue.

The fellowship is particularly valuable for practitioners interested in examining how stories shape communities and how power influences who has the ability to create, control, distribute, and interpret narratives.

Whether working through art as a form of civic participation or critically examining the effects of artificial intelligence and digital systems on collective memory and narrative autonomy, fellows will have an opportunity to contribute to important conversations surrounding the future of ethical storytelling.

Eligible United States-based practitioners with existing projects in storytelling, arts, humanities, civic engagement, or critical technology work should consider applying before the September 13, 2026 deadline.

TITLE: Call for Applications: Takemi Fellowship at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Each year, the Takemi Program in International Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, recruits a small group of mid-career researchers and professionals to spend an academic year at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. The Takemi Program provides participants with the space, time, and flexibility to enhance their capacity for research and leadership. To do this, Fellows are linked to two key resources: the weekly Takemi Seminar Series, and expert faculty. In addition, Fellows have the opportunity for collaboration throughout the Harvard community, and may elect to deepen their knowledge of theory or practice through relevant coursework. Fellows draw on these resources to produce at least one paper of publishable quality.

Since 1984, 282 Fellows from 56 countries have trained in the Takemi Program.

Applications are due by December 31, 2018 at midnight EST.

Follow this link for further information https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/takemi/

TITLE: Communications Manager

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Job opening:

ref: COMMMGR26

The Communications Manager will lead and oversee all aspects of ESF’s communication activities, including corporate and internal communications. This role will be responsible for implementing and refining the organisation’s communication framework, developing tools, and managing relationships with external agencies. In addition, the Communication Manager will supervise and support ESF communication’s team, fostering professional growth and ensuring high-quality, aligned communication practices for project-related activities.

The position will report to Chief Executive.

Key responsibilities

Strategic Communication Management

Develop and implement ESF’s overall communication strategy, ensuring alignment with organisational objectives and ESF’ current strategic plan.

Ensure consistency and quality across all communication channels and materials.

Develop and manage internal communication to promote transparency, engagement, and organisational culture.

TITLE: EA Funds Grants: Apply for $1,000–$500,000 in Funding for High-Impact Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EA Funds provides grant funding to individuals, projects, nonprofit organizations, and institutions working on opportunities that could have a significant positive impact. Through its different funding programs, EA Funds supports initiatives focused on animal welfare, effective altruism infrastructure, transformative artificial intelligence, global health and development, and other high-impact areas.

Eligible applicants can apply for grants ranging from $1,000 to $500,000, depending on the nature, scope, and funding requirements of their proposed work. Applications are accepted on an ongoing basis, meaning there is currently no fixed application deadline listed for the general EA Funds funding opportunity.

The funding opportunity is designed for people and organizations developing projects that address important problems, advance promising research, improve the effectiveness of existing work, or create opportunities to produce significant positive outcomes.

About EA Funds

EA Funds is a funding platform associated with the Effective Altruism community and is focused on directing resources toward projects that are considered potentially high-impact.

The organization operates several funds, each concentrating on a particular area. These include:

Animal Welfare Fund

EA Infrastructure Fund

Transformative AI Fund

Global Health and Development Fund

Each fund has its own area of focus and funding priorities. Applicants are therefore encouraged to identify the fund that most closely matches the objectives and expected impact of their proposed project.

EA Funds is a project of Effective Ventures and works closely with organizations within the broader effective altruism ecosystem, including the Centre for Effective Altruism, GiveWell, and Giving What We Can.

What Funding Does EA Funds Provide?

EA Funds states that grants generally range from:

$1,000 to $500,000

The size of a grant can therefore vary substantially depending on the applicant, project, funding requirement, and the fund under which the application is considered.

The opportunity is not restricted to one particular grant size. Applicants should request an amount that is appropriate for the work they are proposing and should be prepared to explain why the requested funding is necessary.

EA Funds also indicates that applicants can complete the application in less than one hour, although applicants may need additional time to prepare supporting information or develop a strong project proposal.

Who Can Receive Funding?

EA Funds specifically states that it provides funding to:

Individuals

Projects

Nonprofit organizations

Institutions

This means that applicants do not necessarily have to be a registered charity or nonprofit organization to be considered.

The funding opportunity can therefore be relevant to individuals developing high-impact projects as well as established organizations seeking resources to expand or carry out important work.

However, eligibility and suitability can depend on the specific fund and the nature of the proposed project.

Main EA Funds Funding Areas

EA Funds currently highlights several major funding areas. Applicants should carefully review the purpose of each fund before submitting an application.

1. Animal Welfare Fund

The Animal Welfare Fund focuses on opportunities that can effectively improve the well-being of nonhuman animals.

The fund places particular emphasis on areas where additional resources could potentially have substantial impact. Its priorities include:

Work involving relatively neglected geographic regions

Work focused on relatively neglected animals

Promising research related to animal advocacy

Research and activities related to animal well-being

Activities that could make it easier to help animals in the future

Other high-quality opportunities that may significantly improve animal welfare

Projects seeking funding through this area should demonstrate a clear connection to improving outcomes for nonhuman animals.

The fund may be particularly relevant to researchers, advocates, organizations, and project leaders developing evidence-based approaches to animal welfare.

2. EA Infrastructure Fund

The EA Infrastructure Fund aims to improve the ability of projects using effective altruism principles to achieve their objectives.

The fund focuses on improving access to:

Talent

Capital

Knowledge

This means funding can potentially support infrastructure, systems, people, organizations, or initiatives that strengthen the capacity of high-impact projects.

The EA Infrastructure Fund was formerly known as the EA Meta Fund.

Applicants interested in this fund should demonstrate how their proposed work could strengthen the effectiveness of relevant projects, organizations, or communities.

3. Transformative AI Fund

The Transformative AI Fund focuses on issues related to the long-term trajectory of civilization.

One of its major areas of interest is addressing global catastrophic risks, particularly potential risks associated with:

Advanced artificial intelligence

Pandemics

The fund also seeks to support work related to longtermist ideas and initiatives intended to increase the likelihood that future generations will flourish.

Applicants proposing work in artificial intelligence, global catastrophic risk reduction, pandemic preparedness, or related areas may find this fund relevant, provided their work aligns with the fund’s objectives.

Projects should clearly explain the problem being addressed, why the problem matters, and how the proposed work could contribute to reducing relevant risks or improving long-term outcomes.

4. Global Health and Development Fund

The Global Health and Development Fund focuses on global health and development-related opportunities.

However, applicants should note an important current restriction:

The Global Health and Development Fund is currently not accepting applications.

EA Funds directs potential applicants interested in global health and development toward GiveWell as an alternative resource.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the general EA Funds application process is currently open for this specific fund.

What Types of Projects May Be Funded?

EA Funds does not limit its funding to one specific type of activity. Its different funds are designed to support a variety of potentially high-impact opportunities.

Depending on the relevant fund, this can include activities such as:

Research

Advocacy

Organizational development

Infrastructure development

Work addressing global catastrophic risks

Animal welfare initiatives

Artificial intelligence-related projects

Pandemic-related work

Activities designed to improve the effectiveness of other projects

Work that could make future interventions more effective

Other promising high-impact initiatives

The suitability of a project depends heavily on its alignment with the objectives of the relevant fund.

How the EA Funds Application Process Works

Applicants can submit their funding requests through the EA Funds application system.

The organization states that applications can be completed in less than one hour. However, applicants should take the time necessary to clearly explain their proposed work and funding requirements.

A strong application should make it easy for the reviewers to understand:

What you want to do

Clearly describe the project, activity, research, or initiative you want to undertake.

What problem you are addressing

Explain the problem and why addressing it is important.

Why your proposed approach is valuable

Describe how the proposed project could contribute to meaningful outcomes.

Why funding is needed

Explain how the requested funds would be used.

Why the relevant EA Fund is appropriate

Demonstrate how your proposal fits the focus of the fund you are applying to.

Who will carry out the work

Provide relevant information about the people, organization, researchers, or institutions responsible for implementation.

What outcomes you expect

Explain what you expect the funding to accomplish and, where possible, how progress or results could be assessed.

Grant Amounts

EA Funds provides grants ranging from:

$1,000 to $500,000

Applicants should consider the actual financial requirements of their project when determining the amount to request.

The availability of a particular grant amount should not be interpreted as a guarantee that an applicant will receive the full amount requested. Funding decisions depend on the organization’s evaluation of individual applications.

Applicants should therefore provide a clear and reasonable explanation for the amount requested.

Is There an Application Deadline?

No fixed deadline is stated for the general EA Funds application opportunity.

EA Funds describes its funding opportunity as:

Always open to applications

This means applicants can submit applications on an ongoing basis rather than waiting for a specific annual deadline.

Nevertheless, applicants should check the official EA Funds website and application portal for the latest information before submitting an application because individual funds may have different application statuses or requirements.

It is particularly important to note that the Global Health and Development Fund is currently not accepting applications, despite the broader EA Funds application process being open.

Can Applicants Apply for Multiple Projects?

EA Funds provides an FAQ addressing applications for multiple projects and other aspects of the funding process.

Applicants with more than one project should review the current application guidance to determine whether separate applications are appropriate for each project.

Where projects are substantially different, applicants should ensure that the funding request clearly distinguishes the objectives, activities, budgets, and expected outcomes of each initiative.

Application Review and Evaluation

EA Funds has an application evaluation process through which proposals are assessed before funding decisions are made.

Applicants should therefore expect their proposals to be reviewed based on factors such as their fit with the relevant fund and the potential value of the proposed work.

The organization also provides information about its evaluation process through its frequently asked questions.

Applicants should make their proposal as clear and evidence-based as possible and provide enough information for reviewers to understand the project’s objectives, expected impact, costs, and implementation plans.

Can Applicants Speak With EA Funds Before Applying?

EA Funds provides a frequently asked question specifically addressing whether applicants may speak with the organization before submitting a funding application.

Applicants who are uncertain about whether their project fits a particular fund should consult the official guidance and available information before applying.

This can help applicants identify the most relevant funding area and avoid submitting a proposal that does not match the objectives of the selected fund.

How Quickly Are Grant Decisions Made?

The time required to evaluate and process an application can vary.

EA Funds provides information about application decisions and grant disbursement through its FAQ section.

Applicants with time-sensitive projects should review the organization’s guidance regarding expedited evaluation rather than assuming that a decision or payment will occur within a particular timeframe.

Can Funding Be Kept Private?

EA Funds also addresses grant privacy through its frequently asked questions.

Applicants who have concerns about the public disclosure of their grant or project information should review the organization’s privacy guidance and indicate any relevant preferences during the application process where applicable.

Can Applicants Reapply After Rejection?

EA Funds provides information for applicants who have previously submitted a proposal that was not funded.

Applicants whose proposals are unsuccessful should review the organization’s current guidance regarding reapplication and consider whether significant changes, additional evidence, or a revised proposal could improve the fit of a future application.

Do Applicants Need to Be Registered Charities?

According to the information provided by EA Funds, funding is available to people, projects, nonprofits, and institutions.

The organization also provides a specific FAQ addressing whether applicants need to be registered charities.

Therefore, individuals and organizations should review the current eligibility requirements rather than assuming that formal charitable registration is automatically required.

Does EA Funds Support Graduate Studies?

EA Funds also addresses graduate-study funding in its frequently asked questions.

Applicants interested in using funding for graduate studies should review the current official guidance to determine whether their particular educational proposal qualifies and which funding area, if any, would be appropriate.

What Is a Theory of Change?

EA Funds includes a FAQ explaining the concept of a Theory of Change.

A Theory of Change generally describes the reasoning behind how an activity is expected to lead to specific outcomes. For a funding application, this can help explain the connection between the proposed activities, intermediate results, and ultimate impact.

Applicants may benefit from clearly explaining the pathway through which their proposed work is expected to create positive change.

Geographic Eligibility and International Applicants

The information provided does not state that EA Funds funding is restricted to applicants from a particular country or continent.

The listed funding areas include work involving relatively neglected geographic regions, particularly within the Animal Welfare Fund.

However, applicants should check the current requirements of the specific fund they intend to apply to before submitting an application.

There is no specific nationality, race, or continent restriction stated in the provided EA Funds information.

Why Applicants Should Identify the Correct Fund

One of the most important considerations for potential applicants is selecting the funding area that corresponds with the proposed project.

For example:

An animal welfare project may be relevant to the Animal Welfare Fund.

A project strengthening the infrastructure or effectiveness of effective altruism-related work may be relevant to the EA Infrastructure Fund.

A project addressing advanced AI risks, pandemics, or other global catastrophic risks may be relevant to the Transformative AI Fund.

A global health or development project may relate to the Global Health and Development Fund, but this fund is currently not accepting applications.

Selecting the appropriate fund allows applicants to present their proposal in a way that directly addresses the priorities of the relevant funding program.

Important Information Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should:

Review the objectives of each available fund.

Determine which fund most closely matches the proposed project.

Check whether that fund is currently accepting applications.

Clearly describe the problem the project intends to address.

Explain the proposed solution or approach.

Provide a realistic funding request.

Explain how the requested money will be used.

Describe the people or organization responsible for the project.

Explain the expected outcomes and potential impact.

Review the official FAQs for additional requirements and application guidance.

Application Link

Applicants can submit their funding request through the official EA Funds application portal.

Application: EA Funds Funding Application

Official Website

For detailed information about EA Funds, its funding programs, FAQs, grants database, eligibility information, and application guidance, applicants should visit the official EA Funds website.

Website: EA Funds Official Website

For more funding opportunities visit the OFY Website HERE

Deadline

Deadline: Always open to applications

There is no fixed deadline stated for the general EA Funds funding opportunity. However, applicants should verify the status of the specific fund they wish to apply to before submitting an application.

Conclusion

EA Funds offers a potentially significant source of grant funding for individuals, projects, nonprofit organizations, and institutions working on high-impact initiatives. With grants ranging from $1,000 to $500,000, the opportunity can accommodate projects with different levels of financial requirements.

The funding platform currently supports several major areas, including animal welfare, effective altruism infrastructure, and transformative artificial intelligence, while the Global Health and Development Fund is currently not accepting applications.

Because the application process is described as always open, applicants do not need to wait for a traditional annual deadline to submit a proposal. Instead, they should focus on developing a clear project, selecting the appropriate fund, explaining the problem being addressed, presenting a convincing theory of how the work can generate meaningful outcomes, and providing a well-justified funding request.

Potential applicants from different countries and regions should carefully review the current requirements for their chosen fund, as the information provided does not identify a specific nationality, race, or continent restriction.

Anyone considering applying should consult the official EA Funds website and application portal for the most current information before submitting a proposal, particularly because the availability and requirements of individual funds can change.

TITLE: Charles Darwin University RTP Scholarship 2026/27: Research Funding for PhD and Master by Research Students in Australia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Charles Darwin University (CDU) offers Australian Government Research Training Program (RTP) Scholarships to high-performing Higher Degree by Research candidates undertaking a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) or Master by Research in Australia.

The RTP is one of Australia’s principal funding mechanisms for postgraduate research. At Charles Darwin University, scholarships are awarded competitively to candidates who demonstrate strong academic performance, substantial research preparation, high-quality research outputs or research experience, and alignment with CDU’s research priorities. Both domestic and international candidates can meet the general RTP eligibility framework, although the availability of scholarships differs substantially between the two groups and between specific research projects.

For 2026, CDU lists an RTP stipend of:

AUD $35,489 per year for full-time students, tax-free and paid fortnightly.

For part-time recipients, the published 2026 rate is:

AUD $17,744.50 per year, taxable and paid fortnightly.

CDU states that stipend support normally runs for three years for a doctoral degree and two years for a research Master’s degree. Additional benefits can include paid sick leave, maternity leave and a relocation allowance of up to AUD $2,000 for domestic recipients and AUD $2,500 for international recipients, subject to conditions.

However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to an important update before relying on social-media posts advertising a general “2027 RTP Scholarship” with a 30 September 2026 deadline.

Important Application Status Update

The current official CDU information does not support advertising the RTP as a general open application round with a confirmed 30 September 2026 closing date.

CDU’s current RTP information page states that:

Research Training Program Scholarships are by invitation only.

Applicants must first be invited by the CDU Higher Degree by Research team before they can submit the formal RTP scholarship application.

In addition, CDU’s current project-focused scholarship information indicates that scholarship opportunities for 2026/27 are attached to pre-approved research projects and primarily target new HDR candidates. The university’s most recent international scholarship information says the International PhD RTP Scholarship is closed and that no international RTP scholarships remain for Semester 1, 2027, while future opportunities may be announced later.

Therefore, the frequently circulated statement that the “Charles Darwin University RTP Scholarship 2027 is open to all nationalities until 30 September 2026” should not currently be presented as an official CDU deadline.

Applicants should instead follow the live CDU scholarship pages and, where applicable, the instructions associated with a specific research project.

Official CDU RTP information

About the Australian Government Research Training Program

The Research Training Program is funded by the Australian Government and administered through eligible Australian universities.

Rather than students applying directly to the Australian Government, the government provides funding to participating higher education providers, and each university manages its own:

Scholarship application system

Eligibility process

Ranking process

Selection process

Scholarship conditions

The Australian Government confirms that RTP funding supports both domestic and overseas students undertaking research doctorates and research Master’s degrees at eligible Australian higher education institutions.

RTP support can take three broad forms:

Tuition fee offsets

Stipends for general living expenses

Allowances associated with the additional costs of undertaking higher-degree research

At Charles Darwin University, which forms of support a candidate receives can depend on their scholarship type, citizenship status and the particular research opportunity.

What Degrees Are Eligible at Charles Darwin University?

For RTP purposes, CDU defines Higher Degree by Research programmes as:

Doctor of Philosophy

and:

Master by Research

The scholarship is therefore not intended for ordinary coursework degrees such as:

Taught Master’s programmes

Graduate certificates

Graduate diplomas

Undergraduate programmes

CDU’s current eligibility guidelines explicitly state that the relevant HDR programmes are the Doctor of Philosophy and Master by Research.

Charles Darwin University PhD Opportunities

CDU is currently promoting a project-focused scholarship model for 2026/27.

The university lists pre-approved HDR projects across strategic research fields and allows new applicants to submit expressions of interest directly to relevant project supervisors.

Research areas represented across CDU projects include subjects such as:

Indigenous studies

Ecology

Remote health

Energy

Artificial intelligence

Sustainability

Specific eligibility and scholarship availability can differ by project, so candidates should not assume that every PhD project automatically includes the same funding package.

Current Domestic Scholarship Opportunities

For domestic candidates, CDU currently lists opportunities including the:

RTP Domestic PhD Scholarship

which provides approximately the standard CDU RTP stipend together with an RTP fee offset covering PhD tuition fees for up to three years.

CDU also lists a:

DVCRCC Domestic Strategic Project Scholarship

which may combine the standard RTP stipend with an additional top-up of up to approximately AUD $18,000 per year, together with a full fee offset for up to three years.

These project-specific opportunities demonstrate why applicants should review the actual project listing rather than assuming that every CDU research scholarship has identical financial conditions.

Current International Scholarship Position

International candidates need to exercise particular caution.

The general RTP framework does permit international applicants, and CDU’s eligibility rules explicitly state that both domestic and international students can be eligible for consideration.

However, that does not mean that unrestricted international RTP places are always available.

CDU’s current project-focused scholarship page states that the International PhD RTP Scholarship for international applicants is highly limited, while the most recent scholarship listing indicates that it is closed and not accepting applications, with no international RTP scholarships currently left for Semester 1, 2027.

CDU does separately advertise Graduate Full Fee Scholarships for selected international HDR applicants, covering tuition fees for eligible research programmes.

International applicants should therefore distinguish carefully between:

RTP stipend funding

Tuition-only scholarships

Project-specific scholarships

Other international research scholarships

A tuition waiver alone is not the same as receiving an RTP living stipend.

How Much Is the CDU RTP Stipend?

CDU currently publishes the 2026 stipend rate as:

Full-Time Students

AUD $35,489 per year

The stipend is:

Tax-free

Paid in fortnightly instalments

Part-Time Students

AUD $17,744.50 per year

The part-time stipend is:

Taxable

Paid fortnightly

These are CDU’s stated 2026 rates.

Applicants should not automatically describe AUD $35,489 as the confirmed 2027 CDU stipend unless CDU publishes that figure for 2027.

The Australian Government separately establishes indexed RTP base and maximum stipend rates nationally each year. For 2027, the federal minimum full-time RTP stipend rate is listed as AUD $35,550, but universities can set their institutional scholarship rate within the permitted range.

CDU applicants should therefore use the university’s own rate once its 2027 amount is formally published.

How Long Does RTP Funding Last?

CDU’s current scholarship information states that stipend funding normally runs for:

Three years full-time for a doctoral degree

and:

Two years for a research Master’s degree.

The broader Australian Government framework allows universities some flexibility over doctoral RTP support periods, but university-specific scholarship conditions ultimately determine the individual recipient’s funded period.

Candidates should therefore read the CDU scholarship offer and conditions carefully if selected.

Tuition Fee Support

Tuition arrangements differ between domestic and international research candidates.

Domestic RTP Fee Offset

Domestic RTP recipients can receive a:

Full RTP fee offset

which covers eligible research degree tuition costs for the standard funded period.

For project-based domestic PhD scholarships, CDU states that the fee offset can cover PhD tuition fees for up to three years.

International Tuition Fee Support

For international candidates, tuition support is more limited and competitive.

CDU indicates that international applicants awarded an RTP stipend may receive a Graduate Full Fee Scholarship covering international Higher Degree by Research tuition fees for the normal degree period.

CDU’s course information explains that these international tuition fee waivers are limited and normally cover:

Three years full-time for a PhD

Two years full-time for a Master by Research

International candidates who do not receive a fee-waiver scholarship may instead receive an offer as a full fee-paying research student.

For this reason, describing the CDU RTP as automatically covering tuition for every international candidate would be inaccurate.

Relocation Allowance

CDU also identifies relocation support as one of the possible RTP benefits.

The current published maximum allowance is:

Up to AUD $2,000 for domestic students

and:

Up to AUD $2,500 for international students

subject to applicable conditions.

Candidates should review the scholarship terms to determine:

Eligible relocation expenses

Documentation required

Claim deadlines

Whether reimbursement or another payment method applies

Paid Leave Benefits

Additional benefits listed by CDU include:

Paid sick leave

Maternity leave

The precise conditions and entitlements depend on the scholarship rules.

Candidates with family, medical or caregiving considerations should consult CDU’s RTP conditions rather than assuming ordinary employment leave rules apply.

Who Can Be Considered for the CDU RTP Scholarship?

The current CDU RTP eligibility framework requires candidates to satisfy five broad conditions.

Applicants must:

Be a domestic or international candidate.

Meet CDU academic and English-language admission requirements.

Be invited to apply by the CDU HDR team.

Submit a complete RTP scholarship application by the deadline communicated to them.

Not receive equivalent financial support from another source for their HDR studies.

The third requirement is particularly important:

The formal RTP application is invitation-only.

A prospective student therefore cannot necessarily submit an unrestricted scholarship application simply because they meet the academic criteria.

What Counts as a Domestic Student?

CDU defines domestic students as:

Australian citizens

Australian permanent residents

New Zealand citizens

Other applicants are generally categorized as international students.

Academic Requirements for a Master by Research

For scholarship ranking, Master by Research applicants are expected to demonstrate relevant research training.

CDU states that applicants should have completed at least:

Half a semester full-time equivalent

or:

20 credit points of research activity at AQF Level 8 or above

within a relevant qualification.

The university assesses both:

Academic performance

Quality and amount of previous research preparation

Academic Requirements for PhD Applicants

PhD applicants need stronger prior research preparation.

CDU states that candidates should have completed at least:

One semester full-time equivalent

or:

40 credit points of research activity at AQF Level 8 or above.

Relevant evidence can include:

Research thesis

Dissertation

Research units

Honours research

Master’s research components

Applicants must clearly identify which parts of previous degrees involved research and how heavily those units were weighted.

General HDR Entry Standard

For project-focused PhD opportunities, CDU summarizes its HDR academic expectation as a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree with a:

Distinction-level GPA

together with appropriate research preparation.

If a candidate does not meet the research-unit requirement exactly, CDU may consider equivalent research experience where the applicant can demonstrate a sufficiently strong research record.

This flexibility is especially relevant to candidates whose home universities use different programme structures.

International English-Language Requirements

International applicants must also satisfy CDU’s English requirements.

For the current project scholarship campaign, CDU provides an example of:

IELTS 6.5 overall, with no individual band below 6.0

and also notes acceptance of the:

Duolingo English Test

and other approved tests.

Applicants should check the requirements for their specific HDR programme because accepted tests and exemptions can vary.

Scholarship Selection Is Highly Competitive

Meeting the minimum admission conditions does not mean that an applicant will receive an RTP scholarship.

CDU states clearly that:

Australian Government RTP Stipend Scholarships are awarded to students of exceptional research potential and are not automatically granted to all HDR students.

Scholarship applications are ranked competitively.

CDU currently evaluates applicants across four broad areas:

Qualifications and academic performance

Quality research publications and non-traditional research outputs

Research experience or portfolio

Alignment with strategic research priorities

Academic Performance

Academic results form an important part of the ranking process.

CDU expects applicants to demonstrate:

Strong GPA

Relevant Bachelor’s, Honours or Master’s qualifications

Adequate research training

Strong thesis or dissertation performance

International applicants must make their grading systems understandable to CDU.

This may require submitting:

Official transcripts

Grading scale explanations

Course or unit outlines

Thesis information

Official English translations

Research Publications

Research outputs can significantly strengthen an RTP application.

CDU says successful candidates will typically demonstrate recent, high-quality:

Peer-reviewed research publications

as either:

First author

Co-author

The university can also consider eligible:

Non-Traditional Research Outputs

such as creative or discipline-specific research products where appropriate.

Candidates may submit up to four primary outputs demonstrating their research quality, impact and relevance.

Quality Matters More Than Quantity

CDU explicitly advises candidates to focus on:

Quality over quantity.

Listing a large number of publications without evidence of their quality will not necessarily make an application stronger.

Applicants should therefore identify their strongest work and provide evidence such as:

DOI

Journal ranking

Peer-review status

Publisher information

Publication details

Research impact

Publications Must Be Formally Accepted

CDU does not treat all unpublished manuscripts equally.

Outputs must generally be:

Published

In press

Formally accepted after peer review

Manuscripts that are merely:

Submitted

Under review

In revision

are not assessed as completed research outputs for scholarship ranking.

This distinction is especially important for early-career researchers preparing an application close to the scholarship assessment period.

Research Experience

Applicants may also receive credit for broader research experience not already captured by academic qualifications or publications.

Relevant experience can include:

Research employment

Work at a reputable university

Research institute employment

Research-related professional work

Other recognised research outputs

Substantial research portfolio

CDU requires claims to be supported with clear documentation.

Strategic Research Alignment

CDU may give additional weight to research proposals that align with:

University strategic research priorities

Institutional research strengths

Existing research capabilities

This makes supervisor and project fit especially important.

An academically excellent applicant proposing work unrelated to available expertise may be less competitive than a candidate whose research fits strongly within an established CDU team.

What Does a Strong Applicant Look Like?

CDU’s current project scholarship guidance says strong applicants will generally have a combination of:

Excellent academic record

Honours or Master’s research training

High GPA

Research publications

Practical research experience

Skills aligned with the project

The university notes that highly competitive applicants typically have at least one strong publication, such as a quality journal article, or a Master by Research/MPhil with a GPA of around 80% or higher.

This is indicative of competitiveness rather than a universal minimum requirement for every project.

How the Current Application Process Works

The current CDU process is not simply:

“Fill out an RTP scholarship form before September 30.”

For project-focused opportunities, applicants generally begin with an:

Expression of Interest to the lead supervisor.

The EOI should include:

A cover email explaining PhD eligibility, suitability for the research project and motivation

Curriculum vitae

Relevant qualifications and research experience

Up to four strong publications where possible

Postgraduate transcripts

Grading system information

Evidence of thesis or research components

Key Details at a Glance

University: Charles Darwin University

Country: Australia

Funding programme: Australian Government Research Training Program

Study level: Higher Degree by Research

Eligible degrees: Doctor of Philosophy and Master by Research

CDU full-time stipend: AUD $35,489 per year at the published 2026 rate

Part-time stipend: AUD $17,744.50 per year at the published 2026 rate

Payment: Fortnightly

Full-time stipend tax status: Tax-free

Doctoral stipend duration: Normally three years at CDU

Master by Research duration: Normally two years

Relocation allowance: Up to AUD $2,000 domestic / AUD $2,500 international, subject to conditions

Other benefits: Paid sick leave and maternity leave

Domestic eligibility: Australian citizens, Australian permanent residents and New Zealand citizens

International eligibility: International applicants can meet general RTP eligibility, subject to scholarship availability

Formal scholarship application: By invitation only

Current international 2027 status: International RTP availability is extremely limited; CDU’s latest public information indicates no general international Semester 1, 2027 RTP places remain

Tips for Prospective Applicants

1. Find a Suitable Research Project First

CDU’s current scholarship model strongly emphasizes pre-approved projects.

Start by identifying:

Research topic

Faculty

Supervisor

Project fit

before worrying about the formal RTP application.

2. Contact the Lead Supervisor

A strong initial email should explain:

Your research background

Why you meet CDU PhD or Master by Research admission requirements

Why you fit the project

Your strongest research achievements

Why you want to work with that supervisor

Avoid generic mass emails.

3. Make Your Research Training Easy to Assess

International degree structures can differ significantly from Australia’s.

Clearly show:

Which courses were research-based

Credit weighting

Thesis length

Thesis grade

Research methodology training

CDU states that it is the applicant’s responsibility to make this information clear.

4. Provide Your Strongest Research Outputs

If you have publications, prioritize the strongest four.

Explain:

Journal quality

Peer review

DOI

Your contribution

Relevance to the proposed research

5. Do Not Assume Admission Equals Scholarship

An applicant may be academically eligible for a PhD but not competitive enough for RTP funding.

Scholarship selection is substantially more competitive than minimum programme admission.

6. International Applicants Should Check Availability Before Spending Time on a Full Application

This is especially important for 2027.

CDU’s current information indicates very limited or closed international RTP availability for Semester 1, 2027.

Contact the relevant supervisor or CDU HDR team before preparing a large application package.

Conclusion

The Charles Darwin University Research Training Program Scholarship remains an attractive Australian postgraduate research funding pathway for highly competitive candidates pursuing a PhD or Master by Research.

CDU’s published 2026 full-time RTP stipend is AUD $35,489 per year, paid fortnightly and tax-free. Part-time recipients receive AUD $17,744.50 annually, taxable. Scholarship benefits can also include tuition support, paid leave and relocation assistance.

The scholarship is competitive rather than automatic. Applicants are ranked according to factors including academic performance, research preparation, publications, broader research experience and alignment with CDU research priorities.

Importantly, CDU’s current system requires candidates to be invited by the HDR team before submitting a formal RTP application.

Please visit RTP Scholarship Ranking Guidelines before applying.

TITLE: 2026 AWARD Leadership Program for Young African Women in Agricultural Sciences: Apply for the 9-Month Leadership Training

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Women in Agricultural Research and Development (AWARD) has opened applications for the 2026 Leadership Training Program for Emerging African Women in Agricultural Sciences. Funded by the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, formerly Carnegie Corporation of New York, the initiative is designed to strengthen the leadership capacity, confidence, professional visibility and influence of young African women working in agricultural sciences.

The nine-month program seeks to develop a cohort of at least 40 talented African women under the age of 35 and their mentors. Through intensive, non-residential training, participants will develop practical leadership and career skills while strengthening their ability to contribute to agricultural science, gender equality and broader agricultural development.

Opportunity Overview

Program: 2026 AWARD Leadership Training Program for Emerging African Women in Agricultural Sciences

Organiser: African Women in Agricultural Research and Development (AWARD)

Funding: Andrew Carnegie Foundation, formerly Carnegie Corporation of New York

Duration: Nine months

Format: Intensive, non-residential career transformation program

Target: At least 40 young African women under 35, selected competitively, together with their mentors

Application deadline: 20 September 2026 at midnight, East Africa Time (UTC+3)

Application method: Online application form

Eligible countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, Senegal, Tanzania and Zambia

About the AWARD Leadership Training Program

The AWARD Leadership Training Program is intended to invest in the potential of young African women working in agricultural sciences and help them become more competent, confident and influential professionals.

The program recognises that women working in agricultural science can face institutional and professional barriers that affect their career progression. It therefore focuses on building the leadership, communication, networking and strategic skills participants need to navigate these challenges and advance in their careers.

The initiative also promotes greater awareness of gender integration and gender equality in agriculture-related professions. Participants are expected to strengthen not only their individual careers but also their capacity to contribute to broader changes within agricultural research and development.

The selected participants will come from a range of disciplines within the biophysical and social sciences applied to agriculture. The program is also designed to reflect the diversity of African institutions and professional environments, including universities, research centres, government institutions, NGOs, civil society organisations and the private sector.

What Participants Will Gain

The program offers a broad professional and leadership development experience. Selected participants will have the opportunity to:

1. Strengthen leadership skills

Participants will explore different types of effective leadership and develop a stronger understanding of how leadership can be applied within professional and organisational settings.

The training is designed to help emerging women leaders become more confident in taking responsibility, influencing others and contributing meaningfully to their organisations and sectors.

2. Develop a strategic career path

Participants will learn how to define their career direction and make strategic use of professional networks to advance their careers.

This focus can help participants better understand where they want to go professionally and how relationships, collaborations and networks can contribute to achieving their long-term goals.

3. Build a strong personal brand

Another major component of the program is personal branding.

Participants will develop the confidence and practical skills required to communicate their expertise, ideas and achievements effectively. This includes preparing to present or propose promising ideas to funders, financing agencies and potential collaborators.

A stronger professional profile can help researchers and agricultural science professionals increase their visibility and make their work more accessible to potential partners and supporters.

4. Improve team management and organisational skills

The training will provide tools and skills for managing teams effectively.

Participants will explore how to understand organisational dynamics, develop alliances and make carefully considered decisions, including taking calculated risks when appropriate.

These skills are particularly relevant for emerging professionals who aspire to move into management, research leadership or other positions of responsibility.

5. Strengthen gender leadership and negotiation skills

The program also places significant emphasis on gender issues.

Participants will develop a better understanding of gender-related challenges and learn recognised strategies for addressing difficult situations. The training aims to help participants negotiate challenging circumstances and transform obstacles into opportunities for professional success.

6. Expand professional networks

The program brings together young women working across different agricultural science disciplines and professional environments.

This creates opportunities for participants to interact with professionals from universities, research institutions, government, NGOs, civil society and the private sector.

Such connections can contribute to future collaboration, knowledge exchange and professional development.

7. Increase research communication and professional visibility

The program is intended to help participants improve their ability to communicate their research and professional ideas to diverse audiences.

This is particularly valuable for agricultural scientists whose work may need to reach policymakers, funders, development organisations, industry representatives and communities beyond the academic environment.

The 2026 leadership training program specifically targets young African women under the age of 35 who are engaged in agricultural sciences.

Applicants should be working or involved in fields related to agricultural science, including disciplines within the biophysical and social sciences applied to agriculture.

The program can attract women working across different types of organisations, including:

Universities and higher education institutions

Government institutions

Other institutions involved in agricultural research and development

TITLE: Harassment Policy Information

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Physics Department adheres to the policy on harassment set forth by the Institute as found in the publication, Dealing with Harassment at MIT. The publication is available in the Physics Human Resources Office, 4-311 and online at http://hrweb.mit.edu/complaint-guidelines. An abbreviated form of the policy is listed below. However, if you are involved with a harassment case in any capacity, please see the full publication for complete information.

MIT’s Policy of Harassment

Harassment of any kind is not acceptable behavior at MIT; it is inconsistent with the commitment to excellence that characterizes MIT’s activities. MIT is committed to creating an environment in which every individual can work, study, and live without being harassed. Harassment may, therefore, lead to sanctions up to and including termination of employment or student status.

Harassment is any conduct, verbal or physical, on or off campus, that has the intent or effect of unreasonably interfering with an individual or group’s educational or work performance at MIT or that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive educational, work, or living environment. Some kinds of harassment are prohibited by civil laws or by MIT policies on conflict of interest and nondiscrimination. Harassment on the basis of race, color, gender, disability, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, or age includes harassment of an individual in terms of a stereotyped group characteristic, or because of that person’s identification with a particular group.

Sexual harassment may take many forms. Sexual assault and requests for sexual favors that affect educational or employment decisions constitute sexual harassment. However, sexual harassment may also consist of unwanted physical contact, requests for sexual favors, visual displays of degrading sexual images, sexually suggestive conduct, or remarks of a sexual nature.

The Institute is committed under this policy to stopping harassment and associated retaliatory behavior. All MIT supervisors have a responsibility to act to stop harassment in the areas under their supervision. Any member of the MIT community who feels harassed is encouraged to seek assistance and resolution of the complaint. MIT provides a variety of avenues by which an individual who feels harassed may proceed, so that each person may choose an avenue appropriate to their particular situation. Institute procedures are intended to protect the rights of both complainant and respondent, to protect privacy, and to prevent supervisory reprisal. General complaint and grievance procedures are described in Policies and Procedures is available online at https://policies.mit.edu/policies-procedures/70-general-employment-policies.

Options for Dealing with Harassment

MIT’s system for handling complaints is designed to provide choice for the complainants, so that different people may find options for stopping harassment that are appropriate for them. While some people prefer the clarity of a single, formal grievance procedure, many people who have been harassed do not want to lodge a formal complaint. Discussions with colleagues at other universities indicate that as more options for handling complaints become available, more people come forward with their concerns.

Each option has its advantages and disadvantages. Often a formal complaint procedure is preferred for harassment that is considered egregious, and informal complaint resolution is preferred for more subtle, ambiguous, or idiosyncratic harassment. However, choice of option is affected by many factors, including the complainant’s need for privacy and control over the complaint, the complainant’s preferred style of complaint resolution, and what kind of evidence exists.

In many cases, a complainant may change from one option to another–for example, from more formal to less formal, or vice versa. In most cases, however, changing options will require the agreement of both parties to the dispute, as well as the complaint handler.

Formal complaints against students should be made to the IDHR Office. Formal complaints against staff should be made to the immediate or higher supervisor of the alleged harasser, or to Human Resources Officer, Stephen Salk, srsalk@mit.edu, 3-6323.

In addition to the above, if you believe you have been subjected to sexual harassment, you may file a formal complaint with either or both of the government agencies set forth below. Using our complaint process does not prohibit you from filing a complaint with these agencies. Each of the agencies has a short time period for filing a claim.

The United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (“EEOC”)
One Congress Street, 10th Floor
Boston, MA 02114
(617) 565-3200

The Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination (“MCAD”)
One Ashburton Place
Rm. 601
Boston, MA 02108
(617) 994-6000

General Responsibilities of Complaint Handlers and Supervisors

If harassment is observed by, or reported to, the immediate or higher supervisor of an alleged harasser, the supervisor must either act or be assured that appropriate action has been taken to stop any harassment that is occurring. The supervisor should also take reasonable steps to prevent reprisal. Similarly, an administrator who is not in the line of supervision but who can take administrative action must see that any observed or reported harassment ceases to occur, and must take appropriate steps to prevent reprisal.

A supervisor is not necessarily required to initiate a formal investigation and make a decision as to whether harassment actually occurred, except in serious cases. However, as noted above, a supervisor is responsible for either taking reasonable steps to see that any harassment has stopped and that there is no reprisal, or for knowing that effective action has been taken.

All harassment complaints should be addressed as promptly as possible. MIT does not have statute of limitations for concerns of harassment. If a formal complaint is brought long after the fact, it may be unreasonable or impossible to investigate the complaint, but sometimes informal options can help even in these circumstances. Supervisors should inform themselves of the basic information in this policy, including the definition of harassment, and the general principles and options for complaint resolution. Information that is more specific or advice may be obtained from the publication Dealing with Harassment at MIT.

In all cases, a supervisor must take reasonable steps to deal fairly with both parties and strive to maintain, as much as possible, the privacy of all individuals involved in the complaint.

Read also:

Responsible Employee Information: https://idhr.mit.edu/reporting-options/responsible-employees

Guidelines for Responsible Employees: https://idhr.mit.edu/sites/default/files/documents/Web_IDHR%20Responsible%20Employee%20Guide%20v051721.pdf

Information on Complaint Handlers

Role of Complaint Handlers

Below are the MIT guidelines that address the typical action of a compliant handler when dealing with a complaint.

Initial Contact –The complaint handler will listen to the complaint and ask any questions required to fully understand the issue. After having heard the account, they will confirm and review what s/he needs to know to deal fairly and effectively with the concern. Remember that you and the complaint handler can seek advice anonymously if you wish.

Discuss the Possible Options — The complaint handler will review the multiple options for handling complaints including options for the complainant directly, and options for a complaint handler. The person who complains of harassment usually has choices to make as to which option to pursue, but in certain circumstances, for example, if the complaint is so serious that it must be investigated, the complaint handlers must make decisions about how to proceed. If the behavior is egregiously offensive, is a matter of reprisal, or is repeated after a warning, a formal process is appropriate.

Determine What Course of Action to Pursue — If possible, the compliant handler will act in accordance with your wishes. If the complaint handler thinks it necessary to take action not requested by you, the complaint handler should, if possible, discuss this with you.

Resolving a Complaint — It is the complaint handler’s responsibility to see that the complaint is seriously and thoroughly addressed. A complaint can be addressed in a number of different ways–with or without disciplinary action against an offender and with or without a record of the complaint–depending on the course of action pursued and the outcome of the process. After dealing with the complaint, the complaint handler should follow up to ensure that harassment has not recurred and that there is no reprisal.

Reporting and Records — The complaint handler should make sure that both parties are informed of the outcome of a formal or informal intervention by him or her. He or she should also keep a record of the action: a formal record if the complaint was investigated or a statistical record if the complaint was resolved informally.

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

Climate change, caused by a sustained trend of global heating, primarily due to human activity, consists of emissions of greenhouse gasses (known as GHGs), mostly carbon dioxide. Since the industrial revolution, the fossil fuels that have powered the global economy have also altered the atmosphere and are highly likely to cause climate change that may be difficult and expensive to adapt to. About 85 percent of the energy consumed in modern society comes from fossil fuels. The transport sector – trucks, cars, buses, airplanes, cargo ships, railroads – is overwhelmingly dependent on petroleum. Today, transport of goods and people is responsible for about 19 percent of carbon emissions. This course will examine future climate change in the context of climate history, and then consider various strategies for what might be done to deal with it. TITLE: The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship 2027: Paid Remote Science Journalism Program with $6,600 Stipend Open Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027 Early-Career Fellowship Program at The Open Notebook (TON), a paid, remote, part-time professional development opportunity designed for emerging science journalists who want to strengthen their reporting, writing, pitching, interviewing, editing, and career-development skills.

The program runs for 12 months, beginning on February 9, 2027, and provides each selected fellow with a $6,600 stipend. Because the fellowship is fully remote and applicants living outside the United States are explicitly welcome to apply, it represents an accessible international opportunity for aspiring and early-career science journalists around the world.

The deadline to submit the main application is October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time. Reference letters have a separate deadline of November 7, 2026.

About The Open Notebook

The Open Notebook is a U.S.-based nonprofit organization focused on strengthening science journalism through practical training, mentoring, educational resources, professional development programs, and a global community of journalists.

The organization describes itself as a leading online source of training and educational material for journalists who cover science. Its broader work focuses particularly on helping reporters improve coverage of subjects involving science, health, the environment, and technology while strengthening evidence-based journalism more generally.

The organization operates with the broader goal of ensuring that journalists, regardless of geography or financial means, can access resources that help them report complex scientific subjects accurately and effectively.

Its activities include online publications, professional-development programs, mentoring initiatives, workshops, master classes, reporting tools, and other resources aimed at journalists at different stages of their careers.

About the 2027 Early-Career Fellowship Program

The Open Notebook’s Early-Career Fellowship is structured specifically for journalists who are still at an early stage in their professional science-writing careers.

Rather than functioning as a conventional course in which participants mainly attend lectures, the program places fellows directly into The Open Notebook’s editorial environment.

During the 12-month period, fellows work with experienced science-journalism mentors to develop ideas, report stories, write articles, respond to editorial feedback, and prepare work for publication.

This makes the fellowship a combination of professional mentoring, hands-on journalism experience, editorial training, and community participation.

The fellowship is supported by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, which The Open Notebook says has supported the program since 2013.
