What Fellows Will Actually Do

The core of the fellowship is practical journalism.

Each selected fellow is expected to report and write four articles, with individual pieces generally running approximately 1,500 to 2,000 words.

The stories are prepared for publication by The Open Notebook and can include formats such as behind-the-story interviews with journalists and reported features examining some aspect of the craft and practice of science journalism.

This is an important distinction for applicants to understand.

The fellowship is not primarily about reporting new scientific discoveries themselves. The Open Notebook specializes in examining how science journalism is practiced: how reporters find stories, conduct interviews, investigate difficult subjects, structure narratives, use evidence, work with editors, handle ethical challenges, and communicate complex subjects.

Applicants should therefore become familiar with TON’s existing publication before proposing story ideas.

Four Published Journalism Assignments

Completing four substantial articles over a year gives fellows time to move through the full editorial process repeatedly.

That process can involve identifying an appropriate story idea, narrowing the angle, locating sources, arranging interviews, reporting the story, drafting the article, responding to editorial feedback, revising the piece, verifying factual claims, and preparing the final article for publication.

For a journalist still developing professional experience, this repeated cycle can be especially valuable because the learning takes place through actual editorial work rather than hypothetical exercises.

Four articles over 12 months may initially appear modest. However, applicants should recognize that these are not quick news items. They involve substantial reporting, multiple revisions, fact-checking preparation, and collaboration with mentors and editors.

One-to-One Mentorship with an Experienced Science Journalist

A major component of the program is individualized mentorship.

Each fellow is paired with an experienced science journalist and participates in regular phone or video meetings.

The mentor helps the fellow develop story ideas, strengthen reporting techniques, improve drafts, navigate revisions, and think through broader questions about building a career in science journalism.

This mentoring structure means participants receive sustained professional guidance rather than a single workshop or short training intervention.

For early-career journalists, regular access to someone who has already navigated the profession can help clarify issues such as story development, pitching, interviewing, freelancing, editorial relationships, specialization, professional positioning, and long-term career choices.

Become Part of The Open Notebook Editorial Community

Fellows also become part of the wider TON editorial community.

The program includes interaction with current and former fellows, mentors, and editors through a dedicated Slack community.

Fellows participate in cohort-oriented discussions and activities during the program, and membership in this community continues after the fellowship concludes.

This continuing community component is significant because journalism careers frequently depend not only on technical competence but also on professional networks, peer learning, editor relationships, knowledge sharing, and access to trusted colleagues.

The program therefore aims to build both skills and professional connections.

How Much Time Does the Fellowship Require?

The fellowship is officially part-time.

The Open Notebook estimates that most fellows spend approximately 5 to 7 hours per week on average completing fellowship responsibilities. The actual workload can vary depending on the fellow’s experience, work habits, and where a particular story stands in the reporting and editing process.

Some weeks can therefore require considerably more effort than others.

Applicants should not interpret “part-time” as meaning the fellowship can be completed casually whenever spare time becomes available.

The program has real publication deadlines and an intensive editorial process.

Activities Applicants Should Be Prepared to Fit Into Their Schedule

Although the precise weekly workload changes during the year, fellows need sufficient flexibility for several kinds of professional activity.

These include interviewing sources, frequently during normal U.S. daytime hours; holding weekly phone or video conversations with mentors; undertaking multiple rounds of revisions; preparing stories for fact-checking; and participating in fellowship discussions and activities through Slack.

International applicants should pay particular attention to the U.S. daytime interview requirement.

Someone applying from Asia, Africa, Europe, Latin America, or Oceania should consider the time difference and whether their work, studies, family commitments, or other responsibilities will allow sufficient flexibility.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The program is intended for early-career science journalists and aspiring science journalists.

One of the most important eligibility rules is that applicants generally need to have fewer than three years of regular professional science-writing experience.

However, TON makes two important clarifications.

First, internships and student work do not count toward this three-year limit.

Second, exceptions may be considered where an applicant has more than three years of professional science-writing experience but some or all of that experience was conducted in a language other than English.

This provides some flexibility for journalists whose careers developed outside English-language journalism.

You Do Not Need Extensive Experience

Applicants do need some prior exposure to writing for general audiences, but The Open Notebook does not require extensive professional experience.

Some training and/or experience writing about science for the general public is required.

This means the program falls between an absolute beginner opportunity and a mid-career professional fellowship.

An applicant should already be able to demonstrate that they have begun developing relevant skills, but they do not need a long professional publication record.

Experience could potentially come from student journalism, internships, independent reporting, freelance work, journalism training, or another setting that has enabled the applicant to produce public-facing writing.

The decisive issue is whether the applicant can demonstrate an authentic and developing commitment to professional science journalism.

The Fellowship Is for Journalism, Not General Science Communication

Applicants should pay close attention to this distinction.

The Open Notebook gives priority to people whose primary professional ambition is to work as science journalists.

Science journalism and science communication can overlap, but they are not identical.

Science journalists generally report independently for public audiences, interrogate evidence, interview multiple sources, examine uncertainty and disagreement, investigate institutions, and apply journalistic standards of verification and editorial independence.

Science communicators may instead work for research institutions, universities, companies, scientific organizations, government agencies, museums, nonprofits, or individual researchers to communicate science on behalf of those organizations.

Applicants whose main goal is journalism should therefore explain that clearly in their application.

No Specific University Degree Is Listed

The official 2027 eligibility criteria do not state that applicants must possess a bachelor’s degree, master’s degree, doctorate, journalism degree, or science degree.

The emphasis is instead on experience, training, demonstrated writing ability, career stage, and commitment to professional science journalism.

This means candidates should not automatically exclude themselves because they do not hold a specialized journalism qualification.

What matters more is whether their work demonstrates the potential to develop as a science journalist.

International Applicants Can Apply

One of the strongest accessibility features of the fellowship is its global eligibility.

The Open Notebook explicitly states that people living outside the United States are welcome to apply.

Since the fellowship is remote, selected participants can ordinarily complete it from their existing country of residence.

The current call does not provide a restricted list of eligible nationalities.

This makes the program relevant to emerging journalists across Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, the Middle East, the Caribbean, and Oceania, provided they meet the fellowship’s other eligibility and language requirements.

English-Language Requirements

All application materials must be submitted in English.

This includes writing samples and the reference letter.

However, applicants are allowed to provide materials that were originally produced in another language and then translated into English.

The program also recognizes that applicants for whom English is not a first language should not necessarily be expected to write with the same fluency as native English speakers.

Nevertheless, successful participation requires a reasonably strong level of English because fellows must interview sources, write substantial articles, communicate with mentors and editors, and complete multiple rounds of revision in English.

What The Open Notebook Looks for When Selecting Fellows

TON’s published selection criteria emphasize several qualities.

Applicants are expected to demonstrate a serious intention to pursue professional science journalism, some prior experience or training in public-facing science writing, an understanding of the profession and its challenges, familiarity with The Open Notebook, the ability to produce appropriate story ideas, reliability with deadlines, and strong writing ability.

In practical terms, a strong application should demonstrate more than enthusiasm.

It should show that the applicant understands what science journalists actually do, understands the type of journalism TON publishes, can identify worthwhile stories, and has thought carefully about the specific skills they want to develop.

Why Familiarity with The Open Notebook Matters

Applicants are expected to propose stories specifically for TON.

Before applying, candidates should therefore spend meaningful time reading the publication.

A generic science pitch is unlikely to demonstrate strong understanding of the fellowship.

The Open Notebook focuses on the craft of science journalism, so applicants should think about questions such as how journalists report difficult topics, manage ethical challenges, build source networks, use data, cover marginalized communities, investigate scientific institutions, explain uncertainty, structure complex features, or develop sustainable journalism careers.

A good proposal should feel naturally suited to TON rather than like an idea that could be sent unchanged to any science publication.

Application Questions

The application asks candidates to explain why they are interested in the fellowship, what they hope to learn, what previous training or experience they have writing science stories for public audiences, what skills or perspectives they would contribute, and what other commitments they expect to have during the fellowship year.

That final question is especially important.

Because the program requires sustained work over 12 months, applicants should provide a realistic account of how they will balance the fellowship with university study, dissertation work, freelancing, employment, job searching, caregiving, or other responsibilities.

Applicants should avoid creating an unrealistic impression that they have unlimited availability if they do not.

Two Story Proposals Are Required

Applicants must submit two brief story proposals, each approximately 100 words.

These proposals should describe possible TON features or multimedia stories and could take forms such as behind-the-story interviews, reported features about the craft of science writing, roundtable discussions, or another substantial project related to science-journalism practice.

These are intentionally short proposals rather than complete, fully developed pitches.

The challenge is therefore to demonstrate a strong idea efficiently.

A useful 100-word proposal should establish the central question, explain why it matters to science journalists, identify the likely approach or sources, and demonstrate why TON is the right publication for the story.

Resume or CV

Applicants must also provide a resume or curriculum vitae.

For an early-career journalist, the document should focus on relevant professional experience rather than attempting to appear artificially senior.

Relevant information can include journalism employment, freelance assignments, internships, university journalism, publications, fellowships, training programs, multimedia work, scientific expertise, language abilities, awards, and other experiences that help demonstrate suitability.

Where possible, applicants should make it easy for reviewers to understand the relationship between their background and science journalism.

Reference Letter

One reference letter is required.

The referee can be a professor, editor, mentor, supervisor, or another professional colleague who can credibly discuss the applicant’s abilities and characteristics relevant to science journalism and the fellowship.

The best referee is not necessarily the person with the most impressive job title.

An effective referee is someone who knows the applicant’s work sufficiently well to provide detailed observations about qualities such as writing, curiosity, reporting skills, initiative, reliability, openness to editing, ability to meet deadlines, and potential for growth.

The recommendation deadline is November 7, 2026, one week after the main application deadline.

Applicants should therefore contact their referee early rather than waiting until the final application week.

Writing or Multimedia Samples

Applicants may submit up to two writing or multimedia samples intended for general audiences.

Scientific papers and conventional academic writing are not appropriate substitutes because TON wants to evaluate the applicant’s ability to communicate with the public.

Applicants submitting audio or multimedia work can provide relevant links within an uploaded PDF.

Samples must be in English, although translated work is acceptable.

When choosing samples, candidates should prioritize work that demonstrates journalism skills rather than simply selecting the longest or most technically sophisticated material they have produced.

A strong sample might show clear reporting, effective interviewing, accurate explanation of complex information, narrative skill, evidence-based reasoning, or a strong sense of audience.

Optional Background Information

The application also provides candidates with an optional opportunity to share additional information about themselves.

The Open Notebook says it strongly encourages writers from all backgrounds to apply and specifically invites applicants from communities historically marginalized or underrepresented in U.S. journalism to disclose that information if they wish.

Providing such information is completely optional, and TON says information disclosed through this section will be treated confidentially.

Applicants therefore do not need to identify themselves as belonging to any particular demographic group in order to apply.

$6,600 Fellowship Stipend

The 2027 fellowship provides a total stipend of $6,600.

Because the fellowship lasts 12 months and requires an estimated five to seven hours per week on average, candidates should view it as a paid professional-development fellowship rather than full-time employment.

The principal value of the opportunity combines financial support with mentoring, published work, editorial experience, structured skill development, and long-term professional community access.

Applicants should make their own assessment of whether the stipend and professional benefits are appropriate for the time commitment involved.

Fellowship Start Date and Duration

The 2027 fellowship begins on:

February 9, 2027

It continues for:

12 months on a part-time basis

The program is conducted remotely.

Prospective applicants should therefore consider their anticipated commitments throughout most of 2027 and into early 2028 rather than evaluating availability only around the February start date.

Main Application Deadline

The principal deadline is:

October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time

The separate reference-letter deadline is:

November 7, 2026.

International applicants should convert the deadline carefully into their own local time zone rather than assuming that October 31 ends at midnight in their country.

Submitting well before the deadline also reduces the risk of technical problems with document uploads or the application form.

How to Build a Strong Application

A competitive application should show a coherent professional story.

The application components should reinforce one another: the resume should establish relevant experience, the samples should demonstrate ability, the story ideas should show editorial judgment, the written responses should explain motivation and learning goals, and the recommendation should provide independent evidence of the applicant’s potential.

Applicants should avoid approaching each document as an isolated requirement.

For example, someone transitioning from science research into journalism could use the application to explain how scientific expertise has shaped their reporting interests while making clear that their long-term ambition is journalism rather than institutional science communication.

Likewise, someone already freelancing could demonstrate how the fellowship would help them move from short assignments into deeper reported features.

How to Approach the Two 100-Word Story Ideas

The short length makes precision essential.

Start with a specific challenge or question facing science journalists. Then explain why it matters and how the story would investigate it.

Avoid proposing a broad subject such as “how journalists cover climate change.” That topic is too large.

A stronger proposal would isolate a particular reporting problem, practice, ethical dilemma, technique, or emerging challenge and show how interviews with specific kinds of journalists or editors could produce practical insight.

The objective is not simply to select an interesting science subject. It is to identify an interesting science-journalism craft question.

Choosing the Best Writing Samples

Your strongest academic paper is not necessarily your strongest fellowship sample.

The fellowship asks for work intended for a general audience because public-facing journalism requires different skills from scholarly writing.

Select pieces that show that you can make complex subjects understandable without distorting them.

Where possible, choose work that demonstrates reporting rather than pure commentary.

If your strongest material was originally produced in another language, the explicit permission to submit translated samples can make the fellowship particularly accessible to international journalists.

How International Applicants Can Prepare

International applicants should consider several logistical factors even though the program is remote.

Time-zone differences matter because source interviews may need to occur during U.S. daytime hours, and mentor meetings will need mutually workable schedules.

Applicants should also evaluate English-language readiness realistically.

Perfect English is not required, but fellows must be capable of participating in professional editorial discussions, interviewing sources, understanding detailed feedback, and revising substantial articles.

Applicants should treat their geographic perspective as a potential professional asset rather than a disadvantage. Science journalism is global, and reporters working outside major U.S. media centers can bring knowledge of different scientific institutions, communities, reporting environments, languages, and public-health or environmental contexts.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Emerging Science Journalists

Formal pathways into science journalism can be difficult to access, particularly for journalists outside established media centers.

The Open Notebook itself identifies inequitable access to journalism training as an important problem and says its mission includes making professional-development resources available across geography and financial circumstances.

A remote, paid fellowship can help reduce some of those barriers by removing the requirement to relocate to an expensive media hub.

The fellowship also creates something that online courses generally cannot provide: sustained editorial accountability.

Fellows must produce work, meet deadlines, receive professional editing, revise repeatedly, communicate with mentors, and participate in a working journalistic community.

That combination can turn abstract lessons about journalism into habits built through practice.

About the Fellowship’s Track Record

The Open Notebook has operated its early-career fellowship for more than a decade, with listed fellows going back to 2014 and the current roster extending through 2026.

Past fellows have produced articles exploring practical journalism topics including field reporting, disability reporting, reporting during conflict, vaccine hesitancy, sourcing, audio journalism, freelance careers, pitching behavior, internships, investigative reporting, and other elements of the profession.

This history demonstrates that the program is built around practical questions faced by working journalists rather than only theoretical discussion.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through The Open Notebook’s online application form.

Apply for The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship 2027

Applicants should prepare the required responses, two short story proposals, resume or CV, reference arrangements, and up to two qualifying work samples before completing the form.

The official fellowship page should remain the controlling source for requirements or updates:

Official Early-Career Fellowship Program page

Questions that are not already addressed in the program instructions can be sent to editors@theopennotebook.com.

Conclusion

The The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship 2027 offers emerging science journalists an opportunity to spend a full year developing professional reporting and writing skills through real editorial assignments, individualized mentorship, publication experience, and participation in an international journalism community.

The fellowship is particularly accessible because it is fully remote, accepts applicants from outside the United States, does not state a specific university-degree requirement, and allows translated English-language samples from journalists whose previous work was produced in another language.

Selected fellows will receive a $6,600 stipend, work part-time for 12 months beginning February 9, 2027, and complete four substantial articles while working closely with experienced science-journalism mentors. Applicants should nevertheless take the workload seriously: the program estimates an average commitment of roughly five to seven hours per week and expects fellows to meet professional reporting, editing, and revision deadlines.

The main application must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. U.S. Central Time on October 31, 2026, while reference letters are due November 7, 2026.

TITLE: Chevening Scholarship to Study in the UK 2027-2028 (Fully-funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 6, 2026

Applications are open for the Chevening Scholarship to Study in the UK 2027-2028. Chevening is the UK Government’s global scholarship programme that offers future leaders the unique opportunity to study in the UK. These scholarships are awarded to outstanding professionals from all over the world to pursue a one-year master’s degree in any subject at any UK university.

Chevening provides fully-funded scholarships, leaving you free to focus on achieving your academic goals and enjoying the experience of a lifetime. You will live and study in the UK for a year, during which time you will develop professionally and academically, grow your network, experience UK culture, and build lasting positive relationships with the UK.

Scholarship

As Chevening Scholarships are fully-funded, your award includes the following:

university tuition fees

a monthly stipend

travel costs to and from the UK

an arrival allowance

a homeward departure allowance

the cost of one visa application

a travel grant to attend Chevening events in the UK

Eligibility

To be eligible for a Chevening Scholarship you must:

Be a citizen of a Chevening-eligible country or territory.

Commit to returning to your home country for at least two years after your scholarship ends.

Have at least two years of work experience (2,800 hours).

Hold an undergraduate degree that qualifies you for a UK master’s programme.

Apply to three different and eligible  UK university courses. You must have received an unconditional offer from at least one of these course choices by the references and education documents deadline listed on the application timeline.

You are not eligible for a Chevening Scholarship if you:

Hold British or dual British citizenship (unless you are a citizen of a British Overseas Territory or hold BN(O) and are applying from Hong Kong).

Hold refugee status in a country not eligible for Chevening. However, if you are a citizen of an eligible country and hold refugee status in another eligible country, you are eligible for a scholarship.

Are an employee, former employee, or relative of an employee of the UK government, British Embassies/High Commissions, the British Council, the Association of Commonwealth Universities, or sponsoring UK universities. Employees, former employees, or relatives* of an employee of Chevening Partner organisations are eligible to apply, but if the employment took place within the last two years, you cannot receive a Chevening Partner Award from the organisation from which you work, previously worked, or are affiliated with through relatives.

Have previously studied in the UK on a UK government-funded scholarship.

Note that having a master’s degree does not prevent you from applying for a second master’s degree in the UK, providing you can articulate how it aligns with your career goals and will help you to drive positive change in your home country.

Application

To apply, find the awards available in your country/territory. Begin by selecting your country of citizenship. You can then refine your search depending on if you are applying for a scholarship or a fellowship.

TITLE: COBRA Early Career Deep-Sea Expedition Leadership Master Class and Fellowship 2027: Fully Funded Training and Research Leadership Opportunity

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Crustal Ocean Biosphere Research Accelerator (COBRA) is inviting applications for its 2027 Early Career Deep-Sea Expedition Leadership Master Class and Fellowship, an international training and professional development opportunity designed to prepare early career researchers and other emerging professionals to lead deep-sea research expeditions.

The 2027 COBRA Master Class will provide participants with practical knowledge and tools for planning deep-sea oceanographic field research from beginning to end. The programme covers the development of research concepts, funding and proposal writing, expedition preparation, at-sea operations, telepresence, permitting, reporting, data management, ocean law, and engagement with other researchers and stakeholders.

The 12-week programme combines synchronous online training with an in-person final week in Maine, United States. Selected participants will also become COBRA Fellows for the 2027 calendar year and will be eligible for additional COBRA leadership training opportunities.

Importantly, previous hands-on experience in deep-sea research, outreach, or policy is not required, making the opportunity accessible to early career professionals who want to build expertise in deep-sea science, exploration, research leadership, and ocean policy.

About the Crustal Ocean Biosphere Research Accelerator (COBRA)

The Crustal Ocean Biosphere Research Accelerator (COBRA) is an international research coordination network focused on accelerating research into the structure, function, resilience, and ecosystem services of the crustal ocean biosphere.

The network seeks to generate and coordinate research that can contribute to better decision-making, particularly in areas connected to:

Deep-sea mining

Subsea and subseafloor environments

Subsea carbon sequestration

Ocean exploration

Deep-sea ecosystems

Ocean science and policy

COBRA operates internationally and brings together researchers and other interested parties to strengthen research collaboration and improve the translation of scientific findings into practical decision-making.

COBRA is also an endorsed Action of the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development.

COBRA’s Four Primary Activities

COBRA’s mission is organized around four primary activities:

1. Coordinate

COBRA brings together interested parties to identify research priorities and coordinate research planning.

This approach helps researchers and stakeholders work collaboratively rather than operating in isolation.

2. Accelerate

COBRA seeks to accelerate research by:

Leveraging research opportunities

Supporting research exchanges

Connecting researchers

Harnessing existing data

Encouraging collaboration

3. Translate

Scientific findings are most useful when they can inform decisions and be understood beyond the research community.

COBRA therefore works to translate research findings for:

Policymakers

Industry

The public

Other relevant stakeholders

4. Educate

The education component focuses on developing the next generation of ocean researchers and leaders.

The COBRA Master Class is the centerpiece of this education activity.

APPLY HERE

What Is the COBRA Master Class?

The COBRA Master Class is an intensive training programme designed to teach early career researchers (ECRs) how to plan a deep-sea expedition from start to finish.

Rather than focusing only on scientific theory, the Master Class provides practical training in the different stages involved in developing and carrying out deep-sea field research.

Participants will learn how to:

Develop research concepts

Plan deep-sea expeditions

Identify appropriate research assets

Develop funding proposals

Prepare for a research cruise

Plan operations at sea

Use telepresence for research and outreach

Understand permitting requirements

Prepare research reports

Manage data

Understand ocean law

Work collaboratively with other researchers and stakeholders

Communicate research findings to different audiences

Participants will also apply what they learn by developing an independent project during the programme.

Key Areas Covered During the Master Class

The training covers a broad range of skills required to successfully design, propose, conduct, and report deep-sea research.

1. Deep-Sea Research Assets

Participants will learn about the different types of assets and resources available for conducting deep-sea research and exploration.

Understanding available research assets is important when designing an expedition because researchers need to match their scientific objectives with appropriate equipment, platforms, vessels, and technologies.

2. Funding and Proposal Writing

The Master Class will provide guidance on:

Funding opportunities

Developing research proposals

Presenting research ideas

Building strong project concepts

Preparing proposals for potential funders

This component helps participants understand how scientific ideas can be transformed into fundable research projects.

3. Developing Research Concepts

Participants will learn how to develop research concepts while engaging with others in a respectful and reciprocal manner.

This emphasizes collaboration and meaningful engagement when developing research ideas.

4. Cruise Preparation

Planning a deep-sea expedition requires significant preparation before the vessel leaves port.

The Master Class will provide practical guidance on cruise preparation, helping participants understand what needs to be considered before an expedition begins.

5. At-Sea Operations Planning

Participants will learn about planning research activities while an expedition is underway.

This includes understanding how research operations can be organized to ensure that scientific objectives can be achieved during the available time at sea.

6. Telepresence for Research and Outreach

The programme also introduces participants to the use of telepresence in deep-sea research and public outreach.

Telepresence can allow researchers and audiences to engage with deep-sea research activities remotely.

7. Permitting and Reporting

Deep-sea research may involve regulatory and administrative requirements.

Participants will therefore learn about:

Permitting

Reporting requirements

Research-related documentation

Regulatory considerations

8. Data Management

Effective research requires appropriate management of the data generated during an expedition.

Participants will receive training related to data management, helping them understand how research data should be handled as part of a broader research project.

9. Ocean Law

The Master Class also introduces participants to ocean law, giving early career researchers exposure to the legal and policy dimensions of conducting research in marine environments.

International and Collaborative Focus

COBRA is an international network and seeks participation from people around the world.

The programme aims to build a broad collaborative pool of talent capable of contributing to deep-sea research that addresses societal needs.

Participants will learn from a variety of international subject matter experts. These instructors will provide specialist knowledge while also helping participants broaden their professional and research networks.

The programme is therefore not simply a classroom-based course. It is designed to create opportunities for:

Knowledge exchange

Collaboration

Professional networking

Interdisciplinary learning

Research leadership development

International engagement

2027 Partnership With the Schmidt Ocean Institute

The 2027 COBRA Master Class is sponsored by the Schmidt Ocean Institute.

As part of this sponsorship, COBRA will prioritize preparing participants to take advantage of the future cruise track and priorities associated with the RV Falkor (too).

This gives the 2027 programme a particular emphasis on preparing early career researchers to understand and potentially leverage opportunities associated with future deep-sea research expeditions.

Who Is Considered an Early Career Researcher?

COBRA uses a broad definition of Early Career Researcher (ECR).

Under the programme’s definition, an ECR may include:

A senior graduate student

A postdoctoral scientist

Junior faculty who are less than 10 years from their terminal degree

An early career employee of a government institution

An early career employee of a non-governmental organization or nonprofit

An early career employee of a company

Other junior professionals whose work is relevant to the programme

This broad definition means the opportunity is not limited exclusively to university researchers.

Early career professionals working in government, NGOs, nonprofits, companies, research institutions, and related organizations may also fall within the programme’s target group.

Previous Deep-Sea Experience Is Not Required

One of the notable features of the COBRA Master Class is that applicants do not need previous hands-on experience with deep-sea research, outreach, or policy.

This means that an applicant can be interested in entering or developing their career in deep-sea research and related areas without already having extensive practical expedition experience.

The programme is intended to help participants develop the skills required to become more capable researchers and research leaders.

Independent Project

Participants will have the opportunity to apply what they learn through the development of an independent project.

This provides a practical component to the training.

Instead of only receiving information through lectures and discussions, participants will use the knowledge and tools introduced throughout the Master Class to develop their own project.

This can help participants connect the different elements of expedition planning, research design, funding, operations, policy, data management, and communication.

COBRA Fellowship Status

Participants selected for the virtual Master Class will be considered COBRA Fellows for the 2027 calendar year.

Being designated a COBRA Fellow also makes participants eligible for additional COBRA leadership training opportunities.

Therefore, the programme extends beyond the 12-week Master Class itself by connecting selected participants with further leadership-development opportunities within COBRA.

Programme Format and Schedule

The 2027 COBRA Master Class will run for approximately 12 weeks, beginning in January 2027 and concluding in April 2027.

The programme combines:

Synchronous virtual training

Asynchronous learning

Online networking

An in-person final week

Virtual Training

The first 11 weeks will be conducted through synchronous online sessions.

The sessions will take place:

Every Tuesday

12:00 PM–2:00 PM U.S. Eastern Time

Using Zoom

Applicants should take note of the U.S. time change mentioned in the announcement. On March 14, U.S. Eastern Time changes from UTC-5 to UTC-4.

In-Person Final Week

The final portion of the Master Class will take place in person at:

Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences
Maine, United States

The in-person component will take place:

April 12–14, 2027

Participants should also plan for travel days on:

April 11, 2027

April 15, 2027

Attendance at the in-person component is an essential requirement.

Asynchronous Learning and Networking

In addition to the weekly live sessions, participants will engage in asynchronous learning and networking.

These activities will be supported through:

The COBRA Master Class website intranet

A dedicated Slack channel

Participants are expected to complete approximately 30 minutes of asynchronous preparation each week.

This preparation will involve homework distributed through the Master Class website and/or Slack channel.

Weekly Participant Expectations

Each week of the virtual Master Class, participants are expected to:

1. Complete Preparation Work

Participants should dedicate approximately 30 minutes to asynchronous course preparation.

2. Attend the Live Session

Participants are expected to participate in the weekly live training and discussion session through Zoom.

The sessions will be recorded for internal distribution only.

The recordings are intended for participants who:

Cannot attend a particular class

Want to review the material

Want to refresh their learning

Discussion sections will not be made public because COBRA wants to protect vulnerable questions and conversations.

3. Participate in Slack Discussions

Participants will also be expected to communicate with instructors and other participants through the dedicated Slack channel.

This supports continued learning and networking outside the live classroom.

English Language Requirement

The virtual Master Class will be delivered in English.

Participants are expected to communicate in English.

However, the programme will use live transcription to support accessibility and language translation.

Although COBRA is an international network, the instructors are based in the United States. The course itself will nevertheless incorporate:

Non-U.S. resources

International programmes

Guest instructors

Perspectives relevant to different geographic contexts

Technology Requirements

Because much of the Master Class is conducted online, participants are expected to have access to their own:

Computer or other suitable computing device

Microphone

Camera

Internet connection

Participants should also be able to access and use their own:

Google account

Slack account

Zoom account

YouTube

However, COBRA recognizes that hardware and connectivity can be challenging for some participants.

Accommodations for hardware and connectivity support are available where needed.

Applicants who have difficulty meeting these technology requirements should therefore consider the available accommodation options rather than automatically assuming they cannot participate.

Travel Funding for the In-Person Component

Selected participants are eligible to receive travel funds to support their participation in the final in-person week of the Master Class in Maine.

Eligible travel costs include:

Transportation

Accommodation

Allowed per diem for meals

Travel expenses will be reimbursed after participants submit the required expense receipts.

Air Travel

For air travel, reimbursement is limited to economy/coach fares.

The announcement specifies that the most cost-effective route should be used.

Participants should therefore not assume that premium or business-class travel costs will be covered.

Visa Costs

Participants who require a visa to travel to the United States can have the visa costs funded.

However, obtaining the required visa remains the participant’s responsibility.

Participants are expected to work with their home institution to secure the necessary visas.

How Reimbursement Works

Eligible costs are reimbursed after participants submit the required expense receipts.

Payments can be offered through:

Bank account transfer, or

PayPal transfer

Participants must also submit the appropriate U.S. Internal Revenue Service form:

W-9, or

W-8, depending on taxpayer status

These forms are submitted to COBRA’s Managing Director as part of the reimbursement process.

Important: This Is Not an Employment Opportunity

Participation in the 2027 COBRA Master Class does not constitute employment with Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences.

Bigelow Laboratory administers COBRA funding, but participation in the training should not be interpreted as a job or employment appointment at the laboratory.

October 1, 2026

Who Should Consider Applying?

Deep-sea research

TITLE: Caribbean Development Bank IMPPM Scholarship 2026/2027: Fully Funded Master’s in Public Procurement Management at the University of Rome Tor Vergata

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Caribbean Development Bank International Master in Public Procurement Management Scholarship 2026/2027, a major postgraduate funding opportunity for public procurement professionals from eligible Caribbean Development Bank Borrowing Member Countries.

The Caribbean Development Bank, commonly known as CDB, is supporting candidates to pursue the International Master in Public Procurement Management (IMPPM) at the University of Rome Tor Vergata in Italy during the 2026/2027 academic year. The programme is intended to strengthen public procurement capacity across the Caribbean, support the professionalisation of the public procurement workforce, and help participating countries modernise procurement systems in ways that improve value for money, integrity, accountability and development outcomes.

The scholarship package is extensive. It covers the full tuition fee, travel to and from Italy for the in-person study period, accommodation support, subsistence while in Italy, a USD 350 lump-sum allowance toward visa and other essential administrative costs, and in some cases reasonable travel costs associated with completing the visa process outside the applicant’s country of residence.

The application deadline is:

3 October 2026 at 5:00 PM Atlantic Standard Time (AST).

Applications must be submitted in PDF format by email to:

MasterIPPM@caribank.org

This opportunity is aimed at experienced public procurement professionals who are citizens of eligible CDB Borrowing Member Countries and who are currently employed in professional public procurement roles within government or eligible Caribbean public regional institutions.

About the Caribbean Development Bank Scholarship

The Caribbean Development Bank is offering this scholarship as part of its broader commitment to strengthening public financial management systems across its Borrowing Member Countries.

Public procurement plays a critical role in government performance because large amounts of public expenditure pass through procurement systems. Strong procurement institutions can help governments:

Improve value for money

Strengthen accountability

Reduce corruption risks

Improve transparency

Support sustainable development

Improve project delivery

Encourage fair competition

Advance inclusive procurement

Modernise public-sector purchasing

CDB views investment in procurement professionals as an important part of improving the development impact of both nationally financed and CDB-supported projects.

The 2026/2027 academic year marks the fifth consecutive year that CDB has supported this scholarship initiative.

What Is the International Master in Public Procurement Management?

The International Master in Public Procurement Management, or IMPPM, is a full-time postgraduate programme delivered by the:

Faculty of Economics, University of Rome Tor Vergata, Italy.

The programme is designed for professionals working in public procurement and related areas who want to develop deeper expertise in:

Procurement management

Procurement law

Procurement economics

Integrity

Anti-corruption

Negotiation

Sustainable procurement

Innovative procurement

Public-private partnerships

Procurement reform

Strategic procurement

The programme is delivered entirely in:

English.

Programme Structure

The programme runs for approximately one year and combines several different learning components.

These include:

In-person classroom teaching in Rome

Distance learning

A mandatory professional internship

A final dissertation

The academic model is therefore designed to combine theoretical learning with direct professional application.

In-Person Study in Rome

Students are expected to attend:

4.25 consecutive months of in-person classes in Rome.

The programme includes:

13 academic modules

covering important areas of public procurement.

Attendance is compulsory, and students are expected to participate actively in all modules. Each module concludes with an examination intended to assess the skills and knowledge acquired.

For professionals already employed in government or public institutions, this means employer support is particularly important.

Expected Start Date

The 2026/2027 edition is expected to begin in:

Early 2027.

The exact dates will be confirmed by the University of Rome Tor Vergata.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to arrange:

Employer release

Visa documentation

Travel

University documentation

CIMEA or Declaration of Value procedures

soon after selection.

Scholarship Benefits

The CDB scholarship offers a broad financial support package.

Full Tuition Fees

The scholarship covers:

The full tuition fee for the postgraduate programme.

The sponsoring organisation pays the tuition fee directly to the University.

Travel to and From Italy

The scholarship covers:

Travel costs to and from Italy

for the in-person phase of the programme.

It also provides:

A per diem while in transit.

This substantially reduces the financial barrier to attending the residential component in Rome.

Accommodation Support

Scholarship recipients receive:

An allowance for accommodation on campus at the University.

Applicants should understand that the notice describes this as an allowance, rather than simply stating that accommodation itself is automatically prepaid in full.

Living and Subsistence Allowance

The scholarship also provides:

An allowance for subsistence costs while in Italy.

This is intended to support the recipient’s living costs during the 4.25-month period in Rome.

The official notice does not state the exact amount of the subsistence allowance in the material provided, so applicants should not assume a specific monthly figure unless CDB confirms it separately.

USD 350 Administrative Allowance

Selected candidates also receive:

USD 350 as a lump-sum allowance

paid in advance after the scholarship award is confirmed.

This payment is intended to help cover costs such as:

Visa expenses

CIMEA documentation

Declaration of Value

Other essential administrative expenses required to study and travel to Italy

Additional Visa-Related Travel Support

Some selected candidates may need to travel outside their country of residence to complete the Italian visa process.

Where this is necessary, the scholarship may cover reasonable and necessary travel-related costs, including:

Economy airfare

Accommodation

Applicable per diem

for the minimum required visa-processing period.

These costs are arranged or reimbursed by the sponsoring organisation according to its applicable procedures.

Mandatory Professional Internship

A major part of the programme is the required:

500-hour professional internship.

The internship is normally completed within:

The participant’s home organisation, or

Another institution acceptable to the University

This component is designed to ensure that participants apply their new knowledge directly within a professional procurement environment.

Final Dissertation Requirement

Scholarship recipients must also prepare a:

Final dissertation

based on a case study addressing procurement issues relevant to:

Their organisation

Their country

The Caribbean region

This gives participants the opportunity to link academic learning to practical public-sector procurement challenges.

Potential dissertation themes might include:

Sustainable procurement

Procurement digitisation

Procurement transparency

Anti-corruption systems

Procurement law reform

Innovative procurement

Public-private partnerships

Procurement capacity building

Green procurement

Inclusive procurement

Applicants should expect their research to have direct professional relevance.

Employer Release Is Required

Because the in-person study period in Rome lasts approximately 4.25 months, candidates must be:

Formally released from their professional duties

for the full period of in-person study.

Their employer must also support their participation in:

Distance learning

Academic assignments

Other programme requirements

without conflicting professional obligations.

Shortlisted candidates will need written confirmation from their employer granting this release before proceeding to the second stage of evaluation.

Applicants are therefore strongly encouraged to speak with their employers before applying.

Post-Study Employment Commitment

Scholarship recipients must continue serving their employer for at least:

12 months after completing the programme.

This is a formal condition of the award.

An agreement must be reached between the scholarship recipient and their employer stipulating that the full tuition cost must be reimbursed if the recipient leaves before completing the required 12-month service period.

Applicants should therefore consider carefully whether they are willing and able to make this employment commitment.

Why the Return-to-Employer Requirement Matters

The scholarship is designed as a capacity-building investment.

CDB is not only funding an individual academic degree.

It is investing in:

Public-sector institutions

National procurement systems

Regional procurement expertise

Procurement reform

Knowledge transfer

The 12-month service requirement helps ensure that the knowledge gained through the programme is transferred back into the applicant’s professional environment.

Knowledge-Sharing After Graduation

Scholarship recipients are also expected to share what they have learned with colleagues in:

Their home country

Their institution

The broader Caribbean region

Possible activities may include:

Presentations

Training sessions

Professional discussions

Knowledge-sharing workshops

Topics could include:

Sustainable procurement

Digital transformation

Innovative procurement strategies

Approximately 6 to 12 months after graduation, CDB intends to follow up with scholarship recipients to assess the impact of the programme.

Who Can Apply?

Eligibility is relatively specific.

Applicants must satisfy both:

CDB scholarship requirements

University of Rome Tor Vergata admission requirements

Candidates should carefully review all conditions before applying.

Citizenship Requirement

Applicants must be citizens of one of the eligible CDB Borrowing Member Countries.

The eligible countries and territories listed in the official notice are:

Anguilla

Antigua and Barbuda

Barbados

Belize

British Virgin Islands

Cayman Islands

Dominica

Grenada

Guyana

Haiti

Jamaica

Montserrat

Saint Kitts and Nevis

Saint Lucia

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

Suriname

The Bahamas

Trinidad and Tobago

Turks and Caicos Islands

Applicants from countries outside this list are not eligible under the published call.

Employment Requirement

Candidates must be employed:

At the time of application and throughout the programme

in a:

Professional public procurement role

within either:

The government of a CDB Client country, or

A Caribbean public regional institution

This scholarship is therefore not intended for people who are merely interested in procurement but are not professionally working in the field.

Academic Qualification

Applicants must hold at least:

A recognised Master’s-level university degree.

The degree must be equivalent to an Italian two-year:

Master of Science degree

such as the Italian:

Laurea Magistrale

Laurea Specialistica

Laurea vecchio ordinamento

Applicants should be prepared to provide documentation showing equivalency through the appropriate Italian recognition process where required.

Professional Experience Requirement

Applicants should normally have at least:

Five years of relevant procurement experience

including at least:

Two years in public-sector procurement.

This reflects the programme’s professional orientation.

It is designed for practitioners who already understand the basics of procurement and want to strengthen their strategic and technical expertise.

Can Applicants With Less Experience Apply?

Possibly.

The official notice contains an important flexibility provision stating that:

Applicants who are highly motivated but have:

Recently completed a Master’s degree, and/or

Limited procurement experience

may still be considered at the discretion of:

CDB

The University

This means five years of experience is the normal requirement, but there is limited discretion for exceptional candidates.

Applicants with less experience should therefore make a particularly strong case in their motivation letter.

English-Language Requirement

Candidates must be proficient in:

Written English

Spoken English

This is essential because the full Master’s programme is delivered in English.

The notice provided does not specify a mandatory IELTS, TOEFL or other standardized test score, so applicants should not assume one is required unless the University’s separate admission rules state otherwise.

Conflict-of-Interest Requirement

Applicants must not have:

Business or personal relationships with CDB or the University of Rome Tor Vergata

that would create:

An actual conflict of interest

A perceived conflict of interest

Applicants must also sign a declaration confirming that they meet the eligibility requirements and have no relevant conflict of interest.

One Candidate Per Country Rule

The CDB states that:

Only one candidate from the same country may receive a scholarship award in any given year.

This policy is intended to distribute the programme’s benefits more equitably across eligible Caribbean countries.

However, CDB reserves the right to make exceptions where there are insufficient eligible candidates.

Selection Criteria

Meeting the formal eligibility criteria does not guarantee selection.

The evaluation places particular emphasis on:

Relevant professional experience

Leadership potential

Ability to use the programme to improve procurement outcomes

Potential contribution to procurement modernisation

Capacity to apply knowledge in the applicant’s institution

Potential regional impact

CDB particularly highlights areas such as:

Sustainable procurement

Inclusive procurement

Leadership Potential

Applicants should demonstrate not only technical procurement experience but also the ability to:

Influence institutional change

Lead reform

Train colleagues

Strengthen procurement systems

Improve professional standards

Contribute to modernization

A strong application should therefore explain how the candidate will use the degree after returning home.

Sustainable and Inclusive Procurement

CDB specifically highlights:

Sustainable and inclusive procurement

as important areas for future procurement modernisation.

Applicants with relevant experience or future plans in areas such as:

Green procurement

Climate-conscious procurement

Social inclusion

SME participation

Gender-responsive procurement

Sustainable supply chains

may therefore have a strong opportunity to show programme relevance.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted:

By email

to:

MasterIPPM@caribank.org

All documents must be submitted in:

PDF format.

Required Application Documents

Applicants must submit three core documents.

1. Updated Curriculum Vitae

The CV should clearly show:

Education

Procurement experience

Public-sector experience

Current employment

Leadership experience

Procurement reform experience

Relevant training

Professional certifications

Major projects

Regional or international experience

2. Motivational Cover Letter

Applicants must submit a:

Motivational cover letter

explaining their interest in the scholarship programme.

A competitive letter should explain:

Why public procurement matters to the applicant

Why the IMPPM is relevant to their current work

What procurement challenges exist in their country or institution

What reforms they hope to support

How they will apply the knowledge after graduation

How they will contribute to sustainable and inclusive procurement

How the scholarship will benefit their institution and country

3. Signed Eligibility Declaration

Applicants must submit a:

Signed Declaration

confirming that they meet all eligibility conditions.

This includes confirmation that there is no actual or perceived conflict of interest.

The required template is attached to the official Call for Applications and must be completed and signed.

Stage 1: Shortlisting

After the deadline, a CDB evaluation panel will review the applications.

The panel will shortlist up to:

Six candidates

who best satisfy the eligibility and qualification criteria.

Shortlisted candidates will then be contacted by the University for an interview.

At this stage, applicants may need to provide proof that their employer is willing to release them from work for the in-person programme period.

Stage 2: University Interview

The University of Rome Tor Vergata will interview shortlisted candidates to confirm their suitability for the Master’s programme.

In consultation with CDB, the University then identifies final candidates for scholarship awards.

There is one inconsistency in the official notice worth flagging: the overview says CDB is offering scholarships to two candidates, while the selection-stage section says the University will identify three candidates for scholarship awards.

Because the headline and overview explicitly describe two scholarships, applicants should treat two awards as the advertised number unless CDB issues clarification. Anyone needing certainty can contact CDB directly before applying.

Final Scholarship Confirmation

Successful candidates will receive:

An Admission Letter from the University

A Scholarship Offer Letter from CDB

The scholarship is formally confirmed once the recipient satisfies the University’s admission requirements.

Application Deadline

Applications must be received by:

3 October 2026 at 5:00 PM AST.

Applicants in other time zones should convert the deadline carefully.

Because applications are sent by email, it is advisable to submit before the final day and confirm that:

All files are attached

All files are readable

The Declaration is signed

Documents are PDFs

Email address is correct

How to Prepare a Strong Application

1. Connect Your Experience to Procurement Reform

Avoid writing only that you want another degree.

Explain what procurement problem you want to solve.

Possible examples include:

Weak transparency

Delays in procurement

Because leadership is explicitly part of the selection criteria, show examples of situations where you have:

Where possible, explain how your learning could benefit:

Your country

Other Caribbean procurement professionals

4. Highlight Sustainable Procurement

If you have experience involving:

Climate considerations

Social safeguards

Responsible sourcing

include it clearly.

Sustainable procurement is specifically highlighted in the selection criteria.

5. Discuss Employer Support Early

Do not wait until you are shortlisted to tell your employer you may need more than four months away from normal duties.

The official notice explicitly encourages applicants to discuss the possibility of employer release early.

6. Be Ready for the 12-Month Return Commitment

Applicants should understand before applying that they will be expected to remain with their employer for at least one year after completing the programme.

The Caribbean Development Bank International Master in Public Procurement Management Scholarship 2026/2027 offers experienced Caribbean public procurement professionals a rare opportunity to complete an internationally focused postgraduate programme at the University of Rome Tor Vergata with extensive financial support.

TITLE: Research Analyzes the Role of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Exchange in Warming the Arctic Ocean and Reducing Sea Ice

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Randy Showstack

With the Arctic Ocean warming much more rapidly than the global average over the past several decades, the extent and thickness of sea ice in the Arctic has decreased dramatically. Climate models project that these trends will accelerate even more in the future. A new analysis finds that increased ocean heat transport (OHT) into the Arctic through the Barents Sea Opening (BSO) is the primary driver of this warming, with OHT from the Fram and Bering straits also contributing to the warming. (See Figure 1 for a map of the region.)

Figure 1. Map indicating the location of the Arctic gateways where the ocean heat transport is calculated. (Illustration by Natalie Renier, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

The analysis also finds that the projected future OHT changes are driven primarily by warmer inflowing water rather than by changes in the volume of water transported through those three Arctic gateways, according to the journal article, “The Respective Roles of Ocean Heat Transport and Surface Heat Fluxes in Driving Arctic Ocean Warming and Sea Ice Decline,” published in the American Meteorological Society’s Journal of Climate in January 2024.

In addition, the analysis calculates the contributions of ocean-ice and atmosphere-ice heat fluxes to the sea ice heat budget changes (see Figure 2), and determines that the ocean is likely to become the most important source of heat for the ice and hence the most responsible for the melting. “Throughout the entire twentieth century as well as the early twenty-first century, the atmosphere is the main contributor to ice heat gain in summer, though the ocean’s role is not negligible. However, over the course of the 21st century, the ocean progressively becomes the main heat source for the ice as the ocean warms,” according to the article.

Figure 2. Illustration of the factors that contribute to the ocean and sea-ice heat budgets. Credit: Natalie Renier from WHOI Graphics.

“The ocean is expected to play a very important role in driving sea-ice loss in the future. In particular, the increased heat inputs from the different Arctic Ocean gateways, particularly the Barents Sea Opening, the Fram Strait, and the Bering Strait from the Pacific side of the Arctic are going to be very important for driving active ocean warming,” said journal article lead author Dylan Oldenburg, a postdoctoral investigator in physical oceanography at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI). Co-authors are Young-Oh Kwon of WHOI; Claude Frankignoul with WHOI and Sorbonne University; and Gokhan Danabasoglu, Stephen Yeager, and Who M. Kim with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research.

For their heat budget analysis, the researchers defined the Arctic Ocean as the region bounded by the Arctic Ocean gateways, which include the Barents Sea Opening as well as the Barrow, Bering, Fram, and Nares straits. The analysis uses the 100-member Large Ensemble of the state-of-the-art fully coupled Community Earth System Model, version 2 (CESM2), focusing primarily on the period between 1920 and 2100. This Large Ensemble provides researchers with the ability to separate climate change signal variations from natural internal variability.

“The beauty of having so many ensemble members, or simulations, is that when you average them together, there is a lot less noise, and you can remove internal variability that shows up in each ensemble member,” said Oldenburg. “When you look at the Large Ensemble, you can isolate the response of the climate or the Arctic Ocean, for instance, to the greenhouse gas forcing without internal variability masking what is happening due to that forcing.”

Although the model has some minor drawbacks, such as underestimating the Fram Strait OHT relative to observations, overall CESM2 is a good model and the net volume transports through the Arctic gateways are well-represented relative to observations, the article noted. “For limited parts of the historical period, we can rely on observations. However, because observations in the Arctic Ocean are limited and we do not have observations of future conditions, we need to use models,” said Oldenburg. “Our results based on CESM2-LENS indicate an essential role for ocean heat transport in driving Arctic Ocean warming, in line with previous studies.”

The earlier studies have typically examined OHTs that are zonally integrated across a particular latitude, and not based on physical pathways into the Arctic Ocean, according to Oldenburg. The researchers here explicitly calculated the OHT across each of the Arctic gateways to determine the relative importance of OHTs across the gateways. All of the heat flux components are fairly constant in the ensemble mean until about 1980, when the total OHT into the Arctic starts to rapidly increase, eventually strengthening from 0.06 petawatts (PW) from 1961-1980 to 0.10 PW from 2081-2100. The total OHC change over the course of the simulations increases the mean Arctic Ocean temperature from 0.3° to 0.5° Celsius, according to the article. “The increase in the OHT into the Arctic in response to the external forcing results in an Arctic temperature increase which is partly damped by the enhanced heat loss through the sea surface, as found in other climate models.”

In terms of individual gateways, the BSO provides 41% of the total increase in OHT into the Arctic Ocean between 1961-1980 and 2081-2100. The OHT also increases through the Fram and Bering straits, while the Nares Strait OHT is fairly constant until about 2040 when it starts to decrease, and volume transport declines slightly across the Bering Strait.

While thermodynamic (i.e. temperature-driven) changes largely drive the net OHT increase into the Arctic, nonlinear components (i.e. anomalies due to concurrent changes in temperature and velocity) also play a major role. Of the net OHT increase from 1920-80 to 2081-2100, thermodynamic changes contribute 0.03 PW, with nonlinear changes contributing 0.01 PW; dynamic circulation changes act to decrease the net OHT after 2040, with an anomaly slightly smaller than -0.01 PW over the same period due to negative dynamic components from the Nares and Barrow Straits.

The research also looked into the impacts of shortwave (solar) and longwave radiation on the ocean and on sea ice, and looks at the heat budget from the perspective of the ice.

“Essentially, the heat transported into the Arctic Ocean via OHT is primarily used to melt the sea ice until the sea ice coverage declines substantially in the mid-21st century and the exposed ocean surface increases, after which heat begins to flux out to the atmosphere,” the researchers noted.

In terms of heat flux components, while absorbed shortwave radiation strengthens due to decreasing surface albedo with more open ocean and reduced cloud cover, starting in 2040 this increased heat flux is compensated by strengthened outgoing longwave radiation and stronger sensible and latent heat loss reflecting ocean warming and more extended open waters, according to the research. Though incoming longwave radiation also increases over the course of the simulations, that increase is compensated by the strengthened outgoing longwave radiation, which is consistent with the balance in the mean seasonal cycle and which explains the increased ocean cooling due to longwave radiation out to 2100.

“It is very important to understand why the Arctic Ocean is warming and why there are dramatic changes that are being predicted,” Oldenburg said. “This research, which reinforces what has already been found about extreme warming in the Arctic and the loss of sea ice, highlights the importance of ocean heat transport in driving Arctic warming and sea ice decline.”

TITLE: Jesus College Cambridge Science Research Fellowship 2026 (Paid)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026

Applications for the Jesus College Cambridge Science Research Fellowship 2026 are now open. Applications are invited for one Research Fellowship in either Biological Anthropology; Biology/Biological Sciences; Biotechnology; Chemical Engineering; Chemistry; Computer Science; Ecology; Engineering; Environmental Sciences; Mathematics/Mathematical Sciences; Medicine; Natural Sciences; Physics; Psychology or Veterinary Sciences.

Any candidate whose research crosses disciplinary boundaries involving at least one of the subjects listed above (for example, Computer Science and Linguistics) should apply to this competition and not the Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences competition. TITLE: Horizon Fellowship 2027 for Emerging Tech Experts (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 30, 2026

Applications are open for the Horizon Fellowship 2027. The Horizon Fellowship helps emerging technology experts launch their careers in public service. The Horizon Fellowship places experts in AI, biotechnology, and other emerging technologies in federal agencies, congressional offices and committees, and leading think tanks in Washington, DC, for up to two years. Fellows receive comprehensive training, networking opportunities, and access to a supportive community of 100+ other fellows and alumni to launch their careers in public service.

Emerging technologies like AI and biotechnology are rapidly reshaping many domains, from healthcare and science to national security and the economy. The US government plays a critical role in developing and governing these technologies, and it needs people who understand them. Horizon fellows supply that understanding across the institutions that shape technology policy.

Programme Structure

Successful applicants will go through training, matching, and placement phases from January to summer of 2027.

Training (January to March 2027): The selected fellowship cohort completes a part-time, work-compatible remote training on policy work, including the mechanics of the federal government and applied skills like memo writing and policy analysis. The training culminates in an in-person weekend in Washington, DC, where fellows connect with dozens of emerging technology experts from across the policy world. The curriculum and networking prepare fellows to secure strong placement offers and perform high-quality work during their fellowship.

Matching (April to May 2027): After training, fellows begin an individualized matching process. Fellows decide which host organizations to pursue; Horizon supports them with introductions, application feedback, and interview preparation. Most fellows receive multiple offers and choose the placement that best fits their goals. Horizon has a nearly 100% fellow matching rate.

Placement (Spring/Summer 2027 onward): After successfully matching, fellows work with their chosen host organization to finalize a start date (typically during the summer). Horizon provides a full-time salary and benefits once their placement begins. Fellows’ work is fully supervised and directed by their host organization.

Benefits

The provide $78,000 base salary for junior fellows, $130,000 for fellows, and $190,000+ for senior fellows. All fellows also receive a $17,000 benefits-equivalent stipend, a $3,000 professional development stipend, and up to $3,000 for relocation to DC, if needed.

Eligibility

They are looking for people who want to put their expertise to work on the hardest problems in emerging technology policy.

They value attitude, abilities, and knowledge more than formal credentials, and they welcome applicants from diverse and interdisciplinary professional backgrounds. The Horizon Fellowship has helped engineers, data scientists, historians, lawyers, doctors, and many other professionals transition into public service.

Competitive candidates generally have demonstrated subject-matter expertise in their technology area of interest. This could include relevant coursework, work experience, research projects, policy writing, or deep self-study. Prior policy experience is not required.

They support fellows at a range of career stages through three fellowship levels:

Junior fellow: typically less than 3 years of full-time work experience and no PhD. Current students and recent graduates are welcome to apply.

Fellow: typically 3+ years of relevant full-time experience or a PhD.

Senior fellow (new this year): typically 12+ years of full-time experience, including extensive leadership experience. Senior fellows will typically be placed in roles with greater responsibility, such as leading workstreams and advising senior decision-makers.

Application

The bulk of the application consists of administrative questions and a set of brief (max. 100-word) short-answer responses. If you exit without submitting, the application will not save your answers.
