WORKSHOP OVERVIEW

Background and Rationale

For every Higher Education Institution (HEI), the registrar’s office is the axis on which every activity spins and the hub of staff, students and alumni’s data for everything related to them. Due to the vital role of the Registrar’s office in administrative excellence and students’ academic success, the registrar, who is one of the principal officers, should see himself/herself as a peer of academics and a partner in the delivery of educational programs. As the steward of the academic record and the keeper of institutional data, the registrar is in a unique role at the institution. An institution needs good data to advance its initiatives. The registrar, who sits at the crossroads between student service and academic programming, is distinctly suited to use the data at hand to help shape discussions and decisions in the context of desired educational outcomes for the institution and students alike. While serving and advancing higher education by safeguarding the academic integrity of the institution, there are broad professional principles of good practice, management, and conduct that should be followed. When these principles are not being followed, those served by the registrar’s office, majority of whom are students, are the ones that bear the consequences of a disengaged office. The registrar must be current, consistent and professional to ensure the integrity of degrees and maintain the ability to accurately advise students about degree requirements and other administrative requirements. Continuous professional development is central to enabling the registrar perform at optimal level for the overall benefit of his/her institution. It is against this backdrop that the Association of African Universities (AAU) is organizing a capacity building workshop for university registrars in universities and colleges in Africa. The workshop addresses one of AAU’s strategic goals of strengthening the delivery capacity of HEIs through enhanced leadership and management capacity development.

Objectives and Expected Outcomes

The overall goal of this event is to enhance the capacity of the African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) Registrars and Administrators to deliver as custodians of records in HEIs in. The expected outcomes include:

Improved knowledge about staff and students’ records management and processes of records retention, disposal, transcript guide and records archiving.

Improved knowledge of innovative approaches to staff and student recruitment, admission, registration and displacement.

Enhanced awareness of the examination management processes and best practices.

Improved knowledge on how to organise effective online support services for students.

Workshop Modules

The modules to be covered include:

Module 1: Quality Assurance in Registry Services & Systems / Professional Development of Registrars

Module 2: Management of Staff Recruitment/Hiring, Suspensions, Terminations & Retirements

Module 3: Management of Student Recruitment/Admission, Registration and Displacement

Module 4: Staff & Students’ Records Management: Retention, Transcript Guide, Disposal and Archiving

Module 5: Curriculum Management and the Role of the Registrar

Module 6: Examination Management

Module 7: Student Online Services

Module 8: Graduation and Commencement

Methodology

The workshop will be held over a period of three days and will include the use of case studies, focused group discussions, experiential learning (Live Case Study of the University of Dar es Salaam), presentations and sharing ideas, knowledge and skills. The workshop will develop a strategy of follow-up to ensure that university registrars are implementing the good practices to be learned from the workshop at their various institutions of higher learning. The participants will have the opportunity to engage in dialogue with peers on the various challenges at their universities and strategies to overcome them. A post workshop report will be compiled and recommendations made will be integrated into improving subsequent workshops.

Target Participants

Registrars

Enrolment Managers

Provosts

Deans and Faculty

Academic Advisors

Staff of the Registry Departments.

Examination Managers and All who are interested in learning.

TITLE: Formal Announcement of the Passing on of the AAU Director of ICT, Communication and Knowledge Management – Ms Nodumo Dhlamini, a Giant in Africa’s Higher Education

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
It is with profound sadness that the Association of African Universities (AAU), representing over 450 member institutions of higher education in Africa and beyond, announces the passing of Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT, Communications, and Knowledge Management at the AAU Secretariat, who departed on April 25, 2025, in Accra, Ghana.

During her nearly decade-long tenure at AAU, starting July 2015, Ms. Dhlamini demonstrated exceptional leadership, dedication, and expertise, significantly impacting the Association’s core functions and advancing higher education in Africa. As a valued member of the management team, she brought extensive experience, strategic vision, and a commitment to excellence, spearheading key initiatives and shaping effective strategies.

Ms. Dhlamini was known for her transformative leadership in ICT and communications, driving impactful digital solutions that advanced African higher education. She fostered collaboration among diverse stakeholders, leveraged effective communication strategies to strengthen engagements, and demonstrated a commitment to knowledge generation and management, all of which significantly contributed to advancing the objectives of the AAU. Her exceptional blend of intellectual acuity, strategic vision, and warm humanity endeared her to colleagues and earned her a revered place within the AAU community.

Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini believed in empowering the younger generation and ably demonstrated this in her dealings with all who worked with her, going above and beyond to mentor and provide opportunities for them to develop their skills and to advance academically and professionally. As a trailblazing figure in African higher education and a beacon of inspiration to countless individuals across the continent, her enduring legacy will continue to galvanize and shape the future of our collective endeavours. The AAU pays tribute to her remarkable legacy, celebrating her extraordinary contributions and the profound impact made on our community. We invite our stakeholders, partners and various individuals to join us in honouring her memory by sending in your condolence messages via this link: https://aau.org/book-of-condolence-for-madam-nodumo-dhlamini/nodumo-dhlamini/

As a mark of respect and in recognition of Ms. Dhlamini’s outstanding contributions, the Association of African Universities will fly its flag at half-mast at the Secretariat until May 4, 2025.

Early Life and Career Trajectory

Ms. Dhlamini, born on March 23, 1966, in Matobo, Zimbabwe, recorded an illustrious career spanning over 30 years across various sectors, including secondary education, banking, the railway industry, higher education, and agricultural development. Her remarkable journey is marked by strategic leadership, management, and administrative expertise.

Ms. Dhlamini held a degree in Mathematics and Computer Science from the University of Swaziland (1989-1994) and an MBA from Africa University, Zimbabwe (2001-2005). Her professional trajectory began as a teacher in Swaziland and Zimbabwe before transitioning into other sectors and then to higher education.

Throughout her distinguished career, Nodumo held several key positions, her last role being the Director of ICT, Communications, and Knowledge Management at the Association of African Universities Secretariat in Accra, Ghana, where she spearheaded the development of the organization’s key strategic plans, communication strategies, and management information systems. She served previously as Program Manager – ICT at RUFORUM in Kampala, Uganda, overseeing the implementation of ICT projects and knowledge management initiatives. Additionally, she was the Director of the ICT Department at Africa University in Mutare, Zimbabwe, where she provided leadership in ICT adoption, policy development, and project implementation.

Key Impact Areas & Contribution to Africa’s Higher Education

Nodumo’s transformative leadership at the Association of African Universities (AAU) yielded profound impacts on the organization’s operations and Africa’s higher education landscape. Her notable accomplishments include:

– Catalyzing the creation of strategic communities of practice, including communities of ICT directors, communication professionals, and librarians, and implementing targeted capacity-building initiatives to enhance their impact.

– Forging pivotal partnerships that advanced AAU’s mission and strengthened its stakeholder engagements.

– Spearheading the development and implementation of cutting-edge technology platforms, which facilitated seamless interactions between the Secretariat and its stakeholders.

-Establishing a vibrant information clearinghouse for African higher education, by leveraging AAU’s communication services to promote the Association and foster stakeholder engagement

– Providing visionary leadership to AAU’s knowledge management and open science initiatives, and brokering collaborations and partnerships that propelled the Association’s agenda.

The University of Macau (UM) is preparing to welcome applications for its 2027/2028 postgraduate intake, providing prospective students with opportunities to pursue doctoral, master’s and postgraduate certificate programmes in Macau, China.

About the University of Macau Postgraduate Intake

The University of Macau offers postgraduate education through its various academic units, including PhD, Master’s and postgraduate certificate programmes.

Applicants can submit their applications through the university’s official online application system. The system specifically provides registration options for PhD and other doctoral degree, Master’s and postgraduate certificate programmes.

The university’s postgraduate programmes cover multiple academic and professional disciplines, giving prospective students the opportunity to identify programmes that align with their educational background and career goals.

Programmes Available

The 2027/2028 intake includes opportunities in three main categories:

1. PhD Programmes

Doctoral programmes are designed for students seeking advanced research training and an opportunity to develop expertise in their chosen field.

PhD applicants should carefully review the requirements of their intended academic unit because admission conditions can vary by programme.

2. Master’s Programmes

The University of Macau offers a range of master’s-level programmes across different faculties and academic areas.

Applicants generally need to hold a Bachelor’s degree or an academic qualification recognized as equivalent by the University of Macau, although individual programmes may have additional requirements.

3. Postgraduate Certificate Programmes

The intake also includes selected postgraduate certificate programmes. The university publishes programme-specific information covering areas such as the language of instruction and normal duration of study.

Funding Opportunities

One of the most attractive aspects of the University of Macau’s postgraduate opportunities is the availability of financial support for eligible students.

For doctoral students, the university’s published PhD admission guidelines identify the UM PhD Scholarship and UM PhD Teaching Research Assistant as potential sources of stipend support.

Assistantships are also available for master’s students and can serve as a source of stipend support, subject to the applicable funding guidelines.

However, applicants should distinguish between admission to a postgraduate programme and receiving funding. Funding is subject to the relevant programme, scholarship or assistantship conditions and should be confirmed before making financial plans.

Who Can Apply?

The exact eligibility requirements depend on the postgraduate programme selected.

For master’s applicants, the university’s published admission guidelines state that applicants must possess a Bachelor’s degree or an academic background recognized as equivalent by the University of Macau. Some programmes may require additional academic or professional qualifications.

PhD applicants should consult the specific admission guidelines and requirements for their intended doctoral programme.

International applicants should also carefully review the university’s requirements concerning:

Academic qualifications

English or other language proficiency

Programme-specific requirements

Supporting documents

Application fees

Scholarship or assistantship eligibility

Any interview requirements

Application Deadlines

According to the information provided for the 2027/2028 intake, the key deadlines are:

PhD Programmes

First Batch Deadline: 23 October 2026

Master’s & Postgraduate Certificate Programmes

Deadline: 3 December 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin the application process because documents, references and other supporting materials may require additional preparation.

The University of Macau also states that late applications will not be considered and that completed online applications must be submitted through the application system to be processed.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted online through the University of Macau’s official application system.

The process generally involves:

Step 1: Register an Account

New applicants should select the registration option for PhD and other doctoral degree, Master’s and postgraduate certificate programmes.

Applicants are required to provide information including their name as shown on their identification document or passport, identification/passport number, mobile number and valid email address.

Step 2: Receive Your Login Details

After successful registration, applicants receive a reference number and password by email and SMS. These details are required to access the application system.

Step 3: Complete the Application

Applicants should carefully complete the online application form and provide all required information and supporting documents.

Step 4: Submit the Application

Completing the form is not enough. Applicants must click Submit for the application to be processed.

The university states that applications that have been completed but not submitted will not be processed. (UM Sign In)

Step 5: Check for Confirmation

Successful submission should generate an acknowledgement email containing an application number. The university advises applicants to contact the Graduate School if they do not receive the acknowledgement within two days. (UM Sign In)

Applicants should also budget for the postgraduate application fee.

The University of Macau’s published admission rules state that the application fee is MOP 200 per application and is non-refundable.

Applicants should check the applicable admission guidelines for their specific intake and programme before making payment.

Important Application Considerations

Review Your Programme Carefully

Applicants should choose their programme carefully because the university’s online application instructions state that applicants for PhD, master’s and postgraduate certificate programmes cannot change their programme choice after submitting their applications.

Prepare Documents Early

Potential applicants should begin preparing their academic records, identification documents, language certificates, recommendation materials and other programme-specific documents well ahead of the deadline.

Check Funding Separately

Do not automatically assume that admission to a programme means that tuition and living expenses will be fully covered.

Applicants interested in funding should review the specific scholarship or assistantship opportunities associated with their programme.

Monitor Your Email

The university uses email to provide important application information, including registration credentials and application acknowledgement.

Why Consider the University of Macau?

For students considering postgraduate education in Asia, the University of Macau provides an opportunity to pursue advanced academic study in an internationally oriented university environment.

The availability of doctoral scholarships and teaching/research assistantships may also make selected postgraduate programmes particularly attractive to applicants seeking financial support.

TITLE: AAU and RRENs appeal for strengthening of campus network infrastructure

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
ACCRA 6 APRIL 2020

The AAU and the RRENs Call for strengthening of campus network infrastructure so that African Higher Education Institutions can cope with COVID-19 and future global disruptions

Amidst the unprecedented COVID-19 pandemic, many academic and research communities have resolved to work remotely for health and safety reasons. This situation has proved the importance of building strong communications infrastructures for higher education and research institutions, able to support advanced services delivered through high-speed telecommunications networks.

The Association of African Universities (AAU), the UbuntuNet Alliance (UA), the West and Central Africa Research and Education Network (WACREN), the Arab States Research and Education Network (ASREN) and the National Research and Education Networks (NRENs) in Africa are therefore calling for investments to support the development and strengthening of campus networks & research and education networks infrastructure and provision of online/remote teaching and learning platforms/tools for African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). The campus networks, supported by the national and regional research and education networks, are fundamental in transforming methods of teaching, learning and research as a response to the COVID-19 pandemic that has led to the closure of a large majority of African Higher Education Institutions.

This is the opportune time for all of us to come together to support our African HEIs keep their doors of learning, teaching and research open. As a consortium, we appeal to African Governments, Development and Funding Partners and Private Sector to support (financially & in terms of human resources) the development of strong campus networks and the strengthening of National Research & Education Networks so that African HEIs can effectively provide all types of digital services for remote teaching. We especially appeal to African Governments to prioritize the ‘last mile’ solutions in the African countries so that the rural areas have equal access to the internet as those in the urban areas. We appeal to telecommunications companies in Africa to design affordable internet access packages for students as well as staff. We also ask all humanity to support each other to protect our communities and fight the COVID-19 pandemic.

TITLE: University of Cambridge DE-GSJ Free Online Courses 2026: Apply for Fully Funded Sustainability, Climate and International Law Training

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the 2026 Fall Courses under the Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Programme, an international educational initiative co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge. The programme provides learners around the world with free access to specialised education focused on sustainability, international law, public policy, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable development.

For the 2026 Fall offering, applicants can express interest in courses addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the Paris Agreement. The Fall courses will run between September and November 2026, with the full application deadline set for 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST.

The DE-GSJ Programme is particularly valuable for law and policy leaders, government officials, academics, civil society professionals, practitioners and other individuals interested in using law and policy to address some of the world’s most pressing sustainability and justice challenges.

About the Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice Programme

The Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Programme was created to harness the potential of international law to empower governments and communities around the world, with particular attention to highly vulnerable countries facing interconnected global crises.

Co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge, the initiative makes education concerning the law and policy dimensions of sustainability more accessible to learners internationally.

The programme also seeks to train law and policy specialists who can contribute to implementing essential international treaties at different levels of governance.

Rather than approaching sustainability solely as an environmental issue, the programme explores the important relationship between sustainable development, international agreements, governance, public policy and legal frameworks.

This gives participants an opportunity to understand not only major global sustainability challenges, but also how laws, treaties, institutions and policies can be used to translate international commitments into practical action.

2026 DE-GSJ Fall Courses

The DE-GSJ educational offerings page states that applications are open for its Fall Courses 2026.

Three courses are included in the Fall 2026 schedule:

Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law

Course dates: 28 September – 9 October 2026

Key Essentials: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Sustainable Development and the Law

Course dates: 12 October – 23 October 2026

Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law

Course dates: 26 October – 6 November 2026

These dates allow learners to potentially build knowledge across several interconnected areas of international sustainability law during the Fall 2026 period.

1. Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law

The Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law course provides an introduction to emerging approaches and frameworks in sustainable development law.

It is designed for leaders and learners involved in areas such as:

Law;

Policymaking;

Policy analysis;

Legal and policy practice;

Monitoring and reporting;

Government;

Academia;

Civil society; and

Practitioner communities.

The course examines important challenges and possible solutions relating to sustainable development and considers the role that law can play in scaling up implementation globally and within learners’ own jurisdictions.

Learning Objectives

Through the course, learners are introduced to the relevance of sustainable development law and governance.

Participants are encouraged to:

Understand the relevance of sustainable development law and governance;

Think critically about how sustainable development is reflected in legal and governance systems worldwide;

Understand the role of governance within sustainable development law;

Strengthen the role of law and policy in monitoring and reporting; and

Explore opportunities to advance careers related to global sustainability and justice.

Course Modules

The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law course covers:

Module 1: Introduction to the SDGs

Module 2: Sustainable Development Law Principles and Practices

Module 3: Law and Practice of SDGs in the Global Economy

Module 4: Law and Practice of SDGs in the Global Biosphere

Module 5: Law and Practice of SDGs

Module 6: Course Conclusion and Final Remarks

2. Key Essentials: Convention on Biological Diversity, Sustainable Development and the Law

The second Fall 2026 course focuses on biodiversity and the international legal frameworks designed to protect it.

The programme highlights the seriousness of global biodiversity loss and provides learners with an overview of the Global Biodiversity Framework under the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity.

It examines challenges, possible solutions and the role of law in strengthening implementation internationally and within individual jurisdictions.

Learning Objectives

Participants will have the opportunity to:

Examine major biodiversity law and governance challenges;

Explore the Global Biodiversity Framework;

Understand tools available to policymakers and lawmakers, including those relating to finance, transparency and science;

Identify and analyse innovative domestic legal and policy solutions;

Strengthen understanding of monitoring and reporting through law and policy; and

Develop knowledge relevant to careers in sustainability and justice.

What Does the Biodiversity Course Cover?

The course begins with an introduction to its structure and resources and includes engagement with instructors and learners from different parts of the world.

Participants are introduced to the Convention on Biological Diversity, COP15 developments and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

The subsequent modules explore several major areas.

Nature Conservation, Ecosystem Restoration and Biodiversity Protection

Learners examine international goals and targets related to reducing threats to biodiversity, slowing extinction, maintaining genetic diversity and expanding or improving natural ecosystems.

Sustainable Use and Management of Biodiversity

Participants explore international targets concerning sustainable biodiversity use and management, together with examples of regional, national and local policies.

The course also examines international commitments concerning the sustainable use, harvesting and trade of wild species and their relationship with the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

Benefit-Sharing and Traditional Indigenous Knowledge

Learners explore international targets concerning access and benefit-sharing.

The module introduces important international instruments including:

The Nagoya Protocol;

The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture; and

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

It also considers the importance of protecting traditional knowledge.

Biodiversity Finance and Capacity-Building

Another module addresses the resources necessary to implement international biodiversity commitments, including:

Financial resources;

Capacity-building;

Technical cooperation;

Scientific cooperation; and

Access to and transfer of technology.

The course concludes with a live closing session and provides learners with insights into potential career paths related to the Global Biodiversity Framework, sustainable development and law. Learners are also invited to join a course alumni network.

3. Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law

Climate change is another central focus of the Fall 2026 DE-GSJ programme.

The Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law course introduces learners to the Paris Agreement under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

The programme connects climate change with wider social, economic, environmental and human rights challenges and examines the role of law in responding to climate impacts and implementing international commitments.

It is intended for leaders and learners working in law, policymaking, analysis, practice and reporting across governments, academia, civil society and practitioner communities.

Learning Objectives

The course seeks to help learners:

Understand pressing climate change law and governance challenges;

Explore the Paris Agreement;

Understand tools available to policymakers and lawmakers, including climate finance, transparency and science;

Identify innovative domestic policy and legal solutions;

Strengthen the role of law and policy in monitoring and reporting; and

Build knowledge relevant to international careers in sustainability and justice.

What Will Participants Learn About the Paris Agreement?

Course Introduction and Orientation

Participants first become familiar with the course structure, resources, instructors and other learners.

They are also introduced to the major elements, structures and principles of the Paris Agreement under the UNFCCC.

Climate Mitigation and Net-Zero Transitions

Learners examine mitigation obligations under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, including legal commitments relating to the transition towards net zero.

The module examines law and policy measures designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and efforts to limit average global warming.

Climate Adaptation, Resilience and Loss and Damage

Participants explore:

Adaptation commitments under the Paris Agreement;

Nationally Determined Contributions;

National adaptation plans;

Climate resilience;

Legal and governance dimensions of adaptation; and

Loss and Damage provisions and related international developments.

Climate Finance and Carbon Markets

Another module examines climate finance provisions under the Paris Agreement and international efforts to align financial flows with its goals.

Learners are also introduced to carbon-market policy structures and low-greenhouse-gas development pathways.

Climate Compliance, Capacity and Transparency

Participants examine the Paris Agreement’s enhanced transparency framework and the modalities, procedures and guidelines developed through subsequent Conferences of the Parties.

The course also introduces the functions and objectives of the Paris Agreement Implementation and Compliance Committee (PAICC).

The final module includes a live closing session where instructors provide insights into climate law, governance and possible career pathways. Participants are also invited to join an alumni network.

Course Format and Learning Experience

The DE-GSJ courses are designed to combine expert instruction with flexible independent learning.

According to the programme information provided, courses generally involve approximately eight to ten hours of total learning time, with focused modules delivered by University of Cambridge and international experts.

The learning experience can include:

Recorded or focused expert instruction;

Live classroom engagements;

Access to selected learning materials;

Independent reading;

Recommended resources;

Self-paced study;

Assessments; and

Opportunities to engage with instructors and an international community of learners.

For example, the programme describes one of its short courses as providing approximately eight hours of learning across six recorded modules, two live Zoom classroom engagements and approximately two to three hours of independent work.

This structure makes the programme particularly relevant to professionals and learners who want intensive training without enrolling in a conventional full-time academic degree.

Are the DE-GSJ Courses Free?

Yes. The programme is designed to widen access to high-quality education, particularly for learners and professionals in countries that are highly vulnerable to climate and sustainability challenges.

Successful applicants can undertake the course without paying the normal course value.

Each selected learner effectively receives a bursary allowing them to complete the training at no charge. The programme information states that the course is valued at £800.

Importantly, this does not mean that successful participants receive £800 as a cash payment.

Instead, the bursary covers access to the educational opportunity, meaning the selected learner does not have to pay the £800 course value.

What Do Successful Learners Receive?

The DE-GSJ initiative is a non-credit-bearing programme. This distinction is important for applicants who may otherwise assume that completing a course provides academic credits toward a University of Cambridge degree.

However, successful completion offers other valuable professional-development benefits.

Upon successfully completing each course, learners are eligible to receive a certificate from leading expert institutes of the University of Cambridge and global partners.

Successful completion may also provide access to potential further scholarship opportunities for intensive professional development courses through Cambridge Advance Online.

For professionals working in government, law, policy, international development, climate change, sustainability, human rights or civil society, the combination of specialised knowledge, certification and access to an international learning network can provide a useful foundation for continued professional development.

Who Can Participate?

The DE-GSJ Programme is primarily designed to train law and policy leaders.

However, participation is not described as being exclusively restricted to lawyers or policymakers.

Individuals who are committed to making a difference through law and policy in support of sustainable development may also seek to become part of the programme’s wider community of practice.

The individual courses specifically reference leaders and learners involved in:

Government;

Law;

Policymaking;

Policy analysis;

Legal practice;

Policy practice;

Reporting and monitoring;

Academia;

Civil society; and

Practitioner communities.

This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to professionals and emerging leaders whose work intersects with sustainable development, environmental governance, climate action, biodiversity, international development or public policy.

Is the Programme Available Internationally?

Yes. The DE-GSJ Programme describes its mission in global terms and states that it provides free and accessible sustainability law and policy courses to learners from around the world, with particular emphasis on strengthening capacity in highly vulnerable countries.

The supplied programme information does not state a restriction limiting the Fall 2026 courses to one nationality, race or continent.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the application form and individual course requirements before applying.

Language of Instruction

The courses are currently offered only in English.

Prospective participants should therefore consider whether they have sufficient English-language ability to follow expert instruction, complete readings and other independent learning activities, participate in live engagements and successfully complete required assessments.

Certificates and Alumni Network

Successful course completion can provide more than knowledge of a particular international agreement.

Participants may become eligible for a certificate associated with leading University of Cambridge expert institutes and global partners.

Individual courses also indicate that learners can be invited to become part of a course alumni network following completion. For example, both the biodiversity and Paris Agreement course descriptions reference invitations to join a network of course alumni.

Such networks can help participants remain connected to a broader international community interested in sustainability, justice, international law and policy.

How to Apply for the DE-GSJ Fall Courses 2026

The application process begins through the programme’s Educational Offerings section.

Applicants should follow these general steps:

Review the available courses.

Read the course descriptions and identify the Fall 2026 offering or offerings most relevant to your professional interests and development goals.

Submit an Expression of Interest.

Use the Expression of Interest form provided through the DE-GSJ Educational Offerings page.

Check your email.

After submitting the Expression of Interest form, prospective learners should receive further information and detailed instructions for completing the full application.

Submit a separate application where required.

Applicants interested in more than one course should follow the programme’s instructions for submitting the necessary application for each course.

Submit before the deadline.

The programme states that applicants seeking consideration for the Fall Courses must submit their application by 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST.

Wait for the selection decision.

Applications are reviewed by the programme’s selection committee, and applicants are notified by email regarding whether they have been selected.

Because participation is free for successful applicants, prospective learners should provide accurate and thoughtful information demonstrating their interest in the programme and their commitment to applying law and policy knowledge toward sustainable development.

APPLY NOW

Application Deadline

The deadline for full applications to the DE-GSJ Fall Courses 2026 is:

1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST.

Prospective applicants should avoid waiting until the deadline because the process begins with an Expression of Interest, after which additional application instructions are sent by email.

Important Fall 2026 Dates

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

Application deadline: 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST

Sustainable Development Goals and the Law: 28 September – 9 October 2026

Convention on Biological Diversity, Sustainable Development and the Law: 12 October – 23 October 2026

Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law: 26 October – 6 November 2026

Why Consider the DE-GSJ Programme?

The programme provides an unusual opportunity to access specialised international sustainability law and policy education without paying the stated £800 course value.

Potential advantages include:

Free participation for successful applicants;

Learning from University of Cambridge and global experts;

Specialised training in sustainability law and governance;

Flexible online and self-paced learning;

Live classroom engagement;

Exposure to an international community of learners;

Training relating to major international treaties and frameworks;

A certificate following successful completion;

Access to an alumni network through relevant courses;

Potential access to further scholarship opportunities for professional development through Cambridge Advance Online; and

Knowledge that can potentially be applied in government, policy, law, academia, civil society and sustainability-related professional settings.

The programme can be especially relevant for individuals seeking to connect global commitments such as the Sustainable Development Goals, Convention on Biological Diversity and Paris Agreement with practical legal and policy implementation.

Conclusion

The Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Fall Courses 2026 provide an accessible pathway for professionals, emerging leaders and committed learners around the world to deepen their understanding of sustainability through the lens of international law and public policy.

Co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge, the programme is particularly focused on building the capacity of law and policy specialists and empowering communities and governments, including those in highly vulnerable countries, to respond to interconnected global challenges.

With Fall 2026 courses covering the Sustainable Development Goals, Convention on Biological Diversity and Paris Agreement, participants can engage with some of the most consequential international frameworks shaping sustainable development, biodiversity protection and global climate action.

Successful applicants receive access to the training without paying the stated £800 course value, while successful completion can lead to certification, connections with an international alumni community and potential further professional-development scholarship opportunities.

Interested candidates should review the available courses, submit their Expression of Interest and ensure that their full application is completed by 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST.

TITLE: Yale Teaching Fellowship Cohort 3 Applications Open: Full Tuition and a $47,380 First-Year Stipend for Aspiring Teachers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for Cohort 3 of the Yale Teaching Fellowship, an intensive graduate education and teacher-preparation initiative designed to build a strong, diverse and long-term teaching workforce for New Haven Public Schools in Connecticut, United States.

Developed through a partnership among Yale University, New Haven Public Schools, New Haven Promise and Southern Connecticut State University, the program combines fully funded graduate tuition with teacher certification, structured classroom experience, mentorship and a clear route into high-need teaching roles. Depending on the selected track, participants can earn either a Master of Arts in Teaching or a Master of Science from Southern Connecticut State University while preparing to serve New Haven students.

The fellowship concentrates primarily on mathematics, science and special education, which New Haven Public Schools has identified as major teacher-shortage areas. Yale’s current program information states that applications for Cohort 3 are open and must be completed by January 1, 2027.

Yale Teaching Fellowship Cohort 3 at a Glance

Program detail
Information

Program name
Yale Teaching Fellowship

Cohort
Cohort 3

Lead funder
Yale University

Academic institution
Southern Connecticut State University

School district
New Haven Public Schools

Recruitment and applicant support partner
New Haven Promise

Location
New Haven, Connecticut, United States

Main subject areas
Mathematics, science and special education

Available routes
Teacher Pipeline Track and Current Teachers Track

Graduate awards
Master of Arts in Teaching or Master of Science, depending on track

Tuition support
Full tuition for both tracks

Living support
$47,380 during the first fellowship year for Teacher Pipeline Track fellows

Places per fellowship year
Up to 20 Teacher Pipeline fellows and up to five Current Teacher fellows

Service requirement
At least three years of full-time service after completing the relevant degree program

Application deadline
January 1, 2027

Application status
Open

What Is the Yale Teaching Fellowship?

The Yale Teaching Fellowship is a service-linked graduate training program created to address persistent teacher shortages and strengthen teacher retention in New Haven Public Schools. It is not a conventional Yale degree program: fellows complete their graduate degrees at Southern Connecticut State University, while Yale provides substantial financial support and helps sustain the wider fellowship structure.

The fellowship emerged from the Yale & Slavery Research Project and reflects Yale’s broader commitment to New Haven. It is designed to recruit high-quality educators from varied backgrounds and experiences, prepare them for difficult-to-fill teaching areas and support them beyond initial certification so they can build lasting careers in the district.

According to the current Yale Teaching Fellowship program page, the initiative represents a $10 million investment over six years. Across four fellowship years beginning in May 2025, it aims to place up to 100 master’s-qualified educators in New Haven’s public schools. That total is expected to include up to 80 new teachers and up to 20 current teachers gaining a special education cross-endorsement.

The program is already producing cohorts of classroom-ready educators. Yale reported in August 2026 that the first cohort of 20 fellows had completed its preparation year and that the second cohort included 18 participants: eight in special education, six in science and four in mathematics.

Why the Yale Teaching Fellowship Matters

The Yale Teaching Fellowship was built around a straightforward problem: public-school systems need well-prepared teachers, but financial barriers, the cost of graduate education and limited access to extended classroom training can prevent promising candidates from entering or remaining in the profession.

The fellowship addresses those barriers through an integrated model that includes:

Full graduate tuition rather than partial tuition assistance;

A substantial first-year living stipend for eligible Teacher Pipeline fellows;

A degree pathway aligned with Connecticut teacher certification;

Extended clinical experience in New Haven Public Schools;

Guidance from experienced mentor teachers;

A cohort-based learning experience;

A transition from graduate study to responsibility as a teacher of record; and

Ongoing mentorship during the required period of service.

This structure gives aspiring teachers time to develop their skills before assuming full classroom responsibility. It also enables current teachers to gain specialist qualifications in an area where the district has identified a serious need.

The Four Partner Institutions and Their Roles

Yale University

Yale supplies the program’s principal financial investment. It covers full tuition for fellows in both tracks and provides the advertised $47,380 first-year living stipend to Teacher Pipeline Track participants. Yale also supports the cohort experience and the fellowship’s broader mission of serving and strengthening New Haven.

Southern Connecticut State University

Southern Connecticut State University provides the graduate education. Teacher Pipeline fellows work toward a Master of Arts in Teaching and initial Connecticut teacher certification, while eligible current teachers pursue a Master of Science and special education cross-endorsement.

SCSU independently controls admission to its degree programs, so selection as a fellowship finalist does not by itself guarantee university admission.

New Haven Public Schools

New Haven Public Schools identifies the staffing areas that the program should prioritize. The district supplies classroom settings, mentor teachers, residency placements and the employment environment in which fellows complete their required service.

New Haven Promise

New Haven Promise assists with recruitment, application support and professional guidance. Its involvement helps connect the fellowship to New Haven residents, school employees and candidates who have demonstrated a commitment to the city and its young people.

Priority Teaching Areas

Southern Connecticut State University has developed fellowship-aligned academic schedules in three main areas identified by New Haven Public Schools:

Mathematics;

Science; and

Special education.

Science pathways may include biology, chemistry, earth science or physics, subject to the candidate’s academic preparation and SCSU’s admission requirements.

The Teacher Pipeline Track may consider a candidate seeking another licensure area if that person can complete the selected program within the same timeframe as the priority programs. However, the fellowship gives preference to mathematics, science and special education because these represent the district’s greatest teacher shortages.

Teacher Pipeline Track

The Teacher Pipeline Track is the main entry route for college graduates who do not already hold a teaching certificate. New Haven Public Schools paraprofessionals and other student-facing support staff are especially encouraged to consider this pathway, although selected participants must comply with the track’s employment conditions during the first fellowship year.

Up to 20 college graduates may enter this track in each fellowship year. Participants pursue Connecticut teacher certification and a two-year Master of Arts in Teaching at Southern Connecticut State University. The advertised academic sequence covers five terms: fall, spring, summer, fall and spring.

Financial Support for Teacher Pipeline Fellows

Yale provides:

Full tuition for the relevant SCSU graduate program;

A living stipend of $47,380 during the first fellowship year, covering September through August; and

A structured cohort experience.

The published stipend applies specifically to the Teacher Pipeline Track. Applicants should not assume that the Current Teachers Track carries the same living allowance.

Training Sequence

The track deliberately increases classroom responsibility over time:

During the fall of the first year, fellows spend 20 hours per week in a fellowship mentor’s classroom.

During the spring of the first year, fellows undertake a full-time teacher residency in their school.

During the second year, fellows work as full-time teachers of record under Connecticut’s Resident Educator Certificate while continuing the degree pathway.

After completing the degree, fellows commit to at least three years of teaching in New Haven Public Schools and receive ongoing mentorship.

This sequence is designed to avoid placing new teachers into classrooms without sufficient preparation. Fellows first observe and assist, then complete a full-time residency, and finally move into paid professional responsibility as teachers of record.

Current Teachers Track

The Current Teachers Track is designed for eligible full-time teachers already working in New Haven Public Schools. Its purpose is to help qualified educators gain a Connecticut cross-endorsement in special education while earning an SCSU Master of Science.

Up to five certified teachers may enter this track per fellowship year. The graduate program runs across four semesters—summer, fall, spring and summer—and Yale pays full tuition.

Participants continue working as full-time NHPS teachers while completing the program. After earning the Master of Science and cross-endorsement, they must secure and serve in a full-time special education teaching position in the district for at least three years.

This track does not train participants for their first teaching credential. It develops currently certified district teachers for difficult-to-fill special education positions.

Major Benefits of the Yale Teaching Fellowship

Full Graduate Tuition

Both fellowship tracks provide full tuition support for the applicable SCSU master’s degree. This removes one of the largest financial barriers facing prospective and current educators seeking advanced qualifications.

$47,380 First-Year Living Stipend

Teacher Pipeline fellows receive a living stipend of $47,380 during their first year, from September through August. This support is particularly important because the training progresses from a 20-hour weekly placement to a full-time residency.

Master’s Degree and Professional Credential

Depending on the track, participants can earn an SCSU Master of Arts in Teaching with initial Connecticut certification or an SCSU Master of Science with special education cross-endorsement.

Sustained Classroom Experience

The fellowship combines academic learning with direct practice. Pipeline fellows receive mentor-classroom experience, a full-time residency and a supported transition into teaching as the responsible instructor.

Mentorship and Cohort Support

Fellows learn alongside a cohort and receive guidance from experienced educators. Ongoing mentorship continues during the post-degree service period for Teacher Pipeline fellows.

Route Into a High-Need Public-Service Career

The program prepares participants for roles in subjects where qualified teachers are urgently needed. The service commitment links the public investment directly to students and schools in New Haven.

Application Materials

Applicants should prepare a complete application carefully and allow sufficient time for transcripts and recommendations. The published track requirements identify the following materials:

Responses to short-answer questions;

Responses to essay questions;

A résumé or curriculum vitae;

Transcripts from every college or university attended; and

A letter of recommendation.

For Teacher Pipeline applicants, the recommendation should come from a professor, mentor or supervisor. For Current Teachers Track applicants, it should come from an NHPS principal or assistant principal.

Applicants with degrees earned outside the United States should be prepared to provide a certified course-by-course evaluation from World Education Services or Educational Credential Evaluators, as required by the fellowship and SCSU.

The online form allows applicants to save an incomplete application and receive a return link. Candidates should copy or email that link to themselves so they can continue working before final submission. An application should be treated as complete only when every required document, including the recommendation and transcripts, has been received.

Southern Connecticut State University Admission Process

Fellowship finalists must separately apply for admission to the appropriate Southern Connecticut State University graduate program. This is a mandatory second process. SCSU evaluates academic eligibility and retains sole discretion over admission decisions.

For Master of Arts in Teaching programs, the SCSU 2026–2027 graduate catalogue lists a bachelor’s degree from a regionally accredited institution, or a recognized foreign equivalent, with a total undergraduate GPA of at least 2.70.

Depending on the subject, applicants may also need appropriate subject-area preparation, general-education coursework and Praxis Core or qualifying substitute scores.

The current catalogue explains that most MAT concentrations require content preparation in the proposed endorsement area. It also lists 39 general-education credits distributed across five of six subject areas, including a three-credit United States history survey course, for MAT programs other than comprehensive special education.

SCSU may consider applicants with limited outstanding coursework for conditional admission, but university and certification requirements must still be completed.

Applicants should review the exact SCSU concentration requirements that apply to mathematics, biology, chemistry, earth science, physics or comprehensive special education. Minimum eligibility does not guarantee either fellowship selection or university admission.

Academic and Service Obligations

The Yale Teaching Fellowship is a significant funded commitment rather than an unrestricted scholarship. Fellows are expected to:

Maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 3.0 at SCSU;

Complete the approved degree and certification or cross-endorsement pathway;

Participate fully in the required in-person academic and school-based activities; and

Complete at least three years of full-time qualifying teaching service after finishing the degree.

Published fellowship terms also state that a participant who does not complete the required three years of employment may have to repay part of the fellowship funding.

The previously published repayment schedule lists:

$10,000 for completing less than one year;

$6,666 for completing more than one but less than two years; and

$3,333 for completing more than two but less than three years.

Applicants must check the final Cohort 3 agreement before accepting an award because that agreement will control the binding financial and service conditions.

The published terms further explain that if a fellow is not offered a full-time NHPS teaching position by July 31 of the year in which the fellow earns the SCSU degree, the service commitment may be completed in another Connecticut Alliance District after advance notice.

This provision should not be treated as an automatic job guarantee. Applicants should verify its operation directly with the fellowship team.

Yale Teaching Fellowship Cohort 3 Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for Cohort 3 is:

January 1, 2027

Yale’s current program page confirms that applications are open. Because no submission time or late-application policy is stated on the public Yale page, candidates should submit well before the final day.

Transcripts, international credential evaluations and recommendation letters can take time to arrange, and all required materials should be received before the deadline.

How to Apply for the Yale Teaching Fellowship

Applicants can use the following process:

Read the current fellowship overview and compare the two tracks.

Select the track that matches your existing certification and employment status.

Review the relevant SCSU degree and Connecticut certification requirements.

Arrange transcripts from every college or university attended.

Obtain a WES or ECE evaluation if presenting an international degree.

Ask an appropriate recommender early and explain the deadline.

Prepare the short-answer and essay responses with clear evidence of readiness to teach and serve New Haven students.

Upload the résumé or CV and all supporting documents.

Save the in-progress application link securely if the form is not completed in one session.

Submit the complete fellowship application before January 1, 2027.

If selected as a finalist, complete the separate application to Southern Connecticut State University.

Applicants should begin from the official Cohort 3 information page and cross-check updates on the Yale Office of New Haven Affairs program page.

Questions about the fellowship may be directed to Christine Gentry, Director of the Yale Teaching Fellowship, at christine.gentry@yale.edu.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

A competitive application should do more than state a general interest in education. It should demonstrate that the applicant understands the fellowship’s purpose and is ready for its academic, practical and service requirements.

Candidates should consider the following:

Explain why teaching in New Haven Public Schools is a serious long-term commitment rather than a temporary opportunity.

Connect academic background or professional experience to mathematics, science, special education or another demonstrable district need.

Use specific examples of work with children, families, schools or community organizations.

Describe experiences that helped create inclusive, supportive or equitable environments for school-aged children.

Show readiness for an intensive sequence combining graduate study and substantial in-person classroom work.

Address the three-year service obligation directly and realistically.

Proofread every written response and ensure that the résumé, essays and recommendation present a consistent professional story.

If applicable, explain how first-generation or low-income experience has shaped the applicant’s understanding of educational opportunity, without assuming that personal background alone is enough for selection.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the graduate degree awarded by Yale University?

No. Yale funds and supports the fellowship, but the graduate degree is awarded by Southern Connecticut State University.

Does every fellow receive the $47,380 living stipend?

No. The currently advertised living stipend applies to Teacher Pipeline Track fellows during the first fellowship year. The Current Teachers Track advertises full tuition but does not advertise the same stipend.

Can a person apply for a subject other than mathematics, science or special education?

Possibly, under the Teacher Pipeline Track, if the proposed licensure program can be completed within the same timeframe. However, the program gives preference to mathematics, science and special education because those are the principal shortage areas identified by NHPS.

Can current NHPS paraprofessionals or student-facing support employees apply?

Yes. They are specifically encouraged to consider the Teacher Pipeline Track. However, the published Pipeline eligibility conditions state that fellows cannot remain NHPS employees during the first fellowship year, so affected applicants should clarify the employment transition before accepting an offer.

Is the program fully online?

No. It requires in-person study at SCSU and direct work in New Haven Public Schools. Applicants must live, or be able to live by the start of the fellowship, close enough to participate fully.

Does the fellowship guarantee a permanent teaching job?

Applicants should not treat it as an unconditional employment guarantee. The program creates a strong preparation and service pathway, and published terms address what happens if NHPS does not offer a full-time position by a specified date, but candidates should verify employment conditions directly.

When is the deadline?

The Cohort 3 application deadline is January 1, 2027.

Conclusion

The Yale Teaching Fellowship Cohort 3 offers an unusually comprehensive route into high-need public-school teaching. By combining full graduate tuition, Connecticut certification pathways, extensive classroom preparation, mentorship and a substantial first-year stipend for eligible Pipeline fellows, the program reduces both the financial and professional barriers that often prevent talented candidates from becoming teachers.

The opportunity also carries serious responsibilities. Fellows must meet SCSU’s admission and academic standards, participate in an intensive in-person program and complete a multi-year teaching commitment. Prospective applicants should therefore assess their eligibility, location, work authorization, subject preparation and long-term commitment to New Haven before applying.

Applications are open, and all required materials should be submitted by January 1, 2027.

TITLE: Press Release -Strengthening the Capacity of Africa’s Science Granting Councils in Research Management

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nairobi, Kenya and Accra, Ghana (17 August 2020) – Africa faces some of the world’s greatest development challenges and its research capacity is not yet sufficient to meet them. Improving research management within institutions is crucial, if research and innovation is to underpin social and economic development in Africa.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is collaborating with the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) to implement the second phase of the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI) Research Management Project which will strengthen the capacities of Africa’s Science Granting Councils to play their essential roles effectively and efficiently in research, knowledge generation and innovation through training, technical support, and peer-to-peer learning.

Building on the success of the first phase of the SGCI, the Research Management Project is being implemented in 15 sub Saharan African countries, specifically in Ghana, Burkina Faso, Cote d’Ivoire, Senegal, Botswana, Malawi, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Ethiopia, Namibia, and Rwanda. The project will support the development of research and evidence-based policies that will contribute to economic and social development on the continent.

“The overall goal of the project is to fortify the capability of Science Granting Councils in explicit areas of research management, namely research excellence, research ethics, emerging scientific practices (especially open data, open access and scientific citizenship) and development of online grant management systems” said Prof Jonathan Mba, Director of Research and Academic Planning at the AAU.

“Our participation in this project is to complement our efforts to address systemic gaps in the broad research ecosystem so as to create and sustain research environments that enable research to flourish.” said Allen Mukhwana, Research Systems Manager at the AAS.

Africa’s Science Granting Councils are key players and strategic partners in improving the continent’s scientific research outputs and achieving continental policy initiatives such as the African Union’s Science, Technology, and Innovation Strategy for Africa 2024 (STISA-2024), and the Continental Education Strategy for Africa 2016-2025 (CESA 16-25). It is therefore critical that their capacity in research management is regularly built in areas where gaps have been identified. With strengthened capacities in research management, Science Granting Councils in Africa will better play their crucial roles as integrators and brokers of knowledge within their national systems of innovation.

The SGCI is a multi-funder initiative that is funded by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC), South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF) and the German Research Foundation (DFG).

The Association of African Universities and the African Academy of Sciences are strongly committed to working closely with the Science Granting Councils to achieve ‘Research Excellence’ as reflected in their strategic plans. The AAU’s 2020 -2025 Strategic Plan, for instance, prioritizes closer engagement with national policy systems in African Countries, whilst the AAS Strategy emphasizes strengthening of African institutions to become excellent and adaptable to proven needs.

#########################################

Notes to editors

The Association of African Universities

The Association of African Universities (the project lead) is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa. AAU aims to improve the quality of African higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education. It is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 400 HEIs and has three regional offices – North Africa Regional Office (NARO) in Cairo, Egypt; East Africa Regional Office (EARO) in Khartoum, Sudan; and North America Office (NAMO) in Washington DC, USA. The Association is the technical implementing arm of the African Union in higher education – with coverage and mandate across the language divide of Africa. We have influence in the francophone, anglophone, lusophone and arabophone regions. The AAU is the coordinating agency of the Higher Education Cluster of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25) of the African Union Commission (AUC). Through our guidance, our member universities are responsible for implementing the Science, Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024) of the AUC. (Website – https://www.aau.org/ |Facebook – Association of African Universities| Twitter -@aau_67)

Media Enquiries

The Association of African Universities, Accra, Ghana

Felicia Kuagbedzi, fnkrumah@aau.org +233246425147

The African Academy of Sciences

The African Academy of Sciences (AAS) is a non-aligned, non-political, not-for-profit pan African organisation whose vision is to see transformed lives on the African continent through science. Our tripartite mandate is recognising excellence through the AAS’ highly prestigious fellowship and award schemes, providing advisory and think tank functions for shaping Africa’s Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) strategies and policies and implementing key STI programmes addressing Africa’s developmental challenges. The Academy’s five strategic focus areas include: Environment and climate change; health and wellbeing; natural sciences; policy and governance; and social sciences and humanities. Its programmatic unit ,the Alliance for Accelerating Excellence in Science in Africa’s (AESA’s) created in partnership with the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD, has a mission is to catalyse investments, strategies and programmes that promote the brightest minds in Africa, foster scientific excellence, inspire research leadership and accelerate innovation in ways that will improve lives and shift the centre of gravity for African science to Africa.

TITLE: AAU holds Virtual Institutional Quality Assurance (QA) Workshop for Tshwane University of Technology (TUT) QA Directorate

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) held a virtual workshop on quality assurance for the Tshwane University of Technology (TUT), South Africa, from the 16th to 18th November, 2020.

The workshop was facilitated by Dr. Violet Makuku, Quality Assurance Specialist at the AAU, and aimed to assist the university’s Quality Assurance Directorate to produce Quality Assurance standards for Multimodal learning. It was also targeted at building a strong quality culture in the institution and designing a robust Quality Management System (QMS). Important topics such as Quality indicators in Higher Education and the desired personality traits for QA personnel were also covered, among other things.

The nine participants from Tshwane University of Technology were advised to always conduct research whose data should be used to make informed decisions for the Quality Assurance Directorate and the institution at large. “Everything done on Quality Assurance should be based on research to come up with informed decisions”, Dr. Makuku remarked.

She defined Quality Assurance according to Matei and Iwinska (2016:19) as, the systematic internal and external management procedures and mechanisms by which a higher education institution assures its stakeholders of the quality of its systems, processes, products and outcomes and of its ability to manage the maintenance and enhancement of quality. She also added that tools/instruments, policies and practices should form a key part of a robust QMS. “Failure to ensure quality in higher and tertiary education can affect the brand of the institution and quality is everybody’s business but it starts with an individual,” She added.

Dr Makuku urged institutions in need of any form of institutional workshops in any area of interest to use the contact details below for communication. She also indicated that there were two upcoming workshops on Journal Establishment, Management and Sustainability (25/11/2020-17/12/2020) and Digital Marketing for Higher and Tertiary Education (24/11/2020-10/12/2020).
