TITLE: ICCROM Fellowships 2027: Apply for a 3–6 Month Cultural Heritage Research Fellowship in Rome

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the ICCROM Fellowship Programme 2027, offering experienced cultural heritage professionals the opportunity to undertake an independent period of research and study with the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property (ICCROM).

The Fellowship Programme is designed for senior professionals in cultural heritage conservation who want dedicated time to pursue research, exchange knowledge with an international professional community, access ICCROM’s specialist collections, and develop work capable of contributing new perspectives to heritage conservation.

Applications for the 2027 cycle opened on:

15 August 2026

and close on:

15 September 2026

Successful Fellowships will normally be undertaken during 2027, unless another arrangement is agreed with ICCROM.

The programme is open to qualified professionals who are nationals of an ICCROM Member State or who work in an organization located in an ICCROM Member State. Applicants must normally have at least a Master’s degree or higher in a field related to cultural heritage and at least 10 years of professional experience in the heritage field.

Fellows may undertake research at ICCROM headquarters in Rome, Italy, although a Fellowship may be conducted partly online where there is an appropriate justification.

Typical Fellowships last:

3 to 6 months

although ICCROM may consider another timeframe where the applicant provides a convincing justification.

Applicants should note an important financial condition: ICCROM does not currently provide financial support or a living stipend for Fellows because of budgetary constraints. Fellows are responsible for their own travel, accommodation and personal insurance. ICCROM nevertheless provides important institutional and research support, including office facilities, access to its internationally significant conservation library and archives, internet access and engagement with heritage professionals.

About the ICCROM Fellowship Programme

The ICCROM Fellowship Programme is an established professional research opportunity intended to enrich the international field of cultural heritage conservation.

Its purpose is to:

Bring fresh perspectives into ICCROM

Facilitate the exchange of knowledge and ideas

Encourage new lines of research

Strengthen professional relationships

Support research relevant to heritage conservation

Connect senior professionals with ICCROM resources and expertise

The programme is especially appropriate for experienced professionals who already possess substantial knowledge of their field and can independently develop a focused research project.

This is not primarily a training course for beginners or an entry-level internship.

Fellows are expected to arrive with an independent research agenda and use the period at ICCROM to advance it.

What Is ICCROM?

ICCROM is an international intergovernmental organization dedicated to the conservation of cultural heritage.

Its work involves areas such as:

Cultural heritage conservation

Heritage risk management

Capacity building

Research

Policy

Education

Emergency response

Collections

Sites and monuments

Conservation science

Heritage management

Sustainable development

Its international network includes 139 Member States, following San Marino’s accession as the 139th Member State in November 2025. ICCROM’s membership spans countries across Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, the Americas and Oceania.

The Fellowship Programme allows experienced researchers and practitioners from this global network to spend time engaging with the organization and its resources.

Why Apply for an ICCROM Fellowship?

One of the principal advantages of the Fellowship is the opportunity to step away from everyday professional responsibilities and concentrate on independent research in an environment dedicated specifically to cultural heritage.

A Fellowship can provide time and space to:

Develop an existing research project

Investigate a new question

Examine archival sources

Conduct literature-based research

Compare international conservation approaches

Develop policy recommendations

Strengthen a publication

Explore emerging heritage challenges

Build international professional relationships

The Fellowship is particularly valuable because researchers are placed within an international heritage organization rather than a conventional university department.

This creates opportunities to connect academic research with:

Conservation practice

Policy

Institutional experience

International cooperation

Capacity building

Access to One of the World’s Major Conservation Libraries

ICCROM highlights its specialist library as one of the most important resources available to Fellows.

The collection includes material in more than 70 languages and is regarded as one of the world’s major specialized collections in cultural heritage conservation.

Depending on the proposed research, Fellows may use these resources to examine subjects including:

Conservation theory

Restoration

Heritage science

Archaeology

Museum collections

Built heritage

Disaster risk

Heritage policy

Sustainable conservation

Education

Traditional knowledge

Climate-related heritage threats

Access to such a specialist collection can be particularly valuable for researchers working on comparative or international projects.

Access to ICCROM Archives

Fellows also receive access to:

ICCROM’s archives

where relevant to their research.

Archival work can help researchers investigate:

The development of international conservation practice

Historical heritage policies

Institutional cooperation

Past ICCROM programmes

Training and conservation approaches

Evolution of professional standards

Applicants whose proposed project depends on specific ICCROM holdings should explain this connection clearly in the research proposal.

Research Exchange With ICCROM Professionals

The Fellowship is also intended to create opportunities for intellectual exchange.

During the Fellowship, participants may interact with:

ICCROM staff

Other heritage professionals

Researchers

Practitioners

International experts

This exchange can help Fellows:

Test arguments

Receive new perspectives

Discover comparative examples

Develop future partnerships

Identify additional research questions

However, applicants must distinguish professional exchange from formal academic supervision.

ICCROM Fellows Conduct Independent Research

A particularly important condition of the programme is that:

Fellows are expected to conduct independent research.

Applicants cannot request an ICCROM staff member to serve as their research supervisor.

This means candidates should already possess the intellectual and professional experience necessary to:

Formulate their own research question

Design the research

Manage the project independently

Analyze material

Produce the intended outputs

The Fellowship is therefore best suited to established heritage professionals rather than researchers requiring close doctoral-style supervision.

Who Can Apply?

ICCROM welcomes individuals specializing in disciplines related to:

Cultural heritage

Applicants may work as:

Researchers

Teachers

Practitioners

The Fellowship is particularly aimed at senior professionals.

Candidates must satisfy several important requirements.

Master’s Degree Requirement

Applicants must hold at least:

A Master’s degree or higher

in an area related to cultural heritage.

Relevant fields may potentially include areas such as:

Conservation

Heritage studies

Archaeology

Architecture

Art history

Museum studies

Conservation science

Cultural resource management

Historic preservation

Anthropology

Heritage policy

Related disciplines

The exact eligibility of a degree depends on its connection to cultural heritage and the applicant’s proposed research.

Professional Experience Requirement

Candidates must have been professionally active in the cultural heritage field for at least:

10 years

This requirement demonstrates clearly that the ICCROM Fellowship is designed for experienced professionals.

It is generally not intended for:

Recent Bachelor’s graduates

Early-stage Master’s students

Entry-level heritage workers

Professionals with only a few years of relevant experience

Applicants should make their professional experience particularly visible in their CV.

Geographic Eligibility

Applicants must be either:

Nationals of an ICCROM Member State, or

Professionals working in an organization located within an ICCROM Member State

ICCROM’s official membership currently extends across a broad global network of countries.

Examples include countries in:

Africa

Asia

Europe

North America

Latin America and the Caribbean

Middle East

Oceania

Applicants should confirm that their nationality or employer location falls within the official Member States list before applying.

Official Member States list:
https://www.iccrom.org/about/overview/member-states/full-list

Language Requirements

Research during the Fellowship may be conducted in:

Any language

However, Fellows are expected to have good knowledge of at least one of ICCROM’s two official languages:

English

French

This requirement enables Fellows to participate meaningfully in professional exchanges and the institutional life of ICCROM.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating professionally in English or French.

Research Topics

ICCROM welcomes proposals concerning:

Any research topic related to cultural heritage conservation and ICCROM’s mission.

The call is intentionally broad.

Applicants are not required to limit themselves exclusively to the priority themes.

However, applications that align strongly with ICCROM’s current Strategic Directions may receive preference during selection.

Priority Research Areas for 2026–2027

For the 2026–2027 biennium, ICCROM identifies two particularly important thematic areas.

1. Better Heritage Conservation and Risk Management Approaches

ICCROM is interested in research exploring how heritage conservation and risk management can respond more effectively to:

Social change

Emerging hazards

Climate change

Urbanization

Digital transition

Complex crises

New technologies

This priority reflects the fact that cultural heritage is increasingly exposed to rapidly changing and overlapping risks.

Heritage and Climate Change

Changing climate patterns create significant risks for heritage.

Potential areas of research may include:

Extreme weather

Flooding

Drought

Wildfires

Sea-level rise

Heat

Changing humidity

Climate-related deterioration

Climate adaptation for heritage institutions

Risk assessment

Researchers might examine both physical threats to heritage and institutional strategies for addressing them.

Heritage and Urbanization

Rapid urban development can create both opportunities and threats for cultural heritage.

Relevant research could potentially address:

Historic urban landscapes

Development pressure

Urban regeneration

Infrastructure

Community participation

Heritage planning

Sustainable cities

Applicants should link such projects clearly to conservation practice and ICCROM’s mission.

Heritage and Digital Transition

Digital technologies are rapidly changing how heritage is:

Recorded

Preserved

Interpreted

Shared

Managed

Research could examine areas such as:

Digital documentation

Artificial intelligence

Digital archives

Remote sensing

3D technologies

Data management

Digital access

Emerging conservation technologies

ICCROM particularly encourages work considering innovative technologies where they contribute to improved conservation and risk management.

Heritage in Complex Crises

Cultural heritage can be exposed to multiple threats during:

Armed conflict

Natural disasters

Political instability

Humanitarian crises

Displacement

Economic disruption

Research may explore how institutions and communities can prepare for, respond to and recover from these situations.

Priority Area 2: Integrating Heritage Into Broader Policy Agendas

ICCROM also welcomes research examining how heritage can be more effectively incorporated into wider:

National and international policy frameworks.

This priority recognizes that heritage conservation cannot always operate as a separate policy sector.

Instead, heritage increasingly intersects with major policy areas.

Heritage and Climate Action

Researchers may investigate how heritage can be integrated into:

National climate strategies

Climate adaptation

Climate mitigation

Disaster planning

International climate policy

This can include both protecting heritage from climate impacts and examining how heritage knowledge may contribute to climate resilience.

Heritage and Sustainable Development

Another major area is the relationship between heritage and:

Sustainable development

Possible research might examine:

Community development

Sustainable tourism

Cultural industries

Local knowledge

Urban sustainability

Economic development

Social resilience

Heritage and the Sustainable Development Goals

The goal is to better understand how heritage can contribute to development rather than being treated only as an object requiring protection.

Heritage and Education

ICCROM also identifies:

Education

as a policy area in which heritage can play an important role.

Potential subjects include:

Heritage education

Youth engagement

Professional training

Public awareness

Heritage in school curricula

Community learning

Research could investigate how education strengthens conservation while also using heritage as a resource for wider learning.

Heritage, Health and Wellbeing

ICCROM also highlights connections between heritage and:

Health and wellbeing

This opens opportunities for research considering:

Community identity

Mental wellbeing

Social cohesion

Cultural participation

Sense of place

Recovery following crisis

Applicants should demonstrate how these themes connect meaningfully with cultural heritage conservation.

Where Is the Fellowship Based?

Fellowships may be undertaken at:

ICCROM Headquarters in Rome, Italy

Rome offers an especially relevant environment for cultural heritage research because of its concentration of:

Conservation institutions

Museums

Archives

Heritage sites

Academic organizations

International cultural bodies

However, the ICCROM Fellowship itself centers on the applicant’s independent research and use of ICCROM’s institutional resources.

Partially Online Fellowships

A Fellowship may also be conducted:

Partially online

where the applicant provides an appropriate justification.

This does not mean that all applicants should assume the programme can be completed entirely remotely.

Applicants seeking a hybrid arrangement should explain clearly:

Why partial online participation is necessary

Why it remains appropriate for the project

How access to ICCROM resources will be managed

How the Fellowship objectives will still be achieved

Fellowship Duration

The normal Fellowship period is:

3 to 6 months

This provides Fellows with sufficient time to undertake substantial independent research.

However, ICCROM may consider:

Alternative timeframes

where an applicant provides a convincing justification.

Applicants proposing a shorter or longer Fellowship should demonstrate clearly why the research requires that particular schedule.

End-of-Fellowship Research Presentation

At the end of the Fellowship, Fellows are asked to:

Present their research

to:

ICCROM staff

External guests

This presentation allows Fellows to communicate:

Findings

Methods

Emerging conclusions

Implications for conservation practice

Applicants should therefore design projects capable of generating meaningful research outputs within the Fellowship period.

Post-Fellowship Feedback

After completing the programme, Fellows may be contacted by ICCROM to provide feedback concerning:

Their Fellowship experience

Research outcomes

Professional benefits

Wider impact

This helps ICCROM assess and improve the Fellowship Programme.

Financial Support: Important Information

Prospective applicants should pay close attention to the funding arrangements.

ICCROM states clearly that:

Due to current budgetary constraints, it is not able to provide financial support for Fellowships.

Therefore, this is not a funded Fellowship in the traditional sense.

ICCROM does not currently provide:

A salary

Living stipend

Travel allowance

Accommodation funding

Personal insurance funding

Applicants should therefore assess carefully whether they can secure:

Institutional support

Employer funding

External research funding

Personal funding

before committing to a residential Fellowship in Rome.

What Fellows Must Pay For

Fellows are responsible for arranging and financing:

Travel

Applicants must organize travel to and from Italy.

Accommodation

Fellows must pay for their accommodation.

ICCROM may assist, where possible, in identifying reasonably priced accommodation, but accommodation itself is not funded.

Personal Insurance

Fellows must arrange their own insurance.

The programme requires:

Valid major global medical and accident insurance

for the entire Fellowship period.

This is compulsory.

Visa Support

Although ICCROM does not pay travel or visa-related living costs, it can assist successful Fellows with obtaining documents required to:

Enter Italy

Temporarily reside in Italy

This institutional support can help Fellows navigate immigration procedures.

Applicants remain responsible for ensuring they comply with applicable Italian entry and residence requirements.

What ICCROM Provides

Although there is no financial stipend, ICCROM provides substantial research infrastructure.

During the Fellowship, participants receive:

Office space

Computer workstation

Unlimited internet access

Stationery

Documentation services

Library access

Archive access

For established researchers who already have external financial support, these institutional resources may make the Fellowship particularly valuable.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted using ICCROM’s:

Online Fellowship Research Proposal Application form

The application form is available during the application period beginning on:

15 August 2026

Applicants should complete all required sections and upload supporting documentation before the deadline.

APPLY HERE

Required Application Documents

Applicants need several digital files.

The accepted file formats include:

PDF

DOC

DOCX

JPG

JPEG

PNG

TIF

TIFF

Each file must have a maximum size of:

3 MB

The required supporting documentation includes three main components.

1. Updated Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide an:

Up-to-date CV

The CV should demonstrate:

Academic qualifications

Professional history

Heritage specialization

Research experience

Publications

Teaching

Conservation work

Major projects

International experience

Other relevant achievements

Given the 10-year professional experience requirement, applicants should make their seniority and heritage expertise immediately clear.

2. Employer Agreement

Where applicable, applicants must provide:

Confirmation from their employer agreeing to the research period at ICCROM.

This is especially relevant for applicants currently employed by:

Universities

Museums

Heritage agencies

Government institutions

NGOs

Conservation organizations

The document should demonstrate that the employer understands and supports the applicant’s proposed absence or research activity.

3. Three Letters of Reference

Applicants must provide:

Three letters of reference

from people who have:

Direct knowledge of the applicant’s work.

Referees should therefore be capable of commenting credibly on:

Professional expertise

Research ability

Conservation experience

Independence

Contribution to the heritage field

Suitability for the proposed project

Applicants should contact referees well before September 15.

What If You Cannot Use the Online Application Form?

Applicants unable to submit their materials through the online system may contact the Fellowship Programme focal point.

Contact: Alison Heritage
Project Manager, Strategic Planning and Research
ICCROM – Fellowship Programme
Via di San Michele, 13
I-00153 Rome, Italy

Email: fellowships@iccrom.org

Fax: +39 06 58 55 33 49

Applicants should contact ICCROM before the deadline if technical or accessibility issues prevent normal online submission.

Fellowship Selection Process

Applications are assessed by the:

Fellowship Selection Committee

Candidates will be informed of the Committee’s decision in writing once results are available.

ICCROM does not provide a fixed notification date because the timeframe can vary depending on the number of applications received.

How Applications Are Evaluated

ICCROM publishes six major selection criteria.

Understanding these criteria can help applicants prepare much stronger proposals.

1. Overall Quality and Clarity

The proposed research should be:

Clearly written

Logically organized

Well defined

Intellectually coherent

Avoid overly broad topics.

A three-to-six-month Fellowship requires a focused research question.

2. Research Need

The project should address an:

Identified knowledge gap.

Applicants should therefore explain:

What is already known

What remains unclear

Why the gap matters

Why additional research is needed

A proposal that simply summarizes an established topic will likely be less competitive.

3. Quality of Anticipated Results

Applicants should demonstrate how their expected findings will represent:

A useful development

A practical contribution

Intellectual progress

A meaningful advance

for the field of heritage conservation.

Results might potentially take forms such as:

Academic paper

Policy recommendations

Methodological framework

Professional guidelines

Comparative analysis

Research report

Applicants should be specific about anticipated outputs.

4. Feasibility

ICCROM evaluates whether the proposed research can realistically be completed using:

Available resources

ICCROM collections

Fellowship timeframe

Applicant expertise

A highly ambitious project requiring several years of fieldwork would probably not be appropriate for a three-to-six-month Fellowship unless the ICCROM period forms a clearly defined component of a larger project.

5. Dissemination Plan

Applicants must explain how their research findings will be shared with the:

Broader heritage conservation community.

Possible dissemination routes may include:

Open-access publication

Academic journal

Conference presentation

Professional workshop

Institutional briefing

Online resources

Training materials

Policy communication

ICCROM particularly encourages:

Open-access dissemination.

6. Relevance to ICCROM’s Strategic Directions

Applications connected with ICCROM’s current Strategic Directions receive preference.

For 2026–2027, candidates should pay particular attention to the priority themes concerning:

Heritage risk management

Climate change

Urbanization

Digital transition

Complex crises

Innovative technologies

Heritage and climate policy

Sustainable development

Education

Health and wellbeing

A proposal does not necessarily need to fit these themes to qualify, but a strong connection can improve strategic relevance.

Preparing a Competitive ICCROM Fellowship Proposal

1. Identify a Specific Conservation Problem

Avoid proposing a topic such as:

“Climate Change and Cultural Heritage.”

Instead, narrow it to:

A particular heritage type

Specific geographic context

Defined risk

Policy problem

Methodological issue

A focused question is easier to complete within the Fellowship period.

2. Explain Why ICCROM Is Necessary

Do not write a proposal that could just as easily be completed at home.

Explain what ICCROM offers that is particularly valuable.

This might include:

Specialist library holdings

Archives

International conservation literature

Institutional history

Comparative expertise

Professional exchange

3. Demonstrate Professional Experience

The programme requires at least 10 years in the heritage field.

Use your application to show how that experience positions you to undertake genuinely independent research.

4. Connect Research With Practice

ICCROM is strongly practice-oriented.

Where appropriate, explain how your research can improve:

Conservation approaches

Risk management

Policy

Professional practice

Institutional capacity

Community engagement

5. Build a Realistic Research Schedule

A strong proposal should demonstrate what will happen during each phase of the Fellowship.

For example:

Initial literature and archive review

Comparative analysis

Consultation and professional exchange

Drafting

Validation

Final output preparation

6. Develop a Strong Dissemination Plan

Do not leave dissemination as an afterthought.

Explain:

Who needs your findings

How you will reach them

Which platforms you will use

Whether materials will be open access

How the work can continue beyond the Fellowship

7. Prepare Your Funding Plan

Because ICCROM does not provide a stipend, applicants should consider funding before applying.

Potential routes may include:

Employer support

University research funds

External grants

Professional development funds

National heritage institutions

Personal resources

The absence of ICCROM financial support should be factored into the feasibility of the Fellowship.

Important Details at a Glance

Official programme information:
https://www.iccrom.org/get-involved/fellowships

Conclusion

The ICCROM Fellowship Programme 2027 offers an important research opportunity for senior cultural heritage professionals who want to spend dedicated time developing independent research while engaging with one of the world’s leading international organizations for heritage conservation.

The programme welcomes researchers, teachers and practitioners working across cultural heritage disciplines. Applicants must normally hold at least a Master’s degree in a heritage-related field and have at least 10 years of professional experience.

Research may address any topic connected with cultural heritage conservation and ICCROM’s mission. However, the 2026–2027 cycle gives particular preference to projects addressing improved conservation and risk-management approaches, climate change, urbanization, digital transition, complex crises and innovative technologies, as well as research integrating heritage into climate action, sustainable development, education, health and wellbeing.

Fellowships normally last three to six months and may be undertaken at ICCROM headquarters in Rome, with partial online arrangements possible when justified.

Fellows receive office space, a workstation, internet access and full use of ICCROM’s specialist documentation, library and archives. ICCROM’s conservation library includes holdings in more than 70 languages.

Applicants should nevertheless understand that this is currently a self-funded Fellowship. ICCROM does not provide a stipend, travel allowance or accommodation funding because of present budget constraints. Fellows must arrange and finance their own travel, accommodation and mandatory medical and accident insurance.

The application requires an updated CV, employer approval where applicable and three reference letters from people with direct knowledge of the applicant’s work.

Applications opened on 15 August 2026 and must be submitted by 15 September 2026.

TITLE: Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award 2027: PhD Studentship Proposals Across Cambridge, Norfolk, Colchester, Ipswich and Peterborough

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award (CC-EE) is inviting proposals for PhD studentship projects that use collections held by participating cultural and collecting institutions across the East of England.

The programme offers an opportunity for UK university-based academics and staff working within participating collections to develop collaborative doctoral research projects that connect collections with important contemporary and historical questions through arts and humanities methodologies.

For the 2027/28 academic year, the programme plans to allocate five studentships. Each successful PhD project will involve a partnership between at least two CC-EE collections and a UK university, creating a collaborative research environment in which doctoral students can work across institutional boundaries while gaining access to specialist training, research support and dedicated research funding.

The initiative is particularly interested in projects connected to the themes of belonging, resilience and ecologies, while allowing research to address a broad range of collections-related activities, including curatorial work, interpretation, learning and conservation.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award

Programme: Collections & Communities in the East of England (CC-EE)

Opportunity type: PhD studentship proposal / doctoral research opportunity

Studentships available: 5 for 2027/28

Expected PhD start: October 2027

Geographical focus: East of England

Participating collection locations: Cambridge, Norfolk, Colchester, Ipswich and Peterborough

Required methodology: Arts and humanities methods

Key themes: Belonging, resilience and ecologies

Expression of Interest deadline: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Full Application deadline: 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

Application process: Two-stage selection process

About the Collections & Communities in the East of England Programme

The Collections & Communities in the East of England initiative brings together collections and communities across the region with the aim of using collections-based research to engage with significant questions and challenges.

The programme is based around the idea that collections held by museums, archives, galleries and other cultural institutions can provide valuable material for doctoral research. These collections can support research into history, culture, society, heritage, communities, environments and numerous other areas within the arts and humanities.

The Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award provides a structure through which universities and collection-holding institutions can work together to develop doctoral research projects.

Rather than limiting a PhD project to a single university or collection, each studentship is designed around a collaborative partnership involving two or more CC-EE collections and a UK university.

This structure allows doctoral researchers to engage directly with collections and the professionals who care for them while also benefiting from the academic environment and research expertise of a university.

Five PhD Studentships Available for 2027/28

The CC-EE programme plans to allocate five studentships for the 2027/28 academic year.

The resulting doctoral projects are expected to begin in October 2027.

An important feature of the programme is that the studentships themselves will be externally advertised. The current call is therefore focused on identifying and developing suitable doctoral research projects and supervisory partnerships rather than directly inviting individual prospective PhD students to apply for admission at this stage.

Successful proposals will subsequently form the basis for externally advertised PhD opportunities.

This makes the current call particularly relevant to academics and collection professionals who have a strong research idea and are interested in developing it into a collaborative doctoral project.

Where Can Proposed PhD Projects Be Based?

The programme is specifically interested in PhD projects that make use of collections located across the East of England.

The opportunity identifies collections in:

Cambridge

Norfolk

Colchester

Ipswich

Peterborough

The project must involve collaboration between at least two of the participating CC-EE collecting institutions, with the partnership also including a UK university.

Projects involving more than two collections are particularly welcomed.

This multi-institutional structure means that applicants should consider how collections held by different organisations can complement one another and contribute to a coherent doctoral research question.

What Types of Research Projects Are Eligible?

Proposed doctoral research should be based on collections held by participating CC-EE institutions and should employ arts and humanities methodologies.

The programme does not restrict research to a single discipline or one particular type of collections work. Instead, the call provides considerable scope for applicants to develop projects around different aspects of collection-based research.

Potential areas of research may include:

1. Curatorial Research

Projects can investigate how collections are understood, organised, interpreted and presented to the public.

A doctoral project could explore curatorial practices, the development of collections, changing interpretations of objects or materials, or how institutions make decisions about what and how collections are presented.

2. Interpretation

Research may focus on how collections are interpreted for different audiences.

This could include examining exhibitions, displays, interpretive materials, digital interpretation or other ways institutions communicate the significance of collections.

3. Learning and Education

Projects can also explore the relationship between collections and learning.

Research could investigate how museums, archives and other collecting institutions use their collections to support education, public learning, community engagement or knowledge exchange.

4. Conservation

The programme also identifies conservation as a possible area of collections-related research.

Applicants may therefore develop research that examines the cultural, historical or interpretive dimensions of conservation and the ways in which preservation decisions affect how collections are understood and used.

5. Other Collections-Related Research

The examples provided by the programme are not intended to limit the scope of potential projects.

Research may cover other aspects of collections work provided that the project has a strong connection to participating collections and is grounded in appropriate arts and humanities approaches.

Core Research Themes

The CC-EE programme highlights three broad themes that proposed projects may address:

Belonging

Projects may explore questions around identity, community, place, heritage and people’s relationships with collections and cultural institutions.

Research under this theme could examine how collections represent communities, how people relate to cultural heritage, or how institutions contribute to people’s sense of belonging.

Resilience

Research may also consider resilience at individual, community, institutional, cultural or environmental levels.

Projects could investigate how collections document experiences of change, disruption or adaptation, or how collections institutions themselves contribute to resilient communities and cultural practices.

Ecologies

The programme also welcomes projects connected to ecologies.

This theme can provide opportunities for research into relationships between people, collections, landscapes, environments and wider ecological systems, using suitable arts and humanities approaches.

A proposal may fit within one or more of these themes.

Who Is the Call Looking For?

The current opportunity is primarily aimed at potential PhD supervisors and collaborative project partners, rather than individual students applying directly for a PhD.

There are two principal categories of people who can become involved.

Staff at Participating CC-EE Collections

Staff working at one of the participating CC-EE collections can propose to supervise a doctoral student from the collections-based side of the partnership.

Importantly, the programme states that a proposed collections-based supervisor does not need to hold a PhD in order to supervise a PhD student.

This provides an opportunity for experienced professionals working within collections institutions to contribute their practical, curatorial, conservation, learning or other specialist expertise to doctoral research.

Staff at UK Higher Education Institutions

Academics and other relevant staff based at a UK Higher Education Institution can also participate.

University-based applicants are expected to propose a collaboration involving at least two, or preferably more, participating collecting institutions.

The university and collection partners can therefore jointly develop a doctoral project that combines academic research expertise with direct access to collections and professional knowledge.

Collaboration Is Central to the Studentship

One of the defining features of this opportunity is its collaborative nature.

A successful PhD project will not simply be a conventional university-based doctorate. Instead, it will bring together:

A UK university;

At least two CC-EE collecting institutions;

Academic supervisors;

Collections-based supervisors; and

A doctoral researcher.

This model creates opportunities for research to move between academic and professional environments.

Applicants should therefore consider not only whether they have an interesting research idea, but also whether the proposed project can benefit from collaboration between multiple collections.

The programme particularly encourages projects involving more than the minimum two collecting institutions where this strengthens the research.

Support for Supervisors

The CC-EE team recognises that some prospective supervisors may have limited experience with collaborative doctoral supervision.

As a result, training and support are available for people who are new to supervising PhD students.

This is significant for collections professionals who may have extensive expertise in their specialist field but limited previous experience of doctoral supervision.

The programme provides an opportunity to develop supervisory experience while contributing to a substantial research project.

Support Available to Successful PhD Students

Students selected through the resulting doctoral opportunities will receive access to several forms of support.

Consortium Training

Students will have access to training delivered by the Consortium.

This is intended to complement their doctoral research and provide additional skills and knowledge beyond their individual institutional programme.

UK-Wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme Training

Students will also have access to training provided through the UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme scheme.

This gives successful doctoral researchers an opportunity to participate in broader collaborative doctoral training and engage with researchers and institutions beyond their immediate project.

Dedicated Research Funds

The studentships will also provide students with dedicated research funds.

These resources can support the practical requirements of undertaking doctoral research and enable students to develop their projects using the collections and institutional partnerships on which their research is based.

Two-Stage Selection Process

The CC-EE studentship proposal process consists of two stages.

This means prospective supervisors should not wait until the final full application deadline before engaging with the programme.

Stage One: Expression of Interest

The first stage requires applicants to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI).

The deadline is:

26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Applicants who are interested in proposing a doctoral project are strongly encouraged to contact the CC-EE team before submitting the EOI.

The team can discuss the proposed research, provide guidance on developing the project and, where necessary, help connect applicants with relevant collection institutions.

Stage Two: Full Application

Applicants whose Expressions of Interest are successful will be invited to submit a full application.

The deadline for the full application is:

16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

The full application stage provides an opportunity to develop the proposed project in greater depth following the initial assessment.

Applicants Are Strongly Encouraged to Contact the CC-EE Team

The programme strongly recommends that interested prospective supervisors communicate with the CC-EE team before submitting an Expression of Interest.

This preliminary discussion can be particularly useful when an applicant has a research idea but has not yet established all of the necessary institutional partnerships.

The CC-EE team can:

Discuss the proposed doctoral research idea.

Provide support in developing the proposal.

Help applicants understand the requirements of the programme.

Introduce applicants to relevant colleagues within participating collections.

Support the development of collaborative relationships.

Provide training and support for people who are new to PhD supervision.

Applicants should also discuss their proposed project with relevant staff at the collection institution or institutions on which the PhD would be focused.

The programme’s collaborative structure makes early communication particularly important.

How to Develop a Strong Proposal

Prospective applicants should consider several factors when developing an Expression of Interest.

Establish a Clear Research Question

The project should have a clear and meaningful research question that can be investigated through the collections involved.

The proposed research should go beyond simply describing a collection. It should demonstrate why the collections provide valuable evidence or material for answering the proposed research question.

Demonstrate the Value of the Collections

Applicants should clearly explain how the participating collections contribute to the research.

Where multiple collections are involved, the proposal should demonstrate why bringing them together adds value to the project.

Build Genuine Institutional Collaboration

Because collaboration is a central requirement, applicants should identify suitable collection partners and discuss the project with them early.

A successful project should establish a meaningful relationship between the university and participating collection institutions.

Connect With the Programme Themes

Applicants should consider whether their research can contribute to one or more of the programme’s themes:

Belonging

Resilience

Ecologies

Where relevant, the proposal should explain how the research contributes to these broader areas.

Use Arts and Humanities Methodologies

The programme specifically requires the research to use arts and humanities methods.

Applicants should therefore ensure that the methodology is appropriate to the nature of the research question and collections being investigated.

Expression of Interest Form

Applicants who wish to participate in the first stage must complete the official Expression of Interest form.

The form is available through the Collections & Communities in the East of England website.

The programme also provides information and support for prospective supervisors who are considering developing a proposal.

Expression of Interest deadline: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon.

Town Hall Information Session

The CC-EE programme also provided a Town Hall session for prospective applicants.

The session was scheduled for Thursday, 10 September at 2:00 pm and was intended to provide additional information about the studentship proposal process.

The programme states that the session would be recorded and added to the relevant webpage, allowing interested applicants to access the information afterwards.

Prospective applicants should consult the official programme page for the latest availability of the recording and any updated guidance.

Application and Preparation Timeline

Prospective supervisors can use the following timeline to organise their application:

Before 26 October 2026

Develop an initial doctoral research idea.

Identify relevant collections.

Contact potential collection partners.

Discuss the proposed project with the CC-EE team.

Consider how the research relates to belonging, resilience and/or ecologies.

Ensure that the proposed methodology is grounded in the arts and humanities.

Develop and submit the Expression of Interest.

26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Expression of Interest deadline.

Only proposals progressing through the first stage will move forward to the full application stage.

Between the EOI and Full Application Stages

Successful applicants can further develop their proposals and strengthen the collaboration between the university and collection partners.

This stage can be used to refine:

The research question;

Research methodology;

Collection access;

Supervisory arrangements;

Institutional responsibilities;

Project outcomes; and

The relationship between the participating collections.

16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

Full Application deadline.

Successful full applications will contribute to the selection of doctoral projects for the 2027/28 studentships.

October 2027

The resulting PhD studentships are expected to begin.

Who Should Consider This Opportunity?

This opportunity is particularly relevant to people who already work with, research or have specialist knowledge of collections and who would like to develop that expertise into a collaborative doctoral project.

Potential participants include:

Staff working at participating museums and collecting institutions.

Curators interested in doctoral research.

Collections professionals.

Museum and heritage specialists.

Conservation professionals.

Learning and interpretation specialists.

Researchers working with cultural collections.

Academics based at UK universities.

Researchers in arts and humanities disciplines.

University staff seeking collaborative PhD projects with cultural institutions.

Experienced collections professionals interested in PhD supervision.

Potential supervisors seeking training and support in doctoral supervision.

The current call is not primarily a direct scholarship application for individual students. Instead, it is a call for the development of PhD projects and supervisory collaborations that will subsequently lead to externally advertised studentships.

Geographical Eligibility and Participation

The programme is focused on collections in the East of England, particularly participating institutions located in or associated with:

Cambridge

Norfolk

Colchester

Ipswich

Peterborough

University-based collaborators must be based at a UK Higher Education Institution.

For collections-based supervisors, participation is tied to the participating CC-EE collections.

The opportunity is therefore not presented as a general worldwide individual PhD scholarship open directly to applicants from every country. International researchers who are interested in the eventual PhD studentships should monitor the external advertisements when the individual studentship opportunities are announced, as the current proposal call is aimed at supervisors and institutional partners.

Why Collections-Based Doctoral Research Matters

Collections can provide researchers with access to primary materials that can illuminate questions that cannot always be answered through conventional academic sources alone.

Objects, documents, artworks, photographs, archives and other forms of collected material can offer evidence about communities, societies, historical events, cultural practices, environments and changing relationships between people and places.

A collaborative doctoral model can further strengthen this research by allowing a student to work across multiple collections.

For example, collections held in different locations may contain complementary materials relating to the same historical, cultural or social question. Bringing those resources together can create opportunities for comparative research and new interpretations.

The partnership can also allow doctoral researchers to engage with professionals who have specialist knowledge of the collections, their histories, cataloguing, preservation and public interpretation.

Benefits of the Collaborative Model

The CC-EE approach can provide several dimensions of professional and academic development.

For Universities

Universities can develop new doctoral research partnerships with cultural and collecting institutions and give doctoral students access to collections and specialist professional knowledge.

For Collections Institutions

Museums and other collections can contribute their expertise to doctoral research while developing new research relationships with universities.

For Supervisors

Supervisors can work across academic and collections environments, with training and support available to those who are new to doctoral supervision.

For Doctoral Students

Students selected through the resulting projects can gain:

Access to participating collections.

Collaborative supervisory support.

Consortium training.

UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme training.

Dedicated research funds.

Experience working across academic and cultural institutions.

Opportunities to develop specialist research expertise.

How to Apply

Interested prospective supervisors should begin by discussing their research idea with the CC-EE team and relevant staff at the collection institutions they would like to involve.

The programme strongly recommends this preliminary engagement before the Expression of Interest is submitted.

The Expression of Interest form can then be completed and submitted before the first-stage deadline.

Applicants who successfully progress through the EOI stage will be invited to prepare a full application for consideration at the second stage.

The resulting studentships will subsequently be advertised externally for prospective PhD students.

APPLY HERE

Important Deadlines

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

Expression of Interest: 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon

Full Application: 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon

Expected PhD start date: October 2027

Because the programme operates a two-stage selection process, prospective applicants should begin discussions with the CC-EE team and potential collection partners well before the Expression of Interest deadline.

Official Application Resources

Prospective applicants can access the official Expression of Interest Form 2026 through the Collections & Communities in the East of England programme.

They can also consult information about participating collections and further guidance for potential supervisors through the official programme resources.

Applicants are encouraged to rely on the official CC-EE information for the latest requirements, deadlines and application instructions.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award 2027.

Conclusion

The Collections & Communities in the East of England Collaborative Doctoral Landscape Award 2027 provides a structured opportunity for UK university researchers and professionals working within participating collections to develop collaborative PhD projects based on significant collections across the East of England.

With five studentships planned for 2027/28, the programme seeks research projects that bring together two or more CC-EE collections and a UK university and use arts and humanities methodologies to investigate meaningful questions connected to areas such as belonging, resilience and ecologies.

The programme also offers substantial support for the eventual doctoral researchers, including consortium training, UK-wide Collaborative Doctoral Programme training and dedicated research funds. Importantly, support is also available to supervisors who are new to doctoral supervision.

Anyone interested in proposing a project should begin discussions with the CC-EE team and relevant collections as early as possible. The first key deadline is 26 October 2026 at 12:00 noon for Expressions of Interest, followed by the 16 December 2026 at 12:00 noon deadline for full applications for proposals that successfully pass the first stage.

TITLE: Education Endowment Foundation Research Funding Opportunities: Three Calls for Research Proposals in England’s Education Sector

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) has announced three research opportunities inviting legally constituted organisations and research teams to submit proposals examining important issues in education across England. The calls focus on inclusive mainstream education and Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), technical and vocational teaching for learners aged 16–19, and the continuity of exam boards for GCSE resit learners.

These opportunities are particularly relevant to education research organisations, universities, research consultancies, policy institutes, and research consortia with expertise in qualitative research, education, pedagogy, impact evaluation, process evaluation, and the 16–19 education sector.

The three calls seek to generate evidence that can contribute to future EEF guidance, research commissioning, and education policy. Depending on the opportunity, successful research teams may be expected to conduct school or college visits, classroom observations, quantitative analysis, qualitative research, feasibility work, or evaluation activities.

Below is a detailed overview of all three EEF research opportunities, including their objectives, research questions, methodological expectations, eligibility requirements, and application deadlines.

1. Practice Review on the Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies

The Education Endowment Foundation is commissioning a practice review examining how schools in England are developing inclusion strategies and approaching their use of the Inclusive Mainstream Fund (IMF).

The research comes at a time of significant policy development around creating a more inclusive mainstream education system in England, particularly for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities.

Background and Context

The Government’s 2026 Schools White Paper set out an ambition to create a more inclusive mainstream education system in which schools are appropriately equipped and funded to support children with SEND to achieve and thrive within inclusive mainstream settings.

As part of this broader reform agenda, the Department for Education has committed to a package of measures intended to strengthen inclusion within mainstream schools.

One of these measures is the Inclusive Mainstream Fund.

In addition, the Department for Education expects all state-maintained mainstream schools to develop and publish an inclusion strategy on their websites by 31 December each year.

These developments create an opportunity to understand how schools are responding to the new expectations in practice.

The EEF therefore wants to build an evidence base around how schools are developing their inclusion strategies and making decisions concerning the Inclusive Mainstream Fund.

What the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Will Examine

The practice review aims to develop a clearer picture of current practice across different school settings.

In particular, the research will:

Map current approaches to developing inclusion strategies across school settings.

Examine how schools are approaching spending through the Inclusive Mainstream Fund.

Explore differences in practice between schools and settings.

Investigate reported changes in behaviours and beliefs associated with the introduction of the new policies.

Explore changes in decision-making that may be connected to the new inclusion policies.

Identify emerging approaches that may be relevant to future EEF guidance and research.

The research is therefore not simply focused on whether schools have developed inclusion strategies. It is also concerned with understanding the processes behind those strategies and how schools are making decisions about resources and inclusion.

How the Research Findings Will Be Used

The findings from this research are expected to have several applications within education policy, research and practice.

The evidence may inform future development of EEF guidance relating to inclusion, including resources such as the EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching.

The findings may also contribute to:

Future EEF research activity.

The development of additional evidence-based resources.

Understanding of emerging practices in mainstream schools.

Advice provided to policymakers.

Future research priorities concerning inclusive education and SEND.

The main output from the project will be a written research report.

The report is expected to be published by the end of March 2027.

Research Approach

The EEF welcomes proposals capable of addressing both the primary and secondary research questions.

Applicants are encouraged to consider a variety of research methods and may propose innovative approaches where appropriate.

A mixed-methods approach may be suitable for the project, depending on the proposed research questions and methodology.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate clearly how their proposed methodology will allow them to develop a meaningful understanding of:

How schools are developing inclusion strategies.

How schools are approaching Inclusive Mainstream Fund spending.

Whether behaviours and beliefs are changing.

How decision-making may be changing in response to the policies.

How practices vary between different school settings.

Who Can Apply for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Practice Review?

The opportunity is primarily relevant to organisations and research teams with expertise in education research, particularly research involving schools, inclusion, SEND, policy implementation, and qualitative or mixed-methods research.

Potential applicants may include:

Universities and higher education institutions.

Education research organisations.

Research consultancies.

Policy research organisations.

Specialist education research teams.

Consortia bringing together complementary research expertise.

Applicants should carefully review the complete EEF invitation to tender and selection criteria before submitting a proposal.

Deadline for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Opportunity

Completed applications must be submitted through the designated Form Assembly application form by: 12pm on Monday, 19 October 2026.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to review the tender documentation, prepare their methodology and supporting information, and complete the online submission before the deadline.

APPLY HERE

2. Practice Review on 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching

The second EEF research opportunity focuses on teaching practices within technical and vocational education for learners aged 16–19.

The research will investigate current teaching approaches across technical and vocational subject areas and examine how these practices relate to the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework (ITTECF) used in schools.

The project is intended to provide a clearer understanding of what teaching currently looks like in technical and vocational settings.

Project Summary

The practice review will involve detailed observations of teaching practice across a selection of technical and vocational subject areas in the 16–19 sector.

Researchers will examine teaching in classrooms and workshops to build a picture of current practice.

The research is expected to contribute to understanding:

The teaching approaches currently being used.

How frequently particular teaching practices are observed.

Whether practices identified in the schools ITTECF are also used in technical and vocational education.

Whether technical and vocational teachers use other teaching approaches that are not represented in the ITTECF.

Whether there are common patterns among colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas.

The findings may subsequently inform future EEF research commissioning and guidance for the technical and vocational education sector.

Main Research Aims

The project has several interconnected aims.

1. Understand Current Teaching Practice

The research will examine teaching practices currently being used in technical and vocational education settings.

This is intended to provide a practical snapshot of teaching across relevant 16–19 settings.

2. Examine Use of ITTECF Teaching Practices

Researchers will investigate whether teaching practices identified within the schools Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework are being used in technical and vocational education.

The research will also consider whether some of these practices are more prevalent than others.

3. Identify Additional Teaching Practices

The project will look beyond the practices contained in the ITTECF.

Researchers will identify whether there are other teaching practices commonly observed in technical and vocational education that are not included within the ITTECF framework.

4. Explore High-Performing Colleges

The research will also examine whether colleges performing particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas demonstrate common approaches to teaching.

This could include investigating whether successful colleges use particular combinations or amounts of the identified teaching practices.

Main Research Question

The central research question is:

Do vocational and technical teachers use the teaching practices identified from the schools ITTECF in their day-to-day teaching?

This question will provide the foundation for the practice review.

Secondary Research Questions

The research will also investigate several related questions, including:

Are some of the teaching practices more prevalent than others?

Are other teaching practices observed that are not included in the ITTECF?

Do colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas use different combinations of the teaching practices?

Do these high-performing colleges use different amounts of particular teaching practices?

Answering these questions will help the EEF understand whether teaching approaches used in technical and vocational education closely resemble those used in schools or whether there are distinctive practices within the 16–19 sector.

Methodological Expectations

The project will involve primary research intended to provide a snapshot of current teaching practice in vocational and technical education for learners aged 16–19.

The EEF is open to proposals using different research methodologies.

Applicants are encouraged to propose approaches that can effectively answer the primary and secondary research questions.

Innovative research approaches are also welcomed.

However, college visits and observations are expected to be a key component of the research plan.

This means applicants should carefully consider how their proposed methodology will allow researchers to observe teaching directly within technical and vocational settings.

Feasibility Phase

Proposals are expected to include a short feasibility phase.

This feasibility phase should involve a small number of colleges and will help researchers test:

The suitability of the subject areas identified for the research.

The proposed list of classroom teaching practices.

The practicality of the observation approach.

Whether the proposed research design can generate useful data.

Including a feasibility phase will allow the research team to refine its approach before implementing the broader practice review.

Who Should Apply?

The EEF is seeking research teams with:

Experience conducting qualitative research in education.

A strong understanding of the 16–19 education sector.

Knowledge of pedagogy in England.

Experience designing and implementing education research.

The ability to conduct research within colleges and technical or vocational education settings.

Applications can be submitted by either a single research team or a consortium.

Consortia may be particularly appropriate where different organisations can contribute complementary expertise.

However, a consortium must be able to demonstrate that its members can work effectively together and maintain the quality and efficiency of the research project.

Organisations Eligible to Apply

This opportunity is open to legally constituted organisations rather than individuals.

Importantly, applicants do not have to be members of the EEF’s existing panel of evaluators.

The organisation also does not necessarily have to be based in England.

International organisations may apply, provided they can demonstrate that:

Their research outputs will be relevant to the English education system.

The proposed research team has sufficient understanding of the English 16–19 education context.

The proposal represents value for money.

The organisation has the appropriate legal constitution to undertake the work.

This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to eligible education research organisations outside England, provided they can demonstrate appropriate knowledge and contextual expertise.

Deadline for the 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching Research Opportunity

Interested applicants must submit their full research proposals by: 5pm on Friday, 16 October 2026.

Questions relating to the tender and research proposals should be directed to the EEF contact provided in the original tender documentation.

Research proposals should be sent to: post-16@eefoundation.org.uk

3. 16–19 Setting Choices: GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity

The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resits among learners aged 16–19 in England.

The EEF is seeking research proposals to investigate whether maintaining the same exam board between a learner’s original GCSE sitting and their subsequent GCSE resit is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes.

This research forms part of the EEF’s Setting Choices programme.

Overview of the GCSE Resit Research

The project will investigate whether sitting a GCSE resit with the same examination board used for the learner’s initial GCSE sitting affects outcomes in English and mathematics.

The research will compare continuity with changing exam boards.

The central issue is whether maintaining the same examination board provides any measurable difference in outcomes for learners undertaking GCSE resits between the ages of 16 and 19.

Background to the Research

The research takes place against a wider concern about attainment differences during the 16–19 phase of education.

According to the background information provided by the EEF, the socio-economic attainment gap is particularly significant during the 16–19 phase.

The Education Policy Institute’s 2026 annual report reported that the 16–19 disadvantage gap had remained broadly stable at approximately 3.3–3.4 grades, reaching 3.4 grades in 2025.

The EEF describes the 16–19 phase as an important opportunity to improve attainment and strengthen young people’s future life chances.

Within this broader context, the EEF is interested in examining factors that could potentially influence the success of GCSE resit learners.

Why Exam Board Continuity Is Being Studied

The choice of examination board may influence aspects of a learner’s resit experience.

The EEF’s research background notes that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools for English, mathematics, or both.

Other colleges do not maintain this alignment.

The rationale for continuity is that learners may benefit from familiarity with the examination structure and expectations associated with the same exam board.

At the same time, changing examination boards could potentially offer a learner a different approach.

The purpose of the proposed research is not to assume that one approach is beneficial, but to generate evidence about whether continuity is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes.

Existing Evidence and Rationale

The EEF’s background information references the Education Policy Institute’s Drivers of Success report, which identified examination board choice and continuity with a learner’s original examination board as potentially relevant to GCSE resit success.

The EEF has also surveyed its college network, consisting of approximately 90 colleges.

The survey found that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools, while others do not use such alignment.

This variation in practice provides an opportunity to investigate the issue through research.

Main Research Question

The central research question is:

Does sitting a GCSE resit with the same exam board as the initial sitting, compared with using a different exam board, affect English and mathematics outcomes for 16–19 resit learners?

The research is expected to provide evidence capable of assessing the relationship between examination board continuity and learner outcomes.

Expected Research Design

The EEF expects the research to include several important components.

1. Causal Impact Evaluation

The project is expected to include a causal impact evaluation using a quasi-experimental design.

This component is intended to investigate whether differences in exam board continuity are associated with differences in learner outcomes while addressing relevant methodological challenges.

2. Implementation and Process Evaluation

A light-touch Implementation and Process Evaluation is also expected.

This component can help researchers understand how exam board continuity operates in practice and provide context for interpreting the impact evaluation findings.

3. Subgroup Analysis

The research is also expected to include subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners.

This will allow researchers to investigate whether the relationship between exam board continuity and outcomes differs for learners experiencing disadvantage.

Who Should Apply?

The EEF is inviting research teams with experience conducting:

Impact evaluations.

Process evaluations.

Education research.

Research within the 16–19 sector.

Quasi-experimental research.

Quantitative analysis of learner outcomes.

The EEF is interested in expressions of interest from individual research teams as well as consortia with complementary expertise.

Consortia should demonstrate that their members can work effectively together to ensure the quality and efficiency of the research.

Organisational Eligibility

Applications are accepted from legally constituted organisations rather than individuals.

Researchers do not need to be members of the EEF’s panel of evaluators.

Organisations based outside England are also eligible to apply.

However, international organisations must demonstrate that their teams possess the knowledge and expertise necessary to undertake research relevant to the English education system and complete the proposed work effectively.

Conclusion

The Education Endowment Foundation’s three new research opportunities provide organisations with the opportunity to contribute evidence to important questions affecting education in England.

The first opportunity focuses on inclusive mainstream education, examining how schools are developing inclusion strategies and approaching the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. The research is intended to strengthen understanding of current practice and inform future guidance, research and policy.

The second opportunity examines technical and vocational teaching among learners aged 16–19. Researchers will observe teaching practice across selected subject areas and investigate how teaching approaches in technical and vocational settings compare with practices identified in the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework.

The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resit exam board continuity, investigating whether maintaining the same examination board between a learner’s initial GCSE sitting and their resit affects English and mathematics outcomes. The project is expected to use a quasi-experimental impact evaluation alongside a light-touch implementation and process evaluation and subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners.

TITLE: Seasonal dissolved oxygen gas exchange in the California Current Upwelling System

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ren, A.S., Rudnick, D.L., & Nicholson, D.P. (2025). Seasonal dissolved oxygen gas exchange in the California Current Upwelling System. Progress In Oceanography, 103473. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pocean.2025.103473

Image provide by Alice Ren.

Eastern boundary current systems are known for seasonal upwelling that brings water from below the mixed layer to the surface. The process deoxygenates the water column by bringing lower-dissolved oxygen water closer to the surface and oxygenates the water column by driving primary productivity due to the injection of nutrients from deep waters. Here, an observational dataset of 5 years of dissolved oxygen, temperature, and salinity measured to 500 m and from the coast to around 400 km offshore is used to study the seasonal evolution of air-sea exchange of oxygen in an upwelling region. A narrow band of coastal oxygen undersaturation drives dissolved oxygen uptake by the ocean in spring and summer, while in winter dissolved oxygen uptake predominates due to more widespread but less intense oxygen undersaturation. Oxygen outgassing occurs offshore of the nearshore uptake band in spring and summer, driven by warming and primary productivity, such that the cumulative net oxygen gas exchange integrated seaward from shore reaches zero once around one hundred kilometers from the coast. Ventilation of the upper ocean is observed as a result of shoaling isopycnals in the upwelling season. Competing factors causing uptake and outgassing and the seaward extent of the domain determine whether an upwelling zone is a net source or sink of oxygen gas.
