What Is Agenda 2063?

Agenda 2063 is Africa’s long-term development framework and vision for building “The Africa We Want.” It provides a continental framework for transforming Africa economically, socially and politically while promoting inclusive development, sustainable growth, integration and stronger partnerships.

However, understanding Agenda 2063 as a policy or development framework is only one part of the challenge. Its implementation also depends on the actions of individuals and institutions operating in different environments.

This is the central idea behind Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces.

The programme recognizes that important decisions are made every day in many different environments, including:

Governments and public institutions

Businesses and private-sector organizations

Universities and research institutions

Schools and educational organizations

Communities and civil society

Development organizations

Families

Professional networks

Entrepreneurship and innovation spaces

Youth organizations

Other environments where people make decisions and create value

These environments are described as “Power Spaces.”

The programme encourages participants to identify the Power Spaces available to them and consider how they can deliberately use those spaces to contribute to Africa’s long-term transformation.

What Is Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3?

Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3 is a seven-week online traineeship and volunteer learning experience designed to move participants beyond simply knowing about Agenda 2063.

The programme seeks to help participants answer an important question:

How can I personally contribute to achieving The Africa We Want through the spaces in which I have influence?

Rather than treating leadership as something limited to senior government officials, executives or institutional leaders, the programme takes a broader approach.

It recognizes that individuals can create value and influence outcomes from wherever they operate.

A student can influence a university or student organization. An entrepreneur can influence a business ecosystem. A teacher can influence learners and communities. A researcher can influence policy and knowledge. A community leader can influence local development. A communications professional can influence public awareness and engagement.

The programme therefore focuses on developing individual agency and helping participants recognize themselves as potential contributors to Agenda 2063.

Main Objective of the Programme

The central objective is to help participants progress from understanding Agenda 2063 to recognizing themselves as agents capable of contributing to its implementation.

The seven-week journey provides a structured framework through which participants examine:

The value they currently create.

The future they want to help create.

The changes required to move from the present toward that future.

The leadership values required to make meaningful decisions.

The routines needed to turn intentions into action.

The future they want to experience as a result of their efforts.

The lessons they gain and the changes they need to make going forward.

This makes the programme particularly relevant to people interested in leadership, development practice, public policy, entrepreneurship, education, community development and African transformation.

The Seven Leadership Tools Participants Will Develop

One of the most important features of Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3 is its seven-tool leadership architecture.

Throughout the seven-week journey, participants progressively work with seven leadership tools.

1. Contribution Statement – What Value Do I Create?

The first tool encourages participants to identify their personal contribution to Africa’s transformation.

Participants examine their current Power Space and consider the value they create within it.

This may involve asking questions such as:

What am I currently contributing?

Who benefits from my contribution?

What capabilities do I possess?

What problems am I helping to solve?

Where do I have influence?

How does my work or activity connect with Africa’s broader development needs?

The Contribution Statement helps participants understand where they currently fit within the broader transformation agenda.

2. Moonshot – What Future Am I Committed to Creating?

The second tool focuses on developing a sufficiently ambitious vision for the future.

The concept of a “Moonshot” encourages participants to think beyond incremental improvements and identify a consequential future they are committed to helping create.

Participants consider:

What future do I want to see?

What would meaningful transformation look like?

What ambitious outcome would challenge current assumptions?

What future is worth working toward despite present obstacles?

The exercise is intended to help participants challenge the limitations imposed by present circumstances.

3. Delivery – What Must Change?

Having identified a desired future, participants then examine what needs to change to move toward it.

The Delivery tool focuses on the gap between the current situation and the desired outcome.

Participants may consider:

What is preventing progress?

Which systems, behaviours or practices need to change?

What obstacles must be addressed?

Which changes are most critical?

What actions can contribute to the desired transformation?

This stage helps translate vision into a practical understanding of what needs to happen.

4. Leadership Values – Who Must I Be?

The fourth tool focuses on the personal qualities and values required to pursue meaningful change.

Participants reflect on the type of leader they need to become in order to make consequential decisions and remain committed to their goals.

This can involve examining:

Personal values

Integrity

Responsibility

Courage

Accountability

Resilience

Collaboration

Commitment

Respect for others

Willingness to learn and adapt

The emphasis is not simply on what participants want to achieve but also on who they need to be throughout the journey.

5. Leadership Routines – What Must I Repeatedly Do?

A vision only becomes meaningful when it is translated into consistent action.

The Leadership Routines tool helps participants identify repeated behaviours and practices that can gradually produce results.

Participants consider:

What actions must I perform consistently?

Which habits will support my goals?

What behaviours need to become routine?

How can I turn intention into practice?

What repeated actions can accumulate into meaningful results?

This stage emphasizes the importance of sustained action rather than one-time motivation.

6. Letter from the Future – What Does Life Look Like Because I Succeeded?

The sixth tool asks participants to imagine their desired future as though they have already achieved it.

Through a Letter from the Future, participants explore what life looks like because their efforts succeeded.

This exercise can help participants:

Visualize the impact of their contribution.

Understand the consequences of achieving their goals.

Reconsider current choices.

Identify actions that are consistent with their desired future.

Strengthen their connection to their long-term objectives.

The exercise links future aspirations with present-day decision-making.

7. Future Review – What Have I Learned and What Should I Now Revise?

The final tool focuses on reflection, learning and continuous improvement.

Participants are introduced to the practice of:

Return → Review → Revise → Recommit

This process encourages participants to revisit their leadership plans and assess whether their circumstances, experiences and capabilities have changed.

Instead of treating the seven-week programme as an endpoint, participants are encouraged to continue applying the tools after the formal traineeship ends.

What Will Online Volunteers Do?

Online Volunteers will play a supporting role throughout the seven-week traineeship.

Their responsibilities will include the following.

Study the Learning Materials

Volunteers will become familiar with the Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces learning materials, including the Reader and associated resources.

This requires participants to:

Read the provided materials.

Understand the major concepts.

Engage critically with the learning content.

Prepare to support participant learning.

Develop familiarity with the seven leadership tools.

Volunteers are not expected to arrive as experts. The assignment specifically emphasizes curiosity and disciplined engagement with the materials.

Support Participant Engagement

Volunteers will help support participants throughout the seven-week learning journey.

This involves understanding the weekly concepts, questions and exercises and helping participants remain engaged with the programme.

The emphasis is on supporting learning rather than simply delivering course content.

Participate in Small-Group Learning Conversations

Where assigned, volunteers will participate in small-group conversations.

These discussions are intended to encourage participants to connect the leadership tools to their own Power Spaces.

Volunteers should therefore be capable of:

Listening actively.

Encouraging participation.

Asking constructive questions.

Helping participants connect concepts to their own experiences.

Providing concise and useful feedback.

Supporting a collaborative learning environment.

Contribute to the End-of-Cohort Review

Volunteers will also participate in a structured review at the end of the cohort.

They will help identify:

What worked well.

What challenges participants experienced.

What could be improved.

Which learning approaches were effective.

How future cohorts could be strengthened.

How the materials and participant experience could be improved.

This means volunteers can contribute not only to the current cohort but also to the continued development of the programme.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity welcomes applications from people with an interest in Africa’s transformation and related areas.

The requirements specifically mention applicants from a variety of professional and educational backgrounds, including:

Professionals

Development practitioners

Researchers

Entrepreneurs

Educators

Students

Community leaders

Applicants may come from different sectors and Power Spaces.

The programme is therefore not restricted to one profession or academic discipline.

Required Experience and Skills

Candidates should be able to demonstrate a strong interest in one or more areas connected to Agenda 2063 and African development.

Relevant areas include:

Agenda 2063

African development

Leadership

Development practice

Public policy

Business

Education

Community development

Related fields

Applicants should also demonstrate the following capabilities.

Critical Reading and Learning

Candidates should be comfortable reading learning materials and engaging with them critically.

The programme requires volunteers to understand concepts sufficiently to support discussions and participant engagement.

Strong Written Communication

Good written communication is important because volunteers may need to provide feedback, participate in discussions and communicate ideas clearly.

Strong Interpersonal Communication

The role involves interaction with other participants, particularly through small-group learning conversations.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating respectfully and constructively with people from different backgrounds.

Constructive Feedback

Volunteers should be able to provide feedback that is:

Concise

Clear

Constructive

Relevant

Helpful to the learning process

Commitment

Applicants must be able to commit to the assignment throughout the seven-week Cohort 3 period.

The expected workload is 11–15 hours per week, making it important for applicants to assess their availability before applying.

Language Requirement

The listed language requirement is:

English – Fluent, desirable.

Applicants should therefore be able to comfortably understand and engage with English-language learning materials and participate effectively in written and interpersonal communication.

Programme Modality and Time Commitment

The assignment is conducted entirely online.

This makes it suitable for participants who can contribute remotely without needing to relocate to Ethiopia or another physical programme location.

The expected commitment is:

11–15 hours per week for seven weeks.

Applicants should ensure they have sufficient time to:

Study the learning materials.

Participate in learning conversations.

Support participant engagement.

Complete assigned activities.

Contribute to the end-of-cohort review.

What Makes This Opportunity Different?

One of the distinctive features of the programme is that it does not simply present Agenda 2063 as something participants should know.

Instead, it asks participants to consider how they can personally contribute to its implementation.

This approach is important because continental transformation depends not only on governments and large institutions but also on the decisions and actions taken in everyday environments.

The programme’s Power Spaces approach recognizes that individuals have different forms of influence.

A participant does not necessarily need to occupy a senior position to contribute to development.

Their influence could come through:

Their profession

Their organization

Their business

Their research

Their classroom

Their community

Their professional network

Their family

Their youth or civic activities

Their educational institution

This makes the programme relevant to participants at different stages of their careers and lives.

Leadership Portfolio and Letter from the Future

Participants are expected to retain important outputs from the learning journey, including their Leadership Portfolio and Letter from the Future.

These materials can serve as practical references after the seven-week programme.

Rather than treating leadership development as a one-time training activity, the programme encourages participants to revisit their materials periodically as their circumstances, experience, capabilities and Power Spaces evolve.

This creates an opportunity for continuous reflection and development.

Contribution to Future Cohorts

Another important aspect of Cohort 3 is its contribution to the continued improvement of the programme.

Participants and volunteers will help test and improve:

Learning materials

Facilitation approaches

Participant engagement methods

Overall learning experience

Approaches for making the leadership practice accessible to larger numbers of people

Consequently, participation can contribute to the development of future iterations of Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces.

Connection to Sustainable Development Goal 17

The assignment is linked to Sustainable Development Goal 17: Partnerships for the Goals.

SDG 17 emphasizes the importance of partnerships in achieving sustainable development.

The connection is particularly relevant because Agenda 2063 implementation requires collaboration among governments, businesses, communities, civil society, educational institutions, development organizations and individuals.

By encouraging people to identify their Power Spaces and collaborate across different environments, the programme reinforces the importance of partnerships in achieving long-term development objectives.

Is This a Paid Opportunity?

The provided description identifies this as an online volunteer assignment.

It specifically explains that volunteerism involves activities undertaken freely for the public good where monetary reward is not the principal motivating factor.

Therefore, applicants should not approach this as a paid employment opportunity.

The programme is better suited to individuals interested in learning, leadership development, contribution to African development, collaboration and volunteer experience.

Inclusivity and Equal Opportunity

The programme states that United Nations Volunteers is an equal opportunity programme that welcomes qualified applicants.

It is committed to diversity and respect for human rights and individual dignity.

The inclusivity statement specifies that discrimination should not occur on the basis of characteristics including:

Race

Sex

Gender identity

Religion

Nationality

Ethnic origin

Sexual orientation

Disability

Pregnancy

Age

Language

Social origin

Other status

The programme therefore emphasizes an inclusive environment in which qualified individuals from diverse backgrounds can participate.

Who Is the Ideal Candidate?

The ideal candidate is someone who is genuinely interested in contributing to Africa’s long-term development and is willing to learn rather than simply demonstrate existing expertise.

A strong applicant could be someone who:

Has an interest in Agenda 2063 and African development.

Is passionate about leadership and positive change.

Can critically read and understand learning materials.

Communicates clearly in English.

Works effectively with other people.

Can provide constructive feedback.

Is comfortable participating in online learning.

Can dedicate 11–15 hours every week for seven weeks.

Is open to learning from people with different experiences.

Can connect abstract ideas with real-world contexts.

Is willing to reflect on their own contribution and leadership.

Wants to continue applying the programme’s tools beyond the formal traineeship.

Benefits of Participating

Although the opportunity is a volunteer assignment rather than a paid position, participants can gain several forms of professional and personal value.

Leadership Development

The seven-tool framework provides participants with a structured approach to examining their contribution, aspirations, values, routines and future goals.

Understanding of Agenda 2063

Participants gain an opportunity to engage directly with Agenda 2063 and explore its relevance to individual action and African transformation.

Practical Reflection

The programme goes beyond theoretical learning by encouraging participants to apply the concepts to their own Power Spaces.

Collaboration

Small-group learning conversations provide opportunities to engage with people from different professional, educational and community backgrounds.

Communication Skills

Supporting discussions and providing constructive feedback can strengthen written and interpersonal communication.

Development Perspective

The programme can help participants connect individual leadership with broader development objectives.

International Volunteer Experience

Participation in an online UN-linked volunteer assignment can provide experience of contributing to an international development-oriented initiative.

How to Prepare for the Opportunity

Applicants interested in this programme should carefully consider how their existing experience connects with the assignment.

Before applying, it can be useful to reflect on the following questions:

What does Agenda 2063 mean to me?

What aspect of African development interests me most?

What Power Space do I currently operate in?

What value do I create in that space?

What development challenge would I like to help address?

What leadership qualities do I already demonstrate?

What leadership qualities do I need to strengthen?

Can I dedicate 11–15 hours per week for seven weeks?

Can I effectively communicate and collaborate with people online?

How could my professional, academic, entrepreneurial or community experience contribute to the programme?

Applicants should also ensure that their application clearly demonstrates their motivation, relevant interests, communication abilities and commitment.

Important Scam Warning

Applicants should be particularly careful about fraudulent individuals or websites claiming to represent the United Nations.

The opportunity information explicitly warns that the United Nations does not charge application, processing, training, interviewing, testing or recruitment fees.

If anyone requests money in exchange for applying, being shortlisted, receiving training or securing recruitment, applicants should disregard the request.

Applicants should also exercise caution when submitting personal information online because logos, names, addresses and other organizational materials can be copied and reproduced by scammers.

Always verify that an application is being submitted through the legitimate United Nations or UN Volunteers recruitment platform.

Application Deadline

No application deadline is specified in the opportunity information provided.

Applicants should therefore check the official listing for the current application status and any deadline or closing date before submitting an application.

The provided listing also shows an invalid/unspecified expected start date, so applicants should verify the latest programme schedule through the official recruitment platform.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3 provides an opportunity to engage with Africa’s long-term development vision from a personal and practical leadership perspective.

Its central message is that achieving The Africa We Want is not solely the responsibility of governments or major institutions. Transformation can also emerge from the many Power Spaces in which individuals learn, work, build businesses, conduct research, educate others, participate in communities and make decisions.

Over seven weeks, participants will explore seven practical leadership tools covering contribution, vision, delivery, values, routines, future thinking and continuous review. They will also support other learners, participate in group conversations and contribute feedback that can improve future cohorts.

For professionals, students, researchers, entrepreneurs, educators, practitioners and community leaders interested in Africa’s development, this online volunteer assignment can provide a structured opportunity to deepen their understanding of Agenda 2063 while reflecting on how their own work and influence can contribute to the continent’s transformation.

With a commitment of 11–15 hours per week for seven weeks, applicants should ensure that they have sufficient time and motivation to participate fully. Most importantly, successful participation requires more than familiarity with development terminology. It requires curiosity, critical thinking, communication, collaboration and a genuine willingness to connect ideas with action.

The programme ultimately encourages participants to move from asking “What is Agenda 2063?” toward a more personal and consequential question: “What can I contribute to achieving The Africa We Want through the Power Spaces available to me?”

TITLE: Patrick Ledwith ’19, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Patrick Ledwith
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2025-2028
Email: pled@mit.edu
Phone: (267) 421-2726
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, TBA
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Condensed Matter Theory

Research Interests

Patrick is a theoretical physicist who studies quantum many body systems. He is particularly interested in understanding and predicting collective properties that emerge from strongly interacting electrons. He has recently focused on moiré materials, like twisted bilayer graphene at the “magic angle” of 1.1 degrees. These materials often host strongly interacting topological bands. The topology of the band ensures that electrons cannot be localized, which makes exotic correlated motion one of the best ways for electrons to minimize their interaction energy. This correlated motion, in turn, can produce “fractionalized” phases of matter at the macroscale in which the fundamental excitations have electric charge smaller than that of the constituent electrons.

Patrick is also interested in bridging the theoretical gap between strongly correlated electrons in (1) the topological “quantum Hall” setting and (2) the “Mott” setting that is emblematic of high temperature superconductivity and traditionally not topological. He has begun developing new analytical tools for this purpose, with applications to twisted bilayer graphene.

Biographical Sketch

Patrick grew up in North Wales, Pennsylvania in the Philadelphia area. He went to MIT for his undergraduate degree in Physics and Mathematics in 2019. While at MIT he worked with Leonid Levitov on electron hydrodynamics, discovering and elucidating extra-long-lived collective excitations in two dimensional electron gases. He then went to Harvard for his PhD, advised by Asvhin Vishwanath. During his PhD he worked on a variety of topics within moiré materials, including analytical methods for predicting and realizing fractional Chern insulating states.

Selected Publications

P. Ledwith, J. Dong, A. Vishwanath, and E. Khalaf. “Nonlocal Moments and Mott Semimetal in the Chern Bands of Twisted Bilayer Graphene,” Physical Review X, vol. 15, no. 2, p. 021 087, June 2025.

P. Ledwith, A. Vishwanath, and D. E. Parker, “Vortexability: A unifying criterion for ideal fractional Chern insulators,” Physical Review B, vol. 108, no. 20, p. 205 144, Nov. 2023.

T. Devakul, P. Ledwith, L.-Q. Xia, A. Uri, S. C. de la Barrera, P. Jarillo-Herrero, and L. Fu, “Magic-angle helical trilayer graphene,” Science Advances, vol. 9, no. 36, eadi6063, Sep. 2023.

P. Ledwith, G. Tarnopolsky, E. Khalaf, and A. Vishwanath, “Fractional Chern insulator states in twisted bilayer graphene: An analytical approach,” Physical Review Research, vol. 2, no. 2, p. 023 237, May 2020.

P. Ledwith, H. Guo, and L. Levitov, “The hierarchy of excitation lifetimes in two-dimensional Fermi gases,” Annals of Physics, vol. 411, p. 167 913, Dec. 2019, issn: 0003-4916.

TITLE: Call for Expression of Interest – Understanding African universities’ capacity for climate adaptation research: Co-creating and implementing a climate-focused organizational capacity assessment tool (CO-CAT)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
This call for expression of interest seeks to invite African universities and research institutions interested in joining a 24-month initiative to co-create and implement a climate adaptation research-focused institutional capacity assessment tool (Co-CAT). Selected institutions will play an active role in developing, testing, applying, and refining the tool. This will contribute to strengthening the role of African research institutions in driving climate-resilient research and development. The expression of interest should indicate relevant information on institutional strengths, research focus areas, infrastructure, partnerships, and commitment to climate adaptation efforts. For further information, please contact Mrs Ruth Dickson Nyarko and copy Dr Agyemang Darko via aodarko@aau.org and Dr Lorraine Dongo via lorraine.dongo@acu.ac.uk Further details can be accessed below. [The Call For Expression of Interest can also be downloaded HERE ]

Introduction

The “Understanding African Universities’ Capacity for Climate Adaptation Research” project is a 24-month project that seeks to enhance institutional capacity for climate adaptation research in Africa. The project is being funded by the International Development Research Centre (IDRC) and the UK Foreign Commonwealth Development Office (FCDO) and implemented by the Association of African Universities (AAU), the Association of Commonwealth Universities (ACU) and the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM). This project is intended to work with 20 universities across Africa to co-create and implement a climate change adaptation research-focused organizational capacity assessment tool (CO-CAT) through a living lab-based approach. This approach will involve climate adaptation researchers from multiple disciplinary backgrounds, research professional service staff, senior university managers, and non-academic stakeholders such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs), policy makers, government bodies and community members who engage with climate adaptation research.

Through this living lab approach, the project aims to close the communication and collaboration divide among the diverse stakeholders tasked with tackling, or are affected by, the challenges encountered in relation to climate adaptation research in universities and research institutions. By employing the living lab methodology, the project will facilitate the rapid identification of tangible solutions and provide direction on how to implement these solutions.

We are now calling on interested African universities and research institutions that would like to participate in this project.

Eligibility Criteria

Research institutions and universities must meet the following criteria:

a. Institutions must be based in one of the following countries: Algeria, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin, Togo, Central African Republic, RDC, Gabon, Burundi, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda, Namibia, Zambia, and Botswana.

b. Institutional Commitment

Participating universities must demonstrate a strong institutional commitment to sustainability and climate action through established strategies and policies. They should express their active involvement in global or continental initiatives for climate action with clear leadership support and willingness to engage in the proposed project.

c. Research Alignment

Institutions should have ongoing research activities that align with national or continental climate adaptation goals. This includes having dedicated research centres, programs, or experts in climate or environmental science, environmental sustainability, or related fields, with the capacity to contribute to evidence-based policymaking.

d. Partnerships and Collaboration

A strong record of collaboration is essential. Universities and research institutions must have existing partnerships with international academic institutions, NGOs, governments, the private sector, or local communities. Active involvement in multi-stakeholder initiatives and the ability to engage in collaborative knowledge exchange will be highly valued.

e. Infrastructure and Technology

Participating institutions should possess reliable ICT infrastructure that supports online collaboration and data sharing.

f. Credibility and Ethics

Universities must show a credible track record in publishing climate-related research in reputable journals and demonstrate access to internal or external funding for climate research. Ethical research practices and a commitment to transparency and integrity are non-negotiable.

2. Scope of Engagement

The project will employ the methods of engagement outlined below:

a. The selected institutions will be engaged through a series of iterative and collaborative activities involving a diverse group of stakeholders. This will include workshops, focus groups, expert consultations, key informant interviews, and E-surveys, generating evidence to understand the current context.

b. The selected institutions will participate in the joint development of a Climate Adaptation Research-centered Organizational Capacity Assessment Tool (CO-CAT). This tool will be deployed by the selected universities and research institutions, which will also take part in analyzing the findings and initiating pilot projects to tackle the identified needs for capacity building. The process will build on the evidence gathered to ensure that challenges are effectively managed rather than exacerbated.

c) The selected universities and other stakeholders will contribute not only to the refinement and finalization of the CO-CAT but also to the production of user guidelines, and development of case studies of capacity strengthening responses based on tool outcomes.

3. Benefits

This project presents a variety of benefits:

a. An opportunity to engage with a broader community of more than 300 climate adaptation research contributors and organizations across Africa associated with the Climate Change Adaptation Research (CLARE) project across Africa.

b. An opportunity to engage diverse stakeholders on climate change adaptation research

c. Through this project, it is anticipated that institutions will be responsible for common issues identification and proffering of solutions.

d. A seed grant of USD 5,000 will be awarded to selected institutions involved to pilot and contributing to refining the Co-CAT tool.

e. Other benefits include the opportunity for learning activities, training, workshops and exposure to virtual living lab environments and toolkits.

4. Project duration

The implementation phase of the project commenced in January 2025 and is anticipated to conclude in December 2026.

5. Preparation, Submission and Processing of applications

Applicants are expected to respond to the call by filling out this form to express their interest: https://forms.office.com/r/rn7brdKS7n

6. Submission of Applications

The deadline for submissions is Friday, 13th June 2025. Applications received after the deadline will not be considered.

All applications will be received and processed in confidentiality with the acknowledgment of intellectual property rights of the applicants.

All submissions will be evaluated and reviewed by the Project Team and selected based on merit, taking into consideration responses provided.

The review, selection, and communication to applicants are expected to be completed by Friday, 27th June 2025.

7. CONTACT DETAILS:

For further information and inquiries, contact:

Mrs Ruth Dickson Nyarko, Project Officer – rdickson@aau.org

Dr Agyemang Darko, Project Researcher – aodarko@aau.org

Dr Lorraine Dongo, Project Researcher – lorraine.dongo@acu.ac.uk

Or visit the project website via https://clareprogramme.org/project/understanding-african-universities-capacity-for-climate-adaptation-research-piloting-a-climate-focused-organizational-capacity-assessment-tool/

TITLE: Arab Youth Council Global Youth Water Envoys Program 2026

The program will select and prepare 100 young leaders from across the world’s regions for structured, substantive participation in global water governance. Benefits

By completing the program, you will:

Join a global network of 100 Youth Water Envoys.

Benefit from training and mentorship delivered by leading experts and specialists in the water sector.

Contribute to the development of the Global Youth Water Statement.

Build valuable connections with policymakers, international organizations, and leaders across the water sector.

Participate in the 2026 UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi.

Become part of an international alumni network, with ongoing opportunities for collaboration and engagement.

Eligibility

Aged between 18 and 35 years at the time of the 2026 UN Water Conference.

Demonstrate proficiency in English, the program’s primary working language.

Have an interest in or relevant experience in water governance, public policy, climate action, sustainability, innovation, finance, or other water-related fields.

Committed to actively participating throughout the program and representing youth perspectives within their communities.

Complete the full program journey, including all training sessions and engagement activities.

Actively contribute to your assigned Interactive Dialogue track.

Represent youth perspectives in discussions and platforms related to global water governance.

Participate in key program milestones, including the 2026 UN Water Conference, subject to program and logistical arrangements.

Engage with experts, policymakers, and institutional leaders throughout the program.

TITLE: Research Fellow (West Africa) at Chatham House: Full-Time Policy Research Job in London

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Chatham House Africa Programme is inviting applications for a Research Fellow (West Africa) to contribute to independent policy research and convening activities focused on West Africa, with significant work on Nigeria and scope to expand regional coverage over time.

This is a full-time, permanent position based in London, offering an annual salary of £45,000. The successful candidate will join Chatham House’s Africa Programme and contribute to research covering governance, politics, economy and trade, security, and the wider regional and international relationships of African states.

The application deadline is Tuesday, 29 September 2026 at 23:59 BST.

About the Chatham House Africa Programme

The Africa Programme conducts policy research examining issues affecting individual African states as well as their regional and international relations. The programme seeks to produce research that is relevant to policymakers and contributes to discussions on major political, economic, governance and security issues affecting the continent.

As a Research Fellow, the successful applicant will contribute to this work through research projects, publications, stakeholder engagement, events and conferences.

The position is particularly focused on West Africa, including substantial work on Nigeria, while also providing an opportunity for the researcher to expand their regional coverage over time.

The role therefore combines academic and policy-oriented research with practical engagement with stakeholders and the wider policy community.

Research Fellow (West Africa) Role Overview

The Research Fellow will be expected to contribute to the development and delivery of a range of research and convening activities relating to West Africa.

The position covers several major thematic areas, including:

Politics and governance

Economy and trade

Security

Regional affairs

International relations

Policy research and analysis

The successful candidate will also contribute to significant research work concerning Nigeria and will have the opportunity to work across different issues affecting West Africa.

This makes the position suitable for an experienced researcher who can work across multiple policy areas rather than focusing exclusively on one narrow research topic.

Key Responsibilities

1. Designing and Delivering Research Projects

A major responsibility of the Research Fellow will be to help develop and deliver research projects that support the strategic objectives of the Africa Programme and Chatham House.

This includes contributing to research from the initial development stage through to the production and dissemination of findings.

The successful candidate will therefore need to be capable of identifying important research questions, developing research proposals and contributing to projects that have clear policy relevance.

Research projects will be expected to advance understanding of important developments in West Africa and generate findings that can contribute to policy discussions.

2. Producing Policy-Relevant Research

The Research Fellow will produce high-quality research relating to West Africa.

The position specifically covers research across areas such as:

Politics

Governance

Economy

Trade

Security

The role requires more than simply producing academic research. The research should be policy relevant, meaning that the findings should be useful to people involved in understanding, developing or implementing policy.

The researcher will therefore need to demonstrate the ability to analyse complex issues, identify important developments and communicate findings clearly to a policy audience.

3. Research on Nigeria and West Africa

The role includes significant work on Nigeria, alongside broader research covering West Africa.

Nigeria is one of the major areas of focus mentioned in the position, meaning applicants should be prepared to engage deeply with developments affecting the country while also understanding the wider regional context.

The position also provides scope for the successful researcher to expand their regional coverage over time.

This means the role can involve developing expertise beyond an initial area of specialization as the researcher contributes to the broader work of the Africa Programme.

4. Developing Research Proposals

The successful candidate will be expected to have experience developing successful research proposals.

This is an important requirement because research at a policy institute often begins with identifying a relevant issue, developing a research question, establishing an appropriate research approach and presenting a convincing proposal.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate previous experience turning research ideas into structured and deliverable research projects.

5. Supporting Research Events and Conferences

TITLE: Google Apprenticeships 2027: Paid Entry-Level Career Opportunities in Data Analytics, Digital Marketing, IT, Project Management and UX Design

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Google has announced its February 2027 Apprenticeship opportunities for individuals seeking to develop practical, technical and professional skills in some of today’s most in-demand career fields.

The available opportunities cover Data Analytics, Digital Marketing, Project Management, Information Technology and User Experience (UX) Design. These programmes are designed for people interested in beginning a career in technology and related professional fields, particularly those with limited experience who want to gain structured training and practical workplace exposure.

Unlike conventional academic programmes, Google’s apprenticeships combine classroom-style technical instruction with hands-on work experience. Participants will train with a Google team, develop professional skills, receive career-development support and work toward a nationally recognised credential certified by the United States Department of Labor.

The apprenticeships are paid, full-time opportunities requiring participants to dedicate 40 hours per week to the programme. The programmes are expected to begin in February 2027 and last approximately 18 months.

Application deadline: September 21, 2026

Overview of the Google Apprenticeship Programme

Google’s apprenticeship programme is a structured learning and development pathway for individuals who want to enter a professional field but may not yet have extensive work experience or a directly related university degree.

The programme is registered with the United States Department of Labor and is designed to help apprentices build both technical and durable professional skills. Throughout the programme, participants receive a combination of:

On-the-job training.

Related technical instruction.

Track-specific learning.

Career-development workshops.

Professional mentoring and workplace exposure.

Career-readiness support.

Practical experience working with a Google team.

Preparation for future employment, education or other professional opportunities.

The programme begins with an immersive virtual onboarding experience. This onboarding period introduces apprentices to the profession, programme structure, expectations and foundational concepts related to their selected career track.

After onboarding, apprentices join a Google team and continue learning through practical assignments and supervised workplace training. They also participate in technical instruction and career workshops throughout the programme.

At the end of the apprenticeship, successful participants receive a nationally recognised credential certified by the United States Department of Labor.

TITLE: Harvard Takemi Program in International Health 2027–2028: Fully Focused Research Fellowship for Mid-Career Global Health Professionals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Takemi Program in International Health at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health is accepting applications for its 2027–2028 fellowship year, offering mid-career health professionals and researchers an opportunity to spend an academic year at Harvard developing an independent research project, strengthening their research capacity, and advancing their leadership in international health.

The program is particularly relevant to professionals working on health systems, global health, health policy, health financing, disease prevention and control, health equity, public health, and other challenges involving the mobilization and allocation of limited resources for better health outcomes.

Applications for the 2027–2028 program are currently open, and the official deadline is December 31, 2026, at midnight EST (USA).

About the Harvard Takemi Program in International Health

The Takemi Program in International Health is an interdisciplinary research and leadership program at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

The program brings a small group of mid-career health professionals and scholars to Harvard for an academic year to conduct focused research and develop their capacity for research and leadership.

The program’s central focus is on understanding how limited resources can be mobilized, allocated, and managed to improve health and health systems. Its research has a strong emphasis on practical health challenges, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

Since its establishment in 1983, the program has developed a large international network of Takemi Fellows. Harvard currently reports that more than 330 fellows from more than 60 countries have participated in the program.

The program was named after Dr. Taro Takemi, a distinguished Japanese physician-scientist who served as president of the Japan Medical Association for more than two decades.

What Is the Takemi Fellowship?

The Takemi Program is designed for mid-career researchers and health professionals who have already developed substantial professional and research experience and want to dedicate an academic year to advancing a specific research project.

Unlike a conventional degree program, the Takemi Program is centered on an individual research project.

Each fellow works with a Harvard faculty advisor and uses the fellowship year to:

Develop and conduct a focused research project

Analyze existing data

Strengthen research methodology

Engage with Harvard faculty and researchers

Participate in weekly academic seminars

Present research findings and receive feedback

Develop a publication-quality research paper

Strengthen leadership capacity

Build international professional networks

Explore relevant Harvard coursework and academic resources

The program is conducted in person in Boston and does not offer a remote fellowship option.

Who Is the Takemi Program Designed For?

The program is primarily intended for mid-career health professionals and researchers.

Applicants should not view this as a typical early-career fellowship or a postgraduate degree scholarship. Harvard specifically describes the program as being for professionals and researchers who already have an advanced degree, significant work and research experience, publications, and demonstrated leadership potential.

Potential applicants may come from areas such as:

Public health

Medicine

Pharmacy

Nursing

Epidemiology

Health economics

Health policy

Health systems

Global health

Health administration

Nutrition

Health financing

Disease prevention and control

Implementation science

Health services research

Social and behavioral sciences

Other fields relevant to international health

The most important consideration is not simply the applicant’s professional title. The proposed research should fit the program’s broader focus on improving health and health systems through better use of resources, stronger policies, and evidence-based interventions.

What Makes the Takemi Program Different?

The Takemi Program is particularly valuable because it provides fellows with something that can be difficult to obtain while working full-time: dedicated time and an academic environment to focus intensively on research.

Harvard describes the program as providing fellows with the space, time, and flexibility to enhance their research and leadership capacity.

Rather than requiring fellows to complete a conventional curriculum, the program allows them to concentrate on a research project that is relevant to their professional work and future contribution to health policy or practice.

This makes the program especially relevant for professionals who already have a research question, access to data, and a clear idea of how their research could contribute to improving health systems or policy.

Research Focus of the Takemi Program

The program’s research emphasis is broad but strongly connected to real-world international health challenges.

Research can examine questions related to:

Health Systems

Projects may investigate how health systems are organized, financed, managed, or improved.

Health Policy

Applicants may explore policies affecting health outcomes, healthcare delivery, access, equity, financing, or population health.

Health Resource Allocation

A central theme of the program is understanding how scarce resources can be allocated more effectively to achieve better health outcomes.

Disease Prevention and Control

Research may focus on strategies for preventing, controlling, or managing important diseases and health threats.

Health Promotion

Projects may examine interventions designed to improve population health and encourage healthier behaviors.

Global Health

The program is particularly interested in major health challenges affecting low- and middle-income countries and approaches that can produce practical improvements.

Health Equity

Research examining inequalities, access to healthcare, marginalized populations, and equitable distribution of health resources may also fit within the program’s broader research priorities.

Harvard states that Takemi research has a strong practical emphasis and that projects should be closely connected to action and to the fellow’s work after returning home.

A Critical Requirement: Your Data Must Already Be Available

One of the most important requirements for prospective applicants is that their research project must be ready for analysis before the fellowship begins.

Takemi does not support active data collection during the fellowship.

Harvard explicitly states that fellows are expected to conduct their research using data they bring with them and that having the necessary data collected before the program begins is mandatory.

This means applicants should not propose a research project that depends on spending the fellowship year conducting extensive surveys, recruiting participants, collecting laboratory samples, or otherwise gathering primary data.

Instead, a strong proposal should demonstrate that:

The research question has already been defined.

The necessary data are available.

The applicant has access to the data.

The data are sufficiently prepared for analysis.

The proposed methodology can realistically be implemented during the fellowship year.

The research can result in a publication-quality paper.

This requirement is particularly important when designing the research proposal.

Faculty Supervision and Research Mentorship

Each selected fellow is matched with a Harvard faculty advisor based on the fellow’s background and proposed research.

Applicants do not need to independently secure a Harvard faculty supervisor before applying.

Harvard explains that fellows are matched with faculty mentors after selection based on their background and proposed research.

The faculty advisor provides guidance and feedback throughout the research process.

Fellows also receive guidance from the Takemi Program leadership and benefit from interactions with other fellows and the broader Harvard community.

Weekly Takemi Seminar Series

An important component of the program is the weekly Takemi Seminar Series.

The seminars expose fellows to a broad range of research topics, methodologies, and perspectives through presentations by Harvard faculty and distinguished visiting scholars.

The seminars also create opportunities for discussion and intellectual exchange between fellows, faculty, and invited speakers.

This means the fellowship is not simply an individual research residency. Fellows become part of an academic community where they can receive feedback, exchange ideas, and learn from researchers working on different international health challenges.

Research Presentations During the Fellowship

Takemi Fellows are expected to present their research progress during the fellowship.

According to Harvard, fellows participate in:

Preliminary presentations

Mid-year presentations

Final presentations

Final academic poster presentation

These presentations provide opportunities for fellows to receive feedback from faculty advisors and peers as they develop their research.

By the end of the fellowship, fellows are expected to produce a final paper of publishable quality and a research poster.

Opportunity to Audit Harvard Courses

Although the Takemi Program is primarily a research fellowship, fellows may also have opportunities to audit classes at Harvard Chan School.

They are also encouraged to attend Harvard Chan seminars and other academic events.

This can allow fellows to supplement their research experience with additional academic exposure based on their professional and research interests.

Fellowship Duration

The Takemi Program is a full academic-year fellowship.

Harvard states that the fellowship runs from:

August 1 through June 30

Fellows are expected to arrive before the program orientation, which takes place in late August. The certificate ceremony is generally held in early May.

Applicants should therefore plan for a substantial period of residence in Boston rather than treating the fellowship as a short-term visiting researcher position.

What Applicants Need to Submit

The application includes several components designed to assess the applicant’s academic background, professional experience, research capacity, motivation, and leadership potential.

The application requires the following:

1. Eligibility Questionnaire

Applicants must complete the program’s eligibility questionnaire.

This helps establish whether the applicant meets the fundamental requirements for consideration.

2. Proof of English Language Proficiency

Applicants must provide evidence of English proficiency.

The application accepts:

TOEFL

IELTS

Applicants who attended a university where English was the language of instruction may submit a copy of their transcript as evidence, according to the application instructions provided.

3. Statement of Interest

The Statement of Interest is an important component of the application.

Applicants should explain:

Why they are interested in the Takemi Program

Why the fellowship is important at this stage of their career

How the program will contribute to their professional development

What they can contribute to the Takemi community

Why they believe they would succeed in the program

What they hope to gain from the fellowship

What they plan to do after completing the program

A strong statement should connect the applicant’s past experience, current research interests, Takemi fellowship objectives, and future professional plans.

4. Basic Information

Applicants will provide standard personal and application information through the online application portal.

5. Education and Professional Experience

Applicants must provide information about their academic and professional background.

This section allows the program to understand the applicant’s progression and experience in relation to the fellowship.

6. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must upload a current CV in PDF format.

The CV should clearly present relevant:

Academic qualifications

Professional experience

Research experience

Publications

Leadership roles

Awards and recognition

Relevant projects

Professional activities

Because the Takemi Program is designed for mid-career professionals, the CV should clearly demonstrate the applicant’s professional trajectory and research accomplishments.

7. Research Proposal

The research proposal is arguably one of the most important components of the application.

Applicants must submit a research proposal of no more than five pages, excluding the title page and references.

The proposal should be:

Single-spaced

12-point Times New Roman

Submitted as a PDF

The proposal should include the following sections.

Title Page

The title page should clearly identify the proposed research project.

Summary of the Proposed Project

The summary should provide a concise overview of the research, including:

The central research problem

Specific aims and objectives

Potential significance of the research

The application guidance suggests approximately half a page for this section.

Specific Aims

Applicants should clearly explain what the research intends to accomplish.

The suggested length is approximately half a page to one page.

Background and Significance

This section should establish:

What is already known

What problem remains

Why the problem matters

Why the proposed research is important

How the project contributes to existing knowledge

Data Sources

Applicants should identify the data that will be used.

This is particularly important because the program requires the necessary data to already be collected before the fellowship begins.

Research Design and Methods

This section should explain how the research will be conducted.

Applicants should clearly describe:

Research design

Analytical approach

Variables or measures

Methods

Data analysis

Any relevant methodological considerations

The application guidance suggests approximately two pages for this section.

References

The proposal should conclude with relevant references.

8. Publication List

Applicants must provide a list of their publications.

This requirement reflects the program’s emphasis on applicants who already have demonstrated research experience and scholarly output.

Applicants should ensure that the publication list is accurate, clearly organized, and consistent with the CV.

9. Published Document in English

Applicants must provide a document published in English.

This gives the selection committee an opportunity to assess the applicant’s ability to communicate scholarly work in English.

10. Three References

Applicants must provide the names and contact information of three referees.

After the application is submitted, referees receive an automated request to submit their references to the Takemi Program.

Applicants should therefore choose referees who can provide meaningful evidence of their:

Research ability

Professional experience

Leadership potential

Academic development

Contribution to health systems or policy

Capacity to benefit from the fellowship

Who Is Eligible for the Takemi Program?

Harvard’s current application guidance states that applicants should be mid-career researchers and professionals who have:

Completed an advanced degree

Significant work experience

Significant research experience

Publications in internationally recognized journals

Demonstrated potential for leadership in their home countries

Appropriate preparation to benefit from the program

Strong English-language ability

The program is primarily designed for people who are already established in their professional careers rather than recent graduates.

Is the Takemi Program Open to International Applicants?

Yes.

The Takemi Program is explicitly international and brings together professionals and researchers from around the world.

Harvard’s historical fellowship network includes fellows from countries across:

Africa

Asia

Europe

The Middle East

North America

South America

Other regions

Harvard describes the program as having a particular emphasis on fellows from low- and middle-income countries.

Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to U.S. citizens or residents.

Professionals from eligible countries around the world can apply if they meet the program’s academic, professional, research, and leadership requirements.

Is There a Race or Ethnicity Requirement?

The program does not specify a racial or ethnic eligibility restriction.

Its emphasis is instead on professional background, research experience, leadership potential, English proficiency, and the relevance and quality of the proposed research.

Harvard also states that the Takemi Program welcomes research examining issues related to racism, discrimination, marginalization, structural inequality, and other related issues when relevant to international health research.

Preference for Low- and Middle-Income Countries

The Takemi Program has a longstanding commitment to strengthening research and leadership capacity among professionals from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

Harvard states that the program has historically focused on building the capacity of mid-career researchers from LMICs and that most Takemi Fellows have focused their work on LMIC-related challenges.

This makes the program particularly relevant for professionals whose work addresses health challenges in developing and emerging economies.

Financial Support and Funding

Applicants should pay close attention to funding arrangements.

The Takemi Program states that incoming fellows are generally responsible for securing funding to support their fellowship year. Boston is an expensive city, and Harvard encourages accepted candidates to plan carefully for the cost of living and other expenses.

However, limited funding mechanisms are available.

For example, Harvard reports that a contribution from the Japan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association (JPMA) provides partial financial support for up to two fellows from low-income countries each year. Candidates can indicate their interest in this support during the application process.

Importantly, applicants should not assume that the Takemi fellowship automatically provides full funding for the entire year.

Accepted applicants may need to secure funding through other sources, such as:

Employer or professional development funding

Government funding

Research grants

International fellowships

Fulbright funding

Other external funding sources

Harvard provides information about potential external funding sources for incoming fellows.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027–2028 Takemi Program in International Health is:

December 31, 2026

Applications must be submitted by midnight EST (USA) on December 31, 2026.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day because the application includes multiple documents, a research proposal, English-language documentation, publications, and three references.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The Harvard Takemi Program in International Health 2027–2028 represents a significant opportunity for experienced health professionals and researchers seeking dedicated time to conduct high-quality research, strengthen their leadership capacity, and contribute to better health policies and systems.

The program is particularly relevant to mid-career professionals with advanced degrees, substantial research and professional experience, international publications, and demonstrated leadership potential. Its strong emphasis on practical research makes it especially suitable for applicants whose work addresses health challenges in low- and middle-income countries.

The program is also international rather than restricted to U.S. applicants, making it potentially relevant to qualified health professionals and researchers across Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, Europe, and other regions. Harvard’s fellowship network demonstrates its longstanding international reach.

The application deadline is December 31, 2026, at midnight EST (USA). Applicants should begin preparing well in advance because the application requires a research proposal, statement of interest, CV, publication list, English-language documentation, writing sample, and three references.

TITLE: AAU, Highlights the ACE Impact Project’s Mid-Term Review Results

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities, the Regional Facilitation Unit for the ACE Impact Project Highlights the Project’s Mid-Term Review Results

The 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop being hosted in Cotonou, Benin from 14-17 June 2022 featured nine plenary sessions, four parallel sessions and three performance clinics. Close to 300 ACE Impact project stakeholders convened to review the performance of the project, network and reconnect physically for the first time since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The first plenary session on Tuesday 14th June 2022 focused on receiving four presentations that provided an overall update on the progress and status of the ACE Impact Project and highlighted the results from the ongoing mid-term review (MTR) of the project. This session was chaired by Professor Salifu Mohammed who is one of the Project’s Steering Committee members and the Executive Secretary of the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission.

The four presentations were from Dr. Sylvia Mkandawire, the Project Manager of the ACE Impact Project; Mrs. Adeline Addy, the Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Specialist; Ms. Maud Kouadio-IV, the Education Consultant and ACE core team member with the World Bank and Professor Joseph Mutale, one of the Subject Matter Experts supporting the Centres of Excellence.

Regional Facilitating Unit (RFU) Key Project Updates by Dr Sylvia Mkandawire

Dr. Sylvia Mkandawire provided overall project updates, key highlights of each project component, areas needing significant attention and concluded by reflecting on the challenges and opportunities.

The project has realized impressive results that include 3,524 research publications, 4,766 internships and 22,161 enrolled students to date. A total of USD 86.5 million has been mobilized by the Centres as external and additional revenue. The highest research publications were produced in the STEM theme (42%), the highest number of financial resources were raised from grants (75%), and the private sector provided 51% of the internship places for ACE Impact students. The project has exceeded its set targets of enrolling and training PhD and MSc students – by 19% and 8% respectively. A total of 7,214 females (33% of total number of students) have been enrolled as post-graduate students since the project’s inception in 2019 and this is in line with the project’s thrust of increasing the number of women enrolled in post-graduate training programs. As indicated in the presentation, some of these figures are yet to be independently verified.

To support effective implementation of the ACE Impact project, some countries, such as Burkina Faso, Ghana, Nigeria, and The Gambia, have established National Facilitation Units (NFU). Where NFU’s exist, it is evident that those projects are better tracked and supported by their governments. NFU’s also support the procurement of equipment for the Centres, communication to increase project visibility, capacity building for financial management, verification and accreditation of programmes, land acquisition, and recruitment of national subject matter experts among others.

During this reporting period (October 2021 – May 2022), the RFU provided implementation support to the Centres by organizing fourteen in-person missions, twenty virtual missions and preparing the Centres for the mid-term review process. The lessons garnered were that there was need for more in-person implementation support missions to the Centres, prioritization of pending procurements by the Centres, support for the Centres’ accelerated implementation plans and a need for the Centres to strengthen the visibility of their programs and research.

The development impact of the Centres is demonstrated through the publication of key research breakthroughs, such as genetic diversity of SARS-CoV2 infections in Ghana; lessons for the world concerning COVID-19 in Africa; use of drones for data collection; development of solar-powered irrigation system curricula; development of new early growth groundnut seeds for African farmers; and a software application to improve transport and mobility in Ghana. Excellence in leadership continued to be demonstrated through eight prestigious awards won by both Centres’ faculty and students. For example, Ms Atut Chantal Tiku, a student from WACWISA in Ghana won the 2021 University for Development Studies Vice Chancellor’s Business Innovation Award​.

The ACE Impact Project places emphasis on partnerships as a method of building capacities, mobilizing resources, and sustaining the project’s goals. Four partnerships were highlighted by Dr. Sylvia Mkandawire, and these include the collaboration with IBM for Student Internships at IBM’s research laboratories in Kenya and South Africa; the EPFL (Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne) / AAU Centers of Competence in Digital Education (C-CoDE) initiative which is transforming digital education in Africa; The PARTNER IRD​ (Institut de Recherche pour le Développement) initiative that supports four thematic networks, namely, WANIDA, NET-WATER, DSTN and RAMR2D; and the ELSEVIER​ partnership for Capacity Building in Scientific Writing and Publications​.

With support from the World Bank, the RFU has launched an innovative Research Awards initiative called the ACE Impact Students’ Innovative Awards (SIRA). SIRA aims to promote the production of innovative and impactful knowledge through research​; and the generation of scientific and intellectual tangibles that provide solutions to Africa’s problems in the most critical priority areas of development. Fifteen (15) best research projects will be competitively selected and awarded in five ACE Impact thematic areas. Students enrolled in an ACE Impact supported programme at the time of a SIRA call for applications are eligible to participate.

It was highlighted that the challenges faced by the Centres also present opportunities for project implementation redesign. The main challenges faced by the ACE Impact Project, as reported are listed below.

There were disruptive and recurrent strikes and coup d’états at some ACE Impact institutions and countries, leading to delays of some scheduled activities related to Centre workplans and activities.​

Procurement activities at the national level continued to delay the project activities of some Centres.

The centres participating in the C-CoDE Initiative experienced challenges in the procurement of equipment given that these were not readily available in their home countries and needed to be outsourced from manufacturers abroad. ​

There were difficulties in adhering to timelines for the submission of documents by some Centres to the Regional Facilitating Unit mainly relating to Annual Workplans, DLR 5.3 (focused on innovation and entrepreneurship) and DLIs 2 (focused on Development Impact) and DLR 7 (focused on Institutional Impact). This also delayed the review processes and subsequently the implementation of related activities.​

Through the discussions and exchange of ideas during thematic performance clinics and parallel sessions at the ongoing regional workshop, solutions towards addressing the identified challenges will be garnered. The ACE Impact project stakeholders remain committed towards the enhancement of quality education and research as well as harnessing skills to meet Africa’s development needs.

Written By: Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director ICT Services, Communications and Knowledge Management at AAU
