TITLE: UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028: Expression of Interest for Artists, Creative Businesses, Organisations and Cultural Institutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 is creating a major platform for artists, creative businesses, cultural organisations and institutions across the United Kingdom and Nigeria to develop new partnerships, exchange ideas and showcase creative work to international audiences. Delivered by the British Council in partnership with Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy, the Season will run from June to December 2028, with legacy activity continuing into 2029. The programme is designed to strengthen the long-term creative relationship between the UK and Nigeria by creating connections between people, organisations and creative industries in both countries. The initiative is particularly significant because it comes a decade after the landmark 2015/16 UK–Nigeria Season, at a time when Nigeria’s creative economy has expanded considerably and the UK and Nigeria are seeking deeper cultural, commercial and institutional connections.

UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028: What Is It About?

The UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 is a bilateral cultural initiative bringing together creative communities from both countries.

The Season aims to celebrate the creativity, diversity and cultural heritage of the UK and Nigeria while creating opportunities for collaboration that can continue long after the 2028 programme ends.

According to the British Council, the Season is intended to:

Strengthen the creative partnership between the UK and Nigeria.

Build lasting professional and institutional connections.

Create opportunities for creative collaboration.

Open pathways to new markets and audiences.

Showcase the depth and diversity of UK and Nigerian creative talent.

Support knowledge exchange between creative professionals and institutions.

Encourage new artistic commissions and collaborative projects.

Strengthen creative infrastructure and systems.

Support longer-term relationships that can continue beyond the Season itself.

The wider bilateral initiative is also expected to contribute to skills development, institutional capacity, market access and international connections across the creative economy.

When Will the UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 Take Place?

The main Season will take place from:

June to December 2028

Legacy activities are expected to continue into 2029, meaning that the programme is intended to have an impact beyond the main 2028 calendar.

However, creative professionals and organisations do not have to wait until 2028 to become involved. The programme is already seeking ideas, partnerships and potential collaborations during the preparation and incubation period.

The British Council has described the period before the Season as an opportunity for partner engagement, visiting delegations and programme incubation, helping potential collaborations develop before activities take place in 2028.

Five Key Focus Areas of the Season

The UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 is organised around five major focus areas. Applicants and potential partners should consider how their proposed idea connects with one or more of these areas.

1. Cultural Heritage, Identity and Infrastructure

This focus area recognises the importance of cultural heritage and identity while considering the infrastructure required for the creative sector to thrive.

Projects could explore cultural heritage, storytelling, identity, preservation, cultural spaces, creative infrastructure and related issues.

The emphasis is not simply on presenting culture, but also on strengthening the systems and structures that enable cultural and creative activity to develop sustainably.

2. Market Access and Mutual Growth

The Season also aims to create stronger connections between creative industries and markets in both countries.

This focus area is relevant to organisations, entrepreneurs and creative professionals seeking opportunities to:

Reach new audiences.

Build international networks.

Develop commercial partnerships.

Expand into new markets.

Connect with buyers, investors or industry professionals.

Strengthen the international visibility of their creative work or business.

The broader UK–Nigeria creative partnership has also identified international market access and structured engagement as important areas for strengthening the creative economy.

3. Creative Collaboration and Partnerships

Partnership is at the heart of the Season.

The programme is interested in ideas that bring together people, organisations and institutions from the UK and Nigeria to develop meaningful creative collaborations.

A proposed project does not necessarily need to be completely developed before an expression of interest is submitted. The opportunity specifically welcomes both developed project concepts and early-stage ideas.

If you already have a potential partner in the other country, you can indicate this in your response. If you do not yet have a partner, you can still express your interest and describe the type of collaboration you would like to develop.

4. New Artistic Commissions

The Season will also provide a platform for new creative and artistic work.

This could create possibilities for artists and creative organisations to propose original projects, productions, performances, commissions or other forms of creative activity that contribute to the UK–Nigeria cultural relationship.

The emphasis is on developing ideas capable of creating meaningful artistic and cultural value for audiences in both countries.

5. Research, Policy and Knowledge Exchange

The Season is not limited to performances and exhibitions.

Research, policy discussions, professional learning and knowledge exchange are also part of its vision.

This focus area can be particularly relevant to institutions, researchers, cultural policy professionals, academics, practitioners and organisations working on issues affecting the creative and cultural sectors.

It recognises that long-term creative development requires not only artistic activity but also research, evidence, policy development, institutional learning and the exchange of knowledge between countries.

Which Artforms and Creative Disciplines Are Eligible?

One of the notable features of the UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 is its broad approach to creative disciplines.

The Season is open to all artforms and creative disciplines, rather than restricting participation to a single artistic field.

Potential areas include:

Music

Film

Visual arts

Fashion

Literature

Digital creativity

Performing arts

Theatre

Dance

Architecture

Gaming

Gastronomy

Craft

Creative technology

Other creative and cultural disciplines

This broad scope means that the opportunity may be relevant to both traditional and emerging areas of the creative economy.

The British Council’s wider arts work in Nigeria similarly spans areas including architecture, design, fashion, film, literature, music, theatre, dance and visual arts.

Who Is Being Invited to Get Involved?

The opportunity is aimed at people and organisations within the cultural and creative sectors of both the UK and Nigeria.

The invitation specifically mentions:

Artists

Creative businesses

Cultural organisations

Cultural institutions

Creative-sector organisations

Other relevant institutions and creative practitioners

The British Council is looking for people and organisations with an idea for a project, partnership or collaboration that could contribute to the UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028.

You do not necessarily need to have a fully developed project.

The programme welcomes:

Fully formed project proposals.

Early-stage creative ideas.

Potential partnerships.

Collaboration concepts.

Ideas that could be developed with a partner in the other country.

This makes the expression of interest particularly useful for creative professionals who have a strong concept but may still be exploring how to develop it internationally.

Important: This Is Not a Funding Application

One of the most important points for anyone considering submitting an expression of interest is that this stage is not a funding application.

The purpose of the current Expression of Interest is to:

Gather creative ideas.

Identify potential partners.

Understand what the creative sectors in the UK and Nigeria would like to develop.

Start conversations between potential collaborators.

Explore projects that could form part of the wider Season.

Help shape future programme development.

Therefore, applicants should not approach the EOI as though they are applying for a conventional grant.

Instead, the focus should be on clearly communicating who you are, what you would like to do, how your idea connects to the Season and whether you already have a partner in the other country.

What Should You Include in Your Expression of Interest?

The response should be no more than two pages.

It should cover four essential areas:

1. Who You Are

Introduce yourself, your organisation, institution, creative business or relevant professional background.

Explain your role within the cultural or creative sector and provide enough information for the organisers to understand your experience and relevance to the proposed idea.

2. What You Would Like to Do

Describe your project, partnership or collaboration idea.

This does not have to be a fully developed proposal. If the concept is still at an early stage, explain the idea clearly and describe what you hope to develop.

3. Which Focus Area Your Idea Fits

Explain which of the Season’s five focus areas your idea relates to:

Cultural heritage, identity and infrastructure

Market access and mutual growth

Creative collaboration and partnerships

New artistic commissions

Research, policy and knowledge exchange

If your project connects with more than one focus area, you can explain those connections.

4. Whether You Have a Partner in the Other Country

State whether you already have a UK or Nigerian partner.

For example, a Nigerian creative organisation could identify a UK institution it already works with, while a UK artist could describe an existing relationship with a Nigerian creative organisation.

If you do not yet have a partner, explain the type of partner or collaboration you would like to develop.

How to Submit Your Expression of Interest

The Expression of Interest should be submitted by email to:UKNigeria.SeasonofCulture@britishcouncil.org

The response should be two pages or fewer and should address the requested information.

The stated deadline is:

14 September 2026

This deadline is important for anyone intending to have their idea considered as part of the current expression-of-interest process.

For official information and updates, visit the https://www.britishcouncil.org.ng/programmes/arts/uk-nigeria-season-culture-2028

Online Information Sessions for Interested Applicants

Two online sessions are being held to help potential participants understand the Expression of Interest process, the Season and what is expected in a response.

Session 1

Date: Monday, 17 August 2026

Time: 11:00 WAT

Session 2

Date: Monday, 7 September 2026

Time: 11:00 WAT

Both sessions cover the same information, so participants can attend one or both.

If you have questions before attending the sessions, you can contact the Season team by email at:UKNigeria.SeasonofCulture@britishcouncil.org

Why Should Creative Professionals Consider Getting Involved?

The UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 presents an opportunity to engage with a major bilateral cultural initiative at an early stage.

For creative professionals and organisations, early involvement can be particularly valuable because the current process is designed to identify ideas and potential partners before the main Season takes place.

Potential areas of value include:

Developing UK–Nigeria creative partnerships.

Building international professional networks.

Exploring new audiences and markets.

Developing collaborative creative projects.

Connecting creative institutions across both countries.

Contributing ideas to a major international cultural programme.

Exploring new artistic commissions.

Sharing knowledge and expertise.

Strengthening international visibility.

Building relationships that may continue beyond 2028.

The broader bilateral programme is intended to establish lasting partnerships rather than relationships that end when the Season closes. The British Council has highlighted institutional partnerships, skills development, market access and sustainable creative connections as important elements of the wider initiative.

A Major Opportunity for the UK and Nigerian Creative Economies

The Season arrives at an important period for creative industries in both countries.

Nigeria has developed one of Africa’s most internationally visible creative economies, while the UK has a well-established global creative sector spanning music, film, fashion, theatre, literature, design, gaming and other industries.

The Season provides a structured platform for these ecosystems to connect.

Rather than treating cultural exchange simply as a series of performances or exhibitions, the initiative takes a broader approach that includes creative enterprise, partnerships, infrastructure, policy, research, skills and international market access.

The British Council has also described the 2028 Season as part of a wider effort to strengthen creative systems and production infrastructure, develop skills and leadership, improve access to international markets and create lasting relationships between UK and Nigerian creative institutions.

What Happened During the Previous UK–Nigeria Season?

The 2028 programme builds on the earlier UK–Nigeria Season, which ran from September 2015 to March 2017.

The previous Season demonstrated the potential scale of UK–Nigeria cultural collaboration.

According to the British Council, the 2015/16 Season:

Covered nine artforms.

Delivered 31 projects.

Involved 79 partner organisations.

Reached 12 cities.

Attracted more than 446,000 attendees to live events.

Trained 7,135 artists.

The new Season therefore represents a return to a successful model of cultural exchange, while responding to the significant growth and transformation of the creative sector over the intervening decade.

What Makes the 2028 Season Different?

The creative environment in which the 2028 Season is being developed is significantly different from that of the previous Season.

Digital technology, international streaming, gaming, creative entrepreneurship, social media, emerging technologies and rapidly changing global markets have transformed how artists and creative businesses reach audiences.

The 2028 Season is therefore positioned not only as a celebration of culture but also as a platform for developing stronger creative systems and international relationships.

The British Council has identified areas such as emerging technology, creative infrastructure, professional skills, leadership, international markets and institutional partnerships as part of the wider UK–Nigeria creative collaboration agenda.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Expression of Interest

Although the EOI is limited to two pages, applicants should make every sentence count.

Keep the idea clear

Avoid filling the document with unnecessary background information. Clearly explain what you want to do and why it matters.

Explain the UK–Nigeria connection

Since this is a bilateral Season, make the connection between the two countries clear.

Explain how the project could create meaningful collaboration between Nigerian and UK creative communities, institutions, businesses or audiences.

Connect the idea to a focus area

Do not simply name one of the five focus areas. Explain why your idea belongs there.

Be realistic

If your project is still at an early stage, say so. The EOI specifically welcomes early ideas, so there is no need to present an undeveloped concept as though it is already fully formed.

Highlight your experience

Briefly demonstrate why you or your organisation are well positioned to develop the idea.

Relevant previous projects, partnerships, creative work, audiences or institutional experience can help provide context.

Explain your partnership status

Clearly state whether you already have a partner in the UK or Nigeria.

If you do not, explain what type of partner you would like to work with.

Stay within the two-page limit

The request is for a response of two pages or fewer, so concise and structured communication is important.

Who Can Apply or Express Interest?

The opportunity is intended for the cultural and creative sectors in the United Kingdom and Nigeria.

Potential participants include:

Individual artists.

Creative businesses.

Cultural organisations.

Cultural institutions.

Creative-sector organisations.

Other relevant organisations or practitioners with suitable project or collaboration ideas.

There is no specific race or ethnicity requirement stated in the information provided for this Expression of Interest.

The opportunity is geographically centred on the UK and Nigeria, rather than being presented as a general worldwide opportunity for applicants from every country.

Importantly, eligibility is described in terms of participation in the UK or Nigerian cultural and creative sectors. Therefore, prospective participants should focus on demonstrating their connection to the relevant creative sector and explaining how their proposed idea contributes to UK–Nigeria collaboration.

Is This a Grant or Scholarship?

No.

The current Expression of Interest is explicitly not a funding application. It is a process for gathering ideas, identifying partners and initiating conversations about potential projects for the Season.

Participants should therefore not assume that submitting an EOI automatically provides funding, a grant, a scholarship, employment or another financial award.

Any future project development or support arrangements would depend on subsequent discussions and the programme’s development.

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity: UK–Nigeria Season of Culture 2028 – Expression of Interest

Main Season: June–December 2028

Legacy activity: Through 2029

Countries: United Kingdom and Nigeria

Creative disciplines: All artforms and creative disciplines

Who can express interest: Artists, organisations, institutions and creative businesses in the UK and Nigeria

Maximum response length: Two pages

Submission method: Email

Submission email: UKNigeria.SeasonofCulture@britishcouncil.org

Deadline: 14 September 2026

Application type: Expression of Interest, not a funding application

Organisers: British Council and Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy

How to Find More Information

Those interested in participating should consult the official British Council information and follow any updates to the Expression of Interest process.https://www.britishcouncil.org.ng/uknigeria-2015-16-impact-report

TITLE: WFP Ethics Officer P-3 in Rome, Italy: International Professional Job in Ethics, Compliance and Risk Management

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) is inviting applications for an Ethics Officer – P-3 position based at its headquarters in Rome, Italy. This is a full-time International Professional opportunity for an experienced ethics, compliance, legal, risk management or international affairs professional seeking to contribute to ethical governance and accountability within one of the world’s largest humanitarian organizations.

The position is located in the WFP Ethics Office and reports to the Senior Ethics Officer. The successful candidate will help strengthen WFP’s ethical framework by advising employees and management, supporting conflict-of-interest disclosure processes, contributing to ethics-related policies, supporting protection against retaliation, developing training programmes, and strengthening relationships across WFP and the wider United Nations system.

The application deadline is 29 September 2026 at 23:59 Central European Time (Rome).

WFP’s official careers information describes P-3 positions as professional roles involving specialized and analytical responsibilities, with the complexity of responsibilities increasing with grade. International Professional positions generally operate under internationally determined compensation and benefits arrangements.

About the World Food Programme

The World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization. Its work focuses on saving lives during emergencies while using food assistance to support pathways toward peace, stability and prosperity for people affected by conflict, disasters and climate-related impacts.

WFP operates through a large international workforce and a network of country, regional and headquarters offices. Its careers framework emphasizes meaningful work, continuous professional development and a multicultural working environment.

WFP also places strong emphasis on integrity, collaboration, commitment, humanity and inclusion. These values are particularly relevant to an Ethics Officer because the position contributes directly to maintaining trust, accountability and responsible conduct across the organization.

What Is the WFP Ethics Office?

The Ethics Office plays an important role in helping WFP maintain high standards of integrity and ethical conduct.

According to WFP, the Ethics Office is an independent and formal office that assists the Executive Director in nurturing a culture of ethics throughout the organization. It helps employees think through ethical dilemmas, understand relevant rules and policies, and raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

The office’s work includes several interconnected areas:

Ethics advice and guidance

Training, education and outreach

Protection against retaliation

Conflicts of interest and financial disclosures

Ethical standards in policies and organizational practices

Anti-fraud and anti-corruption principles

Confidentiality and data protection considerations

United Nations ethics coordination

Support for ethical decision-making

The WFP Code of Conduct reflects principles including human rights, social justice, dignity, equal rights, competence, integrity, impartiality and discretion. It also addresses areas such as anti-fraud and anti-corruption and protection against sexual exploitation and abuse.

About the Ethics Officer – P-3 Position

The Ethics Officer will work within the Ethics Office at WFP headquarters in Rome and report to the Senior Ethics Officer.

The central purpose of the position is to support the development and maintenance of a robust ethical framework within WFP.

This means the role is not limited to reviewing rules or responding to individual questions. It combines ethics advisory work, policy analysis, conflict-of-interest management, retaliation protection, training, communication, reporting and stakeholder engagement.

The role therefore requires someone who can combine technical knowledge with strong interpersonal skills, discretion, independence and the ability to communicate sensitive issues clearly.

Key Responsibilities of the Ethics Officer

1. Support the Ethics Office Strategy and Work Plan

The Ethics Officer will provide substantive input into the definition and implementation of the Ethics Office’s strategy and work plan.

This involves helping determine priorities, activities and approaches that strengthen ethical standards across WFP.

The role therefore requires an understanding of how ethics functions can be translated into practical organizational systems rather than treated simply as theoretical principles.

2. Provide Ethics Advice and Guidance

A major part of the position involves providing timely advice and guidance to WFP employees and management on ethics and standards of conduct.

The officer will also be responsible for properly tracking and recording ethics-related queries.

This requires the ability to:

Understand complex ethical situations

Identify relevant policies and standards

Provide clear and balanced advice

Maintain confidentiality

Exercise independent judgment

Communicate effectively with different stakeholders

Document advice and follow-up appropriately

The importance of this function is reflected in the broader work of WFP’s Ethics Office. Its 2025 annual report recorded 890 requests for ethics advice and guidance, with 96 percent of respondents to voluntary satisfaction surveys reporting that they were satisfied or very satisfied with the advice received and its timeliness.

3. Support the Annual Conflict-of-Interest Disclosure Programme

The Ethics Officer will contribute to the management of WFP’s annual disclosure programme.

This includes reviewing disclosed conflicts of interest, providing advice and helping ensure the programme operates smoothly.

Conflict-of-interest management is an important part of organizational integrity because employees may sometimes have private interests or outside activities that could conflict with their official responsibilities.

WFP’s Ethics Office explains that its annual disclosure programme is designed to identify and address such conflicts through disclosures involving assets, liabilities, investments and outside activities for certain categories of employees.

For the Ethics Officer, this means applying ethical judgment to real situations and helping employees and management understand how potential conflicts should be identified and addressed.

4. Develop Ethics Training and Learning Programmes

The successful candidate will help develop and deliver:

Ethics training programmes

E-learning modules

Train-the-trainer programmes

Sessions on WFP values

Training on ethical principles

Training on standards of conduct

This responsibility requires more than technical knowledge.

The Ethics Officer must also be able to explain complex concepts to employees with different professional and cultural backgrounds.

WFP emphasizes training and outreach as important components of building an ethical culture because employees need to understand the values, standards and principles expected of them.

5. Advise on Ethics-Related Policies and Regulations

The Ethics Officer will provide advice and review when WFP develops or updates:

Policies

Circulars

Regulations

Other organizational documents involving ethical considerations

The officer may also be requested by other departments to provide ethics advice during policy development.

This makes policy analysis an important component of the role.

The successful candidate must therefore be comfortable reading complex institutional documents, identifying ethical implications and communicating recommendations clearly.

6. Support Protection Against Retaliation

Another major responsibility involves supporting the review of requests for protection against retaliation.

The officer may contribute to:

Reviewing retaliation-protection requests

Preparing memoranda

Drafting responses to complainants

Assessing relevant circumstances

Applying whistleblower protection policies

Maintaining confidentiality

Supporting individuals who raise concerns

WFP states that its Whistleblower Protection Policy is designed to protect employees from retaliation when they engage in protected activities, and that the protection applies to current and former employees regardless of contract type or duration.

This is a particularly sensitive area of the position and requires independence, impartiality, careful listening and sound judgment.

7. Strengthen the Visibility of the Ethics Office

The Ethics Officer will also contribute to enhancing the presence of the Ethics Office through:

WFP internal websites

External websites

Online communication channels

Relevant publications

Other communication platforms

This responsibility shows that the role also has a communication component.

Ethics policies are most effective when employees understand them and know where to seek advice. Therefore, communicating the work of the Ethics Office clearly is part of strengthening an organization’s ethical culture.

8. Support Reporting and Analysis

The position will involve preparing analysis, drafting material and supporting reporting on the overall work of the Ethics Office.

The officer may therefore need to translate complex information into:

Reports

Briefings

Memos

Analytical documents

Policy notes

Communication materials

Strong analytical and writing abilities are consequently important.

9. Build Internal and External Relationships

The Ethics Officer will build positive and effective relationships both within WFP and outside the organization.

External cooperation may include engagement across:

The United Nations system

Other UN entities

Rome-based UN agencies

Professional ethics networks

Relevant institutional partners

WFP’s Ethics Office already works to promote coherence across the United Nations system, including through cooperation with other ethics offices and Rome-based agencies.

The successful candidate will therefore need strong interpersonal and partnership-building abilities.

10. Perform Other Duties as Assigned

The officer may also undertake other responsibilities assigned by the Senior Ethics Officer when necessary to support the mandate of the Ethics Office and strengthen ethics and accountability across WFP.

Minimum Education Requirements

Applicants must have an advanced university degree in one of the following areas or a closely related discipline:

Law

Ethics

Public administration

International affairs

Compliance

Another related field

This educational requirement makes the position particularly relevant to professionals with postgraduate qualifications in legal, governance, ethics, international policy or compliance-related disciplines.

An advanced degree is important because the position requires the ability to interpret policies and regulations, assess ethical risks, advise senior stakeholders and prepare sophisticated written analysis.

Professional Experience Required

Candidates must have at least five years of relevant progressively responsible professional experience.

The experience should be connected to areas such as:

Ethics

Related professional fields

The phrase “progressively responsible” is important. The position is not intended primarily for someone who has only completed an academic programme or gained limited entry-level experience.

Candidates should be able to demonstrate increasing responsibility and professional judgment in their previous roles.

Relevant experience could involve advising organizations, reviewing compliance risks, developing policies, supporting investigations or whistleblower systems, providing ethics guidance, drafting legal or policy documents, or managing institutional risk.

Advisory Skills

Whistleblower Protection Knowledge

This is particularly relevant to the retaliation-protection component of the position.

Because the Ethics Office performs an independent and confidential function, the Ethics Officer must act with:

Integrity

Independence

Impartiality

Professional discretion

The successful candidate must be able to provide objective advice even when dealing with sensitive or difficult situations.

Interpersonal Skills

WFP works with people from diverse professional, national and cultural backgrounds.

The Ethics Officer must therefore be able to establish respectful working relationships and communicate effectively with colleagues from different backgrounds.

Training and Facilitation Skills

Applicants should demonstrate the ability to deliver training to small and medium-sized audiences.

This is important because the role includes developing and facilitating ethics learning programmes.

Active Listening

The position specifically requires the ability to listen attentively to people seeking advice or protection from retaliation.

This is particularly important because ethics-related cases may involve sensitive professional circumstances.

The position is classified as an International Professional role and is open to candidates of all nationalities.

This is an important distinction because the position is not restricted to Italian citizens or citizens of a particular region.

Qualified professionals can therefore come from any country or continent, provided they meet the professional, academic and language requirements.

Meaningful humanitarian work

WFP’s work directly supports people affected by emergencies, conflict, disasters and climate-related challenges.

International working environment

Professional development

WFP invests in employee development through training, accreditation, coaching, mentorship and internal mobility opportunities.

International career opportunities

Nobel Peace Prize recognition

WFP was awarded the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize, recognizing its contribution to efforts to prevent the use of hunger as a weapon of war and to peacebuilding efforts in conflict-affected areas.

Why the Ethics Officer Role Matters to WFP

Ethics may sometimes be viewed as an administrative function, but within a large humanitarian organization, it is closely connected to institutional credibility and operational effectiveness.

WFP works in complex environments and handles significant responsibilities involving humanitarian assistance, partnerships, resources and people.

Maintaining public and internal trust therefore requires strong standards of conduct and accountability.

WFP’s 2025 Ethics Office annual report notes that the organization operates in high-risk environments with a diverse and evolving workforce across more than 120 countries and territories. The report emphasizes the importance of safeguarding WFP’s reputation and credibility and describes the Ethics Office as playing a vital role in providing timely guidance and supporting risk management.

The Ethics Officer therefore contributes to an important institutional function: helping employees make sound ethical decisions and helping WFP maintain confidence in its operations.

Examples of Ethics Work at WFP

The broader work of the Ethics Office provides useful context for understanding this position.

Ethics advice and guidance

Employees can seek confidential advice when facing ethical questions or risks.

Conflict-of-interest management

United Nations coherence

These functions closely correspond to the responsibilities outlined for the Ethics Officer position.

TITLE: Call for Applications – Research Excellence Consultant

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Terms of Reference: Consultant to Develop Training Modules and Develop, Organize and Facilitate Training Workshops Aimed at Strengthening Effective Research Excellence Assessment Capacities within Science Granting Councils (SGCs) in Africa.

About the SGCI

The Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI) is a multi-donor Initiative with Phase 2 (SGCI-2: 2020-2023) supported by Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida), United Kingdom’s Department for International Development (DFID), Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC) and South Africa’s National Research Foundation (NRF).

The overall goal of the SGCI-2 Research Management project is to fortify the capability of Science Granting Councils in explicit areas of research management, namely research excellence (particularly the knowledge and use of tools such as Research Quality Plus framework), research ethics, emerging scientific practices (especially open data, open access and citizen science), Good Financial Grant Practice (GFGP) benchmarking exercise and development of online grant management systems (including databases of peer reviewers).

The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) are the consortium partners for the SGCI-2 Research Management project. Both AAU and AAS are two continental higher education bodies with experience in research management, and the AAU has participated in the SGCI-1 as part of the “Theme 3” Consortium. The SGCI-1 provided the AAU with invaluable experiences and lessons of working with and being part of activities taking place at the level of national science systems.

Assessing research excellence has been identified as one of the new critical work packages for SGCI-2, with cross-cutting dimension. It is well recognized that research excellence is integral and fundamental to the mandate of SGCs all over the world. In order to better appreciate and accurately measure the impact of their activities in funding and supporting national science and innovation systems, SGCs need to be conversant with but more importantly, have a clear understanding and capacity to evaluate and effectively deal with an evolving range of issues beyond those captured in traditional impact metrics.

Assessing Research Excellence by SGCs

Research excellence is integral to the mandate of SGCs all over the world. It is required at all stages of science — from planning and design, production to sharing, use and evaluation, and at each level there are new tools available to measure, promote and safeguard research excellence. These include research ethics, open and collaborative science, open access and Research Quality Plus (RQ+) among others. SGCs need to be familiar with an evolving range of issues beyond those captured in traditional impact metrics. These include legitimacy (whether research is gender transformative, its inclusiveness and engagement with national and local knowledge), importance (its originality and relevance) and positioning for use (accessibility of research data and analysis, actionability and scalability). SGCs’ ability to holistically assess research excellence within the contextual realities of African research ecosystems and within the context of evolving research excellence paradigms to accurately determine SGCs’ contributions and impact within national science systems is the central theme of this project activity. This work package is therefore intended to build capacity within SGCs’ by way of increasing their knowledge, enhancing their capacity in the use of relevant tools and practice of the different dimensions of research excellence. The desired outcome is the development and strengthening of the capacity of SGCs to measure, monitor, report and use research excellence metrics to further the attainment of the mandates of SGCs within their national science systems. This capacity development workstream envisages a paradigm shift from conventional research excellence measurement models which are generally anchored on developed countries’ perceptions of research excellence, norms, nuances, tenets, and practices. These are usually rooted within state-of-the-art, well-resourced research and development ecosystems, which are significantly different from the national science systems within which SGCs on the continent operate. It is expected that this paradigm shift would enable a positive disruption of traditional assessments for research excellence on the continent to reveal the true impact of SGCs’ and Africa’s contributions to research and development through a 360-degree approach to research excellence assessment. This approach is intended to capture all facets of research excellence delving into new and evolving areas that are not typically considered in conventional research excellence assessments, approaches and tools.

From the foregoing, the main objective of this training workshop is to develop and build capacity within SGCs to conduct robust research excellence assessments using the Research Quality (RQ+) framework conceived and developed by IDRC. In broad terms, the successful consultant is required to build on relevant and available reports from SGI-1, further engage with SGCs and build a refined profile of individual SGCs’ capacity needs in research excellence assessment, develop a comprehensive training content that mainly combines theoretical concepts and practical implementation, research excellence assessment tools but with main focus on of the RQ+. Other interrelated areas to consider are monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) outcomes, and a risk assessment and management framework to ensure that by the end of the training, SGCs are able to follow systematic processes in the design and implementation of research excellence assessment projects as part of their core operational mandates and activities. It is further expected that the successful consultant will develop a repository of research excellence resources and materials, provide full access to SGCs and ensure ongoing/post-training professional support or backstopping to SGCs to ensure overall successful knowledge transfer. The key outcomes of these activities will be strengthening and use of the RQ+ framework by each of the SGCs; improved processes of evaluating research excellence by the SGCs and strengthened national science systems in the participating countries.

The specific TORs for this task are outlined below:

Conduct specific needs assessments for capacity development for research excellence assessment for participating SGCs. This should include a survey of the SGCs, and a review of relevant reports on research excellence from SGCI-1 and other sources or resources to identify barriers, key gaps and enablers to research excellence assessment, including practices and protocols within individual SGCs. Any other approach deemed necessary by the consultant, bearing in mind time constraints and the general climate imposed on global business operations by the COVID-19 pandemic should be considered.

Develop training modules and implement/facilitate training and technical support on research excellence assessment, majorly focusing on the use of RQ+ as the preferred tool, and other relevant scientific practices to enable SGCs assess their portfolio of research projects and related activities.

Provide post-training technical support to the SGCs on research excellence assessment to ensure the development of a new culture in the assessment and reporting of research excellence assessments.

Develop training plans, and training evaluations/feedback, while training materials will be shared online.

Ensure at least two SGCs successfully assess their research activities using the RQ+ framework over the project duration and communicate their outcomes with key stakeholders.

Develop a repository of research excellence assessment resources and materials and provide full access to participating SGCs and ensure ongoing professional support or backstopping to ensure successful knowledge transfer. This should include webinar recordings and WhatsApp messages and other platforms that will be synthesized for dissemination.

Develop a risk assessment framework and a monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) framework for this project.

Indicators to Evaluate Consultant’s Performance

The quality and timely delivery of all required tasks as provided for in this term of reference to ensure the successful implementation of this work package.

The submission of monthly progress report summarising the services provided and progress made.

The submission of post-training evaluation report including an evaluation of the use of online resources by SGCs.

The submission of participating SGCs’ research excellence assessment reports using the RQ+ framework.

Desired Competences and Qualifications of Consultant/Service Provider

It is envisaged that the successful consultant would be a subject specialist in research excellence assessments with demonstrable experience in conducting research excellence assessments and trainings. More importantly, the successful consultant should have strong working knowledge and experience in the use of RQ+ in conducting research excellence assessments.

At least 5 years relevant and professional experience including extensive knowledge of research excellence assessments.

Knowledge of research management systems as well as national science systems.

Proven research excellence assessment skills and theoretical and practical knowledge of the use RQ+ and other comparable tools.

Proven and extensive experience in the development of training curricula and materials.

Multidisciplinary skills and the ability to communicate effectively.

Ability to work independently and as part of a team.

Sensitivity to national, political, gender and cultural balance.

A high standard of professionalism.

Technical skills or access thereof to create, evaluate and distribute online content.

Fluency in English (written and spoken) with excellent drafting and communication skills. Ability to communicate in French or Portuguese will be highly desirable.

Submission of Proposals

The AAU and the AAS invite suitably qualified consultants or service providers with advanced technical knowledge and experience in research excellence assessments in general and specifically, practical knowledge of the use of the RQ+ framework in conducting research excellence assessment to submit proposals for this exercise.

How to submit Proposal

Interested Consultants/Specialist/Service providers are requested to submit a detailed application outlining their qualifications and suitability for this task, including proposed solution, budgets and detailed workplan and timeline for completion of this task. Applications should be submitted online via the link: https://bit.ly/3kRUG09

Deadlines

The deadline for submission of the proposals is close of business on Friday, 30th October 2020.

Contact Information

If you have any queries concerning this opportunity, please contact the Association of African Universities Director of ICT Services & Knowledge Management, Ms Nodumo DHLAMINI, Email: rdickson@aau.org with a copy to teckpani@aau.org and to the Deputy Director of Programmes at African Academy of Sciences, Dr Alphonsus Neba, Email: a.neba@aasciences.africa

TITLE: LASU-ACEITSE commences interactive delivery of 6 courses

Professor Peter A. Okebukola, the Center Leader for the Africa Centre of Excellence for Innovative and Transformative STEM Education (LASU-ACEITSE) hosted by Lagos State University in Nigeria, reported that following the advice offered by the World Bank and AAU, he was setting up the interactive online delivery of 6 courses which are expected to begin in April 2020.

TITLE: USIEF’s Historical Landmarks

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
USIEF’s Historical Landmarks

1950

India’s first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, and U.S. Ambassador Loy Henderson sign the “Agreement Between the Government of India and the Government of the United States of America for Financing Certain Educational Exchange Programs,” which established the United States Educational Foundation in India (USEFI) to administer the Fulbright Program.

2008

India’s Foreign Secretary Mr. Shiv Shankar Menon and U.S. Ambassador Dr. David C. Mulford sign a new agreement, whereby India and the United States commit to fund the Fulbright Program as equal partners. USEFI is renamed USIEF (United States-India Educational Foundation), and the core programs become known as Fulbright-Nehru Fellowships to honor India’s first Prime Minister.

2011

USIEF announces call for applications for the U.S.-India 21st Century Knowledge Initiative grant program. The initiative aims to strengthen collaboration and build partnerships between U.S. and Indian institutions of higher education.

2020

USIEF celebrates 70 years of the Fulbright Program in India, showcasing the achievements and contributions of Fulbright alumni across diverse fields.

2021

USIEF celebrates the 75th anniversary of the Fulbright Program with an art exhibit titled “Reciprocation – American Fulbright Artists and India/ Collaborations & Connections.”

2023

USIEF celebrates the 45th anniversary of the Hubert H. Humphrey Fellowship Program by hosting a Global Policy Dialogue led by alumni, focusing on key international issues.

2025

USIEF celebrates 75 years of Fulbright Program in India.

2026

USIEF marks Fulbright 80th Anniversary and Freedom250 through alumni-led panels, seminars and public engagement events across cities in India.

TITLE: Arcadia Impact AI Governance Taskforce 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 31, 2026

Applications are open for the Arcadia Impact AI Governance Taskforce 2026. The AI Governance Taskforce is a 12-week, remote (global), part-time (8 hrs/wk) research programme for experienced professionals working to reduce catastrophic risks, acute and systemic, from advanced AI through policy and governance research. The programme is designed to be compatible with existing commitments.

Research Associates work in multidisciplinary teams of 4, led by a Research Team Leader and working with an expert partner who provides research direction and oversight. Expert partners are senior practitioners in AI safety and governance, contributing in a personal or organisational capacity, drawn from organisations such as the UK AI Security Institute (AISI), GovAI, the AI Incident Database (AIID), MIT’s AI Risk Initiative (AIRI), the Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR), SaferAI, The Future Society (TFS), the Future of Life Institute (FLI) and academia. The work produces policy-relevant research outputs and gives participants the credentials and connections to transition into work in the field.

Participants are not paid; this is a voluntary opportunity designed to support participants’ careers in frontier AI governance.

Eligibility

They look for highly motivated candidates who are driven to transition from established careers into frontier AI governance focused on reducing catastrophic risks, acute and systemic, from advanced AI.

They are interested in candidates from a range of backgrounds, disciplines and experience levels, including law, public policy, economics, other social science and humanities, management, political science, international relations, engineering (of various kinds, e.g. ML, software, mechanical, systems, safety), philosophy and computer science that can be brought to bear with direct or indirect relevance to the projects.

Requirements

Committed to a career reducing catastrophic and systemic risks from frontier AI. This programme is not about general AI risk, corporate AI compliance & AI ethics.

Able to commit at least 8 hours per week across the cohort dates, alongside your existing commitments

Willing to work in a small, structured, remote research team of four alongside a Research Team Leader and an expert partner

Application

For the Autumn 2026 cohort the process has three stages. No writing sample is required at any stage.

General application. Your CV and short written answers. They assess your motivation and readiness to move into the field, your situational awareness of frontier AI risk, your judgement about priorities and interventions, how your existing expertise transfers, your self-direction, and the clarity of your reasoning.

Project application. Shortlisted candidates are given project briefs, and invited to apply to the projects that fit them best, completing a short written task related to their chosen project.

Interview. A remote interview to get to know you, and expand on aspects of your application.

TITLE: University of Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence 2027: Applications Open for Interdisciplinary AI Doctoral Research

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the University of Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence, an interdisciplinary doctoral programme designed for researchers who want to advance artificial intelligence while keeping human needs, capabilities, ethics, governance and social impact at the centre of technological development.

Hosted by the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence (CHIA) within Cambridge’s Institute for Technology and Humanity (ITH), the programme brings together technical AI research with perspectives from the humanities, social sciences, health, ethics, policy and other human-centred disciplines. Its stated goal is to train a new generation of AI researchers, technologists and leaders capable of developing AI that is human-centred, human-compatible, responsible and socially and globally beneficial.

Research areas highlighted by Cambridge include:

Fundamental human-level AI

Social and interactive AI

Cognitive AI

Creative AI

Health and global AI

Responsible AI

The programme is particularly distinctive because it does not treat artificial intelligence as exclusively a computer science problem. Students are expected to engage with the technical, ethical, human, applied and industrial dimensions of AI, making the PhD suitable for ambitious interdisciplinary projects that combine computational research with questions about people and society.

Applications for Michaelmas 2027 entry opened on 9 September 2026.

The main application and course funding deadline is:

8 December 2026

The course is scheduled to begin on:

1 October 2027

Applicants seeking consideration in the Gates Cambridge U.S. round face an earlier funding deadline of:

14 October 2026.

About the Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence

The PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence has been created in response to the rapid expansion of AI across research, industry, government, civil society and everyday life.

Cambridge’s approach recognizes that the future of AI depends on more than increasing computational power or creating more sophisticated algorithms. AI systems interact with people, institutions, cultures and political and economic structures, raising difficult questions about:

Human behaviour

Trust

Responsibility

Governance

Creativity

Cognition

Health

Social interaction

Ethics

Safety

Global inequality

Technology’s effects on institutions and society

The programme therefore takes a deliberately interdisciplinary and cross-disciplinary approach to technical AI. Students are based at CHIA while also potentially working with researchers and facilities across other parts of the University of Cambridge.

Possible arrangements can include:

Cross-disciplinary supervision

Co-supervision

Participation in research seminars

Collaboration with other university units

Access to relevant facilities across Cambridge

The intention is to allow PhD researchers to build projects that are technically serious while also engaging deeply with the human implications of AI.

About the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence

The programme is based in the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence, or CHIA.

CHIA sits within the University of Cambridge’s Institute for Technology and Humanity and provides an interdisciplinary environment for researchers examining artificial intelligence from both technological and human perspectives.

PhD students become part of a broader academic community working on related questions and gain access to CHIA’s research events, seminars and early-career community.

This environment is central to the programme’s design. Cambridge emphasizes that students are not expected to conduct their doctoral research in isolation; they will participate in a wider community of researchers addressing overlapping problems in human-inspired AI.

What Does “Human-Inspired AI” Mean?

The programme’s emphasis on human-inspired AI reflects an approach to artificial intelligence that considers both:

What AI can learn from humans, and
How AI can be developed to work responsibly with and for humans.

This can involve questions about areas such as:

Human cognition

Human communication

Human creativity

Social interaction

Learning

Decision-making

Human-machine collaboration

AI governance

Ethics

Responsible innovation

A project might be technically computational while incorporating insights from psychology or cognitive science.

Another could examine interactive AI systems through technical design and human-computer interaction.

Other researchers might work on health AI, responsible AI or the governance and societal implications of advanced systems.

The programme therefore allows researchers to explore areas in which technical AI intersects with disciplines concerned with human beings, institutions and societies.

Research Areas

Cambridge specifically identifies several broad areas of research training.

Fundamental Human-Level AI

This area may involve foundational questions about AI systems and capabilities associated with forms of intelligence found in humans.

Research could engage with issues related to:

Learning

Reasoning

Decision-making

Generalization

Intelligence

Human-inspired computational mechanisms

Social and Interactive AI

AI increasingly interacts directly with individuals and groups.

Social and interactive AI can therefore involve research into systems capable of:

Communicating with people

Understanding social contexts

Cooperating with users

Supporting decision-making

Functioning in interactive environments

Such research can also raise questions about trust, communication, social behaviour and responsible system design.

Cognitive AI

Cognitive AI explores connections between artificial intelligence and human cognition.

Researchers may draw on areas such as:

Cognitive science

Psychology

Neuroscience

Computer science

Machine learning

to better understand or reproduce cognitive capabilities computationally.

Creative AI

Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of producing:

Text

Images

Music

Designs

Code

Multimedia

Creative AI research can therefore involve both technical development and wider questions about human creativity, collaboration, authorship and innovation.

Health and Global AI

The programme also identifies health and global AI as an important research area.

This may provide opportunities to investigate how AI can be designed and deployed across different healthcare and global contexts while paying attention to issues such as:

Access

Reliability

Equity

Safety

Representation

Human needs

Institutional differences

Responsible AI

Responsible AI is another core area.

This can encompass questions surrounding:

Ethics

Governance

Accountability

Safety

Fairness

Transparency

Human oversight

Social consequences

Cambridge specifically expects doctoral graduates to develop a critical perspective on governance and ethical challenges arising from human-inspired AI and to understand how those challenges interact with wider society.

What the PhD Is Designed to Develop

The programme aims to prepare researchers who can contribute critically and constructively to human-inspired AI.

According to Cambridge, students should develop the ability to:

Work at the frontier of academic research.

Understand advanced AI methods and applications.

Identify interdisciplinary research problems.

Develop technically and methodologically rigorous solutions.

Understand ethical and human dimensions of AI.

Work on complex problems affecting different sectors of society.

The programme therefore emphasizes both specialist expertise and the ability to move between disciplinary perspectives.

Who Might Benefit From the Programme?

Cambridge identifies several broad groups.

The programme may suit students who already want to specialize in human-inspired AI and deepen their:

Technical skills

Methodological skills

Critical research abilities

It may also suit researchers whose intellectual “home discipline” is elsewhere but who want to develop an advanced research project incorporating CHIA’s interdisciplinary approaches.

Finally, the programme is intended to prepare students for careers across:

Academia

Technology

Industry

Government

Public policy

Nonprofit organizations

Research institutions

Consulting

Programme Duration

The PhD can be undertaken:

Full-time: 3–4 years

or:

Part-time: 4–7 years.

It is classified as a research degree rather than a conventional taught doctoral programme.

The full-time course is therefore primarily centred on the student’s individual doctoral research project.

How the PhD Is Structured

Students conduct an individual research project on a topic agreed with CHIA under the guidance of their supervisor.

Although research is the programme’s core, students also participate in structured professional and intellectual development.

PhD researchers are expected to participate in:

Weekly student-led seminars or lab meetings

CHIA Early Career Community seminars during term

Poster presentations at CHIA events

At least one oral presentation at a weekly seminar each year

Students are additionally encouraged to present their research at:

Cambridge events

National conferences

International conferences

Additional Coursework

This is an entirely research-based PhD, but students may sometimes undertake additional academic training.

With supervisor approval, PhD students may be permitted to attend modules from the MPhil in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence when those modules provide useful technical preparation for the doctoral project.

Interdisciplinary researchers may also, where appropriate, audit research-methods classes in other departments.

This provides flexibility for candidates whose doctoral research requires skills outside their original academic discipline.

Supervision

Every PhD student is assigned:

A supervisor

At least one Academic Advisor

Cambridge indicates that supervisor and student are expected to meet individually for approximately 18 hours per year, with additional contact potentially occurring through laboratories, seminars and other research activities.

Supervision therefore combines individual guidance with participation in CHIA’s wider academic environment.

You Must Find a Prospective Supervisor Before Applying

This is one of the most important application requirements.

Applicants are required to contact a prospective supervisor before submitting the formal PhD application.

You should discuss your proposed research with that person and confirm that they are willing and able to accept new PhD students.

Applicants need to propose:

A research area

A topic

A potential supervisory relationship

At least one named supervisor must come from CHIA’s Primary Research Supervisor list.

Where appropriate, applicants may also propose co-supervision involving someone from the Potential Co-Supervisor list.

However, contacting a supervisor does not guarantee admission, and Cambridge notes that final supervisory arrangements are determined by CHIA.

Research Proposal Requirement

Applicants must submit a mandatory research proposal.

The proposal can be:

No more than two A4 pages.

Cambridge expects it to outline:

Intended research topic

Research strategy

Understanding of existing work

An area where new research is needed

Concrete objectives

First-year deliverables

A credible strategy for achieving those objectives

The research proposal may be discussed with the prospective supervisor before the formal application is submitted.

Relevant Experience Statement

Applicants must also complete a mandatory Relevant Experience section limited to:

2,000 characters.

Cambridge specifically asks applicants to explain how their skills and experience have prepared them for the programme’s:

Computational

Mathematical

Programming

components.

This is important because the programme may be interdisciplinary, but it remains a technical AI PhD.

Candidates coming from non-computer-science backgrounds should therefore clearly demonstrate sufficient quantitative and technical preparation.

Reasons for Applying

Applicants also provide a mandatory statement of up to:

1,500 characters

explaining their motivation for applying specifically to the PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence.

A strong response should therefore explain not simply why the applicant wants a PhD or wants to study AI, but why this particular interdisciplinary Cambridge programme is appropriate for the proposed research.

Academic Entry Requirements

Cambridge’s formal course requirements state that applicants should have achieved:

A First-class Honours Degree or international equivalent.

A master’s-level degree, or equivalent work experience or qualifications, is described as highly desirable.

Cambridge accepts applicants from a broad range of academic backgrounds, provided they can demonstrate substantial relevant preparation for the:

Computational

Mathematical

Programming

components of their proposed research.

Important Note on the Master’s Standard

The official Cambridge materials contain an additional statement worth noting.

The course overview says applicants are normally expected to hold a UK Master’s degree with Distinction or an equivalent international qualification. It also says applicants with a Master’s awarded at Merit or Pass level may still be considered if they can demonstrate exceptional relevant experience.

At the same time, the formal Requirements page states that a First-class Honours undergraduate degree is required and describes a master’s-level degree as “highly desirable.”

Prospective candidates whose qualifications do not fit the conventional pattern should therefore assess their credentials carefully and, if necessary, contact the course before applying.

All applications are ultimately considered on their individual merits.

English-Language Requirements

Applicants required to demonstrate English-language proficiency face demanding minimum standards.

IELTS Academic

Required overall score:

7.5

with at least:

Listening: 7.0

Writing: 7.0

Reading: 7.0

Speaking: 7.0

TOEFL Internet-Based Test

Required overall score:

110

with:

Listening: 25

Writing: 25

Reading: 25

Speaking: 25

Cambridge C1 Advanced

Applicants need:

Grade A or B, overall score 193, with no element below 185, plus a Language Centre assessment.

Cambridge C2 Proficiency

Accepted grades are:

A, B or C, with at least 200 overall and no element below 185.

ATAS Requirement for International Students

Cambridge states that applicants who require a visa will need an Academic Technology Approval Scheme (ATAS) certificate if offered admission.

Applicants should not apply for ATAS before receiving an offer.

The relevant CAH3 code needed for the ATAS application will be included in the offer letter.

Application Documents

Applicants should prepare the following:

Two references

Academic transcript

Degree certificate where applicable

CV or résumé

Evidence of English proficiency where required

Research proposal of no more than two A4 pages

Relevant Experience statement

Reasons for Applying statement

Cambridge also asks applicants to upload the grading key associated with their transcript if it is not already clearly included.

References must be submitted by the deadline.

An application is not considered complete until:

The application and documents have been submitted

Any applicable application fee has been paid

The required references have been received

Gates Cambridge Applicants

Applicants who wish to be considered for a Gates Cambridge Scholarship need additional documentation.

This includes:

A Gates Cambridge reference

A research proposal for PhD applicants

The special deadline for applicants in the Gates Cambridge U.S. round is:

14 October 2026.

Other applicants seeking Cambridge funding should pay particular attention to the general course funding deadline of:

8 December 2026.

Is the Cambridge Human-Inspired AI PhD Fully Funded?

Not automatically.

This distinction is important.

The official Finance page currently states:

TITLE: Press Release – Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) to Reward Quality, Applied Research and Innovation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
ACE Impact Launches its First Students Innovation Research Awards (SIRA)

Download the full Press Release from here – English & French

Accra, Ghana, September 15, 2022. The Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) project is announcing a call for applications for its first Students Innovation Research Awards (SIRA). SIRA recognizes and promotes excellent research and innovation which responds to Africa’s developmental challenges. Established by the Regional Facilitation Unit for ACE Impact, the Association of African Universities (AAU), with support from the World Bank, SIRA will deepen the project’s commitment to advancing the production of innovative and impactful knowledge.

The ACE Impact project aims to advance the quality, quantity, and access to post-graduate education within the region. Through this award scheme, the project will recognise exceptional research with both scientific and societal value undertaken by students from the 53 African Centres of Excellence. The practical and long-term impact of the research conducted is essential to the region’s most critical priority areas.

Students are at the heart of this project. As primary ambassadors, SIRA targets students to boost their interest in implementing the skills and knowledge acquired to drive national and regional development and growth. Submissions are accepted under the following thematic areas; health, power generation, and transmission, renewable energy, mining and extractives, sustainable urban planning and transport, sustainable agriculture, environmental sciences, education, and information and communication technology (ICT). For each thematic area, three awards (1st place, 2nd place, and 3rd place) will be presented.

Industry and development partners with an aligned vision to support and improve the next generation of Africa’s highly skilled workforce through mentorship, hands-on training, and funding, among other kinds of support, are invited to collaborate on the SIRA initiative.

Application Details: Only students enrolled in the 53 centres of excellence under the ACE Impact Project are qualified to make a submission under this award. Interested applicants are encouraged to visit https://sira.ace.aau.org/ for further information.

Application Deadline: 30th September 2022

Contact:

For further enquiries related to the Awards, please contact:

• Mr. Schneineda Ankomah via email skankomah@aau.org

• Mr. Enoch Kpaani via email tekpani@aau.org

For Enquiries by the Media, please contact:

• Mrs. Millicent Afriyie via email makyei@aau.org

For Partnership related information, please contact:

• Dr. Sylvia Mkandawire vía email smkandawire@aau.org

Background Information

The Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence (ACE) Project is a World Bank initiative in collaboration with governments of participating countries to support Higher Education Institutions specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Agriculture and Health, Environment, and Social/Applied Science and Education. It is the first World Bank project aimed at the capacity building of higher education institutions in Africa.

The project promotes increased specialization among participating universities, focusing on addressing specific common regional development challenges. It aims to strengthen the capacities of these universities to deliver high-quality training and applied research, closing the skills gap, and meeting the demand required for for Africa’s development. The first phase (ACE I) was launched in 2014 with 22 Centres of Excellence in Nine (9) West and Central African countries; Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, and Togo. The second phase (ACE II) was launched in East and Southern Africa with 24 centers across Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi,

Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia.

Based on the initial successes, the World Bank Group and the French Development Agency (AFD) in collaboration with the African governments, launched the ACE Impact Project in 2019 to further strengthen post-graduate training and applied research in existing fields and support new fields that are essential for Africa’s economic growth. There are 53 ACEs specializing in the broad thematic areas of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), Agriculture, Health, Environment, and Social/Applied Science and Education with a priority focus in sustainable cities; sustainable power and energy; social sciences and education; transport; population health and policy; herbal medicine development and regulatory sciences; public health; applied informatics and communication; pastoral production; entrepreneurship and innovation, among others.

Since its inception, more than 22,000 students have been enrolled under the ACE Impact project. This includes almost 3,000 PhD students, close to 10,000 MSc students, and over 10,000 students enrolled in professional short courses. As a regional initiative, student enrolment extends beyond the participating countries to other African countries including Burundi, and Gabon, among others.

In line with training and meeting the global research standards, the majority of programmes rolled out by the centres

are internationally accredited and centres are provided with enabling teaching, learning, and research environment and facilities, including state-of-the-art equipment and laboratories. For more information on the ACE Impact Project, visit https://ace.aau.org

TITLE: Press Release: Association of African Universities (AAU) set to Convene its 16th Quadrennial General Conference in Rabat Morocco

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Higher Education Stakeholders to Deliberate on Shaping the Future of Higher Education for Innovation and Sustainable Development in Africa

Accra, Ghana, March 12, 2025 – The Association of African Universities (AAU), the apex organization for higher education in Africa, is set to host its 16th Quadrennial General Conference (QGC) in Rabat, Morocco, from July 21st to 25th, 2025. This flagship event is proudly hosted by two esteemed Moroccan AAU member institutions: Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P) and Mohammed V University (UM5).

The General Conference, convened quadrennially, is the Association’s premier gathering, which brings together a diverse range of higher education stakeholders, including representatives of AAU member institutions, associate members, and observers. As the Association’s supreme governing body, the General Conference is responsible for shaping the AAU’s strategic direction and policy framework.

The AAU and its conference hosts invite a diverse range of stakeholders to participate in the Conference, including higher education leaders, such as Vice Chancellors and executive heads of institutions across Africa and beyond, and higher education administrative staff, including but not limited to: Deans, Registrars, ICT directors and officers, Internationalisation and Partnerships Officers. Invitation is also extended to the research and academic community, comprising researchers, educators, and academics. Additionally, development partners, including international organizations, and development institutions, are invited to participate, alongside policymakers, government officials, and ministers. Students and youth, including student leaders and representatives of youth organizations, are also encouraged to attend, as are private sector and industry partners, such as companies and industries interested in higher education and skills development.

Under the theme “Shaping the Future of Higher Education for Innovation and Sustainable Development in Africa,” the AAU 16th General Conference seeks to tackle the pressing challenges facing higher education in Africa. By exploring innovative solutions, it aims to create the platform for stakeholders to converge around key strategies to drive sustainable growth and development, ultimately transforming Africa’s higher education institutions to address the continent’s socio-economic challenges and realize the vision of Africa’s Agenda 2063.

The conference is guided by three core objectives: enhancing access and equity in higher education by reducing barriers to entry and improving retention rates; fostering research and innovation ecosystems by providing funding and support for innovative projects that address local and regional challenges; and integrating Sustainable Development Goals into curricula and institutional practices to ensure that education contributes to sustainable societal transformation.

The conference will delve into nine (9) sub-themes that support the main theme, exploring policy, governance, and advocacy for transforming higher education, as well as the role of artificial intelligence and technology-driven teaching in enhancing education quality. Additionally, the conference will examine curricula re-engineering and credit transfer systems, collaborative research and capacity building, and the impact of climate change on higher education. Furthermore, discussions will focus on the important topics of entrepreneurship skills and competencies, funding infrastructural development, indigenous knowledge and environmental preservation, and the contribution of higher education to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Further information on the theme and subthemes can be obtained from the Conference Concept Note available in Arabic, English, French, and Portuguese.

Professor Olusola Oyewole, Secretary General of the Association of African Universities said “The 16th Quadrennial General Conference promises to be a dynamic and engaging event, featuring a diverse range of activities, including scientific sessions, panel discussions, special sessions coordinated by partner institutions, exhibitions, and an award/recognition session. These sessions will provide a platform for stakeholders to share innovative insights, practical solutions, and best practices”. “The Association of African Universities (AAU) invites all individuals and institutions with aligned visions and interests in advancing higher education in Africa to participate in this momentous event”, he added.

To register or obtain more information about the 16th Quadrennial General Conference, please visit the conference website – https://events.aau.org/gencon/. We look forward to your participation and contributions to shaping the future of higher education in Africa.

Association of African Universities (AAU)

The Association of African Universities (AAU) | www.aau.org

The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organisation created by African universities to promote cooperation among them and between them and the international academic community. It is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 450 higher education institutions, and three regional offices – the North Africa Regional Office (NARO) in Cairo, Egypt; East Africa Regional Office (EARO) in Khartoum, Sudan; and the Southern Africa Regional Office in Zimbabwe (SARO) as well as continental offices hosted in Europe, USA, Latin America among others.
