TITLE: Career Tracking Survey of Doctoral Holders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PUBLICATIONS

Doctorate holders find intellectually satisfying jobs in academia, industry or government, but those in academia are least happy with job security

Wednesday 6 December, 2017 – ESF-Science Connect has published the report with the findings of its 2017 Career Tracking Survey of doctorate holders. The survey, focusing on doctoral graduates of the years 2010 to 2016, was launched in March 2017 and collected over 2,000 of responses, with a response rate of 23 %. The survey studied their employment situation, satisfaction levels, PhD skills utilisation and mobility patterns. This project built on the work of ESF Member Organisation Forum ‘European Alliance on Research Career Development’ (EARCD) and on an ESF pilot study Career tracking of Doctorate Holders (2014) completed in 2015.

Download the Report

The following nine universities and organisations participated in the survey: University of Maastricht, Technical University of Munich, Goethe Research Academy for Early Career Researchers (GRADE) at Goethe University Frankfurt, University of Bucharest, University of Split, University of Luxembourg, Institute of Science and Technology, Austria, and the AXA Research Fund, France. The project enables universities and organisations to monitor careers of their graduates and evaluate their doctoral training and career advice, but also to engage in a discussion on standards, measures and intended outcomes of doctoral training schemes and career development.

“As the central (post) graduate academy of Goethe University Frankfurt, one of our prime goals is to develop and continually improve our program and services so that early career researchers get the best start possible into their future careers at the university or beyond, in industry and society. The Career Tracking Survey coordinated by ESF-Science Connect provides a lot of inspiration and its results will be invaluable for us to achieve our goals”, said Dr. Sybille Küster, Managing Director, GRADE – Goethe Research Academy for Early Career Researchers, Goethe University Frankfurt am Main, Germany.

The findings across all partners included a very high employability of doctorate holders (95%) with a vast majority working as researchers (80%). Doctorate holders also experienced a relatively smooth transition into the job market, with 40 % of them already having a job at graduation, and those without, on average, having found one within four months.

However, the report shows that there is a major difference between academic and non-academic sectors in terms of permanent employment, which indicates a persistent structural problem within academia: only 50 % of those working in universities are permanently employed compared to, for instance, 95 % of those working in industry. University staff are least satisfied with their job security out of graduates in all other workplace categories. Looking at overall job satisfaction levels, doctorate holders working in industry are most satisfied with their jobs, while those working in hospitals and universities are the least satisfied.

About 34 % of all researchers are employed in post-doctorate positions and over 40% in other positions such as research fellows, specialists or Assistant Professors. “While post-doctorate positions are often meant to be temporary – the term “post-doctoral” is not a status, at best a temporal characterization, the lack of more permanent positions for researchers in their later career stages is less acceptable”, says Jean-Claude Worms, ESF Chief Executive.

The majority of respondents work in jobs that are at least partly related to their PhD and are similarly well satisfied with the intellectual challenge offered by their job, whether they work in academia, industry or government.

Overall, respondents see their doctorate as an added value and would do it again if they had to restart their career. However, those engaged in research reported feeling better prepared for their jobs after their doctorate completion than those who took other jobs. The report findings also suggest that organisations could pay more attention to transferable skills training, which are of use both in academia and elsewhere (e.g. communication, networking or project management). This seems especially important since nearly 40 % of researchers are planning to change to a non-research career in the next three years. “Although universities are not the only institutions responsible for ensuring employability of PhDs, they need to adapt their curricula and strategies to help their doctorate holders be even better prepared for professional careers outside academia”, added Jean-Claude Worms.

Among the respondents, a dominant share (60 %) are currently working in the academic field, although it varies across participating organisations (e.g. among the PhD graduates from Technical University of Munich, there are only 35 % who work in academia and nearly 50 % are in industry and other business sector). As the report discusses, growing numbers of doctorate holders in Europe, paucity of permanent positions in academia and low level of transfer to other employment sectors call for more attention on more career guidance informing of alternative career choices.

“We are currently launching a call for universities and research performing organisations to take part in the 2018 survey. There is a clear benefit to continue and scale up career tracking surveys so that we can provide reliable and comparable data to more partner organisations thus building up the benchmarking capacity of the project”, says Julia Boman, Science Officer in charge of career tracking activities at ESF-Science Connect.

TITLE: How to Start a Career in Mental Health Counseling

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mental health counseling is a meaningful career for people who want to help others through some of life’s hardest moments. Counselors support individuals facing anxiety, grief, trauma, depression, relationship conflict, and other challenges that can affect daily life. The profession calls for education, supervised training, licensure, and emotional commitment, but it can also offer purpose, flexibility, and long-term stability.

For people drawn to listening, guidance, and personal connection, this field is worth serious consideration. Understanding what counselors do, what training is needed, and which career paths are available can help you decide whether this profession fits your strengths and goals.

Getting Started

Many people become interested in counseling because they want to make a direct difference in someone’s life. If you have already started exploring the education required to be a mental health counselor, you are already taking an important first step.

Mental health counselors do much more than give advice. Their job is to help clients understand emotions, behaviors, and experiences while developing healthier ways to cope. Some clients seek counseling after a loss, divorce, or personal crisis. Others are dealing with long-term stress, unresolved trauma, or emotional pain that has built over time.

One of the rewarding parts of this work is that progress looks different for every client. For one person, improvement may mean returning to work, school, or social activities. For another, it may simply mean getting through a difficult week with better coping skills. In counseling, both major breakthroughs and smaller steps forward matter.

What Counselors Really Do

At the center of the job is careful listening, thoughtful questioning, and guided conversation. Effective counselors are not passive observers. They help clients identify patterns, set realistic goals, and practice habits that support emotional well-being.

On a typical day, a mental health counselor may meet with clients individually to discuss panic, anger, sadness, trauma, stress, or relationship struggles. They may teach coping strategies, help clients challenge harmful thought patterns, and encourage practical tools clients can use between sessions.

The work also includes responsibilities beyond face-to-face counseling. Counselors document sessions, track client progress, maintain accurate records, and follow legal, ethical, and privacy standards. Depending on the setting, they may also coordinate care with family members, physicians, teachers, or community providers.

This balance of empathy and structure is one of the profession’s defining features. Counselors create a safe space where clients feel heard, but they also guide them toward meaningful change.

Skills That Matter

You do not need to be perfect to become a strong counselor, but several qualities are essential. Empathy is one of the most important. Clients need to feel respected, understood, and emotionally safe, especially when discussing painful or deeply personal experiences.

Patience matters as well. Progress in counseling is rarely quick or predictable. Some clients open up right away and make steady gains, while others need time to trust the process. A good counselor remains supportive even when progress feels slow.

Communication skills are equally important. Counselors must know how to ask useful questions, explain ideas clearly, and pay attention not only to what clients say but also to what they avoid saying. Active listening, emotional awareness, and thoughtful responses help build a productive therapeutic relationship.

Professionalism and resilience are also critical. Counselors hear difficult stories on a regular basis, so they need strong boundaries and healthy ways to manage stress. Caring deeply is part of the work, but protecting your own mental well-being is necessary for long-term success.

Education and Training

The path into mental health counseling usually begins with a bachelor’s degree. Many students major in psychology, social work, human services, or a related field. Undergraduate study builds a foundation in human development, behavior, and mental health concepts.

After earning a bachelor’s degree, most future counselors complete a graduate degree in counseling or a closely related discipline. Graduate programs provide more specialized training in counseling theories, ethics, assessment, diagnosis, and treatment approaches for different populations and concerns.

A major part of this preparation is supervised clinical experience. Through practicum and internship placements, students begin working with real clients under the guidance of experienced professionals. These hands-on experiences are essential because they connect classroom learning to actual practice.

After graduation, licensure requirements vary by state or region. Many areas require candidates to pass a licensing exam, complete a set number of supervised post-graduate hours, and meet approved educational standards. Because requirements differ depending on where you plan to work, it is wise to research local rules early.

Choosing the Right Program

Not every counseling program will fit your goals, schedule, or budget, so comparison is important. Accreditation should be one of the first factors you evaluate. An accredited program meets recognized standards and may make the licensure process more straightforward.

Flexibility is another major consideration. If you are balancing work, family, or other responsibilities, online, hybrid, or evening options may make graduate school more manageable.

Practicum and internship support also deserves close attention. A strong program should help students secure quality supervised placements that provide meaningful clinical experience.

Other factors to compare include tuition, faculty experience, class size, and program focus. Some programs lean more toward school counseling, while others emphasize clinical mental health counseling. Choosing a program that aligns with your long-term plans can make your education more useful and effective.

Career Paths to Explore

One of the profession’s greatest strengths is flexibility. Mental health counselors can work in schools, community clinics, hospitals, nonprofit organizations, and private practice.

In schools, counselors may support students facing academic pressure, behavioral concerns, family issues, or emotional difficulties. In community clinics, they often work with people managing anxiety, depression, addiction, trauma, or financial stress.

Hospital-based roles may involve short-term counseling during crises, psychiatric emergencies, or major medical events. Nonprofit organizations may focus on specific groups such as teenagers, veterans, or underserved families. Private practice can offer more independence, though it often comes after gaining experience and meeting full licensure requirements.

Each setting has its own pace and demands. Some environments are fast-moving and crisis-focused, while others allow for longer-term relationship building. That variety gives counselors the chance to find a work setting that matches both their personality and professional strengths.

Questions to Ask Yourself

Before committing to this path, it helps to reflect honestly. Do you enjoy helping people without needing to control the outcome? Can you stay calm when someone is grieving, angry, or emotionally overwhelmed?

TITLE: Council of Europe EYF Grants 2027: Up to €60,000 for International Long-Term Youth Cooperation Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The European Youth Foundation of the Council of Europe is inviting proposals for international long-term youth cooperation projects beginning in 2027. Through call reference 2027.C6.B, eligible international youth organisations and international networks can request grants of up to €60,000 to implement projects that strengthen democracy, human rights, peaceful and inclusive societies, international solidarity and quality youth work.

The funding is intended for substantial projects lasting up to 18 months. Each proposal must combine at least one international in-person meeting of young people with other connected activities, which may include campaigns, advocacy, research, educational-resource production, capacity development, local actions, regional initiatives and multiplier activities.

The European Youth Foundation, commonly known as the EYF, has announced an indicative total budget of €600,000 for the call. It expects to award approximately 10 grants, each worth no more than €60,000.

However, this is an intention rather than a guarantee. The Foundation may award fewer grants, leave part of the budget unallocated or redistribute the available resources depending on the quality and number of proposals received.

Applications must be submitted through the EYF online grant-management system by October 1, 2026, at 23:59.

Applicants should note a time-zone discrepancy in the official material. The main call text and online call page use CET, while the indicative timetable uses CEST. Because the CEST interpretation produces an earlier UTC cutoff, organisations should treat 23:59 CEST on October 1, 2026 as the safer deadline and submit well in advance. Late applications will not be considered.

Prospective applicants should carefully examine the official call for proposals, the questions and answers updated on August 28, 2026 and the Guide to the Grants of the European Youth Foundation before submitting an application.

About the European Youth Foundation

The European Youth Foundation is a Council of Europe fund established in 1972 to support youth-led civil society initiatives. Its mission is to promote peace, understanding and international cooperation among young people while advancing human rights, democracy and fundamental freedoms.

The Council of Europe is an international organisation headquartered in Strasbourg, France. It has 46 member states and is institutionally separate from the European Union.

The EYF works within the Council of Europe’s youth sector and provides grants to non-governmental youth organisations whose activities reflect Council of Europe standards, priorities and values.

According to the European Youth Foundation’s official overview, its work is built around:

Youth autonomy

Non-formal education and learning

European awareness

International solidarity

Democratic participation

Human rights

Peace and cooperation among young people

This 2027 call is specifically intended to fund long-term international youth cooperation. It does not provide personal financial assistance to individual applicants. Instead, it finances eligible youth organisations to design and implement structured projects involving young people.

Purpose of the 2027 Long-Term Youth Cooperation Call

The call seeks to support international projects that promote understanding and solidarity across borders while contributing to human rights and democracy.

A competitive proposal should address several of the following objectives rather than operating as an isolated event.

Strategic Development of Youth Organisations

Projects may help an applicant organisation, its members and its wider network improve their long-term strategies, methods and institutional capacity in areas connected to EYF priorities.

The project should leave the organisation stronger and better able to continue meaningful youth work after the grant ends.

Strategic development may involve:

Improving governance and youth participation

Developing new organisational strategies

Strengthening international networks

Establishing new cooperation mechanisms

Improving advocacy capacity

Developing sustainable educational methods

Strengthening monitoring and evaluation

Increasing the organisation’s ability to reach excluded young people

Capacity Building and Knowledge Development

The EYF is interested in proposals that develop practical knowledge and capacity within youth organisations.

Possible outputs include:

Youth-work tools and methodologies

Training resources

Manuals and guides

Research reports

Policy recommendations

Advocacy materials

Educational publications

Digital learning resources

Websites and online platforms

Videos or podcasts

Facilitator resources

Replicable non-formal education methods

Outputs should not be produced merely to satisfy a project requirement. Applicants should explain who will use each output, how it responds to a defined need and how it will support longer-term change.

Long-Term Partnerships and Cross-Border Cooperation

Projects can foster strategic relationships among young people and youth organisations across national borders.

The emphasis is on sustained cooperation, shared learning and coordinated action rather than bringing participants together once without a continuation plan.

A strong project may establish:

Long-term cooperation between youth organisations

Shared advocacy platforms

Cross-border learning networks

Joint research or policy initiatives

Youth-led communities of practice

Regional or international follow-up structures

Continued exchange of methods and resources

Knowledge and Skills for Young People

Proposals may strengthen young people’s:

Knowledge of democracy and human rights

Intercultural understanding

Advocacy capacity

Leadership ability

Research and policy skills

Confidence and participation

Media literacy

Digital citizenship

Peacebuilding competence

Ability to organise collective action

The application should explain what young people will learn and how they will apply that learning after participating.

Multiplier Actions and Wider Outreach

The call encourages projects that extend beyond their direct participants.

Educational, awareness-raising, advocacy and cooperation activities may operate at local, national and international levels. Applicants should explain how project knowledge and results will reach additional young people, communities, institutions or decision-makers.

Multiplier actions may include:

Local workshops

Community events

National advocacy campaigns

Training delivered by project participants

Public-awareness activities

Policy meetings

Digital campaigns

Educational-resource distribution

Peer-learning events

Local or regional action grants

Four EYF Funding Priorities for 2024-2027

Every proposal must connect credibly with the Council of Europe’s youth-sector priorities.

Applicants should avoid simply repeating the name of a priority. They must demonstrate how the project responds to a defined challenge, uses relevant Council of Europe standards and produces meaningful results.

The four priorities are explained on the official EYF Youth Sector Priorities page.

Priority One: Revitalising Pluralistic Democracy

This priority includes work that:

Protects young people’s freedom to assemble.

Supports the right to form, join and participate in associations.

Expands civic space for youth organisations.

Removes barriers to youth participation in political processes.

Strengthens youth involvement in public decision-making.

Develops young people’s understanding of artificial intelligence and its democratic effects.

Supports youth participation in artificial-intelligence and internet-governance processes.

Builds the capacity of youth organisations to involve young people in local decision-making.

Gives particular attention to rural youth, minorities and vulnerable groups.

Examines the impact of climate change and environmental degradation on young people and democracy.

Advances young people’s right to a healthy environment.

A democracy-focused proposal should move beyond general civic education. It should identify a genuine barrier to participation or democratic life and explain how young people will analyse, challenge or help remove it.

Priority Two: Young People’s Access to Rights

Projects under this priority may focus on:

Human rights education with and for young people.

Media literacy for children and young people.

Awareness of legal, civic and social rights.

Advocacy for implementing Council of Europe standards on young people’s access to rights.

Social rights for young people living in disadvantaged neighbourhoods.

Practical action enabling marginalised groups to exercise rights that formally exist but remain difficult to access.

Access to information about rights and available services.

Capacity building for young rights advocates.

Strong proposals should identify the difference between recognising a right in principle and enabling young people to exercise that right in practice.

Priority Three: Living Together in Peaceful and Inclusive Societies

This priority covers initiatives addressing:

Discrimination, racism and exclusion, including structural discrimination.

Roma youth participation and antigypsyism.

Inclusion of young refugees and their transition to adulthood.

Multiple discrimination and intersectionality.

Gender equality.

Sexual orientation and gender identity.

Disability inclusion.

Intercultural dialogue.

Peacebuilding and conflict transformation.

Cooperation with neighbouring countries and other world regions.

Participation and inclusion of young people in rural communities.

Mental health and well-being.

Personal development for young refugees and young people affected by war.

Inclusion of young people facing multiple forms of discrimination.

Projects should centre the participation, leadership and agency of the young people concerned rather than treating them solely as passive beneficiaries.

Priority Four: Youth Work

The youth-work priority includes:

Advocacy for recognition and support of youth work.

Action connected to Council of Europe standards on youth work.

Improving the quality and recognition of non-formal education.

Improving non-formal learning practices.

Strengthening capacity-building methodologies.

Developing the skills of youth workers.

Building the institutional capacity of youth organisations.

Supporting youth work in war zones and conflict-affected areas.

Applicants should explain how their methods reflect youth participation, non-formal education, intercultural learning and human rights education.

Activities That Can Be Funded

This is a long-term project grant, so an application should present a connected sequence of activities contributing to shared objectives.

Eligible formats may include:

International youth meetings

Training courses

Seminars and workshops

Youth exchanges or structured learning meetings that are not school exchanges

Campaigns

Advocacy initiatives

Research and evidence gathering

Production of educational materials

Toolkits and manuals

Policy outputs

Local follow-up activities

Regional initiatives

Community engagement

Awareness-raising actions

Digital multiplier activities

In-person multiplier activities

Evaluation and dissemination work

The project should not consist of a loose list of unrelated events. Each activity should contribute logically to the proposed objectives, results and longer-term impact.

Mandatory Four-Day International Meeting

At least one project activity must be an international meeting of young people lasting at least four programme days.

The EYF’s August 2026 questions and answers clarify that this four-day programme must be conducted in person.

Online preparation, follow-up and evaluation can form part of the broader project cycle. However, online sessions do not replace the compulsory in-person international programme.

The meeting must involve participants residing in at least seven Council of Europe member states.

The Q&A also clarifies that the seven-country requirement refers to participants’ countries of residence. Those countries do not all need to be represented by formal partner organisations.

Participant Requirements

For the majority of relevant project activities, participants must meet the following conditions:

Participants must reside in at least seven Council of Europe member states.

Country representation must be adequate and reasonably balanced.

At least 75% of counted participants must be aged 30 or younger.

The project must pay attention to the inclusion of young people with disabilities.

Gender equality must be incorporated into the project.

The social inclusion of young people must be actively considered.

These are mandatory conditions. Applications that fail to comply will not be considered.

The official Q&A provides several important interpretations:

Balanced geographical representation is preferred.

If a few countries have considerably larger groups, the project design should justify the imbalance.

A similar number of participants from each country is presented as a useful rule of thumb.

Balanced participation should support meaningful follow-up in each national context.

Project-team members, trainers and facilitators do not count toward the seven-country requirement.

Team members, trainers and facilitators do not count when calculating whether 75% of participants are aged 30 or younger.

The project team must still be multicultural.

A multicultural project team is generally expected to include members from at least four countries.

Participants from non-member states may be included when justified.

Non-member-state participants do not count toward the required seven Council of Europe countries.

The Q&A does not impose a specific percentage cap on participants from non-member countries.

The applicant must explain why non-member-country participants are relevant in the participant-profile section.

Project activities should, as a general rule, take place in one or more of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states.

Project Duration and Implementation Period

Projects must begin between January 1 and March 31, 2027.

The maximum project duration is 18 months, and the latest permitted end date is September 30, 2028.

The application should include the complete project implementation period, covering:

The official project start

Preparation

Delivery of activities

Follow-up

Evaluation

Multiplier work

Completion of project expenditure

A project completed before the application is submitted will be automatically excluded under the non-retroactivity principle.

Final narrative and financial reports must be submitted within two months after the project ends and no later than November 30, 2028.

Grant Amount and Available Budget

An eligible applicant may request up to €60,000.

The budget must be:

Consistent with the narrative proposal

Accurate

Clear

Complete

Cost-effective

Proportionate to planned activities

Connected to expected results

The indicative total budget for the call is €600,000.

The EYF intends to select approximately 10 projects at a maximum of €60,000 each. It retains discretion over the final number of projects and the distribution of available funds.

Co-Financing Requirement

Every successful organisation must contribute to its project through its own resources or contributions from third parties.

Co-financing may include:

Direct financial contributions

Staff time

Volunteer time

Donated services

Use of premises

Organisational resources

Other properly valued in-kind contributions

The official Q&A states that there is no minimum co-financing percentage.

In-kind contributions are accepted based on a declaration of honour. Nevertheless, applicants should present co-financing transparently and avoid inflated or unsupported valuations.

Projects must also avoid double funding. The same cost, staff time or activity period cannot be charged simultaneously to the EYF and another donor.

Where staff time is included, the Q&A suggests a calculation such as:

Gross salary divided by the number of working days, multiplied by the number of days worked on the project.

Grantee organisations may be audited based on the declarations contained in their applications and reports.

How the Grant Is Paid

The grant is scheduled to be distributed in two stages:

Initial payment: 80% after the grant agreement between the successful organisation and the European Youth Foundation is signed.

Final payment: the remaining balance after the Council of Europe accepts the final narrative and financial reports.

The final grant amount remains subject to satisfactory implementation and reporting. Unsupported, ineligible or improperly documented expenditure may not be accepted.

Because 20% is retained until reporting is approved, applicants should consider whether they have sufficient cash flow to complete the project.

General Eligible-Cost Principles

The EYF grant guide explains that eligible costs should:

Appear in the approved estimated budget.

Be incurred by the grantee during the official implementation period.

Be necessary for the project.

Be identifiable and verifiable.

Be recorded in the organisation’s accounts.

Comply with applicable tax and social-security legislation.

Be reasonable and justified.

Follow sound financial-management principles.

Demonstrate value for money.

Be supported by original documents or certified copies where required.

The general guide permits indirect eligible costs under applicable project-grant rules. It also describes separate arrangements for disability-related accessibility expenditure through the Equal Access Fund.

Applicants should follow the budget template issued specifically for call 2027.C6.B and confirm any additional accessibility-funding mechanism before relying on it.

The guide requires organisations to retain original financial and project evidence for at least 10 years because grants may be audited during or after implementation.

Ineligible Activities

The following activities are expressly excluded:

Commercial or profit-making operations

Purchase of land or buildings

Construction of buildings

Renovation of buildings

Purchase of fixed equipment for buildings

Tourism activities

Scholarships

Sports events and competitions

School exchanges

Activities forming part of a school curriculum

Activities forming part of a university programme

Activities with a strictly vocational character

Projects unrelated to Council of Europe priorities, standards, approaches or resources

Statutory meetings of youth organisations

The Q&A clarifies that voluntary extracurricular work involving secondary-school student parliaments may be eligible. Projects may also train young people to mentor such student parliaments.

The important distinction is that participation must remain voluntary and extracurricular rather than being part of a formal school programme.

A project may also build upon the methodology, results or network of an existing Erasmus+ initiative if it:

Demonstrates additional value for EYF priorities.

Introduces complementary activities.

Does not duplicate costs.

Does not charge the same work to two donors.

Organisations That Can Apply

Direct applications are restricted to organisations registered with the EYF as:

An international non-governmental youth organisation; or

An international network of non-governmental youth organisations.

Individuals, national NGOs, local NGOs, informal groups and universities cannot apply as lead applicants under call 2027.C6.B.

The updated Q&A expressly confirms that a national NGO cannot serve as the lead applicant.

A formal partnership is not compulsory. An eligible international organisation or network can implement the project itself.

Other institutions may be included as partners where relevant, including:

National youth NGOs

Local organisations

Universities

Public authorities

Research institutions

Civil society organisations

Specialist service providers

Their role must be clearly explained. Participation as a partner does not make an otherwise ineligible organisation eligible to submit the lead application.

Organisational Requirements

An applicant must:

Be registered and validated in the EYF online grant-management system under an eligible international category.

Have a bank account capable of receiving euros.

Have stable and sufficient financial resources.

Be able to maintain its activities throughout the grant period.

Contribute financial, human or in-kind resources.

Possess sufficient operational and professional capacity.

Have appropriate staff and volunteers.

Demonstrate the ability to manage an international project.

The EYF grant guide further explains that a youth organisation seeking registration should generally:

Be non-governmental.

Operate on a non-profit basis.

Have its own statute and governance rules.

Demonstrate democratic governance.

Provide meaningful opportunities for youth participation.

Focus primarily on youth-related activities.

Work for and with young people.

Be youth-led in relation to programmes and budgets.

Include people aged 15-30 as the vast majority of its members.

Work in accordance with Council of Europe principles and values.

Be established in a country participating in the European Youth Foundation.

An international youth NGO should normally:

Have legal personality defining its international nature.

Be established in an EYF member country.

Have at least seven member or affiliated youth organisations.

Have those members located in at least seven EYF member countries.

Carry out activities primarily of a multilateral nature.

Work actively and substantially with its members.

Demonstrate that members participate in governance, strategy and project implementation.

An international network may lack separate legal personality. However, it should:

Have a statute or explicit agreement among members.

Have credible governance arrangements.

Have at least seven member or affiliated youth organisations.

Cover at least seven EYF member countries.

Designate a headquarters organisation.

Conduct primarily multilateral activities.

Demonstrate sustained cooperation.

Show shared strategies, resources or funding among members.

Registration Is Required Before Applying

Only organisations registered and validated by the EYF can submit a proposal.

Unregistered organisations must create an account and submit an organisation-registration request through the Support4Youth grant-management system.

The call warns that registration may take up to two weeks.

An unregistered but otherwise eligible organisation should begin registration immediately. Waiting until the final two weeks creates a serious risk that validation will not be completed before the call closes.

Monitoring and evaluation

Define Measurable Results

Applicants should distinguish between:

Activities

Outputs

Results

Longer-term impact

Explain what will change, who will experience that change, how progress will be measured and what evidence will be collected.

Explain Country Representation

Provide a credible recruitment plan involving at least seven member states.

If participation is uneven, explain the reason and demonstrate how meaningful follow-up will take place in all represented countries.

Prevent Double Funding

Map each requested and co-financed cost to its funding source.

Staff time, travel, venue costs, services and activities must never be charged twice.

Assess Cash-Flow Capacity

Because 20% of the grant is retained until reporting is accepted, the organisation should consider whether it can manage project cash flow and any delayed reimbursement.

Complete Registration First

An excellent proposal cannot be submitted if the organisation’s registration has not been validated.

Registration should be treated as the first operational deadline.

Submit Early

Early submission reduces the risks associated with:

Platform problems

Registration delays

Missing attachments

Incomplete forms

Internal approvals

The official CET and CEST discrepancy

Applicants should not plan to upload their applications during the final hours.

Common Reasons an Application May Fail

The lead applicant is a national or local NGO.

The applicant is not an eligible international organisation or network.

The organisation is not registered and validated before the deadline.

The project does not include the mandatory four-day in-person international meeting.

Fewer than seven member-state countries are represented.

The participant age profile does not meet the 75% requirement.

Team members are incorrectly counted as participants.

Activities are disconnected.

The project resembles a one-off event rather than a long-term process.

Alignment with Council of Europe priorities is weak.

The budget is incomplete or unrealistic.

The budget conflicts with the narrative.

Co-financing is omitted.

The same costs are assigned to multiple donors.

The proposed project is commercial or profit-making.

Activities are tourism-focused, curricular or strictly vocational.

The application is incomplete.

Duplicate versions of the same proposal are submitted.

The application is submitted after the deadline.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the maximum grant?

Eligible organisations may request up to €60,000 for one project.

How many projects are expected to receive funding?

The EYF intends to award approximately 10 grants from an indicative €600,000 budget. It may change the number or distribution of awards.

Can an individual apply?

No. The applicant must be an eligible international youth NGO or international network registered with the EYF.

Can a national NGO apply as the lead?

No. National NGOs cannot apply as lead applicants under this call. They may participate as partners in a project led by an eligible international organisation or network.

Are formal partner organisations required in all seven countries?

No. The seven-country test concerns participants’ countries of residence. Each country does not require a formal partner organisation.

Can participants from outside Council of Europe member states join?

Yes, if their participation is justified.

However, those countries do not count toward the minimum seven member states. The Q&A establishes no specific percentage cap but requires the applicant to explain their participation.

What percentage of participants must be young people?

At least 75% of counted participants must be aged 30 or younger.

Project-team members, trainers and facilitators are excluded from this calculation.

Can the four-day international meeting be held online?

No. The required four-day programme must be conducted in person.

Online preparation, follow-up and evaluation may form part of the wider project.

Is co-financing compulsory?

Yes. However, the Q&A does not establish a minimum percentage.

Financial contributions, staff time, volunteer support and in-kind resources may be used.

Can the project build upon an Erasmus+ initiative?

Potentially. It must demonstrate added value for EYF priorities and cannot duplicate activities or costs already financed by Erasmus+ or another donor.

In which languages can the application be submitted?

Applications must be submitted in English or French.

What is the deadline?

Applications must be submitted by October 1, 2026, at 23:59.

Because the official materials inconsistently use CET and CEST, applicants should use 23:59 CEST as the safer interpretation and submit earlier.

Conclusion

The Council of Europe European Youth Foundation call for international long-term youth cooperation projects offers significant assistance to youth-led organisations seeking to strengthen democracy, human rights, inclusion, peace and youth work across borders.

With funding of up to €60,000 and a possible 18-month implementation period, the programme can support considerably more than a single international meeting. It is designed for connected projects that build organisational capacity, develop partnerships, equip young people with knowledge and skills, produce useful resources and extend their impact through advocacy, education and multiplier action.

The opportunity is also highly structured. Only eligible international youth organisations and international networks registered with the EYF can apply directly.

Projects must include an in-person international meeting lasting at least four programme days, involve participants residing in at least seven Council of Europe member states, and ensure that at least 75% of counted participants are aged 30 or younger.

Applicants must also present a realistic budget, provide co-financing, prevent double funding and maintain adequate administrative and financial controls.

Organisations should begin by verifying their EYF registration category, confirming that their bank accounts can accept euros, and assessing their ability to manage an international project and its reporting obligations.

They should then build their proposals around a demonstrated youth need, meaningful youth leadership, clear results and strong alignment with the Council of Europe’s youth-sector priorities.

The application deadline is October 1, 2026, at 23:59. Because registration can take up to two weeks and the official documents contain a CET and CEST inconsistency, waiting until the deadline creates unnecessary risk.

Eligible organisations should register, clarify uncertainties and submit their narrative and budget documents as early as possible.

TITLE: WACA Student Scholars Program 2026: Fully Funded National Conference Opportunity for Undergraduate Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Affairs Councils of America (WACA) Student Scholars Program 2026 offers undergraduate students an exceptional opportunity to gain firsthand exposure to careers in international affairs, global policy, diplomacy, and world affairs. The program is designed to create pathways into careers in world affairs while encouraging students to develop a lifelong interest in international issues. Through the program, 25 undergraduate students from WACA Council communities will be selected to attend the WACA National Conference at no cost. In addition to conference participation, WACA supports the costs associated with students’ travel, room, and board, giving selected scholars the opportunity to participate in a major national gathering without having to carry the full financial burden themselves. The program also includes Scholar Day, an exclusive Washington, DC experience that allows participating students to explore the world of international affairs beyond the conference itself. Students can visit think tanks, embassies, international organizations, and other institutions connected to global affairs. For students considering careers in diplomacy, international relations, public policy, government, international development, economics, security, nonprofit organizations, journalism, or related fields, the WACA Student Scholars Program can provide valuable exposure, professional connections, and a clearer understanding of possible career pathways.

About the WACA Student Scholars Program

The Student Scholars Program was established in 2010 with generous support from the Malú and Carlos Alvarez Family. Since its creation, the initiative has focused on connecting undergraduate students with the broader world affairs community and helping them explore educational and professional opportunities related to international affairs. The program is built around the idea that meaningful exposure to world affairs can help students make informed decisions about their academic and professional futures.

Rather than limiting participation to classroom learning, WACA provides scholars with opportunities to interact with institutions, professionals, and other students who share an interest in global issues.

The program therefore combines:

National conference participation

Professional and educational exposure

Washington, DC institutional visits

Networking opportunities

Career exploration

International affairs education

Engagement with the WACA Council network

What Does the Student Scholars Program Offer?

Selected scholars receive substantial support to participate in the WACA National Conference and related activities.

1. Attendance at the National Conference

WACA selects 25 undergraduate students from Council communities to participate in the National Conference.

The selected students attend the conference at no cost, allowing them to engage with the program without paying the standard conference participation costs.

The National Conference brings students into an environment focused on world affairs and provides opportunities to learn from people working across the international affairs field.

2. Travel and Lodging Support

WACA provides $1,250 to the nominating Council to help defray the Scholar’s travel and lodging expenses.

The funding is intended to help cover:

Travel-related costs

Lodging expenses

Double-occupancy accommodation

The participating Council is responsible for arranging the student’s transportation and hotel reservations.

Importantly, hotel arrangements must cover attendance for all three days of the National Conference.

WACA also helps Councils identify potential roommates by sharing the list of accepted Scholars with sponsoring Councils.

3. Scholar Day in Washington, DC

One of the distinctive elements of the program is Scholar Day, an exclusive excursion designed specifically for Student Scholars.

During this experience, students have the opportunity to explore Washington, DC institutions connected to international affairs.

Potential visits include:

Think tanks

Embassies

International organizations

Other institutions involved in global affairs and policy

This experience can help students move beyond theoretical classroom discussions and see how international affairs operates in professional and institutional settings.

4. Career and Academic Exploration

The program is designed to help students “map their global futures.”

By meeting professionals and visiting organizations involved in international affairs, students can gain a better understanding of potential career directions.

The experience may be particularly valuable for students interested in areas such as:

International relations

Diplomacy

Foreign policy

Global development

International economics

Public policy

Government

International organizations

Nonprofit and civil society work

Global security

International journalism

Research and think tanks

2026 Student Scholars Program Eligibility

The WACA Student Scholars Program has specific eligibility requirements.

Each participating Council may nominate one undergraduate student who is at least 18 years old and attends a local college or university.

Basic eligibility requirements

Applicants must:

Be an undergraduate student.

Be at least 18 years old.

Attend a local college or university within an eligible WACA Council community.

Be selected and nominated by their local WACA Council.

Complete the national application process after being informed that they are the Council’s local nominee.

A critical point for prospective applicants is that students cannot simply submit an application independently and expect WACA to forward it to a local Council.

The Council first conducts its own local selection process. Once a student has been selected as the Council’s nominee, that student can proceed with the national application.

Who Is Not Eligible?

WACA specifically excludes several categories of students from consideration.

The following are not eligible:

High school students

Graduate students

College students in Greater Washington, DC (the DMV)

Prior nominees who were not selected

Therefore, students who are currently pursuing graduate-level studies should not apply, even if they previously participated in an undergraduate program.

Similarly, high school students are not eligible for this particular opportunity.

How Does the Nomination Process Work?

The WACA Student Scholars Program uses a two-stage nomination and application process.

Understanding this process is extremely important because students cannot bypass the local Council selection stage.

Stage 1: Local Council Selection

The local WACA Council identifies and selects its Student Scholar nominee.

Each Council can nominate only one undergraduate student.

Multiple nominees from the same Council will not be considered.

WACA encourages local Councils to promote the opportunity broadly among nearby colleges and universities so that students who may not already be heavily involved with the Council can learn about the program.

Among applicants who are equally qualified and show promise, preference is given to nominees who may not yet have significant local Council involvement.

This means that students should not assume they are at a disadvantage simply because they have not previously been deeply involved with their local World Affairs Council.

Stage 2: National Application

After the local Council has selected its nominee, the nominated student must complete the national application process.

The Council and the student have separate submission requirements.

Documents Required From the Nominating Council

Once a nominee has been selected, the Council must submit:

1. Online Council Nomination Form

The nominating Council must complete the official online nomination form.

2. Professor’s Letter of Recommendation

The Council must also submit a letter of recommendation from a professor of the nominated student.

The student is responsible for making sure that the professor sends the recommendation to the Council in sufficient time for the Council to submit the complete nomination.

Students should therefore contact their professor well before the deadline rather than waiting until the final days.

Documents Required From the Nominated Student

After being selected as the Council’s nominee, the student must submit:

1. Online Student Application Form

The nominated student must complete WACA’s official Student Application Form.

2. Current Resume

Applicants must provide an up-to-date resume highlighting their education, experience, activities, achievements, interests, and other relevant qualifications.

3. Letter of Intent

Applicants must submit a 1–2 page Letter of Intent.

This document provides the student with an opportunity to explain their interests, goals, aspirations, and reasons for wanting to participate in the Student Scholars Program.

Applicants should use the Letter of Intent strategically to demonstrate how participation could contribute to their academic development, professional goals, and interest in world affairs.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the 2026 WACA Student Scholars Program is Friday, September 25, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT. Prospective students should not wait until the deadline to begin preparing their documents. Because the process involves local Council selection, a professor’s recommendation, a Council nomination, and the student’s national application, students should begin by contacting their local WACA Council and asking about its internal selection timeline.

What Happens After Applications Are Submitted?

After applications are submitted, nominated students are reviewed by the WACA national office in consultation with the WACA Board of Directors.

The final selections are expected to be announced within two weeks after the application deadline.

Selected students then participate in the National Conference and associated Student Scholar activities.

To apply click HERE: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSftagIkRIxSyVp09lPabc4PF4U39lLTGznFdHhH4Yhec4PXZw/viewform

Student Scholar Participation Requirements

Selection for the program comes with responsibilities.

As part of their participation requirements, Student Scholars must submit:

A brief evaluation of their experience

A report about their experience

These materials must be submitted no later than two weeks after the National Conference.

This requirement allows WACA to collect feedback from participating students and better understand the value and impact of the Student Scholars experience.

Why Should Undergraduate Students Consider This Opportunity?

The WACA Student Scholars Program offers more than attendance at a conference.

For an undergraduate student interested in global affairs, the experience can provide exposure to people and institutions that may otherwise be difficult to access at the undergraduate level.

Exposure to the World Affairs Community

Students gain an opportunity to become more familiar with the organizations and professionals shaping conversations around international affairs.

Washington, DC Experience

Scholar Day provides students with an opportunity to visit institutions in Washington, DC and gain firsthand insight into the work conducted by think tanks, embassies, international organizations, and other institutions.

Career Exploration

Students can use the experience to investigate potential career paths and better understand how their academic interests connect with professional opportunities.

Networking

Participating alongside other Student Scholars and engaging with the wider WACA community can help students develop relationships that may remain valuable beyond the program.

Professional Development

Preparing a resume, writing a Letter of Intent, communicating with professors, working with a Council, and participating in a national program can all contribute to professional development.

Global Perspective

The program encourages students to think beyond their local academic environment and engage with broader international questions and institutions.

An Important Point About Local Council Selection

One of the most important details applicants should understand is that the Student Application Form is not a substitute for local Council selection.

WACA explicitly explains that the national forms are not intended for local selection and that submissions will not be forwarded to Councils for their own selection process.

Councils must conduct their own local selection and collect the necessary documents.

Therefore, students should:

Identify the WACA Council connected to their local community.

Contact the Council to ask about its Student Scholars selection process.

Follow the Council’s local nomination requirements.

Wait until the Council informs them that they are the selected local nominee.

Complete the national Student Application Form after receiving that confirmation.

Submit the required resume and Letter of Intent.

Ensure that the professor’s recommendation reaches the Council on time.

This process is particularly important because only one student can be nominated by each Council.

Additional links for info here: https://worldaffairscouncils.org/student-scholars-program/

Official Program Resources and Application Links

Students and Councils can access the official WACA resources below:

Students should verify all requirements and deadlines through the official WACA materials before submitting their application.

For more info/ inquiry here:waca@worldaffairscouncils.org

Tips for Prospective Student Scholars

Start With Your Local Council

Do not begin by completing the national application form. First determine which WACA Council serves your area and ask about its local nomination process.

Prepare Your Resume Early

Make sure your resume is current and clearly presents your education, extracurricular activities, leadership experience, research, volunteer work, internships, awards, and relevant interests.

Give Your Professor Enough Time

The recommendation letter is an important part of the nomination process. Contact your professor early and clearly communicate the Council’s deadline.

Make Your Letter of Intent Personal

The Letter of Intent should explain why you are interested in world affairs and how the Student Scholars experience connects with your academic and career goals.

Do Not Assume Previous Council Involvement Is Required

WACA indicates that, among equally qualified applicants of promise, preference may be given to students who do not yet have significant local Council involvement.

Students should therefore consider applying even if they have not previously been highly active in their local Council.

Confirm the Deadline and Time Zone

The final national application deadline is September 25, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT. Applicants should submit their materials before the final hours to avoid technical or document-related problems.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many students will be selected?

WACA offers the opportunity to 25 undergraduate students from Council communities.

Is participation in the National Conference free?

Yes. Selected Student Scholars attend the National Conference at no cost.

Does WACA provide travel and lodging support?

WACA provides $1,250 to the nominating Council to help defray the Scholar’s travel and lodging costs, including double-occupancy accommodation.

Who arranges transportation and hotel reservations?

The participating Council is responsible for arranging transportation and hotel reservations for its Scholar.

Can two students from the same Council be nominated?

No. Each Council may nominate one undergraduate student, and multiple nominees from the same Council will not be considered.

Can graduate students apply?

No. Graduate students are specifically excluded from eligibility.

Can high school students apply?

No. The program is intended for undergraduate students who are at least 18 years old.

Can students in the DMV apply?

No. College students in Greater Washington, DC, commonly referred to as the DMV, are not eligible.

Can a student who was nominated in the past but not selected apply again?

No. Prior nominees who were not selected are listed among those who are not eligible.

Does the program have a nationality restriction?

The provided eligibility requirements do not identify a specific nationality, race, or continental restriction. Eligibility is primarily tied to undergraduate status, age, attendance at an eligible local institution, and nomination through a WACA Council.

When will the results be announced?

WACA states that selections will be announced within two weeks after the application deadline.

Conclusion

The WACA Student Scholars Program 2026 provides undergraduate students with an opportunity to gain meaningful exposure to the world affairs community while participating in the WACA National Conference and an exclusive Scholar Day experience in Washington, DC. With support for conference participation and financial assistance provided through the nominating Council for travel and lodging, the program can give selected students access to professional environments, international organizations, think tanks, embassies, and other institutions that can help shape their understanding of global affairs. The program is particularly valuable for undergraduate students who are beginning to consider careers related to international relations, diplomacy, public policy, government, international development, global economics, research, and other world affairs fields. However, prospective applicants should remember that this is a Council-based nomination program. Students cannot simply submit the national application independently. They must first be selected as the nominee of their local WACA Council. Eligible undergraduate students should therefore begin by contacting their local Council, learning about its internal nomination process, preparing their resume and Letter of Intent, and arranging their professor recommendation well ahead of the final deadline.
