TITLE: Nonprofit Open Source Partnership 2026: Free Technical Support, 800 Hours of Development and Open Source Transformation for Nonprofits

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Nonprofit Open Source Partnership is offering a valuable opportunity for selected nonprofit organizations to transform their existing software and technology projects into publicly accessible, licensed and well-documented open source tools — at no cost to participating organizations. The partnership brings together Bloomberg, Develop for Good, CodeDay and Fast Forward to support a small group of technology-focused nonprofits with the technical expertise, student developer capacity and industry mentorship needed to prepare software for open source use or strengthen projects that are already part of the open source ecosystem. As part of the program, each selected nonprofit will receive a dedicated team of eight vetted and trained college student volunteer developers who will work on the organization’s project for 16 weeks. The program represents approximately 800 hours of technical work per team, supported by weekly check-ins, technical guidance, project management assistance and team coaching. The program is particularly relevant for nonprofits that have developed useful technology but lack the time, staff capacity or specialised expertise required to properly license, document, package and maintain that technology as an open source resource.

Applications for the program close on September 9, 2026.

Nonprofit Open Source Partnership 2026 at a Glance

Program: Nonprofit Open Source Partnership

Organizing partners: Bloomberg, Develop for Good, CodeDay and Fast Forward

Target applicants: Selected technology-focused nonprofit organizations

Project focus: Open sourcing an existing nonprofit software tool or contributing to an existing open source project

Technical support: Eight college student volunteer developers per nonprofit

Program duration: 16 weeks

Technical contribution: Approximately 800 hours per team

Industry mentorship: Bloomberg employee volunteers

Open source guidance: CodeDay

Program support: Develop for Good

Cost: No cost to participating nonprofits

Nonprofit application deadline: September 9, 2026

Selection notification: October 2, 2026

Program kickoff: October 25, 2026

Final delivery: February 20, 2027

What Is the Nonprofit Open Source Partnership?

Many nonprofit organizations build or use technology to deliver their missions, but creating software and preparing it for open source distribution are two different challenges.

A nonprofit may have an existing application, platform, internal tool or other technology that could potentially benefit other organizations. However, making that technology genuinely open source involves much more than publishing code online.

The organization may need to address:

Software licensing

Technical documentation

Code organization

Developer onboarding

Project contribution processes

Technical maintenance

User documentation

Open source best practices

Project management

Quality assurance

Collaboration with external developers

These tasks require time and specialised technical knowledge that many nonprofits may not have available internally.

The Nonprofit Open Source Partnership is designed to help close this gap.

Through the partnership, participating organizations receive a dedicated team of student developers and support from experienced professionals who can help turn an existing technology project into a more accessible and reusable open source resource.

Who Is Behind the Program?

The initiative is a collaboration between four organizations:

Bloomberg

Bloomberg is participating in the partnership through employee volunteers who will provide guidance and mentorship to participating nonprofit projects.

Develop for Good

Develop for Good provides the student development teams and program support. The organization will run weekly check-ins with participating students and provide structured support covering technical work, project management and team coaching.

CodeDay

CodeDay will provide guidance on open source best practices, helping participating nonprofits understand how to prepare their projects for open source use.

Fast Forward

Fast Forward is also part of the partnership, contributing to an initiative designed to strengthen technology capacity within the nonprofit sector.

Together, these organizations provide a combination of student technical talent, professional mentorship, open source expertise and program management support.

What Will Selected Nonprofits Receive?

Selected organizations will receive several forms of support throughout the 16-week program.

1. A Dedicated Team of Eight Student Developers

Each participating nonprofit will receive a team of eight vetted and trained college student volunteer developers.

The students will dedicate their time to the nonprofit’s selected project throughout the 16-week program.

This gives nonprofits access to a substantial pool of technical capacity without the financial cost associated with hiring a conventional software development team.

2. Approximately 800 Hours of Technical Work

The program estimates that each team will contribute approximately 800 hours of technical work.

This can provide significant development capacity for a nonprofit that may otherwise struggle to dedicate internal resources to an open source initiative.

The exact nature of the work will depend on the organization’s project and the objectives established for the program.

Potential work could involve preparing an existing tool for open source publication, improving documentation or contributing to an existing open source project.

3. Weekly Program Check-Ins

Develop for Good will conduct weekly check-ins with students throughout the program.

These check-ins are designed to help teams remain focused, address challenges and maintain progress toward the project’s objectives.

4. Technical Support

Participating teams will receive structured technical support to help them move their projects forward.

This can be especially valuable for organizations that have a strong mission and a useful technology product but do not have extensive internal software engineering capacity.

5. Project Management Support

The partnership also includes project management assistance.

This helps keep the work organized and ensures that the student development team and nonprofit point-of-contact remain aligned on priorities, deliverables and timelines.

6. Team Coaching

Teams will receive coaching designed to support effective collaboration and project execution.

Because the program involves nonprofit staff, student developers and industry mentors, structured coaching can help ensure that different participants remain coordinated throughout the 16-week engagement.

7. Open Source Best-Practices Guidance

CodeDay will provide guidance on open source best practices.

This is particularly important for nonprofits that are making the transition from an internally developed or privately maintained tool to a publicly accessible project.

8. Bloomberg Employee Mentorship

Participating nonprofits will receive weekly guidance from experienced Bloomberg employee volunteers.

These mentors are described as being invested in the success of the projects and can provide an additional professional perspective throughout the program.

9. A Publicly Accessible and Documented Final Product

One of the most important outcomes is a finished project that is intended to be:

Publicly accessible

Properly licensed

Documented

Ready for the nonprofit to use

Potentially useful to other organizations

This can extend the impact of a nonprofit’s technology beyond its immediate internal use.

What Does “Open Source” Mean for Participating Nonprofits?

Open source software is software whose source code is made available under a license that allows others to access, use and, depending on the license, modify and redistribute it under defined conditions.

For a nonprofit, making a tool open source can create opportunities for other organizations, developers and communities to benefit from technology that might otherwise remain limited to the organization that originally developed it.

However, simply uploading software to a public repository does not necessarily mean that a project is ready for meaningful open source collaboration.

A well-prepared open source project generally needs appropriate licensing, clear documentation and enough structure for other users or developers to understand how the project works and how they can engage with it.

That is the gap this partnership is intended to address.

Learn more HERE

What Types of Projects Can Participate?

The program is designed for nonprofits with an existing technology project that is ready to be open sourced or that needs support to contribute to an existing open source project.

A nonprofit may therefore consider applying if it has:

An existing software tool it wants to make open source

A technology project that needs improved documentation

A software project that needs preparation for public release

An existing open source project that requires development support

A technical project that could benefit from a dedicated student development team

The organization should have a sufficiently defined project for the student developers and mentors to work on during the 16-week program.

Apply HERE

What Does the Nonprofit Need to Contribute?

Although the program is offered at no cost to participating organizations, selected nonprofits are expected to commit time and resources in the form of staff participation.

Each participating nonprofit should plan for approximately:

2–3 hours per week for 16 weeks

from a designated point-of-contact.

The nonprofit point-of-contact will participate in activities such as:

Regular check-ins

Providing feedback

Collaborating with student developers

Working with industry mentors

Answering project-related questions

Helping clarify priorities

Reviewing project progress

Supporting decision-making when necessary

This commitment is important because the student developers and mentors need a knowledgeable representative from the nonprofit to provide context and feedback.

How Much Time Should a Nonprofit Expect to Commit?

The stated commitment is approximately 2–3 hours per week for 16 weeks.

Over the entire program period, this represents approximately 32–48 hours of point-of-contact involvement.

Organizations should therefore select someone who can consistently participate throughout the program.

A nonprofit that cannot provide a reliable point-of-contact may struggle to take full advantage of the technical resources being provided.

What Does the Program Cost?

The Nonprofit Open Source Partnership is offered at no cost to participating organizations.

This is one of the program’s major advantages because nonprofits can receive substantial technical support without having to pay for a professional software development team.

The program combines volunteer student developers with industry mentors and structured organizational support to provide the technical capacity needed to advance participating projects.

Why Open Source Can Matter for Nonprofits

Transforming nonprofit software into open source can have benefits beyond the immediate project.

A well-documented and publicly accessible tool can potentially:

Allow other nonprofits to use the technology.

Encourage collaboration among developers.

Reduce duplication of technology development.

Create opportunities for external contributions.

Increase the visibility of the organization’s technical work.

Make the software easier for other organizations to evaluate and adopt.

Build a community around a useful technology project.

Extend the impact of technology developed for a specific nonprofit mission.

The potential impact depends on the quality of the project, the needs of the wider community and the nonprofit’s ability to maintain and support the software after the program concludes.

Program Timeline

The Nonprofit Open Source Partnership has a defined timeline from application through final delivery.

September 9, 2026 — Applications Close

This is the deadline for nonprofit organizations to submit their applications.

Organizations interested in participating should complete their application before this date.

October 2, 2026 — Selected Nonprofits Notified

Organizations selected to participate will be notified on this date.

October 25, 2026 — Program Kickoff

The program officially begins with the kickoff on October 25, 2026.

This marks the beginning of the 16-week collaboration involving the nonprofit, student developers and mentors.

February 20, 2027 — Final Delivery

The program is scheduled to conclude with final delivery on February 20, 2027.

By this stage, participating teams will have worked toward completing the agreed project objectives.

How to Apply for the Nonprofit Open Source Partnership

Nonprofit organizations interested in participating should submit an application through the program’s online application form.

Application deadline: September 9, 2026.

Apply for the Nonprofit Open Source Partnership

Before applying, organizations should make sure they understand the program requirements and can commit the necessary staff time for the entire 16-week period.

How Nonprofits Can Prepare a Strong Application

Although the provided information does not specify a detailed scoring rubric, organizations can prepare by clearly defining the project they want the program to support.

1. Identify the technology project

Determine which existing tool or project you want the student development team to work on.

The project should be sufficiently defined to explain what the team will be expected to accomplish.

2. Explain why the project should become open source

Organizations should be prepared to explain the value of making their technology publicly accessible.

Consider:

Who could benefit from the software?

What problem does the tool solve?

Why would other organizations use it?

What could an open source community contribute?

How could open sourcing the project increase its impact?

3. Define the technical challenges

Identify the areas where your organization needs support.

These could include:

Software development

Documentation

Open source preparation

Technical improvements

Contribution workflows

Existing open source development

A clear understanding of the project’s technical needs can help the development team work more effectively.

4. Identify a reliable point-of-contact

Choose a staff member or representative who can commit 2–3 hours each week for 16 weeks.

The person should have enough knowledge of the project to answer questions and provide meaningful feedback.

5. Consider the project’s sustainability

Open sourcing a project is not necessarily the end of the work.

Organizations should consider how the software will be maintained, documented and supported after the partnership ends.

Thinking about sustainability in advance can help ensure that the project’s results remain useful after February 2027.

Who Should Apply?

The opportunity is especially relevant to nonprofit organizations that have an existing technology or software project and want technical assistance to make it open source or contribute to an existing open source project.

A strong potential applicant may be a nonprofit that:

Has already built a software tool.

Has an existing technology project.

Wants to release its software as open source.

Needs assistance with documentation.

Wants to improve an existing open source project.

Has limited internal technical capacity.

Can provide a dedicated point-of-contact.

Can commit 2–3 hours per week for 16 weeks.

Is prepared to collaborate closely with student developers and mentors.

What the Program Does Not Provide

Applicants should also understand the nature of the opportunity.

This is not described as a cash grant or direct financial award to nonprofits.

Instead, the core support comes in the form of:

Volunteer software development

Technical assistance

Open source guidance

Industry mentorship

Project management support

Team coaching

A structured 16-week development engagement

The primary value is therefore technical capacity and expertise rather than direct funding.

Questions to Ask Before Applying

Before submitting an application, a nonprofit should consider:

Do we have an existing technology project?

Is the project suitable for open source development?

Are we prepared to make the project publicly accessible?

Do we have a clear understanding of what technical work is required?

Can we identify a point-of-contact?

Can that person commit 2–3 hours every week for 16 weeks?

Can our organization provide timely feedback to developers?

Are we prepared to work collaboratively with college student developers?

Can we engage with industry mentors?

Do we have a plan for using or maintaining the project’s output after the program concludes?

If the answer to these questions is generally yes, the partnership may be worth considering.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Nonprofit Open Source Partnership?

It is a collaborative program involving Bloomberg, Develop for Good, CodeDay and Fast Forward that provides selected nonprofits with technical assistance to turn an existing software tool into an open source project or contribute to an existing open source project.

How many student developers does each nonprofit receive?

Each participating nonprofit receives a team of eight vetted and trained college student volunteer developers.

How long does the program last?

The program runs for 16 weeks.

How much technical work is provided?

Each team is expected to contribute approximately 800 hours of technical work.

Does the program charge participating nonprofits?

No. The opportunity is provided at no cost to participating nonprofits.

How much time must the nonprofit contribute?

The nonprofit’s designated point-of-contact should expect to contribute approximately 2–3 hours per week for 16 weeks.

What will the nonprofit representative do?

The point-of-contact will participate in check-ins, provide feedback and collaborate with student developers and industry mentors.

Does the program help with open source best practices?

Yes. CodeDay provides guidance on open source best practices.

Will nonprofits receive professional mentorship?

Yes. Experienced Bloomberg employee volunteers provide weekly guidance throughout the program.

What happens at the end of the program?

The program is scheduled to have its final delivery on February 20, 2027.

The intended outcome is a publicly accessible, licensed and documented project that the nonprofit can use and that may potentially be useful to other organizations.

When is the application deadline?

The nonprofit application deadline is September 9, 2026.

How do I apply?

Applications are submitted through the online application form:

Nonprofit Open Source Partnership application form

Contact Information

Organizations with questions about the program can contact:

Michael Gabrielle
Nonprofit Partnerships Manager
Develop for Good

Email: michael@developforgood.org

Important Dates to Remember

Conclusion

The Nonprofit Open Source Partnership provides selected nonprofits with an opportunity to access significant technical development capacity without paying for it. Through a collaboration involving Bloomberg, Develop for Good, CodeDay and Fast Forward, participating organizations can receive a dedicated team of eight college student developers, industry mentorship, open source guidance and structured project support.

The program is particularly relevant for nonprofits that have already developed a software tool but lack the internal time or technical capacity needed to properly prepare it for open source use. Rather than simply publishing existing code, participating teams can work toward creating a project that is publicly accessible, appropriately licensed and documented for future use.

The commitment from nonprofits is also clearly defined. Each organization should provide a point-of-contact who can dedicate approximately 2–3 hours per week for 16 weeks to check-ins, feedback and collaboration. TITLE: Harvard Environmental Fellows Program 2027: $92,000 Annual Salary for Recent Doctorate Recipients

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Harvard Environmental Fellows Program 2027 is now accepting applications from recent doctorate recipients and scholars with comparable terminal degrees who want to pursue independent environmental research while working with faculty across Harvard University. The two-year fellowship is designed to help early-career scholars use Harvard’s extensive academic and research resources to address complex environmental challenges through research that can connect different disciplines and professional schools.

The program is offered through the Harvard University Center for the Environment (HUCE), a center of the Salata Institute, and is expected to award approximately five fellowships for the 2027 cohort.

With a salary of $92,000 per year, health insurance eligibility, relocation reimbursement, and an annual professional-expenses allowance, the fellowship provides both financial support and access to Harvard’s interdisciplinary research environment.

Harvard Environmental Fellows Program 2027 Overview

The Environmental Fellows Program enables recent doctoral graduates to develop their research at Harvard while working closely with a Harvard faculty host.

Opportunity
Details

Program
Harvard Environmental Fellows Program

Institution
Harvard University Center for the Environment

Cohort
2027

Duration
2 years

Salary
$92,000 per year

Health Insurance
Employee health insurance eligibility

Relocation Support
Up to $2,500

Annual Professional Allowance
$2,500 for travel and other professional expenses

Expected Awards
Approximately 5 fellowships

Eligible Degree Date
May 2023 – August 2027

Application Deadline
December 1, 2026

Research Location
Harvard University

Host Required
Yes

What Is the Harvard Environmental Fellows Program?

The Environmental Fellows Program was created by HUCE to give recent doctorate recipients the opportunity to make use of Harvard’s academic, research, and professional resources while developing work addressing complex environmental issues.

Fellows spend two years working with Harvard faculty members. Importantly, the program is not restricted to one particular Harvard school or department. A fellow can potentially work with a faculty member from a wide range of academic fields.

The program is intended to create connections among researchers working in different disciplines and professional schools. As a result, applicants are encouraged to develop research that can contribute to environmental scholarship or practice while also establishing connections beyond their previous academic work.

Financial Benefits of the Fellowship

Selected Environmental Fellows receive substantial financial and professional support throughout the fellowship.

$92,000 Annual Salary

Each fellow receives a salary of:

$92,000 per year

Because the fellowship lasts two years, the salary component represents approximately $184,000 over the full two-year period, before applicable taxes and deductions.

Health Insurance Eligibility

Fellows are eligible for employee health insurance, providing access to Harvard’s employee benefits structure.

Relocation Reimbursement

The program provides reimbursement of up to:

$2,500 for relocation expenses

This can help eligible fellows with costs associated with relocating for the fellowship.

Professional Expenses Allowance

Fellows also receive:

$2,500 annually

for travel and other professional expenses.

This support can contribute toward activities connected with professional development and research.

Who Can Apply for the Harvard Environmental Fellows Program?

The fellowship is open to individuals who have completed a doctorate or comparable terminal degree within the specified period.

For the 2027 cohort, the degree must have been awarded between:

May 2023 and August 2027

The program therefore targets scholars who are relatively early in their postdoctoral or professional careers.

Eligible terminal degrees can come from a broad range of academic fields. The program specifically notes that fellows and hosts may come from areas including:

Sciences

Economics

Law

Government

Public policy

Public health

Medicine

Design

Humanities

Other relevant disciplines

The diversity of fields reflects the program’s emphasis on environmental research that can extend across traditional academic boundaries.

Interdisciplinary Research Is Encouraged

Applicants do not have to conduct interdisciplinary research to be considered.

However, the program explicitly encourages interdisciplinary projects.

This means applicants working within a single discipline can apply, while researchers who can demonstrate meaningful connections between different areas of scholarship are also encouraged to apply.

For example, an environmental research proposal could potentially connect environmental science with:

Public policy

Economics

Law

Public health

Government

Design

History or other humanities disciplines

The key consideration is whether the proposed research represents a strong and independent contribution to addressing environmental issues.

Research Proposal Requirements

The proposed project is an important part of the selection process.

HUCE faculty evaluate proposals based on several factors, including whether the project:

Represents an independent line of inquiry

Extends beyond the applicant’s doctoral research

Extends beyond the host faculty member’s existing research

Addresses relevant environmental issues

Demonstrates strong potential for intellectual achievement

Can contribute to scholarship or practice

Applicants should therefore avoid simply proposing to continue their PhD research in a slightly different form.

The program specifically looks for research that moves the candidate in a new direction while establishing a meaningful connection with the proposed Harvard host.

Your Project Should Be Distinct From Your PhD Work

One of the important features of this fellowship is the expectation that the proposed research should go beyond the applicant’s previous doctoral work.

The project should represent a new intellectual direction rather than simply being an extension of the PhD dissertation.

This requirement is particularly important for applicants who completed their doctorate recently because the fellowship is intended to help scholars develop new research trajectories.

Harvard candidates are subject to an additional expectation: their proposed research and host arrangements must take them in directions that are significantly distinct from their PhD research.

Harvard Candidates

The program allows candidates who received their terminal degrees from Harvard, as well as postdoctoral researchers currently working at Harvard, to apply.

However, these applicants must demonstrate that the proposed fellowship would take their research in a significantly new direction.

Harvard candidates should:

Propose research substantially different from their PhD work

Establish new research connections within the University

Avoid continuing with the same professors or groups with whom they are currently associated

Avoid simply extending their current research

This is designed to ensure that the fellowship provides a genuinely new research opportunity.

Finding a Harvard Faculty Host

One of the most important steps in preparing an application is identifying a suitable Harvard faculty host.

Applicants are strongly encouraged to begin this process early.

The faculty host will:

Mentor the fellow

Provide office space

Provide basic administrative support

Offer a productive research environment

Support the proposed research project

The host’s commitment is an important component of the application.

Host Support Letter

Every applicant’s proposed host must submit a letter of support of no more than two pages.

The letter should describe:

The faculty member’s commitment to the applicant

Their commitment to the proposed research

Their ability to mentor the fellow

Their support for the candidate’s proposed project

The program notes that Harvard faculty members can receive approaches from many potential applicants and may conduct their own selection process before agreeing to recommend a candidate.

How to Find a Suitable Host

Applicants who are unfamiliar with Harvard faculty can explore potential hosts through the Salata Institute’s faculty resources.

Salata Institute Faculty Directory

When identifying a potential host, applicants should carefully examine the faculty member’s research interests, publications, and academic background.

A strong potential host should be someone whose expertise aligns meaningfully with the proposed research while still allowing the applicant to establish an independent research direction.

Importantly, faculty members from any discipline may potentially serve as hosts, regardless of whether they have previously worked specifically in environmental research or with HUCE.

However, each faculty member can host only one Environmental Fellow at a time.

Faculty Members Not Available as Hosts in 2027

According to the program information provided, the following faculty members are not eligible to host Environmental Fellows in 2027:

Charles Davis

Charles Taylor

Scott Edwards

Le Xie

Robin Kelsey

Phillip Deloria

The program also states that the following faculty members have indicated that they cannot serve as hosts:

Richard Lazarus — Harvard Law School

Joyce Chaplin — History

Applicants should therefore consider host availability before investing significant effort in approaching a particular faculty member.

Selection Criteria

The Environmental Fellows selection process considers the applicant’s previous academic and professional achievements as well as the potential contribution of the proposed research.

Key considerations include:

1. Academic and Professional Success

The committee considers the applicant’s previous academic and professional accomplishments.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate a strong record that supports their potential as an independent scholar or practitioner.

2. Potential Contribution

The committee evaluates the candidate’s potential contribution to:

Scholarship

Environmental research

Professional practice

Broader understanding of environmental issues

3. Strength of the Research Proposal

The proposed project should demonstrate:

Independence

Intellectual ambition

Environmental relevance

A clear departure from previous doctoral research

Potential for meaningful scholarly achievement

4. Host Faculty Commitment

The host’s enthusiasm and commitment are also important.

The committee considers whether the proposed host can:

Mentor the fellow effectively

Support the research

Provide appropriate workspace

Offer a productive research environment

5. Diversity of Research Interests

HUCE aims to create a cohort with a diverse range of:

Academic interests

Skills

Backgrounds

Research approaches

The 2027 cohort is expected to complement fellows selected previously, with the overall cohort consisting of approximately a dozen scholars.

More information click HERE

Interview Stage

After reviewing applications, the selection committee will invite a selected group of applicants to discuss their proposals further.

The interview will take place by video with the selection committee.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to clearly explain:

Their proposed research

Why the project matters

How it addresses an environmental issue

How it differs from their PhD research

Why Harvard is an appropriate environment

Why the proposed faculty host is suitable

What contribution they expect the project to make

Fellowship Community and Harvard Faculty Engagement

The Environmental Fellows Program is not limited to individual research.

HUCE organizes a co-curricular program designed to help fellows become familiar with one another and with each other’s research.

Fellows participate in biweekly dinners involving:

Environmental Fellows

Harvard faculty

A speaker from the Harvard faculty

These activities are intended to strengthen intellectual exchange and help fellows build connections across Harvard.

Other Harvard Environmental Research Opportunities

The program also points prospective applicants toward the Global Change Postdoctoral Fellowship at Harvard University’s Arnold Arboretum.

Global Change Fellows are eligible to participate in the Environmental Fellows cohort at HUCE under the arrangements described by the program.

Applicants interested in this related opportunity can explore the Arnold Arboretum’s program information.

Harvard Arnold Arboretum Global Change Postdoctoral Fellowship

Important Deadline

The application window for the 2027 Harvard Environmental Fellows Program is currently open.

Application Deadline: December 1, 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final deadline to begin looking for a Harvard faculty host.

Because the host relationship and faculty support letter are important parts of the application, prospective applicants should allow sufficient time to:

Identify potential faculty hosts.

Review their research interests.

Contact suitable faculty members.

Discuss the proposed research.

Establish a host relationship.

Develop the research proposal.

Secure the required host support.

Complete the application before the deadline.

There is also an important program-specific note concerning the Department of the History of Science: it has a November 1 deadline for sponsor requests.

Applicants considering a History of Science sponsor should therefore take this earlier date into account.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the final selection is made by the HUCE faculty committee, applicants can use the program’s stated criteria to guide their preparation.

Start With the Research Question

Clearly define the environmental problem or research question you want to investigate.

Your project should demonstrate why the issue deserves scholarly attention and what new contribution your research could make.

Make the Project Independent

Avoid presenting a proposal that simply continues your doctoral dissertation.

Instead, demonstrate how the fellowship would allow you to develop a new line of inquiry.

Identify the Right Harvard Host

Research potential faculty hosts carefully.

Look beyond someone’s job title and examine their:

Publications

Current research

Academic interests

Methodological expertise

Connections to your proposed project

Demonstrate the Harvard Connection

Explain why Harvard’s research environment and the proposed faculty host are particularly useful for your project.

The application should make clear why this research direction benefits from the resources and intellectual environment available at Harvard.

Think Across Disciplines

Interdisciplinary research is encouraged, so applicants may want to identify meaningful connections between their environmental research and other fields.

However, interdisciplinary work is not mandatory. A strong single-discipline proposal can also be considered.

Who Is This Fellowship For?

The Harvard Environmental Fellows Program is particularly relevant to recent doctorate recipients or scholars with comparable terminal degrees who want to establish an independent research direction focused on environmental issues.

The program can be relevant to researchers working across a remarkably broad range of fields, including science, economics, law, government, public policy, public health, medicine, design, and the humanities.

The fellowship may therefore be particularly useful for scholars whose environmental research does not fit neatly into one academic discipline.

Application Information

The official application is available through Harvard University’s academic positions system.

Harvard Environmental Fellows Program Application

For questions about the program, applicants can contact:

Jim Clem
HUCE Managing Director
environmental_fellows@harvard.edu

The main program page is available through the Harvard University Center for the Environment.

Harvard University Center for the Environment – Environmental Fellows Program

Conclusion

The Harvard Environmental Fellows Program 2027 provides recent doctorate recipients with a two-year opportunity to develop independent environmental research within Harvard’s interdisciplinary academic environment. Fellows receive a $92,000 annual salary, health insurance eligibility, relocation support of up to $2,500, and a $2,500 annual allowance for travel and professional expenses.

A particularly important feature of the program is its emphasis on independent research that moves beyond the applicant’s PhD work. Applicants should therefore begin preparing early, especially when identifying a Harvard faculty host and developing a proposal that demonstrates both environmental relevance and intellectual independence.

With approximately five fellowships expected for the 2027 cohort, prospective applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements, establish a suitable host relationship, and prepare their materials well before the December 1, 2026 deadline.

TITLE: 2027 Bee Grant Program: Up to $2,000 and Educational Hive Support for Schools and Nonprofit Organizations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 Bee Grant Program is now open for applications, providing schools and nonprofit organizations with an opportunity to establish, expand, or strengthen educational honey bee programs for students in grades K–12. The program is designed to bring pollinator education to life through hands-on experiences with live honey bee hives, classroom resources, curriculum materials, and other educational support.

The Bee Grant is offered through The Bee Cause Project and Whole Kids, with support from the Whole Foods Market Foundation. It is intended to help educators create meaningful learning experiences that connect students with honey bees, pollinators, environmental conservation, science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics.

For eligible schools and nonprofit organizations in the United States and Canada, the program can provide either a monetary grant or equipment support for developing an educational bee program. Previous Bee Grant recipients may also apply for the separate Renewal Bee Grant, which provides funding and additional program support for continuing and improving existing bee education initiatives.

Applications for both the Traditional Bee Grant and Renewal Bee Grant open on September 1 and close on October 31.

What Is the 2027 Bee Grant Program?

The Bee Grant Program is an educational initiative that helps schools and nonprofit organizations introduce students to the world of honey bees and pollinators.

Rather than limiting bee education to textbooks or conventional classroom lessons, the program encourages hands-on learning through educational hive programs. Students can observe bees, learn about pollination, explore ecosystems, understand environmental stewardship, and develop practical knowledge about the role pollinators play in food systems and natural environments.

Grant recipients can receive financial or equipment assistance to establish or improve their bee programs. In addition, educators gain access to curriculum materials, lesson plans, digital learning resources, and other tools designed to support the integration of pollinator education into the learning environment.

The program is particularly relevant to schools and organizations interested in creating long-term environmental education programs rather than one-time classroom activities.

Who Is Behind the Bee Grant?

The program is brought to educators through The Bee Cause Project and Whole Kids, with support from the Whole Foods Market Foundation.

The Bee Cause Project is dedicated to pollinator education and preservation and works to help students and educators understand the importance of bees and other pollinators.

Through the Bee Grant, participating schools and organizations can create educational experiences that make pollinator science more accessible and practical for students.

What Does the 2027 Bee Grant Provide?

The support available through the program depends on whether an organization applies for the Traditional Bee Grant or Renewal Bee Grant.

For new applicants, the Traditional Bee Grant offers two primary grant options:

1. Monetary Grant

Eligible new applicants can apply for a $2,000 monetary grant to help build and support a live bee education program.

The funding can help an institution develop the infrastructure and activities necessary to establish a meaningful educational bee program.

2. Equipment Grant

Applicants may also choose an Equipment Grant, which includes:

An indoor observation hive

A $1,000 stipend

An indoor observation hive provides students with an opportunity to observe honey bees and learn about hive activity in an educational setting.

This type of equipment can serve as a long-term teaching resource, allowing educators to incorporate bee-related lessons into science, environmental studies, STEAM education, and other areas of the curriculum.

Traditional Bee Grant for New Applicants

The Traditional Bee Grant is specifically intended for new applicants.

It is available to K–12 schools and nonprofit organizations serving students in grades K–12 that are interested in starting a new live bee program or strengthening an existing educational bee program.

Applicants can select between the monetary and equipment options depending on their program needs.

Traditional Bee Grant Options at a Glance

Grant option
Support provided

Monetary Grant
$2,000 to build and support a live bee program

Equipment Grant
Indoor Observation Hive plus $1,000 stipend

The Traditional Bee Grant can therefore be useful for institutions that are at different stages of developing their bee education activities.

A school starting from the beginning may need financial resources to build its program, while another institution may benefit more from having an indoor observation hive that can be incorporated directly into classroom learning.

What Is the Renewal Bee Grant?

The Renewal Bee Grant is designed specifically for previous Bee Grant recipients.

Unlike the Traditional Bee Grant, which is intended for new applicants, the Renewal Bee Grant helps existing Bee Grant programs continue developing their educational bee initiatives.

Previous recipients can use the funding to strengthen, expand, or refresh their existing bee programs.

Renewal Grant recipients receive a $2,000 monetary grant to support the continued growth and development of their Bee Program.

Who Can Apply for the Renewal Bee Grant?

To qualify for the Renewal Bee Grant, an applicant must meet specific previous-recipient requirements.

Applicants must have:

Received a Traditional Bee Grant from the Whole Foods Market Foundation in 2025 or earlier.

Completed the required Bee Grant Progress Report.

An important feature of the Renewal Bee Grant is that live bees are not required in order to apply.

This means previous grant recipients can seek renewal support even if their current program does not have live bees at the time of application.

Additional Support Available to Renewal Grant Recipients

The Renewal Bee Grant goes beyond financial assistance. Recipients can also benefit from additional resources intended to help them maintain and improve their educational bee programs.

One-on-One Program Consultation

Renewal recipients receive personalized support from The Bee Cause Project.

This consultation can assist with areas such as:

Program development

Technical questions

Program planning

Beekeeping guidance where applicable

Strategies for strengthening the educational value of the program

This support can be particularly useful for organizations that have already established a bee program but want guidance on maintaining or expanding it.

Educator Resource Pack

Renewal Grant recipients also receive an educator resource package containing practical materials to support a strong and sustainable Bee Program.

Resources can include:

Standards-aligned lessons and activities

Digital learning experiences

Budgeting and planning tools

Community engagement opportunities

Additional educational resources

These materials can help educators connect bee education to broader learning objectives and create a more structured long-term program.

How the Bee Grant Supports STEAM Education

One of the central educational benefits of the Bee Grant is its connection to STEAM learning.

Students can use the study of honey bees and pollinators to explore concepts across multiple academic areas, including science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics.

For example, students may learn about:

Pollination and plant reproduction

Honey bee behavior

Ecosystems and biodiversity

Environmental conservation

Agricultural systems

Habitat development

Observation and data collection

Problem-solving

Scientific inquiry

Sustainable environmental practices

Because students can interact with a real or observation-based hive environment, educators have opportunities to connect theoretical lessons with practical experiences.

Educational Resources for Bee Grant Applicants

The Bee Cause Project provides resources that can help educators prepare for and develop their bee programs.

The organization recommends building an educational foundation before introducing live bees.

Its Back to School Bee Program provides resources that can be used by educators at different levels of experience, including educators who are completely new to bee education.

The resources are designed to support distance learning, include teacher companion guides, and are mapped to educational standards.

Step One: Educate

The first recommended step is to establish a strong educational foundation.

The Bee Cause Project recommends educators begin with its How to Grow Your Bee Program guide before implementing the Six Week Bee Unit.

The Six Week Bee Unit provides educational materials such as:

Standards-aligned lessons

Teacher guides

Flashcards

Literature circle prompts

These resources can help students develop an understanding of bees and pollinators before the institution introduces or expands a live bee program.

Step Two: Build a Bee Club

The second recommended step is to establish a Bee Club.

A Bee Club can provide structure for students, educators, and members of the wider school community who want to learn more about bees.

It can serve as a platform for activities such as:

Bee-related book discussions

Pollinator education

Campus habitat development

Learning about beekeeping

Student-led environmental activities

Community engagement

Creating a Bee Club can also help an institution build broader support for its bee program.

Step Three: Connect With the Community

The Bee Cause Project encourages schools and organizations to connect their bee programs with their surrounding communities.

Potential community connections can include:

4-H agents

Local beekeeper associations

Farmers

Parents

Educators

Environmental organizations

Other community members with knowledge of pollinators

Community members can participate through in-person visits, educational sessions, and digital field trips.

These interactions can provide students with perspectives beyond the classroom while helping families and community members better understand pollinators and the purpose of the school’s bee program.

Step Four: Expand Pollinator Habitat

A successful bee program is not only about keeping bees. The Bee Cause Project also emphasizes the importance of healthy habitat.

Schools and organizations can explore ways to create environments that support pollinators.

This may involve:

Developing native pollinator gardens

Improving campus habitat

Planting appropriate vegetation

Teaching students about local ecosystems

Learning how pollinators interact with plants

Creating educational conservation projects

The Bee a Friend to Pollinators lesson plan can help educators introduce students to the relationship between pollinators and their surrounding habitats.

Preparing for the 2027 Bee Grant Application

Applicants are encouraged to begin preparing before submitting their final applications.

The Bee Cause Project makes previous application materials available as planning resources so prospective applicants can understand the type of information they may need to provide.

For the Traditional Bee Grant, applicants can review the previous 2026 Traditional Bee Grant application while preparing for the 2027 application cycle.

However, applicants should note that the previous application is provided as a preparation tool. All final 2027 Bee Grant applications must be submitted online.

Applicants should therefore avoid relying solely on a downloaded or previous-year application and should complete the official application through the designated online platform.

How to Apply for the 2027 Bee Grant

Applications are submitted online through the SmartSimple platform.

The general application process involves accessing the online platform, registering the school or organization, and completing the relevant Bee Grant application.

Applicants should make sure they select the appropriate grant type:

Traditional Bee Grant for eligible new applicants.

Renewal Bee Grant for qualifying previous Bee Grant recipients.

Applicants should also prepare the information and materials needed to explain their educational bee program and how the grant support will contribute to their students and organization.

2027 Bee Grant Application Deadline

The application period for both the Traditional Bee Grant and Renewal Bee Grant opens on September 1 and closes on October 31.

Applicants should submit their completed applications before the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

Because online application platforms can experience technical issues or require additional registration steps, organizations interested in the grant may benefit from beginning the application process early.

Bee Grant Application Webinars and Information Sessions

The Bee Cause Project provides webinars and informational resources to help prospective applicants understand the program.

The 2027 Bee Grant Overview Webinar covers areas such as:

Eligibility

Grant costs

Application timelines

Program information

Other important considerations for applicants

The organization also provides access to previous Bee Grant webinars and question-and-answer resources to help applicants prepare for the grant season.

Prospective applicants should also monitor the Bee Cause Project’s official channels for announcements concerning current-year webinars and live Q&A sessions.

Important Considerations for Applicants

Before applying, schools and nonprofit organizations should carefully consider the practical requirements of running an educational bee program.

These may include:

Identifying educators who will oversee the program

Establishing appropriate safety procedures

Determining where educational hive equipment will be located

Planning how students will interact with the program

Identifying potential local beekeeping or community partners

Developing lessons around the hive

Considering habitat and environmental needs

Planning how the program can be sustained beyond the grant period

For applicants pursuing a new bee program, planning is particularly important because the grant represents an opportunity to establish an educational initiative that can continue serving students over time.

Why Schools May Consider Developing a Bee Education Program

A live or observation-based bee program can provide a learning environment where students engage directly with environmental topics.

Rather than studying pollination solely through textbooks, students can observe aspects of a working hive and use those observations as a basis for classroom discussion and inquiry.

A school bee program can potentially support:

Environmental education

Conservation awareness

STEAM learning

Experiential learning

Student engagement

Community participation

Pollinator habitat development

Long-term sustainability education

The program can also help students understand the connection between pollinators, plants, agriculture, ecosystems, and human communities.

Visit HERE to learn more about the 2027 Bee Grant Program.

Conclusion

The 2027 Bee Grant Program provides schools and nonprofit organizations with an opportunity to introduce students to honey bees, pollinators, environmental conservation, and hands-on STEAM learning.

The Traditional Bee Grant offers new applicants a choice between a $2,000 monetary grant and an equipment package consisting of an indoor observation hive and a $1,000 stipend. Meanwhile, previous qualifying Bee Grant recipients can apply for the Renewal Bee Grant, which provides $2,000 along with program consultation and educator resources.

Beyond the financial and equipment support, the program provides access to educational materials, lesson plans, digital learning resources, planning tools, and other resources that can help educators build a structured and sustainable bee education program.

Eligible schools and nonprofit organizations in the United States and Canada should take note of the application timeline. Applications for the 2027 Traditional and Renewal Bee Grants open on September 1 and close on October 31.

TITLE: Application now open for the next competition of the Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program (CADFP)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
DEADLINE: September 30, 2022 at 11:59 PM EST
The Institute of International Education (IIE) is pleased to announce that the next round of competition for the CADFP is now open.

Apply now or share this message with those who might be interested.

What is the CADFP?

The CADFP is a scholar exchange program for African higher education institutions to host a diaspora scholar for 14-90 days for projects in curriculum co-development, research collaboration and graduate student teaching and mentoring. The Association of African Universities (AAU) is a partner of the Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship Program.

Who is eligible?

Accredited universities in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania and Uganda, and member institutions of the African Research Universities Alliance (ARUA) (including Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia; the University of Rwanda; Cheikh Anta Diop University, Senegal; and University of Mauritius) can submit a project request to host a scholar.

Scholars born in Africa, who live in the United States or Canada and work in an accredited college or university in either of those two countries, can apply online to be placed on a roster of candidates for a fellowship. Scholars must hold a terminal degree in their field and may hold any academic rank.

How do I apply?

Links and information about the African host institution project request application, scholar roster application and review guidelines are posted on the CADFP website. Interested parties are invited to register for one of the informational webinars:

Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #1: Wednesday August 3 at 12 noon Eastern US Time

Information for Potential Hosts, Webinar #1: Thursday, August 4 at 12 noon West Central Africa Standard Time

Information for Diaspora Scholars, Webinar #2: Tuesday, August 23 at 2:00 PM Eastern US Time

Information for Potential Hosts, Webinar #2: Wednesday, August 24 at 2:00 PM West Central Africa Time

After the webinars, a recording will be posted on the IIE’s YouTube Channel.

Timeline

The deadline for project requests from host universities and scholar applications for diaspora scholars is September 30, 2022 at 11:59 pm EST. Selection decisions will be made in October-November 2022; project visits can begin as early as January 1, 2023 and must be completed by November 30, 2023.

Benefits

Selected fellows receive a $150/day stipend, visa costs, limited health insurance, round-trip international air travel and ground transportation costs to and from home and the U.S./Canadian airport. Selected Host Fellows and Diaspora Fellows can apply for supplemental funds to be used for fieldwork, publication costs and workshops. The CADFP Team manages the fellowships and payments to fellows. Host institutions are encouraged to provide cost-share for the fellow’s meals, lodging and in-country transportation.

For more information on the fellowship program and application process, as well as the projects of current fellows, please write to AfricanDiaspora@iie.org visit the Programme website and communities on Facebook and Twitter. TITLE: Donor Profile: Yalcin & Serpil Ayasli

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Yalcin (EE ’73) and Serpil Ayasli

by Elizabeth Chadis, MaryGlenn Vincens and Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2008

Serpil & Yalcin (EE ’73) Ayasli
The airy conference room in the new Center for Theoretical Physics (CTP) (now the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)) is named in honor of Dr. Serpil Ayasli, a former postdoctoral fellow in the Physics Department, and the wife of alumnus Dr. Yalcin Ayasli. “I thought it would make a very nice anniversary gift,” Yalcin said.

The couple’s fond memories of the Department during Serpil’s time in the CTP (now CTP-LI) helped shape their decision to support Physics with a naming gift to the Green Center building project.

To Serpil, theirs is a family gift to MIT: “We are, after all, an MIT family.” Not only was Serpil a postdoc (1979–82), but Yalcin earned his PhD from MIT in Electrical Engineering, and one of their three children, daughter Ceylan, earned an S.B. in Economics in 2000.

A surprise dividend to their gift was the discovery that the Serpil Ayasli Conference Room is located in virtually the same place on the third floor of Building 6 as Serpil’s first lab. Serpil wrote at this time (with Prof. Paul Joss) what turned out to be an important 1982 theoretical paper on the modeling of thermonuclear X-ray bursts on neutron stars. Cited nearly 150 times in the literature, it’s a paper that many groups, such as Prof. Deepto Chakrabarty’s, have cited numerous times in their X-ray observational work on neutron stars.

The Drs. Ayasli are originally from Turkey. Yalcin came to the United States to attend graduate school, returning to Turkey to teach. In 1979, he and Serpil came back to the United States together. Yalcin founded and headed Hittite Microwave, a company that develops and markets microwave technologies. Serpil worked for 23 years at Lincoln Laboratory and was an associate group leader when she retired in 2005. During her career there, she served on MIT’s Council on Family and Work.

Yalcin has become a regular at the physics alumni breakfast events, enjoying in particular those featuring astrophysics.

TITLE: Press Release – 10th ACE Impact Workshop: Sustaining Progress and Celebrating a Decade of Change

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
ENGLISH VERSION | VERSION FRANÇAISE

Accra, Ghana (23rd October 2023) – The Africa Higher Education Centre of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) project is set to hold its 10th bi-annual regional workshop in Abidjan, Cote d’Ivoire, from Tuesday, 31 October to Friday, 3 November 2023.

The workshop is being organized with sustainability as its primary theme. This theme holds particular significance due to the recent grant of a no-cost extension, extending the project’s timeline until 2025. This extension period offers an opportunity to operationalize the project’s sustainability plans. Additionally, a crucial highlight of this event will be a dedicated session during which the findings of an impact assessment report for the project will be presented.

In addition, the four-day event will provide a platform to: discuss best practices and implementation plans for the financial and operational sustainability of the project; and provide implementation support to enhance project efficiency and address technical challenges hindering successful project execution.

The Opening ceremony and launch of the ACE @ 10 celebrations will be held on October 31, 2023 (8:00 GMT) at the Latrille Events Center. Hybrid workshop activities (virtual and onsite), including plenary and parallel sessions and steering committee and experts’ meetings, will be held from November 1-2, 2023 at the Noom and Movenpick Hotels concurrently. The closing ceremony is scheduled for November 3, 2023 at the Latrille Events Center.

The 10th regional ACE workshop is co-organised by the French Development Agency (AFD), the World Bank, and the Association of African Universities, in collaboration with the Ivorian Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research.

The workshop cultivates a space for exchanging knowledge and building networks amongst the centers and relevant agencies by bringing together over 400 higher education stakeholders, including vice-chancellors, project team members, subject matter experts, government representatives, and policy think tanks. The workshop offers in-person collaborative opportunities, fostering the exchange of regional insights and learnings. Participants receive essential tools and guidelines for efficient project implementation, promoting long-term sustainability.

As part of the regional workshop, the 10th anniversary of the Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence series of projects (ACEA10) will be launched- celebrating a decade of empowering higher education and fostering innovation across the African continent. “The ACE projects have been a transformative force over the past decade in the tertiary education sector, specifically, training the next generation of Africa’s STEM workforce and fostering cutting-edge research. The projects have made significant strides in addressing Africa’s critical development challenges while tackling brain drain. Since its inception in 2014, the projects have supported over 80 centres, in more than 50 universities, across 20 African nations. As we celebrate ACE@10, it’s evident that its contributions enrich Africa’s academic landscape, enhancing the global competitiveness of African higher education and research to build a more prosperous Africa.” Scherezad Latif, World Bank Practice Manager for Education, Western and Central Africa

The launch will also highlight activities to be rolled out towards the celebrations in 2024. “ACE@10 activities will mark a decade of excellence, collaboration, and transformative impact in African higher education. The ACE @ 10 activities would amplify the project’s impact in African higher education and its crucial role in shaping a prosperous future for Africa.” AAU Secretary-General, Prof. Olusola Oyewole.

“The ACE @ 10 will provide concrete solutions tailored to African development contexts and generated by African research, that can be promoted and disseminated widely” AFD Head of Education, Virginie Delisée-Pizzo.

Prior to the workshop, virtual national-level roundtable implementation support meetings will take place from October 16- 23, 2023.
