TITLE: Global EbA Fund Grants 2026: Up to $500,000 for Ecosystem-Based Adaptation Projects in Developing Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Global EbA Fund Grants 2026 provide an important funding opportunity for organisations working to address climate change, strengthen ecosystem resilience and advance Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) in vulnerable countries.

For the 2026 funding cycle, the Global EbA Fund is inviting organisations to submit innovative and catalytic proposals designed to overcome systemic barriers that prevent Ecosystem-based Adaptation from being adopted, scaled and mainstreamed. The calls place particular emphasis on Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and Least Developed Countries (LDCs), where climate vulnerability is often high while institutional, technical and financial capacity remains constrained.

The 2026 calls provide two grant tracks: Small-Size Grants of up to US$250,000 and Medium-Size Grants of up to US$500,000. Both tracks support projects of up to 24 months and seek initiatives capable of creating lasting enabling conditions for climate adaptation rather than simply financing isolated conservation activities.

What Is the Global EbA Fund?

The Global EbA Fund is a funding mechanism focused on creating an enabling environment for the implementation and scaling of Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

Ecosystem-based Adaptation uses the conservation, restoration and sustainable management of ecosystems to help people and communities adapt to the impacts of climate change. Rather than treating climate adaptation solely as an infrastructure or technological challenge, EbA recognises the important role that healthy ecosystems can play in reducing climate vulnerability.

The Fund supports innovative initiatives that address the systemic obstacles preventing EbA from being effectively adopted and expanded. These obstacles can include gaps in:

Climate and environmental data

Scientific evidence

Technical capacity

Institutional capacity

Governance

Policy implementation

Financing

Investment readiness

Knowledge sharing

Awareness

Partnerships and collaboration

According to the information provided, the Fund has been operational since 2020 and, as of June 2026, had supported 75 projects across 41 countries, with 29 projects completed and 46 at various stages of implementation.

Its portfolio covers a wide range of ecosystems and landscapes, including:

Coastal and marine environments

Drylands

Grasslands

Forests

Mountains

Urban areas

River basins

Wetlands

This broad portfolio demonstrates that Ecosystem-based Adaptation can be applied across different ecological, social and economic contexts.

The Fund’s overall objective is to finance innovative approaches capable of overcoming systemic barriers and enabling EbA to be taken up, scaled and mainstreamed.

Learn More HERE

Why the 2026 Global EbA Fund Call Matters

Climate change is increasing pressure on communities, economies and ecosystems around the world. Rising temperatures, droughts, floods, storms, changing rainfall patterns, sea-level rise and other climate-related hazards are affecting food security, water security, livelihoods and socioeconomic development.

At the same time, many ecosystems are being degraded through unsustainable resource use and other pressures. This creates a double challenge: communities become increasingly exposed to climate risks while the ecosystems that could help protect them become less capable of providing essential services.

Ecosystem-based Adaptation seeks to address these interconnected challenges by strengthening the health and resilience of ecosystems while also reducing vulnerability among people.

The 2026 Global EbA Fund calls are particularly relevant to Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries.

SIDS are highly vulnerable to climate impacts because of factors such as their small land areas, remoteness and close connections between communities, oceans and ecosystems. They can face increasingly frequent and intense tropical cyclones, storm surges, heatwaves, droughts, flooding, changing precipitation patterns and sea-level rise.

LDCs also face significant climate vulnerability. Their economies frequently depend heavily on climate-sensitive sectors, while limited institutional and financial capacity can make it difficult to recover from climate-related shocks or mobilise sufficient resources for adaptation.

The call therefore seeks projects that do more than implement individual adaptation activities. It seeks initiatives capable of strengthening the systems, institutions, knowledge, partnerships and investment mechanisms needed to enable EbA to grow over the long term.

Global EbA Fund Small-Size Grants 2026

The Small-Size Grants Call for Proposals is intended to support innovative and catalytic initiatives that address systemic barriers to scaling Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

Small-Size Grant Amount

The Fund will provide grants of up to US$250,000 per project.

The provided call information indicates that the Small-Size Grants track will support 10 grants, with projects lasting between 18 and 24 months. The official webpage specifies a maximum project duration of 24 months.

Small-Size Grants Deadline

Applications for the Small-Size Grants can be submitted through the online platform from:

28 September to 26 October 2026

The application deadline is 26 October 2026. The call was officially launched on 24 August 2026.

Click HERE to download the Small-size Call for Proposals Document.

What the Small-Size Grants Will Support

The Small-Size Grants call is looking for projects that address upstream or systemic barriers preventing the uptake and scaling of Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

Successful proposals should contribute to one or more areas such as:

1. Strengthening Institutional and Technical Capacity

Projects can address institutional or technical limitations that prevent organisations, governments and other stakeholders from effectively implementing EbA.

This could include initiatives that improve technical expertise, institutional systems, planning capacity or decision-making processes.

2. Improving Data and Evidence

Strong evidence is essential for convincing policymakers, investors and other stakeholders to support adaptation approaches.

The Fund therefore welcomes projects that generate, improve or apply quality data and evidence to resolve specific barriers to EbA implementation and investment.

3. Building Knowledge and Learning Networks

Projects can strengthen systematic knowledge exchange, learning networks and communities of practice that enable practitioners and decision-makers to learn from successful EbA approaches.

4. Improving Investment Readiness

The call encourages initiatives that prepare projects and concepts capable of attracting larger-scale climate financing.

This can include developing investable project pipelines, strengthening financial models and preparing scalable concepts that can eventually move beyond small grant funding.

5. Supporting Innovative EbA Technologies

Projects may adapt or scale tested technological solutions for particular socio-ecological systems.

The emphasis is on technologies that can generate useful lessons for practitioners and decision-makers and contribute to broader EbA uptake.

6. Conducting Applied and Functional Research

The Fund is interested in practical research that addresses specific obstacles to EbA implementation or investment.

Research should therefore have a clear application and contribute to solving real-world adaptation challenges.

7. Creating Synergies With Other Initiatives

Applicants are encouraged to work with existing Ecosystem-based Adaptation and Nature-based Solution initiatives where this can generate operational synergies, strengthen collaboration and create opportunities for co-financing.

These areas are explicitly highlighted in the Small-Size Grants call.

Key Requirements for Small-Size Grant Proposals

A successful Small-Size Grant proposal must demonstrate that the project is genuinely focused on Ecosystem-based Adaptation and has the potential to create an enabling environment for its uptake and scaling.

Projects must:

Qualify as Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

Have catalytic and innovative potential.

Clearly identify the climate impacts being addressed.

Explain how the proposed intervention will address those impacts.

Fall under no more than one Strategic Objective and no more than two Action Pillars of the Global EbA Fund.

Be global, thematic or focused on ODA-eligible countries.

Request no more than US$250,000.

Have a duration of no more than 24 months.

Build on existing work rather than being an entirely standalone initiative.

Demonstrate how results will continue after Fund support ends.

Partner with local institutions and organisations.

Demonstrate relevant experience in the proposed area of work.

Incorporate local communities, Indigenous Knowledge and gender perspectives.

Be led by legally recognised entities.

Meet the Fund’s due-diligence requirements.

Social and Environmental Considerations

The Global EbA Fund places significant importance on ensuring that climate adaptation projects are socially inclusive and environmentally responsible.

Proposals should therefore incorporate:

Gender responsiveness

Meaningful local participation

Respect for Indigenous Peoples’ rights

Environmental and social safeguards

Equitable benefit-sharing

Prevention of maladaptation

Use of local, Indigenous and traditional knowledge where appropriate

Applicants should clearly identify the communities and groups that will benefit from the project and explain how those groups will participate in the initiative.

The evaluation framework also specifically considers the involvement of women, youth, Indigenous Peoples and other marginalised groups. Where Indigenous Peoples may be affected, Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) is expected to be upheld.

Sustainability and Long-Term Impact

The Fund is not simply looking for projects that produce short-term outputs during the grant period.

Applicants must demonstrate how their work will remain viable after the funding period.

A strong proposal should therefore explain:

How local ownership will be established.

How institutions will continue the work.

How project results can be replicated.

How successful approaches can be scaled.

How knowledge and capacities will be retained.

How the initiative connects to relevant national and global policies.

How partnerships will continue after the project ends.

How additional financing can be mobilised.

The Fund specifically evaluates sustainability, including replication, upscaling and links with national and global policies such as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs).

Learn More and Apply HERE

Global EbA Fund Medium-Size Grants 2026

Alongside the Small-Size Grants, the Global EbA Fund has opened a Medium-Size Grants Call for Proposals.

This track provides larger funding for collaborative and innovative initiatives focused on strategic scaling and global influence.

Medium-Size Grant Amount

Each Medium-Size Grant can provide up to US$500,000.

Projects can run for up to 24 months.

Medium-Size Grants Deadline

Applications will be accepted through the online platform from:

12 October to 16 November 2026

The application deadline is 16 November 2026.

The Medium-Size Grants call was officially launched on 24 August 2026.

Click HERE to download the Medium-size Call for Proposals Document.

Medium-Size Grants General Track: Strategic Scaling and Global Influence

The Medium-Size Grants General Track is aimed at proposals that demonstrate collaborative and innovative approaches to advancing Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

The focus is on projects that can address systemic barriers to scalability while contributing to broader learning and policy dialogue.

Projects that strengthen enabling environments and integrate EbA into national frameworks are particularly relevant.

The call identifies three priority themes.

1. Innovative Finance Solutions for EbA

This theme focuses on partnerships with private-sector actors, financiers, innovators, adaptation practitioners and local champions to unlock private capital and blended finance for Ecosystem-based Adaptation.

The underlying objective is to help EbA evolve beyond small-scale or subsistence-level activities and develop business models that are commercially viable, scalable and capable of creating incentives for conservation.

Applicants working in this area should demonstrate how their proposed approach can help overcome financing barriers and make EbA more attractive to investors and other financing partners.

2. EbA for Human Development and Security

This theme explores the connection between climate resilience, human development and security, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected contexts.

Projects should identify specific policy, regulatory, financial or awareness barriers that prevent investment in EbA in high-risk areas.

The Fund is interested in preventive and community-designed interventions that can:

Protect vulnerable populations.

Reduce exposure to climate-related risks.

Strengthen resilience.

Reduce natural-resource-related tensions.

Strengthen social cohesion.

Connect adaptation with humanitarian action.

Support development and peacebuilding objectives.

Strong proposals should establish a measurable pathway showing how targeted EbA investment can contribute to reducing climate-induced fragility.

3. People-Nature-Climate-Land Synergies

The third theme focuses on strengthening connections between climate change, biodiversity, sustainable land management and disaster risk reduction.

The Fund invites proposals led by organisations that actively collaborate with national governments to strengthen operational links between the UNFCCC, Convention on Biological Diversity, UNCCD, Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and other relevant international environmental commitments.

The objective is to connect existing commitments, actors, tools and financing opportunities so countries and communities can reduce duplication and use integrated interventions to achieve multiple environmental and development outcomes.

Who Can Apply for the Global EbA Fund Grants?

The Global EbA Fund is designed primarily for organisations, not individual applicants.

Eligible organisation types include:

Non-governmental organisations (NGOs)

International non-governmental organisations (INGOs)

Intergovernmental organisations (IGOs)

Community-based organisations (CBOs)

Indigenous Peoples’ Organisations

Universities and other academic institutions

Research institutes and think tanks

Private-sector companies, subject to the Fund’s conditions

Consortia of organisations collaborating to create greater impact around EbA

Government entities can participate in consortia, provided that they do not receive funding from the Global EbA Fund. A consortium application must clearly identify its lead organisation, which becomes the responsible contract party if the proposal is successful.

The same broad organisational eligibility structure applies to the Medium-Size Grants.

Learn More and Apply HERE

Local Partnerships and the Role of Local Organisations

One of the important features of the Global EbA Fund is its emphasis on local ownership.

For country-level activities, the call information provided states that a consortium involving one or more local organisations is required, with at least 25% of the project budget allocated to local partners, subject to compliance with applicable standards and due-diligence requirements.

These partnerships should demonstrate:

Capacity transfer

Shared decision-making

Long-term institutional strengthening

Local ownership

Knowledge transfer

Sustainability

Meaningful community participation

This requirement is particularly important for organisations applying from outside the country where project activities will take place.

What Makes a Strong Global EbA Fund Proposal?

The Fund’s evaluation criteria provide applicants with a useful indication of what reviewers will be looking for.

Ecosystem-Based Adaptation — 30%

The proposal must clearly demonstrate that it is an EbA intervention and explain how it will reduce vulnerability or increase the resilience of human communities to climate change.

Applicants should clearly identify:

The main climate hazards.

The climate risks involved.

The affected communities.

Ecosystem vulnerabilities.

The ecosystem services involved.

How the proposed intervention will reduce vulnerability.

The proposal should establish a convincing connection between ecosystem management and climate adaptation outcomes.

Innovative and Catalytic Contribution — 30%

Innovation and catalytic potential are also worth 30% of the evaluation.

The Fund wants interventions capable of producing systemic change.

Examples could include initiatives that:

Influence policy.

Address institutional capacity gaps.

Develop new financing mechanisms.

Improve governance.

Strengthen investment readiness.

Demonstrate approaches that can be replicated elsewhere.

Test approaches in new contexts.

The key question is not simply whether the project is innovative, but whether it can help trigger broader transformation in how EbA is implemented or financed.

Sustainability — 20%

Sustainability accounts for 20% of the evaluation.

Applicants need to explain how activities and results will continue beyond the grant period, including opportunities for replication and upscaling.

Proposals should also demonstrate connections to relevant national and international policies and synergies with other initiatives.

Institutional Arrangements — 20%

Institutional arrangements account for another 20%.

The applicant organisation should have:

An appropriate organisational structure.

Adequate financial capacity.

Strong internal controls.

Qualified and dedicated staff.

Relevant technical expertise.

Previous experience implementing projects of similar scope and complexity.

This means applicants should not focus exclusively on the technical idea. They must also demonstrate that their organisation has the capacity to responsibly manage the proposed funding and deliver the project.

Theory of Change, Logical Framework and SMART Indicators

A strong application should have a clear and logical Theory of Change.

The Fund expects the results chain to demonstrate how proposed activities will lead to outputs and outcomes that create an enabling environment for reducing identified climate risks.

The project design should include:

A logical and coherent results chain.

Feasible activities.

A realistic implementation timeline.

SMART indicators.

Appropriate data sources.

Defined reporting intervals.

A budget that corresponds logically with activities and timelines.

Applicants must also use the Global EbA Fund’s Core Indicator Framework.

At least three relevant indicators from the Core Indicator Framework must be incorporated into the project’s logical framework.

Existing Work Is Important

A key eligibility requirement is that the proposed project must be built on or based on existing work.

Applicants should therefore avoid presenting an entirely disconnected idea with no evidence of previous activity, experience or groundwork.

A stronger proposal can demonstrate:

Previous pilot activities.

Existing partnerships.

Prior research.

Community engagement.

Existing institutional relationships.

Previous data or evidence.

Lessons learned.

Existing projects that can be scaled or replicated.

This helps demonstrate that the proposed investment can move an existing concept toward greater impact rather than starting from zero.

Application Documents

Applicants should carefully prepare the required application package before the relevant submission window opens.

For the Small-Size Grants, the application package includes:

Applicant Declaration

Co-applicant Mandate

Small-Size Grants Application Form

Project Proposal Budget Template

Due Diligence and Financial Capacity Questionnaire

The Fund specifically advises applicants to review the Grants Procedure Manual before developing and submitting their proposal.

The Medium-Size Grants application package similarly includes:

Applicant Declaration

Co-applicant Mandate

Medium-Size Grants Application Form

Project Proposal Budget Template

Due Diligence and Financial Capacity Questionnaire

How to Apply for the Global EbA Fund Grants 2026

Applications must be submitted through the Global EbA Fund’s online platform.

Applicants should not simply complete the downloadable application form and assume that submitting the document itself constitutes an application.

The Fund explicitly states that the application form is intended for drafting purposes and that applications must ultimately be submitted through the online platform.

The Fund strongly recommends that applicants:

Download and review the relevant application materials.

Read the Grants Procedure Manual carefully.

Review the eligibility requirements.

Identify the appropriate Strategic Objective and Action Pillars.

Develop the project’s Theory of Change.

Develop the logical framework and SMART indicators.

Identify at least three relevant Core Indicators.

Establish the climate hazards and risks the project will address.

Demonstrate the project’s EbA approach.

Develop a realistic implementation plan.

Prepare the project budget.

Establish local partnerships where required.

Complete the required due-diligence documentation.

Draft the application offline.

Transfer the completed application to the online platform.

Submit before the applicable deadline.

For the Small-Size Grants, the online submission link is expected to be shared on the Small-Size Grants webpage on 28 September 2026.

For the Medium-Size Grants, the online submission link is expected to be shared on the Medium-Size Grants webpage on 12 October 2026.

Small-Size vs Medium-Size Global EbA Fund Grants

Although both funding opportunities are part of the Global EbA Fund, applicants should carefully consider which track best matches the scale and ambition of their project.

Small-Size Grants

The Small-Size Grants provide up to US$250,000 and are particularly focused on catalytic interventions that overcome barriers to EbA uptake and scaling.

They are well suited to projects addressing issues such as:

Institutional and technical capacity.

Evidence and data gaps.

Knowledge exchange.

Investment readiness.

Applied research.

Innovative EbA technologies.

Synergies with existing EbA and Nature-based Solution initiatives.

The Medium-Size Grants provide up to US$500,000 and have a stronger emphasis on strategic scaling and global influence.

Innovative finance for EbA.

National policy integration.

Global learning.

Policy dialogue.

Collaborative approaches to systemic scaling.

Both tracks require projects to qualify as EbA, demonstrate innovation and catalytic potential, work with local partners and show how project results can be sustained beyond the funding period.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Global EbA Fund 2026 calls may be particularly relevant to organisations working at the intersection of:

Climate change adaptation

Ecosystem restoration

Climate finance

Environmental governance

Climate policy

Community development

Indigenous knowledge

Applied environmental research

Investment readiness

Sustainable technologies

Disaster risk reduction

Human development and resilience

Organisations should, however, ensure that their proposal addresses the Fund’s specific emphasis on Ecosystem-based Adaptation and systemic barriers to its uptake, investment, scaling or mainstreaming rather than presenting a conventional conservation or development project without a clear EbA connection.

Important Tips for Applicants

Before applying, organisations should pay close attention to the following:

Make the climate-adaptation connection explicit

Do not assume that reviewers will automatically understand how an environmental project contributes to climate adaptation. Clearly identify the climate hazard, vulnerability and adaptation pathway.

Demonstrate systemic impact

The Fund is looking for projects capable of changing systems, institutions, policies, financing mechanisms, knowledge or capacity. Explain what barrier exists and how your project will help remove it.

Build on existing work

Use evidence from previous projects, research, partnerships, pilots and community engagement to demonstrate that the proposal is grounded in experience.

Prioritise local ownership

Meaningful participation from local organisations and communities should be integrated into project design rather than treated as an afterthought.

Make gender and social inclusion substantive

Explain how women, youth, Indigenous Peoples and marginalised groups will participate and benefit. Where relevant, incorporate gender-disaggregated information and Indigenous or traditional knowledge.

Think beyond the grant period

Explain who will maintain the results, how activities will be financed after the grant, how knowledge will be retained and how successful approaches could be replicated or scaled.

Prepare early

Because applications must be submitted online and involve several supporting documents, applicants should prepare their materials well before the submission window.

Read the Grants Procedure Manual

The Global EbA Fund strongly recommends reviewing the Grants Procedure Manual before developing a proposal.

Conclusion

The Global EbA Fund Grants 2026 present a significant funding opportunity for organisations seeking to strengthen climate resilience through Ecosystem-based Adaptation. With grants of up to US$250,000 under the Small-Size Grants track and up to US$500,000 under the Medium-Size Grants track, the calls are designed to support initiatives that can address the institutional, technical, financial, knowledge and governance barriers preventing EbA from being scaled.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to organisations working in ODA-eligible Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries, although other ODA-eligible countries may also be considered when proposals demonstrate exceptional ambition and unique opportunities for scaling EbA.

Applicants should remember that the Fund is not simply seeking conventional environmental projects. Strong proposals should clearly demonstrate an Ecosystem-based Adaptation approach, a defined climate-risk pathway, innovative and catalytic potential, meaningful social inclusion, strong institutional arrangements, local partnerships and a credible plan for sustainability and replication.

For organisations preparing applications, early planning will be essential. The Small-Size Grants deadline is 26 October 2026, while the Medium-Size Grants deadline is 16 November 2026. Applicants should carefully review the relevant call documents, Grants Procedure Manual, eligibility requirements, evaluation criteria and Core Indicator Framework before submitting their proposals.

Overall, the Global EbA Fund offers an opportunity not only to obtain project financing but also to help build the policies, institutions, partnerships, evidence, investment mechanisms and local capacities needed to make climate adaptation more sustainable and effective for both people and nature.

TITLE: Community of Experts

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Discover ESF’s

Expert Reviewers delivering impartial evaluations

Since 1974, ESF has developed a network of international academics, science policy experts, and stakeholders across the European and global research landscape. Building on this heritage, we are bringing together the world’s leading researchers to develop the ESF Community of Experts (CoEx). Our CoEx plays a key role in sustaining scientific collaboration and supporting excellence in providing independent research assessments for ESF partners.

It comprises 11,000 international experts across all scientific disciplines, spanning 90 different countries.

Members of the Community of Experts can be invited to act as reviewers for research project proposals, fellowship applications, or academic promotion candidates. They may also be invited to join review panels to select research proposals in a dedicated meeting.

One Community, Two Colleges

College of Expert Reviewers

Members of the College of Expert Reviewers provide scientific assessments and evaluations in their domain of expertise. Expert Reviewers are active researchers who are recognised experts with in-depth scientific knowledge in a specific area and strong credentials in their discipline.

Experts remotely assess the submitted proposals that have been assigned to them, after a preliminary Conflict of Interest check by the ESF scientific staff.

Expert Reviewers for 2024

College of Review Panel Members

The ESF College of Review Panel members is constituted of experts of international stature with a proven record of scientific excellence and a broad knowledge of their disciplinary area. They also have solid experience in committee work and scientific assessment processes.

Review Panel members use their broad expertise to build consensus on the scientific merit of research proposals during dedicated in-person or virtual meetings.

Most members of this College are selected from experienced members of the College of Expert Reviewers.

What our Experts say

“For me, participation in ESF-led peer review exercises has been a fulfilling experience for three reasons. First, because I get the opportunity to appreciate the breadth of the scientific talent that exists across several disciplines. Second, because I meet open-minded and engaging leading experts from other disciplines and countries, all dedicated to fairness and to scientific excellence. Last but not least, because the care demonstrated by ESF in the details of the review procedure, and the fair and equitable way the ethical and social issues that arise from time to time are dealt with, strengthen my belief in the value of the independent peer review process.”

Michael Tsimplis
Professor of Maritime Law and Ocean Sciences
University of Southampton

“It is a great pleasure to work with ESF because of a number of reasons. I have read and evaluated proposals from a wide range of topics. It is very reassuring to see the willingness and the dynamics of the scientific community to push forward the boundaries with excellent proposals to address challenges in their fields. I have not just learnt a lot while helping to assess these proposals, but have also engaged with a large number of fantastic fellow experts from a great variety of scientific and cultural backgrounds who did their best to achieve a fair and rigorous outcome of the peer review process. Further, colleagues from the ESF administration were also always prompt and found quick solutions when needed to resolve matters that arose occasionally”

Prof. Robertus von Fay-Siebenburgen
University of Sheffield, UK

I appreciate serving as a reviewer for ESF, which I have done for several years, and the experience keeps improving. The evaluation procedure is well organized and clearly explained, guidance emails are timely and useful, and the online review form is easy to use. Although the process sometimes requires substantial writing, the outcome is a thorough and objective evaluation, making the effort worthwhile. The online panel meetings are very interesting, bringing together worldwide experts from diverse fields. Unfortunately, time is limited, and in-person meetings would further enrich the experience. I would gladly repeat the experience, as it is always a pleasure to contribute to the advancement of science and technology. Dr. Claudia Wiemer
National Research Council of Italy

What is involved?

Invitations to review project proposals or fellowship applications
Expand
Members of the College have the opportunity to contribute to peer review and research evaluation campaigns ESF conducts for its partner organisations. This entails being ready to receive occasional invitations from ESF to act as an external expert reviewer for research project proposals or fellowship applications.

To support reviewers in providing expert evaluations, ESF has developed the following Reviewers’ Guidelines.

Expert Honoraria
Expand
For the majority of our missions, expert honoraria are paid for timely and substantiated reviews, written according to ESF’s reviewer guidelines prepared for each campaign (including selection criteria, scoring approach, guidance for dealing with biases and Conflicts of Interest, etc.).

An Opportunity to Promote your Work
Expand
Members have the opportunity to promote their work through the ESF Community of Experts network:

Annual publication of reviewers’ names on the ESF website (unless opted-out) for members having provided a review

Certificate of recognition awarded to members having provided a review (upon request).

Join the community

We always look for the best-fit of expertise for each review assignment, taking into consideration the expert’s area of expertise, discipline, experience and availability – and of course potential biases or conflicts of interest.

Experts are asked to upload (or update) their scientific profile on our web portal. This facilitates the efficient assignment of experts to proposals.

Review panel members are selected from experienced members of the College of Expert Reviewers.

TITLE: C. B. Facey Foundation Grants 2026: Funding Opportunities for Arts, Education and Environmental Initiatives in Jamaica

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The C. B. Facey Foundation provides funding and support for initiatives that contribute to the development of communities through its mandated areas of Arts, Education and the Environment. The Foundation accepts grant applications during a specific annual application period, while sponsorship and ticket purchase requests can be submitted throughout the year for consideration.

For organizations, community groups, institutions and other eligible applicants working within the Foundation’s areas of interest, this presents an opportunity to seek financial support for initiatives that align with the Foundation’s mandate.

About the C. B. Facey Foundation

The C. B. Facey Foundation supports activities and initiatives within three principal areas:

Arts

Education

Environment

Its support is structured through different avenues, including annual grant applications, sponsorship requests and specific scholarship arrangements.

Applicants should understand that these avenues have different application procedures and timelines. In particular, the annual grant application period should not be confused with sponsorship requests, which can be submitted year-round.

C. B. Facey Foundation Grant Applications

The Foundation accepts grant applications annually from August 12 to October 12.

This annual application window provides an opportunity for applicants seeking financial support for eligible initiatives to submit their proposals for consideration.

Application period

The annual grant application period is:

Opening date: August 12
Deadline: October 12 each year

APPLY HERE

Applicants interested in receiving grant support should therefore prepare their proposals and supporting information before the application period opens.

Because applications are only accepted during the specified annual period, applicants should pay close attention to the dates and ensure that their submissions are made within the Foundation’s designated window.

Areas Covered by the Foundation

The Foundation’s mandate covers three major areas: Arts, Education and the Environment.

1. Arts

Organizations and initiatives working within the arts may fall within one of the Foundation’s areas of interest.

This may include activities connected to artistic and cultural development, although the information provided does not specify a complete list of eligible arts projects or the maximum amount that can be requested.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed initiative clearly demonstrates its relevance to the Foundation’s arts mandate.

2. Education

Education is another core area supported by the C. B. Facey Foundation.

Applicants seeking support for education-related initiatives should ensure that their proposals demonstrate a clear connection to educational development and fall within the Foundation’s mandated areas.

The Foundation also provides scholarships through specific educational institutions, but these scholarships operate separately from the general grant application process.

3. Environment

Environmental initiatives are also included within the Foundation’s mandate.

However, applicants should distinguish between the Foundation’s general grant applications and the Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant, which is specifically intended for conservation projects.

Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant

The Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant Application is designed for conservation projects.

According to the information provided, the Eco-Grant application is currently closed.

This means applicants interested specifically in conservation funding should not assume that the general C. B. Facey Foundation grant application period automatically applies to the Eco-Grant.

Those interested in future conservation funding opportunities should monitor the relevant application announcements for information about when the Eco-Grant reopens.

Sponsorship Opportunities

The C. B. Facey Foundation also considers sponsorship and ticket purchase requests separately from its annual grant applications.

Unlike the annual grants, sponsorship and ticket purchase requests can be submitted year-round.

Requests must fall within the Foundation’s mandated areas of:

Arts

Education

Environment

Applicants or organizations seeking sponsorship should submit their requests by email to:

cbfacey@panjamaica.com

This means organizations do not necessarily have to wait until the August 12 to October 12 grant application period to request sponsorship or ticket purchase support.

However, submitting a request does not guarantee funding or sponsorship. Requests are subject to consideration by the Foundation.

How Sponsorship Requests Work

Those seeking sponsorship or requesting ticket purchases should prepare their request clearly and explain the purpose of the support being sought.

A strong request should make it easy for the Foundation to understand:

Who is making the request.

What activity, event or initiative is being proposed.

Whether the request relates to Arts, Education or the Environment.

What type of sponsorship or ticket purchase support is being requested.

Why the initiative is relevant to the Foundation’s mandate.

The Foundation can then consider the request based on its own criteria and priorities.

Scholarship Opportunities

The C. B. Facey Foundation also provides scholarships, but these scholarships are not open through a general Foundation application process.

The Foundation specifically states that it grants scholarships only to:

Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts

UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture

This is an important distinction for prospective applicants.

Students interested in these scholarships must apply through the bursaries of the respective institutions.

Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts

Students interested in scholarships associated with the Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts should contact and apply through the institution’s bursary.

Applicants should not send a separate scholarship application directly to the C. B. Facey Foundation unless specifically instructed to do so.

UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture

Students interested in scholarships associated with the UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture must similarly apply through the institution’s bursary.

The Foundation’s information does not indicate that these scholarships are available to students at other universities or colleges.

Important Difference Between Grants, Sponsorships and Scholarships

Applicants should understand the differences between the Foundation’s support mechanisms.

Support Type
Application Period
Main Areas/Recipients

General Grants
August 12 – October 12 annually
Arts, Education and Environment

Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant
Currently closed
Conservation projects

Sponsorships/Ticket Purchases
Year-round
Arts, Education and Environment

Scholarships
Through respective institutions
Edna Manley College and UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture

This distinction is important because each opportunity follows a different process.

For example, someone seeking funding for an eligible organizational project may need to use the annual grant application process, while someone seeking event sponsorship can submit a request by email throughout the year.

Similarly, a student seeking one of the Foundation’s scholarships should approach the relevant institution’s bursary rather than submitting a general scholarship application to the Foundation.

Deadline for C. B. Facey Foundation Grant Applications

The annual grant application deadline is:

October 12 each year

The application period begins on August 12.

Applicants should therefore make sure that their applications are submitted before October 12 rather than waiting until the final day.

For sponsorship and ticket purchase requests, there is no annual deadline, as requests can be emailed year-round.

The Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant is currently closed.

How to Contact the C. B. Facey Foundation

Applicants and interested individuals who have questions or concerns can contact the Foundation directly.

Email: cbfacey@panjamaica.com
Telephone: 876-929-4510

The email address can be used for questions relating to grants, sponsorships, ticket purchase requests and other matters within the Foundation’s mandate.

Visit HERE to learn more about the C. B. Facey Foundation Grants 2026

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity may be relevant to organizations, initiatives and applicants working within the Foundation’s stated areas of interest.

Potential applicants include those involved in:

Arts and cultural initiatives

Educational initiatives

Environmental initiatives

Conservation-related projects, when the relevant Eco-Grant is open

Events or activities seeking sponsorship within the Foundation’s mandated areas

Students should note that the scholarship component is much more specific. According to the information provided, scholarships are limited to students applying through the bursaries of Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts and the UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture.

What Applicants Should Keep in Mind

Before submitting a request, applicants should first determine which type of support best matches their needs.

If you are seeking grant funding, check whether your initiative fits within Arts, Education or the Environment and prepare your application for the August 12–October 12 annual window.

If you are seeking sponsorship or ticket purchases, you can submit your request by email at any time during the year.

If you are seeking a scholarship, confirm whether you are applying through one of the two institutions identified by the Foundation and submit your application through the appropriate bursary.

If your project is specifically focused on conservation, be aware that the Jamaica Conservation Partners Eco-Grant is currently closed and that a separate announcement may be required when applications reopen.

Conclusion

The C. B. Facey Foundation offers several forms of support for initiatives connected to Arts, Education and the Environment. Its main grant application period runs annually from August 12 to October 12, giving eligible applicants a defined window in which to seek grant funding.

Beyond the annual grant programme, the Foundation accepts sponsorship and ticket purchase requests throughout the year by email. Meanwhile, its scholarship support is specifically directed to students at Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts and the UTECH Caribbean School of Architecture, with applications handled through the respective institutions’ bursaries.

Applicants should carefully identify the appropriate funding route before submitting a request and ensure that their initiative falls within the Foundation’s stated areas of support.

Deadline for annual grant applications: October 12 each year.

Contact: cbfacey@panjamaica.com | 876-929-4510

TITLE: Charlotte Community Foundation Fall 2026 Grants | Up to $15,000 for Local Nonprofits

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Charlotte Community Foundation (CCF) has opened its Fall 2026 competitive grant cycle, providing funding opportunities for eligible nonprofit organisations serving Charlotte County, Florida.

The Fall 2026 cycle will distribute $195,000 in donor-designated funding through two grant opportunities focused on specific areas of community need. Eligible organisations can apply for funding supporting work in health care, housing insecurity, seniors, veterans and youth.

Applications opened on September 1, 2026, and must be submitted by September 29, 2026, at 4:59 p.m.

About the Charlotte Community Foundation Fall 2026 Grants

The Charlotte Community Foundation is a philanthropic organisation dedicated to strengthening the quality of life in Charlotte County, Florida.

For the Fall 2026 grant cycle, CCF is offering competitive funding through donor-designated funds supporting specific areas of local nonprofit service delivery.

The cycle includes program grants supporting organisations working in housing insecurity and health care, while the broader designated funding areas for the cycle also include seniors, veterans and youth.

Funding Available

The Fall 2026 cycle includes:

Housing Insecurity

CCF will provide four grants of $15,000 for organisations addressing housing insecurity.

Eligible organisations should provide services such as:

Direct services for people experiencing housing insecurity.

Homelessness prevention programmes.

Housing solutions.

Outreach services.

Support systems aimed at reducing or ending homelessness.

Programmes serving children and youth experiencing homelessness are especially encouraged to apply.

Health Care

CCF will also provide four grants of $15,000 for organisations working in health care.

Eligible applicants may provide:

Direct health-related services.

Access to quality health care.

Initiatives designed to improve health outcomes.

Physical health services.

Mental and behavioural health services.

Preventive and primary care.

Nutrition and wellness programmes.

CCF takes a broad approach to the definition of health and health care for this funding opportunity.

Total Funding

The two $15,000 grant areas described above represent:

$60,000 for Housing Insecurity

$60,000 for Health Care

$120,000 total for these two programme grant areas

The Foundation’s Fall 2026 cycle overall is described as distributing $195,000 in donor-designated contributions through two grant opportunities covering five local nonprofit service areas.

Who Can Apply?

The Fall 2026 grants are intended for nonprofit organisations that meet CCF’s eligibility requirements.

Organisations must:

Be a nonprofit organisation with 501(c)(3) status, unless another status has been approved by CCF.

Have received their tax-exempt determination letter from the IRS.

Align with the mission of the Charlotte Community Foundation.

Be located in or provide services in Charlotte County, Florida.

Use the grant funding within Charlotte County.

An organisation does not necessarily have to be headquartered in Charlotte County. However, the funded activities must take place within the county.

Funding Areas for the Fall 2026 Cycle

CCF identifies five designated areas for its Fall 2026 grants:

Health Care

Housing Insecurity

Seniors

Veterans

Youth

An organisation’s mission and programmes must align with one of the designated funding areas to be eligible for this cycle.

Applicants should carefully review the specific funding opportunity before applying because the cycle uses donor-designated funds and has specific requirements.

Can Faith-Based Organisations Apply?

Faith-based organisations may apply when the proposed funding supports a distinct community outreach programme.

Examples include programmes such as:

Food banks

Homelessness support

Senior support services

However, CCF does not fund activities undertaken for religious purposes, including worship services, religious education, faith-based materials or activities that promote a specific religion.

What Information Is Required?

Applicants will need to provide organisational and programme information as part of the application.

The application process requires information concerning:

Staffing

Organisational mission

Leadership

Board engagement

Budget

Recent financial documents

Existing programmes related to the selected funding area

How the requested funding would strengthen existing programmes

Expected impact on Charlotte County

Importantly, these grants are intended to support or enhance work already underway, rather than provide funding for an organisation to begin working in an entirely new focus area.

Can an Organisation Apply for More Than One Grant?

No.

Each organisation may submit only one application during the Fall 2026 grant cycle.

Organisations should therefore carefully determine which funding opportunity most closely matches their mission and programme activities before submitting an application.

How Applications Are Evaluated

Applications will be reviewed by a Grants Committee consisting of trained community volunteers with relevant area expertise.

The committee will assess applications based on factors including:

Organisational finances

Leadership

Effectiveness of programmes

Community impact

The committee will make recommendations to the CCF Board of Directors for consideration and final approval.

How Long Does the Application Take?

CCF states that the application is designed to take less than two hours to complete.

The programme application for the Housing Insecurity or Health Care funding areas is more detailed. Applicants are encouraged to review the available informational materials before beginning the application.

Grant Information Sessions

CCF strongly encourages prospective applicants to review the Fall 2026 Grant Informational Presentation recording and presentation slides before beginning an application.

The information session provides an overview of:

Eligibility requirements

The grant cycle

Application process

Important dates

Other relevant application information

How to Apply for the Charlotte Community Foundation Grants

Eligible nonprofit organisations can apply through the online grant application portal accessible through the Charlotte Community Foundation’s website.

Before applying, organisations should:

Review the eligibility requirements.

Identify the designated funding area that best matches their existing work.

Review the grant information session and application guidance.

Prepare the required organisational, financial and programme information.

Complete the online application.

Submit the application before the deadline.

Apply through the Charlotte Community Foundation Grants page

Application Deadline

The Fall 2026 grant cycle opened on:

September 1, 2026

The application deadline is:

September 29, 2026 at 4:59 p.m.

CCF states that deadlines are strictly enforced to ensure a fair review process.

When Will Applicants Receive a Decision?

Applicants will receive communication by email regarding the status of their applications in December 2026.

CCF plans for funding to be delivered before the end of December 2026.

Successful applicants will receive an award letter explaining the grant terms, including reporting acknowledgements and disbursement information.

Applicants who are not selected will also receive notification by email and may contact CCF to discuss their application and learn why it was not selected.

Reporting Requirements

Successful grantees will be required to complete an online grant acknowledgement form within two weeks of receiving the award.

One year after receiving the funding, award recipients are invited to submit a concise report of no more than three pages explaining:

How the grant was used.

The impact of the funding.

Progress against projected outcomes.

Relevant qualitative and quantitative data.

About the Charlotte Community Foundation

The Charlotte Community Foundation is dedicated to improving the quality of life throughout Charlotte County, Florida.

The Foundation connects individuals, companies, organisations and advisors with charitable causes and permanent capital to create community impact. It has operated as a community foundation since 2004 and has granted $15 million to nearly every local nonprofit and $1.6 million in scholarships over its 20 years of service.

CCF manages philanthropic resources and supports local nonprofits and students through grants and scholarships.

Conclusion

The Charlotte Community Foundation Fall 2026 Grants provide an opportunity for eligible nonprofits serving Charlotte County to receive financial support for existing programmes addressing important community needs.

The Fall 2026 cycle focuses on five designated areas: health care, housing insecurity, seniors, veterans and youth. The Foundation is particularly offering programme grants of $15,000 for eligible organisations addressing housing insecurity and health care.

Organisations interested in applying should carefully review the eligibility requirements, attend or watch the informational presentation and prepare their application before the deadline.

TITLE: Mastercard Foundation Associates Program Cohort 2 with Jobberman 2026: Apply for 12-Month Paid Work Placements Across West Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Mastercard Foundation Associates Program Cohort 2, implemented in partnership with Jobberman, is offering young professionals an opportunity to gain substantial workplace experience through 12-month paid placements with employers across selected West African countries.

The program is designed to help young people make the often difficult transition from education into meaningful employment. Rather than providing only short-term training, the Associates Program combines practical workplace exposure with professional development, employability training, mentorship, networking, and career-transition support.

The Mastercard Foundation describes the Associates Program as an initiative connecting young Africans with 12-month paid work placements while helping participants build leadership, employability, and entrepreneurship capabilities. More than 1,000 Associates across 22 countries have participated since 2023.

For the Jobberman-led phase, participating countries include Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and The Gambia, with Associates placed with employers offering entry-level professional opportunities.

Application Deadline: 21 October 2026

The current Cohort 2 application window is reported as running from 21 September 2026 to 21 October 2026.

About the Mastercard Foundation Associates Program

The Mastercard Foundation Associates Program was established to address a major challenge affecting young graduates across Africa: obtaining meaningful professional experience after completing their education.

Many graduates possess academic qualifications but find themselves competing for positions that already require prior workplace experience. The Associates Program seeks to bridge this gap by providing structured, longer-term opportunities in real organizations.

According to the Mastercard Foundation, the program connects young Africans with paid professional placements lasting 12 months and combines employment experience with employability development and mentorship.

The program is built around three broad stages:

Recruitment and selection

Placement into internship roles

Transition pathways following the placement

The intention is therefore not simply to give participants temporary work. The broader objective is to strengthen their ability to move into sustainable and fulfilling employment after completing the program.

Jobberman’s Role in the Associates Program

Jobberman serves as a regional placement partner for the Mastercard Foundation Associates Program in Anglophone West Africa.

The Mastercard Foundation identifies Jobberman as one of its official regional placement partners alongside organizations supporting East Africa, Francophone Africa, Southern Africa, and remote placements.

Under the Jobberman component, participating employers provide Associates with meaningful workplace responsibilities, supervision, mentorship, and professional exposure.

For the expanded phase of the program, Jobberman states that participation covers:

Nigeria

Ghana

Liberia

Sierra Leone

The Gambia

The organization describes the initiative as a 12-month professional development and placement program intended for early-career young professionals.

What Selected Associates Will Receive

The Mastercard Foundation Associates Program provides much more than access to a vacancy.

Successful applicants can benefit from a combination of workplace experience, structured professional development, mentorship, and financial support.

1. A 12-Month Professional Placement

One of the most significant features of the program is its duration.

Associates are placed in host organizations for approximately 12 months, allowing considerably more time to build meaningful professional competence than many traditional short-term internships.

The extended placement gives Associates an opportunity to:

Understand workplace systems and processes

Develop technical and professional skills

Work on real organizational assignments

Build professional relationships

Demonstrate performance over an extended period

Learn how organizations operate

Gain references and relevant career experience

Strengthen their prospects of longer-term employment

The Mastercard Foundation officially describes these opportunities as 12-month paid work placements.

2. Monthly Stipend Throughout the Placement

Selected Associates receive financial support while participating in the program.

According to the official applicant guidance, Associates receive a monthly stipend for the full 12-month period.

However, there is no single universal stipend amount. Payment varies according to factors including:

Placement location

Host country

Industry

Nature of the placement

The stipend is normally paid in the local currency of the country where the Associate is placed.

Applicants should therefore be cautious about unofficial websites or social media posts advertising a fixed stipend amount unless that amount is specifically stated in an individual vacancy.

3. Hands-On Professional Work Experience

The program emphasizes practical workplace learning.

Participants are expected to work within real organizations rather than simply complete classroom-based training.

This hands-on structure gives young professionals the opportunity to turn theoretical knowledge into practical competence.

Depending on the host employer and individual position, Associates may gain experience in areas such as:

Administration

Finance

Human resources

Marketing

Communications

Technology

Business development

Operations

Project management

Research

Data

Customer service

Sales

Development programs

Monitoring and evaluation

Other professional and technical functions

Individual responsibilities will vary according to the specific roles advertised through Jobberman’s Cohort 2 portal.

4. Leadership Skills Development

The Associates Program is intended to help participants become more capable professionals and future leaders.

The Mastercard Foundation specifically identifies leadership development as one of the major benefits of the program.

Through professional responsibilities, workplace feedback, mentorship, and structured development activities, participants can improve competencies such as:

Decision-making

Accountability

Teamwork

Professional communication

Problem-solving

Workplace ethics

Initiative

Adaptability

Time management

Stakeholder management

These competencies are valuable regardless of the particular sector in which an Associate eventually builds a career.

5. Employability Skills Development

A major objective of the program is improving employability.

Participants are expected to develop the capabilities needed to compete successfully for future employment opportunities.

The Mastercard Foundation’s applicant guidance confirms that employability training forms part of the Associates Program.

This can be especially important for recent graduates who may have strong academic backgrounds but limited exposure to professional recruitment and workplace expectations.

6. Entrepreneurship Skills Development

The program also incorporates entrepreneurship-related capability development.

This reflects the wider reality of the African employment landscape, where entrepreneurship and self-employment can represent important career pathways alongside formal employment.

Participants may therefore emerge from the program with stronger knowledge of how organizations operate, how value is created, and how professional skills can potentially be applied within entrepreneurial ventures.

The Mastercard Foundation officially lists entrepreneurship skill-building alongside leadership and employability development.

7. Mentorship

Mentorship is another core element of the program.

Associates gain access to professionals who can support their development and help them navigate workplace challenges.

Mentorship can help participants:

Understand professional expectations

Improve performance

Receive career guidance

Reflect on their strengths and weaknesses

Navigate workplace relationships

Develop career plans

Identify future employment pathways

The Mastercard Foundation identifies mentorship and professional networking among the benefits available to Associates.

8. Professional Networking

Participants also gain access to professional networks.

These relationships can become particularly valuable after the placement ends.

Associates may interact with:

Supervisors

Managers

Human resources professionals

Fellow Associates

Industry professionals

Employers

Mentors

Mastercard Foundation network members

Jobberman professionals

Partner organizations

A professional network built through a year-long placement may assist participants with future employment, referrals, mentorship, collaborations, and career opportunities.

9. Career Transition Support

The Mastercard Foundation Associates Program does not treat the completion of an internship as the end of the participant journey.

Career-transition support is explicitly identified as part of the program.

The intention is to help Associates convert the skills and experience gained during the placement into longer-term career opportunities.

Host employers are also encouraged to consider retaining strong-performing Associates after the 12-month placement when possible.

Strong Focus on Long-Term Employment

One of the most important characteristics of the program is its emphasis on transitioning participants toward sustained employment rather than merely increasing the number of completed internships.

Jobberman’s earlier phase demonstrated this approach in practice. Reporting on the program’s expansion, Jobberman and its partners emphasized workplace learning, mentorship, performance reviews, career development, and support throughout Associates’ placements.

Employers are encouraged to give Associates meaningful assignments and opportunities to develop skills that remain relevant after the program.

Inclusive Employment Opportunities

Inclusion is a significant component of the Mastercard Foundation Associates Program.

The Foundation states that the program seeks participation from groups that can face additional barriers in accessing employment, including:

Young women

Persons with disabilities

Refugees

Internally displaced persons

Since the program began, its participant community has included individuals from these groups across multiple African countries.

Host organizations are expected to maintain safe, accessible, inclusive, and supportive workplaces for Associates.

How Host Employers Are Selected

Associates are not intended to be placed randomly with organizations.

Regional partners assess prospective employers to determine whether they can provide an appropriate professional experience.

According to the Mastercard Foundation, participating employers are evaluated based on factors including:

Legal registration and operational status

Workplace structure

Clear reporting arrangements

Supervision capacity

Mentorship capacity

Availability of necessary work resources

Ability to provide a quality professional experience

Employers are expected to provide meaningful assignments, supervision, professional development, performance feedback, and a safe working environment.

Jobberman similarly states that host employers should have structured workplace reporting systems and sufficient capacity to give Associates meaningful work experience.

The PREP2SOAR Training Process

Submitting an application does not automatically result in placement.

Applications are first screened.

According to the official Mastercard Foundation applicant FAQ, candidates who are shortlisted are contacted by the appropriate regional placement partner.

Shortlisted applicants must then participate in mandatory PREP2SOAR training, which is designed to strengthen job readiness and prepare candidates for employer interviews.

This process means applicants should monitor their email closely after applying.

Missing an email requesting participation in training or another selection stage could potentially affect progression.

Recruitment and Selection Process

Although the exact recruitment process may vary between individual roles, the broader journey includes:

Finding relevant Cohort 2 vacancies

Reviewing individual job descriptions

Submitting an application

Initial application screening

Shortlisting

Mandatory PREP2SOAR preparation

Employer consideration and interviews

Placement with a participating employer

Completion of the 12-month professional experience

Career-transition support

Applicants should remember that simply meeting minimum eligibility conditions does not guarantee selection.

Host employers may require specific educational backgrounds, competencies, locations, or technical capabilities depending on the vacancy.

Physical, Hybrid and Remote Work Possibilities

The wider Associates Program allows candidates to indicate preferences for:

Physical/on-site placements

Hybrid placements

Remote placements

However, applicants are not guaranteed their preferred working arrangement.

Candidates interested in remote opportunities must be able to confirm that they have:

A personal laptop

Stable internet connectivity

A reliable electricity supply

These requirements are included in the Mastercard Foundation’s applicant guidance.

Applicants should also apply for positions located in their own country of residence unless the opportunity is explicitly advertised as remote.

Relocation Costs

Prospective applicants should pay particular attention to placement location.

The Mastercard Foundation states that applicants should already satisfy the legal requirements allowing them to work in the city or country where the position is based because relocation expenses are not covered for location-based placements.

Applicants should therefore avoid applying for positions in another country unless they already possess the appropriate legal authorization to work there or the role specifically allows remote participation.

Application Documents

Applicants should prepare an updated CV or résumé.

According to the official applicant FAQ, the résumé can be uploaded in either:

DOC format

PDF format

Candidates who indicate that they are alumni of a Mastercard Foundation-supported initiative may also be required to provide evidence confirming that status.

Important CV File-Naming Requirement

Applicants should also pay attention to how their résumé file is named.

The official guidance states that the CV filename should contain the applicant’s full official name, including first name and family name.

For example:

Firstname_Lastname_CV.pdf

Following seemingly minor application instructions can be important because recruitment systems process large numbers of applications.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Candidates should tailor their application to the specific vacancy rather than submitting the same generic résumé for every position.

Before applying, carefully study:

Required academic qualification

Required field of study

Skills requested

Work-location requirements

Technical competencies

Experience requirements

Employer expectations

Applicants should then clearly demonstrate relevant experience from:

Internships

Volunteering

University projects

National service

Freelance assignments

Student societies

Community projects

Entrepreneurship

Previous employment

Professional certifications

For early-career applicants, evidence of ability and initiative can be important even when formal professional experience is limited.

Why the 12-Month Structure Matters

Many conventional internships last only a few weeks or months.

A 12-month placement provides considerably more time for an individual to become integrated into an organization.

During a year, an Associate may have the opportunity to:

Complete substantial projects

Experience different stages of business cycles

Receive multiple performance reviews

Develop stronger professional relationships

Take on increasing responsibility

Demonstrate measurable improvement

Build a stronger professional portfolio

The employer also has more time to assess the Associate as a potential long-term employee.

This structure supports the program’s wider objective of facilitating meaningful transitions into employment.

Why Employers Participate

The initiative is designed to create value for employers as well as Associates.

Participating organizations gain access to young, pre-trained professionals while contributing to Africa’s emerging workforce.

Jobberman states that employers can benefit by:

Strengthening organizational capacity

Accessing motivated early-career talent

Supporting workforce inclusion

Contributing to youth employment

Developing future talent pipelines

Assessing potential long-term hires

The program also provides financial support toward Associate remuneration, reducing part of the placement cost for host employers.

Application Period and Deadline

Applications for the current Cohort 2 opportunity are open from 21 September 2026 until 21 October 2026.

Application Deadline: 21 October 2026

Candidates should avoid waiting until the final day because individual roles may attract substantial interest.

Applicants should also note that the wider Mastercard Foundation Associates Program publishes opportunities on an ongoing basis, meaning vacancy availability can change as positions are filled or new roles are added.

How to Apply for the Mastercard Foundation Associates Program Cohort 2

Applicants should access the Jobberman Cohort 2 recruitment portal and review the positions currently available.

The official Cohort 2 portal provided for this application cycle is:

Apply through the Jobberman Cohort 2 portal

Candidates should:

Open the Jobberman Cohort 2 recruitment portal.

Review the available positions.

Select opportunities that match their qualifications, interests, location, and experience.

Carefully read the complete job description.

Prepare an updated CV.

Complete the required online application.

Submit the application before the deadline.

Monitor email regularly for shortlisting or PREP2SOAR instructions.

There is no requirement to apply blindly for every vacancy. Candidates should focus on roles for which they can demonstrate a genuine match.

About the Mastercard Foundation

The Mastercard Foundation is an international foundation focused heavily on education and transitions into meaningful work, particularly for young people in Africa.

Through programs such as the Associates Program, the Foundation seeks to help young people develop practical skills, professional experience, leadership capabilities, and pathways toward dignified and fulfilling livelihoods.

The Associates Program is one component of this broader approach to improving the transition from education into sustainable employment.

About Jobberman

Jobberman is a major recruitment and career-development platform operating within Africa’s employment ecosystem.

As a regional partner of the Mastercard Foundation Associates Program, Jobberman is responsible for connecting qualified young professionals with host employers across the participating Anglophone West African markets.

The partnership combines Jobberman’s recruitment infrastructure with the Mastercard Foundation’s broader focus on youth employment and professional development.

Conclusion

The Mastercard Foundation Associates Program Cohort 2 with Jobberman 2026 provides young professionals with an opportunity to move beyond academic qualifications and gain substantial real-world experience through a structured 12-month paid work placement.

Participants can benefit from hands-on professional experience, a monthly stipend, employability development, leadership and entrepreneurship skills, mentorship, professional networking, workplace support, and career-transition assistance.

For young graduates struggling with the familiar challenge of needing experience to obtain a job while needing a job to acquire experience, a structured year-long placement can provide an important bridge into the professional world.

Applicants should review individual vacancies carefully, ensure that their qualifications and location correspond with the requirements, prepare a well-targeted CV, and submit applications through the official Jobberman Cohort 2 portal.
