TITLE: Council on Foreign Relations Fellowships 2026: Transformational Opportunities for U.S. Citizens Pursuing Careers in Foreign Policy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) Fellowships provide prestigious opportunities for individuals seeking to deepen their understanding of international affairs, foreign policy, diplomacy, national security, and global policymaking. Designed to give selected fellows meaningful exposure to new environments and policymaking settings, CFR’s fellowship programs can provide an important platform for professionals committed to building long-term careers in foreign policy.

Through its diverse portfolio of domestic and overseas fellowships, the Council on Foreign Relations connects talented professionals with opportunities to gain practical experience, broaden their perspectives, engage with experts, and contribute to discussions surrounding some of the world’s most important international challenges.

For U.S. citizens with a demonstrated commitment to a career in foreign policy, these fellowships can provide an opportunity to step outside their existing professional environment and gain direct exposure to policymaking institutions, international affairs research, diplomacy, journalism, technology policy, nuclear security, and other areas relevant to America’s engagement with the world.

What Are Council on Foreign Relations Fellowships?

The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) Fellowships are specialized fellowship opportunities intended to broaden the perspectives and professional experiences of individuals working toward careers in foreign policy and international affairs.

According to the information provided by CFR, selected fellows can gain exposure to a new environment in one of several settings, including:

A policymaking environment

The Council on Foreign Relations itself

An overseas professional or policy environment

Specialized institutions and organizations connected to foreign policy

Professional settings related to journalism, technology diplomacy, national security, and international affairs

The objective is not simply to provide a temporary professional placement. CFR describes its fellowships as unique and transformational opportunities through which fellows can develop broader perspectives on foreign affairs.

This makes the programs particularly relevant to professionals who want to expand their understanding beyond their current area of work and gain exposure to the complex processes through which international policy is researched, debated, developed, and implemented.

Why CFR Fellowships Are Important

International affairs increasingly require professionals who understand how different countries, institutions, political systems, economic interests, security priorities, technological developments, and global challenges interact.

A professional working in foreign policy may need to understand diplomacy. A journalist covering international affairs may need deeper knowledge of national security. A technology professional may need to understand how artificial intelligence and emerging technologies affect international relations. Likewise, policymakers may need exposure to academic research, international institutions, media perspectives, and overseas policy environments.

CFR’s fellowship programs are structured around this type of professional development.

By placing fellows in new environments, the programs can expose participants to perspectives and experiences that may not be available through their existing professional roles.

International Affairs Fellowship Programs Overseas

One of the major components of the CFR fellowship portfolio is its collection of overseas fellowship programs.

These programs provide opportunities for selected fellows to gain international exposure while examining foreign policy issues from a different national or regional perspective.

The overseas programs listed in the information provided include:

1. International Affairs Fellowship in Canada

The International Affairs Fellowship in Canada provides an overseas pathway for fellows interested in developing their understanding of international affairs through exposure to the Canadian environment.

Canada is an important partner of the United States, and professional exposure in the country can provide insights into bilateral relations, diplomacy, international cooperation, security, trade, and broader North American affairs.

The fellowship is therefore particularly relevant to professionals whose interests intersect with U.S.-Canadian relations or broader international policy questions.

2. International Affairs Fellowship in India

The International Affairs Fellowship in India provides an opportunity for fellows to gain exposure to one of the world’s most influential countries.

India plays an increasingly important role in global diplomacy, economic affairs, security, technology, and international relations.

Professional experience in India can therefore help fellows develop a broader understanding of South Asian affairs and India’s role in the international system.

3. International Affairs Fellowship in Indonesia

The International Affairs Fellowship in Indonesia offers another overseas opportunity within CFR’s international affairs portfolio.

Indonesia is a major country in Southeast Asia and plays an important role in regional and international affairs.

For fellows interested in Southeast Asian geopolitics, international cooperation, economic relations, regional security, and diplomacy, an overseas fellowship experience in Indonesia could provide valuable exposure to perspectives that differ from those found in the United States.

4. International Affairs Fellowship in Japan

The International Affairs Fellowship in Japan provides an opportunity for fellows to broaden their knowledge of Japan and its position within international affairs.

Japan has an important role in Asian security, global economics, technology, diplomacy, and U.S. foreign policy.

An overseas experience in Japan can therefore be relevant to professionals seeking a stronger understanding of East Asian affairs and the relationships shaping the Indo-Pacific region.

5. Chung Mong-Koo International Affairs Fellowship in the Republic of Korea

The Chung Mong-Koo International Affairs Fellowship in the Republic of Korea is another specialized international opportunity listed among CFR’s overseas programs.

The Republic of Korea occupies a strategically significant position in East Asia. Issues involving regional security, economic relations, technology, diplomacy, and relations with the United States are all important components of the broader international environment surrounding the Korean Peninsula.

This fellowship provides another avenue through which fellows can gain exposure to international affairs outside the United States.

6. Robert A. Belfer International Affairs Fellowship in European Security

The Robert A. Belfer International Affairs Fellowship in European Security focuses specifically on European security.

Security issues in Europe have major implications for international relations, transatlantic cooperation, defense policy, diplomacy, and U.S. foreign policy.

Professionals interested in European security and related foreign policy questions may therefore find this fellowship particularly relevant to their professional development.

Domestic Fellowship Programs

CFR’s fellowship portfolio also includes domestic programs based in the United States.

These opportunities allow fellows to gain exposure to foreign policy and international affairs without necessarily participating in an overseas placement.

The domestic programs listed include the following:

1. International Affairs Fellowship

The International Affairs Fellowship provides an opportunity for professionals committed to foreign policy to broaden their perspectives through a fellowship experience.

The program is part of CFR’s broader mission of developing a stronger and more diverse foreign policy community in the United States.

2. Edward R. Murrow Press Fellowship

The Edward R. Murrow Press Fellowship is particularly relevant to professionals working in journalism and the press.

Journalists play an important role in explaining international developments to the public. Understanding foreign policy, diplomacy, global security, and international institutions can strengthen the quality and depth of reporting on international affairs.

The Murrow fellowship therefore represents an opportunity connected to the intersection of journalism and foreign policy.

3. Stanton Nuclear Security Fellowship

The Stanton Nuclear Security Fellowship focuses on nuclear security.

Nuclear weapons, proliferation, deterrence, arms control, and international security remain significant issues in global affairs.

A specialized fellowship in nuclear security can provide professional exposure for individuals interested in understanding and contributing to policy discussions surrounding these complex issues.

4. Technologist-in-Residence Fellowship

The Technologist-in-Residence Fellowship reflects the increasingly important relationship between technology and international affairs.

Technology is transforming diplomacy, national security, economic competition, communication, intelligence, and international relations.

Professionals with technology backgrounds can therefore contribute valuable technical perspectives to foreign policy discussions.

The fellowship provides a pathway for technological expertise to intersect with the foreign policy community.

Fellowships by Nomination Only

Not every CFR fellowship follows the same application process.

The information provided specifically identifies a group of fellowships that are available by nomination only.

These include:

Historian-in-Residence Fellowship

Military Fellowships

National Intelligence Fellowship

State Department Fellowship on Technology Diplomacy

Because these opportunities are identified as nomination-only programs, interested individuals should not assume that they can apply through the same process used for publicly accessible fellowship opportunities.

This distinction is important for prospective candidates because the application pathway can vary significantly between programs.

Historian-in-Residence Fellowship

The Historian-in-Residence Fellowship provides an opportunity associated with historical expertise and international affairs.

History is an important component of foreign policy because contemporary international relationships are often shaped by historical events, political decisions, conflicts, alliances, treaties, and institutional developments.

A historian working within a foreign policy environment can therefore contribute valuable context to discussions about international affairs.

Military Fellowships

CFR’s Military Fellowships provide another pathway for individuals with military backgrounds to engage with the foreign policy community.

Military experience can offer important perspectives on national security, defense, international conflict, strategic planning, and relations between military institutions and policymakers.

Because the fellowship is identified under CFR’s nomination-only category, interested candidates should carefully review the specific process and eligibility requirements applicable to the program.

National Intelligence Fellowship

The National Intelligence Fellowship is another specialized program within CFR’s fellowship portfolio.

Intelligence plays a central role in national security and foreign policy decision-making. Reliable intelligence can help policymakers understand international developments, assess threats, and make informed strategic decisions.

The fellowship therefore sits at the intersection of intelligence and foreign policy.

State Department Fellowship on Technology Diplomacy

The State Department Fellowship on Technology Diplomacy addresses the growing importance of technology in international relations.

Emerging technologies increasingly influence diplomacy, national security, economic competition, international cooperation, and relations between governments.

Technology diplomacy brings technical and policy perspectives together, making expertise in this area increasingly important to modern foreign policy.

The fellowship provides a specialized opportunity connected to this evolving field.

Who Is Eligible for CFR Fellowships?

Eligibility varies considerably between the individual Council on Foreign Relations fellowship programs.

The general fellowship information provided states that CFR fellowships offer opportunities for U.S. citizens with a demonstrated commitment to a career in foreign policy.

This means prospective candidates should pay close attention to both the general CFR fellowship requirements and the specific eligibility rules for the fellowship they are interested in.

Potential candidates may include professionals whose careers or academic interests are connected to areas such as:

Foreign policy

International affairs

Diplomacy

Journalism

National security

Nuclear security

Military affairs

Intelligence

Technology

Technology diplomacy

European security

International relations

Policymaking

History and international affairs

However, the exact qualifications, professional experience requirements, nomination procedures, and citizenship requirements can differ from one fellowship to another.

Are Applicants From Other Countries Eligible?

The general information supplied for the CFR fellowship portfolio specifically describes the opportunities as being for U.S. citizens with a demonstrated commitment to a career in foreign policy.

Therefore, applicants should not assume that simply being a resident of another country makes them eligible.

At the same time, CFR’s portfolio includes overseas fellowship programs in Canada, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Europe. The location of a fellowship should not automatically be interpreted as meaning that citizens of that country or region can apply.

For example, the existence of an International Affairs Fellowship in India does not, based on the information provided alone, establish that all Indian citizens are eligible.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, or other regions should therefore review the eligibility requirements of the specific fellowship before applying.

What Makes These Fellowships Different?

One of the distinguishing characteristics of the CFR fellowship portfolio is its emphasis on exposure to new environments.

Rather than limiting fellows to their existing professional setting, CFR seeks to provide selected participants with experiences that can broaden their understanding of foreign affairs.

This can involve exposure to:

Policymaking environments

CFR’s professional and research environment

Overseas settings

Journalism and media

Military and national security perspectives

Intelligence

Nuclear security

Technology and technology diplomacy

Regional security

International affairs research and policy discussions

Such exposure can help professionals develop a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that shape foreign policy.

Professional Development and Career Benefits

Participating in a prestigious foreign policy fellowship can contribute to professional growth in several ways.

Broader understanding of international affairs

Fellows can gain exposure to international issues beyond their existing area of expertise.

Exposure to policymaking

The opportunity to work in or around policymaking environments can provide insight into how foreign policy ideas are developed and implemented.

International experience

The overseas fellowship programs can expose fellows to international environments and perspectives.

Cross-sector learning

CFR’s portfolio covers journalism, technology, military affairs, intelligence, nuclear security, history, and diplomacy. This creates opportunities for professionals from different backgrounds to engage with foreign policy.

Professional network development

Working within a foreign policy environment can help fellows develop relationships with other professionals, researchers, policymakers, journalists, and experts.

Greater perspective

Exposure to different institutions and countries can help participants develop a broader understanding of international challenges.

Featured CFR Events and International Affairs Content

The Council on Foreign Relations fellowship page also highlights meetings, expert analysis, and reports related to international affairs.

Among the featured content listed in the provided information is the 2026 International Affairs Fellowship (IAF) Summer Series: Multilateralism Under Pressure, held on July 29, 2026.

The event reflects the type of foreign policy discussion associated with CFR’s broader work and highlights the importance of multilateralism in an increasingly complicated international environment.

The page also features analysis and reports addressing major global issues.

One featured expert take examines how rising deaths from earthquakes in Venezuela tested U.S. disaster relief.

Another article examines U.S. policy surrounding artificial intelligence oversight, demonstrating the growing intersection between technology and national policy.

A report on preventing renewed conflict in Colombia highlights the importance of conflict prevention and international engagement.

These topics demonstrate the breadth of issues connected to the broader foreign policy community.

Council on Foreign Relations and the U.S. Foreign Policy Community

Beyond its fellowship programs, the Council on Foreign Relations maintains a broader ecosystem focused on international affairs.

The CFR website provides access to areas including:

Membership

Fellowships

Careers

Newsletters

CFR Education

Events

Foreign policy analysis

Reports

Expert commentary

International affairs resources

The fellowship program forms part of this wider effort to strengthen the foreign policy community.

CFR also states that it is committed to fostering a foreign policy community in the United States that is more representative of American society as a whole.

This emphasis on representation is an important component of the organization’s fellowship mission.

How to Approach a CFR Fellowship Opportunity

Because CFR operates several different fellowship programs, prospective candidates should avoid treating the fellowship portfolio as a single application.

Instead, applicants should:

Identify the fellowship that most closely matches their professional background and foreign policy interests.

Read the specific eligibility requirements for that fellowship.

Determine whether the program accepts direct applications or operates through nomination or invitation.

Review the required application materials.

Confirm citizenship and professional eligibility requirements.

Check the fellowship’s specific deadline.

Research the focus area of the fellowship.

Prepare application materials that clearly demonstrate a commitment to foreign policy.

Highlight relevant professional, academic, research, journalism, military, technology, or policy experience.

Submit the application through the official CFR process where applicable.

Important Note About Application Deadlines

There is no single overall deadline stated in the information provided for all Council on Foreign Relations fellowships.

Instead, eligibility and application procedures vary among individual fellowship programs.

Applicants should therefore avoid relying on a general CFR fellowship deadline and should check the specific fellowship page for:

Opening date

Closing date

Eligibility requirements

Application procedure

Required documents

Nomination requirements

Citizenship requirements

Fellowship duration

Location

Selection criteria

Potentially relevant candidates include professionals working in:

Government and public policy

Journalism and media

National security

Defense

Why This Opportunity Can Be Valuable for a Foreign Policy Career

Foreign policy careers often require more than academic knowledge.

Professionals may need to understand how governments make decisions, how international institutions operate, how geopolitical relationships evolve, how journalists communicate global developments, how technological changes affect security, and how policymakers respond to emerging threats.

A fellowship that provides exposure to these environments can help bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical understanding.

For professionals committed to foreign policy, the opportunity to work in a new environment can also encourage new perspectives and challenge assumptions developed within a single institution or professional sector.

Applications are open for the FENS/IBRO-PERC Exchange Fellowships Program 2026. In their mutual and strong commitment to support early career researchers and intra-European mobility, with a set goal of advancing neuroscience research and training in Europe, FENS and the IBRO Pan-Europe Regional Committee (IBRO-PERC) are pleased to announce the launch of the FENS/IBRO-PERC Exchange Fellowships Program.

Directed at Master and PhD students as well as early-career postdocs in Europe, this program aims to foster and broaden their scope of methodological training by supporting goal-directed laboratory visits in established European laboratories.

Funding

Maximum grant amount is EUR 4,000. Funds can cover travel (economy class, local public transport) and accommodation during the exchange.

Eligibility

To apply, candidates must:

Be Master or PhD students in neuroscience or early postdoctoral fellows (within 5 years of starting their postdoc) currently based in Europe.

Be members of a FENS member society, individual FENS members, or members of an IBRO organization in the Pan-Europe region that is not a FENS member.

Have acceptance from the host laboratory.

Have recommendation from the home laboratory.

* Eligible organizations include Armenian IBRO Association; Austrian Academy of Sciences; Israel Academy of Sciences & Humanities; Italian Association of NeuroImmunology; Russian Academy of Sciences; Slovak Academy of Sciences; Trisomy 21 Research Society (T21RS, Spain); Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences; Brain Research Society (BARD) in Turkey.

Evaluation Criteria

To ensure transparency and support applicants in preparing strong submissions, note that your application will be evaluated based on the following key criteria:

Scientific and Training Quality

The scientific merit and clarity of your proposed research during the fellowship.

The quality and relevance of the planned training, particularly in terms of new methodologies or skills you will acquire that are not available at your home institution.

Added Value of the Exchange

How clearly and concretely the exchange supports your ongoing or planned research project.

The added value of the fellowship for your home laboratory in terms of collaboration, capacity-building, or new methodological expertise.

Suitability of the Candidate

How well your current methodological expertise and academic background match the proposed training and research.

The recommendation from your home supervisor, including their assessment of your potential and the expected impact of the fellowship.

Expected Outcomes

Clearly defined and realistic scientific and methodological outcomes of the exchange.

The likelihood of achieving the proposed objectives within the planned duration of the stay.

Feasibility and Need

Demonstration of a genuine need for the exchange, both scientifically and financially.

TITLE: Institut Français x Cité Internationale des Arts Residency Program 2027-2028

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 8, 2026

Applications are open for the Institut Français x Cité Internationale des Arts Residency Program 2027-2028. The Institut français x Cité internationale des arts residency program is open to artists and cultural professionals who have been residing outside of France for at least 5 years and who wish to develop a research and creative project in Paris during a three-, six-, or nine-month residency.

Benefits

The Institut français de Paris covers the monthly costs associated with the individual studio apartments at the Cité internationale des arts. These are located in the Marais district (18 rue de l’Hôtel de Ville, Paris 4th arrondissement). They are furnished, equipped with Wi-Fi, and feature a workspace with a sleeping area, a bathroom, and a kitchenette.

The artist’s partner(s) are responsible for submitting applications in response to the call for proposals and agree to cover the following:

A residency stipend (of at least €1,100 per month);

The artist’s international travel;

The artist’s insurance (health, repatriation, liability);

Visa fees, if necessary.

Additional services (accompanying person, rehearsal studios, group workshops, French language classes, etc.) are the responsibility of the artist.

Eligibility

Be supported by one or more associated partners;

Have resided outside French territory on a permanent basis for at least 5 years;

Be engaged in a recognized professional endeavor;

Be free from any professional obligations for the entire duration of the residency;

Demonstrate autonomy and have a professional-level command of French and/or English.

Evaluation Criteria

The candidate’s professional background

The artistic and intellectual quality of the project

The proposed work plan for the residency

The connection to the French and Île-de-France art scenes and professional contacts already established locally

TITLE: Regional Webinar on Leadership and Capacity Building in Food Science and Technology in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: Promoting collaboration and partnership for research development among academic leaders in Food Science and Technology

Date: February 15, 2024

Time: 9 a.m. Eastern Time / 14:00 GMT

Duration: 90 minutes

Register to participate via Zoom: https://bit.ly/48z85CK

Participation is FREE of charge

Concept Note

Introduction

The three main tenets of the International Union of Food Science and Technology (IUFoST) which represents food scientists, technologists, and engineers globally, are Education, Food and Nutrition Security, and Food Safety. To carry out its mission, IUFoST works with the Association of African Universities (AAU), Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), World Health Organization (WHO), United Nations International Development Organization (UNIDO), CGIAR (Consultative Group on Agriculture Research), IFPRI (International Food Policy Research Institute), and many other R&D establishments, academic institutions, industry, non-governmental and governmental organizations, and its national adhering bodies worldwide.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the organization responsible for enhancing the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa and strengthening its contribution to Africa’s development. AAU remains the leading advocate for higher education in Africa, with the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting national, continental, and global needs.

Objectives of the Regional Webinar

The capacity-building webinar, organized by IUFoST and AAU, aims to:

(a) improve the knowledge and understanding of professors and heads of departments of food science and technology within African universities on the collaboration and partnership process, the dimensions, and how collaboration and partnership can be operationalized at a regional level.

(b) disseminate useful insights, guidelines, and resources for successful collaboration and partnership.

(c) create a platform for academic leaders in Food Science and Technology within African Universities to share best practices and challenges encountered in research development in this subject area.

Background

The Association of African Universities (AAU) established the Africa Research, Innovation, and Development (AfRID) as a development platform for empowering African universities and African research teams to leverage research to contribute to development on the continent. The network is bringing together peer African institutions and researchers willing to work together, with a view to generating a critical mass that can effectively support development initiatives on the continent. In the last quarter of year 2022, the Association of African Universities (AAU) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the International Union of Food Science and Technology (IUFoST) for the purpose of organizing training and education for capacity building in Africa, especially in the areas of Food Science, Food Safety and Technology, Agro-food production and processing. The objectives of IUFoST include the encouragement and fostering of: international cooperation and exchange of (scientific) knowledge and innovative ideas among food scientists, engineers, and technologists at a global level; education and training of food scientists, technologists, and engineers; and development of both individual professionalism and professional organization among food scientists, technologists, and engineers for safe, secure, and sustainable technologies globally with local application.

The signed MoU is geared toward finding solutions to future food security challenges and the SDGs through actions to address and thus reduce food losses and waste; mitigating environmental effects through encouragement for innovative and new technologies; improving capacity building and education and training at all levels, especially in combating undernutrition; and providing safe food for all within the continent.

Webinar Modality

The first regional capacity development webinar, coordinated by IUFoST-AAU, holds on February 15, 2024, via Zoom. The duration of the meeting will be approximately 90 minutes. The webinar will feature plenary sessions with simultaneous interpretation (English, French and Arabic). The agenda for the meeting and relevant documentation (including the guides) will be shared with all registered participants in advance to give them enough time to familiarise themselves with the information.

Participation

Expected Participants: Professors and Head of Departments of Food Science and Technology Programmes in African Universities, Executives from AAU and IUFoST, all interested stakeholders.

Agenda

Mentoring in Food Science and Technology.

Promoting Regional Collaboration and Partnership in Food Science and Technology.

Digitalization and Virtual Learning in Food Science and Technology.

The African Research, Innovation and Development Networks – Food Science and Technology Network in Africa.

International Union of Food Science and Technology (IUFoST) focus on Africa

TITLE: University of Salford Postgraduate Research Degrees: PhD and Doctoral Study Opportunities in the UK

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Salford in the United Kingdom offers a broad range of postgraduate research opportunities for students seeking to undertake advanced academic research and develop specialist expertise in their chosen field. Its postgraduate research community spans disciplines including arts and creative technologies, business, management and law, health and society, science, engineering and the environment.

Through its research centres, academic schools and Doctoral School, the University provides postgraduate researchers with opportunities to undertake original research, work with experienced supervisors, develop specialist skills and build academic and professional networks.

For prospective researchers looking to pursue a PhD, professional doctorate, MPhil, MSc by Research or another postgraduate research qualification in the UK, Salford provides multiple research pathways across a wide range of subject areas.

About University of Salford Postgraduate Research

The University of Salford describes its research environment as being focused on addressing complex challenges facing society through pioneering research and solutions-focused enterprise.

Postgraduate researchers become part of a large research community distributed across the University’s research centres and academic schools. Researchers also have access to the University’s Doctoral School, which provides support and training intended to help students develop as researchers.

The University’s postgraduate research environment is designed not only around academic study but also around the development of research skills, professional networks and specialist expertise that can be applied beyond academia.

For international students, the opportunity also provides exposure to the UK’s higher education and research environment while allowing them to work alongside researchers from different academic and professional backgrounds.

What Is a Research Degree?

A research degree is an advanced academic qualification centred on independent investigation rather than primarily classroom-based study.

At the University of Salford, postgraduate research students are expected to investigate an innovative or novel research area and make an original contribution to their chosen field.

Under the guidance of academic supervisors, researchers take significant responsibility for developing and conducting their research. This structure gives students considerable freedom to shape their research questions, methodology and contribution within the requirements of their chosen programme.

Research degrees can be particularly relevant to graduates who want to:

Develop specialist expertise in a particular academic field.

Conduct original research into an emerging or under-researched issue.

Prepare for an academic or research-oriented career.

Develop advanced analytical and problem-solving skills.

Explore an interdisciplinary research topic.

Build an international academic and professional network.

Develop expertise that can also be applied in industry, government, policy, technology, creative industries or other professional environments.

The University offers different types of postgraduate research qualifications depending on the applicant’s academic objectives and selected research pathway.

Postgraduate Research Degrees Available at Salford

The University of Salford offers both master’s-level research degrees and doctoral degrees.

Master’s-Level Research Degrees

Master’s-level research programmes include:

Master of Science by Research (MSc by Research)

Master of Philosophy (MPhil)

These programmes allow students to undertake substantial independent research under academic supervision.

A research master’s degree can be suitable for graduates who want to develop advanced research capabilities or explore a specific topic in considerable depth. It can also provide preparation for further doctoral-level study.

Doctoral Degrees

The University also offers several doctoral-level qualifications, including:

PhD

Doctor of Professional Practice (DProf)

Doctor of Business Administration (DBA)

Doctoral degrees represent the highest academic qualifications awarded by universities in the UK.

A PhD, for example, normally requires the researcher to investigate a specific research question or problem and make an original contribution to knowledge in the field.

The exact duration, structure and requirements of a research degree depend on the specific programme and pathway selected.

Prospective applicants should therefore review the requirements of their chosen course carefully before applying.

Research Opportunities Across Multiple Academic Fields

One of the major features of postgraduate research at Salford is the breadth of research specialisms available.

The University’s research activity is organised across four broad academic areas:

Arts, Media and Creative Technology

Business, Management and Law

Health and Society

Science, Engineering and Environment

This range allows prospective postgraduate researchers to investigate subjects extending from creative technologies and communication to artificial intelligence, business transformation, health, robotics, environmental sustainability and biomedical research.

The School attracts researchers from different parts of the world and promotes collaboration, interdisciplinary research and international networking.

TITLE: European Peer Review Guide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
PUBLICATIONS

Excellence in research depends on the quality of the procedures used to select the proposals for funding. Public and private funding organisations at the national and international levels face the challenge of establishing and maintaining the best procedures to assess quality and potential. This is a demanding task as each proposal is scientifically unique and originates from varying research cultures. As a result, many different systems and criteria are currently in use in European countries. In order

to address the issue of peer review collectively, the common needs have to be specified first. The needs then have to drive development of policies that are both convergent and complementary, whereafter coherent procedures can be conceived, promoted

and implemented.
The Heads of the European Research Councils (EUROHORCs) and the European Science Foundation (ESF) recognised in their Vision on a Globally Competitive ERA and their Road Map for Actions the need to develop common peer review systems that are useable, credible and reliable for all funding agencies. To identify the good practices of peer review, the governing bodies of both organisations invited the ESF Member Organisation Forum on peer review to compile a Peer Review Guide to be disseminated to their members and other interested stakeholders in Europe and beyond. The Forum

included over 30 European research funding and performing organisations from 23 countries, with the partnership of the European Commission and the European Research Council. The Forum established dedicated working groups, ran workshops

and undertook a comprehensive survey on the peer review systems and practices used by research funding and performing organisations, councils, private foundations and charities. The results served to identify good practices across Europe on the evaluation

of grant applications for individual and collaborative research projects.
Consequently, this Peer Review Guide illustrates practices currently in use across the members of ESF and EUROHORCs, while also reflecting the experiences of the European Commission in its Framework Programmes. It describes good practices by setting a minimum core of basic principles on peer review processes commonly accepted at a European level.

In addition to the quality of the basic procedures, peer reviewers and organisations face other challenges such as assessing multidisciplinary proposals and defining the appropriate level of risk inherent in frontier research. The management of peer review

of proposals by large international consortia poses yet another challenge, and this is why the Guide has been designed to address the assessment procedures of large scale programmes such as Joint Programming.
This Guide should serve to benchmark national peer review processes and to support their harmonisation, as well as to promote international peer review and sharing of resources. It should be considered as a rolling reference that can be updated and

revised when necessary.

TITLE: ACCTING

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Inclusive Science Cluster

Image: Freepik/Drazen Zigic

AdvanCing behavioural Change Through an INclusive Green Deal

ACCTING produces knowledge and innovations to advance behavioural change at individual, group, and societal levels, for an inclusive and equal European Green Deal.

The global climate crisis is not only an ecological crisis but also an economic, social and political crisis, with devasting and deadly impacts on individuals, families, collectives of people, economies, and societies. It is increasingly recognised by the scientific and policy communities that while both the impact of climate change and the capacity to mitigate its negative impacts affects all segments of society, they are not evenly distributed either across or within societies; it is the poorer, marginalised and vulnerable groups who are the most acutely affected. Averting, or even mitigating this crisis requires transformative change; changes in societal practices; and, in this frame, in the behaviour of individuals, communities, and organisations.

ACCTING mobilises research experimentation and innovation to advance a gender equal, inclusive and socially just European Green Deal. It specifically focuses on inequalities produced and reproduced in the context of Green Deal policy and interventions. It is based on interdisciplinary conceptual and methodological framework, inspired by strategic policy design-thinking, and collects new data on Green Deal policy interventions at individual, community, organisational and societal levels. Starting with an extensive mapping and comparative analysis of bottom-up environmental initiatives in 34 countries, including the collection of 410 narratives followed by 41 experimental studies from eight research lines, results are fed into multi-sectoral so-called Open Studios to co-create innovative solutions. Results are used for further experimentation, including through pilot actions with mass implementation and high impact potential.

The project relies on a 12 European partner consortium and some hundred researchers in 30+ countries during 2021-2025. It is one of two projects funded under the EU Horizon 2020 grant “Behavioural, social and cultural change for the Green Deal, under the call “Building a low-carbon, climate resilient future: Research and innovation in support of the European Green Deal”.

TITLE: Mosaic 3.0 PhD Scholarship Programme in the Netherlands: €420,000 Funding Available for Researchers from Under-Represented Backgrounds

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The first application round of the Mosaic 3.0 PhD Scholarship Programme is now open, offering researchers from under-represented migrant and recent asylum backgrounds an opportunity to secure funding for a PhD in the Netherlands. The programme, funded by the Dutch Research Council (NWO), provides up to €420,000 per project and supports PhD research across all academic disciplines.

The Mosaic 3.0 PhD Scholarship Programme is a major funding initiative designed to improve access to academic research careers for talented graduates from groups that remain under-represented in Dutch academia.

The updated programme builds on the previous Mosaic 2.0 and Hestia programmes and introduces an expanded target group. In addition to graduates with a non-European migration background, researchers with a recent asylum background are now also eligible under Mosaic 3.0.

Importantly, the programme does not restrict applicants to particular academic disciplines. Any PhD research topic may be proposed, provided the research proposal meets the programme’s assessment requirements and demonstrates the necessary research quality.

The first round of the programme opened on 14 September 2026, with the first major deadline approaching in November 2026.

About the Mosaic 3.0 PhD Scholarship Programme

Mosaic 3.0 is a PhD funding programme of the Dutch Research Council (NWO) aimed at encouraging the recruitment and development of researchers from under-represented groups within Dutch academia.

The programme recognises that diversity within research institutions can contribute to a broader range of perspectives, new ideas and deeper approaches to academic research.

According to NWO, researchers with a non-Western migrant background continue to be under-represented in Dutch academia. Mosaic therefore seeks to support talented researchers from these backgrounds by funding PhD positions at Dutch research institutions.

The programme has now been expanded to include a second target group: junior refugee researchers with a recent asylum background at Master’s level.

This means that Mosaic 3.0 brings together the target groups previously supported through Mosaic 2.0 and Hestia, while establishing separate funding structures for the two groups.

What does the Mosaic 3.0 scholarship fund?

Mosaic 3.0 provides funding for PhD positions in the Netherlands.

The programme is particularly notable because there is no restriction on the subject area of the proposed PhD research.

Applicants can therefore propose research in a wide range of disciplines, provided that the proposed research satisfies the relevant academic and programme requirements.

Potential areas could include, for example:

Health and medical sciences

Nursing and public health

Social sciences

Education

Engineering

Environmental sciences

Climate and sustainability

Economics

Business and management

Law

Political and social research

Information technology and computer science

Artificial intelligence and data science

Natural sciences

Humanities

Agricultural sciences

Development studies

Other recognised academic research fields

The programme does not select projects simply because they belong to a particular discipline. The quality of the research proposal remains decisive in the funding decision.

Two groups are eligible under Mosaic 3.0

A major change introduced under Mosaic 3.0 is the creation of two distinct target groups.

Group 1: Researchers with a non-European migration background

Group 1 focuses on researchers with a non-European migration background.

The programme specifically identifies migration backgrounds from:

Africa

Asia

The Caribbean

Central America

South America

Turkey

Indigenous peoples of North America

Indigenous peoples of Oceania

This means that researchers with an African migration background are within the geographical group specifically identified by the programme, subject to satisfying the other eligibility requirements.

For example, a qualified applicant with a Ghanaian/African migration background who meets the programme’s academic and institutional requirements may be eligible to apply under Group 1.

However, having a qualifying geographical background alone does not automatically guarantee eligibility. Applicants must also satisfy the programme’s complete eligibility conditions.

Group 2: Researchers with a recent asylum background

The second target group consists of researchers with a recent asylum background.

This group specifically focuses on junior refugee researchers at Master’s level.

The programme states that this includes researchers from Ukraine.

This group forms part of the target population previously supported under the Hestia programme, which has now been incorporated into Mosaic 3.0.

Group 2 has its own:

Grant ceiling

Assessment panel

Eligibility criteria

The separate structure is intended to reduce direct competition between the two target groups.

No restriction on PhD research topic

One of the most important features of Mosaic 3.0 is the absence of a specified research subject.

Applicants are not required to select their PhD topic from a predetermined list of disciplines.

Instead, candidates can develop their own research proposal around a topic that is academically appropriate and can be hosted by a suitable Dutch research institution.

This makes the programme potentially relevant to researchers from many academic backgrounds.

However, applicants should not interpret the absence of subject restrictions as meaning that every proposal will be funded. NWO states that the quality of the research proposal is decisive in awarding the scholarships.

Applicants therefore need to develop a strong research project and identify an appropriate academic environment in which the proposed research can be conducted.

Applicants submit their own proposals

Another important feature of Mosaic 3.0 is that candidates submit their own applications.

Depending on the application stage, candidates submit either:

A pre-proposal, or

A full proposal.

The application should not be developed independently of the intended academic supervisors.

Applicants are expected to prepare their applications in consultation with:

The intended supervisor, and

The daily supervisor.

The application must also be accompanied by a statement from the intended supervisor.

This makes establishing an academic connection with a suitable Dutch research institution and supervisor an important part of the application process.

Funding available

The total budget available for this Mosaic 3.0 funding round is:

€7.4 million

The budget is divided between the two target groups.

Group 1

€5 million is allocated to researchers with a migration background from outside Europe.

Group 2

€2.4 million is allocated to researchers with a recent asylum background.

This separate allocation reflects the programme’s two-group structure.

Maximum funding per project

Applicants can request a maximum of:

€420,000 per project

The exact funding available to an individual project will depend on the applicable programme and budgetary conditions.

The funding is intended to support a PhD position rather than simply provide a one-time scholarship payment to an individual student.

PhD funding duration

The maximum duration of the funded PhD position is:

Up to 4 years at 1.0 FTE, or

The equivalent duration of up to 8 years at 0.5 FTE.

The programme therefore allows for either full-time or equivalent part-time arrangements within the maximum funding period.

Applicants should carefully consider the proposed employment/research arrangement when preparing their application with their intended supervisors.

How the Mosaic 3.0 application process works

The application process takes place in two stages.

Stage 1: Pre-application

The first stage requires applicants to submit a pre-application.

The pre-application provides the initial basis on which the proposed research project can be considered.

Pre-application deadline

3 November 2026 at 14:00:00 CEST

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their documents, particularly because the proposal must be developed in consultation with the relevant supervisors.

Stage 2: Full application

Applicants progressing through the process will subsequently submit a full application.

Full application deadline

4 May 2027 at 14:00:00 CET

Applicants should pay close attention to the stated time zones when preparing their submissions.

Important requirements for prospective applicants

Anyone interested in Mosaic 3.0 should begin preparing well before the pre-application deadline.

1. Determine which target group applies to you

First establish whether you fall under:

Group 1: non-European migration background, or

Group 2: recent asylum background.

Each group has its own eligibility criteria.

2. Develop a PhD research idea

Because the programme does not restrict research subjects, applicants have considerable flexibility in developing their research topic.

The proposed project should nevertheless be academically strong and appropriate for a PhD.

3. Identify a suitable Dutch research environment

Applicants should identify a Dutch research institution and academic environment capable of hosting their proposed research.

4. Find an intended supervisor

The application needs to be developed in consultation with the intended supervisor.

Finding an appropriate supervisor can therefore be an important early step in the application process.

5. Work with the daily supervisor

The application is also expected to be prepared in consultation with the daily supervisor.

Applicants should therefore establish the supervisory arrangement before finalising their proposal.

6. Prepare the required statement

The application must include a statement from the intended supervisor.

Applicants should therefore communicate with their intended supervisor early enough to allow the required documentation to be prepared.

7. Prepare the pre-application

The first formal deadline is 3 November 2026 at 14:00:00 CEST.

Applicants should ensure that their pre-application is complete and submitted before the deadline.

8. Prepare for the full application

Applicants who progress to the next stage will need to prepare the full proposal for submission by 4 May 2027 at 14:00:00 CET.

Why Mosaic 3.0 was introduced

The programme forms part of NWO’s broader efforts to promote a more inclusive research environment within Dutch academia.

NWO explains that bringing people with different backgrounds and perspectives together can contribute to new ideas and deeper examination of research topics.

At the same time, the programme acknowledges that inequality continues to exist within academia and that researchers with non-Western migration backgrounds remain under-represented.

Mosaic 3.0 therefore focuses funding specifically on these under-represented groups while expanding eligibility to researchers with a recent asylum background.

How Mosaic 3.0 differs from the previous programmes

Mosaic 3.0 builds on Mosaic 2.0 and incorporates the target population previously supported by Hestia.

The principal change is the broader target group.

Under the updated structure:

Mosaic 3.0 Group 1

Continues the focus on researchers with a non-European migration background.

Mosaic 3.0 Group 2

Adds researchers with a recent asylum background.

Includes junior refugee researchers at Master’s level.

Includes researchers from Ukraine.

The two groups have separate grant ceilings, assessment panels and eligibility requirements.

Number of scholarships expected

NWO expects that a maximum of 18 proposals will receive funding in this round.

This means that applicants should understand that meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not automatically mean that a proposal will receive funding.

The programme explicitly states that research quality is decisive in the awarding of funding.

Applicants should therefore pay particular attention to the academic quality and clarity of their proposed research.

Conclusion

The Mosaic 3.0 PhD Scholarship Programme provides a funding route for researchers from under-represented migrant and recent asylum backgrounds who want to pursue PhD research in the Netherlands.

TITLE: Unveiling the Future of Online Education in Africa: AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS to host Inaugural Edition of e-Learning Summit

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Press Release – Accra, Ghana (March 13, 2024) – AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS has set Thursday, April 18, 2024, to hold the inaugural edition of its e-Learning Summit, a strategic event that seeks to bring together thought leaders in the higher education space to deliberate on emerging trends in online education in Africa.

This insightful summit which starts at exactly 12 pm GMT / 2 pm SAST, will create an important platform for the discussion of challenges, innovations, and opportunities in the ever-changing landscape of online education, with the aim of shaping the future of education in Africa. Scheduled to take place virtually under the theme, Leveraging Modern Trends in Online Education in Africa: A Peek into the Future, the e-Learning Summit will focus on online programme development in higher education, cloud computing, among other pivotal themes. The event will also spotlight significant milestones of the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS project. Stakeholders with aligned vision, who are interested in participating in this important Summit are invited to register by clicking this registration link.

The summit, to be hosted by eLearnAfrica, will empanel experienced educationists and researchers, and other higher-education stakeholders, like the Secretary General of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Prof. Olusola Oyewole; the Chief Executive Officer of eLearnAfrica, Mr. Brook Negussie; the Director of Rhodes Business School, Prof. Owen Skae. Others are the Vice-Chancellor of Nexus International University (NIU), Prof. Magnus Amajirionwu; the ICT Director of Njala University, Sierra Leone, Dr. Thomas Songu; the Director-General of the African Association for Public Administration and Management (AAPAM); Prof. George Scott; Global Channel Marketing Manager, , Mr. Paul Bacanu; and Learning Experience Designer, Tracy McLean.

Participants of this interactive and collaborative summit get the opportunity to engage and tap into the expertise and experiences of these seasoned higher education leaders, as well as contribute to the thought-provoking discussions on online education in the African higher education landscape. They will also get insights into the many benefits they can derive from the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS project and how to leverage these benefits to excel in their academic pursuits and professional development.

The event will also be launched on AAU Talks on AAUTV on Friday, March 15, 2024, at 11 am GMT (1 p.m. SAST) Join the launch via zoom, or use the following details – Meeting ID: 854 6800 3655 & Passcode: 199200. Key issues surrounding the e-Learning Summit 2024 will be discussed during this launch.

About the AAU (Association of African Universities) and eLearnAfrica partnership

In 2016, eLearnAfrica entered into a partnership agreement with the Association of African Universities (AAU), the largest higher education coordinating body in Africa, comprising over 430 member universities across the continent. The agreement, which seeks to enable universities to expand their reach by providing online, distance-learning opportunities to over 10 million African students, has seen significant milestones being achieved over the years.

The partnership now boasts over 140 registered universities and other institutions, as well as individual professors and course holders. It has also had 3 master’s degree programmes and over 200 short courses successfully designed, developed, delivered, and deployed together with its partner universities, such as Rhodes Business School and Njala University.

TITLE: PachiPanda Challenge – Nigeria 2026 (up to ₦10m in prizes)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 28, 2026

Applications for the PachiPanda Challenge – Nigeria 2026 are now open. MTN Nigeria Communications Plc in partnership with the Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF) through its local partner, the Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Nigeria and Deloitte Nigeria have launched the Nigeria PachiPanda Challenge, an innovation challenge designed to provide young people and youth-led SMEs the opportunity to develop innovative, long-term solutions and ideas to pressing environmental challenges and promote sustainability in Nigeria.

Challenge Statements

Climate Change [Solutions focusing on the reduction of greenhouse gases]: Human activities emit greenhouse gases – mainly carbon dioxide and methane, which are the major drivers of climate change. The effects of climate change include, among others, severe drought, water scarcity, rising sea levels, flooding and biodiversity loss.

How can you inspire innovative solutions in Nigeria’s homes and businesses to reduce emissions, fight climate change and build resilience?

Climate Smart Cities and Urban Resilience [Solutions focusing on building cities that can adapt, recover and thrive]: Cities are expected to account for two-thirds of the projected growth of the world’s population by 2050, with most of the remaining one-third of growth concentrated in towns. Nigeria’s urban population is also projected to rise by 70%, increasing pressure on housing, transportation, energy, water, and public infrastructure. Climate impacts such as flooding, extreme heat, erosion, and poor air quality are already affecting urban communities, particularly vulnerable populations. The cities of the future must not only grow but also adapt.

How can you design innovative solutions that help Nigerian cities become more climate-resilient, inclusive, and sustainable in the face of increasing environmental pressures? Prioritising areas such as industrial waste management, flood prediction and response systems, green infrastructure, sustainable transport, smart energy management, climate-resilient housing, urban food systems and sustainable agriculture, community adaptation solutions, and strengthening (inclusive) safeguards against risks, and solutions leveraging AI and frontier tech, enabling local production, integrating soft and hardware innovation with potential to create green jobs and sustainable livelihoods.

Community Conservation [Solutions focusing on biodiversity protection and community-led conservation efforts for improved livelihood]: Conservation is most powerful when it is people-driven, designed to improve livelihood and well-being. Across Nigeria, local communities live closest to nature and hold traditional knowledge and practices that can protect ecosystems. Yet, these same communities often face poverty, limited infrastructure, and restricted access to education or resources, factors that can lead to unsustainable environmental practices.

How can you co-create a future in which communities are empowered to lead conservation efforts and drive change through communal wisdom, innovation, and stewardship?

Pollution [Solutions focusing on improved waste management]: Our activities generate large amounts of waste, with dump sites a common sight in our cities, towns and villages. Despite best efforts at waste management, waste still constitutes significant pollution threats across Nigeria with attendant health and environmental risks.

How can you innovatively transform waste management in Nigeria to reduce pollution, address health and environmental hazards and build sustainability? You can share solutions for business or industrial sectors, behavioural, artistic and tech solutions.

Prizes

First Position – ₦5,000,000

Second Position – ₦ 3,000,000

Third Position – ₦ 2,000,000

The winners will represent Nigeria at the Africa PachiPanda Finale in South Africa, along with winners from other countries.

Eligibility

Open to individuals or teams residing in Nigeria.

Participants should be between 18 and 35.

You may participate as an individual or form a team of a maximum of three members.

Young entrepreneurs or youth-led SMEs with early or idea stage solutions are free to participate, with a maximum of three members.

All participants must register online and submit entries through the designated portal before the deadline.

Participants should provide accurate and complete personal information during registration.

MTN Nigeria, Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Nigeria and Deloitte Nigeria employees, and their immediate families are not eligible to participate.

Application

To submit an entry to any of the challenge statements, answer the following questions:

Briefly describe your innovative idea or solution (Maximum of 200 words)

What makes your idea or solution outstanding and deserving of selection? (Maximum of 200 words)

How would your idea or solution impact people at the community, national and international levels? (Maximum 200 words)

Provide a detailed description of your innovative idea or solution, including evidence or proof of concept (Maximum of 2000 words)

TITLE: CAM-DTP PhD Studentship Opportunities 2027: 39 Supervisor-Led Research Topics for Doctoral Applicants

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Prospective doctoral researchers preparing for PhD study in 2027 can explore a wide range of CAM-DTP supervisor-led PhD topics for 2027 entry, covering research areas such as artificial intelligence, public health, psychology, climate change, education, biodiversity, healthcare, finance, entrepreneurship, energy governance, genomics and social research.

The CAM-DTP Studentship Opportunities for 2027 are being advertised through Route 1, the supervisor-led route. Under this pathway, prospective PhD candidates identify a research topic of interest, contact the relevant supervisory team and discuss the possibility of developing a project proposal before making a formal application.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the application procedure. CAM-DTP does not accept direct applications, and prospective candidates should not submit CVs, research proposals or other documentation directly to CAM-DTP for assessment.

Instead, candidates interested in one of the advertised PhD topics must communicate with the relevant supervisory team and subsequently apply through the CAM-DTP institution of the lead supervisor, following that university’s admissions process and applicable deadlines.

About CAM-DTP PhD Topics for 2027 Entry

The CAM-DTP has published a broad portfolio of supervisor-led PhD topics for students seeking doctoral study beginning in 2027.

The opportunities form part of Route 1, which is specifically based around projects led by supervisory teams.

This means candidates are not expected simply to submit an independent application directly to CAM-DTP. Instead, they should first identify a relevant research topic and establish communication with the supervisors connected to that project.

The available opportunities span a wide variety of disciplines and interdisciplinary research themes, making the programme relevant to prospective researchers from different academic backgrounds.

Areas represented in the 2027 list include:

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

Public health

Healthcare

Psychology

Human behaviour

Climate change

Sustainability

Biodiversity

Education

Architecture

Entrepreneurship

Finance

Cyber resilience

Genomics

Energy governance

Community health

Social research

Leadership

Nature connection

Developmental research

Research methodology

Health inequalities

How the CAM-DTP Supervisor-Led Route Works

Applicants interested in one of the PhD opportunities should follow the process established by CAM-DTP.

1. Review the available PhD topics

Candidates should begin by studying the list of supervisor-led research topics available for 2027 entry.

With 39 topics listed, applicants can identify research areas that align most closely with their academic background, research experience and future doctoral interests.

2. Contact the supervisory team

Students who are interested in conducting a PhD within one of the advertised topics should contact the relevant supervisory team.

This initial communication gives prospective candidates an opportunity to find out more about the project and discuss the development of a possible research proposal.

3. Speak to the supervisory team before applying

CAM-DTP specifically states that an application to conduct a PhD within one of the advertised topics should not be made before speaking to the supervisory team.

Candidates should therefore treat contact with the relevant supervisors as an essential part of the application process.

4. Apply through the lead supervisor’s institution

Once a candidate has discussed the opportunity with the supervisory team, the formal application should be made to the CAM-DTP institution where the lead supervisor is based.

Applicants must follow the admissions procedures and deadlines set by that institution.

5. Interview stage

Supervisory teams will interview candidates who are interested in their respective research topics.

The interview process provides the supervisory team with an opportunity to assess prospective candidates before determining whom to put forward for nomination.

6. CAM-DTP nomination

Following the interview process, supervisory teams will propose selected candidates to their departments for CAM-DTP nomination in early February.

Candidates should therefore begin engaging with supervisors and institutional admissions processes well before this nomination stage.

Important: CAM-DTP Does Not Accept Direct Applications

Prospective candidates should note that CAM-DTP does not take direct applications.

Applicants should therefore not send:

Research proposals directly to CAM-DTP

CVs directly to CAM-DTP

Supporting documentation directly to CAM-DTP

General PhD applications directly to CAM-DTP for review

The appropriate process is to contact the supervisory team associated with the chosen research topic and subsequently apply through the lead supervisor’s institution.

Discuss the research topic and possible project proposal.

Do not formally apply before communicating with the supervisory team.

Determine which CAM-DTP institution hosts the lead supervisor.

Review that institution’s postgraduate admissions requirements and deadline.

Submit the formal PhD application through the relevant university.

Participate in the supervisory team’s interview process if invited.

Successful candidates may then be put forward by the supervisory team for departmental CAM-DTP nomination.

APPLY NOW

Official CAM-DTP Opportunity Page

Prospective applicants should use the official CAM-DTP website to review the opportunities and obtain the latest information about individual projects and supervisory teams:

https://www.cam-dtp.ac.uk/students/current-opportunities/

Important Advice for Prospective Applicants

Because these are supervisor-led projects, selecting a topic should involve more than simply choosing an appealing project title.

Candidates should carefully consider whether a project is aligned with their:

Previous academic study

Research experience

Methodological skills

Subject interests

Career ambitions

Intended area of doctoral specialisation

Prospective applicants should also use their initial communication with supervisors to gain a clearer understanding of the project before beginning a formal application.

Candidates should not assume that the same application deadline, academic requirement or admissions process applies to every project, because applications are submitted through the institution associated with each lead supervisor.

Conclusion

The CAM-DTP PhD Studentship Opportunities for 2027 entry provide prospective doctoral researchers with access to 39 supervisor-led research topics spanning some of today’s most significant academic and societal issues.

From artificial intelligence and machine learning to healthcare, psychology, climate change, biodiversity, education, finance, energy governance, entrepreneurship and social inclusion, the breadth of the available topics creates opportunities for researchers interested in a wide range of interdisciplinary fields.

The most important part of the application process is understanding that CAM-DTP does not accept direct applications.

Prospective candidates must first select a research topic, contact the relevant supervisory team and discuss their proposed PhD project. They should then apply through the CAM-DTP institution of the lead supervisor and comply with that institution’s individual admissions procedures and deadlines.

With supervisory teams expected to put forward candidates for departmental CAM-DTP nomination in early February, prospective applicants interested in 2027 entry should explore the available topics and begin contacting relevant supervisors well in advance.

TITLE: Press Release – African Universities’ Week to shed more light on Digital Transformation in African Higher and Tertiary Education| November 9-13, 2020

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra- Ghana, October 22, 2020 – To mark the 2020 African Universities’ Week, the Association of African Universities and its collaborating institutions will be hosting a series of exciting virtual events focusing on Digital Transformation in African Higher and Tertiary Education.

The African Universities’ Week (AU Week) is celebrated annually by universities in Africa to commemorate the birth of the AAU on the 12th November 1967 in Rabat, Morocco. The Week’s celebration brings together higher education stakeholders across the continent, to discuss contemporary issues pertinent to the improvement of the quality and relevance of higher education to the development of the African continent. The African Universities’ Week Celebrations have become a premier event on the calendar of AAU and has been celebrated by HEIs since 2000.

All higher education institutions and stakeholders across the continent are invited to participate in the celebration of the 2020 African Universities week which comes off from November 9-13, 2020 by registering via https://tinyurl.com/2020AUWeek. For the first time, one continental virtual weeklong event is planned for the 2020 AU Week Celebrations – instead of various physical events in different African Universities. The rich bouquet of programme lined up for the week include keynote addresses and webinars on various topical issues- including Open Access, Blended Education, Leadership by Women, and Geo-Tourism, among others. The programme will also feature sessions dedicated to AAU members and opportunities for collaborating among themselves and with other institutions.

AAU recommends that the management of each member institution circulates information concerning the AU Week Celebrations to Ministries of Education, University Councils, Committees of Vice-Chancellors, and students to ensure their participation. Representatives from diverse sectors including – health, agricultural, financial, and educational industries, Research Institutions and corporate organisations are also invited to actively participate in the celebrations. Other public and private universities in each country which are non-members of the AAU, the media and general public are also invited to join the celebrations to give visibility to the week and promote the activities of higher education institutions in their countries.

This year’s theme, ‘Digital Transformation in African Higher and Tertiary Education’ was aptly chosen to stimulate dialogue on how African HEIs can digitally transform their various business processes – teaching, learning, working spaces, events management, administrative operations (financial, students records, health, accommodation, etc), collaborations, knowledge services, research, community engagement among several other functions of HEIs. Specifically, the theme for the 2020 AU Week links to the African Union Commission’s Digital Transformation Strategy (2020-2030) whose vision is “an Integrated and inclusive digital society and economy in Africa that improves the quality of life of Africa’s citizens, strengthens the existing economic sector, enables its diversification and development, and ensures continental ownership with Africa as a producer and not only a consumer in the global economy”.

‘As the AAU and all higher education institutions come together to celebrate the AU Week, I invite all stakeholders, especially the Heads of HEIs, Government of African States and Development Partners to increase their allocation and investment towards ensuring a holistic digital transformation of the African Higher Education Sector. The COVID-19 pandemic has shown us that this is urgent now, more than ever’ said Prof. Etienne Ehile, Secretary General of the Association of African Universities.

More information about the African Universities’ Week is available in the concept note which is accessible at https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Final-Version-AU-Week-Concept-Note-October-22-2020.pdf

AAU, the Voice of Higher Education in Africa!!

The Association aims to improve the quality of higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education.
