TITLE: AAU creates awareness on available ICT-Driven tools to facilitate teaching and learning by African Higher Education Institutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) continues to devote more time to the education and awareness creation on various available softwares, platforms and applications that can be used during the COVID-19 pandemic by the African Higher Education community. The AAU which is also the African Union Commission’s implementing arm and the coordinator for the Continental Education Strategy (CESA 2016-2025) , took time to study the knowledge and skills gaps that were created by the pandemic as well as the 4th Industrial Revolution and designed targeted staff development and training workshops as a response. This was done through its Workshops Unit headed by Dr. Violet Makuku, a Quality Assurance Specialist and Project Manager-HAQAA Initiative.

Special tools and platforms for teaching in Practical-Oriented Disciplines were also captured under these training programmes. The workshop series has a focus on equipping staff from institutions that offer programmes in disciplines such as Agriculture, Architecture, Music, Dance, Art and Design and Medicine, among others. The positive impact of the workshops held earlier has already been felt as participants indicated from feedback, that they had acquired relevant skills which had improved the quality of their work during the COVID-19 pandemic.

To ensure that top-notch facilitators were engaged to offer these training, the AAU issued an open call for prospective facilitators in various disciplines, and followed a rigorous selection process, to choose the most qualified facilitators.

Capacity Building Workshops Platform for Learning and Exchange

Some of the latest virtual workshops held, which provided the platform for AAU to continue its awareness creation and sensitisation on the available ICT-driven tools included the workshop on ‘ The Teaching of Modern Irrigation Engineering Techniques’ that was facilitated by Tawanda Bangwayo (Water and Irrigation Engineer). Another one was titled ‘ Working in ICT Driven Higher & Tertiary Education Spaces’ and this was facilitated by Dr. Violet Makuku, AAU. All these workshops were organised on the findings from the needs and knowledge and skills gaps analysis that normally precede the planning and execution of each AAU workshop. Participants were encouraged to attend the virtual workshops to enhance their knowledge and to hear from colleagues across the continent on effective teaching and learning methods during the COVID-19 pandemic using the alternative ICT-driven methods rather than adopting a wait and see approach.

The Working in ICT Driven Higher & Tertiary Education Spaces is a workshop series that targeted a number of aspects including the acquisition and use of the SurveyMonkey and Google Forms for data collection, analysis and preservation for later use in research and Monitoring and Evaluation. Short surveys done on the use of the SurveyMonkey during the workshop session indicated that 97% of the 83 participants attending that session never used it. This was a clear indication of the need to carry out thorough training on how to use these tools for different purposes, yet one could easily assume that many Higher & Tertiary Education personnel know and use them frequently. The participants were excited about the fact that these tools could be used to collect both qualitative and quantitative data. They also realized that the creation of questionnaire items is something they could do with more practice.

During the training sessions on how to use Google forms and the SurveyMonkey, individuals and institutions were encouraged to make use of such tools to be more efficient because once a questionnaire is generated, a link can be generated and sent out to many respondents through e-mails and social media, among others. “Gone are the days when lecturers and students would literally move from place to place handing out hard copy questionnaires, collect them and do manual data entry’ said Dr. Makuku, the workshop facilitator, as she reminded participants about the need to swiftly catch up and use e-tools which simplifies teaching, learning and research processes. The advantages that were outlined included the fact that responses are automatically collected, meaning that manual data entry which mainly results in errors, omissions and time consumption can be avoided. These tools also enable data export to other tools, for example, to the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) for analysis while one can also use them for data analysis, to some extent. The SurveyMonkey, for example allows users to select an option where it can send the questionnaire to targeted respondents for a fee.

Lecturers were encouraged to learn how to use the various ICT-driven tools so that they could effectively teach their students and prepare them for the new world of work which now involves working in digitalized workspaces.

AAU’s Recommendation

The AAU highly recommends that institutions take advantage of the available free software, applications and platforms while purchasing others which may not be free for the benefit of staff and students since they can enhance research output and make the practical teaching of research components like data collection and analysis easier. Institutional leaders are encouraged to purchase softwares/applications such as the SurveyMonkey for students and staff and organize institutional workshop training sessions, which the AAU is also ready to handle. The Quality Assurance Specialist and Workshops coordinator at the AAU, Dr. Violet Makuku discourages the use of trial versions since they normally expire and lock in all the work that has been done which may result in data loss. In most cases, the work done becomes permanently inaccessible unless the person subscribes through paying for the software.

AAU encourages stakeholders to invite their colleagues and make them aware of the AAU workshops sessions to enable them update their skills and familiarise themselves with the range of available ICT-Driven tools to improve on their efficiency and effectiveness.

TITLE: Western University Civil and Environmental Engineering Programs in Canada | Undergraduate and Graduate Study Opportunities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
If you are interested in studying civil engineering, environmental engineering, structural engineering, infrastructure, water resources, smart cities, or sustainable development in Canada, the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Western University offers a broad range of undergraduate and graduate study options.

Located in London, Ontario, Canada, Western University’s Civil and Environmental Engineering department combines engineering education with research, industry connections, sustainability, emerging technologies, and real-world project experience. The department offers undergraduate pathways as well as graduate programs leading to Master of Engineering (MEng), Master of Engineering Science (MESc), and PhD degrees. (Western Engineering)

About Civil and Environmental Engineering at Western University

The Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering is part of the Faculty of Engineering at Western University and provides education and research opportunities across several areas of civil and environmental engineering.

The department highlights its strong links with industry and affiliated research centres, including the Boundary Layer Wind Tunnel Laboratory, Geotechnical Research Centre, Institute for Catastrophic Loss Reduction, Centre for Environment and Sustainability, and Wind Engineering, Energy and Environment Research Institute.

Western’s undergraduate Civil Engineering program is accredited through the Canadian Engineering Accreditation Board (CEAB), with the curriculum designed around the graduate attributes expected of accredited engineering programs in Canada. \

Undergraduate Civil Engineering at Western University

Students entering Western Engineering initially complete a Common First Year before moving into their selected engineering discipline.

After completing the common first year, students can enter Civil Engineering and later select from different options and concurrent pathways.

The department’s undergraduate options include:

Structural Engineering

Environmental Engineering

International Development with Structural Engineering

International Development with Environmental Engineering

Civil Engineering and Business

Civil Engineering and Law

Civil Engineering and Artificial Intelligence Systems Engineering, Smart Cities and Structural Engineering

Civil Engineering and Artificial Intelligence Systems Engineering, Smart Cities and Environmental Engineering

The available pathways allow students to combine traditional civil engineering education with areas such as business, law, international development, artificial intelligence, and smart-city technologies.

Structural Engineering

The Structural Engineering option provides students with training in areas related to the analysis and design of structures and infrastructure.

Courses and areas of study include:

Structural theory and design

Reinforced and prestressed concrete design

Steel design

Structural dynamics

Finite element design

Tall buildings

Soil mechanics

Sustainable development

Engineering ethics

Engineering law

This pathway is particularly relevant for students interested in structural and infrastructure engineering and the design of safe and resilient structures.

Environmental Engineering

Western’s Environmental Engineering option focuses on addressing environmental challenges and developing solutions that support a more sustainable future.

Environmental engineers combine knowledge from areas including mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and geology to address problems such as climate change, water management, environmental contamination, and sustainable infrastructure.

Students can explore areas including:

Climate change adaptation

Green infrastructure

Drinking water services

Water resources management

Contaminated-site cleanup

Municipal infrastructure

Environmental policy

Sustainable development

Graduates can pursue careers in consulting, industry, government, non-governmental organisations, and research. (Western Engineering)

Civil Engineering and International Development

Western also provides Civil Engineering pathways that combine engineering education with International Development.

The International Development option exposes students to the social, environmental, political, and economic factors involved in creating safer and more sustainable communities in Canada and developing regions.

A major component is the Summer Community Development Placement and Design Project, through which students can gain practical experience working in developing countries or communities in need in Canada. Western notes that students have undertaken placements in countries including Madagascar, The Gambia, Ghana, China and India.

This pathway can be particularly attractive to students who want to combine engineering with international development and community-focused work.

Civil Engineering and Artificial Intelligence: Smart Cities

Western also offers a five-year concurrent pathway combining Civil Engineering with Artificial Intelligence Systems Engineering (AISE) and Smart Cities.

The programme is designed to equip students with modern AI tools and engineering knowledge that can be applied to challenges in the built environment. Students receive training in areas such as AI fundamentals, deep learning, algorithms, data structures, and the application of AI to engineering problems.

Two highlighted pathways combine AISE and Smart Cities with:

Structural Engineering

Environmental Engineering

The structural pathway explores applications such as design optimisation, structural health monitoring, structural safety, design, and analysis.

The environmental pathway focuses on interdisciplinary solutions related to sustainable development, including sustainable cities, clean energy, clean water and sanitation, responsible consumption, and infrastructure. (Western Engineering)

Practical Learning and Capstone Projects

Western’s Civil and Environmental Engineering programme places emphasis on applying engineering knowledge to practical problems.

The undergraduate programme includes a fourth-year capstone design experience in which students work on real-world engineering projects. The department states that these projects can be identified by the City of London and supported by faculty members and external consulting engineers.

The capstone experience requires students to apply technical knowledge while considering factors such as:

Economic considerations

Health and safety

Environmental impacts

Social considerations

Engineering design

Technical analysis

Professional communication

Students also develop their ability to communicate engineering solutions through reports, drawings, and presentations.

Graduate Programs in Civil and Environmental Engineering

Western University offers three major graduate degree pathways in Civil and Environmental Engineering:

1. Master of Engineering (MEng)

The MEng is a professional graduate degree designed for practicing engineers seeking career advancement as well as graduates who want to strengthen their technical knowledge.

The programme can be completed as either a course-based or project-based degree. The full-time programme is structured over three terms, or approximately 12 months. A part-time option is also available.

The MEng offers specialisations in:

Environmental and Water Resources Engineering

Structural and Infrastructural Engineering

Smart Cities

The Smart Cities specialisation is offered for the Summer term intake.

Students undertaking the course-based MEng complete 10 courses, while the project-based option consists of 8 courses plus an MEng project.

2. Master of Engineering Science (MESc)

The MESc is a thesis-based research degree designed for students interested in conducting independent and innovative research in Civil and Environmental Engineering.

The programme takes approximately two years or six terms and requires a four-year bachelor’s degree in engineering from an accredited university or a similar programme that may be considered. The published minimum admission average is 78% (A- North

Research students work under the supervision of faculty members and can conduct fundamental, computational, or applied research depending on their area of interest.

3. Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)

The PhD in Civil and Environmental Engineering is a research-intensive programme designed for students seeking advanced research training.

The programme is listed as approximately four years or 12 terms. Applicants normally require a master’s degree in engineering from an accredited university or a similar qualification that may be considered, with a published minimum average of 78%.

The PhD is thesis-based and provides opportunities for advanced research under faculty supervision.

Graduate Research Areas

Western’s Civil and Environmental Engineering research activities cover several major areas.

These include:

Environmental and Water Resources

Research and graduate coursework address issues involving water systems, environmental engineering, climate hazards, groundwater, watershed modelling, and related challenges.

Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering

This area focuses on soils, foundations, geotechnical systems, and environmental challenges associated with the ground and subsurface environment.

Structural and Infrastructural Engineering

Research and coursework cover structures, infrastructure, structural health monitoring, design, materials, and related engineering challenges.

Wind Engineering and Environmental Fluid Mechanics

Western has significant research activity in wind engineering and environmental fluid mechanics, supported by specialised facilities and research institutes.

Smart Cities

Smart Cities is another area connected to the department’s growing focus on technology, data, AI, infrastructure, and sustainable urban development.

Graduate Admission Requirements

For the graduate programmes, the published requirements differ according to the degree.

Programme
Typical Duration
Minimum Academic Requirement
Format

MEng
1 year / 3 terms
4-year engineering bachelor’s degree; minimum 70%
Course-based or project-based

MESc

Master’s degree in engineering; minimum 78%
Thesis-based

A similar academic programme may be considered where applicable.

Applicants should always verify the current admission requirements before submitting an application because programme requirements and application procedures can change.

English Language Requirements

International applicants whose first language is not English, or who do not meet Western’s specified prior-English-education exemption, may need to demonstrate English-language proficiency.

The graduate programme information lists the following accepted examinations and minimum scores:

IELTS Academic: 6.5 overall, with no individual section below 6

Duolingo English Test: 115

CAEL: 60

Western English Language Centre: successful completion of the High-Advanced level

Fanshawe College ESL: graduation from Level 10 EAP with a minimum of 80% in all components

Western also lists TOEFL requirements, with the scoring requirement depending on when the test was taken. Applicants should check the current official graduate admissions information before applying. =

Funding Opportunities for Graduate Students

Funding availability depends on the graduate programme.

Western states that funding is available for admissible research students in the MESc and PhD programmes, while funding is not provided for MEng students through the programme.

Students interested in research-based graduate study should therefore investigate available funding and scholarship opportunities as part of the application process.

Career Opportunities

A Civil and Environmental Engineering education can lead to careers across a wide range of sectors.

Western notes that graduates can pursue opportunities in areas including:

Engineering consulting

Municipal government

Provincial government

Federal government

Resource companies

Environmental consulting

Water resources

Infrastructure

Construction

Research

Sustainability

Technology

International development

The department also highlights that its graduates can pursue leadership and entrepreneurship opportunities across multiple professions.

Environmental Engineering graduates, for example, have gone on to work in consulting, government, research and industry, with alumni working at organisations including AECOM, Dillon Consulting, Google, Golder Associates and other companies.

Who Should Consider Studying Civil and Environmental Engineering at Western?

Western’s programmes may be particularly suitable for students and graduates interested in:

Civil engineering

Structural engineering

Environmental engineering

Water resources

Infrastructure

Sustainable development

Climate resilience

Geotechnical engineering

Wind engineering

Smart cities

Artificial intelligence in engineering

International development

Engineering research

Students interested in combining engineering with another discipline can also explore Western’s concurrent and dual-degree options.

How to Apply

Prospective students should use Western University’s official admissions channels to determine the appropriate application route for their chosen programme.

For undergraduate applicants, the Civil and Environmental Engineering department directs prospective students to Western Engineering’s undergraduate admissions and future-student resources.

For graduate applicants, the appropriate route depends on whether the applicant is applying for the MEng, MESc or PhD.

Official Civil and Environmental Engineering Department:

Western University Civil and Environmental Engineering

Graduate programme information:

Western University Civil and Environmental Engieering Graduate Programs

Applicants should carefully review the programme-specific admission requirements, required documents, English-language requirements and application deadlines before submitting an application.

Important Information About Deadlines

The graduate admissions page provides different application deadlines depending on the intended intake and whether the applicant is domestic or international. However, the published page currently contains a Fall international deadline labelled February 10, 2025, which is already past and should not be presented as a current 2026/2027 deadline.

Therefore, applicants should confirm the current deadline directly with Western University before applying, particularly for upcoming intakes.

Conclusion

The Civil and Environmental Engineering programmes at Western University provide students with opportunities to develop engineering knowledge while exploring major challenges involving infrastructure, sustainability, climate change, water resources, structural systems, technology, and urban development.

At undergraduate level, students can choose from structural and environmental engineering pathways and can combine civil engineering with international development, business, law, artificial intelligence, and Smart Cities.

At graduate level, Western offers MEng, MESc and PhD programmes, allowing students to choose between professional training and research-focused study. Research opportunities span environmental and water resources, geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering, structural and infrastructure engineering, wind engineering and environmental fluid mechanics, and Smart Cities.

For students seeking an engineering education connected to real-world infrastructure, environmental sustainability, emerging technology and research, Western University’s Civil and Environmental Engineering department is an option worth exploring.

TITLE: PhD Scholarship at La Trobe University: Research Opportunity on Family Violence Safety for First Nations and Culturally Diverse Families

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
La Trobe University is offering a prestigious PhD scholarship opportunity for a doctoral researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, cultural safety, Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse families, child and family wellbeing, and long-term safety outcomes.

The scholarship forms part of a major Australian Research Council (ARC) Discovery Project examining how safety from domestic and family violence develops and changes for parents involved in family court litigation. The successful PhD candidate will have the opportunity to contribute to an important body of research investigating what helps parents and children move from situations of high risk toward sustained safety, particularly among First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) families.

The PhD will be based at La Trobe University and will be supported by experienced researchers from the University’s Bouverie Centre, alongside cultural consultants and collaborators connected with the Australian family court system.

PhD Scholarship Overview

This doctoral opportunity is particularly suited to applicants who are passionate about understanding family violence and improving outcomes for families navigating complex legal, social and service systems.

The research will focus on experiences of safety among First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents who have been involved in family court proceedings.

Rather than looking only at the presence of family violence or the level of risk experienced by families, the research seeks to understand a broader and equally important question:

What helps families become safer after initially being identified as being at high risk?

The successful candidate will investigate the personal, family, cultural, community, service and court-related factors that may contribute to improved and sustained safety.

This is an opportunity to undertake doctoral research that combines academic research with real-world implications for family courts, family violence services, communities, parents and children.

Scholarship Value

The scholarship provides:

$36,000 per year

Funding for 3.5 years

Full-time PhD study

Research opportunities connected to a major ARC-funded Discovery Project

Supervision from experienced researchers in family violence, family court processes and research methodology

Opportunities to develop expertise in culturally appropriate research methods

Access to the research environment of La Trobe University’s Bouverie Centre

Opportunities to contribute to research intended to improve safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system

The scholarship is funded through La Trobe University’s contribution to the ARC Discovery Project.

About the ARC Discovery Project

The PhD is connected to the Australian Research Council Discovery Project titled:

“Enhancing Safety from Family Violence Through and Beyond Family Court Litigation.”

The wider project will investigate experiences of safety from domestic and family violence among parents involved in Australia’s family court system.

The project is designed to follow families over a period of four years after entry into the family court system, allowing researchers to examine what happens not only while families are under the supervision of the court but also after the court’s direct involvement decreases or ends.

This longer-term approach is important because safety can change over time. A family that is considered high risk when entering court may experience different circumstances several months or years later.

The research therefore seeks to understand:

How safety changes over time.

Which factors are associated with improved safety.

Which factors are associated with continued risk.

Whether court-based triage processes contribute to improved safety.

How family, cultural, personal and social circumstances influence safety.

How court management and family circumstances interact.

What parents themselves identify as contributing to improved safety.

What personal and service-related costs are associated with achieving sustained safety.

Focus of the PhD Research

The PhD will specifically investigate Research Question 2d of the wider ARC Discovery Project:

“To what do First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents attribute improved safety after initial high risk?”

The doctoral candidate will have an opportunity to refine the precise research questions in collaboration with the supervisory team.

The research may explore several important areas.

1. Factors that support sustained safety

The research will examine the factors that help families achieve and maintain safety.

These factors could include:

Family relationships.

Community support.

Cultural connections.

Access to appropriate services.

Personal circumstances.

Social support.

Interactions with government and statutory systems.

Family court processes.

Safety planning.

Service responses to family violence.

Connections to country and community.

Experiences of children and parents.

Access to culturally appropriate support.

The study will consider whether these factors operate differently for First Nations families and culturally and linguistically diverse families.

2. Experiences of mothers following high-risk assessments

Another important aspect of the research concerns how First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse mothers experience safety when they have previously been identified as being at high risk.

The research will seek to understand their experiences over time rather than examining safety at only one point.

This can provide a deeper understanding of how circumstances change during and after family court proceedings.

3. Parents’ explanations of improved safety

The PhD will also explore how parents themselves explain changes in their circumstances.

Instead of relying exclusively on professional assessments or administrative data, the research will provide an opportunity for parents to describe:

What changed in their lives.

What they believe helped them become safer.

Which services were helpful.

Which services were difficult or harmful.

The role of family and community.

The importance of culture.

The role of country and connection.

Their experiences with the family court.

Their interactions with statutory systems.

Their experiences after court involvement decreased.

What helped them protect themselves and their children.

This approach is intended to provide a richer understanding of family safety from the perspective of people who have experienced these circumstances themselves.

Expected Research Approaches and Methods

The PhD is expected to use several complementary research approaches.

The successful candidate will work with the supervisory team to refine the research questions and develop culturally informed methodologies appropriate for the study population.

The proposed PhD-by-publication may involve three major approaches.

1. Review of global Family Court practices

The first component may involve examining family court practices internationally.

The research will investigate practices involving Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse populations that seek to improve:

Cultural safety.

Physical safety.

Psychological safety.

Family safety.

Access to justice.

Appropriate engagement with court processes.

Support for parents and children.

Responsiveness to cultural and community contexts.

This component could help identify practices that may contribute to safer experiences for families throughout family court litigation.

2. Analysis of existing research data

The second component will involve analysis of data that has already been collected.

The available dataset contains information on 214 First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents and their initial safety profiles when they entered the court system.

The candidate may compare these initial safety profiles with those of non-Indigenous parents and examine patterns that could contribute to understanding differences in risk and safety.

This provides an opportunity for the PhD candidate to develop advanced skills in research data analysis and interpretation.

3. Yarning and narrative approaches

The third component is expected to involve a yarning approach with existing cohort participants.

Yarning can provide an opportunity for participants to share their experiences through culturally appropriate forms of conversation.

In this research, the approach is intended to help participants tell their unfolding stories of safety over time.

The research will explore the role of:

Community.

Country.

Family.

Service systems.

Government and statutory systems.

Family courts.

Personal experiences.

Relationships.

Cultural identity and connection.

Experiences of risk and safety.

Other narrative methods may also be considered.

The project specifically notes that approaches such as drawings and artwork are encouraged where appropriate.

This creates an opportunity for the research to move beyond conventional interview-based methods and explore ways of allowing participants to communicate experiences of safety in forms that are meaningful to them.

Why This PhD Research Is Important

Domestic and family violence can have long-lasting effects on parents and children, particularly when families are involved in complex legal proceedings.

Family court litigation can itself be a challenging experience, especially for people who are already dealing with violence, trauma, separation, parenting disputes and concerns about the safety of their children.

For First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse families, additional cultural, social and systemic considerations may influence how they experience the court system and services around it.

Understanding these experiences is therefore essential for developing approaches that are not only legally appropriate but also culturally responsive and genuinely focused on safety.

The research could contribute to improved understanding of:

How families move from high-risk circumstances toward greater safety.

Why some families experience improved outcomes while others continue to experience risk.

How culture influences experiences of safety.

How community and family relationships contribute to wellbeing.

How service systems can better support families.

How family courts can respond more effectively to diverse communities.

How culturally appropriate research methods can improve understanding of family violence.

How parents and children can be better supported during and after court proceedings.

Research Supervisors

The PhD candidate will be supervised by a multidisciplinary research team with expertise in family violence, family relationships, research methodology and family court-related research.

Primary Supervisor: Dr Anna Booth

Dr Anna Booth will serve as the Primary Supervisor for the PhD project.

Co-Supervisors

The candidate will also be supported by:

Dr Felicity Painter

Professor Jennifer McIntosh

Together, the supervisors will provide expertise in research methodology, analysis and the broader field of family violence and family court research.

They will also assist the candidate in developing research outputs and publishing findings from the project.

Cultural Support and Research Mentoring

An important feature of this PhD opportunity is the emphasis on culturally appropriate research.

The candidate will receive cultural support and consultation from Alison Elliott, Bouverie’s First Nations team leader.

The research team will also encourage links with the Family Courts’ Indigenous Advisor at the Melbourne Registry.

This support is particularly relevant because the project involves research with First Nations families and requires approaches that are respectful, culturally informed and appropriate for the communities involved.

The candidate will also be mentored in early-career research through the Bouverie Centre at La Trobe University.

Mental health and wellbeing.

Research methodology.

Indigenous health and wellbeing.

Culturally responsive practice.

Applicants should, however, assess their eligibility against La Trobe University’s formal PhD admission requirements rather than relying solely on their disciplinary background.

What the Successful PhD Candidate Will Do

The successful candidate will become part of a broader research program examining family safety through and beyond family court litigation.

Their responsibilities are expected to include:

Refining the PhD research questions in collaboration with the supervisors.

Developing culturally appropriate research methods.

Reviewing relevant international and Australian literature.

Examining global family court practices.

Analysing existing research data.

Investigating safety profiles of First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents.

Engaging with existing research participants using appropriate approaches.

Conducting qualitative and/or quantitative analyses.

Exploring parents’ experiences and explanations of improved safety.

Examining the influence of family, community, culture, country and service systems.

Developing research publications.

Presenting research findings through appropriate academic and professional channels.

Contributing to the wider ARC Discovery Project.

Completing a PhD by publication.

Skills Applicants Can Develop

This PhD can provide valuable research and professional development opportunities.

Depending on the final research design, the candidate may develop skills in:

Research design.

Qualitative research.

Quantitative research.

Yarning methodologies.

Culturally responsive research.

Indigenous research approaches.

Family violence research.

Family court research.

Academic writing.

Interdisciplinary collaboration.

Community-engaged research.

Research ethics.

Working with sensitive research topics.

These skills can be valuable for future careers in academia, research institutions, government, social policy, health, family services, community organisations and other areas concerned with family wellbeing and safety.

The Wider Stories of Family Safety Study

The PhD is connected to the Stories of Family Safety Study, which forms part of the broader research program.

The wider work is interested in understanding safety as something that can change over time.

Rather than treating safety as a single outcome measured at one point, researchers seek to understand the journey families experience and the factors that contribute to changes in safety.

The research therefore places considerable importance on people’s lived experiences and their explanations of what helped them become safer.

Background to the Research

The project builds on previous research conducted by the team.

This includes the ARC Linkage Project:

“Family Violence Triage in Family Courts: Safety, Efficacy and Benefit.”

That earlier project examined domestic and family violence screening and triage processes within Lighthouse, an innovative approach implemented by the courts to identify family violence risks among litigants.

The earlier work focused on improving safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system.

The new Discovery Project builds on this foundation by examining safety over a substantially longer period.

This creates an opportunity to investigate what happens to families not only during their involvement with the court but also during the period after court oversight and involvement decreases.

Conclusion

The La Trobe University PhD Scholarship attached to the ARC Discovery Project represents a significant opportunity for a researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, Indigenous and culturally diverse families, cultural safety and long-term family wellbeing.

What makes the project particularly valuable is its focus on understanding not only why families experience risk, but also how and why safety can improve over time. By combining existing cohort data with culturally informed research approaches, including yarning and other narrative methods, the PhD candidate will have the opportunity to capture perspectives that may not be visible through conventional court or administrative data.

The research could make an important contribution to family violence prevention, family court practice, culturally responsive services and policies designed to improve the safety and wellbeing of parents and children.

For eligible domestic applicants with a strong interest in this area, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander researchers and candidates whose work aligns with the project’s focus, this is an opportunity to contribute to research with significant academic, social and practical relevance.

TITLE: INVITATION: A conversation with ICT/IT Directors from African Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
On behalf of the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the Association of South African University Directors of Information Technology (ASAUDIT) – you are invited to participate in a webinar where we would be having a conversation with Directors of Information and Communication Technology Departments in African Universities.

This webinar will take place on Thursday 8th October 2020 from 11am GMT – this converts to 12 noon for Nigeria, 1 pm for Southern Africa and 2pm for East Africa. The webinar would last for 2 hours. Please register via this ZOOM link: https://tinyurl.com/ICTDirectorsAfrica

The critical role that ICT/IT Departments in African Universities have played during the COVID-19 pandemic have been widely noted and appreciated, with particular reference to supporting remote teaching and learning and helping educational communities to adapt to the new normal.

Directors of Information and Communication Technology in African Universities play key roles of supporting the technological infrastructure in their institutions – and this includes campus networks, management information systems, cloud services and the maintenance of learning infrastructure and devices. This technology infrastructure enables the integration of technology to support the core businesses of higher educational institutions, which is teaching, learning, research and community engagement. It is important that the work of ICT/IT Directors evolves and goes beyond infrastructure support – but also supports universities to implement effective digital education, support students to have good learning experiences and support their universities to build partnerships in order to sustain the digitization agenda of African Universities.

The “new normal” has elevated the important role of technology in our everyday lives. This has also come with emerging challenges related to accommodating the unconnected, responding to information security, quality assuring online teaching, addressing limited budgets, strengthening institutional digital strategies and the urgent need to train faculty and students to be able to use the digital platforms.

We have lined up several seasoned speakers that include:

Mr Andre le Roux. ICT Director, University of Cape Town, South Africa

Mr Lucas Chigabatia – Chief Information Officer, University of Ghana, Ghana

Ms Val Theron the General Manager of the Association of South African University Directors of Information Technology, South Africa

Ms Nodumo Dhlamini, Association of African Universities, Ghana and Zimbabwe

Topics to be covered include:

Lessons from West Africa that have been learned by ICT/IT Directorates during the COVID-19 pandemic

Emerging Cybersecurity Issues that need to be addressed by African Higher Education Institutions

Tips on implementing Blended Learning Technologies

How ICT/IT Directorates could reposition their roles in African Universities

The long-term goals of such AAU-led webinars is to leverage the power of a community to support less resourced universities in terms of access to technical information and knowledge. There are also opportunities for African IT/ICT Directorates to collaborate in the joint procurement of otherwise expensive IT products and services. In the medium future we would also like to run IT Skills development programs for the benefit of the IT/ICT Directorates. The areas of skills development are anticipated to cover cybersecurity, implementing and maintaining learning management systems, leadership for African IT/ICT Directors, business continuity and disaster recovery planning. We would also like to strengthen the participation of African Universities in their National Research and Education Networks.

For any inquiries please email ndhlamini@aau.org

TITLE: NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship 2026 in Singapore: Up to 4 Years of Funding, SGD 250,000 Research Grant and AI Research Opportunities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship 2026 is a prestigious postdoctoral research opportunity in Singapore designed for outstanding early-career researchers seeking to apply Artificial Intelligence (AI) to scientific discovery and advance research across science, technology, engineering, mathematics and medicine.

Jointly supported by Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and Singapore’s National Research Foundation (NRF), the AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship (AI4X-PDF) seeks to attract promising researchers who can use AI to address important scientific problems and contribute to the development of Singapore’s AI-for-Science ecosystem.

The programme is particularly relevant to researchers working at the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and STEM disciplines, offering a combination of research funding, competitive remuneration, access to advanced computing and research infrastructure, mentorship, AI training and academic career development.

For researchers who have recently completed a PhD and are looking to establish an independent research profile, the fellowship provides an opportunity to develop ambitious research while working within one of Singapore’s leading research universities.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship (AI4X-PDF) 2026

Host institution: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

Location: Singapore

Opportunity type: Postdoctoral Fellowship

Research focus: Artificial Intelligence applied to Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics and Medicine

Funding duration: Up to 4 years

Research grant: SGD 250,000

PhD requirement: PhD or equivalent in a STEM field, conferred in 2023 or later

Mentorship: Project Mentor and AI Mentor

Expected commencement: By 31 March 2027

Application deadline: 30 October 2026 at 23:59 Singapore Time (UTC/GMT+8)

Application method: Online application through NTU’s application portal

About the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship

The NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship is designed around the idea of using Artificial Intelligence as a powerful tool for scientific research and discovery.

Rather than focusing exclusively on conventional AI research, the fellowship encourages researchers to explore how AI can be integrated into other scientific and technological disciplines to address complex research questions.

The programme therefore targets researchers who can demonstrate both strong scientific expertise and a clear vision for applying AI to meaningful scientific challenges.

The fellowship forms part of NTU’s broader research ecosystem and is jointly supported by NTU and Singapore’s National Research Foundation. Successful fellows will be co-funded through the NRF Postdoctoral Award (NRF-PA) framework.

Through this model, fellows can develop research at the intersection of AI and STEM while gaining access to an environment intended to nurture future research leaders.

Why the NTU AI-for-X Fellowship Is a Significant Opportunity

Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used to accelerate scientific discovery, analyse complex datasets, develop predictive models, improve experimentation and address problems that would otherwise require significant amounts of time and resources.

The AI4X-PDF responds to this growing role of AI in scientific research by supporting researchers who can combine disciplinary expertise with AI-driven approaches.

The fellowship can therefore be particularly valuable for researchers who want to:

Develop an independent research programme.

Apply AI techniques to scientific problems.

Build a strong international research profile.

Work alongside researchers across different STEM disciplines.

Access advanced AI platforms and computing infrastructure.

Receive structured mentorship from experienced researchers.

Strengthen their academic career prospects.

Develop research that could contribute to future scientific breakthroughs.

Prepare for future tenure-track or equivalent academic positions.

The programme is positioned not simply as a short-term postdoctoral appointment but as a platform for developing researchers into future scientific and academic leaders.

Key Benefits of the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship

1. Up to Four Years of Funding

One of the major attractions of the fellowship is its potential duration. Selected researchers can receive up to four years of funding, providing a substantial period in which to develop and advance an ambitious research programme.

A longer fellowship period can allow researchers to move beyond preliminary investigations and develop deeper research programmes, publications, collaborations and scientific outputs.

2. Competitive Remuneration and Benefits

Successful fellows will receive competitive remuneration and benefits as part of the fellowship package.

This provides financial support while researchers concentrate on their research and professional development at NTU.

3. SGD 250,000 Research Grant

The fellowship includes a substantial SGD 250,000 research grant.

This research funding can provide an important foundation for developing a research programme, supporting the resources and activities required to investigate the proposed scientific problem.

For early-career researchers seeking to establish a distinctive research profile, access to dedicated research funding can also strengthen their ability to pursue ambitious projects.

4. Continued Funding During a Transition to a Tenure-Track Role

The programme also provides continued funding if a fellow transitions to a tenure-track or equivalent position during the award period, subject to the programme’s conditions.

This feature can make the fellowship particularly attractive to researchers who have long-term academic ambitions.

Rather than treating the postdoctoral period as an isolated stage of a research career, the programme provides a pathway toward broader academic development.

5. Access to NTU AI Platforms and Research Facilities

Fellows will have access to NTU’s AI platforms, research facilities and computing resources.

This is particularly important for researchers whose projects require significant computational capacity, AI infrastructure or access to specialised research facilities.

The availability of institutional infrastructure can enable researchers to test, develop and scale AI-driven approaches to scientific questions.

6. AI Training and Mentorship

Selected fellows will benefit from structured AI training and mentorship involving NTU faculty working across AI and STEM disciplines.

This interdisciplinary approach can be valuable for researchers whose primary expertise lies in a scientific field but who want to strengthen their ability to integrate AI into their research.

7. Teaching and Academic Career Development

The fellowship also includes coaching in university-level teaching.

Teaching development can be particularly useful for researchers preparing for academic careers because successful academics are often expected to demonstrate both research and teaching capabilities.

The teaching component therefore supports the broader transition toward an academic career.

Who Can Apply for the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship?

The fellowship is aimed at early-career researchers who have recently completed a PhD or equivalent qualification in a STEM field.

Applicants must meet several eligibility requirements, including the following:

PhD Qualification

Applicants must hold a PhD or equivalent qualification in a STEM field.

According to the fellowship information, the PhD must have been conferred in 2023 or later.

This means the opportunity is primarily targeted at researchers who are relatively early in their postdoctoral careers rather than established senior researchers.

STEM Background

The applicant’s doctoral background must be in a STEM field.

The fellowship information specifically frames its research scope broadly across:

Science

Technology

Engineering

Mathematics

Medicine

Applicants should therefore consider whether their disciplinary background and proposed research fit within the fellowship’s STEM and AI-for-Science focus.

Strong Academic and Research Record

Candidates are expected to demonstrate a strong academic and research record.

This is a competitive postdoctoral fellowship, so applicants should be prepared to demonstrate evidence of research excellence through their academic achievements, publications and broader research contributions.

AI-Integrated Research Proposal

A central requirement is a compelling research proposal that clearly integrates Artificial Intelligence to solve a scientific problem.

This is one of the most important aspects of the application.

Applicants should not simply propose a conventional scientific research project and mention AI as an additional component. The proposal should clearly explain how AI contributes to addressing the underlying scientific challenge.

A strong proposal should therefore establish a logical connection between:

The scientific problem.

The limitations of existing approaches.

The proposed AI-based approach.

The scientific value of applying AI.

The expected research outcomes.

NTU Project Mentor

Applicants must identify an NTU faculty member as a Project Mentor.

The mentor will provide disciplinary guidance and support the proposed research within the NTU research environment.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider potential faculty mentors whose expertise aligns with their proposed research.

Mentorship Structure

Each selected fellow will be paired with two important forms of mentorship.

Project Mentor

The Project Mentor will support the fellow in their research field and provide disciplinary guidance related to the proposed scientific project.

AI Mentor

The fellow will also receive an AI Mentor, who will be assigned or selected after the award.

The AI Mentor is intended to support the integration of Artificial Intelligence into the fellow’s scientific research.

This dual-mentor model reflects the central purpose of the fellowship: bringing together domain-specific scientific expertise and AI capabilities.

Application Process for the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship 2026

Applications must be submitted electronically through the official NTU Online Application Portal.

Applicants should prepare their documents carefully before submitting the application because the fellowship requires several supporting materials.

Required Application Documents

Applicants are required to submit the following:

1. Cover Letter

A cover letter should accompany the application and provide a clear overview of the applicant’s background, research interests and motivation for applying.

It should complement rather than simply repeat information contained in the CV.

2. Comprehensive CV

Applicants must provide a comprehensive CV.

The CV should include the applicant’s Scopus Author ID and a full publication list.

Researchers should ensure that their academic achievements, publications, research experience and other relevant accomplishments are presented clearly.

3. Official PhD Transcript or Degree Certificate

Applicants must provide an official transcript or degree certificate in English for their PhD.

The documentation should demonstrate the required doctoral qualification.

4. Research Proposal

Applicants must submit a research proposal of no more than two pages.

The proposal is particularly important because the fellowship is focused on applying AI to scientific problems.

The proposal should clearly demonstrate:

The scientific problem being addressed.

Why the problem is important.

The proposed research approach.

How Artificial Intelligence will be integrated.

The expected scientific contribution.

Why the proposed research is suitable for the NTU environment.

Applicants should also follow the official proposal template provided by NTU.

5. Contact Information for Two Referees

Applicants must provide contact information for two referees.

One of the referees must be the applicant’s PhD Supervisor.

Applicants should contact their referees before submitting the application and confirm that they are willing to provide recommendation reports.

NTU will contact the referees after the application has been submitted.

6. Top Three Publications

Applicants are required to submit their top three publications in PDF format.

Applicants should therefore carefully select the publications that best demonstrate their research quality, expertise and potential.

The strongest publications will generally be those most closely connected to the applicant’s research trajectory and proposed AI-for-science project.

7. Mentor’s Support Letter

Applicants must also submit a support letter from their NTU mentor.

The mentor’s support letter should be attached to the research proposal and uploaded as one combined file in the research proposal section of the application.

This makes early engagement with a prospective NTU faculty mentor particularly important.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship 2026 is:

30 October 2026 at 23:59 Singapore Time (UTC/GMT+8).

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their applications, particularly because obtaining mentor support, preparing a two-page research proposal and securing referee agreement can require considerable advance preparation.

Successful applicants must be available to commence the fellowship by 31 March 2027.

Applicants should therefore consider their current employment, research commitments, visa arrangements and other obligations when assessing their ability to take up the fellowship within the required timeframe.

NTU is offering online briefing sessions for prospective applicants.

The sessions are intended to help researchers understand the fellowship and the application process before submitting their applications.

Fellowship objectives.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

The competitive nature of the AI4X-PDF means applicants should approach the application strategically.

1. Develop a Clearly Defined Scientific Problem

The research proposal should begin with a scientifically meaningful problem.

Applicants should demonstrate that the proposed problem is important and that addressing it could produce meaningful scientific or technological value.

2. Explain Why AI Is Necessary

The application should clearly establish why AI is appropriate for the proposed problem.

Rather than simply stating that AI will be used, applicants should explain what AI enables them to accomplish that conventional approaches may not achieve as effectively.

3. Demonstrate Interdisciplinary Potential

Since the fellowship sits at the intersection of AI and STEM, applicants should demonstrate their ability to connect their disciplinary expertise with AI methodologies.

The strongest applications are likely to show a genuine integration rather than treating AI as an unrelated add-on.

4. Identify an Appropriate NTU Mentor

Finding a suitable NTU faculty Project Mentor is a critical part of the application.

Applicants should research NTU faculty members and identify researchers whose expertise, facilities and research interests align with the proposed project.

A strong mentor-project match can help demonstrate that the proposed research can realistically be implemented within the NTU research environment.

5. Select Publications Strategically

Applicants should use the three-publication requirement to showcase their strongest research.

The selected publications should help establish the applicant’s expertise and demonstrate their potential to conduct high-quality independent research.

6. Make the Two-Page Proposal Focused

Because the proposal is limited to two pages, applicants need to communicate their research vision efficiently.

Every section should contribute to answering the central question: What important scientific problem will be solved, and how will AI enable the research?

7. Engage Referees Early

Since two referees are required and one must be the PhD Supervisor, applicants should approach referees well before the deadline.

Referees should agree to provide reports before the application is submitted.

8. Follow the Document Requirements Carefully

Applicants should check file formats, document completeness and submission requirements before submitting.

Who Is Eligible by Country, Race and Continent?

The information provided for the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship does not state a specific nationality, race or country restriction.

Therefore, the published eligibility criteria do not identify the fellowship as being restricted to applicants from a particular African, Asian, European, American or other regional group.

In practical terms, the opportunity is presented as an international research fellowship for eligible early-career researchers, with eligibility primarily determined by academic and research requirements rather than race or geographic origin.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania and other regions may therefore consider applying if they satisfy the fellowship’s stated requirements. However, applicants should rely on NTU’s official eligibility rules for the final determination of their individual eligibility.

Category of People Who Qualify

Early-career researchers.

Recent PhD graduates.

Researchers with a PhD or equivalent in a STEM field.

Researchers whose doctoral qualification was conferred in 2023 or later.

Scientists interested in applying AI to scientific discovery.

Technology and engineering researchers working on AI-enabled scientific problems.

Mathematics researchers developing AI-related scientific applications.

Medical researchers with suitable AI-for-science research proposals.

Researchers with a strong academic and research record.

Applicants capable of developing a compelling AI-integrated research proposal.

Researchers able to identify an NTU faculty member willing to serve as Project Mentor.

Researchers intending to pursue an academic or research leadership career.

Conclusion

The NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship 2026 represents a major opportunity for early-career STEM researchers who want to build research careers at the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and scientific discovery.

With up to four years of funding, a SGD 250,000 research grant, competitive remuneration, access to AI platforms and research facilities, structured AI training, interdisciplinary mentorship and teaching-development support, the fellowship provides researchers with resources to develop ambitious research programmes and strengthen their academic trajectories.

The requirement for an NTU Project Mentor also means that applicants should begin identifying suitable faculty collaborators well before submitting their applications.

Eligible researchers should pay particular attention to the PhD completion requirement of 2023 or later, the need for a strong academic and research record, the two-page AI-integrated research proposal, the three selected publications, referee requirements and mentor support letter.

The application deadline is 30 October 2026 at 23:59 Singapore Time (UTC/GMT+8), while successful fellows must be able to commence the fellowship by 31 March 2027.

For researchers seeking to contribute to the rapidly developing field of AI-for-Science while building an internationally competitive academic research career, the NTU AI-for-X Postdoctoral Fellowship offers an opportunity to combine scientific expertise, Artificial Intelligence, interdisciplinary collaboration and substantial research support within Singapore’s research ecosystem.

TITLE: Gender Equality Plan
