TITLE: UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace 2026: Apply for the UN Youth Peacebuilding Programme in Cyprus

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme 2026 is inviting young people living in Cyprus to apply for an opportunity to develop practical skills in environmental peacebuilding, intercommunal cooperation, youth leadership and sustainable development.

Organized by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) in partnership with the British Council, through its regional Youth Connect programme, the initiative will bring together young people from different communities across the island to learn, collaborate and develop joint environmental actions.

The programme is designed for young people who are interested in environmental protection, peacebuilding, climate action, social cohesion and community development. Participants will take part in immersive workshops, work in intercommunal teams, receive guidance from mentors and develop environmental initiatives that must be implemented by February 2027.

Participation in the programme is free. The application deadline is 20 September 2026.

Overview of the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme

The UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace initiative is being offered for the sixth year by UNFICYP and the British Council. The 2026 edition will focus specifically on environmental peacebuilding and the development of joint actions addressing shared environmental concerns.

Environmental challenges such as climate change, resource scarcity, pollution, environmental degradation and unequal access to resources can affect communities across social, political and geographical divisions. The programme recognizes that environmental issues can also provide opportunities for cooperation, dialogue and trust-building.

Through collaborative learning and practical action, the programme seeks to empower young people in Cyprus to become active contributors to a more peaceful, sustainable and inclusive future.

The initiative will enable participants to:

Explore the relationship between environmental challenges and peacebuilding.

Learn how shared environmental concerns can encourage cooperation.

Develop practical environmental action plans with participants from different communities.

Strengthen leadership, communication and teamwork skills.

Build relationships with environmental and peacebuilding practitioners.

Participate in initiatives that promote intercommunal trust and social cohesion.

Join a wider network of Youth Champions working on environmental and peace-related issues.

According to the official announcement, the programme is taking place at a time when climate change is increasingly contributing to insecurity, inequality and social vulnerability. The initiative therefore emphasizes the importance of acting both locally and collectively to address shared challenges.

What Is Environmental Peacebuilding?

Environmental peacebuilding refers to the use of environmental cooperation, natural-resource management and sustainability initiatives to support peace, prevent conflict and strengthen relationships between communities.

Environmental concerns often affect people regardless of their political, cultural, ethnic or social background. Issues such as water, waste management, biodiversity, climate resilience, land use, food systems and pollution can create shared interests and provide opportunities for constructive cooperation.

Within the UN Youth Champions programme, participants will explore how environmental action can contribute to:

Peaceful relationships between communities.

Mutual understanding and trust.

Sustainable development.

Inclusive youth leadership.

Climate resilience.

Community participation.

Environmental awareness.

Cooperation across the divide in Cyprus.

Rather than focusing only on discussions, the programme encourages participants to work together on practical initiatives that address environmental issues and benefit communities across the island.

Key Dates for the 2026 Programme

Applicants should take note of the important dates and participation requirements.

Programme Activity
Date or Period

Application deadline
20 September 2026

Notification of successful applicants
Expected by 23 September 2026

First workshop day
3 October 2026

Second workshop day
4 October 2026

Third workshop day
10 October 2026

Fourth workshop day
11 October 2026

Environmental action implementation deadline
February 2027

Closing event
End of March 2027

Attendance at all four workshop days is mandatory. Participants are also expected to actively contribute to the development and implementation of their team’s environmental action.

Who Can Apply for the UN Youth Champions Programme?

The programme is open to young people aged 18 to 30 who live in Cyprus and come from any community on the island.

Applicants do not need to have previous professional or academic experience in environmental protection, peacebuilding or activism. However, they should demonstrate genuine interest, motivation and willingness to work collaboratively with people from different communities.

Eligibility Requirements

To be considered, applicants must meet the following requirements:

Be between 18 and 30 years old.

Belong to or live within any community in Cyprus.

Have a strong desire to contribute to a peaceful and sustainable future on the island.

Demonstrate an interest in environmental issues and peacebuilding.

Be willing to become active in environmental and peace-related initiatives.

Commit to attending all four experiential workshop days on 3, 4, 10 and 11 October 2026.

Be willing to work with a team to develop and implement an environmental action by February 2027.

Have a very good knowledge of English.

Be willing to build interpersonal relationships with participants from all communities living in Cyprus.

Be interested in working collaboratively toward a common cause.

Not have previously benefited from a UN Youth Champions programme.

The call is intended to encourage participation from young people across the different communities in Cyprus. The organizers also seek gender diversity and equal representation among participants.

Previous Experience Is Not Required

One of the important features of the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme is that applicants do not need previous experience in environmental peacebuilding, environmental activism or related fields.

This makes the programme suitable for young people who may be new to environmental action but are passionate about sustainability, peace, youth participation, community development or social change.

Applicants do not necessarily need to be environmental scientists, peacebuilding professionals or climate activists. What matters is their:

Interest in the subject.

Willingness to learn.

Commitment to teamwork.

Ability to participate fully.

Motivation to contribute to a peaceful and sustainable Cyprus.

Participants will receive learning opportunities and support from experts, trainers, environmental practitioners, peacebuilding specialists and youth activists.

What Does the Programme Offer?

The UN Youth Champions initiative provides a combination of workshops, collaborative learning, mentoring, practical project development and networking opportunities.

1. Immersive Environmental Peacebuilding Workshops

The programme will include in-person workshops on:

3 October 2026

4 October 2026

10 October 2026

11 October 2026

The workshops will take place at Ledra Palace in the UN buffer zone in Nicosia.

The sessions will focus on experiential and collaborative learning. Participants will engage in interactive discussions, group activities, presentations and practical exercises related to environmental issues and peacebuilding.

The workshops are expected to help participants understand:

The links between environmental challenges and conflict.

The role of youth in peacebuilding.

The importance of environmental cooperation.

The value of inclusive leadership.

Ways to design community-focused environmental actions.

How to work effectively in intercommunal teams.

2. Team-Based Project Development

During the workshops, participants will meet other young people from communities across Cyprus. They will form teams and work together to identify environmental concerns that can be addressed through joint action.

Each team will develop an environmental action idea with support from programme organizers, experts and mentors.

The projects are expected to encourage cooperation across the divide and should be designed to reach people from different communities. Although actions may take place in specific locations, participants are strongly encouraged to develop initiatives that can benefit communities throughout Cyprus.

3. Mentorship and Expert Support

Each team will receive support from a mentor as it develops and implements its environmental action plan.

Mentors and experts may assist participants with:

Refining their project idea.

Identifying the environmental issue to address.

Developing an achievable action plan.

Preparing a simple project proposal.

Organizing implementation activities.

Identifying target beneficiaries.

Strengthening teamwork and communication.

Addressing practical challenges during implementation.

This guidance is intended to help participants transform an initial idea into a realistic and useful environmental initiative.

4. Small Grants for Environmental Actions

After the workshops, teams will be expected to finalize their environmental action ideas and submit a simple proposal.

Each team will receive a small grant to support the implementation of its approved environmental action. The supplied announcement does not specify the exact amount of funding available to each team.

The environmental actions must be implemented by February 2027.

The projects should:

Address a relevant environmental concern.

Encourage cooperation between communities.

Promote sustainability or environmental awareness.

Involve young people or local communities where appropriate.

Contribute to social cohesion and mutual understanding.

Be practical and achievable within the programme timeline.

Reach people across the divide.

The grant is intended to support the implementation of team projects. It should not be interpreted as a personal stipend, salary or individual fellowship award.

5. Networking Opportunities

Participants will have the opportunity to connect with:

Environmental organizations.

Peacebuilding organizations.

Youth networks.

Community activists.

Environmental practitioners.

Peacebuilding experts.

Trainers and facilitators.

Other young people from across Cyprus.

By the end of the programme, participants will become part of the wider UN Youth Champions network, creating opportunities for continued engagement, collaboration and peer learning.

6. Certificate of Participation

Participants who meet the programme requirements may receive a programme certificate.

To receive the certificate, participants must:

Attend all four mandatory workshop days.

Actively participate in the environmental action process.

Fulfil the programme’s participation requirements.

Full compliance with both workshop attendance and environmental action participation is necessary to receive the certificate.

What Will Participants Do During the Workshops?

The workshops will be organized around collaborative learning and practical teamwork.

Participants can expect to take part in activities such as:

Interactive sessions on environmental peacebuilding.

Discussions with environmental and peacebuilding activists.

Presentations from experts and trainers.

Group exercises.

Team-building activities.

Exploration of shared environmental concerns.

Development of environmental action ideas.

Collaborative project planning.

Networking with participants from different communities.

The workshops are designed not only to transfer knowledge but also to help participants develop relationships and learn how to work together across community divisions.

The group work component will be especially important because participants will form teams and develop environmental actions with support from the programme team and experts from across the island.

Implementing Environmental Actions After the Workshops

Following the workshops, each team will be expected to develop its environmental action idea into a simple proposal.

The team will then work toward implementing the action by February 2027.

Potential actions may address shared environmental concerns, although the official announcement does not prescribe a fixed list of project themes. Applicants should therefore remain open to developing practical initiatives that respond to the needs of communities and encourage cooperation.

Examples of possible areas of interest could include:

Environmental education.

Waste reduction and recycling.

Biodiversity conservation.

Climate awareness.

Sustainable communities.

Water conservation.

Green public spaces.

Environmental volunteering.

Sustainable consumption.

Community clean-up activities.

Nature-based cooperation.

Youth-led climate action.

These examples are illustrative rather than an official list of required project topics. The final actions will depend on the ideas developed by selected participants and approved through the programme process.

The organizers encourage actions that reach people across the divide and recommend that initiatives take place throughout Cyprus where possible.

Closing Event in March 2027

The programme will conclude with a closing event expected to take place at the end of March 2027.

All participants are expected to attend the closing event. It will provide an opportunity to reflect on the programme, share experiences, present or discuss environmental actions, celebrate collaboration and recognize the contributions of the Youth Champions.

The closing event may also provide an opportunity for participants to connect with programme partners, environmental organizations, peacebuilding practitioners and other stakeholders.

Programme Location and Attendance Requirements

All programme activities will be held at Ledra Palace, located in the UN buffer zone in Nicosia.

Participation is conditional on applicants being able to enter the UN buffer zone through the relevant crossing points. The official announcement emphasizes that authority over entry through crossing points rests with the respective sides and not with the United Nations.

Applicants must therefore ensure that they possess the required documentation and are able to access the programme venue.

Accommodation Support

Accommodation in Nicosia may be available during the workshop weekends for participants who are unable to commute.

However:

Accommodation is subject to demand.

Availability is limited.

Accommodation is not guaranteed.

Arrangements are subject to confirmation.

Applicants who require accommodation should communicate their needs through the application process or with the programme organizers.

Is Participation Free?

Yes. Participation in the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme is free of charge.

However, applicants should carefully review the practical requirements associated with attending the programme, including:

Travel to the workshop location.

Ability to enter the UN buffer zone.

Availability for all workshop dates.

Participation in team activities.

Ability to contribute to environmental action implementation.

Attendance at the closing event.

The announcement confirms that accommodation may be available for some participants, but it does not state that all travel or personal expenses will be covered.

Important Clarification About the Programme

The UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme is a youth development and community engagement initiative. It is not a job, paid internship or full-time employment opportunity.

Participation is:

Honorary.

Non-remunerated.

Not considered employment with the United Nations or British Council.

Not associated with UN salaries, emoluments or employment benefits.

Not a formal appointment as a UN staff member.

Participants will not receive UN privileges or immunities, and joining the programme does not authorize participants to speak on behalf of the UN, UNFICYP or the British Council.

The programme should therefore be viewed as a learning, leadership, networking and community action opportunity rather than a paid employment placement.

Important Disclaimer for Participants

The views, thoughts and opinions expressed by individuals or groups designated as UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace are expressed in their personal capacity.

These views do not necessarily represent the official views of:

The United Nations.

UNFICYP.

The British Council.

Their officials or personnel.

Participants should therefore understand that being selected as a Youth Champion does not mean they are official spokespersons for the United Nations or UNFICYP.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme 2026 is:

20 September 2026

Applicants are encouraged to submit their forms before the deadline. The official announcement indicates that successful applicants are expected to be notified by 23 September 2026.

Late applications may not be considered, so applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to complete and submit the form.

How to Apply for the UN Youth Champions Programme

Interested applicants should complete the Official Online Application Form before the deadline.

Application Steps

Review the eligibility criteria carefully.

Confirm that you are aged 18–30 and living in Cyprus.

Ensure that you can attend all four workshop days.

Confirm that you can participate in environmental action activities through February 2027.

Ensure that you have a very good knowledge of English.

Check that you have not previously participated in a UN Youth Champions programme.

Complete the online application form.

Submit the application by 20 September 2026.

Official Application Form

Interested applicants can apply through the official application form:

Apply for the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme

Official Programme Information

For the original announcement and additional information, visit:

UNFICYP: Apply Now to Become a UN Youth Champion for Environment and Peace

Contact Information

For questions about the programme or application process, applicants can contact:

Email: unficyp-youthchampions@un.org

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the announcement does not provide a detailed scoring rubric, applicants can improve their applications by clearly demonstrating their motivation and readiness to participate.

A strong application should communicate:

1. Genuine Interest in Environmental Issues

Explain why environmental sustainability, climate action, conservation or related issues matter to you.

Applicants do not need extensive technical knowledge, but they should demonstrate curiosity and a willingness to learn.

2. Commitment to Peacebuilding

Describe your interest in dialogue, community cooperation, social cohesion or building relationships across differences.

The programme is specifically designed to bring together participants from different communities, so applicants should show that they value respect, inclusion and collaboration.

3. Willingness to Work in Teams

The programme requires participants to develop environmental actions as part of a team. Applicants should be prepared to listen, contribute ideas, manage differences and work toward shared goals.

4. Availability for All Programme Activities

Applicants should confirm that they can attend the workshops on:

3 October 2026.

4 October 2026.

10 October 2026.

11 October 2026.

They should also be able to participate in the environmental action implementation process and attend the closing event in March 2027.

5. Interest in Practical Action

The programme is not limited to discussions or classroom learning. Participants will be expected to develop and implement an environmental action.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a willingness to move from learning to practical community engagement.

6. Understanding of the Programme’s Requirements

Applicants should understand that:

Participation is free.

The programme is not paid employment.

Attendance is mandatory.

Environmental actions must be implemented by February 2027.

Entry into the UN buffer zone is the participant’s responsibility.

Accommodation in Nicosia may be limited and is not guaranteed.

A certificate depends on full compliance with programme requirements.

Why This Programme Matters

The UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme responds to two closely connected challenges: environmental sustainability and peaceful coexistence.

Environmental problems do not stop at community boundaries. Climate change, pollution, waste, biodiversity loss and resource pressures can affect people across social and political divisions. Cooperation on these issues can help communities identify common interests and develop practical solutions.

The programme also recognizes the role of young people as contributors to peacebuilding. Rather than treating youth only as beneficiaries, it gives them opportunities to:

Develop leadership skills.

Participate in decision-making.

Build relationships across communities.

Design community initiatives.

Strengthen environmental awareness.

Contribute to sustainable development.

Become involved in peacebuilding processes.

By combining environmental action with intercommunal cooperation, the initiative seeks to show how shared goals can help build trust and strengthen social cohesion.

Visit HERE to learn more about the UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace 2026.

Conclusion

The UN Youth Champions for Environment and Peace Programme 2026 offers young people living in Cyprus an opportunity to gain knowledge, build cross-community relationships and develop practical environmental initiatives that contribute to peace and sustainability.

Organized by UNFICYP in partnership with the British Council, the programme includes immersive workshops, team-based project development, mentoring, small grants for environmental actions and networking with environmental and peacebuilding practitioners.

The programme is open to individuals aged 18 to 30 from any community living in Cyprus. Previous experience in environmental peacebuilding is not required, but applicants must demonstrate motivation, a strong interest in environmental and peace-related issues, good English-language skills and a commitment to attending all workshops and participating in environmental action implementation.

Participation is free, but the programme is honorary and non-remunerated. Applicants must also be able to access the UN buffer zone in Nicosia, where activities will take place.

The application deadline is 20 September 2026. Eligible young people who are passionate about environmental sustainability, peacebuilding, youth leadership and community cooperation are encouraged to apply early and take part in this opportunity to help build a more peaceful and sustainable Cyprus.

TITLE: Undergraduates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
An undergraduate degree in physics at MIT, with its emphasis on learning to solve problems, provides an excellent basis for graduate study in physics and related fields; it is also a great foundation for careers in industry, research, finance, management, law, medicine, or public policy.

The Physics Department offers two tracks to the major, Flexible and Focus, each leading to a Bachelor of Science in Physics:

The Flexible track is selected by most Physics majors: it provides a series of rigorous courses in fundamental physics topics, and its options enable many of our students to complete second majors in other disciplines.

Students who choose the Focus track take a greater number of specific required courses, including two terms of experimental physics, and write a research thesis.

Both pathways are highly suitable for any student planning to pursue graduate school, teaching or research beyond MIT. Degree requirements for each can be found on our Physics Degree Requirements webpage.

Physics subjects for First-years (GIRs)

The Department of Physics has various options for fulfilling the General Institute Requirements (GIRs) of Physics I and Physics II, all based on extensive use of calculus.

Video about the Physics General Institute Requirements
Physics I

Physics I introduces classical (Newtonian) mechanics: space and time; kinematics; Newton’s Laws; particle dynamics; collisions and conservation laws; work and potential energy; universal gravitation; rigid bodies, equilibrium, and rotational dynamics.

8.01: taken by most students, this course uses the Technology Enabled Active Learning (TEAL) format, including group problem-solving and digital content;

8.012: mathematically more advanced than 8.01; is intended for students with strong physics and math background;

8.01L: longer version of 8.01, starts in the fall and continues into January, allowing students additional time to develop problem-solving skills.

Appropriate placement in 8.01, 8.01L, or 8.012 is determined by the results of the Math Self-Assessment test taken during Orientation.

8.011: offered each spring, intended for students who need to retake a version of 8.01; its organization of small lecture sections and weekly quizzes benefits students who learn well in a highly-structured environment.

Physics II

Physics II introduces electromagnetism and electrostatics: electric charge, Coulomb’s law, the electric structure of matter, conductors and dielectrics. Concepts of electrostatic field and potential, electrostatic energy. Electric currents, magnetic fields, and Ampere’s law. Magnetic materials. Time-varying fields and Faraday’s law of induction. Basic electric circuits. Electromagnetic waves and Maxwell’s equations.

8.02: like 8.01, presents material using the TEAL format.

8.021: offered each fall; taught in small lecture sections with weekly quizzes. Enrollment is limited to students who have previously attempted 8.02 or 8.022.

8.022: mathematically more advanced level than 8.02; intended for students with strong physics and math background.

Visit MIT Physics

We welcome hearing from you if you are planning a visit to the Boston area and would like to visit the MIT Physics department! Visits usually involve meeting with our Undergraduate Program Coordinator, who will describe the program and undergraduate activities, and answer questions. We can also arrange for you to meet with a current student. Visit arrangements should be made in advance in order to ensure someone is available to meet with you. To request an appointment, contact physics-undergrad@mit.edu.

While we do not arrange visits with faculty members, you may contact research labs and/or individual faculty directly to ask about a meeting during your visit.

Visitors can also take a campus tour provided by the Admissions Office and read more information about arranging a general visit to MIT.

TITLE: Information on Graduate Course Requirements

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Choosing First Year Graduate Subjects

The Department does not require PhD students to take any subjects other than those needed to satisfy the specialty and breadth requirements described below. However, many students begin by taking some combination of graduate Classical Mechanics (8.309), graduate Quantum Mechanics (8.321 and 8.322), graduate Electricity and Magnetism (8.311), and graduate Statistical Mechanics (8.333). Not only have these subjects been proven to give students a broad view of basic physics, but each of them (with the exception of 8.322) may be used to satisfy the related part of the Written General Exam.

First-year students concerned with the level of their undergraduate preparation are encouraged to consider taking senior-level undergraduate subjects such as Electricity and Magnetism (8.07), Statistical Mechanics (8.08) and Classical Mechanics (8.09). Some first-year students may wish to sample basic graduate subjects in specialty areas: Atomic and Optical Physics (8.421 or 8.422), Solid State Physics (8.511), Systems Biology (8.591J), Plasma Physics (8.613J), Introduction to Nuclear and Particle Physics (8.701), and Astrophysics (8.901 or 8.902). These subjects may later be counted towards one’s specialty or breadth requirements. While planning their first year program, students should keep in mind that the normal subject load for those with full time RAs is two academic subjects, or about 24 units. A student with an RA will also register for Pre-Thesis Research (8.391 in the fall; 8.392 in the spring and summer terms), for 12 or more units, depending on the rest of the course load.

Students are encouraged to visit the website for more information about these requirements.

NuPAX students should take this course in the spring of their first year.

Eligible students from countries with good diplomatic relations can apply for the fully funded scholarships in Japan. Therefore, if you want to pursue postgraduate education in Japan for free, this Japanese Government Scholarship (MEXT) Program is the best opportunity for you!

Students from almost every field can apply, but there are some restricted fields for research. The research fields are traditional entertainment arts, welfare science, medicine, and dentistry. Every year, the application cycle for the MEXT Research scholarship is announced in April and May. TITLE: New AAU Secretary General Assumes Office

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The new Secretary General of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Prof. Olusola Bandele Oyewole assumed office today, Friday October 1, 2021.

He takes over the mantle of leading Africa’s apex continental higher education body, the AAU, from Prof. Etienne Ehilé, who served as the Association’s Secretary General for the last nine years (August 2012 – September 2021).

Prof. Oyewole was appointed the Secretary General following a competitive selection process which had several high-profile applicants participating. The announcement of his appointment was first made at the Extra-ordinary General Conference organized by the Association on August 9, 2021.

Broadly, Prof. Oyewole’s top 10 focus areas are as follows – 1) To demonstrate the value of AAU to its existing Members 2) To increase the AAU’s Membership 3) To promote intellectual engagement to position AAU as the true voice for higher education in Africa 4) To contribute towards building the next generation of academics 5) To consolidate the regional offices and work closely with them for the benefit of stakeholders in those regions 6) To continue strengthening linkages with the diaspora 7) To strengthen partnerships and collaborations between other institutions and the AAU 8) To continue the execution of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa 9) To cultivate new relationships with other development partners and 10) To sustain the Association for the benefit of its members and stakeholders.

Meeting staff of the AAU Secretariat today, Prof. Oyewole appreciated their commitment and hard work which have contributed to the Association’s status. He called on them to cooperate with him, and together collaborate with member institutions and stakeholders to move the Association to the next level.

He assured the meeting of his commitment to creating a conducive environment, promoting a culture of openness, teamwork and excellence, to raise the image of the Association.

On their part, staff of the AAU Secretariat assured the new Secretary General of their commitment and dedication towards realizing his vision of proving to the world that an African Institution can be different and provide excellent leadership to transform the African higher education space.

Professor Olusola Bandele Oyewole is a Nigerian professor of Food Science and Technology, specifically Food Microbiology and Biotechnology. He is not new to the Association, having served as a staff, and subsequently as a Board Member and President of the Association in the past. He is the former Vice Chancellor of the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, Nigeria and has also worked as a Senior Expert in Higher Education at the African Union Commission in Ethiopia. Professor Oyewole’s work experience at the national, regional, and continental levels have endowed him with a wealth of knowledge in coordinating multinational research and development programs. He therefore comes to the AAU fully equipped for the job ahead of him.

Professor Olusola Oyewole’s full profile can be accessed here – https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/New-SG-Prof.-Olusola-Oyewole-CV.pdf

TITLE: Mama Cash Spark Fund 2026: Apply for €5,000–€12,000 Grants for Feminist Groups in the Netherlands and ABCSSS Islands

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Mama Cash Spark Fund 2026, a flexible grant programme supporting self-led feminist groups working for the rights of women, girls, trans people and intersex people in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands: Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao, Saba, Sint Eustatius and Sint Maarten.

The Spark Fund is designed particularly for grassroots and structurally excluded communities working on urgent and contested political issues. Grants range from €5,000 to €12,000 per project and can support work for a period of up to two years. Mama Cash accepts applications from both formal organisations and informal groups, including newly established and volunteer-led initiatives that may have difficulty accessing conventional institutional funding.

The 2026 application period runs from:

20 August 2026 to 20 September 2026

The final deadline is:

20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

Applicants can apply in several accessible formats, including:

Written application

Video application

Audio application

Applications can be submitted in English or Dutch. Groups that would prefer to apply in another language are encouraged to contact Mama Cash at spark@mamacash.org to discuss possible support.

The Spark Fund is especially notable because applicants do not need to be formally registered, do not need an organisational bank account, and do not need a residence permit or official identification in order to apply.

About the Mama Cash Spark Fund

Mama Cash is an international feminist fund with deep roots in feminist movements in the Netherlands.

Through the Spark Fund, the organisation honours its historical connection to the Dutch lesbian feminist activist movement while continuing to support communities working for the rights of:

Women

Girls

Trans people

Intersex people

The Fund is geographically focused on the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands and is intended to help self-led groups pursue bold, grassroots work that challenges structural inequality.

Mama Cash describes the idea behind the programme simply:

A small amount of money can spark major, radical change.

The Fund therefore does not assume that transformative work must come from large, established NGOs.

Instead, it deliberately makes room for:

Informal collectives

New groups

Volunteer-led initiatives

Unregistered movements

Small organisations

Groups without paid staff

Groups without offices

Groups with limited access to flexible funding

This makes the Spark Fund particularly relevant to activists who may struggle to qualify for conventional institutional grants.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Successful applicants can receive between:

€5,000 and €12,000

for a project lasting:

Up to two years.

The flexibility of this range means the Fund can support relatively small grassroots initiatives as well as longer projects that need sustained support.

Importantly, the programme is not structured only around established organisations with professional fundraising departments.

Mama Cash specifically recognises that some activist groups may:

Be newly established

Operate informally

Lack formal organisational structures

Have no long-term strategic plan

Have limited financial infrastructure

but still have a strong idea, urgent political purpose and clear potential for structural change.

What Is the Main Purpose of the Spark Fund?

The Spark Fund supports initiatives:

By and for structurally excluded communities

that work on:

Urgent and contested issues

in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands.

This means the Fund is not designed primarily for neutral service-delivery programmes.

It is particularly interested in groups challenging:

Discrimination

Patriarchal systems

Sexism

Gender inequality

Exclusion

Harmful norms

Unequal access to rights

Structural barriers affecting marginalised communities

Projects should therefore have a clear political or systemic dimension.

The Four Core Eligibility Requirements

Mama Cash sets out four major eligibility criteria.

A group must:

Be self-led by the women, girls, trans people and/or intersex people it serves.

Work from a feminist perspective and/or focus on women’s, girls’, trans rights and/or intersex rights.

Work on urgent and contested political issues in the Netherlands or the ABCSSS islands.

Push for structural and systemic change.

Each of these criteria is important and deserves careful attention before submitting an application.

1. The Group Must Be Self-Led

The people whose rights are at stake must be the people who make decisions about the project.

Mama Cash gives the example of a group supporting women with disabilities.

If the project is focused on the rights of women with disabilities, then women with disabilities should themselves have meaningful leadership over:

Activities

Decision-making

Use of grant funds

Public representation

People without disabilities may participate and provide support, but they should not lead the project.

This principle is central to the Spark Fund.

Mama Cash is not simply looking for organisations that work for marginalised groups.

It prioritises groups that are genuinely led by the communities directly affected by the issues.

Why Self-Leadership Matters

The self-led requirement reflects a broader feminist grantmaking principle: people directly affected by injustice should have power over how solutions are designed.

This means a project may be less competitive if the intended beneficiaries have little influence over:

Strategy

Budget

Leadership

Project design

Communications

Applicants should therefore show clearly who makes decisions inside the group.

A strong application should be able to answer questions such as:

Who leads the group?

Who decides how funds are used?

Who determines project priorities?

Are the affected communities represented in leadership?

Who speaks publicly on behalf of the project?

2. The Group Must Work From a Feminist Perspective

Mama Cash defines feminism broadly.

The organisation understands feminist work as efforts that challenge:

Sexism

Patriarchal gender norms

Inequality

Injustice

and defend the human rights of women, girls, trans and intersex people.

The Fund recognises that gender inequality intersects with many other forms of marginalisation, including:

Race

Ethnicity

Sexuality

Class

Migration status

Disability

Economic status

The Spark Fund therefore supports intersectional approaches where these experiences are central to the project.

What Counts as a Feminist Project?

A project does not need to be about a traditionally defined “women’s issue.”

For example, a project about housing may qualify if it specifically addresses barriers faced by women who are:

Migrants

Queer

Sex workers

Women with disabilities

Rural women

Low-income women

The key point is that their lived experiences and rights must be central to the project rather than included only as a secondary component.

This distinction is important.

A general community housing project that happens to include some women would not automatically meet the Fund’s feminist criteria.

A project designed and led by marginalised women challenging structural barriers to safe and affordable housing may be much more aligned.

3. The Group Must Work on Urgent and Contested Political Issues

The Spark Fund is intended for groups working on issues that may be politically difficult, socially controversial or insufficiently addressed.

Mama Cash gives the example of Muslim women organising to defend their rights and express their concerns in a context where wearing the hijab, niqab or similar forms of religious covering faces criticism from government or public opinion.

Other relevant themes might potentially include:

Reproductive rights

Trans rights

Migrant rights

Disability justice

Sex workers’ rights

Racial justice

Religious discrimination

LGBTQI+ rights

Gender-based violence

Housing inequality

Economic exclusion

These are examples rather than a closed list.

The central requirement is that the issue is politically significant and that the project is rooted in feminist rights-based action.

4. The Project Must Push for Structural and Systemic Change

The Spark Fund is not focused only on helping individual people cope with immediate needs.

Mama Cash wants projects that also challenge the systems creating those needs.

For example, a group of migrant women might offer temporary shelter to other migrant women.

Providing shelter addresses an immediate need.

But to fit the Spark Fund’s structural-change orientation, the same group might also challenge barriers preventing migrant women from accessing:

Housing

Healthcare

Social services

Legal protection

This broader work can create benefits even for people the project cannot support directly.

What Does Structural Change Mean?

Structural change may include efforts to:

Change policy

Challenge discriminatory systems

Shift public attitudes

Improve institutional practices

Expand rights

Strengthen movement power

Reform harmful procedures

Increase representation

Build collective organising capacity

The project does not need to transform an entire national system within one grant period.

But it should have a credible ambition to address causes, not merely symptoms.

Who Gets Priority?

Although many eligible groups can apply, Mama Cash gives particular priority to groups facing barriers to conventional flexible funding.

These include:

Informal groups

Unregistered groups

Newly established groups

Volunteer-led groups

Organisations with limited organisational resources

Groups with no paid staff

Groups without office space

Mama Cash explicitly states that particular consideration is given to groups with limited organisational resources.

This is important because being a small or informal organisation is not automatically a weakness in this competition.

In fact, it may align closely with the Fund’s priorities.

Do Applicants Need to Be Registered Organisations?

No.

The Spark Fund can support:

Informal and unregistered groups.

Your group does not need to be formally registered as a Dutch foundation or other legal organisation in order to apply.

This removes an important barrier faced by grassroots movements.

Do Applicants Need an Organisational Bank Account?

No.

Mama Cash explicitly states that applicants do not need an organisational bank account to submit an application.

Groups should therefore not exclude themselves simply because they have not yet established formal banking arrangements.

If selected, Mama Cash can presumably discuss appropriate payment arrangements directly with the group.

Do Applicants Need a Residence Permit?

No.

The Spark Fund states that applicants do not need a residence permit to apply.

This can be especially important for migrant-led and undocumented communities that may otherwise be excluded from conventional grant programmes.

Do Applicants Need Official Identification?

No.

Mama Cash also states that official identification is not required simply in order to submit an application.

Together, these rules make the Fund particularly accessible to grassroots communities that may lack conventional administrative documentation.

Geographic Eligibility

The Spark Fund is geographically limited.

Projects must operate in:

The Netherlands

Aruba

Bonaire

Curaçao

Saba

Sint Eustatius

Sint Maarten

These islands are collectively referred to by Mama Cash as the ABCSSS islands.

The Spark Fund should therefore not be presented as a global feminist grant.

Groups based elsewhere cannot simply apply for projects in unrelated countries.

The geographic focus is specifically the Netherlands and the six named Caribbean islands.

Can Groups From the Caribbean Apply?

Yes, but only groups working in the specified territories:

Aruba

Bonaire

Curaçao

Saba

Sint Eustatius

Sint Maarten

The Fund does not automatically cover the entire Caribbean.

For example, a group based in Jamaica, Barbados or Trinidad and Tobago would not be eligible simply because it is located in the Caribbean unless it has an eligible structure or programme meeting the specific geographic criteria published by Mama Cash.

Types of Projects That May Fit the Spark Fund

Based on Mama Cash’s criteria, potentially relevant projects might include initiatives addressing:

Migrant Women’s Rights

Projects challenging structural barriers affecting migrant women’s access to housing, healthcare or legal rights.

Disability Justice

Self-led initiatives by women, girls, trans or intersex people with disabilities challenging discrimination or exclusion.

LGBTQI+ Rights

Grassroots organising around the rights and safety of queer, trans or intersex communities.

Anti-Racism and Gender Justice

Initiatives examining how racism and gender inequality intersect.

Sex Workers’ Rights

Self-led organising addressing rights, safety, legal barriers or stigma affecting sex workers.

Religious Freedom and Gender

Projects led by women affected by discrimination linked to religion, clothing or cultural identity.

Housing Rights

Feminist initiatives challenging structural housing barriers experienced by marginalised communities.

Reproductive Justice

Grassroots work defending bodily autonomy, reproductive rights or access to services.

These examples should not be interpreted as guaranteed funding areas. Projects must still meet all Spark Fund criteria.

How to Apply

The 2026 Spark Fund application window is:

20 August to 20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

Mama Cash provides three application formats.

Option 1: Written Application

Applicants can complete the official written form online.

Written Application Form

Option 2: Video Application

Applicants who prefer to speak rather than write can submit through the video recording application.

Video Application Form

Option 3: Audio Application

Applicants can also submit an audio-recorded application.

Audio Application Form

Providing multiple formats reflects Mama Cash’s effort to make the funding process accessible to grassroots activists who may not be comfortable with traditional written grant applications.

What Languages Can Be Used?

Applications can be submitted in:

English

Dutch

Groups that would prefer another language can contact:

spark@mamacash.org

Mama Cash states that it will explore possible support or accommodations where another language would be more suitable.

How Applications Are Reviewed

Mama Cash uses a participatory grantmaking approach.

The process begins with staff reviewing applications against the Spark Fund’s:

Eligibility criteria

Priority areas

Eligible applications then move into a participatory review process involving feminist activists connected to the Mama Cash network and former Spark grantee-partners.

This means decisions are not made solely by professional grant managers detached from activist movements.

People with direct movement experience are involved in deciding which initiatives receive funding.

Who Makes the Final Decision?

According to Mama Cash’s 2026 information, final decisions are made through its participatory grantmaking structure, involving members of the Mama Cash Advisory Network and, in the detailed FAQ, a steering committee of former Spark grantee-partners drawn from feminist activist communities in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands.

This is consistent with Mama Cash’s broader commitment to:

Sharing power and putting decisions in the hands of activists.

When Will Applicants Hear Back?

Mama Cash states in its FAQ that grant decisions are usually announced in:

October.

Applicants should therefore monitor the contact details they provide after submission.

How to Prepare a Strong Spark Fund Application

1. Show That the Group Is Truly Self-Led

Explain clearly:

Who founded the group

Who leads it

Who makes decisions

Who controls the project budget

Who represents the group publicly

Do not merely state that the project “supports women.”

Show that the women, girls, trans or intersex people affected by the issue hold real power.

2. Explain the Structural Problem

A strong application should identify more than an immediate need.

Instead of saying:

“Women in our community struggle to find housing,”

explain:

What barriers cause the problem

How discrimination operates

Which systems reproduce inequality

What the group wants to change

3. Show Why the Issue Is Urgent or Contested

Explain why the issue requires action now.

For example:

Has policy changed?

Is public hostility increasing?

Is a community losing rights?

Is an overlooked group experiencing exclusion?

Is there a new opportunity for movement-building?

Urgency should be concrete.

4. Centre the Community’s Own Priorities

Do not design a project externally and then add marginalised communities afterward.

The people affected should be able to explain:

What they need

What they want changed

How they will organise

What success would look like

5. Explain the Feminist Dimension

Make clear how the project challenges:

Sexism

Patriarchal structures

Gender inequality

Intersectional discrimination

The feminist perspective should be integrated into the project rather than appearing only in one paragraph of the application.

6. Do Not Worry About Being a Small Group

The Fund deliberately prioritises grassroots groups.

If your initiative is:

Volunteer-led

Unregistered

New

Small

Without paid staff

do not hide this.

Explain how flexible funding could help the group strengthen its work.

7. Choose the Application Format That Works Best

A sophisticated written grant proposal is not automatically better than a clear video or audio submission.

Use the format that enables the group to communicate:

Its story

Its purpose

Its leadership

The problem

The proposed change

most effectively.

Key Information at a Glance

Fund: Mama Cash Spark Fund

Grant size: €5,000–€12,000

Funding period: Up to two years

Applications open: 20 August 2026

Deadline: 20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST

Eligible locations: Netherlands, Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao, Saba, Sint Eustatius and Sint Maarten

Target groups: Self-led groups of women, girls, trans people and/or intersex people

Formal registration required: No

Organisational bank account required to apply: No

Residence permit required: No

Official ID required to apply: No

Application formats: Written, video or audio

Application languages: English or Dutch; contact Mama Cash about other language needs

Priority applicants: Informal, newly established, volunteer-led and resource-limited groups

Selection model: Participatory grantmaking

Contact: spark@mamacash.org

Why the Spark Fund Is Different From Many Conventional Grants

Many funding programmes expect applicants to have:

Legal registration

Professional grant-writing capacity

A dedicated bank account

Formal governance structures

Paid staff

Large annual budgets

The Spark Fund deliberately reduces several of these barriers.

That makes it particularly valuable for activist groups whose political relevance may be high even though their institutional infrastructure is small.

Mama Cash’s model recognises that movements often begin as:

Informal collectives

Volunteer networks

Community initiatives

Newly organised campaigns

rather than formal NGOs.

The Fund is therefore designed to support activism at a stage when conventional donors may overlook it.

Conclusion

The Mama Cash Spark Fund 2026 offers grassroots feminist groups in the Netherlands and the ABCSSS islands an opportunity to receive between €5,000 and €12,000 for projects lasting up to two years.

The programme is particularly intended for self-led groups of women, girls, trans and intersex people working on urgent and contested political issues while pursuing structural and systemic change.

Mama Cash gives particular priority to organisations and collectives that have limited access to flexible funding, including informal or unregistered groups, newly established initiatives, volunteer-led groups and organisations with limited resources.

The Fund is especially accessible because applicants do not need to have an organisational bank account, official identification, a residence permit or formal registration as a foundation in order to apply.

Applications can be submitted in writing, by video or by audio, and can be completed in English or Dutch. Applicants needing another language can contact Mama Cash for possible accommodations.

Applications opened on 20 August 2026 and close on:

20 September 2026 at 11:59 PM CEST.

For grassroots groups led directly by communities affected by gender-based and intersectional inequality, the Spark Fund provides an unusually flexible pathway to fund bold feminist activism without requiring the conventional institutional structures expected by many grantmakers.

To know more about this opportunity, visit the official Mama Cash Spark Fund page.

TITLE: Pre-Announcement – The Third Call for Microproject Proposals for the Second Phase of the PRICNAC Project

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
THE PRICNAC PROJECT

PRICNAC is one of the twelve projects funded under the ACP Innovation Fund of the OEACP Research and Innovation Programme with the financial support of the European Union. PRICNAC aims to contribute to an inclusive R&I environment in Central African countries for sustainable development and poverty reduction. It specifically aims to :

Improve access to sustainable solutions generated by R&I and adapted to local realities.

Expand the activities of the PRICNAC network.

This project is executed by a consortium of five institutions: the AUF (Agence Universitaire de la Francophonie) via its Regional Directorate for Central Africa and the Great Lakes based in Yaoundé (coordinator), OBREAL Global Observatory (Observatorio de Relaciones Unión Europea – América Latina), the AAU (Association of African Universities), CAMES ( African and Malagasy Council for Higher Education), and REIFAC (Network of Experts in Training Engineering for Central Africa and the Great Lakes).

PRICNAC is being implemented in eight countries: Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and Sao Tome and Principe, for an implementation period of 4 years (January 2021-December 2024).

PRICNAC’S MICRO-PROJECTS

For its second phase, PRICNAC is about to launch a call for proposals with a view to selecting a maximum of 10 micro-projects for a minimum of 150,000 euros (98,393,550 FCFA) and a maximum of 180,000 euros (118,072,260 FCFA) in funding.

The 10 selected micro-projects will have the following specific objectives:

Strengthen human capital in Central Africa through a regional platform for training, collaboration, and networking;

Better connect the diverse stakeholders that are part of the innovation ecosystem and research in the region to generate sustainable cooperation;

Contribute to regional integration by supporting Central African countries with greater needs and more constraining structural circumstances for research and innovation;

Strengthen existing AUF, AAU, CAMES, and REIFAC programs in Central Africa that aim to improve entrepreneurship capacity and build new bottom-up initiatives, with a view to promoting the role of educational institutions in innovation ecosystems;

Create synergies with/between programs and existing projects, also with the EU (in particular in the framework of the Africa-EU partnership) and other international institutions (World Bank, UN Economic Commission for Africa, UNCTAD …).

It should be stressed that these micro-projects should be inspired by the logic of the Smart Specialization Strategies (3S).[1]

TARGET GROUPS

Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)

Secondary education institutions

Research centers/research networks

Multinational private companies

SMEs (Small and medium-sized enterprises)

National public administrations

Local public administrations

Chambers of Commerce

NGOs and associationsDISTRIBUTION OF ACTIONS BY PRIORITY AREA

The implementation of the second phase of PRICNAC is based on 3 priority areas. Each priority area includes actions whose implementation will contribute to the achievement of PRICNAC’s objectives.

To be accepted, all project proposals must correspond to an action and highlight the gender approach, environmental preservation, and sustainable development. The projects selected under this Call for Proposals will have a duration of 14 months.

Download the full announcement here: https://blog.aau.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Pre-Announcement-PRICNAC.pdf

CONTACT

For information on this call for proposals, please contact:

Agence universitaire de la Francophonie

Central Africa and Great Lakes Regional Directorate (DRACGL)

Yaoundé, Cameroon

Email: pricnac@auf.org

TITLE: InvigoratEU Contest 2026: What Future for the European Continent?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 24, 2026

Applications are open for the InvigoratEU Contest 2026. “What future for the European continent?” is a public contest exploring what a wider European Union could mean for Europe’s security, competitiveness, and citizens. They welcome submissions in three categories: written essays, poetry, and audiovisual works, responding to the theme of Europe’s future and EU enlargement.

TEPSA’s contest “What future for the European continent?” is an invitation to change that. Whatever your background, wherever you are from, if you have a vision for what Europe could become, they want to hear it. Share your ideas and visions through three creative categories: poetry, written essays, and audiovisual works, and contribute to a broader public conversation on the opportunities that a wider EU can bring.

Benefits

Three winners of the contest will be invited to the InvigoratEU final conference on 4-5 November 2026, taking place in Brussels, with travel and accommodation covered up to €500.

Your work will be featured at the InvigoratEU consortium meeting and promoted by TEPSA online, seen by leading researchers, policymakers, and practitioners within the field of EU enlargement.

Eligibility

The contest is open for students, young professionals, and anyone interested in the future of Europe and EU enlargement;

Aged 18 and above;

All nationalities and residencies are welcome to participate.

Requirements

Written Essays: Original written essays (maximum 2000 words) should respond to one of the three guiding questions below:

How can a wider European Union contribute to Europe’s security and resilience?

How can enlargement help build a more competitive and self-sufficient European continent?

How can enlargement create tangible benefits for everyday citizens in both current and future Member States?

Poetry

Original poems should explore, in your own voice, what a wider European Union could mean for Europe’s security, competitiveness, or its citizens. Poems should not exceed 500 words, reflecting the author’s own ideas and creativity.

Audiovisual works

Original audiovisual pieces should be up to 2 minutes in length. They welcome all formats (e.g. interviews, vlogs, animation, or other creative video formats), and submissions can be recorded with any equipment you have.

Your submission should engage with the theme of Europe’s future and/or EU enlargement. You may appear in the video yourself, feature other participants, or rely entirely on visuals, narration, or animation.

Application

Send your submission to communications@tepsa.eu with the subject line “InvigoratEU public contest_LAST NAME” by 24 July 2026.

For more information, visit InvigoratEU Contest.

TITLE: ACT-PREP PhD and Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026: Apply for 25 Funded Research Opportunities in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Apply for 15 ACT-PREP PhD and 10 postdoctoral research fellowships in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness. Review funding, eligibility, research themes, documents, partner universities and September 2026 deadlines.

Applications are open for 25 ACT-PREP research fellowships designed to strengthen Africa’s capacity in clinical trials, infectious-disease surveillance, epidemic preparedness and emergency response.

The current call offers:

15 PhD research fellowships.

10 postdoctoral research fellowships.

The opportunities are available to eligible nationals of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda. Applicants must propose research connected to clinical trials or epidemic preparedness and response while meeting the academic and institutional requirements of their selected fellowship category.

The programme provides tuition support, monthly stipends, research funding, mentorship, specialized training, access to research sites and datasets, and professional networking opportunities. The precise package depends on whether the candidate applies under PhD Round 1, PhD Round 2 or the postdoctoral category.

The official announcement from Makerere University was published on August 14, 2026.

ACT-PREP Research Fellowships at a Glance

Programme detail
Information

Programme
ACT-PREP

Available opportunities
15 PhD and 10 postdoctoral positions

Main fields
Clinical trials and epidemic preparedness and response research

Funding programme
HORIZON-JU-GH-EDCTP3

PhD funding period
Up to three years

Postdoctoral funding period
Up to 12 months

PhD Round 1 deadline
September 15, 2026

PhD Round 2 deadline
September 30, 2026

Postdoctoral deadline
September 30, 2026

Eligible nationalities
DRC, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda

Application languages
English or French

Application method
Submission by email

Number of priority themes
Seven

Female applicants
Strongly encouraged

Application fee
No application fee is stated

What Is ACT-PREP?

ACT-PREP is a multi-country research and capacity-strengthening initiative focused on improving Africa’s preparedness for infectious-disease outbreaks and other public-health emergencies.

The project seeks to strengthen the continent’s ability to conduct timely, ethical and scientifically rigorous clinical research before and during disease outbreaks. It focuses on institutionalizing clinical-trial preparedness within national public-health systems instead of treating research as a separate activity that begins only after an emergency occurs.

According to the official Global Health EDCTP3 project profile, ACT-PREP runs from June 1, 2026, to May 31, 2031. The wider project has been awarded approximately €12.75 million in Global Health EDCTP3 funding.

This amount represents funding for the overall multi-year ACT-PREP project. It is not the individual amount payable to each fellow.

The initiative aims to build clinical research and outbreak-response capacity through:

PhD and postdoctoral research support.

Short- and long-term professional training.

Mentorship programmes.

Research exchanges.

Access to real-world datasets.

Practical training at clinical-trial and surveillance sites.

Training for clinical-trial monitors.

Strengthening of ethics and regulatory-review systems.

Improved surveillance and health-information systems.

Laboratory and data-management upgrades.

Standardized outbreak-research protocols.

Community engagement.

Institutional and regional research partnerships.

The wider project intends to train more than 700 senior researchers in advanced methods, support 15 PhD students and 10 postdoctoral researchers, and train an additional 80 clinical-trial monitors.

Why the ACT-PREP Programme Is Needed

Africa continues to experience a substantial burden of infectious diseases and public-health emergencies.

The official call reports that the African region recorded 2,234 acute public-health events between 2001 and 2022. Approximately 92% were infectious-disease events, while zoonotic outbreaks increased substantially during the period.

Recent outbreaks have repeatedly revealed structural limitations, including:

Fragmented disease-surveillance systems.

Weak integration of human, animal and environmental health information.

Delayed laboratory confirmation.

Limited diagnostic infrastructure.

Slow deployment of outbreak research.

Inadequate readiness to launch clinical trials during emergencies.

Limited research coordination across countries.

Delays in ethics and regulatory review.

Insufficient pharmacovigilance capacity.

Weak integration of research into emergency-response systems.

ACT-PREP seeks to address these gaps by strengthening research, surveillance, ethics, diagnostics, pharmacovigilance, regulation and policy across Africa’s emergency preparedness and response ecosystem.

Diseases and Public-Health Areas Covered

ACT-PREP has a broad infectious-disease and health-security mandate. Its wider programme focuses particularly on:

HIV and AIDS.

Malaria.

Tuberculosis.

Neglected tropical diseases.

Emerging infectious diseases.

Re-emerging infectious diseases.

Epidemic-prone pathogens.

Zoonotic diseases.

Outbreak-related clinical research.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is relevant to the programme’s mandate and to an EDCTP-priority disease or health-security challenge.

Seven ACT-PREP Priority Research Themes

Applicants must align their proposed work with at least one of the following research themes:

1. Clinical Trials and Trial Readiness

This theme can include work on:

Clinical-trial design and implementation.

Trial-site preparedness.

Rapid activation of trials during outbreaks.

Clinical research quality systems.

Participant recruitment and retention.

Trial-monitoring approaches.

Community engagement in clinical research.

Standardized outbreak-trial protocols.

Trial data quality and management.

2. Disease Surveillance, Modelling and Artificial Intelligence

Relevant research may address:

Early-warning systems.

Disease forecasting.

Epidemiological modelling.

Digital surveillance.

Artificial intelligence for outbreak detection.

Integration of surveillance information.

Analysis of routine health data.

Predictive analytics.

Data visualization for emergency response.

Integration with health-information systems such as DHIS2.

3. Ethics and Regulatory Science

This area may include:

Ethics-review procedures during outbreaks.

Regulatory preparedness.

Rapid but responsible research review.

Protection of research participants.

Digital systems for ethics and regulatory authorities.

Regulatory coordination across countries.

Pharmacovigilance regulation.

Ethical governance of emergency research.

Research integrity.

4. Laboratory and Genomic Surveillance

Possible topics include:

Genomic sequencing.

Pathogen detection.

Diagnostic technologies.

Laboratory quality systems.

Molecular epidemiology.

Laboratory-network strengthening.

Data management for genomic surveillance.

Rapid diagnostic confirmation.

Laboratory preparedness for epidemics.

5. One Health

This theme recognizes the connection between human, animal and environmental health. Research can explore:

Zoonotic-disease surveillance.

Human-animal transmission pathways.

Environmental drivers of outbreaks.

Integrated surveillance systems.

Collaboration between medical, veterinary and environmental institutions.

Community-level disease prevention.

Cross-sector emergency preparedness.

6. Health-Systems Resilience

Relevant work may examine:

Health-system continuity during emergencies.

Preparedness of healthcare facilities.

Workforce readiness.

Supply chains during outbreaks.

Integration of research into routine public-health systems.

Emergency governance.

Community trust and engagement.

Equitable access to emergency interventions.

7. Epidemic Preparedness and Response

This broad area can cover:

National and regional preparedness.

Emergency-response systems.

Outbreak investigation.

Rapid research deployment.

Policy responses.

Public-health communication.

Emergency coordination.

Evaluation of preparedness plans.

Lessons from previous epidemics.

PhD Fellowships: Two Application Routes

ACT-PREP has created two separate PhD application rounds. Applicants must select the correct route based on whether they are already enrolled in a doctoral programme.

PhD Round 1: Currently Enrolled Doctoral Researchers

PhD Round 1 is intended for applicants who are already enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.

Applicants must already be conducting or developing doctoral research under one of the seven ACT-PREP priority themes.

PhD Round 1 Eligibility

Applicants should:

Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country.

Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent qualification.

Have an academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related discipline.

Be currently enrolled in a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.

Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme.

Obtain formal endorsement from their home institution.

Provide two suitable referees.

Submit every required document before the closing date.

Commit to research quality, integrity and timely completion.

PhD Round 1 Duration

Fellows are expected to complete their doctoral programme within three years.

A justified no-cost extension may be considered under applicable university policies and approval procedures. Such an extension would not automatically provide additional fellowship funding.

PhD Round 1 Financial and Academic Support

The package may include:

Partial or full tuition and university fees.

A monthly stipend.

A one-time research or clinical-trial grant.

Mentorship from ACT-PREP specialists.

Core training courses.

Specialized courses connected to the research theme.

Access to consortium trial sites.

Access to relevant datasets.

Participation in research and mentorship networks.

Access to alumni opportunities.

The call does not state the monetary value of the monthly stipend or one-time research grant.

PhD Round 1 Deadline

September 15, 2026

PhD Round 2: Applicants Seeking Doctoral Enrolment

PhD Round 2 is intended for candidates who are not necessarily enrolled in a doctoral programme but are eligible and willing to register at an ACT-PREP partner university.

These applicants must commit to completing their doctoral training within three years.

PhD Round 2 Eligibility

Applicants should:

Be nationals of an ACT-PREP partner country.

Hold a relevant master’s degree or equivalent.

Have a suitable academic background in health, biomedical sciences, public health or a related field.

Be eligible to register for a relevant doctoral programme at an ACT-PREP partner university.

Propose work under one of the seven priority themes.

Secure institutional endorsement.

Identify an appropriate host institution and mentor.

Provide two referees.

Commit to completing doctoral training within three years.

Applicants affiliated with an ACT-PREP institution, including eligible junior researchers, will receive priority consideration.

PhD Round 2 Support

The fellowship may provide:

Tuition and university fees.

A monthly stipend.

A one-time research or clinical-trial grant.

Mentorship from ACT-PREP experts.

Core and specialized training courses.

Access to research sites and datasets.

Professional networking.

Alumni and mentorship opportunities.

The fellowship can be supported for up to three years, subject to programme and institutional requirements.

PhD Round 2 Deadline

September 30, 2026

Postdoctoral Research Fellowships

The ten postdoctoral positions are designed to help early-career African researchers develop independent research leadership in clinical trials and epidemic preparedness.

Selected researchers will join ongoing ACT-PREP research activities while developing and leading their own research outputs.

Their work must either:

Integrate appropriate clinical-trial methodologies; or

Address a substantive epidemic preparedness and response topic.

Postdoctoral researchers will be expected to uphold high standards of research quality, ethics and integrity.

Postdoctoral Eligibility

Applicants must:

Be nationals of an eligible ACT-PREP country.

Hold a PhD in a relevant health, biomedical or related field.

Have obtained the PhD within the past five years.

Demonstrate a research record appropriate to their postdoctoral career stage.

Propose research aligned with an ACT-PREP priority theme.

Confirm an appropriate host institution.

Obtain endorsement from the home or host institution.

Identify a suitable mentor.

Provide two referees.

Demonstrate potential for research leadership and scientific independence.

Submit a complete application before the deadline.

Postdoctoral Support

Selected postdoctoral researchers may receive:

A mentored position at a consortium partner institution.

A monthly stipend.

Research support.

Mobility support.

Funding for up to 12 months.

Training in scientific writing.

Training in research leadership.

Training in grant administration.

Specialized methodological training.

Exposure to modelling, bioinformatics and real-world evidence methods.

Support to publish research.

Support to present findings at conferences.

Guidance on securing follow-on research funding.

Mentorship from local and international experts.

The call does not specify the stipend, research-support or mobility-support amounts.

Postdoctoral Deadline

September 30, 2026

Eligible ACT-PREP Countries

Applicants must be nationals of one of the following seven countries:

Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Rwanda.

Senegal.

Somalia.

South Sudan.

Citizenship or nationality is required. Residence in one of these countries without holding an eligible nationality may not satisfy the requirement.

ACT-PREP Partner Universities

The PhD opportunities are connected to the following universities:

Makerere University, Uganda.

Somali National University, Somalia.

Université de Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences, Tanzania.

University of Global Health Equity, Rwanda.
