Units: 3-0-9

The first of a two-term subject sequence that provides the foundations for contemporary research in selected areas of atomic and optical physics. The interaction of radiation with atoms: resonance; absorption, stimulated and spontaneous emission; methods of resonance, dressed atom formalism, masers and lasers, cavity quantum electrodynamics; structure of simple atoms, behavior in very strong fields; fundamental tests: time reversal, parity violations, Bell’s inequalities; and experimental methods.

8.422 Atomic and Optical Physics II

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.05
Units: 3-0-9

The second of a two-term subject sequence that provides the foundations for contemporary research in selected areas of atomic and optical physics. Non-classical states of light- squeezed states; multi-photon processes, Raman scattering; coherence- level crossings, quantum beats, double resonance, superradiance; trapping and cooling- light forces, laser cooling, atom optics, spectroscopy of trapped atoms and ions; atomic interactions- classical collisions, quantum scattering theory, ultracold collisions; and experimental methods.

8.431[J] Nonlinear Optics

G – Spring
(Same subject as 6.6340[J])
Prereq: 6.2300 or 8.03
Units: 3-0-9

See description under subject 6.6340[J].

8.481, 8.482 Selected Topics in Physics of Atoms and Radiation

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.321
Units: 3-0-9

Presentation of topics of current interest, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

8.511 Theory of Solids I

G – Fall
Prereq: 8.231
Units: 3-0-9

First term of a theoretical treatment of the physics of solids. Concept of elementary excitations. Symmetry- translational, rotational, and time-reversal invariances- theory of representations. Energy bands- electrons and phonons. Topological band theory. Survey of electronic structure of metals, semimetals, semiconductors, and insulators, excitons, critical points, response functions, and interactions in the electron gas. Theory of superconductivity.

8.512 Theory of Solids II

G – Spring
Prereq: 8.511
Units: 3-0-9

Second term of a theoretical treatment of the physics of solids. Interacting electron gas: many-body formulation, Feynman diagrams, random phase approximation and beyond. General theory of linear response: dielectric function; sum rules; plasmons; optical properties; applications to semiconductors, metals, and insulators. Transport properties: non-interacting electron gas with impurities, diffusons. Quantum Hall effect: integral and fractional. Electron-phonon interaction: general theory, applications to metals, semiconductors and insulators, polarons, and field-theory description. Superconductivity: experimental observations, phenomenological theories, and BCS theory.

8.513 Many-Body Theory for Condensed Matter Systems

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.033, 8.05, 8.08, and 8.231
Units: 3-0-9

Concepts and physical pictures behind various phenomena that appear in interacting many-body systems. Visualization occurs through concentration on path integral, mean-field theories and semiclassical picture of fluctuations around mean-field state. Topics covered: interacting boson/fermion systems, Fermi liquid theory and bosonization, symmetry breaking and nonlinear sigma-model, quantum gauge theory, quantum Hall theory, mean-field theory of spin liquids and quantum order, string-net condensation and emergence of light and fermions.

8.514 Strongly Correlated Systems in Condensed Matter Physics

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.322 and 8.333
Units: 3-0-9

Study of condensed matter systems where interactions between electrons play an important role. Topics vary depending on lecturer but may include low-dimension magnetic and electronic systems, disorder and quantum transport, magnetic impurities (the Kondo problem), quantum spin systems, the Hubbard model and high-temperature superconductors. Topics are chosen to illustrate the application of diagrammatic techniques, field-theory approaches, and renormalization group methods in condensed matter physics.

8.581, 8.582 Selected Topics in Condensed Matter Physics

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Presentation of topics of current interest, with contents varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

8.590[J] Topics in Biophysics and Physical Biology (New)

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
(Same subject as 7.74[J], 20.416[J])
Prereq: None
Units: 2-0-4 [P/D/F]

Provides broad exposure to research in biophysics and physical biology, with emphasis on the critical evaluation of scientific literature. Weekly meetings include in-depth discussion of scientific literature led by distinct faculty on active research topics. Each session also includes brief discussion of non-research topics including effective presentation skills, writing papers and fellowship proposals, choosing scientific and technical research topics, time management, and scientific ethics.

8.591[J] Systems Biology

G – Fall
(Same subject as 7.81[J])
(Subject meets with 7.32)
Prereq: (18.03 and 18.05) or permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Introduction to cellular and population-level systems biology with an emphasis on synthetic biology, modeling of genetic networks, cell-cell interactions, and evolutionary dynamics. Cellular systems include genetic switches and oscillators, network motifs, genetic network evolution, and cellular decision-making. Population-level systems include models of pattern formation, cell-cell communication, and evolutionary systems biology. Students taking graduate version explore the subject in more depth.

8.592[J] Statistical Physics in Biology

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
(Same subject as HST.452[J])
Prereq: 8.333 or permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

A survey of problems at the interface of statistical physics and modern biology: bioinformatic methods for extracting information content of DNA; gene finding, sequence comparison, phylogenetic trees. Physical interactions responsible for structure of biopolymers; DNA double helix, secondary structure of RNA, elements of protein folding. Considerations of force, motion, and packaging; protein motors, membranes. Collective behavior of biological elements; cellular networks, neural networks, and evolution.

8.593[J] Biological Physics

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
(Same subject as HST.450[J])
Prereq: 8.044 recommended but not necessary
Units: 4-0-8

Designed to provide seniors and first-year graduate students with a quantitative, analytical understanding of selected biological phenomena. Topics include experimental and theoretical basis for the phase boundaries and equation of state of concentrated protein solutions, with application to diseases such as sickle cell anemia and cataract. Protein-ligand binding and linkage and the theory of allosteric regulation of protein function, with application to proteins as stores as transporters in respiration, enzymes in metabolic pathways, membrane receptors, regulators of gene expression, and self-assembling scaffolds. The physics of locomotion and chemoreception in bacteria and the biophysics of vision, including the theory of transparency of the eye, molecular basis of photo reception, and the detection of light as a signal-to-noise discrimination.

8.613[J] Introduction to Plasma Physics I

G – Fall
(Same subject as 22.611[J])
Prereq: (6.013 or 8.07) and (18.04 or Coreq: 18.075)
Units: 3-0-9

See description under subject 22.611[J].

8.614[J] Introduction to Plasma Physics II

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
(Same subject as 22.612[J])
Prereq: 22.611
Units: 3-0-9

See description under subject 22.612[J].

8.624 Plasma Waves

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 22.611
Units: 3-0-9

Comprehensive theory of electromagnetic waves in a magnetized plasma. Wave propagation in cold and hot plasmas. Energy flow. Absorption by Landau and cyclotron damping and by transit time magnetic pumping (TTMP). Wave propagation in inhomogeneous plasma: accessibility, WKB theory, mode conversion, connection formulae, and Budden tunneling. Applications to RF plasma heating, wave propagation in the ionosphere and laser-plasma interactions. Wave propagation in toroidal plasmas, and applications to ion cyclotron (ICRF), electron cyclotron (ECRH), and lower hybrid (LHH) wave heating. Quasi-linear theory and applications to RF current drive in tokamaks. Extensive discussion of relevant experimental observations.

8.641 Physics of High-Energy Plasmas I

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 22.611
Units: 3-0-9

Physics of High-Energy Plasmas I and II address basic concepts of plasmas, with temperatures of thermonuclear interest, relevant to fusion research and astrophysics. Microscopic transport processes due to interparticle collisions and collective modes (e.g., microinstabilities). Relevant macroscopic transport coefficients (electrical resistivity, thermal conductivities, particle “diffusion”). Runaway and slide-away regimes. Magnetic reconnection processes and their relevance to experimental observations. Radiation emission from inhomogeneous plasmas. Conditions for thermonuclear burning and ignition (D-T and “advanced” fusion reactions, plasmas with polarized nuclei). Role of “impurity” nuclei. “Finite-β” (pressure) regimes and ballooning modes. Convective modes in configuration and velocity space. Trapped particle regimes. Nonlinear and explosive instabilities. Interaction of positive and negative energy modes. Each subject can be taken independently.

8.642 Physics of High-Energy Plasmas II

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 22.611
Units: 3-0-9

Physics of High-Energy Plasmas I and II address basic concepts of plasmas, with temperatures of thermonuclear interest, relevant to fusion research and astrophysics. Microscopic transport processes due to interparticle collisions and collective modes (e.g., microinstabilities). Relevant macroscopic transport coefficients (electrical resistivity, thermal conductivities, particle “diffusion”). Runaway and slide-away regimes. Magnetic reconnection processes and their relevance to experimental observations. Radiation emission from inhomogeneous plasmas. Conditions for thermonuclear burning and ignition (D-T and “advanced” fusion reactions, plasmas with polarized nuclei). Role of “impurity” nuclei. “Finite-β” (pressure) regimes and ballooning modes. Convective modes in configuration and velocity space. Trapped particle regimes. Nonlinear and explosive instabilities. Interaction of positive and negative energy modes. Each subject can be taken independently.

8.670[J] Principles of Plasma Diagnostics

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
(Same subject as 22.67[J])
Prereq: 22.611
Units: 4-4-4

See description under subject 22.67[J].

8.681, 8.682 Selected Topics in Fluid and Plasma Physics

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: 22.611[J]
Units: 3-0-9

Presentation of topics of current interest, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when interest is indicated.

Nuclear and Particle Physics

8.701 Introduction to Nuclear and Particle Physics

G – Fall
Prereq: None. Coreq: 8.321
Units: 3-0-9

The phenomenology and experimental foundations of particle and nuclear physics; the fundamental forces and particles, composites. Interactions of particles with matter, and detectors. SU(2), SU(3), models of mesons and baryons. QED, weak interactions, parity violation, lepton-nucleon scattering, and structure functions. QCD, gluon field and color. W and Z fields, electro-weak unification, the CKM matrix. Nucleon-nucleon interactions, properties of nuclei, single- and collective- particle models. Electron and hadron interactions with nuclei. Relativistic heavy ion collisions, and transition to quark-gluon plasma.

8.711 Nuclear Physics

G – Spring
Prereq: 8.321 and 8.701
Units: 4-0-8

Modern, advanced study in the experimental foundations and theoretical understanding of the structure of nuclei, beginning with the two- and three-nucleon problems. Basic nuclear properties, collective and single-particle motion, giant resonances, mean field models, interacting boson model. Nuclei far from stability, nuclear astrophysics, big-bang and stellar nucleosynthesis. Electron scattering: nucleon momentum distributions, scaling, olarization observables. Parity-violating electron scattering. Neutrino physics. Current results in relativistic heavy ion physics and hadronic physics. Frontiers and future facilities.

8.712 Advanced Topics in Nuclear Physics

G – Fall, Spring – Can be repeated for credit (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.711 or permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Subject for experimentalists and theorists with rotation of the following topics: (1) Nuclear chromodynamics– introduction to QCD, structure of nucleons, lattice QCD, phases of hadronic matter; and relativistic heavy ion collisions. (2) Medium-energy physics– nuclear and nucleon structure and dynamics studied with medium- and high-energy probes (neutrinos, photons, electrons, nucleons, pions, and kaons). Studies of weak and strong interactions.

8.751[J] Quantum Technology and Devices

G – Spring
(Same subject as 22.51[J])
(Subject meets with 22.022)
Prereq: 22.11
Units: 3-0-9

See description under subject 22.51[J].

8.781, 8.782 Selected Topics in Nuclear Theory

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.323
Units: 3-0-9

Presents topics of current interest in nuclear structure and reaction theory, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

8.811 Particle Physics

G – Fall
Prereq: 8.701
Units: 3-0-9

Modern review of particles, interactions, and recent experiments. Experimental and analytical methods. QED, electroweak theory, and the Standard Model as tested in recent key experiments at ee and pp colliders. Mass generation, W, Z, and Higgs physics. Weak decays of mesons, including heavy flavors with QCD corrections. Mixing phenomena for K, D, B mesons and neutrinos. CP violation with results from B-factories. Future physics expectations: Higgs, SUSY, sub-structure as addressed by new experiments at the LHC collider.

8.812 Graduate Experimental Physics

G – IAP (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.701
Units: 1-8-3

Provides practical experience in particle detection with verification by (Feynman) calculations. Students perform three experiments; at least one requires actual construction following design. Topics include Compton effect, Fermi constant in muon decay, particle identification by time-of-flight, Cerenkov light, calorimeter response, tunnel effect in radioactive decays, angular distribution of cosmic rays, scattering, gamma-gamma nuclear correlations, and modern particle localization.

8.821 String Theory

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.324
Units: 3-0-9
Credit cannot also be received for 8.251

An introduction to string theory. Basics of conformal field theory; light-cone and covariant quantization of the relativistic bosonic string; quantization and spectrum of supersymmetric 10-dimensional string theories; T-duality and D-branes; toroidal compactification and orbifolds; 11-dimensional supergravity and M-theory. Meets with 8.251 when offered concurrently.

8.831 Supersymmetric Quantum Field Theories

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Topics selected from the following: SUSY algebras and their particle representations; Weyl and Majorana spinors; Lagrangians of basic four-dimensional SUSY theories, both rigid SUSY and supergravity; supermultiplets of fields and superspace methods; renormalization properties, and the non-renormalization theorem; spontaneous breakdown of SUSY; and phenomenological SUSY theories. Some prior knowledge of Noether’s theorem, derivation and use of Feynman rules, l-loop renormalization, and gauge theories is essential.

8.851 Effective Field Theory

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.324
Units: 3-0-9
Credit cannot also be received for 8.S851

Covers the framework and tools of effective field theory, including: identifying degrees of freedom and symmetries; power counting expansions (dimensional and otherwise); field redefinitions, bottom-up and top-down effective theories; fine-tuned effective theories; matching and Wilson coefficients; reparameterization invariance; and advanced renormalization group techniques. Main examples are taken from particle and nuclear physics, including the Soft-Collinear Effective Theory.

8.871 Selected Topics in Theoretical Particle Physics

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: 8.323
Units: 3-0-9

Presents topics of current interest in theoretical particle physics, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

8.872 Selected Topics in Theoretical Particle Physics

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: 8.323
Units: 3-0-9

Presents topics of current interest in theoretical particle physics, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

8.881, 8.882 Selected Topics in Experimental Particle Physics

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: 8.811
Units: 3-0-9

Presents topics of current interest in experimental particle physics, with content varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated.

Space Physics and Astrophysics

8.901 Astrophysics I

G – Spring
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Size and time scales. Historical astronomy. Astronomical instrumentation. Stars: spectra and classification. Stellar structure equations and survey of stellar evolution. Stellar oscillations. Degenerate and collapsed stars; radio pulsars. Interacting binary systems; accretion disks, x-ray sources. Gravitational lenses; dark matter. Interstellar medium: HII regions, supernova remnants, molecular clouds, dust; radiative transfer; Jeans’ mass; star formation. High-energy astrophysics: Compton scattering, bremsstrahlung, synchrotron radiation, cosmic rays. Galactic stellar distributions and populations; Oort constants; Oort limit; and globular clusters.

8.902 Astrophysics II

G – Fall
Prereq: 8.901
Units: 3-0-9

Galactic dynamics: potential theory, orbits, collisionless Boltzmann equation, etc. Galaxy interactions. Groups and clusters; dark matter. Intergalactic medium; x-ray clusters. Active galactic nuclei: unified models, black hole accretion, radio and optical jets, etc. Homogeneity and isotropy, redshift, galaxy distance ladder. Newtonian cosmology. Roberston-Walker models and cosmography. Early universe, primordial nucleosynthesis, recombination. Cosmic microwave background radiation. Large-scale structure, galaxy formation.

8.913 Plasma Astrophysics I

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

For students interested in space physics, astrophysics, and plasma physics in general. Magnetospheres of rotating magnetized planets, ordinary stars, neutron stars, and black holes. Pulsar models: processes for slowing down, particle acceleration, and radiation emission; accreting plasmas and x-ray stars; stellar winds; heliosphere and solar wind- relevant magnetic field configuration, measured particle distribution in velocity space and induced collective modes; stability of the current sheet and collisionless processes for magnetic reconnection; theory of collisionless shocks; solitons; Ferroaro-Rosenbluth sheet; solar flare models; heating processes of the solar corona; Earth’s magnetosphere (auroral phenomena and their interpretation, bowshock, magnetotail, trapped particle effects); relationship between gravitational (galactic) plasmas and electromagnetic plasmas. 8.913 deals with heliospheric, 8.914 with extra-heliospheric plasmas.

8.914 Plasma Astrophysics II

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

For students interested in space physics, astrophysics, and plasma physics in general. Magnetospheres of rotating magnetized planets, ordinary stars, neutron stars, and black holes. Pulsar models: processes for slowing down, particle acceleration, and radiation emission; accreting plasmas and x-ray stars; stellar winds; heliosphere and solar wind- relevant magnetic field configuration, measured particle distribution in velocity space and induced collective modes; stability of the current sheet and collisionless processes for magnetic reconnection; theory of collisionless shocks; solitons; Ferroaro-Rosenbluth sheet; solar flare models; heating processes of the solar corona; Earth’s magnetosphere (auroral phenomena and their interpretation, bowshock, magnetotail, trapped particle effects); relationship between gravitational (galactic) plasmas and electromagnetic plasmas. 8.913 deals with heliospheric, 8.914 with extra-heliospheric plasmas.

8.921 Stellar Structure and Evolution

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Observable stellar characteristics; overview of observational information. Principles underlying calculations of stellar structure. Physical processes in stellar interiors; properties of matter and radiation; radiative, conductive, and convective heat transport; nuclear energy generation; nucleosynthesis; and neutrino emission. Protostars; the main sequence, and the solar neutrino flux; advanced evolutionary stages; variable stars; planetary nebulae, supernovae, white dwarfs, and neutron stars; close binary systems; and abundance of chemical elements.

8.942 Cosmology

G – Fall (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9

Thermal backgrounds in space. Cosmological principle and its consequences: Newtonian cosmology and types of “universes”; survey of relativistic cosmology; horizons. Overview of evolution in cosmology; radiation and element synthesis; physical models of the “early stages.” Formation of large-scale structure to variability of physical laws. First and last states. Some knowledge of relativity expected. 8.962 recommended though not required.

8.952 Particle Physics of the Early Universe

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department)
Prereq: 8.323; Coreq: 8.324
Units: 3-0-9

Basics of general relativity, standard big bang cosmology, thermodynamics of the early universe, cosmic background radiation, primordial nucleosynthesis, basics of the standard model of particle physics, electroweak and QCD phase transition, basics of group theory, grand unified theories, baryon asymmetry, monopoles, cosmic strings, domain walls, axions, inflationary universe, and structure formation.

8.962 General Relativity

G – Spring
Prereq: 8.07, 18.03, and 18.06
Units: 4-0-8

The basic principles of Einstein’s general theory of relativity, differential geometry, experimental tests of general relativity, black holes, and cosmology.

8.971 Astrophysics Seminar

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 2-0-4 [P/D/F]

Advanced seminar on current topics, with a different focus each term. Typical topics: astronomical instrumentation, numerical and statistical methods in astrophysics, gravitational lenses, neutron stars and pulsars. Consult department head.

8.972 Astrophysics Seminar

G – Fall, Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 2-0-4 [P/D/F]

Advanced seminar on current topics, with a different focus each term. Typical topics: gravitational lenses, active galactic nuclei, neutron stars and pulsars, galaxy formation, supernovae and supernova remnants, brown dwarfs, and extrasolar planetary systems. The presenter at each session is selected by drawing names from a hat containing those of all attendees. Offered if sufficient interest is indicated. Consult department head.

8.981, 8.982 Selected Topics in Astrophysics

G – Spring (Not offered regularly; consult department) – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: Permission of instructor
Units: 3-0-9 [P/D/F]

Topics of current interest, varying from year to year. Subject not routinely offered; given when sufficient interest is indicated. Consult department head

8.995 Practical Experience in Physics

G – Fall, IAP, Spring, Summer – Can be repeated for credit
Prereq: None
Units arranged [P/D/F]

For Course 8 students participating in off-campus experiences in physics. Before registering for this subject, students must have an internship offer from a company or organization, must identify a Physics supervisor, and must receive prior approval from the Physics Department. Upon completion of the project, student must submit a letter from the company or organization describing the work accomplished, along with a substantive final report from the student approved by the MIT supervisor. Consult departmental academic office.

8.998 Teaching and Mentoring MIT Students

U – Fall, Spring
Prereq: None
Units: 2-0-1 [P/D/F]

Designed for first-time physics mentors and others interested in improving their knowledge and skills in teaching one-on-one and in small groups, particularly TEAL TAs and graduate student TAs. Topics include: cognition, metacognition, and the role of affect; communication skills (practice listening, questioning, and eliciting student ideas); the roles of motivation and mindset in learning; fostering belonging and self-efficacy through peer mentorship; facilitating small-group interactions to enhance peer instruction and learning; physics-specific learning strategies, such as how to teach/learn problem solving; research-based techniques for effective mentorship in STEM. Includes a one-hour class on pedagogy topics, a one-hour weekly Physics Mentoring Community of Practice meeting, and weekly assignments to read or watch material in preparation for class discussions, and written reflections before class. No required or recommended textbooks

Covers topics in Physics that are not offered in the regular curriculum.

Opportunity for group study of subjects in physics not otherwise included in the curriculum.

Program of research leading to the writing of an SM, PhD, or ScD thesis; to be arranged by the student and an appropriate MIT faculty member.

TITLE: Call for Expression of Interest to Organise Special Sessions, Association of African Universities’ 16th Quadrennial General Conference, 21st – 25th July 2025, Rabat, Morocco

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Organizing Committee of the 16th Quadrennial General Conference of the Association of African Universities (AAU) is pleased to invite institutions, groups, networks, projects, and various categories of organisations to express interest in organising special sessions at the General Conference of the AAU.

The General Conference, convened quadrennially, is the Association’s premier gathering, which brings together a diverse range of higher education stakeholders, including representatives of AAU member institutions, associate members, and observers. Other stakeholders participating in this conference include policy makers, development partners, students and industry representatives. As the Association’s supreme governing body, the General Conference is responsible for shaping the AAU’s strategic direction and policy framework. The conference, themed “Shaping the Future of Higher Education for Innovation and Sustainable Development in Africa,” will take place from July 21st to 25th, 2025, in Rabat, Morocco. The 16th Quadrennial General Conference will be hosted by the Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P), while the AAU Governing Board Meeting preceding the General Conference will be hosted by the Mohammed V University (UM5). This excellent opportunity to organize special sessions will enable institutions to bring together their stakeholders and experts to discuss specific topics, showcase innovative projects, and facilitate networking.

Special sessions can take various formats, including panel discussions, roundtables, meetings, workshops, presentations, and debates, either during the main conference at plenary or parallel sessions, or as side events organized as pre-conference or post-conference events.

Submission Guidelines

To propose a special session, please submit a brief statement of interest or an abstract of 300 -500 words outlining the following:

Session title and brief description

Session format and duration

Key points or topics to be addressed at the session

Relevance of session to Africa’s higher education community

Names and affiliations of session organizers and speakers

Expected outcomes and takeaways

Evaluation Criteria

Proposals will be evaluated based on:

– Relevance to the conference theme or the overall mission of the Association of African Universities

– Originality and innovation, as well as the ability of the session to provide an interactive forum for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to engage in critical dialogue, build networks, or share their innovations and research.

– Clarity and coherence of submission

– Potential for engaging discussions and networking opportunities

Important Dates

– Proposal submission deadline: April 30, 2025

-Notification of acceptance: May 9, 2025

Submissions

Specific details required and submissions should be made via this link – https://forms.office.com/r/zu79YvR1k2

For any inquiries, please contact the conference organisers at – gencon2025@aau.org

Join Us

We encourage you to leverage this opportunity and help shape key conversations through the organisation of special sessions. Submit your proposal by the deadline and be part of this dynamic conference. We look forward to welcoming you to the Association of African Universities’ prestigious 16th General Conference 2025.

Note: To support the conference, organizers of special sessions are required to select a sponsorship package. This contribution will help ensure the overall success of the event. Access the Conference Sponsorship Package here.

TITLE: UN FAO Young Professionals Programme (YPP) 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 7, 2026

Applications are open for the UN FAO Young Professionals Programme (YPP) 2026. The Young Professionals Programme (YPP) is a recruitment initiative targeted at talented, qualified young professionals who are mainly nationals of non or underrepresented members. Priority consideration will be given to candidates from Small Island Developing States (SIDS), Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs) and developing countries in general, to start a career as an international civil servant with FAO.

Under the supervision of a senior staff member, Young Professional Officers work with international and national staff and are involved in the identification, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of FAO activities. Purposes of assignments vary and may have a country-specific, regional, sector-based or thematic focus.

Young Professional Officers are offered two years fixed term contracts subject to a one-year probationary period. They will generally be employed at P-1 step 1 level on initial appointment and will move to P-1 step 2 level for the second year of their assignment.

Eligibility

Candidates for the YPP are selected on a highly competitive basis. The qualifications below are required for consideration:

Candidates should be 32 years of age or younger as of 31 December of the year of application;

Academic qualifications: Advanced university degree (Master’s, Ph.D. or equivalent) in a field relevant to the work of FAO;

A minimum of one year of professional experience in a field relevant to the work of FAO;

Working knowledge of English and limited knowledge of another FAO official language (French, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese or Russian);

Candidates must not bear any of the following relationships to staff members of the Organization: son, daughter, brother or sister.

Application

Visit the list of YPP opportunities currently available in the Organization (for vacancies, click the YPP (Young Professionals Programme) link from the banner at the left of the newly opened page).

Kindly note that the application and selection process will be conducted in English.

For more information, visit UN FAO Young Professionals Programme.

TITLE: KAUST International Internship 2026 in Saudi Arabia | Fully Funded

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Waiting for an international internship opportunity? Apply for the KAUST International Internship in Saudi Arabia 2026. This fully funded internship is offered at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology for at least three to a maximum of 6 months at KAUST. This KAUST research internship is offered to all international students. Internships in Saudi Arabia are highly competitive and welcome all eligible students regardless of race, color, background, and ethnicity. If you are looking for a fully funded internship in Saudi Arabia to enhance your skills and boost your confidence, apply for the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology internship program 2026 now!

TITLE: CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026: Two-Year Technology Policy Fellowship for Leading Academics and Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is now accepting applications from established academics and researchers interested in bringing their scholarly expertise into conversations about technology policy, digital rights, democracy, privacy, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, free expression, and the future of the internet.

Based in Washington, D.C., with remote participation allowed, the program creates a bridge between academic research and real-world public-interest technology policy. Rather than separating academic scholarship from policy development, CDT’s Non-Resident Fellows Program gives researchers an opportunity to engage directly with the organization’s research and policy teams, contribute expertise to emerging technology debates, and strengthen the public-policy impact of their own research.

Applications for the 2026 intake are open until September 18, 2026.

About the Center for Democracy & Technology

The Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) is an organization working at the intersection of technology, public policy, civil liberties, and individual rights.

CDT works to strengthen individual rights and freedoms by defining, promoting, and influencing technology policy and the architecture of the internet that increasingly shapes everyday life. Its areas of focus encompass some of the most significant technology-policy questions facing governments, researchers, companies, civil society organizations, and communities today.

These areas include:

Artificial Intelligence Policy and Governance

Cybersecurity and Standards

Elections and Democracy

Equity in Civic Technology

Free Expression

Government Surveillance

Open Internet

Privacy and Data

Through its research, advocacy, policy engagement, and collaboration with experts, CDT seeks to ensure that technological development and technology policy protect people’s rights and freedoms.

What Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program?

The CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is a two-year engagement designed to connect leading scholars and academics with CDT’s technology-policy work.

The program provides Fellows with opportunities to bring their research and specialist knowledge directly into CDT’s policy conversations. Fellows can exchange ideas with CDT staff, participate in discussions surrounding emerging issues, and help inform how the organization approaches the social, political, economic, legal, and technical implications of rapidly developing technologies.

CDT intentionally brings together Fellows from diverse academic disciplines, institutions, and areas of expertise.

This interdisciplinary approach reflects the reality that technology policy is no longer confined to computer science or law. Technology influences virtually every aspect of modern society, meaning that understanding its effects requires perspectives from numerous disciplines.

CDT therefore welcomes expertise spanning fields such as:

Sociology

Psychology

Computer science

Economics

Communications

Political science

Human-computer interaction

Media studies

Law

Other relevant interdisciplinary fields

Through this diverse community, Fellows can help CDT understand the complex relationship between technology and the institutions, communities, governments, economies, and individuals affected by it.

Bridging Academic Research and Technology Policy

One of the central purposes of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program is to help close the gap between academic research and public-interest technology policy.

Academic researchers can produce significant evidence, theories, frameworks, and findings concerning emerging technologies. However, translating that research into policy discussions and practical public-interest outcomes can require connections between scholars and organizations directly involved in policy development.

The Non-Resident Fellows Program creates opportunities for researchers and technology-policy practitioners to learn from each other.

For academics, this can provide greater exposure to policy discussions and the opportunity to understand how research can contribute to practical debates.

For CDT, Fellows provide access to expertise from leading researchers working across a broad range of disciplines.

The program also places Fellows within a wider community of researchers and technology-policy experts, providing opportunities to establish relationships, exchange ideas, and potentially collaborate on some of the most important questions at the intersection of technology and democracy.

Objectives of the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

The program is designed for researchers who want to engage directly with and contribute to CDT’s policy work.

CDT Fellows volunteer their time to pursue three broad objectives:

1. Inform and Advance CDT’s Research and Policy Work

Fellows contribute academic knowledge, research findings, disciplinary expertise, and perspectives that can strengthen CDT’s research and policy activities.

Their involvement can help the organization consider technology-policy questions through different academic lenses and incorporate relevant scholarly evidence into its work.

2. Amplify CDT’s Voice and Expand Its Expert Network

Fellows can help connect CDT with leading academics and specialists working on relevant issues.

These relationships can strengthen the exchange of information between academic communities and public-interest technology-policy practitioners.

3. Strengthen the Policy Impact of Fellows’ Research

The relationship is intended to benefit Fellows as well.

CDT aims to work with Fellows to strengthen the public engagement and policy impact of their academic research, potentially helping important scholarly work reach audiences involved in technology-policy conversations.

Who Is CDT Looking For?

CDT is seeking researchers from diverse experiences and backgrounds who are advocating for global digital rights.

Applicants may come from a wide variety of disciplines. Relevant backgrounds include, but are not limited to:

Sociology

Psychology

Computer science

Economics

Communication

Political science

Human-computer interaction

Media studies

Law

The breadth of disciplines reflects CDT’s recognition that digital rights and technology policy involve technical, legal, political, social, economic, cultural, and behavioral considerations.

Minimum Qualifications for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility conditions because this opportunity is specifically targeted at established academics rather than students or early-stage postdoctoral researchers.

Qualified applicants must be prepared to commit to a two-year non-resident engagement with CDT.

Applicants must also:

Hold a full-time position at an academic institution.

Have published impactful work in peer-reviewed academic venues.

Have experience working on technology-policy issues relevant to CDT’s areas of work.

Ideally possess a terminal degree, such as a Ph.D., J.D., or equivalent experience within their respective field.

Have relevant expertise that can contribute meaningfully to CDT’s research and policy activities.

Be able to commit to the requirements of the two-year program.

CDT places particular emphasis on candidates whose technology-policy experience relates to developments in the United States and European Union.

Importantly, the program is not open to current students or postdoctoral researchers.

What Will CDT Non-Resident Fellows Do?

Non-Resident Fellows are expected to become active intellectual contributors to CDT’s broader research and policy community.

Their engagement can include participating in policy strategy calls and joining briefings concerning emerging technology-policy issues.

Fellows are also encouraged to:

Contribute original writing to the CDT blog.

Present their research and expertise.

Participate in collaborative projects with CDT’s research and policy teams.

Provide feedback on policy positions.

Contribute perspectives on white papers.

Provide feedback on research.

Review or contribute to other relevant CDT outputs.

These activities provide multiple ways for Fellows to translate academic expertise into practical policy engagement.

Required Contribution During the Two-Year Fellowship

In addition to committing to serve as a Non-Resident Fellow for at least two years, each Fellow agrees to complete at least one specified contribution during the two-year period.

The contribution should concern issues relevant to CDT’s work and be timely.

A Fellow can satisfy this requirement by undertaking at least one of the following:

Co-authoring a CDT blog post or participating in a CDT Tech Talk podcast;

Speaking, presenting, or otherwise contributing to a CDT-branded event; or

Collaborating with CDT on the development of a funding proposal.

These requirements provide Fellows with flexibility to contribute in a way that aligns with their expertise and professional interests.

Participation in CDT Events and Policy Discussions

Fellows may also be invited to participate in CDT-branded events when appropriate.

Examples can include:

CDT Working Groups

Policy roundtables

Public events

Webinars

Other relevant CDT programs and discussions

Fellows are additionally encouraged to promote CDT through their external professional and academic networks.

This can involve sharing relevant CDT outputs, promoting job, internship, and externship opportunities, and connecting CDT with emerging research, policy conversations, events, or experts within Fellows’ academic institutions and professional networks.

Opportunities for Collaborative Research

The fellowship can extend beyond discussions and events into collaborative research.

CDT Non-Resident Fellows may be invited to conduct research alongside CDT on mutually agreed projects connected to the organization’s core research and advocacy priorities.

Fellows may also proactively propose joint research projects they believe would complement CDT’s work.

However, applicants should understand that proposing a project does not necessarily mean it will automatically proceed. CDT evaluates proposed collaborations in the context of its:

Organizational objectives

Current priorities

Available capacity

Resources

This provides room for innovative collaboration while ensuring projects remain aligned with CDT’s broader mission and capabilities.

Memorandum of Understanding for Selected Fellows

Every Non-Resident Fellow will receive a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) at the beginning of their term.

The MOU will establish important aspects of the two-year relationship between the Fellow and CDT.

It will outline:

Key dates during the fellowship;

Expected deliverables for the two-year term; and

Guidelines governing the appropriate use of CDT branding.

This provides Fellows and CDT with a shared framework for expectations and engagement throughout the program.

How CDT Supports Its Non-Resident Fellows

The relationship between CDT and its Fellows is designed to involve active support and engagement rather than simply providing Fellows with a title.

At the beginning of the program, CDT conducts an orientation program.

The orientation includes information concerning:

How Non-Resident Fellows work with CDT;

How CDT promotes Fellows’ research; and

How Fellows can participate in the technology-policy process.

Following orientation, CDT commits to keeping Fellows connected with relevant developments and opportunities.

Access to Technology and Internet Policy Insights

CDT plans to provide Fellows with regular updates regarding important technology and internet-policy developments.

Fellows may also be engaged in relevant working groups and can receive expert insights connected to their research interests.

This exposure can be particularly valuable to academics seeking stronger connections between their research and ongoing policy discussions.

Invitations to CDT Events and Programs

Fellows become active members of CDT’s wider community and can receive invitations to relevant events and programs throughout their participation.

All Fellows are invited as CDT guests to certain public events and webinars, including the organization’s Annual Dinner, Tech Prom.

Fellows will also have opportunities to interact directly with CDT experts.

At the same time, CDT welcomes Fellows’ feedback and recommendations, allowing academics to contribute their perspectives to the organization’s work on developing trends and emerging technology-policy issues.

Is the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program Remote?

Yes. The opportunity is listed in Washington, District of Columbia, United States, but the position allows remote participation.

This is consistent with the structure of the opportunity as a “Non-Resident” Fellows Program.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully assess whether their professional position, expertise, and availability allow them to participate meaningfully in CDT’s activities throughout the two-year engagement.

Duration of the Program

Selected applicants must commit to serving as CDT Non-Resident Fellows for at least two years.

The two-year structure allows Fellows to establish meaningful relationships with CDT researchers and policy professionals rather than participating through a short-term engagement.

The MOU provided at the beginning of the fellowship will establish the key dates and deliverables applicable to each Fellow’s term.

Application Requirements

Applicants must prepare several important documents.

The required application materials are:

1. Full Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide a comprehensive CV demonstrating their academic background, professional appointments, publications, research experience, relevant policy engagement, and other qualifications.

2. Relevant Writing Sample

Candidates must submit a writing sample relevant to the opportunity.

Given CDT’s emphasis on impactful academic work and technology-policy expertise, applicants should consider selecting a sample that effectively demonstrates their research capabilities and relevant subject-matter knowledge.

3. Cover Letter

Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining:

Their interest in becoming a CDT Non-Resident Fellow;

Their relevant experience;

Their qualifications for the opportunity; and

Why their expertise is appropriate for the program.

Applicants should ensure that their cover letter clearly communicates how their academic expertise intersects with technology policy and CDT’s areas of work.

Important Document Submission Requirement

There is an important formatting requirement applicants should not overlook.

The CV, writing sample, and cover letter must be compiled into one PDF or document for submission.

Applicants should therefore not prepare these documents as unrelated individual uploads unless the application system specifically instructs otherwise.

Combining everything into a single organized file before beginning the final submission process can help ensure compliance with CDT’s stated application instructions.

How to Apply for the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026

Interested researchers should complete the application through CDT’s official recruitment system.

A practical application process would involve:

Review the fellowship requirements carefully.

Confirm that you hold a full-time academic position.

Assess whether your research experience relates meaningfully to CDT’s technology-policy priorities.

Update your full academic CV.

Select a relevant and strong writing sample.

Prepare a tailored cover letter explaining your interest, expertise, and qualifications.

Compile the CV, writing sample, and cover letter into one PDF or document.

Access the official CDT careers page and locate the Non-Resident Fellows Program opening.

Select “Apply for this position.”

Complete the required application information and submit the combined document before the deadline.

Applicants with questions about the program or application process can contact CDT’s research team at research@cdt.org.

APPLY NOW

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Center for Democracy & Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 is Friday, September 18, 2026.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to prepare their materials well before the closing date, particularly because the application requires a CV, relevant writing sample, and tailored cover letter compiled into one document.

Why Researchers Should Consider the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program

For academics whose work intersects with digital rights and technology policy, the CDT Non-Resident Fellows Program provides an opportunity to move beyond traditional academic publication and participate in broader policy conversations.

Several aspects distinguish the program.

Direct Engagement With Technology Policy

Fellows can participate in strategy calls, emerging-issue briefings, policy discussions, and other activities that bring academic expertise closer to practical technology-policy work.

Greater Policy Impact for Academic Research

Researchers often seek ways to ensure their scholarship reaches audiences beyond academic journals and conferences.

Through CDT, Fellows can explore opportunities to strengthen the public engagement and policy relevance of their work.

Interdisciplinary Collaboration

Technology policy requires perspectives from numerous fields.

Researchers can become part of a community spanning law, political science, sociology, economics, psychology, communications, computer science, human-computer interaction, media studies, and other disciplines.

Opportunities to Publish and Present

Fellows may contribute to CDT’s blog, participate in Tech Talk, present at CDT events, and engage in other public-facing opportunities.

Potential Research Collaboration

Researchers may have opportunities to collaborate with CDT on mutually agreed research projects and can propose projects relevant to the organization’s priorities.

Access to a Wider Technology-Policy Community

Participation connects Fellows with CDT experts and a broader network of researchers and technology-policy professionals.

Diversity, Equity and Inclusion

CDT states that it is an equal opportunity and inclusive employer and does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, gender, gender expression, age, national origin, disability, marital status, or sexual orientation.

The organization specifically states that it believes diversity enables stronger and more impactful work.

Women, people of color, disabled people, members of low-income communities, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and members of other marginalized communities are strongly encouraged to apply.

Key Details at a Glance

Program: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026

Organization: Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT)

Listed Location: Washington, District of Columbia, United States

Participation: Remote participation allowed

Duration: At least two years

Target Group: Established academics and researchers holding full-time positions at academic institutions

Primary Focus: Technology policy, digital rights, academic research, and public-interest technology policy

Required Documents: Full CV, relevant writing sample, and cover letter

Submission Format: Required materials must be compiled into one PDF or document

Application Deadline: September 18, 2026

Conclusion

The Center for Democracy & Technology Non-Resident Fellows Program 2026 provides established academics and researchers with an opportunity to connect rigorous scholarly research with real-world technology-policy discussions.

As questions surrounding artificial intelligence, privacy, cybersecurity, online expression, surveillance, democracy, data governance, digital equity, and the open internet become increasingly important, interdisciplinary academic expertise has an important role to play in shaping informed public policy.

Through its two-year Non-Resident Fellows Program, CDT aims to bring researchers directly into this environment. Selected Fellows can engage with CDT experts, participate in policy strategy discussions and emerging-issue briefings, contribute original writing and presentations, collaborate on relevant initiatives, and help strengthen the connection between academic evidence and public-interest technology policy.

At the same time, Fellows can benefit from closer exposure to policy conversations, opportunities to strengthen the reach and impact of their own research, and relationships with a broader community of academics and technology-policy professionals.

Researchers with impactful peer-reviewed work, relevant technology-policy experience, and a full-time position at an academic institution should consider preparing their application materials early.

Applications must include a full CV, relevant writing sample, and cover letter compiled into one document, and must be submitted by September 18, 2026.

TITLE: The 7th ACE Impact Workshop Ends After Four Days of Intense Discussions in Cotonou

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 7th ACE Impact Workshop Ends After Four Days of Intense Discussions in Cotonou, Benin – The Gambia is set to host the 8th ACE Impact Regional Workshop in November 2022

The highly successful and productive 7th ACE Impact regional workshop hosted from 14 June 2022 ended on Friday 17 June 2022 with several key outcomes and a way forward forged from the event’s discussion.

As key highlights, the workshop was attended by close to 300 participants comprising government representatives from the 11 participating countries of the project, eminent academics, researchers, development partners from the World Bank, IRD and AFD, team members from the Association of African Universities (AAU), project teams from the African Higher Education Centres of Excellence, students and industry partners, just to mention a few. Aside Africa, participants and experts from the United States of America, Europe, New Zealand, and other countries/continents physically participated in the workshop in Benin. Several other higher education stakeholders also joined the event virtually. Both the closing and opening ceremonies were graced by the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research of the Republic of Benin – Professor Mrs. Eléonore Yayi Ladekan. The workshop, which gathered the crème de la crème of professionals in Africa’s higher education, recorded several technical sessions, including performance clinics, thematic breakout sessions, parallel and plenary sessions.

The four-day workshop also updated participants and featured discussions on overall project updates, monitoring, evaluation and learning, report from the subject matter experts, a focus on entrepreneurship and innovation, the development impact of the centres’ interventions, as well as a report on the progress of the Centres of Competence in Digital Education (C-CoDE) Initiative. Others included a focus on gender , updates on the Data Systems Maturity Survey and updates on regional networks.

The closing remarks, given by the Secretary General of the AAU, Prof. Olusola Oyewole; The Benin Country Manager of the World Bank, who was represented by Dr. Ekua Bentil (the World Bank Senior Education Specialist and Team Leader of ACE Impact) and the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research for Benin, were packed with key messages appreciating all the teams for their outstanding contributions to a successful workshop. Their remarks urged the project’s stakeholders to continue collaboratively working towards the shared goal of achieving development impact to accelerate Africa’s growth.

Specifically, the remarks from the World Bank team paid glowing tribute to the Government of Benin, represented by the Minister of Higher Education & Scientific Research for hosting both the 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop and the Project Steering Committee Meeting. The local organizing committee, Ministers of higher education from across the continent, Vice Chancellors, subject matter experts, partners including the AAU and AFD; Centre leaders and their teams, as well as students from the respective centers, especially those who participated in the workshop’s poster competition were all duly acknowledged. Mrs. Gabrielle Hansen, an officer in charge of logistics at the AAU was specially recognised for her hard work and unwavering dedication to the project, as well as the success of the 7th ACE Impact workshop, despite finding herself in challenging circumstances. The centres were reminded that it was only through their resilience and dedication that the project could achieve its targets. The messages also made a strong call to the centres of excellence to continue innovating, since ‘innovation and impact is what distinguishes them as ACE Centers,’ they were told. Another key point highlighted was the fact that as a regional project, the success of one center was the success of all, and therefore collaboration to ensure that the centres succeed was key. Dr. Ekua Bentil, speaking on behalf of the World Bank Country Manager for Benin, said, that the ACE Impact initiative was not merely a project, but a long-term vision to equip Africa to generate the next cohort of experts, researchers and academics who will contribute to solving Africa’s developmental challenges. She also announced that The Gambia had offered to host the 8th ACE Impact Regional Workshop in November 2022, a gesture for which the project was grateful. This announcement was received with loud applause from the hundreds of participants gathered at Palais des Congrès, the venue for the closing ceremony in Cotonou, Benin.

For his part, the Secretary General of the Association of African Universities, Prof. Olusola Oyewole acknowledged the respective teams for their contributions and active participation throughout the workshop discussions. He highlighted the key areas where centres are remarkably delivering on target (including revenue generation and overall student enrolment) and called for efforts to be stepped up in areas such as accreditation and female student enrolment to foster a complete attainment of the project’s targets. He encouraged the centres to critically identify the challenges that confront them and to invest time and resources towards addressing such challenges. The Centres were also urged to consolidate the gains made so far, by devising innovative mechanisms, strengthening partnerships among themselves and with industry and other sectors, while ensuring sustainability of the project. Prof. Oyewole used the platform to call for the adoption of the brilliant ACE Impact model by other African governments and development partners. He wrapped up by expressing his optimism, about the centres being more that galvanised to meet the project’s targets and to significantly enhance the quality of their research and overall contributions, following all the lively and stimulating discussions over the workshops’ duration.

The guest of honour for the official closing ceremony, the honourable Minister of Higher Education & Scientific Research for Benin, Prof. Mrs. Eléonore Yayi Ladekan was full of praise for the AAU’s facilitative role towards the successful organisation of the workshop, and overall dynamism and contribution to the centres of excellence project. She called on centres to continue prioritising the key tenets underlying the project including the focus on training quality students, achieving institutional impact, generating innovative solutions, prioritising research excellence, and enrolling female students. While thanking all the stakeholders and development partners for facilitating the project and for choosing Benin as the host country for the 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop, she congratulated The Gambia for being the next country to host the gathering of some of Africa’s top intellectuals at the upcoming 8th ACE Impact regional workshop. The minister also invited the participants to explore the beautiful city of Cotonou and to visit some tourism destinations in Benin.

Prof. Joel Tossa, the Centre Leader for CEA-SMIA gave the vote of thanks, on behalf of the Local Organising Committee.

Highlights of the Next Steps of the Project

Giving the Immediate next steps related to activities to be prioritised following the workshop, Dr. Ekua Bentil, the Team Lead for ACE Impact at the World Bank listed the following:

Submission of project extension request letters by the Project Steering Committee Members to their respective governments by end of June 2022

Completion of First ACE Impact re-allocation of Funds and Mid Term Review by end of June 2022

Completion of verification of January -May 2022 results and issuance of disbursement letters to centres (June-August 2022)

Completion of mid-term review assessment of Second ACE Impact countries (June -September 2022)

Subject matter expert site visits and virtual support to the Centres (June – December 2022)

TITLE: AU Internship Program 2026: Communication, Digital Communication & any Digital Fields

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:

Applications are open for the AU Internship Program 2026: Communication, Digital Communication & any Digital Fields. Given the critical role to be played by the AfCFTA in moving the continent forward towards the achievement of its development agenda, it has been deemed necessary to create a platform for a number of African students, possessing the required knowledge and skill levels to be introduced to the work of the AfCFTA, through an internship program.

The internship program is designed to bring highly qualified and motivated students with diverse backgrounds into the Secretariat to work on projects linked to the Strategic Orientations of the Secretariat and to support the corporate functions of the Secretariat. Its main goal is to give successful candidates the opportunity to improve their analytical and technical skills in an international environment. The program is primarily educational and aims to expose participants (interns) to the workings of the AfCFTA at an early stage and strengthen their personal and early professional skills. Eligibility

Be nationals of a Member State of the African Union and residing in Ghana.

Final year students who are enrolled on full-time basis on a fully accredited degree program in a recognized public or private institution of higher learning in any of the following areas: Interpretaion and/or Translation.

Full availability for a minimum of three months, being the duration of the program

A motivation letter be addressed to the Administration and Human Resources Directorate of the Secretariat and indicating what they expect to gain out of the internship program
