TITLE: SEED Solar PV Installation Training 2026: Free Solar Energy Training in Lagos and Abeokuta with COREN Certification

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Siemens Energy Education and Development (SEED) Solar PV Installation (SPVI) Training is offering professionals and technicians an opportunity to strengthen their technical knowledge and practical skills in solar photovoltaic installation and renewable energy technologies. The training is supported by the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP), a technical assistance programme co-funded by the European Union and the German Government and implemented by GIZ.

Designed to respond to the growing demand for technically competent renewable energy professionals, the programme combines classroom-based theoretical instruction with practical, hands-on learning, technical site visits and competency assessments. Successful participants will also receive COREN Certification upon completion of the training.

Importantly, the training itself is offered free of charge, and the cost of certification is also covered. Meals will be provided on training days, although participants will be responsible for their own accommodation and transportation.

The particular training stream covered by the application form will be conducted in Lagos State and Abeokuta, Ogun State, with participants required to attend the training in person for three weeks in September 2026.

About the SEED Solar PV Installation Training

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training is focused on developing practical and technical capacity in the renewable energy sector, particularly for individuals who are working or intending to work in solar photovoltaic installation and related areas.

Solar photovoltaic technology is increasingly important in the transition towards cleaner and more accessible energy. As demand for solar energy systems continues to grow, there is a corresponding need for technicians and professionals who possess the technical competencies required to install, operate and work with solar PV systems safely and effectively.

The training therefore provides an opportunity for participants to develop competencies that can support their professional development and participation in Nigeria’s renewable energy industry.

Rather than being limited exclusively to applicants with conventional academic qualifications, the programme specifically encourages applications from individuals coming through both formal educational pathways and practical or experience-based pathways.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to people who have gained technical knowledge through education as well as those whose skills have been developed through hands-on work and practical experience.

Who Is Organising and Supporting the Training?

The training is associated with the Siemens Energy Education and Development (SEED) initiative and is supported by the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP).

NESP is described in the application information as a technical assistance programme that is:

Co-funded by the European Union.

Co-funded by the German Government.

Implemented by GIZ.

Through this support, the programme is designed to contribute to technical capacity development in Nigeria’s renewable energy sector.

The involvement of these institutions also makes the training relevant to broader efforts to improve technical skills and strengthen the renewable energy workforce.

What Does the Solar PV Installation Training Cover?

The programme is structured around several complementary forms of learning. Participants will not only receive theoretical information but will also have opportunities to apply their knowledge in practical settings.

The training will combine:

1. Theoretical Instruction

Participants will receive theoretical instruction designed to build their understanding of solar PV installation and related technical concepts.

The theoretical component provides an important foundation for practical work because solar PV installation requires technicians to understand how systems function, how different components interact and how installations should be approached from a technical and safety perspective.

2. Hands-On Practical Training

A major component of the programme is practical training.

Participants will have the opportunity to develop their technical competencies through hands-on activities rather than relying solely on classroom instruction. This practical focus can be particularly valuable for people preparing to enter the renewable energy sector or professionals seeking to strengthen existing technical skills.

3. Technical Site Visits

The programme will also include technical site visits.

Site visits can provide participants with exposure to practical applications of renewable energy technologies and help connect theoretical concepts with real-world installations and working environments.

This component is particularly useful for participants who want to understand how solar PV systems and technical processes are applied beyond a classroom setting.

4. Competency Assessments

The training will include competency assessments to evaluate participants’ knowledge and practical capabilities.

Assessment is an important part of technical training because it provides an opportunity to demonstrate that the competencies developed during the programme can be applied effectively.

5. COREN Certification

Participants who successfully complete the training will receive COREN Certification, according to the application information.

The certification component adds an important professional dimension to the programme and may be valuable to individuals seeking to strengthen their professional credentials in the technical and engineering-related space.

Training Locations

For this particular stream, training will take place at two locations:

Lagos State

Abeokuta, Ogun State

Applicants are required to indicate their preferred training location when completing the application form.

The form provides the following location choices:

Abeokuta, Ogun State

Lagos State

Applicants should therefore consider their ability to attend their selected location before submitting the application.

Three-Week In-Person Training Requirement

One of the most important requirements stated in the application form is the ability to attend the programme in person for three weeks during September 2026.

The application specifically asks candidates whether they are able to attend the training physically for three weeks.

This means that the opportunity is not presented as an online training programme. Applicants should be prepared to participate physically at one of the designated training locations.

Before applying, prospective participants should therefore consider:

Their availability throughout the three-week training period.

Their ability to travel to and from the selected training location.

Their ability to arrange accommodation if they live outside the training location.

Their ability to cover transportation costs.

Their ability to attend the required training activities in person.

Is the SEED Solar PV Installation Training Free?

Yes. The training is stated to be free of charge.

The programme information specifically indicates that:

The training is free.

The cost of certification is free.

Meals will be provided on training days.

This significantly reduces the direct cost of participating in the programme and makes the opportunity accessible to individuals who may otherwise find professional technical training financially difficult to pursue.

However, applicants should carefully note that not every participation-related expense is covered.

What Costs Are Not Covered?

While the training and certification are free, GIZ-NESP and Siemens Energy will not provide accommodation or transportation support during the training.

Participants should therefore make their own arrangements for these costs.

This means that applicants travelling from another city or location may need to budget for:

Transportation to and from the training location.

Local transportation where necessary.

Accommodation for the duration of the training, if required.

Any other personal expenses not specifically identified as covered by the programme.

The provision of meals on training days can help reduce daily expenses, but participants should still make adequate arrangements for other costs associated with attending a three-week in-person programme.

Who Is Encouraged to Apply?

The training is designed primarily for individuals interested in developing or strengthening their technical and practical competencies in the renewable energy sector.

The application information specifically describes the target audience as:

Professionals working in the renewable energy sector.

Technicians working in the renewable energy sector.

Professionals seeking to work in the renewable energy sector.

Technicians seeking to work in the renewable energy sector.

Individuals coming through formal educational backgrounds.

Individuals coming through practical or experience-based pathways.

The inclusion of both formal and experience-based pathways is an important feature of the programme.

Applicants should therefore not assume that only people with traditional academic qualifications can apply. The information explicitly encourages candidates with practical or experience-based backgrounds to submit applications.

Formal and Experience-Based Applicants

One of the notable aspects of this opportunity is its recognition of different routes through which people develop technical competencies.

Applicants with Formal Education

Individuals who have acquired relevant knowledge through formal education may find the programme useful for strengthening their technical and practical capabilities.

Academic or technical education can provide theoretical foundations, while practical training can help participants apply that knowledge in real-world settings.

Applicants with Practical Experience

The programme also welcomes applicants who have developed their knowledge and abilities through practical experience.

This is significant for technicians and other individuals who may have gained skills through hands-on work rather than exclusively through formal academic programmes.

The application information therefore takes a broader approach to technical capacity development by recognising both educational and practical pathways.

What Are the Requirements for Applicants?

Based on the information provided in the application form, prospective participants should meet the following key conditions:

Have an interest in working in the renewable energy sector, or already be working in the sector.

Be a professional or technician seeking to develop relevant competencies.

Be willing to participate in the technical and practical components of the programme.

Be able to attend the training in person for three weeks in September 2026.

Select either Lagos State or Abeokuta, Ogun State as the preferred training location.

Be prepared to arrange their own accommodation and transportation.

Be able to commit to the programme’s training requirements.

The application form also requests basic personal and contact information, including the applicant’s full name, gender, phone number and email address.

Information Required on the Application Form

Applicants should be prepared to provide several details when completing the application.

The form requests:

Full Name

Applicants are asked to provide their surname and first name.

Gender

The available options shown in the form are:

Female

Male

Phone Number

Applicants must provide a telephone contact.

Email Address

A valid email address is required for the application.

Preferred Training Location

Applicants can select:

Abeokuta, Ogun State

Lagos State

Availability for In-Person Training

Applicants must confirm whether they can attend the training in person for three weeks from September 2026.

The form identifies the questions as required, meaning applicants should ensure that the requested information is completed before submitting the application.

Important Google Account and Privacy Notice

The application is presented through Google Forms. The form indicates that the name, email address and photo associated with the applicant’s Google Account will be recorded when the applicant uploads files and submits the form.

Applicants should therefore review the information associated with the Google Account they use when accessing the application and ensure that they are comfortable with the information being recorded as part of the submission process.

Why This Training Opportunity Is Valuable

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training provides several potential benefits for people interested in renewable energy and technical careers.

Free Technical Training

The programme removes the tuition cost associated with the training. Participants do not have to pay for the training itself.

Free Certification

The cost of certification is also covered, meaning participants can complete the programme without paying the stated certification costs.

Practical Skills Development

The hands-on nature of the training can help participants develop practical competencies relevant to solar PV installation.

Exposure to Real-World Applications

Technical site visits can provide participants with exposure to practical applications and professional environments within the renewable energy field.

Competency Assessment

Participants will have their competencies assessed as part of the training, providing a structured way of evaluating the knowledge and skills developed during the programme.

COREN Certification

Successful completion comes with COREN Certification, according to the information provided in the application form.

Meals During Training Days

Meals will be provided on training days, helping to reduce some of the daily expenses associated with attending the programme.

Opportunity for Different Educational Backgrounds

The programme encourages applications from both formally educated candidates and individuals whose competencies have been developed through practical experience.

Things Applicants Should Consider Before Applying

Although the training is free, prospective applicants should carefully consider the logistical requirements.

The programme is in person, and participants must attend for three weeks. This makes availability one of the most important considerations before submitting an application.

Applicants should also remember that accommodation and transportation are not provided.

Someone living outside Lagos or Abeokuta, for example, should determine whether they can realistically travel to the training location and remain there for the duration of the programme.

A strong applicant should therefore:

Confirm availability for the full three-week period.

Select a training location they can reasonably access.

Plan transportation in advance.

Arrange accommodation independently if necessary.

Ensure their phone number and email address are accurate.

Review all required application questions before submission.

Use an appropriate Google Account when completing the form.

Submit the application with accurate personal information.

Deadline for the SEED Solar PV Installation Training Application

Deadline: Not specified in the application information provided.

The supplied application form states that the training will take place for three weeks from September 2026, but it does not provide a specific application closing date.

Applicants should therefore verify the application page for any updated closing date or submission instructions before applying. Since the training is scheduled for September 2026, prospective applicants should avoid waiting until the last moment to complete the form.

The application requires candidates to select their preferred location between Abeokuta, Ogun State and Lagos State and confirm that they can attend the training physically for three weeks in September 2026.

Applicants should ensure that all required sections are completed accurately before submitting the form.

Conclusion

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training presents an important opportunity for professionals and technicians who want to strengthen their technical competencies and pursue opportunities in Nigeria’s growing renewable energy sector. Supported through the Nigerian Energy Support Programme and implemented by GIZ, with Siemens Energy involved through the SEED initiative, the programme combines theoretical learning, hands-on practical training, technical site visits and competency assessments.

One of the strongest features of the opportunity is that the training and certification are free, while meals are provided on training days. Participants should, however, be prepared to cover their own accommodation and transportation expenses.

The programme is also notable for welcoming candidates from both formal educational and practical, experience-based backgrounds. This broad approach gives technicians and aspiring renewable energy professionals with different educational pathways an opportunity to develop relevant skills.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the three-week, in-person attendance requirement in Lagos or Abeokuta, Ogun State, and should confirm that they can commit to the programme before applying. Since no specific application deadline is provided in the supplied information, prospective applicants should check the official application form for the latest submission information.

TITLE: AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant 2026: Up to $750,000 for Projects Supporting Older Workers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The AARP Foundation has announced a new grant opportunity aimed at improving access to quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California. Through its Request for Applications (RFA): Quality Employment for Older Workers in California, the Foundation intends to support projects that strengthen workforce systems, improve employment services, and create better pathways to stable and sustainable work for people aged 50 and above who experience financial insecurity.

AARP Foundation plans to invest approximately $2 million in grant funding through this initiative and expects to support between four and eight organizations. Successful applicants may receive grants ranging from $250,000 to $750,000, depending on the size, duration, activities, and expected outcomes of their proposed projects.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations, coalitions, workforce leaders, community organizations, and other eligible entities working to improve how workforce systems serve older workers. Rather than focusing primarily on conventional direct-service delivery, the RFA emphasizes systems change, age-inclusive workforce practices, improved coordination among services, and stronger pathways to quality employment.

About the AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant

The AARP Foundation is seeking innovative projects that can help make workforce systems more responsive to the needs of older adults with low incomes.

Older workers can encounter significant challenges when seeking employment, remaining in work, changing careers, or re-entering the workforce after unemployment. These challenges can include age-related barriers in recruitment, limited access to relevant training, difficulty navigating employment and public-benefit systems, and a lack of coordinated support during periods of job transition.

Through this funding opportunity, AARP Foundation wants to support approaches that address these structural and systemic challenges.

The Foundation is particularly interested in projects that incorporate age-inclusive practices into workforce systems and services and create stronger pathways toward quality employment for adults aged 50 and above.

What Does AARP Foundation Mean by Quality Employment?

For this grant opportunity, quality employment goes beyond simply helping someone find a job.

A quality job should provide conditions that allow an individual to achieve greater financial stability while developing the skills and support necessary to remain employed and progress professionally.

According to the grant description, quality employment includes work that provides:

Stable earnings.

Fair and equitable treatment.

Opportunities to develop skills.

Opportunities for advancement.

Flexibility that helps workers remain employed.

Appropriate support during employment transitions.

Conditions that contribute to longer-term employment sustainability.

This means applicants should think beyond traditional job-placement activities. Strong proposals should demonstrate how their interventions can help improve the broader systems, structures, and services that determine whether older workers can access and maintain quality employment.

Main Areas of Interest

AARP Foundation has identified two major areas that applicants may address through their proposed projects.

1. Age-Inclusive Training, Education, and Employment Services

The first area focuses on improving workforce training, education, and employment services so that they intentionally respond to the needs of older workers.

Many existing workforce programs are designed for broad populations and may not adequately account for the circumstances faced by adults aged 50 and above. AARP Foundation is therefore interested in approaches that redesign or improve these programs to make them more age-inclusive.

Potential activities may include:

Redesigning job-connected training programs to intentionally serve older workers.

Modifying workforce services to better address the needs of adults aged 50 and above.

Developing new approaches for reaching older workers who may not be adequately served by existing employment systems.

Creating recruitment strategies specifically designed to engage older workers.

Helping older adults prepare for quality employment opportunities.

Connecting older workers with employers offering suitable employment opportunities.

Improving the ability of workforce organizations to identify and respond to barriers experienced by older job seekers.

Developing employment pathways that recognize the experience, skills, and needs of older workers.

Applicants should demonstrate how their proposed intervention could improve the effectiveness or inclusiveness of existing workforce systems rather than simply providing temporary assistance to individual participants.

2. Age-Inclusive Workforce Systems and Service Alignment

The second major area of interest focuses on improving coordination among workforce systems, public agencies, community organizations, and other support services.

Older adults experiencing unemployment or employment transitions may need to interact with multiple systems at the same time. These can include workforce development services, unemployment support, employment agencies, community organizations, and public-benefit programs.

When these systems operate independently, individuals may encounter fragmented services, duplicated processes, unclear referral pathways, or difficulty understanding where to obtain appropriate support.

AARP Foundation is therefore interested in projects that strengthen connections between these systems.

Potential approaches could include:

Building stronger connections between unemployment services and workforce development programs.

Improving coordination between reemployment services and other employment-support systems.

Developing stronger referral pathways between public agencies and community-based organizations.

Testing coordinated service models specifically designed to reach older workers.

Improving how older adults navigate multiple benefits and support services.

Creating partnerships among organizations serving older adults experiencing employment transitions.

Developing systems that make it easier for older workers to move between workforce and support services.

Testing approaches that can eventually be replicated or adopted more broadly.

The Grant Is Focused on Systems Change

One of the most important aspects of this opportunity is that applicants should understand the distinction between systems change and traditional direct service delivery.

AARP Foundation specifically states that projects should focus on systems change initiatives rather than direct service programs.

This means an applicant should not simply propose to provide employment services directly to a group of older adults without explaining how the project will change, improve, coordinate, or strengthen the systems through which those services are delivered.

For example, a conventional direct-service project might focus primarily on helping a specific number of individuals prepare résumés or find jobs.

A systems-change project, by contrast, could examine how workforce organizations identify older job seekers, redesign their service models, improve referral systems, coordinate with community organizations, or change workforce practices so that older workers can consistently receive better support.

Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate the broader structural impact their project could have.

Who Should Benefit From the Project?

The proposed projects must primarily benefit older adults aged 50 and above with low incomes or financial insecurity.

The target population is particularly important because the grant is designed around older workers who rely on employment to meet basic needs.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a clear understanding of the employment challenges faced by financially vulnerable older adults and explain how their proposed systems-level intervention will improve access to quality employment.

A strong proposal should establish:

Who the intended older-worker population is.

What employment-related challenges this population experiences.

Why existing systems and services are insufficient.

What systemic barrier the project intends to address.

How the proposed intervention will improve workforce systems.

How the project will ultimately create better employment pathways.

How success will be measured.

Where Must Projects Be Implemented?

The projects supported through this funding opportunity must be implemented in the state of California.

This geographic requirement is central to the RFA. Applicants should ensure that their proposed activities, partnerships, workforce systems, and intended impact are connected to California.

Organizations outside California should carefully review the complete RFA and FAQ before determining whether they are eligible to participate, particularly if they intend to partner with California-based organizations.

The opportunity should not be interpreted as a general international or worldwide employment grant. Its stated purpose is to address quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California.

How Much Funding Is Available?

AARP Foundation expects to invest approximately $2 million through this grant opportunity.

The Foundation anticipates making awards to up to four but no more than eight grantees.

Individual grant awards are expected to range from:

Minimum expected award: $250,000.

Maximum expected award: $750,000.

Applicants are expected to request an amount that is appropriate for the scope of their proposed project, activities, implementation period, and anticipated outcomes.

The grant structure is designed to allow applicants to develop projects of different durations while matching their funding request to the scale of the intervention.

Funding Based on Project Duration

The maximum funding amount depends partly on the proposed implementation period.

12-Month Projects

Projects proposed for a 12-month implementation period may request up to $375,000.

Applicants choosing this duration should ensure that the proposed activities and outcomes can realistically be achieved within one year.

The project should have a clearly defined implementation strategy, measurable outcomes, and a realistic timeline demonstrating how the proposed systems change can occur during the funding period.

24-Month Projects

Projects proposed for a 24-month implementation period may request up to $750,000.

A two-year project may provide greater opportunity to develop partnerships, test new approaches, implement systems changes, evaluate results, and refine interventions.

However, a larger funding request should be supported by a clearly defined scope of work and a strong explanation of why the proposed activities require the requested level of investment.

Important Proposal Considerations

Organizations preparing an application should pay close attention to the central requirements of the RFA.

Focus on Older Workers

The proposed intervention must primarily affect adults aged 50 and above who have low incomes, experience financial insecurity, or depend on employment to meet basic needs.

Demonstrate Systems-Level Impact

The project should be designed to change or improve workforce systems rather than operate solely as a conventional direct-service program.

Address Quality Employment

Applicants should explain how their project will contribute to employment that offers stability, fair treatment, skill development, advancement opportunities, flexibility, and support.

Establish California-Based Impact

The project must be implemented in California, and the proposed activities should clearly demonstrate relevance to the state’s workforce environment.

Develop a Strong Partnership Strategy

Because workforce systems involve multiple organizations and services, applicants should consider how collaboration, referrals, coordination, and service alignment can contribute to the proposed intervention.

Connect Activities to Measurable Outcomes

Applicants should explain what they intend to change and how they will determine whether the project has achieved its objectives.

Rather than simply listing activities, the proposal should establish a logical connection between the identified problem, proposed intervention, expected outputs, and anticipated outcomes.

Application Process

The grant opportunity involves a two-stage application process.

Stage One: Pre-Application

Interested applicants must first submit a pre-application through AARP Foundation’s grant portal.

The pre-application is the initial screening stage of the funding process.

Applicants should review the full RFA carefully before submitting their materials to ensure that the proposed project aligns with the Foundation’s objectives, eligibility requirements, geographic restrictions, target population, and systems-change focus.

The pre-application must be submitted through the AARP Foundation’s Fluxx Grantee Portal.

Stage Two: Full Application

Following the review of pre-applications, selected applicants will be invited to submit a full application.

According to the published schedule, invitations to submit full applications are expected around mid-September 2026.

The full application will provide shortlisted applicants with an opportunity to present their proposed project in greater detail.

Organizations should therefore begin preparing their project concept, partnerships, implementation plan, expected outcomes, and budget before the invitation stage rather than waiting until the full application period begins.

Key Dates and Deadlines

Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates:

Date
Milestone

Application Deadline

The most immediate deadline is:

September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Time / 10:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their pre-application. Technical issues, incomplete information, or difficulties with the grant portal can create unnecessary risks close to the deadline.

Where to Find the Full RFA

The complete grant requirements, application instructions, eligibility information, and additional details are contained in AARP Foundation’s official Request for Applications.

Applicants should read the complete RFA rather than relying solely on summaries because the official document contains the detailed requirements governing the application.

Questions and Technical Support

Applicants who have questions about the RFA or require technical support with submitting an application through the AARP Foundation’s Fluxx Grantee Portal can contact the AARP Foundation Grants Management team.

Email: aarp_foundation_grants@aarp.org

Questions relating to eligibility, proposal requirements, or technical submission issues should be addressed as early as possible so applicants have adequate time to resolve any concerns before the deadline.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can an individual apply for this grant?

The opportunity is structured around projects led by eligible organizations, leaders, and coalitions rather than individual applicants seeking personal financial assistance.

Potential applicants should consult the full RFA for the precise organizational eligibility requirements.

Can organizations outside California apply?

The RFA states that projects must be implemented in California. Organizations considering participation from outside the state should carefully review the full eligibility provisions and FAQ, particularly where partnerships with California-based organizations are involved.

Can multiple organizations collaborate on a proposal?

The RFA includes a question addressing proposals involving multiple partner organizations. Given the focus on workforce-system alignment, partnerships and collaboration may be particularly relevant to projects seeking to improve connections among public agencies, workforce organizations, community organizations, and support services.

Applicants should consult the full RFA for the specific requirements governing collaborative proposals.

What is the difference between quality employment and simply having a job?

The grant opportunity takes a broader view of employment.

Quality employment should provide stable earnings, fair treatment, opportunities for skills development and advancement, flexibility, and sufficient support to help workers sustain employment through subsequent transitions.

Consequently, projects should demonstrate how their proposed systems changes can contribute to these broader employment outcomes.

What does systems change mean in this opportunity?

Systems change refers to interventions that alter or improve the way workforce systems, organizations, services, policies, processes, partnerships, or referral mechanisms operate.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate how their project can produce changes that extend beyond providing temporary services directly to individual participants.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

Organizations considering this opportunity can take several practical steps to strengthen their proposals.

1. Clearly Define the Problem

Begin by identifying a specific workforce-system challenge affecting low-income older adults in California.

Explain the problem using evidence, local knowledge, workforce data, organizational experience, or other credible information.

2. Identify the Systemic Barrier

Do not stop at describing unemployment or financial insecurity.

Explain why the existing workforce system is not adequately addressing the problem and identify the structural or organizational barrier that the project will address.

3. Demonstrate Age Inclusivity

Explain how the proposed approach will intentionally address the circumstances and needs of workers aged 50 and above.

The age-inclusive component should be central to the project rather than an incidental feature.

4. Build a Strong Theory of Change

A strong proposal should demonstrate a logical progression:

Problem → Systemic Barrier → Intervention → System Change → Improved Workforce Services → Better Employment Pathways → Improved Outcomes for Older Workers

This makes it easier for reviewers to understand why the proposed project is likely to produce meaningful results.

5. Develop Meaningful Partnerships

Consider which organizations influence the employment experiences of older workers.

Potential partners could include workforce development organizations, public agencies, community organizations, employers, training institutions, and other relevant stakeholders.

6. Establish Measurable Outcomes

Applicants should identify realistic indicators for determining whether the intervention is successful.

Possible areas of measurement could include improvements in service coordination, referral effectiveness, workforce-system participation, employer engagement, access to training, or pathways to quality employment, depending on the proposed project.

7. Prepare a Realistic Budget

The funding request should correspond with the scope and duration of the proposed intervention.

A larger request should be supported by sufficient activities, staffing, partnerships, evaluation, and expected outcomes to justify the investment.

8. Review the Official RFA Carefully

Finally, applicants should compare their proposed project against every requirement in the official RFA before submitting the pre-application.

The official document should be treated as the authoritative source for eligibility and application requirements.

TITLE: Truist 2027 Credit Internship Program: Paid U.S. Internship Opportunity for Finance and Business Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Truist 2027 Credit Internship Program offers an opportunity for ambitious university students to gain practical experience in financial services while developing their knowledge of credit, risk management, banking, and business operations.

The internship is part of Truist’s broad-based early-career internship programme, which combines education, professional exposure, and practical work experience. Through the Credit track, interns are connected with lines of business within Wholesale Banking, giving them an opportunity to develop an understanding of the day-to-day responsibilities involved in areas such as Commercial & Corporate Banking, Specialized Industries and Wholesale Payments.

The programme is designed for students who are interested in building careers in financial services and who want to complement their university education with hands-on experience in a major banking environment.

The position was posted on August 18, 2026, and is listed as available in five locations across the Truist footprint. The supplied job announcement does not specify a closing date, meaning interested candidates should not wait for a deadline before submitting an application.

About the Truist 2027 Credit Internship Program

The Credit Internship Program is a temporary internship opportunity designed to develop early-career talent for roles connected to Truist’s Wholesale Banking business.

Rather than focusing exclusively on classroom learning, the programme combines structured training with practical assignments and exposure to real business activities.

Interns can expect to participate in:

Educational and professional development sessions.

Business rotations.

Special projects and assignments.

Day-to-day business activities.

Training related to credit and risk.

Team-based projects.

Activities involving internal business partners and external clients.

Exposure to senior leaders and, potentially, executive leaders.

This combination is intended to help interns understand how financial institutions operate while strengthening the technical, analytical, communication, and leadership capabilities required for a career in financial services.

What Is the Credit Track?

The Credit track is specifically aligned with business lines within Wholesale Banking.

Interns may gain exposure to areas such as:

Commercial and Corporate Banking

This area involves supporting businesses and corporate clients with financial services and banking solutions. Interns can gain insight into how financial institutions evaluate business needs, manage relationships, and assess financial and credit considerations.

Specialized Industries

This area focuses on specific industry sectors and their unique financial requirements. Exposure to specialized industries can help interns understand how economic conditions, industry dynamics, and business models influence financial decision-making.

Wholesale Payments

Wholesale Payments focuses on financial solutions and payment services for business and institutional clients. Exposure to this area can help interns understand the role of financial infrastructure and payment systems in supporting businesses.

The specific business area assigned to an intern will depend on the host team and programme placement.

What Can Interns Expect During the Program?

Truist describes the programme as one that combines education, exposure, and experience.

This means successful interns are not simply expected to observe employees. They will have opportunities to participate in work that supports internal business partners and external clients while applying concepts learned during training.

Interns will also be expected to work collaboratively and contribute to projects and activities assigned by their rotational leads.

The programme is therefore suitable for students who want to gain practical experience while developing a deeper understanding of financial services.

Exposure to Truist Senior Leaders

One notable feature of the programme is exposure to Truist senior leadership.

The internship may include sessions involving senior leaders and executive leaders, giving participants an opportunity to learn about the organization, its business operations, and the expectations associated with careers in financial services.

For students preparing for careers in banking, finance, credit, or related areas, this type of professional exposure can provide useful insight into the financial-services industry and corporate leadership.

Key Responsibilities of a Credit Intern

Successful interns will be expected to undertake a range of responsibilities throughout the programme.

1. Learn Credit and Risk Management Concepts

Interns will learn a broad range of concepts related to risk management, enterprise programmes and financial services.

This training is intended to prepare them for assignments within different lines of business.

2. Develop Analytical and Decision-Making Skills

Credit and financial-services careers require employees to evaluate information, identify risks, and make informed decisions.

The programme therefore emphasizes the development of analytical and decision-making capabilities.

Interns will have opportunities to apply these skills through practical projects and business assignments.

3. Strengthen Communication Skills

Effective communication is an important requirement of the internship.

Interns may work with internal business partners, external clients, managers, and other members of their teams. They will therefore need to communicate information clearly and professionally.

4. Develop Leadership Skills

The programme also seeks to strengthen leadership capabilities.

Students can develop leadership skills through project participation, teamwork, initiative, campus involvement, and other professional responsibilities.

5. Complete Special Projects

Interns may be assigned special projects or other tasks outside the formal training programme.

These assignments can provide opportunities to demonstrate initiative, analytical thinking, organization and problem-solving skills.

6. Participate in Business Rotations

Business rotations form an important part of the programme.

Through rotations, interns can work on projects and participate in normal business activities, allowing them to apply concepts and behaviours learned during training.

7. Complete Additional Training

Managers may recommend additional training during or after the internship programme.

This can help interns continue developing relevant skills and knowledge based on their assignments and career interests.

Academic Requirements

The Truist Credit Internship Program is intended for students who are actively pursuing a university degree.

Applicants must be working toward either:

A Bachelor’s degree; or

A Master’s degree.

Truist particularly values candidates studying business-related disciplines, with accounting and finance coursework preferred.

A 3.0 or higher GPA is preferred.

The GPA requirement is described as preferred rather than an absolute minimum, meaning candidates should carefully review the complete application requirements rather than assuming that applicants below 3.0 are automatically excluded.

Graduation Requirement

Another important requirement concerns the expected graduation date.

Applicants should have a scheduled final-degree graduation date between the following:

December 2027 and June 2029.

Students outside this graduation window may therefore not fit the target profile for this particular internship programme.

Prospective applicants should carefully compare their expected graduation date with the requirement before applying.

Skills Truist Is Looking For

The programme is designed for students who can demonstrate a combination of academic preparation, interpersonal abilities, and professional potential.

Important skills and qualities include:

Strong Communication

Candidates should possess excellent interpersonal and communication skills.

This is important because interns may work with multiple stakeholders, participate in meetings, collaborate on projects, and potentially interact with clients.

Initiative

Truist seeks students who demonstrate strong initiative.

Applicants should be able to show situations where they have taken responsibility, identified opportunities, solved problems, or gone beyond basic expectations.

Leadership

Work experience.

Academic projects.

Team activities.

Other situations where the applicant has taken responsibility and influenced positive outcomes.

Students considering this opportunity should therefore be comfortable with travel and potential changes in work location associated with training and programme activities.

Sponsorship for U.S. permanent residence.

Applicants should therefore carefully assess their existing U.S. employment authorization before applying.

This requirement is particularly important for international students studying in the United States who may normally rely on post-study or student-related employment authorization.

English Language Requirement

The job posting identifies English as required.

Candidates should therefore have sufficient English-language proficiency to communicate effectively in a professional banking environment.

This includes the ability to participate in meetings, communicate with colleagues, prepare professional documents and presentations, and interact appropriately with internal and external stakeholders.

Internship Employment Type

The position is classified as temporary.

This is consistent with its structure as an internship programme designed to provide students with professional experience before completion of their degree.

Students should therefore distinguish the programme from a permanent full-time position.

Internship Locations

The job posting states that the Credit Internship Program is available in five locations.

The specific location for an individual intern will depend on the assigned host team and will be communicated in the offer letter.

Because relocation is part of the programme expectations, applicants should be prepared to work at the location assigned to them.

Compensation Information

$25.00 per hour.

The posting provides this figure specifically to comply with Washington, D.C. pay transparency requirements.

Applicants should note that the stated rate applies to Washington, D.C. work locations and should not automatically be assumed to apply to every location where the internship is available.

Benefits Information

The job posting includes a general description of benefits available to eligible Truist employees.

However, it specifically explains that regular employees working 20 hours or more per week may be eligible for benefits, while temporary or contingent workers may not qualify for the same benefits.

The posting therefore advises applicants to review the specific benefits applicable to their employment status and position.

General Truist benefits described in the posting include the following:

401(k) plan.

Vacation.

Paid holidays.

Eligibility for specific benefits depends on employment classification, division, hours worked, and other applicable conditions.

Truist’s Purpose and Values

Truist states that its purpose is to inspire and build better lives and communities.

The company emphasizes caring for clients, empowering teammates, and serving communities.

The organization provides services across areas including:

Consumer banking.

Wholesale banking.

Technology.

Data.

Operations.

Interns are expected to embrace and model Truist’s purpose, mission, and values during the programme.

Equal Employment Opportunity

The company says it does not discriminate based on characteristics including:

Race.

Gender.

Color.

Religion.

Citizenship.

National origin.

Age.

Sexual orientation.

Gender identity.

Disability.

Veteran status.

Other classifications protected by law.

The opportunity, therefore, does not specify a particular race, ethnicity, or continent as a prerequisite.

However, the employment-authorization requirement remains an important condition for applicants.

Who Should Apply?

The opportunity is particularly suitable for students who are:

Studying finance, accounting, business, or a related field.

Pursuing a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree.

Expected to graduate between December 2027 and June 2029.

Interested in banking and financial services.

Interested in credit and risk management.

Comfortable working with Excel and PowerPoint.

Strong communicators.

Analytical and detail-oriented.

Demonstrated leaders.

Proactive and willing to take initiative.

Comfortable working collaboratively.

Willing to travel.

Willing to relocate.

Authorized to work in the United States without requiring sponsorship.

How Applicants Can Prepare a Strong Application

Students interested in the Truist Credit Internship Program should approach the application strategically.

1. Review Your Graduation Date

Confirm that your expected final-degree graduation date falls between December 2027 and June 2029.

2. Highlight Relevant Coursework

TITLE: Google for Startups Immersion EMEA 2026: Apply for the Google x Antler Program for High-Growth Startups

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Google for Startups Immersion – EMEA 2026, an intensive startup development program created for ambitious founders across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) who are already building companies with live products and demonstrated traction.

Powered by Google for Startups and Antler, the 2026 Immersion program combines Google’s technical and product expertise with Antler’s experience in venture building, startup strategy and investment.

Unlike an introductory entrepreneurship course aimed at people who only have a business idea, Google for Startups Immersion EMEA 2026 is targeted at founders who have already moved into execution. Participating startups are expected to have products in the market and evidence of traction.

The program will begin with a series of virtual sessions in October 2026. Following the online phase, 25 startups will be invited to participate in an exclusive in-person Immersion experience in London on December 1, 2026, where selected founders will gain access to Google engineers, Antler mentors, technical support and investor networking opportunities.

The application deadline is October 13, 2026.

About Google for Startups Immersion EMEA 2026

Google for Startups Immersion EMEA is designed to help high-potential startup founders address both the technical and commercial challenges involved in scaling a technology company.

The initiative combines two complementary areas of expertise.

Google brings its technology ecosystem, engineers, product expertise and experience supporting technology companies, while Antler contributes venture-building knowledge, investment perspectives, mentorship and expertise in areas such as fundraising, go-to-market strategy and business economics.

The result is a program that goes beyond generic startup education.

Participants will have opportunities to examine both the technology behind their businesses and the commercial foundations required to build sustainable, scalable companies.

The program is therefore particularly relevant for startup leadership teams seeking to improve their technology architecture, AI capabilities, business strategy, unit economics, fundraising readiness and overall approach to scaling.

How the Google for Startups Immersion Program Works

The 2026 program is structured around two main phases.

Phase One: Virtual Immersion Sessions

The first phase will take place virtually from October 22 to October 28, 2026.

During this stage, participating startups will have access to four online sessions covering technical and business topics.

Importantly, the program uses dedicated or dual tracks designed to address the different responsibilities of startup founders and technical leaders.

The sessions are expected to cover areas including:

Google’s AI and development technologies;

Google Antigravity;

Gemini Enterprise;

AI Studio;

AI investing;

Venture-capital mathematics and strategy;

Unit economics;

Building defensible businesses; and

Technical and commercial considerations associated with scaling a startup.

The structure reflects the reality that scaling a technology startup requires more than building a technically impressive product.

Founders also need to understand whether the business model is sustainable, whether customer acquisition and pricing strategies make sense, how the company can defend its market position and how investors may evaluate its economics.

At the same time, CTOs and technical leaders need to ensure that the underlying technology can support growth.

The virtual phase therefore brings these dimensions together.

Phase Two: In-Person Immersion in London

Following the online phase, 25 startups will be selected and invited to participate in an exclusive in-person Immersion program in London on December 1, 2026.

The London phase takes the program deeper into startup-specific technical and business challenges.

Selected companies can expect opportunities for direct interaction with Google engineers and Antler mentors.

The in-person program is reported to include:

Technical architecture sessions with Google engineers;

Live technical problem-solving and “bug squashing”;

One-on-one Antler mentorship;

Go-to-market strategy discussions;

Pricing guidance;

Fundraising mentorship;

Business-model and scaling discussions; and

A private founder and investor mixer.

This second phase is therefore considerably more targeted than a conventional startup conference.

Rather than simply listening to presentations, selected founders will have opportunities to engage directly with experts around the challenges facing their companies.

Technical Support from Google

Technology is one of the core pillars of the Immersion program.

For founders building AI-enabled or technology-intensive products, scaling can introduce substantial challenges involving infrastructure, product architecture, reliability, integrations and development workflows.

The program gives participating companies exposure to Google’s technical expertise and technology ecosystem.

The virtual curriculum includes technologies such as Google Antigravity and Gemini Enterprise, while the London stage provides selected startups with more direct technical interaction with Google engineers.

For startups already operating live products, this type of engagement can be particularly relevant because technical challenges tend to become more complex as usage increases.

Business and Venture Support from Antler

The second major component of the program comes from Antler.

Antler is a global early-stage venture capital firm and startup ecosystem participant that works with founders in multiple markets.

Through the Immersion program, Antler contributes expertise on the commercial and investment side of building a high-growth startup.

The program covers topics including:

Venture capital strategy;

Startup economics;

Unit economics;

Defensibility;

Go-to-market strategy;

Pricing; and

Fundraising.

For the companies selected for London, this support becomes more personalized through one-on-one mentorship with Antler.

Founder and CTO Tracks

One notable feature of the virtual stage is the use of separate or dual learning tracks.

Startup founders and CTOs frequently face different but interconnected challenges.

A founder or CEO may spend substantial time considering customer acquisition, market positioning, financing, pricing, hiring and investor relationships.

A CTO or technical co-founder may be focused more heavily on architecture, infrastructure, engineering processes, AI implementation, security, product performance and technical scalability.

Google for Startups Immersion addresses both sides rather than treating every member of a startup’s leadership team as having identical development needs.

This approach can help startup leadership teams align technology decisions with commercial objectives.

Who Should Apply?

The program is specifically aimed at ambitious founders across the EMEA region who already have a live product and demonstrated traction.

EMEA refers to:

Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

This means the program is not primarily targeted at aspiring entrepreneurs who are still deciding what company to create.

Applicants should already be building and operating a startup.

Current descriptions of the program emphasize two important characteristics:

A live product: The startup should have moved beyond the purely conceptual stage and have a product in the market.

Traction: Applicants should be able to demonstrate evidence that the company has progressed beyond simply developing an idea.

What Does “Traction” Mean for Startup Applicants?

The official program materials emphasize demonstrated traction, although the publicly available information does not establish one universal numerical threshold that every applicant must meet.

In a startup context, traction can generally refer to evidence that a company is gaining meaningful market validation.

Depending on the business model, evidence may include customers, users, revenue, recurring usage, commercial partnerships, growth or other indicators showing genuine adoption.

Applicants should therefore focus on presenting verifiable indicators appropriate to their own business model rather than assuming that every startup will be assessed using an identical metric.

Who Is This Program Best Suited For?

The program is particularly relevant to founders who have already completed the earliest stages of startup formation and are now confronting questions associated with growth.

This could include companies seeking to:

Improve their technology architecture;

Scale an existing product;

Integrate or expand AI capabilities;

Strengthen unit economics;

Develop stronger go-to-market strategies;

Refine pricing;

Prepare for fundraising;

Improve their understanding of venture capital;

Strengthen their competitive defensibility; or

Connect with other founders, mentors and investors.

Because the program requires a live product and traction, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate that their startup has already progressed beyond the idea stage.

Exposure to Other EMEA Founders

Another component of the Immersion experience is access to other startup founders from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

This creates an environment in which participants can exchange experiences with companies operating in different markets and sectors.

Building a startup in EMEA can involve very different market conditions depending on the founder’s location.

European companies may face one regulatory, investment and customer environment, while startups operating in Africa or the Middle East may encounter different infrastructure, financing and market-access dynamics.

Bringing founders from these regions into the same program creates opportunities for cross-market learning and potentially future collaboration.

Access to Potential Investors

The London phase is also expected to provide selected startups with investor exposure.

A private founder and investor mixer is among the reported elements of the in-person Immersion.

This gives selected founders an additional networking opportunity alongside the program’s technical and business-development activities.

Applicants should nevertheless distinguish between access to investor networking and guaranteed investment.

The available program information does not mean that admission automatically results in investment or funding.

Is Google for Startups Immersion a Funding Program?

The central offering described in the available 2026 program information is technical and business support, mentorship, expert access and networking, rather than a guaranteed cash award.

Accordingly, applicants should not interpret participation as an automatic Google or Antler investment.

The value proposition instead centers on access to expertise, startup development resources, technical guidance, venture mentorship and connections.

Key Program Dates

Applicants should take careful note of the 2026 timeline:

Application deadline: October 13, 2026

Virtual program: October 22–28, 2026

Number of virtual sessions: Four

Startups invited to the in-person phase: Up to 25

TITLE: COVID-19 Pandemic exposes default instructional leadership in African universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Dr Noel Kufaine

The Covid-19 pandemic has managed to separate us individually and limit group gatherings; however, for education in general and higher education in particular, the situation has exposed serious instructional leadership deficiency. There is fidgetiness in higher education institutions as they gradually lose the 2020 academic calendar. Nevertheless, as everybody is striving to salvage the remaining part of the academic calendar, some are passively doing nothing. The active leaders are determined to save the 2020 academic calendar by flipping to teaching and learning using ICT modes. However, whether it’s ‘averse’ attitudes on the part of students and some stakeholders or poor implementation approaches by institutions, the change to the ICT mode of learning is facing resistance from different stakeholders. Reports indicate that implementation in some institutions was initiated before checking whether students who registered on a program to be delivered on face to face are ready to switch to online learning.

Of course, there is a range of ICT applications which are well established and well informed by intensive research, for teaching and learning. However, most of the research, tests and trials were not done in Africa. The COVID19 pandemic has forced university leadership to adopt a different mode of curriculum delivery without proper conceptualisation of the risks to institutions, lecturers, and students in African contexts. Implementing such an important change without initial planning is risky and needs to be addresses.

Technically, students enroll into a program after assessing the program and the mode of delivery; however, with institutions having to suspend physical teaching and learning due to the Covid-19 pandemic, they were forced to switch from one teaching mode to another without properly understanding the technical challenges. It’s excruciating that university leaders are being schooled by student body leaders about the student demographic discrepancies and fragmentation. The lesson here is that African educational institutions must invest in knowing more about their students – e.g. how do they access internet while at home, do they have access to learning devices, where are they domiciled – urban or rural? Unfortunately, the advice from student bodies and other stakeholders is coming while institutions have already confirmed and invested in implementing teaching and learning using ICT.

Fullan and Scot (2009), pointed that when initiating change in higher education, there is need to tap into the aspects of culture. The current dominant culture in higher education is; student engagement, rational persuasion and institutional accountability. Failure to consider dominant culture is a catalyst of frustration, hence, some students are refusing to learn using the so-called strange learning approach.

The student body leadership is a legitimate part of the university, such that in some universities, students are represented in University Councils. Therefore, ignoring them during such change of approach is not exemplary leadership. Reports from some higher education institutions indicate that lecturers were only invited to attend E-learning assessment orientations. One lecturer said; the whole two hours of online meeting was about uploading material on Moodle and designing quiz tests for students. Effective leadership requires that there be consultations, deciding together and considering the inputs of all the concerned stakeholders within an educational institution.

The growth and prevalence of information and communication technologies requires African Universities to develop strategies for effectively harnessing the emerging tools for the benefit of students, lecturers, and universities. When ICT is properly implemented it can result in improving teaching, learning and research.

Instructional leadership is required under such situation to plan how to use the available resources, while cognizant that not all learners have access to the technological facilities. However, in some countries a great deal has been done on access to computers including buying a computer for every new student admitted into the University, while in other countries, the issue of access persists.

Learning online brings a new phenomenon of learning from home. It is worth noting that some homes are not too conducive for learning. There is also the challenge of limited power supply and internet connectivity in various homes. The Sub-Saharan region has a population distribution where more than 70% live in rural areas and more than half of the countries in the region have less than 40% of population powered by electricity, coupled with less than 25% internet connectivity.

The initiative to salvage the remaining 2020 academic calendar is commendable; however, it should not be done for recognition, approval or to be applauded, rather it should enhance achieving the purpose. It is common knowledge that closure of schools is not caused by institutions or students; but starting a teaching mode which is not inclusive is failure by institutional leadership. On the other hand, its poor leadership for universities to remain idle while waiting for government instructions about the next course of action.

Education is a fundamental human right and this is recognized by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. In the same vein access to higher education still remains a priority in this region because of low enrolment rates caused by several challenges including infrastructure and other support services deficit; therefore, denying the already few students access because of challenges beyond their control is a breach of the students’ fundamental rights.

The COVID-19 pandemic and circumstances surrounding it has robbed higher education institutions of their autonomy, because they are now being instructed by governments and health authorities to close or to open schools. One institution in Malawi was closed in the middle of the end of semester examinations. Despite some resistance, institutions are being told to implement or not to implement online delivery. The independence which allows higher education institutions to make informed decisions after systematic research and analysis has been raided. Eventually, university leadership has ignored scholarship of teaching and learning where modes of teaching and learning are evaluated and practiced for the benefit of all students. In this case, focus is on those who can afford. A disturbing case reported is that some institutions are asking students who cannot afford online classes to de-register and register again next year. This is absurd.

It is rational to state that university leadership has permitted the rolling of unfamiliar teaching and learning methods particularly to salvage the 2020 academic calendar. However, the pressure on leadership has been and remains great because there is no knowledge whether the current teaching and learning approach is temporary or permanent. Furthermore, E-learning is not cheap and has sustainability challenges. Simultaneously, leaders have failed to defend higher education autonomy – eventually allowed the higher education institutions’ independence and academic authority to become eroded.

Noel Kufaine PhD

Associate Professor – Namibia University of Science and Technology
