What Is the Brooke Owens Fellowship?

The Brooke Owens Fellowship was created to expand opportunities for undergraduate women and gender minorities who want to become leaders, innovators and contributors within aerospace.

The program is named in honor of Dawn Brooke Owens, an accomplished aerospace professional and pilot whose career included work connected with NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the XPRIZE Foundation, the Federal Aviation Administration’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation and the White House Office of Management and Budget. The initiative was founded by aerospace leaders who knew Brooke personally and wanted to create opportunities for a new generation of people who could bring similar talent, creativity, determination and commitment to service into the industry.

Today, the program focuses on providing career opportunities, mentorship, professional development, industry connections and a strong community for undergraduate women and gender-minority students interested in aerospace.

The organization is a U.S.-registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit and has developed a substantial network of aerospace professionals, executives, mentors, host organizations and alumni.

Applications for the Class of 2027 Are Now Open

The Class of 2027 represents the 11th group of Brooke Owens Fellows, marking more than a decade since the program’s first fellowship class.

Applications opened on September 1 and will remain open until October 4, 2026. The latest official announcement confirms that the opportunity is available to women and gender-minority undergraduate students from all college majors who are interested in careers in aerospace and aviation.

This broad academic approach is important because aerospace is much larger than aerospace engineering alone.

Professionals working in the sector may come from backgrounds including:

Aerospace engineering

Mechanical engineering

Electrical engineering

Computer science

Artificial intelligence

Data science

Physics

Mathematics

Chemistry

Biology

Earth and environmental sciences

Business

Finance

Communications

Public relations

Art and design

Law

Public policy

International affairs

Government

Education

STEM outreach

The program’s FAQ explicitly states that applicants do not have to major in aerospace engineering. Students from engineering, science, business, communications, art, law, policy and other academic fields may apply if they are seriously interested in building a career in aerospace.

What Will Selected Brooke Owens Fellows Receive?

The Brooke Owens Fellowship combines industry exposure with mentorship, community and professional development.

For the Class of 2027, the official announcement states that successful Fellows will:

Participate in a summer internship with a host company.

Receive one-on-one mentorship from professionals aligned with their areas of interest.

Attend a professional development summit with the other Fellows in their class.

The Brooke Owens Fellowship also describes its broader program as providing access to paid internships and executive-level mentorship from senior aerospace figures, including executives, astronauts and industry leaders.

Summer Aerospace Industry Experience

A major element of the program is meaningful exposure to the aerospace industry.

The 2027 program announcement states that accepted Fellows will participate in a summer internship at a host company. This provides students with the opportunity to move from classroom learning into professional aerospace environments and develop practical experience in the sector.

Past Fellows have worked across areas such as:

Rocket propulsion

Satellite operations

Mission planning

Aerospace policy

STEM outreach

Engineering

Software

Space systems

Research

Communications

Other aerospace-related functions.

The fellowship is therefore relevant not only to students pursuing highly technical engineering careers but also to those interested in the business, policy, communications and social dimensions of aerospace.

One-on-One Professional Mentorship

Mentorship is another central feature of the Brooke Owens Fellowship.

Each Fellow is connected with experienced professionals who can provide guidance as the Fellow enters or develops within the aerospace sector.

The Fellowship’s current mentor structure pairs Fellows with hand-selected mentors, with relationships beginning before Fellows start their summer positions. Mentors support Fellows as they prepare for professional roles, navigate workplace challenges and make decisions about their longer-term careers. Many mentor relationships reportedly continue beyond the official summer program.

The program’s mentors have included senior aerospace professionals, astronauts, executives, engineers and other industry leaders.

For a university student preparing to enter a highly specialized sector, this kind of direct professional access can help with:

Career planning.

Understanding aerospace industry pathways.

Developing professional networks.

Navigating early-career decisions.

Preparing for internships and employment.

Learning directly from experienced aerospace leaders.

Building professional confidence.

Identifying future areas of specialization.

Brooke Owens Professional Development Summit

Selected Fellows also participate in the annual Brooke Owens Summit, which brings members of the fellowship class together for professional development.

The 2027 announcement confirms that successful Fellows will attend a professional development summit alongside their cohort.

The summit adds an important cohort component to the program. Rather than completing an internship independently, Fellows become part of a community of students pursuing careers across different parts of aerospace.

This can create valuable relationships that continue as participants move into graduate education, industry, government, entrepreneurship, research and other aerospace careers.

A Long-Term Aerospace Community

The Fellowship is designed to create more than a one-summer experience.

The official Class of 2027 application describes Fellows as joining a lasting community of:

Peers.

Mentors.

Aerospace professionals.

Industry leaders.

This community-based model can be particularly valuable in aerospace, where professional relationships, specialized knowledge and industry networks can play an important role in career development.

The goal stated by the program is not simply to help students obtain their first aerospace opportunity, but to help develop people who may eventually shape the future direction of the industry.

More Than 400 Fellows Have Joined the Program

The Brooke Owens Fellowship has grown significantly since its creation.

According to the program’s September 2026 announcement:

418 undergraduate students have been accepted since the program began.

Fellows have come from nearly 40 U.S. states and territories.

Participants have represented 10 countries.

124 companies have hosted Fellows for summer internships.

105 mentors have helped support Fellows during their early careers.

Fellows have represented 147 schools.

These figures demonstrate that the fellowship has developed into an established pathway connecting undergraduate talent with the aerospace industry.

Detailed Eligibility Requirements

Before beginning an application, candidates should carefully confirm that they satisfy every current requirement.

The official Class of 2027 application page lists four principal eligibility conditions.

1. You Must Be an Undergraduate Student

Applicants must currently be undergraduate students.

They must have completed at least one year of coursework toward a bachelor’s or associate degree by the time they apply.

This means the program is aimed at students who have progressed beyond the very beginning of their undergraduate education.

2. You Must Be Interested in an Aerospace Career

Applicants must demonstrate genuine interest in pursuing a career in the aerospace industry.

Engineering and non-engineering career pathways are both accepted.

Candidates therefore should not assume that admission is restricted to:

Aerospace engineers.

Mechanical engineers.

Scientists.

Technical majors.

Students from other disciplines are encouraged to apply when they can demonstrate a credible connection between their interests and an aerospace career.

3. Applicants Must Identify as a Woman or Gender Minority

The Fellowship is specifically designed to increase opportunities for people underrepresented in aerospace because of gender.

The formal Class of 2027 eligibility criteria require applicants to identify as a woman or gender minority.

The organization’s FAQ specifically notes that this includes women and other gender minorities, including nonbinary and gender-nonconforming individuals.

4. Applicants Must Be at Least 18

Applicants must be 18 years of age or older.

Students From All Academic Majors Can Apply

One of the strongest features of the Brooke Owens Fellowship is that it recognizes the multidisciplinary nature of aerospace.

Students do not have to study aerospace engineering.

The official FAQ specifically welcomes applicants from academic backgrounds such as engineering, science, business, communications, art, law and policy, along with other disciplines.

The critical factor is whether the applicant has a genuine ambition to build a career and create an impact within aerospace.

Is There a Minimum GPA?

No minimum GPA is stated.

The Fellowship deliberately uses a broader approach to identifying talent.

The official application guidance notes that past Fellows have included students with very high GPAs as well as students whose academic records were considerably lower. The organization states that GPA represents only one imperfect way of assessing an applicant’s abilities and potential.

The FAQ similarly states that applications are reviewed holistically, with consideration given to factors including the applicant’s:

Personal statement.

Creative submission.

Recommendation.

Character.

Leadership.

Creativity.

Service.

Alignment with Fellowship values.

Students should therefore not automatically rule themselves out because they do not have a perfect academic record.

Documents You Need to Prepare

The application requires several supporting materials.

Applicants should start preparing these well before the October deadline because the process includes both conventional application documents and original creative work.

Updated Resume or CV

Applicants need their most recent resume or CV.

The Fellowship recommends making sure the document is accurate, polished and carefully proofread.

Relevant experience may include:

Academic activities.

Internships.

Paid employment.

Volunteer activities.

Independent projects.

Leadership positions.

Clubs.

Extracurricular activities.

Relevant community involvement.

Applicants should use the resume to show not merely academic performance but evidence that they could contribute effectively as a teammate and member of the aerospace community.

Academic Transcript

Applicants must submit their latest transcript.

Importantly, an unofficial transcript is acceptable, and the Fellowship actually encourages students to use unofficial versions when obtaining an official transcript would require paying a fee.

The transcript submitted must contain completed, graded coursework. The application guidance says it needs to include at least one full semester of completed grades, rather than only midterm results.

Applicants studying at a new institution who do not yet have an appropriate transcript there may use a transcript from their previous institution where applicable.

Note that the formal Class of 2027 eligibility section separately states that an applicant must have completed at least one year of coursework toward an associate or bachelor’s degree. Applicants should therefore ensure they satisfy the formal eligibility requirement, rather than interpreting the transcript-upload requirement as reducing it to one semester.

One Letter of Recommendation

Only one recommendation letter is required.

The recommender should be someone who genuinely knows the applicant and can provide meaningful evidence about their strengths, achievements and character.

Potential recommenders may include:

Teachers.

Professors.

Coaches.

Mentors.

Supervisors.

Club leaders.

Other appropriate professional or academic contacts.

A family member or personal friend should not be used as the recommender.

The letter should ideally provide evidence of the applicant’s character, creativity, consistency, service and impact in the communities in which they participate.

The official FAQ confirms that applicants need one recommendation and only one will be accepted.

Three Original Application Components

For 2027, applicants are asked to prepare three original works intended to help reviewers understand them beyond their transcript and resume.

These are:

A Personal Statement of no more than 600 words.

A Mission Alignment Essay of no more than 300 words.

A Multimedia Essay in a format other than a conventional written essay.

Together, these submissions are intended to provide insight into three broad dimensions:

Professional and academic interests.

Personal character, values and passions.

Commitment to service, community and creating opportunities for others.

Personal Statement: Maximum 600 Words

The personal statement allows applicants to communicate who they are beyond their academic record.

Applicants are encouraged to discuss the passions, values, experiences, goals and personal qualities that have shaped them and their ambitions.

The objective is not simply to repeat a resume.

A strong personal statement should help reviewers understand:

What motivates you.

What experiences have shaped you.

What matters to you.

What kind of person you are.

Where you want your career to go.

What you would contribute to the Brooke Owens community.

The program specifically encourages applicants to be authentic, specific and reflective.

Mission Alignment Essay: Maximum 300 Words

The 2027 application also includes a Mission Alignment Essay, limited to 300 words.

This component asks candidates to reflect on the Brooke Owens Fellowship’s mission of expanding aerospace opportunities for women and gender minorities.

Applicants should explain why this mission matters to them and how they hope to contribute to it throughout their careers.

Potential themes include:

Creating more inclusive professional environments.

Mentoring future students.

Expanding access to aerospace opportunities.

Addressing structural barriers.

Using leadership positions to support others.

Helping future professionals enter and thrive in aerospace.

The Fellowship encourages applicants to connect their answers with their lived experiences and consider how they could use future leadership or influence to make aerospace more welcoming and equitable.

Multimedia Essay: Show Creativity Beyond a Written Application

The Multimedia Essay is deliberately different from a conventional university application essay.

Applicants must not submit another traditional written essay.

Instead, they should communicate their ideas through a creative digital format.

Past formats have included:

Short videos.

Original songs.

Spoken-word pieces.

Animations.

Graphic designs.

Podcasts.

Comic strips.

Other creative digital formats.

Multimedia Submission Requirements

The submission must:

Be fully digital.

Require no physical mailing.

Be accessible through commonly available software.

Not require passwords or obscure software.

Be reviewable or playable in five minutes or less.

Remain below 250 MB in file size.

2027 Multimedia Essay Prompts

Applicants can respond creatively to one of the prompts listed for the Class of 2027.

The themes focus on:

A situation where the applicant had to be resourceful and work within constraints.

An experience serving a community and the resulting impact.

A project or activity in which the applicant became deeply engaged and demonstrated enthusiasm or creativity.

A situation where the applicant challenged an established system, norm or assumption.

How intentional decision-making has influenced the applicant’s actions and outcomes.

These prompts are designed to reveal qualities such as:

Resourcefulness.

Creativity.

Values.

Service.

Teamwork.

Enthusiasm.

Courage.

Independent thinking.

Leadership.

Self-awareness.

Intentionality.

Important File Submission Rules

Applicants should carefully test every file before submitting the application.

The Fellowship specifically warns that an application cannot be edited after submission.

Before submitting:

Test video links.

Confirm that file-sharing permissions work.

Make sure reviewers will not encounter access restrictions.

Check that all files open correctly.

Verify multimedia runtime.

Keep files below the required 250 MB limit.

Proofread written documents.

Confirm that the correct versions have been uploaded.

The application page also recommends including the relevant prompt directly with each original work so reviewers can easily identify the question being addressed.

One detail worth noting is that the current page explicitly identifies three original works, including the 300-word Mission Alignment Essay, while its later file-submission checklist lists the resume, transcript, recommendation letter, personal statement and multimedia essay without repeating the mission essay. Applicants should follow the live application portal carefully and prepare the Mission Alignment Essay because it is expressly listed as a required original work earlier on the official 2027 application page.

Are International Students Eligible?

Yes.

U.S. citizenship is not required.

The official FAQ states that students of all nationalities are welcome to apply, while the official application portal describes the fellowship as bringing together undergraduate students from around the world.

There is, however, an important practical qualification for international applicants.

Some aerospace opportunities may be subject to U.S. export-control or International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) restrictions. These requirements can limit eligibility for particular jobs or host-company roles based on citizenship or immigration status.

The Fellowship states that it works with Fellows individually to identify opportunities that fit their circumstances.

International students should therefore not interpret ITAR restrictions as a general ban on applying. They are eligible for the Fellowship itself, although the range of specific industry placements available to them may differ.

Virtual Information Sessions for the Class of 2027

The Fellowship is also hosting virtual information sessions for prospective applicants.

The published Class of 2027 sessions, with times given in EDT, are:

September 13, 2026 at 2:00 PM EDT

September 19, 2026 at 12:00 PM EDT, featuring international students

September 28, 2026 at 10:00 PM EDT

The session specifically featuring international students may be particularly useful for applicants with questions about citizenship requirements, aerospace placements and participation from outside the United States.

Ask a Brookie Application Support

Applicants who want advice from someone who has previously completed the fellowship process can use the program’s Ask a Brookie resource.

Past Fellows can provide guidance about matters such as:

Their fellowship experience.

How they approached application essays.

Internship preparation.

Joining the Fellowship community.

General application strategy.

For formal questions concerning eligibility, applicants are advised to use the Fellowship’s official eligibility information or contact its administration rather than relying solely on peer advice.

How Applicants Are Selected

The program emphasizes holistic assessment rather than relying on one numerical indicator.

According to its FAQ, applications are reviewed by aerospace professionals and Brooke Owens alumni.

The program considers the overall application, including personal and creative materials, recommendations and alignment with the Fellowship’s values. There is no published minimum GPA cutoff and no single factor automatically determines selection.

This makes it important for applicants to submit a coherent application where the different components reinforce one another.

For example:

Your resume shows what you have done.

Your transcript gives academic context.

Your recommendation provides an outside perspective.

Your personal statement shows who you are.

Your Mission Alignment Essay explains how your values connect with the program.

Your multimedia project demonstrates creativity, character and perspective.

What Makes a Strong Application?

While there is no guaranteed formula, applicants should pay particular attention to the qualities the Fellowship repeatedly emphasizes.

Be Authentic

Do not attempt to construct what you imagine a stereotypical aerospace candidate should look like.

The application is specifically designed to identify talent that may not always be recognized through conventional recruitment methods.

Demonstrate Service

Community involvement is an important theme throughout the application.

Show what you have actually done for other people, organizations or communities.

Demonstrate Aerospace Interest

You do not need to study aerospace engineering, but your application should make it credible that aerospace is genuinely part of your intended career direction.

Show Creativity

This matters particularly in the multimedia submission.

Use a format that strengthens your message rather than selecting something elaborate simply because it appears impressive.

Explain Your Values

The program wants to understand what motivates your decisions and how your values affect the way you work with others.

Proofread Everything

A creative application can still be weakened by avoidable mistakes, inaccessible links or unclear writing.

Start Early

The application includes several components requiring substantial reflection, plus a recommendation from another person. Waiting until the final day substantially increases the risk of an incomplete or technically flawed application.

Application Timeline

Applications officially opened at 12:00 AM EDT.

September 13, 2026

Application deadline at 11:59 PM EDT.

The Fellowship’s FAQ indicates that semifinalists are typically contacted within several weeks after applications close, with finalists subsequently selected through interviews and the complete class announced during the winter.

How to Apply for the Brooke Owens Fellowship Class of 2027

Prospective applicants should:

Confirm that they meet the Class of 2027 eligibility requirements.

Review the entire official application guide.

Create an account in the application portal.

Prepare an updated resume or CV.

Obtain an appropriate academic transcript.

Select one recommender and provide sufficient time for the recommendation.

Draft the Personal Statement within the 600-word limit.

Prepare the Mission Alignment Essay within the 300-word limit.

Select one multimedia prompt.

Create an original non-prose multimedia submission.

Confirm that the multimedia content is reviewable in five minutes or less.

Keep the relevant digital file under 250 MB.

Check links, permissions and file accessibility.

Review the entire application carefully.

Submit before October 4, 2026 at 11:59 PM EDT.

Do not wait until the final minutes because applications cannot be corrected after submission.

Apply for the Brooke Owens Fellowship Class of 2027

Why Students Interested in Aerospace Should Consider Applying

The Brooke Owens Fellowship offers something difficult to reproduce through an ordinary internship application: a combination of industry experience, structured mentorship, professional development and access to a continuing aerospace community.

The program’s record now includes hundreds of Fellows, more than one hundred host organizations and more than one hundred mentors. Its alumni network extends across aerospace research, engineering, operations, policy, technology, entrepreneurship and other areas.

For students who are serious about aerospace but have not traditionally seen themselves represented in the industry, the program is designed to create both access and a support structure for long-term career development.

Conclusion

Applications for the Brooke Owens Fellowship Class of 2027 provide undergraduate women and gender-minority students with an opportunity to build professional experience, receive mentorship from experienced aerospace professionals, participate in professional development and join an established community of emerging aerospace leaders.

The program is intentionally multidisciplinary. Applicants do not need to major in aerospace engineering, there is no published minimum GPA, and U.S. citizenship is not required. What matters is that applicants meet the undergraduate and age requirements, identify within the gender groups the program serves, and demonstrate genuine interest in pursuing an aerospace career.

The application is more extensive than a conventional internship form. Candidates need to prepare a resume or CV, academic transcript, one recommendation letter, a Personal Statement, a Mission Alignment Essay and a creative Multimedia Essay. Applicants should therefore start preparing their materials early.

Applications close October 4, 2026 at 11:59 PM EDT.

TITLE: Blue Catalyst Fund 2026: Funding and Technical Support for High-Quality Mangrove Conservation and Restoration Projects

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Blue Catalyst Fund 2026 is now accepting applications from eligible mangrove conservation and restoration projects around the world. The initiative is designed to help high-quality blue carbon projects overcome the technical, financial and development barriers that often prevent promising coastal ecosystem projects from reaching implementation and investment readiness.

Led by Fair Carbon and Finance Earth, the Blue Catalyst Fund combines catalytic funding with specialist technical expertise, project development assistance, financial and transaction advisory services, and capacity building. The initiative is particularly focused on helping credible mangrove projects move from early-stage feasibility and development toward projects that can attract larger-scale investment.

Applications are open globally, providing an important opportunity for organizations and project developers working to protect, restore and sustainably manage mangrove ecosystems and other coastal and marine environments.

The deadline for applications is 19:00 BST / 20:00 CEST on Thursday, 1 October 2026.

What Is the Blue Catalyst Fund?

The Blue Catalyst Fund is an initiative focused on accelerating the development of high-quality blue carbon projects, particularly those involving mangrove conservation and restoration.

Blue carbon refers to carbon captured and stored by coastal and marine ecosystems. Mangroves are particularly important because they can store significant amounts of carbon while simultaneously providing ecological, economic and social benefits to coastal communities.

Despite their importance, many potentially impactful mangrove and blue carbon projects struggle to progress beyond the early development stage. Project developers may have a strong conservation concept but lack the financial resources, technical expertise, data, regulatory knowledge or investment preparation needed to turn that concept into a bankable project.

The Blue Catalyst Fund is intended to address this gap by providing support throughout different stages of project development.

The Fund is open to eligible projects globally, including projects that are still establishing feasibility as well as projects that have already progressed beyond the feasibility stage and require additional support to become investment-ready.

Why Is the Blue Catalyst Fund Important?

Coastal ecosystems face significant environmental pressures, while the development of high-quality blue carbon projects remains relatively limited compared with the potential of these ecosystems.

According to information presented by the Fund, coastal ecosystems can sequester substantially more carbon per hectare than terrestrial forests. At the same time, a significant proportion of the world’s coastal wetlands has already been lost.

Mangrove degradation also has major climate implications. The destruction and degradation of mangroves releases carbon that had previously been stored within these ecosystems while reducing the ability of coastal areas to provide important environmental services.

Coastal wetlands are also closely connected to fisheries and the livelihoods of coastal populations. Healthy mangrove ecosystems can provide habitat and nursery grounds for marine species, help protect coastlines and contribute to climate adaptation.

The Fund therefore recognizes that investment in mangrove conservation and restoration can deliver benefits that extend well beyond carbon markets.

Key challenges facing blue carbon projects include:

High project development costs.

Complex technical requirements.

Difficulty establishing project feasibility.

Regulatory and policy uncertainty.

Limited access to appropriate early-stage finance.

Lack of technical expertise in some project locations.

Challenges preparing projects for investment.

A gap between early-stage project development and larger-scale capital.

Limited availability of high-quality blue carbon projects in the voluntary carbon market.

The Blue Catalyst Fund has been established to help address these barriers and create a pathway through which credible projects can progress toward implementation and investment.

What Support Does the Blue Catalyst Fund Provide?

One of the major strengths of the Blue Catalyst Fund is that it is not simply a conventional grant programme. Instead, it offers a combination of financial support, technical assistance, capacity building and investment-readiness support.

This integrated approach is intended to help project developers address multiple challenges at the same time.

1. Specialist Technical and Project Development Support

Selected projects can receive specialist technical and project development support covering different stages of the project-development process.

This can include assistance with establishing feasibility, project design and validation.

Technical support is particularly important for blue carbon projects because successful project development requires reliable environmental information, credible carbon accounting, appropriate methodologies, strong project design and consideration of regulatory and ecological requirements.

By providing access to specialist expertise, the Fund aims to help project developers improve the technical quality and credibility of their projects.

2. Early-Stage Catalytic Funding

The Blue Catalyst Fund provides early-stage catalytic funding to project developers.

Early-stage finance can be one of the most difficult forms of funding for conservation and nature-based projects to secure. Projects may have strong long-term potential but may not yet be sufficiently developed to attract conventional commercial investment.

Catalytic funding can help bridge this early-stage financing gap by supporting activities necessary to move a project toward greater technical and financial maturity.

3. Financial and Transaction Advisory

The Fund also provides financial and transaction advisory support.

This is important because developing a technically sound conservation project does not automatically make it investment-ready.

Project developers may need assistance understanding financial structures, preparing for investment, developing appropriate transactions and positioning their projects to attract follow-on capital.

The Fund’s financial and transaction advisory component is therefore designed to help projects move closer to the point where they can secure larger-scale investment.

4. Blue Carbon Academy and Capacity Building

The programme also includes capacity building through the Blue Carbon Academy.

Developing local technical expertise is an important component of creating sustainable blue carbon markets.

Rather than relying entirely on external technical expertise, capacity building can help strengthen knowledge and capabilities among people and organizations working in the project locations.

This can contribute to stronger local ownership and improve the long-term ability of project developers and stakeholders to manage and expand blue carbon initiatives.

How Does the Blue Catalyst Fund Financing Work?

The Fund’s financial support has an important distinction from a traditional grant.

Funding is provided as an unsecured contingent loan. The Fund does not take equity in the project, and repayment is required only if follow-on investment is secured.

This structure is designed to align the interests of the Fund with the success of the supported project.

For project developers, this can provide access to early-stage capital without requiring them to give up equity ownership in their project.

The contingent nature of the financing also means that repayment is linked to the project’s ability to secure subsequent investment.

Applicants should carefully review the official Applicant Information Pack to understand the specific financial arrangements, conditions and requirements applicable to their project.

What Types of Projects Is the Fund Looking For?

The current call is focused on high-quality mangrove conservation and restoration projects.

Projects can be at different stages of development. This means the opportunity is not restricted exclusively to projects that are already fully developed.

Eligible projects can range from those that are

Establishing feasibility;

Developing their project concept;

Progressing through project development;

Working toward project design and validation;

Seeking technical assistance;

Requiring early-stage catalytic funding; or

Preparing to progress toward investment readiness.

The Fund’s objective is to support credible projects through the development of barriers that stand between an early-stage concept and a project capable of attracting larger-scale investment.

Global Eligibility

One of the notable features of the 2026 call is its global scope.

Applications are open to eligible projects globally. Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to applicants from a particular country or continent.

This global approach is particularly relevant for mangrove conservation because mangrove ecosystems are distributed across tropical and subtropical coastal regions in many parts of the world.

Organizations and project developers working in eligible locations should therefore assess their projects against the Fund’s requirements rather than assuming that their country or region is excluded.

However, being located in an eligible country or region alone does not guarantee eligibility. Applicants should review the official Applicant Information Pack and complete the Fund’s eligibility process to determine whether their specific project qualifies.

Who Can Apply for the Blue Catalyst Fund?

The Blue Catalyst Fund is not primarily an individual scholarship or fellowship opportunity.

Instead, it is designed for project developers and organizations developing eligible mangrove conservation or restoration projects.

The relevant applicants are therefore expected to have a credible project rather than simply an individual interest in blue carbon or environmental conservation.

Potential applicants may include organizations and project-development entities working on mangrove conservation, restoration and related blue carbon activities, provided their projects meet the Fund’s eligibility requirements.

The opportunity may be particularly relevant to:

Mangrove conservation organizations;

Mangrove restoration initiatives;

Blue carbon project developers;

Environmental and conservation organizations;

Nature-based solutions organizations;

Organizations developing coastal ecosystem projects;

Public, private or nonprofit entities involved in eligible project development; and

Partnerships or project teams working toward investment-ready blue carbon projects.

Because the Fund uses a two-stage application process, applicants should carefully assess their project’s eligibility before submitting an application.

Application Process

The Blue Catalyst Fund uses a two-step application process.

Step 1: Eligibility Questionnaire

Applicants first need to complete an initial Eligibility Questionnaire.

This stage is intended to determine whether the proposed project meets the Fund’s basic eligibility requirements.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they have sufficient information about their project before beginning the application.

Step 2: Full Assessment

Projects that successfully pass the initial Eligibility Questionnaire will be invited to complete a more detailed Full Assessment.

The Full Assessment provides an opportunity for the Fund to examine the project in greater depth.

Because the process involves multiple stages, applicants are encouraged to apply early rather than waiting until the final deadline.

What Should Applicants Do Before Applying?

Potential applicants should take time to understand the programme before submitting their application.

The Fund specifically recommends reading the Applicant Information Pack before applying. This document provides important information about eligibility, the support available and the information applicants will need to provide at the different stages of the process.

Applicants should consider the following steps:

Read the Applicant Information Pack carefully.

This should be the first step before starting the application.

Assess project eligibility.

Confirm that the proposed project falls within the scope of the Fund.

Understand the project’s current development stage.

Applicants should be able to explain whether the project is establishing feasibility, progressing through development or approaching investment readiness.

Prepare project information.

Gather relevant technical, environmental, financial and organizational information.

Identify the project’s development needs.

Consider whether the project requires technical assistance, catalytic funding, capacity building, financial advisory or transaction support.

Complete the Eligibility Questionnaire.

Eligible projects that pass this initial stage may be invited to proceed to the Full Assessment.

Apply early.

Because the application process has two stages, applicants should not wait until the final day to begin.

Blue Catalyst Fund Impact Goals

The Blue Catalyst Fund has established ambitious long-term goals for coastal and marine ecosystem protection and restoration.

By 2035, the Fund aims to:

Protect or restore 150,000 hectares of coastal and marine ecosystems;

Avoid or remove 32 million tonnes of CO2e over the lifetime of supported projects; and

Unlock $275 million in private investment for coastal ecosystems and communities.

These targets demonstrate that the Fund is intended to operate beyond individual projects. Its broader objective is to contribute to the development of a stronger pipeline of high-quality coastal ecosystem projects capable of attracting private investment.

Why Mangrove Conservation Matters

Mangroves are among the world’s most valuable coastal ecosystems.

They provide important ecological services while also supporting communities that depend on coastal resources.

Climate mitigation

Mangroves capture and store carbon, making them important ecosystems in efforts to address climate change.

Protecting existing mangroves can also help prevent the release of carbon associated with ecosystem degradation.

Coastal protection

Mangrove forests can help reduce the impacts of waves, storms and coastal erosion.

This makes mangrove conservation relevant not only to climate mitigation but also to climate adaptation and resilience.

Fisheries and biodiversity

Mangrove ecosystems provide habitat and nursery areas for numerous marine and coastal species.

Healthy coastal wetlands can therefore contribute to fisheries productivity and broader biodiversity conservation.

Community livelihoods

Coastal communities may depend on mangrove ecosystems for fisheries, natural resources and other livelihood opportunities.

Well-designed conservation and restoration projects can therefore potentially deliver environmental benefits alongside social and economic benefits.

Organizations Behind the Blue Catalyst Fund

The Blue Catalyst Fund is led by Fair Carbon and Finance Earth, working alongside specialist technical partners.

Fair Carbon

Fair Carbon is a nonprofit organization focused on accelerating the protection and restoration of blue carbon ecosystems by addressing technical, financial and policy barriers that restrict the growth of the blue carbon market.

Finance Earth

Finance Earth is a regulated social enterprise providing advisory services to private, public and nonprofit organizations. According to the Fund’s information, the organization has advised on more than 100 projects across more than 30 countries.

NIKA

NIKA is a Singapore-based company providing carbon technical services using technologies and approaches including artificial intelligence, remote sensing and geospatial analysis.

TerraCarbon

TerraCarbon specializes in blue carbon and wetland restoration and has experience in developing nature-based carbon offset projects.

Silvestrum

Silvestrum specializes in nature-based solutions and brings together policy, scientific, technical, financial and legal expertise.

Together, these organizations provide the specialist expertise required to support projects through different aspects of blue carbon project development.

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Project Developers

The Blue Catalyst Fund offers more than a single source of financing.

For an eligible project, the combination of technical expertise, capacity building, catalytic finance and investment advisory can potentially address several of the major challenges faced during project development.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant for projects that have strong environmental potential but require additional support before they can attract larger-scale investment.

The Fund may be especially valuable for project developers that are struggling with the transition from:

Concept → Feasibility → Project Development → Validation → Investment Readiness → Follow-on Investment

By supporting this development pathway, the programme aims to help create a stronger pipeline of credible and investable coastal ecosystem projects.

Deadline for Applications

The deadline for applications to the current Blue Catalyst Fund call is

Thursday, 1 October 2026, at 19:00 BST / 20:00 CEST.

Applicants are encouraged to submit their applications early because the process consists of an initial Eligibility Questionnaire followed by a more detailed Full Assessment for projects that pass the first stage.

How to Apply

Interested project developers should first read the official Applicant Information Pack to determine whether their project is eligible and understand what information will be required.

Applications can then be submitted through the official Blue Catalyst Fund application process.

Applicants should rely on the official Fund documentation for the most detailed and authoritative eligibility and application requirements.

Visit HERE for more information about the Blue Catalyst Fund 2026.

Conclusion

The Blue Catalyst Fund 2026 represents an important opportunity for organizations and project developers working to protect and restore mangrove ecosystems and develop high-quality blue carbon projects.

Rather than focusing solely on financial support, the Fund takes a broader approach by combining technical expertise, project development assistance, catalytic funding, capacity building, financial advisory and transaction support. Its financing structure is also designed to support project development without taking equity, with repayment of the contingent loan required only when follow-on investment is secured.

With a goal of protecting or restoring 150,000 hectares of coastal and marine ecosystems, avoiding or removing 32 million tonnes of CO₂e, and unlocking $275 million in private investment by 2035, the initiative is positioned to contribute to the development of a stronger global blue carbon market.

Eligible mangrove conservation and restoration projects around the world should carefully review the Applicant Information Pack, assess their eligibility and begin the two-stage application process as early as possible.

TITLE: Prince Casper Foundation Impact Grant 2026/2027: ₦6 Million Education Grant for Educators Supporting Underserved Rural Communities in Nigeria

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Prince Casper Foundation Impact Grant 2026/2027 is an educator-led funding opportunity designed to support teachers and other education-sector professionals working to improve learning outcomes for children and young people in underserved and educationally disadvantaged communities across Nigeria.

The grant provides a total of ₦6 million to successful applicants across three funding tiers. Funding is intended to help educators address practical challenges affecting teaching and learning, including access to learning resources, digital technology, school infrastructure, teacher development, student-focused initiatives, inclusion, and other locally relevant educational needs.

Applications for the 2026/2027 cycle opened on 21 September 2026 and close on 6 November 2026.

About the Prince Casper Foundation Impact Grant

The Impact Grant is established by the Prince Casper Foundation, a nonprofit organization focused on advancing equitable and quality education, particularly for children and young people in underserved communities.

Rather than providing general-purpose funding, the Impact Grant is designed to place resources directly in the hands of educators who understand the educational challenges facing their students and communities.

The Foundation describes the grant as an opportunity to fund work that is already taking shape in classrooms and communities and help educators carry those initiatives further. The overarching purpose is to improve educational outcomes for students in rural, underserved, or otherwise educationally disadvantaged communities in Nigeria.

What the Impact Grant Supports

The 2026/2027 Impact Grant is organized around four priority focus areas. Applicants’ proposed projects should demonstrate relevance to one or more of these areas.

1. Learning Access

The Learning Access focus area addresses barriers that prevent students from participating effectively in education.

Projects may seek to improve:

Classroom readiness

Access to essential learning materials

Literacy development

Student attendance

Learning environments

Resources that help students participate more effectively in school

The objective is to address practical barriers that can interfere with students’ ability to learn and remain engaged in education.

2. Digital Innovation

Digital Innovation focuses on using technology to address educational challenges and prepare students for an increasingly technology-driven economy.

Potential initiatives may include:

Digital learning resources

ICT infrastructure

Digital literacy

Technology-enabled teaching

E-learning initiatives

Innovative approaches to classroom learning

Projects designed to reduce the digital divide

The Foundation’s broader education programmes also identify digital literacy training, ICT infrastructure, e-learning, blended learning, and mobile learning as areas of interest.

3. Educator Excellence

The Educator Excellence category focuses on improving teaching quality, classroom engagement, and educational leadership.

Projects can address areas such as:

Teacher professional development

Instructional improvement

Classroom engagement

Teaching resources

School leadership

Professional learning

Practical approaches that strengthen educational delivery

This reflects the Foundation’s wider emphasis on teacher development, continuous professional development, teaching grants, and recognition of educators.

4. Inclusive Empowerment

Inclusive Empowerment focuses on educational equity and initiatives that help students and families overcome barriers to participation and long-term development.

This may include projects that:

Reduce student dropout

Promote educational inclusion

Support vulnerable learners

Address barriers affecting disadvantaged students

Improve opportunities for girls and other underserved groups

Build longer-term resilience within families and communities

The Foundation’s broader mission also includes supporting girls, children with disabilities, inclusive education, and initiatives that address socioeconomic and geographic barriers to education.

How Much Funding Is Available?

A total of ₦6 million is available for the 2026/2027 Impact Grant cycle.

The funding will be distributed among 26 successful applicants across three grant tiers. Applicants do not choose which tier they want to receive. Instead, the selection committee determines the appropriate funding level based on factors such as the proposed project’s:

Scope

Cost

Educational need

Relevance

Potential impact

Grant Tier 1: Trailblazer

Grant amount: ₦500,000 per successful applicant

Number of grantees: 7

Total allocation: ₦3,500,000

The Trailblazer tier is intended for larger or more transformational projects capable of producing sustainable educational change and potentially inspiring similar initiatives elsewhere.

Grant Tier 2: Catalyst

Grant amount: ₦200,000 per successful applicant

Number of grantees: 6

Total allocation: ₦1,200,000

The Catalyst tier is designed to support promising initiatives with potential for development, growth, and longer-term impact.

Grant Tier 3: Launchpad

Grant amount: ₦100,000 per successful applicant

Number of grantees: 13

Total allocation: ₦1,300,000

The Launchpad tier provides smaller-scale seed funding intended to help educators turn early-stage concepts and classroom needs into practical initiatives.

Who Can Apply?

The Impact Grant is primarily designed for educators and education-sector professionals in Nigeria who are directly contributing to the learning, development, or educational outcomes of children and young people in primary or secondary education.

According to the Foundation’s current eligibility criteria, applicants must:

Be actively involved in the education sector in Nigeria.

Applicants should be directly involved in or contributing to the education, learning, development, or educational outcomes of children and young people in primary or secondary education.

Work in an underserved or disadvantaged community.

The applicant must be serving or working within a rural, underserved, or otherwise educationally disadvantaged community in Nigeria.

Demonstrate genuine financial need.

Applicants must show that financial constraints are affecting their ability to support or improve teaching and learning outcomes.

Present a relevant educational initiative or need.

The proposed project should address a genuine educational challenge and align with the Foundation’s mission and one or more of its four focus areas.

Demonstrate capacity to deliver the proposed project.

The selection process considers the applicant’s track record and evidence that they can realistically implement the proposed initiative.

Prince Casper Fellows are also eligible to apply, although the Foundation states that priority will be given to applicants who have not previously received the Impact Grant.

What Kind of Applicants Is the Grant Looking For?

The opportunity is particularly relevant to educators who are already working directly with students and have identified a specific problem that additional funding could help address.

Examples could include educators seeking resources for:

Classroom learning materials

Science or other subject-specific equipment

Digital learning initiatives

Technology and ICT resources

Literacy programmes

Student support initiatives

Teacher training or professional development

Infrastructure improvements

Projects addressing barriers to school participation

Initiatives supporting vulnerable or underserved learners

Practical projects designed to improve educational outcomes

The Foundation’s previous grant projects illustrate the range of interventions that can be supported. Previous initiatives have included practical science laboratory equipment, classroom resources, learning recovery programmes, student transportation solutions, and other education-focused interventions.

How Applications Are Evaluated

The Impact Grant uses a merit-based evaluation framework. The Foundation identifies several criteria that are considered when reviewing applications.

1. Demonstration of Need — 20%

Applicants should clearly establish the educational challenge they are addressing and explain the severity and urgency of the problem.

A strong application therefore needs to make the problem understandable rather than simply stating that additional funding is required.

2. Relevance and Alignment — 10%

The proposed initiative should align with the Impact Grant’s focus areas and the broader mission of the Prince Casper Foundation.

3. Impact Potential and Sustainability — 30%

This is the largest component of the published evaluation framework.

Applicants should demonstrate how the project can create meaningful educational change and whether its benefits can continue beyond the period of grant funding.

4. Feasibility and Implementation Plan — 20%

The Foundation considers whether the proposed project can realistically be delivered.

Applicants should therefore provide a credible plan, appropriate activities, and a realistic timeline that matches the identified educational need.

5. Applicant Capacity and Track Record — 10%

The Foundation considers evidence that the applicant has the ability and experience necessary to implement the proposed initiative.

This component may be assessed during the interview and reference-check stages.

6. Budget Clarity and Accountability — 10%

The proposed budget should be properly costed and proportionate to the project.

Applicants should also demonstrate that they can account responsibly for grant funds.

Application Requirements

The application process is conducted online through the Foundation’s application portal.

Applicants are expected to provide supporting information and documentation as part of their submission. The Foundation currently identifies the following key materials:

Letter of Intent

Applicants are required to submit a 500–750 word Letter of Intent explaining:

The educational challenge they are addressing

Their proposed solution

The expected impact of the project

The letter should provide a clear connection between the identified problem, the proposed intervention, and the expected educational outcomes.

Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide a CV containing relevant information such as:

Professional background

Teaching experience

Relevant achievements

Educational or community involvement

The application instructions also request a recent headshot.

Supporting Materials

Applicants may upload additional materials demonstrating their qualifications, experience, previous work, or potential impact.

The Foundation requests that supporting materials be submitted as a single PDF where applicable.

APPLY HERE

Application Timeline and Deadline

The current 2026/2027 application period is:

Opening date: 21 September 2026

Closing date: 6 November 2026

Deadline: 6 November 2026

The Foundation has listed the announcement of winners as TBA, meaning a specific winner-announcement date has not yet been provided on the current grant page.

Applicants should therefore prepare their materials in advance rather than waiting until the final day of the application period.

Read Full Details About This Opportunity HERE

Why This Grant Matters for Rural Education

Many education challenges are highly localized. A teacher working directly with students may understand a classroom’s needs more clearly than an outside organization because they experience those challenges every day.

The Impact Grant is structured around this principle by directing funding toward educators who are already working within the communities they seek to support.

Previous recipients provide examples of how this model can translate funding into practical educational interventions. The Foundation’s published 2025 Impact Grant results show projects involving science laboratory equipment, classroom learning materials, student support, and other community-specific initiatives.

For example, one previous project equipped a Biology laboratory to provide students with opportunities for practical science learning rather than relying solely on theoretical instruction.

Another published project involved responding to disruption affecting students’ physical learning space in the Makoko waterfront community by establishing a temporary educational location.

These examples demonstrate the range of educational challenges that educator-led funding can address.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants should focus on clearly communicating the connection between the educational problem and the proposed solution.

A useful application should clearly establish:

The problem: What specific educational challenge exists in your school or community?

The affected learners: Who is experiencing the problem and how?

The proposed intervention: What exactly will the grant fund?

The expected results: What changes should occur after implementation?

The budget: How much will each activity or resource cost?

The implementation plan: When and how will the project be delivered?

Sustainability: How can the benefits continue after the grant is used?

Your experience: What evidence demonstrates that you can successfully deliver the project?

This approach is particularly relevant because the Foundation’s evaluation framework gives substantial attention to impact potential, feasibility, demonstrated need, applicant capacity, and budget accountability.

Conclusion

The Prince Casper Foundation Impact Grant 2026/2027 provides a funding opportunity for educators working to address educational challenges in underserved and rural communities across Nigeria.

With ₦6 million available across 26 grants, the programme covers three funding levels and four major educational focus areas: Learning Access, Digital Innovation, Educator Excellence, and Inclusive Empowerment. The grant is intended for education-sector professionals who understand the needs of their students and can demonstrate a practical, feasible plan for creating meaningful educational impact.

The application deadline is 6 November 2026. Prospective applicants should review the official eligibility requirements, prepare their Letter of Intent, CV, supporting documents, and project information carefully before submitting their application.

TITLE: Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice 2026: African Storytellers Can Receive Up to US$4,000 in Funding

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice 2026 initiative, a major opportunity for African journalists, content creators, podcasters, vloggers, muralists, data visualizers and other storytellers who want to reshape public conversations about climate justice across the continent.

Delivered by Africa No Filter (ANF) in partnership with Comic Relief, Voices for Climate Justice is a 12-month storytelling initiative designed to support African creators to develop compelling, research-informed narratives that connect some of the continent’s most urgent challenges: climate change, climate finance, debt, gender inequality and fossil fuel extraction.

The program will select approximately 15 to 20 storytellers and provide them with training, mentorship, content amplification and grants of up to US$4,000 to produce stories capable of generating public discussion, improving understanding of climate justice and inspiring action.

Application Deadline: September 25, 2026, at 6:00 PM GMT

Applications are being considered on a rolling basis, meaning eligible applicants are encouraged to submit their applications well before the final deadline rather than waiting until the last day.

About the Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice Initiative

Climate change is not only an environmental problem. Across Africa, it is closely connected with economic inequality, public debt, access to natural resources, development financing, gender inequality and the long-term consequences of fossil fuel extraction.

Africa No Filter’s Voices for Climate Justice initiative seeks to make these complex relationships easier for ordinary people to understand through effective storytelling.

One of the central issues highlighted by the initiative is the way climate finance reaches African countries. Although Africa has historically contributed a relatively small share to the global climate crisis, many African countries continue to face severe climate impacts while receiving a significant proportion of climate-related financing through loans rather than grants.

According to the framing of the Voices for Climate Justice call, increased reliance on loans can deepen existing debt pressures on African governments. In some cases, countries already facing heavy debt obligations may subsequently depend on oil, gas and mineral resources as financial or economic assets, potentially encouraging further extraction.

The consequences can extend far beyond government finances. Fossil fuel extraction, drilling and associated development can affect communities that depend on land, agriculture, water and local ecosystems for their livelihoods.

The initiative particularly wants storytellers to explore how these issues affect women and girls, who may experience disproportionate consequences when communities lose access to agricultural land, water resources or livelihoods.

Voices for Climate Justice therefore aims to help African audiences understand that conversations about climate change cannot be separated from questions about debt, gender, development, justice, economic systems and fossil fuels.

What Does the Program Want Storytellers to Do?

Africa No Filter is seeking creators who can turn complicated climate justice issues into stories that are understandable, compelling and relevant to communities.

Applicants are encouraged to propose original storytelling ideas exploring the relationship between:

Climate justice

Climate finance

Public and national debt

Gender

Fossil fuel extraction

Community livelihoods

Climate reparations

Economic inequality

Environmental justice

African communities’ experiences of climate change

The proposed content should not simply describe environmental problems. Successful ideas are expected to help audiences understand how these different issues are connected and why those connections matter.

Storytelling can potentially take several formats, including:

Journalism and written articles

Digital content

Video storytelling

Podcasts

Vlogs

Murals and public art

Data visualization

Social media storytelling

Other creative and accessible storytelling formats

Selected storytellers will create content that is relevant to their country or community while Africa No Filter helps amplify the resulting work to reach broader audiences.

What Will Selected Participants Receive?

The Voices for Climate Justice initiative provides considerably more than financial support.

1. Grants of Up to US$4,000

Successful participants may receive grants of up to US$4,000 to develop and produce their approved storytelling projects.

The funding is intended to help storytellers turn their proposed concepts into substantive content capable of contributing to the climate justice conversation.

2. Climate Justice Training

Selected storytellers will receive training designed to strengthen their understanding of climate justice.

This is important because the initiative addresses technically and politically complex issues involving climate finance, public debt, gender, natural resources and fossil fuels.

3. Data Storytelling Training

Participants will also learn how to use evidence and data effectively in storytelling.

Rather than producing content based solely on opinion, participants will be encouraged to translate research and evidence into stories that audiences can understand.

4. Narrative Framing Support

Africa No Filter places considerable emphasis on how Africa is represented.

Participants will therefore receive support in narrative framing, helping them develop stories that avoid simplistic or stereotypical descriptions of African communities.

5. Mentorship

The initiative will provide mentorship to participating storytellers throughout the program, helping them strengthen their ideas and storytelling approaches.

6. Collaboration With Researchers and Partners

Participants will work with researchers and relevant partners to create content that is accurate and informed by evidence.

This can be particularly valuable for storytellers addressing topics such as climate finance, debt or fossil fuel extraction, where technical accuracy is essential.

7. Content Amplification

Africa No Filter will support the amplification of participants’ stories, potentially allowing their work to reach audiences beyond their existing platforms or communities.

8. Participation in a 12-Month Initiative

Voices for Climate Justice runs for approximately 12 months, giving successful applicants an extended period to develop their knowledge, produce content and participate in the initiative.

Overall, between 15 and 20 storytellers are expected to receive support through the program.

Who Is Africa No Filter Looking For?

Africa No Filter is particularly interested in storytellers capable of combining creativity with public engagement.

Potential applicants include:

Journalists

Content creators

Podcasters

Vloggers

Data visualizers

Muralists

Digital storytellers

Creators using visual, written, audio or multimedia storytelling

Applicants should already have an established platform or demonstrated way of reaching an audience.

The program is therefore particularly suited to people who are already producing content and now want to use their skills and audience to explore climate justice issues in greater depth.

Detailed Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility conditions before submitting an application.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be over 18 years old.

Individual Applicants Only

The initiative is designed for individual storytellers.

Organizations and agencies are not eligible to apply as applicants.

Geographic Requirement

Applicants must be based in one of the following countries:

Mozambique

Uganda

Nigeria

Angola

Chad

Republic of the Congo

Tanzania

South Sudan

Malawi

Zambia

The call specifically seeks African storytellers from these countries.

Platform and Audience Requirements

Applicants must have an active and engaged platform through which they can reach an audience.

Examples include:

Podcast

YouTube channel

TikTok

Instagram

Publication or media outlet

Data visualization portfolio

The platform should have been consistently active for more than one year.

Minimum Audience for Content Creators and Data Visualizers

Content creators and data visualizers should have a combined audience of at least 5,000 followers across platforms such as:

Instagram

TikTok

Twitter/X

Snapchat

Journalists may demonstrate their reach differently, such as through the circulation or audience reach of the publication for which they produce content.

Content Commitment

Applicants must be willing to produce sustained content rather than a single isolated post.

Successful applicants are expected to commit to sharing a minimum of four pieces of content addressing the program’s gender, debt and fossil fuel themes over a period of at least six months.

Applicants should therefore consider whether they have sufficient time, audience access and commitment to continue working on the subject after selection.

Requirement for Independent Content Creators

Content creators must be unsigned, meaning they should not be represented by an agent.

Journalists may be associated with a media organization or publication, provided that the work they submit and the relevant content rights remain their own.

This requirement is important because applicants need sufficient ownership and control over the content created through the initiative.

What Topics Should Proposed Ideas Address?

Proposed storytelling ideas must connect meaningfully with the initiative’s core thematic areas:

Climate Justice

The story should help audiences understand who is responsible for climate change, who experiences its consequences, and whether climate responses distribute costs and benefits fairly.

Debt

Applicants can examine how government borrowing, debt repayment and climate finance affect national development choices and communities.

Gender

Stories should consider how women, girls and different groups experience climate impacts differently, including questions surrounding livelihoods, land, water, unpaid care work and economic vulnerability.

Fossil Fuels

Applicants can explore the relationship between debt, economic pressure and the extraction of oil, gas or other resources.

The strongest proposals are likely to demonstrate how these subjects overlap rather than treating them as completely separate issues.

Africa No Filter’s Approach to Better Representation

A major component of the program is Africa No Filter’s wider mission to transform narratives about Africa.

The organization argues that damaging narratives are not changed simply by producing more content. Instead, the underlying stories and assumptions shaping perceptions of Africa must also change.

Africa No Filter describes its approach around the idea of both telling stories better and telling better stories.

Telling stories better involves producing nuanced, ethical and balanced narratives about African societies.

Telling better stories involves creating new narratives capable of expanding how Africa and Africans are represented rather than repeatedly relying on narrow stereotypes.

Participants in Voices for Climate Justice are therefore expected to approach storytelling ethically and avoid representations that present African communities merely as passive victims.

The initiative particularly emphasizes ethical and survivor-centered storytelling when discussing gender-related impacts.

What Makes a Strong Application?

Africa No Filter indicates that grantees will be assessed according to several important factors.

Originality

The proposed story should offer an original angle rather than repeating familiar climate narratives.

Relevance to Africa No Filter’s Mission

Applicants should demonstrate an understanding of Africa No Filter’s commitment to storytelling that challenges stereotypes and presents African people with complexity and agency.

Alignment With the Gender-Debt-Fossil Fuel Focus

Ideas must clearly connect to the program’s key themes rather than addressing climate change only in general terms.

Audience Reach or Community Standing

Applicants should demonstrate that they have an existing audience, platform or meaningful standing within the community they intend to reach.

Community Access

The proposed idea should involve communities to which the applicant has realistic access.

Applicants should therefore avoid proposing projects dependent on communities or locations they cannot practically reach.

Application Requirements

Applicants are expected to prepare a storytelling pitch describing their thinking around climate reparations and climate justice and explaining how their proposed story could influence the way debt, gender and climate justice are discussed and understood.

The official application portal also requires a short written explanation of no more than 300 words explaining why the applicant believes their proposed narrative should be selected for the Voices for Climate Justice campaign.

Applicants will also need to provide:

An online application through the official portal

Information about their proposed storytelling concept

Links to their platforms

Relevant social media, publication or community network details

Information about the audience or community they intend to reach

Evidence demonstrating platform reach or engagement

A description of how the proposed story addresses the campaign themes

The official portal currently refers to a written pitch deck as part of the expression of interest. Applicants should follow the exact fields and format displayed on the live Africa No Filter submission portal when applying.

Language Requirements

Content produced under the initiative must be delivered in either:

English

French

Applicants should therefore be capable of developing the required content in at least one of these languages.

Application and Selection Timeline

The official timeline is as follows:

Applications Open

August 12, 2026

Applications are being accepted and reviewed on a rolling basis.

Final Application Deadline

September 25, 2026, at 6:00 PM GMT

Applicants should not assume that submitting close to the deadline provides any advantage because applications are already being reviewed as they arrive.

Shortlisting and Virtual Interviews

Following the application review, a selection committee will shortlist candidates.

Shortlisted candidates will then meet the jury through virtual interviews.

Notification

Only shortlisted candidates will receive notification regarding their application status, with this expected by the first week of October 2026.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Africa No Filter will review applications submitted through its official application portal.

The assessment is expected to consider:

How well the idea addresses gender, debt and fossil fuels.

The originality and creativity of the storytelling concept.

Alignment with Africa No Filter’s mission.

The applicant’s platform reach.

Audience analytics or publication circulation.

Community reach or influence where relevant.

The applicant’s ability to communicate the proposed narrative effectively.

Commitment to ethical storytelling.

Access to communities relevant to the proposed story.

Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Applications That Will Not Be Considered

Africa No Filter has identified several circumstances that can make a submission ineligible.

Applications may be rejected if they are:

Incomplete

Submitted through post instead of the official application system

Submitted by email instead of the official portal

Based on inappropriate or unethical material

Vulgar, racist, sexist or homophobic

Reinforcing harmful stereotypes about Africa or Africans

Presenting African communities in ways that deny them agency

Associated with accounts or posts where audience engagement has been artificially increased through paid boosting

Applicants should therefore make sure that both their application and existing platform activity are consistent with the values of the initiative.

Why the Voices for Climate Justice Initiative Matters

The Voices for Climate Justice program recognizes that public understanding of climate change depends significantly on the stories people encounter.

Technical discussions around climate finance, debt sustainability, fossil fuel extraction and gender inequality can be difficult for broad audiences to follow.

Storytellers can bridge this gap.

A journalist can investigate how climate debt affects government spending.

A data visualizer can transform complicated financing information into accessible graphics.

A podcaster can document the experiences of communities affected by extraction.

A muralist can translate climate justice into public art.

A digital creator can explain complex relationships between gender, debt and fossil fuels to thousands of people through social platforms.

By bringing different forms of storytelling together, Voices for Climate Justice aims to strengthen African voices within debates that directly affect the continent.

Important Advice for Applicants

Because applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, prospective applicants should consider applying before the final deadline.

Applicants should also avoid submitting a broad proposal that merely states that climate change is a serious problem.

A more competitive concept is likely to identify a specific community, specific problem, clear narrative angle and defined audience.

The application should show:

What story you want to tell

Why that story matters

Who is affected

How gender, debt and fossil fuels connect to the issue

Who your audience is

How you will reach that audience

What storytelling format you will use

Why your existing platform makes you well positioned to tell the story

How your approach challenges stereotypes rather than reinforcing them

What meaningful conversation or action you hope the story will generate

Where possible, applicants should also have verifiable audience statistics, publication circulation information or other evidence of community reach ready before beginning the application.

Deadline

The final deadline for the Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice 2026 opportunity is:

September 25, 2026, at 6:00 PM GMT

Applications opened on August 12, 2026 and are being assessed on a rolling basis. Applicants are therefore strongly encouraged to submit ahead of the deadline.

Conclusion

The Africa No Filter Voices for Climate Justice 2026 initiative offers an important opportunity for African storytellers who want to combine storytelling, research and climate advocacy.

With up to US$4,000 in grant support, professional training, mentorship, collaboration with researchers, narrative development assistance and content amplification, the 12-month program gives selected creators the resources to develop stories capable of reaching audiences and influencing conversations about climate justice.

For journalists, content creators, podcasters, vloggers, muralists and data visualizers based in the eligible African countries, this initiative provides an opportunity not simply to document climate change but to explain the deeper relationships between climate finance, debt, fossil fuels, gender and justice.

Applicants with an established audience, an original storytelling concept and a clear commitment to nuanced and ethical African narratives should consider preparing their submission as early as possible before the September 25, 2026 deadline.
