TITLE: MIASA Fellowships 2026–2028 at the University of Ghana: Research Fellowships in Sustainable Governance, Democracy, Peace and Environmental Transformation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Maria Sibylla Merian Institute for Advanced Studies in Africa (MIASA) at the University of Ghana is offering a range of residential research fellowship opportunities for scholars in the Humanities and Social Sciences whose research aligns with the Institute’s overarching theme of Sustainable Governance.

Based at the University of Ghana’s Legon campus in Accra, MIASA provides an interdisciplinary research environment where scholars can dedicate time to developing, analysing and writing their research while engaging with researchers from Ghana, Germany, other African countries, Europe and beyond.

The Institute offers several fellowship models, including Interdisciplinary Fellow Groups, Individual Fellowships, Tandem Fellowships, Artists in Residence and Self-funded Fellowships. These different formats allow researchers to participate either independently, collaboratively across disciplines, or through research partnerships between Africa and Germany.

For the current 2026–2028 opportunities, MIASA’s open calls include four residential fellowships within the Interdisciplinary Fellow Group on Sustainable Democracy, up to five individual residential fellowships for the 2027/28 academic year, and an ongoing opportunity for self-funded residential fellowships. The current official MIASA fellowship page lists the application deadline for the first two calls as 15 October 2026.

About the Maria Sibylla Merian Institute for Advanced Studies in Africa

The Maria Sibylla Merian Institute for Advanced Studies in Africa, commonly known as MIASA, was established in 2018 within the College of Humanities at the University of Ghana, Legon.

The Institute was created through a collaboration between the University of Ghana and a consortium of German research and higher-education institutions, including:

University of Freiburg

Goethe University Frankfurt

German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA)

German Historical Institute Paris (GHIP/DHIP)

MIASA is dedicated to strengthening high-quality research in the Humanities and Social Sciences while creating stronger intellectual connections between African and European research communities.

The Institute is funded through German federal research funding, with co-funding from the University of Ghana. Its fellowship programme is administered in collaboration with the University of Freiburg.

MIASA’s Central Research Theme: Sustainable Governance

At the heart of MIASA’s intellectual programme is the concept of Sustainable Governance.

MIASA approaches governance broadly. Rather than viewing governance only through governments, states and formal institutions, the Institute examines the interaction between formal and informal rules and practices that shape public affairs.

These practices are understood within their historical, social, material and cultural contexts and as part of everyday life.

This broad understanding makes MIASA particularly suitable for interdisciplinary research.

Researchers can investigate how institutions, communities, cultures, social movements, political systems and everyday practices influence the way societies are governed and how more sustainable forms of governance can be developed.

MIASA’s Three Main Research Areas

MIASA’s research programme is organised around three major thematic corridors.

1. Sustainable Environmental Transformation

This area examines questions surrounding environmental sustainability and the transformation of societies in response to environmental challenges.

Potential research may explore relationships between:

Environmental change and governance.

Sustainability and public policy.

Communities and natural resources.

Political institutions and environmental transformation.

Social practices and sustainability.

Local knowledge and environmental governance.

Development and environmental justice.

2. Sustainable Conflict Management and Peace

The second major research corridor focuses on conflict, peace and sustainable approaches to managing social and political tensions.

Research in this area can examine:

Conflict management.

Peacebuilding.

Social cohesion.

Political conflict.

Community-level conflict resolution.

Institutions and peace.

Traditional and informal mechanisms of conflict management.

Post-conflict societies.

The relationship between governance and sustainable peace.

3. Sustainable Democracy

The third major research corridor focuses on democracy and democratic governance.

MIASA’s current Sustainable Democracy call highlights questions surrounding the interaction between formal and informal institutions, citizenship, political life, knowledge systems, languages, cultures, historical experiences, indigenous governance practices and decolonial approaches to democracy.

Researchers may therefore investigate topics involving:

Democratic institutions.

Citizenship.

Political participation.

Traditional authorities.

Religious organisations.

Civil society.

Grassroots movements.

NGOs.

Community governance.

Indigenous governance systems.

Decolonial approaches.

Political cultures.

Knowledge systems and democracy.

Everyday democratic practices.

Cross-Cutting Research Topics

MIASA’s research programme extends beyond its three main thematic corridors.

The Institute also welcomes research addressing important intersectional and cross-cutting issues, including:

Landownership and land acquisition.

Migration and mobility.

Restitution of colonially acquired cultural objects.

African cities.

Human rights.

These areas can be examined independently or in connection with the broader themes of environment, democracy and peace.

The interdisciplinary nature of MIASA means that researchers can approach these questions from different disciplinary and methodological perspectives.

MIASA Fellowship Types

MIASA operates several different fellowship models. Each has a different structure and purpose.

1. Interdisciplinary Fellow Groups

The Interdisciplinary Fellow Group (IFG) programme is one of MIASA’s central mechanisms for bringing researchers from different academic backgrounds together around a shared research question.

MIASA funds two IFGs per year.

An IFG generally brings together a group of four fellows, including two convenors. One of the two convenors must be from the University of Ghana.

The groups normally work together for four months.

The purpose is to investigate research questions that cannot be adequately addressed from a single academic discipline.

An IFG could therefore bring together researchers with expertise in areas such as political science, history, anthropology, sociology, law, environmental studies, cultural studies or related Humanities and Social Sciences disciplines.

How IFGs are selected

Selection takes into consideration:

Academic excellence.

The composition of the group.

Fit with MIASA’s main theme or sub-themes.

Originality of the proposed research theme.

Interdisciplinary character.

Feasibility of the research plan.

International character.

Potential contribution to the intellectual environment at MIASA and the University of Ghana.

The current IFG opportunity is focused on Sustainable Democracy.

Current Sustainable Democracy IFG

MIASA is currently inviting applications for four residential fellowships within the Interdisciplinary Fellow Group on “Sustainable Democracy” (IFG 16).

The fellowship period is:

1 September – 31 December 2027

The current application deadline is:

15 October 2026 at 24:00 UTC

Successful candidates are expected to be informed in March 2027.

The current call describes Sustainable Democracy as one of MIASA’s three major research corridors and encourages research examining institutions, citizenship, everyday political life, knowledge systems, languages, cultures, historical experiences, indigenous governance and decolonial perspectives.

Research Requirements for the Current IFG

Applicants are expected to provide a research project that clearly fits the Sustainable Democracy theme.

The application dossier includes:

A front page with general applicant and project information.

A project proposal of no more than five pages.

A CV in tabular form of no more than two pages.

A publication list highlighting the applicant’s most important publications.

The front page should include information such as:

Name.

Email address.

Webpage, where applicable.

Date of doctorate.

Current position and affiliation.

Institution and business address.

Research field.

Project title.

Research project abstract of no more than 150 words.

The two most important reasons the research project fits the Sustainable Democracy IFG.

Whether the applicant would like to serve as a co-convenor.

The project proposal should address:

Project title.

Project abstract.

Aims.

Theoretical framework.

Methodology.

Work and time plan.

Innovative potential.

Originality.

Relevance to Sustainable Democracy.

Added value of conducting the research at MIASA and the University of Ghana.

Added value of conducting the research collaboratively as a team.

Bibliographical references.

Applications must comply with the specified formatting requirements, including Arial, 11-point font, 1.5 line spacing and 2.5 cm margins.

2. Individual Residential Fellowships

MIASA also offers Individual Residential Fellowships, allowing scholars to work on their own research projects while becoming part of the Institute’s intellectual community.

The current open call provides up to five individual residential fellowships for the 2027/28 academic year.

Each fellowship lasts between:

3 and 6 months

The earliest possible start date is:

1 September 2027

The latest possible end date is:

31 August 2028

The application deadline is:

15 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC

Successful candidates are expected to be informed in March 2027.

Who can apply for the Individual Fellowship?

The current call is open to scholars at both junior and senior levels who have been awarded their doctoral degree at least three months before the beginning of the fellowship.

Applications are welcomed from disciplines within the Humanities and Social Sciences, provided that the proposed research fits MIASA’s intellectual programme.

What Can Individual Fellows Research?

Individual fellows can develop a research project connected to MIASA’s thematic areas.

The research project may be:

At the conceptual stage.

In the middle of the research process.

At the final stage.

Focused on analysing existing data.

Focused on writing up research findings.

An important point is that data collection cannot be the main purpose of a MIASA fellowship.

The fellowship is primarily designed to provide researchers with time and space for intellectual work, reflection, discussion and writing.

Residential Nature of the Fellowships

MIASA’s fellowships are residential.

This means successful fellows are expected to be physically present at the Institute at the University of Ghana, Legon campus in Accra.

The residential structure is intended to encourage:

Academic exchange.

Research collaboration.

Intellectual discussion.

Writing.

Interdisciplinary interaction.

Networking.

Participation in MIASA activities.

For the current fellowship programmes, only limited periods of absence are normally permitted and must be approved in accordance with MIASA’s requirements.

This is an important consideration for international applicants because the fellowship is not simply a remote research grant.

3. Tandem Fellowships

MIASA’s Tandem Fellowship programme is designed to strengthen research relationships between Africa and Germany.

A tandem consists of:

One researcher based at an African institution or country.

One researcher based at a German institution.

The two researchers work together on a joint research project.

The fellowship normally lasts between 3 and 5 months, according to MIASA’s fellowship programme information.

The central objective is to strengthen sustainable research partnerships between African and German scholars in the Humanities and Social Sciences.

What makes a strong tandem proposal?

MIASA places particular importance on:

The fit of the research topic with MIASA’s intellectual programme.

Alignment with the overall aims of MIASA.

Academic excellence.

Quality and originality of the research.

Potential contribution to a sustainable Africa-Germany research alliance.

The tandem model is therefore particularly valuable for researchers who already have, or are developing, meaningful academic collaboration across Africa and Germany.

4. Artists in Residence

MIASA also has an Artists in Residence programme.

This programme recognises that artists can contribute important perspectives to academic research.

Artists can work alongside Interdisciplinary Fellow Groups and researchers and use artistic approaches to engage with complex global issues.

The programme is based on the idea that art can introduce disruptive or alternative ways of thinking into academic discussions, while scientific research can also stimulate and enrich artistic practice.

Artist-in-residence stays are generally three months.

Potential areas of artistic engagement include issues connected with:

Sustainability.

Environment.

Conflict and peace.

Democracy.

African cities.

Restitution.

Migration.

This fellowship type is particularly relevant to artists whose creative practice engages with social, political, cultural or environmental questions.

5. Self-Funded Residential Fellowships

MIASA also accommodates researchers who have their own financial support.

The Self-funded Residential Fellowship is intended for researchers who either:

Have external funding for their stay; or

Are on paid leave from their home institution, such as during a sabbatical.

The fellowship lasts between:

3 and 6 months

Applicants must have been awarded their doctoral degree at least three months before the start of the fellowship.

There is no fixed annual deadline for this opportunity.

Applications can be submitted at any time, but they must be submitted at least four months before the intended fellowship start date.

The earliest possible start date currently listed is 1 September 2026.

What does MIASA provide to self-funded fellows?

Self-funded fellows receive:

Office space.

Organisational assistance.

Access to the MIASA research environment.

The opportunity to participate in the Institute’s intellectual activities.

Because this is a self-funded arrangement, applicants need to demonstrate that they have funding available for their fellowship period.

A full-time presence at MIASA is required, subject to the Institute’s rules on approved periods of absence.

Funding and Financial Support

Funding arrangements differ according to the type of fellowship.

For the current individual residential fellowship programme, MIASA indicates that fellows affiliated with an institution may have salary or teaching-substitution costs covered for the fellowship period, with payments made directly to their home institution, subject to the programme’s maximum amount.

The current published information lists a maximum of €6,925 per month for such arrangements. Fellows who do not have employment may receive an individual monthly grant.

For fellows coming from outside Accra, MIASA may provide an accommodation allowance of up to €1,500 per month and reimburse travel costs at the beginning and end of the fellowship, subject to the programme’s conditions. Family allowances may also be available for fellows relocating to Accra with family members.

Applicants should carefully check the specific financial terms of the fellowship call they are applying for because funding conditions may vary between fellowship types.

The Importance of Interdisciplinary Research at MIASA

One of MIASA’s distinguishing characteristics is its emphasis on interdisciplinary research.

Many of the major challenges facing African societies cannot be adequately understood through one academic discipline.

Questions about democracy, migration, environmental transformation, conflict, land ownership or human rights often involve political, economic, historical, social and cultural dimensions simultaneously.

MIASA therefore creates an environment where researchers from different academic backgrounds can exchange perspectives and develop research that crosses conventional disciplinary boundaries.

This can be particularly valuable for researchers whose projects require:

Comparative perspectives.

Historical analysis.

Social research.

Political analysis.

Cultural interpretation.

Interdisciplinary methodologies.

African and European perspectives.

Local and global approaches.

MIASA’s Commitment to African Knowledge Production

A major objective of MIASA is to contribute to reducing global asymmetries in knowledge production.

The Institute also aims to bridge cultural and intellectual divides between Anglophone and Francophone Africa.

This is particularly significant because African research is often discussed within international academic systems in which knowledge production, funding and publication networks can be unevenly distributed.

MIASA seeks to provide a platform where African researchers and international scholars can interact, collaborate and develop research on questions that are relevant to African societies while contributing to broader global scholarship.

Research Networking and Collaboration

MIASA serves as a hub for exchange and collaboration among researchers from:

Ghana.

Germany.

Other African countries.

European countries.

Other regions of the world.

The residential model helps facilitate sustained interaction between fellows.

Researchers can exchange ideas through:

Seminars.

Workshops.

Research discussions.

Public lectures.

Conferences.

Collaborative projects.

Informal academic interaction.

This makes the fellowship valuable not only for completing an individual research project but also for building long-term academic networks.

MIASA Events and Academic Activities

MIASA’s activities extend beyond its fellowship programme.

The Institute organises a wide range of academic and public events, including:

Thematic conferences in Ghana and other African countries.

Policy conferences.

The Annual Anton Wilhelm Amo Lecture.

Writing workshops for early-career African researchers.

Publishing workshops.

Female Academic Careers in Africa workshops.

Research seminars.

Public lectures and other scholarly activities.

These programmes contribute to MIASA’s broader goal of connecting academic research with society, policy and the arts.

Publication and Dissemination of Research

MIASA supports researchers in disseminating their findings through several channels.

Research produced through the Institute may be shared through:

MIASA’s working paper series.

UGSpace.

MIASA’s academic blog.

Peer-reviewed academic journals.

Books.

External research publications.

This provides fellows with opportunities to communicate their work to both academic and wider audiences.

For Individual Fellowships

The current 2027/28 individual fellowship call is open to junior and senior scholars who hold a doctoral degree awarded at least three months before the start of the fellowship. Applicants should work within the Humanities or Social Sciences and propose research that fits MIASA’s thematic programme.

For Interdisciplinary Fellow Groups

IFGs can include both junior and senior researchers.

Junior researchers are expected to have successfully completed their doctorate by the time the fellowship agreement is concluded, with the published requirements specifying that the doctorate should have been completed at least three months before the fellowship begins.

The research must fit the IFG’s specific theme and demonstrate academic quality, originality and interdisciplinary value.

For Self-Funded Fellowships

Self-funded fellowships are open to junior and senior scholars who have completed their doctorate at least three months before the fellowship begins and who have their own external funding or paid leave from their home institution.

For Artists in Residence

The Artist in Residence route is intended for artists whose creative work can meaningfully interact with MIASA’s research themes and fellow groups.

Countries, Regions and Nationality

MIASA’s fellowship programme has a strong international and Africa-focused orientation.

The Institute’s collaborations involve Ghana, Germany, other African countries and European institutions, and its stated objectives include strengthening research exchange between Africa and Europe.

However, the current open calls provided by MIASA do not state a race or ethnicity restriction, nor do they state that applicants must be citizens of a particular African country.

For the individual fellowship, the published eligibility criteria focus on the applicant’s doctoral qualification, research level, academic excellence and fit with MIASA’s thematic programme rather than nationality.

The Tandem Fellowship is more geographically specific because it requires a pair consisting of one researcher based in Africa and one based in Germany.

Applicants should therefore distinguish between nationality and institutional location: for some programmes, where a researcher is based can be more important than citizenship.

Languages of Application

MIASA accepts applications in English and French for the self-funded fellowship and has used both languages across its fellowship programme.

This reflects the Institute’s objective of strengthening intellectual connections across Anglophone and Francophone Africa.

Applicants should nevertheless check the specific call they are applying to for the applicable language requirements.

How Applications Are Evaluated

MIASA states that fellows and groups are selected by its distinguished Academic Advisory Board.

Selection is merit-based and takes into consideration factors such as:

Academic excellence.

Quality of the research proposal.

Originality.

Relevance to MIASA’s research programme.

Interdisciplinary potential.

Feasibility.

Composition of research groups.

International character.

Potential contribution to the intellectual environment at MIASA and the University of Ghana.

For individual fellowships, particular importance is placed on the academic excellence of the applicant and the quality and innovation of the fellowship proposal. MIASA also states its commitment to gender balance.

What a Strong MIASA Research Proposal Should Demonstrate

A strong proposal should go beyond describing an interesting topic.

It should clearly establish:

The research problem — What important issue is being investigated?

The research question — What specifically will the researcher seek to understand?

The theoretical framework — Which concepts or theories guide the research?

The methodology — How will the research be conducted?

Originality — What makes the research new or distinctive?

Relevance — Why does the research matter?

MIASA fit — Why is MIASA the appropriate environment for the project?

University of Ghana connection — What value does conducting the research at Legon provide?

Feasibility — Can the project realistically be advanced during the fellowship?

Contribution to academic life — How can the fellow contribute to discussions and activities at MIASA?

The proposal should make it easy for reviewers to understand why the project belongs within MIASA’s intellectual environment.

Residential Research at the University of Ghana

The location of the fellowship is an important part of the programme.

MIASA is based on the Legon campus of the University of Ghana in Accra.

Researchers are expected to work from the Institute and participate actively in its academic environment.

This means the fellowship is particularly suitable for scholars who value:

Face-to-face academic discussion.

Interdisciplinary collaboration.

Research seminars.

Networking.

Academic writing.

Intellectual exchange.

Engagement with African research environments.

It is not simply a financial award for research that can be undertaken entirely from the applicant’s home country.

Apply HERE

Can Former MIASA Fellows Apply Again?

Yes.

MIASA allows former fellows to apply for a second research stay provided that the new application is for a different fellowship type.

For example, a former Interdisciplinary Fellow Group participant can subsequently apply for an individual fellowship.

This provides researchers with the possibility of maintaining a longer-term relationship with MIASA while pursuing different research formats.

Current Open Calls and Deadlines

The current MIASA fellowship page lists the following open opportunities:

Sustainable Democracy Interdisciplinary Fellow Group

Four residential fellowships

Fellowship period: 1 September–31 December 2027

Location: University of Ghana, Legon

Theme: Sustainable Democracy

Application deadline: 15 October 2026 at 24:00 UTC

Successful candidates expected to be informed: March 2027

Individual Residential Fellowships

Up to five fellowships

Learn More About This Opportunity HERE

Why Consider a MIASA Fellowship?

It provides an opportunity to become part of an international academic environment based in Ghana while engaging with researchers working on some of the most important questions facing African societies and the wider world.

The fellowship can help researchers:

Advance an existing research project.

Develop a new research idea.

Complete academic writing.

Analyse existing research material.

Strengthen interdisciplinary perspectives.

Develop international research networks.

Collaborate with researchers from different countries.

Connect with African and European academic communities.

Participate in seminars and public academic activities.

Develop future collaborative research projects.

Contribute to debates around sustainable governance.

For researchers based in Africa, the programme can also provide an opportunity to strengthen connections with international research networks without separating the research from African academic environments.

For international researchers, MIASA offers an opportunity to conduct research within the intellectual environment of the University of Ghana and develop deeper connections with African scholarship and research communities.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should carefully consider several factors before preparing an application.

1. Your research must fit MIASA

A strong academic project may still be unsuitable if it does not connect clearly with Sustainable Governance or one of MIASA’s research areas.

2. The fellowship is residential

Applicants should be prepared to spend the required period at MIASA in Accra.

3. Data collection should not be the main purpose

For the individual fellowship, the programme is primarily designed for research development, analysis, reflection and writing rather than using the entire fellowship period for primary data collection.

4. Read the specific call carefully

Different fellowship types have different requirements.

An applicant should not assume that the requirements for an individual fellowship are identical to those for an IFG, tandem fellowship or self-funded fellowship.

5. Demonstrate MIASA’s added value

Applicants should explain why conducting the research at MIASA and the University of Ghana would strengthen their project.

This could involve access to intellectual networks, interdisciplinary exchange, African scholarship, academic events or potential collaborators.

Conclusion

The Maria Sibylla Merian Institute for Advanced Studies in Africa (MIASA) offers a distinctive platform for researchers seeking to advance high-quality scholarship in the Humanities and Social Sciences while engaging with questions of sustainable governance, democracy, peace, environmental transformation and other major issues affecting African societies.

Its fellowship programme is particularly notable for its commitment to interdisciplinary research, international collaboration and the strengthening of African knowledge production.

Through Interdisciplinary Fellow Groups, researchers can work collectively on complex questions requiring expertise from different disciplines. Through Individual Fellowships, scholars can dedicate several months to their own research projects within the stimulating environment of the University of Ghana. Tandem Fellowships create structured research partnerships between scholars based in Africa and Germany, while Artists in Residence bring creative perspectives into academic discussions. Researchers who already have external funding can also make use of the Self-funded Residential Fellowship pathway.

The current open calls provide particularly timely opportunities for researchers interested in Sustainable Democracy and for junior and senior scholars seeking individual residential research fellowships for the 2027/28 academic year. Both major current calls have an application deadline of 15 October 2026, while the self-funded fellowship accepts applications throughout the year provided they are submitted at least four months before the intended start date.

For researchers whose work fits MIASA’s intellectual programme, the opportunity represents a chance to do more than complete a research project. It offers access to an international community of scholars, interdisciplinary exchange, academic networking, the University of Ghana’s Legon research environment and a platform for contributing to broader debates about Africa, governance, sustainability, democracy, peace and social transformation.

Applicants should therefore approach the opportunity strategically: select the fellowship type that best matches their career stage and research plans, develop a strong and original proposal, demonstrate clear alignment with MIASA’s themes, and explain convincingly why the research would benefit from being undertaken within the MIASA and University of Ghana environment.

TITLE: EvalYouth Asia 2026 Core Group: Call for Applications for Young and Emerging Evaluators

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EvalYouth Asia (EYA) has opened applications for its 2026 Core Group, inviting passionate young and emerging evaluators to take an active leadership role in strengthening evaluation practice, youth leadership, networking, and collaboration across the Asia-Pacific region.

This is a volunteer leadership opportunity for individuals who are passionate about evaluation and evidence-informed decision-making and who want to contribute to a regional network supporting the next generation of evaluation professionals.

Selected Core Group members will have the opportunity to contribute to strategic planning, develop initiatives for young and emerging evaluators, strengthen national and regional networks, build partnerships, and help shape the future direction of EvalYouth Asia.

About EvalYouth Asia

EvalYouth Asia is a regional platform that works to strengthen the participation and leadership of young and emerging evaluators (YEEs) within the evaluation community across Asia and the Pacific.

Established in 2019, EvalYouth Asia has focused on creating opportunities for young and emerging evaluators to connect with one another, develop their professional capacities, exchange knowledge, and participate meaningfully in the wider evaluation community.

The network is driven by volunteers who contribute their time, expertise, and ideas to create a stronger and more connected community of emerging evaluation professionals.

Through its activities, EvalYouth Asia seeks to provide young evaluators with opportunities to:

Build professional networks across the Asia-Pacific region.

Exchange knowledge and experiences in evaluation.

Develop their leadership and professional skills.

Participate in regional and global evaluation discussions.

Engage with evaluation associations and other professional organizations.

Strengthen youth participation in the evaluation field.

Contribute to the development of the next generation of evaluation leaders.

For 2026, EvalYouth Asia is seeking new Core Group members who can contribute their skills, perspectives, leadership, and commitment to the continued development of the regional network.

What Is the EvalYouth Asia 2026 Core Group?

The Core Group is a volunteer leadership group responsible for helping guide and implement the activities of EvalYouth Asia.

Joining the Core Group is more than simply becoming a member of a professional network. Successful applicants will be expected to actively participate in planning, decision-making, community engagement, partnerships, and the development of initiatives benefiting young and emerging evaluators across the region.

Core Group members will work collaboratively with other volunteers and regional partners to help strengthen the evaluation community and create opportunities for young professionals.

Key Responsibilities of Core Group Members

Selected members will contribute to a range of strategic, programmatic, networking, and community-building activities.

1. Provide Strategic Leadership

Core Group members will help provide strategic leadership for the EvalYouth Asia network.

This includes contributing ideas, participating in discussions about the network’s direction, and helping identify activities and initiatives that can strengthen opportunities for young and emerging evaluators throughout the Asia-Pacific region.

Members will therefore have an opportunity to contribute not only to individual activities but also to the broader development and direction of the regional network.

2. Design and Implement Regional Initiatives

Core Group members will help design and implement initiatives that support young and emerging evaluators.

These initiatives may contribute to areas such as:

Professional development.

Capacity building.

Knowledge exchange.

Networking.

Youth leadership.

Engagement within the evaluation community.

Collaboration between young evaluators and established evaluation organizations.

Members will be able to contribute their own ideas and expertise while working collaboratively with other members of the Core Group.

3. Strengthen National and Regional EvalYouth Networks

Another important responsibility will be supporting the development and strengthening of EvalYouth networks at both the national and regional levels.

Core Group members will work to encourage collaboration among existing networks and support efforts to establish new country chapters where appropriate.

This provides an opportunity for individuals interested in regional network development and youth-led professional communities to contribute to a broader evaluation movement.

4. Build Partnerships With Key Stakeholders

Core Group members will also contribute to partnership-building efforts.

They will work to establish and strengthen relationships with:

Evaluation associations.

Development organizations.

Professional evaluation networks.

Other relevant stakeholders.

Regional and international partners.

The objective is to expand opportunities for youth engagement and create stronger connections between young and emerging evaluators and the wider evaluation ecosystem.

5. Collaborate With Regional Evaluation Organizations

The Core Group will work closely with organizations and networks involved in evaluation across the region.

This includes collaboration with the Asia Pacific Evaluation Association (APEA), Voluntary Organizations for Professional Evaluation (VOPEs), and other regional partners.

Such collaboration can help create stronger links between young and emerging evaluators and established evaluation institutions and professional networks.

6. Participate in Monthly Core Group Meetings

Core Group members are expected to participate in monthly Core Group meetings.

These meetings provide an important space for members to:

Discuss ongoing activities.

Plan future initiatives.

Make decisions.

Coordinate responsibilities.

Share updates.

Discuss challenges and opportunities.

Contribute ideas for strengthening the network.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to maintain an ongoing commitment throughout their term.

7. Engage With EvalYouth Asia Members

Core Group members will also be expected to regularly engage with the wider EvalYouth Asia community.

This includes supporting community-building activities and helping maintain an active, connected, and collaborative network of young and emerging evaluators across the region.

Community engagement is an important part of the role because the Core Group’s activities are intended to respond to the needs and interests of the wider EvalYouth Asia membership.

Volunteer Commitment

The EvalYouth Asia Core Group is a voluntary leadership opportunity.

Selected members are expected to dedicate approximately 20 hours per month to Core Group responsibilities.

This means applicants should carefully consider whether they have sufficient time and availability to make a meaningful contribution alongside their existing academic, professional, or other commitments.

In addition to the regular monthly commitment, each Core Group member is expected to lead or co-lead at least one major EvalYouth Asia initiative or workstream during their term.

This requirement emphasizes the active leadership component of the opportunity.

Applicants should therefore be prepared not only to attend meetings but also to take responsibility for delivering a substantial initiative or area of work.

Who Should Apply?

EvalYouth Asia is looking for young and emerging evaluators across the Asia-Pacific region who are interested in contributing to the development of evaluation practice and youth leadership.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to individuals who demonstrate the following qualities:

Passion for Evaluation

Applicants should have a genuine interest in evaluation and evidence-informed decision-making.

An interest in understanding what works, generating and using evidence, improving programs, and supporting better decision-making can be particularly relevant to the role.

Commitment to the Evaluation Community

Applicants should be committed to strengthening the evaluation community within the Asia-Pacific region.

This includes an interest in supporting other young and emerging evaluators and contributing to a stronger regional evaluation ecosystem.

Collaborative Approach

Core Group work involves collaboration with other volunteers, evaluation organizations, development organizations, and regional and international partners.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable working with others and contributing constructively to collaborative initiatives.

Proactive and Willing to Contribute

The role requires active participation rather than passive membership.

Applicants should be willing to contribute their:

Time.

Skills.

Knowledge.

Ideas.

Professional experience.

Leadership.

The expected commitment of approximately 20 hours per month makes availability and willingness to contribute important considerations.

Interest in Regional and International Collaboration

Applicants should be interested in working with diverse partners across the Asia-Pacific region and potentially engaging with regional and international organizations connected to evaluation and development.

Why Join the EvalYouth Asia Core Group?

Becoming part of the Core Group can provide an opportunity to contribute to the development of a regional professional community while gaining practical experience in leadership, collaboration, networking, and initiative management.

Key areas of potential professional development include:

Regional Networking

Members can engage with young and emerging evaluators and evaluation stakeholders across the Asia-Pacific region.

Leadership Experience

Core Group members will participate in strategic decision-making and are expected to lead or co-lead a major initiative or workstream.

Program and Initiative Development

Members can gain practical experience in designing and implementing activities intended to support young evaluators.

Partnership Building

Working with evaluation associations, development organizations, VOPEs, APEA, and other partners can provide exposure to regional professional networks.

Knowledge Exchange

The network provides a platform for sharing ideas, experiences, and knowledge related to evaluation.

Youth Leadership in Evaluation

The Core Group provides an avenue for young and emerging evaluators to contribute directly to the development of the evaluation community and strengthen youth leadership within the field.

Geographic Scope of the Opportunity

The Core Group opportunity is intended for young and emerging evaluators across the Asia-Pacific region.

The announcement does not provide a specific list of eligible countries. Therefore, applicants should interpret the geographic eligibility according to EvalYouth Asia’s definition and scope of the Asia-Pacific region and confirm any country-specific requirements through the official application information.

There is also no race, ethnicity, or racial-group restriction stated in the announcement.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the EvalYouth Asia 2026 Core Group is:

October 1, 2026

Applicants should ensure that they submit their applications before the stated deadline.

Because the announcement provides the deadline only as October 1 and does not specify a particular time or time zone, applicants should check the official application instructions for the exact submission time and any additional requirements.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants should carefully consider how their experience, interests, and skills align with the responsibilities of a Core Group member.

When preparing an application, it can be useful to demonstrate:

Your interest in evaluation and evidence-informed decision-making.

Your experience or involvement in evaluation, where applicable.

Your interest in youth leadership and professional community development.

Your ability to collaborate with people from different backgrounds and organizations.

Your availability to contribute approximately 20 hours per month.

Your leadership potential, particularly examples of initiatives, projects, or activities you have helped organize or lead.

Your interest in regional collaboration across the Asia-Pacific region.

Your ideas for supporting young and emerging evaluators and strengthening the EvalYouth Asia network.

Applicants should also consider which skills they could contribute to the Core Group, whether in research, evaluation, communications, partnerships, project management, community engagement, training, networking, or another relevant area.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The EvalYouth Asia 2026 Core Group is a volunteer leadership opportunity for young and emerging evaluators interested in strengthening evaluation practice, youth leadership, networking, and collaboration across the Asia-Pacific region.

Since its establishment in 2019, EvalYouth Asia has worked to create opportunities for young and emerging evaluators to connect, develop their capacities, exchange knowledge, and participate meaningfully in the evaluation community. The 2026 Core Group will continue this work by bringing together committed volunteers who can provide leadership, develop initiatives, strengthen national and regional networks, build partnerships, and engage with members.

Selected members will be expected to dedicate approximately 20 hours per month and lead or co-lead at least one major initiative or workstream during their term.

Young and emerging evaluators across the Asia-Pacific region who are passionate about evaluation, evidence-informed decision-making, collaboration, and regional professional development are encouraged to consider applying.

TITLE: Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship 2026: Apply for Up to $5,000 in Project Funding and Global Mentorship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship 2026, a year-long leadership and impact programme powered by the PeaceJam Foundation. The programme is designed to help emerging young changemakers strengthen projects addressing peace, justice, equity, human rights, environmental protection and other urgent social challenges.

Selected participants will receive structured mentorship, tailored coaching, access to an international community of peacebuilders and up to US$5,000 in project funding. The funding is intended to help fellows develop, improve or expand work they have already started.

This programme is particularly relevant to emerging leaders whose projects have moved beyond the idea stage but have not yet achieved significant scale. Applications officially opened on September 1, 2026, and the official deadline is September 28, 2026.

Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship 2026 at a Glance

Programme name: Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship 2026

Organiser: Billion Acts of Peace, powered by the PeaceJam Foundation

Programme duration: One year

Delivery format: International programme with virtual sessions and opportunities to participate in PeaceJam events

Financial support: Up to US$5,000 in project funding

Mentorship: Ten monthly sessions with experienced mentors

Additional support: Tailored one-to-one coaching

Applications opened: September 1, 2026

Official application deadline: September 28, 2026

Official application page: Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship

About the Billion Acts of Peace Initiative

Billion Acts of Peace is an international movement associated with the PeaceJam Foundation. It encourages individuals, youth groups and organisations to address the root causes of challenges affecting their communities through practical and measurable acts of peace.

PeaceJam’s wider model brings together young people, community leaders and Nobel Peace Laureates to encourage peaceful leadership, social responsibility and community action. Rather than treating peace only as the absence of violence, the initiative approaches peacebuilding through justice, inclusion, education, human rights, environmental sustainability and equitable access to essential resources.

The Changemaker Fellowship builds on this approach by investing in emerging leaders who have already begun implementing solutions. It combines financial assistance with mentorship, leadership development, project support and international community-building.

What the Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship Offers

The fellowship provides several connected forms of support intended to help early-stage projects become stronger, more sustainable and more effective.

1. Up to US$5,000 in Project Funding

Selected fellows can receive up to US$5,000 to develop and grow their peacebuilding projects.

The funding is intended for the work being developed by each fellow. Depending on the nature of the project, funds may potentially support activities such as:

Community outreach and mobilisation

Educational workshops and awareness campaigns

Project materials, supplies and equipment

Digital tools and communications

Research or community data collection

Volunteer coordination

Pilot activities

Training programmes

Monitoring and evaluation

Organisational development

Expansion into additional communities

Applicants should understand that this is project funding of up to US$5,000, not a guaranteed US$5,000 personal stipend. The amount awarded may depend on the project, its proposed use of funding and the organisers’ assessment.

The published information does not separately promise a salary, living allowance, international travel funding, accommodation or visa support.

2. Year-Long Mentorship

The fellowship includes a year-long mentorship structure intended to help participants become more capable and effective leaders.

According to PeaceJam’s 2026 programme announcement, fellows will participate in ten monthly sessions with world-class mentors. These sessions are expected to combine leadership learning, professional guidance, networking and project development.

The mentorship model draws upon competencies and lessons connected with PeaceJam’s Nobel Peace Laureates and broader network of experienced changemakers. However, applicants should not assume that every session will be delivered personally by a Nobel Peace Laureate.

3. Tailored One-to-One Coaching

In addition to group mentorship sessions, the official programme announcement identifies tailored one-to-one coaching as one of the fellowship benefits.

This individual support may help fellows examine challenges specific to their projects, including:

Clarifying the project’s strategy

Strengthening leadership and decision-making

Defining intended outcomes

Identifying operational weaknesses

Developing partnerships

Improving project sustainability

Measuring community impact

Planning responsible growth

Individual coaching can be especially useful for early-stage founders and community organisers who may not yet have access to experienced advisers.

4. A Global Community of Changemakers

Fellows will join a wider international community that may include:

Other Billion Acts of Peace fellows

PeaceJam participants and alumni

Community organisers

Youth leaders

Nonprofit professionals

Mission-driven entrepreneurs

Business professionals

Peacebuilding practitioners

PeaceJam network members

Nobel Peace Laureates

This network can provide fellows with peer learning, encouragement, collaboration opportunities and exposure to projects working on similar challenges in other countries.

The community element is a core part of the programme. Applicants should therefore be prepared not only to receive support but also to contribute ideas, experience and constructive feedback to other participants.

5. PeaceJam Conferences and Virtual Events

Fellows may be invited to participate in PeaceJam conferences, virtual events and other opportunities aligned with their goals.

These activities may allow participants to:

Present their work to broader audiences

Meet experienced changemakers

Learn from projects operating in different contexts

Build international relationships

Identify potential partners

Increase the visibility of their initiatives

Explore future leadership and development opportunities

An invitation to an event should not automatically be interpreted as a guarantee that travel or accommodation costs will be covered. Applicants should review the conditions of each event separately.

6. Recognition Through an Award Ceremony

The official 2026 announcement also identifies an award ceremony celebrating the impact of participating changemakers. This recognition may provide fellows with additional visibility and an opportunity to communicate the progress achieved through their projects.

The Ten Key Issue Areas

Projects considered for the fellowship must relate to at least one of the ten issue areas identified by Billion Acts of Peace:

Advancing Women and Children

Projects may address gender equality, women’s empowerment, maternal welfare, protection from violence, child rights, girls’ education or economic opportunities for women.

Alleviating Extreme Poverty

Initiatives may focus on livelihoods, food security, economic inclusion, employment, entrepreneurship, access to essential services or support for underserved communities.

Clean Water for Everyone

Relevant work may include access to safe drinking water, sanitation, hygiene education, water conservation or community water infrastructure.

Conflict Resolution

This area includes dialogue, reconciliation, mediation, violence prevention, social cohesion and peaceful solutions to community conflict.

Education and Community Development

Projects may improve access to education, literacy, youth development, vocational training, digital skills or community participation.

Ending Racism and Hate

Initiatives may challenge discrimination, xenophobia, hate speech, prejudice, racial injustice or exclusion based on identity.

Global Health and Wellness

This area can include mental health, public health education, disease prevention, disability inclusion, healthcare access and community well-being.

Human Rights for All

Projects may advance civil rights, social justice, legal awareness, freedom, dignity, equality or the protection of marginalised groups.

Non-Proliferation and Disarmament

Relevant initiatives may address nuclear disarmament, weapons reduction, gun violence, arms control and education about the human consequences of armed conflict.

Protecting the Environment

Projects may focus on climate action, conservation, biodiversity, waste management, environmental education, pollution prevention or sustainable use of natural resources.

A project may address more than one issue area. However, applicants should identify the areas most directly connected to their activities rather than selecting several categories without demonstrating a clear relationship.

The Six PeaceJam Leadership Competencies

The fellowship’s mentorship and leadership-development activities are structured around six PeaceJam competencies.

Positive Power and Purpose

This competency helps participants understand their strengths, values and sense of purpose. Fellows are encouraged to use their influence responsibly and direct their abilities toward meaningful change.

Creating Inclusive Communities

Participants explore how to build teams and communities where different people can contribute and feel respected. The competency covers collaboration, participation, supportive relationships and inclusive leadership.

Compassionate Leadership

Fellows are encouraged to lead with empathy, fairness and concern for the experiences of others. Compassionate leadership does not mean avoiding difficult decisions; it means making decisions while recognising their human consequences.

Peacebuilding

This competency develops the ability to understand conflict, address root causes, encourage constructive dialogue and promote justice. It treats lasting peace as something that must be actively created.

Global Citizenship and Interconnectedness

Participants consider how local decisions connect with wider regional and global issues. This competency promotes awareness of shared humanity, responsibility toward the planet and cooperation across borders.

Change Agent

The final competency focuses on taking action. Fellows are expected to move beyond identifying problems and demonstrate that they can organise, advocate, implement solutions and encourage others to participate.

The Type of Projects the Programme Seeks

The programme is not restricted to formally registered charities. Projects may take several forms, including:

Emerging nonprofit organisations

Grassroots community initiatives

Activist projects

Youth-led campaigns

Community-based programmes

Social enterprises

Mission-driven businesses

Educational initiatives

Advocacy movements

Informal but organised community projects

What matters most is that the initiative already exists in some form and is addressing a real problem. A concept that has not yet been tested or implemented is unlikely to demonstrate the level of progress expected by the fellowship.

The ideal project is somewhere between having recently started and gaining early traction. It should be serious and active but not yet significantly scaled.

Evidence of progress could include:

Activities already delivered

People or communities reached

Partnerships established

Volunteers recruited

Testimonials from participants

Photographs or videos of activities

Social media or website links

Early impact data

Pilot results

Media coverage

Letters of support

Application Process

Applicants should use the official Billion Acts of Peace fellowship page and follow the application instructions provided there.

The application form is reported to request information covering:

Personal and contact details

Country of residence and time zone

The name of the applicant’s project

A concise description of the peacebuilding project

The problem the project is addressing

The length of time the project has been operating

The project’s current stage of development

The Billion Acts issue areas connected to the project

The applicant’s motivation for joining the programme

What could be achieved with up to US$5,000

The applicant’s definition of success after one year

The most difficult challenge currently faced by the project

Links or evidence demonstrating the applicant’s work

Availability to participate in fellowship sessions

Any accessibility or participation support required

Applicants should check the live form carefully because individual questions and word limits may be updated.

How Applications Will Be Assessed

The programme indicates that applications will be assessed primarily on their substance and alignment with the fellowship rather than polished English or sophisticated writing.

A competitive application should demonstrate:

A genuine commitment to peace, justice, equity or social change

An existing initiative rather than an untested idea

A clear understanding of the problem being addressed

Evidence that the applicant has already taken action

A realistic explanation of how funding would strengthen the work

Openness to mentorship, feedback and accountability

Willingness to collaborate with other fellows

Capacity to participate throughout the programme

Potential for meaningful and sustainable community impact

The organisers encourage applicants to communicate in their own authentic voices and advise against relying on generative artificial intelligence to write application answers. Applicants should therefore use personal examples, actual experiences and evidence from their work.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Explain the Problem Clearly

Describe the specific challenge affecting the community. Avoid relying only on broad statements such as “poverty is a major issue.” Explain who is affected, where the problem exists and why current responses are insufficient.

Demonstrate Existing Action

Show what has already been done. Even a small pilot activity is stronger than a large plan with no evidence of implementation.

Connect the Project to the Issue Areas

Identify the Billion Acts issue area most closely connected to the project. Explain the relationship through the project’s actual activities and intended outcomes.

Present a Practical Funding Plan

Although a detailed formal budget may not be required at the initial stage, applicants should be prepared to explain how the funding would be used. The proposed activities should be realistic within the maximum US$5,000 allocation.

Define Measurable One-Year Results

Applicants should explain what success would look like after one year. Strong outcomes could include people trained, communities reached, partnerships developed, services delivered or measurable improvements experienced by participants.

Be Honest About Current Challenges

The fellowship is intended to provide support. Applicants should not pretend that their projects have no weaknesses. A thoughtful explanation of operational, financial or leadership challenges can demonstrate self-awareness and readiness for mentorship.

Show Commitment to the Full Programme

The fellowship is more than a funding opportunity. Applicants should demonstrate that they value coaching, monthly sessions, peer learning, accountability and participation in the international community.

Application Deadline and Important Clarification

Applications officially opened on September 1, 2026.

The official Billion Acts of Peace fellowship page and PeaceJam Foundation’s official LinkedIn announcement both state that applications close on:

September 28, 2026

The official landing page does not currently specify an exact closing time or time zone. At least one secondary report states that the linked application form displays a later date. Applicants should not rely on that later date and should submit no later than September 28, 2026, preferably several days early.

Important Points to Remember

The maximum financial support is US$5,000, not a guaranteed fixed payment.

Funding is intended for project development and expansion.

Applicants must already be building or leading meaningful work.

Idea-stage concepts without implementation are not the programme’s primary focus.

A formally registered organisation is not listed as mandatory.

Participation, collaboration and accountability are central expectations.

The programme offers mentorship and coaching in addition to funding.

The published information does not specify the number of fellows who will be selected.

Applicants should use their own voices when completing the form.

All information should be checked again on the official page before submission.

Conclusion

The Billion Acts of Peace Changemaker Fellowship 2026 offers an important development pathway for emerging young leaders who are already responding to real problems in their communities. Its combination of up to US$5,000 in project funding, ten monthly mentorship sessions, individual coaching, international networking and leadership development can help promising initiatives move from early progress toward stronger and more sustainable impact.

The programme is best suited to applicants who can demonstrate that they have already taken action, understand the community they serve and are prepared to learn openly from mentors and fellow changemakers. Interested applicants should review the official requirements carefully and submit their applications before September 28, 2026.
