TITLE: Mitacs Globalink Research Award 2026: Up to $12,000 for International Research Internships in Canada and Eligible Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Mitacs Globalink Research Award (GRA) provides an opportunity for senior undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows to participate in international research collaborations between Canada and eligible countries and regions. Through the program, successful applicants can undertake a research internship under the joint supervision of a home-country and host-country professor, gaining international research experience while developing academic and professional connections across borders. The program supports research projects lasting between 12 and 24 weeks for one internship unit, while applicants receiving two internship units can undertake a longer research period or complete two separate research projects, subject to the program’s rules.

For students and postdoctoral researchers interested in international academic collaboration, this program can provide access to research environments outside their home institution, international academic networks, and financial support toward eligible project-related costs.

What Is the Mitacs Globalink Research Award?

The Mitacs Globalink Research Award is designed to facilitate international research collaboration and academic mobility. It brings together researchers from eligible Canadian and international institutions so that interns can conduct research in another country under the supervision of academic researchers.

Successful applicants work under the joint supervision of a home supervisor and a host supervisor. This structure allows participants to remain connected to their home institution while gaining experience conducting research in an international academic environment.

The program is particularly relevant to students and postdoctoral fellows who already have a research direction and are able to identify suitable academic supervisors and an appropriate host institution.

Mitacs Globalink Research Award Streams

The program is offered through two principal streams.

1. Allocation Stream

Under the Allocation Stream, participating Canadian universities receive a designated number of internship units each year.

Each Canadian university manages its own allocation, meaning that rules, conditions, and availability may differ between institutions. Applicants are therefore encouraged to contact their local Mitacs Advisor before developing their project so they can determine whether the proposed research fits their institution’s available allocation and requirements.

2. Quantum Stream

The Quantum Stream is open to all Canadian universities.

Unlike the Allocation Stream, there is no limit on the number of projects a Canadian university can submit through the Quantum Stream, and projects submitted under this stream do not count toward the university’s regular internship allocation.

Projects under the Quantum Stream must focus on the quantum sector. Areas mentioned by the program include:

Quantum computation, including hardware

Quantum algorithms

Quantum software

Quantum communication

Quantum networks

Quantum cryptography

Quantum metrology

Quantum sensing

Quantum imaging

Quantum materials

Applicants whose research falls within the quantum field may therefore want to investigate the Quantum Stream separately when planning their application.

How Much Funding Does the Mitacs Globalink Research Award Provide?

The program provides $6,000 per internship unit. Depending on the number of internship units awarded, participants can receive either $6,000 or $12,000 in research award funding.

One Internship Unit

One internship unit provides:

$6,000 research award

One research project lasting 12 to 24 weeks

Research conducted in the other country

Two Internship Units

Two internship units provide:

$12,000 research award

Either one research project lasting 24 to 48 weeks, or

Two separate research projects, each lasting 12 to 24 weeks

Awards are offered in partnership with Mitacs’s Canadian academic institution partners and remain subject to available funding.

Applicants should also be aware that the award may not necessarily cover every expense associated with international research travel. The program encourages applicants to seek additional sources of financial support and to use prudence when budgeting for travel and accommodation.

What Can the Mitacs Funding Be Used For?

Mitacs funding must be spent according to the budget included in the application and in accordance with eligible Tri-Agency expenses. The program’s funding administration also allows funds to support eligible direct research costs and other approved project-related expenses.

Following approval, Mitacs sends the funds to the Canadian institution’s Office of Research Services or equivalent administrative office. The institution then administers the funding as a research grant in the Canadian supervisor’s name.

Potential applicants should therefore carefully review their university’s policies regarding research expenditures and funding administration before finalizing their project budget.

Additional International Partner Funding

The program information also notes that some international partners may provide additional funding.

However, such funding is outside Mitacs’s purview. Applicants interested in partner-specific funding are expected to contact the relevant partner organization directly.

The supplied program information identifies partner information for countries including India and South Korea.

Who Can Apply for the Mitacs Globalink Research Award?

The program is aimed at researchers at different stages of higher education and early research careers.

Eligible interns include:

Full-time senior undergraduate students

Full-time graduate students

Postdoctoral fellows

Applicants must be registered at an eligible Canadian or eligible international institution and must remain registered in the relevant status throughout their Globalink Research Award.

Postdoctoral Eligibility

Postdoctoral fellows may apply when:

Their PhD graduation date is no more than five years before the proposed research project start date; and

They hold postdoctoral status at an eligible institution.

Other Important Applicant Requirements

Applicants must also satisfy several additional conditions.

They:

Must not undertake their research project at an institution where they previously completed a degree.

Cannot conduct the research project in a country where they hold citizenship.

Must be at least 18 years old, meeting the legal age of majority requirement in Canada.

Must meet travel requirements for their destination, including applicable visa, immigration, and documentation requirements.

Cannot hold more than two Globalink Research Awards or Mitacs-JSPS Summer Program Awards during their academic lifetime.

Cannot participate in more than one Mitacs internship simultaneously.

There are also specific rules for Canadian citizens and permanent residents enrolled at institutions outside Canada, as well as Canadian-enrolled students who hold citizenship in an eligible country.

Who Can Serve as a Supervisor?

The program also establishes eligibility requirements for supervisors.

A supervisor must:

Hold a faculty position at an eligible university.

Be eligible to supervise graduate students.

For supervisors at Canadian institutions, be eligible to hold Tri-Agency funding.

Applicants should therefore identify appropriate academic supervisors before progressing too far with their application.

An important point is that Mitacs does not connect interested interns with academic supervisors. Participants are responsible for connecting with one another and discussing research interests.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

The Mitacs Globalink Research Award has broad international reach.

According to the supplied program information, research and travel are supported between Canadian academic institutions and institutions in most countries, subject to the program’s country and travel-advisory restrictions.

For outbound mobility from Canada, applicants cannot travel to countries classified by the Government of Canada under the relevant “Avoid all travel” or “Avoid non-essential travel” categories.

For inbound mobility to Canada, the program states that all countries are eligible except Russia and North Korea.

Because travel advisories can change, applicants must verify the status of their intended destination both when submitting their application and before travelling.

Is There a Specific Nationality or Race Requirement?

The program information does not identify a race-based eligibility requirement.

Eligibility is instead structured around factors such as:

Citizenship and destination

Enrollment at an eligible institution

Academic status

Institution eligibility

Research project requirements

Travel eligibility

Supervisor eligibility

Importantly, applicants generally cannot undertake their research project in a country where they hold citizenship.

Therefore, applicants should assess their eligibility based on their institution, academic status, citizenship, intended research destination, and the specific mobility rules rather than assuming that the program is restricted to one nationality or continent.

How to Apply for the Mitacs Globalink Research Award

The application process can vary depending on the Canadian university and its available internship-unit allocation.

Applicants should first contact their local Mitacs Advisor to determine whether their proposed project meets the funding requirements for their institution and to obtain the appropriate GRA Application Portal link.

The program recommends applying at least 16 weeks before the planned project start date. The formal submission guidance also states that complete applications should be submitted 12–16 weeks before the project start date.

Step 1: Review the Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review both:

Mitacs eligibility and award guidelines; and

The requirements established by their Canadian institution.

University-specific requirements can affect the application process, particularly for projects submitted through the Allocation Stream.

Step 2: Identify and Connect With Supervisors

Potential interns and supervisors need to connect with each other and discuss research interests and potential projects.

Mitacs does not serve as a matchmaking service for interns and academic supervisors, so applicants should take responsibility for establishing the academic collaboration themselves.

Step 3: Obtain Canadian University Endorsement

For supervisors at Canadian institutions, the appropriate institutional endorsement must be obtained before the application is prepared.

Applicants should contact their local Mitacs Advisor to understand the specific rules and internal process applicable at their Canadian university.

Step 4: Prepare the Application

Applicants must complete the required fields in the application portal.

The application also requires:

A research proposal

A Mitacs Pre-Departure form

Personal information from all participants

Responses to a research security question

Required participant sign-offs

The research security question is visible only to the relevant participant, and each participant must personally log in and provide their response.

Step 5: Obtain All Required Signatures

Once the application is complete, all participants must log in again and sign off on the project.

The Canadian university signature requirements depend on the stream.

For the Allocation Stream, the project must count toward the university’s internship allocation, and the Vice President Research or designate signature is required.

For the Quantum Stream, projects do not count against the university’s allocation and the Vice President Research or designate signature is not required.

However, the Office of Research Services or its designate must provide a signature on completed applications from either stream.

Applicants should allow approximately one to three weeks to obtain the appropriate university signatures.

Step 6: Submit the Complete Application

The complete application should be submitted 12–16 weeks before the intended project start date.

Only certain participants are authorized to submit the application through the portal, including:

Local Mitacs Advisors

Academic supervisors at Canadian institutions

The intern who created the application

Once the application has been submitted, participants receive a confirmation email.

Learn more HERE

What Happens After You Apply?

Applicants should understand that approval is not the only requirement before travelling.

The program explicitly states that interns cannot travel until Mitacs has issued both an outcome and an award letter.

If the application is approved:

Funding is provided to support eligible travel and accommodation expenses, research-related expenses, and stipend.

Funds are transferred to the Canadian institution’s research administration office.

The Canadian supervisor administers the funding as a research grant.

The project must begin within one year of the outcome letter being issued.

If a second internship unit is awarded, the project must end within two years of the start date of the first unit.

Interns are generally expected not to leave the host country during an internship unit.

All participants must complete an exit survey at the end of the project.

FAQS HERE

Mitacs Globalink Research Award Deadline

The supplied program information does not provide a single fixed calendar deadline for the Globalink Research Award.

Instead, applications are tied to the proposed research project start date. Applicants are advised to submit their complete application 12–16 weeks before the project begins, and the program recommends applying at least 16 weeks before the planned start date.

This means applicants should not wait for a single annual deadline. Instead, they should plan backward from their intended project start date and allow sufficient time for:

Finding a research supervisor

Developing the project

Preparing the research proposal

Completing the application

Obtaining institutional endorsement

Securing university signatures

Completing the submission process

Receiving the Mitacs outcome and award letter

Completing necessary travel and immigration arrangements

Because institutional allocation and funding availability can affect the process, prospective applicants should contact their local Mitacs Advisor as early as possible.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

Before applying, prospective participants should pay attention to several important program conditions.

Funding Is Subject to Availability

The award is offered in partnership with Mitacs’s Canadian academic institution partners and is subject to available funding.

Applicants Need to Find Their Own Academic Collaboration

Mitacs does not connect interns and supervisors. Applicants need to establish the appropriate academic relationship themselves.

University Requirements Can Differ

The application process can vary depending on the Canadian university and whether the project is being submitted through the Allocation or Quantum Stream.

Travel Restrictions Matter

Applicants must meet the travel, visa, immigration, and documentation requirements of their intended destination.

They must also check current travel advisories because country eligibility can change.

Do Not Travel Before Receiving the Required Approval

An intern must wait until Mitacs has issued both an outcome and award letter before travelling for the project.

Why This Opportunity Can Be Valuable for Researchers

The Mitacs Globalink Research Award combines international mobility with academic research collaboration.

For eligible students and postdoctoral fellows, the program can provide an opportunity to:

Conduct research in another country

Work under joint academic supervision

Build international research relationships

Gain experience in a different academic environment

Develop a structured international research project

Access up to $12,000 in award funding, depending on the number of internship units

Participate in research collaborations involving Canadian and international institutions

Develop experience that can strengthen an academic or research career

The program is particularly relevant for applicants who already have a defined research interest and can identify appropriate home and host supervisors.

Final Takeaway

The Mitacs Globalink Research Award is an international research mobility opportunity connecting Canadian and international academic institutions. It supports eligible senior undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows who want to undertake collaborative research abroad under the joint supervision of academic researchers.

Funding can reach $12,000, depending on whether an applicant receives one or two internship units, while research projects can range from 12 to 48 weeks depending on the structure of the award.

There is no single fixed annual deadline stated in the supplied information. Instead, applicants should plan to submit their complete applications 12–16 weeks before the intended project start date, with Mitacs recommending that applicants begin the process at least 16 weeks ahead. Because university allocation, institutional procedures, funding availability, supervisor eligibility, and international travel rules can affect an application, prospective applicants should begin early and consult their local Mitacs Advisor before developing and submitting their project. For eligible researchers seeking international academic experience and collaborative research opportunities, the Mitacs Globalink Research Award can serve as a pathway to develop research projects across borders while building connections between Canadian and international academic communities.

TITLE: Why Is the monsoon coastal upwelling signal subdued in the Bay of Bengal?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Abbott, K., Mahadevan, A. (2024). Why Is the Monsoon Coastal Upwelling Signal Subdued in the Bay of Bengal?; Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans, 129(12), e2024JC022023. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JC022023

Figure provided by Katy Abbott.

A conceptual schematic of how the surface signature of upwelling differs in the western coastal Arabian Sea (left) and Bay of Bengal (BoB) (right). In the AS, alongshore winds are typically upwelling-favorable for the duration of the Southwest Monsoon (June-August, JJA), and coastal upwelling brings cold waters to the surface as a result of the temperature-controlled density structure in the upper 150 m. In the BoB, alongshore winds show much greater intraseasonal variability, and while winds are still upwelling favorable, the region experiences a higher frequency of wind relaxation during JJA. Because stratification is controlled by salinity near the surface, upwelled waters are salty and only somewhat cooler than surface waters, so the sea surface temperature (SST) signature of upwelling is small in comparison with the AS. These differences in stratification are quantified by calculating the thermal and haline components of the buoyancy frequency. The average near-coast profiles of the buoyancy frequency (white solid line), thermal component of the buoyancy frequency (red dashed line) and haline component of the buoyancy frequency (dark blue dashed line) are plotted for JJA. A consequence of the very different summertime SSTs in the two basins is that deep moist convection only develops over the BoB, increasing cloudiness. Clouds obscure infrared SST measurements and likely lead to an underestimate of upwelling magnitude in satellite SST products, an effect that would be magnified in the BoB.

TITLE: D-Prize Competition 2026: Win Up to $20,000 to Launch a Social Enterprise Distributing Proven Poverty Solutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The D-Prize Competition 2026 is now open for entrepreneurs, innovators and changemakers who want to launch new organizations that distribute proven solutions to poverty. The competition provides seed funding of up to US$20,000 to selected applicants seeking to expand access to interventions that can improve lives in underserved communities.

D-Prize is built around a simple but important development challenge: many effective poverty solutions already exist, but they do not reach enough people who need them. The competition supports entrepreneurs who can build organizations focused on the distribution, delivery and scaling of evidence-based solutions.

Rather than funding the invention of entirely new products, D-Prize prioritizes ideas that can help deliver existing, proven interventions to people living in poverty. Successful applicants are expected to launch a pilot, demonstrate that their distribution model works and build an organization capable of expanding its impact.

The Global Competition launches on 14 September 2026. Applicants can submit their proposals through the early, regular or extension submission deadlines.

What Is the D-Prize Competition?

D-Prize is a global competition that supports entrepreneurs who want to establish organizations dedicated to distributing proven poverty solutions.

The programme is based on the principle that development interventions can have a greater impact when they are effectively delivered to communities that lack access to them. These interventions may already be supported by research and evidence, but distribution challenges can prevent them from reaching the last mile.

D-Prize seeks entrepreneurs who can answer a central question:

How can an existing, evidence-based poverty solution be distributed more effectively to people who need it most?

Selected entrepreneurs receive seed funding to launch a new organization, test their distribution model and begin building a scalable operation.

The competition focuses on the practical delivery of solutions rather than simply identifying social problems. Applicants must demonstrate how their proposed organization will move a proven intervention from existing supply channels to underserved populations.

How the D-Prize Model Works

The D-Prize model is structured around three main stages:

1. Identify a Proven Poverty Solution

Applicants select an intervention from the D-Prize challenge list or propose another evidence-based intervention that is not currently listed.

The intervention should have credible evidence demonstrating that it can improve outcomes related to poverty, health, education, agriculture, livelihoods, water, public services or other development priorities.

2. Build a Distribution Organization

Applicants develop a plan for launching an organization that will distribute the selected intervention to underserved communities.

The proposed organization may focus on activities such as:

Delivering products to hard-to-reach communities.

Connecting vulnerable populations with existing services.

Improving access to essential health interventions.

Supporting farmers with proven agricultural inputs or services.

Expanding access to education and learning interventions.

Connecting low-income households with public services.

Providing information, training or support that improves access to proven solutions.

3. Pilot and Scale the Organization

Selected entrepreneurs use the seed funding to launch a pilot and test whether their distribution model works.

After demonstrating initial results, entrepreneurs are expected to raise additional funding and expand their organizations to reach thousands or potentially millions of people.

D-Prize therefore seeks applicants who are not only passionate about social impact but also capable of building practical, sustainable and scalable organizations.

D-Prize Funding: Up to US$20,000

Selected entrepreneurs can receive up to US$20,000 in seed funding to launch a new organization distributing a proven poverty solution.

The funding is intended to help applicants move from an idea to early implementation. Depending on the proposed intervention and operating model, the award may support activities such as:

Initial programme implementation.

Distribution of products or services.

Community outreach.

Recruitment and training.

Pilot operations.

Monitoring and evaluation.

Local partnerships.

Transportation and logistics.

Early organizational expenses.

Testing and refining the distribution model.

Applicants should explain how the funding will be used to launch and test their organization. The award is designed as seed capital rather than long-term operational funding.

Entrepreneurs are expected to use the pilot stage to generate evidence, demonstrate effectiveness and position their organization for future fundraising and growth.

Who Is D-Prize Looking For?

D-Prize is particularly interested in entrepreneurs who want to establish new organizations focused on distributing evidence-based poverty interventions.

Most awardees are described as first-time entrepreneurs who have not yet launched an organization or raised significant outside funding. Applicants do not necessarily need to have an established nonprofit, company or extensive organizational history.

The competition is especially encouraging applicants from low- and middle-income countries, where distribution gaps may prevent proven poverty solutions from reaching vulnerable populations.

Potential applicants may include:

Social entrepreneurs.

Development practitioners.

Public health innovators.

Education entrepreneurs.

Agricultural entrepreneurs.

Community organizers.

Researchers interested in implementation.

Nonprofit founders.

Youth-led social impact teams.

Early-stage innovators.

Professionals seeking to launch a poverty-focused organization.

The key requirement is not simply having a good idea. Applicants must propose a credible plan to distribute a proven intervention and demonstrate the potential to reach people living in poverty.

Eligibility Requirements

D-Prize prioritizes new organizations and early-stage entrepreneurs.

New Organizations

The competition is primarily designed for applicants who have not yet launched an organization or who are still at the earliest stage of development.

Most awardees are first-time entrepreneurs who:

Have not yet launched their proposed organization.

Have not raised substantial outside funding.

Are developing a new distribution-focused organization.

Want to test and scale a proven poverty solution.

Existing Organizations

Existing organizations may be considered, but only under specific conditions.

An existing organization may be eligible if its core focus is distributing an existing, evidence-based poverty intervention.

However, organizations with:

More than 18 months of full-time operations, or

More than US$30,000 raised,

are typically not supported.

Applicants with established organizations should carefully review the official eligibility guidance and frequently asked questions before applying.

Geographic Encouragement

D-Prize especially encourages applications from entrepreneurs based in low- and middle-income countries.

The supplied competition information does not state that applicants must be citizens of a particular country or continent. However, the programme’s emphasis is on poverty-focused distribution models that can serve underserved populations, particularly in low-resource settings.

Applicants should confirm any additional geographic or operational requirements in the official application materials.

D-Prize Intervention Areas

Applicants can choose from several intervention categories. These challenges cover a broad range of sectors connected to poverty reduction, health, education, agriculture, livelihoods and public services.

The listed categories include:

Agriculture.

Custom interventions.

DMPA-SC.

Education.

Health.

Livelihoods.

Public services.

Water.

Each intervention page provides a specific challenge question and an application packet that explains the problem, the intervention and the distribution opportunity.

Available D-Prize Challenges

The D-Prize website lists multiple intervention challenges. Applicants should review the available options and select an intervention that matches their interests, skills, local context and distribution capacity.

1. Childhood Diarrhea Treatment

This challenge focuses on distributing oral rehydration salts, commonly known as ORS, and zinc to households before children become sick.

Childhood diarrhea remains a serious threat to children under five, particularly where families lack timely access to treatment. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop a distribution model that helps ensure households can access ORS and zinc when needed.

Potential distribution approaches may involve:

Community health workers.

Pharmacies and local retailers.

Health facilities.

Household education.

Community-based distribution.

Partnerships with health organizations.

Applicants should review the official challenge packet for the specific intervention and evidence requirements.

2. DMPA-SC: Reaching Underserved Populations

This challenge focuses on distributing DMPA-SC, a self-injectable contraceptive method, to underserved populations.

The goal is to improve access to reproductive health services and ensure that people who face barriers to conventional healthcare delivery can access appropriate contraceptive options.

Applicants may consider distribution models involving:

Community-based providers.

Health facilities.

Outreach programmes.

Local health networks.

Training and referral systems.

Supply-chain partnerships.

Any proposed model must comply with applicable health regulations and clinical requirements.

3. DMPA-SC: Improving Provider Training

This intervention focuses on improving mandatory provider training for DMPA-SC.

The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop ways to strengthen the training, knowledge and preparedness of providers responsible for delivering DMPA-SC services.

Potential activities may include:

Improving training delivery.

Expanding access to provider education.

Developing training-support systems.

Strengthening assessment and supervision.

Improving training completion and quality assurance.

Applicants should consult the official challenge materials for the required training standards and implementation expectations.

4. DMPA-SC: Last-Mile Inventory Management

This challenge focuses on improving the management of DMPA-SC supplies at the last mile.

Weak inventory management can lead to stockouts, wastage, delays and limited access to essential health products. Applicants are encouraged to develop distribution solutions that improve visibility, availability and management of supplies.

Possible areas of focus include:

Inventory tracking.

Stock monitoring.

Demand forecasting.

Supply-chain coordination.

Reporting systems.

Distribution planning.

Stockout prevention.

5. DMPA-SC: Medical Waste Management

This challenge asks entrepreneurs to improve the safe disposal of DMPA-SC needles.

The intervention focuses on reducing risks associated with medical waste and improving the safe handling and disposal of used injection equipment.

Applicants may explore solutions involving:

Safe collection systems.

Disposal partnerships.

Provider training.

Community awareness.

Waste tracking.

Appropriate disposal infrastructure.

All proposed approaches must follow relevant public health and medical waste regulations.

6. Reading Glasses

This challenge focuses on distributing non-prescription reading or working glasses to people who need them.

Many individuals experience difficulty reading or performing close-up tasks but may not have access to affordable vision support. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to develop a distribution model that can make suitable reading glasses more accessible.

Potential target groups may include:

Older adults.

Workers who require close-up vision.

Low-income households.

Rural communities.

People with limited access to optical services.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed model includes appropriate screening, product quality and referral pathways where necessary.

7. Childcare

The childcare challenge focuses on helping low-income families access quality childcare services.

Affordable and reliable childcare can support children’s development while enabling parents and caregivers to work, study or participate in economic activities.

Applicants may consider distribution or access models involving:

Community childcare networks.

Childcare referrals.

Local service providers.

Subsidized access systems.

Parent information platforms.

Partnerships with existing childcare organizations.

8. ConnectEd Phone-Based Tutoring

This education challenge focuses on distributing a phone-based intervention designed to improve learning outcomes.

The model may be particularly relevant in areas where students have limited access to formal tutoring, educational technology or qualified teachers.

Applicants may explore ways to deliver phone-based learning support through:

Mobile phones.

Voice calls.

SMS-based systems.

Local education partnerships.

Teacher or tutor networks.

Community learning programmes.

The specific intervention requirements should be reviewed in the official challenge packet.

9. Teaching at the Right Level

This challenge focuses on improving foundational literacy and numeracy in resource-limited classrooms.

Teaching at the Right Level is an approach that organizes instruction according to students’ actual learning levels rather than only their age or grade.

Applicants may develop distribution models that help schools and education systems access:

Teacher training.

Instructional materials.

Assessment tools.

Classroom support.

Implementation guidance.

Monitoring systems.

The goal is to help children develop foundational reading, writing and numeracy skills.

10. Road Safety

The road safety challenge focuses on replicating a proven public transport safety campaign to reduce road deaths.

Applicants are expected to identify ways to distribute or implement evidence-based road safety messaging and practices among transport operators, passengers, communities or other relevant groups.

Potential approaches may include:

Driver education.

Passenger awareness.

Public transport partnerships.

Community campaigns.

Safety communication.

Behaviour-change initiatives.

11. Government Transparency

This challenge focuses on monitoring and reporting data to reduce corruption and improve public service delivery.

Applicants may develop organizations that help communities, civil society groups or public institutions collect, analyze and use information to strengthen accountability.

Potential areas of work include:

Public service monitoring.

Community reporting.

Data collection.

Transparency platforms.

Citizen feedback.

Public expenditure tracking.

Accountability mechanisms.

12. Poverty Graduation

The poverty graduation challenge focuses on providing coaching, capital and social support to help people move out of extreme poverty.

A graduation approach typically combines several forms of support, which may include:

Livelihood assistance.

Business or income-generation support.

Coaching.

Financial services.

Skills development.

Social protection.

Community support.

Applicants should review the challenge packet to understand the specific intervention and evidence base expected by D-Prize.

13. Agriculture: Propose Your Own

Applicants can propose the distribution of an evidence-based agricultural intervention that is not already included on the D-Prize challenge list.

The proposed intervention should have credible evidence and address a clear agricultural or rural development need.

Potential areas could include:

Improved agricultural practices.

Farmer training.

Quality inputs.

Market access.

Climate-smart agriculture.

Livestock services.

Agricultural technologies.

Soil improvement.

Smallholder productivity.

Applicants must demonstrate why the intervention is evidence-based and explain how their organization will distribute it effectively.

14. Post-Harvest Support

This challenge focuses on providing smallholder farmers with post-harvest loans and storage technologies that have been shown to be effective.

Post-harvest losses can reduce farmer income, food availability and market stability. The challenge encourages distribution models that help farmers preserve, store or finance agricultural produce after harvest.

Potential components may include:

Storage technologies.

Post-harvest financing.

Farmer training.

Market linkages.

Warehouse partnerships.

Loss-reduction services.

15. Quality Agricultural Inputs

This challenge focuses on providing smallholder farmers with quality agricultural inputs and training to increase harvests.

Applicants may explore ways to improve access to:

Quality seeds.

Fertilizers.

Agricultural tools.

Crop protection products.

Farmer training.

Extension services.

Input distribution networks.

The proposed model should prioritize affordability, quality assurance and effective access for smallholder farmers.

16. Water Filters

This challenge focuses on distributing ceramic water filters to people living in areas without reliable access to clean water.

Applicants are expected to develop a distribution model that makes water filtration technology accessible to underserved households.

Potential activities may include:

Community distribution.

Household education.

Retail partnerships.

Installation and maintenance support.

Water, sanitation and hygiene awareness.

Monitoring of filter use.

17. Kangaroo Care

This health challenge focuses on improving access to Kangaroo Care, a proven but underused intervention for infants born too soon or too small.

Kangaroo Care involves practices that support the care and development of vulnerable newborns, including skin-to-skin contact and related supportive care approaches.

Applicants may explore distribution and awareness models involving:

Hospitals.

Maternity facilities.

Midwives.

Community health workers.

Parent education.

Newborn-care networks.

18. Oxygen

This challenge focuses on developing a team of technicians who can service and repair existing oxygen concentrators.

Medical oxygen is essential for treating several serious health conditions, but equipment failures can limit access in health facilities. The challenge asks entrepreneurs to improve the maintenance and availability of oxygen concentrators.

Potential activities may include:

Training technicians.

Establishing repair networks.

Providing maintenance services.

Supporting health facilities.

Managing spare parts.

Developing equipment-monitoring systems.

19. Patient Identification

This challenge focuses on identifying patients who need treatment for conditions such as:

Obstetric fistula.

Cervical cancer.

Clubfoot.

Cataracts.

The proposed organization would then connect identified patients with existing treatment services in their area.

Possible activities may include:

Community screening and awareness.

Patient referral systems.

Health-worker partnerships.

Case identification.

Transport coordination.

Treatment navigation.

Follow-up support.

20. Maternal Health

This challenge focuses on training birth attendants to administer misoprostol to help prevent maternal deaths caused by postpartum hemorrhage.

Applicants may explore distribution models involving:

Birth attendants.

Community health workers.

Maternal health organizations.

Training programmes.

Health facilities.

Referral networks.

Because this intervention involves medication and maternal healthcare, applicants must follow national clinical, regulatory and public health requirements.

21. Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission

This challenge focuses on counselling and motivating HIV-positive pregnant women to adhere to antiretroviral therapy and reduce the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission.

Potential distribution models may involve:

Community health workers.

Maternal health clinics.

HIV support networks.

Patient counselling.

Treatment adherence systems.

Referral and follow-up services.

22. Child Immunization

This challenge focuses on directing caregivers to bring children to health facilities for routine immunizations that might otherwise be missed.

Applicants may develop systems involving:

Community mobilization.

Reminder services.

Health-worker outreach.

Parent education.

Immunization tracking.

Referral and follow-up.

Partnerships with health facilities.

23. Sugar Daddy Awareness

This challenge focuses on teaching sugar daddy awareness to eighth-grade classes to reduce unwanted teenage pregnancies and HIV infections.

Applicants may explore ways to distribute an evidence-based educational intervention through:

Schools.

Teachers.

Youth organizations.

Parent engagement.

Peer education.

Community health programmes.

The intervention should be implemented in ways that are age-appropriate, culturally sensitive and aligned with relevant education and safeguarding standards.

24. Propose Your Own Intervention

D-Prize also accepts proposals for evidence-based poverty interventions that are not included on its standard challenge list.

Applicants choosing this route must identify:

A clear poverty-related problem.

An existing intervention with credible evidence.

The population that lacks access to the intervention.

The distribution gap.

The proposed organization’s delivery model.

The expected social impact.

The plan for piloting and scaling.

The proposed intervention should not simply be a new idea without evidence. D-Prize is specifically interested in distributing solutions that have already demonstrated effectiveness.

D-Prize Application Process

The D-Prize selection process consists of several stages.

Round 1: Concept Note and Résumé Submission

Applicants begin by submitting:

A two-page concept note.

Résumé or résumés of the applicant or founding team.

The concept note should explain the proposed organization and distribution model. D-Prize receives more than 3,000 submissions per competition, so applicants need to communicate their ideas clearly and directly.

A strong concept note should explain:

Which intervention will be distributed.

Why the intervention matters.

Who lacks access to it.

Where the organization will operate.

How distribution will take place.

Why the applicant or team is well positioned to implement the model.

How the pilot will be launched.

How the organization could scale.

What the funding will make possible.

Round 2: Written Questions

The top 5% of entrepreneurs are invited to answer a set of short written questions.

Selected applicants generally have approximately two weeks to prepare and submit their responses.

At this stage, applicants may be asked to provide more detail about:

Their proposed intervention.

Their target population.

Their distribution strategy.

Their operational plan.

Their understanding of the local context.

Their team’s capabilities.

Their expected impact.

Their plans for using the seed funding.

Final Round: Interviews

Top entrepreneurs proceed to phone and email interviews.

The final stage allows D-Prize to assess the applicant’s motivation, understanding of the problem, entrepreneurial ability, proposed distribution model and readiness to launch.

Applicants should be prepared to discuss:

Why they selected the intervention.

How they will reach underserved communities.

What risks they anticipate.

How they will measure results.

How they will build partnerships.

How they will manage operations.

How they will use the award responsibly.

How they plan to raise additional funding.

Award and Launch

The top 1% of entrepreneurs receive up to US$20,000 to launch their organization.

Awardees are expected to spend the following months:

Piloting their distribution idea.

Establishing their organization.

Testing their operating model.

Reaching initial beneficiaries.

Measuring results.

Refining their approach.

Preparing for future growth.

The long-term goal is to build organizations that can scale their impact to reach thousands or millions of people.

How to Download the D-Prize Application Packet

Applicants should select an intervention from the official D-Prize challenge list and download the corresponding application packet.

The application packet provides information about the selected challenge and helps applicants understand the problem, intervention and expectations.

Applicants can also download the general application packet from the D-Prize website:

Download the D-Prize Application Packet

Applicants should read the relevant packet carefully before preparing their concept note.

How to Prepare a Competitive D-Prize Application

Because D-Prize receives thousands of submissions, applicants should ensure that their proposal is specific, practical and evidence-based.

1. Select the Right Intervention

Choose an intervention that:

Addresses a significant poverty-related need.

Has credible evidence of impact.

Is relevant to the target population.

Can realistically be distributed in the proposed location.

Matches the applicant’s skills and experience.

Has potential for scale.

Applicants should avoid choosing an intervention only because it sounds interesting. The proposed distribution model must be realistic within the local context.

2. Define the Distribution Gap

Explain why the intervention is not reaching enough people.

Possible barriers may include:

Geographic distance.

High costs.

Limited information.

Weak supply chains.

Lack of trained providers.

Poor community awareness.

Inadequate referral systems.

Stockouts.

Limited trust.

Weak coordination between service providers.

A strong proposal should identify the specific last-mile problem the organization intends to solve.

3. Identify the Target Population

Applicants should clearly describe who will benefit from the intervention.

This may include:

Low-income households.

Rural communities.

Smallholder farmers.

Children.

Pregnant women.

Patients with limited access to care.

Students in resource-limited schools.

Vulnerable newborns.

Underserved populations.

Communities lacking access to clean water.

The target population should be specific rather than described broadly as “everyone in need.”

4. Explain the Delivery Model

Applicants should describe exactly how the intervention will reach beneficiaries.

The proposal should answer questions such as:

Who will distribute the intervention?

Where will distribution occur?

How will beneficiaries be identified?

What partnerships are needed?

How will products or services be transported?

How will quality be maintained?

How will demand be generated?

Why D-Prize Is Different from a Traditional Grant

D-Prize is different from many conventional grants because it emphasizes the creation of new organizations and the distribution of proven solutions.

Traditional grants may support established programmes, research projects, institutional activities or general organizational operations. D-Prize, by contrast, is designed primarily to support entrepreneurs who want to launch a new organization focused on delivering evidence-based interventions.

Distribution rather than invention.

Practical implementation rather than theory alone.

Early-stage entrepreneurship.

Measurable social impact.

Last-mile access.

Organizational growth.

Long-term scalability.

Conclusion

The D-Prize Competition 2026 offers entrepreneurs and changemakers an opportunity to receive up to US$20,000 to launch organizations that distribute proven poverty solutions to underserved communities.

The competition is built on the understanding that effective interventions already exist in areas such as health, education, agriculture, water, livelihoods and public services, but many people still lack access to them. D-Prize seeks innovative distribution models that can close these gaps and deliver practical solutions to the last mile.

Applicants can choose from a wide range of intervention challenges, including childhood diarrhea treatment, maternal health, child immunization, water filters, agricultural inputs, post-harvest support, education, road safety, government transparency and poverty graduation. They may also propose their own evidence-based intervention if it is not included on the existing list.

The competition is particularly suitable for early-stage entrepreneurs and first-time founders, especially those based in low- and middle-income countries. Applicants should be able to demonstrate a clear understanding of the distribution problem, a practical delivery model, a realistic pilot plan and the potential to scale their impact.

Research Interests

Kathryn Neugent studies massive stars across the HR Diagram from hot OB and Wolf-Rayet stars, to cool yellow and red supergiants.

As primarily an observer, Kathryn regularly travels to telescopes in Chile, Hawaii and Arizona to better constrain the numbers and types of these stars in the Local Group galaxies M31, M33 and the Magellanic Clouds.

There is no single worldwide application deadline. Every participating location works through a designated regional partner, and application dates, award amounts, legal-status requirements and project conditions can vary.

The Pacific Northwest application closed on February 17, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

The Belgium application closed on February 12, 2026.

The United States application portal administered by Charities Aid Foundation of America is no longer available.

The Toronto partner has announced the 13 organizations selected for support.

The Nike overview directs eligible organizations to look for application opportunities beginning in January.

Dates for the next application cycle have not yet been published on Nike’s main initiative page. Prospective applicants should monitor the official page and the appropriate regional partner, particularly around January.

What Is the Nike Community Impact Fund?

The Nike Community Impact Fund, commonly referred to as NCIF, is designed to strengthen community-level efforts that use sport and physical activity to improve the lives of children and young people.

The initiative is based on the understanding that participation in quality sport and play can help young people:

Develop confidence and resilience.

Build communication, leadership and teamwork skills.

Improve their physical and mental well-being.

Form stronger connections with their peers and communities.

Gain access to positive coaches, mentors and role models.

Overcome social isolation and exclusion.

Participate in safe, structured and inclusive activities.

Discover opportunities that may otherwise remain inaccessible.

Rather than applying one uniform model to every location, Nike works through local institutions that understand the legal, social and administrative conditions of their respective communities.

How the Nike Community Impact Fund Works

The initiative generally follows a five-stage process:

Regional applications open

Starting around January, organizations operating in participating communities can submit applications through their designated regional partner.

Applications undergo an eligibility review

The regional administrator confirms whether the applicant has an acceptable legal status, operates in an eligible area and proposes activities aligned with the relevant funding priorities.

Nike employees receive application-review training

Volunteer committees include Nike employees from offices, logistics centres, Air Manufacturing and Innovation sites, and other local operations.

Local committees assess the proposals

Committee members use their knowledge of local needs and communities to review applications and recommend projects for support.

Applicants receive decisions

Nike’s main timetable indicates that applicants are generally notified and approved funding is distributed by the end of May. Certain regional schedules may vary.

Applicants do not need to know or obtain the support of a Nike employee before applying. The Pacific Northwest frequently asked questions explicitly confirm that knowing a Nike employee is not an application requirement.

Eligible Nike Community Impact Fund Locations

The current Nike initiative page identifies the following participating communities:

Who Can Apply?

Nike’s main initiative page describes the intended applicants as local nonprofit organizations and schools that are creating lasting community change and making play possible for young people.

However, exact legal requirements differ by location.

Pacific Northwest Requirements

Under the official 2026 Pacific Northwest guidelines, applications were accepted from:

Organizations recognized as 501(c)(3) public charities.

Federally recognized Indian Tribes under IRC Section 7871.

Government entities.

Organizations without their own eligible tax-exempt status when applying through an appropriately qualified fiscal sponsor.

A project had to serve at least one of the following areas:

Multnomah County, Oregon.

Clackamas County, Oregon.

Washington County, Oregon.

Yamhill County, Oregon.

Columbia County, Oregon.

Linn County, Oregon.

Benton County, Oregon.

Marion County, Oregon.

Polk County, Oregon.

Clark County, Washington.

An organization waiting to receive nonprofit status could not apply without an eligible fiscal sponsor.

Belgium Requirements

The official Belgium call document accepted applications from nonprofit associations, nongovernmental organizations and clubs operating in Antwerp, Limburg or Flemish Brabant.

The proposed project had to:

Encourage vulnerable children and young people up to 21 years old to move, play or participate in sport.

Be a concrete local initiative rather than a commercial project.

Explain how the activities would remove barriers to participation.

Demonstrate accessible delivery arrangements.

Seek a lasting effect instead of being limited to a one-time activity.

Identify measurable quantitative and qualitative results.

Begin implementation no later than September 2026.

Aim to operate for approximately 12 months.

Schools and local authorities could participate as project partners, but they could not submit an application directly under the Belgium call. The application had to be led by an eligible nonprofit organization or nongovernmental organization.

The Netherlands Requirements

The Netherlands regional page focuses on local organizations helping to advance youth sport in Amsterdam, Amersfoort, Hilversum and Utrecht.

Organizations must review the regional selection criteria before applying because eligibility, documentation and project requirements are administered through the King Baudouin Foundation rather than through one universal Nike application.

Toronto Requirements

Applications for Toronto are administered through the Jamaal Magloire Foundation. Its current Nike Community Impact Fund page confirms that 13 organizations have been selected and that support ranging from $5,000 to $15,000 was awarded for initiatives providing young people with positive experiences in sport and physical activity.

The Toronto page is presently displaying the selected recipients rather than accepting new submissions.

Funding Priorities

While detailed criteria vary among regions, competitive projects generally need to show how they will provide meaningful and inclusive opportunities for young people to participate in sport, active play or other forms of physical activity.

For the Pacific Northwest, all 2026 awards were directed toward projects that get more children active. Particular priority was placed on organizations that:

Provide quality coaching.

Increase the participation of girls in sport and physical activity.

Address social barriers that keep young people from participating.

Intentionally serve communities of colour.

Have boards and staff that represent the communities being served.

Respond to a clearly demonstrated local need.

Use a creative approach or an established method with evidence of effectiveness.

Present clear objectives and a realistic sustainability plan.

Submit a reasonable and proportionate project budget.

Receive support through partnerships, financial contributions or in-kind assistance.

Have not received support from the initiative during the previous 24 months.

Serving children with higher levels of need can make an application more compelling. However, the Pacific Northwest guidance explains that schools serving a general population can still apply if the proposed project is innovative, addresses an important need and demonstrates strong community support.

Barriers That Projects May Address

The Belgium guidance gives useful examples of the obstacles that may prevent young people from participating in sport and play. These include:

Poverty or financial hardship.

Language barriers.

Educational or learning disadvantages.

Cultural differences.

Refugee or migration backgrounds.

Mental-health challenges.

Behavioural difficulties.

Physical or intellectual disabilities.

Inaccessible facilities.

Transportation or mobility limitations.

Lack of equipment.

Inappropriate opening hours.

Complicated registration procedures.

Limited access to qualified coaches.

Activities that are not adapted to participants’ language or learning needs.

Applicants should explain not only that a barrier exists, but also how the proposed activities will practically reduce or remove it.

Examples of Relevant Community Projects

The Belgium call offered several examples of activities that could align with its objectives:

Mobile sport or circus activities delivered in underserved neighbourhoods.

Football initiatives that combine sport with homework assistance.

Programs that train young participants to become assistant coaches.

Sporting activities for young people affected by domestic or family violence.

Training for participants aged 16 and above to become community coaches.

Skateboarding lessons for autistic children in a low-stimulation environment.

The 2026 Pacific Northwest awards provide further practical examples, including:

After-school sport for low-income middle-school students.

Outdoor recreation for underrepresented young people.

Physical activities for young people experiencing homelessness.

Inclusive summer camps for participants with intellectual or developmental disabilities.

Girls’ sport participation through free, culturally responsive training.

Youth bicycle camps.

Community football, baseball, softball and soccer programs.

Recreation opportunities for foster youth.

Therapeutic recreation.

Movement and dance workshops.

Sport-based mentoring and leadership development.

These examples should be treated as guidance rather than a fixed list. A project can use any suitable sport or physical activity if it responds to a genuine local need and satisfies the applicable regional criteria.

Regional Award Amounts

There is no universal award amount across all participating locations.

Pacific Northwest

The 2026 Pacific Northwest awards ranged from $5,000 to $25,000 per organization.

The Oregon Community Foundation states that Nike employees work with the foundation to award at least $550,000 annually in the Metropolitan Portland region, Northern Willamette Valley and southwest Washington. The 2026 award list records 29 awards totalling $550,000.

Belgium

Selected Belgium projects could request:

Up to €6,000 per project.

Funding from a total available budget of €140,000.

Co-financing was considered an advantage, although the guidance did not state that it was mandatory.

The Netherlands

The Netherlands regional page states that selected projects could receive between €5,000 and €20,000.

Toronto

The Jamaal Magloire Foundation reports awards displayed as ranging from $5,000 to $15,000 for the selected Toronto organizations.

Applicants should never assume that an amount published for one location applies to another. The appropriate regional rules must be consulted before preparing a budget.

Activities Not Supported Under the Pacific Northwest Rules

The Pacific Northwest guidelines exclude the following requests:

Assistance provided directly to individuals.

Scholarships, stipends, fellowships or personal financial assistance.

Individual or group travel.

Research projects.

Fundraising-event sponsorship.

Elite or private sport camps, teams or programs.

Standalone one-day events, unless they are the culmination of a wider program.

Endowments or memorial funds.

Organizational budget deficits.

Fundraising activities.

Religious programs without a secular and community-focused purpose.

Lobbying, political or fraternal activities.

Most capital projects, unless the requested award would provide the final funding needed.

Projects or events taking place before the award is distributed.

Projects outside the designated geographic area.

Organizations that discriminate based on age, race, ethnicity, political affiliation, religion, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, disability or national origin.

Organizations that received support from the fund during the preceding two years.

The exclusions above come from the Pacific Northwest rules. Other locations may impose different or additional restrictions.

2026 Regional Timeline

General Nike Process

Applications generally begin: January.

Employee review and recommendation process: following the application period.

Applicant notification and disbursement: by the end of May.

Pacific Northwest

Application opened: January 8, 2026.

Information session: January 21, 2026.

Application deadline: February 17, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time.

Award distribution: week of May 25, 2026.

Current status: closed.

Belgium

Call opened: December 18, 2025.

Application deadline: February 12, 2026.

Selection announcement: mid-May 2026.

Project implementation required to begin no later than September 2026.

Intended project duration: approximately 12 months.

Current status: closed.

Applicants interested in a future round should not rely on these dates as the schedule for the next cycle. They should wait for a new official notice.

How Applications Are Evaluated

The central selection model combines formal assessment with local knowledge.

Nike employees serving on review committees receive training before assessing submissions. They then use their understanding of the community to review projects and develop funding recommendations.

In the Belgium process, selection involved two stages:

An independent panel of experts conducted a preliminary assessment against the published selection criteria.

A panel of Nike employees evaluated the preselected applications and made the final selection based on the criteria and available budget.

Reviewers generally look for detailed and clearly written applications that demonstrate:

A well-defined community problem.

A clear connection between the problem and the proposed activities.

Meaningful benefits for children and young people.

Accessible and inclusive implementation.

Realistic targets.

Measurable results.

Appropriate use of the requested funds.

Strong partnerships.

Potential for lasting impact.

A credible plan for continuing or sustaining the work.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

Organizations preparing for a future application cycle can take the following steps:

Confirm geographic eligibility

Verify that the organization and proposed beneficiaries are located within an officially supported community.

Review the correct regional rules

Do not rely solely on Nike’s general overview. Read the guidelines issued by the regional partner responsible for the relevant location.

Confirm the applicant’s legal status

Determine whether the organization can apply directly or needs an eligible fiscal sponsor or nonprofit partner.

Define the local problem with evidence

Explain which young people are excluded from sport, why they are excluded and how the organization knows that the need exists.

Connect activities to measurable results

State how many children will participate, how frequently activities will take place and what changes the project expects to achieve.

Explain accessibility arrangements

Address participation costs, transportation, location, equipment, language, disability access, opening hours, safeguarding and registration procedures.

Describe coaching quality

Explain how coaches will be recruited, trained, supervised and supported to provide a safe and positive experience.

Show how girls and underserved young people will be included

Identify practical measures for reaching groups that remain underrepresented in sport.

Prepare a realistic budget

Every major cost should connect directly to a proposed activity or expected result. The requested amount should be proportionate to the number of participants and likely community impact.

Document partnerships

Include the contribution of schools, community organizations, local authorities, volunteers or other supporters where relevant.

Demonstrate sustainability

Explain what will remain after the funded period, such as trained coaches, reusable equipment, continuing partnerships, established programs or improved access.

Create the online account early

New applicants to the Oregon Community Foundation were advised to create their nonprofit account in advance because profile setup and guidance on the next steps could take up to one week.

Submit before the regional deadline

Applicants should allow enough time for technical problems, missing documents and final internal approval.

Reporting Responsibilities

Reporting requirements also differ by region.

For Pacific Northwest recipients, a report is due by email within one year after the funding is distributed. It must include:

The number of children or young people served.

Participant information by age and gender.

Significant changes made to the project after approval.

An impact story describing something achieved, learned or changed for participants.

Applicants should therefore design a simple monitoring system before project implementation begins. Attendance records, participant demographics, activity logs, coaching records, photographs obtained with appropriate consent, surveys and beneficiary stories can help demonstrate results.

Official Application Information

Organizations should begin with the official Nike Community Impact Fund page and select the link for their eligible location.

Regional information is available through:

King Baudouin Foundation – The Netherlands

King Baudouin Foundation – Belgium

Oregon Community Foundation – Pacific Northwest

Jamaal Magloire Foundation – Toronto

Organizations in Atlanta, Mid-South/Memphis and St. Louis should use the Charities Aid Foundation of America link provided on Nike’s official page when a new application round becomes available.

Conclusion

The Nike Community Impact Fund offers locally rooted organizations an opportunity to expand access to sport and physical activity for children and young people. Its employee-led review system places community knowledge at the centre of funding decisions, while regional partnerships ensure that applications are administered according to local conditions.

The strongest applicants will be those that can demonstrate a clear local need, practical removal of participation barriers, inclusive and accessible activities, quality coaching, measurable results, a reasonable budget and a plan for lasting impact.

The published 2026 rounds are now closed, and the next application dates have not yet been announced. Interested organizations should prepare their project plans and supporting evidence in advance and begin monitoring the official Nike and regional partner pages around January.

Successful PhD students will receive:

A stipend to support their graduate studies and living expenses.

Tuition coverage, helping reduce the financial burden associated with pursuing a doctoral degree.

Health insurance as part of the funding package.

Conference travel support, providing opportunities for students to participate in academic and research conferences and share their work with the wider scientific community.

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

Deep learning

Reinforcement learning

Unmanned aerial vehicles

Unmanned ground vehicles

Autonomous navigation

Robotic agricultural applications

This research area provides opportunities to explore how intelligent machines can operate in agricultural environments with reduced human intervention.

Students working in this area may explore computational representations and simulations of agricultural systems as tools for research, analysis and decision-making.

The announcement identifies AI and machine learning, computer vision and multimodal sensing, robotics and autonomous systems, and digital twins and simulation for agricultural systems as key areas of research interest.

The International Criminal Police Organization, commonly known as INTERPOL, facilitates international police cooperation between its member countries.

Because INTERPOL operates across national borders and deals with sensitive information and cooperation between different jurisdictions, its activities require a substantial legal and regulatory framework.
