TITLE: Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 2026: 12-Week Hybrid Fellowship for Young Leaders in Tanzania and Kenya

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 is now inviting applications from young people aged 18 to 35 who are interested in or have experience in neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), One Health, community engagement, advocacy, health systems, and related areas.

Organized by One Health Society (OHS), Tanzania, in partnership with the Global Alliance for NTDs Elimination (GANE), Kenya, the 12-week hybrid fellowship is designed to equip young leaders with practical knowledge, skills, mentorship, and opportunities to contribute to NTD elimination efforts.

The fellowship brings together young people who are interested in addressing NTD-related challenges and strengthening community and health-system responses. Participants will receive guidance from expert mentors and work collaboratively on team-based capstone projects.

Application Deadline: 25 September 2026

About the Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2

The Youth NTDs Fellowship is a 12-week hybrid leadership and capacity-building programme focused on preparing young people to contribute meaningfully to efforts to eliminate neglected tropical diseases.

The programme combines learning, mentorship, practical skill development, community-focused approaches, and collaborative project work.

For Cohort 2, participants will have the opportunity to develop practical skills across several interconnected areas, including:

One Health

NTD elimination

Community engagement

Advocacy

Health systems integration

Solution development

Rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge, the fellowship is structured to support young people in developing practical skills that can be applied to real-world NTD and One Health challenges.

The programme also provides participants with access to expert mentors and opportunities to work with other young leaders through team-based capstone projects.

What Are Neglected Tropical Diseases?

Neglected tropical diseases, commonly referred to as NTDs, are a group of diseases that disproportionately affect populations and communities facing conditions such as poverty and limited access to healthcare and other essential services.

Addressing NTDs requires more than medical interventions alone. Community participation, health-system strengthening, advocacy, awareness, prevention, and collaboration across different sectors can all contribute to effective disease elimination efforts.

This is why the Youth NTDs Fellowship incorporates a One Health approach, connecting human health with broader community and health-system considerations.

What Will the Fellowship Focus On?

The Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 is designed around several major areas of learning and practical development.

1. One Health

Participants will develop an understanding of the One Health approach, which recognizes the interconnected nature of health and the importance of collaboration across different sectors and disciplines.

This perspective can help young leaders understand NTD challenges within their wider community and health-system context.

2. NTD Elimination

The fellowship focuses specifically on neglected tropical disease elimination, helping participants strengthen their understanding of the challenges and approaches associated with NTD control and elimination.

Participants with existing experience or interest in NTDs can use the fellowship as an opportunity to deepen their engagement in this area.

3. Community Engagement

Community involvement is an important part of addressing NTD-related challenges.

The fellowship will equip young leaders with practical skills related to community engagement, helping them consider how communities can be meaningfully involved in health initiatives and solutions.

4. Advocacy

Participants will also develop skills in advocacy, enabling them to better understand how young people and community actors can contribute to raising awareness and supporting action around NTD-related issues.

5. Health Systems Integration

The programme also focuses on health systems integration, helping fellows understand how NTD-related interventions and solutions can connect with broader health systems.

This provides an opportunity for participants to consider NTD elimination from a wider health-system perspective rather than as an isolated issue.

6. Solution Development

A further focus of the fellowship is solution development.

Through collaborative activities and capstone projects, fellows will have an opportunity to apply their learning to practical challenges and work together to develop potential solutions.

Expert Mentorship and Capstone Projects

One of the key components of the fellowship is the combination of expert mentorship and team-based capstone projects.

Participants will be supported by expert mentors throughout the fellowship while working with other fellows on collaborative projects.

The capstone component provides an opportunity to move beyond learning and apply skills to practical challenges related to NTDs, One Health, community engagement, advocacy, health systems integration, or solution development.

Working in teams can also allow participants to learn from peers with different experiences and perspectives.

Fellowship Duration and Time Commitment

The Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 will run for 12 weeks.

The fellowship is structured as a hybrid programme, meaning participants will engage through a combination of formats as determined by the programme organizers.

Applicants should be prepared to commit approximately:

6–8 hours per week for 12 weeks.

This means applicants should consider their existing academic, professional, community, or other commitments before applying and ensure that they can dedicate the required time throughout the fellowship.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is intended for young people aged 18–35 from Tanzania and Kenya who have an interest or experience in areas related to:

Neglected tropical diseases

One Health

Public health

Community engagement

Health advocacy

Health systems

Related fields

Applicants do not necessarily need to be established NTD specialists. The opportunity is aimed at young people who have an interest or experience in NTDs, One Health, or related fields and want to strengthen their skills and contribution in these areas.

Applicants Particularly Encouraged to Apply

The organizers particularly encourage applications from several groups, including:

Young People from NTD-Endemic Communities

Young people who come from communities affected by NTDs are especially encouraged to apply.

Their community experience can provide valuable perspectives on the challenges associated with NTDs and potential approaches to addressing them.

People With Lived Experience of NTDs

People with lived experience of neglected tropical diseases are also especially encouraged to apply.

Their direct experiences can contribute important perspectives to discussions around NTD elimination and community-focused solutions.

People With Disabilities

The fellowship particularly encourages applications from people with disabilities.

Women

Women are specifically encouraged to apply to the fellowship.

Community Actors

Young community actors with an interest or experience in NTDs, One Health, or related fields are also encouraged to apply.

Why Participate in the Youth NTDs Fellowship?

The fellowship offers young participants an opportunity to strengthen practical skills while engaging with other young leaders working around NTD and One Health-related issues.

Key areas of development include:

Practical One Health skills

Understanding of NTD elimination

Community engagement approaches

Advocacy skills

Health systems integration

Solution development

Team-based project experience

Mentorship from experts

Exposure to other young people working in related areas

The combination of structured learning, mentorship, and a capstone project can provide participants with an opportunity to connect knowledge with practical application.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 is:

25 September 2026

Applicants should ensure that they submit their application by the stated deadline.

Because the deadline is approaching, eligible young people interested in the programme should review the requirements and prepare their application information in advance.

Important Information for Applicants

Applicants are asked to provide accurate information in the application form.

According to the fellowship announcement, the information provided will be used for purposes including:

Selection

Fellowship planning

Mentorship

Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL)

Related programme purposes

Applicants should therefore ensure that the information they provide is complete and accurate.

APPLY HERE

How to Prepare for the Fellowship Application

Before applying, prospective fellows should consider the following:

Confirm your age eligibility
Applicants should be between 18 and 35 years old.

Confirm your country eligibility
The fellowship is intended for young people from Tanzania and Kenya.

Review your relevant experience or interest
Consider your experience or interest in NTDs, One Health, public health, community engagement, advocacy, health systems, or related fields.

Consider your availability
The programme requires approximately 6–8 hours per week over 12 weeks.

Reflect on your community experience
Applicants can consider how their experiences, community involvement, or professional interests connect with NTDs and One Health.

Provide accurate information
Ensure that all information submitted through the application form is truthful and accurate.

Submit before the deadline
The deadline is 25 September 2026.

Conclusion

The Youth NTDs Fellowship Cohort 2 provides young people from Tanzania and Kenya with a structured 12-week opportunity to strengthen their knowledge and practical skills in One Health, neglected tropical disease elimination, community engagement, advocacy, health systems integration, and solution development.

Through expert mentorship and team-based capstone projects, the fellowship is designed to connect young leaders with practical experiences and collaborative learning.

Young people aged 18–35 with an interest or experience in NTDs, One Health, or related fields are encouraged to consider applying. The organizers particularly encourage applications from NTD-endemic communities, people with lived experience of NTDs and/or disability, women, and community actors.

With a commitment of 6–8 hours per week for 12 weeks, applicants should ensure they have sufficient availability to participate fully.

Data is an essential component for effective planning, decision-making, and policy development in higher education. However, across many African universities and higher education commissions, the lack of strong, institutionalized data management systems remains a significant challenge. The absence of reliable infrastructure for data collection often hampers the ability of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) to monitor performance, plan effectively, and respond to emerging trends. One of the key hurdles faced by these institutions is the fragmented and inconsistent data on faculty across the region, which directly impacts faculty staffing and performance monitoring. This inability to establish reliable data management systems prevents HEIs from making evidence-based decisions and limits their capacity to address the rapidly changing demands of education in Africa. To address these issues, the Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with Education Sub-Saharan Africa (ESSA), the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA), and the Population Reference Bureau (PRB), launched the Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community (DAF EAC Phase II) project, running from November 2023 – October 2025. This initiative aims to address significant data gaps, strengthen the capacity of HEIs to manage and collect data, and advocate for the adoption of best practices in data management.

As part of the activities under DAF EAC project, the AAU hosted a webinar on Thursday, 27th February 2025, under the theme: Building Sustainable Higher Education Data Management Systems for Informed Decision-Making. The event featured key stakeholders who discussed the challenges faced by East African HEIs in managing and utilizing data, and the ways forward for addressing these issues.

Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director for ICT Services, Communications & Knowledge Management at the AAU, delivered the opening remarks on behalf of the Secretary-General. She reaffirmed AAU’s commitment to supporting evidence-based policies and advocacy for data management in higher education.

The session was moderated by Dr. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, the Senior Communications Officer at the AAU who guided the discussions on the progress and findings of the DAF project.

Dr. Marlene Lee, representing the Population Reference Bureau (PRB) highlighted that the institution was founded in 1929, and has been instrumental in compiling and harmonizing demographic data, providing significant contributions to the development of data management systems in higher education across Africa. Dr. Lee underscored the role of PRB in the current project, stating that the organization has been actively involved in demographic data collection and analysis in East, West, and Central Africa, and has extensive experience working in Kenya.

Dr. Lee also reflected on the pilot phase of the DAF project, which was hosted in Ghana in collaboration with AAU and ESSA. The pilot project focused on aggregating data and developing a base methodology for projecting faculty staffing. Dr. Lee praised the collaboration and how it benefited the East African community, offering valuable insights that informed the current phase of the DAF project. The second phase of the DAF project, running from 2023 to 2025, aims to bridge the data gaps identified in the first phase and develop harmonized guidelines for standardized data collection and management across the region, she added.

Dr. Salome Guchu, Principal Innovations and Outreach Officer at IUCEA, made a presentation titled – DAF-EAC Project – Insights from Phase 1, Progress in Phase 2, and the Path to Harmonized Guidelines. She stated that the study, initiated in 2021 and concluded in 2023, focused on faculty demographics across East African higher education institutions, including faculty numbers, gender distribution, and subject areas. Dr. Guchu outlined the findings, which highlighted critical gaps in faculty availability, gender representation, and adherence to policy norms. These findings, as highlighted, are essential for understanding student-teacher ratios, faculty demands, and future planning for faculty staffing in the region.

A significant issue discussed was the student-teacher ratio, and the implications of this ratio on data gaps in higher education. The conversation also delved into the challenges surrounding data governance at HEIs, specifically the need to address data fragmentation and inconsistency in data standards and definitions. Dr. Guchu identified key challenges in data collection processes and shared key insights from a benchmarking exercise conducted as part of the project. The goal is to establish a framework that improves data governance, ensures data quality, and supports better decision-making in faculty planning. One of the primary challenges in higher education data management, as projected, is the fragmentation and lack of integrity in data systems. Inconsistent data standards and definitions, limited automation, and issues of data accuracy and reliability were discussed as major barriers to effective decision-making.

Associate Professor Robert Wamala, from Makerere University, Uganda, presented strategies to harmonize and institutionalize higher education data collection processes. He discussed the need for a standardized data collection framework and the development of integrated data management systems, which could include the use of digital tools to replace outdated paper-based records. Prof. Wamala emphasized the importance of developing data governance policies and quality assurance mechanisms to ensure that data collected by institutions is reported accurately and appropriately.

The discussion on institutional data policies raised concerns about the absence of centralized data policies and standardized processes across HEIs. A proposed solution is to develop harmonized guidelines that would enhance data accountability and improve decision-making. These guidelines include standardized indicators, data sources, and collection methods, which are crucial for planning, resource allocation, and tracking faculty and student performance metrics. Additionally, the importance of engaging stakeholders in the process was emphasized, particularly in terms of involving faculty and administrative staff in data collection and analysis.

The challenges related to data integration and fragmentation were further explored, with suggestions made for creating a centralized data framework that would streamline institutional reporting. The integration of digital tools and the adoption of data-driven decision-making practices were identified as key solutions to address these issues. A case study from Makerere University, showed the MakData centralized dashboard, as a successful example of data integration. Starting in 2023, this project serves as a model for the East African Community (EAC), offering valuable lessons on overcoming data fragmentation and enhancing institutional management. The closing remarks were made by Ms. Joan Akua Iyoha, Project Officer for the DAF EAC project at the AAU, who acknowledged the contributions of various stakeholders and project partners , in advancing data management in higher education. Participants were encouraged to take proactive steps towards establishing robust data management systems, which would aid in data-driven decision-making in their institutions. The DAF Project has made significant strides in improving data management in East African higher education institutions. The ongoing second phase of the project, funded by the Carnegie Corporation of New York, is focused on addressing critical data gaps, promoting best practices, and fostering stakeholder collaboration.

The webinar reinforced the importance of sustainable data management systems to support informed decision-making, enhance faculty planning, and contribute to the long-term sustainability of higher education in the region. With continued efforts, the DAF project is poised to play a transformative role in shaping the future of higher education data management across Africa

TITLE: Become an Ambassador at the 2027 AFS Youth Assembly: Apply by September 18, 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program is an opportunity for young leaders who have previously participated in the AFS Youth Assembly to take on a representative and leadership role within the global AFS Youth Assembly community.

The program is designed for young people who want to become pioneers in their communities, amplify youth voices on the global stage, promote youth participation in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and represent the mission and programs of the AFS Youth Assembly.

Ambassadors serve as official representatives of the AFS Youth Assembly for a one-year term. During this period, they are expected to promote Youth Assembly programs and initiatives, encourage other young people to participate, and nominate youth to become delegates.

Applications are currently open, and interested candidates must complete the application process before the stated deadline.

AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program 2027

The AFS Youth Assembly is a global platform focused on cultivating a network of young leaders and changemakers through exchange, education, action and impact.

The Ambassador Program builds on this mission by giving previous Youth Assembly delegates an opportunity to remain engaged with the organization and contribute to its wider youth leadership network.

According to the program, ambassadors are expected to become pioneers in their communities, help young people have a voice at the global level, and represent the mission of the AFS Youth Assembly.

Successful ambassadors serve as official representatives of the Youth Assembly and take part in activities that promote its programs and initiatives.

What Does an AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Do?

An ambassador serves for a one-year term and has an active role in promoting the AFS Youth Assembly.

The main responsibilities include:

Representing the AFS Youth Assembly
Ambassadors serve as official representatives and help communicate the organization’s mission, programs and opportunities to young people in their communities and networks.

Promoting Youth Assembly Programs
Ambassadors are responsible for disseminating information about AFS Youth Assembly programs and initiatives.

This may involve communicating opportunities through personal networks, schools, universities, youth organizations and digital platforms.

Nominating Young People
Ambassadors are expected to nominate youth who may be interested in becoming delegates at the AFS Youth Assembly.

Conducting Engagement Activities
Ambassadors may promote and represent the Youth Assembly through activities such as:

Speaking at events

Participating in radio programs

Appearing on podcasts

Participating in television shows

Writing blogs

Creating social media posts

Conducting other engaging promotional activities

These activities provide ambassadors with opportunities to communicate with different audiences and encourage greater youth participation in the Youth Assembly.

Qualifications for the 2027 AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program

The Ambassador Program has several specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants should carefully review these requirements before submitting an application.

Previous AFS Youth Assembly Participation

Applicants must have attended the AFS Youth Assembly as a Delegate.

This is an important requirement because the Ambassador Program is specifically geared toward youth who have previously participated in the Youth Assembly.

Current Education or Organizational Affiliation

Applicants must either:

Be currently pursuing an undergraduate, graduate or postgraduate degree at a recognized academic institution during the present academic year; or

Be affiliated with or represent an organization with a mission similar to that of the AFS Youth Assembly.

This allows the program to consider both students and young people actively connected with relevant organizations.

Active Role in School or Community

Applicants should demonstrate that they have an active role within their school or community.

This may include participation in youth initiatives, community activities, leadership programs, organizations or other forms of civic engagement.

Knowledge and Experience With the Sustainable Development Goals

Applicants should have experience and knowledge in working on the Sustainable Development Goals.

The program is therefore particularly relevant to young people who have already engaged with global development, sustainability, community development or related initiatives.

Commitment to Youth Empowerment

Candidates should demonstrate a commitment to:

Youth empowerment

The Sustainable Development Goals

Giving young people greater opportunities to participate

Supporting youth voices and leadership

Self-Starter and Problem Solver

The program seeks candidates who are proactive and capable of identifying and addressing challenges independently.

Being a self-starter is important because ambassadors are expected to actively promote the Youth Assembly and carry out activities during their one-year term.

Social Media and Content Creation Skills

Applicants should be social media savvy and have experience creating content.

The program specifically identifies experience with formats such as:

Short videos

TikTok content

Social media posts

Other digital content

These skills are relevant because ambassadors will play a role in communicating Youth Assembly opportunities and initiatives through different platforms.

Communication and Coordination Skills

Excellent communication and coordination skills are also required.

Ambassadors may communicate with young people, organizations, event audiences, media platforms and the Youth Assembly team, making effective communication particularly important.

Fundraising and Sponsorship Experience

Experience in fundraising and sponsorship development is listed as a plus.

This means it is beneficial but is not presented as a mandatory qualification.

Candidates with experience developing partnerships, raising funds or securing sponsorships may therefore have an additional strength in their application.

Responsibilities and Standards for AFS Ambassadors

Being selected as an ambassador involves ongoing responsibilities throughout the one-year term.

Ambassadors are expected to complete their assigned activities and maintain appropriate standards when representing the Youth Assembly.

Reporting and Measuring Progress

Ambassadors must complete an online report and present their strategy and progress using:

Metrics

Photos

Specific activities conducted

This means successful ambassadors should be prepared to document their activities and demonstrate what they have accomplished during their term.

Completing Assignments

Ambassadors are expected to complete assignments fully and before the applicable deadlines.

Reliability and timely completion are therefore important elements of the ambassador role.

Using the Official Promotional Materials

Ambassadors must use the Youth Assembly’s communication promo kit and follow the relevant protocols when presenting information about Youth Assembly programs.

This helps ensure consistency and accuracy when ambassadors communicate publicly about the organization.

Providing Accurate Information

Ambassadors must always present accurate information about Youth Assembly programs.

This is particularly important when promoting opportunities to potential delegates and other young people.

Following the Code of Conduct

Ambassadors are expected to follow the organization’s code of conduct and uphold its stated values.

These include:

Professionalism

Integrity

Respect for Diversity

Friendship

Benefits of Becoming an AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador

The Ambassador Program provides several potential benefits for selected participants.

Certificate of Recognition

Ambassadors can receive a Certificate of Recognition for their dedication and work with the AFS Youth Assembly.

This provides formal recognition of their contribution during the ambassador term.

Potential Speaking Opportunities

Ambassadors may receive potential opportunities to speak at events.

These experiences can help young leaders strengthen their public speaking and communication skills.

Conference Fee Waivers

Ambassadors may receive complimentary AFS Youth Assembly conference fee waivers, subject to applicable conditions.

Delegate Discounts

Ambassadors may also receive discounts for delegates attending the AFS Youth Assembly, subject to conditions.

Professional Networking

The program provides opportunities to build a professional network.

Ambassadors can interact with other young leaders, Youth Assembly participants and individuals connected to the broader AFS network.

Professional Development

Ambassadors have opportunities to enhance their skills and professional development through their activities and engagement with the Youth Assembly.

Opportunities to Attend AFS Youth Assemblies

The program provides opportunities for ambassadors to attend AFS Youth Assemblies, subject to applicable conditions.

Youth Leadership Experience

Serving as an ambassador provides a leadership opportunity for young people who want to inspire and engage other youth around global challenges and the Sustainable Development Goals.

Opportunity to Publish Online

Ambassadors may have opportunities to publish content online as part of their engagement with the Youth Assembly.

Outstanding Ambassador Recognition

The program also provides additional recognition for ambassadors who perform their responsibilities with excellence.

Outstanding Ambassadors will receive Outstanding Ambassador recognition.

According to the program information, outstanding ambassadors will also receive special mention at the Youth Assembly and may be promoted through the Youth Assembly’s social media platforms.

Ambassador status and recognition are determined based on factors including:

Quality of work

Level of activity in promoting the Youth Assembly

Effectiveness of promotional activities

Completion of assigned tasks

Communication with the Youth Assembly team

Efforts to promote and support the Youth Assembly

Quality of Youth Assembly nominees submitted according to procedures

Overall delegation the ambassador will bring to the next Youth Assembly session

This means simply being selected as an ambassador does not automatically guarantee outstanding recognition. Performance throughout the ambassador term is an important factor.

How to Apply for the 2027 AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program

The application process consists of two steps.

Step 1: Written Application

Interested candidates must first complete and submit the application form for consideration.

Applicants should provide information demonstrating that they meet the required qualifications and have the experience, motivation and skills needed to serve as an ambassador.

Step 2: Online Interview

Shortlisted candidates will proceed to an online interview.

Only candidates who are shortlisted will receive an interview request from the AFS Youth Assembly staff.

If the interview is successful, selected candidates will receive further information and instructions.

First-Come, First-Serve Application Review

Applicants should pay particular attention to the way applications will be reviewed.

The program states that applications will be reviewed on a first-come, first-serve basis.

The first 200 applications will be prioritized.

Applications submitted after the first 200 may be placed on a waitlist and reviewed as needed.

This makes early application particularly important. Candidates who meet the eligibility requirements should not necessarily wait until the deadline to submit their application.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the 2027 AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program is September 18, 2026.

Applicants should submit their application before the deadline and, importantly, consider applying early because the first 200 applications are prioritized.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity may be particularly suitable for previous AFS Youth Assembly delegates who are already active in their schools, universities, communities or youth organizations.

Strong candidates are likely to be young people who can demonstrate a combination of:

Previous AFS Youth Assembly participation

Youth leadership experience

Community engagement

SDG knowledge and experience

Commitment to youth empowerment

Communication skills

Social media experience

Content creation abilities

Organizational and coordination skills

Initiative and problem-solving ability

Interest in representing a global youth platform

Applicants with fundraising or sponsorship development experience may have an additional advantage because the program identifies this experience as a plus.

Why This Opportunity Can Be Valuable for Young Leaders

The Ambassador Program can be particularly valuable for young people who want to build a stronger international leadership profile.

Rather than participating only as a delegate, ambassadors take on an ongoing responsibility to represent and promote the Youth Assembly.

This can provide experience in areas such as:

Leadership

Ambassadors are responsible for promoting programs, engaging other young people and representing the Youth Assembly.

Public Communication

Speaking at events and participating in media activities can help ambassadors develop their communication and public-speaking abilities.

Digital Communication

Social media and content creation experience can be strengthened through practical promotional activities.

Networking

Ambassadors can expand their professional and youth leadership networks.

SDG Engagement

The role provides an opportunity to remain actively engaged with the Sustainable Development Goals and youth-led development initiatives.

Community Impact

By nominating young people and promoting Youth Assembly programs, ambassadors can help create opportunities for other young people in their communities.

Tips for Potential Applicants

Candidates preparing their application should ensure that they can clearly demonstrate the requirements stated by the program.

Highlight Your Previous Youth Assembly Experience

Because previous participation as a Youth Assembly delegate is required, make this experience clear in your application.

Demonstrate Community Engagement

Explain your current role in your school, university, organization or community and provide concrete examples of activities you have undertaken.

Show Your SDG Experience

Do not simply state that you are interested in the SDGs. Demonstrate how you have worked on or contributed to SDG-related activities.

Highlight Your Digital Skills

If you have created social media campaigns, short videos, TikTok content, blogs or other digital materials, highlight this experience.

Demonstrate Initiative

Provide examples that show you can independently identify opportunities, solve problems and take action.

Emphasize Communication Skills

The ambassador role involves communicating with different audiences, so examples of public speaking, coordination, media engagement or community outreach can strengthen your application.

Apply Early

Because the first 200 applications are prioritized, submitting early is particularly important.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The 2027 AFS Youth Assembly Ambassador Program provides previous Youth Assembly delegates with an opportunity to move beyond participation and take on an active leadership and representation role.

Successful ambassadors serve for one year and help disseminate information about AFS Youth Assembly programs, nominate young people to become delegates, participate in promotional activities and represent the Youth Assembly within their communities and wider networks.

The program is particularly suited to young leaders who are active in their schools, communities or organizations, have experience with the Sustainable Development Goals, understand youth empowerment and possess strong communication and social media skills.

Selected ambassadors can benefit from recognition, networking, professional development, potential speaking opportunities, opportunities to attend Youth Assemblies, online publishing opportunities and other forms of engagement, subject to applicable conditions.

One of the most important points for prospective applicants is that applications are reviewed on a first-come, first-served basis, with the first 200 applications prioritized. Therefore, eligible previous AFS Youth Assembly delegates should consider submitting their application well before the September 18, 2026 deadline.

For young leaders who want to continue contributing to the AFS Youth Assembly community while developing their leadership, communication and professional networks, the Ambassador Program offers a meaningful way to represent and advance youth participation on a global platform.

TITLE: Cornell University Postdoctoral Associate in Political Economy and Technology 2026/2027: PhD Research Opportunity in Communication, AI and Technology

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a recent PhD graduate with a strong background in empirical research, social science, Science and Technology Studies (STS), communication, technology, history, political economy, or a related field? Cornell University is inviting applications for a Postdoctoral Associate in Political Economy and Technology within its Department of Communication.

The position offers an exciting opportunity for an early-career researcher to develop an independent research project examining how technology is reshaping political and economic systems while also becoming part of an active research team led by Dr. danah boyd.

Unlike many postdoctoral positions that primarily allow researchers to continue developing their dissertation projects, this fellowship-style research appointment is specifically designed for scholars who are ready to put their dissertation project temporarily on the backburner and investigate a new, original empirical research question.

The successful candidate will conduct original fieldwork and data collection, collaborate with Dr. boyd and her research team, mentor graduate students, participate in the intellectual life of Cornell’s Department of Communication, and contribute to broader research activities.

Applications are being accepted until November 1, 2026 at 03:59 AM GMT, although applicants should be aware that the review of applications will begin much earlier, on October 16, 2026.

Cornell University Postdoctoral Associate Opportunity at a Glance

University: Cornell University

College: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS)

Department: Department of Communication

Position: Postdoctoral Associate

Research Area: Political Economy and Technology

Related Areas: Communication, Communication Technology, Artificial Intelligence, Science and Technology Studies, Social Science and Technology

Location: Ithaca, New York, United States

Position Type: Postdoctoral

Duration: 1 year

Possible Renewal: Up to an additional 1 year

Salary: $64,000–$70,000 per year

Application Deadline: November 1, 2026 at 03:59 AM GMT

Application Review Begins: October 16, 2026

Start Date: Flexible, but no later than August 30, 2027

Application Platform: Academic Jobs Online

Position ID: Cornell-Department of Communication-POLECONOMYTECHPOSTDOC [#32502]

About the Cornell University Department of Communication

The position is housed within Cornell University’s Department of Communication and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

Cornell’s College of Agriculture and Life Sciences describes itself as a purpose-driven college working across disciplines to address major challenges facing society. Its research and educational work spans complex systems, communities, the environment, technology, agriculture, and other areas with significant social impact.

The Department of Communication provides the academic environment for this postdoctoral appointment, while the successful candidate will work closely with Dr. danah boyd and her research team.

The position is particularly suitable for researchers interested in understanding the relationship between technology and society rather than studying technology solely as a technical phenomenon.

What Is the Political Economy of Technology?

The central intellectual focus of the position is the political economy of technology.

Broadly, this area examines how technological systems interact with institutions, markets, governments, communities, organizations, workers, and social structures.

Researchers may investigate questions such as:

Who controls emerging technologies?

How do technology companies influence governments and institutions?

How do digital platforms change markets?

How does artificial intelligence transform industries?

How do technological systems redistribute power?

How do communities respond to technological change?

How do contracts, infrastructure and technology vendors affect public institutions?

How does technology reshape ideas about risk, governance, ownership and economic value?

Cornell is particularly interested in applicants who can identify new and understudied questions rather than simply reproducing existing research.

Main Purpose of the Postdoctoral Position

The successful Postdoctoral Associate will be expected to propose, develop and execute an independent empirical research study focused on a novel question related to the political economy of technology.

The researcher will also become an active member of Dr. boyd’s research team.

This means the position combines three major components:

Independent research

Collaborative research

Participation in the broader intellectual and academic community

The appointment is therefore not simply a continuation of a candidate’s PhD research. Cornell is looking for someone capable of developing a new research agenda and producing rigorous empirical work.

Important Difference From a Traditional Postdoctoral Position

One of the most important features of this opportunity is that applicants should be prepared to put their dissertation project on the backburner.

Many social science postdoctoral positions are designed to help researchers transform their doctoral dissertations into books or continue their existing dissertation research.

This position takes a different approach.

Dr. boyd’s philosophy is that stepping away from the dissertation project can give an early-career scholar the intellectual space needed to:

Develop a stronger dissertation-derived book later

Explore a completely new research question

Build additional methodological experience

Develop a broader academic research profile

Establish new research collaborations

Produce research that can strengthen their long-term academic career

Applicants should therefore be comfortable starting a new empirical research project rather than simply extending their doctoral dissertation.

Expected Division of Time

The appointment has a clearly defined distribution of responsibilities.

1. Independent Primary Research — 50%

Approximately half of the Postdoctoral Associate’s time will be devoted to their proposed research project.

Activities may include:

Conducting fieldwork

Conducting interviews

Collecting original data

Coding qualitative data

Analyzing research findings

Writing academic papers

Developing the research project

Presenting findings

Giving talks focused on the project

Developing theoretical contributions from the research

The research project should be sufficiently focused and realistic to be completed during the postdoctoral appointment.

2. Supporting Dr. danah boyd’s Research — 25%

Approximately 25% of the position will involve supporting research conducted by Dr. boyd.

Potential responsibilities include:

Conducting interviews

Coding qualitative data

Editing academic papers

Helping develop research projects

Assisting with grant writing

Supporting ongoing research activities

Contributing to research outputs

Depending on the candidate’s level of involvement in specific projects, there may also be opportunities for co-authorship.

3. Intellectual Community and Mentoring — 25%

The remaining 25% will involve contributing to the broader intellectual community of the research team and department.

Responsibilities may include:

Attending academic talks

Helping organize events

Mentoring graduate students

Co-mentoring other principal investigators

Participating in research discussions

Supporting intellectual development within the research team

Contributing to field-building activities

Although the position does not include formal supervisory responsibilities, the Postdoctoral Associate should expect to play a meaningful mentoring role.

Who Should Apply?

The opportunity is particularly suitable for researchers who are interested in the intersection of:

Technology and society

Artificial intelligence

Communication technology

Political economy

Science and Technology Studies

Social theory

Digital platforms

Technology governance

Public-sector technology

Technology and labor

Technology and markets

Technology and communities

Institutional change

Digital economies

Technology policy

Applicants should have demonstrated their ability to conduct serious empirical research and should be able to propose an original research question with a realistic methodology.

Academic Requirements

Applicants must meet several important requirements.

PhD Requirement

Applicants must have a PhD in the social sciences, Science and Technology Studies (STS), history, or another relevant field.

The PhD must be completed and officially in hand by the start date of the position.

Applicants who have not yet completed their PhD by the start date would therefore not satisfy this requirement.

Recent PhD Requirement

Applicants must be no more than two years post-completion of their PhD.

This makes the opportunity particularly appropriate for very early-career researchers who have recently completed doctoral studies.

Applicants should carefully assess their PhD completion date against Cornell’s two-year requirement before applying.

Empirical Research Experience

Applicants must have conducted significant empirical research as part of their doctoral work.

The position is strongly research-oriented and requires the successful applicant to be capable of conducting original data collection and rigorous qualitative analysis.

Having a PhD alone is therefore not sufficient. Candidates need to demonstrate meaningful empirical research experience.

Research Methodology Requirements

Cornell has provided particularly detailed expectations concerning the methodology of the proposed project.

Qualitative Research Is Central

The proposed research should be a qualitative empirical study involving original data collection.

Cornell gives particular preference to:

Ethnographic research

Interview-based research

Fieldwork

Other methodologies may be incorporated as complementary approaches.

For example, researchers may use:

Computational methods

Content analysis

Surveys

Quantitative data

Digital data

However, these approaches should not be the primary method of the proposed study.

This is an important consideration for applicants whose research background is primarily quantitative or computational.

Ethnographic Research Is Especially Encouraged

Applicants proposing ethnographic projects may receive particular consideration.

Ethnographic research can allow researchers to closely examine how people, institutions and organizations experience and respond to technological systems in real-world settings.

For example, a project could involve spending substantial time observing:

Technology workers

Government agencies

Agricultural communities

Local businesses

Public institutions

Digital platform users

Industry organizations

Technology implementation teams

However, applicants are not required to conduct ethnography if they can present a strong interview-based or other qualitative empirical design.

Original Data Collection

A major requirement is that the project should involve new, original data collection.

Applicants should therefore explain precisely how they will obtain the information needed to answer their research question.

A strong proposal should demonstrate:

What data will be collected

Who will provide the data

Where the research will take place

How participants will be accessed

How interviews or fieldwork will be conducted

How the data will be analyzed

Why the chosen methodology is appropriate

What ethical considerations may arise

Access to Research Participants and Field Sites

Cornell places significant emphasis on research access.

This is because ethnographic and interview-based research can fail if a researcher cannot obtain access to the relevant people, organizations or institutions.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a viable pathway to access.

For example, an applicant studying a technology company’s relationship with local government agencies should explain how they could realistically gain access to government officials, procurement staff, technology vendors or other relevant stakeholders.

Simply identifying an interesting research question is not enough.

The applicant needs to show that the proposed research can actually be conducted.

Theoretical Requirements

The successful applicant should have strong theoretical foundations.

Cornell gives preference to applicants with deep grounding in areas such as:

Science and Technology Studies

Political economy

Social theory

Applicants should demonstrate that they understand the theoretical debates relevant to their research question.

The proposal should therefore not merely describe a social problem. It should explain:

What theoretical issue the research addresses

Which scholars or theoretical traditions inform the research

What existing assumptions the research challenges

What the study could contribute to existing scholarship

Why the research question matters academically

Projects Near Ithaca Are Especially Encouraged

Cornell particularly encourages research projects where data can be collected within driving distance of Ithaca, New York.

This is intended to help the Postdoctoral Associate remain an active member of the Cornell academic community.

Applicants proposing research requiring extensive travel should therefore carefully explain why that travel is necessary and how they will still meet the expectation of spending significant time in Ithaca.

The position requires at least 50% of the candidate’s time to be spent in Ithaca.

Living in Ithaca during the academic year is a requirement.

Examples of Research Projects

Cornell provides several examples to illustrate the kind of research it considers appropriate.

These examples are not mandatory topics. They are intended to demonstrate the type of original question the department is seeking.

AI and Agricultural Technology

One example examines how AI-based agricultural technology, such as self-milking cow machines, changes the political economy of the dairy industry.

Such research could investigate how automation affects:

Farmers

Workers

Dairy production

Business models

Ownership

Labor

Technology companies

Agricultural governance

Betting Markets and Technology

Another example explores how betting markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi may change norms surrounding:

Risk

Assetization

Gambling

Governance

Financial markets

Technology platforms

The broader point is to investigate how emerging technological systems create new economic and political arrangements.

Technology Vendors and Local Governments

A third example asks how technology vendors can make local government agencies dependent on their systems and contractual arrangements.

This could potentially examine:

Procurement

Government contracts

Technology infrastructure

Vendor relationships

Public-sector dependence

Institutional decision-making

Technology governance

Again, these are examples rather than prescribed research topics.

What Cornell Really Wants From the Research Proposal

The university emphasizes that the most important factor is novelty combined with feasibility.

Applicants should ask themselves:

What important question about the political economy of technology is not being adequately studied?

The ideal project should be:

Original

Important

Empirically researchable

Theoretically grounded

Methodologically rigorous

Realistic within the appointment period

Supported by a credible access strategy

A highly ambitious project that cannot realistically obtain participants or complete data collection may be weaker than a narrower project with exceptional access and a clear research strategy.

Travel and Location Expectations

The position is based in Ithaca, New York.

The successful applicant must be willing to relocate to Ithaca and remain based there.

Depending on the proposed research project, significant travel may be necessary.

However, Cornell requires that the project be designed so that at least 50% of the candidate’s time is spent in Ithaca.

Living in Ithaca during the academic year is specifically identified as a requirement.

This means the opportunity may not be suitable for applicants who want to remain permanently outside the United States or conduct the majority of their research remotely from another country.

Funding and Research Support

The Postdoctoral Associate will receive some project and travel support.

However, the successful candidate will also be encouraged to pursue external funding opportunities.

The researcher may contribute to Dr. boyd’s grant proposals as part of their professional and academic development.

This can potentially help the researcher:

Build grant-writing experience

Develop a stronger academic profile

Expand research funding

Establish research collaborations

Gain experience with externally funded research

The announcement notes that the Postdoctoral Associate will not be eligible to serve as a Principal Investigator (PI).

Salary

Cornell lists the CALS hiring range for this position at:

$64,000–$70,000 per year

The final hiring rate may be determined based on factors such as:

Prior relevant work or industry experience

Education level where relevant to the position

Academic discipline

Unique applicable skills

Applicants should therefore understand that the stated range represents the hiring range rather than necessarily guaranteeing one specific salary for every successful candidate.

Duration of the Appointment

The initial appointment is for one year.

There is a possibility of a one-year renewal.

The start date is flexible, but the appointment must begin no later than August 30, 2027.

Applicants should indicate their desired start date in their cover letter.

Application Deadline

The official application deadline is:

November 1, 2026 at 03:59 AM GMT

However, applicants should not wait until the final deadline.

Cornell states that the review of applications will begin on October 16, 2026.

Applications will then continue to be reviewed as they are received until a suitable applicant is identified.

This means early submission could be strategically important.

Required Application Documents

Applicants are required to submit several materials through Academic Jobs Online.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Your CV should clearly demonstrate:

PhD qualifications

Academic background

Research experience

Empirical research experience

Publications

Conference presentations

Research methods

Teaching or mentoring experience

Relevant professional experience

Awards and fellowships

Other academic accomplishments

Because this is a research-intensive postdoctoral appointment, applicants should make their research profile particularly clear.

2. Cover Letter

Applicants should submit a 1–2 page cover letter.

The cover letter should describe:

Broader research interests

Intellectual interests

Theoretical background

Methodological background

Approach to collaboration

Desired start date

The cover letter should help Cornell understand how the applicant’s academic background connects with the position and Dr. boyd’s research environment.

3. Two-Page Project Proposal

Applicants must submit a 2-page project proposal.

This is one of the most important parts of the application.

The proposal should focus on:

Research question

Research approach

Data collection

Research access

Theoretical framework

Applicants should demonstrate that the project is both intellectually ambitious and realistically executable.

The proposal should clearly answer:

What are you studying?

Why does the question matter?

What is novel about the project?

What data will you collect?

How will you collect it?

Who will you interview or observe?

How will you gain access?

What theories will guide the analysis?

Why is the project feasible?

Why is Cornell an appropriate environment for the research?

4. Dissertation Chapter and Dissertation Cover Letter

Applicants must submit:

One substantial dissertation chapter

A separate one-page dissertation cover letter

The dissertation cover letter should explain:

The dissertation project as a whole

Why the applicant chose the research approach

How challenges were addressed during the dissertation

The selected chapter should be a substantial internal chapter that demonstrates the applicant’s intellectual ability and research quality.

Applicants should therefore avoid automatically selecting the introduction or literature review unless it is genuinely the strongest representation of their scholarly work.

5. Article-Length Academic Paper

Applicants must also submit an example article-length paper.

The paper should be written for publication in a journal or conference proceedings.

If the paper is co-authored, applicants should attach a note explaining their specific contribution.

This requirement allows the selection committee to evaluate the applicant’s ability to produce publication-quality academic work.

6. Three References

Applicants must provide the names and contact information for three references.

The announcement specifies that applicants should provide:

Name

Email address

Contact information

Actual recommendation letters are not required at the application stage.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Based on the requirements in the announcement, strong applicants are likely to demonstrate several qualities.

Strong empirical research experience

Applicants should be able to demonstrate that they have successfully conducted substantial empirical research.

A genuinely original research question

The project should not simply repeat an existing research agenda.

Applicants should identify a research question that could open a new perspective on technology and political economy.

Methodological rigor

The proposed methodology should be appropriate, detailed and realistic.

Strong theoretical grounding

Applicants should demonstrate familiarity with relevant theoretical traditions, particularly STS, political economy and social theory.

Realistic access

The applicant should provide convincing evidence that they can actually reach the people, organizations or communities needed for the research.

Feasibility

The project should be achievable within the postdoctoral appointment.

Collaborative ability

Because 25% of the position involves supporting Dr. boyd’s research and another 25% involves participating in the intellectual community, applicants should demonstrate that they can work effectively with others.

International Applicants

The announcement does not state that applicants must be citizens or residents of the United States.

Cornell also states that it is an equal opportunity employer and indicates that employment decisions are not made on the basis of legally protected characteristics, including national or ethnic origin, citizenship and immigration status, race, color, religion, sex, age, disability and other protected characteristics.

Therefore, qualified international applicants may apply.

Researchers from Africa and other regions outside the United States are not excluded simply because of their nationality or location.

However, an international applicant must be prepared to meet the practical requirements of the position, particularly relocation to Ithaca and any applicable U.S. employment or immigration requirements.

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Early-Career Researchers

This position could be particularly valuable for a researcher seeking to build an academic career around technology and society.

Potential benefits include:

Conducting an independent research project

Developing a new research agenda

Working with an established research team

Collaborating with Dr. danah boyd

Accessing Cornell’s academic environment

Gaining additional fieldwork experience

Conducting original qualitative research

Developing interview and ethnographic skills

Mentoring graduate students

Participating in academic events

Developing grant-writing experience

Potentially contributing to co-authored publications

Strengthening an academic research profile

Building professional networks

Developing research that can contribute to future publications

The opportunity is particularly distinctive because it deliberately encourages researchers to step outside their dissertation project and develop a new line of inquiry.

Important Things Applicants Should Consider Before Applying

Before beginning an application, prospective candidates should carefully assess whether they meet the essential requirements.

Ask yourself:

Do I have a PhD in a relevant discipline?

Will my PhD be officially completed by the position start date?

Am I within two years of PhD completion?

Have I conducted significant empirical research?

Can I conduct qualitative research?

Can I collect original data?

Do I have a realistic strategy for accessing research participants?

Is my proposed research related to the political economy of technology?

Is my research question genuinely novel?

Do I have sufficient theoretical grounding?

Can I relocate to Ithaca?

Can I spend at least 50% of my time in Ithaca?

Am I comfortable putting my dissertation project on hold temporarily?

Can I collaborate effectively with a research team?

Can I provide all required application materials?

If the answer to these questions is largely yes, the opportunity may be worth serious consideration.

Pro Tip for Applicants

The two-page project proposal should receive significant attention.

Do not simply submit a broad statement such as “I want to study AI and society.”

Instead, develop a specific, compelling and researchable question.

A strong proposal should make the reader quickly understand:

the problem → the research question → why it is novel → who you will study → how you will gain access → what data you will collect → how you will analyze it → what theoretical contribution the research could make.

Because Cornell specifically emphasizes novelty and viability, an original project with a convincing access strategy is likely to be more persuasive than an extremely broad project that would be difficult to execute.

Application Link

Applications should be submitted online through AcademicJobs Online.

Applicants should prepare all required materials before beginning the submission process, including the CV, cover letter, research proposal, dissertation materials, writing sample and three references. Visit HERE for more information

Application Deadline: November 1, 2026 at 03:59 AM GMT

Application Review Begins: October 16, 2026

Conclusion

The Cornell University Postdoctoral Associate in Political Economy and Technology is a highly specialized opportunity for recently graduated PhD researchers interested in understanding the relationship between technology, society, institutions, markets and power.

The position stands out because it is not simply intended to help a researcher turn an existing dissertation into a book. Instead, the successful candidate will be expected to develop a new empirical research project that offers an original perspective on the political economy of technology.

The researcher will spend approximately half of their time conducting independent research, while the remaining time will involve supporting Dr. danah boyd’s research activities and contributing to Cornell’s broader intellectual community.

Applicants should have a relevant PhD, substantial empirical research experience, strong theoretical and methodological foundations, and a convincing plan for conducting qualitative research and gaining access to appropriate research participants or field sites.

International applicants can apply, as the announcement does not impose a nationality, country or continental restriction. Nevertheless, applicants must be prepared to relocate to Ithaca, New York, and meet the position’s requirement to be based there during the academic year.

With a salary range of $64,000–$70,000, an initial one-year appointment with possible renewal, access to Cornell’s academic environment, opportunities for collaboration and research support, and the chance to develop an entirely new research agenda, this position represents a strong opportunity for an eligible early-career scholar working at the intersection of technology, communication, AI, political economy and society.

Prospective applicants should begin preparing their materials early because application review starts on October 16, 2026, even though the listed application deadline is November 1, 2026 at 03:59 AM GMT.

TITLE: Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award: $3,000 Stipend for Students and Recent Graduates in Government Internships

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award provides financial support to students and recent graduates who are pursuing internships or fellowships in government. The award offers a $3,000 stipend to help recipients gain valuable public-sector experience while developing their professional careers.

Applications are accepted three times each year, corresponding with the fall, spring and summer semesters.

For students interested in public service, government and public-sector careers, the award provides an opportunity to gain practical experience while receiving financial support during their internship.

About the Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award

The Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award is designed to support students and recent graduates undertaking qualifying government internships.

The award recognizes the importance of gaining practical experience in government and public service. Through the program, eligible applicants can receive a $3,000 stipend while completing an approved government internship.

The award is particularly intended to help students who may face barriers to accessing internship opportunities, including paid internships.

Award Benefits

Successful recipients receive:

$3,000 stipend to support their government internship experience.

An opportunity to gain practical public-sector work experience.

Exposure to government operations and public service.

An opportunity to develop professional skills and experience relevant to future careers in government and public service.

Participation in a cohort of other award recipients during the relevant semester.

The award can therefore provide both financial assistance and professional development for students pursuing careers connected to public service.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

Applicants must meet the eligibility requirements established for the award.

To qualify, applicants must:

Be enrolled in an undergraduate or graduate program; or

Be a junior or senior in an undergraduate program; or

Have graduated within the last two years.

Have already secured a government internship.

Applicants must have a qualifying government internship in place in order to be considered for the award.

Priority Consideration

The program gives priority to applicants who have historically experienced barriers to accessing internships or paid internship opportunities.

This includes:

First-generation students

Nontraditional students

Pell Grant recipients

Meeting one of these priority characteristics does not replace the core eligibility requirements. Applicants must still meet the program’s requirements, including securing an eligible government internship.

What Counts as a Government Internship?

A key requirement of the award is that the internship must be with a qualifying government organization.

The internship employer must be one of the following:

A local government office or agency

A state government office or agency

A federal government office or agency

Internships with organizations that do not fall within these categories are not eligible for the award.

Internship Time Requirements

The program also establishes minimum requirements for the amount of time interns must work.

For part-time fall and spring internships, the internship must:

Require at least 10 hours per week

Last for a minimum of 12 weeks

For a summer internship, the internship must:

Require at least 15 hours per week

Run for a minimum of 8 weeks

Applicants should ensure that their internship satisfies these requirements before applying.

Internships That Are Not Eligible

Not every internship qualifies for the Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award.

In particular, the program states that:

Internships at a university are not eligible.

Internships at a nonprofit organization are not eligible.

The employer must instead be a local, state or federal government office or agency.

APPLY HERE

How to Apply

Applicants can submit their applications through the official application form.

The application collects several categories of information, including:

1. Applicant Information

Applicants will be asked to provide their personal and relevant application information.

2. Professional Experience

Applicants must provide their professional experience, including a resume.

3. Short Answer Responses

Applicants must respond to three short-answer prompts.

Each response should be between 100 and 300 words maximum.

These responses provide applicants with an opportunity to explain their experiences, motivations and interest in public service.

4. Internship Information

Applicants must provide information about their secured government internship.

This information is important because the eligibility of the internship is a central requirement of the award.

Application Deadlines for 2026

The Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award accepts applications during three cycles each year: summer, fall and spring.

The 2026 application schedule is:

Application Cycle
Applications Open
Application Deadline

Summer 2026
February 23, 2026
April 17, 2026

Fall 2026
June 1, 2026
September 14, 2026

Spring 2027
October 16, 2026
November 20, 2026

For applicants seeking consideration in the fall 2026 cycle, the deadline is September 14, 2026.

The next listed cycle is the spring cycle, with applications opening on October 16, 2026 and closing on November 20, 2026.

What Makes a Strong Application?

The program indicates that strong applications should be:

Well organized

Thoughtfully composed

Clear and authentic

Motivated by a genuine interest in public service

Applicants should present a compelling narrative explaining the values that drive their public-service aspirations.

The program is particularly interested in seeing:

Clarity in communication

Authenticity

Motivation

An understanding of public-service values

Resilience

Determination

A demonstrated commitment to public service

Applicants should therefore use their written responses to clearly communicate why public service matters to them and how their internship connects to their longer-term goals.

When Will Applicants Hear Back?

Applicants can generally expect to receive a decision approximately three weeks after the application deadline.

Award recipients typically receive their funds no later than one month after decisions are announced.

Applicants should therefore monitor their communication channels after submitting their application and ensure that the information provided in their application is accurate.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award

Conditions for Award Recipients

Selected recipients have several responsibilities associated with accepting the award.

Each award recipient must:

Sign an acknowledgement letter.

Complete a W-9 form.

Provide a headshot for promotional purposes.

Provide a biography for promotional purposes.

Participate in a virtual check-in with the awardee cohort for that semester.

Complete an exit survey.

These requirements are intended to help the program support awardees throughout their internship experience and gather feedback about the program.

Application Preparation Tips

Applicants should ensure that their application clearly connects their government internship with their interest in public service.

Before submitting an application, applicants should:

Confirm that their internship is with a local, state or federal government office or agency.

Verify that their internship meets the required weekly hours and duration.

Prepare an updated resume.

Carefully answer all three short-answer questions.

Stay within the 100–300 word limit for each response.

Clearly communicate their motivation for pursuing public service.

Highlight experiences that demonstrate resilience, determination and commitment.

Review the application carefully before submitting it.

Application Link

Interested applicants can access the application form through the official award application portal:

Apply for the Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award

Conclusion

The Paul A. Volcker Government Internship Award offers a valuable opportunity for eligible students and recent graduates who have secured government internships and want to gain practical experience in public service.

Through a $3,000 stipend, the award helps provide financial support while recipients undertake qualifying internships with local, state or federal government offices and agencies.

The program also places priority on students who have historically faced barriers to accessing internships, including first-generation students, nontraditional students and Pell Grant recipients.

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements, confirm that their internship meets the program’s definition of a government internship and prepare thoughtful responses that demonstrate their commitment to public service.

For the fall 2026 cycle, applications close on September 14, 2026. The following spring cycle opens on October 16, 2026, with a deadline of November 20, 2026.
