TITLE: UN Women HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster: Remote Consultancy Opportunity for Gender Equality Experts

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Professionals with expertise in gender equality, equitable masculinities, male allyship, social norm change, human rights, training and community engagement can explore a consultancy opportunity with UN Women through the HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster.

The opportunity is designed to establish a pool of qualified and pre-vetted facilitators who can support the delivery and contextual adaptation of the HeForShe Barbershop Toolkit across different countries, languages and communities.

The consultancy is home-based and primarily remote, although selected consultants may be required to undertake short-term in-person facilitation assignments or field missions depending on programme requirements.

Unlike a conventional full-time employment position, inclusion in the consultant roster does not guarantee an immediate assignment. Instead, successful candidates become part of a pre-vetted pool that UN Women can draw upon when programmes, country offices, regional offices or implementing partners require qualified Barbershop facilitators.

About UN Women

UN Women is the United Nations entity dedicated to gender equality and the empowerment of women.

The organization works toward the elimination of discrimination against women and girls, the empowerment of women, and the achievement of equality between women and men as partners and beneficiaries of development, human rights, humanitarian action, and peace and security.

The Barbershop Facilitator opportunity sits within UN Women’s Strategic Partnerships Division, specifically the Private Sector Partnerships Section.

The Private Sector Partnerships Section leads UN Women’s engagement with:

Private-sector organizations

Corporations

Philanthropic organizations

Foundations

Individuals

The section also supports and drives several major global initiatives, including:

HeForShe

Women’s Empowerment Principles

Unstereotype Alliance

Its broader objective is to develop and sustain high-quality, impact-focused partnerships that contribute to gender equality and women’s empowerment.

What Is the HeForShe Barbershop Toolkit?

The Barbershop Toolkit is a participatory HeForShe programme designed to engage men and boys in discussions and learning around gender equality, equitable masculinities and social norms.

The programme is rooted in the Transforming Patriarchal Masculinities (TPM) approach.

Through facilitated discussions, participants can explore how social expectations and norms surrounding masculinity affect individuals, relationships, communities and broader society.

The initiative is intended to operate across multiple countries and languages. Because of this, UN Women is seeking qualified facilitators who can not only deliver Barbershop sessions but also help adapt the programme to different local environments and communities.

What Is the Consultant Roster?

The consultant roster is a mechanism used by UN Women to maintain a pool of pre-vetted experts with particular areas of specialization.

The purpose is to make it easier for UN Women headquarters, regional offices and country offices to quickly access qualified expertise when new programmes need to be launched, existing programmes need additional support, or urgent assignments require rapid deployment.

For this particular opportunity, successful consultants can potentially be called upon to support Barbershop programming based on demand from UN Women and its implementing partners.

However, applicants should understand an important distinction:

Being accepted into the consultant roster does not guarantee employment or an assignment.

Actual engagements depend on:

Programme needs

Requests from implementing partners

Availability of resources

The geographic requirements of a particular assignment

The need for specific expertise

Consultants are therefore engaged on an as-needed basis, with the duration and frequency of assignments potentially varying over time.

Working Arrangement

The consultancy is structured as a home-based assignment.

Consultants will primarily work remotely and may receive assignments depending on UN Women’s programme requirements.

However, the work is not necessarily exclusively virtual.

Where necessary, consultants may be asked to undertake:

Short-term in-person facilitation assignments

Field missions

National travel

International travel

Travel requirements will be determined on a case-by-case basis according to the needs of the programme and the location where Barbershop sessions are being implemented.

APPLY HERE

When Will Barbershop Sessions Begin?

The consultant roster onboarding process includes mandatory webinars and preparation activities.

The actual Barbershop Toolkit sessions are expected to begin in Q4 2026.

Consultants will report to the Partnerships Engagement and Special Initiatives Advisor and Global Head of HeForShe, who will serve as the focal point for contractual and payment-related matters.

Once engaged, consultants are expected to work independently while following the established Barbershop methodology, facilitation standards, implementation protocols and monitoring and evaluation framework.

Consultant Responsibilities and Deliverables

The consultancy includes several stages, beginning with onboarding and preparation and continuing through session delivery, monitoring, evaluation and knowledge sharing.

1. Complete Mandatory Barbershop Onboarding

Consultants must participate in mandatory Barbershop orientation and coordination webinars.

They are expected to attend at least 80% of the mandatory webinars organized by UN Women.

The purpose of these sessions is to ensure that facilitators understand and can properly apply:

Barbershop methodology

Facilitation standards

Implementation protocols

Curriculum objectives

Reporting requirements

Consultants must also review relevant materials, including:

The facilitation toolkit

Safeguarding guidance

Implementation framework

After completing the onboarding process, consultants are expected to confirm their understanding of the curriculum objectives and reporting requirements.

The onboarding webinars are envisioned to take place during 2026.

Importantly, the supplied information states that the first six months from roster onboarding are not paid activity and that the webinars are not compensated. Consultants may spend up to 10 hours per year participating in mandatory onboarding and knowledge-exchange webinars, with that participation time not compensated.

2. Prepare Adapted Barbershop Session Materials

Before delivering sessions, consultants will be responsible for reviewing the standard Barbershop curriculum and adapting the content where necessary.

The adaptation process may involve considering:

Local language

Cultural context

Socio-cultural environment

Participant profile

Specific setting

Partner requirements

Available logistics

The consultant must ensure that adaptations remain aligned with the core objectives and methodology of the Barbershop programme.

Consultants will also coordinate with UN Women or the relevant implementing partner to ensure that the session design is appropriate and that all necessary preparations have been completed.

The finalized adapted materials must be submitted at least 7 working days before the workshop delivery date.

3. Deliver Barbershop Sessions

The central responsibility of the facilitator is to conduct Barbershop sessions with groups of men and boys.

Sessions must be delivered according to the standardized curriculum and approved guidelines.

Facilitators will be expected to:

Conduct Barbershop sessions

Facilitate discussions about gender equality

Explore equitable masculinities

Use the approved curriculum

Create a safe and inclusive learning environment

Maintain respectful dialogue

Adapt facilitation techniques to group dynamics

Preserve the core learning objectives of the programme

Facilitators must therefore be able to manage group discussions effectively while creating an environment where participants can engage in sensitive conversations in a constructive and respectful manner.

4. Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting

Following each workshop, consultants must complete a structured monitoring and evaluation process.

The post-workshop report must align with the Barbershop Monitoring and Evaluation Framework.

The report should document:

Session delivery

Participant attendance

Participant engagement

Participant profiles

Key discussion themes

Outcomes

Facilitation observations

Challenges encountered

Lessons learned

Recommendations for future sessions

Suggested improvements

The post-workshop monitoring and evaluation report must be submitted within 5 working days after the workshop has been completed.

5. Contribute to the Barbershop Community of Practice

Consultants are also expected to contribute their knowledge and experience to the broader Barbershop community of practice.

This can include:

Sharing facilitation insights

Sharing lessons learned

Sharing good practices

Participating in community-of-practice platforms

Participating in debrief sessions

Providing written input for guidance notes

Contributing to supplementary facilitation materials

Recommending improvements to future Barbershop sessions

Providing recommendations for implementation approaches

Submitting facilitator testimonials

Providing reflective statements for potential use in UN Women communications and advocacy materials

This element of the consultancy means that facilitators are not only expected to deliver sessions but can also contribute to improving and strengthening the broader Barbershop initiative.

Core Values Expected From Consultants

UN Women identifies several core values that consultants are expected to demonstrate.

These include:

Integrity

Professionalism

Respect for Diversity

These values are particularly relevant to a programme that involves discussions around gender, social norms, identity and cultural contexts.

Core Competencies

Applicants should also demonstrate a range of professional competencies relevant to facilitation and gender equality programming.

These include:

Awareness and Sensitivity Regarding Gender Issues

Facilitators must understand the sensitive nature of gender-related discussions and be able to engage participants respectfully.

Accountability

Consultants must take responsibility for delivering agreed activities, meeting deadlines and completing required reporting.

Creative Problem Solving

Facilitators may encounter different cultural, logistical and group-dynamic challenges and should be able to develop appropriate solutions.

Effective Communication

Strong communication skills are essential for facilitating discussions and ensuring participants understand the subject matter.

Inclusive Collaboration

Consultants must be capable of working constructively with UN Women, implementing partners, participants and other stakeholders.

Stakeholder Engagement

The role requires the ability to engage effectively with different stakeholders involved in programme delivery.

Leading by Example

Facilitators are expected to demonstrate the principles and professional standards promoted through the programme.

Functional Skills and Expertise Required

Beyond the general competencies, the consultancy requires specialized knowledge and experience.

Applicants should have a strong understanding of:

Gender equality

Equitable masculinities

Social norm change approaches

Strong interpersonal, communication and facilitation abilities are also required.

Applicants should be capable of:

Managing groups

Resolving conflicts

Facilitating difficult conversations

Adapting content to different contexts

Working with diverse populations

Adjusting content to different literacy levels

Working across different languages and cultures

Experience in monitoring, evaluation and reporting for training or community-engagement programmes is considered an asset.

Knowledge of the UN system and familiarity with intergovernmental processes are also considered assets.

Experience with the HeForShe Initiative and Barbershop Toolkit is an additional advantage.

Educational Requirements

Applicants are generally required to have a Master’s degree or equivalent.

The preferred fields include:

Social Sciences

Human Rights

Gender Studies

Women’s Studies

International Development

Related disciplines

However, an alternative pathway is available.

A first-level university degree combined with two additional years of qualifying experience may be accepted instead of an advanced university degree.

Professional Experience Requirements

Applicants must have a minimum of 5 years of work experience.

In addition to the general experience requirement, candidates must have experience facilitating:

Trainings

Workshops

Dialogue-based programmes

The experience should specifically relate to areas such as:

Gender equality

Male allyship

Equitable masculinities

This is an important requirement because the role is not simply an administrative consultancy. Consultants are expected to have the professional experience necessary to lead structured conversations and learning sessions with groups of men and boys.

Language Requirements

Fluency in written and spoken English is required.

Knowledge of an additional language is highly desirable.

Additional language skills can be particularly valuable where the facilitator needs to adapt the Barbershop Toolkit and supporting materials to regional or local contexts.

UN Women Diversity and Inclusion Commitment

UN Women states that it is committed to creating a diverse and inclusive environment based on mutual respect.

The organization states that recruitment, employment, training, compensation and promotion are carried out without discrimination based on factors including:

Race

Religion

Colour

Sex

Gender identity

Sexual orientation

Age

Ability

National origin

UN Women states that employment decisions are based on qualifications, competence, integrity and organizational need.

Candidates who require reasonable accommodation during the recruitment and selection process are encouraged to include that information in their application.

Safeguarding and Standards of Conduct

UN Women maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward conduct that is incompatible with the aims and objectives of the United Nations and UN Women.

This includes:

Sexual exploitation and abuse

Sexual harassment

Abuse of authority

Discrimination

Selected candidates are expected to comply with UN Women’s policies and procedures and the standards of conduct applicable to UN Women personnel.

Candidates who are selected may also be subject to rigorous reference and background checks.

These checks can include verification of:

Academic credentials

Employment history

Other information required for the recruitment process

Selected candidates may be required to provide additional information to complete the background-check process.

Important Point About the Consultant Roster

Prospective applicants should understand that this is a consultant roster opportunity rather than a guaranteed employment position.

Being accepted into the roster means the consultant becomes part of a pool of pre-vetted experts whom UN Women may approach when suitable assignments become available.

Actual assignments depend on:

Programme demand

Partner requests

Available funding and resources

Required expertise

Location and implementation needs

Consequently, inclusion in the roster does not automatically mean that a consultant will receive a specific number of assignments or a guaranteed workload.

Remote Work and Potential Travel

The position is advertised as home-based and remote, making it potentially suitable for qualified professionals who are not based at UN Women offices.

However, candidates should be prepared for the possibility of travel.

Depending on programme requirements, assignments may involve short-term in-person facilitation or field missions.

Travel can potentially be:

Within the consultant’s country

International

The exact travel requirements will depend on the assignment and will be determined on a case-by-case basis.

Timeline and Key Dates

The supplied opportunity information indicates that:

Mandatory onboarding webinars are envisioned for 2026.

The first six months from roster onboarding involve onboarding activity that is not paid.

Barbershop Toolkit sessions are expected to begin in Q4 2026.

Adapted session materials must be submitted at least 7 working days before the relevant workshop.

Post-workshop M&E reports must be submitted within 5 working days after workshop completion.

No specific application deadline is stated in the supplied information.

Who Should Consider This Opportunity?

This consultancy is particularly suited to established professionals who have already developed substantial experience in gender equality and facilitated learning or dialogue programmes.

Potentially suitable candidates may include professionals working in:

Gender equality

Women’s rights

Human rights

Social sciences

International development

Gender studies

Community development

Social norm change

Male allyship

Gender-transformative programming

Training and facilitation

Community engagement

Advocacy

Peace and development

International development programmes

However, applicants should carefully compare their qualifications with the stated requirements, particularly the 5-year professional experience requirement and the requirement for experience facilitating programmes related to gender equality, male allyship and equitable masculinities.

Conclusion

The UN Women HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster provides an opportunity for experienced gender equality and facilitation professionals to become part of a global pool of pre-vetted experts supporting the expansion of the Barbershop Toolkit.

The programme focuses on engaging men and boys in conversations about gender equality, equitable masculinities and social norm change. Successful consultants may support the adaptation and delivery of sessions across different languages, cultures and communities.

The consultancy is home-based and primarily remote, while short-term national or international travel may be required for particular assignments. Consultants will be expected to complete onboarding, adapt session materials, facilitate worksho

s, conduct monitoring and evaluation, meet reporting deadlines and contribute to the wider Barbershop community of practice.

Applicants should have a relevant advanced degree or an accepted combination of a first-level degree and additional experience, at least five years of professional experience, demonstrated experience facilitating gender-related dialogue or training programmes, and fluency in English.

Importantly, inclusion in the consultant roster does not guarantee employment or future assignments. Consultants are engaged according to UN Women’s programme needs, partner requests and available resources.

TITLE: ASTRAIOS

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Space Science Cluster

Image: Freepik/Serg Nivens

Analysis of Skills, Training, Research, And Innovation Opportunities in Space

The goal of the ASTRAIOS project is to provide an exhaustive view and understanding of the current and future offer of space curricula and courses in the EU-27, characterise the demand from European space industry in the next 10-15 years, and identify actionable ways towards the alignment of the European space sector’s curricula and qualification capabilities with skills required by the sector to foster innovation and increase EU competitiveness.

These goals will be achieved by mapping the educational offer across the EU-27 at Bachelor, Master, postgraduate, and continuing education levels and measuring the average time and cost required for a degree leading to a career in the space sector. A socio-economic analysis of the population of students enrolled in space-related studies will be performed, which together with the education data will create a Europe-wide space competencies and skills taxonomy to support the identification and analysis of the excellences and shortcomings within the European academic offer for the space sector.

The project will analyse future trends and challenges of the EU space sector through desk research, direct industry consultation and automated methods. The analysis will cover current and future needs in both, technical/hard skills and soft skills such as collaborative working, multidisciplinary approaches, and creative thinking that future European students need to develop. Final outputs will include recommendations of actions towards a better alignment between the European space sector’s curricula and the skills required by the future EU space sector, new materials to promote space related jobs and careers, and educational material developed for the Copernicus and Galileo sectors. The consortium in place to achieve this has extensive coverage of the EU-27 space education and industry sector.

TITLE: University of Cambridge NERC-Funded PhD Studentships 2027: 15 Fully Funded CREATES Doctoral Opportunities in Environmental Science

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Cambridge is offering 15 NERC-funded PhD studentships for students starting in October 2027 through the Cambridge Research Experience and Advanced Training for Environmental Scientists (CREATES) Doctoral Landscape Award (DLA). Each studentship is designed to support 3.5 years of doctoral research in environmental science, with research opportunities hosted across relevant University of Cambridge departments and the British Antarctic Survey.

The CREATES programme is the University of Cambridge’s new environmental science doctoral training programme under the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) Doctoral Landscape Awards. It succeeds the previous C-CLEAR programme and is designed to develop researchers working across major environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity, conservation, Earth sciences and environmental processes.

For prospective PhD students interested in environmental research, climate science, conservation, geology, biodiversity, environmental modelling, plant sciences, zoology, archaeology and related areas, the 2027 CREATES DLA provides an opportunity to pursue doctoral study at Cambridge while being considered for NERC funding.

University of Cambridge CREATES NERC PhD Studentships 2027

The Cambridge Research Experience and Advanced Training for Environmental Scientists (CREATES) is built around interdisciplinary environmental science research. The programme brings together the University of Cambridge and the British Antarctic Survey as hosts and works with a wider network of partners from areas including government, industry and the third sector.

The programme addresses environmental challenges that have major implications for society, including:

Climate change and environmental change

Biodiversity loss

Conservation

Food production and land-use pressures

Environmental and natural hazards

Earth-system processes

Polar and cryospheric science

Environmental modelling and informatics

Ecosystem processes

Evolutionary and ecological research

The CREATES programme is organised around three broad research themes:

Solid Earth and Geological Hazards

Climate Change and Environmental Processes

Biology and Conservation

These themes reflect the breadth of environmental research available through the programme.

What Does the NERC-Funded PhD Opportunity Offer?

For students beginning their studies in October 2027, Cambridge will offer:

15 NERC-funded PhD studentships

3.5 years of doctoral funding

Research opportunities across eligible Cambridge departments and the British Antarctic Survey

Access to the CREATES doctoral training environment

Interdisciplinary environmental science training

Opportunities to work with supervisors whose research aligns with NERC’s remit

Development of research, professional, technical and transferable skills

The official programme states that the 2027 studentships will form part of a five-cohort CREATES programme replacing the previous C-CLEAR doctoral training programme.

The wider CREATES programme also connects students with collaborative partners, providing opportunities for networking, professional development and, where applicable, internships and partner-led activities.

Research Areas and Departments

One of the major features of the CREATES DLA is the range of environmental research areas available to applicants.

Current CREATES supervisors are associated with departments and research environments including:

Department of Archaeology

British Antarctic Survey

Department of Chemistry

Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics

Department of Earth Sciences

Department of Genetics

Department of Geography

Department of Plant Sciences

Scott Polar Research Institute

Department of Zoology

This means prospective applicants can approach the programme from different academic backgrounds, provided their proposed research fits within the relevant environmental science and NERC remit.

Examples of Potential Research Areas

The current supervisor directory includes research areas such as:

Climate and climate change

Atmospheric science

Ocean circulation

Polar physical oceanography

Palaeoenvironments

Palaeobiology

Conservation ecology

Ecosystem-scale processes

Environmental informatics

Evolutionary biology

Population genetics

Behavioural ecology

Marine ecology

Plant and crop science

Environmental physiology

Geochemistry

Volcanology

Geological hazards

Earth-surface processes

Environmental microbiology

Archaeology

Quaternary science

Cryosphere and climate research

Applicants should examine the current supervisor and topic information carefully because the specific research interests and available supervision areas vary between academics.

How the CREATES Research Topics Work

An important feature of this PhD opportunity is that applicants are not necessarily applying to a completely finalised PhD project title.

Instead, applicants are expected to identify topics and supervisors that particularly interest them. The final research project can then be developed with the supervisory team during the first term of doctoral study.

This means applicants should focus on demonstrating:

Their research interests

Their understanding of the relevant environmental research area

Why the topic interests them

Which supervisors they would like to work with

How their academic background relates to the proposed area

Their potential to undertake independent doctoral research

The programme strongly recommends contacting prospective supervisors before submitting an application. This allows applicants and supervisors to explore whether their research interests are compatible and can also provide useful advice about the application.

What If a Prospective Supervisor Does Not Respond?

The programme recognises that contacting academics can sometimes be difficult, particularly if a potential supervisor is conducting fieldwork or otherwise unavailable.

Applicants who are interested in a particular area but cannot establish contact with a suitable supervisor can contact the CREATES DLA Administrator, who can help connect them with an academic.

The administrator can be contacted at:

dtp-admin@esc.cam.ac.uk

NERC Research Remit Requirement

Applicants seeking CREATES NERC DLA funding must ensure that at least one of their proposed research topics falls within the NERC research remit.

Applicants may identify projects or research areas that fall under other UK Research Councils, but they will only be considered for CREATES DLA funding if at least one proposed subject area fits within NERC’s remit. If admitted and funded through the DLA, the research topic must continue to remain within that remit during the development of the project.

This makes it particularly important for applicants to understand the environmental science focus of NERC before selecting their preferred research topics.

Cambridge PhD Admission Requirements

Before applying for the NERC funding, applicants must first ensure that they meet the University’s requirements for admission to the relevant PhD programme.

According to the CREATES application guidance, applicants are expected to have:

1. A Strong Relevant Degree

Applicants should normally have at least a 2.1 Honours degree from a UK university, or an equivalent qualification from an overseas university.

The guidance gives CGPA 3.5/4.0 as an example of an equivalent overseas academic standard, although applicants should check the specific requirements applicable to their circumstances and chosen course.

2. Two Outstanding References

Applicants need to provide two outstanding references.

The programme recommends requesting references well in advance of the application deadline so that referees have enough time to prepare and submit them.

3. English-Language Proficiency

Applicants must meet the University’s English-language requirements.

The exact evidence required can depend on the applicant’s circumstances, previous education and course, so prospective international applicants should consult Cambridge’s official English-language requirements before submitting their application.

How to Apply for the Cambridge CREATES NERC PhD

Applicants must apply through the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal and select the PhD course relevant to their preferred supervisor.

The application process involves several important stages.

Step 1: Research Supervisors and Topics

Begin by examining the available CREATES topics and supervisors.

Applicants are encouraged to:

Identify research areas that match their interests.

Review potential supervisors’ research interests.

Identify more than one suitable topic where appropriate.

Contact prospective supervisors.

Discuss research interests and potential project directions.

Develop a prioritised list of preferred supervisors and topics.

The programme recommends providing a prioritised list because academic staff can act as lead supervisor for only one CREATES studentship per application round. Applicants may also identify supervisors in different departments.

Step 2: Check the NERC Remit

At least one proposed topic must fit within NERC’s remit if the applicant wants to be considered for CREATES DLA funding.

Step 3: Apply for the Relevant Cambridge PhD

The application must be submitted through Cambridge’s Applicant Portal.

Applicants should select:

Michaelmas Term 2027 start — 1 October 2027.

Step 4: Request Funding Consideration

When the application asks:

“Do you wish to apply for funding?”

applicants should select:

“Yes — I wish to apply for funding.”

Applicants should also indicate that they wish to be considered for the NERC Doctoral Landscape Award and identify their preferred CREATES topics and supervisors.

Research Summary Required for the Application

Applicants seeking DLA funding will need to provide information about their planned research interests.

This includes:

Prospective supervisor or supervisors

Proposed topic or topics

A 250-word summary of the area or areas of research they are interested in

Some Cambridge departments may request a longer research proposal as part of their own admissions process, but the CREATES DLA specifically focuses on the applicant’s 250-word research-interest summary.

Applicants should therefore make sure that their 250-word summary is focused, relevant to NERC’s remit and clearly connected to the research interests of their preferred supervisors.

Where Should Applicants Enter Their Research Information?

The exact structure of the Cambridge application form varies depending on the department and course.

Applicants may encounter sections such as:

Research

Other Information

Course-Specific Questions

Additional Information to Support Your Application

If a Research section is available, applicants should use it to provide information about their proposed supervisors, topics and research summary.

If the Research section is not available, applicants should look for research-related questions under Course-Specific Questions.

The Additional Information to Support Your Application section can also be used where applicants need more space to explain their preferred combinations of topics and supervisors.

Applicants Should Complete the Entire Cambridge Application

The CREATES guidance emphasises that the instructions concerning topics, supervisors and the 250-word summary do not replace the other questions in the University’s PhD application.

Applicants should answer all other questions required by their chosen Cambridge course.

The funding section should also clearly indicate the applicant’s interest in NERC funding and include preferred supervisors where requested.

Funding and Financial Support

The CREATES opportunity is a NERC-funded PhD studentship. The 2027 call provides 15 studentships, each lasting 3.5 years.

The current Cambridge CREATES funding information explains that NERC studentships can cover tuition and provide a maintenance allowance and Research Training Support Grant. It also states that a limited number of studentships can be offered to international students, with UKRI funding covering the UK-rate fees, maintenance allowance and Research Training Support Grant; Cambridge has agreed to waive the difference between international and home fees for DLA students. Applicants should check the latest funding guidance for the precise conditions applying to the 2027 intake.

International applicants should also note that certain expenses, such as visa and health-related surcharges, may not be covered by the DLA funding itself. Cambridge recommends that international applicants also consider other funding opportunities where appropriate.

Important Application Deadlines

The CREATES NERC DLA deadline is tied directly to the funding deadline for the applicant’s chosen Cambridge course.

For the 2027 entry cycle, the relevant deadline will be either 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027, depending on the course. Applicants must check the deadline for their first-choice course carefully.

The final CREATES DLA deadline is therefore:

8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027, depending on the chosen Cambridge course.

All supporting documentation, including references, must be submitted by the applicable deadline.

Applicants should not assume that every Cambridge department uses the same deadline.

Earlier Funding Deadlines

Some other Cambridge funding schemes may have earlier deadlines.

The CREATES guidance specifically highlights:

The Department of Chemistry may have an earlier deadline for other PhD funding.

The Department of Geography may have an earlier deadline for other PhD funding.

US-based applicants seeking Gates Cambridge funding should apply by 14 October 2026, including references.

Applicants interested in multiple funding sources should therefore research each relevant funding deadline rather than relying solely on the CREATES deadline.

CREATES 2027 Application Timeline

The programme has provided the following expected timeline for the 2027 intake:

Supervisor Information

Supervisor pages for the 2027 entry cycle were scheduled to be updated by:

1 September 2026

Application Deadline

Depending on the selected course:

8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027

All supporting documents and references must be submitted by the relevant deadline.

Interviews

Online interviews are anticipated to take place during the week of:

22 February 2027

Offers

Initial offers are expected to begin being communicated in late February 2027.

The NERC Universal Acceptance Date is:

Noon, 17 March 2027

What Does the CREATES Programme Look For in Applicants?

Beyond minimum admission requirements, the CREATES DLA assessment process considers several aspects of a candidate’s potential.

The programme’s assessment framework includes:

Academic Excellence

Applicants are assessed on factors such as:

Degree results or predicted results

Achievement in relevant subjects

Academic achievements

Research experience

Evidence of advanced knowledge in the proposed research area

Awareness of knowledge gaps and relevant methodologies

Originality and Independence

The programme looks for evidence of:

Independent working ability

Self-motivation

Problem-solving

Critical decision-making

Independence during research or project work

Communication Skills

Applicants should be able to:

Communicate clearly

Explain complex ideas logically

Provide precise and detailed answers

Demonstrate enthusiasm for environmental science

Preparedness for Doctoral Study

The assessment also considers:

Intellectual curiosity

Ability to evaluate personal strengths and weaknesses

Awareness of skills gaps

Ability to identify challenges

Ability to develop strategies for overcoming challenges

Understanding of how doctoral study fits into future career plans

Importantly, CREATES states that contextual information can also be taken into account. This can include adversity, caring responsibilities, employment undertaken alongside study, and differences in access to research opportunities.

Why Contacting a Supervisor Before Applying Matters

A strong supervisor match is an important part of the CREATES application process.

Because applicants are expected to identify potential research areas and supervisors, contacting academics before applying can help applicants:

Understand whether their research interests align.

Learn more about potential projects.

Discuss possible research directions.

Determine whether a supervisor is accepting students.

Decide which topics to prioritise.

Develop a more focused research-interest statement.

The programme itself strongly advises applicants to contact prospective supervisors before submitting an application.

How to Prepare a Strong CREATES Application

Applicants can begin preparing well before the deadline.

1. Research the Supervisors

Read the profiles of potential supervisors carefully and identify academics whose research connects closely with your academic background and interests.

2. Identify Several Potential Topics

Do not necessarily limit yourself to one research area. The programme encourages applicants to provide a prioritised list of topics and supervisors they would consider.

3. Check the NERC Remit

Make sure at least one proposed research area clearly falls within NERC’s remit.

4. Prepare Your 250-Word Research Summary

The summary should communicate:

What area you want to research

Why the area interests you

What environmental problem or research question motivates you

How your interests relate to the supervisor

Why the proposed area is appropriate for environmental science research

5. Request References Early

Because two references are required, applicants should approach referees well before the relevant deadline.

6. Check the Exact Course Deadline

The CREATES deadline is not necessarily identical across every Cambridge course. Applicants must identify the course associated with their first-choice supervisor and check whether the deadline is 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027.

7. Consider Other Cambridge Funding

Applicants are encouraged to complete the Cambridge Trust and Gates Cambridge sections where relevant so they can be considered for additional sources of funding. However, some of these schemes have earlier deadlines.

An Opportunity for Environmental Science Researchers

The CREATES DLA is designed around major environmental challenges and interdisciplinary scientific research. Its participating departments span areas from Earth sciences and climate research to biodiversity, conservation, genetics, plant sciences, zoology, archaeology and environmental modelling.

The programme’s broader training environment also aims to develop researchers who can work beyond academia. CREATES has collaborative relationships with organisations across government, industry, conservation and the third sector, creating opportunities for networking and professional development alongside doctoral research.

Frequently Asked Questions

The programme is for students beginning in October 2027, with the application guidance specifying a 1 October 2027 Michaelmas Term start.

There are 15 NERC-funded PhD studentships for the 2027 entry.

Not necessarily. Applicants identify topics and supervisors, while the final project is intended to be developed with the supervisory team during the first term.

Yes. The guidance allows applicants to choose supervisors across more than one department, although applicants should provide a prioritised list.

Do I need a research topic within NERC’s remit?

Yes, if you want to be considered for CREATES NERC DLA funding, at least one proposed topic must fall within the NERC remit.

Is an English-language requirement applicable?

Yes. Applicants must meet Cambridge’s English-language requirements where applicable.

When is the application deadline?

The applicable CREATES deadline is the same as the funding deadline for the applicant’s chosen course: 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027.

When are interviews expected?

Online interviews are anticipated during the week of 22 February 2027.

When will offers be made?

Initial offers are expected from late February, with the NERC Universal Acceptance Date at noon on 17 March 2027.

Conclusion

The University of Cambridge CREATES NERC-funded PhD Studentships 2027 provide an opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers to pursue advanced environmental science research within one of the world’s leading research universities. The programme offers 15 funded 3.5-year PhD studentships, with research opportunities spanning climate change, environmental processes, biology, conservation, Earth sciences, geological hazards and other areas within the NERC remit.

Applicants should begin by identifying relevant research topics and supervisors, checking that at least one proposed area falls within NERC’s remit, contacting prospective supervisors, preparing their 250-word research summary and arranging their two references well ahead of the deadline.

Because the final application deadline depends on the chosen Cambridge course, prospective applicants should check carefully whether their deadline is 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027. Early preparation is particularly important for applicants who also want to be considered for other Cambridge funding schemes with earlier deadlines.

For applicants with a strong academic background and a clear interest in environmental research, the CREATES DLA provides a structured route toward doctoral research, specialist training and interdisciplinary engagement in areas addressing some of the world’s most significant environmental challenges.

Its primary goal is to build capacity of mid-level professionals to control, prevent, detect, and respond to disease threats and outbreaks by employing science, policy, and data-driven interventions and programs effectively and efficiently whilst learning from best practices across the continent. The African Epidemic Service has three tracks namely, Epidemiology, Laboratory Leadership Fellowship and Public health informatics.

The African Epidemic Services – Epidemiology track is a full-time two-year competency based applied epidemiology training program with three months in-person didactic training in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and 21 months of applied training in a site hosted by an African Union Member State. The program aims to strengthen the disease prevention and response capacity of African Union Member States. Successful applicants will participate in experiential Core Activities of Learning (CALs) that include, but are not limited to, data analysis, surveillance system evaluation, and outbreak investigation. The AES-Epidemiology fellow will have the support of an expert supervisor and or a mentor who will provide support throughout the fellowship programme.

Benefits

Africa CDC will provide all learning and development materials and cover costs associated with the fellowship, including travel-related costs, stipends, hardware, software and health insurance.

Eligibility

Applicants for the Fellowship must:

Be a citizen of an African Union Member State.

Be a youth as defined by the African Union, i.e., an individual under the age of 35.

At the time of application, be employed in an African country with permission from employing government institution to attend the two years training, with guarantee to return to employment post training;

Have a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree from an accredited university in the one health or related fields such as human medicine, nursing veterinary medicine, environmental sciences, public health or related fields or other doctoral-level training;

Demonstrate satisfactory completion of coursework in epidemiology or quantitative research methods; and biostatistics

Have at least three years of recent full-time public health post graduate experience in an African country.

Demonstrate ability to read and prepare technical medical and epidemiological communication materials such as scientific publications, scientific conference presentations etc

Proficiency in at least one of the African Union’s official languages (English, French, Arabic, Portuguese, Spanish, or Kiswahili) is required. Knowledge of an additional AU official language is an asset

Note: Advanced FETP Fellows and Graduates are not eligible to apply.

Application

All applications must be submitted using the online application form. Incomplete applications will not be considered. All applicants must provide the following information:

A national passport from an African Union Member State.

An official letter of support with permission from a government institution to attend the two-year training programme with the right to return post training.

Letters of recommendation from two reputable professional referees.

An official copy of degree certificate and transcripts of your bachelor’s or master’s degree.

Brief curriculum vitae using the AU template.

Motivation statement (maximum 500 words), outlining why this program would be a good fit, and further outlining how this training will impact your country.

Optional: Evidence of additional relevant qualifications.

TITLE: WHO 2026 Urban Health Training: Apply for the Urban Health Capacity Assessment and Response Kit Training

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is inviting qualified urban health professionals, policymakers, city practitioners, and experienced facilitators of multi-sectoral processes to apply for its 2nd WHO Training on the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Kit.

This four-week online training is designed to strengthen the ability of professionals and cross-sectoral teams to understand, assess, and respond to urban health challenges through collaborative approaches. The programme focuses on the practical use of the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit, which helps policymakers and practitioners identify existing capacities, recognize gaps, develop response strategies, and work collaboratively across different sectors to improve health and wellbeing in cities.

The training will take place online through four sessions scheduled for 17 September, 24 September, 1 October and 8 October 2026. Each session will run for two hours from 14:00 to 16:00 CET, with participants also expected to dedicate additional time to preparation and assignments.

According to the WHO announcement, the training is intended for professionals who are actively involved in shaping urban environments, public policy, health, infrastructure, transport, housing, climate resilience, food systems, security, economic development and other areas that influence the health and wellbeing of urban populations.

About the WHO Urban Health Capacity Training

Urbanization is transforming the way people live, work and access essential services. As cities continue to grow, policymakers and practitioners face increasingly complex challenges involving public health, infrastructure, climate change, inequality, housing, transport, food systems, governance and access to basic services.

The WHO’s Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit is designed to help professionals respond to these interconnected challenges by taking a whole-of-city and intersectoral approach.

The resource recognizes that urban health cannot be addressed by the health sector alone. Decisions involving transportation, urban planning, housing, infrastructure, environmental management, economic development, food systems, governance and public safety can all have direct or indirect effects on population health.

The training therefore provides participants with the knowledge and practical skills needed to assess the capacities available within urban systems, identify weaknesses and strengths, and develop strategies for addressing capacity gaps.

Why Urban Health Capacity Building Matters

Rapid urbanization, climate change and socio-economic inequalities are creating increasingly complex pressures on cities.

Urban health challenges often involve several sectors at the same time. For example, improving health outcomes in a city may require coordinated action involving public health authorities, transport planners, housing agencies, environmental institutions, local government, community organizations and economic actors.

The WHO resource kit is intended to support this kind of collaboration.

It can help professionals working to influence areas such as:

Transportation and mobility

Urban planning

Housing and real estate development

Infrastructure and basic services

Public health

Governance

Food systems and nutrition

Climate resilience

Environmental management

Safety and security

Economy and livelihoods

Community participation

By identifying what capacities already exist and where gaps remain, practitioners can develop more targeted and practical responses to urban challenges.

The training will therefore be particularly relevant to professionals who are seeking to connect health considerations with broader urban development policies and interventions.

Who Should Apply for the WHO Urban Health Training?

The WHO has identified two main categories of applicants for the 2026 training.

1. Cross-Sectoral Teams of Urban Practitioners

The WHO is encouraging applications from teams of three to four individuals who share a common urban health goal.

A qualifying team should include professionals from at least two different sectors or organizations. This is intended to ensure that participants bring different perspectives and areas of expertise to the training.

Potential sectors may include:

Built environment and infrastructure

Health and social services

Environment and climate resilience

Safety and security

Food systems and nutrition

Economy and employment

Transportation

Urban planning

Housing

Other sectors that influence urban health

The team members may come from public or private institutions, including:

Local government agencies

National government agencies

Civil society organizations

Other relevant institutions

Teams that already have a shared urban health objective are particularly well suited to the programme because they can apply the Resource Kit collaboratively to a real-world urban challenge.

2. Individual Facilitators of Intersectoral Processes

Individual applicants can also apply if they have significant experience facilitating multi-sectoral processes.

The WHO is looking for professionals who have experience with activities such as:

Joint planning exercises

Stakeholder dialogues

Inter-agency collaborations

Multi-sectoral projects

Cross-sectoral coordination

Urban health planning processes

Individual applicants should also have a close working relationship with a local government.

They may work within:

Local government

Academia

Private organizations

Civil society organizations

However, the organization should have a primary focus on improving urban living conditions and health where applicable.

Approximately 50 participants are expected to take part in the training.

WHO Urban Health Training Eligibility Requirements

Applicants are expected to meet several professional and academic requirements.

Professional Background

The training is open to professionals working in policy-making and city-level practice, particularly those whose work influences urban health.

Relevant professionals may include those working in:

Public health policy

Urban policy

Transport and mobility

Housing and real estate

Infrastructure and services

Economy and livelihoods

Security and justice

Urban development

Other fields connected to urban health

Applicants should have experience working in multi-sectoral environments and facilitating or participating in multi-sectoral processes.

Academic Qualifications

Applicants should have:

A bachelor’s-level university degree; and

At least five years of professional experience, or three years of experience combined with an advanced degree.

Applicants should also demonstrate an interest in or experience with urban health and capacity building.

Language Requirement

Participants must have an excellent command of English, as English is the working language of the training.

Preference for Cross-Sectoral Teams

The WHO states that preference will be given to teams.

To qualify as a team, the application group should consist of three to four individuals who meet the stated eligibility requirements and come from at least two different sectors or organizations.

For example, a team could combine professionals from the following:

Public health and transportation

Local government and civil society

Urban planning and environmental management

Health and infrastructure

Food systems and nutrition and local government

The purpose of this arrangement is to encourage participants to apply the training through different professional perspectives and strengthen collaboration between sectors.

What Will Participants Learn?

The training will focus on developing practical competencies that can be applied to real urban health challenges.

Participants will learn how to use the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit to understand their existing capacities, identify weaknesses and develop appropriate strategies.

Key learning areas include:

1. Informed Decision-Making, Monitoring and Evaluation

Participants will learn how evidence and data can support urban health policies and decision-making.

This component emphasizes the importance of using reliable information to understand urban challenges, monitor interventions and evaluate whether policies and programmes are achieving their intended outcomes.

2. Policy Coherence and Multi-Sectoral Governance

Urban health challenges frequently cross institutional and sectoral boundaries.

The training will therefore examine ways of strengthening governance structures and improving collaboration among sectors so that policies and interventions work toward shared objectives rather than operating in isolation.

3. Sustainable Financing and Resource Mobilization

Participants will also explore ways of identifying financing mechanisms and strategic investments that can support urban health initiatives.

This is particularly important because urban health interventions often require sustained resources, coordination and investment across multiple institutions.

4. Partnerships and Participation

The programme will emphasize stakeholder engagement and partnerships.

Participants will learn about approaches for bringing different partners and stakeholders into urban health initiatives and strengthening participation in decision-making and implementation.

Key Competencies Participants Will Develop

By the end of the training, participants are expected to strengthen their ability to:

Conduct urban health capacity assessments using the Resource Kit.

Identify critical strengths and capacity gaps within urban systems.

Develop actionable response strategies suited to local circumstances.

Work effectively across different sectors to address urban health challenges.

Use participatory approaches to strengthen urban governance.

Integrate health equity considerations into urban policies and interventions.

These competencies are intended to help participants move beyond identifying urban health problems toward developing practical, coordinated and locally appropriate responses.

Main Objective of the Training

The primary objective of the WHO training is to develop awareness of the cross-disciplinary capacities required for effective urban health action and policy-making.

Particular emphasis will be placed on areas such as:

Data analysis

Policy coherence

Community engagement

Financing strategies

Cross-sectoral collaboration

Urban governance

The training also aims to build a cohort of professionals capable of applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit in their respective settings.

Additional Objectives

Beyond the primary objective, the programme seeks to:

Build a professional cohort skilled in applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit.

Strengthen participants’ ability to identify, assess and address urban health challenges using a capacity-based approach.

Encourage collaboration among professionals working in urban health.

Facilitate peer-to-peer learning and knowledge exchange.

Support the development of strategic responses to urban health challenges.

These objectives make the programme relevant not only for individual professional development but also for organizations seeking to improve their approaches to urban health and cross-sectoral planning.

Training Format and Schedule

The WHO training will be delivered entirely online.

The programme consists of four online sessions, each lasting two hours.

The scheduled sessions are:

17 September 2026

24 September 2026

1 October 2026

8 October 2026

Each session will take place from 14:00 to 16:00 CET.

In addition to the live sessions, participants should expect approximately 4 to 6 hours of offline preparation and assignment work.

Online Delivery Through Zoom

The programme will be delivered through Zoom and will combine different learning approaches, including:

Expert presentations

Breakout discussions

Interactive exercises

Practical application of the Resource Kit

Case studies

Collaborative exercises

Participants will therefore be expected to take an active role rather than simply attend lectures.

Participation and Attendance Requirements

Successful applicants will be expected to actively participate throughout the programme.

The WHO requires participants to:

Attend 100% of the training sessions.

Participate actively in the sessions.

Complete assigned preparation and other required assignments.

Engage in collaborative and interactive exercises.

Participants who meet the attendance and engagement requirements will receive a certificate of completion.

What Do Applicants Need to Submit?

Applicants must prepare three main components for their application.

1. Letter of Interest

Applicants must submit a letter of interest of no more than 500 words.

The letter should explain:

The applicant’s relevant professional experience.

Their motivation for participating in the training.

Their interest in applying the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit.

Applicants should use the letter to demonstrate how their professional background aligns with the objectives of the programme.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide an up-to-date CV highlighting their academic qualifications, professional experience and relevant work in urban health, multi-sectoral collaboration, policy-making, facilitation or related areas.

The CV should clearly demonstrate that the applicant meets the programme’s professional and academic requirements.

3. Personal Video Statement

Applicants are required to submit a personal video statement of no more than five minutes.

The video must respond to the question:

Why do you want to participate in this training and apply the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit?

Applicants must also answer two of the scenario-based questions provided by the WHO.

Scenario Questions for the Video Statement

Applicants can choose two of the following scenarios.

Scenario 1: Urban Health Multi-Sectoral Project

Applicants may describe an urban health multi-sectoral project they have worked on.

They should explain:

The objective of the project.

Who was involved.

How the project was implemented.

This question provides an opportunity to demonstrate practical experience in working across sectors.

Scenario 2: Multi-Sectoral Coordination Challenge

Applicants may describe a challenge they encountered while facilitating or coordinating a multi-sectoral project.

They should explain:

What the challenge was.

Who was involved.

How they addressed the challenge.

How the issue was ultimately resolved.

This allows applicants to demonstrate problem-solving, coordination, communication and facilitation skills.

Scenario 3: Relevant Strengths and Skills

Applicants can alternatively discuss their strengths and skills in relation to the objectives of the training.

They should explain:

Which skills they consider critical for conducting an urban health capacities assessment and response exercise.

How they developed those skills.

Examples of situations where they have applied those skills.

Applicants should use concrete professional examples wherever possible.

How to Apply for the WHO Urban Health Training

Applicants are required to submit their:

Letter of interest

CV

Personal video statement

The application should be sent by email to the WHO at urbanhealth@who.int, with copies to obandof@who.int and macauleym@who.int.

The required email subject line is:

“Urban health capacities Training Application”

Applicants should ensure that all required materials are included before submitting their application.

APPLY HERE

WHO Urban Health Training Deadline

There is an important deadline discrepancy in the WHO announcement that applicants should be aware of.

The announcement headline states:

Deadline for submissions: 4 September 2026.

However, the detailed submission instructions state that applications should be submitted by 28 August 2026.

Because the detailed submission instructions provide the earlier date, applicants should treat 28 August 2026 as the safer deadline and submit as soon as possible rather than waiting for 4 September.

Is the WHO Training Free?

Yes. The WHO states that participation in the training is free.

The working language of the programme is English.

Applicants should nevertheless take into account any personal costs associated with internet access, equipment and participation in the online sessions, as the source does not specify financial support for such expenses.

Countries and Regions Eligible to Apply

The WHO announcement does not specify a restricted list of eligible countries or a particular continent from which applicants must originate.

The opportunity is therefore presented as an international professional training opportunity for eligible professionals, with the WHO specifically stating that women and professionals from low- and middle-income countries are especially encouraged to apply.

The emphasis on low- and middle-income countries makes the opportunity particularly relevant to professionals working in developing urban environments where rapid urbanization, climate pressures, infrastructure gaps and socio-economic inequalities can create complex health challenges.

Who Is Most Likely to Benefit From This Training?

The programme could be particularly valuable for professionals whose work involves influencing urban policies, programmes or systems.

Potential applicants include:

Urban health professionals

Public health policymakers

City practitioners

Local government officials

Urban planners

Transport and mobility professionals

Housing and infrastructure practitioners

Environmental and climate resilience professionals

Food systems and nutrition professionals

Social service professionals

Security and justice practitioners

Economic development professionals

Civil society practitioners

Academics working on urban health

Professionals facilitating multi-sectoral partnerships

Professionals involved in inter-agency collaboration

Practitioners working to improve urban living conditions

The strongest applicants are likely to be those who can demonstrate both professional experience and an ability to work collaboratively across sectors.

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Professionals

The WHO training offers participants an opportunity to strengthen their understanding of how different urban systems interact with health.

Rather than approaching urban health as the responsibility of one institution or profession, the programme promotes a collaborative model in which multiple sectors contribute to healthier urban environments.

Participants can potentially benefit from:

Developing practical urban health assessment skills.

Learning how to identify capacity gaps and existing strengths.

Improving multi-sectoral coordination skills.

Strengthening policy and governance approaches.

Learning about sustainable financing and resource mobilization.

Developing stakeholder engagement and participation skills.

Applying evidence and data to urban health decision-making.

Learning through case studies and collaborative exercises.

Connecting with other professionals working in urban health.

Receiving a certificate of completion after meeting the programme requirements.

The programme’s emphasis on practical application means that participants can potentially use the Resource Kit within their own professional and urban contexts after completing the training.

Visit HERE for more information about the WHO 2026 Urban Health Training.

How Applicants Can Prepare a Strong Application

Although the WHO announcement does not provide a ranking formula for applications, prospective applicants can strengthen their submissions by clearly connecting their experience to the programme’s objectives.

Applicants should consider demonstrating:

Relevant Professional Experience

Explain previous work involving urban health, city development, public policy, infrastructure, community engagement, environmental management or another field affecting urban health.

Multi-Sectoral Experience

Clearly describe experience working with people or institutions from different sectors. This is particularly important because cross-sectoral collaboration is central to the training.

Facilitation and Coordination Skills

Applicants applying as individual facilitators should emphasize experience organizing stakeholder dialogues, joint planning activities, inter-agency collaborations or other multi-sectoral processes.

A Clear Urban Health Challenge

Applicants who apply as teams should identify a specific urban health goal that the team shares. They should also demonstrate how the members’ different sectoral backgrounds contribute to addressing that goal.

Practical Examples

For the video statement, applicants should avoid relying only on general statements about their skills. The scenario questions provide an opportunity to demonstrate practical experience through specific examples, including challenges encountered, actions taken and results achieved.

Important Information for Team Applicants

Professionals interested in applying as a team should consider forming a group of three or four eligible individuals before submitting their application.

The team should:

Include three to four professionals.

Ensure members meet the stated eligibility criteria.

Include individuals from at least two different sectors or organizations.

Identify a shared urban health goal.

Demonstrate experience or interest in addressing urban health challenges.

Prepare an application that communicates how the team could benefit from applying the Resource Kit together.

Because preference is given to teams, eligible professionals who already collaborate across sectors may wish to consider a team application.

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity: 2nd WHO Training on Urban Health Capacity Assessment and Response Kit

Organiser: World Health Organization

Category: Training / Professional Development Opportunity

Format: Online

Platform: Zoom

Duration: Four weeks

Training dates: 17 September, 24 September, 1 October and 8 October 2026

Session time: 14:00–16:00 CET

Session length: Two hours per session

Additional commitment: Approximately 4–6 hours for offline preparation and assignments

Expected participants: Approximately 50

Cost: Free

Working language: English

Academic requirement: Bachelor’s-level university degree

Experience requirement: At least five years of professional experience, or three years plus an advanced degree

Additional experience: Multi-sectoral work and facilitation, plus demonstrated interest or experience in urban health and capacity building

Team option: Three to four people from at least two sectors or organizations

Application documents: Letter of interest, CV, and personal video statement

Letter limit: Maximum 500 words

Video limit: Maximum five minutes

Certificate: Awarded to participants who meet attendance and engagement requirements

Priority encouragement: Women and professionals from low- and middle-income countries

Deadline stated in announcement header: 4 September 2026

Deadline stated in detailed submission instructions: 28 August 2026

Conclusion

The WHO 2026 Urban Health Capacity Assessment and Response Kit Training presents an opportunity for professionals and cross-sectoral teams to strengthen their ability to address the increasingly complex health challenges associated with urbanization.

The programme recognizes that healthier cities require cooperation across multiple areas, including health, transportation, housing, infrastructure, climate resilience, food systems, governance, economic development and community participation. Through the Urban Health Capacities Assessment and Response Resource Kit, participants will learn how to assess existing capacities, identify gaps, develop practical response strategies and strengthen collaboration across sectors.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to professionals with experience in urban development, public policy, public health, local government and multisectoral facilitation. Teams of three to four professionals from different sectors are encouraged, while experienced individual facilitators with strong local government connections can also apply.

Since the source contains different dates for the submission deadline, prospective applicants should exercise caution and follow the earlier 28 August 2026 deadline stated in the detailed submission instructions unless the WHO confirms otherwise.

For professionals seeking to strengthen their expertise in urban health, intersectoral collaboration and evidence-based urban policy, this free WHO training offers an opportunity to gain practical skills, engage with peers and apply a structured resource to real-world urban health challenges.
