TITLE: AEE 2026 Fellowship: Research, Learning and Preservation of Ebira Knowledge, Culture and Heritage

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The AEE 2026 Fellowship is an opportunity for students, researchers, graduates, writers, creatives, early-career professionals and other individuals interested in Ebira history, culture, language, heritage and contemporary issues to engage in structured learning, research and knowledge production.

Held under the theme “Research, Learning and the Preservation of Ebira Knowledge, Culture and Heritage,” the fellowship is designed to encourage deeper exploration and documentation of Ebira knowledge and cultural heritage while giving participants an opportunity to develop research ideas and produce written work based on their interests.

The application process requires prospective fellows to provide information about their personal background, education, professional experience, research interests, motivation and availability to participate in the fellowship. Applicants are also expected to indicate their willingness to undertake an individual research project, produce a scholarly article and actively participate in fellowship activities.

About the AEE 2026 Fellowship

The AEE 2026 Fellowship focuses on the relationship between research, learning, cultural knowledge and heritage preservation. Through the programme, participants are expected to explore subjects connected to Ebira society and contribute to the documentation and preservation of knowledge that may be important to present and future generations.

The fellowship provides a platform for participants with different educational and professional backgrounds to identify areas of interest and develop them into research topics or ideas. The application form specifically invites applicants to consider subjects including Ebira history, culture and tradition, language, literature, heritage preservation, history, political and development studies, as well as contemporary issues.

Rather than limiting applicants to a single academic discipline, the fellowship appears to encourage multidisciplinary engagement with Ebira knowledge and heritage. This allows participants to approach the study of Ebira society from different perspectives, depending on their academic background, professional experience, creative interests or research goals.

Fellowship Theme

The official theme of the programme is:

“Research, Learning and the Preservation of Ebira Knowledge, Culture and Heritage.”

The theme highlights several interconnected areas:

Research: Encouraging participants to investigate topics relating to Ebira history, culture, language, heritage and contemporary society.

Learning: Providing an environment in which participants can develop their understanding of research and knowledge production.

Knowledge preservation: Supporting the documentation and continuation of Ebira knowledge for current and future generations.

Cultural heritage: Promoting research and engagement with traditions, historical experiences, language, literature and other aspects of Ebira heritage.

Knowledge production: Encouraging participants to transform their interests and research ideas into structured written work.

Areas of Interest Covered by the Fellowship

Applicants are asked to identify the areas in which they have an interest. These include:

1. Ebira History

Participants can explore historical aspects of Ebiraland, including important events, communities, historical figures, social developments and other subjects that contribute to an understanding of Ebira history.

Research in this area may involve examining historical records, oral histories, community narratives or other sources of knowledge.

2. Ebira Culture and Tradition

The fellowship also provides an avenue for exploring Ebira culture and traditional practices. Applicants interested in this area may consider different aspects of cultural identity, customs, traditions, social practices and community knowledge.

3. Ebira Language

Language is an important component of cultural preservation. Applicants may therefore develop research ideas relating to the Ebira language, including its preservation, use, development, documentation, literature or role in cultural identity.

4. Heritage and Cultural Preservation

Applicants can investigate ways in which Ebira cultural heritage and knowledge can be documented, protected and passed to future generations.

This area may be particularly relevant to individuals interested in cultural documentation, heritage studies, community-based research and preservation initiatives.

5. Literature

The fellowship welcomes interests relating to literature. Applicants may explore literary works, storytelling, oral traditions, written literature or the relationship between literature and Ebira identity and culture.

6. History

Beyond specifically defined Ebira historical subjects, applicants can also indicate a broader interest in history and develop a research idea relevant to the fellowship theme.

7. Political Studies

Political issues and political developments are also included among the listed areas of interest. Applicants can therefore propose research examining political questions connected to Ebira society or relevant contemporary contexts.

8. Development Studies

Development-related research is another area identified in the application form. Potential research interests may examine social, economic, institutional or community development issues relevant to Ebiraland.

9. Contemporary Issues

The fellowship also recognizes the importance of studying current issues affecting Ebira communities and society. Applicants can therefore develop research proposals addressing contemporary challenges, developments or emerging questions.

10. Other Areas

Applicants are also given an “Other” option, allowing them to identify an area of interest that is not explicitly included in the listed categories.

Who Can Apply for the AEE 2026 Fellowship?

The application form accommodates people at different stages of their academic, research, professional and creative journeys. Applicants are asked to select their current status from the following categories:

Undergraduate students

Postgraduate students

Researchers

Graduates

Early-career professionals

Writers and creatives

Other applicants whose status does not fit the listed categories

The form also asks applicants to provide their institution or organisation, course of study or area of specialization, and highest educational qualification.

Educational Qualifications

Applicants are asked to indicate their highest educational qualification from the following options:

Secondary School

OND/NCE

HND/Bachelor’s Degree

Master’s Degree

PhD

Other qualifications

This indicates that the application form is structured to accommodate applicants with different levels of educational attainment rather than being restricted solely to postgraduate researchers or degree holders.

Ebira Indigene Requirement

One of the specific questions in the application form asks:

“Are you an indigene of Ebiraland?”

Applicants are required to select either Yes or No.

Those who answer yes are subsequently asked to specify which part or Local Government Area of Ebiraland they are from.

Because the application form specifically asks about Ebira indigene status and the applicant’s part/LGA of Ebiraland, prospective applicants should pay close attention to this section and provide accurate information about their background.

Research Experience and Knowledge Production

The AEE 2026 Fellowship places significant emphasis on research, writing and knowledge production.

Applicants are asked whether they have previous experience in:

Research

Writing

Cultural activities

Knowledge production

They can respond either Yes or No.

Previous experience is therefore directly addressed in the application, although the form does not state that applicants must already have extensive research experience.

This makes it important for applicants to accurately describe any relevant experience they have, whether it comes from academic research, independent writing, cultural activities, community engagement, documentation, creative work or other forms of knowledge production.

Proposed Research Topic

A major component of the application involves identifying what the applicant would like to research.

Applicants are asked:

“What aspect of Ebira history, culture, language, heritage or contemporary issues would you like to research?”

They are then required to briefly describe their proposed research topic or idea.

This section gives applicants an opportunity to demonstrate the subject they would like to investigate during the fellowship.

A strong response should clearly communicate:

The subject the applicant wants to investigate.

The specific issue or question they are interested in.

Why the subject is relevant to Ebira knowledge, culture, history, language, heritage or contemporary society.

What they hope to understand, document or contribute through the research.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed topic is realistic and sufficiently focused to be developed into an individual research project during the fellowship.

Why Participate in the AEE 2026 Fellowship?

The application form indicates that participants will be expected to engage in a structured eight-week fellowship involving research, learning and other activities.

Potential areas of engagement include:

Research Development

Participants will have an opportunity to develop an individual research project around an aspect of Ebira history, culture, language, heritage or contemporary issues.

Scholarly Writing

Participants are expected to write and submit a scholarly article based on their research. This can provide practical experience in transforming a research idea into a structured written output.

Knowledge Preservation

By researching and documenting aspects of Ebira knowledge, culture and heritage, participants can contribute to broader efforts to preserve cultural knowledge.

Discussions and Presentations

The fellowship requires participants to take part in discussions, presentations, assignments and other programme activities. This creates opportunities for participants to engage with ideas and communicate their research interests.

Research and Cultural Engagement

Participants can use the fellowship as an opportunity to deepen their engagement with subjects relating to Ebira identity, history, language, traditions and contemporary development.

Eight-Week Fellowship Commitment

Applicants must confirm whether they are available to participate in the eight-week fellowship every Saturday and Sunday.

This is an important consideration before applying. Prospective applicants should ensure that they can consistently participate throughout the programme period.

The application form asks applicants to confirm their availability by selecting either:

Yes

No

Applicants should provide an accurate response because successful participation is expected to require a sustained commitment over the eight-week period.

Individual Research Project

Participants are asked whether they are willing to complete an individual research project during the fellowship.

The research project is a central component of the programme and connects directly to the fellowship’s broader emphasis on research, learning and preservation of Ebira knowledge.

Applicants should therefore consider their potential research interests before completing the application and think about a topic that they could realistically investigate during the programme.

Scholarly Article Requirement

The fellowship also asks applicants whether they are willing to write and submit a scholarly article based on their research.

This means participants should be prepared not only to identify a research topic but also to develop their findings into a written scholarly output.

For prospective applicants, this requirement makes writing ability, willingness to conduct research and commitment to completing written work particularly relevant to the fellowship.

Participation in Fellowship Activities

Applicants are required to indicate whether they are willing to participate in:

Discussions

Presentations

Assignments

Other fellowship activities

Participation is therefore not limited to independent research. Successful fellows are expected to engage with the wider programme and its activities.

Previous Fellowship and Training Experience

The application form also asks whether applicants have previously participated in:

Fellowships

Research programmes

Training programmes

Similar programmes

Applicants can answer either Yes or No.

Those with previous experience should provide truthful information when completing the application. Applicants without previous fellowship or research programme experience can also indicate that they have not participated in such programmes.

What Applicants Hope to Gain

The application includes a question asking:

“What do you hope to gain from the AEE 2026 Fellowship?”

This gives applicants an opportunity to explain their expectations and learning objectives.

Applicants may wish to discuss goals connected to research development, scholarly writing, cultural knowledge, heritage preservation, academic development, networking, knowledge production or gaining practical experience in investigating and documenting Ebira-related subjects.

The strongest response should connect the applicant’s personal or professional objectives with the focus of the fellowship.

Personal and Contact Information Required

Applicants must provide several pieces of personal information as part of the application process.

These include:

Full name

Date of birth

Gender

Phone number

Email address

State of residence

Local Government Area

Ebira indigene status

Part/LGA of Ebiraland, where applicable

Applicants should carefully check these details before submitting the form to ensure that all information is accurate.

Academic and Professional Information Required

The education and professional section asks applicants to provide:

Current status

Institution or organisation

Course of study or area of specialization

Highest educational qualification

The current-status options include undergraduate student, postgraduate student, researcher, graduate, early-career professional, writer/creative and other.

Application Declaration

Before submitting the application, candidates are required to confirm that the information they have provided is true and correct to the best of their knowledge.

The declaration also acknowledges that participation in the AEE 2026 Fellowship requires commitment to:

The fellowship programme

The research project

Other fellowship activities

Applicants should therefore review their responses carefully before submitting the form.

How to Apply for the AEE 2026 Fellowship

Interested applicants should complete the AEE 2026 Fellowship Application Form and provide the requested personal, educational, professional and research information.

The application process involves the following general steps:

Complete the personal information section.

Provide your educational and professional background.

Identify your areas of interest.

Explain your motivation for joining the fellowship.

Indicate whether you have previous research, writing, cultural or knowledge-production experience.

Identify the aspect of Ebira history, culture, language, heritage or contemporary issues you would like to research.

Describe your proposed research topic or idea.

Confirm your availability for the eight-week weekend fellowship.

Confirm your willingness to undertake an individual research project.

Confirm your willingness to write and submit a scholarly article.

Confirm your willingness to participate in discussions, presentations, assignments and other activities.

Provide information about previous fellowship, research or training experience.

Explain what you hope to gain from the programme.

Complete the declaration and submit the application.

Applicants should ensure that their responses are accurate, complete and relevant to the fellowship’s theme.

APPLY HERE

AEE 2026 Fellowship Deadline

Deadline: Not specified in the provided application form.

The supplied AEE 2026 Fellowship application information does not state a closing date. Applicants should therefore check the official application page or announcement for any deadline or subsequent update before submitting their application.

Important Information for Applicants

Only shortlisted applicants will be contacted, according to the application form.

Applicants should therefore:

Provide accurate contact information.

Ensure all required questions are answered.

Clearly explain their motivation for applying.

Present a focused research topic or idea.

Demonstrate genuine interest in Ebira knowledge, culture, heritage or related contemporary issues.

Consider whether they can commit to the eight-week Saturday and Sunday schedule.

Be prepared to undertake an individual research project.

Be prepared to write and submit a scholarly article.

Be willing to participate in discussions, presentations and assignments.

Review all information carefully before submitting the form.

Visit HERE to learn more about the AEE 2026 Fellowship.

Conclusion

The AEE 2026 Fellowship provides a research- and learning-focused platform centred on the preservation of Ebira knowledge, culture and heritage. The programme brings together individuals with interests spanning history, culture, language, literature, heritage preservation, political studies, development studies and contemporary issues.

The fellowship’s emphasis on an individual research project and scholarly article makes research and writing important components of the programme. At the same time, its broad range of eligible educational and professional backgrounds allows students, researchers, graduates, early-career professionals, writers and creatives to engage with subjects connected to Ebira knowledge and heritage.

Prospective applicants should carefully consider the programme’s eight-week weekend commitment and ensure they are prepared to participate in research, discussions, presentations, assignments and other activities. Since the provided application form does not specify a deadline, applicants should verify the latest application information through the official fellowship announcement before submitting their forms.

TITLE: University of Saskatchewan Toxicology MSc and PhD 2026–2027: Funded Graduate Study in Canada With Guaranteed Stipends

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Saskatchewan (USask) Toxicology Graduate Program is accepting applications for its research-intensive Master of Science (M.Sc.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) programs in Toxicology in Canada. The program is particularly attractive to students interested in environmental health, contaminant science, ecological risk assessment, human health, wildlife toxicology, analytical toxicology, molecular toxicology, and related scientific fields.

One of the most important features of the program is its funding structure. The University of Saskatchewan states that all graduate students accepted into the Toxicology Graduate Program are guaranteed funding, with current minimum stipends of CAD 23,000 for master’s students and CAD 26,000 for doctoral students. The Toxicology Centre separately describes accepted students as receiving full funding once they have secured a research supervisor and satisfied admission requirements.

Another major advantage is application flexibility. There is no fixed application deadline for the Toxicology M.Sc. or Ph.D. programs. Applications are accepted continuously throughout the year, and students may start their studies in January, May, or September.

Both Canadian and international applicants can apply, subject to academic, English-language, research, and admission requirements.

About the University of Saskatchewan Toxicology Graduate Program

The Toxicology Graduate Program is an interdisciplinary research program at the University of Saskatchewan. It offers research-based M.Sc. and Ph.D. pathways designed to prepare students to investigate the effects of contaminants and potentially harmful physical or chemical agents on human beings, animals, ecosystems, and biological systems.

Research and postgraduate education in toxicology are coordinated through the University of Saskatchewan Toxicology Centre and involve academics from numerous university departments as well as scientists from government research institutions. This multidisciplinary structure allows graduate students to work across conventional disciplinary boundaries rather than being restricted to one narrow scientific field.

The Toxicology Centre’s broader mission is to train highly capable toxicologists who can contribute to emerging human and environmental health challenges while strengthening research, public engagement, technical outreach, and international leadership in toxicology.

Degrees Available

Applicants can pursue either a Master of Science or Doctor of Philosophy degree.

Program
Typical duration
Format
Delivery

M.Sc. in Toxicology
Approximately 2 years
Research/thesis-based
In person

Ph.D. in Toxicology
Approximately 3–4 years; USask lists 4 years as the expected length
Research/dissertation-based
In person

The program is therefore designed primarily for students seeking advanced scientific research training rather than a classroom-only postgraduate qualification.

Why Study Toxicology at the University of Saskatchewan?

Toxicology sits at the intersection of environmental science, biology, chemistry, medicine, veterinary science, ecology, public health, and risk assessment. Students can investigate how pollutants and contaminants move through environmental systems, how living organisms respond to chemical exposure, how toxic substances affect human and animal health, and how scientific evidence can inform environmental regulation and risk management.

USask highlights three broad strengths of its program: exposure to numerous areas of toxicology, interdisciplinary research involving university faculty and government scientists, and preparation for careers in government, consulting, industry, public health, and academia.

The program has a particularly strong environmental and aquatic toxicology component, while faculty research spans a considerably broader spectrum.

Toxicology Research Areas and Specializations

Depending on supervisor availability and the applicant’s research interests, potential areas of graduate specialization include:

Analytical toxicology

Aquatic toxicology

Ecotoxicology

Immunotoxicology

Molecular and biochemical toxicology

Nutritional toxicology

Soil toxicology

Environmental contaminant research

Ecological and human-health risk assessment

Veterinary toxicology

Human toxicology

Wildlife toxicology

Forensic toxicology

Radiation toxicology

Molecular biology related to toxicological mechanisms

Contaminant exposure and environmental chemistry

The official University Catalogue confirms that the interdisciplinary program extends across areas such as analytical, aquatic, ecological, forensic, immunological, nutritional, radiation, veterinary, and wildlife toxicology.

Examples of Research Available Through USask Toxicology

The breadth of the faculty provides potential research opportunities involving topics such as heavy-metal neurotoxicity, exposure modelling, contaminant effects on aquatic organisms, livestock toxicology, environmental pollutants, computational chemistry, reproductive and developmental toxicology, food-web contamination, biomagnification, pesticides, northern ecosystems, metal bioaccumulation, selenium and human health, emerging contaminants, soil ecotoxicology, air pollution, cardiovascular effects, environmental genetics, DNA damage, and chemical mixtures.

This interdisciplinary environment is particularly valuable for students whose research interests cross environmental, biological, chemical, veterinary, or human-health disciplines.

Research Supervisors

The University strongly recommends identifying and contacting a prospective supervisor before submitting an application.

Applicants should review the faculty members associated with the Toxicology Graduate Program and identify researchers whose expertise aligns closely with their proposed area of study. Prospective students are encouraged to contact an appropriate faculty member with information about their academic background, research interests, and proposed graduate goals.

If the faculty member is accepting new students and considers the applicant potentially suitable, the prospective supervisor may then advise the student to proceed with the formal application. Supervisor approval is described by the program as highly recommended before applying.

This step should not be treated as a formality. For a research-based master’s or Ph.D., the fit between the applicant’s interests and the supervisor’s active research program can be central to admission, research funding, and successful completion of the degree.

Guaranteed Funding for Accepted Toxicology Graduate Students

Funding is one of the strongest aspects of this opportunity.

According to the official graduate-program page, all graduate students are guaranteed funding if accepted into the Toxicology program. The minimum stipend levels currently stated are:

Degree
Minimum stipend

M.Sc.
CAD 23,000

Ph.D.
CAD 26,000

The Toxicology Centre further states that once a student has been accepted by a supervisor for their research program and has met the admission requirements, graduate students are guaranteed full funding. Basic health-insurance coverage is also identified as guaranteed by the Centre.

Applicants should understand an important distinction: guaranteed funding does not mean that tuition and university fees disappear. Students are still assessed tuition and student fees. The stipend and other funding support should therefore be considered alongside the actual cost of enrollment.

Additional Scholarships and Awards

Graduate students may also have access to other University of Saskatchewan funding opportunities. Across the university, the College of Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies administers more than CAD 14 million in scholarships annually, with funding originating from governments, university programs, donors, and individual academic units.

The Toxicology Centre also lists program-specific awards and scholarships. These include opportunities such as an entrance scholarship for incoming M.Sc. and Ph.D. students, academic awards, research-presentation travel funding, and a Student Support Fund. Individual awards have their own eligibility criteria and deadlines and should not be confused with the standard guaranteed funding package attached to admission.

M.Sc. in Toxicology Admission Requirements

Applicants seeking admission to the master’s program must generally hold a relevant undergraduate qualification.

For the Toxicology M.Sc., USask requires a four-year honours degree or equivalent from a recognized university or college in an academic discipline relevant to the intended field of study, together with a minimum cumulative weighted average equivalent to 70% in the final two years of study. Proof of English-language proficiency may also be required.

The Toxicology Centre provides additional academic guidance, indicating that applicants should normally have an undergraduate background in the life or natural sciences. Preparation in biology, chemistry, biochemistry, physiology, and statistics is particularly relevant, while previous study in environmental chemistry, ecology, pharmacology, or toxicology can be advantageous.

Meeting the minimum academic threshold does not automatically guarantee admission.

Ph.D. in Toxicology Admission Requirements

Applicants seeking direct admission to the Ph.D. program normally require a master’s degree or equivalent from a recognized institution in a discipline relevant to toxicology.

The applicant must also generally have a cumulative weighted average of at least 70% on the USask grading-equivalent scale in the relevant master’s coursework. English-language proficiency requirements may apply to international applicants and applicants whose first language is not English.

As with the master’s program, applicants should also demonstrate the capacity for independent academic research and advanced graduate study.

M.Sc. Degree Requirements

The M.Sc. is a research-based program. According to the 2026–2027 University Catalogue, students must maintain continuous registration in the required research course and complete relevant graduate ethics, seminar, research, and academic-course requirements.

The program includes a minimum of nine credit units of core coursework, selected in consultation with the student’s advisory committee and approved by the graduate chair. Additional ethics requirements apply where human or animal research is involved.

The degree is therefore structured around both formal graduate study and substantial independent research.

Ph.D. Degree Requirements

The Ph.D. places greater emphasis on independent original research.

Doctoral students must maintain continuous registration in their designated research course, complete required research and ethics components, participate in the toxicology seminar requirement, and complete at least six credit units selected in consultation with the advisory committee.

Ph.D. candidates must also successfully complete a doctoral candidacy assessment and dissertation defense.

English-Language Requirements for International Applicants

Because instruction and examination at the University of Saskatchewan are conducted in English, applicants may be required to establish English proficiency.

Applicants should verify the current test requirements immediately before applying because language-testing systems and university thresholds can change.

Additional Student Fees

Full-time on-campus students may also be assessed fees supporting services such as health and dental coverage, transit, and other student services.

For the 2026–2027 academic year, the program page currently lists student fees of CAD 617.36 for Fall 2026, CAD 854.96 for Winter 2027, and CAD 46.75 each for Spring and Summer 2027, subject to university policies and the student’s enrollment circumstances.

Applicants should therefore budget using both tuition and student fees rather than relying only on the tuition figure.

Application Deadline

There is no fixed application deadline.

The University of Saskatchewan states that Toxicology applications are accepted on a year-round, continual basis. Students can begin the program in:

January, May, or September.

Because a research supervisor is highly recommended and international applicants may require significant time for study-permit processing, applying well ahead of the intended start term is prudent even though there is no formal program deadline.

Application Process

A prospective applicant should first investigate the available research areas and identify an appropriate Toxicology faculty member whose work aligns with their interests. After discussing potential supervision, the applicant can submit the formal University of Saskatchewan graduate application.

The online application requests personal details, the applicant’s complete post-secondary academic history, and information for three referees. Two referees must be academic contacts, while the third may be either academic or professional. The university estimates that the initial online application takes approximately 30 minutes and allows applicants to save their progress before submission.

Application Fee

The application will not proceed to processing until the required fee has been paid.

Documents Applicants Should Prepare

After submitting the online application and paying the fee, applicants receive access to the Supplemental Items & Documents section of the application system.

Applicants are initially required to upload unofficial PDF transcripts from each post-secondary institution they attended. Documents must include the institution’s grading information or legend, and all pages of each transcript should be combined into one PDF. Transcripts issued in languages other than English need a certified English translation. Official transcripts are generally requested from applicants who receive an offer of admission.

Depending on the applicant and program assessment, additional documentation can include a current CV or résumé, a statement or letter of intent describing experience and interest in toxicology, English-language test evidence where required, and letters of recommendation.

What to Include in a Strong Statement of Intent

For a research-based program of this nature, applicants should avoid sending a generic statement that simply says they are interested in science or environmental protection.

A strong statement should clearly establish the applicant’s academic preparation, previous research or laboratory exposure, proposed area of toxicology, methodological interests, reasons for choosing USask, and the connection between those interests and a potential supervisor.

Applicants should also explain how their previous academic or professional experience prepares them for independent graduate research and what they hope to accomplish through the M.Sc. or Ph.D.

International Students and Canadian Study Permits

International students are explicitly considered within the University’s graduate admission process.

For current Canadian immigration procedures reflected on the USask website, master’s and doctoral students applying for a Canadian study permit do not require a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL). USask advises international applicants to review current federal study-permit requirements before applying because immigration policies can change independently of university admission rules.

Admission to the university and approval of a Canadian study permit remain separate processes.

Indigenous and Under-Represented Applicants

The Toxicology Graduate Program specifically states that it encourages applications from Indigenous students and individuals from under-represented groups.

USask explains that incorporating diverse perspectives and knowledge systems can improve the relevance and impact of environmental and toxicological research.

This is an encouragement and inclusion statement, however, rather than a restriction: the general Toxicology M.Sc. and Ph.D. programs are not limited to applicants from a particular racial or ethnic group.

Career Opportunities After a Toxicology Graduate Degree

The interdisciplinary nature of toxicology can prepare graduates for positions across environmental science, regulatory work, research, industry, health, and academia.

USask specifically identifies potential employment pathways in government, environmental consulting, industry, public health, and academic research. The Toxicology Centre also states that its graduates are prepared for careers with government agencies, consulting organizations, industrial employers, universities, and further postgraduate research.

Career possibilities can vary considerably depending on the student’s research specialization, laboratory capabilities, quantitative skills, publications, professional network, and regulatory expertise.

Important Funding Clarification

Applicants should not interpret the phrase “guaranteed funding” as meaning that there are no costs associated with studying at USask.

The Toxicology program provides a guaranteed minimum stipend for accepted students, while the university separately charges tuition and student fees. Prospective students should therefore calculate the net financial position after tuition, university fees, living costs, insurance arrangements, transportation, housing, and other expenses.

This distinction is especially important for international M.Sc. students because the published international master’s tuition is higher than the domestic master’s rate.

Conclusion

The University of Saskatchewan Toxicology M.Sc. and Ph.D. programs offer a strong opportunity for students seeking advanced, interdisciplinary research training in environmental, human, wildlife, analytical, aquatic, molecular, veterinary, and ecological toxicology.

The combination of guaranteed graduate funding, minimum stipends of CAD 23,000 for M.Sc. students and CAD 26,000 for Ph.D. students, year-round applications, multiple annual entry points, and eligibility for international students makes the program particularly noteworthy for prospective researchers seeking graduate study in Canada.

Prospective applicants should begin by identifying an appropriate research supervisor, assessing whether their academic background aligns with the program, preparing a focused research-oriented statement of intent, and completing the formal USask graduate application.

There is no fixed application deadline, but applicants should apply sufficiently early for their intended January, May, or September start date, particularly if international study-permit processing will be required.

TITLE: University College London Online Courses

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you looking for online courses from one of the world’s leading universities? If yes, then the University College London Online Courses are an excellent opportunity for learners who want to develop new skills, pursue their interests, or advance their careers. These free online courses provide flexible learning opportunities through the FutureLearn platform and cover a wide range of subjects, including healthcare, education, medicine, psychology, technology, sustainability, research, and social sciences. Whether you want to improve your professional skills, explore a new academic field, or gain knowledge in a specific subject, the University College London Online Courses offer valuable learning opportunities from a globally recognized university.

University College London (UCL) was founded in 1826 and became the first English university established after Oxford and Cambridge. It was also the first university in England to open university education to people who had previously faced exclusion. UCL introduced systematic teaching in fields including law, architecture, and medicine. Today, UCL has more than 35,000 students from 150 countries and over 11,000 staff, with an annual income of more than £1 billion.

The University College London free courses are available through the FutureLearn online learning platform. Learners can choose from 55 courses covering different academic and professional areas. UCL also offers an ExpertTrack, including a series of courses designed to help learners specialise their skills. The UCL free online courses range from short three-week programs to longer options, with study requirements generally between 2 and 5 hours per week depending on the course.

These 2026 online courses cover a variety of subjects, including English grammar, education, healthcare, medicine, research methods, urban mobility, sustainability, social media, economics, blockchain, machine learning, and mental health. Some courses offer free digital upgrades, while others are included in FutureLearn Unlimited or available as premium courses. Learners can select courses according to their interests, professional goals, and learning needs. If you want to learn from a leading UK university without enrolling in a full-time degree program, these international UCL online courses are worth exploring.

TITLE: Durham University Sir William Luce Fellowship 2027: Funded Middle East Research Fellowship Covering Travel, Accommodation and Meals in the UK

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027 Sir William Luce Fellowship at Durham University, a prestigious visiting research opportunity for scholars and experienced professionals working on the politics, society, economy, history and security of the Middle East and adjacent regions that were central to the career of Sir William Luce.

The Fellowship is administered by the Sir William Luce Memorial Fund and hosted jointly by the Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies and Trevelyan College at Durham University in the United Kingdom.

For the 2027 cycle, the Fellowship will run from:

26 April to 25 June 2027

during Durham University’s Easter term.

The programme is open to people working at postdoctoral or equivalent professional level, including:

Postdoctoral scholars

Academics

Diplomats

Politicians

Business executives

Other appropriately experienced researchers or practitioners

The geographic focus is specifically on areas connected with Sir William Luce’s professional career:

The Gulf monarchies

Yemen

Iran

Sudan

South Sudan

The Fellowship is particularly interested in applicants whose research can bring fresh perspectives on political, social, economic or security issues in these countries and regions.

Successful Fellows receive substantial practical support during their stay in Durham. The Fellowship covers:

Travel to and from Durham

Accommodation

All meals during the Fellowship period

Access to Durham University facilities

Access to research collections and libraries

Limited additional funding to consult Sir William Luce papers held at the Gulf Studies Centre at the University of Exeter

In addition, the Fellow will receive a £1,000 honorarium after submitting the final paper for publication.

The application deadline is:

Wednesday, 7 October 2026

Applicants must submit a CV of no more than two pages, a two-to-three-page research proposal, and contact details for two referees.

Applications should preferably be sent by email to:

luce.fund@durham.ac.uk

About the Sir William Luce Fellowship

The Sir William Luce Fellowship is an annual research fellowship designed to support high-level research on the parts of the Middle East and surrounding region with which Sir William Luce was closely associated during his career.

The Fellowship brings a selected researcher or practitioner to Durham University during the University’s Easter term.

Its purpose is not simply to provide an individual with time away from their usual position.

Instead, the programme is designed to create a period of intensive research and intellectual engagement in which the Fellow can:

Develop a focused research project

Use Durham’s specialist Middle East collections

Engage with scholars at the University

Participate in the academic life of the Institute

Interact with the Trevelyan College community

Deliver a major public lecture

Produce a final paper for publication

The Fellowship therefore combines the characteristics of:

A visiting research fellowship

An academic residency

A professional exchange

A publication opportunity

It may be particularly attractive to established or emerging experts whose work would benefit from access to archival collections and an interdisciplinary Middle East research environment.

Fellowship Dates for 2027

The 2027 Fellowship will take place from:

26 April to 25 June 2027

The Fellow is hosted at Durham University during the Easter term.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they are available to spend the Fellowship period in Durham and participate fully in the intellectual and collegiate life associated with the programme.

Research Focus of the Fellowship

The Sir William Luce Fellowship is not a general international relations fellowship covering the whole world.

Its geographic remit is relatively specific.

Research should relate to one or more of the following:

Gulf monarchies

Yemen

Iran

Sudan

South Sudan

The Committee is particularly interested in work that provides new or original perspectives on important issues affecting these areas.

Possible dimensions include:

Politics

Society

Economics

Security

Research may be:

Historical, or

Contemporary

This means both historians and scholars examining current political or socio-economic developments may be suitable candidates.

The Gulf Monarchies

Research relating to the Gulf monarchies may potentially examine issues such as:

Political institutions

Governance

State-society relations

Economic diversification

Energy

Security

Regional diplomacy

Social transformation

Labour

Migration

Foreign policy

Gulf political economy

Historical state formation

Applicants should, however, develop their own original question rather than treating these examples as predetermined Fellowship themes.

Yemen

Applicants working on Yemen may potentially contribute new perspectives concerning:

Political conflict

State institutions

Regional intervention

Society

Humanitarian conditions

Economic change

Security

Historical political development

Because the Fellowship explicitly welcomes both historical and contemporary work, proposals can vary substantially in period and methodological approach.

Iran

Research focused on Iran may potentially address:

Domestic politics

Foreign policy

Political economy

Security

State-society relations

Regional politics

Institutional change

Historical developments

The Fellowship does not prescribe a single theoretical or disciplinary approach.

What matters is that the proposed research falls meaningfully within the programme’s geographic and intellectual remit.

Sudan and South Sudan

The inclusion of both Sudan and South Sudan is particularly important because Durham University holds distinctive archival resources relevant to the region.

Research could potentially investigate:

Political history

State formation

Conflict

Peace processes

Governance

Security

Political economy

Society

Regional relations

Historical administration

The University’s Sudan Archive is especially relevant to researchers whose projects depend on documentary and archival materials.

Fresh Perspectives Are Encouraged

The Fellowship Committee states that it wants to appoint someone whose work can provide:

Fresh perspectives

on the regions covered by the Fellowship.

Applicants should therefore avoid proposing projects that simply summarize an established body of literature.

A strong proposal should ideally show:

An original question

New evidence

A distinctive interpretation

A useful comparative approach

A new conceptual perspective

An under-researched issue

The Fellowship is designed to create new scholarship rather than merely provide a platform for already completed work.

Who Can Apply?

The Fellowship is unusual because eligibility is not restricted solely to university academics.

Potential applicants include:

Scholars at postdoctoral level

Academics

Diplomats

Politicians

Business executives

This broad eligibility reflects the Fellowship’s interest in combining scholarship with practical professional knowledge.

A diplomat with significant regional expertise, for example, may bring perspectives different from those of an academic historian.

Likewise, an experienced business executive working in the Gulf could potentially offer valuable analysis of regional economic or institutional developments.

The key requirement is that the candidate’s work must be relevant to the geographical and thematic scope of the Fellowship.

Is a PhD Required?

The call describes the Fellowship as available to a:

Scholar at post-doctoral level, diplomat, politician, academic or business executive.

For candidates applying through an academic route, this means the Fellowship is primarily aimed at researchers who have already reached postdoctoral level rather than current undergraduate or early-stage doctoral students.

However, the wider list of eligible professional categories demonstrates that possession of a PhD is not necessarily the only route to eligibility for experienced diplomats, politicians or business executives.

Applicants should demonstrate an appropriate level of:

Professional expertise

Research capacity

Regional knowledge

Intellectual independence

What Does the Fellowship Cover?

The Sir William Luce Fellowship provides substantial practical support for the successful Fellow.

Travel to and From Durham

The Fellowship covers:

The cost of travel to and from Durham.

This is particularly valuable for international applicants who may otherwise face significant travel expenses.

Applicants should consult the Fellowship organizers regarding the exact travel arrangements and reimbursement procedures if selected.

Accommodation

The Fellowship covers:

Accommodation for the duration of the Fellowship.

Fellows normally reside at:

Trevelyan College

during their time at Durham University.

This allows the Fellow to remain integrated into the University community rather than arranging accommodation independently.

Meals

The Fellowship also covers:

All meals for the duration of the Fellowship.

This significantly reduces the day-to-day cost of spending approximately two months in the United Kingdom.

£1,000 Honorarium

The successful Fellow will receive a:

£1,000 honorarium

However, this payment is not simply an upfront stipend.

It is paid:

On submission and receipt of the final paper for publication.

Applicants should therefore distinguish the honorarium from the Fellowship’s travel, accommodation and meal support.

The £1,000 payment is linked to the Fellow completing the required scholarly publication output.

Is There a Monthly Stipend?

The Fellowship announcement does not state that Fellows receive a monthly living stipend or salary.

Instead, financial support is structured primarily around:

Travel

Accommodation

Meals

Access to facilities

Limited research travel funding

£1,000 honorarium after submission of the final paper

It would therefore be inaccurate to advertise the opportunity as offering a large cash stipend in addition to these benefits.

Research Funding for the Luce Papers at Exeter University

The Sir William Luce Memorial Fund may also provide:

Limited funding

for the successful Fellow to visit the Luce papers held at the Gulf Studies Centre at the University of Exeter.

This is particularly relevant for researchers whose project would benefit from archival work connected directly to Sir William Luce or broader Gulf research.

Applicants whose proposal requires this material should explain why access to the Exeter collection would strengthen their research.

Access to Durham University Facilities

The Fellowship is held jointly within:

Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies

Trevelyan College

The Fellow receives full access to relevant University facilities.

These include:

University Library

Computing and Information Services

Departmental facilities

Specialist research collections

This institutional access is one of the central benefits of the Fellowship.

Access to the Sudan Archive

One of Durham University’s particularly distinctive resources is the:

Sudan Archive

Researchers whose work concerns Sudan, South Sudan or related historical issues may find this collection especially valuable.

The Fellowship Committee specifically expects Fellows to engage with the distinctive resources available at Durham.

Applicants should therefore investigate the relevant collections before writing their research proposal.

A strong proposal should demonstrate not only that Durham is an attractive university, but why the specific resources available there are necessary for the proposed research.

Middle East and Gulf Documentary Collections

Durham also possesses extensive documentary and library collections related to:

Middle East

Gulf region

These resources can support historical and contemporary research across several disciplines.

Candidates should identify collections relevant to their project whenever possible.

Engagement With Durham Academic Staff

Fellows are expected to engage with academic staff at Durham.

The Fellowship is not designed as a private writing retreat.

Instead, the Fellow is expected to become part of the University’s intellectual community during the residency.

Potential forms of engagement may include:

Research discussions

Seminars

Informal academic exchanges

Meetings with specialists

Participation in Institute activities

This can provide valuable opportunities to test arguments and develop new research networks.

Participation in the Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies

The Fellow is encouraged to participate in the full range of academic and social activities organized by the:

Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies

This is an important component of the residency.

The Fellowship therefore suits applicants who are interested in active academic exchange rather than spending the entire period working independently.

About the Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies

Durham University’s Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies was established in:

1962

It has developed an international reputation for its broad expertise in Middle Eastern studies.

Its research and teaching interests have included substantial work concerning:

Politics

Economy

Society

International relations

History

of the Middle East.

The Institute also has a large graduate programme with particular strengths in the politics and economy of the region.

In September 2002, the Institute moved into a purpose-built building donated by H.H. Sheikh Dr Sultan Bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah.

For visiting Fellows, the Institute provides an academic environment specifically oriented toward the region covered by the Sir William Luce Fellowship.

Trevelyan College

The Fellowship is also held in association with:

Trevelyan College

Trevelyan is one of Durham University’s constituent colleges.

It is located within walking distance of:

University libraries

Teaching departments

The Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies

Several other colleges

Durham Botanic Gardens

The College has an active:

Senior Common Room

bringing together academics and other senior members of the University community.

Participation in the Senior Common Room

Sir William Luce Fellows are encouraged to participate actively in the life of Trevelyan College’s Senior Common Room.

This could include activities such as:

Informal seminars

Lectures

Discussions with Fellows

Engagement with students

College events

The expectation is that the Fellow will contribute to the intellectual life of the College rather than simply use it as accommodation.

College Facilities Available to the Fellow

As a member of Trevelyan College, the Fellow may access facilities including:

Senior Common Room

Computer facilities

Library

Common spaces

Other College facilities

The Fellowship therefore provides both academic and collegiate integration.

The 2027 Sir William Luce Lecture

One of the major responsibilities of the Fellow is to deliver the:

2027 Sir William Luce Lecture

The lecture will be based on the research conducted during the Fellowship.

This is an important scholarly output and one of the central public components of the residency.

The lecture allows the Fellow to present:

Research findings

New arguments

Emerging evidence

Policy or historical insights

to an academic audience.

Publication in the Durham Middle East Papers Series

Following the Fellowship, the Fellow’s work will be published online by the Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies through its:

Durham Middle East Papers series.

This gives the Fellowship a concrete publication outcome.

For researchers, this can be valuable because the residency is connected to both:

Public presentation

Published research output

The final paper also triggers payment of the £1,000 honorarium.

Previous Sir William Luce Fellows

The Fellowship has attracted prominent scholars, diplomats and regional specialists.

Recent Fellows have included:

Mark Katz

Edward Thomas

Helen Lackner

Richard Barltrop

Ambassador John W. Limbert

Dr Altea Pericoli

Professor Simon Smith

The backgrounds of previous Fellows illustrate the programme’s combination of:

Academic expertise

Diplomatic experience

Regional specialization

Policy knowledge

Application Requirements

The 2027 application is relatively focused.

Candidates must submit three main components:

Curriculum vitae

Research proposal

Contact details for two referees

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants need to submit a:

CV of no more than two pages.

The page limit is important.

Candidates should prioritize information directly relevant to the Fellowship.

Depending on their professional background, this may include:

Academic qualifications

Current position

Research experience

Publications

Regional expertise

Diplomatic experience

Professional appointments

Policy work

Relevant business experience

Languages

Major awards

Applicants should avoid filling the limited space with information unrelated to the Fellowship.

2. Research Proposal

Applicants must submit a:

Two-to-three-page outline of their proposed research.

The proposal should establish what the Fellow intends to investigate during the residency.

A strong proposal should ideally explain:

Research question

Geographic focus

Background

Why the issue matters

Original contribution

Method or analytical approach

Durham resources to be used

Expected output

Why the work is suitable for the Sir William Luce Fellowship

Because the residency is relatively short, the project should also be realistic.

Using Durham Collections in the Research Proposal

Applicants should pay particular attention to the Fellowship’s explicit expectation that Fellows engage with Durham’s distinctive resources.

A strong application could identify materials from:

Sudan Archive

Middle East collections

Gulf collections

Documentary holdings

University Library

where relevant.

If the Luce papers at Exeter University are important, applicants may also explain this.

A proposal demonstrating specific archival preparation is likely to be more convincing than one merely stating that Durham has “excellent resources.”

3. Two Referees

Applicants must provide:

Contact details for two referees.

The announcement asks for referee contact details rather than stating that reference letters must necessarily accompany the initial application.

Candidates should choose referees who can credibly comment on their:

Research ability

Professional expertise

Regional knowledge

Academic or policy contribution

How to Apply

Applicants are asked to submit their materials, preferably by email, to:

luce.fund@durham.ac.uk

Applications are addressed to:

The Honorary Secretary
Sir William Luce Memorial Fund
School of Government and International Affairs
Durham University
United Kingdom
DH1 3TU

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted by:

Wednesday, 7 October 2026

Candidates should prepare their proposal well before the deadline, particularly if they plan to identify specific Durham archival materials relevant to their research.

Does the Committee Have to Make an Award?

No.

The Committee administering the Sir William Luce Memorial Fund:

Reserves the right not to appoint a Fellow.

This means the Fellowship is competitive and an appointment is not guaranteed merely because eligible applications are received.

The Committee may decide not to make an award if applications do not meet the expected standard.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Make the Geographic Fit Obvious

Your research must clearly concern one or more of:

Gulf monarchies

Yemen

Iran

Sudan

South Sudan

Do not make reviewers search for the regional connection.

State it clearly from the beginning.

2. Develop a Fresh Perspective

The Committee specifically seeks new perspectives.

Explain what your project contributes that existing work has not adequately addressed.

This could involve:

New evidence

New archives

Comparative analysis

Practitioner insight

Historical reassessment

New conceptual framework

3. Explain Why Durham Matters

This is especially important.

Do not write a proposal that could be conducted equally well anywhere.

Identify the value of:

Sudan Archive

Gulf materials

Middle East documentary holdings

Durham academic expertise

Luce papers at Exeter

where relevant.

4. Keep the Project Feasible

The Fellowship lasts approximately two months.

Do not propose several years of new empirical research.

Instead, design a project that can make substantial progress during the period from late April to late June 2027.

5. Show What You Will Contribute to Durham

The Fellowship is reciprocal.

Durham provides:

Accommodation

Meals

Travel

Research facilities

Academic community

The Fellow is expected to contribute through:

Intellectual exchange

Seminar participation

College life

The Sir William Luce Lecture

Publication

Your application should show that you are ready to participate actively.

6. Think About the Final Paper From the Beginning

Because the Fellowship culminates in a published Durham Middle East Paper, the project should be capable of generating a clear written output.

The proposal should therefore contain a coherent question that can lead to a substantive paper.

Important Details at a Glance

Conclusion

The 2027 Sir William Luce Fellowship at Durham University offers a distinctive research opportunity for postdoctoral scholars and experienced professionals working on the Gulf monarchies, Yemen, Iran, Sudan or South Sudan.

Hosted jointly by Durham University’s Institute for Middle Eastern & Islamic Studies and Trevelyan College, the Fellowship will run from 26 April to 25 June 2027 and is designed to encourage original research and fresh perspectives on the political, social, economic, security and historical dimensions of these regions.

TITLE: SHE-CAN Scholar Program 2026-2027 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 1, 2026 (Cambodia & Guatemala) / November 1, 2026 (Liberia)

Applications are invited for the SHE-CAN Scholar Program 2026-2027. SHE-CAN seeks talented young women leaders from Cambodia, Liberia, and Guatemala who have few opportunities but incredible potential and passion for change.

As a SHE-CAN scholar, you will be supported in winning a full-ride scholarship to a top U.S. college. Through access to a world-class college education, mentorship, and leadership training in the U.S., they will provide you with the tools and support needed to return and make change in your home country.

Funding

SHE-CAN aims to support low-income young women who would not otherwise have the opportunity to study in the U.S. and get the tools needed to return home and step into leadership roles in their countries. Funding for SHE-CAN scholars is provided by:

College-Funded Scholarship: Every scholar applies for and is awarded a full-ride scholarship from a U.S. college, which pays for the cost of tuition, a place to live, and meals while in school.

SHE-CAN: The organization funds test preparation classes and costs not covered by your scholarship that your family can’t afford, including passport and visa fees, flight (one to U.S. and one home), textbooks, health insurance, etc.

Scholar & Family: Scholars fund travel to and from test preparation classes in your country’s capital city. When you arrive in the U.S., you are expected to work on campus to fund your personal expenses (toothpaste, shampoo, etc.). While SHE-CAN funds your health insurance, the organization is unable to fund medical expenses outside of what the insurance covers, including dental and vision expenses.

Eligibility

Open to a woman between the ages of 17-20

Passionate about improving your country

High school graduate or graduating high school by June 2027

Access to capital city if selected for an interview (Note: Guatemala location is dependent on applicants)

From a low-income household

Interested in pursuing an undergraduate degree at a U.S. college or university (SHE-CAN does not work with students seeking graduate degrees)

Have less than 1 year of university or other post-secondary credits

Already a leader in your school or community

A strong English speaker: Your ability to speak and write in English is critical because all U.S. universities require a high score on an official language exam, such as the TOEFL, IELTS or Duolingo. Therefore, if your English is not strong, they recommend that you spend a year studying and apply next year

Academically strong: Consistently ranked high in your class with strong grades and a strong score on National Exam or WAEC/WASSCE

Dedicated to this program: Able to dedicate your days in January – June to SHE-CAN’s pre-college program (accepted scholars must not work full-time during this period)

Able to access a strong internet connection and computer daily to check emails

Application

You will need the following to apply:

High school transcripts for grades 10, 11, and 12

National exam score report or WAEC score report

English translations of transcripts or exam scores if necessary (can be self-translated)

Estimate of family’s monthly income

Score reports for the SAT, ACT, IELTS, TOEFL if you have taken them

No application fee – free to apply!

Apply by Country

Cambodia Apply Here

Guatemala Apply Here

Liberia Apply Here

TITLE: British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026-2027 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 30, 2026

Applications for the British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026-2027 are now open. The British Academy is inviting proposals from early-career researchers in the humanities and social sciences wishing to pursue an independent research project, towards the completion of a significant piece of publishable research.

The British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowship offers outstanding early-career researchers the opportunity to strengthen their experience of research and teaching in an academic environment. This scheme aims to help develop the award-holder’s curriculum vitae and boost their prospects of obtaining a permanent academic post. The primary emphasis is on the completion of a significant piece of publishable research, and the integration of the award holder into the community of established scholars within their field.

The Fellowship is non-renewable and funded by the Department for Science, Innovation & Technology (DSIT).

Benefits

The scheme is covered under the Full Economic Costing (FEC) regime. Currently, the Academy funds 80 per cent of salary costs, directly allocated and indirect costs under FEC. The Fellowship is tenable for three years, starting from Autumn 2027 in a UK-based university or higher education institution.

Eligibility

The applicant must be a researcher from the humanities and social sciences and be based at an eligible university or research organisation for the duration of the Fellowship. Suitable institutions include any UK university or recognised research organisation based in the UK. British citizens and any nationals from the EEA are eligible, regardless of where their doctorate was obtained.

Anyone of any nationality who has a doctorate from a UK university is eligible. If an applicant does not meet the prior categories, they may be accepted if they can demonstrate ‘strong prior association’ with the UK academic community.

Eligible applicants are expected to be at an early stage of their career. Applicants are expected to have completed their Viva Voce examination between 1st April 2024 to 1st April 2027. The applicant must already be of postdoctoral status at the time when the Research Awards Committee meets.

Additionally, no applicant who has been appointed to a permanent academic post in an institution of higher education at any time in their career, whether in the UK or overseas, will be eligible. This includes positions held before the award of a doctorate.

Application

The deadline for submissions and UK institutional approval is Wednesday, 30 September 2026 (17:00 BST).
