TITLE: PhD at INSAIT in Bulgaria: Fully Funded Doctoral Fellowship of €39,684 Per Year for International Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you an aspiring researcher in computer science, artificial intelligence, data science, mathematics, physics, statistics, or electrical engineering looking for a fully funded PhD opportunity in Europe? The Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology (INSAIT) in Sofia, Bulgaria, is offering talented doctoral candidates the opportunity to pursue a world-class PhD while receiving a full doctoral fellowship of €39,684 gross per year.

The INSAIT PhD programme is designed for ambitious students who want to develop into independent scientists, researchers, technology leaders, and deep-tech innovators. Successful candidates work closely with leading researchers from INSAIT and affiliated international institutions, while undertaking advanced research in computer science and artificial intelligence.

Unlike many scholarship programmes that have a fixed annual deadline, INSAIT uses a rolling admission process, meaning prospective doctoral candidates can submit applications throughout the year.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: PhD at INSAIT

Category: Scholarship / Fully Funded PhD Fellowship

Host Institution: INSAIT – Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology

Location: Sofia, Bulgaria

Study Level: Doctoral / PhD

Fields: Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Mathematics, Physics, Statistics and Electrical Engineering

Funding: €39,684 gross per year

Programme Duration: Up to 5 years

Application System: Rolling admissions

Deadline: No fixed deadline; applications are accepted throughout the year

Language: English

Degree Issuing Institution: INSAIT at Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski”

Eligible Applicants: International applicants are welcome

About INSAIT

INSAIT is the Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology, located in Sofia, Bulgaria. The institute was established in 2022 in partnership with leading technical universities including ETH Zurich and EPFL and operates as a special unit of Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski.” Its mission is to build a world-class research and education environment focused on computer science, artificial intelligence and related technologies.

The institute aims to attract outstanding researchers and train the next generation of scientists and technology leaders. Its research ecosystem has connections with internationally recognized academic and technology institutions, making the PhD programme particularly attractive to candidates seeking international research exposure.

For doctoral candidates, the programme goes beyond classroom-based education. Students are expected to become active researchers, work with experienced advisers, contribute to high-quality research and develop the expertise necessary to pursue careers in academia, industry, entrepreneurship and advanced research laboratories.

What Does the INSAIT PhD Fellowship Offer?

One of the most significant features of the programme is its financial support.

All admitted doctoral candidates receive a full PhD fellowship worth €39,684 gross per year. This financial support is intended to allow students to concentrate fully on their doctoral research rather than having to seek unrelated employment to finance their studies.

INSAIT also notes that doctoral fellowships may be available through major technology companies, including DeepMind and Amazon Web Services.

The fellowship therefore provides an opportunity for qualified researchers to pursue advanced doctoral studies while receiving substantial financial support.

Key financial benefit

€39,684 gross per year

Full doctoral fellowship for admitted candidates

Financial support can continue during the first two years for candidates who enter with a Bachelor’s degree and complete their Master’s degree within the programme

Students are expected to dedicate themselves full-time to doctoral research

There is no requirement to repay the fellowship if a candidate ultimately fails the doctoral programme, according to INSAIT’s FAQ.

It is important to understand that the stated amount is gross, rather than net, meaning the amount received after applicable taxes or deductions may be lower.

Who Is Eligible for the INSAIT PhD?

INSAIT is looking for talented candidates with strong academic backgrounds who have obtained, or will have obtained by the time they begin the doctoral programme, a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree.

The institute generally considers applicants with academic backgrounds in:

Computer Science

Data Science

Mathematics

Physics

Statistics

Electrical Engineering

Candidates who are currently completing their Bachelor’s or Master’s degrees may also be considered, provided they obtain the relevant degree before beginning the doctoral programme. Recent Bachelor’s and Master’s graduates are therefore encouraged to apply if they meet the academic requirements.

Applicants with only a Bachelor’s degree

An important feature of the programme is that applicants do not necessarily need to already hold a Master’s degree.

A candidate who has a Bachelor’s degree but does not yet have an MSc can be admitted with the expectation that they will complete their Master’s degree during the first two years of the INSAIT doctoral programme.

During this period, the student remains financially supported through the €39,684 gross annual fellowship and is expected to continue toward the second part of the PhD programme if successful.

This makes the opportunity particularly interesting for outstanding Bachelor’s graduates who want to move directly into an advanced research environment.

Are International Students Eligible?

Yes. International applicants are explicitly welcome.

INSAIT states that it aims to become an international, world-class research and education institution and embraces diversity. English is the working language, and communications within the programme take place in English.

Therefore, the programme is not restricted to Bulgarian citizens.

Qualified candidates from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania and other parts of the world can be considered, provided they meet the academic and programme requirements.

For international candidates, however, immigration requirements should be considered. INSAIT notes that visa applications and work-permit procedures can sometimes affect the timing of a student’s start date.

What Research Areas Can PhD Students Pursue?

Applicants do not necessarily have to commit to one highly specific PhD research topic before submitting their application.

INSAIT allows candidates to identify several areas of interest. Students are encouraged to have a general idea of the research directions they would like to explore, but their interests can evolve during the programme.

The institute also encourages interdisciplinary research and collaboration, meaning a final PhD topic may combine several areas of computer science, artificial intelligence, mathematics or related disciplines.

This approach is particularly useful for candidates who have strong technical interests but are still exploring the precise research problem they want to investigate.

How Long Is the INSAIT PhD Programme?

The doctoral programme can last up to five years and is divided into two major stages.

Part I: Up to two years

During the first part, the student works on research with their adviser while exploring potential research directions.

The objective is to develop sufficient expertise and research understanding to formulate a specific PhD thesis topic.

By the end of this stage, the candidate is expected to define the theme of their doctoral research and defend it before an INSAIT graduate committee.

The first two years are not necessarily limited to one research topic. Students are encouraged to gain exposure to multiple areas and collaborate with other researchers.

Part II: Up to three years

After successfully completing the first stage, the student proceeds to the second part of the programme.

The focus then becomes deeper research into the selected thesis topic, with the objective of producing significant and original research results.

INSAIT explains that, as a rule of thumb, a PhD thesis should be based on at least three publications in top academic venues. However, the final thesis should form a coherent body of academic work rather than simply being a collection of previously published papers.

Students are also expected to contribute to the broader research environment by collaborating with other doctoral researchers and potentially supervising or working with Master’s students.

World-Class Mentorship and Research Supervision

A major advantage of the INSAIT PhD is access to experienced researchers and international mentors.

Students are mentored by INSAIT faculty members as well as affiliated mentors. The institute’s broader research network includes researchers associated with leading institutions around the world.

For students who are supervised primarily by an external adviser, INSAIT has a structure designed to facilitate close collaboration with the adviser’s research group.

An externally supervised student may spend approximately three months per year visiting the adviser’s institution. According to INSAIT, these visits are fully covered by the institute.

The arrangement can allow students to work directly with established research groups while maintaining their connection to INSAIT.

External advisers are also expected to visit INSAIT several times per year and provide regular technical guidance to their doctoral students.

This international supervision model can provide doctoral students with exposure to different research environments and international academic networks.

Who Issues the PhD Degree?

INSAIT is legally part of Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski.”

Consequently, the official doctoral degree is issued by INSAIT at Sofia University.

This means students are participating in INSAIT’s specialized research environment while the degree is institutionally connected to Sofia University.

Required Application Documents

Candidates should prepare a strong application package before applying.

The main documents requested by INSAIT include the following.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants should provide a detailed academic and professional CV.

The CV should highlight:

Universities attended

Degrees obtained or currently being completed

Academic achievements

Relevant professional experience

Research experience

Publications, where applicable

Technical achievements

Extracurricular achievements

Awards and distinctions

Other accomplishments relevant to doctoral research

For a competitive PhD application, candidates should ensure that the CV demonstrates evidence of research potential rather than simply listing educational qualifications.

2. Degree Certificates

Applicants who have already graduated should submit official copies of their Bachelor’s and/or Master’s degree certificates.

Candidates still completing their degrees should ensure that their graduation timeline is compatible with the expected start of the doctoral programme.

3. University Transcripts

Applicants must provide official university transcripts showing their academic coursework, academic hours and grades.

Strong academic performance can be important because INSAIT evaluates the quality of a candidate’s coursework and grades as part of the admissions process.

4. Recommendation Letters

Recommendation letters are listed as optional, but candidates can submit two letters from individuals who can attest to their academic and scientific achievements.

Ideally, referees should be able to provide meaningful evidence of the applicant’s:

Research ability

Academic performance

Technical skills

Intellectual curiosity

Problem-solving ability

Independence

Potential for doctoral research

Recommendation letters should include the full contact details of the recommender.

5. Motivation Letter

The motivation letter is an important component of the application.

Candidates should clearly explain:

Why they want to pursue a PhD

Why they are interested in INSAIT

Their general research interests

Their academic and research objectives

Their long-term goals

Relevant experiences or achievements

Why INSAIT’s research environment is appropriate for their ambitions

INSAIT recommends that the motivation statement generally be no more than two A4 pages.

6. English Language Proficiency

Applicants are expected to have a strong command of English.

Where available, candidates can provide formal evidence of English-language proficiency, such as:

IELTS

TOEFL

Cambridge English qualifications

Other recognized English-language certificates

INSAIT’s working language is English, so candidates should be comfortable conducting academic communication and research in English.

Important Document Requirement

All application documents must either be issued in English or translated into English.

Applicants should therefore make sure that documents originally issued in another language are accompanied by appropriate English translations.

INSAIT also explains that official documents are accepted for initial admission, but documentation may need to be legalized when the doctoral contract is issued.

How Is the Application Assessed?

INSAIT evaluates applicants based on several factors rather than relying on one qualification alone.

The assessment may consider:

Academic qualifications

Quality of university coursework

Academic grades

Extracurricular achievements

Motivation

Recommendation letters

Research potential

Alignment with the institute’s research interests

Performance during technical assessments or interviews

Strong grades can help demonstrate academic preparation, but applicants should also use their CV and motivation letter to show evidence of curiosity, technical ability and research potential.

Technical Interview

Candidates who successfully progress through the initial assessment may be invited to a technical interview.

The interview may be conducted by the faculty member or members who are interested in the candidate’s profile.

This stage provides the research group with an opportunity to assess the candidate’s technical preparation, research interests and suitability for doctoral-level work.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to discuss their academic background, technical knowledge, previous projects, research interests and reasons for applying to INSAIT.

When Will Applicants Receive a Decision?

INSAIT states that applicants should receive notification of the application result within two months of applying.

If an adviser or several advisers are interested in the candidate, the applicant may be contacted for further steps, including technical interviews and assessments.

Successful progression can ultimately result in a working PhD contract.

Is There an Application Deadline?

There is no fixed annual deadline for the INSAIT PhD programme.

INSAIT uses a rolling admissions process, allowing candidates to apply at any point during the year.

Deadline: Rolling Admissions

Because applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, prospective applicants should not interpret the absence of a fixed deadline as a reason to delay.

Candidates should apply when they have a strong application package ready, particularly because the programme is competitive and applicants may be contacted by potential advisers after submission.

What Happens If You Are Admitted?

Successful candidates can expect to begin the doctoral programme as soon as possible, subject to the relevant administrative requirements.

For international students, visa and work-permit procedures can affect the start date.

Once the doctoral programme begins, students are expected to dedicate themselves fully to research at INSAIT.

The programme specifically requires PhD students to be 100% focused on their doctoral research and not work other jobs alongside their studies.

Career Opportunities After the PhD

The INSAIT PhD is designed not only to award a doctoral degree but also to prepare students for high-level careers in research and technology.

According to INSAIT, graduates may pursue opportunities including:

University research and academic careers

Professorships

Research scientist positions

Artificial intelligence research

Big-tech research laboratories

Industrial research and development

Engineering R&D departments

Deep-tech entrepreneurship

Technology startups

International research collaborations

Potential employers and research environments mentioned by INSAIT include major technology and research organizations such as DeepMind, Google Brain, Microsoft Research and Amazon, among others.

For candidates interested in becoming research scientists or technology entrepreneurs, the combination of advanced research, international mentorship and industry connections can provide a strong foundation for future career development.

Why This PhD Opportunity Stands Out

There are several reasons qualified candidates may want to consider the INSAIT doctoral programme.

1. Full financial support

The €39,684 gross annual fellowship provides substantial financial support throughout the doctoral programme.

2. International research environment

International applicants are welcome, and English is the working language.

3. Strong academic mentorship

Students have access to INSAIT faculty and affiliated international mentors.

4. Flexible research direction

Students can explore several research areas before settling on a final PhD topic.

5. International research exposure

Students working with external advisers may have opportunities to spend approximately three months per year at the adviser’s institution, with visits covered by INSAIT.

6. Five-year programme structure

The programme allows up to five years for exploration, thesis development and advanced research.

7. Opportunity for Bachelor’s graduates

Applicants who have only a Bachelor’s degree can potentially enter the doctoral programme and complete a Master’s degree during the first two years.

8. Strong career potential

The programme is designed to prepare graduates for academic careers, research laboratories, startups and industrial R&D.

How to Apply for the INSAIT PhD

Interested candidates should first review the official PhD programme information and identify the research areas that align with their academic and professional interests.

Applicants should then prepare their application documents, including their CV, academic records, degree certificates where applicable, motivation letter and supporting recommendation letters.

The application is submitted through INSAIT’s online recruitment platform.

Candidates who encounter difficulties accessing the application platform can contact INSAIT through the contact details provided on the official programme page.

APPLY HERE

How to Make Your Application More Competitive

Although there is no single formula for gaining admission, prospective candidates can take several practical steps to strengthen their applications.

Demonstrate academic strength

Highlight courses and academic projects that are directly relevant to your intended research area.

For example, applicants interested in machine learning could emphasize coursework in:

Algorithms

Linear algebra

Probability

Statistics

Optimization

Machine learning

Artificial intelligence

Programming

Highlight research experience

Research experience can help distinguish an applicant from candidates who have only completed coursework.

Include:

Research projects

Undergraduate or Master’s theses

Publications

Preprints

Research internships

Technical projects

Open-source contributions

Conference participation

Laboratory experience

Write a targeted motivation letter

Avoid submitting a generic statement that could be sent to any university.

Explain specifically why INSAIT’s research environment appeals to you and identify broad research areas that interest you.

Your statement should connect your previous experience, current interests and future research ambitions.

Choose recommenders carefully

If submitting recommendation letters, choose people who know your academic or research capabilities well.

A detailed letter from someone who has directly supervised your research can generally provide more meaningful evidence than a generic letter from someone who knows you only superficially.

Prepare for technical interviews

Candidates who progress to the interview stage should be prepared to explain their previous projects and demonstrate their technical understanding.

Review the fundamentals relevant to your intended research area and be ready to discuss why particular research problems interest you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I apply if I have not yet completed my Master’s degree?

Yes. INSAIT can consider applicants who have a Bachelor’s degree but not a Master’s degree. Such students are expected to complete the Master’s degree during the first two years of the doctoral programme.

Can international students apply?

Yes. INSAIT explicitly welcomes international applicants and conducts its academic communication in English.

Do I need to choose my exact PhD topic before applying?

No. Candidates can identify several areas of interest, and their research interests may evolve during the programme. INSAIT also encourages interdisciplinary research.

Is the fellowship fully funded?

Admitted candidates receive a full doctoral fellowship of €39,684 gross per year.

How long does the PhD take?

The programme can last up to five years, divided into an initial period of up to two years and a second period of up to three years.

Is the PhD full-time?

Yes. Students are expected to be fully focused on their doctoral research and not hold other jobs during the programme.

Does INSAIT have a fixed application deadline?

No. The programme operates on a rolling admissions basis, so applications can be submitted throughout the year.

When will I receive an application decision?

INSAIT states that applicants will be notified within two months of applying.

What language are the studies conducted in?

English is the working language at INSAIT, and communications take place in English.

Is it necessary to legalize documents?

Official documents are accepted for initial acceptance, but documentation may need to be legalized when the doctoral contract is issued.

What happens if I fail the doctoral programme?

According to INSAIT’s published FAQ, candidates are not required to repay the salary or fellowship they received before failing the programme.

Conclusion

The INSAIT PhD programme in Bulgaria represents a significant opportunity for ambitious researchers seeking fully funded doctoral study in computer science, artificial intelligence and related technical disciplines.

With a €39,684 gross annual doctoral fellowship, a programme lasting up to five years, international mentorship, opportunities for collaboration with leading research groups and an English-language research environment, the programme is particularly suited to candidates who want to build careers in advanced research, academia, artificial intelligence, deep technology or technology entrepreneurship.

The absence of a fixed annual deadline is another important advantage because INSAIT uses rolling admissions and allows qualified candidates to apply throughout the year. However, prospective applicants should still prepare carefully and submit a strong application rather than waiting unnecessarily.

For candidates with a strong background in computer science, mathematics, data science, physics, statistics or electrical engineering, this programme could provide the financial support, mentorship and international research exposure needed to progress toward becoming an independent scientist or technology leader.

Applicants should review the official programme requirements carefully, prepare a research-focused CV and compelling motivation letter, gather their academic documents and submit their application through the official INSAIT application platform.

TITLE: Professor Frederick Ato Armah, Director of Research and Programmes at AAU, Elected Fellow of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) proudly announces that Professor Frederick Ato Armah, Director of Research and Programmes at the AAU, has been elected as a Fellow of the prestigious Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences. His election was confirmed during the 219th General Meeting of Fellows on October 30, 2024. This honour recognizes individuals for their outstanding contributions to the fields of arts and sciences, and Prof. Armah’s inclusion reflects his significant impact in environmental and sustainability science in Ghana and beyond.

The Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences, established in 1959, has been instrumental in shaping the intellectual and policy landscape of Ghana and beyond. With a vision to be the foremost merit-based learned society committed to national development and global advancement, the Academy strives to make its wealth of knowledge and expertise accessible to both national and global audiences. Notable early members include Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s former president, among its twenty Foundation Fellows.

Professor Frederick Ato Armah joined the AAU in November 2023 and has since served as the Director of Research and Programmes. He is a distinguished Professor of Environmental and Sustainability Science with extensive experience in institutional development, project management, and research. Since 1995, he has taught at all educational levels—basic, secondary, and tertiary. His leadership in designing, managing, and evaluating various development projects across Africa and beyond over the past 20 years is noteworthy. Prof. Armah has managed several multi-million-dollar research grants and collaborated with national, regional, and international stakeholders to enhance management tools and policies, conduct research, and address environmental, health, and social issues.

Prof. Armah’s academic and professional credentials are extensive. He holds numerous certificates in university leadership, project planning, and governance. He has consulted widely for organizations such as USAID, the World Bank, and the United Nations Environment Programme. As a prolific author, his works are published extensively in peer-reviewed journals of international repute. He was an Ontario Trillium Scholar in Canada from 2011 to 2015 and won the Association of American Publishers Awards for Professional and Scholarly Excellence (PROSE) in Environmental Sciences in 2020. Prof. Armah also served as the Director of Research, Innovation, and Consultancy at the University of Cape Coast, Ghana, from April 2019 to July 2022. Additionally, he is a Senior Research Fellow of the Earth Systems Governance initiative of the International Science Council and a member of the Intergovernmental Science Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).

The AAU celebrates Prof. Armah’s election to the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences as a testament to his contributions to environmental and sustainability science, leadership, and academic excellence.

In addition to Prof. Armah, the following distinguished individuals were also elected as Fellows of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences:

Prof. Samuel Egyir Aggrey: An expert in poultry nutrigenomics, genetics, and gut health.

Prof. Joe-Nat Afutu Clegg-Lamptey: Renowned as the leading breast surgeon in Ghana and the West African sub-region.

Prof. Samuel Nii Ardey Codjoe: A professor of Geography and Soil Science, with research encompassing geography, population studies, and climate change.

Prof. Godfred Darko: A professor of Chemistry and recipient of the 2016 Young Research Award by the Egyptian Academy of Scientific Research and Technology.

Prof. Emmanuel Bekoe Larbi: A retired professor of medicine and Fellow of various prestigious medical societies.

Prof. Frederick Yeboah Obese: A professor of Animal Science and research scientist at the Animal Research Institute (ARI) of the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR).

Prof. (Mrs) Ibok Nsa Ekpenyong Oduro: A professor of Postharvest Technology at KNUST in Ghana.

The AAU extends its heartfelt congratulations to all the new Fellows for their exceptional contributions to the arts and sciences, and for their ongoing commitment to advancing knowledge and development in their respective fields.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Suzanne Z. Deutsch

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Suzanne Z. Deutsch,
A Bequest to the Physics Department

by Elizabeth Chadis, Director of Development // MIT Physics Annual 2006

Suzanne Deutsch and Yong-ll Shin, 2005 recipient of the Martin Deutsch Student Award for Excellence in Experimental Physics

In her estate plans, Suzanne Deutsch has established a fully endowed fellowship to honor the memory of her late husband, MIT Professor of Physics Martin Deutsch. By doing so, she will ensure that young scientists have the opportunities and experiences so critical to their success. Additionally, she will help the Department of Physics reach its goal of full fellowship support for all incoming graduate students.

“One day, I came home from work and found Martin lying at the top of the staircase in front of the cellar blowing smoke rings,” recounts Suzanne Deutsch, widow of former MIT Professor Martin Deutsch. Her first thought was that he had lost his mind, but as it turned out there was something wrong with the furnace and Martin was “trying to determine the airflow.” Common day-to-day problems such as this were not only to be solved, but in the process of doing so, to be mined for any fresh ideas or insights that may not have been foreseen. While the attendant diversions and delays often entailed in these activities led Suzanne to question whether Martin was procrastinating, they came to be dubbed for what they really were—“experiments” in the household. For Suzanne, they also became an introduction to that which fascinated and gave meaning to Martin’s life: the need to understand the forces of nature and to share the excitement of scientific inquiry with students.

Martin Deutsch was born in Vienna on January 29, 1917 as the only child of parents who were doctors. Helene and Felix Deutsch were psychoanalysts, significant members of Freud’s inner circle. Martin saw himself as “a product of the intellectual culture of Vienna.” In 1935, he came to the U.S. planning to complete a baccalaureate program in two years and enter a doctoral program in one of two fields—chemistry or physics—yet to be determined. He earned his SB in two years, taught and conducted research at MIT for a couple of years before going to Los Alamos to work on the Manhattan Project. After the war, he joined other scientists in speaking out against the proliferation of nuclear weapons. In 1946, Martin returned to MIT where Viki Weisskopf and Bruno Rossi had joined the Physics faculty. His studies in radioactive decay led him to the discovery of positronium in 1951. Martin spent most of his career researching and teaching. From 1973 to 1979, Martin was head of the MIT Laboratory for Nuclear Science.

Martin had a sensitive eye for talented and dedicated students…. Therefore, I want to endow a fellowship as the most fitting way to honor and perpetuate his memory.
Suzanne Deutsche

From the earliest days at MIT, Martin found the scientific environment and collegial spirit of the Physics Department attractive. Thus, increasingly his attachment to physics deepened and became the center of his life’s work. While he made many scientific contributions during his career, many of them significant, he believed his real accomplishment was as an educator. Martin had a sensitive eye for talented and dedicated students, supporting and recruiting then as circumstances dictated. Therefore, Suzanne wants to endow a fellowship as the most fitting way to honor and perpetuate his memory. She feels strongly that Martin would be pleased to know that each year a talented and dedicated person will come to MIT on a fellowship bearing his name.

A single Overseas Student Health Care Policy and relocation allowance of up to AUD $2,000 for international applicants.

TITLE: DIV Fund Grants 2026: Up to US$1.5 Million to Scale Evidence-Based Innovations in Low- and Middle-Income Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The DIV Fund is offering funding opportunities for organizations developing, testing, evaluating, and scaling innovative solutions that can meaningfully and measurably improve the lives of people living in poverty around the world.

Through its tiered, evidence-based funding model, the DIV Fund provides financial support to innovators and researchers at different stages of development. Funding is designed to help promising innovations move from early-stage real-world piloting to rigorous testing and, ultimately, large-scale implementation.

Depending on the maturity and evidence base of an innovation, successful applicants may receive funding of up to US$200,000 for Stage 1, US$500,000 for Stage 2, or US$1.5 million for Stage 3. In exceptional cases, Stage 2 funding may reach US$750,000.

The fund is deliberately open to innovations across sectors and does not limit applicants to a particular type of technology, product, service, policy, or development intervention. Instead, the central focus is whether a proposed solution has the potential to generate significant development impact in a cost-effective and sustainable way.

What Is the DIV Fund?

The DIV Fund is a tiered, evidence-based, open innovation fund focused on identifying and supporting solutions that have the potential to improve the lives of millions of people living in poverty.

Its approach is designed to function as a discovery engine for global development by building a pipeline of evidence-driven innovations capable of achieving impact at scale.

Rather than providing the same type or amount of funding to every applicant, the DIV Fund adjusts its funding requirements according to the stage of development of an innovation.

At the earlier stages, applicants are assessed primarily on the potential of their idea, theory of change, cost-effectiveness prospects, and ability to achieve scale. At later stages, applicants are expected to provide increasingly strong evidence that their innovation works, is cost-effective, and can be sustained at a large scale.

This creates three principal funding stages:

Stage 1 – Piloting

Stage 2 – Testing and Positioning for Scale

Stage 3 – Transitioning to Scale

Applicants do not necessarily have to begin at Stage 1. Organizations with innovations that already meet the requirements of a later stage may apply directly for that stage, provided they can demonstrate that they have credibly satisfied the relevant requirements of earlier stages.

What Does the DIV Fund Support?

The DIV Fund supports innovators and researchers that are piloting, rigorously testing, or scaling solutions capable of meaningfully and measurably improving people’s lives.

One of the fund’s defining characteristics is its broad interpretation of innovation.

An innovation does not necessarily have to be a completely new invention. It may include:

A new product

A service

A policy

A program

A delivery model

A new method of implementing an existing solution

A process improvement

An evidence-generation approach for an already widely used development intervention

The key consideration is whether the solution has real potential to generate impact at scale more affordably or efficiently than existing approaches.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to present a groundbreaking technological invention. A relatively simple change in the way an existing service is delivered may qualify if it can demonstrate the potential to generate significantly better development outcomes at scale.

Where Does the DIV Fund Operate?

The DIV Fund supports innovations addressing challenges in low- and middle-income countries, according to the World Bank’s income classifications.

The fund prioritizes proposals according to their expected social return and gives greater weight to improvements expected to benefit people with lower incomes.

Consequently, applicants should clearly demonstrate not only what their innovation does, but also who will benefit, how significant those benefits could be, and why the proposed intervention represents an effective use of resources.

Who Can Apply for DIV Fund Grants?

The DIV Fund accepts applications from a broad range of organizations.

Eligible applicants include:

Non-profit organizations

Social enterprises

Universities

Research institutions

Technical assistance providers supporting government innovation

Businesses

Partnerships involving multiple types of organizations

However, individuals cannot apply directly. The fund specifically states that it is unable to support individuals.

Organizations that are public or legal entities but are uncertain about their eligibility are encouraged to contact the DIV Fund for clarification.

Geographic Eligibility

The opportunity is intended for organizations working on challenges in low- and middle-income countries as classified by the World Bank.

The source does not specify eligibility according to race, ethnicity, nationality, or continent. Eligibility is instead primarily linked to the organization type and the location or development context addressed by the proposed innovation.

Therefore, applicants from eligible countries should focus on demonstrating how their proposed solution addresses a significant development challenge affecting people living in poverty.

The Three Core Principles of DIV Fund Investment

Every DIV Fund application is assessed around three central principles:

Evidence of impact

Cost-effectiveness

Potential for durable scale

These principles become increasingly demanding as applicants progress through the three funding stages.

1. Evidence of Impact

The DIV Fund places significant emphasis on evidence.

Applicants are expected to present a credible theory of change explaining how their activities and intervention are expected to produce meaningful improvements in development outcomes.

The stronger the existing evidence supporting the theory of change, the stronger the application is likely to be.

The fund ultimately values outcomes such as

Improved health

Higher earnings

Academic achievement

Other meaningful improvements in people’s lives

Intermediate outcomes may also be considered where rigorous evidence already demonstrates their relationship to important development outcomes. For example, increasing vaccination rates may be relevant where there is already a strong causal evidence base connecting vaccination to improved health outcomes.

The DIV Fund distinguishes between correlation and causation. Rigorous evidence should demonstrate that an innovation caused measurable improvements rather than simply being associated with positive results.

2. Cost-Effectiveness

The second major principle is cost-effectiveness.

The DIV Fund is interested in innovations capable of generating greater impact per dollar than the status quo or viable alternatives.

Cost-effectiveness does not simply mean that an intervention is inexpensive.

An innovation may become more cost-effective by:

Reducing its costs while maintaining impact

Increasing its impact without proportionately increasing costs

Reducing costs and increasing impact simultaneously

Applicants should therefore understand both the current cost of their intervention and how those costs are expected to change as the solution reaches larger numbers of people.

They should also explain the assumptions behind their cost projections and the evidence supporting their expected impact.

3. Potential for Durable Scale

The third principle is scale.

The DIV Fund generally defines “at scale” as improving the lives of at least one million people over ten years.

However, the fund may consider particularly compelling innovations capable of generating exceptionally large benefits for a somewhat smaller population.

Applicants must therefore think beyond the initial pilot.

They need to demonstrate:

Who could eventually adopt the innovation

How many people could benefit

How the intervention would be financed

Who would implement it

What partnerships would be necessary

How long-term operations would be sustained

How the solution could continue growing without indefinite dependence on DIV Fund support

The fund accepts different pathways to scale, including public, commercial, and hybrid models.

DIV Fund Funding Stages

The DIV Fund offers three principal funding tiers corresponding to different stages of innovation development.

Stage 1: Piloting – Up to US$200,000

Stage 1 funding is designed for early-stage innovations that are ready for real-world testing.

The innovation must already be beyond the prototype stage. Ideas that remain purely conceptual or are still being developed in a laboratory are considered too early for DIV support.

Stage 1 projects are typically tested with at least hundreds or thousands of people, allowing organizations to determine whether the innovation works in a practical setting.

What Can Stage 1 Funding Support?

Potential activities include:

Assessing demand

Assessing willingness to pay

Exploring alternative delivery models

Conducting user testing

Conducting market testing

Documenting social outcomes

Measuring real-world implementation costs

Refining the innovation

Establishing whether the model is viable in practice

By the end of a Stage 1 grant, the fund wants applicants to have a much clearer understanding of whether people will actually use the innovation, how it performs in real-world conditions, and whether it demonstrates enough promise to justify further investment.

Stage 1 Evidence Requirements

Stage 1 applicants are not required to have causal evidence of impact.

However, they must provide:

A strong theory of change

A compelling rationale for expected development impact

A plan for collecting data

A plan for analyzing that data

A strategy for using evidence to test the assumptions underlying the theory of change

For innovations intended to scale through public or philanthropic funding, applicants should explain how the pilot will prepare the innovation for rigorous testing of causal impact and cost-effectiveness.

Commercially oriented innovations should focus on assessing customer demand, willingness to pay, and initial market viability.

Hybrid innovations must address the requirements applicable to both their public/philanthropic and commercial components.

Stage 1 Scale Expectations

Even at the pilot stage, applicants must demonstrate that their innovation has the potential to reach millions of people.

They should explain:

How the innovation could eventually be financed

Who might pay for it

Who could adopt it

Which organizations might implement it

What partnerships may be required

Whether relationships with potential partners already exist

Existing partnerships are not necessarily required at Stage 1, but applicants should demonstrate that they understand the ecosystem needed to achieve scale.

Stage 2: Testing and Positioning for Scale – Up to US$500,000

Stage 2 funding is designed for innovations that have already undergone successful pilot testing and are ready for more rigorous evaluation or market validation.

The general funding ceiling is US$500,000, although in rare and especially compelling cases, the DIV Fund may consider awards of up to US$750,000.

At this stage, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate whether their innovation:

Meaningfully improves people’s lives

Has measurable impact

Is cost-effective

Is market viable where relevant

Has a credible pathway to scale

Stage 2 grants may also support operational expansion designed to position an innovation for future scale.

Stage 2 and Rigorous Evidence

For innovations following a public pathway to scale, applicants without existing rigorous causal evidence may be expected to generate such evidence during the DIV Fund award.

The initial application may require information about the proposed study design, including:

Treatment and comparison groups

Unit of assignment

Power calculations

Minimum detectable effects

Primary outcomes

The evaluation should be capable of providing credible information about both impact and cost.

A credible counterfactual is required. Examples include a randomized controlled trial or an appropriately designed quasi-experimental approach such as a regression discontinuity design.

Commercial Pathway at Stage 2

Commercially scaling innovations do not necessarily need causal evidence of impact at this stage.

Instead, they should demonstrate:

A credible theory of change

Evidence supporting the expected development impact

Plans for collecting usage data

Appropriate measures of social outcomes

Evidence of market viability

A plan to validate market viability during the grant period

Applicants should demonstrate that the innovation could potentially generate sufficient revenue to cover its fully loaded costs at scale.

This includes costs such as

Customer acquisition

Distribution

Headquarters operations

Capital costs

Depreciation

Product or service delivery

Applicants may also demonstrate market viability by showing that the innovation could reasonably attract commercial capital on market terms by the end of the Stage 2 period.

Hybrid Pathway at Stage 2

Hybrid innovations combine commercial revenue with public or philanthropic subsidy.

Applicants following this model must demonstrate that the subsidy component is justified by the additional social value it generates.

In other words, the applicant needs to establish both commercial viability and a compelling social justification for the portion of funding that cannot be covered by commercial revenue.

Stage 2 Cost-Effectiveness

Applicants should either have already assessed the cost-effectiveness of their intervention or provide a credible plan for doing so during the grant period.

They should identify:

Current costs

Projected costs

Major cost drivers

Expected costs at scale

Impact measurements

Cost-per-impact comparisons

How the innovation compares with alternatives

For commercially oriented innovations, relevant commercial and financial information should also be presented.

Stage 2 Partnerships and Scale

Stage 2 applicants must explain what financial resources will be needed to scale their innovation and how those resources will ultimately be secured.

Applications are stronger when organizations already have relationships with potential scaling partners.

Examples may include:

Distribution partnerships

Large customer orders

Government relationships

Memoranda of Understanding

Relationships with long-term funders

Implementation partnerships

The goal is to demonstrate that the innovation is moving beyond proof of concept toward a realistic scale-up strategy.

Stage 3: Transitioning to Scale—Up to US$1.5 Million

Stage 3 represents the DIV Fund’s highest funding tier, with grants of up to US$1.5 million.

This stage is intended for innovations that have already demonstrated strong evidence or market viability and are ready to address the operational challenges involved in moving toward widespread implementation.

For public or philanthropic scaling, applicants should already have:

Rigorous causal evidence of impact

A credible counterfactual

Evidence that the intervention is cost-effective at scale

For commercial scaling, applicants should already have demonstrated market viability.

Hybrid applicants should demonstrate the appropriate combination of impact evidence and commercial viability.

What Can Stage 3 Funding Support?

Stage 3 funding may support activities such as

Adapting an innovation to new contexts

Accelerating scale-up

Providing technical assistance for public-sector implementation

Testing whether an innovation’s impact remains effective in new settings

Expanding successful approaches into new markets

Addressing operational barriers to growth

The ultimate objective is for the innovation to operate at scale in a way that is financially sustainable over the long term.

Stage 3 Evidence Requirements

For public or philanthropic pathways, applicants must demonstrate rigorous causal evidence and a convincing case that the intervention is cost-effective at scale.

Commercial applicants should already meet the relevant market-viability requirements.

The DIV Fund also expects applicants to clearly explain why its investment would generate a high social return.

For example, DIV support might:

Unlock additional capital

Enable entry into new markets

Remove barriers to expansion

Accelerate adoption

Enable greater scale

Increase the overall social impact of an existing solution

Stage 3 funding is therefore intended to be catalytic rather than simply financing ordinary ongoing operations.

Stage 3: Cost-Effectiveness and Sustainability

Stage 3 applicants should have a strong understanding of the cost of delivering their innovation.

They should be able to estimate:

Cost per person reached

Cost per outcome achieved

Cost structure at scale

Factors affecting unit costs

Expected changes in costs as the innovation expands

Applicants should also demonstrate that the cost structure can support large-scale implementation.

This could occur because the innovation is already inexpensive enough to remain cost-effective at scale or because there is concrete evidence that costs will decrease as production, distribution, or implementation expands.

Public, Commercial and Hybrid Pathways to Scale

An important feature of the DIV Fund is that it does not require every innovation to follow the same route to scale.

Public Pathway

An innovation follows a public pathway when it is expected to scale through:

Government funding

Donor funding

Philanthropic funding

Public-sector systems

Applicants using this pathway should explain how governments or philanthropic systems could ultimately adopt, finance, and sustain the intervention.

Commercial Pathway

A commercial pathway involves scaling through revenue generated from:

Customer payments

Advertising

Commercial investment

Other private-market mechanisms

Applicants need to establish that the business model can eventually support the full cost of the innovation at scale.

Hybrid Pathway

A hybrid pathway combines commercial revenue with public or philanthropic funding.

For example, customers may cover part of the cost while a subsidy covers the remainder.

The applicant must demonstrate both that customers are willing and able to pay the commercial portion and that the subsidy creates additional social value that justifies the remaining support.

How the DIV Fund Assesses Expected Social Return

Across all funding stages, the DIV Fund seeks to maximize expected social returns.

This means it considers the overall benefit expected from investing in an innovation relative to the size of the proposed grant.

The assessment considers factors such as

Impact per person

Unit costs

Potential scale

Probability of achieving scale

How DIV funding could increase the likelihood of successful adoption

The long-term social benefits of the intervention

An innovation may therefore be attractive even if its initial pilot appears only moderately cost-effective, provided there is a credible possibility that DIV support could help it achieve very large-scale adoption.

For example, a solution producing a modest benefit per person could generate enormous total social value if it eventually reaches tens or hundreds of millions of people.

This illustrates why applicants should not focus exclusively on the immediate size of their pilot. They should explain how the proposed investment could unlock much greater impact over time.

Focus on People Living in Poverty

The DIV Fund specifically seeks to support people living in poverty.

When assessing income-related interventions, the fund considers improvements relative to people’s existing living standards rather than simply looking at the absolute dollar value of the income increase.

This means an increase in income can carry greater value when it represents a larger improvement in the living standards of a poorer person.

For health interventions, comparable health improvements are valued similarly across populations, while the overall disease burden and number of lives that could plausibly be improved or saved are important considerations.

Applicants should therefore clearly explain:

Who benefits from the innovation

The socioeconomic circumstances of beneficiaries

The expected magnitude of the improvement

How many people could ultimately benefit

Why the intervention represents an efficient use of resources

Grant Duration

DIV Fund awards may have a maximum duration of five years.

Applicants are encouraged to propose a timeline that aligns realistically with their objectives and the development stage of their innovation.

The fund also emphasizes catalytic funding. Applicants should clearly explain why they are seeking DIV support at the current point in their development and how the grant would enable results that would otherwise be difficult or impossible to achieve.

APPLY HERE

Why This Opportunity Could Be Valuable for Development Innovators

The DIV Fund provides a distinctive funding pathway because it can support an innovation as it progresses through different stages of development.

Rather than focusing solely on established organizations or fully proven interventions, the fund can support:

Early real-world pilots

Rigorous evidence generation

Market validation

Cost-effectiveness analysis

Scale preparation

Adaptation to new contexts

Public-sector adoption

Commercial expansion

Evidence generation for widely used approaches

This creates an opportunity for organizations to obtain funding appropriate to their current level of development while demonstrating progressively stronger evidence of impact.

Visit HERE for more information about the DIV Fund Grants 2026.

Key Funding Amounts at a Glance

Stage 1 – Piloting: Up to US$200,000

Stage 2 – Testing and Positioning for Scale: Up to US$500,000

Exceptional Stage 2 cases: Up to US$750,000

Stage 3 – Transitioning to Scale: Up to US$1.5 million

Maximum award period: Up to five years

The funding amounts are ceilings rather than guaranteed awards. Applicants are encouraged to request only the amount genuinely needed for their proposed activities. Co-funding is valued where appropriate, although it is not mandatory.

What Applicants Should Demonstrate

Organizations considering the DIV Fund should ensure their proposal clearly addresses the following areas:

The problem: What significant development challenge is being addressed?

The innovation: What is the proposed product, service, policy, program, delivery model, or process improvement?

Theory of change: Why should the innovation produce meaningful development outcomes?

Evidence: What existing evidence supports the proposed approach?

Impact measurement: How will the organization determine whether the intervention actually works?

Cost-effectiveness: How does the intervention compare with existing alternatives in terms of cost and impact?

Scale: How could the innovation eventually reach at least one million people or generate an exceptionally large benefit for a somewhat smaller population?

Financing: Who will ultimately pay for the intervention?

Partnerships: Which governments, businesses, funders, distributors, implementers, or other organizations will be required?

Sustainability: How will the innovation continue operating after DIV Fund support ends?

Catalytic role: Why is DIV funding particularly important at this stage, and what would the funding unlock that would otherwise not happen?

These considerations are especially important because the DIV Fund evaluates proposals based on their potential to generate substantial and durable social returns rather than simply assessing whether an intervention is innovative.

Deadline

No specific application deadline is stated in the provided DIV Fund Request for Proposals.

Applicants should therefore consult the official DIV Fund application information for current submission procedures and any applicable application timelines.

Conclusion

The DIV Fund Request for Proposals presents a significant funding opportunity for organizations developing evidence-based solutions to poverty and development challenges in low- and middle-income countries.

With funding of up to US$1.5 million, the opportunity can support innovations at multiple stages, from early real-world pilots to rigorous testing and large-scale implementation.

The fund’s approach is centered on three fundamental questions: Does the innovation work? Is it cost-effective? And can it achieve durable scale?

Organizations applying should therefore go beyond describing an interesting idea. They should demonstrate a clear theory of change, explain how impact will be measured, provide realistic cost projections, identify a credible pathway to scale, and show how the intervention can ultimately become financially sustainable.

For early-stage innovations, Stage 1 provides an opportunity to establish real-world viability. For innovations with successful pilots, Stage 2 offers support for rigorous testing, market validation, and preparation for scale. For proven solutions ready for widespread implementation, Stage 3 provides substantial funding to overcome operational barriers and transition toward sustainable scale.

Ultimately, the DIV Fund is particularly suited to nonprofits, social enterprises, universities, research institutions, businesses, technical assistance providers, and partnerships that have a promising solution capable of improving the lives of large numbers of people living in poverty and that can make a compelling case for measurable, cost-effective, and sustainable impact.

TITLE: Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship 2027–2028: Fully Funded Ph.D. Fellowship with $45,000 Stipend, Full Tuition and Paid Internship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship for the 2027–2028 academic year, an opportunity designed to support exceptional doctoral students conducting advanced research in data science, artificial intelligence, machine learning and related technical fields.

Bloomberg is inviting outstanding Ph.D. students working in relevant areas of study to apply for the fellowship. The program connects doctoral researchers with Bloomberg’s AI and machine learning research community, where researchers and engineers work on complex scientific and engineering challenges associated with Bloomberg technology and the Bloomberg Terminal.

The Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship provides a comprehensive package of financial and professional support. Selected fellows receive 100% tuition coverage, a USD 45,000 stipend, mentorship from Bloomberg professionals, career support and a paid 14-week research internship at Bloomberg. Fellows may also have an opportunity to renew their fellowship annually for up to three years, subject to Bloomberg’s discretion.

Applications, including all required documents and reference letters, must be submitted by Friday, September 25, 2026, at 11:59 PM Anywhere on Earth (AoE).

About the Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship

The Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship is an academic engagement initiative aimed at supporting Ph.D. candidates whose research can contribute to advances in data science, artificial intelligence, machine learning and other areas relevant to Bloomberg’s technology and research ecosystem.

The fellowship’s broader goal is to encourage doctoral researchers to produce meaningful research outputs. Bloomberg specifically highlights groundbreaking research publications, open-source contributions and other forms of research dissemination as outcomes that the fellowship is intended to encourage.

Rather than offering financial support alone, Bloomberg combines funding with professional and research development opportunities. Fellows receive mentorship, career counseling and access to research internships, creating opportunities to connect academic research with practical technical challenges.

Bloomberg has operated previous cohorts of its Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship, including cohorts for the 2018–2019 through 2024–2025 academic years.

Research Areas and Topics of Interest

Applicants should be pursuing doctoral research relevant to Bloomberg’s areas of interest.

For the current call, Bloomberg has identified a broad range of research topics. The list is not necessarily exhaustive, meaning applicants working in closely related fields may also have research that fits the program.

The stated topics of interest include:

Agentic AI, Tool Use and Agent Infrastructure

Research involving autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents, the tools used by AI systems and the infrastructure required to develop and operate agent-based systems.

Agent Evaluation and LLM Judges

Research exploring methods for evaluating AI agents and the use, reliability and development of large language models as evaluators.

Code Generation, Semantic Parsing and Text-to-API

Work involving AI-assisted programming, translation of natural language into structured representations and systems that convert textual instructions into API interactions.

Efficient Models, Distillation and Inference

Research focused on improving the efficiency of machine learning models, model compression and distillation, and efficient inference techniques.

Human-AI Collaboration, Data Annotation and Data-Centric AI

Research examining how people and artificial intelligence systems interact, methods for improving data annotation and approaches that prioritize the quality and management of data used in AI development.

Information Retrieval, RAG and Agentic Search

Research covering information retrieval, retrieval-augmented generation and advanced AI-driven search systems.

Information Synthesis, Summarization and Generation

Work examining how AI systems can identify, combine, summarize and generate useful information from different sources.

Knowledge Graphs, Structured and Neuro-symbolic Reasoning

Research involving structured knowledge representations and systems that combine neural methods with symbolic reasoning.

LLM Post-training, Domain Adaptation, Reasoning and Alignment

Research exploring how large language models can be improved after initial training, adapted to particular domains, enhanced in their reasoning capabilities and aligned for intended uses.

Multimodal Models and Document Intelligence

Research involving models capable of processing multiple forms of information and technologies for understanding complex documents.

Time-series Modeling, Forecasting and AI for Finance

Research involving temporal data, predictive modeling, forecasting and applications of artificial intelligence within financial contexts.

Trustworthy, Responsible and Secure AI

Research addressing the reliability, responsibility, security and trustworthiness of artificial intelligence systems.

These research areas make the fellowship particularly relevant to doctoral researchers working at the intersection of computer science, data science, artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, information retrieval and related disciplines.

Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship Benefits

One of the major attractions of the Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship is its combination of academic funding and professional research experience.

Selected fellows will receive the following benefits:

1. 100% Tuition Coverage

Bloomberg states that the fellowship will cover 100% of the recipient’s tuition.

This provides substantial financial support for doctoral candidates during the fellowship period and allows selected researchers to focus more extensively on their academic and research responsibilities.

2. USD 45,000 Stipend

Each recipient will receive a USD 45,000 stipend.

Bloomberg states that the stipend can support:

Living expenses;

Attendance at professional conferences; and

Research-related expenses, including computer hardware.

The ability to use the funding for professional conferences and research equipment gives fellows additional flexibility in supporting their academic development.

3. Bloomberg Mentorship

Recipients will be connected with Bloomberg mentors.

This mentorship component provides fellows with professional connections to individuals working within Bloomberg’s research and technology environment while they continue their doctoral research.

4. Paid 14-Week Summer Internship

Fellows are required to complete a 14-week paid summer internship at Bloomberg for every year in which they are a fellow.

For the incoming fellowship cohort, the internship requirement begins in Summer 2027.

The internship will be research-focused and may take place in:

New York;

London; or

Toronto.

This component provides fellows with the opportunity to undertake practical research within Bloomberg while continuing to build their doctoral research experience.

5. Potential Fellowship Renewal for Up to Three Years

Recipients may have the opportunity to renew the Bloomberg fellowship annually for up to three years.

However, renewal is not automatic and remains at Bloomberg’s discretion.

Who Is Eligible for the Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship?

Bloomberg has established specific eligibility requirements that applicants should review carefully before preparing an application.

Full-Time Doctoral Student Requirement

Applicants must be full-time doctoral students during the 2027–2028 academic year.

They must also have an expected Ph.D. graduation date in or before the end of 2030.

Continued Full-Time Enrollment

Successful applicants must remain enrolled as full-time students throughout the duration of the grant.

Bloomberg states that if a fellow fails to maintain full-time student status, the remaining portion of the grant will be forfeited.

Academic Year Kickoff Event

Recipients are required to attend the fellowship’s academic-year kickoff event each fall at Bloomberg Headquarters in New York, unless Bloomberg conducts the event entirely online.

Bloomberg will cover expenses associated with the fellow’s attendance at this event.

Mandatory Summer Research Internship

Recipients must complete a 14-week summer internship during each year of their Bloomberg fellowship.

Internships may take place in:

New York;

London; or

Toronto.

Bloomberg states that these are paid, research-focused internships.

Restrictions on Other Industry Fellowships

Recipients cannot simultaneously receive support from another industry fellowship during the Bloomberg fellowship.

However, Bloomberg indicates that non-industry funding may be permitted on a case-by-case basis.

Outside Employment Restrictions

Fellows may not be employed outside their university during the fellowship unless they have received explicit permission from Bloomberg.

These requirements mean applicants should carefully review any existing funding arrangements, employment responsibilities or external fellowship commitments before applying.

Important U.S. Visa and Work Authorization Requirement

International applicants should pay particular attention to Bloomberg’s visa policy.

Bloomberg will not provide sponsorship for any U.S. visa for this fellowship.

Required Application Documents

Finalize their research proposal;

Enter referee information;

Complete the online application.

When Will Successful Applicants Be Announced?

Bloomberg expects to inform fellowship recipients by:

Friday, December 18, 2026.

How to Apply for the Bloomberg Data Science Ph.D. Fellowship

Applications are submitted online through Bloomberg’s designated fellowship application platform.

Applicants should:

Review the fellowship eligibility criteria carefully.

Confirm that they will be a full-time doctoral student during the 2027–2028 academic year.

Confirm that their expected Ph.D. graduation date is no later than the end of 2030.

Review Bloomberg’s listed research topics and assess the relevance of their proposed research.

Prepare an updated curriculum vitae.

Format the research proposal according to Bloomberg’s required Overleaf template.

Hotel accommodation throughout the conference period.

Daily allowance covering meals and incidental expenses.

Official observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation.

Guidance from experienced members of the CCCCC delegation before, during and after COP31.

Pre-COP preparation, role definition and post-conference knowledge-sharing activities.

Youth organisation

Non-governmental organisation

Community-based organisation

Private-sector organisation

Public-sector institution; or

Other organisation working in climate, development or public engagement.

The applicant’s commitment to the Caribbean’s climate agenda

The potential professional value of the fellowship

The quality of the proposed institutional knowledge-transfer plan

The potential for the fellowship to create impact beyond COP31
