TITLE: Field Studies Council Youth Panel 2026: Join the UK-Wide Youth Environmental Leadership Panel

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Field Studies Council Youth Panel 2026, an exciting opportunity for young people in the United Kingdom to contribute their ideas, experiences and perspectives to one of the UK’s leading environmental education charities.

The Youth Panel brings together young people who are passionate about nature, the outdoors and environmental education. Panel members have the opportunity to influence how the Field Studies Council engages with young people, participate in discussions with staff and trustees, develop valuable transferable skills, meet other young naturalists and environmentalists, and contribute to content and projects focused on youth engagement.

Applications opened on 14 September 2026, and eligible young people are encouraged to submit their applications before the deadline of 9:00 pm on Sunday, 27 September 2026.

About the Field Studies Council Youth Panel

The Field Studies Council Youth Panel is a UK-wide group of young people that helps shape nature education and youth engagement through strategic insight and feedback.

Youth Panel members play an important role within the Field Studies Council by bringing young people’s perspectives into organisational discussions. Rather than simply participating in environmental activities, members can contribute their views on how young people can be better engaged with nature, outdoor learning and environmental education.

The opportunity is particularly suitable for young people who want to become a stronger voice for their generation while gaining practical experience in communication, decision-making, teamwork and influencing.

The role is voluntary, meaning that successful applicants will not be employed or paid as Youth Panel members. However, the position provides opportunities for personal development, networking, training and involvement in the work of the Field Studies Council.

What Does a Youth Panel Member Do?

Youth Panel members are expected to actively contribute to the Panel and participate in activities that support the Field Studies Council’s youth engagement work.

The Panel provides young people with an opportunity to have their voices heard in discussions concerning the organisation’s provision for young people. Members can provide feedback, share ideas, participate in meetings and contribute to projects based on their interests and skills.

The Field Studies Council describes its Youth Panel members as key members of the organisation who can engage in high-level discussions about its provision for young people.

This makes the opportunity particularly valuable for young people interested in:

Environmental education

Nature and conservation

Youth engagement

Environmental leadership

Communication and content creation

Decision-making

Advocacy and representation

Biodiversity

Outdoor learning

Community engagement

Developing leadership and teamwork skills

Key Benefits of Joining the Youth Panel

Being selected for the Field Studies Council Youth Panel can provide a combination of environmental, leadership, communication and personal-development experiences.

1. Participate in a Funded Residential Weekend

Youth Panel members will have the opportunity to attend a funded residential weekend at a Field Studies Council field centre in the UK.

For the 2026 intake, the residential weekend is scheduled to take place from Friday 6 November to Sunday 8 November 2026 at Preston Montford, Shropshire. The costs associated with the residential are covered.

This residential experience provides an opportunity for members to meet other participants in person and take part in Youth Panel activities.

2. Access Training Opportunities

Youth Panel members can participate in training opportunities during their time on the Panel.

These include heavily subsidised Biodiversity Courses, which may be offered online and in person. Such opportunities can help young people expand their understanding of biodiversity and develop knowledge that complements their interest in nature and the environment.

3. Network With Other Young Environmentalists

The Youth Panel provides an opportunity to meet other young people who are passionate about nature.

Throughout their term, members will have opportunities to connect with other young naturalists and environmentalists. This can create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge exchange and building relationships with peers who share similar interests.

4. Develop Transferable Skills

One of the important benefits of the Youth Panel is the opportunity to develop practical skills that can be useful beyond environmental activities.

The Field Studies Council specifically identifies skills such as:

Meeting skills

Decision-making

Influencing

Collaboration

Communication

Participation in organisational discussions

These experiences can be valuable for young people who are considering future education, volunteering, employment or leadership opportunities.

5. Create Content for Social Media and Blogs

Youth Panel members can also contribute to communications activities.

Members may have opportunities to create content for social media and blogs that can be shared through Field Studies Council channels as well as through their own channels.

This element of the role may be particularly useful for young people interested in digital communication, journalism, social media, content creation, environmental storytelling or public engagement.

6. Represent Young People in Decision-Making

Youth Panel members can represent young people’s perspectives in decision-making meetings involving Field Studies Council staff and trustees.

They may also have opportunities to represent the Field Studies Council at events or conferences.

This provides participants with exposure to organisational decision-making and gives them an opportunity to contribute directly to conversations concerning young people and environmental education.

Duration of the Youth Panel Role

Members recruited during autumn 2026 are expected to serve on the Youth Panel for two years.

The role is voluntary, and successful applicants will therefore need to be prepared to make a sustained commitment to the Panel throughout this period.

A two-year commitment can allow members to build meaningful experience over time rather than participating in a one-off activity. It also gives participants the opportunity to develop their skills and contribute to projects throughout their period of service.

Meetings and Time Commitment

Youth Panel members participate in both online and in-person activities.

The Panel holds an in-person residential once a year at a Field Studies Council centre. For the 2026 cohort, the annual residential is scheduled for 6–8 November 2026 at Preston Montford. Applicants are expected to confirm their availability for this date.

In addition, monthly online meetings are held. These meetings alternate between weekday evenings and generally take place on Mondays, Wednesdays or Thursdays from 6:00 pm to 7:15 pm.

The Field Studies Council recognises that young people may require greater flexibility at certain times of the year.

Youth Panel members are expected to attend a minimum of four meetings per year and contribute to associated tasks and projects.

This means applicants should consider their existing commitments, including school and other activities, before applying.

Who Can Apply for the Field Studies Council Youth Panel 2026?

The opportunity is open to young people who meet the specific requirements set by the Field Studies Council.

Applicants must:

Be aged between 16 and 18 at the time of applying.

Be based in the United Kingdom.

Be able to attend the in-person Youth Panel residential from Friday 6 November to Sunday 8 November 2026 at Preston Montford, Shropshire.

Be able to commit approximately a couple of hours per month to meetings and related tasks.

The Field Studies Council states that it welcomes applications from young people regardless of their experience or background.

It also indicates that it is particularly interested in representatives from Scotland and Wales, while the Youth Panel itself is UK-wide.

Country and Continent Eligibility

The opportunity is restricted geographically to young people based in the United Kingdom.

Therefore, applicants from the following UK nations can potentially apply, provided they meet the other requirements:

England

Scotland

Wales

Northern Ireland

The source specifically highlights Scotland and Wales as areas from which the Field Studies Council is especially keen to receive representation.

The eligible continent is Europe, but the actual eligibility requirement is more specific: applicants must be based in the UK. The opportunity is not presented as open to applicants from Europe generally.

No Previous Experience Is Required

An important feature of the opportunity is that applicants do not need to demonstrate extensive previous experience.

The Field Studies Council welcomes applications from young people regardless of their experience or background.

This means applicants should not assume that they need an extensive environmental, conservation or leadership record to be considered. Instead, they should use their application to explain who they are, what motivates them, what they hope to learn and what they can contribute to the Panel.

What Is Required in the Application?

The application consists of three main questions designed to help the Field Studies Council understand applicants, their motivations and the contribution they could make to youth engagement.

Question 1: Tell Us About Yourself and Your Motivation

Applicants are asked to explain something about themselves, their experiences and what motivates them to join the Field Studies Council Youth Panel.

The maximum response length is 200 words.

Applicants may consider discussing:

Their connection with the outdoors

Previous volunteering roles

Areas they would like to become involved in

Their motivation for representing young people

Their interest in the Field Studies Council

The organisation is looking for insight into the applicant as an individual and an understanding of why they want to become part of the Youth Panel.

Question 2: What Do You Hope to Learn?

The second question asks applicants to explain what they hope to learn from participating in the role.

The maximum response length is 200 words.

Applicants can consider discussing:

Skills they want to develop

What excites them about joining the Youth Panel

How the opportunity could support their future

Personal or professional development goals

This is an opportunity for applicants to demonstrate that they have thought about how Youth Panel participation could contribute to their growth.

Question 3: What Can You Bring to the Panel?

The third question asks applicants what they could contribute to the Panel and what they hope to achieve as a Panel member.

The maximum response length is 300 words.

Applicants can discuss:

Particular skills they possess

Relevant experiences

What distinguishes them from other applicants

Ideas they could contribute

Their goals as a Youth Panel member

How they would balance Panel responsibilities with school and other commitments

This question is particularly important because it allows applicants to demonstrate both their potential contribution and their understanding of the responsibilities involved in joining the Panel.

Application Tips

The Field Studies Council recommends preparing responses in Microsoft Word or Google Docs before copying and pasting them into the online application form.

This approach can make it easier for applicants to draft, edit and review their answers before submitting the application.

Applicants should ensure that their responses directly answer each question while remaining within the specified word limits.

Young people should also consider demonstrating genuine motivation rather than simply listing achievements. Since the Field Studies Council welcomes applicants regardless of their experience or background, applicants can focus on their interests, perspectives, aspirations and willingness to contribute.

Alternative Application Format for Applicants Who Find Online Forms Difficult

The Field Studies Council provides an alternative way to respond to the application questions.

Applicants who find completing online forms difficult and would prefer to talk through their answers can record their responses in video or audio format.

Each question can be answered in a recording of up to three minutes.

Applicants choosing this option are instructed to email their files to youth.engagement@field-studies-council.org.

This provides an alternative route for young people who may communicate their ideas more effectively through spoken responses.

Application and Selection Timeline

The Field Studies Council has provided a clear application and selection timeline for the 2026 Youth Panel recruitment.

Applications Open

Applications open at midday on 14 September 2026.

Application Deadline

Applications close at 9:00 pm on Sunday, 27 September 2026.

Applicants should ensure that their application is submitted before the deadline rather than waiting until the final minutes.

APPLY HERE

Application Outcome

Applicants will hear about the outcome of their application at the start of October 2026.

Virtual Interviews

Shortlisted candidates will be invited to a short virtual interview taking place on 13 or 14 October 2026.

The Field Studies Council indicates that there is flexibility for alternative arrangements. The interview is intended to allow the organisation to get to know shortlisted candidates and also give candidates the opportunity to ask questions of a current Youth Panel member.

Importantly, interview questions can be shared with candidates in advance.

Residential Weekend

Successful applicants need to be available for the Youth Panel residential from Friday 6 November to Sunday 8 November 2026 at Preston Montford in Shropshire.

The costs of the residential are covered.

What Makes This Opportunity Valuable?

The Field Studies Council Youth Panel provides young people with a combination of environmental engagement, youth representation and personal development.

Rather than simply attending an environmental programme, participants can become part of a group that contributes to the organisation’s approach to youth engagement.

Members can gain insight into the workings of an environmental education charity while participating in high-level discussions concerning provision for young people.

The opportunity can therefore be particularly valuable for young people who are considering future interests or careers related to:

Environmental science

Conservation

Biodiversity

Environmental education

Sustainability

Communications

Media and content creation

Youth development

Advocacy

Leadership

Public engagement

Community development

A Platform for Youth Voice and Representation

One of the central aspects of the Youth Panel is representation.

Young people have the opportunity to provide perspectives on issues affecting youth engagement and contribute to organisational discussions. Members can represent young people at meetings involving Field Studies Council staff and trustees and may also represent the organisation at events and conferences.

This creates an opportunity for participants to practise expressing ideas, listening to different perspectives, contributing constructively to discussions and communicating the interests of young people.

Opportunities to Develop Through the Role

The Field Studies Council notes that the Youth Panel is shaped by its members and that there will be opportunities to expand skills and experiences according to individual areas of interest.

This means that the experience does not necessarily have to be limited to one particular area. Members may be able to explore interests connected to environmental education, communication, biodiversity, youth engagement, content creation, decision-making and other areas relevant to the Panel’s activities.

The combination of regular online meetings, annual residential activities, training opportunities and projects can provide a sustained environment for learning and participation.

Important Commitment to Consider Before Applying

Although the Youth Panel offers numerous development opportunities, applicants should understand that it is a two-year voluntary commitment.

Successful applicants are expected to contribute time each month and attend at least four meetings per year, in addition to associated tasks and projects.

They must also be able to attend the annual residential and participate in monthly online meetings.

Young people should therefore consider their school schedules, extracurricular activities and other responsibilities before applying. The Field Studies Council acknowledges that participants may sometimes require flexibility during particularly busy periods.

How to Apply for the Field Studies Council Youth Panel 2026

Eligible young people can apply through the official Field Studies Council application process.

The application form is available through the Field Studies Council’s Youth Panel application page, and applications opened on 14 September 2026.

Applicants should prepare thoughtful responses to all three questions and make sure their answers remain within the required word limits.

Those who have difficulty completing the online form can instead submit video or audio responses of up to three minutes per question by email to the Youth Engagement team.

Application deadline: 9:00 pm, Sunday, 27 September 2026.

TITLE: Call for Hosting the Association of African Universities (AAU) General Conference 2029

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) will hold its 17th Quadrennial General Conference (QGC) in July 2029. The QGC, comprising representatives of members, associate members and observers, is the supreme authority of the Association and is responsible for determining the general policies of the Association. It is normally a five-day event centered around issues of relevance to higher education in Africa.

The QGC comprises two parts; the first is the business session, which evaluates the performance of the AAU in the preceding four years and approves of the programmes in the subsequent four years. The business session also incorporates the election of a new 15-member Board to steer the affairs of the Association for the next four years.

The second part of the QGC is the scientific discussions of the theme and sub-themes of the Conference under the biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and Rectors of African Universities (COREVIP). At the 17th General Conference, the 24th COREVIP will be held.

These events are jointly organised by the AAU and a member institution in good reputation with the Association (i.e. having zero arrears in annual subscription payment). It should be noted that the co-hosting of this most important event in the calendar of the African higher education community provides very high-level visibility and exposure to the host institution and country because of the calibre and number of academic leaders, policymakers, researchers, development partners, and other stakeholders that usually attend it, and it is, therefore, a highly sought-after event.

2029 QGC THEME

Yet to be finalized.

CALL FOR HOST

The AAU hereby invites applications from member institutions for the co-hosting of this prestigious quadrennial Conference.

The Host’s Responsibilities

The host university will be expected to contribute to the organisation of the Conference, financially or in kind, in the areas of:

• Local transportation for participants.

• Airport “meet and greet” (reception and facilitation of immigration procedures).

• Traditional items as gifts to presenters and sessional chairs.

• Welcome Reception or Dinner for participants.

• Publicity and media coverage (local press, radio and TV, conference photographer).

• Arrangement of courtesy calls by the Governing Board on appropriate government authorities in the host country.

• Arranging excursion visits by delegates.

• Providing the Secretariat for the Conference (equipment and supplies).

• Decorations, banners, invitations to Opening/Closing Ceremony and receptions.

• Cultural display during open and closing ceremonies.

The main Campus is situated on the Great East Road, 9 km from the Lusaka City Centre while the Ridgeway Campus is on John Mbita Road, 4 km South East of Lusaka.

The University of Zambia is the leading Higher Education Institution in Zambia and one of the market leaders in the provision of higher education in the region. It has thirteen (13) Schools, three (3) Directorates, three (3) Institutes and offices in ten (10) Provincial Centres. The University has a staff complement of 2000 employees comprising of 900 academic staff and 1100 non-academic staff. The student population stands at more than 18,000 in both undergraduate and postgraduate programmes.

The University’s programmes and activities are driven by its motto of “Service and Excellence”.

The University of Zambia is proudly a member of the Association of African Universities (AAU).

TITLE: 22nd Academy of African Business and Development (AABD) Annual Conference | May 17 -21, 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Posted on Behalf of the University of Professional Studies, Accra (an AAU Member)

Conference Theme – Sustainable Development Beyond Aid: The Focus for Africa

The Academy of African Business and Development (AABD) invites researchers, business practitioners, consultants, community leaders, and policy makers to participate in the 22nd AABD annual conference to be held at the University of Professional Studies, Accra, Ghana, from May 17 to May 21, 2022.

The AABD annual conferences aim at facilitating multidisciplinary research by stimulating collaborations between Africa based researchers and professionals and their counterparts around the world, by broadening and deepening global understanding of various issues relevant to Africa’s business and development, as well as advancing solutions to some of her challenges.

Background

Africa has been and continues to be reliant on international aid for its development. Though the volume of international aid received may be relatively small compared to its total annual expenditure, it represents a substantial part of the discretionary funds available to governments once statutory payments, wages, and salaries, and debt repayments have been set aside. International aid, therefore, is one of the key sources of funding for ongoing development projects in many nations.

Studies on aid effectiveness abound, but the contradictory nature of the research findings calls for more discussion and further research on the subject. Amidst the growing criticism of negative effects of international aid to Africa, the President of the Republic of Ghana, Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo has proposed a Ghana Beyond Aid vision, urging the creation of “…a Ghana that is beyond dependence on the charity of others to cater for the needs of its people, but instead engages with other countries competitively through trade and investments and political cooperation for enhanced regional and global peace and security.” It is argued that the emphasis is on the efficient and effective mobilization and use of resources to grow out of the dependence on aid rather than a rejection of aid (Ghana Beyond Aid Charter and Strategy Document, Government of Ghana, 2019).

A Zambian economist, Dambisa Moyo, in her book, Dead Aid: Why Aid is Not Working and How There is a Better Way for Africa, opined that the greatest myth of our time is that billions of dollars in aid sent from wealthy countries to developing African nations has helped to reduce poverty and increase growth. Much like President Akufo-Addo, she advocates for institutional change and an Asian Development model – a focus on Foreign Direct Investments and Trade not Aid.

The Director-General of the WTO, Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, argues that we should move from simplistic debate such as aid versus private sector, aid versus trade, etc. The issue she opined should be about how to get collaborative, multifaceted models that brings a partnership of governments, non-governmental organizations, donors, the private sector, and ordinary African people taking charge of their own lives. She argued that developed countries utilize Aid to better their economies, citing the example of Spain which got 10 billion dollars in Aid from the EU.

The conference theme, “Sustainable Development Beyond Aid: The Focus for Africa?” calls for further consideration of this new orientation. Should it be the focus of sustainable development of Africa? If so, how is this to be achieved? What are the challenges to implementation? These and many other issues require the critical attention of researchers, business practitioners, community leaders, and policy makers.

TITLE: 2026 UN Youth Townhall in Germany: Open Call for Young People Aged 18–35 to Join the UN Youth Townhall

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations Youth Office is inviting young people from diverse backgrounds to apply for participation in the 2026 UN Youth Townhall, a flagship youth engagement gathering taking place in Heidelberg, Germany, from 8 to 10 December 2026.

The Townhall is designed to bring young people together with governments, the United Nations, civil society, the private sector and other partners to move beyond dialogue and develop concrete recommendations, partnerships and opportunities for action.

For the 2026 gathering, the UN Youth Office will support a limited number of eligible young people aged 18 to 35 to participate in person. The selection process aims to promote diversity, including geographical representation, gender balance and participation from underrepresented and marginalized youth.

The application deadline is 7 September 2026 at midnight ET.

2026 UN Youth Townhall at a Glance

Opportunity detail
Information

Opportunity
2026 UN Youth Townhall

Organizer
UN Youth Office with support from partners

Location
Heidelberg, Germany

Dates
8–10 December 2026

18–35 years

Successful applicants will be notified; if no notification is received by 8 October 2026, applicants are encouraged to explore other opportunities

Application platform

What Is the 2026 UN Youth Townhall?

The 2026 UN Youth Townhall is described as the first convening of its kind and is a flagship gathering of the UN Youth Compass.

The event is intended to create a space where young people can engage meaningfully with decision-makers and other important stakeholders on issues affecting young people and the wider world.

Rather than limiting youth participation to discussion and consultation, the Townhall aims to generate tangible outcomes.

These include:

Concrete recommendations;

Partnerships;

Opportunities for action;

Continued engagement between young people and institutions; and

Stronger connections between youth and decision-makers.

The Townhall will bring together young people from diverse backgrounds with representatives from governments, the United Nations, civil society, the private sector and other partners.

This makes the event particularly relevant to young people interested in youth participation, international development, policymaking, peace and security, sustainable development, human rights and global affairs.

Where and When Will the UN Youth Townhall Take Place?

The 2026 UN Youth Townhall will take place in:

Heidelberg, Germany

The event is scheduled for:

8–10 December 2026

Selected young participants will therefore need to be available to participate in person during the Townhall dates.

The source specifically states that the UN Youth Office will support a limited number of young people to participate in person.

Who Is the UN Youth Townhall Looking For?

The open call is aimed at young people between the ages of 18 and 35.

However, age alone does not determine selection.

The UN Youth Office states that the selection process will consider several factors to help ensure meaningful and diverse youth representation.

These include:

Gender balance;

Geographical representation;

Participation of youth from underrepresented groups;

Participation of youth from marginalized groups;

Engagement with grassroots organizations; and

Previous engagement with the United Nations.

The selection process will be conducted by the UN Youth Office, with support from online volunteers and the Youth Advisory Group to the UN Youth Townhall.

Preference for Grassroots Youth Engagement

One particularly important aspect of the call is the preference given to young people who are engaged in grassroots organizations.

The UN Youth Office also indicates that preference will be given to applicants who have had limited or no prior engagement with the United Nations.

This is significant because the Townhall is designed to broaden youth participation rather than simply bring together young people who already have extensive experience within international institutions.

Young people who are actively contributing to their communities through grassroots initiatives may therefore find this opportunity particularly relevant.

Representation of Underrepresented and Marginalized Youth

The UN Youth Office aims to ensure that the Townhall reflects the diversity of young people.

The selection process will therefore consider participation from underrepresented and marginalized groups.

The application form specifically asks applicants whether they belong to or identify with particular rights-holder communities, including:

LGBTQIA+ communities;

Indigenous communities;

Migrants and internally displaced people;

Persons with disabilities;

Youth facing work- and descent-based discrimination;

Young people living with HIV; and

Refugees.

Applicants are given the opportunity to identify with these communities in the application.

The form also asks applicants with disabilities whether they require reasonable accommodation to participate.

Why the UN Youth Townhall Matters

The Townhall is designed around the principle that young people should have meaningful opportunities to contribute to discussions and decisions affecting their lives and communities.

The event is anchored in several major United Nations youth and international policy frameworks.

These include the:

UN Youth Compass;

UN Secretary-General’s 2023 Policy Brief on Meaningful Youth Engagement;

Youth2030: The UN Youth Strategy;

Pact for the Future;

UN Security Council Resolution 2250 (2015) on Youth, Peace and Security; and

UN Security Council Resolution 2807 (2025) on Youth, Peace and Security.

These frameworks provide the broader policy context for the Townhall.

The event therefore represents an opportunity for young participants to engage with international youth policy and contribute perspectives that can inform recommendations and future action.

What Can Participants Expect From the Townhall?

The source emphasizes that the Townhall will go beyond dialogue.

Participants will have an opportunity to connect with a range of stakeholders, including:

Governments

Young participants can engage with government representatives and contribute youth perspectives to policy discussions.

United Nations

The Townhall provides an opportunity for youth to interact with UN representatives and contribute to the organization’s broader youth engagement efforts.

Civil Society

Civil society organizations play an important role in youth participation and community action. The Townhall will provide opportunities for young people to connect with civil society actors.

Private Sector

The event will also connect young people with private-sector stakeholders, creating potential opportunities for collaboration and partnerships.

Other Partners

The gathering will bring together additional organizations and stakeholders working on youth-related issues.

The resulting connections can potentially extend beyond the three-day event, as the Townhall aims to create opportunities for continued engagement after the gathering.

The UN Youth Townhall Is Designed to Generate Action

A major feature of the event is its emphasis on moving from conversation to action.

Rather than simply asking young people to express their views, the Townhall seeks to produce:

Concrete recommendations that can inform future work;

Partnerships between young people and relevant stakeholders; and

Opportunities for action that can continue beyond the Townhall.

This approach places young people not only in the position of participants but also as contributors to solutions and future initiatives.

Application Eligibility

Applicants should carefully review the official application guidance before submitting their applications.

Based on the supplied call, applicants should meet the following central criteria:

Age

Applicants must be between 18 and 35 years old.

Participation

Selected applicants are expected to participate in person at the Townhall in Heidelberg, Germany.

Language

The application asks whether applicants have a working knowledge of English.

Applicants are also asked whether they would require interpretation support and, if so, which language and what scope of support would be required.

Youth Engagement

The opportunity is intended for young people who can contribute meaningfully to the Townhall and its objectives.

The selection process considers the diversity of youth representation and gives preference to young people involved in grassroots organizations.

Important Restriction for Current UN Contractors

There is an important eligibility consideration that applicants should not overlook.

The UN Youth Office states that it is unable to sponsor youth who are currently under contract with the United Nations.

Applicants who are currently working under a UN contract should therefore carefully consider this restriction before applying.

What Information Does the Application Form Request?

The application form contains several sections designed to help the UN Youth Office understand applicants’ backgrounds, circumstances and participation needs.

Personal Information

Applicants are asked to provide basic personal information, including:

First name;

Last name;

Date of birth;

Gender identity;

Email address;

Country of nationality;

Country of residence; and

City of residence.

The form states that personal information collected in this section will not be disclosed to third parties.

Gender Identity

Applicants are asked about their gender identity.

The options displayed in the form include:

Woman;

Man;

Non-binary; and

Prefer not to say.

This information forms part of the application process and can contribute to the organizers’ consideration of gender balance in participant selection.

Rights-Holder Community Information

Applicants can indicate whether they belong to or identify with any of the rights-holder communities listed in the form.

These include:

LGBTQIA+;

Indigenous Community;

Migrants and Internally Displaced People;

Persons with Disability;

Youth Facing Work and Descent Based Discrimination;

Young People Living with HIV; and

Refugees.

Applicants should provide this information according to their circumstances and the options available in the application form.

Applicant Category

The application asks candidates which category they most closely associate with.

The listed options are:

Youth-led entity/organisation;

Youth-serving entity/organisation; or

Individual young person aged 35 and below.

This allows the organizers to understand whether an applicant is participating as an individual or through an organization or entity connected to youth work.

Organization of Affiliation

Applicants are also asked to provide their organization of affiliation, if they have one.

This is particularly relevant to applicants involved in:

Youth organizations;

Grassroots initiatives;

Civil society organizations;

Community initiatives; or

Other youth-related entities.

Applicants without an organizational affiliation can provide the information requested according to their individual circumstances.

Disability and Reasonable Accommodation

The application asks applicants whether they consider themselves a person with a disability.

If the answer is yes, applicants can specify the reasonable accommodation they would need to participate in the UN Youth Townhall.

This allows the organizers to consider accessibility requirements when planning participation.

Applicants who require accommodations should provide sufficient information to help the UN Youth Office understand what support may be needed.

Safety and Security Considerations

The application also provides applicants with an opportunity to identify any safety measures that should be considered to ensure their secure participation in the Townhall.

Examples given in the application include:

Avoiding the display of an applicant’s full name;

Using a specific travel route; or

Other precautions the applicant may require.

This section is particularly relevant for applicants who may have specific safety or privacy concerns connected to their participation.

English Language and Interpretation Support

Applicants are asked whether they have a working knowledge of English.

The form also asks whether selected participants would require interpretation support.

If interpretation is required, applicants can indicate:

The language they require; and

The scope of interpretation support needed.

This information can help organizers plan appropriate support for participants.

How Long Does the Application Take?

The UN Youth Office estimates that completing the application will take approximately:

30–45 minutes

Applicants should therefore avoid beginning the application immediately before the deadline.

It is advisable to set aside sufficient uninterrupted time to read the questions carefully and provide thoughtful responses.

Application Deadline for the 2026 UN Youth Townhall

The application deadline is:

7 September 2026 at midnight ET.

Applications should be submitted before the deadline.

Because the selection process is expected to attract a large number of applications, prospective participants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit.

When Will Applicants Be Notified?

The UN Youth Office states that, due to the anticipated large number of applications, it will only be able to notify successful applicants.

Applicants who do not receive communication from the office by:

8 October 2026

are encouraged to explore other opportunities.

This means applicants should not necessarily expect an individual rejection notification if they are not selected.

How to Apply for the 2026 UN Youth Townhall

Applicants should first read the Official Application Guidance carefully before completing the form.

Step 1: Review the Application Guidance

The UN Youth Office provides an official application guidance document explaining the call and application process.

Applicants should read this before starting the form.

Step 2: Confirm Your Eligibility

Check that you meet the age requirement and consider the other selection factors and restrictions outlined in the call.

Step 3: Prepare Your Information

Have your basic personal, nationality, residence and organizational information available.

You should also consider in advance whether you need:

Reasonable accommodation;

Interpretation;

Specific safety measures; or

Other participation support.

Step 4: Complete the Application Form

The application is submitted through the online form provided by the UN Youth Office.

Step 5: Submit Before the Deadline

Ensure that the completed application is submitted by:

7 September 2026 at midnight ET.

Applicants should allow enough time for any technical issues and for reviewing their responses before submission.

Youth2030 and Continued Engagement

The UN Youth Townhall is connected to the wider Youth2030 framework and the UN’s efforts to strengthen meaningful youth participation.

Participants will not simply be brought together for a single event. The Townhall aims to create opportunities for continued engagement beyond the gathering.

This means the value of participation can extend beyond the three days in Heidelberg.

Young people can potentially use the experience to:

Strengthen connections with other youth leaders;

Develop relationships with institutions;

Who Should Consider Applying?

Between 18 and 35 years old;

Active in youth-led or youth-serving organizations;

Working with grassroots communities;

Interested in youth participation;

Interested in international development;

The call does not suggest that applicants must have previously participated in UN programmes. In fact, limited or no previous UN engagement is identified as a preference.

How to Strengthen Your Application

While selection is competitive, applicants can improve the quality of their submission by approaching the application thoughtfully.

Demonstrate Meaningful Youth Engagement

Explain clearly how you engage with young people, your community or an issue affecting youth.

Highlight Grassroots Experience

If you are involved in a grassroots organization or community initiative, clearly explain your role and the impact of your work.

Explain Your Perspective

The Townhall seeks diverse youth representation. Applicants should clearly communicate the perspectives, experiences and issues they can contribute to the gathering.

Be Clear About Accessibility Needs

If you require reasonable accommodation, interpretation or specific safety measures, provide the relevant information in the appropriate section of the application.

Review Before Submitting

Because the application takes approximately 30–45 minutes, applicants should reserve enough time to review their answers carefully before submission.

A Global Youth Participation Opportunity

The 2026 UN Youth Townhall is structured to bring together young people from diverse geographical and social backgrounds.

Geographical representation is specifically included among the selection considerations.

The call does not identify a restricted list of eligible countries in the supplied information. Applicants are therefore encouraged to review the official application guidance and form carefully to determine whether they meet all requirements.

Conclusion

The 2026 UN Youth Townhall in Heidelberg, Germany provides young people aged 18–35 with an opportunity to participate in a major United Nations youth engagement gathering focused on turning youth dialogue into recommendations, partnerships and action.

Taking place from 8–10 December 2026, the Townhall will connect young people with governments, the United Nations, civil society, the private sector and other partners.

The UN Youth Office intends to support a limited number of young people to participate in person, with selection considering gender balance, geographical representation and participation from underrepresented and marginalized groups. Preference will also be given to young people involved in grassroots organizations and those with limited or no previous engagement with the United Nations.

The application deadline is 7 September 2026 at midnight ET, and applicants should expect the form to take approximately 30–45 minutes to complete.

Prospective applicants should carefully review the official application guidance, confirm their eligibility, prepare the requested personal and participation information, and submit their application well before the deadline.

TITLE: ACE Impact in motion !

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Following the success of the first phase of the ACE Project, the World Bank and governments of participating countries recognized the need to escalate the success and expand the benefits accrued to the Centres and their countries. Consequently, the third phase of the Project titled the ACE for Development Impact (or simply ACE

Impact) has been approved by World Bank. There are 12 participating countries; including Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Cote d’Ivoire, Djibouti, Ghana, Guinea, Senegal, The Gambia, Togo, Niger and Nigeria.

ACE Impact seeks to increase the quality and relevance of post- graduate education in selected universities through regional specialization, applied research, upfront university-industry linkage and better regional and international

coordination.

In September this year, a Call for Proposals was advertised in national newspapers in the participating countries. Subsequently, a hundred and ten (110) proposals were submitted to AAU by the higher education agencies of participating countries consisting of new and renewal proposals (from existing ACEs).

These proposals were carefully reviewed by experts in the various thematic fields of Health, Agriculture, Environment, Social Sciences and STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics). Following the desk and remote panel evaluations, 65 proposals were shortlisted, and onsite visits were undertaken to the higher educational institutions which submitted them. The goal was to find out more about the institutions in terms of their readiness and commitment to host the potential Centres of Excellence.

To finalize the process will be the selection of the ACE Impact Centres of Excellence by the Project Steering Committee at its meeting at the AAU Secretariat, Accra, Ghana on November 2, 2018

TITLE: Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant 2026: Apply for Up to AUD 350,000 to Develop Climate Finance Solutions in Southeast Asia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Asia Climate Solutions (ACS) Design Grant 2026 is now accepting applications from organizations and consortiums developing innovative blended finance solutions that can mobilize private capital for climate action across Southeast Asia. Delivered through Convergence Blended Finance, the programme combines catalytic grant funding with acceleration support to help promising climate finance solutions progress from early-stage design and feasibility work toward implementation, investment readiness, and scale.

Supported by the Australian Government through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), the current funding cycle focuses specifically on solutions addressing climate-resilient agriculture, food security, and nature-based solutions in eligible Southeast Asian markets.

Selected organizations can access catalytic grants of up to AUD 350,000, depending on the maturity and type of project proposed. In addition to financial support, successful applicants can receive technical guidance, connections to investors and ecosystem partners, access to blended finance knowledge and data, training opportunities, and peer learning through the Convergence network.

The deadline to submit concept notes is September 28, 2026 at 9:00 PM ET, corresponding to September 29, 2026 at 9:00 AM SGT.

About the Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant

The Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant is part of Convergence’s regional blended finance accelerator initiatives. Its overarching objective is to catalyze innovative financial solutions capable of mobilizing substantial private investment into climate mitigation and adaptation activities in developing Asian markets.

Blended finance can play an important role in addressing investment barriers by strategically combining public, philanthropic, and private capital. Through the ACS Design Grant, Convergence aims to support commercially viable models that can use this approach to unlock investment while delivering measurable climate and development outcomes.

For the current funding cycle, particular attention is being placed on climate-resilient agriculture and nature-based solutions across Southeast Asia.

Agriculture remains critical to Southeast Asia’s economies, livelihoods, employment, and food security. It accounts for approximately 10% of regional GDP and employs roughly one-third of the workforce. At the same time, Southeast Asia holds around 30% of the world’s potential for nature-based solutions.

However, climate change, environmental degradation, and persistent financing gaps continue to limit investment in resilient agricultural systems and natural ecosystems. Women farmers can face additional challenges, including barriers to finance, productive resources, and markets.

The ACS Design Grant seeks to address these challenges by supporting innovative blended finance models capable of attracting capital into solutions that strengthen resilience while creating environmental, social, and economic benefits.

Who Supports the Asia Climate Solutions Programme?

Asia Climate Solutions is a multi-donor funded programme.

Its supporters include:

Australian Government through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)

Olayan Group

UBS Optimus Foundation

The Rockefeller Foundation

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)

DFAT is supporting the current funding cycle focused on climate-resilient agriculture and nature-based solutions in Southeast Asia.

What Does the ACS Design Grant Offer?

The Accelerator provides two major forms of assistance to selected organizations:

Catalytic Grant Funding

Acceleration Support

Together, these components are intended to help organizations develop stronger blended finance structures, overcome early-stage barriers, engage potential investors, and move promising financial vehicles toward launch and scale.

1. Catalytic Grant Funding of Up to AUD 350,000

Eligible organizations can seek catalytic funding to support the development of blended finance solutions from feasibility and early-stage scoping through proof-of-concept activities.

Depending on the stage of development, funding may support activities such as:

Financial structuring

Legal structuring

Market scoping

Investment pipeline development

Stakeholder consultations

Investor outreach

Fundraising

Piloting

Governance framework development

Impact measurement framework development

Refinement of investment models

Preparation for potential vehicle launch

Funding levels depend on whether an applicant is seeking support for a Feasibility Study or a Proof-of-Concept.

2. Acceleration Support

Successful applicants will receive more than grant funding. Convergence also provides acceleration assistance intended to strengthen the investment model and help teams progress toward mobilizing capital.

Acceleration support may include:

Ongoing technical feedback and guidance to refine investment models and strategies

Opportunities to connect with Convergence’s network of investors and ecosystem partners

Support in expanding partnerships and identifying opportunities to mobilize resources for climate action

Access to Convergence member training

Access to blended finance data

Market insights and intelligence

Peer-learning opportunities

This combination of capital and technical assistance can be particularly valuable for organizations attempting to take an innovative climate finance concept and develop it into an investable and scalable structure.

Types of Asia Climate Solutions Design Grants

Applicants can apply under one of two principal grant categories based on the maturity of their proposed blended finance solution.

Feasibility Study Grant

The Feasibility Study Grant is designed for solutions at an earlier stage of development where organizations need to explore and validate whether a proposed blended finance vehicle is feasible.

Applicants should already have an initial design and structure for their proposed blended finance vehicle, an impact and investment thesis, and evidence of early stakeholder engagement.

What Can Feasibility Study Funding Be Used For?

Activities can include:

Scoping and refining the design of the proposed vehicle

Developing or refining the financial structure

Developing or refining the legal structure

Conducting market scoping

Building an initial investment pipeline

Conducting stakeholder consultations

Developing draft impact assessment frameworks

Developing governance frameworks

Feasibility Study Funding Amount

Organizations applying for a Feasibility Study Grant can seek up to AUD 200,000.

The funding is provided as a non-repayable grant.

Proof-of-Concept Grant

The Proof-of-Concept Grant targets solutions that have progressed further in their development.

At this stage, funding can support the design and structuring work necessary to prepare a blended finance vehicle for its possible launch.

Applicants should generally have already refined areas including their:

Financial model

Capital structure

Impact analysis

Governance approach

They should also demonstrate advanced engagement with potential investors.

What Can Proof-of-Concept Funding Support?

Examples include:

Advancing fundraising activities

Conducting investor outreach

Refining the blended finance vehicle’s design

Refining the vehicle’s legal structure

Strengthening governance arrangements

Refining impact frameworks

Developing the investment pipeline

Undertaking other structuring work needed to prepare the vehicle for potential launch

Proof-of-Concept Funding Amount

Proof-of-Concept applicants can seek up to AUD 350,000.

Funding may be provided as either a non-repayable or conditionally repayable grant.

What Types of Blended Finance Solutions Are Eligible?

Proposals must demonstrate a clear need for catalytic grant support for the design and/or launch of an innovative blended finance vehicle.

The proposed solution must be a financial instrument incorporating a blended finance structure.

Examples of potentially eligible structures include:

Funds

Project finance vehicles

Private companies

Bonds

Results-based financing structures

Financing facilities

Other suitable financial instruments incorporating blended finance

Importantly, proposed vehicles must demonstrate the potential to mobilize private investment at scale while generating development impact in Southeast Asia.

Solutions must also target climate mitigation and/or climate adaptation within the eligible sectors for this funding cycle.

Eligible Countries for the ACS Design Grant 2026

Proposed solutions must target one or more of the following Southeast Asian countries:

Cambodia

Indonesia

Lao PDR

Malaysia

Myanmar

Philippines

Thailand

Timor-Leste

Vietnam

A solution may operate within a single eligible country or across several eligible countries.

An important feature of the programme is that the applicant organization itself does not have to be domiciled in one of these countries.

However, the end beneficiaries and activities targeted by the proposed solution must be located within the eligible markets.

This means organizations based outside Southeast Asia may potentially participate provided their proposed blended finance solution satisfies the programme’s geographic and other eligibility requirements.

Priority Sector 1: Climate-Resilient Agriculture and Food Security

One of the major priorities for this funding round is developing financial models capable of improving resilience throughout agriculture and food systems.

Eligible areas include:

Climate-Smart and Regenerative Agriculture

Solutions may address climate-smart agricultural practices, regenerative agriculture, sustainable aquaculture, and related approaches that increase resilience while reducing environmental impacts.

Agricultural Value Chains

The programme can support blended finance solutions targeting agricultural value chains, including processing and improved market access.

Farmer, Cooperative and Agri-SME Finance

Solutions can focus on improving access to finance for farmers, agricultural cooperatives, and small and medium-sized enterprises operating within agricultural systems.

Agricultural Insurance and Climate Risk Management

Innovative financing structures that improve agricultural insurance or help communities and businesses manage climate-related risks may also qualify.

Agri-Tech and Smart Farming

The programme also identifies agricultural technology, biotechnology, and smart farming as eligible areas.

Priority Sector 2: Nature-Based Solutions

The ACS Design Grant also seeks innovative financing approaches that can unlock capital for nature-based solutions.

Eligible areas include:

Sustainable forestry

Landscape restoration

Ecosystem management

Carbon markets

Natural capital finance

Biodiversity finance

Blue carbon

Biodiversity conservation

Ecosystem restoration

Coastal protection

Watershed management

Ecosystem resilience

Applicants proposing solutions within these areas should demonstrate how blended finance can overcome investment barriers and help mobilize public, philanthropic, and private capital.

Eligibility Requirements for Applicant Organizations

Applications are only accepted from organizations or consortiums of organizations.

Potentially eligible organizations include:

Asset owners

Asset managers

Advisory firms

Foundations

Not-for-profit organizations

Private enterprises

Consortiums comprising eligible organizations

The lead organization must be capable of providing:

Proof of incorporation

Financial statements for the previous fiscal year

Individual applicants are therefore not the target applicants for this funding opportunity.

Beyond organizational eligibility, applicants must demonstrate that their proposed solution meets the programme’s purpose, geographic, sectoral, and blended finance requirements.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Convergence evaluates eligible proposals against seven major areas. Organizations preparing concept notes should carefully consider each of these criteria because they provide a strong indication of what assessors will be looking for.

1. Development Impact and Gender Considerations

Proposed blended finance solutions should deliver inclusive, measurable, and significant environmental and social impact.

Gender considerations should be intentionally integrated into areas such as:

Design

Governance

Implementation

Stakeholder engagement

Applicants should establish clear key performance indicators and include gender-related indicators where appropriate.

Recognized global standards should also be used to measure, monitor, and report impact.

2. Track Record and Capabilities

Evaluators will consider the applicant organization’s ability to successfully develop and manage the proposed solution.

Considerations include:

Relevant experience designing investment vehicles

Experience managing investment vehicles

Commitment of the core project team

Local presence within target markets

Partnerships within eligible countries

Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate that their team has the experience, resources, partnerships, and commitment required to move the proposal forward.

3. Additionality

Applicants need to explain why blended finance is necessary.

The proposal should demonstrate:

A clear market gap

A strong rationale for using blended finance

Potential to unlock capital in the targeted markets

Potential to create new investable opportunities

Strategic use of ACS catalytic funding

Strategic use of ACS acceleration support

The grant is intended to address genuine barriers rather than simply replace capital that could readily be obtained elsewhere.

4. Scalability and Replicability

Convergence is seeking solutions with the potential to grow beyond a small pilot or isolated intervention.

Applicants should demonstrate:

A clear capital structure

A credible fundraising strategy

Potential to mobilize significant private capital

A realistic pathway to reach the proposed target size

Potential to scale the solution

Opportunities to replicate the model across additional markets

Solutions with a credible pathway to expansion and replication can potentially generate a broader demonstration effect across the climate finance ecosystem.

5. Innovation and Demonstration Effect

The proposed solution should have the potential to generate useful lessons for the broader blended finance field.

Innovation could involve creating an entirely new financing model or applying an existing model within a new market or context.

Evaluators will consider whether other practitioners could learn from, adapt, or replicate the approach.

6. Likelihood of Achieving Financial Close

Applicants should demonstrate that the proposed structure has a credible pathway toward financial close.

This includes consideration of:

Bankability

Alignment with potential investors’ risk-return expectations

Progress already made toward financial close

Clear next steps

Appropriate risk management

Robust governance arrangements

A strong proposal should demonstrate not only an innovative idea but also a realistic pathway toward becoming an operational and investable vehicle.

7. Stakeholder Support

Applicants should demonstrate support from relevant internal and external stakeholders within the target country or region.

Proposals should show:

Engagement with important local partners

Support from key stakeholders

Clearly defined roles

A credible stakeholder engagement strategy

Appropriate partnerships to support the proposed launch

Local relationships can be particularly important in demonstrating market understanding and implementation capability.

Importance of Gender Considerations

Gender inclusion is specifically incorporated into the programme’s evaluation framework.

Applicants should consider how women and other relevant groups may experience different barriers within agricultural, financial, environmental, and climate systems.

For example, women farmers may encounter constraints in accessing finance, productive resources, and markets. Proposed financing solutions should therefore consider whether their design can address these barriers and produce inclusive outcomes.

Where appropriate, proposals should include measurable gender-related indicators and explain how gender considerations will influence the solution’s governance, implementation, and stakeholder engagement.

Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant Information Session

Convergence and Australia’s DFAT will host a virtual information session on September 10, 2026 for prospective applicants.

The session will provide an opportunity to learn more about:

Convergence’s Blended Finance Accelerator

The Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant

Current funding priorities

Grant eligibility requirements

Evaluation criteria

The application process

Prospective applicants are encouraged to participate, particularly organizations that need additional clarification about the programme’s requirements before preparing their concept notes.

For detailed evaluation criteria and scoring, refer to the Evaluation Criteria document

Application Deadline

The deadline to submit concept notes for the Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant is September 28, 2026 at 9:00 PM Eastern Time (ET), equivalent to September 29, 2026 at 9:00 AM Singapore Time (SGT).

Organizations interested in applying should avoid waiting until the final day, particularly where consortium partners, supporting documentation, financial information, and internal approvals need to be coordinated.

How to Apply for the Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant 2026

Interested organizations should review the full eligibility and evaluation requirements before beginning an application.

Applicants should particularly ensure that:

The applicant is an eligible organization or consortium.

The lead organization can provide proof of incorporation.

The lead organization can provide financial statements for the previous fiscal year.

The proposed solution incorporates a genuine blended finance structure.

There is a clear rationale for catalytic grant funding.

The solution targets climate mitigation and/or adaptation.

Target activities and beneficiaries are located in one or more eligible Southeast Asian countries.

The solution falls within climate-resilient agriculture, food security, or eligible nature-based solution sectors.

The proposed vehicle demonstrates potential to mobilize private capital.

The team can demonstrate relevant capabilities, partnerships, and a credible pathway toward implementation and scale.

Applicants should then prepare and submit their concept note through the official ACS Design Grant application platform.

APPLY NOW

https://www.convergence.finance/accelerator/acs

https://www.convergence.finance/calendar/3TJSC0ZOZnYpgy5kYMy3dP/view

Applicants should rely on the official Convergence website and application materials for the final requirements, documentation, terms, and any programme updates before submitting.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Climate Finance in Southeast Asia

The Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant addresses one of the most significant challenges facing climate action: transforming promising ideas and climate solutions into investable structures capable of attracting capital at meaningful scale.

Agriculture, food systems, forests, coastlines, watersheds, and natural ecosystems are deeply connected to economic development and community resilience across Southeast Asia. Yet investment gaps can prevent promising solutions from reaching the scale required.

By combining catalytic funding with technical assistance, investor connections, market knowledge, and blended finance expertise, the ACS Design Grant aims to help bridge the gap between early-stage financial innovation and commercially viable investment vehicles.

The emphasis on private capital mobilization is particularly significant. Rather than relying exclusively on grant funding to finance climate activities, the programme seeks to use catalytic resources to develop financial structures capable of attracting substantially larger pools of investment.

For organizations already developing innovative climate finance vehicles, the programme therefore offers an opportunity not only to secure funding for design and structuring but also to strengthen the foundations needed to reach investors and eventually achieve financial close.

Conclusion

The Asia Climate Solutions Design Grant 2026 offers a significant funding and acceleration opportunity for organizations developing innovative blended finance solutions addressing climate-resilient agriculture, food security, and nature-based solutions across Southeast Asia.

With Feasibility Study Grants of up to AUD 200,000 and Proof-of-Concept Grants of up to AUD 350,000, the programme can support organizations at different stages of developing their blended finance vehicles. Successful applicants can also benefit from Convergence’s technical expertise, investor and ecosystem networks, training, blended finance data, market insights, and peer-learning opportunities.

Strong proposals will need to demonstrate meaningful climate and development impact, intentional gender considerations, organizational capabilities, additionality, scalability, innovation, a credible pathway toward financial close, and strong stakeholder support.

Organizations do not have to be headquartered in the eligible Southeast Asian markets, but their proposed activities and end beneficiaries must target Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and/or Vietnam.

Interested organizations should carefully review the programme requirements, consider attending the September 10 information session, and begin preparing their concept notes well ahead of the September 28, 2026 at 9:00 PM ET / September 29, 2026 at 9:00 AM SGT deadline.

TITLE: Press Release – 53 Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence Convene In-person for the First Time Post-Covid to Enhance the Drive toward Achieving Development Impact 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop to hold from June 13-17, 2022

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop to hold from June 13-17, 2022

Download Press Release in English and in French

Accra, Ghana (May 30, 2022) – The 7th bi-annual meeting of the Africa Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact) is scheduled to take place from 13th-17th June 2022 in Cotonou, Benin. Considering the impact and mobility restrictions posed by the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, the ACE Impact stakeholders are meeting for the first time in-person in two years (the last in-person meeting was held in February 2020 in Abuja, Nigeria).

The meeting, which will make provision for virtual participation is bringing together leaders of the fifty-three (53) Centres of Excellence, government representatives from the 11 participating countries, key higher education stakeholders, policy think tanks, and partners such as the World Bank, the French Development Agency (AFD) and the Association of African Universities (AAU).

Committed to enhancing the capacity of universities to deliver high-quality training and applied research to address regional development challenges, the ACE Impact project is convening stakeholders to accelerate project implementation by measuring the impact accrued and exploring ways to address bottlenecks. With the project reaching its Mid-Term Review (MTR) in 2021, results of the MTR process will be evaluated during the upcoming workshop, with the teams finalizing recommendations and next steps. ACE Impact is being implemented over a five-year duration, 2019 -2024.

The workshop will further provide an opportunity for peer-learning and regional knowledge sharing among the centers and strengthen partnerships and networks to drive successful project implementation and sustainability. The meeting seeks to provide implementation support and share global best practices with centers on the project objectives, especially development impact, entrepreneurship and innovation, gender initiatives, digital transformation, and institutional impact activities.

In addition, selected students from the three centers in Benin will be given the opportunity to share their innovative research outputs during a poster exhibition on 14th June 2022 at the Palais des Congrès. The opening and closing sessions of the workshop will be held on 14th and 17th June, respectively, at 10:00 GMT+1.

The ACE Impact project remains committed to training and providing Africa with the needed skills in the fields of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM); Agriculture, Environment, Applied Social Science, Education, and Health to realize its economic transformation.

– END –

Note to Editors

A press conference will be held virtually/in person on 14th June 2022 at the Palais des Congrès in Cotonou. Benin To participate or for further information, kindly contact Millicent Afriyie via email makyei@aau.org.

TITLE: GDPC Spotlight Research Grants Program 2026 (up to $10,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 31, 2026

Applications are open for the GDPC Spotlight Research Grants Program 2026. The GDPC Spotlight Research Grants Program, in partnership with the French Red Cross Foundation, provides funding to university researchers for projects focused on principled and accountable use of technology in humanitarian action. This program specifically supports researchers from low- and middle-income countries.

Awards provide $10,000 USD for research lasting up to eight months, with a completion deadline of June 30, 2027. This program supports applied and impactful research that can inform policy, planning, humanitarian programming, community action, and so on. Research must be original, and plagiarism will result in immediate disqualification at any stage of the grant process. Research can be conducted in English or French.

Research Topics

The program seeks to stimulate new knowledge in priority research questions under the following topics:

Topic 1: Community Needs & Digital Realities

Topic 1.1 Needs-Aligned ICTs: What are the priority needs and concerns of affected people regarding digital tools used in humanitarian service delivery?

Topic 1.2 Community Adaptation of ICTs: How do technologies get repurposed or reinterpreted by communities to be utilized for humanitarian purposes? How or why do communities maintain, adapt, or abandon technologies over time?

Topic 2: ICT Solution Feasibility & Implementation

Topic 2.1 Operational Constraints: What are the operational constraints (infrastructure, skills, funding, governance) to implementing ICT solutions in LMIC humanitarian contexts? How do these impact successful design and use of these ICTs?

Topic 2.2 Digital Maturity Context: How do variations in digital maturity across communities and organizations affect implementation and humanitarian outcomes in different settings?

Topic 2.3 Humanitarian Principle Alignment: How does proactive alignment of technology design and implementation with humanitarian principles affect outcomes (and address risks)?

Topic 3: Data Protection in Humanitarian Action

Topic 3.1 Personal Data Handling: How do disaster-affected people understand, experience, and respond to the collection and use of their personal data in humanitarian programmes and how can this inform policy and practices?

Topic 3.2 Data Privacy & Accountability: What two-way communication mechanisms (feedback loops, complaint systems) are most effective for data privacy and accountability in ICT-enabled humanitarian programs?

Topic 3.3 Community Trust: How do incidents (e.g., data breaches, misinformation) affect trust in humanitarian actors and programs?

Grant

The research grants are USD $10,000.

Eligibility

Applicants must be affiliated with an accredited university at the time of submission, including PhD candidates, post-doctoral researchers, and faculty members. Teams of researchers are welcome to submit proposals.

Researchers should come from disciplines in social sciences and humanities, such as sociology, anthropology, law, human geography, management, behavioral studies, psychology, etc.

Applications are open to researchers who are nationals of low- and middle-income countries, including least developed and upper-middle-income nations. Research must be focused on these countries.

Proposed research projects must align with one of the the program’s defined topics and clearly demonstrate how they contribute to the selected area of focus.

Projects must be feasible for completion within the eight-month program timeline, running from 1 November 2026 to 30 June 30 2027.

Researchers may conduct their research in any language, but the final research paper must be submitted in English or French. If translation into English is needed, the budget proposal should include estimated costs for translation services.

Application

The complete application package must include:

Applicant Information: This includes professional affiliation details.

Project Summary: A concise project abstract and key information.

Project Description: Detail on the research background, rationale, objectives, methodology, scientific merit, broader impact, and ethical considerations.

Research Team Composition: Include information about the Principal Investigator (PI) and key co-investigators, along with their CVs.

Budget: A budget proposal in US Dollars, including a detailed breakdown of expenses and budget justification.

Letters of Collaboration: For projects involving partnerships with institutions or organizations outside the applicant’s primary affiliation, a letter of support from each partner institution is required.
