TITLE: Global Youth & Survivor Summit 2026 in Manila: Applications Open for Young Leaders and Survivor Advocates to End Violence Against Children

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children 2026, an international gathering designed to place young people and survivor advocates at the centre of global conversations about preventing and ending violence against children.

The Summit will take place on 15–16 November 2026 in Manila, Philippines, at the Marriott Manila Hotel. It will bring together young people, survivor leaders, advocates and other stakeholders to exchange experiences, develop policy recommendations, strengthen networks and influence international action on ending violence against children.

The event is being organised ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, which will also take place in Manila in November 2026. This positioning gives participants an important opportunity to contribute youth- and survivor-led perspectives at a time when governments, international organisations and civil society actors will be discussing how to accelerate global progress on child protection.

About the Global Youth & Survivor Summit 2026

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is intended to provide a dedicated platform where young people and people with lived experience can help shape the international agenda for ending violence against children.

Rather than treating young people and survivors simply as participants in discussions led by institutions, the Summit is structured around their leadership, perspectives and experiences. The organisers want young people and survivor advocates to engage directly with policymakers, donors, civil society organisations, faith-based organisations and other actors working on child protection.

The Summit comes at a critical time. According to the organisers, an estimated one billion children around the world experience some form of violence every year. At the same time, governments and other stakeholders have made hundreds of commitments aimed at strengthening child protection.

The challenge is therefore not limited to obtaining new commitments. It also involves ensuring that existing pledges are translated into meaningful, sustained and accountable action — with the people most affected by these issues involved in determining what effective action should look like.

Summit Dates and Location

The main event details are:

Event: Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children

Dates: 15–16 November 2026

Venue: Marriott Manila Hotel

Location: Manila, Philippines

Working language: English

Application deadline: 25 September 2026

Deadline time: 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8)

Registration fee: None

Interpretation support may be considered depending on the needs of confirmed participants and the availability of appropriate resources.

What Is the Purpose of the Youth & Survivor Summit?

The Summit has been developed to strengthen the role that young people and survivor advocates play in international efforts to end violence against children.

One of its central objectives is to gather policy recommendations directly from young people and survivor advocates. These recommendations can contribute to wider discussions taking place around the Second Global Ministerial Conference.

The Summit is also expected to help participants establish stronger connections with youth-led and survivor-led organisations, networks and movements operating in different parts of the world.

Broadly, the event focuses on three interconnected objectives.

1. Strengthening Global Connections and Solidarity

Youth- and survivor-led organisations often work within different communities, countries and policy environments. The Summit aims to connect these networks and create opportunities for longer-term collaboration.

Participants will have opportunities to meet other advocates, exchange approaches, identify shared priorities and explore possibilities for collective advocacy beyond the event itself.

The intention is therefore not simply to organise a two-day meeting in Manila, but to strengthen relationships that can continue after participants return to their respective communities and organisations.

2. Putting Youth and Survivor Leadership at the Centre

A defining feature of the Summit is its focus on ensuring that people affected by violence against children have opportunities to influence discussions about the policies and programmes designed to address it.

Young people and survivor advocates will be able to share experiences, research, solutions and recommendations while engaging with decision-makers, funders and other stakeholders.

This approach is intended to move beyond symbolic participation and towards meaningful involvement in policy discussions and advocacy efforts.

The Summit therefore provides a platform for participants to contribute not only personal perspectives but also practical ideas about how governments, organisations and communities can strengthen the prevention of violence against children.

3. Turning Shared Priorities into Collective Action

The organisers also want the Summit to translate discussions into common priorities and calls for action.

By identifying areas where youth leaders, survivors and child-protection advocates have shared concerns, participants can develop stronger collective messages that may subsequently be used for advocacy, accountability and engagement with decision-makers.

These priorities are expected to support continued action beyond Manila rather than ending when the Summit concludes.

What Participants Can Expect

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is designed as an interactive space rather than a conventional conference dominated entirely by formal presentations.

Participants can expect opportunities to:

Connect with youth leaders and survivor advocates from different communities and backgrounds.

Exchange experiences and perspectives related to preventing violence against children.

Share research, community-based solutions and advocacy approaches.

Discuss policy priorities with other participants and stakeholders.

Contribute ideas that may influence wider discussions surrounding the Global Ministerial Conference.

Strengthen international networks and solidarity among youth- and survivor-led movements.

Participate in cross-generational dialogue with policymakers, donors, civil society representatives and other actors.

Develop collective priorities and advocacy messages for continued action after the Summit.

Restless Development has also highlighted leadership development and meaningful dialogue as important elements of the gathering.

Connection With the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children

The Youth & Survivor Summit is taking place immediately before the broader international discussions associated with the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children.

The official Ministerial Conference is scheduled for 18–19 November 2026 in Manila and is co-organised by the Government of the Philippines, World Health Organization and UNICEF, in collaboration with the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General on Violence Against Children.

The Ministerial Conference will bring together governments and a broad range of international stakeholders to accelerate action against violence affecting children.

Its agenda includes prevention-focused approaches such as support for parents and caregivers, safer schools and stronger response systems. Attention will also be given to emerging and escalating concerns including technology-facilitated violence, humanitarian and climate-related contexts, and the relationship between violence against children and violence against women.

The Youth & Survivor Summit is intended to make sure that youth and survivor perspectives contribute to this wider global moment.

However, applicants should understand an important distinction:

Selection for the Youth & Survivor Summit does not automatically provide access to the Second Global Ministerial Conference.

Participation and registration for the two events are separate. Being accepted to the Youth & Survivor Summit should therefore not be interpreted as an invitation to attend the official Ministerial Conference.

Is the Global Youth & Survivor Summit Fully Funded?

There is no registration fee to participate in the Summit.

Meals and refreshments during the official programme will also be provided.

However, the standard participation arrangement does not automatically cover international travel and other attendance expenses.

Unless an applicant receives a fully funded place, participants or their supporting organisations are responsible for costs including:

International or domestic travel

Accommodation

Visa expenses

Travel insurance

Local transportation

Personal expenses

The organisers have confirmed that a limited number of fully funded places are available for participants aged 18 and above who would otherwise be unable to attend the Summit.

These funded places are not guaranteed. Funding decisions will depend on eligibility, individual circumstances, demonstrated support needs and the amount of funding available to the organisers.

Applicants who require financial support should therefore clearly and accurately explain their circumstances when completing the application.

Special Conditions for Applicants Aged 15–17

Applicants aged 15 to 17 years are permitted to participate, but specific safeguarding requirements apply.

Anyone in this age group must be:

Nominated by a partner organisation;

Fully funded by that organisation; and

Fully supported by the organisation for participation in the Summit.

Therefore, applicants between 15 and 17 cannot rely on the Summit’s limited funding mechanism available to participants aged 18 and above. Appropriate organisational support must already be in place.

How Will Applications Be Assessed?

Submitting an application does not guarantee that an applicant will receive a place.

The Summit Organising Committee will review applications while considering available capacity and several selection factors.

According to the official application information, these factors include:

Diversity and representation

Applicant motivation

Relevant experience

Potential contribution to the Summit

Individual support requirements

Availability of places

Applicants should therefore use the application form to demonstrate why participation is relevant to their experience, advocacy, community work or professional activities and how they could contribute meaningfully to discussions.

Applicants with relevant lived experience, youth leadership activities, child-protection advocacy, community organising, policy work, research or similar experience should clearly explain that background rather than providing only general statements about their interest in attending.

Safeguarding and Mental Health Support

Given the sensitive subject matter of violence against children and the involvement of people with lived experience, safeguarding forms an important part of the Summit.

The organisers state that they intend to create an environment that is safe, inclusive and respectful for participants irrespective of characteristics including age, gender, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation or disability.

Sessions and activities are intended to follow trauma-informed approaches.

Participants, speakers and partners will also be invited to participate in a safeguarding briefing before the Summit.

During the event, participants are expected to have access to:

On-site mental health support

First-aid support

A wellbeing space where participants can step away and decompress when necessary

Identifiable Summit team members who can respond to safeguarding concerns

A mechanism for confidential or anonymous reporting of concerns

These provisions are particularly significant for a conference involving survivors and potentially sensitive discussions about violence, exploitation, abuse and child protection.

Who Is Organising the Summit?

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit is co-organised by:

Restless Development

Brave Movement

Global Youth-Led Movement on Ending Violence Against Children

The event is also being guided by a Summit Organising Committee composed of young advocates and professionals with experience across areas including human rights, survivor advocacy, public policy, child protection, youth participation, gender equality, communications, research and community-based development.

Why This Summit Matters

Violence against children is a global challenge that intersects with education, health, justice, gender equality, technology, humanitarian crises, social protection and human rights.

Effective solutions require more than institutional discussions between governments and development organisations. Young people and survivors can provide perspectives about how policies and interventions operate in practice, where protection systems fail and what changes communities actually need.

By providing a dedicated platform for youth and survivor leadership immediately before a major international Ministerial Conference, the Global Youth & Survivor Summit offers participants an opportunity to connect grassroots experience with international policy dialogue.

For young advocates, survivor leaders and people working to protect children, the Summit can therefore serve as both a global networking platform and a space for substantive advocacy.

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted by:

25 September 2026 at 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8).

Applications received after the deadline should not be assumed to be considered, so interested candidates are encouraged to complete the official form before the closing time.

Apply for the Global Youth & Survivor Summit 2026

Applicants can also review the official Summit information before submitting an application.

Visit the Official Youth & Survivor Summit Website

Conclusion

The Global Youth & Survivor Summit on Ending Violence Against Children 2026 provides an important international platform for young people, survivor leaders and child-protection advocates to participate directly in discussions that affect children and communities worldwide.

Taking place in Manila, Philippines, on 15–16 November 2026, the Summit will create opportunities for participants to build international connections, exchange evidence and lived experiences, develop shared priorities and contribute to advocacy surrounding global efforts to end violence against children.

With no registration fee and a limited number of fully funded opportunities available for eligible participants aged 18 and above, the Summit may be particularly valuable for youth and survivor advocates who would otherwise have limited access to high-level international forums.

Interested applicants should carefully review the eligibility and funding requirements and submit their application no later than 25 September 2026 at 23:59 Philippine Time (UTC+8).

TITLE: KNOW YOUR CONTINENT QUIZ – Join us on May 25, 2022 as we celebrate Africa Day

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities Television (AAU TV) presents; the “Know Your Continent Quiz” Competition to commemorate this year’s Africa Day – 25th May 2022. The day is observed annually to celebrate the founding of the organization of African Unity (OAU), which later evolved into the African Union (AU).

The quiz competition by AAU TV is also being hosted to create awareness and educate stakeholders about the aspirations, goals, and policies of the African Union towards the development of the African Continent as enshrined in Agenda 2063.

Hosted under the theme “The Year of Nutrition – Strengthening resilience in nutrition and food security on the African Continent”, the quiz will provide the opportunity for Africans to enrich our knowledge on related key topics such as Agro-Food Systems, Health and Social Protection Systems for acceleration of human, social and economic capital development, among others.

As format the quiz will feature exciting and educational Q&A sessions in a live show set up with live audience at the studios of the Association of African Universities TV (AAU TV STUDIOS), located at Trinity Avenue, East-Legon, Accra, Ghana. Additionally, stakeholders can join via zoom to participate by registering via this link – https://bit.ly/3MnYGms

The whole event will also be streamed online via YouTube and Facebook (Association of African Universities)

Winners will be rewarded and given massive visibility through a broadcast on AAU TV, which will further be disseminated among the AAU’s wider network.

Additional Information

The Association of African Universities is the apex African higher education body, with a membership of about 400 higher education institutions from 46 countries in Africa. It’s aim is to be the lead advocate for higher education in Africa with the capacity to provide support for its member institutions in meeting national, continental, and global needs. In line with fulfilling its mission to enhance the relevance of Higher Education in Africa, the AAU TV was established to disseminate real-time information on education-related issues, as well as discuss issues of relevance to Africa’s development.

The Association of African Universities Television/Media (AAU TV ) was set up to also leverage the wealth of research and development knowledge that higher education institutions and their collaborators have churned out over the years, thereby creating a space where both the academic community and general public can access the benefits that these innovations hold for the continent.

TITLE: EPFL AI Center and Swiss AI Initiative Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026-2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 9, 2026

Applications are open for the EPFL AI Center and Swiss AI Initiative Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026-2027. The EPFL AI Center Postdoctoral Fellowship Programme, supported in part through funding from the Swiss AI Initiative, gives outstanding and highly motivated young researchers the chance to collaborate with a broad range of EPFL faculty on furthering the capabilities and applications of AI techniques in a variety of scientific domains.

The Fellowship programme focuses on excellence and collaborative research endeavours. Therefore, Fellows will work with several laboratories at EPFL and will be granted ample freedom to develop their own research agenda. This will include contributing to and participating in the various community activities and strategic initiatives associated with the EPFL AI Center.

Funding

The fellowship covers a contribution to the salary of the postdoctoral researcher of appr. 50% per year (EPFL salary scales apply). The remaining part of the salary is covered by the EPFL host laboratories. EPFL Human Resources guidelines and practices apply with regard to social security.

A maximum amount of CHF 5’000 per fellowship year can be granted for research costs, open research data costs, open access publication costs, travels and conferences. These costs need to be justified in the budget and in the financial report. Any additional costs for research expenses, travel, etc. need to be covered by the host Professor(s).

The host laboratories commit to making the necessary infrastructure available to the postdoctoral researcher (e.g., office space, laboratory space and equipment, administrative support).

Eligibility

Applications are encouraged by researchers at the postdoctoral level.

Applicants must have obtained a PhD diploma in computer science, physics, engineering, applied mathematics, or another field relevant to artificial intelligence, no more than two years before the submission deadline.

Doctoral students in the last year of their doctoral studies are eligible to apply (senior PhD students), provided that they will have successfully completed their PhD diploma by the time they start the fellowship.

Applicants must have the support of two EPFL host professors who are Faculty members affiliated with the EPFL AI Center. Applicants should therefore contact potential host Professor(s) from this list and discuss and agree on a potential collaboration before submitting their application.

Priority will be given to external candidates. However, senior PhD students and junior postdocs, who are already at EPFL are eligible to apply.

This programme is highly competitive, and the primary evaluation criterion is excellence, as measured by academic records and professional accomplishments. Candidates applying for the AI Center fellowship are expected to have excellent grade transcripts.

Applicants may submit only one application.

Citizens of any nationality may apply for the AI Center & Swiss AI Initiative postdoctoral fellowship programme. No age restrictions apply

Applications from candidates of all genders and backgrounds are strongly encouraged.

Application

Explore the Application toolkit and read carefully the application guidelines. All documents must be submitted in English.

All required documents must be submitted on the online submission platform.

For more information, visit EPFL AI Center and Swiss AI Initiative Postdoctoral Fellowships.

TITLE: Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program 2026: Up to $50,000 for Organisations Supporting Young People’s Positive Futures in Australia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications will soon open for the Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program 2026, offering eligible Australian charitable organisations the opportunity to apply for funding of up to $50,000 for projects lasting up to one year.

The 2026 Annual Open Grant Program is focused on Young People’s Positive Futures, with funding intended to support organisations helping young adults aged 16 to 24 navigate significant transitions in their lives, particularly young people experiencing multiple and interconnected forms of disadvantage.

The grant round seeks to support organisations that help young people overcome barriers to:

Wellbeing

Social participation

Education

Employment

Economic engagement

Community participation

Independence

Positive life transitions

Particular attention is given to young people facing circumstances such as:

Poverty

Homelessness

Substance use

Trauma

Health challenges

Leaving out-of-home care

Exiting the justice system

Finishing formal education

Transitioning into employment

Other complex barriers to participation and independence

Importantly, this funding opportunity is not available directly to individual young people. Applications must come from eligible organisations registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) and holding Deductible Gift Recipient (DGR) Item 1 status at the time of application.

The grant process involves two stages. Organisations must first submit an Expression of Interest (EOI). Selected organisations will then be invited to submit a full application.

The EOI round opens on:

Friday, 11 September 2026 at 9:00 AM

and closes on:

Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 PM midday

EOI applicants are expected to receive notification of the first-stage outcome on:

Wednesday, 7 October 2026

Eligible organisations are encouraged to review the Gandel Foundation’s FY26–29 Strategy, Grant Guidelines and Funding Exclusions before preparing an application.

About the Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program

The Gandel Foundation provides philanthropic support to organisations seeking to create positive social outcomes in Australia.

Many of the Foundation’s other grant opportunities are primarily proactive or invitation-based. However, the Annual Open Grant Program provides an opportunity for eligible organisations to apply through an open competitive process.

For the current round, the Foundation has selected:

Young People’s Positive Futures

as the central funding focus.

The programme recognizes that the period between adolescence and adulthood can be particularly significant.

For many young people, the years between 16 and 24 involve major transitions involving:

Education

Employment

Housing

Independence

Relationships

Community participation

Financial responsibility

Health

Identity

Interaction with public institutions

Young people who have access to stable support systems may be able to navigate these transitions successfully.

Others, however, may encounter significant barriers.

The Annual Open Grant Program is designed particularly to support organisations working with those young people whose transitions toward adulthood are complicated by disadvantage.

Focus of the 2026 Grant Round: Young People’s Positive Futures

The 2026 Annual Open Grant Program focuses specifically on:

Young adults aged 16–24

who are moving through significant developmental and life transitions.

Gandel Foundation recognizes that this period can shape a young person’s future trajectory.

The right support during an important transition may help a young person:

Remain connected to education

Find meaningful employment

Maintain stable housing

Build supportive relationships

Improve wellbeing

Participate in society

Avoid re-entry into the justice system

Develop greater independence

Build confidence and skills

The programme therefore seeks organisations capable of providing meaningful, appropriately timed support.

Priority for Young People Experiencing Multiple Disadvantages

The grant programme particularly emphasizes young people experiencing:

Multiple and interconnected forms of disadvantage.

This distinction is important.

The Foundation is not only interested in addressing a single isolated barrier.

Some young people may simultaneously experience combinations of:

Financial hardship

Unstable housing

Family disruption

Trauma

Mental or physical health challenges

Substance use

Justice-system involvement

Educational disengagement

Limited employment opportunities

Social exclusion

When several barriers overlap, the transition to independent adulthood can become significantly more difficult.

The grant programme therefore prioritizes organisations supporting particularly vulnerable and marginalized young people.

Supporting Young People Experiencing Poverty

Poverty can affect multiple areas of a young person’s life.

Financial insecurity may make it harder to:

Continue studying

Travel to education or employment

Maintain stable accommodation

Participate socially

Access services

Prepare for employment

Meet basic needs

Projects seeking to improve young people’s longer-term pathways may therefore address economic barriers alongside broader social and developmental needs.

Supporting Young People Experiencing Homelessness

Young people facing homelessness or unstable accommodation may encounter significant barriers to education, employment, health and social participation.

Organisations working with homeless or housing-insecure young people may potentially fit the objectives of the programme where their work supports positive transitions and longer-term outcomes.

The Foundation’s focus is on helping young people navigate barriers that prevent them from realizing their potential.

Supporting Young People Affected by Trauma

Experiences of trauma can have long-term effects on:

Mental health

Education

Relationships

Employment

Trust

Decision-making

Participation in community life

The programme recognizes trauma as one of several factors that can contribute to interconnected disadvantage.

Organisations supporting trauma-affected young people may therefore be relevant where their programmes align with the wider goal of building positive future pathways.

Health Challenges

Health challenges are also identified as one of the possible forms of disadvantage affecting young adults.

These may interact with:

Housing insecurity

Economic participation

Education

Employment

Social engagement

The programme’s broader approach recognizes that barriers affecting young people are often interconnected rather than neatly separated.

Substance Use

The Foundation also acknowledges that substance use can form part of the complex circumstances affecting young people’s transition toward adulthood.

Organisations addressing substance use alongside broader issues of wellbeing, employment, housing or social participation may therefore potentially align with the programme’s priorities.

Transition From Out-of-Home Care

One important transition explicitly highlighted by Gandel Foundation is:

Leaving out-of-home care.

Young people leaving care may face major changes in:

Housing

Financial responsibility

Education

Employment

Support networks

Access to services

Independent living

The move from structured care arrangements toward independent adulthood can be particularly difficult where stable family or community support is limited.

The programme therefore welcomes organisations helping young people make this transition successfully.

Young People Exiting the Justice System

Another transition specifically identified is:

Exiting the justice system.

Young people leaving the justice system may encounter barriers involving:

Employment

Education

Housing

Social stigma

Family relationships

Community participation

Re-engagement with services

Support during this period may help create stronger pathways toward stability and social participation.

Organisations working with young people transitioning out of justice-system involvement may therefore find the grant particularly relevant.

Transition From Education

The Foundation also highlights young people who are:

Finishing formal education.

The transition out of school, vocational education or another educational setting can be challenging, especially when young people lack clear pathways into:

Employment

Further study

Training

Community participation

Programmes that help vulnerable young people move from education into sustainable next steps may align with the funding focus.

Transition Into Employment

Employment can be a major element of the transition into adulthood.

Yet young people experiencing multiple disadvantages may encounter barriers including:

Limited work experience

Educational disruption

Lack of professional networks

Housing instability

Health problems

Justice-system involvement

Financial hardship

Projects that help young people navigate the transition into employment may be suitable where they contribute to broader wellbeing and economic engagement.

Grant Amount

The Annual Open Grant Program offers grants of:

Up to $50,000

for projects lasting:

Up to one year

The supplied information does not explicitly label the currency as AUD, although the Foundation and programme operate in Australia. Applicants should confirm the exact financial terms in the official Grant Guidelines before finalizing budgets.

The maximum grant amount should also not be interpreted as an automatic award of $50,000 to every successful applicant.

Applicants should develop a budget appropriate to the actual scale and needs of their proposed project.

Grant Duration

Funding is available for:

Up to one year

This means applicants should develop projects that can reasonably deliver their proposed activities and outcomes within a 12-month period.

A strong project should therefore have:

Clearly defined objectives

Realistic activities

Appropriate staffing

Measurable outcomes

A realistic budget

A practical implementation timeline

Two-Stage Application Process

The Gandel Foundation Annual Open Grant Program uses a:

Two-stage application process

This is important because organisations do not initially submit the full grant proposal.

The process begins with an:

Expression of Interest

or:

EOI

Only organisations selected during the first stage will be invited to move to the second stage.

Stage 1: Expression of Interest

The EOI allows the Foundation to identify organisations and project concepts that best align with:

The programme’s focus

Eligibility requirements

Strategic priorities

Funding objectives

Organisations should use the EOI to communicate clearly:

The problem they are addressing

The young people they serve

The transition point involved

The disadvantages faced by the target group

The proposed response

Why the intervention matters

The outcomes expected

Stage 2: Full Application

Invited to submit a full application.

The full application is likely to require additional information about areas such as:

Project design

Budget

Outcomes

Implementation

Organisational capacity

Evaluation

Friday, 11 September 2026 at 9:00 AM

Thursday, 1 October 2026 at 12:00 PM midday

Portal issues

Internet problems

Missing attachments

Last-minute revisions

Wednesday, 7 October 2026

Who Can Apply?

The programme is designed for:

Eligible charitable and not-for-profit organisations

rather than individuals.

Two organizational eligibility requirements are specifically identified.

Applicants must:

Be registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission.

Hold Deductible Gift Recipient Item 1 status when applying.

Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Registration

Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission

commonly known as:

at the time of application.

Individuals Cannot Apply

The Gandel Foundation explicitly states:

Individuals cannot be funded.

This means the programme is not a direct grant for:

Individual young people

Students

Young entrepreneurs

Researchers

Individual community leaders

Young people aged 16–24 are the intended beneficiaries of funded programmes, not the direct grant applicants.

One Application Per Organisation

The Foundation will accept:

No more than one application per organisation.

Organisations operating multiple programmes must therefore decide which proposed project best aligns with the grant round.

Geographic Focus

The programme supports work across Australia, but geographic preferences apply.

The Foundation states that:

Preference is given to Victorian organisations and programmes.

This means organisations and projects based in:

Victoria, Australia

may receive particular consideration.

However, organisations outside Victoria are not automatically excluded.

Organisations Outside Victoria

Address a broader community issue

Funding Exclusions

Before submitting an EOI, organisations should carefully review the Foundation’s general funding exclusions.

Several important exclusions apply.

No Funding for Individuals

No Retrospective Funding

Retrospective funding

No Recurrent Administrative Costs

Recurrent administrative costs

No Continuous Funding

Gandel Foundation states that it does:

Not provide continuous funding to organisations.

No Duplicate Services

Duplicate existing services.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate what is distinctive about their proposed intervention.

They should be able to explain:

What gap currently exists

Why existing services do not adequately address it

How the proposed programme adds value

No Auspiced Applications

Auspiced applications.

Government bodies.

Environment

Personal expenses.

1. Clearly Identify the Young People You Serve

3. Explain the Barriers

Confidence

Independence

5. Demonstrate That the Programme Does Not Duplicate Existing Services

6. Develop a Realistic One-Year Plan

7. Build a Justified Budget

$50,000

but applicants should request what is genuinely required.

Staffing

Participant support

Delivery expenses

Evaluation

What Makes This Grant Different?

TITLE: Stakeholders meet in Cairo, Egypt for AAU’s Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and President’s of African Universities (COREVIP 2019)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Higher Education stakeholders from Africa and across the world are meeting in Egypt from 8-11 July 2019 to discuss critical issues and priorities for the advancement of this sector of the African economy. The 20th COREVIP is organized by the Association of African Universities in collaboration with the Arab Republic of Egypt and Al-Azhar University. Over 1,400 participants gathered for the opening ceremony which took place at the Al-Azhar International Conference Center in Egypt.

Participants of this well-attended conference include various rectors, vice chancellors, and presidents of African universities, as well ministers of education, development partners, student associations, service providers of higher education and industry players. Representatives from sub-regional, regional and international organisations are also in attendance.

The theme for this year’s conference is “The Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting the Continental Education for Strategy for Africa (CESA 16 -25).” The seven subthemes of the conference reflect the strategic objectives of CESA 16-25. They focus on science and mathematics curricula, expanding TVET opportunities at tertiary levels, revitalizing and expanding tertiary education, research and innovation, promoting mobility through harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation systems, among other key themes.

The Conference is providing an excellent opportunity for leaders of African higher education institutions, particularly the current member institutions of the AAU, to exchange experiences and draw on the lessons and discussions of the conference themes. It is also providing the opportunity for the various stakeholders to collectively chart the way forward and come out with practical ways of ensuring that they work towards the achievement of the goals of CESA 16 -25, and the African Union’s Agenda 2023 – The Africa We Want.

In his speech, the President of Al-Azhar University, Prof. Mohamed El-Mahrasawy, warmly welcomed participants to Egypt and elaborated on the various initiatives being implemented by the Al-Azhar University in collaboration with the AAU. He referenced the African Universities Olympics, and the hosting of the North Africa Regional Office ( NARO) of the AAU. He indicated the commitment of the university to ensure that they work hand in hand with all North African Higher Education Institutions under the AAU NARO office.

Addressing participants, Prof. Orlando Quilambo, the President of the Association of African Universities called on all stakeholders to contribute effectively, in their own small ways, to ensure that Higher Education in Africa, is among the best in the world. He urged institutions to involve students and other stakeholders, through reforms in curricula, pedagogy and research, to engender more innovations that change lives of societies. Prof. Quilambo encouraged the inculcation of relevant skills such as critical thinking, effective communication, entrepreneurship and adaptability, to enhance the employability of graduates. He called on governments, industry and policy making institutions, to ‘work to improve investments in higher education to help achieve the African Union’s Vision of an integrated, prosperous and peaceful Africa, driven by its own citizens and representing a dynamic force in the global Arena’.

For his part, the Secretary General of the AAU, Professor Etienne Ehile mentioned how crucial it was for academics to position themselves strategically to take advantage of the various opportunities presented by CESA and other global and continental agendas, initiatives and agreements. He reiterated the AAU’s commitment to working closely and collaboratively with all stakeholders in education to achieve the targets of CESA in the most efficient way and within the assigned time-frames to improve the current state of the quality of Higher Education in Africa.

The Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research of Egypt, Prof. Khaled Abdel Ghaffar expressed their excitement in hosting the rest of the African higher education community in their country and called for more collaboration between African Universities in moving the continent forward.

AAU and the conference participants appreciated Egypt for its commitment and effort made in favour of Higher Education in Egypt and on the continent in general. Egypt was also praised for the unrivalled hospitality extended to all participants since the beginning of the conference.

Sub-Theme 1: Focus on the science and mathematics curricula in youth training and disseminate scientific knowledge and culture in society

Sub-Theme 2: Expand TVET opportunities at tertiary levels and strengthen linkages between the world of work and education and training systems

Sub-Theme 3: Revitalize and expand tertiary education, research and innovation to address continental challenges and promote competitiveness.

Sub-Theme 4: Promote peace education and conflict prevention and resolution at all levels of education and for all age groups.

Sub-Theme 5: Improve management of education systems as well as build and enhance capacity for data collection, management, harness the capacity of ICT to improve access, quality and management of education and training systems.

Sub-Theme 6: Promoting mobility through harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation systems.

Sub-Theme 7: Identifying new directions in improving management of education through enhanced capacity for data collection and management, research and scholarship and efficient governance of HEIs in Africa.

TITLE: Holger Jannasch

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
“Science is an adventure, not a career,” said Holger Jannasch, a WHOI biologist who lived up to those words.

In the 1960s, inspired by the surprisingly edible condition of a bologna sandwich that survived for months while Alvin was stuck underwater, Holger Jannasch and his colleagues were the first to identify the effect of pressure on microbial metabolism in the deep sea.

He designed and developed a variety of highly sophisticated sea-going instruments for collecting, culturing, and sampling bacteria from deep-sea depths. This research yielded valuable insights into the fragile nature of deep-sea food chains and the use of the ocean as a repository for mankind’s wastes.

After the discovery of deep-ocean hydrothermal vents in the late 1970s, Jannasch confirmed his early theory of the existence of deep-sea bacterial organisms. Jannasch passed away in 1998, but his work lives on at WHOI.

Learn more about this inspiring Ocean Pioneer: go.whoi.edu/holger-jannasch

TITLE: DoSomething DoCrew: Paid Youth Leadership Opportunity for Emerging Changemakers in the United States

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
DoSomething is inviting passionate young people across the United States to apply for its inaugural DoCrew, a unique paid leadership opportunity designed for emerging young adult leaders who want to use their voices, experiences, creativity, and personal stories to inspire others to take action on issues that matter to their communities and generation.

The DoCrew will bring together four young leaders who will become part of DoSomething’s efforts to engage young people around important social issues. Selected members will represent different areas of focus, create content for DoSomething’s digital platforms, share their perspectives, participate in leadership and media development activities, and encourage other young people to get involved in causes they care about.

Unlike opportunities that require applicants to already be famous influencers, professional content creators, or nationally recognized activists, the DoCrew is designed to give authentic young people an opportunity to tell their stories and demonstrate how they are making a difference.

Most importantly, this is a paid opportunity. Each selected DoCrew member will receive $250 every two weeks, subject to applicable tax and legal requirements, for successfully completing the agreed responsibilities during the six-month pilot.

Applications are currently open, and interested applicants should submit their applications before the stated deadline.

About the DoCrew

The DoCrew is a new initiative from DoSomething focused on identifying and supporting emerging young leaders who can help demonstrate what youth leadership and civic participation look like in everyday life.

DoSomething believes that taking action does not necessarily mean leading a major national movement or having thousands of followers. Young people can make a difference through the choices they make, the issues they care about, the communities they support, and the ways they encourage others to participate.

The inaugural DoCrew will consist of four selected young people. Each member will represent one of four areas connected to DoSomething’s broader mission.

As a DoCrew member, participants will have the opportunity to:

Represent an issue or cause that is important to them.

Create social media content for DoSomething.

Share personal perspectives and experiences.

Highlight issues affecting young people and their communities.

Encourage other young people to take meaningful action.

Develop their storytelling and communication abilities.

Work directly with DoSomething staff.

Participate in training, coaching, and virtual meetings.

Contribute to campaigns and media opportunities.

Build a portfolio of published content and campaign work.

Become part of a small community of four emerging changemakers.

Help shape how DoSomething engages with its members.

The Four DoCrew Focus Areas

Applicants will have the opportunity to connect their interests and experiences to one of four DoSomething focus areas.

1. Walk the Walk

This area focuses on:

Equity

Justice

Economic mobility

Belonging

Community service

Applicants who are passionate about creating more equitable communities, improving access to opportunities, supporting marginalized communities, or encouraging young people to serve others may find this area particularly relevant.

2. No Planet B

This focus area is centered on:

Climate action

Sustainability

Environmental justice

Young people who care about climate change, environmental protection, sustainability, environmental inequality, conservation, or encouraging communities to take environmental action can connect their experiences to this pillar.

3. Thrive On

This area focuses on:

Mental health

Safety

Wellbeing

Applicants can use this area to highlight their interest in creating safer and healthier communities and supporting young people in areas related to wellbeing and safety.

4. Be Heard

This pillar focuses on:

Community voice

Democracy

Advocacy

Civic participation

Young people interested in civic engagement, democratic participation, advocacy, community organizing, public issues, or encouraging others to make their voices heard may be particularly suited to this focus area.

What Will DoCrew Members Do?

Selected members will play an active role in helping DoSomething communicate with and inspire its community of young people.

Their responsibilities will include creating and submitting digital content, participating in virtual meetings and coaching sessions, responding to feedback, supporting campaigns, and sharing reflections about their experiences.

The content may include:

Short-form videos

Photos

Social media posts

Written reflections

Blog-style content

Campaign-related materials

Other approved digital storytelling

DoCrew members will also have their content reviewed according to DoSomething’s content review process and applicable organizational guidelines.

This means successful applicants should be comfortable communicating their ideas publicly and working collaboratively with an organization to develop content.

Do You Need to Be an Influencer?

No.

One of the notable features of the DoCrew opportunity is that applicants do not need to be professional influencers, content creators, or nationally recognized activists.

DoSomething is looking for authentic young people with:

Genuine stories

Strong ideas

Personal perspectives

Curiosity

Initiative

Community involvement

A willingness to learn

An interest in inspiring others

The organization is interested in discovering young leaders whose contributions may not already be publicly recognized.

Therefore, applicants should focus on demonstrating who they are, what they care about, what they have done, and what they could inspire others to do.

Benefits of Joining the DoCrew

Selected participants will receive several professional and personal development benefits in addition to financial compensation.

Leadership and Media Training

DoCrew members will receive leadership and media training designed to strengthen their ability to communicate ideas, tell stories, advocate for causes, and engage audiences.

National Platform

Members will have an opportunity to share their voices with DoSomething’s community of more than 1 million members.

This provides an opportunity for emerging leaders to gain exposure and communicate their ideas on a significant national platform.

Hands-On Content Creation Experience

Participants will gain practical experience creating different forms of digital content, potentially including:

Social media content

Videos

Blogs

Campaign materials

Written reflections

This experience could be particularly valuable for applicants interested in communications, advocacy, social media, public relations, nonprofit work, digital storytelling, or community engagement.

One-on-One Mentorship

Selected members will receive mentorship and ongoing support from the DoSomething team.

This can provide participants with guidance as they develop their leadership, communication, and storytelling skills.

Paid Leadership Experience

The DoCrew is not simply a volunteer position.

Each selected member will receive $250 every two weeks, subject to tax and legal requirements, for successfully completing the agreed responsibilities during the six-month pilot.

Portfolio Development

Participants will have the opportunity to build a portfolio through published content and campaign work.

This may be useful when applying for future leadership programs, jobs, fellowships, internships, communications roles, nonprofit positions, or other opportunities requiring evidence of practical experience.

Community of Changemakers

The inaugural cohort will consist of only four young leaders, giving members an opportunity to work closely with other passionate individuals.

Opportunity to Influence DoSomething’s Engagement

DoCrew members will contribute their perspectives and experiences to help shape how DoSomething engages with its members and communicates with young people.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet several requirements to be considered for the DoCrew.

Applicants must:

Be at least 18 years of age when the DoCrew term begins in October 2026.

Live in the United States.

Be a current DoSomething member or create a free DoSomething account before applying.

Be available to actively participate as a DoCrew member.

Be available for the virtual orientation scheduled for Saturday, October 10, 2026, from 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM ET.

Be available to participate in regular virtual check-ins.

Be willing to create short-form digital content.

Be comfortable creating videos, photos, written reflections, and social media posts.

Be comfortable having approved content shared through DoSomething’s website, social media, email, fundraising materials, and other communications.

Demonstrate a meaningful connection to at least one DoSomething pillar or civic engagement.

Agree to follow DoSomething’s community standards.

Follow the organization’s brand guidelines and content review process.

Have reliable access to a smartphone or another device capable of recording video.

Have access to a device capable of participating in virtual meetings.

Be willing to comply with DoSomething’s applicable policies and guidelines.

Comply with policies concerning confidentiality, privacy, social media, intellectual property, appropriate online conduct, and use of the organization’s name.

Complete all required application, consent, and participation documents.

Complete the required agreement before beginning the program.

Be legally eligible to work in the United States.

Who Is DoSomething Looking For?

DoSomething is looking for emerging young adult leaders who have authentic stories, strong ideas, and a genuine desire to make a difference.

Applicants do not need to be famous or have thousands of social media followers.

Strong candidates may demonstrate:

A meaningful connection to a particular social issue.

Community involvement.

Curiosity about important issues.

Initiative and willingness to take action.

Strong communication skills.

Storytelling potential.

Reliability.

Willingness to learn.

Ability to collaborate with others.

A desire to inspire other young people.

Applicants whose leadership may not always receive public recognition are encouraged to apply.

Time Commitment

DoCrew members should expect to spend approximately 15 to 20 hours per month participating in the program.

This time may be spent on:

TITLE: Setting sail during the Southwest Monsoon

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
by Katy Abbott

This summer, I got the opportunity to spend six weeks at sea in the Bay of Bengal during the Southwest Monsoon. Although I have studied wind-driven processes in this region during my PhD, it is one thing to make plots of high wind stress from the comfort of a desk on land — and another thing entirely to experience it firsthand in the middle of the ocean.

The TN-445 science party aboard the R/V Thompson, on a beautiful sunny day during a break in the monsoon! Image courtesy of Katy Abbott.

The cruise took place on the R/V Thompson, a global-class UNOLS research vessel operated by the University of Washington. Our science party was a powerhouse team of marine microbiologists, chemical oceanographers, isotope biogeochemists and, yours truly, a humble physical oceanographer. The primary science mission, led by chief scientists Annie Bourbonnais (University of South Carolina) and Maria Pachiadaki (WHOI), was to study nitrous oxide (N2O) production and nitrogen cycling in oxygen deficient zones, or ODZs. ODZs are regions of the ocean where oxygen concentrations are low (“hypoxic”) or even undetectable (“anoxic”). Under these low oxygen conditions, nitrate is used as a substitute electron acceptor for microbial respiration, in a process called denitrification. During the denitrification process, N2O, a powerful greenhouse gas, is produced. Studies predict that ODZs will expand under a warming climate, so it is important to quantify rates of N2O production and understand the pathways by which it is produced. To study this, our science party employed a suite of methods including in situ and shipboard rate measurements, incubation experiments and filtration of large volumes of water from Niskin bottles.

There are several physical and biological processes responsible for the formation of ODZs. They are often associated with highly productive coastal upwelling systems, because remineralization of the productive organic matter by microbes consumes oxygen in the process. However, coastal upwelling in the Bay of Bengal is relatively unproductive. Instead, the ODZ here is thought to be a consequence of weak vertical mixing in the basin. The Bay of Bengal is strongly stratified, and a thick lens of freshwater at the surface inhibits mixing of oxygen-rich surface water into the interior. Below about 75-100 m, oxygen concentrations sharply decrease and drop to nearly zero.

There are still many avenues for oxygen to make its way into the oxygen-starved ODZ — including small-scale eddy processes that mix and stir properties along density surfaces. In my research, I study interactions between these eddy processes, which transport surface organic carbon and oxygen to the interior ocean, and the microbes that consume this carbon and oxygen. One important parameter for my work is the respiration rate, which measures how quickly microbes use oxygen to oxidize organic carbon. During this cruise, I measured the respiration rate across a range of oxygen concentrations, which will allow us to understand how rapidly the oxygen that is supplied by eddy processes is “used up”.

Sampling during the monsoon comes with its challenges. Even on a large research vessel like the Thompson, many of us spent the first week or more getting over seasickness as a result of the high wind and waves. Weather delays were prevalent. But as a physical oceanographer, getting to observe the summer monsoon at sea was also a dream come true. In the Bay of Bengal, the monsoon is characterized by active phases — with strong winds, atmospheric convection and high precipitation — and break phases, where the winds die down. This variability occurs on 10-60 day timescales.

We left port right in the middle of an active phase, with a long transit to the northern bay. I spent a lot of the transit time in the CTD control room and out on deck, watching as we passed through atmospheric cold pools that showed up as sudden drops in air temperature in the meteorological data and the huge gusts of wind and bursts of rain on the back deck. Over the next six weeks, we witnessed some dramatic weather changes, including the transition from an active to break phase, where the skies cleared and the ocean was as calm as I have ever seen it, and the switch back to another active phase that was made especially stormy with the remnants of Tropical Storm Wipha rolling through the bay.

Convective clouds during a sunset at sea. Image courtesy of Katy Abbott.

Because the CTD was being deployed nearly around the clock, we were able to observe changes in the upper ocean structure directly linked to these meteorological processes we were experiencing. For me, this is one of the many thrills of seagoing oceanography that never gets old. Six weeks is a long time to be at sea. But there’s something remarkable about getting to do science in an environment like this — every day, you wake up and learn a little more about the secrets that the ocean contains.

TITLE: Nineteenth century global wind data from historical New England whaling ship voyages (1820-1900 CE)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Ummenhofer, C. C., Sander, N., Wimberly, F., Gordon, H., Giacoppo, T., Münch, B., Bice, C., & Walker, T. D. (2026). Nineteenth century global wind data from historical New England whaling ship voyages (1820-1900 CE). Scientific Data. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-07437-3

Maritime weather data from historical ship logbooks are used to assess 19th century surface wind conditions. Housed across several New England archives, logbooks of U.S. whaling voyages contain systematic weather observations (e.g., wind strength/direction, sea state, precipitation) at (sub-)daily temporal resolution. Here, qualitative wind descriptions by the whalers from ~200 ship logbooks are quantified to generate a dataset with ~81,000 daily records of wind strength and direction en route and covering key whaling grounds in the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian, and Southern Ocean during the period 1820–1900 CE (Figure 1). Following extensive quality control, we find good agreement in wind strength and direction for the whaling records when compared with 20th Century Reanalysis winds for mean and seasonal conditions (Figure 2). For the North Atlantic with the densest coverage of whaling records, interannual variations in the basin-wide wind field associated with different phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation are also captured in the whaling records. Our results demonstrate that the historical records provide an important long-term context for maritime wind patterns in ocean regions lacking direct observational data during the 19th century. The dataset described in this study is available through the WHOI Library Dataverse at https://doi.org/10.26027/DATAWJBAVU.

Figure 1: (a) Global plot of all usable daily wind records (i.e., 80,653 daily records in the Tier 4 dataset with infilling) retrieved from New England whaling voyage logbooks during the period 1820–1900 CE. Locations of usable wind records are colored according to the year. (b–e) Global plot with wind records sorted by season for (b) DJF with 21,656 daily records, (c) MAM with 19,243 daily records, (d) JJA with 18,602 daily records, and (e) SON with 21,152 daily records. [From Ummenhofer et al. 2026]

Figure 2: Comparison of usable daily wind records between whalers and 20CR over the North Atlantic. (a) Scatterplot of wind speed in Beaufort scale recorded by the whalers, with the box-and-whisker plot comparison of whaler wind recordings (green) to 20CR (blue) on the same days and for the nearest grid point in the individual 20CR ensemble members. (b) North Atlantic wind directions split into 20° longitude × 10° latitude boxes. The number of whaling records (N) with usable directional wind data available per box are indicated at the bottom of each box. Following meteorological convention, the blue (green) wind roses show the prevailing wind directions that the wind is coming from for 20CR (whaling) data. The background shading shows the long-term mean wind direction obtained from the 20CR for the period 1826–1913 CE. The 20CR wind speed/directional data in (a,b) is selected for the same days and for the nearest gridbox to the whaler wind recordings. [From Ummenhofer et al. 2026]

TITLE: Executive Director’s Message

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Celebrating the Power of Cultural Exchange: A Message from the Executive Director

Senator J. William Fulbright once described the cultural exchange programs bearing his name as “probably the most important and potentially rewarding of our foreign-policy activities,” emphasizing their role in fostering world peace and order. His words resonate strongly today, in an era where traditional diplomacy often seems intensely competitive. Fulbright’s vision underscores the vital need for nations to come together—to share knowledge, express passions, and most importantly, to listen and learn from one another in the pursuit of mutual understanding.

Since the inaugural agreement in February 1950, signed by Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and U.S. Ambassador Loy W. Henderson, the Fulbright Program in India has facilitated academic and cultural exchanges for approximately 22,000 citizens of India and the United States. This enduring partnership has become a cornerstone of U.S.-India relations.

The United States-India Educational Foundation (USIEF), which administers these programs, has undergone significant growth and transformation since its inception. In 2008, the organization was renamed from the United States Educational Foundation in India (USEFI) to USIEF, reflecting the Indian government’s commitment to becoming an equal partner in funding and governance, and truly embodying the binational essence of the program.

Under this renewed partnership, the scope of exchanges has expanded, tripling the size of the program and fostering the creation of innovative initiatives. Today, India boasts the largest Fulbright Scholar Program in the world, as well as one of the largest student research programs globally.

As Executive Director of USIEF, I have the privilege of leading a team of 40 dedicated professionals in Delhi and across our regional offices in Mumbai, Kolkata, and Chennai. Our collaborative efforts with the Indian Ministry of External Affairs, the American Embassy, and numerous academic institutions ensure that the Fulbright Program continues to thrive. Amid the daily responsibilities—overseeing operations, participating in interview panels, visiting institutions, and maintaining the historic Fulbright House—it’s easy to become immersed in the tasks at hand.

Yet, I remain deeply grateful for the tireless contributions of the USIEF staff, whose commitment and intelligence drive the success of our programs. The support of our alumni—our most passionate advocates—further amplifies our impact. Their enthusiasm for sharing knowledge and experience is contagious, spreading the benefits of cultural exchange far and wide. Each year, I am inspired by the talent and humanity of the students and scholars who participate in these programs. They consistently exceed expectations, enriching not only their own lives but also the lives of those they touch during their time abroad.

As we celebrate the 80th anniversary of the Fulbright Program, we reaffirm our dedication to fulfilling Senator Fulbright’s goal of bringing “a little more knowledge, a little more reason, and a little more compassion into world affairs.” Together, we continue to advance the possibility that nations will learn to live in peace and friendship.

Adam J. Grotsky
Executive Director

Area of Physics

Astronomy / Astrophysics

Research Interests

Nicholas Kern’s work lies at the interface of experiment and theory of high redshift astrophysics and cosmology. Broadly, Nicholas is interested in problems related to precision radio interferometry, data analysis and optimal signal extraction, and cosmological parameter inference. Specifically, his research aims to understand when and how the first stars and galaxies in the universe formed and the way this process was tied to cosmological structure formation. In particular, Nicholas uses low-frequency radio telescopes that map the distribution of primordial hydrogen in the distant universe in order to shed light on these processes. His PhD work focused on the development of data analysis algorithms and pipelines for a new radio experiment, the Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array (HERA), which aims to make a first measurement of such radio emission from the Epoch of Reionization. Nicholas’ background spans a wide range of sectors within the experiment, including hardware commissioning, data quality management, instrument calibration, data compression, and connections to astrophysical theory. His research goals at MIT are to establish these experiments as novel cosmological probes and to design the next generation of experiments that will provide new tests of the cosmological standard model.

Nicholas is also invested in teaching and student mentoring. During his PhD, he developed an introductory class on computer programming and data analysis for undergraduate students beginning research in astrophysics, which is hosted online and publicly accessible. He is also an instructor and student mentor for HERA’s summer research bootcamp and internship, which pairs students from California state and community colleges with summer projects at premier research institutions.

Biographical Sketch

Nicholas Kern was born and raised in Ann Arbor, Michigan. In 2015, he received his B.S. in physics and astrophysics from the University of Michigan working on galaxy cluster dynamical mass estimation. In 2020, he completed his PhD in astrophysics at UC Berkeley working with Aaron Parsons on 21 cm cosmology and the tomographic mapping of the Epoch of Reionization. In his free time, Nicholas enjoys traveling, running, gardening, and raising his cats.

TITLE: Press Release – Climate Change and Health Innovation Hub for West and Central Africa (CHINNOVA) Project Kicks Off: Strengthening Resilience of Health Systems to the Impacts of Climate Change in West and Central Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana, February 10, 2025 – The Climate Change and Health Innovation hub for West and Central Africa (CHINNOVA) project has commenced. The implementation of the project is in response to the escalating threat of climate change to health systems in West and Central Africa, a region disproportionately burdened by climate-related diseases and disorders. Download the announcement in English and French (COMMUNIQUÉ DE PRESSE).

CHINNOVA is a 4.8 million Canadian dollar project funded by the International Development Research Centre (IDRC), Canada, and the UK Foreign Commonwealth Development Office. It is being implemented from 2025–2028 by a consortium led by the Association of African Universities in partnership with the West African Science Service Centre on Climate Change and Adapted Land use (WASCAL), Institut Pasteur de la Côte d’Ivoire (IPCI), and the University of Omar Bongo (Université Omar Bongo) in Gabon.

The Climate Change and Health INNOVation hub for West and Central Africa (CHINNOVA) is a network of networks designed to strengthen resilience in health systems to climate change through improving data availability, fostering interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral collaborations, and building the capacity of the health workforce to anticipate and respond to the outbreak of diseases and disorders related to climate change. Climate change continues to pose significant challenges to public health, including the spread of vector-borne diseases, heat-related illnesses, and disruptions to healthcare delivery systems, particularly in vulnerable regions such as West and Central Africa. To mitigate these impacts, innovative solutions are urgently needed, making CHINNOVA’s mission critical to the region.

Several key activities will be implemented under this initiative, including funding up to 10 innovative projects through an open call for proposals, accompanied by technical, administrative, and methodological support to sub-grantees. The initiative will also build capacity to address common challenges and foster collaboration among projects, with a strong emphasis on integrating gender equality and inclusion principles. Additionally, CHINNOVA will establish a robust knowledge management system and a network for systematic climate change and health data collection, ultimately enhancing the availability of disaggregated and interoperable climate and health data to inform research and services in West and Central Africa.

Prof. Olusola Bandele Oyewole, Secretary General of the AAU, stated, “We are pleased to lead the implementation of CHINNOVA, a pivotal project that marks a significant step towards building climate-resilient health systems in West and Central Africa. Our commitment to inclusivity ensures that the needs of the most vulnerable populations, including displaced persons, refugees, and indigenous communities, are integrated into the development of innovative climate-health solutions. This is a veritable opportunity to foster multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary partnerships to generate knowledge that responds adequately to the critical development needs of academia, government, civil society, industry and communities”

Prof. Frederick Ato Armah, Principal Investigator of CHINNOVA and the Director of Research and Programmes at the AAU, noted, “CHINNOVA employs a multi-stakeholder approach to develop inclusive and sustainable solutions. A critical element of CHINNOVA is its emphasis on linguistic plurality and integration, evidenced-informed decision making based on quality disaggregated and context-specific data, and indigenous knowledge systems. We anticipate that all relevant stakeholders will be deeply involved in this comprehensive research program focused on climate change and health policy engagement, knowledge management, and the establishment of an international conference series on climate change and health”. Professor David Teye Doku, a core team member of CHINNOVA, shared similar sentiments.

Professor Kehinde Ogunjobi, Deputy Director of WASCAL and Director of the Competence Centre, Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, commented “CHINNOVA will integrate diverse datasets from various disciplines—such as meteorology, environmental science, epidemiology, and social science—to promote collaboration and advance the creation of accurate, localized predictions. By working together, our research team will refine models, identify vulnerable areas, and track health outcomes linked to climate shifts. CHINNOVA will also contribute to sharing data, improving predictive capabilities, and designing interventions that are grounded in robust, real-time data. Ultimately, CHINNOVA will ensure that climate health strategies are informed, effective, and adaptable to changing conditions. As WASCAL, we are deeply committed to harnessing the power of CHINNOVA to drive meaningful impact in West and Central Africa”

Dr. Andre Toure Offianan, Director of Research, Institut Pasteur de la Cote d’Ivoire, said “Climate change poses significant challenges to health systems by increasing the prevalence of diseases, disrupting food security, and straining resources. Through this project, we aim to generate evidence to guide policy, improve health system resilience, and ensure interventions address the needs of vulnerable populations. By sharing knowledge and resources, we also aim to strengthen the capacity of health workers and foster more equitable, effective responses to climate-related health issues”.

Dr. Aba’a Ibrahim, Core Team Member and Researcher, Universite Omar Bongo, Gabon emphasized, “In Central Africa, where climate vulnerability and complex health challenges intersect, collaborative research is crucial. CHINNOVA will enhance local capacity for climate data collection, monitoring, and response, enabling governments and health systems to develop targeted, region-specific strategies that tackle the intertwined challenges of climate change and public health.”

The commencement of CHINNOVA marks a pivotal moment in our quest to undertake groundbreaking policy-relevant research that comprehensively addresses the devastating impact of climate change on health systems in West and Central Africa. By harnessing the power of innovative solutions, collaborative research, and capacity building, CHINNOVA is poised to drive transformative change in the region’s healthcare landscape. With a deep commitment to inclusivity and equity, the project partners are dedicated to ensuring the achievement of CHINNOVA’s targets and look forward to working closely with stakeholders to protect the most vulnerable populations from the debilitating impacts of climate-sensitive diseases and disorders.

– END –

The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organisation created by African universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. WASCAL is the West African Science Service Centre on Climate Change and Adapted Land Use. It aims to enhance the capacity of West African countries to manage climate change impacts and improve land use practices. WASCAL focuses on scientific research, education, and capacity building in areas such as climate change adaptation, agriculture, and natural resource management, with the goal of supporting sustainable development in the region. The center collaborates with universities, research institutions, and governmental organizations across West Africa.
