TITLE: 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship: Training and Supporting the Next Generation of Journalist Safety Leaders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship is an opportunity for journalists in the United States who are passionate about improving the safety and well-being of fellow journalists and strengthening safety practices within local newsrooms. The fellowship is organized by the International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) with support from Press Forward as part of an expanded effort to strengthen safety infrastructure for local journalism across the United States.

Through the fellowship, selected Safety Ambassadors will receive specialized knowledge, practical tools, mentoring, and experience in journalist safety. The program is designed to prepare participants to become trusted resources within their journalism communities and help local journalists and newsrooms respond to the increasingly complex physical, digital, and psychosocial risks associated with journalism.

The initiative forms part of the IWMF’s broader Newsroom Safety Across America program, which aims to train approximately 3,000 local journalists across the United States while helping small newsrooms develop and implement effective safety policies.

About the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship

Journalists today face a wide range of risks while performing their professional responsibilities. These risks can include physical threats, online harassment and digital security challenges, as well as psychosocial pressures associated with reporting, particularly in difficult or high-risk environments.

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship seeks to help address these challenges by developing a network of journalists who have the knowledge and skills to support their peers.

Safety Ambassadors will receive training that provides a holistic understanding of journalist safety, including:

Physical safety risks

Digital and online security threats

Psychosocial safety concerns

Risk assessment and management

Safety planning for journalists and newsrooms

Approaches for communicating safety information to peers

Training and facilitation skills

The program is intended to create a sustainable network of safety-focused journalism professionals who can continue supporting their colleagues beyond the fellowship itself.

What Is the Newsroom Safety Across America Initiative?

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship is connected to the IWMF’s Newsroom Safety Across America initiative.

With support from Press Forward, the initiative is expanding its efforts to provide safety training to thousands of local journalists throughout the United States. It also seeks to assist small newsrooms in developing and implementing safety policies that can help protect their staff and strengthen their overall preparedness.

A central component of this work is the development of Safety Ambassadors.

Rather than limiting safety knowledge to a small number of specialists, the initiative aims to create journalists within local communities who can share safety expertise with colleagues and help establish stronger safety practices throughout the profession.

Role of a Safety Ambassador

Participants selected for the fellowship will be expected to develop into knowledgeable resources for journalists and newsrooms within their communities.

After successfully completing the program, Safety Ambassadors will be equipped to provide support and share their knowledge with other journalism professionals.

Their expected activities include:

1. Delivering Safety Workshops

Safety Ambassadors will be prepared to deliver both virtual and in-person workshops covering relevant areas of journalist safety expertise.

These workshops can help journalists better understand the risks associated with their work and learn practical approaches to managing those risks.

The ability to deliver training is therefore an important component of the fellowship.

2. Supporting Fellow Journalists

Ambassadors will serve as resources for their peers within the journalism profession.

By sharing knowledge gained through the program, they can contribute to stronger safety awareness among journalists and help colleagues navigate physical, digital, and psychosocial safety challenges.

3. Supporting Future Safety Ambassadors

The fellowship is designed to create a continuing network of safety professionals within journalism.

Successful participants will therefore have opportunities to contribute to future cohorts of Safety Ambassadors by sharing their experience and expertise.

4. Representing the IWMF at Industry Events

Safety Ambassadors may also be featured by the IWMF at journalism conferences, trainings, and other industry events.

This provides participants with opportunities to contribute to broader conversations about journalist safety and share their expertise with professional audiences.

Benefits of the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship

The fellowship offers participants several forms of professional development and support.

Individualized Mentoring

Fellows will receive individualized mentoring and advice from leading experts in journalism safety.

This mentorship can provide participants with an opportunity to strengthen their understanding of safety issues while learning from professionals with experience in the field.

Stipend

Participants will receive a small stipend intended to support their participation in the fellowship program.

The stipend provides financial assistance during the six-month commitment period.

Potential Paid Opportunities

Following successful completion of the fellowship, participants may have access to potential paid opportunities with the IWMF and its partners.

These opportunities are subject to availability and successful completion of the program and therefore should not be interpreted as guaranteed employment.

Professional Development

The fellowship provides participants with specialized knowledge in journalist safety, risk assessment, training, and peer support.

For journalists interested in newsroom leadership, professional development, journalist wellbeing, digital security, physical safety, or journalism capacity building, these skills can complement their existing professional experience.

Opportunity to Build a Professional Network

Participants will become part of a cohort focused on improving journalist safety.

The experience can facilitate professional connections with other journalists, safety experts, trainers, and organizations working to strengthen journalism safety.

Fellowship Commitment

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship requires a meaningful time commitment from selected participants.

Fellows must be willing to commit 10 hours per month over a six-month period.

This means applicants should consider whether they can consistently dedicate time to training, mentoring, learning, and other fellowship-related activities before applying.

Participants must also commit to delivering four training sessions after successfully completing the program.

The training requirement is an important component of the fellowship because the program is designed not only to develop individual expertise but also to create journalists who can share safety knowledge with their wider professional communities.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The fellowship is intended for people already working in journalism who have a strong interest in helping make journalism safer.

Potential applicants may include journalists working in local newsrooms and other journalism professionals who are interested in developing their expertise in safety and becoming trainers or resources for their peers.

Applicants should particularly consider the opportunity if they:

Work professionally in journalism.

Have a strong interest in journalist safety.

Want to help colleagues understand and manage safety risks.

Are interested in teaching or training other journalists.

Are willing to learn from safety experts.

Can dedicate approximately 10 hours each month for six months.

Are prepared to deliver four training sessions after completing the program.

Want to contribute to stronger safety practices within local newsrooms.

Are interested in physical, digital, and psychosocial safety issues affecting journalists.

Diversity and Geographic Representation

The IWMF states that it seeks diversity of lived experiences as well as geographic diversity within the Safety Ambassador program.

This means the fellowship is intended to build a cohort that reflects a variety of experiences and geographic communities within the United States.

The program is also open to journalists of all genders.

About the International Women’s Media Foundation

The International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) is an organization that works to support journalists and strengthen journalism safety.

The foundation describes itself as a leading provider of identity-informed and holistic safety training and resources for journalists and newsrooms, with a particular focus on women and nonbinary reporters in the United States and globally.

Through its safety work, the IWMF has trained thousands of journalists to strengthen their safety both online and offline.

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship builds on this broader body of work by developing journalists who can extend safety knowledge within their own professional communities.

Why Journalist Safety Training Matters

The risks faced by journalists are not limited to what happens while reporting in the field.

Modern journalism can expose professionals to multiple categories of risk simultaneously.

Physical Safety

Journalists may encounter physical risks while covering protests, conflicts, disasters, crime, political events, public demonstrations, or other potentially dangerous situations.

Understanding risk assessment and appropriate safety procedures can help journalists prepare more effectively for these assignments.

Digital Safety

Journalists increasingly depend on digital systems for communication, research, publishing, source management, and collaboration.

Digital threats can therefore affect both individual journalists and entire newsrooms.

Developing knowledge of digital safety can help journalists understand potential vulnerabilities and adopt stronger practices.

Psychosocial Safety

Journalism can also involve exposure to traumatic events, harassment, threats, intense workloads, and other pressures.

A holistic approach to safety therefore needs to consider psychosocial wellbeing alongside physical and digital security.

The Safety Ambassador Fellowship specifically emphasizes this broader understanding of journalist safety.

What Successful Participants Will Be Expected to Do

The fellowship is not simply a training opportunity. Participants are expected to use what they learn to benefit the wider journalism community.

Successful participants will therefore need to be prepared to:

Participate actively in the six-month fellowship.

Dedicate approximately 10 hours per month to the program.

Develop their understanding of journalist safety and risk assessment.

Learn from experienced journalism safety professionals.

Share relevant safety knowledge with colleagues.

Complete the fellowship successfully.

Deliver four training sessions after completing the program.

Contribute to the broader Safety Ambassador community where appropriate.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate not only an interest in learning but also a willingness to teach and support others.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship is Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at 7:00 AM.

Applicants should ensure that they submit their applications before the stated deadline. It is advisable to begin preparing the required application information well in advance rather than waiting until the final hours.

APPLY HERE

How to Prepare for the Application

Applicants can strengthen their preparation by reflecting on their professional experience and interest in journalist safety.

Before applying, prospective candidates should consider the following:

Demonstrate Your Journalism Experience

Applicants should clearly communicate their current involvement in journalism and explain the nature of their professional work.

Explain Your Interest in Safety

A strong application should clearly communicate why journalist safety matters to the applicant and why they want to develop expertise in this area.

Highlight Teaching and Training Potential

Because Safety Ambassadors will ultimately deliver training sessions, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate an interest in teaching, mentoring, facilitating workshops, or sharing professional knowledge.

Previous experience conducting workshops, training colleagues, speaking at professional events, mentoring journalists, or leading learning activities may be relevant.

Consider Your Availability

Applicants must be able to commit approximately 10 hours each month for six months.

They should therefore make sure they can accommodate the fellowship alongside their existing professional responsibilities.

Think About Your Local Journalism Community

The fellowship is intended to strengthen safety within journalism communities, particularly local newsrooms.

Applicants should consider how the knowledge and skills gained through the fellowship could be shared with colleagues and other journalists in their communities.

Visit HERE for more information about the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship.

Conclusion

The 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship provides an opportunity for U.S.-based journalists to develop specialized expertise in journalist safety and become resources for their professional communities.

Supported by Press Forward and implemented through the International Women’s Media Foundation’s broader Newsroom Safety Across America initiative, the fellowship focuses on developing a network of Safety Ambassadors capable of understanding and addressing physical, digital, and psychosocial risks facing journalists and newsrooms.

Participants will receive individualized mentoring from journalism safety experts, a small participation stipend, and potential access to paid opportunities with the IWMF and its partners following successful completion. They will also gain the knowledge and tools needed to conduct safety workshops and support fellow journalists.

The program requires a commitment of 10 hours per month for six months, followed by a commitment to deliver four training sessions after successful completion.

For journalists based in the United States who are passionate about improving safety within the profession and are interested in learning, teaching, and supporting their peers, the 2027 Safety Ambassador Fellowship offers a structured pathway to develop these capabilities and contribute to stronger safety practices across local journalism communities.

TITLE: Celebrating the First Female Prime Minister for Tunisia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
On the 29th of September 2021, the President of Tunisia, President Kais Saied, appointed Professor Najla Bouden (also referred to as Professor Najla Romdhane) to form and lead the Tunisia government as Prime Minister. This is a first in Tunisia for a woman to be appointed at this high level of political leadership. She joins a growing list of past and present female presidents and prime ministers across the world.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) conveys its heartiest congratulations to Professor Najla Romdhane. Three universities in Tunisia are members of the prestigious AAU – Institut Des Hautes Etudes De Tunis, Université Centrale, Tunisia and Université Du 7 Novembre A Carthage, and therefore we deem it necessary to wish them the very best under the new leadership. More importantly, the AAU strongly supports the empowerment of women and girls, as well as their equal participation in the leadership of higher education and other areas of society.

Professor Najla Romdhane has contributed greatly to the higher education sector in several capacities, including previously serving in the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research in Tunisia. She is an engineer (geologist) by profession and a professor of higher education at the National Engineering School of Tunis at Tunis El Manar University. She holds a Ph.D. from the École des Mines de Paris in earthquake engineering.

She also led the $70 million World Bank-funded program called “PromEssE” to reform and “modernize” university education to help lessen the prevalent joblessness among Tunisian graduates.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the apex continental organisation and voice of higher education in Africa established 54 years ago. The AAU prioritises strengthening intellectual engagement and discussions on topical issues that addresses Africa’s developmental goals – and one of such key issues relates to gender inclusiveness.

The AAU is leading the equal participation of women and young girls in the higher education sector. Cognizant of the gender imbalances in African higher education, the AAU has been dedicated to ensuring gender inclusiveness in its various initiatives and projects, including hosting its flagship Women in Leadership Positions in Higher Education (WoLPHE) Conference regularly. The promotion of gender equality is firmly rooted in the AAU’s Strategic Plan, which was carefully crafted to help Higher Education Institutions respond to the realisation of the targets of continental and global strategies, agendas and frameworks such as the African Union’s (AU) Agenda 2063, the Continental Education Strategy for Education (CESA 16 -25) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

To consolidate and to take our gender inclusivity promotion role a step further, the AAU launched the African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN) on 8th July 2021 during its General Conference which brought together higher education stakeholders, development partners and members of the AAU Network. Over 1,000 stakeholders participated in this conference. WoHEN is among others, engaging similar minded bodies to ensure that it adds value to issues related to all women in the African Higher education space, both teaching and non-teaching. Stakeholders interested in joining WoHEN are encouraged to sign up to the WoHEN database and mailing list via this link to receive updates from the Network: http://eepurl.com/hDw5Sv

TITLE: Youth Travel Grants to attend UNEP’s 1st International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals (GFC IC-1) 2026 in Geneva, Switzerland

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 29, 2026

Open call for applications for delegates to represent the children and youth constituency at the upcoming First International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals (GFC IC-1), scheduled from 16-20 November 2026 in Geneva, Switzerland. The GFC IC-1 is an important opportunity for young people to participate directly in global chemicals and waste governance. It will be preceded by the 4th Global Youth Forum on Chemicals and Waste from 14-16 November.

On behalf of the Chemicals and Waste Youth Platform (CWYP), UNEP is currently inviting applications for travel grants to support youth participation at the conference. As the body coordinating youth engagement in the Global Framework on Chemicals, the Chemicals and Waste Youth Platform will contribute collective children and youth policy recommendations to GFC IC-1. Youth delegates can be expected to deliver spoken and written interventions during the negotiations, meet with country and stakeholder delegations to discuss youth priorities, and engage in the 3-day Youth Forum on Chemicals and Waste, a special event of GFC IC-1.

ABOUT THE GLOBAL FRAMEWORK ON CHEMICALS

The Global Framework on Chemicals – For a Planet Free of Harm from Chemicals and Waste (GFC) is a comprehensive policy plan adopted in September 2023 at the 5th International Conference on Chemicals Management (ICCM5). It addresses a broad range of chemical safety issues – from highly hazardous pesticides to endocrine disrupting chemicals to pharmaceutical pollutants – and replaces the earlier Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM). Building upon SAICM’s legacy, the GFC provides a more concrete set of 5 strategic objectives and 28 targets, most of which are set to be achieved by 2030-2035. While voluntary (not legally-binding), the GFC serves as a centralized strategy connecting governments, civil society stakeholders, academia, and the private sector to enhance global coordination, mobilize political will, and drive action on safer chemicals management, from innovation to production to disposal.

Benefits

If you select the Fully-Funded Travel Grant option:

Roundtrip international airfare

Accommodations with included breakfast, and reimbursement of meals

Transportation and visa fee.

Open to children and youth from low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) and/or Indigenous youth from any region.

If you select the Partially-Funded Travel Grant option:

Benefits include: in-country / in-region (Europe) low cost airfare/train ticket (up to 150 CHF roundtrip) and accommodations with included breakfast. Open to all children and youth (any country/region).

If you select the Non-Funded Registration Support option:

You confirm that you will be responsible for your own travel expenses during your time in Geneva for GFC IC-1, and may be asked for additional details on how you plan to finance your travel and stay. CWYP will support you with an accreditation letter / registering to the GFC IC-1 conference only. Open to all children and youth (any country/region).

Eligibility

All travel grants and registration support applications are open to youth meeting the following criteria, without exceptions:

Are age 35 or younger at the time of application;

Are available to travel and be present in Geneva from 13-20 November (inclusive), and are committed to participating in the full duration of the programme; and

Have submitted this completed application form by the deadlines indicated in the header.

No prior UN or policy experience is required; applicants with experience or interest in chemicals and waste through advocacy, science/research, journalism, storytelling, education, or other avenues are encouraged to apply

*Note: Minors (under the age of 18) must confirm the name and contact information of the parent or legal guardian who will accompany them for the entire duration of GFC IC-1. CWYP will support with registration of the parent or legal guardian, but will only cover travel expenses of the minor participant.

TITLE: Improving Higher Education Recruitment through the African Jobs Board Project

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Jobs Board is a project which seeks to create a central Academic Jobs Board for African universities and Higher Education Institutions to actively recruit for various Academic and Non-Academic roles in their institutions. In a survey carried out by the Association of African Universities, we realised that a high number of universities and Higher Education bodies have staffing gaps which they want to fill with experts in those fields, however their adverts go on for so long with many of these staffing gaps still not being filled after months and years of advertisement. TITLE: BRYOMOLECULES

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Materials Cluster

Image:

Bioprospection and production of bioactive molecules from European bryophytes

The BRYOMOLECULES project aims to explore the untapped potential of EU bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) to develop innovative, sustainable bioactive compounds for use in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals while contributing to the EU Green Deal.

Bryophytes, including mosses and liverworts, have long been overlooked in the world of biotechnology. However, these ancient plants hold a treasure trove of biologically active compounds (BACs) with immense potential for bioeconomy. The BRYOMOLECULES project, a groundbreaking research initiative funded by the European Union within the Horizon Europe program, aims to explore and harness this potential, driving innovation in the cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries.

The BRYOMOLECULES project employs cutting-edge biotechnological approaches. By establishing innovative methods for cultivating bryophytes and engineering their metabolic pathways in controlled environments, the project aims to produce high-value BACs without relying on overharvesting natural populations. This dual strategy not only ensures a steady supply of these valuable compounds but also aligns with the European Union’s commitment to environmental sustainability and resource efficiency, paving the way for a greener, more sustainable bioeconomy.

Over the next three years, BRYOMOLECULES will provide groundbreaking insights into the vast untapped potential of European bryophytes, making significant contributions towards the European Green Deal, namely by:

Advancing knowledge of European bryophytes and how they can be used in bioeconomic development, particularly in the cosmetic and pharmaceutical sectors;

Developing innovative biotechnological methods to produce BACs, enabling new, greener biochemical routes that contribute to decreasing environmental impact;

Driving economic growth by creating new, marketable, and patentable bio-based innovations that will support the development of sustainable industries in Europe, contributing to the circular economy;

Engaging the public through educational initiatives to raise awareness about the ecological and economic value of bryophytes;

Promoting the valorisation of the biotechnological capacity of European bryophytes by providing alternative methods for producing BACs, and at the same time reducing the pressure on natural populations by promoting conservation and preventing biodiversity loss;

Active collaboration between academic and industrial partners, enhancing the competitiveness of European biotech companies and BAC producers. This collaborative approach will drive innovation and ensure that Europe remains at the forefront of bioeconomic development.

The ultimate goal of the BRYOMOLECULES project is to unlock the biotechnological potential of European bryophytes and support a transition to a greener, more sustainable economy.

TITLE: PRESS RELEASE: Addressing Female STEM Lecturers’ Underrepresentation in Leadership in Technical Universities in Ghana – New Initiative Aims to Break Down Systemic Inequalities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana, March 5, 2025 – Ho Technical University (HTU), The University of Nottingham (UoN), and the Association of African Universities (AAU) announce the commencement of a new project targeted at addressing the underrepresentation of female STEM lecturers in leadership positions in Ghana’s 10 technical universities.

Significant gender-based inequalities continue to persist in Sub-Saharan Africa, thwarting the aspirations of female academics seeking leadership positions and hindering their career progression. Women in academia still face substantial barriers to career progression, including slower promotion rates, under-representation in senior roles, and constraints in publishing and disseminating their research, which can impact their visibility and career advancement. The challenges are particularly pronounced in technical universities, where women in STEM fields encounter unique barriers.

To address these disparities, the ‘Addressing Female STEM Lecturers’ Underrepresentation in Leadership’ project targets bridging the existing knowledge gap and providing targeted support to female academics with background in STEM fields in Ghana’s technical universities. This project is funded by the British Council and aligns with global efforts to promote gender equity in academia. The specific aim of the project is to explore the experiences of female STEM lecturers in Ghanaian technical universities in attaining leadership positions and to identify the macro and micro level processes that perpetuate the inequities they face in academia. Additionally, the project will examine the impact of capacity-building strategies, including writing workshops and mentorship, in addressing gender-based obstacles. It aims to also put forward recommendations to redress the disparities and achieve gender equity in technical universities in Ghana.

Running through January 2025 – February 2026, the project targets achieving these goals through undertaking research-driven interventions to deepen understanding of the underlying issues impeding women’s progression to leadership, inform evidence-based policy, foster supportive mentorship, and deliver a targeted capacity-building workshop and a mentorship programme. Upon completion, this project is poised to achieve far-reaching outcomes, notably enhancing research output and visibility of female academics, and significantly boosting leadership capacities among female STEM lecturers in Ghana’s Technical Universities. This transformation will be marked by increased representation in leadership positions, amplified voices in policy formulation, and greater recognition within their institutions. The project will also generate actionable research insights, informing evidence-based policies and institutional practices that promote gender equality, ultimately paving the way for a more inclusive and equitable academic environment in Ghana’s Technical Universities.

Prof. Ben Q. Honyenuga, the Vice-Chancellor of Ho Technical University said that “this British Council funded initiative addresses a core challenge in academia in Ghana and across Sub-Saharan Africa. At Ho Technical University (HTU), we have remained committed to excellence and inclusivity in technical and vocational education and training (TVET). Through this initiative, HTU in collaboration with the implementing partners is hopeful that systemic barriers affecting female STEM lecturers would be addressed. HTU remains resolute in its commitment to implementing the project’s recommendations, integrating them into policies, and ensuring that they lead to sustainable change in the academic landscape of Ghana’s technical universities”.

“This project exemplifies the University of Nottingham’s commitment to global engagement and partnership. By collaborating with Ho Technical University in Ghana and the Association of African Universities, with the support of the British Council, we are fostering meaningful knowledge exchange and contributing to the advancement of gender equity in Ghanaian Technical Universities. We are confident that the project will have a significant impact on the lives of female STEM lecturers, helping them overcome obstacles and advance in their careers,” said Professor Volker Wedekind, Head of School (Professor in Education), Faculty of Social Sciences, University of Nottingham (UoN)”.

Prof. Olusola Oyewole, Secretary General of the Association of African Universities commented “At the AAU, we are dedicated to fostering an inclusive academic environment by advancing gender equity through research, capacity building, and collaborative initiatives. This project represents a pivotal step in addressing the structural barriers that hinder female STEM lecturers from attaining leadership positions. Through our extensive network of higher education institutions across Africa, we will leverage this initiative to not only support women’s professional growth but also to advocate for evidence-based policies that promote gender inclusivity. By partnering with Ho Technical University and the University of Nottingham, and with the support of the British Council, we are reinforcing our commitment to empowering female academics and ensuring their voices shape the future of technical education in Ghana and beyond.” This project is a critical step towards breaking systemic barriers and fostering a more inclusive academic environment.

About the Project Funder

This project is supported by funding from the British Council’s Going Global Partnerships Programme. Going Global Partnerships supports universities, colleges and wider education stakeholders around the world to work together towards stronger, equitable, inclusive, more internationally connected higher education, science and TVET.

Through international partnerships, system collaborations and opportunities to connect and share, we enable stronger transnational education, more collaborative research, higher quality delivery enhanced learner outcomes and stronger, internationalised, equitable and inclusive systems and institutions. This leads to stronger higher education, research and TVET systems around the world that can support fairer social and economic growth and address national and global challenges – all backed up by mutually beneficial international relationships.

About the Project Partners

Ho Technical University (HTU)| http://www.htu.edu.gh/

Ho Technical University (HTU) is a publicly funded university in Ghana, with a mandate to train highly competent human capital to the highest level possible through career-focused education, skills training and research, in partnership with stakeholders. Ho Technical University started as a Technical Institute in 1968 with the primary objective of providing pre-technical education. However, in 1986, the Institute became a Polytechnic. The passage of the Technical Universities Act 2016 (Act 922) as amended by Act 2018 (Act 974), gave Ho Technical University the mandate to award degrees, diplomas, certificates and other qualifications to the highest level in Engineering, Science and Technology based disciplines, Technical and Vocational Education and Training, Applied Arts and related disciplines. Its vision is to become a hub of practical education and innovation advancing sustainable global development, and its mission is to develop highly competent human capital through career-focused education, skills training, research and innovation in partnership with stakeholders. As a leading technical university, HTU has been actively working towards creating a more inclusive academic environment. Acknowledging the importance of gender equity, the University in 2022 set up a dedicated Gender Affairs Office, which plays a crucial role in implementing gender policies, advocating for female representation and addressing challenges that hinder women’s career progression within the University.

In terms of faculty leadership, HTU has taken concrete steps to advance gender equity. Prior to becoming a University, the Institution had a female Vice-Rector in 2012/13. The University, in 2024, promoted its first female Associate Professors, and both occupy very significant offices in the University. Additionally in 2022, the University appointed a female Dean of Students Affairs, a significant achievement in promoting female representation in leadership roles within the institution. For two conservative times, the Office of International Programmes and Institutional Linkages in the University has been headed by female academics and they exhibit quality leadership in this position. We have a history of female leadership in other office space, both in the teaching and the administration fields.

It is noteworthy that beyond faculty and administrative female leadership, HTU also supports initiatives that encourage women’s participation and professional growth in male-dominated fields. One such initiative is the Women in Engineering (WINE) Association, which provides mentorship, networking opportunities, and advocacy for female students and faculty in engineering.

TITLE: Ford Foundation NYC Good Neighbor Grant 2027: Funding for New York City Community Organizations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Ford Foundation New York City Good Neighbor Committee Grant 2027 is an annual funding opportunity designed to support community-based organizations carrying out local work across New York City. The initiative provides unrestricted funding to a small group of eligible organizations working in areas that align with the Good Neighbor Committee’s priorities, including arts and culture, education, and human services.

The program is particularly focused on organizations and initiatives that address inequality, expand opportunities for communities, and contribute to the quality of life and well-being of people across New York City’s five boroughs.

Applications for the 2027 open call are being accepted from September 1, 2026, through September 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM EST.

About the Ford Foundation NYC Good Neighbor Committee

The New York City Good Neighbor Committee is an initiative of the Ford Foundation established to strengthen the foundation’s relationship with organizations and communities located around its New York City base.

Beyond providing financial support, the committee also gives Ford Foundation employees who are not directly involved in grantmaking an opportunity to gain experience with the foundation’s core philanthropic work.

The committee seeks to apply approaches to grantmaking that emphasize:

Flexible support

Transparency

Trust-based relationships

Accountability

Responsiveness to communities

Reduced administrative burden for grantee organizations

Through this approach, the Good Neighbor Committee aims to support organizations in ways that allow them to concentrate on their community work rather than being unnecessarily constrained by funding requirements.

What the NYC Good Neighbor Grant Supports

Each year, the Good Neighbor Committee provides unrestricted funding to a relatively small number of community-based organizations working locally in New York City.

The funding is concentrated in three main areas:

1. Arts and Culture

Organizations working in arts and culture may be eligible if their activities contribute to stronger, more inclusive and accessible communities.

This broad area can include community-oriented cultural programs, creative initiatives, artistic activities and organizations using arts and culture to address social and community needs.

2. Education

Education is another major priority of the Good Neighbor Committee.

Organizations undertaking local educational initiatives may be considered where their work contributes to greater opportunity, reduces barriers to participation or improves outcomes for New York City communities.

3. Human Services

The committee also supports organizations operating in human services.

This area encompasses community-based work intended to improve people’s well-being, respond to local needs and address barriers that can prevent individuals and communities from accessing opportunities and resources.

What Types of Work Are Prioritized?

While applicants must work within one of the three priority areas, the Good Neighbor Committee has an additional emphasis on initiatives that address inequality and create opportunities.

The committee prioritizes work that:

Reduces barriers caused by inequality

Creates opportunities for individuals and communities

Improves quality of life

Supports community well-being

Responds directly to local community needs

Demonstrates accountability to the people and communities being served

This means organizations should clearly demonstrate how their work connects with the needs of New York City communities and how their activities contribute to positive local outcomes.

Who Can Apply for the Ford Foundation Good Neighbor Grant?

The opportunity is intended for community-based organizations located in New York City, rather than individual applicants.

To be considered, an applicant organization must satisfy the committee’s eligibility requirements.

New York City Location Requirement

The organization must be based in New York City and primarily support local work within the city’s five boroughs.

Consequently, organizations whose principal activities are outside New York City do not meet this location requirement.

501(c)(3) Status

Applicants must either:

Have 501(c)(3) status, or

Work with a fiscal sponsor that has 501(c)(3) status.

Organizations using a fiscal sponsor therefore have a potential pathway to eligibility provided the other requirements are also satisfied.

Priority Thematic Area

The applicant must work in at least one of the Good Neighbor Committee’s three priority areas:

Arts and Culture

Education

Human services

Organizations whose work falls outside these areas are not eligible under the stated selection criteria.

Existing Ford Foundation Grant Status

Applicants must not be current grantees of other Ford Foundation programs.

This is an important requirement for organizations considering whether to submit an application because current participation in another Ford Foundation program can affect eligibility.

Community Accountability

Applicants are expected to be responsive and accountable to the communities they support.

Organizations should therefore be able to demonstrate a meaningful connection with the communities they serve and show that their programs and activities respond to identified local needs.

Annual Organizational Budget

Eligible organizations must have an annual budget of between:

$50,000 minimum, and

$5,000,000 maximum

Organizations with annual budgets outside this stated range will not meet the committee’s eligibility requirements.

Eligibility Summary

Before beginning an application, organizations should check that they meet all of the following conditions:

Be based in New York City.

Primarily conduct or support local work within New York City’s five boroughs.

Have 501(c)(3) status or operate with a qualifying fiscal sponsor.

Work in arts and culture, education or human services.

Not currently receive grants from another Ford Foundation program.

Be responsive and accountable to the communities served.

Have an annual organizational budget between $50,000 and $5 million.

The Ford Foundation states that organizations that do not meet these criteria will not be considered for funding.

Funding Is Unrestricted

One of the notable characteristics of the NYC Good Neighbor Committee opportunity is that the funding is described as unrestricted.

Unrestricted funding can provide organizations with greater flexibility to direct resources toward their operational and programmatic priorities, rather than restricting every dollar to a narrowly defined project.

For community-based organizations, this type of support can be particularly relevant because local needs may change and organizations may require flexibility to respond effectively.

The Good Neighbor Committee’s approach also emphasizes flexible support, transparency and trust in its relationships with grantee organizations.

How to Apply for the 2027 NYC Good Neighbor Grant

Organizations interested in applying must submit their applications through the official Good Neighbor Grant Application.

The application window for the 2027 open call is:

Opening date: September 1, 2026

Deadline: September 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM EST

Applicants should submit their materials before the stated deadline through the official application page.

APPLY HERE

Important Application Considerations

Eligible organizations should carefully review the requirements before submitting an application.

In particular, applicants should ensure that their organization can clearly demonstrate:

New York City presence

The organization should be based in New York City and primarily serve communities within the five boroughs.

Nonprofit eligibility

The organization should have 501(c)(3) status or an appropriate fiscal sponsor.

Alignment with the priority areas

The organization’s work should clearly fall within arts and culture, education or human services.

Community connection

Applicants should be able to demonstrate that their work is responsive and accountable to the communities they serve.

Appropriate organizational budget

The organization’s annual budget should fall between $50,000 and $5 million.

Ford Foundation grant status

Organizations should verify that they are not current grantees of another Ford Foundation program.

2026 NYC Good Neighbor Committee Grantees

The Ford Foundation’s 2026 NYC Good Neighbor Committee grantees included organizations working across different areas of community development, arts, social services and related fields.

The organizations listed for the 2026 cycle were:

Artistic Freedom Initiative

Dance to Unite

Echoes of Incarceration

Friends of the Material of the Arts

Los Herederos

One Love Community Fridge

SNACC

St. Ann’s Corner of Harm Reduction

Street Vendor Project, Urban Justice Center

The Drawing Center

UnLocal

The list provides examples of the types of community-based organizations that have received support through the NYC Good Neighbor Committee.

Ford Foundation Good Neighbor Committees Beyond New York

The Good Neighbor Committee concept is not limited to New York City.

The Ford Foundation notes that regional offices in Asia, Africa and Latin America have established their own versions of Good Neighbor Committees over time. These regional committees are designed to respond to the particular needs of communities surrounding those offices.

Organizations interested in learning about regional opportunities are encouraged to contact the relevant Ford Foundation regional office directly.

The Ford Foundation also points organizations interested in creating their own Good Neighbor Committee toward the GrantCraft publication Building Community Inside and Out with a Good Neighbor Committee.

Why Community-Based Organizations Should Review the Opportunity

The NYC Good Neighbor Grant is structured specifically around local community organizations rather than individuals. Its focus on unrestricted funding means eligible organizations can potentially receive support that offers flexibility in responding to their organizational and community priorities.

The program’s three thematic areas also provide a clear framework for organizations to determine whether their activities fit the committee’s focus.

Organizations should, however, first verify every eligibility condition because the location, nonprofit status, thematic focus, existing Ford Foundation grant status and annual budget requirements are all part of the stated selection criteria.

Deadline for the Ford Foundation NYC Good Neighbor Grant 2027

The application deadline is: September 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM EST.

The application period began on September 1, 2026, giving eligible organizations until the end of September to submit their applications.

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours of the application period, particularly if they need to verify their nonprofit status, fiscal sponsorship arrangements or other organizational information.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Ford Foundation NYC Good Neighbor Grant 2027.

Conclusion

The Ford Foundation NYC Good Neighbor Grant 2027 provides an opportunity for eligible New York City community-based organizations to seek unrestricted support for locally focused work in arts and culture, education, and human services. The initiative places particular emphasis on efforts that reduce inequality, create opportunities and improve the quality of life and well-being of New York City communities.

To qualify, organizations must be based in New York City, primarily serve communities within the five boroughs, have 501(c)(3) status or an eligible fiscal sponsor, operate within one of the three priority areas, maintain an annual budget between $50,000 and $5 million, and meet the committee’s other eligibility requirements.

Organizations that meet the criteria should review the official application requirements carefully and submit their applications before the September 30, 2026, 5:00 PM EST deadline.

TITLE: Warming and lateral shift of the Gulf Stream from in situ observations since 2001

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Todd, R. E., & Ren, A. S. (2023). Warming and lateral shift of the Gulf Stream from in situ observations since 2001. Nature Climate Change. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01835-w

Since the turn of the 21st century, the Gulf Stream has warmed and gradually shifted closer to the US East Coast. To identify these long-term trends, Todd and Ren (2023) combined more than 25,000 profiles of temperature, salinity, and density collected with Spray autonomous underwater gliders and Argo profiling floats. The Gulf Stream region west of 68°W along the US East Coast has experienced surface-intensified warming due to heat uptake from the atmosphere at a rate exceeding that of the global ocean. At the same time, the Gulf Stream’s frontal structure has moved shoreward at a rate of about 5 km per decade. The study provides observational confirmation of a shift in the position of an oceanic western boundary current, which has been predicted by simulations of a warming climate. (Image provided by Robert Todd)
