TITLE: European Union Youth Sounding Board (YSB) – Kenya 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 31, 2026

Are you passionate about shaping policies and strengthening the voice of young people in Kenya? Do you have experience working with youth groups, civil society organizations, networks, or community initiatives? This is your opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to the EU–Kenya partnership.

The European Union Delegation to Kenya, through the Meaningful Engagement – Transformative Action (META) for Structured CSO Dialogue in Kenya project, is pleased to invite applications for the second cohort of the Youth Sounding Board (YSB).

The YSB brings together 15 young people from across Kenya to advise the European Union Delegation on youth participation and empowerment, contribute to structured dialogue between young people, civil society, and the EU, and help ensure that EU partnerships with Kenya are more inclusive, relevant, and responsive to the needs and aspirations of young people.

Benefits

Being part of the EU Youth Sounding Board will be a transformative experience, offering a blend of personal growth, professional development, and opportunities to make a meaningful impact in Kenya. The benefits of being part of the YSB will include but are not limited:

Experience in Youth-led Advocacy and Policy Influencing: Members of the YSB will have the opportunity to advise the EU Delegation to Kenya by sharing insights and perspectives that will contribute to making EU programming, EU Communication campaigns, the EU Youth Action Plan, and policy design more participatory, relevant, and effective for young people in Kenya.

Voice and Representation: The board members will have the opportunity to represent the views of a diverse range of young people, and engage with youth networks and initiatives at the local, national, regional, and global level fostering connections and exchange.

Networking Opportunities: YSB members will come from diverse backgrounds and representation and interact with diverse stakeholders ensuring a rich exchange of ideas and perspectives and offering an opportunity for members to connect with peers, mentors, and professionals from various fields.

Capacity-strengthening: Participating in YSB will allow members to enhance their leadership abilities, communication skills, strategic thinking and planning, knowledge, and understanding of the EU-Kenya partnership.

Eligibility

Be a Kenyan citizen.

Be between 18 and 30 years of age during the project implementation period, ending in March 2028.

Be residing in Kenya and available to actively participate in Youth Steering Board meetings and related activities throughout the duration of the mandate.

Have a good command of English and/or Swahili.

Demonstrate active engagement and experience in youth participation, civic engagement, advocacy, volunteerism, or community organizing through a youth-led organization, civil society organization, community-based organization, network, movement, or other recognized collective platform.

Demonstrate collaborative leadership, the ability to work effectively with diverse stakeholders, and a commitment to representing the interests of broader youth constituencies throughout the mandate.

Possess effective communication skills, including writing skills and appropriate use of social media.

Demonstrate an interest in policy advocacy, governance, and the EU–Kenya partnership.

Application

Click here to apply

For more information, visit European Union Youth Sounding Board.

TITLE: New America Future of Work Reporting Fellowship 2026 ($5,000 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 4, 2026

Applications are open for the New America Future of Work Reporting Fellowship 2026. The Future of Work Reporting Fellowship, co-organized by Work Shift and New America’s Future of Work & Innovation Economy initiative, supports journalists telling these essential stories: how education, workforce development, and the innovation economy intersect in real communities, and what it means for people’s lives and livelihoods.

Fellows must complete a place-based reporting project, such as an in-depth article, series, or multimedia project that examines the intersection of education, workforce development, and the innovation economy in specific communities or regions.

Benefits

Each Fellow in the Work Shift & New America Reporting Fellowship will receive:

$5,000 stipend for project completion

$1,500 expense budget for travel, research, and other reporting expenses

Professional development and editorial support including coaching, editing, and peer learning opportunities from Work Shift editors and New America leaders

A virtual workshop organized by New America to deepen understanding of the intersection of education, industrial policy, and tech-driven economic development

Access to expert sources and data resources to support high-quality, informed reporting

Eligibility

Open to U.S.-based journalists whose work includes reporting on education (K-12 or postsecondary), workforce development, economic development, technology, industrial policy, or related social and public policy issue.

They particularly encourage applications from local and regional reporters covering the workforce and education impacts of advanced manufacturing, semiconductor, next generation energy, and other technology investments in their communities. National reporters are also eligible if their work focuses on place-based stories and on-the-ground impacts.

Potential fellows will be early- and mid-career journalists (approximately 1-15 years of professional reporting experience) interested in deepening and expanding their understanding of how education systems connect to technology-driven economic development and the future of work.

Print, online, radio, TV and multimedia reporters and editors from local and national publications and digital-only news platforms are eligible. So are independent news podcasters, newsletter writers, and freelancers who target nonpartisan media outlets.

Your application should state your intended outlet and its commitment to run your project. Work Shift is open to co-publishing or being the primary publisher on some projects. If you would like us to be the primary or secondary publisher of your work, there will be a space for you to indicate that in the application.

Application

A complete application consists of these required components:

Basic applicant information (personal and professional details)

Statement of interest / Project proposal (500-750 words)

One letter of recommendation OR a statement of qualifications

Résumé

Links to three (3) work samples (provide links to three work samples published within the past five years. Samples should be your best recent work.)

TITLE: UNICEF Thailand Young Professionals Programme 2026: Communication Internship in Bangkok for University Students and Recent Graduates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
UNICEF Thailand is accepting applications for its Young Professionals Programme (Communication) 2026, a structured early-career opportunity for university students and recent graduates who want practical experience in communications, digital advocacy, youth engagement, knowledge management, and children’s rights.

Based at the UNICEF Thailand Country Office in Bangkok, the programme gives selected Young Professionals the opportunity to work alongside experienced UNICEF colleagues while contributing to real communication and advocacy activities. Participants will gain hands-on exposure to the development and humanitarian sector, receive one-on-one guidance, strengthen professional skills, and build a portfolio through assignments connected to UNICEF’s work for children.

The programme is designed as a 4–6 month, part-time placement of approximately 15–20 hours per week, with flexible working arrangements intended to accommodate academic schedules.

UNICEF is looking particularly for third-year or above university students and recent graduates from relevant disciplines such as communications, social sciences, international relations, digital media, and related fields. Candidates should demonstrate an interest in children’s rights, development, or humanitarian work and need strong communication and writing skills in both Thai and English.

The application deadline is 3 September 2026, Southeast Asia Standard Time.

About UNICEF

UNICEF works in more than 190 countries and territories to protect children, defend their rights, support their development, and help them reach their full potential from early childhood through adolescence.

Its work covers areas including:

Child protection

Education

Health

Nutrition

Social policy

Humanitarian response

Advocacy

Communication

Youth participation

UNICEF emphasizes that promoting the rights of every child is central to its mission.

The organization also aims to provide professional and personal development opportunities for people working within its programmes, while maintaining an inclusive and multicultural working environment.

About UNICEF Thailand’s Young Professionals Programme

The UNICEF Thailand Young Professionals Programme is intended to give students from diverse academic backgrounds an opportunity to gain practical experience in the development and humanitarian sector.

Participants will work alongside UNICEF professionals and contribute directly to ongoing activities rather than participating only in classroom-style training.

The programme combines:

Practical assignments

Professional guidance

Mentorship

Exposure to UNICEF operations

Skills development

Career learning

Opportunities to contribute to children’s rights

The broader goal is to help young professionals understand how communications, advocacy, digital engagement, volunteer management, and knowledge-sharing activities are used to advance UNICEF’s mission.

Duration of the Programme

The placement lasts:

4 to 6 months

Participants are expected to work:

15 to 20 hours per week

The programme is:

Part-time

UNICEF states that working arrangements will be flexible in order to accommodate participants’ academic schedules.

This structure may be especially useful for current university students who want practical professional experience while continuing their studies.

Duty Station

The official duty station is:

Bangkok, Thailand

The opportunity is advertised through the UNICEF Thailand Country Office.

Although flexible working arrangements are mentioned, the posting does not describe the opportunity as a fully remote international programme. Applicants should therefore be prepared for the requirements associated with the Bangkok-based assignment.

Main Areas of Work

Participants may support UNICEF Thailand across four major areas:

Digital content creation and publishing

Digital advocacy and public campaigns

Volunteer engagement

Knowledge management and communication

These areas make the programme particularly relevant to students and recent graduates interested in communications, international development, media, advocacy, youth engagement, or public-interest campaigning.

1. Digital Content Creation and Publishing

Young Professionals may contribute to developing and publishing digital content for UNICEF platforms.

This can include content for:

Social media

UNICEF websites

Digital stories

Internal communication platforms

External communication channels

Participants may therefore gain practical exposure to how an international organization develops communication materials for different audiences.

This work can involve adapting messages to suit particular platforms while maintaining accuracy, clarity, and alignment with UNICEF’s communication standards.

Digital Communication Skills

The programme can help participants build experience in areas such as:

Digital storytelling

Social-media communication

Audience-focused messaging

Editorial preparation

Online publishing

Advocacy communication

Candidates with existing familiarity with social media and digital platforms may be especially well positioned to contribute.

2. Digital Advocacy and Public Campaigns

Participants will also support public advocacy campaigns.

Potential responsibilities include:

Participating in brainstorming sessions

Developing campaign ideas

Creating content

Recommending communication approaches

Suggesting techniques for reaching youth audiences

Supporting broader public engagement

This component can provide valuable insight into how UNICEF transforms children’s rights priorities into public-facing communication campaigns.

Reaching Youth Audiences

The programme places particular emphasis on communication with young people.

Participants may help UNICEF identify communication approaches that can make campaigns more relevant and accessible to youth audiences.

This could involve considering:

Platform choice

Tone

Format

Visual storytelling

Audience preferences

Participation

Digital engagement

Young Professionals can therefore bring their own perspectives as members of younger generations into UNICEF’s communication work.

3. Volunteer Engagement

The programme also includes responsibilities linked to the I Am UNICEF volunteer platform.

Participants may support:

Community management

Volunteer engagement

Youth activities

Event coordination

Communication with participants

This gives Young Professionals exposure not only to communications but also to community-building and volunteer engagement.

Supporting Youth and Volunteer Events

Participants may help facilitate administrative procedures connected with organizing and documenting:

Volunteer events

Youth events

Engagement activities

This may involve supporting logistical coordination, documentation, information management, or follow-up.

Candidates should therefore be comfortable working on both creative communication tasks and practical administrative responsibilities.

4. Knowledge Management and Knowledge Sharing

Knowledge management is another important component of the placement.

Participants may assist with:

Archive management

Organizing information

Knowledge sharing

Internal learning activities

Organizing sessions on different topics

Knowledge management helps organizations ensure that important information, experience, learning, and documentation remain accessible and usable.

For students interested in international organizations, this component can provide useful exposure to the behind-the-scenes systems that support programme continuity and institutional learning.

Learning and Development

UNICEF Thailand describes the Young Professionals Programme as an opportunity for participants to receive:

Hands-on mentorship

Exposure to UNICEF’s work

Practical professional experience

Opportunities to develop a portfolio

Experience contributing to high-impact initiatives

Participants will be able to work on projects reaching audiences in Thailand and potentially beyond.

This makes the programme more than an observational placement. Selected Young Professionals are expected to make meaningful contributions to ongoing work.

Certificate of Completion

Participants who successfully complete the programme will receive a:

Certificate of Completion from UNICEF

The certificate recognizes the participant’s contribution and experience during the programme.

This can be a useful addition to the professional profile of students and early-career applicants interested in:

United Nations careers

International development

Communication

Advocacy

NGOs

Humanitarian work

Public policy

International organizations

Who Can Apply?

Applicants should be:

Current university students in their third year or above, or

Recent university graduates

Relevant academic backgrounds may include:

Communications

Social sciences

International relations

Digital media

Related fields

The examples given are not necessarily exhaustive.

Applicants from other academic disciplines may still have relevant profiles if they can demonstrate strong alignment with the programme’s communication and children’s rights focus.

Interest in Children’s Rights

Candidates should demonstrate a genuine interest in:

Children’s rights

International development

Humanitarian work

This interest is important because the communication responsibilities are directly connected with UNICEF’s mandate.

Applicants should therefore avoid presenting themselves simply as people looking for general social-media experience.

A stronger application will explain why communication for children’s rights and social impact is meaningful to the candidate.

Thai and English Language Requirement

Applicants need:

Strong communication and writing skills in Thai and English

This is one of the most important practical eligibility requirements.

The programme involves communication activities in the Thailand Country Office, so candidates need to be comfortable creating and communicating information in both languages.

Applicants should make their language abilities clear in their CV and cover letter.

Digital Skills

Candidates should have familiarity with:

Digital platforms

Social media

UNICEF does not provide a long list of required software or technical programmes in the posting.

Applicants should therefore not assume advanced technical production skills are mandatory unless additional requirements appear in the application portal.

However, experience using social-media platforms, creating digital content, managing online communication, or supporting digital campaigns may strengthen an application.

Multicultural Working Environment

Candidates should demonstrate a willingness to:

Learn

Collaborate

Work with different perspectives

Operate in a multicultural environment

This is particularly relevant because UNICEF is an international organization whose personnel, partners, and programmes span diverse backgrounds and professional cultures.

UNICEF’s Core Values

Applicants are expected to align with UNICEF’s core values, summarized through the acronym CRITAS:

Care

Respect

Integrity

Trust

Accountability

Sustainability

These values guide how UNICEF expects personnel and participants to approach their work and relationships.

UNICEF Competencies

The posting identifies seven important competencies.

1. Builds and Maintains Partnerships

Participants should be able to develop respectful and productive relationships with colleagues and stakeholders.

2. Demonstrates Self-Awareness and Ethical Awareness

Candidates should demonstrate maturity, professionalism, and awareness of ethical responsibilities.

3. Drive to Achieve Results for Impact

UNICEF places emphasis on producing meaningful outcomes rather than simply completing tasks.

4. Innovates and Embraces Change

Communication environments evolve quickly.

Candidates should therefore be open to new ideas, technologies, platforms, and approaches.

5. Manages Ambiguity and Complexity

International development work can involve changing priorities and complex environments.

Participants should be adaptable.

6. Thinks and Acts Strategically

Even junior professionals should understand how individual communication activities connect with broader organizational objectives.

7. Works Collaboratively With Others

Teamwork is particularly important because participants will work closely with UNICEF Thailand colleagues.

UNICEF’s Work for Children

The posting emphasizes several fundamental rights that UNICEF works to protect.

Survival

Every child should have access to:

Basic healthcare

Peace

Security

Development

Children should have opportunities for:

Education

Adequate nutrition

Supportive homes

Healthy development

Protection

Children must be protected from:

Abuse

Neglect

Trafficking

Child labour

Exploitation

Participation

Children should have the opportunity to:

Express opinions

Be heard

Participate in decisions that affect them

Communication and advocacy play an important role in advancing all of these rights.

Application Requirements

Applicants are requested to submit:

A CV

A brief cover letter

The cover letter may be submitted in:

Thai, or

English

The application should be submitted through UNICEF’s official recruitment platform.

What to Include in Your CV

A strong CV should highlight:

Academic background

Current year of study or graduation date

Communications experience

Social-media experience

Digital content experience

Writing

Volunteer activities

Student leadership

Youth engagement

Development or humanitarian experience

Thai and English language skills

Applicants do not need years of professional employment to demonstrate relevance.

University projects, volunteering, student organizations, campaigns, publications, digital content, or relevant coursework may also help demonstrate suitable experience.

How to Write the Cover Letter

The cover letter is described as brief, so applicants should prioritize relevance.

A strong structure could address:

Why you are interested in UNICEF Thailand

Why children’s rights matter to you

Your relevant communication or digital experience

Your ability to work in Thai and English

What you can contribute

What you hope to learn

Avoid repeating your CV word for word.

Instead, use the cover letter to explain the connection between your experience and UNICEF’s communication work.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

3 September 2026

The vacancy was advertised on:

20 August 2026

The official listing specifies the deadline according to Southeast Asia Standard Time.

Applicants should submit well before the closing time rather than waiting until the final hours.

How to Apply

Applications should be submitted through UNICEF’s official recruitment system.

Position: UNICEF Thailand – Young Professionals Programme (Communication)

Job Number: 595210

Duty Station: Bangkok, Thailand

Apply through UNICEF

Selection Process

Only shortlisted applicants will be contacted and invited to advance to the next stage of the recruitment process.

Candidates should therefore ensure their initial application clearly communicates their strongest relevant qualifications.

UNICEF may conduct:

Reference checks

Academic credential verification

Employment-history verification where applicable

Background checks

Selected candidates may also be asked to provide additional information during these procedures.

Safeguarding and Professional Conduct

UNICEF has a zero-tolerance approach to conduct incompatible with the goals of the United Nations and UNICEF.

This includes:

Sexual exploitation and abuse

Sexual harassment

Abuse of authority

Discrimination

UNICEF also applies strict child-safeguarding principles.

All selected candidates are expected to comply fully with these standards.

Diversity and Inclusion

UNICEF states that its workforce should reflect the diversity of the children and communities it serves.

The organization emphasizes inclusion regardless of characteristics including:

Race or ethnicity

Age

Disability

Gender identity

Sexual orientation

Religion

Nationality

Socio-economic background

UNICEF also provides reasonable accommodation for candidates with disabilities during the recruitment process and, where appropriate, during assignments.

Applicants who require accommodation are encouraged to disclose this through the relevant recruitment procedures.

Visa and Health Insurance

The vacancy contains standard UNICEF language stating that selected candidates are responsible for ensuring that any required:

Visa

Health insurance

remain valid for the assignment period where applicable.

Applicants who are not already able to work or reside in Thailand should therefore pay particular attention to immigration and insurance requirements.

The posting does not state that UNICEF will provide visa sponsorship for this programme.

Is the Programme Paid?

The supplied vacancy information does not state a stipend, salary, or financial allowance for the Young Professionals Programme.

Applicants should therefore not assume that the placement is paid unless UNICEF provides compensation information elsewhere in the application process.

The clearly stated benefits relate primarily to:

Professional experience

Mentorship

Skills development

Portfolio building

UNICEF exposure

Certificate of completion

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Show Relevant Work Even If It Was Not Paid

Students may not have long professional histories.

Relevant examples can include:

University campaigns

Student media

Volunteer projects

Social-media accounts

Student organizations

Communication assignments

Photography

Video

Writing

Event communication

2. Demonstrate Both Thai and English

Because both languages are explicitly required, mention them prominently.

Where relevant, include examples showing that you have written or created content in both languages.

3. Connect Communication With Children’s Rights

UNICEF is not simply recruiting a social-media intern.

Your application should demonstrate why communication can be used to advance:

Children’s rights

Advocacy

Youth engagement

Social development

4. Show Digital Awareness

Be ready to explain how younger audiences consume information and how organizations can communicate effectively with them.

5. Demonstrate Creativity

The role includes brainstorming and content creation.

Examples of projects where you generated original communication ideas can strengthen your profile.

6. Highlight Youth or Volunteer Engagement

Experience working with:

Youth groups

Volunteer networks

Student organizations

Community initiatives

may be particularly relevant to the I Am UNICEF responsibilities.

7. Keep the Cover Letter Brief and Specific

A focused letter tailored to UNICEF Thailand will be stronger than a generic UN application letter.

Important Details at a Glance

Organization: UNICEF

Office: UNICEF Thailand Country Office

Programme: Young Professionals Programme – Communication

Job number: 595210

Duty station: Bangkok, Thailand

Duration: 4–6 months

Workload: 15–20 hours per week

Arrangement: Part-time with flexible scheduling

Target group: Third-year or above university students and recent graduates

Relevant fields: Communications, social sciences, international relations, digital media and related disciplines

Languages: Strong Thai and English required

Certificate: Certificate of completion provided

Advertised: August 20, 2026

Deadline: September 3, 2026

Conclusion

The UNICEF Thailand Young Professionals Programme (Communication) 2026 provides university students and recent graduates with an opportunity to gain practical exposure to communications and advocacy within one of the world’s most recognized organizations working for children.

Over a period of four to six months, selected participants will work approximately 15–20 hours each week while contributing to digital content, advocacy campaigns, volunteer engagement, event support, and knowledge management.

Participants will work alongside UNICEF professionals, receive mentorship, contribute to real projects, strengthen their professional portfolios, and receive a UNICEF certificate of completion at the end of the programme.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to students and graduates in communications, international relations, social sciences, digital media, and related disciplines who have strong Thai and English skills and an interest in children’s rights, development, or humanitarian action.

Applicants must submit a CV and brief cover letter in Thai or English.

The application deadline is September 3, 2026, Southeast Asia Standard Time.

Research Interests

Sean P. Robinson’s primary research interests are in quantum field theory, general relativity, and the various points of connection between these subjects. Current work involves the use of quantum anomalies to understand black hole thermodynamics. He is also heavily involved in physics education, focusing on advanced laboratory instruction in experimental physics.

Biographical Sketch

Sean P. Robinson received an SB in Physics from MIT in 1999 and a PhD in Theoretical Particle Physics from MIT in 2005. He has held staff positions in the MIT Physics Department since 2005, with a focus on education and academic programs administration. From 2005-2007 he represented the Physics Department as Space and Renovation Manager in the PDSI project management, leading to the construction of the Green Center for Physics. He is currently the head laboratory instructor in the MIT Physics Helena Foundation Junior Laboratory.

He was awarded the 2022 Jonathan F. Reichert and Barbara Wolff-Reichert Award for Excellence in Advanced Laboratory Instruction by the American Physical Society for “leading and helping to develop Junior Lab, MIT’s advanced physics laboratory, and for pedagogical excellence that extends to the broader advanced physics laboratory community”.

TITLE: Invitation to the WoHEN Side Event at the 16th AAU Quadrennial General Conference

Venue: University Mohammed VI Polytechnic (UM6P), Rabat, Morocco

Background

Women across Africa are making significant contributions to innovation and sustainability, two central goals of African higher education. As African nations integrate the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into their education systems, women’s participation in tertiary education, especially STEM disciplines, continues to rise. This focus has created a vibrant and dynamic academic landscape that addresses skill gaps and promotes gender equity. According to UNESCO, approximately 30% of science professionals in Africa are women, and female enrollment in STEM courses is steadily increasing (Garwe and Chikwiri, 2021).

Despite these advances, women in African HEIs still face numerous gender-based obstacles and socio-cultural and institutional barriers that limit their access to leadership and recognition. This hinders their full impact on innovation and sustainable development (Founou et al., 2023). Overcoming these challenges requires systemic commitment to gender parity, not only for fairness but as a vital driver of Africa’s sustainable development. Achieving leadership parity is, as Nalova and Ayuk-Etang (2020) note, “critical to sustainable development.”

Introduction

The African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN) was established by the AAU and its partners in 2021 to advocate for gender equity in African higher education through advocacy, research, capacity-building, and policy dialogues. Launched at the 15th AAU General Conference, WoHEN continues to empower women across HEIs by providing platforms for exchange, visibility, and leadership, including commemorating International Women’s Day and other impactful initiatives.

Aligned with its vision and mission and to further solidify its impact, WoHEN will host a dedicated side event at the AAU’s 16th Quadrennial General Conference (QGC), taking place at UM6P, Rabat, Morocco, from 21st to 25th July 2025. The overall conference theme is “Shaping the Future of Higher Education for Innovation and Sustainable Development in Africa,” with a dedicated focus on the subtheme “Contribution of Higher Education to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).”

Recognizing gender equity as a critical SDG (SDG 5), the WoHEN event will highlight women’s leadership and contributions to transforming African higher education for innovation, sustainability, and inclusive progress.

Side Event: Women’s Contribution to Higher Education in Africa: Driving Change for Innovation and Sustainability

This WoHEN side event will explore the vital role of women in advancing innovation, sustainability, and gender-responsive leadership in African higher education institutions. The event will encourage participants to exchange knowledge, best practices, and actionable strategies to support women’s leadership and enhance gender equity in HEIs.

Specifically, we will focus on:

Women’s contributions in HEIs toward achieving the SDGs.

How gender inequality may limit women’s impact in HEIs.

WoHEN as a catalyst for empowering women in HEI leadership.

This 2-hour event offers a valuable opportunity for networking, knowledge exchange, and identifying collaborative actions that will support women’s advancement and promote gender equality across African higher education. Participants will gain insights from experienced leaders, engage in focused discussions, and explore innovative approaches to achieving equity.

Proposed Programme

Welcome

Keynote Presentation – Delivered by a distinguished expert highlighting the current landscape of women’s contributions to innovation and sustainable development in African HEIs (e.g. STEM, research, leadership).

Panel Discussion & Interactive Q&A – Women leaders from diverse disciplines and career stages will share their personal stories, strategies for navigating challenges, and achieving success in academia.

SDG Impact Showcases – Presentations on up to four high-impact projects addressing SDG challenges led by women across African HEIs.

WoHEN Network Overview – Presentation by WoHEN representatives on the network’s mission, achievements, and resources for its members.

Group Discussion – Interactive group work to identify concrete actions to promote gender equity and support women’s leadership across HEIs.

What actions can African HEIs take to advance gender equity?

How can we leverage local and international networks to accelerate progress?

What policy changes are needed to support African women’s leadership in HEIs?

Closing & Call to Action

Why Attend?

This WoHEN side event provides an invaluable opportunity for vice-chancellors, academics, policymakers, students, and international partners to share knowledge, make new connections, and leave with practical tools for promoting gender parity and sustainability in African higher education. Attendees will gain deeper insight into the systemic challenges facing women in academia, learn best practices from across Africa, and help shape a concrete roadmap for action.

We look forward to welcoming you to Rabat as we leverage these platforms for strategic dialogues, policy engagements, knowledge sharing, and collaborative initiatives that will empower women leaders and strengthen Africa’s higher education systems.

For inquiries, please contact:

Dr. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, Organizing Team — WoHEN

Email: fnkrumah@aau.org

TITLE: Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program 2027: Fully Funded Master’s Scholarships for Developing Country Nationals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program (JJ/WBGSP) 2027 is offering a major opportunity for experienced development professionals from eligible developing countries to pursue a master’s degree in a development-related field at participating universities around the world.

The scholarship is part of the World Bank’s broader effort to strengthen human capacity, knowledge, and development leadership in developing countries. It is designed for professionals who already have academic qualifications and meaningful work experience in development-related fields and who want to acquire advanced skills that they can use to contribute to the social and economic development of their home countries.

For the 2027 cycle, the World Bank has announced two application windows for developing-country nationals. Window 1 will run from January 18 to February 26, 2027, while Window 2 will run from March 29 to May 21, 2027.

The program provides substantial financial support, including tuition, a monthly living allowance, round-trip economy-class airfare, health insurance, and travel allowances. However, applicants must first secure admission to one of the designated JJ/WBGSP participating master’s programs before they can apply for the scholarship.

Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program 2027 at a Glance

Scholarship: Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program

Cycle: 2027

Study level: Master’s degree

Study areas: Development-related fields

Eligible applicants: Nationals of eligible developing countries

Number of participating programs: 44 master’s programs

Participating universities: 24 universities

Study destinations: United States, Europe, Africa, Oceania and Japan

Application Window 1: January 18 to February 26, 2027

Application Window 2: March 29 to May 21, 2027

Funding: Tuition, monthly living stipend, health insurance, round-trip airfare and travel allowance

Degree requirement: Bachelor’s degree or equivalent

Professional experience: At least three years of paid development-related employment

Post-study expectation: Scholars are expected to return to their home countries and contribute to social and economic development

The World Bank currently lists 44 participating master’s programs at 24 universities for the 2027 cycle. Applicants must be admitted to one of these designated programs to be eligible for JJ/WBGSP scholarship consideration.

What Is the Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program?

The Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program, commonly known as JJ/WBGSP, supports professionals from eligible developing countries who are pursuing graduate-level education in development-related fields.

The program is intended for people who have already established themselves professionally and have demonstrated an interest in contributing to development in their countries or communities.

Rather than being an undergraduate scholarship or a general scholarship for any master’s degree, JJ/WBGSP is specifically connected to approved master’s programs that address development-related challenges.

The World Bank states that the program is open to citizens of certain developing countries who have relevant professional experience and a history of supporting their countries’ development efforts.

The scholarship therefore combines three important elements:

Advanced graduate education

Professional development

Application of acquired knowledge to development in the scholar’s home country

A key condition of the program is that developing-country scholars are expected to return to their home countries after completing their studies and use their new knowledge and skills to contribute to their countries’ social and economic development.

What Does the JJ/WBGSP 2027 Scholarship Cover?

One of the major attractions of the JJ/WBGSP is its comprehensive financial support.

Successful scholars receive several forms of assistance designed to make it possible to complete their master’s degree abroad.

1. Full Tuition Support

The scholarship covers the tuition fees associated with the approved graduate program.

This means successful applicants do not have to independently finance the tuition cost of their participating master’s degree through the scholarship.

The tuition support applies specifically to the approved JJ/WBGSP participating program for which the scholar has been selected.

2. Monthly Living Allowance

Scholars receive a monthly subsistence allowance to support living expenses while studying.

The allowance is intended to cover expenses such as:

Accommodation

Food

Books and other basic study-related living expenses

Other ordinary living costs

The amount of the monthly allowance varies according to the host country.

3. Round-Trip Airfare

The scholarship provides economy-class air travel between the scholar’s home country and the host university.

The airfare support covers travel:

At the beginning of the study program

Immediately after completion of the scholarship period

In addition, scholars receive a US$600 travel allowance for each trip.

4. Health Insurance

JJ/WBGSP provides coverage for basic medical insurance obtained through the university.

This support helps reduce the financial burden associated with basic health coverage during the master’s program.

5. Travel Allowance

In addition to the round-trip economy airfare, the scholarship provides the specified travel allowance associated with the trips to and from the host university.

6. Scholarship Duration

The JJ/WBGSP scholarship covers the duration of the graduate program or two years, whichever is less.

Applicants should therefore understand that the scholarship is designed around the normal duration of the approved master’s program and does not automatically extend beyond two years.

What Does the JJ/WBGSP Scholarship Not Cover?

Although the scholarship provides extensive financial support, it does not cover every possible expense associated with studying abroad.

According to the World Bank, the scholarship does not cover:

Visa application costs

Expenses associated with bringing or supporting family members

Extracurricular courses or training

Courses that do not meet the minimum credits required for the graduate degree

Language training that is not provided by the graduate program

Additional travel during the study program

Research-related expenses

Supplementary educational materials

Field trips

Workshops and seminars

Internships

Educational equipment such as computers

Resident permit fees

Applicants should therefore prepare a realistic financial plan for expenses outside the scholarship’s coverage.

What Master’s Programs Are Eligible?

A critical feature of the JJ/WBGSP is that applicants cannot choose just any master’s degree and expect it to qualify for the scholarship.

The program is restricted to designated JJ/WBGSP participating master’s programs.

For 2027, the World Bank lists 44 participating master’s programs across 24 universities in several regions, including the United States, Europe, Africa, Oceania and Japan.

The participating programs cover a broad range of development-related subjects.

Examples from the 2027 lists include programs in:

Public policy

Economic policy

Development practice

Global health

Public health

Environmental management

Climate change

Environmental and resource economics

Taxation policy and management

Development studies

Development economics

International policy

Water and sustainable development

Sustainable cities

Infrastructure management

Agricultural development

International health

Refugees and forced migration

Public administration

The precise programs differ between the two application windows.

Window 1 Participating Programs

The 2027 Window 1 list includes programs at institutions such as:

Brandeis University

Columbia University

Johns Hopkins University

KIT/Royal Tropical Institute and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

University of California, Berkeley

University of Tsukuba

Williams College

Yale University

The World Bank’s official Window 1 listing includes programs such as global sustainability policy and management, global health policy and management, public policy, economic policy management, global leadership, development practice, public health, public policy, policy economics and systemic risk.

Window 2 Participating Programs

The 2027 Window 2 list includes universities and institutions such as:

Australian National University

Columbia University

Erasmus University

IHE Delft Institute for Water Education

Keio University

London School of Economics and Political Science

National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies

Saitama University

SOAS University of London

Stanford University

Université Clermont-Auvergne/FERDI

University of Leeds

University of Oxford

University of Tokyo

Yokohama National University

Programs include climate change, environmental and resource economics, public policy, global urban change, development studies, water and sustainable development, taxation policy, development management, global health policy, international social and public policy, development economics, international policy, public health, sustainable cities, water and sanitation, sustainable food systems, refugees and forced migration, international health, agricultural development and infrastructure management.

Applicants should carefully review the official participating-program list because admission to a master’s program that is not on the JJ/WBGSP participating-program list does not make an applicant eligible for the scholarship.

Who Can Apply for the JJ/WBGSP 2027 Scholarship?

The main 2027 scholarship track described here is intended for Nationals of Eligible Developing Countries.

However, meeting the nationality requirement alone is not sufficient.

Applicants must satisfy a series of academic, professional, employment, admission and personal eligibility requirements. The World Bank states that these criteria are strictly applied and that there are no exceptions.

1. Citizenship of an Eligible Developing Country

Applicants must be nationals of a World Bank member developing country appearing on the official JJ/WBGSP eligible-country list.

The current list includes countries across multiple regions of the developing world, including many countries in:

Africa

Asia

Latin America and the Caribbean

Middle East

Europe

Pacific Island states

The list includes Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Malawi, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Bangladesh, India, Indonesia and many others.

Because the eligibility list is subject to change between scholarship cycles, applicants should check the official 2027 list rather than relying on an older list.

2. No Dual Citizenship of a Developed Country

Applicants must not hold dual citizenship of a developed country.

This requirement is part of the program’s nationality criteria and should be carefully reviewed by anyone who holds more than one nationality.

3. Bachelor’s Degree

Applicants must hold a bachelor’s degree or equivalent university qualification.

For the 2027 cycle, the bachelor’s degree must have been earned at least three years before the relevant application deadline.

This means the scholarship is not designed primarily for individuals who have just completed their undergraduate degree.

Instead, the program targets professionals who have had time to gain meaningful post-bachelor’s work experience.

4. Development-Related Professional Experience

Applicants must have at least three years of paid development-related employment after obtaining their bachelor’s degree.

The experience must have been acquired within the six years preceding the relevant application deadline.

The World Bank provides guidance on what constitutes development-related work and identifies relevant development topics in the application materials.

Examples of areas that can be relevant include economic policy, public policy, health, education, infrastructure, environmental sustainability, social development and other development-related sectors.

Applicants should consult the relevant 2027 Application Guidelines when determining whether their professional experience qualifies.

5. Current Full-Time Employment

At the time of submitting the scholarship application, applicants must be employed in paid, full-time development-related work.

This requirement distinguishes JJ/WBGSP from many graduate scholarships that accept applicants immediately after completing university.

The program is specifically designed to support professionals who already have development-related work experience and are seeking advanced training to strengthen their contribution to development.

The World Bank notes that there is a special consideration for nationals of countries classified as fragile and conflict-affected states because employment opportunities in those countries may be limited.

6. Admission to a Participating Master’s Program

Applicants must be admitted unconditionally, except for funding, to at least one of the designated JJ/WBGSP participating master’s programs for the upcoming academic year.

The master’s program must be:

A JJ/WBGSP participating program

Located outside the applicant’s country of citizenship

Located outside the applicant’s country of residence listed when the scholarship call opens

The admission letter must be uploaded as part of the scholarship application.

This is one of the most important requirements in the entire application process.

7. Good Health

Applicants are required to be in good health as part of the broad eligibility criteria.

8. World Bank Group Employment Restrictions

Applicants cannot be an Executive Director, alternate, or staff member of the World Bank Group under the relevant eligibility rules.

The restriction also applies to specified close relatives of individuals covered by this rule.

The World Bank defines the relevant close relatives to include:

Mother

Father

Sister

Half-sister

Brother

Half-brother

Son

Daughter

Aunt

Uncle

Niece

Nephew

Applicants should review the official application guidelines for the full wording of this restriction.

9. Previous JJ/WBGSP Scholarship

Individuals who were previously offered a JJ/WBGSP scholarship but declined it are not eligible to apply again.

Similarly, individuals who previously received a JJ/WBGSP scholarship but did not graduate are not eligible to reapply.

Is There a Race Requirement?

The JJ/WBGSP eligibility requirements are primarily based on nationality, academic qualifications, professional experience, employment, admission and other program criteria.

The World Bank’s eligibility criteria do not specify a race or ethnicity requirement for the developing-country nationals track.

The program’s geographical eligibility is instead determined through its official list of eligible developing countries.

Applicants should therefore focus on whether their nationality, academic history, professional experience and intended master’s program meet the published requirements.

What Countries Can Apply?

The official 2027 eligible-country list contains a broad range of developing countries.

Among the African countries listed are:

Angola

Benin

Burundi

Kenya

Madagascar

Malawi

Mali

Mauritania

Mauritius?

The current official list should be used rather than reproducing an incomplete regional list. It also includes eligible countries in Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East, Europe and the Pacific.

For accuracy, applicants should consult the World Bank’s official JJ/WBGSP Eligible Countries page before preparing an application because eligibility is determined by the current published country list.

Two Application Windows for 2027

The 2027 JJ/WBGSP application process for developing-country nationals is divided into two windows.

This arrangement is designed to accommodate the different academic calendars and admission timelines of participating universities.

Application Window 1

Opening date: January 18, 2027

Closing date: February 26, 2027

Window 1 includes participating programs at universities such as Brandeis University, Columbia University, Johns Hopkins University, KIT/Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, UC Berkeley, University of Tsukuba, Williams College and Yale University.

Application Window 2

Opening date: March 29, 2027

Closing date: May 21, 2027

Window 2 includes participating programs at institutions such as Australian National University, Columbia University, Erasmus University, IHE Delft, Keio University, LSE, GRIPS, Saitama University, SOAS, Stanford University, Université Clermont-Auvergne/FERDI, University of Leeds, University of Oxford, University of Tokyo and Yokohama National University.

Applicants should identify which participating program they want to pursue and determine which application window applies to that program.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program 2027.

How the JJ/WBGSP Application Process Works

The JJ/WBGSP application process is different from a typical scholarship where an applicant first submits a scholarship form and then waits to be considered for university admission.

Instead, applicants must first secure admission to an eligible participating master’s program.

The process broadly involves the following stages:

Step 1: Identify an Eligible Master’s Program

Applicants should review the official 2027 JJ/WBGSP participating-program lists.

They should identify programs that match their academic background, professional experience and long-term development interests.

Step 2: Apply to the University

Applicants must apply directly to the university offering the participating master’s program.

They should carefully review that university’s own admission requirements, deadlines, application fees, English-language requirements and supporting-document requirements.

Step 3: Obtain Unconditional Admission

Before applying for the JJ/WBGSP scholarship, applicants must have been admitted unconditionally except for financing to an eligible participating master’s program.

This is a crucial distinction.

Simply applying to a participating university is not enough.

Being interested in a participating master’s program is not enough.

Being conditionally admitted in a way that does not satisfy the JJ/WBGSP requirements is also not sufficient.

The applicant needs the required admission status before submitting the scholarship application.

Step 4: University Shortlisting

The participating university identifies and shortlists candidates who meet the relevant requirements.

The World Bank states that the JJ/WBGSP scholarship application link is communicated only to candidates who have been admitted to a participating master’s program and shortlisted as eligible JJ/WBGSP applicants by the participating university.

Step 5: Submit the JJ/WBGSP Scholarship Application

Shortlisted candidates then receive access to the relevant JJ/WBGSP application process.

Applicants must submit the required information and documentation within the applicable application window.

How Are JJ/WBGSP Applications Selected?

The scholarship selection process evaluates eligible applications using four principal factors.

The World Bank states that two qualified assessors independently review each eligible application and score it on a scale of 1 to 10.

The four main assessment factors are:

Quality of professional experience — 30%

Quality of professional recommendations — 30%

Quality of commitment to the applicant’s home country — 30%

Quality of education background — 10%

The assessment therefore does not focus solely on academic grades.

Professional experience, recommendations and evidence of commitment to development in the applicant’s home country account for the majority of the assessment framework.

Other Factors Considered During Selection

After the assessment process, the JJ/WBGSP Secretariat considers additional factors when selecting finalists.

These include:

Maintaining reasonable geographical distribution of awards

Maintaining reasonable gender distribution

Unusual circumstances or hardships

Giving consideration, all else being equal, to applicants with limited access to financial resources for graduate study abroad

The final list of finalists is presented to the JJ/WBGSP Steering Committee, which includes members of the World Bank Board of Directors and World Bank management, for approval. Winners are notified after the Steering Committee’s approval.

What Happens After Completing the Master’s Degree?

JJ/WBGSP is not simply intended to help scholars obtain international master’s degrees.

A central component of the program is the expectation that developing-country scholars will return to their home countries after their studies and use their acquired skills to contribute to social and economic development.

This makes the scholarship particularly relevant to professionals who have a clear connection to development work and can explain how advanced graduate training will strengthen their contribution to their communities, institutions or countries.

Development Fields Covered by the Scholarship

The scholarship is intended for master’s programs connected to development.

The 2027 participating programs demonstrate the breadth of this definition.

Relevant areas include:

Economic Policy and Economics

Programs in economic policy management, development economics, policy economics and related areas can prepare professionals to work on economic policy, public-sector reform, development planning and related challenges.

Public Policy and Public Administration

Several participating universities offer programs focused on public policy, public administration, international policy and policy management.

Health and Public Health

JJ/WBGSP also supports master’s programs in public health, global health policy, international health and health equity.

Environment and Climate

Programs include climate change, environmental management, environmental economics, sustainable development and related areas.

Water and Infrastructure

The 2027 lists include master’s programs related to water and sustainable development, infrastructure management, sustainable cities and other infrastructure-related development challenges.

Development Studies

Development studies and development practice remain important areas within the participating-program portfolio.

Tax Policy and Public Finance

The scholarship also supports programs focused on taxation policy, public finance and economic management.

International Development and Social Policy

Other participating programs address social policy, international social and public policy, refugees and forced migration, and related development concerns.

Applicants should remember that the scholarship is not open to every master’s program at the participating universities. Only programs officially designated as JJ/WBGSP participating programs qualify.

Important Financial Consideration

Although JJ/WBGSP is commonly described as a fully funded scholarship, applicants should read the official coverage carefully.

The scholarship provides:

Tuition

Basic medical insurance through the university

Monthly subsistence allowance

Economy-class round-trip airfare

US$600 travel allowance for each trip

However, several expenses remain outside the scholarship’s coverage, including visa application costs, resident permit fees, family expenses, computers, additional travel, research expenses, extracurricular courses, internships and certain educational activities.

Applicants should therefore distinguish between the scholarship’s substantial core funding and the expenses that they may still need to finance independently.

Can the Scholarship Be Combined With Other Funding?

The JJ/WBGSP scholarship may supplement but does not duplicate another source of financial support or fellowship.

If an applicant receives another scholarship or fellowship, the applicant must provide the relevant documentation to the JJ/WBGSP Secretariat.

Applicants should therefore disclose other financial awards rather than assuming that multiple scholarships can automatically be combined.

Separate 2027 Opportunity for Japanese Nationals

The World Bank also operates a separate JJ/WBGSP application track for Japanese nationals.

For the 2027 cycle, the Japanese nationals application window is scheduled for February 15 to April 16, 2027.

The Japanese nationals track has different eligibility requirements from the developing-country nationals track.

Among its requirements, applicants generally must:

Be Japanese nationals

Hold a bachelor’s degree earned at least three years before the application deadline

Have at least three years of paid development-related employment

Have obtained that experience after earning their bachelor’s degree and within the specified six-year period

Be admitted unconditionally or currently enrolled in an eligible graduate program outside Japan in a development-related field, or meet the applicable employment requirement relating to development work in developing countries

Meet the relevant World Bank Group employment and family restrictions

Japanese nationals should therefore use the dedicated Japanese-national application guidance rather than applying under the developing-country nationals requirements.

Important Things Applicants Should Know Before Applying

The scholarship application is not the first step

Applicants should not wait for the JJ/WBGSP scholarship application before applying to universities.

The university admission process needs to be addressed first because the scholarship application is linked to admission and university shortlisting.

Not every master’s program qualifies

A university may have hundreds of graduate programs, but only the programs officially designated as JJ/WBGSP participating programs qualify.

Applicants should verify the exact master’s degree title against the 2027 participating-program list.

Admission must be outside the applicant’s country

For developing-country nationals, the participating master’s program must be outside both the applicant’s country of citizenship and country of residence as listed when the scholarship call opens.

Professional experience matters substantially

Because professional experience carries a 30% assessment weight, applicants should be able to clearly document their development-related employment and explain how it connects with their intended master’s study.

Commitment to the home country matters

Another 30% of the assessment focuses on commitment to the applicant’s home country.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate how their professional trajectory, development interests and proposed graduate training connect with future contributions to their country.

Application Deadlines for the JJ/WBGSP 2027 Cycle

For developing-country nationals, there are two application windows:

Window 1 – Application Guidelines

January 18, 2027 to February 26, 2027

Window 2 – Application Guidelines

March 29, 2027 to May 21, 2027

The appropriate window depends on the participating master’s program the applicant is pursuing.

Applicants should also remember that university admission deadlines can be earlier than the JJ/WBGSP scholarship deadline. Consequently, prospective scholars should begin the university application process well in advance.

Recommended Preparation Strategy

Applicants interested in the 2027 scholarship cycle can begin preparing long before the scholarship windows open.

1. Check Your Country Eligibility

Confirm that your nationality appears on the official 2027 JJ/WBGSP eligible-country list.

2. Review the Participating Programs

Study the official list of 2027 participating master’s programs and identify degrees that match your professional development goals.

3. Check the University Requirements

Once you identify a suitable participating program, review the university’s admission requirements and deadlines.

4. Prepare Academic Documents

Organize your bachelor’s degree certificate, academic transcripts and any other documents required by the university.

5. Document Your Professional Experience

Because the program requires at least three years of paid development-related work experience, prepare accurate records of your employment history.

6. Strengthen Your Professional Recommendations

Professional recommendations carry significant weight in the selection process. Identify appropriate referees who can provide evidence of your professional performance, development experience and potential.

7. Develop a Clear Development Narrative

Applicants should be able to connect:

Past experience → master’s degree → new skills → return home → development contribution.

A coherent professional story can help demonstrate why the proposed master’s degree is relevant to the applicant’s career and development goals.

8. Start Early

The most important practical consideration is timing.

University admission and scholarship applications involve separate stages. Waiting until the JJ/WBGSP application window opens may leave insufficient time to obtain the necessary university admission.

Official Application Resources

The World Bank provides separate official resources for the two 2027 developing-country application windows.

For Window 1, applicants can consult the official 2027 Application Guidelines and FAQ provided by the World Bank.

For Window 2, the World Bank provides a separate 2027 Application Guidelines document and FAQ.

Applicants should also review the official participating-program lists before beginning their university application process.

Click HERE to learn more about the Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program 2027.

Conclusion

The Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship Program 2027 is a major graduate scholarship opportunity for experienced development professionals from eligible developing countries who want to pursue master’s-level training in development-related fields.

The program combines tuition support, a monthly living allowance, health insurance, round-trip economy airfare and travel allowances, while also connecting scholars with master’s programs at participating universities in the United States, Europe, Africa, Oceania and Japan.

However, the scholarship has strict eligibility requirements. Applicants generally need an eligible developing-country nationality, a bachelor’s degree earned at least three years before the relevant deadline, at least three years of paid development-related professional experience, current full-time development-related employment, and unconditional admission to an approved JJ/WBGSP participating master’s program outside their country of citizenship and residence.

The 2027 application process for developing-country nationals opens in two windows: January 18 to February 26, 2027 for Window 1, and March 29 to May 21, 2027 for Window 2.

Prospective applicants should begin with the participating-program list, identify an appropriate master’s degree, check the university’s admission requirements, and work toward securing the required unconditional admission before the relevant scholarship deadline.

The most important point is that JJ/WBGSP does not fund just any master’s degree. Applicants must be admitted to one of the officially designated participating programs. Careful planning, early university applications, strong documentation of development-related professional experience, and a clear connection between graduate study and future contribution to the applicant’s home country are therefore central to preparing for the 2027 cycle.

For the latest country eligibility list, participating programs, application guidelines, FAQs and official deadlines, applicants should always consult the World Bank’s official JJ/WBGSP resources because program information can change between application cycles.

TITLE: YOU-DARE

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Inclusive Science Cluster

YOUth Debunking the gendered Arguments of far-Right Extremism

YOU-DARE brings together interdisciplinary expertise from across Europe to investigate how far-right youth groups construct and mobilise gender identities, and how these narratives erode democratic values and behaviours.

In recent years across the globe, far-right movements have increasingly utilised gender identities to promote exclusionary ideologies, simultaneously undermining democratic values. The YOU-DARE project seeks to illuminate this paradox by examining these dynamics through an intersectional lens that uncovers both the complexities and contradictions of gender constructions within far-right youth movements.

Key focus areas

Intersectional Analysis: Challenging oversimplified views of far-right ideologies on gender by exposing the nuanced interplay between hyper-masculine/feminine tropes and pro-equality rhetoric within anti-immigration campaigns.

Youth Leadership: Exploring how youth leaders, including online influencers, shape far-right gender discourses.

Local and Transnational Dimensions: Conducting comparative case studies across eight countries-Denmark, Spain, the United Kingdom, France, Hungary, Italy, Romania, and Sweden-to understand how local dynamics connect to global trends.

Policy and Practice Innovation: Establishing a Policy Lab to co-design and pilot-test practical solutions for reducing the appeal of far-right ideologies among youth.

Through its work and results, YOU-DARE will demonstrate the need for intervention across society. The YOU-DARE Toolkit and policy recommendations are designed to help policymakers tackle the spread of extremist gender ideals. The project will also offer powerful mutual learning opportunities through the Open Policy Lab, capacity-building workshops, and a Knowledge Sharing Platform. By clearly illustrating the influence of (hyper-)masculinity and femininity models within identity politics and presenting innovative solutions, the initiative will strengthen cross-national networking and collaboration among those working to prevent the spread of far-right ideologies among young people. It will also provide policymakers with the knowledge and evidence required to safeguard democratic values against the corrosive impact of far-right gender narratives.

Project partners

The YOU-DARE consortium brings together organisations from across Europe, combining diverse expertise in social sciences, gender studies, far-right politics, and participatory research. Partners include the European Science Foundation (project coordinator), Aalborg University in Denmark, Smart Venice, Goldsmiths University of London, Stockholm University, University of Glasgow, Universitat Oberta de Catalunya, Political Capital, University of Bucharest, ALDA (European Association for Local Democracy), and NetHood. Together, the consortium gathers decades of experience in research, policy design, and community engagement, and will collectively address the challenges posed by far-right youth movements.

TITLE: Pre-Conference Workshop – Driving Policy through Research, Communication and Partnerships for Institutional Transformation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Workshop by the Association of African Universities (AAU) in partnership with the University of Cape Coast, Ghana

Hosted by Mohammed V University in Rabat, Morocco

19th to 20th July 2025 | Venue: Rabat, Morocco

Pre-Conference Event to the AAU 16th General Conference

Workshop Title: Driving Policy through Research, Communication and Partnerships for Institutional Transformation

Registration Link – https://forms.office.com/r/uJ7STBxa8J

Background

An adeptly communicative African higher education institution holds the power to bridge the gap between research and action, enabling policymakers and stakeholders to make well-informed decisions while positioning/reaffirming itself as a trusted source of expertise. This strategic positioning is crucial in attracting multiple partners to an institution.

With research playing a pivotal role in informing policymaking and shaping reforms, policymakers often rely on research findings, debates, and discourses to make informed decisions. The effective packaging, dissemination, and communication of research findings are essential in ensuring their relevance and impact on policy formulation. Policy briefs have emerged as a valuable tool for disseminating research findings and providing advice on potential policy options. A policy brief is a concise document that presents research findings and recommendations to a non-specialist audience, aiming to evaluate policy options and provide evidence-based actionable recommendations that align with the practical constraints policymakers face.

Scholars such as Young and Quinn (2007) emphasize the importance of succinctness in policy briefs, defining them as short documents tailored for non-specialist readers. Eisele (2006) views policy briefs as neutral summaries of information related to specific issues or problems. The crafting of a policy brief demands two critical technical skills. Firstly, the ability to judiciously select relevant information and findings from research that align with recommended policy options. Secondly, the skill to present this information in a concise, purpose-driven, and accessible manner that resonates with non-research audiences. Strong and effective communication skills, therefore, become crucial in this process.

Moreover, in an increasingly dynamic and interconnected world, effective communication is paramount for organizations to thrive. The concept of strategic communication goes beyond conventional practices, emphasizing the need for a purposeful, cohesive, and forward-thinking approach to communication that aligns with an institutions’ mission and goals. By strategically managing communication and building strong relationships with stakeholders, African Higher Education Institutions can enhance their competitiveness, foster organizational success, and positively influence their reputation.

Strategic communication requires the intentional and purposeful use of communication by organizations to fulfill their mission. This approach to communication has been recognized as a crucial element in achieving competitive advantage, organizational effectiveness, and the establishment of lasting relationships with stakeholders. Several scholars have emphasized its significance in shaping the communication processes of an organization. Notably, the research field of strategic communication thrives when specific research objectives, perspectives, and institutional manifestations contribute to a cumulative body of knowledge.

On a parallel front, the concept of Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) as cooperative arrangements between public and private partners has gained significant attention and relevance in recent years. Researchers, such as Kwak et al. (2009) defined PPPs as strategic alliances that seek to leverage the unique capabilities of both sectors, facilitating the attainment of shared objectives while mitigating individual limitations. Likewise, Rybnicek et al. (2020) emphasize the growing popularity of PPPs as a means to establish synergies, bridging the gap between the public and private spheres in tackling complex societal issues.

PPPs by their very design, allow institutions from both sides to combine their strengths and resources to achieve common social, economic, and environmental objectives. In such partnerships, both parties share risks, responsibilities, and rewards, fostering a collaborative approach towards addressing modern challenges and unlocking new opportunities for sustainable development. Collaborating with private enterprises enables universities to leverage resources, expertise, and innovation from the business sector, enhancing the quality of education, research capabilities, and employability of graduates. Such partnerships facilitate the alignment of academic programs with industry needs, promoting relevant skill development and entrepreneurship. Moreover, joint initiatives stimulate economic growth, knowledge transfer, and technology diffusion while fostering a culture of innovation that supports Africa’s aspirations for inclusive and diversified advancement. The need to therefore sharpen staff skills in this area is crucial.

Objectives: The main objectives of the workshop are to:

Equip participants with practical skills in crafting policy-oriented research and developing concise and persuasive policy briefs.

Demonstrate the significance of research evidence in informing policymaking and driving meaningful policy change.

Showcase the role of organizational PPPs in fostering collaborative partnerships and addressing modern challenges for sustainable development.

Explore the principles and practices of strategic communication to enhance organizational competitiveness, reputation, and stakeholder relationships.

Facilitate the integration of writing research for policy, organizational PPPs, and strategic communication for a holistic approach to driving sustainable policy change and organizational success.

Expected Outcomes:

Participants will leave the workshop with enhanced skills in crafting compelling policy briefs that effectively communicate research findings to influence policy agendas.

They will have the ability to package complex research information concisely and persuasively, catering to the needs of non-research audiences, and offering evidence-based recommendations for policy change.

By equipping participants with strategic communications skills and insights, the workshop will enable institutions to effectively engage stakeholders, build strong relationships, and navigate the complexities of an interconnected global landscape.

Participants will be equipped with the knowledge to identify and cultivate mutually beneficial partnerships with private enterprises, leading to enriched research opportunities, industry-relevant curriculum development, and increased funding attraction to their institutions.

Expected Participants

1. Academics and Researchers from African universities

2. University Administrators: Leaders and managers from African higher education institutions.

3. Policy Makers: Government officials, policymakers, and stakeholders who would benefit from research-informed policy decisions.

4. Communication Professionals: Staff from African universities responsible for strategic communication, public relations, and stakeholder engagement.

5. Research Officers: Professionals involved in research and policy analysis.

6. Partnership and Collaboration Experts: Individuals involved in developing and managing public-private partnerships (PPPs) in African higher education institutions

The registration fees cover the conference package, including training materials, certificates, tea/coffee, and lunches for the duration of the workshop and conference. Participants will be responsible for their own dinners.

Under the theme “Shaping the Future of Higher Education for Innovation and Sustainable Development in Africa”, the event aims to unite higher education stakeholders — including university leaders, researchers, policymakers, students, and industry partners — to address challenges and explore strategies for sustainable development in line with Africa’s Agenda 2063.

The conference will feature scientific sessions, panel discussions, and exhibitions, all focused on enhancing access to education, fostering innovation, and aligning curricula with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
