TITLE: Press Release: Coalition for Digital Africa Turns Focus to Universal Acceptance

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Collaboration with African Universities Lays Groundwork for Multilingual Internet

Nairobi, Kenya – 13 April 2023 – The Coalition for Digital Africa has launched another major initiative aimed at strengthening Internet infrastructure across the continent. Undertaken in collaboration with the Association of African Universities (AAU), the project focuses on making websites, applications, and email systems within Africa’s higher education institutions ready to support all domain names and email addresses.

Universal Acceptance (UA) allows all valid domain names, unique addresses like https://www.icann.org – and email addresses to be accepted, validated, stored, processed, and displayed correctly and consistently, regardless of script, language, or character length. It is a fundamental requirement for achieving a multilingual Internet, where Internet users around the world can navigate entirely in local languages and scripts.

The new project will create awareness of UA within higher education institutions across Africa. Training will be provided for these institutions to configure and make their websites, applications, and email systems UA-ready, and incorporate the concepts of UA into their curricula. This is critical to academic work in various ways, including being able to access vital content from the Internet for research and learning.

“ICANN is committed to ensuring that the Internet continues to grow safely in Africa, to bring communities, cultures, and economies together,” said Sally Costerton, Interim President and CEO of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN). “That’s why collaboration among Internet access providers, manufacturers, content providers, and academia is so important. We must work together to support the development of Africa’s digital economy.”

More than 2,000 languages are spoken in Africa. Expanding the number of languages and scripts which can be used in domain names is an important step toward building a more useful and empowering Internet.

“This work truly lays the foundation for a more inclusive Internet,” said Professor Olusola Bandele Oyewole, Secretary General of the AAU. “By enabling the use of local languages and scripts, users here in Africa and around the world will be able to more readily access important content online – from within the continent and beyond – for academic purposes.”

Stakeholders in higher education and research institutions are encouraged to participate in the work of the Universal Acceptance Steering Group (UASG), a volunteer-led group supported by ICANN. The UASG is working to achieve UA-readiness, in which Internet applications, devices, and systems treat all domain names in a consistent manner.

Conceived and initiated by ICANN, the Coalition for Digital Africa is an alliance of like-minded organizations committed to building a robust and secure Internet infrastructure to bring more Africans online. More information is available at www.coalitionfordigitalafrica.africa.

About the AAU

Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa. It aims to improve the quality of African higher education and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education. The AAU is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 400 Higher Education Institutions and is the technical implementing arm of the African Union Commission (AUC) on matters related to higher education in Africa. The Association is the Coordinator for the implementation of The Higher Education Cluster of the AUC’s Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25).

About ICANN

ICANN’s mission is to help ensure a stable, secure, and unified global Internet. To reach another person on the Internet, you need to type an address – a name or a number – into your computer or other device. That address must be unique so computers know where to find each other. ICANN helps coordinate and support these unique identifiers across the world. ICANN was formed in 1998 as a nonprofit public benefit corporation with a community of participants from all over the world.

TITLE: Call for Applications: Africa CDC Continental Immunization Advisory Council Membership 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 21, 2026

Africa CDC invites expressions of interest from distinguished African leaders, experts, and advocates to serve as members of the Continental Immunization Advisory Council (CIAC). The CIAC is a high-level strategic advisory and action-oriented platform established to accelerate the delivery of the Africa CDC Continental Immunization Strategy 2026–2030 (CIS) and broader Continental Immunization priority issues in Africa. The CIS Strategy positions immunization as a foundational pillar of resilient, epidemic-ready primary health care, health security, equity, and sustainable development across Africa.

Roles of the CIAC Members

CIAC members will serve as senior strategic advisors, advocates, and accelerators for the implementation of the Continental Immunization Strategy. Members will be expected to bring independent judgment, leadership experience, technical insight, political influence, financing expertise, community perspectives, or institutional networks that can help drive momentum in advancing immunization in Africa.

Members will provide high-level strategic advice to Africa CDC on opportunities, risks, and bottlenecks affecting immunization systems; champion immunization as a priority for primary health care, health security, equity, and human capital; and support advocacy for sustainable domestic financing, partner alignment, and accountability. They may also be invited to contribute to targeted working groups, policy dialogues, problem solving, advocacy engagements, or follow-up actions linked to CIAC recommendations.

Members will provide:

Strategic guidance on continental immunization priorities, risks, opportunities, and implementation of bottlenecks.

Decisive action and problem solving including on complex issues requiring political commitment, leadership and ownership

Advocacy support to keep immunization high on political, parliamentary, financing, partner, and public health agendas.

Advice on sustainable financing, equity-focused delivery, zero-dose and under-immunized children, outbreak prevention, and integration with primary health care and health security systems.

Support for accountability by reviewing progress updates and recommending actions to accelerate results linked with the Continental Immunization Forum.

Use of members’ networks and influence to advance Continental Immunization priorities, while respecting Africa CDC and Member State leadership.

Eligibility

Africa CDC seeks expressions of interest from individuals with recognized leadership, credibility, and influence in areas that are critical to advancing immunization outcomes across Africa. CIAC membership will aim to bring together a bold and balanced mix of political leadership, technical expertise, financing insight, implementation experience, community voice, and strategic advocacy capacity.

Political, parliamentary, diplomatic, or policy influence that can help elevate immunization on national, regional, and continental agendas.

Senior leadership experience in public health, immunization, primary health care, health security, or broader health systems strengthening.

Demonstrated expertise in immunization policy, vaccine-preventable disease control, zero-dose and under-immunized populations, outbreak prevention and response, or life-course vaccination.

Experience in public finance, domestic resource mobilization, health financing, innovative financing, budgeting, investment cases, or sustainable financing for health and immunization.

Experience with community engagement, civil society leadership, demand generation, risk communication, gender equity, youth engagement, or reaching underserved and marginalized populations.

Strong understanding of implementation challenges in African contexts, including fragile, conflict-affected, cross-border, humanitarian, urban poor, remote, and hard-to-reach settings.

Capacity to convene, advocate, build consensus, and mobilize action across governments, regional bodies, partners, communities, academia, the private sector, and civil society.

Commitment to equity, accountability, transparency, ethical conduct, and effective solutions for sustainable immunization impact.

Application

Interested individuals are invited to submit an expression of interest package that includes:

a brief biography and

a letter of interest outlining their relevant experience, expertise, motivation for serving on the CIAC, and the specific contribution they would bring to advancing continental immunization priorities.

Members must maintain a resolute urgency for immunization progress in Africa. Please do not apply if you do not bring this.

Submissions should be sent no later than 21 July 2026. Africa CDC will review submissions against the desired expertise, leadership profile, regional and gender balance, and overall composition required for an effective and representative Council.

TITLE: Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program 2027: Funded Research Opportunities With Stipends of Up to $65,000 Per Year

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program 2027 is now accepting applications from graduate students, doctoral candidates, postdoctoral researchers, and senior scholars seeking to conduct independent research using the Smithsonian Institution’s internationally significant collections, facilities, field stations, archives, libraries, laboratories, and expert staff.

Through the program, selected researchers can undertake full-time, primarily in-residence research at an appropriate Smithsonian museum, research institute, center, office, or field station. Depending on the applicant’s academic level and research discipline, financial support ranges from a $10,000 stipend for a ten-week graduate appointment to an annual stipend of up to $65,000 for eligible postdoctoral and senior researchers in Earth and Planetary Sciences.

The Smithsonian welcomes research proposals across the sciences, humanities, history, art, anthropology, environmental studies, materials research, molecular biology, and other disciplines connected to the Institution’s work. Interdisciplinary proposals and projects that broaden or diversify research within Smithsonian fields are particularly encouraged.

Applications for the 2027 cycle must be submitted through the Smithsonian Online Academic Appointment System by October 15, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

About the Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program

The Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program supports independent research and advanced study directly connected to the Smithsonian’s collections, research interests, facilities, and professional expertise.

The program is administered by the Smithsonian’s Office of Academic Appointments and Internships. Successful applicants work with Smithsonian research professionals who serve as principal advisors, hosts, co-advisors, or consultants during the appointment.

A successful proposal must do more than describe an interesting academic topic. Applicants must demonstrate why the Smithsonian is the appropriate institution for the proposed work. This ordinarily requires identifying specific Smithsonian collections, archives, laboratories, equipment, field stations, library resources, research programs, or staff expertise that are essential to the project.

Researchers are expected to spend most of the appointment at the Smithsonian. Approved fieldwork or research travel may form part of the project where justified, but the program is fundamentally designed as an in-residence research experience.

Research Areas Supported by the Smithsonian

The Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program accepts proposals connected to disciplines actively pursued across the Institution. Applications of an interdisciplinary nature are also encouraged.

Supported research areas include:

Animal behavior

Ecology and environmental science, with particular interest in tropical research

Anthropology

Archaeology

Cultural anthropology

Astrophysics and astronomy

Earth sciences

History of science and technology

History of art

Decorative arts

Social and cultural history of the United States

Applicants should consult the Smithsonian’s official Fields of Research information and the publication titled Smithsonian Opportunities for Research and Study before selecting a host unit or proposed advisor.

Researchers who intend to work specifically at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory should review that observatory’s separate procedures because its application requirements and deadlines may differ from the central program.

Fellowship Levels, Duration, and Financial Support

The appropriate application level depends on the applicant’s academic status and the date on which the qualifying degree was or will be completed.

Ten-Week Graduate Student Appointment

This option is intended for students who are formally enrolled in a graduate degree program but have not yet advanced to doctoral candidacy.

Applicants must:

Be enrolled in a graduate program at a degree-granting institution when applying.

Remain enrolled when the Smithsonian appointment begins.

Have completed at least one full-time semester, or its equivalent, before the appointment starts.

Not yet have advanced to doctoral candidacy if enrolled in a doctoral program.

Master’s students and eligible early-stage doctoral students may apply.

The appointment lasts ten weeks and provides a stipend of $10,000. Graduate student recipients are not eligible for the separate research allowance and should not submit a research budget justification.

Predoctoral Appointment

The predoctoral option is intended for doctoral candidates who need to conduct research for their dissertations.

By the time the appointment begins, the applicant’s university must:

Approve the proposed dissertation research at the Smithsonian.

Confirm that the applicant has satisfied all doctoral requirements other than completion of the dissertation.

Recognize the applicant as a candidate for a PhD or an equivalent doctoral degree.

Predoctoral appointments normally last between three and twelve months.

The stipend is $45,000 per year, prorated when an appointment is shorter than twelve months. Eligible applicants may also request a research allowance of up to $5,000 per year, subject to approval of the proposed budget and justification.

Postdoctoral Appointment

Applicants must complete their doctorate or equivalent degree before the Smithsonian appointment begins. A person who is still completing a doctorate at the time of application may apply if all degree requirements will be completed before the proposed starting date.

Postdoctoral appointments ordinarily last between three and twelve months. Postdoctoral applicants working in science may request an appointment of up to 24 months, subject to program approval and available funding.

The standard stipend is $60,000 per year. Eligible postdoctoral researchers in Earth and Planetary Sciences may receive $65,000 per year.

A research allowance of up to $5,000 per year may also be requested. Stipends and research allowances are prorated where applicable.

Senior Researcher Appointment

Senior applicants must have held a PhD or equivalent qualification for at least five years. For the current cycle, applicants who received their qualifying degree before October 15, 2021, fall within the senior category.

The standard senior stipend is $60,000 per year. Eligible senior researchers in Earth and Planetary Sciences may receive $65,000 per year.

Senior appointments are generally offered for periods of three to twelve months, with a possible research allowance of up to $5,000 per year.

Researchers who are five or more years beyond their doctorate but experienced a substantial leave of absence from research may request consideration under the postdoctoral category. They must explain the circumstances in the additional-information section of the application.

Research and Relocation Support

Eligible predoctoral, postdoctoral, and senior applicants may request up to $5,000 per year for research-related expenses. The proposed costs must be necessary for completing the research and clearly explained in the budget justification.

Potentially eligible expenses may include:

Research equipment

Essential supplies and materials

Research-related travel

Specialized services required for the project

Other justified research costs

The research budget must not include the applicant’s stipend, temporary relocation expenses, or the cost of directly hiring personnel. If a project requires more than the maximum research allowance, the applicant must identify the expected source of the additional funding.

Separate support for temporary relocation to the Smithsonian may be available. Applicants should not place relocation expenses in the research allowance budget.

The Smithsonian does not provide funding for the travel or living expenses of a fellow’s dependants.

All Smithsonian fellowship funds, including stipends and any research or travel allowances, may be subject to taxation. The stipend is intended to support research and study; it is not classified as salary or employment compensation.

Academic and General Eligibility Requirements

In addition to the academic requirements for each appointment level, applicants must satisfy the following general conditions:

The proposed project must fall within a research discipline pursued at the Smithsonian.

The application must contain a specific and detailed research proposal.

The applicant must explain why Smithsonian resources and expertise are necessary for the research.

The applicant must be able to carry out full-time research during the proposed appointment.

Applicants whose native language is not English must be able to write and communicate fluently in English.

Every application document must be submitted in English.

Academic records issued in another language must be accompanied by English translations.

Past and current Smithsonian fellowship recipients may apply for another award.

Former Smithsonian employees or contractors must ordinarily complete one full year of separation before applying.

A current Smithsonian employee or contractor cannot simultaneously hold a fellowship without prior approval from the Office of Academic Appointments and Internships.

The Smithsonian states that it does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, pregnancy, national origin, age where legally protected, disability, genetic information, parental status, or military service.

Finding a Smithsonian Advisor and Host Unit

Identifying an appropriate Smithsonian advisor is one of the most important parts of the application process.

Applicants are strongly encouraged to contact potential advisors before submitting their applications. Early communication can help determine:

Whether the proposed research is feasible at the Smithsonian.

Whether the required collections, archives, library materials, laboratories, equipment, data, or facilities will be available.

Whether the proposed advisor will be in residence during the intended appointment period.

Whether the research timeline is realistic.

Whether additional permissions will be required.

Which Smithsonian unit should be selected in SOLAA.

The Smithsonian’s Opportunities for Research and Study publication lists research staff, educational backgrounds, specializations, and departmental research interests.

Smithsonian research staff may serve as principal advisors, co-advisors, or consultants. Conservation staff may serve as principal advisors for conservation projects or as co-advisors and consultants. Affiliated research staff may normally serve as co-advisors or consultants when they will be present for a substantial portion of the proposed appointment.

The host unit must be the unit of the proposed principal advisor. This unit must also match the “preferred unit” entered in the SOLAA application. If the proposed advisor later becomes unavailable, the Smithsonian may assign another advisor within the selected host unit.

Contacting an advisor does not guarantee selection. However, a proposal is likely to be stronger when it demonstrates that the applicant has investigated the availability of the relevant Smithsonian expertise and resources.

Conditions of the Research Appointment

Selected researchers must devote full-time effort to the approved project. Fellows are expected to remain in residence at the Smithsonian except during authorized fieldwork, research travel, or other approved absences.

Appointments for the 2027 cycle must begin between June 1, 2027, and May 30, 2028. The start date must fall on either the first or third Monday of a month.

Before proposing dates, applicants should consider:

Their academic calendar

Preliminary examinations

Coursework requirements

Dissertation or degree-completion schedules

Availability of the proposed Smithsonian advisor

Availability of collections, laboratories, equipment, and facilities

Time required for visas or relocation

Any scheduled fieldwork or research travel

Applicants should agree on the proposed dates with their prospective principal advisor before submission.

Researchers may receive additional financial support from other sources for matters such as equipment or research travel, provided that the additional funding does not impose duties that interfere with the full-time Smithsonian appointment. Written approval is required before accepting additional stipend support.

Submitting an application does not legally oblige a successful candidate to accept the appointment.

Facilities and Research Resources Available to Fellows

Selected fellows are generally provided with research space in the Smithsonian department or unit where they are based. The exact level of administrative, technical, equipment, and support services depends on the host department’s capacity and policies.

Applicants should discuss their requirements with the proposed advisor before applying, especially where the project depends on specialized equipment, laboratories, collection access, data, imaging facilities, or other limited resources.

Fellows can also receive access to Smithsonian Libraries and Archives services, including:

Library borrowing privileges

Interlibrary loans

Document delivery

Database searches

Reference assistance

Specialized research collections

Access to particular collections, specimens, archives, datasets, equipment, or restricted materials may require additional permission.

Selection Criteria

Applications are evaluated by scholars working in appropriate fields. Selection is based primarily on the quality and feasibility of the proposed research rather than on the applicant’s financial need.

Reviewers consider:

Scholarly merit of the proposal: The project should address an important question and make a meaningful contribution to its discipline.

Applicant’s ability: The applicant’s education, research experience, publications, achievements, and previous work should demonstrate the ability to complete the project.

Feasibility: The methodology, timeline, resources, and proposed duration should be realistic.

Smithsonian relevance: The application must clearly establish how Smithsonian collections, facilities, staff expertise, archives, laboratories, or other resources will contribute to the research.

Potential contribution to professional goals: Reviewers consider how the appointment would support the applicant’s development and broader scholarly objectives.

The number of appointments offered each year depends on the availability of program funding. Meeting the basic eligibility criteria therefore does not guarantee selection.

Documents Required for the Application

Application documents must be uploaded individually through SOLAA. Supported formats include BMP, DOC, DOCX, GIF, JPEG, JPG, PDF, PNG, RTF, TIF, TIFF, TXT, XLS, and XLSX. Each uploaded file is subject to a 3 MB limit.

1. Research Abstract

Applicants must submit an abstract that:

Does not exceed one page.

Is double-spaced.

Clearly summarizes the proposed research.

Identifies the main question, approach, Smithsonian connection, and expected significance.

2. Full Research Proposal

The research proposal must not exceed six double-spaced pages. The six-page limit includes tables, figures, and images but excludes the separate abstract and bibliography.

The proposal should:

Use pages approximately 8.5 by 11 inches or 210 by 297 millimetres.

Have margins of at least one inch.

Use a font size of at least 11 points.

Describe the proposed research in detail.

Explain the methodology.

Discuss the importance of the research to the wider discipline.

Explain how the project supports the applicant’s scholarly goals.

Justify why the research must be conducted at the Smithsonian.

Identify the Smithsonian resources that will be used.

Identify the proposed principal advisor and any co-advisors or consultants.

Address required permissions for collections or facilities outside the advisor’s unit.

3. Research Timeline

The timeline should divide the proposed appointment into clear research phases and explain the expected period required for each phase.

Applicants requesting a two-year science postdoctoral appointment must provide a timeline covering the complete proposed period.

4. Budget and Budget Justification

Applicants requesting a research allowance must provide an itemized budget and explain why each cost is necessary.

The budget may cover equipment, supplies, research-related travel, and other direct research support. It must not include stipend costs, relocation expenses, or funding for direct hires.

Graduate student applicants should not submit a research budget because the ten-week graduate appointment does not include a research allowance.

5. Bibliography

Applicants must provide a bibliography of literature relevant to the proposed project. It should demonstrate familiarity with the existing scholarship and position the proposed research within its academic field.

6. Curriculum Vitae

The CV must:

Be current.

Not exceed four pages.

Include relevant education and research experience.

Identify previous and current fellowships, grants, awards, publications, and professional accomplishments.

Explain the applicant’s level of English reading, writing, and speaking proficiency if English is not their native language.

7. Academic Transcripts

Unofficial transcripts are acceptable. Applicants may upload up to three transcript files, with each file subject to the 3 MB limit.

Transcript requirements differ by level:

Graduate student applicants must provide undergraduate and graduate transcripts.

Predoctoral applicants must provide graduate transcripts.

Postdoctoral applicants must provide graduate transcripts.

Senior applicants are not required to submit transcripts.

Documents issued in languages other than English must be accompanied by translations.

8. Two Academic or Professional References

Applicants must provide the names and email addresses of two people familiar with their research abilities and academic or professional work.

The proposed Smithsonian advisor, co-advisor, or consultant should not be used as a referee.

SOLAA sends an electronic request to each referee. Applicants may send these requests before completing the rest of the application. Referees cannot view the candidate’s application.

References should preferably be submitted by the application deadline. SOLAA may accept a reference after the deadline, but there is no guarantee that a late letter will reach reviewers before the evaluation begins. Applicants should monitor their accounts and follow up with referees whose letters remain outstanding.

Additional Requirements for Research With Indigenous Communities

Applicants proposing work involving Indigenous communities should explain:

The current status of consultation or collaboration.

The appropriate community contacts.

How the research will respect relevant rights holders and knowledge holders.

How findings will be communicated or shared with the participating communities.

A letter of approval or endorsement from a tribal community, community representative, knowledge holder, artist, or other appropriate rights holder can strengthen the application and may be submitted as an additional reference.

How to Apply for the Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program 2027

Applications must be submitted electronically through the Smithsonian Online Academic Appointment System.

Applicants should follow these steps:

Create or access a SOLAA account.

Complete the required general profile information.

Select “Fellowship” as the appointment type.

Select the Office of Academic Appointments and Internships.

Locate the Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program.

Enter 2027 as the application cycle.

Select the correct academic level: graduate, predoctoral, postdoctoral, or senior.

Select the preferred Smithsonian unit that corresponds to the proposed principal advisor.

Upload every required document as an individual file.

Enter the names and email addresses of two referees.

Send the reference requests through SOLAA.

Review the application for completeness, accuracy, formatting, and file-size compliance.

Submit the complete application before the deadline.

Continue monitoring SOLAA to confirm whether the reference letters have been received.

Applicants should not wait until the final day to upload documents. Technical problems, oversized files, formatting issues, and incomplete reference information could prevent timely submission.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

October 15, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time

Applicants must enter 2027 as the cycle year in SOLAA. The deadline is stated in Eastern Time, so international applicants should carefully confirm the corresponding date and time in their own country.

The Smithsonian expects to communicate decisions through SOLAA in mid-March. Successful appointments must begin between June 1, 2027, and May 30, 2028.

Practical Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

A strong application should establish a direct and convincing connection between the proposed project and the Smithsonian.

Applicants should:

Contact a potential advisor well before the deadline.

Identify the precise collections, facilities, archives, laboratories, datasets, field stations, or staff expertise required.

Avoid presenting a generic proposal that could be completed equally well at any institution.

Explain the project’s wider scholarly importance.

Use a realistic methodology and timeline.

Match the proposed duration to the amount of work required.

Follow every page, margin, font, format, and file-size requirement.

Obtain any necessary preliminary permissions.

Select referees who can evaluate the applicant’s research ability in detail.

Give referees sufficient time to prepare strong letters.

Ensure the preferred Smithsonian unit matches the principal advisor’s unit.

Present a proportionate, itemized, and well-justified research budget.

Submit the application early enough to correct any technical problems.

Applicants should also prepare every part of the submission in their own words. The Smithsonian treats plagiarism in applications seriously and may disqualify a candidate if copied or improperly attributed work is identified.

Contact Information

Questions about the application may be directed to:

Office of Academic Appointments and Internships

Email: InternsAndFellows@si.edu

Official information: Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program

Application portal: Smithsonian Online Academic Appointment System

Conclusion

The Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program 2027 offers a significant opportunity for researchers to undertake independent, full-time work within one of the world’s most extensive networks of museums, laboratories, research centers, archives, libraries, and field stations.

With appointments available for graduate students, doctoral candidates, postdoctoral scholars, and established senior researchers, the program supports projects across the natural sciences, social sciences, history, anthropology, art, culture, environmental research, and numerous interdisciplinary fields.

Financial support includes stipends ranging from $10,000 for a ten-week graduate appointment to as much as $65,000 per year for eligible Earth and Planetary Sciences researchers. Qualified applicants may also request research and temporary relocation support.

A competitive application must clearly explain not only what the applicant intends to study, but why the Smithsonian’s particular collections, facilities, resources, and professional expertise are essential to the project. Candidates should identify and contact a potential advisor early, develop a focused and feasible proposal, and submit all documents through SOLAA before October 15, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

TITLE: Clean Slate Initiative Policy Coordinator Job 2026 | Apply for Remote Policy Position in the USA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Clean Slate Initiative (CSI) is seeking a Policy Coordinator to support its policy team through project management, policy research, technical assistance and knowledge management.

The full-time position offers an annual salary of $56,000–$62,000 and is a remote role open to candidates based in the United States. Applicants must be authorised to work in the U.S. without requiring current or future visa sponsorship. The application deadline is September 15, 2026.

About The Clean Slate Initiative

Founded in 2019, The Clean Slate Initiative (CSI) works across the United States and in Congress to advance laws that automatically seal eligible criminal records for people who have completed their sentences and remained crime-free.

The organisation also works to expand eligibility for record sealing and promote policies that provide people with records a fair opportunity to work, pursue education, contribute to their communities and achieve their full potential.

According to the supplied opportunity information, 14 states and Washington, D.C. have passed Clean Slate laws impacting more than 18 million people. CSI works with bipartisan leaders and organisations and focuses on policy design, implementation and campaign strategies that centre lived experience.

About the Policy Coordinator Position

The Policy Coordinator will support CSI’s Policy Department through project management, policy research and technical assistance.

Reporting to the Public Policy Director, the successful candidate will help maintain knowledge of record-relief policies across all 50 states, support cross-functional initiatives and develop resources that inform CSI’s policy, campaign and implementation work.

The role is particularly suited to someone who is highly organised, detail-oriented and interested in translating complex policy information into practical resources that help teams make informed decisions.

Key Responsibilities

The Policy Coordinator will contribute to the Policy Department’s operations and strategic projects.

Project Management and Coordination

Responsibilities include:

Supporting the Policy Department’s day-to-day operations.

Coordinating meetings and tracking tasks.

Contributing to both small-scale initiatives and larger strategic policy projects.

Ensuring project timelines and deliverables remain on track.

Policy Tracking and Knowledge Management

The successful candidate will create, maintain and update internal policy tracking tools, legislative comparison frameworks and knowledge templates related to record-relief laws across all 50 states.

The role also involves tracking legislative developments using PolicyNote and maintaining accessible summaries of state policy landscapes, implementation questions and emerging trends.

Policy Research

The Policy Coordinator will conduct research on record-relief and related policies, including:

Record sealing

Expungement

Automated relief

Petition-based relief

The candidate will also compile and organise information concerning eligibility rules, exclusions, waiting periods, procedural requirements, implementation structures and other important policy choices.

Technical Assistance and Partner Support

The role will involve responding to policy questions from CSI staff and supporting technical assistance, coalition and partner meetings when required.

Who Should Apply?

CSI is looking for a candidate with experience in policy, legislative, legal or public policy research.

The ideal candidate should be:

Highly organised and intellectually curious.

Interested in researching and understanding detailed policy issues.

Strong in project management and organisation.

Exceptionally attentive to detail.

Able to manage multiple priorities and meet deadlines.

Comfortable working in a collaborative, fast-paced environment.

A strong written and verbal communicator.

Passionate about equitable criminal justice policy and CSI’s mission.

Familiar with tools such as Asana, Google Workspace, PolicyNote and Airtable, or equivalent platforms.

What Success Looks Like

CSI identifies several indicators of success for the Policy Coordinator.

The successful candidate will be expected to:

Maintain accurate and up-to-date policy tracking systems and legislative resources.

Produce high-quality policy research that informs campaign strategy, implementation and technical assistance.

Keep Policy Department projects organised and progressing through effective project management and follow-through.

Provide timely and accurate responses to policy questions.

Build strong cross-functional relationships.

Contribute to a collaborative and high-performing Policy team.

Clean Slate laws continue to evolve across different states, creating an opportunity for the Policy Coordinator to develop expertise in a rapidly changing policy environment.

The role provides an opportunity to build systems, strengthen knowledge management and become a trusted internal resource on record-relief policy.

$56,000–$62,000 per year

Pre-tax transportation benefits.

Paid holidays.

Paid vacation.

Paid sick leave.

Paid casual time off.

The Policy Coordinator position is full-time and remote.

CSI is location-agnostic regarding where candidates are based within the United States. Candidates who live near the organisation’s Orlando office may discuss a hybrid or in-office arrangement.

The successful candidate must:

Be authorised to work in the United States.

Work collaboratively with colleagues across different time zones.

Live close to a major airport and be able to travel approximately 10–15%.

Attend required on-site planning meetings at least twice a year in various locations.

TITLE: JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program 2026: Fully Funded Japan Visit for African Animation Professionals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program – Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) offers African animation professionals an opportunity to travel to Japan for an approximately 12-day international exchange and professional learning experience focused on animation production, industry exposure, networking, cultural exchange, and collaboration.

Organized by the Japan International Cooperation Center (JICE) as part of the Japan-Africa Youth Program, the initiative is designed to bring together African animation professionals and Japanese anime creators, companies, organizations, and educational institutions.

For selected participants, program participation and travel expenses are free of charge, making this a significant opportunity for professionals seeking international exposure and connections within Japan’s globally influential animation industry.

The application deadline is Tuesday, September 8, 2026, at 23:59 Japan Standard Time (JST).

About the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program

The Japan-Africa Youth Program is an international exchange initiative promoted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan and implemented as part of efforts to strengthen mutual understanding and relationships between young people from Japan and Africa.

The broader program focuses on allowing young people from both regions to learn from one another through direct interaction, observation, cultural experiences, and professional exchange.

The Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) forms part of this wider initiative and focuses specifically on professionals working in Africa’s animation industry.

The program recognizes the growing importance of animation and anime as creative industries capable of connecting cultures, creating economic opportunities, developing talent, and encouraging international collaboration.

Through the Japan visit, African participants will have the opportunity to gain first-hand exposure to Japan’s animation ecosystem while building relationships with Japanese professionals and organizations.

What Is the JICE Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation?

The Professionals Japan Visit Program for Co-creation (Animation Production) is an international exchange and professional development initiative specifically designed for African animation professionals.

JICE plans to invite 20 individuals working at anime production companies in Africa to Japan for approximately 12 days.

Rather than being simply a tourism or cultural visit, the program is structured around professional exposure, networking, learning, cultural exchange, and the development of future partnerships between African and Japanese animation stakeholders.

Participants are expected to explore Japan’s anime production environment and learn more about the country’s animation-related industries and educational institutions.

The program also aims to create opportunities for African participants to connect directly with Japanese companies and creators, potentially laying the groundwork for future cooperation and co-creation.

Key Objectives of the Program

The initiative has several interconnected objectives.

1. Strengthen Japan-Africa professional networks

One of the central goals is to establish stronger relationships between animation professionals from Africa and Japan.

By bringing professionals together in Japan, the program provides an environment where participants can exchange ideas, discuss industry developments, identify areas of mutual interest, and explore potential future collaboration.

2. Increase exposure to Japan’s animation industry

Japan has an internationally recognized anime and animation ecosystem.

The visit is intended to provide African professionals with an opportunity to experience aspects of this ecosystem directly, including exposure to animation production sites, related industries, companies, and educational institutions.

This type of first-hand experience can provide insights that may be difficult to obtain through online research alone.

3. Encourage co-creation

The program is specifically framed around co-creation, meaning that the goal is not simply for African professionals to observe Japan’s animation sector.

Instead, the initiative seeks to encourage relationships through which professionals from both regions can exchange ideas and potentially develop future projects together.

This makes networking and relationship-building important components of the experience.

4. Promote cultural understanding

Participants will also have opportunities to deepen their understanding of Japanese culture, values, mindset, and cultural heritage.

At the same time, interaction between African and Japanese participants can contribute to greater awareness of Africa’s own creative industries and cultural perspectives.

5. Support future African leaders

The broader Japan-Africa Youth Program seeks to empower young people to become leaders capable of contributing to Africa’s future development.

For animation professionals, this means combining professional development with international exposure and intercultural exchange.

What Will Participants Experience in Japan?

The program is expected to last approximately 12 days, during which selected participants will take part in activities connected to animation, professional exchange, and cultural learning.

Although the exact itinerary should be confirmed in the official Draft Standard Itinerary and Application Guidelines, the announcement indicates that participants will have opportunities to explore:

Anime production sites.

Animation-related industries.

Japanese animation companies and organizations.

Educational institutions connected to the animation sector.

Japanese cultural and social environments.

Professional networking opportunities.

Cultural exchange activities.

Discussions and interactions with Japanese creators and industry stakeholders.

The program is therefore particularly relevant to professionals who want to understand how Japan’s animation ecosystem operates and how African and Japanese creative professionals could collaborate.

Who Is the Program Looking For?

The call is specifically aimed at African anime creators and professionals working within anime production companies or organizations in Africa.

JICE intends to accommodate 20 participants in total.

However, the application structure is particularly important.

Applications are being sought from interested companies and organizations, with participation limited to a maximum of 10 companies in total.

Each participating company can send no more than two individuals.

The two participants are expected to consist of:

One company executive

The first participant should be a company executive who will act as the decision-maker.

This role is important because the program is designed to encourage organizational and business-level collaboration in addition to individual professional development.

One creative professional

The second participant should be a creative professional working in the animation field.

This allows the program to bring both organizational decision-making perspectives and hands-on creative expertise into the Japan-Africa exchange.

Geographic Eligibility: Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is specifically targeted at Africa.

JICE describes the initiative as targeting African anime creators, and the program is intended for young professionals in the animation industry from Africa.

Therefore, professionals and organizations operating within the African animation sector should pay particular attention to this opportunity.

However, the announcement provided does not list every eligible African country individually. Applicants should therefore consult the official Application Guidelines to confirm whether their specific country, organization, and professional circumstances meet all requirements.

In other words, the opportunity has a clear Africa-wide focus, but applicants should not assume that every organization automatically qualifies without checking the detailed guidelines.

How Many Participants Will Be Selected?

The program intends to invite 20 individuals to Japan.

At the organizational level:

Up to 10 companies or organizations can participate.

Each company can nominate a maximum of two participants.

The two participants should include a company executive/decision-maker and a creative professional.

This structure means that the program is not simply seeking 20 unrelated individual applicants. It is designed to engage animation companies and organizations and facilitate meaningful professional connections between African and Japanese stakeholders.

Major Benefits of the JICE Japan Visit Program

Participating in the JICE Japan-Africa Youth Program can offer several professional and personal advantages.

1. Fully Covered Program Participation and Travel Expenses

One of the most significant benefits is that participation in the program and travel expenses are free of charge.

This can substantially reduce the financial barrier associated with participating in an international professional exchange program.

However, applicants should carefully distinguish between expenses covered by the program and personal expenses that remain their responsibility.

2. International Exposure

Selected professionals will travel to Japan and gain direct exposure to one of the world’s most influential animation ecosystems.

This can broaden their understanding of:

Animation production.

Creative industry structures.

Professional practices.

Industry collaboration.

Animation-related education.

Cultural influences on creative production.

Potential international partnerships.

3. Networking With Japanese Animation Professionals

Networking is one of the core elements of the initiative.

Participants will have opportunities to interact with Japanese animation creators and related organizations.

For African animation professionals, these relationships could potentially contribute to future:

Partnerships.

Creative collaborations.

Knowledge exchange.

Business relationships.

Co-production opportunities.

Professional networks.

The program is particularly valuable for professionals interested in building connections beyond their domestic markets.

4. Exposure to Animation Production Sites

Participants are expected to have opportunities to discover Japanese anime production sites and related industry environments.

First-hand exposure can help professionals understand how animation projects are developed, produced, managed, and supported within Japan’s creative ecosystem.

5. Access to Animation-Related Institutions

The program also intends to expose participants to animation-related industries and educational institutions.

This can be useful for professionals interested in understanding the relationship between education, skills development, creative production, and the commercial animation sector.

6. Cross-Cultural Learning

The program is also designed to deepen participants’ understanding of Japan’s:

Values.

Mindset.

Culture.

Cultural heritage.

Social systems.

At the same time, participants bring their own African professional and cultural experiences into the exchange.

This creates a two-way learning process rather than a one-sided study visit.

7. Potential for Future Co-Creation

The concept of co-creation is central to the program.

African and Japanese animation professionals can use the exchange to identify shared interests and explore ways of working together.

TITLE: Call for Co-Hosting – Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) will hold its 24th Biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors, and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) in July 2027. The AAU hereby invites applications from member institutions for the co-hosting of this prestigious conference.

COREVIP is an assembly of the Chief Executive Officers of AAU member institutions or their representatives. It is held once every two years with the purpose of:

collectively examining themes identified as common concerns and priorities for the development of higher education in member institutions and Africa in general,

making recommendations primarily to members, as well as to the Governing Board of the Association, and to the Secretariat, and

acting as a mid-term forum for taking stock of the implementation of the decisions of the previous AAU General Conference and recommending corrective actions.

The AAU’s statutory conferences, such as the COREVIP, are normally jointly organized with a member institution in good standing, ie. having zero arrears in annual subscription payment. In light of this, the AAU invites applications from its member institutions in good standing for the co-hosting of this prestigious biennial conference. It should be noted that the co-hosting of this most important event on the calendar of the African higher education community provides very high-level visibility and exposure to the host institution and country because of the calibre and number of academic leaders, policymakers, researchers, development partners, industry, and other stakeholders that usually attend it, and it is, therefore, a highly sought-after event.

Theme for COREVIP 2027: To be determined.

The Host’s Responsibilities

The host university will be expected to contribute to the organisation of the Conference, financially or in kind, in the areas of:

Local transportation for participants.

Airport “meet and greet” (reception and facilitation of immigration procedures).

Traditional items as gifts to presenters and sessional chairs.

Welcome reception or dinner for participants.

Publicity and media coverage (local press, radio and TV, conference photographer).

Arrangement of courtesy calls by the Governing Board on appropriate government authorities in the host country.

Arrangement of excursion visits by delegates.

Providing the Secretariat for the Conference (equipment and supplies).

Decorations, banners, invitations to Opening/Closing Ceremony and receptions.

Cultural display during open and closing ceremonies.

Institutions interested in co-hosting the 24th Biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) should officially apply by filling this form: https://forms.office.com/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=ZDIG_HEQC0elgxzC-lC4v5zOX9CysWZCtVAlnK39wBxUOFZTVUJQTlQyM1FNOEdaUEVUQ05FWTk3SC4u

TITLE: Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship 2026: Up to $20,000 for Documentary Filmmakers Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship is an exciting funding opportunity for documentary filmmakers who want to tell compelling, cinematic stories about the rapidly evolving world of psychedelics.

The fellowship is designed to support filmmakers producing documentaries that explore the science, policy, business and culture surrounding psychedelics. Through substantial production funding, the program seeks to help a new generation of filmmakers bring important and underreported stories to audiences through film.

For 2026, the fellowship offers two different grant opportunities: a Feature-Length Documentary Grant providing up to $20,000 to selected filmmakers and a Short-Form Documentary Grant providing up to $10,000 to selected filmmakers.

The application deadline is October 5, 2026.

The fellowship is a project of the U.C. Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics and is intended to foster a diverse group of filmmakers documenting a field that is undergoing significant scientific, cultural, political and social change.

About the Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship

The psychedelic field is developing rapidly, with growing public interest in areas such as psychedelic-assisted therapy, scientific research, drug policy, cultural practices, business and emerging approaches to mental health and wellness.

The Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship seeks filmmakers capable of transforming these developments into strong cinematic narratives.

Rather than simply funding general filmmaking activities, the fellowship is interested in projects with compelling stories that can engage audiences while providing deeper insight into the issues surrounding psychedelics.

According to the fellowship, it is looking for groundbreaking narratives fit for cinematic storytelling, particularly untold stories that can illuminate the science, policy, business and culture of this emerging era.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to filmmakers who have identified an important story that has not yet received sufficient attention.

What Funding Is Available?

The fellowship has two distinct funding tracks.

1. Feature-Length Documentary Grant

The Feature-Length Documentary Grant will provide:

Up to $20,000 per filmmaker

Three documentary filmmakers will be selected

Funding can support the production or post-production of a feature-length documentary

The documentary must be more than 40 minutes in length

The project should be a documentary or nonfiction film rather than fiction.

The feature-length grant is particularly suited to filmmakers who already have a substantial documentary project underway and need additional resources to complete production or post-production.

The application materials indicate that applicants should be the director of the project, have relevant prior work samples, have access to participants and locations, and be independently producing the project.

What can the funding help with?

Depending on the project’s needs, documentary production funding can potentially help a filmmaker cover costs associated with completing the project, such as:

Production activities

Post-production

Filming

Editing

Other legitimate project-related costs

Costs necessary to move the documentary toward completion

The fellowship does not require grantees to submit individual expenses for reimbursement. However, successful applicants are expected to provide a report explaining how the grant was spent and what was accomplished on the project.

2. Short-Form Documentary Grant

The Short-Form Documentary Grant will provide:

Up to $10,000 per filmmaker

Up to five documentary filmmakers may be selected

Funding is intended for the production of short-form documentaries

The film must be 40 minutes or less

This track is particularly important for emerging filmmakers because it can provide meaningful financial support for a shorter documentary project.

The fellowship specifically encourages student filmmakers currently enrolled in graduate programs to consider the Short-Form Documentary Grant, although additional eligibility requirements apply to student applicants.

Special Opportunity for Student Filmmakers

Students should pay particular attention to the eligibility requirements because the fellowship does not treat student applications in the same way as applications from established independent filmmakers.

For the student route, eligible applicants must be enrolled in a U.S.-based undergraduate or graduate-level film or journalism program at an intermediate level or higher and must have a faculty advisor supporting the project. The faculty advisor must provide a letter of support by the application deadline.

The fellowship’s FAQ further clarifies that only graduate-school-level student films are eligible for the Short-Form Documentary Grant.

Therefore, prospective student applicants should carefully check the current application requirements before preparing their submission.

Important student restriction

A current student cannot apply for the Feature-Length Documentary Grant under the current rules.

Who Can Apply?

One of the most attractive aspects of this opportunity is its international eligibility.

The fellowship confirms that both grants are open to filmmakers worldwide, regardless of nationality or citizenship status.

This means filmmakers from:

Africa

Asia

Europe

North America

South America

Central America

The Caribbean

Oceania

Other parts of the world

may apply, provided they satisfy the relevant grant’s project and applicant requirements.

There is no stated nationality or citizenship restriction preventing international filmmakers from applying.

For example, a qualified documentary filmmaker based in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Uganda, Rwanda, India, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Brazil or another country can potentially apply.

However, being from an eligible country alone does not guarantee eligibility. Applicants must also meet the requirements for their chosen grant.

Eligibility Requirements for Documentary Filmmakers

For the feature-length production/post-production route, the application requirements indicate that applicants should satisfy several important criteria.

1. You must be the director

The applicant must be the director of the documentary project.

This is important because the funding is intended to support individual filmmakers who are directly responsible for the creative direction of the project.

2. You need relevant previous work

Applicants must have prior work samples in which they played a principal role, such as:

Director

Co-director

Producer

Co-producer

Therefore, applicants should be prepared to demonstrate their filmmaking experience through previous work samples.

3. The project must be documentary or nonfiction

The project must be a:

Documentary

Nonfiction film

Hybrid documentary

The fellowship does not support fiction films.

4. Feature projects must meet the required length

For the feature-length grant, the project must be at least 40 minutes in length according to the application materials.

5. The project should already be in production or post-production

The feature production/post-production grant is designed for projects that have progressed beyond the earliest development stage.

The application recommends that applicants have at least 10% of their footage shot by the application date, although applicants should consult the current FAQ for clarification about project stages.

6. You must have access to the story

Applicants must have confirmed access to:

Participants

Locations

This is important because the selection committee wants to see that the proposed documentary is realistically achievable.

7. The project must be independently produced

The documentary must be independently produced.

Works produced as “work for hire” are not eligible for the relevant production/post-production grant.

8. Only individuals can apply

Applications must come from individual filmmakers.

Organizations such as:

Universities

Foundations

Nonprofit businesses

Other organizations

cannot apply on behalf of a project.

What Types of Stories Is the Fellowship Looking For?

The fellowship is intentionally broad in its thematic scope.

It is interested in documentary stories examining different dimensions of psychedelics, including:

Science

Projects may explore scientific research and the developing understanding of psychedelic substances and their effects.

Policy

Filmmakers can examine laws, regulations, drug policy and the changing political environment surrounding psychedelics.

Business

Stories can investigate the growing commercial ecosystem surrounding psychedelic research, services, companies and related industries.

Culture

Documentaries may examine how psychedelics intersect with culture, communities, traditions and changing social attitudes.

The fellowship is particularly interested in untold and compelling narratives rather than generic treatments of the topic.

A strong application should therefore demonstrate why the proposed story matters and why audiences should care about it.

International Applicants Are Welcome

International filmmakers should take particular note of this opportunity.

The official FAQ explicitly states that filmmakers residing outside the United States can apply, and that both grants are open worldwide regardless of nationality or citizenship status.

Therefore, you do not have to be a U.S. citizen to apply.

However, international applicants should be aware that receiving fellowship funds may have tax implications, particularly for foreign nationals working in the United States. UC Berkeley may require documentation through its tax compliance process, and foreign nationals receiving fellowship payments may be subject to withholding depending on their circumstances.

Can the Documentary Be in Another Language?

Yes.

A filmmaker can produce a documentary in a language other than English, provided that the finished film will have English subtitles.

However, the application itself must be written in English because the selection committee does not have the capacity to evaluate applications in other languages.

This is particularly useful for filmmakers documenting psychedelic-related stories within communities where English is not the primary language.

Important Restrictions Applicants Should Know

Before applying, filmmakers should carefully consider several restrictions.

Fiction films are not eligible

The fellowship does not fund fiction films. The proposed project must be documentary, nonfiction or an eligible hybrid documentary.

Cannabis stories are not eligible

The fellowship’s FAQ states that it does not fund stories about cannabis and directs applicants to its definition of what qualifies as a psychedelic substance.

First-person illegal-substance experiences are not eligible

Applicants should not pitch stories centered on personally taking illegal substances and reporting on the experience. The fellowship specifically states that such stories cannot be supported for legal reasons.

Previously publicly distributed films are not eligible

A project that has already been publicly distributed is not eligible. This includes previous:

Theatrical screenings

Festival screenings

Educational screenings

Community screenings

Applicants should therefore ensure that the project they submit has not already been publicly distributed in these ways.

You cannot submit multiple stories

Each applicant may submit only one story pitch.

You cannot apply to both grant categories

Applicants must choose between the Feature-Length Documentary Grant and the Short-Form Documentary Grant.

You cannot apply to both grants during the same year.

Can Filmmakers Apply as a Team?

Yes, filmmakers can work with collaborators, co-directors or colleagues.

However, the fellowship requires one primary applicant to submit the application.

If awarded, the funds will be distributed to the primary applicant, who can then distribute funds to other members of the filmmaking team as appropriate.

This means a collaborative project does not necessarily have to be completed by one person, but the application needs to identify a primary applicant.

What Happens If You Are Selected?

Grant recipients have several responsibilities after receiving funding.

Successful fellows are expected to:

Attend 3–4 virtual cohort meetings.

Submit a written report within six months of the initial grant issuance.

Explain how the grant money was spent.

Describe what has been accomplished on the documentary.

Share the finished film with the Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics once it is completed.

Credit the Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship in the finished film.

Student filmmakers also have additional expectations relating to completion of their film as part of their graduate-level coursework and faculty-advisor supervision.

How Will the Grant Money Be Paid?

The payment structure differs between the two grants.

Feature-Length Documentary Grant

Feature-length awardees receive:

Half of the award upfront

The remaining half six months later, after completing a project-update memo.

Short-Form Documentary Grant

Short-form awardees receive:

The full grant amount upfront.

The fellowship does not require recipients to submit individual expenses for reimbursement, although a six-month report explaining spending and project progress is required.

Is There an Application Fee?

No.

The application is free to submit.

This makes the opportunity particularly accessible to emerging filmmakers who may not have substantial resources available for application fees.

What Should Applicants Prepare?

A strong application should be built around a compelling documentary idea and demonstrate that the filmmaker has the experience, access and ability to execute it.

Applicants should be prepared to provide information about areas such as:

The documentary’s working title

Project stage

Story concept

Topic and context

Filmmaker background

Previous work

Artistic approach

Connection to the story

Access to participants and locations

Funding received so far

Project budget

Production plans

The application materials also ask filmmakers to explain the creative and narrative direction of their projects.

For student applicants, the application includes areas such as a logline, topic summary, story or concept summary, filmmaker statement, artistic approach, connection and access, and funding to date.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although no application can guarantee funding, filmmakers can strengthen their submissions by paying close attention to the fellowship’s priorities.

1. Lead with the story

Do not make the application simply a discussion about psychedelics.

Instead, identify the human story at the center of the documentary.

Explain who the audience will follow, what is at stake and why the story is important now.

2. Demonstrate cinematic potential

The fellowship specifically seeks narratives suitable for cinematic storytelling.

Explain what viewers will see, hear and experience.

3. Show that you have access

If your documentary depends on specific people, communities, locations or institutions, explain how you will access them.

4. Demonstrate your filmmaking ability

Previous work samples are important, particularly for applicants seeking the feature-length funding.

Choose work that demonstrates your ability to tell compelling nonfiction stories.

5. Make the project’s relevance clear

Explain why the story matters within the larger conversation around psychedelics.

Consider the scientific, cultural, political, economic or social implications of the story.

6. Be realistic about production

A compelling concept needs a credible execution plan.

Make sure your proposed budget and production strategy are realistic.

7. Follow the eligibility rules carefully

Do not submit a project that falls into one of the excluded categories, such as fiction, cannabis-focused stories or previously publicly distributed films.

8. Remember the language requirement

If your film will be produced in another language, plan for English subtitles and prepare the application in English.

Important Information for Applicants Working With Collaborators

If several people are developing the documentary together, applicants should decide who will serve as the primary applicant before submission.

The fellowship does not split the application into multiple primary applicants. One person should submit the application and receive the funds, with the primary applicant then able to distribute funds to other team members.

Can You Reapply?

Yes.

Applicants who are unsuccessful may reapply if their project has undergone significant new developments since the previous application.

If reapplying, filmmakers should clearly explain what has changed or progressed since their earlier submission.

When Will Applicants Hear Back?

According to the current FAQ, applicants will be notified of award decisions by December 2026.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Mycoskie–UC Berkeley Psychedelic Documentary Fellowship is:

October 5, 2026

Applicants should submit their materials before the deadline because the fellowship states that extensions cannot be provided.

Support initiatives designed to improve ways of working.

This area is suitable for students who enjoy identifying problems, simplifying complex processes and developing practical solutions.

Who Should Apply?

TITLE: Press Release – Association of African Universities joins SCOSS to help secure the future of Open Science

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities, AAU, (https://www.aau.org) has joined the Global Sustainability Coalition of Open Science Services (SCOSS) bringing essential African representation to the effort.

AAU, which represents more than 400 higher education institutions across the five regions of Africa, provides a platform for research, consultation, debates, and collaboration on a wide range of issues pertaining to higher education in Africa.

Nodumo Dhlamini, Director of ICT Services and Knowledge Management at AAU, said the association is pleased to be joining the coalition. “We believe this collaboration will help in strengthening the structures and infrastructure that exists to disseminate research findings and preserve global scholarly knowledge.”

SCOSS functions by providing a framework for libraries, policymakers and other stakeholders to collectively fund and secure the growing infrastructure of noncommercial services on which, in many ways, the OA and OS community at large depend. Officially launched in late 2017, SCOSS is in the midst of its first round funding call for two Board-approved services: the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and SHERPA/RoMEO. The next search for potential services to fund in a second funding cycle is now getting underway.

To date, SCOSS has attracted pledged funding totaling in excess of 750,000 Euros from library consortia, individual libraries, as well as research institutes and universities in Europe, Australia, Africa and North America.

“Gaining AAU as a member is a key win for SCOSS,” said SPARC Europe Director Vanessa Proudman. “It brings us one significant step closer to our goal of global representation, which we need if SCOSS is to succeed long-term. And AAU’s expansive role in Africa means they will bring a wealth of invaluable insights to the coalition.”

With the addition of AAU, SCOSS’s members now span four continents: Europe, Australia, North America and Africa.

For additional information, including a full and current list of global institutions that have pledged funding thus far, and for details on how to join them — visit www.scoss.org.

About SCOSS: The Global Sustainability Coalition for Open Science Services (SCOSS) represents a community-led effort to help maintain, and ultimately secure, the vital infrastructure on which Open Access and Open Science depend.

TITLE: CirculaRise Accelerator in Kenya 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 31, 2026

Applications for the CirculaRise Accelerator in Kenya 2026 are now open. The CirculaRise Accelerator in Kenya supports growth stage social businesses to develop and scale inclusive circular solutions. Through the CirculaRise Accelerator Framework, they guide entrepreneurs in bridging the gap between economic viability, environmental responsibility and social impact and enable them to implement validated circular solutions.

The CirculaRise Accelerator is implemented by Yunus Environment Hub in different country contexts, adapting the program framework to local ecosystems while maintaining a consistent approach across implementations.

In Kenya, the CirculaRise Accelerator is supported by the Employment promotion for women for the green transformation in Africa (WE4D) programme, which is funded by the German government and the IKEA Foundation and implemented by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH. It supports businesses that are driving circular economy solutions or are ready to integrate circular principles into their business models, with a particular focus on advancing women’s economic participation and leadership.

Program Details

The program is designed to help participating businesses strengthen their circular strategy, improve customer readiness, and scale their impact while remaining grounded in financial sustainability, with a particular focus on advancing women’s economic participation.

Over the course of six months, each participating business is required to take part with two designated individuals who must be the founder(s) and CEOs. Both participants receive personalised coaching, take part in expert-led trainings, and engage in structured peer learning with other participating businesses.

At least one of the two participants must be directly involved in strategic decision-making to ensure the business has the internal capacity to develop and implement a circular strategy.

Eligibility

The CirculaRise Accelerator in Kenya is designed for businesses that meet the following criteria:

Registered legal entities in Kenya

Operational for at least three years

SMEs by size, employing between 10 and 250 people

Active in, or interested in transitioning towards, circular economy practices

Demonstrated commitment to social impact

Women-led, women-owned, or women-managed businesses, or businesses that demonstrably support women’s economic participation
