TITLE: IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme 2026/2027: Fully Funded Master’s Scholarship for Women in Nuclear-Related Fields

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme (MSCFP) is an international scholarship initiative designed to encourage and support young women who want to build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology, nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear medicine, nuclear law and other nuclear-related disciplines.

Established by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the programme provides financial support to selected female students pursuing master’s degrees in nuclear-related fields at accredited universities. In addition to financial assistance for master’s studies, selected students may also have access to limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA.

The programme is particularly valuable for women who want to develop specialist expertise in a field where women remain underrepresented and subsequently contribute to the peaceful, safe and secure applications of nuclear science and technology.

The IAEA MSCFP is therefore more than a conventional university scholarship. It is an opportunity to obtain advanced academic training while positioning yourself for a future career in the international nuclear sector.

About the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme

The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme was created to inspire more young women to pursue educational and professional opportunities in nuclear-related fields.

The programme recognizes the importance of developing a highly skilled workforce capable of contributing to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology.

Through the MSCFP, selected students receive financial assistance toward their master’s studies in approved nuclear-related disciplines. The programme may also provide limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, allowing eligible students to gain exposure to professional environments connected to their academic specialization.

The initiative is named after Marie Skłodowska-Curie, one of history’s most influential scientists and a pioneer in the study of radioactivity.

The programme’s broader objective is to encourage the next generation of women scientists, engineers, researchers, legal experts and professionals to enter and contribute to the nuclear field.

The IAEA has reported substantial participation in the programme since its launch. Its 2025 reporting stated that 760 students from 129 Member States had been selected since the programme began in 2020, with recipients studying in 76 countries.

What Does the IAEA MSCFP Scholarship Cover?

One of the major attractions of the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme is the level of financial support available to successful applicants.

Selected students may receive:

Up to €20,000 for tuition costs

Up to €20,000 for living costs

Potential internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA

Exposure to an international professional and academic network in nuclear-related fields

This means that the maximum support described under the programme can reach up to €40,000, consisting of up to €20,000 toward tuition and up to €20,000 toward living expenses.

The actual amount awarded can depend on the applicant’s circumstances and the programme’s assessment of the financial support required.

Applicants who already have another scholarship for their master’s programme must declare it to the IAEA. Where additional scholarship funding exists, the IAEA’s financial support may be adjusted accordingly.

The programme’s financial arrangements are therefore designed to prevent undisclosed duplication of scholarship support.

Who Can Apply for the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship?

The MSCFP has specific eligibility requirements, and applicants should carefully review them before beginning an application.

1. Applicants must be female

The programme is specifically designed to encourage more women to pursue careers in nuclear-related disciplines.

Therefore, the programme is open to female candidates who meet the academic and programme requirements.

2. Applicants must be from an IAEA Member State

The programme is open to students from IAEA Member States.

This means that eligibility is determined by the applicant’s country being a Member State of the International Atomic Energy Agency rather than by a particular continent or region.

Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East, the Pacific and other regions may therefore be eligible if their country is an IAEA Member State.

3. Applicants must be accepted into or enrolled in a master’s programme

Applicants must either:

Have been accepted into an accredited university master’s programme; or

Already be enrolled in an accredited university master’s programme.

The master’s programme must be related to an eligible nuclear-related field.

An applicant who has not yet secured admission to an eligible master’s programme should therefore pay particular attention to the admission requirement before applying.

Academic Requirements

Academic performance is an important component of the MSCFP selection process.

The programme indicates that preference is given to candidates with above-average academic credentials, specifically:

75% or above, or

A GPA greater than 3.0 out of 4.0.

Meeting the academic benchmark does not necessarily mean an applicant will automatically receive the fellowship. Selection also considers other factors, including educational background, previous achievements, motivation, career objectives and commitment to public service.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that academic grades alone determine the outcome.

Eligible Fields of Study

The IAEA MSCFP supports master’s programmes in fields connected to nuclear science, nuclear technology and the wider peaceful applications of nuclear energy.

Eligible or relevant fields include areas such as:

Nuclear Engineering

Nuclear engineering focuses on the design, operation, safety and technological development of nuclear systems and facilities.

Students interested in reactor technology, nuclear energy systems and related engineering applications may find this field particularly relevant.

Nuclear Physics

Nuclear physics examines the properties, structure and interactions of atomic nuclei.

It is an important foundation for many applications of nuclear science and technology.

Nuclear Chemistry

Nuclear chemistry involves the study of radioactive materials, nuclear reactions, radioisotopes and chemical processes associated with nuclear science.

Nuclear Medicine

Nuclear medicine uses radioactive materials for diagnosis, imaging and treatment of disease.

This area is particularly relevant to students interested in the intersection between healthcare and nuclear technology.

Isotopic Techniques

Isotopic techniques have applications across areas such as medicine, agriculture, environmental science, hydrology, food safety and scientific research.

Radiation Biology

Radiation biology examines the effects of ionizing radiation on living organisms and biological systems.

This field is important in areas including radiation protection, medicine and nuclear research.

Nuclear Safety

Nuclear safety focuses on preventing accidents and minimizing risks associated with nuclear facilities, materials and technologies.

Nuclear Security

Nuclear security concerns measures designed to prevent, detect and respond to unauthorized access, theft, misuse or other malicious activities involving nuclear and radioactive materials.

Nuclear Non-Proliferation

Nuclear non-proliferation deals with efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons while supporting peaceful applications of nuclear technology.

Nuclear Law

Nuclear law combines legal principles with the regulatory requirements surrounding nuclear activities.

It can involve areas such as nuclear safety, nuclear security, liability, safeguards, regulation and international nuclear cooperation.

The IAEA provides a broader list of eligible and related fields, meaning applicants should not automatically assume that their programme is ineligible simply because its title does not exactly match one of the examples above.

Why the Field of Study Matters

Applicants should understand that the MSCFP is not a general master’s scholarship.

The programme is specifically connected to the IAEA’s mandate and therefore focuses on disciplines that can contribute to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology.

For example, a general master’s programme that has no meaningful connection to nuclear science, technology, safety, security, medicine, law or another relevant area may not qualify.

Applicants should therefore carefully compare their intended programme with the IAEA’s list of supported fields before applying.

Required Application Documents

Applicants are required to submit supporting documents in addition to completing the online MSCFP application form.

The required documents include the following:

1. Passport or National ID

Applicants must provide a copy of an accepted identification document, such as:

Passport; or

National identification document.

Applicants should ensure that the document submitted is clear and readable.

2. University Admission or Acceptance Letter

Applicants must provide an official acceptance or admission letter from the university where they will undertake their master’s programme.

The document should indicate:

The university;

The master’s programme;

The nuclear-related field of study; and

The duration of the programme.

This is an important document because the IAEA needs to establish that the applicant has been accepted into an appropriate programme.

3. Tuition Fee Statement

Applicants must submit documentation showing the tuition costs associated with the master’s programme.

This may include an official statement or confirmation from the university detailing the applicable tuition fees.

4. Information About Other Scholarships

If the applicant has received or is receiving another scholarship for the master’s programme, documentation relating to that scholarship must also be submitted.

Applicants are required to disclose other scholarship funding because the IAEA may adjust its financial support when another scholarship is available.

5. Reference Form

Applicants must arrange for referees to complete the required IAEA reference template.

At least one reference is mandatory, while a second reference is preferred.

An important point is that the references must be sent directly by the referees to the MSCFP email address by the application deadline.

Applicants should therefore contact their potential referees early rather than waiting until the final day of the application period.

All Application Documents Must Be in English

The IAEA requires application documents to be submitted in English.

If an applicant’s original documents are written in another language, the applicant must also provide an official English translation.

This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because incomplete documentation or missing translations can affect the assessment of the application.

The IAEA explicitly states that incomplete applications will not be considered.

Applicants should therefore review their application carefully before submission and ensure that every required document has been provided.

See Application Form HERE

How the IAEA MSCFP Selection Process Works

The selection process is competitive.

Applications are reviewed by the IAEA MSCFP Technical Selection Committee.

The committee assesses applications against several selection criteria rather than considering academic performance alone.

The assessment includes:

Meeting the programme’s entry requirements;

Educational background;

Previous academic and professional achievements;

Motivation for pursuing the programme;

The potential impact of the fellowship on the applicant’s career goals;

Commitment to public service.

The IAEA may also consider factors such as:

Geographic diversity;

Field-of-study diversity;

Linguistic diversity; and

Other programme-related considerations.

This means applicants should prepare an application that tells a clear story about their academic background, professional ambitions and intended contribution to the nuclear field.

What Should Applicants Emphasize in Their Applications?

Because the selection process goes beyond grades, applicants should make sure their application clearly explains why they want to pursue a nuclear-related career.

A strong application should demonstrate a logical connection between:

Previous education → chosen master’s programme → nuclear-related career goals → potential impact on society → commitment to public service.

Applicants should also explain how receiving the fellowship could help them contribute to their country, region or the wider international community.

For example, an applicant interested in nuclear medicine could explain how advanced training could contribute to improved access to nuclear diagnostic or therapeutic technologies.

Similarly, someone interested in nuclear safety could explain how specialist training could contribute to stronger safety systems, regulation or technical capacity.

Internship Opportunities

The MSCFP also provides limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA.

These opportunities can provide students with exposure to professional environments connected to nuclear science and technology.

The IAEA has reported that MSCFP graduates have subsequently been confirmed for internships within IAEA departments and laboratories as well as external organizations, including IAEA Collaborating Centres and other public and private sector partners.

Internship opportunities can be particularly valuable because they may allow students to complement academic study with practical professional exposure.

However, applicants should understand that the fellowship’s primary purpose is master’s-level study and that internship opportunities are described as limited.

Commitment to Public Service

Commitment to public service is one of the factors considered during the selection process.

This is significant because the programme is intended not simply to finance individual education but to contribute to the development of a skilled workforce capable of supporting the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology.

Applicants should therefore consider how their education and future career can contribute to areas such as:

Public health;

Nuclear safety;

Radiation protection;

Energy security;

Scientific research;

Environmental protection;

Nuclear security;

Nuclear regulation;

Nuclear medicine;

Food and agriculture;

Water resources;

International cooperation; or

Other peaceful applications of nuclear technology.

Financial Support and Other Scholarships

Applicants who already have financial support from another scholarship must disclose that funding to the IAEA.

The IAEA explains that its financial support may be reduced where another scholarship exists.

In particular, the IAEA may provide only tuition support rather than both tuition and living-cost support for the relevant period.

Transparency is therefore essential.

Applicants should not omit information about other scholarships in an attempt to receive additional funding.

Failure to provide relevant information in a timely and transparent manner may lead to suspension of the IAEA’s financial support.

Fellowship Acceptance

Successful applicants will receive an offer from the IAEA.

Selected candidates are required to confirm acceptance of the fellowship within one week.

The fellowship offer will contain important information concerning:

The value of the award;

Payment arrangements;

Expected commitments;

Administrative requirements; and

Other arrangements relating to the fellowship.

Successful applicants should therefore carefully read the fellowship offer before accepting it.

Obligation to Complete the Master’s Programme

The MSCFP is intended to support students through their master’s education.

Selected students are therefore expected to successfully complete the master’s programme.

Failure to graduate or failure to meet the requirements associated with the scholarship can have serious financial consequences.

According to the programme information, failure to meet the scholarship requirements may result in termination of the award and an obligation to repay tuition and living-cost support received from the IAEA upon request.

Applicants should therefore apply only when they are prepared to commit themselves fully to completing the master’s programme.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The IAEA MSCFP may be particularly suitable for women who want to pursue advanced education and careers in areas such as:

Nuclear engineering;

Nuclear physics;

Nuclear chemistry;

Nuclear medicine;

Radiation biology;

Nuclear safety;

Nuclear security;

Nuclear non-proliferation;

Nuclear law;

Isotopic techniques; and

Other fields connected to the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology.

It may also be relevant to students who want to combine nuclear expertise with broader careers in research, healthcare, regulation, international development, public policy or scientific innovation.

Why This Fellowship Is a Valuable Opportunity

The MSCFP stands out because it combines financial support, advanced academic training and potential professional exposure.

For eligible women, the programme can help remove some of the financial barriers associated with pursuing an international or specialized master’s degree.

The potential benefits include:

Financial assistance

The programme offers up to €20,000 toward tuition and up to €20,000 toward living expenses, subject to the programme’s terms and the applicant’s circumstances.

Specialized education

Students can pursue master’s-level education in highly specialized areas connected to nuclear science and technology.

International exposure

The programme brings together students from IAEA Member States and supports the development of an internationally connected nuclear workforce.

Professional development

Eligible recipients may have access to internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, providing potential practical exposure alongside academic study.

Career development

Specialized master’s-level training can help prepare graduates for careers in scientific research, healthcare, engineering, regulation, nuclear safety, nuclear security, international organizations and other related sectors.

Contribution to society

The programme is designed around the broader objective of strengthening human capacity for the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology.

Read details about this Opportunity HERE

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Applicants should begin preparing well before the deadline.

Start with university admission

Because an official admission or acceptance letter is required, prospective applicants should identify suitable master’s programmes and begin the university application process early.

Confirm that your programme is nuclear-related

Do not rely solely on the title of your master’s programme.

Review the programme curriculum and compare it with the IAEA’s eligible fields.

Prepare your academic documents

Make sure your academic records clearly demonstrate your educational background and achievements.

Applicants with grades meeting or exceeding the stated academic preference should highlight their academic strengths.

Choose referees early

Since at least one reference is mandatory and the reference must be sent directly by the referee, applicants should approach referees well in advance.

Develop a strong career narrative

Clearly explain:

Why you want to study the chosen field;

Why the field matters to you;

How the master’s programme fits into your career;

How the fellowship will help you achieve your goals; and

How you intend to contribute to society after completing your studies.

Demonstrate public-service motivation

Because commitment to public service is part of the selection criteria, applicants should clearly communicate how their future expertise can benefit their community, country, region or the international community.

Check every document

Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Before submitting, applicants should confirm that they have included all required documents and that documents originally issued in other languages have appropriate English translations.

Conclusion

The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme represents a significant opportunity for women who want to pursue advanced education and build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology and related disciplines.

With financial support of up to €20,000 for tuition and €20,000 for living costs, the programme can substantially reduce the financial burden associated with master’s-level study. Beyond financial assistance, the programme can provide a pathway toward professional development and potential internship exposure within the wider international nuclear community.

However, this is a specialized fellowship rather than a general master’s scholarship. Applicants must be female, come from an IAEA Member State, and be accepted into or enrolled in an accredited master’s programme in a nuclear-related field. Strong academic performance is preferred, with the programme indicating 75% or above or a GPA greater than 3.0/4.0 as the preferred academic benchmark.

Applicants should also pay close attention to the supporting-document requirements, English-language requirements, reference process, disclosure of other scholarships and the obligation to complete the master’s programme.

For women interested in nuclear engineering, nuclear physics, nuclear medicine, radiation science, nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear law, non-proliferation and other related areas, the MSCFP can provide an important opportunity to gain advanced education and develop expertise that can contribute to the safe, secure and peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology.

Because application dates can change from one cycle to another, prospective applicants should always verify the current application deadline and latest eligibility requirements on the official IAEA MSCFP page before submitting an application.

Its members contribute to the spreading and strengthening of the Institute’s values: excellence, freedom, interdisciplinarity.

The Cercle des Mécènes is open to individual donors who commit to the Institute with a one-off donation of at least €15,000, or €20,000 over 3 years, as well as to representatives of corporate sponsors. Being a member of the Cercle des Mécènes of IHES means contributing to the development of fundamental research by supporting the peculiar model of IHES. It is also a way to create a special relationship with the Institute, including the possibility to interact with researchers and offering extraordinary access to the Institute, according to your needs.

TITLE: Advanced Standing Exams and Transfer Credit

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
MIT Physics offers two kind of credit for knowledge demonstrated through exams or for previous work:

Advanced Standing credit can be given for successfully passing an exam demonstrating mastery of the material from an MIT course. Current subjects for which Advanced Standing Exams (ASEs) are available are 8.01, 8.02, 8.03, and 8.04.

Transfer credit is given for course work completed at another university; a Validation Exam to demonstrate mastery of the material is required for 8.01 or 8.02 transfer credit.

Upcoming Exams Schedule

Note: Due to the increasing use of LLMs, the Physics department no longer offers ASEs online. All exams will now be in-person only.

Summer 2026 Advanced Standing/Validation Exams schedule:

All ASEs will be offered in-person only

8.01 August 31st from 8-11AM

8.02 September 2nd from 1:30-4:30PM

8.03 September 8th from 9-12AM

8.04 September 8th from 1-4PM

To register for ASEs, see information below.

Questions? Contact Michal Holland (holland3@mit.edu)

Note: Locations of exams will be sent via email to registered students.

More on Advanced Standing Credit

MIT’s first-level Physics courses in Classical Mechanics (8.01) and Electricity & Magnetism (8.02) provide a rigorous, in-depth study of these topics at a level offered by few other schools. A student who believes that pre-MIT work has prepared the student with strong knowledge of the subject matter in 8.01 and/or 8.02 may take an Advanced Standing Exam.

A passing grade on an MIT Advanced Standing Exam entitles a student to full credit for the subject, as well as placement in the next subject in a sequence. A student may only take an Advanced Standing Exam in a class for which they had never registered nor attended at MIT.

Obtaining Advanced Standing Credit

For January Exams:

All students, including new transfer students:

Register for ASEs using the ASE petition form.

Be sure to sign the petition yourself and obtain your advisor’s signature, then forward it to Physics Assistant Director Shannon Larkin for instructor signatures.

For August Exams:

Incoming first-year students:

Register for 8.01 and 8.02 ASE exams through the form on the Office of the First Year website.

All continuing students and new transfer students:

Register for 8.01, 8.02, 8.03 and 8.04 ASEs using the ASE petition form.

All students, both exam dates:

Read the “What you need to do” section of the MIT Registrar’s Office website on ASEs.

After obtaining a signature from your Academic Advisor, and signing the petition yourself, send the petition to physics-undergrad@mit.edu to obtain an instructor signature from Shannon Larkin, Physics Assistant Director.

Once you receive your signed form, submit it to the Registrar’s Office (send to records@mit.edu) for verification that you have not previously been enrolled in the class. Forms must be submitted to the Registrar’s Office by the deadline posted in the Academic Calendar.

Additional information about MIT’s Advanced Standing Exams policy and practice.

Advanced Standing Grading

First-semester first year students: P grade for passing the exam; no grade posted for failing the exam.

A, B, or C letter grades will appear on your spring term record and transcript for ASEs taken in January. These grades are not included in your GPA calculation.

Sophomores, juniors, and seniors (including new transfer students): letter grades will appear on transcript, but not factor into the GPA.

A student who fails an advanced standing exam cannot retake it, and should enroll in the appropriate subject.

Accommodations for ASEs / Transfer Validation Exams

In order to be granted extended time, a distraction-free space, or any other needed accommodation for the exams offered, students need to get approval from the Disabilities and Access Services Office (das-student@mit.edu). Students also need to contact the Physics Course Manager at physics-course-manager@mit.edu to coordinate the logistics of the accommodation requested.

Resources to help prepare for the ASEs

8.01 textbook

8.02 textbook

8.01 and 8.02 Review Videos

More on Transfer Credit

MIT’s first-level Physics courses in Classical Mechanics (8.01) and Electricity & Magnetism (8.02) provide a rigorous, in-depth study of these topics at a level offered by few other schools. A student who has not yet completed the Physics GIRs at MIT may wish to take a course at another college or university (e.g., during a summer session) and apply for transfer credit; students transferring to MIT may have already taken such a course. In order to qualify for MIT credit, the course must:

be calculus-based and directed toward science or engineering majors;

use a text at a level comparable to that of texts used at MIT (see below);

be the equivalent of one MIT term in the number of lecture hours, number of assignments, etc.; have content matching that of 8.01 (Mechanics) or 8.02 (Electricity and Magnetism).

The principal topics usually included in such a course are listed below. Additional information can be found on the individual course websites.

Obtaining transfer credit

To request transfer credit for any Physics subject, consult with Physics Assistant Director of Academic Programs Shannon Larkin, who serves as the Department’s Transfer Credit Examiner and will determine whether the course meets MIT Physics’ standards. Students requesting transfer credit should send:

a copy of or link to the official catalog description of the course;

a detailed syllabus including the title and author of the textbook and the chapters covered, as well as topics covered week to week;

a transcript from the institution where the course was taken (NOTE: a grade of B or better is required to receive transfer credit).

Requesting credit for 8.01 or 8.02:

The student must validate the transfer credit by passing an MIT 8.01 or 8.02 Validation Exam. Exams are given during Orientation week prior to the fall term and in the last week of IAP prior to the spring term, or arranged to the mutual convenience of the student and exam administrator. To register for an exam, submit a petition (PDF) to the Academic Programs Office.

After passing the Validation Exam, request transfer credit by submitting a Request for Additional Credit (PDF) to the Transfer Credit Examiner.

Requesting credit for courses beyond the GIRs:

Based on the materials sent to the Transfer Credit Examiner, a decision will be made on what transfer credit will be awarded; no exam is required for subjects above 8.02. Transfer credit may be in the form of direct credit for a specific MIT Physics subject, if the previous course covers the same curriculum with the same rigor, or may be in the form of units of academic credit, in cases where no analogous MIT course exists.

Once credit has been approved, submit a Request for Additional Credit (PDF) to the Transfer Credit Examiner.

Transfer Credit Grading

Transfer credit appears on the transcript with a grade of “S.” Transfer credit entitles the student to placement in the next subject in a sequence.

A student who fails an 8.01 or 8.02 Validation Exam will have no grade noted on the transcript, but may not repeat the exam and must enroll in the MIT course.

Potential Topics for Placement Exams

Physics ASEs and Validation Exams are three-hour, closed-book exams covering calculus-based introductory Classical Mechanics (8.01) or Classical Electromagnetism (8.02). Exams are modelled on final exams in 8.01 and 8.02, with problems based on a selection of the topics listed below. Suggested texts for study include University Physics by Young and Freedman; Physics by Halliday, Resnick and Krane; and Physics for Scientists and Engineers by Serway. Calculators may not be used during these exams; formula sheets are often provided but are not guaranteed.

TITLE: Next-Geo Program 2027: Pan-European Research and Training Fellowship in Geoeconomics for PhD Students and Early Postdocs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Next-Geo Program 2027 is inviting applications from advanced PhD students and early Postdoctoral researchers working in economics and closely related quantitative fields who are conducting research on geoeconomics. Now entering its second year, Next-Geo is a one-year pan-European research and training programme designed to support the next generation of researchers working at the intersection of economics and geopolitics.

The programme is coordinated by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in cooperation with CEPR, Bocconi University through the Institute for European Policymaking, and the Oxford University Department of Economics, with funding from Stiftung Mercator. Each year, the programme brings together a carefully selected cohort of approximately 10 junior scholars to develop their research expertise, strengthen their professional networks and advance a research or policy project in geoeconomics.

Applications submitted by October 31, 2026 are guaranteed full consideration for the 2027 cohort. The organisers aim to finalise the selection of successful candidates by the end of November 2026.

About the Next-Geo Program 2027

The Next-Geo Program is a specialised research and training programme focusing exclusively on the growing field of geoeconomics.

The programme responds to the increasing importance of the relationship between economic policy and geopolitics in a rapidly changing global environment. While demand for researchers and policy experts with expertise in geoeconomics is growing, the programme notes that systematic training specifically focused on the field remains limited. Next-Geo was established to help address this gap by providing advanced research training, mentoring, policy-oriented development and networking opportunities for promising early-career researchers.

The programme is intended to complement, rather than replace, the doctoral or postdoctoral training participants receive at their home universities or research institutions.

It provides a dedicated environment where researchers can focus specifically on geoeconomic questions while remaining enrolled or employed at their existing European institution.

What Is Geoeconomics?

Geoeconomics broadly examines the relationship between economic activity, economic policy and geopolitical power.

The Next-Geo programme recognises that economic and geopolitical developments are increasingly interconnected. Issues such as international trade, economic security, sanctions, industrial policy, energy transitions and global financial flows can have implications that extend beyond traditional economic analysis.

The programme therefore welcomes research addressing a broad range of geoeconomic topics.

Potential research areas include:

Economic security

Trade coercion

Trade fragmentation

Industrial policy

Sanctions design

Sanctions evasion

Global financial flows

Economic aid

Climate transition

Energy transition

Defence economics

The list is not presented as an exhaustive set of research topics, meaning applicants working on other questions that fit within the broader field of geoeconomics may also be relevant to the programme.

Purpose of the Next-Geo Program

The programme has two closely connected objectives: research development and community building.

Supporting the Next Generation of Geoeconomists

Next-Geo aims to support highly promising PhD students and early Postdoctoral researchers whose work focuses on geoeconomics.

The programme recognises that young researchers working in this area can be geographically dispersed across Europe and may sometimes be isolated within departments or academic communities that do not have specialised expertise in geoeconomics.

By bringing these researchers together, Next-Geo seeks to create a stronger network connecting early-career scholars with each other and with leading senior researchers across institutions and countries.

A One-Year Add-On Fellowship Programme

Next-Geo has a one-year duration and is structured as an add-on fellowship programme.

This distinction is important.

The programme is designed to complement participants’ existing PhD or Postdoctoral work rather than replacing their home institution.

Participants remain enrolled or employed at their existing university or research institution throughout the programme. Next-Geo does not provide a formal degree and does not create an employment relationship with the Kiel Institute.

The programme therefore provides an additional research and training environment specifically focused on geoeconomics.

What Does the Next-Geo Program Offer?

Selected participants become part of a competitive cohort of junior researchers and receive research training, mentoring, networking opportunities and practical research support.

The programme combines online and in-person activities throughout the academic year.

Key elements include:

1. Advanced Coursework and Research Training

Participants receive lectures and training covering research at the frontier of geoeconomics.

The teaching is delivered by:

Internationally renowned external scholars

Researchers at the Kiel Institute

Leading experts working in the field

The objective is to expose participants to current research and strengthen their understanding of advanced questions in geoeconomics.

2. Research Feedback and Senior Mentoring

Participants develop their own research or policy project during the programme.

They receive feedback and mentoring from senior researchers and leading experts in geoeconomics.

This provides participants with an opportunity to refine their projects, strengthen their research design and receive input from experienced scholars working in the field.

3. Research Assistant Support

Promising research projects may receive support from a pool of four Next-Geo student research assistants.

These research assistants are specifically hired at the Kiel Institute to support Next-Geo junior researchers.

Support can be provided:

In person at the Berlin office

Remotely

Or through a combination of these arrangements

This research assistance can provide additional capacity for participants developing substantial research projects.

4. Funding for Data and AI Subscriptions

Promising projects may also receive funding for research-related resources.

This can include:

Data purchases

Subscriptions to frontier large language models and AI tools

The programme specifically gives Claude and OpenAI as examples of AI services that may be supported.

This component is intended to provide researchers with practical resources that can contribute to the development of their projects.

5. Travel and Accommodation Support

The programme provides support for travel and accommodation expenses associated with in-person modules.

On-site participation is expected, so this support is an important part of the programme’s structure.

Participants can therefore take part in the programme’s physical workshops and modules without being expected to independently cover the stated travel and accommodation costs associated with those activities.

Engagement With the Kiel Institute

Participants also have the opportunity to become familiar with the work and activities of the Kiel Institute, which the programme describes as one of the leading institutions working on geoeconomics.

The institute’s activities and initiatives include:

The annual Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics

The LSE-Kiel-CEPR Conference on Defence Economics

The Kiel Institute-led CEPR Research Policy Network on Geoeconomics and Security

The Ukraine Support Tracker

The Kiel Research Center on Geoeconomics

This provides participants with opportunities to engage with research networks and initiatives connected to geoeconomics and related policy questions.

Research and Policy Project Outcomes

A central objective of the programme is for participants to complete a substantial research or policy project in geoeconomics.

By the end of the programme, participants are expected to have developed a high-quality project.

The strongest projects may have opportunities to be:

Published as Kiel Institute working papers

Published as CEPR working papers

Developed into policy briefs

Presented at conferences

Presented at workshops

Participants also receive a certificate of programme participation.

The programme therefore places emphasis not only on training but also on producing a tangible research or policy output.

Opportunities to Engage With Policymakers and Practitioners

Next-Geo also connects researchers with people working outside traditional academic environments.

Participants can engage with:

Policymakers

Think tanks

Practitioners

Academic researchers

Policy experts

These interactions take place through events and workshops at the Kiel-CEPR Research Hub in Berlin and at partner institutions.

This policy-facing element is particularly relevant for researchers interested in producing work that can contribute to public-policy discussions in addition to academic debates.

Programme Structure and Timeline

The Next-Geo programme runs across one academic year and combines virtual learning with several in-person modules.

The programme begins with an online kick-off during winter and progresses through research training, workshops and networking activities before concluding with the Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics in autumn.

Winter: Online Kick-Off

The programme begins with an online meeting in winter.

During this stage, participants:

Meet the other members of the cohort

Present their research or policy project ideas

Receive an introductory lecture

Learn about the foundations of geoeconomics

This initial stage establishes the basis for collaborative learning and project development.

Spring: Lecture and Research Training

The spring stage is titled “Best of Geoeconomics @ Kiel Institute.”

This is a multi-day in-person module held in Kiel and/or Berlin.

Activities include:

Advanced academic lectures

Lectures delivered by leading scholars

Training in producing high-quality policy-relevant research

Structured feedback on participants’ research projects

This stage is designed to deepen participants’ academic understanding and help them improve their research designs and methodologies.

Summer: Research and Policy Workshop

The summer stage consists of a hands-on, multi-day Research and Policy Workshop.

The workshop takes place in Berlin and/or another European location.

Activities include:

Presenting ongoing research projects

Receiving feedback

Interacting with policymakers

Engaging with think tanks

Connecting with practitioners

Developing research communication skills

Developing policy engagement skills

Strengthening public outreach abilities

The workshop is therefore intended to help researchers think beyond the academic paper and develop the skills needed to communicate research to policy and public audiences.

Autumn: Geoeconomics Conference and Networking

The programme concludes in autumn with the Kiel-CEPR Conference on Geoeconomics in Berlin.

Participants will:

Attend the leading academic conference in the field

Potentially present their research projects to an international expert audience

Compete with peers for the best research paper or best policy brief

Network with scholars

Engage with political decision-makers

The opportunity to potentially present research at the conference provides a further platform for participants to communicate their work to an international audience.

European Institutional Affiliation Requirement

The programme is designed for researchers conducting their PhD or Postdoctoral work at a European institution.

Applicants must therefore generally be enrolled or employed at a European university or research institution.

The call also states that European nationals at overseas institutions may be eligible in selected cases.

This distinction is important because nationality and institutional affiliation are treated differently in the eligibility requirements.

What the Next-Geo Programme Does Not Provide

Applicants should understand the distinction between research support and personal financial support.

The programme does not provide:

An employment contract

A stipend

A living-expense allowance

A formal degree

Instead, it provides funding for:

Travel for on-site modules

Accommodation for on-site modules

Research support

Research assistant access

Data purchases and/or AI subscriptions for promising projects

Participants remain fully enrolled or employed at their home institution and do not receive employment or enrollment status at the Kiel Institute.

This means that applicants should not regard Next-Geo as a replacement for their existing PhD funding or Postdoctoral employment.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their applications through the designated application form.

Applications submitted by October 31, 2026 are guaranteed full consideration.

The application must include the following materials:

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a CV demonstrating their academic and research background.

Given the programme’s emphasis on an excellent track record, applicants should ensure that their CV clearly presents their research experience, publications where applicable, academic achievements and other relevant accomplishments.

2. Cover Letter

A cover letter is required as part of the application.

The letter should help explain the applicant’s motivation for joining the programme and demonstrate the relationship between their research and Next-Geo’s focus on geoeconomics.

3. One-Page Research Project Sketch

Applicants must submit a one-page research project sketch.

This document should present the proposed research or policy project that they intend to develop during the programme.

Because the programme focuses specifically on geoeconomics, applicants should clearly demonstrate how their project fits within the field.

Potential topics can include areas such as economic security, trade, sanctions, industrial policy, financial flows, energy, climate transition and defence economics.

4. Writing Sample

Applicants must provide a writing sample.

Examples identified by the programme include:

A third-year paper

A job market paper

The writing sample provides an opportunity for applicants to demonstrate the quality of their academic research and writing.

5. Two Potential References

Applicants must provide the names of two potential references.

The programme states that contact information in the applicant’s CV is sufficient for this purpose.

Additional Documents for Successful Candidates

Successful candidates will subsequently need to provide evidence of their institutional status.

This includes:

Proof of enrollment or employment

Written permission from the employer if the applicant is employed

The employer’s written permission is required where applicable because the Next-Geo programme is an add-on programme alongside the participant’s existing employment or academic affiliation.

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications that are guaranteed full consideration is October 31, 2026.

Applicants should prepare their CV, cover letter, one-page research project sketch, writing sample and two references well in advance of the deadline.

Important Date

Application Deadline: October 31, 2026

The organisers aim to finalise the selection of the 2027 cohort by the end of November 2026.

Read Full Details About This Opportunity And Apply HERE

Why the Next-Geo Programme Is Relevant to Geoeconomics Researchers

The programme brings together several components that are directly relevant to researchers seeking to develop expertise in geoeconomics.

First, it provides specialised research training in a field where the programme identifies a shortage of systematic training.

Second, it connects early-career researchers who may otherwise be working independently across different European institutions.

Third, participants receive access to senior researchers and international experts who can provide feedback and mentoring.

Fourth, the programme provides practical resources, including research assistant support and potential funding for data and AI subscriptions.

Finally, it creates opportunities for participants to interact with policymakers, think tanks and practitioners and potentially present their research at an international conference.

Research Support for Promising Projects

One of the practical components of the programme is support for promising participant projects.

Researchers may receive access to the programme’s pool of student research assistants, while additional funding may be available for project-specific data and AI subscriptions.

This can provide researchers with additional resources for conducting empirical analysis, gathering data, developing research outputs and advancing their projects during the programme year.

The programme does not state that every participant will automatically receive all forms of research support. The call refers specifically to promising research projects as being eligible for such support.

Research, Policy and Public Engagement

Next-Geo extends beyond academic research training by incorporating policy engagement and public outreach.

During the summer Research and Policy Workshop, participants interact with policymakers, think tanks and practitioners.

The autumn conference also creates an opportunity for researchers to engage with an international expert audience and political decision-makers.

This structure encourages participants to develop skills not only in conducting research but also in communicating research findings to audiences beyond academia.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants considering Next-Geo should make sure their application demonstrates a clear relationship between their academic background, current research and the field of geoeconomics.

1. Establish Your Geoeconomics Focus

Your research should clearly connect to geoeconomics. Applicants can consider how their work relates to issues such as economic security, trade, sanctions, industrial policy, global finance, energy, climate transition or defence economics.

2. Prepare a Strong Research Project Sketch

The one-page project sketch should clearly communicate the research or policy project you intend to develop.

The limited length means that applicants should present the central idea clearly and avoid unnecessary detail.

3. Demonstrate Research Quality

The CV and writing sample should provide evidence of your academic and research track record.

A writing sample such as a third-year paper or job market paper can demonstrate your ability to formulate and investigate a research question.

4. Select Appropriate References

Choose two potential references who can credibly speak to your academic or research capabilities.

5. Explain Your Motivation

6. Confirm Your Institutional Eligibility

TITLE: Hinrich Foundation Research Grant 2026: Call for Research Proposals on Global Trade Issues

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Hinrich Foundation has opened its Call for Research Proposals 2026, inviting researchers and research organizations to submit proposals for research projects that advance understanding of global trade issues and contribute to policy development.

Through its international trade research program, the Foundation supports research across a broad range of trade-related sectors. Proposals are particularly encouraged in areas including trade governance, the geopolitics of trade, foreign direct investment, global supply chain resilience and security, digital trade and technology, environmental sustainability, workforce and education, industrial competitiveness, natural resources, and trade logistics and services.

The upcoming submission deadline is October 31, 2026.

About the Hinrich Foundation Research Programme

The Hinrich Foundation is an independent Asia-based philanthropic organization dedicated to advancing mutually beneficial and sustainable global trade.

Its international trade research program seeks to promote research that can strengthen understanding of global trade challenges and support policy development.

Researchers and research organizations are invited to propose projects addressing significant trade-related questions. The Foundation reviews proposals twice each year, following the closing of each submission cycle.

The annual submission deadlines are:

May 31

October 31

The next opportunity to submit a proposal is October 31, 2026.

Priority Research Areas

The Foundation supports research across several areas of international trade. Its stated priority areas, in order, are:

1. Trade Governance

Research examining trade governance and the systems, institutions and policies that shape international trade.

2. The Geopolitics of Trade

Research exploring the relationship between geopolitics and international trade and the ways political developments influence global trade.

3. Foreign Direct Investment

Research focused on foreign direct investment and its relationship with international trade and economic activity.

4. Global Supply Chain Resilience and Security

Projects examining the resilience and security of global supply chains and issues affecting their reliability and stability.

5. Digital Trade, Innovation and Technology

Research examining digital trade, innovation and technology and their growing influence on international commerce.

6. Trade and Environmental Sustainability

Research investigating the relationship between international trade and environmental sustainability.

7. Trade Workforce and Education

Projects examining workforce and education issues connected to international trade and economic development.

8. Industrial Competitiveness and Economic Development

Research exploring industrial competitiveness and the contribution of trade to economic development.

9. Natural Resources in Trade

Research examining the role of natural resources within international trade.

10. Trade Logistics and Services

Research addressing trade logistics and services that support international commerce.

Who Can Submit a Proposal?

The call invites:

Individual researchers

Groups of researchers

Research organizations

The provided call does not state a specific nationality, citizenship or country requirement for applicants. Researchers and organizations should therefore focus on whether their proposed research fits within the Foundation’s international trade research priorities and meets the submission requirements.

What Should the Research Proposal Include?

The Hinrich Foundation asks researchers to include specific information in their proposals.

1. Name and Credentials of the Researcher or Researchers

Applicants should provide the names and relevant credentials of the researcher or researchers responsible for the proposed project.

This section should help demonstrate the researcher’s expertise and ability to undertake the proposed work.

2. Synopsis of the Proposed Research

The proposal should include a clear synopsis of the research being proposed.

The Foundation encourages researchers to:

Address major trade-related themes.

Identify the central issue the research will investigate.

Present two to four key questions that the research seeks to answer.

Explain the proposed research approach.

Specify whether the research will use primary or secondary research.

Researchers should make the proposed research questions clear and demonstrate how the project will contribute to understanding an important trade issue.

Research Format and Publication

The Hinrich Foundation generally publishes research in two formats:

White papers: Approximately 4,000 words

Articles: Approximately 1,600 words

All research products will be subject to the Foundation’s editorial review.

Researchers may propose either a new research project or an overview or summary of existing work.

New Research Project

A researcher may propose a new research project that includes any combination of article and/or white paper deliverables.

Existing Research

Researchers may also propose an overview or summary of existing work, including research that has already been published elsewhere.

It is important to note that the final decision to publish research rests entirely with the Foundation.

Deliverable Timetable

The Foundation encourages research projects to be completed within four months from the point of commission.

During the project, the researcher should provide updates to the Foundation at mutually agreed regular intervals.

Researchers are also encouraged to consider feedback from the Foundation’s research program team regarding the progress and findings of the project.

In some cases, researchers may be asked to produce one or two interim articles of approximately 1,600 words before completing the full research project. These interim articles may summarize findings from the research that is still underway.

Funding Request

Funding for successful research projects is negotiable.

The Foundation may provide full or partial financial support for successful proposals.

Funding is typically paid at the point of completion of the project.

Researchers should therefore clearly communicate their funding requirements when submitting their proposal.

How to Prepare a Strong Proposal

Researchers interested in submitting should ensure that their proposal clearly explains the proposed research and its relevance to global trade.

A strong submission should:

Clearly identify the researcher or research team.

Provide relevant credentials and expertise.

Explain the proposed research topic.

Identify two to four key research questions.

Explain whether the research will use primary or secondary research.

Identify the expected research outputs.

Provide a realistic project timetable.

Clearly state the requested funding.

Demonstrate relevance to one or more of the Foundation’s priority research areas.

How to Apply

Researchers and research organizations interested in the call should first review the Hinrich Foundation application guidelines and then submit their research proposal through the designated submission form.

The Foundation has provided a dedicated submission process for researchers to submit their proposals.

Upcoming submission deadline: October 31, 2026

Applicants should ensure that their proposals are completed and submitted before the deadline.

Important Considerations

The Foundation’s call states that successful proposals may receive full or partial financial support. However, funding is negotiable and is typically paid upon completion of the project.

Researchers should also be aware that receiving support does not automatically mean that a research product will be published. All research products are subject to editorial review, and the Foundation retains the final decision regarding publication.

Conclusion

The Hinrich Foundation Call for Research Proposals 2026 offers researchers and research organizations an opportunity to develop research addressing important global trade issues and contributing to policy development.

The programme covers a wide range of subjects, including trade governance, trade geopolitics, foreign direct investment, supply chain resilience, digital trade, environmental sustainability, workforce and education, economic development, natural resources, and logistics.

Researchers with relevant expertise are encouraged to develop clear research questions, explain their methodology, outline their proposed deliverables and identify their funding requirements.

The next submission deadline is October 31, 2026.

Interested researchers should review the application guidelines and submit their proposals through the official submission form before the deadline.

About the Committee to Protect Journalists

Founded in 1981, the Committee to Protect Journalists, commonly known as CPJ, is an independent nonprofit organisation that works to defend journalists and advance press freedom around the world.

CPJ monitors, verifies and reports attacks against journalists and media workers. Its work includes documenting press freedom violations, advocating for imprisoned or threatened journalists, supporting journalists facing emergencies and encouraging legal and policy reforms that protect freedom of expression.

Over more than four decades, CPJ has contributed to efforts that have:

Secured the early release of imprisoned journalists.

Helped advance accountability for the murders of journalists.

Supported legal reforms in countries where freedom of expression has deteriorated.

Raised international awareness of attacks on journalists.

Produced widely cited research, databases and reports concerning press freedom.

Provided assistance to journalists facing physical, digital, legal and psychological threats.

Although CPJ is headquartered in New York City, its staff members and contributors work across different regions. The organisation seeks employees who can collaborate effectively across countries, cultures and time zones.

Position One: Program Coordinator, Eastern Europe/Central Asia

Position Overview

The Program Coordinator will lead CPJ’s research, documentation, advocacy and journalist-support activities relating to Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

The position sits within CPJ’s Europe and Central Asia programme and reports to the Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia. It is classified within CPJ’s Management II job band.

CPJ is looking for an experienced professional with extensive knowledge of press freedom conditions in Russia and Eastern Europe and a strong understanding of the wider regional political, human rights and media environment.

The selected candidate will coordinate regional contributors, oversee press freedom monitoring, support journalists facing danger and represent CPJ before media organisations, government representatives, civil society partners and other stakeholders.

This is a leadership position requiring both strategic oversight and hands-on involvement in research, reporting, advocacy, crisis response and team management.

Team Coordination and Leadership Responsibilities

The Program Coordinator will provide day-to-day leadership and supervision to staff members and regional contributors. Responsibilities will include:

Establishing clear expectations for staff and contributors.

Assigning and delegating work according to programme priorities.

Monitoring the quality, accuracy and timeliness of regional work.

Coaching and developing team members.

Addressing performance or conduct concerns when necessary.

Promoting an inclusive, accountable and high-performing team culture.

Supporting the recruitment and onboarding of employees and contributors.

Managing researchers, correspondents, contractors and other regional contributors.

Ensuring that regional work aligns with CPJ’s organisational strategy and standards.

Deputising for senior regional leadership when required.

Supporting the implementation of wider regional strategies and priorities.

Providing crisis-management leadership during urgent or high-risk press freedom situations.

Applicants should demonstrate experience supervising people, coordinating distributed teams and maintaining professional standards under pressure.

Press Freedom Monitoring, Research and Data Responsibilities

A major part of the position involves ensuring that CPJ receives reliable, current and well-documented information concerning attacks on journalists.

The Program Coordinator will be expected to:

Monitor press freedom developments across Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

Document and report attacks, threats and restrictions affecting journalists.

Maintain oversight of press freedom case-tracking and advocacy pipelines.

Ensure that CPJ’s records concerning imprisoned, missing, killed or targeted journalists remain accurate and current.

Identify emerging threats and trends affecting journalists and media organisations.

Propose, commission, supervise and conduct regional research.

Produce daily reporting, longer analytical reports and multimedia content.

Prepare timely news alerts, statements, videos and expert analysis.

Develop factual social media material in coordination with CPJ’s communications and social media teams.

Contribute to annual regional assessments, planning documents and strategic reviews.

The successful candidate must be capable of moving between immediate breaking-news responses and deeper, long-term research projects.

Advocacy Responsibilities

The Program Coordinator will play a leading role in developing and implementing advocacy strategies intended to improve protections for journalists.

Duties will include:

Designing regional and country-level press freedom advocacy strategies.

Advocating for the release of journalists who have been imprisoned because of their work.

Supporting efforts to end impunity in cases involving the killing of journalists.

Producing advocacy briefings and other supporting materials.

Overseeing the preparation of advocacy content.

Developing new projects in response to emerging political and media developments.

Presenting CPJ’s research to media outlets, policymakers and other stakeholders.

Using evidence and documented cases to influence public and policy discussions.

Applicants should understand how research, public communication, stakeholder engagement and policy advocacy can be combined to produce practical pressure for change.

Representation and External Engagement

The position requires the selected candidate to represent CPJ publicly and maintain a strong network of regional contacts.

The Program Coordinator will:

Act as a CPJ spokesperson when required.

Engage with media outlets, governments, civil society groups and partner organisations.

Develop and maintain relationships with policymakers and journalists.

Strengthen CPJ’s network of regional media contacts.

Establish relationships with human rights defenders and other relevant stakeholders.

Develop collaborations, joint initiatives and coalition-based activities.

Represent CPJ at national and regional meetings, forums and events.

Travel within the region when required.

Strong professional judgment will be essential because the position may involve communication about politically sensitive cases and engagement with journalists experiencing serious threats.

Journalist Assistance and Safety Responsibilities

The Program Coordinator will also support journalists who are experiencing threats, trauma or emergency situations.

Responsibilities include:

Developing journalist-assistance and advocacy plans.

Reviewing requests for assistance from journalists.

Assessing urgent cases and identifying appropriate responses.

Providing first-responder support and feedback.

Coordinating assistance with CPJ’s Journalist Assistance team.

Preparing case-related documentation and reports.

Working with the Emergencies team to monitor dangerous situations.

Responding to new threats affecting journalists.

Supporting the delivery of timely and appropriate assistance.

Experience supporting people affected by trauma, persecution or emergency conditions is particularly valuable for this role.

Internal Coordination and Reporting

The Program Coordinator will work with CPJ teams responsible for advocacy, research and journalist assistance to ensure that regional activities contribute to the organisation’s wider objectives.

The selected candidate will prepare activity reports, assessments and internal updates and may be assigned other responsibilities consistent with CPJ’s research and advocacy mandate.

Required Qualifications for the Program Coordinator

Applicants must possess the following qualifications and competencies:

A bachelor’s degree or equivalent professional experience.

At least seven years of experience in media or advocacy work connected to regional press freedom issues.

Extensive knowledge of Russia, Eastern Europe and the wider Europe and Central Asia region.

A deep understanding of the regional geopolitical environment.

Demonstrated ability to analyse political, policy and freedom-of-expression issues.

The ability to connect political developments with their consequences for journalists and press freedom.

Strong research, analysis and reporting skills.

Experience writing concise and high-quality reports.

The ability to interpret, assess and accurately summarise reports and data.

Fluency in spoken and written English.

Fluency in spoken and written Russian.

Working proficiency in other relevant regional languages.

Excellent written and verbal communication skills.

Strong interpersonal, negotiation and conflict-resolution skills.

Excellent organisational abilities and close attention to detail.

Strong time-management skills and a record of meeting deadlines.

Effective analytical and problem-solving abilities.

The capacity to work with integrity, professionalism and confidentiality.

Experience leading teams and working with senior managers.

Willingness and ability to travel occasionally within the region.

Proficiency in Google Workspace applications.

Because the role includes emergency response and politically sensitive work, candidates must be able to make careful decisions, protect confidential information and remain effective in high-pressure situations.

Preferred Qualifications for the Program Coordinator

CPJ considers the following qualifications desirable:

Knowledge of additional regional languages.

An established network of professional contacts across the region.

Expertise concerning online or digital harms, including surveillance.

Experience contributing to policy development.

Multimedia or data-journalism experience.

Experience supporting journalists or other individuals affected by trauma.

Experience managing journalist-assistance cases.

Applicants who meet all essential requirements should not necessarily exclude themselves merely because they do not possess every preferred qualification.

Work Location and Schedule

The Program Coordinator position is:

Fully remote.

Located in Europe.

Intended for a candidate based in the Europe and Central Asia region.

Filled through an Employer of Record.

Subject to occasional regional travel.

Required to attend meetings conducted on United States Eastern Time when necessary.

The vacancy does not state that CPJ will sponsor a visa, work permit or relocation.

Country of employment.

Cost of living.

£72,250 to £84,000

Position Two: Researcher, Western and Northern Europe

Position Overview

CPJ is also recruiting a Researcher focusing on Western and Northern Europe. The position is part of the Europe and Central Asia programme and reports to the Program Coordinator for Europe and Central Asia.

The position is classified within the Researchers and Associates I job band and identified as a mid-level role.

The Researcher will monitor, investigate, verify and document attacks on the press and other developments affecting media freedom. The position also involves preparing research and advocacy materials, supporting regional strategy, representing CPJ when required and assisting journalists facing threats or emergencies.

The successful candidate must have substantial knowledge of media, press freedom and human rights issues in Europe and Central Asia, with particular strength in Western and Northern Europe.

Monitoring, Data Collection and Documentation Responsibilities

The Researcher will be responsible for tracking press freedom developments and ensuring that CPJ’s reporting is supported by verified evidence.

Responsibilities include:

Monitoring press freedom developments across Europe and Central Asia.

Focusing particularly on Western and Northern Europe.

Investigating and documenting arrests of journalists.

Monitoring censorship and restrictions on media organisations.

Recording physical attacks and threats against journalists.

Examining legal harassment directed at journalists and media outlets.

Monitoring transnational repression affecting journalists.

Documenting other threats to press freedom.

Maintaining current information in CPJ’s databases.

Updating records concerning imprisoned, missing, killed or targeted journalists.

Monitoring breaking news and emerging developments.

Alerting the Program Coordinator promptly when an urgent issue arises.

Developing and maintaining databases of media, government and civil-society contacts.

Candidates must be able to verify information carefully and distinguish credible evidence from incomplete, misleading or politically motivated claims.

Research and Writing Responsibilities

The Researcher will produce content for CPJ’s reporting, advocacy and public communications.

The selected candidate will:

Initiate and write reports concerning regional press freedom.

Produce advocacy documents and background materials.

Write timely news alerts and public statements.

Prepare expert analysis concerning regional developments.

Conduct original research on press freedom issues.

Prepare research notes in accordance with CPJ standards.

Write factual and engaging social media content.

Coordinate public-facing material with CPJ’s social media team.

Contribute to longer-term research and reporting initiatives.

Excellent English writing and reporting skills are essential. Applicants must be able to produce accurate material quickly without sacrificing verification or journalistic standards.

Advocacy Responsibilities

The Researcher will support and participate in CPJ’s regional advocacy activities.

Responsibilities will include:

Participating in meetings with government authorities.

Engaging with journalists, partner organisations and policymakers.

Helping develop advocacy strategies for Europe and Central Asia.

Implementing advocacy activities in coordination with the Program Coordinator and Regional Director.

Participating in online and in-person meetings that advance CPJ’s press freedom objectives.

The role requires candidates who can explain complex political and media issues clearly to different audiences.

Stakeholder Engagement and Coordination

The Researcher will build relationships with people and organisations relevant to CPJ’s work.

This includes:

Developing relationships with journalists.

Maintaining contacts with human rights organisations.

Engaging with civil society and other regional stakeholders.

Coordinating joint activities that advance CPJ’s objectives.

Collaborating with CPJ’s advocacy, research and assistance teams.

Presenting CPJ research to media outlets and other stakeholders.

Helping influence coverage of important press freedom developments.

A strong regional network is preferred, although it is not listed as an absolute requirement.

Journalist Assistance Responsibilities

The Researcher will support CPJ’s work with journalists who require assistance.

Duties include:

Preparing assistance documentation in accordance with CPJ’s internal framework.

Coordinating with the Emergencies team.

Experience with trauma-related cases or journalist-assistance work is considered an advantage.

Translation and Additional Support

The Researcher may be asked to translate interviews, documents and other materials between English and relevant regional languages.

The selected candidate may also perform other responsibilities that fall within CPJ’s research and advocacy mandate.

Required Qualifications for the Researcher

Applicants must possess:

At least five years of experience researching, reporting and publishing on global human rights and political issues; or equivalent experience in advocacy and humanitarian assistance.

Strong knowledge of Europe and Central Asia.

A solid understanding of regional media and human rights issues.

The capacity to work with minimal supervision.
