TITLE: Bank of America Global Capital Markets 2027 Summer Analyst Programme in London: DCM, ECM, Leveraged Finance and Sustainable Solutions Group

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Bank of America Global Capital Markets 2027 Summer Analyst Programme is an exciting opportunity for university students seeking to build a career in investment banking, capital markets, corporate finance, sustainable finance and related areas. Based in London, United Kingdom, the programme provides successful candidates with the opportunity to gain practical experience within one of four major Global Capital Markets businesses: Debt Capital Markets (DCM), Equity Capital Markets (ECM), Leveraged Finance (LevFin), or the Sustainable Solutions Group (SSG).

The programme is designed to expose participants to real-world financial transactions, sophisticated capital markets solutions, senior-level clients and professionals across Bank of America. Successful interns will receive formal training, on-the-job development, mentorship and opportunities to build a professional network within one of the world’s leading financial institutions.

Applications are currently open, and interested candidates should submit their applications by October 11, 2026. Because recruitment takes place on a rolling basis and assessments may begin before the stated deadline, prospective applicants are strongly encouraged to apply as early as possible.

Opportunity Overview

Organisation: Bank of America

Programme: Global Capital Markets 2027 Summer Analyst

Business Areas: Debt Capital Markets, Equity Capital Markets, Leveraged Finance and Sustainable Solutions Group

Location: London, United Kingdom

Programme Type: Summer internship

Job Reference: JR-14521

Application Deadline: October 11, 2026

Age Requirement: Applicants must be at least 18 years old

Expected Graduation Window: June 2027 to July 2028

Degree Requirement: Bachelor’s or Master’s degree from an accredited college or university

Academic Requirement: Minimum expected 2:1 degree classification or equivalent

Language Requirement: Fluency in English

Potential Outcome: Successful interns may receive an offer for full-time employment beginning in July 2028, with some business areas potentially offering January or April start dates

About Bank of America

Bank of America is a major global financial institution serving individuals, businesses, institutional investors and governments across a broad range of financial services. The organisation states that its purpose is to help make financial lives better through the power of every connection.

The bank places significant emphasis on what it describes as Responsible Growth, which involves delivering value to clients, employees, communities and shareholders while maintaining a strong focus on sustainable and responsible business practices.

For students and recent graduates, Bank of America’s early-career programmes provide opportunities to develop technical knowledge, professional skills and practical experience while working alongside experienced professionals.

The organisation also highlights its commitment to creating an inclusive workplace in which people from different backgrounds, experiences and perspectives can contribute to its business.

What Is the Global Capital Markets Business?

Bank of America’s Global Capital Markets business helps organisations access financial markets and develop financing strategies that meet their specific objectives.

The business includes four major areas:

Debt Capital Markets (DCM)

Equity Capital Markets (ECM)

Leveraged Finance (LevFin)

Sustainable Solutions Group (SSG)

Although each group has a different area of expertise, the teams work closely with clients and other parts of the bank to develop and execute financing solutions.

Clients can include investment-grade and sub-investment-grade corporations, financial institutions, private equity firms, sovereign issuers and supranational organisations.

1. Debt Capital Markets

Debt Capital Markets focuses on helping clients raise financing through debt-related instruments and develop strategies for managing their liabilities and financial obligations.

DCM products covered by the programme include:

Bonds

Loans

Capital products

Liability management

Foreign exchange solutions

Interest-rate solutions

Students interested in corporate finance, fixed income, credit markets, economics and financial markets may find DCM particularly relevant.

During the internship, participants can gain insight into how organisations determine their financing requirements, evaluate market conditions and structure debt transactions.

2. Equity Capital Markets

Equity Capital Markets helps companies access capital through equity-related transactions and other solutions connected to equity markets.

ECM products and transactions mentioned by Bank of America include:

Initial Public Offerings (IPOs)

Accelerated bookbuilds

Rights issues

Convertible bonds

Bespoke derivatives transactions

Working in ECM can provide exposure to the process through which companies raise capital from investors and navigate public and private financial markets.

Students interested in investment banking, corporate finance, equity markets, valuation and financial transactions may find this area particularly attractive.

3. Leveraged Finance

Leveraged Finance focuses on financing solutions for sub-investment-grade companies and private equity-backed businesses.

The team works with transactions involving:

Leveraged loans

High-yield bonds

Acquisitions

Leveraged buyouts

Take-private transactions

Dividend recapitalisations

Refinancing of existing debt

Private equity portfolio companies

Bank of America specifically notes that applicants interested in Leveraged Finance are preferably expected to have previous coursework or internship experience in finance.

This makes relevant academic and professional preparation particularly valuable for candidates who want to express a preference for the Leveraged Finance team.

4. Sustainable Solutions Group

The Sustainable Solutions Group focuses on sustainability-related issues that can influence financing, valuation and strategic decision-making.

The team works with professionals across Investment Banking, Debt Capital Markets and Equity Capital Markets to develop sustainable finance solutions and provide insights that can support clients’ long-term objectives.

This area may be particularly relevant to students interested in the intersection of:

Finance

Sustainability

Environmental, social and governance considerations

Corporate strategy

Sustainable investment

Capital markets

Long-term business transformation

Candidates interested in sustainability should be prepared to demonstrate an understanding of how sustainability considerations increasingly influence investors, companies and financial markets.

What the 2027 Summer Analyst Programme Offers

The Global Capital Markets Summer Analyst programme is structured to give participants broad exposure to the capital markets business while allowing them to indicate a preferred area.

Applicants can express a preference for:

Debt Capital Markets

Equity Capital Markets

Leveraged Finance

Sustainable Solutions Group

Following the selection process, successful candidates may be placed in any one of these four teams.

This means that while candidates can communicate their interests, they should remain open to being assigned to another Global Capital Markets group.

The programme also provides opportunities to interact with professionals across the wider bank, allowing interns to understand how different business units collaborate to deliver financial solutions to clients.

Training and Professional Development

Training and development are central components of the programme.

Successful candidates receive extensive formal training at the beginning of the internship. This training is supplemented by practical learning and professional support throughout the programme.

Participants can benefit from:

Formal training

On-the-job learning

Educational speaker events

Mentorship

Professional networking

Exposure to experienced financial professionals

Practical experience with capital markets transactions

Interaction with clients and senior professionals

This combination of classroom-style learning and practical experience can help students understand how concepts learned at university are applied in real financial markets.

Responsibilities of a Global Capital Markets Summer Analyst

As a Summer Analyst, participants may support a wide range of activities. Responsibilities can vary depending on the team to which an intern is assigned.

Key responsibilities may include the following.

Working With Product Specialists and Clients

Interns may work alongside product specialists and interact with clients, including senior management-level representatives.

This provides exposure to the process of understanding a client’s financial objectives and developing appropriate financing strategies.

Understanding Financial Markets

Participants are expected to develop a strong understanding of market fundamentals.

They may need to follow financial market developments and understand how market conditions affect financing decisions.

The ability to connect market developments with client needs is therefore an important part of the role.

Developing Client Presentations

Summer Analysts may be involved in preparing highly tailored presentations for clients.

These presentations can address financing requirements such as:

General corporate purposes

Acquisition financing

Sustainable-themed financing

Other customised financing solutions

This means candidates should be comfortable working with data, financial information and presentation materials.

Working on Live Transactions

One of the most valuable aspects of the internship is exposure to live transactions.

Interns may work alongside experienced professionals while transactions are being developed and executed.

This can provide practical insight into the pace, complexity and collaborative nature of capital markets work.

Collaborating Across the Bank

The programme involves interaction with professionals from multiple areas of Bank of America.

Summer Analysts may work closely with:

Investment Banking

Corporate Banking

Global Markets

Sales teams

Trading teams

Global Research

Capital Markets specialists

This cross-business exposure can help interns understand how different financial teams work together to support clients.

Understanding Sustainable Investment

Participants may also develop an understanding of how investors incorporate sustainability considerations into investment decisions.

This is particularly relevant for candidates interested in the Sustainable Solutions Group and the growing role of sustainability within capital markets.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

Applicants must satisfy the programme’s academic, graduation, language and other requirements.

Candidates should be:

Currently pursuing a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree.

Studying at an accredited college or university.

Expected to complete their degree between June 2027 and July 2028.

On track to achieve at least a 2:1 degree classification or equivalent.

Fluent in English.

At least 18 years old.

Available to join the bank at the required start date if subsequently offered a full-time position.

The stated completion requirement means candidates must have completed all final examinations, coursework and other outstanding requirements necessary for graduation within the specified timeframe.

Bank of America reserves the right to request evidence confirming the expected completion date before extending an employment offer.

What Academic Backgrounds Are Accepted?

One of the notable aspects of the programme is the broad range of academic disciplines accepted.

Applicants do not necessarily need to have studied finance, economics or business.

Bank of America states that applications are accepted from disciplines including:

Arts and humanities

Economics

Mathematics

Science

Engineering

Other relevant academic disciplines

This means students from non-traditional finance backgrounds may still be considered if they can demonstrate genuine interest in financial markets and the skills required for the role.

However, applicants interested in Leveraged Finance may benefit from previous finance coursework or internship experience, as this is identified as a preference for that business area.

Skills and Qualities Bank of America Is Looking For

Academic performance is only one part of the selection process. Candidates are also expected to demonstrate a combination of analytical, interpersonal and professional qualities.

Genuine Interest in Financial Markets

Applicants should be able to demonstrate why they are interested in financial markets and capital markets.

A strong application should go beyond simply stating that investment banking is prestigious or competitive. Candidates should demonstrate an understanding of the work involved and explain why a particular capital markets area interests them.

Analytical and Problem-Solving Skills

Capital markets work involves analysing information, assessing financial situations and helping develop solutions to complex client requirements.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate strong analytical and problem-solving abilities.

Teamwork

Global Capital Markets is highly collaborative.

Analysts may work with colleagues from multiple business units, meaning candidates should be comfortable contributing to teams and communicating with people with different areas of expertise.

Leadership

Bank of America also identifies leadership as an important quality.

Leadership does not necessarily require holding a formal leadership position. Candidates can demonstrate leadership through university activities, projects, societies, internships, community initiatives, employment or other experiences in which they took responsibility and influenced outcomes.

Creativity and Innovation

The ability to think creatively can be valuable when developing tailored financing solutions for clients.

Applicants should demonstrate that they can approach challenges from different perspectives and contribute ideas.

Ability to Work in a Fast-Paced Environment

Capital markets can involve rapidly changing market conditions and multiple competing priorities.

Candidates should therefore demonstrate an ability to:

Manage multiple tasks

Work under pressure

Prioritise responsibilities

Adapt to changing circumstances

Maintain attention to detail

Communicate effectively

Language Requirements

Fluency in English is essential for the programme.

Proficiency in another European language is considered highly desirable.

For regional roles, the relevant local language may also be required.

Candidates should therefore ensure that their application accurately communicates their language capabilities.

Microsoft Office Skills

Competence in Microsoft Office is listed as a desired qualification.

Relevant applications include:

Microsoft Word

Microsoft Excel

Microsoft PowerPoint

Microsoft Outlook

Excel and PowerPoint can be particularly useful in financial and investment banking environments because analysts frequently work with data, financial information and client presentations.

Candidates who have developed these skills through university projects, internships, part-time employment or other experiences should consider highlighting them in their application.

Potential Full-Time Employment Opportunity

The internship can potentially serve as a pathway into a full-time career with Bank of America.

Candidates who perform well during the summer internship may receive an offer for full-time employment beginning in July 2028.

Depending on the relevant line of business, some successful candidates may also have the possibility of starting in January or April.

However, candidates who receive an offer must be available for one of the applicable start dates because Bank of America states that deferrals cannot be offered.

Therefore, students applying for the internship should consider their post-graduation availability before applying.

Recruitment Process

Bank of America conducts analyst internship and full-time recruitment on a rolling basis after applications open.

This is an important point for prospective applicants.

Although the official application deadline is October 11, 2026, assessments may begin before the deadline.

As a result, waiting until the final day to submit an application could reduce the opportunity to be considered during earlier stages of the recruitment process.

Applicants are therefore encouraged to submit their applications as early as possible.

Why Apply for the Bank of America Global Capital Markets Internship?

The programme offers several potential advantages for students interested in financial markets and investment banking.

1. Practical Capital Markets Experience

Participants can gain exposure to real-world financing strategies and live transactions rather than relying exclusively on classroom learning.

2. Exposure to Multiple Financial Businesses

The programme connects participants with DCM, ECM, Leveraged Finance and Sustainable Solutions Group professionals.

3. Professional Networking

Interns can build relationships with professionals across Bank of America, including colleagues in Investment Banking, Corporate Banking, Global Markets and Research.

4. Mentorship and Training

Participants receive formal training, mentorship and on-the-job support.

5. Client Exposure

The internship may provide opportunities to work alongside professionals serving major corporate, institutional and other clients.

6. Potential Pathway to Full-Time Employment

High-performing interns may be considered for full-time employment following the programme.

7. Exposure to Sustainable Finance

The Sustainable Solutions Group provides an opportunity to understand the growing relationship between sustainability, financing, valuation and strategic decision-making.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Because Bank of America’s recruitment process can begin before the official closing date, applicants should prepare their materials carefully and apply early.

1. Tailor Your CV

Your CV should clearly demonstrate the skills most relevant to Global Capital Markets.

Where applicable, highlight:

Financial or economic coursework

Investment or finance internships

Analytical projects

Excel skills

PowerPoint experience

Research experience

Leadership roles

Team projects

Client-facing experience

Problem-solving achievements

Relevant extracurricular activities

Students from arts, humanities, science and engineering backgrounds should focus on transferable analytical, communication and problem-solving skills.

2. Demonstrate Your Interest in Capital Markets

Applicants should research the differences between DCM, ECM, Leveraged Finance and sustainable finance.

Understanding these businesses can help candidates articulate a credible reason for applying.

For example, an applicant interested in DCM should understand how companies use debt markets to raise capital, while someone interested in ECM should understand equity issuance and public-market transactions.

3. Research Current Market Developments

Candidates should develop a basic understanding of financial markets and be prepared to discuss major market developments.

This could include developments involving:

Interest rates

Inflation

Corporate financing

Bond markets

Equity markets

IPO activity

Credit markets

Private equity

Sustainable finance

4. Prepare for Competency-Based Questions

Applicants should prepare examples demonstrating:

Leadership

Teamwork

Problem-solving

Initiative

Adaptability

Creativity

Working under pressure

Managing competing priorities

Using specific examples can make responses more credible and memorable.

5. Improve Excel and PowerPoint Skills

Candidates should ensure they are comfortable with fundamental Microsoft Office functions.

Excel skills can help with analysing and organising information, while PowerPoint skills are particularly relevant to preparing professional client presentations.

Workplace Inclusion and Equal Opportunity

Bank of America states that it is committed to creating an equal and inclusive workplace.

The organisation welcomes applicants from diverse backgrounds and states that selection decisions are based on candidates’ skills, qualifications and experience.

The bank’s equal opportunities statement covers a wide range of characteristics, including:

Gender

Gender identity or reassignment

Marital or civil partner status

Race

Religion or belief

Colour

Nationality

Ethnic or national origin

Age

Sexual orientation

Pregnancy or maternity

Socio-economic background

This means candidates should not assume they are excluded based on their nationality, race, ethnicity, religion or other protected characteristic.

Workplace Adjustments

Bank of America also states that it is committed to ensuring its online application process provides equal employment opportunities.

Applicants who require workplace adjustments or assistance with:

Searching for a job opening

Completing an application

Completing a video interview

can contact the bank’s Junior Talent EMEA team at juniortalentemea@bofa.com to discuss the support they require.

The organisation states that it aims to respond to such enquiries within two business days.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Bank of America Global Capital Markets 2027 Summer Analyst Programme in London is October 11, 2026.

However, applicants should not wait until the deadline.

Because recruitment takes place on a rolling basis and assessments may begin before the closing date, submitting an application early is strongly recommended.

How to Apply

Interested candidates should apply through the official Bank of America careers platform and search for the Global Capital Markets 2027 Summer Analyst (DCM, ECM, Leveraged Finance, and SSG) – London position using Job Reference JR-14521.

International Migration: Comparative analysis of immigration and integration policies in the areas of refugee resettlement and asylum, immigrant integration (including labor market integration and social cohesion), labor migration, borders and mobility, migration and development, and returns and reintegration.

U.S. Immigrant Integration: Issues related to early childhood education and care; Dual Language Learners and English Learners; K-12 immigrant education; adult education, training, and workforce development; state and local immigration/integration policy and services; and language access policy.

Latin America and Caribbean Initiative: Assessing policy responses to mixed migration flows, with a focus on northern Central America and Venezuela; evaluating migration management systems in key host countries, including Mexico, Costa Rica, and Colombia; tracking regional and international development policies; and identifying integration challenges and opportunities. Written proficiency and oral fluency in Spanish are required.

Refugee and Forced Displacement Initiative: Research and analysis of policy and programmatic approaches that privilege refugee agency, lived experience, refugee livelihoods and self-reliance, host-country integration, and the role of faith in global responses.

Within each of these substantive areas, research intern duties include:

Contributing to overall MPI research efforts, including through independent quantitative and/or qualitative research and policy analysis

Writing paper drafts and preparing literature summaries

Providing events support

Summarizing hearings and other relevant public and private events

Light administrative tasks.

Communications Internships: MPI offers a communications internship, providing essential dissemination and other support across the Institute and with the ability to experience the breadth of its work across research areas.

Communications intern duties include:

Media tracking

Development of social media campaigns and visual assets

Assisting with events organization and execution

Assisting with promotion of the Migration Information Source magazine

Short-form writing and possible multimedia editing.

Benefits

A $1,472 biweekly stipend is offered to full-time interns and a prorated stipend to part-time interns. Students also may arrange to obtain credit for their work. MPI does not cover relocation expenses. Internships can be remote or in person.

Eligibility

Applicants do not need not be a U.S. citizen to apply; however, all applicants must be U.S. work authorized before the internship begins, unless they reside and work from outside the United States throughout the internship cycle. MPI is not designated by the State Department to be an exchange visitor sponsor and therefore cannot provide the supporting documents to apply for H-1B, J-1, H-3, or F-1 visas.

For all positions, applicants must be at least a junior in college and possess excellent oral and written communication skills.

Current students, college graduates, graduate students, and early-career professionals are welcome to apply.

Those without college experience who can demonstrate substantial relevant work experience will also be considered.

Foreign language skills and proficiency in key Office and other software programs are helpful, as are strong quantitative skills.

Minority applicants and/or applicants from immigrant or refugee backgrounds are strongly encouraged to apply.

Application

Interested applicants should fill out the online form. Separately, applicants should send the following materials by October 15, 2026, to InternshipApplications@migrationpolicy.org, including in the subject line “First Name Last Name_Spring 2027”:

CV/Resume

Cover letter (maximum 2 single-spaced pages) describing your personal or professional interest in migration and/or another public policy issue; specify which MPI program area(s) you wish to be considered for and describe relevant research, academic, and/or professional experiences.

Writing sample (maximum 5 single-spaced pages in English) demonstrating your ability to write clearly and analytically about migration, integration, refugee issues, or other public policy topics. Acceptable writing samples include course papers, policy memos, research reports, or published articles. If submitting an excerpt from longer works, include the sections that demonstrate your writing or analytical skills the best.

Transcript (official or unofficial) from all colleges/universities attended, showing courses and grades.

No AI policy: To fairly evaluate all applicants, they require application materials that reflect your authentic abilities and voice. Using AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) to write or substantially revise your application will result in disqualification.

TITLE: CDC Advancing Active People, Healthy Nation Through Science – Physical Activity Fellowship 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is offering a research and training opportunity through the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE) for qualified researchers and graduate-level professionals interested in physical activity promotion, public health, community design, implementation science, epidemiology, data analysis, policy, and related fields.

The CDC Advancing Active People, Healthy Nation Through Science – Physical Activity Fellowship, referenced as CDC-2026-0033, provides an opportunity for an eligible participant to train with CDC’s National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (NCCDPHP), specifically within the Division of Nutrition, Physical Activity, and Obesity (DNPAO) in Atlanta, Georgia.

This fellowship is particularly relevant to individuals interested in using scientific research, data, policy, community partnerships, and evidence-based interventions to increase physical activity and improve public health outcomes.

About the CDC Physical Activty Fellowship

The fellowship is connected to Active People, Healthy Nation, a national CDC initiative designed to help 27 million Americans become more physically active by 2027.

The initiative recognizes physical activity as an important component of population health and seeks to create environments and systems that make physical activity easier and more accessible.

As an ORISE participant, the selected fellow will work alongside multidisciplinary teams at CDC and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The training experience will involve research, evidence translation, partnership development, communication, evaluation, policy analysis, and dissemination activities related to physical activity promotion.

A major area of focus is activity-friendly community design. This involves identifying, evaluating, and communicating evidence-based approaches that increase opportunities for people to:

Walk

Bicycle

Use public transportation

Access everyday destinations through active transportation

Engage in other forms of routine physical activity

The fellowship therefore goes beyond traditional exercise promotion. It examines how communities, transportation systems, policies, urban environments, and public health strategies can be designed to support healthier and more physically active populations.

Research Project

The selected ORISE participant will be placed within CDC’s National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, in the Division of Nutrition, Physical Activity, and Obesity.

The research and training experience will contribute to nationally significant public health initiatives that aim to generate, interpret, translate, and communicate scientific evidence.

The fellow will contribute to efforts supporting Active People, Healthy Nation and may participate in activities involving:

Scientific research

Evidence reviews

Implementation science

Evaluation

Policy analysis

Data analysis

Community-level strategies

Evidence translation

Scientific writing

Dissemination

Partnership development

Public health communication

The fellow will also have opportunities to work with experts and organizations across several disciplines, creating an interdisciplinary training environment.

Key Learning Objectives

One of the strongest features of this fellowship is the breadth of professional and research skills participants can develop.

Under the supervision and guidance of experienced mentors, the selected fellow will have opportunities to develop the following competencies.

1. Scientific Evidence Reviews

The participant will learn how to support scientific evidence reviews, coordination, and communication activities that may contribute to future updates of the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd Edition.

This experience can provide valuable exposure to the process of reviewing scientific evidence and translating research findings into public health guidance.

2. National Partnership Development

The fellow will learn how to engage with national partners in support of updates to the National Physical Activity Plan.

This can involve working with organizations and stakeholders whose activities influence physical activity, health promotion, community development, transportation, and related areas.

3. Scientific Writing and Publications

The fellowship provides opportunities to develop experience in authoring or co-authoring:

Peer-reviewed scientific manuscripts

Scientific reports

Conference presentations

Evidence summaries

Other scientific communication products

This is particularly valuable for candidates interested in establishing or strengthening a research and academic career.

4. Implementation Science

Participants will build knowledge and skills in implementation science, which focuses on understanding how evidence-based interventions, programs, and policies can be effectively translated into real-world practice.

This may include examining why certain interventions work in particular communities and how successful strategies can be implemented or scaled.

5. Evaluation and Dissemination Research

The fellow will have opportunities to gain experience in evaluation and dissemination research.

These skills are important in determining whether public health programs and strategies are achieving their intended objectives and how evidence can be effectively communicated to organizations, policymakers, professionals, and communities.

6. Policy Analysis

The fellowship includes opportunities to understand policy analysis and evaluation related to community design and physical activity promotion.

This can involve examining how policies and community-level decisions influence opportunities for physical activity.

7. Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis

Participants will learn to apply both quantitative and qualitative analytical methods.

Depending on project needs, this may include working with:

Statistical data

Qualitative data

Mixed-method approaches

R

Python

GIS

Spatial analysis

Emerging analytical approaches

Candidates with existing data-analysis experience may therefore find this opportunity particularly relevant.

8. Interdisciplinary Collaboration

The fellow will work in interdisciplinary groups and interact with professionals from fields such as:

Public health

Physical activity

Tribal health

Urban planning

Epidemiology

Community planning

Transportation planning

Policy

Research

This provides an opportunity to understand public health problems from multiple professional perspectives.

9. Qualitative Research

The participant will build skills in qualitative methodology, including opportunities related to qualitative data collection, methodology, and analysis.

10. Data Analysis and Evidence Translation

The fellowship will provide opportunities to analyze data and translate scientific findings into products that can be understood and used by different audiences.

Participants may contribute to manuscripts and other materials addressing physical activity and community-level interventions.

11. Public Health Communication

The fellow will gain experience developing materials such as:

Infographics

Fact sheets

Evidence summaries

Messaging materials

Other communication products

These materials may be designed for policymakers, public health professionals, leadership, professionals in other sectors, and the general public.

12. Presentation Skills

Participants will also develop their ability to prepare and deliver presentations to internal and external audiences.

This can strengthen communication skills that are essential for researchers and public health professionals.

Preferred Skills and Experience

Although the opportunity has specific eligibility requirements, CDC has also identified several preferred skills that can strengthen an applicant’s profile.

The preferred candidate may have experience in:

Strong oral and written communication

Scientific writing

Peer-reviewed publications

Scientific reports

Scientific communication

Teamwork

Partner engagement

Physical activity

Active transportation

Land-use planning

Parks and recreation

Related public health sectors

Qualitative data

Qualitative research methodology

Qualitative data analysis

Translating scientific findings into plain language

R

Python

Tribal organizations and communities

Implementation science

Evaluation methods

Mixed-methods research

GIS/spatial analysis

Community planning

Transportation planning

Data visualization

Applicants do not necessarily need to possess every preferred skill. The fellowship is designed as a training experience, and candidates should highlight the relevant skills and experiences they already possess.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The opportunity has a specific eligibility requirement that applicants should carefully review before beginning an application.

Citizenship Requirement

The fellowship is available to U.S. citizens only.

This means that individuals who are citizens of other countries but do not hold U.S. citizenship are not eligible for this particular opportunity.

There is no race or ethnicity restriction stated in the eligibility requirements. However, the citizenship requirement is mandatory.

Academic Requirement

Applicants must have:

A master’s degree, or

A doctoral degree

in one of the eligible disciplines.

The degree must have been received within the previous 60 months.

Alternatively, applicants who are currently pursuing a qualifying master’s or doctoral degree may be eligible if they anticipate graduating by January 27, 2027.

Eligible Academic Disciplines

The listed eligible disciplines fall into two broad categories:

Life, Health and Medical Sciences

Applicants with relevant academic backgrounds within the life, health, and medical sciences may qualify, depending on how their degree aligns with the fellowship’s requirements.

Social and Behavioral Sciences

Applicants from relevant social and behavioral science disciplines may also qualify.

Because the fellowship focuses on physical activity, public health, community design, policy, implementation, evaluation, and behavioral and population-level interventions, candidates should carefully demonstrate how their academic background connects with the fellowship’s research objectives.

Where Is the Fellowship Located?

The research opportunity is based at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta, Georgia, USA.

The fellow will participate in a full-time training appointment and work with CDC and HHS teams involved in physical activity and public health initiatives.

Fellowship Duration

The appointment is initially expected to last one year.

However, the appointment may be renewed upon the recommendation of CDC and depending on the availability of funding.

The anticipated start date is listed as September 31, 2026, although the opportunity states that the start date is flexible and will depend on several factors.

Applicants should note that September has only 30 days. Therefore, the stated September 31 date appears to be a date-entry inconsistency in the announcement, and applicants should rely on the official application information or contact the listed point of contact if the exact start date is important to their application.

Learn More About This Opportunity HERE

Level of Participation

This is a full-time appointment.

The selected participant will therefore be expected to devote full-time participation to the fellowship and its research and training activities.

Participant Stipend

The fellowship provides a participant stipend.

However, the announcement does not provide one fixed stipend amount.

The stipend rate may vary according to several factors, including:

The specific opportunity

Location

Educational background

Experience

Other applicable factors

Candidates who reach the interview stage may ask about the exact stipend rate.

If selected, the official appointment offer will state the applicable monthly stipend.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming a specific dollar amount unless it is provided directly by ORISE or in their appointment offer.

Health Insurance and Participant Status

ORISE participants do not become employees of CDC, the U.S. Department of Energy, or ORAU.

The fellowship also does not provide traditional employment-related benefits associated with being a CDC employee.

Proof of health insurance is required for participation.

Health insurance may be obtained through ORISE.

Prospective applicants should therefore understand that this is a structured research and training appointment rather than a standard CDC employment position.

Environmental, Safety and Health Requirements

Successful applicants will be required to comply with the environmental, safety, and health requirements applicable to the hosting facility.

These requirements may include health and safety measures established by the facility, including applicable COVID-19-related requirements such as:

Facial covering

Physical distancing

Testing

Vaccination

Applicants should be prepared to comply with the requirements applicable at the time of their appointment.

How to Apply

A complete application must contain all required components.

Applicants should prepare the following:

1. Application Form

Complete and submit the official application through the designated ORISE application system.

Apply HERE

2. Academic Transcripts

Applicants must provide the required transcripts.

The announcement specifies that applicants should review the detailed ORISE transcript guidelines to determine what constitutes an acceptable transcript.

If documents are not in English, an official English translation must be included.

3. Current Resume or CV

The resume/CV should be current and should clearly present relevant academic and professional experience.

It should include information such as:

Academic history

Employment history

Relevant research or professional experience

Publications, where applicable

Relevant technical skills

Other experiences related to the fellowship

Candidates should tailor their CV to the research focus rather than submitting a generic resume whenever possible.

4. Recommendation

Applicants must provide one educational or professional recommendation.

This is an important requirement.

The application will be considered incomplete and will not be reviewed until at least one recommendation has been submitted.

Applicants should therefore contact their recommender early enough to ensure the recommendation is submitted before the application is reviewed.

Language Requirement

All application documents must be submitted in English.

If an applicant’s documents are in another language, they must include an official English translation.

This requirement applies particularly to academic documents and other materials submitted as part of the application.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

September 11, 2026, at 3:00 PM Eastern Time.

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Because applications may be reviewed before the final deadline, applicants should not wait until September 11 to submit their materials.

A strong strategy is to prepare the CV, transcripts, recommendation, and other application materials well in advance and submit a complete application as early as possible..

Why This Fellowship Could Be Valuable

This opportunity offers more than a traditional academic research placement.

A successful participant could gain exposure to the way a major U.S. public health agency uses research evidence to influence programs, policies, community strategies, and public health communication.

Some of the major professional development areas include:

Public health research

Scientific writing

Evidence synthesis

Policy analysis

Implementation science

Evaluation

Data analysis

Qualitative research

GIS and spatial analysis

Scientific communication

Public health messaging

Community design

Active transportation

Partnership development

Interdisciplinary collaboration

Conference presentations

Peer-reviewed publications

For researchers interested in population health and physical activity, the fellowship could provide an opportunity to work at the intersection of science, policy, community planning, and public health practice.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This fellowship may be particularly suitable for eligible U.S. citizens who are pursuing or have recently completed graduate-level education in areas connected to health, medicine, life sciences, social sciences, behavioral sciences, public health, epidemiology, or related disciplines.

Candidates with experience in any of the following areas may find the opportunity especially relevant:

Public health

Epidemiology

Physical activity research

Health promotion

Behavioral science

Community health

Implementation science

Program evaluation

Qualitative research

Quantitative research

Mixed-methods research

Urban planning

Transportation planning

GIS

Data science

Policy analysis

Health communication

Scientific writing

The strongest applicants should demonstrate not only academic qualifications but also an ability to work collaboratively, communicate scientific findings, analyze information, and connect research evidence with real-world public health practice.

Application Preparation Tips

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should carefully check that their materials demonstrate a clear connection between their background and the fellowship.

Tailor your CV

Emphasize research, publications, data analysis, public health projects, community work, presentations, and other experiences relevant to the fellowship.

Demonstrate research skills

If you have experience with R, Python, GIS, qualitative research, quantitative analysis, mixed methods, or data visualization, make those skills easy for reviewers to identify.

Highlight scientific communication

Publications, research reports, conference presentations, policy briefs, infographics, fact sheets, and other communication products can demonstrate your ability to translate evidence for different audiences.

Connect your experience to physical activity

Experience involving physical activity, active transportation, community planning, parks, land use, health promotion, or related sectors can be particularly valuable.

Secure your recommendation early

Because the application will not be reviewed until a recommendation has been submitted, applicants should not leave this requirement until the last minute.

Apply early

The opportunity uses rolling review. Submitting a complete application early may therefore be preferable to waiting until the final deadline.

CONCLUSION

The CDC Advancing Active People, Healthy Nation Through Science – Physical Activity Fellowship is a specialized research and training opportunity for eligible U.S. citizens with a recent or forthcoming master’s or doctoral degree in a relevant discipline.

The fellowship combines public health research, physical activity promotion, community design, policy analysis, implementation science, evaluation, data analysis, scientific writing, and evidence translation. Participants will have the opportunity to work with multidisciplinary professionals while contributing to initiatives connected to CDC’s Active People, Healthy Nation campaign.

With a full-time initial appointment of one year, a participant stipend, opportunities for professional development, and potential exposure to peer-reviewed research and national public health initiatives, the fellowship can be particularly valuable for graduate-level researchers seeking experience in applied public health science.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. The opportunity is restricted to U.S. citizens, requires a qualifying master’s or doctoral degree obtained within the past 60 months or anticipated by January 27, 2027, and requires a complete application containing the application form, transcripts, current CV/resume, and at least one educational or professional recommendation.

Most importantly, applicants should remember the September 11, 2026, 3:00 PM Eastern Time deadline and the fact that applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. Preparing and submitting a complete, carefully tailored application early can help ensure that the application is available for consideration.

TITLE: Call for Applications – AAU/IUFoST Young Scientists Innovation Competition

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Scaling UP Food Processing in Africa – The Role of Young Scientists

Background and Rationale

The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the International Union of Food Science and Technology (IUFoST), recognizes the vital role of young and early-career food scientists in shaping Africa’s food security and sustainable development goals. Supporting innovation, fostering excellence, and providing platforms for leadership development will strengthen Africa’s capacity for research, entrepreneurship, and industrial development in food systems.

This programme aims to create opportunities for emerging talent to showcase their innovative ideas, connect with mentors and industry leaders, and receive recognition for outstanding contributions.

Objectives

To encourage innovation and excellence in food science and technology among young and early-career scientists in Africa.

To provide a platform for showcasing research and innovation in scaling up food processing in Africa.

To foster leadership, entrepreneurship, and career development opportunities for early-career food scientists.

To honour and celebrate the achievements of young scientists who are contributing to Africa’s food security and industrial growth.

Scaling Up Food Processing in Africa – The Role of Young Scientists

Africa’s food processing landscape requires creative and practical solutions that integrate smallholder farmers, informal markets, and formal supply chains. The ‘One Mile’ approach – focusing on the immediate community and local market integration is critical to achieving scalable, sustainable food processing solutions that begin at the grassroots level.

The AAU, in partnership with IUFoST is organising a Young Scientist Competition to encourage early career food scientists and students to demonstrate real-life case studies of food processing innovation using the One Mile approach. The competition will promote creativity, critical thinking, and storytelling while showcasing how local food systems can be transformed through simple, practical innovations that support food safety and market access.

Competition

* Eligibility

African food scientists under 35 years or within 5 years of completion of their PhD/MSc.

* Submission Requirements

A one-page summary of innovation or research with clear impact potential for food processing scale-up in Africa.

* Application Deadline

18 May 2025. Applications should be emailed to secretariat@iufost.org

* Selection Process

Shortlisting of 10 candidates by the review committee.

Final selection of 5-6 for presentations during the Roundtable event on 30 May 2025.

Awards and Recognition

1st Prize: Plaque, mentorship opportunity, seed grant (US$1,000), and AAU/IUFoST innovation certificate.

2nd Prize: US$250.00, Plaque, mentorship opportunity, and innovation certificate.

3rd Prize: US$100.00 Certificate of participation and special mention.

Next Steps (Post-Competition)

* Winners to be featured in AAU and IUFoST newsletters.

* Opportunity to present at future regional or continental conferences.

* Invitation to join AAU/IUFoST mentorship and leadership programmes.

Application Deadline: May 18, 2025

Decision Notification: By May 22, 2025

Note: Finalists will present for 4-5 minutes on May 30th at an upcoming roundtable

TITLE: Sepehr Ebadi, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Sepehr Ebadi
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2024-2027
Email: sebadi@mit.edu
Phone: (617) 253-6074
Office: MIT Department of Physics
77 Massachusetts Avenue, 26-407
Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

Experimental Nuclear & Particle Physics/Atomic Physics

Research Interests

The Standard Model, a triumph of physics in the twentieth century, fails to explain some cosmological observations such as the origin of dark matter or matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe, hence motivating a broad search for physics beyond the standard model. While the energy frontier directly studies high energy particles (e.g. LHC at CERN), the precision frontier aims to indirectly access the effects of heavy particles with smaller experiments. Sepehr is broadly interested in using techniques from the field of atomic, molecular, and optical physics, combined with recent advances in nuclear physics to push the experimental precision frontier in search for new physics.

At MIT, I aim to develop techniques for laser-cooling of molecules with heavy, deformed nuclei to dramatically increase the sensitivity of future physics searches and the study of so-far unexplored nuclear and particle physics with tabletop experiments. These molecules, for instance Radium Fluoride (RaF), benefit from large enhancements stemming from large intramolecular electric fields, and large intrinsic sensitivity of the nucleus to symmetry-violating moments. Once laser-cooled, a few ultracold molecules can act as a quantum sensor in search of physics at 100TeV scale.

Biographical Sketch

Sepehr was born in Iran, and later immigrated to Toronto, Canada where he finished high school. He then received his bachelor of engineering science (physics option) at University of Toronto.

During his bachelor’s degree, he came to MIT for a professional experience year (PEY), working towards creating an ultracold gas of the lightest bi-alkali molecule. He later returned to Boston, where he obtained his PhD in physics from Harvard, working on quantum simulation and quantum information processing with neutral atom arrays.

Outside of physics, Sepehr is interested in phase transitions of complex organic matter in extreme environments — otherwise known as the science of cooking.

TITLE: Green Climate Fund Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group 2027–2030: Call for Nominations for Indigenous Peoples Representatives

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Green Climate Fund (GCF) has opened a call for nominations for its Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group (IPAG) for the 2027–2030 term, providing an opportunity for Indigenous Peoples’ representatives to contribute to dialogue, coordination, and engagement between Indigenous Peoples, the Green Climate Fund, and its partners on climate action and climate finance.

For the 2027–2030 term, the GCF is seeking nominations to fill one vacancy in each of four regions: Africa, Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Pacific. The nomination process is specifically designed as an Indigenous Peoples-led self-selection process, meaning nominations are expected to come through relevant Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, organizations, networks, and regional Indigenous Peoples’ caucuses.

The call is particularly relevant to Indigenous Peoples’ organizations and representatives working on climate action, environmental issues, Indigenous Peoples’ rights, sustainable development, climate finance, community development, and related areas.

Nomination deadline: 9 October 2026

About the Green Climate Fund Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group

The Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group (IPAG) was established under the Green Climate Fund’s Indigenous Peoples Policy to strengthen coordination and engagement between Indigenous Peoples and the Green Climate Fund and its partners.

The group provides a mechanism through which Indigenous Peoples’ perspectives can be brought into the GCF’s work. Its membership consists of Indigenous Peoples’ representatives from regions of developing States where the Green Climate Fund may fund activities.

Rather than being an ordinary employment position, IPAG membership is part of the GCF’s broader institutional approach to Indigenous Peoples’ participation and engagement.

The current call follows recommendations arising from the eighth meeting of the Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group, after which the GCF Secretariat began the process of filling vacancies for the next 2027–2030 term.

What Is the Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group?

The Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group is a mechanism for strengthening interaction between the Green Climate Fund and Indigenous Peoples.

This is particularly significant in the context of climate action because Indigenous Peoples and their communities are frequently closely connected to land, forests, water, biodiversity, natural resources, and ecosystems that are affected by climate change and climate-related interventions.

Through IPAG, Indigenous Peoples’ representatives can participate in a structured advisory mechanism connecting Indigenous Peoples’ perspectives with the GCF and its partners.

The group therefore provides an avenue for Indigenous Peoples’ institutions and representatives to contribute perspectives relevant to climate action, inclusion, environmental sustainability, and the interests and concerns of Indigenous Peoples in developing regions.

Regional Vacancies for the 2027–2030 Term

For the 2027–2030 IPAG term, the Green Climate Fund has identified four regional vacancies.

There is one vacancy in each of the following regions:

1. Africa

Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, organizations, networks, and regional Indigenous Peoples’ caucuses in Africa may submit nominations for the African regional vacancy.

The nominee should be an Indigenous Peoples’ representative from a developing State where the GCF may fund activities.

2. Eastern Europe and Central Asia

The second vacancy is for the Eastern Europe and Central Asia region.

Relevant Indigenous Peoples’ institutions and organizations in this region may nominate an appropriate Indigenous Peoples’ representative who meets the requirements and considerations established in the IPAG Terms of Reference.

3. Latin America and the Caribbean

The third vacancy covers Latin America and the Caribbean.

Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, organizations, networks, and regional caucuses may participate in the self-selection process by submitting qualified nominations for this regional position.

4. Pacific

The fourth vacancy is for the Pacific region.

Indigenous Peoples’ organizations and institutions from eligible developing States in the Pacific may submit nominations for consideration.

The GCF notes that where no eligible nomination is received from one of these four regions, the Secretariat may consider eligible nominations from underrepresented sub-regions or groups, consistent with advice from the Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group.

Who Can Be Nominated?

This opportunity is specifically focused on Indigenous Peoples’ representatives rather than applicants from the general public.

The nominee should be a representative from an Indigenous Peoples’ institution, organization, body, network, or related structure in an eligible developing State where the Green Climate Fund may fund activities.

Importantly, individuals do not simply submit a personal application independently. The nomination must come through an appropriate Indigenous Peoples’ institution, body, or organization.

The nominating organization must also formally confirm that the individual has been nominated or endorsed by the organization’s head or designated focal point.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to individuals who already have an established connection with Indigenous Peoples’ organizations or representative structures.

What Experience Should the Nominee Demonstrate?

The nomination must include a statement demonstrating how the nominee satisfies the criteria and factors for IPAG membership contained in the group’s Terms of Reference.

The nomination should also include a short CV or biography highlighting the nominee’s experience and contributions that are relevant to areas such as:

Indigenous Peoples’ issues

Climate action

Environmental issues

Climate-related development

Community-level initiatives

Indigenous Peoples’ participation

Related areas of relevance to the work of the Green Climate Fund

The GCF specifically requests that the nominee’s relevant experience and contributions be clearly presented.

This means that a generic CV may not be sufficient on its own. The information submitted should help demonstrate the nominee’s connection to Indigenous Peoples’ issues and/or climate action and explain why the person is appropriate for representation on the Advisory Group.

Nomination Must Come From an Indigenous Peoples’ Organization

One of the most important aspects of this call is that it is an organization-led nomination process.

Individuals interested in being considered should therefore first establish whether an eligible Indigenous Peoples’ institution, organization, body, network, or regional caucus is able and willing to formally nominate or endorse them.

The nominating organization is responsible for providing information about itself and the nominee and for confirming that the nomination is formally supported.

The organization must identify the region for which the nomination is being submitted.

Information Required From the Nominating Organization

The Green Climate Fund has specified the information that must accompany each nomination.

1. Information about the nominating organization

The submission should include:

The name of the Indigenous Peoples’ institution, body, or organization.

Contact details of the organization.

The region for which the nomination is being submitted.

This information allows the GCF to establish the institutional source of the nomination and the relevant regional context.

2. Information about the nominee

The submission must provide:

The nominee’s full name.

The nominee’s contact details.

Email address.

Telephone number.

The nominee’s information should be accurate and current because the nomination process may involve subsequent communication with the individual and the nominating organization.

3. Formal confirmation of nomination or endorsement

The nomination must include confirmation from the head or designated focal point of the nominating Indigenous Peoples’ institution, body, or organization.

This confirmation should establish that the nominee has been formally nominated or endorsed by the organization.

This is an important distinction because the opportunity is not structured as an open individual application.

4. Statement demonstrating eligibility and suitability

The nominating organization must provide a statement demonstrating how the nominee meets the criteria and factors to be considered for IPAG membership as established in the Terms of Reference.

This statement should therefore go beyond simply saying that the person is experienced.

It should connect the nominee’s experience, knowledge, representation, and contributions to the requirements and considerations for IPAG membership.

5. Short CV or biography

The nomination should include a short CV or biography of the nominee.

The GCF specifically asks that this document highlight the individual’s:

Experience relating to Indigenous Peoples’ issues;

Contributions to Indigenous Peoples’ communities or organizations;

Experience in climate action;

Relevant experience in related areas.

A strong biography should therefore make the nominee’s relevant experience immediately clear rather than focusing primarily on unrelated professional achievements.

6. Additional endorsements

Endorsements from other Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, or organizations within the respective region are highly encouraged.

Although the GCF does not state that these additional endorsements are mandatory, they can form part of the regional self-selection process and demonstrate broader institutional support for the nominee.

Organizations considering a nomination may therefore wish to explore whether additional Indigenous Peoples’ organizations within their region are willing to provide endorsements.

How the Indigenous Peoples-Led Self-Selection Process Works

The call is based on an Indigenous Peoples-led self-selection process.

This means that the selection mechanism is designed to involve Indigenous Peoples’ institutions and representative structures in identifying nominees for the regional vacancies.

The process is therefore different from a conventional recruitment exercise in which individuals compete for a job by submitting applications directly to an employer.

The GCF is specifically asking relevant Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, organizations, networks, and regional Indigenous Peoples’ caucuses to submit nominations.

The regional dimension is also important. Each of the four listed regions has one vacancy, and nominations should identify the region for which the nomination is being submitted.

What Do IPAG Members Do?

The detailed IPAG Terms of Reference describe the group’s role and functions, membership arrangements, competencies and factors to be considered, the self-selection process, working arrangements, and provisions relating to revision and termination of the Terms of Reference.

The Terms of Reference therefore provide the principal framework for understanding the responsibilities and expectations associated with IPAG membership.

Potential nominees and nominating organizations should review the Terms of Reference carefully before preparing a submission.

The GCF’s announcement specifically directs prospective nominators to the Terms of Reference when demonstrating how a nominee meets the criteria and factors considered for IPAG membership.

Is IPAG Membership a Paid Position?

No.

IPAG members serve on a voluntary and non-remunerated basis.

This means that the opportunity should not be treated as a salaried employment position or paid consultancy.

However, the GCF indicates that where in-person participation is required, travel-related arrangements may be supported in accordance with applicable GCF policies and procedures.

This distinction is important: the membership itself is voluntary and unpaid, but certain travel-related arrangements associated with required in-person participation may receive support under applicable GCF rules.

How Often Do IPAG Members Meet?

IPAG members can expect to participate in:

Two in-person meetings each year

Monthly online meetings

Additional online meetings where specific activities require them

The frequency of participation means that nominees should be prepared to make a sustained commitment throughout the 2027–2030 term.

The opportunity is therefore not simply an honorary designation. It involves ongoing participation in the group’s work.

Working Language

The working language of the Green Climate Fund is English.

Consequently, nominees should be able to participate in the group’s activities within this working-language environment.

Organizations preparing nominations should take this into account when identifying and supporting nominees.

Duration of the Appointment

The call concerns the 2027–2030 term of the Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group.

This means that nominees are being considered for participation in the Advisory Group during this multi-year period rather than for a short-term event or one-time consultation.

The expected meetings and activities described by the GCF indicate that members should be prepared for continued engagement throughout their term.

Important Deadline

The deadline for submitting nominations is:

9 October 2026

Nominations must be sent to:

IPAGnomination@gcfund.org

The Green Climate Fund’s official announcement specifies that nomination submissions must reach this email address no later than 9 October 2026.

Organizations should therefore allow sufficient time to identify the nominee, obtain the required organizational confirmation, prepare the supporting statement, compile the nominee’s CV or biography, and obtain any additional endorsements they wish to include.

How to Prepare a Strong Nomination

Organizations interested in submitting a nomination should carefully organize their materials before sending them.

Step 1: Identify the relevant regional vacancy

First determine whether the nomination relates to:

Africa;

Eastern Europe and Central Asia;

Latin America and the Caribbean; or

the Pacific.

The nominating organization should clearly identify the region for which the nomination is being submitted.

Step 2: Identify an appropriate Indigenous Peoples’ representative

The nominee should have a clear connection to Indigenous Peoples’ representation and relevant experience.

Organizations should consider the individual’s experience with Indigenous Peoples’ issues, climate action, environmental matters, community engagement, and other areas relevant to the IPAG mandate.

Step 3: Review the IPAG Terms of Reference

Before preparing the nomination statement, the organization should review the official IPAG Terms of Reference.

The Terms of Reference explain the role and functions of IPAG, membership, competencies and factors to be considered, the self-selection process, working arrangements, and other institutional provisions.

This review is particularly important because the GCF requires the nomination to include a statement demonstrating how the nominee meets the relevant criteria and factors.

Step 4: Prepare the nominee’s CV or biography

The CV or biography should focus attention on experience and contributions relevant to:

Indigenous Peoples;

climate action;

environmental issues;

community development;

Indigenous representation; and

related areas.

Relevant achievements should be presented clearly and in a way that demonstrates the nominee’s connection to the purpose of the Advisory Group.

Step 5: Obtain formal organizational endorsement

The organization’s head or designated focal point should formally confirm the nomination or endorsement.

This confirmation should be included in the submission.

Step 6: Consider additional regional endorsements

The GCF highly encourages endorsements from other Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, or organizations in the relevant region.

Where appropriate, organizations may therefore seek additional endorsements to demonstrate broader regional support.

Step 7: Submit before the deadline

The completed nomination should be sent to IPAGnomination@gcfund.org no later than 9 October 2026.

Organizations should avoid leaving the submission until the final day because obtaining organizational confirmation and additional endorsements may require coordination with multiple people.

Why This Opportunity Is Significant for Indigenous Peoples’ Representatives

The IPAG nomination process provides a structured avenue for Indigenous Peoples’ representatives to participate in engagement with one of the major international institutions working on climate finance.

The Green Climate Fund is focused on mobilizing and delivering climate finance for developing countries, and its work includes climate-related investments and partnerships across developing regions. The Fund currently reports activities across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, Eastern Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East, and Latin America and the Caribbean.

The IPAG mechanism specifically recognizes the importance of Indigenous Peoples’ participation in this broader climate-finance context.

For Indigenous Peoples’ organizations, therefore, the nomination process is an opportunity to put forward representatives who can contribute perspectives and experience relating to Indigenous Peoples and climate action.

Who Should Consider This Opportunity?

This call is particularly relevant to:

Indigenous Peoples’ institutions;

Indigenous Peoples’ organizations;

Indigenous Peoples’ representative bodies;

Indigenous Peoples’ networks;

regional Indigenous Peoples’ caucuses;

Indigenous Peoples’ representatives with experience in climate action;

Indigenous Peoples’ representatives working on environmental issues;

Indigenous Peoples’ advocates involved in climate and sustainable-development discussions; and

eligible Indigenous Peoples’ representatives from developing States where the GCF may fund activities.

It is important to emphasize that the call is not a general application opportunity open to anyone interested in climate change.

The nomination must come through a relevant Indigenous Peoples’ institution, body, or organization, and the nominee must be an Indigenous Peoples’ representative from an eligible developing State.

Regional and Geographic Eligibility

The call specifically identifies four regions:

Africa, Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Pacific.

The nominee should come from a developing State where the Green Climate Fund may fund activities.

This means that geographic eligibility is tied to both the four regional vacancies and the GCF’s framework concerning developing States where it may finance activities.

The GCF’s announcement provides a link to its countries and regions information for determining the relevant geographic context.

Important Documents to Review

The Green Climate Fund has published two principal documents associated with this call:

Main Call for Nominations – provides the details of the 2027–2030 nomination process, regional vacancies, nomination requirements, and submission deadline.

IPAG Terms of Reference – provides the framework covering the role and functions of IPAG, membership, competencies and factors to be considered, self-selection, working arrangements, and other provisions.

Potential nominators should review both documents carefully before preparing their submission.

Conclusion

The Green Climate Fund Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group 2027–2030 call for nominations provides an institutional pathway for Indigenous Peoples’ representatives to contribute to engagement between Indigenous Peoples, the Green Climate Fund, and its partners.

The opportunity is particularly distinctive because it is not structured as a conventional job, fellowship, scholarship, or individual application. Instead, it uses an Indigenous Peoples-led nomination and self-selection process, with relevant Indigenous Peoples’ institutions, bodies, organizations, networks, and regional caucuses playing a central role.

Four regional vacancies are available for the upcoming term, covering Africa, Eastern Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Pacific. Nominees should be Indigenous Peoples’ representatives from developing States where the GCF may fund activities and should be able to demonstrate relevant experience and contributions, particularly in relation to Indigenous Peoples’ issues, climate action, or related fields.

IPAG members serve on a voluntary, non-remunerated basis, but the role involves ongoing participation, including monthly online meetings and two in-person meetings each year. Travel-related arrangements for required in-person participation may be supported in accordance with applicable GCF policies and procedures.

Organizations intending to nominate a representative should begin the process early, carefully review the IPAG Terms of Reference, prepare the required organizational and nominee information, develop a clear statement addressing the membership criteria, and consider obtaining additional regional endorsements.

The deadline for nominations is 9 October 2026, and submissions should be sent to IPAGnomination@gcfund.org.

For the official announcement and supporting documents, visit the Green Climate Fund’s official call for nominations.
