TITLE: Remote and regional drivers of the Indonesian Throughflow under future warming: Implications for Inter-Basin Freshwater Transport

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Wang, S., Waitzmann, D., Ummenhofer, C. C., & Oppo, D. W. (2026). Remote and Regional Drivers of the Indonesian Throughflow Under Future Warming: Implications for Inter-Basin Freshwater Transport. Geophysical Research Letters, 53(1), e2025GL119514. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL119514

The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) is an important passageway through which warm, fresh waters from the Pacific are carried into the Indian Ocean. There are large uncertainties on how individual pathways of the ITF will change over the course of the 21st century because models used in climate change studies often do not have sufficient horizontal resolution to accurately represent these narrow passageways. Here we use state‐of‐the‐art climate model simulations to investigate how the ITF is projected to change. We find that transport through the three inflow pathways is expected to weaken in the 21st century due to influences from equatorial Pacific winds and the Atlantic overturning circulation. The wind changes contribute to the ITF decline in the surface layer, while Atlantic circulation changes explain the subsurface decrease in transport. Despite a weakened ITF, the amount of freshwater this current system carries into the Indian Ocean increases because of enhanced rainfall in the Western Pacific. Our results highlight the remote and regional changes that are expected to impact the exchange of volume and freshwater between the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

(a) Bathymetry of the Indonesian seas (in kilometers) with main ITF inflow and outflow pathways, Pacific upper ocean currents, and the Karimata Strait Throughflow shown as black arrows. The transects used to analyze Makassar Strait, Maluku Sea, Halmahera Sea, and ITF outflow transport are indicated by blue, purple, green, and orange lines, respectively. Transport magnitudes (in Sverdrups) averaged over the 1850–1950 period are also shown along with future (2080–2100) transport changes in parenthesis. Positive values denote southward/westward transport along the direction of the ITF. (b) Full‐depth transport anomalies (relative to 1850–1950) calculated for all three inflow passageways, (d) the sum of inflows and the ITF outflow. (c) Profiles of velocity trends spanning 2005–2100 for all three inflow pathways, (e) the sum of all three inflow profiles, and the ITF outflow. Velocity is multiplied by strait width at each depth. The 95% confidence intervals of velocity trends in (c), (e) are also shown (shading). Figure from Wang et al. (2026).

TITLE: Patti Grace Smith Fellowship 2027 | Paid Aerospace Internship for Black Undergraduates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Patti Grace Smith Fellowship Class of 2027 is now accepting applications from talented Black undergraduate students seeking to launch their careers in the aerospace industry.

The fellowship is designed to help extraordinary students gain their first meaningful work experience in aerospace, while providing mentorship, financial support, professional connections and a supportive community of peers and industry professionals.

Students interested in aviation, space, engineering, science, business, policy, journalism and other aerospace-related fields are encouraged to apply.

About the Patti Grace Smith Fellowship

The Patti Grace Smith Fellowship celebrates and supports Black Excellence in Aerospace by helping talented undergraduate students who have not yet entered the aerospace workforce access career opportunities and professional networks.

Through the programme, Fellows can be connected with aerospace employers for paid summer internships and receive ongoing mentorship and community support. The fellowship also provides a cash grant and an annual leadership summit.

Benefits

Selected Patti Grace Smith Fellows can receive:

Paid summer internship opportunities with leading aerospace companies, startups and institutions.

$2,500 or more cash grant to support tuition, school fees, professional development and other academic or career-related expenses.

Two mentors, including an experienced aerospace industry leader and an early-career professional.

Leadership development opportunities, including the fellowship’s annual summit.

Professional networking opportunities with aerospace companies, industry leaders and fellow students.

Lifelong community and alumni support from talented Black professionals pursuing careers in aerospace.

The programme is open to students interested in areas beyond engineering, including business, policy, communications and other fields relevant to the aerospace industry.

Eligibility Requirements

To be eligible for the Patti Grace Smith Fellowship Class of 2027, applicants must:

Be currently enrolled in a bachelor’s degree programme or an associate’s degree programme.

Be a U.S. citizen, U.S. permanent resident, U.S. national, qualifying refugee or qualifying asylee and legally permitted to work in the United States.

Not yet be part of the aerospace workforce. The fellowship typically serves students seeking their first paid aerospace internship, although certain exceptions may apply.

Demonstrate strong moral character and commitment to the mission and community of the fellowship.

Required Application Materials

Applicants should prepare the following:

1. One-Page Résumé

Submit an updated one-page résumé highlighting your education, projects, clubs, work experience, internships, leadership activities and other relevant achievements.

The résumé should be submitted as a PDF and named:

2027PGSF_Lastname_Firstname_Resume.pdf

2. Latest Transcript

Applicants must provide their most recent school transcript. Unofficial transcripts are accepted at the application stage.

File name:

2027PGSF_Lastname_Firstname_Transcript.pdf

3. Two Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must provide two letters of recommendation.

One letter should discuss your aptitude, skills, passion and potential in your chosen field.

The second should focus on your character, creativity and consistency.

Both recommendation letters must be submitted by the application deadline.

4. Written Essay

Applicants must submit an original 500–750 word essay addressing the following question:

What can the global aerospace industry do to better serve communities who currently feel unconnected to and underrepresented in aerospace?

Applicants should include at least one specific, achievable idea that could make a difference for an underserved community.

The essay should be submitted as a PDF using:

2027PGSF_Lastname_Firstname_Essay.pdf

5. Multimedia Essay

Applicants must also submit a multimedia response addressing:

“GPAs and college transcripts don’t paint a complete picture of a person. What else do we need to know about you?”

Applicants can choose a format that reflects their personality and creativity, such as a video, spoken-word performance, song, animation, fiction, comic or another suitable format.

The submission must be reviewable within approximately five minutes and should preferably be below 250 MB.

6. Additional Essay or Multimedia Response

Applicants must answer one additional question from the fellowship’s selection of prompts. The response can be submitted as either a written essay or multimedia piece.

The prompts explore areas such as:

Personal decision-making when dealing with difficult industry situations.

A project you started independently.

A technology, policy or business model that could transform aerospace.

An act of service that has had a meaningful impact.

How you would help develop an aerospace startup.

An aerospace topic you could passionately explain.

How you have grown since a previous fellowship application.

7. Previous Aerospace Experience

Applicants who have already worked in aerospace but believe they would still benefit significantly from the fellowship may explain their circumstances in a 250–500 word essay.

Applicants without previous aerospace employment can skip this section.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is particularly suitable for talented Black undergraduate students who:

Want to build a career in aerospace, aviation or space.

Are looking for their first paid aerospace internship.

Want to gain practical industry experience.

Are interested in engineering, science, business, policy, journalism or related fields.

Want access to mentors and a strong professional network.

Want to connect with other talented Black students and professionals in aerospace.

Application Deadline

Deadline: October 4, 2026

Applications must be submitted by 11:59:59 PM Eastern Time on Sunday, October 4, 2026. Both recommendation letters must also be submitted by the deadline.

How to Apply

Interested students can submit their application through the official online application portal.

Apply here: Patti Grace Smith Fellowship Class of 2027 Application

Applicants can also access free application guides and join the fellowship’s applicant community for additional guidance and support.

Conclusion

The Patti Grace Smith Fellowship provides talented Black undergraduates with an opportunity to gain valuable experience, mentorship, financial support and professional connections as they begin their aerospace careers.

If you are an eligible undergraduate interested in aviation, space, engineering, science, business, policy, journalism or another aerospace-related field, consider applying for the Class of 2027.

Don’t wait until the deadline to begin preparing your application.

Application Deadline: October 4, 2026.

TITLE: Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship 2026: CAD $4,000 Stipend and Reporting Support for Journalists in Global South Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship 2026 is now accepting applications from journalists in ODA-recipient countries who are interested in producing powerful, fact-based journalism about local solutions to global crises, with a particular focus on gender.

Launched by the Equality Fund in partnership with Canadian Journalists for Free Expression (CJFE) and African Women in Media (AWiM), the inaugural fellowship is designed to support journalists who are reporting directly from the communities affected by major social, economic, environmental, political and human rights challenges.

The programme will select up to five journalists for a fellowship running from January to September 2027, providing a CAD $4,000 stipend, up to CAD $500 in reporting expenses, professional learning opportunities, safety training, expert-led online sessions and an in-person convening with travel expenses covered.

For journalists looking for opportunities to strengthen their reporting, develop an important investigative or solutions-focused story, expand their professional networks and highlight community-led responses to global challenges, the fellowship provides a structured platform to undertake this work.

About the Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship

The inaugural Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship was created in response to the need for strong, independent and fact-based journalism at a time when communities around the world are experiencing interconnected crises.

The programme is particularly interested in stories that move beyond simply documenting problems and instead explore local solutions to global crises. Its central focus is on identifying and amplifying initiatives, people and approaches within communities that are responding to challenges and creating meaningful change.

The fellowship’s core objective is for each journalist to produce and publish at least one story focused on local solutions to a global crisis, with gender serving as an important lens.

The Equality Fund describes the fellowship as an opportunity to support journalists who are reporting from their own communities and whose work can help bring locally developed solutions into wider public view.

What Does the Fellowship Focus On?

The fellowship is not limited to one specific type of crisis. Applicants can explore a broad range of issues affecting communities around the world.

Potential areas include:

Climate change and environmental challenges

Gender-based violence

Authoritarianism

Anti-rights movements

Sexual and reproductive health and rights

Economic injustice

War and armed conflict

Human rights

Democracy and civic space

Other interconnected global crises where communities are developing locally relevant responses.

The emphasis, however, is not simply on reporting the existence of these crises. Fellows are expected to investigate and report on solutions emerging from within affected communities.

This means a strong fellowship proposal could potentially examine how women, grassroots organisations, community leaders, activists, local institutions, first responders, farmers, entrepreneurs or other community actors are responding to major challenges.

Key Objective of the Fellowship

The central objective of the Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship is straightforward: each fellow should produce at least one published story about local solutions to global crises, with a focus on gender.

The fellowship therefore combines financial support with professional development and editorial opportunities.

Rather than functioning solely as a training programme, the fellowship is structured around the production of journalism. Successful applicants will have the opportunity to develop their proposed story while receiving support, mentorship, training and access to experts throughout the programme.

The programme is scheduled to run from January through September 2027, with six months of programming followed by an additional three months for fellows to finalise publication.

What Does the Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship Offer?

Successful fellows will receive a combination of financial, professional and networking support.

1. CAD $4,000 Fellowship Stipend

Each selected journalist will receive a CAD $4,000 stipend.

The stipend is intended to support fellows during their participation in the programme and enable them to dedicate time and resources to developing their journalism project.

According to the official guidelines, freelance journalists who are already being paid a publication fee by their publishing outlet may retain that publication fee in addition to the fellowship stipend. Full-time staff journalists, meanwhile, will be required to notify their newsroom about the fellowship stipend.

2. Up to CAD $500 for Reporting Expenses

In addition to the stipend, fellows can receive up to CAD $500 in reporting expenses.

This additional support can help facilitate the practical reporting process associated with developing and producing the fellowship story.

For journalists reporting from their own communities, this may provide useful additional resources for gathering information, conducting interviews and carrying out field reporting connected to their proposed project.

3. Six Months of Fellowship Programming

The core fellowship programming will run for approximately six months.

The programme is scheduled to begin in January 2027, followed by an additional three-month period during which fellows can finalise their publications.

Overall, the fellowship programme and publication period will run through September 2027.

4. Monthly Online Meetings

Fellows will participate in monthly online meetings featuring journalists and experts.

These sessions are designed to expose fellows to different areas of journalism practice, reporting, ethics, safety and coverage of complex global issues.

The programme’s listed contributors include:

Nina Lakhani, a climate journalist associated with The Guardian and Drilled.

Kelly Kimball, a journalism and ethics professor at the City University of New York.

Professionals involved in journalist safety training from the International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF).

Experts associated with the Freedom of the Press Foundation.

These sessions can provide fellows with opportunities to develop their professional knowledge while working on their fellowship projects.

5. Journalism Safety Training

Safety is an important component of the fellowship.

Selected journalists will receive safety-related training involving organisations working in the field of journalist protection, including the International Women’s Media Foundation and Freedom of the Press Foundation.

This is particularly relevant for journalists covering sensitive subjects such as conflict, human rights violations, gender-based violence, political repression or other challenging environments.

6. One In-Person Convening

The fellowship will also include one in-person convening.

The specific location and timing of the gathering have not yet been determined, but travel expenses will be covered.

The convening will give fellows an opportunity to meet in person, build professional relationships and exchange experiences arising from their reporting work.

Who Can Apply for the Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for working journalists in ODA-recipient countries.

Importantly, applicants do not have to be employed full-time by a traditional newsroom.

The programme is open to:

Full-time journalists.

Independent journalists.

Freelance journalists.

Journalists working across different media platforms.

Journalists producing text-based reporting.

Digital journalists.

Video journalists.

Audio journalists.

The fellowship specifically encourages journalists to report on their own communities and geographies.

Minimum Eligibility Requirements

The official 2026 application guidelines provide additional requirements that applicants should carefully review before applying.

Applicants must have at least three years of journalism experience.

Candidates are required to demonstrate a minimum of three years of journalism experience.

Applicants should therefore be able to show a sustained track record of journalistic work rather than relying solely on academic qualifications or an interest in journalism.

Applicants must be located in an ODA-recipient country

Applicants should be located in an ODA-recipient country and should be reporting on communities in those countries.

The fellowship uses the OECD framework for determining ODA-recipient countries.

Applicants must provide three journalism samples.

Candidates are required to submit three strong journalism samples demonstrating a range of relevant work.

Applicants should therefore select portfolio pieces that best demonstrate their reporting ability, storytelling skills, editorial judgement and experience covering issues relevant to the fellowship.

English proficiency is required.

The official application guidelines state that applicants must be fluent in English, which is the Equality Fund’s working language.

Applicants must be able to participate in meetings in Eastern Standard Time.

Because the fellowship includes online programming, applicants must be able to accommodate meetings taking place during daytime hours in Eastern Standard Time.

Prospective applicants should therefore consider the time-zone difference between their location and Eastern Standard Time before applying.

Applicants need a bank account capable of receiving international transfers.

Applicants should have access to a bank account capable of accepting international Electronic Wire Transfers.

This requirement is important because the fellowship includes financial support.

Gender and Diversity Eligibility

The fellowship is designed to be inclusive.

The original fellowship announcement states that applications are welcomed from:

Women

Men

LGBTQI+ people

The detailed application guidelines further state that women, non-binary and trans people are encouraged to apply. The guidelines also reference the Equality Fund’s values around equality and diversity across areas including race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, ethnicity, national origin and disability.

This means applicants do not need to belong to one particular gender category to be considered.

Eligible Countries and Regions

The Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship is open to journalists based in ODA-recipient countries.

The opportunity therefore has a broad geographical scope covering eligible countries across the Global South rather than being restricted to one particular region.

Applicants should verify that their country appears on the relevant OECD DAC list of ODA recipients before submitting an application.

For African journalists, this makes the fellowship particularly relevant to journalists working in eligible African countries, while the programme also extends to eligible countries in other parts of the Global South.

What Kind of Story Should Applicants Propose?

One of the most important aspects of the fellowship is the proposed journalism story.

The programme is looking for reporting that explores local solutions to global crises, particularly through a gender-focused perspective.

Applicants should therefore think beyond simply identifying a problem.

A strong concept could explore questions such as

What major crisis is affecting the community?

How is the crisis affecting women or other groups differently?

What local individuals, organisations or communities are responding?

What practical solution has emerged?

What evidence exists that the approach is working or producing meaningful results?

What barriers are limiting the solution?

What lessons could other communities learn from the experience?

Potential stories could focus on women farmers developing responses to climate-related challenges, community-led responses to gender-based violence, local approaches to economic injustice, grassroots responses to conflict or initiatives protecting human rights.

The programme’s emphasis on local solutions means applicants should demonstrate a clear connection between the proposed story and the community in which they work.

Editorial Independence

An important feature of the fellowship is that fellows will retain complete editorial independence.

This means journalists remain responsible for their journalistic work and editorial decisions.

The official guidelines also state that fellows retain intellectual property rights over their work, while the Equality Fund retains the right to publish or reproduce the work for purposes of promoting the fellowship.

This distinction is important for journalists who are concerned about ownership and editorial control when participating in externally funded journalism programmes.

Editorial Commitment From a News Outlet

The fellowship uses a phased application process.

Shortlisted applicants will be asked to provide a letter of editorial commitment from a news outlet.

This demonstrates that there is an intended publication pathway for the proposed journalism.

For applicants who are self-publishing, the guidelines indicate that the editorial commitment may, in some cases, be replaced by a fact-checking plan.

Applicants should therefore think carefully about how their proposed story will ultimately reach an audience.

AI Use in the Application and Journalism Process

Applicants should pay particular attention to the fellowship’s rules concerning artificial intelligence.

According to the official fellowship announcement:

AI use is not permitted in the proposal and application.

AI use during the journalistic process must be disclosed to the programme.

Such use must be approved in advance.

This is an important requirement for applicants preparing their submissions and developing their fellowship stories.

Applicants should read the official guidelines carefully and follow the programme’s requirements rather than assuming that general AI policies from other journalism organisations apply.

Additional Expectations for Fellows

Beyond producing a story, fellows should be prepared to follow responsible journalism practices.

The application guidelines state that fellows should be willing to:

Follow trauma-informed reporting best practices.

Conduct community roundtables where possible.

Maintain editorial independence.

Work collaboratively with the fellowship community.

Participate in the programme’s online meetings and learning activities.

These expectations reflect the fellowship’s focus on reporting complex issues involving communities that may be experiencing significant social, political, economic or humanitarian pressures.

Fellowship Timeline

The Equality Fund expects the programme to follow this general timeline:

Stage
Timeline

Application period
2026

Application deadline
November 8, 2026

Fellowship begins
January 2027

Core programming
Six months

The official application guidelines specify that applications close on November 8, 2026 at midnight Eastern Standard Time.

What Applicants Should Prepare

Before applying, prospective candidates should prepare the required materials and information.

A useful application preparation checklist includes:

Confirm country eligibility
Verify that your country is included among ODA-recipient countries.

Document your journalism experience
Ensure you can demonstrate at least three years of relevant journalism experience.

Select three strong journalism samples
Choose work that demonstrates your reporting range and ability to cover relevant issues.

Develop a clear story concept
Identify a compelling local solution to a global crisis and explain how gender is connected to the story.

Identify the community you will report on
The fellowship expects journalists to report on their own communities and geographies.

Consider your publication pathway
If you work with a news organisation, consider how you can secure an editorial commitment. Freelancers and self-publishing journalists should review the alternative requirements carefully.

Review the AI rules
Applicants should understand the restrictions on AI use in the application and the disclosure and approval requirements for AI use during the journalistic process.

Check your availability
Make sure you can participate in online meetings during the required Eastern Standard Time hours.

Confirm your banking arrangements
Ensure your bank can receive international electronic wire transfers.

Review the official application guidelines
Applicants should read the full guidelines before submitting their application.

Why This Fellowship Is Relevant to Journalists in the Global South

The fellowship is specifically designed around journalists reporting from communities in ODA-recipient countries.

That local perspective is central to the programme. Instead of relying exclusively on international correspondents or external observers, the fellowship seeks to support journalists who already understand the communities they are covering.

This can be particularly important when reporting on subjects such as gender inequality, climate change, economic injustice, conflict, human rights and gender-based violence, where local knowledge and relationships can provide important context.

The programme’s focus on solutions journalism also provides an opportunity to investigate how communities are responding to difficult circumstances rather than focusing exclusively on the challenges themselves.

About the Fellowship Partners

The Equality Fund is implementing the journalism fellowship in partnership with two organisations with experience in journalism and media advocacy.

Canadian Journalists for Free Expression

The Equality Fund has partnered with Canadian Journalists for Free Expression (CJFE), an organisation focused on supporting freedom of expression and journalism.

The partnership brings an additional journalism and press-freedom dimension to the fellowship.

African Women in Media

The fellowship also partners with African Women in Media (AWiM).

AWiM’s involvement is particularly relevant to the programme’s focus on gender equality, journalism and media systems across Africa and beyond.

Fellowship Financial and Professional Benefits at a Glance

Successful applicants can expect:

CAD $4,000 stipend

Up to CAD $500 for reporting expenses

Six months of structured programming

Three additional months to finalise publication

Monthly online meetings

Access to experienced journalists and experts

Journalism and ethics learning

Journalist safety training

One in-person convening

Travel expenses for the in-person convening

Editorial independence

Retention of intellectual property rights over fellows’ work, subject to the Equality Fund’s stated publication/reproduction rights

Opportunity to produce and publish at least one major story focused on local solutions to global crises and gender.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the Equality Fund Global Journalism Fellowship 2026 is November 8, 2026, at midnight Eastern Standard Time. The official application guidelines also describe the closing time as 11 p.m. Eastern Standard Time in the application instructions, so applicants should submit well before the final day to avoid any time-zone or technical issues.

Because the programme is competitive and requires several supporting elements, including journalism samples and potentially an editorial commitment, applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their submissions early.

Applicants should carefully review all eligibility requirements, documentation requirements, editorial expectations and AI-related rules before submitting their application.

Conclusion

The Equality Fund Journalism Fellowship 2026 provides an opportunity for experienced journalists in ODA-recipient countries to receive financial support, professional development, safety training and networking opportunities while producing journalism focused on local solutions to global crises through a gender lens.

The programme is open to journalists working across text, digital, video and audio platforms, including both full-time and independent freelance journalists. Successful fellows will receive a CAD $4,000 stipend, up to CAD $500 in reporting expenses, access to monthly expert-led sessions, safety training and an in-person convening with travel expenses covered.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the additional requirements: a minimum of three years of journalism experience, three strong journalism samples, English fluency, availability for meetings in Eastern Standard Time and the ability to receive international electronic wire transfers. The programme also places strong emphasis on reporting from journalists’ own communities and maintaining editorial independence.

TITLE: Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant 2026: Up to US$12,000 for Journalists, Filmmakers, Photographers and Audio Storytellers in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant 2026 is inviting experienced journalists, filmmakers, photographers and audio storytellers to develop high-quality, publishable stories that examine conservation through the experiences, realities and perspectives of people across Africa.

The grant is designed for storytellers who can move beyond conventional wildlife and conservation narratives and produce thoughtful, evidence-based stories that explore how conservation interacts with communities, livelihoods, rights, governance, economies, health, culture, land use and coexistence with wildlife.

With funding of up to US$12,000, applicants can seek support through three funding tiers depending on the scale and requirements of their proposed story. The next application round opens on 1 September 2026, with applications closing on 29 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT.

This opportunity is particularly relevant to established storytellers who already have the professional skills, editorial experience and access necessary to produce work suitable for publication, broadcast or distribution through an established media outlet or independent platform.

Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant 2026 at a Glance

Opportunity
Details

Opportunity name
Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant

Funding
Up to US$12,000

Funding tiers
Tier 1: Up to US$5,000; Tier 2: Up to US$8,000; Tier 3: Up to US$12,000

Application opens
1 September 2026

Application deadline
29 September 2026

Deadline time
23:59 GMT

Geographical focus
Africa

Target applicants
Experienced journalists, filmmakers, photographers and audio storytellers

Story focus
Conservation through human-centred perspectives

Application method
Online

Publication requirement
Applicants must demonstrate a credible publication, broadcast or distribution pathway

Previous applicants
Eligible to apply again

What Is the Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant?

The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant is a commissioning grant intended to support high-quality and publishable storytelling about conservation in Africa.

The central idea behind the grant is that conservation should not be presented solely through ecological or wildlife perspectives. Conservation policies and projects affect real people, communities and economies, and those human realities can be essential to understanding whether conservation efforts succeed, fail or produce unintended consequences.

The grant therefore seeks stories that investigate conservation through issues such as:

Human rights

Community livelihoods

Governance

Resource access

Land use

Local economies

Health

Culture

Food systems

Energy

Climate adaptation

Wildlife coexistence

Community decision-making

Conservation-related trade-offs

Social and political realities surrounding conservation

Rather than encouraging simplistic narratives, the grant is looking for storytellers who can demonstrate depth, curiosity, careful reporting and respect for complexity.

Successful stories may examine situations where human-centred conservation is producing positive outcomes, situations where it is failing, or the complicated space between success and failure.

Why Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Matters

Conservation stories are sometimes presented in highly simplified ways. A project may be portrayed as an uncomplicated success, or a conservation challenge may be presented as an uncomplicated failure.

However, conservation frequently involves competing interests and difficult decisions.

For example, a conservation initiative can have positive ecological outcomes while simultaneously creating challenges for communities whose livelihoods depend on land or natural resources. Similarly, community participation can contribute to better conservation outcomes, but only when participation is meaningful and communities have a genuine role in decision-making.

The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant seeks to bring these realities into public discussion.

The supported stories can therefore help audiences understand:

Who is affected by conservation decisions

Who benefits from conservation initiatives

Who bears the costs

How communities interact with natural resources

How conservation policies affect livelihoods

How governance influences conservation outcomes

How people coexist with wildlife

What happens when conservation principles are absent

How communities innovate in response to environmental challenges

What can be learned from both successful and unsuccessful conservation efforts

This makes the opportunity particularly valuable for professional storytellers interested in producing journalism and creative work that contributes to a deeper understanding of conservation in African societies.

What Kind of Stories Is the Grant Looking For?

The grant does not prescribe one particular format or storytelling angle.

Instead, applicants are encouraged to develop strong, original stories that place people and context at the centre of conservation narratives.

Proposed stories may explore three broad areas.

1. Where Human-Centred Conservation Works

Applicants can investigate examples where conservation approaches that recognise human realities have contributed to better outcomes.

A story might explore:

How community participation improves conservation

How local knowledge influences environmental management

How conservation supports livelihoods

How communities and wildlife successfully coexist

How inclusive governance improves conservation outcomes

How locally led initiatives produce sustainable solutions

The important element is not simply to celebrate a successful project but to investigate what made the approach work and what can be learned from it.

2. Where Human-Centred Conservation Falls Short

The grant is also interested in stories that critically examine situations where conservation approaches have failed to adequately account for people and their realities.

Such stories could investigate:

Exclusion of communities from decision-making

Conflicts over natural-resource access

Displacement or livelihood challenges

Governance failures

Unintended consequences of conservation policies

Tensions between conservation goals and local economic needs

Gaps between conservation policy and implementation

These stories should provide appropriate context rather than simply portraying conservation as either good or bad.

3. The Tensions and Trade-Offs Between Success and Failure

Some of the most compelling conservation stories may not fit neatly into either success or failure.

The grant welcomes stories that explore the complexities, contradictions and trade-offs surrounding conservation.

For example, a story could examine how a conservation initiative produces environmental benefits while creating economic challenges for certain communities, or how communities balance wildlife protection with food security.

The objective is to encourage storytelling that reflects conservation as it is actually experienced by people.

Potential Themes for Applicants

Applicants do not have to select from a fixed list of themes. However, the grant indicates that stories could engage with areas such as:

Conservation governance

Natural-resource use

Community livelihoods

Wildlife and human coexistence

Food systems

Energy

Health

Climate adaptation

Land-use decisions

Community rights

Local knowledge

Conservation economics

Environmental justice

Community resilience

Social and political dimensions of conservation

The subject matter should ultimately connect back to the central principle: putting people and their lived realities at the heart of conservation storytelling.

What the Grant Is Not Looking For

Understanding what is excluded is just as important as understanding what is encouraged.

The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant is not intended to support the following types of work:

Promotional or advocacy content

The grant is not designed to finance material primarily intended to promote an organisation, campaign, conservation project or institution.

Generic wildlife stories

A wildlife story without a strong human dimension is unlikely to meet the grant’s central purpose.

Oversimplified conservation narratives

Stories presenting conservation as purely successful or purely failing without investigating the underlying complexities are not the intended focus.

Stories without social, political or economic context

Applicants are expected to explore the wider circumstances in which conservation takes place.

Organisational marketing material

Content primarily produced for organisational communications or marketing purposes is outside the grant’s intended scope.

Applicants should therefore approach their proposal as independent, thoughtful storytelling, rather than as promotional communications for an organisation.

Who Is the Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant For?

The grant is aimed at experienced professional storytellers with the ability to produce work that meets established editorial and professional standards.

The opportunity specifically identifies:

Journalists

Filmmakers

Photographers

Audio storytellers

The ideal applicant should already have the relevant skills, experience and access necessary to take a story from concept to a professional, publishable or broadcast-ready product.

This is important because the grant is not primarily a training or capacity-building programme.

The organisers indicate that they are unlikely to support proposals requiring extensive editorial development, capacity-building or technical assistance before the work can reach publishable quality.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate previous work and professional readiness.

Publication, Broadcast or Distribution Requirement

One of the most important eligibility requirements is that applicants must already have a credible pathway for their proposed story to reach an audience.

Because of the high level of interest in the grant, applications must demonstrate an established route to publication, broadcast or distribution.

Applicants must meet at least one of the following conditions:

1. Confirmed commitment from an established media organisation

The applicant may have a confirmed commitment from an established:

Media outlet

Broadcaster

Distribution platform

to publish, broadcast or distribute the proposed story.

2. Applying through a media outlet or platform

An applicant may apply on behalf of, or have publishing or commissioning authority within, the organisation that will eventually publish, broadcast or distribute the story.

3. Established independent platform

Applicants may also intend to publish, broadcast or distribute the story through their own established independent channel or platform, provided that the platform already has an existing audience.

Applicants will be required to provide evidence of the relevant publication or distribution pathway.

This means that having a strong story idea alone may not be enough. Applicants should begin thinking about where the finished work will appear and how it will reach its intended audience.

Funding Available: Up to US$12,000

The grant offers three different funding levels.

Tier 1: Up to US$5,000

Applicants with smaller-scale storytelling projects can apply for funding of up to US$5,000.

Tier 2: Up to US$8,000

Applicants requiring a larger budget can seek up to US$8,000.

Tier 3: Up to US$12,000

The highest funding category provides up to US$12,000 for suitable storytelling projects.

Important note about the funding tiers

Applicants do not have to request the maximum amount available under a particular tier.

Budgets are assessed according to:

Realism

Proportionality

The requirements of the proposed project

The scale of the proposed storytelling work

Applicants should therefore prepare a budget that is clearly connected to the proposed story rather than simply requesting the largest possible amount.

What Should Applicants Submit?

Applications are submitted online and require several important components.

Applicants should prepare:

1. A short story pitch

The pitch should communicate the central idea of the proposed story and explain why it is important.

A strong pitch should make clear:

What the story is about

Who is at the centre of the story

What conservation issue is being explored

Why the story matters

What makes the story original

What human realities the story will reveal

2. Examples of previous work

Applicants must demonstrate their professional storytelling experience through examples of previous work.

These examples are important because the grant is aimed at experienced storytellers who can work to professional editorial standards.

3. Evidence of a publication or distribution pathway

Applicants should provide evidence showing where the proposed story can be published, broadcast or distributed.

This could involve:

A confirmed media commitment

A commissioning arrangement

Evidence of authority within a media organisation

An established independent platform with an existing audience

4. A summary budget

Applicants must provide a budget corresponding to the funding tier they are applying for.

The budget should be realistic and proportional to the proposed work.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

The selection panel will assess applications according to several key criteria.

1. Quality and clarity of the story pitch

The proposed story should be clearly presented and demonstrate a compelling narrative idea.

The selection panel will need to understand what the applicant intends to investigate and why the story deserves support.

2. Alignment with Human-Centred Conservation

The story should clearly demonstrate that conservation will be examined through a human-centred perspective.

Applicants should avoid proposals that focus solely on wildlife or ecological issues without adequately addressing people, communities and context.

3. Professional experience and editorial readiness

The applicant should demonstrate the experience and skills necessary to produce a professional-quality story.

Previous work samples are therefore an important part of the application.

4. Feasibility and budget realism

The proposed project should be achievable within the requested funding amount.

Applicants should demonstrate that their budget is appropriate for the scale and requirements of the story.

Is the Grant Competitive?

Yes.

The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant is a competitive funding opportunity.

Meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not guarantee funding.

The organisers state that only applications meeting the eligibility requirements will be considered for review, and not all eligible applications will receive funding.

Applicants should therefore make their proposals as clear, compelling and well-supported as possible.

Can Previous Applicants Apply Again?

Yes.

Applicants who applied during the previous round are welcome to apply again.

However, previous applicants should not simply resubmit their old application.

Because the organisers have made changes to the application form and the information requested, previous applicants must:

Complete a new application.

Provide the information requested for the current round.

Ensure their proposed story meets the current eligibility requirements.

Provide updated evidence where necessary.

Important Dates for the 2026 Grant

The application timeline is straightforward.

Application opening date

1 September 2026

Application deadline

29 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit their application.

Because the application requires a story pitch, previous work samples, publication or distribution evidence and a budget, prospective applicants should begin preparing their materials before the deadline.

How to Apply for the Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant

Applications are submitted online through the grant’s application platform.

Applicants should prepare the required materials before beginning the submission process.

Application checklist

Before submitting, make sure you have:

A clear and compelling story pitch

Examples of your previous professional work

Evidence of your publication, broadcast or distribution pathway

A realistic budget

A clear connection to Human-Centred Conservation

A proposal that places people and context at the centre

A story that is suitable for professional publication, broadcast or distribution

Application deadline: 29 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT.

Apply HERE

Official Grant Information and Terms

Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the full terms and conditions before submitting an application.

The official grant page provides information about the opportunity, application process and eligibility requirements.

Visit the Official Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant page HERE

Applicants should also review the full Terms and Conditions before applying.

For questions concerning eligibility or the application process, applicants can contact info@jamma.co. The organisers advise applicants to first review the grant page and Terms and Conditions because many common questions are already addressed there. Individual feedback on applications will not be provided.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the grant is competitive, applicants can improve their applications by focusing on the elements the selection panel is looking for.

1. Develop a genuinely human-centred story

Do not simply take a conventional wildlife or conservation story and add a human-interest element.

Instead, build the story around the people whose lives, decisions, rights, livelihoods or communities are connected to the conservation issue.

2. Demonstrate complexity

Avoid portraying conservation as simply a success story or a failure.

Show the tensions, trade-offs, contradictions and realities that exist on the ground.

3. Explain why the story matters

Your pitch should make the significance of the story immediately understandable.

Explain what audiences can learn from the story and why the issue deserves greater attention.

4. Demonstrate professional readiness

Choose previous work samples that best demonstrate your ability to investigate, report, photograph, film or otherwise tell complex stories professionally.

5. Establish your distribution pathway early

This is particularly important.

Before applying, identify where the story could realistically be published, broadcast or distributed and obtain appropriate evidence of that pathway.

6. Keep the budget realistic

Do not automatically request US$12,000 simply because it is the maximum.

Your budget should correspond to the actual requirements of your story.

Conclusion

The Human-Centred Conservation Storytelling Grant 2026 presents an important opportunity for experienced African-focused storytellers to investigate conservation beyond conventional wildlife narratives.

With funding of up to US$12,000, the grant can support journalists, filmmakers, photographers and audio storytellers who have the professional experience and access needed to produce high-quality work for established media outlets, broadcasters or independent platforms.

The strongest proposals will be those that place people at the centre of conservation stories while maintaining the complexity of the social, political, economic and environmental realities involved. Applicants should demonstrate professional experience, a compelling story pitch, a realistic budget and a credible pathway for publication, broadcast or distribution.

The 2026 application period opens on 1 September 2026 and closes on 29 September 2026 at 23:59 GMT. Prospective applicants should begin preparing their story pitch, previous work samples, distribution evidence and budget well before the deadline.

TITLE: Science for Policy Exchange: a new project to connect researchers and policymakers across Europe

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects | Project News | Science Policy Support | Science Policy Support

S4PXchange, a new project funded under the Horizon Europe programme, launched on 1st June 2026 to strengthen connections between science and policymaking across Europe, where practices still vary from country to country. Coordinated by the European Science Foundation (ESF), the three-year project brings together partner organisations from six countries to build shared tools, networks, and training that put scientific evidence into the hands of the people shaping policy decisions.

“S4PXchange represents an important step forward in connecting science and policy communities across Europe. By building shared understanding, tools, and networks, we aim to strengthen the role of evidence in policymaking,” commented Adam Brandstetter-Kunc, ESF, Project Coordinator.

“The contribution of S4Pxchange to the ERA Policy Agenda and its action, ‘Strengthening the European Science for Policy Ecosystem’, is warmly welcomed to build lasting capacity and trust in evidence-informed policymaking. By bringing together diverse actors working at the science for policy interface, harnessing open science principles, and deploying practical tools, S4PXchange has the potential to make S4P practice the norm across Europe”, stated Joanna Drake, Deputy Director-General of the European Commission’s DG Research & Innovation.

A strong European partnership

The S4PXchange consortium brings together six organisations from six EU member states, combining expertise in evidence-informed policymaking, science-policy linkages, public administration, policy mapping, and analysis:

European Science Foundation (France),(opens in new tab)

APRE – Italian Agency for the Promotion of European Research (Italy),(opens in new tab)

Leiden University (Netherlands),(opens in new tab)

Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation(opens in new tab) Research ISI (Germany),(opens in new tab)

Austrian Institute of(opens in new tab) Technology (Austria),

European Future Innovation System Centre (Belgium).(opens in new tab)

S4PXchange will work closely with the European Commission’s DG Research & Innovation (DG RTD) and collaborate with existing relevant initiatives, such as the Community of Practice on Evidence-Informed Policymaking and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC).

“Scientific knowledge and the academic system that produces it are an integral aspect of evidence-informed policymaking (EIPM). There are many barriers holding it back from realising its full potential for informing policy. The initiatives of S4PXchange are a welcome boost to the growing momentum in Europe to invest in the people, processes and institutions that enable EIPM,” said David Mair, Head of Unit of JRC S.2 (Science for Democracy, Public Governance and Administration).

Looking ahead

Over the coming months, S4PXchange will begin its online community building activities by involving relevant researchers, policymakers, and knowledge brokers, the first of several milestones over the project’s three-year lifetime. Organisations and individuals interested in following or engaging with the project are invited to get in touch using the details below.

TITLE: MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship 2026: ₹70,000 Monthly Stipend and Research Funding for Young Scholars Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Manav Rachna University (MUJ) has launched its Post-Doctoral Fellowship (PDF) program to encourage theoretical and conceptual advancements across disciplines while attracting promising young research talent from around the world. The program is designed to support outstanding scholars from India and abroad who have demonstrated strong academic and research achievements and are ready to undertake advanced post-doctoral research.

The MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship provides financial support through a monthly stipend of ₹70,000, along with two annual contingency grants worth ₹50,000 each. Together, these provisions are intended to support researchers with living costs, professional conferences, presentations, publication expenses, research consumables and necessary equipment.

The fellowship is particularly competitive because applicants must already hold a PhD, be under 35 years of age, and have published at least four papers in Q1/Q2 journals within the previous two years.

MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Overview

The MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship has been established to strengthen research and encourage young scholars to contribute to theoretical and conceptual developments in different academic disciplines.

The program is open to scholars from all nationalities, making it an international post-doctoral research opportunity. Applicants are expected to demonstrate strong research credentials and a recent publication record before they can be considered.

The fellowship initially lasts for one year, with the possibility of an additional year depending on satisfactory research performance and progress.

Key features include:

Monthly stipend of ₹70,000

Annual Contingency Grant – Part I of ₹50,000

Annual Contingency Grant – Part II of ₹50,000

Fellowship initially awarded for one year

Possibility of a one-year extension

Applications invited throughout the year

Monthly interviews for shortlisted candidates, subject to expert panel availability

Dedicated supervision and research-progress monitoring

Opportunity to undertake academic responsibilities related to teaching and learning

International eligibility with applicants from all nationalities welcome

MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Financial Benefits

One of the major attractions of the MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship is the financial package provided to successful fellows.

1. Monthly Stipend of ₹70,000

Selected Post-Doctoral Fellows will receive a monthly stipend of ₹70,000.

This financial support is intended to provide fellows with regular funding throughout the fellowship and enable them to focus on their research activities.

Over an initial 12-month fellowship period, the monthly stipend amounts to ₹840,000, before considering the additional contingency grants.

2. Contingency Grant – Part I: ₹50,000 Per Year

MUJ provides an annual ₹50,000 Contingency Grant – Part I.

According to the fellowship guidelines, this funding can be used for research-related professional activities such as:

Attending professional conferences

Presenting research at conferences

Covering publication charges

This component can therefore help fellows participate in academic activities beyond their immediate research environment and disseminate their findings through professional and scholarly channels.

3. Contingency Grant – Part II: ₹50,000 Per Year

Fellows will also receive a ₹50,000 annual Contingency Grant – Part II.

This component is intended for research-related requirements, including:

Procurement of consumables

Necessary equipment

The two contingency grants provide a combined annual allocation of ₹100,000, in addition to the monthly stipend.

Who Is Eligible for the MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship?

The MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship has specific eligibility conditions that applicants must satisfy.

Candidates should carefully review each requirement before applying because the fellowship is intended for young researchers who have already demonstrated substantial research achievement.

1. Open to All Nationalities

The fellowship is open to applicants of all nationalities.

This means the opportunity is not restricted to Indian citizens. Scholars from other countries are also eligible to apply, provided they meet the academic, age, publication and other fellowship requirements.

2. Age Requirement

Applicants must be under 35 years of age at the time of application submission.

The age requirement is therefore assessed at the point when the application is submitted.

3. PhD Requirement

Applicants must hold a PhD from a recognized institute in India or abroad.

This means that the fellowship is specifically designed for researchers who have already completed doctoral-level study and are seeking to continue developing their research careers through post-doctoral work.

4. Additional Requirement for MUJ PhD Graduates

Candidates who completed their PhD at MUJ must have at least one year of post-PhD experience in a relevant field outside MUJ.

This requirement specifically applies to candidates whose doctoral degree was completed at MUJ.

5. Publication Requirement

Applicants must have published at least four papers in Q1/Q2 quartile journals during the last two years.

This is one of the fellowship’s most significant research requirements.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate a recent and substantial publication record rather than relying solely on publications from earlier stages of their academic careers.

6. No Other External Financial Support

Applicants must not be receiving another form of:

External grant

Financial aid

Research assistance

during the fellowship.

Candidates who are already receiving external research funding or financial assistance should carefully consider this condition before applying.

7. No Other Employment During the Fellowship

Selected fellows must not undertake part-time or full-time employment, whether remunerative or honorary, for the entire duration of the fellowship.

The fellowship therefore requires the fellow to comply with the employment restriction throughout the fellowship period.

Duration of the MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship

The MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship is initially awarded for one year.

However, fellows may have the opportunity to continue for another year if their performance and research progress are considered satisfactory.

The possible extension is not automatic. Research performance and progress will be reviewed by a committee before an additional year can be granted.

This structure provides researchers with the possibility of undertaking a longer post-doctoral research program while maintaining a formal performance-review process.

Academic Responsibilities During the Fellowship

Although the primary purpose of the fellowship is research, fellows may also be assigned academic responsibilities related to teaching and learning.

Such responsibilities may be allocated within the relevant department according to its requirements.

Prospective applicants should therefore understand that the fellowship may involve both research activities and certain academic responsibilities, depending on departmental needs.

MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Application and Recruitment Process

MUJ invites applications from eligible candidates throughout the year, according to announcements made on its official website.

Applicants must complete the online application using the prescribed format and provide the required supporting materials.

Required Application Materials

Applicants must submit:

1. Two Recommendation Letters

Candidates must provide recommendation letters from two referees.

Applicants should therefore identify appropriate referees who can provide meaningful assessments of their academic and research capabilities.

2. Academic and Research Credentials

Applicants must provide copies of their relevant:

Academic credentials

Research credentials

Supporting evidence of their research achievements

These documents allow the selection committee to assess the candidate’s academic and research background.

3. Statement of Purpose

Applicants must submit a Statement of Purpose of at least 500 words.

The Statement of Purpose should provide an opportunity for applicants to explain their academic and research background, their research interests and their motivation for pursuing the post-doctoral fellowship.

Because the selection committee considers the applicant’s proposed research area, candidates should ensure that their application presents a clear and coherent research direction.

MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Selection Process

After applications are submitted, they are reviewed and evaluated by a designated MUJ PDF Selection Committee.

The committee evaluates candidates based on several factors, including:

Academic credentials

Research credentials

Publication record

Proposed research area

Candidates who successfully pass the initial review may be shortlisted for an interview.

Monthly Interview Schedule

Shortlisted candidates will be invited for an interview.

The interviews are conducted once a month during the first week, subject to the availability of expert panel members.

This means applicants should be prepared for an interview as part of the selection process rather than expecting selection to be based solely on their written application.

Who Is on the MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Selection Committee?

The fellowship guidelines specify the composition of the selection committee.

The committee includes:

Pro President — Chairperson

Dean RIAA

Concerned Academic Dean

Concerned Associate Dean

Concerned Heads of Department (HoDs)

Prospective Supervisors

Director Research — Member Secretary

The involvement of academic leaders, department representatives, prospective supervisors and research leadership means that candidates are evaluated from both academic and research perspectives.

Successful applicants will receive a formal letter of award from MUJ.

Research Supervision and Progress Monitoring

Each Post-Doctoral Fellow will be assigned a supervisor.

The supervisor will monitor:

Research progress

Administrative compliance

The supervision arrangement is intended to ensure that fellows remain on track with their research objectives while also meeting the administrative requirements associated with the fellowship.

Quarterly Progress Reports

Fellows are required to submit a quarterly progress report to their supervisor.

These reports should outline the research activities undertaken during the relevant period.

The process involves several levels of review:

The fellow prepares and submits the quarterly progress report.

The supervisor reviews the research progress.

The Head of Department provides feedback.

The reports and feedback are submitted to the Directorate of Research (DoR).

The Directorate of Research evaluates the progress.

This reporting structure creates a formal mechanism for monitoring research performance throughout the fellowship.

Expected Research Outcomes

The fellowship has a clear publication expectation.

By the end of the fellowship, fellows are expected to publish or have accepted at least two research papers in Q1/Q2 journals.

This requirement reinforces the program’s emphasis on high-quality research output and aligns with the requirement that applicants already demonstrate a strong publication record before entering the fellowship.

Prospective applicants should therefore consider whether their proposed research can realistically generate high-quality scholarly outputs within the fellowship period.

Intellectual Property and Research Outputs

An important condition of the fellowship concerns ownership and affiliation of research outcomes.

The guidelines state that outcomes such as:

Research findings

Publications

Monographs

Patents

Other research outputs

must be affiliated with and remain the intellectual property of MUJ.

Applicants should understand this requirement before accepting the fellowship, particularly if their proposed research is likely to generate intellectual property, commercialisable research, patents or other valuable outputs.

Technology Transfer Opportunities

Where relevant, fellows are also expected to explore opportunities for technology transfer.

This is particularly relevant for research that could have practical, technological or commercial applications.

The requirement encourages fellows to consider how research findings and innovations might potentially move beyond academic publication toward practical implementation or broader use.

Is There an Application Deadline?

The MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship guidelines state that applications are invited throughout the year, as announced on the University’s official website.

Therefore, the provided fellowship information does not specify one fixed annual application deadline.

Deadline: Applications are accepted throughout the year, subject to announcements by MUJ.

Applicants should nevertheless monitor the official MUJ website for current calls and application instructions.

Why Researchers Should Consider the MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship

The fellowship offers several features that may appeal to early-career researchers who have already established a strong research profile.

The combination of a monthly stipend, research-related contingency funding, academic supervision and opportunities for high-quality publication makes the fellowship particularly relevant to researchers seeking to strengthen their post-doctoral research careers.

The opportunity can potentially help fellows:

Continue advanced research after completing a PhD

Develop an independent research profile

Produce additional Q1/Q2 journal publications

Participate in professional conferences

Present research findings

Cover eligible publication costs

Obtain research consumables and equipment

Work with an academic supervisor

Build connections within an academic department

Explore technology-transfer opportunities

Gain further academic experience through possible teaching and learning responsibilities

Key Requirements Applicants Should Check Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should confirm that they satisfy the major conditions:

You are under 35 years old when you submit the application.

You hold a PhD from a recognized institution in India or abroad.

You have at least four Q1/Q2 journal papers published during the previous two years.

If you earned your PhD from MUJ, you have completed at least one year of relevant post-PhD experience outside MUJ.

You will not receive another external grant, financial aid or research assistance during the fellowship.

You will not undertake part-time or full-time employment, including honorary employment, throughout the fellowship.

You are prepared to submit two recommendation letters.

You can provide your academic and research credentials.

You can prepare a Statement of Purpose of at least 500 words.

You are prepared to participate in the interview process if shortlisted.

You understand the quarterly progress-reporting requirements.

You are prepared to work toward the expected minimum of two Q1/Q2 publications by the end of the fellowship.

How to Prepare a Strong MUJ Post-Doctoral Fellowship Application

Applicants can improve their preparation by approaching the application as a research-focused academic opportunity rather than simply another post-doctoral position.

Develop a Clear Research Direction

Your proposed research area is one of the factors considered by the selection committee. Make sure your research direction is clearly articulated and demonstrates a meaningful academic purpose.

Highlight Your Recent Publications

Because the fellowship requires at least four Q1/Q2 papers from the last two years, applicants should clearly document their recent publication record.

Prepare Strong Recommendations

Choose referees who are familiar with your research and can provide credible assessments of your academic and research achievements.

Write a Strong Statement of Purpose

The Statement of Purpose must contain at least 500 words. It should be carefully prepared and should clearly communicate your research background, academic motivation and proposed direction.

Prepare for the Interview

Shortlisted applicants are invited to an interview, so candidates should be prepared to discuss their research credentials, publication record and proposed research area.

Understand the Fellowship Restrictions

Applicants should carefully consider the restrictions on external funding and employment before applying. Successful fellows cannot receive other external grants, financial aid or research assistance and cannot undertake part-time or full-time employment during the fellowship.

Applicants must be under 35, hold a recognized PhD and have published at least four Q1/Q2 papers within the previous two years. They must also be prepared to meet the fellowship’s restrictions concerning external financial support and employment.

Research outputs will remain affiliated with and be the intellectual property of MUJ, while fellows may also be expected to explore technology-transfer opportunities where relevant.

TITLE: Job Announcement- Policy Specialist

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) was established in November 1967 with the cardinal functions of coordinating and networking Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) at the continental level, and providing leadership in developing and promoting a common vision for African higher education. The AAU is an international non-profit higher education organisation dedicated to enhancing the quality and relevance of higher education in Africa. Currently, AAU has a membership of about 400 HEIs from 46 African countries. Given its continental scope of operation, inclusiveness, capacity and experience, AAU is the main advocate for and convener of all stakeholders on general matters of Higher Education (HE) in Africa. The AAU collaborates with a number of international organizations and development partners in an effort to fulfil its mandate to the African higher education community. The Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25) aims to reorient and provide qualitative and quantitative improvements to African education and training systems and provide the continent with the requisite human resources for achievement of the African Union’s Vision and Agenda 2063. The AAU is the Coordinator of the Higher Education Cluster of CESA and the Manager of the African Quality Rating Mechanism (AQRM) database of the African Union.

The AAU is part of a consortium on Harmonisation, Quality Assurance and Accreditation (HAQAA) Initiative funded by the European Union Commission whose key objective is to

improve the quality and harmonisation of African higher education and support students’ employability and mobility across the continent. Pursuant to this Quality Assurance (QA)

Initiative, AAU is creating a Policy-Data Unit, which is a centralized structure within AAU that will be responsible for all data related activities, with particular reference to the HAQAA Initiative. As a result of the volume of envisaged activities under the Policy-Data Unit, the AAU seeks to recruit a Policy Specialist.

The AAU Policy-Data Unit will undertake a number of activities, including but not limited to:

-Driving data collection on key themes linked of the objectives of CESA 25, specifically those related to higher education, as covered by CESA Higher Education Cluster

-Interacting with key stakeholders in African higher education, at regional and national level, so as to better understand existing data sources and build upon them.

-Producing policy analysis reports, based on data collection activities, which will serve the CESA Clusters and ultimately help to assess the goals of CESA, particularly in higher

education.

-Participating in CESA Higher Education Cluster meetings, so as to receive feedback on data collection and also present findings.

-Setting up and hosting the African Higher Education Database, with key information on Trends in higher education in Africa.

-Contributing, where called upon, to other important studies carried out by the CESA Higher Education Cluster, led by its Co-Coordinators (AAU and INHEA) and the

coordinators of its subclusters.

-Overseeing the data intake from the AQRM and assessing its possible integration into the African HE Database and into Policy reports and studies.

-Communicate activity with the AUC regarding the coordination of data to assess and develop policies at the African level for higher education, via the CESA platform.

Main Responsibilities of the Policy Specialist:

The Policy Specialist will be a member of the AAU project management team and will report to the Secretary General of the AAU and consult regularly the Director of Research & Academic Planning (DRAP) and the Director of ICT and Knowledge Management (DIKM), as well as other relevant governing structures, including the AAU Governing Board. S/he will be responsible for the day-to-day execution of the policy related activities of the AAU Data-Policy Unit under the guidance of DRAP, DIKM and the HAQAA Initiative coordinator, OBREAL Global.

The main duties of the Policy Specialist will include:

– Drafting an annual workplan for discussion within the AAU, with key stakeholders and the PDU Steering Committee;

-Conducting background policy research and analysis as well as synthesizing research findings to identify and recommend best practices.

-Canvassing existing data sources, research and reports and ensuring the added value of the PDU’s work toward the CESA framework;

– Coordinating and analyzing the results of policy surveys in cooperation with a Data Specialist;

-Developing one-pagers and policy briefs based on data collection and analysis;

-Assisting in enhancing the policy department’s collaborations and communications on integrated activities with other CESA Clusters and Higher Education Subclusters;

-Contributing professional expertise and experience concerning science policy, higher education policy, and other policy areas most relevant to the AUC and other higher

education stakeholders;

-Writing annual HE policy reports;

-Preparing other written communications on a variety of topics of importance to AUC and higher education stakeholders, based on the work of the PDU;

-Interacting/coordinating communication with the PDU Steering Committee so as to integrate its feedback in the PDU’s work;

-Identifying new fields policy research relevant for the CESA framework;

-Performing any other duties or project management assignments that the Secretary-General may assign, in consultation with the HAQAA2 Implementing Team and the Coordinator of the CESA HE Cluster.

Requirements of the Policy Specialist

– A higher education degree or academic qualification in Public Policy Studies, International Relations, African Studies, Education/Higher Education, Regional

Integration Studies or a relevant discipline;

-Having held academic and/or management position with experience in public policy, policy development and assessment and/or international higher education for a minimum of 8 years, with extended period outside home country;

-High experience with the African higher education environment and higher education regional and sub-regional bodies as well as with African Union policy making;

-Ability to work in a multi-cultural environment;

-Ability to prepare and manage project budgets and produce project reports;

-Ability to analyze existing tools and databases;

-Excellent written communication skills and report writing experience;

-Exceptional team player with a strong ability to contribute positively to a team environment;

-Have good management, presentation and interpersonal skills;

-Excellent verbal communication skills.

-Fluency in English and French. Competency in at least one other AU language will be an advantage (Arabic or Portuguese).
