TITLE: WIPO Internship 2027 in Geneva: Paid Economics, Data Science and Innovation Research Internship at WIPO

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) is inviting applications for a Category II Internship within its Composite Indicator Research Section, Department for Economics and Data Analytics (DEDA), under the IP and Innovation Ecosystems Sector (IES).

This six-month internship will be based at WIPO Headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, and is designed for qualified candidates with an academic background in economics, data science or a related field who have strong interests in statistical analysis, econometrics, data visualization, innovation economics and policy research.

The selected intern will contribute to major WIPO research publications, including the Global Innovation Index (GII) 2027 and the World Intangible Investment Highlights (WIIH) 2027.

The internship is expected to begin on January 4, 2027, and provides a monthly stipend of CHF 2,170, together with medical insurance, annual leave and sick leave benefits.

The application deadline is September 15, 2026, at 11:59 PM CEST.

About the WIPO Internship Program

The WIPO Internship Program is designed to help students and recent graduates complement their academic education with practical professional experience in an international organisation.

Through participation in the workplace, interns can apply their academic knowledge to real-world projects while developing professional skills and competencies.

The programme also provides opportunities for learning through:

Practical work experience.

Exposure to an international working environment.

Supervision and feedback from experienced colleagues.

Technical mentoring.

Structured courses and learning programmes where available.

Experience working within the United Nations common system.

For candidates interested in international organisations, economics, innovation, data analytics and public policy, this internship provides an opportunity to gain practical experience while working on internationally relevant research and publications.

About the Host Department

This internship is hosted by the Composite Indicator Research Section within the Department for Economics and Data Analytics (DEDA) of WIPO’s IP and Innovation Ecosystems Sector (IES).

The intern will work under the supervision of the Head of the Composite Indicator Research Section.

The section’s work involves economic and data analysis, including research associated with innovation and intangible investment.

The internship therefore combines several areas, including:

Economics

Statistics

Data analytics

Econometrics

Innovation research

Economic publications

Data visualization

Policy research

Digital communications

Main Objectives of the Internship

The internship has several key objectives.

APPLY HERE

Apply Academic Knowledge

The intern will have an opportunity to apply knowledge of economics, statistics and data analytics to practical work involving economic publications and policymaking.

This means the internship is not purely administrative. Candidates will be expected to contribute analytical skills to research and publication-related activities.

Receive Technical Supervision and Mentoring

The intern will work under the guidance of experienced WIPO staff.

This provides an opportunity to receive technical supervision and mentoring while developing practical research and analytical skills.

Gain United Nations System Experience

The internship provides experience working within a United Nations common system organization.

This can give successful candidates exposure to the working environment, processes and professional standards of an international organisation.

Key Research Projects

The successful intern will contribute to work associated with two major publications.

Global Innovation Index 2027

One of the primary areas of work will be the Global Innovation Index (GII) 2027.

The Global Innovation Index is associated with research and analysis concerning innovation performance.

The intern may contribute analytical inputs and other research-related activities supporting the preparation of the 2027 edition.

This can provide practical experience in using data and economic analysis to support an internationally recognised research publication.

World Intangible Investment Highlights 2027

The intern will also contribute to the World Intangible Investment Highlights (WIIH) 2027.

This work focuses on measuring investment in intangible assets and communicating findings through research publications and related materials.

The combination of the GII and WIIH projects means that the intern can gain exposure to economic research, data analysis, innovation and intangible investment.

Duties and Responsibilities

Under the supervision of the Head of the Composite Indicator Research Section, the intern will contribute to several areas of work.

1. Research and Analytical Contributions

The intern will provide analytical inputs to the production of:

Global Innovation Index 2027.

World Intangible Investment Highlights 2027.

This may involve working with economic and statistical information and supporting research used in the preparation of the publications.

2. Data Visualization

The intern will provide support for data visualization.

This is particularly relevant for candidates interested in communicating complex datasets and economic findings through clear and accessible visual formats.

Applicants with experience using modern data visualization tools may therefore have an advantage.

3. Social Media and Website Content

The intern will also support the preparation of content for:

WIPO’s social media platforms.

The WIPO website.

This work will be carried out under editorial guidance.

Candidates with experience creating digital content, drafting web content or preparing social media materials may therefore find this aspect of the internship particularly relevant.

4. Event Organisation

The intern will assist with the organisation of events connected to the two major publications.

Responsibilities may include preparing:

Presentations.

Talking points.

Background materials.

Other event-related documentation.

This provides exposure to the communication and event-management side of international research projects.

5. Logistical and Administrative Support

The intern may also perform other related tasks as required.

Examples include:

Drafting invitations.

Coordinating event logistics.

Supporting administrative processes.

Providing general logistical assistance related to research activities and events.

The internship therefore combines analytical, communication, research and organisational responsibilities.

Educational Requirements

The essential educational requirement is an:

Advanced university degree (master’s degree) in economics, data science or a related field.

Candidates should therefore have an appropriate postgraduate academic background relevant to the work of the Composite Indicator Research Section.

Relevant academic areas may include economics, data science and related disciplines where the candidate has developed strong quantitative, analytical or research capabilities.

Statistical and Programming Experience

Applicants must have experience using specialised software and programming languages for statistical or econometric analysis.

The announcement specifically highlights:

R

Python

Experience with either R, Python or both is therefore particularly relevant to the position.

Candidates should be able to demonstrate practical experience using these tools for statistical analysis, econometric work, data processing or related research activities.

Data Visualization Skills

Familiarity with modern data visualization tools is an essential requirement.

Applicants should also have an interest in developing their data visualization skills further.

This suggests that candidates should be comfortable working with data and interested in transforming analytical findings into understandable visual outputs.

Desirable Skills and Experience

Several additional qualifications are listed as desirable rather than essential.

These include:

Applied Economics

Knowledge of or experience with applied economics is an advantage.

Candidates with experience applying economic concepts and analytical methods to real-world economic questions may therefore be particularly well suited.

Innovation Economics

Experience or knowledge of innovation economics is also desirable.

This is particularly relevant given the internship’s connection to the Global Innovation Index and WIPO’s broader work on innovation ecosystems.

Social Media and Web Content

Experience drafting content for social media and web use is another advantage.

Candidates who can combine technical research skills with strong digital communication abilities may therefore be able to contribute across several areas of the internship.

Communication Skills

The position also values:

Strong oral communication.

Strong written communication.

Strong interpersonal skills.

The ability to communicate effectively is important because the intern will contribute to research publications, digital content, presentations and events.

Multicultural Working Environment

Candidates should have the ability to work effectively in a multicultural environment.

Because WIPO is an international organisation, interns are expected to work respectfully and effectively with colleagues from different professional, cultural and national backgrounds.

Professional Integrity

Sound judgement and integrity are also listed among the desirable competencies.

Language Requirements

Excellent written and spoken English is an essential requirement.

Candidates must therefore be able to communicate effectively in English in both professional and written settings.

Knowledge of other official United Nations languages is desirable.

Additional UN languages may therefore strengthen an applicant’s profile, although they are not listed as essential.

Organisational Competencies

WIPO identifies several organisational competencies relevant to the internship.

Candidates should demonstrate the ability to:

Communicate effectively

Show team spirit

Demonstrate integrity

Value diversity

Produce results

Show service orientation

See the big picture

Seek change and innovation

Develop yourself and others

These competencies reflect the professional behaviours expected within the organisation.

Internship Duration

The internship has an expected duration of:

Six months

The internship may be renewed, subject to the applicable conditions.

The minimum duration is six months, while the maximum total duration is 12 months.

Expected Start Date

The expected start date is:

January 4, 2027

Candidates should therefore be prepared to undertake the internship from this date if selected.

Location and Remote Work

The internship will take place at:

WIPO Headquarters, Geneva, Switzerland

Importantly, this internship cannot be carried out remotely.

The selected candidate will therefore need to work physically from WIPO’s headquarters in Geneva.

Internship Working Hours

The stipend stated in the vacancy is based on a full-time internship of 40 hours per week.

Candidates should therefore be prepared to commit to a full-time schedule for the duration of the internship.

Stipend and Benefits

The selected intern will receive a monthly stipend of:

CHF 2,170

In addition to the stipend, the internship provides:

Medical insurance.

Annual leave.

Sick leave benefits.

The stipend amount applies to the full-time 40-hour-per-week internship.

The internship is therefore a paid opportunity rather than an unpaid placement.

Eligibility Requirements

This position falls under Category II of the WIPO Internship Program.

Under the eligibility rules provided in the opportunity, the following individuals may qualify:

Category II Eligibility

Option A: Students Pursuing Their First Advanced University Degree

Individuals who are pursuing their first advanced university degree may qualify if they have:

Completed their coursework.

Not yet completed their final thesis.

Option B: Individuals Pursuing a Subsequent Degree

Individuals who have already obtained their first advanced university degree and are currently pursuing a subsequent university degree may also qualify.

Option C: Recent Advanced Degree Graduates

Individuals who obtained their most recent advanced university degree less than two years before the date of their internship application may also qualify.

Applicants should carefully determine which of these three categories applies to their situation before applying.

Who Should Apply?

The internship is particularly suited to candidates who combine postgraduate academic training with practical quantitative and analytical skills.

A competitive candidate would ideally have:

A master’s degree or qualifying advanced university degree in economics, data science or a related field.

Experience with R and/or Python.

Experience in statistical or econometric analysis.

Familiarity with modern data visualization tools.

Excellent written and spoken English.

An interest in economics, innovation, data analytics and policy research.

Strong communication skills.

The ability to work in a multicultural environment.

Additional experience in applied economics, innovation economics, social media, web content and data communication would be advantageous.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit two essential documents:

1. Motivation Letter

The motivation letter should explain the candidate’s interest in the internship and demonstrate their suitability for the position.

Candidates should use the letter to connect their academic background, technical skills and professional interests with the work of the Composite Indicator Research Section.

2. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must also submit a current CV.

The CV should clearly present relevant:

Educational qualifications.

Statistical and econometric experience.

Programming skills.

Data visualization experience.

Professional experience.

The CV and cover letter must be combined into one single PDF file when submitting through LinkedIn Easy Apply.

September 15, 2026, at 11:59 PM CEST

TITLE: ProPublica Emerging Reporters Program 2026-2027 ($9,000 stipend)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: August 17, 2026

Applications are open for the ProPublica Emerging Reporters Program 2026-2027. The Emerging Reporters Program is specifically designed for talented aspiring journalists who find investigative journalism inaccessible for financial reasons.

ProPublica has a vested interest in developing more journalists from a wide range of backgrounds, particularly those who are economically disadvantaged. They consider it crucial to the future of the industry and to their own ability to fulfill their mission, which is to expose abuses of power and produce journalism that provokes change.

Without the voices and points of view of more journalists from diverse backgrounds, there is every reason to believe that important stories are being overlooked. Barriers that keep aspiring journalists from entering the field include financial constraints and lack of access to mentors and training. The Emerging Reporters Program is aimed at lowering those barriers and encouraging the next generation of journalists.

Benefits

The Emerging Reporters Program provides $9,000 stipends, along with mentoring and a trip to a journalism conference, such as the Investigative Reporters & Editors conference.

Accommodations and other expenses for the conference will be covered by ProPublica. The dates of the conferences are to be determined.

Eligibility

Open only to students who are eligible to file U.S. taxes and are able to provide a completed W-9 form, including U.S. citizens or U.S. residents. The W-9 form requires that each participant provide a valid Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number. They will not make any exceptions to this rule.

All students who will be undergraduate juniors or seniors in college this academic year are eligible to apply, and students from groups that are traditionally underrepresented in journalism are especially encouraged to do so.

Application

This year’s program will run from late September to June, during which time mentors and program participants will be in contact by phone and email.

TITLE: Young Leaders Programme 2026 in Vietnam: Fully Funded Opportunity for Emerging Leaders Interested in Regional Cooperation and Maritime Security

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Young Leaders Programme 2026, an international leadership opportunity taking place alongside the 18th South China Sea International Conference in Hanoi, Viet Nam, from 6–8 October 2026.

The programme, themed “Regional Cooperation and Next-Generation Solutions,” offers an exceptional platform for promising young leaders, researchers, scholars, and policy enthusiasts to engage with some of the most important geopolitical and maritime security issues shaping the Indo-Pacific region.

Selected participants will have the opportunity to attend one of the region’s leading forums on maritime security and geopolitics, interact with prominent scholars and policymakers, exchange ideas with fellow young leaders, and contribute their perspectives on promoting peace, stability, cooperation, and prosperity in the South China Sea.

Importantly, the selected Young Leaders will receive comprehensive sponsorship covering round-trip economy-class airfare, accommodation, local transportation, and meals, making this an excellent opportunity for qualified young people interested in international affairs and regional cooperation.

A total of eight Young Leaders will be selected to participate in the programme.

About the Young Leaders Programme 2026

The Young Leaders Programme is organized as part of the annual South China Sea International Conference, hosted by the Diplomatic Academy of Viet Nam. The conference has established itself as one of the leading regional platforms for discussions surrounding maritime security, geopolitics, international cooperation, and developments affecting the South China Sea and the broader Indo-Pacific region.

Each year, the South China Sea International Conference brings together an impressive community of scholars, policymakers, practitioners, researchers, and experts from different parts of the world. The forum provides participants with an opportunity to discuss emerging geopolitical developments, exchange research findings, and explore possible solutions to complex regional and international challenges.

Recognizing the importance of involving younger generations in conversations about the future of the region, the Young Leaders Programme was established to create a dedicated platform for emerging leaders to participate in these discussions.

The programme aims to empower the next generation of thinkers and decision-makers by providing them with opportunities to:

Engage directly with complex issues surrounding the South China Sea.

Learn from experienced scholars and policy experts.

Exchange perspectives with other promising young leaders.

Build professional and academic networks.

Develop ideas related to peace, cooperation, and regional development.

Participate actively in high-level discussions.

Present innovative policy ideas.

Gain exposure to international academic and policy environments.

Participants in the programme will become part of a growing network of young scholars and leaders interested in contributing meaningful ideas toward the future of the South China Sea and the wider Indo-Pacific region.

Theme of the Young Leaders Programme 2026

The 2026 programme will focus on the theme:

Regional Cooperation and Next-Generation Solutions

The theme recognizes the increasingly important role that young people will play in shaping future responses to geopolitical, security, environmental, economic, and international cooperation challenges.

The South China Sea remains one of the world’s most strategically important maritime regions. Issues surrounding maritime security, international law, territorial disputes, economic development, environmental sustainability, freedom of navigation, and regional cooperation continue to attract significant international attention.

Addressing these complex challenges requires innovative thinking, constructive dialogue, and meaningful cooperation between different stakeholders.

Through the Young Leaders Programme, emerging researchers and leaders will be encouraged to explore creative and practical ideas that can contribute to a peaceful, stable, and prosperous regional environment.

The programme particularly emphasizes the importance of next-generation perspectives and recognizes that young scholars and professionals can bring fresh ideas to discussions that have traditionally been dominated by established policymakers and experts.

About the South China Sea International Conference

The South China Sea International Conference of the Diplomatic Academy of Viet Nam is an annual forum focusing on important geopolitical and maritime issues affecting the region.

Over the years, the conference has developed into a respected platform for dialogue and knowledge exchange, attracting participants from:

Universities

Research institutions

Think tanks

Government institutions

International organizations

Policy communities

Diplomatic circles

Academic institutions

The conference features presentations and discussions led by experienced experts and thought leaders working on issues related to international relations, maritime security, international law, regional cooperation, and geopolitics.

For Young Leaders Programme participants, attending the conference provides a valuable opportunity to observe and engage with high-level discussions involving some of the leading voices in the field.

Participants will also gain exposure to current research, emerging policy debates, and different perspectives on issues affecting the South China Sea and the broader Indo-Pacific.

What Will Selected Young Leaders Do?

The Young Leaders Programme is designed to ensure that participants are not merely observers at the conference.

Selected participants will have opportunities to actively engage with the programme and contribute their own perspectives.

1. Attend the 18th South China Sea International Conference

Young Leaders will receive full access to participate in the conference and follow presentations and discussions taking place across different sessions.

This will enable participants to gain firsthand exposure to contemporary debates and discussions involving leading scholars, practitioners, and policymakers.

2. Learn From Leading Experts

One of the major highlights of the programme is the opportunity to interact with experienced thought leaders and experts.

Participants will have opportunities to learn from individuals working in areas such as:

International relations

Maritime security

International law

Geopolitics

Regional cooperation

Foreign policy

Strategic studies

Indo-Pacific affairs

These interactions can provide valuable academic and professional insights for young people seeking to build careers in related fields.

3. Participate in the Young Leaders Special Session

Young Leaders will have their own dedicated Special Session during the Conference.

During this session, participants will be given the opportunity to present their policy pitches before fellow participants and members of the audience.

This provides a significant opportunity for emerging leaders to articulate their ideas, propose solutions, and contribute to conversations surrounding peace and cooperation in the South China Sea.

Participants will be encouraged to think creatively about how future challenges can be addressed through innovative and constructive approaches.

4. Engage in Side Events and Deep Discussions

Young Leaders will also participate in side events associated with the South China Sea International Conference.

These events will create additional opportunities for deeper engagement with speakers and experts.

Participants may engage in discussions surrounding issues addressed during the main conference and explore topics in greater depth.

Such interactions can help young researchers develop a stronger understanding of the practical and policy dimensions of international affairs.

5. Exchange Ideas With Other Young Leaders

The programme will bring together a small but highly selected group of young people with shared interests in international affairs and regional cooperation.

This creates an opportunity for participants to exchange perspectives, learn from different experiences, and establish meaningful professional relationships.

The diversity of perspectives can contribute to richer discussions and encourage participants to think beyond their individual academic or national contexts.

Benefits of the Young Leaders Programme 2026

The Young Leaders Programme offers both financial support and significant academic and professional benefits.

Fully Sponsored International Participation

One of the most important benefits is the comprehensive sponsorship provided to selected participants.

The organizers will cover key costs associated with attending the programme in Hanoi.

The sponsorship includes:

Round-trip economy-class airfare.

Three nights of accommodation.

Local transportation.

Meals during the programme.

The accommodation period is scheduled around the conference dates of 6–8 October 2026.

This financial support allows talented young leaders to participate regardless of the financial barriers that might otherwise prevent them from attending an international conference.

Full Participation in the 18th South China Sea International Conference

Selected participants will receive the opportunity to fully participate in one of the region’s important forums on maritime security and geopolitical affairs.

Participants will be able to follow discussions, attend sessions, and gain exposure to current debates involving international experts.

Opportunity to Present a Policy Pitch

Young Leaders will have the opportunity to present their ideas during the programme’s dedicated Special Session.

This is particularly valuable for young researchers and professionals who want to:

Develop policy communication skills.

Present ideas before an international audience.

Receive exposure to diverse perspectives.

Practice articulating solutions to complex challenges.

Build confidence in academic and policy discussions.

Networking With International Scholars and Experts

Universities

Research institutions

Policy organizations

Building such networks can be highly beneficial for young professionals and researchers seeking future opportunities for collaboration, research, academic development, and professional growth.

Certificate of Attendance

This certificate can serve as a valuable addition to an individual’s academic or professional portfolio, particularly for those pursuing careers related to:

International affairs

Political science

International law

Security studies

Public policy

Research

Regional cooperation

Membership in the Alumni Network

Selected participants will become part of the South China Sea Conference Young Leaders Programme Alumni Network.

Being part of an alumni network provides the possibility of maintaining connections beyond the duration of the programme.

Such networks can create opportunities for:

Continued knowledge exchange.

Professional networking.

Academic collaboration.

Future partnerships.

Participation in related initiatives.

Who Can Apply for the Young Leaders Programme 2026?

The programme is seeking young people with a strong interest in issues surrounding maritime security, international relations, and regional cooperation.

Applicants must meet several eligibility requirements.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be between 20 and 35 years old at the start of the programme.

Candidates should therefore ensure that they fall within the specified age range by the beginning of the Young Leaders Programme in October 2026.

English Language Proficiency

Candidates must be able to use English fluently.

Since the programme will bring together participants and experts from different countries and backgrounds, English will be essential for:

Networking with participants.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable communicating and expressing their ideas in English.

Relevant Academic Background

Applicants should possess background knowledge in relevant fields.

Interest in Maritime Security and Related Issues

Applicants should demonstrate a genuine commitment to maritime security and related issues.

This could be reflected through:

Academic studies.

Publications.

Advocacy work.

Participation in relevant conferences or initiatives.

Independent research and analysis.

Applicants should demonstrate that their interest extends beyond simply attending an international event and show how their experiences or aspirations connect to the broader issues addressed by the programme.

How Many Participants Will Be Selected?

The Young Leaders Programme is highly competitive.

A total of only eight Young Leaders will be selected from the pool of applicants.

The small cohort size means that successful candidates will likely benefit from more meaningful engagement with fellow participants and opportunities for closer interaction with experts.

Because of the limited number of available places, applicants are encouraged to prepare thoughtful and compelling application responses that clearly demonstrate:

TITLE: Observations and Recommendations by the ACE Impact Subject Matter Experts

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
At the ongoing 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop holding in Benin from June 14-17, 2022, one key group of stakeholders that is represented is the Subject Matter Experts. As part of the strategy to effectively implement the ACE Impact for Development Project, the Regional Facilitation Unit (RFU) – the AAU, has identified and is coordinating a team of subject matter Experts who contribute to the operational and technical implementation support and supervision of the ACE Impact Centers. These independent Experts are selected based on their academic and/or disciplinary expertise relative to the ACE Impact Centers, and their international experience in higher education and/or university leadership. Experts are appointed to support specific Centers and to contribute to the ACE Impact project.

Each ACE Impact Center has been assigned a primary Expert who provides implementation support and supervision to the Center. Experts are supporting and guiding the ACE Impact Centers so that they attain scientific excellence, quality, relevance, and impact. Each Expert provides his/her inputs in close coordination and guidance from the ACE Impact RFU.

The key tasks of the subject matter experts include:

Reviewing and providing expert insight and advice on the ACE Impact Centers’ implementation plans

Reviewing and providing expert insight and advice on the ACE Impact Centers’ annual work plans.

Mentoring the ACE Impact Centers as needed.

Undertaking supervision and implementation Centre support visits which may either be in-person or virtual.

Reviewing the research publications of the ACE Impact Centers to ensure compliance with ACE Impact objectives.

Supporting the ACE Impact Centers by connecting them to potential university and industry partners, and potential funding opportunities.

Reporting supervision findings to the Project Steering Committee during its Meetings.

Participating in the ACE Impact Regional Workshops.

Liaising with the RFU on any key factors that may hinder the success of Centers or the ACE Impact project.

Providing ongoing advice and support to the RFU and the World Bank on the ACE Impact project.

Professor Joseph Mutale represented the subject matter experts on Tuesday 14th June 2022 to provide feedback from the subject matter experts to the ACE Impact Centres. He congratulated all the Centres for sustaining performance at the peak of the difficult Covid 19-season and for navigating new challenges by developing innovative ways to deliver education. He acknowledged that the Centres had adopted digital and blended learning methods to address the challenges posed by the Covid 19 era. He also stressed that as subject matter experts they were confident that the Centres would successfully address all their future challenges effectively, having learnt some lessons and gained experience over this period.

Professor Mutale shared key observations and recommendations for the Centres to consider towards ensuring the timely delivery of the project’s milestones. He advised that attention needed to be paid to the annual work plans and project management by assigning dedicated personnel to support these areas. New ACE Impact Centres were advised to start the self-evaluation processes early enough, to give them ample time to prepare towards international accreditation of their programs. It was indicated, that the research strategies for the Centres must clarify priorities, objectives, and available resources to support research. Centres were advised to effectively use their sectoral advisory boards and international scientific committees to strengthen their research strategies. Again, effective communication at all levels, especially with students, was singled out as extremely important for the effective implementation of the project. Enhancing regional dimensions in terms of internships, research, publications, and student recruitment was said to be a key way of ensuring the project’s success.

It was mentioned that the success of the ACE Impact project depends on the effective involvement of all team members and therefore the Centre leaders need to pay attention to this aspect. Increased engagement of university leadership to facilitate procurement and to address the causes of underspending were singled out as being equally important.

In conclusion, Professor Mutale called on the Centres to seize the opportunity of meeting physically for the first time after the COVID-19 outbreak to reconnect, exchange ideas and look for solutions to push the project forward. He stressed that the next six months were critical for the achievement of time bound project results. He pledged the commitment of all the subject matter experts to “remain available and committed to work” with all the ACE Impact Centres to enable them achieve the project objectives.

Written By: Ms Nodumo Dhlamini, Director – ICT Services, Communications and Knowledge Management at AAU

TITLE: PhD Candidate in Hydroinformatics at IHE Delft: Uncertainty-Aware Optimisation for Robust Water Distribution System Operation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a Master’s graduate with a strong background in hydroinformatics, water engineering, civil or environmental engineering, applied mathematics, operations research, or computer science? Are you interested in artificial intelligence, optimisation, hydraulic modelling, uncertainty analysis, digital twins, and intelligent water systems?

The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education is offering an exciting PhD Candidate position in Hydroinformatics as part of the Horizon Europe Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Network i3WaterS – Intelligent, Innovative and Integrative Water Systems.

This four-year doctoral research opportunity is designed for an ambitious researcher who wants to contribute to the future of intelligent, resilient, sustainable, and data-driven drinking-water distribution systems.

The selected candidate will be based in Delft, the Netherlands, and will work within IHE Delft’s Hydroinformatics and Socio-Technical Innovation Department. The research will focus specifically on developing uncertainty-aware optimisation approaches that can help water utilities make better operational decisions when hydraulic models, operational data, water demand, and other inputs are uncertain.

The position combines academic research, advanced computational methods, artificial intelligence, optimisation, water-system modelling, international collaboration, and practical engagement with water utilities.

Opportunity Overview

The PhD candidate will undertake research within the Horizon Europe-funded i3WaterS Doctoral Network, which brings together universities, research institutions, technology developers, and water utilities.

The broader i3WaterS network will train 15 Doctoral Candidates in developing advanced approaches for intelligent water systems. The programme integrates:

Monitoring data

Expert knowledge

Hydraulic models

Water-quality models

Digital twins

Optimisation

Artificial intelligence

Machine learning

Decision-support systems

Uncertainty analysis

Data-driven modelling

The goal is to develop innovative approaches that can help drinking-water distribution systems become more intelligent, resilient, efficient, and sustainable.

For this particular PhD project, the successful candidate will investigate how uncertainty can be explicitly incorporated into operational optimisation.

PhD Research Topic

Uncertainty-Aware Optimisation for Robust Water Distribution System Operation

Water distribution systems are complex infrastructure networks. Their operation depends on many variables, including water demand, hydraulic conditions, network characteristics, operational decisions, and information obtained from monitoring systems.

However, these variables are not always known with complete certainty.

Hydraulic models may contain uncertainties, operational data may be incomplete or inaccurate, and water demand can fluctuate significantly. Consequently, an operational decision that appears optimal under one set of assumptions may not perform as expected when actual conditions differ.

This PhD research will address this challenge by developing uncertainty-aware, model-based, multi-objective optimisation methodologies for drinking-water distribution systems.

The research will explicitly account for uncertainty in hydraulic models and operational data and investigate how different sources of uncertainty influence operational decisions.

An important part of the research will involve identifying which uncertainties are significant enough to justify further investigation or additional information gathering.

The project will therefore make use of Value of Information (VoI) concepts to determine which uncertainty sources are worth resolving and which may not materially affect decisions.

The ultimate goal is to advance computational methods that enable robust and potentially real-time operational optimisation for water distribution systems.

Main Research Objectives

The successful PhD candidate will be expected to contribute to several major research objectives.

1. Identify Important Sources of Uncertainty

The research will develop methodologies and reproducible computational tools for determining which uncertainty sources have a meaningful impact on operational decisions.

Not every uncertainty within a water distribution system will necessarily need to be resolved.

The candidate will therefore investigate how uncertainties can be assessed and prioritised, including through Value of Information approaches.

This can help water utilities focus their resources on collecting, improving, or resolving information that has the greatest influence on decision-making.

2. Develop Robust Optimisation Methods

The project will develop methods for optimising water-distribution-system operations while accounting for uncertain inputs.

Rather than assuming that all model parameters and operational conditions are perfectly known, the research will investigate optimisation approaches capable of producing decisions that remain effective under uncertainty.

This will involve robust and potentially stochastic multi-objective optimisation approaches.

3. Develop Reproducible Code

An important expected outcome of the PhD will be the development of reproducible research methodologies and software.

The candidate is expected to produce:

Reproducible code for identifying influential uncertainty sources

Computational approaches for uncertainty-aware decision-making

Code for robust optimisation of water distribution system operations

Methods that can potentially support real-time operational decision-making

Reproducibility will be important because the resulting methodologies should be useful for future research and potentially transferable to practical water-management applications.

4. Validate the Research Using a Real Utility Case

The research will not remain purely theoretical.

The developed methodologies will be validated using a real water utility case.

The candidate will assess how the proposed methods perform under realistic operational conditions and evaluate their potential benefits and limitations.

The validation will include an assessment of:

Operational performance improvements

Robustness of decisions

Practical applicability

Limitations of the proposed methods

Effects of uncertainty on operational outcomes

This real-world component provides an opportunity for the doctoral research to connect advanced computational research with practical water-utility challenges.

Expected Results of the PhD

The project identifies three major expected outcomes.

Expected Result 1: Uncertainty Identification Methodology

The candidate will develop a methodology and reproducible code capable of identifying uncertainty sources that materially affect operational decisions.

Expected Result 2: Robust Optimisation Methodology

The candidate will develop a methodology and associated code for robust optimisation of water-distribution-system operations under uncertain inputs.

Expected Result 3: Real-World Validation

The developed research will be tested using a real utility case, with an assessment of performance improvements and limitations.

Together, these outputs are expected to contribute to more reliable and intelligent operational decision-making within drinking-water distribution systems.

IHE Delft is an international institution specialising in water education, research, and capacity development.

The doctoral researcher will work within an interdisciplinary environment connecting water engineering, hydroinformatics, data science, artificial intelligence, modelling, optimisation, and socio-technical innovation.

The position provides an opportunity to conduct doctoral research while collaborating with academic researchers, water-sector professionals, technology developers, and other doctoral researchers within the i3WaterS network.

TITLE: The Foundation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
IHES was created in 1958 at a key stage in the history of science and the world. Léon Motchane, a Russian businessman, loved mathematics to the extent that he submitted his doctoral thesis in 1954. Determined to offer exceptional scientists a place conducive to the unfettered development of their research, he took inspiration from the model of the Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) in Princeton and created IHES, dedicated to theoretical sciences: mathematics, physics and their interactions.

From the Institute’s inception, Motchane enlisted the emblematic support of Robert Oppenheimer – then Director of IAS – who joined the Scientific Committee and remained a member all his life. The first contributors, won over by this scientific project, came from both the public and the private sectors, in France and abroad. The wide range of the Institute’s partners reflects lasting universal appeal.

Excellence is the privilege of no single nation and for the past half century, IHES has been a link in the global chain of knowledge development. The Institute was created for researchers – both permanent and invited – who transcend the borders of mathematics and theoretical physics. More than 200 scientists come to IHES from all over the world every year for research visits.

IHES directors

1958 – 1971 : Léon Motchane, a Russian born business man who loved mathematics, was the Institute’s founder and first director.

1971 – 1985 : Nicolaas H. Kuiper, Dutch mathematician

Nicolaas Kuiper showed a marked interest in his research for topology and geometry in many forms, from immersion theory to dynamic systems, from flexahedron theory to taut immersions.

1985-1994 : Marcel Berger, French mathematician

A wide spectrum Riemannian geometer, Marcel Berger is particularly noted for the 1/4 pinching theorem, which became a cornerstone for global geometry. He was the President of the Société Mathématique de France from 1979 to 1981.

1994-2013 : Jean-Pierre Bourguignon, French mathematician

Jean-Pierre Bourguignon has a strong preference for differential geometry, especially its links to partial differential equations and mathematical physics. He has focused his work on the Ricci curvature, both for its mathematical aspects and the role it plays in general relativity.

Since 2013 : Emmanuel Ullmo, French mathematician

His area of mathematical research is algebraic geometry and arithmetic. He is an alumnus of École Normale Supérieure de Cachan (class of 1985) and holds a PhD in Mathematical Sciences from Université Paris-Sud (1992).

Renaud de la Genière, Banque de France (1978-1985)

Marcel Boiteux, Électricité de France (1985-1994)

TITLE: Why we should harmonise higher education data for a sustainable future in East Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
By Daniel Omanyo, ESSA and Paul Odhiambo

On Africa Universities’ Day, celebrated on 12th November, we recognise the power of harmonised higher education data to build resilient and inclusive educational systems in East Africa. Higher education data is critical for creating responsive and effective systems that benefit stakeholders and society. In a rapidly evolving digital world, data is crucial for decision-making, competitiveness and progress, including in higher education.

The East African Community (EAC) Vision 2050 prioritises improving access to education and completion rates, particularly at higher levels. Realising this vision depends on reliable and comprehensive higher education data. EAC member states must harmonise their data laws and standards. The EAC Data Governance Policy Framework will improve digital integration and security, and support regional data harmonisation. The Policy Framework aims to harmonise data governance across EAC member states to foster secure, efficient and inclusive digital systems for sustainable economic growth and regional integration. Aligned with the 2022 African Union Data Policy Framework, the EAC Data Policy Framework seeks to advance resilient and inclusive education systems, a fitting focus as we celebrate Africa Universities’ Day and its theme of building an African fit for the 21st century.

EAC policies recognise that a well-educated population is essential for productivity and innovation. While education is an important foundation of the EAC’s economic and social development, lack of sufficient higher education data hinders policy development, resource allocation, and educational equity. As the EAC expands, harmonising higher education data becomes essential for creating quality, relevant learning opportunities across diverse educational systems, supporting Africa Universities’ Day’s mission of fostering access to lifelong, high-quality education. Moreover, higher education data is critical for informing the development and implementation of Science, Technology and Innovation policies in the region. EAC member states often collect disjointed data using different methods, which complicates regional comparisons. The region must harmonise data collection and management now that it has designated itself as a common higher education area. The Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) is collaborating with Education Sub Saharan Africa (ESSA), Population Reference Bureau (PRB), and the Association of African Universities (AAU) to develop guidelines for harmonisation, which are a significant step forward. This effort is part of the ongoing project titled Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community, funded by the Carnegie Corporation of New York. This collaboration, spearheaded by organisations such as AAU—the institution that facilitates and organises events to mark the Africa Universities’ Day—demonstrates the commitment to building systems that support resilient and accessible higher education across the continent.

Despite these efforts, insights from ESSA show substantial data gaps across EAC member states, highlighting the need for continued focus on data harmonisation. Data availability varies significantly, and there are inconsistencies in discipline classification and national-level faculty data. Inconsistent measures within countries further complicate national-level estimates. As the IUCEA develops harmonised guidelines, it is imperative to prioritise key indicators, establish data collection departments in each higher education institution, and involve all stakeholders. Equally crucial is building university staff capacity in data collection approaches, storage, use, and dissemination, recognising that diverse users of higher education data include parents, students, investors, and other universities. Operationalisation of the harmonised guidelines will ensure data uniformity, enable cross-country comparison, and facilitate effective decision-making at national and regional levels. In addition, they will support the development of a regional higher education information management system, promoting data sharing and learning. The full realisation of this initiative requires collaboration across EAC institutions and higher education stakeholders in the region.

As we commemorate Africa Universities’ Day, the urgency to harmonise higher education data is evident. This is not just about data; it is about empowering every learner in East Africa. A unified data framework can drive equitable policies, foster innovation, and build resilient communities. Collaboration among governments, institutions, and communities is essential to transform education for sustainable development.

Dr. Omanyo is the Research Policy Manager at Education Sub Saharan Africa (ESSA). He leads the implementation of the Demographics of African Faculty project in the East African Community. Email: daniel@essa-africa.org. Mr. Odhiambo is an independent consultant on foreign policy, governance and higher education. Email: odhiodongo@gmail.com.

Introduction and Background: As part of the numerous benefits offered by the Association of African Universities (AAU) to its members, and in line with strengthening the capacity of leaders in Africa’s higher education ecosystem, the AAU is organizing a workshop for senior officers in African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) concerned with strengthening partnerships for their institutions, including those from the International Offices and Partnerships Units.

International relations is crucial for African universities for various reasons, including facilitating academic collaborations, promoting the engagement of African universities in joint research projects and exchange programmes, fostering the attraction of international students and faculty, promoting collaborative teaching initiatives and generally broadening the academic horizon. The exposure to global best practices through engagements and partnerships with other institutions helps to enrich the overall educational experience and contribute substantially to the sustainability of institutions. Through a strengthened international office and partnership unit, African universities can tap into global funding opportunities, grants, and scholarships among others. Such resources, once available to institutions, support various initiatives, including research development, infrastructure improvements, and academic program enhancements. With stakeholders of Africa’s Higher Education calling in HEIs to lead the transformation of the continent’s economies, collaborations and partnerships to generate cutting edge research and innovative solutions have become even more crucial in recent years.

Access to global research networks and resources helps African universities stay at the forefront of scientific and technological advancements. Active engagement in international relations boosts the global visibility and reputation of African universities, enhancing institutions’ standing and influence. Additionally, international relations foster cultural exchanges, enriching the campus environment with diverse perspectives. This exposure helps students and faculty develop a global mindset and intercultural competencies, preparing them for the increasingly interconnected world. Continuous training of officers and leaders in charge of international partnerships and relations, in alignment with a university’s goals helps to enhance the institution’s global engagement and impact, leading to more effective partnerships and collaborations.

This upcoming workshop, being organised by the Association of African Universities, aims to provide the much needed platform for the heads and other officials in the Offices of International Relations, International Education, Partnerships and other related offices in Africa’s higher education to share best practices, explore opportunities, and discuss ways of overcoming common challenges, while fostering peer-to-peer learning, to enhance the quality and global relevance of higher education in Africa.

TITLE: Wongani Mulanga from Malawi is OD Young Person of the Month – August 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Wongani Mulanga is a Malawian Environmental Scientist and the Co-Founder and Executive Director of Green Minds Malawi, a youth-led organisation working at the intersection of climate education, clean energy access, and community engagement. She also runs Her Climate Lab, a girl-led climate education programme at a secondary school in Mangochi.

Background and Work

Growing up, Wongani watched students around her work hard with very little to show for it, not because they lacked ability, but because they lacked electricity to study by, resources to learn with, and spaces that reflected their potential back at them. She carried that observation through school and into university, and when she finished her BSc in Environmental Science, she decided she was not going to wait for a job before doing something about it. Together with three other young people, she co-founded Green Minds Malawi and launched the Green Ed Initiative almost immediately after finishing university. Green Ed is built on the conviction that educational inequality and environmental degradation share the same root. Students studying by kerosene lamp are breathing harmful fumes and falling behind academically because the light is poor, and both problems have the same solution. Through the initiative, Green Minds distributes solar lamps to students from households without reliable electricity, works with schools to establish environmental clubs, introduces waste management through bin donations and clean-up campaigns, and plants trees. Young people are treated as thinkers who are already part of the climate story, not as passive recipients waiting to be educated. The initiative has engaged over 100 students across four partner schools, three primary schools and one secondary school, through environmental education, club activities, and clean energy access. The work has also extended beyond Green Minds. Through Her Climate Lab, Wongani facilitated a session on solar energy and clean technology with a group of young women studying at a secondary school in Mangochi, connecting climate science to the energy choices their families make every day.

How It Started
There was no single dramatic moment, it was just an accumulation of things observed over years, students relying on kerosene to read at night, environmental issues treated as secondary in communities already carrying too many burdens, young people left out of conversations about changes affecting their lakes, their farms, and their futures. What pushed Wongani to act was recognising that the gap was not in awareness. Most people already know the environment is under pressure. The gap was in practical tools and platforms that would allow young people to do something about it, and she did not want to be someone who wrote reports about that gap without trying to close it.

Successes So Far
Green Minds has distributed solar lamps to students from households without electricity, enabling them to study at night while adopting clean energy in ways that feel personal and immediate rather than abstract. Four school partnerships have produced environmental clubs, clean-up campaigns, waste management initiatives, and tree planting activities. The organisation has also been documenting climate stories from communities living on the shores of Lake Malawi, capturing flood experiences and recovery through its Climate Witness project.

Challenges and How They Were Faced
Like most youth-led startups, the hardest thing has been funding. Green Minds is still largely self-funded, with the founding team working voluntarily and relying on personal contributions alongside a small pool of dedicated volunteers to keep operations running. There is no comfortable budget to fall back on, and every activity requires finding creative ways to make limited resources go further. The team has navigated this by being deliberate about commitments, only promising what can actually be delivered, and building partnerships that contribute in-kind where cash is not available. The other challenge has been fair distribution of lamps. School-level recommendations do not always reflect household realities, because favouritism and limited information mean that the students who need support most are not always the ones put forward. Green Minds responded by introducing household visits before distribution decisions are made, so the team sees conditions directly rather than relying on second hand nominations.

Plans for the Future
The goal is to expand Green Ed to more schools across Malawi, prioritising districts where energy poverty and limited environmental education overlap most. An instalment-based model for lamp access is being developed so that students whose households can contribute something can do so over time, making the programme more financially sustainable without removing the full donation model for those who cannot contribute at all.

Words of Advice for Young Changemakers
Do not wait until conditions feel right, because they rarely do. Start where you are, stay close to the communities your work is meant to serve, and find at least one person who believes in what you are doing but will also tell you the truth when something is not working. Proximity and honesty are what make impact last beyond a single project or funding cycle.

TITLE: Europlanet 2024 RI

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Research Infrastructure Cluster

Image:

Europlanet 2024 Research Infrastructure

The Europlanet 2024 Research Infrastructure (RI) provided the pan-EU infrastructure needed to address the major scientific and technological challenges facing modern planetary science and strengthen Europe’s position at the forefront of space exploration.

Europlanet 2024 RI built on the foundations of a series of highly successful EU-funded projects that have created the leading Virtual Observatory for planetary data and the largest, most diverse collection in the world today of field and laboratory facilities capable of simulating and analyzing planetary environments. Europlanet 2024 RI provided Transnational Access (TA) to an enhanced set of world-leading field and laboratory facilities, Virtual Access (VA) to state-of-the-art data services and tools linked to the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC), and Networking Activities (NA) to widen the user base and draw in new partners from Under Represented States (URS), non-EU countries, industry and interdisciplinary fields, and to train the next generation of RI leaders and users.

With 53 beneficiaries, from both industry and academic sectors, providing access to 29 TA facilities on 5 continents and 4 VA services linking over 100 data services and catalogues, Europlanet 2024 RI represented a step-change in ambition for planetary science worldwide. Innovations included the establishment of a ground based observation network to support space based missions, the launch of an interactive mapping service to provide virtual exploration of planetary surfaces, and the development of machine learning tools for data mining to fully exploit and analyze planetary data sets. Europlanet 2024 RI established global collaborations and an international userbase for the RI through inclusion of partners in Africa, Asia and South America. Ultimately, Europlanet 2024 RI supported the transition of this unique infrastructure to a sustainable future within the structure of the Europlanet Society.

Project partners

The Europlanet 2024 RI consortium was led by the University of Kent, UK, and had 53 beneficiary institutions from 21 countries in Europe and around the world, with a further 44 affiliated partners. The project drew on the resources of the Europlanet Society to disseminate activities and outcomes and develop a more diverse community of users.

TITLE: Nationwide Tracer Study on Most Viable Career Pathways Among Ghanaian Graduates

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Brighter Investment, a social enterprise that provides full financial support to talented students in developing countries, in partnership with the Ministry for Business Development of the Republic of Ghana, and the Association of African Universities (AAU) will be conducting a nationwide career tracer study on most viable career pathways among Ghanaian graduates in August, 2020. The study broadly seeks to identify the most viable career paths and factors contributing to career development and success among graduates in Ghana.

Graduates from Ghanaian Universities, Polytechnics and Colleges of Education between 2010 and 2019 are eligible to participate in this study. Respondents will be required to fill a structured questionnaire which will only take five minutes to complete. The outcome of this study will provide policymakers with the needed data to make informed decisions regarding financing education, graduate employability, and business development in Ghana.

Through its partnering organizations, Brighter Investment will be conducting this nationwide tracer study specifically to:

Utilize the results to make informed decisions with regard to higher education in the country and in Africa as a whole.

Determine what education programs hold the highest career prospects for students.

Expand supported programs and institutions and support more students.

Inform decisions and create policies to increase employment and empower individuals to tow the path of entrepreneurship where and when necessary

It is important to note that Information provided during this study will be used for research purposes and to aid informed decision-making for the collaborators involved in the study. All partners hold a data protection certificate and will therefore treat data provided by respondents with anonymity and not use it for any other purposes outside the purposes stated above.

About Brighter Investment (BI): Brighter Investment has tested an investment-led funding model for higher education financing over the last five years in Ghana. The results to date show that BI students have outperformed their peers, increased their incomes and are less likely to be unemployed with their degrees. These positive first results suggest that BI’s investment model is a viable solution to improve access to higher education in Ghana. By providing financial support with income-based repayment, more brilliant but needy students in some Ghanaian universities have been supported in their University education.

For more information on Brighter Investment please visit their website www.brighterinvestment.com

For more information about the Ministry for Business Development of the Republic of Ghana please visit their website https://mobd.gov.gh/

For more information about the Association of African Universities, please visit their website www.aau.org
