TITLE: Good Assessment Practices in Higher Education – Baze University, Abuja , Nigeria

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The dawn of the twenty-first century is being recognized as a knowledge era, of which higher education plays a crucial role. For a country to succeed economically, culturally, and politically, it must have a strong postsecondary sector[1]. This has called for a tremendous increase in demand for higher education. In countries where a decade ago 10,000 students attended higher education institutions, that figure has grown many times over to become hundreds of thousands. This has led to the raising of concerns regarding the quality of education measured by teaching and learning outcomes.

In such a globalized and competitive world, students need to know not only the basic reading and arithmetic skills, but also lifelong skills that will allow them to face a world that is continually changing. They must be able to think critically, to analyze, and to make inferences. This has made assessment an integral part of teaching and learning. Teachers’ instructional and classroom assessment practices have become a means by which the education system is enhanced and defined[2].

Assessment of students’ learning is very critical because effective teaching decisions are based on the ability of teachers to understand their students and to match actions with accurate assessments. However, past research has shown that there are many problems associated with teachers’ classroom assessment practices.

These include but not limited to teachers’ lack of an adequate knowledge base regarding the basic testing and measurement concepts[3], and failure of teachers to employ and adhere to measurement guidelines they learned in measurement courses4.

An important consideration when designing a learning experience, course, or programme is to ensure assessments and instructional strategies are aligned with the intended learning outcomes. Creating an aligned design focuses instructional strategies on development of knowledge, skills, and values while providing formative feedback and preparing learners for formal assessment.

In Higher Education Institutions, assessments are indispensable part of the teaching and learning process. It is considered a key component for effective teaching and learning, as it determines whether or not the goals of education are being met. It again enables teachers to amass relevant educational information about students’ progress as well as the extent to which methods of instruction used are helping students to achieve the intended learning outcome. It also affects decisions about grades, placement, advancement, instructional needs, curriculum, and, in some cases, funding.

Assessment goes beyond the mere rating of academic tasks either qualitatively or quantitatively. Its boundary stretches beyond using it as a gauge to determine whether learning objectives are achieved or met. It simply drives and guides the entire teaching and learning process.

It also inspires us (lecturers) to evaluate ourselves by asking these hard questions: “Are we teaching what we think we are teaching?” “Are students learning what they are supposed to be learning?” “Is there a way to teach the subject better, thereby promoting better learning?” “Are our assessments linked with approaches vis a vis objective?” It helps us to frequently evaluate our approach to teaching and learning which results in improvement.

In order to enhance teaching and learning in our higher institutions, the Association of African Universities (AAU) is offering a four-day training workshop titled Good Assessment Practices in Higher Education: Aligning Outcome, Instruction and Assessment that seeks to equip teaching staff with the basic knowledge and skills in assessment to help improve teaching and learning.

The AAU believes that revitalizing the teaching profession by equipping teachers with assessment skills and knowledge will contribute to quality higher education in Africa.

2. OBJECTIVES

The aim of this workshop is to equip teaching staff in higher education with the requisite skills and knowledge they need in students’ assessment, which will yield a significant improvement in teaching and learning.

The specific objectives of the workshop are to;

Introduce participants to the various forms of assessment, its limitations and strengths as well as how they impact on teaching and learning.

Expose participants to the various feedback systems and assessment practice when used efficiently will improve teaching and learning.

Expose participants to assessment practices that either deflate or inflate students’ test scores from reflecting their actual score on an academic task.

3. EXPECTED OUTCOMES

It is expected that at the end of the workshop:

Participants will be equipped with the basic assessment knowledge and skills that will make them effective and efficient in their teaching assignments.

Participants will also acquire knowledge on efficient and alternative ways of communicating assessment feedbacks to various stakeholders (parents, students, school administrators, educationists and employers).

4. WORKSHOP MODULES

The workshop modules will include the following:

Aligning assessments with teaching approaches and outcomes

Test format

Test construction

Test administration

Test score analysis

Grading Practices

Feedback Systems

5. TARGET AUDIENCE

This workshop is meant for all staff of higher education institutions connected with students’ assessments including Professors, Associate Professors, Quality Assurance Specialists, Senior Lecturers, Lecturers, Assistant Lecturers and Teaching Assistants.

6. ORGANIZATION OF WORKSHOP

Workshop content is covered through direct lectures, case studies, demonstrations, reading, listening, thinking, problem-solving, group discussion and video presentation. Active participation is expected. Every effort will be made to teach the workshop as a seminar with substantial participation from the class. Participants, therefore, should come to class prepared to ask questions, contribute ideas, and share experiences.

DATE AND VENUE

The workshop will take place on: 31st March – 3rd April 2020 at Baze University, Abuja, Nigeria

WORKSHOP LANGUAGE

The working language of the workshop is English.

TITLE: How to Invest in Foreign Currencies

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Foreign currencies can help investors diversify assets, protect purchasing power and prepare for international expenses. However, buying dollars, pounds or euros does not guarantee profit. Exchange rates move in both directions, transaction costs reduce returns, and speculative trading can cause serious losses. Investors must therefore understand the available options, their objectives and the risks involved.

Understanding Foreign-Currency Investment
Foreign-currency investment involves converting domestic money into another currency or buying assets linked to foreign markets. Its value changes with the exchange rate. An investor who buys United States dollars may gain if the dollar strengthens against the local currency and lose if it weakens. Exposure can be direct, through holding the currency, or indirect, through international shares, bonds, funds and other regulated products.

Why People Invest in Foreign Currencies
A major reason is protection against domestic currency depreciation. When a local currency loses value, imported goods, foreign education, travel and international business become more expensive. Holding part of one’s savings in a relatively stable currency may reduce this pressure. Foreign currencies also support diversification. Keeping all wealth in one currency ties an investor to one economy, while holding assets in several currencies spreads exposure across different markets. Diversification does not remove risk, but it can reduce dependence on one country. Foreign-currency savings may also help meet future expenses abroad. A student planning to study in Britain may save in pounds, while an importer buying from the United States may hold dollars. International shares, bonds and funds can additionally provide access to companies and industries unavailable locally.

Foreign-Currency Bank Accounts
One of the simplest methods is a regulated foreign-currency savings or deposit account. Such accounts may hold dollars, pounds or euros and can support education, travel, business or family expenses abroad. Before opening one, an investor should examine interest rates, maintenance fees, minimum balances, withdrawal rules, exchange rates and transfer charges. It is also important to confirm whether the funds are covered by a deposit-protection scheme.

International Bonds and Investment Funds
International bonds may be issued by governments, development institutions or companies. Investors may receive interest and repayment at maturity. However, the issuer may experience financial difficulty, while the currency may fall against the investor’s domestic currency. A profitable bond can therefore deliver a weaker return after conversion. Foreign shares expose investors to both a company and the currency in which it trades. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds may hold shares in many international companies, spreading money across businesses, industries and countries. For many beginners, diversified funds are easier to manage than individual shares. Investors should still examine fees, geographical focus, strategy and currency risk. A foreign investment may perform well locally but produce a lower return if the currency weakens before conversion.

Currency Exchange-Traded Products
Currency exchange-traded products provide exposure to one currency or a group of currencies. Some hold foreign deposits, while others use futures, derivatives or complex arrangements. Before investing, an individual should understand what the product owns, how its value is calculated, whether it uses leverage and how closely it tracks the currency.

Direct Foreign-Exchange Trading
Direct foreign-exchange trading involves buying one currency while selling another. Traders attempt to profit by predicting which currency in a pair will strengthen. This is usually short-term speculation rather than long-term investment. Prices can move rapidly because of interest rates, inflation, elections, conflicts and economic reports. Many platforms also offer leverage, allowing traders to control positions larger than their deposits. Although leverage can increase gains, it magnifies losses, and a small unfavourable movement may erase the entire deposit. Forex trading is therefore unsuitable for people who do not understand the market or cannot afford to lose their money.

Contracts for Difference
Contracts for Difference, or CFDs, allow individuals to speculate on currency movements without owning the currencies. They are complex, leveraged products in which losses can occur quickly. Anyone seeking to preserve savings should distinguish between holding genuine foreign currency and speculating through CFDs.

Establishing a Clear Objective
Before investing, an individual should identify the purpose of the foreign-currency exposure. The goal may be to protect savings, pay foreign tuition, finance travel, support an import business or diversify a long-term portfolio. Different objectives require different approaches. Someone saving for university fees may prefer a foreign-currency account, while a long-term investor may consider diversified international funds. A person seeking short-term profits is accepting much greater risk. A clear objective helps investors avoid products chosen only because they appear popular or promise unusually high returns.

Building Financial Security First
Foreign-currency investment should not replace emergency savings. Money needed for rent, food, healthcare, school fees, debt repayment and other essential expenses should remain easily accessible in the currency used for daily living. Only money that will not be needed immediately should be exposed to exchange-rate movements. Otherwise, an investor may be forced to convert the foreign currency at an unfavourable rate during an emergency.

Using a Regulated Provider
Investors should use banks, brokers and platforms authorised by the appropriate regulator. Regulation does not guarantee profits, but it provides greater accountability and consumer protection. The company’s legal name, address, registration details and licence should be confirmed through the regulator’s official records. Unregulated platforms may refuse withdrawals, manipulate balances or disappear after receiving investors’ money. Caution is essential when dealing with unfamiliar online operators.

Understanding Costs and Investing Gradually
Foreign-currency investment often involves charges that reduce returns. Banks may offer different buying and selling rates, creating an immediate cost. Other expenses may include account fees, transfer charges, commissions, fund management fees, withdrawal costs, taxes and overnight financing charges.
An investment should not be judged only by the expected currency movement. The investor must determine whether the possible return is enough to cover all costs. Investing gradually can reduce the risk of converting a large amount at an unfavourable rate. Instead of buying in one transaction, an investor may divide the amount into smaller purchases over several weeks or months. This does not guarantee profit, but it reduces the pressure of trying to identify the perfect rate.

Developing an Exit Plan
Every investor should decide how and when the investment will be used, reviewed or converted. The decision may be linked to a specific goal, target exchange rate or fixed investment period. Without an exit plan, an investor may continue holding a falling currency in the hope that it will recover. Regular reviews help determine whether the original purpose remains valid and whether the investment still suits the investor’s circumstances.

Major Risks
Exchange-rate risk is the possibility that the foreign currency will lose value against the domestic currency. Inflation, interest rates, political stability, government borrowing and trade performance can all affect currency values. No currency rises continuously, including those considered strong. Inflation risk also matters. Holding foreign cash does not automatically create wealth. If the money earns little interest, inflation in the foreign country may reduce its purchasing power. Long-term investors may therefore prefer assets capable of producing income or growth rather than holding only cash. Political and regulatory decisions can affect access to foreign-currency investments. Governments may introduce capital controls, taxes, transfer restrictions or limits on withdrawals. Foreign investors may also receive different legal protection from local investors. Liquidity risk arises when an investment cannot be converted into cash quickly without accepting a lower price. Major currencies are generally easier to trade than less widely used currencies, but some foreign bonds and funds may be difficult to exit. Leverage presents one of the greatest dangers. It allows traders to control positions larger than their deposits, meaning a minor market movement can create a significant loss or eliminate the entire account balance.

Avoiding Foreign-Currency Fraud
Foreign-currency scams often promise guaranteed profits, daily income, automated trading success or high returns without risk. Some promoters claim to use secret strategies, artificial intelligence or professional traders who never lose. No legitimate investment can guarantee continuous high returns. Investors should be suspicious of pressure to invest immediately, requests to send money to personal accounts or cryptocurrency wallets, and operators who discourage independent research. Another warning sign is a platform that accepts deposits easily but prevents withdrawals. Investors should not pay additional charges simply because an unregulated operator claims that taxes, verification fees or account upgrades are required before money can be released.

Conclusion
Foreign currencies can support financial planning by helping people prepare for international expenses, diversify investments and reduce exposure to domestic currency depreciation. However, currency values can fall, fees can reduce returns and speculative trading can destroy capital. A responsible investor should establish a clear objective, build emergency savings, use regulated institutions, understand all costs and avoid risking money needed for essential expenses. For most beginners, foreign-currency accounts and diversified international funds may be more suitable than leveraged forex trading. Foreign currencies should be treated as one part of a broader financial strategy rather than a shortcut to wealth. Successful investing requires research, patience, diversification and realistic expectations. Anyone uncertain about the financial, legal or tax implications should seek qualified professional advice before investing.

For the Spring 2027 cycle, applications must be submitted by September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

The spring and fall OSTEM internships generally run for approximately 15 weeks, while summer internships generally last around 10 weeks.

What Do NASA OSTEM Interns Do?

NASA OSTEM interns work on projects that contribute to the agency’s mission.

Depending on the specific internship, responsibilities can vary considerably. NASA offers opportunities across a broad range of academic and professional disciplines.

Interns may have the opportunity to:

Work on real NASA projects

Conduct research and analysis

Support scientific or engineering activities

Develop technical solutions

Analyze data

Assist with communications and outreach

Contribute to technology development

Work with NASA scientists, engineers, researchers, and other professionals

Develop professional and workplace skills

Gain practical experience related to their academic field

Participate in a professional NASA work environment

Importantly, NASA states that its internship opportunities are not limited exclusively to STEM majors. NASA also offers opportunities for students from non-STEM disciplines, depending on the available projects and NASA’s workforce needs.

This means students should not automatically assume that they are ineligible simply because their degree is not in engineering, physics, computer science, or another traditional STEM discipline.

Key Benefits of a NASA OSTEM Internship

A NASA internship can provide several important benefits for students seeking to build their academic and professional careers.

1. Gain Hands-On Professional Experience

One of the major advantages of the OSTEM program is the opportunity to move beyond classroom learning.

Interns can work on projects and activities that provide practical experience and help them understand how their academic knowledge can be applied in a professional environment.

2. Work on Real NASA Projects

OSTEM internships are designed around actual NASA projects rather than purely theoretical assignments.

Students can contribute to work related to NASA’s broader mission in areas such as science, technology, aeronautics, and space exploration.

3. Learn From NASA Professionals

Interns have the opportunity to work with NASA experts and mentors.

This can expose students to professional approaches to:

Research

Problem-solving

Project management

Technical work

Communication

Collaboration

Innovation

4. Strengthen Your Resume

Having hands-on experience with NASA can be a valuable addition to a student’s academic and professional profile.

The experience can demonstrate exposure to:

Professional project environments

Research or technical work

Team collaboration

Problem-solving

Innovation

Mission-oriented work

Students can subsequently use the experience when applying for graduate programmes, scholarships, research opportunities, jobs, and other internships.

5. Develop Technical and Professional Skills

NASA describes OSTEM internships as opportunities to build both technical skills and career readiness.

Depending on the project, students may develop skills related to their discipline while also strengthening transferable skills such as communication, teamwork, organization, critical thinking, and professional problem-solving.

6. Explore Careers at NASA

An OSTEM internship can also help students understand what it is like to work within NASA and explore potential career paths.

For students interested in eventually pursuing careers in aerospace, science, engineering, research, technology, communications, administration, or other NASA-related fields, an internship can provide useful exposure to the organization.

Who Can Apply for the NASA OSTEM Internship?

NASA’s current eligibility requirements specify that OSTEM candidates must meet several requirements.

Applicants must:

Be a U.S. citizen

Be at least 16 years old at the time of application

Have a minimum 3.0 cumulative GPA on a 4.0 scale

Be a full-time or part-time college student, from undergraduate through graduate level

Be enrolled in a degree-granting programme at a U.S. Department of Education-accredited college or university

Be studying in a course of study aligned with NASA’s needs

NASA also indicates that educators who are enrolled as students can be eligible to apply.

Students who have recently graduated may also be eligible for internships taking place during the three internship sessions immediately following their graduation, subject to NASA’s eligibility requirements.

Do You Need to Study a STEM Subject?

Not necessarily.

The name “Office of STEM Engagement” might lead some applicants to believe that only STEM students can apply. However, NASA explicitly states that it offers internships for non-STEM majors as well.

The key consideration is whether the applicant’s academic programme and qualifications align with the requirements of the particular internship opportunity.

Therefore, students from fields outside traditional STEM disciplines should review the individual project descriptions rather than automatically ruling themselves out.

How Long Is the NASA OSTEM Internship?

The length of the internship depends on the session.

NASA’s current programme information indicates:

Spring: approximately 15 weeks

Summer: approximately 10 weeks

Fall: approximately 15 weeks

The exact dates and working arrangements can vary according to the specific internship project.

Is the NASA OSTEM Internship Paid?

Yes.

NASA describes OSTEM internships as paid internships.

This makes the opportunity particularly attractive to students who want to gain high-level professional experience while receiving financial compensation during the internship.

Applicants should review the specific opportunity listing for the details applicable to the position they are applying for.

Is the NASA Internship Available to International Students?

This is an important point for international applicants.

For the standard NASA OSTEM Internship Program, NASA’s current eligibility requirements state that applicants must be U.S. citizens.

Therefore, students living in countries such as Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa, India, the United Kingdom, Canada, or other countries generally cannot apply for the standard Spring 2027 OSTEM internship solely on the basis of being international students.

NASA previously operated international internship arrangements through its International Internship (I²) programme. However, NASA’s current international internship page states that the International Internship (I²) programme is not being offered at this time.

Students who are not U.S. citizens should therefore carefully distinguish the standard OSTEM programme from any separate NASA international opportunities that may become available in the future.

Important Citizenship Requirement

The citizenship requirement is particularly important because some online posts about NASA internships may make the opportunity appear open to students worldwide.

For the current OSTEM programme, NASA explicitly states:

U.S. citizenship is required.

International students should not assume that studying at a U.S. university automatically makes them eligible for OSTEM. The official eligibility requirement is U.S. citizenship.

What Academic Level Is Eligible?

NASA’s OSTEM programme is intended for students at multiple levels of higher education.

Eligible students can include:

Undergraduate students

Graduate students

Other college-level students who meet NASA’s requirements

The programme requires applicants to be enrolled in an eligible degree-granting programme at a U.S.-accredited institution.

The minimum age is 16 years old at the time of application.

GPA Requirement

Applicants must have a minimum cumulative GPA of:

3.0 out of 4.0

This is an important eligibility requirement and should be checked before submitting an application.

Applicants should also review the requirements listed on each individual internship opportunity because individual projects may have additional qualifications or preferences.

Application Deadline for NASA Spring 2027 Internships

The most important date for students interested in this opportunity is:

September 14, 2026

The official NASA internship page specifies that applications for the Spring 2027 OSTEM session close at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on September 14, 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their applications.

Technical problems, incomplete information, missing documents, or last-minute application issues can create unnecessary risks.

How to Apply for the NASA Spring 2027 OSTEM Internship

Applicants should begin by reviewing the available NASA OSTEM internship opportunities and identifying projects that match their academic background, interests, skills, and career goals.

The general process is:

Step 1: Review the Available Opportunities

Look through the NASA OSTEM internship listings and identify projects that match your interests and qualifications.

Step 2: Check the Eligibility Requirements

Before spending significant time on an application, confirm that you meet the basic requirements, including:

U.S. citizenship

Minimum age

GPA

Student status

Educational institution requirements

Academic field requirements

Step 3: Identify the Best-Fit Projects

Do not simply apply randomly.

Review the project description and consider:

What skills are requested?

What academic background is preferred?

What responsibilities are involved?

Step 4: Prepare Your Application

Make sure your application accurately communicates your:

Academic background

Relevant experience

Skills

Research interests

Career objectives

Relevant projects

Leadership or extracurricular activities

Step 5: Submit Before the Deadline

Applications for Spring 2027 must be submitted by:

September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to complete and review their application before the deadline.

A Note for International Applicants

International students should pay particular attention to the citizenship requirement before investing time in an OSTEM application.

The current NASA OSTEM requirements state that candidates must be U.S. citizens.

NASA’s International Internship programme page also currently states that the International Internship (I²) programme is not being offered at this time.

NASA does, however, encourage international students to explore certain NASA student challenges and citizen science projects.

Therefore, international students should monitor NASA’s official pages for other opportunities rather than assuming that the Spring 2027 OSTEM programme is open internationally.

Conclusion

The NASA Spring 2027 OSTEM Internship Program provides eligible students with an opportunity to gain paid, hands-on experience while contributing to projects connected to NASA’s mission.

The programme is designed for students at different stages of higher education and can accommodate a broad range of academic disciplines, including some non-STEM fields. Interns can develop technical and professional skills, gain practical workplace experience, work with NASA professionals, and strengthen their career readiness.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. The current OSTEM programme requires applicants to be U.S. citizens, at least 16 years old, enrolled in an eligible programme at a U.S.-accredited institution, and have a minimum 3.0 GPA.

TITLE: 2026 AFD CSO Call for Expressions of Project Intentions: Funding Opportunity for Civil Society Organizations in Developing Countries

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Agence Française de Développement (AFD) has opened the 2026 Call for Expressions of Project Intentions for Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), providing an opportunity for eligible civil society organizations to submit projects for potential AFD co-financing in 2027.

The call is designed to strengthen the contribution of civil society organizations to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), international solidarity, local development and policy change. For the 2026 edition, AFD has introduced a single call covering both French CSOs and locally governed CSOs, with the objective of identifying projects led by civil society organizations in partner countries that could receive financing in 2027.

The call is particularly relevant for eligible CSOs working on development, social transformation, international solidarity, climate vulnerability, civic engagement and other areas aligned with sustainable development priorities.

Applications must be submitted through AFD’s OSCar online platform, and organizations that do not already have an OSCar account must request account creation by September 15, 2026.

The final deadline for submitting project intentions is October 9, 2026, at 6:00 PM Paris time.

Overview of the 2026 AFD CSO Call

The 2026 CSO Call for Expressions of Project Intentions is part of AFD’s CSO Initiatives mechanism, which supports projects led by civil society organizations.

The mechanism recognizes the role of civil society in identifying development challenges and designing initiatives that respond to the needs of communities. Rather than limiting CSOs to projects defined by external institutions, AFD’s framework recognizes the right of initiative, allowing eligible organizations to propose projects that they have developed themselves.

For the 2026 call, AFD is seeking project intentions that can potentially be shortlisted for financing in 2027.

The initiative aims to achieve two closely connected objectives:

Strengthen civil society organizations in France and AFD intervention countries.

Generate concrete development impacts for beneficiary populations while contributing to local policy and sustainable development.

What Is the AFD CSO Initiatives Mechanism?

The CSO Initiatives (CSO-I) mechanism is an AFD financing mechanism for projects led by French and locally governed civil society organizations.

It is designed to support the capacity and effectiveness of civil society actors while enabling them to implement initiatives that contribute to development and international solidarity.

Through this mechanism, AFD can support CSOs that are working to address development challenges and create meaningful, measurable benefits for communities.

The mechanism is therefore particularly relevant to organizations that already have the institutional capacity, project experience and development-oriented mission needed to implement a substantial initiative.

Objectives of the 2026 Call

The 2026 call operates within France’s broader development and international solidarity framework.

It falls under France’s 2021 Framework and Programming Act on Development and International Solidarity, adopted on August 4, 2021. It also aligns with France’s Strategy for Civil Society and Civic Engagement for 2023–2027, the conclusions of the Presidential Council for International Partnerships from April 2025, and AFD Group’s 2025–2030 Strategy.

The call consequently forms part of a wider effort to strengthen civil society participation in sustainable development and international cooperation.

Key objectives include:

Supporting the role of civil society organizations in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

Strengthening the institutional and operational capacity of CSOs.

Supporting initiatives developed by civil society organizations themselves.

Generating concrete benefits for communities and beneficiary populations.

Contributing to local policy development.

Supporting international solidarity and sustainable development.

Increasing the participation of locally governed CSOs in development financing.

Who Can Apply for the AFD CSO Call?

The call is open to eligible civil society organizations, rather than individual applicants.

Two broad categories of CSOs are relevant:

1. French Civil Society Organizations

French CSOs are eligible under the CSO Initiatives mechanism and can submit project intentions in accordance with the requirements of the call.

2. Locally Governed Civil Society Organizations

Locally governed CSOs in countries eligible for Official Development Assistance (ODA) can also be eligible for direct AFD financing under specific conditions.

This represents an important feature of the 2026 call because locally governed organizations are not automatically excluded from AFD financing simply because they are based outside France.

Eligibility Requirements for Locally Governed CSOs

According to the call, locally governed CSOs, including unions, are eligible provided that they have previously received financing at least once for a completed project from an eligible AFD Group entity or through certain qualifying mechanisms.

Previous financing may have been received:

Directly from the CSO-I mechanism.

Through AFD’s Operations Directorate.

From Expertise France.

From Proparco.

From the French Facility for Global Environment (FFEM).

From the Fund for Innovation in Development (FID).

Through an FSOF intermediary funding mechanism.

From a French embassy, where the annual financing received was more than €100,000.

The previous financing may have been received either directly by the locally governed CSO or through a lead CSO, provided the project has been completed.

The eligibility requirement applies regardless of the amount of qualifying AFD Group financing received.

This means that organizations should carefully review their previous institutional funding history before beginning the application process.

Which Countries Are Eligible?

The geographical scope of the 2026 AFD CSO call is broad.

Countries eligible for the opportunity are countries included on the OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) list of ODA recipients.

This means that eligibility is not restricted to one particular African subregion or a small group of countries.

However, the call gives priority to Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change.

Organizations operating in eligible developing countries should therefore examine how their proposed project responds to development needs, climate vulnerability and other strategic priorities.

Projects in France

Projects located in France may also be eligible, but under specific programmes:

Global Citizenship and International Solidarity Education (ECSI).

Civil Society Capacity Building (SMA).

Organizations proposing projects in France should therefore determine whether their project fits within one of these eligible programmes.

What Types of Projects May Be Relevant?

The call is intended for projects that contribute to sustainable development, international solidarity, civil society strengthening and concrete benefits for communities.

While the supplied call information does not provide a simple list of every eligible thematic sector, applicants should ensure that their proposed initiative clearly connects with the objectives of the CSO Initiatives mechanism and the broader development priorities reflected in the call.

Projects are particularly relevant when they:

Address clearly identified development challenges.

Respond to the needs of beneficiary populations.

Demonstrate potential for concrete and measurable impact.

Strengthen civil society participation.

Contribute to local policy or institutional development.

Support sustainable development objectives.

Address challenges affecting vulnerable populations.

Respond to climate vulnerability where relevant.

Demonstrate a strong understanding of the local context.

Are designed and led by civil society organizations with appropriate institutional capacity.

Important Funding Consideration

The 2026 call is a project financing and co-financing opportunity for eligible CSOs.

However, the information supplied for this call does not state one universal maximum grant amount that every successful applicant can receive.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the programme offers a fixed amount of funding to every organization.

Instead, organizations should consult the official call documentation and methodological guide to understand the specific financing arrangements, co-financing requirements and financial conditions applicable to their proposed project.

How the Application Process Works

The application process is conducted through OSCar, AFD’s online platform dedicated to the submission of documents relating to the CSO Initiatives mechanism.

Project intentions submitted outside the OSCar platform will not be considered.

This makes it important for applicants to begin the administrative process early rather than waiting until the final deadline.

Step 1: Confirm organizational eligibility

Before preparing the project intention, the organization should determine whether it qualifies under the call.

Locally governed CSOs should pay particular attention to the requirement concerning previous qualifying financing and completed projects.

Step 2: Review the official call documentation

Applicants should carefully read the official call document and methodological guidance.

These documents provide important information about the procedures and requirements for preparing and submitting project intentions.

Step 3: Prepare an OSCar account

CSOs need a user account to access and use OSCar.

An authorization to use the platform is required when creating the account.

Organizations that already have an OSCar account should ensure that their account remains accessible and that the relevant users have the necessary permissions.

Step 4: Request an account if you do not already have one

Organizations that do not yet have an OSCar account must submit a request to create their account no later than September 15, 2026.

This is an important administrative deadline because it occurs before the final project submission deadline.

Organizations should not interpret October 9 as the only date they need to worry about.

Step 5: Prepare the project intention and administrative documents

Applicants should prepare the required project intention documentation and supporting administrative documents in accordance with the official templates and guidelines.

For locally governed CSOs, AFD provides a specific Project Intention Sheet.

Step 6: Submit through OSCar

The completed project intention and required administrative documents must be submitted directly through OSCar.

Only submissions made through the designated platform will be considered.

Important Application Deadlines

There are two important dates to remember for this call.

September 15, 2026 — OSCar Account Request Deadline

CSOs that do not already have an OSCar account must submit their account creation request by:

September 15, 2026

Organizations should therefore start the registration process well before this date.

October 9, 2026 — Final Project Submission Deadline

The final deadline for submitting project intentions is:

October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time

Applications must be submitted through OSCar before the deadline.

Waiting until the final hours could create unnecessary risks, particularly if organizations encounter account, document or technical issues.

Documents and Resources Available to Applicants

AFD has provided several resources to help CSOs understand and complete the application process.

1. 2026 Call for Expressions of Project Intentions

The official call document explains the framework and requirements for the 2026 CSO financing initiative.

2. Project Intention Sheet for Locally Governed CSOs

Locally governed CSOs can access the relevant project intention template provided by AFD.

3. Methodological Guide

AFD provides a methodological guide explaining the procedures for co-financing projects submitted by French and locally governed CSOs.

This guide can help organizations understand the recommended approach to preparing their project intention.

4. Authorization for Use of OSCar

Organizations creating an OSCar account need the relevant authorization document.

5. OSCar User Guide

AFD also provides a user guide explaining how CSOs can use the OSCar platform and follow the recommended submission procedures.

Applicants should make use of these resources before submitting their applications.

Why the Opportunity Matters for Civil Society Organizations

The AFD CSO call is significant because civil society organizations often have close relationships with communities and can identify challenges that may not always be visible through traditional institutional structures.

By recognizing the right of initiative, the mechanism gives eligible organizations an opportunity to propose projects based on their own understanding of development needs.

The call can therefore be particularly valuable for CSOs that have:

A strong record of community engagement.

Experience implementing development projects.

Established relationships with local communities.

Institutional experience with donor-funded projects.

Evidence of previous project results.

Capacity to manage project finances and reporting.

A clear development or international solidarity mission.

A project concept aligned with sustainable development priorities.

How to Prepare a Strong Project Intention

A competitive project intention should do more than describe a good idea.

The organization should demonstrate why the project is necessary, who will benefit, what will be achieved and why the organization is capable of delivering the proposed results.

1. Clearly define the problem

Begin by identifying the development challenge the project intends to address.

Explain:

What the problem is.

Who is affected.

Where it occurs.

Why it matters.

What evidence demonstrates the need for intervention.

2. Identify the beneficiaries

Clearly describe the populations that will benefit from the proposed project.

Where possible, explain the characteristics of the target population and why they require support.

3. Demonstrate local relevance

A strong project should be grounded in the realities of the country or community where it will be implemented.

Applicants should demonstrate that the organization understands the local context and has meaningful relationships with the communities involved.

4. Explain the proposed solution

Describe how the project will respond to the identified problem.

The proposed activities should logically connect to the expected results.

5. Demonstrate organizational capacity

Applicants should show why their organization is capable of implementing the proposed initiative.

Relevant evidence can include:

Previous projects.

Organizational experience.

Staff expertise.

Partnerships.

Previous donor funding.

Community relationships.

Previous project results.

6. Connect the project to sustainable development

Applicants should demonstrate how the proposed project contributes to relevant Sustainable Development Goals and broader development priorities.

7. Consider climate vulnerability

Because the call gives priority to countries particularly vulnerable to climate change, organizations in such contexts should clearly explain relevant climate-related challenges where appropriate.

8. Focus on measurable impact

Avoid presenting only activities.

Explain the expected changes resulting from the project and how those changes will benefit communities.

Key Advantages of the 2026 AFD CSO Call

The opportunity offers several important advantages for eligible civil society organizations.

Access to Potential Project Financing

Selected projects may be considered for AFD financing in 2027, giving eligible organizations an opportunity to secure support for development initiatives.

Support for Civil Society

The CSO Initiatives mechanism is specifically designed to strengthen civil society stakeholders and their ability to contribute to development.

Opportunity for Locally Governed Organizations

Eligible locally governed CSOs can potentially access AFD financing under the conditions established by the call.

Alignment with Global Development Goals

The mechanism is explicitly connected to the Sustainable Development Goals and international solidarity.

Potential Policy Impact

The initiative is also intended to contribute to local policy, meaning that well-designed projects can potentially influence wider systems and development approaches beyond individual beneficiaries.

Important Things Applicants Should Know

There are several details that applicants should not overlook.

This is not an individual scholarship or fellowship

The opportunity is intended for civil society organizations, not individual students, researchers or job seekers.

Individuals cannot apply in their personal capacity unless they are applying on behalf of an eligible organization in accordance with the call requirements.

Previous financing matters for locally governed CSOs

Locally governed organizations should carefully examine the previous-financing requirement before investing substantial time in preparing a submission.

The OSCar account deadline comes first

Organizations without an existing OSCar account must request one by September 15, 2026.

The final deadline is October 9, 2026

The complete project intention must be submitted by October 9, 2026 at 6:00 PM Paris time.

External submissions are not considered

Project intentions must be submitted through OSCar. Sending the project through another channel does not satisfy the application requirement.

Official Application Platform

Eligible organizations should submit their project intention through the official OSCar platform.

Access the OSCar application platform

Organizations that need to create an account should begin the process as early as possible and observe the September 15, 2026 account-request deadline.

For additional guidance, applicants can consult the official AFD call documentation and methodological resources.

View the official AFD 2026 CSO Call

Contact and Further Assistance

Organizations requiring assistance with the OSCar platform can use the official OSCar contact channel provided by AFD.

Contact the OSCar team

Applicants should also consult the official documentation before contacting the support team, as many procedural questions are addressed in the available guides.

TITLE: UNICEF Club Registration 2026–2027: How to Start or Renew a UNICEF USA Club and Take Action for Children

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The UNICEF USA Club Registration for the 2026–2027 school year is now open for students and schools interested in taking action for children in the United States and around the world.

The initiative provides an opportunity for students to establish or continue a UNICEF Club and participate in activities that support child rights, awareness, advocacy, fundraising, and UNICEF’s broader mission for children.

Both new and returning UNICEF Clubs are required to complete the official registration process in order to be recognized as active UNICEF Clubs for the 2026–2027 school year.

What Is the UNICEF USA Club Registration?

The UNICEF USA Club Registration is the official process through which schools and student groups register a UNICEF Club for the upcoming academic year.

UNICEF USA works with communities and young people to build awareness and support for children’s rights. Through UNICEF Clubs, students can organize activities and campaigns that help raise awareness about issues affecting children and encourage their peers and communities to become involved.

For the 2026–2027 school year, UNICEF USA is inviting both newly established and returning clubs to complete the registration form.

Registration is important because a club must be approved by the UNICEF USA team before it can become an active UNICEF Club.

Who Should Consider Registering?

The registration opportunity is particularly relevant to:

Students interested in children’s rights and global development.

Students who want to organize a UNICEF Club at their school.

Existing UNICEF Clubs returning for the 2026–2027 school year.

Student leaders interested in advocacy and community engagement.

School communities interested in supporting UNICEF’s mission.

Individuals who want to raise awareness about challenges facing children around the world.

Students who want practical experience in leadership, organization, communication, teamwork, advocacy, and community activities.

Whether you are establishing a UNICEF Club for the first time or continuing an existing club, UNICEF USA states that both new and returning clubs must complete the registration form.

What Can a UNICEF Club Do?

A UNICEF Club can provide students with a structured platform to become involved in issues affecting children.

Depending on the activities organized by a particular club, students may have opportunities to:

Raise awareness about children’s rights.

Educate fellow students about challenges affecting children.

Organize school or community activities.

Support UNICEF-related campaigns.

Encourage advocacy for children.

Participate in fundraising or awareness initiatives.

Develop leadership and organizational skills.

Work collaboratively with other students and an advisor.

Engage their school community around issues affecting children.

Connect local student action with UNICEF’s work for children around the world.

The club structure can therefore be particularly valuable for students who want to combine education, leadership and community involvement.

Requirements Before Starting the Registration

One of the most important things prospective applicants should know is that the registration form requires information about the club’s leadership and advisor.

UNICEF USA requires the contact information of:

Four club leaders

One club advisor

Applicants should therefore collect all necessary contact information before starting the registration form.

This is especially important because UNICEF USA states that there is no save-and-return option on the registration form.

In other words, applicants should make sure they have the required information available before beginning the application.

Information You Should Prepare

Before accessing the registration form, prospective clubs should have the details of their four club leaders and one advisor ready.

It is advisable to verify the information carefully before submitting the form to avoid unnecessary delays or mistakes.

Applicants should also make sure that everyone involved understands their role within the club and is prepared to provide accurate contact information.

UNICEF Club Registration Process

The UNICEF USA registration page contains a multi-stage webform. The registration process is organized into several sections.

According to the registration page, applicants will move through the following stages:

1. Find Your School or Organization

The first stage involves identifying the school or organization associated with the UNICEF Club.

Applicants should provide the requested information so UNICEF USA can associate the club with the appropriate educational institution or organization.

2. Get Started

After identifying the school or organization, applicants proceed to the next stage of the registration process.

This section begins the formal club registration questionnaire.

3. Questionnaire

Applicants will complete the questionnaire provided as part of the UNICEF Club registration process.

It is important to read each question carefully and provide accurate information.

4. Advisor Information

The registration process requires information about the club’s advisor.

As noted by UNICEF USA, each club must provide information for one advisor.

Prospective clubs should therefore have their advisor’s required information available before starting.

5. Enter Your Leader Information

This section requires information about the club’s student leaders.

UNICEF USA requires contact information for four club leaders.

Clubs should therefore select their leadership team and collect the required information before beginning the registration form.

6. Back-2-School Kit

The webform also includes a section relating to the Back-2-School Kit (B2SK).

This forms part of the UNICEF Club registration process for the 2026–2027 school year.

7. Confirm and Submit

After completing the required sections, applicants will reach the confirmation and submission stage.

Before submitting, clubs should carefully review the information entered to ensure that it is accurate and complete.

8. Complete

Once the registration process has been successfully submitted, the application enters the UNICEF USA review process.

Applicants should retain any confirmation information provided after submission.

What Happens After You Register?

Submitting the registration form does not mean that the club is immediately approved.

UNICEF USA states that registrations are reviewed by its team.

Once the registration has been approved, the club will receive an approval email within 7–10 business days.

The approval email will include links to helpful resources that can assist the club with its activities.

This means prospective club leaders should monitor the email address provided during registration after submitting their application.

Opportunity to Win UNICEF USA Merchandise

An additional benefit mentioned on the registration page is the opportunity for registered clubs to start winning UNICEF USA merchandise.

This provides an added incentive for clubs to remain engaged and active after completing the registration process.

Students should therefore not view registration simply as an administrative requirement. It can be the starting point for an ongoing school-based effort supporting UNICEF’s mission.

Important Registration Tips

Applicants should pay close attention to UNICEF USA’s instructions when completing the form.

Prepare all information first

Because there is no save-and-return option, do not begin the form until you have collected the required information for:

Four club leaders

One advisor

Your school or organization

Use the form’s Previous button

If you need to return to an earlier section, UNICEF USA specifically advises applicants to use the “previous” button within the form rather than the browser’s back arrow.

This is an important technical instruction because using the browser’s back button could potentially interfere with the form.

Double-check contact information

Make sure names, email addresses, telephone numbers and other requested details are entered correctly.

Incorrect contact information could make it difficult for UNICEF USA to communicate with club leaders or the advisor.

Monitor your email

After submitting the registration, watch the relevant email account for the approval notification.

UNICEF USA indicates that approval emails are expected within 7–10 business days.

Keep your leadership team informed

Since four club leaders and one advisor are required, it is helpful to ensure everyone involved knows that their information is being submitted as part of the official UNICEF Club registration.

Is There a Registration Deadline?

The information provided on the UNICEF USA registration page does not specify a fixed calendar deadline for the 2026–2027 UNICEF Club Registration.

The page simply invites eligible clubs to register for the 2026–2027 school year.

Therefore, applicants should not assume that there is a particular deadline unless UNICEF USA subsequently announces one.

For the most accurate and current registration information, applicants should check the official UNICEF USA registration page before submitting their application.

Registration period: For the 2026–2027 school year; no specific closing date is stated on the provided registration page.

Support and Questions

Applicants who experience problems while completing the registration or have questions about UNICEF Clubs can contact UNICEF USA.

The registration page provides the following email address for assistance:

volunteer@unicefusa.org

This contact is intended for registration issues and other UNICEF Club-related questions.

SMS Notifications

The UNICEF USA website also provides an option for supporters to receive SMS notifications concerning UNICEF’s humanitarian relief efforts during emergencies.

According to the website, individuals who provide their mobile number agree to receive SMS notifications from UNICEF USA.

Message frequency can vary, and standard message and data rates may apply. Users can reply STOP to cancel or HELP for assistance.

The website also provides links to its terms and privacy information relating to SMS notifications.

Why This Opportunity Can Be Valuable for Students

Joining or establishing a UNICEF Club can provide more than simply participation in a school organization.

Students can potentially develop practical skills that are valuable for academic, professional and community leadership.

Leadership experience

Running a student organization requires students to coordinate activities, work with other people and take responsibility for projects.

Communication skills

Club activities can help students practice public speaking, written communication, awareness campaigns and communicating important issues to their peers.

Teamwork

A UNICEF Club requires collaboration between student leaders, members and an advisor.

Project and event organization

Organizing awareness campaigns, school activities and other initiatives can expose students to practical planning and coordination.

Advocacy experience

Students interested in children’s rights, international development and social impact can gain experience communicating important causes and encouraging others to take action.

Community engagement

UNICEF Clubs can give students a platform to connect issues affecting children globally with their own school and local communities.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is intended for school-based UNICEF Clubs in the United States, including both new and returning clubs, for the 2026–2027 school year.

The registration information specifically refers to UNICEF Clubs in the USA and requires a school or organization, four club leaders and one advisor.

Therefore, this is not presented as an open global scholarship, fellowship, internship or individual funding opportunity.

Students outside the United States should carefully review the official UNICEF USA requirements before assuming that they can establish a UNICEF USA Club through this registration system.

Geographic Eligibility

Primary geographic scope: United States of America.

The provided registration information is specifically for UNICEF Clubs in the USA.

It does not state that individuals from every country or continent can independently register a UNICEF USA Club through this form.

Applicants outside the United States should contact UNICEF USA directly if they are unsure whether their school or organization qualifies.

Race, Nationality and Equal Participation

The registration information provided does not specify a race, ethnicity or racial restriction.

It also does not identify a particular nationality or ethnic group as the exclusive beneficiary.

The key eligibility distinction described on the page is the club’s connection to a school or organization in the United States, together with the required leadership and advisor information.

Applicants should therefore focus on meeting the stated organizational requirements rather than assuming that the opportunity is restricted to a particular race or ethnicity.

Category of People Who Qualify

The opportunity is primarily relevant to:

Students in the United States who want to establish a UNICEF Club.

Existing student UNICEF Clubs continuing into the 2026–2027 school year.

Four designated student club leaders.

A designated school or organization advisor.

Schools and student organizations interested in children’s rights and UNICEF-related action.

The provided page does not state a specific minimum age, academic grade, GPA requirement, academic qualification or field of study.

How to Register

Interested applicants should complete the official UNICEF USA Club Registration form HERE for the 2026–2027 school year.

Visit the official website HERE

Before beginning, make sure you have the required information for four club leaders and one advisor.

Applicants should also remember that the form does not offer a save-and-return option.

Visit the OFY Website HERE for more social clubs

Conclusion

The UNICEF USA Club Registration for 2026–2027 provides students and school communities in the United States with an opportunity to organize around children’s rights and take meaningful action for children.

Both new and returning clubs must complete the registration process to become active UNICEF Clubs for the new school year. Clubs should prepare the contact information of four club leaders and one advisor before beginning because the registration form does not provide a save-and-return option.

After submission, UNICEF USA states that approved clubs will receive an email within 7–10 business days, along with helpful resources and opportunities to participate in UNICEF USA activities and potentially win UNICEF USA merchandise.

Students interested in leadership, advocacy, children’s rights, community engagement and international development may find the UNICEF Club structure particularly valuable. Anyone considering registration should carefully review the official requirements and submit accurate information through the UNICEF USA registration page.

Important: The provided registration page does not state a fixed application deadline, so prospective clubs should check the official page for any subsequent deadline or registration updates.

TITLE: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at Arizona State University 2027-2028 (Fully-funded)

Applications for the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at Arizona State University 2027-2028 are now open. The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program, in partnership with Arizona State University, is offering 30 graduate study opportunities for students admitted for the 2027–2028 academic year to pursue select master’s degree programs focused on technology and innovation.

The scholarship supports a traditional, in-person, two-year graduate degree experience at ASU’s Tempe campus in Arizona, United States. The scholarship covers full tuition, on-campus housing, healthcare coverage, and comprehensive support throughout the graduate program.

In addition to financial support, Mastercard Foundation Scholars participate in leadership development, mentorship, community engagement, professional development, and other enrichment opportunities. Full tuition, required books, and student fees

Applicants must be between the ages of 18 and 33 on or before the application deadline.

Applicants must demonstrate a record of leadership, service, and a commitment to creating positive change in their communities.

Applicants must not have previously enrolled in or completed a graduate or master’s degree program.

TITLE: European Science Foundation Appoints Dr. Angelika Kalt as New President

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
ESF News | News

Strasbourg, France – The General Assembly of the European Science Foundation (ESF) has appointed Dr. Angelika Kalt as its next President, succeeding Professor Véronique Halloin after two terms in office (July 2020 – July 2026). Dr. Kalt took office on Thursday, 2 July 2026, following an independent selection process led by a three-member Search Committee and unanimously endorsed by the ESF Executive Board.

A Strong Legacy Under Professor Véronique Halloin

Under Professor Halloin, Secretary General of the Fonds de la Recherche Scientifique (FNRS, Belgium), ESF’s budget more than tripled from €4.4 million to €15 million and its staff grew from 32 to 53. Her tenure also included ESF’s 50th anniversary in June 2024 and the adoption of the ESF Strategy 2023-2028, cementing the organisation’s role as a premier independent partner for research evaluation, programme management, and scientific cooperation.

Reflecting on her tenure, Professor Halloin said:

“It has been an honour to serve as President of the European Science Foundation over the past six years. Together with our members, partners, and dedicated team, we have significantly strengthened ESF’s role in the European research ecosystem. I am confident that under Dr. Kalt’s leadership, ESF will continue to innovate and expand its impact in support of excellent science.”

Incoming President: Dr. Angelika Kalt

Dr. Kalt was a professor of petrology and geodynamics before joining the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) in 2008 as Deputy Director, becoming Director in 2016, a role she held until 2025. There, she led major institutional developments, including strengthened evaluation processes and modernised funding schemes, while overseeing support for thousands of research projects.

Commenting on her appointment, Dr. Kalt said:

“I am deeply honoured to be entrusted with the presidency of ESF at such a dynamic time for science in Europe. Building on the strong foundations established in recent years, I look forward to working with ESF team and members to further develop its role as a trusted partner in research. Together, we will explore new opportunities, including those offered by artificial intelligence, while strengthening collaboration across the European scientific landscape.”

Looking Ahead

With the support of the ESF senior leadership team, Dr. Kalt will lead the organisation through strategic opportunities and challenges in the years ahead. A key priority will be adapting ESF’s activities to the rapidly evolving European research landscape, including exploring how emerging tools and technologies can further strengthen ESF’s role as a facilitator and enabler of research.

Alongside this, ESF will focus on strengthening and expanding its membership base and partnerships across the European and international research ecosystem. Looking further ahead, Dr. Kalt will guide the development of the next ESF Strategy for 2029-2034, building on the foundations established in recent years while positioning the organisation to meet future scientific and societal challenges.

About the European Science Foundation

Since 1974, ESF (European Science Foundation) has been a non-profit, non-governmental organisation committed to advancing high-quality research across Europe and beyond. With a strong track record across all research disciplines, ESF offers expert, independent management and support throughout the entire research lifecycle, from conception and implementation to evaluation, sustainability, and impact.

Backed by a dynamic, highly qualified international team, ESF is a key partner for research endeavours, ensuring scientific networks and organisations have the resources they need to focus on impactful research and collaboration.
