TITLE: GCHERA celebrates WACCI Director

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
On 28 October Professor Eric Danquah Director of the West Africa Centre for Crop Improvement (WACCI) at the University of Ghana received the GCHERA World Agriculture Prize 2018 at a ceremony at Nanjing Agricultural University, Peoples Republic of China. With this award GCHERA (Global Confederation of Higher Education

Associations for Agricultural and Life Sciences) recognized Professor Danquah’s exceptional and significant life time achievements in the field of agricultural and life sciences. John Kennelly, President of GCHERA, in presenting

the award said: “Eric Danquah established the West Africa Centre for Crop Improvement (WACCI), led a maize breeding program which has released three high yielding maize varieties in Ghana, created the Seed Science and Technology International MPhil degree program, and significantly contributed to the establishment of

the Biotechnology Centre at the University of Ghana.

The establishment of WACCI by Prof Danquah provided an environment where young people were inspired to pursue careers in plant breeding. Over 100 students from 19 African countries have had the life transforming opportunity to receive a world class education in plant breeding. His encouragement and support of women

to study in this area has been especially noteworthy as today over one third of the students enrolled in the program are women. Many of the graduates have gone on to develop improved varieties of commercial and indigenous

crops in their home countries. These highly trained professionals will continue to produce improved varieties of the staple crops of Africa for decades, thus extending the legacy of WACCI in improving the lives of small farmers as

well as contributing to global food and nutritional security.

The World Bank and Association of African Universities congratulate Prof. Danquah on this remarkable achievement.

TITLE: Public Health Digital Communication Fellowship: Six-Month Fellowship for Health Experts, Researchers, Clinicians and Policy Leaders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Public health information plays an increasingly important role in how people understand their health, make decisions, access healthcare services, and respond to health-related issues. However, having strong expertise in public health, medicine, research, or health policy does not automatically mean that this expertise is reaching the public in a clear, engaging, and accessible way.

A new six-month fellowship for health experts, researchers, clinicians, policy leaders, and evidence-based communicators offers an opportunity for professionals who want to turn their public health expertise into stronger public-facing communication and build a more effective digital presence.

The fellowship is designed for individuals who already have expertise in health-related fields and want to learn how to communicate accurate and credible information effectively in today’s digital environment.

Participants will work alongside established digital communicators to develop accurate and engaging content that reflects how people discover, understand, and act on health information today.

About the Public Health Digital Communication Fellowship

The fellowship is a six-month professional development opportunity focused on the intersection of public health expertise and digital communication.

Rather than focusing only on developing technical knowledge in public health, the fellowship emphasizes the ability to translate existing expertise into content that can be understood and used by the public.

This distinction is particularly important in today’s digital environment, where people increasingly encounter health information through online platforms.

Health experts may have extensive knowledge, research findings, clinical experience, or policy expertise, but communicating that information effectively requires additional skills.

The fellowship is therefore intended to help participants bridge the gap between:

Public health expertise → Digital communication → Public understanding → Informed action

Through collaboration with established digital communicators, fellows will have the opportunity to develop content that is both accurate and engaging, while considering how people search for, consume, understand, and respond to health information online.

Why Public Health Communication Matters

Public health information can be complex.

Research papers, clinical evidence, health policies, epidemiological data, and technical recommendations are often written for professional audiences. However, members of the public may need to understand the same information in much simpler and more practical terms.

Effective public health communication helps make complex information more accessible.

For example, a health professional may understand a research finding in technical detail, while a member of the public may need to know:

What does this information mean?

Does it affect me?

What should I do?

Where can I find reliable information?

How can I distinguish evidence from misinformation?

What action should I take based on the available evidence?

The fellowship’s focus on creating accurate, engaging digital content is designed around this challenge.

What the Fellowship Focuses On

The central objective is to help health professionals and experts develop a stronger public-facing digital presence.

This means participants will work on communicating their expertise beyond traditional professional or academic audiences.

The fellowship brings together two important areas:

1. Public Health Expertise

Participants are expected to bring existing knowledge and expertise from areas such as:

Public health

Clinical practice

Health research

Health policy

Evidence-based communication

Other relevant health-related fields

2. Digital Communication

Participants will work alongside established digital communicators to develop content that is suitable for today’s digital information environment.

This involves thinking about how audiences:

Find health information.

Understand health information.

Engage with health content.

Decide whether information is credible.

Use information to make health-related decisions.

The combination allows participants to transform their existing expertise into communication that can reach broader audiences.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The fellowship specifically identifies several groups of professionals who may benefit from the opportunity.

Health Experts

Health experts with established knowledge in public health or related areas can use the fellowship to improve how they communicate their expertise to wider audiences.

Researchers

Researchers who produce evidence and scientific findings may benefit from learning how to translate complex research into accessible public-facing content.

This can help researchers communicate findings beyond academic publications and professional conferences.

Clinicians

Clinicians possess valuable practical knowledge based on their professional experience and interaction with patients.

The fellowship can support clinicians who want to develop a stronger digital presence and communicate evidence-based health information to wider audiences.

Policy Leaders

Health policy leaders can use effective digital communication to explain policies, evidence, and public health issues in ways that are more accessible to non-specialist audiences.

Evidence-Based Communicators

The opportunity also specifically welcomes individuals working in evidence-based communication.

For these professionals, the fellowship provides an opportunity to further develop their ability to communicate credible health information through digital channels.

Building a Stronger Public-Facing Digital Presence

One of the central goals of the fellowship is helping participants establish or strengthen their public-facing digital presence.

A digital presence allows professionals to communicate directly with audiences outside traditional professional settings.

For health experts, this can mean creating content that makes their expertise easier to discover and understand.

Instead of limiting communication to:

Academic papers

Professional conferences

Technical reports

Institutional publications

Specialist audiences

participants can explore ways to communicate health information through digital content designed for broader audiences.

The fellowship therefore focuses on helping professionals take their expertise and make it more accessible in the environments where people increasingly search for information.

Working With Established Digital Communicators

An important feature of the fellowship is the opportunity to work alongside established digital communicators.

This provides participants with exposure to professionals who understand how digital audiences consume information.

The collaboration can help bridge the gap between knowing health information and knowing how to communicate that information effectively online.

Participants will be able to work in an environment where health expertise and digital communication come together.

The focus is not simply on producing more content. It is on developing content that is:

Accurate

Evidence-based

Engaging

Accessible

Relevant to public audiences

Creating Accurate Health Content

Accuracy is particularly important when communicating health information.

Health misinformation can create confusion and make it difficult for people to distinguish credible information from unsupported claims.

The fellowship specifically emphasizes the creation of accurate content.

This means that participants’ existing health expertise can serve as the foundation for developing trustworthy public-facing communication.

For researchers and clinicians, this may provide an opportunity to communicate evidence in formats that are easier for non-specialists to understand.

For policy leaders and health communicators, it can provide a framework for explaining complex health topics to broader audiences.

Creating Engaging Health Content

Accuracy alone does not necessarily guarantee that people will read, understand, or engage with health information.

Digital audiences are exposed to large amounts of information every day. As a result, health information also needs to be presented in ways that capture attention and encourage understanding.

The fellowship therefore combines accuracy with engagement.

This means participants will be working toward content that communicates evidence without unnecessarily losing the audience’s attention.

The goal is to make health information easier for people to discover, understand, and use.

Understanding How People Find Health Information

The fellowship is designed around the realities of modern digital information consumption.

People increasingly search online when they want answers to health-related questions.

The way people discover information can therefore influence which health messages they encounter.

Understanding how people find health information is an important part of developing an effective digital communication strategy.

Professionals participating in the fellowship can use this perspective to think more strategically about how their expertise is presented and made accessible to audiences.

Helping People Understand Health Information

Finding health information is only the first step.

People also need to understand what the information means.

Technical terminology and highly specialized explanations can make health information difficult for non-specialist audiences to interpret.

The fellowship focuses on developing content that is engaging and accessible while maintaining accuracy.

This can help health professionals communicate complex ideas in ways that are easier for broader audiences to understand.

Supporting Informed Action

The fellowship description also highlights how people act on health information.

This means the communication process extends beyond simply publishing information.

Effective health communication should consider what audiences do after encountering a health message.

The fellowship therefore brings together three stages of the digital health-information journey:

Finding health information.

Understanding health information.

Acting on health information.

This approach positions digital communication as an important part of public health engagement.

Potential Benefits of the Fellowship

Participants can potentially gain several professional benefits from taking part in the six-month fellowship.

Strengthen Digital Communication Skills

Participants can develop their ability to communicate health expertise in digital formats designed for public audiences.

Build a Public-Facing Professional Profile

The fellowship is specifically intended for professionals who want to build a stronger public-facing digital presence.

Learn From Established Communicators

Working alongside established digital communicators provides an opportunity to gain practical exposure to digital communication approaches.

Translate Expertise Into Accessible Content

Participants can learn to transform specialized knowledge into content that broader audiences can understand.

Improve Public Engagement

Developing accurate and engaging content can help health professionals communicate more effectively with people outside traditional professional settings.

Expand the Reach of Health Expertise

A stronger digital presence can help health experts make their knowledge more discoverable to audiences looking for reliable health information.

Why This Opportunity May Be Relevant to Health Professionals

Many health professionals have substantial expertise but limited opportunities to develop public-facing communication skills.

A researcher may be highly experienced in conducting studies but less experienced in communicating findings through digital platforms.

A clinician may have extensive patient-care experience but may not have developed a structured online communication strategy.

A policy leader may understand complex health systems and policies but may need additional tools for explaining them to the public.

This fellowship addresses that gap by bringing health expertise together with digital communication expertise.

Six-Month Fellowship Structure

The opportunity is described as a six-month fellowship.

The six-month duration provides participants with an extended period in which to develop their public-facing communication capabilities rather than treating digital communication as a one-time workshop or short training.

The fellowship’s collaborative model involves working alongside established digital communicators throughout this period.

However, the announcement provided does not specify the exact monthly schedule, number of participants, training format, meeting frequency, or individual fellowship activities.

Therefore, prospective applicants should consult the official fellowship announcement or application materials for those details when available.

Who Can Benefit From the Opportunity?

The fellowship may be particularly relevant to professionals who already have a strong foundation in health-related knowledge and now want to become stronger communicators.

It may be suitable for individuals who want to:

Develop a professional digital identity.

Communicate research findings to wider audiences.

Explain health issues in accessible language.

Increase the visibility of evidence-based health information.

Develop engaging health content.

Connect with digital communication professionals.

Strengthen public engagement with their expertise.

Application Deadline

No application deadline is provided in the information supplied for this opportunity.

Applicants should check the official fellowship announcement or application page for the deadline and application timeline before applying.

Application Information

The information provided describes the fellowship and its intended audience, but it does not include specific application instructions.

The supplied announcement does not state:

The application opening date.

The application deadline.

The application website.

Required application documents.

Selection criteria.

Number of fellows selected.

Fellowship stipend or financial support.

Location or residency requirements.

Whether participation is online, in person, or hybrid.

These details should be verified through the official fellowship source before publication or application.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The six-month Public Health Digital Communication Fellowship is designed for health professionals and experts who want to turn their knowledge into public-facing communication that is accurate, engaging, and relevant to the way people consume health information today.

By bringing together health experts, researchers, clinicians, policy leaders, and evidence-based communicators with established digital communicators, the fellowship focuses on an increasingly important skill: communicating credible health expertise effectively in the digital environment.

Participants will have the opportunity to work on developing content that considers how people find, understand, and act on health information, while also building a stronger public-facing digital presence.

For professionals who already possess health expertise but want to expand their ability to communicate with wider audiences, this six-month fellowship represents an opportunity to connect subject-matter expertise with modern digital communication.

Prospective applicants should review the official fellowship information carefully for application requirements, eligibility details, funding information, geographic restrictions, and the application deadline, as these details are not included in the announcement provided here.

TITLE: Equality Fund CONNECT Grant 2026: Up to CAD $1 Million Per Year for Feminist and Allied Movement Collaborations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Equality Fund has opened applications for its CONNECT funding stream, a major grant opportunity designed to strengthen collaboration among feminist, women’s rights, gender-expansive, and allied social justice movements around the world.

Through the 2026 CONNECT Expression of Interest (EoI), selected collaborations can receive between CAD $500,000 and CAD $1 million per year for an initial period of two years, with the possibility of additional years of support. The Equality Fund expects to distribute approximately CAD $4 million per year through this funding round and anticipates supporting between five and seven collaborations.

The CONNECT funding stream is particularly focused on organizations and movements that recognize that many of today’s challenges cannot be addressed by individual organizations or movements working independently. Instead, it seeks to support cross-movement relationships, shared strategies, trust, infrastructure, and collective capacity that can enable movements to work together toward gender equality, social justice, democracy, human rights, and broader systems change.

The Expression of Interest application period runs from August 31 to September 16, 2026, closing at 17:00 EDT (UTC-4).

Opportunity at a Glance

Detail
Information

Opportunity
Equality Fund CONNECT Funding Stream

Opportunity Type
Grant

Application Stage
Expression of Interest (EoI)

Grant Size
CAD $500,000–CAD $1,000,000 per year

Total Funding
Approximately CAD $4 million per year

Expected Number of Grants
5–7 collaborations

Initial Grant Duration
Two years

Potential Extension
Additional years may be possible

Expected Grant Start Date
February 1, 2027

EoI Opens
August 31, 2026

EoI Deadline
September 16, 2026

Closing Time
17:00 EDT (UTC-4)

Application Method
Equality Fund Community Portal

Languages
English, French, or Spanish

Priority
Collaborations with lead organizations based in the Global South or East

What Is the Equality Fund?

The Equality Fund is a global initiative focused on sustainably resourcing women’s rights organizations and feminist movements. Its work combines global grantmaking, gender-lens investing, policy advocacy, and feminist philanthropy to move resources toward people-powered movements, particularly across the Global South.

The organization was launched in 2019 and, according to the CONNECT guidelines, has since disbursed more than $125 million to over 1,800 organizations across more than 100 countries.

The Equality Fund works with governments, foundations, philanthropic organizations, feminist funds, grassroots organizations, and social movements to strengthen efforts toward gender equality and social transformation.

Its funding approach recognizes that organizations working directly within communities often have important knowledge about the problems affecting them and are therefore well positioned to develop locally relevant solutions.

The Equality Fund currently operates four major funding programs:

Catalyze – Provides resources to individual women’s rights and feminist organizations.

Activate – Provides resources to Feminist Funds.

Prepare, Respond & Care – Supports women’s rights and feminist organizations working in difficult crisis environments, including political, humanitarian, conflict, and post-conflict contexts.

CONNECT – Supports relationships, infrastructure, collaboration, and collective capacity that enable feminist and allied movements to build power together.

The CONNECT opportunity therefore represents a distinct approach to movement funding because it focuses not only on individual organizations but also on the relationships and infrastructure connecting different movements.

What Is the Equality Fund CONNECT Grant?

CONNECT is a pilot funding stream created to support collaborations between feminist movements and allied movements that want to work together toward shared goals.

The program is based on the idea that many of the major challenges facing communities today are interconnected.

Issues involving:

Gender equality

Human rights

Democracy

Social justice

Political participation

Economic inequality

Discrimination

Gender-based oppression

Anti-rights movements

Authoritarianism

Social exclusion

often overlap and cannot be effectively addressed through isolated interventions.

The Equality Fund therefore wants to support collaborations that can bring together different actors and movements that may not have historically worked together but now recognize the value of building a common strategy.

CONNECT seeks to strengthen the relationships, trust, infrastructure, shared strategy, and collective capacity needed for such collaboration.

Why Was CONNECT Created?

According to the Equality Fund, anti-rights, anti-democracy, anti-gender, and authoritarian movements have become increasingly coordinated.

These developments affect multiple communities, issues, and movements simultaneously.

At the same time, philanthropic funding is often organized into separate thematic categories. While thematic funding can be useful, it can also create silos in which organizations working on related problems have limited opportunities to collaborate.

CONNECT attempts to address this problem by investing in cross-movement collaboration.

The underlying idea is that movements can achieve more when they understand their shared challenges and develop coordinated responses.

For example, a feminist organization may work primarily on gender equality while another organization focuses on democracy, human rights, environmental justice, racial justice, youth rights, or economic justice. CONNECT creates space for such movements to identify common interests and develop equitable ways of working together.

What Does CONNECT Aim to Fund?

CONNECT is intended to support the infrastructure that makes collective action possible.

This can include strengthening:

Relationships between movements

Trust between organizations

Shared strategies

Collaborative structures

Movement infrastructure

Collective leadership

Cross-movement networks

Joint advocacy capacity

Organizational collaboration

Communication and coordination

Collective learning

Shared approaches to addressing common threats

The emphasis is therefore not simply on funding individual projects in isolation.

Instead, CONNECT is interested in how movements work together and what they need to build stronger collective power.

The Equality Fund describes this as an investment in the infrastructure of collective action.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The CONNECT funding round has a significant funding envelope.

The Equality Fund expects to distribute approximately:

CAD $4 million per year

to approximately:

Five to seven collaborations.

Each successful collaboration may receive:

CAD $500,000 to CAD $1 million per year.

The precise grant amount will depend on factors including:

The nature of the proposed collaboration

The scope of the proposed work

The needs identified by the collaboration

The proposal itself

The financial management experience of the organization managing the grant

This means applicants should not simply focus on requesting the maximum amount. The proposed budget should be connected to the actual needs and activities of the collaboration.

How Long Will the CONNECT Grants Last?

CONNECT grants will initially run for two years.

The expected start date for the grants is: February 1, 2027.

The guidelines also indicate that there may be potential for additional years of funding, although continued funding should not be assumed as automatic.

Applicants should therefore develop realistic strategies that demonstrate how the requested funding can contribute to meaningful and sustainable collective capacity.

Who Can Apply for the Equality Fund CONNECT Grant?

CONNECT is designed for collaborations, rather than individual applicants.

The Equality Fund is looking for collaborations that bring together:

Feminist actors

Women’s rights organizations

Gender-expansive movements

Allied social justice movements

Other organizations or groups that can contribute to shared movement goals

The collaboration should demonstrate why working together is important and how the participating actors can collectively address challenges that individual movements may not be able to tackle alone.

Importantly, the Equality Fund recognizes that collaborations can take different forms.

There is no single model of collaboration that applicants must follow.

Different collaborations may have different:

Structures

Relationships

Leadership models

Geographical arrangements

Movement partners

Shared objectives

Organizational roles

The application therefore uses open-ended questions intended to allow movement actors to explain what matters most in their particular context.

Who Is Not Eligible to Receive CONNECT Funding?

The guidelines clearly identify several categories that cannot receive funding.

The following are not eligible for funding:

Political parties

Government bodies

For-profit organizations

Individuals

These entities may nevertheless participate in or engage with activities associated with a collaboration on their own accord, but they cannot be the funded applicant organization.

This distinction is important for collaborations that involve multiple stakeholders.

A collaboration may work with government institutions, political actors, private-sector organizations, or individuals where appropriate, but the grant itself must be managed through eligible lead organization(s).

Lead Organization Requirements

For operational purposes, a CONNECT collaboration must have either:

Option 1: One Lead Organization

A single organization can serve as both:

Programmatic Lead

Financial Lead

This organization would assume both the programmatic and financial responsibilities associated with the grant.

Option 2: Two Separate Lead Organizations

A collaboration may instead identify:

A Programmatic Lead, and

A Financial Lead

In this arrangement, responsibilities are divided between the two organizations.

Responsibilities of the Programmatic Lead

The Programmatic Lead is responsible for:

Submitting the application

Signing the grant agreement alongside the Financial Lead

Submitting financial and narrative reports on behalf of the collaboration

Responsibilities of the Financial Lead

The Financial Lead is responsible for:

Signing the grant agreement alongside the Programmatic Lead

Receiving and distributing funds

Ensuring proper financial management

Completing financial reporting

Sharing financial reports with the Programmatic Lead

The Equality Fund states that it will prioritize collaborations whose lead organization is based in the Global South or East.

This is therefore an important consideration for organizations planning their application structure.

Eligibility Requirements for the Programmatic Lead

The Programmatic Lead must satisfy a number of requirements.

The organization must be primarily:

Governed by local women, youth, girls, and/or non-binary people from the Global South and East

Led and directed by people from these communities

Women, youth, girls, and/or non-binary people must also constitute a majority of the organization’s leadership and board or coordinating committee.

In addition, the organization’s primary mission must involve the promotion of the rights of:

Women

Youth

Girls

Non-binary people

This work must be central to the organization’s mission rather than simply being one component of a broader portfolio.

Feminist and Women’s Rights Focus

The Programmatic Lead must work from a feminist and/or women’s rights perspective and pursue structural change concerning issues affecting women, youth, girls, and/or non-binary people.

The organization should also demonstrate a commitment to:

Feminist movement building

Collaboration

Women’s rights

Gender equality

Gender-expansive movements

Intersectional approaches

Structural change

The organization should be willing to collaborate with other:

Women-led organizations

Youth organizations

Gender-expansive organizations

Black, Indigenous and People of Color (BIPOC) organizations

Feminist organizations

Allied social justice movements

Geographic Eligibility

The Programmatic Lead must be registered or operate in an ODA-eligible country, with the exception of Afghanistan.

The Equality Fund explains that much of its funding comes from bilateral donors whose funding requirements include restrictions concerning Official Development Assistance (ODA)-eligible countries.

As a result, the majority of resources supported through these funds must be invested in ODA-eligible countries.

There is a limited consideration for organizations led by diaspora women or gender-expansive people that are headquartered in a non-ODA-eligible country but work exclusively in an ODA-eligible country.

However, applicants in this situation should carefully review the official guidelines and assess whether their specific structure meets the requirements.

Important Afghanistan Restriction

Organizations in Afghanistan should note that the Equality Fund currently cannot provide CONNECT grants in Afghanistan because of Canadian sanctions and laws relating to financing terrorism.

The Equality Fund states that it continues to advocate with the Canadian government regarding the importance of supporting work outside strictly humanitarian assistance.

Language Requirements

The Programmatic Lead must have the ability to complete:

Proposal documents

Narrative reports

Financial reports

in one of the following languages:

English

French

Spanish

The organization must also be able to communicate verbally in at least one of these languages.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to operate primarily in English, provided they can meet the required communication and documentation requirements in English, French, or Spanish.

Requirements for the Financial Lead

The Financial Lead has a different set of eligibility requirements.

The organization must:

Have valid legal registration.

Have externally audited financial reports for the previous two fiscal years.

Have managed annual expenditure of at least CAD $325,000 in one of the previous two fiscal years.

Have the capacity to ensure that participating organizations can receive, manage, and report on CONNECT funds appropriately.

The financial management requirement is particularly important because CONNECT grants can be substantial.

Applicants should therefore select a Financial Lead capable of responsibly managing the funds and supporting participating organizations with financial reporting and compliance.

Financial Audit Documentation

At the Expression of Interest stage, the Financial Lead will be required to submit externally audited institutional financial reports covering the previous two fiscal years.

These documents are intended to help the Equality Fund verify whether the organization satisfies the financial eligibility requirements.

There is, however, a provision for organizations that do not strictly meet the institutional audit requirement.

If the organization:

Managed or expended at least CAD $325,000 in one of the previous two fiscal years, and

Has other audit-related documentation, such as project audits,

the Equality Fund may ask the organization to submit those documents along with a short explanation of why it does not have externally audited institutional financial reports.

This provides some flexibility while still allowing the Equality Fund to assess the organization’s financial management capacity.

Existing Equality Fund Grantees

Current Equality Fund grantee partners may participate in a CONNECT collaboration.

However, an existing Equality Fund grantee partner cannot serve as the lead organization of a CONNECT application.

Importantly, the participation of a current Equality Fund grantee partner will not negatively affect the consideration of the application.

This means existing grantees can potentially contribute to a broader collaborative effort without being the formal lead.

How to Apply for the Equality Fund CONNECT Grant

The CONNECT application process consists of multiple stages.

The Equality Fund has deliberately designed the process to reduce the amount of time organizations spend developing full proposals when they are unlikely to proceed to the next stage.

The process begins with an eligibility assessment.

Step 1: Complete the Eligibility Quiz

Before submitting an Expression of Interest, applicants should complete the Equality Fund’s eligibility quiz through its Community Portal.

The quiz is intended to help applicants determine whether their collaboration meets the basic eligibility requirements.

If the collaboration is eligible, applicants will be directed to the Community Portal login page.

Applicants who do not already have an account can select the “Sign-up” option.

After creating an account, applicants will receive an email containing a link to the Community Portal.

Applicants should bookmark the Community Portal for future access.

Step 2: Submit the Expression of Interest

Eligible collaborations must submit their Expression of Interest between:

August 31 and September 16, 2026

The application closes at:

17:00 EDT (UTC-4)

The EoI must be submitted through the Equality Fund’s Community Portal.

The Expression of Interest is intended to provide the Equality Fund with an understanding of the collaboration, including its:

Vision

Mission

Context

Work

Cross-movement relationships

Commitment to women’s rights

Approach to gender equality

Shared goals

Collaborative work

Applicants should use this stage to communicate the core value of their collaboration rather than attempting to provide an unnecessarily elaborate full proposal.

Expression of Interest Templates

The Equality Fund provides Expression of Interest templates to help applicants prepare their responses.

Templates are available in:

English

French

Spanish

The template can allow members of a collaboration to work together offline before transferring their final responses to the Community Portal.

This may be particularly useful for collaborations involving multiple organizations because it provides an opportunity to discuss and agree on responses before the final online submission.

What Happens After the Expression of Interest?

The CONNECT application process has a second stage known as the Advanced Application.

Only selected collaborations will be invited to proceed to this stage.

The Equality Fund expects to invite up to 18 collaborations to submit Advanced Applications.

These organizations will be asked to provide more detailed information concerning:

Their context

Collaborative priorities

Strategies

Proposed actions

Budget

Organizational documentation

Financial management

Partnership arrangements

Supporting documents may include:

Registration documents

Financial Management Manual

Memorandum of Understanding

Other relevant organizational documentation

The Advanced Application stage will therefore require considerably more detail than the initial Expression of Interest.

Advanced Application Timeline

Organizations shortlisted for the Advanced Application stage are expected to receive invitations by:

November 1, 2026.

Those invited will have:

Four weeks

to complete their Advanced Application.

The Equality Fund emphasizes that only organizations selected to proceed will receive an invitation.

Because of the expected volume of applications, the Equality Fund will not be able to provide individual status updates regarding Expression of Interest applications.

Reference and Endorsement Checks

The Advanced Application stage will also include reference and endorsement checks.

These checks may involve organizations, allies, and funders that have previously worked with the applicant.

This means organizations should ensure that their previous partnerships and relationships accurately reflect their organizational experience and credibility.

Applicants should also make sure that relevant partners and allies understand the collaboration and are prepared to confirm their relationship if contacted.

Final Grant Selection

Following the selection process, the Equality Fund expects to award approximately:

5–7 CONNECT grants.

Successful grants are expected to begin on:

February 1, 2027.

Given that up to 18 collaborations may be invited to submit Advanced Applications but only five to seven grants are expected to be awarded, applicants should recognize that advancing to the second stage will not guarantee funding.

How Will Applications Be Selected?

The Equality Fund uses a participatory selection process.

The selection of successful Expressions of Interest and Advanced Applications will be guided by a participatory advisory model.

The process will involve perspectives from:

Activists

Regional women’s funds

Professionals

Community representatives

People with expertise in movement infrastructure

The objective is to ensure that funding decisions are informed by the realities, priorities, knowledge, and experiences of movements and communities.

This is consistent with the Equality Fund’s broader approach to trust-based and participatory grantmaking.

What Does Cross-Movement Collaboration Mean?

Cross-movement collaboration is central to CONNECT.

The concept involves building relationships with movements beyond traditional feminist circles so that different groups can create a united response to common challenges.

Rather than organizations working independently on separate issues, cross-movement collaboration encourages them to identify areas where their goals overlap.

For example, organizations working on gender equality may collaborate with movements focused on:

Democracy

Human rights

Economic justice

Youth empowerment

Racial justice

Indigenous rights

Environmental justice

Disability rights

Social justice

Political participation

The exact combination will depend on the context of each collaboration.

The important consideration is whether the organizations can demonstrate a meaningful shared purpose and a reason for working collectively.

What Is Movement Infrastructure?

Movement infrastructure refers broadly to the resources, people, skills, relationships, and systems that support an entire movement ecosystem.

This may involve:

Organizations

Networks

Leaders

Knowledge

Skills

Relationships

Communication structures

Collaborative platforms

Shared resources

Collective strategies

CONNECT recognizes that strong movements require more than individual organizations.

They also require strong relationships between organizations and communities.

Equality Fund’s Approach to Grantmaking

CONNECT is based on feminist, intersectional, trust-based, participatory, and non-extractive grantmaking principles.

The Equality Fund aims to build partnerships that extend beyond simply providing financial resources.

Its approach may include:

Accompaniment

Learning

Exchanges

Joint strategies

Collective advocacy

Resource mobilization

Movement strengthening

The intention is to develop longer-term relationships with grantee partners rather than treating funding as a purely transactional arrangement.

Guidance on Using Artificial Intelligence in the Application

The Equality Fund explicitly addresses the use of artificial intelligence in the application process.

Applicants may use AI as a supportive tool, but the organization wants to see the applicant’s actual experiences, ideas, thinking, and understanding of its context.

The Equality Fund recommends that applicants:

Write their first draft themselves.

Use AI to refine ideas or polish communication if desired.

Ensure the final responses genuinely represent their own experience and thinking.

Applications will not be assessed primarily on writing quality.

Instead, the Equality Fund is interested in:

Quality of ideas

Strength of collaboration

Understanding of context

Movement experience

Shared goals

Proposed approach

Applicants whose first language is not English, French, or Spanish may also use AI for translation purposes.

This is an important distinction: AI can help improve clarity and language, but applicants should avoid submitting generic, AI-generated narratives that do not accurately reflect their organization’s actual work.

Sanctions Screening and Due Diligence

Organizations invited to the Advanced Application stage will undergo sanctions screening as part of the Equality Fund’s due-diligence process.

The Equality Fund uses software known as Sanctions.io for this purpose.

Screening may cover:

The organization

Key organizational contacts

Grant agreement signatories

Fiscal sponsor contacts, where applicable

Senior management contacts, where necessary

The purpose is to safeguard against exposure to:

Terrorism

Human rights abuses

Money laundering

Fraud

Other criminal activity

The Equality Fund notes that credible sanctions-screening flags are rare.

If a credible match is identified, the organization may be asked to provide identification documentation for the relevant individual so that the Equality Fund can determine whether the match is genuine.

Important Deadline for the CONNECT Grant

Organizations interested in this opportunity should pay close attention to the application deadline.

Expression of Interest Deadline

September 16, 2026 at 17:00 EDT (UTC-4)

The application period began on August 31, 2026.

Because the deadline is based on Eastern Daylight Time, organizations applying from other parts of the world should convert the closing time to their local time zone well in advance.

Applicants should also avoid waiting until the final hours to complete their submission, particularly where multiple organizations are involved in preparing a collaborative application.

Recommended Preparation Strategy for Applicants

Organizations considering applying should begin by examining their collaboration against the eligibility requirements.

1. Confirm that the collaboration is genuinely cross-movement

The application should demonstrate why different movements need to work together.

Applicants should avoid presenting a conventional single-organization project if the collaboration does not genuinely involve cross-movement work.

2. Identify the correct lead structure

Determine whether the collaboration will use:

One organization as both Programmatic and Financial Lead, or

Separate Programmatic and Financial Leads.

3. Verify Programmatic Lead eligibility

Review requirements concerning:

Leadership

Governance

Mission

Feminist perspective

Women’s rights

Movement building

Geographic eligibility

Language capacity

4. Verify Financial Lead eligibility

Check:

Legal registration

Audited financial reports

Annual expenditure

Financial management systems

Ability to manage and report on grant funds

5. Gather financial documentation early

Because externally audited reports may be required, organizations should not wait until the deadline to locate financial documents.

6. Complete the eligibility quiz

The eligibility quiz should be completed before investing significant time in the EoI.

7. Develop the application collaboratively

Since CONNECT is designed around collaboration, participating organizations should have an opportunity to discuss and agree on the application’s key messages.

8. Keep the application authentic

The Equality Fund wants to understand the actual collaboration, its context, and the thinking of the people involved.

Applicants should therefore prioritize authentic experiences and concrete examples over generic development-sector language.

9. Use AI carefully

AI can be used to improve clarity, grammar, structure, or translation, but the core ideas should come from the applicant.

10. Submit before the deadline

Do not leave the submission until September 16, 2026, especially if several organizations need to approve the final application.

Why the CONNECT Grant Could Be Significant for Feminist Movements

The CONNECT grant represents a different approach to movement funding because it focuses on the connections between movements.

Many organizations possess significant expertise within their own areas of work, but they may lack the resources, infrastructure, or relationships needed to coordinate effectively with other movements.

By supporting collaboration, CONNECT aims to help movements develop stronger collective responses to interconnected challenges.

The potential funding level is also significant. With grants ranging from CAD $500,000 to CAD $1 million per year, selected collaborations could have substantial resources to strengthen their collective infrastructure over the initial two-year grant period.

However, the program is highly competitive, with only approximately five to seven collaborations expected to receive grants.

Applicants should therefore focus on demonstrating a compelling reason why their collaboration is necessary, what shared challenge they are addressing, and how their collective work can strengthen broader movement power.

Frequently Asked Questions About the Equality Fund CONNECT Grant

What is the Equality Fund CONNECT opportunity?

CONNECT is a grantmaking stream of the Equality Fund that supports collaborations between feminist and allied movements working together toward shared goals related to gender equality, social justice, and broader systems change.

How much funding can a successful applicant receive?

Selected collaborations can receive between CAD $500,000 and CAD $1 million per year, depending on the proposal and the financial management experience of the organization responsible for managing the grant.

How many collaborations will receive funding?

The Equality Fund expects to award approximately five to seven grants in this funding round.

How long is the grant?

The initial grant period is two years, with the possibility of additional years.

When are grants expected to begin?

The expected grant start date is February 1, 2027.

Can an individual apply?

No. Individuals are not eligible to receive CONNECT funding.

Can a government organization apply?

No. Government bodies are not eligible to receive the funding.

Can a political party apply?

No. Political parties are not eligible for CONNECT funding.

Can a for-profit company apply?

No. For-profit organizations are not eligible for funding.

Can different organizations apply together?

Yes. CONNECT is specifically designed to support collaborations involving feminist actors and allied movements.

Can an existing Equality Fund grantee participate?

Yes. Existing Equality Fund grantee partners can participate in a collaboration, but they cannot serve as the lead organization for a CONNECT application.

Is there a geographic restriction?

Yes. The Programmatic Lead generally needs to be registered or operating in an ODA-eligible country, with Afghanistan excluded under the current restrictions.

Are organizations in the Global South prioritized?

Yes. The Equality Fund states that it will prioritize collaborations whose lead organization is based in the Global South or East.

What languages can applicants use?

The required application and reporting work can be completed in English, French, or Spanish, and the Programmatic Lead must be able to communicate verbally in one of these languages.

Can applicants use artificial intelligence?

Yes, but with limitations. The Equality Fund recommends that applicants write their own first draft and use AI primarily to refine ideas, improve communication, or translate content. The application should reflect the organization’s real experiences and ideas.

What is the first step in applying?

Eligible organizations should first complete the Equality Fund’s Eligibility Quiz through the Community Portal before submitting an Expression of Interest.

Equality Fund CONNECT Grant 2026: Key Takeaways

The CONNECT funding stream is particularly relevant to organizations and movements that recognize the importance of working beyond traditional organizational or thematic boundaries.

The most important points to remember are:

It is a grant opportunity, not an individual scholarship or fellowship.

It is designed for collaborations, rather than individual applicants.

Approximately CAD $4 million per year will be distributed.

Individual grants can range from CAD $500,000 to CAD $1 million per year.

Grants will initially last two years.

The expected grant start date is February 1, 2027.

Approximately five to seven collaborations are expected to receive grants.

Up to 18 collaborations may be invited to the Advanced Application stage.

Political parties, government bodies, for-profit organizations, and individuals cannot receive funding.

The Programmatic Lead must meet specific feminist, leadership, governance, mission, geographic, and language requirements.

The Financial Lead must meet specific legal and financial-management requirements.

The Equality Fund will prioritize lead organizations based in the Global South or East.

Applicants must first complete an eligibility quiz.

The Expression of Interest deadline is September 16, 2026 at 17:00 EDT (UTC-4).

The application process has two principal stages: Expression of Interest and Advanced Application.

AI may be used for refinement and translation, but applicants are expected to provide their own ideas and experiences.

Successful applications will be assessed through a participatory selection process involving diverse movement and community perspectives.

Conclusion

The Equality Fund CONNECT Grant 2026 provides a major funding opportunity for feminist organizations, women’s rights movements, gender-expansive actors, and allied social justice movements seeking to strengthen collective action.

Rather than focusing exclusively on individual organizations or isolated projects, CONNECT seeks to invest in the relationships, trust, infrastructure, shared strategies, and collective capacity that allow different movements to work together effectively.

With potential funding of CAD $500,000 to CAD $1 million per year, an initial two-year grant period, and approximately CAD $4 million in annual funding available, the opportunity could provide significant support to eligible collaborations working toward gender equality and social justice.

However, the opportunity is highly competitive and has strict eligibility requirements. Potential applicants should carefully assess their collaboration, confirm the eligibility of their Programmatic and Financial Leads, complete the Equality Fund’s eligibility quiz, prepare their Expression of Interest collaboratively, and ensure that their submission accurately reflects their real experience and shared goals.

Organizations that meet the requirements should take particular note of the September 16, 2026 deadline at 17:00 EDT (UTC-4) and begin the application process as early as possible.

TITLE: Why a Mastercard Foundation Scholarship May Be the Best Fit for You

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
I received the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship after facing 17 rejections. Seventeen rejection emails could easily have convinced me that perhaps I was not qualified, prepared or fortunate enough to receive a major international scholarship. But rejection did not end my story. It strengthened it. The day you open a rejection email can be just as sunny, bright or cold as the day you eventually open an acceptance email. The major difference is that, on the day the acceptance arrives, your perseverance, persistence and determination have finally created the opportunity you refused to stop pursuing. Today, I am studying Africa and International Development at the University of Edinburgh as a Mastercard Foundation Scholar. Looking back, I am grateful that I continued applying, learning and believing that there was still a place for me somewhere. While the core benefits are well-known, there are numerous unadvertised perks and community-driven dynamics that completely transform the student experience, rendering this one of the most comprehensive scholarships available globally.

Financial Coverage and Secure Housing
Foremost among the structural benefits of this scholarship is the comprehensive financial peace of mind it establishes from day one, allowing scholars to immerse themselves entirely in their academic pursuits without the looming anxiety of historical or ongoing educational debt.

The foundation takes full responsibility for complete tuition fees, eliminating the substantial financial barriers that often prevent top-tier global talent from accessing world-class instruction. In tandem with tuition coverage, scholars receive a regular monthly stipend designed to comfortably meet the cost of living in Edinburgh. This ensures that textbook purchases, dietary needs, local transit, and daily incidentals are entirely taken care of.

This financial framework extends directly to student accommodation, which is meticulously planned, fully paid for, and coordinated by the program administration before arrival. Rather than leaving international students to navigate the highly competitive and stressful local rental market from afar, the foundation secures housing in prime areas of the town. These residential spaces are selected with strict criteria in mind, ensuring a high level of physical security, modern domestic comfort, and a pristine, quiet study environment optimized for rigorous academic focus.

Strategic Career Transitions and Executive Mentorship
The true value of this scholarship lies in its forward-looking design, which actively rejects the idea that a funding package should merely cover a degree and then dissolve. From the very moment a scholar is handed their official admission letter, the Mastercard Foundation implements a strategic framework aimed at preparing the individual for life beyond graduation. Central to this effort is direct access to a dedicated transitions coordinator. This professional’s entire mandate is to help students think critically about their long-term professional trajectories, identify hidden career avenues, and strategically position themselves within the global workforce. This guidance prevents post-graduation panic by transforming the academic year into a continuous launchpad for future leadership. To facilitate a smooth departure from university life when the time comes, the program provides a comprehensive transitions fee. This is a lump-sum financial cushion explicitly intended to offset the immediate logistical costs of moving, relocating, or establishing a professional base. This remains true whether a scholar chooses to utilize their chance to remain in the United Kingdom or return immediately to their home country. Furthermore, scholars gain unparalleled, first-hand advisory access to highly successful team members working directly within the Mastercard network. These industry professionals, who have built illustrious careers across diverse corporate, technological, and developmental fields, offer direct mentorship. They share operational insights and provide a realistic view of what it takes to drive systemic change on a global scale.

Cutting-Edge Technology and Entrepreneurial Support

I won the scholars enterprise fund providing me with funding to expand my work.

To ensure that every student can participate equally in a high-tech, fast-paced academic landscape, the scholarship equips recipients with top-tier hardware immediately upon arrival. The latest version of a MacBook is handed directly to each scholar to support their academic research, multimedia assignments, and coursework. This hardware provision ensures that no one is ever disadvantaged by outdated technology, allowing students to seamlessly manage intensive data analysis and complex projects with premium equipment and 24 hours internet. Having this level of technological support is foundational to daily productivity and academic confidence. For scholars who possess an entrepreneurial spirit and a desire to build tangible ventures, the program offers concrete avenues to turn theoretical business models into operational realities. Through the Mastercard Enterprise Fund, students are invited to compete and pitch their innovative business ideas, social enterprises, or technological start-ups in a supportive funding environment. Winning scholars are awarded crucial seed capital to launch or scale their businesses, directly addressing the chronic lack of early-stage financing that plagues young African entrepreneurs. Beyond the potential capital injection, the fund provides an intensive, 10-week business mentorship training program. This curriculum covers vital operational skills such as financial forecasting, market verification, legal compliance, and pitch design, ensuring that student ventures are built on sustainable organizational foundations.

Global Experiential Learning and Student-Led Summits
The educational model championed by the Mastercard Foundation and the University of Edinburgh extends far beyond the traditional boundaries of the Scottish capital, incorporating mandatory experiential learning trips that broaden a scholar’s global perspective. One of the most significant highlights of the academic calendar is a fully funded trip to Johannesburg, South Africa to participate in the Climate Enterprise School. This immersive program brings together on-campus students in Edinburgh and online scholars studying from various regions across the African continent. Working side-by-side in a collaborative environment, students analyze pressing environmental challenges, explore sustainable agricultural technologies, and design localized climate adaptation strategies. This experiential learning is further reinforced by the Climate Enterprise Leadership Summit, an event entirely led, organized, and executed by the students themselves. This summit provides an empowering platform where scholars are given the chance to present original research, deliver talks, lead panels, and engage in meaningful conversations with international climate experts. This experience directly refines public speaking capabilities and institutional leadership skills before an international audience.

Balancing Rigour with Rest: Pastoral Care and Wellness
Recognizing that intense academic work can easily lead to burnout if not balanced with intentional periods of rest, the program builds dedicated wellness retreats directly into the academic year. Mid-way through the semester, when assignments and exam pressures peak, scholars embark on an immersive trip to The Burn, a historic and peaceful country estate located near Aberdeen. This time away from the bustling university campus serves as a vital psychological release valve, allowing students to completely cool off from academic stressors, reconnect with nature, and enjoy time away from the shadow of impending deadlines. The retreat to The Burn is intentionally structured to serve as a moment of collective reflection and a feedback loop. It offers a safe space where peers can discuss their university experiences, share coping mechanisms for culture shock, and think collectively about their personal and professional growth. This focus on holistic well-being is backed by comprehensive pastoral care and structured mental health infrastructure, ensuring that every student feels profoundly supported on a personal level. Scholars are granted direct, confidential access to mental health support and dedicated therapy sessions conducted by trained therapists whenever they need them. This setup ensures that any psychological struggles, emotional distress, or feelings of isolation are addressed immediately with empathy and clinical expertise. Furthermore, the foundation provides complete security and travel support in the case of personal distress, ensuring that scholars can take trips back to their home country immediately if an emergency arises.

Radical Authenticity: The Freedom to Be Yourself
Ultimately, perhaps the most profound yet frequently underrated perk of the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship is the explicit freedom it gives you to be your authentic self and bring your unique, unfiltered talents to the table. In many elite academic environments, international students often feel an unspoken pressure to assimilate, to alter their accents, or to suppress their distinct cultural viewpoints to fit into Western institutional paradigms. The culture established within this scholarship program actively fights against this conformity. As Dr. Maya Angelou famously observed, “If you are always trying to be normal, you will never know how amazing you can be.” Every single day that you walk into a Mastercard scholarship gathering, you are struck by how uniquely talented every individual is. More importantly, you observe how intentionally everyone is guided to ensure they are not trying to copy someone else or morph into a predefined stereotype of success. This deliberate celebration of individuality is incredibly special. It instills a deep sense of self-worth and confidence, validating the idea that a scholar’s specific background, local knowledge, and unique lived experiences are precisely what make them a valuable asset to the global development discourse.

Launching Global Futures: Dissertation Fieldwork Support
As the academic journey nears its conclusion, the scholarship continues to offer empowering autonomy regarding a scholar’s next steps. To facilitate the final academic requirement of the degree, the program offers specialized placement-based dissertation and research support. Rather than forcing students to conduct secondary literature reviews from a library in Scotland, the foundation provides full flight fees and a dedicated research stipend to support field placements. This incredible support was put into action during my own coursework when my research took me to Sierra Leone, a country I was stepping into for the very first time. Navigating an entirely new country for fieldwork could easily have been an overwhelming and logistically daunting experience for any student. However, Mastercard completely stepped in and took up the full flight costs, smoothing the path and helping to dynamically navigate the moment. Future scholars should know that this is the level of backing they can expect, an institution that removes logistical hurdles so you can focus entirely on producing impactful, primary field research on the ground. When you look at the entirety of this program from the full financial coverage and executive mentorship to the experiential travel opportunities and deep commitment to personal well-being it becomes clear that the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship is much more than an educational fund. It is a profound door to new global opportunities. For those currently drafting applications and facing the daunting wall of potential rejections, remember that perseverance is the definitive catalyst that turns a closed door into an open gateway. Trust the value of your unique story, stay persistent through every setback, and take the leap, because an extraordinary future is waiting for you to claim it.

Student Agency and Leadership: Building the Scholars Safe Space (3S)

The diversity and cultural richness of the scholar community constitutes one of the most transformative elements of the entire Edinburgh experience. By bringing together a wide range of individuals from dozens of different African nationalities, the scholarship creates a vibrant miniature community that mirrors the complexity and talent of the entire continent. Interacting daily with peers from West, East, Central, and Southern Africa breaks down regional silos, enhances cross-cultural communication skills, and fosters deep collaborative teamwork. Within this space, scholars meet incredible people, find intellectual partners, and make lifelong friends, building a powerful network of future African leaders who are deeply bonded by their shared experience in Scotland. What truly sets this scholarship apart, however, is that Mastercard actively trusts its scholars to take on bold institutional initiatives. A prime example of this student agency is the creation of the Scholars Safe Space, affectionately known as 3S. Rather than being a top-down program handed down by administrators, 3S was built entirely from scratch by us scholars. Alongside my brilliant peers Alasana, Yusra, Usman, and Ismail, we took the lead in designing a dedicated ecosystem specifically tailored to our community’s needs. We built 3S to bring scholars together to play, reflect, create, have fun, and garner beautiful, shared experiences during our demanding study times. It serves as a confidential, supportive environment where students can openly share their vulnerabilities, celebrate victories, navigate personal hurdles, and uplift one another without fear of judgment. Knowing that the foundation backs you not just to study, but to launch your own community initiatives, provides a deep sense of ownership and leadership that carries over into your professional life.

TITLE: Harpswell Leadership Resident Program 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 18, 2026

Applications are open for the Harpswell Leadership Resident Program 2027. The Leadership Residency is a four-to-eight-month professional development opportunity based in Harpswell’s leadership centers in Phnom Penh. LRs are women with university degrees who support, mentor, teach and collaborate with Harpswell’s Cambodian Women’s Leadership students and alumnae.

Leadership Residents (LRs) become integral members of the community, joining the Harpswell sisterhood and broader alumnae network. Through their work, LRs can expect to refine their professional interests, define their leadership style and engage in hands-on social impact.

Responsibilities

Engage as active participants in life at the leadership centers, prioritizing cultural exchange and building meaningful relationships with students and alumnae. Community building is the primary function of the role.

Host weekly office hours to support students and alumnae as needed. (This may look like editing job applications, practicing English conversation or reviewing university papers, for example.)

Facilitate 1-2 weekly critical thinking classes centered on current events, supporting student presenters in preparation and execution of classes.

Teach weekly Core Curriculum courses as needed. (Note: LRs teach a suite of six in-house courses ranging from Health & Nutrition to Analytical Writing, each 6-8 weeks long, throughout each calendar year. Curriculum and teaching materials are provided.)

Plan and execute at least one enriching cultural activity for students and alumnae per month.

Benefits

Professional Development

LRs and LR Fellows have the opportunity to develop their professional skills through hands-on experience supporting students’ learning, facilitating discussions, and building their teaching skills.

In addition, all Harpswell alumnae have access to ongoing virtual development opportunities, from professional mentorship to expert-led learning sessions.

Cultural Exchange

LRs and LR Fellows live immersed in Khmer culture at Harpswell’s leadership centers, celebrating traditional holidays and enjoying fresh Khmer food daily alongside our students and staff.

During their time at Harpswell, all LRs will have the chance to travel to the provinces for a homestay with a Harpswell student and their family.

Living Expenses

In addition to full room and board plus travel insurance, LRs and LR Fellows receive a monthly stipend reflective of cost-of-living in Phnom Penh:

LR: $330 USD

LR Fellow: $420 USD

Both LRs and LR Fellows are asked to make their own travel arrangements to and from Cambodia.

Eligibility

Open to women only;

Have experience living and working cross culturally, and a posture of curiosity and respect in regard to cultural differences;

Self-starter with the ability to be resourceful and flexible;

Excellent English language skills, both spoken and written;

A commitment to women’s empowerment and leadership development;

Willingness to work nontraditional hours (weeknights and weekends);

Teaching experience preferred but not required;

University graduate.

TITLE: Remote Internships vs In-Person Internships: The Honest Comparison

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Imagine this: you’ve just graduated and have no idea what your next steps are. You’ve studied for three to four years, and you’re now ready to enter the working world. So where do you begin? This blog is where all your answers will be.

Internships sound like a good start. You come across two types of internships, an in-person one and a remote one, and you’re unsure of which one to apply for. Both have their advantages and disadvantages. So here’s an honest breakdown of both.

In-Person Internships

Some may think that an internship will consist of running up and down getting lunch orders for your superiors and barely getting hands-on experience; this is an outdated view, and a real in-person internship means the internship will focus on giving you real experience you will use to do the job to the best of your ability. You’ll be exposed to real daily work operations; you’ll be able to collaborate with your colleagues, build professional relationships and connect with people on a face-to-face level.

You will be required to show up every day for work, where you’ll have your set working hours and a set time for when you leave. Once you join, you’ll be assigned to a supervisor who will oversee your work and ensure you become accustomed to the work, the office culture, and the company’s SOP (standard operating procedure). In-person internships offer you a tangible work experience. If you’re considering an in-person internship, it’s important to understand that it can lead to full-time employment. According to NACE’s 2025 Internship & Co-op Report, employers extended full-time offers to 62% of their 2024 interns.

Pros of an In-person Internship

Interns may find it easier to talk to people when they’re face-to-face rather than being behind a screen. They’ll find it easier to form real connections with their colleagues and meaningful relationships with their peers and mentors.

An in-person internship provides a structured work environment that’s built around schedules and punctuality; these structures allow for streamlined teamwork and instant communication with each other.

There’s also the possibility of receiving travel allowance for you to make your way to the office.

When working on-site, you have complete access to your mentors; you’re able to receive hands-on guidance on anything you may be struggling with or have any confusion cleared up instantly. Mentors can provide you with immediate feedback.

Unlike remote internships, companies will provide equipment to their interns such as laptops, headset and or phones.

Cons of In-person internships

In an In-person internship, there is not much room for flexibility; you have fixed hours. This means you will need to adjust your schedule accordingly.

If your internship is far from where you live, this may cause some constraints for you: travelling to the office, finding the right routes to take and having to wake up early in order to arrive on time.

Some interns may find the hustle and bustle of the office distracting, making it harder to focus; this could affect your work quality and your work output.

Remote internships

A remote internship often means you’ll be more than likely working for an overseas company. These types of internships are offered to students who either aren’t able to or simply don’t want to relocate but still want the experience that an internship overseas would give them. This means your entire internship is conducted online, through virtual meetings, emails and companywide messaging platforms.

When we think of an internship, most of us might have the idea of being stuck grabbing coffee for the higher-ups, sitting in meetings taking notes or printing pages till you and the printer are best friends; however, with remote internships, that worry is taken out of the equation completely. Graduates are offered the opportunity to gain valuable experience they otherwise wouldn’t be exposed to with companies from around the world, giving them insights and unique perspectives.

Pros of Remote Internships

This internship type offers you more flexibility with your time, meaning you decide your hours and where you want to work; you’re able to curate a work environment that best suits you.

When working remotely, you’ll be able to save on travel costs, whether you’re familiar with taking public transport or driving yourself around; working remotely cuts that aspect of your mornings out completely.

Some virtual internships even offer you travelling allowance in the instance where you may want to go to a cafe or a shared workspace to work at.

Remote internships offer you a different set of skills that an in-person internship wouldn’t be able to offer you, such as being tech-savvy, working on multiple different work platforms and thinking dynamically.

Cons of Remote Internships

Weak communication or a lack thereof could set you and the team back; when interns don’t communicate with their team on issues or problems or choose not to speak up when confused could push production back by days or even weeks.

A weak mentor could also lead you to feeling lost, confused, anxious and unsure of how to proceed; this would then affect the quality of work you’re putting out.

When working remotely, you’ll have to be your own motivator. It’s easier to get into that working spirit when surrounded by other people working, but with remote internships, there isn’t that motivator, which means you need to hold yourself accountable and ensure your work is complete and of good quality.

Remote vs In-person Internships: Side-by-side comparison.

Factors Remote Internships In-Person Internships
FlexibilityAble to work whenever and wherever they want Fixed working hours
Cost and travelSpends a lot less on travel feesHigher travelling costs
Mentorship Mentors are less hands-on, no micromanaging Hands-on mentorship
Networking Meet people from around the world but no face-to-face interactions Better opportunity to connect with colleagues in meaningful ways
Pay potential Can be paid or unpaid. Depends Often paid, especially at larger companies
Skill building Improves digital, independent work and communication skills Hands-on experience and understanding office work culture

Where to apply for an internship?

Now that you know the main difference between an in-person and remote internship, where should you be searching for these opportunities? A few places you should always keep in your rotation are job boards or job search engines. Such as LinkedIn, which advertises plenty of remote and in-person internships within a wide variety of roles. Next to consider would be Indeed; similar to LinkedIn, you can find an array of job ads along with a wide range of internship opportunities, both remote and in-person.

If you want to go through a facilitator to help you find and curate your internship search, then checking out places like Recruitable and Capital Placement are great options to help you through the entire process of finding an internship that suits your needs and interests.

Conclusion

Finding an internship can be hard, but it doesn’t need to be. Once you’ve done the proper research, finding one that suits you and fits your needs, then landing that interview and internship will be easy. Both internship types have their pros and cons; understanding your strengths and knowing where you may need improvement may be what helps you in choosing the right fit for you. So now that you have the comparison of an in-person internship vs a remote one, which one will you be applying for?
