TITLE: 2027-2028 Fulbright-Nehru Academic and Professional Excellence Fellowships

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications submitted prior to February 18, 2026 will NOT BE considered.

The Fulbright-Nehru Academic and Professional Excellence Fellowships are designed to provide Indian faculty, researchers, and professionals with the opportunity to teach, conduct research, or engage in a combination of both research and teaching at U.S. institutions. Depending on the specific host institution, grantees may contribute to the academic environment by developing curriculum, as well as conducting workshops and seminars. These fellowships are for four to nine months. We encourage proposals that are futuristic, innovative and technology focused.

Fields of Study

1. Critical Minerals and Supply Chains

Geology

Materials Science

Mining Engineering

4. Science and Research Collaboration

Bioengineering

Artificial Intelligence

Semiconductor Engineering

2. Defense and Security

Cybersecurity

Aerospace Engineering

Robotics and Autonomous Systems

5. Space Cooperation

Astrophysics

Planetary Science

Space Systems Engineering

Satellite Communications

3. Energy Security

Energy Engineering

Petroleum Engineering

Energy Innovation and Technology Commercialization

6. Technology and Innovation

Data Science

Quantum Computing

Electrical and Electronics Engineering

Fellowship Categories

Research

Applicants must justify the relevance of the proposed research to both India and/or the U.S., demonstrating its potential benefits for their home institution.

The feasibility of completing the research within the fellowship’s time frame (4 to 9 months) is crucial.

The applicant must explain the need to carry out the research in the U.S. and how the research aligns with the goals of the fellowship.

Teaching

Indian academics and professionals contribute to the internationalization of the curriculum at their U.S. host institutions and the understanding of recent developments not just in India but globally. The applicant should explain what they propose to teach in the U.S. within this context.

Applicants must provide the details of their current/previous teaching experience including the courses taught and teaching methodologies.

They should also indicate any involvement in curriculum or course designing, thesis guidance or any academic leadership responsibilities undertaken. The applicant should explain how this experience will be relevant to the proposed teaching in the U.S.

The applicant must explain the expected outcome and impact of their teaching on both their home and U.S. institutions and more widely to the community and professional field.

The applicant must indicate if the course/s will be individual or team taught.

Research and Teaching

Applicants can opt for a mix of research and teaching activities.

The project statement must clearly define the time allocation for each activity. For example, an applicant may allocate 60% of their time for research and 40% for teaching.

The teaching component may involve courses (individually or team-taught) or conducting a series of seminars at the U.S. institution

Affiliation

The applicant will be affiliated with one U.S. host institution. USIEF strongly recommends all applicants to indicate affiliation preference, and to correspond, in advance, with potential host institutions. If the applicant has secured a letter of invitation from a U.S. institution, they must include it as a part of the online application.

Grant Benefits

The fellowships provide a J-1 visa support, a monthly stipend, Accident and Sickness Program for Exchanges per U.S. Government guidelines, round-trip economy class air travel, a modest settling-in allowance, and a professional allowance. Subject to availability of funds, in case of grantees on eight or nine-month grants, a dependent allowance and international travel may be provided for one accompanying eligible dependent provided the dependent is with the grantee in the U.S. for at least 80 percent of the grant period.

Eligibility Requirements

In addition to the General Prerequisites

Faculty/researchers must have a Ph.D. degree with at least five years of relevant teaching/research/professional experience;

Professionals outside academe must have a master’s degree and at least five years of relevant experience;

The applicant should upload a recent significant publication (copy of paper/article) on the online application (not exceeding 30 pages);

If the applicant is employed, they must follow the instructions carefully regarding employer’s endorsement. The employer must indicate that leave will be granted for the fellowship period. The applicant must obtain the endorsement from the appropriate administrative authority on the Letter of Support from Home Institution; and

Employees of the Government of India and Indian State Governments are not eligible for any Fulbright-Nehru Fellowships. This includes civil servants in central services (such as IAS, IPS, IRS, IFS, and allied services), state government services (including state civil services), and bureaucratic staff employed in central and state ministries or departments. However, researchers, scientists, and academicians from CSIR, ICAR, ICGEB, DRDO, ISRO, ICMR, DBT institutions, DST laboratories, BARC, IISc, and IITs, as well as other centrally funded government institutions and universities, are eligible to apply.

Application Process

Please carefully review the FNAPE Applicant Instructions before starting your online application

Please refer to FNAPE Applicant Checklist before submitting the application.

In addition, you must complete and upload the FNAPE Applicant Annexure and FNAPE Letter of Support from Home Institution on your online application.

TITLE: 2027 NDMC Bursary South Africa: Apply for Disaster Management and Fire Technology Studies Before 30 September 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The National Disaster Management Centre (NDMC), through the Department of Cooperative Governance (DCoG), has opened applications for its 2027 Bursary Programme, providing an opportunity for qualifying students who intend to pursue studies in disaster management, fire technology, or fire engineering at recognised public higher education institutions in South Africa.

The NDMC bursary is aimed at supporting students pursuing relevant qualifications that contribute to the development of skills and expertise in disaster risk management and fire-related fields. The opportunity covers selected undergraduate and postgraduate-level programmes for the 2027 academic year.

Students who meet the stated academic and eligibility requirements are encouraged to prepare their supporting documents and submit their applications before the closing date.

2027 NDMC Bursary Programme

The Department of Cooperative Governance (DCoG), through the National Disaster Management Centre (NDMC), is inviting applications from qualifying students for the 2027 academic year.

The bursary is specifically intended for students who plan to study a qualifying programme in:

Disaster Management

Fire Technology

Fire Engineering

Eligible applicants may pursue an Undergraduate, Post-Graduate Diploma, Advanced Diploma, or full Master’s programme, provided that the programme falls within the relevant fields and is offered by a recognised public higher education institution in South Africa.

The programme does not include certificate qualifications or PhD programmes.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to students seeking to build academic and professional careers in areas associated with disaster preparedness, disaster risk reduction, emergency management, fire safety, fire technology, fire engineering and related areas.

What Is the NDMC Bursary?

The NDMC Bursary Programme is an educational funding opportunity administered through the National Disaster Management Centre under the Department of Cooperative Governance.

The programme is designed around academic programmes relevant to disaster management and fire-related disciplines. By supporting students in these fields, the initiative seeks to contribute to the development of individuals with the knowledge and skills required in areas connected to disaster management and fire services.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their intended qualification is directly aligned with one of the fields specified in the bursary advertisement before submitting an application.

Fields of Study Covered

The 2027 NDMC bursary focuses on qualifications in the following broad study areas:

1. Disaster Management

Students interested in disaster management may consider eligible programmes dealing with areas such as disaster risk reduction, disaster preparedness, emergency management, disaster response, recovery, resilience and related disaster management disciplines.

Applicants should verify that their specific programme is recognised as a qualifying Disaster Management qualification under the bursary requirements.

2. Fire Technology

The bursary also welcomes qualifying students pursuing Fire Technology programmes.

Fire Technology is relevant to the technical and operational aspects of fire prevention, fire protection and fire-related safety systems.

Students interested in this area should confirm that their chosen qualification meets the NDMC’s requirements.

3. Fire Engineering

Students pursuing qualifying Fire Engineering programmes may also apply.

Fire Engineering involves technical and engineering approaches to fire safety, fire prevention, fire protection and related areas.

As with the other fields, applicants should ensure that their qualification is offered by a recognised public higher education institution in South Africa and meets the requirements of the bursary programme.

Qualifications Covered by the Bursary

The NDMC states that applicants may pursue several levels of qualification during the 2027 academic year.

These include:

Undergraduate programmes

Post-Graduate Diploma programmes

Advanced Diploma programmes

Full Master’s programmes

However, there are important exclusions.

The bursary does not cover:

Certificate qualifications

PhD qualifications

Applicants considering programmes outside the listed qualification levels should carefully check the official bursary advertisement before applying.

Minimum Academic Requirements

Academic performance is an important requirement for the 2027 NDMC Bursary Programme.

Applicants must provide their most recent academic results, statement of results or academic transcript.

The stated minimum averages are:

Undergraduate, Post-Graduate Diploma and Advanced Diploma applicants

Applicants for Undergraduate, Post-Graduate Diploma and Advanced Diploma programmes must have a minimum average of 60%.

Master’s applicants

Applicants applying for Master’s-level study must have a minimum average of 65%.

This means prospective applicants should carefully review their latest academic results before beginning the application process.

Meeting the minimum academic average does not necessarily guarantee selection, as applicants must also satisfy the other requirements of the bursary programme and provide all requested documentation.

Supporting Documents Required

Applicants are required to submit supporting documentation together with their bursary application.

The NDMC application system specifies the documents that should be attached and downloaded underneath the application form in the required sequence.

Applicants should prepare the following documents:

1. Certified Copy of South African Identity Document

Applicants must provide a certified copy of their South African Identity Document.

The document should meet the certification requirements specified for the application.

Prospective applicants should make sure that the copy is clear and legible before uploading it.

2. Certified Copy of Matric Certificate

A certified copy of the applicant’s Matric Certificate is also required.

Applicants should ensure that the document is properly certified and that all relevant information can be clearly read.

3. Most Recent Academic Results

Applicants must provide their most recent academic results, statement of results or academic transcript.

This document is particularly important because the NDMC specifies minimum academic averages for different qualification levels.

The requirement is:

60% minimum average for Undergraduate, Post-Graduate Diploma and Advanced Diploma applicants.

65% minimum average for Master’s applicants.

Applicants should therefore submit their most recent available academic record.

4. Proof of Application, Acceptance or Registration

Applicants must also provide proof of application, acceptance or registration.

This document should demonstrate the applicant’s status with the relevant higher education institution.

Depending on the applicant’s circumstances, this may be proof that they have applied to, been accepted by, or registered with the relevant institution.

Applicants should make sure that the document clearly identifies the institution and the relevant programme.

5. Curriculum Vitae for Master’s Applicants

Master’s applicants are required to provide a brief Curriculum Vitae (CV).

The CV must be no longer than two pages.

This requirement specifically applies to Master’s applicants, so applicants at other qualification levels should pay attention to the distinction in the application requirements.

A concise CV should focus on relevant academic background, experience, skills, achievements and other information that may demonstrate the applicant’s suitability for postgraduate study.

6. Master’s Research Proposal

Applicants applying for Master’s programmes must also submit a research proposal.

The research proposal must focus on one of the 16 Priority Thematic Areas identified by the NDMC.

This is an important requirement for Master’s applicants and should not be overlooked.

Applicants should review the official research agenda and ensure that their proposed research topic falls within one of the specified priority thematic areas.

16 Priority Thematic Areas for Master’s Research

Master’s applicants are required to develop their research proposal around one of the NDMC’s 16 Priority Thematic Areas.

Prospective Master’s students should therefore review the official research agenda before preparing their proposal.

The research agenda is available through the NDMC bursary application system and should be consulted carefully to understand the priority areas and ensure that the proposed research is appropriately aligned.

Applicants can access the NDMC Research Agenda through the official application system’s research agenda document.

Where Can Successful Applicants Study?

The bursary is intended for qualifying programmes offered at a recognised Public Higher Institution of South Africa.

Applicants should therefore pay close attention to the type of institution they intend to attend.

The information provided by the NDMC specifically refers to recognised public higher education institutions in South Africa.

Students should verify the status of their institution and programme before submitting an application.

Important Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027 NDMC Bursary application has been updated.

Application deadline: 30 September 2026 at 23:59.

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit their applications.

Preparing documents such as certified identification, Matric certificates, academic transcripts, proof of university application or registration and, where applicable, a Master’s research proposal can take time.

It is therefore advisable to begin the application process early and ensure that all required documents have been correctly prepared and uploaded before the deadline.

Important: The Application System Does Not Support Mobile Devices

One of the most important technical instructions provided by the NDMC is that the application system does not support mobile devices.

The notice specifically states that the system does not support:

Android devices

Apple devices

Applicants should therefore avoid relying on a smartphone or tablet to complete their application.

Instead, applicants should use a desktop or laptop computer to access and complete the online application.

This is particularly important because attempting to submit an application through an unsupported device could result in technical difficulties or prevent the applicant from completing the process successfully.

How to Apply for the 2027 NDMC Bursary

Applicants who meet the requirements can apply through the NDMC Bursary Management System.

Step 1: Confirm Your Eligibility

Before beginning the application, confirm that:

You are applying for the 2027 academic year.

Your intended programme is in Disaster Management, Fire Technology or Fire Engineering.

Your qualification falls within the eligible qualification levels.

Your institution is a recognised public higher education institution in South Africa.

You meet the applicable academic average requirement.

You have the required supporting documentation.

Step 2: Prepare Your Supporting Documents

Prepare the required documents before starting the online application.

These include:

Certified South African Identity Document.

Certified Matric Certificate.

Most recent academic results, statement or transcript.

Proof of application, acceptance or registration.

Two-page maximum CV for Master’s applicants.

Master’s research proposal aligned with one of the 16 Priority Thematic Areas, where applicable.

Having the documents ready in advance can make the application process easier and reduce the risk of submitting an incomplete application.

Step 3: Access the NDMC Bursary Application System

Applications are submitted online through the NDMC Bursary Management System.

Applicants should use a supported computer rather than an Android or Apple mobile device.

Step 4: Complete the Application Form

Applicants should provide accurate information when completing the online application.

Make sure that information entered into the application corresponds with the information contained in the supporting documents.

Step 5: Upload the Required Documents

Upload the requested supporting documents according to the instructions provided by the NDMC.

Applicants should check that:

Documents are clear and readable.

Certified copies are properly certified.

The correct academic record has been provided.

Proof of application, acceptance or registration is included.

Master’s applicants include their CV and research proposal.

All required attachments have been submitted.

Step 6: Submit Before the Deadline

Once the application has been completed and all supporting documents have been uploaded, submit it before:

30 September 2026 at 23:59.

Applicants should avoid leaving submission until the last minute because technical problems, internet connectivity issues or missing documents could prevent timely submission.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity is particularly relevant to students who are planning to build academic and professional careers in disaster management, fire technology or fire engineering.

It may be suitable for:

Students pursuing eligible Undergraduate qualifications.

Students pursuing eligible Post-Graduate Diplomas.

Students pursuing eligible Advanced Diplomas.

Students pursuing eligible Master’s programmes.

Students interested in disaster management and related disciplines.

Students interested in fire technology.

Students interested in fire engineering.

Master’s applicants whose proposed research can be aligned with one of the NDMC’s 16 Priority Thematic Areas.

Applicants should nevertheless review the complete official requirements before applying.

Why This Opportunity Is Important

Disaster management and fire-related fields play an important role in protecting communities, infrastructure and public safety.

Training professionals in these disciplines can contribute to areas such as:

Disaster preparedness

Disaster risk reduction

Emergency planning

Disaster response

Recovery and resilience

Fire prevention

Fire safety

Fire protection

Fire engineering

Public safety

Risk management

For students interested in these areas, pursuing a relevant qualification can provide an opportunity to develop specialised knowledge that can be applied in government, emergency services, disaster management structures, fire services, private organisations, research institutions and other related sectors.

Tips for a Strong NDMC Bursary Application

Applicants can take several practical steps to reduce avoidable mistakes.

Check your academic average

Make sure your latest academic results meet the relevant threshold before applying.

Remember:

60% minimum for Undergraduate, Post-Graduate Diploma and Advanced Diploma applicants.

65% minimum for Master’s applicants.

Verify your programme

Do not assume that every programme with a similar title will automatically qualify.

Confirm that your intended programme falls within the specified areas of Disaster Management, Fire Technology or Fire Engineering.

Prepare certified documents early

Certification can take time, particularly when several documents are required.

Prepare your certified copies well before the deadline.

Master’s applicants should start their research proposal early

A Master’s research proposal requires considerably more preparation than simply completing an online form.

Applicants should first review the 16 Priority Thematic Areas and then develop a research proposal that clearly aligns with one of them.

Keep the Master’s CV within the required length

The NDMC specifies a maximum of two pages for the Master’s applicant CV.

Avoid submitting an unnecessarily long CV.

Use a computer

Because the application system does not support Android or Apple mobile devices, applicants should complete the application using a suitable desktop or laptop computer.

Do not wait until the final hours

The deadline is 30 September 2026 at 23:59.

Submitting early gives applicants more time to address technical issues or correct missing information.

Since its launch, the forum has brought together young people from different regions and backgrounds to exchange ideas, develop partnerships and contribute youth perspectives to discussions about the global energy transition.

The IRENA Youth Forum 2027 will focus particularly on the technologies, policies, financing and skills needed to integrate greater amounts of renewable energy into electricity systems.

The programme will provide participants with opportunities to engage with governments, international organisations, businesses, researchers, investors and other young leaders working to accelerate the transition to clean energy.

IRENA Youth Forum 2027 Theme

The theme for the 2027 forum is:

“Youth Energising the Future: Grids, Storage and Flexibility for Renewable Energy Systems”

The theme highlights the growing importance of modern electricity grids, energy storage and system flexibility as countries increase their use of renewable energy.

Participants will explore how young innovators and professionals can contribute to:

Renewable energy integration

Grid modernisation

Energy storage solutions

Flexible energy systems

Sustainable energy access

Climate and energy policy

Clean technology innovation

Financing the energy transition

Objectives of the IRENA Youth Forum

The forum aims to strengthen the role of young people in shaping the global energy transition.

Key objectives include:

1. Amplify Youth Voices

The forum will provide young people with opportunities to contribute to global energy and climate policy discussions and ensure youth perspectives are represented in decision-making.

2. Develop Knowledge and Skills

Participants will deepen their understanding of energy grids, storage technologies and system flexibility, including the policy and regulatory frameworks required to support renewable energy deployment.

3. Support Youth Innovation

The programme will help young people develop the knowledge, skills and networks needed to design, implement and scale innovative renewable energy solutions.

4. Explore Financing Opportunities

Participants will examine the role of young entrepreneurs and innovators in financing the energy transition, including ways to access capital and scale clean energy solutions.

5. Build Global Partnerships

The forum will connect youth with stakeholders from governments, the private sector, academia and international organisations, creating opportunities for collaboration and knowledge exchange.

IRENA Youth Forum 2027 Programme

The programme will take place across several activities in Abu Dhabi.

6–7 January 2027 – IRENA Youth Forum

The main Youth Forum will take place in Abu Dhabi and will include a High-Level Opening, interactive workshops and youth-focused discussions.

8 January 2027 – Closing Session

The Youth Forum closing session will take place during the Seventeenth IRENA Assembly at the St. Regis Saadiyat Island.

9–13 January 2027 – Youth-Led Activities

Selected participants will also have opportunities to take part in youth-led activities, including the Youth Booth and Lounge at the St. Regis and activities at the IRENA Pavilion during Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week at ADNEC.

The opportunity is open to young people aged 18 to 35 at the time of the forum.

Applicants should:

Be actively engaged in renewable energy, sustainability, climate action, innovation or related fields.

Be leading or contributing to a project, startup, research initiative, advocacy campaign or other activity supporting the energy transition.

Demonstrate a strong interest in collaborating with other young leaders and stakeholders.

Be motivated to contribute to the development and acceleration of sustainable energy solutions.

Applications are welcome from young people of all nationalities and countries.

The selection process will consider factors including geographic diversity, gender balance and demonstrated commitment to the energy transition.

All applications must be completed in English.

TITLE: AAU Welcomes New Governing Board Members

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana (9th August 2021) – The Association of African Universities, today inaugurated a 17-member Governing Board during its extra-ordinary General Conference which was hosted virtually.

As per its constitution, the Association of African Universities (AAU) concluded a process of nominations and election for the new Governing Board Members, following the expiration of the tenure of the old Board. The outgoing President of the AAU Governing Board, Professor Orlando Antonio Quilambo (also the Rector of Eduardo Mondlane University, Mozambique) presented the new board members to AAU’s stakeholders and called for support to enable them deliver on their core mandate.

The new Board, which assumes office immediately, and to be led by Professor Saeed Bakri Osman, President of Sudan International University, Sudan, has a key mandate of implementing the decisions made by the AAU General Conference, the supreme authority of the Association responsible for determining its general policies and direction.

Professor Quilambo (outgoing President) acknowledged the Government of Ghana for its support to the Association over the years. He also paid tribute to the outgoing Board Members for their commitment and contributions to the growth of the Association. He thanked Professor Etienne Ehouan Ehile the outgoing Secretary General for his visionary leadership and recognized the good work of the AAU Secretariat in leading the innovative process of virtual elections – which was a first for the AAU.

The constitution of the AAU allows for the following governing board positions – the President, 3 Vice Presidents, 2 Board Members from each of the 5 regions, 1 Alternate Board Member from each of the 5 regions, as well as a position for the immediate past President and the current Secretary General. The composition of the new Governing Board considers regional representation, gender balance and the profile of the different members of the Association according to the AAU byelaws.

About the Association of African Universities, AAU (https://www.aau.org/)

The Association of African Universities is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa. AAU aims to improve the quality of African higher education, and to strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflection and consensus building on issues affecting higher education. It is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, has a membership of more than 400 HEIs and has three regional offices – North Africa Regional Office (NARO) in Cairo, Egypt; East Africa Regional Office (EARO) in Khartoum, Sudan; and North America Office (NAMO) in Washington DC, USA. The Association is the technical implementing arm of the African Union in higher education – with coverage and mandate across the language divide of Africa. We have influence in the francophone, anglophone, lusophone and arabophone regions. The AAU is the coordinating agency of the Higher Education Cluster of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25) of the African Union Commission (AUC). Through our guidance, our member universities are responsible for implementing the Science, Technology and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024) of the AUC

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Organizers: Daniel Harlow, Shu-Heng Shao, Ross Dempsey, Daine Danielson and Elliot Gesteau
Held every Wednesday, 3:00 pm — 4:15pm EST., Cosman Room, 6C-442

Speaker: TBA

*Tuesday, September 15 at 12:30pm (Different day and time this week only)
Speaker: Jordan Cotler
Title: The “State” of Quantum Cosmology
Abstract: I will review why the Hartle-Hawking state coupled to a slow-roll inflaton appears to make an incorrect prediction for our universe. There are at least two possible explanations: (i) we are misinterpreting the probabilistic content of the Hartle-Hawking state and need a better formulation of quantum mechanics in quantum cosmology; or (ii) our universe is not described by the Hartle–Hawking state, raising the broader question of how inflation should be embedded nonperturbatively in quantum cosmology. I will pursue both directions: first, by studying the closed-universe inner product and its probabilistic interpretation; and second, by developing a more nonperturbative picture of inflation in quantum cosmology through a somewhat surprising connection to Liouville theory.

Wednesday, September 23
Speaker: Nikita Sopenko, IAS
Title: On the extended split property in quantum field theory
Abstract: In a quantum field theory, the Hilbert space does not factorize into degrees of freedom inside and outside a region, as reflected in the UV divergence of the entanglement entropy across the entangling surface. However, this failure is rather mild: as soon as two regions are separated by an arbitrarily small but finite distance, there is a factorization of the Hilbert space in which observables of the two regions act on different tensor factors. This property is known as the split property.

In this talk, I will discuss whether this splitting can be performed simultaneously at infinitely many locations. This is a sharp form of the question of which field theories can be realized on a lattice. It asks for an exact locality-preserving identification of the observables of the continuum theory with those of a lattice system with infinite-dimensional on-site Hilbert spaces. I will show that such an identification exists in many theories. On the other hand, I will argue that the gravitational anomaly provides a fundamental obstruction to its existence. I will also explain how this question is related to the classification of topological phases of matter in one dimension higher.

Based on joint work with Corey Jones and Ryan Thorngren.

Wednesday, September 30 (Remote talk)
Speaker: Jorge Santos, DAMTP
Title: The Low Energy Limit of BFSS Quantum Mechanics
Abstract: We investigate the low-energy regime of BFSS quantum mechanics using its holographic dual. We identify three distinct thermodynamic phases (black holes) and analyse their thermodynamic properties extensively, including phase transitions amongst the several phases. While the properties of the canonical ensemble align with existing conjectures on BFSS thermodynamics, we uncover intriguing and unexpected behaviour in the microcanonical ensemble. Specifically, for sufficiently low energies, we observe the dominance of the localised phase. Surprisingly, we also identify an energy range where the non-uniform phase becomes dominant. The transition between these phases is mediated by a Kol-type topology-changing phenomenon.

Friday, October 9 *Note day change this week only
Speaker: Raphael Bousso, UC Berkeley
Title: Quantum State of a Gravitating Region
Abstract: We propose that any compact dd-manifold with elliptic data, JJ, prepares a quantum state ∣J⟩∣J⟩ on its (d−1)(d−1)-boundary σσ. Elliptic data consists of metric and field values, or their conjugates, but not both. No asymptotic structure is required. Inner products and traces are evaluated by the gravitational path integral with closed boundary conditions obtained by gluing elliptic data manifolds. In particular, we give a prescription for the Rényi entropies SnSn​ of a subregion of σσ. In a class of examples, we find that SnSn​ is nonnegative and nonincreasing with nn, as required for consistency. We obtain the von Neumann entropy by analytic continuation and find agreement with the minimal surface prescription of Bousso and Penington.

Wednesday, February 4 (informal seminar)
Speaker: Tom Banks
Title: Diamonds in the Bulk and Large-N Scaling in AdS/CFT
Abstract: Quantum Field Theory (QFT) introduced us to the notion that a causal
diamond in space-time corresponded to a subsystem of a quantum mechanical system
defined on the global space-time. Work by Jacobson [1], Fischler and Susskind [2] and
particularly Bousso [3–5] suggested that in the quantum theory of gravity this subsystem
should have a density matrix of finite entropy. These authors formalized older intuitive
arguments based on black hole physics. Although mathematically, Type II von Neumann
algebras admit finite entropy density matrices, the black hole arguments suggest that the
number of physical states in these subsystems is finite. The conjecture that de Sitter (dS)
space has a finite number of physical states was first made in [6, 7]. Leutheusser and Liu
[8] showed that, in the N= ∞limit, causal diamonds with finite area in AdS radius units
had Type III1 von Neumann sub-algebras of the full operator algebra. They claimed that
this was true for finite values of the UV cutoff, and that the algebra was the algebra of
bulk local fields in the diamond. We will argue that the second part of this conjecture is
incorrect and that the bulk field algebra emerges only in a double scaled limit, where the
boundary UV cutoff is taken to infinity as N is taken to infinity. There is never a bulk
field theory description that resolves distances smaller than the AdS radius.

Wednesday, February 11
Speaker: Christoph Kehle, MIT
Title:The moduli space of dynamical spherically symmetric black hole spacetimes and the extremal threshold
Abstract: We study the moduli space of spherically symmetric, asymptotically flat solutions of the Einstein–Maxwell equations coupled to a real scalar field. Near the Reissner–Nordström family, I will present a proof showing that the black hole region in the moduli space is foliated by codimension-one stable manifolds of constant charge-to-mass ratio, and that the black hole formation threshold coincides exactly with the set of asymptotically extremal black holes. We further establish universal scaling laws near this threshold: the final horizon area, location of the event horizon, and final temperature (surface gravity) scale with critical exponent 1/2. This is based on upcoming joint work with Y. Angelopoulos (BIMSA) and R. Unger (Berkeley).

Wednesday, February 18 (Zoom talk), 2pm *Note different time for this week*
Speaker: Mark Van Raamsdonk, University of British Columbia
Title: 3D holographic cosmologies”
Abstract: In this talk, I’ll describe the construction of fully back-reacted cosmological solutions in three-dimensional gravity with negative cosmological constant and heavy particle matter. Focusing on time-symmetric big-bang / big-crunch closed universe cosmologies, we decribe how there is often a simple analytic continuation to an AdS Euclidean wormhole solution, but also an infinite family of other related Euclidean solutions that can give rise to the same cosmology as part of the Lorentzian continuation. We discuss possible holographic CFT constructions that can give rise to these cosmology/wormhole solutions and discuss necessary conditions on the construction for obtaining the cosmology as a dominant saddle. Based on 2601.10906, 2503.12227, and 2411.14673

Wednesday, February 25 at 3 pm (Zoom Talk)
Speaker: Ping Gao
Title: Probing Stringy Horizons with Pole-Skipping in Non-Maximal Chaotic Systems
Abstract: In this talk, we will study pole-skipping in non-maximally quantum chaotic systems. Using Rindler conformal field theories and the large-q SYK chain as illustrative examples, we argue that the pole-skipping points of few-body operators organize into trajectories in the complex frequency-momentum plane, with the leading trajectory encoding the quantum Lyapunov exponent. We further propose that these trajectories admit a natural interpretation as Regge trajectories of stringy excitations in a dual stringy black hole geometry. From this perspective, pole-skipping for an individual operator can be viewed as tracking the stringy horizon through the response of a single excitation. Our results suggest that pole-skipping reflects intrinsic properties of quantum chaotic systems and may be deeply connected to the structure of horizons in the stringy regime.

Wednesday, March 4
Speaker: Xi Yin, Harvard
Title: Revisiting Matrix String Theory
Abstract: I will revisit matrix string theory as a possibly non-perturbative formulation of the superstring S-matrix, and discuss its implications and tests.

Wednesday, March 11
Speaker: Cyuan-Han Chang, U. Chicago
Title: Seeing through the confinement screen: DGLAP/BFKL mixing and light-ray matching in QCD
Abstract: We argue that collider observables such as hadron number flux can be matched onto a linear combination of detectors/light-ray operators in perturbative QCD. The spectrum of light-ray operators in QCD is subtle, due to recombination between the DGLAP and BFKL trajectories. We explain how to define and renormalize these trajectories at one-loop, systematically incorporating their recombination. Combined with our light-ray matching hypothesis, the anomalous dimensions of recombined DGLAP/BFKL detectors yield a prediction for the energy dependence of the number of particles in a jet, as well as other predictions for more general energy-weighted hadron measurements.

Wednesday, March 18 (Zoom talk)
Speaker: Stefan Hollands, University of Leipzig
Title: Entropic Energy Conditions
Abstract: Entropic energy conditions are generalizations of the energy conditions in classical general relativity (GR) implying fundamental properties of gravity such as topological censorship, singularity formation, bounds on time-delay, positivity of gravitational mass, and more. These generalizations often involve entropic quantities reflecting the quantum nature of spacetime excitations. In this talk, I outline recent progress regarding the proofs of some of these conditions including the Quantum Null- and the Quantum Dominant Energy conditions. Mathematically, these proofs yield non-trivial theorems about von Neumann algebras.

Wednesday, April 1
Speaker: Juan Maldacena, IAS
Title: Comments on wormholes based on massless scalars
Abstract: The simplest flat space wormholes are based on massless scalar fields. In Euclidean space, they involve imaginary values for these fields. Similar wormholes exist in AdS spacetimes. We propose an interpretation of these wormholes. Namely, that they are imposing a limit on the analytic continuation of the couplings of the boundary theory. In addition, we will relate various wormholes that were previously discussed in the literature, and discuss a connection to the weak gravity conjecture.

Based on work in progress with Alex Maloney and Brian McPeak.

Wednesday, April 8
Speaker: Miguel Montero, CSIC Spain (Zoom talk)
Title: Adventures in the Riemann-Flat Landscape
Abstract: String/M-theory compactifications on Riemann-flat manifolds are a relatively unexplored corner of the string landscape where leading quantum effects on the potential can be computed explicitly and corrections are unusally well-controlled. I will describe recent explorations of this corner in the string landscape, including a de Sitter maximum in four dimensions, no-go theorems for dS minima, and constructions of AdS scale-separated vacua.

Wednesday, April 15
Speaker: Brandon Rayhaun, IAS
Title: Anomalies of Defect Parameter Spaces and a Spin-Flux Duality
Abstract: I will explain how the irreversibility of the renormalization group, together with anomalies, including anomalies in the space of coupling constants, can be used to constrain the IR phases of defects in familiar quantum field theories. As an example, I will use these techniques to provide evidence for a conjectural “spin-flux duality” which describes how certain line operators are mapped across particle/vortex duality in 2+1d.

Wednesday, April 22
Speaker: Zhenbin Yang, Tsinghua University
Title: Quantum Channel Capacity of Traversable Wormhole
Abstract: We formulate the Gao-Jafferis-Wall traversable wormhole protocol as a quantum channel and compute its quantum channel capacity. We show that this capacity is governed by the time derivative of an out-of-time-ordered correlator, hence by operator size growth in the holographic dual, and that its growth is bounded above by the Einstein gravity limit. The channel capacity therefore provides a natural benchmark for quantum simulations of traversable wormholes.

Wednesday, April 29
Speaker: Anna Biggs, Princeton
Title: A melonic quantum mechanical model without disorder
Abstract: I will describe a quantum mechanical model involving N interacting fermions without disorder that has a large N melonic expansion. In particular, it has the same Schwinger-Dyson equations and low energy physics as the \mathcal{N} = 2 supersymmetric SYK model. The model is SU(2) invariant, and the supercharge involves the SU(2) 3j symbol. I will conceptually explain why the model has a melonic expansion, discuss various solvable corners, and present some results of exact diagonalization for small values of N. Expanded around states with maximal angular momentum, the model is approximated by a two dimensional CFT. The BPS states have a simple description in that regime. Based on arXiv:2601.08908 with L. Lin and J. Maldacena.

Wednesday, May 6
Speaker: Andreas Schachner, Cornell
Title: The Road Goes Ever On: Corrections to de Sitter Uplifts
Abstract: I will begin with a brief status update on de Sitter constructions in string theory, focusing on uplift scenarios from supersymmetric AdS minima in Type IIB flux compactifications. The viability of such constructions depends on the stability of the uplifted vacuum, which in turn requires control over corrections beyond leading supergravity. I will then discuss a class of higher-derivative D-brane corrections relevant to this problem. The main part of the talk will present a computation of protected (\alpha’)^2 couplings on the D3-brane worldvolume action using Schwinger proper time in M-theory. The calculation is formulated as a one-loop eleven-dimensional superparticle amplitude in an M5-brane background compactified on a two-torus. I will describe the resulting modular completion, including D-instanton effects, and explain how these corrections enter the analysis of anti-D3-brane uplifts.

Wednesday, May 13
No Seminar

Wednesday, May 20 at *1pm
Speaker: Henry Lin, Princeton
Title: The sign problem and the bootstrap
Abstract: I will discuss the sign problem in BFSS/D0 branes and related super Yang Mills theories using an effective field theory approach. I will then discuss the matrix bootstrap approach to the D0 brane theory which does not suffer from the sign problem. The talk should be accessible to people unfamiliar with BFSS.

Monday, September 15 at 11am *Special Seminar: note different day and time*
Speaker: Herman Verlinde, Princeton
Title: Comments on de Sitter Holography
Abstract: In this talk I will discuss aspects of de Sitter holography using the correspondence between the double scaled SYK model and pure 3D de Sitter gravity as a guide.

Wednesday, September 17 (Zoom talk)
Speaker: Lorenz Eberhardt, University of Amsterdam
Title: Evaluating one-loop string amplitudes
Abstract: I will explain a general technique that evaluates one-loop string amplitudes exactly in terms of an infinite series originating from certain Lorentzian singularities in moduli space. It is based on a non-holomorphic extension of the Rademacher procedure that applies to any integral of a modular function (with certain boundedness conditions). I will then discuss the concrete example of the one-loop four-graviton scattering amplitude for type II superstrings and the physics we can extract from these methods. This talk is based on joint work with M.M. Baccianti, J. Chandra, T. Hartman and S. Mizera.

Wednesday, September 24
Speaker: Zimo Sun, IAS
Title: The $epsilon$-expansion and Boundary/Defect CFTs
Abstract: The $\epsilon$-expansion is a widely used technique to study aspects of renormalization group flows and critical phenomena. In this talk, I will discuss recent developments of the $\epsilon$-expansion in the study of boundary and defect universality classes of the O(N) model in d dimensions, with particular focus on the so-called ordinary and normal transitions. I will also discuss comparisons with numerical approaches, such as conformal bootstrap, Monte Carlo simulations and fuzzy sphere regularizations.

Wednesday, October 1
Speaker: Thomas Grimm, Universiteit Utrecht
Title: Tameness and Complexity in Quantum Field Theory and String Theory
Abstract: Inspired by the idea that physical systems should exhibit only finite complexity, I present a framework to quantify the logical information required to specify functions and sets. The central concept is tameness: the requirement that physical theories and observables are definable within o-minimal structures and their sharp refinements. These mathematical frameworks forbid overly wild behavior and guarantee a description of finite geometric complexity. I explain that tameness is realized in a broad class of effective field theories and recall its conjectured link to a UV completion. One application is to perturbative quantum field theory, where tameness constrains amplitudes. In string theory, effective theories arising from compactifications naturally follow these principles. Compatible with many ideas about finiteness, this perspective points toward the existence of universal complexity bounds for UV-consistent theories.

Wednesday, October 8
Speaker: Ahmed Almheiri, NYU Abu Dhabi
Title: Black hole disappearance
Abstract: Not much is known about what happens at the end of black hole evaporation. Pushing the semi-classical evolution well beyond its regime of validity suggests that the final Cauchy slice breaks into a piece that remains behind the event horizon, anchored to the point where the singularity meets the horizon, and a piece that detaches from the horizon to become a Cauchy slice for all future time evolution in slightly perturbed empty space. The evidence for this picture, however, remains scant. In fact, it is disputed by evaporating AdS black holes in two dimensions. I will offer a new scenario by analyzing evaporating black holes in a modified version of JT gravity that admits both empty AdS and black hole solutions. I will argue that the key to black hole disappearance is the emission of a baby universe that extracts the matter that formed the black hole, using the same mechanism for global symmetry violation in quantum gravity. This non-perturbative transition transforms the black hole into an excited state without a horizon that proceeds to disappear through reliable semi-classical evolution. This talk is based on work in progress with Shadi Ali Ahmad, Simon Lin, and Shoy Ouseph.

Wednesday, October 15
Speaker: Kasia Budzik, Harvard University
Title: Finite-N indices from branes and negative branes
Abstract: Finite-N effects in large-N gauge theories, such as trace relations, are expected to be dual to non-perturbative phenomena in quantum gravity, such as Giant Graviton branes. A convenient setting to study these effects are BPS indices of U(N) (and U(N|M)) invariants. I will review the recent progress on the so-called Giant Graviton expansions, which express the finite-N indices as a series of corrections to the infinite-N result, and discuss another expansion in terms of branes and negative branes. I will also propose a physical interpretation of Murthy’s Giant Graviton Expansion in terms of “Koszul-dual” branes and negative branes. This talk is based on arXiv:2509.20451 and work in progress with Davide Gaiotto.

Wednesday, October 22
Speaker: Wayne Weng, Cornell
Title: Replica manifolds, pole skipping, and the butterfly effect
Abstract: Black holes are strongly chaotic quantum systems: small perturbations to its state grow exponentially in time. In holographic theories, this can be quantified by the butterfly velocity, defined using out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) or entanglement wedge reconstruction, which can in principle be different. There are many explicit calculations showing that the two velocities are in fact equal, including in theories with higher curvature corrections, but there was no general explanation for this apparent coincidence. We show that it follows from a deeper relationship

between replica manifolds, shockwaves, and the so-called pole skipping mode in the thermal two-point function.

Based on [2504.08139] with Wan Zhen Chua and Thomas Hartman.

Wednesday, October 29
Speaker: Thomas Dumitrescu, UCLA
Title: 2+1 Dimensional QED in a Magnetic Field
Abstract: I will discuss massless Dirac fermions integrating with a relativistic photon in 2+1 spacetime dimensions. After reviewing what is known about the dynamics of this strongly-coupled theory in the Lorentz-invariant vacuum, I will study it in the presence of a uniform magnetic field. When the field is sufficiently strong, this problem can be solved exactly. The resulting ground state spontaneously breaks some of the global symmetries, and we can precisely compute the spectrum of excitations and the low-energy effective action in this state. I will discuss parallels with quantum Hall ferromagnets in condensed matter physics.

Wednesday, November 5
Speaker: Jonah Kudler-Flam, IAS
Title: Stringy algebras, stretched horizons, and quantum-connected wormholes
Abstract: While the supergravity limit of AdS/CFT has been extensively explored, the regime in which stringy dynamics dominate is far less understood. Working in the small g_s (but finite alpha’) regime, I will demonstrate that the resulting Hagedorn spectrum leads to the breakdown of the split property, a strengthening of the locality principle, for regions that are within a string length of each other. This leads to a precise algebraic definition of stretched horizons and stretched quantum extremal surfaces. When stretched horizons exist, there is an associated nontrivial horizon algebra. Furthermore, applying the algebraic ER=EPR proposal leads to the emergence of type III0 von Neumann factors, which characterizes how regions can have a quantum Einstein-Rosen bridge even if they are geometrically disjoint. Based on 2510.01556 with Aidan Herderschee.

Wednesday, November 12
Speaker: Arvin Shahbazi-Moghaddam, UC Berkeley
Title: Constraints on the resolution of spacetime singularities
Abstract: What happens at spacetime singularities is poorly understood. The Penrose-Wall singularity theorem constrains possible scenarios, but until recently its key assumption–the generalized second law (GSL)–had only been proven perturbatively, severely limiting this application. We highlight that recent progress enables a proof of the GSL in holographic brane-world models, valid non-perturbatively at the species scale
cG (with c the number of matter fields and G Newton’s constant). This enables genuine constraints: an outer-trapped surface in the Einstein gravity regime implies geodesic incompleteness non-perturbatively at the species scale. Conversely, any genuine resolution must evade Penrose’s criteria. We illustrate both possibilities with explicit examples: the classical BTZ black hole evolves to a more severe singularity, while a null singularity on the Rindler horizon is resolved, both by species-scale effects. Subject to the GSL, these constraints on singularity resolution apply beyond brane-worlds: namely, in any theory with a geometric UV scale–roughly, where the metric remains well-defined but classical Einstein gravity breaks down.

Wednesday, November 19
Speaker: Andreas Karch, University of Texas
Title: Sharp Transitions for Subsystem Complexity
Abstract: The circuit complexity of time-evolved pure quantum states
grows linearly in time for an exponentially long time. This behavior has
been proven in certain models, is conjectured to hold for generic
quantum many-body systems, and is believed to be dual to the long-time
growth of black hole interiors in AdS/CFT. Achieving a similar
understanding for mixed states remains an important problem. We
demonstrate that holography predicts several sharp transitions in the
time evolution of subsystem complexity and show that at least some of
these transitions are also realized in random quantum circuits.

Wednesday, November 26
No Seminar This Week

Wednesday, December 3
SPECIAL INFORMAL SEMINAR
Speaker: Alon Faragg
Title: Toward stable de Sitter vacua in string theory
Abstract: In addition to the supersymmetric vacua in 10 dimensions, heterotic-string theory gives rise to non-supersymmetric vacua that contain physical tachyons in compactifications to 4 dimensions. These tachyons can be projected out by the GSO projections, and produce string amplitudes that are finite at one—loop. Over the past few years, we developed systematic methods to analyse the spectrum of the tachyon free non-supersymmetric heterotic-string vacua and study their phenomenological properties. We analysed the would be Fayet-Iliopoulos term in non-supersymmetric heterotic string vacua and a D-term uplift of the vacuum energy from negative to positive energy. Examples of positive uplift are found for models with explicitly broken supersymmetry as well as models with Scherk-Schwarz breaking. The moduli space of the string compactifications will be discussed and vacua with positive vaccum energy and in which all geometrical moduli are fixed will be presented, with the eventual aim being to produce a string model with stable moduli and positive vacuum energy.

*Monday, December 8 at 4pm – note different day and time
SPECIAL SEMINAR
Speaker: Pau Figueras
Title: The Endpoint of the Gregory Laflamme Instability of Black Strings in Higher Derivative Gravity
Abstract: In this talk I will present ongoing work on the endpoint of the Gregory-Laflamme(GL) instability of five dimensional black strings in higher derivative theories of gravity. As is well-known, in general relativity, the endpoint of the GL instability is likely to be a naked singularity, which forms in finite asymptotic time. This instability is generic in higher dimensions in the sense that it does not require fine-tuning and it affects black strings in Kaluza-Klein spaces as well as rapidly spinning black holes in asymptotically flat spaces and in AdS. Therefore it is important to understand its endpoint. It is expected that higher derivative corrections should affect the dynamics close to the singularity. In this talk I will quantify the latter using numerical relativity tools and I will discuss how the sign of the coupling affects the formation of the singularity at the endpoint.

Wednesday, December 10
Speaker: Sahand Seifnashri, IAS
Title: Symmetry Transmutation
Abstract: We begin with a review of generalized global symmetries and their various applications. Next, we describe the phenomenon of symmetry transmutation, in which an ordinary global symmetry in the UV theory transmutes into a generalized higher-form symmetry in the effective low-energy theory. Notably, transmuted symmetries are exact rather than accidental. We then discuss gauge theory examples in which the anomaly of the UV symmetry is matched by the anomaly of the transmuted symmetry in the IR. Finally, we discuss symmetry transmutation in QCD and its implications for confinement.

Wednesday, February 12
Speaker: Sarah Harrison, Northeastern
Title: Comments on Non-Invertible Symmetries in K3 CFTs and the Conway Moonshine Module
Abstract: There is an established connection between discrete symmetry groups of K3 non-linear sigma models and a distinguished N=1 chiral SCFT called the Conway moonshine module. More specifically, all symmetry groups of K3 NLSMs preserving the N=4 superconformal algebra can be obtained as subgroups of “Conway zero”, the group of symmetries of the Conway module, and their explicit action on the BPS spectrum can (almost always) be obtained via traces in the Conway module. A natural question is whether this relation extends to fusion category symmetry of these theories. I will discuss positive evidence in this direction, by exploring examples of non-invertible topological defect lines in K3 NLSMs and the Conway module. This is based on work in progress with R. Angius, S. Giaccari, and R. Volpato.

Wednesday, February 19
Speaker: Hee-Cheol Kim, Postech
Title: Finite Landscape of 6d (1,0) Supergravity
Abstract: I will talk about a bottom-up proof of the finiteness of the number of massless fields in any 6d supergravity theories preserving 8 supercharges. From this, sharp bounds on the number of tensor multiplets and the rank of gauge algebras will be derived. I will also show that these bounds are saturated by specific theories realized through F-theory compactifications on elliptic Calabi-Yau threefolds.

Wednesday, February 26
Speaker: Diandian Wang, Harvard
Title: Ensemble of 2d BCFTs and Open-closed 3d Gravity
Abstract: I will discuss extensions of recent developments on interpreting 3d gravity as a CFT ensemble, focusing on the case of CFTs with boundary (BCFTs). In alignment with the spirit of AdS/BCFT, the 3d theory now involves end-of-the-world branes. We propose an action for the brane that matches Takayanagi’s original proposal at large-c but deviates at finite-c. We argue that the proposed action gives an open-closed extension of Virasoro TQFT upon quantization.

Wednesday, March 5
Speaker: Sean Colin-Ellerin, Berkeley
Title: Generalized entropy of gravitational fluctuations
Abstract: Quantum corrections to holographic entanglement entropy are well-understood for ordinary quantum matter in a classical gravitational background. These famously lead to a unitary Page curve for evaporating black holes in AdS (coupled to a bath). However, the correct treatment of quantum fluctuations of the metric, including graviton excitations, is a longstanding problem. I will provide a gauge-invariant prescription for the generalized entropy of gravitons in anti-de Sitter space in terms of areas and bulk entanglement entropy, generalizing the quantum extremal surface prescription to accommodate fluctuations in the semiclassical spacetime geometry. I will give some justification for the prescription using covariant phase techniques and explicitly check it in a non-trivial example. Along the way, I will identify a class of perturbative graviton states that have parametrically larger generalized entropy, in the small G_N expansion, than any low-energy excitations of an ordinary quantum field.

Wednesday, March 12
Speaker: Matthew Dodelson, Harvard
Title: Quasinormal ringdown in the SYK model
Abstract: Thermal correlators in large N systems equilibrate at late times, but the precise late-time behavior is unknown away from holographic and free field limits. In this talk I will analyze this problem in the case of the SYK model away from the low-temperature limit. I will then explain how to think about the result in terms of a stringy black hole.

Wednesday, March 19
Speaker: Beatrix Muehlmann, IAS
Title: The complex Liouville string
Abstract: I will introduce a new 2d gravity/matrix integral duality. The bulk theory is a two-dimensional string theory defined by coupling two copies of Liouville CFT with central charges c = 13 \pm is on the worldsheet. We call this string theory the complex Liouville string. I will argue that the complex Liouville string admits a dual description in terms of a double-scaled two-matrix integral. The string amplitudes, which are the main observables of the complex Liouville string, can be interpreted as cosmological correlators of massive particles, integrated over the metric at future infinity of dS3 to define gauge invariant observables. Furthermore we obtain evidence that the dS3 Gibbons-Hawking entropy can be reproduced exactly by counting the degrees of freedom in the dual matrix integral.

Wedesday, March 26
No Seminar, Spring Break

TUESDAY, April 1 at 12:00**
Speaker: Julian Sonner, University of Geneva
Title: Chaos and stochasticity in holography
Abstract: We employ a probabilistic mesoscopic description to draw conceptual and quantitative analogies between Brownian motion and late-time fluctuations of thermal correlation functions in generic chaotic systems respecting ETH. In this framework, thermal correlation functions of `simple’ operators are described by stochastic processes, which are able to probe features of the microscopic theory only in a probabilistic sense. We apply this formalism to the case of semiclassical gravity in AdS3, showing that wormhole contributions can be naturally identified as moments of stochastic processes. We reinterpret the gravitational results from the boundary perspective, promoting the OPE data of the CFT to probability distributions. The outcome of this study shows that semiclassical gravity in AdS can be naturally interpreted as a mesoscopic description of quantum gravity.

Wednesday, April 9
Speaker: Gary Horowitz, UC Santa Barbara
Title: Smooth extremal horizons are the exception not the rule
Abstract: TBDWednesday, April 16
Speaker: Ji Hoon Lee, ETH Zurich
Title: On Branes and Trace Relations
Abstract: We propose and study a holographic relation between the states of giant graviton branes in anti-de Sitter space and trace relations in the dual gauge theory. In a computation of the partition function of half-BPS states in AdS5 x S5, we find that the maximal giant is an unstable saddle point and that its Lefschetz thimble corresponds to the quantization of an imaginary phase space. The states resulting from the quantization of this phase space contribute negatively to the partition function. The cohomological treatment of trace relations in N=4 SYM suggests that these D-brane states can be regarded as bulk duals of trace relations. We suggest that the Lefschetz trace formula, which computes bulk observables as an alternating sum of the expectation values in an ensemble of states built on each classical open string vacuum, may be a useful way to formulate the holographic map at finite N.

Wednesday, April 23
Speaker: Zohar Komargodski, Simons Center
