Actions that will have clear, measurable outcomes. They look for applications that have given careful consideration to the indicators that will be used to evidence impact.

Sustainable projects that will continue well beyond the Whitley Award. Successful proposals will demonstrate long-term planning.

Projects that demonstrate value for money and ability to manage funding at the Whitley Award level (£50,000).

Work that would benefit from greater visibility, particularly projects that could gain momentum through media exposure and wider recognition.

TITLE: Michael Sunmoni from Nigeria is OD Young Person of the Month – July 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Michael Sunmoni is a health entrepreneur and youth development advocate from Ikorodu, Lagos, Nigeria. He is the founder of SerielleHealth, a digital maternal health platform that improves access to maternal healthcare for women in underserved communities across Lagos, with plans to expand its reach across Nigeria. His work is driven by the belief that no woman’s chances of surviving pregnancy or childbirth should depend on where she lives. Through SerielleHealth, he is working to close gaps in access to maternal health information and care for women who are too often left behind.

Learn more about his work and be inspired

Michael’s interest in maternal health grew out of his own experiences in Ikorodu. Growing up, he saw how women in many communities struggled to access reliable health information and timely medical care. He watched families delay seeking treatment because services were unavailable, unaffordable, or simply too far away. He became particularly concerned about women who faced pregnancy with little support. Many did not recognise the warning signs of complications, while others reached health facilities only after their conditions had worsened. These experiences convinced him that many maternal deaths and complications could be prevented if women received the right information early enough. That conviction led him to establish SerielleHealth.

Building SerielleHealth
SerielleHealth is a digital maternal health platform designed to connect women with trusted health information, practical guidance, and support throughout pregnancy and after childbirth. From the beginning, Michael developed the platform with underserved communities in mind. It responds to everyday realities such as poor internet access, shared mobile phones, and varying literacy levels. Rather than expecting women to adapt to technology, SerielleHealth was designed around the circumstances in which they live. Alongside his work in digital health, Michael has participated in youth-led initiatives, health outreach programmes, and community engagement activities that encourage young people to contribute to improving healthcare in their communities. He believes that young people have an important role to play in strengthening health systems across Africa.

Challenges Along the Way
Building a health enterprise has come with significant challenges. One of the greatest has been earning the trust of communities that have experienced years of inadequate healthcare services. Michael understands that lasting change depends as much on relationships as it does on technology. Like many young founders, he has also had to overcome limited funding opportunities and the difficulty of securing partnerships in a highly competitive sector. Despite these challenges, he has remained committed to building practical solutions that respond to the needs of the communities he serves.

Leadership and Recognition
Michael has participated in several leadership and entrepreneurship programmes, including the Young African Leaders Initiative (YALI, Cohort 44), the Millennium Fellowship, Clinton Global Initiative University, United People Global, and the African Business Coalition for Health Entrepreneurs. His work has received recognition both in Nigeria and internationally. He received the Ten Outstanding Persons Award for Scientific and Technological Development from JCI Nigeria, University of Lagos. SerielleHealth was recognised by the Savvy Fellowship and selected among the Top 10 participants at the Design4Health Designathon 2026. He was also invited to the Presidential Mentorship Youth Retreat 6.0 by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, where he joined other young leaders working across different sectors in Nigeria. His selection among the Top 12 finalists at ODIC 2025 further strengthened his commitment to building solutions that improve maternal healthcare in underserved communities.

Looking Ahead
Michael’s goal is to strengthen SerielleHealth’s impact across Lagos while preparing for expansion into other parts of Nigeria. He is focused on building evidence that demonstrates how accessible digital health tools can improve maternal health outcomes. He is equally committed to supporting young innovators and encouraging more young people to develop practical solutions to the challenges facing their communities. As part of his professional growth, he continues to pursue opportunities that deepen his knowledge of health innovation, entrepreneurship, and social impact.

His Perspective
Michael believes that communities often described only by their challenges also possess the ideas, talent, and determination needed to create lasting change. Through SerielleHealth and his wider work, he hopes to contribute to a future where every woman, regardless of her location or income, can access the information and care she needs for a safe pregnancy and childbirth.

TITLE: Cairo Prepares to host the 20th Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
As the dates for the 20th COREVIP of the Association of African Universities approaches, all hands are on deck in Cairo, in preparation to host Africa’s topmost Chief Executive Officers of various Higher Education Institutions.

AAU’s 20th COREVIP is holding in Cairo, Egypt from July 8 -11, 2019 and is envisaged to draw over 1,500 higher education stakeholders, including Vice Chancellors, Presidents, Rectors, Academics, Government Representatives and Industry Representatives.

In line with this, a team of senior officials from the AAU Secretariat embarked on a site visit to Cairo, from 27th – 30th May, 2019 to among others, ensure that arrangements are advanced towards the hosting of the Conference.

A series of meetings with the Local Organizing Committee and other stakeholders, as well as site visits to the Conference venue, selected hotels and other key venues selected for the Conference also ensued. The team concluded, that indeed, the colleagues in Cairo had been busy with full preparations for the Conference.

The team from AAU also participated in a major side event “Al-Azhar forum for African-Arab Network” which is organized by AAU Northern African Regional Office (NARO). This meeting was attended by various institutions who are keen to participate in COREVIP, including higher education institutions, Banks, NGOs, ministries’ representatives, international organizations, TVET Egypt, journalists and several others.

Addressing participants at the Arab-Africa Network forum, the Secretary General of the AAU, Prof. Etienne Ehile, thanked all key stakeholders and individuals, including Prof. Ahmed El-Tayeb, the Al-Azhar Grand Imam, Prof. Mohamed El-Mahrasaway, the Al-Azhar University President and Prof. Amany El-Sharif, NARO director for their immense contribution to hosting the 2019 COREVIP in Egypt.

Background

The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the Arab Republic of Egypt and Al-Azhar University, is organising its 20th biennial Conference of Rectors, Vice Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) at the Al-Azhar International Conference Centre, in Cairo, Egypt from 8-11 July 2019.

Conference Theme and Subthemes

This year’s conference is being held under the theme ‘The Role of Higher Education Institutions in Promoting the Continental Education for Strategy for Africa’ and is set to convene distinguished scholars and practitioners to discuss and exchange experiences on the main conference theme and the subthemes indicated below;

Sub-Theme 1: Focus on the science and mathematics curricula in youth training and disseminate scientific knowledge and culture in society

Sub-Theme 2: Expand TVET opportunities at tertiary levels and strengthen linkages between the world of work and education and training systems

Sub-Theme 3: Revitalize and expand tertiary education, research and innovation to address continental challenges and promote competitiveness.

Sub-Theme 4: Promote peace education and conflict prevention and resolution at all levels of education and for all age groups.

Sub-Theme 5: Improve management of education systems as well as build and enhance capacity for data collection, management, harness the capacity of ICT to improve access, quality and management of education and training systems.

Sub-Theme 6: Promote mobility through harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation systems.

Sub-Theme 7: Identify new directions in improving management of education through enhanced capacity for data collection and management, research and scholarship and efficient governance of HEIs in Africa.

The over 1500 expected participants of the COREVIP will comprise executive heads of AAU member institutions, top-notch African scholars, representatives of student bodies, as well as representatives of sub-regional, regional and international organisations. Members from the donor and development agencies that partner with the AAU in carrying out its mandate of improving the quality of higher education in Africa will also be in attendance. In addition, Ministers of Higher Education and other higher education policy think tanks will partake in this august conference.

About COREVIP

The Conference of Rectors, Vice-Chancellors and Presidents of African Universities (COREVIP) is an assembly of the Chief Executive Officers of AAU member institutions or their representatives. The Conference is held every two years with the purpose of collectively examining themes identified as common concerns and priorities for the development of higher education in member institutions and Africa in general; making recommendations primarily to members, as well as to the Governing Board of the Association, and to the Secretariat; and acting as a mid-term forum for taking stock of the implementation of the decisions of the General Conference and recommending corrective actions.

TITLE: Caribbean Biodiversity Fund Board of Directors 2026: Call for Expressions of Interest and Nominations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF) is inviting expressions of interest and nominations from suitably qualified individuals who may be considered for appointment to its Board of Directors. The opportunity provides individuals with an interest and experience in conservation, biodiversity protection, sustainable development and regional environmental governance with an opportunity to contribute to the strategic direction of an important Caribbean environmental fund.

The proposed Board appointment will run for a maximum of two years, with the proposed term beginning on 1 October 2026.

Applications and nominations must be submitted by 7 September 2026.

About the Caribbean Biodiversity Fund

The Caribbean Biodiversity Fund (CBF) is a regional environmental fund established to provide stable, long-term financial resources for conservation, ecosystem-based adaptation and biodiversity protection across the Caribbean.

The Fund plays a role in supporting long-term approaches to environmental conservation and sustainable development throughout the region. Its work involves the mobilization and management of financial resources intended to support biodiversity and ecosystem-related priorities.

As a regional institution handling resources for environmental and conservation purposes, effective governance and oversight are important to ensuring that the Fund operates responsibly and achieves meaningful strategic impact.

It is within this context that the CBF Governance Committee has opened a formal call for individuals who may be considered for vacant positions on its skills-based Board of Directors.

CBF Board of Directors Opportunity

The CBF is seeking expressions of interest and nominations from suitably qualified individuals for possible appointment to its Board of Directors.

The Board is described as skills-based, meaning that the selection process is intended to identify individuals whose knowledge, experience and professional capabilities can contribute to the governance and strategic oversight of the Fund.

The appointment is proposed for a maximum period of:

Two years

Proposed start date: 1 October 2026

Application deadline: 7 September 2026

The opportunity is therefore intended for individuals who are interested in contributing at a governance and strategic level to a regional organization focused on biodiversity conservation and environmental financing.

Why Serve on the CBF Board?

Serving on the Caribbean Biodiversity Fund Board provides an opportunity to contribute directly to the governance and strategic development of a regional institution working on biodiversity and conservation.

According to the opportunity announcement, Board members can contribute to several important areas.

1. Help Shape the Strategic Direction of the CBF

Directors will have an opportunity to contribute to the strategic direction of the Caribbean Biodiversity Fund.

Board-level participation can therefore involve contributing perspectives and expertise that help guide the institution’s priorities and long-term development.

The Board plays an important role in ensuring that the Fund continues to develop in a way that supports its conservation and biodiversity objectives.

2. Support Strong Governance

The CBF is seeking Board members as part of efforts to ensure:

Robust fiduciary oversight

Objective governance

Strategic impact

This makes Board participation particularly important because the Fund is responsible for managing resources intended to support environmental and conservation priorities.

Directors can contribute to the governance structures and oversight needed to support responsible institutional decision-making.

3. Contribute to Regional Conservation

The CBF’s work is focused on conservation, ecosystem-based adaptation and biodiversity protection across the Caribbean.

Board members therefore have the opportunity to contribute to an institution whose activities are connected to some of the region’s broader environmental priorities.

The position provides an opportunity to support efforts aimed at protecting biodiversity and strengthening long-term financing for conservation.

4. Engage With Regional and International Partners

Board service can also provide opportunities for Directors to engage with partners working in conservation and sustainable development.

The announcement notes that Directors may have opportunities to represent the CBF at:

Regional meetings

International meetings

Convenings

Other strategic engagements

Where appropriate, these engagements may also involve travel.

This can provide Board members with opportunities to participate in discussions involving Caribbean and international partners committed to conservation and sustainable development.

Nature of the Board Appointment

The CBF Board opportunity is different from a conventional employment position.

Board service is voluntary and does not carry remuneration.

This means individuals appointed to the Board should understand that they will not receive a salary or regular remuneration for their Board service.

However, Directors may have opportunities to represent the CBF through regional and international engagements, including meetings and other strategic activities.

The announcement specifically notes that travel may be involved where appropriate.

Appointment Term

The proposed appointment is for a maximum of two years.

The proposed commencement date is:

1 October 2026

Applicants should therefore be prepared for the possibility of serving on the Board during the proposed two-year period, subject to the terms and conditions of the appointment.

Who Is This Opportunity For?

The CBF is specifically seeking suitably qualified individuals who may be considered for vacant positions on its skills-based Board of Directors.

The announcement emphasizes that the Board is skills-based, indicating that professional knowledge, expertise and relevant capabilities are important considerations.

However, the information provided in the announcement does not specify a detailed list of educational qualifications, years of professional experience, specific professional disciplines or individual technical skills required from applicants.

Therefore, applicants should carefully review the official application materials and nomination process for any additional requirements that may apply.

Geographic Eligibility

The Caribbean Biodiversity Fund is a regional Caribbean environmental fund, and the Board opportunity is connected to its work across the Caribbean.

However, the supplied announcement does not explicitly state a nationality restriction or provide a specific list of countries from which applicants must come.

It also does not provide a specific race or ethnicity requirement.

Applicants should therefore refer to the official CBF application materials for any additional geographic or eligibility requirements that may apply.

Application Deadline

The deadline for submitting an expression of interest or nomination is:

7 September 2026

Interested individuals should ensure that their applications or nominations are submitted before the stated deadline.

Because the opportunity is for Board-level service and the appointment is proposed to begin on 1 October 2026, interested candidates should allow sufficient time to review the requirements and prepare their submission.

Proposed Start Date

The proposed start date for the Board appointment is:

1 October 2026

The appointment is expected to run for a maximum of two years.

How to Apply

Individuals interested in being considered for the CBF Board of Directors should submit their expression of interest or nomination through the official application process.

Application deadline: 7 September 2026

Apply Now:
CBF Board of Directors Expression of Interest Application

Applicants should carefully review the official application form and provide the information requested as part of the expression-of-interest or nomination process.

Important Information for Potential Applicants

It is a Board appointment opportunity, rather than a conventional employment vacancy.

The call for Board members is closely connected to the CBF’s need for strong institutional governance.

The Fund was established to provide long-term financial resources for:

Because these areas involve significant regional environmental priorities, the Board has an important role in supporting responsible governance and strategic decision-making.

The proposed Board term is up to two years, beginning on 1 October 2026. Board service is voluntary and unpaid, although Directors may have opportunities to represent the CBF at regional and international meetings, convenings and other strategic engagements, including travel where appropriate.

TITLE: KHK CURE Fellowships 2027/2028 in Germany: Funded Research Fellowships Offering Up to €7,200 Per Month

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the 2027/2028 Käte Hamburger Centre for Cultural Practices of Reparation (KHK CURE) Fellowship Programme at Saarland University in Germany. The internationally oriented programme will offer up to 12 research fellowships to scholars working in cultural studies, the humanities, and social sciences for the academic year running from October 2027 to September 2028. The fellowships are offered pending approval by the German Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR).

Successful applicants can spend between six and twelve months in Saarbrücken, Germany, conducting an independent research project while participating in the interdisciplinary intellectual life of KHK CURE. Depending on the applicable funding arrangement and the Fellow’s qualifications, financial support may take the form of a monthly stipend of approximately €6,100 to €7,200 before taxes, or institutional compensation to enable a salaried scholar to take leave from their home institution. Travel to and from Saarbrücken is also reimbursed once in accordance with the applicable Saarland travel-expense rules.

The application deadline is 30 November 2026. Applicants must have completed, submitted, and successfully defended their doctorate by that date.

About the Käte Hamburger Centre for Cultural Practices of Reparation

The Käte Hamburger Centre for Cultural Practices of Reparation, commonly referred to as KHK CURE, is an institute for advanced study located at Saarland University in Saarbrücken, Germany.

The Centre has been funded by the German Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space since 2024 and brings together international scholars from different academic traditions to investigate questions surrounding reparation and irreparability.

The Fellowship Programme is a central component of the Centre’s work. Each year, KHK CURE brings up to 12 international scholars from disciplines concerned with culture to Saarland University as visiting researchers. Fellows work alongside the Centre’s directors, academic staff, and other Fellows while pursuing their own research projects.

The Centre aims to establish an international and comparative research environment in which scholars from different intellectual traditions can examine how societies respond to historical, social, environmental, political, and cultural forms of harm.

KHK CURE Fellowship 2027/2028 Research Theme: “Things”

For the 2027/2028 academic year, applicants must develop a project related to the annual theme:

Things

The 2027/2028 theme places particular emphasis on the material dimensions of reparation. KHK CURE is interested in objects, artefacts, material environments, and practices through which repair, reuse, mending, and related processes acquire cultural and political meaning.

Applicants should therefore consider how material objects and environments can participate in processes of reparation, both practically and symbolically.

The “Things” theme forms part of a four-year thematic sequence within the Centre:

2024/2025: Theory

2025/2026: Society

2026/2027: Bodies

2027/2028: Things

Applicants for the current call must specifically apply for the October 2027 to September 2028 Fellowship year.

Understanding KHK CURE’s Research on Reparation and Irreparability

KHK CURE’s broader research programme examines the fundamental problem that many forms of damage cannot simply be reversed.

Examples include:

Destruction of cultural heritage caused by colonialism

Consequences of war and violence

Historical injustice

Individual and collective trauma

Displacement

Environmental destruction

Climate change

Damage to social and cultural worlds

The Centre approaches reparation not merely as an attempt to restore a previous state, but as a process of building a future while recognizing that the consequences of past harm may remain visible, experienced, or remembered.

Economic compensation and legal remedies may be important aspects of addressing injustice, but KHK CURE’s research focuses particularly on cultural and social practices of reparation.

These can include:

Oral narratives

Written narratives

Literature and poetry

Linguistic practices

Rituals

Music

Visual art

Film

Theatre

Exhibitions

Historiography

Public discourse

Scientific and scholarly practices

Other forms of knowledge production

The Centre investigates how these practices can respond to damage and create possibilities for future life even when past harms cannot be completely repaired.

Three Main KHK CURE Research Areas

Applicants must connect their proposed project to at least one of the Centre’s three principal research areas while also engaging with the 2027/2028 annual theme of “Things.”

1. History

The history research area deals particularly with memory politics and cultural responses to traumatic or suppressed pasts.

Relevant areas may include:

Colonialism

Genocide

War

Historical violence

Suppressed collective memories

Cultural heritage

Historical injustice

Commemoration

Memory practices

Researchers may investigate how societies remember, reinterpret, display, preserve, reconstruct, or negotiate histories of damage.

2. Experience

The experience research area examines lived experiences of damage, loss, injury, alienation, and displacement.

This can include issues such as:

Physical injuries

Psychological trauma

Experiences of war

Political displacement

Forced migration

Loss

Alienation

New forms of community

Changing forms of subjectivity

Projects may consider how individuals or communities experience harm and how cultural practices contribute to rebuilding social relations and future possibilities.

3. Nature/Culture

The third area considers transformations in relationships between humans, nature, technology, and their environments.

It includes questions concerning:

Environmental loss

Climate-related damage

Cultural ecology

Loss of habitats

Environmental insecurity

Future habitability

Technology

Human self-understanding

New information technologies

KHK CURE particularly encourages perspectives that connect history, experience, and nature/culture rather than treating the fields as completely separate.

Who Can Apply for the KHK CURE Fellowships?

The general CURE Fellowship is open to scholars working in:

Cultural studies

Humanities

Social sciences

Applicants must have completed their PhD, meaning that the doctoral thesis must have been both submitted and successfully defended by the application deadline of 30 November 2026.

Candidates must also be professionally active in academia or research.

However, holding a formal university position is not mandatory. Independent scholars and freelancers may apply as long as they remain professionally active in academic or research work.

Can Artists Apply?

Yes, but the academic Fellowship has specific requirements for artists.

Artists are encouraged to apply if they:

Hold a completed doctorate;

Have experience collaborating with academic researchers; and

Propose an independent, research-based project connected to KHK CURE’s central research questions.

An artistic practice alone without the required doctorate does not satisfy the eligibility criteria for this particular Fellowship call.

KHK CURE separately hosts artists-in-residence, including artists, authors, musicians, and filmmakers, but that arrangement is distinct from the academic Fellowship described in the current call.

Who Is Not Eligible?

The following groups cannot apply for the 2027/2028 KHK CURE Fellowship:

Retired individuals, including professors emeriti

Scholars who have not completed their doctorate by the deadline

Artists who have not completed a doctorate

Members or employees of Saarland University

Applicants based elsewhere in Germany are not automatically excluded. German nationals and researchers employed at other German universities may apply as long as they satisfy all other eligibility requirements.

International Applicants Are Welcome

The KHK CURE Fellowship is internationally oriented and welcomes applications from qualified researchers regardless of nationality.

The Fellowship Programme is specifically designed to bring researchers from around the world to Saarland University and create an international and interdisciplinary cohort.

There is therefore no general restriction limiting applications to Germany, Europe, or European Union nationals.

Eligible researchers may apply from countries across:

Africa

Asia

Europe

North America

South America

Oceania and the Pacific

Other regions worldwide

International applicants who need immigration authorization for Germany may require a research visa under Section 18d of the German Residence Act. KHK CURE states that successful Fellows will receive advice and support with the visa process.

Fellowship Duration

KHK CURE Fellowships are awarded for:

A minimum of six months and a maximum of twelve months.

Fellowships begin on:

1 October 2027

The relevant Fellowship year continues until:

30 September 2028

Applicants should therefore propose a project that can realistically be completed within the selected Fellowship duration.

Up to 12 Fellowships Available

KHK CURE expects to welcome up to 12 Fellows for the 2027/2028 academic year.

Selection is competitive. The Centre notes that the number of applications normally considerably exceeds the number of available positions.

One Fellowship is specifically allocated through the University of the Greater Region (UniGR), while the remaining Fellowships are funded through Saarland University and the German Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space.

Financial Support: €6,100 to €7,200 Per Month

One of the most significant aspects of the KHK CURE programme is its substantial financial support.

The Fellowship guidelines provide two principal funding models.

Funding Option 1: Monthly Stipend

Fellows who take unpaid leave from their home institution, as well as eligible independent scholars, may receive financial compensation through a stipend.

According to the official call, the stipend is approximately:

€6,100 to €7,200 per month before taxes, depending on the Fellow’s qualifications.

The Fellowship FAQ states that Fellows taking unpaid leave receive a monthly scholarship of at least €6,100 before taxes, depending on experience and qualifications.

The final financial arrangement will therefore depend on the successful applicant’s circumstances and qualifications.

Funding Option 2: Teaching Replacement

A Fellow who maintains their existing salary and employment benefits may instead have KHK CURE compensate their home institution for the cost of a teaching replacement during their stay at the Centre.

Financial arrangements under this route are coordinated individually with the Fellow’s institution.

Travel Support

KHK CURE reimburses expenses associated with travelling:

To Saarbrücken at the beginning of the Fellowship; and

From Saarbrücken when the Fellowship concludes.

The reimbursement is made once in accordance with the Saarland Travel Expense Act.

Applicants should note that ordinary research or business travel undertaken during the Fellowship is not funded by KHK CURE.

Office and Research Facilities

Every Fellow receives a fully equipped individual workspace at the Centre.

In addition, Fellows gain access to Saarland University’s wider interdisciplinary research environment and become part of KHK CURE’s international academic community.

The University has extensive European and cross-border networks, including:

University of the Greater Region

Transform4Europe

Cluster for European Studies

These structures contribute to the Centre’s wider international and interdisciplinary setting.

Accommodation in Saarbrücken

Modern accommodation at Saarland University may be arranged upon request.

For individual Fellows, accommodation is currently indicated at approximately:

€1,250 per month.

Fellows must generally pay their accommodation costs themselves.

The Centre’s FAQ separately states that Fellows whose partners or children live with them full-time in Saarbrücken can receive suitable family accommodation free of charge, along with assistance in locating childcare or schools.

Family Allowances

Family members may accompany Fellows to Saarbrücken.

Where eligible family members reside with the Fellow full-time during the Fellowship, the Centre states that additional monthly support may include:

€100 per month for a partner

€400 per month for the first child under 18

€100 per month for each additional child under 18

Travel expenses for accompanying family members are not covered by KHK CURE.

Costs Fellows Must Cover Themselves

The Fellowship should not be described as covering every personal expense.

Fellows remain responsible for costs including:

Ordinary rent where applicable

Health insurance

Public liability insurance

Personal accident insurance

General living expenses

Research or business travel during the Fellowship

Applicable taxes

Health insurance is legally required in Germany, and Fellows must ensure that appropriate coverage is in place.

The FAQ gives a broad indication that food expenses in Germany may range from approximately €400 to €800 per month, depending on household size and individual circumstances.

Fellows Must Live in Saarbrücken

This is not a remote Fellowship.

Successful applicants are expected to reside in Saarbrücken, Germany, for the Fellowship period and participate actively in the Centre’s research programme.

Fellows are expected to engage in activities such as:

Colloquia

Working groups

Conferences

Workshops

Centre events

Research discussions

Publications

Extended absences for long research trips or outside stays are not compatible with the programme.

With approval from the Centre’s Executive Committee, Fellows may also organize workshops or participate in teaching and other academic events with CURE’s research and cultural cooperation partners.

Independent Research Project Requirement

Every application must propose an independent research project to be carried out during the Fellowship.

The project must:

Relate substantively to CURE’s broader research programme on reparation and irreparability.

Connect to at least one of the three research areas: history, experience, or nature/culture.

Engage meaningfully with the 2027/2028 annual theme of “Things.”

Be academically original and feasible within the proposed Fellowship period.

The project’s intellectual fit with the Centre is a significant element of the selection process.

What Should the Project Description Contain?

The official FAQ provides particularly useful guidance on preparing the project proposal.

Applicants should include:

A clearly formulated research question

A clear research objective

Engagement with the annual theme

Explanation of the project’s relevance to reparation

Theoretical positioning within existing scholarship

Definitions of important concepts where necessary

A clearly explained methodology

Description of the corpus, sources, material, or object of investigation

A coherent academic argument

Bibliography

The entire project description, including the bibliography, must not exceed five A4 pages.

KHK CURE explicitly asks applicants to submit writing that reflects their own individual scholarly voice and states that AI-generated application texts are discouraged.

Application Documents Required

Applicants must submit their application through CURE’s official online application system by 30 November 2026.

The submission consists of several components.

Online Application Form

Applicants must complete the official CURE form, including an abstract and personal and academic information.

First PDF

Applicants must upload one PDF containing:

A motivation letter of no more than one A4 page

A curriculum vitae of no more than three A4 pages

A publication list

Second PDF

Applicants must upload a separate PDF containing:

Project description

Bibliography

The project document must not exceed five A4 pages and must clearly demonstrate how the proposed research connects with CURE’s programme, one or more of its research fields, and the annual theme.

Formatting Requirements

Application materials must comply with the following formatting specifications:

Minimum font size: 11

Minimum line spacing: 1.15

Project proposal: Maximum five A4 pages including bibliography

Motivation letter: Maximum one A4 page

CV: Maximum three A4 pages

Photographs: Do not include photographs

Applicants should ensure that their documents comply exactly with these limits.

Languages Accepted

Applications may be submitted in any of the following languages:

English

German

French

Candidates are therefore not restricted to submitting their materials in German.

Selection Criteria

Applications will be evaluated by the KHK CURE Academic Advisory Board.

Important assessment factors include:

Academic quality of the proposed research

Originality

Conceptual relevance to CURE’s research programme

Applicant’s qualifications

Applicant’s motivation

Career stage

Contribution to an intellectually balanced and internationally diverse cohort

The Centre also seeks diversity in academic traditions and cultures when creating each cohort.

Diversity and Equal Opportunity

KHK CURE expressly welcomes applications regardless of:

Gender

Nationality

Ethnic origin

Social origin

Religion

Worldview

Disability

Age

Sexual orientation

Sexual identity

Applicants are assessed according to the Fellowship’s academic and formal criteria rather than nationality or ethnicity.

Special UniGR Fellowship

One of the available positions is designated as the University of the Greater Region Fellowship.

The applicant must satisfy all standard CURE Fellowship requirements and must also be employed in an academic position at one of the following institutions when applying:

University of Trier

University of Liège

University of Luxembourg

University of Lorraine

RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau

Applicants must submit proof of employment.

Employees of Saarland University are specifically excluded.

The UniGR candidate is assessed through a parallel selection process by the same Academic Advisory Board.

Important Application Timeline

The principal dates for the 2027/2028 Fellowship cycle are:

Stage
Date

Application deadline
30 November 2026

Selection outcome
By the end of April 2027

Fellowship begins
1 October 2027

Maximum Fellowship period ends
30 September 2028

Applicants are asked not to contact the Centre about their application status before the announced notification period.

Application Confirmation

After submitting the online application, candidates should receive an automatic confirmation email.

Anyone who does not receive confirmation should contact KHK CURE directly using the contact details provided on the official application page.

Why the KHK CURE Fellowship Is a Significant Research Opportunity

The programme combines substantial financial support with an extended period of protected research time in an interdisciplinary Institute for Advanced Study.

For selected scholars, the Fellowship provides an opportunity to:

Develop an independent research project

Work alongside an international cohort

Participate in interdisciplinary scholarly exchange

Contribute to conferences, workshops, and publications

Access Saarland University’s research environment

Explore theoretical and comparative approaches to reparation

Strengthen international academic networks

Spend six to twelve months focusing extensively on research

Its international scope and relatively broad disciplinary eligibility make the Fellowship particularly relevant to researchers whose work crosses conventional disciplinary boundaries.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

Because the programme receives substantially more applications than available Fellowships, applicants should not submit a generic research proposal.

A competitive application should demonstrate a clear intellectual connection between the candidate’s existing scholarship and CURE’s research agenda.

In particular, applicants should ensure that the project clearly answers four questions:

Why reparation?
Explain precisely how the research contributes to questions of reparation, irreparability, damage, repair, or future-building.

Why “Things”?
Demonstrate a substantive rather than superficial relationship with the 2027/2028 theme.

Why CURE?
Show how the project’s theoretical and methodological approach benefits from engagement with the Centre.

Why this applicant?
Use the CV, publications, and motivation letter to establish the scholarly expertise required to complete the proposed project.

Because CURE specifically requests individually authored academic work and discourages AI-generated application text, applicants should prepare their proposal in their own scholarly voice.

Application Deadline

The final deadline to apply for the KHK CURE Fellowship 2027/2028 is:

30 November 2026

Applications must be submitted through the official online application form.

Official KHK CURE Fellowship Application Page

Conclusion

The KHK CURE Fellowships 2027/2028 at Saarland University provide an exceptional opportunity for established and early-to-mid-career postdoctoral researchers in cultural studies, the humanities, and social sciences to pursue an independent project in Germany within a highly international research environment.

With up to 12 Fellowships, a duration of six to twelve months, financial support potentially ranging from €6,100 to €7,200 per month before taxes, reimbursement of arrival and departure travel, dedicated workspace, and access to an interdisciplinary academic community, the programme provides substantial support for scholars studying reparation, irreparability, culture, history, experience, nature, and materiality.

For the 2027/2028 cohort, projects must engage with the annual theme “Things” and connect to at least one of the Centre’s research areas. Applicants must have completed and defended a doctorate by the 30 November 2026 deadline, and successful candidates will begin their Fellowship in Saarbrücken on 1 October 2027.

TITLE: LEVEL Youth Policy Program 2027: Fully Funded Public Policy and Leadership Training for Indigenous and Racialized Youth in British Columbia

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The LEVEL Youth Policy Program (YPP) 2027 is an eight-month leadership and public policy development program designed for Indigenous and racialized immigrant and refugee youth living in British Columbia, Canada. The program provides participants with practical training, mentorship, policy development skills and opportunities to understand how public policy is created and influenced.

Organized through LEVEL, a youth engagement initiative of the Vancouver Foundation, the program is designed to help young people build the knowledge, confidence and practical skills needed to participate in public policy discussions and advocate for issues affecting their communities.

Applications for the 2027 cohort are currently open, giving eligible young people an opportunity to join a cohort of emerging leaders from across British Columbia.

LEVEL Youth Policy Program 2027 Overview

The LEVEL Youth Policy Program brings together young people who are interested in leadership, advocacy and public policy. Participants explore how government works, how policy decisions are made, who influences those decisions and how communities can advocate for meaningful policy and systems change.

The program also places importance on Indigenous governance, cultural awareness, trauma-informed learning and respectful engagement with people from different backgrounds and lived experiences.

Rather than focusing only on classroom-based learning, the program combines training, practical activities, mentorship, community engagement and the development of an individual policy project.

By the end of the program, participants will have developed a policy ask addressing an issue that affects their community. LEVEL will support participants in turning their policy ask into a professionally designed and printed policy ask booklet.

There is no final examination.

What Participants Will Learn

Through the LEVEL Youth Policy Program, participants will have the opportunity to develop a deeper understanding of public policy and advocacy.

Key areas of learning include:

Understanding the meaning and importance of public policy

Exploring how public policy is developed and implemented

Understanding the different levels of government in Canada

Learning about Indigenous governance structures

Identifying public policy issues affecting communities in British Columbia

Understanding the stakeholders involved in policy development

Learning how to engage with decision-makers and other stakeholders

Developing strategies for influencing public policy

Building capacity for policy advocacy and systems change

Exploring storytelling and new narratives as tools for shaping policy

Developing a policy ask around an issue affecting the participant’s community

The program also encourages participants to reflect on what it means to conduct policy and advocacy work on unceded Indigenous territories.

A Practical and Community-Based Learning Experience

The LEVEL Youth Policy Program is designed to be interactive rather than purely theoretical.

Participants will join a cohort of other young leaders from across British Columbia and take part in individual and group-based learning activities.

Activities may include:

Short readings and learning materials

Educational videos

Hands-on policy activities

Meetings with mentors and coaches

Interviews with members of local communities

Examination of existing advocacy campaigns

Group discussions and collaborative activities

Personal learning reflections

Development of a policy project

Participants are expected to complete assigned readings, activities and projects on time and actively participate throughout the program.

Trauma-Informed and Culturally Conscious Learning Environment

An important feature of the LEVEL Youth Policy Program is its emphasis on creating a culturally conscious and trauma-informed learning environment.

Participants will have opportunities to learn from and engage with Elders, mentors, counsellors, faculty members and other leaders with experience in public policy and community advocacy.

The program is designed to create a learning environment where participants can engage in meaningful conversations while respecting the different identities, experiences and journeys of members of the cohort.

LEVEL states that it also provides support for participants to access Elders and trauma-informed therapists during the program.

Final Policy Project

One of the most important components of the LEVEL Youth Policy Program is the final policy project.

Participants will identify a public policy issue that affects their community and develop a policy ask intended to advance change on that issue.

Participants receive support from mentors, subject-matter experts and a writing coach while developing their policy asks.

The final policy ask will be turned into a professionally designed and printed policy ask booklet.

Previous cohorts have developed policy projects covering a wide range of issues, including housing, immigration, Indigenous communities, migrant workers, social services, education, family support and racial equity.

The Policy Project Library published by LEVEL provides examples of projects produced by previous cohorts.

$1,500 Policy Project Stipend

The LEVEL Youth Policy Program does not provide a general participation honorarium. However, participants receive a $1,500 stipend to support the development of their individual policy ask.

This funding is intended to assist participants as they research, develop and complete their policy projects.

LEVEL also provides design, editing, printing and other support for producing the final project.

Fully Funded Participation

There is no cost to participate in the LEVEL Youth Policy Program.

The program provides participants with training materials, including a workbook containing learning objectives, readings, assignments, videos and other resources.

LEVEL also provides support for travel associated with required in-person program activities.

Participants who live outside Metro Vancouver can receive support for:

Travel

Accommodation

Meals during in-person modules and gatherings

For participants living within Metro Vancouver, LEVEL provides transit tickets to assist with transportation costs.

During in-person gatherings, LEVEL also provides refreshments and meals and makes efforts to accommodate dietary requirements.

Support for Participants With Work or Study Commitments

Applicants who are studying or working can still apply.

Successful applicants can request a confirmation letter from LEVEL explaining the purpose of the program and the leadership opportunity it provides. This letter can be used when requesting time away from school or work.

However, participants remain responsible for making arrangements to catch up on missed assignments, examinations or work responsibilities.

Childcare and Caregiving Support

LEVEL recognizes that participants may have childcare or caregiving responsibilities.

An Institutional Workshop is a capacity building workshop organized by the AAU for staff of a particular institution. TITLE: What drives the mean along-shelf flow in the Northwest Atlantic coastal ocean?

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Chen, K., & Yang, J. (2024). What Drives the Mean Along-Shelf Flow in the Northwest Atlantic Coastal Ocean? Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans, 129(7), e2024JC021079. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JC021079

Upper panel: along-shelf transport at the four cross-shelf sections: Middle Labrador Shelf, Southern Labrador Shelf, Scotian Shelf, and Middle Atlantic Bight. Results from three scenarios are shown: control experiment (ctrl, black circle), no wind stress experiment (noWind, red square), and no continental runoff experiment (noRiver, blue diamond). Transport is integrated from surface to bottom, from the coast to 200 m isobath. Lower panel: the influence of wind (ctrl-noWind) and buoyancy (ctrl-noRiv) on the along-shelf transport. Image provided by Ke Chen.

A long-standing hypothesis is that the steady along-shelf circulation in the Northwest Atlantic (NWA) coastal ocean is driven by buoyancy input from continental freshwater runoff. However, the influence of freshwater runoff has not been adequately evaluated or compared with other potential driving mechanisms. This study investigates the roles of both wind stress and freshwater runoff in driving the mean along-shelf flow in the NWA coastal ocean and examines other potential drivers using a newly developed high-resolution regional model with realistic forcing conditions. The results reveal that wind stress has a greater impact than freshwater runoff on the overall mean circulation and along-shelf sea-level gradient on the NWA shelf. While continental freshwater consistently contributes to equatorward along-shelf flow and a higher sea level along the coast, wind stress is more effective in setting up the broad-scale circulation pattern, driving the along-shelf flow on the Labrador Shelf and opposing it in the Mid-Atlantic Bight and the Scotian Shelf. In addition to local wind and freshwater runoff, sub-Arctic inflow from higher latitudes is an essential component of the NWA shelf circulation system. This remote driver directly influences the along-shelf flow and helps insulate the shelf flow from the Gulf Stream on the southern shelves.

TITLE: CRAFT-OA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
EU Projects

Science Policy Support

Image: iStock/Ismagilov

Creating a Robust Accessible Federated Technology for Open Access

After several decades of evolving, Open Access (OA) publishing is now at the centre of scientific communication, providing access to scientific publications without barriers. In Diamond Open Access, authors can publish free of charge as the institutional sector with universities, research institutions or libraries provide the necessary technological infrastructure. While the commercial model of Open Access dominates in anglophone journals from the Global North, the Diamond OA model shows a much higher level of diversity and origin. However, the Diamond OA landscape continues to be fragmented, is often underfunded, and is not always technically proficient enough to develop its full potential for science and society. The CRAFT-OA project aims to consolidate the Diamond OA publishing landscape.

The project focuses on four threads of activities to improve the technical and organisational infrastructure of Diamond OA:

Provide technical improvements for journal platforms and journal software

Build communities of practice to foster overall infrastructure improvement

Increase visibility, discoverability and recognition for Diamond OA publishing

Integrate Diamond OA publishing with EOSC and other large-scale data aggregators.

CRAFT-OA’s 23 consortium partners from 14 European countries are all engaged in institutional publishing and its infrastructures, and committed to sustaining and developing capacities in the field. Many CRAFT-OA partners are leading organisations at national and European levels in terms of open publishing, and represent internationally visible centres of expertise in Open Science and FAIR implementation with strong connections to EOSC.

Within 36 months, CRAFT-OA will deliver technical and community tools, training events, training materials, information, and services for the Diamond OA institutional publishing environment. It will foster communities of practice with the capacity to sustain the project improvements over time.

TITLE: Sign up now to enroll in the Theories of International Relations course

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Course Name: Theories Of International Relations

Duration: 1 week

Target group:

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE

This course focuses on ideas about, and explanations of, international relations, concentrating mainly (but not exclusively) on introductions to the major theoretical approaches in the academic study of international relations since 1945. The key theories and approaches to be examined include realism and neo-realism; theories about war, security and the use of force in international relations; classical liberalism, globalization, and transformation in world politics; theories about inter-state cooperation and transnationalism; the concept of international society; constructivism and the impact of law and norms in international relations; neo-Marxist and critical theory approaches to international relations; and normative theory and international ethics. The course seeks to provide not only an overview of the key theoretical debates but also a ‘toolkit’ of concepts that students can use to analyze international relations. Throughout the course, an emphasis will be placed on the need to marry empirical analysis and normative reflection in the study of international relations. In order to add specific content to the theoretical structure, a ‘real world’ example has been chosen for reflection in the final week (The trade War between China and the USA), where the theories can be assessed as they are applied.

At the end of this course, the student / participant will be able to:

Understand the international system and its actors.

Demonstrate an understanding of a range of theories underpinning international relations.

Discuss critically, and write knowledgeably about, major IR theories, relating these both to

contemporary events and historical processes.

TITLE: New UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report Fellowship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
A new UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Report Fellowship programme has just been launched thanks to the support of the Open Society Foundations. The Fellowship aims to strengthen the evidence base on comparative education.

The first call for fellowships is online with applications expected by September 28. Such calls will be issued twice a year with the aim of hosting an average of three fellows per year in the team. Fellowships will typically provide or contribute to the funding for fellows to conduct their research and build their networks for one year, of which at least one month would be spent at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris.

Based on the successful model of the Thomas J. Alexander Fellowships at the OECD, the GEM Report Fellowship programme will support academic researchers and research-oriented policy makers to carry out studies in the area of international and comparative education with a special focus on:

utilizing the GEM Report’s data resources, notably those household and school surveys linked to the World Inequality in Education database, to strengthen analyses of global, regional and national education trends on issues of access, equity, inclusion and quality;

strengthening the content of the GEM Report with respect to its coverage of important issues at the regional and national level, through evidence-based analyses of educational policy and practice;

helping advance the SDG 4 monitoring agenda, especially on issues related to the global and thematic indicator framework that have been highlighted in previous reports; and

supporting the themes of forthcoming GEM reports, i.e. inclusive education in 2020(including a special focus on (i) disability (ii) Latin America) and the role of non-state actors in education in 2021.

The fellowships are open to exceptional individuals who have quantitative research skills, demonstrate a potential for transformational impact in their domain, and share a commitment to provide more people with better educational opportunities. Learning from their experience with the team, the fellows will also be able to participate in and influence the work of the GEM Report. A stipend of up to $25,000 for the duration of the fellowship and full travel costs for at least one month to be spent in Paris will be provided to each of the fellows.

Please share the news with your networks and visit the online call for proposals to find out more.

TITLE: World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 26, 2026

Applications are open for the World Bank Group Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge 2026. As of 2025, more than 2 billion people remained offline. Over the next decade, 1.2 billion young people in the Global South will reach working age yet current trends point to only 420 million new jobs being created to meet them.

Artificial intelligence is changing what is possible in development. But most AI tools have been built for a world with reliable connectivity, a smartphone in hand, and a user already fluent in how to interact with AI. The Small AI for Development Hackathon Challenge is an open call to young innovators worldwide to build AI solutions that work in the real conditions facing developing economies, where the people with the most to gain are the furthest from the tools being built.

Three winners will be selected from the entries generated at the hack-a-thon, one from each of the categories – Agriculture, Health, and Tourism. Open to applicants aged 18 to 35, in line with the UN definition of youth, across the World Bank member countries.

TITLE: Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027: Up to $3,000 Project Funding Plus $3,600 Stipend for Indigenous Women Leaders

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027 – Cohort V, a year-long leadership and community development opportunity designed to support emerging Indigenous women leaders who are creating meaningful change within their communities.

Through its Indigenous Women’s Program, Land is Life is inviting Indigenous women from around the world to submit applications for the 2027 fellowship cohort. The program is particularly focused on women who are committed to advancing Indigenous Peoples’ rights, gender equality, land and resource rights, environmental justice, community well-being and sustainable livelihoods.

Successful fellows will receive a comprehensive package of support that combines personalised mentorship, technical assistance, leadership development, international networking opportunities and financial support. Fellows can receive up to USD $3,000 to design and implement a community-level project, in addition to a USD $3,600 stipend to support their participation throughout the fellowship.

Applications opened on 25 August 2026 and must be submitted by 24 September 2026 at 11:00 PM EST.

About the Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027

The Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship is an initiative of Land is Life, a global coalition of Indigenous Peoples working to advance self-determination and collective rights for Indigenous Peoples across the world’s seven sociocultural regions.

Land is Life established its Indigenous Women’s Program in 2022. The program was designed and is led by Indigenous women, with a focus on strengthening the ability of Indigenous women and their organisations to assert their individual and collective rights.

Its work particularly supports Indigenous women in Africa, Asia and throughout the Americas in their efforts to access, use and control land and natural resources, strengthen their livelihoods, and promote and protect the rights of their peoples.

Through the Indigenous Women’s Program, participants have received support including funding, stipends, mentorship and training opportunities. This assistance has also helped Indigenous women leaders participate in international spaces where decisions affecting Indigenous Peoples and their communities are discussed.

The fellowship component began in 2023 and has since supported more than 15 women in successfully implementing community projects.

Purpose of the Indigenous Women’s Fellowship

The year-long fellowship seeks to nurture the next generation of Indigenous women leaders.

Rather than focusing exclusively on theoretical learning, the fellowship supports women who are already taking innovative steps within their communities and gives them the resources, knowledge and networks needed to turn their ideas into practical projects.

The fellowship particularly supports initiatives that contribute to:

Gender equality;

Recognition and protection of Indigenous Peoples’ land and resource rights;

Community well-being;

Indigenous women’s leadership;

Protection and promotion of Indigenous Peoples’ rights;

Stronger community livelihoods;

Environmental and climate justice;

Indigenous governance and autonomy; and

Greater participation of Indigenous women in decision-making.

An important part of the fellowship is the implementation of a community-level project. Applicants are therefore expected to identify an issue affecting their community and propose an achievable initiative that responds to that challenge.

What Does the Land is Life Fellowship Offer?

Selected participants in the 2027 Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship will receive a combination of financial, technical and professional development support.

1. Up to USD $3,000 in Community Project Funding

Each fellow can receive funding and technical support of up to USD $3,000 to design and implement a community-level project.

The project should address issues relevant to Indigenous Peoples and place particular attention on the rights, experiences and needs of Indigenous women and girls.

This component gives fellows the opportunity to translate their leadership ideas into tangible initiatives within their own communities.

2. USD $3,600 Fellowship Stipend

Selected fellows will also receive a USD $3,600 stipend.

The stipend is intended to support each fellow’s participation throughout the program, providing additional financial support as they undertake fellowship activities and work on their community projects.

3. Personalised Mentorship

Participants will receive personalised mentoring from experienced Indigenous women leaders with demonstrated experience in advancing Indigenous Peoples’ rights.

This mentorship gives fellows an opportunity to learn directly from women who have practical leadership, advocacy and community experience.

4. Technical Support

In addition to financial assistance, fellows will receive technical support for the design and implementation of their community projects.

This can help participants develop realistic, achievable projects and strengthen their capacity to manage initiatives that produce meaningful results for their communities.

5. Bimonthly Training and Knowledge Sharing

Fellows will participate in bimonthly training sessions addressing important topics related to Indigenous Peoples’ rights.

These learning opportunities are designed to strengthen participants’ knowledge while encouraging the exchange of ideas, experiences and approaches between Indigenous women from different communities and regions.

6. Leadership Development

Leadership development is a central part of the fellowship.

The program seeks to strengthen the voices of Indigenous women and increase their decision-making power within their communities and beyond.

Participants will have opportunities to develop skills and confidence that can support their continued work as community leaders and advocates.

7. Networking Opportunities

Fellows will be able to build and strengthen relationships with local, regional and global partners and allies.

These networks can be valuable beyond the fellowship itself, particularly for women seeking to expand community initiatives, exchange knowledge or collaborate with other Indigenous leaders and organisations.

8. Advocacy Support

The fellowship also provides advocacy support that can help participants engage in national and international decision-making spaces.

This creates opportunities for Indigenous women leaders to contribute their perspectives and community experiences to wider discussions concerning Indigenous rights and related issues.

Six Central Themes of the Indigenous Women’s Program

Applicants must develop a community project aligned with the central themes identified by the Indigenous Women’s Program.

The six areas are:

1. Climate Change and Environmental Justice

Projects can address issues such as:

Climate change adaptation and mitigation;

Biodiversity protection; and

Critical examination of false climate solutions.

Indigenous communities are often directly connected to their territories and natural resources, making Indigenous leadership particularly important in discussions about environmental protection and climate resilience.

2. Land Rights and Territorial Defence

Projects may focus on protecting Indigenous territories from threats such as:

Extractive activities;

Forced evictions;

Illegal logging;

Illegal mining; and

Other pressures affecting Indigenous territories.

This theme also encompasses Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) protocols.

3. Food Sovereignty and Livelihoods

Potential initiatives can address:

Agroecology;

Seed sovereignty; and

Economic alternatives to industrial agribusiness.

Projects under this theme can explore ways Indigenous communities can strengthen control over their food systems while protecting traditional practices and developing sustainable livelihoods.

4. Health and Well-Being

Projects can address a range of community health and well-being priorities, including:

Access to traditional medicine;

Mental health support following disasters;

Maternal health;

Child health; and

Violence prevention.

5. Economic Empowerment and Livelihood Strengthening

This theme can include projects related to:

Community enterprises;

Market access;

Sustainable income generation; and

Women’s economic leadership.

The focus is on strengthening economic opportunities in ways that support Indigenous communities and women’s leadership.

6. Governance

Projects can also support Indigenous organisations and communities in strengthening governance.

Areas may include:

French; or

Panama;

Ecuador;

Peru;

Mali;

Step 3: Obtain a Letter of Recommendation

An Indigenous Peoples organisation;

An equivalent official source.

The Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship is distinctive because it combines leadership development with practical community action.

Successful applicants are not simply participating in training sessions. They will have an opportunity to design and implement their own community projects while receiving financial resources, technical support and mentorship from experienced Indigenous women leaders.

The Land is Life Indigenous Women’s Program Fellowship 2027 – Cohort V offers an important opportunity for emerging Indigenous women leaders to strengthen their leadership abilities while implementing practical projects in their own communities.

With personalised mentorship, bimonthly training, technical assistance, networking and advocacy opportunities, up to USD $3,000 in community project funding and a USD $3,600 participation stipend, the fellowship provides both financial and capacity-building support.

The program is particularly relevant for Indigenous women working on issues connected to climate and environmental justice, territorial and land rights, food sovereignty, health and well-being, economic empowerment, sustainable livelihoods and Indigenous governance.

Eligible Indigenous women between the ages of 18 and 35 who can communicate fluently in English, French or Spanish and have not previously participated as a Land is Life fellow are encouraged to review the requirements carefully and prepare their community project proposals.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Hale Bradt

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Hale Bradt PhD ’61,
Professor of Physics Emeritus

by Elizabeth Chadis, MaryGlenn Vincens and Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2008

Hale Bradt PhD ’61, Professor of Physics, Emeritus, poses with his Benjamin Franklin Award for his book Wilber’s War. Photo courtesy of Hale Bradt.
This year, Professor Hale Bradt established a Fund from his IRA to support the Department’s graduate students. The Fund, named in honor of Mrs. Barbara E. Thomas, undergraduate administrator in the physics education office from 1931–65, was established by Hale in appreciation of the physics department support staff: past, present and future.

“MIT has provided a wonderful environment for me to teach and to carry out research. I am exceptionally grateful for that and happy to be in a position to give back,” says Hale. Besides,” he adds, “I am told you cannot take it with you.” From Hale’s perspective, MIT’s faculty retirement and associated savings plans have been sufficiently generous to enable him to have more than enough financial assets to live upon and to pass onto his children. He thus decided to take advantage of the 2006 tax law allowing for charitable IRA distributions by making a $100,000 gift to the Physics Department, and incurring no tax hit from the IRS by doing so.

Hale Bradt entered MIT as a graduate student in 1955 and joined Bruno Rossi’s cosmic-ray group as a research assistant the following year. “The group was small with only a half-dozen faculty and a similar number of students. Sputnik was launched and the group was soon involved in space experiments with rockets, balloons and satellites. The beginnings of celestial X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy took root in Cambridge, as did the exploration of interplanetary space. Bruno Rossi provided the primary inspiration and our immediate supervisors were younger faculty or staff members: Bill Kraushaar, George Clark and Herbert Bridge, among others. We were soon joined by radio astronomers Alan Barrett and Bernard Burke, plus theorist Phil Morrison, who broadened our perspective. Today, the astrophysics division of the department is a thriving community of faculty, postdocs and graduate students. I cast my lot with X-ray astronomy in 1966 and had a wonderfully exciting time observing the X-ray sky from space until my retirement in 2001.” Hale recently completed his second textbook in astrophysics, Astrophysics Processes (Cambridge University Press), and has taken up the violin again with mixed results.

When Hale started lecturing 8.01 and 8.02 in 1961—his earliest years on the faculty—Mrs. Barbara Thomas was the “matriarch” of the Undergraduate Physics Office. At the time, she was an “elderly lady (born 1897), with an outsized, warm personality, who ran the office single-handedly. She managed the undergraduate courses, prepared course preparation materials, exams and grade assignments. It wasn’t easy work: typewriters, mimeograph and ‘ditto’ machines were the technology of the day.”

Barbara E. Thomas (1897–1988)

For over three decades, Barbara Thomas was the principal face of the Physics Department administration for thousands of undergraduates. Until she retired in 1965, her warm greeting to each and every student was undeniably a major asset for the physics ‘mission.’ She revered the senior faculty in residence when she first arrived, always referring to them by title, as in “Professor Sears” or “Professor Frank.” In contrast, the next generation of faculty, whom she had then known since they were students, went by their first names: department chairman William Buechner was “Bill” to her. Needless to say, junior faculty were mincemeat if they did not adhere to her strict guidelines for efficient course management, as Hale Bradt quickly discovered! Any recollections from members of the MIT physics community who knew Barbara are warmly encouraged, and can be emailed to physics@mit.edu.

Hale Bradt decided to support the department’s graduate students understanding full well the value of fellowships for entering students. As a former MIT physics graduate student, he can easily empathize with their situation. Fellowships provide more flexibility in the exploration of research fields as compared to research and teaching assistantships, and they help MIT compete for the best students.

His decision to name the fellowship in honor of Barbara Thomas evolved gradually. Last year, when the Physics Undergraduate Education Office (now known as Physics Academic Programs) moved to the Infinite Corridor during the renovation of the Green Center for Physics and the creation of the Pappalardo Community room, Hale says, “It struck and saddened me that the memory of the previous location (building 4-352), that was the focus of so many undergraduates over the years, would gradually be lost to memory. This then led me to think about Mrs. Thomas and the many staff who interface with our students and help make MIT physics a receptive and productive environment.” He hopes others will join him in supporting the Barbara E. Thomas Fund and honor the dedicated staff of the Physics Department. Once the fund reaches $1 million, it will be able to support a graduate student every year in perpetuity.

The Barbara E. Thomas Fund in support of physics graduate students has been established in the MIT Department of Physics. You may contribute to the Fund (#3312250) online at the MIT web site giving.mit.edu, by selecting “Give Now,” then “Physics.”

For more information about this fund, other physics funds and naming opportunities in the department, please contact Erin McGrath Tribble, Director of Development for the Department of Physics at 617.452.2807 or emcgrath@mit.edu.
