TITLE: Linking Quality Assurance to Institutional Performance and Development

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN) and Association of African Universities (AAU) invite stakeholders to participate in an upcoming workshop with the following details:

Date & Time: Thursday, 28 August 2025 , 9:00 GMT

Venue: Virtual (via Zoom)

Registration Link: http://bit.ly/46r6q3Z

Background and Rationale

Higher education institutions across Africa are increasingly recognizing that robust Quality Assurance (QA) systems are not just regulatory tools, but strategic levers for institutional performance and long-term development. However, many institutions still struggle to move from process-based QA to performance-oriented systems that demonstrate measurable impact.

This virtual workshop will examine how QA frameworks can be effectively integrated with institutional performance indicators and development goals, thereby fostering a culture of continuous improvement and evidence-based decision-making.

“Quality Assurance in Africa’s institutions is no longer just about meeting standards—it’s about transforming how we teach, research, and innovate to drive real societal impact. This workshop provides the opportunity for stakeholders to jointly rethink QA as a strategic engine that powers institutional excellence, aligns with Africa’s bold development goals, and prepares graduates for the future. It targets unlocking how better data, smarter processes, and genuine stakeholder engagement can move us from compliance to performance-driven growth.”

Workshop Overall Objectives

The Strategic goal is to “Transform QA from a regulatory obligation into a strategic lever for institutional excellence, innovation, and development.”

The workshop aims to emphasize the importance of Quality Assurance (QA) in driving institutional performance and sustainable development within African Higher Education Institutions. It will assist African HEIs in understanding how both internal and external QA mechanisms can be effectively aligned with institutional goals to inform evidence-based decision-making and enhance teaching, learning, and student outcomes. Additionally, the workshop seeks to cultivate a culture of continuous improvement, strengthen accountability and transparency, and guide institutions in identifying and applying context-relevant key performance indicators. By linking QA to innovation, institutional growth, and preparedness for the national and regional accreditation process, the workshop will promote peer learning and the exchange of good practices tailored to the African Higher Education context, ultimately contributing to improved quality and relevance across the continent’s institutions.

Workshop-Specific Objectives

By the end of this workshop, participants will:

Understand the role of QA in enhancing institutional performance and strategic development.

Identify performance indicators that align with QA standards.

Learn practical tools for integrating QA into institutional planning and monitoring.

Engage in peer learning to share best practices and lessons across institutions.

Develop draft institutional action points for improving QA-performance alignment.

Target Participants

Quality Assurance Officers and Directors

University Senior Management (VCs, DVCs, Registrars)

Academic Leaders (Deans, HODs)

Institutional Planners and M&E Officers

Higher Education Policy Makers

Accreditation and Regulatory Agency Staff

Workshop Structure and Agenda

Session 1 (09:00 – 10:30 GMT)

Opening and Keynote Address

Topic: Understanding the Strategic Role of QA in Institutional Development

The shift from compliance to impact

QA as a catalyst for excellence and sustainability

QA’s influence on funding, partnerships, and rankings

Facilitator: Distinguished QA/HE Policy Expert Q&A (Live Chat and Verbal)

Break (10:30 – 10:45 GMT)

Session 2 (10:45 – 12:00 GMT)

Topic: QA and Performance Indicators: Aligning Tools and Metrics

What should institutions be measuring?

Mapping QA to Teaching, Research, and Institutional Effectiveness

Sample institutional KPI dashboards and case examples

Interactive Activity: Breakout group discussion on institutional gaps

Lunch Break (12:00 – 13:00 GMT)

Crafting practical next steps for QA alignment

Embedding QA responsibilities into departmental operations

Reporting and communicating QA outcomes

Summary of key insights

Participant reflections and chat testimonials

Announcement of follow-up activities (e.g., virtual QA clinic, community of practice)

Vote of thanks

Expected Outcomes

Shared understanding of QA’s role in institutional transformation

Cross-institutional exposure to best practices and common challenges

Draft QA-Performance Integration Action Plans

Enhanced virtual collaboration among African QA stakeholders

The discussions will make one thing clear: quality assurance is the linchpin for Africa’s higher education transformation. But it only works when it’s integrated, innovative, and inclusive—when institutions own it and communities benefit.

TITLE: IIE Scholar Rescue Fund 2026: Fully Supported Fellowships for Threatened Scholars Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Institute of International Education Scholar Rescue Fund (IIE-SRF) provides fellowship support to professors, researchers, and public intellectuals whose lives, academic careers, or ability to continue their work are threatened in their home countries or countries of residence.

Through the programme, threatened and displaced scholars can receive support to undertake temporary academic appointments at universities, colleges, research institutions, think tanks, museums, and other approved higher education or research institutions in safe locations around the world.

The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund is designed to protect academic freedom, preserve knowledge, and enable scholars to continue teaching, researching, publishing, and contributing to intellectual and public life despite serious threats.

Unlike conventional scholarships, the programme is not intended to finance students who want to begin or continue a degree. It is specifically focused on established scholars and public intellectuals who require urgent support to continue their academic or intellectual work in safety.

What Is the IIE Scholar Rescue Fund?

The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund is a global programme administered by the Institute of International Education. It arranges, funds, and supports fellowships for threatened and displaced scholars through partnerships with higher education and research institutions.

The programme was established to respond to situations in which academics and intellectuals are unable to continue their work because of persecution, repression, violence, censorship, imprisonment, intimidation, harassment, political instability, or other serious threats.

IIE-SRF seeks to provide more than short-term financial assistance. It helps scholars:

Relocate or establish themselves in a safer academic environment.

Continue research and teaching.

Maintain professional and intellectual activity.

Rebuild academic networks.

Access professional development and career guidance.

Contribute to host academic communities.

Prepare for future academic or professional opportunities.

The programme accepts applications from scholars around the world and across academic disciplines. According to the official programme information, fellowships are awarded on a rolling basis, with selection decisions generally made quarterly.

IIE-SRF Fellowship 2026: Key Details

Programme: IIE Scholar Rescue Fund

Organising institution: Institute of International Education

Opportunity type: Fellowship and temporary academic placement

Eligible applicants: Threatened professors, researchers, and public intellectuals

Nationality: Scholars from any country may qualify

Academic disciplines: All academic fields and disciplines

Fellowship duration: Typically 9–12 months

Potential renewal: A second and final year may be possible in many cases

Fellowship grant: Up to US$30,000

Additional support: Health insurance, relocation assistance, professional development, and academic networking

Application system: Rolling applications

Important deadline: October 11, 2026, for possible consideration at the December 2026 Selection Committee meeting

Application method: Email the required materials to srf@iie.org

Programme location: Safe host institutions worldwide, subject to placement and programme approval

The official application page states that applications submitted by October 11, 2026 may be considered at the IIE-SRF Selection Committee meeting in December 2026. Because the programme accepts applications throughout the year, this is a consideration deadline rather than a permanent annual closing date.

What Does the IIE Scholar Rescue Fund Provide?

The IIE-SRF fellowship package is intended to support a scholar’s temporary academic placement and help them continue their work in a safe environment.

1. Temporary Academic Appointment

The programme supports a yearlong research and/or teaching appointment at a partnering higher education or research institution in a safe location.

Potential host institutions may include:

Universities.

Colleges.

Research centres.

Think tanks.

Museums.

Other approved institutions of higher learning or research.

The exact nature of the appointment depends on the scholar’s academic background, research interests, professional experience, host institution, and available placement opportunities.

The fellowship is designed to enable scholars to continue activities such as:

Teaching university courses.

Conducting academic research.

Writing journal articles or books.

Completing ongoing research projects.

Publishing scholarly work.

Supervising students, where appropriate.

Participating in seminars and academic events.

Contributing to research groups and institutional projects.

2. Fellowship Grant of Up to US$30,000

The IIE-SRF fellowship includes a grant of up to US$30,000 to support a temporary academic appointment of up to one year.

The final amount may depend on factors such as:

The location of the host institution.

The cost of living in the host country.

The length and structure of the fellowship.

Contributions from the host institution.

Additional support available from other sources.

The grant is not necessarily paid as a single lump sum directly to the scholar. In many cases, funds are sent to the host institution, which disburses the support through a salary or stipend arrangement. In certain situations, IIE-SRF may provide funds directly to the scholar in instalments.

3. Health Insurance

The fellowship package includes individual health insurance coverage for the fellow.

This support is intended to help the scholar access necessary healthcare during the fellowship period. Applicants should review the specific insurance arrangements and conditions that apply to their placement.

4. Relocation Support

IIE-SRF provides funding for relocation to the host institution.

Relocation assistance may help address some of the costs associated with moving from a threatened or displaced situation to a new academic environment. The specific arrangements depend on the scholar’s circumstances, host location, and programme requirements.

5. Professional Development

The programme provides professional development support to help fellows sustain and advance their academic careers.

This may include:

Resource guides.

Access to academic networks.

CV and cover-letter review.

Career mentorship.

Professional advising.

Guidance on post-fellowship opportunities.

In some cases, financial support for conference attendance.

In some cases, support for language training.

These services are important because scholars may need assistance not only during their fellowship but also when transitioning to future academic or professional opportunities.

6. Academic Visibility and Networking

IIE-SRF and its partners may provide opportunities for fellows to share or promote their academic work.

These opportunities may include:

Academic events.

Partner activities.

Media engagements.

Public discussions.

Scholarly presentations.

Opportunities to speak about the scholar’s home country or area of expertise.

Such activities can help fellows maintain professional visibility, expand their networks, and contribute to discussions about academic freedom, displacement, conflict, and knowledge preservation.

7. Ongoing Support

IIE-SRF and its partners provide support before, during, and after the fellowship.

This may include assistance related to:

Fellowship placement.

Academic integration.

Relocation.

Professional development.

Networking.

Career planning.

Transitioning after the fellowship.

The programme also works with host institutions to help fellows adjust to their academic and local environments.

Fellowship Duration and Renewal

The IIE-SRF fellowship generally lasts between 9 and 12 months, although the precise duration depends on the needs and arrangements of the fellow and host institution.

In many cases, fellows may apply for a second and final year of financial support. Renewal is not automatic and depends on the programme’s assessment, available funding, the fellow’s circumstances, and the host arrangement.

The fellowship does not necessarily need to begin at the start of an academic semester. Fellows may begin their appointments at different points during the year, depending on the host institution and placement arrangements.

Who Can Apply for the IIE Scholar Rescue Fund?

IIE-SRF accepts applications from scholars who meet the programme’s academic and threat-related requirements.

Professors

University and college professors who are unable to continue teaching or conducting research safely may qualify.

Applicants should provide evidence of:

Their current or previous academic appointment.

Teaching responsibilities.

Research experience.

Academic publications.

Professional contributions.

The threats preventing them from continuing their work.

Established Researchers

Researchers working at universities, research institutes, policy centres, think tanks, laboratories, or other recognised institutions may be eligible.

Relevant applicants may work in areas such as:

Social sciences.

Humanities.

Natural sciences.

Medicine and health.

Engineering.

Education.

Law.

Economics.

Political science.

Environmental studies.

Technology.

Arts and cultural research.

Other academic or intellectual disciplines.

The programme does not limit eligibility to a particular academic field or discipline.

Public Intellectuals

Select public intellectuals may also qualify, even where their work does not fit a conventional university faculty position.

A public intellectual may be a recognised writer, scholar, commentator, researcher, or thought leader whose work contributes significantly to public debate, intellectual life, social understanding, or academic inquiry.

Applicants in this category should demonstrate the quality and relevance of their work, their professional accomplishments, and the threats they face.

Academic Qualifications and Experience

Preference is given to applicants who demonstrate strong academic qualifications and professional experience.

Applicants are generally expected to have some combination of the following:

A PhD or the highest degree available in their academic field.

Significant teaching experience at a university, college, or other higher education institution.

Significant research experience.

An established record of academic publications.

Evidence of scholarly accomplishment or promise.

A clear academic research agenda.

Experience contributing to academic or professional communities.

A record of teaching, publishing, supervising, presenting, or conducting research.

Holding a PhD is strongly preferred, but the programme’s eligibility language also refers to scholars who hold the highest degree in their field. Applicants should explain their qualifications clearly, particularly if their discipline or professional pathway does not follow a traditional PhD route.

Threats and Circumstances That May Qualify

The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund focuses on scholars who face threats that prevent them from safely continuing their academic or intellectual work.

Qualifying circumstances may include:

Targeted persecution.

Intimidation.

Harassment.

Repression.

Censorship.

Arrest or imprisonment.

Violence.

Threats to personal safety.

Threats connected to scholarship, identity, or beliefs.

General insecurity, instability, or civil conflict that significantly affects the scholar’s ability to continue their work.

The programme assesses both the nature and urgency of the threat. Applicants must explain clearly why they cannot continue their work in their home country or current country of residence.

A general lack of funding, insufficient research resources, limited career advancement, or a desire to access better professional opportunities does not, by itself, qualify an applicant for IIE-SRF support.

Preference Given During Assessment

Although scholars from any country and discipline may qualify, IIE-SRF gives preference to applicants who demonstrate several important characteristics.

Preference may be given to scholars who:

Hold a PhD or the highest degree in their field.

Have significant teaching or research experience at a higher education institution.

Have an established record of published research.

Demonstrate strong academic achievement or potential.

Face immediate and targeted threats to their lives or careers.

Have recently fled threats in their home country or country of residence.

Can contribute meaningfully to their host academic community.

May also benefit their home academic community through continued research, teaching, collaboration, or knowledge exchange.

Meeting the eligibility criteria does not guarantee an award. Due to the high demand for assistance and limited resources, IIE-SRF cannot support every applicant who meets the basic requirements.

Who Is Generally Not Eligible?

The programme identifies several categories of applicants it typically cannot consider.

1. Students Seeking to Continue Their Studies

IIE-SRF generally does not support individuals who are seeking funding to:

Begin a PhD.

Continue PhD studies.

Complete a degree programme.

Undertake academic training.

Continue as students without an established academic career.

The programme is intended for professors, established researchers, and select public intellectuals rather than students seeking educational funding.

2. Scholars Displaced for More Than Two Years

Applicants who have been displaced or have resided outside their home countries for more than two years are generally not eligible.

However, an exception may apply if the applicant is experiencing a renewed or continuing threat in the country where they have been displaced.

Applicants should explain their displacement history accurately and provide relevant dates.

3. Individuals with Safe Second-Country Citizenship or Permanent Residency

Applicants who hold citizenship or permanent residency in a safe second country are generally not eligible.

This rule reflects the programme’s focus on scholars who lack a safe alternative from which to continue their academic work.

4. Applicants with Two Years of Comparable Fellowship Support

Individuals who will have completed two years on a comparable fellowship or programme for threatened scholars are generally not eligible for further IIE-SRF support.

Applicants should disclose previous fellowships, academic rescue programmes, or similar support.

5. Applicants Seeking General Career Advancement

The programme is not intended for scholars who simply want to improve their career prospects, obtain better research funding, access a more prestigious institution, or leave their country for professional convenience.

The central requirement is a credible and serious threat that prevents the scholar from continuing their work safely.

Special Note for Ukrainian Applicants

The official eligibility information includes a specific note concerning Ukrainian applicants.

IIE-SRF states that, within the context of the war in Ukraine and its effects on the academic community, the programme is focusing its support on fellowships undertaken in Eastern or Central Europe.

The programme indicates that it is unable to consider applications from Ukrainian scholars seeking placements elsewhere in Europe, including Western Europe, under the stated policy.

Applicants affected by this policy should consult IIE-SRF directly for the latest guidance before preparing or submitting an application, as programme approaches may change in response to developments and available resources.

Required Application Materials

Applicants must submit a set of documents that demonstrate their academic background, professional experience, scholarly work, personal circumstances, and need for assistance.

The required materials include the following.

1. Completed Application Form

Applicants must complete the official IIE-SRF application form.

The form is available through the programme’s application instructions page.

2. Current CV or Résumé

The CV should provide a detailed account of the applicant’s academic and professional background.

It should include:

Academic degrees.

Degree-granting institutions.

Academic fields.

Dates degrees were awarded.

Current position.

Current institution and location.

Dates of employment.

Professional title.

Current responsibilities.

Previous academic positions in chronological order.

Locations and dates of previous appointments.

Professional responsibilities.

Academic publications.

Journal articles.

Books and book chapters.

Exhibitions, where relevant.

Thesis supervision.

Conference presentations.

Grants.

Honours and awards.

Professional affiliations.

Other relevant academic work.

Publication entries should include full citations where possible, including:

Publication name.

Authors.

Title of the work.

Date of publication.

Page numbers, where available.

A detailed CV is important because IIE-SRF assesses the applicant’s academic experience, scholarly quality, and potential contribution to a host institution.

3. Academic Statement

Applicants must submit an academic statement of at least one page.

The statement should explain:

The applicant’s academic background.

Professional experience.

Research interests.

Academic achievements.

Previous teaching and research activities.

Publications and scholarly contributions.

The work the applicant would undertake during the fellowship.

Proposed research, teaching, publishing, or other academic activities.

The academic statement should demonstrate that the applicant has a clear scholarly identity and a realistic plan for continuing productive academic work during the fellowship.

4. Personal Statement

Applicants must submit a personal statement of at least one page explaining why they are seeking IIE-SRF support.

The statement should include:

The applicant’s reasons for applying.

The threats or risks they are facing.

The circumstances preventing them from continuing their work safely.

The reasons they cannot remain in or return to their home country at the present time.

The urgency of their situation.

How the fellowship would help them continue their academic or intellectual work.

This statement should be specific, factual, and detailed. Applicants should explain their circumstances clearly rather than relying on general descriptions of insecurity or professional difficulty.

5. Reference Letters

The application requires reference letters that address both the applicant’s academic background and personal circumstances.

The application instructions state that IIE-SRF requires a minimum of three reference letters, although the detailed breakdown identifies:

Two academic or professional reference letters.

Two personal reference letters.

Applicants should therefore prepare for the possibility that four letters may be required or requested.

Academic or Professional References

Two academic or professional colleagues should provide letters discussing:

The applicant’s research.

Publications.

Teaching.

Academic experience.

Professional contributions.

Areas of expertise.

Contributions to specific intellectual questions or fields.

Personal References

Two personal references should come from colleagues or other individuals who understand the applicant’s circumstances and can describe the threats they have faced.

Reference letters should be original and specific to the applicant. Each referee should write from their own knowledge and should not use identical or AI-generated text.

Where possible, referees should prepare letters on official letterhead and send them directly to IIE-SRF at srf@iie.org.

6. Copy of PhD or Highest Degree

Applicants must provide a copy of their PhD or highest academic degree.

If the applicant does not hold a PhD, they should provide documentation of the highest degree relevant to their academic or professional field and explain their qualifications where necessary.

7. Samples of Recent Research Publications

Applicants must submit samples of their most current research publications.

These samples help IIE-SRF assess:

The quality of the applicant’s scholarship.

Research competence.

Academic contribution.

Relevance of the applicant’s work.

Potential for continued scholarly activity.

8. Host Institution Commitment Letter, If Available

Applicants who have already secured a commitment from a university or other institution to host their fellowship may submit a letter confirming the institution’s intent to host them if they receive an award.

However, a host commitment is not required at the initial application stage.

This is important because applicants may apply before identifying or securing a host institution. IIE-SRF may assist with placement and host arrangements after reviewing the application.

Initial Materials Required for Assessment

To begin assessing an application, IIE-SRF must receive the following four items:

Completed application form.

Current CV or résumé.

Academic statement.

Personal statement.

The remaining materials may be submitted later.

Applicants should nevertheless aim to prepare the complete application package as early as possible, particularly because reference letters, degree certificates, and publication samples may take time to obtain.

Important Rules for Application Materials

All application materials must be original and specifically prepared for the applicant’s academic background and personal circumstances.

IIE-SRF states that it will not accept academic or personal statements that:

Use identical language to statements submitted by other applicants.

Contain copied material without proper attribution.

Present generic or fabricated accounts.

Fail to reflect the applicant’s actual circumstances.

Any information or language borrowed from online sources must be properly cited.

The programme also strongly discourages applicants from using artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT, to create application materials or responses to application questions. Suspected AI-generated language may negatively affect the assessment of an application.

Applicants should therefore write their statements in their own words, provide accurate details, and ensure that all claims are truthful and personally relevant.

Special Guidance for Spouses Applying Together

If two spouses may both qualify for IIE-SRF and intend to apply, they should submit their applications at the same time.

The programme notes that if one spouse submits an application after the other spouse has already been awarded an IIE-SRF fellowship, the second application may not be considered.

Each spouse must submit a complete and unique application package. Even if both applicants are experiencing similar circumstances, their academic statements, personal statements, and supporting materials must reflect their individual backgrounds and situations.

How to Apply

Applicants should follow the official application process carefully.

Step 1: Review the Eligibility Criteria

Confirm that you meet the academic, professional, geographic, and threat-related requirements.

Pay particular attention to:

Your academic status.

Your degree and research experience.

Your publication record.

The nature of the threats you face.

Your displacement history.

Your citizenship or permanent residency status.

Any previous comparable fellowship support.

Step 2: Download the Application Form

Obtain the official IIE-SRF application form from the programme’s application instructions page.

Step 3: Prepare the Four Initial Documents

Prepare the following:

Completed application form.

Current CV.

Academic statement.

Personal statement.

These are the documents IIE-SRF needs to begin assessing an application.

Step 4: Gather Supporting Materials

Prepare:

Reference letters.

Degree certificate.

Recent publication samples.

Host institution letter, if available.

The remaining materials may be submitted after the initial four documents, but applicants should not delay unnecessarily.

Step 5: Submit by Email

Send the application materials to:

srf@iie.org

If a scholar cannot submit the application personally, a third party may send the materials on the scholar’s behalf.

If email access is unavailable, the programme also permits materials to be sent by fax or post.

APPLY HERE

Postal Address

Scholar Rescue Fund

Institute of International Education

One World Trade Center, 36th Floor

New York, New York 10007

USA

Fax: +1-212-205-6425

Application Deadline and Rolling Admissions

IIE-SRF accepts applications on a rolling basis, and fellowships are awarded quarterly.

For possible consideration at the IIE-SRF Selection Committee meeting in December 2026, applications must be submitted no later than:

October 11, 2026

Applicants who wish to be considered during this cycle should submit their materials before the stated date. Applications submitted after the deadline may be considered for a later selection cycle, depending on programme capacity and timing.

Because the programme receives a high volume of applications, interested scholars should begin preparing their materials as early as possible. Reference letters, publication samples, degree documents, and evidence of threats may require additional time to assemble.

How IIE-SRF Reviews Applications

IIE-SRF conducts a detailed assessment of each application.

The review considers:

Academic qualifications.

Professional experience.

Quality of scholarly work.

Publication record.

Academic potential.

Nature of the threats faced.

Urgency of the applicant’s circumstances.

Ability to continue productive academic work.

Potential benefit to a host institution.

Potential benefit to the applicant’s home academic community.

IIE-SRF may contact references or other sources, including independent experts familiar with:

The applicant’s academic field.

The applicant’s country of origin.

The applicant’s reported circumstances.

The nature of the threats described.

The programme states that it will not share identifying information about an applicant without permission.

In some cases, IIE-SRF may contact applicants directly to request additional information about their academic work or personal situation. This may be necessary to understand the applicant’s background and assess the urgency and credibility of the request.

Selection Committee and Award Decisions

After the initial assessment, selected applications may be presented to the IIE-SRF Selection Committee.

The Selection Committee makes the final decisions on fellowship awards. The committee meets four times per year.

However, not every applicant who meets the eligibility criteria will necessarily be presented to the committee or receive funding. The programme has limited resources and must prioritise cases according to academic merit, urgency, threat level, placement possibilities, and available support.

Host Institution Matching and Financial Contributions

IIE-SRF works with higher education and research institutions that can host fellows and support their academic work.

Host institutions may include:

Universities.

Colleges.

Research centres.

Think tanks.

Museums.

Other institutions of higher learning or research.

The host institution is expected to provide an academic environment in which the scholar can continue teaching, research, writing, or other appropriate work.

IIE-SRF generally requires the host institution to provide financial support equal to or greater than the IIE-SRF fellowship award. This matching support may take the form of:

Stipend.

Salary.

Housing.

Airfare.

Health insurance.

Other direct benefits that offset living expenses.

In-kind contributions such as office space, computer access, library access, or laboratory fees may strengthen the overall support package but generally do not count as matching financial support.

In certain cases, IIE-SRF may consider waiving the full host-funding requirement, particularly where a fellowship is undertaken within the scholar’s home region or in a country with a lower cost of living.

Can Applicants Apply Without a Host Institution?

Yes. Applicants do not need to have already secured a host institution before applying.

If an applicant has already obtained a host commitment, they may submit a letter from the institution. However, the letter is optional at the initial stage.

Applicants without a host institution may still be considered for support, subject to eligibility, academic assessment, urgency, available funding, and the possibility of arranging a suitable placement.

Global Eligibility and Geographic Coverage

The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund is global in scope.

Scholars from:

Africa.

Asia.

Europe.

North America.

Latin America.

The Caribbean.

The Middle East.

Oceania.

Other regions worldwide.

may qualify, provided they meet the programme’s academic and threat-related criteria.

There is no restriction to a particular race, nationality, continent, or academic discipline in the general eligibility criteria. However, specific placement policies or regional restrictions may apply in certain circumstances, such as the programme’s current guidance concerning Ukrainian applicants.

Applicants may apply from any location, although the programme generally focuses on scholars who are facing threats and who have not been safely settled outside their home country for an extended period.

Learn More HERE

Important Considerations Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should consider the following:

Be Clear About the Threat

Explain the threat in concrete terms. Describe what has happened, when it happened, how it affects your work, and why you cannot safely continue your academic activities.

Demonstrate Academic Continuity

Show that you have a clear plan for continuing research, teaching, publishing, or other academic work during the fellowship.

Provide Evidence of Scholarly Achievement

Include a detailed CV, publication list, degree documentation, and recent research samples.

Use Original Statements

Write the academic and personal statements in your own words. Avoid generic language, copied text, or statements that do not reflect your personal experience.

Prepare References Early

Reference letters may take time to secure. Choose referees who know your academic work and, where relevant, understand the threats or circumstances you face.

Do Not Present the Fellowship as a Study Scholarship

The programme is intended for established scholars and public intellectuals. Applicants should focus on continuing their academic work rather than seeking funding for a new degree.

Contact IIE-SRF Directly When Unsure

Questions about eligibility should be directed to:

srf@iie.org

Applicants should contact the programme directly if they are uncertain about their academic status, displacement history, country situation, host institution, or the nature of their circumstances.

Official Links and Contact Information

Official IIE Scholar Rescue Fund website: https://www.scholarrescuefund.org/

Eligibility criteria: https://www.scholarrescuefund.org/applicants/eligibility-criteria/

Application instructions: https://www.scholarrescuefund.org/applicants/instructions-and-application/

Application and scholar information: https://www.scholarrescuefund.org/for-scholars/

Application email: srf@iie.org

Telephone: +1-212-205-6486

Fax: +1-212-205-6425

Conclusion

The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund 2026 provides a vital opportunity for threatened professors, researchers, and public intellectuals to continue their academic and intellectual work in a safer environment. Through temporary academic appointments, financial assistance of up to US$30,000, health insurance, relocation support, professional development, and academic networking, the programme helps protect scholars whose work and personal safety are at risk.

The opportunity is open to qualified scholars from any country and academic discipline, but applicants must demonstrate both a strong academic or intellectual background and a credible threat that prevents them from continuing their work safely.

Applications are accepted on a rolling basis. Scholars seeking possible consideration at the December 2026 Selection Committee meeting should submit their applications by October 11, 2026. Applicants should prepare original and detailed materials, explain their circumstances truthfully, and contact IIE-SRF directly if they need clarification about eligibility or the application process.

TITLE: World Bank Young Professionals Program (YPP) 2027: Fully Funded Global Career Opportunity, Eligibility, Application Deadline & How to Apply

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Bank Group’s Young Professionals Program (YPP) is its flagship leadership development initiative for highly talented individuals who are passionate about global development.

The Young Professionals Program offers a unique opportunity to build technical expertise, gain international experience and contribute to projects that address the world’s most pressing development challenges.

World Bank YPP Highlights

Global and competitive selection

Initial start at headquarters followed by field rotations in various World Bank Group offices

Initial two-year program followed by a five-year contract upon successful performance

Working experience across the World Bank, IFC and MIGA through rotations

Tailored training in coaching, mentorship and leadership

Opportunities to engage with senior leaders and build strategic professional networks

Exposure to global operations and diverse development challenges

Program Features

TITLE: 2027 Mandela Washington Fellowship for Young African Leaders – Fully Funded Leadership Opportunity in the United States

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2027 Mandela Washington Fellowship for Young African Leaders will open for applications on September 22, 2026, giving young African leaders an opportunity to participate in a prestigious leadership development and professional exchange program in the United States.

The Fellowship is the flagship program of the U.S. Government’s Young African Leaders Initiative (YALI) and is designed for accomplished young leaders who are already making a difference in their communities, countries, and professional sectors.

For the 2027 Fellowship, eligible applicants may apply to one of three tracks:

Business and Trade

Emerging Technologies

Governance and Security

The program brings together emerging African leaders for intensive learning, professional networking, leadership development, and engagement with American institutions and professionals.

About the Mandela Washington Fellowship

Established in 2014, the Mandela Washington Fellowship has developed a growing network of young African leaders from across Sub-Saharan Africa. The official Fellowship website reports that nearly 7,800 young leaders from all 49 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa have participated since the program began.

The Fellowship is intended for accomplished young professionals and leaders with demonstrated experience in leadership, innovation, public service, business, civic engagement, or other areas of community impact.

Rather than being a traditional academic degree program, the Fellowship combines leadership development, practical learning, professional networking, and cultural exchange.

2027 Fellowship Tracks

Applicants for the 2027 program will be able to apply to one of three specialized tracks.

1. Business and Trade

The Business and Trade track is designed for leaders working in areas connected to entrepreneurship, business development, trade, investment, economic growth, and related fields.

Participants can use the Fellowship to develop practical knowledge, exchange ideas with peers, and build professional relationships with organizations and leaders in the United States.

2. Emerging Technologies

The Emerging Technologies track focuses on leaders working in technology and emerging areas shaping economies and societies.

The track provides an opportunity for participants to explore innovative approaches, strengthen professional skills, and connect with others working at the intersection of technology, leadership, and development.

3. Governance and Security

The Governance and Security track is intended for leaders working in areas related to governance, public service, security, policy, and related fields.

Participants have opportunities to exchange perspectives with other African leaders and engage with U.S. institutions and professionals.

What Does the Fellowship Include?

The Mandela Washington Fellowship includes an intensive six-week Leadership Institute at a U.S. college or university. Fellows participate in academic and practical activities while sharing experiences and perspectives with their peers and U.S. communities.

Depending on the Fellowship cycle and participant selection, program activities can include:

Leadership and professional development

Academic and practical learning

Networking with other African leaders

Engagement with U.S. businesses, organizations, and professionals

Community and cultural activities

Opportunities to exchange ideas and experiences across sectors

Continued engagement through the Fellowship’s alumni network

The broader Fellowship also includes professional and reciprocal exchange opportunities designed to strengthen relationships between African and U.S. participants.

Who Should Apply?

The Mandela Washington Fellowship is aimed at young African leaders aged 25 to 35 who have established records of leadership and accomplishment. The official Fellowship describes its participants as accomplished innovators and leaders who have demonstrated positive impact in their communities and countries.

Previous Fellowship eligibility requirements have included applicants who:

Are between 25 and 35 years old at the time specified by the application cycle, although exceptional applicants aged 21–24 may be considered;

Are citizens and residents of an eligible Sub-Saharan African country;

Are proficient in English;

Are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents;

Are eligible to receive a U.S. J-1 visa;

Are not employees or immediate family members of employees of the U.S. Government; and

Have not previously participated in the Mandela Washington Fellowship.

Important: Applicants should check the official 2027 application instructions once applications open on September 22, 2026, as eligibility requirements and application details may change from previous Fellowship cycles.

What Makes a Strong Applicant?

The Fellowship is highly competitive and looks for applicants with evidence of leadership, achievement, service, and professional experience.

Previous official application guidance has emphasized several areas, including:

Demonstrated leadership and accomplishment

Applicants should be able to show what they have achieved through their professional, entrepreneurial, civic, or community work.

Commitment to community or public service

Experience in volunteering, mentoring, community service, or initiatives that benefit others can strengthen an application.

Relevant experience in your chosen track

Your professional and leadership experience should connect clearly to the Fellowship track you select.

For example, an applicant choosing Emerging Technologies should be able to demonstrate meaningful experience or engagement in technology or a related field.

Clear goals

Applicants should explain how participating in the Fellowship would contribute to their current work and future goals.

Commitment to Africa

Previous Fellowship guidance has emphasized the importance of applicants’ plans to use their skills and experience to contribute to their communities and countries in Africa.

How Competitive Is the Fellowship?

The Mandela Washington Fellowship is a competitive international leadership program. Applications are reviewed against established selection criteria, with emphasis on leadership experience, community or public service, relevant professional experience, and the applicant’s goals for participating in the Fellowship.

Applicants should therefore avoid treating the application as simply an academic application. Your application should demonstrate what you have done, the impact you have achieved, what you have learned, and how the Fellowship connects to your future work.

The official Fellowship recommends using concrete examples and real-world experiences when responding to application questions.

How to Prepare Before Applications Open

With applications opening on September 22, 2026, prospective applicants can begin preparing now.

1. Identify your Fellowship track

Consider which of the three 2027 tracks most closely reflects your professional experience and leadership activities:

Business and Trade | Emerging Technologies | Governance and Security

2. Update your CV

Make sure your CV clearly highlights:

Leadership positions

Professional achievements

Community involvement

Awards and recognition

Entrepreneurial or professional initiatives

Volunteer and mentoring experience

Relevant projects and measurable results

3. Start identifying your strongest examples

Think about specific situations where you demonstrated leadership, solved a problem, created an initiative, supported your community, or achieved measurable results.

4. Connect your experience to your goals

Be prepared to explain why the Fellowship is relevant to your work and what you intend to do with the knowledge, skills, and connections gained from the program.

5. Follow the official instructions

The application should be completed according to the requirements published for the 2027 Fellowship. Previous official guidance has stressed that applications must be submitted online and in English.

Application Opening Date

Application opens: September 22, 2026

The application portal and official 2027 instructions should be consulted when the application period opens.

Prospective applicants should check the official Mandela Washington Fellowship website for the 2027 deadline, detailed eligibility requirements, application questions, and supporting information.

How to Apply

Applications for the Mandela Washington Fellowship are submitted online through the official Fellowship application system.

Application opens September 22, 2026.

Applicants should use only the official application portal and should not pay anyone to submit an application on their behalf. Previous official guidance confirms that the Fellowship application is online and free of charge.

Learn more: mandelawashingtonfellowship.org

For further details, visit our Application Resources and Frequently Asked Questions pages.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the 2027 Mandela Washington Fellowship application open?

The 2027 Mandela Washington Fellowship application opens on September 22, 2026.

What are the 2027 Fellowship tracks?

Applicants may apply to one of three tracks: Business and Trade, Emerging Technologies, or Governance and Security.

Who is the Fellowship for?

The Fellowship is designed for accomplished young African leaders, generally ages 25–35, from Sub-Saharan Africa.

Is the Mandela Washington Fellowship fully funded?

The Fellowship is a U.S. Government-funded leadership and exchange program. Applicants should review the official 2027 program information for the specific benefits and arrangements provided to selected Fellows.

Can I apply if I have never participated in YALI before?

Yes. Previous participation in other YALI programs does not automatically mean an applicant has participated in the Mandela Washington Fellowship. Applicants should review the 2027 eligibility requirements when they are published.

Where will the Fellowship take place?

The Leadership Institutes take place at U.S. colleges and universities. The official Fellowship describes the Institute as a six-week experience combining learning, leadership development, and engagement with U.S. communities.

Start Preparing Now

If you are a young African professional, entrepreneur, public servant, technology leader, or community changemaker, the opening of the 2027 Mandela Washington Fellowship application is an opportunity to prepare your application early.

Start by identifying your strongest leadership experiences, updating your CV, reviewing your achievements, and thinking carefully about how your work connects to your preferred Fellowship track.

Applications open September 22, 2026.

Bookmark this page and check the official Fellowship website for the latest 2027 application information and deadline once the application portal opens.

Learn more: mandelawashingtonfellowship.org

For further details, visit our Application Resources and Frequently Asked Questions pages.

TITLE: MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme 2026 at Academy of Art and Design Basel FHNW, Switzerland

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme 2026 at the Academy of Art and Design Basel FHNW (HGK Basel) offers an opportunity for artists, designers, curators, publishers and cultural organisers to pursue doctoral research through interdisciplinary and practice-based approaches.

Hosted by the Critical Media Lab at the Institute Experimental Design and Media Cultures in Basel, the PhD programme is organised in partnership between Basel and Linz and brings together artistic research, critical media practices, experimental design, publishing, cultural production and critical approaches to infrastructures.

The programme is particularly suited to applicants whose research does not fit neatly within conventional academic disciplines and who want to investigate complex cultural, technological, institutional or social questions through creative and practice-based research.

The pre-proposal application deadline is September 27, 2026.

About the MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme

The MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme is built around the principles of flexibility, self-determination, creativity and interdisciplinarity. Rather than prescribing a single research methodology or disciplinary framework, the programme supports doctoral projects that use experimental, artistic and critical approaches to generate knowledge.

The PhD is carried out through a partnership between Basel and Linz, with the programme hosted by the Critical Media Lab at the Institute Experimental Design and Media Cultures in Basel.

Doctoral candidates receive joint supervision from faculty members at both institutions. The programme combines individualised mentoring with collective academic and research activities.

Its structure includes:

Individualised mentoring

Joint supervision from faculty in Basel and Linz

Monthly colloquia

An annual assembly

Public events

Collaborations with external partners

Interdisciplinary research and exchange

The programme is designed to create an environment where doctoral researchers can develop independent research projects while also participating in a broader intellectual and creative community.

Three Core Areas of Research

Applicants should develop projects that engage with at least one of the programme’s principal areas of concern. These areas provide a framework for understanding the kinds of research the MAKE/SENSE programme is interested in supporting.

1. Situated Artistic Research

The first area is Situated Artistic Research.

This strand supports artistic and research practices that question dominant ways of producing and validating knowledge. It places particular emphasis on forms of inquiry that are embodied, affective and experimental.

Rather than treating knowledge as something produced exclusively through conventional academic methods, situated artistic research can explore how knowledge emerges through:

Artistic practice

Embodied experience

Affective engagement

Experimentation

Creative processes

Situated perspectives

Alternative epistemologies

Applicants interested in this area may therefore consider how artistic practice itself can function as a method of investigation and knowledge production.

The approach is particularly relevant for projects that seek to challenge established assumptions about whose knowledge counts, how knowledge is generated, and how different forms of experience can contribute to research.

2. Infrastructural Critique

The second area is Infrastructural Critique.

This strand examines infrastructures not simply as technical or institutional systems but as spaces where power, knowledge, organisation and social relations are produced and contested.

Research may engage with:

Institutional infrastructures

Technological infrastructures

Research infrastructures

Systems of organisation

Institutional practices

Technologies and their social consequences

Alternative forms of collective organisation

The programme describes these infrastructures as potential sites of critique, abolitionist intervention, collective reimagining and world-making.

This makes the area relevant to researchers interested in examining how systems and structures shape everyday life, knowledge production, cultural practice or institutional relationships.

Applicants could therefore develop research that not only analyses existing infrastructures but also considers possibilities for transforming, reimagining or creating alternatives to them.

3. Critical Media

The third area is Critical Media.

This area explores how knowledge is:

Read

Written

Mediated

Published

Circulated

Interpreted

Produced through different formats

The programme supports practice-based approaches to reading and writing, publishing and expanded media formats.

This means that applicants may explore not only conventional written research but also alternative ways of producing and communicating knowledge.

Projects could potentially engage with questions surrounding publishing, media practices, experimental writing, cultural circulation and the ways different media formats influence how knowledge is understood and shared.

Interdisciplinary and Practice-Based Research Environment

A major feature of the MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme is its interdisciplinary character.

The programme welcomes applicants whose practices may cross traditional disciplinary boundaries. This makes it relevant to professionals working across areas such as art, design, publishing, curating and cultural organisation.

Instead of requiring applicants to fit their research entirely within a conventional academic discipline, the programme provides space for projects that combine different practices and perspectives.

The combination of individual mentoring, monthly colloquia and an annual assembly also means that doctoral researchers are expected to develop their individual projects while engaging with a wider research community.

Public events and collaborations with external partners further extend the programme beyond its core academic environment.

What Applicants Must Submit

The first stage of the selection process is the pre-proposal round.

Applicants are required to submit a number of documents demonstrating their academic qualifications, professional background and proposed doctoral research.

The required application materials are as follows:

1. Motivation Letter

Applicants must submit a two-page A4 motivation letter.

The letter must include:

The applicant’s motivation for pursuing the PhD

Two preferred supervisors

The rationale for selecting those supervisors

Plans for financing the PhD

Any need for support with external funding applications

External funding or grants the applicant plans to apply for

Applicants should therefore carefully consider the research interests and expertise of potential supervisors before selecting their preferred supervisors.

The rationale for choosing each supervisor should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s proposed research and the supervisor’s expertise.

2. Project Outline

Applicants must provide a 2–3 page A4 project outline, excluding references.

This is one of the most important components of the pre-proposal because it introduces the proposed doctoral research project.

The project outline should contain:

Research Question

Applicants need to clearly identify the central question their proposed research will investigate.

A strong research question should establish what the project is trying to understand, explore, challenge or develop.

State of the Art

The proposal should include a short state-of-the-art section.

This demonstrates the applicant’s understanding of existing research, debates, practices or knowledge related to the proposed project.

Relevance and Topicality

Applicants must explain the relevance and topicality of their project in relation to at least one of the programme’s areas of concern.

The proposal should therefore make a clear connection to one or more of:

Situated Artistic Research

Infrastructural Critique

Critical Media

Proposed Methods

The project outline must explain the methods the applicant intends to use.

Because the programme supports artistic and practice-based research, applicants should clearly communicate how their creative, artistic, design, curatorial, publishing or other research practices will contribute to the investigation.

Proposed Outcomes

Applicants must also explain the expected outcomes of the research.

These outcomes should communicate what the doctoral project intends to produce, discover, develop or contribute.

References should be included where appropriate but do not count toward the 2–3 page limit.

3. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a CV outlining their academic and professional background.

The CV should provide relevant information about the applicant’s experience and demonstrate how their previous work relates to the proposed doctoral project.

For creative professionals, relevant artistic, design, curatorial, publishing, cultural or research experience can be particularly important in demonstrating the applicant’s profile.

4. Portfolio

Applicants must submit a portfolio.

The call specifically identifies the following types of material:

Art samples

Design samples

Curatorial work

Writing samples

The portfolio provides applicants with an opportunity to demonstrate their existing practice and show how their previous work connects with their proposed research.

Applicants should therefore select portfolio materials strategically rather than treating the portfolio simply as a collection of unrelated work.

5. Academic Diplomas and Transcripts

Applicants must provide:

MA diploma

MA transcript

BA diploma

BA transcript

The MA qualification should be equivalent to 120 ECTS or meet the programme’s equivalent qualification requirement.

Applicants with qualifications from outside the European higher education system should ensure that their academic documentation clearly demonstrates the level and scope of their qualifications.

PhD Supervision

Applicants are required to identify two preferred supervisors in their motivation letter.

The programme’s current list of PhD supervisors is available through the official MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme page.

Applicants should review the available supervisors carefully and identify individuals whose research interests, expertise and methodological approaches connect meaningfully with their proposed project.

The motivation letter should then explain why those two supervisors have been selected.

Important Funding Information

One of the most important considerations for prospective applicants is that doctoral positions in the programme are not funded.

This means that admission to the programme does not come with a funded doctoral position.

Applicants therefore need to think carefully about how they will finance their studies.

The application specifically requires applicants to explain their plans for financing the PhD.

Applicants should also indicate:

Whether they require support identifying external funding

Whether they intend to apply for external grants

Which external funding opportunities they plan to pursue

How they intend to support themselves during the doctoral programme

This makes financial planning an important component of the application rather than something that can be considered only after admission.

Selection Process and Important Dates

The MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme uses a two-stage selection process.

First Round: Pre-Proposals

The first stage involves submitting the required pre-proposal materials.

Deadline: September 27, 2026

Applicants should ensure that the motivation letter, project outline, CV, portfolio and academic documents are prepared before the deadline.

Notification of Results

Applicants will be notified of the outcome of the first round in:

Mid-November 2026

Applicants who progress to the second stage will then be invited to prepare a full proposal.

Second Round: Full Proposal

The second stage requires shortlisted applicants to develop and submit a full proposal.

Deadline: December 18, 2026

The full proposal stage provides applicants with an opportunity to develop the research project introduced during the pre-proposal stage in greater depth.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to further develop their research question, theoretical and contextual framework, methodology and expected outcomes.

Interviews

Interviews are scheduled for:

Mid-January 2027 — Week 2/3

Applicants who reach this stage should be prepared to discuss their proposed research project and explain its relationship to the MAKE/SENSE programme.

Final Notification

The final admission notification is scheduled for:

End of January 2027

This marks the conclusion of the selection process.

What Makes the Programme Distinctive?

The MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme is structured around a research environment that combines creative practice, critical inquiry and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Rather than separating artistic practice from research, the programme creates space for applicants to develop research through artistic, design, media, curatorial, publishing and cultural practices.

Its three research areas provide several possible entry points:

Situated Artistic Research for projects investigating embodied, affective and experimental knowledge practices.

Infrastructural Critique for projects examining institutional, technological and research infrastructures and possibilities for their transformation.

Critical Media for projects exploring reading, writing, publishing, mediation and alternative forms of knowledge circulation.

This framework can accommodate doctoral projects that engage with contemporary cultural, technological, institutional and social questions through experimental methodologies.

Potential Applicants Should Consider

Before applying, prospective candidates should carefully assess whether their professional and academic background fits the programme.

A prospective applicant should consider:

Academic eligibility — Do you hold an MA worth 120 ECTS or an equivalent qualification?

Professional profile — Do you have a background in art, design, curating, publishing or cultural organisation?

Research alignment — Does your proposed project connect with at least one of the three programme areas?

Research question — Can you formulate a clear and meaningful research question?

Methodology — Can you explain how your proposed methods will investigate the question?

Portfolio — Can you demonstrate relevant previous creative, design, curatorial or writing practice?

Supervision — Have you identified two potential supervisors whose expertise relates to your project?

Funding — Do you have a realistic plan for financing an unfunded doctoral position?

Documentation — Do you have your BA and MA diplomas and transcripts available?

Timeline — Can you prepare a strong pre-proposal before September 27, 2026?

How to Prepare a Strong Pre-Proposal

Applicants should approach the first-round application as more than an administrative submission. The pre-proposal should communicate the relationship between the applicant’s previous practice, proposed research and the intellectual environment of MAKE/SENSE.

A useful preparation process would involve:

Step 1: Identify Your Research Interest

Begin with the question, problem or phenomenon you genuinely want to investigate.

Step 2: Connect It to the Programme

Determine whether your project is most strongly connected to:

Situated Artistic Research

Infrastructural Critique

Critical Media

A project may potentially intersect more than one area, but the relationship should be clear.

Step 3: Research Potential Supervisors

Review the current supervisor list and identify two academics whose expertise is relevant to the proposed research.

Step 4: Develop the Research Question

Turn the broad research interest into a focused research question that can realistically be investigated at doctoral level.

Step 5: Develop the Project Outline

Prepare the required:

Research question

State of the art

Relevance and topicality

Proposed methods

Proposed outcomes

References

Step 6: Prepare the Portfolio

Select work that demonstrates the applicant’s practice and supports the proposed research direction.

Step 7: Develop a Funding Plan

Because the doctoral positions are not funded, applicants should investigate external grants, scholarships and other sources of financial support.

Step 8: Complete the Application Documents

Ensure that the motivation letter, project outline, CV, portfolio and academic documentation are complete before submission.

Deadline

The deadline for the MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme 2026 pre-proposal application is September 27, 2026.

Applicants interested in applying should begin preparing their proposal and supporting documents well before the deadline, particularly because the application requires both a research project outline and a portfolio.

The second-stage full proposal deadline is December 18, 2026, followed by interviews in mid-January 2027 and final notifications at the end of January 2027.

Conclusion

The MAKE/SENSE PhD Programme 2026 provides a doctoral research environment for artists, curators, publishers, designers and cultural organisers interested in developing interdisciplinary and practice-based research. Hosted by the Critical Media Lab at the Institute Experimental Design and Media Cultures in Basel and conducted in partnership between Basel and Linz, the programme brings together individual mentoring, joint supervision, monthly colloquia, an annual assembly, public events and external collaborations.

The programme’s three central areas — Situated Artistic Research, Infrastructural Critique and Critical Media — offer different pathways for investigating how knowledge is created, embodied, mediated, organised and circulated.

Applicants must hold an MA degree of 120 ECTS or an equivalent qualification and submit a motivation letter, research project outline, CV, portfolio and academic documents. They must also identify two preferred supervisors and explain their financing plans.

A particularly important consideration is that the doctoral positions are not funded, meaning prospective candidates need to develop a realistic financial plan and explore external funding opportunities where appropriate.

For applicants whose professional practice and research interests align with the programme’s interdisciplinary and experimental approach, the pre-proposal stage represents the first opportunity to present a doctoral research project for consideration.

TITLE: PwC Student and Graduate Opportunities 2026: Graduate Jobs, Internships, Apprenticeships and Early-Career Career Programs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Starting a career after university can be challenging, particularly for graduates who are looking for an opportunity that combines professional training, practical experience, mentorship, and exposure to a global business environment. PwC offers a range of student and graduate opportunities designed to help university students and recent graduates transition into professional careers while developing the technical, business, leadership, and interpersonal skills required in today’s workplace.

The PwC student and graduate opportunities include several pathways for different stages of academic and professional development. These include graduate opportunities for recent university graduates, the China Sourcing Initiative for eligible students studying in the United States and Canada, the Deals—Edge graduate programme, the Assurance Remote Team Member programme, the Hong Kong Assurance Apprenticeship Programme, internships, and the LEAP programme.

These opportunities can be particularly valuable for students and graduates interested in professional services, accounting, auditing, business advisory, deals, and other corporate career pathways. Depending on the programme, applicants may receive structured training, career coaching, work-buddy support, practical project experience, exposure to experienced professionals, professional development opportunities, and potential pathways into longer-term employment.

The programmes have different eligibility requirements, academic levels, locations, and starting periods. Therefore, prospective applicants should carefully review the requirements for the specific programme they intend to pursue before submitting an application.

PwC Student and Graduate Opportunities at a Glance

PwC’s student and graduate opportunities are divided broadly into opportunities for graduates and opportunities for undergraduate or current university students.

Graduate Opportunities

The graduate-level opportunities featured include:

General Graduate Programme

China Sourcing Initiative

Deals—Edge

Assurance Remote Team Member (RTM)

Undergraduate and Student Opportunities

The student-focused opportunities include:

Apprenticeship

Internship

LEAP

This structure allows students to identify an opportunity according to their current stage of education, expected graduation year, academic background, and career interests.

1. PwC General Graduate Opportunities

The PwC General Graduate Programme is designed for recent graduates who are ready to begin their professional careers and develop into trusted business advisers.

PwC describes the programme as an opportunity for individuals who are passionate about teamwork, making a difference, and working in a firm that provides opportunities across a broad range of industries.

One of the major advantages of the graduate programme is its focus on structured professional development. Successful applicants receive training connected to the service area to which they are allocated.

The programme also provides support from experienced professionals, including a career coach and work buddy. This can help graduates understand their responsibilities, adapt to the professional environment, and develop their careers from the beginning.

According to the opportunity information, PwC welcomes applications from graduates of 2025, 2026, and 2027 who hold a bachelor’s degree or above. All majors are eligible.

What Does the PwC Graduate Programme Offer?

The programme is structured to help graduates make a successful transition from university into professional employment.

Key features include:

Entry-level professional training.

Training related to the applicant’s allocated service area.

Support from an experienced career coach.

Guidance from a work buddy.

Exposure to a broad range of industries.

Opportunities to work collaboratively as part of a professional team.

Development of skills needed to become a trusted business adviser.

For graduates who have limited professional experience, the combination of structured training, coaching, and practical workplace exposure can provide an important foundation for their careers.

PwC General Graduate Application Process

The application journey consists of several stages:

Online application

Online assessment

Meeting with PwC

PwC Superday

Receiving an offer

Offer celebration

The first step is the online application. Applicants are required to provide basic personal information as well as academic achievements and professional background information relevant to the job requirements.

When Does the General Graduate Programme Start?

The information provided states that the programme starts from August 2026.

General Graduate Eligibility

Applicants should have:

Graduated in 2025, 2026, or 2027.

A bachelor’s degree or above.

Any academic major, as all majors are eligible.

The source does not specify a particular nationality, race, or African-country eligibility requirement for the General Graduate Programme. Therefore, applicants should consult the specific vacancy and application conditions for the relevant PwC location.

2. PwC China Sourcing Initiative

The China Sourcing Initiative, commonly referred to as CSI, is a graduate programme designed for overseas students who want to begin their professional careers with PwC in Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong SAR, or Macau SAR.

The initiative specifically targets students in the United States and Canada who aspire to join PwC in full-time Associate positions.

An important feature of the programme is its remote application process. Eligible candidates do not need to travel back to Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong SAR, or Macau SAR during the application process because PwC facilitates the application through online assessments and virtual interviews.

Who Can Apply for the China Sourcing Initiative?

According to the provided information, applicants must:

Be studying at a university in the United States or Canada.

Hold a bachelor’s degree or above, or be pursuing such a degree.

Graduate between August 2025 and August 2027.

Meet the relevant work eligibility requirements.

Be eligible to work in Chinese Mainland and Macau SAR without a working visa.

For selected Associates working in Hong Kong SAR, PwC will provide Hong Kong SAR working visa sponsorship.

CSI Application Process

The China Sourcing Initiative application journey includes:

Online application.

Online assessment.

Information session.

Virtual interviews.

Receiving an offer.

Starting with PwC.

Applicants provide personal details together with their academic and professional background as part of the application process.

CSI Starting Period

The source states that the opportunity starts from August 2026.

3. PwC Deals—Edge Graduate Programme

The Deals—Edge programme is a graduate opportunity within PwC Deals EMEA and Asia Pacific.

It is designed to attract, develop, and retain talented graduates and help them build early-career skills in the Deals business.

The programme is particularly relevant to graduates who are interested in developing careers as Deals advisers and working in an international professional-services environment.

PwC describes Edge as a programme intended to launch graduate careers in an international Deals environment. It combines professional development with practical exposure and opportunities to work across different areas of the Deals business.

What Does the Deals—Edge Programme Include?

The programme features a combination of:

International development opportunities.

Rotations across different Deals business units.

Potential international rotations.

Regular professional learning.

Technical learning.

Opportunities to complete a professional qualification.

Development of early-career Deals skills.

Exposure to an international Deals environment.

Some rotations may be international, giving participants the possibility of gaining experience across different markets and business environments.

The programme is intended to help participants develop into the next generation of highly valued Deals advisers who can deliver sustainable outcomes and build trust with clients.

Who Is Eligible for PwC Edge?

PwC welcomes applications from:

2025 graduates.

2026 graduates.

2027 graduates.

Applicants with a bachelor’s degree or above.

Applicants from all academic majors.

Online assessment.

Meeting with PwC.

PwC Superday.

Offer celebration.
