TITLE: Bloomberg Fellows Program 2026–2027 at Johns Hopkins: Fully Funded MPH and DrPH Degrees for U.S.-Based Public Health Professionals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Bloomberg Fellows Program at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, a major public health leadership and graduate education initiative that provides selected professionals with full scholarship support to pursue either a Master of Public Health (MPH) or Doctor of Public Health (DrPH) degree while continuing to address some of the most urgent health challenges facing communities across the United States.

The Bloomberg Fellows Program is part of the Bloomberg American Health Initiative and is specifically designed for people already working on the front lines of public health and related social challenges. Rather than functioning as a conventional scholarship in which funding is based only on an individual student’s academic record, the programme creates a three-way partnership between the Fellow, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, and the Fellow’s employing organization.

Selected Fellows receive tuition and fee support for their Johns Hopkins degree. MPH Fellows also receive a fellowship stipend intended to offset costs such as travel, books and attendance at required in-person activities in Baltimore.

Applications for the current cycle close on:

December 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time.

Applicants must complete both the Johns Hopkins degree application and the separate Bloomberg Fellows application process. Admission to the relevant MPH or DrPH degree is a prerequisite for receiving the Fellowship.

About the Bloomberg Fellows Program

The Bloomberg Fellows Program was created to strengthen the capacity of organizations and professionals confronting major public health challenges in the United States.

The programme does not treat graduate education as separate from public health practice. Instead, it seeks to train professionals who are already embedded in organizations working directly with communities and systems affected by complex health and social problems.

Fellows pursue graduate training at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health while maintaining a formal relationship with a qualifying collaborating organization. After graduation, they must return to or continue working with that organization for at least one year so that the knowledge and skills developed through the degree can be applied directly to real-world public health challenges.

This makes the programme particularly relevant to professionals working in areas such as:

Public health departments

Community-based organizations

Nonprofit organizations

Health systems

Schools and education organizations

Criminal justice organizations

Environmental organizations

Housing and community development organizations

Food systems organizations

Violence-prevention programmes

Addiction and overdose prevention initiatives

Collaborating organizations do not necessarily need to be traditional public health institutions. What matters is that their work directly connects with one of the programme’s five priority areas.

Five Priority Areas

Applicants must select one of the Bloomberg American Health Initiative’s five focus areas.

These are:

Addiction and Overdose

Adolescent Health

Environmental Challenges

Food Systems for Health

Violence

The applicant’s professional responsibilities, collaborating organization and proposed academic development should all have a meaningful connection to the selected focus area.

1. Addiction and Overdose

This focus area is relevant to professionals addressing substance use, overdose and associated public health challenges.

Potential applicants may work in fields such as:

Harm reduction

Addiction treatment

Overdose prevention

Substance-use policy

Recovery programmes

Behavioral health

Community health

Public health surveillance

The Fellowship can help professionals deepen their ability to develop, evaluate and implement evidence-based responses to addiction and overdose.

2. Adolescent Health

The Adolescent Health focus area concentrates on improving the health and well-being of young people.

Relevant professional work may involve:

Schools

Youth-serving organizations

Mental health

Sexual and reproductive health

Youth development

Prevention programmes

Adolescent health policy

Community programmes for young people

Applicants do not need to work for a traditional health department. A school, nonprofit, community organization or other institution working directly on adolescent well-being may potentially serve as the collaborating organization if it satisfies Fellowship requirements.

3. Environmental Challenges

The Environmental Challenges focus area addresses the relationship between environmental conditions and population health.

Professionals may be engaged in areas such as:

Environmental justice

Climate and health

Air quality

Water safety

Housing conditions

Environmental policy

Community resilience

Environmental exposure and health

This area is particularly relevant for professionals interested in strengthening the public health response to environmental risks.

4. Food Systems for Health

This focus area examines how food systems influence population health.

Applicants might work in areas including:

Food access

Food insecurity

Nutrition

Agricultural systems

Community food systems

Healthy food policy

Neighborhood development

Institutional food systems

Johns Hopkins specifically notes that even an organization focused on neighborhood development could potentially qualify if its work meaningfully relates to food systems and health.

5. Violence

The Violence focus area supports professionals seeking to prevent violence and reduce its health consequences.

Relevant areas might include:

Community violence prevention

Intimate partner violence

Youth violence

Firearm injury prevention

Criminal justice

Trauma

Violence intervention

Community safety

Organizations working to reduce community violence can qualify even if they are not formally categorized as public health agencies.

Two Degree Pathways: MPH and DrPH

Bloomberg Fellows can pursue either:

Master of Public Health (MPH)

or:

Doctor of Public Health (DrPH)

Applicants must select one programme during a given application cycle. They cannot apply simultaneously to both the MPH and DrPH for Fellowship consideration in the same cycle.

Bloomberg Fellows MPH

The Johns Hopkins MPH option is available in both:

Full-time format

Part-time format

The full-time MPH takes approximately 11 months, beginning in late June and ending the following May. It is based primarily in Baltimore.

The part-time MPH combines:

Online coursework

In-person components

and typically takes approximately two to three years to complete.

Both formats are eligible for the Bloomberg Fellows Program.

Full-Time MPH Fellows

Full-time MPH Fellows generally take a leave of absence from their collaborating organization to complete the intensive 11-month programme.

The leave arrangement must be agreed between the Fellow and the employer.

The Fellow remains connected to the organization through the Fellowship structure and ultimately completes the required service obligation following graduation.

Part-Time MPH Fellows

Part-time MPH Fellows generally continue working:

Full-time with their collaborating organization

while completing their academic programme.

This model may be particularly attractive to professionals who want to continue contributing directly to their organization while pursuing graduate training.

MPH Scholarship Coverage

Bloomberg Fellows pursuing the MPH receive scholarship support covering:

Tuition and fees for up to 80 credits.

MPH Fellows also receive a stipend.

The stipend is intended to help offset Fellowship-related costs including:

Travel

Books

Other programme-related expenses

Costs associated with attending required in-person coursework in Baltimore

The Fellowship page confirms that the stipend is available to both full-time and part-time MPH Fellows.

The official programme page does not currently publish a universal stipend amount, so applicants should not rely on unofficial figures circulated elsewhere.

MPH Admissions Requirements

Receiving the Fellowship requires admission to the Johns Hopkins MPH programme.

For students beginning the MPH in June 2027 or later, Johns Hopkins lists several important requirements.

Applicants generally need relevant health-related professional preparation and must satisfy one of the programme’s experience pathways. The standard route requires at least:

Two years of full-time, paid, post-baccalaureate health-related professional experience.

Alternative qualifying pathways include certain doctoral degrees or U.S. post-baccalaureate professional health training.

MPH Coursework Prerequisites for 2027 Entry

For applicants beginning in June 2027 or later, the MPH requires:

One mathematics course, such as calculus, algebra or statistics

One health-related science course

Examples of acceptable health-related sciences can include:

Biology

Microbiology

Cellular biology

Nutrition

Anatomy and physiology

Epidemiology

Psychology

Environmental science

Neuroscience

Genetics

Kinesiology

These courses must be completed satisfactorily at an accredited institution by matriculation.

Standardized Tests for the MPH

Johns Hopkins currently states that standardized test scores such as the:

GRE

GMAT

LSAT

MCAT

are optional for the MPH programme.

Applicants who do not submit test scores are still expected to demonstrate adequate quantitative and analytical ability through other parts of the application.

Bloomberg Fellows DrPH

The Doctor of Public Health is designed for experienced professionals seeking advanced public health leadership roles.

The programme is predominantly:

Part-time

and combines online study with summer and winter institutes and other academic requirements.

It is intended for individuals who already have an MPH or another relevant graduate degree and who plan to pursue leadership positions in public health practice.

DrPH Scholarship Coverage

Bloomberg Doctoral Fellows receive support covering:

All tuition and fees for up to 70 credits.

Unlike MPH Fellows, the official Fellowship information does not state that DrPH Fellows receive the MPH Fellowship stipend.

The stipend described by Johns Hopkins is specifically for Bloomberg Fellows enrolled in the MPH programme.

This distinction is important when promoting the programme.

The DrPH is fully tuition-funded under the Fellowship, but applicants should not assume that the same additional stipend applies.

DrPH Academic Requirements

Applicants to the DrPH must hold:

An MPH or another relevant graduate degree

by the time they matriculate.

Examples of potentially acceptable graduate degrees include:

MPH

MHA

MHS

MPP

MSPH

MS or ScM

Health-focused MBA

Other relevant graduate degrees

DrPH Professional Experience Requirement

DrPH applicants must have at least:

Three years of full-time professional experience in public health, healthcare or a closely related field

by the December 1 application deadline.

This makes the DrPH pathway more appropriate for professionals who already have substantial applied experience.

Who Can Apply for the Bloomberg Fellows Program?

At the Fellowship level, applicants must satisfy several important requirements.

They must be:

Currently based in the United States

Working full-time for a qualifying organization

Working in one of the five priority areas

Performing that relevant work in the United States

Applying to either the Johns Hopkins MPH or DrPH

Admitted to the relevant degree programme

Supported by their collaborating organization

Applicant Must Be a Full-Time Employee

Applicants cannot participate merely as volunteers.

Johns Hopkins states that the collaborating organization is the applicant’s employer and that the applicant must be employed full-time by that organization when applying.

The Fellowship FAQ further states that applicants should have worked for the collaborating organization for:

More than one year at the time of application.

This is an important eligibility condition.

What Is a Collaborating Organization?

The collaborating organization is the applicant’s employer.

It can be a:

Public organization

Private organization

Nonprofit

Government agency

Health organization

School

Community organization

Criminal justice organization

Housing organization

Environmental organization

Other institution

provided its work connects meaningfully with one of the five Bloomberg American Health Initiative focus areas.

The organization itself and the relevant work must be based in the United States.

The Organization Must Participate in the Application

The collaborating organization is not simply listed as an employer.

It must actively participate in the application.

The organization completes a separate:

Collaborating Organization Form

and confirms its support for the applicant.

If the Fellow is selected, the organization must also sign a:

Letter of Commitment

pledging in good faith to employ the Fellow for at least one year after graduation.

Service Obligation After Graduation

A central requirement of the Bloomberg Fellows Program is the:

Service Obligation.

After completing the MPH or DrPH, Fellows must work as full-time employees of their collaborating organization in the selected focus area for at least:

One year.

The service must begin within 12 months of completing the degree requirements.

This requirement reflects the programme’s central philosophy: Johns Hopkins invests in professionals who will take advanced public health skills back into organizations already working on urgent U.S. health challenges.

Important Grant Repayment Condition

Applicants should understand that the Fellowship funding is linked to completion of the degree and the Service Obligation.

For MPH Fellows, Johns Hopkins states that failure to satisfy the terms of the Grant Agreement can require repayment of the full grant award. The programme describes the Fellowship as a grant that can convert to a loan if the requirements are not met.

The stated loan arrangement can extend for up to 15 years at an annual interest rate of 1%.

Applicants should therefore read the Grant Agreement carefully before accepting the award.

Can International Applicants Apply?

Yes.

Applicants do not have to be U.S. citizens.

However, this should not be confused with being globally open regardless of residence.

International applicants must still be:

Currently based in the United States

Employed full-time by a qualifying organization

Performing qualifying work in the United States

The collaborating organization’s relevant work must also be based in the United States.

Therefore, someone living and working in Kenya, India, Nigeria, Brazil, Germany or another country would not qualify simply because international citizens are technically eligible.

Nationality is flexible; current professional location is not.

Existing Johns Hopkins MPH or DrPH Students Are Not Eligible

The Fellowship is intended for people who are newly applying to the relevant degree.

Applicants who are already matriculated in the MPH or DrPH programme are not eligible to apply for the Bloomberg Fellowship.

This means prospective Fellows should apply for the Fellowship at the same time they seek admission to Johns Hopkins.

You Must Apply to the Degree and Fellowship Separately

There are two separate processes.

Step 1: Apply to Johns Hopkins

Applicants must submit an application to either:

MPH

DrPH

through SOPHAS, the Schools of Public Health Application Service.

Step 2: Apply to the Bloomberg Fellows Program

Applicants must separately submit:

Bloomberg Fellows applicant form

Collaborating Organization form

through the Fellowship application platform.

Completing only the degree application is not enough.

Completing only the Fellowship application is also not enough.

Admission Is Required Before Fellowship Selection

Being interested in the Fellowship does not override the academic admissions process.

An applicant must be admitted to the relevant Johns Hopkins degree to remain eligible for Fellowship consideration.

For DrPH applicants, those placed on the admission waitlist are not considered for the Fellowship because Fellowship review operates on a separate fixed timeline.

MPH and DrPH Start Dates

Selected Fellows begin according to the programme they choose.

MPH

Bloomberg MPH Fellows begin in:

June

DrPH

Bloomberg DrPH Fellows begin in:

August

For the 2027–28 academic cycle, the Johns Hopkins admissions calendar lists December 1, 2026 as the deadline for both the relevant June 2027 MPH intake and the DrPH programme.

Required In-Person Study in Baltimore

Although significant portions of some programmes can be completed online, Bloomberg Fellows should not assume the Fellowship can be completed entirely remotely.

All Bloomberg Fellows must complete at least:

Five in-person academic credits in Baltimore.

Applicants should therefore plan for the associated travel and scheduling requirements.

For MPH Fellows, the stipend is partly intended to help offset costs connected with these in-person requirements.

Fellowship Orientation

New Fellows must participate in a Fellowship orientation.

Johns Hopkins states that orientation generally takes place in:

Early to mid-June

and is typically conducted virtually via Zoom.

Bloomberg American Health Summit

Fellows are also expected to participate in the annual:

Bloomberg American Health Summit

which usually takes place near the end of the year.

The Summit brings together:

Fellows

Alumni

Faculty

Collaborating organizations

Public health leaders

Initiative partners

and provides an opportunity for cross-sector learning and networking.

Problem-Focused Networks

One of the distinctive features of the Fellowship is participation in professional networks associated with the five priority areas.

These networks bring together:

Fellows

Alumni

Johns Hopkins faculty

Organizations

to:

Identify common challenges

Develop collaborative research

Share information

Implement evidence-based policies

Develop programmes

The network therefore continues beyond the academic degree itself.

Enrichment and Professional Development

Bloomberg Fellows also receive access to special learning and professional-development opportunities.

These can include:

Seminars

Speakers

Training

Professional networking

Fellowship activities

Cross-focus-area learning

This makes the Fellowship more than simply a tuition scholarship.

MPH Practicum and Capstone

For MPH Fellows, the programme directly connects academic requirements with the collaborating organization.

Fellows must work with their organization to develop:

Practicum

Capstone project

that benefits both the Fellow and organization and relates to the Fellow’s selected priority area.

This helps ensure that the graduate degree remains grounded in practical public health work.

Can Applicants Change Their Collaborating Organization?

This is highly restricted.

The Fellowship is awarded based on the combination of:

Applicant

Collaborating organization

If a selected Fellow changes organizations after receiving the award, during onboarding, before starting, or within the specified early programme period, the Fellowship can be rescinded.

Applicants should therefore be confident about their relationship with their organization before applying.

Can Fellows Defer the Award?

No.

The Bloomberg Fellows Program does not permit Fellowship deferrals.

Selected applicants must either:

Accept the award for the specified cycle, or

Decline it

They cannot automatically move the Fellowship to the following year.

Dual and Joint Degrees Are Not Eligible

The Bloomberg Fellows Program is specifically intended for applicants pursuing either the:

MPH

DrPH

It does not support Fellows enrolled in dual or joint degree programmes.

Application Deadline

The current Fellowship application closes:

December 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST.

Johns Hopkins also lists December 1, 2026 as the relevant admissions deadline for:

DrPH

MPH full-time 2027 entry

MPH online/part-time June 2027 entry

Applicants should not wait until the deadline because they need to coordinate both the degree application and the collaborating organization component.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

1. Demonstrate Clear Alignment With One Priority Area

Do not merely select a focus area because it sounds interesting.

Explain how your current professional work already addresses:

Addiction and overdose

Adolescent health

Environmental challenges

Food systems for health

Violence

Your role should show genuine frontline engagement.

2. Explain Why Graduate Training Will Strengthen Your Existing Work

The Fellowship is not simply designed for someone who wants a prestigious public health degree.

Explain how Johns Hopkins training will help you:

Improve programmes

Develop stronger evidence

Lead organizations

Evaluate interventions

Design policy

Improve systems

Strengthen community health

3. Work Closely With Your Employer

Your collaborating organization is an integral part of your application.

Before applying, make sure organizational leadership understands:

The Fellowship structure

Degree format

Time requirements

Service Obligation

Organization form

Letter of Commitment

4. Explain How Your Organization Will Benefit

Strong applications should demonstrate mutual benefit.

Explain how the degree will strengthen:

Organizational capacity

Programme design

Leadership

Research

Evaluation

Community impact

5. Prepare Early

Because the application has multiple components, applicants should allow enough time for:

SOPHAS

Academic transcripts

Recommendations

Johns Hopkins requirements

Collaborating organization documentation

Fellowship essays/forms

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: Bloomberg Fellows Program

Institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health

Country: United States

Degrees: MPH or DrPH

MPH formats: Full-time or part-time

MPH scholarship: Tuition and fees for up to 80 credits

MPH stipend: Yes, for both full-time and part-time Fellows

DrPH scholarship: Tuition and fees for up to 70 credits

DrPH stipend: No general stipend stated on the official Fellowship page

Priority areas: Addiction and overdose; adolescent health; environmental challenges; food systems for health; violence

Residence requirement: Applicant must currently be based in the United States

Employment: Full-time with qualifying collaborating organization

Employer tenure: Applicants should have been employed by the organization for more than one year when applying

Nationality: U.S. citizenship not required

Post-graduation requirement: At least one year of employment with collaborating organization

In-person requirement: At least five credits in Baltimore

MPH start: June

DrPH start: August

Deadline: December 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST

To know more about this opportunity, please visit the OFFICAL WEBSITE.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Bloomberg Fellows Program 2026–2027 at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health is a substantial opportunity for professionals who are already working to address major public health challenges in the United States and want advanced graduate training without assuming the full tuition burden of an MPH or DrPH.

Selected MPH Fellows receive tuition and fee coverage for up to 80 credits, while DrPH Fellows receive tuition and fee support for up to 70 credits. MPH Fellows additionally receive a stipend designed to help offset Fellowship-related expenses.

The Fellowship is built around five focus areas: addiction and overdose, adolescent health, environmental challenges, food systems for health, and violence. Applicants must already work full-time for a U.S.-based organization engaged in one of these areas, and both the applicant and relevant organizational work must be based in the United States.

Importantly, this is not simply a tuition award. The programme establishes a long-term partnership among the Fellow, Johns Hopkins and the collaborating organization. Fellows must remain engaged with their organization during their studies as appropriate to their programme format and complete at least one year of full-time service with the organization after graduation.

Applications require separate submissions to the MPH or DrPH programme and the Bloomberg Fellows Program, together with participation from the collaborating organization.

The deadline is:

December 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST.

Prospective applicants should begin coordinating with their employer and preparing the Johns Hopkins admission application well before the deadline.

To discover more global fellowship opportunities, VISIT HERE.

TITLE: AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers 2026 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 16, 2026

Applications are open for the AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers 2026. This grant is generously funded by the German Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and with the support of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation (AvH).

This AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grant for Junior Researchers aims to strengthen the scientific capacity and networking of young researchers in sub-Saharan Africa through the active cooperation of AGNES and potential AGNES members (serving as supervisors for the awardees of this grant). It further supports the alumni of the AvH Foundation in their efforts towards mentoring high potential junior researchers, helping them to access international networks of scientific excellence.

AGNES is operating two Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers for which application may be submitted directly by interested and qualified candidates from sub-Sahara Africa:

General AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers (Generally for MALE and FEMALE candidates)

Special AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants for Junior Researchers (For FEMALE candidates ONLY)

Funding

1 Month: up to EUR 2,300

1.5 Months: up to EUR 2,650

2 Months: up to EUR 3,000

Eligibility

Direct applications from junior researchers having published at least one article from their thesis work (in a non-predatory journal) will be considered for both AGNES Mobility Grants.

The applicant:

may be from any academic discipline but must be officially registered for a doctoral degree at a university/tertiary institute in sub-Sahara Africa at the time of application

must be a national of a sub-Saharan African country, and

must have, at least one already published paper from his/her earlier thesis work (in a non-predatory journal). For the avoidance of doubt, they will only consider journals that are indexed by SCOPUS and Web of Science.

The applicant must clearly demonstrate that their work is relevant towards development in sub-Saharan African countries and cannot be conducted in the home country.

Only applicants with an identified scientific host and mutually agreed-upon proposal/work schedule will be considered for the Grant.

Application

Complete applications MUST include the following:

A short research/project proposal which MUST be in ENGLISH language (not more than 5 pages) from the junior scientist (applicant) with a short outline of the proposed research activity and a work schedule for achieving the aim(s) of the research project at the host institution. The scientific host must agree in writing to the proposal and time schedule.

A standard CV of the applicant which MUST be in ENGLISH language (use the AGNES template). The AGNES CV template can be obtained from here: Download 2026 AGNES Intra-Africal Mobility CV-Template.

Official proof of registration for the postgraduate degree (only current doctoral students are eligible).

A copy of the official academic transcripts of the applicant, reflecting the grades obtained in the undergraduate and any postgraduate studies. If your transcript is in another language, supply the official explanation of the grading system in English language.

A list of published articles in non-predatory journals with SCOPUS or Web of Science links (URL) to each publication (include an e-copy of the first page showing the title, authors and the abstract). Both the list of publications and the first page of each publication should be merged into a single PDF document. The document should begin with a descriptive title on the first page (e.g., “LIST OF PUBLICATIONS FOR JOHNSON JAMES”), followed by the list of publications (with the link to each publication included after the title and other details of the publication). The first page of each publication should then follow in the same PDF document.

Travel costs (by land or economy class flight): supply two quotes for the journey (including return travel) between the applicant’s country of residence and the country of the host institute).

Estimated cost of living (rent, meals, local transport, health insurance) at the host institute. Applicants are expected to conclude a valid health insurance for the research stay. Scientific hosts and host institutes are expected to assist applicants in finding affordable accommodation and advise them on establishing subsistence estimates.

Letter of invitation from the scientific host (MUST be in English language): (i) confirming that a place to work will be available at the indicated period, (ii) a binding declaration from the host institution requesting an amount of the research cost allowance. The amount of EUR 100 per month and EUR 200 per month, respectively, will be deducted from the total grant amount for Humanities & Social Sciences, and Natural & Life Sciences and Engineering Sciences, to cover bench fees.

Click here to apply

For more information, visit AGNES Intra-Africa Mobility Grants.

TITLE: Graduate Admissions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Admissions Information for Prospective Graduate Students

Thank you for considering the PhD program in Physics at MIT. Information regarding our graduate program and our application process can be found below and through the following webpages and other links on this page. If your questions are not answered after reviewing this information, please contact us at physics-grad@mit.edu.

Here are some links to pages relevant to prospective students:

Material Required for a Complete Application, and information about When/How to Apply can be found below on this page.

We have an FAQ which should help to answer many questions, and we provide Application Assistance from staff and students if you don’t find what you need in the FAQ.

Additional Guidance about the application itself, along with examples, can be found on a separate page. The graduate application is available at https://apply.mit.edu/apply/.

General information about the graduate program and research areas in the physics department may also be of use.

MSRP (MIT Summer Research Program) is designed to give underrepresented and underserved students access to an MIT research experience, pairing each student with a faculty member who will oversee the student conducting a research project at MIT.

Statement regarding COVID grading policies

MIT has adopted the following principle: MIT’s admissions committees and offices for graduate and professional schools will take the significant disruptions of the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020 into account when reviewing students’ transcripts and other admissions materials as part of their regular practice of performing individualized, holistic reviews of each applicant.

In particular, as we review applications now and in the future, we will respect decisions regarding the adoption of Pass/No Record (or Credit/No Credit or Pass/Fail) and other grading options during the unprecedented period of COVID-19 disruptions, whether those decisions were made by institutions or by individual students. We also expect that the individual experiences of applicants will richly inform applications and, as such, they will be considered with the entirety of a student’s record.

Ultimately, even in these challenging times, our goal remains to form graduate student cohorts that are collectively excellent and composed of outstanding individuals who will challenge and support one another.

Questions or concerns about this statement should be directed to the Physics Department (physics-grad@mit.edu).

Applying to the MIT Department of Physics

We know that the application process can be time-consuming, stressful, and costly. We are committed to reducing these barriers and to helping all applicants receive a full and fair assessment by our faculty reviewers. Help is available from the Physics Graduate Admissions Office at physics-grad@mit.edu and additional assistance from current students is offered during the admissions season. Further details are described at the end of this page in our Assistance for Prospective Applicants section.

The list below describes the important elements of a complete application. Please reach out to us at physics-grad@mit.edu if you have a concern or logistical difficulty that could prevent you from providing your strongest application.

Required for a Complete Application

1. Online Application and Application Fee

MIT Graduate Admissions Online Graduate Application

Application Fee: $90

2. University Transcript(s)

Unofficial transcripts are sufficient for our initial review, with final transcripts required as a condition of matriculation for successful applicants. Applicants should include a scan of their transcript(s) and, if a degree is in progress, should include a list of the class subjects being taken in the current semester. The portal will allow applicants to log back into the application after the deadline to add their Fall term grades when they are available.

Note: We will respect decisions regarding the adoption of Pass/No Record (or Credit/No Credit or Pass/Fail) and other grading options during the unprecedented period of COVID-19 disruptions, whether those decisions were made by institutions or by individual students.

3. Standardized Test Results

GRE Tests: The Physics GRE (PGRE) is recommended but not required for graduate applications. All applications will be given full consideration with or without GRE scores.

TOEFL or IELTS Test, Cambridge English, or Duolingo English Test or a waiver is required for non-native English speakers. MIT’s TOEFL school code is 3514; the code for the Department of Physics is 76. IELTS does not require a code. Eligibility for English Language Proficiency Test waivers is in our FAQ section.

Self-reported scores are sufficient for our initial application screening, with official scores required for admitted students as a condition of their offer. Applicants should attach a scanned copy of their test score report.

4. Letters of Recommendation

Letters should include any individual work applicants have done and/or areas where they have special strengths. It is possible to submit up to 6 total letters, but 3 are sufficient for a complete application and committee members may evaluate applications based on the first three letters that they read.

5. Statement of Objectives

Research is central to graduate study in physics. The Statement of Objectives/Purpose should include descriptions of research projects, aptitude and achievements as completely as possible. This important part of the application provides an opportunity to describe any interests, skills, and background relative to the research areas selected on the application form. Applicants should share anything that prepares them for graduate studies and describe their proudest achievements.

Additional Application Materials

Research, Teaching, and Community Engagement – Any special background or achievement that prepares the applicant for Physics graduate studies at MIT. This may include research at their undergraduate school as part of their Bachelor or Master degree, or summer research at another program or school. We also value our student’s contributions to their community on a variety of scales (from institutional to societal) and we encourage applicants to tell us about their teaching and community engagement activities. The “experience” questions are intended to provide a CV-like listing of achievements, some of which may be elaborated on in the “Statement of Objectives” and/or the optional “Personal Statement”.

Publications, Talks, and Merit Based Recognition – Recognition of success in research, academics, and outreach can take many forms, including publications, talks, honors, prizes, awards, fellowships, etc. This may include current nominations for scholarships or papers submitted for publication.

Optional Personal Statement – Members of our community come from a wide variety of backgrounds and experiences. We welcome any personal information that will help us to evaluate applications holistically and will provide context for the applicant’s academic achievements. This statement may include extenuating circumstances, significant challenges that were overcome, a non-traditional educational background, description of any advocacy or values work, or other information that may be relevant.

Detailed instructions for each application section, and many examples, can be found on the “Additional Guidance” page. The detailed instructions are lengthy, and are intended to be read only “as needed” while you work on your application (i.e., you don’t need to go read the whole thing before you start).

When/How to Apply

When: Applications can be submitted between September 15 and December 15 by 11:59pm EST for the following year.

How: The application is online at https://apply.mit.edu/apply/

Application Assistance

Faculty, students, and staff have collaborated to provide extensive guidance to prospective applicants to our graduate degree program, which we detail below:

Our website provides answers to many frequently asked admissions questions

Admissions staff are available for questions at physics-grad@mit.edu. We encourage students to send their questions early in the application process, as staff become increasingly busy with requests as the application deadline approaches!

The Physics Graduate Application Assistance Program (PhysGAAP) is run by current graduate students and offers online webinars, office hours, and one-on-one mentoring. Registration is now open for Fall 2025, and more information is provided below.

Physics Graduate Application Assistance Program (PhysGAAP)

PhysGAAP is a program offering resources for students applying to graduate school, and it was first started to reduce the barriers for application to the MIT Physics PhD program and address the underrepresentation of students from historically excluded communities. Our services include annual webinars about the application process, office hours to answer questions, and a one-on-one mentoring program for students who would benefit from more in-depth, individual assistance.

Visit the PhysGAAP website for more information!

Webinars

The Fall 2025 webinars will be held on October 22nd at 9-10am and 4-5pm. Zoom and Slido information will be sent 1 week before the webinar to applicants who have registered for PhysGAAP using this form.

Recordings of past webinars can also be found on our website. Please note past webinars may contain outdated information about some topics, such as GRE requirements.

Office Hours

Our Office Hours are a space where you can briefly chat with an MIT Physics graduate student about questions you may have about applying to graduate school. For example, if you have questions about the specifics of applying to MIT Physics, what materials you need for your application, or other questions that only require a one-time meeting, office hours may be a good option for you.

Information about the Office Hours program will be sent out to those who register for PhysGAAP through this form.

1-on-1 Mentorship

1-on-1 mentoring is offered for students who would benefit from more in-depth individual assistance. Our capacity is limited, so we will give preferential consideration to PhysGAAP Mentorship applicants who would most benefit from the program and can demonstrate that they are a good fit. We therefore ask prospective applicants to start by asking their questions at our webinars and office hours program.

If applicants want further assistance, they may apply to the PhysGAAP Mentorship Program, which pairs prospective graduate school applicants with current graduate students who can provide feedback on their application and insight into graduate school and the MIT Physics PhD program.

Applications for the PhysGAAP Mentorship Program will open later in the Fall and are expected to close in early-mid November. To stay up to date on when the applications open, please register for PhysGAAP through this form.

Please note that participation in PhysGAAP is not considered during admissions review. It helps applicants put forward their strongest materials, but does not guarantee admission into our graduate program.

Admissions/Application FAQs

Our Frequently Asked Questions provide further information about degree requirements, funding, educational background, application deadlines, English language proficiency, program duration, start dates and deferrals, and fee waiver requests.

The MOST Frequently Asked Question…

What is included in a strong graduate application for Physics at MIT?

Applications are assessed holistically and many variables are considered in the application review process. The following four main factors are required for a complete application.

the applicant’s statement of objectives or purpose,

transcripts of past grades,

score reports of any required standardized tests,

three letters of reference.

In addition, any past research experience, publications, awards, and honors are extremely helpful, particularly if they are in the area(s) of the applicant’s interest(s). Applicants may also include a personal statement in their application to provide context as the materials are assessed.

Applications are routed to admission committee members and other faculty readers using the “areas of interest” and any faculty names selected from the menu as well as based on the research interests included in the statement of objectives. Please select the areas of interest that best reflect your goals.

Instructions are available in the application itself, with further guidance on our Additional Guidance page. The Physics Admissions Office will respond to questions sent to physics-grad@mit.edu.

General Questions Regarding the PhD Program in Physics

Must I have a degree in physics in order to apply to this graduate program?

Our successful applicants generally hold a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics, or have taken many Physics classes if they have majored in another discipline. The most common other majors are astronomy, engineering, mathematics, and chemistry. Bachelor of Science degrees may be 3-year or 4-year degrees, depending on the education structure of the country in which they are earned.

What are the requirements to complete a PhD?

The requirements for a PhD in Physics at MIT are the doctoral examination, a few required subject classes, and a research-based thesis. The doctoral examination consists of a written and an oral examination. The written component may be satisfied either by passing the 4 subject exams or by passing designated classes related to each topic with a qualifying grade; the oral exam will be given in a student’s chosen research area. The Physics Department also requires that each student take two classes in the field of specialization and two physics-related courses in fields outside the specialty. Research for the thesis is conducted throughout the student’s time in the program, culminating in a thesis defense and submission of the final thesis.

Can I take courses at other schools nearby?

Yes. Cross-registration is available at Harvard University and Wellesley College.

How many years does it take to complete the PhD requirements?

From 3 to 7 years, averaging 5.6 years.

How will I pay for my studies?

Our students are fully supported financially throughout the duration of their program, provided that they make satisfactory progress. Funding is provided from Fellowships (internal and external) and/or Assistantships (research and teaching) and covers tuition, health insurance, and a living stipend. Read more about funding.

Note: For more detailed information regarding the cost of attendance, including specific costs for tuition and fees, books and supplies, housing and food as well as transportation, please visit the Student Financial Services (SFS) website.

How many applications are submitted each year? How many students are accepted?

Although the number varies each year, the Department of Physics usually welcomes approximately 45 incoming graduate students each year. Last year we received more than 1,700 applications and extended fewer than 90 offers of admission.

What are the minimum grades and exam scores for admitted applicants?

There are no minimum standards for overall grade point averages/GPAs. Grades from physics and other related classes will be carefully assessed. Under a special COVID-19 policy, MIT will accept transcripts with a variety of grading conventions, including any special grading given during the COVID-19 pandemic.

PGREs (Physics subject GRE) is not required for graduate applications but is recommended.

Our program is conducted in English and all applicants must demonstrate their English language proficiency. Non-native English speakers should review our policy carefully before waiving the TOEFL/IELTS requirements. We do not set a minimum requirement on TOEFL/IELTS scores; however, students who are admitted to our program typically score above the following values:

IELTS – 7

TOEFL iBT26 – 5

TOEFL (computer based) – 200

TOEFL (iBT) – 100

TOEFL (standard) – 600

The Application Process

When is the deadline for applying to the PhD program in Physics?

Applications for enrollment in the fall are due each year by 11:59pm EST on December 15 of the preceding year. There is no admission cycle for spring-term enrollment.

The COVID-19 pandemic has made it difficult for me to take tests in person. Can I still apply?

PGRE (Physics subject GRE) is not required for graduate applications but is recommended.

Non-native English speakers who are not eligible for a test waiver should include their results from either an in-person or online version of the TOEFL or IELTS test.

Does the Department of Physics provide waivers for the English language exam (TOEFL/IELTS)?

The language of instruction at MIT is English and *all* applicants must include proof of their English language proficiency in their application. Therefore, an English language exam (IELTS, TOEFL, TOEFL iBT, Duolingo English, or the C2 Cambridge English Proficiency exam) is required of all applicants who are from a country in which English is not the primary language or attended a non-English-speaking college or university (see below for info).

Ways to demonstrate English Language Proficiency:

‘Native English Speaker’. Applicant was born and raised in a country where English is the official language used and where schools are taught in English. Examples include the USA, United Kingdom, and Australia.(Country of birth and life-long residence.)

’Non-Native English Speaker.’ Applicant attended an English-speaking college or university in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, or New Zealand and attained an undergraduate (or equivalent) degree from that institution within the last 5 years.

Applicants who do not fit any of the above categories and who demonstrate their English language proficiency through TOEFL or IELTS standardized tests, including the remote or online versions. Applicants should include self-reported test scores with the application materials and provide official test scores if an acceptance offer is made. (Interviews may also be conducted.)

Note: The applicant should decide which of the above categories will best demonstrate their English language skills. We receive many hundreds of applications and English language proficiency is carefully assessed as part of our admissions selection process. If there is any lack of clarity in demonstrating your English skills, please consider taking the TOEFL or IELTS tests. Your application can include the unofficial, self-reported results from the remote on-line version and we will contact you if we need official scores sent.

The Physics Admissions committee may conduct video interviews as part of an English language assessment or when finalizing their decisions. All incoming non-native English speakers or students who did not attend an English-speaking college or university within the last 5 years are required to demonstrate their language proficiency upon the start of their MIT studies.

Does the Department of Physics provide application fee waivers?

Although we do not want the MIT application fee to be a barrier to admission, we cannot provide application fee waivers to all who request one.

The Department of Physics has a limited number of fee waivers to grant. To request a fee waiver, you must be ineligible to request an OGE fee waiver or have been denied an OGE fee waiver.

Fee waiver requests will only be considered *before* an applicant has submitted the application, but *after* they have completed all parts of the application, including transcript uploads, statement, and requests for letters of recommendation. Fee waiver requests for incomplete applications will not be considered.

Fee waiver requests will be considered on a first-come-first-served basis, and not after December 1. Furthermore, applications lacking the paid fee or a fee waiver by 11:59pm EST on December 15 will not be reviewed or considered for admission.

Can I arrange a visit to the Physics Department or a specific research area?

We are not currently hosting or meeting with outside visitors in person, nor are we facilitating visits to our classrooms. Current graduate students and prospective applicants should direct any questions by email to physics-grad@mit.edu.

Applicants are invited to send specific questions to the Physics Admissions Office and some questions may be forwarded to current students for further information.

Admitted students will be invited to attend an in-person open house.

Can I receive an update on the status of my application?

Candidates can check on the status of their application at apply.mit.edu/apply at any time. It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure that all items are sent.

When will I be notified of a final decision?

Applicants will be notified via email of decisions by the end of February. If you have not heard from us by March 1, please send email to physics-grad@mit.edu.

We do not provide results by phone.

Can admitted students start in a term other than the next Fall semester?

Applications submitted between September 15 and December 15 by 11:59pm EST are assessed for the following Fall semester. We do not provide a separate admission review cycle for the Spring semester. Individual research supervisors may invite incoming students to start their research during the summer term a few months earlier than their studies would normally begin. All other incoming students start their studies in late August for the Fall term.

Once admitted, applicants may request a one-year deferral to attend a specific academic program or for another approved reason, with single semester deferrals for the following Spring term granted only rarely.

NATO is inviting qualified professionals to apply for its Temporary Staff (NATO HQ) candidate pool, offering opportunities to work at NATO Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium.

The recruitment process is designed to create a pool of qualified candidates who may be considered for temporary positions that arise periodically across different functions within NATO’s International Staff. Rather than recruiting applicants for one specific vacancy or assignment, NATO will use the candidate pool when temporary staffing needs emerge.

The opportunity may be particularly relevant to professionals with experience in areas such as administration, communications, project management, human resources, finance, information technology, cybersecurity, legal affairs, logistics, public diplomacy, political affairs, graphic design, event management, social media, research and analysis, and other specialized functions.

Opportunity Overview

NATO Headquarters occasionally needs professionals to fill temporary positions across its International Staff structure.

The Temporary Staff (NATO HQ) recruitment process allows NATO to maintain a database of candidates who have relevant professional skills and may be available to take on temporary assignments.

This means that applicants are not applying for one particular job description. Instead, they are applying to become part of a candidate pool from which NATO can identify suitable professionals when temporary staffing requirements arise.

Temporary positions may become available in a wide variety of professional disciplines, depending on NATO’s operational and organizational needs.

Because these assignments can arise unexpectedly and may need to be filled quickly, NATO places particular emphasis on candidates who are capable of being available at short notice.

Who Can Apply for the NATO Temporary Staff Positions?

The most important eligibility requirement is nationality.

Applicants must be nationals of a NATO member state.

Therefore, being professionally qualified alone is not sufficient. Candidates must also meet NATO’s nationality requirements.

Applicants should also have:

TITLE: Past and future modulation of the ENSO teleconnection to Southeast Asian rainfall by interbasin interactions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Le Roy, E. J., & Ummenhofer, C. C. (2025). Past and Future Modulation of the ENSO Teleconnection to Southeast Asian Rainfall by Interbasin Interactions. Geophysical Research Letters, 52, e2024GL111916. https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL111916

a) Modeled 13-year running correlation coefficient of Mainland Southeast Asia (MSEA) precipitation for March-May (year 0) with the Niño3.4 index for December-February (year -1) in LENS2 for the individual ensemble members (light gray and pink lines) and ensemble mean (thick black line). b) Relationship between the December-February (year -1) Niño3.4 index and March-May (year 0) precipitation (right y-axis) and precipitation anomalies (left y-axis) averaged over the MSEA region in LENS2 (1900–2014). c) December-February (year -1) SST anomalies (shading; °C) and 850-hPa wind anomalies (vectors; 1 m/s) during positive phases of the Tropical Tripole Pattern, when ENSO and MSEA precipitation are uncorrelated, for 13-year periods in LENS2 (1900-2014). d) Same as (c ) but during negative phases of the Tropical Tripole Pattern, when ENSO and MSEA precipitation are strongly correlated. e) March-May (year 0) precipitation anomalies (shading; mm/month) and total, vertically-integrated, precipitable water (contour lines; kg/m2) during positive phases of the Tropical Tripole Pattern for 13-year periods in LENS2 (1900-2014). f) Same as (e ) but during negative phases of the Tropical Pattern. Image provided by E.J. Le Roy.

ENSO’s teleconnection with rainfall in mainland Southeast Asia (MSEA) indicates a large degree of variability on decadal timescales. This study uses the Community Earth System Model version 2 Large Ensemble (LENS2) to identify conditions that amplify or dampen the ENSO teleconnection to rainfall in the MSEA region. Composite analyses reveal that decades with a strong ENSO-rainfall relationship are characterized by a tripolar pattern in sea surface temperatures spanning the Indian Ocean, central Indo-Pacific Warm Pool, and western Pacific regions, and an overall wetter mean state. Because the ENSO teleconnection is asymmetric, negative phases of the tripolar pattern enhance wet conditions during La Niña events whereas dry conditions during El Niño events are not similarly exacerbated during positive phases. By 2100, future projections indicate the emergence of a positive tripole pattern and a weakening of ENSO’s influence on rainfall in the MSEA region. As a result, ENSO indices, such as the Niño-3.4 index, will become less reliable for predicting springtime rainfall in this area.

TITLE: BRYOMOLECULES explores the potential of bryophytes for the cosmetic and pharmaceutical sector

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
News | Project News

BRYOMOLECULES aims to uncover natural compounds hidden within bryophytes widely available in Europe. The initiative develops sustainable, cutting-edge approaches to harness bioactive compounds (BACs) from these small plants for applications in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals.

By advancing knowledge and novel applications of bryophytes, the project strives to drive economic growth by creating marketable, patentable bio-based innovations, contributing to the circular economy and supporting the development of sustainable industries in Europe.

After 18 months of research and collaboration involving academic and industry partners, the BRYOMOLECULES project is making progress in exploring bryophytes, the mosses and liverworts that grow quietly across forests, wetlands, and rocky landscapes.

Watch our documentary to discover the project and its vision.

Collecting and cultivating liverwort and mosses

Our partners at Lund University (Lunds Universitet) have established axenic cultures of 50 moss accessions and 50 liverwort accessions, which will serve as the foundation for many of the project’s downstream studies. The selected accessions collection represents a wide diversity of liverwort and moss species, with most of the plant material collected in Sweden, with additional samples gathered in Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and Italy.

To ensure clean and controlled laboratory conditions, the plant material undergoes a careful sterilisation process before being grown in specialised culture media. These sterile cultures allow scientists to study the plants without interference from other microorganisms. The cultures are maintained under controlled light and temperature conditions, providing a stable resource for future biological and chemical analyses.

Explore the collection of liverworts in our project deliverables:

D1.1 List of moss accessions

D1.2 List of new liverworts collected

D1.3 Inclusion of 40+ axenic liverwort accessions to the bryophyte culture collection

Metabolomic Analysis of Bryophytes

Another important part of the project has been taken on by our partner at the Medical University of Lublin (Uniwersytet Medyczny w Lublinie), where researchers are analysing the chemical composition of moss and liverwort extract samples.

So far, 57 moss accessions (from axenic cultures) and 86 liverwort accessions (49 samples grown in sterile laboratory cultures and 37 collected directly from the wild) have been studied. The liverwort specimen includes several samples of Marchantia polymorpha, one of the most well-known liverwort species, representing its different subspecies.

Read our publication about Marchantia polymorpha

The plant material is carefully processed to extract its biochemical compounds, which are then analysed using advanced mass spectrometry and chromatography techniques. These methods allow scientists to identify and catalogue the metabolomic profile of the plant samples, meaning the wide range of molecules produced by the bryophytes.

The results are helping researchers build a growing library of bryophyte-derived compounds that may later be investigated for potential use in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and other applications.

More details are available in the relevant project deliverables:

D2.1 Report on phytochemical profile of 50 moss accessions

D2.2 Report on phytochemical profile of 80 collected liverwort accessions

Mapping Bryophyte Genetics

In addition to phytochemical studies, the project is also exploring the genetic profile of bryophytes to gain insights into the role of gene activity in how these plants produce their bioactive molecules.

Researchers from the Edmund Mach Foundation (Fondazione Edmund Mach) have produced data referencing the assemblies of 102 bryophyte transcriptomes generated from the Illumina platform. The transcriptome assemblies were reconstructed from raw sequences (RNA-Seq) generated on the Illumina platform, which will be available through the GenBank Short Read Archive, ensuring they can support both current and future research.

Learn more from the deliverables generated by the project:

D3.1 Raw sequences for 90 bryophyte transcriptomes

D3.2 Assemblies of 90 bryophyte transcriptomes

Results exploitation

Building on the technical progress, Fondazione Hub Innovazione Trentino (HIT) has advanced the project’s exploitation preparation activities by leading the development of a comprehensive Exploitation Plan. This effort has included a detailed market analysis on natural fragrances and cosmetics, providing in-depth insights into key industry actors and supporting the upcoming external stakeholder engagement plan. Moreover, HIT has established an IPR Management Plan to monitor, in collaboration with the partners, the status of the expected exploitable results: i) optimized liverworts cultivation protocols, ii) methods for sustainable, optimal production/extraction of BACs, iii) BACs biosynthesis in metabolically engineered factories, iv) new bioactive ingredients for the cosmetic and pharmaceutical industry, v) database on novel BACs and biosynthetic genes/pathways and bioprospecting pipeline.

At the halfway point of the project, BRYOMOLECULES has already built an important scientific foundation: collections of cultivated bryophytes, large datasets on their chemistry and genetics, and an initial understanding of how these plants produce their unique compounds. This foundation is crucial for the future stages of the project, including the assessment of compounds’ bioactivity, the enhancement of specific biosynthetic pathways and the identification of specific hit molecules.

Over the coming months, the partners will continue to explore how these discoveries can be translated into sustainable applications for the cosmetic and pharmaceutical sectors.

Moreover, the next phase in the project results’ exploitation plan will involve engaging the different target groups across the value chain, depending on the technological maturity of the project’s results, and collaborating with the project partners.

Submit an article

Submission of an article to the Publications mathématiques de l’IHES is done on the journal’s Editflow webpage.

Submitted papers must be in .pdf format, and prepared according to the instructions found on the publisher’s page.

History of the review

The Publications mathématiques de l’IHES was created in 1959 under the leadership of Léon Motchane, founder and director of the institute, and Jean Dieudonné, professor at the institute.

Issues were first published at irregular intervals and in four languages: French, English, German and Russian. Today, German and Russian are discontinued. Gradually, IHES published two annual volumes totalling 800 pages. Today, the journal has had a circulation of 80 printed copies. It is also available ­online and on numdam.org.

The Publications mathématiques de l’IHES is an international journal publishing papers of highest scientific level. Thanks to its worldwide distribution (it can be found in the libraries of the major mathematical institutions in the world), to its tradition of publishing landmark articles and to its broad coverage of the discipline, it has won international recognition.

Jean Dieudonné was the journal’s first editor-in-chief. Jacques Tits succeeded him in 1980 to 1998, followed by Etienne Ghys until 2009.

The editorial board has expanded over the years. Pierre Deligne, Dennis Sullivan, René Thom, all IHES professors, were the first to join the committee in 1980.

They were followed by Mikhail Gromov in 1982, Jean Bourgain in 1987, Maxim Kontsevich in 1996, Laurent Lafforgue in 1999 and Claire Voisin in 2007.

Les Publications mathématiques de l’IHES was managed in 2010 and 2011 by Claire Voisin and Sergiu Klainerman and by Claire Voisin from January 2012 until June 2019. It is then on Nicolas Bergeron’s initiative, editor-in-chief from 2019 to 2022, that Les Publications mathématiques de l’IHES became diamond open access (more information here). Sébastien Boucksom has been the editor-in-chief since July 2022.

Since January 1, 2026, the Publications mathématiques de l’IHÉS have been distributed by the Mersenne Center, a diamond open-access platform.

This decision marks a further step toward the free dissemination of scientific results for the journal: distributed between 1979 and 2000 by the Presses Universitaires de France and Springer, and since 2001 by Springer alone, it has been published in open access with no APCs since 2021. In early 2026, the journal joined the Mersenne Center. This policy ensures the broad and equitable dissemination of cutting-edge mathematical research.
