TITLE: Fully Funded PhD Studentship at Edinburgh Law School 2026: Apply to Research AI, Algorithms and Legal Decision-Making

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Edinburgh, through Edinburgh Law School and the Leverhulme Centre for Algorithmic Life, is inviting applications for a fully funded PhD studentship focused on the rapidly evolving relationship between artificial intelligence, algorithmic technologies, law and decision-making.

The opportunity is offered through the “Decisions” Cluster of the Leverhulme Centre for Algorithmic Life, with the successful candidate working with Professor Nehal Bhuta at Edinburgh Law School while also becoming part of the wider interdisciplinary research community of the Leverhulme Centre for Algorithmic Life, based at Durham University.

This PhD opportunity is particularly relevant to applicants interested in how algorithmic and AI technologies are transforming legal decision-making, governance, norms, accountability and responsibility. The research environment encourages collaboration across law, social sciences, humanities and sciences, making it potentially suitable for candidates whose interests extend beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries.

Applications must be submitted by 5pm on 30 September 2026.

About Edinburgh Law School

Edinburgh Law School is part of the University of Edinburgh and provides research opportunities across a broad range of legal and criminological subjects.

The School has an established community of approximately 100 PhD students, creating an environment in which doctoral researchers can participate in the intellectual and academic life of the institution while developing their own independent research.

According to the information provided by Edinburgh Law School, the School was ranked third in the UK for law for the quality and breadth of its research based on the 2021 Research Excellence Framework. The School also reports that 80% of its research outputs were rated as world-leading or internationally excellent, while its research environment received a 100% world-leading rating in the REF2021 exercise.

For prospective doctoral researchers, this provides an opportunity to undertake research within an established academic environment with access to experienced supervisors, research training and a wider community of scholars.

About the Fully Funded PhD Studentship

The studentship is part of the Decisions Cluster of the Leverhulme Centre for Algorithmic Life (CAL).

The successful candidate will be supervised by Professor Nehal Bhuta at Edinburgh Law School and will also be integrated into the wider research environment of the Leverhulme Centre for Algorithmic Life.

The centre takes an interdisciplinary approach to studying algorithmic technologies and their implications for human life, knowledge, perception and action.

One of the central questions guiding the centre’s research is how society should live with and alongside algorithmic technologies. Rather than focusing exclusively on individual technological projects, the centre examines broader and fundamental questions surrounding algorithmic life and how emerging technologies interact with social, legal and human systems.

This makes the studentship particularly relevant at a time when algorithmic systems are increasingly involved in areas such as public administration, welfare, security, military decision-making and other areas where decisions can have significant consequences for individuals and society.

What the Decisions Cluster Researches

The Decisions Cluster, led by Professor Nehal Bhuta, examines how algorithmic technologies are changing the nature and character of decision-making.

The cluster is interested in the interaction between human and algorithmic forms of knowledge and decision-making. As automated and machine-based systems become increasingly integrated into human institutions, questions arise concerning who or what makes decisions, how those decisions are justified, and how responsibility and accountability should be understood.

Research within the cluster considers areas including:

Algorithmic decision-making.

Artificial intelligence and law.

Automated decision systems.

Legal decision-making.

Accountability and responsibility.

Ethical approaches to automated decisions.

Norms and normativity.

AI-enabled military and security technologies.

Welfare and public administration.

Human-machine interactions in decision-making.

The changing role of legal concepts in algorithmic environments.

The cluster also seeks to develop new approaches to understanding decisions in an increasingly algorithmic world.

An important aspect of the research involves high-risk domains where automated technologies may influence decisions with substantial social, legal or political consequences. These include areas such as AI-enabled warfare, military technologies, security and public administration.

What the PhD Involves

A PhD at Edinburgh Law School is based on independent research culminating in the production of a substantial doctoral thesis.

The standard Edinburgh Law School PhD involves submitting a thesis of up to 100,000 words. The thesis is expected to constitute an original piece of research that makes a significant contribution to knowledge within the selected field and contains material of a standard suitable for publication.

For this particular studentship, the successful candidate will develop a research project connected to the broad themes of algorithmic technologies, AI, law and decision-making.

The precise research direction is expected to be developed through the application and subsequent academic discussions. Applicants are therefore encouraged to focus their proposal on clearly defined research questions and explain why those questions are important.

Interdisciplinary Research Environment

One of the distinctive features of this PhD studentship is its interdisciplinary character.

The opportunity is not limited to applicants following a conventional legal research pathway. The centre encourages researchers to develop their disciplinary expertise while collaborating with scholars from other academic fields.

Potential applicants may come from backgrounds including:

Law and legal theory
Candidates may be interested in how AI and algorithmic systems are changing legal concepts, legal reasoning, legal practice or legal decision-making.

Socio-legal studies
Researchers may explore how algorithmic systems influence institutions, social relationships, governance and the operation of law.

Computer science
A computer scientist could investigate machine learning and law, including the technical and social development of legal reasoning through algorithmic systems.

Sociology
Applicants with an interest in algorithmic social systems may explore theoretical questions concerning legal concepts, governance and social organisation.

Humanities and social sciences
Researchers from other relevant disciplines may investigate how algorithmic technologies are reshaping concepts of humanity, knowledge, responsibility, authority and decision-making.

The opportunity therefore provides scope for research that crosses traditional academic boundaries.

Funding and Financial Support

The studentship is described as a fully funded PhD opportunity for eligible applicants.

The funding package includes:

Tuition fees at the UK Home Fee rate.

An annual stipend in line with UK Research and Innovation rates, currently stated as approximately £21,805 per year.

Stipend payments made in equal monthly instalments.

Funding for 3.5 years, subject to satisfactory academic progress.

Additional research funding to support training and development.

The studentship is specifically restricted to candidates who qualify for Home fee status.

According to the opportunity information, eligible Home-fee candidates include applicants from the United Kingdom, Republic of Ireland, and EU-EEA applicants with Pre-settled status.

Applicants who do not meet the stated Home-fee eligibility requirements should carefully assess their fee status before applying, as the funding provided through this studentship is not described as covering international tuition fees.

Candidate Profile and Academic Requirements

The opportunity is aimed at applicants with a strong academic background and a demonstrable interest in the relationship between law and algorithmic or AI technologies.

Successful candidates are expected to have excellent grades in both undergraduate and postgraduate taught degrees, with at least one of those degrees being in law.

Applicants should also demonstrate a strong interest in questions concerning how AI and algorithmic technologies interact with law.

Relevant interests may include:

The influence of AI on legal decision-making.

Algorithmic governance.

The production and transformation of legal norms.

Normativity and algorithmic systems.

Automated decision-making.

Legal responsibility for decisions made or influenced by algorithms.

Accountability in AI systems.

The changing nature of legal practices.

AI and national legal systems.

AI and international law.

AI and global legal structures.

Algorithmic technologies in high-risk domains.

The School notes that any field of law may potentially be relevant, provided that the proposed research connects appropriately with the themes of the studentship.

English Language Requirements

Applicants must demonstrate proficiency in English, both written and spoken.

For candidates whose first language is not English, the stated requirement is an overall IELTS score of 7.0, with:

At least 7.0 in writing.

At least 6.5 in each of the other components.

The University may also accept another recognised English-language qualification at an equivalent standard.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they have appropriate evidence of English-language proficiency where this is required for their application.

Communication and Teamwork Skills

In addition to academic qualifications and research interests, applicants should demonstrate strong communication and teamwork skills.

Although a PhD involves substantial independent research, this particular studentship places the researcher within a wider interdisciplinary environment.

The successful candidate will have opportunities to engage with:

Other PhD researchers.

Postdoctoral researchers.

Academic collaborators.

Researchers from different disciplines.

University and research partners.

External partners in academia.

Industry partners.

Charitable organisations.

Arts-sector organisations.

The ability to communicate research ideas clearly and collaborate effectively across disciplinary boundaries can therefore be important to succeeding within the research environment.

Duration of the Studentship

The studentship is funded for 3.5 years, subject to satisfactory progress.

The precise duration may depend on the training requirements associated with the PhD project and any periods involving placement or collaborative work.

The successful applicant is expected to begin the PhD in either:

January 2027, or

September 2027.

Applicants should therefore consider their availability and preferred start period when preparing their application.

How to Apply

Applicants must apply through the University of Edinburgh’s admissions system, EUCLID, and select the PhD Law programme.

An important application instruction is that applicants should enter Professor Nehal Bhuta in the proposed supervisor section of the EUCLID application.

The application must be completed by 5pm on 30 September 2026.

Interviews are expected to take place online in late October 2026.

Applicants should make sure that all required documents are submitted before the deadline because incomplete applications will not progress to the academic selectors.

Required Application Documents

Applicants are expected to provide several documents as part of the application.

1. Degree Transcripts and Certificates

Applicants must submit their academic transcripts and degree certificates.

Where documents are not in English, certified translations should also be provided where applicable.

2. Evidence of English Language Ability

Applicants who are required to demonstrate English proficiency should provide the appropriate English-language qualification or evidence.

The stated IELTS requirement is an overall score of 7.0, including 7.0 in writing and at least 6.5 in each remaining component, unless an equivalent accepted qualification is used.

3. Research Proposal

Applicants must submit a short research proposal of no more than two pages.

The proposal should focus particularly on:

The research questions the applicant intends to investigate.

The proposed approach to the research.

Why the research questions are important.

How the proposed research relates to the broader themes of the studentship.

A strong proposal should therefore demonstrate a clear understanding of the research problem rather than simply providing a general discussion of artificial intelligence.

4. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide a full CV outlining their academic and professional background, research experience, relevant skills and other information that demonstrates their suitability for doctoral research.

5. Cover Letter

The application also requires a cover letter of no more than two pages.

The cover letter should explain:

The applicant’s academic and professional background.

Their suitability for the PhD.

Their research interests.

Their interest in the themes of the studentship.

Relevant experience that demonstrates their ability to undertake the proposed research.

6. Two Recent References

Applicants must provide two recent references.

It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure that the reference letters are received before the application deadline.

Applicants should therefore contact their referees well in advance rather than waiting until the final days before submission.

Important Document Submission Requirement

The University provides an important instruction concerning the research proposal, CV and cover letter.

These three documents should be uploaded as one combined document within the application portal.

Applicants should therefore check the final uploaded file carefully before submitting the application to ensure that all required sections are included and readable.

The application should also contain all other required supporting documentation, including transcripts, certificates, English-language evidence where applicable and references.

Application Timeline

Key dates and expected stages include:

Application deadline: 5pm, 30 September 2026.

Interviews: Expected to take place online in late October 2026.

Potential PhD start: January 2027 or September 2027.

Funding duration: 3.5 years, subject to satisfactory progress.

Because the deadline is specific to the hour, applicants should not wait until the final minutes to submit their applications.

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly relevant to candidates who have a strong academic record and are interested in the intersection of law, artificial intelligence and algorithmic technologies.

Applicants should generally have:

Excellent undergraduate and postgraduate academic results.

At least one degree in law.

A demonstrable interest in AI and algorithmic technologies.

An interest in how these technologies interact with law and legal decision-making.

Strong written and oral English skills.

Strong communication and teamwork abilities.

An interest in interdisciplinary research.

The ability to develop a focused and meaningful doctoral research question.

Eligibility for UK Home fee status under the funding conditions.

The opportunity can potentially accommodate researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds, provided their proposed research connects meaningfully with the themes of algorithmic life, law and decision-making.

Eligible Countries and Fee Status

The funding is not open on an unrestricted worldwide basis.

The studentship is specifically available to applicants who qualify for UK Home fee status.

The information provided identifies eligible candidates as:

Applicants from the United Kingdom.

Applicants from the Republic of Ireland.

EU-EEA applicants with Pre-settled status, where they meet the relevant Home-fee eligibility requirements.

Applicants from other countries should not assume that they qualify for the funding simply because they meet the academic requirements. They should first establish whether they meet the University’s applicable Home-fee status requirements.

Why This Research Area Matters

Artificial intelligence and algorithmic technologies are increasingly influencing decisions that were traditionally made exclusively by humans.

These developments create significant questions for law and society.

For example, when an algorithm contributes to a decision, questions may arise concerning who is responsible for the outcome, how the decision can be challenged, whether the reasoning behind it can be explained, and what legal standards should govern the use of automated systems.

These questions become particularly significant in areas where decisions can affect people’s rights, access to services, security or welfare.

The Decisions Cluster provides an academic environment for investigating these issues at a fundamental level. Researchers can examine not only how algorithmic systems operate but also how concepts such as responsibility, accountability, ethics and legal decision-making may need to evolve alongside technological change.

Research Training and Support at Edinburgh Law School

PhD students at Edinburgh Law School benefit from a structured research environment designed to support both specialist research and broader academic development.

The School’s PhD programme provides:

Expert supervision in the candidate’s research area.

Training in legal and criminological research methods.

Transferable research and professional skills.

Opportunities for advanced specialist training.

Interaction with established researchers.

Participation in a wider scholarly community.

Opportunities to communicate research findings to different audiences.

The broader Leverhulme Centre environment also offers opportunities for interdisciplinary engagement, allowing doctoral researchers to develop connections beyond their primary academic discipline.

Career Development Opportunities

The PhD is designed not only to develop advanced research expertise but also to contribute to the candidate’s longer-term professional development.

Researchers can benefit from specialist training and engagement with academic and external partners.

The wider Edinburgh Law School PhD community includes graduates who have pursued careers in different areas, including:

Academic careers in law and criminology.

Private legal practice.

National governments.

International organisations.

Research and policy-related careers.

For researchers working at the intersection of law and emerging technologies, interdisciplinary experience may also provide a foundation for engaging with organisations and institutions dealing with AI governance, technology policy, regulation and algorithmic decision-making.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants should begin preparing their application well before the deadline.

A useful preparation process is to:

Review the research themes carefully.

Make sure your proposed topic genuinely connects with algorithmic technologies, law and decision-making.

Develop focused research questions.

The proposal is limited to two pages, so applicants should prioritise clear and researchable questions rather than attempting to cover an overly broad subject.

Explain why the research matters.

Demonstrate the legal, theoretical, social or practical importance of the proposed research.

Demonstrate interdisciplinary potential.

If your research draws on computer science, sociology, political science, philosophy or another field, clearly explain how that discipline contributes to the project.

Check your academic eligibility.

Confirm that you meet the required academic standards and that at least one of your undergraduate or postgraduate taught degrees is in law.

Check your fee-status eligibility.

Because the funding is restricted to Home fee-status candidates, this should be established before submitting the application.

Prepare your references early.

Contact referees in advance and ensure they understand the submission deadline.

Combine the required documents correctly.

The research proposal, CV and cover letter should be uploaded as one combined document.

Review the entire application.

Missing documents can prevent an application from progressing to academic selection.

Submit before the deadline.

Number of winners: 1

Number of winners: 2

This category recognises pioneering institutions that address gender equality together with at least two other social categories, including racial or ethnic origin, disability, sexual orientation, or social origin.

Number of winners: 1

Who Can Apply?

The award is open to eligible:

Higher education institutions

Universities

Research organisations

Organisations conducting research and innovation

Eligible organisations must be based in EU Member States, Associated Countries, or countries currently holding EU candidate status, according to the applicable rules of the contest.

Prize

The 2026 EU Award for Gender Equality Champions has a total prize value of €400,000.

29 September 2026

Application Deadline: 29 September 2026

Prize Fund: €400,000

Application Platform: EU Funding and Tenders Portal

Eligible Applicants: Universities, higher education institutions, research organisations and other eligible research and innovation organisations

Apply Here

Gender equality remains an important part of building a more inclusive and effective European research and innovation system. TITLE: Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund 2026: Up to £500,000 to Strengthen Employment Outcomes for Young People in the UK

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Nuffield Foundation has launched the Essential Employment Skills Fund, a major new funding initiative offering grants of up to £500,000 to build robust evidence about how young people facing significant barriers to employment can develop the skills, attributes and behaviours needed to access and progress into good jobs.

The fund focuses specifically on young people aged 16–24 living in the United Kingdom who face significant barriers to entering the labour market. Rather than simply supporting skills programmes, the initiative seeks to establish high-quality evidence about which interventions work, why they work, for whom they work, and how successful approaches can ultimately be expanded or adapted to different settings.

The outline application deadline is 10 December 2026, according to the Nuffield Foundation’s announcement of the fund. Shortlisted applicants will subsequently be invited to submit full applications in 2027.

About the Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund

The Essential Employment Skills Fund has been established in response to a major challenge facing the UK: many young people, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds or facing substantial barriers to work, do not have equal opportunities to develop the skills that employers value.

The Nuffield Foundation argues that employment-related skills development needs to be more effectively integrated across education, training and youth-support systems. At the same time, these interventions need to be supported by stronger evidence about what actually works.

Through the new fund, the Foundation therefore aims to support the rigorous evaluation of existing UK programmes that help young people aged 16–24 develop essential employment skills and move toward good employment.

Grants of up to £500,000 are available for evaluation, with the Foundation anticipating that most evaluation awards will fall between approximately £200,000 and £400,000. There is also potential for additional support toward programme-delivery costs where those costs cannot be covered from other sources, including through partnership funding arrangements.

Why Has the Essential Employment Skills Fund Been Created?

Youth unemployment and economic inactivity represent serious long-term challenges.

Young people who struggle to enter the labour market or gain meaningful employment experience during early adulthood may face consequences extending far beyond their first few years of working life. These can affect their longer-term career trajectories, earnings and well-being.

At the same time, employers continue to report difficulties finding young people with the skills they need.

The Nuffield Foundation identifies an important disconnect: although employers and educators increasingly recognize the importance of essential employment skills, these competencies do not necessarily receive sufficient emphasis within curricula, assessment and accountability systems.

Opportunities to develop these skills can consequently vary substantially according to a young person’s circumstances and background.

The Essential Employment Skills Fund aims to address an important evidence gap: Which approaches actually help young people facing significant barriers to work develop essential employment skills and progress toward sustainable employment?

What Are Essential Employment Skills?

For this funding programme, the Nuffield Foundation uses “essential employment skills” as an inclusive term covering a broad range of transferable skills, attributes and behaviours valued by employers across industries and occupations.

These skills are associated with important labour-market outcomes such as gaining employment, progressing at work, job satisfaction and earnings.

The Foundation highlights research identifying areas such as:

Collaboration

Communication

Creative thinking

Information literacy

Organising, planning and prioritising

Problem solving

Decision making

Other established frameworks cover comparable competencies, including speaking, listening, creativity, adapting, planning, leadership and teamwork.

Applicants do not have to adopt one particular skills framework. They may use an appropriate existing framework that suits their programme.

However, proposals must clearly identify the specific essential employment skill or skills that the intervention intends to develop.

Importantly, the Fund is not intended to finance the creation of new definitions or frameworks for essential employment skills.

Main Aim of the Fund

The central purpose of the Essential Employment Skills Fund is to strengthen the evidence base concerning effective approaches for helping young people aged 16–24 who face significant employment barriers develop essential skills and ultimately gain access to good jobs.

The Nuffield Foundation intends to achieve this by supporting rigorous evaluations of relevant programmes and facilitating the dissemination of findings and practical learning.

The longer-term objective is not merely to determine whether individual projects succeed. The Foundation wants the evidence generated through funded projects to help successful practices be:

Expanded;

Replicated;

Adapted to different contexts;

Incorporated into wider education and employment systems; and

Used to reduce inequalities in young people’s employment outcomes.

The Foundation is also interested in projects that improve mechanisms for sharing learning or advance methods for measuring essential employment skills.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The Essential Employment Skills Fund offers substantial financial support.

Maximum grant for evaluation: Up to £500,000

The Foundation expects most evaluation grants to fall within the range of approximately:

£200,000 to £400,000

In appropriate circumstances, there may also be additional funding available to contribute toward programme-delivery costs when these cannot be funded from other sources.

Organizations considering requesting delivery funding are encouraged to contact the Nuffield Foundation before submitting their application to discuss the proposed arrangements.

Who Can Apply?

The Essential Employment Skills Fund is primarily designed around organizational partnerships rather than applications from individual young people.

This distinction is important.

The young people aged 16–24 are primarily the target beneficiaries of the programmes being evaluated, rather than individual applicants for the £500,000 grants.

For this particular fund, successful teams will require expertise in two major areas:

Independent evaluation and research expertise

Frontline programme delivery expertise

The Nuffield Foundation therefore anticipates receiving applications from partnerships between an evaluator/research organization and a delivery organization.

The partnership must already have been established before an application is submitted, and the research design should be developed jointly.

Applicants must also clearly explain the division of roles and responsibilities and demonstrate how the evaluation will retain sufficient independence and impartiality.

The Foundation expects the evaluation partner to act as the lead applicant.

Who Should the Programmes Support?

Funded programmes must work with young people aged 16–24 living in the UK, although applicants may choose to concentrate on a narrower age group within this range.

For example, an intervention could specifically target people aged 16–19.

However, the central emphasis must remain on young people who face significant barriers to employment.

Applicants are expected to clearly identify their intended target population and provide a persuasive justification for selecting that group.

Young People Facing Significant Barriers to Work

The Foundation identifies several circumstances that may increase the likelihood of a young person struggling to access employment.

Projects could, for example, focus on young people experiencing one or more factors such as:

Low or no academic qualifications;

Persistent absence from school;

School exclusion;

Special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), particularly young people with an Education, Health and Care Plan;

Mental health difficulties;

Experience of the care system;

Young parenthood;

Responsibilities as a young carer;

Membership of Gypsy, Roma or Traveller communities; or

Residence in geographic areas experiencing comparatively high youth unemployment.

These examples should not be interpreted as a requirement that every funded programme must cover every listed group.

Instead, applicants need to define their particular target population and provide evidence explaining why the selected group faces meaningful barriers to employment.

Reaching Young People Who Need Support Most

The Nuffield Foundation places particular emphasis on recruitment and sustained engagement.

Applicants must provide a realistic strategy explaining how they will:

Identify eligible young people;

Recruit them into the programme;

Maintain their participation and engagement; and

Avoid restricting participation to individuals who are comparatively easy to reach.

This is significant because programmes intended to reduce employment inequality can fail to achieve their purpose if they primarily attract individuals who are already comparatively well connected to education, training or employment services.

What Types of Programmes Can Be Funded?

An eligible programme must have an explicit objective of developing at least one essential employment skill among participating young people.

Many programmes will naturally address several skills simultaneously.

The development of essential employment skills may form part of a broader programme containing other forms of support.

Potential activities could include:

Literacy, numeracy or digital-skills development;

Vocational education or training;

CV preparation;

Interview preparation and employment support;

Enterprise and entrepreneurship training;

Mentoring;

Coaching;

Volunteering;

Community activities;

Work experience;

Work-based learning;

Peer support;

Mental-health support; and

Assistance with practical barriers such as housing or benefits.

This provides applicants with considerable flexibility in designing or adapting programmes, provided that essential employment skills remain an explicit and measurable component.

Existing and Promising Programmes Are Prioritized

Organizations should note that the Fund is not primarily designed to finance entirely new programmes developed from scratch.

Given the level of funding available and the emphasis on rigorous evaluation, the Nuffield Foundation expects to support existing programmes that already demonstrate some evidence of promise.

Projects may nevertheless adapt or refocus an established intervention.

For example, an organization could propose testing an existing programme within a different environment, population or delivery context.

The programme should be based on a clear and convincing theory of change, supported by previous testing, relevant evidence and/or theoretical literature.

Robust Impact Evaluation Is Essential

Evaluation is not an optional addition to this funding opportunity; it is one of its defining requirements.

Funded programmes must include a robust impact evaluation.

At minimum, the evaluation must examine:

Changes in the targeted essential employment skills; and

Participants’ progress toward employment.

Progress toward employment could include outcomes such as:

Starting a job;

Beginning an apprenticeship;

Accessing voluntary employment;

Participating in a supported internship;

Completing work experience; or

Enrolling in further training.

The appropriate evaluation methodology will depend on the intervention and its stage of development.

However, the Foundation expects sufficiently large samples for robust analysis and credible evidence that observed outcomes can be attributed to the programme rather than unrelated external factors.

Depending on the programme, this may require control or comparison groups or high-quality qualitative impact methodologies.

Process and Implementation Evaluation

Applicants must also include process and implementation evaluation.

This recognizes that even a well-designed programme may achieve different outcomes when delivered in different real-world environments.

Factors influencing implementation may include:

Organizational culture;

Stakeholder priorities;

Practical constraints;

Physical circumstances;

Government policy;

Regulation;

Local labour-market conditions; and

Wider political or institutional environments.

Evaluation should therefore examine not only whether an intervention works but also how it is implemented and what contextual factors influence its effectiveness.

Young People’s Voices Must Influence the Programme

The Fund also requires applicants to consider the contemporary experiences and perspectives of young people themselves.

Proposals should demonstrate how evidence from young people has informed—or will inform—the programme’s design and delivery.

Organizations may establish a youth advisory board or youth engagement group, although this specific structure is not compulsory.

What matters is that applicants can explain how young people’s own perspectives on employment barriers and potential solutions are incorporated meaningfully into the programme.

Partnership and Collaboration

Another important ambition of the Fund is to strengthen partnerships around youth employment.

Funded projects may bring together stakeholders including:

Employers;

Education institutions;

Training providers;

Third-sector organizations;

Research and evaluation organizations;

Local government; and

Regional government.

The Foundation hopes these collaborations can continue supporting young people beyond the lifespan of an individual funded project.

Support Available from the Nuffield Foundation

Potential applicants can seek feedback before submitting a formal application.

The Foundation welcomes a brief one-page project description from prospective applicants seeking initial feedback.

Delivery organizations that do not yet have an evaluation partner may also request information about potential evaluators who have agreed to be approached by applicants to the programme.

Successful projects will receive additional support from the Nuffield Foundation during implementation, including assistance relating to communications and impact.

The Foundation also intends to connect grant holders with other funded organizations and its wider stakeholder network, enabling organizations to exchange learning and promote effective practice.

Essential Employment Skills Fund Application Timeline

The current timetable is:

Outline application deadline: 10 December 2026

Shortlisting decisions: February 2027

Full application deadline: April 2027

Final funding decisions: July 2027

Earliest possible project start: September 2027

Applicants should also check the official funding page for updates and FAQs before finalizing their submissions.

How to Apply

Applicants must follow the Nuffield Foundation’s Outline Application process and carefully review the Foundation’s Guide for Applicants before submitting.

The Foundation expects the evaluation partner to be the lead applicant.

Prospective applicants should therefore establish their evaluator-delivery organization partnership before applying and jointly develop the proposed research and evaluation design.

Apply for the Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund

Why This Funding Opportunity Matters

The Essential Employment Skills Fund is particularly significant because it combines youth-employment intervention with rigorous evidence generation.

Many organizations already deliver employability, mentoring, training, work-experience and youth-development programmes. However, policymakers and practitioners need stronger evidence about which approaches produce measurable improvements, particularly for young people who are furthest from the labour market.

The Fund is therefore designed to move beyond simply financing individual interventions.

Its wider ambition is to generate knowledge capable of informing future education, training, youth-support and employment systems, allowing promising interventions to be improved, scaled or adapted.

The initiative also recognizes that employability is not determined solely by technical qualifications. Communication, collaboration, planning, creativity, problem solving, adaptability, teamwork and similar transferable competencies can play an important role in helping young people navigate an increasingly complex labour market.

Conclusion

The Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund 2026 represents a substantial funding opportunity for organizations working at the intersection of youth employment, education, training, research and programme evaluation in the United Kingdom.

With up to £500,000 available for evaluation, and potential additional support toward programme-delivery costs in appropriate circumstances, the Fund aims to generate robust evidence about how young people aged 16–24 who face significant employment barriers can develop essential skills and ultimately access good jobs.

Strong proposals will require more than an innovative idea. Applicants should have an established and promising intervention, a compelling theory of change, an appropriate target population, credible plans for reaching young people facing significant barriers, a strong independent evaluation design, meaningful engagement with young people’s perspectives, and an established partnership between frontline delivery and evaluation expertise.

Organizations considering applying should begin preparing well ahead of the 10 December 2026 outline application deadline, particularly because partnerships should be established and the research design co-developed before the application is submitted.

The abstract should provide a clear overview of the proposed project.

2. Project Statement

Applicants must submit a 1,000–2,000-word project statement explaining their proposed research.

The statement should address:

Research objectives

Research approach

Overall importance of the study

The central research questions or issues

The significance of the proposed work

Applicants may also include a one-page bibliography containing the key sources relevant to their proposed research.

3. Two Writing Samples

Applicants must provide two samples of writing.

The samples may be:

Published works

Unpublished works

These samples allow the Institute to assess the applicant’s research and writing ability.

4. Letter of Interest

Applicants must provide a letter of interest explaining their interest in the fellowship and their proposed research.

5. Curriculum Vitae

A current CV should be included with the application, presenting the applicant’s academic, research, professional, and publication background.

6. Referees

Applicants must provide the contact details of three referees.

The Institute will contact the referees directly to request letters of reference.

Applicants should therefore ensure that the contact information provided is accurate and that their referees are appropriate individuals who can comment meaningfully on their academic or professional work.

How to Choose the Right Fellowship

Applicants should carefully match their academic background and proposed research to the fellowship’s thematic focus.

Choose the Toni Morrison Senior Fellowship if:

Your work focuses on African diaspora literature, literature, culture, humanities, cultural studies, or critical theory, and you are an established scholar, author, or public intellectual.

Choose the Ali A. Mazrui Senior Fellowship if:

You are an established scholar working broadly in African and African diaspora studies, particularly across the humanities and social sciences.

Choose the Okwui Enwezor Postdoctoral Fellowship if:

You recently completed your Ph.D. and your research focuses on visual culture, performance studies, art history, art criticism, or critical humanities.

Choose the Fatema Mernissi Postdoctoral Fellowship if:

You recently completed your Ph.D. and your research focuses on gender, feminism, social sciences, cultural studies, visual cultures, and their relationship to Africa or the African diaspora.

Fellowship Location

All four fellowships are based in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates.

The fellowships are structured as residency programmes, meaning successful fellows are expected to undertake their research on a full-time basis at the Institute.

The senior fellowships are generally one-year residencies, while the postdoctoral fellowships are generally two-year residencies.

The typical fellowship period runs from September to June.

Why This Fellowship Opportunity Is Significant

The Africa Institute’s fellowship programme is particularly relevant to researchers seeking a dedicated environment for advanced work on Africa and the African diaspora.

The programme brings together different areas of scholarship, including:

African and African diaspora studies

Humanities

Social sciences

Literature

Cultural studies

Gender and feminism

Visual culture

Performance studies

Art history

Critical humanities

For established scholars, the Senior Fellowships provide an opportunity to pursue focused research at an advanced stage of their careers.

For recently graduated Ph.D. researchers, the Postdoctoral Fellowships provide an opportunity to develop their research within an institution specifically dedicated to African and African diaspora studies.

Important Deadline

The application deadline for the 2027 The Africa Institute Senior and Postdoctoral Fellowships is:

September 30, 2026

Applicants should prepare their research proposal, writing samples, CV, letter of interest, and referee information well before the deadline.

How to Apply

Applicants should prepare all required application materials and submit their application through the official fellowship application process.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The 2027 The Africa Institute Senior and Postdoctoral Fellowships provide a research opportunity for established scholars and emerging postdoctoral researchers whose work contributes to the study of Africa and the African diaspora.

With four specialised fellowships covering African diaspora literature and cultural studies, global African studies, visual culture and performance studies, and social and cultural studies, the programme offers different pathways for researchers with diverse academic interests.

The fellowships are based in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, and provide full-time research residencies ranging from one to two years depending on the fellowship.

Researchers interested in applying should ensure that their proposed project clearly aligns with the relevant fellowship, prepare a strong research statement and writing samples, and submit their application before the September 30, 2026 deadline.

TITLE: IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026: Funding for New Neuroscience Societies and Thematic Networks in Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026, an international funding opportunity designed to help groups of scientists and organizations take the first practical steps toward establishing sustainable neuroscience societies, sub-societies, regional chapters and thematic research networks.

Offered by the International Brain Research Organization (IBRO), the programme focuses specifically on regions where stronger formal structures for neuroscience collaboration could expand scientific exchange, professional networking, representation and long-term research capacity.

Applications are open to eligible initiatives in:

Africa

Asia-Pacific

Latin America

The 2026 application window runs from:

1 September 2026 to 30 September 2026

The application deadline is therefore:

30 September 2026

Applications must be submitted through the official IBRO Grants Portal.

Apply for the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants

Read the official programme information

About the IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants

The IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants are intended to provide early-stage financial support for scientists who want to create stronger and more formal neuroscience communities.

The programme recognizes that in some countries or regions, neuroscientists may already be collaborating informally but lack:

A formal professional society

An organizational structure

Governance arrangements

A sustainable membership system

A dedicated regional chapter

A network focused on a particular neuroscience discipline

IBRO therefore provides funding for the inaugural activities needed to move from informal scientific collaboration toward a formal, sustainable structure.

This can include activities such as:

Governance planning

Strategic workshops

Organizational development

Discussions on leadership and membership

Planning the structure of a new neuroscience society

Developing a thematic scientific network

Establishing a regional or sub-national neuroscience chapter

The central purpose is not simply to organize another scientific event. Instead, the funding should help scientists create something that continues beyond the initial funded activity.

What Is the Main Aim of the Programme?

The official aim of the programme is to:

Support the development of emerging neuroscience societies or thematic networks.

IBRO wants to empower local neuroscientists and organizations to come together, establish common objectives and build the governance structures necessary for a sustainable scientific community.

The programme can therefore support initiatives that lead to the creation of:

National neuroscience societies

Regional neuroscience societies

Formal neuroscience sub-societies

Regional chapters

Thematic neuroscience networks

The programme is particularly valuable where researchers are already interested in building a collaborative community but lack the financial resources needed to organize the planning process.

What Types of Neuroscience Communities Can Be Created?

The programme is broader than the establishment of a traditional national neuroscience society.

Applicants may also propose a formal community focused on a specific neuroscience field.

IBRO gives examples such as:

Computational neuroscience

Glial research

Other thematic networks may potentially fit the programme where they represent a genuine unmet need and are consistent with the call requirements.

A thematic network could be useful where researchers in a specialized field are spread across several institutions or countries but do not yet have a recognized body through which to:

Coordinate activities

Build research collaborations

Support early-career scientists

Share resources

Organize training

Advocate for their research field

Develop regional scientific capacity

Who Can Apply?

IBRO welcomes applications from:

Emerging Neuroscience Societies

Groups that already function informally as a neuroscience community but have not yet become a formally established society may apply.

Groups of Scientists

A group of researchers actively planning to form a neuroscience society, chapter, sub-society or thematic network may submit an application.

Scientific Organizations

Organizations representing the interests of the neuroscience community may also apply where their proposed activities are directed toward establishing a formal neuroscience structure.

Groups in Regions With Limited Neuroscience Infrastructure

The programme particularly fits areas where there is:

Little formal neuroscience organization

Limited opportunity for scientific exchange

No functioning neuroscience society

Limited representation of a specific neuroscience discipline

Applicants With a Concrete Establishment Plan

Applicants should have a clear and actionable plan for moving from the initial funded activity to an actual formal society or network.

This is crucial.

IBRO is not looking simply for groups that say they may eventually form an organization. The proposal should demonstrate that the funded activities are part of a genuine process toward establishment.

Geographic Eligibility

The programme is open in three broad regions:

Africa

Groups of neuroscientists and eligible organizations based in African countries may apply where they meet the programme criteria.

Asia-Pacific

Eligible scientific groups and organizations from the Asia-Pacific region may also participate.

Latin America

The programme is additionally open to qualifying initiatives based in Latin America.

The official programme information provided does not list a single closed country-by-country eligibility table in the text supplied. Applicants should therefore check the IBRO Grants Portal or contact the IBRO programmes team if there is any uncertainty about whether their location falls within the relevant IBRO regional structure.

What if a National Neuroscience Society Already Exists?

The existence of an established national neuroscience society does not automatically prevent an application, but the rules become significantly more restrictive.

In countries where a national neuroscience society already exists, including an IBRO member society, applicants may apply only where they are formally seeking to establish something distinct, such as:

A neuroscience sub-society

A specialized thematic body

A regional chapter

The proposed activity must focus on the planning and governance required to launch that new structure.

Applicants must also demonstrate that the proposed organization provides clear added value.

For example, it could address:

An underserved geographic area

A specialized neuroscience subfield

A group of scientists not adequately represented by the existing society

A particular scientific or professional need that the national organization does not currently meet

Creating a duplicate organization without a convincing reason is unlikely to fit the purpose of the programme.

A New Society Must Address an Unmet Need

Where an existing neuroscience society already operates, applicants should clearly explain:

What is missing from the existing scientific ecosystem

Which researchers are underserved

Why a new sub-society or regional chapter is needed

How the proposed group complements rather than competes unnecessarily with the existing organization

What scientific or regional value the new structure will add

This is particularly important for thematic groups.

For example, if a national neuroscience society exists but there is no organized community for computational neuroscience, a proposal to create a formal computational neuroscience network may be relevant if the applicants can demonstrate a real scientific need.

What Activities Can the Grant Support?

The programme is intended for inaugural and organizational activities that directly contribute to the creation of a sustainable neuroscience body.

Examples can include:

Governance Planning

Applicants may organize activities to determine:

Organizational structure

Leadership arrangements

Executive roles

Decision-making procedures

Membership models

Constitutions or bylaws

Internal governance processes

Governance is central because a sustainable professional society needs more than an informal network of scientists.

Strategic Workshops

A funded planning workshop could bring together researchers to decide:

The mission of the new society

Scientific priorities

Membership strategy

Leadership model

Future activities

Regional representation

Funding plans

Diversity and inclusion commitments

The workshop should produce a practical outcome rather than ending simply as a discussion event.

Community-Building Activities

Early activities may also help identify and connect neuroscientists who could become founding members.

This could involve:

Mapping researchers

Creating institutional links

Engaging universities

Developing communication structures

Establishing working groups

The ultimate goal should still be the formal establishment of a society or network.

Standalone Conferences Are Not Eligible

One of the most important restrictions is that the Seeding Neuroscience Grants are not ordinary conference grants.

IBRO explicitly states that the programme:

Does not support standalone conferences or scientific meetings where the sole purpose is event organization.

This means applicants should not submit a proposal simply to fund:

A symposium

Scientific congress

Research conference

Workshop with no follow-up structure

Academic meeting unrelated to formal organization-building

An event may form part of the proposal, but it must be tied to a clear and actionable plan to establish a:

Society

Sub-society

Regional chapter

Thematic network

The organizational outcome must be central.

Example of an Eligible Approach

Imagine neuroscientists from several universities in one country have never had a national professional society.

They could propose a planning workshop bringing together representatives from universities, research institutes and hospitals.

The workshop might focus on:

Agreeing on a constitution

Electing an interim steering group

Defining membership rules

Identifying scientific priorities

Developing a two-year strategic plan

Agreeing on registration procedures

If the outcome is a concrete pathway toward establishing a recognized national neuroscience society, that would align much more closely with the programme than simply holding a research conference.

Example of a Weak Proposal

A group proposes a two-day neuroscience symposium with:

Keynote speakers

Poster sessions

Scientific presentations

Networking

but provides no real plan for creating a continuing organization afterward.

Even if the conference is scientifically strong, it would not meet the fundamental purpose of the Seeding Neuroscience Grants.

The programme is about institution-building, not simply event delivery.

Building Sustainable Neuroscience Communities

Sustainability is an important underlying principle of this funding opportunity.

IBRO wants the initial grant to help create a neuroscience community that can continue functioning after the funded activities end.

Applicants should therefore think beyond the first workshop.

A strong proposal should consider questions such as:

Who will lead the society after establishment?

How will membership be maintained?

How will future activities be financed?

How will early-career researchers participate?

How will leadership transition occur?

How will institutions across the region be represented?

How will communication between members continue?

How will the network measure its development?

The stronger the pathway from the initial activity to a functioning organization, the more convincingly the proposal will reflect the purpose of the programme.

Diversity and Inclusion

Building a neuroscience community also requires thinking carefully about who is included.

Although the material supplied does not reproduce every detailed review criterion from the full call, the programme’s broader community-building approach makes representation and participation highly relevant.

Applicants should consider diversity across areas such as:

Gender

Career stage

Institution

Geography

Neuroscience discipline

Professional background

A national or regional society dominated by one institution may struggle to represent the wider neuroscience community effectively.

Applicants can strengthen their proposals by demonstrating meaningful participation from a broad range of researchers.

Supporting Early-Career Neuroscientists

Emerging societies can play an important role in supporting:

Graduate students

Postdoctoral researchers

Early-career academics

Young clinicians

New research groups

A sustainable scientific society can give these researchers access to:

Mentoring

Networking

Training

Collaboration

Leadership experience

Scientific visibility

Applicants may therefore consider how their proposed society or network will create opportunities for emerging researchers.

Strengthening Regional Scientific Collaboration

The Seeding Neuroscience Grants can also help overcome fragmentation between institutions.

In some regions, neuroscientists may work in:

Universities

Hospitals

Medical schools

Psychology departments

Biomedical laboratories

Engineering departments

Computational research centres

without having a common platform.

A formal neuroscience society or network can create stronger links between these communities.

This can contribute to:

Interdisciplinary collaboration

Shared research initiatives

Training

Resource exchange

Regional visibility

International partnerships

Thematic Networks and Specialized Neuroscience Fields

Thematic networks are particularly useful when researchers share a scientific specialization but are geographically dispersed.

IBRO explicitly welcomes proposals for new formal thematic networks that do not yet exist as recognized bodies.

Examples cited by IBRO include:

Computational neuroscience

Glial research

A successful thematic network could potentially:

Connect laboratories

Develop shared research priorities

Organize specialist training

Create mentorship relationships

Support collaborative publications

Advocate for investment in the field

The proposal should still explain how the network will become formal and sustainable.

Grant Amount

The official programme page identifies the:

Maximum grant amount: “See call details.”

The public text supplied does not specify a numerical maximum.

For accuracy, applicants should therefore consult the current 2026 call documents and IBRO Grants Portal for the applicable funding ceiling rather than relying on older grant figures or unofficial third-party summaries.

Open the official IBRO application portal

Grant Type

IBRO classifies the Seeding Neuroscience Grants under:

Event organization

However, the purpose is more specific than ordinary event funding.

The funded event or organizational activity must contribute directly to establishing a formal neuroscience:

Society

Sub-society

Regional chapter

Thematic network

Applicants should therefore avoid interpreting the “event organization” classification as general conference support.

Application Period

The 2026 application period is:

1 September 2026 to 30 September 2026.

Applicants should prepare their proposal well before the final day because first-time users will need to create an account on the IBRO Grants Portal.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the:

IBRO Grants Portal

Apply for the 2026 Seeding Neuroscience Grants

First-time portal users must create an account.

Create an IBRO Grants Portal account

Applicants experiencing technical difficulties can use the customer support mechanism available through the Grants Portal.

IBRO also recommends consulting the portal FAQ where necessary.

Before Starting an Application

Applicants should first determine whether the proposed initiative truly fits the programme.

Consider the following questions:

Are we actively trying to establish a formal neuroscience society, sub-society, regional chapter or thematic network?

Is our group genuinely representative of an emerging neuroscience community?

Is there an unmet scientific or organizational need?

Do our planned activities result in concrete governance or institutional outcomes?

Will the proposed structure continue after the grant?

If another neuroscience society already exists, can we explain why our proposed group adds value?

Are we applying for organization-building rather than simply funding a conference?

If the answer to these questions is unclear, the project may need further development before submission.

What a Strong Proposal Should Demonstrate

1. A Clear Need

Explain why the proposed society or network is necessary.

Provide context about:

Existing neuroscience activity

Institutional gaps

Geographic fragmentation

Lack of formal networking structures

Underrepresented neuroscience disciplines

2. A Concrete Establishment Plan

Avoid vague ambitions such as:

“We hope to create a neuroscience community.”

Instead, explain what will actually happen.

For example:

Convene founding members

Draft governance rules

Establish an interim executive committee

Develop membership procedures

Register the organization

Adopt a strategic plan

Launch formal communication channels

3. Clear Outcomes

The project should produce outcomes that can be demonstrated.

Possible outcomes could include:

Approved constitution

Founding committee

Membership framework

Formal society registration process

Strategic plan

Regional chapter structure

Thematic network governance system

4. Sustainability

Explain how the community will continue after IBRO support ends.

Potential sustainability mechanisms could include:

Membership dues

Institutional support

Future sponsorship

Partnerships

Volunteer leadership

Future grants

5. Broad Community Engagement

Demonstrate that the initiative represents more than a small circle of colleagues where possible.

The proposal can be strengthened by engaging researchers from:

Different institutions

Different cities or regions

Different career stages

Relevant neuroscience disciplines

Applications From Countries With Existing Societies

Applicants in countries where a formal national neuroscience society already exists should be especially careful.

They should clearly establish that they are pursuing:

A formal sub-society

A thematic organization

A regional chapter

and that the proposed body serves a need not currently met by the existing society.

The proposal should not appear to create unnecessary duplication.

It should instead demonstrate:

Complementarity and added value.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

30 September 2026

The application period opened on:

1 September 2026

Applications must be completed through the official IBRO Grants Portal.

Future Application Rounds

IBRO indicates that the next application round is expected to open around the same period next year.

Scientists who are not ready to submit in 2026 may therefore consider:

Developing their founding group

Building institutional partnerships

Clarifying the scientific focus

Drafting governance structures

Joining the IBRO newsletter

so that they are better prepared for a future call.

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants

Organizer: International Brain Research Organization

Purpose: Establishing new neuroscience societies, sub-societies, regional chapters and thematic networks

Grant type on IBRO website: Event organization

Eligible regions: Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America

Applications open: 1 September 2026

Deadline: 30 September 2026

Eligible applicants: Groups of scientists and organizations working toward the formation of a formal neuroscience community

Examples of supported activities: Governance planning, strategic workshops and other inaugural organizational activities

Standalone conferences: Not eligible unless connected to an actionable society/network establishment plan

Countries with an existing society: Applicants may seek support for a new formal sub-society, regional chapter or thematic network where clear added value and unmet need can be demonstrated

Maximum grant amount: Not numerically stated in the supplied public-page text; applicants should consult the active call details

Application method: IBRO Grants Portal

Conclusion

The IBRO Seeding Neuroscience Grants 2026 provide an important opportunity for scientists in Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America to move from informal scientific collaboration toward the establishment of formal, sustainable neuroscience communities.

Unlike a conventional conference grant, the programme is specifically designed to support the organizational foundations required to create new:

National neuroscience societies

Regional neuroscience societies

Formal sub-societies

Regional chapters

Thematic neuroscience networks

Funding may support inaugural activities such as governance discussions, strategic workshops and other organizational steps that lead directly to the establishment of a durable scientific body.

The programme is particularly relevant in regions where neuroscience researchers currently lack a formal structure for collaboration and professional exchange. It may also support specialized groups in countries where a national neuroscience society already exists, provided the proposed new structure addresses an unmet need and offers clear added value.

The most important principle for applicants is that the proposed activity must lead somewhere concrete. A standalone conference or scientific meeting is not enough. Applicants need to demonstrate an actionable pathway toward establishing a society, chapter, sub-society or thematic network.

Applications opened on 1 September 2026 and must be submitted through the IBRO Grants Portal by: 30 September 2026.
