TITLE: University of the Witwatersrand PhD and LLM Bursaries 2027: Up to R200,000 for African Law Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the 2027 PhD and LLM by Research bursaries at the University of the Witwatersrand School of Law, offering postgraduate funding for researchers interested in equality, socio-economic rights, land rights, housing, social justice, and African human rights law.

The bursaries are offered through the NRF-funded South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice, based at the School of Law, University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University), Johannesburg, South Africa.

Successful applicants will undertake either a PhD or an LLM by Research beginning in 2027 under the supervision of the Chair or associated academics.

The opportunity is particularly significant for postgraduate researchers from South Africa and other African countries whose proposed research aligns with one of the Chair’s identified areas of interest.

For 2027, the bursary value is approximately:

R200,000 for PhD candidates who qualify for the higher level of NRF support

R190,000 for LLM candidates who qualify for the higher level of NRF support

Approximately R150,000 for PhD candidates qualifying at the lower funding level

Approximately R145,000 for LLM candidates qualifying at the lower funding level

The higher funding level is linked to the NRF’s means-tested funding provisions or applicants with academic averages of 75% or higher, while students with a minimum academic average of 65% may qualify for partial bursary amounts.

Applicants must study full-time at Wits University, meet the relevant academic and age requirements, and successfully complete several stages of approval involving the SARChI Chair, the National Research Foundation, and the Wits School of Law.

The application deadline is 30 September 2026.

About the Wits University School of Law Postgraduate Funding Opportunity

The funding opportunity is offered through the South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice, commonly referred to as a SARChI Chair.

The Chair is supported by the National Research Foundation of South Africa (NRF) and is hosted within the School of Law at the University of the Witwatersrand.

The 2027 call seeks postgraduate researchers who want to undertake sustained research on questions related to:

Equality

Law

Social justice

Socio-economic rights

Land rights

Housing

Vulnerable groups

African regional institutions

African human rights mechanisms

The funding is available for two research-degree routes:

PhD

LLM by Research

Applicants should therefore be interested in completing an advanced research degree rather than a coursework-only programme.

Research Areas Available for 2027

Applicants must propose research that fits within one of the areas identified by the SARChI Chair.

The five research areas are:

Intergenerational equity and women’s land rights

Impact of intergenerational injustice on the right to housing

Contributions of African regional bodies to the development and enforcement of economic, social and cultural rights

The role of economic, social and cultural rights in addressing inequalities among vulnerable groups in Africa

Advancing equality and social change through the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights

These research areas place the opportunity firmly within broader debates about law, justice, rights, inequality, and African legal institutions.

1. Intergenerational Equity and Women’s Land Rights

One of the research areas concerns:

Intergenerational equity and women’s land rights.

Applicants interested in this field would need to develop a research question addressing the relationship between gender, land rights, justice across generations, and relevant legal frameworks.

The call itself does not prescribe a specific research question, country case study, legal jurisdiction, or methodology.

Applicants therefore need to formulate their own focused research problem within this broader theme.

The one-to-two-page summary research proposal required at the initial application stage should clearly identify the legal or socio-legal issue the candidate intends to investigate.

2. Intergenerational Injustice and the Right to Housing

A second research area is:

The impact of intergenerational injustice on the right to housing.

This theme connects questions of historical or inherited inequality with legal protections concerning housing.

Applicants should propose a clearly defined research problem rather than merely stating that they want to research housing rights.

The Chair is looking for a concise proposal demonstrating that the candidate has identified a substantive question appropriate for advanced postgraduate research.

3. African Regional Bodies and Economic, Social and Cultural Rights

The third research area focuses on:

The contributions of African regional bodies to the development and enforcement of economic, social and cultural rights.

Economic, social and cultural rights are often abbreviated as ESC rights.

This research area is particularly relevant to candidates interested in African regional human rights law and institutions.

The call does not prescribe which regional body, particular right, or country should form the focus of the research, so applicants will need to define an appropriate research scope themselves.

4. ESC Rights and Inequality Among Vulnerable Groups in Africa

Another priority is:

The role of economic, social and cultural rights in addressing inequalities among vulnerable groups in Africa.

This theme combines:

Rights

Inequality

Social justice

Vulnerability

African legal and policy contexts

Applicants will need to identify which rights, groups, legal frameworks, or inequalities their proposed study will address.

The research should remain closely aligned with the broader work of the Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice.

5. African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights, Equality and Social Change

The fifth research area concerns:

Advancing equality and social change through the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

This provides a particularly strong avenue for applicants interested in:

African human rights law

Regional judicial institutions

Equality

Rights enforcement

Legal approaches to social change

Again, the call identifies the broad research field rather than providing a predetermined dissertation project.

Candidates are expected to formulate their own viable research question.

Degree Options

The funding opportunity supports two postgraduate research degrees.

PhD

Applicants may apply to undertake a doctoral degree under the supervision of the SARChI Chair or associated scholars.

The PhD bursary may provide approximately:

R200,000

for candidates meeting the applicable higher-level NRF funding criteria.

For applicants with the minimum qualifying academic average of 65%, the funding may instead be approximately:

R150,000

or the applicable part thereof.

LLM by Research

The opportunity also supports candidates undertaking an:

LLM by Research

This is distinct from a coursework-based LLM.

The LLM by Research bursary may be approximately:

R190,000

for applicants qualifying for the higher NRF funding level.

For candidates with a minimum academic average of 65%, the amount may be approximately:

R145,000

or part thereof.

Understanding the 2027 Bursary Amounts

Applicants should pay close attention to the way the funding is structured.

The call states that the approximate 2027 NRF bursary values are:

Higher funding level

PhD: Approximately R200,000

LLM: Approximately R190,000

This higher level applies under the relevant NRF means-tested funding criteria or for students with academic averages of:

75% or higher

Lower or partial funding level

Applicants meeting the minimum average of:

65%

may qualify for approximately:

R150,000 for PhD

or:

R145,000 for LLM

or the applicable part thereof.

Applicants should therefore not assume that every successful candidate automatically receives the maximum stated amount.

Actual funding is subject to NRF eligibility and approval.

The Bursary Must Be the Primary Funding

The call states that the NRF bursary should be held as the applicant’s:

Primary funding towards the degree.

Candidates who already have another major funding source should therefore consult the relevant NRF rules to determine whether the funding can be combined with other awards.

The detailed NRF Postgraduate Funding Framework should be reviewed carefully by applicants who have questions about concurrent funding or other financial conditions.

Who Can Apply?

Applicants must meet several important requirements.

They must:

Intend to undertake either a PhD or LLM by Research

Study full-time

Study at the University of the Witwatersrand

Work under the supervision of the Chair or associates

Be South African or come from another African country

Meet the required minimum academic average

Meet the NRF age requirement

Submit a research proposal aligned with one of the five listed areas

This is therefore a targeted postgraduate research funding opportunity rather than a general scholarship open to all programmes at Wits University.

Full-Time Study Requirement

Successful applicants must undertake their degree:

Full-time

at:

Wits University

The funding is therefore not presented as support for part-time postgraduate study.

Applicants should be prepared to commit to the academic requirements of a full-time research programme.

Academic Requirements

The call specifies a minimum academic average of:

65% in the applicant’s previous degree

The qualifying previous degree is generally:

LLB for relevant LLM applicants

LLM for PhD applicants

The 65% threshold is the minimum requirement for NRF bursary eligibility under this opportunity.

Applicants with academic averages of 75% or above may potentially qualify for the higher funding level identified in the call.

Age Requirements

The NRF funding also includes maximum age requirements.

LLM Applicants

Applicants must be:

30 years old or younger in 2027

The announcement states that candidates must not be older than 30 in 2027.

PhD Applicants

Applicants must be:

32 years old or younger in 2027

Candidates must therefore not be older than 32 in 2027.

These are important eligibility conditions.

A strong academic record does not override the age requirements stated for the NRF bursary.

Nationality and Geographic Eligibility

The opportunity is open to:

South African applicants

Applicants from other African countries

This makes the bursary a continentally accessible postgraduate opportunity rather than one restricted only to South African nationals.

Applicants from African countries outside South Africa must still meet all academic, programme, funding, and admission requirements.

Required Application Documents

Applicants must prepare six main components.

1. Covering Letter

Candidates must submit a letter explaining:

Why they are interested in the bursary.

The letter should therefore be tailored specifically to the SARChI Chair opportunity.

A strong covering letter should connect:

The applicant’s academic background

Research interests

Proposed topic

Interest in equality, law and social justice

Long-term academic or professional goals

Reasons for wanting to work with the Chair

Candidates should avoid sending a generic postgraduate funding letter.

2. One-to-Two-Page Research Proposal

Applicants must provide a:

One-to-two-page summary research proposal

The proposal should clearly specify:

The issue the applicant wishes to research.

This is one of the most important components of the application.

Because the proposal is short, candidates need to present their idea concisely.

A useful structure may include:

Proposed title

Research problem

Main research question

Brief background

Relevance to one of the Chair’s research areas

Proposed legal or research approach

Expected contribution

Applicants should remain within the required one-to-two-page length.

Choosing a Research Topic

The research proposal should align directly with one of the five announced areas.

Candidates should avoid proposing a broad topic such as:

“Human rights in Africa”

or:

“Women’s rights.”

Instead, the proposal should identify a specific and researchable legal issue.

The application should make clear why the project belongs within the Chair’s programme on:

Equality, Law and Social Justice.

3. Copy of ID or Passport

Applicants must provide either:

Identification document, or

Passport

This helps establish identity and relevant nationality information.

International African applicants should ensure their passport documentation is clear and valid.

4. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit an updated CV.

For an academic postgraduate funding application, the CV should highlight information such as:

Education

Academic results

Research experience

Dissertation or thesis experience

Publications, if any

Research assistant work

Mooting or legal research

Internships

Relevant professional experience

Awards

Conferences

Teaching or tutoring

Community or public-interest work

Candidates should prioritize experiences connected to law, rights, equality, social justice, or their proposed research field.

5. Full Academic Records

Applicants must provide:

Full academic records

This is essential because the NRF bursary has explicit minimum academic thresholds.

Candidates should ensure the submitted record clearly demonstrates their academic performance.

6. Two Academic Referees

Applicants must provide:

Contact details for two academic referees.

Referees should ideally be academics who know the applicant’s research or academic abilities well.

Potential referees might include:

Thesis supervisor

Dissertation supervisor

Research project supervisor

Lecturer

Professor familiar with the applicant’s work

The announcement asks for contact details rather than stating that recommendation letters must be submitted with the initial application.

Applicants should follow any subsequent instructions they receive from the Chair.

Application Process: Three Important Stages

Applicants should understand that acceptance by the SARChI Chair is not the final funding decision.

The process involves multiple stages.

Stage 1: Apply to the SARChI Chair

Applicants first submit the required documents to the Chair’s application contact.

The application will be evaluated for:

Research alignment

Academic eligibility

Bursary criteria

Suitability for supervision

Stage 2: Apply to the NRF

Candidates accepted by the Chair will subsequently need to submit an application through the:

National Research Foundation online system

Acceptance by the Chair remains subject to NRF approval.

The SARChI Chair will provide additional details to candidates who reach this stage.

Stage 3: Apply to the Wits School of Law

Successful bursary candidates must also obtain admission to the appropriate:

Wits School of Law programme

This means that being selected for consideration by the Chair does not automatically constitute formal admission to Wits University.

Candidates must successfully satisfy the academic admission requirements for the relevant:

PhD, or

LLM by Research

programme.

Important Conditional Nature of the Award

Applicants should therefore understand that final funding depends on:

Acceptance by the SARChI Chair

NRF approval

Successful admission to the relevant Wits School of Law programme

All three elements matter.

How to Submit the Application

Applications must be sent to:

Judy Mafika

judy.mafika@wits.ac.za

Candidates are encouraged to submit:

As soon as possible

and no later than:

30 September 2026

Late applications will not be considered.

Incomplete applications will also not be considered.

Applicants should therefore confirm that all required documents are attached before sending their application.

Application Deadline

The final deadline is:

30 September 2026

This is the deadline for the initial application to the SARChI Chair.

Applicants should not confuse this deadline with later NRF or Wits University processes that may apply after selection.

When Will Applicants Hear Back?

The announcement states that applicants who do not receive communication by:

The end of October 2026

should consider their application to the Chair unsuccessful.

This provides candidates with a relatively clear timeline for the first stage of the process.

Enquiries About Research Scope

Applicants who have questions about the research areas or whether their proposed project fits the Chair’s programme may contact:

Professor Cathi Albertyn

cathi.albertyn@wits.ac.za

or:

Professor Lilian Chenwi

lilian.chenwi@wits.ac.za

Questions concerning the scope of the research area or bursary criteria should be directed to these contacts.

About the SARChI Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice

The postgraduate bursaries are connected to the:

South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice

at the University of the Witwatersrand.

The Chair’s 2027 research themes show a strong focus on the relationship between law and structural inequality.

Across the five identified areas, recurring themes include:

Equality

Intergenerational justice

Women’s rights

Land rights

Housing

Economic, social and cultural rights

Vulnerable groups

African institutions

Regional human rights law

Social change

This makes the bursary particularly relevant to students interested in legal research that examines how law interacts with inequality and social transformation.

Why the Opportunity Is Particularly Relevant to African Researchers

The programme explicitly welcomes candidates from:

South Africa and other African countries.

Research topics are also heavily centered on African legal and human rights questions.

This combination provides opportunities for researchers to examine legal issues within African contexts while being based at a major South African university.

The identified themes encourage research relating to:

African rights institutions

African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights

Vulnerable groups in Africa

Regional approaches to ESC rights

Equality and social justice

Understanding ESC Rights

Several of the research themes refer to:

ESC rights

This stands for:

Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

Within the context of this call, applicants may be interested in examining how legal frameworks and institutions contribute to developing, enforcing, or using such rights to respond to inequality.

The specific right, jurisdiction, population, or institutional focus must be defined by the applicant’s proposal.

Preparing a Competitive Application

1. Start With the Research Fit

The first question applicants should ask is not:

“How much funding can I receive?”

Instead, ask:

“Does my research genuinely fit one of the five themes?”

Strong thematic alignment is fundamental.

2. Make the Research Problem Specific

A one-to-two-page proposal does not allow space for an extremely broad topic.

Clearly state:

What problem exists

What legal question you want to answer

Why the question matters

Where the research is situated

What contribution the project could make

3. Connect the Project to Equality and Social Justice

Even when choosing a specific area such as land, housing, or the African Court, applicants should make the connection with the Chair’s overarching concern with:

Equality, Law and Social Justice

clear.

4. Demonstrate Academic Readiness

The minimum average is 65%, but a competitive application should communicate more than numerical eligibility.

Candidates can highlight:

Previous dissertation work

Research methods

Academic writing

Relevant coursework

Publications

Conference work

where applicable.

5. Choose Strong Academic Referees

Your referees should be capable of discussing your ability to undertake independent postgraduate research.

A famous academic who barely knows your work may be less useful than a lecturer or supervisor familiar with your academic strengths.

6. Check the Age Requirement Before Applying

The age limits are explicit:

Applicants should verify this condition before investing substantial time in preparing the application.

7. Submit a Complete Application

The call states explicitly:

Incomplete applications will not be considered.

Before submitting, check that your application contains:

Covering letter

Research proposal

ID/passport

CV

Full academic records

Two academic referees

Application Checklist

Before sending your application, confirm that you have:

Written a tailored covering letter.

Prepared a one-to-two-page research proposal.

Selected one of the five relevant research areas.

Included your ID or passport.

Updated your CV.

Attached full academic records.

Provided two academic referee contacts.

Checked that your previous-degree average is at least 65%.

Confirmed that you meet the NRF age requirement.

Confirmed that you can study full-time at Wits University.

Confirmed that you are South African or from another African country.

Submitted everything by September 30, 2026.

Applicants accepted by the Chair will subsequently receive information concerning their NRF and Wits School of Law applications.

The University of the Witwatersrand PhD and LLM Bursaries 2027 provide an important postgraduate funding opportunity for African researchers interested in law, equality, socio-economic rights and social justice.

TITLE: The Promise of the Universal Acceptance in Academic Institutions Initiative

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Nodumo Dhlamini, Director, ICT Services & Knowledge Management, Association of African Universities

Abdul Manaf Sulemana, UA Project Officer, Association of African Universities

Universal Acceptance (UA) is a foundational requirement for a truly multilingual Internet, one in which users around the world can navigate entirely in local languages. To achieve UA, all Internet-enabled applications, devices, and systems, must regard all top-level domains (TLDs) in a consistent manner, including new generic TLDs (gTLDs), internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), and IDN country-code TLDs by accepting, validating, storing, processing, and displaying all valid domain names and email addresses.

The AAU-Led Initiative for Promoting UA in Academic Institutions

Launched in Accra on 13 April 2023 by the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) under the Coalition for Digital Africa, the UA in Academic Institutions initiative is part of a broader goal to expand Internet access in Africa.

The initiative aims to foster collaborative community outreach and engagement, enhancing UA readiness across AAU’s 400+ member universities. This ensures equitable treatment of all domain names, including IDNs, and email addresses across Internet-enabled applications and systems. As key agents of UA principles adoption, these institutions are supported in updating their systems and integrating IDN and UA concepts into their IT and computer science curricula.

Key Milestones achieved to date.

The AAU observed the UA Day on 28 March 2023 which attracted 48 in-person participants from 7 higher education institutions in Ghana physically attending the event and 153 virtual participants globally. This event was also broadcast live on the AAU TV which is viewed across 27 African countries.

Two technical workshops were held for ICT Directors and CTOs from African higher education institutions. The first was held in Accra, Ghana, on 14 April 2023, and the second in Windhoek, Namibia, on 3 July 2023, aligning with the AAU COREVIP pre-conference activities. These workshops, attended by 43 individuals from 11 universities and 2 governmental bodies in Accra and 26 participants from seven countries respectively, focused on UA, including programming and email administration, to enhance UA-compliance in their university systems.

On 15 and 16 February 2024, webinars in English and French languages were held to discuss strategies for updating computer science curricula in African higher education institutions to include concepts around IDNs and UA. Leaders in academia were the target participants for this webinar – 249 participants joined for the English session, and 34 participants joined the French session.

Upcoming Activities

A third technical workshop is scheduled for 26 April 2024 in Rabat, Morocco on the sidelines of the Middle East DNS Forum 2024 to further discuss inclusion of the IDN and UA concepts into the computer science and information technology curricula.

Challenges and Opportunities

The configuration of UA-compliant email systems and websites requires appropriate skills and capacities. There is a need to continuously train the technical staff by running workshops in the five official languages of the continent. Interpretation costs increase the expenses of delivering virtual or in-person training.

During discussions on strategies for updating computer science and information technology curricula to include UA concepts, academic staff were concerned about who would teach the topics concerning IDNs and UA. This demonstrated the importance of investing in the training of academic staff so that they would be confident in delivering the new curricula.

The bureaucratic process of updating curricula in African higher education institutions might hinder the building of the capacities of computer science and information technology students. The curriculum is designed into micro learning modules to help mitigate such challenges. Still, a multi-pronged approach is recommended involving the holding of UA-curriculum seminars on campuses and using such platforms to raise awareness and build the capacities of faculty members.

A significant number of African Universities use Yahoo, Gmail and related email systems as their official emails. However, this does not mean that such universities do not have institutional email systems. This poses a challenge of testing the institutional emails for UA-compliance because time is spent ascertaining the institutional email addresses.

Testing websites running on content management systems (CMS) for UA-readiness required the AAU-ICANN team to broker a collaboration with the CMS to achieve the effective testing of the concerned websites.

As echoed by AAU Secretary General, Prof. Olusola Oyewole during the launch, “The Universal Acceptance in Academic Institutions initiative is a vital project as it is aligned to AAU’s strategic priority of strengthening the institutional capacities of its stakeholders to be able to implement the required changes to their digital platforms so that Africa is part of an inclusive internet. With a platform of 420 universities, the AAU remains strategically positioned to champion the required changes towards achieving universally accepted email systems and websites.”

TITLE: Become a Young European Ambassador: Join the YEA Network and Connect Youth Across Europe and the Eastern Neighbourhood

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Young European Ambassadors (YEA) initiative is a youth network that brings together young people from the European Union and the Eastern Partnership countries to promote youth participation, awareness, dialogue, solidarity, and connections across borders.

The initiative is part of the work of EU NEIGHBOURS east, which provides news, information and opportunities relating to the European Union’s cooperation with its Eastern partners: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine.

For young people interested in European affairs, youth engagement, community initiatives, democracy, human rights, environmental issues, gender equality, international cooperation and cross-border networking, the Young European Ambassadors initiative provides an opportunity to become part of a growing regional community.

The network is celebrating its 10th anniversary in 2026, marking a decade of youth-led activities, connections, campaigns, community initiatives and cooperation.

What Is the Young European Ambassadors Initiative?

The Young European Ambassadors initiative is a network that gives young people a platform to become active in their communities while connecting with peers across the Eastern Neighbourhood and the European Union.

Since its launch, YEAs have worked to raise awareness about the EU’s partnership with its Eastern neighbours, promote shared values and communicate opportunities available to young people.

The initiative has also supported youth-led activities addressing issues such as:

Democracy and civic participation

Human rights

Environmental protection

Gender equality

Youth empowerment

European integration and cooperation

Community development

Solidarity and social engagement

Awareness of educational and professional opportunities

Cross-border youth networking

Rather than being limited to one particular type of activity, the YEA network provides a space where young people can develop connections and participate in initiatives that respond to issues affecting their communities and the wider region.

A Decade of Young European Ambassadors

The YEA network was officially launched on 16 June 2016, when the first 100 Young European Ambassadors were selected from the six Eastern partner countries and the European Union.

The six Eastern partner countries represented in the initiative are:

Armenia

Azerbaijan

Belarus

Georgia

Republic of Moldova

Ukraine

The initiative began with activities designed to connect young people with their communities and increase awareness of EU values, cooperation and opportunities.

One of the early activities involved visits to schools across the Republic of Moldova, where Young European Ambassadors engaged with students and raised awareness about European Union values and opportunities.

Over the following decade, the network expanded substantially, developing a broader regional and international community.

Young European Ambassadors and Regional Cooperation

An important part of the YEA initiative has been creating connections among young people from different countries.

For example, in 2019, activities marking the 10th anniversary of the Eastern Partnership brought 100 Young European Ambassadors to Brussels for the Eastern Partnership 10th Anniversary Launch Event.

The YEAs organised a flashmob in front of the European Commission, featuring national costumes and the flags of the six Eastern partner countries and the European Union.

Similar activities were also organised by Young European Ambassadors across the six partner countries.

These activities demonstrate the network’s emphasis on youth-to-youth connections, cultural exchange, public engagement and regional cooperation.

Community Engagement and Grassroots Impact

The Young European Ambassadors network has a strong grassroots dimension.

YEAs have participated in activities intended to bring information, opportunities and discussions closer to young people in local communities.

Through school visits, campaigns, public activities, community initiatives and youth engagement, members have helped create opportunities for young people to discuss issues affecting their societies.

This grassroots approach allows Young European Ambassadors to connect broader European and regional discussions with local communities.

The initiative’s activities have included work around:

Youth participation

Education and learning opportunities

Community engagement

Awareness campaigns

Human rights

Democracy

Environmental issues

Gender equality

European cooperation

Social solidarity

Supporting Solidarity and Youth Action

The network has also responded to major developments affecting communities across the region.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Young European Ambassadors across the partner countries and the European Union mobilised solidarity activities.

These included awareness-raising events, solidarity actions and volunteer initiatives supporting Ukraine.

The YEA network has subsequently continued to provide a platform for youth engagement around issues affecting the region.

The initiative also highlights the importance of youth voices in conversations surrounding European enlargement, particularly following applications for EU membership by Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia in 2022.

A Growing International Youth Network

The scale of the YEA network has grown considerably since its establishment.

According to EU NEIGHBOURS east, as the network reaches its tenth anniversary in 2026, it has almost 1,000 active members, while more than 3,000 people have served as Young European Ambassadors since the initiative began in 2016.

This provides current and former members with an extensive network of people who have participated in youth initiatives across the Eastern Neighbourhood and Europe.

The network therefore extends beyond individual activities. Members can develop relationships with peers, alumni and other participants whose experiences can continue to be valuable after particular YEA activities have ended.

What Do Young European Ambassadors Do?

Young European Ambassadors have participated in a wide range of activities depending on their communities, interests and the issues being addressed.

Examples of YEA engagement include:

1. Raising Awareness

YEAs communicate information about the European Union, its partnership with Eastern neighbours and opportunities available to young people.

This can involve conversations, campaigns, public activities, educational engagement and digital communication.

2. Supporting Community Initiatives

Young European Ambassadors can participate in activities that address issues within their communities.

This grassroots dimension enables members to translate broader ideas into practical local engagement.

3. Promoting Democracy and Human Rights

The YEA network has supported awareness around democracy and human rights, including efforts to keep these issues visible within youth and community discussions.

4. Environmental Engagement

Young European Ambassadors have also participated in activities connected to environmental awareness and the importance of protecting the environment.

5. Promoting Gender Equality

Gender equality has been among the issues addressed through YEA campaigns and activities.

6. Building Youth Connections

A central part of the initiative is connecting young people from different countries and communities.

These relationships can create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge exchange and continued engagement.

7. Supporting Solidarity

The network has demonstrated its capacity to organise solidarity activities and volunteer initiatives in response to regional developments.

Examples of YEA Experiences

The 10th-anniversary campaign highlights experiences from current and former Young European Ambassadors, illustrating the different ways participants have engaged with the initiative.

One example comes from Dmytro, whose highlighted experience involved bringing opportunities closer to young people in Poltava and engaging youth councils and student self-governments.

His experience demonstrates how YEA participation can involve direct work with youth organisations and local institutions.

Another example comes from Tatevik, who highlighted a 2019 Human Rights Day campaign involving free morning coffee for passers-by as a way of creating everyday conversations around human rights.

Her experience also reflects the network’s broader emphasis on creating meaningful conversations through accessible community activities.

The initiative also features the experience of Ambroise, who described gaining a strong network of people, support and experiences that continued to remain valuable after his participation.

His experience illustrates how relationships developed through the network can extend beyond individual activities and locations.

The Importance of the YEA Network in 2026

The tenth anniversary provides an opportunity to reflect on the development of the initiative while looking toward its future.

Over ten years, the YEA network has moved from its initial group of 100 ambassadors to a community involving thousands of current and former members.

Today, YEAs remain active across the region and within the European Union.

Their activities include:

Promoting awareness of EU opportunities

Supporting solidarity with Ukraine

Discussing European enlargement

Raising awareness of democracy

Highlighting human rights issues

Connecting young people across countries

Supporting youth-led activities

Strengthening community networks

The anniversary campaign is built around the theme of connections that last, highlighting friendships, networks, experiences and community relationships developed through the initiative.

Why Join the Young European Ambassadors Network?

Becoming part of a youth network such as the YEA initiative can provide opportunities to participate in activities beyond one’s immediate community.

Participants can potentially benefit from exposure to:

Regional and International Networking

The network connects young people from the Eastern partner countries and the European Union, creating opportunities to meet peers with different backgrounds and experiences.

Youth Leadership and Engagement

Participation can provide practical experience in organising and supporting youth activities, awareness campaigns and community initiatives.

Cross-Border Collaboration

The network provides a platform for young people to work with peers across national borders and contribute to regional activities.

Community Experience

Young people can engage with schools, youth organisations, student groups, community members and other stakeholders.

Exposure to European Opportunities

The YEA initiative also promotes awareness of opportunities connected to education, training, work and wider EU cooperation.

Long-Term Connections

With thousands of people having participated in the initiative since 2016, joining the network can provide access to a community that extends beyond individual campaigns or activities.

Who Can Be Part of the Young European Ambassadors Network?

The YEA initiative is specifically focused on young people connected to the European Union and the Eastern Partnership region.

The Eastern partner countries identified by EU NEIGHBOURS east are:

Armenia

Azerbaijan

Belarus

Georgia

Republic of Moldova

Ukraine

The initiative also has a connection to young people in the European Union.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the official YEA application information and eligibility requirements when an application round is open, as specific requirements may vary depending on the particular recruitment cycle.

How to Apply to Become a Young European Ambassador

Young people interested in joining the network should follow the official Young European Ambassadors channels for application announcements.

The official EU NEIGHBOURS east YEA platform provides information about the initiative and directs interested young people to relevant application opportunities.

Prospective applicants should:

Visit the official Young European Ambassadors website.

Read the information about the initiative and its activities.

Check whether a current application round is open.

Carefully review the eligibility requirements.

Prepare the requested personal, educational, professional or community-engagement information.

Submit the application through the official application channel before the stated closing date.

Follow the YEA and EU NEIGHBOURS east communication channels for future opportunities if applications are not currently open.

Interested young people can also subscribe to EU NEIGHBOURS east updates to receive information about opportunities as they are published.

APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

No specific application deadline is stated in the information provided for the general Young European Ambassadors initiative.

Because YEA recruitment can take place through specific application rounds, interested candidates should check the official application page for the latest opening and closing dates before applying.

A Network Built Around Youth Voices

The Young European Ambassadors initiative demonstrates how youth networks can connect local community engagement with broader regional cooperation.

Since its launch in 2016, the network has grown from its first 100 ambassadors into a community involving almost 1,000 active members and more than 3,000 people who have served as YEAs.

Its activities have covered education, community engagement, democracy, human rights, environmental issues, gender equality, solidarity and awareness of European opportunities.

As the initiative enters its second decade, its emphasis remains on building connections among young people, strengthening communities and providing opportunities for youth voices to contribute to discussions across the European Union and the Eastern Neighbourhood.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Become a Young European Ambassador.

Conclusion

The Young European Ambassadors initiative offers young people an opportunity to become part of a regional and European youth network focused on connection, community engagement, awareness and cooperation.

With a history dating back to 2016, the network has created opportunities for young people to participate in campaigns, community activities, awareness initiatives, solidarity actions and cross-border youth engagement.

Its tenth anniversary in 2026 marks an important milestone, with almost 1,000 active members and more than 3,000 people having served as Young European Ambassadors since the initiative began.

Young people from the European Union and the Eastern partner countries who are interested in youth engagement, European cooperation, community initiatives, democracy, human rights, environmental issues and international networking should monitor the official Young European Ambassadors platform for current and upcoming application opportunities.

For official information and future application announcements, applicants should rely on the EU NEIGHBOURS east and Young European Ambassadors platforms.

TITLE: Energy Transition Academy 2026 for Latin America and the Caribbean: Free Online Programme, Certification and Application Guide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the 2026 Energy Transition Academy for Latin America and the Caribbean (ATE LAC), a free online regional training programme designed to strengthen knowledge and capacity around the energy transition.

The programme brings together the technical, economic, political and social dimensions of energy transition, giving participants an opportunity to understand how energy systems are changing and what those changes mean for countries, communities, economies, industries and citizens across Latin America and the Caribbean.

The Academy is designed for young people, students, professionals, civil society representatives and other people interested in energy and climate issues. Importantly, previous academic or professional experience in the energy sector is not required. The programme is intended to make energy-transition knowledge accessible to people from different educational and professional backgrounds.

The 2026 programme will run from 15 October to 26 November 2026 and will consist of seven online sessions covering 12 thematic classes and a high-level closing panel. Participants will explore topics ranging from renewable energy, electricity grids and electrification to electromobility, industrial decarbonisation, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, strategic minerals, energy poverty, climate policy, energy economics and regional energy integration.

The programme is 100% online and free of charge, and eligible participants who satisfy the applicable participation and assessment requirements can receive certification issued by the University of Chile.

Application Deadline: 30 September 2026

What Is the Energy Transition Academy 2026?

The Energy Transition Academy for Latin America and the Caribbean (ATE LAC) is a regional training programme intended to bring energy-sector knowledge closer to a broader range of people.

The Academy seeks to strengthen the capacities needed for more people to participate actively in the transformation of energy systems across the region. Its stated objective is to develop people capable of contributing to the implementation of national energy and climate commitments while strengthening regional climate cooperation.

Rather than treating energy transition as a subject that belongs only to engineers or energy specialists, ATE LAC approaches it as a multidisciplinary issue involving:

Technology

Economics

Public policy

Climate action

Infrastructure

Social development

Communities

Investment

Regulation

Employment

Energy access

Regional cooperation

This comprehensive approach is important because changing an energy system involves much more than installing renewable-energy technologies. Governments, businesses, communities, researchers and civil society organizations must also address questions surrounding infrastructure, investment, affordability, regulation, employment, energy security and social equity.

Why Energy Transition Matters in Latin America and the Caribbean

Latin America and the Caribbean are entering an important period of energy-system transformation.

Countries across the region need to translate climate and energy commitments into practical policies, infrastructure investments, regulations and projects. At the same time, they need to consider energy security, energy access, economic development and the specific circumstances of different territories.

The transition is also creating new technological, economic and social opportunities. These developments require people who can understand complex energy choices and participate meaningfully in their implementation.

ATE LAC is designed to respond to this need by providing participants with a broad understanding of the forces shaping the energy transition.

The programme does not focus exclusively on one technology or one professional discipline. Instead, it examines how different parts of the energy system interact.

Main Objective of ATE LAC

The main objective of the Academy is to strengthen the capacities needed for more people to actively participate in transforming the region’s energy systems.

The programme also seeks to develop leaders who can contribute to national commitments and goals while helping consolidate regional climate cooperation.

This means that the Academy is not simply intended to provide theoretical knowledge. It is designed to help participants understand the practical conditions surrounding energy transformation and develop the capacity to engage with the challenges involved.

About the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe

The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe is a major intergovernmental security organization bringing together 57 participating States across North America, Europe and Asia.

Its work is based on the principle that security cannot be viewed purely through military or political considerations. Instead, lasting peace and stability also depend on economic development, environmental protection, democratic institutions, human rights, good governance and cooperation between states.

The OSCE organizes much of its work around three broad dimensions:

The politico-military dimension;

The economic and environmental dimension; and

The human dimension.

The organization works to promote stability, peace and security for more than one billion people through political dialogue and practical programmes implemented across its region.

Understanding the OSCE Economic and Environmental Dimension

The internship specifically focuses on the OSCE’s Economic and Environmental Dimension, sometimes referred to as the organization’s second dimension.

The foundations of this dimension can be traced to the Helsinki Final Act, where participating States recognized the importance of cooperation in economics, science, technology and environmental affairs.

The principle behind this work is that economic and environmental problems can have consequences extending well beyond development policy. When issues such as corruption, economic inequality, poor natural-resource governance, environmental degradation or ineffective waste management are not adequately addressed, they can contribute to instability and tensions within or between countries.

Development of the OSCE’s Economic and Environmental Work

The OSCE’s economic and environmental mandate has evolved over several decades.

An important milestone was the Conference on Economic Co-operation in Europe held in Bonn in 1990, where participating States emphasized common objectives such as sustainable economic growth, improving living standards and quality of life, creating employment, using economic resources efficiently and protecting the environment.

The OSCE subsequently developed institutional mechanisms addressing economic and environmental security, including the work of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities and the Economic and Environmental Forum.

Another major milestone came during the 2003 Maastricht Ministerial Council meeting, when participating States adopted the OSCE Strategy Document for the Economic and Environmental Dimension.

This strengthened cooperation in fields including:

Economic development;

Good governance;

Sustainable development;

Environmental protection; and

Economic and environmental security.

The internship therefore sits within a substantial policy framework connecting economics and environmental issues with wider international security and stability.

What Does the Economic and Environmental Dimension Work On?

Through this dimension, the OSCE assists participating States with challenges that can potentially affect security and stability.

Relevant areas include:

Good governance;

Environmental awareness;

Anti-corruption initiatives;

Sustainable development;

Natural-resource management;

Sharing of natural resources;

Environmental waste management;

Economic governance;

Environmental protection;

Economic and environmental security; and

Related policy and programme development.

Interns may therefore gain exposure to topics that connect international relations with economics, sustainability and environmental governance.

What Can the OSCE Internship Programme Offer?

The internship provides young professionals with an opportunity to experience the daily working environment of a major multilateral organization.

1. Practical Exposure to an International Organization

Interns can gain direct insight into how the OSCE Secretariat operates and how international institutions translate policy commitments into programmes, research, meetings, projects and administrative activities.

2. Professional Skills Development

The internship gives participants opportunities to strengthen skills such as:

Policy research;

Report writing;

Analytical writing;

Project management;

Financial analysis;

Communications;

Stakeholder engagement;

Event management;

Administrative coordination; and

International teamwork.

3. Multinational Working Environment

Interns work in an institution involving professionals from different national, cultural and professional backgrounds.

This exposure can be particularly valuable to students and graduates interested in international organizations, diplomacy, development, environmental policy or multilateral cooperation.

4. Professional Mentorship and Learning

Participants may work alongside experienced OSCE professionals, creating opportunities to learn from colleagues with expertise across policy, programme management, administration and international affairs.

5. Professional Networking

The programme also gives interns opportunities to meet other young professionals with similar interests and establish professional connections within an international environment.

Internship Duration

Successful applicants may be appointed for periods ranging from two to six months.

The precise starting date will depend on the operational requirements of the relevant hiring office.

Applicants should also understand that the maximum cumulative internship period with the OSCE is six months.

This means that an individual who has already completed six months of internship service with the OSCE cannot subsequently undertake another OSCE internship, even if the second position is located at another duty station.

Full-Time Working Arrangement

OSCE internships are normally undertaken on a full-time basis of approximately 40 hours per week.

However, the vacancy indicates that flexible arrangements involving part-time internships may be approved in special circumstances.

Applicants should therefore generally prepare for full-time participation unless an alternative arrangement is specifically agreed with the OSCE.

Tasks and Responsibilities of OSCE Economic and Environmental Interns

Interns may be assigned a broad range of responsibilities depending on the department, programme and operational needs of the OSCE Secretariat.

The vacancy provides examples of the assignments interns may undertake.

1. Research and Policy Writing

A significant portion of an intern’s work may involve research and drafting.

Assignments can include preparation of:

Research papers;

Policy reports;

Concept papers;

Briefing papers;

Internal memoranda;

Talking points;

Speeches;

Background documents;

Newsletters;

Presentations; and

Other policy or programme materials.

This aspect of the internship makes strong analytical, research and writing skills particularly valuable.

2. Project Management and Implementation

Interns may assist with the design, management and implementation of OSCE projects.

Possible tasks include:

Supporting preparation of project proposals;

Assisting with project budgets;

Monitoring project implementation;

Compiling information from project activities; and

Preparing progress reports for donors.

This can provide practical experience with the project cycle used by international organizations and donor-supported programmes.

3. Thematic Research and Analysis

Interns may conduct research on subjects relevant to OSCE activities.

Depending on the assignment, this could include:

Thematic policy research;

Legal research;

Assisting with reviews of legal documents;

Supporting preparation of legal opinions;

Media monitoring;

Surveys;

Financial analysis; and

Compilation and interpretation of data.

Candidates with strong research and analytical capabilities may therefore find the internship especially relevant.

4. Communications and Outreach

Some interns may support communications-related activities.

Possible responsibilities include:

Updating websites;

Preparing publications;

Developing booklets;

Producing leaflets;

Supporting outreach campaigns; and

Producing audio-visual material for social media.

This creates opportunities for candidates with communications and digital-content capabilities alongside their substantive academic background.

5. Event and Conference Support

The OSCE regularly organizes meetings and international events.

Interns may help organize:

Meetings;

Regional workshops;

Press conferences;

Round-table discussions;

Conferences; and

Other professional events.

Responsibilities can range from preparing background materials to logistical and administrative coordination.

6. Participation in OSCE Meetings

Depending on their placement, interns may attend meetings involving OSCE decision-making or related bodies.

Tasks may include:

Taking minutes;

Preparing meeting summaries;

Drafting official records;

Writing reports; and

Supporting follow-up activities.

This can provide valuable exposure to multilateral decision-making processes.

7. Administrative and Operational Support

Internships are not limited to substantive policy work.

Participants may also support operational departments responsible for areas such as:

Human resources;

Financial services;

Procurement;

Supply-chain activities;

Travel management;

Information technology;

Communications technology; and

General administration.

These responsibilities can help participants understand how a major international institution functions beyond its visible policy activities.

8. Supporting Senior Management

Interns can also assist senior managers in preparing for:

Official travel;

Bilateral meetings;

Country visits;

External meetings; and

Other engagements.

This may involve preparing briefing packages, compiling background materials, supporting logistical arrangements and communicating with internal and external stakeholders.

Educational Requirements

Applicants are expected to meet the OSCE’s academic requirements.

Candidates should have either:

Completed at least two years of full-time post-secondary education; or

Graduated from an eligible academic programme within two years before the application deadline.

The applicant’s educational background should be relevant to the work of the internship.

Fields specifically identified by the OSCE include:

Economics;

Environmental science;

Development studies;

International development;

Finance; or

Other comparable fields.

Applicants studying closely related areas may also be suitable where their academic background aligns with the internship’s economic and environmental work.

Age Requirement

Candidates must not be older than 30 years of age on December 31, 2026, which is the closing date of the vacancy.

Applicants should assess their eligibility according to their age on the official deadline rather than their age on the day they submit the application.

English-Language Requirement

Applicants are expected to have professional fluency in English, both written and spoken.

They should be able to communicate information clearly and concisely.

Candidates should also be prepared to demonstrate their communication capabilities during the recruitment process because interviews may form part of the selection procedure.

Other Skills and Competencies Required

In addition to academic qualifications, the OSCE is looking for candidates demonstrating strong personal and professional capabilities.

Applicants should possess:

High motivation;

Open-mindedness;

Flexibility;

Ability to work collaboratively;

Capacity to build effective professional relationships;

Ability to work with individuals from different national, cultural and religious backgrounds;

Impartiality;

Objectivity;

Awareness of gender considerations in professional work; and

Computer literacy.

Candidates should be familiar with standard Microsoft Office applications, particularly:

Microsoft Excel;

Microsoft PowerPoint;

Word-processing software; and

Email applications.

Additional Experience That Can Strengthen an Application

Certain qualifications are considered assets rather than mandatory requirements.

These include:

Relevant Work Experience

Previous professional, volunteer, research or internship experience connected with economics, environmental affairs, development, finance or international organizations can strengthen a candidate’s profile.

Multicultural or Multilateral Experience

Experience working in an international, multicultural or multilateral environment is advantageous.

Organizational Skills

Candidates who can manage multiple assignments simultaneously and maintain attention to deadlines may have a stronger profile.

Analytical and Research Skills

Research, analytical reasoning and the ability to translate information into well-structured written outputs are useful for many of the assignments associated with the internship.

Drafting Skills

Strong professional writing skills are valuable because interns may contribute to reports, briefings, concept notes, presentations and policy documents.

Additional OSCE-Region Language

Knowledge of another language spoken within the OSCE region is regarded as an advantage, although professional English remains the central language requirement identified in the vacancy.

Internship Locations: Vienna and Prague

The primary duty location listed for this internship is the OSCE Secretariat in Vienna, Austria.

The vacancy also identifies Prague, Czechia, as an additional potential location.

The actual placement of a successful applicant will depend on the hiring office and organizational requirements.

Is the OSCE Internship Paid?

Applicants should understand the funding conditions carefully.

The OSCE states that its internships do not provide a salary or remuneration, and the organization does not reimburse an intern’s travel expenses associated with relocation to or from the duty station.

However, the receiving OSCE office is expected to contribute toward the cost of living for eligible international and national interns who are non-residents of the duty station.

If a receiving office is unable to provide such a cost-of-living contribution, it may instead accept interns who are already residents of the duty station.

Applicants should therefore not describe this programme as a salaried internship and should consider accommodation, travel and personal financial requirements carefully before accepting an offer.

Insurance Arrangements

Selected interns must have health insurance that is valid at their assigned duty station.

If an intern does not already possess appropriate health coverage, the individual may participate in the relevant group health-insurance scheme at their own expense.

The OSCE, however, provides life and disability insurance for interns under the conditions described in the vacancy.

Visa Support

Some selected candidates may require a D visa or another appropriate authorization to undertake the internship at the OSCE Secretariat.

Where such documentation is required, the OSCE indicates that it can support the selected intern by providing an appropriate support letter.

Candidates remain responsible for ensuring they comply with applicable immigration and entry requirements.

Does the Internship Lead to Employment?

No guarantee of future employment is attached to the internship.

The OSCE explicitly states that participation in an internship lasting two to six months does not constitute a commitment to future employment with the organization.

Candidates should therefore view the programme primarily as a professional-learning and practical-experience opportunity.

How to Apply for the OSCE Economic and Environmental Dimension Internship

Candidates who meet the eligibility requirements must submit their application through the official OSCE online recruitment system.

Applicants should carefully complete all information requested through the application platform.

Importantly, the vacancy specifically asks candidates to mention their availability dates in their cover letter.

An effective application should therefore clearly indicate:

The applicant’s earliest available starting date;

The period during which they can undertake the internship;

Their academic background;

Their interest in the Economic and Environmental Dimension;

Relevant research, analytical, policy, environmental, economic or project experience;

Relevant language and technical skills; and

How the internship fits their academic or early-career objectives.

Applications should be submitted through the official OSCE vacancy page before the deadline.

Selection Process

Submission of an application does not guarantee an interview.

The OSCE states that only candidates selected to proceed to subsequent stages of the recruitment process will be contacted.

Applicants should therefore make sure their application clearly demonstrates how they meet the essential criteria rather than relying on generic statements about their interest in international organizations.

Diversity and Inclusion at the OSCE

The OSCE states that it is committed to building a diverse and inclusive workforce.

Qualified women and men from different:

Religious backgrounds;

Ethnic backgrounds; and

Social backgrounds

are encouraged to apply, provided they satisfy the nationality and other eligibility criteria.

Successful candidates are also expected to maintain the standards required of international civil servants, including professionalism, integrity, independence, impartiality and appropriate ethical conduct.

Important Warning About Application Fees

Applicants should be alert to recruitment scams.

The OSCE explicitly states that it does not request payment at any stage of the application or review process.

Any request demanding money in exchange for submitting, reviewing or progressing an OSCE internship application should therefore be treated with caution.

Application Deadline

The official closing date for the OSCE Internship – Economic and Environmental Dimension is:

December 31, 2026

The vacancy was originally issued on July 3, 2026 and lists multiple available internship posts.

Why This OSCE Internship Is Worth Considering

For young professionals seeking careers in international development, environmental governance, economics, sustainability, multilateral organizations or international public policy, this internship provides exposure to the way economic and environmental questions are addressed within a comprehensive international-security framework.

The breadth of possible assignments is particularly valuable. An intern could potentially contribute to policy research on one project, assist with donor reporting on another, participate in an international meeting and support communications or administrative work.

This combination gives participants an opportunity to understand not only the subject matter of international organizations but also the institutional processes behind their work.

The programme may be especially useful for students and recent graduates interested in future careers with:

International organizations;

Government institutions;

Development agencies;

Environmental organizations;

Research institutions;

International NGOs;

Multilateral development organizations;

Public-policy organizations;

International financial institutions; or

Diplomatic and foreign-policy institutions.

Tips for Preparing a Competitive Application

Applicants should avoid submitting a generic cover letter that simply states an interest in the OSCE.

A stronger application should connect the candidate’s academic and practical experience directly to the vacancy.

Consider emphasizing:

Relevant university coursework;

Research projects;

Academic papers;

Sustainability or environmental projects;

Economic or financial analysis;

Project-management experience;

Policy-writing experience;

International-development exposure;

Volunteer experience;

Multicultural teamwork;

Data-analysis capabilities;

Knowledge of Excel and other Microsoft Office applications;

Strong drafting and research abilities; and

A clear understanding of the relationship between economic, environmental and security issues.

Candidates should also explicitly state their availability dates, as requested by the OSCE.

Conclusion

The OSCE Economic and Environmental Dimension Internship 2026 offers students and recent graduates an opportunity to gain practical professional experience within one of the world’s leading regional security organizations.

With placements potentially available in Vienna and Prague, successful candidates can gain exposure to economic governance, environmental security, sustainable development, anti-corruption, natural-resource management, research, programme implementation, communications and international institutional operations.

The programme is particularly relevant to candidates studying or recently graduated in economics, environmental science, development studies, international development, finance or related disciplines.

Internships last between two and six months, with multiple positions available. Although the programme is not salaried and travel expenses are not reimbursed, eligible non-resident interns may receive a contribution toward living costs from the receiving office under the conditions set by the OSCE.

Applicants must meet the academic, age, language and nationality requirements and should submit a carefully prepared application through the official OSCE recruitment system.

The application deadline is December 31, 2026.

TITLE: Max Weber Programme (MWP) at the European University Institute 2027-2028 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 16, 2026

Applications are open for the Max Weber Programme (MWP) at the European University Institute 2027-2028. The Max Weber Programme (MWP) at the European University Institute (EUI) is a unique postdoctoral programme in the historical, humanities and social sciences.

The Programme is highly selective, with an annual acceptance rate of <2%. A cohort consists typically of around 65 Fellows across the different academic units of the EUI (Economics, History, Law, Political and Social Sciences, the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies or the Florence School of Transnational Governance). Preference is given to applicants who have only just completed their doctorate and have not had a postdoctoral fellowship before. Selected Fellows will benefit from the stimulating combination of a global programme located in the heart of Europe offering a broad menu of multidisciplinary and disciplinary activities.

Benefits

The grant provided by the Fellowship is currently 2,500 EUR per month plus – when appropriate – family allowances. Further benefits include health insurance and mission and research funds. During the second year, qualifying fellows will have the possibility of applying for a Part-time assistant professor contract (level ASSPR6/3) for 12 months involving some teaching duties and mentoring Ph.D. researchers: net remuneration would be approximately 850 EUR in addition to the monthly grant.

Fellows are required to live in the area of Florence for the duration of their Fellowship so that they may play an active part in the programme and in the academic activities of their academic unit.

Eligibility

Candidates of any nationality are eligible for the Max Weber Fellowships.

Candidates must have received their Ph.D. within the past 5 years or have official approval to defend their thesis by the time of the start of the programme (1 September). This means to apply for 2027-28 candidates should have received or submitted their Ph.D. between 01/09/2022 and 01/09/2027 and the Ph.D. defence should take place no later than 31/12/2027.

Extensions to the five-year rule are allowed for applicants whose academic career has been interrupted for maternity or paternity leave, illness or mandatory military service. Cite circumstances in the application form in the field ‘Additional Notes’. Successful candidates will be asked to provide supporting documents.

Early-stage researchers who are at the EUI at the time of the application deadline are not eligible for the Max Weber Fellowship. This refers to those enrolled in the EUI Doctoral Programme, or employed by or on a fellowship hosted by the EUI. Those who have formerly been at the EUI can apply for a Fellowship after having been continuously away from the EUI in a full-time occupation or fellowship for at least one year by the application deadline.

The expected level of English proficiency is level C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR). An English certificate is not requested as part of the application, but successful candidates will be requested to provide a certificate/supporting document on registration. This can be one of the international certificates listed below, or a document showing that the candidate has written the doctorate, or published an article or a book chapter of at least 6,000 words, in English, or has pursued post-graduate studies in an English language degree programme. Native English speakers are exempt from proof.

Application

Requested Documents include:

CV with a list of publications in PDF.

‘Academic career statement’ (1 page) as a PDF. The purpose of this statement is for you to indicate why you think the MW Programme, particularly the Academic Practice Activities, will benefit you. It should indicate your research and teaching interests and experience, and career plans.

‘Research proposal’ (2 pages) as a PDF. The proposal must be clear and well structured, with well-defined and realistic goals that can be achieved within the duration of the fellowship. If you are applying for a 24-month Fellowship, you should indicate in the research proposal what you aim to achieve 1) in the first 12 months and 2) what you hope to do in months 13-24. Also include a reflection on how gender and diversity are relevant to your proposed research during your Max Weber Fellowship. In the context of the social sciences and humanities, this may involve examining how categories such as gender, racial or ethnic background, class, sexuality, age, religion, disability, or other dimensions of identity and inequality shape your research topic, questions, theoretical framework, methodology, sources, or expected findings. If such aspects are not central to your project, you are encouraged to briefly explain why or reflect on how they might relate to the broader context or implications of your work.

A copy of your passport (JPEG).

Use standard international fonts, do not use macros, special characters, password-protection.

The Academic career statement and Research proposal should also meet the requirements established by the EUI Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence for Research. In particular, candidates should refrain from having Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) autonomously write substantial or integral parts of the documents. When using AI to produce novel content, they must acknowledge and reference the parts of the content that have been AI-generated.

Letters of Reference:

Applicants should provide the names of a minimum of two and a maximum of three academic referees and ensure that at least two letters of reference are submitted online directly by the referees by the deadline 16 October 2026 (14:00 CEST). References will not be accepted after the deadline.

References from current full-time or part-time EUI professors will not be accepted.
