TITLE: Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The interface between particle theory and early-universe cosmology has been a lively area of research since the 1970’s, when physicists realized that hot big bang cosmology would imply that fundamental properties of our universe — from the abundance of chemical elements to maybe also the density of baryons — were determined by high-energy physics processes in the nascent universe. In the present day, our understanding of the universe seems to require “dark energy” and “dark matter” components, which do not have any simple explanation in the Standard Model of particle physics.

Inflationary cosmology, pioneered by Alan Guth in 1980-81, proposed that early-universe particle physics could be responsible for the production of essentially all the matter in the universe, explaining the uniformity of the universe and predicting its average mass density. It was soon discovered that quantum fluctuations during inflation might be responsible for the ripples in the mass density of the early universe—ripples that formed the seeds for structure formation, and which are now visible in the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The inflationary prediction of the mass density has now been confirmed to an accuracy of about half a percent, and the patterns of ripples seen in the CMB agree very well with the predictions of simple inflationary models.

At the same time, the CMB and other probes have allowed us to measure the amount of dark matter in the universe to percent-level precision. Physicists have established that dark matter must have mass and exert gravity, but it must also be relatively slow-moving, and its interactions (other than gravity) with known particles must be weak or absent. This leaves open a huge range of possibilities for dark matter, from new particles tens of orders of magnitude lighter than even neutrinos, through to primordial black holes formed in the first instants of the universe’s existence.

Mikhail Ivanov uses cosmological large-scale structure to understand dark matter, dark energy, and inflation. The new generation of galaxy surveys will allow for precision tests of these sectors through their imprints on the observed matter distribution. An accurate theoretical understanding of these imprints will be key to harvesting new cosmological information from large-scale structure in this novel regime of high precision.

The cosmology and particle astrophysics program in the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) focuses on implications for fundamental physics and applications of field-theoretic techniques, complementing the work of our colleagues in the Laboratory for Nuclear Science and the MIT Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research.

Research on inflation

David Kaiser and Alan Guth are continuing to pursue the connection between particle theory and early-universe cosmology. Much of the work of Kaiser and his group has centered around understanding the dynamics and the predictions of inflationary models that include realistic features from high-energy physics: multiple interacting fields, each with nonminimal gravitational couplings. His group has also developed novel techniques to study the dynamics of inflationary models before and after inflation, including conditions under which the universe may enter an inflationary phase even amid significant inhomogeneities, and the mechanisms by which inflation ends during the “reheating” epoch, when the universe becomes filled with ordinary matter in thermal equilibrium at a high temperature. Alan Guth and collaborators have recently worked on models of inflation at a very low energy scale, and on the cosmology of axions. Guth’s recent research has also included the study of eternal inflation, with the issues it raises concerning the definition of probabilities. Guth and Kaiser are both working with a group of postdocs, graduate students, and undergraduates to study the possibility of the production of primordial black holes in the context of a particular type of inflation, called hybrid inflation.

Simulation of the onset of inflation. Citation: J. K. Bloomfield, P. Fitzpatrick, K. Hilbert, and D. I. Kaiser, Phys. Rev. D 100, 063512 (2019).

Testing the foundations of quantum mechanics

In a separate line of investigation, David Kaiser and Alan Guth have both been part of the international “Cosmic Bell” collaboration, which has tested the foundations of quantum mechanics by conducting experimental tests of Bell’s inequality using real-time astronomical observations of high-redshift quasars to determine which measurements to perform on entangled particles. Kaiser has also worked with Joseph Formaggio in the Laboratory for Nuclear Science to use data on neutrino oscillations to test the Leggett-Garg inequality across unprecedented length-scales.

Telescopes at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory on La Palma, Canary Islands, used for the “Cosmic Bell” test of Bell’s inequality. Credit: Calvin Leung

Astrophysical and cosmological dark matter signals

In Search of Dark Matter at the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)
Video by Bill Lattanzi | CTP-LI
Annihilations or decays of dark matter could modify the thermal and ionization history of the universe, with possible observational consequences for nucleosynthesis, the cosmic microwave background and the redshifted 21cm line. In the present era, the same phenomena could provide striking signals from regions of high dark matter density. Tracy Slatyer’s group works extensively on the interpretation of such signals, developing new constraints and identifying possible signatures of dark matter physics, from radio to gamma-ray wavelengths, with a particular focus on data from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope and signals from the early universe.

TITLE: Strengthening Educational Technology Skills in African Universities

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
AAU and Partners Pilot Training Universities on the use of the Moodle Learning Management System

The huge impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on face-to-face education has accentuated the need for African Universities to build the capacities of their faculty on the effective use of educational technologies to facilitate learning.

The Association of African Universities (AAU) has identified, that though some Universities in Africa have installed the Moodle Learning Management System (LMS), their academic faculty have limited or no skills to use it. These Universities also have limited technical expertise to administer and manage their Moodle platforms.

In response, the AAU and its partners are piloting a virtual capacity building of the Moodle LMS for 170 academic staff of Lupane State University based in Zimbabwe. The open content being used for the Virtual Moodle Training for all academic staff at Lupane State University was developed as part of the EdTech-UEM project for academic staff capacity building. The content was developed by Eduardo Mondlane University and the Centre for Innovation in Learning and Teaching (CILT) at the University of Cape Town (UCT) – and funded by Sida. e/merge Africa, which is funded by the Carnegie Corporation is a partner in the adaptation of the EdTech-UEM workshop resources.

The Think Modular – Digital Solutions GmbH (Austria), are also be offering their Big Blue Button video conferencing system for this training. This platform is open source and can be integrated to Moodle.

In addition, over 93 Moodle Experts signed up to assist with delivering the virtual capacity building sessions. The volunteering Moodle Experts are from Egypt, Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Macedonia, Eswatini, South Africa, Austria, Pakistan, India, UK and Australia and they will be helping the AAU pilot this training.

The training, which runs from 26th May to 24th July 2020 is targeted at building the proficiencies of the participating academics in using Moodle. Each week of the training will have a lead facilitator, 4 support facilitators and 4 mentors.

Why this pilot is important?

This will help us to understand how to deploy future virtual trainings in Africa that are scalable. The AAU plans to train thousands of academic faculty in Africa to effectively use the educational technologies. To do this in an effective and quality assured manner, it is important to undergo this pilot phase, working with the academics of one institution. The institution was selected based on an earlier request for AAU to conduct this type of training for them.

Next Steps

If an African Higher Education institution is interested in having its academic faculty trained, they should contact the AAU via the Secretary General (secgen@aau.org) and copy Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini, Director -ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management (ndhlamini@aau.org).

TITLE: Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate Democracy at the University of Helsinki, Finland – €3,700–€4,000 Monthly Salary

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Helsinki in Finland is inviting applications for a fixed-term Postdoctoral Researcher position focusing on climate democracy and community-based democratic responses to climate turbulence.

The position offers an opportunity for an early-career researcher to contribute to an interdisciplinary research project examining how communities and democratic institutions can respond to the climate crisis.

The successful candidate will work across environmental sciences and social sciences and will contribute to research involving areas such as deliberative assemblies, food and energy systems, disaster and climate adaptation responses, ecological urban design, environmental justice, and democratic innovations.

The position is connected to the Finnish Research Council Profi9-supported Climate Democracy project, led by Professor David Schlosberg, and is expected to begin in January 2027.

The appointment is initially for three years, with a possibility of extension depending on continued project funding and the continuation of the research programme.

Postdoctoral Researcher in Climate Democracy at University of Helsinki

The University of Helsinki is seeking a collaborative and proactive researcher to join its interdisciplinary Climate Democracy project.

The research position is based within either:

The Department of Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences; or

The Discipline of Social and Public Policy, Faculty of Social Sciences.

The project brings together environmental and social science perspectives to investigate democratic responses to climate turbulence and the ways communities can participate in developing responses to climate-related challenges.

The successful applicant will have the opportunity to conduct both independent and collaborative research while working with researchers, community organizations, project partners and international research networks.

About the Climate Democracy Project

The position is linked to a project supported by the Finnish Research Council Profi9 programme.

The Climate Democracy project is led by Professor David Schlosberg, whose research background includes environmental politics, environmental justice and democracy.

The project explores democratic and community-based responses to the climate crisis.

Rather than focusing only on the scientific or technological dimensions of climate change, the project examines how democratic processes, communities and institutions can contribute to responding to climate-related challenges.

The research may cover several interconnected areas, including:

Deliberative assemblies

Community-based democratic innovations

Food systems

Energy systems

Disaster response

Climate adaptation

Ecological urban design

Environmental justice

Political responses to climate change

Public participation

Community-based experiments

Democratic approaches to climate turbulence

This interdisciplinary focus means that candidates from different academic backgrounds may be considered, provided their research experience is relevant to the broader field of climate democracy.

Faculties: Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Faculty of Social Sciences

TITLE: In Memoriam – Mildred Dresselhaus

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mildred “Millie” Dresselhaus

November 11, 1930 – February 20, 2017

Name: Mildred “Millie” Dresselhaus
Title: Former Institute Professor
Former Professor of Physics, Emerita
Former Professor of Electrical Engineering, Emerita

Research Areas

Condensed Matter Experiment

Biographical Sketch

Storied Women of MIT: Mildred ‘The Queen of Carbon Science’ Dresselhaus
Courtesy of TeachingExcellence MIT | YouTube
Professor Mildred Dresselhaus, “The Queen of Carbon”, is a native of the Bronx, New York City, where she attended the New York City public schools through junior high school, completing her high school education at Hunter College High School in New York City. She began her higher education at Hunter College in New York City and received a Fulbright Fellowship to attend the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge University (1951-52). Professor Dresselhaus received her master’s degree at Radcliffe College (1953) and her Ph.D. at the University of Chicago (1958).

Professor Dresselhaus began her MIT career at the Lincoln Laboratory. During that time she switched from research on superconductivity to magneto-optics, and carried out a series of experiments which led to a fundamental understanding of the electronic structure of semi-metals, especially graphite.

A leader in promoting opportunities for women in science and engineering, Professor Dresselhaus received a Carnegie Foundation grant in 1973 to encourage women’s study of traditionally male dominated fields, such as physics. In 1973, she was appointed to The Abby Rockefeller Mauze chair, an Institute-wide chair, endowed in support of the scholarship of women in science and engineering.

Professor Dresselhaus has greatly enjoyed her career in science. On her experience working with MIT students, she says, “I like to be challenged. I welcome the hard questions and having to come up with good explanations on the spot. That’s an experience I really enjoy.” Thus far, she has graduated over 60 Ph.D. students.

This biographical text was adapted from Harvard Magazine’s January-February 1980 feature article on Professor Mildred S. Dresselhaus.

TITLE: SCOSS Launches Second Funding Cycle

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Global Sustainability Coalition for Open Science Services (SCOSS) has launched its second funding cycle with three vetted “vital open infrastructure” services being presented to the international scholarly community for funding:

The Directory of Open Access Books (DOAB), a digital directory of peer reviewed Open Access books and Open Access book publishers; and Open Access Publishing in European Networks (OAPEN), a growing repository of freely accessible academic books; and

The Public Knowledge Project (PKP), a university initiative that creates open source software and services, including Open Journal Systems (OJS), which is used to publish more than 9,000 OA journals worldwide.

OpenCitations, a scholarly infrastructure service that provides open bibliographic and citation data;

With the launch, SCOSS is appealing to academic institutions and their libraries, research institutes, funding organisations, national and regional governments, international organisations, learned societies and service providers—everyone who is invested in Open Access and Open Science—to consider helping support one or more of these services through a three-year commitment.

SCOSS was formed in early 2017 with the purpose of providing a new coordinated cost-sharing framework for enabling the broader OA and OS community to support the non-commercial services on which it depends. In its pilot funding cycle, more than 1.5 million euros have been pledged by more than 200 institutions worldwide to help secure the Directory of Open Access Journals and SHERPA Ro/MEO.

For more details about the services, and the specifics of the suggested funding levels, visit www.scoss.org.

TITLE: Quantum Gravity and Field Theory

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Calabi-Yau string geometry landscape.
Credit: W. Taylor
Quantum physics and Einstein’s theory of general relativity are the two solid pillars that underlie much of modern physics. Understanding how these two well-established theories are related remains a central open question in theoretical physics. Over the last several decades, efforts in this direction have led to a broad range of new physical ideas and mathematical tools. In recent years, string theory and quantum field theory have converged in the context of holography, which connects quantum gravity in certain space-times with corresponding (conformal) field theories on a lower-dimensional space-time. These developments and connections have deepened our understanding not only of quantum gravity, cosmology, and particle physics, but also of intermediate scale physics, such as condensed matter systems, the quark-gluon plasma, and disordered systems. String theory has also led to new insights to problems in many areas of mathematics.

Holographic entanglement wedge.
Credit: N. Engelhardt, D. Harlow
The interface of quantum physics and gravity is currently leading to exciting new areas of progress, and is expected to remain vibrant in the coming decade. Researchers in the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) have been at the forefront of many of the developments in these directions. CTP-LI faculty members work on string theory foundations, the range of solutions of the theory, general relativity and quantum cosmology, problems relating quantum physics to black holes, and the application of holographic methods to strongly coupled field theories. The group in the CTP-LI has close connections to condensed matter physicists, astrophysicists, and mathematicians both at MIT and elsewhere.

Strange metals and AdS_2.
Credit: N.Iqbal
In recent years a set of new developments has begun to draw unexpected connections between a number of problems relating aspects of gravity, black holes, quantum information, and condensed matter systems. It is becoming clear that quantum entanglement, quantum error correction, and computational complexity play a fundamental role in the emergence of spacetime geometry through holographic duality. Moreover these tools have led to substantial progress on the famous black hole information problem, giving new avenues for searching for a resolution of the tension between the physics of black holes and quantum mechanics. CTP-LI faculty members Netta Engelhardt and Daniel Harlow have been at the vanguard of these developments, which also tie into the research activity of several other CTP-LI faculty members, including Aram Harrow, whose primary research focus is on quantum many-body dynamics.

Minimal area metric on punctured torus.
Credit: B. Zwiebach
Holographic dualities give both a new perspective into quantum gravitational phenomena as encoded in quantum field theory, and a way to explore aspects of strongly coupled field theories using the gravitational dual. CTP-LI faculty have played a pioneering role in several applications of holographic duality. Hong Liu and Krishna Rajagopal are at the forefront of efforts that use holography to find new insights into the physics of the quark-gluon plasma. Liu was among the first to point out possible connections between black hole physics and the strange metal phase of high temperature superconductors, and in recent years has been combining insights from effective field theories, holography, and condensed matter physics to address various issues concerning far-from-equilibrium systems including superfluid turbulence, entanglement growth, quantum chaos, thermalization, and a complete formulation of fluctuating hydrodynamics. Gravitational effective field theories play a key role in the interpretation of gravitational wave observations. Mikhail Ivanov works at the intersection of these fields with the aim of testing strong field gravity at a new precision frontier.

False vacuum bubble.
Credit: A.Guth
Even though we understand string theory better than we did in decades past, there is still no clear fundamental description of the theory that works in all situations, and the set of four-dimensional solutions, or string vacua, is still poorly understood. The work of Washington Taylor and Barton Zwiebach combines physical understanding with modern mathematical methods to address these questions, and has led to new insights into how observed physics fits into the framework of string theory as well as the development of new mathematical results and ideas. Alan Guth‘s foundational work on inflationary cosmology has led him to focus on basic questions about the physics of the multiverse that arises naturally in the context of the many string theory vacua, and which provides the only current natural explanation for the observed small but positive cosmological constant.

Tensor network for the non-invertible duality symmetry in lattice gauge theory. Credit: P. Gorantla
Symmetry has long been a guiding principle in the study of quantum field theory and gravity. Shu-Heng Shao’s research focuses on generalizations of global symmetries in field theory and lattice systems. These new symmetries and their anomalies lead to various new dynamical constraints on (de)confinement, scattering amplitudes, renormalization group flows, and more. They also unify different conjectures in quantum gravity and holography. The microscopic lattice realizations of these new symmetries are naturally expressed through tensor networks, indicating an intriguing link to quantum information theory.

TITLE: Strengthening Research Excellence and Ethics – SGCI Research Management Workshop Empowers African Institutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Livingstone, Zambia, 14 – 17, August, 2023 – In an effort to fortify research excellence, promote ethical practices, and enhance grant management capabilities, a four-day Training of Trainers (ToT) workshop is currently underway in Livingstone, Zambia. The workshop, organized under the Research Management Project of the Science Granting Councils Initiative (SGCI), has convened stakeholders from 14 out of the 17 participating countries of the initiative. It aims to equip participants with the essential skills and knowledge in research excellence, ethics, and grant practices, fostering a robust research ecosystem in sub-Saharan Africa. The initiative is a culmination of the SGCI Research Management Project’s success, designed to further amplify its impact and sustain positive changes.

Organised by the Association of African Universities (AAU) and the African Academy of Science (AAS) and graciously hosted by the National Science and Technology Council (NSTC) of Zambia, the workshop’s comprehensive agenda encompasses three key themes – Research Ethics, Research Excellence (RQ+ for Researchers) and the Good Financial Grant Practices (GFGP). The sessions on Research Excellence (RQ+ for Researchers) are geared towards equipping participants to facilitate the RQ+ for Researchers course, which focuses on preparing researchers to adhere to the RQ+ guidelines in crafting robust research proposals and grant applications. The lead facilitator for this theme – Dr. Isabel Tarling, the managing director of Limina, is also practically engaging participants and broadening their knowledge and understanding of the Research Quality Plus (RQ+) framework, an innovative tool designed to enhance research quality and evaluation.

Under the research ethics theme, participating Science Granting Councils (SGCs) will be empowered to effectively implement the research ethics frameworks, address barriers and strengthen enablers, while gaining insights into monitoring and evaluating research ethics practices. This theme will be facilitated by Dr. Rakeshnie Ramoutar-Prieschl.

Given the importance of financial governance and management of grant funding to the SGCs, the workshop will also provide insights into the Good Financial Grant Practice (GFGP) Standard. SGCs will engage in discussions surrounding financial management, human resources, procurement, and governance, with an aim to improve their grants management practices. The GFGP sessions are facilitated by the African Academy of Sciences.

TITLE: Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship 2027: Fully Funded PhD Scholarship in Canada for International and Canadian Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship 2027 is now accepting applications from exceptional doctoral students whose research falls broadly within the humanities and social sciences and addresses important issues relevant to Canada and the wider world.

The prestigious doctoral scholarship provides substantial financial support, research and travel funding, mentorship, experiential learning opportunities, and access to a multidisciplinary community of Scholars, Fellows, Mentors, and alumni.

For the 2027 competition, applicants must first complete an eligibility verification process before they can access the full scholarship application. The deadline to request eligibility confirmation is October 2, 2026, while the final application deadline is November 6, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. ET.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation PhD Scholarship 2027

Category: Scholarship

Study level: PhD/Doctoral

Fields: Humanities and Social Sciences

Study location: Canada, with specific eligibility provisions for Canadian students studying abroad

Scholarship duration: Three years

Annual stipend: Up to $50,000

Research, networking and travel allowance: Up to $20,000 per year

Eligibility verification deadline: October 2, 2026

Reference deadline: October 30, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. ET

Complete application deadline: November 6, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. ET

Application process: Two steps

Official organization: Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation

About the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship

The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation PhD Scholarship is designed to support outstanding doctoral researchers whose work can contribute to important conversations and challenges affecting Canada and society.

The Foundation is not simply looking for students with excellent grades. Its selection approach considers the broader potential of applicants, including their intellectual curiosity, leadership potential, engagement with society, ability to communicate knowledge, and capacity to create meaningful impact beyond academia.

Successful Scholars become part of a multidisciplinary community where academic research is connected with public dialogue, mentorship, experiential learning, networking, and societal engagement.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant for doctoral students who want their research to have an influence beyond academic publications and contribute to wider discussions about major social, environmental, political, cultural, and human challenges.

Scholarship Benefits

One of the major attractions of the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship is its combination of financial support and professional development.

1. Annual stipend of up to $50,000

Selected Scholars can receive up to $50,000 per year for three years to support tuition and living expenses associated with their doctoral studies.

Over the three-year scholarship period, this represents potential stipend support of up to $150,000.

The funding is intended to give doctoral researchers greater financial stability while they concentrate on their studies and research.

2. Research, networking and travel allowance

Scholars can also receive up to $20,000 per year for three years to support activities connected to their doctoral work.

This allowance can help support:

Research-related activities

Academic and professional travel

Networking

Participation in relevant events

Activities connected with Foundation programming

Other research-related opportunities

This additional funding can be particularly valuable for researchers whose projects require fieldwork, conferences, collaboration, or engagement beyond their home institution.

3. Mentorship and experiential learning

The scholarship goes beyond financial assistance by providing Scholars with opportunities to engage with Mentors and Fellows.

The Foundation’s programming can include:

Meetings

Masterclasses

Seminars

Conferences

Leadership development

Experiential learning

Interdisciplinary exchanges

Public policy discussions

These opportunities are designed to broaden Scholars’ perspectives and help them connect their academic research with practical societal challenges.

4. Multidisciplinary community

Successful applicants become part of a community involving Scholars, Fellows and Mentors working across different disciplines and sectors.

This community can provide opportunities to:

Exchange ideas across academic disciplines

Develop professional relationships

Learn from experienced researchers and leaders

Share research with broader audiences

Explore interdisciplinary approaches

Participate in conversations about major societal issues

5. Alumni network

Scholars also become part of the Foundation’s alumni network, which includes more than 500 alumni.

This creates a long-term professional and intellectual network that can continue beyond the three-year scholarship period.

Fields of Study and Research Themes

Applicants must be pursuing doctoral research broadly related to the humanities or social sciences.

However, being in one of these broad academic fields is not enough. The proposed PhD research must also address issues relevant to Canada’s future and align with at least one of the Foundation’s four foundational themes.

The four themes are:

1. Human Rights and Dignity

This theme focuses on issues surrounding human rights, dignity, equality, justice, inclusion, and the conditions necessary for individuals and communities to live with dignity.

Potential research areas may include questions related to:

Human rights

Social justice

Equality

Inclusion

Discrimination

Rights and freedoms

Vulnerable populations

Human dignity

2. Responsible Citizenship

This theme concerns citizenship, participation, democratic life, civic engagement, and the responsibilities individuals and institutions have within society.

Research connected to this theme may explore:

Democracy

Civic participation

Citizenship

Governance

Political engagement

Social responsibility

Community participation

Public institutions

3. Canada and the World

This theme examines Canada’s relationship with the international community and Canada’s role in global affairs.

Relevant research could address:

International relations

Globalization

Diplomacy

Migration

International development

Global governance

Canada’s international role

Cross-border social and political issues

4. People and Their Natural Environment

This theme explores relationships between people, society and the natural environment.

Potential research areas may include:

Environmental policy

Climate change

Sustainability

Environmental justice

Human-environment relationships

Natural resource governance

Ecological challenges

Sustainable development

Applicants should therefore ensure that their research proposal clearly demonstrates how their doctoral project connects with at least one of these four themes.

Who Can Apply for the 2027 Scholarship?

The Foundation has established specific citizenship and enrollment requirements.

Eligible applicants must fall into one of three categories:

Canadian students enrolled at a Canadian university

Canadian students enrolled at a university outside Canada

International students enrolled at a Canadian university

This means international students can apply, but they must be enrolled in a doctoral program at a Canadian university.

Importantly, international students who are residing outside Canada and enrolled at a university outside Canada are not eligible for this particular scholarship.

Therefore, applicants should carefully distinguish between citizenship and university enrollment when determining eligibility.

PhD Stage Requirements

The 2027 scholarship is specifically targeted at early-stage doctoral researchers.

At the time of application, candidates must be either:

In the first year of their PhD program, or

In the second year of their PhD program.

Applicants who are beyond the second year of their doctoral program should therefore carefully assess whether they meet the Foundation’s requirements before beginning the application.

There is no age limit for applying to the scholarship.

What Does the Foundation Look For?

Academic excellence is important, but the Foundation evaluates applicants more broadly.

The strongest candidates are expected to demonstrate several qualities.

Academic Excellence

Applicants should have an outstanding academic record and demonstrate strong intellectual ability.

Academic performance is assessed across the application, including:

Academic transcripts

Research proposal

Letters of recommendation

Overall application quality

The Foundation states that successful applicants stand out through the quality of their research and their academic excellence.

Intellectual Curiosity

The Foundation seeks doctoral researchers who demonstrate genuine curiosity and an ambition to explore important questions.

Your application should therefore demonstrate not only what you are researching, but also:

Why the question matters

What makes the research intellectually significant

What knowledge gap you are addressing

What new perspectives your work could contribute

Leadership Potential

Applicants should demonstrate potential to contribute positively beyond their immediate academic environment.

Leadership does not necessarily have to mean holding a formal leadership position. It can be demonstrated through:

Community initiatives

Research collaborations

Advocacy

Professional activities

Student leadership

Public engagement

Projects that have produced meaningful results

Commitment to Society

The Foundation places considerable emphasis on applicants who are interested in connecting research with society.

Strong applications should show how the applicant’s work could contribute to broader conversations or help address significant societal challenges.

Potential for Impact Beyond Academia

Applicants should think carefully about how their research can reach audiences outside universities.

This could involve:

Public policy

Communities

Civil society

Government

Professional organizations

Practitioners

Public education

Knowledge translation

The Foundation specifically emphasizes the importance of sharing knowledge and creating meaningful impact beyond academia.

Collaboration and Knowledge Sharing

The Foundation also values applicants who are willing to engage in dialogue, interdisciplinary collaboration, and knowledge exchange.

A strong candidate should therefore be able to demonstrate an openness to learning from people working in other disciplines and sectors.

Letters of Reference

Applicants must provide three letters of reference.

The three referees must include:

One PhD supervisor

One additional academic referee

One referee from outside academia

The inclusion of a non-academic referee is particularly important because the Foundation is interested in applicants’ broader engagement and potential impact beyond academia.

Applicants should therefore select referees strategically rather than simply choosing individuals based on academic seniority.

A good referee should ideally be able to provide specific evidence of your:

Academic ability

Research potential

Leadership

Community or professional engagement

Communication skills

Commitment to societal impact

Potential for future contribution

How the 2027 Application Process Works

The 2027 competition introduces a two-step application process.

Step 1: Eligibility Verification

Applicants must first complete a short eligibility verification form.

This initial step allows the Foundation to confirm whether an applicant meets the scholarship’s eligibility requirements.

The eligibility verification request must be submitted by:

October 2, 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final day if they can avoid it. Reviewing the eligibility requirements in advance can help identify potential problems before submission.

Step 2: Full Scholarship Application

Only applicants whose eligibility has been confirmed will receive access to the full application form.

This means applicants cannot simply skip the eligibility verification stage and proceed directly to the full application.

The Foundation states that applications that do not meet the eligibility criteria will not be reviewed.

Important 2027 Scholarship Deadlines

Applicants should keep track of all dates rather than focusing only on the final application deadline.

September 1, 2026

The 2027 application process opens, including the eligibility verification form.

October 2, 2026

Deadline to submit an eligibility confirmation request.

This is the first major deadline and should not be confused with the final application deadline.

Weeks of October 5 and October 12, 2026

Mandatory information sessions.

Eligible applicants should pay attention to instructions from the Foundation regarding participation in these sessions. October 30, 2026 — 9:00 a.m. ET

Deadline for all three reference letters to be received.

Applicants should contact referees well in advance because the letters must be received by the deadline.

November 6, 2026 — 4:00 p.m. ET

Final deadline for submitting the complete scholarship application.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Because the scholarship is highly selective, applicants should approach the application strategically.

1. Confirm Your Eligibility Early

Before investing significant time in the application, check:

Your citizenship status

Your university’s location

Your current PhD year

Your field of study

Your research topic

Your alignment with the four Foundation themes

This is especially important for international applicants because international students must be enrolled at a Canadian university.

2. Develop a Clear Research Narrative

Your research proposal should make it easy for reviewers to understand:

The problem you are investigating

Why the problem matters

The research gap

Your research questions

Your approach

The expected contribution

The relevance of your work to Canada and society

How your research connects to the Foundation’s themes

Avoid presenting your project as merely an academic exercise. Explain why the research matters in the real world.

3. Clearly Connect Your Research to a Foundation Theme

Do not assume reviewers will automatically see the connection.

Explicitly explain how your research relates to one or more of:

Human Rights and Dignity

Responsible Citizenship

Canada and the World

People and their Natural Environment

A well-developed thematic connection can help demonstrate that your project fits the Foundation’s objectives.

4. Demonstrate Impact

Think beyond publications and academic conferences.

Explain how your research could potentially influence:

Public policy

Communities

Institutions

Professional practice

Public understanding

Social debates

Government decision-making

5. Choose Your Referees Carefully

Because three references are required and one must come from outside academia, applicants should begin approaching potential referees early.

Give referees sufficient information about:

Your research

The scholarship

Your achievements

Your goals

The Foundation’s themes

Why you believe you are a strong candidate

This makes it easier for referees to write detailed and relevant recommendations.

6. Demonstrate Engagement Beyond Academia

If you have participated in community projects, professional initiatives, policy discussions, advocacy, public communication, volunteering, or other activities related to your research, explain their relevance.

The Foundation is interested in researchers who can connect knowledge with society.

Why This Scholarship Is Different from a Conventional PhD Scholarship

Many doctoral scholarships primarily focus on financial support. The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship combines financial assistance with an extensive intellectual and professional development component.

The Foundation describes its scholarship as more than financial support, emphasizing mentorship, experiential learning, community engagement and knowledge sharing.

A Scholar therefore gains access to:

Substantial doctoral funding

Research and travel support

Mentorship

Leadership opportunities

Interdisciplinary discussions

Experiential learning

Professional networking

A multidisciplinary community

A long-term alumni network

For doctoral students interested in connecting academic research with real-world challenges, this broader model can be particularly valuable.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can international students apply?

Yes. International students are eligible if they are enrolled in a doctoral program at a Canadian university.

International students residing outside Canada and enrolled at universities outside Canada are not eligible.

Can Canadian students studying outside Canada apply?

Yes. Canadian students enrolled at universities outside Canada can apply, provided they meet the other eligibility requirements.

Can students in their third year of a PhD apply?

No. For the 2027 competition, applicants must be in their first or second year of doctoral studies at the time of application.

Is there an age limit?

No. The Foundation states that there is no age limit for applicants.

Do applicants have to speak both English and French?

No. Applicants do not need to be fluent in both official languages. However, they must be able to communicate effectively in either English or French.

How much is the scholarship worth?

The scholarship provides up to $50,000 per year for three years, plus up to $20,000 per year for research, networking and travel.

Is the scholarship renewable?

The scholarship is structured as a three-year program.

Can Scholars receive other scholarships?

Yes, but the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship may be adjusted depending on funding received from other organizations, universities or institutions. Scholars must declare additional sources of income each year.

The Foundation states that, regardless of other funding, Scholars continue to receive the annual research allowance, while the annual stipend has a minimum level of $25,000.

Application Link

Applicants should begin by reviewing the official eligibility requirements and then completing the eligibility verification process.

Applicants with questions about the 2027 scholarship can contact the Foundation at scholarship2027@trudeaufoundation.ca.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship 2027.

Conclusion

The Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation Scholarship 2027 is a major opportunity for early-stage doctoral researchers in the humanities and social sciences who want to combine academic excellence with leadership, public engagement and meaningful societal impact.

The scholarship offers up to $50,000 annually for three years, an additional $20,000 per year for research, networking and travel, mentorship, experiential learning, interdisciplinary engagement and access to a community of more than 500 alumni.

However, applicants should pay close attention to the eligibility requirements. The opportunity is open to Canadian students studying in Canada or abroad, as well as international students enrolled at Canadian universities. Applicants must also be in the first or second year of their PhD and their research must fall broadly within the humanities or social sciences while aligning with at least one of the Foundation’s four themes.

The first critical deadline is October 2, 2026, when applicants must submit their eligibility confirmation request. Those who pass the eligibility stage must then ensure their three references are received by October 30, 2026, and submit the complete application by November 6, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. ET.

For prospective Scholars, the key to a competitive application is not simply demonstrating strong academic performance. Applicants should present a compelling research project, clearly articulate its relevance to Canada and society, demonstrate leadership and engagement, and show how their work can create impact beyond academia.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Mark Mueller

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Mueller makes a lead gift to endow a fellowship in honor of his undergraduate thesis advisor, Professor of Physics Emeritus Arthur Kerman.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2011

Mark Mueller ’78
Mark Mueller ’78 studied theoretical physics as an undergraduate with Arthur Kerman in the 1970s. After a long hiatus and career in the financial services industry, Mark has reconnected with Arthur, MIT, and the Center for Theoretical Physics1. He shares his journey from physics to finance and back, and why it was important to make a gift in Arthur’s name.

“I knew I was a physicist at a young age. I loved trying to understand things around me and it dawned on me that they could be described by mathematics. I fell in love with MIT when I visited as a senior in high school. I remember attending a class on electrodynamics where [Professor of Physics Emeritus] Earle Lomon was the instructor; my office is now next to his in the Center for Theoretical Physics1. Even though Caltech had Feynman, I just felt MIT was where I belonged. During my junior year, I started working with Arthur and in my senior year I began doing research with him that led to my undergraduate thesis. Arthur has great taste in problems and I’m still really proud of the work I did with him.”

After MIT, Mark attended Stanford University (Ph.D. ’84, Physics) for graduate school, and went on to do postdocs at the Institute for Advanced Study, the University of Pennsylvania, and Harvard. He segued into finance after auditing some classes at the Harvard Business School. This was also the time when the Superconducting Super Collider was cancelled, and Mark started interviewing on Wall Street. He joined Morgan Stanley and became a quant2, then worked at Goldman Sachs and later at Grantham Mayo Van Otterloo and Co. (GMO) in Boston. Mark really liked the culture at GMO, and it was a rewarding experience, during which he spent 12 years and became a partner. While at GMO, Mark co-founded an algorithmic trading group that was involved in high-frequency trading. The new trading division was very successful in running strategies with high return-to-risk ratios. At this point, as Mark says, “I hit my number (everyone in finance has their number),” and he knew it was time to retire from finance and return to physics.

There is nothing that gives me more pleasure than working with students and it has been a joy to work with Mark again after all these years.

Professor of Physics Emeritus Arthur Kerman

Mark first reconnected as a donor to the Physics Department when he joined the Patrons of Physics Fellows Society. He enjoyed getting to know the student who was the recipient of his graduate fellowship and continues to cultivate that relationship to this day. “Graduate students are fearless; I know, I was one. They think they can solve these intense problems and attack them head-on, and it gives me great joy to bounce ideas back and forth with them.” Mark joined the Society because he’d heard that graduate fellowship support was the top priority for the Department. His involvement with the department deepened as he felt he was treated not just as a donor, but as a member of the physics community.

Even though Mark had retired from finance he still felt the pull of physics and wondered how he could find his way back in. He continued with his physics research interests and became a visiting scientist in MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics (CTP)1. At the CTP1, Mark was pleased to find that his former advisor Arthur Kerman was still involved in research, as well as scientific consulting. For Mark, it was a delight to come back and work with his greatest mentor in physics and return to the types of problems he was working on with Arthur so many years ago. Mark also expressed his appreciation of the CTP1, a community that he believes needs to be sustained. He has a great admiration for the faculty members in the Physics Department and feels they have a deep respect for the students that is clearly apparent. Mark says, “Faculty members are mentors, but they act like colleagues, and as a student you don’t feel marginalized or dismissed. The Department fosters creativity and innovation and is open to good ideas from the top level to the students; it’s a great example of what makes MIT a meritocracy. For me, this has been more evident at MIT than any other place. For that reason, I wanted to give back to MIT physics and create a permanent endowed fellowship in Arthur’s name.”

1. On May 28, 2025, the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics (CTP) was renamed the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP – LI).
2. A person working in financial markets, in roles such as a researcher, trader, or portfolio manager, who uses quantitative methods and models with the goals of making profits and managing risks. Quants come from areas such as engineering, computer science, operations research, mathematics, and physics, and apply their skills to quantitative problems in a wide variety of global financial markets. The now ubiquitous use of computers and electronic trading, as well as the use and abuse of complex derivative securities, has made quantitative literacy an indispensable part of modern finance. [M.M.]

TITLE: AAU Secretary General’s Message – 2020 Open Access Week Celebration

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: “Open with Purpose: Taking Action to Build Structural Equity and Inclusion”

Dear Colleagues in the research and Knowledge management fraternity and indeed the HEI community in Africa, I bring you greetings from the Secretariat of the Association of African Universities. Once again, the month of October is soon to be with us! And we are glad to remind ourselves of our desire to promote sharing of information and knowledge openly for the benefit of humanity. Existing and new threats on the planet makes the point ever clearer that if we act as islands of knowledge instead of steppingstones, we will all expire quickly.

Openness has propelled building of equitable systems of knowledge sharing. Over the past few years, the Open Access celebrations have focused on underscoring the urgent need for action on equity and inclusion, as well as the need to make our spaces and systems support the open sharing of knowledge. For instance, the 2018 celebration focused on “Designing Equitable Foundations for Open Knowledge” whiles that for 2019 was “Open for Whom? Equity in Open Knowledge”. Coming from a legacy that suffered discrimination, and exclusion- conditions that persist in various forms, it is important that these injustices are addressed by rebuilding research and scholarship to be open by default. The events of the year 2020 has presented a unique opportunity to re-construct our foundations to fundamentally make our systems and spaces more equitable within the academic community on the continent, to support our development together. The theme for the year “Open with Purpose: Taking Action to Build Structural Equity and Inclusion” therefore is more than apt. With the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, the continent was caught off balance and many of our academic institutions could not respond to changing their operations to digital forms immediately. While we are recovering from the shock, it is pertinent that we begin to build the culture of developing systems that will support open sharing of knowledge and experience among the HEI community. We must re-evaluate who these spaces and systems are designed for, who is missing out, who is excluded by the business models we adopt, and whose interests are prioritized as research institutions. As we work together to rebuild these structures, we need to commit to moving from conversations to concrete commitments and to hold one another accountable for making real progress.

I urge all our member institutions numbering over 400 and other HEIs and research institutions on the continent to re-evaluate their business models and /or systems and to take concrete steps to make their systems support open sharing of knowledge. As we celebrate Open Access Week from October 19th through the 25th, Let us prioritize integrating Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion into the fabric of the open community – from how our infrastructure is built, through to how we organize community discussions and to the governance structures we use.

During the weeklong celebrations I urge institutions to host discussions around this year’s theme and whenever is most suitable during the year and to take action to adapt the theme and activities to their local context. Let us use the opportunity to kickstart new conversations and form new connections across and between communities that will facilitate and advance progress towards building more equitable foundations.

I wish you all a fruitful planning sessions and successful open access week celebration!!

TITLE: Carnegie China Fellowship 2027: Apply for a $20,000 Fellowship to Conduct Policy-Oriented Research on China and U.S.-China Relations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Carnegie China Fellowship 2027 is now accepting applications from eligible American scholars, practitioners, journalists, lawyers, and other public intellectuals interested in developing original research on China’s rise, its global implications, and its relationship with the United States.

Organized through the University of Maryland School of Public Policy’s Center for International and Security Studies at Maryland (CISSM/CUSP context as presented in the fellowship guidelines), the one-year, non-residential fellowship is designed to connect rigorous research with public policy. Selected fellows receive a $20,000 stipend that can support activities such as teaching release, research-related travel, and research assistant compensation.

The fellowship provides an opportunity for researchers and professionals to investigate important questions concerning China while engaging with policymakers and the broader policy community in Washington and internationally. Fellows are expected to produce a policy-focused research paper and present their findings at the annual Carnegie China Conference at the University of Maryland.

Deadline: January 4, 2027

5

About the Carnegie China Fellowship

The Carnegie China Fellowship is a one-year, non-residential research fellowship intended to support rising American scholars and other qualified public intellectuals conducting research related to China.

The fellowship focuses on understanding:

China’s rise and development

The effects of China’s emergence on the wider world

China’s relationship with the United States

Issues of importance to public policy

Questions that can contribute to policymakers’ understanding of China and related global developments

Rather than limiting applicants to a single academic discipline, the program encourages proposals that approach China-related questions from different perspectives and that can communicate their findings beyond a narrowly specialized academic audience.

During the fellowship period, successful applicants are expected to undertake original, policy-oriented research and participate actively in the policy community. This can include engagement with policymakers in Washington and elsewhere.

The fellowship also requires fellows to produce a policy-focused research paper based on their work and present their findings at the annual Carnegie China Conference at the University of Maryland.

What the Carnegie China Fellowship Offers

One of the central components of the fellowship is a $20,000 stipend.

The stipend is intended to provide financial support that can help fellows dedicate time and resources to their proposed research project. According to the fellowship guidelines, the funding may be used for purposes such as:

Buying out teaching responsibilities

Research-related travel expenses

Research assistant compensation

Other activities directly connected to conducting the proposed research

Applicants should note that the fellowship does not provide all personal or research-related expenses. Fellows remain responsible for their own health insurance and for managing their own research-related travel logistics.

The fellowship also may not be deferred, meaning applicants should be prepared to undertake the fellowship during the designated period if selected.

Who Is Encouraged to Apply?

The Carnegie China Fellowship welcomes applications from a broad range of professionals whose work can contribute to a deeper understanding of China and its implications for international affairs and public policy.

The program specifically invites applications from:

Scholars

Practitioners

Journalists

Lawyers

Other public intellectuals

Applicants may come from different academic and professional backgrounds. The program specifically identifies areas such as:

Economics

Researchers working in economics may explore issues involving China’s economy, international economic relations, trade, development, financial systems, economic policy, or China’s role in the global economy.

Humanities

Applicants from the humanities may approach China-related questions through disciplines such as:

Area studies

Cultural studies

History

Related humanities fields

Historical and cultural research can qualify where the proposed project demonstrates meaningful relevance to public policy.

Law

Lawyers and legal scholars may propose projects examining China’s legal institutions, international law, regulatory developments, governance, or other legal questions connected to China and its relationship with the United States or wider world.

Social Sciences

The fellowship also welcomes researchers working in social sciences, including:

Anthropology

Political science

Sociology

Related social science disciplines

The program is not restricted to these fields, and applicants from other relevant areas may also apply.

The Fellowship Encourages Interdisciplinary Research

A notable feature of the Carnegie China Fellowship is its interest in projects that go beyond narrow disciplinary boundaries.

The program particularly welcomes research that:

Transcends narrow academic specialties

Moves beyond methodological debates that are primarily relevant within one discipline

Examines understudied issues

Connects academic research to broader public-policy questions

Can be communicated effectively to policymakers and non-specialist audiences

This means that applicants should think carefully about how their research can contribute to conversations outside their immediate academic field.

A strong proposal should make the significance of the research understandable to readers who may not have specialized knowledge of the applicant’s discipline.

Policy Relevance Is an Important Consideration

Applicants are expected to demonstrate the public-policy relevance of their proposed research.

Policy relevance does not mean that the project must be narrowly focused on current government policy. The guidelines specifically indicate that historical, sociological, and other forms of research can be relevant.

The important consideration is whether the project’s findings or lessons could help policymakers better understand an important topic.

Applicants should therefore explain clearly:

What question their research will investigate.

Why the question matters.

What is original about the proposed research.

How the research could contribute to understanding an issue of public importance.

Why the findings could be useful to policymakers or the broader policy community.

Applicants should also be prepared to interact with policymakers in Washington as part of the fellowship experience.

Eligibility Requirements

The Carnegie China Fellowship has specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants must:

Be U.S. citizens.

Have received a PhD or JD from an accredited university.

Hold the qualifying degree at the time of application.

Submit a complete application in English.

Develop a research proposal that meets the fellowship’s requirements.

An institutional affiliation is not required to apply. This means that eligible applicants do not necessarily need to be currently affiliated with a university, research institution, or other organization.

The application form specifically asks applicants to provide information about their U.S. citizenship, PhD or JD qualification, awarding institution, year the degree was awarded, and primary academic discipline.

Who Is Not Eligible or What Projects Are Excluded?

The fellowship guidelines also identify several categories of applications and projects that will not be accepted.

The program will not accept:

Applicants currently working toward a PhD or JD

Partisan proposals

Advocacy-oriented proposals

Rewritten doctoral dissertations

Projects primarily involving the editing of texts, papers, or documents

Preparation of textbooks

Preparation of anthologies

Preparation of translations

Preparation of memoirs

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed project represents a distinct research undertaking rather than simply revising an existing doctoral dissertation or undertaking an editorial project.

The distinction between research and advocacy is particularly important. Applicants should formulate research questions objectively and demonstrate that their conclusions will emerge from the investigation rather than being predetermined.

Carnegie China Fellowship Selection Process

Applications that meet the initial eligibility requirements undergo a multi-stage review process.

The process includes internal evaluations by the relevant University of Maryland program and consideration by a selection committee that includes experts from inside and outside the University of Maryland.

The review process considers several dimensions of an applicant’s research and professional record.

1. Significance and Originality of the Research

Reviewers consider the importance of the proposed project and whether it offers an original contribution.

Applicants should therefore explain why their research question matters and what makes their proposed study different from existing work.

A proposal should make clear:

The problem being investigated

Why the problem deserves attention

What is already known

What remains unclear

What the applicant intends to discover

What new contribution the research could make

2. Policy Relevance

The proposal should explain how the research can contribute to policymakers’ understanding of the issue under investigation.

As noted in the guidelines, policy relevance does not require a project to be purely contemporary or governmental. Historical, sociological, cultural, and other research can qualify when its findings or lessons have potential relevance to public-policy understanding.

3. Quality of the Project Proposal

The quality of the proposal is another important consideration.

Applicants are encouraged to present their ideas with:

Clear definitions

Strong organization

Logical structure

Clarity

Appropriate scope

A clearly defined research problem

A coherent methodology

A persuasive explanation of the project’s importance

The proposal should explain what reviewers will learn from the research and why that knowledge matters.

Applicants are also encouraged to articulate a clear hypothesis or step-by-step argument around a central problem where appropriate.

4. Methodology

The research methodology should be clearly explained.

Applicants should identify:

The approach they intend to use

Why the chosen approach is appropriate

How they will gather the information or data required

What sources they will consult

What archives or collections they may use

What techniques will be used to analyze the evidence

How the methodology will allow them to address the research question

Because reviewers may come from fields different from that of the applicant, the proposal should explain specialized research methods in accessible language.

5. Applicant’s Capabilities and Achievements

The selection process also considers the applicant’s professional and academic record.

Applicants need to demonstrate that they possess the skills, knowledge, experience, and background necessary to complete the proposed project successfully.

However, the proposal should not present the project’s conclusion as predetermined.

Instead, applicants should demonstrate that the research involves a genuine inquiry and that there is something meaningful to investigate.

The application should give reviewers confidence that the proposed project is feasible and that the applicant has a realistic plan for completing it.

6. Contribution to CUSP’s Mission

The program also considers whether the candidate can contribute to the broader life, priorities, and mission of the center.

An important aspect of this is the ability to make expert research accessible to a broader audience.

Applicants should therefore consider how they can communicate their research beyond academic specialists and contribute to conversations connecting scholarship with public affairs.

Carnegie China Fellowship Application Requirements

All applications must be submitted online.

The program states that it will not accept application materials submitted by email or through other means, with the exception of the required reference letters, which are to be sent by the referees to the designated email address.

A complete application must be submitted in English.

Applicants are required to prepare the following materials:

1. Project Proposal

The project proposal is one of the most important components of the application.

It must:

Be no more than five single-spaced typed pages

Use 12-point type

Be submitted in PDF format

Clearly explain the proposed research project

The proposal should address several specific elements.

Detailed Description of the Topic

Applicants should provide a detailed explanation of the research topic and its importance.

The proposal should establish the central issue and explain why it deserves investigation.

Originality of the Study

Applicants must explain what makes their proposed study distinctive.

This can involve addressing an understudied question, approaching an established issue from a new perspective, examining new evidence, or developing a research approach that contributes something different.

Basic Ideas and Hypotheses

The proposal should explain the core ideas behind the research and identify the main hypotheses where appropriate.

The research question and argument should be sufficiently clear that a reviewer outside the applicant’s specific discipline can understand what the project is attempting to establish.

Methodology

The applicant should explain how the research will be conducted.

This includes describing the activities required to gather evidence and the methods that will be used to analyze the evidence.

Current Research Status

Applicants should also explain the current status of their research.

This should include information about:

Work already completed

Relevant collections or archives already consulted

Existing research or evidence gathered

What remains to be done

What the applicant expects to accomplish during the fellowship

This helps reviewers understand both the project’s current stage and how the fellowship would contribute to its completion.

2. Current CV or Resume

Applicants must submit a current CV or resume.

The CV/resume must not exceed three pages.

There is an important exception regarding publications, presentations, or events. A list of publications, presentations, or events placed at the end of the CV/resume does not count toward the three-page limit.

The CV should provide a clear overview of the applicant’s academic and professional background and demonstrate relevant achievements and capabilities.

3. Two Letters of Reference

Applicants must arrange for two letters of reference to be submitted by the deadline.

The letters should be written by people who are familiar with the applicant and their work.

Importantly, referees should receive a copy of the applicant’s project description so that their letters can address:

The proposed research

The applicant’s qualifications

The applicant’s ability to undertake the project

The applicant’s proposed contribution to the fellowship

How the applicant and/or their research could contribute to bridging academic learning and public affairs

The reference letters must be written in English.

Applicants are specifically advised not to submit letters originally written for another purpose, such as employment applications.

The applicant is responsible for ensuring that both reference letters reach the program by the application deadline.

Applicants are strongly encouraged to contact their referees before the deadline to confirm that the letters have been submitted.

Reference letters should be sent by the referees to:

cusp@umd.edu

Information Required in the Online Application

The online application form requests several categories of information.

Contact Information

Applicants are required to provide information including:

First name

Last name

Email address

Phone number

Permanent address

City or town

State or province

ZIP/postal code

Eligibility Information

The application asks applicants to affirm that:

They are a U.S. citizen.

They hold a PhD or JD awarded by an accredited institution.

Applicants must also provide:

Name of the awarding institution

Year the degree was awarded

Primary academic discipline

Project Information

Applicants must provide:

Project title

Project proposal

The proposal must be uploaded as a PDF and must comply with the five-page limit and formatting requirements.

The application specifies a 100 MB file limit for the proposal.

CV/Resume

Applicants must also upload their current CV or resume in PDF format.

The CV/resume is subject to the three-page requirement and has a stated 100 MB file limit.

Recommendation Confirmation

Applicants must confirm that they will request their two recommenders to submit their letters of recommendation to cusp@umd.edu by the deadline.

Applicants must also affirm that the information supplied in the application is true and accurate.

The form additionally asks applicants how they heard about the Carnegie China Fellowship.

Important Application Considerations

Prospective applicants should pay close attention to the distinction between a strong academic research proposal and a proposal written exclusively for specialists.

The Carnegie China Fellowship explicitly encourages applicants to make their projects understandable to individuals outside their own fields.

A proposal should therefore avoid unnecessary technical language and explain specialized concepts when they are necessary.

Applicants should focus on demonstrating:

A clearly defined research problem

An important and original research question

A logical research strategy

A suitable methodology

A realistic plan

Evidence of preparation and relevant expertise

Potential public-policy relevance

A willingness to engage with policymakers

The ability to communicate research findings to broader audiences

Why the Research Proposal Matters

The five-page proposal gives applicants limited space to communicate a substantial research project, making clarity and organization particularly important.

A well-structured proposal can help reviewers understand the relationship between the research question, methodology, evidence, expected contribution, and policy relevance.

Applicants should avoid treating the proposal simply as a summary of their previous academic work. The fellowship is intended to support a research project with its own purpose and contribution.

Similarly, applicants should avoid presenting a predetermined conclusion. The guidelines emphasize the importance of demonstrating that there is a genuine inquiry at stake.

Connecting Scholarship With Public Affairs

A central theme of the Carnegie China Fellowship is the relationship between research and public affairs.

The program is designed for people who can contribute rigorous knowledge while engaging with the policy community.

This makes the ability to communicate research findings beyond an academic audience an important component of the fellowship.

Selected fellows are expected to engage with the policy community in Washington and abroad and eventually present their findings at the annual Carnegie China Conference at the University of Maryland.

The fellowship therefore provides a structure in which research can move from academic investigation toward broader discussions involving policymakers and other public audiences.

Fellowship Timeline and Deadline

The current Carnegie China Fellowship application round is open now.

The application deadline is: January 4, 2027

Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin preparing their materials because the application includes several components that require coordination, particularly the two external reference letters.

Before submitting, applicants should ensure that:

The project proposal is within the five-page limit.

The proposal is formatted using 12-point type and single spacing.

The proposal is submitted as a PDF.

The CV/resume does not exceed three pages.

Both reference letters have been requested.

Referees understand that letters must reach CUSP by the deadline.

The application is completed in English.

The applicant satisfies the U.S. citizenship and PhD/JD requirements.

The research project is not one of the excluded project types.

All information submitted is accurate.

How to Apply for the Carnegie China Fellowship

Interested applicants should complete the online application through the University of Maryland School of Public Policy.

Applicants should carefully review the fellowship guidelines and application requirements before submitting their materials.

A part of this Japan-Africa Youth Program is destinated to 20 young professionals in the animation industry from Africa. It offers opportunity to discover anime production sites or anime-related industry and educational institutions, aiming to inspire them and to foster connections between these professionals from Africa and Japanese companies. It provides participants with opportunities to deepen their understanding of Japanese values, mindset, and cultural heritage.

Costs

Participation in the program and travel expenses are free of charge.

Note: Participants are responsible for personal expenses, including transportation between your home and the airport and passport issuance fees.

Eligibility

Open to African anime creators.

They are currently calling for applications from interested companies and organizations (up to 10 companies in total). Please note that the maximum number of participants per company is two (one company executive who will act as the decision-maker and one creative professional).

Application

Application Deadline: Tuesday, September 8, 2026, at 23:59 (Japan Standard Time – JST)

Note: The application system will automatically close at 23:59 JST. Be mindful of time zone differences when submitting your application.
