Breadth Subject Requirements (pre Fall 2023)

Breadth Subject Requirements (pre Fall 2023)

To enrich knowledge about physics outside of one’s own research field, students must complete two breadth requirement subjects. At least one of these must be from the list below. Both must be passed with a grade of B- or better.

If only one breadth requirement is taken from this list, students may request approval of a second course that is not on the list if it genuinely satisfies the two stated objectives of the breadth requirement: 1) learning about physics and 2) being outside the student’s research field.

To request approval for a course, a student should write a short but clear email or letter explaining why the course satisfies these two objectives. If the course is in another department, the message should tersely explain on the basis of the course description or curriculum, why it should be considered learning about physics. The student should also succinctly state his or her research specialty and thesis topic, and explain why the course should be considered as being outside this research area. A short paragraph is sufficient to convey the necessary information.

Physics graduate students may wish to arrange an internship in an industrial or national laboratory at some time during their graduate career. Internships may be scheduled during either summer or academic terms and can be used, with approval of the student’s academic advisor, to satisfy one of the Departmental breadth requirements, even if the internship is in the student’s research field; internships may not be used to satisfy the specialty requirement. The Department recognizes that the demands of MIT research may make it difficult for students to consider this opportunity, but it also believes that the benefits can outweigh the possible conflicts. Students seeking internships should discuss the issue with their research supervisor and schedule the internship to minimize disruption of research.

The advisor should then forward the request, with his or her approval, to the General Examination and Requirements Coordinator who will send notification of the decision.

X indicates the subject is not allowed as a breadth requirement for students in this area

Research

Most graduate students are supported by Research Assistantships. RAs become involved in a research project as soon as they begin their assistantship, and this often leads to a thesis topic. Students should look for a research group during the first year, and confirm the supervisor by March 1. Prior to thesis research, students get academic credit for their research by registering for Pre-Thesis Research (8.391 or 8.392), which is taken every semester that research is conducted until thesis research formally commences.

Starting with the semester after a student passes the oral exam, registration changes from Pre-Thesis Research to Thesis (8.THG). While many students stay with their first research group, some register for Pre-Thesis Research in two or more research areas before finding a research topic suitable for a thesis. Pre-Thesis Research is graded on a Pass/Fail basis.

All graduate students conduct research that eventually leads to a thesis, but there are many different paths to gaining a research project. Students are expected to register for thesis and be assigned a thesis committee by the first term of their fourth year of graduate school (see Thesis section below).

Research Supervision

Any person who holds a Faculty or Senior Research Scientist appointment in the Physics Department may serve as a research supervisor. Under special circumstances, a faculty member outside the Department may supervise a student (this includes other MIT departments). All proposals for working with a faculty member outside the department must be approved by the Associate Department Head.

Prior to embarking on a research project with an outside supervisor, the student must obtain a Physics co-supervisor. The co-supervisor will maintain close contact with the research as it progresses, guide the student through the oral exam and thesis committee formation, guarantee funding for the student, and must ultimately co-sign the thesis. The student should submit a Research Co-Supervision Form (PDF), which requires the signatures of the research supervisor and co-supervisor. This form must be submitted to Academic Programs. No funding will be administered by the Department of Physics until this form is submitted.

Students will not be permitted to have advisors at other universities, including Harvard, except through well established collaborations i.e. the Center for Ultra-cold Atoms.

Research Internship

Physics graduate students may wish to arrange an internship in an industrial or national laboratory at some time during their graduate career. Internships may be scheduled during either summer or academic terms and can be used, with approval of the student’s academic advisor, to satisfy one of the Departmental breadth requirements, even if the internship is in the student’s research field; internships may not be used to satisfy the specialty requirement. The Department recognizes that the demands of MIT research may make it difficult for students to consider this opportunity, but it also believes that the benefits can outweigh the possible conflicts. Students seeking internships should discuss the issue with their research supervisor and schedule the internship to minimize disruption of research. Internships must be arranged six months ahead of time.

Thesis

Ph.D. Thesis

Schedule of upcoming physics PhD Thesis Defenses. If you are defending this term and do not see your information listed, please contact Jennifer Roesch.

Students must register for thesis and be assigned a thesis committee no later than one term after that in which they pass their oral exam. Students should consult with their Research Supervisor to discuss the Doctoral Thesis Committee Proposal Form which will list the committee chair and selected readers of the Physics Doctoral Committee and a descriptive draft thesis title. A third reader from the Physics faculty, who is not in the same research area, but whose interests, background, or special knowledge make him or her an appropriate member of the committee, is assigned by the Graduate Student Coordinator. When the departmentally-assigned reader has been selected, it is the student’s responsibility to convene an initial thesis committee meeting no later than four weeks before the last day of classes.

At that meeting the student makes an oral presentation to the thesis committee of a detailed proposal for a research program that would subsequently become the Ph.D. thesis. The student should demonstrate a thorough knowledge of relevant literature, explain the significance of the research to progress in the field, and present a well-thought-out program of research, including contingency plans. After that meeting, and based on the discussion, the student may develop a written proposal consisting of a one- or two-page description of the body of work that is to comprise the thesis.

Subsequent changes in title, scope, supervisor(s), or readers may be made with the written approval of the Graduate Student Coordinator.

In some cases, the thesis research may be in a borderline field between physics and some other field of science or engineering. In these cases, a joint committee, including members of another department may be formed. This requires approval by the Dean for Graduate Education.

Students who have not submitted a thesis proposal by the end of the first term after passing their oral exam will be prevented from registering for classes until they do.

After the initial oral presentation to the thesis committee, each student must make at least one substantial oral presentation of progress to the thesis committee every 12 months. The scheduling of this presentation is arranged by the student.

Students wishing to have more than one advisor, or to work with an advisor outside of Physics must submit a Research Co-Supervision Form to the APO.

Master’s Thesis

Students pursuing a Master’s degree are required to submit a written thesis. No oral defense is necessary. When work on the thesis commences, each student must submit a Master’s Thesis Proposal Form (PDF) with the proposed title of the thesis and the signature of the research supervisor to Academic Programs, 4-315. The student should begin registering for 8.THG immediately. A second reader will be assigned by the Graduate Student Coordinator and the student will be subsequently notified. Upon completion of the thesis, the research supervisor will submit a letter grade for the work to Academic Programs.

MIT Degree List

A student may be recommended for his or her degree in any term, but MIT only awards degrees three times a year – in February, May and September. A student must submit an Application for Advanced Degree at the beginning of the term in which he or she plans to graduate, and must be registered in residence during that term. Those on the September and February degree lists may participate in commencement the following June. A student must register for thesis as long as he or she is doing thesis research, including the summer terms. No specified number of research units is required, although the combined number of registered units each term should not be fewer than 36.

Student status and RA appointment are terminated upon receipt of the thesis document. Students with prospective employers may request a letter confirming completion of all degree requirements from the APO.

Thesis Oral Defense

The thesis defense is an oral presentation of the thesis research. The defense should take place at least two weeks before Departmental deadline (the last day to go off the degree list in a given semester). This oral presentation is based on an acceptable written draft of the thesis, which is provided to the thesis committee at least two weeks prior to the defense. The student is responsible for scheduling the thesis defense and arranging for the room in which it is to be held. The student should then notify the Graduate Coordinator in Academic Programs of the day, time, and place of the defense; the Graduate Coordinator will send notice to the Physics community. The defense is public and all members of the MIT community may attend. Immediately following the public presentation there will be a mandatory private session involving only the student and the thesis committee.

Thesis Copies

After passing the thesis defense and incorporating the suggested changes, students must submit to Academic Programs:

-A PDF/A-1 of your final thesis document (without signatures)
-Signature page

Please note: Files must be named according to this scheme: authorLastName-kerberos ID-degree-dept-year-type_other.ext

Thesis PDF: macdonald-mssimon-phd-physics-2024-thesis.pdf
Signature Page: macdonald-mssimon-phd-physics-2024-sig.pdf

In addition, The Libraries’ Thesis Form must be completed by the day of graduation.
The information you provide must match the title page and abstract of your thesis. You will be asked to confirm or provide:
Your name as it appears on your thesis (Family Name, Given Name Middle Name)
Thesis title
Department or Program
Degree(s)
Abstract
Supervisor(s)
ORCID iD
ProQuest opt-in (for Graduate and Doctoral candidates only)

Details of the required thesis, abstract, and title page formats are provided in Specifications for Thesis Preparation. Care should be taken to follow the presented format. The student should determine whether or not the supervisor, fellowship sponsor, etc. require additional copies. For advanced degrees submitted to the Physics Department, copyright is usually granted to MIT instead of retained by the student. The “Chair” signature line on the thesis cover page should be that of Professor Scott Hughes, Associate Department Head. This signature is obtained by the Academic Programs Office after the student submits the thesis.

Students should also be aware that a thesis archival fee will be charged to their student account. The Institute requires that this, and all outstanding charges, be paid before the final degree is approved.

Career Counseling

Although the MIT Physics graduate program is primarily focused on training students for careers in physics research, the pursuit of an advanced degree in physics is an excellent preparation for a variety of careers, both in physics and in other fields. If you have questions, or if you need someone to talk to about your career, there are many people available and willing to help. Every incoming student is assigned an academic advisor with whom they can discuss their course schedule and professional plans. Students in research groups have excellent resources in their research supervisor and other graduate students, and teaching assistants can talk to the professors for whom they are teaching. Students can also get advice from their course instructors. The MIT Career Advising and Professional Development (CAPD, E17-294) has a variety of resources for graduate students.

TITLE: PASSENGER project concludes: advancing Europe’s autonomy in producing permanent magnet materials

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
News | Project News

As Europe faces growing pressure to secure its clean technology supply chains, the PASSENGER project marks a major milestone toward industrial independence and sustainability. After four years of work, PASSENGER – funded by the EU’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme – successfully concludes today, having demonstrated that high-performance permanent magnets for strategic applications can be produced entirely without rare earth elements.

Learn more about PASSENGER

Europe currently imports almost 100% of its rare earths magnets, with recycling rates below 1%, leaving its industries and green transition exposed to geopolitical risks and volatile markets. PASSENGER offers a concrete, European-based solution: developing improved Strontium Ferrite (Sr-ferrite) and Manganese-Aluminum-Carbon (MnAlC) alloys as sustainable, rare-earth-free alternatives for permanent magnets, based on materials abundantly available in Europe.

Breakthrough Results for European Industry

Through eight pilot plants across Europe, PASSENGER has achieved multiple firsts:

Manganese-Aluminium-Carbon (MnAlC) magnets: The consortium achieved the first-ever industrial-scale production of 158 kg of MnAlC magnetic powder in its strongest τ-phase, combining excellent remanence (>2.0 kG) and coercivity (>3.5 kOe).

Improved Strontium Ferrite (Sr-ferrite) magnets: Over 4 tonnes of improved ferrite material were produced, maintaining high magnetic performance across temperature ranges without lanthanum or cobalt, commonly used in commercial magnets.

Validation in real applications: The new materials were successfully integrated into water pump and e-scooter prototypes, achieving performance comparable to conventional rare-earth-based systems.

These results demonstrate the potential for a complete European value chain, from raw materials and alloy production to finished magnet components, enabling a transition from laboratory research to pre-industrial manufacturing.

Reducing environmental and social impacts

The project’s environmental assessments show that rare-earth-free magnets developed within PASSENGER could reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 80% and human toxicity impacts by 74% compared with conventional NdFeB magnets.

Health and safety analyses indicate that replacing neodymium-based magnets could significantly reduce workplace risks, with 3-12 times fewer potential worker accidents, eliminating hazardous substances such as neodymium dust and hydrochloric acid from production processes.

By using locally sourced materials and designing for recyclability, PASSENGER contributes to Europe’s circular economy and supports the objectives of the European Green Deal.
Economic and Strategic Benefits for Europe

PASSENGER demonstrates that rare-earth-free magnet production can be economically viable, with life cycle cost analyses showing lower manufacturing costs than those of rare-earth-based magnets.

By relying on raw materials from European sources, including deposits in Ukraine, Norway, Iceland, and Spain, the project contributes to reducing strategic dependencies and enhancing supply chain security.
Over its duration, the project has invested €8.8 million across 20 partners in eight European countries, reinforcing research capacity and creating the basis for new industrial and employment opportunities in sustainable manufacturing.

A European pathway for sustainable innovation

The PASSENGER consortium has shown that technological excellence, environmental responsibility, and strategic autonomy can advance together. Its integrated approach – combining materials research, industrial scale-up, life cycle assessment, and socio-economic analysis – provides a model for future European collaborations in the field of critical materials and sustainable manufacturing.

“PASSENGER has demonstrated that Europe can lead the development of rare-earth-free magnet technologies, ensuring both sustainability and industrial competitiveness,” said Rodolfo Miranda, the project coordinator, from IMDEA. “Our results show that Europe’s green and digital transitions can be supported by solutions fully developed and produced within Europe.”

About PASSENGER

PASSENGER (Pilot Action for Securing a Sustainable European Next Generation of Efficient RE-free magnets) is funded by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme under grant agreement no. 101003914. The project brings together leading research institutions and industry partners to develop and scale rare-earth-free permanent magnets for electric mobility, wind energy, and other strategic applications.

More information and scientific publications are available at:

TITLE: London Mathematical Society (LMS) Mathematics in Africa Grant 2026 (up to £2,000)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 15, 2026

Applications are open for the Mathematics in Africa Grant 2026. The London Mathematical Society (LMS) offers a number of different grants schemes to support mathematics, including research grants for mathematicians and computer scientists working at the interface of Maths and computer science; education grants for teachers and other educators; and travel grants to attend conferences, among others.

The objective of the Mathematics in Africa grant is to provide partial support for mathematical activities based in Africa. Activities can include:

Attendance to mathematical conferences or workshops.

The organisation of mathematical conferences or workshops.

Mathematical research collaborations.

Grant

The maximum award is £2,000 (this amount is the upper limit, not the standard award) and covers:

Mathematical activities based in Africa.

Travel, accommodation and subsistence expenses.

In addition, the Society allows the use of the grant award to cover Caring Costs for those attendees who have dependents.

Visa costs are regarded as part of normal travel expenses.

The grant will be split into two payments. Half of the value of the grant can be claimed in advance of the activity. The balance of the grant, up to the actual cost of the expenses incurred, will be paid upon receipt of a satisfactory financial and academic report.

Grants will be paid to a university or institution only; payments will not be made to individual bank accounts.

Eligibility

Grant applicants can be mathematicians based anywhere in the world but grants will only be awarded for activities taking place within Africa.

Note that PhD students are not eligible to apply for a Mathematics in Africa grant.

Criteria

The Society will support only mathematical activities which take place in Africa.

Conference and Workshop organisers should note the following advice on diversity.

Application

Download the application form in PDF or Word and submit applications and any enquiries to: grants@lms.ac.uk

For more information, visit Mathematics in Africa Grant.

TITLE: Salzburg Global Library Internship 2027 in Austria

The internship is offered by Salzburg Global and is open to students and recent graduates who are eager to gain international experience. Through this internship in Europe, interns will get the chance to polish their skills and further their career. All interns will assist with one or more active programs, offering exposure to the organization’s global initiatives and events. With the Salzburg Global internship, candidates with a background in Library Information Science or a relevant area are encouraged to apply. For more details about this European internship, make sure to read till the end.

Similarly, Salzburg Global Library Internship is a full time three-month internship that will take place in Austria. The library internships are available in mid-January, early July, and late September. Hence, offering multiple options. This internship in Austria offers many benefits, although it is not a paid internship; interns will get boarding and lodging at Schloss Leopoldskron, a return ticket for their country of origin and various networking opportunities.

Throughout the duration of this internship in Austria, candidates will be responsible for different tasks, including archival duties, library duties and program related support. Interns will play a key role in managing and organizing the organization’s historical records. The role focuses on archival management, library maintenance, and oversight of the institution’s periodicals collection. They will also contribute to building and creating Salzburg Global’s institutional archives while ensuring the private library remains up to date and well-managed.

This internship for students offers a valuable opportunity to gain practical experience in digital archiving, including sorting, systematizing and shaping electronic documents into a functional and accessible archive. Therefore, you would not want to miss the Salzburg Global Library Internship. Everyone from around the world can apply for this Austria internship and German language skills are not required.

TITLE: The African Higher Education Community Mourns the Passing of Prof. Tolly Mbwette, Former AAU Governing Board Member

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the entire African higher education community are deeply saddened by the news of the passing of Prof. Tolly Salvatory Augustin Mbwette. Prof. Mbwette was a celebrated Professor of Engineering, and the former Vice Chancellor of the Open University of Tanzania.

Due to his strong track record as an achiever and a leader, Prof. Mbwette was elected as a governing board member of the AAU and served the association from year 2013 to 2017 as the representative of the East African Region. He worked tirelessly with his team members to improve African Higher Education and to promote it to the rest of the world.

He also served the AAU in various capacities, including chairing of sessions at the AAU’s statutory conferences, representing the AAU and advocating for its interests at international meetings, being part of the panel for the recruitment of the AAU Secretary General, as well as contributing to the implementation of projects such as the World Bank funded Africa Centres of Excellence (ACE) Projects. He served as an evaluator in the selection of some Centres of Excellence in both the ACE I and ACE Impact Projects. He also played active roles in the AAU African Quality Assurance Network (AAU/AfriQAN) activities.

On behalf of the Governing Board of the AAU, the 400-member universities of the Association, Staff of the AAU Secretariat and all stakeholders of the African Higher Education community, the Association extends its heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family, and commiserates with the Tanzanian Ministry of Education as well as the entire citizenry of Tanzania, and Africa on this sad event.

We fondly remember him for his immense contribution to academic scholarship in Africa. Indeed, Africa has lost a great scholar and leader.

May His Dear Soul Rest in Perfect Peace!

BACKGROUND INFORMATION ON PROF. TOLLY MBWETTE

(Source – Open University of Tanzania)

Prof. Mbwette held various positions in higher learning institutions. Between January 2004 and April,2005, he was the Deputy Vice Chancellor (Academic) at the Open University of Tanzania. He also served as the Vice Chancellor, Open University of Tanzania following his re-appointment for a further five-year period, starting 3rd April 2010. He was the Chairman of the IUCEA Governing Board for two years (2007-2009) and the Foundational Chairman of TERNET Council between April 2007 and April 2010. Between December 2006 and December 2009, Prof. Mbwette was the Chairman of the Tanzania Commission for Universities (TCU). He was also the Vice Chairperson of the Executive Board of the African Council on Distance Education (ACDE) between July 2008 and July 2011 as well as one of the two Vice Chairpersons of the IUCEA Governing Board from July 2008 to June 2010. From September 2009, Prof. Mbwette was an Honorary Advisor to the Commonwealth of Learning (COL). In July 2011, Prof. Mbwette was duly elected as the President of ACDE for a period of three (3) years. Prof. Mbwette was the team leader of various multi-disciplinary research teams responsible for treatment of both drinking and wastewater treatment systems that rely on bio-systems. He had a broad experience in management of higher education institutions initially through being an Associate Dean responsible for Research, Publications and Postgraduate Studies for three years in the former Faculty of Engineering at the University of Dar es Salaam after which he assisted the UDSM Vice Chancellor in Coordinating the much acclaimed University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM) Transformation Programme for eight years, between July 1994 and April, 2002. Prof. Mbwette was also involved in co-ordination of a number of co-operation programmes between Europe and America and Universities in Africa ranging from East, Central and Southern Africa.

TITLE: Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program 2026: Funding Opportunity for Nonprofit Organizations Supporting Food Access and Environmental Stewardship

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program provides financial support to qualifying nonprofit organizations working to address important needs in communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores. The program is designed to empower Whole Foods Market team members to support local organizations whose work reflects the company’s broader purpose of nourishing people and the planet.

For eligible nonprofit organizations seeking funding for community-based initiatives, the program offers an opportunity to receive financial support for activities related to food access, environmental stewardship and other closely related community needs.

Applications are submitted through the Whole Foods Market Community Engagement Portal and are considered during designated voting cycles throughout the year.

What Is the Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program?

The Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program is a community giving initiative through which Whole Foods Market provides financial support to eligible nonprofit organizations.

The program is locally oriented. Rather than supporting individuals or unrestricted organizations globally, the initiative focuses on nonprofit programs serving communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores.

The program is particularly relevant to organizations whose work addresses areas such as

Food access and food security

Environmental stewardship

Community-based initiatives

Other needs closely related to Whole Foods Market’s community priorities

Programs aligned with Whole Foods Market’s Core Values

Whole Foods Market states that financial support is provided biannually, with specific application and voting periods during the year.

2026 Whole Foods Market Store Giving Deadlines

Organizations interested in applying should pay close attention to the 2026 application and voting calendar.

Quarter 2 Vote

Application deadline: April 12, 2026

Voting period: April 28 – May 10, 2026

The Quarter 2 application deadline has already passed.

Quarter 4 Vote

Application deadline: October 11, 2026

Voting period: October 27 – November 8, 2026

The October 11, 2026, deadline is the upcoming application deadline listed for the 2026 Store Giving Program.

Organizations that intend to seek consideration during the Quarter 4 cycle should ensure that their applications are submitted through the appropriate Community Engagement Portal before the deadline.

Who Can Apply for the Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program?

The program is specifically designed for registered nonprofit organizations, rather than individuals or commercial businesses.

According to the published eligibility guidelines, applicants must be able to demonstrate verified nonprofit status.

Eligible organizations include:

Registered U.S. 501(c) (3) nonprofit organizations

Registered Canadian charitable organizations

UK charitable incorporated organizations

Applicants must therefore have an appropriate recognized nonprofit or charitable status in one of the eligible jurisdictions.

Which Countries and Regions Are Eligible?

This is an important consideration for organizations outside North America and the United Kingdom.

The Store Giving Program specifically identifies eligible organizations as

United States—registered 501(c) (3) nonprofit organizations

Canada—registered charitable organizations

United Kingdom—charitable incorporated organizations

Therefore, the program is not presented as an open global grant opportunity for nonprofit organizations worldwide.

For example, an organization based solely in Kenya or another African country would not meet the stated organizational eligibility requirement based on the guidelines provided.

Organizations should also consider the program’s local-community focus: donations must support nonprofit programs in communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores.

What Areas Does Whole Foods Market Fund?

The program identifies several priority areas, with a particular emphasis on initiatives that contribute to community well-being and align with Whole Foods Market’s values.

1. Food Access

Organizations working to improve access to food may be relevant to the program.

Potential examples could include nonprofit initiatives addressing:

Access to nutritious food

Food insecurity

Community food programs

Food distribution initiatives

Community-based food access projects

Organizations should clearly demonstrate the community need being addressed and how their proposed program contributes to improving food access.

2. Environmental Stewardship

Environmental initiatives are another area identified by the program.

Organizations working on environmental stewardship may seek support for projects that address relevant environmental needs within eligible communities.

The strongest applications should demonstrate a clear connection between the proposed activity, the community being served and environmental stewardship.

3. Closely Related Community Needs

The program also allows consideration of other closely related needs.

However, applicants should not assume that every type of charitable activity qualifies. Projects should demonstrate alignment with Whole Foods Market’s stated priorities and core values.

Key Eligibility Requirements

Before submitting an application, organizations should carefully review the program’s eligibility requirements.

Verified nonprofit status

Applicants must be able to demonstrate that they are legally recognized nonprofit or charitable organizations within the jurisdictions specified by Whole Foods Market.

Community-based impact

Funding must be designated for nonprofit program support in communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores.

This means organizations should be able to clearly explain:

Where the project will take place

Which community will benefit

What needs the project addresses

How the organization will deliver the proposed activities

What impact the funding is expected to create

Alignment with Whole Foods Market Core Values

Proposed activities should align with Whole Foods Market’s core values.

Applicants should therefore familiarize themselves with the company’s values and demonstrate a meaningful connection between those values and their proposed project.

Funding from the Whole Foods Market Foundation

Receiving funding from the Whole Foods Market Foundation does not automatically disqualify an organization from consideration under the Store Giving Program.

However, applicants should distinguish between the Store Giving Program and the Foundation’s separate funding activities.

Organizations That Are Not Eligible

The program clearly identifies several categories that it does not support.

Whole Foods Market does not donate through this program to:

Individuals

Political candidates

Political organizations

For-profit businesses

Organizations that discriminate against any racial, ethnic or cultural group

This means the opportunity is intended specifically for qualifying nonprofit organizations rather than individuals seeking personal financial assistance or commercial businesses seeking funding.

Important Consideration for Organizations That Have Received Previous Funding

Previous support from Whole Foods Market does not guarantee that an organization will receive funding again.

Applicants should therefore treat every application cycle as a new opportunity for consideration and demonstrate the current relevance and impact of the proposed request.

Organizations that have previously received support should not assume that past funding creates an automatic entitlement to future donations.

Priority Consideration for Organizations Without Recent Sponsorship

Whole Foods Market states that priority consideration will be given to organizations that have not received another sponsorship or donation within the calendar year.

This does not necessarily mean that organizations that received other funding are automatically excluded.

Instead, organizations without another sponsorship or donation during the calendar year may receive priority consideration.

Importantly, funding from the Whole Foods Market Foundation is specifically stated to be non-disqualifying.

Can an Organization Submit the Same Request to Multiple Locations?

No.

The program’s system does not allow the same request to be submitted to various locations.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider the appropriate location for their request and avoid attempting to duplicate the same application across multiple Whole Foods Market locations.

How Does the Application Process Work?

Organizations interested in requesting support should follow the application process established by Whole Foods Market.

Step 1: Review the eligibility guidelines.

Before starting an application, confirm that the organization:

Has verified nonprofit status

Falls within one of the eligible organizational categories

Is seeking support for an eligible nonprofit program

Serves a community surrounding a Whole Foods Market store

Aligns with Whole Foods Market’s relevant values and priorities

Step 2: Prepare the funding request.

Applicants should have sufficient information available to explain their nonprofit program and the purpose of the requested support.

A strong request should make it easy for reviewers to understand:

The organization

The community it serves

The problem being addressed

The proposed program

The purpose of the requested funding

The expected community benefit

Step 3: Submit through the Community Engagement Portal

Requests for Whole Foods Market Store Giving must be submitted through the company’s Community Engagement Portal.

Whole Foods Market Community Engagement Portal

Applicants should use the official portal for submission rather than sending requests through unrelated channels.

Step 4: Monitor the application.

Organizations that receive support will be notified during the relevant funding cycle.

Applicants can also log into their online profile to check their application status.

What Happens After an Organization Is Selected?

Organizations that receive support are subject to additional requirements concerning their relationship with Whole Foods Market.

One important requirement concerns publicity and communications.

Recipients must not issue or permit publicity, advertising, press releases, public statements, announcements or other public communications about the relationship with Whole Foods Market or the resulting agreement without prior written approval from Whole Foods Market.

Recipients must also obtain prior written consent before using Whole Foods Market’s:

Name

Trade name

Service marks

Trademarks

Trade dress

Logo

Organizations should therefore carefully review the applicable recipient requirements before publicly announcing or promoting a Whole Foods Market donation.

APPLY HERE

Donation Payment Process

Whole Foods Market states that donations to qualifying organizations are made through Versaic grants disbursement through the Benevity platform, a service owned and provided by Benevity, Inc.

This means successful organizations should be prepared to follow the relevant procedures associated with the donation-disbursement system.

The payment mechanism is separate from the initial application process and does not change the requirement that organizations submit their requests through the Whole Foods Market Community Engagement Portal.

How Competitive Is the Program?

Whole Foods Market notes that it receives a high volume of inquiries, meaning that it is not possible to fulfill every request.

Consequently, satisfying the basic eligibility requirements does not guarantee funding.

Organizations should focus on presenting a clearly defined community need and demonstrating how the proposed program aligns with the program’s priorities.

Applicants should also make their requests specific rather than relying on broad descriptions of their organization’s mission.

How to Strengthen Your Application

Although funding is not guaranteed, organizations can take practical steps to make their requests clearer and more compelling.

1. Clearly explain the community need.

Begin with the problem.

Explain what challenge exists in the community and why the proposed intervention is necessary.

Where possible, provide concrete information demonstrating the scale or urgency of the issue.

2. Connect the project to Whole Foods Market’s priorities.

Applicants should clearly demonstrate how their proposed project relates to areas such as

Food access

Environmental stewardship

Community wellbeing

Other closely related needs

Avoid presenting a project without explaining its relevance to the program.

3. Identify the beneficiaries

Clearly describe who will benefit.

For example, explain:

The number of people expected to benefit

The geographic community being served

The characteristics of the target population where relevant

How beneficiaries will participate in or benefit from the program

4. Explain exactly what the funding will support.

A funding request should make the intended use of the donation clear.

Rather than simply stating that funding will support “community programs,” explain the specific activities, resources or program costs that the donation would contribute toward.

5. Demonstrate measurable impact

Where possible, identify measurable outcomes.

Examples include:

Number of beneficiaries reached

Number of meals or food-support interventions delivered

Number of community members participating

Environmental outcomes achieved

Number of program activities implemented

Percentage or number of intended beneficiaries reached

Clear outcomes can help reviewers understand the practical impact of the proposed project.

6. Confirm nonprofit eligibility before applying

Organizations should verify their legal charitable status before investing significant time in preparing an application.

This is particularly important for international organizations because the program’s eligibility rules specifically identify U.S., Canadian and UK charitable organizations.

Important Restrictions Applicants Should Understand

Applicants should be aware that the Store Giving Program has several restrictions beyond the basic eligibility requirements.

The program does not support:

Individuals

Political candidates

Political organizations

For-profit businesses

Organizations that discriminate against racial, ethnic or cultural groups

Additionally, successful recipients face restrictions on publicizing their relationship with Whole Foods Market without prior written authorization.

Applicants should therefore read the complete guidelines before submitting a request.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity may be relevant to organizations that meet all of the core requirements, particularly:

U.S. 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations

Registered Canadian charitable organizations

Organizations serving communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores

Nonprofits working on food access

Organizations outside the specified eligible jurisdictions should also carefully review the requirements before attempting to apply.

Conclusion

The Whole Foods Market Store Giving Program 2026 offers financial support to qualifying nonprofit organizations addressing community needs connected to food access, environmental stewardship and related priorities. The initiative is particularly focused on nonprofit programs serving communities surrounding Whole Foods Market stores.

For the remaining 2026 funding cycle, the application deadline is October 11, 2026, followed by voting from October 27 to November 8, 2026.

Organizations interested in applying should first confirm their nonprofit eligibility, geographic eligibility and alignment with the program’s priorities. They should then prepare a clearly defined funding request explaining the community need, proposed activities, beneficiaries, expected outcomes and intended use of the donation.

TITLE: ESDC Internship 2027 in Brussels, Belgium: EUR 1,500 Monthly Allowance for EU Security and Defence Policy Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The European Security and Defence College (ESDC) has opened applications for its 2027 internship programme, offering students the opportunity to gain practical experience within an EU institutional environment in Brussels, Belgium. The programme provides two internship periods in 2027 and is designed for students pursuing relevant bachelor’s or master’s degree programmes who want practical exposure to the European Union’s Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) and the wider Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP).

Selected interns will receive a monthly allowance of EUR 1,500, while eligible expenses for occasional duty trips outside Brussels may also be reimbursed. Applications must be submitted by 12:00 CET on 14 October 2026.

About the European Security and Defence College Internship

The ESDC is a European Union institution focused on education and training in the area of the EU’s Common Security and Defence Policy within the broader framework of the Common Foreign and Security Policy.

According to the official 2027 internship call, the programme is intended to give students an opportunity to work directly with the ESDC and contribute to the organisation and implementation of its activities. Through this practical experience, interns can develop a stronger understanding of CSDP and CFSP while applying knowledge gained through their academic studies.

The ESDC operates as a network that brings together civilian and military institutes, universities, academies and other organisations working in the fields of security and defence. Its activities therefore provide interns with exposure to a broad institutional and international environment.

The ESDC works under the overall responsibility of the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, while the European External Action Service (EEAS) supports the High Representative in carrying out responsibilities relating to the EU’s foreign and security policy.

For students interested in international relations, diplomacy, security studies, defence policy, European affairs and related disciplines, the internship provides an opportunity to gain experience in an environment directly connected to these areas.

ESDC Internship 2027 Overview

Here are the key details applicants should know:

Host institution: European Security and Defence College (ESDC)

Location: Brussels, Belgium

First internship period: 18 January – 14 May 2027

Second internship period: 29 March – 30 July 2027

Monthly allowance: EUR 1,500

Application deadline: 12:00 CET, 14 October 2026

Application method: Email

Required application documents: CV and motivation letter

Application language: English or French

CV format: European CV/Europass format

Target applicants: Students currently enrolled in relevant bachelor’s or master’s degree programmes

Citizenship requirement: Applicants must be nationals of an EU Member State

Working languages: English or French, with knowledge of another language considered an asset

ESDC Internship Periods for 2027

Applicants can apply for one of the two internship periods announced for 2027.

First Internship Period

The first internship will run from

18 January – 14 May 2027

Second Internship Period

The second internship will run from

29 March – 30 July 2027

Applicants are required to indicate their preferred or available internship period as part of their application.

The ESDC also indicates that a third internship period, running from 1 September to 31 December 2027, is expected to be published in March 2027. This third period is therefore not part of the current application call.

What Will ESDC Interns Do?

The internship is designed to provide practical experience rather than purely academic exposure. Successful candidates will support the ESDC Secretariat and contribute to a range of activities associated with security and defence policy training and education.

The official call identifies several responsibilities that interns may undertake.

1. Support Courses, Seminars and Conferences

Interns will assist with the preparation, implementation and post-processing of ESDC courses, seminars and conferences.

These activities may take place in Brussels or abroad and focus on CSDP and the broader CFSP framework.

This means interns can gain exposure to the planning and delivery of institutional events involving stakeholders working in European security and defence.

2. Prepare Course Materials and Background Documents

Interns may be responsible for helping prepare:

Course materials

Background briefs

Reports

Supporting documentation

This responsibility can provide useful experience in policy research, institutional writing, briefing preparation and information management.

3. Provide Meeting and Administrative Support

Interns will provide logistical and administrative assistance for meetings involving ESDC bodies, topic-focused configurations and ESDC stakeholders.

They may also:

Attend meetings

Take meeting notes

Help prepare meetings

Support post-meeting activities

Assist with coordination and follow-up

This aspect of the internship can be particularly relevant to students interested in diplomacy, international organisations, public administration, foreign affairs and policy coordination.

4. Support eLearning Activities

The ESDC also expects interns to support the revision of its eLearning modules.

This could expose interns to institutional digital learning content, training development and the review of educational materials.

5. Maintain the Annual Training and Course Catalogue

Interns may assist in maintaining the ESDC’s annual training and course catalogue.

This involves supporting the organisation and management of information relating to the College’s training activities.

6. Contribute to the ESDC Annual Report

Interns may also support the drafting of the ESDC Annual Report.

This can provide practical exposure to institutional reporting, information gathering, drafting and documentation.

7. Support Knowledge Management

Another important responsibility involves supporting the ESDC Secretariat’s internal Lessons Identified / Lessons Learnt and knowledge-management processes.

This component can give interns insight into how international institutions capture experience, document lessons and use organisational knowledge to improve future activities.

8. Proofread Documents and Draft Social Media Posts

The internship also includes communication-related responsibilities.

Interns may be expected to:

Proofread institutional documents

Draft social media posts

Support the preparation of communications content

This makes the opportunity potentially relevant not only to security and international-relations students, but also to students whose academic backgrounds combine international affairs with communications, public information, digital media or related fields, provided their programme is considered relevant to ESDC activities.

Who Can Apply for the ESDC Internship 2027?

The ESDC has established specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants must meet all applicable eligibility criteria outlined in the official call.

1. EU Citizenship Is Required

Applicants must be nationals of a Member State of the European Union.

This is an important requirement for prospective applicants from outside the European Union. The official call does not establish general eligibility for nationals of non-EU countries.

Therefore, applicants from African, Asian, American, Middle Eastern or other non-EU countries would not meet the stated nationality requirement unless they are also nationals of an EU Member State.

2. Current Bachelor’s or Master’s Students

Candidates must currently be enrolled at an academic institution or university with a view to obtaining a:

Bachelor’s degree;

Master’s degree; or

Equivalent qualification.

Their field of study must be relevant to the activities of the ESDC.

The internship is therefore aimed primarily at currently enrolled students, rather than applicants who have already completed their studies and are no longer enrolled.

3. Students Must Remain Enrolled Throughout the Internship

Applicants must remain enrolled at their academic institution or university for the entire duration of the internship.

This means applicants should carefully consider their expected graduation date before applying.

A student whose enrolment ends before the completion of the selected internship period may not satisfy this requirement.

4. Health and Accident Insurance

Candidates must have insurance covering sickness and accidents for the entire duration of the internship.

Applicants should therefore ensure that appropriate coverage will be available throughout their selected internship period.

5. Language Requirement

Applicants must have a thorough knowledge of at least one EU working language: English or French.

Knowledge of another language is considered an additional asset.

What Academic Backgrounds May Be Relevant?

The official call does not provide an exhaustive list of qualifying degree programmes. Instead, it requires candidates to be enrolled in a field relevant to ESDC activities.

Given the College’s mandate and the responsibilities listed in the internship call, potentially relevant academic areas may include fields connected to:

International relations

Diplomacy

Security studies

Defence studies

European studies

Political science

Foreign policy

International security

Strategic studies

Peace and conflict studies

Public policy

International law

European affairs

Related social sciences and policy disciplines

Applicants should rely on the ESDC’s official assessment of whether their particular academic profile is relevant rather than assuming that a specific degree automatically qualifies.

Selection Criteria

Meeting the minimum eligibility requirements does not necessarily guarantee selection.

The ESDC states that applicants will be assessed based on several qualifications, including:

Academic achievements

Academic profile

International profile

Work experience

This means applicants should present their academic and professional background clearly and demonstrate how their studies and experience relate to the work of the ESDC.

Students with relevant international exposure, academic projects, internships, research activities or work experience may wish to make those aspects clear in their application where applicable.

What Does the ESDC Internship Offer?

One of the most significant features of the programme is the financial allowance.

EUR 1,500 Monthly Allowance

Selected interns will receive a monthly allowance of EUR 1,500.

The call also explains how the allowance interacts with certain external grants.

For example, if an intern receives a grant such as an Erasmus+ grant, the ESDC will reimburse the difference up to the EUR 1,500 monthly amount.

Reimbursement for Certain Duty-Trip Expenses

Interns may participate in ESDC duty trips outside Brussels, subject to budget availability.

The ESDC states that interns will be reimbursed for expenses associated with occasional duty trips outside Brussels.

This provides an additional opportunity for selected interns to gain exposure to ESDC activities beyond the institution’s Brussels base.

Internship Mentorship and Responsibilities

Interns will be placed under the responsibility of a mentor.

They are expected to follow instructions provided by their mentors and ESDC superiors and maintain high standards of:

Personal integrity

Impartiality

Courtesy

Interns are also required to keep a careful record of their activities and submit a report to their mentor at the end of the internship.

After completing the internship, the ESDC will provide a certificate confirming the internship.

Working Hours and Leave

Interns will work the same working hours as ESDC staff and will have the same official public holidays as ESDC employees.

They are also entitled to two working days of leave per month.

These provisions provide applicants with a clearer understanding of the institutional nature of the internship and the expectations associated with participating in the programme.

Equal Opportunities and Inclusion

The ESDC states that it is committed to an equal-opportunities policy for its staff and applicants.

The College says it is committed to:

Promoting gender equality;

Preventing discrimination on any grounds;

Welcoming qualified candidates from diverse backgrounds; and

Maintaining the broadest possible geographical representation among EU Member States.

Candidates with disabilities may request assistance or reasonable accommodation during the selection process.

The official call instructs candidates requiring accommodation to contact the ESDC vacancies address so that appropriate support can be considered.

Documents Required to Apply

Applicants must submit:

A CV

A motivation letter

The documents must be submitted in English or French and should be provided in PDF or Word format.

The ESDC specifically requests applicants to use the European CV format.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their CV clearly communicates their academic background, relevant experience, international exposure, language abilities and other information relevant to the internship.

How to Apply for the ESDC Internship 2027

Applications must be submitted by email only.

Applicants should send their application to:

esdc-vacancies@eeas.europa.eu

The application process involves screening applications against the internship requirements. The most suitable candidates may subsequently be invited to an interview by the ESDC.

Applicants must also:

Indicate their availability for the internship period.

Identify a point of contact or supervisor at their academic institution or university.

Submit all required documents.

Ensure that the application is complete.

Submit the application before the specified deadline.

The ESDC explicitly states that incomplete applications will not be considered.

ESDC Internship 2027 Application Deadline

The application deadline is

14 October 2026 at 12:00 CET

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their documents because applications must be complete and sent through the specified email channel.

The official ESDC webpage and internship call both confirm the 14 October 2026, 12:00 CET deadline.

APPLY HERE

Important Points Applicants Should Check Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should verify that they satisfy the core requirements.

Eligibility checklist

Applicants should confirm that they:

Are nationals of an EU Member State.

Are currently enrolled in a bachelor’s, master’s or equivalent degree programme.

Are studying a field relevant to ESDC activities.

Will remain enrolled throughout the entire internship.

Have sickness and accident insurance covering the entire internship.

Have a thorough knowledge of English or French.

Can provide a CV in the requested European format.

Can prepare a motivation letter in English or French.

Can identify an academic institution/university contact or supervisor.

Can commit to one of the announced internship periods.

Can submit a complete application before the deadline.

Why This Internship May Be Relevant to International Affairs Students

The ESDC internship combines academic learning with practical institutional work in an area closely connected to European and international security policy.

Interns can potentially gain experience in several areas, including:

International security and defence policy

European foreign and security policy

Policy-oriented research

Institutional coordination

International conferences and seminars

Meeting management

Briefing and report preparation

Knowledge management

eLearning

Strategic communication

Social media content development

Administrative and logistical coordination

The combination of these functions can provide a broad institutional perspective for students whose studies are connected to international affairs and related disciplines.

Visit HERE for more information about the ESDC Internship 2027 in Brussels, Belgium.

Academic qualification

Applicants must:

Be currently enrolled at an academic institution or university;

Be pursuing a bachelor’s, master’s or equivalent degree;

Be studying a field relevant to the ESDC’s activities; and

Remain enrolled for the entire duration of the internship.

Nationality and geographical eligibility

The opportunity is restricted to nationals of European Union Member States.

Therefore, nationality is a significant eligibility condition. Being a student at a European university by itself does not satisfy the stated nationality requirement.

Applicants from non-EU countries who do not also hold nationality of an EU Member State are not eligible under the nationality criterion in this particular call.

Conclusion

The ESDC Internship 2027 provides eligible students with an opportunity to gain practical experience within a European Union institutional environment focused on security and defence policy. Based in Brussels, Belgium, the programme offers two internship periods in 2027 and includes a EUR 1,500 monthly allowance.

The internship involves a broad range of activities, including supporting courses and conferences, preparing briefing materials and reports, assisting with meetings, contributing to eLearning and knowledge-management activities, supporting the annual report and drafting social media content.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to students whose academic studies connect with international relations, security and defence, European affairs, diplomacy, foreign policy, public policy and related areas. However, applicants must carefully note the nationality requirement: candidates must be nationals of an EU Member State, must remain enrolled in their academic programme throughout the internship and must satisfy the language, insurance and other eligibility requirements.

Applications must include a CV and motivation letter in English or French and must be submitted by email to the ESDC vacancies address. The final deadline is 12:00 CET on 14 October 2026.

TITLE: Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) Scholarship 2027-2028

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 10, 2026

Applications are open for the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) Scholarship 2027-2028. The Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) hereby invites suitably qualified nationals of the East African Community (EAC) to apply for Cohort 4 of the KfW-funded Scholarships to pursue Master’s studies in an EAC Partner State other than their own.

The EAC Scholarship Programme (EACSP) is a regional initiative of the East African Community (EAC) and the Federal Republic of Germany. Implemented by the Inter-University Council for East Africa, the Programme seeks to develop future leaders who will contribute to regional integration and sustainable development by supporting students to pursue Master’s studies in an EAC Partner State other than their country of citizenship.

Scholarship

Up to 120 scholarships are available under this cohort.

The scholarship package includes:

One return economy-class air ticket between the scholar’s home country and the host country upon commencement and completion of studies.

Full tuition fees payable directly to the host university.

Arrival allowance EUR 200 upon arrival in the study country and opening a bank account in that country (Where feasible, scholars are encouraged to open a EUR-denominated bank account to facilitate the receipt of the allowance and reduce potential losses arising from currency exchange fluctuations and conversion charges).

A monthly stipend of EUR 380 to cover accommodation, meals, local transport and other living expenses.

A lump-sum allowance of EUR 650 for study materials

A one-time EUR 1,500 study and research allowance.

Medical insurance coverage for the duration of the scholarship.

Visa/ Entry fee: Where payment of entry pass into the host country or student pass is required.

Participation in at least one extracurricular event

Eligibility

Be a citizen of any of the 8 EAC Partner States;

Be below 35 years of age at the time of application;

Apply to study in an EAC Partner State other than their country of citizenship;

Possess a Bachelor’s Degree, with a minimum of Second Class Upper Division, Distinction or equivalent qualification;

Have applied for admission to an eligible Master’s programme offered by partner university;

Submit a complete scholarship application within the stipulated application period.

Application

Complete the online EAC Scholarship Application Form and submit all required supporting documents before 10 September 2026 at 17:00 East African Time.
