TITLE: IACHR Internship Program 2027: Apply for the Winter/Spring Human Rights Internship in Washington, D.C. and National Offices

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) Internship Program 2027 is offering students and recent graduates from Organization of American States (OAS) Member States an opportunity to gain practical professional experience in international human rights, law, communications, technology, translation, international cooperation, fundraising, and related fields.

The program provides participants with the opportunity to work alongside professionals and staff of the IACHR Executive Secretariat while developing a deeper understanding of the Inter-American human rights system and the mechanisms used to promote and protect human rights throughout the Americas.

For the upcoming 2027 Winter/Spring Session, applications are open from August 24 to September 11, 2026, while the internship itself will run from January 14, 2027, to April 30, 2027.

Importantly, the IACHR internship is unpaid, meaning participants should plan for their own living, travel, accommodation, and other expenses associated with participation.

IACHR Internship Program 2027 at a Glance

Program: IACHR Internship Program

Organization: Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR)

Parent organization: Organization of American States (OAS)

Opportunity: Professional internship

2027 Session: Winter/Spring Session

Locations: Washington, D.C. and National Offices

Application period: August 24 – September 11, 2026

Internship period: January 14 – April 30, 2027

Duration: Approximately three and a half months

Funding: Unpaid; no payment or stipend is provided

Eligible applicants: Students and recent graduates from OAS Member States

Primary fields: Law, international cooperation, fundraising, journalism, graphic design, web design, computer information technology, and translation

Application method: OAS Internship Program online application

Application requirement: Applicants must indicate their interest in the IACHR during the application process

What Is the IACHR Internship Program?

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) is a principal human rights body within the inter-American system. Its work focuses on promoting and protecting human rights in the Americas.

The IACHR Internship Program is managed in conjunction with the broader OAS Internship Program. It is designed to give young students and recent graduates an opportunity to gain first-hand experience with the work of the Commission and understand how the inter-American human rights protection system operates in practice.

Rather than being limited exclusively to law students, the program provides opportunities for people from several academic and professional backgrounds whose skills can contribute to the work of the Commission.

Participants have the opportunity to interact with professionals working within the IACHR Executive Secretariat and contribute to activities assigned during the internship.

This makes the program particularly valuable for individuals interested in careers involving:

International human rights

International law

Human rights advocacy

Public policy

International organizations

Diplomacy

Civil society

Journalism and communications

Digital communications

Graphic design

Web design

Information technology

Translation

International cooperation

Fundraising

IACHR Internship 2027 Application Deadline

The application window for the 2027 Winter/Spring Session is:

August 24 – September 11, 2026

Therefore, applicants interested in participating in the January 2027 to April 2027 session should complete and submit their applications during this period.

Important deadline

Application deadline: September 11, 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day if they can submit earlier. The application process requires applicants to provide documentation, so prospective interns should review the requirements carefully and prepare their materials before beginning the online application.

When Will the Internship Take Place?

The selected interns for this session will participate from:

January 14, 2027 – April 30, 2027

The IACHR internship program operates according to established sessions and dates. Applicants should therefore ensure that they are available for the specified internship period before applying.

Individuals who need an internship to fulfill a specific university requirement should pay particular attention to the duration requirements.

The program states that participants fulfilling a university internship requirement for a specific length of time must provide documentation from their university confirming the required internship duration.

Where Is the IACHR Internship Based?

The 2027 Winter/Spring opportunity covers:

Washington, D.C.

National Offices

Washington, D.C. is particularly significant because it is home to the IACHR headquarters at:

1889 F Street N.W., Washington, D.C., U.S.A. 20006

Applicants should carefully review the OAS Internship Program information for the specific placement arrangements applicable to their application.

Who Can Apply for the IACHR Internship?

The program is aimed at students and recent graduates from OAS Member States.

The IACHR specifically identifies several categories of applicants who may be suitable for internship opportunities.

1. Law Students

Law students are among the primary groups targeted by the program.

This opportunity can be particularly relevant to students interested in:

International human rights law

International law

Public international law

Constitutional law

Human rights advocacy

Human rights litigation

Refugee and migration issues

International organizations

Regional human rights systems

Students interested in building a career in international human rights can potentially gain valuable exposure to how a regional human rights institution operates.

2. Recently Graduated Lawyers

The program also welcomes recently graduated lawyers.

For graduates who want to move into international human rights work, the internship can provide practical exposure that complements their academic legal training.

Experience at an international human rights institution can be relevant for future work with:

Human rights organizations

Civil society organizations

Government institutions

Ombudsmen’s offices

International organizations

Legal advocacy organizations

International law practices

Human rights litigation organizations

3. International Cooperation and Fundraising Students and Graduates

The IACHR also identifies opportunities for students and recent graduates working in international cooperation and fundraising.

This makes the program relevant beyond traditional legal careers.

Applicants with an interest in international development, institutional partnerships, resource mobilization, donor engagement, and international cooperation may find the experience particularly valuable.

4. Journalism Students and Recent Graduates

The IACHR Press Office receives students and recent graduates in journalism.

This provides an opportunity for communications-oriented applicants to gain experience in promoting awareness of human rights issues and communicating the work of an international institution.

Journalism applicants may benefit from exposure to:

Human rights communications

International affairs reporting

Institutional communications

Public information

Media relations

Human rights advocacy

Digital communications

5. Graphic Design Students and Graduates

The program also welcomes students and recent graduates in graphic design.

Graphic designers can potentially contribute to communications and promotional activities associated with the IACHR’s work.

This is particularly relevant for applicants who want to combine creative skills with international affairs and human rights communications.

6. Web Design Students and Graduates

The IACHR Press Office also offers opportunities for students and recent graduates with web design backgrounds.

This provides a potential pathway for individuals interested in using digital communication and web-based platforms to support human rights advocacy and public information.

7. Computer Information Technology Students and Graduates

The IACHR also receives students and recent graduates specializing in computer information technology.

This demonstrates that the internship program is not exclusively focused on legal or communications careers.

Applicants with technical skills may be able to gain experience within an international organization while applying their IT knowledge in support of institutional activities.

8. Translation Students and Graduates

The IACHR also provides opportunities for students and recent graduates in translation.

Translation applicants should be capable of working in at least two of the four official languages of the OAS:

English

Spanish

Portuguese

French

This requirement is especially relevant because the inter-American human rights system operates across multiple linguistic environments.

Which Countries Can Apply?

The opportunity is intended for students and recent graduates from OAS Member States.

The Organization of American States is a regional organization bringing together countries from across the Americas. Therefore, eligibility is based on membership in the OAS rather than being restricted to a particular country or nationality within one subregion.

Applicants should verify that their country is an OAS Member State and review the official OAS Internship Program requirements before submitting an application.

The information provided for this opportunity does not establish a separate racial or ethnic eligibility requirement. The OAS also states that it is committed to equal employment opportunity and does not discriminate against individuals on the basis of race, color, marital status, religion, age, gender, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, or parental status.

What Will Interns Do?

During the internship, participants will have opportunities to work with professionals and staff from the Executive Secretariat of the IACHR.

Specific assignments are determined by the Executive Secretariat and may vary according to the needs of the Commission, the participant’s academic or professional background, and the particular internship placement.

The experience is therefore intended to provide practical exposure rather than simply classroom-based learning.

Depending on their field, interns may be exposed to activities connected to:

Human rights research

Legal and policy work

Human rights communications

Press and media activities

Graphic design

Web-related activities

Information technology

Translation

International cooperation

Fundraising

Other activities carried out by the Executive Secretariat

The exact duties are assigned by the IACHR.

Objectives of the IACHR Internship

The central objective of the internship is to provide eligible students and recent graduates with the opportunity to learn about the work of the Commission and gain practical training.

For law students and recent law graduates, this can mean gaining greater familiarity with the functioning of the inter-American human rights system.

The program can also help participants understand how human rights institutions interact with victims, civil society, governments, legal professionals, and other stakeholders.

The program’s objectives include:

Providing practical professional training
Participants gain experience working with professionals within an international human rights institution.

Introducing participants to the IACHR’s work
Interns can develop a better understanding of the Commission’s mandate and activities.

Building knowledge of the inter-American human rights system
Participants can learn how regional human rights protection mechanisms operate.

Supporting professional development
The knowledge and experience gained can contribute to future careers in human rights, law, international organizations, communications, technology, and related fields.

Creating a multiplying effect in participants’ home countries
One of the program’s broader objectives is for participants to take the knowledge they acquire during the internship back to their home countries and apply it professionally.

Why Is This Internship Valuable?

The IACHR internship can be particularly valuable because it combines academic knowledge with practical experience in an international institutional environment.

For a law student, for example, studying human rights law in university provides theoretical knowledge. Working alongside professionals at a regional human rights institution can provide a different perspective by showing how human rights mechanisms function in practice.

Similarly, a journalism student can gain insight into communicating human rights issues, while a graphic designer or web designer can see how creative and digital skills can support institutional advocacy.

The experience may therefore strengthen both technical and professional skills.

Professional development

Participants can develop skills that may be useful for future employment and further study.

International exposure

Working within the IACHR provides exposure to a major regional human rights institution.

Human rights knowledge

Participants can develop a deeper understanding of human rights protection mechanisms within the Americas.

Practical experience

The program provides an opportunity to move beyond academic study and gain hands-on experience.

Networking

Interns have the opportunity to work with professionals and staff of the IACHR Executive Secretariat.

Home-country impact

The program emphasizes the potential for participants to return home and use the knowledge acquired during their internship.

How the Internship Can Support a Future Career

The experience gained at the IACHR can be relevant to a wide range of professional pathways.

Former interns and fellows have gone on to work in areas including:

Human rights advocacy

Legal representation of victims

Civil society

International human rights organizations

Government institutions

Ombudsmen’s offices

Human rights litigation

International law

International development

Journalism

Communications

Technology

Translation

International cooperation

According to the program information, former participants have used their knowledge of the inter-American system in their home countries, including by representing victims of human rights violations, filing petitions and requests for precautionary measures with the Commission, advising civil society organizations, and working with government bodies and Ombudsmen’s Offices.

This illustrates the longer-term professional value that the program can potentially provide.

Is the IACHR Internship Paid?

No.

The IACHR Internship Program is unpaid.

The program is administered by the General Secretariat of the OAS, and the internship does not provide a salary, payment, or stipend.

This is an important consideration for international applicants, particularly those who may need to relocate or travel to Washington, D.C.

Applicants should therefore consider the financial implications of participating, including possible costs associated with:

International travel

Accommodation

Food

Local transportation

Visa or immigration-related expenses, where applicable

Insurance

Personal expenses

Prospective applicants should independently verify any additional financial or logistical requirements with the OAS before making travel arrangements.

How to Apply for the IACHR Internship 2027

Interested applicants must apply through the OAS Internship Program.

The electronic application becomes accessible during the designated application periods.

Applicants should follow these steps:

Step 1: Review the OAS Internship requirements

Before beginning the application, carefully review the eligibility criteria and documentation requirements for the OAS Internship Program.

Step 2: Prepare the required documents

Applicants should ensure that all documents requested by the OAS Internship Program are ready before submitting the application.

Step 3: Complete the online application

Submit the application through the OAS Internship Program’s electronic application system during the open application period.

Step 4: Indicate your interest in the IACHR

This is particularly important.

Applicants interested in an IACHR placement should clearly indicate their interest in the IACHR in the electronic application.

Step 5: Upload all required documentation

Applicants must upload the required supporting documentation to the electronic application form.

Step 6: Submit before the deadline

The application period for this session ends on:

September 11, 2026

Applicants should submit before the deadline rather than waiting until the final hours.

Application Link

Applications are submitted through the OAS Internship Program’s electronic application system.

OAS Internship Application: http://www.oas.org/interns/

Applicants should also review the official OAS Internship Program webpage for the current requirements and application instructions.

See the OFY Website HERE for more internship programs

Important Information for University Students

Students who want to use the internship to satisfy a university requirement should pay special attention to the program’s duration rules.

The IACHR explains that participants who need to complete an internship of a specific length as part of their university requirements must provide documentation from their university specifying the required length.

Therefore, if your university requires you to complete a particular number of weeks or months, make sure you obtain the appropriate documentation before applying.

Official Languages of the OAS

The four official languages referenced by the program are:

English

Spanish

Portuguese

French

This is particularly important for translation applicants, who must be able to work in at least two of these four official languages.

Applicants in other fields should also recognize that multilingual ability can be highly relevant in an international and regional organization operating across the Americas.

Equal Employment Opportunity

The IACHR and OAS state that they are committed to equal employment opportunity based on individual merit.

The organization states that it does not discriminate against individuals on the basis of:

Race

Color

Marital status

Religion

Age

Gender

Disability

Sexual orientation

Gender identity

Parental status

Applicants should therefore be evaluated within the framework of the organization’s stated equal employment policy and the applicable internship requirements.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be particularly suitable for:

Law students interested in human rights

Recent law graduates

Students interested in international law

Graduates pursuing careers in human rights

International cooperation students and graduates

Fundraising students and graduates

Journalism students

Recent journalism graduates

Graphic design students and graduates

Web design students and graduates

Computer information technology students and graduates

Translation students and graduates who meet the language requirement

Young professionals interested in international organizations

Students seeking practical international human rights experience

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although meeting the eligibility requirements is essential, applicants should also make sure their application clearly communicates why they are interested in the IACHR.

1. Clearly explain your field of interest

Connect your academic background or recent professional experience to the type of work carried out by the IACHR.

2. Demonstrate genuine interest in human rights

Applicants should be able to explain why human rights and the inter-American system are relevant to their academic or professional goals.

3. Highlight relevant experience

Where applicable, emphasize experience involving:

Legal research

Human rights

Policy

Advocacy

Journalism

Communications

Graphic design

Web design

IT

Translation

International development

Fundraising

Civil society

4. Show how the internship fits your career plans

A strong application should demonstrate that the internship is part of a broader professional development journey.

5. Pay attention to documentation

Incomplete applications or missing documents can create unnecessary problems. Review the OAS requirements carefully before submitting.

6. Apply early

Because the application period ends on September 11, 2026, applicants should prepare their materials in advance and avoid leaving submission until the last minute.

Key Dates to Remember

Applications open: August 24, 2026

Application deadline: September 11, 2026

Internship begins: January 14, 2027

Internship ends: April 30, 2027

Applicants should save these dates and make sure they can commit to the full internship period.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the IACHR Internship Program open to international applicants?

The program is intended for students and recent graduates from OAS Member States. Applicants should confirm that their country is an OAS Member State and review the current OAS internship eligibility requirements.

Is the IACHR internship paid?

No. The internship is unpaid and does not provide a payment or stipend.

When is the application deadline?

The deadline for the 2027 Winter/Spring Session is September 11, 2026.

When does the internship take place?

The internship runs from January 14, 2027, to April 30, 2027.

Do I have to study law to apply?

No. Although law students and recent lawyers are specifically mentioned, opportunities are also available for students and recent graduates in international cooperation and fundraising, journalism, graphic design, web design, computer information technology, and translation.

Can journalism students apply?

Yes. The IACHR Press Office receives students and recent graduates in journalism.

Can graphic designers apply?

Yes. Graphic design students and recent graduates are among the fields identified by the IACHR.

Can IT students apply?

Yes. The IACHR receives students and recent graduates in computer information technology.

What languages are relevant to the program?

The OAS has four official languages: English, Spanish, Portuguese, and French. Translation applicants should be able to work in at least two of these languages.

Can a student use the internship to meet a university requirement?

Potentially, yes. However, if a university requires a specific internship duration, the applicant must provide documentation from the university specifying the required length.

Where do I apply?

Applicants should apply through the OAS Internship Program’s electronic application system and indicate their interest in the IACHR.

Final Takeaway

The IACHR Internship Program 2027 presents an opportunity for students and recent graduates from OAS Member States to gain practical experience within a major regional human rights institution.

Although the program is unpaid, its potential professional value extends beyond the internship period. Participants can gain practical exposure to the work of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, interact with professionals in the Executive Secretariat, strengthen their understanding of regional human rights mechanisms, and develop experience that can support future careers in law, human rights, international organizations, communications, journalism, technology, translation, international cooperation, and related fields.

The opportunity is also broader than a traditional legal internship. Students and recent graduates in journalism, graphic design, web design, computer information technology, translation, international cooperation, and fundraising may also find relevant opportunities within the program.

For eligible applicants, the most important dates to remember are August 24 to September 11, 2026, when applications are accepted, and January 14 to April 30, 2027, when the internship takes place.

Anyone considering applying should carefully review the OAS Internship Program requirements, prepare all required documentation, clearly indicate their interest in the IACHR, and submit their application before the September 11, 2026 deadline.

TITLE: New Phase of the Demographics of African Faculty Project to Enhance Data Management Culture for Faculty Planning in the East African Community

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Kampala, Uganda, 12 June 2024 – The Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community (DAF EAC) project, funded by Carnegie Corporation of New York (G-21-58066), has launched its second phase. Building upon evidence collected during the inaugural phase (2021-2023), this phase addresses data gaps and incorporates lessons learned from the pilot phase in Ghana in 2018. The pilot phase was funded by Mastercard Foundation, and Dubai Cares.

Phase 1 of the DAF EAC project identified significant data gaps at institutional, national, and regional levels, revealing fragmented and inconsistent faculty data in higher education institutions (HEIs). Key findings included:

University Projections:

Burundi: According to projections from the DAF model, the University of Burundi would require an additional faculty of 1,400 by the year 2030 to bridge the gap (Base year: 2021).

South Sudan: The University of Juba would need an additional faculty of 620 by 2030 to achieve policy norms for Student Teacher Ratios (Base year: 2021).

Uganda: Makerere University requires an additional 5,800 faculty members by 2030 to meet the increased student enrollment ratio (Base year: 2019).

Country-Level Projections:

Kenya: Projections indicate that Kenya will require an additional faculty of 26,000 by 2030 to meet Student Teacher Ratio goals, considering population growth (Base year: 2017).

Rwanda: The projections estimate that Rwanda will need an additional faculty of 12,600 by 2030 (Base year: 2021).

Tanzania: To achieve policy norms for Student Teacher Ratios by 2030, Tanzania requires an additional faculty of 33,300 (Base year: 2021).

Across Burundi, Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, education was the discipline with the highest Student Teacher Ratio.

The second phase focuses on closing these gaps by establishing a comprehensive approach to institutionalising data collection and management. This approach will link university data systems through national bodies and to the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA), a regional intergovernmental agency.

This launch coincides with the 4th Biennial Conference on Catalysing Systemic Social Transformation Through Research and Innovation, hosted by the Commission for University Education in Kenya, highlighting the project’s alignment with ongoing academic advancements.

The Demographics of African Faculty in the East African Community Project is implemented by a consortium comprised of the IUCEA, the Association of African Universities (AAU), Education Sub Saharan Africa (ESSA), and Population Reference Bureau (PRB).

Running from 2023 to 2025, DAF EAC phase 2 project aims to develop harmonised guidelines for unified data collection and management in the EAC. The project will also promote best practices for data collection and management in the region and beyond. Additionally, the project will engage in advocacy to highlight the importance of harmonised data collection and management guidelines within the East African Community and beyond.

Prof. Gaspard Banyankimbona, IUCEA Executive Secretary said, ‘‘The findings of the first phase of DAF EAC portrayed a dire situation and overall weak culture for higher education data collection and management in the EAC countries. The commitment to redress the situation is aligned to the IUCEA mandate to advise Partner States on all matters of higher education and research. The phase 2 of this project will promote and inculcate a culture of higher education data collection and management through application of a multifaceted approach. This will foster good practices and processes, as well as application of emerging technologies in higher education data collection and management.’’

Prof. Olusola Oyewole, Secretary General of the AAU, remarked, ‘‘The AAU has been involved in the DAF project since its Ghana pilot phase because we strongly believe that reliable and quality data is critical for decision-making by African higher education institutions and key stakeholders, including governments and development partners. Through this current phase of the project, we aim to establish a continental Higher Education Data Working Group that will work closely with the project team to address the data challenges in East Africa while contributing to solving the higher education data collection challenges across the continent. This DAF Project will also be associated with the Data Work Area activities under the Harmonisation of African Higher Education, Quality Assurance, and Accreditation (HAQAA 3) Project’’.

Dr. Lucy Heady, CEO of ESSA, commented: ‘‘Collectively we have identified a systemic issue—a scarcity of data on faculty and higher education systems in the region. Ultimately, Phase 2 funding underscores the significance of the Demographics of African Faculty work and the consortium’s capability to deliver. ESSA is excited to be working alongside its valued partners to take this collaboration to the next phase, to nurture a culture of data collection and collaboration. This is critical for a coordinated and unified approach to data in higher education and to support policymakers to design and implement reforms that enhance the quality of education in universities.’’

Dr. Jennifer D. Sciubba, President and Chief Executive Officer of PRB, stated, ‘‘Meeting the rapidly growing demand for higher education is critical for EAC member states to harness the benefits of the demographic dividend. In phase 1 of this project, PRB was privileged to support IUCEA-appointed researchers from EAC member states to project the future demand for faculty in higher education—a crucial piece of assessing the future workforce in the world’s youngest region. Moving into phase 2, we look forward to improving on these projections by supporting IUCEA to identify key data on students and faculty to be collected and disseminated by EAC member states.’’

The consortium aims to establish a coordinated and unified data collection system to inform higher education decisions at both the national and regional levels by the end of the implementation of DAF EAC phase 2.

TITLE: Erasmus University Rotterdam PhD Candidate Position 2026: Study the Transimperial History of Women’s Work

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you passionate about history, gender studies, colonial societies, archival research, or digital humanities? Erasmus University Rotterdam is offering an exciting fully funded PhD opportunity for highly motivated researchers interested in investigating the transimperial history of women’s work between 1600 and 1900.

The Erasmus School of History, Culture and Communication (ESHCC) is seeking two PhD candidates to join an ambitious research project examining how European colonial expansion influenced ideas, practices, and experiences surrounding women’s labour across different regions of the world.

The successful candidates will become part of an interdisciplinary and internationally oriented research team led by Dr. Natália da Silva Perez. The project combines traditional historical and archival research with innovative computational approaches, including handwritten text recognition, multilingual datasets, digital humanities methods, natural language processing, statistical analysis, and qualitative historical research.

The positions provide an exceptional opportunity for emerging scholars to pursue doctoral research while receiving a competitive monthly salary, professional development opportunities, extensive employment benefits, research experience, teaching exposure, and access to an international academic environment in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

About the Erasmus University Rotterdam PhD Research Project

The PhD project focuses on the relationship between European colonial expansion and changing ideas about women’s work between 1600 and 1900.

European colonialism created extensive political, economic, social, and cultural connections between European metropolitan centres and territories across Africa, the Americas, and other parts of the world. These connections influenced how labour was organised, represented, regulated, and understood.

Women played crucial roles within colonial and transimperial economies and societies. However, ideas about women’s work were often shaped by gender, race, class, colonial power, slavery, migration, and social hierarchies.

This research project seeks to investigate these complex historical relationships by examining both normative ideas about gendered labour and the lived experiences of women.

Rather than studying colonial societies in isolation, the project adopts a transimperial perspective. This approach explores how ideas, people, texts, institutions, and understandings of labour moved between different colonial territories and European metropolitan centres.

The selected PhD candidates will conduct independent doctoral research while contributing to a broader collaborative project.

The research will focus on one of two historical cases:

Pernambuco

Atlantic Africa, including potential research areas such as Senegambia, the Gold Coast, or Angola

Through these historical cases, the PhD researchers will explore important questions surrounding women’s labour, colonial societies, gender relations, and the circulation of ideas across imperial boundaries.

Understanding the Transimperial History of Women’s Work

The central objective of the project is to understand how women’s lived experiences of work either conformed to or diverged from dominant ideas about gendered labour.

Historical societies often developed expectations regarding what types of work women should perform. However, these expectations did not always reflect the realities of women’s everyday lives.

Women participated in numerous forms of economic, domestic, agricultural, commercial, and social labour. Their work could be influenced by factors including:

Gender

Colonial rule

Social class

Race

Enslavement

Migration

Family structures

Economic systems

Religious institutions

Legal regulations

Cultural traditions

The research project will investigate how ideas about women’s work circulated between European metropolitan centres and colonial territories.

By examining archival records from multiple regions and imperial contexts, researchers will be able to explore similarities, differences, exchanges, and transformations in historical understandings of gendered labour.

This makes the PhD particularly relevant for scholars interested in:

Colonial history

Early modern history

Women’s history

Gender history

African history

Atlantic history

Labour history

Social history

Digital humanities

Historical archives

Computational research methods

Intersectionality

Social reproduction theory

Research Areas Available for PhD Candidates

Applicants will be expected to focus their doctoral research on one of the project’s two major historical cases.

1. Pernambuco

One possible research focus is Pernambuco, a historically significant region in Brazil with a complex colonial past.

Researchers choosing this case may investigate historical sources relating to women’s work, labour systems, colonial societies, economic structures, and the circulation of ideas between Pernambuco and European metropolitan centres.

Applicants interested in the Pernambuco case may benefit from knowledge of languages such as:

Portuguese

Dutch

Spanish

Depending on their proposed research direction, candidates may also be encouraged to develop additional linguistic skills relevant to the archival material.

2. Atlantic Africa

The second research focus concerns Atlantic Africa.

Angola

This research case offers an opportunity to investigate women’s work and gendered labour within historically interconnected African and Atlantic worlds.

Researchers may examine the movement of people, ideas, economic systems, and institutional practices across African regions, colonial territories, and European metropolitan centres.

Portuguese

Dutch

French

English

Danish

Candidates are not necessarily expected to possess expertise in every language listed. However, strong knowledge of at least one language relevant to the chosen historical case is required, and willingness to develop additional language skills will be viewed positively.

What Will the Selected PhD Candidates Do?

The successful candidates will undertake independent doctoral research while contributing to the wider collaborative project.

The PhD programme is designed to combine traditional historical research with modern computational and digital methodologies.

Selected researchers will be expected to carry out several important academic and research activities.

Build and Curate Historical Datasets

One of the major responsibilities will involve contributing to the development of multilingual and transimperial historical datasets.

These datasets will focus on evidence relating to women’s work and gendered labour.

The materials may include:

Researchers will contribute to the organisation and curation of these materials across different geographical locations and historical periods.

The project is particularly innovative because it combines historical evidence from multiple imperial and linguistic contexts.

Conduct Archival Research

Archival research will form a central component of the doctoral project.

PhD candidates will identify, examine, interpret, and analyse primary historical materials relevant to their selected research case.

Applicants will also be required to demonstrate an awareness of relevant archives when applying for the position.

The PhD candidates will work with Transkribus, a platform commonly used for the transcription and analysis of historical handwritten documents.

Researchers may use handwritten text recognition technologies to convert archival documents into searchable and analysable text.

However, automated transcription is not always perfect.

Candidates will therefore also be expected to manually review and correct transcription results.

This combination of digital technology and human expertise provides an opportunity to develop advanced skills in computational historical research.

TITLE: SEACAF Research Fellowships on Empowering Academic Freedom in Southeast Asia 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 20, 2026

Applications are open for the SEACAF Research Fellowships on Empowering Academic Freedom in Southeast Asia 2026. Academic freedom in Southeast Asia is increasingly under threat, closely tied to the region’s broader trend of democratic backsliding. Like other human rights defenders, academics and students who speak out on issues of social justice face constant risk – including state surveillance, administrative penalties, criminalization of dissent, and informal restrictions on what may be taught, researched, or published.

These threats are even more acute in areas affected by armed conflict or where governments invoke national security to justify tighter control over academic spaces. The rise of youth movements in recent years in countries like Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand are the cases in question where they face harsh state repression.

Research Fellowships on Empowering Academic Freedom in Southeast Asia brings together an annual cohort of 6 early-career researchers and advocates for ten to twelve months of structured inquiry, expert mentorship, and peer exchange — producing original research and policy proposals that matter to the region.

Research Themes

For 2026, SEACAF will support six research fellowship that fall under one of the following themes:

Neoliberal Higher Education and Its Impacts on Academic Freedom: Neoliberal policies governing higher education contribute to the erosion of academic integrity and independence. Grounded in case studies, research under this theme will investigate how such neoliberal higher education affects academic freedom in practice. The findings will inform policy advocacy aimed at securing higher education institutions as space for critical knowledge development and enquiries.

Developing Regional Indicators for Academic Freedom: The research under this theme will engage stakeholders to design regional context-sensitive indicators and propose mechanisms for academic freedom monitoring in the region. The outcomes will be the basis of SEACAF’s future work to establish a robust academic freedom monitoring and documentation system in Southeast Asia.

Participatory Action Research for Training Modules on Academic Freedom (OPENED FOR RESEARCH TEAM ONLY): This research theme focuses on collaborative engagement with academic communities and student groups to co-develop training modules on academic freedom. Using participatory action research methods, the fellow will develop training modules and educational materials and test the modules through participatory workshops.

Funding

Theme 1: Neo-liberal Higher Education – $12,000 per project

Theme 2: Developing Regional Indicators – $12,000 per project

Theme 3: Participatory Action Research for Training Modules – $15,000 per project

TITLE: Press Release – The Association of African Universities (AAU) and the University of Nottingham sign a Memorandum of Understanding to Advance Academic Excellence in Africa and Europe

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana and UK, February 7, 2023 – The Association of African Universities (AAU), Africa’s apex higher education organization established in November 1967, has signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding with the University of Nottingham, a top-ranked university in the UK founded as University College Nottingham in 1877 and granted a royal charter in 1948, to promote collaborations that will mutually benefit higher education institutions in both Africa and Europe.

This MoU mandates the University of Nottingham to provide an office space with a dedicated Desk Officer to centrally coordinate AAU’s existing and emerging partnerships in Europe while the two institutions also work together to develop mutually acceptable proposals as co-applicants to potential funders. Equally important, the MOU obliges the AAU to provide guidance to Nottingham on the Association’s new focal areas, including but not limited to the promotion of technical and vocational education and training; the promotion of the AAU Africa Research, Innovation and Development (AFRID) Network that seeks to mobilise African institutions and researchers to generate a critical mass of human resources to support continental initiatives; and the strengthening of the AAU multimedia platform, the AAU Television, as Africa’s premier continental television station that promotes African scholarly works. The two institutions have also agreed, under the MOU, to collaborate in specific areas to advance academic excellence such as staff, researchers and students’ capacity building, quality assurance, resource mobilization, ICT and other infrastructural development.

The AAU Secretary-General, Prof. Olusola Bandele Oyewole, and the Pro-Vice Chancellor for Global Engagement of the University of Nottingham, Prof. Robert Mokaya OBE, respectively appended their signatures to the agreement for their institutions. Expressing his excitement about the Agreement, Prof. Oyewole noted that despite the AAU having a number of partnerships with institutions in Europe, “University of Nottingham has become a home and focal point to AAU member universities and its other networks for effective partnerships with European counterparts, particularly with the University of Nottingham itself that has emerged as a world-class, research-intensive university whose research transforms lives and shapes futures.

The partnership will be hosted by the University of Nottingham’s School of Education and led by Professor Juliet Thondhlana, who is also the UNESCO Chair in International Education and Development. Juliet Thondhlana, Professor of International Education and Development at the University of Nottingham said: “International collaboration is essential to teaching and research. The university is developing a new strategy for engaging with partners in Africa, at the core of which is developing equitable partnerships with collaborators, so we are delighted to be partnering with the AAU to advance research and innovation across our continents. I look forward to seeing what we can achieve together as our collaboration grows further.”

About the Partnering Organizations

The Association of African Universities (AAU)

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the apex higher education organization in Africa and represents the voice of Africa’s higher education on regional and international bodies. Established in Rabat (Morocco) in 1967, the AAU currently has a membership of over 400 institutions of higher learning across all the linguistic and geographic divides of Africa. Its headquarters is in Accra, Ghana and it currently has two regional offices – East Africa Regional Office ( hosted by the University of Khartoum in Sudan) and the North Africa Regional Office (hosted by the Al Azhar University in Egypt), as well as a Country Office in Abuja, Nigeria. It also has agreements with institutions in North America and China to establish nodal Desk Offices.

The AAU supports African universities to deliver quality higher education and, as its niche, creates a platform for networking among its members. The Association enjoys a unique capacity for convening most of the higher education community in Africa to reflect and consult on key issues affecting education on the continent. The thrust of its base is the nimble deploying of advocacy, commissioning of studies, and acting and becoming the clearing house and intelligence arm for these higher education institutions on the continent.

The AAU operates in four languages namely, English, French, Arabic and Portuguese. It endeavours to raise the quality of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by fostering collaboration among its member institutions; providing support to their core functions of teaching, learning, research, and community engagement; and facilitating critical reflection on, and consensus-building around, issues affecting higher education and the development of Africa.

https://aau.org/

2. The University of Nottingham

Ranked 18th in the UK by the QS World University Rankings 2023, the University of Nottingham is a founding member of Russell Group of research-intensive universities. Studying at the University of Nottingham is a life-changing experience as it prides itself on unlocking the potential of students. It has a pioneering spirit, expressed in the vision of its founder – Sir Jesse Boot, which has seen it lead the way in establishing campuses in China and Malaysia – part of a globally connected network of education, research and industrial engagement.

The University is among the best universities in the UK for the strength of its research, positioned seventh for research power in the UK according to REF 2021. The birthplace of discoveries such as MRI and ibuprofen, its innovations transform lives and tackle global problems such as sustainable food supplies, ending modern slavery, developing greener transport, and reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

The University is a major employer and industry partner – locally and globally – and its graduates are the second most targeted by the UK’s top employers, according to The Graduate Market in 2022 report by Highfliers Research. It led the Universities for Nottingham initiative, in partnership with Nottingham Trent University, a pioneering collaboration between the city’s two world-class institutions to improve levels of prosperity, opportunity, sustainability, health and wellbeing for residents in it’s city and region.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Robert Lourie

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Robert Lourie ’82, PhD ’86 understands the importance of basic science research and graduate fellowships in the Physics Department.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2015

Robert Lourie ’82, PhD ’86

Robert Lourie ’82, PhD ’86 was born and raised in Newton, MA, just outside of Boston. He was not particularly studious in his youth, and left high school in the 11th grade to join the Navy. Robert spent six years on active duty, with almost five of them as a radar technician aboard the USS Ranger (CV-61). Radar sparked his interest in technology and engineering such that he originally thought he would go for an electrical engineering degree after discharge. However, during one leave Robert visited a friend who happened to have on hand the Scientific American issue with Sheldon Glashow’s article on quarks. Robert read it, was hooked, and now attributes his newfound interest in physics to this one event. (At the time, he had no idea that protons were even made of anything!)

After that, and until his discharge, Robert spent as much time teaching himself math and physics as he possibly could. He took his SATs while still on the aircraft carrier and received early admission to MIT in 1978. He arrived at MIT wanting to do experimental physics and because of the opportunities provided in his first IAP period, took a tour of the Bates Linear Accelerator Center. Again, he was hooked, and in the second semester of his freshman year he started working with Prof. Bill Bertozzi, who eventually supervised both Robert’s senior thesis and PhD research.

After earning his PhD, Robert spent another two great years at MIT as a postdoc with the Bertozzi group. Finally, he had to leave the nest and in 1988 he joined the faculty of the University of Virginia. As well as being very involved in the new electron accelerator CEBAF (now Jefferson Lab) in Virginia, Robert continued to do research at Bates. Then, in one of those totally unexpected turns in life, he took a sabbatical to work in finance at Renaissance Technologies, a company founded by his cousin (and fellow MIT alum) Jim Simons ‘58. The work turned out to be as technically challenging as anything Robert had ever done in physics. The job also brought him back to the East Coast and closer to family, and Robert’s original six-month sabbatical is now in its 21st year.

Basic science is one of the highest forms of human endeavor and MIT’s Physics Department is unrivaled in the excellence of its pursuit.
Robert Lourie ’82, PhD ’86

Robert has supported the Physics Department with the renovation of the Lourie Common Room in the Laboratory for Nuclear Science (LNS), along with graduate student fellowship support, which is a top need for the Department. When asked what made him get involved in supporting the Department, he replied, “Simply put, I would not be who I am or where I am today without the experience of MIT. I feel tremendous gratitude towards the Institute that exposed me to so much, taught me so much, and allowed me the opportunity to work with so many brilliant, caring and encouraging people. I am thrilled to give back to those who gave me so much.”

Robert knows the importance of basic science research and how graduate fellowships help with that. He encourages others to support the Physics Department. “Basic science is one of the highest forms of human endeavor and MIT’s Physics Department is unrivaled in the excellence of its pursuit. It is a privilege to be able to participate by means of my support. More practically, financial support, particularly in the form of fellowships, can make a big difference in the life of a budding young scientist. It allows earlier and deeper involvement in their research. If you yourself were once the recipient of a graduate fellowship, take a moment to remember its importance to you.”

TITLE: 2030STEM Fellowship 2026: Apply for a US$10,000 Career Development Award for STEM Researchers and Professionals

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the 2030STEM Fellowship 2026, a career-development opportunity designed to support early- to mid-career researchers and professionals working across science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and related STEM fields.

For the 2026 cycle, 2030STEM is seeking five STEM professionals to serve as Fellows, with each selected Fellow receiving a US$10,000 award that can be used to advance their professional career. The fellowship is intended to provide flexible career-development support while recognizing STEM professionals who demonstrate leadership, community building, knowledge translation, and the potential to contribute to meaningful change within the STEM ecosystem.

The funding can support a range of professional-development needs, including conference participation, research-related expenses, childcare, and other costs connected with career advancement. Rather than prescribing one single route to professional development, the program acknowledges that STEM professionals may face different financial, institutional, professional, and personal barriers at different stages of their careers.

2030STEM Fellowship 2026 at a Glance

Application Status

The current application form does not display a formal closing date. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that applications will remain open indefinitely and should consider submitting as early as possible after confirming that they meet the intended applicant profile.

What Is the 2030STEM Fellowship?

2030STEM describes the initiative as a catalytic resource intended to advance the careers of STEM researchers and professionals.

The central idea behind the fellowship is that scientific and technological progress depends not only on institutions, laboratories and funding mechanisms but also on the people conducting research, communicating scientific knowledge, building professional communities and providing leadership.

The program therefore seeks professionals who can advance their own careers while also contributing to improvements in the broader culture and structure of STEM.

According to the 2026 application, successful candidates are expected to have demonstrated a strong history in three important areas:

Building community.

Translating knowledge.

Demonstrating innovative leadership in STEM.

These elements indicate that applicants should present themselves not simply as technically qualified scientists or professionals but as individuals whose work has influenced colleagues, communities, institutions, research environments or wider audiences.

About 2030STEM

2030STEM is an initiative working toward systemic change within science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

Its broader work focuses on areas including:

Full inclusion in STEM.

Leadership development.

Institutional change.

Access to capital.

Professional advancement.

Community development.

Improved pathways for historically underrepresented STEM professionals.

2030STEM states that its work takes a systems-level approach to strengthening professional self-efficacy, STEM and cultural identities, self-advocacy, leadership pathways and institutional structures.

The organization particularly emphasizes increasing representation and leadership opportunities for Black, Latino/a/x, Indigenous and other people of color throughout STEM disciplines and sectors. Its broader strategy includes improving access to professional networks, capital, leadership opportunities and institutional support.

Why the 2030STEM Fellowship Matters

Career advancement in STEM can require resources that traditional research grants, university funding or employer budgets do not always cover.

Researchers and professionals may need financial support to:

Attend important scientific conferences.

Conduct or advance research.

Access professional-development opportunities.

Build collaborations.

Travel to laboratories, institutions or meetings.

Obtain equipment or other resources connected with professional advancement.

Manage childcare responsibilities while participating in professional activities.

Strengthen their professional networks.

Explore new research directions.

Position themselves for future leadership opportunities.

The 2026 fellowship addresses this challenge by providing selected professionals with US$10,000 toward their career development.

Importantly, the application itself specifically identifies conference travel, research expenses and childcare as examples of potential career-development needs.

How Much Funding Is Available?

Each selected 2030STEM Fellow will receive:

US$10,000 toward career advancement.

The 2026 call states that five STEM professionals are being sought for the fellowship.

This represents a potential combined allocation of US$50,000 across the five selected Fellows, although applicants should understand that the official application describes the award individually as US$10,000 for each Fellow.

What Can the US$10,000 Be Used For?

The fellowship is designed around career development rather than one narrowly prescribed research project.

The application specifically provides examples including:

Conference Travel

Funding could help a Fellow participate in professional or scientific conferences that are important for:

Presenting research.

Networking with collaborators.

Learning about emerging developments.

Meeting prospective mentors.

Connecting with employers or research institutions.

Building visibility within a specialist field.

Research Expenses

The award may also contribute to expenses associated with advancing the Fellow’s research or professional work.

The application does not provide an exhaustive list of eligible research costs, so applicants should explain clearly how their proposed expense will contribute to their professional advancement.

Childcare

One particularly notable aspect of the fellowship is the explicit recognition of childcare as a potential career-development expense.

Professional travel, conferences, fieldwork and other career activities can create additional care responsibilities. By explicitly mentioning childcare, the fellowship recognizes that career barriers are not limited to laboratory or academic costs.

Other Career-Development Needs

The application uses the phrase “including but not limited to,” indicating that the stated examples are not necessarily the only possible uses.

Applicants should therefore identify the career-development expenditure that is most relevant to their circumstances and clearly explain how the US$10,000 would produce a meaningful professional outcome.

What Type of Applicants Is 2030STEM Looking For?

The 2026 call specifically describes its target group as early- to mid-career STEM researchers and professionals.

The strongest candidates are expected to demonstrate a history of:

Building meaningful professional or scientific communities.

Communicating or translating knowledge.

Exercising innovative leadership.

Advancing science or STEM practice.

Supporting broader improvements within STEM environments.

Applicants should therefore think beyond conventional achievements such as publications, degrees or job titles.

The fellowship questions suggest that reviewers are interested in understanding:

Where the applicant wants their career to go.

What motivates their STEM career.

How the applicant contributes to other people or communities.

How they communicate knowledge.

What kind of leadership they demonstrate.

How funding would change or accelerate their career trajectory.

2030STEM’s Approach to STEM Inclusion

The broader mission of 2030STEM is closely connected with improving representation and opportunity across the STEM ecosystem.

The organization argues that STEM institutions benefit when professionals from different backgrounds participate fully in scientific research, decision-making and leadership.

Its stated work places substantial emphasis on improving opportunities for Black, Latino/a/x, Indigenous and other people of color in STEM, including by addressing structural barriers that can affect recruitment, retention, promotion, leadership and access to financial resources.

However, applicants should distinguish the organization’s broader mission from the formal requirements displayed on the current 2026 application form. The live 2026 form does not present a race or ethnicity field as an explicit eligibility condition.

Application Requirements

The 2030STEM Fellowship application requests a combination of personal details, professional information, career reflections and supporting documentation.

Applicants should be prepared to provide the following.

1. Full Name

Applicants must provide their first and last name.

Use the same professional name that appears on your CV, publications, institutional profile and other professional records wherever possible.

2. Email Address

A valid email address is required.

Applicants should preferably use an email account that they monitor regularly because fellowship communications and potential follow-up regarding the selection process may be sent to this address.

3. Phone Number

Applicants are required to provide a valid telephone number.

4. Highest Level of Education

The application asks applicants to identify their highest completed level of education.

The current 2026 form does not, within the publicly accessible text reviewed, state a specific minimum degree requirement.

Applicants should therefore report their educational background accurately rather than assuming that the qualification requirements from a previous fellowship cycle automatically apply to the 2026 call.

5. Current Field or Area of Expertise

Applicants must state their current field or professional area of expertise.

This is an important part of establishing the applicant’s connection to STEM.

Applicants should use a specific description where possible. Instead of simply writing “science,” for example, an applicant may identify areas such as:

Molecular biology.

Environmental science.

Artificial intelligence.

Engineering.

Chemistry.

Astronomy.

Biomedical research.

Climate science.

Data science.

Mathematics.

Physics.

Public health research.

Computer science.

Scientific communication.

Engineering education.

The exact field should reflect the applicant’s genuine professional background.

6. Current Affiliation

Applicants must provide their present institutional or professional affiliation.

This could potentially include a university, research institution, government entity, company, laboratory, nonprofit organization or other professional organization, depending on the applicant’s circumstances.

Five-Year Career Vision

One of the application questions asks applicants to explain where they see themselves professionally over the next five years.

Applicants are also asked to discuss:

The type of science they expect to be doing.

The people or types of professionals with whom they hope to collaborate.

This question gives applicants an opportunity to demonstrate that they have a meaningful career direction.

A strong response should connect:

Current position → professional development need → fellowship support → five-year objective.

Applicants should avoid writing only about a desired job title. Instead, they can describe the scientific or professional impact they want to create.

Explain the Pivotal Moment Behind Your STEM Career

Applicants are asked to:

Share a pivotal moment or experience that significantly influenced their decision to pursue their current STEM career path.

This question is more personal than a conventional CV-based application question.

The objective appears to be understanding the applicant’s motivation, trajectory and relationship with their chosen STEM field.

Applicants may consider discussing an experience such as:

Exposure to an important scientific problem.

A research experience.

A mentor who influenced their career.

A community challenge that inspired their work.

An academic breakthrough.

An internship or professional experience.

A personal experience that led to a scientific question.

A problem the applicant became determined to solve.

The response should remain authentic and directly connected to the applicant’s career development.

Demonstrate Community Building, Knowledge Translation and Leadership

This is one of the most important components of the application.

Applicants must explain how they or their work have contributed to:

Building community.

Translating knowledge.

Innovative leadership in STEM.

Applicants should support their answer with concrete examples.

Potential evidence may include:

Creating research networks.

Mentoring students or younger researchers.

Leading professional groups.

Developing interdisciplinary collaborations.

Communicating scientific research to non-specialist audiences.

Working with communities affected by scientific or technological issues.

Translating research findings into policy or practice.

Developing new scientific initiatives.

Creating inclusive professional environments.

Leading institutional changes.

Developing innovative research methods or approaches.

Simply describing yourself as a leader will generally be less persuasive than demonstrating what you led, who benefited and what changed.

Explain How You Would Use the US$10,000

Applicants are specifically asked:

If selected, how will you use the funds toward advancing your career?

This response should be clear, realistic and connected with professional development.

A strong answer could explain:

What the funding would purchase or support.

Why that particular expenditure is necessary.

Why existing institutional resources cannot fully cover it, where applicable.

What professional outcome the expenditure would produce.

How that outcome connects with the applicant’s longer-term STEM career.

Applicants should avoid treating the US$10,000 simply as a financial prize. The application frames the funding specifically around career advancement.

Three Professional References Are Required

Applicants must provide the name and email address of three references.

Importantly, the application states that references will only be contacted if the applicant progresses to the second round.

Applicants should therefore select references carefully.

Suitable references will generally be people who can credibly discuss the applicant’s:

STEM expertise.

Research or professional accomplishments.

Leadership.

Community contributions.

Collaboration.

Communication skills.

Professional potential.

Applicants should obtain permission from references before listing their contact information and make sure the email addresses entered in the application are accurate.

Resume or CV Requirement

Applicants are also asked to upload a resume or curriculum vitae.

The CV should reinforce the story presented throughout the application.

Relevant sections could include:

Education.

Current position.

Research experience.

Professional experience.

Publications.

Presentations.

Fellowships.

Awards.

Grants.

Professional leadership.

Community engagement.

Science communication.

Mentoring.

Professional societies.

Relevant projects.

Applicants should ensure that dates, affiliations and accomplishments mentioned in their written responses are consistent with the information appearing on their CV.

Additional Information Section

The application concludes with an optional question asking whether there is anything else the selection team should know about the applicant.

Applicants should use this space strategically.

Rather than repeating information already stated elsewhere, it may be useful for providing context that is genuinely relevant to the application but has not been captured by the previous questions.

How Applicants Can Strengthen Their Application

The current application does not publish a numerical evaluation rubric. The following points should therefore be treated as practical application guidance rather than official scoring criteria.

Demonstrate Impact, Not Only Achievement

Instead of simply listing accomplishments, explain the effect of those accomplishments.

For example:

Who benefited?

What problem was addressed?

What changed?

What was created?

What did the applicant personally contribute?

Connect Your Career Vision With the Funding

The five-year career question and the funding-use question should support one another.

If an applicant wants to become a leader in a particular research area, the proposed use of funding should logically move them toward that objective.

Provide Evidence of Community Building

Since community building is specifically mentioned by 2030STEM, applicants should identify concrete examples of how they have supported colleagues, students, professional communities or other stakeholders.

Explain Knowledge Translation

Knowledge translation can involve turning specialist research into information that can be understood or applied by:

Policymakers.

Communities.

Students.

Industry.

Healthcare professionals.

Educators.

Other researchers.

The general public.

Applicants should demonstrate actual communication or application rather than merely saying that science communication is important.

Show Innovative Leadership

Leadership does not necessarily require holding a senior management position.

Applicants may demonstrate leadership by initiating projects, solving problems, creating collaborations, mentoring others, changing institutional practices or introducing new scientific approaches.

Previous 2030STEM Fellowship Context

2030STEM previously operated the 2030STEM × Burroughs Wellcome Fund Fellowship.

The 2025 program also focused on advancing early- to mid-career STEM professionals and provided US$10,000 to Fellows.

The earlier fellowship included a two-year professional-development structure involving cohort meetings, career-development workshops and access to the 2030STEM Champions network.

However, these specific features are not stated on the current 2026 application form, so applicants should not assume that every condition, benefit or eligibility rule from the 2025 cycle applies automatically to the 2026 fellowship.

The current application should always take precedence for the 2026 competition.

Important Note About Eligibility for 2026

The archived 2025 fellowship webpage required applicants to be late-stage PhD candidates or hold a PhD or graduate equivalent such as an MD or JD, and it stated that only U.S.-based professionals would be considered.

The current 2026 application form does not display those restrictions.

Instead, it asks applicants to provide their highest education level, STEM field and current affiliation.

Therefore, applicants should not automatically treat the archived 2025 requirements as confirmed 2026 eligibility requirements.

Anyone uncertain about eligibility should rely on the current application and any additional instructions issued directly by 2030STEM.

Application Deadline

No application deadline is stated on the live 2030STEM Fellowship Application 2026 form reviewed on September 4, 2026.

Because the organization is selecting only five Fellows, interested candidates should prepare and submit their applications promptly rather than waiting for an unconfirmed closing date.

Applicants should also recheck the application page before submitting in case a deadline or additional instructions are subsequently added.

How to Apply for the 2030STEM Fellowship 2026

Applicants can follow these steps:

Review the fellowship description carefully.

Prepare your current resume or CV.

Confirm your highest educational qualification.

Clearly identify your current STEM field or area of expertise.

Provide your current professional or institutional affiliation.

Develop a clear five-year career vision.

Identify a pivotal experience that influenced your STEM career.

Prepare examples demonstrating community building.

Explain how you translate scientific or technical knowledge.

Demonstrate innovative leadership.

Develop a specific plan for using the US$10,000 award.

Select three appropriate professional references.

Obtain their correct names and email addresses.

Complete all required sections of the online form.

Upload your resume or CV.

Review the application carefully.

Submit the application while the form remains open.

Application and reference link:

Apply for the 2030STEM Fellowship 2026

The shortened reference link directs applicants to the official 2030STEM Fellowship Application 2026 hosted on Jotform.

Why STEM Professionals Should Consider Applying

The 2030STEM Fellowship differs from many conventional research opportunities because its focus is the professional themselves and their career advancement, rather than solely funding a tightly defined research proposal.

The US$10,000 support can potentially help selected Fellows overcome practical barriers that prevent them from pursuing important professional opportunities.

For an early- or mid-career STEM professional, access to funding at the right stage could help support research, participation in an important conference, collaboration-building or another strategic professional-development activity.

At the same time, the application clearly signals that 2030STEM is interested in people who contribute beyond their individual technical work.

Applicants who can demonstrate a combination of scientific capability, professional ambition, community engagement, communication and innovative leadership may be particularly aligned with the program’s stated objectives.

Application Checklist

Before submitting, applicants should make sure they have:

Full name.

Active email address.

Valid telephone number.

Highest level of education.

Current field or area of expertise.

Current professional affiliation.

A clear five-year career vision.

Information about the type of science or STEM work they plan to pursue.

Potential collaborators or collaboration goals.

A meaningful pivotal STEM career experience.

Examples of community building.

Examples of knowledge translation.

Examples of innovative leadership.

A clear plan for using the US$10,000.

Names of three references.

Email addresses of all three references.

Updated resume or CV.

Any useful additional information not already covered elsewhere in the application.

Conclusion

The 2030STEM Fellowship 2026 provides an important career-development opportunity for early- to mid-career researchers and professionals seeking resources to advance their work and expand their impact within STEM.

2030STEM is selecting five Fellows, with each successful applicant receiving US$10,000 toward career advancement. Potential uses identified in the application include conference travel, research expenses, childcare and other career-development needs.

The application places significant emphasis on more than academic credentials alone. Candidates are asked to demonstrate their career vision, motivation for pursuing STEM, contribution to community building, ability to translate knowledge and record of innovative leadership.

Applicants are also required to explain how the US$10,000 would advance their career, provide three professional references and upload a resume or CV.

No deadline is currently displayed on the live 2026 application form, so prospective applicants should consider applying as soon as they have prepared a strong submission rather than relying on an unconfirmed closing date.

TITLE: About USIEF
