About USIEF

The United States – India Educational Foundation (USIEF) is dedicated to fostering mutual understanding between the people of India and the United States through educational exchanges involving outstanding scholars, professionals, and students.

Since its establishment in 1950, USIEF has awarded over 22,000 fellowships, funded by the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. Department of Education, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), and other key entities.

USIEF’s core activities include

Administering Fulbright-Nehru and other fellowships for Indian and American students, faculty, researchers and professionals.

Advancing U.S. leadership in higher education, research, and innovation through EducationUSA India, a U.S. Mission-supported platform promoting academic engagement between India and the United States.

Serving as a resource for fostering linkages between higher education institutions in the United States and India.

Our offices in Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata host academic and professional workshops, forums, mentoring sessions, and policy dialogues on contemporary issues, connecting academic communities, higher education institutions, and civil society in both countries. We actively engage Fulbright alumni in these sessions, amplifying the impact of their outstanding work across various disciplines.

As we celebrate 75 years of fostering educational exchange and mutual understanding, USIEF remains dedicated to expanding opportunities for scholars, students, and institutions in both countries. Marking this milestone on February 2, 2025, we reaffirm our commitment to strengthening the U.S.-India educational partnership. Through Fulbright and EducationUSA programs, we continue to support academic excellence, facilitate cross-cultural dialogue, and advance shared priorities in higher education, working closely with both the Indian and U.S. governments to shape the future of global learning and collaboration.

TITLE: KOHA Training Workshop in Malawi

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) in collaboration with Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources (LUANAR) in Malawi presents a training Workshop on KOHA (an open source Integrated Library Management System) to be held at the Crossroads hotel in Lilongwe, Malawi from September 3- 6, 2018.

The KOHA Workshop is for both Librarians and library IT support staff of University libraries, and other Information and Knowledge Management professionals especially those from Southern and Eastern countries of the continent and beyond.

The objective of the workshop is to unbundle the KOHA open source Integrated Library System (ILMS) to participants and institutions.

Koha is a highly sophisticated web-based ILS, with a SQL database backend and accessible via Z39.50. Koha has a highly configurable and adaptable user interface that can also support many languages. Koha has most of the features that would be expected in an ILS, including:

Web 2.0 facilities like tagging, comment, Social sharing and RSS feeds

Union catalogue facility

Customizable search

Circulation and borrower management

Full acquisitions system including budgets and pricing information

Ability to cope with any number of branches, patrons, patron categories, item categories, items, currencies and other data

Reading lists for members

UNICODE and library standards compliant

Export/import and backup/restoration facilities

This workshop will also introduce the Linux operating system to the participants to acquaint them with the installation of Koha on server class machines and provide extensive hands-on-training for both librarians and the library IT support staff. Participants will be equipped with capacity to manage Koha as LMS at institutions with large collections.

The registration fee for the 4-day event is $400 for AAU Member institutions and $500 for Non- AAU member Institutions. This will cover workshop attendance fee, snacks and lunches, e-training material and other logistics.

Interested participants are kindly requested to register online at https://www.research.net/r/KOHA-3-09-2018

For further information please contact Millicent Afriyie via email makyei@aau.org, Cc: Abednego Coeletey aclortey@aau.org and Nodumo Dhlamini ndhlamini@aau.org

Supporting sustainable Institutional Changes to promote Citizen Science in Science and Technology

TIME4CS (Supporting sustainable Institutional Changes to promote Citizen Science in Science and Technology) aims at supporting and facilitating the implementation of sustainable Institutional Changes in Research Performing Organisations (RPOs) to promote Public Engagement (citizens and citizens associations) and Citizen Science in science and technology. TIME4CS has identified 4 Intervention Areas (IAs) that alone or combined can stimulate the Institutional Changes necessary to promote Public Engagement in R&I activities: i) Research; ii) Education and Awareness; iii) Support resources and Infrastructure; iv) Policy and Assessment.

Institutional Changes should be: i) irreversible, ii) comprehensive, iii) inclusive and iv) contextualized. Bearing this in mind, TIME4CS will establish a knowledge transfer and mutual learning programme between Front-Runners (FRs) and Implementers (Is). The first ones are RPOs with a comprehensive expertise in Citizen Science and that have already undergone Institutional Changes. The latter are TIME4CS beneficiaries still in the early stages of the implementation of Institutional Changes to support Citizen Science, willing to face the challenge of introducing CS activities in their structures. The mutual learning programme will lead to the development of specific and tailored roadmaps for each implementing organisation including a set of specific and detailed actions to follow (Grounding Actions). The whole process will be supported by two facilitator partners supporting the knowledge transfer and the definition of the Grounding Actions.

European Facility for Airborne Research (EUFAR)

EUFAR is the European distributed infrastructure for airborne research. Established in 2000, it serves as a network for the European airborne research community, aiming to support scientists by providing access to research aircraft and instruments not readily available in their respective countries. This fosters equal opportunities for scientists across Europe to conduct various atmospheric and in situ measurements onboard research aircraft.

Over time, EUFAR has expanded its scope, incorporating new activities and objectives to establish itself as the primary network and portal for airborne research in Europe’s environmental and geosciences field. The organization’s initiatives now encompass organizing summer schools and expert workshops, serving as an interactive information hub, maintaining a central data archive, and developing tools and standards for data collection, processing, and analysis. Through these efforts, EUFAR continually enhances the operational environment for conducting airborne research.

TITLE: BOLD Science Communication Fellowship 2027: Fully Remote Global Fellowship with CHF 5,000 Stipend

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship 2027, an international, fully remote opportunity designed for early-career researchers working in the field of children’s learning and development.

The six-month program provides selected researchers with professional training, expert mentorship, practical science communication experience, opportunities to publish their work for a global audience, and a CHF 5,000 stipend to support the time and resources required to participate in the Fellowship.

Launched by BOLD as the platform celebrates a decade of communicating scientific knowledge about child learning and development, the Fellowship seeks researchers who want to take their scientific expertise beyond traditional academic audiences and make evidence-based knowledge accessible to caregivers, educators, and other people who directly support children.

The Fellowship is fully remote and part-time, meaning participants can take part from anywhere in the world while continuing their existing research or professional responsibilities. Up to three researchers will be selected for the inaugural Fellowship cohort.

Applications opened on 1 September 2026 and will close on 31 October 2026.

About BOLD

BOLD is a global platform dedicated to sharing scientific knowledge that can improve children’s learning and development.

The platform connects researchers, journalists, practitioners, educators, and other specialists interested in understanding how children learn, develop, and thrive.

Rather than limiting important scientific findings to academic journals or specialist conferences, BOLD aims to make rigorous research understandable and useful to wider audiences.

Its content focuses on evidence-based information that caregivers and educators can use to make informed decisions when supporting children and young people.

BOLD covers areas connected with:

Child and youth development

Learning and education

Psychology

Neuroscience

Genetics

Mental and physical health

Learning environments

Education systems

Technology and learning

Parenting and childcare

Teaching methods

Equity and inclusion

Society and child development

BOLD describes itself as a global scientific knowledge platform that empowers caregivers and educators with information and tools that can help children learn and develop. Its wider network includes researchers, journalists, and practitioners committed to communicating current scientific thinking in accessible ways.

About the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship was created to help researchers become more effective communicators of scientific knowledge.

Researchers often produce valuable evidence that could influence education, parenting, child development, and public understanding. However, academic research can be difficult for non-specialist audiences to understand because findings are commonly communicated through technical papers, specialist terminology, statistical language, and academic conferences.

The BOLD Fellowship aims to help bridge this gap.

Selected Fellows will learn how to translate complex scientific ideas into accessible and engaging information for audiences outside academia.

This includes communicating with people such as:

Parents and caregivers

Teachers

Education professionals

Practitioners

Members of the public

Other audiences interested in child learning and development

During the six-month program, Fellows will receive dedicated mentoring and training while simultaneously putting those skills into practice by creating content for BOLD’s audience.

Rather than functioning only as a classroom-style training course, the Fellowship combines professional development with real publishing experience. Fellows will develop articles, interviews, videos, or other agreed content that can ultimately appear on BOLD’s website and social media platforms.

BOLD Science Communication Fellowship Stipend

One of the major features of the program is its financial support.

Each selected Fellow will receive a CHF 5,000 stipend.

According to BOLD, the stipend is intended to cover the time and resources participants invest in fulfilling the requirements of the Fellowship.

Payment will be made in two stages:

50% of the stipend will be awarded when the Fellowship begins.

50% will be awarded at the end of the Fellowship after the Fellow successfully completes the required activities, tasks, and milestones.

This means the total available financial support for each Fellow is CHF 5,000.

Applicants should understand that this funding is connected to participation and completion of the Fellowship requirements rather than being described as an unrestricted research grant.

Fully Remote and Part-Time Program

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship has been structured to make participation possible for researchers based around the world.

The program is:

Fully remote: Participants do not need to relocate to another country or travel to a physical BOLD office to complete the Fellowship.

Part-time: The Fellowship has been designed to fit alongside a participant’s existing research or professional role.

BOLD expects Fellows to dedicate approximately six hours per month to content development and participation in virtual training sessions.

This relatively flexible structure means selected researchers can continue their existing academic or professional commitments while participating in the program.

Fellowship Duration

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship will run for approximately six months.

The official program dates are:

Fellowship begins: 4 January 2027

Fellowship ends: 30 June 2027

Fellows will also be expected to participate in a virtual introduction during January 2027.

How Many Fellows Will Be Selected?

The program is highly focused and will select up to three researchers.

These researchers will participate in the six-month Fellowship while receiving individualized training, mentorship, and opportunities to develop public-facing content.

Because only a small number of researchers will be selected, prospective applicants should prepare their application materials carefully and demonstrate both their scientific expertise and their interest in communicating research to audiences beyond academia.

What Selected BOLD Fellows Will Receive

Successful applicants will gain access to several professional-development opportunities covering writing, editing, public communication, and multimedia science communication.

1. Writing Workshop with BOLD’s Editor-in-Chief

Fellows will participate in a writing workshop led by BOLD’s Editor-in-Chief.

The workshop is expected to help researchers improve their ability to translate scientific concepts into clear and compelling language for general audiences.

Academic writing and public science communication require different approaches. A research paper may prioritize methodology, precision, technical terminology, and citations, while public communication must often explain the same concepts clearly without overwhelming readers with specialist language.

The workshop will therefore provide practical experience in adapting scientific knowledge for non-academic audiences.

2. Editing Training

Fellows will receive training in editing both:

Their own work

The work of their colleagues

Learning to edit effectively is an important science communication skill because good communication involves more than generating an initial draft.

Researchers must learn how to identify unnecessary complexity, clarify arguments, improve structure, strengthen explanations, and ensure scientific accuracy while making material understandable to non-specialists.

The peer-editing element can also help Fellows develop skills in giving constructive editorial feedback.

3. Monthly Writing Club

Selected Fellows will participate in a monthly writing club with the BOLD team.

This provides a regular structure for practicing science communication, receiving input, developing ideas, and remaining engaged with the Fellowship community throughout the six-month program.

4. Training in Science Communication Videos

Modern science communication increasingly takes place through digital and social media.

The Fellowship therefore includes expert training on producing science communication videos for social media.

This aspect of the program can help researchers learn how to explain complex topics in formats suitable for platforms where audiences often consume information quickly and visually.

Participants can consequently develop communication capabilities extending beyond traditional academic writing.

5. Training in Writing for General Audiences

Fellows will also receive expert instruction in writing scientific information for general audiences.

This training is particularly important because the primary audience for BOLD includes caregivers and educators rather than only scientists.

Participants will need to communicate evidence accurately without assuming that readers have specialist knowledge of statistics, psychology, neuroscience, education research, or other technical fields.

What Fellows Are Expected to Do

Participation in the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship comes with specific responsibilities.

Selected researchers will be expected to:

Attend a virtual introduction in January 2027.

Dedicate approximately six hours per month to content development and participation in virtual training activities.

Produce at least three pieces of content during the Fellowship.

Depending on discussions with BOLD’s Editor-in-Chief, these outputs may include:

Articles

Interviews

Videos

The final pieces will be published through BOLD’s website and social media channels.

This publication component is particularly valuable because Fellows are not simply practicing communication exercises privately. They have the opportunity to produce work intended for real audiences.

Who Can Apply for the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship?

The Fellowship is intended for scientists researching children’s learning and development.

According to the official eligibility criteria, applicants must:

Be a scientist studying an aspect of children’s learning and development

Be an active researcher

Be no more than 10 years post-PhD

However, an important aspect of the eligibility rules is that applicants do not need to hold a PhD to apply.

This means the program is aimed broadly at early-career researchers rather than being exclusively restricted to people who already hold a doctoral qualification.

Do You Need a PhD to Apply?

No.

BOLD explicitly states that applicants do not need a PhD to apply.

The reference to being no more than 10 years post-PhD establishes an upper career-stage limit for researchers who have completed a doctorate, but it does not make a doctorate mandatory.

Applicants must nevertheless be active researchers working on areas related to children’s learning and development.

Relevant Research Fields

BOLD does not restrict eligibility to one narrowly defined academic discipline.

Researchers may potentially work across fields connected to children’s learning and development, provided their research is relevant to the Fellowship’s focus.

Potential areas may include, depending on the applicant’s research topic:

Developmental psychology

Education

Educational psychology

Neuroscience

Cognitive science

Child development

Learning sciences

Language development

Mental health

Child and adolescent development

Education technology

Social development

Behavioral science

Genetics and development

Teaching and learning

Public health topics connected to child development

The key requirement is that the applicant is a scientist studying an aspect of children’s learning and development. Applicants should therefore explain clearly how their research connects with BOLD’s mission and audience.

Applicants from All Countries Can Apply

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship is a global opportunity.

BOLD specifically states that applicants are welcome from anywhere in the world.

Because the Fellowship is conducted remotely, successful candidates can participate without relocating internationally.

There is no country-specific restriction stated on the official Fellowship page.

This gives eligible researchers from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, and other regions an opportunity to compete for the Fellowship, provided they satisfy the research and career-stage criteria.

Application Requirements

Applications must be submitted in English through BOLD’s official application form.

Applicants need to prepare three principal components.

1. Science Communication Sample

Applicants must provide either a sample article or video explaining a scientific concept relevant to BOLD in a way that is accessible to caregivers.

The recommended maximum length is:

Approximately 500 words for an article, or

Approximately three minutes for a video

Applicants who have already written or presented something for a public audience can provide a link to that work.

Those who do not already have a suitable public-facing science communication example can instead upload a written piece.

2. Written Statement

Applicants must submit a written statement of up to 500 words.

The statement should explain:

Why the applicant wants to participate in the Fellowship

Why the applicant believes they would be a good fit for the program

This is an important opportunity to demonstrate motivation, communication ability, alignment with BOLD’s mission, and a genuine interest in translating research for caregivers and educators.

3. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must also submit their CV.

The CV should include any previous science communication experience.

Researchers who have communicated science through public articles, talks, videos, podcasts, workshops, social media, outreach events, teaching, or related activities may therefore want to ensure that relevant experience is clearly presented.

Application Language

All required application materials must be submitted in English.

This includes the science communication sample, written statement, and associated application materials submitted through the official form.

Who Will Review the Applications?

Applications will be reviewed by:

Annie Brookman-Byrne, Editor-in-Chief of BOLD

and

Gemma Wirz, Learning Outreach Lead at the Jacobs Foundation.

The involvement of both editorial and learning-outreach leadership reflects the Fellowship’s emphasis on combining scientific quality with effective communication for public audiences.

BOLD Science Communication Fellowship 2027 Timeline

Applicants should take note of the following official dates:

1 September 2026: Applications open

31 October 2026: Applications close

November 2026: Applications reviewed

1 December 2026: Selected Fellows informed

4 January 2027: Fellowship begins

30 June 2027: Fellowship ends

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship is:

31 October 2026

Applicants should prepare and submit their materials before the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

Because a science communication sample and a tailored statement are required, candidates should allow sufficient time to prepare strong materials that demonstrate their ability to explain scientific concepts clearly.

How to Apply for the BOLD Science Communication Fellowship

Applications are submitted online through the official application form linked from BOLD’s Fellowship page.

Before beginning the application, candidates should prepare:

A science communication article of ideally no more than 500 words or a video of ideally no more than three minutes

A written statement of up to 500 words explaining their motivation and suitability

A current CV including relevant science communication experience

Applicants should ensure that all application materials are prepared in English.

The official Fellowship page provides access to the application form and should be used as the primary source for application instructions and any future updates.

Why This Fellowship Is Valuable for Early-Career Researchers

Scientific expertise alone does not guarantee that research will influence practice.

For evidence to benefit families, educators, policymakers, or communities, research findings need to be communicated in a way that non-specialists can understand and use.

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship addresses this challenge by giving scientists practical experience in translating their research expertise into accessible public communication.

The combination of mentoring, writing instruction, editing practice, video training, publishing opportunities, and financial support makes the Fellowship particularly relevant for researchers who want to develop a stronger public-facing profile.

For an early-career scientist, these skills may be useful across multiple professional pathways, including:

Academic research

Public engagement

Science journalism

Education

Research communications

Policy engagement

Knowledge translation

Non-profit organizations

Public-facing science platforms

Research outreach

Opportunity to Build a Published Science Communication Portfolio

Another significant feature of the Fellowship is that participants will create at least three pieces of content for BOLD.

Depending on the format agreed with the Editor-in-Chief, these may include articles, interviews, or videos.

Having published examples of science communication can help researchers demonstrate that they are able to translate technical knowledge for wider audiences.

For researchers interested in science communication, public engagement, journalism, policy translation, or outreach roles, this type of portfolio can be professionally valuable.

Commitment Required from Fellows

The program is intended to complement, rather than replace, a researcher’s existing professional role.

Fellows should expect to commit approximately six hours each month to training and content-development activities.

However, applicants should not interpret the relatively modest monthly time requirement as meaning that participation requires little effort.

Successful Fellows will be expected to:

Engage seriously with training

Participate in the program’s virtual activities

Develop publishable content

Respond to editorial feedback

Complete agreed milestones

Produce at least three final pieces of content

Completion of required tasks and milestones is also relevant to receiving the second half of the CHF 5,000 stipend.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Applicants should pay particular attention to the science communication sample because it provides direct evidence of their ability to explain research to a non-specialist audience.

A strong submission should generally aim to:

Explain one clear scientific idea

Minimize unnecessary technical terminology

Define technical concepts that cannot be avoided

Make the topic relevant to caregivers or educators

Maintain scientific accuracy

Use clear and engaging language

Demonstrate an understanding of BOLD’s audience

The motivation statement should complement the communication sample rather than simply repeating the applicant’s CV.

Applicants should explain why science communication matters to them, what they hope to learn from the Fellowship, how their research relates to children’s learning and development, and how they intend to use the communication skills gained through the program.

Key Details at a Glance

Program: BOLD Science Communication Fellowship

Cohort: 2027

Host: BOLD

Supported by: Jacobs Foundation

Program format: Fully remote

Participation: Part-time

Number of Fellows: Up to three researchers

Stipend: CHF 5,000

Payment arrangement: 50% at the beginning and 50% after successful completion of required Fellowship tasks and milestones

Approximate commitment: Six hours per month

Program start: 4 January 2027

Program end: 30 June 2027

Application opens: 1 September 2026

Application deadline: 31 October 2026

Application language: English

Geographic eligibility: Worldwide

PhD required: No

Main target group: Active researchers studying children’s learning and development

Career-stage limit: No more than 10 years post-PhD for applicants who hold a PhD

Required outputs: At least three articles, interviews, or videos agreed with the Editor-in-Chief and published through BOLD’s website and social media channels.

Conclusion

The BOLD Science Communication Fellowship 2027 offers an excellent opportunity for early-career researchers studying children’s learning and development to build practical skills in communicating science beyond academia.

With a CHF 5,000 stipend, expert training in writing and editing, guidance on science communication videos, a monthly writing club, professional mentoring, and opportunities to publish content for BOLD’s international audience, the program combines structured learning with hands-on communication experience.

Its fully remote and part-time format also makes the Fellowship accessible to eligible researchers around the world without requiring relocation or interruption of their existing research careers.

Applicants do not need to hold a PhD, although they must be active researchers studying an aspect of children’s learning and development and fall within the program’s early-career criteria.

Applications opened on 1 September 2026 and the final deadline is 31 October 2026. Successful Fellows will be informed on 1 December 2026, with the Fellowship beginning on 4 January 2027 and continuing until 30 June 2027.

Researchers who are passionate about making scientific evidence understandable and useful to caregivers, educators, and wider public audiences are encouraged to prepare their applications carefully and apply before the deadline.

TITLE: Making a Deeper Impact in African Higher Education Through Technology

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Technology and technologically facilitated means of working has changed the work systems and operations of the African higher education sector, following an increase in its adoption since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, along with its various restrictions. The Association of African Universities, for instance, moved most of its physical events – workshops, meetings, conferences, webinars etc, to virtual platforms. Platforms such as Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams, were among those adopted. The result has been a tremendous increase in the number of stakeholders the AAU engaged and impacted through these virtual means of collaboration.

On its ZOOM platform alone, 193 webinars and virtual workshops were hosted with a total of 40,163 participants being recorded between 1st July 2020 to 30th June 2021. In contrast, the figures reported in the AAU’s Annual Report for the previous year (July 2019 -June 2020), showed that 28 physical workshops were held with a total of 1,156 higher education stakeholders benefiting from those capacity building interventions. The percentage increase stands at a whooping figure of over 3,400%. This implies that more people got involved in AAU’s programmes and activities, more people benefited and had the opportunity to contribute towards AAU’s vision and goals of transforming Africa’s higher education sector.

Again, the ZOOM platform statistics indicated that a total of 931 all-type meetings were hosted between July 2020 and June 2021 – amounting to 2,377,274 meeting minutes and 103,134 participants. These statistics are only one example of how the Association has made deeper impact and worked smarter through technologically facilitated means.

Also worth highlighting is the fact that physical engagements are equally important as some aspects of the higher education work processes are more hands on and require a face-to-face engagement. Therefore, where possible, the adoption of blended approaches is a recommended option.

Despite all the downsides of COVID-19, it can be said that institutions have also been presented with opportunities that were largely neglected during the normal times – the adoption of virtual approaches of collaboration in general organisational processes. The convenience and cost effectiveness of technologically facilitated means of working cannot be left unmentioned here.

Additionally, E-learning (the innovative use of digital tools, technologies, and practices during teaching and learning) has been magnified and become very critical for higher education institutions during this COVID-19 period. Learning Management Systems (LMS), which enable universities and educational institutions to plan, assess, facilitate, implement, and monitor the learning and teaching processes of both students and teachers have also now been widely adopted more than ever before.

As part of its contribution, the AAU officially launched a Learning Management System, in collaboration with e-LearnAfrica, called the AAU-eLearnAfricaLMS (https://www.elearnafricalms.com/) in 2021. This platform is supporting the efforts of higher education institutions in Africa, through the provision of FREE eLearning tools to make online education accessible. African Universities can easily adopt this platform without the need to invest in e-learning infrastructure. By the end of 2021, the AAU/eLearn Africa online platform recorded a total of 56 Universities and corporate institutions sign-ups, 83 courses uploaded and 53 Professors signed up, excluding corporate executives who are facilitating various courses on the platform.

Online education is rapidly becoming the norm, and many African Universities are focusing on mainstreaming e-learning. Professors are collaborating across universities thanks to advancements in educational technology. New high-growth technologies have entered the online education marketplace, making learning more interactive.

Again, technology has made it very easy to access publications electronically, increasing the readership of such publications, as compared to hard prints.

Many faculty and students have strived to adopt the requisite skills to facilitate their effective use of technology and the various technological platforms due to the enormous benefits technology offers, including the ability to make them work smarter.

African Higher Education institutions have continued to undertake their core duties of teaching, learning, research, and community engagement, through the support of various mediums including technologically facilitated ones. Simple and widespread technologies such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Television and Radio have been used by African higher education institutions to keep educational activities going on. It is significant to note that technology and technological applications require continuous learning processes and therefore individuals and institutions are encouraged to strive to remain up to date to make a deeper/wider impact in their fields of expertise.

Written By: Miss Selikem Agbadi

National Service Attaché – Ghana Institute of Journalism, Ghana

Article Reviewed by Mrs. Felicia Kuagbedzi & Ms. Nodumo Dhlamini (Directorate of ICT, Communications and Knowledge Management, AAU)

TITLE: EJN Story Grants to Report on Business Responses to Climate Change in Thailand 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: July 19, 2026

Applications are open for the EJN Story Grants to Report on Business Responses to Climate Change in Thailand 2026. Internews’ Earth Journalism Network’s (EJN) Business and Climate and Media Initiative (BCMI) aims to increase the quality and quantity of reporting on the private sector’s contribution to climate change, as well as its role in advancing climate mitigation, adaptation and innovative financing solutions.

EJN is pleased to offer up to 10 story grants of up to EUR 1,500 to selected journalists to produce in-depth reports on business response to climate change in Thailand. In addition to financial support, selected grantees will receive editorial guidance and mentorship from experienced journalists throughout the reporting and production process.

Story Themes

They welcome pitches for stories that focus on, but are not limited to, the following topics:

Business responses to Thailand’s climate policies, including the draft Climate Change Act, Thailand Taxonomy, carbon pricing mechanisms and the country’s pathway toward carbon neutrality and net zero.

How Thai businesses are adapting to international sustainability requirements, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), supply chain due diligence regulations and evolving ESG expectations.

Climate finance and investment, including green and sustainability bonds, blended finance, transition finance and the role of financial institutions in supporting decarbonization.

Carbon markets, including voluntary carbon markets, blue carbon, forest carbon projects and questions of integrity, equity and benefit sharing.

Corporate climate commitments, emissions disclosures and greenwashing, including scrutiny of net-zero claims, offsets and environmental reporting.

Innovative technologies, business models and locally led solutions that help businesses reduce emissions, build climate resilience or accelerate a just transition.

The opportunities and challenges facing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as they navigate the transition to a low-carbon economy.

They particularly encourage proposals that adopt a solutions journalism approach while maintaining rigorous, evidence-based reporting and accountability. Stories should examine not only promising innovations and business practices but also their effectiveness, scalability, trade-offs and unintended consequences.

Grant

They expect to award up to 10 story grants of up to 1,500 EUR each.

Eligibility

Applicants must come from Thailand. While this opportunity is open to all eligible journalists, priority will be given to participants of EJN’s Thailand Business and Climate Net Zero workshop held in June 2026.

Applications are open to journalists working in any medium (online, print, television or radio) and other professional content producers with demonstrated reporting experience. They welcome applications from both early-career and experienced journalists, including freelancers and staff from international, national, local and community-based media organizations.

Applications from teams of journalists are welcome. However, each team must designate one lead applicant, who will serve as the primary point of contact with EJN and, if selected, will be responsible for receiving and administering the grant on behalf of the team.

Applications may be submitted in either English or Thai. Applicants should have a working knowledge of English or arrange for translation support to facilitate communication with EJN staff throughout the grant period.

EJN reserves the right to disqualify applicants found to have engaged in unethical or improper professional conduct, including, but not limited to, submitting AI-generated content as their own work.

Judging Criteria

Applicants should consider the following points when devising their proposals.

Relevance: Does the proposal meet the criteria and objectives of the call? Why does this story matter and to whom? Is the main idea, context and overall value to the target audience clearly defined?

Angle: If the report has been covered, does your proposal bring new insights to the topic or offer a fresh angle?

Reach: Does the proposed media outlet have a wide reach? Journalists publishing their work at outlets that typically restrict content behind paywalls are encouraged to secure commitments to publish from additional outlets, or request an exception to ensure their EJN-supported report remains accessible to audiences.

Impact: Does the proposal have a compelling narrative or in-depth element that will inform and engage, draw attention, trigger debate and spur action?

Innovative storytelling: The use of creative approaches, multimedia and data visualization will be considered a plus.

Plan for timely publication: Journalists whether freelance or employed at a media outlet, will need to include a letter of support from an editor in their application, committing to publish the reports by October 31, 2026.

TITLE: UNU-MERIT MMPAF Programme 2026: Apply for Online Training in Migration and Asylum Policy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Moving the Migration Policy Agenda Forward (MMPAF) Programme 2026 is an online capacity-building opportunity offered by the United Nations University – Maastricht Economic and Social Research Institute on Innovation and Technology (UNU-MERIT) for professionals involved in migration and asylum policy and management.

The programme is particularly designed for government officials working in the fields of migration and asylum, while also providing an opportunity for other practitioners and students with an interest in migration and asylum policies to develop relevant knowledge and practical skills.

Funded by the European Union (EU) through the Migration Partnership Facility (MPF) of the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD), the MMPAF programme provides intensive, tutor-led online learning focused on major migration policy issues.

For 2026, participants can take part in two specialised courses: Irregular Migration and Migration and Development. Each course is delivered online over one full-time week and combines lectures, interactive learning, practical exercises and Problem-Based Learning (PBL).

About the UNU-MERIT MMPAF Programme

UNU-MERIT is an international research and training institute that forms part of the United Nations University system. Its work covers economic and social research, innovation, technology, development and public policy.

The Moving the Migration Policy Agenda Forward (MMPAF) programme contributes to capacity development in migration management by giving participants the opportunity to strengthen their understanding of important migration policy challenges.

Rather than relying exclusively on traditional lectures, the programme uses a combination of teaching and assessment approaches. Participants are expected to actively engage in online sessions, discussions, practical exercises and workshops.

The programme places particular emphasis on Problem-Based Learning (PBL), an approach that allows participants to work through practical policy-related challenges and apply concepts to real-world situations.

MMPAF Programme 2026 Courses

The 2026 programme consists of two separate online courses. Each course lasts one week and is delivered on a full-time basis.

1. Irregular Migration

Dates: 23–27 November 2026

The Irregular Migration course will be taught by Dr. Lalaine Siruno.

The course is intended to strengthen participants’ understanding of irregular migration and the policy challenges associated with managing migration movements.

Through interactive learning and practical exercises, participants can explore migration policy issues and develop their ability to approach complex challenges from a policy and management perspective.

2. Migration and Development

Dates: 30 November–4 December 2026

The Migration and Development course will be taught by Prof. Khalid Koser.

This course focuses on the relationship between migration and development and provides participants with an opportunity to examine migration through a broader policy and development lens.

The course is particularly relevant to professionals who need to understand how migration interacts with development policies, institutions and wider socioeconomic processes.

How the MMPAF Courses Are Delivered

Both courses are delivered entirely online, allowing selected participants to participate without travelling to a physical campus.

However, the online format does not mean that the programme is self-paced. The courses are structured as intensive, full-time learning programmes.

Each one-week course is divided into smaller learning blocks to make the programme structured and manageable. These learning blocks combine different forms of teaching and evaluation.

Participants may be involved in:

Online lectures

Interactive sessions

Practical exercises

Problem-Based Learning activities

Workshops

Self-preparation and independent study

Other tutor-led learning and evaluation activities

The programme requires a significant time commitment. Participants are expected to dedicate approximately 40 hours per week to the course, including online contact hours and time spent preparing independently.

Applicants should therefore ensure that they can make the necessary time available before applying.

Who Can Apply for the MMPAF Programme?

The MMPAF programme is primarily targeted at government officials and civil servants working in migration and/or asylum in the eligible countries and regions.

The programme is also open to other practitioners and students who have an interest in migration and asylum policy, although the stated eligibility criteria specifically require applicants working as government officials in the relevant fields and eligible locations.

Applicants should meet the following requirements:

English Language Requirement

Applicants must be fluent in spoken and written English.

Because the programme is delivered online and involves interactive sessions, participants need to be comfortable communicating, listening, reading and writing in English.

Academic Qualification

Applicants must hold at least a Bachelor’s degree.

This means that a recognised undergraduate degree is the minimum academic qualification specified for the programme.

Identification Document

Applicants must provide a copy of a valid passport or identification document as part of their application.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their identification document is valid and that they can provide a clear copy when submitting their application.

Computer Skills

Applicants must be sufficiently confident with computers to participate in an online education programme.

Since the courses are delivered online and involve interactive sessions and practical activities, participants should be able to use the technology required for online learning.

Professional Background

The programme is specifically intended for government officials working in migration and/or asylum.

Eligible officials must work in the relevant fields in one of the programme’s designated geographical areas.

Applicants who are government employees must also have full and written support from their employers confirming that they will not be expected to perform their normal work duties during the period of the MMPAF programme.

This requirement is important because each course is full-time and requires approximately 40 hours of commitment per week.

TITLE: Physics Major

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The undergraduate curriculum allows students to acquire a deep conceptual understanding of fundamental physics through its core requirements. Students then choose one of two options to complete the degree, the Flexible track or the Focus track. Both options lead to the same degree, a Bachelor of Science in Physics. And both options are superb preparation for any student planning on applying to graduate school in Physics.

Students may choose either option at any time in their undergraduate career, but many determine their choice during sophomore year in order to have enough time to craft a program that best suits their individual needs. Each option provides time for exploration through electives.

Flexible Track

The Flexible track is based on a series of rigorous courses in fundamental physics topics, and its options enable many of our students to complete second majors in other disciplines. Below is an overview; students may obtain more detailed information in the MIT Bulletin.

The Flex track requires:

8.03, 8.04 or 8.041, 8.044, 18.03 (Differential Equations)

8.21 Physics of Energy or 8.223 Classical Mechanics II (choose one)

8.033 Relativity, 8.05 or 8.051 Quantum Physics II, or 8.20 Introduction to Special Relativity (choose one)

8.13 Experimental Physics (a similarly rigorous lab subject from another department can be substituted with permission, or less frequently, an experimental project or experimentally-oriented externship may substitute be allowed to substitute). Note that 8.13 satisfies the lab requirement that is part of the GIRs.

At least one elective Physics subject beyond 8.02

Two CI-M Subjects from this list: 8.06, 8.13, 8.14, 8.226, 8.287J, 8.225J.

In addition, students in the Flex track complete a group of three related subjects, similar to a concentration, subject to the approval of Flex Major Coordinator Dr. Sean Robinson. This group of subjects is known as a “focus area.” Examples of possible focus areas include, but are not limited to:

astronomy

biology / biophysics

computer science / engineering

chemistry

electrical engineering

history of science

mathematics

materials science

science teaching

philosophy

quantum physics

Focused Track

This option—which includes three terms of quantum mechanics, 36 units of laboratory experience, and a thesis—constitutes strong preparation for a career in physics. It is comprised of three required parts: specifically required subjects; restricted electives; and a research thesis.

The Focus track requires:

8.03, 8.033, 8.04 or 8.041, 8.044, 8.05 or 8.051, 8.06, 8.223, 18.03 (Differential Equations)

8.13 and 8.14 Experimental Physics I and II; note that both 8.13 and 8.14 satisfy the lab requirement that is part of the GIRs.

restricted electives:

one subject given by the Mathematics Department beyond 18.03;

two additional subjects given by the Physics Department beyond 8.02 including at least one of the following: 8.07, 8.08, 8.09

a thesis based on research supervised by a faculty member:

Students should have an idea for a thesis topic by the middle of junior year; many thesis projects grow organically out of UROP projects. A thesis proposal must be submitted by Add Date of senior year, and students must register for units of 8.ThU (Undergraduate Thesis) in the senior year. See the Senior Thesis section below for more details.

Two CI-M Subjects from this list: 8.06, 8.13, 8.14, 8.226, 8.287J, 8.225J.

Double Major in Physics

A frequent question of undergrads is whether a double major is possible with Physics. It definitely is, and in fact the majority of our undergraduates pursue major studies in Physics and another department, or a minor, or both. Popular second majors for our Physics students include: Mathematics, Computer Science, Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Nuclear Science and Engineering.

A second major can only be declared after three terms. Students with two majors must complete the requirements of both departments. More general information about double majoring.

To apply for a double major:

Flex majors only

Meet with Dr. Sean Robinson, the Physics Flex Plan Coordinator, to discuss how you will meet all the requirements of the Flex major.

All Physics majors

Fill out the double major petition and submit it by emailing physics-undergrad@mit.edu or by delivering it to the Academic Programs Office, 4-315, for a signature. Please note that we will not sign your petition until you’ve obtained your advisor’s signature first.

After obtaining the necessary signatures, submit the signed petition to the Committee on Curricula (curricula@mit.edu) to be processed. Once approved, the Physics Undergraduate Program Coordinator will reach out to you with a welcome.

Communications Requirement for the Physics Major (CI-M 8)

Each MIT undergraduate must take two subjects within their major that have been designated as communications-intensive (CI-M). CI-Ms teach the specific forms of written, oral, and/or visual communication appropriate to the field’s professional and academic culture. Students may write in teams; prepare and present oral and visual research reports for different audiences; learn audience analysis and peer review; or go through the experience of proposing, writing, and extensively revising a professional journal article. Most students complete their CI-Ms during the junior and senior year.

The Physics Department offers the following CI-Ms for both Flex and Focus students:

8.06 Quantum Physics III

8.13 Experimental Physics I

8.14 Experimental Physics II

8.225J Einstein, Oppenheimer, Feynman: Physics in the 20th Century

8.226 Forty-three Orders of Magnitude

8.287J Observational Techniques of Optical Astronomy

8.THT Thesis Tutorial plus 8.THU Thesis (NEW) – contact J. Conrad

Students occasionally petition to substitute a CI-M from another department in place of one of these subjects; the department may support such a petition if the proposed substitution forms a natural part of the student’s individual program. Petitions are approved by the MIT Subcommittee on the Communications Requirement (SOCR).

Senior Thesis

Research is an integral part of any student’s experience as an MIT Physics major. Students who have had the opportunity to delve deeply into an area of research over time are encouraged to write a Senior Thesis describing their work and their conclusions.

Senior Thesis Submission Dates

Senior Thesis Proposal form (PDF) due by Add Date the term before you complete your thesis

Senior Thesis Title form (PDF)

Submission dates for academic year 2024-25

Candidates on May 2025 degree list: Friday, May 9, 2024

Senior Thesis Policies

All Physics Focus students must write an undergraduate thesis; students on the Physics Flex track may choose to write a thesis, but are not required to.

Any Physics Department faculty member or research staff member is an acceptable thesis supervisor.

To write a thesis under the supervision of an MIT professor outside the Physics Department, or a non-MIT professor, you must have a departmental faculty member as a co-supervisor. Contact the Academic Programs Office for more information.

You must be registered for thesis units (8.THU) in the term you plan to submit your thesis. The standard number of units is 12; a student with an unusual situation may register for up to 24 units, but should discuss with the thesis supervisor why this thesis requires more effort than a standard 12-unit subject.

During the term you are enrolled in 8.THU, you may not also conduct a UROP project that contributes or relates to the thesis work, or vice versa (MIT UROP policy).

Formatting

For a list of formatting requirements and details for writing your senior thesis, see the MIT Libraries’ MIT Specifications for Thesis Preparation page, which contains links to several sections on thesis preparation, as well as MIT Thesis FAQs.

Formatting requirements for undergraduate theses are the same as for Ph.D. theses except:

Abstracts are not required for undergraduate theses.

No ProQuest/UMI form is required.

Senior Thesis Title form (PDF): use this template to format your title page.

Required Signatures and Submission Guidelines

Your thesis will be signed by you, your thesis supervisor, and the Associate Head of the Physics Department. After your thesis supervisor has read your thesis completely, provided feedback or corrections, and approved the final version for submission:

Submit your thesis in a PDF attachment via email to physics-undergrad@mit.edu.

Copy your thesis supervisor(s) on the email.

Your supervisor then provides a signature via Docusign.

Once this is done, the staff of the Academic Programs Office will be responsible for obtaining the signature of the Associate Head.

Digital Submission Guidelines

Do not print OR physically sign and scan your thesis to us. Follow the signing instructions written below.

When the final version of your thesis is completed, submit your thesis in a PDF attachment via email to physics-undergrad@mit.edu.

You must copy your thesis supervisor(s) on the email.

Once you’ve submitted your thesis and your supervisor has given their approval via Docusign, then the Associate Head will review it.

Advising

Each year, a group of faculty members are designated as academic advisors to an incoming cohort of sophomore Physics majors. In July, rising sophomores are provided information about the available advisors and are asked to indicate their top choices, and matches are then made by the Academic Administrator. Students who join the department after this initial set of assignments will then be matched with one of the advisors for the student’s class; these students may make specific requests which will be considered along with the current advising loads of each advisor.

Your advisor can assist with:

Course selection and sequencing

Changes to subject choices after Registration

Academic progress

Academic or personal support resources

Advice about graduate school in physics or other disciplines

Internship and career advice

Our advising program’s goal is for Physics majors to retain their advisor throughout the undergraduate program, but students are welcome to request a change of advisor if circumstances warrant by contacting the Assistant Director Shannon Larkin.

FAQ for Prospective Undergraduate Students

Does the Physics Department accept AP credit?
Yes. The Physics Department awards credit for 8.01 to incoming students who score a 5 on both parts of the AP Physics C test. No credit is given for the Physics B test or for a qualifying score on only one part of the Physics C test.

Does the Physics Department grant credit for the International Baccalaureate or G.C.E. “A” Level Exams?
Entering students may receive 8.01 credit for qualifying scores on A-level exams, IB exams, the German Arbitur, and similar tests. For full details on Physics credit awarded for international exams and how to request it, see information on the website of the Office of the First Year.

If I have 8.01 credit already through an exam, do I have to take the Math Self-Assessment?
Yes. The Math Self-Assessment serves a dual purpose. In addition to providing advice for the appropriate level of Physics I for the majority of entering first-year students who must take a version of 8.01, Math Self-Assessment scores also validate AP credit for Mathematics courses.

How can I receive Physics transfer credit?
Requests for transfer credit for Physics courses taken at other institutions can be made through Physics Assistant Director Shannon Larkin. Please read our Transfer Credit page for complete details on how to apply for credit. This page also has information on the scheduling of exams and on topics covered.

May I take 8.02 before passing 8.01?
No. All students must receive credit for 8.01 before registering for any version of 8.02. The sole exception to this policy is for second-semester seniors who have not yet completed either 8.01 or 8.02. A senior who needs to complete both 8.01 and 8.02 in the final term should contact the Assistant Director, Shannon Larkin.

Can I switch between the various versions of 8.01 or 8.02?
Yes. Students can switch between 8.01 and 8.01L, or 8.011 and 8.012 (as well as between 8.02 and 8.022) before Add Date. Instructors of the subject a student wishes to switch into can provide additional information on any written work to be submitted or tests to be taken to facilitate such a change.

Can I take graduate classes as an undergrad?
Yes, many undergrads take graduate courses, but we take prerequisites and appropriate preparation very seriously. Whether you are taking a first-year Physics course or an advanced graduate course, we want to be sure you are set up for success.

Are there any study-abroad programs?
Yes. Most study-abroad opportunities are handled by MIT’s Global Education and Career Development Office. The MISTI program is most specifically aimed towards science and technology initiatives.

TITLE: Rio Changemakers Call for Funds: Apply to Join the First Global Climate and Nature Investment Cohort

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Rio Changemakers is inviting impact funds focused on climate and nature to apply to become part of the first cohort featured on a new global marketplace designed to connect trusted investment opportunities with investors and locally led projects.

The initiative aims to strengthen connections between climate and nature-focused capital and credible organizations working on solutions in emerging markets and developing economies. Funds selected for the first cohort will have the opportunity to help shape the platform while increasing their visibility among potential investors and accessing a growing pipeline of locally led projects seeking financing.

Priority consideration deadline: 26 September 2026

About Rio Changemakers

Rio Changemakers is an AI-enabled, science-guided marketplace being developed by the Government of Luxembourg and the Global Landscapes Forum (GLF).

The platform is being designed to address an important challenge in climate and nature finance: connecting credible, locally led initiatives with appropriate financing partners.

The marketplace aims to make it easier for:

Investors to discover trusted climate and nature investment opportunities.

Locally led projects to connect with potential financing partners.

Impact funds to increase their visibility among investors.

Capital to reach organizations and communities already leading climate and nature action.

The initiative places particular emphasis on locally led action across emerging markets and developing economies.

What Is the Rio Changemakers Call for Funds?

Rio Changemakers is looking for impact funds that invest in climate and nature solutions and are committed to supporting locally led action.

Selected funds will become part of the platform’s first cohort.

This means selected organizations will have an early opportunity to interact with and test the marketplace while contributing feedback that can help improve the platform before it grows further.

The call is therefore not simply an opportunity for funds to gain visibility. It is also an opportunity to participate in the development of a global financing platform intended to improve access to capital for locally led climate and nature initiatives.

Who Should Apply?

The call is specifically aimed at impact funds rather than individual applicants, NGOs applying for grants, students, researchers or individual entrepreneurs.

Funds should have an investment strategy focused on climate and/or nature solutions and demonstrate a commitment to supporting locally led action.

Rio Changemakers particularly welcomes funds that support:

Indigenous Peoples

Local communities

Women-led organizations

Youth-led organizations

Other locally led initiatives

Priority will also be given to funds investing in specific regions of the Global South and other emerging and developing markets.

Priority Regions

Rio Changemakers states that priority will be given to funds investing in:

Africa

Asia

Latin America

The Pacific

The Caribbean

Funds working across multiple regions may therefore be particularly relevant, especially where their investment strategies support locally led climate and nature solutions.

What Types of Funds Are Encouraged to Apply?

The initiative is looking for funds whose investment activities align with climate, nature and locally led development.

Potentially relevant funds may include those investing in areas such as:

Climate solutions

Nature-based solutions

Biodiversity

Conservation

Sustainable land management

Sustainable agriculture

Climate resilience

Community-led environmental initiatives

Locally led development

Women’s climate initiatives

Youth-led climate initiatives

Indigenous-led environmental initiatives

Other climate and nature-related solutions

The key consideration is whether the fund’s investment strategy aligns with the objectives of Rio Changemakers.

Why Join the First Rio Changemakers Cohort?

Being selected for the first cohort can provide several potential benefits to participating funds.

1. Early Access to the Marketplace

Selected funds will be among the first organizations to use the Rio Changemakers platform.

They will have an opportunity to create their fund profile and experience the platform before it expands further.

2. Increased Visibility

As Rio Changemakers develops its global marketplace, participating funds will have an opportunity to increase their visibility among investors looking for credible climate and nature investment opportunities.

A presence on the platform could help funds communicate their:

Investment strategy

Areas of focus

Geographic priorities

Climate and nature objectives

Approach to locally led investment

3. Access to a Growing Project Pipeline

The platform is intended to connect funds and investors with a growing pipeline of credible, locally led climate and nature projects seeking financing.

For participating funds, this could create opportunities to discover potential investment opportunities that align with their strategies.

4. Help Shape the Platform

First-cohort participants will not simply use the platform.

They will also be asked to test key features and provide feedback.

Their feedback can help inform the development of a marketplace that better serves both:

Investors and impact funds; and

Locally led organizations seeking financing.

5. Contribute to a Global Public Good

Rio Changemakers describes the marketplace as a public good intended to help make it easier for capital to reach local people and organizations already leading climate and nature action.

By participating, funds can therefore contribute to a broader effort to improve the connection between capital and locally led climate and nature solutions.

How the Application Process Works

Interested impact funds are asked to complete an online questionnaire.

The questionnaire is designed to help Rio Changemakers understand the applicant’s:

Fund structure

Investment strategy

Areas of focus

Geographic priorities

Approach to climate and nature investment

Commitment to locally led action

Readiness to participate in the first cohort

Applicants should provide accurate and complete information.

Where a question provides several options, applicants should select all applicable options unless the question specifically states otherwise.

How Long Does the Application Take?

The organizers estimate that the questionnaire will take approximately 15–20 minutes to complete.

Applicants are encouraged to prepare the relevant information about their fund and investment strategy before beginning the questionnaire.

Application Review Process

Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to wait until the final deadline to apply.

However, Rio Changemakers encourages interested funds to submit their applications by:

26 September 2026

for priority consideration.

Funds interested in joining the first cohort should therefore consider submitting their applications as early as possible.

What Happens If Your Fund Is Selected?

Selected funds will become part of the first Rio Changemakers cohort.

As a participating organization, your fund will have the opportunity to:

Create a profile on the marketplace.

Test important platform features.

Provide feedback on the platform.

Help identify ways the marketplace can better serve investors and locally led organizations.

Increase visibility among potential investors.

Potentially connect with a growing pipeline of locally led climate and nature projects seeking financing.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to funds that want to play an active role in shaping the future of climate and nature finance.

Why Locally Led Climate and Nature Finance Matters

One of the central ideas behind Rio Changemakers is the need to improve connections between financing and the people and organizations closest to climate and nature challenges.

Locally led organizations often have deep knowledge of their communities and ecosystems and may be directly involved in developing and implementing solutions.

The marketplace is intended to make it easier for investors to discover credible opportunities while helping locally led initiatives connect with financing partners.

This approach places local actors at the center of climate and nature action rather than treating them simply as beneficiaries of externally designed projects.

Geographic Focus

Although the initiative has a global ambition, priority will be given to funds investing in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Pacific and the Caribbean.

Funds with significant investment activity in these regions should therefore pay particular attention to this opportunity.

The geographic focus also makes the call especially relevant to impact funds supporting climate and nature solutions in developing and emerging economies.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Application Deadline

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

For priority consideration, impact funds are encouraged to apply by:

26 September 2026

The questionnaire takes approximately 15–20 minutes to complete.

Conclusion

The Rio Changemakers Call for Funds offers climate and nature-focused impact funds an opportunity to become part of the first cohort of an emerging global marketplace connecting investors with credible, locally led projects.

The initiative is particularly relevant to funds investing in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Pacific and the Caribbean, as well as funds supporting Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women-led organizations, youth-led organizations and other locally led initiatives.

Selected funds will gain an opportunity to create a profile, test the platform, provide feedback, increase their visibility among investors and potentially connect with a growing pipeline of climate and nature projects seeking financing.

With applications reviewed on a rolling basis, interested impact funds are encouraged to submit their applications by 26 September 2026 for priority consideration.

TITLE: Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS) 2027-2028

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: November 16, 2026

Applications are open for the Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS) 2027-2028. The program will select early-career scholars from around the world to be in residence at Princeton for an academic year (10 months) and to engage in research and discussion around a common theme.

The fellowships will be awarded to those employed outside the United States who have a faculty appointment or a professional research appointment, and they will be expected to return to their positions at the conclusion of the fellowship. Lastly, they must have demonstrated outstanding scholarly achievement and unusual intellectual promise. Early-career scholars will be appointed at the rank of Visiting Research Scholar.

Democratic governance faces mounting pressure around the world. The rise of populist movements, declining trust in institutions, polarization, disinformation, and democratic backsliding (including in democracies once considered as consolidated) have prompted renewed debate about whether democracy’s ascendance in the late 20th century was more fragile than assumed. At the same time, democracies have proven resilient in unexpected ways—through grassroots mobilization, institutional safeguards, judicial independence, and civic renewal—raising the question of what, precisely, allows some democratic systems to weather crisis while others erode or collapse.

During the 2027-28 academic year, the program theme will be “Democracy in Crisis?” They invite applications from scholars who study the challenges confronting democratic governance and/or the sources of democratic resilience. TITLE: Is the regime shift in Gulf Stream warm core rings detected by satellite altimetry? An inter-comparison of eddy identification and tracking products

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Perez, E., Andres, M., Gawarkiewicz, G. (2024). Is the Regime Shift in Gulf Stream Warm Core Rings Detected by Satellite Altimetry? An Inter-Comparison of Eddy Identification and Tracking Products; Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans, 129(10), e2023JC020761. https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JC020761

Figure provided by Elena Perez.

The evolution of a warm core ring (WCR)-like eddy from the META2.0 data product (matched to a July 1995 WCR from the regional Ring Census) is shown at four stages. (a) The eddy was first identified a few days before the ring in the Ring Census in June 1995 near 41°N, 64°W. (b) The eddy moves westward to about 41°N, 65°W, and a sea surface height (SSH) bridge to the Gulf Stream starts to form in August 1995. (c) The eddy is still connected to the Gulf Stream via an SSH bridge on 20 September 1995 near 40°N, 65°W. (d) The SSH bridge has disappeared, and the META2.0 WCR-like eddy continues to be tracked for 4 more months to its demise near 40°N, 70°W in December 1995. The background color shading indicates sea surface temperature, the thin black contours are the absolute dynamic topography of SSH, and the thick black line is the trajectory of the feature. The light blue circle is the center of the eddy on the given day, and the thick blue line is the Gulf Stream path, identified by the 25 cm SSH contour.
