TITLE: 2026–2028 EdRedesign Cradle-to-Career Fellowship at Harvard: Tuition-Free 18-Month Leadership Program – Apply by October 6, 2026

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The EdRedesign Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Education is accepting applications for the 2026–2028 EdRedesign Fellowship for Cradle-to-Career Partnership Leaders, a competitive, tuition-free, 18-month professional development opportunity created for new and aspiring leaders working to improve outcomes for children, young people, and families through place-based, cross-sector partnerships.

Applications for the new cohort opened on August 28, 2026, and the official application deadline is October 6, 2026, at 11:59 PM EST.

The program is designed for leaders working at the intersection of education, community development, health, government, philanthropy, nonprofit organizations, social services, housing, economic mobility, and other sectors. Rather than focusing on a single institution or service, the Fellowship develops leaders who can bring organizations and stakeholders together around shared community-level goals.

Participants will receive an extensive combination of in-person learning, virtual leadership development, executive coaching, mentoring, peer networking, specialized training, and practical project implementation. Importantly, tuition and the costs of travel, accommodation, and meals associated with mandatory Fellowship activities are covered for Fellows.

About the EdRedesign Fellowship for Cradle-to-Career Partnership Leaders

The EdRedesign Fellowship was established in response to the complex challenges affecting children and families in communities across the United States, including disparities in education, health, well-being, income, and economic mobility.

EdRedesign’s approach recognizes that major community challenges cannot generally be addressed effectively by one organization or sector acting independently. Place-based partnerships therefore bring together stakeholders such as:

Government agencies

Educational institutions

Nonprofit organizations

Businesses

Philanthropic organizations

Community organizations

Youth organizations

Faith-based organizations

Health and social-service providers

Housing and community-development organizations

These partnerships work within specific geographic communities and seek to align resources, services, opportunities, and institutional efforts around common outcomes. The model also emphasizes incorporating the experiences and voices of residents, young people, and families into decision-making.

The Fellowship aims to strengthen the leadership capacity required to manage these complicated collaborations.

Why the Cradle-to-Career Approach Matters

A cradle-to-career strategy considers the entire developmental journey of children and young people rather than treating individual challenges in isolation.

This can include areas such as early childhood development, school readiness, primary and secondary education, postsecondary education, workforce preparation, employment, health, family support, community development, and long-term socioeconomic mobility.

The underlying principle is that improving outcomes for children often requires coordination among multiple systems.

For example, an education challenge may also be connected with housing stability, family income, transportation, healthcare, childcare, community safety, or access to employment. Effective place-based partnerships therefore seek to develop a coordinated ecosystem of support rather than a collection of disconnected programs.

The EdRedesign Fellowship helps leaders develop the capabilities needed to lead these kinds of systems-level initiatives.

Duration of the 2026–2028 Fellowship

The program runs for approximately 18 months.

Rather than functioning as a short conference or one-time training course, the Fellowship combines structured learning with ongoing professional practice.

Fellows remain involved in their existing organizations and communities while completing Fellowship activities. The structure is intended to allow participants to immediately apply new knowledge, leadership tools, and strategies to real challenges within their communities.

Fellows should expect to dedicate approximately 10 to 12 hours per month to Fellowship activities.

What Fellows Will Learn

The Fellowship aims to strengthen participants’ ability to lead complex community partnerships and systems-change initiatives.

Through the program, Fellows are expected to improve their ability to:

1. Lead Across Different Sectors

Participants will develop their capacity to work across organizations, sectors, programs, and cradle-to-career systems.

This is particularly important because leaders of community partnerships frequently have to coordinate stakeholders who have different institutional mandates, funding arrangements, operating structures, and priorities.

2. Use Data for Decision-Making

Fellows will strengthen their ability to make decisions based on evidence and measurable outcomes.

The Fellowship emphasizes the importance of combining quantitative and qualitative information with meaningful engagement from young people and families.

3. Center Youth and Family Voices

Effective place-based leadership requires understanding the experiences of the communities being served.

The program therefore emphasizes authentically incorporating youth and family perspectives into planning, implementation, and decision-making.

4. Use Personal and Professional Leadership Strengths

Participants will examine how their professional experience, expertise, personal strengths, and leadership style can contribute to community-level change.

5. Align Resources Around Common Goals

Fellows will strengthen their ability to identify, generate, and coordinate:

Human resources

Financial resources

Organizational capacity

Technical expertise

Community assets

Partnerships

The objective is to align these resources around shared community outcomes rather than allowing organizations to operate independently.

6. Lead Without Formal Authority

One of the most important competencies emphasized by the program is the ability to lead organizations and partners even where the Fellow does not have direct managerial authority over them.

Place-based partnership leaders often rely on influence, trust, shared objectives, evidence, communication, and relationship management rather than traditional organizational authority.

Fellows will develop strategies for sustaining collaboration and navigating challenges and setbacks while keeping partners focused on collective goals.

2026–2028 Fellowship Program Components

The 18-month program combines several complementary learning formats.

Three In-Person Cohort Convenings

Fellows will participate in three in-person cohort convenings.

The program begins and concludes with convenings at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It will also include a site visit to a community demonstrating an exemplary cradle-to-career place-based approach.

Exact convening dates are expected to be announced before the Fellowship begins.

Monthly Virtual Learning Sessions

Between the in-person convenings, Fellows will participate in virtual learning sessions covering cradle-to-career strategies, cross-sector collaboration, leadership skills, and related topics.

These sessions generally last approximately three to four hours.

According to the program information, virtual learning sessions are expected approximately every four to six weeks, generally on Tuesdays from 12:00 PM to 4:00 PM Eastern Time.

A virtual orientation is scheduled to begin on Tuesday, January 26, 2027, with additional dates to be provided before the Fellowship launches.

Peer Learning Groups

Fellows will also participate in smaller peer groups.

These groups are intended to provide an environment for:

Reflection

Collaborative problem-solving

Brainstorming

Peer consultation

Discussion of leadership challenges

Sharing practical experiences

Peer groups are expected to rotate two or three times during the Fellowship, giving participants an opportunity to build relationships with different members of their cohort.

StriveTogether Training Hub

Participants will complete specially selected modules through the StriveTogether Training Hub.

The modules are designed to develop foundational capabilities relevant to collaborative systems change, including:

Improving outcomes

Changing systems

Influencing institutional change

Understanding one’s leadership role

Engaging community partners

Supporting collective action

The Training Hub component supplements the Fellowship’s broader leadership-development curriculum.

Community-Based Project

Every Fellow will design and advance a project that is meaningful to their own community.

This makes the Fellowship highly practice-oriented.

Rather than learning leadership concepts only theoretically, participants will have an opportunity to apply those concepts to an initiative directly connected with the community or partnership they lead.

The community project can therefore serve as a practical vehicle for translating Fellowship learning into measurable local change.

Executive Coaching

Participants will have access to executive coaching throughout their Fellowship journey.

Executive coaching can assist Fellows in strengthening leadership capabilities, navigating organizational challenges, making strategic decisions, and applying the Fellowship curriculum to their professional responsibilities.

Mentoring and Expert Support

Fellows will also have access to tailored project coaching and opportunities to engage with EdRedesign’s By All Means Senior Fellows, who bring extensive experience in relevant fields.

This provides participants with access to both structured learning and experienced practitioners who understand the realities of leading complex cross-sector initiatives.

Cost of the Fellowship

One of the most significant aspects of this opportunity is that participation in the mandatory Fellowship components is provided at no cost to the Fellow.

According to EdRedesign, the program covers:

Fellowship tuition

Accommodation for mandatory activities

Meals associated with mandatory activities

Travel for mandatory Fellowship components

Partner organizations may occasionally invite Fellows to additional events. Those events are optional and their costs are not covered by EdRedesign unless otherwise specified.

Therefore, applicants should distinguish between the required Fellowship program and separate optional opportunities that may arise through partner organizations.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The program primarily targets experienced professionals who either currently lead or are preparing to lead cross-sector, cradle-to-career place-based partnerships.

The principal target groups include:

New Executive Directors

Executive Directors who are relatively new to leading a place-based partnership’s backbone or intermediary organization are encouraged to apply.

Aspiring Executive Directors

Senior-level professionals who have substantial leadership and decision-making responsibilities and aspire to become an Executive Director or CEO may also qualify.

An applicant does not necessarily need to carry the formal title of Executive Director.

Senior leaders overseeing cradle-to-career place-based strategies may qualify when their responsibilities demonstrate significant organizational leadership and decision-making authority.

Leadership Qualities EdRedesign Is Seeking

The program describes several characteristics of competitive applicants.

Deep Connection to a Particular Place

Candidates should work within and demonstrate commitment to a clearly defined U.S. geography, which may include:

An urban neighborhood

A suburban community

A rural community

A town

A city

A county

A region

Competitive candidates are expected to possess meaningful knowledge of the communities they serve and trusted relationships with residents, colleagues, organizational leaders, and partners.

Demonstrated Impact

Candidates should be able to demonstrate that their leadership has contributed to meaningful outcomes.

EdRedesign specifically emphasizes measurable and data-informed results.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to explain not merely what activities they have conducted but what changes or results those activities produced.

Decision-Making Authority

Applicants should currently occupy leadership positions involving meaningful decision-making responsibility.

Mid-Career Professional Experience

Most Fellows are expected to have approximately 10 or more years of professional experience.

However, EdRedesign explicitly states that exceptionally qualified applicants with fewer than 10 years of experience may also be considered.

Strategic and Multi-Sector Leadership

Candidates should understand that challenges affecting economic and social mobility cannot generally be solved by one institution acting independently.

Competitive applicants are therefore expected to demonstrate an ability and willingness to build sustainable partnerships across sectors.

Potential to Expand Their Impact

The program particularly seeks individuals at a significant stage of professional development who already possess meaningful leadership experience but recognize areas in which they need additional knowledge, networks, and skills.

Integrity and Growth Mindset

EdRedesign also looks for leaders whom others want to work with.

This includes candidates who demonstrate:

Humility

Integrity

Willingness to learn

Openness to different perspectives

Collaborative leadership

Capacity to inspire others

Commitment to personal and professional growth

Organizational Requirements

The Fellowship is specifically structured for leaders involved in cross-sector, cradle-to-career, place-based partnerships.

Such organizations typically coordinate multiple institutions and stakeholders rather than simply delivering one service independently.

For example, an eligible partnership might coordinate government agencies, schools, community organizations, nonprofits, health organizations, businesses, philanthropic institutions, and other stakeholders around shared outcomes for children and families.

Organizations that operate exclusively as direct-service providers or work only with one or two partners are less likely to satisfy the program’s criteria.

Importantly, an organization does not necessarily need to have fully developed its cradle-to-career model before its leader applies.

EdRedesign confirms that applicants may still be considered where their organization is pursuing a cradle-to-career place-based strategy but is continuing to develop the breadth and depth of its work.

Can Leaders From Established Organizations Apply?

Yes.

The Fellowship is not restricted to newly established organizations.

An applicant may be considered where their organization or partnership has existed for some time but the applicant:

Is relatively new to their leadership role; or

Is overseeing a significant expansion or transformation of the partnership; or

Needs additional knowledge, skills, and professional networks to effectively manage a new phase of organizational development.

EdRedesign explicitly encourages such leaders to consider applying.

Selection Criteria

Fellows will be selected through a competitive process.

EdRedesign indicates that reviewers will consider factors including:

Leadership experience.

Commitment to the applicant’s community.

Readiness to grow through the Fellowship.

Ability to collaborate effectively with others.

Commitment to equity.

Demonstrated impact involving children, youth, and families.

Potential to strengthen the applicant’s local partnership.

Potential to contribute to the broader cradle-to-career field.

Applicants should therefore use their application to provide concrete examples and evidence rather than relying on generalized statements about leadership or community engagement.

2026–2028 Application Requirements

Applicants must complete an online application through the official EdRedesign application portal.

The application has three major components.

1. Background Information

Applicants must answer short questions about themselves and the place-based partnership or organization with which they are involved.

Applicants should be prepared to clearly explain their:

Current position

Leadership responsibilities

Organization or partnership

Geographic focus

Community served

Cross-sector activities

Leadership experience

2. Seven Essay Questions

Candidates must respond to seven application questions.

Each response may be submitted either:

In writing, with a maximum of approximately 250 words per question; or

Through an audio or video submission of approximately two minutes per question.

This format provides applicants with flexibility in presenting their experience and motivation.

3. Resume or CV

Applicants must upload a resume or CV in PDF format as part of the application.

Application and Selection Timeline

The major dates for the 2026–2028 selection process are:

Application opening: August 28, 2026

Application deadline: October 6, 2026, at 11:59 PM EST

Interview notification: Candidates selected to progress are expected to be notified by October 29, 2026.

Interview format: Approximately 45 minutes, conducted virtually.

Final Fellow selection: Expected in mid-December 2026.

Onboarding: Begins in January 2027.

Employer Commitment Letter

Candidates do not appear to need to submit the organizational commitment letter with their initial application.

Instead, selected Fellows will be required during onboarding to obtain a signed commitment letter from organizational leadership.

The required support involves the Fellow’s:

Direct supervisor; and

Organization’s CEO or Board Chair.

The purpose is to confirm that the organization understands and supports the time the employee will need to dedicate to the Fellowship as part of their current professional role.

This requirement is particularly important because Fellows are expected to dedicate approximately 10–12 hours per month to Fellowship activities in addition to attending required convenings.

Organizations Behind the Fellowship

The Fellowship is led by The EdRedesign Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and was developed in collaboration with several national organizations working in place-based and cradle-to-career systems change, including:

Partners for Rural Impact

Purpose Built Communities

StriveTogether

William Julius Wilson Institute at Harlem Children’s Zone

This collaboration ensures that the program is informed by practical experience from organizations actively working on community-level systems change.

Previous Fellowship Cohort

The Fellowship was first launched in 2024.

Its inaugural 2024–2026 cohort included leaders working across a broad range of community settings.

According to EdRedesign, the first cohort included representatives from 15 U.S. states, including leaders serving urban, rural, mixed urban/suburban/rural, neighborhood, regional, county, city, and town partnerships.

The diversity of partnership models demonstrates that the program is not limited to one type of community structure.

Why This Fellowship Is Significant for Community Leaders

Leading a place-based partnership involves a distinctive set of challenges.

Unlike a conventional organizational leader, a partnership leader may need to coordinate dozens of stakeholders without having formal authority over them.

These stakeholders may include public agencies, schools, businesses, nonprofit organizations, foundations, families, residents, health systems, community organizations, and elected officials.

Successful leadership therefore requires more than conventional organizational management.

It requires the ability to:

Establish common objectives.

Build trust across organizations.

Manage competing priorities.

Coordinate funding and resources.

Develop measurable outcomes.

Use data intelligently.

Engage communities authentically.

Maintain collaboration over long periods.

Navigate institutional and political challenges.

Influence organizations without direct authority.

The Fellowship is explicitly structured around developing these competencies.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted through the official 2026–2028 Cradle-to-Career Fellowship for Partnership Leaders application portal.

Applicants who have never used the application platform must first register for an account. Returning users can log into an existing account before beginning the application.

Apply for the 2026–2028 EdRedesign Fellowship

Applicants are strongly advised to begin well before the deadline because the application requires seven substantive responses in addition to background information and a PDF resume or CV.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2026–2028 EdRedesign Fellowship for Cradle-to-Career Partnership Leaders is October 6, 2026, at 11:59 PM EST.

Applicants should submit their materials before the deadline rather than relying on a last-minute submission, particularly where video or audio responses are being uploaded.

Contact for Questions

Applicants with questions about the Fellowship or application process may contact:

Denisse Arias
Director of Cradle-to-Career Leadership and Learning
The EdRedesign Lab, Harvard Graduate School of Education

The application portal also identifies Jessica Bernstein as an additional contact for application-related questions.

Conclusion

The 2026–2028 EdRedesign Fellowship for Cradle-to-Career Partnership Leaders offers an unusually comprehensive professional-development opportunity for leaders working to improve outcomes for children, young people, and families through coordinated community action.

Its 18-month structure combines Harvard-based cohort convenings, virtual learning, peer groups, StriveTogether training, executive coaching, mentoring, and implementation of a real community project. With tuition and the travel, accommodation, and meals required for mandatory program activities covered, the Fellowship removes significant financial barriers to participation.

For experienced leaders working in U.S. place-based partnerships—and particularly professionals preparing for Executive Director or CEO-level leadership—the program provides an opportunity to strengthen cross-sector leadership capabilities while becoming part of a national network of practitioners working on cradle-to-career systems change.

Interested candidates should carefully review the eligibility requirements, prepare evidence of their leadership and measurable community impact, and complete their application by October 6, 2026, at 11:59 PM EST.

TITLE: AU-EU Youth Action Lab Grants 2026: Funding for Youth-Led Initiatives in Africa and Europe

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The AU-EU Youth Action Lab is launching its final Call for Proposals for youth-led initiatives seeking financial support to address global challenges in their communities. The programme supports young people and youth initiatives across Africa and Europe, providing funding designed to help turn innovative ideas, solutions, and advocacy efforts into practical action.

For the final cohort, eligible youth initiatives can apply for one of two grant opportunities: Innovation Grants or Entrepreneurship Grants. Both grant types are designed around a “powershifting” approach that places young people at the centre of decisions about the initiatives intended to benefit them.

The grants will support selected initiatives for 12 months, from January 2027 to December 2027.

Application deadline: 23 September 2026 at 13:00 Central African Time (CAT).

Important: Applicants can apply to only one of the two grant opportunities.

About the AU-EU Youth Action Lab

The AU-EU Youth Action Lab is focused on strengthening cooperation between young people in Africa and Europe. The programme creates opportunities for youth initiatives to connect with peers, exchange experiences, develop ideas, collaborate across contexts, and bring youth perspectives and solutions to decision-makers.

The initiative recognises the role young people can play in addressing major challenges within their communities and beyond.

Through its Youth Action Lab grants, the programme provides funding for youth-led initiatives that are developing solutions to global challenges or working to create more supportive environments for young people.

The final Call for Proposals is specifically open to eligible youth initiatives in selected African countries.

What Is the Purpose of the Youth Action Lab Grants?

The grants are designed to help young people move from ideas and advocacy to practical implementation.

The AU-EU Youth Action Lab is particularly interested in initiatives that can contribute to addressing global challenges within their own contexts.

Rather than simply providing conventional project funding, the programme describes its grant approach as “powershifting.”

This approach is built around three key principles:

1. Nothing About Youth Without Youth

Young people should have a meaningful role in decisions concerning youth initiatives.

To support this principle, a Youth Advisory Board of the Youth Action Lab will review and select proposals for funding.

This means the grant-selection process is designed to give young people a direct role in determining which initiatives receive support.

2. Organisational Capacity

The programme seeks to provide grants that do more than support individual activities.

According to the AU-EU Youth Action Lab, the funding aims to facilitate and nurture:

Organisational stability

Resilience

Financial security

Organisational capacity

This approach can help youth initiatives strengthen their ability to operate effectively and sustain their work.

3. Simplified Application and Reporting

The Youth Action Lab also aims to make its application and reporting processes appropriate for youth initiatives.

The programme emphasises application and reporting mechanisms that make sense for youth-led organisations and initiatives.

This is intended to reduce unnecessary complexity and make the funding process more accessible to the initiatives the programme seeks to support.

Two AU-EU Youth Action Lab Grant Opportunities

For the final Call for Proposals, the Youth Action Lab is offering two different types of grants.

Although each grant has a different focus, both are intended to support youth-led initiatives through the programme’s powershifting approach.

1. Innovation Grants

The Innovation Grants are designed to support youth initiatives that want to design, test and/or scale innovations linked to global challenges.

This grant category is particularly relevant to youth initiatives developing new approaches, ideas, models, tools, projects, or solutions to challenges affecting their communities.

An initiative may be at a stage where it is:

Designing a new solution;

Testing an existing idea;

Developing an innovative approach; or

Seeking to scale an innovation that has already demonstrated potential.

The central focus is on innovations connected to global challenges and their application within the initiative’s specific context.

Applicants interested in this funding stream should review the official Innovation Grants information before preparing their application.

Innovation Grants:

2. Entrepreneurship Grants

The Entrepreneurship Grants are designed to support youth initiatives that advocate for an enabling environment for young entrepreneurs.

This grant type is therefore focused on initiatives working to improve the conditions in which young entrepreneurs can start, develop, and sustain their activities.

Potential applicants should review the specific requirements and focus of the Entrepreneurship Grants before deciding whether this is the most appropriate funding stream for their initiative.

Entrepreneurship Grants:

Each grant will run for 12 months.

The final cohort’s grant period is scheduled to run from:

January 2027 to December 2027

Applicants should take this timeframe into consideration when developing their project plans and determining what they realistically intend to accomplish during the funding period.

Who Can Apply?

The opportunity is intended for youth-led initiatives in the eligible countries.

The call describes its target audience broadly as young people and youth initiatives in their diversity that are working on solutions to global challenges or seeking to improve conditions for young entrepreneurs.

What Makes These Grants Different?

One of the distinguishing features of the AU-EU Youth Action Lab grants is the programme’s emphasis on youth participation in decision-making.

The programme does not simply position young people as beneficiaries. Its powershifting approach is intended to give youth a meaningful role in shaping decisions about funding and initiatives.

The Youth Advisory Board’s involvement in reviewing and selecting proposals is an important example of this approach.

The programme also recognises that youth initiatives need more than short-term project financing. Its emphasis on organisational capacity means the grants are intended to contribute to the stability, resilience, financial security, and broader capacity of youth initiatives.

Potential Benefits of the AU-EU Youth Action Lab Grants

For successful youth initiatives, the grants can provide an opportunity to:

Obtain financial support for a youth-led initiative.

Develop, test, or scale innovative solutions to global challenges.

Support advocacy aimed at creating better conditions for young entrepreneurs.

Strengthen organisational capacity.

Connect with youth initiatives and peers across Africa and Europe.

Share ideas and experiences with other young people.

Strengthen youth participation in decision-making.

Implement a supported initiative over a 12-month period.

23 September 2026 at 13:00 Central African Time (CAT)

You can apply to only one grant opportunity at a time.

This means an initiative should carefully assess whether its project is better suited to the Innovation Grant or the Entrepreneurship Grant before submitting an application.

Applicants should not attempt to submit applications to both categories simultaneously.

How to Decide Which Grant Is Right for Your Initiative

The distinction between the two grant categories provides a useful starting point.

Choose the Innovation Grant if:

Your youth initiative is focused on developing, testing, or scaling an innovative solution connected to a global challenge.

For example, the initiative may involve developing a new approach, testing a solution in a particular community, or expanding an existing innovation.

Consider the Entrepreneurship Grant if:

1. Clearly Define the Problem

Explain the challenge your initiative is addressing and why it matters in your community or context.

2. Demonstrate Youth Leadership

Because the programme is specifically focused on youth-led initiatives, clearly explain how young people lead, design, implement, or make decisions within the initiative.

3. Choose the Correct Grant Category

Do not apply simply because a grant is available.

Determine whether your initiative genuinely fits the Innovation Grant or Entrepreneurship Grant.

Describe what your initiative intends to do, how it will work, and how it responds to the challenge you have identified.

The grant period lasts from January to December 2027. Applicants should therefore propose activities that can realistically be delivered during the 12-month period.

Explain what makes your initiative relevant, useful, innovative, or capable of contributing to meaningful change.

Carefully review the official information and application guide before submitting. Make sure all required information is provided and that the application is submitted through the appropriate process.

Oxfam

European Youth Forum

The programme is therefore providing a significant opportunity for eligible youth initiatives to secure support for projects that address global challenges or strengthen the environment for young entrepreneurs.

With grants running for a full year from January to December 2027, successful applicants will have a defined period within which to implement their initiatives and pursue their intended objectives.

The powershifting approach is also central to the programme. By involving a Youth Advisory Board in proposal review and selection, emphasising organisational capacity, and simplifying application and reporting mechanisms, the programme seeks to create a funding process that is more responsive to youth initiatives.

The AU-EU Youth Action Lab Grants 2026 provide funding opportunities for youth-led initiatives in selected African countries that are working to address global challenges or promote a more enabling environment for young entrepreneurs.

For the final Call for Proposals, applicants can choose between two grant categories: Innovation Grants, which support initiatives developing, testing, or scaling innovations linked to global challenges, and Entrepreneurship Grants, which support initiatives advocating for an enabling environment for young entrepreneurs.

Workshop Fee: AAU member institutions: 700 USD and Non-AAU member institutions: 800 USD

BACKGROUND

In recent decades, there have been growing demands on higher education institutions from several actors including regulators, students, and donors, requiring them to be more compliant with legal and policy frameworks in the performance of their functions. This increasing demand has exposed universities to considerable legal risk. As such, Higher education institutions must be very mindful of the legal environment in which they operate.

The Legal Issues in Higher Education program is an annual training program instituted by the Association of African Universities in 2017 in response to this growing need. Four training sessions have so far been held over three years in Mauritius, Botswana, and Rwanda. These training programs explored several themes relating to the legal context of higher education governance and management. The COVID pandemic in 2020 led to the truncation of this initiative.

During this lull, there have been significant legal developments in higher education. In the past five years alone, close to fifteen (15) African countries have enacted data protection legislation as well as intellectual property laws. Most of these laws raise legal issues linked to the interface of university processes to data and technology. Also, there has been significant progress in artificial intelligence in the year 2023. Generative AI in particular has provided tools that have significantly transformed innovation and inventions. This has implications for claims by Higher Education Actors to intellectual property and technology transfer. This workshop will focus on the key legal issues arising from this evolving environment. The purpose is to generate ideas and share perspectives on emerging legislative frameworks that address these concerns. It will also introduce participants to data management and protection policies that effectively respond to the demands imposed by legislation. The training will review related case studies based on reported litigation from the Courts.

GENERAL OVERVIEW:

The thematic areas to be focused on comprise matters relating to the interface between law, Digital Technology, Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Assets. The training will also explore judicial attitudes towards these issues.

METHODOLOGY/ MODE OF DELIVERY

The training session would employ the use of presentations, case studies on policy approaches, expert discussions, cohort deliberations, and open sessions, amongst others, to ensure effective facilitation, interaction, and communication of the ideals underpinning the training.

ABOUT THE FACILITATORS:

SOLOMON FAAKYE, ESQ: Solomon Faakye is the Head of Legal and General Counsel for the University of Cape Coast. He has also provided specialized corporate counsel to many reputable organizations including the Ghana Heritage Conservation Trust. Mr. Faakye has deep understanding of the legal and policy environment in which higher education operates. He has broad expertise in public law and technology law. He has published widely in peer reviewed journals both local and international and provided lectures, trainings and consultancies to several reputable national and international institutions. Mr. Faakye is a recipient of several prestigious academic and professional fellowships including the Erasmus Mundus Fellowship (European Union), Quota Scholarship (Government of Norway) and Mandela Washington Fellowship (US Department of State).

PROF. ERIK NIKLAS LAVESSON : Prof. Niklas Lavesson is a Full Professor of software engineering and Artificial Intelligence at the Blekinge Institute of Technology (Hogskola), Sweden. He has held several positions in various Higher Education Institutions across Sweden. From 2017 to 2021, he was a full professor of Computer Science at the Jonkoping University, Sweden. Between 2021 to 2022, he was the senior adviser to Hamrin Foundation, Jonkoping in Sweden. Prof. Lavvesson has also published in several journals including the Journal of Data Science and Analytics and the Journal of Wireless Mobile Networks, Ubiquitous Computing and Dependable Application. His works have focused on the creation of technology, its use and implications on different aspects of society.

TRAVEL, ACCOMMODATION, AND VISA

Participants will be responsible for their own accommodation and travel-related costs, such as flights and or local transportation. AAU will provide invitation letters to support the visa application process of participants from countries that require visas to enter Tanzania.

Participants are encouraged to confirm their participation early enough to ensure they have enough time to process their visas. It is suggested that participants arrive latest on the Monday evening, as the training starts on Tuesday morning.

The main training language is English. However, an English French-English interpretation service will be provided for French speaking participants.

ABOUT THE TRAINING PROGRAMME ORGANISER – The Association of African Universities –https://aau.org/

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is an international non-governmental organization set up by the universities in Africa to promote cooperation among them and between them and the international academic community. With over 440 members across the African continent, AAU is the largest and most comprehensive organization representing Universities and Higher Education bodies in Africa. It is also the apex organization and forum for consultation, exchange of information, and cooperation among institutions of higher education in Africa, and represents the voice of higher education in Africa on regional and international bodies and supports networking by institutions of higher education in teaching, research, information exchange, and dissemination. The AAU, with headquarters in Accra, Ghana, was founded in 1967, following recommendations made at an earlier conference organized by the United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) in Antananarivo, Madagascar in September 1962 for the formation of such an apex organization. The mission of the AAU is to raise the quality of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to African development by fostering collaboration among its member institutions.

TITLE: National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs 2026: One Young World Opportunity for Young South African Entrepreneurs.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Young South African entrepreneurs with businesses capable of creating significant employment opportunities have an opportunity to connect with a global network of young leaders through the One Young World National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs 2026.

The programme has been created as part of One Young World’s wider commitment to addressing one of South Africa’s most pressing challenges: youth unemployment. It seeks to identify and support young entrepreneurs who are not only building businesses but are also creating pathways to employment and livelihoods for other young people.

Applications for the programme opened on 11 August 2026, and the application deadline is 12 September 2026.

Selected participants will have the opportunity to join the global One Young World community and participate in the One Young World Summit in Cape Town, South Africa, from 3–6 November 2026.

About the One Young World National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs

The National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs has been developed in connection with the One Young World Summit taking place in Cape Town.

One Young World describes the programme as part of a legacy commitment designed to respond to youth unemployment in South Africa through practical, business-led approaches to employment and job creation.

The programme recognises that young people are not only future employees. They can also be powerful creators of employment within their communities when they have the right businesses, networks, knowledge and opportunities to scale.

The initiative therefore focuses on entrepreneurs whose businesses have the potential to generate significant numbers of jobs and contribute meaningfully to economic opportunities for young people.

Rather than focusing solely on entrepreneurship as an individual career pathway, the programme places particular emphasis on entrepreneurs as job creators.

Why the Programme Was Created

Youth unemployment remains an important challenge in South Africa, and the programme aims to contribute to solutions that place young entrepreneurs at the centre of employment creation.

The information provided by One Young World highlights research indicating that 35% of young South Africans identify the creation of new, well-paying jobs as one of the most important steps Africa can take to progress. According to the programme information, this was the highest response among the 16 countries surveyed.

This finding reinforces the relevance of a programme focused on entrepreneurs who can create employment opportunities.

The One Young World Summit in Cape Town is therefore intended to be more than a global gathering. Through initiatives such as this programme, the Summit is also positioned as an opportunity to support practical solutions to national and regional challenges.

What the Programme Is Looking For

The programme is designed for young South African entrepreneurs who are actively leading businesses or enterprises and have the potential to create significant employment opportunities.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate that they are not simply interested in entrepreneurship but are already taking a leadership role within an organisation or business.

The programme specifically requires applicants to:

Lead a business or enterprise.

Have significant job-creation potential within their business.

Have direct decision-making authority within their organisation or company.

Be South African nationals and residents.

Meet the programme’s age requirements.

Be available to attend the One Young World Summit in Cape Town.

The focus on job creation makes this opportunity particularly relevant to entrepreneurs whose businesses are growing or have the potential to scale and employ more people.

Connection to the One Young World Global Community

One of the major aspects of the programme is its connection to the wider One Young World Ambassador Community.

Participants can become part of a global network of more than 20,000 young leaders across more than 190 countries.

This creates opportunities for young entrepreneurs to connect with individuals working on different social, economic and community challenges around the world.

Being part of such a network can expose participants to different approaches to entrepreneurship, employment creation, leadership and social impact.

The programme is therefore not only focused on the individual business of an entrepreneur. It also seeks to connect young business leaders with a broader international community of people working to create positive change.

Opportunities Available to Participants

The programme information states that participants will have access to several opportunities through their connection to One Young World.

These include:

1. Access to a Global Network

Participants will be connected to a global community of more than 20,000 young leaders from over 190 countries.

This international network brings together young people working across different sectors, industries and areas of social impact.

For entrepreneurs, such a network can provide exposure to new ideas, perspectives and potential professional relationships.

2. Ambassador Opportunities

Participants can gain access to exclusive opportunities available to One Young World Ambassadors.

These may include:

Speaking opportunities.

Regional networking opportunities.

Mentoring sessions.

Other engagement opportunities within the Ambassador Community.

These activities can support continued leadership development beyond the Summit itself.

3. Understanding the Youth Unemployment Challenge

The programme will also provide participants with an opportunity to improve their understanding of solutions to the youth unemployment crisis.

This is particularly relevant to entrepreneurs whose businesses already contribute to employment or have the potential to create additional jobs.

By engaging with other young leaders and the wider One Young World community, participants can explore different approaches to employment, entrepreneurship and economic participation.

4. Strengthening Enterprise Growth

Another important focus is increasing participants’ capacity to scale their enterprises as generators of employment opportunities.

The programme therefore connects entrepreneurship with the broader objective of creating sustainable jobs.

For a business leader, this can mean thinking beyond the survival of an individual enterprise and considering how business growth can translate into opportunities for other people.

One Young World Summit 2026 in Cape Town

Successful participants are expected to participate in the One Young World Summit in Cape Town, South Africa, from 3–6 November 2026.

The Summit provides an international platform where young leaders can connect, exchange ideas and engage with other people working on significant social and economic challenges.

For participants in the National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs, the Cape Town Summit will provide an opportunity to engage with a global leadership community while contributing perspectives from South Africa’s entrepreneurship and employment landscape.

The Summit is therefore a central component of the programme and applicants must be available to participate during the specified dates.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements before submitting an application.

To be eligible for the National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs, an applicant must:

Be between 18 and 30 years of age.

Be a national of South Africa and resident in South Africa.

Be leading a business or enterprise with the potential for significant job creation.

Have direct decision-making authority within their organisation or company.

Be available to participate in the One Young World Summit from 3–6 November 2026.

Applicants Over 30

The programme notes that most delegates participating in the One Young World Summit are between 18 and 30.

However, applicants older than 30 may be considered where they can demonstrate appropriate levels of:

Personal impact.

Initiative.

Willingness to engage.

Applicants who will be under 18 at the time of the Summit, which takes place from 3–6 November 2026, cannot apply.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This programme may be particularly relevant to young South African entrepreneurs who are already running businesses and are interested in expanding their impact through employment creation.

Potential applicants could include entrepreneurs whose businesses operate in areas where growth can directly lead to new employment opportunities.

The key consideration is not simply having a business idea. The eligibility requirements specifically refer to applicants leading a business or enterprise that has the potential for significant job creation.

Applicants should therefore consider how their business contributes, or could contribute, to employment opportunities and economic participation.

The Importance of Direct Leadership

Another important eligibility requirement is that applicants must have direct decision-making authority within their organisation or company.

This means the opportunity is intended for entrepreneurs who have meaningful leadership responsibility rather than individuals who are simply employees or passive participants in a business.

Applicants should be able to demonstrate their role in making decisions and leading the organisation.

Nationality and Residency Requirement

The National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs is specifically focused on young entrepreneurs in South Africa.

Applicants must be both:

A national of South Africa; and

Resident in South Africa.

The opportunity information provided does not identify other countries as eligible.

Consequently, entrepreneurs from other African countries or other regions should not assume that they qualify for this particular national programme unless One Young World provides additional eligibility information.

Age Requirement

The standard age range for the programme is 18 to 30 years.

The programme does, however, allow for consideration of applicants over the age of 30 where there is evidence of appropriate personal impact, initiative and willingness to engage.

There is also a firm restriction concerning applicants under 18. The programme states that applications cannot be accepted from individuals who will be under 18 at the time of the One Young World Summit.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs is:

12 September 2026

The application period opened on 11 August 2026.

Applicants should ensure that they submit their applications before the stated deadline and carefully review the official application requirements before completing their submission.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the official One Young World application platform.

Interested applicants should use the official application link provided on the programme page and complete the application process before the deadline.

Apply for the National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs

Applicants should ensure that the information they provide accurately reflects their entrepreneurial leadership, business activities and potential for job creation.

APPLY HERE.

Key Dates to Remember

The most important dates associated with the opportunity are:

Application opening date: 11 August 2026

Application deadline: 12 September 2026

One Young World Summit: 3–6 November 2026

Summit location: Cape Town, South Africa

Applicants should pay particular attention to the 12 September 2026 application deadline.

For more information, Visit HERE.

Why Job-Generating Entrepreneurs Matter

Entrepreneurship can play an important role in addressing unemployment by creating businesses that provide opportunities for other people.

A successful enterprise can generate direct employment while also supporting wider economic activity through suppliers, customers, service providers and other businesses.

The National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs reflects this approach by focusing on entrepreneurs who have the potential to create significant numbers of jobs.

The programme therefore places the entrepreneur within a wider economic and social context: building a business is not only about personal success but can also become a pathway to employment and livelihoods for others.

What Makes This Opportunity Different?

The programme stands out because of its specific focus on job-generating entrepreneurship.

While many entrepreneurship opportunities focus on developing business ideas, skills or individual enterprises, this initiative specifically seeks young entrepreneurs whose businesses can contribute to solving the employment challenge.

It also combines national entrepreneurship priorities with international leadership development through the One Young World network.

Participants can therefore connect a local challenge, namely youth unemployment in South Africa, with a global community of young leaders.

International Networking and Exposure

Joining the One Young World community can provide participants with an international perspective on leadership and social impact.

The network includes young leaders from more than 190 countries, creating an environment where participants can encounter different approaches to entrepreneurship, innovation, community development and employment creation.

For South African entrepreneurs, international exposure can also provide opportunities to learn from businesses and leaders working in different economic environments.

Leadership Development

The programme is also connected to One Young World’s wider focus on young leadership.

Through networking, speaking opportunities, mentoring and engagement with other Ambassadors, participants can continue developing their leadership capabilities.

The experience may be particularly valuable for entrepreneurs who want to strengthen their ability to lead organisations while increasing their social and economic impact.

What Entrepreneurs Should Highlight in Their Applications

Eligible entrepreneurs should ensure that their applications clearly communicate the aspects of their work that align with the programme’s objectives.

Important areas to demonstrate include:

The business or enterprise they lead.

Their role and decision-making authority.

The problem their business addresses.

Current or potential employment opportunities created by the business.

The potential for the enterprise to scale.

Their personal leadership and impact.

Their contribution to their community or wider society.

Their availability to participate in the One Young World Summit.

The strongest applications should make it clear how the applicant’s entrepreneurial work connects with the programme’s central focus on job creation.

Important Information for Prospective Applicants

Before applying, prospective candidates should carefully assess whether they meet the programme’s requirements.

In particular, applicants should confirm that they:

Are South African nationals.

Currently reside in South Africa.

Meet the age requirements.

Lead a business or enterprise.

Have direct decision-making authority.

Can demonstrate significant job-creation potential.

Can attend the One Young World Summit in Cape Town from 3–6 November 2026.

Meeting these requirements is important because the programme is specifically designed for young South African entrepreneurs who can contribute to the objective of creating employment opportunities.

Conclusion

The One Young World National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs 2026 provides a platform for young South African entrepreneurs whose businesses have the potential to create significant employment opportunities.

By connecting participants to the One Young World community of more than 20,000 young leaders across more than 190 countries, the programme provides an opportunity to engage with an international leadership network while addressing a critical national challenge.

The initiative places particular emphasis on entrepreneurs as drivers of employment, recognising that young business leaders can contribute directly to creating livelihoods and expanding economic opportunities for other young people.

Eligible entrepreneurs should carefully review the requirements and submit their applications before the 12 September 2026 deadline.

The One Young World Summit will take place in Cape Town from 3–6 November 2026, providing selected participants with an opportunity to engage with a global community of young leaders while contributing to conversations and solutions around entrepreneurship, employment and youth unemployment.

TITLE: AAU TO HOST EXECUTIVE LEADERSHIP WORKSHOP ON DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION FOR HIGHER EDUCATION LEADERS IN AFRICA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Press Release – Accra, Ghana, March 9, 2025 – The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with eLearnAfrica, is pleased to announce a flagship Executive Leadership Workshop titled “Digital Transformation in Practice: From Strategy to Execution,” scheduled to take place from 20th to 24th July 2026, at the AAU Secretariat in Accra, Ghana. Click to register here: https://forms.office.com/r/TYpPR74DT3

This four-day intensive workshop is designed to bring together senior leaders and institutional change agents from across the African higher education ecosystem. The primary objective is to equip participants with the strategic vision and practical tools necessary to lead effective digital transformation initiatives within their institutions. The programme will focus on strengthening institutional capacity in three critical pillars: Cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance, and Digital Skills productivity.

Workshop participants will engage in strategic keynotes, scenario-based workshops, hands-on labs, and collaborative capstone projects covering cybersecurity risk assessment, ethical AI integration, digital productivity tools, and the development of personalized 12-Month Digital Transformation Action Plans, culminating in the launch of the AAU Digital Leaders Network. A core deliverable for each participating institution will be the development of a tailored Institutional Action Plan, providing a concrete roadmap for advancing digital transformation upon return to their home universities. Additionally, participants will gain membership in a pan-African network of digital leaders, fostering ongoing collaboration and peer support across the continent.

The workshop addresses the urgent need for African universities to build institutional readiness in the face of rapid technological change. By focusing on cybersecurity and institutional risk management, AI adoption and governance, and digital skills productivity, the programme aims to produce tangible outcomes, including:

Enhanced institutional capacity for digital transformation.

Improved cybersecurity readiness and risk mitigation.

Responsible adoption and governance of AI technologies.

Stronger continental collaboration among African universities.

This integrated workshop represents a critical step in translating online learning into on-the-ground impact. It empowers the very staff who drive African universities, equipping them with the skills, tools, peer connections, and strategic plans needed to lead their institutions through a responsible and effective digital transformation.

The workshop participation fee is $400 per participant. This fee covers:

Accommodation

Workshop materials and resources.

Daily feeding (lunch and refreshments).

Certification upon completion.

Access to the pan-African Digital Leaders Network.

Administrative and logistical support.

Note: Travel arrangements are the responsibility of participating institutions or individuals.

Interested stakeholders are invited to register for the workshop here: https://forms.office.com/r/TYpPR74DT3. Payment deadline is 26th June 2026.

AAU and eLearnAfrica Partnership

In 2016, eLearnAfrica entered a partnership with the Association of African Universities (AAU), the largest higher education coordinating body in Africa, representing over 430 member universities across the continent. This collaboration aims to provide online, distance-learning opportunities to over 10 million African students, supporting universities in expanding their reach.

The partnership has made significant strides, now boasting over 140 registered users (universities, institutions, as well as individual professors and course holders). It has successfully designed, developed, delivered, and deployed three master’s degree programs and over 200 short courses in collaboration with institutions such as Rhodes Business School and Njala University.

TITLE: Call for Members: Global Young Academy Cohort of 2027

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 15, 2026

Apply now to join the Global Young Academy Cohort of 2027. Applications are sought from young, independent scholars who combine the highest level of research excellence with a demonstrated passion for delivering impact.

The GYA is a global organisation that places a high value on its diversity. They encourage applications from all qualified candidates. All applicants receive consideration and will not be discriminated against with regard to race, colour, ethnicity, religion, creed, sex, marital status, ancestry, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, physical or mental disabilities, or other factors. They aim to avoid any single institution being overrepresented in our membership. They especially encourage women and applicants from different minority groups, and from diverse disciplines including the natural, physical and social sciences as well as the arts and humanities and people working in government, industry, and non-governmental sectors to apply.

Benefits

GYA does not give stipends to members. Depending on the funds available to the GYA, they aim to financially support members with travel co-funding for the Annual General Meetings and provide some seed funding for GYA-internal projects in their four thematic areas.

Eligibility

Open to all scholars working in any research-based discipline, including the natural, physical and social sciences, as well as the arts and humanities. Applicants working in government, industry, and non-governmental sectors are also welcome.

Applicants must be able to demonstrate a high level of excellence in their discipline, ascertained by a proven track record and expected future achievements. Moreover, applicants must demonstrate a clear commitment to making a difference in society. A PhD or an equivalent degree is a requirement for applicants.

The Global Young Academy is committed to a broad range of programmes around the world to support young scholars, promote science to a broad audience, engage in policy debate, and foster international and interdisciplinary collaboration. Applicants should provide evidence of interest or experience in one or more of these areas.

Applicants should be in the early to middle years of their independent careers. Applicants born in or after 1986 and holding a PhD are eligible without any restrictions. Applicants born before 1986 must have obtained their PhD in 2019 or later. Applicants born before 1986 with a PhD obtained before 2019 must submit a detailed justification of why they should be considered.

Each GYA member is encouraged to attend the GYA Annual General Meeting each year. As member-led organisation, GYA relies in members contributions, thus expected to actively contribute a minimum of 6 hour per month to one or more of the organisation’s programmes (projects and committees), which may include participation in science-for-policy or policy-for-science activities, supporting science outreach and education at national or international levels, engaging in science diplomacy, or collaborating with the world’s young academies and further GYA partners. In the event that applicants are selected as new GYA members, they should be available to attend the next Annual General Meeting, which is scheduled for 21 – 25 June 2027 in Indonesia.

Application

The following documents must be uploaded with your online application, as PDF documents:

CV
Maximum length of 4 pages. The Selection Committee members are instructed to ignore any material over the 4-page limit. Your CV should contain a brief education and employment history and make your achievements clear to a general audience. For example, a few words summarising your most significant publications are more useful than a complete list of every paper that you have authored. Applicant may add hyperlinks only at applicable achievements.

Letter(s) of support
Arrange for the submission of at least one letter of support for your application directed to the GYA. Letters created for a different purpose cannot be accepted. Your referee(s) should be familiar with your research career and able to comment on your standing as one of your country’s leading academics.
Individuals that you may contact for reference letters could be from one of your employers or a superior, your research institution, or another professional person familiar with your work. They may also come from a young academy (in case you are an active member).
Send in at least one, but no more than three reference letters. One may highlight your excellence in your academic field. Another may focus on your societal engagement. Aim to find a referee/referees that can provide a comprehensive picture of who you are and what you excel at in your career and additional engagements.
Personal or character references are not required. Letters should be written personally by your referee(s) in their own words.

Supply the document “Instructions for Referees” to your referees.

Data Protection / Declaration / signature of applicant

TITLE: Doctoral Requirements

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Spring 2022 Written Examinations

Exams will be administered this fall: date, time, and order of topics to be announced.
You must apply via the button below, at least a week in advance of the test date.
Updated information will be posted here when available.

Application Form

General Doctoral Requirements Information

The General Requirements assess doctoral students’ readiness to progress through the stages of the PhD program. While the Department believes strongly that all students admitted to the program are capable of succeeding in it, it is important for each student to demonstrate their expertise at specified points during the program.

There are two parts to the General Doctoral Requirements:

a set of Physics Core requirements consisting of four sections: Classical Mechanics, Electricity and Magnetism, Quantum Mechanics, and Statistical Mechanics. Each section may be satisfied either through taking a designated course, or by passing a Written Exam that indicates whether a student already has sufficient mastery of a particular area. These courses and exams are taken during the first two years of graduate study. Satisfying the Physics Core requirements demonstrates a student’s sufficient grasp of four basic areas of Physics which are the building blocks for future research. The four sections of the Physics Core together constitute an important foundation required for all PhD students, regardless of the particular topic of their thesis research.
an Oral Exam of approximately two hours. The Oral Exam is given in the student’s area of research specialty in the second or third year of graduate study, and it is designed to assess the student’s deep understanding of central ideas in the specialty area. Passing the Oral Exam indicates the student’s readiness to move on to thesis research in the designated area.

All the courses that satisfy the Physics Core Requirements are offered annually. The Physics Core Written Exams and the Oral Exam are each offered in both the Fall and Spring terms.

Core Requirements Information

The four courses that satisfy the Core Requirement sections are:

Classical Mechanics (8.309) offered every fall
Electricity and Magnetism (8.311) offered every spring
Quantum Mechanics (8.321) offered every fall
Statistical Mechanics (8.333) offered every fall

A student satisfies any section by completing the corresponding course with a grade of B+ or higher.

Alternatively, a student may choose to satisfy one or more sections of the Physics Core Requirements by taking an exam. The Physics Core Written Exam is scheduled in the week prior to the start of each fall and spring term. Entering students may choose to take the exam upon arrival, or may wait until the spring-term exam in late January to attempt the exam for the first time. In practice, most students do choose to make their first attempt upon entering the program.

After the first term, for any section of the Core Requirements not yet satisfied:

the student is required to attempt all remaining sections of the next Core Written Exam;
if there are remaining sections still to be completed at any time after the exam in the student’s first January, the student must enroll in the corresponding course the next time it is offered.

The deadline for satisfying all four sections of the Core Requirements is the end of a student’s second year. This timeline allows a student two attempts to complete the Core Requirements by passing the corresponding courses with a B+ or better, as well as four opportunities to satisfy the requirements through the Core Written Exams (first August, first January, second August, second January).

Students experiencing unusual circumstances (e.g., serious health issues, family emergency), may request a delay of their deadline. (See the section below on Schedule Postponements.)

If a student has not passed all sections of the Physics Core Requirement by the appropriate deadline, an ad hoc committee will form to consider the student’s individual case. This committee will report to the Associate Department Head and will consist of:

the student’s academic and research advisors
the Faculty Graduate Program Coordinator
the General Exam and Requirements Coordinator
the chair of the Written Exam Committee

The likely recommendation would be to switch the student to Master’s degree status and set a schedule for completing an SM thesis. However, in unusual cases and with strong support from the student’s advisors, this committee may recommend that the student be allowed to do prescribed further study and/or to have one additional attempt to complete the outstanding section by course or exam at the next opportunity. The final decision would be made by the Associate Department Head. No further extensions would be allowed.

Structure of the Written Exam

Students planning on taking the Written Exam in any term should file an Exam Application with the Academic Programs Office no later than one week prior to the exam.

Each exam consists of two questions; the student selects one of the two questions to solve in a 75-minute period. The questions are prepared by a committee of four Physics faculty members, and are reviewed before the exam is finalized by additional faculty who are each assigned to grade one section of the exam.

There is no pre-determined or fixed percentage of students who pass, nor is there a fixed passing score. The difficulty of the examination may vary somewhat from year to year, and this is taken into account in determining the pass/fail line.

Exams with grades near the deciding line are reviewed in detail by all members of the Exam Committee and by the graders. If a student is repeating an exam, the earlier performance is also considered.

Exam results are communicated to students and their advisors individually by email in time for the results to be considered in the selection of classes for the upcoming term.

Sample Written Exams

Sample exams, with solutions, are available as study aids for the Written Exam. The current format of four 75-minutes sections was first administered in fall 2015. Prior to 2015 our Qualifying Exams were given in 3 parts: Parts I and II comprised the Written Exam, and the Oral Exam was known as Part III.

Pre-2015 sample exams labeled ‘Part II’ with the 4 sections presented as a single 5-hour exam continue to be useful for Written Exam study, if reviewed as separate 75-minute topics.

Oral Exam Information

The purpose of the oral portion of the general exam is to test students’ broad general knowledge within their field, which is the same as that of their research supervisor; only a minor portion of the exam will concern the student’s specific research topic.

The Oral Exam, taken in the second or third year, allows the student to demonstrate deep knowledge of a specialty area.

Two attempts at the Oral Exam are allowed.
The first attempt at the oral exam must be taken by the first term of the third year.
If a second attempt is needed, it must be taken in the term immediately following the first attempt. (If a first, failed attempt was taken in the first term of the second year, or earlier, the student may postpone the second attempt until the beginning of the third year.)

Structure and Content of the Oral Exam

Students planning on taking the Oral Exam in any term should file an exam application with the Academic Programs Office by September 15 for the fall term and February 15 for the spring term.

At the start of the academic year, each Division appoints one committee for each research field to examine all students in that field who will take the exam within the coming year. The oral exam committee consists of:

the chairperson
two other faculty members
an alternate faculty member if the student’s research supervisor is a member of the standing exam committee

The Academic Programs Office notifies all students about the members of their committee; the student is then responsible for scheduling the exam with the committee and notifying Academic Programs of the exam day, time, and place. Exams are generally administered in the second half of the term.

The Committee Chair in each area should communicate exam expectations to the students taking the exam that term. Ideally, this should be done in a meeting of all examinees at the start of the term.

Content of the exam:

The first question should be in the student’s specific area. The Chair should have received this question from the supervisor and provided it to the student a week before the exam.
The oral examination continues in the student’s general field.
Discussion of a student’s research, when applicable, comprises no more than the final quarter of the examination.

The research supervisor may observe the exam and may provide input only if solicited by committee members. The supervisor and student will be asked to leave the examination room when the final decision is discussed. The committee should inform them of the result as soon as a decision is reached.

CMT Oral Exam FAQs

Am I responsible for contacting the committee to schedule the exam?
Yes. Send a Doodle poll to all of your committee members (usually 3 of them) to pick the time for your exam; usually towards the end of the semester works best. Suggest many days as options, and on each day, make 2-hour slots, with 1-hour increments. Once the time of the exam is agreed upon, book one of the conference rooms for the exam, and email the time and place to your committee members. Also, just in case, send them a reminder email about two days prior to the exam. Ask Graduate Coordinator Sydney Miller to send you a grade sheet for the exam, print it out, and bring it with you to the exam.
Will there be a question given to me to prepare in advance? Who will give it to me, and when will I receive it?
Yes. Ask your research advisor to give you one prepared question, which the committee will use to start the exam. He or she needs to give you this question about a week before the exam. Please email the question to the committee members as soon as you have it.
Will I be expected to talk about my own research?
No, not beyond the research question from your advisor.
Which subjects cover the content that the exam questions will require me to know? Which texts?
Any material from: Ashcroft & Mermin, Solid State Physics
Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics
Kerson Huang, Intro to Stat Mech.

…is fair game for the exam. In addition, the student will start by giving a short presentation on a question prepared by their research advisor. The committee is allowed to ask questions on that also, but only assuming the knowledge of the material covered in 1, 2, and 3 above.

Will I receive the results of the exam immediately? What kind of feedback will I receive if I don’t pass?
You will receive the results of the exam immediately. The feedback will be given either immediately, or within the few days immediately after the exam.
What are some tips for the exam? Solve the advance problem (from your adviser) in a number of different ways. Make sure that you can present and discuss the simple intuitive solutions.
Be prepared to present your solution without notes (except for the problem statement from your research advisor, which you should print out for yourself and the exam committee).
Make sure that you listen to the questions being asked during the examination. Sometimes it helps to rephrase the question in your own words. This helps to ensure that you understand the question and it also gives you more time to prepare your response.
After giving an answer, confirm that you have addressed the question.
It is ok if you don’t know all of the answers. It is better to say “I don’t know” than to say something that is not true. Even better would be to say, “I don’t know the answer to that question, but I could figure it out by doing…”

Schedule Postponements

Postponements for completing any part of the General Doctoral Requirements can be granted if a student is experiencing unusual circumstances. Requests for postponement of the Physics Core Requirement must be submitted at least one month prior to the start of the next term in which a Written Exam or corresponding course would be required.
