TITLE: EU No Child Left Behind Grant 2026: Up to €1 Million for NGOs Supporting Children with Disabilities in Egypt

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The European Union has opened a major new call for proposals titled “No Child Left Behind: Inclusion and Protection for Children with Disabilities”, inviting eligible nonprofit organisations to develop projects that advance the rights, protection, participation and well-being of children with disabilities in Egypt.

Published under reference EuropeAid/186723/DD/ACT/EG, the opportunity is designed to strengthen the environments in which children with disabilities live, learn and participate. It combines a rights-based approach to disability with practical interventions around child protection, inclusive education, community participation, family support, accessibility, social protection and institutional capacity. The EU Delegation to Egypt has confirmed that eligible NGOs are invited to apply and that the deadline is 30 September 2026.

The call has three major priority areas:

Human rights and protection of children with disabilities

Social inclusion and participation

Family and enabling environments

Applicants must address at least one of these priority areas, although proposals integrating more than one priority will be viewed particularly favourably during evaluation.

Detailed call information reproduced by funding databases indicates an overall budget of approximately €3.9 million, with individual grants ranging from €650,000 to €1 million and projects generally lasting 24 to 36 months. Funding is reported to cover between 51% and 95% of eligible project costs, meaning most applicants will need to demonstrate an appropriate financing structure for the balance where the EU grant does not cover the full budget.

A particularly important feature of the call is its emphasis on strengthening local organisations. At least 60% of eligible action costs is reported to be intended for financial support to third parties, such as Egyptian civil society organisations, community-based organisations and organisations of persons with disabilities. The normal maximum amount of support per third-party recipient is reported as €60,000, unless a higher amount can be appropriately justified.

The deadline for submission is:

30 September 2026

Applicants should consult the official EU Funding & Tenders/EuropeAid documentation referenced by the EU Delegation to Egypt before submitting, since the full guidelines govern eligibility, partnership structure, budget rules, documentation and application procedure.

View the EU Medbridge opportunity page

About the No Child Left Behind Call for Proposals

The programme responds to continuing gaps in the realisation of children’s rights in Egypt, particularly for children affected by overlapping disadvantages such as disability, poverty, social exclusion, geographic isolation and limited access to appropriate services.

Egypt ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1990, and its 2014 Constitution affirms the state’s commitment to protecting children. National policies have subsequently sought to improve education, health and child-protection outcomes. Nevertheless, children with disabilities continue to experience barriers that can affect their ability to participate fully in family, school and community life.

The call therefore moves beyond a narrow service-delivery model.

Its overall objective is to contribute to the full realisation of the:

Rights

Dignity

Well-being

Participation

Equality

of children with disabilities in Egypt.

It aims to achieve this by supporting inclusive social environments, strengthening families and communities, and improving the institutional and systemic capacity needed to deliver accessible and equitable services.

Why This Funding Opportunity Matters

Children with disabilities can experience disadvantages at several different levels simultaneously.

These can include:

Discrimination within families or communities

Exclusion from schools

Violence or neglect

Limited access to health and social services

Stigma

Inaccessible public spaces

Limited participation in community activities

Barriers to social protection

Insufficient family support

Lack of opportunities to express their views

The programme is therefore deliberately broad.

It recognizes that inclusion cannot be achieved by concentrating only on the child as an individual.

Effective disability inclusion also depends on:

Parents

Caregivers

Schools

Health workers

Community organisations

Religious and community leaders

Government services

Social-protection systems

Accessible physical environments

Public attitudes

The call is designed to support interventions capable of working across those interconnected levels.

Global Objective of the Call

The programme’s global objective is to contribute to the:

Full realisation of the rights, dignity and well-being of children with disabilities in Egypt.

It intends to do so by:

Promoting inclusive social environments

Strengthening families

Strengthening communities

Improving institutional capacity

Improving systemic capacity

Expanding access to equitable services

Expanding access to accessible services

This makes the call relevant to organisations working in both direct service delivery and systems change.

Specific Objective 1: Protecting the Rights of Children With Disabilities

The first specific objective seeks to promote a:

Rights-based approach

to disability and child protection.

The programme aims to protect children with disabilities from:

Discrimination

Neglect

Violence

Abuse

while promoting equality.

This framing is important because disability programmes can sometimes treat beneficiaries only as recipients of care.

The EU call instead emphasizes children with disabilities as rights-holders.

That approach can involve ensuring children and their families understand:

Their legal rights

Available services

Social-protection entitlements

Mechanisms for reporting abuse

Available support systems

It also means institutions and communities should understand their responsibility to respect and uphold those rights.

Specific Objective 2: Inclusion and Participation

The second objective is focused on ensuring that children with disabilities can participate meaningfully in:

School

Peer groups

Community life

It also aims to challenge:

Stigma

Harmful social norms

Discriminatory attitudes

that restrict children’s development, participation or voice.

Participation should therefore not be interpreted simply as physical presence.

A child may technically attend school but still be excluded from learning, friendships, recreation or decision-making.

Meaningful inclusion involves enabling children to:

Participate

Communicate

Learn

Play

Build friendships

Develop skills

Express opinions

Influence decisions affecting their lives

Specific Objective 3: Strengthening Families and Caregivers

The third objective recognizes the critical role played by:

Parents

Caregivers

Families

Community actors

in enabling children with disabilities to thrive.

The programme seeks to strengthen their capacity while supporting family- and community-based environments that promote the child’s:

Development

Well-being

Inclusion

Participation

This can involve practical caregiving support as well as:

Counselling

Training

Peer support

Financial resilience

Links to social protection

Community rehabilitation

Priority Area 1: Human Rights and Protection of Children With Disabilities

The first priority focuses on protecting children with disabilities from harm while ensuring equal treatment.

Eligible or relevant activities may include promoting:

Non-discrimination and equality

within:

Families

Schools

Communities

This could potentially involve:

Rights-awareness campaigns

Community dialogue

Training for teachers

Child-protection mechanisms

Referral systems

Strengthening safeguarding practices

The call is not limited to these examples, but proposed activities should clearly contribute to the programme objectives.

Preventing Violence, Neglect, Abuse and Exploitation

Projects under Priority Area 1 may work to prevent and respond to:

Violence

Neglect

Abuse

Exploitation

affecting children with disabilities.

The call specifically includes the promotion of:

Positive parenting and non-violent discipline

within families.

This can be particularly important because children with disabilities may face heightened protection risks while also experiencing barriers to reporting mistreatment.

Strong proposals might therefore combine:

Prevention

Awareness

Identification

Referral

Response

Family support

rather than focusing only on awareness campaigns.

Building the Capacity of Frontline Community Actors

The call also highlights the importance of increasing awareness among frontline actors such as:

Teachers

Religious leaders

Health workers

Community volunteers

These groups frequently interact with children and families and can play a central role in recognizing:

Abuse

Exclusion

Service needs

Protection risks

Projects may therefore strengthen their ability to understand and uphold the rights of children with disabilities.

Helping Families Access Integrated Service Cards

Another possible intervention is helping children with disabilities and their families obtain:

Integrated service cards

and understand the rights and entitlements associated with them.

This illustrates the practical nature of the call.

A rights-based programme is not only about advocacy at national level.

It can also help individual families navigate administrative systems and access benefits for which they are already eligible.

Priority Area 2: Social Inclusion and Participation

The second priority addresses the barriers that keep children with disabilities from fully participating in school and community life.

Actions may support access to:

Inclusive education

Recreation

Community activities

School participation

TITLE: Workshop on Leadership, Governance, Resource Mobilisation and Digital Transformation of HEIs in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Date: 5th February – 8th February 2024 | Workshop Duration: 4 Days | Venue: Kigali, Rwanda

Participants: Registrars, Enrollment Managers, Academic Advisors, Staff of the Registry, Examination Managers, Project Managers and Officers, Staff Responsible for Resource Development, Partnership & Policy Managers, and Planning Officers

Registration Link: https://forms.office.com/r/hmxXWK6u8h

Introduction

From time immemorial, a university has always been seen as a collegial organisation, governed and managed by a community of scholars. However, in the last few decades, the collegial governance and management system was dismantled in part because of forces of globalisation and the need for universities to become publicly accountable, not just to their governing bodies and internal stakeholders, but to broader society and donor agencies. This trend has revolutionized not only the operations of the University of the past but has also recreated a new university governance and management model. Universities are important institutions in the 21st century and are essential to the way that training and education are provided.

They play a crucial role in practice, policy, and public discourse in addition to offering knowledge, information, and evidence. The higher education environment is dynamic and for the last 20 years, global university rankings have been a major and growing factor in higher education around the world. There is still more work to be done, even though rankings may have encouraged some universities to raise their standards. To support quality and improvement in all universities, promote sector-wide planning pertinent to national and regional contexts, accommodate a more diverse ecosystem of differentiated universities, and uphold and strengthen universities’ mandates to serve the global common good, academics and university leaders must comprehend and contextualize university rankings. For universities, funding for postsecondary education is a constant challenge.

Examining the mobilization of financial resources for higher education systems is necessary, with an emphasis on two fundamental issues that must be addressed by all systems: what proportion of financial resources should be increased for higher education, and where will these funds originate? In addition, to be able to respond to societal needs, Africa’s higher education landscape requires visionary leadership, effective governance, sustainable resource mobilization, and seamless digital integration. Registrars are pivotal to maintaining the smooth functioning of the universities and play a key role in the above functions. Registrars typically serve as key administrative officers, overseeing various aspects related to student affairs, academic records, and institutional governance. Their responsibilities are diverse and essential for maintaining order and efficiency within the university. Their work schedule, roles, and responsibilities contribute significantly to the overall success and reputation of the institution. However, given the increasing complexity of the environment of HEIs, leading and managing such institutions requires unique and transformational leadership, management, and digital competencies, which some university managers are lacking. It is against this backdrop that the Association of African Universities (AAU) is organizing a capacity-building workshop for university registrars and administrators in universities.

General objective

The workshop aims to bring together key stakeholders, including academic leaders, registrars, and administrators, to deliberate on and concretise strategies for enhancing leadership, governance, resource mobilization, and digital transformation in Higher Education Institutions. This workshop seeks to empower participants with the knowledge and tools needed to lead transformative change in their respective institutions, fostering a collaborative and innovative higher education landscape in Africa.

Specific Objectives

Provide participants with a deep understanding of the key elements—leadership, governance, resource mobilization, and digital transformation—that shape the trajectory of HEIs in Africa.

Showcase successful models and best practices from institutions that have successfully navigated challenges and achieved transformative growth.

Equip participants with practical skills and strategies to lead and implement positive change within their respective institutions.

Engage participants on the importance, merits, and demerits of university ranking systems and context-specific application of ranking metrics and indicators

Facilitate networking opportunities for participants to engage in meaningful discussions, share experiences, and explore potential collaborations and partnerships.

Expected outcomes

The expected outcomes include:

Enhanced understanding of effective leadership, governance, resource mobilization, and digital transformation in the context of African HEIs.

Identification of actionable strategies and best practices for immediate implementation.

Networking opportunities for potential collaborations and partnerships.

Development of a collective commitment to drive positive change in African higher education.

Course Fee:

$950 per participant(excluding hotel accommodation)

Methodology

The workshop has adopted a strategic methodology that will include effective approaches, such as the use of case studies, focused group discussions, experiential learning (case studies from universities in various regions in Africa), presentations, and sharing of ideas, knowledge, and skills. The participants will have the opportunity to engage in dialogues with peers on the various challenges at their universities and map out strategies to overcome them.

Summary of the Course Content

Leadership in Higher Education

Define the characteristics of effective and transformational leadership in the context of HEIs.

Discuss the importance of fostering leadership skills among academic and administrative staff.

Develop Leadership Skills for HEI Professionals

Case Studies: Successful Leadership Models in the contexts of universities in Africa

Governance in Higher Education

Analyze the role of governance structures in ensuring accountability, transparency, and efficient decision-making.

Explore models of governance that align with the unique challenges and opportunities faced by African HEIs.

Best Practices Showcase: Governance Models from Successful HEIs

Resource mobilisation

Examine the current state of resource mobilization in African HEIs.

Understand Resource Mobilization Systems, the Donor Environment, Donor Characteristics and Expectations

Key Observations and Elements in Formulating Convincing Proposals for Resource Mobilization

Strategic Models for Sustainable Resource Mobilization

Discuss strategies for diversifying funding sources, including public-private-philanthropic partnerships, alumni engagement, and international collaborations.

Digital transformation

Assess the current level of digitalization in African HEIs and identify gaps.

Explore the role of e-learning, online platforms, and data analytics in improving the overall quality of education.

Critical steps needed to digitally transform HEIs in Africa

The confluence of Artificial Intelligence and Academic Integrity

Case Studies: Successful Integration of Technology in Education

About the Organization

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is an international non-governmental organisation set up by the universities in Africa to promote cooperation among them and between them and the international academic community. With over 400 members across the African continent, AAU is the largest and most comprehensive organization representing Universities and Higher Education bodies in Africa. It is also the apex organization and forum for consultation, exchange of information, and cooperation among institutions of higher education in Africa, and represents the voice of higher education in Africa on regional and international bodies ,and supports networking by institutions of higher education in teaching, research, information exchange, and dissemination. The AAU, with headquarters in Accra, Ghana, was founded in 1967, following recommendations made at an earlier conference organized by the United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) in Antananarivo, Madagascar in September 1962 for the formation of such an apex organization. The mission of the AAU is to raise the quality of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to African development by fostering collaboration among its member institutions.

TITLE: Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027: Global Graduate Jobs, Rotations and Career Opportunities in Wealth Management

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a recent university graduate looking to build an international career in banking, finance, wealth management, technology, data science, business administration, management, law, risk, or related fields? The Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 offers an opportunity for talented graduates to begin their professional careers with one of the world’s established wealth management institutions.

Julius Baer is opening recruitment for its 2027 Graduate Programme, providing graduates with structured professional development, practical experience and exposure to different areas of the financial sector.

The programme is designed around an 18-month graduate journey featuring three rotations, allowing participants to gain experience across different functions while developing their professional knowledge and skills.

Recruitment for the April 2027 cohort opens in September 2026, while applications for the October 2027 cohort open in February 2027. This makes the programme particularly relevant for university graduates who are planning their transition from higher education into the financial services industry.

Importantly, Julius Baer encourages graduates from a broad range of academic backgrounds to consider the programme. Although specific study profiles are highlighted, candidates whose degrees fall outside the listed fields are also encouraged to apply if they have an interest in the financial sector and specialized knowledge that could contribute to the organization.

What Is the Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027?

The Julius Baer Graduate Programme is a structured early-career programme designed to help university graduates develop the knowledge, experience and professional capabilities required to establish a career in wealth management and financial services.

Rather than placing graduates into a single function for the entire programme, the graduate journey includes three rotations over 18 months.

This rotational structure gives participants the opportunity to gain exposure to different teams and areas of the organization.

Through the programme, graduates can explore where their academic background, professional interests and skills are best suited within the broader financial services environment.

The programme’s overall philosophy is captured by Julius Baer’s graduate recruitment message: “Be the future. Be Bär.”

The programme therefore represents an opportunity for young professionals to learn, contribute and develop their careers while gaining exposure to the future of wealth management.

Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 Key Features

The 2027 programme offers several features that make it attractive to graduates seeking structured entry into the financial sector.

1. An 18-Month Graduate Programme

Participants undertake an 18-month programme designed to provide a structured transition from university into professional employment.

The length of the programme provides graduates with sufficient time to develop practical skills, understand different business functions and build professional relationships.

Rather than treating graduate recruitment as a short-term placement, the programme provides an extended development journey.

2. Three Professional Rotations

A central feature of the programme is its three rotations.

During the 18-month period, graduates have the opportunity to work across different areas of the organization.

Rotations can help participants:

Develop practical professional experience.

Understand how different teams contribute to wealth management.

Discover areas that align with their skills and interests.

Develop cross-functional knowledge.

Build relationships with colleagues across the organization.

Gain a broader understanding of financial services.

Strengthen their professional profile for future career opportunities.

The rotational structure can be particularly valuable for graduates who have strong academic foundations but are still determining which area of financial services they would like to pursue long term.

3. Exposure to the Wealth Management Industry

The programme is positioned within the wealth management sector, providing graduates with the opportunity to develop knowledge of an industry that combines finance, investment, advisory services, technology, risk management and client-focused solutions.

This exposure can help participants understand how different professional disciplines work together to support financial services organizations.

4. Focus and Flex Tracks

Julius Baer indicates that its Graduate Programme includes focus and flex tracks.

The programme brochure provides further information about these tracks, what the programme offers and the requirements for candidates.

This structure allows graduates to learn more about the possible career pathways available to them and identify opportunities that correspond with their academic and professional interests.

Study Profiles Accepted by Julius Baer

Julius Baer highlights several academic study profiles for its graduate opportunities.

These include:

Accounting, Banking and Finance

Graduates with backgrounds in accounting, banking and finance may find opportunities in areas such as:

Finance;

Advisory;

Markets; and

Portfolio Management.

These areas are particularly relevant for candidates who enjoy working with numbers, financial analysis, markets and investment-related concepts.

Graduates interested in financial markets may find the programme useful for developing practical knowledge beyond what is acquired through academic study.

Business Administration, Management and Law

Candidates with backgrounds in business administration, management or law may explore opportunities connected with areas such as:

Transformation;

Business Management;

Risk; and

Legal functions.

These disciplines are valuable within financial institutions because successful wealth management organizations require professionals who understand organizational strategy, business operations, regulatory considerations, governance and risk.

Data Sciences and Information Technology

Julius Baer also highlights Data Sciences and Information Technology as important study profiles.

Graduates with expertise in these areas can explore opportunities within technology and data-focused teams.

As financial services become increasingly dependent on technology, data, digital platforms and advanced analytical capabilities, professionals with technical expertise can play an important role in the evolution of wealth management.

Graduates From Other Academic Fields Can Also Apply

One of the most important aspects of the Julius Baer Graduate Programme is that candidates should not automatically exclude themselves simply because their degree is not one of the study profiles listed by the organization.

Julius Baer specifically states that university graduates with degrees in fields not mentioned in the highlighted study profiles should not be allowed to be discouraged from considering the programme.

The organization says it is always looking for young talent interested in the financial sector and possessing specialized knowledge in other areas.

This means that graduates from nontraditional academic backgrounds may still have an opportunity if they can demonstrate relevant skills, knowledge, motivation and an interest in financial services.

Candidates should therefore evaluate their overall profile rather than focusing exclusively on whether the exact name of their degree appears on the list.

What Can Graduates Gain From the Programme?

The Julius Baer Graduate Programme is designed to provide more than an entry point into employment.

Participants can potentially develop a combination of technical knowledge, professional experience and transferable skills.

Practical professional experience

Graduates can move from academic learning into a professional environment where they can apply their knowledge to real organizational activities.

Cross-functional exposure

Three rotations can provide broader exposure than a conventional entry-level position limited to one department.

Career exploration

Rotations allow graduates to understand different functions and identify areas where their strengths and interests are best aligned.

Professional development

An 18-month structured programme provides an extended period in which participants can develop their professional capabilities.

Industry knowledge

Participants can gain exposure to wealth management and the broader financial services industry.

Networking

Working across different teams can allow graduates to establish professional relationships with colleagues and other professionals within the organization.

Technology and innovation exposure

Graduates in data science and information technology can potentially contribute to technology-driven developments within financial services.

Opportunities for specialized talent

The programme’s openness to graduates from academic fields beyond the specifically highlighted disciplines creates room for candidates with specialized knowledge to bring different perspectives to the financial sector.

Julius Baer Graduate Programme 2027 Recruitment Timeline

Julius Baer has identified two recruitment periods for the 2027 graduate cohorts.

April 2027 cohort

Recruitment for the April 2027 cohort opens in September 2026.

Candidates interested in beginning the programme with this cohort should monitor the relevant graduate job announcements and submit applications once positions become available.

October 2027 cohort

Applications for the October 2027 cohort open in February 2027.

Graduates who are not applying for the April intake can therefore consider the later 2027 cohort.

Because the recruitment windows are different, applicants should pay attention to the specific cohort and job announcement for which they are applying.

Is There a Fixed Application Deadline?

The information provided by Julius Baer specifies the opening periods for the two 2027 cohorts rather than one universal closing deadline.

Therefore:

April 2027 cohort: Applications open in September 2026.

October 2027 cohort: Applications open in February 2027.

Candidates should check the individual graduate job announcements for the applicable closing date and specific application requirements.

APPLY HERE

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Julius Baer Graduate Programme may be particularly suitable for graduates who:

Have recently completed or are completing a university degree.

Want to establish a career in wealth management or financial services.

Are interested in banking, finance or investment.

Have an academic background in accounting, banking or finance.

Have studied business administration or management.

Have a background in law.

Are interested in risk, legal or business management.

Have studied data science or information technology.

Enjoy analytical and quantitative work.

Are interested in technology’s role in financial services.

Have specialized knowledge from another academic discipline and want to apply it within the financial sector.

Are interested in learning through practical experience and rotations.

Want exposure to multiple areas of a global wealth management organization.

How the Three-Rotation Structure Can Help Graduates

For someone entering the workforce directly after university, deciding on a long-term career specialization can be challenging.

A graduate may have studied finance but discover that they prefer advisory work rather than portfolio management. Another candidate with a technology background may discover a stronger interest in data analytics within financial services.

The rotational structure can help address this challenge.

Instead of requiring graduates to make a permanent career decision immediately, the programme provides exposure to multiple areas.

A participant can use each rotation to develop a better understanding of:

The responsibilities of different functions.

The skills required in each area.

The relationship between departments.

The type of work they enjoy.

The professional skills they need to strengthen.

The areas in which they can make the strongest contribution.

This makes the programme particularly useful for graduates who want both professional development and career discovery.

Why Data Science and Information Technology Graduates Should Pay Attention

Financial services are undergoing significant technological transformation.

Data analytics, digital platforms, information technology, automation and other technological capabilities increasingly influence how financial institutions operate and deliver services.

Julius Baer’s inclusion of Data Sciences and Information Technology among its study profiles demonstrates the relevance of technical expertise within its graduate recruitment strategy.

Graduates with technical backgrounds can therefore consider how their knowledge can be applied to financial services rather than limiting their career search to traditional technology companies.

A candidate with skills in data analysis, software, information systems or related technical disciplines may be able to bring specialized expertise to the wealth management environment.

Why Graduates From Non-Finance Backgrounds Should Not Self-Exclude

Many graduates assume that careers in banking or wealth management are exclusively reserved for people with finance or economics degrees.

The Julius Baer Graduate Programme provides an important reminder that financial institutions also require professionals with expertise in areas such as technology, data, management, law, risk and other specialized disciplines.

The organization explicitly encourages graduates whose degrees are not included in the highlighted study profiles to consider applying.

For such candidates, the key is to demonstrate how their specialized knowledge can be relevant to the financial sector.

For example, a graduate from a technology discipline could emphasize data and digital skills, while a law graduate could demonstrate knowledge relevant to legal and regulatory environments.

The strongest applications are likely to connect the applicant’s academic background and skills with the needs of the financial services industry.

Accra, Ghana – (November 22, 2025) —

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is proud to announce the official launch of its Digital Empowerment Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) Initiative, a strategic intervention designed to propel the technological advancement of higher education across Africa.

The platform was unveiled by the AAU Secretary-General, Professor Olusola Oyewole, on November 14, 2025, during the closing ceremony of the Africa Universities’ Day celebrations. In his address, Professor Oyewole called for a fundamental shift in how universities harness technology, urging institutions to expand their digital capacity-building efforts beyond faculty and students to include administrators and all staff within the academic value chain. This initiative delivers on that vision by providing accessible, scalable, and high-quality training in three critical domains: (1) Cybersecurity Fundamentals for University Systems (2) AI Essentials for Teaching and Administration (3) Digital Literacy for Modern Academia

The initiative is designed to equip university staff across Africa with critical digital skills, strengthen institutional capacity, and enhance the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity practices in teaching, research, and administration. It forms part of AAU’s broader strategy to strengthen digital competencies among academic and administrative staff across its 450 member universities, supporting the African Union’s Agenda 2063 vision of a knowledge-driven, digitally empowered Africa.

The Digital Empowerment MOOCs will be delivered in a blended format, combining three-week self-paced online sessions with a day’s contact session (virtual) with facilitators, followed by an optional one-week in-person practical workshop to maximize participation and impact.

The first online cohort runs from from February 2 to 20, 2026. Registration for the online sessions is free and can be completed via https://forms.office.com/r/JLb6fkHWeF.

The in-person workshop will take place in April, 2026, at the AAU Secretariat, located on the Trinity Avenue, East Legon, Accra, Ghana It focuses on advanced strategic planning, leadership in digital transformation, and technology adoption. The workshop fee, USD 400, covers facilitation, materials, and meals. Payment can be made via https://pay.aau.org/digital-empowerment-moocs.

Participants will engage in video lectures, interactive simulations, case studies, discussion forums, and capstone projects, enabling practical application of acquired skills. The MOOCs initiative aims to deliver measurable benefits to staff and institutions across Africa, with at least 80% of participants expected to improve proficiency in digital, AI, and cybersecurity tools. It also aims to help institutions to reduce minor cybersecurity incidents by 50% while accelerating AI-driven processes within 12 months. Successful participants will be awarded certificates, enhancing professional visibility and institutional benchmarking.

The programme was designed with subject matter experts, strategic partners, university staff, and ICT directors to deliver practical and contextually relevant content. The AAU is, thus, by this release, inviting university administrators, teaching staff, ICT professionals, students, and sector partners to participate in this transformative initiative. We believe that by building a digitally empowered workforce, African universities will enhance innovation, strengthen operational resilience, and contribute meaningfully to Africa’s long-term development goals.

TITLE: The Fanyi Zhao Award

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Fanyi Zhao Award

Postdoctoral Researcher Dr. Fanyi Zhao was a rising star in the area of nuclear and particle theory who tragically passed away on January 24, 2024 at the age of 27.

The MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) honors Fanyi’s memory each year with the Fanyi Zhao Award for postdoctoral researchers in the CTP-LI who have promoted collaboration and interactions between different CTP-LI research groups, including scientific and/or social connections.

Recipients:

Dr. Thomas Steingasser 2024

Dr. Neill Warrington2025

Dr. Jamie Sullivan2026

In Memory of Fanyi Zhao

Fanyi Zhao
Postdoctoral Researcher Dr. Fanyi Zhao, a rising star in the area of nuclear and particle theory, tragically passed away on January 24, 2024 at the age of 27. She had joined the MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics (CTP) (now MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)) in September 2023.

Born in 1996 in China, Fanyi received her B.S. in Physics in 2018 from the University of Science and Technology in Anhui, China before heading to UCLA where she completed her PhD in Physics under the supervision of Professor Zhong-bo Kang. Her PhD thesis was titled “3D Imaging via Polarized Jet Fragmentation Functions and Quantum Simulation of the QCD Phase Diagram.”

During her time, at UCLA, she impressed in many ways with her research in QCD theory and phenomenology, and in quantum simulation to QCD and strong interactions. She was a recipient of the Mani L. Bhaumik Institute Nina Byers Summer Fellowship in Theoretical Physics and a fellowship in quantum information science. In addition to efforts in conference organizing and diversity and outreach she also found time to mentor undergraduate students at UCLA, a number of whom went on to PhD programs in Physics, including one at MIT.

Joining the CTP (now CTP-LI) in the September 2023, Fanyi’s research involved using quantum field theory to investigate nucleon structure, including things like transverse momentum distributions, energy-energy correlators, and jets as a member of the research team of Professor Iain Stewart. Her work also continued to involve a significant component on quantum information science as applied to problems in nuclear physics.

She is remembered by Center members and other colleagues outside of MIT as a funny, generous, kind and thoroughly committed scientist with a great love of physics. Beyond her scientific passion, she embraced life fully, with passions ranging from music and martial arts to running and drawing. We are all greatly saddened by her passing.

In May 2024, the Center for Theoretical Physics will honor Fanyi’s memory with the announcement of the recipient of the first Fanyi Zhao Award for postdoctoral researchers in the CTP who have promoted collaboration and interactions between different CTP research groups, including scientific and/or social connections.

In the Fall of 2024, there will also be the Fanyi Zhao Memorial Lecture established at the UCLA Department of Physics and Astronomy. This lecture series will be awarded yearly to a young physicist, recognizing outstanding achievements in nuclear and particle physics.

Any donations made to the CTP-LI to honor the memory of Fanyi Zhao will be used to support the award named in her honor.

A reminder to all that MIT’s MyLife Services for staff, postdocs and faculty (844-405-5433), and Student Mental Health and Counseling for students (617-253-4481, Option 2), are available 24/7 including on the weekend.

TITLE: Richard Nally, Pappalardo Fellow

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Name: Richard Nally
Title: Pappalardo Fellow in Physics: 2024-2027
Email: rnally@mit.edu

Cambridge, MA 02139

Related Links:
Pappalardo Fellowships in Physics

Area of Physics

String Theory

Research Interests

Richard Nally’s research is centered on string theory and its compactifications to four dimensions. String theory is defined in ten dimensions. To connect this theory to our familiar four dimensions, we take six of the ten dimensions to be compact, and the shape of the compact dimensions determines the physics in the four large dimensions. In the best-studied framework for these compactifications, we take the compact dimensions to be a special type of shape called a Calabi-Yau manifold. Richard’s research concerns these shapes and the physics of their compactifications.

A fundamental fact about our universe is that its expansion is accelerating. The leading proposal for how to realize this behavior in a string compactification was made by Kachru, Kallosh, Linde, and Trivedi (KKLT) in 2003, but an actual example of their proposed mechanism remained elusive for twenty years. In recent work, Richard and his collaborators constructed the first completely explicit examples of string compactifications realizing the KKLT mechanism for obtaining an accelerating universe in string theory. This work will be the starting point for Richard’s future research activities.

In addition to his work on constructing realistic solutions of string theory, Richard is also interested in connections between string theory and mathematics. In particular, he has worked extensively on relating special solutions of string theory to number theory, and has established physical criteria for the modularity of certain Calabi-Yau manifolds.

Biographical Sketch

Richard was born and raised in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. He went to Brown University for college, where he received an ScB in Mathematical Physics. While at Brown, he pursued research in both experimental and theoretical aspects of Large Hadron Collider physics, under the mentorship of Profs. Meenakshi Narain and Chung-I Tan, respectively.

After Brown, Richard proceeded to get his PhD from Stanford University. Working with Prof. Shamit Kachru, Richard explored connections between string theory and number theory, and in particular worked to understand the role number theoretic objects called modular forms play in string theory. He additionally pursued projects in holography and aspects of theoretical condensed matter research.

From Stanford, Richard was awarded a Klarman Fellowship to pursue postdoctoral research at Cornell University. At Cornell, he worked with Prof. Liam McAllister to study explicit string compactifications and their physics. This productive collaboration led to the construction of the first-ever de Sitter vacua in Calabi-Yau compactifications of string theory.

Outside of physics, Richard is passionate about coffee, fashion, and cooking.

TITLE: Harvard Academy Scholars Program 2027–2028: Fully Funded Postdoctoral Fellowship at Harvard University

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Harvard Academy Scholars Program 2027–2028 is now accepting applications from outstanding early-career scholars who have recently completed, or are nearing completion of, a PhD or equivalent doctoral degree in the social sciences.

Hosted by the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies at Harvard University, the Academy Scholars Program is a prestigious two-year, in-residence postdoctoral fellowship designed for researchers whose work combines strong social science scholarship with deep knowledge of countries or regions outside the United States and Canada.

The programme provides selected scholars with substantial financial support, research assistance, mentoring, access to Harvard’s academic community and dedicated time to develop ambitious research and publication projects. For the 2027–2028 cohort, the application deadline is September 18, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

The Harvard Academy is highly selective. It receives more than 500 applications in many years and normally selects only five or six Academy Scholars for each cohort.

About the Harvard Academy Scholars Program

The Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies is housed within the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University.

Its mission is to promote innovative social science research while deepening understanding of the experiences and practices of different regions and countries around the world.

The Academy Scholars Program was established to support outstanding researchers at the beginning of their academic careers whose work combines:

Excellence in a social science discipline

Strong regional or country expertise

Knowledge of languages relevant to their research where appropriate

Original and innovative research

Comparative, transnational or domestic research questions

The potential to develop a successful career in a research university or international institution

The programme is particularly interested in scholars whose research connects disciplinary expertise with knowledge of regions outside the United States and Canada.

What Is the Harvard Academy Scholars Program?

The Academy Scholars Program is a two-year, in-residence postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Each year, approximately five to six scholars are selected for two-year appointments. Selected scholars receive an annual stipend of US$80,000, in addition to US$6,000 in annual research support.

The fellowship provides scholars with the time and resources necessary to undertake substantial research, writing and professional development during the early stages of their academic careers.

Academy Scholars become part of a select interdisciplinary community and participate in academic activities with other scholars and Harvard faculty members.

The programme also provides opportunities for scholars to interact with the Harvard Academy’s Senior Scholars, who serve as mentors and members of the selection committee.

Harvard Academy Scholars Program 2027–2028 Benefits

The fellowship provides several important benefits designed to support scholars during their two-year appointment.

1. Annual Stipend of US$80,000

Each Academy Scholar receives an annual stipend of US$80,000.

This substantial financial support allows fellows to dedicate significant time to research, writing and academic development without the financial pressures that can accompany early-career research.

2. Annual Research Support of US$6,000

In addition to the annual stipend, Academy Scholars receive US$6,000 per year in research support.

This funding can help facilitate research-related activities associated with the scholar’s approved academic work.

3. Two-Year Fellowship

The appointment is structured as a two-year postdoctoral fellowship.

The fellowship provides an extended period for scholars to develop their research programmes, publish academic work and establish themselves as independent researchers.

The Academy notes that the two years must be completed within a three-year window.

4. Research and Writing Opportunities

The programme is specifically designed to provide scholars with time to undertake significant research and writing.

Scholars may use the fellowship period to develop work based on their doctoral research, prepare a dissertation for publication or begin a new research project.

5. Mentorship

Academy Scholars are mentored by the Harvard Academy’s Senior Scholars.

These faculty members participate in Academy activities and support fellows as they develop their research and academic careers.

6. Interdisciplinary Academic Community

Academy Scholars participate in dinners, seminars and informal academic gatherings.

These activities encourage scholars from different disciplines and regional specializations to exchange ideas and develop interdisciplinary approaches to research.

7. Harvard University Research Environment

Being based at Harvard University provides Academy Scholars with access to a major international academic environment and opportunities to interact with researchers, faculty and other scholars.

The programme is particularly suited to researchers who would benefit from an intellectually intensive period dedicated to research and publication.

Who Is Eligible for the Harvard Academy Scholars Program 2027–2028?

The Academy Scholars Program is open to scholars from all countries and citizenships.

However, applicants must meet specific doctoral and disciplinary requirements.

The programme is intended for scholars who have recently completed or are nearing completion of a PhD or equivalent degree in the social sciences. Equivalent degrees include programmes such as the DPhil and SJD where applicable.

Applicants Who Have Already Completed Their PhD

If you have completed your PhD, your degree must have been completed within two years of the fellowship’s August 1, 2027 start date.

For the September 18, 2026 application deadline, applicants who have already completed their PhD must have completed it on or after August 1, 2025.

Current PhD Candidates

Applicants who are still completing their doctoral degree may also apply.

However, they must be sufficiently advanced in their programme and able to provide official degree-conferral documentation from their university registrar by June 30, 2027.

This requirement is important because successful applicants must be able to begin the fellowship on the required schedule.

Applicants Who Have Previously Held a Postdoctoral Fellowship

Individuals who hold or have completed another postdoctoral fellowship are not eligible to apply.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider their previous postdoctoral experience before submitting an application.

Eligible Fields of Study

The Harvard Academy does not accept applications from every academic discipline.

The programme focuses on the social sciences, particularly research that examines regions and countries outside the United States and Canada.

Eligible social science fields include:

Anthropology

Economics

Ethnic Studies

Geography

Government

History

History of Science

International Relations

Law

Political Economy and Government

Political Science

Psychology

Public Policy

Social Policy

Social Studies

Sociology

Women, Gender, and Sexuality

Applicants from regional studies disciplines may also be considered when their research is clearly grounded in one or more of the accepted social science disciplines.

Regional Studies Fields That May Be Eligible

The Academy welcomes applicants from several regional studies fields when the research is appropriately designed around the accepted social science disciplines.

These include:

African Studies

Asian Studies

Central Asian Studies

East Asian Languages and Civilizations

Eastern European Studies

Inner Asian and Altaic Studies

Latin American and Iberian Studies

Middle East Studies

Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations

Russia Studies

Slavic Languages and Civilization

South Asian Studies

Southeast Asian Studies

Ukraine Studies

Western European Studies

The key consideration is not simply the name of the degree programme. The applicant’s research must clearly engage with one or more of the Academy’s eligible social science disciplines.

Fields That Are Not Accepted

The Harvard Academy also identifies a number of areas that are not eligible.

The list includes:

Research focused on the United States or Canada

Archaeology

Architecture

Art History

Business

Classics

Global Health

Linguistics

Literature

Management

Medieval Studies

Religion

The Academy notes that this list is not exhaustive.

Applicants should therefore carefully compare their doctoral field and research focus with the official eligibility criteria before applying.

A Major Requirement: Research Must Focus Outside the United States or Canada

Applicants should pay close attention to the Academy’s regional focus.

The programme seeks scholars whose work combines social science expertise with knowledge of countries or regions outside the United States or Canada.

Therefore, an otherwise eligible scholar may not qualify if the proposed research is primarily focused on the United States or Canada.

This regional requirement is central to the intellectual purpose of the programme and distinguishes the Academy Scholars Program from many other postdoctoral fellowships.

Harvard Academy Scholars Program Application Requirements

Applicants must submit a complete online application containing several important documents.

1. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a CV that includes their academic and professional background as well as a list of publications.

The CV should provide a clear overview of the applicant’s:

Academic qualifications

Research experience

Publications

Awards and recognitions

Teaching experience where applicable

Fellowships

Professional appointments

Relevant academic activities

2. Research Proposal

Applicants must submit a research proposal of no more than 2,000 words.

The proposal should explain the intellectual objectives of the research and the methodological and disciplinary work the applicant plans to undertake.

The Academy’s selection committee is particularly interested in:

The relevance of the proposed research

Its contribution to the applicant’s discipline

The originality of the research

The researcher’s plans for the two-year fellowship

Future publication plans

Future research plans

References and citations do not count toward the 2,000-word limit.

3. Scholarly Writing Sample

Applicants must submit one scholarly writing sample.

Examples include:

A chapter from a PhD dissertation

A peer-reviewed academic journal article

Another substantial scholarly work

The writing sample must:

Be written in English

Be no longer than 50 pages

Represent approximately the length of a single PhD dissertation chapter or academic journal article

Be submitted as one sample only

A published or unpublished work may be used.

Co-authored work is permitted provided that the applicant’s contribution is clearly identified and the work is not co-authored with an academic adviser.

4. PhD Program Transcript

Applicants must submit a copy of their PhD programme transcript.

For applicants who studied at universities outside the United States, the Academy advises that applicants provide as much official transcript-like documentation as their university registrar can provide for their graduate studies, including relevant Master’s and PhD records.

5. Three Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must provide three letters of recommendation.

The letters must be uploaded directly and confidentially by the recommenders through the online application system.

Importantly, applicants must first submit their application before the recommendation upload link is sent to the recommenders.

This means applicants should contact their potential recommenders well in advance of the deadline.

The recommendation letters have a later submission deadline than the main application materials: they must arrive no later than September 28, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

The main application deadline is:

September 18, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

Harvard Academy states that late applications are not accepted.

All application materials other than the recommendation letters must be received by this deadline.

Recommendation letters must arrive by:

September 28, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

Important 2027–2028 Application Timeline

Key dates include:

September 18, 2026, 11:59 PM EDT: Main application deadline

August 1, 2027: Fellowship start date

Where Is the Fellowship Located?

The Harvard Academy Scholars Program is based at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States.

The Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies is located within the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at:

1727 Cambridge Street

Cambridge, MA 02138

USA

The fellowship is an in-residence programme, meaning Academy Scholars are expected to participate actively in the Harvard academic community during the formal programming period.

Residency and Fieldwork Requirements

Academy Scholars are expected to be in residence and participate fully in the scholarly community during the formal programming period, which runs approximately from late August through the end of April.

Scholars can conduct extensive fieldwork during the winter, spring and summer breaks.

Short trips for conferences and other academic engagements may be permitted provided that they do not interfere with Harvard Academy obligations.

This requirement is important for applicants whose research involves extensive international fieldwork.

The fellowship is designed around participation in an active academic community at Harvard rather than being a fully remote research fellowship.

Can the Fellowship Start Date Be Deferred?

No.

Successful applicants cannot postpone or defer the August 1, 2027 start date.

Year 1 must begin no later than the fall immediately following the fellowship offer.

The two fellowship years must also be completed within the programme’s specified three-year window.

Applicants should therefore apply only if they will be able to commit to the required timeline.

How Competitive Is the Harvard Academy Scholars Program?

The Academy Scholars Program is extremely competitive.

The Harvard Academy states that it receives more than 500 applications in many years but typically selects only five or six scholars.

Historical statistics demonstrate the selectivity of the programme. For example:

Fall 2016: 716 completed applications, 4 selected

Fall 2019: 585 completed applications, 5 selected

Fall 2022: 350 completed applications, 5 selected

Fall 2024: 533 completed applications, 6 selected

Fall 2025: 522 completed applications, 5 selected

These figures demonstrate why applicants need to present a highly focused research agenda and compelling evidence of scholarly potential.

How to Prepare a Strong Harvard Academy Application

Because the programme is highly selective, applicants should approach the application strategically.

1. Develop a Clear Research Question

Your research proposal should communicate exactly what problem you intend to investigate.

Avoid presenting a broad topic without a clear research question.

Explain:

What you want to study

Why the question matters

What is already known

What gap your research addresses

What contribution you intend to make

How you will conduct the research

2. Demonstrate Disciplinary Contribution

The Academy specifically emphasizes the relevance and contribution of the proposed research to the applicant’s discipline.

Your proposal should therefore make the academic contribution explicit rather than assuming that the committee will infer it.

3. Explain Your Two-Year Research Plan

Applicants should explain how they intend to use the fellowship period.

For example, a scholar may use the first year to develop doctoral research into a book or series of articles and use the second year to begin a new research project.

If you plan to move in a new research direction, explain how the new project connects with or expands upon your doctoral research.

4. Select Your Writing Sample Carefully

The writing sample is an important demonstration of your scholarly ability.

Choose one piece that clearly demonstrates:

Strong argumentation

Original thinking

Research competence

Evidence-based analysis

Clear academic writing

Strong methodological reasoning where relevant

Do not submit multiple writing samples because the Academy specifically requests only one.

5. Contact Recommenders Early

Since recommendation letters must be submitted separately, applicants should contact their recommenders well before the application deadline.

Waiting until the final days can create unnecessary risks, especially if a recommender is unavailable or encounters technical difficulties.

6. Check Your Regional Fit

One of the most important elements of the Academy Scholars Program is its focus on regions outside the United States and Canada.

Applicants should clearly demonstrate how their research engages with a specific country, region or broader comparative question that fits the Academy’s mission.

Why This Fellowship Is Valuable for Early-Career Researchers

The transition from completing a PhD to establishing an independent academic career can be challenging.

Researchers often need time to transform doctoral research into publications while developing new research projects and establishing an independent scholarly identity.

The Harvard Academy Scholars Program addresses this need by providing:

A two-year research environment

A substantial annual stipend

Dedicated research funding

Mentorship

An interdisciplinary scholarly community

Opportunities for academic exchange

Time to develop publications

Access to the Harvard academic environment

The programme is particularly valuable for researchers whose work sits at the intersection of social science discipline and regional expertise.

Important Advice for International Applicants

International applicants are explicitly welcome, regardless of citizenship or where they completed their graduate studies.

However, applicants studying outside the United States should ensure that their academic documentation is sufficiently detailed.

The Academy advises international applicants to obtain official transcript-like documentation for their graduate studies from their university registrar where necessary.

Applicants should also consider the practical implications of an in-residence fellowship in Cambridge, Massachusetts, including the requirement to participate in the programme’s formal activities.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Harvard Academy Scholars Program may be particularly suitable for an applicant who:

Has recently completed a PhD in an eligible social science field

Is an advanced doctoral candidate nearing completion

Has a strong academic record

Has a clearly defined research agenda

Conducts research focused on a region outside the United States or Canada

Has demonstrated scholarly potential

Has strong writing and research experience

Wants to develop doctoral research into publications

Is planning an independent research project

Can commit to a two-year in-residence fellowship

Has not previously completed a postdoctoral fellowship

Researchers from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and other regions may apply because the programme accepts scholars of all nationalities, provided they satisfy the academic and research requirements.

How to Apply for the Harvard Academy Scholars Program

Applications are submitted online through the Harvard Academy’s application system.

Applicants should prepare the required documents before beginning the submission process:

Curriculum vitae with publication list

Research proposal of no more than 2,000 words

One English-language scholarly writing sample of no more than 50 pages

PhD programme transcript

Three confidential letters of recommendation

All application materials are submitted online as PDF documents.

The application should be completed and submitted by September 18, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT, while recommendation letters must arrive by September 28, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

Applicants can access the application through the official Harvard Academy website.

Official Harvard Academy Scholars Program:

Visit the Harvard Academy Scholars Program page

Online Application:

Apply through Harvard’s online application portal

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Harvard Academy Scholars Program fully funded?

The programme provides substantial financial support, including an annual US$80,000 stipend and US$6,000 annual research support. It is therefore a highly funded postdoctoral fellowship, although applicants should review the official terms carefully rather than assuming that every possible personal expense is covered.

Can applicants from Africa apply?

Yes. The Academy states that the programme is open to scholars from all countries and citizenships. African applicants are eligible provided they meet the doctoral, disciplinary, regional and other programme requirements.

Can current PhD students apply?

Yes. Advanced doctoral candidates can apply if they will be able to submit official degree-conferral documentation from their university registrar by June 30, 2027.

Can someone with a PhD apply?

Yes, provided the PhD was completed within two years of the August 1, 2027 start date. For the current application cycle, the PhD must have been completed on or after August 1, 2025.

Can someone who has already completed another postdoctoral fellowship apply?

No. Individuals who hold or have completed another postdoctoral fellowship are not eligible.

Is there an age limit?

The official eligibility information focuses on the timing of PhD completion or expected completion rather than specifying a general age limit. Applicants should therefore assess eligibility primarily according to their doctoral status and completion date.

Can the fellowship be deferred?

No. The August 1, 2027 start date cannot be postponed or deferred.

Can Academy Scholars conduct research outside Cambridge?

Yes, but extensive fieldwork should generally be scheduled during winter, spring or summer breaks. Scholars are expected to remain in residence and participate in the Academy’s formal programming during the main academic period.

How many scholars are selected?

The Academy generally selects approximately five to six scholars each year, although the exact number can vary.

Conclusion

The Harvard Academy Scholars Program 2027–2028 represents a highly competitive opportunity for emerging social scientists seeking dedicated time, financial support and an exceptional academic environment to advance their research.

The two-year in-residence postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard University provides selected scholars with an US$80,000 annual stipend, US$6,000 in annual research support, mentorship from Senior Scholars and opportunities to participate in an interdisciplinary scholarly community.

The programme is open to applicants from all countries and citizenships, making it accessible to qualified researchers worldwide. However, applicants must meet the programme’s strict academic requirements, including having recently completed or being close to completing a PhD or equivalent degree in an eligible social science field. Their research must also demonstrate meaningful expertise in countries or regions outside the United States or Canada.

Because only a small number of Academy Scholars are selected each year, prospective applicants should invest considerable time in developing a compelling research proposal, selecting a strong scholarly writing sample, preparing an academic CV and securing high-quality recommendation letters.

For the 2027–2028 cohort, the main application deadline is September 18, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT, while recommendation letters must arrive by September 28, 2026, at 11:59 PM EDT.

Eligible researchers should begin preparing their applications well in advance and carefully review the official Harvard Academy requirements before submitting. This is particularly important for international and regional studies applicants, as the programme’s disciplinary and geographic focus is central to the selection process.

TITLE: PO Department features prominently in 2026 Woods Hole Sea Grant Educator workshop, Fishing for Data: Real world applications for oceanographic observations

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
by Caroline Ummenhofer

The Woods Hole Sea Grant Educator workshop, Fishing for Data: Real world applications for oceanographic observations, took place on January 23, 2026, in Woods Hole, MA. It was targeted at educators in STEM fields for grades 6-12 and focused on ecosystem dynamics and how biotic and abiotic factors intersect. Educators learned how scientists and fishermen are working together to document and understand the rapidly changing ocean conditions off the Northeast U.S. and its impacts on fisheries. The Educator workshop related to a collaborative project “Tracking local ocean conditions through a new partnership with the fishing community to support sustainable Cape Cod fisheries on a changing New England shelf” (PIs: Caroline Ummenhofer, Glen Gawarkiewicz, and Svenja Ryan) between PO and Cape Cod Commercial Fishermen’s Alliance (CCCFA) and included presenters from both, as well as NOAA Fisheries. Presentations and hands-on tutorials were led by Caroline Ummenhofer and Finn Wimberly in PO. In addition to learning about various oceanographic concepts, educators participated in hands-on tank experiments to explore ocean stratification, were given an opportunity for exploration of the Cape Cod Ocean Watch dashboard that visualizes various datasets, and examples were given how educators and students can use the data collected by the fishing community to engage with oceanographic concepts.

Finn Wimberly presents the Cape Cod Ocean Watch dashboard to ~25 STEM educators from across New England at the Woods Hole Sea Grant Educator workshop. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

During the afternoon, the educators were given a tour of Clark South and David Center, led by Jessica Kozik. During the tour, they had the opportunity to learn more about oceanographic instrumentation and technological developments first-hand by visiting the Argo/Float labs and UNOLS Wire Pool at WHOI, as well as a tour of the R/V Neil Armstrong in Woods Hole. They heard about the Argo program from Bill Dullea, gliders from Patrick Deane, and the UNOLS WirePool and mooring operations from Andrea Harvey and Barbara Callahan.

Jessica Kozik leads the tour of labs and facilities for the educators, here introducing a CTD in the Clark South high bay area. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

Bill Dullea explains the Argo program to the educators, pointing out the suite of new floats to be deployed. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

Patrick Deane showcases various gliders to the STEM educators. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

STEM educators learn about the UNOLS WirePool and mooring operations from Andrea Harvey and Barbara Callahan. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

Barbara Callahan demonstrates how mooring cables are evaluated by undergoing a break test in the David Center. Photo credit: Caroline Ummenhofer (WHOI).

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Manchester Metropolitan University (Manchester Met) is providing a range of fellowship opportunities designed to support researchers at different stages of their academic careers. The university’s fellowship portfolio includes schemes covering areas such as early-career research, engineering, science and technology, artificial intelligence, humanities and social sciences, biological sciences, and interdisciplinary research.

Manchester Met states that it is committed to the development of early-career researchers and supports outstanding candidates seeking externally funded research opportunities. Its fellowship portfolio includes both opportunities currently open for applications or expressions of interest and previously advertised schemes.

For applicants interested in pursuing an academic research career in the United Kingdom, the university’s fellowship opportunities provide potential routes to develop independent research, strengthen research records, build collaborations and progress toward longer-term academic careers.

About Manchester Metropolitan University’s Fellowship Opportunities

Manchester Metropolitan University is based in Manchester, United Kingdom, and has established a broad research environment focused on innovation, knowledge exchange and societal impact.

The university describes its research as being driven by a desire to make an impact on the world, building on its position in Manchester while pursuing national and global impact. It also highlights its facilities, research activities and academic environment as important elements of its research offering.

Its fellowship opportunities are particularly relevant to researchers looking for structured support to develop their research careers and pursue externally funded schemes.

The university’s fellowship page currently highlights several schemes, including:

Leverhulme Trust Early Career Fellowships

STFC Ernest Rutherford Fellowships

Royal Academy of Engineering Research Fellowships

British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowships

Leverhulme Trust Research Leadership Awards

BBSRC Fellowships

The Sir Robert Boyd Fellowship

Third Century Fellowship Scheme

However, applicants should carefully check the status of each scheme because the page contains both currently open and closed opportunities.

Featured Current Opportunity: Leverhulme Trust Early Career Fellowship

Among the opportunities listed by Manchester Met, the Leverhulme Trust Early Career Fellowship is identified as having Expressions of Interest now open.

The scheme is intended for early-career researchers who already have a research record but have not yet held a full-time permanent academic post. The fellowship enables successful researchers to undertake a significant piece of publishable research.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to researchers who are building their academic careers and want dedicated time and institutional support to develop a substantial research project.

How the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship Works

The scheme operates through a joint-support model.

Under this arrangement:

The Leverhulme Trust contributes part of the total salary cost.

Manchester Metropolitan University provides the remaining salary cost as match funding.

Because there is a limit to the number of proposals that can be supported, Manchester Met conducts an internal selection process.

Applicants need support from a prospective host School or Department.

Researchers interested in applying should contact the relevant School or Department Research contact to discuss the potential for Manchester Met to host their proposed research and receive support with the Expression of Interest form.

This means prospective applicants should not treat the process as a straightforward direct application to the external funder. Manchester Met first conducts an internal selection process before selected candidates proceed to the external fellowship application.

Key Deadline for the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship

The current Manchester Met Expression of Interest deadline is

Friday, 9 October 2026

Applicants are required to submit their Expressions of Interest to the relevant School or Department contact by this date.

Following submission, the Schools and Departments will nominate their selected candidates for internal review.

The internal selection panel is scheduled to meet on:

5 November 2026

Manchester Met expects to select up to two applications to progress to submission to the Leverhulme Trust.

Successful candidates will then be notified following the internal panel and supported by a mentor and the Research Development Team as they prepare for external submission.

The external submission is scheduled for:

18 February 2027

Who Is the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship For?

The fellowship is specifically designed for early-career researchers who have an established research record but have not yet held a full-time permanent academic position.

The purpose is to enable these researchers to undertake a significant piece of publishable research. The scheme is intended to support researchers at a relatively early point in their academic careers and may help position them for a future permanent academic role.

The fellowships are tenable for three years.

Research and Career Development Through the Fellowship

The Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship is structured around the development of independent research.

Rather than simply providing short-term research support, the scheme is intended to give an early-career researcher the opportunity to undertake a substantial project capable of producing significant publishable work.

The fellowship may therefore be valuable for researchers seeking to:

Develop an independent research profile.

Complete a substantial research project.

Produce publishable research.

Strengthen their academic track record.

Develop their position within their research field.

Work toward a longer-term academic career.

Establish connections with a UK university research environment.

Benefit from institutional mentoring and research development support.

Manchester Met notes that the fellowship is intended to assist researchers at a relatively early stage of their academic careers and expresses the hope that the appointment can lead to a more permanent position for the individual, either at the same university or elsewhere.

Important Consideration for Prospective Applicants

Researchers considering the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship should understand the distinction between the Manchester Met Expression of Interest stage and the external Leverhulme Trust application.

The Manchester Met process involves:

Identifying a suitable Manchester Met School or Department.

Discussing the research proposal and potential hosting arrangements with the relevant research contact.

Preparing and submitting the Expression of Interest.

Participating in Manchester Met’s internal selection process.

If selected, receiving institutional support to develop the external application.

Preparing for submission to the Leverhulme Trust by the external deadline.

Because Manchester Met states that there is a limit on the number of proposals it can support, applicants should carefully engage with the relevant School or Department before submitting their EOI.

Other Fellowship Opportunities at Manchester Metropolitan University

Manchester Met’s fellowship portfolio extends beyond the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship.

STFC Ernest Rutherford Fellowships

The STFC Ernest Rutherford Fellowships support outstanding early-career researchers seeking to establish independent research careers within the Science and Technology Facilities Council’s core science programme.

Manchester Met’s page identifies the 2026 opportunity as open and invites potential applicants to submit an Expression of Interest to the university.

Applicants should note that this deadline has already passed.

Royal Academy of Engineering Research Fellowships

Manchester Met invited prospective applicants to submit Expressions of Interest for this scheme, but the university page states that the call is now closed.

UKRI Future Leaders Fellowships

Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action Postdoctoral Fellowships
