UKRI Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowship

The UKRI Turing AI Pioneer Interdisciplinary Fellowship is aimed at established researchers across the UKRI remit who do not have a background in core artificial intelligence research.

The opportunity is designed for researchers who want to:

Build domain-relevant AI capability.

Develop advanced AI approaches.

Apply AI approaches to a specific research challenge in their chosen field.

Work across disciplinary boundaries.

The Manchester Met page currently identifies this opportunity as closed.

The British Academy Postdoctoral Fellowships are designed for early-career researchers in the humanities and social sciences.

The Manchester Met page currently identifies this opportunity as closed.

Tools and technologies underpinning biological research

The Dowager Countess Eleanor Peel Trust (DCEPT) Sir Robert Boyd Fellowship was another fellowship opportunity featured on the Manchester Met page.

The referenced 2024 EOI deadline was 26 August 2024, and the page currently identifies the opportunity as closed.

Third Century Fellowship Scheme

The Third Century Fellowship Scheme was launched by Manchester Metropolitan University in connection with its 200th anniversary in 2024.

The fellowship was aimed at exceptional researchers in the early stages of their postdoctoral careers who wanted to establish themselves in their field through independent research.

The university described the target candidates as emerging research leaders with significant experience and a notable record of research outputs.

Who Qualifies for These Opportunities?

Because Manchester Met’s fellowship page contains several different schemes, eligibility varies from one fellowship to another.

For the currently highlighted Leverhulme Trust Early Career Fellowship, the stated target group is:

Early-career researchers.

Researchers who already have a research record.

Researchers who have not yet held a full-time permanent academic post.

Researchers seeking to undertake a significant piece of publishable research.

Researchers who can secure the support of a prospective Manchester Met host School or Department.

The source provided does not state a specific nationality, race or continental restriction for the Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship on the page excerpt. Therefore, applicants should consult the official Leverhulme Trust guidance for the complete external eligibility requirements before applying.

For the other fellowships, eligibility is scheme-specific. For example, the British Academy fellowship focuses on humanities and social sciences, the Royal Academy of Engineering fellowship focuses on engineering, and the BBSRC scheme focuses on biotechnology and biological sciences.

Application Process for the Current Manchester Met Opportunity

Researchers interested in the currently open Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship should approach the application strategically.

18 February 2027

3. Support Communication and Coordination

The successful candidate may be required to help ensure that information is communicated effectively, stakeholders are coordinated and programme activities are properly organized.

4. Provide Administrative Support

The Graduate Professional will also contribute to administrative tasks required by programme staff.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable managing multiple responsibilities, keeping track of deadlines and supporting organizational processes.

Responsible Research and Innovation in the Western Balkans

The overall aim of WBC-RRI.NET is to foster the application of Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) principles at the territorial level in Western Balkan Countries (WBCs), so as to then promote a multi-level steering R&I governance framework. The RRI principles will act as enablers to the shared learning and diffusion of R&I governance innovations at the territorial level and this in turn can lead to enhancing R&I planning, including the existent or upcoming Smart Specialisation Strategies (S3) in the WBCs.

This framework will be based on a ‘smart directionality’ approach ─been indicated as beneficial to regional ecosystems─ as well as on a regional and local innovation planning, a concept to which citizens will also be brought closer through the RRI principles. R&I planning and S3 strategies will thus have the potential to be characterised by an RRI-driven open and inclusive approach, entailing a comprehensive stakeholder involvement and engagement with a focus on citizens’ participation. The approach described is also based on the rationale that the RRI concept ─mostly adapted to the level of research institutions ─can also be applied to the level of regional and territorial research and innovation governance.

Operationally, RRI activities will be performed throughout the entire course of the project (horizontal aspect), raising an active dialogue in the wider WB region and fostering the comprehension of all RRI pillars under a holistic framework. Alongside, a set of RRI ‘anchor’ initiatives (vertical aspect) will touch-in depth specific RRI keys in 5 WB territories:

Kune-Vain- Tale Lagoon wetland ecosystem (Albania)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Universal quadratic field equations via homotopy algebras

Christoph Chiaffrino, Raji Ashenafi Mamade and Barton Zwiebach
August 11, 2026, arXiv:2608.11307
Abstract: (click to show)
We explain how the 'bar-cobar' construction for homotopy algebras reformulates the equations of motion of arbitrary gauge theories as gauge-covariant quadratic equations for an extended set of fields. The linear term of the new equations encodes the interactions of the original theory, while the quadratic term is universal. The extended fields include type-I multilocal fields, which depend on a set of coordinates and type-II multilocal fields, which depend on several sets of coordinates. The new equations of motion are the Maurer-Cartan equations of a differential graded associative algebra or Lie algebra. We show that every solution of the new equations is gauge equivalent to a solution with only type-I fields, that represents a solution of the original equations of motion. In string theory type-I fields are entangled states of the associated CFT, to be inserted across multiple punctures of a Riemann surface. General type-II states can also represent disconnected Riemann surfaces.

Vacuum polarization in QED with an electromagnetic background from the lattice

En-Hung Chao
August 11, 2026, arXiv:2608.10457
Abstract: (click to show)
We propose a framework to determine the vacuum polarization functions in QED in the presence of an electromagnetic background field in the spacelike region on the lattice. This method consists in reweighting lattice Monte Carlo data generated without the background with the fermion determinant ratio evaluated in the continuous spacetime using worldline formalism. This proposal can be further extended to other applications in lattice gauge theory, such as QCD in finite chemical potential.

Quantum Chinese Remainder Clock

Ivri Nagar, Alioscia Hamma, Mikel Palmero, Matthew Radzihovsky, Shouzhuo Yang et. al.
August 8, 2026, arXiv:2608.07938
Abstract: (click to show)
The Chinese remainder theorem is used in metrology for extending the range of quantum clocks/radar/interferometry, where the phase of a signal is known relative to a set of oscillators with different periods. This paper investigates the performance of a quantum-mechanical Chinese remainder clock, consisting of atoms/oscillators with pairwise coprime periods. We provide the optimal initial state and the optimal Heisenberg-limited quantum measurements for measuring time up to the product of the periods. We introduce a novel fault-tolerant post-processing protocol that allows reconstruction of the correct time even in the presence of errors in the remainders.

Sample Variance Cancellation for Future Spectroscopic Surveys

James M. Sullivan and Martin White
August 7, 2026, arXiv:2608.07339
Abstract: (click to show)
High-redshift spectroscopic galaxy surveys will be the scientific engines of the next generation of large-scale structure cosmology. The clustering signal of high redshift, star-forming Lyman-$α$ emitters (LAEs) will be of key importance for obtaining high-redshift constraints on the growth of structure and redshift-space distortions. The complex radiative transfer (RT) of Lyman-$α$ photons alters the symmetry group respected by the overdensity field constructed from these galaxies, and so the observed large-scale clustering of LAEs may have an angular dependence that differs significantly from that of linear theory, possibly biasing inference of cosmological parameters. While such an effect has been seen in simulations, its amplitude in nature and its detailed form remains unclear. In the restricted context of a linear, Gaussian model, we outline a procedure for pinning down the type and amplitude of such changes in angular dependence on large scales due to unknown RT or a more general unmodeled angular effect in the hypothetical scenario in which an observer is presented with LAE data containing such an effect. We show that if a second tracer without the modified angular dependence is available for cross correlation with the LAEs at the same redshifts (e.g., Lyman-break galaxies), then, with a high redshift survey of modest size, it is possible to rapidly identify: 1) the presence of a nontrivial angular functional form of radiative transfer (by a conditional field-level realization), 2) the functional form itself (with an optimal filter that we derive), and 3) the value of its amplitude with an uncertainty (via an adaptation of the standard quadratic estimator). Such sample-variance-cancellation strategies therefore provide a statistical solution to unknown astrophysical or systematic angular clustering dependence, including from RT.

Baryogenesis via the CKM Matrix with Minimal Flavor Violation

Innes Bigaran, Gordan Krnjaic, Kevin Langhoff and Huangyu Xiao
August 5, 2026, arXiv:2608.05269
Abstract: (click to show)
It is often claimed Standard Model CP violation is insufficient for baryogenesis. We present a counterexample using minimal flavor violation (MFV) in which all CP-violating effects arise from the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix. Our scenario involves a leptoquark field with MFV-preserving interactions whose decays to Standard Model particles yield the observed baryon asymmetry in the early universe. Unlike previous efforts to realize baryogenesis through the CP violation of the CKM matrix, our scenario does not require any time-variation of model parameters.

Zhiyao Lu and Shu-Heng Shao
August 3, 2026, arXiv:2608.02728
Abstract: (click to show)
We present a fermionic lattice Hamiltonian that exactly realizes the $mathrm{U(1)}_mathrm{L}times mathrm{U(1)}_mathrm{R}$ global symmetry and the associated chiral anomalies of a massless Dirac fermion in 1+1 dimensions. The construction couples Villain bosons to a Kitaev chain of Majorana fermions, where the bosonic fields are essential for evading Nielsen-Ninomiya-type no-go theorems. For two copies of our model, we realize the anomaly-free $mathrm{U(1)}_{3450}$ global symmetry and construct symmetric boundary conditions. We analytically demonstrate symmetric mass generation by mapping the symmetry-preserving six-fermion interactions to fermion bilinear terms using fermionic T-duality. Finally, by gauging general anomaly-free global symmetries, we obtain a broad class of lattice chiral gauge theories. As nontrivial applications, we compute the mass spectra of the lattice Schwinger model and the 3450 gauge theory, finding agreement with the corresponding continuum results.

Ramp, Plateau, and Wormholes without Averaging, and Hyper-non-perturbative Structures in Gravity

Hong Liu
August 3, 2026, arXiv:2608.02743
Abstract: (click to show)
Universal hallmarks of quantum chaos---such as the ramp and plateau in the spectral form factor---and the ramp's gravitational duals involving wormholes are widely interpreted as consequences of spectral or ensemble averaging. In this paper, following an earlier proposal of~cite{Liu25c}, we develop an alternative approach: these phenomena arise as macroscopic smooth structures hidden within erratic microscopic data, which can be isolated through a smooth filter projection. Using the semiclassical Gutzwiller trace formula as a paradigmatic example, we illustrate how many features characteristic of random matrix models---including the ramp, the plateau, the spectral curve, and single-eigenvalue instantons---can be derived in the semiclassical limit without invoking ensemble or explicit spectral averages. We postulate the existence of a minimal Gutzwiller-like structure in the large-$N$ limit of holographic systems and explore its consequences. Beyond deriving the ramp and the plateau, this Gutzwiller-like structure predicts universal rapid macroscopic oscillations in the density of states and the possible existence of hyper-instantons, both of which involve double exponentials in $1/N^2$. On the gravity side, we demonstrate how spacetime wormholes enable the construction of emergent hyper-non-perturbative objects---such as baby-universe and wormhole condensates---which yield double exponential effects in $G_N$. This mirrors the postulated boundary Gutzwiller-like structure and provides a dual gravitational derivation of the universal rapid macroscopic oscillations in the density of states and the spectral plateau.

GGI Lectures on Large-Scale Structure Perturbation Theory (Effective Field Theory)

Mikhail M. Ivanov
July 30, 2026, arXiv:2607.28314
Abstract: (click to show)
These notes are an introduction to non-linear perturbation theory for cosmological large-scale structure. They are aimed at undergraduate and beginning graduate students and do not require any cosmology or quantum field theory background. All necessary concepts are developed from scratch. The lectures are intended to explain all key ingredients needed to model the observed clustering of galaxies in real and redshift spaces. After a brief pedagogical introduction to the ideas of effective field theory (EFT), we develop large-scale structure EFT in the context of Newtonian cosmology using symmetry principles. We discuss in detail the shortcomings of Standard Perturbation Theory, the non-linear evolution of baryon acoustic oscillations and its relation to the equivalence principle, counterterms and renormalization of the loop diagrams, and stochastic effects. Then we develop EFT for galaxy bias and redshift space distortions. We also highlight some important facts about redshift-space stochasticity, relevant for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Finally, we introduce Lagrangian Perturbation Theory.

July 30, 2026, arXiv:2607.28445
Abstract: (click to show)

Our results demonstrate that the tension between current observational data and the Starobinsky, Higgs, and simplest $α$-attractor models holds only for $Λ$CDM, and can be mitigated in extended cosmological models. We discuss implications of these findings for inflationary models in an open universe and/or with dynamical dark energy, including scenarios with quantum tunneling and non-standard topology. Furthermore, we briefly describe a special class of $α$-attractor models, where one can make $n_s$ arbitrarily large, and we describe the $α$-attractor quintessence model. Abstract: (click to show)

This modifies cosmology in two ways. First, if any of these axion towers interact with the standard model (SM) plasma, they can significantly alter the freeze-in production of the cosmological abundance of tower states. Freeze-in to graviton and axion towers can provide all of dark matter (DM) for an axion decay constant in $10^{12} \text{ GeV }\lesssim f_a\lesssim 10^{16}\,\text{ GeV }$ and reheating temperatures $5\text{ MeV }\lesssim T_{\rm RH} \lesssim O(1)\,\text{ GeV }$. Second, different towers fragment into each other and redistribute energy; each tower’s fraction of energy at late times is fixed by their interactions. If there are $N\gg1$ axion towers, the energy visibly injected into the SM by any decaying tower is diluted by a factor of $N$. This suppression offers a simple realization of how dark dimension dark matter can avoid strong cosmological constraints which rule out the simplest models. In the process of this exploration we develop a continuum approach to evaluating tower fragmentation which offers insight and aids numerical calculations by reducing the problem to quadrature.

In particular, we study the Sudakov shoulders in the trijet region, originating from the incomplete cancellation of infrared singularities between final states with different parton multiplicities, and resum the induced large logarithms to all orders. The shoulder resummation yields sizable corrections and improves the perturbative stability of the distribution. Our results provide state-of-the-art predictions for heavy jet mass in $H \to gg$ and $H\to q\bar{q}$ and can be applied to precision Higgs measurements at future $e^+e^-$ colliders.

Abstract: (click to show)

Abstract: (click to show)

Abstract: (click to show)

Financial assistance for eligible master’s-level education in nuclear-related subjects.

What Does the IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme Offer?

One of the major features of the MSCFP is the level of financial assistance available to selected students.

Successful applicants may receive:

Up to €20,000 toward tuition costs for their master’s programme.

Up to €20,000 toward living costs during their master’s programme.

Potential access to limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA.

The opportunity to advance their education in a nuclear-related discipline relevant to the IAEA’s mission.

Support toward developing a professional career within the nuclear sector.

This means the maximum potential scholarship support can reach €40,000, although the actual amount awarded will depend on the applicant’s circumstances and the terms of the individual fellowship offer.

Financial Support for Tuition Costs

Selected fellows can receive up to €20,000 to cover tuition costs associated with their master’s degree.

Applicants are required to provide documentation confirming their tuition costs as part of the application process. This allows the IAEA to assess the level of financial assistance required.

Candidates should therefore make sure they obtain an official statement of tuition fees or another acceptable document confirming the cost of their studies from their university.

Financial Support for Living Costs

In addition to tuition assistance, the fellowship can provide up to €20,000 for living expenses during the master’s programme.

This can make the programme particularly valuable for students who may otherwise face financial barriers to pursuing postgraduate studies in nuclear-related disciplines.

However, applicants must disclose any additional scholarships they receive for the same master’s programme.

Where an applicant receives another scholarship, the IAEA may adjust its financial contribution accordingly. According to the programme information, this could mean that IAEA support covers tuition costs rather than living expenses for the duration of the programme.

Applicants must therefore provide complete and transparent information regarding other scholarship funding.

Failure to disclose additional financial support in a timely and transparent manner may result in the suspension of IAEA financial assistance.

Limited IAEA Internship Opportunities

The Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme also provides limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA.

These opportunities complement the academic component of the fellowship by potentially allowing participants to gain additional exposure to the international nuclear field.

Applicants should note that internship opportunities are described as limited. Candidates should therefore not assume that receiving the scholarship automatically guarantees an internship.

Who Can Apply for the IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme?

The MSCFP is open to students from IAEA Member States who satisfy the programme’s entry requirements.

Applicants must meet the following principal eligibility conditions:

The applicant must be female.

The applicant must come from an IAEA Member State.

The applicant must have been accepted into or already be enrolled in an accredited university.

The applicant must be studying toward a master’s degree.

The master’s programme must be in a nuclear-related field.

Candidates should carefully review these requirements before beginning an application.

Academic Performance and Preference

Meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not necessarily guarantee selection.

The IAEA states that preference will be given to applicants with above-average academic credentials.

In particular, preference is given to candidates with:

Academic results of 75% or above, or

A GPA greater than 3.0 on a 4.0 scale.

Applicants with strong academic records should therefore make sure that their educational achievements are clearly reflected in their submitted documentation.

The academic threshold is described as a preference rather than one of the basic entry requirements. Candidates should therefore carefully distinguish between the programme’s eligibility criteria and the factors that can strengthen an application.

Eligible Fields of Study

The MSCFP supports women studying subjects connected to nuclear science, technology and other areas relevant to the work of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The IAEA’s work focuses on advancing the safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology.

Examples of relevant areas of study include:

Nuclear engineering

Nuclear physics

Nuclear chemistry

Nuclear medicine

Isotopic techniques

Radiation biology

Nuclear safety

Nuclear security

Nuclear non-proliferation

Nuclear law

These examples are not necessarily exhaustive. The IAEA provides additional information on eligible or relevant fields of study through its official MSCFP resources.

Students studying interdisciplinary subjects connected with nuclear technologies should consult the IAEA’s official Fields of Studies document to determine whether their programme falls within an appropriate area.

How to Apply for the IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme

Applications must be completed through the MSCFP online application form.

Candidates should prepare their supporting documentation carefully before submitting their application.

The IAEA emphasizes that incomplete applications will not be considered.

Applicants should therefore allow sufficient time to collect official university documents, identification documents, tuition information and references before submitting the application.

Documents Required for the Application

In addition to completing the online application form, candidates must provide several supporting documents.

1. Passport or National Identification Document

Applicants must submit a copy of their:

Passport, or

National identification document.

Candidates should ensure that the document submitted is clear, valid and contains the necessary identifying information.

2. Official University Acceptance or Admission Letter

Applicants must provide an official acceptance or admission letter from their university.

The letter must confirm admission into the relevant master’s programme and should indicate:

The nuclear-related field of study; and

The duration of the master’s programme.

Because acceptance into or enrolment in an accredited university master’s programme is a core eligibility requirement, this document is particularly important.

3. Statement of Tuition Fees

Applicants must provide a statement or confirmation showing the tuition costs associated with their master’s programme.

This information helps determine the level of financial support that may be provided toward tuition.

4. Information About Other Scholarships

Candidates who have already received other scholarship funding for the master’s programme for which they are requesting MSCFP support must provide documentation relating to that funding.

Applicants must be transparent about other scholarships because additional financial assistance may affect the level or type of support offered by the IAEA.

5. Reference Form

References are an important part of the application process.

The IAEA requires:

One reference as mandatory.

A second reference is preferred.

Importantly, the completed reference templates must be sent directly to the MSCFP by the referees by the application deadline.

Applicants should therefore contact their referees well in advance and ensure that they understand the submission requirements.

Waiting until the final days before the deadline to request references could put an otherwise strong application at risk.

English-Language Application Requirement

All application documents must be submitted in English using the MSCFP online application form.

If an applicant’s original documents are issued in another language, the applicant must also provide an official English translation.

Candidates should factor the time required to obtain official translations into their application preparations.

Submitting untranslated documents when an English translation is required could make an application incomplete.

Incomplete Applications Will Not Be Considered

The IAEA specifically states that incomplete applications will not be considered.

Candidates should therefore perform a detailed review before final submission.

A useful application checklist should include confirmation that:

The online application form has been fully completed.

A passport or national ID copy has been included.

The official university admission or acceptance letter has been included.

The letter identifies the relevant master’s programme and its duration.

Tuition cost documentation has been included.

Any other scholarship funding has been declared.

Supporting scholarship documents have been provided where applicable.

At least one referee has completed and directly submitted the required reference form.

A second reference has been arranged where possible.

All required documents are in English or accompanied by official English translations.

How Are Applicants Selected?

Applications are evaluated by the IAEA MSCFP Technical Selection Committee.

The assessment considers several factors rather than focusing on only one aspect of an applicant’s profile.

Selection criteria include:

Whether the candidate meets the programme’s entry requirements.

Educational background.

Previous achievements.

Motivation for applying.

The potential impact of the fellowship on the candidate’s career goals.

Commitment to public service.

The selection process also takes broader diversity considerations into account.

These include:

Geographic diversity.

Diversity of fields of study.

Linguistic diversity.

Other relevant factors considered during the selection process.

Candidates should therefore use their application to clearly demonstrate not only their academic capabilities but also how the fellowship could contribute to their professional development and future impact.

Why Motivation and Career Goals Matter

Academic performance is important, particularly because preference is given to applicants with above-average academic credentials. However, the selection process also considers the applicant’s motivation and the potential impact of the fellowship on her career.

A strong application should therefore clearly communicate:

Why the applicant chose her nuclear-related field.

What she hopes to accomplish professionally.

How master’s-level education will help achieve those goals.

How the MSCFP could contribute to her development.

How she intends to use her knowledge and expertise in the future.

Her commitment to contributing to society and public service.

Candidates should avoid treating these elements as secondary to academic results. They form part of the IAEA’s stated selection considerations.

Notification of Results

Following the selection process, all applicants will be notified of the decision by email.

Candidates should therefore ensure that the email address included in their application is accurate and regularly monitored.

It may also be useful to check spam or junk folders periodically so that important correspondence from the programme is not overlooked.

What Happens If You Are Selected?

Successful candidates will receive a fellowship offer from the IAEA.

Selected applicants will be required to confirm acceptance of the fellowship within one week.

This is a relatively short response period, so successful candidates should review their offer promptly.

The fellowship offer will provide information concerning:

Award details.

Payment arrangements or modality.

Expected commitments.

Administrative requirements.

Relevant programme arrangements.

Candidates should carefully read the complete offer before accepting it.

Responsibilities of Fellowship Recipients

Receiving an MSCFP award also comes with important obligations.

Students who receive scholarship support are expected to successfully complete their master’s programme.

Recipients must comply with the requirements associated with their fellowship award.

According to the IAEA, failure to graduate from the master’s programme or failure to meet the requirements of the scholarship may result in:

Termination of the MSCFP award; and

An obligation to repay tuition and living-cost support already received, if requested by the IAEA.

Applicants should therefore view the fellowship as a serious academic and financial commitment.

Obligation to Disclose Other Scholarships

Financial transparency is another significant obligation.

Applicants must disclose whether they have additional scholarships supporting the master’s programme for which they are seeking MSCFP funding.

If another scholarship exists, supporting documentation must be provided.

The IAEA may then reduce its own financial assistance accordingly.

Failure to disclose this information in a timely and transparent manner may lead to the suspension of IAEA financial support.

Application Deadline

The information supplied does not state a specific application deadline.

Prospective applicants should check the official IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme application page for the current application cycle and confirm the applicable deadline before preparing or submitting an application.

This is particularly important because reference forms must also be received directly from referees by the application deadline.

Applicants should not assume that submitting their own online application is sufficient if the mandatory reference has not also been submitted correctly and on time.

Important Tips Before Applying

Prospective applicants can strengthen their preparation by taking several practical steps.

Start Collecting Documents Early

Official university letters, tuition statements, identification documents and translations can take time to obtain.

Begin gathering documents as early as possible.

Contact Your Referees in Advance

At least one reference is mandatory, while a second is preferred.

Because referees must send their completed reference templates directly to the MSCFP, applicants should contact suitable referees early and provide them with enough time to complete the process.

Check Whether Your Master’s Programme Is Relevant

The degree must be in a nuclear-related field.

Applicants whose programmes are interdisciplinary should review the official IAEA list of relevant fields before applying.

Explain Your Long-Term Career Goals

The selection committee considers the potential impact of the fellowship on an applicant’s career.

Candidates should clearly demonstrate how their studies relate to their future professional ambitions.

Highlight Academic and Professional Achievements

Previous achievements and educational background form part of the assessment.

Relevant academic distinctions, research experience, projects, professional experience and other accomplishments should therefore be clearly presented where the application permits.

Be Transparent About Other Funding

Candidates who have other scholarships should disclose them and submit the appropriate documentation.

Having another scholarship should not be hidden in an attempt to maximize funding, as failure to provide the information can result in suspension of financial support.

Review Everything Before Submission

Because incomplete applications are not considered, applicants should carefully verify every section and supporting document before submitting.

Why the IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme Is an Important Opportunity

The MSCFP offers more than financial assistance.

It provides women pursuing advanced studies in nuclear-related disciplines with support that can help reduce the financial barriers associated with postgraduate education.

With potential funding of up to €20,000 for tuition and €20,000 for living expenses, the programme can provide substantial assistance during a master’s degree.

The possibility of limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA adds another valuable dimension by connecting academic development with potential professional exposure.

The programme is particularly relevant to women seeking careers in fields such as nuclear engineering, physics, chemistry, medicine, radiation sciences, nuclear safety, security, non-proliferation and nuclear law.

Official Application Information

Prospective candidates should consult the International Atomic Energy Agency’s official Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme website for application information, forms, eligible fields of study and updates regarding the current application cycle.

Applicants can also access the official reference form and the IAEA’s detailed list of relevant fields of study through the programme website.

APPLY NOW

Conclusion

The IAEA Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme is a significant international opportunity for women who want to build careers in nuclear science, technology and related disciplines.

Open to eligible female students from IAEA Member States, the programme supports candidates who have been accepted into or are already enrolled in accredited master’s programmes in nuclear-related fields.

With financial assistance of up to €20,000 for tuition and up to €20,000 for living expenses, successful candidates may receive as much as €40,000 in total support, subject to the conditions of their individual award and any other scholarship funding they receive.

The programme also offers limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, potentially helping fellows complement their postgraduate studies with valuable exposure to the international nuclear sector.

Prospective applicants should pay particular attention to the documentation requirements. At least one reference is mandatory, documents must be submitted in English or accompanied by official English translations, and incomplete applications will not be considered.

Candidates with strong academic credentials may have an advantage, with preference given to applicants achieving at least 75% or a GPA above 3.0 on a 4.0 scale. However, academic performance is only part of the assessment. Educational background, previous achievements, motivation, career impact and commitment to public service are also considered.

Women seeking to advance their expertise in nuclear engineering, nuclear physics, nuclear chemistry, nuclear medicine, radiation biology, nuclear safety, nuclear security, non-proliferation, nuclear law and other relevant disciplines are encouraged to review the official programme requirements carefully and prepare their applications well in advance of the applicable deadline.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.

TITLE: New Workshop Series on Journalism and Media Studies by the AAU Kicks Off

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Association of African Universities (AAU) has started a new workshop series on Journalism and Media Studies in response to demands by some stakeholders for attention to be paid to this area. Looking at the needs analysis report, the AAU, through its Workshops Unit, realized that offering such a workshop would yield an opportunity to reconfigure and rejuvenate Journalism and the associated specialized areas degree programmes offered in African Higher and Tertiary Education.

Through the AAU Workshops Coordinator, Dr Violet Makuku, an arrangement was made with Dr. Stanford Mukasa, based in the United States of America (USA) to roll out the workshop series from the 5th of August 2021 to the end of October 2021. Dr Mukasa is highly experienced in this field of study and has worked with many countries around the globe. He retired from The University of Pennsylvania, Indiana, USA where he taught Journalism and Media Studies for Africa for more than 10 years. He also taught the same discipline online to Somalis and other African countries. The initial cohort of participants was drawn from several African countries including Ghana, Malawi, Zambia, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zimbabwe, Nigeria, Cameroon, Tanzania and Kenya, among others. The number of participants at the sessions has increased from just 20 to more 150 participants and continues to rise.

Each workshop series is punctuated by at least an exercise that participants do within the two (2) hours allocated to the workshop. The highly interactive sessions also give the participants opportunities to ask questions and make contributions that are very helpful and useful to almost everyone. Participants testified that the information provided during the session was spot on, and highly enlightening. Participants from hard sciences and STEM disciplines, who initially thought that the workshop was meant for those in humanities, journalism and related areas, also testified that the workshop was equally relevant to them. They realized that they could improve their writing and communication skills through the workshop. They also noted that they could add value to the published scientific journal articles through featuring them in a layman’s language for the benefit of students and the society at large. They also learnt a lot about the nature and structure of different pieces of writing depending on where and when they would be publish, as well as the readership.

“The workshop series came in handy at a time when we started a radio station not long ago (beginning of 2021). The radio station has proved to be an effective and moderate means to reach out to students, given the restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic”, said Ms. Tsitsi Gate from the Bindura University of Science Education (BUSE). She added that the workshop series will go a long way in supporting those operating the radio station in their university with more knowledge and skills.

It is highly commendable to note that there are a number of Higher Education institutions in Africa which have such radio stations, and thus will benefit greatly from this workshop series through their participation. These institutions include but are not limited to the University of Kisangane (Democratic Republic of Congo), Great Zimbabwe University (Zimbabwe), University of Ghana (Ghana), Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Reedemers’ University (Nigeria), University of Ilorin, 2009 (Nigeria), Federal University of Agriculture Abeokuta, 2015 (Nigeria) Ho Technical University (Ghana), University of Namibia (Namibia), University of Ibadan (Nigeria), and Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia.

In addition, there are African Universities which are already offering degree programmes in Journalism and Media Studies and these include but are not limited to Ghana Communication Technology University, Ghana; The Great Zimbabwe University, Zimbabwe and The Ghana School of Journalism. South Africa alone has got numerous universities which offer programmes in Journalism, Communication and Media Studies including The University of Pretoria, University of Johannesburg, University of Cape Town, University of Witwatersrand, among others. In East Africa, The Tanzania Open University also offers similar programmes online while in West Africa, institutions like the Ghana School of Journalism in Ghana, University of Ilorin and Mountain Top University, Nigeria, also offer programmes in Communication, Journalism and Media Studies though they are named differently. All these institutions will definitely benefit immensely from the international flavour, brought in by the facilitator, Dr. Mukasa, as well as contributions by fellow participants attending the workshop sessions from different countries, which they can blend with their own. This can be through curricula review, designing of new related curricula through the enlightenment that the workshop series would bring. The workshop series is meant to also generate information that can result in students and staff exchange programmes. Furthermore, the AAU hopes that besides the workshop facilitation, some meaningful partnerships may also be birthed through this activity. Additionally, the workshop series will enlighten the African Higher Education stakeholders in this area and urge them to catch up with the rest of the world in Journalism and Media Studies.

The AAU remains committed to continue to contribute towards better quality education as spelt out in the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 on Quality Education. Institutional workshops in this speciality and others, can also be organized for whole departments, faculties, students and academic support staff based on their requests. The advantages of such workshops include but are not limited to mass training for a shared vision and total empowerment of large groups of personnel. It is also more affordable without travel and accommodation costs for many participants. Moreover, the institution can start implementation soon after the workshop due to the capacity building and development of a large number of personnel who can combine their efforts and share tasks associated with the implementation of action plans. Furthermore, given the international nature of the workshops that the AAU organizes, such platforms readily promote the sharing of ideas, networking and collaborations that can assist institutions to move to the next level. TITLE: An overview of the first two Days of the ACE Meetings in Djibouti

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
At least 450 Higher Education stakeholders (representing over 30
nationalities) gathered in Djibouti to attend a string of meetings under the
banner of the Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence (ACE) Project from
18 – 26 February 2019. The various meetings included the Project Steering
Committee Meetings for the ACEI Project and the new ACE IMPACT Project, the 10th
ACE I workshops and the ACE IMPACT Bootcamp.

On the 18th
February 2019 the day zero activities were at the Kempinski Hotel and they
focused on the 14th Project Steering Committee Meeting for ACE I and
the 1st ACE IMPACT Project Steering Committee
Meeting. Here is the 14th ACE I PSC Meeting Agenda (English);
14th ACE I PSC Meeting Agenda (French)
and the ACE Impact PSC Meeting Agenda (English)

Day one activities were hosted by the University of Djibouti on the 19th
February 2019.

In his opening remarks, Mr Andreas Blom, ACE IMPACT Task team Leader
with the World Bank welcomed all the participants and encouraged them to use
the opportunity to engage and learn from their colleagues. He also praised the
ACEI institutions for the amazing results that they had achieved to date. The
ACE IMPACT Project, valued at over USD350 million, is a result of the success
of the ACEI Project. The World Bank and the French Development Agency (AFD) in
collaboration with the African governments, have conditionally identified 44
ACEs (26 new ones and 18 from ACE I); 5 Emerging Centres; and 5 Colleges and
Schools of Engineering for funding through this new phase called “ACE
IMPACT”.

Professor Djama Hassan Mohamed, the Vice Chancellor of the University of
Djibouti also welcomed all the participants – saying that despite all the
problems that abound, the African continent was changing. He called for strong
bonds of collaboration between and among the Centres of Excellence. He
emphasized the need for universities to actively mentor their students, expose
them to quality research and allow them to explore new frontiers of knowledge.

The plenary on “Creating Strong Regional Networks” was chaired by
Prof Fahmi Ahmed and facilitated by Gen Xavier Michel. This session exposed the
ACE Centers to selected and relevant regional networks that they could learn
from or collaborate with.

TITLE: Invitation to Regional Workshop on KOHA-An Open-Source Integrated Library Management Software (ILMS)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Is your library still using manual systems to deliver services to your clientele?

Is your university burdened by hefty yearly subscription fees of hundreds of dollars for proprietary library management software?

Are you seeking an enterprise-level library management solution for modernising your digital library operations?

Do you wish to eliminate yearly subscription costs and embrace an open-source alternative?

Would you like to integrate electronic article surveillance and enhance security within your library premises?

If your answer to any of the above is YES, then this workshop is for you!!!

The Association of African Universities (AAU), warmly invites you to its regional training workshop on KOHA, an open-source Integrated Library Management System. The objective of the workshop is to unbundle the KOHA open-source Integrated Library System (ILMS) to participants and institutions.

KOHA is an enterprise level web-based ILS, accessible via Z39.50 protocol, with highly configurable and adaptable user interface that can also support many languages. It has most of the features that would be expected in an ILS, including:

Web 2.0 facilities like tagging, comment, social sharing and RSS feeds

Union catalogue facility

Customizable search

Automated circulation and borrower management

Self-check-in/check-out capacity

Full acquisitions module that manages budgets and pricing information

Ability to handle multiple branches, patrons, patron categories, item categories, items, currencies, and other data

Reading lists for members

UNICODE and library standards compliant

Export/import and backup/restoration facilities

Offline support

Integrating security gates and electronic article surveillance

This workshop will also introduce the Linux operating system to participants to acquaint them with the installation of KOHA on server class machines and provide extensive hands-on-training for both librarians and library IT support staff. Participants will be equipped with the requisite capacity to manage KOHA as LMS at institutions with large collections.

TARGET AUDIENCE

There will be two parallel sessions for the workshop.:

Librarian Session for KOHA management

IT session for installation, customising, and configurations.

These sessions will be of immense benefit to LIS professionals working in any type of library. The number of participants will be restricted to 30 per session, and admission will be strictly on a first-come-first-served basis. The Workshop will be handled by experts with extensive practical experience in Linux and Koha.

WORKSHOP FEES:

The registration fees for the 4-day event

AAU Member Institutions – $800

Non – AAU Member Institutions – $1000

Ghanaian Institutions: Subsidized Fee – $400

This will cover workshop attendance fee, snacks and lunches, training material, certificates and other logistics.

REGISTRATION LINK: https://forms.office.com/r/pPNeZu8Fy9

WORKSHOP DATE AND VENUE

This workshop will be held on 28th -31st May, 2024 at the Secretariat of the Association of African Universities (AAU), Accra -Ghana.

CONTACT DETAILS: +233 26 417 3153/ elaari@aau.org and membership@aau.org

VENUE: AAU Secretariat, Accra, Ghana

TRAVEL, ACCOMMODATION, CONFERENCING AND VISA

Participants will be responsible for their own accommodation and travel-related costs, such as flights and or local transportation. AAU will provide invitation letters to support the visa application process of participants from countries that require visas to enter Ghana.

Participants are encouraged to confirm their participation early enough to ensure they have enough time to process their visas. TITLE: Funded traineeships for young graduates at the EU Delegation to the United States – Apply by 14 September

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a young graduate interested in international relations, diplomacy, European affairs, politics, communications, environment, economics or public policy? The European Union Delegation to the United States is offering funded traineeships for young graduates across several sections of its Washington, D.C. delegation.

The traineeships can last up to six months, with the tentative start date set for November 2026, subject to budget availability.

Application deadline: 14 September 2026.

EU Delegation USA Funded Traineeships 2026 – Quick Overview

Opportunity
Details

Host organisation
EU Delegation to the United States

Location
United States of America

Duration
Up to 6 months

Tentative start
November 2026

Category
Traineeship

Funding
Monthly grant

Deadline
14 September 2026

Eligibility
Young graduates with at least a Bachelor’s degree

Language
Excellent English

Work schedule
Full-time, Monday–Friday

Are you a young graduate interested in international relations? Are you curious to learn more about work of a diplomatic mission and how the EU Delegation represents EU interests and values in United States of America?

What is offered:

Traineeships of up to 6 months within the following sections of the EU Delegation to the United States, subject to availability of the budget. The tentative start date is November 2026.

Traineeship in the Administration Section (ADMIN):

The Administration section provides support services to the Delegation staff, building, and residences. It encompasses Human Resources, Accounting & Finance, Infrastructure, and Information Technology. It liaises with authorities in Europe and the United States on protocol and administrative matters related to EU officials. As a trainee in the Admin section, you will work on the following tasks:

Main tasks:

Support the logistical coordination and organization of meetings, events, workshops, and official visits, including escorting visitors to the Delegation.

Receive, organize, and maintain office stationery, supplies, and other materials.

Maintain accurate records of suppliers, orders, deliveries, and expenditures.

Provide general administrative and clerical support to the Section, including filing, correspondence, scheduling, and document management.

Attend internal and external meetings and prepare minutes, action points, and follow-up records.

Assist with maintaining organized records and ensuring that administrative activities are completed efficiently and on time.

Assist with market surveys

Traineeship in the Global Issues and Innovation section (GIN):

The Global Issues and Innovation section monitors and analyses U.S. political, economic, and regulatory developments in the areas of transportation, energy and environment, research and innovation, space, food safety (which includes plant and animal health and animal welfare), public health, and consumer protection. As a trainee in the Global Issues and Innovation section, you will work on the following tasks:

Main tasks:

Researching U.S. regulatory developments in the areas of transportation, climate, energy and environment, research and innovation, space, food safety, public health, and consumer protection.

Attending U.S. Congressional hearings and other public events related to section policy areas and writing summaries for the section.

Support the preparation of the Delegation’s outreach activities within the GIN section areas.

Preparing minutes of section meetings.

Traineeship in the Head of Delegation section (HOD):

The Head of Delegation Section (HOD) supports the work of both the Ambassador and Deputy Ambassador in promoting positive relations with the United States.

The HOD team coordinates with all Sections across the Delegation to establish priorities for the Ambassador’s agenda, ensure briefing for all scheduled meetings and engagements, coordinate a high number of social and diplomatic functions at the EU residence (dinners, lunches, receptions and events), and plan several State Outreach visits per year to build relationships at the State level with elected officials, business leaders and civil society. The HOD team also works with the wider Delegation to ensure the Ambassador’s participation in all high-level visits from Headquarters, and prepares the monthly coordination meetings of EU Ambassadors and Deputy Ambassadors as well as a monthly briefing call with EU Consuls General serving as EU Local Chairs around the US. The HOD intern will primarily be tasked to assist on State Outreach planning and events hosted by the Ambassador at the official EU Residence. As a trainee in the HOD section, you will work on the following tasks:

Main tasks:

State Outreach:

Conducting preliminary research to identify suitable meetings/events/partner in the destination State

Assisting with pre-trip planning calls with contacts in the destination State

Briefing assembly

Post-trip follow-up correspondence

Support to Social Secretary for Events at EU Residence

Ad Hoc special projects at request of Ambassador

Traineeship in the Political section (POL):

The Political Section follows all aspects of the transatlantic agenda and closely monitors the work of Congress and the U.S. Administration on foreign, security, and defence policy, counterterrorism and home affairs, and human rights, as well as U.S. domestic policy and U.S. elections. The section maintains regular contact with a broad range of Washington-based NGOs, think tanks, and civil society organizations. As a trainee in the Political section, you will work on the following tasks:

Main tasks:

Attending virtual U.S. Congressional hearings and writing summaries.

Attending think tank events and writing summaries of topics covered.

Researching and writing reports on foreign policy, security, and development cooperation issues for the section.

Contributing to briefings on issues related to the section’s priorities.

Assisting with the organization of outreach events and activities related to political, security and development issues.

Traineeship in the Press and Public Diplomacy section (PPD):

The Press and Public Diplomacy section aims to highlight the work of the EU to various audiences in the U.S. As a horizontal section, PPD is the key coordinator of all the Delegation’s public outreach activities. The section is also responsible for the Delegation’s media relations and communications strategy. In addition, the section manages people-to-people initiatives and is in charge of the EU’s cultural diplomacy in the U.S. As a trainee in the Press and Public Diplomacy section, you will work on the following tasks:

Main tasks:

Assisting with the organization of public diplomacy events.

Assisting with media monitoring and analysis and support for press events.

Supporting the section with social media communication and digital content creation (website and social media).

Monitoring events organized by think tanks and other organizations for reporting purposes.

Providing research assistance as needed in areas related to the section’s priorities.

Preparing minutes of meetings and assisting with drafting briefings.

Answering general information requests.

Qualifications or special requirements:

Must have at least a Bachelor’s Diploma and background in relevant disciplines (International Affairs, European Affairs, Political Science, Law, Communications, Environment, Health, Science, Economics and other related policy areas).

Excellent command of the English language.

Be available full time, Monday through Friday.

How to apply?

Candidates must apply to the e-mail address delegation-usa-internships@eeas.europa.eu and send the following documents:

A detailed standard Europass curriculum vitae (CV) https://europa.eu/europass/en (CVs in other format will not be considered)

a cover letter describing why you want to participate in a EU traineeship

and an application form

Please mention in the subject of your e-mail: Funded Traineeship – ADMIN, GIN, HOD, POL, or PPD (you may only apply to 1 traineeship per delegation, however based on your profile, the delegation could offer you a traineeship in another section).

Important information to read before applying

Before applying you are requested to examine the dedicated website as well as the general eligibility criteria for a paid traineeship (Article 8 of the Decision ADMIN(2017)28 – Paid traineeship).

Each selected trainee will receive a monthly grant to cover living expenses. All costs related to travels, visa, insurance, accommodation must be borne by the trainee.

Applications from non-eligible candidates will not be considered. After the evaluation of all applications, shortlisted candidates will be contacted and invited for an interview. Unsuccessful candidates will be notified by email. In case the selected candidates are not able to present the required documents, their application will be rejected.

The traineeships can only be offered in compliance with the local legislation as well as the legislation of the country of origin.

Citizens from EU Member states:

must provide proof that they will be covered against the risk of a pandemic and the costs of repatriation;

must hold a relevant entrance visa and / or temporary residence permit where applicable, based on the traineeship agreement, the duration of the traineeship, and in compliance with the local legislation.

TITLE: Advanced Diplomacy, Protocol and Etiquette Certificate Workshop

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
14 -17 May ,2019 / Reduit, Mauritius

Institutions are largely intercultural, interconnected and continuously seeking for innovative ways of delivering value to the global society. In addition to this, they are expected to be able to confront challenging and new situations confidently, particularly when dealing with high ranking officials. Such demands require staff who can act in line with internationally accepted practices of diplomacy, etiquette and protocol. This workshop will bridge your knowledge about diplomacy, protocol and etiquette – and will demonstrate how all these are applied to all the sectors of society.
Protocol is a rule of diplomatic procedure, ceremony and etiquette observed by Heads of State/Government, diplomats, government dignitaries and intergovernmental organizations. It is an especially important art for low, middle and higher-level personnel, tasked with portfolios that involve diplomacy, protocol and etiquette. The Cambridge Dictionary website defines Diplomacy as the skill in dealing with people without offending or upsetting them: Typically, diplomacy is associated with careers of Government officials, diplomats and other dignitaries around the world.
The Management Study Guide website describes ‘etiquette’ as the guidelines which control the way a responsible individual should behave in the society. There are several types of etiquette and these include social etiquette, corporate etiquette, business etiquette, meeting etiquette, telephone etiquette and several others.

This workshop will introduce participants to the ceremonial aspects of protocol procedures, principles and rules that define diplomacy, rules of courteousness in society and respect for precedence. It also seeks to equip participants with the requisite tools to guide them to better understand the expected conduct or behaviour of ranked officials, including managers, and leaders, that they work closely with.
This course is designed to equip you with skills to become thoughtful and empower you with critical skills to succeed in today’s everchanging, multicultural and demanding workplace.

Course Learning Outcomes
At the end of the course, participants should;
1. Be able to explain the principles and set of rules that define diplomacy
2. Be able to react in an appropriate and proactive manner to arising protocol and etiquette related issues and challenges
3. Be able to apply the critical skills required for hosting important events and dignitaries
4. Be able to appraise and evaluate securities in protocol
5. Develop action plans to enhance their written and oral communication skills, diplomacy skills, protocol skills and etiquette skills.

Workshop Approach

The workshop is going to be highly interactive and participatory. It will adopt a practical approach in addressing issues related to protocol, diplomacy and etiquette. It will be facilitated by highly experienced professionals in this sector who will use real life case studies and scenarios during their delivery.

TITLE: Centres of Excellence Explore More Effective Ways to Accelerate Development Impact in the Region

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
To propel the overarching goal of the Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence for Development Impact (ACE Impact), and to ensure that the research outputs of higher education institutions address national and regional challenges, the Disbursement Linked Indicator (DLI 2) was instituted. The DLI2 indicator measures the development impact that Centres are having, both nationally and regionally in terms of the extent of their contribution to their respective sectors/industries. It supports the advancement of applied research, training of quality post graduates, industry linkages and innovativeness aimed at tackling societal challenges. Its evaluation criteria include the number of student internships recorded by a centre, number of graduates hired in the sector, number of short courses delivered in response to sectoral stakeholder requests and an evaluation of Sectoral Advisory Board annual reports, as well as feedback obtained from interviews with sectoral stakeholders. The DLI 2, is coordinated by Technopolis in close collaboration with the Regional Facilitation Unit -the Association of African Universities and the World Bank.

At the ongoing 7th ACE Impact Regional Workshop, a session on Development Impact was held to provide the opportunity for an interactive discussion on how the centres are progressing towards achieving development impact in line with the project objectives. Chaired by Dr. Joshua Atah, the Focal Member for Nigeria, the session benefited from panel discussions involving Prof. Gordon Awandare from the West Africa Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogen (WACCBIP), Prof. Emenike Ejiogu, Center leader for Africa Center of Excellence for Sustainable Power and Energy Development (ACE_SPED) and Prof. Daouda Mama, Center leader for the Africa Center of Excellence for Water and Sanitation (C2EA).

A presentation by the main speaker, Ms. Anneloes de Ruiter, a Senior Consultant with the Technopolis Group, noted that the primary goal of the ACE Impact project to enhance regional capacity and to produce high-quality research for sustainable solutions to solving the challenges within the region, has heightened the need to assess the key and long-term effects of centres achievements and activities. She provided insights to observations made during the verification of centres for the DLI 2 prior to the 7th regional workshop. She emphasized that some centres have well-established academic and industry connections; distinct research, innovation, and education policies; adaptable and flexible responses to the pandemic as well as excellent understanding of the added value and positioning in the international/ regional/national research landscape. She further added that using existing opportunities, the ACEs must fully engage their alumni and include grooming them to serve as ambassadors, future faculty, and collaborators. She encouraged centres to forge partnerships for collaborative efforts toward making effective impact.

Highlighting WACCBIP’s strategy for public and community engagement, Prof. Awandare explained that the centre prioritized the establishment of a communication and public engagement unit to facilitate research communication and interactions with the public and the media. He noted that the unit has been a major game-changer in enhancing the centre’s visibility. Some key activities have included communicating complex research outputs in simple and relatable language that is easily digestible by the public. In addition, the unit has been at the forefront of organizing fora, press engagements and community outreach programs aimed at publicizing the centre’s research outputs.

Speaking on impact, Prof. Ejiogu noted that ACE-SPED’s impact has focused on its immediate environment- the university. He emphasized the centre’s efforts to tackle power challenges at the University of Nsukka, Nigeria through extensive research and prudent measures. He added that the centre has leveraged partnerships with local power and energy companies to access internship opportunities for students. In terms of regional partnerships, ACE-SPED had signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the West Africa Power Pool – a specialized agency of ECOWAS targeting the generation of a self-reliant regional power market which delivers abundant affordable electricity to all member states.

Prof. Mama emphasized C2EA’s partnerships with both the public and private sectors. He stated that the centre’s partnership with the Water Management Authority in Benin enables them to conduct research and share its findings to advise policymakers on water and sanitation.

Additionally, panel members also shared challenges faced by their centres in addressing developmental challenges. Key areas of concern were related to procurement delays, financial and administrative bureaucracies, lack of effective policies to facilitate scientific research and the timely acquisition of science equipment.

Centres were advised by Ms. De Ruiter to ensure that their activities are strategically executed to provide a sustainable long-term impact that transcends the academic community. In addition, centres were encouraged by the panel members to invest in high-quality staff, foster regional and international collaborations and empower young people in their teams as well as maximize the potential of their strengths to achieve their goals.

In his closing remarks, the Chair entreated centres to put in place efficient measures for project sustainability beyond the World Bank funding.

Written By: Millicent Afriyie Kyei, ACE Impact Communications Officer

TITLE: Max Planck Institute Visiting Researchers Program 2027 | Research Opportunity in Germany

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies (MPIfG) is inviting applications for its Visiting Researchers Program for the summer semester 2027. The program offers an opportunity for doctoral researchers, postdoctoral researchers and professors to spend between two and twelve months conducting research at the Institute in Cologne, Germany.

The Visiting Researchers Program is intended for scholars working in the fields of economic sociology and comparative and international political economy. Applicants are expected to propose a research project that relates closely to the MPIfG’s research program and that they wish to pursue during their stay at the Institute.

The Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies conducts basic research into the governance of modern societies. Its research seeks to develop empirically based theories of the social and political foundations of modern economies by examining the relationships between social, economic and political action.

Max Planck Institute Visiting Researchers Program 2027

The MPIfG Visiting Researchers Program provides scholars with an opportunity to become part of the Institute’s academic environment and pursue an independent research project related to its research agenda.

The Institute’s research program draws particularly on sociology and political science and combines approaches from new economic sociology with comparative and international political economy.

Visiting researchers will work in a collaborative academic environment and will be assigned to an MPIfG director or research group leader during their stay.

Applicants are therefore required to identify a preferred MPIfG director or research group leader as part of their online application.

Fields of Research

The program is specifically open to scholars whose research falls within:

Economic sociology

Comparative political economy

International political economy

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research project has a clear connection to the MPIfG’s research program.

The Institute encourages research that relates to its broader interest in understanding the social, economic and political foundations of modern economies and the governance of modern societies.

Duration of the Visiting Research Stay

Visiting researchers can generally undertake stays ranging from:

2 months

Up to 12 months

The exact dates of an agreed visiting researcher stay must be carefully considered before applying.

According to the program information, agreed dates cannot be postponed or split. If a successful applicant is subsequently unable to attend during the agreed period, they may reapply for the following year.

Who Can Apply?

The Visiting Researchers Program is open to:

Professors

Postdoctoral researchers

Doctoral researchers

Applications are welcome from scholars based in Germany as well as researchers from abroad.

Applicants should have a research project that they wish to pursue at the MPIfG and that relates to the Institute’s research program.

Research Proposal Requirements

A central component of the application is the research proposal.

Applicants are expected to submit a research proposal of up to three pages outlining the project they intend to pursue during their time at the MPIfG.

The proposal should clearly communicate the research project and demonstrate its relevance to the Institute’s research program.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider:

The research question they intend to investigate.

How the project relates to economic sociology or comparative and international political economy.

Why conducting the research at the MPIfG would be relevant to the project.

The proposed research activities during the visiting period.

The academic contribution or objectives of the research.

Funding for the Visiting Research Stay

An important requirement of the program is that visiting researchers must provide their own funding.

Applicants are required to submit a funding plan for their proposed stay.

The MPIfG does not indicate in the provided announcement that the visiting researcher position itself provides funding. Instead, successful applicants receive a letter of invitation that they can use when approaching funding institutions.

Researchers who require external financial support should therefore investigate suitable funding opportunities and develop their funding plans alongside their application.

Academic Environment

Successful visiting researchers become part of the MPIfG’s collaborative and collegial working environment.

During the program, each visiting researcher is assigned to an MPIfG director or research group leader.

Applicants are asked to indicate their preferred director or research group leader in the online application. This allows applicants to identify an academic connection between their research interests and the Institute’s research community.

The program can therefore provide an opportunity for researchers to pursue their own projects while engaging with scholars working within the Institute.

Selection Process

Successful candidates are selected on the basis of:

Scholarly excellence

The quality and relevance of the proposed research project

The connection between the proposed project and the MPIfG research program

The research proposal can be up to three pages and should outline the project the applicant intends to pursue at the Institute.

Because the MPIfG is a small research institute, only a limited number of visiting researcher positions can be offered each year.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their research proposal is clearly developed and demonstrates a strong connection with the Institute’s academic focus.

Application Language

Applications may be submitted in:

English

German

The Institute states that applications must be submitted online.

Applications sent by email will not be considered.

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications to the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies Visiting Researchers Program is:

October 31, 2026 at 23:59 UTC+1

Applicants should ensure that their online application is completed and submitted before the stated deadline.

How to Apply

Interested researchers should prepare their application through the official MPIfG online application system.

The application process involves presenting the proposed research project and identifying a preferred MPIfG director or research group leader.

Applicants should also prepare their own funding plan because visiting researchers are expected to provide their own funding.

The official application page should be used to submit the application. Applications sent by email are not accepted.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants can take several steps to prepare before submitting their application.

1. Identify a relevant research topic

Develop a research project that falls within economic sociology or comparative and international political economy and has a clear connection to the MPIfG’s research program.

2. Develop the research proposal

Prepare a concise proposal of no more than three pages that clearly explains the project to be pursued during the visiting period.

3. Identify a suitable MPIfG research connection

Review the Institute’s research program and identify the director or research group leader whose expertise is most relevant to the proposed project.

4. Prepare a funding plan

Because visiting researchers are expected to provide their own funding, applicants should identify possible funding institutions and develop a realistic plan for financing their stay.

5. Plan the visiting period carefully

Applicants should consider the proposed dates carefully because agreed visiting periods cannot subsequently be postponed or divided.

6. Submit the application online

Complete the online application in English or German before the October 31, 2026 deadline.

Equality, Diversity and Inclusion

The MPIfG states that it is committed to equality of opportunity and a diverse and inclusive working environment.

The Institute welcomes applications from people of different backgrounds and highlights its commitment to equality of opportunity.

It also identifies compatibility between career and family as an important concern and supports the employment of people with disabilities.

About the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies

The Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies is a research institute of the Max Planck Society located in Cologne, Germany.

Its research focuses on the governance of modern societies and the social and political foundations of modern economies.

The Institute’s research draws on sociology and political science, with particular emphasis on new economic sociology and comparative and international political economy.

The Visiting Researchers Program provides an opportunity for scholars whose research aligns with these areas to spend an extended period working within the Institute’s research environment.

Important Information for Applicants

Before submitting an application, prospective visiting researchers should carefully consider the following:

The program is for the summer semester 2027.

Stays generally range from two to twelve months.

Applications are open to professors, postdoctoral researchers and doctoral researchers.

Applicants may be based in Germany or abroad.

Research should relate to economic sociology or comparative and international political economy.

The proposed project should relate to the MPIfG research program.

The research proposal can be up to three pages.

Applicants must provide their own funding and a funding plan.

Successful applicants receive an invitation letter that can be used when approaching funding institutions.

Applicants should identify a preferred MPIfG director or research group leader.

Applications can be submitted in English or German.

Applications must be submitted online.

Applications by email are not considered.

The application deadline is October 31, 2026 at 23:59 UTC+1.

Only a limited number of visiting researcher positions are available each year.

Conclusion

The Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies Visiting Researchers Program 2027 offers an opportunity for doctoral researchers, postdoctoral researchers and professors to pursue research within a leading academic environment focused on the governance of modern societies and the relationship between social, economic and political action.

The program is particularly relevant to scholars working in economic sociology and comparative and international political economy who have a research project that aligns with the MPIfG’s research program.

Prospective applicants should prepare a research proposal of up to three pages, identify a suitable MPIfG director or research group leader, and develop a funding plan for their proposed stay.

Applications must be submitted online in English or German by October 31, 2026 at 23:59 UTC+1.
