TITLE: Bank of America Campus Programs 2026: Internships, Analyst and Associate Opportunities for University Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
University students and recent graduates seeking to begin a career with one of the world’s leading financial institutions can explore a wide range of early-career opportunities through the Bank of America Campus Experience.

Bank of America’s campus recruitment platform is designed to help university and advanced-degree students gain practical professional experience, build industry knowledge, develop technical and interpersonal skills, and potentially transition into full-time careers with the organization.

Rather than representing one single program, the Bank of America Campus Experience brings together a range of opportunities, including summer internships, pre-internship programs, industrial placements, analyst positions, associate opportunities and other early-career pathways across different business divisions and geographical regions.

Students interested in banking, finance, investment banking, technology, operations, corporate functions, wealth management and related areas can explore opportunities based on their academic background, career interests and location.

Bank of America states that candidates for its campus opportunities must generally be currently enrolled in a college, university or advanced-degree program. Individual programs may have additional academic, technical, language, graduation-date or work-authorization requirements.

About the Bank of America Campus Experience

The Bank of America Campus Experience is designed to provide students and emerging professionals with exposure to the bank’s workplace, employees, business operations and professional development resources.

Successful applicants can gain more than conventional classroom learning. Depending on the program, participants may receive structured training, practical assignments, professional mentorship, networking opportunities and exposure to employees working across different areas of Bank of America.

The bank describes its campus experience as an environment where motivated and ambitious students can develop their skills while gaining practical insight into professional life.

Bank of America highlights several important elements of the campus experience, including mentorship, training, networking, orientation, community-building opportunities, professional events and interaction with other early-career participants.

Why Students May Consider Bank of America Campus Opportunities

Starting a professional career can be challenging for university students because employers frequently look for candidates who can combine academic knowledge with practical workplace skills.

Bank of America’s student programs are structured to help bridge this gap.

Through its campus programs, students may have opportunities to understand how a major global financial institution operates while learning directly from professionals in their chosen field.

Participants can potentially develop experience in areas such as financial services, technology, business operations, investment banking, corporate functions, risk, client services and wealth management.

For students who eventually want to join Bank of America on a full-time basis, internships may also represent an important route into the company’s graduate recruitment pipeline. Bank of America states that its summer internship class is a primary source of candidates for its full-time campus programs.

What Does the Bank of America Campus Experience Offer?

1. Professional Mentorship

Participants may receive guidance from experienced professionals working in their areas of interest.

This can help students better understand professional expectations, career development and the practical application of concepts they have studied at university.

Mentorship can be particularly valuable for individuals entering industries such as investment banking, technology, financial markets and corporate services, where learning directly from experienced professionals can complement academic study.

2. Training and Skills Development

Bank of America emphasizes professional training as an important part of its student experience.

Participants can develop skills extending beyond what they have learned in university.

Depending on the program and business area, this may involve learning about financial products, technology systems, business processes, client relationships, analytical work, teamwork and professional communication.

3. Networking Opportunities

Campus participants can interact with employees and other students across Bank of America.

Networking can help students better understand different career paths and develop professional relationships with people from various teams and divisions.

Participants may also interact with other interns or members of their program cohort.

4. Orientation and Onboarding

Students joining Bank of America programs may receive structured onboarding designed to introduce them to the organization, its working environment and their responsibilities.

A well-developed orientation process can help participants adjust more quickly when moving from an academic environment into a professional workplace.

5. Culture and Community

The campus experience also gives participants opportunities to build relationships with other students entering the organization.

Cohort-based programs can allow participants to share experiences, learn collaboratively and develop professional networks that may continue beyond the duration of the program.

6. Professional and Social Events

Depending on the program and location, participants may have access to activities specifically designed for interns and early-career professionals.

These can complement formal work experience by providing additional opportunities for engagement with colleagues and the broader organization.

Bank of America Internship Opportunities

Internships represent one of the main pathways available through Bank of America’s campus recruitment system.

Summer internships typically target students in the penultimate year of university who expect to begin full-time employment after completing their degree.

Bank of America states that these internships typically last approximately 10 weeks, although program length can differ by region and specific opportunity.

Interns may work directly within a Bank of America business team rather than participating only in classroom-based activities.

This can enable participants to experience actual working conditions, contribute to projects, receive feedback and better understand whether a specific career path suits their professional ambitions.

In the Asia-Pacific region, Bank of America states that summer internships usually run for approximately eight to ten weeks. Timing differs by market: internships in India generally take place between April and May, while many other APAC locations run summer internships between June and August. Australia follows a different schedule, with summer internships typically lasting about 11 weeks between November and February.

Full-Time Analyst Opportunities

Bank of America’s full-time analyst programs are designed primarily for students approaching university graduation and preparing to begin full-time professional employment.

Analyst positions are generally associated with candidates studying toward a bachelor’s or master’s degree.

Because recruitment can take place before a student’s final semester, potential applicants should begin researching programs well before graduation rather than waiting until their degree has been completed.

The exact qualification, graduation date and technical requirements depend upon the specific analyst position and geographical region.

Associate-Level Opportunities

Bank of America also provides associate-level opportunities for candidates with more advanced academic backgrounds.

Associate programs are generally aimed at students pursuing qualifications such as an MBA, PhD, master’s degree or another relevant advanced degree, depending on the position and region.

These opportunities may be appropriate for individuals who have developed specialized academic knowledge or previous professional experience and are ready to enter the organization at an advanced early-career level.

Major Career Areas Available

Bank of America’s student opportunities span several major areas of the organization.

Banking, Markets and Finance

Students interested in financial services may explore opportunities involving customers, businesses and institutional clients.

Potential areas can include:

Retail banking

Investment banking

Global markets

Wealth management

Corporate banking

Other customer- and client-focused financial services

These opportunities can be particularly relevant for students studying finance, economics, accounting, business, mathematics or related subjects, although individual job descriptions should always be reviewed for specific academic requirements.

Corporate Functions

Bank of America’s corporate functions support the strategic and operational management of the organization.

Opportunities can include areas such as auditing, digital solutions and other corporate services.

Students interested in governance, administration, finance, risk, audit, strategy or business support functions may find relevant opportunities within this area.

Technology and Operations

Technology plays a major role in modern financial institutions, and Bank of America also recruits students for technology and operational positions.

These teams support the infrastructure, technology platforms, information-security capabilities and operational systems needed to provide financial services to customers and clients.

Technology-related opportunities may therefore appeal to students studying computer science, information technology, cybersecurity, engineering, data-related disciplines and similar fields.

General Eligibility Requirements

Although every Bank of America campus program can establish its own requirements, there is one important general eligibility condition.

Applicants must normally be currently enrolled in a college, university or advanced-degree program to be considered for campus opportunities.

Individuals who are no longer students can instead explore Bank of America’s professional or experienced-hire opportunities.

Additional eligibility requirements can depend on factors such as:

Degree level

Expected graduation date

Academic performance

Relevant technical skills

Language ability

Program location

Business division

Work authorization

Professional experience

Specific requirements contained in the individual job description

Applicants should therefore never assume that satisfying the general student requirement automatically makes them eligible for every Bank of America program. The specific vacancy description remains the controlling source for the requirements of an individual opportunity.

What Kind of Candidates Is Bank of America Looking For?

Bank of America indicates that there is not one rigid candidate profile applicable to every opportunity.

The bank says it values differences in areas such as thought, culture, experience and working style.

Candidates should demonstrate genuine interest in the business and an ability to work effectively with others.

Depending on the region and program, qualities that may be relevant include strong academic ability, professional and extracurricular achievement, integrity, teamwork, leadership, intellectual curiosity, communication abilities and interest in the relevant area of banking or business.

Certain positions may also require specific technical or language capabilities.

EMEA Academic Requirements

Students interested in opportunities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) should pay particular attention to the regional requirements.

For analyst opportunities, Bank of America states that candidates generally need to have obtained, or realistically expect to obtain, at least a 2:1 degree or equivalent.

For MBA-level opportunities, completion of an MBA or equivalent advanced degree is required.

Applicants for certain pre-internship opportunities should generally have achieved, or be on track to achieve, ABB or higher at A-level or an equivalent qualification. Bank of America notes that applicants whose results were affected by extenuating circumstances can provide relevant information in their application.

Bank of America Application Process

The precise recruitment process varies according to region, program and business division, but applicants can generally expect several stages.

First, candidates should research the available opportunities and select the program that best matches their education, interests, location and expected graduation date.

They then submit their application through Bank of America’s recruitment platform.

Depending on the program, the application can include a CV or résumé, competency-related questions and a digital or on-demand video interview.

Candidates who successfully complete the initial screening process may progress to further interviews or assessments.

These can take place by telephone, video, on campus or at a Bank of America office.

Final-stage assessments can involve interviews with representatives from the business division to which the applicant has applied. Some programs or regions can also include exercises or additional assessments designed to evaluate relevant competencies and aptitude.

Important Application Advice

Bank of America uses rolling recruitment for a number of its programs.

This means applicants should not necessarily wait until the published final deadline.

Assessments can begin while applications are still open, so applying earlier can be important where applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Applicants should carefully review the individual opportunity before submitting an application and confirm that they meet the academic, graduation-date, technical, language and location-specific requirements.

Candidates should also ensure that all required components of the application are completed before the relevant deadline.

Application Deadline for Bank of America Campus Programs

There is no single global deadline for the Bank of America Campus Experience because the page covers multiple programs, countries and regions.

Deadlines vary according to the opportunity.

For the United States and Canada, application periods vary by line of business throughout the year and applications can be reviewed on a rolling basis. Bank of America advises candidates to check the individual program page for the applicable deadline.

For Latin America, internship recruitment takes place on a rolling basis, with specific deadlines varying by program.

For Europe, the Middle East and Africa, applications for the 2026 recruitment cycle for Summer, Off-Cycle and Full-Time programs opened on September 1, 2026 and are scheduled to close on:

October 11, 2026

Bank of America states that recruitment is conducted on a rolling basis and encourages candidates to submit applications early.

For Asia-Pacific, recruitment schedules vary by program and country.

For Asia-Pacific markets excluding Australia, India and Japan, the currently published general recruitment windows include:

Banking Connections: February to March

Industrial Attachment: July to October

Summer Internship: July to October

Full-Time Program: July to October

For Australia, the published recruitment windows are generally February to August for Summer Internships and February to April for Full-Time Programs.

Candidates seeking opportunities in India are advised to consult their university careers service, while candidates interested in Japan should consult Bank of America’s dedicated Japan recruitment information.

Because individual vacancies can have different closing dates, applicants should always verify the deadline shown on the specific position before applying.

Work Authorization and International Applicants

International students should carefully examine work-authorization requirements for the country where they want to work.

Policies vary considerably by location.

For Asia-Pacific opportunities, Bank of America states that candidates may be considered for summer internships and full-time positions even if they do not currently have work authorization for the relevant country. However, visa-sponsorship practices remain subject to business requirements and applicable local laws.

According to Bank of America’s current APAC guidance, the bank can currently assist with work sponsorship for opportunities in Hong Kong, Singapore and Japan, while it does not currently support work sponsorship for opportunities in Australia.

Applicants should not assume that the same sponsorship policy applies to another region or country. They should review the specific vacancy and local recruitment information before applying.

Can Previous Applicants Apply Again?

Yes.

Bank of America states that candidates who previously applied may potentially apply again, subject to regional application limits.

For example, the main campus page states that applicants may generally apply to one office and one division per year, and candidates who are unsuccessful for a summer program may apply for a Full-Time program the following year.

Different regional rules can apply. For example, Bank of America’s APAC guidance currently permits candidates to submit two applications per year.

Applicants should therefore check the applicable rules for their region before submitting multiple applications.

Benefits for Interns, Analysts and Associates

Benefits vary according to employment type and location.

Bank of America states that student internships do not qualify for its complete employee benefits package.

However, eligible full-time analyst and associate positions may qualify for employment benefits such as health insurance, retirement-related benefits and other benefits applicable to the employee’s position and location.

The specific compensation and benefits associated with an individual opportunity should be confirmed from the relevant vacancy or offer documentation.

Equal Employment Opportunity

Bank of America states that qualified candidates are considered for employment without regard to characteristics including race, religion, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, national origin, ancestry, citizenship, protected veteran status or disability status, subject to applicable law.

This means the Campus Experience is not presented as an opportunity limited to applicants of a particular racial or ethnic group. Eligibility instead depends primarily on the requirements of the relevant position, academic status and applicable employment or immigration requirements.

How to Apply

Applicants should visit the official Bank of America Campus Experience website and explore the available student opportunities.

Official website:

https://careers.bankofamerica.com/en-us/students/campus-experience

Before applying:

Identify the region where you want to work.

Select your preferred career area.

Determine whether you are applying for an internship, analyst, associate, placement or another student program.

Review the degree and graduation-date requirements.

Check technical or language requirements.

Review work-authorization or visa requirements where relevant.

Confirm the exact application deadline for the individual vacancy.

Prepare an updated CV or résumé.

Complete all required online application stages.

Apply as early as possible where recruitment operates on a rolling basis.

Final Thoughts

The Bank of America Campus Experience provides university students and advanced-degree candidates with access to a broad portfolio of early-career opportunities across banking, financial markets, corporate functions, technology and operations.

The programs are particularly relevant for students who want to combine their academic education with practical experience inside a major international financial institution. Depending on the opportunity, participants can receive professional training, mentorship, networking opportunities, hands-on experience and exposure to Bank of America’s working environment.

Students should remember that the Campus Experience is not one standardized global program. Eligibility requirements, recruitment periods, work-authorization conditions and application deadlines differ significantly by country, business division and program.

Prospective applicants should therefore identify the specific opportunity that matches their degree level, graduation date, geographical preference and career interests, then carefully review the official vacancy before applying.

For candidates interested in EMEA opportunities, the currently published closing date for the main Summer, Off-Cycle and Full-Time 2026 recruitment cycle is October 11, 2026, and Bank of America recommends applying early because recruitment takes place on a rolling basis.

TITLE: WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants 2026–2027: Up to US$15,000 for Implementation Research in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa and TDR have opened applications for the 2026–2027 Joint WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants for Implementation Research for Regional Priorities.

The programme will provide funding of up to US$15,000 per selected project to support public health-oriented implementation research in the WHO African Region. Proposed studies must address practical barriers affecting the delivery, scale-up, sustainability or impact of existing health interventions, particularly those connected with infectious diseases of poverty.

The funding is aimed at researchers and institutions capable of producing actionable evidence that can strengthen health systems, improve access to essential interventions and translate research findings into policy and practice. Proposals may address person-centred primary healthcare, digital transformation, climate-sensitive diseases, antimicrobial resistance, One Health, emergency preparedness and other specified regional priorities.

Applications must be submitted through the eTDR platform by 15 September 2026. The official summary and WHO AFRO’s public announcement give the deadline as 17:00 CEST. Applicants should use the earlier CEST interpretation and submit well ahead of the closing time. Official WHO AFRO call

WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants 2026–2027 at a Glance

Item

About WHO AFRO and TDR

The WHO Regional Office for Africa, commonly known as WHO AFRO, is responsible for WHO’s work with Member States assigned to the African Region.

TDR is the UNICEF/UNDP/World Bank/WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases. It supports research and strengthens research capacity to address infectious diseases of poverty and associated global health challenges.

The Impact Grants are implemented jointly by TDR and WHO regional offices. Projects are carried out by researchers in developing countries, while the regional offices help implement and manage the grants. Implementation research has been the central focus of the scheme since 2014. TDR Impact Research Grants Scheme

The 2026–2027 call aligns with the TDR Strategy 2024–2029, which focuses on building locally led research solutions to improve global health. It seeks to strengthen health systems, improve access to interventions and respond to challenges such as climate change, infectious disease threats and pandemics. TDR Strategy 2024–2029

Why the WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants Are Important

The WHO African Region continues to face persistent health-system weaknesses that affect the availability, accessibility, quality and sustainability of health services.

New drugs, vaccines, diagnostics and other health technologies remain important. However, developing an effective intervention does not automatically ensure that it reaches the people who need it.

Implementation barriers may include:

Weak referral systems

Fragmented health programmes

Inadequate supply chains

Shortages of essential medicines and diagnostics

Poor laboratory capacity

Insufficient use of health information

Limited community participation

Weak coordination among health-sector institutions

Environmental and climate-related pressures

Difficulties moving successful pilot interventions to national scale

Poor integration of disease programmes into primary healthcare

Inadequate translation of research evidence into policy and practice

Implementation research examines these practical problems. It seeks to understand why proven interventions are not working as intended in a particular context and what changes could make their delivery more effective, equitable, scalable and sustainable.

TDR’s implementation research materials emphasize identifying system bottlenecks and relevant stakeholders, formulating appropriate research questions, conducting the study and preparing a plan for putting the findings into practice. TDR Implementation Research Training Materials

Main Objectives of the Impact Grants

The 2026–2027 Impact Grants have three principal objectives.

1. Strengthening Research Capacity

The programme seeks to strengthen the capacity of relevant researchers, health professionals and institutions to conduct operational and implementation research.

The funding is intended to help build sustainable country-level research capacity rather than support research that is disconnected from national health priorities.

2. Producing Actionable and Context-Specific Evidence

Projects should generate findings that countries can use to:

Strengthen health systems

Improve the implementation of health programmes

Expand access to existing interventions

Address delivery bottlenecks

Improve quality of care

Develop context-specific implementation strategies

Tackle infectious diseases of poverty

Inform health policies and operational decisions

A successful proposal should demonstrate how its findings could lead to practical action rather than ending only as an academic publication.

3. Encouraging Intersectoral Dialogue and One Health

The programme encourages cooperation among health authorities, researchers, communities and institutions working in related sectors.

One Health approaches recognize the relationship between human health, animal health and the shared environment. Projects addressing zoonotic diseases, climate-sensitive infections, antimicrobial resistance or emerging threats may therefore require collaboration beyond the traditional health sector.

Research Priority One: Person-Centred Service Delivery Across the Life Course

The first priority supports implementation research that helps health systems move away from fragmented and isolated disease programmes toward integrated, person-centred primary healthcare.

Research should examine how services addressing infectious diseases of poverty can be integrated into comprehensive healthcare models that respond to people’s needs throughout their lives.

Potential areas include:

Communicable Diseases

Research may focus on the implementation and integration of interventions relating to:

Tuberculosis

Malaria

Neglected tropical diseases

Other infectious diseases of poverty

Projects should not merely describe the burden of disease. They should examine a practical implementation challenge and test or assess a strategy for improving service delivery.

Referral Systems

Research could investigate:

Delays in referral

Patient loss between different levels of care

Communication between community, primary and specialist services

Referral completion

Feedback mechanisms

Continuity after referral

Barriers preventing patients from reaching appropriate care

Continuity of Care

Relevant questions may include how health systems can maintain continuous care for patients with long-term or recurring conditions and how communicable disease services can be integrated with maternal, child, adolescent or adult healthcare.

Quality Improvement Within Integrated Models

Projects may assess practical strategies for improving service quality when previously separate programmes are combined within person-centred primary healthcare.

Scalable and Sustainable Innovations

Proposals may examine whether an innovation can:

Operate in routine health-system conditions

Be expanded beyond a pilot site

Remain affordable

Be sustained after initial funding ends

Be integrated into existing primary healthcare structures

Maintain quality when implemented at a larger scale

Research Priority Two: Health-Systems Strengthening, Innovation and Digital Transformation

The second priority focuses on systemic barriers that limit the scale, sustainability and impact of interventions for controlling or eliminating infectious diseases.

Access to Essential Medicines

Projects may investigate implementation barriers affecting:

Availability of medicines

Affordability

Procurement

Distribution

Stock management

Last-mile delivery

Rational use

Equity of access

Diagnostics and Laboratory Strengthening

Research could address:

Access to diagnostic services

Sample referral systems

Turnaround time

Quality assurance

Laboratory information systems

Integration of laboratory networks

Diagnostic capacity at primary healthcare level

Links between testing and clinical decision-making

Health Supply Chains

Potential studies may focus on forecasting, procurement, inventory control, distribution, stock-outs, data visibility or coordination among institutions responsible for health commodities.

Quality-of-Care Improvement

Projects may test or evaluate strategies for improving:

Adherence to clinical standards

Patient safety

Health-worker performance

Respectful and person-centred care

Monitoring and supervision

Accountability

Use of quality indicators

Digital Health and Health Information Systems

Relevant implementation research may address:

Electronic health records

Disease surveillance platforms

Digital reporting

Interoperability

Data quality

Data use by managers

Decision-support systems

Community-level digital tools

Appropriate uses of artificial intelligence

Privacy, governance and responsible implementation of digital systems

The call refers specifically to appropriate AI-supported tools. A proposal should therefore demonstrate that the proposed technology addresses a defined health-system problem and can be implemented responsibly in the local context.

Innovative Service-Delivery Models

Proposals may assess new ways of organizing or delivering health services, provided that they address an implementation problem and are relevant to infectious diseases of poverty.

Emergency Preparedness Integration

Projects can examine how emergency preparedness and response functions can be integrated into routine health systems rather than operating only during a crisis.

Community-System Strengthening

Research may explore how community health workers, local organizations, civil society and community structures can improve programme implementation, surveillance, service uptake, accountability or continuity of care.

Cross-Sector Collaboration

Projects may investigate how health authorities can work more effectively with environmental, agricultural, veterinary, education, technology or local government institutions.

Research Priority Three: Environmental Health, Climate Change, One Health and Emerging Threats

The third priority addresses the environmental, ecological and multisectoral factors influencing infectious diseases of poverty.

Climate-Sensitive Diseases

Projects may examine how climate variability and environmental change affect disease transmission, service demand, programme delivery or community vulnerability.

Research can also test community-based adaptation strategies that help populations and health systems prepare for climate-related health risks.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene

Projects may address the integration of water, sanitation and hygiene interventions into primary healthcare, disease-control programmes or community health systems.

Antimicrobial Resistance

Research may focus on:

Rational use of medicines

Antimicrobial stewardship

Prescribing practices

Community use of antimicrobials

Surveillance

Diagnostic stewardship

Infection prevention and control

Coordination across human, animal and environmental health systems

Zoonotic and Emerging Diseases

One Health projects may examine how human health, animal health and environmental institutions can work together to prevent, detect and respond to zoonotic and emerging or re-emerging diseases.

Surveillance, Preparedness and Response

Implementation research may assess strategies for strengthening:

Early detection

Community surveillance

Laboratory surveillance

Data sharing

Multisectoral coordination

Risk communication

Emergency response

Preparedness at national and subnational levels

Funding Amount and Financial Conditions

Each selected project may receive up to US$15,000.

Applicants should understand that “up to US$15,000” is a maximum limit rather than a guaranteed award amount. The proposed budget should reflect the actual cost of the study and must be expressed in United States dollars.

Domestic or external co-funding is encouraged. However, the official call does not describe co-funding as a mandatory eligibility condition.

The public announcement does not specify:

The number of grants expected to be awarded

A minimum grant amount

The payment schedule

Detailed eligible and ineligible cost categories

Whether indirect institutional costs are permitted

A fixed co-funding percentage

Applicants should use the prescribed application form and request clarification from WHO where a proposed expense may be uncertain.

Project Duration

The maximum study duration is 12 months.

In addition to the 12-month limit:

The entire research project must be completed by the end of 2027.

A no-cost extension will not be permitted.

The proposed work plan must therefore be realistic and achievable within both limits.

Applicants should account for ethics review, administrative approval, data collection, analysis, stakeholder validation, reporting and knowledge translation when preparing the timeline.

A technically ambitious project that cannot realistically be completed within the available budget and timeframe is unlikely to present a strong implementation plan.

Detailed Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet all applicable conditions.

Application Language

The proposal and Principal Investigator information must be submitted in one of the following languages:

English

French

Portuguese

Geographic Location of the Research

The proposed study must be conducted in the WHO African Region.

Institutional Base

The Principal Investigator and most members of the research team must be based at an institution in a WHO African Region country or territory.

Eligible institutional settings may include:

National tropical disease programmes

National communicable disease-control programmes

Ministries of health

Academic institutions

Universities

Research institutes

Nongovernmental organizations

Public health or healthcare-service institutions

Alignment with the Call

The research must relate directly to the objectives, scope and priority areas of the call.

Implementation or Operational Research Experience

Applicants must demonstrate relevant experience in operational or implementation research and the ability to conduct research independently.

Evidence may include:

Previous operational or implementation research

Formal implementation research training

Completion of the TDR Implementation Research Toolkit

Completion of the TDR implementation research massive open online course

Another recognized research training programme

Relevant publications

Leadership of previous research projects

Evidence of applying research findings in policy or practice

The call does not prescribe a particular university degree, academic rank, age limit or minimum number of years of experience. The decisive requirement is credible evidence of implementation or operational research capacity.

Authorization for Research in a Health Centre

If the proposed research will be implemented in a health centre, the application requires an authorization letter from the relevant public health manager or director.

Programme Acknowledgement Letter

The proposal must include an acknowledgement letter signed by the manager of the programme area or the person responsible for the programme connected with the research.

The signatory may be based at:

A primary healthcare unit

A municipal health authority

A state or provincial health department

A national ministry or secretariat of health

Another appropriate level of the public health or healthcare system

This letter is important because the call is intended to support implementation research connected with real health programmes and decision-makers.

Equality, Diversity and Inclusion

WHO AFRO and TDR encourage eligible researchers to apply irrespective of:

Gender identity

Sexual orientation

Ethnicity

Religion

Cultural background

Social background

Disability status

Applications are particularly encouraged from:

Early-career researchers

Women

Applicants based in least-developed countries

These groups are encouraged, but the call does not state that eligibility is restricted to them.

Selection Process

Applications will be assessed competitively by external reviewers and staff from WHO AFRO and TDR.

The three stated scoring areas are:

Scientific Excellence

Reviewers will assess whether the research question, methodology, analysis and overall scientific approach are sound and appropriate.

Public Health Impact

The proposal should explain how the results could improve health programmes, strengthen systems, address infectious diseases of poverty or inform policy and practice.

Project Implementation Plan

The proposal should present a credible work plan, timeline, management approach, budget and strategy for completing the project within 12 months and before the end of 2027.

Principal Investigators are expected to be informed of the results within three months after the application deadline.

Ethical Approval

Funding is conditional on obtaining ethical approval from the relevant research ethics committees in the WHO African Region and the country where the study will be conducted.

The WHO application instructions also list ethical approval among the documents to be combined into the final application PDF. Applicants should therefore initiate the ethics process early and confirm exactly what approval or evidence must accompany the initial submission.

Ethical review should not be treated as an administrative formality. A strong proposal should address:

Participant protection

Informed consent, where applicable

Privacy and confidentiality

Data security

Risks and benefits

Community engagement

Protection of vulnerable populations

Responsible use of digital health or artificial intelligence tools

Relevant national and institutional requirements

Application Documents

Applicants should prepare the following materials.

1. Completed and Signed Research Proposal Form

The prescribed WHO form must be used. It must be completed fully and signed appropriately.

WHO states that applications that do not fully complete the required proposal form will not be considered for funding.

2. Principal Investigator’s Curriculum Vitae

The PI’s CV must not exceed one page.

It should clearly provide:

Institutional affiliation

Complete address

Mobile telephone number

WhatsApp number

Email address

Other affiliated institutions

Full name, with the family name underlined

Gender

Date of birth

Nationality

Qualifications

Current position

Previous positions

A standard multi-page academic CV should not be uploaded without first adapting it to these requirements.

3. Project Budget

The project costing must be included and expressed in United States dollars.

The budget should align with:

The proposed activities

The research timeline

The methodology

The number and location of study sites

Data collection requirements

Analysis

Stakeholder engagement

Reporting and dissemination

4. Ethical Approval

The required ethics documentation should be included as directed by the call and applicable ethics committees.

5. Acknowledgement Letter

The application requires the signed acknowledgement letter from the appropriate programme manager or responsible health-service official.

6. Health-Centre Authorization Letter

If the research will be implemented in a health centre, obtain authorization from its public health manager or director.

How to Apply for the WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants

Step 1: Read the Complete Official Call

Review the official WHO AFRO announcement, research priorities, eligibility rules and required supporting documents.

Step 2: Create or Access an eTDR Account

Applications must be submitted through the official eTDR application portal.

Existing users should sign in. New users must create an account before beginning the submission.

Applicants should create the account early enough to resolve registration, password or portal-access problems before the deadline.

Step 3: Download the Correct Application Form

Official forms are available in three languages:

English application form

French application form

Portuguese application form

Step 4: Complete and Sign the Proposal

Every mandatory field should be completed. Do not substitute an independently designed proposal for the official form.

Step 5: Finalize the Budget

Prepare the budget in US dollars and make sure the costs are reasonable, necessary and directly connected with the proposed activities.

Step 6: Obtain the Required Letters and Approvals

Secure the programme acknowledgement letter, health-centre authorization where applicable and ethics documentation.

Step 7: Prepare the One-Page PI CV

Reduce the CV to one page while retaining every item specifically required by WHO.

Step 8: Combine Everything Into One PDF

The following documents must be combined into a single PDF:

Completed and signed research proposal

Ethical approval documentation

Project budget

One-page PI CV

Signed acknowledgement letter

Health-centre authorization, where applicable

Do not upload the documents as separate files unless the portal specifically instructs otherwise.

Step 9: Name the PDF Correctly

The filename must use the applicant’s name followed by “SGS2026.”

WHO provides the following example:

SmithJ_SGS2026.pdf

Applicants should use a similarly clear format based on the PI’s family name and initial.

Step 10: Upload and Submit Through eTDR

Upload the final PDF, complete all portal fields and formally submit the application before the deadline.

Saving a draft is not the same as submitting an application. Applicants should verify that the portal records the application as submitted and retain any confirmation or reference number.

Application Deadline and Time-Zone Warning

The application deadline is:

15 September 2026 at 17:00 CEST

This is equivalent to 15:00 UTC.

The call’s summary and WHO AFRO’s official social announcement use CEST. One paragraph in the detailed application section uses CET, which differs by one hour. To avoid any risk, applicants should treat 17:00 CEST as the controlling deadline and submit earlier. WHO AFRO official deadline announcement

Practical Tips for a Strong Application

The following recommendations are based on the stated evaluation criteria and application requirements.

Define a Genuine Implementation Problem

Do not submit a proposal that only measures disease prevalence or describes a public health problem. Explain what intervention already exists, what implementation barrier is preventing impact and how the study will generate evidence to address that barrier.

Demonstrate Policy or Programme Relevance

Involve the responsible health programme or service manager early. The acknowledgement-letter requirement signals that institutional ownership and policy relevance are important.

Select One Clear Priority Area

The proposal should align convincingly with at least one of the three priorities. Avoid adding unrelated themes simply to make the project appear broader.

Keep the Study Feasible

The project must fit within:

A maximum US$15,000 budget

A maximum 12-month implementation period

The final completion deadline at the end of 2027

A focused study with a realistic implementation pathway is likely to be stronger than an overly ambitious multi-country project.

Explain the Expected Public Health Impact

Show who will use the findings, how the evidence will reach decision-makers and what programme or policy decision the research could influence.

Include Knowledge Translation

Build dissemination and evidence-use activities into the work plan rather than treating publication as the only final output.

Address Equity and Community Engagement

Explain how the study will consider underserved groups, gender, disability, geographic inequalities and community perspectives where relevant.

Prepare Ethics and Authorization Documents Early

Waiting until the final days to obtain signatures or institutional approvals creates a serious risk of an incomplete application.

Check the Final PDF Carefully

Before submission, confirm that:

The official form has been used

Every required field is complete

All signatures are present

The CV is no more than one page

The budget is in US dollars

All required letters are included

Ethics documentation is included

The file opens correctly

The filename follows the required format

The application has been submitted rather than merely saved

Publication and Data Requirements

Publications and data produced through funded projects must comply with the WHO Policy on Open Access.

Outputs should clearly acknowledge support from the WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants for Regional Priorities and include the relevant grant number.

WHO’s policy generally seeks to ensure that WHO-funded research outputs are freely accessible and reusable. It also addresses the deposit of research data in appropriate repositories. Applicants should consider publication, data management and open-access requirements while preparing the study budget and dissemination plan. WHO Policy on Open Access

Official Contact Information

For questions about the call:

Dr Constance Assohou-Luty: assohoulutyc@who.int

Mrs Ritah Nakuya Turay: nakuyar@who.int

For technical problems involving the eTDR portal:

Ms Elisabetta Dessi: dessie@who.int

eTDR support: etdr@who.int

Applicants should use the technical contacts only for portal-related problems and direct programme or eligibility questions to the call contacts.

Conclusion

The 2026–2027 Joint WHO AFRO/TDR Impact Grants provide an important funding opportunity for researchers and public health institutions seeking to solve practical health-service and implementation problems in the WHO African Region.

With funding of up to US$15,000, the programme can support focused implementation research on person-centred primary healthcare, infectious diseases of poverty, health-system strengthening, digital transformation, climate-sensitive diseases, antimicrobial resistance, One Health and emerging public health threats.

A competitive application will need more than a relevant topic. It must define a clear implementation problem, demonstrate scientific quality, explain its potential public health impact, involve the appropriate health programme and present a realistic plan that can be delivered within 12 months.

Eligible applicants should begin by selecting the appropriate research priority, securing programme support and ethical documentation, preparing the required one-page CV and completing the prescribed application form. The complete application must be combined into one correctly named PDF and submitted through the eTDR portal before 15 September 2026 at 17:00 CEST.

TITLE: 2027 Hoover Fellows Program at Stanford University

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Hoover Institution at Stanford University is seeking outstanding early-career scholars for the 2027 Hoover Fellows Program, an opportunity for researchers whose work has implications for public policy.

Hoover Fellows will be based at the Hoover Institution in Stanford, California, where they will have the opportunity to pursue scholarly research, publish academic work, and contribute to the intellectual life of one of Stanford University’s leading research centers.

The fellowship is particularly suited to scholars working in fields such as economics, history, international relations, national security, political science, and public policy.

According to the 2027 opportunity information provided by the Hoover Institution, appointments are for one to three years, and the position carries no teaching responsibilities.

About the Hoover Fellows Program

The Hoover Institution is a research center at Stanford University focused on research and scholarship with relevance to public policy. Hoover scholars contribute to research and intellectual discussions on issues including economics, national security, international relations, and governance.

The Hoover Fellows Program provides early-career scholars with an opportunity to concentrate on their research and scholarly writing while participating in the intellectual community at Hoover and engaging with Stanford’s broader research environment.

During the fellowship, Fellows are expected to produce scholarly articles and books that have implications for public policy. They are also expected to contribute to the intellectual life of the Hoover Institution.

Unlike some academic fellowships, the position does not include teaching responsibilities, allowing Fellows to focus primarily on research and publication.

Fellowship Benefits

The 2027 Hoover Fellow position offers a highly competitive compensation package.

Salary

Selected Fellows will receive a 12-month base salary ranging from $169,950 to $230,000.

Housing Allowance

In addition to the base salary, Fellows will receive a $20,000 annual housing allowance.

Research Environment

Fellows will be based at the Hoover Institution on Stanford University’s campus in Stanford, California. They will also be encouraged to engage with Stanford’s wider research community in their respective fields.

This provides Fellows with an opportunity to interact with scholars and researchers beyond Hoover while developing their own academic research agendas.

Fellowship Duration

The 2027 opportunity specifies an appointment term of one to three years.

The position is based at the Hoover Institution, Stanford, California, and Fellows are expected to participate in the Institution’s intellectual community while pursuing their research.

Areas of Research

The Hoover Fellows Program is open to scholars working in relevant academic and policy fields.

Examples of eligible fields include:

Economics

History

International Relations

National Security

Political Science

Public Policy

Applicants from related disciplines may also be considered where their research aligns with the Hoover Institution’s mission and has meaningful implications for public policy.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must be early-career scholars who hold a Ph.D. or equivalent degree in a relevant field, or who expect to complete the degree by September 1, 2027.

The opportunity is therefore particularly relevant to doctoral candidates approaching completion of their Ph.D. as well as scholars who have already completed their doctoral studies.

Applicants should have an academic and research background that demonstrates their potential to produce significant scholarly work.

Candidates are expected to show how their research can contribute to broader discussions relevant to public policy.

What Will Hoover Fellows Do?

Selected Fellows will primarily focus on research and scholarly activities.

During the fellowship, they are expected to:

Conduct research in their area of specialization.

Produce scholarly articles and other academic publications.

Develop books or book-length research where appropriate.

Pursue research projects with implications for public policy.

Contribute to the intellectual life of the Hoover Institution.

Engage with Stanford’s broader research community.

Participate in scholarly discussions connected to their research interests.

Because the position carries no teaching responsibilities, Fellows can devote their time primarily to research, writing, and intellectual engagement.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit several documents as part of their application.

1. Cover Letter or Statement of Interest

Applicants should provide a cover letter or statement of interest describing their academic background and experience.

This document should clearly communicate the applicant’s research interests, academic preparation, and reasons for seeking the Hoover Fellowship.

2. Recent Scholarly Work

Applicants must submit one or more recent publications, working papers, or draft book chapters.

These materials allow the selection committee to assess the applicant’s research quality, scholarly writing, and potential for future contributions.

3. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide an up-to-date CV outlining their academic background, research experience, publications, professional experience, awards, and other relevant achievements.

4. Future Research Statement

Applicants must submit a statement describing their future research plans.

The research statement must be no more than two pages and should clearly explain the research the applicant intends to pursue during the fellowship and its potential significance.

5. Three Letters of Recommendation

Applicants are required to provide three letters of recommendation.

The letters should address the candidate’s research accomplishments and potential for future research.

Applicants should therefore select recommenders who can provide meaningful assessments of their academic and research capabilities.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is particularly suitable for early-career researchers who are developing independent research programmes and want to work in a leading research environment.

Potential applicants include:

Ph.D. candidates nearing completion of their degrees.

Recent Ph.D. graduates.

Early-career scholars in economics and related disciplines.

Researchers working on international relations and national security.

Political scientists and historians.

Public policy researchers.

Scholars whose research has clear implications for public policy.

Applicants should have a strong research profile and be prepared to demonstrate their potential for future scholarly contributions.

Location

The Hoover Fellows Program is based at:

Hoover Institution

Stanford University

Stanford, California, USA

The Hoover Institution is located in the heart of Stanford University’s campus, providing Fellows with access to a broader academic and research environment.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027 Hoover Fellows Program is:

November 17, 2026

Time: 11:59 PM Pacific Time

Applicants are encouraged to prepare their application materials well in advance of the deadline, particularly because the application requires three recommendation letters and several research documents.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted online through the Hoover Institution’s application platform.

Application Portal: Apply for the 2027 Hoover Fellows Program

Applicants should ensure that all required documents and recommendation letters are submitted according to the instructions before the deadline.

For questions about the fellowship, applicants can contact hooverfellowship@stanford.edu. The Hoover Institution notes that this inbox is checked only periodically.

Important Information for Applicants

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should make sure they:

Hold a Ph.D. or equivalent degree, or expect to complete it by September 1, 2027.

Have a research background in a relevant academic field.

Prepare a strong cover letter or statement of interest.

Include recent scholarly work, working papers, or a draft book chapter.

Prepare an updated academic CV.

Develop a focused future research statement of no more than two pages.

Identify three appropriate referees.

Allow enough time for recommendation letters to be submitted.

Submit the complete application before November 17, 2026, at 11:59 PM PT.

Why Consider the Hoover Fellowship?

For early-career scholars, the fellowship provides an opportunity to dedicate substantial time to research and scholarly publication while becoming part of the intellectual community at the Hoover Institution.

The combination of a competitive salary, housing allowance, research-focused responsibilities, and access to Stanford’s broader scholarly environment makes the opportunity particularly attractive to researchers seeking to advance an academic or policy-oriented career.

The fellowship can also provide a valuable platform for scholars whose research seeks to connect academic scholarship with important public policy questions.

Conclusion

The 2027 Hoover Fellows Program at Stanford University offers an exciting opportunity for early-career scholars to pursue research in a prestigious academic and policy research environment.

Successful Fellows will be expected to produce high-quality scholarly work, contribute to the intellectual life of the Hoover Institution, and engage with Stanford’s wider research community. The position offers a 12-month base salary of $169,950 to $230,000, plus a $20,000 annual housing allowance, and carries no teaching responsibilities.

Researchers in economics, history, international relations, national security, political science, public policy, and related fields who meet the doctoral degree requirement are encouraged to consider applying.

Discover more opportunities on the OFY Webpage.

TITLE: Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships 2027: Up to $20,000 for Environmental Photographers Worldwide

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships 2027 are inviting photographers and visual storytellers from around the world to develop long-term documentary photography projects focused on environmental and conservation challenges.

The programme is designed to support photographers who use visual storytelling to explore environmental issues while highlighting the people, communities and organizations working to protect the planet, wildlife and natural habitats.

In 2027, Vital Impacts plans to award one $20,000 fellowship to an established environmental photographer, six $5,000 fellowships to emerging photographers from around the world, and ten mentorships for photographers whose work demonstrates strong potential and would benefit from additional professional guidance.

The programme emphasizes long-term documentary storytelling, meaningful relationships with communities and ethical approaches to photography. Prior publication experience is not required.

About Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships

Vital Impacts is a nonprofit organization that uses journalism and visual storytelling to amplify the work of communities protecting people, wildlife and habitats around the world.

Its Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships provide financial support, mentorship and creative independence to photographers developing significant bodies of work around environmental and conservation issues.

The programme is particularly interested in projects that move beyond simply documenting environmental problems. Applicants are encouraged to tell stories about the people, communities and initiatives developing solutions to environmental and conservation challenges.

Each fellowship supports one photographer and one documentary project during the fellowship and mentorship period. Recipients receive time, financial support and guidance from the Vital Impacts mentorship community while developing their proposed project.

At the end of the programme, recipients are expected to have made meaningful progress on their proposed project and developed a substantial body of work that could be suitable for publication, exhibition or other forms of public engagement.

Vital Impacts Photography Fellowships 2027 Awards

For 2027, the programme will provide three categories of support:

One $20,000 Fellowship

One $20,000 fellowship will be awarded to an established environmental photographer.

Six $5,000 Fellowships

Six $5,000 fellowships will be awarded to emerging photographers from around the world.

Ten Mentorships

Ten photographers will receive mentorship support. These applicants should demonstrate strong potential and have work that would benefit from additional guidance and professional support.

The combination of financial support and mentorship is intended to give photographers the opportunity to spend significant time developing their projects and producing thoughtful, deeply reported visual stories.

New Exhibition Opportunity in Italy

Vital Impacts has expanded its partnership with the Festival of Ethical Photography to create an additional opportunity for one of the seven fellowship recipients.

One fellowship recipient will be selected at a later stage to exhibit their work at the 2027 Festival of Ethical Photography in Lodi, Italy.

The selected photographer will benefit from the Festival’s international platform for documentary photography and photojournalism focused on important social and environmental issues.

The Festival will cover:

The full costs of producing the exhibition.

Installation costs.

International travel for the selected photographer.

Accommodation to attend the Festival.

The opportunity to present the work in person.

This partnership can provide the selected fellow with an opportunity to reach an international audience and connect with photographers, editors, conservationists and members of the public interested in environmental and social issues.

Who Should Apply?

Vital Impacts is particularly interested in photographers who have developed meaningful and established relationships with the people, places and issues they document.

The programme places strong emphasis on photographers who take time to:

Listen to communities.

Build trust.

Understand local context.

Develop meaningful relationships.

Return to stories over time.

Produce long-term documentary work.

Vital Impacts strongly encourages applications from photographers documenting environmental and conservation stories within their own communities.

Local photographers can bring knowledge, access, relationships and perspectives that may provide greater depth and authenticity to the stories being documented.

However, applicants do not necessarily need to live permanently in the location they propose to document.

The programme will also consider photographers who can demonstrate sustained knowledge and engagement through:

Recurring travel.

Long-term collaborations.

Professional experience.

Academic experience.

Other meaningful relationships with the community or issue.

Applicants should clearly explain why they are the right person to tell their proposed story, including what they know, who they know, what relationships they have developed and what unique perspective they bring.

What Does Vital Impacts Look For?

Successful applications should demonstrate the ability to communicate the complexity of environmental and conservation challenges while also showing potential solutions.

Vital Impacts is looking for photographers who can demonstrate:

Meaningful Relationships

Applicants should have a meaningful and sustained relationship with the community, environmental issue or conservation initiative they intend to document.

Understanding of the Issue

Applicants should demonstrate a clear understanding of the environmental issue and explain its wider significance.

A Realistic Project Plan

Applicants should present a thoughtful and realistic plan for developing the project over a 12-month period.

Existing Access and Trust

Where appropriate, applicants should demonstrate existing access to the community or issue and evidence of established trust.

Ethical Storytelling

Applicants must demonstrate a commitment to ethical and responsible storytelling.

Strong Photography

Applications should demonstrate distinctive visual approaches and strong photographic ability.

Public Impact

The proposed project should have potential to contribute meaningfully to public understanding of environmental and conservation issues.

Is Previous Publication Experience Required?

No.

Prior publication experience is specifically stated as not being a requirement for applicants.

This means photographers should focus on demonstrating the strength of their visual work, their relationship with the proposed subject or community, their understanding of the issue and their ability to develop a meaningful long-term documentary project.

Ethical Storytelling Requirements

Ethics are an important part of the Vital Impacts programme.

All winners are required to comply with the Vital Impacts Code of Ethics throughout the application, fellowship or mentorship, production and delivery of their project.

Applicants are expected to review the Code of Ethics before applying and agree to comply with it if selected.

Vital Impacts may assess ethical compliance through several mechanisms, including:

Review of submitted work and project materials.

Review of the applicant’s project statement.

Assessment of the applicant’s relationship with the community or issue.

Regular check-ins.

Communications with mentors and the Vital Impacts team.

Review of concerns or complaints.

Requests for additional information or clarification.

Review of project materials, captions, metadata and other documentation where necessary.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed projects are based on responsible, respectful and ethical documentary practices.

What Will Fellowship Recipients Do?

The fellowship or mentorship period is intended to give recipients the time and support needed to develop a substantial documentary project.

During the programme, recipients will work on their proposed projects while receiving guidance from the Vital Impacts mentorship community.

The expected outcome is meaningful progress toward a substantial body of work that can potentially be:

Published.

Exhibited.

Presented to the public.

Used to increase understanding of environmental and conservation issues.

Key Benefits of the Programme

The programme provides different forms of support depending on the award received.

Key opportunities include:

A $20,000 fellowship for one established environmental photographer.

Six $5,000 fellowships for emerging photographers worldwide.

Ten mentorship opportunities.

Ongoing guidance from the Vital Impacts mentorship community.

Financial support for developing a documentary photography project.

Creative independence during project development.

An opportunity to develop a substantial long-term body of work.

Potential publication, exhibition and public engagement opportunities.

A special exhibition opportunity at the 2027 Festival of Ethical Photography in Lodi, Italy for one selected fellowship recipient.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Photographers interested in applying should pay particular attention to the relationship between their proposed story, their existing experience and their ability to access and document the issue responsibly.

1. Choose a Strong Environmental Story

Select an environmental or conservation issue that has clear significance and where there are people, communities or initiatives working toward solutions.

2. Demonstrate Your Relationship to the Story

Explain your existing relationship with the people, community, location or issue.

The programme places considerable emphasis on sustained engagement and trust.

3. Present a Long-Term Approach

Avoid presenting the project as a short-term photography assignment. Explain how the story can develop over the proposed 12-month period.

4. Show Your Visual Strength

Your portfolio and proposed project should demonstrate a distinctive visual approach and strong photographic ability.

5. Explain Your Ethical Approach

Show that you understand the responsibilities involved in documenting people and communities and that you are prepared to follow the Vital Impacts Code of Ethics.

6. Focus on Solutions

While environmental challenges are important, Vital Impacts specifically seeks stories that also illuminate the people and initiatives working toward solutions.

7. Explain the Potential Impact

Describe how the completed project could help audiences better understand the environmental or conservation issue.

Application Timeline

The programme page currently indicates that the opportunity is open for submissions. Applicants should consult the official application page for the exact submission timeline and current closing date before applying.

Applications are hosted through Picter, which provides the submission platform for the Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowship 2027.

How to Apply

Interested photographers should first review the programme information, timeline, FAQ and terms before starting their submission.

Applicants can access the official submission platform and begin their application through the Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowship 2027 application page.

The programme page provides a “Start submission” option for applicants.

Applicants should also review the Vital Impacts Code of Ethics before submitting.

Conclusion

The Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships 2027 offer photographers an opportunity to develop long-term documentary projects focused on environmental and conservation challenges and the people working to address them.

The programme combines financial support, mentorship and creative independence, with awards ranging from a $20,000 fellowship for an established photographer to six $5,000 fellowships for emerging photographers, alongside ten mentorship opportunities.

The programme is particularly suitable for photographers who have meaningful relationships with the communities or issues they document and who are committed to ethical, long-term storytelling.

Photographers should carefully develop their project concept, demonstrate their connection to the proposed story and explain how their work can contribute to greater public understanding of environmental and conservation issues.

Discover more fellowship opportunities like this on the OFY Webpage.
