The National Youth Council of Ireland (NYCI) is accepting applications for a Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer, an opportunity for an experienced education, training, youth work, or global citizenship professional to contribute directly to the organisation’s Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme.

Based in Dublin, Ireland, the full-time position combines training and facilitation, educational resource development, project coordination, stakeholder engagement, monitoring and evaluation, and work supporting the integration of Global Citizenship Education and Global Youth Work across Ireland’s youth sector.

The successful candidate will join the Youth 2030 team and contribute to efforts to ensure that young people become better informed about global challenges and more actively engaged in advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The position comes with an annual salary of €35,779 to €48,408, depending on qualifications and experience, together with hybrid working arrangements, 27 days of annual leave, pension contributions, professional development opportunities, family-friendly working provisions, and a range of additional employee benefits.

Application Deadline: 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026

Applicants should note that NYCI’s general vacancy announcement gives a later deadline of 5:00 p.m. on the same date, but the organisation’s live recruitment and application page states 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026. Candidates are therefore strongly advised to treat 2:00 p.m. as the effective deadline and submit well before that time.

About the National Youth Council of Ireland

The National Youth Council of Ireland works to support and strengthen the youth sector in Ireland while promoting policies, services, programmes, and opportunities that improve the lives of young people.

Its work spans areas including youth work, global youth work, equality and intercultural engagement, youth health, international engagement, digital youth work, youth arts, child protection, advocacy, education, and professional development.

For professionals passionate about youth participation, equality, sustainability, social justice, global issues, and education, working with NYCI provides an opportunity to contribute to programmes capable of influencing practice across the wider youth sector.

The organisation also places significant emphasis on creating an inclusive workplace and states that it values different identities, perspectives, and experiences while providing opportunities for staff learning and professional growth.

About the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme

The successful Project Officer will work within Youth 2030, NYCI’s major Global Youth Work and Development Education programme.

Youth 2030 is funded by Irish Aid and is intended to increase the integration, quality, and reach of Global Youth Work and Development Education throughout non-formal youth work organisations, programmes, and projects.

The programme is led by the National Youth Council of Ireland as part of a consortium involving Concern Worldwide, Trócaire, and Maynooth University.

At its core, Global Youth Work encourages young people to understand both their role within their local communities and their connection to an increasingly globalised world.

It gives young people opportunities to examine complex global issues including:

Poverty

Inequality

Hunger

Injustice

Climate change

Sustainable development

Global interconnectedness

Social and economic justice

Equality

International development

Rather than simply presenting information about these challenges, Global Youth Work seeks to encourage critical thinking, participation, and action among young people.

Purpose of the Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer Role

The Project Officer will play a key role in delivering the outcomes of NYCI’s Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme.

A central objective is ensuring that Global Youth Work becomes more fully integrated into non-formal youth work programmes and activities carried out by NYCI member organisations and the wider youth sector.

The programme aims to help young people become better informed about global challenges while empowering them to become active participants in efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.

The role will also contribute to ensuring Global Youth Work is incorporated into professional youth and community work training at third-level education institutions.

Another important area of work involves supporting innovation, research, and capacity development throughout the youth sector. This includes identifying and responding to challenges and opportunities that can broaden and deepen Global Youth Work, while developing stronger connections with the Global South.

Main Responsibilities of the Project Officer

This is a diverse role involving training, project administration, resource development, stakeholder engagement, monitoring, evaluation, and external representation.

Planning and Delivering Global Citizenship Education Training

One of the most significant responsibilities will involve working with Youth 2030 colleagues to identify training needs throughout the youth sector.

The Project Officer will then help plan, coordinate, design, and deliver workshops and training interventions addressing those needs.

Training will be delivered at different levels of the youth sector, meaning the successful candidate will need to adapt material and facilitation methods to different audiences and professional contexts.

Training delivery will take place through both in-person and virtual formats, while bespoke training may also be designed in response to specific organisational requirements.

Managing Training Administration

The position is not restricted to facilitation.

The successful applicant will also be responsible for administrative processes associated with training activities, including management of the programme’s training booking system.

Effective administration will therefore be important for ensuring that programmes are properly scheduled, coordinated, communicated, and delivered.

This means candidates should be comfortable moving between outward-facing facilitation responsibilities and detailed administrative work.

Developing Educational Resources

Another significant responsibility involves devising and developing educational resources for Ireland’s youth sector.

These resources can help youth workers, educators, organisations, and young people engage more effectively with Global Citizenship Education, sustainable development, global justice, and related issues.

The role therefore provides an opportunity for someone with experience translating complex social or global issues into accessible learning materials.

Educational resource development is particularly important because Youth 2030 seeks not only to deliver individual training sessions but also to strengthen the long-term capacity of youth workers and youth organisations.

Supporting the Global Youth Work Educators Network

The Project Officer will facilitate and support the Global Youth Work Educator’s Network.

Professional networks can provide important opportunities for educators and practitioners to exchange experiences, learn from one another, identify emerging challenges, develop good practice, and improve the overall quality of Global Youth Work.

The successful candidate will therefore need strong facilitation and relationship-management abilities alongside technical knowledge of Global Citizenship Education and youth work.

Building Relationships Across the Youth Sector

Stakeholder engagement represents another major dimension of the position.

The Project Officer will engage with NYCI member organisations and with the broader youth and Development Education community.

This will involve maintaining relationships with existing stakeholders while potentially developing new connections and collaborative opportunities.

The work may include interaction with youth organisations, educational institutions, trainers, educators, youth workers, community organisations, development organisations, and other actors involved in Global Citizenship Education and Global Youth Work.

Contributing to the Youth 2030 Team

The successful applicant will become an integral member of the NYCI Youth 2030 Global Youth Work team.

They will contribute both to the specific objectives of the Youth 2030 programme and to implementation of NYCI’s wider strategic direction.

This means the role requires someone capable of looking beyond isolated training activities and understanding how individual projects, resources, partnerships, and capacity-building initiatives contribute to wider organisational outcomes.

The Project Officer will work toward the objectives established within the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Results Framework while contributing to the delivery of NYCI’s Strategic Plan.

Monitoring, Evaluation and Impact Measurement

Monitoring and evaluation forms a defined part of the role.

The Project Officer will work with other staff to implement the programme’s monitoring and evaluation framework and help assess the effectiveness and impact of Youth 2030 activities.

This may involve gathering evidence, reviewing programme outcomes, assessing training effectiveness, analysing feedback, and contributing information that helps the organisation understand whether its interventions are creating the intended results.

This dimension makes the position particularly interesting for professionals who combine training and facilitation experience with an interest in evidence-based programme management.

NYCI’s original vacancy announcement specifically asks whether prospective candidates have experience using monitoring and evaluation tools, demonstrating the importance of this capability to the position.

External Representation

The selected candidate will also represent Youth 2030 externally within Global Citizenship Education arenas.

External representation may involve engaging with professional networks, partner organisations, educational institutions, development-sector stakeholders, youth organisations, and other communities involved in Global Citizenship Education.

As a result, the successful applicant will be expected to represent NYCI and Youth 2030 professionally while communicating effectively with different audiences.

Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals

The position has a particularly strong connection with sustainable development.

Youth 2030 aims to ensure that young people become more informed about global challenges and more active in helping achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.

Through training, education, capacity building, youth participation, and resource development, the Project Officer will therefore contribute to creating greater awareness of issues connected with global justice, sustainability, climate change, inequality, and development.

The position provides an opportunity to translate the SDGs from international policy frameworks into practical youth education and engagement activities.

Training and Continuous Professional Development

Training and continuous professional development are established elements of NYCI’s Global Youth Work activities.

Youth 2030 provides tailor-made training designed to strengthen the knowledge and practical capabilities required to deliver high-quality Global Youth Work.

The wider programme also supports learning through initiatives including online education, professional development activities, and educational programmes developed with partner institutions.

The Project Officer will therefore operate within an established training ecosystem rather than developing activities in isolation.

Location and Working Arrangements

The position is based at:

National Youth Council of Ireland

3 Montague Street

Dublin 2

Ireland

Travel will be required as part of the role.

NYCI is also currently operating a hybrid working model, which provides some flexibility between office-based and remote work.

Candidates should nevertheless understand that this is not advertised as a fully remote position.

The role involves in-person training, stakeholder engagement, travel, and other professional responsibilities requiring physical presence.

Working Hours

The position is full-time and involves:

35 hours per week

Some flexibility will be required, including the possibility of working during evenings and weekends when programme activities require it.

Applicants should therefore consider whether they can accommodate occasional working patterns outside conventional office hours.

Contract Duration

The position is offered on a one-year contract running to December 2027.

There is potential for the contract to be extended, but any extension will be dependent on continued funding.

The recruitment documentation describes the appointment as a specified-purpose contract.

This means applicants should not interpret the vacancy as an automatically permanent appointment.

Salary

The advertised annual salary range is:

€35,779 – €48,408 per annum

The actual salary offered will depend on the successful applicant’s qualifications and relevant professional experience.

This gives experienced candidates some scope to enter above the bottom point of the advertised salary range, subject to NYCI’s assessment and applicable employment arrangements.

Employee Benefits

NYCI provides employees with a substantial package of benefits and professional supports intended to contribute to financial security, personal wellbeing, professional development, and work-life balance.

Benefits listed for this position include:

27 days of annual leave

Access to sick leave arrangements

Parental leave schemes

Bereavement leave provisions

Employee Assistance Programme

Death-in-service benefit equivalent to four times salary

Family-friendly flexible working hours

Hybrid working arrangements

Tax Saver commuter ticket arrangements

Cycle to Work Scheme

Staff supervision

Staff training and professional development opportunities

Pension contributions

NYCI states that these benefits and supports are intended to enhance staff wellbeing and promote a healthy balance between professional and personal responsibilities.

Support for Candidates Attending Interviews

NYCI has introduced a practical measure intended to reduce financial barriers for applicants attending face-to-face interviews.

Candidates invited to attend an in-person interview may receive reimbursement for public transport costs within Ireland, subject to providing receipts.

The organisation specifically connects this measure with the financial challenges that people on lower incomes can experience when attending interviews and with wider cost-of-living pressures.

Child Safeguarding Responsibilities

Because the role involves the youth sector and activities affecting children and young people, safeguarding responsibilities are particularly important.

The successful applicant will be required to demonstrate a commitment to protecting children and young people.

This includes:

Participating in relevant safeguarding training

Undergoing required Garda vetting

Following child safeguarding policies and procedures

Following relevant reporting arrangements

Ensuring that the safety and wellbeing of young people remain paramount

Candidates should therefore understand that safeguarding is a substantive professional responsibility attached to the position rather than merely an administrative recruitment requirement.

Reporting Arrangements

The successful Project Officer will report directly to the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme Manager at the National Youth Council of Ireland.

Overall accountability sits with the Director and Board of NYCI.

This structure places the position within a wider programme and organisational accountability framework.

Probationary and Notice Periods

The position comes with a:

Six-month probationary period

and a:

One-month notice period.

Applicants should take these employment conditions into consideration when assessing the opportunity.

Expected Starting Date

NYCI expects the successful applicant to commence the role in:

November 2026.

Because recruitment is taking place during September 2026, shortlisted candidates should be prepared for a relatively quick appointment process.

Recruitment Timeline and Interviews

According to the live recruitment portal, shortlisted applicants are expected to be informed by 1 October 2026, with face-to-face interviews anticipated during the week beginning 5 October 2026.

There is an inconsistency in NYCI’s separate vacancy announcement, which states that interviews are expected during the week beginning 12 October 2026.

Applicants should therefore remain available for further instructions from NYCI rather than relying exclusively on either indicative interview week.

Application Process

Applications must be completed through NYCI’s online recruitment system.

The organisation clearly states that applications submitted through other methods will not be accepted.

The application form requests substantial information from candidates, including educational background, professional training, employment history, voluntary experience, availability to take up the position, references, driving-licence status, and information demonstrating how the applicant meets the specific requirements of the role.

Candidates are also asked whether they currently have the right to work in Ireland.

Applicants should therefore allow sufficient time to complete the application carefully rather than treating it as a simple CV upload.

The application form also asks for two referees, with one normally being the applicant’s current or most recent employer and at least one referee having knowledge of the candidate in a working environment, whether paid or unpaid.

Apply for the NYCI Project Officer Position

Applications can be submitted through the official NYCI recruitment portal:

Apply for the Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer position

Application Deadline

Candidates should submit their applications no later than:

2:00 p.m., Monday, 28 September 2026

The live NYCI recruitment portal gives this as the deadline.

NYCI’s accompanying news article instead states 5:00 p.m. on 28 September 2026.

Because the two official pages conflict and the recruitment portal is where applications are actually submitted, prospective applicants should use the earlier 2:00 p.m. deadline to avoid any risk of submitting too late.

Why This Opportunity Stands Out

The Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer position offers a distinctive combination of practical training, education, sustainable development, youth engagement, project management, stakeholder relations, research, and monitoring and evaluation.

The successful applicant will not simply deliver workshops. They will contribute to strengthening the capacity of the wider youth sector to engage young people with some of the most important global issues of the present decade.

The opportunity may be particularly meaningful for professionals who want their training and education experience to contribute directly to social justice, equality, sustainability, global citizenship, and youth participation.

The position also offers the chance to work within an established national programme supported by Irish Aid and delivered with major organisations including Concern Worldwide, Trócaire, and Maynooth University.

At the same time, the combination of a competitive salary, hybrid working, 27 days of annual leave, pension contributions, professional development support, and family-friendly working provisions strengthens the overall employment package.

Conclusion

The NYCI Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer 2026 position presents a significant professional opportunity for an experienced trainer or education practitioner seeking to advance Global Citizenship Education, Global Youth Work, sustainable development, and youth participation in Ireland.

Based in Dublin and working within the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme, the successful applicant will design and deliver training, develop educational resources, coordinate training activities, strengthen professional networks, build relationships with youth-sector stakeholders, contribute to monitoring and evaluation, and represent Youth 2030 within the wider Global Citizenship Education community.

With an annual salary ranging from €35,779 to €48,408, hybrid working, substantial annual leave, pension contributions, staff development opportunities, and a role directly connected with the Sustainable Development Goals, this position offers both professional development and an opportunity to contribute to meaningful social change.

Candidates interested in applying should prepare their online application carefully and submit it through NYCI’s recruitment portal before 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026.

TITLE: Elizabeth “Betty” Thompson Bunce

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Elizabeth “Betty” Thompson Bunce

April 25, 1915 – December 13, 2003

WHOI Geophysicist and first woman to go to sea on a WHOI research ship

The saddest day in my life was when I was very young and I was told I was a girl and there were things that boys could do which girls couldn’t. That meant I couldn’t be a sailor.

The saddest day did not change Elizabeth “Betty” Thompson Bunce’s desire or determination. A native of Mineola, NY, the woman who would be referred to later in life as the “flinty explorer of the ocean’s depths,” had her life and career path altered by a short weekend break in July 1944.

Bunce was a 1937 graduate of Smith College where she majored in physical education. Her interests lay in sports, government, and constitutional law. In 1939, she received her master’s degree in physical education from Smith and found herself teaching physical education at a New Jersey girls’ school where she also became involved in wartime efforts as an air raid warden, a WAVES physical instructor, and a student of armed forces advanced-rating courses.

Betty Bunce (second from right). (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
During a July 4, 1944 holiday to visit a friend who was working at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), Bunce made a life-altering decision. The friend worked on the third floor at WHOI, the “third floor” being an employees’ only area that was restricted to those with appropriate security clearance. The “third floor” was heavily involved in the wartime effort – it was where classified underwater explosive research was being conducted. Always curious and intrepid, Bunce truly wanted to see exactly what was happening on the “third floor.” She discovered that WHOI job applicants could potentially receive access to the “third floor.” Thus, Bunce filled out a job application and was pleasantly surprised to discover that she was one of a select few that was offered an interview. It appears that Bunce’s wartime coursework did the trick-she had participated in a rigorous crash course in electronics-spending three hours a night for eight weeks to complete it. Bunce was interviewed and offered a job – and got to see the “third floor.”

Teaching was no longer appealing to Bunce but she had to complete the fall semester as promised so she began her new job at WHOI on January 1, 1945. She found herself on the “third floor” working as a technician on air blast explosive experiments in the underwater explosive group. The name of the group was Navy 7 and was under the leadership of J. Bracket Hersey. In the 7, they studied different types of high explosives detonated in the air. The data collected was used for combat and the Manhattan Project-it determined at what altitude the bombs did the most damage and this was done, in part, photographically. While working on the project, Bunce did not know how the data would be used but when she discovered her work played a role in nuclear fission and the Manhattan Project after the bombings in Japan, she felt compelled to learn more.

Betty Bunce in main lab of R/V Bear. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)

Betty Bunce on the R/V Atlantis II looking at bathy-track chart atlas. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
After the war, Bunce returned to Smith College to earn her master’s degree in physics and mathematics. Degrees in hand, Bunce became an instructor in physics at Smith in 1949, returning to WHOI each summer. Unfortunately (or fortunately), Smith College eliminated her position due to policy changes and, learning of an open position at WHOI under J. Bracket Hersey, Bunce contacted him. She arrived back at WHOI in July 1951 as a Research Associate in Physics (1951-1964) and started testing out acoustic instruments. In 1956, she began a two-year seismic study with the Army Corps of Engineers and in 1959, she was made the Chief Scientist of her BEAR research cruise-the first American woman chief scientist for a major oceanographic expedition. Throughout her WHOI career she would serve on BEAR, as well as ASTERIAS, CHAIN, ATLANTIS II, and many others.

Betty Bunce and unidentified Man on the Glomar Challenger. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Bunce would serve as the chief scientist on many cruises throughout the 1960s and 1970. In 1964, Bunce was made Associate Scientist in Physics and Geophysics at WHOI, and then, in 1971, she was the first American chosen as a chief scientist-and the first woman to share chief scientist-on a deep sea drilling cruise on GLOMAR CHALLENGER. This Indian Ocean cruise laid the groundwork for the Joint Oceanographic Institutions for Deep Earth Sampling (JOIDES) and helped to prove the theory of plate tectonics and seafloor spreading. Bunce would travel around the world with WHOI and her studies of the Puerto Rican Trench-a fault line between North America and the Caribbean-would find her receiving the honor of having the deepest trench in the Atlantic named for her-The Bunce Fault-just before her death. In 1975, Bunce was made WHOI Senior Scientist and upon her retirement in 1980, Scientist Emeritus.

Betty Bunce and Ed Laine analyzing seismic data. (Photo by Vicky Cullen © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Betty Bunce had a remarkable career at WHOI. She authored or co-authored over twenty-five papers on marine geophysics and her research primarily focused on crustal structure, marine seismology, reflection and refraction, and underwater acoustics associated with seafloor studies. She was a member of Sigma Xi, the American Geophysical Union, the Seismological Society, the Society of Exploration Geophysics, and a fellow of the Geological Society of America and the American Association of Petroleum Geologists. She remained active in athletics throughout her life by participating and coaching and in 1995, WHOI honored her at its Second Women Pioneers in Oceanography.

Betty Bunce waits for a sediment core to come up, aboard R/V Chain circa 1958. One of the first woman oceanographers, Bunce (1915-2003) was kind and loyal as well as forthright and tough, according to those who knew her—and famous for using a punching bag on research cruises. A geophysicist interested in tectonics and seismic studies, she was the first WHOI female oceanographer to go to sea for more than a day, be chief scientist on a WHOI ship, or serve as Department Chair. She received the 1995 Women Pioneers in Oceanography Award, and geologist colleagues honored her by naming a deep-sea fault after her. (Photo courtesy of WHOI Archives © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Elizabeth Thompson Bunce was a woman of “firsts.” She was the first woman to dive on ALVIN (1965), the first western woman to lecture on marine geophysics at the International Union of Geology and Geophysics, the first woman to serve as a WHOI interim department chair in Geology and Geophysics, the first woman scientist to go to sea routinely, and the first woman chief scientist to go to sea routinely. She was a “world class straight talker,” and known as a jack-of-all-trades who brought a punching bag aboard ship to keep in shape. An avid rower, squash player, and birder, Bunce designed her own home and was even a contestant in the 1960s on “To Tell the Truth” where she fooled three of the four contestants-they could not identify her as an oceanographer.

As her good friend, and the wife of a colleague said, “Whatever she does, she attacks wholeheartedly . . . She has been extremely loyal to WHOI . . .” She is considered one of WHOI’s eminent scientists and was truly a pioneer who inspired, and continues to inspire, women in the sciences.

Betty Bunce began working for Navy 7 in the summer of 1944, when she was teaching in a private school. She later joined the geophysics group full time and in 1959 was the first WHOI woman to go to sea on an Institution vessel. She also served as chief scientist aboard a Bear cruise that year. This picture was taken in the Atlantis II main lab in 1977. (Photo by Vicky Cullen © Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
Jascin N. L Finger July 2022

TITLE: African Nutrition Leadership Programme (ANLP) 2027: Apply for the 10-Day Nutrition Leadership Development Programme in Africa

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Nutrition Leadership Programme (ANLP) is a leadership development initiative focused on strengthening nutrition leadership capacity across the African continent. Based at North-West University in South Africa, the programme works to develop the leadership abilities of early- and mid-career nutrition professionals and other stakeholders whose work contributes to improving nutrition and health outcomes in Africa. The ANLP has been successfully delivering its flagship 10-day Leadership Development Programme since 2002, bringing together professionals from a broad range of nutrition-related disciplines and sectors. Through an intensive leadership development experience, the programme aims to equip participants with the knowledge, skills, perspectives and leadership capabilities needed to contribute more effectively to nutrition programmes, policies, institutions and initiatives across Africa. Applications and further information are available for the 2027 ANLP programme.

About the African Nutrition Leadership Programme

The African Nutrition Leadership Programme was established around the goal of developing both individual and institutional leadership capacity in nutrition at different levels across Africa.

Nutrition challenges on the continent are complex and often require collaboration between professionals working in health, agriculture, education, policy, research, community development, government, international organisations and other sectors. Effective leadership is therefore an important part of developing and implementing sustainable nutrition solutions.

The ANLP seeks to respond to this need by providing leadership development opportunities for professionals who are already working in, or are closely connected to, the nutrition sector.

The programme is based at North-West University in South Africa and has a particular commitment to developing the leadership potential of early- and mid-career professionals.

What Is the ANLP 10-Day Leadership Development Programme?

The flagship ANLP programme is an intensive 10-day leadership development programme for individuals.

Since 2002, the programme has brought together participants from a wide variety of nutrition-related backgrounds. Rather than focusing exclusively on one profession or sector, the ANLP welcomes a multidisciplinary approach to nutrition leadership.

This creates an environment where participants can engage with people who approach nutrition challenges from different professional and institutional perspectives.

The programme is intended to strengthen participants’ leadership capacity so they can become more effective contributors within their organisations, professional networks and the wider nutrition community.

Who Participates in the African Nutrition Leadership Programme?

One of the notable features of the ANLP is the diversity of professional backgrounds represented among its participants.

According to the programme description, previous participants have come from a wide range of nutrition-related disciplines and sectors, including:

Government institutions

United Nations organisations

Civil society organisations

Academic institutions

The private sector

Individual consultants

Other nutrition-related professional fields and stakeholder groups

This multidisciplinary participation is important because nutrition is influenced by many interconnected areas, including health, food systems, agriculture, public policy, education, research and community development.

By bringing professionals from different sectors together, the programme provides an opportunity for participants to learn from different experiences and perspectives while developing their own leadership approaches.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The ANLP is particularly relevant to early- and mid-career nutrition professionals and related stakeholders working in Africa.

Potential applicants may include professionals whose work, research, programmes or institutional responsibilities are connected to nutrition or related areas.

The programme may be particularly valuable for individuals who:

Work in nutrition-related roles within government.

Work with United Nations agencies or other international organisations.

Work for civil society or non-governmental organisations involved in nutrition.

Are involved in nutrition-related academic or research activities.

Work in the private sector in areas connected to nutrition.

Work as independent consultants in nutrition or related fields.

Have responsibilities that require them to influence nutrition policies, programmes or initiatives.

Are developing their leadership capabilities as early- or mid-career professionals.

Want to strengthen their ability to lead, collaborate and contribute to nutrition-related initiatives across Africa.

Applicants should consult the official 2027 application information to confirm the specific eligibility and selection requirements applicable to the upcoming programme.

African Focus of the Programme

The African Nutrition Leadership Programme has a continent-wide focus.

Its purpose is not simply to develop individual professional skills but to contribute to broader leadership capacity within the African nutrition community.

The programme recognises that African countries face diverse nutrition challenges and that effective solutions require leadership that is responsive to local and regional realities.

By developing professionals from different African countries and professional environments, the ANLP contributes to a wider network of nutrition leaders who can apply their learning within their own organisations and communities.

Individual and Institutional Leadership Development

A key aspect of the ANLP is its focus on leadership at both the individual and institutional levels.

Individual leadership development can help professionals become more effective in their roles, communicate more effectively, work across professional boundaries and take greater responsibility for initiatives within their organisations.

At the institutional level, stronger leadership can help organisations improve how they plan, coordinate and implement nutrition-related activities.

The ANLP therefore goes beyond the idea of leadership as simply managing people. Its broader objective is to strengthen leadership capacity that can contribute to improved nutrition action across different levels of the African nutrition sector.

Tailor-Made Leadership and Functional Capacity Development

In addition to the 10-day programme for individual participants, the ANLP also offers tailor-made leadership and functional capacity development programmes.

These programmes are designed around the needs of particular stakeholders or institutions.

This means that the ANLP’s work extends beyond an individual training model. Organisations and stakeholders can potentially engage with the programme to address specific leadership and functional capacity development needs within their institutions.

The tailor-made approach allows capacity development to be connected more closely to an organisation’s particular circumstances, priorities and requirements.

Why Leadership Matters in Nutrition

Nutrition is a multidisciplinary field, and addressing nutrition challenges often requires cooperation among many different actors.

A nutrition professional may need to work with government officials, researchers, community organisations, international agencies, healthcare professionals, businesses and other stakeholders.

Leadership skills can therefore be important for:

Building effective partnerships.

Coordinating people and institutions.

Communicating ideas and priorities.

Influencing decision-making.

Managing complex programmes.

Supporting collaboration across sectors.

Responding to changing nutrition challenges.

Strengthening organisational capacity.

Contributing to evidence-informed policy and programmes.

The ANLP’s leadership-focused approach is intended to help professionals become better equipped to operate within this complex environment.

What Makes the ANLP Significant?

The programme has a substantial history of delivering leadership development opportunities for nutrition professionals.

The 10-day individual programme has been successfully hosted since 2002, meaning that the initiative has a long-standing presence in African nutrition leadership development.

Its multidisciplinary participant base is another important feature. Participants have historically represented government, the UN, civil society, academia, the private sector and consultancy.

This broad professional representation creates the potential for participants to gain perspectives beyond their immediate professional environments.

Application for the ANLP 2027 Programme

Individuals interested in participating in the 2027 African Nutrition Leadership Programme can access the application form provided by the programme.

Applicants should carefully review the application requirements and provide the requested information when completing the form.

Important Information for Prospective Applicants

Before applying, prospective participants should consider the following:

African connection: The ANLP is designed around developing nutrition leadership capacity across the African continent.

Multidisciplinary participation: Previous participants have represented government, the UN, civil society, academia, the private sector and consultancy.

Leadership focus: The programme is specifically concerned with leadership development rather than being solely a technical nutrition course.

Conclusion

The African Nutrition Leadership Programme (ANLP) provides an opportunity for nutrition professionals and related stakeholders across Africa to strengthen their leadership capacity and contribute more effectively to the development of nutrition initiatives on the continent. Based at North-West University in South Africa, the ANLP has been developing individual leadership capacity through its 10-day programme since 2002. Its participants have come from diverse professional environments, including government, the United Nations, civil society, academia, the private sector and consultancy. For early- and mid-career professionals seeking to strengthen their leadership abilities while engaging with a multidisciplinary African nutrition community, the 2027 ANLP programme represents an opportunity worth exploring.

TITLE: The Association of African Universities (AAU), in collaboration with the African Quality Assurance Network (AfriQAN) presents a Virtual workshop on Institutional Quality Assurance for Impact

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Date 29-30 April 2025 | Venue: ZOOM – http://bit.ly/4jrGnwX

Target audience

Quality Assurance Officers from universities, colleges, and other higher education institutions (HEIs), Directors/Heads of Quality Assurance Units, Higher Education Institution Leaders, National QA Agencies, Accreditation Bodies, Institutional Researchers, Monitoring & Evaluation Officers, Curriculum Developers and Academic Program Reviewers, Ministry of Education Officials / Policymakers Involved in national education policy and QA regulatory frameworks, Postgraduate Students and Researchers.

Registration link: http://bit.ly/4jrGnwX

Registration is FREE

General overview of the workshop

In an increasingly complex global landscape, there is a growing need for institutions to demonstrate their impact amid increasing worldwide demands for transparency and accountability. In higher education, Quality Assurance (QA) is essential not just for meeting standards but for driving broader outcomes like improved educational quality, institutional development, and societal progress. In sub-Saharan Africa, unique challenges and opportunities exist in aligning QA with meaningful impact. The upcoming workshop, “Institutional Quality Assurance for Impacts,” aims to provide participants with strategies, tools, and insights to strengthen QA processes and better measure, assess, and communicate institutional impacts across multiple dimensions.

Objectives

The primary objectives of the workshop are:

Enhance Understanding: To deepen participants’ understanding of institutional quality assurance and its role in driving impactful outcomes.

Tool and Strategy Development: To provide practical tools and methodologies for assessing and enhancing institutional impact through quality assurance.

Best Practices Sharing: To facilitate the exchange of best practices and experiences among institutions to strengthen quality assurance frameworks.

Action Plan Creation: To guide participants in developing actionable plans to implement or enhance quality assurance processes within their institutions for greater impact.

Workshop Structure

The workshop will be organized over two days, featuring a mix of keynote presentations, panel discussions, interactive sessions, and group activities.

Day 1: Introduction to Institutional Quality Assurance

Overview of quality assurance frameworks

The role of quality assurance in institutional effectiveness

Aligning quality assurance with institutional mission and goals

Defining and operationalizing “impact” within institutions

Day 2: Enhancing Quality Assurance for Greater Impact

Best practices in quality assurance for impact

Leveraging technology in quality assurance

Strategies for communicating impact to stakeholders

Tools and techniques for impact measurement

Methodology

The workshop will employ a mix of instructional methods to engage participants actively:

Lectures and Presentations: Delivered by experts in quality assurance and institutional development.

Interactive Discussions: Facilitated discussions to explore challenges and opportunities in institutional quality assurance.

Case Studies: Real-world examples to illustrate the successful implementation of quality assurance for impact.

Group Work and Exercises: Collaborative activities to apply learning to participants’ contexts.

Action Plan Development: Guided sessions for participants to develop tailored action plans for their institutions.

Expected Outcomes

By the end of the workshop, participants will:

Have a clear understanding of the importance of quality assurance in achieving institutional impact.

Be equipped with practical tools and methodologies to assess and enhance institutional impact.

Gain insights into best practices and successful strategies from other institutions.

Leave with a draft action plan to implement or improve quality assurance processes in their institutions.

TITLE: SUSTAIN Seminar 2026 in Slovakia: Fully Supported Rural Youth Leadership and Policy-Making Opportunity for Young Europeans

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The SUSTAIN Seminar 2026 is inviting motivated young people from across Europe to participate in an international learning and networking event focused on strengthening rural youth organisations, developing sustainable youth networks, and increasing the participation of rural communities in decision-making.

Organised by Rural Youth Europe (RYE) and the Rural Youth Parliament in Slovakia (VPMS), the SUSTAIN Seminar will take place from 8 to 13 November 2026 in Hokovce, Slovakia, with the main seminar programme running from 9 to 12 November.

The event will bring together 25 young people from across Europe for peer learning, organisational development, policy engagement, networking and practical planning. The activity forms part of the Rural Youth Forward project, which is co-funded by the Erasmus+ Programme of the European Union.

SUSTAIN Seminar 2026 Overview

The SUSTAIN Seminar is designed for young people who are actively involved in rural communities, youth organisations, youth work, farming, community initiatives or networks and who want to learn how to make such organisations more resilient, representative and influential.

Participants will examine the challenges faced by rural youth organisations and explore practical approaches to:

Strengthen organisational structures.

Improve leadership and governance.

Engage and retain volunteers.

Develop sustainable financing models.

Build partnerships.

Improve communication.

Encourage generational renewal.

Increase youth participation in policy-making.

Connect grassroots concerns with national and European decision-making processes.

The seminar will use a highly participatory approach, allowing participants to learn from one another while developing practical solutions that can be applied in their own communities and organisations.

What Is the SUSTAIN Seminar?

The SUSTAIN Seminar is an international seminar focused on sustaining and growing local and national rural youth organisations and networks and strengthening their European dimension.

Rural youth organisations play an important role in creating opportunities for young people to participate in their communities and make their voices heard in decision-making. However, many organisations face challenges such as dependence on short-term funding, limited volunteer capacity, informal organisational structures and difficulties transferring knowledge between generations.

The SUSTAIN Seminar seeks to address these challenges by helping participants understand what is required not only to establish rural youth organisations, but also to maintain and grow them over the long term.

The event will bring together 25 selected participants for several days of peer learning, organisational reflection and practical policy work.

About the Rural Youth Forward Project

The SUSTAIN Seminar is organised within the Rural Youth Forward project, which aims to cultivate resilient rural youth networks capable of contributing to more inclusive and participatory policy-making.

The project recognises that young people in rural areas need meaningful opportunities to influence decisions affecting their communities.

Through activities such as research, study visits, mentoring and seminars, the project seeks to strengthen the ability of rural youth organisations to:

Represent the interests of rural young people.

Develop sustainable organisational structures.

Participate in policy processes.

Build stronger networks.

Create meaningful opportunities for youth participation.

Contribute to local, national and European policy discussions.

What Will Participants Learn?

The SUSTAIN Seminar has been designed around practical organisational and policy challenges.

Participants will explore several important areas.

1. Organisational Sustainability

Participants will examine what makes a rural youth organisation healthy, resilient and capable of operating effectively over time.

Areas of discussion will include:

Organisational vision.

Governance.

Membership.

Programmes and services.

Feedback mechanisms.

Risk management.

Knowledge transfer.

Organisational development.

The aim is to help participants identify strengths and weaknesses within their own organisations or initiatives and develop practical approaches for improvement.

2. Leadership and Volunteer Engagement

Strong leadership is essential to maintaining youth organisations, particularly where organisations depend heavily on volunteers.

The seminar will explore sustainable approaches to:

Leadership development.

Volunteer engagement.

Generational renewal.

Knowledge sharing.

Organisational growth.

Building stronger teams.

Participants will have opportunities to exchange experiences and learn from the approaches used by other rural youth organisations across Europe.

3. Financing and Partnerships

Financial sustainability is another important issue for rural youth organisations.

Participants will examine approaches to:

Sustainable financing.

Partnership development.

Organisational growth.

Communication.

Building relationships with relevant stakeholders.

The seminar will encourage participants to think beyond short-term project funding and consider how organisations can develop stronger and more sustainable foundations.

4. European Union Youth Participation Tools

Participants will also learn about and explore European participation mechanisms that can help rural young people engage in policy-making.

These include:

Have Your Say.

The European Citizens’ Initiative.

Citizens’ panels.

Public consultations.

Petitions to the European Parliament.

These tools can provide avenues through which young people can move from identifying challenges in their communities to contributing to wider policy discussions.

5. Civic Dialogue

The programme will include a Civic Dialogue with European and national stakeholders.

The dialogue will be supported by Europe Direct and an invited Team Europe expert.

This component will give participants an opportunity to engage directly with stakeholders and better understand how youth perspectives can be brought into policy discussions.

6. European Parliament Simulation

Participants will take part in a simulation of the European Parliament.

Through this activity, participants will experience elements of policy negotiation and collaborative decision-making while working toward a shared Rural Youth Resolution.

This provides a practical way to understand how different perspectives can be brought together to develop common policy positions.

7. Organisational Action Plans

The seminar will not focus only on discussion and theory.

Participants will work on practical organisational action plans and recommendations that can contribute to the final policy paper of the Rural Youth Forward project.

This means participants will have the opportunity to translate what they learn during the seminar into concrete ideas and actions for their organisations and communities.

Learning Approach

The SUSTAIN Seminar will use an interactive and participatory learning model.

Rather than relying solely on traditional presentations, the programme will combine several learning methods, including:

Short expert inputs.

Peer-to-peer exchange.

Case studies.

Organisational self-assessment.

Workshop stations.

Civic Dialogue.

Policy simulation.

Collaborative drafting.

Group discussions.

Practical organisational planning.

Participants will therefore be expected to actively contribute their own experiences, knowledge, ideas and perspectives.

Key Project Resources

Participants will work with two important outputs from the Rural Youth Forward project:

Recommendations to Support Meaningful Youth Participation in Rural Areas

This resource provides recommendations intended to strengthen meaningful participation by young people in rural communities.

Quality Standards for Piloting and Mentorship Systems

Participants will also work with quality standards developed around piloting and mentorship systems.

During the seminar, participants will examine these resources in relation to their own organisational realities and explore how they can be transformed into practical next steps.

Who Can Apply?

The SUSTAIN Seminar is aimed at young people who have a connection to rural communities and rural youth development.

The organisers are particularly interested in applicants who fall into one or more of the following categories:

Active members of Rural Youth Europe member organisations or partner organisations.

Rural young people involved in local groups or community initiatives.

Young farmers.

Young people involved in emerging rural organisations.

Members of national rural youth networks.

Youth workers.

Youth leaders.

Youth practitioners.

People supporting rural youth through NGOs.

People involved in informal youth groups.

Individuals working with public institutions supporting rural youth.

Applicants may have experience or an interest in:

Youth work.

Education.

Rural development.

Youth participation.

Organisational sustainability.

Policy-making.

Community development.

Age Requirement

Applicants should be between 18 and 30 years old at the time of the seminar.

SUSTAIN Seminar 2026 Dates

The event will take place according to the following schedule:

Arrival: 8 November 2026

Main seminar programme: 9–12 November 2026

Departure: 13 November 2026

Overall dates, including travel: 8–13 November 2026

Location

The seminar will take place in:

Hokovce, Slovakia

Hokovce will serve as the setting for the international gathering of rural youth representatives, youth workers, leaders and practitioners from across Europe.

Travel, Accommodation and Meals

The organisers will provide substantial support for selected participants.

Accommodation

Shared accommodation will be covered by the organisers.

Meals

All meals will be covered from dinner on 8 November through breakfast on 13 November 2026.

Travel Reimbursement

Travel to and from Hokovce will be reimbursed in accordance with the project’s travel guidelines.

Further information regarding travel arrangements and accommodation will be provided to selected participants.

Participation Fee

There is no participation fee for the SUSTAIN Seminar.

Applicants should nevertheless wait until their participation has been officially confirmed before making travel or other arrangements.

How to Apply for the SUSTAIN Seminar 2026

Interested applicants must complete the official application form.

APPLY HERE

Application deadline: 25 September 2026.

Participation is by selection only, meaning that completing the application does not automatically guarantee a place at the seminar.

Selected applicants will receive a confirmation email following the selection process.

Applicants are specifically advised not to make travel arrangements or other commitments until their participation has been confirmed.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

25 September 2026

Applicants should ensure that their application is completed and submitted before the deadline.

Because participation is competitive and limited to only 25 participants, interested applicants are encouraged to prepare their applications early rather than waiting until the final day.

Important Information for Applicants

Before applying, prospective participants should make sure that they can satisfy the main participation requirements.

Applicants should be prepared to:

Demonstrate a connection to rural communities.

Show an interest or experience in rural youth work, community development, youth participation, organisational development or policy-making.

Participate in the entire programme from 8–13 November 2026.

Communicate and participate actively in English.

Share relevant experiences, practices or perspectives with other participants.

Demonstrate motivation to apply what they learn after the seminar.

Wait for official confirmation before making travel arrangements.

Why This Seminar Matters for Rural Youth

Rural young people often face challenges related to access to opportunities, participation in decision-making, organisational resources and representation.

Youth organisations can help address these challenges by creating structures through which young people can organise, communicate their concerns and participate in community and policy processes.

However, simply creating an organisation is not enough. Organisations need sustainable leadership, effective governance, committed volunteers, reliable partnerships and mechanisms for transferring knowledge between generations.

The SUSTAIN Seminar therefore focuses on the longer-term question of how rural youth organisations can remain effective, representative and influential.

By bringing together participants from different European countries, the seminar also creates an environment in which young people can compare experiences and identify solutions that may be adapted to their own local contexts.

Networking and International Exposure

One of the important aspects of the SUSTAIN Seminar is the opportunity to meet other young people working on rural youth issues across Europe.

Participants can exchange experiences with:

Rural youth leaders.

Young farmers.

Youth workers.

Community activists.

NGO representatives.

Youth practitioners.

Members of rural youth networks.

This international environment can encourage new partnerships, ideas and approaches to rural youth development.

Practical Outcomes for Participants

The seminar is designed to produce practical results rather than only providing theoretical knowledge.

Participants will have opportunities to develop:

Organisational action plans.

Recommendations.

Policy ideas.

New approaches to youth participation.

Strategies for organisational sustainability.

Ideas for volunteer engagement.

Approaches to partnership development.

Knowledge of European participation mechanisms.

Participants are also encouraged to use their learning and networks to support concrete actions after the seminar.

Organisers

The SUSTAIN Seminar is organised by:

Rural Youth Europe (RYE)

Rural Youth Parliament in Slovakia (VPMS)

The activity forms part of the Rural Youth Forward project and is co-funded by the European Union through EACEA under the Erasmus+ programme.

Important Disclaimer

The activity is part of the Rural Youth Forward project, co-funded by the European Union through EACEA. The views and opinions expressed by the organisers and participants are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the European Union or EACEA. Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.

Learn more about this opportunity HERE

Conclusion

The SUSTAIN Seminar 2026 in Hokovce, Slovakia offers a valuable opportunity for young people involved in rural communities and youth development to strengthen their organisational, leadership and policy-making skills.

With 25 participants from across Europe, the seminar will combine peer learning, practical workshops, organisational assessment, policy engagement, Civic Dialogue and a European Parliament simulation. Participants will also have the opportunity to develop practical action plans and contribute to recommendations for strengthening rural youth organisations.

The organisers will cover shared accommodation and meals, while travel will be reimbursed according to the project’s travel guidelines. There is also no participation fee, making the opportunity accessible to eligible young people who are committed to rural youth development.

Those interested should ensure they meet the age, country, rural-community connection, English-language and participation requirements and submit their application by the 25 September 2026 deadline.

TITLE: UNDP Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces Cohort 3: 7-Week Online Leadership and African Development Opportunity

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is inviting applications for Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3, a seven-week online learning and volunteer opportunity designed to help participants strengthen their leadership capacity and identify how they can contribute to achieving Agenda 2063: The Africa We Want.

The programme provides participants with practical tools to move beyond simply understanding Agenda 2063 and instead identify the influence, opportunities and responsibilities they have within their own “Power Spaces” — including governments, businesses, universities, communities, schools, development organizations, families and professional networks.

The opportunity is conducted entirely online and requires approximately 11–15 hours per week.

About the Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces Programme

Agenda 2063 represents Africa’s long-term development vision and focuses on building The Africa We Want. However, achieving this vision requires more than awareness of continental development frameworks.

The UNDP-led programme focuses on helping participants recognize that meaningful transformation can take place through the everyday environments where people make decisions, influence others, and create value.

These environments are referred to as “Power Spaces.”

The programme therefore encourages participants to ask:

What contribution can I make to Africa’s transformation?

What future am I committed to creating?

What needs to change to achieve that future?

What leadership values do I need?

What actions should I consistently take?

What would success look like?

How can I continue improving after the programme?

What Participants Will Learn

During the seven-week journey, participants will develop seven practical leadership tools:

1. Contribution Statement

Participants identify the value they currently create through their Power Space and consider how their work, activities or influence can contribute to Africa’s transformation.

2. Moonshot

Participants define an ambitious and meaningful future they are committed to helping create rather than simply accepting current circumstances.

3. Delivery

Participants identify the important changes required to move from their current situation toward their desired future.

4. Leadership Values

Participants explore the values they need to guide important decisions and actions throughout their leadership journey.

5. Leadership Routines

Participants translate their intentions into practical and repeatable behaviours that can gradually produce meaningful results.

6. Letter from the Future

Participants imagine their desired future as if it has already been achieved and use that perspective to reconsider the choices they are making today.

7. Future Review

Participants learn a continuous improvement approach based on:

Return → Review → Revise → Recommit

This enables them to continue using the programme’s leadership tools after the formal seven-week experience has ended.

What Will Online Volunteers Do?

Selected Online Volunteers will participate in the learning experience while also supporting the delivery and improvement of the cohort.

Their responsibilities will include:

Studying the Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces Reader and related learning materials.

Supporting participant engagement throughout the seven-week programme.

Becoming familiar with weekly concepts, questions and exercises.

Participating in small-group learning conversations where assigned.

Helping participants connect the leadership tools to their own Power Spaces and circumstances.

Providing constructive and concise feedback.

Contributing to the end-of-cohort review.

Identifying what worked well and suggesting areas that could improve future cohorts.

Importantly, applicants do not need to be experts on every aspect of Agenda 2063. The programme emphasizes curiosity, disciplined engagement with the provided materials and the willingness to help others apply the concepts to their own contexts.

Programme Format and Time Commitment

This is a fully online opportunity, meaning volunteers can participate remotely.

Duration: 7 weeks
Modality: Online
Time commitment: 11–15 hours per week
Host organization: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
Assignment country: Ethiopia
Sustainable Development Goal: SDG 17 – Partnerships for the Goals
Recruitment: Competitive

The assignment focuses on learning, participant engagement, leadership development and contributing to the improvement of future cohorts.

Who Should Apply?

The opportunity is particularly suitable for people who have a strong interest in areas such as:

Agenda 2063 and Africa’s development

Leadership and development practice

Public policy

Business and entrepreneurship

Education

Community development

Social impact

African transformation

Applicants may come from different professional and educational backgrounds. The programme specifically welcomes:

Professionals

Development practitioners

Researchers

Entrepreneurs

Educators

Students

Community leaders

Applicants should also demonstrate strong written and interpersonal communication skills and the ability to engage critically with learning materials.

Required Skills and Experience

Candidates should demonstrate:

Strong interest in African development and Agenda 2063 or related areas.

Critical reading skills and the ability to engage meaningfully with learning materials.

Strong written and interpersonal communication skills.

Ability to provide concise and constructive feedback.

Commitment to completing the assignment throughout the seven-week Cohort 3 period.

Language Requirement

English: Fluent level is desirable.

Important Application Information

The recruitment is competitive, and applicants should be prepared to commit to the full duration of the assignment.

Application deadline: 4 September 2026 at 03:00.

The programme is expected to run for seven weeks, with participants working remotely and contributing approximately 11–15 hours per week.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Why This Opportunity Is Valuable

The Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces programme can provide participants with an opportunity to:

Develop practical leadership skills.

Better understand their potential contribution to Africa’s long-term development.

Connect personal leadership with Agenda 2063.

Strengthen communication and collaboration skills.

Learn how to turn ideas into practical action.

Engage with people working across different sectors and Power Spaces.

Develop a personal leadership portfolio and future-oriented leadership practice.

Contribute feedback that can help improve future cohorts.

The programme is particularly relevant for individuals who want to connect their career, community involvement, education, entrepreneurship or professional influence with broader African development goals.

Conclusion

The UNDP Agenda 2063 in Power Spaces – Cohort 3 offers a structured seven-week online leadership journey for individuals interested in contributing to Africa’s transformation. Rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge of Agenda 2063, the programme encourages participants to identify their own areas of influence and develop practical ways to create value within them.

With a commitment of 11–15 hours per week and a deadline of 4 September 2026, interested applicants should review the requirements carefully and submit their applications before the recruitment period closes.

TITLE: Global Studies University UAE Admissions 2027: MA and PhD Programs, Scholarships, Fees, Eligibility and Deadlines

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are open for the Fall 2027 graduate intake at Global Studies University in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates. Prospective students can apply for the two-year Master of Arts in Global African Studies or the five-year Doctor of Philosophy in Global Studies. The university also offers shorter certificate courses in Arabic, Amharic, Hausa and Kiswahili, with a separate Fall 2026 registration schedule.

Global Studies University, commonly abbreviated as GSU, presents an unusual academic proposition: postgraduate education designed around Africa, its global connections and the movement of ideas, people, cultures and institutions across regions. Rather than treating history, politics, culture, diplomacy, literature, heritage and language as isolated fields, GSU brings them together through interdisciplinary teaching and research.

The Fall 2027 degree application deadline is Tuesday, October 27, 2026. Applications opened on Monday, August 3, 2026. The first 40 applicants who submit complete applications for either graduate program are eligible for an application-fee waiver worth AED 365, according to the respective program pages. Applicants should therefore prepare and submit all required documents as early as possible.

For learners interested in a shorter language course, registration for the Fall 2026 Arabic, Amharic, Hausa and Kiswahili certificates has been extended to September 13, 2026, subject to available places. Classes run from September 14 to December 17, 2026.

This guide explains the programs, specializations, curriculum, admission requirements, English-language standards, tuition fees, scholarship support, application process, campus experience and important deadlines. Applicants should confirm the latest details through the official Global Studies University academic programs page before submitting an application.
