TITLE: 2026-2027 Fulbright Specialist Program for Indian Institutions

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Program Description

The Fulbright Specialist Program offers Indian universities and institutions of higher education a valuable opportunity to engage with U.S. scholars and professionals, fostering meaningful collaboration and institutional partnerships with American counterparts.

Specialist grants focus on strengthening and supporting the development needs of institutions and broadening institutional cooperation. Fulbright Specialists work in their areas of expertise as they enhance their understanding of the cultural and educational contexts of the host country through engagement with the host community.

Eligible Institutions

Host institutions should be involved in university-level teaching or training, the expansion of partnerships between universities and specialized institutions, and the promotion of international and cross-institutional cooperation.

According to Government of India regulations, Fulbright scholars must be affiliated with recognized institutions of higher education approved by the Indian Ministry of Education, including institutions accredited by the UGC, AICTE, or other apex regulatory bodies, as well as medical institutions accredited by the relevant authorities.

Possible Fulbright Specialist Activities

The Fulbright Specialist Program encourages host institutions to tailor projects to their own needs. However, all projects should have an education or training focus. Due to the short-term nature of the exchange, projects should have concrete objectives that can be achieved over the course of the Specialist’s visit. Past Specialists have supported host institutions by conducting activities such as:

Delivering seminars or workshops

Consulting on faculty or workforce development

Developing academic or training curricula and materials

Lecturing at the graduate or undergraduate level

Conducting needs assessments or evaluations for a program or institution

Note: Personal research projects, including clinical medical research or projects involving patient contact, are not eligible for funding under the Fulbright Specialist Program.

Grant Length

The length of a Fulbright Specialist project must be a minimum of 14 days and a maximum of 42 days, including travel days and weekends.

Program Costs

Fulbright and the host institution share costs for Fulbright Specialist grants. Fulbright covers international airfare and an honorarium for the Specialist. The host institution is responsible for the cost of housing, meals, and any necessary, program- related, in-country transportation. In-country costs may be supplied by the host institution as in-kind services and/or funds paid directly to the specialist. Note that in-country transportation refers to transportation once the Specialist has arrived in the city of the activity, and not to flights taken as part of the international travel.

Eligible Fields

Eligible fields include: Agriculture • American (U.S.) Studies • Anthropology • Archaeology • Biology Education • Business Administration • Chemistry Education • Communications and Journalism • Computer Science and Information Technology • Economics • Education • Engineering Education • Environmental Science • Law • Library Science • Math Education • Peace and Conflict Resolution Studies • Physics Education • Political Science • Public Administration • Public/Global Health • Social Work • Sociology • Urban Planning.

Download sub-disciplines in each eligible field.

Priority Areas for 2026-27: In addition to the above-mentioned eligible fields, projects in the following areas will be prioritized:

Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Business, entrepreneurship, management, and supply chains

Cybersecurity and IT

Disaster response

STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics)

Free speech and open debate

Energy security and critical minerals; and

Cultural heritage (preservation, anti-trafficking, and enforcement).

Celebrating the United States’ 250th Anniversary of Independence

All projects must include a component celebrating the 250th anniversary of the United States (Freedom 250). Institutions may participate as follows:

A. Submit a project request focused on a Freedom 250 topic. This may include, but is not limited to, the following:

American Studies, including American society and values and American cultural traditions

American History, including the Declaration of Independence, Constitutional studies, federalism, military history, local/regional history, etc.

American values, including freedom of speech and open debate

Cultural heritage preservation and archival research on topics of American interest

Political Science, such as an introduction to U.S. government and American political thought

Military and strategic studies

Law, including constitutional law

Philosophy, including founding-era political thought, and civic virtue

Religious Studies, including religious freedom, religious liberty and founding

Education, specifically teaching of American history, civics, etc

Public Policy/Leadership Studies, including U.S. foreign policy and American global leadership

American business and economics

B. Add Freedom 250 programming by including some type of community engagement activities that celebrate America. Examples of such activities could include, but are not limited to:

Delivering a lecture on American excellence in, or contributions to, the Specialist’s field of study.

Hosting an event highlighting the United States or key themes from its 250-year history.

Conducting outreach activities at local schools, organizations, or community groups to share information about America.

Requesting a U.S. Scholar

Specialists, who represent a wide range of professional and academic disciplines, are competitively selected to join the Fulbright Specialist Roster based on their knowledge, skill sets, and ability to make a significant contribution to projects overseas. Those individuals that have been approved to join the Fulbright Specialist Roster are then eligible to be matched with approved projects designed by host institutions. Host institutions have the following options for requesting a U.S. scholar:

Roster Named Requests identify Specialists already on the Roster in the project application. The host institution and the Specialist have been in contact and mutually agreeable project dates and goals are included in the project application.

Named Requests identify an individual that is not on the Roster, but specifically requested by the host institution. The host institution and the Specialist candidate have been in contact and mutually agreeable project dates and goals are included in the project application. A candidate may apply to the Roster before a project application is submitted, but will need to be peer reviewed and approved. Candidates not on the Roster who are in contact with host institutions are strongly encouraged to immediately apply to the Roster by visiting the following link: : https://world-learning-npsp.my.site.com/FSP/

Open Requests do not identify a candidate in the project proposal. USIEF and World Learning will assist with identifying an individual with suitable technical or professional experience that is approved by the host institution.

Also refer to: https://fulbrightspecialist.worldlearning.org/eligibility-foreign-institutions.

IMPORTANT – India Specific Guidelines for Submitting Applications

Please read the following guidelines carefully before proceeding further.

Applications requesting multiple visits for specialists will not be approved. Therefore, please do not select this option when submitting the form.

No more than one application in a field from an institution should be submitted.

Funding is not available to cover any part of the local hospitality expense on behalf of the host institution. Local hospitality (housing, meals, local transportation, and program-related in-country travel) must be borne by host institutions. Therefore, please do not select options that will make your application ineligible.

Grants are limited. Preference will be given to institutes/university departments that have not hosted a Fulbright Specialist in the last three years.

All selected applicants will be notified of the result by August 2026.

Processing of the selected applications typically takes 4-5 months after the deadline. Grant dates should be between January 1 and September 30, 2027.

Application Procedure

Interested institutions may download the Host Institution Project Proposal (Application) Template. This document includes all questions that host institutions must complete when they submit the required online application through the Fulbright Specialist Program Portal (FSP). This document would be helpful in reviewing all of the required information before submitting the online application.

Applications must be submitted online through FSP Portal – https://world-learning-npsp.my.site.com/FSPHost/

Note: Project proposals submitted via post/courier or email as a Word or PDF attachment will not be accepted. All project proposals must be submitted online through the FSP Portal only.

Last date of submission of application on the portal is May 31, 2026

For any query, please write to Dr. Girish Kaul at girish@usief.org.in.

TITLE: CTP-LI Travel Guidelines

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Guidelines for Travel for Postdocs & Students in the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)

Update for September 2026
Hi. Here are some guidelines to follow when booking travel for submitting receipts for reimbursement. We have limited time to process the many requests for we receive so please review and follow the rules/guidance below.

For students only—weeks before traveling, you must turn in a travel request form to request CTP-LI funds to Scott Morley (6-307) for your proposed trip. Scott has the form. You will need your advisors sign-off on the form. The form will then be reviewed and signed off on. Graduate students can take one trip per year, after their first year, and receive up to $500 for a domestic trip and up to $1000 for an international trip. You should request of your advisor additional funds if you incur additional costs on your trip. It is at their discretion if they will cover it. All such travel must be endorsed by the student’s research supervisor, who is responsible for making certain that the school, conference or workshop is relevant to the student’s research program.

If you are in your first year, travel needs the approval of a faculty member the student has started doing research with and the Director.

Once a year, the Director will ask for requests for travel funds a program to provide modest ancillary funding amounts to CTP-LI graduate students for needs and initiatives that are not already funded through other sources. Each year, subject to continued availability of funding, we provide several grants for amounts in the range of $10 – $1000 for purposes such as conference travel beyond that already supported, books, inviting visitors that complement graduate student needs (please confirm we have space for them before inviting), etc.

A reminder to all that you need to register your international trips if that trip was paid for or will be reimbursed by MIT funds. You can do this at the Travel Registry site.

For postdocs only—Your budget for the year is the one in your offer letter. If you have additional expenses that extend beyond that level, you should work out with your advisor in advance to see if they can cover your additional costs. If so, that should be relayed to Scott Morley.

For Postdocs and Students–
1. In the email for reimbursement
All requests must contain the following: where you went (conference name, workshop name, collaborative visit with X, etc.) and the dates of your travel. The email must also have an itemized list of the costs you are seeking reimbursement for.

Example:
Attended: Fantastic Conference 2026. Paris, France.
Dates of Travel: September 1 – September 5, 2026
Request for Reimbursement:
Air. Boston-Paris Roundtrip. Delta. $600.
Conference Fee: $300
Lodging not covered by Conference Organizers: $500.
Uber: $40 (receipt not needed it under $70)
Taxi: $35 receipt not needed it under $70)
Etc.
Request for reimbursement without the above will be returned.

Note: If a foreign trip, no need to convert Euros, etc. MIT has a daily currency calculator for when we process each travel report.

REMEMBER: get your requests for approved reimbursements right away when you return from your trip. MIT mandates travel be submitted within 60 days of the conclusion of the trip. Not doing that means they will not reimburse.

Send the email to Charles Suggs (csuggs@mit.edu) and cc morley@mit.edu

2. Each item needing reimbursement needs its own pdf. Do not group them into one pdf. Receipts grouped in one pdf will be returned to you.

3. Air travel
Receipts for air travel. A receipt is one that shows the flights, the airline, the class of flight (coach or economy only unless you pay for the difference yourself and show what the difference between business and coach/economy is), and delineation of all costs, including if you incurred a baggage fee you seek reimbursement for.

ALL travel conducted where you are seeking reimbursement from a Federal grant account (most of our travel is paid that way) MUST utilize US Air Carriers when flying over an ocean (Atlantic, Pacific, etc.) AND when flying to Canada or Mexico. You can book on a US carrier and fly on a non-US carrier partner as a code share.

If you are making a side trip within a region (Amsterdam to Vienna, for example) you may use a non-US carrier for that leg of the trip if that is more convenient and/or cost effective.

Some travel is paid on non-Federal money and if that is the case (check in advance), non-US carriers can be used in those circumstances for convenience/lower cost.

Do not use Orbitz, Priceline, etc. !! They do not provide enough info for the Travel office to okay for reimbursement. If Travel will not put through, we cannot reimburse you!!

Special Note on Air Travel: If you are traveling to place X for a research trip but also say going to place Y for a week’s vacation after, you must when booking your air source and also save for when you turn in your receipts a sample fare would have been from Boston to X to Boston for the dates of the conference. as if that was the sole activity you were doing. Travel accounting requires these comparisons to make a determination of fair reimbursement for the conference travel itself.

4. Train, taxi, Uber/Lyft and subway travel
We need pdf scans of the tickets or rideshare receipts. Train receipts should have to, from and a breakdown of the total cost.

5. Hotel reimbursements
If you are seeking lodging reimbursements, we need the bill from the hotel, etc. As with air bookings, Orbitz, Priceline, etc email receipts are not acceptable to MIT’s Travel Office.

Hotel bills need to have the hotel name and location, dates of your stay, the itemized cost per night, the name of the person staying and total amount paid.

6. Conference fee reimbursements
If you are seeking reimbursement for a conference fee, we need a receipt that states the amount, the name of the conference and the dates of the conference.

TITLE: Invitation to  Participate – AAU Organised Capacity Building Workshop for Registrars and Administrators

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
In line with the Association of African Universities’ (AAU) commitment to enhancing the wide array of benefits available to its members, the AAU is organizing a workshop for Registrars and Administrators of its member Universities. The AAU is therefore inviting institutions of higher learning to nominate staff to participate in this high-level executive training. The participation fee and accommodation costs are covered (by the AAU) for one participant from each member university in good standing, i.e – institutions who are up to date with their subscriptions (not universities with two years deficits), provided that the institution is also paying for the participation of at least one other participant. The workshop is holding as part of activities to mark the 2023 Africa Universities’ Day (weeklong) celebrations. This year, the AAU is turning 56 years.

REGISTRATION LINK: https://forms.office.com/r/F7Sy3FSH7v

CONTACT DETAILS: elaari@aau.org and membership@aau.org

VENUE: AAU Secretariat, Accra, Ghana

DATES: The workshop dates are 7th& 8th November , 2023. However, attendees are invited to participate in the main Africa Universities’ Day Celebration, holding on 9th November on the theme – Artificial Intelligence in African Higher Education.

WORKSHOP FEES: AAU will sponsor one participant from each of its member universities in good standing (up to date with payment of their subscription fees), provided that the institution is also paying for the participation of at least one other participant. The sponsorship package covers the following costs: Tea/Coffee Breaks, Lunch + Refreshments, Certificates, Workshop Training Materials, and Local Transport. Accommodation will also be provided for sponsored participants on the following three days only – November 6, 2023 (arrival) and November 7-8, 2023 (Workshop Days). Participating Higher Education Institutions are to contribute to this capacity building initiative by covering the air tickets and other related costs to facilitate effective participation of delegates.

Member Universities with additional attendees/participants will be charged a fee of US $400.00 per participant. Similarly, Non-Members of the AAU are invited to participate at a fee of US $700.00. Participants in these two categories are responsible for their accommodation as well as air tickets.

COORDINATOR: Ms. Edith Laari (Membership Officer)

BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

For every Higher Education Institution (HEI), the registrar’s office is the axis on which every activity spins and the hub of staff, students and alumni’s data. Due to the vital role of the Registrar’s office in ensuring administrative excellence and students’ academic success, the registrar, who is one of the principal officers, should see himself/herself as a peer of academics and a partner in the delivery of educational programs. As the steward of the academic record and the keeper of institutional data, the registrar is in a unique role at the institution, since institutions require accurate and current data to drive their initiatives forward. The registrar, who sits at the crossroads between student service and academic programming, is distinctly suited to use the data at hand to help shape discussions and decisions in the context of desired educational outcomes for the institution and students alike.

While serving and advancing higher education by safeguarding the academic integrity of the institution, there are broad professional principles of good practice, management, and conduct that should be followed. When these principles are not being followed, those served by the registrar’s office, majority of whom are students, are the ones that bear the consequences of a disengaged office. The registrar must be current, consistent and professional to ensure the integrity of degrees and maintain the ability to accurately advise students about degree requirements and other administrative requirements. Continuous professional development is central to enabling the registrar perform at optimal level for the overall benefit of his/her institution. It is against this backdrop that the Association of African Universities (AAU) is organizing a capacity building workshop for university registrars and administrators in universities and colleges in Africa. The workshop addresses one of AAU’s strategic goals of strengthening the delivery capacity of HEIs through enhanced leadership and management capacity development.

OBJECTIVES AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES

The overall goal of this workshop is to enhance the capacity of the African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) Registrars and Administrators to deliver as custodians of records in HEIs in Africa. The expected outcomes include:

Improved knowledge about staff and students’ records management and processes of records retention, disposal, transcript guide and records archiving.

Improved knowledge of innovative approaches to staff and student recruitment, admission, registration and

Enhanced awareness of the examination management processes and best practices

Improved knowledge of how to organise effective online support services for students

MODULES FOR THE WORKSHOP

The modules for the AAU-organised capacity building workshop for university registrars and administrators include:

MODULE 1: PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT OF REGISTRARS

This module is intended to set the grounds for personal assessment of the participants, identify areas where improvement is needed, and set goals for the future. The module also introduces registrars and administrators to the fundamental principles of good practices in their field. It offers insights into industry standards, ethical considerations, and best practices that should guide their roles and responsibilities. Module 1 fosters a transformative journey, equipping participants with the tools for professional development while nurturing a deeper understanding of their potential within academia. It lays the groundwork for subsequent workshop modules, ensuring that registrars and administrators are better prepared to excel in their crucial roles at their respective universities.

MODULE 2: MANAGEMENT OF STAFF RECRUITMENT/HIRING, SUSPENSIONS, TERMINATIONS & RETIREMENTS

This module delves into the critical and multifaceted aspects of managing personnel within higher education institutions. It is designed to equip university registrars and administrators with the knowledge and skills necessary to handle various personnel-related processes effectively and efficiently. Good practices in the documentation and handling of information related to the above will also be tackled. Module 2 seeks to promote the adoption of efficient processes, ethical standards, and best practices, ultimately contributing to a well-structured and harmonious work environment within African HEIs.

MODULE 3: MANAGING STUDENT RECRUITMENT/ADMISSION, REGISTRATION AND DISPLACEMENT

This module looks at good practices in students’ enrolment, administration and registration. It considers responsibilities, ranging from registration and academic scheduling to detecting credentials’ fraud. The module also explores how students, who are displaced by acts of violence, natural disasters, sexual assault, financial displacement, school closings, pandemic outbreaks, and military intervention, can be integrated back into the system for smooth academic operation and to ensure the academic success of such students.

MODULE 4: STAFF & STUDENTS’ RECORDS MANAGEMENT: RETENTION, TRANSCRIPT GUIDE, DISPOSAL AND ARCHIVING

This session will involve sharing of best practices in records management and will provide guidance for developing or revising institutional records retention and disposition schedules. The session will further provide recommendations to assist college and university personnel with the challenging decisions surrounding records management and provide a comprehensive set of best practice recommendations to develop and modify student records management policy, practice, and the application of technology. Specifically, the session will provide an overview of the complex issues facing student records managers today, how registrars can develop or modify their own records retention and disposition schedule. The session will also provide some examples from specific institutions by type, state guidelines, accrediting body guidelines, and other samples for special categories of records. Finally, the session will address the myriad of security considerations around student records management.

MODULE 5: EXAMINATION MANAGEMENT

This module aims to empower participants with the expertise and competencies required to navigate the multifaceted landscape of examination management. It will effectively focus on the processes of organising university examinations to ensure its smooth running and avoidance of timetable clashes. By emphasizing the maintenance of examination integrity, efficiency, and best practices, the session will also explore the roles of examination managers which include the prevention and detection of examination fraud.

MODULE 6: STUDENT ONLINE SERVICES

This module will serve as a catalyst for empowering participants with the knowledge and strategies required to create and manage dynamic online systems that provide robust support services to students. By embracing technology in this manner, universities can enhance the overall student experience, fostering a climate of accessibility, engagement, and academic excellence within their institutions.

METHODOLOGY

The workshop has adopted a strategic methodology which will include effective approaches, such as the use of case studies, focused group discussions, experiential learning (case studies from universities in the various regions in Africa), presentations and sharing of ideas, knowledge and skills. The workshop will develop a strategy of follow- up to ensure that university registrars are implementing the good practices to be learned from the workshop at their various institutions of higher learning. The participants will have the opportunity to engage in dialogues with peers on the various challenges at their universities and map out strategies to overcome them. A post workshop report will be compiled, and recommendations made will be integrated into improving subsequent workshops.

Registrars

Enrolment Managers

Provosts

Deans and Faculty

Academic Advisors

Staff of the Registry

Examination Managers and

All stakeholders interested in learning

A BRIEF BACKGROUND OF THE AAU

The Association of African Universities (AAU) founded in 1967 with an initial membership of 34 universities, currently has more than 400 member institutions spread across 46 African countries. The Association represents the voice of higher education in Africa and draws its membership from all five sub-regions of Africa and operates in four official languages, namely English, French, Portuguese and Arabic. The Association’s mandate as an apex organization for higher education in Africa is to promote cooperation, academic linkages and exchange of information on higher education issues across the continent. The mandate further extends to support members in their core functions of teaching, learning, knowledge generation and its dissemination through fundamental and applied research and community engagement. The AAU also plays a key role in setting up dialogue platforms, advocacy and raising awareness for and about the major needs of African higher education institutions and coordinates the means by which these needs are met. The Association also acts as a catalyst for increased networking between and among its members and the wider African and international higher education academic community. In pursuit of its mandate, AAU coordinates and facilitates one of the World Bank’s biggest Education Projects; the Africa Higher Education Centres of Excellence (ACE) Project. The AAU also serves as the Coordinator for the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA), among other high-profile projects and initiatives. The AAU frequently identifies areas where member institutions require capacity building through its training programmes that are tailor-made to address such needs.

Guiding Ethical Authorship in Collaborative Research

Authorship is more than a name on a publication: it signifies intellectual contribution, responsibility, and accountability. It encompasses the creation of ideas, the writing process, and the ethical principles that ensure transparency and fairness in collaborative research. Beyond recognition, authorship carries legal implications through intellectual property rights (IPR), granting authors control over the reproduction, distribution, and use of their work. It also serves as a safeguard against plagiarism and unauthorized use.

Recurring challenges observed across multiple EU-funded projects have highlighted the need for clear, practical guidance on authorship. This document responds to that need. Drawing on established frameworks such as the Horizon Europe Programme, the Annotated Grant Agreement, and the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, it consolidates key legal provisions, ethical standards, and best practices. Its purpose is to help research teams:

Understand the legal and ethical dimensions of authorship;

Apply consistent criteria for identifying authors and contributors;

Prevent disputes through transparent agreements;

Ensure fair recognition of all contributions.

While this guideline does not aim to be exhaustive, it provides a practical reference for navigating authorship in interdisciplinary and international collaborations. By promoting clarity and integrity, it supports the values of responsible research and strengthens trust among partners.

TITLE: Co-operatives UK Youth Advisory Group 2026: Paid Opportunity for Young People Aged 16–30 to Shape the Future of the Co-operative Movement

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Co-operatives UK Youth Advisory Group 2026, a paid youth participation opportunity for young people aged 16 to 30 who want to help influence the future of the co-operative movement, strengthen youth participation, and contribute ideas on how co-operative values can respond to some of the challenges facing younger generations.

Established in 2024, the Youth Advisory Group, commonly referred to as the YAG, brings together young people from different backgrounds to provide strategic input into the work of Co-operatives UK and to develop independent projects designed to increase engagement among young people both within the co-operative movement and across wider society.

Importantly, applicants do not need to have previous experience with co-operatives. Applications are welcomed from young people already involved in co-operative organizations as well as those who are completely new to the movement.

Members of the Youth Advisory Group are paid for their time, reflecting both the commitment expected from participants and Co-operatives UK’s intention to reduce barriers that could otherwise prevent young people from participating.

Applications may be submitted in several formats. Candidates can respond through:

Written text

Video

Audio

The application process is designed to be accessible to people with different levels of experience and different communication styles.

Applications close at:

23:59 on Sunday, 6 September 2026.

Applicants must complete the official application form and send it to:

youth@uk.coop

About Co-operatives UK

Co-operatives UK is an organization representing and supporting the co-operative movement.

Co-operatives are organizations or businesses owned and controlled by their members rather than primarily by outside investors. Depending on the type of co-operative, members may include:

Workers

Consumers

Residents

Community members

Producers

Businesses

Other stakeholders

The broader co-operative movement is based on ideas such as:

Democratic participation

Shared ownership

Fairness

Community

Mutual support

Collective decision-making

Economic participation

Social responsibility

Co-operatives UK’s Youth Advisory Group is intended to ensure that younger people have a meaningful role in conversations about how these ideas should develop in the future.

What Is the Co-operatives UK Youth Advisory Group?

The Youth Advisory Group is a group of young people aged 16–30 who work with Co-operatives UK to bring youth perspectives into the organization’s work.

The group was established in:

2024

It was launched through Co-operatives UK’s National Youth Summit as part of the organization’s strategic commitment to:

Empowering young people.

The group has two broad functions:

Providing strategic advice and youth perspectives to Co-operatives UK.

Developing or supporting projects that increase young people’s participation in the co-operative movement.

The YAG is therefore more than a discussion forum.

Members are expected to contribute ideas, challenge assumptions, advocate for youth participation, and help connect co-operative principles with the priorities and experiences of younger generations.

Why the Youth Advisory Group Was Created

Co-operatives UK recognizes that young people face significant uncertainty in areas such as:

Employment

Economic security

Climate change

Community resilience

Housing

Business models

Social inequality

Participation in decision-making

At the same time, many young people may know relatively little about co-operatives and the alternative approaches they can provide to ownership, work, business, and community action.

The Youth Advisory Group was therefore created to help bridge this gap.

Its members can help Co-operatives UK understand:

What young people care about

What prevents young people from engaging with co-operatives

How co-operative ideas can be communicated more effectively

What types of opportunities would interest younger generations

How the movement can become more accessible and relevant

The Role of Youth Advisory Group Members

The official description of the Youth Advisory Group organizes its work around two major areas:

Advise and enrich

Advocate and engage

1. Advise and Enrich

Young people can bring perspectives that established organizations may not otherwise hear.

Youth Advisory Group members are therefore expected to help Co-operatives UK:

Understand younger generations

Generate new ideas

Challenge established ways of thinking

Improve youth participation

Make decisions that better reflect young people’s needs

Include youth perspectives in organizational discussions

The group provides strategic input into Co-operatives UK’s work.

This means members may be asked to comment on ideas, priorities, activities, communication, or wider questions affecting the co-operative movement.

Bringing New Perspectives

A central purpose of the YAG is to ensure that young people are not merely discussed as an audience but are included in conversations about the future of the movement.

Young members may bring perspectives shaped by:

Education

Employment

Entrepreneurship

Climate concerns

Community involvement

Social movements

Digital culture

Youth networks

Cost-of-living pressures

Changing expectations about work and business

These experiences can help established organizations identify blind spots and reconsider traditional approaches.

Championing Youth Voice

Youth Advisory Group members work alongside Co-operatives UK to:

Champion the youth voice.

This means advocating for young people to be meaningfully involved in the co-operative movement rather than included only symbolically.

Participants can help promote:

Youth participation

Youth leadership

Intergenerational collaboration

Representation

Accessible opportunities

New ways of engaging younger audiences

The group therefore serves as both an advisory mechanism and a platform for youth representation.

2. Advocate and Engage

The second major role of the Youth Advisory Group is advocacy.

Co-operatives UK notes that younger generations are facing an uncertain future, including challenges related to:

Climate anxiety

Job insecurity

Economic pressures

The organization believes that co-operative approaches can contribute to a fairer future but recognizes that many young people are not yet familiar with the co-operative movement.

Members of the YAG therefore help:

Raise awareness of co-operatives

Promote co-operative values

Connect with youth networks

Encourage participation

Explain alternative approaches to business and ownership

Increase engagement beyond existing co-operative communities

What Issues Might Interest Applicants?

Although applicants do not need to have a specific professional or academic background, the opportunity may be particularly attractive to young people interested in issues such as:

Fairness

Climate action

Community development

Social justice

Ethical business

Alternative business models

Youth empowerment

Sustainability

Social enterprise

Economic democracy

Employment

Community ownership

Candidates do not need to be experts in these issues.

The application is designed to identify young people who have ideas, motivation, relevant perspectives, or useful experiences to contribute.

You Do Not Need Previous Co-operative Experience

One of the most important features of the application call is that previous involvement with co-operatives is not required.

Applications are welcomed from:

Young people already active in co-operatives

Young people familiar with the movement

Young people with limited co-operative experience

Young people completely new to co-operatives

This makes the opportunity accessible to a broader range of applicants.

The group is intentionally designed to bring together people from across the co-operative landscape as well as people who may offer entirely new perspectives.

Members Are Paid for Their Time

Youth Advisory Group members are:

Paid for their time.

This is an important feature of the opportunity.

Co-operatives UK states that payment is intended to:

Recognize the commitment involved

Reduce barriers to participation

Value young people’s contributions

Support meaningful participation

The supplied call does not specify the exact payment rate or total amount.

Applicants should therefore consult the official information pack for precise details about:

Payment arrangements

Expected hours

Meeting frequency

Duration of membership

Other participation conditions

The National Youth Summit

The Youth Advisory Group was launched at the:

Co-operatives UK National Youth Summit

in 2024.

The National Youth Summit is an annual event intended to:

Increase young people’s understanding of co-operatives

Build enthusiasm for co-operative approaches

Create opportunities for learning

Provide networking opportunities

Bring young co-operators together

The establishment of the YAG created a more ongoing mechanism for young people to influence the organization beyond the annual summit.

Who Can Apply?

The main age requirement is clear:

Applicants must be aged 16 to 30.

The official announcement emphasizes that applications are welcomed from young people with:

All levels of experience and skills.

There is no requirement in the supplied call for applicants to hold:

A university degree

A professional qualification

Previous employment experience

Leadership experience

Previous co-operative membership

This makes the opportunity considerably more accessible than many formal youth leadership programmes.

Experience Level

Applicants may be:

Students

Recent graduates

Young professionals

Workers

Volunteers

Entrepreneurs

Co-operative members

Community organizers

People completely new to the co-operative movement

The key requirement is not a particular career status.

Instead, the application is intended to understand:

Who you are

Why you want to join the Youth Advisory Group

What skills you can contribute

What experience or perspective you bring

What Co-operatives UK Wants to Know About Applicants

The short application form asks candidates to provide information about:

Who they are

Why they want to become a Youth Advisory Group member

Their skills

Their experience

This means applicants should focus on authenticity rather than trying to present themselves as established experts.

A strong application should clearly communicate:

What matters to you

Why youth participation matters

What perspective you would bring

Why you are interested in co-operative ideas

How you might contribute to the group

Applications Can Be Written, Video or Audio

Applicants are not limited to traditional written responses.

Co-operatives UK accepts applications through:

Written text

Video

Audio

This can make the process more accessible to applicants who may communicate more effectively through different formats.

Candidates should choose the format that allows them to present their ideas most clearly and authentically.

Written Applications

Candidates who prefer writing can complete the application in text format.

A strong written response should be:

Clear

Specific

Personal

Concise

Relevant

Applicants do not need to use highly formal corporate language.

The application is designed to understand the person behind the submission.

Video Applications

Young people who communicate more naturally on camera may submit responses through video.

A good video application might explain:

Why you want to join

What issues matter to you

What perspective you can contribute

How you would help strengthen youth engagement

Applicants should consult the application form and information pack for any technical requirements concerning video submissions.

Audio Applications

Audio responses are also accepted.

This can be particularly useful for candidates who are comfortable expressing their ideas verbally but do not want to appear on video.

Again, applicants should check the official application materials for format and submission instructions.

How to Apply

Applicants need to:

Download and review the Youth Advisory Group information pack.

Download the official application form.

Complete the application.

Choose written, video, or audio format where appropriate.

Send the completed application to the official email address.

Applications should be sent to: youth@uk.coop

Official Application Resources

Applicants should consult two documents before applying:

Youth Advisory Group Information Pack

The information pack provides additional details about the opportunity and what participation involves.

Official information pack:

https://www.uk.coop/sites/default/files/2026-08/YAG_2026_Information_pack_web.pdf

Youth Advisory Group Application Form

Applicants must complete the official application form.

Application form:

https://www.uk.coop/sites/default/files/2026-08/YAG_Application_Form_2026.pdf

Application Deadline

Applications close at:

23:59 on Sunday, 6 September 2026.

Applicants should send their submissions before the deadline.

Because applications may involve video or audio files, candidates using those formats should avoid waiting until the final minutes in case they encounter:

File-size problems

Upload difficulties

Email issues

Technical delays

Why Young People Should Consider Applying

The Youth Advisory Group offers a relatively unusual opportunity for young people to contribute directly to the strategic thinking of an established national organization.

Participants can potentially gain experience in:

Advisory work

Youth advocacy

Strategic discussion

Collaboration

Public engagement

Co-operative development

Leadership

Community engagement

Social and economic policy conversations

Unlike programmes that focus primarily on training participants, this opportunity asks young people to contribute their existing experiences and perspectives to real organizational discussions.

Opportunity to Influence an Established Movement

The co-operative movement includes organizations operating across many sectors of society and the economy.

Young people participating in the YAG can contribute to discussions about how the movement evolves and responds to changing expectations.

This could be particularly valuable for candidates interested in questions such as:

What should ethical business look like?

How can workers have more influence?

How can communities own local assets?

How should organizations respond to climate change?

How can young people participate more meaningfully in economic decision-making?

What alternatives exist to traditional business ownership?

Applicants do not need to arrive with answers to these questions.

A willingness to engage with them can itself be valuable.

Skills Participants May Develop

Although the supplied call does not present a formal training curriculum, participation could help members strengthen transferable skills through practical involvement.

These may include:

Communication

Teamwork

Strategic thinking

Advocacy

Public speaking

Collaboration

Idea development

Constructive challenge

Community engagement

Stakeholder engagement

Members may also develop a stronger understanding of how organizational decision-making and youth participation operate in practice.

Building Networks

The Youth Advisory Group brings together young people from:

Existing co-operatives

The wider co-operative movement

Different youth networks

Backgrounds outside co-operatives

This creates opportunities for participants to meet peers with different experiences and perspectives.

For young people interested in:

Social enterprise

Co-operatives

Sustainability

Community development

Youth leadership

Alternative business models

the group may provide useful professional and personal connections.

Preparing a Strong Application

1. Explain Why the Opportunity Matters to You

Avoid giving a generic response such as:

“I want to develop my leadership skills.”

Instead, explain what specific issue motivates you.

Perhaps you care about:

Climate action

Fair employment

Communities

Ethical business

Youth voice

Economic inequality

Connect that interest with why the YAG appeals to you.

2. You Do Not Need to Pretend to Be a Co-operative Expert

The call explicitly welcomes applicants who are completely new to co-operatives.

If you are unfamiliar with the movement, say so honestly.

You could instead explain:

Why you want to learn

What perspective you bring from outside the movement

What issues already matter to you

Being new to co-operatives is not presented as a disadvantage.

3. Give Concrete Examples

When discussing your skills, use examples.

Instead of saying:

“I am a good communicator,”

you might explain how you:

Organized a student project

Spoke at a community event

Ran social media for a group

Volunteered with young people

Participated in a campaign

Helped resolve a disagreement

Evidence makes an application stronger.

4. Explain What Young People Need

The YAG exists partly to make Co-operatives UK more responsive to younger generations.

Think about:

What young people currently worry about

What opportunities they need

Why traditional institutions may not engage them

How co-operatives could become more relevant

Your perspective does not need to match everyone else’s.

The purpose of an advisory group is partly to hear different views.

5. Choose the Best Application Format for You

You can apply using:

Writing

Video

Audio

Do not automatically choose written text because it seems more formal.

Use whichever format lets you communicate most effectively.

Important Details at a Glance

Organization: Co-operatives UK

Programme: Youth Advisory Group

Abbreviation: YAG

Established: 2024

Applicant age: 16–30

Previous co-operative experience: Not required

Experience level: All levels welcome

Payment: Members are paid for their time

Application formats: Written, video, or audio

Application email: youth@uk.coop

Deadline: 6 September 2026 at 23:59

Information: https://www.uk.coop/news/applications-now-open-co-operatives-uks-youth-advisory-group

Conclusion

The Co-operatives UK Youth Advisory Group 2026 offers young people aged 16 to 30 an opportunity to have a meaningful voice in discussions about the future of the co-operative movement.

Established in 2024, the group works alongside Co-operatives UK to provide strategic advice, generate new ideas, challenge existing thinking, advocate for youth participation, and increase awareness of co-operative approaches among younger generations.

The opportunity is deliberately accessible. Applicants do not need previous co-operative experience, a university degree, a particular profession, or extensive leadership credentials. Young people with all levels of skills and experience are encouraged to apply.

The group may be particularly relevant to young people interested in fairness, climate action, community development, youth participation, sustainability, or alternative approaches to business and ownership.

Importantly, Youth Advisory Group members are paid for their time, recognizing both their contribution and the commitment involved.

Applications can be submitted in written, video, or audio format, allowing candidates to choose the communication method that works best for them.

Applicants must complete the official application form and send it to youth@uk.coop.

The application deadline is 23:59 on Sunday, 6 September 2026.

TITLE: Humanity AI Open Call 2026 | Grants of Up to $1 Million for Community-Led AI Initiatives

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Humanity AI has launched a first-of-its-kind Open Call for Proposals seeking community-led efforts that shape how artificial intelligence is built, governed, and used for the common good.

The initiative comes at a time of growing public concern about the impact of AI on people’s lives, jobs, and communities. Humanity AI is particularly interested in supporting communities that are not simply being consulted about AI but are actively setting the agenda and leading efforts to determine how AI affects them.

The Open Call will provide grants ranging from $75,000 to $1,000,000, with applicants able to propose projects lasting up to three years.

About the Humanity AI Open Call

The Humanity AI Open Call is designed to support community-led work addressing the social, economic, cultural, and technological implications of artificial intelligence.

The initiative seeks applications from communities and organizations where those most affected by technological change are defining the goals, shaping the approach, and driving the work.

This includes communities of:

Workers

Artists

Students

Educators

Writers

Scholars

Cultural heritage workers

Other communities working in the humanities and culture

Humanity AI is also actively seeking applicants who may not traditionally have considered themselves participants in shaping the impact of AI.

Eligible Issue Areas

The Open Call focuses on three key issue areas.

1. Education

The education component supports efforts to shape AI around the interests of students, educators, and communities.

Projects may focus on developing and expanding knowledge, strengthening how people learn, and safeguarding people against risks associated with AI.

Humanity AI is particularly interested in work led by students, educators, and organizations representing them.

2. Labor and Economy

The labor and economy area focuses on ensuring that AI enhances rather than simply replaces workers.

The initiative seeks efforts that help create an economy where people can thrive and benefit from technological developments.

Humanity AI is particularly interested in work led by workers and worker-focused organizations.

3. Humanities, Arts, and Culture

The third issue area focuses on enhancing human creativity and understanding of the human experience while protecting artists and creators.

Humanity AI is particularly interested in projects led by:

Artists

Writers

Scholars

Cultural heritage workers

Other people working in culture and humanities

Organizations representing these communities

Eligible Approaches

Within the three issue areas, Humanity AI is funding community-led work that follows one of three approaches.

1. Shaping How AI Is Governed and Used

This approach supports efforts by communities and advocates to strengthen safeguards around AI and help define the rules governing AI deployment at local, regional, or national levels.

Examples could include educators establishing AI guidelines for schools or workers organizing around enforceable standards for responsible AI use in the workplace.

2. Building AI on Community Terms

This approach supports technical efforts that place community needs ahead of profits and focus on developing AI systems and infrastructure that communities can shape and control.

Examples include:

Evaluations centred on overlooked communities

Auditing approaches to ensure AI systems work as intended

Datasets supporting broad and consensual participation in AI development

Artistic and creative approaches to community-led AI infrastructure

Projects that reimagine, audit, or challenge AI systems

Humanity AI prioritizes technical proposals focused on AI infrastructure. AI products using novel approaches may also be considered when they address a community gap and are co-designed with the communities they serve.

3. Challenging AI That Doesn’t Serve Communities

This approach supports community efforts to challenge AI deployments that are imposed on communities or do not align with their values and needs.

The goal is to elevate approaches that place human agency at the centre of decision-making about AI.

Examples include artists and cultural organizations using creative interventions to challenge dominant narratives about AI, or worker coalitions challenging AI surveillance in workplaces.

Priority Consideration for Open-Weight and Open-Source AI

Projects can be eligible whether or not they incorporate AI.

However, when AI models are central to the proposed methodology or deliverables, priority will be given to open-weight and/or open-source models rather than closed models.

Areas Out of Scope

Applicants should carefully consider whether their proposed project falls within the scope of the Open Call.

The following areas are specifically excluded:

AI Literacy

Projects primarily focused on providing people with knowledge and skills to use AI tools are out of scope.

AI Adoption

Projects primarily focused on promoting the spread of particular AI tools or systems are not eligible.

Research-Only Projects

Projects primarily focused on research without advancing community leadership and action are also out of scope.

Eligibility Requirements

The Humanity AI Open Call welcomes applications from:

U.S.-based organizations

U.S.-based collaborations

U.S.-based individuals with eligible proposals focused on U.S.-based communities

Lead organizations must have 501(c)(3) status.

Individuals can apply with the support of a fiscal sponsor or another 501(c)(3) intermediary.

Applicants based outside the United States should carefully review the official FAQ and eligibility requirements before preparing an application, as the call specifically states that applicants and proposed work must meet the U.S.-based requirements.

Funding Amount

Humanity AI will provide grants ranging from $75,000 to $1,000,000.

Applicants can select the funding tier that best matches the resources required for their proposal.

Tier One: $75,000–$150,000

This tier may be suitable for:

A fiscally sponsored project involving an individual practitioner

A focused proposal

A two-partner collaboration undertaking exploratory work

An emerging organization launching an early initiative

An established organization running a contained pilot

Tier Two: $150,000–$500,000

This tier may be suitable for projects involving:

Individual practitioners whose work requires sustained time or production resources

Collaborations requiring meaningful coordination or development costs

Emerging organizations with full-time teams working on defined initiatives

Established organizations dedicating staff capacity to a new area of work

Tier Three: $500,000–$1,000,000

This tier may be suitable for:

Coalitions requiring substantial coordination and dedicated staffing

Multi-year initiatives with significant technical development or infrastructure costs

Emerging organizations building full-time teams around major initiatives

Established organizations launching ambitious, resource-intensive pilots

Humanity AI is not pre-allocating funding between the tiers. Applicants are encouraged to request the level of funding their proposal actually requires.

Grant Duration

Applicants may propose projects lasting up to three years.

Where feasible, grants will be disbursed at the beginning of the grant period to support early resourcing.

Application Process

The application process consists of two phases.

Phase 1: Initial Application

Eligible applicants must submit their initial application by:

October 21, 2026, at 4:59 p.m. PT / 7:59 p.m. ET.

Applications will first undergo an eligibility screening by reviewers at Lever for Change, which is supporting the Open Call.

Eligible applications will then be evaluated according to the Open Call’s evaluation criteria.

Phase 2: Finalist Round

Top-rated applicants will be invited to submit additional application materials.

These materials may include:

A detailed budget

A measurement plan

Additional information about the proposed work

Some applicants may also be invited to participate in an interview with Humanity AI staff and funders.

Application Timeline

September 10, 2026

Launch

Initial applications opened.

September 14, 2026

Applicant Webinar

An informational webinar is scheduled for prospective applicants.

October 21, 2026

Initial Applications Due

Applications must be submitted by 4:59 p.m. PT / 7:59 p.m. ET.

December 2026

Finalists Notified

Finalists will be contacted and invited to provide additional materials.

Early Spring 2027

Grantee Awards Announced

Humanity AI expects to announce the successful grantee awards.

The dates are estimates and may change. Humanity AI states that updates will be communicated as early as possible.

Evaluation Criteria

Proposals will be evaluated according to five major criteria:

Vision for the Proposal

Vision for Community Leadership

Clarity and Feasibility

Potential for Impact

Credibility and Experience

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposals clearly communicate their vision, demonstrate meaningful community leadership, explain how the project can realistically be delivered, describe its potential impact, and establish the credibility and experience of those involved.

How to Apply

Prospective applicants are encouraged to begin by reviewing the organizational readiness tool to assess their eligibility.

Applicants can also review the complete list of application questions before submitting their proposal.

Start Application: Humanity AI Open Call application portal

Assess Eligibility: Humanity AI organizational readiness tool

Download Questions: Humanity AI Open Call application questions

Who Should Consider Applying?

This Open Call is particularly relevant to U.S.-based organizations, collaborations, and eligible individuals working with U.S.-based communities on projects involving:

Education and AI

Labor and the future of work

Humanities, arts, and culture

AI governance

Community-led AI infrastructure

Open-source or open-weight AI

Community-led challenges to harmful AI deployment

Human-centred approaches to AI development and use

The strongest fit will be projects where affected communities are not merely consulted but are actively defining the goals, shaping the approach, and leading the work.

Important Information for Applicants

Before applying, prospective applicants should carefully assess whether their project meets the Open Call’s requirements.

Applicants should pay particular attention to:

U.S.-based eligibility requirements

501(c)(3) requirements for lead organizations

The need for a fiscal sponsor for eligible individual applicants

The three eligible issue areas

The three eligible approaches

Areas that are specifically out of scope

The preference for open-weight and open-source AI when AI models form part of the core methodology or deliverables

The appropriate funding tier

The maximum three-year grant duration

The October 21, 2026 application deadline

APPLICATION PORTAL

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Humanity AI Open Call 2026 provides a major funding opportunity for U.S.-based communities, organizations, collaborations, and eligible individuals working to shape the development, governance, and use of artificial intelligence.

With grants ranging from $75,000 to $1 million and project durations of up to three years, the initiative is designed to support community-led efforts across education, labor and the economy, and humanities, arts, and culture.

Applicants should ensure that their proposals place communities at the centre of the work and clearly demonstrate a strong vision, community leadership, feasibility, potential impact, and relevant experience.

Discover more on the OFY Webpage.

TITLE: British Red Cross Youth Engagement & Early Careers Internship 2026: Paid London Opportunity for Young People

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The British Red Cross Youth Engagement & Early Careers Internship 2026 offers young people an opportunity to gain practical workplace experience while contributing to projects designed to improve opportunities, career development and resilience for young people.

Based in London, with hybrid working between home and the British Red Cross offices, this six-month internship provides hands-on experience in youth engagement, early careers, recruitment data, project support and resource development.

The internship offers a salary of £24,479 per annum, with an additional Inner London Weighting (ILW) of £3,344 pro rata for eligible employees residing and working in London. The position is full-time at 35 hours per week, Monday to Friday, and is scheduled to run from November 2026 to May 2027.

Applications are currently open, and interested candidates should submit their applications before the 27 September 2026 deadline.

British Red Cross Youth Engagement & Early Careers Internship 2026 Overview

The internship is designed for young people who want to develop their professional experience while helping create meaningful opportunities for other young people.

As a Youth Engagement & Early Careers Intern, the successful candidate will work alongside colleagues across the British Red Cross and contribute to projects focused on improving young people’s access to opportunities.

The role combines practical workplace experience with youth-focused project work. Interns will have opportunities to engage directly with young people, collect feedback and insights, support events and workshops, analyse recruitment information and help develop resources related to youth engagement and early careers.

Key Details

Organisation: British Red Cross

Position: Youth Engagement & Early Careers Intern

Location: London, United Kingdom

Working arrangement: Hybrid, between home and the London offices

Office location: EC2Y 9AL

Salary: £24,479 per annum

London weighting: £3,344 pro rata, where applicable

Working hours: 35 hours per week

Working days: Monday to Friday

Contract: Fixed-term

Duration: Six months

Expected period: November 2026 to May 2027

Application deadline: 27 September 2026 at 23:59

Assessment Centre: Expected to take place in London during the week commencing 5 October 2026

About the Youth Engagement & Early Careers Internship

The internship focuses on helping young people access opportunities, develop confidence and strengthen their career resilience.

The successful intern will contribute to work that seeks to understand the experiences and needs of young people and identify ways to make paid opportunities more accessible and inclusive.

Rather than being limited to administrative tasks, the position involves several areas of practical project work, including youth engagement, events, data analysis, research, resource development and communication.

The role can therefore provide experience across different areas of organisational work while maintaining a strong focus on young people and early-career development.

What Will a Youth Engagement & Early Careers Intern Do?

The intern will support several activities throughout the placement.

1. Engage With Young People

A key responsibility will be engaging with young people and gathering their feedback.

The information collected through these interactions can help the British Red Cross understand young people’s experiences and use those insights to shape projects, resources and opportunities.

This may give the intern experience in:

Youth engagement

Gathering feedback

Listening to young people’s perspectives

Understanding user experiences

Supporting project development

Contributing to improvements in youth-focused opportunities

The role therefore places young people’s experiences at the centre of some of the work the intern will support.

2. Support Youth Engagement Events and Workshops

The intern will also help with youth engagement events, workshops and activities.

This could provide practical experience in supporting activities that involve groups of young people and colleagues from across the organisation.

Through this work, the intern can develop skills in areas such as organisation, communication, event support and relationship building.

3. Analyse Recruitment Data

Another important part of the position involves analysing recruitment data relating to young people.

The purpose is to help identify ways of improving access to paid opportunities.

This gives the intern exposure to the relationship between data and organisational decision-making. Instead of simply collecting information, the role involves looking at what the information can reveal and considering how it could inform improvements.

4. Develop Resources and Case Studies

The intern will contribute to the development of:

Resources

Case studies

Insights

Youth engagement materials

Career resilience materials

Early-career opportunity resources
