TITLE: Press Release: AAU Gears Up for Africa Universities’ Day 2023 and 56th Anniversary—Focusing on Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Accra, Ghana, October 5, 2023 – The Association of African Universities (AAU) is calling on all higher education institutions across the continent to join the commemoration of this year’s Africa Universities’ Day. A week-long schedule of activities, slated for Monday November 6, through to Friday November 10, 2023, have been lined up for the celebrations, which also marks 56 years of the AAU’s existence and service to Africa’s higher education sector. This year’s theme, “Artificial Intelligence (AI) in African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)”, underscores the critical need for HEIs in Africa to adopt progressive strategies to guide the usage and integration of emerging technologies such as AI and use these opportunities to improve educational outcomes.

The Africa Universities’ Day is a key statutory event on the AAU’s calendar, observed annually to commemorate the founding of the Association on November 12, 1967, in Rabat, Morocco, as well as to highlight the contributions of the higher education sector to the development of the African continent. It also seeks to bring together academic leaders, policymakers, students, and industry experts to deliberate on key challenges and opportunities facing African universities. With the rapid advancement of technology and the increasing importance of AI in various sectors, this year’s theme was aptly chosen to discuss advancements in augmented reality, virtual reality, natural language processing, the internet of things, and other emerging technologies – and how these impact teaching, learning, research, collaboration, lifelong learning, ethics and privacy, and the administrative functions of African HEIs.

“Over the span of 56 years, the AAU has been at the forefront of higher education excellence, making significant strides in the transformation of Africa’s higher education landscape. As we proudly commemorate this remarkable milestone and celebrate the 2023 Africa Universities’ Day, we acknowledge the invaluable contributions and unwavering support of our member universities and stakeholders. Their dedication has played an instrumental role in strengthening the AAU, establishing it as the authentic voice of higher education in Africa. We look forward to the continued collaboration and commitment of our stakeholders as we chart, with lucidity and pragmatism, the path towards the Association’s future.” – Prof. Olusola Oyewole, Secretary General, AAU.

In line with the AAU’s ongoing commitment to enhance the experience and accommodate the diverse needs of our esteemed participants, this year’s event will seamlessly blend in-person and virtual components. The virtual events will be held via the AAU Zoom platform and streamed live on AAU TV as well as our social media pages on Facebook and YouTube. The physical venue is the AAU Secretariat Office in East Legon, Accra, Ghana while the final event to climax the weeklong celebrations will hold at a selected AAU member university campus in Ghana.

This year’s commemoration will feature a series of insightful high-level panel discussions and keynote presentations by experts, scholars, and leaders from academia, industry, and the public sector. There will also be a student engagement forum organized by the AAU TV as well as a members-only training workshop for university registrars and administrators. Further details on the theme and topics to be discussed are highlighted in the concept notes which can be accessed in ENGLISH, FRENCH, ARABIC and PORTUGUESE. The registration link is made available here – https://bit.ly/44MysCN.

The 2023 Africa Universities Day promises to be an engaging and thought-provoking event that will provide the much-needed platform for deliberations on Artificial Intelligence in higher education in Africa. African higher education institutions are encouraged to commemorate the day within their campuses by arranging engaging events in the form of seminars, debates, exhibitions, social media dialogues, conferences, webinars, and other activities, aimed at exploring the theme and maximizing Africa’s gains from Artificial Intelligence. Alternatively, in cases where such initiatives are not feasible, higher education institutions and other stakeholders are urged to participate in the AAU Secretariat’s planned activities.

AAU encourages the management of universities, to circulate information concerning the 2023 Africa Universities Day celebrations to the Ministries of Education, University Councils, Committees of Vice-Chancellors, and all institutions involved in the management of Higher Education Institutions for their attention and participation in the events. Other public and private universities in each country which are non-members of the AAU, research institutions, the media and public should also be invited to join the celebrations to give visibility to the Africa Universities Day and promote the activities of Higher Education Institutions in each country.

AAU – The Voice of Higher Education in Africa!!

—————————————————————————————————————

Media Contact

Mrs. Felicia Nkrumah Kuagbedzi, Senior Communications and Publications Officer, AAU- fnkrumah@aau.org

Ms. Naomi Darko, Communications Assistant, AAU – ndarko@aau.org

About the Association of African Universities

The AAU is an international non-profit, non-governmental organization created by African Universities to promote cooperation among them on the one hand, and between them and the international academic community on the other. Created in 1967, the AAU is the voice of higher education in Africa and aims to improve the quality of African higher education and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by supporting the core functions of higher education institutions and facilitating critical reflections and consensus building on issues affecting higher education. The AAU headquartered in Accra, Ghana has a membership of more than 400 Higher Education Institutions and is the technical implementing arm of the African Union Commission (AUC) in higher education. The Association is also the coordinating agency of the Higher Education Cluster of the Continental Education Strategy for Africa (CESA 16-25). Through our guidance, our member universities are also responsible for implementing the AUC’s Science, Technology, and Innovation Strategy for Africa (STISA 2024).

TITLE: Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships 2026: $3,000 for American History Research in New York City

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the Gilder Lehrman Institute Scholarly Fellowships 2026, offering short-term research funding to doctoral candidates, university and college faculty members, and independent scholars conducting research in the field of American history.

The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History awards annual short-term research fellowships valued at $3,000 each to support scholars who need to conduct research using historical collections and resources in New York City.

For the 2026 competition, the Institute expects to award ten Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships. While research projects covering all aspects of American history are eligible, the Institute has identified three areas that will receive particular attention during the current application cycle:

Colonial American history

Slavery and abolition studies

Cold War studies

Three of the ten fellowships are specifically connected to these priority fields:

John Winthrop Fellowship with a Focus on Colonial History

Scholarly Fellowship in Slavery and Abolition Studies

Scholarly Fellowship in Cold War Studies

Preference will be given to strong applications in these fields, but researchers working on other periods and subjects in American history are still encouraged to apply.

The fellowship is open internationally. Eligible applicants include doctoral candidates, academic faculty members at every rank, and independent scholars.

Successful applicants must complete their funded research in New York City within one year of notification of the award.

Applications must be submitted online by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Monday, October 26, 2026.

About the Gilder Lehrman Institute Scholarly Fellowships

The Gilder Lehrman Institute provides its Scholarly Fellowships to support researchers undertaking original work in American history.

The programme has a long record of supporting historians and other scholars at different stages of their academic careers. Since the fellowship programme began in 1994, the Institute has awarded 723 fellowships.

Rather than limiting support exclusively to established professors, the programme deliberately includes several categories of researchers:

Doctoral candidates

College faculty

University faculty

Independent scholars

International scholars

This makes the fellowship particularly valuable for researchers who need relatively short-term financial assistance to complete archival research connected with a dissertation, book project, article, or other substantial scholarly work.

Fellowship Value

Each Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowship provides:

$3,000

The fellowship is designed as short-term research support.

The Institute does not describe the award as a full scholarship covering every cost associated with travel, accommodation, and living expenses. Applicants are therefore required to include an anticipated budget within their project proposal explaining how they expect to use the fellowship funds.

Researchers should plan carefully for costs associated with conducting research in New York City.

Number of Fellowships Available

For the 2026 competition, the Gilder Lehrman Institute plans to award:

Ten Scholarly Fellowships

Among these ten awards, three are linked to specific thematic research priorities.

The remaining fellowships remain open to high-quality research covering the broader field of American history.

Research Field: American History

The programme is specifically intended for scholars working in:

American history

The Institute welcomes applications examining a wide variety of themes, periods, populations, institutions, movements, events, and historical processes.

Although the 2026 call gives preference to three particular fields, applicants should not assume that projects outside those areas are ineligible.

The official call explicitly states that:

Projects on all aspects of American history are welcome.

This creates opportunities for researchers working across a broad range of subjects.

Potential fields may include political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic, military, intellectual, legal, gender, labor, racial, transnational, or environmental history, provided the project makes a meaningful contribution to the study of American history.

Special Priority Area 1: Colonial American History

One of the special awards available in 2026 is the:

John Winthrop Fellowship with a Focus on Colonial History

The fellowship specifically supports research concerning the colonial era.

The award is funded by John Winthrop, a descendant of John Winthrop, the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

The Gilder Lehrman Collection includes an important 1634 letter written by Winthrop describing life in Boston, helping connect the fellowship with the Institute’s historical holdings.

Researchers whose work focuses on colonial America may therefore have a particularly strong opportunity during the 2026 competition.

Relevant research could potentially engage with topics such as:

Colonial government

Indigenous-colonial relations

Religion

Migration

Atlantic history

Settlement

Law

Gender

Labor

Trade

Race

Political culture

Everyday life

Applicants should still formulate an original research project rather than relying only on the broad priority area.

Special Priority Area 2: Slavery and Abolition Studies

The Institute is also offering a:

Scholarly Fellowship in Slavery and Abolition Studies

Projects examining the histories of slavery, emancipation, resistance, abolition, race, African American communities, and related themes may receive particular consideration.

This priority reflects the importance of slavery and abolition to understanding American political, social, economic, and cultural development.

Researchers could potentially work with archival material concerning:

Enslaved people

Abolitionist organizations

Resistance

Slaveholding societies

Emancipation

Reconstruction

African American communities

Political debates

Legal structures

Memory of slavery

The exact research question remains up to the applicant.

Special Priority Area 3: Cold War Studies

The third designated fellowship is the:

Scholarly Fellowship in Cold War Studies

Researchers studying the Cold War and its political, military, social, diplomatic, technological, cultural, or ideological dimensions are encouraged to apply.

Potential topics could include:

U.S. foreign policy

Nuclear politics

Civil defense

International relations

Anti-communism

Propaganda

Intelligence

Domestic politics

Civil rights

Cultural diplomacy

Scientific competition

Projects do not necessarily need to follow traditional diplomatic-history approaches if they contribute meaningfully to understanding the American experience of the Cold War.

Other American History Topics Remain Eligible

Applicants should not interpret the three special fellowships as meaning that only colonial history, slavery and abolition, or Cold War research will be funded.

The Institute explicitly states that:

All areas of American history remain eligible.

The thematic priorities simply mean that applications in those three fields may receive particular attention.

A strong project outside the priority areas can still compete for one of the general Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships.

Who Can Apply?

The Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships are open to three principal groups.

1. Doctoral Candidates

Current PhD candidates working on American history can apply.

This may be especially useful for doctoral researchers who:

Need additional archival material

Are completing dissertation chapters

Need to verify primary sources

Are developing a substantial dissertation argument

Require short-term research access in New York City

The call does not state that doctoral candidates must be enrolled at a U.S. university.

International doctoral researchers are explicitly eligible.

2. College and University Faculty

Faculty members may apply regardless of academic rank.

This means eligibility is not restricted only to:

Full professors

Tenured professors

Senior scholars

Researchers at other academic ranks may also apply.

This broad eligibility allows faculty members at different career stages to seek support for research projects in American history.

3. Independent Scholars

Researchers who are not currently employed in a traditional university faculty position may also qualify as:

Independent scholars

This is particularly important because many research fellowships limit eligibility to scholars holding formal university appointments.

The Gilder Lehrman programme explicitly recognizes independent scholarship as an eligible category.

International Scholars Are Eligible

The programme explicitly states that:

International scholars are eligible to apply.

There is therefore no requirement that applicants:

Be U.S. citizens

Be permanent residents of the United States

Study at a U.S. university

Hold an American academic appointment

Applicants from universities, research institutions, and independent scholarly communities outside the United States may apply.

However, successful Fellows must be able to conduct their research in New York City within the required period.

Applicants should therefore consider immigration, travel, and logistical requirements when developing their project and anticipated budget.

Research Must Be Conducted in New York City

Successful Fellows are required to complete their research in:

New York City

The research must be completed within:

One year of notification of the fellowship award

This means applicants should already have a reasonably clear understanding of:

Which archives they need

Which collections they intend to consult

Why those materials are necessary

How much research time they expect to need

How the $3,000 award will support the research visit

The fellowship is therefore not simply a general award for producing scholarship from the applicant’s home institution.

It is specifically connected with a research trip to New York City.

Primary Sources Are Central to the Application

Applicants must include a list of the:

Primary sources they expect to consult

within their project proposal.

This requirement is important because it helps the selection committee determine whether the proposed research trip is genuinely necessary and well planned.

Candidates should therefore investigate collections before submitting their applications.

A strong application should identify specific archival materials rather than saying only:

“I plan to consult archives in New York.”

Applicants should demonstrate that they know what materials exist and how those materials connect with their research questions.

Fellowship Responsibilities

Receiving the fellowship involves several responsibilities beyond conducting archival research.

Successful Fellows must:

Complete their research within one year of notification.

Conduct their fellowship research in New York City.

Meet with the Director of the Scholarly Fellowship Program during their research trip.

Submit a written essay after the fellowship.

Provide documentation regarding the archival collections consulted.

These requirements ensure that the Fellowship contributes not only to the scholar’s individual project but also to the Institute’s broader scholarly mission.

Meeting With the Fellowship Programme Director

During their research trip to New York City, Fellows are required to meet with the:

Director of the Scholarly Fellowship Program at the Gilder Lehrman Institute

Applicants should therefore plan their research visit in coordination with the Institute.

Post-Fellowship Essay

Successful Fellows are required to submit an essay of:

750–1,000 words

The essay should concern the Fellow’s research topic.

This creates an opportunity for Fellows to communicate aspects of their scholarship in an accessible format.

Archival Collections Statement

In addition to the essay, Fellows must provide:

A separate paragraph documenting the archival collections consulted during the fellowship period.

Researchers should therefore maintain a careful record of archives and collections used during their research trip.

Application Requirements

Applications require three major components:

Project proposal

Curriculum vitae

Two recommendation letters

Project Proposal

Applicants must submit a project proposal of:

2–5 pages

The proposal should include several specific elements.

Current Contact Information

Applicants should include current contact details as required by the application instructions.

Project Description

The proposal should explain:

The research topic

Central research question

Historical significance

Current stage of the research

Scholarly contribution

Why archival research is needed

Primary Sources

Applicants must list the primary sources they expect to consult.

This should demonstrate preparation and feasibility.

Anticipated Budget

The proposal must also include an:

Anticipated budget

Applicants should explain how fellowship funds are likely to be used.

Depending on the applicant’s location and circumstances, this might include expenses associated with:

Travel

Accommodation

Local transportation

Research-related costs

Candidates should develop a realistic rather than inflated budget.

Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a:

Curriculum vitae

There is:

No stated page limit

The official call specifically says that the CV may be of any length.

However, applicants should still present information clearly and professionally.

Relevant sections may include:

Academic education

Doctoral research

Academic appointments

Publications

Conference presentations

Awards

Fellowships

Research experience

Teaching

Professional affiliations

Public history work

Two Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must arrange:

Two letters of recommendation

The letters should come from:

Established scholars

Applicants should identify recommenders who understand both their research abilities and the importance of the proposed project.

Strong recommenders may be able to comment on:

Research originality

Historical knowledge

Archival competence

Scholarly potential

Feasibility of the project

Importance of the research

Candidates should contact recommenders well before the deadline.

Application Deadline

Applications must be submitted online by:

11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Monday, October 26, 2026

Applicants outside the United States should carefully convert the deadline into their local time zone.

Submitting several days early can help avoid problems involving:

Recommendation letters

Uploads

Application-system errors

Time-zone confusion

How to Apply

Applications are submitted online through the Gilder Lehrman Institute fellowship portal.

Official fellowship information

APPLY HERE

Contact Information

Questions about the programme can be directed to:

Email: fellowships@gilderlehrman.org

Telephone: 646-366-9666, ext. 129

Candidates with eligibility or application questions should use the official contact information rather than relying solely on third-party fellowship listings.

Examples of Current Fellows and Research Topics

The range of projects supported by the programme demonstrates the breadth of American history scholarship considered eligible.

Current Fellows include researchers working on subjects such as:

Numbers and the formation of American political identity

U.S. governance in the Panama Canal Zone

The history of American civil litigation

African American internationalism

Slavery and violence in South Carolina

Black midwives in early America

Civil defense during the Cold War

African American children during the Civil War

Revolutionary-era political figures

Women and urban economic life

This diversity demonstrates that the programme supports work extending across:

Early America

Colonial history

Nineteenth-century history

African American history

Legal history

Diplomatic history

Political history

Social history

Cold War history

Applicants should therefore focus on the quality and archival foundation of their research rather than assuming that only highly traditional historical topics are competitive.

Importance of Archival Preparation

Because the fellowship supports short-term research rather than a long residential appointment, applicants should arrive with a clear archival plan.

Before applying, candidates should identify:

The specific collections they need

Relevant documents

Archive opening schedules

Potential restrictions

Research priorities

Expected time needed

A four-week research plan, for example, should identify what can realistically be accomplished during that period.

A strong proposal demonstrates that the Fellowship will enable work that could not easily be completed without access to the relevant New York collections.

Preparing a Competitive Project Proposal

1. Define a Clear Historical Question

Avoid proposing a topic that is too broad.

Instead of:

“Slavery in America”

a competitive research proposal should identify a focused problem, period, archive, population, or historical debate.

2. Explain the Scholarly Contribution

Reviewers should understand what the project adds to existing knowledge.

Applicants may explain whether their work:

Challenges an existing interpretation

Introduces new archival material

Reframes a historical debate

Connects previously separate literatures

Examines an overlooked community

3. Identify Specific Primary Sources

The application explicitly requires a list of primary sources.

This is not a minor administrative detail.

Applicants should demonstrate that they have already researched the collections relevant to their project.

4. Explain Why the Research Must Be Done in New York

A strong application should establish why access to New York City collections is essential to the project.

Reviewers should not be left wondering why the applicant needs to travel.

5. Create a Realistic Budget

Because the fellowship provides $3,000, applicants should present a credible plan for how the funding will support their research.

The budget should correspond to the scope and duration of the proposed visit.

6. Use the Special Priority Areas Strategically

Applicants working on:

Colonial America

Slavery and abolition

Cold War history

should make that connection visible.

Why the Gilder Lehrman Fellowship Can Be Valuable for PhD Candidates

TITLE: Participate in the AAU Policy Webinar Series| Implications of the AfCFTA Agreement for HEIs in Africa| Monday, November 25, 2019

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
ASSOCIATION OF AFRICAN UNIVERSITIES

POLICY WEBINAR SERIES| MONDAY, NOVEMBER 25, 2019

AFRICAN CONTINENTAL FREE TRADE AREA (AfCFTA) AGREEMENT: IMPLICATIONS FOR HIGHER EDUCATION IN AFRICA

Synopsis

Consistent with the African Union’s Agenda 2063, the African Union Summit in 2012 decided on Boosting Intra-African Trade (BIAT) and fast-tracking the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The AfCFTA has the overarching aim of creating a single continental market for goods and services, with free movement of business persons and investments, paving the way for accelerating the establishment of the continental Customs Union. Ninety-eight percent of member states have so far signed the AfCFTA with 27 African countries ratifying the agreement and bringing it into force. With the completion of the phase 1 (trade in services based on five priority areas namely: Transport, Communication, Financial Services, Tourism and Business Services), attention has been shifted to phase 2 (investments, competition policy and intellectual property rights). At a time when the world is moving apart, Africa is getting closer and integrating faster. It is perhaps the biggest single intervention on the continent and with a combined population of 1.2 billion (projected to reach 1.4 billion by 2040) and a combined GDP of USD 3 trillion, it is perhaps the world’s largest Free Trade Area with commercial significance, second only to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in terms of the number of Member States. Africa can negotiate from position of strength with the rest of the world and improve terms of trade going forward. More importantly, it overcomes the historic fragmentation and isolation of her economies as well as ending the cycle of exporting raw material only to re-import them after value addition. Greater economic transformation hinged on productivity growth, consumption and income growth on the continent are anchored on the theories of comparative advantage and economies of scale. That said, AfCFTA must work for the common good (narrow the rising inequality on the continent) and not tiny Africans (Africa 4 Africa) and serious effort must be garnered to overcome both tariff and non-tariff barriers whilst avoiding race to the bottom in competing for foreign direct investment and other ‘pull him down’ syndrome.

Optimizing AfCFTA for Africa requires addressing both hard and soft infrastructure deficits in anchoring greater reforms to boost intraregional trade with far reaching implications for tertiary education. African universities must play a pivotal role in training graduates ready to take up the challenge and opportunities AfCFTA offers. Scaling up labour productivity informed by appropriate skill set in upskilling and reskilling and consistent with the Fourth Industrial Revolution predicated on network readiness will be critical. This must be supported by cutting-edge research to guide implementation and reforms going forward. It requires closer collaboration between African universities and AfCFTA implementation protocols agencies and stakeholders. Reforms must be informed by empirical evidence that is relevant for the continent.

It is in this light that the Association of African Universities (AAU), the apex higher education body in Africa, is creating a common platform through its webinar series for academics and education stakeholders to dialogue and map out strategies to support the implementation of the AfCFTA.

Objectives

The objectives of the webinar are to:

Shed light on the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and discuss its implication for African universities (Teaching-Learning, Research and Community Engagements).

Stimulate ideas, identify gaps and opportunities in the implementation of the AfCFTA.

Dialogue on the key roles of African higher education and other key stakeholders in the implementation of the AfCFTA.

TITLE: Mechanisms of tropical Pacific decadal variability

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Capotondi, A., McGregor, S., McPhaden, M., Cravatte, S., Holbrook, N., Imada, Y., Sanchez, S., Sprintall, J., Stuecker, M., Ummenhofer, C., Zeller, M., Farneti, R., Graffino, G., Hu, S., Karnauskas, K., Kosaka, Y., Kucharski, F., Mayer, M., Qiu, B., Santoso, A., Taschetto, A. S., Wang, F., Zhang, X., Holmes, R. M., Luo, J.-J., Maher, N., Martinez-Villalobos, C., Meehl, G. A., Naha, R., Schneider, N., Stevenson, S., Sullivan, A., van Rensch, P., & Xu, T. (2023). Mechanisms of tropical Pacific decadal variability. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00486-x

Subtropical cells influence on tropical Pacific decadal variability and two different mechanisms are illustrated schematically: (a) equatorward advection of temperature anomalies within the pycnocline (the vbarT’ hypothesis) is schematically illustrated in the upper panel as the advection of spiciness anomalies (pink shading) by the mean circulation (black arrows) on the 25.0kg mm−3 isopycnal surface. The lower panel depicts zonally averaged isopycnal depths (from 23 kg m−3 to 25.5 kg m−3 with a spacing of 0.5 kg m−3; solid lines: 23, 24 and 25 kg m−3; dashed lines: 23.5, 24.5 and 25.5 kg m−3), and the flow of equatorward spiciness anomalies along isopycnal surfaces. (b) As in (a), but for anomalous upwelling that can also drive TPDV via changes in the transport of the subtropical cells (the v’Tbar hypothesis) is schematically illustrated with mean (black arrows) and anomalous (red arrows) flows, which reveal how flow along isopycnal surfaces connects the subtropics to the tropics. Both mechanisms are proposed as potential contributors to TPDV. EUC, equatorial undercurrent; LLWBC, low-latitude western boundary current. [Adapted from Capotondi et al., 2023] (Figure provided by Caroline Ummenhofer)

Naturally occurring tropical Pacific variations at timescales of 7-70 years – tropical Pacific decadal variability (TPDV) – describe basin-scale sea surface temperature (SST), sea-level pressure and heat content anomalies. Several mechanisms are proposed to explain TPDV, which can originate through oceanic processes, atmospheric processes, or as an El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) residual. In this Review, we synthesize knowledge of these mechanisms, their characteristics and contribution to TPDV. Oceanic processes include off-equatorial Rossby waves, which mediate oceanic adjustment and contribute to variations in equatorial thermocline depth and SST; variations in the strength of the shallow upper-ocean overturning circulation, which exhibit a large anti-correlation with equatorial Pacific SST at interannual and decadal timescales; and the propagation of salinity-compensated temperature (spiciness) anomalies from the subtropics to the equatorial thermocline. Atmospheric processes include midlatitude internal variability leading to tropical and subtropical wind anomalies, which result in equatorial SST anomalies and feedbacks that enhance persistence; and atmospheric teleconnections from Atlantic and Indian Ocean SST variability, which induce winds conducive to decadal anomalies of the opposite sign in the Pacific. Although uncertain, the tropical adjustment through Rossby wave activity is likely a dominant mechanism. A deeper understanding of the origin and spectral characteristics of TPDV-related winds is a key priority.

TITLE: Call for Research Proposals: Economic Opportunities for Women and Men — How Regulation and Fiscal Policy Shape Economic Opportunities in Latin America and the Caribbean

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Gender and Diversity Lab (GDLab), an initiative of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Group, has launched a new Call for Research Proposals on “Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy.”

The call seeks research proposals that can generate rigorous, credible, and policy-relevant evidence on one of the most important questions facing economies in Latin America and the Caribbean: how government regulations, financial systems, fiscal policies, and labor-market reforms affect the economic opportunities available to women and men, and how public policy can help reduce gender differences in economic outcomes.

Through this initiative, GDLab and the IDB’s Institutions for Development Sector are looking to support research that goes beyond describing gender gaps. Instead, the call emphasizes causal research capable of determining whether particular policies, reforms, regulations, or interventions actually produce different outcomes for women and men.

Researchers are encouraged to develop studies that can provide practical evidence for governments, private-sector organizations, and multilateral institutions seeking to design more effective policies and programs.

The deadline for applications is September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon).

Key Details at a Glance

Opportunity
Details

Organizer
GDLab, an IDB Group initiative, in collaboration with the IDB’s Institutions for Development Sector

Opportunity
Call for Research Proposals

Research theme
Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy

Geographic focus
Latin America and the Caribbean

Eligible research countries
One or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries

Research approach
Rigorous quantitative causal research

Accepted methodologies
Experimental, quasi-experimental, and structural models

Qualitative research
Considered only when supporting the quantitative analysis

Funding
Available under the funding categories specified in the official brochure

Application platform
Oxford Abstracts

Deadline
September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon)

Research outputs
External peer review; potential consideration for the IDB Working Paper Series; academic publication encouraged

About the Research Call

Gender differences in economic opportunities can emerge from many aspects of economic and institutional systems. Regulations can influence whether women and men can enter particular occupations, establish businesses, access financial services, participate in the labor market, or benefit equally from economic reforms.

Similarly, fiscal policy can affect households, workers, businesses, and entrepreneurs differently depending on gender, income, employment status, family responsibilities, and access to economic resources.

The new GDLab call is designed to support research that investigates these relationships systematically.

Rather than simply asking whether a gender gap exists, researchers are expected to examine questions such as:

What causes differences in economic opportunities between women and men?

Which regulations create or reduce barriers to women’s economic participation?

Do financial policies affect women and men differently?

How do fiscal reforms influence women’s and men’s labor-market outcomes?

What happens when governments introduce a particular policy or regulatory reform?

Which interventions are effective at reducing gender disparities?

Are some policies more effective for certain groups of women or men?

What policy instruments can governments use to expand economic opportunities?

How can governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations use evidence to design more effective interventions?

The emphasis on causal research is particularly important because the organizers are seeking evidence that can help distinguish correlation from actual policy effects.

Main Objective of the Call

The central objective is to support rigorous causal research addressing two broad areas.

1. Understanding how reforms affect women and men differently

The call seeks research examining how regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms affect economic opportunities for women and men.

This could include studying whether a particular reform changes:

Labor-force participation

Employment

Earnings

Entrepreneurship

Business creation

Access to finance

Business growth

Occupational opportunities

Formal employment

Access to economic resources

Productivity

Economic mobility

Other relevant measures of economic opportunity

Researchers should be able to establish credible relationships between the policy or reform being studied and the resulting outcomes.

2. Identifying policies that can reduce gender differences

The second major objective is to understand how policy instruments can improve economic opportunities and reduce differences between women and men.

This moves the research from diagnosis toward solutions.

The strongest studies may therefore demonstrate not only that a gender gap exists, but also identify which policy interventions can effectively address the gap and under what circumstances.

What Topics Will the Research Call Prioritize?

The call focuses broadly on the relationship between economic opportunity, gender, regulation, fiscal policy, financial systems, and labor-market policies.

Researchers may investigate how different forms of government intervention influence women and men differently.

Potential research areas can include the following.

1. Regulatory Reforms

Regulations can have significant effects on people’s ability to participate in economic activity.

Research could examine how changes in regulations affect women and men in areas such as:

Employment

Entrepreneurship

Business registration

Business ownership

Occupational access

Labor-market participation

Business operations

Access to markets

Formalization

Economic activity

A strong proposal could investigate whether a regulatory reform removes barriers to women’s participation or unintentionally creates new constraints.

2. Financial Policies and Access to Finance

Access to financial services is another important component of economic opportunity.

Researchers could examine whether women and men experience different outcomes from:

Credit policies

Financial inclusion programs

Lending reforms

Access to business finance

Financial regulations

Credit guarantees

Digital financial services

Other financial policy instruments

The research could investigate whether financial reforms improve women’s ability to start, operate, or expand businesses and whether the effects differ from those experienced by men.

3. Fiscal Policy

Fiscal policies can influence economic decisions and opportunities through taxation, government spending, transfers, subsidies, and other mechanisms.

Researchers could examine whether fiscal reforms have different effects on women and men.

Possible questions could include:

Does a particular tax reform affect women and men differently?

Do government transfers increase women’s economic participation?

Can fiscal incentives encourage women’s entrepreneurship?

Do public spending programs improve women’s access to economic opportunities?

How do fiscal policies interact with household responsibilities?

Are certain fiscal instruments more effective at reducing gender disparities?

The objective would be to produce evidence that can inform future fiscal-policy decisions.

4. Labor-Market Reforms

Labor-market policies are directly connected to economic opportunity.

Researchers could study the effects of reforms involving:

Employment regulations

Labor-market participation

Working conditions

Employment protections

Formal employment

Wages

Hiring

Occupational mobility

Other labor-market outcomes

The research should examine whether particular policies create different effects for women and men and whether reforms can reduce existing disparities.

Why Causal Research Is Central to This Opportunity

One of the most important requirements of this call is that proposals use rigorous quantitative methods capable of establishing causal relationships.

This means that applicants should not simply present descriptive statistics showing that women and men have different economic outcomes.

For example, a study showing that women earn less than men would demonstrate a gender difference, but by itself it would not establish what caused that difference.

The call is interested in research that can answer stronger questions such as:

What was the effect of a specific policy, regulation, or reform on women’s economic outcomes compared with what would have happened without that intervention?

This distinction makes the methodological component of the proposal extremely important.

Methodologies That May Be Used

The call specifically identifies several rigorous quantitative approaches.

Experimental Designs

Experimental research can be used when researchers can credibly introduce or evaluate an intervention and compare outcomes between relevant groups.

For example, researchers could evaluate whether a particular policy intervention changes economic outcomes for women compared with an appropriate comparison group.

Quasi-Experimental Designs

Quasi-experimental methods can be particularly useful when researchers cannot randomly assign policies or interventions.

Depending on the research question and available data, appropriate approaches could include methods designed to exploit:

Policy changes

Regulatory reforms

Eligibility thresholds

Geographic variation

Timing differences

Other institutional or policy changes

The key requirement is that the chosen methodology must provide a credible strategy for identifying causal effects.

Structural Models

The call also allows the use of structural models.

These approaches can be useful when researchers want to model economic behavior and simulate how alternative policies or reforms could affect outcomes.

A structural approach may therefore allow researchers to examine not only the effect of an existing policy but potentially the implications of alternative policy scenarios.

Role of Qualitative Research

The call does not completely exclude qualitative research.

However, qualitative components will be considered only to the extent that they support the implementation of the quantitative analysis.

This means that a proposal centered primarily on qualitative interviews, focus groups, narratives, or descriptive case studies may not align well with the call’s methodological expectations.

A stronger approach would be to use qualitative information strategically to:

Inform the design of the quantitative research

Help understand the institutional context

Support interpretation of quantitative findings

Improve implementation of the research strategy

Help explain mechanisms behind quantitative results

The quantitative causal component should remain central.

Geographic Scope: Latin America and the Caribbean

A critical eligibility condition is the geographic focus of the research.

Only proposals analyzing one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries will be considered.

This means researchers should ensure that their proposed study has a clear connection to an eligible IDB borrowing member country.

Applicants should therefore verify the IDB’s official list of borrowing member countries before developing their proposal.

The geographic requirement is important because the call is designed to generate evidence directly relevant to economic and policy challenges in the Latin America and Caribbean region.

What Makes a Strong Proposal?

Although the final proposal should follow the detailed requirements in the official brochure, the description of the call provides several clear indications of what the organizers are seeking.

A competitive proposal should ideally demonstrate:

1. A clear research question

The proposal should clearly explain what economic or policy question it intends to answer.

2. A strong gender dimension

The research should meaningfully examine differences between women and men rather than simply mentioning gender as a secondary variable.

3. A clearly defined policy or reform

The study should identify the relevant regulation, financial policy, fiscal reform, labor reform, or other policy instrument being evaluated.

4. A credible causal identification strategy

The proposal needs to explain how the researchers will establish a causal relationship.

5. Appropriate quantitative data

Applicants should demonstrate that the necessary data are available or realistically obtainable.

6. Policy relevance

The research should have potential implications for real-world decision-making.

7. Actionable recommendations

The call particularly encourages proposals that can generate recommendations for:

Governments

Private-sector organizations

Multilateral organizations

This makes policy applicability an important feature of a potentially competitive proposal.

Potential Research Questions Applicants Could Explore

The following examples illustrate the type of questions that could fit within the broad theme of the call. They are illustrative research directions, not an official list of required topics.

Regulation

How does a change in business registration regulation affect women’s business creation?

Do regulatory reforms affect female-owned businesses differently from male-owned businesses?

Which regulatory barriers have the greatest effect on women’s participation in formal economic activity?

Finance

Does improved access to formal credit increase women’s entrepreneurship?

Do financial reforms produce different business outcomes for women-owned and men-owned enterprises?

What types of financial interventions most effectively reduce gender gaps in access to capital?

Fiscal Policy

How do changes in taxation affect women’s labor-force participation?

Do government transfers have different employment effects for women and men?

Can targeted fiscal policies increase women’s participation in economic activity?

Labor Markets

How do labor regulations influence women’s formal employment?

Do changes in employment protections affect women and men differently?

Which labor-market reforms are most effective at reducing gender disparities?

Again, the strongest proposal would need to translate such a question into a rigorous causal research design.

Why This Research Matters

Gender differences in economic opportunity are not simply individual-level issues. They can affect households, businesses, labor markets, productivity, income distribution, and broader economic development.

When women face barriers to employment, entrepreneurship, finance, or economic participation, economies may fail to use a significant portion of their available human capital.

Understanding which policies actually improve economic opportunities can therefore help governments allocate resources more effectively.

This is particularly important because policies that appear gender-neutral on paper can sometimes have different effects on women and men.

For example, a policy may technically apply equally to both groups but interact differently with:

Household responsibilities

Existing employment patterns

Access to financial resources

Business ownership

Occupational segregation

Labor-market participation

Access to formal institutions

Rigorous causal research can help policymakers identify these differences and design more effective interventions.

Policy Impact Is a Major Component

The call explicitly encourages research capable of generating actionable recommendations.

This means the ultimate value of a successful study should extend beyond academic publication.

Research findings could potentially help policymakers understand:

Which policies work

Which policies do not work

For whom policies work

How large the effects are

Whether effects differ by gender

What unintended consequences may exist

How policies could be improved

Whether an intervention can be scaled

How limited public resources could be allocated more effectively

The findings may also be relevant to private-sector organizations and multilateral institutions.

Potential Benefits for Selected Researchers

Selected studies will undergo external peer review, which can provide an additional layer of academic and methodological scrutiny.

Selected research may also be considered for publication in the IDB Working Paper Series.

In addition, the call encourages publication in academic journals.

For researchers, this means the opportunity can potentially provide more than research funding. A successfully completed project could also contribute to:

Academic research

Policy evidence

Regional economic policy discussions

Gender-equality research

Government decision-making

Institutional research outputs

Peer-reviewed publications

Funding Available

The call provides funding under categories specified by the organizers.

Because the exact funding amounts and corresponding requirements are detailed in the official brochure, applicants should review the brochure carefully before preparing their budgets and submitting their proposals.

Researchers should pay particular attention to:

Available funding categories

Maximum funding amounts

Eligible expenses

Research team requirements

Proposal requirements

Methodological expectations

Application documentation

Submission procedures

Applicants should not rely solely on summaries of the call when preparing a submission. The official brochure should be treated as the authoritative source for the complete funding and eligibility conditions.

Click HERE to learn more.

How to Apply

Applications must be submitted online through the Oxford Abstracts platform.

The application process should be approached carefully because the proposal needs to demonstrate both substantive relevance and methodological rigor.

Step 1: Review the Official Call

Begin by reading the official brochure carefully.

Pay particular attention to:

Eligibility

Research priorities

Funding categories

Proposal requirements

Evaluation criteria

Submission requirements

Key dates

Step 2: Select an Eligible Country

Make sure the research analyzes one or more of the 26 IDB borrowing member countries.

Step 3: Define the Research Question

Develop a precise question related to economic opportunities for women and men and the role of:

Regulation

Financial policy

Fiscal policy

Labor-market reform

Other relevant policy instruments

Step 4: Develop the Causal Strategy

Explain exactly how the research will establish causal effects.

The proposal should identify the appropriate quantitative methodology and demonstrate why it is suitable for the research question.

Step 5: Demonstrate Data Feasibility

Applicants should consider whether the necessary data exist and whether they can realistically be accessed and analyzed within the project’s scope.

Step 6: Explain Policy Relevance

Clearly explain how the findings could inform policy decisions.

Step 7: Develop Actionable Recommendations

Where possible, demonstrate how the research could translate evidence into recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral organizations.

Step 8: Submit Through Oxford Abstracts

The completed application must be submitted through the designated Oxford Abstracts application platform before the deadline.

Application Deadline

The deadline is:

September 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. ET (noon).

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their proposals. Researchers should allow sufficient time to:

Review eligibility requirements

Develop the research question

Finalize the methodology

Verify data availability

Prepare the research team information

Develop the budget

Review supporting documentation

Complete the online application

Resolve any technical issues with submission

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The GDLab Call for Research Proposals on Economic Opportunities for Women and Men: The Role of Regulation and Fiscal Policy offers an important opportunity for researchers studying gender differences in economic participation and the effectiveness of public policy in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The call is particularly suited to research teams capable of conducting rigorous quantitative causal analysis rather than purely descriptive or qualitative studies. Its emphasis on regulatory, financial, fiscal, and labor reforms creates a broad research space for investigators examining how policy decisions shape economic opportunities for women and men.

A particularly strong application is likely to combine a well-defined policy question, a credible causal identification strategy, appropriate quantitative data, a clear gender dimension, and strong policy relevance. Researchers are also encouraged to ensure that their findings can translate into actionable recommendations for governments, businesses, and multilateral institutions.

TITLE: How to Write a Winning Mastercard Foundation Scholarship Essay

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applying for the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program can feel overwhelming, especially when you know that thousands of talented young people may be applying for the same opportunity. It is easy to assume that the strongest application belongs to the person with the highest grades, the biggest organisation, the most difficult life story or the longest list of achievements. That is not necessarily the case. A good application is one that helps the person reading it understand you. By the time they finish your essays, they should know where you are coming from, what matters to you, what you have already done with the opportunities available to you, what has stood in your way, what you still need to learn and what you hope to do with that learning. Your application should not feel like several unrelated essays written to answer different questions. It should feel like different parts of the same story. From my experience winning the Mastercard Foundation Scholarship, here are 24 tips to help you write a strong essay.

1. Know What You Are Applying For
Before writing your essays, spend time understanding the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program. Do not begin with the questions on the application form. Begin with the scholarship itself. The programme is interested in young people who have demonstrated academic potential, leadership and service to others, particularly those who have faced significant barriers to education. At Edinburgh, there is also a strong focus on climate justice and on the contribution scholars can make to their communities and home countries. This matters because it tells you that academic results alone will not carry an application. Neither will financial need on its own. Leadership without evidence of service is also not enough. The selectors are trying to understand the person behind the qualifications. They want to know what you care about, why you care about it and what you have done about it.

2. Find the Story That Connects Everything
Before you start writing, look at your experiences and ask yourself what connects them. Perhaps you grew up in a farming community and became interested in food security because you saw what unpredictable rainfall did to families around you. Maybe your experience of struggling to stay in school led you to begin supporting other girls to continue their education. Perhaps volunteering in a health centre showed you how difficult it was for people in rural communities to access basic healthcare. There should be a reason your past experiences, current work, chosen master’s programme and future plans belong in the same application. You do not need to force every achievement you have ever had into your essays. In fact, trying to mention everything can make an application weaker because the reader finishes without knowing what really matters to you. Choose the experiences that best explain your journey. Your application should make it possible for someone to say, after reading it, “I understand why this person is doing this work, why they want this degree and what they want to do afterwards.”

3. Tell Your Story Without Writing Your Entire Life History
One of the easiest mistakes to make is turning the personal essay into an autobiography. You do not need to begin with the year you were born and take the reader through primary school, secondary school, university and every organisation you have joined since then. Choose the moments that mattered. Maybe there was one experience that completely changed how you understood a problem in your community. Maybe there was a period when continuing your education became uncertain. Maybe something you witnessed pushed you to start volunteering or organising other young people. Tell us what happened, but do not stop there. Explain what you did afterwards. That is where the real story begins. Two people can experience the same difficulty and respond completely differently. What helps a selection committee understand you is not only the challenge you faced, but the decisions you made afterwards.

4. You Do Not Need the Saddest Story
The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program pays particular attention to applicants who have faced barriers to education, so it is important to explain the difficulties you have experienced. But there is a difference between explaining hardship and building your entire application around suffering. Do not try to compete over who had the hardest childhood. If your family struggled financially, explain what that meant for your education. Perhaps you worked while studying, depended on scholarships, travelled long distances to school or sometimes went without things you needed. If you experienced another type of barrier, explain that honestly too. What matters is the effect the barrier had and how you responded to it. There is no need to exaggerate a difficult experience or turn it into something more dramatic than it was. There is also no need to invent hardship because you think that is what the Foundation wants to hear. Your real story is enough. And remember that if you progress to an interview, somebody may ask you about what you wrote. Every part of your application should therefore be something you can talk about comfortably and truthfully.

5. Do Not Tell Them You Are a Leader. Show Them.
One of the most important parts of a Mastercard Foundation application is leadership. Leadership does not mean listing every position you have ever held. Being a founder, president, coordinator or team leader is useful information, but the title itself tells the selection committee very little. What did you actually do? Perhaps you noticed that girls were dropping out of school and organised a mentoring programme. Maybe you realised farmers in your community had no access to useful information and brought together volunteers to support them. Perhaps you saw something going wrong within an organisation and helped change the way the programme worked. Tell that story. What was the problem? What did you do? Who did you bring on board? What was difficult? What happened in the end? That is leadership.

6. Be Clear About What You Personally Did
Community work usually involves teams, and there is nothing wrong with saying “we”. In fact, good leadership requires working with other people. But the reader still needs to know what you did. If you write, “We trained 500 girls,” the obvious question is: what was your role? Perhaps you developed the programme, recruited volunteers, raised the funding, facilitated sessions or negotiated with community leaders. Say so. You can then explain what the whole team achieved together. This allows the person reading your application to understand both your contribution and your ability to work with others.

7. Use Numbers When They Help Tell the Story
Specific details make an application stronger. Instead of writing that your initiative “had a major impact,” tell the reader what happened. How many people participated? How many completed the programme? Did participants go back to school? Did businesses start? Did community leaders make commitments? Did the initiative expand to another community? Numbers are useful because they make your work easier to understand. But do not make numbers bigger simply because you think bigger sounds more impressive. If ten young people were involved and something meaningful happened for those ten people, tell that story well. Ten real people are better than 10,000 invented beneficiaries.

8. Small Acts of Leadership Still Count
Applicants sometimes assume that they need to have founded an NGO or run a national campaign before they can talk about leadership. You do not. You may have organised students at your university, mentored younger people, volunteered in your community, started a small business, coordinated an outreach programme or solved a problem at work. What matters is what you did with the responsibility you had. A small project that you genuinely understand and can reflect on may tell the selection committee much more about you than a large initiative where your actual role was unclear.

9. Do Not Just Tell Them What You Did. Tell Them What You Learned.
This is where many essays stop too early. An applicant describes an impressive project, gives the numbers and moves on. But the interesting question is often what happened inside you because of the experience. Maybe you learned that the solution you originally imagined was not what the community wanted. Perhaps a project failed the first time and forced you to listen differently. Maybe working with government officials showed you that community programmes alone could not solve the problem and that policy change was also necessary. Those lessons matter. They show that you are not simply collecting achievements. You are paying attention to what your experiences are teaching you.

10. It Is Fine to Talk About Something That Did Not Work
You do not have to present yourself as someone who has never made a mistake. Sometimes the best leadership stories involve something that went wrong. Perhaps attendance dropped halfway through a programme. Perhaps the first approach you tried was ineffective. Maybe you underestimated the importance of involving parents, local leaders or another group. Explain what happened and what you changed. A person who can recognise that something is not working, listen to feedback and make changes often demonstrates more leadership than someone who claims that everything they touch succeeds.

11. Think About What Remains After You Leave
Another useful question is whether the work continues without you. Did you train other young people to take over? Did the community create a committee? Did a school continue the programme? Did an organisation adopt something you introduced? Did participants go on to train others? This is important because leadership is not about making yourself indispensable. Sometimes the strongest sign that you led well is that other people are able to continue without you

12. Take the Climate Justice Question Seriously
Anyone applying to the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at Edinburgh should understand that climate justice is now an important part of the programme. However, that does not mean everybody suddenly needs to start writing about planting trees. Your task is to understand how climate change relates to the work you already care about. If you work in education, consider what happens to children’s schooling when floods destroy homes or when drought reduces family income. If you work with women and girls, think about how climate shocks can increase unpaid care work, displacement, poverty or vulnerability. If you work in agriculture, the connection may be much more direct: changing rainfall, declining yields, food insecurity or the need for climate-resilient farming. Climate justice is also about fairness. Who suffers most when climate disasters happen? Who has the least money to recover? Who is often left out when decisions about climate responses are made? Those questions can help you find an honest connection between your work and climate justice. Do not add climate change to your essay simply because you know the programme wants to see it. The connection should make sense.

13. Explain Why You Need a Master’s Degree Now
Another important part of the application is explaining why you need further study. Saying that you have always dreamed of studying abroad is not enough. Ask yourself what you have reached in your work that you cannot solve with your current knowledge. Perhaps you have spent years implementing community programmes but now need to understand how policy is made. Maybe you work with small businesses but need stronger knowledge of finance and entrepreneurship. Perhaps you have experience advocating for girls’ education but need better research skills to produce evidence that can influence government. This is the gap your master’s degree should fill. When this part of the application is written well, the degree feels like the natural next step rather than simply another qualification you want to collect.

14. Research the Course Properly
Do not choose a programme and then write that you want to attend a university because it is a prestigious university. For example, almost every applicant knows Edinburgh University has an international reputation. Instead, look closely at the master’s programme itself. Read the course descriptions. Look at the modules. Understand the research opportunities. Find out whether there are centres, lecturers or areas of work connected to what you want to do. Then explain why those things matter to you. If there is a course that will help you understand a particular issue better, say so. If the programme will teach you a research method you need for your future work, explain that. The point is not to praise the school. The point is to show that you have thought carefully about what you need to learn and why Edinburgh is a good place to learn it.

15. Be Clear About What You Want to Do Afterwards
“I want to give back to my community” is a good intention, but it is not yet a plan. What does giving back look like? Do you want to return to an organisation you already work with? Expand an existing programme? Join government? Build a social enterprise? Conduct research? Work on policy? Train other young people? Tell the reader. You do not need to know exactly what your life will look like ten years from now, but there should be a direction. Your plans should also grow out of work you have already started whenever possible. If somebody has spent years working in education and suddenly announces in the final paragraph that they plan to become a renewable-energy entrepreneur, the reader will naturally wonder where that ambition came from. Your future should make sense when placed beside your past.

16. Think Beyond What the Scholarship Will Do for You
Of course receiving a fully funded scholarship can change your life. But your application should not end there. Think about who else benefits. If you gain new knowledge, what will you do with it? Which community, organisation, sector or group of people could benefit from what you learn? The Mastercard Foundation is investing in people, but it is also interested in what those people will go on to contribute. The strongest applications make that wider benefit easy to see.

17. Do Not Hide Your Academic Story Behind Your Grades
Good academic results are important, but your transcript does not tell the whole story. Explain what you have enjoyed learning and how your academic interests developed. If you completed research that changed how you understood a problem, mention it. If a particular course led you into your current field, explain why. If your grades were affected by difficult circumstances, you can provide context without turning the section into a long defence of your transcript The question the selection committee ultimately needs to answer is whether you are ready to succeed academically at Edinburgh. Give them enough information to believe that you are.

18. Explain Financial Need Properly
If the application asks about financial circumstances, be specific. “My family cannot afford my education” is understandable, but it leaves many questions unanswered. What has the financial situation meant in practical terms? Maybe you worked while attending university. Perhaps family income could cover tuition but not accommodation. Maybe you depended on bursaries throughout your undergraduate education. Perhaps studying overseas would simply be impossible without full funding. Explain your circumstances clearly and without embarrassment. Financial need does not make you less capable. It simply explains why talent and opportunity have not always existed in equal measure.

19. Write Like Yourself
You do not need complicated vocabulary to win a scholarship. In fact, writing becomes weaker when every paragraph is filled with words such as “transformative”, “catalytic”, “multifaceted”, “groundbreaking” and “impactful”. Tell the story plainly. Instead of saying that you “spearheaded a transformative intervention that empowered marginalised youth,” you can often say exactly what happened: “I organised weekly sessions for 40 young people who had dropped out of school and worked with two local businesses to place 12 of them in apprenticeships.” The second sentence is easier to believe because the reader can see it. Good scholarship writing is not about sounding important. It is about being clear.

20. Answer the Question You Were Asked
This sounds obvious, but many applicants lose valuable space because they tell a good story without fully answering the question. Scholarship questions often contain several parts. If the question asks about an experience that shaped you, what you learned and how you will contribute to the Scholars community, all three parts matter. Before writing your answer, separate the question into its individual parts. Then check your finished essay against them. Beautiful writing cannot compensate for an unanswered question.

21. Do Not Waste Your Word Count
Most scholarship essays are short, which means every paragraph needs to earn its place. Do not spend 300 words giving background when the most important part of the story is what you did. Give enough context for the reader to understand the situation and then move quickly to your actions, results and learning. If a sentence could appear in almost anybody’s scholarship essay, ask whether you really need it. Phrases such as “education is the key to success” and “young people are the leaders of tomorrow” use words without telling the reader anything about you. Use that space for your own story.

22. Prepare Your Referees
Choose referees who actually know you. A famous person who met you twice may provide a weaker reference than a lecturer, supervisor or mentor who has watched you work over several years. Let your referees know what you are applying for. Share your CV and explain the master’s programme you hope to study. Tell them about your plans. A good reference should add something to your application rather than simply repeat that you are hardworking.

23. Remember That Your Application May Become Your Interview
If you are invited for an interview, your essays will likely shape some of the conversation. That is another reason to write honestly. Know the stories you included. Know your numbers. Be able to explain what your role was and what you learned. You do not need to memorise your essays. You should simply know your own experiences well enough to talk about them naturally.

24. Read the Entire Application Before You Submit
Once you have finished all the essays, do not review them only one at a time. Read the whole application from beginning to end. Does it feel like the same person wrote every section? Does the reader understand what you care about? Can they see evidence that you have already done something about it? Does your chosen master’s programme make sense? Do your future plans follow naturally from the experiences you describe? Most importantly, can they see what the opportunity would allow you to do that you cannot currently do? If those answers are clear, your application is moving in the right direction.

One Final Thing to Remember
A strong Mastercard Foundation application is not a promise that you will suddenly become committed to your community after receiving a scholarship. Your life should already contain some evidence of the values you are writing about. You may still be early in your journey. Your work may still be small. You may have made mistakes along the way. That is fine. What matters is that there is already something to build on. Your application should help the reader see that you have started somewhere, learned from what you have done, reached a point where you need more knowledge and have thought seriously about what you would do with that knowledge. The scholarship then becomes part of a journey already underway, rather than the beginning of one. That is the story worth telling.

I hope you get in, am rooting for you!
