TITLE: Braiding Seeds Fellowship 2027–2028: $50,000 Stipend and Mentorship for Beginning BIPOC Farmers in the U.S.

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Braiding Seeds Fellowship is an 18-month fellowship designed to support beginning farmers and land stewards through financial assistance, professional development, mentorship, coaching, and opportunities to strengthen community-based agricultural and land stewardship projects.

Founded by Soul Fire Farm Institute in partnership with the Federation of Southern Cooperatives/Land Assistance Fund, the fellowship draws inspiration from the history of ancestral grandmothers who braided seeds into their hair before being forced onto transatlantic slave ships. The programme carries forward this legacy by supporting farmers working to sustain and pass on land-based knowledge, food systems, and community resources.

Applications are currently open for the 2027–2028 cohort, with the application deadline set for September 25, 2026, at 11:59 PM EST.

What Is the Braiding Seeds Fellowship?

The Braiding Seeds Fellowship is a programme for beginning farmers and land stewards who are developing projects connected to farming, food production, ecological stewardship, and community impact.

The fellowship was created to provide resources to Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) beginning farmers whose work contributes to the development and continuation of land-based livelihoods.

The programme seeks to support farmers not simply through financial assistance, but through a combination of:

Financial support

Professional development

One-to-one mentorship

Individualized coaching

Farm finance support

Business planning assistance

Workshops

Cohort gatherings

Community and professional networking

The fellowship is intended to help farmers strengthen their projects and livelihoods while contributing to broader community-based agricultural work.

The Historical Meaning Behind the Fellowship

The Braiding Seeds Fellowship takes its name and inspiration from a story of resilience and preservation.

The programme honours ancestral grandmothers who, according to its stated purpose, braided seeds and promises into their hair before being forced onto transatlantic slave ships. The seeds represented a belief that their descendants would survive and would eventually inherit, plant, and pass on those seeds.

The fellowship connects this historical legacy to contemporary farming and land stewardship.

Its purpose is therefore not only to provide funding to individual farmers. It also seeks to support the continuation of agricultural knowledge, relationships with land, food sovereignty, and community-based farming practices.

The programme’s previous cohorts include fellows working across the Southeast and Northeast United States, including areas associated with the Underground Railroad and the Great Migration.

The fellowship describes its broader goal as helping to bridge North-South connections and generations of farmers, including legacy-returning generations.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed to Support?

The Braiding Seeds Fellowship is specifically intended for beginning farmers and land stewards who are Black, Indigenous, or People of Color.

Applicants must also meet the programme’s experience requirements and geographic requirements.

The fellowship is designed for people who are already engaged in farming or land stewardship rather than individuals who have no experience with a farming or land-based project.

Minimum Experience Requirement

Applicants must have:

At least one year of farming or land stewardship experience

No more than three years of experience running their own farm or land stewardship project

Applicants must also be 18 years of age or older.

What Does “Farmer” Mean for This Fellowship?

The fellowship uses a broad definition of what constitutes a farmer.

For the purposes of the programme, a farmer is someone whose livelihood involves working collaboratively with an ecosystem to produce things such as:

Food

Forage

Seeds

Medicine

Crops

Other land-based products

The programme recognizes that people involved in this type of work may use different terms to describe themselves or their activities.

Examples listed in the fellowship information include:

Peasant

Urban grower

Campesino

Farmworker

Row crop farmer

Shepherd

Herb grower

Schoolyard gardener

Nonprofit farmer

Ocean farmer

Orchardist

Fiber farmer

The common element is the relationship between the person’s work and the land or ecosystem as a means of securing the necessities of life.

The fellowship is particularly interested in farmers producing at a scale capable of supporting a wider community, rather than projects intended only to provide for one household or a small group of family members and friends.

$50,000 Fellowship Stipend

One of the major features of the Braiding Seeds Fellowship is its $50,000 stipend.

This financial support is intended to help fellows dedicate time and resources toward their farming and land stewardship work during the fellowship period.

The stipend forms part of a broader support package that also includes professional development, mentorship, coaching, and farm business assistance.

Professional Development and Mentorship

Financial support is only one component of the fellowship.

Fellows receive access to a menu of professional development opportunities that includes:

One-to-one mentorship

Workshops

Farm finance support

Business plan support

Individualized coaching

Cohort gatherings

Professional networking

These resources are designed to help fellows strengthen both the practical and organizational aspects of their projects.

Individualized Coaching

Fellows receive individualized coaching throughout the programme.

This can provide a space to discuss challenges, goals, project development, and other issues connected to their farming or land stewardship work.

The fellowship also requires regular one-to-one check-in meetings with fellowship staff.

Cohort-Based Learning and Networking

The programme includes both online and in-person cohort gatherings.

These gatherings provide opportunities for fellows to:

Build relationships with other farmers

Exchange experiences

Develop professional connections

Participate in professional development

Learn from other land-based practitioners

Build longer-term networks

The cohort model is an important component of the programme because fellows are not participating in isolation. They become part of a wider group of farmers and land stewards.

Fellowship Duration and Dates

The Braiding Seeds Fellowship is an 18-month programme.

For the upcoming cohort, the fellowship is scheduled to begin on:

January 15, 2027

The programme is scheduled to end on:

June 15, 2028

This extended period allows fellows to work on their projects while participating in professional development and mentorship activities.

Fellowship Obligations

Applicants should understand that receiving the fellowship involves responsibilities in addition to receiving financial support.

Farming as the Main Work

Farming will be the primary work of fellows.

During the growing season, fellows are expected to dedicate a minimum average of:

20+ hours per week

to their farms.

Professional Development Requirement

Fellows must complete at least:

50 hours of professional development over 18 months

The professional development hours can be completed through the menu of opportunities provided by the fellowship, including mentorship, workshops, farm finance assistance, and business planning support.

Cohort Participation

Fellows are expected to attend online and in-person cohort gatherings.

These gatherings are designed for networking and professional development.

Feedback to the Programme

Fellows are also asked to provide feedback and suggestions that can help inform future years of the fellowship.

Regular Check-Ins

Fellows will participate in regular one-to-one meetings with fellowship staff.

These check-ins provide ongoing contact between fellows and programme staff throughout the fellowship.

The application process for the upcoming cohort follows a specific schedule.

Applicants should prepare several supporting materials before beginning the online application.

The fellowship recommends gathering the following materials.

1. Three References

Applicants must provide a list of three references.

Each reference should include:

References can come from a variety of relationships and settings.

4. Letter of Recommendation

Applicants need:

5. Detailed Budget

Applicants who prefer to prepare their responses before entering them into the online form can review the non-fillable English application PDF and Spanish PDF provided by the programme.

Applicants can also access the recording and presentation slides.

The fellowship recommends attending or reviewing this information session before booking individual technical assistance.

One-to-One Application Technical Assistance

Applicants can receive technical assistance with specific questions about the application.

The fellowship offers one 30-minute one-to-one technical assistance session per applicant.

can contact the fellowship team for assistance.

How Are Fellows Selected?

Applications are reviewed by a selection committee made up of alumni and representatives from Black- and Indigenous-centered farming organizations in the Northeast and Southeast.

The selection group includes representatives associated with organisations such as:

Federation of Southern Cooperatives

Land Loss Prevention Project

National Black Food and Justice Alliance

Native American Food Sovereignty Alliance

Northeast Farmers of Color Land Trust

New Communities Inc./SW GA Project

Black Church Food Security Network

Southeastern African American Farmers’ Organic Network

Farms to Grow

Black Farmer Fund

Farm School NYC

Sierra Seeds Cooperative

Jubilee Justice

Sipp Culture

Intertribal Agriculture Council

Each application is assigned to at least two reviewers, with reviewers assigned randomly.

The review process considers both the applicant’s eligibility and the quality and readiness of the proposed project.

Application Review Criteria

The fellowship provides a detailed review rubric.

Reviewers consider whether applicants demonstrate:

Clear Project Description

Applicants should clearly describe their farm or land stewardship project.

Commitment to the Project

The application should demonstrate the applicant’s commitment or ability to commit to the project.

Alignment With Fellowship Values

Reviewers consider whether the project’s mission and approach align with the fellowship’s stated commitment to:

The flourishing of Black agrarianism

Indigenous sovereignty

Liberation of people impacted by racial capitalism and settler colonialism

Authentic Responses

The application includes a question for which reviewers specifically assess whether the applicant has provided a thorough and authentic response.

Food Sovereignty

Reviewers consider whether the project has an intersectional vision and approach to food sovereignty.

Community Involvement and Impact

Applicants should demonstrate strong community involvement and potential community impact.

Recommendation Letter

The applicant’s reference letter is also considered in relation to community involvement.

Long-Term Impact

Reviewers consider whether the project is positioned to continue producing community impact over the long term.

Goals and Timeline

Applicants should identify:

Clear goals

A timeline

Planned next steps

The reviewers also consider whether these goals, timelines, and next steps are realistic and attainable.

Project Readiness

Applicants should demonstrate readiness to undertake and sustain the project.

Financial Need

The application considers whether the project has financial or other support needs that are unlikely to be met without the fellowship.

Land Access

Applicants should have a clear plan for accessing land.

Project Support

Reviewers consider whether applicants have adequate support, including:

Collaborators

Partners

Team members

Other relevant support systems

to realistically implement their stated project goals.

Why Does the Fellowship Have a Strong Focus on Black Farmers?

The fellowship explicitly explains its focus on rebuilding Black agrarianism in the context of historical land dispossession.

According to the programme’s information, Black farmers owned between 16 and 19 million acres of farmland at their peak in 1910, representing approximately 14% of U.S. farm operators.

The fellowship states that more than 90% of this land was lost during the 20th century, citing factors including:

State-sanctioned violence

Discriminatory lending practices

Vulnerabilities associated with heirs’ property

Systematic legal exclusion

The programme states that Black farmers today own less than 3 million acres and represent just over 1% of U.S. farmers.

Within this context, the fellowship reserves awards for Black fellows as part of its stated effort to rebuild Black agrarianism.

Allocation of Fellowship Spaces

The programme states that it normally provides:

7 awards reserved for Black fellows

2–3 awards reserved for Indigenous fellows

1 space usually reserved for other People of Color

The fellowship explains that this structure reflects its focus on addressing historical dispossession and supporting Black agrarianism while working in solidarity and collaboration with Indigenous peoples.

Language and Spanish-Speaking Applicants

The fellowship recognizes that applicants come from communities with different experiences relating to:

Race

Gender

Immigration status

Class

Language

The programme states that it celebrates and uplifts the diversity of languages spoken by applicants.

A Spanish-language application is available.

However, the fellowship is conducted primarily in English. The programme acknowledges that this can create limitations for some applicants and states that it aims to support non-native English speakers while recognizing that there may be gaps in available resources.

$2,500 Seed Grants

In addition to the fellowship positions, the programme will also award 12 Seed Grants of $2,500 each.

These seed grants provide another form of financial support for farming and ecological land stewardship projects.

Importantly, receiving a seed grant does not positively or negatively affect an applicant’s likelihood of receiving the fellowship in the future.

Seed Grant Requirements

Seed Grant recipients must:

Use the funds by December 2027

Use the funds for charitable and/or educational purposes

Use the funds in connection with farming and/or ecological land stewardship

Complete a short questionnaire explaining how the funds were used

The Seed Grant programme is separate from the main fellowship award.

The programme notes that future cohorts may have a different geographic focus.

Preparing a Strong Application

TITLE: APRM Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation 2027: Virtual Training on Agenda 2063 and the SDGs

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The African Peer Review Mechanism (APRM) has announced its Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTrC) for Sustainable Development, a virtual capacity-building programme designed to strengthen African expertise, peer learning and partnerships for sustainable development.

Under the theme “Accelerating the Implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs in a Changing Global Order,” the training will explore how South-South and Triangular Cooperation can be used to advance Africa’s development priorities, strengthen institutional capacity, mobilize resources and support implementation of the African Union Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

The third edition is scheduled to start on 1 November 2027 and will be delivered virtually, making it accessible to eligible participants across Africa and to Africans in the diaspora.

APRM Third Continental Training 2027: Programme Overview

The training is being organized as part of APRM’s efforts to strengthen knowledge and practical capacity around South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTrC).

South-South Cooperation generally refers to collaboration and knowledge exchange among countries of the Global South, while Triangular Cooperation involves collaboration among developing countries with support from an additional development partner, institution or organization.

The programme recognizes the importance of these approaches in helping African countries and institutions respond to changing global economic, political and development dynamics.

Key programme details

Programme: APRM Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation

Theme: Accelerating the Implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs in a Changing Global Order

Starting date: 1 November 2027

Modality: Virtual/Online

Organizer: African Peer Review Mechanism (APRM)

Focus: South-South and Triangular Cooperation, Agenda 2063, SDGs, development partnerships, financing, knowledge management, youth, gender and inclusive governance

Geographic focus: Africa, with participation also identified for Africans in the diaspora

The official APRM announcement does not currently state an application deadline. Therefore, applicants should monitor the official announcement for application procedures, registration details and any future deadline.

What Is South-South and Triangular Cooperation?

South-South and Triangular Cooperation has become an increasingly important mechanism for countries and institutions in the Global South to exchange knowledge, technology, expertise, resources and development solutions.

Rather than relying exclusively on traditional development cooperation models, SSTrC encourages countries and institutions to learn from one another and develop partnerships based on shared experiences and complementary capabilities.

For Africa, this can include cooperation in areas such as:

Economic development

Education and skills development

Healthcare

Agriculture and food security

Technology and digital transformation

Climate action

Governance

Public-sector reform

Youth development

Gender equality

Infrastructure

Trade and investment

Sustainable development

The APRM training is therefore designed to help participants understand how these cooperation mechanisms can contribute to Africa’s long-term transformation.

Main Objectives of the APRM Training

The programme has several interconnected objectives.

1. Strengthen capacity for South-South and Triangular Cooperation

Participants will develop a stronger understanding of SSTrC concepts, approaches and practical applications.

This can help professionals and institutions identify opportunities for cooperation, develop partnerships and contribute more effectively to development initiatives.

2. Promote peer learning and exchange of best practices

The training will provide an opportunity for participants to learn from experiences across different African contexts and from other development stakeholders.

Peer learning can help participants identify approaches that can potentially be adapted to their own institutions, countries or communities.

3. Enhance implementation of Agenda 2063 and the SDGs

A major focus of the programme is connecting South-South and Triangular Cooperation with the implementation of Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals.

This is particularly important because Africa’s development priorities require coordinated action across governments, civil society, development organizations, academia, communities and the private sector.

4. Foster multi-stakeholder partnerships

The programme also seeks to encourage collaboration between different stakeholders working toward sustainable development.

Participants may gain a better understanding of how governments, development partners, civil society organizations, academia, communities and other actors can work together to advance development priorities.

APRM SSTrC Training Programme Modules

The training consists of five major modules, with a new module on Youth, Gender and Inclusive Governance included in this third edition.

Module I: South-South and Triangular Cooperation in a Changing Global Order

The first module will examine the background and evolution of South-South and Triangular Cooperation within a changing global environment.

Topics include the role and influence of:

The G20

BRICS and other emerging blocs

Global South cooperation

Changing international development partnerships

New geopolitical and economic dynamics

Emerging models of international cooperation

This module is intended to help participants understand the broader environment in which SSTrC operates.

Module II: SSTrC, Agenda 2063 and the SDGs

The second module focuses on the relationship between South-South and Triangular Cooperation and Africa’s development frameworks.

Participants will explore how SSTrC can contribute to:

Agenda 2063 implementation

SDG implementation

National development priorities

Regional development

Institutional cooperation

Knowledge and technology exchange

Sustainable development initiatives

This module is particularly relevant for professionals involved in development planning, policy, programme implementation and partnerships.

Module III: Financing the Africa We Want

The third module focuses on financing development through South-South and Triangular Cooperation programmes.

Access to sustainable financing remains a major issue for development initiatives across Africa. The module therefore examines how cooperation mechanisms can contribute to mobilizing resources and supporting development programmes.

Potential areas of interest include:

Development financing

Partnership financing

Resource mobilization

Cooperation programmes

Financing for Agenda 2063

Financing for sustainable development

Module IV: Monitoring, Evaluation and Knowledge Management

The fourth module focuses on monitoring, evaluation and knowledge management in SSTrC.

Effective cooperation requires more than establishing partnerships. Stakeholders must also be able to measure results, document lessons and use evidence to improve future programmes.

Participants will therefore explore the importance of:

Monitoring development programmes

Evaluating outcomes

Measuring impact

Documenting lessons learned

Managing institutional knowledge

Sharing best practices

Improving future cooperation initiatives

Module V: Youth, Gender and Inclusive Governance

The fifth module is a new component of the programme.

It focuses on:

Youth participation

Gender equality

Inclusive governance

Participation in development processes

Representation of diverse groups

Community-level development

Inclusive approaches to SSTrC

The inclusion of this module recognizes that sustainable development requires meaningful participation from young people, women and other groups that contribute to Africa’s transformation.

Who Can Participate?

The APRM identifies a broad range of potential participants. The programme is not limited to government officials.

Target participants include:

Individuals working within or connected to APRM National Structures are among the intended participants.

The programme specifically identifies youth and women as target participant groups, particularly those involved in development, governance, community initiatives or Agenda 2063-related activities.

Africans in the diaspora are also identified as a target group, creating an opportunity for Africans living outside the continent to engage with the programme.

This makes the programme relevant to individuals working at both institutional and grassroots levels.

Geographic Eligibility: Who Can Apply?

Based on the APRM’s stated target participants, the opportunity is primarily designed for Africans and people working on Africa’s development, including Africans in the diaspora.

The announcement does not provide a specific list of eligible African countries. It identifies Africans in the diaspora as a target group and refers broadly to APRM structures, African development stakeholders, civil society, academia, development partners, practitioners and community leaders.

Therefore, interested applicants should check the official registration or application instructions once released to confirm any specific nationality, residency or institutional requirements.

There is no indication in the announcement that eligibility is restricted by race or ethnicity. The geographic emphasis is on Africa and Africans in the diaspora.

Why This Training Matters

The programme is particularly relevant at a time when African countries are navigating significant changes in the global development and geopolitical environment.

South-South and Triangular Cooperation can provide opportunities for African countries and institutions to:

Exchange practical knowledge

Share successful development models

Build institutional partnerships

For individual participants, the training can also strengthen their understanding of international development cooperation and partnership-building.

The APRM Third Continental Training on South-South and Triangular Cooperation for Sustainable Development presents an important learning opportunity for African development practitioners, young people, women, civil society actors, academics, community leaders, development partners and Africans in the diaspora.

For professionals and community leaders working to advance sustainable development in Africa, the programme can provide a useful platform for strengthening knowledge, learning from peers and understanding how partnerships can be used to translate development commitments into practical action.

TITLE: Berenson Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard University’s I Tatti: $5,200 Monthly Funding for Renaissance Scholars in Florence, Italy

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Berenson Fellowship at Harvard University’s Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies offers an exceptional residential research opportunity for scholars whose work explores the connections between Italy and the wider world during the Renaissance.

Supported by The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund, the fellowship is designed to encourage research into “Italy in the World” by examining the transnational exchanges, encounters, dialogues, and cultural relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance, broadly understood as the period from the 14th through the 17th century.

The fellowship is particularly interested in research that moves beyond a narrowly European understanding of the Renaissance and examines Italy’s relationships with cultures and societies across regions such as Africa, the Mediterranean, Latin America, and Asia.

Selected Fellows will be based in Florence, Italy, where they will have dedicated time for research, access to Harvard’s extensive scholarly resources at I Tatti, and opportunities to participate in the intellectual life of the Center. The fellowship provides USD 5,200 per month, in addition to a relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

Up to four Berenson Fellowships are awarded each year, making this a highly selective opportunity for established and emerging scholars working on original research related to the Renaissance and its global connections.

What Is the Berenson Fellowship?

The Berenson Fellowship is a residential research fellowship hosted by Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies in Florence.

The fellowship takes its name from Bernard Berenson, an influential scholar and art historian associated with I Tatti. In his 1956 statement, “On the Future of I Tatti,” Berenson expressed a vision in which scholars would come from different parts of the world and develop a broad understanding of the Mediterranean and its surrounding regions.

The Berenson Fellowship builds on this vision by encouraging scholarship that examines the Renaissance from a geographically expansive perspective.

Rather than treating the Renaissance solely as a European phenomenon, the fellowship seeks to support research investigating the connections between Italy and other cultures and regions.

These connections may include:

Cultural exchanges between Italy and Africa.

Italy’s historical relationships with Mediterranean societies.

Connections between Italy and Asian cultures.

Transnational relationships involving Latin America.

Intellectual exchanges across geographical boundaries.

Movement of ideas, artistic traditions, texts, technologies, and people.

Cross-cultural interactions during the Renaissance and early modern period.

The influence of non-European cultures on Italian Renaissance developments.

Italy’s role within wider networks of the early modern world.

The fellowship therefore offers an opportunity for scholars to develop research that places the Italian Renaissance within a broader international and intercultural context.

Berenson Fellowship Research Theme: “Italy in the World”

The central theme of the fellowship is “Italy in the World.”

Applicants are expected to propose projects that address transnational dialogues between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance.

The Renaissance is interpreted broadly for purposes of this fellowship, covering approximately the 14th to 17th centuries.

This broad chronological and geographical approach allows researchers to investigate subjects that cross conventional disciplinary and regional boundaries.

A strong project should therefore demonstrate how Italy was connected to wider intellectual, cultural, artistic, political, scientific, or social networks.

For example, research could examine:

Italian artistic exchanges with other regions.

Mediterranean intellectual networks.

African-Italian cultural encounters.

Italian relationships with Asian societies.

The circulation of Renaissance texts across borders.

Music and musical traditions moving between cultures.

Scientific knowledge exchanged between Italy and other regions.

Philosophical interactions between Italian and non-Italian thinkers.

Architectural influences crossing geographical boundaries.

Literary connections between Italian writers and writers from other cultures.

Trade, travel, migration, and their influence on Renaissance culture.

The movement of artistic techniques, manuscripts, objects, and ideas.

Cross-cultural encounters involving the Mediterranean and its hinterlands.

The key consideration is that the project should contribute to a broader understanding of the Renaissance as a connected and geographically expansive historical phenomenon.

Academic Fields Supported by the Fellowship

The Berenson Fellowship welcomes scholars working across the range of disciplines supported by I Tatti.

Applicants may come from fields including:

Architecture and the Arts

Researchers can investigate architecture, painting, sculpture, visual culture, material culture, artistic exchange, and related areas.

Projects may explore how artistic ideas, styles, techniques, or objects moved between Italy and other parts of the world.

History

Historical research may examine political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic, or intellectual relationships between Italy and other regions during the Renaissance.

Philosophy

Philosophical projects may explore intellectual exchanges, circulation of ideas, philosophical traditions, and relationships between Italian thinkers and intellectual traditions elsewhere.

Literature

Researchers may examine texts, literary movements, translation, cultural exchange, multilingual literary networks, and relationships between Italian and non-Italian literary traditions.

Music

Music scholars can investigate musical exchange, performance traditions, composers, instruments, musical theory, and the movement of music across geographical and cultural boundaries.

History of Science

Projects may investigate scientific knowledge, technologies, discoveries, instruments, scholarly networks, and intellectual exchanges linking Italy with other parts of the world.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed project clearly fits within the intellectual scope of I Tatti while addressing the fellowship’s emphasis on transnational connections.

Why the Berenson Fellowship Is a Valuable Research Opportunity

The fellowship is designed to provide scholars with something that is increasingly difficult to obtain: extended, uninterrupted time to focus primarily on research.

I Tatti emphasizes a combination of substantial scholarly resources and relatively few obligations.

Fellows can devote their time to developing their research project rather than balancing it with extensive teaching or administrative responsibilities.

The fellowship provides:

A residential research appointment in Florence.

A grant of USD 5,200 per month.

A relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

Access to the scholarly resources of Harvard’s I Tatti Center.

Access to the Biblioteca Berenson.

A dedicated desk or carrel in the library.

Opportunities to participate in the intellectual community at I Tatti.

Participation in selected activities organized at the Center.

Opportunities to attend conferences, lectures, and concerts.

Interaction with scholars from different countries and academic disciplines.

A research environment designed to minimize interruptions and obligations.

These resources can be particularly valuable for scholars preparing a major scholarly publication, completing an extensive research project, or developing research that requires access to specialized materials available in Florence.

Fellowship Duration

The Berenson Fellowship is a residential fellowship lasting either four or six months.

Applicants are asked to indicate their preferred fellowship period:

Fall: September through December.

Winter-Spring: January through June.

The exact fellowship arrangement will depend on the appointment offered.

Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows are expected to live in the Florence area and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti.

This requirement reflects the Center’s goal of creating an active scholarly community in which Fellows interact with other researchers and participate in the intellectual life of the institution.

Financial Support and Fellowship Grant

One of the major attractions of the Berenson Fellowship is its substantial financial support.

Selected Fellows receive:

Monthly Grant

The fellowship provides a grant of:

USD 5,200 per month

This provides substantial financial support during the residential research period.

Relocation Support

In addition to the monthly grant, Fellows can receive a one-time relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

The supplement is intended to assist with expenses associated with relocating to Florence for the fellowship.

Housing

Because the fellowship is residential, Fellows must live in the Florence area.

When possible, I Tatti will set aside an apartment for the Fellow’s use. The apartment is provided rent free, although the Fellow is responsible for utility charges.

If an I Tatti apartment is not available, the Center will provide a housing subsidy to help offset rental expenses.

This housing arrangement can significantly reduce the cost of relocating to Florence for the fellowship period.

Access to Harvard’s Scholarly Resources

Berenson Fellows enjoy the privileges available to Fellows at I Tatti.

One of the most important resources is the Biblioteca Berenson, which Fellows can use seven days a week.

This access is particularly important for scholars whose research requires specialized Renaissance materials and scholarly resources.

Fellows also have their own desk or carrel in the Library.

However, Term Fellows do not receive a separate private office or study.

The research environment is therefore centered around the library and broader scholarly community of I Tatti.

Participation in the I Tatti Intellectual Community

Although Fellows receive substantial freedom to focus on their research, the fellowship is not intended to be an isolated research experience.

Selected activities at I Tatti are reserved for Fellows, and Fellows are expected to become part of the wider scholarly community.

They are expected to participate in activities such as:

Conferences.

Academic lectures.

Concerts.

Scholarly gatherings.

Other intellectual activities organized by I Tatti.

This community-oriented approach allows researchers to exchange ideas with scholars working across different disciplines and geographical areas.

For applicants interested in building international academic networks, this aspect of the fellowship can be particularly valuable.

Berenson Fellowship Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy several important eligibility requirements.

PhD Requirement

At the time of application, candidates must already hold a PhD.

Applicants will be required to upload a scan of their PhD certificate as part of the application process.

This means the fellowship is not intended for doctoral students who are still completing their first PhD.

Applicants Cannot Be Pursuing a Second PhD

Candidates may not be working on a second PhD at the time of application.

This requirement should be carefully considered by applicants who have completed one doctoral degree but are enrolled in another doctoral programme.

Research Project Requirement

Applicants must apply with a specific research project.

The proposed project should align with the Berenson Fellowship’s central focus on Italy in the World and the transnational relationships between Italy and other cultures during the Renaissance.

The proposed research can form part of a larger scholarly project.

However, applicants must be able to demonstrate that the specific project presented in the application is sufficiently developed and appropriate for the fellowship period.

Full-Time Research Commitment

Successful Fellows are expected to work solely on the project for which they applied.

They are not permitted to simultaneously work on editing other book or article projects.

This is an important condition because the fellowship is designed to provide uninterrupted time for a particular research project.

Applicants should therefore select a project that can benefit substantially from four or six months of concentrated research.

English and Italian Language Requirements

Applicants must be:

Conversant in English, and

Familiar with Italian.

The language requirement is important because the fellowship is based at an Italian Renaissance research center in Florence and involves engagement with Italian scholarly resources and the wider academic community.

Research Must Be Feasible in Florence

Applicants must demonstrate that it is possible to conduct most of their research in Florence.

This does not necessarily mean that every source required for the project must be located in Florence.

Rather, the proposed research should be sufficiently connected to the resources available in Florence to justify a residential appointment at I Tatti.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider the research materials, archives, libraries, collections, and scholarly resources they will need during the fellowship.

Priority for Early- and Mid-Career Scholars

The fellowship gives priority to early- and mid-career scholars.

This does not mean that senior scholars are necessarily excluded. Rather, the selection process gives particular consideration to applicants at earlier and middle stages of their academic careers.

Candidates should therefore explain clearly how the fellowship would contribute to the development and advancement of their research.

Global Eligibility: Scholars From All Nations Can Apply

The Berenson Fellowship welcomes applications from scholars from all nations.

There is no stated restriction limiting applications to a particular country, nationality, continent, or racial group.

The fellowship specifically gives special consideration to candidates who do not have regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to scholars based outside Italy who would significantly benefit from spending an extended research period at I Tatti.

Who Can Apply?

In general, the opportunity is aimed at:

Scholars who already hold a PhD.

Researchers working in relevant Renaissance and early modern fields.

Early-career scholars.

Mid-career scholars.

Scholars researching transnational relationships involving Italy.

Researchers working in architecture and the arts.

Historians.

Philosophers.

Literature scholars.

Music scholars.

Historians of science.

Scholars whose projects can be substantially researched in Florence.

Researchers conversant in English and familiar with Italian.

Scholars from any country or nationality.

The fellowship is therefore international in scope, and scholars from Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, Oceania, the Middle East, and other regions may apply, provided they meet the academic and research requirements.

Who Is Not Eligible?

Potential applicants should take note of several restrictions.

You may not qualify if:

You do not yet have a PhD at the time of application.

You are currently working toward a second PhD.

Your proposed project cannot be substantially researched in Florence.

You are unable to work in English and do not have familiarity with Italian.

You intend to use the fellowship period to work simultaneously on unrelated books or articles.

You plan to take on teaching or other professional obligations during the fellowship.

You have previously held a Term Fellowship at I Tatti, except if you previously held a Graduate Fellowship.

You have already used the fellowship opportunity in a way that conflicts with the Term Fellowship’s one-time restriction.

Applicants should carefully review the official application requirements before submitting their application.

Previous I Tatti Appointments and One-Time Fellowship Rule

Term Fellowships at I Tatti can be held only once.

They also cannot be deferred.

The fellowship is intended for scholars who have not previously held appointments at I Tatti, with the exception of Graduate Fellows.

This means previous affiliation with I Tatti is an important factor to consider before applying.

Restrictions During the Fellowship

The residential fellowship comes with several obligations and restrictions.

No Teaching Positions

Fellows may not take on other obligations such as teaching positions, including part-time teaching, during any part of the fellowship period.

Applicants who currently teach should therefore consider whether they can fully comply with this requirement.

No Simultaneous Fellowship or Award

The Berenson Fellowship may not be held concurrently with another fellowship or award.

Applicants who receive external funding should carefully consider whether it can be held alongside the I Tatti fellowship.

Outside Grants and Salary

If an applicant receives a partial salary or outside grant, this information must be disclosed either:

In the application, or

In subsequent correspondence with the Director.

Permission must also be received where required.

Applicants should therefore be transparent about other sources of financial support.

Visa and Health Insurance Responsibilities

International Fellows are responsible for handling their own immigration and health-related arrangements.

The Fellow is responsible for obtaining:

A visa, where required.

A permesso di soggiorno where applicable.

Health coverage.

Appropriate documentation for accompanying family members, where relevant.

Applicants must determine whether they require a visa and, if one is necessary, obtain it before travelling.

Prospective international applicants should therefore begin investigating Italian immigration requirements well before the fellowship start date.

Application Process for the Berenson Fellowship

Applications are submitted electronically.

Applicants can prepare their application in either:

English, or

Italian.

Candidates should ensure that all required application materials are completed and submitted through the designated online application system.

The application should present a compelling research project and demonstrate the applicant’s scholarly ability and potential contribution to I Tatti’s intellectual community.

What Makes a Strong Application?

Although selection is competitive, several elements are explicitly important in the evaluation process.

The selection committee pays particular attention to:

The strength of the proposed project

The potential of the project to produce original results

The candidate’s curriculum vitae

The candidate’s ability to contribute collegially to I Tatti’s intellectual life

Applicants should therefore avoid treating the application as simply a funding request.

Instead, the application should demonstrate:

A clearly defined research question.

A strong understanding of existing scholarship.

A convincing explanation of the project’s originality.

A realistic research plan.

A strong connection to the “Italy in the World” theme.

A clear reason why Florence and I Tatti are important for the research.

Evidence of the applicant’s scholarly achievements.

The potential significance of the expected results.

Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must arrange for two scholars who know their work well to submit recommendations online.

The recommendation letters may be written in:

English, or

Italian.

The referees must submit their recommendations electronically by:

November 21, 2026

Applicants are strongly encouraged to register their referees early through the reference section of the application system.

Once registered, referees will receive an email explaining how to access the system and submit their recommendations.

Applicants are responsible for informing their referees about:

The nature of the proposed research project.

The fellowship being applied for.

The application deadline.

The separate recommendation deadline.

Giving referees adequate notice can help ensure that recommendations are submitted on time.

Berenson Fellowship Deadlines

There are two important dates applicants should remember.

Main Application Deadline

November 16, 2026

Applications must be submitted electronically by midnight Cambridge, Massachusetts time on November 16, 2026.

Recommendation Letter Deadline

November 21, 2026

The two required recommendation letters must be submitted online by November 21, 2026.

Because the recommendation deadline comes after the main application deadline, applicants should not wait until the last minute to register their referees.

Important Application Restriction

Scholars may apply for only one type of I Tatti Fellowship per academic year.

Applicants considering multiple I Tatti fellowship categories should therefore carefully determine which fellowship best matches their research and career circumstances before submitting an application.

How to Prepare a Competitive Application

Applicants interested in the Berenson Fellowship should approach the application strategically.

1. Develop a Clearly Defined Research Project

Your project should have a clear research question and demonstrate why the subject matters.

Avoid presenting a project that is too broad to complete meaningful work on during a four- or six-month residential fellowship.

2. Demonstrate the Transnational Dimension

Because the fellowship focuses on “Italy in the World,” applicants should make the international or cross-cultural dimension of their research clear.

Explain how the project examines relationships between Italy and another culture, region, society, intellectual tradition, or geographical area.

3. Explain Why Florence Matters

A strong application should establish why conducting research at I Tatti and in Florence is important.

Applicants should identify the resources, collections, scholarly environment, or research networks that make Florence particularly valuable for the project.

4. Emphasize Originality

The selection committee specifically considers the potential of the proposed project to produce original results.

Applicants should clearly explain what their research contributes that existing scholarship does not adequately address.

5. Present a Strong CV

The curriculum vitae is an important component of the evaluation.

Applicants should clearly present relevant:

Academic qualifications.

Publications.

Research experience.

Previous scholarly achievements.

Fellowships and awards.

Relevant academic positions.

Conference participation.

Other evidence of research ability.

6. Choose Appropriate Referees

The two recommenders should know the applicant’s scholarly work well enough to provide meaningful assessments.

Applicants should give referees sufficient information about the proposed project so that their recommendations can address the candidate’s research ability and potential.

Clean and sustainable water

Quality education

Fundamental healthcare

The Foundation’s approach is centered on supporting organizations that can create sustainable and measurable impact for communities that lack access to essential resources.

AJA Foundation – How to Apply

TITLE: Best practices for Core Argo floats-Parts 1 and 2

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Morris, T., Scanderbeg, M., West-Mack, D., Gourcuff, C., Poffa, N., Bhaskar, TVSU, Hanstein, C., Diggs, S., Talley, L., Turpin, V., Liu, Z., and Owens, B., (2024) Best practices for Core Argo floats – part 1: getting started and data considerations. Front. Mar. Sci. 11:1358042. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2024.1358042

Morris, T., Scanderbeg, M., West-Mack, D., Gourcuff, C., Poffa, N., Bhaskar, TVSU, Hanstein, C., Diggs, S., Talley, L., Turpin, V., Liu, Z., and Owens, B., (2024) Best practices for Core Argo floats – Part 2: physical handling, deployment and metadata considerations. Front. Mar. Sci. 11:1358048. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2024.1358048

The primary objective of the Argo Program, established with the first Argo float deployments in 1999, was to uniformly deploy Argo floats in all the ocean basins, acquiring data from the upper 2000 dbar of the world’s ocean every 10 days (Roemmich et al., 2019). The Core Argo Mission has significantly advanced our understanding of the upper 2000 dbar of the global oceans (Wong et al., 2020). This paper looks to highlight the Core Argo float mission, and to encourage the continued and enhanced support of established Core Argo members (be they countries, regions or research teams), but also to engage with and encourage new users to the program. New users are able to provide deployment opportunities in regions difficult to access, procure new Argo floats to work towards the OneArgo targets or make use of the freely available data acquired thus far by Argo, showing its worth to existing funders. TITLE: SCIANCE project kicks off: Shaping AI in Science, by Scientists, for Europe

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
News | Project News

[Brussels, 13 January 2026]

The SCIANCE project – AI for Science – has its official kick-off meeting today in Brussels, Belgium.

Coordinated by ESF, the SCIANCE project – AI in Science – will support the development of Resource for AI Science in Europe (RAISE) and coordinate AI-enabled scientific research across Europe through a bottom-up approach. The project mobilises leading European scientific organisations and research infrastructures across five pilot areas – fundamental physics and astronomy, materials science, life science, earth sciences, and social sciences and humanities – together with AI research centres and e-infrastructures. SCIANCE will identify AI-in-science research and innovation priorities and pilot the structure of the RAISE Secretariat for AI in science.

Key outcomes

SCIANCE key outcomes include:

a Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda (SRIA) for AI in Science

an implementation roadmap for infrastructure upgrades

and the RAISE Secretariat for AI in science, to support long-term collaboration, capacity building, and alignment with European policy objectives.

Led by ESF, the SCIANCE consortium includes 13 leading European organisations and research infrastructures: EGI Foundation, OpenAIRE AMKE, CNR-ISTI, Euro-BioImaging ERIC (affiliated entity: EMBL), EMBL, CU, MU, UT-ITC, Nikhef, DFKI, SZTAKI, BDVA

Coordinated by ESF

As coordinator, ESF will be providing overall strategic direction, governance and sustainability. ESF also leads the co-creation of the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda and associated implementation roadmaps through expert working groups and stakeholder workshops, and will host the RAISE Secretariat for AI in Science, supporting cooperation across Europe and ensuring long-term impact of the project’s outcomes.

“SCIANCE represents a unique opportunity to coordinate AI-enabled science across Europe – connecting research communities, infrastructures and AI expertise in a way that truly reflects scientific priorities,” said Jonas L’Haridon, Project Coordinator, ESF.

What is RAISE?

RAISE – the Resource for Artificial Intelligence Science in Europe – is a new European virtual institute designed to accelerate the adoption of AI in scientific research. It brings together computing power, data, expertise and funding to support scientists in developing and applying AI for transformative discoveries across all research fields. As a flagship initiative related to the European Strategy for AI in Science, RAISE will help position Europe as a global leader in AI-enabled research.

1 Ubuntu Leader position is available for an eligible applicant currently based in either the United Kingdom or Zimbabwe.

Applicants should therefore pay close attention to their current country of residence, as the application form specifically asks applicants to identify whether they are based in Kenya, the UK or Zimbabwe.

Duration of the Role

The Global Kinship Leader position is a six-month role.

This means successful applicants will have the opportunity to contribute to Girl Up EMEA programming over an extended period rather than participating in a one-time event or short-term activity.

The role may also be renewed, providing the possibility of continued engagement beyond the initial six-month period.

However, applicants should understand that renewal is described as a possibility rather than a guaranteed extension.

Working Hours

The position is part-time, requiring approximately:

15–20 hours per week.

This structure may make the opportunity particularly suitable for young people who are balancing leadership activities, education, work or other responsibilities.

Nevertheless, applicants should be prepared to commit the required time consistently throughout the six-month period.

The ability to manage time effectively and communicate reliably with the Girl Up EMEA team will therefore be important.

Who Is Eligible to Apply?

The stated age requirement is:

19–22 years old.

Applicants must also currently be based in one of the three eligible locations:

Kenya

Zimbabwe

United Kingdom

The application form specifically requests applicants to provide their country of residence and includes these three countries as the available choices.

Applicants should therefore carefully check both the age requirement and geographic requirement before beginning the application.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Young Leaders

The Global Kinship Leader role provides more than a title.

It offers young people the opportunity to gain practical experience supporting a youth-centred international initiative.

Through their involvement, successful applicants can potentially develop experience in:

Youth leadership

Programme coordination

Community engagement

Digital communications

Storytelling

Youth network development

Gender equality programming

Collaborative leadership

International youth development

Social impact initiatives

For a young person considering a future career in international development, civil society, advocacy, communications, gender equality or youth leadership, this type of practical experience can be particularly valuable.

Girl Up and Youth Leadership

Girl Up is a youth-focused movement associated with the United Nations Foundation that works to support girls and young people as leaders and advocates for gender equality.

The organisation’s model places young people at the centre of leadership and encourages them to develop the skills, networks and confidence needed to create change.

The Global Kinship Leaders opportunity fits within this broader approach by giving young people a structured role in supporting youth leadership programming and the Girl Up movement.

The opportunity is therefore especially relevant to applicants who already demonstrate an interest in youth-led change and want to contribute to a wider network of young leaders.

What Kind of Experience Could Be Relevant?

The information provided for this recruitment does not specify a formal university degree or professional qualification requirement.

Instead, the role is positioned as a youth leadership opportunity for eligible young people.

Applicants may therefore want to highlight experiences that demonstrate their ability to contribute effectively to the role.

Relevant experiences could include:

Participation in youth leadership programmes

Leadership of a Girl Up club or youth organisation

Volunteer experience

Community service

Advocacy campaigns

Gender equality initiatives

Youth empowerment projects

Social media management

Digital content creation

Storytelling

Event coordination

Programme support

Community mobilisation

Peer education

Student leadership

Non-profit or civil society engagement

Applicants should focus on demonstrating what they have actually done and the impact of their involvement.

Importance of Youth Leadership and Community Engagement

A central feature of this opportunity is its focus on youth leadership.

The Global Kinship Leader is not simply expected to attend activities. The selected individuals will support programmes, engage with clubs, contribute to storytelling and assist with coordination.

Applicants should therefore consider how their previous experiences demonstrate:

Initiative

Responsibility

Teamwork

Communication

Creativity

Community engagement

Problem-solving

Leadership

Commitment to positive social change

Even relatively small community initiatives can be useful examples if the applicant can clearly explain their role and the results achieved.

Digital Storytelling and Communication

The digital storytelling component makes communication skills particularly relevant.

Young people today use digital platforms to tell stories, mobilise communities and increase awareness of social issues.

Applicants who have experience creating content or communicating through digital platforms can highlight relevant experience in areas such as:

Social media

Video production

Photography

Graphic design

Blogging

Writing

Campaign communication

Digital advocacy

Online community management

Youth-focused communications

However, applicants should ensure that they present their experience honestly and focus on the skills they can genuinely contribute.

Programme Coordination Experience

Applicants should also consider any experience they have supporting or organising programmes.

This does not necessarily have to come from formal employment.

Examples could include:

Organising youth events

Coordinating school activities

Supporting workshops

Managing volunteers

Organising advocacy campaigns

Coordinating community projects

Supporting conferences or webinars

Planning club activities

Working with youth organisations

Such experiences can demonstrate the applicant’s ability to plan, communicate and work with others.

Terms of Reference

Applicants are specifically instructed to review the Terms of Reference before completing the application.

This is an important part of the application process because the Terms of Reference provide the detailed expectations associated with the Global Kinship Leader role.

Prospective applicants should therefore read the document carefully before submitting their application.

Terms of Reference: Girl Up EMEA Global Kinship Leaders Terms of Reference

Applicants should use the Terms of Reference to understand the responsibilities and expectations of the position and to determine whether their experience and interests align with the role.

Information Required in the Application

The application form begins with a section requesting basic information from applicants.

Applicants are asked to provide:

Full name

Email address

Country of residence

City or region

Age

The country-of-residence section identifies:

Kenya

UK

Zimbabwe

The age field explicitly states the eligibility range of 19–22 years old.

Applicants should ensure that all information submitted is accurate.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the Girl Up EMEA Global Kinship Leaders 2027 application is:

September 21, 2026.

Applicants should submit their applications before the deadline and avoid waiting until the final day.

Early submission is particularly advisable because applicants should have enough time to review the Terms of Reference, prepare their responses and ensure that all information is accurate.

Location of the Opportunity

The opportunity has a multi-country eligibility structure.

The available locations are:

Kenya

Zimbabwe

United Kingdom

One position is specifically allocated to Kenya, while the second position covers the UK/Zimbabwe recruitment category.

Applicants must currently be based in one of these locations to be eligible under the stated recruitment criteria.

Is This a Full-Time Opportunity?

No.

The Global Kinship Leader role is explicitly described as a part-time position.

The expected commitment is approximately 15–20 hours per week for six months.

This makes the opportunity different from a full-time employment position and may allow eligible young people to balance the role with other commitments.

Is the Role Permanent?

No.

The initial appointment is for six months, with the possibility of renewal.

Applicants should therefore view the opportunity as a fixed-term leadership engagement rather than a permanent position.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the application form begins with basic information, applicants should approach the opportunity strategically.

Review the Terms of Reference Carefully

The first step should be to read the Terms of Reference carefully.

Applicants should understand:

What the Global Kinship Leader role involves

What responsibilities are expected

What type of contribution Girl Up EMEA is seeking

Whether their experiences align with the role

What commitment will be required

Identify Your Strongest Leadership Experiences

Think about experiences where you took responsibility rather than simply participated.

For example:

Did you lead a youth project?

Did you organise an event?

Did you coordinate volunteers?

Did you create a community campaign?

Did you manage a club?

Did you mentor other young people?

Did you lead a digital campaign?

These examples can help demonstrate leadership.

Highlight Your Youth Engagement Experience

Because the role focuses on youth leadership and Girl Up club engagement, applicants should clearly demonstrate their experience working with or for young people where applicable.

Demonstrate Communication Skills

Digital storytelling and programme coordination require strong communication.

Applicants should therefore highlight experiences involving writing, speaking, social media, storytelling, advocacy or community mobilisation.

Show Commitment to Positive Change

The role is connected to a wider youth-centred movement.

Applicants should demonstrate that they are motivated by more than personal career development and are interested in contributing to meaningful change.

What Applicants Should Avoid

Applicants should avoid submitting generic applications that simply list activities without explaining their contribution.

Instead of writing:

“I participated in several youth programmes.”

It is more useful to explain:

What the programme was

What your role was

What you contributed

Who benefited

What you learned

What changed as a result

Applicants should also avoid exaggerating their experience.

The strongest applications should provide a genuine picture of the applicant’s leadership, interests and ability to contribute.

Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, eligible applicants should confirm that they:

Are 19–22 years old.

Currently live in Kenya, Zimbabwe or the United Kingdom.

Understand that the role is part-time.

Can commit approximately 15–20 hours per week.

Can commit to the initial six-month period.

Have reviewed the Terms of Reference.

Have prepared their full name and email address.

Can provide their country of residence.

Can provide their city or region.

Have entered their correct age.

Have reviewed their application carefully before submitting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Girl Up Global Kinship Leaders opportunity?

It is a youth leadership opportunity within the Girl Up Kinship Network through which selected young people support Girl Up EMEA’s youth leadership programming, club engagement, digital storytelling and programme coordination.

How many positions are available?

There are two Ubuntu Leader positions for this recruitment cycle.

One is for Kenya, while the other is for the UK/Zimbabwe category.

How long is the role?

The initial role lasts six months, with the possibility of renewal.

Is it full-time?

No. It is a part-time role requiring approximately 15–20 hours per week.

What age must applicants be?

Applicants must be 19–22 years old.

Which countries are eligible?

Applicants must currently be based in Kenya, Zimbabwe or the United Kingdom.

Do I need a university degree?

The information provided for the application does not state a university degree requirement.

Applicants should therefore focus on the stated eligibility criteria and the requirements outlined in the Terms of Reference.

What will the selected leaders do?

They will support youth leadership programming, Girl Up club engagement, digital storytelling and programme coordination with the Girl Up EMEA team.

Can the role be renewed?

Yes. The opportunity states that renewal is possible, although renewal is not guaranteed.

When is the application deadline?

The deadline is September 21, 2026.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should first review the Terms of Reference and ensure they meet the age and location requirements.

They can then proceed with the Girl Up EMEA application and provide the requested basic information.

Terms of Reference: https://bit.ly/3SZBlA2

Applicants should ensure that their information is accurate and that they submit their application before September 21, 2026.

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Girl Up EMEA Global Kinship Leaders 2027 opportunity provides an exciting pathway for young people in Kenya, Zimbabwe and the United Kingdom to take on a structured youth leadership role within the Girl Up Kinship Network.

With two Ubuntu Leader positions available, the six-month, part-time role will allow selected young leaders to support youth leadership programming, engage Girl Up clubs, contribute to digital storytelling and assist with programme coordination.

The opportunity can be particularly valuable for young people interested in youth development, gender equality, advocacy, communications, community engagement, international development and social impact. It provides an opportunity to contribute to a recognised youth-centred movement while gaining practical experience in leadership and programme support.

Eligible applicants should carefully review the Terms of Reference, assess how their experiences align with the role and prepare their applications well before the September 21, 2026 deadline.

The key requirements are straightforward but important: applicants must be 19–22 years old, currently based in Kenya, Zimbabwe or the UK, and able to commit 15–20 hours per week for six months. For young people who meet these requirements and are passionate about youth leadership and creating positive change, this is an opportunity worth considering.
