TITLE: NextGen@ICANN88 Programme 2026: Fully Supported Opportunity for Young Students Interested in Internet Governance

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The NextGen@ICANN88 Programme 2026 is inviting eligible young students to apply for an opportunity to participate in the global Internet governance community through the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN).

The programme is designed for young people who are interested in Internet governance, the future of the Internet, digital policy, technology and other issues addressed within the ICANN ecosystem. Selected participants will receive coaching, guidance and travel support to attend an ICANN meeting, giving them an opportunity to learn directly from experts, engage with the international ICANN community and begin building a pathway toward long-term participation in Internet governance.

For the current application round, the programme is associated with the ICANN88 Community Forum, which will take place in Lisbon, Portugal, from 13–18 March 2027. Applications are open from 31 August 2026 until 9 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC.

What Is the NextGen@ICANN Programme?

The NextGen@ICANN Programme is a youth-focused initiative established to encourage greater participation by young people in ICANN and the wider Internet governance ecosystem.

ICANN recognizes that the future of the Internet depends not only on established experts and institutions, but also on bringing new generations of people into discussions about how the global Internet operates and evolves. The NextGen@ICANN Programme therefore seeks to identify young people who have the potential to become future contributors to the ICANN community.

The programme introduces participants to important areas of ICANN’s work while helping them understand the bottom-up, multistakeholder model used in Internet governance. Participants can learn how different stakeholders contribute to discussions and decision-making processes that affect the Internet at regional and global levels.

For students interested in technology, digital transformation, cybersecurity, Internet policy, communications, governance, law, computer science, public policy or related areas, the programme can provide an opportunity to gain exposure to an international environment where important conversations about the Internet take place.

Why Consider NextGen@ICANN88?

Participating in NextGen@ICANN can provide more than attendance at an international conference. The programme is structured to help young participants understand the ICANN ecosystem and gradually become involved in the wider Internet governance community.

Selected participants receive coaching and guidance, as well as financial support associated with attending the relevant ICANN meeting. This makes the programme particularly valuable for students who want international exposure but may otherwise find it difficult to attend a major global meeting independently.

ICANN describes participation in a NextGen@ICANN meeting as an ideal first step for young people beginning their journey into the ICANN ecosystem. Participants are expected not simply to attend but to engage meaningfully with the programme and meeting activities.

Some of the potential benefits include:

International exposure: Participants can interact with members of an international Internet governance community.

Coaching and guidance: Selected students receive support intended to help them understand ICANN and its broader ecosystem.

Travel support: The programme provides financial support toward attending the ICANN meeting.

Economy-class airfare: The support grant covers the cost of economy-class airfare.

Hotel accommodation: Selected participants receive support for hotel costs associated with participation.

Stipend: Participants are provided with a stipend as part of the programme’s support package.

Internet governance knowledge: Participants gain a deeper understanding of Internet governance and issues discussed within the ICANN community.

Networking opportunities: The programme can introduce young students to people working and participating in different areas of the global Internet ecosystem.

Opportunity to present a project: Selected participants are required to prepare and deliver a 5–10-minute presentation at the meeting.

Potential long-term engagement: The programme is intended to encourage young people to become future members and contributors to the ICANN community.

What Is the ICANN88 Community Forum?

The current NextGen application round is for ICANN88, the Community Forum scheduled to take place in Lisbon, Portugal, from 13 to 18 March 2027.

ICANN meetings rotate among different geographic regions. The ICANN88 meeting falls within the Europe region. According to the programme’s eligibility requirements, applicants generally need to be living and studying in the region of the respective ICANN meeting.

This means that students interested in applying for the current ICANN88 NextGen opportunity should carefully verify that they meet the geographic requirement for the Europe-based meeting.

Who Can Apply for NextGen@ICANN88?

The NextGen@ICANN Programme has specific eligibility requirements. Applicants should carefully review these conditions before beginning an application.

1. Applicants Must Be Students

Applicants must be currently enrolled as an undergraduate, graduate or doctoral student.

This means the programme is intended for people who are actively pursuing higher education rather than applicants who have already completed their studies and are no longer enrolled.

Eligible study levels include:

Undergraduate students

Graduate students

Doctoral students

The source does not limit eligibility to a single academic discipline. Therefore, applicants should focus on demonstrating how their studies, research, activities or interests connect with Internet governance, the future of the Internet or subjects relevant to ICANN.

2. Applicants Must Be Between 18 and 30 Years Old

Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years of age at the time of the ICANN meeting.

For ICANN88, the relevant meeting takes place in March 2027, so applicants should ensure that they satisfy the age requirement at the time the meeting occurs, rather than looking only at their age on the application date.

3. Applicants Must Live and Study in the Relevant Region

A major requirement is that applicants must be currently living and studying in the region of the respective ICANN meeting.

ICANN rotates its meetings through five geographic regions:

Africa

Europe

North America

Latin America

Asia Pacific

For the current NextGen@ICANN88 application, the meeting is scheduled for Lisbon, Portugal, in the Europe region. Consequently, the regional eligibility requirement is particularly important for applicants considering this round.

ICANN also notes that if applications are accepted from regions other than the region in which a particular meeting is taking place, that information will be made publicly available before applications open for that meeting.

4. Applicants Should Have an Interest in Internet Governance

Applicants should demonstrate an interest in Internet governance, the future of the Internet and other topics covered at ICANN meetings.

This is important because the programme is not simply a general international travel opportunity for students. Applicants are expected to have a genuine interest in the issues addressed by ICANN and the Internet governance ecosystem.

An applicant can therefore strengthen their application by clearly explaining their connection to Internet-related issues through their studies, research, projects, professional activities, public discussions or other relevant engagements.

What Will Selected Participants Be Expected to Do?

Being selected for NextGen@ICANN comes with active participation requirements.

Participants are expected to attend the relevant ICANN meeting and required events and to participate actively throughout the programme. The opportunity is therefore best suited to students who are genuinely interested in learning, engaging and contributing rather than simply attending the event as observers.

Participants Must Present a Project

One of the notable requirements is that selected participants must be willing to deliver a 5–10-minute project presentation at the meeting.

The presentation can focus on different types of work, including

Research the applicant is currently working on

Research the applicant has already completed

An activity connected to ICANN’s work

An ICANN-related website with which the applicant is affiliated

A thesis project

Another relevant project connected to the programme’s themes

This requirement provides applicants with an opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge, interests and ability to communicate an Internet-related subject to an international audience.

Applicants should therefore think carefully about the project they could present if selected.

What Financial Support Does NextGen@ICANN Provide?

One of the major attractions of the programme is the financial support available to selected participants.

Each selected participant receives a grant of support covering:

Economy-class airfare

Hotel accommodation

A stipend

This support is designed to enable selected students to attend the ICANN meeting and participate in the required programme activities.

However, applicants should be aware that the support does not cover every travel-related expense.

Visa Costs

Participants are responsible for securing their own visas for travel, and the cost of obtaining the visa is at the participant’s own expense.

Applicants should therefore investigate visa requirements well in advance if they are selected, particularly because international travel arrangements may require additional documentation and processing time.

Travel and Health Insurance

If a participant wishes to obtain travel insurance or health insurance, those costs are also the participant’s responsibility.

Applicants should take this into consideration when planning for participation.

How Are NextGen@ICANN Applicants Selected?

Meeting the basic eligibility requirements does not automatically guarantee selection.

ICANN evaluates applications using a number of selection criteria designed to identify applicants who demonstrate genuine interest in Internet governance and the potential to contribute to the community.

The selection criteria include:

Demonstrated Interest in ICANN and the Internet Ecosystem

Applicants should demonstrate their interest in ICANN and the broader Internet ecosystem through examples of their current work, activities, studies, research or public dialogue on the web.

This means applicants should not simply state that they are interested in Internet governance. They should provide evidence that supports that interest.

Value of Participation to the Applicant and Their Community

Applicants are assessed on how clearly they explain the value that participating in NextGen@ICANN would provide to them personally and to a wider community.

The wider community could include a:

University

Country

Region

Other relevant community

Applicants should therefore consider not only what they hope to gain, but also how they could use the experience and knowledge gained through participation to benefit others.

Quality of the Applicant’s View on an Internet Topic

The application also considers the applicant’s ability to express their views on an Internet-related topic.

This makes the quality of written responses particularly important. Applicants should aim to communicate their ideas clearly, demonstrate genuine understanding and present thoughtful perspectives on relevant Internet issues.

Desire to Join the ICANN Community

Applicants should demonstrate that they genuinely want to become part of the ICANN community.

The programme is intended to support future engagement, so applicants who can clearly explain their interest in continuing to participate in Internet governance may be better positioned to demonstrate alignment with the programme’s objectives.

Long-Term Interest in ICANN-Related Topics

ICANN also considers whether an applicant has demonstrated a long-standing interest in topics related to ICANN’s work.

Applicants should therefore consider how their academic background, research, projects, professional interests or other activities demonstrate sustained engagement with Internet-related subjects.

Desire to Understand and Engage With Regional ICANN Work

Applicants are also assessed on their desire to engage with and improve their understanding of ICANN’s work in their region.

This reinforces the importance of explaining why participation is relevant not only to the applicant personally but also to the Internet governance environment in their region.

How to Prepare a Strong NextGen@ICANN Application

Although selection is competitive, applicants can take practical steps to make their applications stronger.

Demonstrate Genuine Interest

Avoid relying on generic statements about loving technology or wanting international exposure. Instead, connect your experience to specific Internet governance issues.

For example, an applicant could discuss relevant:

Academic research

University projects

Digital policy activities

Internet-related initiatives

Research publications

Technology projects

Online discussions

Community activities

Thesis work

Professional activities related to Internet governance

The objective should be to show evidence of genuine engagement rather than simply claiming interest.

Explain the Impact of Participation

Applicants should clearly explain why NextGen@ICANN matters to their personal development and how participation could benefit their university, country or region.

A strong response should make a clear connection between:

Current experience → ICANN opportunity → knowledge gained → future contribution.

This can help demonstrate alignment with the programme’s objective of developing future members of the ICANN community.

Prepare a Relevant Project

Because selected participants are expected to present a project for 5–10 minutes, applicants should consider what work they could potentially showcase.

A thesis, research project, Internet-related initiative, relevant website or other activity may provide a suitable foundation for the presentation.

Demonstrate Your Regional Perspective

Since eligibility and participation are linked to ICANN’s geographic regions, applicants should consider how Internet governance issues affect their own region.

Explaining a regional Internet challenge, policy issue, digital inclusion question, cybersecurity concern or other relevant subject may help demonstrate the applicant’s understanding of the broader Internet ecosystem.

Application Requirements and ICANN Account

Applicants should be aware that an ICANN Account is required to apply for the NextGen@ICANN Programme.

The application is submitted through ICANN’s application platform, and prospective applicants should make sure they have the necessary account access before attempting to submit their application.

Applicants can access the official application route through the NextGen@ICANN programme page and should follow ICANN’s instructions for the relevant application round.

NextGen@ICANN88 Application Deadline

The NextGen@ICANN88 application period opened on 31 August 2026 and closes on 9 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC.

This is the key deadline prospective applicants should keep in mind.

The selection announcement for ICANN88 is scheduled for 17 December 2026.

Important Dates at a Glance

Application opening date: 31 August 2026

Application deadline: 9 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC

Selection announcement: 17 December 2026

ICANN88 Community Forum: 13–18 March 2027

Location: Lisbon, Portugal

ICANN region: Europe

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their applications. Creating an ICANN Account, reviewing eligibility, preparing application responses and identifying a suitable project for presentation can all take time.

APPLY HERE

Geographic Eligibility: Which Countries Can Apply?

The programme’s eligibility is based primarily on ICANN geographic regions, rather than a simple worldwide open application model.

ICANN identifies five meeting regions:

Africa

Europe

North America

Latin America

Asia Pacific

Applicants are generally expected to be living and studying in the region of the respective ICANN meeting.

For ICANN88, the meeting is scheduled in Lisbon, Portugal, and the listed region is Europe. Therefore, the current application round is aimed at eligible students living and studying in the Europe region, subject to any specific announcement by ICANN concerning applications from other regions.

The source does not provide a country-by-country list of eligible countries for ICANN88, so applicants should use ICANN’s official regional classification rather than assuming that every country is eligible based solely on geographical proximity.

There is also no race-based restriction stated in the eligibility information provided. The requirements focus on age, student status, residence and study location, interest in Internet governance, ability to attend and willingness to participate and present a project.

What Makes NextGen@ICANN Different?

Many international opportunities provide students with funding or access to events, but NextGen@ICANN places significant emphasis on participation and long-term engagement.

The programme is designed to help young people understand the Internet governance ecosystem and progressively become involved in the ICANN community.

This makes it particularly relevant to students who want to develop expertise in areas where technology intersects with policy, governance and international cooperation.

The opportunity can be especially valuable for students interested in fields such as

Internet governance

Digital policy

Technology policy

Information and communication technologies

Computer science

Cybersecurity

Law and technology

Public policy

Digital rights

Internet infrastructure

Communications

Digital development

Technology governance

International relations

Research involving the Internet ecosystem

The programme itself does not restrict applicants to these fields in the eligibility information provided, so applicants should focus on demonstrating their genuine connection to ICANN-related topics.

Visit HERE for more information about the NextGen@ICANN88 Programme 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions About NextGen@ICANN88

Is NextGen@ICANN a scholarship?

No. It is not a traditional academic scholarship. It is a youth participation and development programme that provides selected students with coaching, guidance and financial support to attend an ICANN meeting.

The support includes economy-class airfare, hotel accommodation and a stipend.

Do applicants have to be university students?

Yes. Applicants must be enrolled as an undergraduate, graduate or doctoral student.

What is the age requirement?

Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years old at the time of the ICANN meeting.

Can applicants from any country apply?

Not necessarily. Eligibility is linked to the region of the ICANN meeting. For ICANN88, the meeting is in Lisbon, Portugal, within the Europe region, and applicants are expected to be living and studying in the relevant region.

Does ICANN cover airfare?

Yes. Selected participants receive a support grant covering economy-class airfare.

Does ICANN provide accommodation?

Yes. The support grant covers hotel accommodation for selected participants.

Is a stipend provided?

Yes. The NextGen@ICANN support package includes a stipend.

Does ICANN pay for visas?

No. Participants must secure their own visas and pay the associated costs themselves.

Are participants required to present?

Yes. Selected participants must be willing to present a project lasting 5–10 minutes during the meeting.

When does the ICANN88 application close?

The application closes on 9 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC.

Conclusion

The NextGen@ICANN88 Programme 2026 offers eligible young students an opportunity to move beyond simply studying technology and become more actively involved in conversations about the future of the Internet.

Through coaching, guidance, travel support, accommodation and a stipend, selected participants can attend the ICANN88 Community Forum in Lisbon and engage directly with the international Internet governance ecosystem. The programme also provides participants with an opportunity to present their own research or project and begin developing a longer-term relationship with the ICANN community.

The opportunity is particularly relevant for students who are 18–30 years old, currently enrolled in undergraduate, graduate or doctoral studies, living and studying in the relevant ICANN meeting region, and genuinely interested in Internet governance and the future of the Internet.

For the current ICANN88 round, eligible applicants should take note of the 9 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC deadline and prepare their applications carefully. Beyond meeting the basic eligibility requirements, applicants should demonstrate their existing interest in ICANN and Internet-related issues, explain how participation would benefit them and their wider community, and show their potential to become an engaged member of the ICANN ecosystem.

For young students seeking international exposure, knowledge, networking and a structured introduction to global Internet governance, NextGen@ICANN88 represents a valuable opportunity to learn, participate and contribute to discussions shaping the future of the Internet.

TITLE: USDA Spring 2027 Internship Program in Washington, D.C.: Applications Open for U.S. Citizens Interested in Public Service, Agriculture, Policy and Rural Development

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Applications are now open for the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Spring 2027 Internship Program, offering emerging professionals an opportunity to gain practical experience inside one of the largest departments of the U.S. federal government.

The Spring 2027 cohort will run from January 25 through April 30, 2027, with applications due by November 13, 2026. The program is an unpaid, in-person volunteer internship based in Washington, D.C. USDA does not provide housing or relocation assistance.

Unlike many internships that are limited to currently enrolled university students, USDA’s current Internship Program does not require applicants to be enrolled in school or to hold a college degree. According to USDA’s official FAQ, applicants must be U.S. citizens and at least 18 years old at the time of application. Candidates from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds may therefore be considered.

The program provides participants with direct exposure to public service and federal government operations while allowing them to contribute to work related to agriculture, food systems, conservation, rural communities, communications, research, public policy, stakeholder engagement and other areas central to USDA’s mission.

About the USDA Internship Program

The U.S. Department of Agriculture describes its Internship Program as a public-service and leadership-development experience intended to introduce emerging leaders to USDA’s work and help prepare them for careers in public service, agriculture, science, policy and community development.

USDA’s mission reaches far beyond farming alone. The Department works across areas including:

Agriculture and agricultural markets

Food and nutrition

Food safety

Rural economic development

Natural-resource conservation

Forestry and environmental stewardship

Agricultural research

Data and economics

International agricultural trade

Communications

Public policy

Congressional relations

Civil rights

Community partnerships

Stakeholder engagement

Interns may therefore have opportunities to work in areas aligned with a broad range of academic interests, professional skills and career ambitions.

USDA states that interns may contribute to activities such as research, program operations, data analysis, communications, outreach and stakeholder engagement. Exact responsibilities depend on the mission area or staff office in which an intern is placed.

Spring 2027 USDA Internship Dates

The current application is specifically for the Spring 2027 cohort.

Program period: January 25, 2027 – April 30, 2027

Application deadline: November 13, 2026

USDA’s application information states that applicants should be available during the program period. The application form itself also allows candidates with limited availability to explain their circumstances, although applicants should expect the program to require substantial in-person participation.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider academic, employment, transportation and housing commitments before applying.

Is the USDA Spring 2027 Internship Paid?

No.

The current USDA Spring 2027 Internship Program is explicitly described as an unpaid volunteer internship. Applicants will not receive a salary from USDA through this program.

This distinction is important because USDA also operates other student employment initiatives, including Pathways opportunities, some of which may be paid. The internship advertised on the USDA page linked above, however, is the USDA Volunteer Internship Program and is unpaid.

USDA encourages applicants to explore whether their educational institutions or relevant nonprofit organizations can provide funding or academic support.

Applicants should also be aware that outside income, funding or housing assistance associated with the internship may require prior approval from USDA.

Housing and Relocation Assistance

USDA does not provide housing specifically for interns under this program.

Participants are responsible for finding and paying for their own accommodation for the duration of the internship.

USDA also states on the Spring 2027 application page that the program provides no housing or relocation assistance.

Candidates who do not already live within commuting distance of Washington, D.C., should therefore calculate expected costs before accepting an internship, including:

Housing

Transportation

Meals

Local commuting

Relocation expenses

Personal living expenses

Because the position is unpaid, financial planning will be particularly important for applicants relocating to Washington.

Internship Location: Washington, D.C.

The USDA Internship Program is conducted in person in Washington, D.C.

Interns are expected to work onsite at USDA’s Whitten Building, where they participate directly in departmental operations and interact with USDA personnel.

USDA specifically states that remote participation is not available for this program.

Applicants should therefore not apply on the assumption that they will be permitted to complete the internship remotely from another U.S. state or another country.

Expected Internship Schedule and Working Hours

Most USDA internships under this program operate on a Monday-to-Friday schedule, typically within approximately 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

Some flexibility may be available for interns who have academic or other program requirements.

USDA states that interns considered full-time are generally expected to work the equivalent of approximately 4.5 days per week, although limited adjustments may be permitted where appropriate.

Applicants should therefore view the opportunity as a substantial professional commitment rather than a few-hours-per-week volunteer placement.

What Will USDA Interns Do?

Specific duties will depend heavily on the intern’s assigned mission area or staff office.

USDA identifies potential internship activities including:

Conducting research

Supporting program operations

Analyzing data

Drafting communications

Assisting with outreach activities

Supporting stakeholder engagement

Developing briefing materials

Supporting meetings and events

Conducting policy-related research

Helping coordinate projects

Participating in departmental programming

This structure allows interns to gain practical experience while contributing to ongoing federal government activities.

Leadership and Professional Development

The program is not intended to consist solely of administrative assignments.

USDA describes it as a leadership-development and public-service experience designed to help young and emerging professionals better understand federal service.

Interns participate in department-wide programming, including lunch-and-learn sessions featuring USDA leaders and subject-matter experts.

Through these activities, interns may gain exposure to:

Federal decision-making

Government leadership

Agriculture and food policy

Public administration

Interagency operations

Stakeholder engagement

Professional networking

Career development

Public-service culture

USDA Mission Areas and Offices Available to Applicants

As part of the application, candidates must list their top three preferred USDA Mission Areas or Staff Offices.

USDA’s official Office Opportunities document identifies a wide range of potential placement areas.

1. Farm Production and Conservation

Farm Production and Conservation (FPAC) serves as a major focal point for farmers, ranchers and other stewards of private agricultural and forest lands.

Its work includes programs related to:

Crop insurance

Agricultural conservation

Farm safety nets

Lending

Disaster programs

Risk mitigation for agricultural producers

This area may be particularly relevant for applicants interested in agricultural economics, environmental policy, farming systems, risk management or public administration.

2. Food and Nutrition Administration

The Food and Nutrition Administration focuses on reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition security in the United States.

Its work includes administration of federal domestic nutrition-assistance programs as well as science-based nutrition guidance, policy coordination and nutrition education.

This area may appeal to applicants interested in food security, nutrition, social policy, public health or program management.

3. Food Safety and Inspection Service

The Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) is USDA’s public-health agency responsible for helping ensure the safety of meat, poultry and egg products.

Its work includes food-safety oversight and implementation of federal laws governing meat, poultry, egg products and humane animal handling.

Students and professionals interested in food science, public health, veterinary science, regulatory policy or compliance may find this mission area particularly relevant.

4. Marketing and Regulatory Programs

Marketing and Regulatory Programs (MRP) supports domestic and international agricultural markets while protecting U.S. plant and animal health.

Its responsibilities include:

Agricultural marketing

Plant health

Animal health

Biotechnology regulation

Animal-welfare administration

Wildlife-damage management

Participation in national and international standards development

5. Research, Education and Economics

The Research, Education and Economics (REE) mission area supports research, analysis and education related to a safe, competitive and sustainable U.S. food and agricultural system.

Its work also addresses communities, families and young people.

Applicants interested in science, statistics, economics, research, data analysis or education may find REE especially relevant.

6. Rural Development

USDA Rural Development supports rural communities through loans, grants and loan-guarantee programs.

Its work includes investments relating to:

High-speed internet

Electricity

Transportation infrastructure

Businesses

Healthcare

Education

Housing

Community facilities

This placement could be highly relevant for students of economics, finance, infrastructure, public policy, community development or business administration.

7. Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs

Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs (TFAA) works to expand international opportunities for American farmers and ranchers.

Its responsibilities include international agricultural trade policy, market intelligence, trade promotion and export development.

USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service maintains a global network covering numerous countries, while the U.S. Codex Office coordinates American participation in international food-standard setting.

This area may be particularly attractive to applicants interested in international relations, economics, trade, diplomacy, agriculture or global food policy.

8. Natural Resources and Environment

The Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) mission area focuses on maintaining the health, diversity and productivity of U.S. forests and grasslands.

It works with states, tribes and communities across the country to steward natural resources.

Applicants with interests in environmental studies, forestry, climate policy, conservation, sustainability or natural-resource management may consider this placement.

USDA Staff Offices Offering Internship Exposure

Applicants can also express preferences for USDA staff offices.

Office of the Secretary

The Office of the Secretary provides leadership and strategic direction across USDA.

Interns may support:

High-level policy coordination

Research

Briefing materials

Departmental decision-making

Senior leadership meetings

Major events

This placement provides particularly close exposure to senior-level federal policy and executive decision-making.

White House Liaison Office

The White House Liaison Office connects USDA with the Executive Office of the President.

Its responsibilities include personnel matters, political appointments, leadership onboarding and coordination with the White House.

Interns may assist with research, personnel processes, organizational analysis, briefings and leadership engagements.

Office of Communications

The Office of Communications manages public information and strategic communication across USDA.

Internship work may involve:

Writing and editing

Press support

Briefing materials

Digital content

Media monitoring

Event support

Visual storytelling

Strategic messaging

It may be particularly suitable for applicants interested in journalism, public relations, communications, digital media or public affairs.

Office of Congressional Relations

The Office of Congressional Relations acts as USDA’s main liaison with the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.

Interns may gain experience in:

Legislative research

Tracking congressional hearings

Monitoring legislation

Preparing background materials

Congressional communications

Supporting departmental engagements with lawmakers

Office of the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights

The Office of the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights (OASCR) leads USDA’s work relating to civil-rights compliance and equal treatment.

Potential intern activities include:

Civil-rights policy research

Data analysis

Training-material preparation

Outreach

Compliance-related work

Office of Partnerships and Public Engagement

The Office of Partnerships and Public Engagement (OPPE) works with rural and underserved communities and helps connect stakeholders with USDA programs and resources.

Interns may assist with:

Outreach strategy

Partnership development

Community-needs research

Event coordination

Stakeholder engagement materials

Who Can Apply?

One of the distinctive features of the current USDA internship is its relatively broad educational eligibility.

According to USDA:

Applicants must be at least 18 years old.

Applicants must be U.S. citizens.

Applicants do not need to be currently enrolled in school.

Applicants do not need to hold a college degree.

People from a wide range of educational and professional backgrounds may apply.

The online application provides education-status options including:

Currently enrolled in high school

Currently enrolled in college or university

Recently graduated

Not currently enrolled in school

This confirms that the program is not restricted solely to university students.

Does an Applicant Need a Specific Major?

No specific academic major is identified as a universal requirement for the program.

The application nevertheless asks candidates to identify their major or field of study, where applicable. Applicants who are not currently enrolled may provide their most recent field of study or indicate that the question is not applicable.

Given USDA’s broad responsibilities, potentially relevant backgrounds include—but are not limited to:

Agriculture

Agricultural economics

Economics

Finance

Business administration

Public administration

Public policy

Political science

International relations

Law

Communications

Journalism

Data science

Statistics

Computer science

Food science

Nutrition

Public health

Environmental science

Forestry

Biology

Animal sciences

Rural development

Sociology

Community development

Applicants should choose office preferences that align logically with their interests, abilities and professional goals.

Is a Minimum GPA Required?

The application asks candidates to provide a GPA, but USDA marks the GPA field as optional.

The current program page therefore does not establish a universal minimum GPA requirement for the Spring 2027 Volunteer Internship Program.

USDA Internship Application Requirements

The application must be submitted through USDA’s official online portal.

Hard-copy applications sent by mail are not accepted.

Applicants will need to complete several sections.

Section 1: Personal Information

Applicants provide details including:

Full name

Street address

City, state and ZIP code

Telephone number

Email address

Section 2: Education

Applicants indicate their education status and provide applicable details such as:

Current school or university

Major or field of study

Expected graduation date

GPA, if they choose to provide it

Section 3: Spring 2027 Availability

Applicants must indicate whether they are available for the full Spring 2027 semester or have limited availability.

Candidates selecting limited availability must provide an explanation.

Section 4: Statement of Interest

The application requires substantive written responses addressing several topics.

Applicants are asked to explain:

Why they are interested in an internship with USDA.

What skills and experiences they could bring to USDA.

Which issues affecting agriculture, food systems, conservation or rural communities they want to learn more about and why.

What public service means to them and how they have demonstrated commitment to their community.

A personal accomplishment they are proud of and how it shaped their perspective on success.

The application also asks whether applicants have previously volunteered or worked for a:

Political campaign

Elected official

Government official

Applicants answering yes are asked to describe their role and the relevant campaign, office or official as well as the year or years involved.

Importantly, USDA states separately that political preference is not used as a deciding factor in internship application review.

Section 5: Office Preferences

Candidates must identify their top three USDA Mission Areas or Staff Offices where they would prefer to intern.

Applicants should research these offices before selecting preferences because their choices can help communicate their career interests and indicate where their skills may best fit USDA’s needs.

Section 6: References

Applicants must provide at least two references who can discuss their:

Qualifications

Character

Work ethic

Commitment to public service

USDA suggests potential references such as:

Professors

Supervisors

Mentors

Community leaders

Applicants should provide complete contact information for each reference.

Recommendation letters are optional and may be uploaded as PDF documents if applicants wish to include them.

All required reference information must be submitted by the application deadline.

USDA notes that applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, which makes early submission advisable.

Resume Requirement

Applicants must upload a resume.

The application portal currently accepts:

PDF

DOC

DOCX

The maximum upload size shown on the application form is 20 MB.

Candidates should tailor their resume to demonstrate relevant experience rather than using a generic resume whenever possible.

Useful information may include:

Education

Work experience

Volunteer experience

Leadership activities

Community involvement

Research projects

Public-service activities

Relevant technical skills

Communication skills

Data or analytical experience

Policy experience

Agriculture, food or environmental interests

How Applicants Can Strengthen Their Application

Because the program seeks individuals interested in public service, candidates should demonstrate more than academic achievement alone.

Strong applications should provide concrete evidence of:

Interest in USDA’s mission

Commitment to public service

Community involvement

Leadership

Initiative

Research or analytical skills

Communication ability

Professional maturity

Interest in agriculture, food systems, conservation or rural communities

When answering the statement-of-interest questions, applicants should avoid vague claims such as “I am passionate about agriculture.”

Instead, they should explain why a particular issue matters to them, what they have already done in that area, what they hope to learn and how USDA experience fits their longer-term professional objectives.

Political Experience and Political Preference

Applicants are specifically asked whether they have worked or volunteered for a political campaign, elected official or government official.

However, USDA states that political preference itself is not considered in the application review process.

Applicants should answer the application questions accurately and transparently.

What matters is their ability to demonstrate commitment to USDA’s public-service mission and responsibilities toward farmers, rural communities and the American public.

Important Financial Considerations Before Applying

Because the Spring 2027 internship is unpaid and based in Washington, D.C., candidates should evaluate the financial implications carefully.

Before applying or accepting an offer, consider:

Whether you can live in or commute to Washington, D.C., from January through April 2027.

Whether your college or university can provide academic credit or financial assistance.

Whether you qualify for support from an external nonprofit organization.

Your housing costs.

Transportation and commuting costs.

Food and personal expenses.

Whether outside funding would require USDA approval.

The absence of compensation does not diminish the professional exposure available through the program, but applicants should make a realistic financial assessment before committing.

Why Consider the USDA Spring 2027 Internship?

The program may be particularly valuable for individuals interested in understanding how federal institutions operate in practice.

Participants may gain firsthand exposure to:

Federal public administration

Agricultural policymaking

Policy research

Data analysis

Rural-development programs

Food and nutrition programs

Environmental conservation

International agricultural trade

Congressional relations

Communications

Civil-rights compliance

Community engagement

Executive-branch operations

Because internship placements span both policy-focused and operational offices, the program can be relevant to candidates from many academic and professional backgrounds.

The experience may also help applicants determine whether a longer-term career in public service, agriculture, federal policy or related sectors is appropriate for them.

Application Deadline

The official deadline for the USDA Spring 2027 Internship Program is November 13, 2026.

USDA notes that applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, so interested candidates should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their materials.

How to Apply for the USDA Spring 2027 Internship

Applications must be submitted electronically through the official USDA Internship Application portal.

Apply for the USDA Spring 2027 Internship

Applicants can review the main program information here:

USDA Internship Program Official Website

Before submitting, candidates should make sure they have:

Completed all personal and educational information.

Confirmed their Spring 2027 availability.

Prepared strong responses to the statement-of-interest questions.

Selected three preferred USDA mission areas or offices.

Provided two appropriate references with current contact information.

Prepared an updated resume.

Uploaded any optional recommendation letters they wish to include.

Reviewed their application carefully for accuracy.

Conclusion

The USDA Spring 2027 Internship Program provides U.S. citizens interested in public service with an opportunity to work directly within the U.S. Department of Agriculture in Washington, D.C.

Running from January 25 to April 30, 2027, the program offers exposure to federal government operations, leadership, policymaking, agriculture, food systems, conservation, communications, rural development and other areas central to USDA’s national mission.

A major advantage of the current program is its broad educational eligibility: applicants do not have to be currently enrolled in college and do not need a university degree. USDA requires applicants to be U.S. citizens and at least 18 years old.

At the same time, prospective applicants should understand the financial commitment involved. The internship is unpaid, fully in person in Washington, D.C., and provides neither intern housing nor relocation assistance.

Candidates who can meet those requirements and want practical exposure to federal public service should prepare their materials early. Applications for the Spring 2027 cohort must be submitted by November 13, 2026.

TITLE: Donor Profile: Leinweber Foundation

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
$20 million gift supports theoretical physics research and education at MIT

Gift from the Leinweber Foundation, in addition to a $5 million commitment from the School of Science, will drive discovery, collaboration, and the next generation of physics leaders.

by Julia C. Keller // MIT Physics Annual 2025

Larry Leinweber
Courtesy of Leinweber Foundation

A $20 million gift from the Leinweber Foundation, in addition to a $5 million commitment from the MIT School of Science, will support theoretical physics research and education at MIT.

Leinweber Foundation gifts to seven institutions, exceeding $100 million, will establish the newly renamed MIT Center for Theoretical Physics – A Leinweber Institute within the Department of Physics, affiliated with the Laboratory for Nuclear Science at the School of Science, as well as Leinweber Institutes for Theoretical Physics at four other top research universities: Stanford University, the University of Michigan, the University of California at Berkeley, and the University of Chicago, as well as a Leinweber Forum for Theoretical Physics at the California Institute of Technology and a Leinweber Forum for Theoretical and Quantum Physics at the Institute for Advanced Study.

“MIT has one of the strongest and broadest theory groups in the world,” says Professor Washington Taylor, the director of the newly funded center and a leading researcher in string theory and its connection to observable particle physics and cosmology.

“This landmark endowment from the Leinweber Foundation will enable us to support the best graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to develop their own independent research programs and to connect with other researchers in the Leinweber Institute network. By pledging to support this network and fundamental curiosity-driven science, Larry Leinweber and his family foundation have made a huge contribution to maintaining a thriving scientific enterprise in the United States in perpetuity.”

The Leinweber Foundation’s investment across seven institutions — constituting the largest philanthropic commitment ever for theoretical physics research, according to the Science Philanthropy Alliance, a nonprofit organization that supports philanthropic support for science — will strengthen existing programs at each institution and foster collaboration across the universities. Recipient institutions will work both independently and collaboratively to explore foundational questions in theoretical physics. Each institute will continue to shape its own research focus and programs, while also committing to big-picture cross-institutional convenings around topics of shared interest. Moreover, each institute will have significantly more funding for graduate students and postdocs, including fellowship support for three to eight fully endowed Leinweber Physics Fellows at each institution.

“This gift is a commitment to America’s scientific future,” says Larry Leinweber, founder and president of the Leinweber Foundation. “Theoretical physics may seem abstract to many, but it is the tip of the spear for innovation. It fuels our understanding of how the world works and opens the door to new technologies that can shape society for generations. As someone who has had a lifelong fascination with theoretical physics, I hope this investment not only strengthens U.S. leadership in basic science, but also inspires curiosity, creativity, and groundbreaking discoveries for generations to come.”

Theoretical physics may seem abstract to many, but it is the tip of the spear for innovation. It fuels our understanding of how the world works and opens the door to new technologies that can shape society for generations. As someone who has had a lifelong fascination with theoretical physics, I hope this investment not only strengthens U.S. leadership in basic science, but also inspires curiosity, creativity, and groundbreaking discoveries for generations to come.

Larry Leinweber, founder and president of the Leinweber Foundation

The gift to MIT will create a postdoc program that, once fully funded, will initially provide support for up to six postdocs, with two selected per year for a three-year program. In addition, the gift will provide student financial support, including fellowship support, for up to six graduate students per year studying theoretical physics. The goal is to attract the top talent to the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics – A Leinweber Institute and support the ongoing research programs in a more robust way.

A portion of the funding will also provide support for visitors, seminars, and other scholarly activities of current postdocs, faculty, and students in theoretical physics, as well as helping with administrative support.

“Graduate students are the heart of our country’s scientific research programs. Support for their education to become the future leaders of the field is essential for the advancement of the discipline,” says Nergis Mavalvala, dean of the MIT School of Science and the Curtis (1963) and Kathleen Marble Professor of Astrophysics.

The Leinweber Foundation gift is the second significant gift for the center. “We are always grateful to Virgil Elings, whose generous gift helped make possible the space that houses the center,” says Deepto Chakrabarty, head of the Department of Physics. Elings PhD ’66, co-founder of Digital Instruments, which designed and sold scanning probe microscopes, made his gift more than 20 years ago to support a space for theoretical physicists to collaborate.

“Gifts like those from Larry Leinweber and Virgil Elings are critical, especially now in this time of uncertain funding from the federal government for support of fundamental scientific research carried out by our nation’s leading postdocs, research scientists, faculty, and students,” adds Mavalvala.

Professor Tracy Slatyer, whose work is motivated by questions of fundamental particle physics, particularly the nature and interactions of dark matter, will be the subsequent director of the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics – A Leinweber Institute beginning in fall 2025. Slatyer will join Mavalvala, Taylor, Chakrabarty, and the entirety of the theoretical physics community for a dedication ceremony planned for the near future.

The Leinweber Foundation was founded in 2015 by software entrepreneur Larry Leinweber, and has worked with the Science Philanthropy Alliance since 2021 to shape its philanthropic strategy. “It’s been a true pleasure to work with Larry and the Leinweber family over the past four years and to see their vision take shape,” says France Córdova, president of the Science Philanthropy Alliance. “Throughout his life, Larry has exemplified curiosity, intellectual openness, and a deep commitment to learning. This gift reflects those values, ensuring that generations of scientists will have the freedom to explore, to question, and to pursue ideas that could change how we understand the universe.”

TITLE: Tulane University Postdoctoral Fellow 2027: 18-Month Position in Communication, Digital Media and the Future of Work

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Tulane University is inviting applications for an 18-month Postdoctoral Fellow in Communication, Digital Media, and Influence, beginning on January 5, 2027, in New Orleans, Louisiana.

Hosted by the Department of Communication at Tulane University, the position is designed for early-career researchers whose scholarship examines the changing relationships between technology, society, politics, culture, digital media, influence, and the future of work.

The selected Postdoctoral Fellow will become an inaugural affiliate of a developing interdisciplinary initiative focused on the future of work. Through both research and teaching, the Fellow will help contribute to the intellectual foundations of what Tulane describes as a prospective new interdisciplinary center.

The role combines an active independent research agenda with undergraduate teaching, faculty mentorship, participation in departmental intellectual life, and access to Tulane University’s institutional and library resources.

The appointment is full-time for 18 months and carries a 2-2 teaching load, meaning that the Fellow will teach two courses per semester. Tulane emphasizes that the position also includes protected research time so that the successful candidate can continue developing publications and a broader scholarly profile.

Salary will be commensurate with experience, and the position includes a full benefits package.

There is no fixed final application deadline stated in the vacancy. However, review of applications will begin on October 15, 2026 and continue until the position is filled. Candidates are therefore strongly encouraged to submit their materials before the first review date.

About the Tulane University Postdoctoral Fellow Position

The Postdoctoral Fellow in Communication, Digital Media, and Influence is being recruited by Tulane University’s Department of Communication in anticipation of a broader interdisciplinary initiative examining the future of work.

Rather than focusing on one narrow definition of work, the position welcomes researchers studying how contemporary changes in digital technologies, platforms, information systems, media, politics, and culture are transforming the way work is organized, experienced, governed, represented, and monetized.

The successful Fellow will contribute through two complementary areas:

Independent academic research

Undergraduate teaching

The Fellow will also participate in the intellectual development of the emerging future-of-work initiative.

This makes the opportunity especially relevant to scholars interested in combining a traditional academic postdoctoral appointment with participation in a new institutional research agenda.

Position at a Glance

Institution: Tulane University

Department: Communication

Position: Postdoctoral Fellow in Communication, Digital Media, and Influence

Location: New Orleans, Louisiana, United States

Employment: Full-time

Appointment duration: 18 months

Start date: January 5, 2027

Teaching load: Two courses per semester

Research time: Protected research time included

Salary: Commensurate with experience

Benefits: Full benefits package

Application review begins: October 15, 2026

Closing: Applications continue to be reviewed until the position is filled

Contact: Dr. Vicki Mayer, vmayer@tulane.edu

Research Focus: Technology, Society and the Future of Work

Tulane is particularly interested in researchers whose work can advance critical debates concerning the ways the future of work intersects with technology, society, politics and culture.

The call deliberately leaves room for a wide variety of substantive topics and methodological traditions.

Potential research areas specifically identified by the Department include:

Digital employment

Work platforms

Emerging and new technologies

Big data applications

Influence campaigns

Advertising

Political economy of attention

Social media

Digital policy

Changing information environments

Technology and labor

Digital communication

The list is illustrative rather than narrowly prescriptive.

Applicants whose research connects meaningfully with the broader themes of digital communication, influence, emerging technologies and the future of work may therefore have a strong fit even if their exact project does not use one of these specific labels.

Digital Employment and Work Platforms

One potential research direction concerns the expansion of digitally mediated employment.

Digital technologies increasingly organize how people:

Find work

Complete work

Are managed

Are evaluated

Communicate professionally

Develop careers

Build professional identities

Researchers examining digital labor or work platforms could therefore find this position particularly relevant.

Potential topics could include platform economies, algorithmic management, remote work, digital labor, creator economies, online freelancing, gig work or changing relationships between workers and technological infrastructures.

Tulane does not require applicants to work on any one of these topics, but digital employment is specifically included among the areas of interest.

Emerging and New Technologies

The future-of-work initiative also welcomes scholarship examining new and emerging technologies.

This could potentially include research on technological developments affecting:

Communication

Employment

Management

Media production

Information circulation

Organizational culture

Political communication

Advertising

Public discourse

Because the position is situated in Communication, applicants should be able to demonstrate how their work contributes to questions relevant to media, communication, influence, technology or related social processes.

Big Data Applications

Big data is another research area highlighted by the Department.

Researchers may investigate how large-scale data systems are reshaping communication, organizations, platforms, labor practices, surveillance, targeting or decision-making.

Potential questions could involve:

Data-driven management

Algorithmic systems

Digital surveillance

Data analytics

Targeted advertising

Platform governance

Data and workplace power

Again, these are potential directions rather than formal requirements.

Influence Campaigns and Advertising

The position places particular emphasis on influence.

Researchers working on advertising, persuasion, political communication, digital influence, information campaigns or platform-based communication may therefore be particularly well aligned.

Influence can operate across multiple areas, including:

Political campaigns

Commercial advertising

Social-media promotion

Digital persuasion

Branding

Influencer cultures

Public communication

Organizational communication

The successful Fellow may investigate these topics through critical, qualitative, quantitative, computational, historical or mixed-method approaches.

Political Economy of Attention

Tulane also identifies the political economy of attention as a relevant research area.

The contemporary digital environment increasingly treats attention as an economic and political resource.

Researchers may examine how platforms, advertisers, media institutions, creators, employers and other actors compete for and monetize attention.

This could raise questions about:

Platform capitalism

Advertising systems

Algorithmic visibility

Monetization

Digital labor

Audience measurement

TITLE: United Nations – Nippon Foundation Fellowship on Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea 2027 (Funded)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 13, 2026

Applications are open for the United Nations – Nippon Foundation Fellowship on Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea 2027. The United Nations – Nippon Foundation Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea Fellowship (OALOS) provides Government officials and other mid-level professionals from developing States with advanced training on ocean affairs and the law of the sea, as well as related disciplines, including marine science in support of management frameworks.

Fellows will learn about international legal frameworks, key issues and best practices in ocean affairs, become familiar with the work of the United Nations, and develop professional skills. Fellows will also conduct individual research, under academic supervision, and develop a written thesis on a topic selected by them.

Upon completion of the Fellowship, Fellows are expected to return to their home countries and use their in-depth knowledge and extended experience to assist in formulating comprehensive ocean policy and in implementing the legal regime set out in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and related instruments, including through designing, implementing and/or evaluating specific improvement projects.

Programme Phases

The UNNF OALOS Fellowship is a nine-month programme consisting of two phases:

Phase One: A three-month training programme at OLA/DOALOS, United Nations Headquarters, New York (24 March to 30 June 2027).

Phase Two: A six-month research placement at an academic Host Institution participating in the UNNF Programmes, selected based on its expertise in the Fellow’s research area (1 July to 17 December 2027).

Benefits

Fellows will receive a monthly stipend during their Fellowship, both during their time in New York and, for the United Nations – Nippon Foundation Fellowship on Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea (UNNF-OALOS) Fellows, participating in the 9-month programme, during their time at the second phase host institution.

Fellows will be provided with a round-trip economy class airline ticket for travel between their home country and New York to undertake the Fellowship.

Selected Fellows must be medically cleared by the United Nations Medical Service and their award is contingent on such clearance.

Eligibility

To qualify, applicants must:

Be between 25 and 45 years of age.

Hold at least a first university degree or an equivalent qualification.

Demonstrate the ability to undertake advanced academic research and study.

Be a national of a developing State.

Be a mid-level government official or mid-level professional working directly on ocean affairs and/or the law of the sea, including but not limited to:

Implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and related instruments;

Implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly SDG 14;

Maritime zones and maritime boundary delimitation;

National and regional ocean policy;

Coastal zone management;

Conservation and sustainable management of marine living resources;

Maritime transport and shipping;

Maritime security;

Protection and preservation of the marine environment; and

Marine science and related fields.

Have a strong command of spoken and written English. All Fellowship activities are conducted in English and require in-person participation. Training materials in French and Spanish are available upon request, subject to availability. The research project may be undertaken in English or French, provided that the Host Institution is able to offer supervision in the chosen language.

Application

Before completing the Indico.UN online Personal History and Proposed Research/Study Programme Application Form, applicants must:

Download, complete and sign the 2027 UNNF OALOS Application Form – Personal History and Proposed Research/Study Programme. Fill in all the fields electronically and apply your electronic or handwritten signature and use the “Save” option to save your changes.

Each question must be answered clearly and completely in order to ensure that the application will be processed. While completing the form, candidates should pay particular attention to sections 16, 17 and 18.

Complete the 2027 UNNF OALOS Fellowship Nomination Form, signed and stamped by the nominating authority.

Kindly upload the completed documents in either Word or PDF format.

Have a copy of your valid national passport ready for upload.

All three documents should be uploaded in the Indico.UN Platform.

CFR assists fellows in finding a host organization that matches their proposed work in Canada. However, all placements are made at the discretion of the host institution. CFR cannot guarantee placement at any specific agency or organization. The fellowship will be a full-time, in-person experience. Fellows should expect to work on-site with their host organization in Canada at least four days per week.

Eligibility

Applicants must be U.S. citizens.

Applicants must be mid-career professionals.

Applicants must have a strong record of professional achievement.

Applicants must have a demonstrated commitment to a career in foreign policy and have an interest in U.S.-Canada relations.

Applicants must hold at least a bachelor’s degree.

Applicants must have a U.S. passport, valid through six months after the fellowship end date.

Selection Criteria

Selection as an IAF in Canada is based on the following criteria:

Scholarly qualifications and/or professional experience

The merits and feasibility of a research proposal on some aspect of U.S.-Canada relations

Character and personal qualities conducive to promoting cross-cultural communication and cooperation

The contribution the fellowship will make to the applicant’s career development

Applications are open for the GEAF Ambassador Programme 2027. The GEAF Ambassador Programme by the Green Earth Action Foundation is a 6-month global initiative for individuals committed to taking action on environmental and climate challenges within their communities.

Through mentorship, capacity building, and guided project implementation, GEAF Ambassadors design and lead locally relevant initiatives that address environmental challenges within their communities. These initiatives are fully funded and implemented across GEAF’s five thematic areas: Waste Reduction & Pollution Prevention, Marine & Water Protection, Environmental Education & Community Empowerment, Climate-Smart Agriculture Advancement, and Forest & Biodiversity Protection.

GEAF Ambassadors are supported by the GEAF team throughout their journey, with training sessions delivered by subject-matter experts. Previous training sessions have been facilitated by representatives from the ILO, IISD, CCC, SAIIA, UNEP, UNDP, WIPO, and other leading organisations.

Benefits

Full funding to design and deliver a community climate project

Expert-led capacity building from international think tanks and UN affiliates

One-to-one mentorship throughout the programme

Recognition for their affiliated organisation as a key collaborator

A global platform through participation in 4.29 Green Earth Action Day

Eligibility

Be at least 18 years old at the time of the application;

Strong understanding and passion for sustainability and environmental justice;

Strong written and spoken communication skills;

Experience in community outreach and implementing local initiatives;

Fluency in French or English (basic understanding of English is mandatory for all participants);

Be available to participate fully in the six-month Programme, with an expected commitment of approximately 5–10 hours per week.

Application

Required documents:

Passport – A scan of the information page of your passport.

CV – The CV should include past and current experiences, diplomas and languages and should be a maximum of 2 pages.

Motivation Letter – This document should include what this Programme means to you, why you would be a good fit, and how it will help you achieve your goals and should be a maximum of 1 page.

Project Proposal – This document should include: a project overview with a clear description of the project goals, expected outcomes and relevance to your local community. An implementation strategy with a step-by-step plan including timelines. A stakeholder engagement section with a list of potential partners. TITLE: Texas Aerospace Scholars Research Brief Development Opportunity at NASA Johnson Space Center: Apply for the Spring 2027 Program

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Are you a university student with strong writing, communication, research, education, engineering, science, or STEM interests and a passion for space exploration? NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) is offering an opportunity to contribute to the Texas Aerospace Scholars (TAS) program through research, educational content development, and NASA-focused projects connected to the agency’s Moon-to-Mars exploration objectives.

The Texas Aerospace Scholars – Research Brief Development position is designed for students who want to gain practical experience in a professional NASA environment while helping develop educational resources for high school students interested in aerospace, science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

Based at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, the position involves developing research briefs, educational materials, newsletters, digital content, and other resources that translate complex NASA initiatives into engaging and accessible learning experiences.

The program is scheduled for the Spring 2027 session, with registration opening on June 12, 2026, and closing on September 14, 2026.

About the Texas Aerospace Scholars Opportunity

The Texas Aerospace Scholars program is connected to NASA’s broader efforts to engage students in STEM education and inspire the next generation of aerospace professionals.

The Research Brief Development position provides an opportunity for a student intern to support the development of educational and research content for TAS participants. A major focus of the assignment will be NASA’s Moon-to-Mars exploration objectives and how these objectives can be transformed into meaningful research projects for high school students.

The selected student will work alongside TAS mentors and subject matter experts at NASA Johnson Space Center to research, write, edit, design, and develop educational resources.

Rather than simply observing NASA operations, the student will be expected to make tangible contributions to the TAS program through the creation of professional-quality educational materials.

NASA describes its internships as educational, hands-on experiences that provide participants with opportunities to gain NASA-related research and operational experience.

For broader information about NASA internships, applicants can visit NASA Internships.

What Will the Selected Student Work On?

One of the central responsibilities of the position will be the development of comprehensive research briefs for Texas Aerospace Scholars students.

The intern is expected to develop approximately 5–7 two-page research briefs aligned with NASA’s Moon-to-Mars exploration objectives.

These research briefs are expected to contain several important components, including:

Detailed descriptions of research projects.

Scientific and technical background information.

Exploratory activities designed for high school students.

Clearly defined learning outcomes.

Professionally formatted educational content suitable for distribution during TAS program sessions.

Information that connects NASA exploration objectives with practical student research activities.

The work therefore combines research, writing, editing, education, communication, STEM knowledge, and content development.

Key Responsibilities

The selected participant will undertake a broad range of communications, research, education, and content-development responsibilities.

1. Develop Educational Content

The intern will research and create educational materials that help Texas Aerospace Scholars students understand complex aerospace and STEM concepts.

This requires the ability to take technical information and transform it into content that is clear, engaging, accurate, and appropriate for a high school audience.

2. Prepare Research Briefs

A major responsibility will be developing the 5–7 research briefs associated with the TAS program.

The briefs will connect student research activities with NASA’s Moon-to-Mars exploration goals and provide students with structured opportunities to investigate relevant topics.

3. Research NASA Moon-to-Mars Initiatives

The intern will research NASA initiatives associated with human exploration and the Moon-to-Mars pathway.

This may require reviewing technical and scientific information and identifying the most relevant material for educational use.

4. Write and Edit TAS Materials

The position involves writing content for a variety of Texas Aerospace Scholars communication and educational materials.

This includes content for:

TAS educational resources.

Newsletters.

Digital platforms.

Research materials.

Student-facing resources.

Other program communications.

5. Translate Complex Information for Students

An important part of the role is making complex technical concepts understandable to high school audiences.

The successful applicant should therefore be able to communicate scientific and technical information without unnecessarily complicated language while maintaining accuracy.

6. Support TAS Engagement Events

The intern will also support Texas Aerospace Scholars engagement activities and events.

This may involve helping prepare materials, supporting educational activities, assisting with program logistics, or contributing to other initiatives connected to student engagement.

7. Collaborate With Mentors and Subject Matter Experts

The position provides an opportunity to work with TAS mentors and subject matter experts at Johnson Space Center.

Collaboration will be important because the intern will need to gather information, receive feedback, refine content, and ensure that educational materials meet program expectations.

8. Contribute to Special Projects

In addition to the primary research-brief assignment, the intern may assist with special projects related to the Texas Aerospace Scholars program.

This makes adaptability and the ability to manage multiple assignments particularly important.

Work Schedule and Location

The opportunity is an in-person, full-time position at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

The stated working schedule is:

Location: Houston, Texas

NASA Center: Johnson Space Center

Format: In-person

Schedule: Full-time

Working hours: 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Hours per week: 40 hours

Session: Spring 2027

Because the position is fully on-site, applicants should be prepared to participate in the program physically at Johnson Space Center rather than remotely.

Skills NASA Is Looking For

The opportunity is particularly suitable for students who can combine strong communication skills with research, analytical, technical, educational, or STEM capabilities.

The listing highlights several desired skills.

Strong Writing, Editing and Proofreading

The ability to write clearly and professionally is central to the position.

Applicants should be comfortable researching information, drafting content, editing their own work, proofreading documents, and producing polished materials for students and program stakeholders.

Ability to Work in a Fast-Paced Environment

The position may involve several assignments and changing priorities. Applicants should therefore be capable of adapting quickly while maintaining accuracy and quality.

Multi-Project Management

Strong organizational and time-management abilities will therefore be valuable.

Graphic Design

Applicants who can combine writing with visual communication may be particularly well suited to the role.

Communication

Problem Solving and Critical Thinking

Microsoft Office 365

This is one of the defining aspects of the position because the research briefs are intended for high school students.

NASA Mission or STEM Education Familiarity

While this is described as a preferred area rather than the sole basis for eligibility, applicants who understand NASA’s mission, aerospace exploration, STEM education, or Moon-to-Mars objectives may be better positioned to demonstrate their suitability.
