TITLE: Donor Profile: Jim and Sylvia Earl

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Jim ’53, PhD ’57 has had a lifelong passion for physics and he and his wife Sylvia have been great friends and supporters of the MIT Physics Department. They have named their gifts in honor of people that were important to them.

by Erin McGrath // MIT Physics Annual 2017

Jim and Sylvia Earl before the
The Helena Foundation Junior Laboratory

After Jim graduated from Omaha Central High School in 1949, he entered MIT expecting to study electrical engineering. However, two events in his freshman year convinced him to study physics instead. The first occurred during freshman physics laboratory, which was supervised by a graduate student named Robert Noyce—who later co-founded Intel Corporation—and who introduced Jim to the concept of experimentation. The second event was the arrival from Europe of Stanislaw Olbert—who became an MIT physics faculty member—and who lived in Jim’s fraternity house and became a trusted mentor.

As Bruno Rossi’s student, Olbert introduced Jim to the cosmic ray research group, which included William Kraushaar; he supervised Jim’s bachelor’s thesis on the properties of a large ionization chamber. Jim’s graduate work continued under Kraushaar at the Agassiz Air Shower Experiment at the Harvard College Observatory, where he studied the muonic component of extensive air showers.

While at MIT, Jim met Sylvia, a native of Newton, MA, and a student at Wheelock College, where she said it was her good fortune to have met Jim. After they married, the Earls lived at the Westgate barracks for two years. Between two babies, she performed in a play as the moon goddess Selene, which took place in the Little Theatre of MIT’s Kresge Auditorium. Sylvia recalls being perched on top of a stepladder for the duration of the play.

After MIT, Jim spent a year as a Second Lieutenant with the Army Signal Corps Laboratory at Fort Monmouth, New Jersey, working on the Vanguard 2 weather satellite. However, before it was launched Jim left for an academic position at the University of Minnesota. There, Jim began a series of experiments using cloud chambers to study cosmic rays at the top of the atmosphere. (Earlier, Edward Ney had pioneered this approach to space research.) It led to a very notable result: Jim’s discovery of primary cosmic ray electrons.

After a few years, Jim left Minnesota for the University of Maryland, where he began experiments using balloons to carry Geiger tube hodoscopes to visualize and identify particles at the top of the atmosphere. Results of this research were an early determination of the spectrum of cosmic electrons at very high energies and the discovery of the J = AT law, which describes the spectrum of solar modulated protons.

Later in his career, after a sabbatical at the California Institute of Technology, Jim turned to theoretical studies of energetic particle propagation in random magnetic fields. These resulted in a simple explanation of the J = AT law and the identification of a coherent mode of propagation that explained observations of “scatter-free” solar particle events.

To confirm theoretical results on propagation, Jim carried out extensive Monte Carlo simulations of particle propagation on the Massively Parallel Processor at Goddard Space Flight Center. This computer was quite primitive, but it could track the behavior of enormous numbers of particles. Consequently, statistical errors were minor and comparison with theoretical results provided convincing verification.

Jim has had a lifelong passion for physics, and he and Sylvia have been great friends and supporters to the MIT Physics Department. They have supported The Helena Foundation Junior Laboratory, and a number of fellowships including the Clark (1952) Fellowship Fund, Boldt (1953 Fellowship Fund), and the Bruno Rossi Fellowship Fund.

The Earls have named their gifts in honor of people that were important to them. As a graduate student, Jim worked on the air shower experiment with George Clark, who was then a recent PhD graduate. Jim notes: “I learned a tremendous amount from him. Later, George dramatically upgraded the junior laboratory. The Clark fellowship is our attempt to recognize him for these personal and institutional contributions.” Jim continues: “Elihu Boldt and I were members of the MIT class of 1953 and as graduate students members of Rossi’s group. When Sylvia and I came to Maryland, we continued our friendship with Elihu and his family. By this time, Elihu had begun his brilliant career at Goddard Space Flight Center. He was an outstanding scientist worthy of recognition by the Boldt fellowship.” And, Jim says, “As you can see from above, Bruno Rossi had a profound impact on my life. For this reason and more general ones, it is certainly appropriate for graduate fellowships to be named after him.”

Outside of physics, Jim has a strong interest in art. At Maryland, he earned two additional undergraduate degrees in studio art and computer science. After retiring in 1999, Jim renewed his interest in art by creating intaglio prints in the print shop at Anne Arundel Community College. Jim notes: “My art has appeared in many shows around Annapolis; a highlight was a one-person show at St. John’s College library, and a few of my etchings have won awards. I also do watercolors and pen and ink drawings in sketchbooks, one of which I always carry in my pocket.”

Sylvia shares, “Jim and I are the parents of four sons and nine grandchildren. Over the years, sixty-two in all, I’ve enjoyed attending MIT reunions, which gave us the opportunity to rekindle old friendships. During Jim’s career, we have attended conferences all over the world and taken sabbaticals in this country and abroad. A memorable one was at Kiel University in West Germany, during which we and our two youngest sons became quite fluent in German.”

Now in retirement, Jim and Sylvia are both busy with the Helena Foundation supporting MIT and other organizations, as well as their special interests in physics, the arts and the environment.

TITLE: How I Won a Fully Funded Study Abroad Scholarship and How You Can Too

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
A scholarship can be the door you have been waiting for. A year ago, I received a fully-funded Mastercard scholarship, and I did that after receiving 17 rejections. Now, I will show you how I did that and how you can too. First, picture this: there are 15,000 people and 50 people need to be selected for a scholarship worth £80,000. Why should that scholarship body decide to invest in you? Why are you the best person to be invested in, and why should they invest in you now? Why should you be one of the 50 people selected? Don’t think they must invest in you just because you want to get it. Think about it as a journey in which you have already made a lot of progress. You need to get the door open. Here is how I opened mine, and here is what I would do differently if I was starting from rejection number one again.

1. Know Your Story Before Anyone Else Does
Many scholarships would need you to share your story. Your past, your present, and your future, especially as it relates to your career. Your understanding of your own personal journey, story, life, and trajectory would be a shaping force for you to define where you are headed. This isn’t just about writing a nice paragraph for the personal statement. It’s about actually sitting down, sometimes for weeks, and asking yourself hard questions: Where did I start? What shaped my choices? What am I really working towards, and why? For me, that meant going back to why I even chose my field in the first place, tracing it through the projects I had taken on, the setbacks, and connecting all of that to the future I wanted the scholarship to help me build. If you can’t tell your own story to yourself in a way that makes sense, you won’t be able to convince a panel of strangers either.

2. Do the Work, Not Just the Application
You don’t want to go around lying about things you did not do. You want to reflect on what you have done and how that leads you to a future, and how, with a scholarship, you would leverage that to be and do even more. Make sure you are telling an authentic story of your own work.
Make sure it is verifiable, and make sure you are doing it from a place of something you are truly invested in and not because you just want a scholarship. After applying 17 times over three years, I realised that my courage for the work I was doing had not waned because of rejections, and even now, I find the need to leverage all I am learning to do and be more. What kept me going wasn’t the scholarship itself, it was the work. I kept publishing, kept volunteering, kept building, even after rejection number 10, number 14, number 17. By the time I got that yes, I had a body of work that could speak for itself, not because I planned it that way, but because I never stopped. Get the work done!

3. Show, Don’t Tell
It’s very sweet to write a beautiful story, but make sure that as you are telling stories, you are showing what you have done and adding the numbers, the impact, the journey, and everything. An example is saying “I led a project” versus “I led a project that reached 500 students and raised £10,000.” The second one gives the panel something to picture and something to verify. Go through your own CV and personal statement and ask yourself, for every line, can I attach a number, an outcome, or a name to this? If a reader can’t picture what you did or measure its impact, that line application probably needs more work.

4. Network
Get close to people who have walked that path, understand their journey, understand how they got in, and leverage that knowledge. This can be as simple as sending a message on LinkedIn to a past scholar and asking for 15 minutes of their time. Most people who have won something like this remember what it felt like to be on the outside, and many are willing to share what worked for them, what they’d do differently, and sometimes even review your application. I did this myself, and some of the most useful feedback I got on my personal statement came from people who had sat in that exact interview room before me.

5. Research
The truth is, every scholarship knows who they are looking for. The day I got into the interview room for my scholarship, I was as convinced as anything that this scholarship was looking for me. The scholarship is also looking for the right fit; that is why they put out a call for applications. So, research, research. What is this programme about, who is it for, what kind of people have been getting in in the past, what does it cover, who would likely not get this, where do I fall? Research extensively about the programme you want to get into, the university, the place, the country, the scholarship. Look at past cohorts if the information is public. Look at the kind of work previous winners were doing before they got selected. Look at what the scholarship body says about itself, its mission, its values, and see how your own story genuinely lines up with that, not how you can force it to line up. Research is also crucial because it would help you filter which scholarships you should be applying to and where you stand a greater chance.

Next week, I will share with you more tips on how you can win, learning from my own experience. So, stay tuned. I am rooting for you. Disclaimer – All views shared here are strictly my views and from my experience, and do not reflect the views of any scholarship body.

TITLE: Advancing Paediatric Cancer Research in Europe

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Grant Evaluation | News | Programme Management | Research Assessment News

In 2019 several European childhood cancer foundations launched the Fight Kids Cancer programme, an initiative created to address the urgent need for innovation in paediatric oncology.
Learn how ESF played a key role in its success – supporting its implementation, guiding project assessment, and managing post-award processes.

A Collaborative Model for Advancing Paediatric Cancer Research in Europe

Launched in 2019, the Fight Kids Cancer (FKC) initiative was created to address the pressing need for innovation in paediatric oncology. The programme supports translational research and clinical trials focused on improving survival rates, reducing treatment toxicity, and restoring young patients to full health. It prioritises interdisciplinary and collaborative research, particularly on paediatric brain tumours, leukaemia, and solid tumours-while also aiming to advance fundamental scientific knowledge and build scientific capacity across Europe.

FKC brings together three founding funders – KickCancer (Belgium), Imagine for Margo (France), and The Kriibskrank Kanner Foundation (Luxembourg) -recently joined by two other partners: the CRIS Cancer Foundation (Spain, France, UK) and KiKa (Netherlands).

By pooling resources, these organisations have funded 38 projects and one innovation award over the past five years, totalling nearly €30 million. With a budget of €12 million in 2025, FKC is making significant strides in paediatric cancer research by supporting innovative treatments, enhancing clinical trial design, and fostering closer collaboration between clinical and laboratory researchers across Europe.

The Role of ESF

Faced with an urgent need, the founders knew that accelerating support was critical and were determined to act fast. With ESF’s dual expertise in managing funds and grant evaluation, the path forward quickly became clear.

“ESF’s involvement was a game-changer,” recalls Delphine Heenen, co-founder of Fight Kids Cancer and Director of KickCancer (Belgium). “It allowed us to launch FIGHT KIDS CANCER without having to create a whole new legal entity, which saved time while simplifying the process. Their support allowed us to pool funds effectively and structure our collaboration without cumbersome legal complexities.”

ESF has since played a pivotal role in the FIGHT KIDS CANCER initiative by assisting with the definition of scientific objectives and ensuring an independent selection process.

Selection Process & Post-Award Grant Management

The independent project selection process managed by ESF has been critical in upholding fairness and credibility. Given that paediatric oncology is a small and highly specialised research area, managing conflicts of interest (CoI) can be complex.

“Paediatric cancer is a small research area, and managing CoI is always a challenge,” says Heenen. “ESF’s independent selection procedure, combined with their effective CoI management, has been essential in maintaining the integrity of our calls and ensuring that the best projects are funded.”

Post-award, ESF has also ensured that grant-making remains efficient and transparent. Through regular annual reviews and project monitoring, ESF helps FKC track progress and address any implementation challenges.

“ESF’s role in project follow-up and financial reviews has made it possible for us to track the progress of our funded projects accurately and efficiently”, Heenen adds.

Toward €25 Million in Funding

Since its launch, FKC has scaled its funding capacity from €3 million to €12 million annually and continues to invest in both translational research and clinical trials that bring new treatments closer to young patients. In line with its goal to foster future generations of paediatric oncology researchers, the programme has also introduced the Innovation Award-providing flexible funding to early-career scientists.

Looking ahead, FKC aims to double its annual funding to €25 million and expand its network and impact across Europe. ESF’s role will continue to be vital as FIGHT KIDS CANCER scales up its operations. With enhanced tracking tools and strengthened grant-making processes, FKC will be better equipped to scale its impact. As Heenen notes:

“The toolkit developed by ESF for FIGHT KIDS CANCER has set a benchmark. Their ability to structure and manage multi-partner funding calls could easily be adapted for other disease areas. It has helped us create a sustainable model for paediatric cancer research, and we often recommend ESF to other organisations in similar rare disease sectors.”

A Model for Research Support in Paediatric Oncology

The FIGHT KIDS CANCER initiative, fuelled by collaboration and strategic funding, has proven to be a model for effective research support in paediatric oncology. This collaborative grant-making model-underpinned by structured management and independent selection processes-offers strong potential for broader application, particularly in rare diseases and other underserved research areas.

By overcoming the fragmentation of funding across borders, it delivers real added value to end users-whether patients, practitioners, or society at large.

TITLE: Call for expression of interest in the creation of inter-ACE thematic network on Health

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Through the ACE Impact regional project, targeting 12 countries in West, Central and Sahel countries (Burkina

Faso, Gambia, Guinea, Cameroon, Nigeria, Niger, Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Togo, Benin, Ghana, Djibouti), the World

Bank and AFD are financing 53 centers of excellence (ACE) competitively selected after an independent

evaluation, for a total amount of more than 350 million USD. AFD is financing ACE programs in Côte d’Ivoire,

Benin and Nigeria for a total amount of 78 million USD.

In this context and in accordance with the ACE Impact Project Managers, starting with the World Bank and the

Association of African Universities in charge of the regional coordination of the project, the AFD is granting

additional funding dedicated to the creation of ACEPartners, an inter-ACE thematic network on health-related

issues.

The ACEPartners project aims to:

Strengthen research networking on common research health-related interests between eligible ACEs.

Build sustainable Health Research Networks with a broader spectrum that goes beyond the current

ACE frameworks by opening participation to non-core ACE actors (emerging ACEs, faculties and

universities from ACE Impact countries, international research organizations, private sector, NGOs,

etc.)

The IRD (French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development) will be in charge of the implementation of the project.

1. Objectives and Contents of ACEPartners :

1.1 Thematic Scope

The regional health network will be based around the following:

• Core actors: ACEs and emerging centers on common or complementary thematic areas, with an ACE in

coordination (through the recruitment of a coordinator financed by ACEPartners);

• First circle of academic and scientific partners, composed of faculties and laboratories from other ACE

programs, partner universities, research performing organizations (RPO) in the North ;

• Second circle of non-academic partners, such as NGOs, private sectors, foundations, etc.

1.2 ACEPartners’ Components

The ACEPartners project aims to provide and co-finance mobility grants, PhD scholarships, scientific events and

expertise in the following four areas:

Component 1: Strengthening Research Capacities

The networks will be expected to (1) define and implement a common scientific strategy through

applied research programs, (2) establish research teams which will be funded through research projects

whose calls for proposals will be launched within networks, (3) mutualize and optimize the use of

scientific equipment by ACEs (computing centers, databases, digital tools, etc.) and (4) design and

implement training cycles adapted to the needs of the scientific communities in order to increase the

skills of researchers on the following three pillars:

Conduct and publish their research (workshops for writing scientific articles, bibliographic

research, research methodologies…),

Fund their research (grant writing, lobbying in specific fields of research),

Promote and disseminate their research (media training, expertise, maximize research results and impacts) in partnership with the private sector.

Component 2: Strengthening Higher Education Training Capacities

Networks will be expected to (1) create joint training programs (master’s programs, doctoral schools,

continuing education…) for the reinforcement of existing training programs and their adaptation to the

need of socio-economic partners, (2) bridge the gap between higher education and research (creation

of short and long inter-ACE training cycles at the regional level, workshops and thematic conferences,

etc.). A mobility program (thesis, master and exchange programs between academic and administrative

staff) will be implemented inside the network.

Component 3: Strengthening Innovation Capacities and Ties with the Non-academic Sector.

Networks will be expected to (1) involve relevant socio-economic actors in existing or upcoming

training and research activities through the use of innovative tools for analyzing the needs of the socioeconomic sector (round tables with companies, students / employers training bank, alumni follow-up,

social networks, doctoral programs). We aim for the creation of specialized academic modules and the

development of a policy of support for innovation and research transfer for students (creation of startups, business / research / student collaborations, etc.), (2) formalize services and platforms for

innovation and research transfer toward the private sector within the network and Centers (training

program for ACEs’ research transfer managers, implementation of multi-actors projects).

Component 4: Ensuring the Network’s Sustainability

Networks will be expected to (1) identify and respond to funding opportunities (call for research

project, call for expertise, etc.) from various financing actors (African and European Union, think tanks,

development banks, government, foundations…) and (2) develop resource-generating activities

(training dedicated to professionals, expertise, etc.).

Network support cost is estimated around 375 000 euros maximum per year over four year (1.5 M EUR

total). Support will comprise four types of activities: expertise through missions and services,

scholarships, scientific events and outputs.

Fiduciary management (and all procurement – equipment, scholarship, services) will be undertaken by the

IRD. ACE involved in the thematic network will determine activities and objectives through its Workplan

(common scientific program, common events and training, targeted technical assistance, scholarships, etc.). The

IRD will mobilize its current procurement scheme and will launch new procurement in order to respond to the

thematic network Workplan needs. The IRD will also manage allocated scholarships.

2. Expected Impacts

The main objective of the network will be the enhancement of Research and Academic collaborations between

ACEs, whose impact will be subject to a review through an evaluation framework and a final independent

assessment. The Health Network will have specific goals in terms of (1) creating common training and research

programs, (2) workshop activities (3) collaboration with socio-economic partners, (4) external revenue

generation. ACEPartners’ goal is also to impact indirectly on ACEs achievements. 3. How to express interest:

Interested ACE should send a general description (4/5 pages max) of the proposed thematic network to the

following address: acepartners@ird.fr indicating:

The roles of centers involved in the network and potential network’s leader ;

The scientific, academic and partnership approaches of the network ;

How the network will help centers involved in reaching their DLIs ;

A general implementation plan (calendar and budget).

Deadline for submission: April 15th.

For any additional questions, please contact acepartners@ird.fr

TITLE: CERN Junior Digital Communications Officer 2027: Apply for a 12-Month Administrative Student Position in Geneva

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
CERN is inviting applications for an exciting Junior Digital Communications Officer opportunity within its Digital Communications team in Geneva, Switzerland. Designed for university students who want to develop professional experience in digital communications, social media, science communication, and technology-related content, the position offers the chance to spend 12 months working at one of the world’s most internationally recognised scientific organisations.

The position forms part of the CERN Administrative Student Programme and is expected to begin on 1 June 2027. Successful applicants will work closely with communications professionals responsible for telling CERN’s stories to audiences around the world through digital platforms, social media, campaigns, science communication, and multimedia content.

Application Deadline: 16 October 2026

The CERN Administrative Student Programme application portal currently specifies that applications must be submitted by 23:59 Geneva time on 16 October 2026.

About CERN

CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, is one of the world’s leading centres for scientific research. Based near Geneva, Switzerland, CERN brings together scientists, engineers, technicians, administrators, communications professionals and other specialists from many countries to advance fundamental knowledge and develop technologies with wider benefits for society.

CERN’s mission extends beyond scientific discovery. The organisation also promotes technological innovation, education, international collaboration and the development of future generations of scientists, engineers and professionals. Its work includes operating major scientific facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider while creating an international environment in which people from diverse professional and cultural backgrounds collaborate on global scientific challenges.

For a student interested in digital communications, this creates an unusual professional environment: rather than promoting a conventional commercial product or service, the selected student will help communicate research, science, technology, innovation, education and international collaboration to global audiences.

About the Junior Digital Communications Officer Position

The selected Junior Digital Communications Officer will join the CERN Digital Communications team.

This team works alongside CERN’s Press team and Web team within the Media and Digital Communications section, which is part of the Education, Communications and Outreach group in CERN’s Stakeholder Relations sector.

The position therefore offers direct exposure to an integrated communications environment covering areas such as:

Digital communications

Social media management

Science communication

Digital campaign development

Content creation

Content curation

Online community management

Social media moderation

Communications monitoring

Media and digital communications evaluation

Science and technology writing

Video-oriented communications

Public engagement

Students will be able to apply academic knowledge to real communications activities while learning how a large international scientific organisation communicates complex subjects to different audiences.

Main Responsibilities

The Junior Digital Communications Officer will support a broad range of activities within CERN’s Digital Communications team.

1. Supporting CERN’s Social Media Activities

A major component of the position involves contributing to CERN’s social media presence.

Responsibilities can include:

Community management

Creating content for CERN’s digital audiences

Curating appropriate content

Moderating online interactions

Monitoring social media activity

This provides the successful applicant with practical experience in managing the digital presence of a highly visible international scientific organisation.

2. Developing Digital Communications Campaigns

The student will contribute to implementing digital communications campaigns surrounding some of CERN’s major stories and activities.

The campaigns may cover subjects including:

Physics

Particle accelerators

Scientific detectors

Computing

Technology transfer

International relations

Education

The selected candidate will work collaboratively with colleagues across the relevant section and group to transform these topics into communications suitable for digital audiences.

This aspect of the role could be particularly valuable for students interested in learning how complex scientific or technical information is translated into accessible, engaging communications.

3. Contributing to Communications for the 2027 CERN Open Days

One particularly notable element of the position is the opportunity to contribute to the digital communications campaign for the 2027 CERN Open Days.

The selected student will therefore have the opportunity to gain experience supporting communications around a major CERN public-engagement activity.

Experience of this nature can provide valuable practical exposure to event communications, audience engagement, campaign planning, social media coordination and content production.

4. Writing Science and Technology Content for Social Media

Applicants interested in science communication should pay particular attention to this responsibility.

The Junior Digital Communications Officer will help write science and technology social media posts using existing CERN news items and will also contribute content for CERN’s regular digital series.

The role therefore requires more than simply knowing how to use social media platforms. Candidates should be capable of understanding information, identifying the most relevant points and transforming potentially technical material into accurate and engaging digital content.

5. Monitoring and Evaluating Communications Activities

The successful candidate will also contribute to the evaluation and monitoring of CERN’s media and digital communications activities.

This provides an opportunity to understand the analytical side of communications, including how organisations assess communication activities, audience engagement and the effectiveness of digital content and campaigns.

For students interested in data-informed communications strategy, this element can provide experience beyond traditional content creation.

Skills and Experience CERN Is Looking For

CERN has identified several skills and experience areas relevant to the Junior Digital Communications Officer position.

Science and Technology Writing Experience

Applicants should have some experience in science and technology writing, particularly writing intended for digital platforms.

This could be particularly relevant for students who have previously worked on:

University science communications

Digital publications

Science blogs

Online magazines

Social media content

Research communication

Student publications

STEM outreach activities

Digital journalism

Institutional communications

Strong Interest in Social Media

Candidates should demonstrate strong motivation and interest in social media.

CERN specifically highlights an interest in the online video environment, indicating that awareness of how video-based content functions within contemporary digital communications would be valuable.

Communications or Marketing Experience Related to STEM

Some previous experience in communications and/or marketing connected with science, technology, engineering or mathematics is also requested.

Applicants should therefore consider highlighting any relevant academic, voluntary, freelance, university, society, internship or professional activities involving the communication of STEM subjects.

Experience in Multicultural and Multidisciplinary Environments

Previous experience working in a multicultural environment would be an advantage.

Experience working in multidisciplinary teams would similarly strengthen an application.

This is particularly relevant because CERN operates as a highly international organisation, bringing together people from numerous countries, academic disciplines and professional backgrounds.

Language Requirements

Applicants must have a very strong command of English.

The vacancy specifically states that candidates must be proficient in English at least at C2 level and should be willing to learn French.

The wider CERN Administrative Student Programme normally requires applicants to have a good knowledge of English or French, but candidates applying specifically for the Junior Digital Communications Officer role should pay attention to the higher English requirement stated in the individual vacancy.

Personal and Professional Competencies

The successful candidate should be capable of:

Working independently when required

Collaborating effectively as part of a team

Communicating clearly

Managing responsibilities in an international environment

Working effectively in a fast-paced setting

Contributing proactively to communications activities

CERN specifically identifies the ability to work both independently and collaboratively and the ability to thrive in a fast-paced environment among the required attributes.

Educational and Student Status Requirements

Because the position is offered through CERN’s Administrative Student Programme, applicants need to satisfy the programme’s student eligibility conditions.

Candidates must have completed at least 18 months, or three semesters, of their overall studies in the relevant field by the time of selection.

The vacancy is designed for students undertaking Bachelor’s or Master’s-level studies, and the selected applicant must remain enrolled as a full-time student for the entire duration of the CERN studentship.

PhD students and individuals who already hold a PhD are not eligible for the Administrative Student Programme.

Students studying communications or a closely related discipline and who can demonstrate relevant experience with digital communications, STEM communications, marketing, science writing or social media are likely to be particularly aligned with this specific position.

Duration and Expected Starting Date

This particular position is intended to last for 12 months.

The target starting date is:

1 June 2027

Although CERN’s broader Administrative Student Programme can host students for periods ranging from approximately four to twelve months, the Junior Digital Communications Officer vacancy specifically advertises a 12-month student position.

Students should consequently ensure that their university enrolment and academic arrangements would permit them to remain registered as full-time students throughout the placement.

CERN Administrative Student Programme Financial Support and Benefits

Students accepted through CERN’s current Administrative Student Programme receive a range of benefits designed to support their stay in Geneva.

According to CERN’s current programme information, benefits include:

A monthly net allowance of CHF 3,486

30 days of paid leave per year

An additional two-week annual CERN closure

Coverage through CERN’s comprehensive health insurance scheme, with the relevant contribution deducted from the student’s allowance

A possible family supplement depending on individual circumstances

Travel expenses to Geneva upon joining CERN, depending on individual circumstances

These provisions make the programme particularly valuable for students seeking substantial international professional experience while continuing their university studies.

Applicants should nevertheless consult the official CERN application portal for the conditions applicable to their individual circumstances.

Training and Professional Development Value

Beyond the financial support, one of the strongest aspects of this opportunity is its training value.

The successful applicant will have the opportunity to learn more about CERN’s scientific activities while working at the laboratory associated with major developments in science and technology, including the invention of the World Wide Web and the discovery of the Higgs boson.

The student will also gain exposure to:

Current physics developments at CERN

Engineering advances

Technological developments

Science communication

International digital communications

Social media strategy and implementation

Communications campaign development

Communication monitoring and evaluation

Another important benefit is professional networking.

According to the vacancy, the successful student will have opportunities to interact with and expand their network among:

Social media officers

Science communicators

Scientists

Technology specialists

Communications professionals from CERN Member States

Professionals from CERN Associate Member States

International communication and scientific communities

For students considering future careers in science communication, digital communications, international organisations, STEM outreach or institutional communications, this exposure could be particularly valuable.

Application Documents

Applicants applying through the CERN Administrative Student Programme should be prepared to submit a CV in English or French.

CERN’s current programme information also identifies the following documents as possible application materials:

CV in English or French

Academic reference letter, which is currently listed as optional

Academic transcript, which is currently listed as optional

Other documents that the applicant considers relevant to the application

Candidates applying specifically for this communications position should ensure that their CV clearly demonstrates relevant experience with digital communications, writing, social media, marketing, STEM communication or related projects.

How to Apply for the CERN Junior Digital Communications Officer Position

Applicants must complete two important steps.

Step 1: Apply Through the CERN Administrative Student Programme

Submit an application to CERN’s Administrative Student Programme before the deadline.

When completing the application, candidates interested in this specific position must clearly state:

SR-ECO-PRD

This is the reference provided by CERN for the Junior Digital Communications Officer opportunity.

Step 2: Send Your CV to the CERN Digital Communications Team

In addition to submitting the official Administrative Student Programme application, applicants must send their CV by email to:

social-media-admin@cern.ch

The purpose of this additional step is to inform the Digital Communications team that the applicant is specifically interested in the Junior Digital Communications Officer studentship.

Applicants should therefore not rely solely on emailing their CV. The formal CERN Administrative Student Programme application must also be completed.

Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

16 October 2026

CERN’s current Administrative Student Programme portal specifies a deadline of 16 October 2026 at 23:59 Geneva time.

Applicants are encouraged to prepare their documentation sufficiently early rather than leaving the application until the deadline.

Important Dates at a Glance

Application deadline: 16 October 2026

Target start date: 1 June 2027

Duration: 12 months

Location: CERN, Geneva area, Switzerland

Programme: CERN Administrative Student Programme

Specific position reference: SR-ECO-PRD

Why Consider the CERN Junior Digital Communications Officer Opportunity?

This position combines several areas that are increasingly important in professional communications: digital storytelling, social media, science communication, online video, content strategy, community engagement and communications analytics.

Students will not simply observe CERN’s communications activities. The vacancy indicates that they will contribute directly to social media management, digital campaigns, science and technology content, communications monitoring and CERN’s 2027 Open Days campaign.

The position may therefore be particularly attractive to students who want to build careers in areas such as:

Digital communications

Social media management

Science communication

STEM communications

Digital journalism

Content strategy

Institutional communications

International organisation communications

Public engagement

Communications analytics

Digital campaign management

Working within CERN also provides the opportunity to develop these skills in an environment where communications professionals interact directly with scientists, engineers, technology specialists, educators and international stakeholders.

Conclusion

The CERN Junior Digital Communications Officer opportunity for 2027 offers university students an exceptional chance to develop practical experience at the intersection of digital communications, science, technology and international engagement.

The 12-month position will allow the selected student to contribute to CERN’s social media activities, produce science and technology content, support major digital campaigns, assist with communications for the 2027 CERN Open Days and participate in the monitoring and evaluation of CERN’s media and digital communication activities.

With a target starting date of 1 June 2027, a current monthly net allowance of CHF 3,486 under the Administrative Student Programme, and extensive opportunities for professional learning and international networking, the programme provides substantial professional development for students seeking careers in communications and science-related fields.

Interested candidates should complete the CERN Administrative Student Programme application, specify SR-ECO-PRD in their application, and separately send their CV to social-media-admin@cern.ch.

Applications must be submitted by 16 October 2026.

TITLE: NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme 2027 Call for Proposals: Funding for Multi-Year Projects and Scientific Events

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The NATO Science for Peace and Security (SPS) Programme has opened its 2027-1 Call for Proposals, inviting scientists, experts, researchers and eligible institutions from NATO member countries and selected NATO partner countries to submit proposals addressing emerging security challenges through scientific research, technological innovation and international knowledge exchange.

The programme provides opportunities for Multi-Year Projects (MYPs) and SPS-supported scientific events, including Advanced Research Workshops, Advanced Training Courses and Advanced Study Institutes. Successful activities can receive funding, expert advice and programme support to develop practical, civil security-relevant solutions that contribute to NATO’s strategic objectives.

The 2027-1 call places particular emphasis on emerging areas such as countering unmanned systems, critical infrastructure protection, hybrid threats, energy resilience, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and space technologies.

The deadline for full proposals is 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

About the NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme

The NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme promotes dialogue and practical cooperation between NATO member states and partner countries.

Through scientific research, technological innovation and knowledge exchange, the SPS Programme brings together scientists, experts and officials to collaborate on security challenges that have implications for NATO and its partner countries.

The programme is designed to support practical, civil security-relevant activities that align with NATO’s strategic priorities. It enables researchers and experts from different countries to work together, develop innovative solutions and establish long-term professional and scientific partnerships.

Funding and support through the SPS Programme can help participating institutions conduct collaborative research, organize specialized scientific events, develop technologies and strengthen cooperation between NATO member states and eligible partner countries.

What Does the 2027-1 NATO SPS Call for Proposals Support?

For this call, the SPS Programme is accepting applications under two broad categories:

1. Multi-Year Projects

Multi-Year Projects are collaborative research and development activities designed to address security-related challenges through practical scientific and technological solutions.

Projects typically run for 24 to 36 months. Shorter implementation periods may also be considered where applicants provide adequate justification.

The programme expects project results to improve upon the existing state of the art and generally aims for results reaching Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 3–6.

This means projects should go beyond theoretical research and demonstrate a meaningful pathway toward practical application.

2. SPS Events

The call also supports specialized scientific and expert events, including:

Advanced Research Workshops

Advanced Training Courses

Advanced Study Institutes

Applicants proposing events are expected to demonstrate that the activity will generate outcomes beyond simply organizing a meeting, workshop or training programme.

The proposal should explain how the event will contribute to NATO-relevant objectives and how its findings, recommendations, research outputs or other results will reach relevant stakeholders and communities of interest.

Networking can be an important part of an SPS-supported event, but networking alone cannot be the primary objective.

Key Areas of Interest for the 2027-1 Call

Applications aligned with any of the SPS Programme’s Key Priorities are welcome.

However, the 2027-1 call identifies several topics of particular interest.

Non-Kinetic Mitigation Measures Against Unmanned Systems

The programme is interested in innovative approaches to addressing security challenges associated with unmanned systems.

Applicants may explore scientific, technological or operational approaches that can help mitigate risks associated with unmanned systems without relying exclusively on conventional kinetic measures.

Protection of Critical Infrastructure, Supplies and Personnel

Another area of interest is the protection and resilience of critical infrastructure, essential supplies and personnel.

This includes particular attention to:

Critical infrastructure protection

Maritime infrastructure resilience

Undersea infrastructure resilience

Protection of essential supplies

Protection of personnel

Systems and technologies that can maintain essential functions during disruptions

Deterrence and Defence Against Hybrid Tactics

The call encourages proposals addressing hybrid security challenges.

Potential projects may focus on:

Technologies for addressing hybrid threats

New approaches to deterrence and defence

Cross-sector coordination

International cooperation

Technologies and systems that strengthen resilience against hybrid tactics

Innovative Energy Generation, Storage and Distribution

Energy resilience is another priority area.

The programme is particularly interested in innovative approaches to energy generation, storage and distribution, including technologies and systems that enable critical facilities and deployed systems to continue operating during prolonged interruptions to energy supplies.

Projects may therefore address the resilience of energy systems and the ability of critical infrastructure to function despite extended disruptions.

Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence

The call identifies biotechnology as an area of particular interest, including the convergence between biotechnology and artificial intelligence.

Researchers and experts working at the intersection of biotechnology and AI may therefore find opportunities to develop collaborative projects addressing relevant security challenges.

Space Technologies

Space-related technologies are also highlighted.

Topics of interest include:

Space awareness

Positioning

Navigation

Timing

Technologies supporting resilient space-enabled capabilities

Applicants working on innovative space technologies with clear links to security objectives may consider the SPS Programme as a potential source of collaborative research and development support.

Who Can Apply?

The NATO SPS Programme has specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants must meet all applicable eligibility criteria to have their proposals considered.

A proposal must:

Contribute to NATO’s strategic objectives and have a clear connection to security.

Address at least one of the SPS Key Priorities.

Be jointly developed by scientists or experts from at least one NATO member country and at least one eligible NATO partner country.

Include the required NATO and partner-country Project Directors.

Be developed and implemented by eligible institutions.

Include realistic plans and budgets.

Follow the rules and regulations contained in the relevant SPS handbooks.

Required Project Directors

Each proposed activity must include two key leadership roles.

NATO Country Project Director

The activity must include a NATO country Project Director (NPD).

The NPD must:

Be a scientist or expert;

Be a resident in a NATO member country; and

Be employed in a NATO member country.

Partner Country Project Director

The activity must also include a Partner country Project Director (PPD).

The PPD must:

Be a scientist or expert;

Be a resident in an eligible NATO partner country; and

Be employed in an eligible NATO partner country.

For Multi-Year Projects, additional Co-Directors from NATO member countries or eligible partner countries may also participate.

Eligible Institutions

Projects must be developed and implemented by Co-Directors who are employed by eligible organizations.

These include:

Governmental institutions

Academic institutions

Other non-profit institutions

For-profit private companies are not eligible for SPS funding.

This institutional requirement is particularly important for applicants considering participation through private-sector organizations. A proposal involving a for-profit private company as the institution responsible for the SPS-funded activity would not meet the stated eligibility requirements.

Eligible Countries

The programme allows participation from specified NATO member countries and eligible NATO partner countries.

NATO Member Countries

Eligible NATO member countries include:

Important: Ghana is not included in the eligible NATO member or NATO partner country lists provided in this call. Therefore, individuals and institutions based in Ghana would not be eligible to participate as the required country Project Director or participating institution under this specific call unless their circumstances otherwise satisfy the programme’s country eligibility rules.

Funding Available Under Multi-Year Projects

The NATO SPS Programme does not establish a strict maximum budget for Multi-Year Projects.

However, the call states that budgets for projects lasting 36 months are typically around €400,000.

Higher budgets may be considered where they are adequately justified, particularly for:

Activities aligned with priority deliverables; and

Proposals involving large consortia of institutions.

Applicants should therefore develop budgets based on the actual work required to achieve the proposed results rather than simply attempting to request the largest possible amount.

Co-Financing

Applicants may choose to use co-financing.

The call indicates that a reasonable amount of co-financing is up to one-third of the total grant amount.

SPS may consider higher levels of co-financing on a case-by-case basis where the proposal provides sufficient justification.

Project Duration

The typical duration of an SPS Multi-Year Project is:

24 to 36 months

Shorter projects may be considered if the applicant provides a convincing justification.

Applicants should also account for anticipated procurement timelines when developing the project schedule.

This is important because procurement and other administrative processes can affect the actual time required to deliver a project.

What Makes a Strong SPS Proposal?

Applicants are encouraged to thoroughly research the existing state of the art before submitting their proposal.

A strong application should demonstrate:

Awareness of existing academic research;

Awareness of relevant industrial developments;

Understanding of current technologies and approaches;

A clear explanation of what is innovative about the proposed activity;

Evidence that the proposed work differs from existing work;

Appropriate and recent literature references;

A realistic implementation plan;

A realistic budget;

Clear security relevance;

Alignment with NATO strategic objectives; and

A credible pathway toward practical results.

Applicants should clearly explain how their proposed work improves upon or differs from existing efforts.

The state-of-the-art analysis does not necessarily need to become the main objective of the activity. Instead, it should demonstrate that the applicants understand the existing research and technology landscape and can clearly identify the contribution of their proposed work.

Technology Readiness Levels

For Multi-Year Projects, the SPS Programme expects project results to aim for Technology Readiness Levels 3–6.

Applicants should therefore consider how their research can progress toward practical technological development rather than remaining entirely theoretical.

Projects should demonstrate how the proposed work can improve the state of the art, including where relevant through improvements over commercially available off-the-shelf solutions.

Requirements for Multi-Year Project Applications

A complete Multi-Year Project proposal must include the application submitted through the SPS grant platform along with the required supporting documentation.

Applicants should prepare:

A completed SPS application form;

A project schedule, such as a Gantt chart or another suitable project timeline;

An end-user commitment letter for each project end-user;

A brief overview of participating institutions;

SPS MYP Detailed Budget in the required Excel format;

SPS MYP Acceptance of Funds;

SPS MYP Agreement for Joint Research; and

An SPS MYP Sample Intellectual Property Rights Agreement or an IPR waiver agreed upon by all participants and their institutions.

These documents form an important part of a complete application.

Requirements for SPS Events

For Events, applicants must submit a complete application through the SPS grant platform together with the required supporting documentation.

The required documents include:

SPS Events Budget;

SPS Events Acceptance of Funds; and

SPS Events Cooperation Agreement.

Applicants should also clearly explain the purpose of the event, its relevance to NATO and its expected impact on relevant stakeholders and communities of interest.

How to Apply for the NATO SPS 2027-1 Call

Applications must be submitted through the official NATO SPS grant platform.

Proposals submitted through other means, including email, will not be considered. Read the full proposal HERE

Step 1: Register

Applicants should first create an account on the SPS grant platform.

Step 2: Find the Opportunity

After registering, applicants should identify the relevant available opportunity on the platform homepage.

Step 3: Start the Application

Applicants should select “Start application” and choose the appropriate grant mechanism.

This may be a Multi-Year Project or an eligible SPS Event.

Step 4: Complete the Proposal

Applicants should provide all required information and upload the relevant supporting documents.

Step 5: Review the Application

Before submission, applicants should carefully check that:

All required fields have been completed;

The correct grant mechanism has been selected;

All supporting documents have been included;

The project budget is realistic;

The project schedule is achievable;

The proposal demonstrates security relevance;

The proposal addresses an SPS Key Priority;

The required NATO and partner-country Project Directors are included; and

The participating countries and institutions meet eligibility requirements.

Step 6: Submit Before the Deadline

Applicants are strongly advised not to wait until the final hours to submit their proposals.

The programme specifically advises applicants against last-minute submissions.

Proposal Evaluation Process

After submission, proposals undergo an evaluation process.

The proposal will be evaluated by the SPS Office and the Independent Scientific Evaluation Group (ISEG).

Proposals recommended for funding by the ISEG are then shared with the NATO Partnerships and Cooperative Security Committee (PCSC) for approval.

Applicants should therefore expect a detailed review process rather than an immediate funding decision.

How Long Does the Evaluation Take?

The SPS Programme states that a funding decision can take up to nine months following an application deadline.

Applicants should take this timeframe into account when proposing dates for their projects or events.

This is particularly important for events because applicants should avoid proposing an activity date that would occur before sufficient time has been allowed for the review and funding process.

Important Rules on Multiple Submissions

There are restrictions on the number of proposals an individual can lead.

Co-Directors are limited to one proposal per call.

This means that an individual cannot serve as Co-Director on multiple proposals under the same call.

Rules for Ongoing SPS Activities

Applicants who are already directing an SPS activity must ensure that the existing activity has been formally closed before applying as a Co-Director for a new activity.

A person cannot simultaneously serve as Co-Director of multiple activities.

However, Co-Directors of ongoing activities may participate in new proposals as participants, provided that doing so does not interfere with their existing work.

Budget Planning

Applicants should ensure that proposed budgets are balanced and realistic.

The call specifically states that each Co-Director’s institution should receive an appropriate portion of the project budget.

Applicants should therefore make sure that the budget reflects the actual responsibilities, activities, resources and contributions of participating institutions.

A strong budget should be closely connected to the proposed work plan and should provide a reasonable justification for major expenses.

Intellectual Property Considerations

Multi-Year Project applicants must address intellectual property rights as part of the application.

The proposal must include either:

An SPS MYP Sample Intellectual Property Rights Agreement; or

An IPR waiver agreed upon by all participants and their institutions.

This ensures that participating institutions understand and agree on how intellectual property arising from the collaborative research will be handled.

End-User Participation

Multi-Year Projects must include an end-user commitment letter for each project end-user.

This requirement emphasizes the practical orientation of SPS-supported projects.

Applicants should therefore consider who will ultimately use, implement or benefit from the project’s results and demonstrate meaningful engagement with those end-users.

Diversity and Inclusion

The NATO SPS Programme states that it is committed to diversity and inclusion.

Eligible applicants are welcomed regardless of:

Gender

Age

Nationality

Ethnicity

Religion or belief

Cultural background

Sexual orientation

Disability

However, applicants must still meet the programme’s specific country, institutional and project eligibility requirements.

Deadline for the NATO SPS 2027-1 Call for Proposals

The deadline for submitting full proposals is:

15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET

Applications must be submitted through the SPS grant platform before the deadline.

The call warns that data relating to incomplete applications will be lost after the deadline.

Applicants are therefore strongly encouraged to submit their proposals well before the closing time.

Where to Get More Information

Applicants should familiarize themselves with the relevant SPS documentation before preparing their proposals.

In particular, applicants are encouraged to review:

The SPS Events Handbook;

The SPS Multi-Year Project Handbook;

SPS grant application templates;

SPS budget documents;

SPS acceptance of funds documents;

SPS cooperation and joint research agreements; and

Guidance on managing SPS grants.

The official NATO SPS resources provide further information on the programme and the management of SPS-supported activities.

Applicants with questions before submitting an application should direct their enquiries to the SPS Programme through the contact form provided on the NATO SPS website.

Key Takeaways

The NATO Science for Peace and Security 2027-1 Call for Proposals provides an opportunity for eligible scientists, experts and institutions to collaborate internationally on practical security-related scientific and technological challenges.

The most important points to remember are:

The programme supports Multi-Year Projects and Events.

Multi-Year Projects typically run for 24–36 months.

Typical funding for a 36-month Multi-Year Project is around €400,000, although there is no fixed hard budget limit.

Higher budgets may be considered where properly justified.

Projects should generally target Technology Readiness Levels 3–6.

Proposals must have a clear connection to security and NATO strategic objectives.

Proposals must address at least one SPS Key Priority.

Projects must involve eligible participants from at least one NATO member country and one eligible NATO partner country.

A NATO country Project Director and Partner country Project Director are required.

Co-Directors must work for governmental, academic or other non-profit institutions.

For-profit private companies are not eligible for SPS funding.

Applicants must submit through the official SPS grant platform.

Proposals submitted by email or other methods will not be accepted.

Co-Directors may submit or lead only one proposal per call.

The funding decision process can take up to nine months after the deadline.

The full proposal deadline is 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

Conclusion

The NATO Science for Peace and Security 2027-1 Call for Proposals offers a significant opportunity for eligible researchers, scientists, experts and non-profit institutions to develop international collaborations addressing some of the most important emerging security challenges.

The call is particularly relevant to researchers and institutions working in areas such as unmanned systems, critical infrastructure resilience, hybrid threats, energy security, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and space technologies.

However, eligibility is highly structured. Applicants must establish a qualifying partnership between a NATO member country and an eligible NATO partner country, appoint the required Project Directors, work through an eligible institution and demonstrate a clear connection between the proposed activity and NATO’s strategic security objectives.

Potential applicants should begin developing their partnerships, research concept, project schedule, budget and supporting documentation well before the deadline. Given the detailed evaluation process and the possibility of decisions taking up to nine months, applicants should also plan their proposed project or event dates carefully.

Deadline: 15 November 2026 at 23:59 CET.

All proposals must be submitted through the designated NATO SPS grant platform before the deadline.

TITLE: University of Bayreuth Centre of International Excellence “Alexander von Humboldt” Short Term Grants Programme 2026 (up to €3,500)

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: September 15, 2026

Applications are open for the University of Bayreuth Centre of International Excellence “Alexander von Humboldt” Short Term Grants Programme 2026. The University of Bayreuth Centre of International Excellence “Alexander von Humboldt”, in short “Bayreuth Humboldt Centre” (BHC), promotes excellent research at the University of Bayreuth (UBT) and advances the internationalisation of research and networking with the best universities worldwide. Effective immediately, the BHC is offering Short Term Grants for the year 2026.

They invite the Short Term Grantees to carry out their own research projects in cooperation with a local host at UBT. Prior to submission of the application, applicants are required to identify a host in Bayreuth with whom they aim to carry out their research project. The Short Term Grant programme aims at the direct contact between the researchers themselves, therefore the Administrative Office of the Bayreuth Humboldt Centre cannot and should not be involved in the search for a host at the University of Bayreuth. The research projects shall benefit both the candidate and the host. The local hosts provide their grantees with appropriate office and lab space and an up-to-date infrastructure.

Grants

Short Term Grants (intended for stays of about 1-3 weeks duration) include the reimbursement of travel expenses between the home institution and Bayreuth as well as accommodation costs in Bayreuth. The costs will be refunded up to a maximum of €3,500. Short Term Grants are available to researchers regardless of their field of research.

Eligibility

They award Short Term Grants to individuals affiliated with institutions abroad with challenging and innovative research projects of top academic quality through a highly competitive, strictly merit-based selection process.

Applicants must have a PhD, and it is indispensable that the PhD procedure is fully completed (including PhD diploma).

The all-important selection criteria are the academic excellence of both the applicant and the cooperative project as well as the potential for networking with the University of Bayreuth beyond the local host.

They view the diversity of awardees as an asset and are expressly committed to the goal of gender equality. Female scholars and anyone who can help make the research profile of the university more diverse are strongly encouraged to apply.

Application

Submit your complete application via the online form by September 15, 2026. Note that you will need to register with an email address and a password.
