TITLE: Orr Fellowship 2027: Launch Your Career With a Two-Year Corporate Fellowship in Indianapolis or Evansville

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Orr Fellowship 2027 offers ambitious college graduates and early-career professionals looking for more than a traditional entry-level position the opportunity to combine full-time professional employment with structured leadership development, mentorship, business training and access to an established professional community.

Applications are now open for the 2027 Orr Fellowship cohort, a two-year corporate fellowship programme designed to connect high-achieving college graduates with meaningful roles at innovative partner companies in Indiana. Successful Fellows gain real-world professional experience while participating in intentional career and leadership development designed to accelerate their transition from college into the workplace.

Fellows can be placed with partner companies in either Indianapolis or Evansville, Indiana, where they work full-time while becoming part of the wider Orr Fellowship community. The programme provides exposure to industries including technology, healthcare, finance, consulting, marketing and operations, with partner organisations ranging from high-growth startups to established companies.

The application deadline for the 2027 cohort is September 25 at 11:59 p.m.

What Is the Orr Fellowship?

Orr Fellowship is a two-year corporate fellowship programme created for high-achieving college graduates and young professionals preparing to begin their careers.

Rather than separating professional development from employment, Orr Fellowship combines the two. Fellows are matched with partner companies where they take on full-time roles and gain practical workplace experience from the beginning of the programme.

At the same time, Fellows participate in structured professional and leadership development activities that complement their responsibilities at their partner companies.

The programme is therefore designed for graduates who want to begin building a professional career while receiving additional training, mentorship, networking opportunities and exposure to business leaders.

According to Orr Fellowship, participants receive two years of full-time, on-the-job experience alongside professional and leadership development.

Why Consider the Orr Fellowship 2027?

Starting a career after college can involve more than simply securing a first job. New graduates may also need to develop professional networks, learn how organisations operate, strengthen communication skills, understand different career pathways and determine where their strengths can create the greatest impact.

Orr Fellowship is structured to help participants navigate this transition.

Fellows receive opportunities for:

Full-time professional employment and real-world work experience.

Leadership and career development.

Business and communication skills development.

Workshops and speaker series.

Mentorship.

Cohort-based learning.

Exposure to executives and business leaders.

Connections with peers and Orr Fellowship alumni.

Experience working across teams and business functions.

Long-term professional networking.

The combination of employment and structured development is one of the programme’s defining features.

Two Years of Full-Time Professional Experience

Orr Fellows are not simply attending workshops or participating in a short-term training programme.

They work in full-time roles with Orr Fellowship partner companies.

Fellows may be placed across numerous industries and professional functions depending on partner-company needs and the Fellow’s skills and strengths. The Fellowship specifically highlights opportunities across fields such as:

Technology

Healthcare

Finance

Consulting

Marketing

Operations

The partner network includes both high-growth startups and more established organisations.

This gives Fellows an opportunity to develop practical skills within real organisations while simultaneously building their broader professional capabilities.

Hiring, Compensation and Benefits

Successful Orr Fellows are hired as full-time employees by their partner companies.

They receive competitive compensation and employee benefits aligned with entry-level employment while contributing to meaningful professional work.

This distinction is important for prospective applicants: Orr Fellowship provides a structured development experience alongside actual full-time employment rather than functioning solely as an academic or classroom-based fellowship.

The Fellow’s work at their partner company provides the practical component of the experience, while Orr Fellowship programming supports broader professional growth.

Professional and Leadership Development

The Orr Fellowship programme is intentionally designed to complement each Fellow’s full-time position.

Development programming focuses on areas such as:

Leadership development

Career development

Business skills

Communication skills

Executive exposure

Cross-functional exposure

Programming takes place during dedicated development days or outside core working hours, allowing Fellows to continue fulfilling their responsibilities as full-time employees.

Fellows can also access ongoing training through workshops, speaker series, mentorship and cohort-based learning.

The intention is to develop capabilities that extend beyond the Fellow’s immediate job description and can continue benefiting them throughout their careers.

Mentorship and Ongoing Support

Another major component of the Fellowship is the support available throughout the two-year experience.

Early-career professionals can encounter challenges ranging from adjusting to professional environments to determining career direction and building confidence in communicating with senior colleagues.

Orr Fellowship provides participants with mentorship, structured programming and a peer community that can help them navigate these early-career experiences.

If questions or challenges arise during the Fellowship, Orr also serves as a resource for Fellows and partner companies.

This support structure means Fellows have access not only to their employer but also to the wider Orr Fellowship ecosystem throughout the programme.

Build a Professional Network Early in Your Career

Professional relationships can play an important role in long-term career development, and networking is incorporated into the Orr Fellowship experience.

Fellows can build relationships with:

Other members of their cohort

Fellows from other cohorts

Orr Fellowship alumni

Mentors

Business leaders

Executives

Partner-company representatives

Professionals across different industries

The programme specifically highlights access to a network of peers, alumni and business leaders as one of the experiences available to Fellows.

After completing the two-year programme, Fellows become part of the Orr Fellowship alumni network, extending the community beyond the formal Fellowship period.

Who Can Apply for the Orr Fellowship 2027?

Orr Fellowship welcomes applicants from a wide range of academic backgrounds.

Importantly, applicants are not required to have completed a particular major or degree discipline. The programme states that Fellows come from diverse academic fields and are connected by qualities such as drive, curiosity and leadership potential.

Strong candidates typically demonstrate:

Interest in professional and leadership development.

Previous internship experience.

Campus, extracurricular or other relevant work experience.

Leadership involvement in academic, professional or community settings.

Strong potential to contribute within a professional environment.

A willingness to live in Indiana.

U.S. work authorisation.

The programme also identifies a GPA of 3.2 or above as typical among strong candidates. However, applications are reviewed holistically, and flexibility may be considered.

This means applicants should consider their complete profile rather than assuming that one individual factor automatically determines their chances.

Do You Need a Specific College Major?

No specific major is required.

This makes the Orr Fellowship relevant to graduates from a variety of academic disciplines rather than limiting participation to business, entrepreneurship or another particular field.

Applicants should instead consider how their experiences demonstrate leadership potential, curiosity, initiative, professional readiness and a desire to develop.

U.S. Work Authorisation Requirement

Prospective applicants should pay particular attention to the employment eligibility requirement.

Strong candidates are expected to have U.S. work authorisation and be willing to live in Indiana.

Because Fellows become full-time employees of partner companies, applicants should ensure they meet the programme’s work-authorisation requirements before applying.

Orr Fellowship Locations: Indianapolis and Evansville

Applicants can pursue the Fellowship through two Indiana chapters:

Indianapolis Chapter

The Indianapolis chapter is positioned for candidates interested in beginning their careers in a larger market.

It offers access to expansive professional networks, diverse roles and longer-term opportunities across industries.

Evansville Chapter

The Evansville chapter provides the same core Fellowship programming while offering the experience of developing professionally within a smaller market.

The programme highlights meaningful impact, leadership visibility and a strong regional identity among the characteristics of the Evansville experience.

Both chapters provide the same core professional-development experience. The primary differences relate to location, community size and local industry presence.

How the Orr Fellowship Recruitment Process Works

Candidates should be prepared for a structured recruitment and matching process rather than a single application followed immediately by an employment decision.

Recruitment generally takes place from August through December and involves a four-stage process incorporating:

Application

Interviewing

Networking

Final placement

Throughout the process, candidates may interact with Orr Fellowship alumni, partner organisations and other applicants.

The process is designed not simply to select applicants but also to match candidates with partner organisations where their skills and strengths align with hiring needs.

How the Company Matching Process Works

Orr Fellowship uses a mutual matching process between candidates and participating companies.

At Finalist Day, candidates may interview with multiple partner companies whose recruitment needs align with their skills and strengths.

Many candidates may receive offers on Finalist Day, although placements can continue afterward.

The Fellowship also notes that, in certain circumstances, a candidate may be placed directly within a partner company as an Orr Fellow instead of proceeding through the traditional selection process. Such placements depend on candidate qualifications and company needs.

Candidates are typically informed about their next steps within a few weeks following each stage.

What Do You Need to Apply?

The initial application requirements are relatively straightforward.

According to the programme’s application information, candidates need:

A resume.

Basic personal information.

These materials are required to get the application process started.

Applicants should nevertheless take time to prepare a strong resume that clearly demonstrates relevant internships, work experience, campus involvement, extracurricular activities, leadership responsibilities and other experiences that demonstrate their professional potential.

Application Deadline for the Orr Fellowship 2027

Deadline: September 25 at 11:59 p.m.

The Orr Fellowship application page states that applications for the 2027 cohort close September 25 at 11:59 p.m.

Prospective candidates should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their application. Applying early provides additional time to review application information, prepare a polished resume and address any technical issues that could arise during submission.

How to Apply for the Orr Fellowship 2027

Applicants can apply separately depending on which Orr Fellowship chapter they wish to pursue.

The official application page provides application routes for:

Indianapolis

Evansville

Candidates should first review the programme requirements and determine which location best aligns with their professional and personal goals.

The official Orr Fellowship application page is available through the programme’s website under Apply to Orr Fellowship.

Applicants who are interested in more than one chapter should carefully review the programme’s chapter information and application instructions.

APPLY NOW

Not Ready to Apply Yet?

Students who are interested in Orr Fellowship but are not yet ready or eligible to join can remain connected with the organisation.

The Fellowship specifically encourages sophomores, juniors and other future candidates to request additional information.

By doing so, prospective future applicants can:

Receive programme updates.

Learn about future application deadlines.

Hear from current Fellows and alumni.

Remain informed until they become eligible to apply.

This can be particularly useful for students who want to use their remaining time at university to strengthen their internship experience, leadership involvement and professional profile.

Why the Orr Fellowship Can Be Valuable for Early-Career Professionals

The Orr Fellowship is particularly notable because it brings together several aspects of early-career development within one two-year experience.

Participants are able to build their careers through real employment, rather than relying exclusively on simulated business exercises or classroom learning. At the same time, their employment is supplemented by structured development opportunities that may help broaden their professional perspective.

For graduates who want exposure beyond the responsibilities of a single entry-level position, the programme offers opportunities to learn from business leaders, engage with peers, strengthen leadership and communication capabilities and build a professional network early in their careers.

The Fellowship can therefore appeal to applicants who want both immediate professional responsibility and a wider framework for long-term career development.

Conclusion

The Orr Fellowship 2027 offers high-achieving college graduates and young professionals an opportunity to launch their careers through a combination of full-time employment, two years of professional experience, leadership development, mentorship, business training and community.

Successful Fellows work as full-time employees at partner companies in Indianapolis or Evansville, Indiana, while participating in structured programming designed to strengthen leadership, career, business and communication capabilities.

With opportunities spanning industries such as technology, healthcare, finance, consulting, marketing and operations, the programme is open to applicants from diverse academic disciplines. Candidates are evaluated holistically, although strong applicants typically bring internship or extracurricular experience, leadership involvement, professional-development ambitions and a GPA around 3.2 or higher. Applicants must also have U.S. work authorisation and be willing to live in Indiana.

For college graduates seeking an entry point into meaningful professional work while developing a strong network and leadership foundation, the Orr Fellowship provides a structured pathway from university into the professional world.

Applications for the 2027 Orr Fellowship cohort close September 25 at 11:59 p.m.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.

TITLE: NNF-IAS Fellowship 2027-2029 for Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Deadline: October 1, 2026

Applications are open for the NNF-IAS Fellowship 2027-2029. The eight Nordic Institutes for Advanced Studies are pleased to announce the first call for fellowships in the NNF-IAS fellowship programme on Health and Sustainability, supported by the Novo Nordisk Foundation.

This call is the first of four calls. The first sub-theme is: Inequity in Health.

In this first call, five fellowships are available for curiosity-driven, talented international researchers from any discipline. The five fellowships are distributed among the four main partner institutes and start on September 1, 2027, lasting for 23 months until July 2029.

Benefits

Salary: Fellows are offered a full-time salary based on seniority. Employment conditions and wages are regulated through the collective union agreements in the Nordic country of the hosting institute.

Travel and research costs: The fellowship covers relocation travel expenses (amount subject to prior approval by the hiring institute) and offers relocation assistance. The fellowship also includes a budget for research costs of up to EUR 20,000.

Working environment: Fellows will have office space at the hosting institute and can participate in academic training activities, conferences and workshops at the institute. Fellows will also be affiliated with the other Institutes for Advanced Studies in the Nordic countries.

Eligibility

Applicants apply individually, but the selected candidates are also expected to work together as a group during the fellowship and occasionally travel to the other Nordic Institutes for Advanced Studies. The fellowship call is open for curiosity-driven researchers and welcomes applications from researchers:

of any nationality and from all academic disciplines with research profiles within the thematic scope of the call.

who have a career experience of 2 to 10 years after completion of the PhD (PhD training period will not be considered in the calculation of experience).

who comply with a mobility demand as applicants must not have resided or carried out their main work activity in the country of priority for more than 12 months in the two years immediately prior to the deadline of the call.

who are excited about taking part in an interdisciplinary, cross-Nordic research endeavor.

who demonstrate mobility and are willing to reside in the country of the hosting institute for the duration of the fellowship.

Application

In the application, applicants must prioritize their desired hosting institute for the duration of the fellowship. In the ‘Guide for Applicants’, you can find the detailed application requirements, and information on the structure of the online application system and on the selection criteria and process.

TITLE: Nuffield Medical Fellowships 2026 at the University of Oxford: Fully Funded Medical Research Fellowship for Early-Career Researchers

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The University of Oxford has launched the Nuffield Medical Fellowships, a new research fellowship programme designed to support exceptional early-career researchers who are transitioning to independent research careers or who have recently established full research independence.

Established in 2026, the Nuffield Medical Fellowships provide an opportunity for outstanding biomedical researchers to develop and lead ambitious research programmes within the Medical Sciences Division of the University of Oxford. The programme is particularly significant for researchers whose work has the potential to advance medical knowledge and generate outcomes that improve human physical or mental health.

A distinctive feature of the fellowship is its international and collaborative dimension. Applicants must propose a research programme that includes a collaborative link with a research institution located in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom. This requirement creates an opportunity for researchers to build meaningful international partnerships while conducting high-level medical research at Oxford.

The inaugural cohort will support two Fellows, with successful candidates expected to take up their fellowship positions in early 2028.

About the Nuffield Medical Fellowships

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships were established in 2026 by the Nuffield Medical Trust to support researchers with outstanding potential at an important stage of their academic careers.

The programme is aimed at researchers who are moving toward, or have recently achieved, full research independence. Rather than focusing solely on established senior researchers, the fellowship is intended to provide substantial support to researchers who are capable of developing and leading an ambitious programme of independent medical research.

Successful Fellows will be hosted by a suitable department within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. During the selection process, applicants will be matched with a department that can provide an appropriate academic and research environment for their proposed programme.

The fellowship is designed to provide both career support and research funding, enabling successful candidates to dedicate themselves to developing a substantial programme of medical research.

What Does the Nuffield Medical Fellowship Fund?

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships are intended to provide robust financial support for both the Fellow and the proposed research programme.

Each Fellowship will provide:

A full salary for the Fellow, in line with the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade.

Generous funding for the research programme.

The opportunity to conduct independent biomedical research within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

An academic environment in which Fellows can develop their research programme and collaborate with researchers across disciplines.

Opportunities to establish or strengthen international research partnerships through the required Commonwealth-country collaboration.

Support for research aimed at advancing medical knowledge and improving human physical or mental health.

The combination of salary support and research funding makes the programme substantially different from opportunities that provide only a research stipend or limited project funding.

Who Can Apply for the Nuffield Medical Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for exceptional early-career researchers who are either transitioning to full research independence or have recently achieved full research independence.

Applicants are expected to demonstrate outstanding research potential and submit a compelling proposal that clearly establishes the significance and potential impact of their proposed work.

The programme is open to both:

Practicing clinicians, and

Non-clinical researchers.

This means that applicants do not necessarily need to be practicing medical doctors. Researchers from appropriate biomedical and medical research backgrounds can also be considered, provided their proposed research meets the fellowship’s requirements.

Eligible Research Areas

One of the important features of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship is the breadth of research fields that can be considered.

The proposed research must be in a biomedical field and should seek to advance medical knowledge in a way that is expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

Eligible areas include:

Clinical medicine

Surgery

Neuroscience

Epidemiology

Population health

Primary care

Physiology

Biochemistry

Pharmacology

Psychiatry

Experimental psychology

The programme is therefore relevant to researchers working across a broad spectrum of medical and biomedical disciplines.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is clearly connected to medical advancement and has a credible pathway toward improving human health.

International Collaboration Requirement

A particularly important eligibility feature is the requirement for an international research collaboration.

The proposed research programme must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

This means that applicants need to demonstrate more than an interest in international research. Their proposed programme must incorporate a meaningful collaborative relationship with an eligible research institution located in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom.

This element of the programme can be particularly relevant to researchers whose work addresses global health, population health, health inequalities, infectious diseases, environmental health, clinical research, public health, or other areas where international collaboration can strengthen research outcomes.

Applicants should therefore consider carefully how their proposed partnership contributes to the research programme rather than treating the collaboration as an additional or separate component.

Research Proposal Expectations

A strong research proposal is central to the Nuffield Medical Fellowship application.

Applicants are expected to submit a compelling research proposal that demonstrates how their work will advance medical knowledge.

The proposal should therefore clearly communicate the research problem, the proposed approach and the expected contribution of the research.

When developing a proposal, applicants should be prepared to explain:

The medical or biomedical problem being addressed.

The research question or questions.

Why the research is important.

The existing knowledge or evidence surrounding the problem.

The proposed research approach.

How the research will contribute to advancing medical knowledge.

The expected outcomes of the research.

How those outcomes could contribute to improvements in human physical or mental health.

The applicant’s capacity to lead the research independently.

The role of the proposed Commonwealth-country research collaboration.

Why the University of Oxford provides an appropriate environment for the proposed programme.

The proposal should also demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s research trajectory and the programme they intend to establish at Oxford.

University of Oxford Medical Sciences Division

Successful Fellows will be hosted within the Medical Sciences Division of the University of Oxford.

The Medical Sciences Division brings together a wide range of medical and biomedical research departments and provides an environment for interdisciplinary research.

As part of the fellowship selection process, applicants will be matched with an appropriate department that can host their proposed research programme.

This means that applicants should consider how their research aligns with the expertise, facilities and research environment available within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

The institutional fit is particularly important because the fellowship is intended to support a substantial research programme rather than a short-term research placement.

Number of Fellowships Available

For the inaugural cohort, the Nuffield Medical Trust is providing funding for two Fellowships.

The first Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.

The programme is also intended to become an ongoing annual fellowship scheme. Going forward, the Trustees expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows each year through an annual recruitment round.

This makes the 2026 programme the first cohort of what is intended to become a continuing fellowship opportunity.

Who Is the Fellowship Suitable For?

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships may be particularly relevant to researchers who are at a career stage where they are moving from supervised or collaborative research toward independent leadership.

Potential applicants may include:

Early-career biomedical researchers.

Researchers who have recently achieved full research independence.

Researchers transitioning into independent research leadership.

Practicing clinicians with strong research programmes.

Non-clinical biomedical researchers.

Researchers working in clinical or translational medicine.

Researchers working in population health or epidemiology.

Neuroscience researchers.

Researchers in physiology, biochemistry or pharmacology.

Researchers working in psychiatry or experimental psychology.

Researchers whose work addresses human physical or mental health.

Researchers able to establish an appropriate collaborative relationship with an eligible Commonwealth-country research institution outside the UK.

Applicants should nevertheless assess their individual circumstances and the detailed application requirements before applying.

Countries and Nationalities: Who Can Apply?

The information provided by the University of Oxford describes the international collaboration requirement in terms of the location of the collaborating research institution, rather than restricting applicants to a particular nationality or race.

The key geographical requirement stated by the programme is that the proposed research must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

Therefore, the important distinction is between the applicant’s nationality and the location of the required research collaboration.

Researchers should consult the official fellowship application guidance for the complete eligibility requirements and any additional restrictions concerning applicants, host institutions or collaborating institutions.

The opportunity is not presented as being restricted to a particular race.

Why the Commonwealth Collaboration Matters

The international collaboration component gives the fellowship a distinctive global dimension.

Medical research increasingly depends on collaboration between institutions, researchers and health systems across different countries. Partnerships can provide access to different populations, research environments, expertise, datasets, clinical settings and scientific perspectives.

For researchers whose work has an international or global-health dimension, a collaboration with an institution in a Commonwealth country could strengthen the practical relevance and reach of the proposed programme.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a substantive research rationale for the partnership and explain how the collaboration contributes to achieving the objectives of the proposed research.

Expected Research Impact

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships are designed around research that can make a meaningful contribution to medical knowledge.

The programme specifically requires research proposals to pursue outcomes expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

This means applicants should think beyond simply describing a technically interesting research question. They should also explain the broader significance of the research and how the expected findings could contribute to improved understanding, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, management or other aspects of human health, depending on the field.

The nature of the potential impact will naturally differ between disciplines. For example, an epidemiological project may generate evidence relevant to population health, while a neuroscience project could contribute to understanding neurological processes or disorders.

Career Development and Research Independence

One of the central purposes of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship is to support researchers at the transition to research independence.

For an early-career researcher, developing an independent research programme can require substantial resources, including salary support, research funding, institutional infrastructure, collaborators and an environment capable of supporting ambitious scientific work.

The Fellowship is structured to provide these elements together.

By funding the Fellow’s salary while also providing research programme funding, the scheme is designed to enable successful candidates to concentrate on developing and leading their research programme within Oxford.

How the Selection and Hosting Process Works

Applicants are expected to propose research that fits strategically with a department within the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

During the selection process, applicants will be matched with a suitable department that will host their Fellowship.

This makes institutional alignment an important consideration when preparing an application.

Researchers should carefully consider the relationship between:

Their research expertise.

Their proposed research programme.

The scientific environment at Oxford.

The relevant Medical Sciences Division department.

Potential collaborators.

The Commonwealth-country institutional partnership.

The anticipated contribution of the research to medical knowledge and human health.

A coherent connection between these elements can help demonstrate why the proposed programme is suitable for the Fellowship.

How to Apply

Applicants interested in the Nuffield Medical Fellowships should review the official How to Apply information provided by the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

The application process should be approached carefully because the programme is intended for researchers proposing substantial independent research programmes.

Applicants should review all application instructions, eligibility conditions, proposal requirements and supporting-document requirements before submitting their application.

It is also advisable to ensure that the proposed research programme is clearly developed before beginning the application, particularly where an international institutional collaboration is required.

Fellowship Timeline

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships were established in 2026, making this the programme’s inaugural recruitment cycle.

The first cohort will consist of two Fellows, and the inaugural Fellows are expected to begin their positions in early 2028.

The Trustees subsequently expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows per year through an annual recruitment process.

Deadline

Applicants should check the official University of Oxford application page for the current application deadline, as the programme information supplied does not state a specific deadline.

Because recruitment dates can change, prospective applicants should rely on the official Oxford fellowship page and application portal for the authoritative deadline and submission instructions.

About the Funder: Nuffield Medical Trust

The Nuffield Medical Trust is the funder behind the Nuffield Medical Fellowships.

The Trustees have committed to establishing a robust and well-funded programme capable of supporting high-potential researchers and ambitious medical research programmes.

The funding commitment for the inaugural cohort includes support for two Fellows, with the programme intended to continue through future annual recruitment rounds.

Key Features of the Nuffield Medical Fellowship

The major features of the opportunity include:

Established in 2026.

Hosted by the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division.

Designed for exceptional early-career researchers.

Supports researchers transitioning to or recently achieving full research independence.

Open to practicing clinicians and non-clinical researchers.

Research must be in a biomedical field.

Research must aim to advance medical knowledge.

Proposed outcomes should be expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

Eligible areas include clinical medicine, surgery, neuroscience, epidemiology, population health, primary care, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.

Requires a collaborative link with a research institution in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

Provides a full salary for the Fellow according to the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade.

Provides generous funding for the research programme.

Two Fellowships are available in the inaugural cohort.

Successful Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.

The Trustees expect to appoint one to two Fellows annually in future recruitment rounds.

Tips for Prospective Applicants

Researchers considering this fellowship should begin preparing well in advance.

1. Develop a clear independent research programme

The Fellowship is intended to support researchers moving into independent research leadership. Your proposal should therefore demonstrate that you have a coherent research vision rather than simply describing a single isolated study.

2. Clearly establish the medical significance

Explain why the research matters and how it can contribute to medical knowledge and, ultimately, human physical or mental health.

3. Build a meaningful international collaboration

Because collaboration with a Commonwealth-country institution outside the UK is a central programme requirement, applicants should carefully consider the institution and researchers with whom they intend to collaborate.

The partnership should have a clear scientific purpose and contribute directly to the proposed research programme.

4. Demonstrate research independence

Applicants should clearly communicate their research achievements, expertise, intellectual contribution and capacity to lead an independent programme.

5. Consider Oxford’s departmental fit

Think carefully about which area of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division best aligns with the proposed research. The Fellowship includes a departmental hosting component, making institutional fit an important part of the overall application.

6. Explain expected outcomes

Avoid focusing exclusively on research methods. Explain what the research is expected to discover, develop or demonstrate and why those outcomes matter.

7. Check the official requirements

Before submitting an application, applicants should carefully review the official University of Oxford information, including the application instructions and frequently asked questions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Nuffield Medical Fellowship fully funded?

The Fellowship provides a full salary for the Fellow in line with the appropriate University of Oxford staff grade, together with generous funding for the Fellow’s research programme.

How many Fellowships are available?

Two Fellowships are being supported in the inaugural cohort.

When will the successful Fellows begin?

The inaugural Fellows are expected to take up their positions in early 2028.

Is the Fellowship only for doctors?

No. The programme can support both practicing clinicians and non-clinical researchers, provided they meet the fellowship requirements and propose eligible biomedical research.

What research areas are eligible?

The programme covers a broad range of biomedical fields, including clinical medicine, surgery, neuroscience, epidemiology, population health, primary care, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.

Does the research have to benefit human health?

Yes. The proposed research should aim to advance medical knowledge through outcomes expected to benefit human physical or mental health.

Is international collaboration required?

Yes. The proposed research programme must involve a collaborative link with a research institution based in a Commonwealth country outside the UK.

How many Fellows will be selected each year?

The inaugural cohort will have two Fellows. In subsequent years, the Trustees expect to appoint approximately one to two Fellows annually.

Where will the Fellow be hosted?

Successful applicants will be hosted by a suitable department within the University of Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. Applicants will be matched to a department during the selection process.

Is there a stated application deadline?

The programme information provided does not specify a deadline. Applicants should consult the official Oxford application page for the current deadline and submission instructions.

Conclusion

The Nuffield Medical Fellowships at the University of Oxford offer a major research opportunity for exceptional early-career biomedical researchers who are ready to develop or have recently developed independent research programmes.

Established in 2026, the Fellowship combines salary support with substantial research programme funding and places successful researchers within Oxford’s Medical Sciences Division. The programme covers a wide range of biomedical disciplines, from clinical medicine, surgery and neuroscience to epidemiology, population health, pharmacology, psychiatry and experimental psychology.

A defining feature of the Fellowship is its international collaboration requirement. Applicants must develop a research programme that includes collaboration with a research institution in a Commonwealth country outside the United Kingdom. This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to researchers interested in building international research partnerships and addressing medical challenges through collaborative research.

The inaugural programme will support two Fellows, with successful candidates expected to begin in early 2028. With the Nuffield Medical Trust intending to continue the programme through annual recruitment rounds, the Fellowship is designed to provide sustained support for emerging research leaders and ambitious medical research programmes.

Researchers who meet the eligibility requirements and have a strong, independent biomedical research vision should review the official University of Oxford application guidance carefully, identify an appropriate departmental fit, develop a compelling research proposal and ensure that the required Commonwealth-country collaboration is meaningfully integrated into their programme.

TITLE: Invitation to Join the 2024 International Women’s Day Celebration By WoHEN, AAU & WUA

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: ‘Invest in Women in African Higher Education: Accelerate Progress’

The African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN), hosted by the Association of African Universities (AAU) in collaboration with the Women’s University in Africa (WUA), will host a webinar to commemorate the 2024 International Women’s Day. The theme for the celebration is “Invest in Women in African Higher Education: Accelerate Progress.” This webinar holds on Friday, March 8, 2024, from 10:00 a.m. GMT to 12:00 p.m. GMT and will provide the platform to highlight the gender inequalities in higher education institutions in Africa, track progress in addressing these, discuss the best possible ways to invest in women, and promote a gender-responsive and inclusive African higher education community. All stakeholders of African higher education, both men and women, are invited to participate in this important and insightful event and to contribute to the key discussions. The registration link is available here for reference by our stakeholders – https://tinyurl.com/9d8yt6z9

Background

According to UN Women, investing in women is a human rights issue and cornerstone for building inclusive societies. Hence, progress for women in African higher education institutions (HEIs) can benefit the continent by contributing to the attainment of Agenda 2030 and African Union Agenda 2063. Although the primary responsibility for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) lies at the country level, HEIs in the respective countries are well placed to make a significant contribution to the 2030 Agenda (UNESCO, 2023)). Again, although institutional efforts to increase the representation of women in academia are increasing across the region, they tend to focus on increasing female enrollment in undergraduate studies rather than the hiring and retention of women in senior leadership positions (Afua-Klege, 2022). A 2020 report by the United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) showed that only 24% of females are academic personnel in tertiary educational institutions across Sub Saharan Africa.

Gender inequalities have also been reported in STEM within higher education. For example, the African Union Development Agency reports that in 2016, the overall rate of women’s participation inequalities in STEM research was 34% across the African continent. The implicit gender bias towards men during the hiring process, inadequate institutional oversight of women’s representation in STEM activities, and limited institutional initiatives to facilitate work-life balance for females in STEM are some barriers that hinder the participation of women in HEIs. The African Union Development Agency further reports that women experience longer delays in finishing their postgraduate studies, such as Masters’ and Doctoral Degrees, while female researchers and academics struggle to build a solid publishing record due to societal and gender conventions. The African Education Research Database indicates that, out of 2,510 African-led studies surveyed by the database, only 32 % were led by women. Obstacles such as structural barriers, traditional beliefs and norms, societal expectations, gender stereotypes, and the patriarchal nature of many African academic institutions make it challenging to make any significant progress. Lack of leadership skills, lack of and ineffective mentorship, inadequate resources, limited networking opportunities, unfavourable organizational climate are other additional barriers to gender equality in higher education (Adewale & Potokri, 2023). Fostering networks and communities of women in academia can help create a supportive environment for sharing experiences and best practices. Education Sub-Saharan Africa (ESSA) highlights that the region is losing huge gains by underinvesting in women in universities and colleges. ESSA also highlights the lack of evidence about the role of universities and colleges in equipping women with leadership skills and opportunities.

There is also a shortage of sex-disaggregated data which poses a challenge in policy proposition and progress monitoring of women’s participation in developing innovations in the context of HEIs. In some countries, while gender data is present, they are often infrequent, sparse, and out of date, leading to low reliability of information (UN Women, 2023). In African countries where gender policies in HEIs exist, it is reported that they tend not to focus on the structural conditions that disadvantage women and by implication their limited participation in higher education or Science, Technology & Innovation (Nakayiwa et al., 2020). For instance, the gender criteria in HEI policies focus more on the gender dimension of team composition, the project beneficiaries and the project outcomes, instead of prioritising women for research fund allocation. Mainstreaming gender into research funding, technological innovations, and progress is underpinned by the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (UN Women).

In view of these highlighted challenges, the Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN) in collaboration with the Women’s University in Africa is hosting a webinar to commemorate the 2024 International Women’s Day.

Objectives

The webinar seeks to:

Raise awareness about the impact of gender inequalities in HEIs

Create a platform for various actors—educators, policymakers, and partners—to discuss pertinent issues related to the promotion of equality in higher education in Africa.

To establish strategies in which to invest more in women in African HEIs

To document best practices promoting inclusive African HEIs

Expected Outcomes

Documentation of the Challenges, Opportunities and Best Practices for investing in women in African Higher Education.

Documentation of the pragmatic actions that can be undertaken by African HEIs towards ensuring gender equality in their systems and practices.

Generation of a communique at the end of the event for dissemination and further engagement with stakeholders.

Target Audience:

Female and male VCs, Pro-VCs, Presidents, Rectors, Provosts, Registrars, Deans, Directors, Deputy Directors, Lecturers, Non-academic staff, Students and CSOs who are interested in the theme.

Organizers:

African Women in Higher Education Network (WoHEN)

WoHEN was established to support women to participate effectively in the higher education sector, and across all the higher education thematic areas – leadership, management, administration, agriculture, business, health, STEM, education, humanities, social sciences, and technical and vocational education. This Network is being hosted by the Association of African Universities (AAU). Membership to the Network is open to females on the continent – that is female students, female lecturers/professors, female researchers, female personnel, female administrators, and female leaders in higher, tertiary, and vocational training institutions.

Association of African Universities (AAU)

The Association of African Universities (AAU) is the apex higher education organization in Africa and represents the voice of Africa’s higher education on regional and international bodies. Established in Rabat (Morocco) in 1967, the AAU currently has a membership of over 400 institutions of higher learning across all the linguistic and geographic divides of Africa. Its headquarters is in Accra, Ghana.

The AAU supports African universities to deliver quality higher education and, as its niche, creates a platform for networking among its members. The Association enjoys a unique capacity for convening most of the higher education community in Africa to reflect and consult on key issues affecting education on the continent. The thrust of its base is the nimble deploying of advocacy, commissioning of studies, and acting and becoming the clearing house and intelligence arm for these higher education institutions on the continent. The AAU operates in four languages namely, English, French, Arabic and Portuguese. It endeavours to raise the quality of higher education in Africa and strengthen its contribution to Africa’s development by fostering collaboration among its member institutions; providing support to their core functions of teaching, learning, research, and community engagement; and facilitating critical reflection on, and consensus-building around, issues affecting higher education and the development of Africa.

Women’s University in Africa (WUA)

The Women’s University in Africa’s vision is to be the best University in Africa in relation to the promotion of gender equity and equality in higher education. Its mission is to reduce gender disparity by providing gender-sensitive and socially responsible educational training and research. WUA is the only women’s university in the region that is directly tackling the problem of women’s access to university education. Its enrolment policy of 85% women and 15% men is contributing towards the 50:50 gender participation ratio enunciated in the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development and the Constitution of Zimbabwe. The University currently has three faculties, namely: Agricultural, Environmental and Health Sciences, Management and Entrepreneurial Sciences and Social and Gender Transformative Sciences and two Centres, namely the Gender and Diversity Centre and the Research, Innovation and Postgraduate Centre.

Contact : ndarko@aau.org /fnkrumah@aau.org

TITLE: Financial Support for Graduate Students

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Types of Financial Support

PhD students in Physics are typically funded in each year they are in the program and remain in good standing. Financial support provides for full tuition, a monthly living stipend, and 12 months of health insurance.

Note: For more detailed information regarding the cost of attendance, including specific costs for tuition and fees, books and supplies, housing and food as well as transportation, please visit the Student Financial Services (SFS) website.

There are three sources of financial support:

Fellowships (internal and external)

Research Assistantships

Teaching Assistantships

General Information:

Full-time registration for all PhD students, whether funded by fellowship or by a research or teaching assistantship, is 36 academic units. The normal course load for students with a full-time RA or TA who have not yet completed their qualifying exams is two academic subjects; students supported by a fellowship in the first year, before joining a research group, sometimes enroll in three subjects.

Students with an RA or TA are expected to spend full time on education and assigned duties, and may not engage in any other activity for compensation without the specific approval of the Department Head.

Annual and monthly stipend rates for RAs and TAs are published in the Graduate Student Union Collective Bargaining Agreement. While there are varying levels of stipend funding allowed by MIT, it is the policy of the Physics Department that all our students are provided the same stipend in any individual academic year.

If a student loses RA support because of termination of a research contract, the Department will provide support for one additional term (in the form of a TA) and will make every effort to help the student identify a new source of support.

The periods for graduate appointments are as follows:

Fellows: Fall: 9/1 to 1/15; Spring: 1/16 to 5/31; Summer: 6/1 to 8/31

RAs: Fall: 9/1 to 1/15; Spring: 1/16 to 5/31; Summer: 6/1 to 8/31

TAs: Fall: 9/1 to 1/15; Spring: 1/16 to 5/31

Fellowships

The Physics Department provides internal fellowship funding to a number of the students admitted each year. The majority of these internal, donor-funded fellowships are for the first year in the program, covering twelve months; a small number of three- and five-year fellowships are also awarded. There is no application process for departmental fellowships; all admitted candidates are considered for them.

A student beginning PhD study with a fellowship has a great deal of flexibility in planning his or her graduate program and in seeking out a research group. Each fellowship recipient is responsible for finding a research group that will provide funding once the fellowship support has been used; students with multi-year fellowships are expected to have joined a research group by the beginning of the second year. Additional information on fellowships for graduate students in physics is available through the Office for Graduate Education.

External Fellowships:

1. Students interested in applying for an outside fellowship and receiving a departmental top-up should submit the Pre-award Fellowship Top-up Application. This helps us calculate whether a fellowship top-up is possible.

2. If you are successful in an external fellowship which covers 45% of a 9 month cost (tuition + stipend), the Department can supplement (top-up) the remainder, contingent upon our funding situation, and if we have received a top-up application.

3. Physics also has a policy where any student who receives an outside fellowship covering 45% or more of a 9 month cost will also receive a $1,500 discretionary fund from the Department.

4. There are programs which are titled “Fellowship” which do not cover tuition and stipend – students should carefully review all terms before accepting a fellowship. The KITP Fellowship is an example of this. Students thinking of applying for the KITP Fellowship should read the departmental policy document carefully before making their decision.

5. The Department will support a maximum of 5 years on fellowship. Any time spent at MIT after that should be as an RA or TA.

Several external fellowships require departmental nomination and have a limited number of available spots. If you are interested in one of these fellowships, you should speak to your research supervisor about your interest. These fellowships are typically full tuition plus stipend, and therefore do not require a top-up. Some of the most common are listed here:

Apple AI The PhD fellowship in AI/ML was created as part of the Apple Scholars program to support the work of outstanding PhD students from around the world, who are pursuing cutting edge research in machine learning and artificial intelligence. Managed by the OGE.

Google AI Google PhD Fellowships directly support graduate students as they pursue their PhD, as well as connect them to a Google Research Mentor. Google PhD Fellows are a select group recognized by Google researchers and their institutions as some of the most promising young academics in the world. The Fellowships are awarded to students who represent the future of research in the following fields: Algorithms and Theory, Distributed Systems and Parallel Computing, Health & Bioscience, Human-Computer Interaction and Visualization, Machine Intelligence, Machine Perception, Natural Language Processing, Networking, Quantum Computing, Security, Privacy and Abuse Prevention, Software Engineering, Software Systems, Speech Processing. Managed by the OGE.

Mathworks These graduate fellowships provide support to graduate students within the School of Science with a preference for students who are active users of MATLAB and/or Simulink. Managed by MIT School of Science.

Pillar AI A program for final-year Masters or PhD students in AI, Machine Learning, and Data Science, the MIT-Pillar AI Collective Fellowship provides funding and support to promote the commercialization of their innovations.

Two Sigma Two Sigma’s PhD Fellowship is open to all doctoral students who are expanding frontiers in a STEM field such as statistics, applied mathematics, computer science, and physics.

Research Assistantships (RAs)

Research assistants receive full tuition, living stipend, and health insurance in exchange for conducting research on behalf of a faculty member. This faculty member also serves as the supervisor of the student’s individual research project that will become the PhD thesis.

RA work generally covers the full academic year, including summer. The amount of time spent on RA duties depends on the time needed for required course work as well as the requirements of the research group. For new graduate students taking classes and preparing for the general examination, research duties normally require 20 hours per week or less. After two to three years, research usually becomes full-time.

In addition to courses, students conducting research register each term for a research subject, providing academic credit for research work. The number of units varies from 12 to 36 according to the approximate time spent weekly on research. Research subjects include:

Pre-Thesis Research (8.391, fall; 8.392, spring and summer): students who have not yet completed the General Examinations

Thesis Research (8.THG); all students after passing the Oral Exam

Note: For more detailed information regarding the cost of attendance, including specific costs for tuition and fees, books and supplies, housing and food as well as transportation, please visit the Student Financial Services (SFS) website.

Teaching Assistantships (TAs)

Teaching assistants receive full tuition, living stipend, and health insurance in exchange for supporting the Department’s teaching program. TA responsibilities can include grading homework and exams, tutoring, conducting office hours, or, less often, teaching sections of a course. TA work requires up to 20 hours per week in addition to research or class work the student is engaged in.

Having a TA appointment can serve a variety of purposes:

support departmental teaching needs

encourage students who wish to hone their teaching skills

help alleviate funding pressures on the faculty

facilitate a student’s transition to a different research group

TA assignment process:

Students may request nomination as a TA, or they may be assigned a term as a TA by their research supervisor.

Each of the four divisions in the department has a standard guaranteed number of TA positions per term. Research supervisors submit names of students to be considered for TAs to the Division Head, who compiles the division’s list and provides it to the Academic Programs Office.

Students on the department’s TA list are asked to select their top choices among the subjects offered in the upcoming term, and every effort is made by the TA Faculty Coordinator to match student requests when possible. Teaching faculty may also request a specific student to be assigned to their course.

While TA appointments are typically made only after the first year, very occasionally a first-year graduate student will be supported by a nine-month (fall and spring) TA appointment. Students with a first-year TA normally join a research group and are supported by an RA beginning in their first summer.

Note: For more detailed information regarding the cost of attendance, including specific costs for tuition and fees, books and supplies, housing and food as well as transportation, please visit the Student Financial Services (SFS) website.

Teaching Resources:

Teaching Assistant handbook

Switching Research Groups

While many students continue from their first RA to a thesis in the same group, others elect to change research groups, for a variety of reasons. An RA who wishes to change groups or research direction should feel comfortable reaching out to talk to other professors about different opportunities.

However, students are responsible for notifying their current supervisor of their intention to leave a group, and they are expected to continue working in the research group as long as it is providing funding. They should also be cautioned that acceptance into another group is dependent upon the student’s academic preparation and the advisor’s funding.

To facilitate a transition between research groups, each student is guaranteed one semester of transitional funding in the form of a TA appointment.

Students who wish to discuss their interest in changing their research group are welcome to talk with Academic Administrator Shannon Larkin or with Graduate Student Advocate Claude Canizares at any time.
