TITLE: Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowships 2027–28: $3,000 Monthly Funding for PhD Scholars and ABD Researchers in Chicago

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowships 2027–28 are now open for applications, offering scholars an opportunity to spend one to two months in residence at the Newberry Library in Chicago, United States, conducting intensive research using the institution’s unique and extensive collections.

The fellowship is designed for PhD-holding scholars and PhD candidates who have reached ABD (All But Dissertation) status or its equivalent and whose research requires access to specific materials held in the Newberry’s collections. Successful fellows receive a $3,000 monthly stipend to help cover housing, travel, and other living and research-related expenses associated with their residency in Chicago.

The program is particularly valuable for researchers whose work depends on primary sources, rare books, manuscripts, maps, historical documents, and other specialized materials that may be difficult to access remotely.

Deadline: December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time.

About the Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowship

The Newberry Library is an independent research library in Chicago with millions of historical sources and materials documenting people, cultures, places, and events across time.

Its fellowship program provides researchers with the time, resources, and scholarly environment needed to undertake intensive research. Fellows do not simply receive financial support; they also become part of the Newberry’s scholarly community during their period of residence.

The Short-Term Fellowship program specifically supports researchers who need to examine particular items in the Newberry’s collections for a defined scholarly project.

Unlike the Newberry’s Long-Term Fellowships, which support four to nine months of research, Short-Term Fellows generally spend one month in residence. Certain named fellowships can provide two months of support, depending on the fellowship.

For researchers who have identified specific Newberry materials that are essential to their work, this can provide an efficient way to spend concentrated time working directly with those sources.

Fellowship Benefits

Successful Short-Term Fellows receive several important benefits.

1. $3,000 Monthly Stipend

Short-Term Fellows receive $3,000 per month.

The stipend is intended to help cover the costs associated with undertaking research in Chicago, including:

Housing

Travel

Living expenses

Other costs associated with the research residency

The Newberry Library does not provide housing, so fellows are responsible for arranging their own accommodation during their fellowship.

2. One to Two Months of Research Residency

The majority of Short-Term Fellowships provide one month of support.

However, some specific fellowships provide longer support:

Jody Enders Fellowship: 2 months

Frances C. Allen Fellowship: 1–2 months

Lester J. Cappon Fellowship in Documentary Editing: 1–2 months

The exact duration therefore depends on the fellowship for which an applicant is considered.

3. Access to Newberry Collections

The central benefit of the fellowship is the opportunity to conduct research directly with materials in the Newberry’s collections.

Applicants should therefore have a clear reason for needing to consult specific Newberry collection items rather than simply wanting general research time in Chicago.

The Newberry has millions of collection items, including materials relevant to areas such as American history and culture, maps and cartography, books, manuscripts, performing arts, and American Indian and Indigenous Studies.

4. Participation in a Scholarly Community

Fellows become part of the Newberry’s scholarly community during their residency.

This creates opportunities to interact with other researchers and engage with the intellectual environment surrounding the library’s collections and research programs.

For scholars working on specialized historical or humanities research, this environment can provide valuable academic connections and opportunities to develop their work.

What Fields of Study Are Eligible?

One of the major advantages of the fellowship is that applicants can come from any academic field, provided that their proposed project demonstrates a genuine need to work with materials in the Newberry collection.

This means applicants should not assume that they must be studying one particular discipline.

Potentially relevant fields may include areas such as:

History

Literature

Cultural studies

American studies

Indigenous studies

Anthropology

Sociology

Religious studies

Philosophy

Political history

Art history

Musicology

Theatre and performance studies

Linguistics

Medieval and Renaissance studies

Early modern studies

Cartography and the history of maps

Archival studies

Documentary editing

Genealogy

Other humanities and related disciplines

However, simply belonging to one of these disciplines does not automatically make an applicant competitive.

The research project itself must demonstrate a specific need to consult Newberry materials.

What Makes a Strong Fellowship Project?

A strong application should make a clear connection between the applicant’s research and the Newberry’s collections.

Applicants should be able to explain:

What they are researching

Why the research matters

Which Newberry materials they need

Why those materials are important to the project

What they intend to accomplish during the residency

Why the research needs to be conducted in person

This is particularly important because the Short-Term Fellowship is not simply a general travel grant.

The purpose is to enable scholars to conduct focused research using specific collection items at the Newberry.

Applicants should therefore investigate the Newberry’s collections and research guides before preparing their proposal. The library provides collection descriptions and research resources to help scholars identify relevant materials.

Application Requirements

The Newberry processes fellowship applications through its SlideRoom online application portal.

The general Short-Term Fellowship application includes several components designed to give reviewers a detailed understanding of the researcher, project, and need for a Newberry residency.

1. Personal, Demographic and Professional Information

Applicants will need to provide personal and professional information relevant to their academic or research background.

This can include information concerning:

Academic institution

Academic rank or professional position

Department

PhD-granting institution

Date of PhD award

Previous fellowships

Previous Newberry fellowship applications or awards

Current PhD candidates should provide their anticipated completion date where applicable.

2. Research Project Information

The research project is one of the most important parts of the application.

Applicants should clearly explain the proposed project and establish the relationship between the project and the Newberry’s collections.

A strong proposal should demonstrate that the applicant has done sufficient preliminary research to identify the materials they need to consult.

The Newberry advises applicants with questions about its materials to contact its librarians.

3. Selective Secondary Source Bibliography

Applicants are required to submit a one-page selective secondary-source bibliography related to or contextualizing their research project.

This should demonstrate that the applicant understands the existing scholarship surrounding the proposed research.

The bibliography should be submitted in Word or PDF format.

4. Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must submit a current CV of no more than five pages.

The Newberry provides specific terminology for describing forthcoming publications:

In progress: not yet completed or submitted

Submitted: currently under review

Accepted: contracted for publication and undergoing revision

In press: with a copy editor, typesetter, or printer

Applicants should therefore make sure their CV accurately represents the status of their publications.

5. Fellowship Duration Requested

Applicants will indicate how many months of support they are requesting.

The majority of Short-Term Fellowships provide one month, while certain fellowships may support two months.

6. Letter of Recommendation

One letter of recommendation is required for Short-Term Fellowship applicants.

The recommendation should address:

The scholarly contribution of the proposed project

The value of a Newberry residency to the applicant

The applicant’s qualifications

The recommendation must be submitted in English.

Importantly, recommendation letters may be submitted for up to 10 days after the fellowship application deadline. For the 2027–28 cycle, the stated deadline for recommendation letters is December 14, 2026.

Fellowship Period and Timing

Awards can be taken at any point within the 15-month period between June of the awarding year and August of the following year.

This provides successful fellows with some flexibility when planning their research residency.

However, applicants should carefully plan their proposed dates around:

Collection access

Research needs

Academic schedules

Housing availability

Travel arrangements

The Newberry’s operating schedule

The Newberry notes that fellowship orientations occur on Tuesdays and that the library is closed on Sundays and holidays, while Special Collections and other reading rooms are closed on Mondays.

Special Short-Term Fellowship Opportunities

In addition to the general short-term fellowship funding, the Newberry offers several fellowships with specific eligibility or research preferences.

John S. Aubrey Fellowship

This fellowship supports scholars who demonstrate a specific need to use the Newberry’s collections.

It is therefore one of the general opportunities potentially available to researchers across fields.

Lester J. Cappon Fellowship in Documentary Editing

This fellowship supports researchers working on historical editing projects that are being prepared for scholarly editions.

It is specifically open to postdoctoral scholars and can provide one or two months of support.

Jody Enders Fellowship

The Jody Enders Fellowship supports exceptional scholars at any career stage whose projects relate to:

Medieval theatre

Renaissance theatre

Other live art forms

Rhetoric

Translation

Preference is given to projects focused on areas outside Britain.

This fellowship provides two months of support.

Fellows’ Fellowship

The Fellows’ Fellowship supports scholars who demonstrate a specific need for the Newberry’s collections.

Preference is given to early-career scholars in all fields whose research relates to:

Women’s studies

Spirituality

Venice

Applicants do not necessarily need to be working directly in these areas to be considered for the broader Short-Term Fellowship program.

Society of Mayflower Descendants in the State of Illinois Fellowship

This fellowship supports projects relating to:

Early American history

Transatlantic history

It is another example of how the Newberry’s named fellowships can provide targeted opportunities within the broader Short-Term Fellowship program.

Fellowships with Additional Membership Requirements

Some Newberry Short-Term Fellowships have additional eligibility requirements.

Midwest Modern Language Association Fellowship

This fellowship supports scholars who:

Are members of the Midwest Modern Language Association

Are working on projects in literary and cultural criticism

Applicants must indicate their interest on the Short-Term Fellowship application form, after which the Newberry will confirm membership status with the MMLA.

Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies Consortium Fellowships

The Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies supports two awards:

One for a postdoctoral scholar

One for a PhD candidate

Projects should focus on:

Medieval studies

Renaissance studies

Early modern studies

Applicants must come from institutions participating in the Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies Consortium.

Eligible postdoctoral applicants can include full-time faculty members, adjunct faculty, librarians, and curators.

Fellowships for Indigenous Scholars

The Newberry also offers specialized fellowships for Indigenous scholars.

The Frances C. Allen Fellowship and Susan Kelly Power and Helen Hornbeck Tanner Fellowship support scholars who are:

Citizens of federally recognized U.S. tribal nations;

Documented descendants of federally recognized U.S. tribal nations; or

Native Hawaiian individuals.

Importantly, research does not have to focus specifically on American Indian or Indigenous Studies for these fellowships.

The Frances C. Allen Fellowship supports female scholars and can provide one or two months of support, while the Power and Tanner Fellowship is open to all qualifying scholars and provides one month of support.

These are specialized opportunities within the broader Newberry fellowship ecosystem and should not be confused with the general Short-Term Fellowship eligibility.

Is the Fellowship Fully Funded?

It is important to understand what the $3,000 stipend means.

The fellowship provides $3,000 per month, intended to support:

Housing

Travel

Living expenses

Other expenses connected to residing in Chicago

However, the Newberry does not provide housing.

Therefore, applicants should not automatically describe this as a fully funded fellowship covering every possible expense.

Instead, it is more accurately described as a funded short-term research fellowship providing a $3,000 monthly stipend.

Researchers should prepare a realistic budget, particularly if they are traveling internationally to Chicago.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027–28 Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowship is:

December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time.

Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin the application because the process involves preparing a research proposal, bibliography, CV and securing a recommendation letter.

Recommendation letters or other required supporting materials must be submitted no later than December 14, 2026, according to the Newberry’s application guidance. How to Apply

Applications are submitted online through the Newberry Library’s SlideRoom portal.

Apply Here

Before applying, prospective applicants should:

Review the Short-Term Fellowship eligibility requirements.

Explore the Newberry’s collections and research guides.

Identify the specific collection materials needed for the project.

Develop a clear research proposal.

Prepare the selective secondary-source bibliography.

Update the academic CV to a maximum of five pages.

Identify an appropriate recommender.

Ensure the recommender understands the scholarly purpose of the proposed Newberry residency.

Complete the SlideRoom application.

Submit the application before the December 4 deadline.

Confirm that the recommendation letter is submitted by December 14.

Applicants who have questions about Newberry materials for their project can contact the library’s research staff. The fellowship page lists research@newberry.org for fellowship-related questions.

Why This Fellowship Is Valuable for Researchers

The Newberry Short-Term Fellowship can be especially valuable for researchers whose work depends on primary-source research.

A scholar may have a strong research question but need to physically examine historical documents, manuscripts, maps, books, archival records, or other specialized materials that cannot be adequately studied through digital copies or secondary literature.

A concentrated residency provides the researcher with dedicated time to:

Examine primary sources

Take research notes

Compare archival materials

Verify historical evidence

Develop chapters or articles

Strengthen a dissertation

Prepare a scholarly edition

Advance a book project

Build relationships with other researchers

Develop new interpretations based on primary sources

The Newberry describes its broader fellowship program as providing researchers with the time, space and community needed to pursue innovative scholarship.

Important Tip for Applicants

One of the strongest ways to improve an application is to avoid presenting the fellowship simply as an opportunity to “visit Chicago” or “conduct research at a prestigious library.”

Instead, demonstrate a specific scholarly need.

For example, your proposal should make it clear:

“My project requires consultation of these particular Newberry collection materials because…”

Then explain how examining those materials will advance your research.

Applicants should also research the collections carefully before applying. The Newberry recommends its research guides, bibliographies, checklists and collection descriptions as resources for identifying relevant materials.

The more precisely you can connect your research question, the specific collection materials and the expected research outcomes, the stronger the rationale for a short-term residency becomes.

Other Newberry Opportunities

Researchers who do not meet the Short-Term Fellowship eligibility requirements may still find other Newberry opportunities.

Artists-in-Residence Fellowships

Writers, artists and other creative researchers who do not hold a PhD or ABD status may be better suited to the Newberry’s Artist-in-Residence Fellowship program.

NCAIS Fellowships

Faculty members and graduate students from institutions affiliated with the Newberry Consortium in American Indian and Indigenous Studies (NCAIS) may qualify for NCAIS fellowships and research awards. These programs have separate application requirements and deadlines.

Tribal Research Fellowships

Researchers conducting work on behalf of a U.S. federally recognized tribal nation can explore the Tribal Research Fellowship. That program supports individuals or small groups working with federally recognized tribal nations and can provide up to $10,000 depending on the project.

Long-Term Fellowships

Researchers who need substantially more time may consider the Newberry’s Long-Term Fellowships. These provide four to nine months of research support and offer $5,000 per month. Applicants must already hold a PhD at the time of application. The 2027–28 deadline is November 20, 2026.

The Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowships 2027–28 provide an excellent opportunity for PhD researchers and ABD doctoral candidates who need direct access to specialized primary sources in one of America’s major research libraries.

Applicants should identify the specific materials they need, explain why those materials are essential to their research and demonstrate what they expect to accomplish during their residency.

The application deadline is December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time. Recommendation letters may be submitted until December 14, 2026.

TITLE: U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029: Paid Two-Year Opportunity for Recent College Graduates in International

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury is recruiting candidates for its International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029, a highly selective, fixed two-year program designed for new college graduates interested in international economic policy, finance, public policy, international relations, and related fields.

The fellowship provides an opportunity to work within Treasury’s Office of International Affairs (IA) and contribute to issues that shape U.S. international economic policy. Junior Fellows can gain exposure to international financial and economic developments, policy analysis, government decision-making, and bilateral and multilateral engagement involving major international institutions and forums.

Unlike a conventional entry-level position focused on a single function, the Junior Fellowship is structured to provide fellows with exposure to multiple policy issues and opportunities to develop practical analytical, policy, and professional skills. Fellows may contribute to policy proposals, analytical studies, international economic and financial analysis, and preparations for high-level meetings involving organizations and forums such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, G7, and G20.

The program is particularly relevant for recent undergraduate graduates who want to build careers in government, international economic policy, public policy, international relations, finance, or related areas.

Application deadline: October 31, 2026

About the U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship

The International Affairs Junior Fellowship is a highly selective, two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of International Affairs.

The program is designed specifically for new college graduates and offers fellows the opportunity to gain firsthand experience in the development and implementation of international economic policy for the United States.

During the two-year appointment, Junior Fellows can expect to work on a variety of assignments and policy questions rather than being limited to one narrow area of responsibility. This can include examining international economic and financial developments, developing policy proposals, conducting analytical research, and supporting senior Treasury officials in international engagements.

The program can therefore serve as a strong early-career pathway for graduates who want to understand how international economic policy is developed within the U.S. government.

According to the program description, previous fellows have gone on to pursue diverse career and academic paths, including:

Employment with the U.S. Department of the Treasury

Other positions within the U.S. government

Careers in the private sector

Graduate education

Law

Public policy

International relations

Finance and business

This makes the fellowship potentially valuable not only as a two-year professional experience but also as a foundation for longer-term careers in international affairs and economic policy.

What Do International Affairs Junior Fellows Do?

Junior Fellows are exposed to multiple policy issues and are given opportunities to strengthen their knowledge and professional capabilities through practical work.

Their responsibilities typically include several areas of policy and analytical work.

1. Developing Policy Proposals

Fellows may contribute to the development of policy proposals relating to international economic and financial issues.

This can involve understanding a policy problem, reviewing relevant information and developments, analyzing potential approaches, and contributing to recommendations or proposals for consideration by Treasury officials.

For graduates interested in public policy, this provides exposure to how policy ideas are developed in a major U.S. government department.

2. Analyzing International Economic and Financial Developments

Another important component of the fellowship is monitoring and analyzing international economic and financial developments.

This may require fellows to follow developments affecting international economies and financial systems and assess their implications for U.S. economic policy and international engagement.

Such experience can be particularly relevant for individuals interested in:

International economics

Global finance

Macroeconomic policy

Financial policy

International development

Global economic relations

Public policy

3. Conducting Analytical Studies

Junior Fellows may also conduct analytical studies as part of their responsibilities.

This gives participants an opportunity to apply academic knowledge to real-world policy questions and develop skills in research, analysis, evidence assessment, and policy-oriented writing.

4. Supporting Bilateral and Multilateral Meetings

Fellows can support bilateral and multilateral meetings involving senior Treasury officials.

The program specifically highlights engagements involving major international institutions and forums, including:

International Monetary Fund (IMF)

World Bank

G7

G20

Junior Fellows often participate in these meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad.

This component can provide valuable exposure to international economic diplomacy and the practical processes involved in high-level government engagement.

Where Are Junior Fellows Placed?

Junior Fellows are placed in either a regional office or a functional office within Treasury’s Office of International Affairs.

The two types of offices provide exposure to different aspects of international economic policy.

Regional Offices

Regional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries around the world.

Working in a regional office can therefore provide exposure to U.S. economic relationships with specific countries or regions and the policy issues associated with those relationships.

Depending on their assignment, fellows may gain experience understanding:

International economic relationships

Government-to-government engagement

Economic policy developments in other countries

Regional economic issues

Engagement with foreign finance ministries and treasuries

Bilateral policy discussions

Functional Offices

Functional offices focus on engagement with international financial institutions and broader Treasury policy issues.

The program identifies areas including:

International financial institutions

International trade

Export credits

Foreign exchange

Functional assignments can therefore provide fellows with exposure to policy questions that extend across individual countries or regions.

A Unique Opportunity to Work in International Economic Policy

For graduates interested in international affairs, the fellowship provides an opportunity to move beyond classroom learning and gain practical experience in U.S. international economic policy.

The program sits at the intersection of several disciplines, including:

Economics

Finance

International relations

Public policy

International economic policy

Government

Global financial affairs

This multidisciplinary nature means that candidates do not necessarily need to pursue a narrowly defined career path within economics. Applicants with relevant academic preparation and interests in related policy fields may also be well positioned for the program.

International Exposure and Potential Travel

One of the distinctive aspects of the Junior Fellowship is the opportunity to engage with international issues and, potentially, international meetings.

The program states that Junior Fellows may participate in meetings involving international institutions and major multilateral forums and may have opportunities to travel abroad.

However, international travel should not be understood as an automatic component of every fellow’s experience. The opportunity will depend on the fellow’s office, duties, assignments, and program requirements.

The international exposure can nevertheless be particularly valuable for graduates seeking careers in:

International organizations

Government

Diplomacy

International development

Global finance

Economic policy

International relations

Who Should Consider Applying?

The program is particularly suited to recent college graduates who are interested in understanding and contributing to international economic policy.

Strong candidates may have academic backgrounds or relevant coursework in:

Economics

Public policy

Finance

International relations

Related fields

The Treasury specifically notes that strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor’s degree with relevant coursework in these areas.

The program also states that, because of its structure, preference is given to undergraduates.

International Affairs Junior Fellowship Eligibility and Qualifications

The formal qualifications are particularly important for applicants to understand before preparing an application.

Candidates should meet the following key requirements.

Bachelor’s Degree

Candidates should have recently received, or be close to receiving, a bachelor’s degree.

Relevant coursework may include:

Economics

Public policy

Finance

International relations

Related disciplines

Preference for Undergraduates

The program explicitly states that preference is given to undergraduates because of the structure of the Junior Fellowship.

This means candidates should carefully consider how their educational stage aligns with the program before applying.

Relevant Experience

Applicants must also demonstrate 52 weeks, or 2,080 hours, of relevant paid or unpaid experience.

Importantly, this experience does not have to come exclusively from conventional employment.

The application instructions specifically allow relevant experience to include:

Paid employment

Unpaid work

Volunteer experience

Extracurricular activities

Work-study experience

Other professional or extracurricular activities relevant to the duties described by the program

This makes it important for applicants to review their entire background rather than considering only formal full-time jobs.

How to Document the Required 52 Weeks of Experience

One of the most important aspects of the application is demonstrating the required 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant experience.

Applicants are instructed to provide sufficient detail in their resumes to demonstrate this experience.

The resume should explain the duties performed in each relevant professional or extracurricular activity.

Candidates should include:

The position or activity

The organization or setting

The period during which the activity took place

The number of hours per week

The duties performed

How the duties relate to the fellowship

For example, the application guidance gives the format of specifying dates and weekly hours, such as:

June 1, 2025 to August 31, 2025, 30 hours per week

Applicants should therefore avoid simply listing an organization and job title without describing what they actually did.

The purpose is to make it possible for reviewers to determine whether the applicant has the relevant experience required by the program.

Resume Requirements

The Treasury provides specific instructions regarding the resume.

Maximum Length: Two Pages

The resume should not exceed two pages.

This is particularly important because candidates need to demonstrate the required 52 weeks of experience while remaining within the two-page limit.

Applicants should therefore prioritize:

Relevant responsibilities

Analytical experience

Policy-related activities

Research

International affairs exposure

Economics or finance-related experience

Public policy experience

Government or nonprofit experience

Relevant volunteer activities

Relevant extracurricular activities

Rather than merely listing responsibilities, candidates should explain the work they performed and demonstrate its relevance to the Junior Fellowship.

Application Documents Required

Candidates must submit several materials by email.

The application package should include:

Cover letter

Resume

One recommendation letter

Transcript(s) demonstrating academic qualifications and career potential

These documents should be sent to:

IAFellows@treasury.gov

The application deadline is October 31, 2026.

Additional Information Required in the Application Email

In addition to submitting the required documents, candidates must provide specific information in their application email.

Applicants must:

1. Indicate Their Desired Start Date

Candidates should state when they would ideally like to begin the fellowship.

2. Confirm U.S. Citizenship

Candidates must confirm that they hold U.S. citizenship and must be able to provide documentation proving their citizenship.

3. Note Veterans’ Preference

Candidates should indicate whether they are eligible for veterans’ preference, if applicable.

4. Demonstrate the Required Experience

The submitted resume must demonstrate the required 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience.

What Happens After You Apply?

The selection process does not end with submission of the initial application.

Candidates who pass the first round of screening will be asked to respond to two short essay questions.

This means applicants should be prepared to demonstrate not only their academic and professional qualifications but also their ability to communicate clearly about their interests, experiences, and suitability for the fellowship.

The application materials are expected to be evaluated in December 2026.

Selected Fellows are expected to begin in summer 2027, although an alternative start time may be mutually agreed upon.

International Affairs Junior Fellowship Timeline

The key timeline for the 2027–2029 recruitment cycle is:

Stage
Timeline

Application deadline
October 31, 2026

Application evaluation
December 2026

Fellowship begins
Summer 2027

Program duration
Two years

Expected program period
2027–2029

Candidates should not wait until the final day to assemble their materials because the application requires multiple documents, including a recommendation letter and transcript(s).

National Security Clearance Requirement

An important condition of the fellowship is that candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance.

This requirement should be taken seriously by applicants.

A candidate may meet the educational and experience requirements but still need to satisfy the applicable security-clearance requirements to participate in the program.

Applicants should therefore understand that selection for the fellowship is not necessarily the only consideration in determining eligibility to serve in the position.

Salary and Employment Benefits

Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits.

This makes the program distinct from unpaid academic fellowships or many short-term graduate programs.

The fellowship combines:

A two-year professional appointment

Work within the U.S. Department of the Treasury

International economic policy exposure

Potential international travel

Professional development

Standard Treasury benefits

Experience working with senior officials and international counterparts

For recent graduates, this combination can provide substantial exposure to public-sector economic policymaking.

Career Opportunities After the Fellowship

The fellowship can provide a strong foundation for a range of future career paths.

According to the Treasury’s description, former fellows have pursued opportunities including employment at Treasury, other U.S. government positions, private-sector careers, and graduate education.

Potential longer-term directions include:

U.S. government careers

International economic policy

Public policy

International relations

Finance

Business

Law

Graduate study

International affairs

Economic analysis

The fellowship can therefore be viewed as an early-career platform for graduates who want to build expertise in international economic and financial policy.

Apply here

Information Sessions for Prospective Applicants

The Junior Fellows recruiting committee plans to host three information sessions before the application deadline.

These sessions are intended to help prospective applicants better understand the program and hear directly from current fellows.

The sessions will be led by current Junior Fellows from different International Affairs offices.

Participants will have an opportunity to:

Ask questions about the Junior Fellowship

Hear about current fellows’ experiences

Learn more about working in Treasury International Affairs

Gain insight into the fellowship from people currently participating in the program

The Treasury states that date and registration information for these sessions will be available on the relevant page in late summer 2026.

Why the Information Sessions Could Be Valuable

Prospective applicants should consider attending the information sessions if possible.

Because the Junior Fellowship is highly selective, understanding the program from current fellows can help candidates gain a clearer picture of:

The nature of the work

Different International Affairs offices

The experience of working at Treasury

Potential responsibilities

The transition from college to government policy work

The expectations associated with the fellowship

Candidates can also use the opportunity to ask questions before submitting their applications.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Although the Treasury sets out the formal application requirements, applicants can strengthen their preparation by making sure every document clearly demonstrates relevance to the fellowship.

1. Tailor Your Resume to International Affairs

A generic graduate resume may not effectively communicate your suitability.

Focus on experiences involving:

Economic analysis

Research

Policy

Finance

International affairs

Government

Public-sector work

Data analysis

Writing

International organizations

Development

Volunteer activities

Relevant extracurricular activities

2. Clearly Demonstrate the 2,080-Hour Requirement

Do not make the reviewer calculate your experience themselves.

Where appropriate, clearly state:

Start and end dates

Hours per week

Position/activity

Responsibilities

This is especially important for candidates whose experience is spread across internships, volunteering, extracurricular activities, part-time employment, or work-study.

3. Keep the Resume Within Two Pages

The two-page requirement means candidates need to be selective.

Prioritize experiences that demonstrate capabilities relevant to the responsibilities of an International Affairs Junior Fellow.

4. Make the Cover Letter Specific

The cover letter should explain why the applicant is interested in:

International economic policy

The U.S. Department of the Treasury

International Affairs

The Junior Fellowship

The specific skills and experiences they bring

A generic statement about wanting a government job is unlikely to communicate the same level of fit as a carefully targeted application.

5. Prepare for the Essay Stage

Candidates who pass the initial screening will be asked to answer two short essay questions.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to discuss their:

Academic background

Professional experience

Policy interests

Analytical skills

International interests

Motivation for joining Treasury

Career goals

For more details please visit here

What Makes This Fellowship Different?

Several features distinguish the International Affairs Junior Fellowship from a typical graduate recruitment opportunity.

Two-Year Structure

The fellowship is a fixed two-year program, providing more time for fellows to develop substantive professional expertise than a short internship.

International Economic Policy Focus

The program is specifically focused on international economic policy, making it highly relevant to graduates interested in global economic affairs.

Exposure to Major International Institutions

Fellows may support meetings involving organizations and forums such as the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20.

Regional and Functional Career Exposure

Fellows can be placed in either regional or functional offices, exposing them to different dimensions of international policy.

Potential International Travel

Junior Fellows may have opportunities to participate in meetings and travel abroad depending on their assignments.

Government Experience

The program provides direct experience within the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

Potential Long-Term Career Pathways

Former fellows have gone on to careers in Treasury, elsewhere in the U.S. government, the private sector, and graduate education.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the International Affairs Junior Fellowship?

It is a highly selective, fixed two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of International Affairs for new college graduates interested in international economic policy.

How long is the Junior Fellowship?

The program lasts two years, with the current recruitment cycle covering 2027–2029.

When is the application deadline?

The application deadline is October 31, 2026.

When will the selected Fellows begin?

Fellows are expected to begin in summer 2027, although an alternative start time may be mutually agreed upon.

What degree is required?

Strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor’s degree with relevant coursework.

What subjects are relevant?

The Treasury identifies economics, public policy, finance, international relations, and related fields.

Is preference given to undergraduate students?

Yes. The program specifically states that preference is given to undergraduates due to the structure of the program.

Is previous work experience required?

Candidates must demonstrate 52 weeks (2,080 hours) of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience.

Can volunteer or extracurricular experience count?

Yes. The application instructions specifically allow relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, and extracurricular experience.

How long can the resume be?

The resume should not exceed two pages.

Is U.S. citizenship required?

Yes. Candidates must confirm that they hold U.S. citizenship and must be able to provide documentation.

Is a security clearance required?

Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance.

Are Fellows paid?

Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level and receive standard Treasury benefits.

Can Fellows travel internationally?

Junior Fellows may have opportunities to travel abroad, depending on their work and assignments.

Will there be interviews or additional selection steps?

Candidates who pass the first screening stage will be asked to respond to two short essay questions.

When are applications evaluated?

The applications are expected to be evaluated in December 2026.

Where should applications be submitted?

Applications should be emailed to IAFellows@treasury.gov.

Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should ensure they have:

A cover letter

A resume of no more than two pages

One recommendation letter

Transcript(s)

Evidence of the required 52 weeks/2,080 hours of relevant experience

Desired start date included in the email

Confirmation of U.S. citizenship

Veterans’ preference information, if applicable

Detailed descriptions of relevant duties and activities

Dates and weekly hours for relevant experiences

Prepared for the possibility of two short essay questions

Considered their ability to obtain and maintain a national security clearance

Important Deadline

The deadline to apply for the U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 is:

October 31, 2026

Applicants should prepare their recommendation letter, transcripts, resume, and cover letter well before the deadline. The requirement to document 52 weeks or 2,080 hours of relevant experience also means candidates should carefully review their past work, volunteer, and extracurricular activities before submitting their application.

Conclusion

The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 offers recent college graduates an opportunity to begin a career in international economic policy through a structured, two-year professional program.

The fellowship combines analytical work, policy development, international economic research, and exposure to bilateral and multilateral engagements. Junior Fellows may work in regional or functional offices and can gain experience with issues involving international financial institutions, trade, export credits, foreign exchange, and international economic relationships.

The opportunity is particularly relevant for graduates with backgrounds in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields who want to develop careers in government, international affairs, public policy, finance, or global economic policy.

With placements within the U.S. Treasury’s Office of International Affairs, potential exposure to institutions such as the IMF and World Bank and forums such as the G7 and G20, and the possibility of international travel, the program can provide substantial early-career exposure to international policymaking.

Candidates should pay close attention to the specific application requirements, particularly the two-page resume limit, 52-week/2,080-hour experience requirement, U.S. citizenship requirement, recommendation letter, transcripts, and national security clearance requirement.

For eligible applicants, this is an opportunity to gain meaningful professional experience at one of the United States’ key economic policy institutions while building a foundation for future careers in government, international relations, finance, public policy, or further graduate study.

TITLE: Wallace Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard’s I Tatti: $5,200 Monthly Stipend for Scholars Researching the Italian Renaissance

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Wallace Fellowship 2027–2028 at Harvard’s I Tatti: $5,200 Monthly Stipend for Scholars Researching the Italian Renaissance

The Wallace Fellowship at Harvard University’s Villa I Tatti – The Harvard University Center for Italian Renaissance Studies offers scholars an opportunity to dedicate several months to advanced research on the historiography, influence, transformation, and continuing impact of the Italian Renaissance in the modern era.

Supported by a generous grant from The Lila Wallace – Reader’s Digest Fund, the Wallace Fellowship is designed for scholars whose research explores how the Italian Renaissance has been understood, interpreted, transformed, and represented from the 19th century through the 21st century.

The fellowship provides selected scholars with a residential research period in Florence, Italy, allowing them to concentrate on their proposed projects while benefiting from access to Harvard’s scholarly resources and the intellectual community at I Tatti.

Up to four Wallace Fellowships are awarded each year, and the residential fellowship can last either four or six months.

Applications for the fellowship must be submitted by November 16, 2026, while letters of recommendation must be submitted by November 21, 2026.

About the Wallace Fellowship

The Wallace Fellowship is intended for scholars conducting research into the Italian Renaissance and its relationship with the modern era.

The fellowship recognizes that the Renaissance continues to have a significant influence on modern scholarship, culture, artistic production, architecture, literature, music, philosophy, political thought, museums, collecting practices, and other areas of intellectual and cultural life.

Rather than limiting applicants to one specific academic discipline, the fellowship welcomes a broad range of research projects that examine the ways the Renaissance has survived, been interpreted, transformed, or commented upon during the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries.

This makes the fellowship potentially relevant to researchers working across multiple fields, provided that their proposed project has a meaningful connection to the historiography or impact of the Italian Renaissance in the modern era.

Research Areas Covered by the Wallace Fellowship

Applicants can propose projects addressing a wide range of topics connected to the Renaissance and modernity.

Potential areas of research include:

Historiography of the Italian Renaissance

The impact of the Renaissance on modern thought and culture

Modern interpretations of the Italian Renaissance

Reactions to Renaissance ideas and traditions

Transformations of Renaissance concepts in the modern era

Commentary on the Renaissance and its relationship with modernity

Museum history

Collecting history

Renaissance influences on modern art

Renaissance influences on modern architecture

Photography

Landscape architecture

Literature

Music

Philosophy

Political thought

History

Material culture

Religion

Science

The fellowship therefore provides considerable intellectual scope for researchers whose work connects Renaissance studies with developments and debates in the modern period.

Apply HERE

A Residential Research Opportunity in Florence

One of the defining features of the Wallace Fellowship is its residential nature.

Fellows are expected to live in the Florence area during their fellowship and spend at least three days per week at I Tatti.

This arrangement is intended to give scholars the time and environment necessary to concentrate deeply on their research.

I Tatti describes the fellowship environment as providing Fellows with valuable time to pursue their studies with a minimum of obligations and interruptions, while also giving them access to substantial scholarly resources.

The combination of dedicated research time and access to an active academic community makes the fellowship particularly suitable for scholars who need an extended period of concentrated research.

Learn more HERE

Life and Academic Community at I Tatti

Wallace Fellows are not isolated researchers. They become part of the broader scholarly environment at I Tatti.

Each year, certain activities organized at the center are reserved for Fellows, and Fellows are expected to participate in the wider intellectual community.

This includes joining:

Conferences

Lectures

Concerts

Other scholarly and cultural activities organized at the center

The expectation of collegial participation means that applicants are evaluated not only on the quality of their research but also on their potential contribution to the intellectual life of the Harvard Center.

Wallace Fellowship Duration

The Wallace Fellowship is a residential fellowship lasting either:

Four months, or

Six months

Applicants are asked to indicate their preferred fellowship period when applying.

They must choose between:

Fall: September through December

Winter-Spring: January through June

Applicants should therefore consider their research schedule carefully before selecting their preferred term.

Wallace Fellowship Financial Support

Selected Fellows receive significant financial support during their residence in Florence.

The fellowship provides:

Monthly Grant

Fellows receive:

USD 5,200 per month

This monthly grant is intended to support the Fellow during the residential research period.

Relocation Supplement

In addition to the monthly grant, Fellows may receive a one-time relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800.

This additional support is intended to help offset relocation expenses associated with moving to Florence for the fellowship.

Housing Support in Florence

Because the Wallace Fellowship is residential, housing is an important part of the fellowship arrangement.

When possible, an apartment will be set aside for the Fellow’s use rent-free, although the Fellow will be responsible for utility charges.

If an apartment is not available, a housing subsidy will be provided to help offset rental costs.

This arrangement can substantially reduce the financial burden associated with living in Florence during the fellowship.

However, applicants should understand that housing is subject to availability and that Fellows may need to use the housing subsidy if an apartment cannot be provided.

Access to Harvard’s Resources

Wallace Fellows enjoy the privileges available to Fellows at the Harvard Center.

One particularly important resource is the Biblioteca Berenson, which Fellows can use seven days a week.

Fellows also have the opportunity to participate in lunch with other appointees from Monday through Friday.

Although Term Fellows do not receive a private office or study, they are provided with their own desk or carrel in the Library.

This arrangement is designed to provide scholars with a dedicated workspace while keeping them connected to the research environment of the center.

Important Restrictions During the Fellowship

Applicants should carefully consider the fellowship’s requirements before applying.

Wallace Fellows are expected to devote themselves to the research project for which they were selected.

During the fellowship:

Fellows must work solely on the project with which they applied.

They may not simultaneously work on editing other books or article projects.

They may not take on other obligations such as teaching positions, including part-time teaching.

The fellowship cannot be held concurrently with another fellowship or award.

The fellowship cannot be deferred.

Term Fellowships can be held only once.

These conditions emphasize that the fellowship is intended to provide scholars with dedicated time for one substantial research project.

Who Can Apply for the Wallace Fellowship?

Applicants must meet several academic and professional requirements.

At the time of application, scholars must already have a PhD.

Applicants will be required to upload a scan of their PhD certificate as part of the application process.

Applicants also:

Must not be working toward a second PhD at the time of application.

Must be prepared to work solely on their proposed fellowship project.

Must be conversant in English.

Must have familiarity with Italian.

Should have a research project that falls within the fellowship’s thematic scope.

Must be able to conduct most of their research in Florence.

The fellowship gives priority to early- and mid-career scholars.

Applicants From All Nations Are Welcome

The Wallace Fellowship is open to scholars from all nations.

The program does not restrict applications to scholars from a particular country or continent.

Importantly, I Tatti gives special consideration to candidates who do not have regular access to research materials and facilities in Italy.

This means that scholars who face limited access to Italian research resources may receive particular consideration during the selection process.

Academic Fields Eligible for Consideration

The fellowship has a broad interdisciplinary focus.

Proposed projects may address the Renaissance’s historiography or impact in fields including:

Art

Architecture

Landscape architecture

History

Literature

Material culture

Music

Philosophy

Religion

Science

Applicants should therefore focus on demonstrating a strong intellectual connection between their proposed research and the Italian Renaissance’s role, interpretation, influence, or transformation in the modern era.

How Applications Are Evaluated

Applications are evaluated by international scholars.

The selection process considers several elements of an applicant’s academic profile and proposed research.

Particular attention is given to:

The strength of the proposed project

The research proposal should present a strong and compelling scholarly project.

Potential for original results

Applicants should demonstrate that their research has the potential to produce original findings or meaningful scholarly contributions.

Curriculum vitae

The applicant’s academic and research background is an important component of the evaluation.

Contribution to the intellectual community

The selection committee also considers the candidate’s ability to contribute collegially to the intellectual life of the Harvard Center.

Applicants should therefore think beyond simply presenting a strong research topic. They should also demonstrate that they can participate constructively in the scholarly community at I Tatti.

Previous Appointments at I Tatti

The Wallace Fellowship is intended primarily for scholars who have not previously held appointments at I Tatti.

Term Fellowships can only be held once.

However, there is an exception for Graduate Fellows.

Applicants who have previously held an appointment at I Tatti should therefore carefully review the eligibility conditions before preparing an application.

Visa, Residence Permit, and Health Coverage

International scholars selected for the fellowship are responsible for arranging the documentation and coverage required for their residence in Italy.

The Fellow is responsible for obtaining:

A visa, where required

A permesso di soggiorno (residence permit)

Health coverage

Appropriate documentation and arrangements for accompanying family members, where applicable

Applicants should determine whether they require a visa and, if necessary, obtain it before traveling to Italy.

These immigration and health-related responsibilities should be considered when planning for the fellowship.

Outside Funding and Salary

Applicants who receive a partial salary or outside grants must disclose this information.

Such funding should be indicated either:

In the application, or

In subsequent correspondence with the Director

Permission must be received if the applicant has partial salary or outside grant support.

Applicants should therefore provide accurate information about any other sources of financial support connected to their research or professional circumstances.

Application Language

Applications for the Wallace Fellowship may be written in either:

English, or

Italian

This gives eligible scholars flexibility in presenting their research proposal and other application materials.

However, applicants are expected to be conversant in English and have familiarity with Italian.

Wallace Fellowship Application Deadline

The main application deadline is:

November 16, 2026

Applications must be submitted electronically by midnight, Cambridge, Massachusetts time, on November 16, 2026.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their materials because technical or administrative problems could potentially interfere with a timely submission.

Recommendation Letter Deadline

Letters of recommendation have a separate deadline:

November 21, 2026

Applicants must have two scholars who know their work well submit recommendations online by this date.

The recommendation letters may be written in:

English, or

Italian

Applicants are strongly encouraged to register their referees as early as possible through the reference tab so that the referees have sufficient time to complete and submit their recommendations.

Choosing Recommendation Writers

Applicants should select two scholars who know their academic and research work well.

A strong recommendation can help provide the selection committee with additional insight into:

The applicant’s academic ability

Research experience

Scholarly potential

Quality of previous work

Capacity to undertake the proposed project

Applicants should also make sure that their referees understand the nature of the proposed project and the relevant submission deadline.

The applicant is responsible for informing the scholars writing on their behalf about the project and recommendation deadline.

One Fellowship Type Per Academic Year

Scholars can apply for only one type of fellowship at I Tatti per academic year.

Applicants should therefore carefully consider which I Tatti fellowship best corresponds to their research profile before submitting an application.

Submitting applications for multiple fellowship types during the same academic year is not permitted.

How to Prepare a Strong Wallace Fellowship Application

Because the selection committee pays particular attention to the proposed project, applicants should make the research proposal one of the strongest parts of their application.

A well-prepared application should clearly communicate:

1. The central research question

Explain exactly what the project seeks to investigate.

2. The connection to the Italian Renaissance

Clearly establish how the proposed research relates to the historiography, influence, transformation, survival, or interpretation of the Italian Renaissance in the modern era.

3. The modern-era dimension

The Wallace Fellowship focuses specifically on the relationship between the Renaissance and the modern era. Applicants should make this connection clear.

4. The potential for original results

Explain what new contribution the research could make and why the project has the potential to produce original findings.

5. Why Florence is important

Since applicants must be able to carry out most of their research in Florence, it is useful for the proposal to demonstrate why access to resources in Florence and at I Tatti is important for the project.

6. A clear research plan

Applicants should have a realistic understanding of what they intend to accomplish during their four- or six-month residential period.

Why the Wallace Fellowship Is a Significant Research Opportunity

The Wallace Fellowship combines several elements that can be valuable for scholars undertaking advanced research.

The fellowship provides:

A dedicated residential research period in Florence

USD 5,200 per month

Up to USD 1,800 in relocation support

Potential rent-free apartment accommodation when available

Housing subsidy when an apartment is unavailable

Access to the Biblioteca Berenson seven days a week

A dedicated desk or carrel in the Library

Participation in the intellectual community at I Tatti

Access to conferences, lectures, concerts, and other activities

The opportunity to work alongside scholars and other appointees

A research environment designed to minimize competing obligations

For scholars whose work requires substantial engagement with Italian Renaissance materials and resources in Florence, these features can provide a valuable environment for concentrated academic research.

Important Dates to Remember

Applicants should keep the following dates in their calendars:

November 16, 2026: Main application deadline. Applications must be submitted electronically by midnight Cambridge, Massachusetts time.

November 21, 2026: Deadline for the two online letters of recommendation.

Because the recommendation deadline comes after the main application deadline, applicants should contact their referees well in advance rather than waiting until the application deadline approaches.

Final Checklist Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective applicants should make sure that they:

Hold a PhD at the time of application.

Have a scan of their PhD certificate ready to upload.

Are not pursuing a second PhD.

Have a project directly relevant to the fellowship’s research scope.

Can conduct most of their research in Florence.

Are conversant in English.

Have familiarity with Italian.

Understand that the fellowship is residential.

Can live in the Florence area and spend at least three days each week at the center.

Are prepared to work exclusively on the proposed project.

Do not plan to take on teaching or other obligations during the fellowship.

Have identified two scholars who can provide recommendations.

Have registered their referees early enough for them to submit their recommendations.

Have selected their preferred fall or winter-spring term.

Have considered visa, residence permit, and health coverage requirements.

Have disclosed any partial salary or outside grant support where applicable.

Are applying for only one type of I Tatti fellowship during the academic year.

Submit the application before November 16, 2026.

Ensure both recommendation letters are submitted by November 21, 2026.

Conclusion

The Wallace Fellowship at Harvard’s I Tatti provides a highly focused residential research opportunity for scholars investigating the historiography and continuing impact of the Italian Renaissance in the modern era.

With a monthly grant of USD 5,200, a relocation supplement of up to USD 1,800, potential housing support, access to the Biblioteca Berenson, and participation in the scholarly community at I Tatti, the fellowship is structured to give selected researchers substantial time and resources to advance an important academic project.

The fellowship welcomes scholars from all nations and supports interdisciplinary research spanning art, architecture, history, literature, material culture, music, philosophy, religion, science, and other fields connected to the Renaissance and modernity.

Prospective applicants should pay particular attention to the research proposal, as the selection committee places significant emphasis on the strength of the proposed project, its potential to produce original results, the applicant’s curriculum vitae, and the candidate’s potential contribution to the intellectual life of the Harvard Center.

Interested scholars should begin preparing early, particularly because two recommendation letters are required. The main application deadline is November 16, 2026, while recommendation letters must be submitted by November 21, 2026.

TITLE: Graduate Admissions – Additional Guidance

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
This page includes detailed instructions for each section in the MIT Physics Graduate Admissions portal. The main graduate admissions page has a broader description of the admissions process, and an FAQ.

Program Information

The high-level information provided in this section helps the admissions committee to guide your application through the admissions process. The research areas of interest and “suggested faculty readers” are particularly important to ensuring that your application is read by the admissions committee members (and possibly other faculty) most able to appreciate your research background and interests. The “suggested faculty readers” may include faculty that you would be interested in working with, or may simply represent areas of research that you find interesting or have worked in. Research areas in the MIT Physics Department are described here, and each area page includes a list of associated faculty. The physics department hosts a wide and diverse collection of labs, centers and groups that operate within and across research areas. Finally, the faculty webpage lists all faculty, and allows you to select based on the research area, lab and/or center.

The following examples are of applicants with a fairly tight research focus. This narrow focus is just for the sake of making simple examples and is not typical or expected of all applicants.

Example A, an applicant interested in the particle nature of dark matter, and dark energy’s role in cosmology:

Area 1: High Energy and Nuclear Physics (Theory)

Area 2: High Energy and Nuclear Physics (Experimental)

Lab/center/group: MIT Center for Theoretical Physics — a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI)

Suggested Faculty Readers: Winslow, Slatyer, Guth

Example B, an applicant interested in galaxy formation, black holes and dark matter dynamics:

Area 1: Astrophysics Theory

Area 2: Astrophysics Observation, Instrumentation, and Experiment

Lab/center/group: MIT Kavli Institute for Astrophysics & Space Research (MKI)

Suggested Faculty Readers: Necib, Vogelsberger, McDonald

Area 2: Atomic and Optical Physics

Area 3: Quantum Information Science

Lab/center/group 1: Center for Ultracold Atoms (CUA)

Lab/center/group 2: MIT Kavli Institute for Astrophysics & Space Research (MKI)

Suggested Faculty Readers: Mavalvala, Evans, Vuletic

Personal Background

The information requested in these sections allows us to contact you, provide you with information that may be relevant to the application process, and understand our applicant pool with the aim of improving our admissions process.

MIT is a diverse and supportive community committed to the inclusion of all gender identities. The Physics Department is committed to upholding both the MIT Nondiscrimination Policy and the Physics Community Values.

Test Scores

GREs and/or PGREs (Physics subject GREs) are not required for graduate applications but are recommended. All applications will be given full consideration with or without GRE scores.

English is the language of instruction at MIT and all students must demonstrate their English language proficiency. Non-native English speakers are expected to provide results from the IELTS or TOEFL with their application, though a waiver may be requested in some circumstances (see the FAQ for more information).

Graduate Record Examination (GRE)

GREs and PGREs are optional but recommended.

Academic History

Your academic experience and performance is an important part of your application. In this section you are asked to provide information about academic institutions that you have attended. Most of the requested information should be self-explanatory, but there are a few points that might require clarification.

Your academic experience and performance is an important part of your application. In this section you are asked to provide information about academic institutions that you have attended. Most of the requested information should be self-explanatory, but there are a few points that might require clarification.

Institution Name and Location: Please find your institution in the database using the text search function. Finding your institution in our database will greatly help the admissions committee! If your institution is not in the database, you may enter the institution’s name and address manually.

Academic Calendar: Please indicate if this institution uses a Semester (2 academic terms per year, i.e. fall and spring), Trimester (3 terms: fall, winter, spring) or Quarter (4 terms: fall, winter, spring, summer) system. Optional/special academic terms, like optional summer classes or MIT’s “Independent Activity Period” in January, can be ignored for the purposes of this question.

Dates of Attendance: Please indicate the dates you attended (or expect to attend) this institution. The end date may be a few months in the future, and will probably be similar to your expected degree date (requested under Degree information).

Contact Hours: Please estimate the average number of “contact hours” per week (i.e., time in class) during your time at this institution. For many US colleges and universities the number of credits given for a class is equal to the number of contact hours per week (see the Carnegie Unit System), such that the requested value is just the number of credits on your transcript divided by the number of semesters you attended the institution. For example, 15 hours per week (and thus 15 credits per term) would lead to 120 credits total after 4 years (8 semesters). There are a wide range of course credit systems used internationally, and some utilities for unit conversion exist (e.g., University of Arizona and a wiki page for the EU).

Level of Study, and Degree Expected/Awarded: Please indicate the degree you received (or expect to receive soon) from this institution. The list of majors is standardized and quite long: most applicants to the Physics Department should choose “Physics, General” or “Physics and Astronomy”.

Numerical GPA: Please enter your cumulative GPA as listed on your transcript. If your institution does not provide a numerical GPA, but you can compute yours from the courses on your transcript, please do so. Otherwise, enter “N/A.”

Grading System: While most educational institutions provide numerical grades or letter grades, the relationship between these numerical scales and performance varies widely. In the US, common numerical scales have a range of 0 to 4.0, 0 to 4.3 and 0 to 5. Internationally, numerical scales may have a range of 0 to 10, 0 to 20, 0 to 100, etc. In order to provide the admissions committee with a clearer understanding of your GPA, and other grades on your transcript, we request that applicants guide our interpretation of your grades.

TITLE: Invitation to In-person Training Workshop (Institutional Repositories) at Catholic University of Eastern Africa, CUEA, Kenya, from 26 – 30 July 2021

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Theme: Strengthening Institutional Repositories to support teaching, learning and research

The covid-19 pandemic has shown why it is urgent that African Universities have E-content in our institutions to support the academic environment. The covid19 pandemic exposed our inadequacies in having enough E-resources to support virtual learning/teaching in African HEIs. Some African HEIs and their students had no online resources they could rely on and even where it was available, its completeness and ease of access by students and faculty proved to be a challenge . The need to have online E-content has also been further highlighted by the unfortunate fire outbreaks that has destroyed the physical content of some HEIs on the continent. It is time for all in the knowledge management Creators Cycle (researchers) and Managers (Information Professionals) to critically look at building strong platforms to support E-content development and make them available online to support the core mandates (teaching, learning and research) of our HEIs.

In line with reducing these inadequacies and building a more resilient higher education system, the Association of African universities is collaborating with the Catholic University of Eastern Africa, CUEA, Kenya, to organize a workshop on strengthening Institutional Repositories to provide the platform for building a critical mass of E-content for our institutions. This is an in-person training workshop and participants are expected to be onsite.

Why is this workshop being held in-person in a pandemic and social distancing era

The workshop is totally hands-on with on-site guidance for real time implementation

Experience from previous hands-on training shows participants coming with computers that require fixing because of the different operating systems, before it can be used in the training (this fixing is difficult to carry out online)

There will be a day when each participating institution will have personal reviews of plans and also repository reviews for institutions that have an existing platform

Who should attend the workshop?

Directors of Research, Researchers, Librarians, IT Staff supporting Libraries, and Information Professionals. Institutions with the following challenges are especially encouraged to attend.

Institutions with repositories that have gone silent in the wake of the covid19 pandemic.

Institutions that have been unable to update their repositories for earlier versions

Institutions having problems with making their repositories harvestable

Institutions having challenges with their advocacy and copyright policies

Institutions having difficulty with digitizing records for upload unto their repositories

The workshop will also provide the avenue to discuss taking steps to safeguard physical collections against disasters.

Participants will be required to attend the workshop with a laptop. Those coming from institutions with repositories should have administrative access to their institutional repository. There will be two (2) days dedicated to holding clinics with each participating institution, where their repository will be reviewed with them. Institutions looking to set up their repositories are also welcomed to attend

Covid19 Protocols will be strictly adhered to in all sessions

Workshop dates are July 26 – 30, 2021.

Rate is $500 per participant (Covers conference package which includes meals, cost of conference venue and conference material)

Registration Link is here https://event-mgt.aau.org/event/52/

About the PASSENGER Project

PASSENGER – Pilot Action for Securing a Sustainable European Next Generation of Efficient RE-free Magnets – is a Horizon 2020 innovation action that addressed Europe’s dependency on rare-earth elements (REs) in the production of permanent magnets (PMs). These magnets are essential for clean and emerging technologies such as electromobility, wind energy, and high-efficiency industrial systems.
The project developed innovative pilot lines to produce high-performance magnets using abundant, sustainable materials, thereby reducing environmental impact while securing Europe’s industrial and technological independence. Bringing together 20 partners from eight EU countries, including leading research institutes, SMEs, and large industrial players, PASSENGER had a strong industrial orientation, focusing on delivering real-world, scalable solutions.

Learn more about the project

ESF’s role in PASSENGER

ESF led the work package on dissemination, ensuring that PASSENGER’s results are widely communicated through digital materials, press releases, videos, events, and publications, making the project’s achievements visible to both expert and general audiences.

Insights through Factsheets

As part of its communication efforts, ESF produced a series of factsheets showcasing the results and technological progress achieved by each pilot plant and work package within the PASSENGER project.
These factsheets highlight key outcomes, industrial validations, and sustainability results, offering concise and accessible overviews of the innovations developed throughout the project. They form an integral part of PASSENGER’s outreach. They are designed to inform industrial stakeholders, researchers, policymakers, and the general public about how Europe is pioneering next-generation, rare-earth-free permanent magnet technologies.
