TITLE: 2026 Impact Grant: €50,000 in Unrestricted Funding for Arts Nonprofits Supporting Underrepresented Emerging Artists

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The 2026 Impact Grant by The Supporting Act Foundation is an opportunity for eligible nonprofit arts organizations that are working to support emerging artists from underrepresented groups and communities facing systemic barriers in the creative and cultural industries.

The grant is specifically designed for organizations that provide non-financial support to emerging artists. Rather than funding individual artists or specific projects, the Impact Grant supports nonprofit organizations whose ongoing work helps artists develop their practices, improve their living conditions, gain greater visibility, and build confidence in their creative careers.

For the 2026 funding cycle, 10 organizations will receive unrestricted grants of €25,000 per year for two years, providing a total of €50,000 per selected organization.

Applications are open to eligible nonprofit arts organizations based in Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom, as well as organizations registered elsewhere that work with an eligible fiscal host.

The application deadline is October 1, 2026, at 11:00 AM CET.

About the 2026 Impact Grant

The Impact Grant is an initiative of The Supporting Act Foundation, which seeks to support organizations contributing to meaningful change in the creative and cultural sector.

The 2026 grant focuses on nonprofit arts organizations that work with underrepresented emerging artists. These may be artists who face systemic barriers to accessing opportunities, visibility, professional development, networks, resources, or other forms of support within the creative and cultural industries.

The program recognizes that emerging artists often need more than direct financial assistance. Organizations can play an important role by providing mentoring, professional development, platforms for visibility, community-building opportunities, access to networks, guidance, and other forms of non-financial support.

Through the Impact Grant, The Supporting Act Foundation aims to strengthen organizations that are already doing this work and help them increase their long-term impact.

The program’s intended impact includes:

Improving the living conditions of artists.

Enabling emerging artists to dedicate more time to developing their artistic practices.

Increasing the visibility of artists and their work.

Supporting artists who face systemic barriers within the creative and cultural industries.

Strengthening artists’ confidence in their work and professional development.

Supporting nonprofit organizations that create meaningful opportunities for underrepresented artists.

Helping organizations sustain and expand their contribution to the arts ecosystem.

What Does the 2026 Impact Grant Provide?

The 2026 Impact Grant will provide 10 unrestricted grants.

Each selected nonprofit organization will receive:

€25,000 per year

Funding for two years

€50,000 total per organization

Unrestricted funding intended to support the organization’s work rather than a specific project proposal

The unrestricted nature of the funding is particularly relevant for organizations that require flexibility to respond to the needs of the artists and communities they serve.

Instead of restricting the grant to one predetermined project, unrestricted support can give eligible organizations greater flexibility in strengthening their existing work and organizational activities.

A total of 10 nonprofit organizations will be selected for the 2026 Impact Grant.

Who Is the 2026 Impact Grant For?

The Impact Grant is intended for nonprofit arts organizations, rather than individual artists.

Eligible organizations should have an established focus on supporting emerging artists from underrepresented groups or artists who experience systemic barriers to opportunities in the creative and cultural industries.

Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate that their organization is actively providing non-financial support to emerging artists.

Examples of such support may include professional development, mentoring, artistic platforms, networking opportunities, community support, visibility initiatives, career guidance, capacity building, or other forms of assistance that do not constitute direct financial grants to artists.

Organizations should be able to demonstrate this work through publicly available information on their websites.

2026 Impact Grant Eligibility Criteria

Organizations interested in applying must satisfy the eligibility requirements established by The Supporting Act Foundation.

1. The applicant must be a nonprofit arts organization

The opportunity is intended specifically for nonprofit organizations operating within the arts and cultural sector.

Organizations must have been registered as a nonprofit arts organization between 2016 and 2024.

The organization must also be registered in one of the eligible countries listed below.

2. The organization must be based in an eligible country

The applicant organization must be registered in one of the following countries:

Belgium

France

Germany

Greece

Ireland

Italy

The Netherlands

Portugal

Spain

United Kingdom

Organizations registered outside these countries may also be eligible if they can provide a letter of intent from a fiscal host that is registered as a nonprofit organization in one of the eligible countries.

This means that organizations outside the listed countries should not automatically assume that they are excluded. However, they must meet the fiscal-host requirement specified by the program.

3. A qualifying bank account is required

Applicants must be able to provide a bank account number with an IBAN in the name of either:

The applicant organization; or

An eligible fiscal host located in one of the listed countries.

Organizations should ensure that they can meet this requirement before beginning the application process.

4. The organization must meet the annual expenditure requirement

Eligible organizations must have a total annual expenditure of between €50,000 and €300,000, or the equivalent amount in the organization’s local currency, during the current fiscal year.

This requirement is intended to ensure that applicants have an established level of organizational activity and financial operations.

Organizations should therefore review their current financial information before applying.

5. The organization must have an updated website

Applicants must have an updated website that provides publicly available evidence of the organization’s active work.

The website should demonstrate that the organization provides non-financial support to emerging artists from underrepresented groups or to artists facing systemic barriers to opportunities in the creative and cultural industries.

This makes the organization’s online presence an important part of demonstrating eligibility.

Applicants should ensure that their website clearly communicates:

What the organization does.

Who it supports.

How it supports emerging artists.

The communities or groups it works with.

Examples of active or recent programs.

Evidence of its contribution to the creative and cultural sector.

Who Cannot Apply for the Impact Grant?

The 2026 Impact Grant is not open to everyone working in the arts sector.

According to the program information, the open call is not intended for:

Individual artists.

Commercial organizations.

Ongoing projects.

Project proposals.

Current The Supporting Act Foundation grantees.

Past The Supporting Act Foundation grantees.

The grant is focused on eligible nonprofit arts organizations rather than individual creative projects.

Organizations that previously applied but were unsuccessful may apply again in 2026, provided they meet all current eligibility requirements.

The Supporting Act Foundation states that it can only accept applications that satisfy the eligibility criteria and cannot make exceptions to those requirements.

What Does “Non-Financial Support” Mean?

A central element of the 2026 Impact Grant is the focus on organizations that provide non-financial support to emerging artists.

This means that the organization’s contribution to artists does not necessarily have to involve giving artists direct grants or financial awards.

Instead, organizations may support artists through activities and services that help them build sustainable creative careers.

This could include areas such as:

Mentorship.

Professional development.

Artistic development.

Training.

Networking.

Career guidance.

Exhibitions and showcases.

Performance opportunities.

Community-building.

Access to professional networks.

Platforms that increase artists’ visibility.

Creative workshops.

Knowledge-sharing.

Industry connections.

Support for artists facing systemic barriers.

Opportunities to develop and present artistic work.

Applicants should focus on demonstrating what their organization actually does and the impact its support has on emerging artists.

Why the Impact Grant Matters for Arts Organizations

Many emerging artists face barriers that go beyond access to funding.

An artist may have the creative ability and ambition to develop professionally but still lack access to networks, mentorship, platforms, professional opportunities, training, or visibility.

Arts nonprofits can help address these gaps by creating supportive environments where emerging artists can develop their skills and practices.

The Impact Grant is designed around this broader understanding of impact.

The Supporting Act Foundation identifies several desired outcomes, including improving artists’ living conditions, giving artists more time to develop their practices, increasing the visibility of their work, and strengthening their confidence.

For nonprofit organizations already working in these areas, the grant provides an opportunity to strengthen their organizational capacity and continue their work over a two-year funding period.

How Much Funding Can Organizations Receive?

The 2026 Impact Grant offers substantial unrestricted support.

Each selected organization will receive:

€25,000 per year for two years

This amounts to:

€50,000 total funding per selected organization.

There will be:

10 grants available.

Because the grant is unrestricted, the funding is not presented as support for a single project proposal. Instead, it is designed to support eligible organizations and their broader work.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the official open call guide to understand the Foundation’s expectations regarding the use and administration of the funding.

2026 Impact Grant Application Timeline

Applicants should pay close attention to the official timeline because the application window is limited.

September 1, 2026 — Call Opens

The 2026 Impact Grant open call officially opened on September 1, 2026.

Eligible organizations can begin preparing and submitting their applications through the designated application platform.

October 1, 2026 — Application Deadline

The application deadline is:

October 1, 2026, at 11:00 AM CET.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their applications.

Organizations should allow sufficient time to review their eligibility, prepare supporting information, complete the application form, and ensure that all required information has been submitted correctly.

October 2026 — Application Review

Applications will be reviewed during October 2026.

Late October 2026 — Applicant Notifications

All applicants are expected to receive notifications regarding their applications in late October 2026.

November 2026 — Final Review of Shortlisted Applicants

Shortlisted applications will undergo a final review during November 2026.

January 2027 — Public Announcement and First Installment

The public announcement of selected organizations and the transfer of the first installment are scheduled for January 2027.

Applicants should consult the official open call guide for the more detailed timeline.

How to Apply for the 2026 Impact Grant

Interested organizations should first establish that they meet all eligibility requirements.

The application process can be approached in several stages.

Step 1: Review the Eligibility Requirements

Before starting the application, confirm that your organization:

Is a nonprofit arts organization.

Was registered between 2016 and 2024.

Is registered in one of the eligible countries or has an eligible fiscal host.

Can provide the required IBAN bank account.

Has annual expenditure between €50,000 and €300,000.

Has an updated website.

Provides non-financial support to emerging artists from underrepresented groups or artists facing systemic barriers.

Is not an excluded applicant type.

Step 2: Read the Open Call Guide

Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the official open call guide and preview the application form before applying.

The guide can help organizations understand the requirements and prepare their application properly.

Download the 2026 Impact Grant Open Call Guide

Step 3: Review the Frequently Asked Questions

Applicants should also review the Impact Grant FAQ, particularly if they are uncertain about their organization’s eligibility, application process, use of funding, or selection and evaluation process.

This can help organizations determine whether their questions have already been addressed before contacting the Foundation.

Step 4: Prepare the Application

Organizations should prepare their application carefully and make sure that the information they provide accurately reflects their activities, organizational structure, financial position, and work with emerging artists.

Particular attention should be given to demonstrating the organization’s actual impact and its approach to supporting underrepresented artists.

Step 5: Submit Through the Official Application Platform

Applications should be submitted through the official open call platform.

Applicants should ensure that their submission is completed before the October 1, 2026, 11:00 AM CET deadline.

APPLY HERE

Tips for Preparing a Strong Impact Grant Application

Although eligibility is the first requirement, applicants should also make sure that their application clearly communicates the organization’s work and impact.

Clearly explain your organization’s mission

The application should make it easy for reviewers to understand what your organization does, why it exists, and which communities it serves.

Demonstrate your work with emerging artists

Applicants should provide clear evidence that they actively support emerging artists rather than simply stating that they do so.

Where appropriate, describe programs, initiatives, platforms, partnerships, training, mentorship activities, exhibitions, performances, or other forms of support.

Explain the barriers faced by the artists you support

The program specifically focuses on underrepresented groups and artists facing systemic barriers.

Organizations should therefore clearly explain the context in which they operate and the barriers their artists or communities encounter.

Make your website work for your application

Because applicants are required to have an updated website with publicly available evidence of their activities, organizations should review their online presence before applying.

Make sure that key programs and activities are clearly presented and easy to find.

Check your financial eligibility

Confirm that the organization’s current annual expenditure falls within the required €50,000 to €300,000 range.

Check the country and fiscal-host requirements

Organizations should carefully verify whether their registration country qualifies.

If an organization is registered outside the listed countries, it should determine whether it can satisfy the fiscal-host requirement before submitting an application.

Do not leave the application until the deadline

The closing time is specifically stated as 11:00 AM CET on October 1, 2026.

Applicants should account for the time-zone difference and submit early enough to resolve any technical or administrative issues.

Selection Committee for the 2026 Impact Grant

Applications are reviewed by an independent selection committee.

The 2026 committee includes professionals from the arts, culture, music, film, creative practice, and nonprofit sectors.

The committee members listed by The Supporting Act Foundation are:

Adwoa Amoah — Artist and curator

Federico Bomba — Artistic director of Sineglossa

Maka Chkhaidze — Founder of InForm and 2025 Impact Grant recipient

Marie McPartlin — Director of Somerset House Studios

Nicolas Derné — Co-founder of Association Zofi and 2025 Impact Grant recipient

Rocío Mateo-Sagasta — Head of Music & Film at La Casa Encendida

Tamar Guttmann — Founder of Cue Collective and 2025 Impact Grant recipient

The independent selection committee is responsible for reviewing applications and determining which organizations will receive the grant.

Frequently Asked Questions About the 2026 Impact Grant

Is the Impact Grant available to individuals?

No. The Impact Grant is designed for eligible nonprofit arts organizations. Individual artists are not eligible to apply under this open call.

Can commercial organizations apply?

No. Commercial organizations are specifically excluded from the open call.

Can an organization apply for a specific project?

The Impact Grant is not intended for ongoing projects or project proposals. It is designed to support eligible nonprofit arts organizations whose ongoing work provides non-financial support to emerging artists.

Can organizations outside the listed countries apply?

Organizations registered outside the eligible countries may be able to apply if they can provide a letter of intent from a qualifying fiscal host registered as a nonprofit in one of the eligible countries.

How much is the grant worth?

Each selected organization receives €25,000 per year for two years, for a total of €50,000.

How many organizations will receive funding?

The 2026 Impact Grant will provide funding to 10 nonprofit organizations.

Can previous unsuccessful applicants apply again?

Yes. Organizations that previously applied unsuccessfully may apply again, provided they meet all of the current eligibility requirements.

Are current or previous Supporting Act Foundation grantees eligible?

TITLE: Buoy Lunch: WHOI in the Old Days by George Tupper

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
George Tupper gives a talk about what WHOI was like in the old days at a recent Buoy Lunch. Picture by Andrea Harvey.

Last month’s Buoy Lunch, presented by George Tupper, was an exciting peek into a time when the approaches to physical oceanography were different, or, perhaps, comfortingly similar, to the ways in which things are done today. “Buoy Lunch: WHOI in the Old Days” attracted an audience of more than 45 people and included photos, charts, memories, and lore from a rich and storied nearly six-decade long sea-going career. Buoy Lunch itself was recognized as a long-standing PO department tradition, which was first instituted by Robert H. Heinmiller, then head of the Buoy Operations Group. Dr. Ferris Webster gave a Buoy Lunch talk on July 17, 1967, which was also George’s first day of employment at WHOI. Ferris and his wife, Jackie, attended last month’s Buoy Lunch.
George recalled life on the R/V Gosnold, explained how instruments were used at sea, and presented a chart showing a drastic decrease in lost moorings from 1968 onward. Coincidence? Perhaps not.

In classic Tupper form, humor was woven throughout the presentation and laughter erupted when a photo of Al Vine’s solution to Eel Pond maintenance appeared, which showed people being ferried from the Iselin Dock to Water Street on what looked like massive inner tubes rigged up to a rope pulley system.

In addition to a brief history of iconic research vessels, aircraft, and people, George shared his own sentiments with witty and moving anecdotes. “Buoy Lunch: WHOI in the Old Days” was a treat to all who attended. Thank you, George!

TITLE: Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027: Apply for $30,000 to Build Bold Social Justice Ideas

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027 is now accepting applications from social justice changemakers in the United States who have bold, early-stage ideas aimed at creating meaningful social change. The six-month fellowship provides selected fellows with a $30,000 award, a $1,000 healthcare stipend, coaching and mentorship, peer support, and fully funded travel to three in-person fellowship convenings.

Unlike many traditional funding opportunities, the Voqal Partners Fellowship is specifically designed for people who are still developing an idea. Applicants do not need to have an established organization, completed product, fully developed campaign, or comprehensive business plan. Instead, Voqal Partners is interested in individuals who recognize a systemic problem, have a compelling vision for changing it, and are ready to begin testing, developing, and learning from their idea.

Applications for the 2027 cohort close on October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Opportunity Overview

Opportunity: Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027

Category: Fellowship

Fellowship duration: Six months

Award: $30,000

Healthcare support: $1,000 healthcare stipend

Additional support: Coaching, mentorship, peer learning and community

Travel: Fully funded travel to three in-person convenings

Childcare support: Available for fellows with dependents under 18

Location requirement: United States

Project focus: Social justice and systemic change

Application deadline: October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time

Fellowship period: April–September 2027

What Is the Voqal Partners Fellowship?

The Voqal Partners Fellowship is a six-month program designed to support people who are developing ambitious ideas for social justice and systemic change.

The fellowship recognizes that many potentially transformative ideas never receive funding because they are considered too early, too unconventional, or too difficult to fit into traditional philanthropic funding models. Voqal Partners takes a different approach by supporting people at the dream or idea stage and giving them the resources and environment they need to explore what their ideas could become.

The program is therefore not necessarily looking for applicants with an established nonprofit organization or an already successful initiative. An applicant may still be determining the best structure for their project, testing assumptions, exploring a new approach, or figuring out how a promising idea could be implemented.

The central question is whether the applicant has a strong vision for creating a more equitable future and a realistic starting point for exploring that vision.

During the fellowship, selected fellows receive financial support, coaching, mentorship, peer learning opportunities, and access to a community of other changemakers. The program is intended to help fellows move their ideas from an early concept toward real-world experimentation.

What Does the $30,000 Fellowship Award Cover?

Each selected fellow receives a $30,000 award, generally distributed as a lump sum at the beginning of the fellowship.

One of the distinctive features of the Voqal Partners Fellowship is the flexibility attached to the funding. Fellows are not restricted to spending the money only on narrowly defined project expenses.

The funding can support expenses such as:

Living expenses

Equipment

Contractors or additional assistance

Travel

Project implementation

Research and experimentation

Other costs that help the fellow develop their idea

If a particular expense helps the fellow move their idea forward, it is generally considered an appropriate use of the fellowship funding.

Voqal Partners can also work with fellows who prefer to receive their funding according to a particular schedule, such as through monthly payments. The organization indicates that the full award can be distributed according to an agreed timeline as long as the entire amount is provided by the end of the fellowship.

This flexible funding structure allows fellows to determine what they need most during the six-month period rather than having every expense predetermined by the funder.

$1,000 Healthcare Stipend

In addition to the $30,000 fellowship award, selected fellows receive a $1,000 healthcare stipend.

This additional support recognizes that personal wellbeing and health can affect a person’s ability to pursue demanding social justice work. The stipend provides an additional financial resource for fellows during the fellowship period.

Fully Funded Travel to Three Fellowship Convenings

The fellowship includes three in-person convenings scheduled during the program.

These gatherings are an important component of the fellowship because they provide opportunities for fellows to:

Meet and learn from other fellows

Participate in peer learning

Work with coaches and advisors

Develop relationships with members of the Voqal community

Reflect on their work

Collaborate around challenges and opportunities

Strengthen their ideas through collective learning

Voqal Partners covers the travel costs associated with these gatherings.

Fellows with dependents under the age of 18 can also receive childcare support, helping reduce one of the practical barriers that can prevent caregivers from participating fully in professional development and fellowship programs.

Coaching, Mentorship and Professional Support

Financial support is only one part of the Voqal Partners Fellowship.

Selected fellows gain access to coaches, advisors and mentors who can help them think through the challenges involved in turning an early-stage idea into something that can be tested in the real world.

This support can include discussions around:

Strategy

Operations

Organizational development

Structural challenges

Project development

Experimentation

Leadership

Community engagement

Future opportunities

Because fellows may be working on ideas that challenge existing systems, the coaching component can provide an important opportunity to examine assumptions, identify obstacles and determine practical next steps.

A Small Cohort of Social Justice Changemakers

Voqal Partners selects only eight fellows each year.

The small cohort model allows fellows to develop close relationships with one another and create a community around shared learning.

Rather than going through the fellowship experience independently, participants learn alongside other people who are also attempting to develop ambitious ideas for social change.

Past fellows remain connected through an active alumni network, creating opportunities for relationships and knowledge-sharing to continue after the formal six-month fellowship ends.

Who Is Voqal Partners Looking For?

The Voqal Partners Fellowship is aimed at people who are deeply connected to the communities and issues they are working to address.

The organization emphasizes that applicants should not simply approach communities from the outside with solutions. Instead, it prioritizes people who are part of the communities they serve and who have a strong understanding of the challenges those communities face.

Voqal Partners particularly values:

Community leaders

Organizers

Builders

Visionaries

People with lived experience

People developing unconventional approaches to social justice

Individuals working alongside communities affected by systemic problems

People seeking to support historically excluded communities

The fellowship also encourages applications from individuals and communities that have traditionally had difficulty accessing philanthropic funding.

These include, among others:

LGBTQIA+ individuals

Women

Indigenous peoples

People of color

People with disabilities

The emphasis is not simply on demographic identity. Voqal Partners also wants to understand an applicant’s relationship with the community, their lived experience, their vision for change, and their ability to contribute meaningfully to the work.

What Does Dream-Stage or Idea-Stage Mean?

One of the most important aspects of the Voqal Partners Fellowship is its focus on dream-stage and idea-stage projects.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to have everything figured out before applying.

For example, an applicant might:

Have identified a major social problem but still be determining the best solution.

Have a new approach they want to test.

Be exploring how a community-led initiative could work.

Have an early concept for a campaign or project.

Have an idea for disrupting an existing system.

Be developing a new model for organizing or community participation.

Need time and resources to determine whether an unconventional idea can work.

The fellowship is designed to provide space for this kind of exploration.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that their idea is “too early” simply because they do not yet have a finished organization, product, campaign or business plan.

What Types of Projects Does Voqal Partners Support?

Voqal Partners seeks ideas that have the potential to challenge or disrupt systems rather than simply making existing systems easier to navigate.

The organization is particularly interested in projects with a compelling vision for the future.

Projects may be:

Hyperlocal

Community-based

National in scope

However, the work must focus on communities in the United States.

The scale of the project is therefore less important than the quality of the vision, the relationship with the affected community, and the potential for the proposed work to contribute to meaningful systemic change.

Key Qualities Voqal Partners Looks For

Applicants should consider five major characteristics when assessing whether their project fits the fellowship.

1. Dream-stage or idea-stage work

The idea may still be developing.

Applicants do not need to present a finished initiative. What matters is having a bold vision and being ready to explore how that vision could become reality.

2. A compelling vision

Voqal Partners is interested in ideas that challenge the status quo.

The organization seeks approaches that can potentially disrupt systems through transformative solutions rather than simply creating small interventions that make existing systems more comfortable.

3. A path forward

Having a big idea is not enough.

Applicants should also demonstrate that they have some thoughts about where they could begin.

This could include identifying:

What they want to test

What they want to learn

What they want to build

Which assumptions they need to explore

What initial steps they could take during the fellowship

The path does not need to be completely developed because the fellowship itself is intended to provide space for learning and experimentation.

4. Alignment with the fellowship

Applicants should explain why the Voqal Partners Fellowship is appropriate for their idea.

The application should demonstrate how the fellowship’s funding, coaching, mentorship and community could help move the project forward.

5. Connection to community

Applicants should be able to explain their relationship with the people most affected by the issue they are addressing.

Voqal Partners places significant emphasis on community connection and the role an applicant plays in advancing the work.

Fellowship Responsibilities

The Voqal Partners Fellowship provides substantial freedom, but fellows are also expected to actively participate in the program.

Fellows are expected to:

Work on their fellowship project from April through September 2027.

Attend three in-person convenings.

Participate in monthly cohort calls.

Engage with coaches and advisors.

Share what they learned at the conclusion of the fellowship.

The three convenings are scheduled for:

April 2027: Opening convening

July 2027: Middle convening

September 2027: Closing convening

Although fellows are permitted to pursue other employment or responsibilities during the fellowship, Voqal Partners asks them to make their fellowship project a priority.

This flexibility may be particularly useful for applicants who have existing professional, family or community responsibilities.

Do Fellows Keep Ownership of Their Ideas?

Yes.

Fellows retain full ownership of intellectual property developed during the fellowship.

Voqal Partners does not claim ownership of a fellow’s ideas, products or creations.

This is an important consideration for applicants developing innovative concepts because it means the fellowship does not require fellows to surrender ownership of intellectual property created as part of their work.

Can Previous Applicants Apply Again?

Yes.

Previous applicants are encouraged to apply again.

Voqal Partners recognizes that strong ideas can evolve over time. Applying in a previous year does not prevent someone from submitting a new application or returning with an idea that has developed further.

The organization also indicates that previous applications do not negatively affect future consideration.

Can Previous Fellows Apply?

The supplied fellowship information includes this question in the FAQ section, but does not provide a complete answer in the provided material. Applicants who have previously participated as fellows should therefore verify their eligibility directly with Voqal Partners before submitting an application.

Can Fellows Have Other Jobs?

Yes.

Fellows are permitted to pursue other work during the fellowship.

Voqal Partners recognizes that fellows may have employment, family obligations and other responsibilities. However, the organization expects the fellowship project to remain a priority throughout the program.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to leave their existing employment to participate.

Application Process

The Voqal Partners Fellowship application is divided into four primary sections.

Section 1: Eligibility

The first part of the application contains questions designed to establish whether the applicant meets the fellowship’s core eligibility requirements.

Applicants should carefully review these requirements before investing significant time in the application.

Section 2: Basic Details

This section collects fundamental information about the applicant and their proposed project.

Applicants may be asked for:

Information about how they found the fellowship

Their project name

Brief project descriptions

Basic personal details

Section 3: The Specifics

This is the central part of the application.

Applicants will need to explain the future they are trying to create, how they envision moving toward that future, and what kind of support they would need from the fellowship.

This section is likely to be particularly important because it gives applicants an opportunity to demonstrate the strength of their vision and their connection to the issue they are addressing.

Applicants should focus on clearly communicating:

The problem they are addressing

Why the problem matters

Their vision for change

What makes their approach different

What they want to explore or test

What they hope to learn

Why they are well positioned to pursue the idea

How Voqal Partners could help

Section 4: Additional Details

The final section provides space for additional information.

Applicants may be asked about:

Their use of artificial intelligence

Previous experience with coaches

Additional information relevant to their application

Links

Supporting documents

Other details they believe the selection team should know

The Fellowship Budget

Applicants must also submit a budget explaining how they anticipate using the $30,000 fellowship award.

Importantly, Voqal Partners states that the budget is not used to evaluate the application.

Instead, the budget helps the organization understand where the applicant currently stands in their planning.

A budget template is provided as part of the application.

Applicants should therefore use the budget to provide a realistic picture of what they believe they will need rather than attempting to create an artificially sophisticated financial plan.

Application Resources

Applicants can prepare for the application using resources provided by Voqal Partners, including:

The application guide

The fellowship question list

The online application

Virtual information sessions

Reviewing the application guide and question list before beginning the application can help applicants understand what information they will need and organize their responses in advance.

Voqal Partners Fellowship Information Sessions

Voqal Partners is offering two virtual information sessions for prospective applicants.

The organization states that both sessions will cover the same information, meaning applicants only need to attend one.

Session 1

Date: September 18, 2026

Time: 12:00 p.m. Eastern / 9:00 a.m. Pacific

Format: Virtual

The first session will be recorded, with the recording expected to be shared afterward.

Session 2

Date: October 14, 2026

Time: 4:00 p.m. Eastern / 1:00 p.m. Pacific

Format: Virtual

Applicants who cannot attend the first session can participate in the second session.

2027 Fellowship Timeline

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

Applications Open

First Tuesday after Labor Day 2026

Applications Close

October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time

Interviews

January 2027

Fellows Selected

February–March 2027

Opening Convening

April 2027

Fellowship Programming

April–September 2027

Middle Convening

July 2027

Closing Convening

September 2027

Because the application deadline is specific to a time zone, applicants should avoid waiting until the final day and should submit well before the stated closing time.

How to Strengthen Your Voqal Partners Fellowship Application

Although there is no guaranteed formula for selection, applicants can take several practical steps to make their application clearer and more compelling.

Clearly explain the future you want to create

Do not focus exclusively on describing what is wrong.

Explain what the world, system or community could look like if your idea succeeds.

Demonstrate your connection to the community

Explain your relationship with the people affected by the issue.

If you have lived experience, community organizing experience or another meaningful connection to the issue, make that relationship clear.

Show why your idea is different

Voqal Partners is interested in bold ideas that can challenge existing systems.

Explain what makes your proposed approach different from conventional solutions.

Be honest about what you do not know

Because the fellowship is designed for early-stage ideas, applicants do not need to pretend that every detail has already been solved.

Instead, identify the questions you need to answer and the assumptions you want to test.

Explain what you would do with the fellowship

Be specific about how the six months could help you move from an idea toward experimentation.

Consider explaining:

What you would investigate

What you would build

Who you would engage

What you would test

What resources you need

What you hope to learn

Prepare a realistic budget

Even though the budget does not determine the evaluation of your application, it should demonstrate that you have thought carefully about how the fellowship resources could support your work.

Use the application guide

Review the official application guide and question list before submitting.

This can help you understand the application structure and avoid overlooking important questions.

Examples of Previous Fellows’ Work

The fellowship has previously supported projects addressing civic participation, grassroots organizing and worker advocacy.

Andrea Hart — City Bureau

Andrea Hart worked on a civic newsroom model designed to train residents to report on local government and conduct community-driven investigations.

The example illustrates how the fellowship can support approaches that strengthen community participation in civic life and local accountability.

Erick Garcia — #GAMETHESYSTEM

Erick Garcia developed a gamified approach to grassroots organizing, using digital tools to increase participation and accessibility.

This demonstrates the type of experimentation that can emerge when technology and organizing are combined in unconventional ways.

Rich Wallace — Equity & Transformation

Rich Wallace organized workers in the informal economy to pursue policy protections at city and state levels.

The project demonstrates another dimension of the fellowship’s focus: supporting efforts that seek structural and policy-level change for communities that may otherwise have limited access to institutional power.

Why the Voqal Partners Fellowship Is Different

The fellowship stands out because of its willingness to fund ideas before they have become fully established projects.

Traditional funding opportunities frequently require applicants to demonstrate previous results, organizational infrastructure, detailed implementation plans or established programs.

The Voqal Partners model is more focused on the person, their vision and the possibility of what their idea could become.

Its approach combines:

Flexible funding

Personal financial support

Healthcare assistance

Coaching

Mentorship

Peer learning

Community

Fully funded travel

Continued alumni engagement

The result is an opportunity for social justice changemakers to dedicate meaningful time and resources to exploring an idea that may otherwise struggle to receive conventional funding.

Who Can Apply?

The fellowship is intended for social justice changemakers who meet the organization’s eligibility requirements and have a bold vision for creating a more equitable future.

Applicants must:

Be 18 years of age or older.

Be based in the United States.

Be able to receive funds in the United States.

Be working on an idea connected to communities in the United States.

Have a social justice-oriented vision or idea.

Be prepared to dedicate the fellowship period to developing and testing the idea.

Be willing and able to participate in the fellowship’s required activities, including the three in-person convenings.

Voqal Partners does not provide visa sponsorship.

The organization particularly encourages applications from people with lived experience and individuals connected to communities historically excluded from philanthropy.

APPLY HERE

Geographic Eligibility

This is not a worldwide fellowship.

The fellowship requires applicants to be based in the United States and able to receive funds in the United States.

Projects may be local, regional or national in scope, but the work must focus on communities within the United States.

Therefore, applicants living in countries outside the United States, including applicants from African countries such as Kenya, do not meet the stated geographic eligibility requirement unless they independently satisfy Voqal Partners’ U.S.-based eligibility requirements.

Important Deadline

The application deadline for the Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027 is October 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.

Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their application. Technical problems, incomplete responses or missing documents can create unnecessary difficulties close to the deadline.

A good strategy is to complete the application ahead of time, review every response, check the budget and submit before the final day.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should use the official Voqal Partners application portal to begin their application.

Before applying, prospective fellows should also review the official application guide and question list so they understand what is expected.

Applicants who have questions can contact Voqal Partners through fellowship@voqalpartners.org.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Voqal Partners Fellowship fully funded?

The fellowship provides a $30,000 award, a $1,000 healthcare stipend and covers travel costs associated with the three required in-person convenings. Childcare support is also available for fellows with dependents under 18.

Do I need an established organization to apply?

No. The fellowship specifically welcomes dream-stage and idea-stage work. Applicants do not need a finished organization, product, campaign or business plan.

Can I use the $30,000 for living expenses?

Yes. The funding has no stated restrictions on how fellows use the award, provided the expenses support the fellow and their work. This can include living expenses, equipment, contractors, travel and implementation costs.

Do I keep ownership of my intellectual property?

Yes. Fellows retain ownership of intellectual property developed during the fellowship.

Can I work another job during the fellowship?

Yes. Other work is permitted, although fellows are expected to prioritize their fellowship project.

How many fellows are selected?

Voqal Partners selects eight fellows each year.

Are previous applicants allowed to apply?

Yes. Previous applicants are encouraged to apply again.

Does Voqal Partners sponsor visas?

No. The organization does not offer visa sponsorship.

Must I attend the in-person convenings?

Yes. Attendance at all three convenings is a core part of the fellowship experience.

What happens to my application information?

Voqal Partners states that applications are reviewed by a select group of community members, including program alumni, staff and partners. Access is limited to the evaluation period, and the organization states that it will not share applicants’ ideas or details beyond this process without their knowledge.

Conclusion

The Voqal Partners Fellowship 2027 offers a distinctive opportunity for social justice changemakers who have ambitious ideas but may not yet have the organizational infrastructure, funding or resources needed to turn those ideas into reality.

With $30,000 in flexible funding, a $1,000 healthcare stipend, coaching and mentorship, peer support, fully funded travel to three convenings and access to an alumni community, the fellowship is designed to give selected changemakers the time and resources to explore, test and develop new approaches to systemic change.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to people with lived experience and strong connections to the communities they serve, especially individuals from groups historically excluded from traditional philanthropy.

However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to the geographic requirement. The fellowship is U.S.-based, applicants must be 18 or older, based in the United States and able to receive funds in the U.S., and Voqal Partners does not provide visa sponsorship.

For eligible applicants with a bold social justice idea, the October 31, 2026 deadline provides an important opportunity to seek support for an idea that may be too early or unconventional for traditional funding programs.

Applicants should begin by reviewing the application guide and question list, developing a clear explanation of the future they want to create, identifying what they want to test or learn during the six-month fellowship, and preparing a realistic budget for the $30,000 award.

TITLE: Afya na Haki Doctoral/Post-Doctoral Fellowship 2026: Fully Remunerated Global Health Research Opportunity

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Afya na Haki is inviting applications for a full-time Doctoral/Post-Doctoral Fellow to join the Ubingwa Think Tank for Global Health. This one-year, competitively remunerated opportunity is designed for doctoral researchers and recently qualified PhD holders who want to contribute to research, evidence generation, policy analysis and African thought leadership across health, human rights and global health.

The selected Fellow will work within an Africa-centred research environment that seeks to strengthen the visibility and influence of African knowledge, contextual evidence and leadership in global health policy, practice and public discourse. The appointment will commence in October 2026 and will be based at the Afya na Haki Secretariat.

According to Afya na Haki’s official announcement, the fellowship is particularly relevant to researchers working in Law, Public Health, Social Sciences, Gender Studies, Human Rights, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights, Development Studies, Political Science, International Relations, Economics and other disciplines connected to the Think Tank’s mandate. About Afya na Haki

Afya na Haki, commonly referred to as Ahaki, is an African research and training institution working across health, human rights and Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights. Its approach centres African knowledge, experience, agency and leadership in addressing health and justice challenges affecting the continent.

The institution seeks to co-create and advance African solutions to African problems by engaging African researchers, practitioners, advocates, policymakers and communities. Its vision is to see African potential effectively harnessed and amplified in the realization of health, human rights and sexual and reproductive health and rights.

Afya na Haki’s mission is to facilitate Africentric learning and innovation in these fields. Its institutional values include Pan-Africanism, Ubuntu, innovation, African agency and participation, excellence, integrity, transparency, accountability, learning and reflection. Afya na Haki’s vision, mission and objectives

These priorities make the fellowship particularly relevant to researchers who are interested in producing scholarship that is not disconnected from African realities. Successful research is expected to consider the historical, political, economic, cultural and structural conditions that influence health systems, human rights and social justice across Africa.

About the Ubingwa Think Tank for Global Health

The Ubingwa Think Tank for Global Health operates at the intersection of Afya na Haki and the Ahaki Institute. It was established to address the systemic exclusion or underrepresentation of African perspectives, evidence and leadership in global health.

The Think Tank draws on African knowledge and contextual understanding to help ensure that global health policies and practices reflect the distinctive historical, cultural, political and structural realities of African societies.

Its work is organized around four interconnected thematic areas:

Reproductive Justice

Health Technologies and Digital Justice

Governance of Complex Health Emergencies

Health, Trade and Economics

Within these broader areas, the Think Tank also engages with subjects including:

Global mental health

Maternal health policy

Global health justice

Access to medicines

Digital health

Climate justice

Health equity

Human rights

Social justice

African health policy and governance

The Think Tank connects these areas to wider continental development ambitions, including the realization of the African Union’s Agenda 2063. Ubingwa Think Tank for Global Health

Purpose of the Doctoral/Post-Doctoral Fellow Position

The central purpose of the position is to strengthen the work of the Ubingwa Think Tank through rigorous research, knowledge generation, evidence development, scholarship, critical analysis, thought leadership and strategic engagement.

The Fellow will help advance African perspectives and evidence in global health while supporting efforts to increase the influence of African knowledge in policy, practice and international debate.

This is therefore not limited to an individual academic research project. It is an applied research and policy-oriented role that connects scholarship with contemporary health, human rights and social justice challenges.

The successful candidate will be expected to work across academic, policy, legal and practice-based sources, converting complex evidence into material that can inform policymakers, researchers, advocates, practitioners and other decision-makers.

Main Research Responsibilities

1. Conducting and Supporting Research

The Fellow will conduct or contribute to research relevant to the mandate of the Ubingwa Think Tank. This may include:

Developing relevant and researchable questions

Conducting literature reviews

Undertaking evidence reviews

Gathering and assessing information

Analysing quantitative or qualitative data, where appropriate

Contributing to research design and implementation

Supporting the preparation of research outputs

Identifying gaps in existing evidence

Connecting academic research with policy and practice

The position requires a researcher who can move beyond simply collecting information. The Fellow must be able to evaluate the strength, relevance and limitations of evidence and determine what it means for African health systems, human rights and global health governance.

2. Evidence Generation, Synthesis and Analysis

The Fellow will generate, synthesize and analyse evidence from different types of sources, including:

Peer-reviewed academic literature

National and regional policies

Laws and legal decisions

Government documents

Institutional reports

Practice-based evidence

Civil society research

Global health frameworks

Contextual and community knowledge

Other credible sources relevant to the research question

The resulting evidence will be used to support scholarship, policy engagement, institutional strategy and public thought leadership.

3. Scholarship Across the Think Tank’s Core Themes

The selected Fellow may contribute to research and scholarship across the Think Tank’s four principal areas:

Reproductive Justice

This area may examine how legal, economic, social, political and health systems affect reproductive autonomy, access to services, maternal health, sexual and reproductive rights and reproductive justice.

Health Technologies and Digital Justice

Research under this theme may explore access to digital health systems, the governance of health technologies, digital inequalities, data rights, artificial intelligence in health, technology-related exclusion and the equitable use of health innovations.

Governance of Complex Health Emergencies

This area may cover pandemics, epidemics, health emergencies, preparedness, emergency governance, community participation, institutional accountability and the protection of human rights during crises.

Health, Trade and Economics

Work may consider access to medicines, health financing, trade policy, intellectual property, economic barriers to healthcare, market structures and the relationship between economic policy and health equity.

The Fellow may also contribute to related work on global mental health, maternal health policy, global health justice, digital health, access to medicines and climate justice, depending on their expertise and the Think Tank’s institutional priorities.

Critical Analysis from African Perspectives

An important part of the position is the ability to examine health and global health issues through African perspectives.

The Fellow will be expected to consider:

Historical influences on African health systems

Colonial and post-colonial structures

Cultural and community contexts

Political institutions and power relations

Economic inequalities

Structural barriers to health and human rights

The treatment of African evidence in international policy processes

The role of local and Indigenous knowledge

African leadership in health policy and decision-making

This means that candidates should be able to question assumptions in conventional global health scholarship and examine whether dominant policies adequately reflect African realities.

Monitoring Emerging Health and Human Rights Developments

The Fellow will monitor important developments at multiple levels, including:

National developments

Regional African developments

Pan-African policy processes

International health policy

Human rights developments

Global health governance

Emerging legal and regulatory issues

New technologies and health innovations

Changes affecting health equity and social justice

The Fellow must identify the possible implications of these developments for Africa and translate them into timely research, commentary, recommendations or briefing materials.

Policy, Legal and Contextual Analysis

Depending on the Fellow’s academic and professional background, the role may involve:

Analysing laws and regulations

Reviewing public policies

Examining legal judgments

Assessing policy implementation

Comparing regional and international frameworks

Identifying institutional or regulatory gaps

Developing evidence-informed policy recommendations

Explaining the likely effects of policies on African communities

The role is suitable for scholars who can connect theoretical or legal analysis with practical policy consequences.

Development of Knowledge Products

The Fellow will contribute to a broad range of written outputs. These may include:

Research papers

Discussion papers

Policy briefs

Analytical articles

Commentaries

Institutional reports

Briefing notes

Conference materials

Evidence summaries

Other academic or policy-oriented publications

Candidates must therefore demonstrate a strong ability to write clearly, accurately and persuasively.

The Fellow should be capable of producing rigorous academic material while also translating technical evidence into accessible language for non-academic audiences such as policymakers, advocates, civil society organizations and practitioners.

Participation in Policy and Intellectual Engagements

The role will involve more than desk-based research. The Fellow may contribute to:

Policy dialogues

Academic conferences

Seminars

Roundtable discussions

Strategic meetings

Intellectual exchanges

National policy engagements

Regional and Pan-African forums

Global health discussions

Through these engagements, the Fellow will help present evidence, promote African perspectives and support the Think Tank’s contribution to global health policy and decision-making.

Amplifying African Knowledge and Leadership

A major objective of the position is to strengthen the visibility and influence of African voices in global health.

The Fellow will support efforts to:

Amplify African research and scholarship

Document African health experiences

Promote African leadership in policy debates

Integrate local and contextual knowledge into global health practice

Challenge the marginalization of African evidence

Strengthen Africa-centred policy recommendations

Support more equitable global health decision-making

This dimension of the role makes it particularly suitable for researchers whose work is grounded in African contexts or who can demonstrate a serious, evidence-based appreciation of African knowledge and leadership.

Partnership and Network Development

The Fellow will contribute to relationships with stakeholders such as:

Universities

Individual researchers

Academic networks

Think tanks

Civil society organizations

Policymakers

Government institutions

Health practitioners

Human rights advocates

Regional and international institutions

Other stakeholders working in related fields

The Fellow must be comfortable working across professional and disciplinary boundaries and contributing constructively to collaborative research and policy initiatives.

Interdisciplinary Collaboration and Institutional Learning

The position requires openness to interdisciplinary approaches. Global health problems frequently involve law, economics, politics, public health, technology, culture, gender, human rights and social policy at the same time.

The Fellow will therefore be expected to:

Work with colleagues from different disciplines

Contribute to collaborative research

Engage respectfully with different methodological approaches

Participate in institutional learning

Share research knowledge with colleagues

Identify emerging research opportunities

Explore innovative approaches relevant to the Think Tank’s mandate

Undertake other reasonable responsibilities assigned by the supervisor

The complete responsibilities are provided in the official Doctoral/Post-Doctoral Fellow job frame.

Required Academic Qualifications

Candidates must satisfy one of the following doctoral-stage requirements:

Hold a PhD that was awarded within the last two years; or

Be at the research or dissertation stage of a doctoral degree.

The doctoral qualification or ongoing doctoral research should be in one of the following fields:

Law

Development Studies

Economics

Another discipline relevant to the mandate of the Ubingwa Think Tank for Global Health

Candidates from related interdisciplinary fields may also be considered where they can clearly demonstrate how their research connects with the Think Tank’s work.

Required Academic or Professional Experience

Applicants must demonstrate academic or professional engagement with one or more relevant areas, including:

Health

TITLE: Dynamics of inertial particles in flows with stochasticity

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
Rogers, M., & Rypina, I. (2025). Dynamics of inertial particles in flows with stochasticity. Journal of Physical Oceanography. https://doi.org/10.1175/jpo-d-24-0117.1

Image provided by Mason Rogers

In this paper we derive and test a simple advection-diffusion model for the evolution of distributions of small, rigid, non-neutrally-buoyant particles in fluid flows with a stochastic turbulent component. Three different tracers are released in an idealized simulation of three-dimensional turbulence: (a) a passive fluid tracer, (b) a buoyant fluid tracer that is advected at the sum of the fluid velocity and a rising velocity, and (c) a distribution of small, solid particles with the same buoyancy as the buoyant fluid tracer. Tracers are injected at a constant rate via a Gaussian source at the center of the domain. Snapshots of horizontal slices of the concentration fields of each tracer p(x,y) are plotted at the (top row) surface, (middle row) mid-depth, and (bottom row) bottom boundary of the domain. The inertia of the small, solid particles causes their motion to deviate from that of the buoyant fluid tracer. The resulting discrepancies between the concentration field of the buoyant tracer and that of the inertial particles are depicted as p'(x, y) in column (d). At small scales, inertial effects may cause particles to cluster near some flow features and evacuate others. In this example, local differences between the inertial particle and buoyant tracer distributions are on the order of 10%.

TITLE: New peer-reviewed book “The Indian Ocean and Its Role in the Global Climate System” published

OPPORTUNITY TEXT:
The Indian Ocean represents one of the great frontiers in climate science and oceanography. Bordered by nearly 40 countries, and home to a third of the global population, changes to climate in this area of the world could have major societal and economic impacts. Currently, the Indian Ocean and its surrounding countries stand out globally as the region with the highest risk of natural hazards, with coastal communities vulnerable to weather and climate extremes. However, given its unique characteristics and the fact it has historically been understudied, we have limited knowledge about its inner workings.

In a new book published by Elsevier, The Indian Ocean and Its Role in the Global Climate System, an interdisciplinary team of experts take a deeper dive into recent warming trends and extreme events, such as marine heatwaves, ocean acidification, and deoxygenation. The book contains 20 peer-reviewed chapters, and more than 175 figures, 3,000 references, 100 educational resources and links directing readers to more in-depth information, and 100 glossary entries of key concepts.

Several oceanographers from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) Physical Oceanography Department were involved in the book: Associate Scientist Caroline Ummenhofer was one of the two editors of the book and led a chapter on the past, present, and future of the South Asian monsoon, as well as a chapter on regional and global impacts of the Indian Ocean. Assistant Scientist Viviane Menezes was a co-author on the Indian Ocean circulation chapter, and Senior Scientist Lisan Yu co-authored the Indian Ocean Observing System chapter.

“The Indian Ocean is particularly susceptible to human-induced climate change. Robust warming trends and pronounced changes in heat and freshwater are being observed there,” said one of the book’s editors, oceanographer Caroline Ummenhofer. “The Indian Ocean is unusual among tropical ocean basins. It has seasonal reversal of monsoon winds and ocean currents in turn. It’s also landlocked to the north, limiting the ability for tropical heat to escape to higher latitudes.”

“The advent of new technologies, an expanded observation system, and rapid advances in environmental predictions and forecasting capabilities in recent decades open new and exciting opportunities for improved environmental and climate risk management,” said Raleigh Hood, the book’s co-editor and biological oceanographer at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science. “In a region particularly vulnerable to changing conditions, it’s important to be collaborating and compiling this information. This book contains everything from the history of the region to all parts of the climate system including geology, hydrology, biogeochemistry, atmosphere, and oceanography.”

Contributions by more than 90 authors from around the world with expertise across a wide range of fields underpin the content of this textbook. Furthermore, all chapters were peer-reviewed by at least two experts in the field. The textbook identifies new understandings and technologies, providing stakeholders with relevant knowledge for more informed decision-making, encouraging students, practitioners, and researchers to overcome some of these pressing knowledge gaps.

The Indian Ocean and Its Role in the Global Climate System is available now. Published by Elsevier.
